CONSULIBUS, PROCONSULIBUS, QUÆSTORIBUS, OECONOMO, TOTIQUE simul AUGUSTO SENATUI Inclytæ & Antiquissimæ TIGURINORUM REIPUBLICÆ, Patriæ Patribus, Ecclesiæ Nutriciis, Legitimis Electoribus, Veritatis Defensoribus, DOMINIS SUIS Gratiosissimis, Gratiam & Pacem à Deo Patre Jesu Christi precatur Author!
units.tr: To the most magnificent, noble, ample, learned, and prudent men, the Lords Consuls, Proconsuls, Quaestors, and Treasurer, and to the whole venerable Senate of the renowned and most ancient Republic of the Tigurini, the fathers of the country, nurses of the Church, lawful electors, defenders of the truth, my most gracious Lords: the Author prays for grace and peace from God the Father of Jesus Christ!

units.la: Eminem certè, & Vos, Viri Amplissimi, Consultissimi, Domini mei Gratiosissimi, omnium minime latet, multum in Electionibus Personalibus, Ecclesiasticis, Politicis, quibuscunque situm esse, atque haud parum, quales eæ sint, referre Perfectè quidem bonas & sanctas, in ista hominum Viatorum jam sine exceptione omnium imperfectione, quæ imperfecta reddit humana omnia, addo, in quorundam etiam ; ut bonis ubique mali mixti sunt; perversitate, frustra quis requirat. Ubi tamen pii Proceres plerunq; dignos digné eligunt, & regulæ legésque SanSanctæ & inviolatæ manent, & plùs possunt merita genere sine meritis, & virtus ambitionem superat, & bonæ qualitates magis respiciuntur quàm munera, ibi de Electionibus & Electis gaudet Civitas, juvatur Ecclesia, floret Respublica, promoventur etiam omnibus modis commoda publica. Contraria autem omnia accidunt contrariis: Atque hinc dicere ausim: Quales Electiones, talis ferè est Respublica. Bonæ etenim bonos provehunt, malæ non nisi per accidens, proin rarius; Multùm autem interest, à qualibus regamur, & uberior Dei gratia adest dubio procul bene electis. Hinc non infima merito Electionum in omni statu cura est, atque eò major, quò melior haberi, quò felicior esse cupit Respublica, in qua Electiones fiunt, quò magis aliis præstare volunt Eligentes, quò arctioribus ad Electiones sanctas vinculis constringuntur, quò denique majores & sanctiores sunt Dignitates, ad quas Electiones diriguntur. Proin, si quæ esse deberet in Orbe dignitas, quæ non tantùm dignitates quasvis alias, sive Ecclesiasticas, sive Politicas, infinitis fere parasangis superaret, utpote haud minùs involvens Monarchiâ Universali Ecclesiastico-Politicâ, propter Successionem in locum Christi, ad parem, imò majorem, quàm ipse in terris existens exercuit, potestatem, ab omnibus omninò Christianis sub periculo damnationis æternæ in habente eam dignitatem agnoscendam atque devenerandam, & quæ adeò totius Religionis Christianæ vi successionis per Electiones fundamentum foret, sed quæ & insuper hac singulari etiam laude decoranda esset, quòd Electiones ad eam singulari Divinâ providentiâ & Spiritûs S. gratiosâ assistentiâ dirigantur: Necessarium certè foret, ut non tantùm certò constaret, talem dignitatem dari, & per Electiones tales vel tales continuari debere, sed & ut Electiones ad eam cumprimis dignitatem Sanctæ essent, id est, dignitati tantæ respondentes, Capiti & Sponso Ecclesiæ, Successori & Vicario Jesu Christi convenientes, jactantiæ de singulari Providentia & Spiritùs S. assistentia aptæ, Electoribus dignæ, verbo, tales, ut Divinum sic Opus peragi manifestum fiat omnibus. Sin verò contrà demonstrari posset, & dignitatem talem in rerum natura atque, ubi jactatur, non existere, potestatémque talem usurpationem meram esse, & Electiones, quæ ad eam dignitatem atque potestatem fingantur, dignitati atque potestati minimè convenire, & præ aliis ad longè inferiores dignitates longè majoribus nævis urgeri, aliáque omnia potiùs quàm jactatam Spiritûs S. peculiarem assistentiam spirare; eádem profecto operâ jam probatum esse, quàm malè Electiones ad talem dignitatem sacræ jactentur, quàm cariosum proinetiam sit Religionis, quæ iis superstruitur, fundamentum, & quòd in tanta támque manifesta contrarietate, ubi tamen maxima similitudo jactatur, & alter Christus ostenditur, Antichristianismus non esse non posset. Atque illud ipsum est, Viri Amplissimi, Consultissimi, Domini mei Gratiosissimi, quod hîc ago, Opus, in quo pretium operæ, credo, est, si improbas sub nomine Christi contra Christum impostura (quatenus enim Papa Princeps in suo territorio secularis est, eatenus is nihil ad nos; ) detegere, si Christum & Ecclesiam Christi ab iis aliquo modo vindicare, si ipsa Papismi fundamenta evertere, si ita non sine æterno animarum periculo errantes convincere, si ita in aliis fidei Antichristianismo oppooppositæ πλνεῳροεἰαν augere, non abs re est. Agitur illud opus eò justius, quòd (quos hîc impetere videmur, sed quos revera de suis erroribus salutariter bonóque suo monemus) Pontificii, nihil magis amant, nihílque frequentius jactantiúsque agunt, quàm quòd nobis ob Electiones nostras Ecclesiasticas Personales, Reformatorum nostrorum, Ministrorúmque aliorum, quasi nullæ, nullam planè à Deo vocationem, nullam planè, electos & alios authoritate publica eatenus destitutos inter, differentiam involventes fuerint, & sint, miserè turpitérque insultant. Quibus proin haud immeritò, & præter alias quoad Reformatores, Ministrósque subsequentes & solidum Christiani Magistratus Christianæque plebis in ejusmodi Electionibus jus, vindicias, reponimus etiam, quòd inepte & hîc cæcus in luscum dicat, & ne quidem comparatio similium nævorum propter excessum ab illorum parte hîc institui posit, ut nulla etiam est, ex hypothesi, proportio dignitatum, & quòd illæ ipsæ Electiones, à quibus & Electiones Ecclesiasticas reliquas, & in Religione reliqua omnia legitimari, authoritatémque, si quam habere velint, accipere debere ajunt, sint omnium vel maximè illegitimæ. In qua tamen, ut sic loquar, recriminatione etiam valde necessaria iniquéque nobis sæpe sæpiùs extorta ita æquo animo versari lubuit, ut offensionis evitandæ, veritatísque sine calumnia proferendæ ergo assertiones nostras partim ratione probàrim, partim testimoniis non inidoneis, quippe vel (& maximam quidem partem) Authorum inter Pontificios receptorum, celebrium, magni nominis magnæque authoritatis, vel aliás rerum Romanarum peritissimorum atque gnarissimorum, simúlque nihil nisi aut vulgò cognita, aut jam ab aliis tradita, aut traditis ab aliis plane similia proferentium, nullásque calumniandi, ut quidem, quoad plerosque, adulandi causas habentium, confirmârim: Quemadmodum etiam nihil hîc opus fuit, præter rei, de qua fere in omnibus inter omnes consensus, expositionem, Consequentiarúmque inde manantium deductionem, rationi, Legibus receptis, Scripturæ & Antiquitati consentaneam, utpotè quibus Mysterium Iniquitatis in hoc etiam jam satis supérque revelatur; Utut permulti etiam sint, qui illud videre nolunt, cùm tamen videre possent clarissimè; Imò etiam irascuntur ostendentibus, & talia proferentibus, quamvis nullo sanè merito, quando, ut dixi, causa & occasio non desunt, & res personaeque meliores sisti non possunt, quàm contingere & esse solent, híque proin soli in culpa sunt, à quibus, dum ipsi mali sunt, mala proficiscuntur, & totum hoc salutis ipsorum studio declaratur. Quod dum facere instituí, ad Vos venio, Viri Amplissimi, Consultissimi, Domini mei Gratiosissimi! Vos etenim, dum ceu Christiani Magistratus Ecclesiaeque Nutricii Christum & Veritatem ejus sincerè amatis, non potestis non odisse opposita mendacia & impostturas, quibus ea colorantur, vanissimúmque (quo tamen magna pars Orbis, quia vult, decipitur;) de Pontificum Romanorum ad talem Monarchiam Ecclesiastico-Politicam Electione praetextum; Et dum praecipui apud nos Electores estis, facillimè etiam animadvertitis Electionis, qua de agitur, irregularitates fere innumeras, & quòd, quae ab Electionibus sanctis abesse deberent quàm longissimè, illa ipsa sunt, quae in Electione ea, sanctissima scilicet, quàm maximè obtinent, atque eò magis evitari & impediri pediri debent, quia sunt artes Antichristianæ, Babylonicæ; Et dum Patriæ Patres estis, optimi quoque in ea Veritatis, Veritatisque in ea defensorum, Defensores estis; Estis haud minus & fuistis hactenus Domini & Evergetæ mei Gratiosissimi, quibus idcirco multis hoc, quicquid est Operis, debetur, offertur, consecratur nominibus, & datur Territorii Dominis, quod in eo, si non conceptum, saltem completum atque ad lucis publicæ usuram editum est. Accipite modò, Viri Amplissimi, Consultissimi, Domini mei Gratiosissimi, juxta petitionem meam humillimam, quod offero, serenis frontibus, æquis animis, parique gratiâ meæ de ea fiduciæ & ad obsequia Vestra & ad vota pro Vobis debitæ promptitudini: Quâ denique supremum Numen, supremum Electorem, Electionumque omnium, ut rerum aliarum quoque omnium, supremum Arbitrum, Sanctarum Approbatorem, perversarum Vindicem, longanimum, sed justum, supplex veneror, ut Vobis & Regioni cumprimis Vestræ nullum unquam exoriatur deinceps ab Electione Antichristiana, aut similibus, lethale periculum, & ut contrà per Electiones sanctas, Vobis opitulantibus, ad annos multos, & jam jam, Deo longanimitatem suam continuante, secuturo cumprimis, maneat sub dignis Proceribus salva & integra Vestra Respublica! Ita vovebam, scribebam, in Musæo meo, pridie Kal. Januarij in fine Anni juxta Æram Christianam vulgarem MDCXCI.
units.tr: Surely it is not least known to you, most ample and most learned Gentlemen, my most gracious Lords, how much depends on personal, ecclesiastical, and political elections of every kind, and how much it matters what sort they are. Elections that are perfectly good and holy are, I add, nowhere to be found among these wayfaring men, since all human affairs are imperfect and none is free from imperfection; and in some men, as good and evil are everywhere mixed, perversity is also found, so that one would seek in vain for elections without it. Yet where pious leaders usually choose the worthy worthily, and the rules and laws remain holy and inviolate, where merit prevails over birth without merit, virtue overcomes ambition, and good qualities are regarded more than offices, there the state rejoices in its elections and its elected, the Church is helped, the Republic flourishes, and the public welfare is advanced in every way. All the contrary things happen when the opposite causes operate. Hence I would venture to say: such as the elections are, such for the most part is the Republic. For good elections advance good men, while bad ones do so only by accident, and therefore more rarely. It matters greatly by what sort of men we are ruled, and without doubt richer grace of God is present to those who are well chosen. Hence the care of elections is rightly of no small importance in every state, and it is the greater the better and happier the Republic wishes to be in which the elections are held; the more the electors wish to excel others, the more tightly they are bound by ties to holy elections; and finally the greater and holier the dignities are to which the elections are directed. Therefore, if there were to be in the world a dignity which far surpassed, by almost endless leagues, all other dignities, whether ecclesiastical or political, as it would comprise no less than a universal ecclesiastical-political monarchy, by succession into the place of Christ, exercising a power equal or even greater than that which he himself exercised on earth, a power which all Christians without exception must, on pain of eternal damnation, acknowledge and revere in the one who holds that dignity, and which would thus be the foundation of the whole Christian religion by the force of succession through elections; and if this dignity were moreover to be adorned with this singular praise, that its elections are directed by a singular divine providence and the gracious assistance of the Holy Spirit, then it would certainly be necessary not only that it be firmly established that such a dignity is to be given, and that it ought to be continued through such or such elections, but also that the elections to that dignity above all be holy, that is, answer to so great a dignity, be fitting to the Head and Spouse of the Church, the Successor and Vicar of Jesus Christ, be suited to the boast of a singular providence and the assistance of the Holy Spirit, and be worthy of the electors; in a word, be such that the divine work is manifestly seen to be carried out among all. But if on the contrary it could be demonstrated that such a dignity does not exist in the nature of things, where it is boasted of, and that such a power is mere usurpation, and that the elections which are feigned for that dignity and power are in no way fitting to the dignity and power, but are burdened, beyond others, with the greatest blemishes, far more than those belonging to much lower dignities, and that all else breathes rather than the boasted peculiar assistance of the Holy Spirit; then by the same work it would surely already be proved how wickedly elections to such a dignity are boasted of, how rotten is the foundation of the religion built upon them, and that in so great and so manifest a contrariety, where nevertheless the greatest likeness is boasted of and another Christ is displayed, Antichristianism cannot but be present. And this very thing, most ample and most learned Gentlemen, my most gracious Lords, is what I am doing here: a work in which, I believe, it is worth the effort, if I may, under the name of Christ, expose the impostures against Christ (for insofar as the Pope as Prince is secular in his own territory, so far it is nothing to us), if I may in some way vindicate Christ and the Church of Christ from them, if I may overthrow the very foundations of Papism, if I may thus convict those who err, not without eternal peril to souls, and if I may thus increase, in other points of faith opposed to Antichristianism, the [πλνεῳροεἰαν] of the truth. This work is all the more justified because the Papists, whom we seem here to assail, but whom in truth we warn for their own salvation and good about their errors, love nothing more, and do nothing more frequently or more boastfully, than to insult us miserably and basely, saying that our elections, both of our Reformers and of other ministers, are as if they were no elections at all, involve no difference whatever in God's calling, and that the elected and others so far destitute of public authority were and are such. To these men, not undeservedly, and besides other matters concerning the Reformers and the ministers who followed them, and the solid right and vindication of the Christian magistrate and the Christian people in such elections, we reply also that the blind man speaks foolishly in calling the one-eyed man blind; and that no comparison of similar blemishes can be made here, since on their side the excess is so great that, on their own hypothesis, there is no proportion between the dignities; and that those very elections, from which they say all other elections of the Church and everything else in religion must be legitimated, and must receive their authority, if they are to have any, are of all the most illegitimate. Yet in this recrimination, which, if I may so speak, has been very necessarily and unjustly forced upon us again and again, I have been pleased to proceed with a calm mind, so that to avoid giving offence and to set forth the truth without calumny, I have confirmed our assertions partly by reasoning, partly by testimonies not unfit, namely by those of authors received among the Papists, famous, of great name and great authority, or otherwise most skilled and expert in Roman affairs, who at the same time set forth nothing but what is commonly known, or already handed down by others, or what is wholly similar to what others have handed down, and who have no grounds for calumny or, as far as most of them are concerned, for flattery. Just as there was no need here, beyond the exposition of the matter, on which there is almost universal agreement among all, and the deduction of the consequences flowing from it, to add anything more consistent with reason, with the accepted laws, with Scripture and with antiquity, since in these the Mystery of Iniquity is already revealed here fully enough and more; although there are very many who are unwilling to see it, though they could see it most clearly; indeed they are even angered by those who show it and set such things forth, though without any real merit on their part; since, as I have said, the cause and the occasion are not lacking, and the matters and persons cannot be presented in a better light than they are and usually are; and therefore those alone are at fault from whom evils proceed, so long as they themselves are evil; and all this is declared out of concern for their salvation. While I have set about doing this, I come to you, most ample and most learned Gentlemen, my most gracious Lords! For you, as Christian magistrates and nurses of the Church, since you sincerely love Christ and his truth, cannot but hate the lies and impostures set against them, by which they are dressed up, and the most empty pretext (by which, however, a great part of the world is deceived, because it wishes to be) for the election of the Roman Pontiffs to such an ecclesiastical-political monarchy. And since you are the chief electors among us, you very easily perceive the almost countless irregularities of the election in question, and that those things which ought to be as far as possible from holy elections are precisely those which prevail most in that election, which is most holy in its own estimation, and which for that reason ought all the more to be avoided and prevented, because they are Antichristian, Babylonian arts. And since you are Fathers of the country, you are also the best Defenders of Truth and of those who defend it in it. You are, and have hitherto been, no less my most gracious Lords and benefactors, to whom therefore, under your names, what there is of this work is owed, is offered, is dedicated, and is given to the lords of the territory, since in it, if not conceived, at least it has been completed and brought out into the use of public light. Accept now, most ample and most learned Gentlemen, my most gracious Lords, in accordance with my most humble petition, what I offer, with serene brows, with equal minds, and with the same favour toward me, of that trust which is owed to your service and of the readiness owed to prayers on your behalf; by which, lastly, I humbly worship the Supreme Deity, the Supreme Elector, the Supreme Arbiter of all elections as of all other things, the Approver of the holy, the Avenger of the perverse, patient yet just, that no deadly peril from an Antichristian election, or from similar things, may ever arise for you and for your region above all, and that, on the contrary, through holy elections, with your help, for many years and for years yet to come, God continuing his forbearance, your Republic may remain safe and whole under worthy leaders, above all in the time to follow! Thus I vowed and wrote, in my Museum, the day before the Kalends of January, at the end of the year according to the common Christian era, 1691.

units.la: Magnificentissimis & Amplissimis Nominibus Vestris, In Domino obsequentissimus
units.tr: To your most magnificent and ample names, most obedient in the Lord.

units.la: JOH. GEORGIUS FUESLINUS, S.S. Theol. Doct. & Evangelii Jesu Christi Præco.
units.tr: JOH. GEORGIUS FUESLINUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology, and Herald of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

units.la: PRÆFATIO ad Lectorem Christianum, Veritatisque Studiosum.
units.tr: PREFACE to the Christian Reader, and Lover of Truth.

units.la: Extus jam annus labitur, Lector Benevole! ex quo me linguam Italicam, saltem ad intelligentiam Authorum, addiscendi cupido incessit. Dúmque ei satisfacere laboravi, in manus meas pervenerunt primos inter Authores Conclavi de' Pontefici Romani. De quibus in ipso Opere Differt. IV. Sect. 3. n. 29. 30. ago prolixiús. Vixdum legere incœpi, & mentem subiit cogitatio, operæ forte pretium fore, si quis de Electione Pontificum Romanorum scriberet, & quæ ibi secundùm ordinem Conclavium habentur, in locos certos dispositá exhiberet, sicque ostenderet Orbi diligentiús, quales sint Electiones Pontificum. Aperui mentem meam Viris Doctissimis juxta ac Clarissimis nonnullis, simúlque, num non jam eam quis operam plenè navârit, investigavi. Addiderunt calcar jam currere volenti, & Authores aliquot, qui thema attingunt potiús, quàm plenè & ex professo tractant, partim indicârunt, partim etiam exhibuerunt. Quibus præter alia in investigatione ulteriori reperta ad pleniorem tractationem uti potui. Eam ita ordinare statim visum est, ut non tantùm ostendatur, Electiones Pontificum Romanorum in formis, Electoribus, principiis, accidentibus, Electis, & consequentibus suis næuis laborare plurimis, sed & ante omnia demonstretur, Electiones tam vitiosas nullo insuper etiam solido fundamento niti, neque veram sanctámque Dei ordinationem esse dignitatem, ad quam instituantur; Petrum, quem post Christum primum ad eam electum esse ajunt, ad talem Monarchiam Ecclesiastico-Politicam, & quidem Romanam, minimè electum esse, atque aliàs etiam Pontificum Romanorum Electionem non æstimari posse successionem in locum & dignitatem Petri, Petróque tributam. Visum & hoc, totam hanc tractationem convenire Stationi, in qua apud Exteros tunc temporis eram, & in qua Studiosos S. Ministerio destinatos cumprimis in Theologia Sacra & Historia Ecclesiastica juvare incumbebat. Quibus proin ex Antithesi genuinam Electionis Ministrorum N. T. rationem declarare & in horis Theologiæ destinatis Theologica hæc non minima, in horis Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ attributis Historica hæc, ad quæ juxta filum Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ aliàs sæpe recurrendum fuisset, propinare, & in Disputationibus hebdomadariis omnia porrò illustrare aptè licuit. Sic crevit, sic tandem confectum est opus; Quod jam sub initium anni M DC LXXXVII. approbationes, etiam à Celeberrimis nostris Theologis Tigurinis, quibus à me transmissum fuerat, non sine ulterioribus ad Editionem maturandam stimulis, accepit luculentas, scriptas, laude ex amore nata plenas, proin non publicandas. Atque jam jam prelo peregrino submitti debuisset, quando mense Julio anni M DC LXXXVIII. ejus Typum Disputatione publicâ: De legitima Ministrorum N. T. vocatione, & oppositâ ei Pontificum Romanorum Electione; Tiguri (Patriam enim tunc invisebam) exhibui, nisi paulò post ex improviso irruens bellica calamitas & Editionem apud Exteros impedivisset, & me in Patria manere, variásque mutationes, ceu tot à studiis avocationes, subire jussisset. Quamprimùm autem denuò pede fixo stare & sacro aliquo otio frui mihi contigit, denuò etiam de Opere nondum edito cogitavi. Jamque Editionem pactus fueram & coeperam, quando nuntiatum fuit, Clarissimum Virum, Jo. Fridericum Mayerum, Doctorem & Professorem Theologum, in Universitate Kilonienși & Gymnasio Hamburgensi, Hamburgensis itidem Ecclesiae ad D. Jacobi Pastorem & Scholarcham, de Pontificum Romanorum Electione librum Commentarium nuperrimè edidisse. Quo nuntio accepto, cogitavi equidem, jam laborem meum frustraneum fore, neque post Homerum Iliada scribi debere, & parùm mihi forte à tanto Nomine in hac materia relictum esse. Hæc animo volvens emi librum, frontispicium suprà positum vidi, in lectione τῶν σπεγλεγομένων pergens Cl. Kortholtum Kiloniensem S. Theologiæ Professorem Primarium & Academiæ Pro-Cancellarium Epitomen libri ita egregiè enuntiantem audivi: Nempe hæc Romana methodus servatur in Urbe: Sic Ordo eligitur, cujus successio certa Esse basis debet Sacri indubitanter ovilis. O quale & quantum in Romanis rebus inane est! Quàm confusa ibi cuncta, Deóque invisa hominique!
units.tr: For a year now, Kind Reader, I have been eager to learn the Italian language, at least enough to understand its authors. While I was working at this, I came across, among the first of these authors, the Conclave of the Roman Pontiffs. I discuss these at greater length in the work itself, Dissert. IV, Sect. 3, nn. 29, 30. I had barely begun to read them when the thought came to me that it might be worth the effort for someone to write on the Election of the Roman Pontiffs, and to set out in a fixed order what is found in the conclaves, so as to show the world more carefully what the elections of the Pontiffs are like. I shared my plan with some learned and distinguished men, and at the same time I enquired whether anyone had already fully carried out such a task. They spurred me on as I was already eager to run, and some authors who touch on the subject rather than treating it fully and expressly, some of them pointed out, others actually set out. From these, along with other material found in my further research, I was able to draw for a fuller treatment. I immediately decided to arrange it so that it would show not only that the elections of the Roman Pontiffs labour under many defects in their forms, electors, principles, accidents, persons elected and consequences, but above all that it would demonstrate that such defective elections rest on no solid foundation, that the dignity to which they install men is not a true and holy ordination of God, that Peter, whom they say was the first elected after Christ to that ecclesiastical-political monarchy, and indeed the Roman one, was by no means elected to it, and that otherwise the election of the Roman Pontiffs cannot be regarded as a succession to the place and dignity of Peter, which they ascribe to him. I also thought this whole treatment suited the post I then held among foreigners, where my duty was chiefly to help students destined for the holy ministry, especially in sacred theology and ecclesiastical history. So, by way of contrast, I was able to set out the genuine manner of electing ministers of the New Testament, to serve up this material as theology in the hours set for theology and as history in the hours given to ecclesiastical history, to which I would otherwise often have had to return along the thread of ecclesiastical history, and to make everything clear in the weekly disputations. So the work grew, and so at last it was finished. At the beginning of the year 1687 it received approvals, excellent and written, full of praise born of affection, from our most celebrated theologians of Zurich, to whom I had sent it, along with further urging to hasten the edition; these were therefore not to be published. And it was almost ready to be sent to a foreign press when, in July 1688, I presented its type in a public disputation, On the Lawful Calling of the Ministers of the New Testament, and the Election of the Roman Pontiffs set against it, at Zurich (for I was then visiting my homeland). But soon afterwards an unexpected war-calamity broke in and prevented the edition abroad, and ordered me to remain in my homeland and to undergo various changes, as many distractions from my studies. However, as soon as I was again able to stand on a settled foot and enjoy some sacred leisure, I once more thought about the work, not yet published. And I had already contracted for its edition and had begun it when word came that the most distinguished man, Johann Friedrich Mayer, Doctor and Professor of Theology in the University of Kiel and the Hamburg Gymnasium, likewise Pastor of St. James's and Scholarch of the Church of Hamburg, had very recently published a commentary-book on the Election of the Roman Pontiffs. On receiving this news, I did indeed think that my labour would now be in vain, and that one should not write a second Iliad after Homer, and that perhaps little had been left to me after so great a name in this subject. Turning these thoughts over in my mind, I bought the book, saw the title-page above, and while reading through [τῶν συγγεγραμμένων] the works, I heard the epitome of the book expressed so admirably by Kortholt of Kiel, Chief Professor of Sacred Theology and Pro-Chancellor of the University: namely, that this Roman method is observed in the City: thus an order is chosen whose certain succession must be the foundation of the holy flock beyond doubt. Oh, how empty and how great are Roman affairs! How confused everything is there, hateful to God and to man!

units.la: Sed & paulò post talia scribenti remunerationem Romanam abjudicantem, meliorem promittentem: Hæc quoque Roma quidem grates non solvet, opinor, Propterea, nec vel Papam, vel purpurâ amictum Carnalem Te constituet, vel Præsulis ullam Imponet mitram; plaudit tamen Orbis ubique Doctus, amans veri.
units.tr: But also a little later, to one who wrote such things, he denied a Roman reward and promised a better one: "Rome, I suppose, will not pay thanks for this either, and therefore will not make you a Pope, or a carnal man clothed in purple, nor will she place upon you any bishop's mitre; nevertheless the learned world everywhere, lovers of the truth, applauds."

units.la: In Præfatione Authoris stimulos à Celeberrimo Conringio non sine vero de pondere Thematis nondum plenè à quoquam tractati judicio Eidemsic additos inveni: Tuum de electione Paparum propositum laudo. Satis est enim vel illud unum evertenda Anti-Christiana Monarchia, me quidem judice: ac nihilominus tamen. tamen à quàm paucis Protestantium argumentum hoc vel tactum fuit. Dixi quidem ipse nonnulla de monstrosò illo negotio, in libro uno alteroque, jam edito, ac jam pridem affecta habeo longè plura, sed hactenus negotia editurum prohibuerunt, nunc præter illa etiam morbida mea senectus istam curam jubet deponere. Gaudeo igitur, abs Te insigne hoc negotium suscipi, qui vales & ætate, & supra ætatem accurato judicio, singularique industria. Nec verò dubito, etiam hoc in campo præstiturum Te adversariis verè Majorem &c. Postquam verò ipsum Cl. Mayeri Commentarium perlegissem diligentius, reperi, ut diversorum diversa sunt cogitata, ita etiam diversos esse non modò loquendi, sed & aliâs tractandi modos, diversa, etiam de rebus iisdem, lumina, diversa, idem etiam probandi, media. Nihil Cl. Mayerus habet de Electione Petri ad talem Monarchiam Romanam, nihil de Electione Pontificum, quatenus esse debet successio in locum & dignitatem Petri, distinctè; Præsupponit horum falsitatem, quam ego ostendo prolixiùs; Nonnisi ferè innuit, qui de Cardinalibus scripserint, quos ego ceu hodiernos Electores solos, solos Eligibiles, Papas in potentia, ut ex iis jam, quales eorum Electiones & Electi ab & ex iisdem esse possint, constaret, pluribus, & tamen in compendio Authorum, qui hactenus de iis scripserunt, describendos esse duxi. Nævos ratione Eligentium non ita distinctè omnes proponit & urget. Non agit de vitiosis eligendi principiis, nihil habet de Factionibus præter pauca de Regum concursu & authoritate, nihil, præter solum de Aphorismis Card. Azzolini indicium, de regulis eligendi vitiosis, quales Electoribus & eligendis ab Authoribus Pontificiis præscriptæ sunt, nihil de artificiosis molitionibus, nihil de artibus indignis, nihil de Simoniacis, nihil de violentis Electionibus, neque ita Pontificios ex ipsis Electionum accidentibus quibuscunque convincit, quod, meo quidem judicio, in ista tractatione palmarium & maximè essentiale est; Nihil affert de Electionibus Schismaticis, quas ego, cùm in iis non minimus sit Electionis Pontificum Romanorum nævus, imò nævorum confluxus, generaliùs & specialiùs fusè & compendiosè tamen prosequor, nihil de Ominibus Electionem interdum antecedere jactatis. Plùs quoque habemus, quæ ex Authoribus Gallicis & Italicis; Sic etiam de Johanna Papissa vitium Sexûs habente, de vitio ratione ætatis duplici, de nævis ratione Patriæ & statûs antecedentis plenior est nostra tractatio, & multò plenior illa de nævo ratione probitatis, eruditionis & prudentiæ electorum, nec non & illa de Electionis consequentibus, inter quæ non exponit ipse Nepotismum, ut prolixior contra est in explicandis partibus vestitûs Pontificii & Episcopalis, in capite de Avenione, in citationibus prolixis, in quibusdam aliis, dum tamen haud habet in universum vel quartam materiæ nostræ partem. Atque ita in Opere meo longè plurima esse deprehendi, quæ ipse vel plane non habet, vel minùs plenè exposita; contrà nihil feré est in ipsius Commentario, quod huc pertinere debeat, & non etiam fuerit in meo. Jmò fuerit; Neque enim exscripsi demum ex Commentario, quæ in eo reperi, quod facilè patebit ex collatio ibus, nisi longè paucissima & ea quidem contrahendo, quod non insolens & Cl. Mayero quoq; de meis licuisset & licere constitisset, si prius edita fuissent; Addidi autem, quando & alia in recentiore Lectione subinde notata, & ob Electiones recentiores duorum Pontificum addenda. Sed pleraque, quæ communia habemus, ceremonialia, ex iisdem Cæremonialis Romani & Cæremonialis Gregorij XV. fontibus haurimus uterque, & communia nobis non esse non potuissent commune Thema tractantibus. Quæ omnia non eo animo commemorare instituì, qui vel minimam meritorum & laudis Cl. Mayeri partem detrahere velit; Magnus & hic est, & quæ habet, egregia sunt, non simplici, sed florente stylo tradita, à veterano contrà Romanenses milite, dudum enim, quo eum Cl. Kortholtus in subscriptione carminis Gratulatorij elogio ornat, De Romana Curia, ingrata licèt, non pessimè meritus est. Scriptis etiam aliis, in quibus omnibus pari zeli fervore errores & abusus ejus prosternit. Sed mihi constitutum tantùm est, rationem reddere, cur post Commentarium à Tanto Viro editum & meum de Electione Pontificum Romanorum opus appareat, prius fortè conceptione, licèt non nativitate publicâ, & quoad eam jam non sine exemplo isthoc Thema perstringens maximè arduum, in quo tamen non aliena modò repeto, sed Mysterium Iniquitatis conjunctim multò quam hactenus à quocunque alio factum plenius expono. Quod, ut spero, ita invenies, Lector Benevole! Vale & labore meo qualicunque ad Dei in Antichristianismi Romani detestatione & veritatis oppositæ ferventiore amore gloriam, ipso nobis gratiosè cooperante, ut libet, fruere!
units.tr: In the Author's Preface I found that he had been spurred on by the most celebrated Conring, who, with a true judgement of the weight of the subject, which no one has yet fully treated, added these words: "I praise your purpose concerning the election of the Popes. For, in my judgement, that one thing is enough to overthrow the Antichristian monarchy. And yet, how few of the Protestants have even touched on this argument! I myself have said some things about that monstrous business in one or two books already published, and I have long held far more on the matter in hand, but up to now my affairs have prevented me from publishing them; now, besides those, my sickly old age bids me lay this care down. I am glad, therefore, that you have taken up this remarkable business, you who are strong both in age and beyond your age in accurate judgement and singular diligence. Nor do I doubt that you will show yourself, even in this field, truly superior to your adversaries, etc." But when I had read through Mayer's own commentary more carefully, I found that, as different men have different thoughts, so they also have different modes not only of speaking but also of treating matters; different lights on the same things, and also different means of proof. Mayer has nothing about the election of Peter to that Roman monarchy, nothing about the election of the Pontiffs insofar as it ought to be a succession to the place and dignity of Peter, as a separate point; he presupposes their falsity, which I show at greater length. He only hints at what those who wrote about the Cardinals have said, whom I, as the present electors, the only ones eligible, Popes in potency, judged should be described, in the compendium of the authors who have so far written about them, so that from these it might be clear how their elections and the elected could be and what they could be from and by these men, and yet I thought this should be done. He does not set out and press all the defects on the part of the electors so distinctly. He does not treat the defective principles of electing; he has nothing about factions except a few things on the concurrence and authority of kings, nothing, except only an indication from the Aphorisms of Cardinal Azzolino, on the defective rules of electing, such as the Papist authors prescribe for electors and those to be elected; nothing on artful schemes, nothing on unworthy arts, nothing on the Simoniacal, nothing on violent elections; nor does he convince the Papists so thoroughly from the accidents of the elections themselves, which, in my judgement, is the chief and most essential point in this treatment. He brings nothing on Schismatic Elections, in which, since there is no small defect of the election of the Roman Pontiffs, indeed a confluence of defects, I follow them more generally and specially, fully and briefly. Nothing on the omens which are sometimes boasted of as preceding an election. We also have more matter from French and Italian authors; thus our treatment of Pope Joan, who had the defect of sex, of the twofold defect of age, of the defects of country and previous condition, is fuller, and much fuller is that on the defect of the probity, learning and prudence of the electors, and also that on the consequences of the election, among which he does not set out Nepotism itself, whereas the contrary is fuller in explaining the parts of Papal and Episcopal vestments, in the chapter on Avignon, in the lengthy citations, and in certain other things, though he does not have in general even a quarter of our material. And so in my work I found very many things which he either does not have at all or sets out less fully; on the other hand there is almost nothing in his commentary which ought to pertain to this and which is not also in mine. Indeed, there is; for I did not finally copy out from his commentary whatever I found in it, as will easily be clear from the comparisons, except very few things, and those by condensing, which would not have been unusual and would have been allowable for Mayer too, to use from mine, had mine been published first. I added, however, both other things noted from time to time in later reading, and things to be added on account of the more recent elections of two Pontiffs. But most of what we have in common, the ceremonial matters, we both draw from the same sources, the Ceremonial of the Romans and the Ceremonial of Gregory XV; and we could not fail to have things in common, since we treat a common subject. I did not set out to mention all these things with the intention of detracting even the smallest part of the merit and praise of Mayer; he is great, and what he has is excellent, delivered not in a plain but in a flourishing style, by a veteran soldier against the Romanists, for he has long, as Kortholt honours him in the subscription of his congratulatory verse, deserved not badly of the Roman Curia, though an ungrateful one. He also has other writings, in all of which he overthrows its errors and abuses with an equal fervour of zeal. But my only purpose is to give an account of why my work, On the Election of the Roman Pontiffs, appears after the commentary published by so great a man, having been conceived earlier, perhaps, though not yet published, and taking up a subject which is, in this respect too, not without precedent, most arduous; yet in it I not only repeat what is not my own, but I set out the Mystery of Iniquity together, far more fully than anyone else has done so far. This, as I hope, you will find so, Kind Reader! Farewell, and enjoy my labour, such as it is, for the glory of God in the detestation of Roman Antichristianism and in a more fervent love of the opposite truth, with Him graciously cooperating with us, as He pleases!

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS PRIMÆ SECTIO
units.tr: FIRST SECTION OF THE FIRST DISSERTATION

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA,
units.tr: SECTION ONE,

units.la: Quæ agit, partim de magnitudine rei tractandæ, sive de Electionis Pontificum Romanorum dignitate, ex hypothesi, partim de necessitate certæ hic cognitioni, partim denique de eo, quòd Petrum authoritatem Scripturæ allegantes jactant; Breviarium.
units.tr: Which deals partly with the greatness of the matter to be treated, namely the dignity of the election of the Roman Pontiffs, taken as a hypothesis; partly with the need for certain knowledge here; and finally partly with what the Papists boast of when they allege Peter's authority from Scripture. A summary.

units.la: I. Magnitudo rei tractanda ostenditur primò ex dicto Bellarmini de Primatu Pontificis. II. Ex Conclavium duorum exordiis, & dicto Cardinalis Tarentini. III. Explicatur & examinantur horum dicta, de electione Vicarii Christi & alterius in terris Dei. IV. Infertur, ex priori maximè Epitheto, Romanenses Christum facere quasi primum Pontificem Romanum.
units.tr: I. The greatness of the matter to be treated is shown first from Bellarmine's saying about the Primacy of the Pontiff. II. From the prefaces of two Conclaves and the saying of Cardinal Tarentinus. III. Their sayings are explained and examined, concerning the election of the Vicar of Christ and of another God on earth. IV. It is inferred, chiefly from the first epithet, that the Romanists make Christ, as it were, the first Roman Pontiff.

units.la: V. Infertur porrò, certè igitur constare debere de illo Christi Vicario. VI. Cujus certa cognitionis necessitas ex imparibus illustratur, & simul ostenditur, neque naturam aut rationem, neque etiam miraculosam demonstrationem, neque etiam testimonialem de illo Vicario nos edocere; non posse nos edoceri hic ab ulla traditione non scripta; scriptam claram esse debere. VII. Quod porrò ostenditur, & dicitur, Scriptura testimonia ostendere velle Pontificios, licèt contrà propria principia sic agant. VIII. Allegantes ea, quæ de Petro, vel saltem ad Petrum in Scriptura dicta sunt. Ubi, quantum Petrum jactent, & ubique Successionem ejus crepent, pluribus ostenditur. IX. Et causæ hujus, cúrque potiùs Petrum, quàm alios Antecessores allegent hodierni, exponuntur. X. Difficultas ipsis proponitur, quomodo nimirum simul immediati Vicarii Christi & simul etiam nonnunquam Vicarii Petri esse velint Pontifices.
units.tr: V. It is further inferred that it must therefore be certain concerning that Vicar of Christ. VI. The necessity of certain knowledge is illustrated from unequal cases, and at the same time it is shown that neither nature nor reason, nor even miraculous demonstration, nor testimony teaches us about that Vicar; we cannot be taught here by any unwritten tradition; it must be clearly written in Scripture. VII. It is further shown and said that the Papists wish to show this from Scripture testimonies, although in acting so they go against their own principles. VIII. They allege those things which are said in Scripture about Peter, or at least to Peter. Where, and how much they boast of Peter and everywhere trumpet his succession, is shown at length. IX. The causes of this are explained, and why today's men allege Peter rather than the other predecessors. X. The difficulty is put to them, namely how Popes wish to be at once the immediate Vicars of Christ and at the same time sometimes Vicars of Peter.

units.la: I. ARduum molimur opus de Pontificum Romanorum Electione scripturi; Etenim de qua re agitur? Est quæstio Bellarmini Præfat. in libr. de Pont. Rom. quoad Primatum Pontificum; ad quam statim ipse respondet Brevissimè dicam; de summa rei Christianæ; Id enim quæritur, debeátne Ecclesia diutiùs consistere, an verò dissolvi & concidere. Quid enim aliud est quærere, an oporteat ab ædificio fundamentum removere, à grege pastorem, ab exercitu Imperatorem, solem ab astris, caput à corpore, quàm, an oporteat ædificium ruere, gregem dissipari, exercitum fundi, sydera obscurari, corpus jacere? Si tantum in Romanorum Pontificum Primatu situm est, si, Bellarmino judice, rei Christianæ summa, Christianismi fundamentum est, certè haud parùm situm etiam eric in Romanorum Pontificum Electione, quae hujus fundamenti fundamentum est, & quae, quale sit illud fundamentum, qualis ei inaedificata domus, homines edocere potest, & per quam iste Primatus & potestatis quaedam infinitudo conferri dicitur.
units.tr: I. I am undertaking a difficult work in writing about the election of the Roman Pontiffs. For what is the matter at issue? It is the question Bellarmine raises in his Preface to the book on the Roman Pontiff, concerning the Primacy of the Pontiffs; to which he himself immediately replies, "I will say very briefly," that it concerns the sum of the Christian religion. For what is asked is whether the Church ought to continue longer or rather be dissolved and collapse. For what else is it to ask whether one ought to remove the foundation from a building, the shepherd from a flock, the emperor from an army, the sun from the stars, the head from the body, than to ask whether the building ought to fall, the flock be scattered, the army be dispersed, the stars grow dim, and the body lie dead? If the sum of the Christian cause lies in the primacy of the Roman Pontiffs, if, by Bellarmine's judgment, the sum of the Christian religion is the foundation of Christianity, then certainly no small part of it will also lie in the election of the Roman Pontiffs, which is the foundation of this foundation, and which can teach men what kind of foundation that is and what kind of house is built upon it, and through which this primacy and a certain infinitude of power is said to be conferred.

units.la: II. Nec mirum est, quod, qui ista revera per Electionem Pontificibus conferri credunt, magnifice etiam de ea & sentiunt & loquuntur, & quod in specie Conclavium Scriptores (de quibus & Conclavibus, & Scriptoribus plura suo loco dicenda erunt;) nonnunquam a rei, quam describendam susceperunt, momento ordiuntur: La creatione del Pontifice, ita incipit Conclave Innocentii IX. è senza alcun dubio &c. Id est; Creatio Pontificis est sine omni dubio gravissima & maxime ardua actionum, qua in mundo fiunt, quandoquidem de gradu Cardinalatus, tam alto & eminenti; sed qui absolutam potestatem in neminem exercet, plerumque ad sublimissimum & excelsissimum solium & ad supremam in terris in animas & etiam in corpora, opes, principatus, regna, imperia, potestatem, persona ordinaria, nonnunquam etiam ex infima plebe nata evehitur &c. Nec est dissimile exordium Conclavis Sixti V. Omnia autem in Conclavi Nicolai V. paucis complexus est Cardinalis Tarentinus, Collegis festinationem in Electionis actu dissuadens, hoc argumento, quod agatur de eligendo (un altro Dio in terra,) altero in terris Deo.
units.tr: II. Nor is it surprising that those who truly believe these things are conferred on Pontiffs through election think and speak magnificently of it, and that the writers of the Conclaves in particular (about whom, and about the Conclaves, more will be said in its place) sometimes begin with the weight of the matter they have undertaken to describe. "La creatione del Pontifice": so begins the Conclave of Innocent IX, "è senza alcun dubio," and so on. That is: "The creation of the Pontiff is without doubt the most grave and most arduous of all the actions that take place in the world, since it concerns the rank of Cardinal, so high and eminent; yet he who exercises absolute power over no one is for the most part raised to the most sublime and lofty throne, and to the supreme power on earth over souls and also over bodies, wealth, principalities, kingdoms, empires and power; an ordinary person, sometimes even born of the lowest common people," and so on. The opening of the Conclave of Sixtus V is not dissimilar. Cardinal Tarentinus, in dissuading the college from haste in the act of election, summed up everything in the Conclave of Nicholas V with this argument, that the matter concerns electing (another God on earth,) "another God on earth."

units.la: III. Magna profecto haec sunt, & tanta, quanta mortalium a condito hoc universo nulli alii (θεάνθρωπον si excipias) unquam fuerunt attributa. Huic autem se pares faciunt hujus, ut haberi volunt, Vicarii, quo quidem titulo non in tenui illo sensu insigniuntur, in quo Vicarios Christi vocare liceret Evangelii praecones quoscunque, tanquam ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύοντες, nomine Christi legatione fungentes 2.Cor. V.20. & Ministerium Verbi a Christo sibi demandatum, habentes; sed in omni vocis emphasi, & quatenus successionem in regno & potestatem absolutam legislationis, remissionis & dispensationum caeterarum salutis aeternae involvit, imo etiam talia, quae Christus tanquam Doctor & Moderator Ecclesiae non habuit, non exercuit; Pauper ipse; non eximii & magni Imperii temporalis Gubernator; subditus ipse; non, supremam in terris, etiam in corpora, opes, Principatus, regna, imperia, potestatem exercens; uno verbo talis, cujus regnum οὐκ ἐστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, non ex hoc mundo Joh.XVIII. 36. Sic plura, quam quae Christus Ecclesiae Doctor & Moderator habuit, exercuit, (glorificati autem qua tali Vicarius, vel Successor esse non potest;) sed non minora, plenitudinem potestatis Christi, qui, ex quo in coelum ascendit, (licet praesentiam, nimirum quoad spiritualem gratiae influxum & potentiam contra quoscunque hostes tuitivam & verbi Sacramentorumque ministerium ἕως τῆς συντελείας τῶν αἰώνων, usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 20. promiserit, & tanquam Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedec habeat ἀπαρέγκλητον τὸν ἱερωσύνην, sacerdotium non transiens, in hoc etiam potior sacerdotibus Aharonicis, quòd illi quidem plures facti sunt Sacerdotes, quia mors prohibebat eos permanere, cùm ille contrà maneat εἰς τ᾽ αἰῶνα, in aeternum, πάντοτε ζῶν, semper vivens, Hebr. VII. 23.24.25. Τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ἔσχατος, A & O, primus ille & ultimus ille ζῶν εἰς τὰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, vivens in secula seculorum, claves adhuc habens, etiam inferorum & mortis: quemadmodum ipse ad Johannis & Ecclesiarum solatium ne minimâ quidem talis Vicarii mentione factâ Apoc. I. 8. 11. 18. testatur) qui inquam, ex quo in coelum ascendit, his hominibus aut non regnat, aut in coelo tantum, dum Pontifex alter Deus in terris (quod elogium etiam Julius II in Concilio Lateranensi sess. 4. & 9. Marcello insigniente audiit) sive (quod Paulus V. admisit) Vice-Deus rebus praeest, quem etiam, si Augustino Steucho Bibliothecario de Donat. Constat. pag. 141. fides habenda, Constantinus uti Deum, uti Christi & Petri successorem adoravit: Divinos honores ei, quoad ejus potuit, contulit, velut vivam Christi imaginem veneratus est; & de quo Joh. de Turrecremata Eccles. Hier. p. 2. l. 5. p. 298. ait: Tenemur Pontificem Christi Personam in Ecclesia sustinentem, ceu ipsius Ecclesiae fundamentum & basin perpetua cum veneratione venerari & sanctissimum velut numen excolere; Quemadmodum etiam idem Tribunal Christi & Papae esse in Concilio Tridentino Lainezius Jesuitarum Generalis asseruit, & eundem utrique honorem deberi Augustinus de Ancona summ. de Pot. Eccles. q. 9. art. 1. p. 93. concludit, & promiscuè loca de Christi potestate & honore ei debito Papis applicant.
units.tr: III. These things are indeed great, and as great as any ever attributed to any mortal since this universe was made, except the God-man (θεάνθρωπον), if you exclude him. Those who want to be held as this one's Vicars make themselves equal to him. They are marked with this title not in that slight sense in which it would be lawful to call any preachers of the Gospel Vicars of Christ, as "acting as ambassadors on behalf of Christ" (ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύοντες), discharging the office of envoy in Christ's name (2 Cor. 5:20), and having the ministry of the Word entrusted to them by Christ. Rather, they are marked in the full emphasis of the word, and insofar as it involves succession in the kingdom and absolute power of legislation, of remission and of the other dispensations of eternal salvation; indeed, also such things as Christ, as Teacher and Governor of the Church, did not have and did not exercise. He himself was poor; he was not the governor of a distinguished and great temporal empire; he himself was a subject; he did not exercise "supreme power on earth, even over bodies, wealth, principalities, kingdoms, empires." In a word, his kingdom is "not of this world" (οὐκ ἐστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου), John 18:36. Thus they have more than Christ had and exercised as Teacher and Governor of the Church, though glorified as such he cannot be a Vicar or Successor. But they have no less than the fullness of power of Christ, who, since he ascended into heaven (though he promised his presence, namely the spiritual influx of grace and protective power against all enemies, and the ministry of the Word and Sacraments, "until the end of the age," ἕως τῆς συντελείας τῶν αἰώνων, Matt. 28:20; and as "a priest according to the order of Melchizedek" he holds an unchangeable priesthood, ἀπαρέγκλητον τὴν ἱερωσύνην, "not passing on," which in this too is greater than the Aaronic priests, in that "indeed they were made priests in greater numbers, because death prevented them from continuing, whereas he remains" for ever, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, "always living," πάντοτε ζῶν, Heb. 7:23-25; "the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last," ζῶν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, "living for ever and ever," still holding the keys even of hell and death, as he himself, for the comfort of John and the Churches, bears witness without making the slightest mention of any such Vicar, Rev. 1:8, 11, 18), who, I say, since he ascended into heaven, either does not reign over these men, or reigns only in heaven, while the Pontiff, "another God on earth" (an elogium which Julius II also heard applied to himself by Marcellus at the Lateran Council, sessions 4 and 9), or (as Paul V admitted) "Vice-God," presides over affairs. Constantine, if one may trust the librarian Augustinus Steuchus, On the Donation of Constantine, p. 141, "worshipped him as God, as successor of Christ and Peter; he conferred divine honours on him as far as he could, venerating him as a living image of Christ." Of him John de Torquemada says (Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, part 2, book 5, p. 298): "We are bound to venerate with perpetual reverence the Pontiff who sustains the person of Christ in the Church, as the very foundation and base of the Church itself, and to honour him as a most holy deity." Just so, Lainez, General of the Jesuits, asserted at the Council of Trent that the tribunal of Christ and of the Pope is the same; and Augustinus de Ancona, in his Summa on Ecclesiastical Power, q. 9, art. 1, p. 93, concludes that the same honour is due to each. They apply indiscriminately to the Popes the passages about Christ's power and the honour due to him.

units.la: IV. Ut etiam sic satis superque dicatur: Ecce hic est Christus! imò, quemadmodum paucis ostendimus quoque aliqua ratione: Hic est plus quàm Christus! & in texendo Romanorum Pontificum Catalogo secundùm istas hypotheses primus illi locus assignandus foret, quemadmodum etiam Platina Historiam de vitis Pontificum scripturus, juxta titulum eam merito à vita Christi auspicatus est, & Jesum Christum aequè in frontispicio posuit, ac post ipsum D. Petrum, & in fine historiae Christi de lectione historiae suae dixit, eam tanquam irriguum fontem ab Imperatore Christianorum in Pontifices Romanos per ordinem derivari. Interim Christum verbis apertis Pontificem Romanum facere hactenus reformidant, dum tamen rem ipsam sedulò inculcare non erubescunt. Nam quòd Romæ non fuit Christus, id solùm obstare hîc non posset; siquidem constat, per 70. annos, quibus captivitas Babylonica, sub N. T. Italorum appellatione, duravit passivè respectu Papārum (quamvis alii etiam activè malint, & terminos ultrà extendant;) Pontifices æquè aliis Romanos Avenione sedisse; Sed his multùm immorari non est opus.
units.tr: IV. So that it may be said well enough, and more than enough: "Behold, here is Christ!" Indeed, as we show briefly in some way: "Here is more than Christ!" And in drawing up the catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs on these hypotheses, the first place would have to be assigned to him. Platina too, about to write the history of the lives of the Pontiffs, according to its title "rightly began it from the life of Christ," and placed Jesus Christ on the frontispiece equally with, and after him, St Peter. At the end of the history of Christ he said, about reading his own history, that "it is derived in order, like water from an irrigating fountain, from the Emperor of the Christians into the Roman Pontiffs." Meanwhile they hesitate to make Christ Roman Pontiff in plain words, though they do not blush to inculcate the thing itself diligently. For that Christ was not at Rome cannot be an obstacle here; for it is established that during the seventy years of the "Babylonian captivity," under the New Testament name of Italians, the Popes, passively speaking, sat at Avignon like other Romans (though some prefer to make it active too and extend the limits further). But there is no need to dwell long on these things.

units.la: V. Illud saltem hic notâsse sufficiat, horum Successorum & Vicariorum Christi Electionem haud obscura divinitatis indicia postulare, quando benignissimus Servator; non se ipsum glorificavit, ut Pontifex fieret, sed is qui dixerat ei, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te; Et alibi, Tu es Sacerdos in æternum, secundùm ordinem Melchisedk. Heb. V.5.6. Ut etiam Divina ejus Electio partim Scripturis Propheticis, partim apparitione Spiritûs, partim voce bis cœlitùs missa, Matth III.17. XVII.5. partim Testimoniis Piorum, partim Doctrinæ præstantiâ, partim Signorum efficaciâ, partim plane irreprehensibili vitâ, & ut omnia verbo dicam, exactissimâ eorum omnium, quæ talem decebant, & à tali exspectari poterant, præstatione hominibus approbata fuit. Quibus proin similia circa Vicariorum & Successorum ejus constitutionem haud immerito desideres, talium certè, quibus omnes subjici necesse est, & qui indemonstrabilia loqui, nec effata sua aliorum examini submittere, qui tantam potestatem exercere, qui honorem tantum accipere volunt; id saltem, ut clarissimis testimoniis Christus, cujus Successionem & Vicariatum jactant, eorum institutionem notârit, firmârit.
units.tr: V. It will be enough to note here that the election of these successors and vicars of Christ does not admit of obscure signs of divinity. The most gracious Saviour "did not glorify himself to be made a high priest, but he who said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee"; and elsewhere, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec" (Heb. 5:5, 6). His own divine election was approved to men partly by the prophetic Scriptures, partly by the appearance of the Spirit, partly by the voice sent twice from heaven (Matt. 3:17; 17:5), partly by the testimonies of the godly, partly by the excellence of his teaching, partly by the power of his signs, partly by a plainly blameless life, and, to say everything in a word, by the most exact performance of all those things that befitted such a person and could be expected from one such as he. Accordingly, one may rightly expect similar things concerning the appointment of his vicars and successors: at the very least, men to whom everyone must submit, who claim to speak things that cannot be demonstrated, who will not submit their pronouncements to the examination of others, and who wish to exercise such great power and receive such great honour. At the very least, let Christ, whose succession and vicariate they boast of, have marked and confirmed their appointment by the clearest testimonies.

units.la: VI. Utique rei magnitudo desiderium hocce ab æquitate commendat; si enim prudentiæ regula nobiscum nata nos nihil temerè credere jubet, & in aliis minoris longè momenti negotiis obtinet illud Epicharmi: Νᾶφε ... φρενῶν; quantò magis opus erit cauto in eo, quod plurimùm nocere potest malè creditum, æternùm nocere potest? At jam hunc vel illum esse talem Christi Vicarium, certè naturâ non cognosco, non enim inter κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, notiones communes, hæc assertio locum habet, neque id merâ humanâ ratiocinatione colligere possum; esset enim, si vel omnia largiremur, arbitrii duntaxat Divini, quod citra revelationem cognosci nequit, quando enim ea, quæ sunt hominis nemo scit, nisi Spiritus hominis, qui in ipso est; multò magis ea, quæ Dei sunt, nemo novit, nisi Spiritus Dei I.Cor II.11. Et hîc in specie ratio dictat; quemadmodum ante Pontifices natos sine tali Vicariatu & Μοναρχίᾳ mundum gubernari Deus sit passus, ita & post mero sane arbitrio ejus relictum esse, num unum aliquod toti mundo caput dare velit, aut non dare; imo docet, plurimum admissa Potestate Pontificia omnes humanas res publicas privatasque ab eo, quod alias recepti & vulgo inter homines cogniti est juris, variare; ut temerarium foret nova illa & nusquam hactenus audita, omnemque fidem superantia, spretis iis, quorum ratio ab orbe condito omnibus fuit mortalibus probata, sine certa & evidenti demonstratione laudare & in usum transferre. Quae demonstratio proin hic omnino est necessaria; sive miraculosa, quam personae tantae & usque adeo extraordinariae requirere plane videntur, praesertim cum Deus Prophetas suos & Apostolos, qui longe minora de se quam Vicarii isti de se credi voluerunt, ea commendarit; Sed operum miraculosorum patrandorum vim sibi deesse ultro largiuntur Pontifices hodierni, id est, se plane praeter naturae ordinem institutos mundi Gubernatores, & quos Deus ab omnibus tanquam suos Pro-Reges coli velit, non tamen aliqua Majestate diviniore ornatos esse, non viros ὡς ἡ Θεὸς εἰς ἡμᾶς ἀποδεδειγμένους δυνάμεσι, καὶ τέρασι καὶ σημείοις, a Deo ad nos demonstratos virtutibus & prodigiis & signis; sive testimonialis per verbum; Tertiam enim viam in talibus non dari, ipse Papa Innocentius III. lib.V. Decretalium tit.7. cap.12. agnovisse videtur. Cum interior missio, inquit, sit occulta, non sufficit cuiquam nude tantum asserere, quod ipse sit missus a Deo, cum hoc quilibet haereticus asseveret, sed oportet, quod adstruat illam infallibilem missionem per viam miraculi, vel Scripturae testimonium speciale. Ad Scripturam merito provocat, cum sit, quod vulgo ajunt, fama malum, & sint litera, Livio Annal. l.6. teste, una custodia fidelis memoriae rerum gestarum. Traditiones contra incertae, variae & quae hic adducuntur, ab ipsis Pontificibus, de quorum hic constitutione quaeritur, demum auctoritatem suam habere dicantur, & hic maxime applicari meretur Bonifacii VIII. in Extra. Com. de Elect. verba: Asserenti, se cum mandatis Principis venisse, credendum non est, nisi hoc scriptis probaverit; Nec similiter creditur, se asserenti legatum. Nunquam enim Apostolica sedi moris fuit, absque signatis apicibus undecunque legationem suscipere; Sed nec dicenti se delegatum Sedis ejusdem creditur vel intenditur, nisi de mandato Apostolico fide doceat oculata. De ista autem testimoniali demonstratione per verba scripta ante omnia necesse est, ut clara sit. Lex erit de tali Vicario, cui subesse, omni humana creatura esse de necessitate salutis, declaravit, definivit & pronunciavit Bonifacius VIII. Extrav. Unam sanctam &c. ipse, si credere fas est, talis; neque enim tantùm consilia dantur de rebus tantis, cùm nullius quamvis exiguæ civitatis regimen ita institui aut soleat, aut possit; Et si vel consilium esset, Dei esset, proin vice legis: Perspicuitatem autem debere esse cujuslibet legis, siquidem vim obligandi nancisci velit, dotem, inter ea est, quæ homines sine omni pene magistro discimus, qualem tamen hic ex superfluo audire possumus Gratianum, vel potiùs Isidorum, cujus ille hæc verba in Decretum Dist.4. recepit: Erit autem lex manifesta quoque, ne aliquid per obscuritatem in captionem contineat.
units.tr: VI. Surely the greatness of the matter commends this desire to fairness. For if the rule of prudence, born with us, bids us believe nothing rashly, and in other matters of far smaller weight the saying of Epicharmus holds: "Be sober ... of mind" [Νᾶφε ... φρενῶν]; how much more caution will be needed in that matter, where a wrongly believed thing can do the greatest harm, and can harm eternally? But that this or that man is such a vicar of Christ, I certainly do not know by nature, for this assertion does not belong among the common notions [κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι], nor can I gather it by mere human reasoning. It would be a matter of the divine will alone, even if we granted everything, which cannot be known without revelation; for "the things of a man no one knows, except the spirit of man which is in him; much more the things of God no one knows, except the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2:11). And here in particular reason dictates that, just as God allowed the world to be governed before the Pontiffs were born, without such a vicariate and monarchy [Μοναρχίᾳ], so too it has been left entirely to his free decision whether he will give the world one head or not. Indeed, it teaches that, with the Papal power admitted, all human public and private affairs would be altered from the law that is otherwise received and commonly known among men. So it would be rash to praise and put into practice those new and never-before-heard-of things, which surpass all belief, while setting aside those things whose reasoning has been approved by all mortals since the foundation of the world, without a certain and evident demonstration. Therefore a demonstration is absolutely necessary here: either a miraculous one, which such great and so extraordinary a person plainly seems to require, especially since God commended by such means his prophets and apostles, who claimed far less for themselves than these vicars wish to be believed about themselves; but today's Pontiffs freely claim for themselves the power of performing miracles, that is, that they are rulers of the world appointed quite beyond the order of nature, whom God wishes to be honoured by all as his own vice-kings, yet they are not adorned with any more divine majesty, not men "shown to you by God with powers and wonders and signs" [ὡς ἡ Θεὸς εἰς ἡμᾶς ἀποδεδειγμένους δυνάμεσι, καὶ τέρασι καὶ σημείοις]; or else a testimonial one, by the word. For that Pope Innocent III himself seems to have acknowledged that there is no third way in such matters, in Book 5 of the Decretals, title 7, chapter 12: "Since the inner mission is hidden, it is not enough for anyone merely to assert baldly that he has been sent by God, since any heretic can assert this; but he must show that infallible mission by way of a miracle or a special testimony of Scripture." He rightly appeals to Scripture, since, as people commonly say, "report is a bad thing, but letters are a faithful custodian of the memory of deeds," as Livy witnesses (Annals, book 6). Traditions, by contrast, are uncertain and various, and those adduced here are said to have their authority only from the very Pontiffs whose constitution is in question here; and the words of Boniface VIII in the Extra Commune, On Elections, apply most fittingly here: "One who asserts that he has come with the commands of a prince is not to be believed unless he proves it by writing; nor is one who claims to be a legate believed in the same way. For it has never been the custom of the Apostolic See to receive a legation from anywhere without sealed letters; nor is one who says he is a delegate of that same See believed or heeded, unless he proves by clear sight that it is by Apostolic command." Moreover, concerning this testimonial demonstration by written words, it is above all necessary that it be clear. The law will concern such a vicar, to whom "it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject," as Boniface VIII declared, defined and pronounced in the Extravagant Unam sanctam, if it is right to believe that he is such. For such great matters do not give rise merely to counsels, since no government even of the smallest city is usually or can be set up in such a way; and even if it were a counsel, it would be of God and so have the force of law. Now, clarity is a requirement of any law, if it wishes to acquire the power of binding; this is among those things that we learn without almost any teacher, though here we may hear it superfluously from Gratian, or rather from Isidore, whose words Gratian received into the Decretum, Dist. 4: "A law shall be manifest also, lest it contain anything by obscurity that entraps."

units.la: VII. Oportet igitur, ut in Verbo Dei scripto de Electione sive constitutione horum Pontificum agatur, & quidem perspicuè; oportet, ut ex eo cognoscere possim, quæ illorum potestas, quis illis debitus honos, quæ obedientia debita; quis eorum primus esse meruerit, quomodo successio cæterorum constare queat, ne aliâs regulam fidei meæ ignorem, Legislatorem rejiciam, præscripta extra Verbum salutis media vilipendam, alterum in terris Deum Christíque in Regno suo Vicarium contemnam, & extra Pastoris summi curam & erratorum meorum veniam misere & æternùm peream. Consentiunt ipsæ Pontificiorum hypotheses, dum nimirum Scripturam ideò perfectam dici, ajunt, quòd ad Ecclesiam, id est, stylo partis majoris, ad Papam, Doctorem infallibilem nos quasi manu ducat. Mira perfectio Verbi, quod ipsum potest σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν, sapientem facere ad salutem, & quod ipsum utile est, ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, qua est in justitia, ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος, ut perfectus sit Dei homo ad omne bonum opus perfectè instructus 2.Tim.III.15.16.17. si nobis ostendit Doctorem aliquem, qui ne quidem ex illo verbo, placita sua demonstrare vult, & omnia necessaria ex eo demonstrari posse negat! Similis ferè perfectio, cum perfectione cæci de vidente loquentis, pauperis alienas divitias cognoscentis! Interim tamen manet ipsorummet voluntate, Scripturas nobis Doctorem istum ostendere debere, de ejus constitutione loqui, & evidenter. Complures certè, nonnullis aliis cum Valeriano Capucino &c. Ingenuè fatentibus, infallibilem hunc Doctoratum & Vicariatum sepositâ Traditionis Infallibilitate non esse demonstrabilem, id est, Doctorem suum non nisi ex proprio testitestimonio cognosci posse, in eo sunt, ut hinc causae suae fidem faciant, id est, volunt probare primum per secundum, incognitum per magis incognitum, Papam, à cujus infallibili dictamine Scripturae Divinitas & sensus pendent, per Scripturam, quae secundùm eos nonnisi agnita jam Papae authoritate intelligi potest & authoritatem habere; id est, porrò volunt sibi contradicere in eo, quòd ex Scriptura, quam perspicuam esse negant, testimonia perspicua producere volunt; quod eos non facere demum concedemus, quando nobis ante probaverint, Scripturae testimonia illa solùm perspicua esse, quae Papae authoritatem probent, caetera tenebris involvi densissimis, perspicuum esse illud: Tu es Petrus &c. obscurum illud: Adorabis Dominum Deum tuum, & ipsi soli servies Matth.IV.10. obscurum & illud: Colliginus igitur fide justificari hominem absque operibus legis, Rom.III.28. Obscura caetera omnia, paucissimis tantùm quae pro constitutione infallibilis sui Doctoris adducunt, exceptis; obscura usque adeò, ut etiam Dei invocato nomine, adhibitâ omni diligentiâ, considerato scopo, spectatis antecedentibus & consequentibus, collatis denique Scripturae partibus aliis lucem mutuò dantibus, homo pius ad propriam convictionem & fratrum admonitionem sensum in necessariis sine hoc Doctore indemonstrabilia loquente assequi neutiquam valeat, cùm contrà haec pauca ita perspicua esse debeant, ut sine Doctoris illius, utpote cujus constitutio & authoritas adhuc probanda est, authorirate illorum sensus omni Christiano sit evidens. Quaeramus istam evidentiam & Pontificum Romanorum in Scriptura certam Electionem atque Constitutionem.
units.tr: VII. It is necessary, therefore, that the constitution or election of these Pontiffs be treated in the written Word of God, and that clearly. It is necessary that from it I may know what their power is, what honour is due them, what obedience is owed; who among them has deserved to be first, and how the succession of the others can be established. Otherwise I would be ignorant of the rule of my faith, reject the Lawgiver, despise the means prescribed outside the Word of salvation, scorn the one God on earth and Christ's vicar in his kingdom, and, outside the care of the supreme Shepherd and the pardon of my errors, perish wretchedly and eternally. The very hypotheses of the Papists agree with this, since they say that Scripture is called perfect for this reason: that it leads us by the hand to the Church, that is, in the style of the greater part, to the Pope, the infallible Teacher. What a remarkable perfection of the Word, which can "make wise unto salvation" [σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν], and which is profitable "for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works" [ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος] (2 Tim. 3:15, 16, 17), if it shows us some teacher who does not even wish to demonstrate his opinions from that very Word, and denies that everything necessary can be demonstrated from it! It is a perfection much like the perfection of a blind man compared with a seeing man speaking of colours, or of a poor man recognising the riches of others! Yet it remains, by their own will, that the Scriptures must show us that Teacher and speak of his constitution, and do so evidently. Indeed, many, along with some others who frankly confess, with Valerianus the Capuchin and others, that this infallible teaching office and vicariate cannot be demonstrated apart from the infallibility of tradition, that is, that their Teacher can be known only from his own testimony, are engaged in this: that they wish to make good their cause by this route, that is, to prove the first by the second, the unknown by the still more unknown; the Pope, on whose infallible dictum the divinity and sense of Scripture depend, by Scripture, which according to them can be understood and has authority only once the authority of the Pope is already recognised. In other words, they wish to contradict themselves in this: that from Scripture, which they deny to be clear, they wish to produce clear testimonies. We shall grant that they do not do this only when they have first proved to us that only those testimonies of Scripture are clear which establish the authority of the Pope, and that all the rest are wrapped in the thickest darkness. Clear, they say, is "You are Peter, etc." Obscure is "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve" (Matt. 4:10); obscure also is "We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law" (Rom. 3:28). All the other passages are obscure, except the very few that they adduce for the constitution of their infallible Teacher; obscure to such a degree that even when the name of God has been invoked, all diligence applied, the aim considered, what goes before and after observed, and finally the parts of Scripture compared, each giving light to the others, a godly man cannot in any way grasp the sense, in matters necessary to salvation, for his own conviction and for the admonition of his brothers, without this Teacher who speaks things that cannot be demonstrated. Whereas, on the contrary, these few passages ought to be so clear that their sense is evident to every Christian without the authority of that Teacher, whose constitution and authority is still to be proved. Let us seek this evidence, that the election and constitution of the Roman Pontiffs is certain in Scripture.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Producunt in scenam Petrum, Primum, ex ipsorum sententia, Pontificem Romanum, semper & magno cum studio clamitantes, quoque: Hic est Petrus! Sanctiones suas omnes accipiendas esse tanquam ipsius Divinâ voce Petri firmatas; pertendunt C. sic omnes dist.19. Ecclesiae suae infallibilitatem perpetuam gratiâ & auxilio Petri adjudicant; Agatho P. epist.6. Synod. Const. Act. 4. impositum à sede sua jugum vix ferendum, tamen ferendum esse in memoriam B. Petri censent C. in Memor. Dist. 19. Constantinum illis coronam suam ex auro purissimo & gemmis pretiosis, qua uterentur, pro honore B. Petri, concessisse, frenum equi Papae tenuisse, pro reverentia B. Petri stratoris officium illi exhibentem, fingunt in Donatione C. Constantinus dist.96. Imperatorem Petro jurantem de defendenda secundum suum posse terra Petri introducunt
units.tr: They bring Peter onto the stage as the first Roman Pontiff by their own judgment, and they cry out constantly and loudly: Here is Peter! They assert (C. Sic omnes, dist. 19) that all their decrees are to be received as if confirmed by the living voice of Peter himself. They assign to their Church perpetual infallibility by the grace and help of Peter. Agatho, in his letter (Synod of Constantinople, Act 4), speaks of a yoke laid down from his see, scarcely to be borne, yet to be borne. Out of remembrance of blessed Peter they hold (C. in Memor., dist. 19) that Constantine granted them his crown of purest gold and precious stones, to be worn for the honour of St Peter, and that he held the bridle of the Pope's horse, performing the office of groom out of reverence for St Peter. They feign in the Donation of Constantine (dist. 96) that the emperor swore to Peter to defend the land of Peter to the best of his power, and they introduce him doing so.

units.la: Allegantes ea, quae de Petro & ad Petrum dicta sunt. Ubi, quantum Petrum jactent, ostenditur; cunt S. Cerem. Eccles. Rom. l.1. §. 10. Archiepiscopis Pallium de corpore B. Petri sumptum mittunt & vendunt C. Quoniam quidam dist. 100. & S. Cerem. Eccles. Rom. l.1. §. 10. Episcopos, & eos etiam qui dignitates alias accipiunt, ut promittant obedientiam suam & fidem etiam S. Petro adigunt C. Ego N. Episc. Extra. de jure jur. & Felin Com. Imò, quod vel maximè notari meretur, in formula jurisjurandi, quæ, ut in jure Canonico descripta exstat, ad defensionem Regularum S. Patrum obligat, hodie, prout jam olim facere coeperunt, verbis mutatis defensionem Regalium S. Petri exigunt; Ut nempe hic & ubique Petrus ipsis ante oculos sit (& ô utinam in claritatem ejus transformarentur!) quemadmodum ægrotanti illi figura sua propria obversabatur semper. Petrus ipsis est α & ω, siquidem in Principio Bullarum ordinario legitur: authoritate S. Petri; In fine plerumque habetur; Datum apud S. Petrum; signantur Annulo Piscatoris, id est, Petri; Petrus ipsis sic est λίθος πέτρα, forte lapis ille pretiosus, quo se mulier inaurâsse dicitur Apoc. XVII. 4. sic Philosophicus illis lapis est nomen Petri, quo sua omnia, vilissima licèt, in aurum purissimum transsubstantiare conantur. Petrum sic omnibus modis commendant, ut cum eo beatiores ipsi fiant, simili cum illo Hortensii studio, qui, Cicerone teste, Eloquentiam summis laudibus ad coelum extulit, ut cum ea in coelum ipse ascenderet.
units.tr: They allege what has been said about Peter and to Peter, and in this it is shown how much they boast of Peter. (S. Cerem. Eccles. Rom. l.1, §10.) They send to archbishops a pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, and they sell it. (C. Quoniam quidam, dist. 100; S. Cerem. Eccles. Rom. l.1, §10.) They force bishops, and even those who receive other dignities, to promise obedience and faith even to St Peter. (C. Ego N. Episc.; Extra, de jure jurando; Felinus' commentary.) Indeed, what is most worthy of note is this: in the oath formula, as it stands described in canon law, the swearer is bound to defend the Rules of the holy Fathers. Today, as they began to do long ago, they change the words and demand that he defend the Regalia of St Peter.
