So, namely, here and everywhere Peter may stand before their eyes (O that they might be transformed into his brightness!), just as the figure of his own face always appeared to that sick man. Peter is their alpha and omega: at the beginning of their ordinary bulls it is read by the authority of St Peter; at the end it is usually found Given at St Peter's; they are sealed with the Fisherman's Ring, that is, Peter's. Peter is thus for them λίθος πέτρα [lithos petra], perhaps that precious stone by which the woman is said to have adorned herself (Apoc. XVII. 4). Thus their philosophers' stone is the name of Peter, by which they try to transmute all their own things, however vile, into the purest gold. They commend Peter in every way so that they may become more blessed through him, with the same eagerness as Hortensius, who, as Cicero testifies, extolled eloquence to the heavens with the highest praise, so that he himself might ascend to heaven with it.

units.la: IX. Neque quis miraretur frustra, cur tantopere Petrum crepent, & ejus se Successores esse dicant non item caeterorum, quibus tamen ex hypothesi Pontificia. (Vide etiam Baron. ad a. 971.3.) Potestas æquè convenit, nisi statim cuilibet obvium foret, de Petro multa in Scripturis in bonam partem dici, electionem ejus saltem ad aliquod munus idque eminentissimum ibi tradi, eúmque talem fuisse, quali se nemo non simillimum optaret, cum contrà de aliis & Scriptura in bonam partem plane sileat, & multi eorum tales fuerint Antecessores immediati, quorum Successores merito pudere potuit, & quibus nonnunquam etiam aliàs quasi data opera contrariari studuerunt. Igitur ut illustrem Prædecessorem nominantes splendorem sibi conciliant, non obscuri manent, aut obscuriores fiant quorumlibet Successionem præ se ferentes, unanimi consilio Petrum Antecessorem jactant; non autem Christum ordinario (aliquando eos id audere jam ostendimus, uti etiam cum principiis eorum convenit, dum Christum verè primum illam potestatem habuisse dicunt, non Petrum majorem suâ aut cujuscunque que alius Pontificis, à quo tamen denominari nolunt;) tum quia eum Romæ non fuisse ipsimet agnoscunt, tum quia magis aperta esset illa impudentia, quæ tamen satis aperta, quando talis Vicarius etiam pro plenario Successore haberi debet.
units.tr: IX. Nor need anyone wonder in vain why they so loudly trumpet Peter and say that they are his successors, but not those of the others, to whom nevertheless, on the Papist hypothesis, the same power would equally belong. Unless it were obvious to anyone at once that much is said about Peter in Scripture in a good sense, and that his election to some office, and that the most eminent one, is set out there, and that he was such a man as everyone would wish most to resemble; whereas on the contrary Scripture plainly keeps silent about the others in a good sense, and many of them were such immediate predecessors that their successors might well be ashamed of them, and against whom they have sometimes studied, as if on purpose, to act in opposition. (See also Baron. ad a. 971.3.) Therefore, in naming an illustrious predecessor, they win for themselves splendour, while those who claim succession from any obscure persons remain obscure, or become more obscure. By unanimous counsel they boast of Peter as their predecessor, but not of Christ as a rule. We have already shown that they sometimes dare this, and it also agrees with their principles, since they say that Christ truly held that first power, greater than Peter's, than their own, or than that of any other Pontiff, though they do not wish to be named after him. This is so both because they themselves acknowledge that he was not at Rome, and because that impudence would be more open, though it is open enough, when such a Vicar must be taken even for a full successor.

units.la: X. Sed quomodo idem simul immediatus Christi Vicarius esse potest & simul etiam Vicarius Petri? Utroque elogio se exornant in diversis locis. Si immediati Christi Vicarii sunt, quomodo sunt igitur Vicarii Petri? Quomodo Vicarii Petri, qui ipse Vicarius, cùm statuant & probent Canonistæ, Vicarium non posse facere Vicarium? quomodo Vicarii sunt Petri, quos ille non constituit? Quomodo Vicarii Petri, cui tantùm in munere succedere volunt eadem cum potestate? Si Vicarii Petri, cur non etiam aliorum prædecessorum tot Vicariorum quilibet Vicarius, quot ante ipsum Papæ fuerunt? Ast eandem ob causam se Vicarios Petri interdum vocant, ob quam se pro Successoribus ejus venditant, & quæ § praced. notata est.
units.tr: X. But how can the same man be at once the immediate Vicar of Christ and also the Vicar of Peter? They adorn themselves with each title in different places. If they are immediate Vicars of Christ, how then are they Vicars of Peter? How are they Vicars of Peter, when Peter himself was a Vicar, and the canonists lay down and prove that a Vicar cannot make a Vicar? How are they Vicars of Peter whom he did not appoint? How are they Vicars of Peter, whose office they wish to succeed to with the same power? If they are Vicars of Peter, why is not every Vicar of the many other predecessors also a Vicar, as many as there were Popes before him? But for the same reason that they sometimes call themselves Vicars of Peter, namely the one for which they peddle themselves as his successors, and which is noted in the preceding §.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA,
units.tr: SECOND SECTION,

units.la: In qua, Petrum ad talem Pontificatum minimè electum esse, probatur ex suprema & æquali Apostolorum potestate in Scripturis tradita, à Patribus summo cum consensu asserta, ab ipsis Pontificiis agnita. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which it is proved, from the supreme and equal power of the Apostles set out in Scripture, asserted with the greatest unanimity by the Fathers and acknowledged by the Papists themselves, that Peter was by no means elected to such a Pontificate. Summary.

units.la: 1. Petrum ad talem Pontificatum Romanum non electum esse, ostenditur primò ex Scriptura, & iis maximè, quæ ante Christi Ascensionem dicta aut facta sunt; II. Ex iis, quæ post Ascensionem Christi contigerunt; III. Secundò ex Patrum pro æqualitate Apostolorum testimoniis nonnullis; IV. Quibus robur etiam ex Ludovici Elia du Pin, Doctoris Sorbonici allegatione & attestatione accedit, eâque occasione primâ de Authore isto & ejus Dissertationibus haud ita pridem editis ex dedicatione, præfatione & approbationibus quibusdam adducuntur; V. Tertiò ex Pontificiorum ipsorummet de Apostolorum suprema potestate & æqualitate testimoniis; Ubi primò testis adducitur Cl. du Pin; VI. Secundò ipse Bellarminus; VII. Ostenditur, Scriptura, Patrum, & Pontificiorum ista testimonia cum sententia Romana Ecclesia neutiquam convenire; VIII. Neque consensum efficere Bellarmini distinctiones & tentatas Conciliationes, quæ proponuntur. IX. Specia-
units.tr: 1. That Peter was not elected to such a Roman Pontificate is shown first from Scripture, and especially from what was said or done before Christ's Ascension; II. from what happened after Christ's Ascension; III. Secondly, from some testimonies of the Fathers on the equality of the Apostles; IV. to which strength is also added by the citation and attestation of Louis Ellies du Pin, Doctor of the Sorbonne, and on this occasion, first, concerning this author and his Dissertations published not long ago, are adduced from the dedication, preface and certain approvals; V. Thirdly, from the testimonies of the Papists themselves concerning the supreme power and equality of the Apostles; where first the witness, the learned du Pin, is adduced; VI. Secondly, Bellarmine himself; VII. It is shown that these testimonies of Scripture, of the Fathers and of the Papists by no means agree with the opinion of the Roman Church; VIII. Nor do Bellarmine's distinctions and attempted reconciliations, which are proposed, produce agreement. IX. Specifically

units.la: § praced. — ...
units.tr: § preceding. — ...

units.la: IX. Speciatim refutantur ; Primò illa, Apostolos tamen à Petro cum aliqua subjectione pependisse ; X. Secundò illa ; Apostolos extraordinarios, Petrum verò ordinarium Ecclesia universalis Pastorem fuisse ; Vbi etiam similis ad utramque Doct. du Pin [Greek] adducitur.
units.tr: IX. The following are refuted in particular: first, the claim that the Apostles nevertheless depended on Peter with some subjection; X. secondly, the claim that the Apostles were extraordinary ministers, while Peter was the ordinary Pastor of the universal Church; where a similar passage from the Doctor du Pin [Greek] is also adduced.

units.la: I. VIdeamus de Petro, quia Petrum jactant; Sive jam sint Successores tantum, sive etiam Vicarii, eum electum vocatum esse ex Scripturis evidens est; Sed an forte etiam, eum electum, vocatum esse ad talem Pontificatum Romanum? Negamus, ejusmodi Electionem ex Scriptura probari posse, nimirum per quam constitutus sit Vicarius sive Successor Christi in plenitudine potestatis, Monarcha Ecclesiae talis, quales hodierni esse volunt, Dominus caeterorum omnium in & ex Cathedra Romana. Vocatus fuit ad Apostolatum, ad quem & alii vocati fuerunt. Atqui constat, Apostolatum esse summam, quae sub Christo hominibus obtigit, potestatem Ecclesiasticam, adeoque Petrum nullam superiorem caeteris habuisse, caeteros eo non inferiores fuisse, constat evidenter ex Scriptura, quae Deum in Ecclesia [Greek] primum Apostolos posuisse 1.Cor. XII.28. testatur. Quomodo autem primùm Apostolos tanquam praecipuos dedit, si Petrus illis major? Si illis major, cur non dicitur; primùm Petrum, secundò Apostolos? Sed juvabit adducere plura pro aequalitate Apostolorum Scripturae testimonia. Vocantur immediatè pariter à Christo, ad idem officium, ut nempe sint Piscatores hominum Matth. IV. 18. 19. pariter mittuntur ad perditas Israelis oves eâdem potestate donati Matth. X.25. ad docendum omnes gentes, ad praedicandum Evangelium omni creaturae cap. XXVIII.19.20. Marc. XVI.15. pari potestate peccata remittendi aut detinendi mittuntur à Christo, sicut ipsum Pater misit Joh. XX.21.23. pariter donantur Spiritu Ib. & Act. II. pariter in regeneratione sessuri in 12. thronis & judicaturi 12. tribus Israelis Matth. XIX.28. pariter fundamenta, quibus inaedificandi erant fideles Eph. II.10. ut etiam eorum nomina pariter 12. nova Hierosolymae fundamentis inscripta sunt Apoc. XXI.14. & pariter à Christo de Primatu contendentes audiverunt: Reges gentium dominantur eis, & qui inter eos potestatem habent, vocantur benefici, [Greek]. Vos autem non sic, sed major inter vos, fiat ut junior, & ductor, ut ministrans Luc. XXII.25. seq. & Petro quoque dicitur, ut, si frater contra eum peccet, dicat Ecclesiae Matth. XVIII.17.
units.tr: I. Let us look at Peter, since they boast of Peter. Whether they are now only Successors or also Vicars, it is plain from Scripture that he was chosen and called. But was he perhaps also chosen and called to such a Roman Pontificate? We deny that such an election can be proved from Scripture, namely by which he would have been appointed Vicar or Successor of Christ in the fullness of power, a Monarch of the Church of the kind they now wish to be, the Lord of all others, in and from the Roman Chair. He was called to the Apostleship, to which others also were called. Now it is established that the Apostleship is the highest ecclesiastical power that men have received under Christ; and so it is clear from Scripture that Peter had no authority over the others, nor were the others inferior to him. Scripture testifies that God placed first in the Church apostles (1 Cor. 12.28) [πρῶτον ἀποστόλους]. But how could he have given apostles first, as the most eminent, if Peter were greater than they? If he were greater than they, why is it not said: first Peter, second the Apostles? But it will help to adduce more Scripture testimonies for the equality of the Apostles. They are called immediately by Christ alike, to the same office, namely to be fishers of men (Matt. 4.18, 19); they are likewise sent to the lost sheep of Israel, endowed with the same power (Matt. 10.25); to teach all nations, to preach the Gospel to every creature (Matt. 28.19, 20; Mark 16.15); with equal power they are sent by Christ to forgive or retain sins, as the Father sent him (John 20.21, 23); they are likewise given the Spirit (ibid. and Acts 2); likewise they will sit in the regeneration on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19.28); likewise they are the foundations on which the faithful are to be built (Eph. 2.20); and likewise their names are written on the twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21.14). And likewise, when they contended about primacy, they heard from Christ: The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors [εὐεργέται]. But you are not so; rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves (Luke 22.25ff.). And it is also said to Peter: if your brother sins against you, tell it to the Church (Matt. 18.17).

units.la: II. Si autem per ista omnia paritas Apostolorum, &c, Petrum non ad Monarchiam electum esse, probatur, certè non minùs probatur per ea, quæ sequuntur post Ascensionem Christi facta; Non enim Petrus Monarchicam suam potestatem unquam exercuisse legitur, multa contrà occurrunt, quæ ei planè repugnant. Non maxima & omnes spectantia solus supremâ authoritate egisse reperitur, non cæteri quicquam nomine & authoritate ejus fecisse leguntur; Paritatem spirant omnia. Ecclesia eligit Apostolum Act. I. & Diaconos cap. VI. ipse mittitur æquè ac Johannes cap. VIII. 14. reddit rationem c. XI. in Concilio primus quidem loquitur, sed sententiam fert Jacobus; Διò ἐγὼ κρίνω quare ego judico, Act. XV. in faciem ei resistit Paulus, ὅτι κατεγνωσμένῳ ἦν, quia reprehensibilis erat Gal. II. 11. ἀλλ' ὅτε ἦλθον ... quia non recte incedebat secundum veritatem Evangelii v. 14. idem Paulus & illos reprehendit, qui à Petro denominari volebant 1. Cor. I. incestuosum sine allegatione authoritatis Petri excommunicat cap. V. de se testatur, se plùs cæteris laborâsse cap. XV. 10, curam omnium Ecclesiarum habere 2. Cor. XI. 28. Apostolum οὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων, οὐδὲ δι' ἀνθρώπου, non ab hominibus, neque per hominem esse Gal. I. 1. honoratiores nihil sibi addidisse cap. II. 6. sed agnovisse, sibi Evangelium præputii concreditum fuisse, καθὼς quemadmodum Petro circumcisionis v. 7. cùm idem in utroque apud diversos efficax fuerit v. 8. quare etiam Jacobus, Cephas (Petrus) & Johannes, qui columna habebantur, sibi & Barnabæ δεξιὰς κοινωνίας dextras societatis dederint v. 9.
units.tr: II. If, however, from all these things the equality of the Apostles, and that Peter was not chosen to a Monarchy, is proved, it is certainly proved no less from what followed after Christ's Ascension. For we do not read that Peter ever exercised a monarchical power; on the contrary, many things occur that plainly contradict it. He is not found acting alone with supreme authority in the greatest matters that concern everyone; nor are the others read to have done anything in his name and authority. Everything breathes equality. The Church elects an Apostle (Acts 1) and Deacons (ch. 6); he himself is sent, just as John is (Acts 8.14); he gives an account (ch. 11); in the Council he indeed speaks first, but James gives the judgment: Wherefore I judge [Διὸ ἐγὼ κρίνω] (Acts 15). Paul resisted him to his face, because he was to be blamed [ὅτι κατεγνωσμένος ἦν] (Gal. 2.11); but when they came… because he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel [ἀλλ' ὅτε ἦλθον] (v. 14). The same Paul also rebukes those who wanted to be named after Peter (1 Cor. 1). He excommunicates the incestuous man without citing any authority of Peter (ch. 5). He testifies of himself that he laboured more than the others (ch. 15.10), and that he has care of all the Churches (2 Cor. 11.28). He is an Apostle not from men, nor through man [οὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων, οὐδὲ δι' ἀνθρώπου] (Gal. 1.1). The more honoured men added nothing to him (ch. 2.6), but acknowledged that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to him, just as [καθὼς] to Peter that of the circumcision (v. 7), since the same power was effective in each among different peoples (v. 8). Therefore also James, Cephas (Peter) and John, who were held to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship [δεξιὰς κοινωνίας] (v. 9).

units.la: III. Constat eadem veritas, quòd nimirum Apostoli pares fuerint, & Petrus non ad Monarchiam electus sit, evidenter ex Patribus. Cyprianum audiamus clarissimè nobis adstipulantem. Ita ille, lib. de unitate Ecclesiæ: Quamvis Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam parem potestatem tribuat. Hoc erant utique & cæteri Apostoli, quod fuit Petrus, pari consortio praditi & honoris & potestatis. Eadem est sententia Hieronymi lib. 1. adversus Jovinianum. At dicis, inquit, super Petrum fundatur Ecclesia, licèt hoc ipsum alio in loco super omnes Apostolos fiat, & cuncti claves regni cœlorum accipiant, & ex æquo super eos Ecclesiæ fortitudo solidetur. Hinc etiam Apostoli omnes à Patribus dicuntur Vicarii Christi. Constat, inquit Hilarius Diaconus in epist. 1. ad Cor, Apostolos esse Dei adjutores, quia Vicarii sunt Christi. Et Chrysostomus, explicans illud Pauli; Pro Christo legatione fungimur; ait; omnes Apostolos illius loco officium ejus suscepisse: Mitto illud omniomnibus notum praefationis Missae Apostolorum: Quos Operis Tui Vicarios eidem contulisti praesse Pastores.
units.tr: III. The same truth is established, namely that the Apostles were equals and that Peter was not chosen to a Monarchy, plainly from the Fathers. Let us hear Cyprian, who clearly agrees with us. Thus he writes in his book On the Unity of the Church: although after his resurrection he gave all the Apostles equal power, the other Apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honour and power. The opinion of Jerome is the same, in his first book Against Jovinian: But you say, he writes, that the Church is founded on Peter, although in another place the same is done on all the Apostles, and all receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the strength of the Church is equally established on them. Hence all the Apostles are also called by the Fathers Vicars of Christ. It is established, says the deacon Hilary in his first letter to the Corinthians, that the Apostles are God's helpers, because they are Christ's Vicars. And Chrysostom, explaining Paul's words, We act as ambassadors for Christ, says: All the Apostles took up his office in his place. I pass over that well-known preface of the Mass of the Apostles, which is known to everyone: whom you appointed as Vicars of your Work, to be Pastors over the same.

units.la: IV. Sed quid longa probatione opus est? Nulla plane opus fuisset, nisi liquido patere deberet, quam strenuè non tantum Scripturae & piae Antiquitati, sed & sibimet hic contradicant Pontificii. Fatentur ab una parte omnes Apostolorum aequalitatem; Quae pro ea jam jam adduxi, Patrum testimonia ex Doctore Pontificio, cujus etiam propria verba adhibere malui, & qui tanquam inter Pontificios de praefatione Missae Apostolorum tanquam de re omnibus nota loquitur, adducta sunt, testimonia, qualia, ut ipse ait, dantur multa & aperta. Est is Ludovicus Ellies du Pin, Sacra Facultatis Theologiae Parisiensis Doctor, qui An. 1686. Parisiis Dissertationes Historicas de antiqua Ecclesiae Disciplina septem cum Privilegio Regis & decem Theologorum Parisiensium (qui avitam in iis doctrinam a Christo per Apostolos eorumque Successores transmissam & terminos a Patribus positos, antiquam Gallicanae Ecclesiae ac Facultatis Sacrae sententiam a malevolorum calumniis ac sciolorum ratiunculis liberatam & sincerum ardensque veritatis ac pacis singulari cum eruditione conjunctum studium, ita ut Author uni veritati aperiendae atque illustrandae intentus, ubique personas a causa secernat, neutri, quod sui juris, adimat, neutri, quod alterius, concedat, in opere nihil exuberet, ac nihil desideretur, nec quicquam habeat, quod inoffenso pede decurri non possit; agnoverunt & laudant, oblectationem animi in iis volvendis eam, qua major vix dari possit, depraedicant, adeoque cum ita feliciter ea omnia, quae ad Ecclesiasticam atque civilem potestatem spectant, plene & dilucide in unum veluti doctrinae corpus redegerit Author, ex operis lectione plurimum fructus & utilitatis iis, qui missis praejudiciorum falsis persuasionibus soli Christo loquenti & Ecclesiae ejus Sponsae definienti aures cordis accommodaturi sint; promittunt;) approbationibus in lucem emisit, & in iis praefixo ad Lectorem Monito protestatus est, se Sedem Apostolicam, & qui in ea sedeat, Innocentium XI. Pontificem venerari, Ecclesiam Romanam ut caeterarum omnium caput, vero & sincero honore prosequi, ejus communionem, quam studiosissime possit, fovere & amplecti, nec unquam vel latum anguem a debita ipsi obedientia recessurum; & qui Dissertationes suas ad adjungendos ei multorum animos utiles valde ac necessarias fore judicavit, & Rom. Pontificis Primatum & Authoritatem, intra justos limites coh ibe ri, non eam odiosam & gravem Regibus & populis ostentari debere, censuit, quemadmodum etiam anno 1682. Cleri Gallicani Patres, non tam tam ad Libertates suas propagandas, quàm ad vindicandam Ecclesiæ Romanæ dignitatem congregati fuerint, & liceat utique Romani Pontificis authoritatem, quam alii invidiosam reddant, ab hujusmodi opprobrio vindicare; quem scopum etiam in Dedicatione ad Illustrissimum Virum D. D. Dionysium Talæum, S. Consistorii Consiliarium, & in Senatu Parisiensi Advocatum Generalem prodidit, significans illi opus suum deberi tanquam Libertatum Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Vindici, quique ex eorum ordine, quorum operâ, studio, adhortatione Senatus Parisiensis, eorum, qui novas & peregrinas opiniones inducere conabantur, molitionibus semper obstiterit & veterem doctrinam vindicaverit, quomodo præcipuè Illustrissimi Parentis ipsius vigilantiâ non semel ambitiosi Curiæ Romanæ conatus repressi sint; Et ipse, cùm annis superioribus Theologi quidam velut suæ patriæ obliti, & Curiæ Romanæ nimiùm addicti, nova dogmata, potestati Regiæ, Conciliorum authoritati & libertati Ecclesiæ contraria disseminâssent, maximâ authoritate malum ingruens repressêrit, maximâ libertate Regni & Ecclesiæ jura defenderit, maximâ vehementiâ contraria eis dogmata proscripserit, & maximâ demum arte ipsum Theologia ordinem quasi è somno excitârit & ad antiquæ doctrinæ defensionem commoverit, testibus hujus rei semper futuris sex illis articulis ab eo tum temporis Senatui Parisiensi ipso annuente & adhortante oblatis.
units.tr: IV. But why is a long proof needed? None would be needed at all, were it not that it should be plain how vigorously the Papists here contradict not only Scripture and pious antiquity, but also themselves. On the one hand, they all admit the equality of the Apostles. The testimonies of the Fathers which I have just adduced for this, drawn from a Papist doctor, whose own words I have preferred to use, and who speaks, as among the Papists, of the preface of the Mass of the Apostles as a matter known to all, have been cited: testimonies, such as, as he himself says, are given in many and clear form. He is Louis Ellies du Pin, Doctor of the Sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris, who in the year 1686 at Paris published Seven Historical Dissertations on the Ancient Discipline of the Church, with the Royal Privilege and that of ten Parisian Theologians (who acknowledge and praise the ancestral doctrine transmitted to them by Christ through the Apostles and their Successors, and the limits set by the Fathers, the ancient opinion of the Gallican Church and of the Sacred Faculty, freed from the calumnies of ill-wishers and the petty arguments of half-learned men, and the sincere and ardent study of truth joined with singular learning, so that the Author, intent on unfolding and illustrating the one truth, everywhere separates persons from the cause, takes from neither what is his own, concedes to neither what is another's, nothing superfluous in his work, nothing lacking, and nothing that cannot be run through without stumbling; and they proclaim that the delight of mind in turning these pages is as great as can hardly be given; and since he has so happily gathered into one body of teaching all that pertains to ecclesiastical and civil power, they promise that much fruit and profit will come from reading the work to those who, putting aside false prejudices, will lend the ears of their heart to Christ speaking alone and to his Church, his Bride, defining). He published these with approvals, and in them, in a Notice prefixed to the Reader, he declared that he venerates the Apostolic See and him who sits in it, Pope Innocent XI; that he honours the Roman Church as the head of all others with true and sincere honour, that he cherishes and embraces her communion as earnestly as he can, and that he will never withdraw even a little from due obedience to her. He judged that his Dissertations would be very useful and necessary for winning over the minds of many, and he held that the primacy and authority of the Roman Pontiff ought to be kept within just limits, and not displayed as odious and burdensome to kings and peoples, just as the Fathers of the Gallican clergy assembled in the year 1682, not so much to extend their liberties as to defend the dignity of the Roman Church; and it is surely allowed to defend the authority of the Roman Pontiff, which others render hateful, from this kind of reproach. He revealed the same aim in the Dedication to the most illustrious man, Denis Talon, Councillor of the Holy Consistory and Advocate General in the Parisian Senate, signifying to him that his work is owed to him as the Defender of the Liberties of the Gallican Church, who from among their order, by whose work, zeal and encouragement the Parisian Senate has always resisted the schemes of those who tried to introduce new and foreign opinions and has defended the old doctrine; and how, especially through the vigilance of his most illustrious father, the ambitious attempts of the Roman Curia were more than once put down. He himself, when in former years certain Theologians, as if forgetful of their country and too devoted to the Roman Curia, had spread new doctrines contrary to royal power, to the authority of Councils and to the liberty of the Church, had with the greatest authority repressed the threatening evil, had with the greatest freedom defended the rights of the kingdom and the Church, had with the greatest vehemence condemned the doctrines contrary to them, and had finally, with the greatest skill, as though from sleep, roused the order of Theology itself and moved it to defend the ancient doctrine, the six articles then offered by him to the Parisian Senate, with its consent and encouragement, being witnesses of this matter for ever.

units.la: V. In Dissertationum harum quarta agit de Primatu Romani Pontificis, & cap.1. de Primatu B. Petri. Sect.3. ex parte ostendere vult, nihil obstare Petri Primatui Apostolorum inter se aqualitatem; quam primò proponit, post etiam allatis Patrum testimoniis confirmat, in fine autem hæc verba emphatica habet, quæ licèt partem argumentationis nostræ ex Scriptura præmissæ contineant, heic tamen inserere non abs re erit: Et certè, inquit, quoad regimen prima illa Ecclesia Aristocratia usa est; nihil enim solus Petrus statuit, sed simul cum Apostolis & Senioribus; sic cùm eligendi fuerunt Diaconi, communi Apostolorum consilio & authoritate id factum est; cùmque de circumcisionis & legalium observatione longè gravior difficultas foret exorta, illa non Petri authoritate, sed Apostolorum Seniorúmqûe Hierosolymis congregatorum judicio definita est. Atque adeò verum, Petrum non fuisse absolutum Monarcham aliorum Apostolorum, ut Paulus non sit veritus, ei in faciem resistere, cùm Gentes ad Judaicas ceremonias observandas vellet impellere. Constat ergò, Petri Primatum non fuisse Monarchiam absolutam aut dominatum in cæteros Apostolos. In quo quidem sententiæ communis Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ genuinum se interpretem præbet.
units.tr: V. In the fourth of these Dissertations he deals with the Primacy of the Roman Pontiff, and in chapter 1, on the Primacy of Blessed Peter, Sect. 3, he seeks in part to show that the Primacy of Peter does not stand in the way of equality among the Apostles. He first sets this out, then confirms it with the testimonies of the Fathers. At the end he has these emphatic words, which, although they contain part of our own argument drawn from Scripture, it will not be out of place to insert here: And certainly, he says, the first Church used an aristocracy in its government. For Peter alone decided nothing, but always together with the Apostles and the elders. So when deacons had to be chosen, this was done by the common counsel and authority of the Apostles. And when a much more serious difficulty arose about circumcision and the observance of the law, it was settled not by the authority of Peter but by the judgment of the Apostles and elders gathered at Jerusalem. Thus it is true that Peter was not an absolute monarch over the other Apostles, so much so that Paul did not hesitate to resist him to his face when he tried to force the Gentiles to observe Jewish ceremonies. It is therefore clear that the Primacy of Peter was not an absolute monarchy or a lordship over the other Apostles. In this, indeed, he shows himself a genuine interpreter of the common opinion of the Gallican Church.

units.la: VI. Sed eam hic nobiscum sentire miratur valdè nemo, quando constat, ut suo loco etiam plenius dicam, eam immensam illam, quam cæteri Pontificibus Romanis adscribunt, potestatem minimè admittere. Mirandum multò magis est, Cardinalem Bel-larminum (Ast quàm acer ille Romanæ omnipotentiæ defensor fuit!) quoad supremam adeóque æqualem Apostolorum potestatem eadem nobiscum dicere, Libri nimirum de Pont. Rom. quarti cap.23. cui primò titulus; Apostolos à Christo jurisdictionem omnem accepisse; In ipsa tractatione dicit; Locum Joh.20. Sicut misit me Pater & ego mitto vos; Patres, Chrysostomum & Theophylactum sic exponere, ut aperte dicant, factos esse his verbis Apostolos Christi Vicarios, immò ipsum Christi officium & authoritatem accepisse; Addit; addere Cyrillum in locum, his verbis proprie creatos esse Apostolos & orbis totius Doctores, & ut intelligeremus in Apostolica Auctoritate contineri omnem potestatem Ecclesiasticam, ideò adjecisse Christum: Sicut misit me Pater, siquidem Pater Filium misit potestate summâ praditum. Subjungit Cypriani verba, quibus Christus Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam parem potestatem tribuisse testatur. Et concludit: Ubi vides idem dari Apostolis per illa verba: Ego mitto vos, quod Petro fuerat promissum, per illud: Tibi dabo claves, & postea exhibitum per illud: pasce oves meas. Constat autem per illa, Tibi dabo claves, & per illud; pasce oves, intelligi jurisdictionem plenissimam etiam exteriorem.
units.tr: VI. But no one should be surprised that he agrees with us here, since, as I will say more fully in its place, it is clear that he does not admit that immense power which the others ascribe to the Roman Pontiffs. Much more remarkable is that Cardinal Bellarmine (and how fierce a defender of Roman omnipotence he was!) says, on the supreme and therefore equal power of the Apostles, the same things as we do. Certainly in the fourth book of his work on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 23, whose title is first: The Apostles received all jurisdiction from Christ. In the treatment itself he says: On John 20: As the Father sent me, I also send you, the Fathers, Chrysostom and Theophylact, expound this so as to say plainly that by these words the Apostles were made Vicars of Christ, indeed that they received Christ's own office and authority. He adds: Cyril adds in the same place that by these words the Apostles were properly created and teachers of the whole world, and that we might understand that all ecclesiastical power is contained in the apostolic authority, Christ therefore added: As the Father sent me, since the Father sent the Son endowed with supreme power. He adds the words of Cyprian, by which he testifies that Christ, after his resurrection, gave equal power to all the Apostles. And he concludes: Here you see that the same thing was given to the Apostles by the words I send you which had been promised to Peter by the words I will give you the keys, and afterwards conferred by the words feed my sheep. But it is clear that by the words I will give you the keys and by feed my sheep is meant the fullest jurisdiction, even external.

units.la: VII. Jam quæro, quomodo hæc consistere queant cum illo Pii V. in sentent. Declar. contra Elisabetham Angliæ Reginam effato: Regnans in excelsis, cui data est omnis in cœlo & in terra potestas, unam, sanctam, Catholicam, & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, extra quam nulla est salus, UNI SOL I in terris, videlicet Apostolorum Principi, Petro, Petri Successori Romano Pontifici, cum potestatis plenitudine tradidit gubernandam? Quomodo hæc consistere queant cum illa Monarchia, ad quam Petrum electum esse operosè contendunt, ipse Bellarminus, Baronius, alii, subjectionem cæteris Apostolis, & quòd sub Petro fuerint, à Petro pendere debuerint, aperte tribuentes? Quomodo hæc consistere queant, cum illa potestate absoluta, quam cum Successione Petri sibi vendicant Pontifices Romani, ita ut cæteri Ecclesiarum Rectores, Apostolorum in potestate ordinaria Successores omnes, ab illis potestatem suam accipere, illis obedientiam jurare, in omnibus præstare teneantur, illis se opponere nulli unquam audeant, ipsi tam inæquales Papæ, quando Apostoli tam æquales Petro?
units.tr: VII. Now I ask how these things can stand together with the statement of Pius V in his sentence of declaration against Elizabeth, Queen of England: The One reigning on high, to whom all power in heaven and earth has been given, committed one, holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, outside which there is no salvation, to be governed on earth by ONE, namely to the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, and to the Roman Pontiff, Peter's successor, with the fullness of power? How can these things stand together with that monarchy to which Bellarmine, Baronius and others strive laboriously to show that Peter was chosen, openly attributing to the other Apostles subjection and the fact that they were under Peter and ought to depend on Peter? How can they stand together with that absolute power which the Roman Pontiffs claim for themselves through the succession of Peter, so that all the other rulers of the churches, successors of the Apostles in their ordinary power, are bound to receive their power from them, to swear obedience to them, and to render them everything, and never dare to oppose them at all? How can such unequal popes be reconciled with Apostles so equal to Peter?

units.la: VIII. Vidit certè Bellarminus difficultatem, hinc loco citato subjecit: Quomodo autem haec non impediant Petri Principatum, aliàs satis ostendimus. Dubio procul respicit ad lib. 1. cap. 11. circa finem: Omnes fuerunt capita, ibi inquit, Rectores & Pastores Ecclesiae universa, sed non eodem modo. Illi enim habuerunt summam & amplissimam potestatem ut Apostoli, seu legati, Petrus autem ut Pastor ordinarius. Deinde ita habuerunt plenitudinem potestatis, ut tamen Petrus esset caput eorum, & ab illo penderent, non è contrario. Atqui hoc est, quod promittitur Petro Matth. 16. cùm ei soli coram aliis dicitur: super hanc Petram &c. Respicere etiam potuit ad cap. 12. §. Dices, si non, ubi eadem fere repetit, nempe summam potestatem collatam esse Apostolis omnibus, ut Legatis, non ut Pastoribus ordinariis, & cum quadam subjectione ad Petrum, cui etiam Apostolorum, Fratrum suorum commissa sit cura.
units.tr: VIII. Bellarmine certainly saw the difficulty, and so he added in the passage cited: How these things do not hinder the Primacy of Peter we have shown elsewhere. He doubtless refers to book 1, chapter 11, near the end: All of them, he says there, were heads, rulers and pastors of the universal Church, but not in the same way. For they had the highest and most ample power as Apostles, or legates, while Peter had it as ordinary pastor. Again, they had the fullness of power in such a way that Peter was nevertheless their head, and they depended on him, not the reverse. Now this is what is promised to Peter in Matthew 16, when it is said to him alone, in the presence of the others: upon this rock, etc. He could also have referred to chapter 12, § Dices, si non, where he repeats almost the same thing, namely that the highest power was conferred on all the Apostles as legates, not as ordinary pastors, and with a certain subjection to Peter, to whom the care of his brother Apostles was also entrusted.

units.la: IX. Egregiè scilicet difficultatem solvit, contradictionem manifestam tollit, tollit, solvit, si solvi illa, tolli haec potest continuatione in contradictione, suppositionibus non fundatis, & manifestè falsis, & praerogativa, quae nulla est! Continuatio est contradictionis, quòd Apostolos Christi Vicarios, Capita, Rectores & Pastores Ecclesiae universa, ipsum Christi officium & authoritatem habentes, & in authoritate sua omnem Ecclesiasticam, parem potestatem, plenitudinem potestatis, qui idem cum Petro, jurisdictionem etiam plenissimam, etiam exteriorem acceperint, nihilominùs à Petro Capite & Monarcha cum quadam, (sic individuum vagum exprimit, qualis enim ista subjectio fuerit, dicere nemo potest) subjectione pendere atque illius cura concreditos esse, & non vicissim illum, curae eorum; affirmat; quam contradictionem ut effugerent Rhemenses, in Matth. XVI. Petro datam esse dixerunt supereminentem potestatem, quae collata cum potestate aliis Apostolis, Episcopis & Pastoribus data, vocari possit plenitudo potestatis; Sic à Bellarmino dissentientes & Apostolis supremam dignitatem denegantes. Sed istam Apostolorum subjectionem à Monarchicis consensu traditam unanimi, multò adhuc absurdior reddere potest consideratio & illa, quod Johannes Apostolus, adhuc sub Domitiano superstes, secundùm istas hypotheses non tantum Petro, sed ejus etiam, quos vocant, Successoribus, Lino, Cleto, Clementi subjectus esse debuerit, cùm contrà Eusebius Hist. Eccl. l. 3. c. 6. jure meritóque augustiùs multò de Johannis quàm verò de Clementis Episcopi Romani ministerio loquatur, scribens, Clementem Romanam gubernâsse Ecclesiam: ac Johannem Apostolum adhuc huc in Asia vitam traducentem Ecclesias ibi administrasse. Hic scilicet tanquam illius Legatus ab illo pendens, illi subjectus cuncta fecit! Absurditatem etiam auget, consideratio haec, quo nimirum loco ultimorum seculorum, si vera narrant, Petri in Monarchia Successores quosvis in orbe terrarum Ecclesiarum Rectores, Apostolorum in potestate ordinaria Successores habeant, quos a se omnibus modis pendere, non juris Divini, sed Pontificii tantum esse contendunt.
units.tr: IX. Certainly he resolves the difficulty excellently, he removes the manifest contradiction, he removes it, resolves it, if it can be resolved and removed by a continuation within the contradiction itself, by unfounded and manifestly false suppositions, and by a prerogative which does not exist! It is a continuation of the contradiction that he affirms that the Apostles, Vicars of Christ, heads, rulers and pastors of the universal Church, having Christ's own office and authority, and in their authority every ecclesiastical power, an equal power, the fullness of power, who received the same jurisdiction, even the fullest, even external, as Peter, nevertheless depend on Peter as their head and monarch with a certain subjection (he expresses this vague and indeterminate thing in this way, for no one can say what sort of subjection that would be), and that they were entrusted with his care, and not he with theirs. To escape this contradiction, the Rhemists said on Matthew 16 that Peter was given a supereminent power, which, compared with the power given to the other Apostles, bishops and pastors, could be called the fullness of power. Thus they dissent from Bellarmine and deny the Apostles their supreme dignity. But the consideration that Peter's supposed monarchy would make this subjection of the Apostles, which they all hold unanimously, far more absurd, is this: according to these hypotheses, the Apostle John, still surviving under Domitian, ought to have been subject not only to Peter but also to his so-called successors, Linus, Cletus and Clement. Yet Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 6, rightly and deservedly speaks far more fully of the ministry of John than of the ministry of Clement, Bishop of Rome, writing that Clement governed the Church at Rome, and that John the Apostle, still living his life here in Asia, administered the churches there. So here John, as legate of that man, depending on him and subject to him, did everything! The absurdity is increased by this further consideration: if the accounts of the last ages are true, Peter's successors in the monarchy have in every part of the world rulers of churches, successors of the Apostles in their ordinary power, whom they claim depend on them in every way, and this is not of divine right but only of papal right.

units.la: X. Suppositiones non fundatae & manifeste falsae sunt illae, Petrum in eo caeteris Apostolis tamen majorem manere, quod Pastor Ecclesiae ordinarius fuerit, id est, juxta Gretseri in loci Bellarminiani defensione explicationem, quod ei in plenitudine Clavium, hoc est, potestatis successum est, & succedetur usque ad finem mundi, cum summam & amplissimam habuerint reliqui, ut Apostoli & Legati. Quae praerogativa primo respectu Petri nulla est, & Primatui ejus tali Apostolorum aequalitatem non obstare haud docet. Eximia certe praerogativa, quam ut cito habeant alii, ille, cui tribuitur, cito mori debet! Ut taceam, Ministros extraordinarios ordinario ordinarii is majores esse, fuisse Mosen Aarone, Samuelem summo Sacerdote, Prophetas Leviticis, Apostolos aliis in N. T. Ministris. Secundo, gratis haec omnia finguntur & dicuntur, Petrum nimirum ordinarium Pastorem fuisse; Apostolum, id est, Legatum aeque ac caeteros (vide Joh. XX.21. 2.Cor. V.20.) ostendimus fuisse; Atqui munus Apostolicum extraordinarium fuerat; Successores habuisse in alio sensu, quam in quo & caeteris Apostolis succedatur; Apostolos enim aeque in potestate ordinaria Successores habere, in plenitudine autem potestatis suae neminem, nec Petro, nec aliis successisse, inferius docendum erit. Hic autem addere jubet Doctissimi & supra laudati du Pin loco etiam citato ad istam a Bellarmino & plerisque aliis Petro tributam posteriorem praerogativam Pnxeion nostrae simillimam. Haec responsio, inquit, nimirum Apostolicam illam authoritatem ad tempus tantum datam fuisse caeteris, & Petro concessam ut ad Successores ejus permanaret, mihi videtur esse fictitia, & Petri Primatui non parum derogare. Fictitia quidem est, quia nulla ratione, nullo Testimonio Scripturae aut Traditionis docemur, potestatem Apostolatus Petri ad ejus Successores permanasse, non autem potestatem caeterorum Apostolorum, cum ex aequo Ecclesiarum Apostolicarum Episcopi dicantur eorum Apostolorum, a quibus Ecclesiae sunt fundatae, Successores, imo omnes Episcopi Episcopi Apostolorum omnium Successores esse perhibeantur. Deinde hæc opinio Primatui Petri derogat, nam ex ea sequitur quidem, Petri Successores præferri debere cæteris Episcopis, at Petrum propterea inter Apostolos Primatum habuisse, non convincitur.
units.tr: X. Those suppositions are unfounded and manifestly false, namely that Peter nevertheless remained greater than the other Apostles in this respect, that he was the ordinary pastor of the Church, that is, according to Gretser's explanation in his defence of Bellarmine's passage, that the succession to him in the fullness of the keys, that is, of power, has passed and will pass to the end of the world, whereas the others, such as the Apostles and legates, had the highest and most ample power. This prerogative, in the first place, does not exist with respect to Peter, and does not teach that equality of the Apostles is no obstacle to his Primacy of this kind. Indeed, it is an remarkable prerogative, which others must quickly have, but he to whom it is attributed must quickly die! Not to mention that extraordinary ministers are greater than ordinary ones: Moses was greater than Aaron, Samuel than the high priest, the prophets than the Levites, and the Apostles than other ministers in the New Testament. Secondly, all these things are invented and asserted without grounds, namely that Peter was the ordinary pastor; we have shown (see John 20:21 and 2 Corinthians 5:20) that he was an Apostle, that is, a legate, just as the others were. But the apostolic office was extraordinary, and it cannot be said that it had successors in the same sense in which it is said to have successors in the case of the other Apostles. For that the Apostles equally have successors in their ordinary power, but that none has succeeded to the fullness of his power, neither Peter nor the others, must be taught below. Here the very learned Du Pin, praised above, bids us add, in the passage cited, to this second prerogative, which Bellarmine and most others attribute to Peter, something very close to our own Pnxeion. This answer, he says, namely that that apostolic authority was given to the others only for a time, but was granted to Peter so that it would pass on to his successors, seems to me to be fictitious and to detract not a little from the Primacy of Peter. It is fictitious, because we are taught by no reason and no testimony of Scripture or tradition that the apostolic power of Peter passed on to his successors, but not the power of the other Apostles, since the bishops of the apostolic churches are equally called successors of those Apostles by whom the churches were founded, and indeed all bishops are said to be successors of all the Apostles. Moreover, this opinion detracts from the Primacy of Peter, for it follows from it that the successors of Peter ought to be preferred to the other bishops, but it is not thereby shown that Peter had the Primacy among the Apostles.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA, In qua, Petrum ad talem Pontificatum minimè electum esse, ex invaliditate argumentorum Pontificiorum ostenditur, & maximè locus Matth. XVI. 18. examinatur.
units.tr: SECTION THREE, in which it is shown from the invalidity of the Papists' arguments that Peter was by no means chosen to such a Pontificate, and especially Matthew 16:18 is examined.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Transitus fit ad argumenta Pontificiorum, quibus Petri electionem ad Pontificatum talem, sive Monarchiam probare conantur. Et primò quid m detorsiones locorum Luc V. 4. & 10. redarguuntur, & de plerisque Petri apud Bellarminum prærogativis judicium fertur. II. Posthac loca eorum præcipua Matth. XVI. & Joh. XXI. indicantur, & ad ea aliquid in genere annotatur. III. Speciale examen loci Matth. XVI. & quidem verborum priorum: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram &c. incipit, eorúmque quatuor, quæ apud Patres etiam occurrunt, expositiones notantur; IV. Primæ expositionis Authores, qui per Petram fidem & confessionem Petri intelligunt, & rationes indicantur; V. Secundæ, quâ per Petram Christus designari dicitur, Authores proponuntur; VI. Fundamenta exponuntur; VII. Tertiæ, quâ per Petram Petri personam intelligunt, Authores pariter indicantur; VIII. Eam Monarchiam Petri non involvere ostenditur, etiam M. Ant. de Dominis verbis; IX. Doctiss. du Pin judicio; X. Quæ porrò explicantur; XI. Quartæ expositionis, quâ per Petram sive Apostolos, sive fideles quosvis intelligi dicitur, Authores nominantur, eorúmque testimonia proferuntur; XII. Erasmus, expositionis approbator & ille, à Bellarmini exceptionibus vindicatur. XIII. Turrecremata, tandem vim argumenti in eo solo ponenti, quòd hæc verba ad Petrum cæteris præsentibus dicta sunt, occurritur. XIV. Expositionum harum vicinia & convenientia adstruitur; XV. Atque Πλεονεξίας generalior subjungitur.
units.tr: I. We now turn to the Papists' arguments by which they try to prove that Peter was chosen to such a Pontificate, or Monarchy. First, the distortions of Luke 5:4 and 10 are refuted, and a judgment is passed on most of Peter's prerogatives as listed by Bellarmine. II. Next, their chief passages, Matthew 16 and John 21, are pointed out, and something is noted about them in general. III. A special examination of Matthew 16 begins, namely of the first words, "You are Peter, and upon this rock," and the four interpretations of them, which also occur among the Fathers, are noted. IV. The authors who understand by the rock the faith and confession of Peter are named, and their reasons are indicated. V. The authors who say that Christ is designated by the rock are presented. VI. The foundations are explained. VII. For the third interpretation, by which the rock is taken to be the person of Peter, the authors are likewise indicated. VIII. It is shown that this does not involve Peter's Monarchy, including by the words of Marco Antonio de Dominis. IX. The judgment of the most learned du Pin. X. Further points are explained. XI. The authors of the fourth interpretation, by which the rock is said to be understood as either the apostles or all the faithful, are named, and their testimonies are offered. XII. Erasmus, an approver of this interpretation, is defended against Bellarmine's objections. XIII. Finally, Turrecremata is met, who places the whole force of the argument solely in the fact that these words were spoken to Peter while the others were present. XIV. The proximity and agreement of these interpretations is established. XV. And a more general complaint about covetousness is added.

units.la: LAtis hactenus probavimus, Petrum non ad Monarchiam Ecclesiasticam electum esse, argumento maximè ab æqualitate & suprema potestate Apostolorum desumpto, in S. Scriptura optimè fundato, Patrum etiam testimoniis illustrato, propriâ non minùs Pontificiorum Confessione confirmato, & denique ab exceptioceptionibus Bellarminianis vindicato. Copiis sic nostris lustratis, etiam castra adversariorum explorari debent, & in re tanti momenti videndum est quoque, quibus ab altera parte armis pugnetur, quomodo probare velint, Petrum ad talem Pontificatum Romanum electum esse. Jam in prima vocatione ad Christum hujus rei indicia ostendere conantur nonnulli; Nam quòd Petro Luc. V. 4. dictum, ut duceret in altum, ibíque retia expanderet, illud Innocentio III. (cui ad stabiliendam Paparum potestatem, maximè temporalem, S. Scriptura turpiter abuti solenne fuit;) interprete Serm. 2. in Fest. Petr. ei significavit, ut ascenderet Romam, qua altum habeat Dominium super gentes, & inde per omnes terrarum rationes retia in capturam possint laxari. Quomodo certè Christus jam ipsam Monarchae spiritualis sedem designâsset! Et verba ejusdem historiae v.10. illa: Ex nunc Piscator hominum eris. Reginaldus Polus ita explicat, sive corrumpit: Tu Successoresque tui dominationem habebitis in omnes homines & potestatem Regibus atque Imperatoribus imperandi, eos citandi atque ejiciendi. Quâ ratione extremum potestatis Pontificiae jam tunc collatum fuisset, potestas nempe in omnes & supra omnes temporalis à Petro nunquam, nunquam etiam ab ullo per misse annos Romano Pontifice ita exercita! Sed ineptae sunt istae expositiones, imò impiae Scripturarum Sanctarum detorsiones, quibus se ex eorum numero esse produnt, qui Scripturas torquent ad propriam perniciem 2. Pet. III. 16. Responsionem nullam merentur, cùm manifestâ suâ absurditate Lectorem jam satis offendant; Quemadmodum etiam praerogativae illae, quas Bellarminus studiosè Petro conquisivit ex Scriptura S. viginti, ex aliis Scriptoribus octo, quatenus nimirum ad probandum Petri Primatum talem eas adduxit. Scilicet probandus est vanis allegoriis, praerogativis, quae partim nullae, partim leves, & quibus majores, & aequè magnas apud alios reperias, partim incertae & manifestè falsae, omnes insufficientes sunt, & jam abundè ab aliis refutatae; Agnoscente illud quoque Doctiss. du Pin Dissert. cap. 1. in fine scribens: Omitto quasdam alias praerogativas, quas fusè digerit Bellarminus, nam ex illis nonnulla sunt gratis conficta, alia nihil omninò ad Primatum Petri pertinent; hoc facile esset demonstrare, sed in his immorari taedet, cùm unusquisque possit earum levitatem vel eas percurrendo statim perspicere. Talibus itaque, cùm Theologo, maximè in retanti momenti, plane indigna sint, missis, ad palmaria, quibus pro Electione Petri ad Pontificatum talem cum specie aliqua utuntur, vel abutuntur potiùs, loca progredior accuratiùs examinanda.
units.tr: Thus far we have proved that Peter was not chosen to an ecclesiastical Monarchy. We based this chiefly on the argument from the equality and supreme power of the apostles, which is well founded in Holy Scripture, illustrated by the testimonies of the Fathers, confirmed by the very confession of the Papists, and finally defended against Bellarmine's objections. With our forces thus reviewed, the camps of the opponents must also be explored, and in a matter of such great importance we must also see with what weapons the other side fights, and how they wish to prove that Peter was chosen to such a Roman Pontificate. Now some try to show indications of this matter in Peter's first calling to Christ. For when Luke 5:4 says to Peter, "that he should launch out into the deep and there let down his nets," Innocent III (for whom it was customary to abuse Holy Scripture shamefully in order to establish the power of the Popes, especially the temporal power) explained this in his Sermon 2 on the Feast of St Peter as meaning that he should go up to Rome, where he has the "deep" dominion over the nations, and from there the nets could be let down for a catch through all regions of the earth. Surely in this way Christ would already have designated the seat of the spiritual Monarch! And the words of the same story, verse 10, "From now on you will be a fisher of men," Reginald Pole explains, or rather corrupts, thus: "You and your successors shall have dominion over all men, and power to command kings and emperors, to summon them and to cast them out." By this reasoning the full extent of the papal power would already have been conferred at that time, namely a power over all and above all, which temporal power was never, never exercised by Peter, nor by any Roman Pontiff in so many years! But these interpretations are foolish, indeed impious distortions of the holy Scriptures, by which they show themselves to be among those "who twist the Scriptures to their own destruction" (2 Peter 3:16). They deserve no answer, since by their plain absurdity they already offend the reader enough. Likewise those prerogatives which Bellarmine has diligently gathered for Peter, twenty from Holy Scripture and eight from other writers, insofar as he has brought them forward to prove Peter's Primacy of that kind. Clearly they are to be tested by empty allegories and prerogatives, some of which are non-existent, some slight, and for which you may find greater and equally great ones among others; some are uncertain and manifestly false. All are insufficient and have already been sufficiently refuted by others. The most learned du Pin also acknowledges this, writing in the Dissertation, chapter 1, at the end: "I omit certain other prerogatives which Bellarmine sets out at length, for some of them are invented without grounds, and others have nothing at all to do with Peter's Primacy. This would be easy to demonstrate, but it is tedious to dwell on these, since anyone can see their lightness at once simply by running through them." Since such things are wholly unworthy of a theologian, especially in a matter of such moment, I pass them over and proceed to the chief passages, which they use, or rather abuse, with some show of support for Peter's election to such a Pontificate, to be examined more carefully.

units.la: Il. Cajeta-
units.tr: II. Cajeta-

units.la: II. Cajetanus, postquam Tract. de Rom. Pont. Instit. Cap.1. dixisset, ex sacris literis pendere omnem quaestionis hujus de Primatu Petri & Pontificis veritatem; (quod notari, & cum iis, quae Sect.1. §. 6. ad demonstrationem ex Scriptura dixi, etiam conferri velim) subjungit, duos esse praecipue textus de eo Mysterio expresse loquentes, Matth.XVI. & Joh. Ultimo. Qui textus quoque praecipui sunt ex Bellarminianis, imo soli speciem quandam habentes. Possemus examen horum etiam Textuum, post tot, non tantum ex nostris maximi nominis, sed etiam Gallorum Theologorum, qui hic nobiscum junctis copiis pugnant, contra Monarchicorum πrgεqμηνέως vindicias omittere, & sine ablegatione Lectoris ad nostros forsan ei vel hoc solo indicio satisfacere, quod Ecclesia Gallicana non infima Romanae Communionis pars in istis Textibus electionem Petri ad Pontificatum & Primatum talem minime continepи, non tantum fateatur ingenuè, sed & ex sanctis quoque Patribus ostendat egregiè; Et quidem hanc ob causam, ne post Homerum quod ajunt, Iliada scribamus, infinitis ferè Patrum testimoniis excribendis non immorabimur. Interim tamen ne diffidere causae nostrae, & in re tanti momenti aliquid neglexisse videamur, videamus & ipsi, quàm expresse hi Textus de isto sive pietatis, sive iniquitatis mysterio loquantur.
units.tr: II. Cajetan, after saying in the first chapter of his Treatise on the Institution of the Roman Pontiff that "the whole truth of this question about the Primacy of Peter and of the Pontiff depends on the sacred letters" (which should be noted, and I would also like it compared with what I said in Section 1, §6 about the demonstration from Scripture), adds that "there are two chief texts speaking expressly about that mystery, Matthew 16 and the last chapter of John." These texts are also the chief ones among the Monarchists, indeed the only ones that have any appearance. We could, after so many, not only of our own men of the greatest name but also of the French theologians, who here fight with us in united forces, leave out the examination of these texts and defend the exegesis of the Monarchists, and perhaps, without sending the reader away to our writers, satisfy him with this single indication: that the Gallican Church, no small part of the Roman communion, not only freely admits that in these texts the election of Peter to the Pontificate and such a Primacy is by no means contained, but also shows this admirably from the holy Fathers too. And indeed, lest we write, as they say, an Iliad after Homer, we will not linger on copying out almost endless testimonies of the Fathers. Meanwhile, lest we seem to distrust our cause, or to have neglected something in a matter of such moment, let us see for ourselves how expressly these texts speak about this mystery, whether of piety or of iniquity.

units.la: III. Prior, qui habetur Matthaei XVI.18.19. ubi nimirum Christus ad Petrum, post editam ab eo egregiam confessionem, dicit: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam &c. Tibi dabo claves Regni caelorum; & in duobus versibus duo etiam continet, ex quibus duplici etiam modo argumentantur Monarchici. Primò argumentantur ex eo, quòd dicitur: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram, &c. Ajunt evidenter hic Petrum Petram, cui inaedificanda sit Ecclesia, vocari, & per consequens Ecclesiae Monarcham, & Rectorem universalem constitui. Haec igitur est clara illa Scriptura, quae arduam hanc de constitutione Pontificum talium, saltem Petri, quaestionem decidere debet. Haec est prima par; literarum, ut sic loquar, credentialium, quibus Petrus supremus Ecclesiae Rector populo Christiano proponitur. Sine dubio sensus horum verborum unicus legitimus apud Lectorem vel Auditorem ullum Christianum, de ullo alio dubium non relinquet. Ast quatuor sunt, quas Bellarminus l. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap.10. memorat, verborum istorum expositiones. Satis quidem subdole tres à sua diversas sub nomine mine Erasmi, Calvini, Lutheri proponit, quasi nimirum hi primi sic exponant, & fere soli, verùm, quando quatuor Bellarmino & sequacibus declarimus Patrum celeberrimorum, quorum authoritas in Ecclesia Pontificia, Verbo Dei, verbis saltem, & facto, ubi lubet, tantùm non æquatur, diversas expositiones, quarum nulla illud, quod Bellarminus & alii Hierarchici ex isto loco erucre conantur, continet, jam satis constare poterit, eum ad probandum illum, vel Petri, Pontificatum talem minimè idoneum esse.
units.tr: III. The first text is Matthew 16:18–19, where Christ, after Peter has made an outstanding confession, says to him: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church... I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." In these two verses there are two things, on the basis of which the Monarchists argue in a twofold way. First, they argue from the words "You are Peter, and upon this rock," etc. They say that Peter is here evidently called the rock on which the Church is to be built, and consequently that he is appointed Monarch and universal Ruler of the Church. This, then, is that clear Scripture which ought to settle this difficult question about the appointment of such Pontiffs, at least of Peter. This is, so to speak, the first of the credentials of letters by which Peter is presented to the Christian people as the supreme Ruler of the Church. Without doubt, the one legitimate sense of these words will leave no doubt for any Christian reader or hearer about any other sense. But there are four interpretations of these words, which Bellarmine mentions in book 1 of De Pontifice Romano, chapter 10. Rather craftily, he sets out three of them under the names of Erasmus, Calvin and Luther, as if these first men interpreted in this way, and almost alone. Yet when we show Bellarmine and his followers that four interpretations are held by the most celebrated Fathers, whose authority in the Papist Church, at least in words and in practice wherever it pleases, is hardly equalled to the Word of God, and that none of these different interpretations contains what Bellarmine and the other hierarchs try to extract from that passage, it will already be sufficiently clear that it is by no means suitable for proving that Peter, or the Pontificate of that kind, is his.

units.la: IV. Proponamus illas eo ordine, quo à doctissimo du Pin proponuntur. Primò dicit; non paucos ex sanctis Patribus per Petrum (Petram) hic intelligere fidem & confessionem Petri. Citat pro ea expositione Hilarium, Gregorium Nyssenum, Ambrosium, Chrysostomum, Augustinum, Acacium Melitenum, Cyrillum Alexandrinum, Juvenalem Hierosolymitanum, Theodoritum, Anonymum in Catena Niceta, Gregorium M. Isidorum Hisp. Bedam, Druthmarium, Hincmarum, Tostatum, ei favere testatur & alios. De Dominis de Rep. Eccl. l.1. c.6. §. 12. addit Epiphanium, Victorem Antiochenum, Theophylactum, Jonam Aurelianensem, ex Pontificibus Rom. Eutychianum, Leonem M. Felicem III. Adrianum I. Nicolaum I. Johannem VIII. Stephanum VI. Innocentium II. porrò Patres Concilii Suessionensis. An. 909. & dicit potuisse se plurima adhuc sanctorum Patrum loca afferre, et am effugere conantem Bellarminum retinet, & loci Augustiniani, qui Romanu adeò non placuerit, ex Breviario deletionem, alius decurtationem, & contrà sub Chrysostomi nomine currentis Apocryphi cujusdam suppositionem, in quibus Breviarii deformationibus potiùs, quàm reformationibus bona fides desideretur, memorat. Forbesius Instruct. Hist. Theol. l.15. c.7. § 2. addit Basilium Seleucien-sem, Paulum Emisenum, Joh. Damascenum, Germanum Constantinopolitanum, Authorem Glossæ dist. 19. Can. Ita Dominus. & Ludovicum Vives, ex quibus omnibus multos expositionem Pontificiam non attulisse, ipse etiam testis est. Ut certè mirari liceat fraudem Bellarmini, qui hanc sententiam Luthero, Centuriatoribus, aliisque ejusdem ordinis simpliciter tribuit. Miratur certè Magnus Launojus Epist. T. V. 7. sententiam, in qua plures compareant Pontifices Rom. Lutheranis tribui, usque adeò ut exclamet: O fucatam & perversam scribendi methodum, in qua damnatur, quod laudandum est, nempe Lutheranos illam Scripturæ expositionem recipere & amplecti, quam tot antiqui Patres & Pontifices Romani suis monumentis consignarunt! Si Lutherani, ita porrò argumentantur, sunt Novatores, quâ parte S. Patrum sequuntur traditionem, Novatores, tores, opinor, non erunt, cùm re ipsâ Novatores erunt. Ad has necessariò deveniendum est ineptias, cùm à Christiana disputandi simplicitate deflectimus. Et duabus antehac paginis: Ut expositionem reddat odiosam Bellarminus factioni Lutheranorum addicit; etiamsi veterum Patrum testimoniis confirmari posse fateatur. Et pergens ingenuitatem Tissii laudat, qui Luthero hic responderit, aedificatam supra Petri confessionem Ecclesiam esse, à nemine Catholicorum negari, hoc est, à Doctoribus pene cunctis ad mille, seu neminem esse, qui apertè recusárit. Fundamento etiam illa non caret; Confessionem quippe in praecedentibus suo & aliorum nomine edidit Petrus, quae profectò Ecclesiae Christianae fundamentum est, per quam fideles Christo inseruntur, qui & sanctissima sua fidei, Jud. v. 20. se inaedificare dicuntur, ut etiam perpetuò illa in Ecclesia manere debet; Eam etiam nec novam, nec profanam esse, jamjam laudatus Launojus l. c. probat.
units.tr: IV. Let us set these out in the order in which the most learned du Pin presents them. First, he says that not a few of the holy Fathers understand by Peter (the Rock) here the faith and confession of Peter. In support of this interpretation he cites Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Augustine, Acacius of Melitene, Cyril of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Theodoret, the anonymous author in the Catena of Nicetas, Gregory the Great, Isidore of Spain, Bede, Drutmar, Hincmar, Tostatus, and he testifies that others also favour it. From De Dominis, De Rep. Eccl. l.1. c.6. §12., he adds Epiphanius, Victor of Antioch, Theophylact, Jonas of Orléans; from the Roman pontiffs Eutychian, Leo the Great, Felix III, Adrian I, Nicholas I, John VIII, Stephen VI, Innocent II; and further the fathers of the Council of Soissons in the year 909. He says that he could bring forward very many more passages of the holy Fathers. Trying to escape Bellarmine's objection, he also records the passage of Augustine, which so displeased the Romanists that it was deleted from the Breviary in one place, shortened in another, and on the contrary a certain apocryphal work circulating under the name of Chrysostom was put in its place; in these deformations of the Breviary, rather than its reformations, good faith is lacking. Forbes, Instruct. Hist. Theol. l.15. c.7. §2., adds Basil of Seleucia, Paul of Emesa, John Damascene, Germanus of Constantinople, the author of the Gloss on dist. 19, Can. Thus De Dominis. And Ludovicus Vives; and from all of these, he himself also bears witness, many did not bring forward the Papist interpretation. One may certainly marvel at the dishonesty of Bellarmine, who simply ascribes this opinion to Luther, the Centuriators and others of the same kind. Magnus Launoy certainly marvels, in Epist. T. V. 7., that an opinion in which many Roman pontiffs appear is ascribed to the Lutherans, to such an extent that he exclaims: O false and perverse method of writing, in which what is to be praised is condemned, namely that the Lutherans receive and embrace that interpretation of Scripture which so many ancient Fathers and Roman pontiffs have confirmed in their writings! If the Lutherans, he goes on to argue, are Innovators, insofar as they follow the tradition of the holy Fathers, they will not, I think, be Innovators, since in fact they will be Innovators. We must come to these absurdities whenever we depart from the Christian simplicity of disputing. And two pages earlier: In order to make the interpretation odious, Bellarmine attaches it to the faction of the Lutherans, even though he admits it can be confirmed by the testimonies of the ancient Fathers. And continuing, he praises the candour of Tissius, who answered Luther here that the Church is built upon Peter's confession, something denied by none of the Catholics, that is, by almost all the teachers, numbering a thousand, or that there is no one who has openly refused it. Nor is this interpretation lacking in foundation: Peter had indeed given the confession in the preceding words in his own name and that of the others, which is truly the foundation of the Christian Church, through which the faithful are grafted into Christ; they are also said to build themselves up on their most holy faith, Jude v. 20, and this confession must always remain in the Church. That it is neither new nor profane, the aforementioned Launoy proves in the same place.

units.la: V. Ait Doctissimus du Pin, ab ista expositione (de Petra fide, vel confessione Petri) non multùm abludere eos, qui Petrum (Petram) interpretantur Christum, quem Petrus erat confessus. Citat pro ea Hieronymum & praecipuè Augustinum, qui Retract. l. 1. c. 21. testatur se verba illa semel de Petro, sapissimè de Christo exposuisse, & subjungit: Harum duarum sententiarum quae sit probabilior eligat Lector; Theodoritum, Bedam, & alios, qui videri possint apud Launojum Ep. part. 5. Ep. ad Voellum. Exprimit de Dominis l. c. § 9. & seqq. porrò Cyrillum Alexandrinum, Tarasium Constantinopolitanum, Glossam interlinearem, quae supra hanc Petram Christum habeat, in quem credis; Subdit, Petrum à Petra Christo vocabulum hoc sortitum esse communi omnium fere Patrum, Hieronymi, Tertulliani, Augustini, Ambrosii, sive Prosperi, Gregorii M. Leonis I. Bedae, Nicolai I. Gregorii VII. Gratiani, Alphonsi de Castro, &c. sententiâ, qui omnes expositioni illi aptè favère deprehendantur. Forbesius loc. citato adjungit Hilarium, Gregorium Nyssenum, Modestum Archiepiscopum Hierosolymitanum. Ut & hic similem Bellarmini fraudem mirari liceat, qui sententiae hujus Authorem Calvinum, & per consequens hos sanctos Patres & Viros celebres omnes hac in parte Calvinianos facit. Ita autem rursus Doctiss. Launojus; Calvino tribuere, ut de hujus Sectarii nomine reddatur suspecta, atque sic in Calvino crimen fuisse, eam amplecti explicationem, quam Hieronymus &c. sint amplexi.
units.tr: V. The most learned du Pin says that those who interpret the Rock as Christ, whom Peter confessed, do not differ much from this interpretation (of the Rock as the faith or confession of Peter). In support of it he cites Jerome and especially Augustine, who, in Retract. l. 1. c. 21., testifies that he had explained those words once of Peter and very often of Christ, and adds: let the reader choose which of these two opinions is the more probable; he also cites Theodoret, Bede and others, who may be seen in Launoy, Ep. part 5, Ep. ad Voellum. He sets out De Dominis, l. c. §9. and following; further Cyril of Alexandria, Tarasius of Constantinople, the Interlinear Gloss, which has the Christ upon this Rock in whom you believe. He adds that Peter received this name from the Rock Christ, according to the opinion of nearly all the Fathers: Hilary, Tertullian, Augustine, Ambrose, or Prosper, Gregory the Great, Leo I, Bede, Nicholas I, Gregory VII, Gratian, Alphonsus de Castro, etc., all of whom are found to favour that interpretation. Forbes, in the passage cited, adds Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Modestus, Archbishop of Jerusalem. Here too one may marvel at a similar dishonesty of Bellarmine, who makes Calvin the author of this opinion, and consequently makes all these holy Fathers and celebrated men Calvinists in this point. Launoy again: to ascribe it to Calvin, so that the name of this sectarian becomes suspect, and so that the crime lies in Calvin for embracing the explanation which Jerome etc. embraced.

units.la: VI. Et ista quidem sententia à multis etiam rationibus commendatur. Christus enim Petra est, divinisque personis in Scriptura hoc nomen ordinariò tribuitur, Christo, qui Petra salutis, Psalm. XCV. 1. quem Architecti rejecterunt, Psalm. CXVIII. 22. qui in Zione positus
units.tr: VI. This opinion is also commended by many reasons. For Christ is the Rock, and in Scripture this name is ordinarily given to the divine persons: to Christ, the Rock of our salvation, Psalm 95.1; whom the builders rejected, Psalm 118.22; who is laid in Zion

units.la: Secundae Authores; Fundamenta; positus, lapis probatus, pretiosus lapis, angularis, fundatissimus Esaj. XXVIII. 16. (quamvis locum hunc de Papa in Prafat. ad libros de Rom. Pont. prolixè ita explicet Bellarminus, ut parum à blasphemiis absit, & aperte repugnet ipsi Petro, qui 1.Ep.II.v.6. locum Esaj. de Christo explicat; Ubi nullum effugium, præter ordinarium esse poterit, nempe quæ de Christo dicuntur, etiam Papis, ejus Vicariis convenire, in quo quidem impietas impietate excusatur;) Sic etiam Paulus Christum vocat fundamentum, præter quod aliud poni non possit, 1.Cor.III.11. & Petram, cap.X.4. utpote qui non tantum in natura omnia portat verbo potentiæ suæ, Heb.I.3. sed & Ecclesiæ gratiam & tutelam efficaciter largitur, & imbecillitatem suorum potenter sustentat, & quem Petrus jamjam confessus fuerat, Filium Dei viventis, v.16. Cui explicationi etiam favere videtur illud, quòd Evangelista Θεόπνευστος, vocem unam non retinuit, sed diversimodè Πέτρον & Πέτρᾳ dixit; quódque Christus apud Evangelistam non simpliciter dicit; Tu es Petrus, & super TE ædificabo; vel: Tu es Petra, &c. vel; & super te Petram ædificabo; Sed: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram ædificabo; quâ ratione commodè ad se ipsum respicere potuit, juxtà similes loquendi formulas, Joh.II.13. Job.XIX.26. 1.Cor.XV.53.
units.tr: laid, a tested stone, a precious stone, a corner-stone, a most sure foundation, Isaiah 28.16 (although Bellarmine, in his preface to the books on the Roman Pontiff, explains this passage about the Pope at such length that he is barely free from blasphemy, and openly contradicts Peter himself, who in 1 Peter 2.6 explains the passage of Isaiah about Christ; where there is no escape except the usual one, namely that what is said of Christ also belongs to the Popes, his Vicars; in which impiety is excused by impiety). So too Paul calls Christ the foundation, other than which no one can lay, 1 Cor. 3.11, and the Rock, 1 Cor. 10.4, since he not only bears all things by the word of his power, Heb. 1.3, but also effectively bestows grace and protection on the Church, and powerfully sustains the weakness of his people; and whom Peter had just confessed, the Son of the living God, v. 16. The fact that the divinely inspired [θεόπνευστος] Evangelist did not keep one word but wrote Peter [Πέτρον] and rock [Πέτρᾳ] in different forms also seems to favour this explanation; and that Christ, according to the Evangelist, does not simply say, You are Peter, and upon YOU I will build; or You are the Rock, etc.; or and upon you, the Rock, I will build; but: You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build; by which reasoning he could fittingly refer to himself, according to similar forms of speech, John 2.13, Job 19.26, 1 Cor. 15.53.

units.la: VII. Tertia expositio est, ait Doctissimus du Pin, nomine Petræ ipsum Petrum intelligi.
units.tr: VII. The third explanation is, says the most learned du Pin, that Peter himself is meant by the name Rock.

units.la: Hanc expositionem esse Catholicorum, dicit Bellarminus, & alibi: Omnes Patres docere, super Petrum fundatam esse Ecclesiam. Sed rectè Clarissimus Launojus T.V. epist.7. p.9. seq. in his verbis fucum observat, & addit: Nisi Author iste (Bellarminus) mentiatur, ἀμετρεία εἰς ἀνθρώπους, nemo mentietur unquam (quod quidem parùm convenit cum eo, quòd effigiei Cardinalis appositum, eum nullius in tota vita mendacii sibi conscium fuisse;) At idem etiam Clariss. Launojus 4. sententias plurimis Patrum testimoniis firmatas exhibet. Patres hanc dederunt expositionem aliquot; Augustinus tamen ei expresse aliam, teste ipso Bellarmino, antepo-suit, & judice de Dominis. l. c. §25. hanc ut improbabiliorem ac propemodum retractandam fermè rejecit. Ipse de Dominis tamen eam contrà probabiliorem vocat, & probat, ita tamen ut dua illa Sanctorum Patrum interpretationes, quæ Petra vocabulo vel Christum intelligunt, vel fidem, & fidei divinitatis Christi confessionem, adhuc ut probabiles maneant, & nihil Ecclesiæ Catholicæ contrarium, liberámque hic esse electionem. L. c. Doctissimus du Pin similiter eam probabiliorem esse judicat, imò ex nostris Doctissimus Camero, quem quoque sequuntur alii, in Myrothecio ad hunc l. eam studiose vindicat atque defendit.
units.tr: Bellarmine says this explanation belongs to the Catholics, and elsewhere: All the Fathers teach that the Church is founded upon Peter. But the most distinguished Launoy rightly notes the deceit in these words (T.V. epist. 7, p. 9 ff.) and adds: Unless this author lies, [ἀμετρία εἰς ἀνθρώπους] immoderation towards men, no one will ever lie. (This agrees poorly with the inscription under the Cardinal's portrait, that he was never conscious of any lie in his whole life.) Yet the same most distinguished Launoy sets out four opinions, each supported by many testimonies of the Fathers. Some Fathers did give this explanation, but Augustine expressly preferred another, as Bellarmine himself testifies, and de Dominis, in the same place (§ 25), almost rejected it as less probable and nearly to be retracted. De Dominis himself, however, calls it more probable and argues for it, yet so that those two interpretations of the holy Fathers, which understand by Rock either Christ or the faith and the confession of Christ's divinity, remain probable, nothing contrary to the Catholic Church, and the choice here is free. (Ibid.) The most learned du Pin likewise judges it to be more probable, and indeed among our own people the most learned Cameron, whom others also follow, in the Myrothecium on this passage zealously vindicates and defends it.

units.la: VIII. Sed multùm abest, ut omnes hujus expositionis approbatores simul absolutam Petri Monarchiam probent, & in hoc loco Petrum ad eam electum, eam illi vel promissam, vel exhibitam esse, cognoscant, quod cum expositione ista indissolubili nexu conjunctum esse Bellarminus, Baronius, aliique somniant, & vel maximè hic in quæstione est; Ut lepidus sit certè præcipuè Baronius, qui, postquam à se probatum esse, sibi certò persuasisset, Petrum hic per Petram denotari, confestim totus in triumphos resolvitur, ut jam Victor exultat, epinicíumque canit, ad annum Ch.33. n. 27. c.2. Qui eadem planè cum ipso cæterisque sentiunt, certè nihil minùs, quàm Catholici sunt, cùm eos & venerandæ antiquitatis imò propriorum in aliis fidei Sociorum, ut de aliis nihil dicam, consensus destituat. Nam fuitne ullus ex his Patribus (qui de Petri Persona explicant Petram) qui Petrum Petram & fundamentum ædificanda Ecclesiæ dictum, cum Illustri de Dominis l. c. § 30. loquor, sub hac Metaphora constitutum, aut designatum Principem & Monarcham Ecclesiæ intellexerit? Certè hi omnes & cum illis plures Petrum fundamentum Ecclesiæ eo sensu acceperunt, quòd vel fidem divinitatis Christi primus solenniter promulgavit, in qua tota fundatur Ecclesia, vel quòd fidei soliditatem retinuerit, vel quod primus & præcipuus ex duodecim Evangelium per mundum sparserit, sed ex his nullus consurgit Petri Primatus, nisi ad summum excellentiæ cujusdam, & dignitatis personalis. Quod si quis, ex Patribus antiquioribus, Petrum facit propterea solum totius Ecclesiæ Primatem & Monarcham, quia super ipsum dicatur ædificanda Ecclesia, eum producant; Nos enim nullum prorsus id aut censuisse, aut protulisse, aut innuisse putamus.
