Adeò enim difficile, ne dicam impossibile, est, suprematum hunc Petri ex illis præcisè promissis super hanc Petram &c. colligere, aut confirmare, ut vel ipsi Monarchici nostri, quò se vertant, non inveniant, ut in nomine, seu Metaphora fundamenti primatûs inveniant authoritatem, & Petri supremam præfecturam.
units.tr: VIII. But it is far from the case that all who approve this explanation also prove that Peter was at once given an absolute monarchy, and recognise that in this passage Peter was chosen for it, or that it was promised or shown to him. Bellarmine, Baronius and others dream that this is bound up with the explanation, and this is precisely what is in question. Baronius is especially comical: after he had, as he had persuaded himself, proved that Peter is here denoted by Rock, he at once dissolves entirely into triumph, and exults like a victor, singing his song of victory (at the year of Christ 33, n. 27, c. 2). Those who think exactly as he does and as the rest are certainly no more Catholic, since they lack the consensus of venerable antiquity, and indeed of their own fellow-believers in other matters, not to say anything of others. For was there any one of those Fathers (who explain Rock of the person of Peter), who understood Peter, called the Rock and foundation on which the Church is to be built, to be a Prince and Monarch of the Church, set up or designated under this metaphor? I speak with the illustrious de Dominis (ibid., § 30). Certainly all these, and with them many more, took Peter to be the foundation of the Church in the sense that he was the first to proclaim solemnly the faith in Christ's divinity, on which the whole Church is founded, or that he kept the firmness of the faith, or that he was the first and chief of the twelve to spread the Gospel through the world. But from these there arises no primacy of Peter, except as a high degree of a certain excellence and personal dignity. If anyone, from the more ancient Fathers, makes Peter the sole primate and monarch of the whole Church because the Church is said to be built upon him, let him produce them. For we think that none of them has either held, or put forward, or hinted at that. Indeed it is so difficult, not to say impossible, to infer or confirm this supremacy of Peter from those promises alone, upon this rock and so on, that our own Monarchists, whichever way they turn, cannot find in the name or metaphor of the foundation any authority for the primacy and Peter's supreme headship.

units.la: IX. Concinit planè Doctissimus du Pin, cujus hæc sunt verba: Et certè ratio fundamenti hic consistit in promulgatione Evangelii & Ecclesiarum administratione; sed hac non secus Apostolis cæteris ac Petro data sunt, & illi non secus ac Petrus hoc sensu dicuntur fundamentum Ecclesiæ. Ephes. 2. ædificati supra fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum. Et Apoc. c.21. Et murus civitatis habens fundamenta
units.tr: IX. The most learned du Pin agrees entirely, and his words are these: And indeed the force of the foundation here consists in the promulgation of the Gospel and the administration of the Churches; but these were given to the other Apostles no less than to Peter, and they are called the foundation of the Church in this sense no less than Peter. Eph. 2. built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets. And Rev. 21. And the wall of the city having foundations

units.la: Ema Monarchiam Petri non involvere, ostenditur etiam M Ant. de Dominis verbis
units.tr: That the Monarchy of Peter is not involved in this exposition is also shown by the words of M. Antonius de Dominis.

units.la: Doctiss. du Pin judicio menta duodecim, & in ipsis duodecim nomina, duodecim Apostolorum agni. Nec aliud probant allata à Bellarmino testimonia; quae vindicat & addit : Itaque posito , quòd hæc verba; & super hanc Petram; à Christo de persona Petri dicta sint, ut ego probabilius esse arbitror, nihil aliud hic sibi vult Christus, quàm Petrum ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ, hoc est, fidelium conversionem & Ecclesiarum administrationem plurimùm laboraturum. Ad Summum igitur inde deduci potest, eum primum ac præcipuum fore inter eos, qui Evangelium erant annunciaturi: sed inde colligi minimè potest cum Bellarmino,Petro totius Ecclesiæ regimen esse commissum, præsertim circa fidem.
units.tr: According to the judgment of the most learned du Pin, the twelve foundations, and on the twelve themselves the names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb. Nor do the testimonies cited by Bellarmine prove anything else; which he vindicates and adds: Therefore, granting that these words, and upon this rock, were spoken by Christ concerning the person of Peter, as I judge more probable, Christ means nothing else here than that Peter will labour very much for the building of the Church, that is, for the conversion of believers and the administration of the Churches. So at most it can be deduced from this that he will be the first and chief among those who are to proclaim the Gospel; but it cannot at all be inferred, with Bellarmine, that the governance of the whole Church was committed to Peter, especially concerning the faith.

units.la: X. Et hæc quidem optimè se habent Doctissimorum Virorum judicia. Quid enim Petro hic diceretur, quod non & aliis, & de aliis dici potuerit, imò revera dictum sit? Si solus ita dictus fuisset an hoc majorem quàm gradûs alicujus differentiam involveret ? Quemadmodum , dum Zebedæi filii Boanerges dicuntur, cæteros in concionando fulminatores fuisse non ideò negatur. Sed quid in appellatione Petræ illustrius fundamenti significatione? Atqui vidimus commune hoc esse Apostolorum Epitheton; Imò vidimus Hieronymi testimonium, quòd super omnes ex æquo Ecclesiæ fortitudo solidetur. Differentiam quidem Bellarminus assignare conatur,sed cui jam occurrimus. Petra sæpe de Deo dicitur,si igitur homini applicari debet, pro statu etiam hominis explicari debet, quod etiam Ambrosius pulchrè monet Serm.4. Petra, inquit,Petrus pro devotione dicitur,& Petra pro virtute Dominus nuncupatur; Et quod, eodem in Evang. Luca l. 6. Com. penult. notante, circa alia vocabula, quæ Christi gratia discipulis ipsis donavit sua, lucis ,panis, vitis rectè fit, & fieri debere Chrysostomus in hom. post captum Eutropium monuit, utpote quæ tunc potiùs significent τηλὼ ονόμαλ@·, quàm verò φύσιν πεφύγμαλ@·, in Deo rem declarent, in hominibus honorem nominis. Ita certè Petrus non aliter potuisset Petra vocari super quam ædificanda foret Ecclesia, quàm verò de Abrahamo Genes.XII.3. legitur,in eo benedictum iri omnes gentes; Quod quidem in omni emphasi complementum in Christo accepit,Abrahami semine primario, sed etiam in ipso Abrahamo , quatenus nimirum cum fideli Abrahamo & post eum & in imitatione fidei ejus gentes benedictionem consequuntur. Eodem modò hic Petro promitteretur,eum non tantùm suo commodo vivum lapidem fore in ædificio Domûs Dei, sed & aliis instrumentum communis salutis,fundamentum inter inter fundamenta nobile, diceretur illi; quandoquidem jam antea nomen Petri acceperit, & modò eximia confessione suâ ei respon-derit, ut etiam in posterum ei respondere pergat, fructu optato il-lud neutiquam carituram, sed multos sic ad Christum adductum iri, & cum in illis victorem contra Diaboli quosvis insultus, exti-turum esse. Quibus etiam eventus respondisset, Et sanè non ali-ter hæc promissio accipienda foret, ac prout res postea contigerunt; Ast, juxta dicta & dicenda, nihil aliud de Petro occurrit quàm, quòd multam & primam quasi in ædificanda Ecclesia Christi ope-ram Divinâ efficaciter cooperante gratiâ præstitit, & primum qua-si domûs Christianæ lapidem posuit, primos Judæos Act.I. &, pe-culiari revelatione de eo edoctus, etiam primos fere ex gentibus, Act.X. ad fidem Christi adduxit; Dico fere primos ex Gentibus, cùm Paulus statim post suam ante Cornelii conversionem etiam Gentibus Christum annuntiârit, & Andronicus & Junia, verisimi-liter etiam ex gentibus, ante eum in Christo fuerint.
units.tr: X. These judgments of the most learned men are altogether sound. For what would be said to Peter here that could not also be said to others, and about others, and indeed has not really been said? If he alone had been so called, would this involve a difference of more than some degree? Just as when the sons of Zebedee are called Boanerges, it is not denied that the others were also thunderers in preaching. But what is more distinguished in the appellation of Rock than the meaning of foundation? Yet we have seen that this is a common epithet of the Apostles; indeed we have seen the testimony of Jerome, that the strength of the Church is equally strengthened upon all of them. Bellarmine does try to assign a difference, but we have already met it. Rock is often said of God; if therefore it must be applied to a man, it must also be explained according to the man's state, as Ambrose wisely warns (Serm. 4): Peter, he says, is named for his devotion, and the Lord is named Rock for his virtue. And what Chrysostom, in his homily after the fall of Eutropius, rightly notes should be done, and ought to be done, with the other names that Christ gave his disciples out of his grace, such as light, bread, and vine: these then signify rather mere names [ὀνόματα] than natural qualities [φύσιν πεφυκότα], declaring in God a reality and in men only the honour of a name. So certainly Peter could not have been called Rock in any other way than that upon him the Church was to be built. Just as it is read of Abraham (Gen. 12:3) that all nations would be blessed in him, which indeed received its full fulfilment in Christ, the chief seed of Abraham, but also in Abraham himself, in so far as, with the faithful Abraham, and after him and in imitation of his faith, the nations obtain the blessing. In the same way it would be promised here to Peter that he would be not only a living stone in the building of God's house for his own good, but also an instrument of common salvation for others; he would be called a noble foundation among foundations, since he had already received the name Peter and had now answered with his outstanding confession, and would go on answering so in future. He would not at all lack the desired fruit, but many would thus be led to Christ, and he would be a conqueror in them against all the assaults of the Devil. To these things the outcome would also have corresponded. Indeed this promise ought not to be understood otherwise than as things afterwards turned out. But according to what has been and will be said, nothing else about Peter appears than this: that in the building of Christ's Church he performed much first work, with divine grace effectively cooperating, and laid the first stone, as it were, of the Christian house, when he brought the first Jews to the faith of Christ (Acts 1), and, instructed by a peculiar revelation about him, almost the first of the Gentiles (Acts 10). I say almost the first of the Gentiles, since Paul, immediately after his conversion, before Cornelius, also proclaimed Christ to the Gentiles, and Andronicus and Junia, probably also from the Gentiles, were in Christ before him.

units.la: XI. De quarta expositione sic loquitur Doctissimus du Pin:
units.tr: XI. Du Pin, the most learned man, speaks thus about the fourth explanation:

units.la: Denique non hoc tantùm de Petro, sed & de aliis Apostolis dictum esse, af-firmant plerique. Citat Origenem, qui tamen & latiùs verba illa ex-tendere videtur, de quovis Christi discipulo & imitatore ea explicans; quæ etiam explicatio literalis est, non mera, ut Bellarminus pertendit, allegoria, cùm expresse dicat: Quòd si super illum unum Petrum tantùm existimas ædificari totam Ecclesiam, quid dicturus es de Johanne filio Tonitrui & Apostolorum unoquoque? Tract.1. super cap.16. Matth. Citat porrò Cyprianum, qui ep.27. de omnibus Episcopis id dictum esse dicat; Hieronymum, super omnes Apostolos Ecclesiam fundatam esse, omnes Psal.86. Ecclesia fundamenta vocari, dicentem; Augustinum item, Theodoretum & Paschasium Ratbertum. Quibus addi etiam potest Ambrosius l. supra cit. Ubi & hæc verba: Qui carnem vicerit, Ecclesia fundamentum est, & si æquari Petro non poterit, imitari poterit. Et ex his quoque concludi potest, non ita bene Bellarminum hanc expositionem sub Erasmi nomine proferre.
units.tr: Finally, many affirm that these words were said not only of Peter but also of the other Apostles. He cites Origen, who nevertheless seems to extend those words more widely, explaining them of any disciple and imitator of Christ. This explanation is also literal, not a mere allegory, as Bellarmine contends, since he expressly says: But if you think the whole Church is built upon that one Peter alone, what will you say about John, the son of thunder, and about each of the Apostles? Tract. 1 on Matthew 16. He next cites Cyprian, who in Epistle 27, on all bishops, says that this was said; Jerome, who, saying that the Church is founded upon all the Apostles, calls all of them the foundations of the Church (Psalm 86); likewise Augustine, Theodoret and Paschasius Radbertus. To these may also be added Ambrose in the work cited above, where he also says: Whoever has conquered the flesh is a foundation of the Church, and if he cannot be made equal to Peter, he can imitate him. And from these things it can also be concluded that Bellarmine does not do well in putting this explanation under the name of Erasmus.

units.la: XII. Qui etiam non ita bene contra hanc sententiam argumentatur.
units.tr: XII. He also argues not very well against this opinion.

units.la: Nam, quòd ait, Christum expressè Petri Personam designare & describere; illud tantùm probat, Petrum quoque talem Petram, imò in ordine quodam primam, & cæterorum typum fuisse fidelium; Et quòd pergit: Si omnes fideles sunt ista Petra, fundamentum istud, ubi erunt parietes? &c. illud ex distinctione fidelium singulorum, sub diversis respectibus & totius Ecclesiæ corporis solvitur; quivis fidelis dici potest Petra, super quam Ecclesia ædificatur, quatenus fidelis confessione veritatis ædificans, adeóque primò habito ad alios respectu; secundò etiam sine respectu ad alios, quatenus fundamentalem tenet & profitetur veritatem, & huic alias superstruit, fundamentum existit, & super singulos fideles Ecclesiam ædificari, dici potest, quatenus nimirum ex singulis fidelibus totum Ecclesiæ corpus consistit; Et quòd Bellarminus tandem contra hanc sententiam addit; Erasmum absurdum esse censere, super hominem Petrum ædificari Ecclesiam, & proin multò minùs eam super singulos fideles ædificari posse; illud totum ex male intellecta Erasmi sententia venit, qui post Origenem non negat, Petrum dici posse Petram, sed solum sic sensu Pontificio dici, dum Petrum & unumquemque fere fidelem, quisquis jam ille sit, Petram esse, sensu jamjam indicato, judicat.
units.tr: For when he says that Christ expressly designates and describes the person of Peter, this proves only that Peter too was such a rock, indeed in a certain order the first, and a type of the other faithful. And when he goes on: If all the faithful are that rock, where will the walls be, that foundation? etc., this is resolved by the distinction between individual believers under different respects and the whole body of the Church. Any believer can be called a rock upon which the Church is built, insofar as, by confessing the truth, he builds others up, and so first in relation to others; and secondly even without relation to others, insofar as he holds and professes the fundamental truth and builds other things upon it, he exists as a foundation. And it can be said that the Church is built upon each individual believer, insofar as the whole body of the Church consists of individual believers. And when Bellarmine finally adds against this opinion: Erasmus is absurd to think that the Church is built upon the man Peter, and therefore much less can it be built upon single believers, all this comes from a misunderstanding of Erasmus's view. For, following Origen, he does not deny that Peter can be called a rock; he only holds that it can be said in the Papist sense, when he judges that Peter and almost every believer, whoever he may be, is a rock, in the sense just indicated.

units.la: XIII. Quæ in Apostolos præcipuè quadrare posse ex præcedentibus liquet, & omnibus non minùs quàm Petro eandem competere Metaphoricam fundamenti rationem, senserunt judice de Dominis l. c. § 45. &c. Patres fere omnes Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Propugnatores.
units.tr: XIII. As is clear from what precedes, this can apply especially to the Apostles, and that the same metaphorical sense of foundation belongs to all no less than to Peter: nearly all the Fathers, the defenders of the Catholic Church, have thought so, as the judge Dominis holds in the work cited, §45 etc.

units.la: Citat Ignatium, Tertullianum, Hieronymum, Origenem, Hilarium, Cyrillum, Augustinum, Ambrosium, Chrysostomum, Concilium Aquense, Nicolaum tertium, Cardinalem Cusanum, Epistolas Decretales Anacleti, Sixti I. Eusebii, Melchiadis, Julii I. Ægyptiorum epistolam ad Felicem. Et subdit: Quid mirum igitur, si ipsimet Monarchici in hoc manus dare, ac propemodum huic primo loco ad confirmandam Petri Monarchiam, dum ad paucula respiserent, aptissimo judicato cedere, illúmque è manibus sibi elabi, sponte pati, consentiant? Eos id facere, probat ex loco Joh. de Turrecremata, Ecclesiæ Rom. Cardinalis & Protectoris singularis, qui l. 2. de Eccl. cap. 11. sic loquitur: Non sumus argumentati, Petrum primatum habuisse, quia dictus fuit fundamentum, sive Petra Ecclesia, sed ideò, quia singulariter Petrum, aliis præsentibus Apostolis, Christus Petram nominavit Ecclesia: Hoc autem neutiquam probare, quemadmodum quidem Turrecrematæ videtur, Petrum principale fundamentum sive potestatis, sive majoris universalitatis respectu fuisse, quamvis fundator ministerialis inter duodecim principalis esse potuerit, & prout v.g. inter Medicos aliquis cæteros in arte sua antecellit, qui tamen ob id cæterorum Dominus non est, manifestum est, & pariter, cùm omnes Christus interrogárit, Petrus etiam, quod & alibi fecerat, omnium nomine præ cæteris
units.tr: He cites Ignatius, Tertullian, Jerome, Origen, Hilary, Cyril, Augustine, Ambrose, Chrysostom, the Council of Aachen, Nicholas III, Cardinal Cusanus, the Decretal Epistles of Anacletus, Sixtus I, Eusebius, Melchiades, Julius I, and the letter of the Egyptians to Felix. And he adds: What wonder, then, if the monarchists themselves give way on this point, and, when they look only at a few passages, judge that this first place, the most suitable for confirming the monarchy of Peter, yields, and willingly consent to let it slip from their hands? That they do so he proves from a passage of John de Turrecremata, Cardinal of the Roman Church and its special protector, who in book 2 On the Church, chapter 11, speaks thus: We have not argued that Peter had the primacy because he was called the foundation or rock of the Church, but because Christ named Peter alone, with the other Apostles present, the Rock of the Church. But that Peter was the principal foundation, either of power or of greater universality, is by no means proved, as Turrecremata seems to think. It is clear that a foundation can be the principal one, while being only a ministerial founder among the twelve, just as one physician among others excels in his art, and yet for that reason is not the lord of the others. And likewise, since Christ questioned all of them, Peter also answered on behalf of all, as he had done elsewhere, before the others and for the others. Hence, that the promise which followed also applies to all should be beyond doubt, even though Christ directed his speech expressly to one man, whose zeal stood out above the zeal of the rest and who answered for all, and alluded particularly to the name given to him.

units.la: Turrecremata, vim argumenti in speciali tantum Petri alloquio ponenti, occurrit; teris & pro cæteris,inde etiam ⲁⲣⲭⲏⲅⲟⲥ ⲕⲁⲓ ⲣⲉⲧⲁ ⲥⲟⲙⲁ ⲱⲛ ⲡⲁⲗⲁⲓⲱⲛ pralocutor & os Apostolorum Patribus dictus,responderit;(quod ad evitandam confusionem , quæ omnibus simul respondentibus exoriri potuisset,& ad significandam, quod Patres addunt, Ecclesiæ unitatem , testandúmque illorum de Christo consensum,fieri debuit, & cùm Pater jam mysteria fidei patefecit, hoc est, discipulis revelaverit Matth.XI.25. & cùm dubio procul jam ahtea sæpe de his sermones commiscuerint, fieri potuit;) hinc promissionem etiam subsecutam omnes spectare, extra dubium esse debet licèt Christus ad unum, cujus Zelus præ Zelo cæterorum eminebat, quique pro omnibus responderat, sermonem suum expresse direxerit, & ad nomen ei datum peculiariter alluserit.
units.tr: Turrecremata meets the force of the argument only in its special address to Peter, and answers that he was called the leader and spokesman of the Apostles [ἀρχηγὸς καὶ ῥήτωρ τῶν ἀποστόλων] by the Fathers, in the same way, on behalf of the rest and in place of the rest. This had to happen to avoid the confusion that would have arisen if all had answered at once, and to signify, as the Fathers add, the unity of the Church, and to bear witness to their agreement about Christ. And when the Father had already revealed the mysteries of faith, that is, had disclosed them to the disciples (Matthew 11:25), and when without doubt they had often before discussed these matters among themselves, it could happen. It should be beyond doubt that the promise which followed concerns all of them, although Christ directed his speech expressly to one, whose zeal stood out above the zeal of the others, who answered for all, and alluded particularly to the name given to him.

units.la: XIV. Sed non oportet nimiùm separare istas quatuor expositiones; Subordinatæ sunt aliquomodo, & amicè inter illas convenit. Etenim juxta primam expositionem talis confessio Petri intelligitur, quam (quod quarta favet) nomine omnium exhibuerat, ut omnes ejusdem confessionis socios, Apostolos cumprimis, pariter ac loquentem Petrum,Petram vocare liceat; Petrus autem juxta tertiam expositionem Petra fuit , non certè ratione naturæ humanæ,cui, maximè cùm corrupta sit, & à vita Dei aliena, augusta illa elogia neutiquam conveniunt, & quæ Petro illud,propter quod Christus eum beatum prædicavit,non revelaverat, nec etiam, ut Pontificii volunt, ratione supremi & absoluti Rectoratûs Ecclesiæ universæ,qui Rectoratus vel maximè controvertitur, imò ordinationi Christi contrarius est, & quem Petrus per paucos annos habuisse supponitur, & in quo Successores nulli in Scripturis memorantur, & qui esse volunt, nec nomine nec re Petri, vel Petræ sint, & fidei meritum præ aliis , quod Petrum Petram fecisse, Bellarminus ait,non habent , sed demum postquam fundamenta Ecclesiæ facta sint,mutari finguntur multi per totam vitam pessimi, quidam in ipsa morte Athei,sine quo Rectoratu Ecclesia subsistere potest, & cum quo, si spiritualis gratia desit, esse nequit. Verùm tertiò ratione spiritualis gratiæ sive fidei per confessionem ostensæ, quò etiam dubio procul respexit Erasmus in Schol. in Hieron. dicens : Non super Roma, arbitror, ædificata est Ecclesia, nam fieri potest,ut Roma denegaret, sed super illam fidem, quam Petrus professus est. Sed illa gratia,fides & confessio rursus non potest spectari & Petra dici, sive appellationis hujus fundamentum, quatenus in Petro fuit, Virtus Petri, nam in Petro imperfecta valde fuit, & immediate posthac gravissimum errorem & tempore passionis foedissimam abnegationem admisit, & in multis, qui Petri Successores, & post eum Petrae, fundamenta Ecclesiae esse volunt, plane non est, & illa quidem Petro prodesse, caeterum Ecclesiam sustentare non potest, cum justus ex fide sua vivere debeat, & cuivis dictum sit; Si confiteris ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & credis in corde tuo, quod Deus eum e mortuis resuscitaverit, salvus eris; Igitur intelligitur illud spiritualis gratiae, fidei & confessionis donum, (favet hoc rursus quarta expositioni) quod Ecclesiae membra ita habent, ut per illud talia sint, & habeantur, & Deo placeant, & Satanae resistant, & mundum vincant; quod denuo non per ullam virtutem communem ullorum hominum fit, cum illi effectus hominum viribus longe majores sint, sed totum dependet a Christo, quem juxta secundam expositionem, & Petrus confessus, & a quo, quod ipsa impudentia non audet negare, denominatus erat, & omnes confiteri, & Authorem salutis suae agnoscere, & in eo reperiri, & in eo salvari debent, Filio Dei viventis, qui est Petra salutis omnibus ad eum confugientibus, & confessores suos in mundo habet & habebit, & tandem de omnibus hostibus suis gloriose triumphabit. Sic igitur comprehendimus Petrum aliosque Apostolos & fideles fundamenta ministerialia, fidei confessionem instrumentale, Christum reale. Et modo quis illa nobiscum agnoscat, quam, vel quas caeterum, expositionem, vel expositiones praeferat, haud multum interereit, cum omnia in idem recidant. Et certe nullum ex dictis per Petram sine respectu proximo ad reliqua omnia intelligi potest; Quare etiam S. Patres iidem pro diversis expositionibus allegari solent. Interim diversae illorum hac etiam in parte expositiones & loquendi formulae ostendere possunt sufficienter, partim quam difficile sit, illorum cognoscere sententias, partim, quam non illi etiam ob sententiarum differentias pro fidei regula haberi possint.
units.tr: XIV. But these four explanations should not be separated too much. They are in some way subordinate to one another, and they agree well together. For according to the first explanation, that confession of Peter is understood, which he had made in the name of all, so that it is permitted to call all the companions of the same confession, the Apostles above all, as well as the speaking Peter, a rock. But Peter, according to the third explanation, was a rock not indeed by reason of human nature, to which those majestic praises by no means apply, since it is corrupt and alien to the life of God; nor was it because of that which Christ had praised him as blessed for, namely that he had not revealed it; nor, as the Papists wish, by reason of the supreme and absolute rule of the universal Church. This rule is especially disputed, and indeed it is contrary to the ordinance of Christ. It is supposed that Peter held it for only a few years, and the Scriptures mention no successors to it, and those who want to hold it are neither Peter nor a rock, either in name or in fact. They do not have the merit of faith above others, which Bellarmine says made Peter a rock; but many wicked men, some even atheists at death, are imagined to change only after the foundations of the Church have been laid. The Church can exist without this rule, and with it, if spiritual grace is lacking, it cannot exist. But thirdly, by reason of spiritual grace or faith shown through confession, which Erasmus undoubtedly had in view in his Scholia on Jerome, saying: I think the Church was built not upon Rome, for Rome could deny it, but upon that faith which Peter professed. But that grace, faith and confession cannot again be regarded as a rock, or as the foundation named by this appellation, insofar as the power of Peter was in Peter. For in Peter it was very imperfect, and immediately afterwards he committed a most grievous error and, at the time of the passion, a most shameful denial. And in many of those who want to be the successors of Peter, and after him rocks, the foundations of the Church, it plainly is not present. Faith benefits Peter himself, but it cannot sustain the Church, since the righteous shall live by his faith, and it has been said to everyone: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved (Romans 10:9). Therefore that gift of spiritual grace, faith and confession is understood (this again favours the fourth explanation) which the members of the Church have in such a way that through it they are such, and are regarded as such, and please God, and resist Satan, and overcome the world. This again does not come about through any common power of human beings, since those effects are far greater than human strength; but everything depends on Christ, whom Peter confessed according to the second explanation, and from whom he was named, as even impudence itself does not dare to deny. All must confess him, acknowledge him as the author of their salvation, be found in him and be saved in him: the Son of the living God, who is the rock of salvation for all who flee to him, who has and will have his confessors in the world, and who at last will triumph gloriously over all his enemies. Thus we understand Peter and the other Apostles and the faithful as ministerial foundations, the confession of faith as instrumental, and Christ as real. Now, whether someone acknowledges these things with us, or which explanation or explanations he prefers, does not matter much, since all come to the same thing. And certainly nothing said of the Rock can be understood without close reference to all the rest. Therefore the same Fathers are usually cited for different explanations. Meanwhile, their different explanations and forms of speech in this matter can sufficiently show how difficult it is to know their opinions, and how, because of their differences of opinion, they cannot be taken as the rule of faith.

units.la: XV. Qualiscunque autem ex expositionibus datis praeferatur, nondum ideo cum Monarchicis sentitur.
units.tr: XV. However any of the explanations given above is preferred, one does not thereby agree with the Monarchists.

units.la: Audiamus de eo porro Doctissimum du Pin: His de loci hujus expositione praemissis, ait, inquirendum, quo pacto & qualis inde Primatus Petri posset colligi. Ex prima & secunda expositione nulla fere Petri supra caeteros Apostolos praerogativa colligitur; nam ex iis minime sequitur, Petrum esse fundamentum Ecclesiae, imo id vel Christo, vel confessioni & fidei, quam emiserat Petrus, trus, adaptatur. In tertia expositione Petrum fateri oportet esse fundamentum Ecclesia; sed inde non videtur sequi, eum Apostolis omnibus superiorem fuisse, cùm ex quarta expositione constet, idem de omnibus Apostolis dictum &c. En igitur Catholicorum hîc consensum! Tantúsne ille, ut soli, Erasmus, Lutherus, Calvinus sententias ab illa, quæ Petrum Monarcham facit, diversas tueantur? Quàm parùm hîc de ulla Monarchia etiam Petri, nedum Paparum? Quàm multùm verba Christi differunt ab his: Tu es Petrus, & Tibi promitto principatum, & tu eris Papa, Princeps & Monarcha, & regnabis Romæ cum omnibus, qui te sequentur, Urbis illius Episcopis? Quàm ineptè Christi verba exponuntur ita, ut; edificare Ecclesiam; explicetur per; committere regimen; & super hanc Petram, per; Petro atque Successoribus ejus Romanis!
units.tr: Let us hear further from the most learned du Pin on this point. Having laid out these things about the explanation of this passage, he says, we must inquire in what way, and of what kind, a primacy of Peter could be inferred from it. From the first and second explanations almost no pre-eminence of Peter over the other apostles is inferred, for it does not at all follow from them that Peter is the foundation of the Church; rather, this is applied either to Christ, or to the confession and faith which Peter had made. In the third explanation we must admit that Peter is the foundation of the Church, but it does not seem to follow from this that he was superior to all the apostles, since from the fourth explanation it is clear that the same was said of all the apostles, etc. Behold, then, the consensus of the Papists here! Is it so great that only Erasmus, Luther and Calvin defend opinions different from that which makes Peter a monarch? How little is said here of any monarchy even of Peter, let alone of the popes! How far do Christ's words differ from these: You are Peter, and to you I promise the principate, and you will be the Pope, Prince and Monarch, and you will reign at Rome over all who follow you, the bishops of that city? How absurdly Christ's words are explained thus: to build the Church is explained as to commit governance; and upon this rock as upon Peter and his Roman successors!

units.la: SECTIO QUARTA, In qua, Invaliditas argumentorum Pontificiorum pro Electione Petri ad talem Pontificatum, instituto examine loci Matth. XVI. 19. porrò ostenditur.
units.tr: SECTION FOUR, in which the invalidity of the Papists' arguments for Peter's election to such a pontificate is further shown, by a close examination of Matth. XVI. 19.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Verborum posteriorum ex Matth. XVI. Et tibi dabo Claves &c. examen incipit. II. Claves tantùm promittuntur; III. Promittuntur Petro; IV. Sed non soli, quod tamen sine periculo admittere possemus; V. Quomodo etiam aliis; explicatur, atque ita Doctiss. du Pin, ita Patres apud eum, & alios, maximè autem apud Doct. Launojum, cujus testimonia adducuntur, sentire; VI. Confirmatur primò ex eo, quòd verba sunt quasi responsoria ad Confessionem communi nomine editam; VII. Occurritur exceptionibus Bellarminianis; VIII. Atque respondetur ad distinctionem, dum Cardinalis contendit, historicè, non parabolicè Petrum hîc Ecclesiam repraesentâsse; IX. Ostenditur contrà eundem, Primatum talem, neque in repraesentatione, neque in ipsa Clavium promissione involvi, & neque ex accurata Petri in praecedentibus descriptione, neque etiam ex sequentibus verbis ad Petrum directis: Vade post me &c. probari posse; X. Neque etiam ex eo, quòd praesentibus reliquis hîc sermonem Christus ad Petrum solum expresse direxit; XI. Confirmatur secundò ex eo, quòd idem Matth. XVIII. 18. aliis dictum fuit; Neque enim verba: Tibi dabo Claves regni coelorum; quæ tantùm Matth. XVI. occurrunt, distinctam potestatem continent; XII. Quod ex ipso Bellarmino contra Cajetanum, MaldoMaldonatum, Stapletonum, Baronium ostenditur; propositâ eorum sententiâ; XIII. Quam Bellarminus refutat; XIV. Atque ita nobis arma contrà se suppeditat valida, licèt infirmare ea conetur; XV. Confirmatur tertiò ex eo, quòd Ioh. XX. v. 21. eadem potestas data fuit Apostolis omnibus; Non obstante exceptione Bellarmini, quæ proponitur; XVI. Refutatur; XVII. Conclusiones Doct. du Pin ratione verborum illorum posteriorum. XVIII. Quibus additur conclusio Authoris, ex Bellarmini explicatione horum verborum Matth. XVI. 19. manifestum esse, priora quoque ab ipso inconvenienter nimis arctè ad Petrum restringi. XIX. Ad Conclusionem quartam Doctissimi du Pin aliquid annotatur. XX. Discordia inter Bellarminum ab una, Turrecrematam & Iacobatium ab altera parte, respectu quaestionis: An Apostoli à Christo immediatè, vel à Petro clavium potestatem acceperint? XXI. Dissensus Monarchicorum in aliis quoque; XXII. Defectio ab Orthodoxia in explicatione perversa illius potestatis clavium.
units.tr: I. The examination of the later words of Matth. XVI, "And I will give you the keys" etc., begins. II. Only the keys are promised; III. they are promised to Peter; IV. but not to him alone, although we could admit this without danger; V. it is explained how they are also given to others, and so the most learned du Pin, the Fathers cited by him and others, and especially the learned Launoy, whose testimonies are adduced, hold; VI. it is first confirmed from the fact that the words are like a response to the Confession made in the name of all; VII. the objections of Bellarmine are met; VIII. and the distinction is answered, when the Cardinal contends that Peter here represented the Church historically, not figuratively; IX. it is shown, against the same man, that such a primacy is involved neither in the representation nor in the promise of the keys itself, and cannot be proved either from the careful description of Peter in what precedes, or from the following words addressed to Peter, "Get behind me" etc.; X. nor from the fact that Christ addressed his speech expressly to Peter alone while the others were present; XI. it is confirmed secondly from the fact that the same words of Matth. XVIII. 18 were said to the others; for the words "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," which occur only in Matth. XVI, do not contain a separate power; XII. which is shown from Bellarmine himself against Cajetan, Maldonatus, Stapleton and Baronius, with their opinion set out; XIII. which Bellarmine refutes; XIV. and so he supplies us with strong weapons against himself, although he tries to weaken them; XV. it is confirmed thirdly from the fact that the same power was given to all the Apostles in John XX. 21, notwithstanding the objection of Bellarmine that is put forward; XVI. this is refuted; XVII. the conclusions of du Pin from the sense of those later words; XVIII. to which is added the author's conclusion that, from Bellarmine's explanation of these words of Matth. XVI. 19, it is clear that he has also restricted the earlier words to Peter far too narrowly; XIX. something is noted on the fourth conclusion of the most learned du Pin; XX. the disagreement between Bellarmine on one side, and Torquemada and Jacobatius on the other, on the question: did the Apostles receive the power of the keys from Christ immediately, or from Peter? XXI. the disagreement of the Monarchists among themselves on other matters too; XXII. the departure from orthodoxy in the perverse explanation of that power of the keys.

units.la: I. VIdeamus autem, an Monarchicis magis faveat altera loci Matth. XVI. pars ista: Et tibi dabo Claves regni Cœlorum, & quicquid ligaveris in terra, ligatum erit in cœlis, & quicquid solveris in terra, solutum erit in cœlis. De hac loci parte altera Emanuel à Schelstrate fatetur, majorem esse difficultatem circa illius sensum, quàm prioris de Petra. Non igitur exiguam hîc experientur difficultatem. Videamus. Non autem fert animus, locum hunc hîc plenissimè, quoad fieri posset, exponere, & quid per illam Clavium potestatem, per illud solvere & ligare intelligatur, & quomodo hæc in Ecclesia fiant, accuratius annotare, Pontificiorumque hac in parte errores omnes prolixè taxare; Nec etiam illud instituti nostri ratio exigit; Sed tantùm ea hîc spectabimus, quæ ad refutanda Monarchicorum ex hoc loco argumenta sufficere poterunt; Sufficere autem poterit, probè indicâsse præcipuè, cui hîc & alibi Claves Regni Cœlorum promissæ & datæ sint.
units.tr: I. Let us see whether the other part of Matth. XVI, namely "And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven," favours the Monarchists more. Emmanuel à Schelstrate admits that the difficulty over its meaning is greater than that of the earlier part about the rock. So we shall not meet a small difficulty here. Let us see. I do not, however, feel inclined to expound this passage here as fully as possible, nor to note accurately what is understood by that power of the keys, by that loosing and binding, and how these things are done in the Church, nor to list at length all the errors of the Papists in this respect; nor does the plan of our work require it. We shall look only at what will suffice to refute the Monarchists' arguments drawn from this passage. It will be enough to have shown clearly, above all, to whom here and elsewhere the keys of the kingdom of heaven are promised and given.

units.la: II. Claves hîc tantùm promissas, non etiam datas esse, evidentissimè apparet. Non enim dicitur: Et do tibi Claves &c. Sed: Et dabo tibi Claves &c. Ut à veritate planè alienum ac licentiæ pictoriæ Poeticæque adscribendum sit, quòd in picturarum quodam volumine, quod inscribitur: Non recedet volumen legis ab ore tuo; Romæ An. 1577. excusò, non tantùm Christus Claves Petro eique soli tradens depingitur, sed & versus additur: Pastorum Princeps esto, Tibi jus datur uni Claudere cœlestes & reserare fores.
units.tr: II. That the keys are here only promised, not also given, appears most plainly. For it is not said, "And I give you the keys" etc., but "And I will give you the keys" etc. So it must be attributed to a pictorial and poetic licence, far from the truth, that in a certain volume of pictures, entitled "The book of the law shall not depart from your mouth," printed at Rome in 1577, Christ is depicted handing the keys to Peter alone, and a verse is added: "Be the prince of shepherds; to you alone is given the right to shut the heavenly gates and to open them."

units.la: Quà pictura, quoque versu si lis decidenda foret, jam certè contra nos manifestè pronunciatum & extra controversiam esset, Petrum saltem vi hujus loci ad Monarchiam Ecclesiæ & Pontificatum, qualem ei primò attribuunt, à Christo electum & solenniter institutum esse. Ast & à Pictore, & à Poeta ad Scripturam & venerandam traditionem attento rationis scrutinio consulendas appellamus.
units.tr: If the dispute were to be settled by that picture and that verse, then surely it would already have been declared clearly against us and beyond controversy that Peter, at least by the force of this passage, was chosen and solemnly instituted by Christ for the Monarchy of the Church and the pontificate in the form in which they first attribute it to him. But we appeal from the painter and the poet to Scripture and to venerable tradition, to be consulted with a careful scrutiny of reason.

units.la: III. Docet nos vel primus loci aspectus, hîc Petro aliquid promitti, & quando dubitatur à multis, utrum Petrus in priori hujus loci parte per Petram, cui inædificanda erat Ecclesia, intelligatur, quia quidem dictum: Et super hanc Petram; sed non: Et super te Petram; nomini tamen dubitare licet, utrum hîc Petro Claves promissæ sint, cùm apertè Christus dicat: Tibi dabo Claves &c. Ut proin Bellarminus non nisi aerem verberet, dum ita ferè argumentationem suam instituit, ac si negaremus, Petro in Textu Claves regni cœlorum promissas esse.
units.tr: III. The first look at the passage shows us that something is promised to Peter here. And although many doubt whether in the earlier part of this passage Peter is meant by the rock on which the Church was to be built, because it is said "And upon this rock" and not "And upon you, rock", yet one may doubt whether the keys are promised to Peter here, since Christ plainly says "I will give you the keys" etc. So Bellarmine merely beats the air when he builds his argument almost as if we denied that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were promised to Peter in the text.

units.la: IV. Ast multùm differunt hæ duæ quæstiones; Utrum Claves promissæ sint? Et; utrum ei soli promissæ sint? Ad priorem unanimi consensu affirmando respondetur: quod ad posteriorem, Pontificii affirmativam tenent, nos negativam sententiam. Et quidem longè hîc à periculo abest nostra causa, quæ nihil amitteret, si in Textu illo soli Petro Claves promissæ essent, quando vel ex adversariorum concessione constat, eas, vel potiùs ea quæ per eas denotari solent, alibi aliis promitti, imò cui nihil etiam decederet, si ne quidem alibi aliis hæc promissa forent, dum eâdem certitudine cognoscimus, ea reapse aliis unâ cum Petro collata; Quorum ultimum etiam sine prioribus argumentationem ex verbis Christi pro constitutione Monarchæ satis refellere potest. Verùm omninò pertendimus, etiam hîc claves aliis & non tantùm Petro promitti, & verba Origenis: Hæc velut ad Petrum dicta, sunt omnibus communia, ut & verba Doctissimi de Dominis l. c. 7. § 3. nostra facimus: Monstri simile sit, negare hoc loco Dominum cum ipsamet Petri (persona) loqui, eique promittere claves, quas postea etiam ipsi infallibiliter concesserit; Sed monstri adhuc fortasse majoris simile fuerit ad Petrum solum hanc promissionem ipsiusque executionem adeò arctare, ut claves Apostolis aliis neque fuerint promissa à Christo, neque data.
units.tr: IV. But these two questions differ greatly: whether the keys were promised, and whether they were promised to him alone. To the first we answer with one voice, Yes. As to the second, the Papists hold the affirmative and we the negative. And indeed our cause is far from danger here, for it would lose nothing even if the keys in that text were promised to Peter alone; since it is clear, even from the concession of our opponents, that they, or rather what they are usually taken to denote, are promised to others elsewhere. Indeed, our cause would lose nothing even if these things were not promised to others elsewhere, since we know with the same certainty that they were in fact conferred on others together with Peter. The latter point alone, even without the former, can sufficiently refute the argument from Christ's words for the institution of a monarch. But we insist absolutely that here too the keys are promised to others and not to Peter only, and we make our own the words of Origen: "These things, spoken as if to Peter, are common to all"; and the words of the most learned de Dominis (l. c. 7. § 3.): "It would be monstrous to deny that the Lord here speaks with Peter himself as a person, and promises him the keys, which he later also infallibly granted to him; but it would perhaps be even more monstrous to restrict this promise and its execution so closely to Peter alone that the keys were neither promised nor given by Christ to the other Apostles."

units.la: V. Nimirum ita sentimus, Christum unâ cum Petro etiam reliquis Apostolis, Ecclesiæ Christianæ quasi primitiis, claves hîc & alibi expressiùs fidelibus omnibus totīque Ecclesiæ promisisse.
units.tr: V. Assuredly we think this way: that Christ, together with Peter, promised the keys here and elsewhere, more expressly, to all believers and to the whole Church, and to the other Apostles as the first fruits of the Christian Church.

units.la: Sed non soli ita sentimus, nec est opinio ista χῷὲς ἡ σεύχῷες, aut nobiscum, aut cum Luthero & Calvino, quod Bellarminus l. c. c.12. somniat, nata. Doctissimus du Pin & hic veritatis testis est, dum ita ad posteriorem, in qua consideranda jam versamur, loci partem transit. Atque id, nimirum Petrum quidem primum & praecipuum futurum fuisse, sed non ei, quod minimè cum Bellarmino colligere liceat, totius Ecclesiæ regimen praesertim circa fidem commissum esse;) aliunde confirmatur ex sequentibus Christi verbis, quibus exponit id, quod dixerat, aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Tibi, inquit, dabo claves regni coelorum, & quodcunque ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum & in coelis. Hanc enim potestatem clavium, quam Christus Petro hic promittit, isdem deinde verbis omnibus omninò Apostolis promittit, Matth.XVIII. & deinceps cunctis largitur, Matth.XVIII. & Joh.XX. Illi igitur oppidò falluntur, qui soli Petro datas claves esse autumant; At non ita antiqui, qui unanimi consensu tradunt, claves istas in persona Petri toti Ecclesia datas. Subjungit testimonia Tertulliani, Cypriani, Hieronymi, Optati, Gaudentii Brixiensis, Ambrosii, (qui id centies inculcet;) Augustini, & (ex quo pauca attulisse satis sit;) S. Leonis, Fulgentii Augustini discipuli, Theophylacti, Eucherii, Bedæ, Rabani, Lyrani, Hincmari, Odonis, Petri Blesensis, aitque, alios innumeros idem testari, quos referre longius foret. Videri possunt eadem loca expressa & à responsionibus Bellarmini vindicata, contra testimonia, quæ pro se ex Patribus allegat, refutata apud de Dominis lib. c. c.7. Witackerum lib.c. c. 5. Forbes.Instruct. Historico-Theolog. lib.16. cap.3. §. 5. &c. alios, sed vel maximè apud Doctiss. Launojum qui postquam T.2. Epist.5. de subjecto clavium ex Doctoribus antiquis egit prolixissimè, ostendens, id non esse personam Petri, sed ipsammet sub persona Petri Ecclesiam, hanc traditionem à parum sinceris Bellarimini impetitionibus suscepit defendendam, in antecessum de hoc suo labore observans, eo nihil esse facilius, hoc insuper addito, Authoris verba simpliciter referre, idem esse ac simpliciter confutare, usque adeò veritati & æquitati ea adversari. Postea sententiam Synodi, ut vocat, Smalcaldica Parisiensium sententiam esse dicit, claves nimirum principaliter & immediatè Ecclesiæ datas esse, quæ per traditionem à S. Patribus (longa serie recensitis:) derivata & illorum articulis definita sit. Subjungit; Bellarminum ut Parisiensium sententiam tacitus infamet, & sua doctrina novitatem multet, Gorgoneíque capitis adspectu horribiliorem efficiat, illud ascribere hominibus, qui seorsim à Romanis per Religionem sentiant. Heu prisca Christianorum integritas! (exclamat) apud quos ex fide persona, non ex persona fides probatur: Et paulò post: Augustini dissimulat testimonia, nonnulla tamen refert, & hac minùs expressa & sæpiùs truncata, quò hac facilius excogitatas in Velatica Turrecremata & Cajetani Academia distinctiones admittant. Et porrò; Bellarminus Augustini doctrinam in Lutheri & Calvini os intrudit, ut inde prodeat virulenta, & de haereticorum nomine ac origine censeatur! O consilium perversum! Profectò mihi nunquam persuadebit, hoc artificii genere defensum iri Ecclesiam, vel Augustinum liberaliter tractari, cùm doctrina illius invidiosa redditur, quòd ea haeretici vel utantur, vel abutantur. Tum Bellarminus non parùm impingit in fidei Tridentinæ regulam, seu professionem, qua tenetur quisque Scripturam S. juxta Patrum unanimem consensum accipere & interpretari. Sacramentum hoc insuper habet; quia etiam è tanta nube Patrum ne duos quidem adfert, qui locum accipiunt, ut in illius opinione accipiendus est. Tum demum, quando certa quædam testimonia Patrum edit, hæc ad sacrorum canonum normam & ad Ecclesiastica disciplinæ solem effugiunt, & Authori suo vehementer incommodant. Item. Facessant ergo Joh. Turrecremata, Dominici Jacobatii, Th. Cajetani, Rob. Bellarmini & sectatorum præstigiæ, quibus, quod sole clarius est, inobscurare conantur. Augustini libros non evolverunt, nec loca cum locis contulerunt, ut veram S. Doctoris sententiam expiscarentur, inquirerent, agnoscerent. Unum aut alterum locum è reliquo contextu avulsum legerunt, & examinandum sibi sumpserunt, ut B. Augustino de sua, non ut sibi de B. Augustini sententia accommodarent, in summa B. Augustinum pro discipulo, non pro Magistro habuerunt. Hoc vitium in Turrecremata, Jacobatio, Cajetano, Bellarmino & sectatoribus notâsse, illos confutâsse est. Si tamen, cùm ita se erga B. Augustinum gesserint, digni sunt, qui confutentur. Et iterum: Bellarminus sibi canit, non Augustino, cujus loca non refert integra, ne in Doctori Sancto illata deprehendatur, sed, quod adhuc indignius est & insignius, Aug. doctrinam ex ore Lutheri & Calvini prodeuntem inducit, ut illius minuatur authoritas, & velut suspecta reddatur, aut certè cavenda proponatur.
units.tr: But we are not alone in this view, and this opinion is neither new nor peculiar to us or to Luther and Calvin, as Bellarmine dreams in l. c. c.12. The very learned du Pin is also a witness to the truth here, when he moves on to the latter part of the passage, which we are now considering. He says that Peter was indeed to be the first and chief, but that the governance of the whole Church, especially as regards the faith, was not committed to him, as Bellarmine wrongly infers. This is confirmed from the words of Christ that follow, in which he explains what he had said, "I will build my Church." "To you," he says, "I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven also." For the power of the keys that Christ here promises to Peter, he later promises to all the Apostles in the same words, Matt. 18, and to all of them in the same way, Matt. 18 and John 20. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who maintain that the keys were given to Peter alone. The ancient writers, however, did not think so; with one voice they hand down that those keys were given to the whole Church in the person of Peter. He adds the testimonies of Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, Optatus, Gaudentius of Brescia, Ambrose (who repeats it a hundred times), Augustine, and (to name only a few) St. Leo, Fulgentius, a disciple of Augustine, Theophylact, Eucherius, Bede, Rabanus, Lyra, Hincmar, Odo, and Peter of Blois, and he says that countless others bear the same witness, too many to list. The same passages may be seen, set out and defended against Bellarmine's replies, and refuted against the testimonies he cites from the Fathers in his favour, in de Dominis lib. c. c.7., Witaker lib. c. c. 5., Forbes Instruct. Historico-Theolog. lib. 16, cap. 3, §5, etc., and others; but most of all in the most learned Launoy, who, after T. 2, Epist. 5. treated at great length the subject of the keys from the ancient teachers, showing that it is not the person of Peter but the Church itself, under the person of Peter. He undertook to defend this tradition against the not very sincere attacks of Bellarmine, observing beforehand about this his labour that nothing is easier, adding this besides: to report an author's words plainly is the same as to refute him plainly, so greatly do those things oppose truth and fairness. Afterwards he says that the view of the so-called Smalcald Synod is the view of the Parisians, namely that the keys were given principally and immediately to the Church, and that this was handed down by tradition from the holy Fathers (recounted in a long series) and was defined by their articles. He goes on: Bellarmine, wishing silently to discredit the Parisian view and to fine its doctrine for novelty, and to make it more horrible than the sight of the Gorgon's head, ascribes it to men who think differently in religion from the Romanists. Alas for the old integrity of the Christians! (he exclaims), among whom faith is proved by the person, not the person by faith. And a little later: He conceals the testimonies of Augustine; yet he reports some of them, and these less clearly and often cut short, so that the distinctions devised in Turrecremata's Velatica and the Academy of Cajetan can be admitted more easily. And further: Bellarmine thrusts Augustine's doctrine into the mouths of Luther and Calvin, so that it may come forth tainted, and be counted as coming from the name and origin of heretics! O perverse design! Truly he will never persuade me that the Church is defended by this kind of trickery, or that Augustine is treated generously, when his doctrine is made odious because heretics either use it or abuse it. Then Bellarmine not a little offends against the rule of faith of Trent, or the profession by which each person is bound to take and interpret Holy Scripture according to the unanimous consent of the Fathers. Moreover he has this fault: though from so great a cloud of Fathers he does not bring forward even two who take the passage as it must be taken on his view. Finally, when he does put forward certain testimonies of the Fathers, these flee from the standard of the sacred canons and the sun of ecclesiastical discipline, and cause great embarrassment to their author. Likewise: Let then the tricks of John Turrecremata, Domenico Jacobazzi, Thomas Cajetan, Robert Bellarmine and their followers depart, by which they try to obscure what is clearer than the sun. They have not unrolled Augustine's books, nor compared passage with passage, so as to draw out, inquire into and recognize the true opinion of the holy Doctor. They have read one or another passage torn from the rest of the text, and have taken it upon themselves to examine it, so as to adapt it to St. Augustine's view of himself rather than his view of them; in short, they have regarded Augustine as a pupil, not as a master. To have noted this fault in Turrecremata, Jacobazzi, Cajetan, Bellarmine and their followers is to have refuted them. Yet if, having so behaved towards St. Augustine, they are worthy of being refuted... And again: Bellarmine sings to himself, not to Augustine, whose passages he does not give whole, lest they be detected as being brought against the holy Doctor; but, what is even more unworthy and more striking, he brings in the doctrine of Augustine as it comes from the mouths of Luther and Calvin, so that its authority may be diminished and it may be made as it were suspect, or at any rate set forth as something to be avoided.

units.la: VI. Sed videamus, quàm bene post tot Viros in Ecclesia citiùs, seriùs, magis & minùs celebres ita sentiamus. Et quidem sententiam illorum & nostram primò juvare contendimus illud, quòd verba Christi hæc quasi responsoria sunt ad confessionem à Petro cæterorum etiam nomine editam. Id quod & jam ex parte probatum est, & porrò probandum. Denuò illud colligimus ex interrogatione Christi ad omnes directa, ex eo, quòd nullus alius pro more, Joh. VI.68. Act.II.14. respondit, nec tamen concipi potest, cæteros simul interrogatos aut superbos, aut perversos, aut saltem officii sui immemores fuisse, & postea Christus non, quid reliqui de se sentiant, sciscitari perrexit, nec etiam tacentes reprehendit, nec Petro, sed omnibus, ne cuiquam dicerent, ipsum esse Jesum Christum, interdixit.
units.tr: VI. But let us see how well we hold this view, after so many men in the Church, earlier and later, more and less famous. And indeed we contend that both their view and ours is helped, first, by the fact that the words of Christ are a kind of response to the confession which Peter made also in the name of the others. This has already been proved in part, and is to be proved further. Again we infer it from Christ's question addressed to all, from the fact that no one else answered, as was the custom (John 6:68; Acts 2:14); and yet it cannot be conceived that the others, when questioned together, were proud, perverse, or at least forgetful of their duty. Afterwards Christ did not go on asking what the rest thought of him, nor did he rebuke those who kept silent; and he forbade not Peter but all of them to tell anyone that he himself was Jesus Christ.

units.la: VII. Quis igitur ei hanc pro caeteris respondendi provinciam imposuit? Est interrogatio Bellarmini.
units.tr: VII. Who, then, assigned him this task of answering on behalf of the others? This is Bellarmine's question.

units.la: Possemus multò magis quaerere, quis illi imposuit provinciam pro Pontificibus Romanis respondendi? Illorúmne Legatus aut Vicarius fuit? Sed respectu Apostolorum: Illi ipsi, nisi Petrum temerè & extra ordinem locutum esse temerè judicare velimus, qui aliás ei istam hic provinciam imposuerunt Apostoli, & licèt illud non expresse memoretur, facilè tamen concipi potest, vel nutu factum esse, imposuit ei quoque hanc provinciam Zelus & fervor ejus singularis, hinc à Chrysostomo apud Bellarminum, gnarus nimirum de consensu reliquorum, confestim prosiluisse & prævenisse dicitur. At, excipit Bellarminus, quando pro aliis respondit, pro aliis etiam se respondere indicavit dicens. Nos credimus & cognovimus. Respondemus: Non necessariam fuisse illam formulam hic, ut nimirum explicaret actum credendi & personas credentes, ut nec de seipso dixit; Ego credo; partim, quia aliàs cognosci potuit omnium nomine responderi, partim quia jam antea illâ ipsâ formulâ, hanc communem omnium fidem esse, testatus erat. Et quòd hic non, ut Joh. VI. Judam Christus excipit, cui Bellarminus porrò insistit, illud pariter non necessarium fuit, cùm & ille unâ cum reliquis confiteri potuerit & persuasionem forsan etiam, quòd Jesus sit Filius Dei viventis, habuerit, & Christus Joh. VI. non tam eum à confessione excluserit, quàm verò sceleus ejus exaggeraverit, suo tempore patrandum, Diabolum eum vocando, eò quòd prodituros erat, quem Filium Dei tum per os Petri appellaverat. Haud minùs obest, quòd Bellarminus contra communionem confessionis allegat revelationem patris cœlestis. Nam illa non excludit consultationem omnem, cùm per medium consultationis & seriae ad dicta Prophetarum & facta Christi attentionis, accedente Dei gratiâ, proin non à carne & sanguine, sed revelante Deo, notitiam suam quoad hoc accepisse, & Petrum, & caeteros verisimile sit, & si vel immediata & extraordinaria revelatio cuivis aut Petro tantùm obtigisset, tamen de ea post inter se conferre potuissent; Non autem Petro soli istam revelationem lationem obtigisse, cateros istam veritatem nescivisse, quod Bellarminus nos docet. Jam enim crediderunt multi, inquit ipsemet, c.10. Christum esse Filium Dei. B. Virgo, Simeon, Zacharias, Joannes Baptista, Apostoli & discipuli cateri. Et certè parùm honorificè de Apostolis sentit, qui eos hîc ignaros fingit. Quid? Annon Johannes, non Jacobus, non Andreas, non quisquam alius hoc sciverit? Annon se invenisse Messiam, & se Messiæ discipulos esse crediderunt, dixerunt? Annon Messiam Filium Dei agnoverunt? Quin Nathanaël jam antè, Philippo præsente & audiente, professus est idem, quod post Petrus, Christum nimirum esse Filium illum Dei Joh.1.50. Imò annon agnoverint Apostoli illud, quod confitentes Dæmones ante audierant, quod ipsi vectores & nautæ agnoscere coacti fuerant? Quod Petrus, ipso Bellarmino urgente, antea se omnes credere & agnovisse nomine omnium professus fuerat?
units.tr: We might ask much more pointedly who assigned him the task of answering on behalf of the Roman Pontiffs. Was he their legate or vicar? But consider the matter in relation to the Apostles. Unless we are willing to judge rashly that Peter spoke rashly and out of turn, the Apostles themselves, who on other occasions gave him this role here, may have assigned it to him. Even though this is not expressly recorded, it can easily be imagined that it was done by a nod, or that his singular zeal and fervour assigned him this role as well. Hence, according to Chrysostom, as quoted by Bellarmine, knowing of course the agreement of the rest, he is said to have leapt forward at once and anticipated them. But, Bellarmine objects, when he answered on behalf of the others, he also showed that he was answering for the others too, by saying: We believe and have come to know. We reply: that formula was not necessary here, namely to express the act of believing and the persons believing, just as he did not say of himself, I believe. This was partly because it could be known that he answered in the name of all, and partly because he had already declared, by that very formula, that this faith was common to all. And as for the fact that here Christ does not except Judas, as in John 6, on which Bellarmine insists further, that too was equally unnecessary. Judas could have confessed together with the rest, and perhaps also had the conviction that Jesus is the Son of the living God. And in John 6 Christ did not so much exclude him from the confession as aggravate his wickedness, which he was to carry out at his appointed time, by calling him a devil, because he was going to betray the one whom he had then called the Son of God through Peter's mouth. Bellarmine's appeal against the common confession to the revelation of the heavenly Father is no less unhelpful. For that revelation does not exclude all consultation. It is likely that Peter and the others received their knowledge of this matter through the medium of consultation and serious attention to the words of the Prophets and the deeds of Christ, with God's grace assisting, and so not from flesh and blood, but with God revealing it. And even if an immediate and extraordinary revelation had fallen to Peter alone or to anyone else, they could still afterwards have compared notes with one another about it. But that this revelation fell to Peter alone, and that the others did not know this truth, is what Bellarmine teaches us. For he himself says, c.10: Many had already believed that Christ is the Son of God: the Blessed Virgin, Simeon, Zechariah, John the Baptist, the Apostles and the other disciples. And certainly he thinks rather meanly of the Apostles when he pretends here that they were ignorant. What? Did John not know it, nor James, nor Andrew, nor anyone else? Did they not believe and say that they had found the Messiah, and that they were the disciples of the Messiah? Did they not recognise the Messiah as the Son of God? Indeed Nathanael, earlier, in the presence and hearing of Philip, professed the same thing that Peter did afterwards, namely that Christ is that Son of God (John 1:50). Indeed, did the Apostles not recognise that which the demons had confessed and which the passengers and sailors had been compelled to acknowledge? Did Peter not, at the urging of Bellarmine himself, profess in the name of all that they had all believed and recognised this beforehand?

units.la: VIII. Quoad Ecclesiam totam, fatetur quidem Bellarminus, Petrum ejus personam gessisse, sed historicè, non parabolicè. Doctissimus Launojus lib. c. ita de hac distinctione judicat: Bellarminus collatorum inter se locorum splendorem ferre non potest, tenebras quærit in duobus adverbiis, Historicè, Parabolicè, & à Petro historicè personam Ecclesiæ gestatam esse, recipit; quo nihil est à B. Augustini & caterorum Patrum mente alienius.
units.tr: VIII. As for the whole Church, Bellarmine indeed admits that Peter bore her person, but historically, not parabolically. The most learned Launoy, in the work cited, judges this distinction as follows: Bellarmine cannot bear the brightness of passages compared with one another; he seeks darkness in the two adverbs, historically and parabolically, and accepts that Peter bore the person of the Church historically. Nothing is more alien to the mind of blessed Augustine and the other Fathers.

units.la: Sed admittimus nos, si id tantùm dicere vult Bellarminus, Petrum ita clavium potestatem penes Ecclesiam figurâsse, ut & ipse acceperit (quamvis in explicatione hujus distinctionis accuratior esse potuisset, neque enim Abrahamus duos filios habens Dei personam gessit, neque res figurata semper tempore posterior & adhuc gerenda est, cùm Deus in Abrahamo simul cum semine ejus fœdus inierit, & ubi aliquid figuratur, id eatenus parabolicè fit;) Igitur Petrus etiam accepit claves; Quis negat? Sed in ejus persona etiam Ecclesiam simul suscepisse, & verba hæc æquè ac alia nisi relata ad Ecclesiam, cujus ille in figura personam gestâsse agnoscatur, illustrem intellectum non habere, testatur Augustinus in Psal.108. de quo rectè de Dominis §23. Hebes est, qui non videt, Petrum ab Augustino verè & propriè exui in quibusdam locis Evangelicis & S. Scriptura à persona propria, & induitantùm persona universalis Ecclesia, ut ipsius sit & typus & figura. Non igitur intellexit de constitutione Monarchæ quoad Petrum, quis enim intellectus illustrior esse posset? Sed ita arbitratus est, quod & nos arbitramur, repræsentasse Ecclesiam, cui convenit potestas clavium principaliter ter & in summo gradu, formaliter, in qua semper conservatur, cùm aliâs præcipuum ejus cum Petro, saltem ad tempus interiisset, & cum quovis Papa interire & ipsum potestatis hujus fontem exsiccari sæpe statuere debeant, & eatenus Petro nonnisi materialiter claves promissas esse, quemadmodum Abrahamus quidem formaliter duos filios, sed non istos duos populos, interim tamen etiam formaliter ipsum claves accepisse, partim quatenus unus, imò primus ex figuratis fuerit, partim quia post resurrectionem cum cæteris Apostolis, quando eis dictum : (sicut misit me pater &c.) formalissimè claves acceperit, primus etiam, ut Tertullianus loquitur, claves imbuerit. Illustrat rem simili Illustris de Dominis l. c. § 26. dum ait : Sicuti si Duci Venetorum quis cederet jus & dominium alicujus civitatis, vel Regni, Dux certè accipit, dominium & jus hoc, non sibi soli, sed indirectè, consecutive & inclusivè, (quatenus scilicet ipse quoque unus est ex nobilibus illius Reipublica) (non Monarcha) sed toti nobilitati Venetæ, principaliter & directè, quam totam ille repræsentat. Ita Petrus accepit claves toti Ecclesiæ principaliter & directè, hoc est, omnibus Prælatis ipsius, consecutive & indirectè etiam sibi.
units.tr: But we grant, if Bellarmine means only this, that Peter so figured the power of the keys as belonging to the Church that he himself also received it (although in explaining this distinction he could have been more precise. For Abraham, having two sons, did not bear the person of God, and a figured matter is not always later in time nor still to be carried out, since God entered into covenant with Abraham together with his seed; and where something is figured, it is done in a parabolic manner only so far). Therefore Peter also received the keys. Who denies it? But that in his person he also took up the Church at the same time, and Augustine bears witness in Psalm 108 that these words, like the others, have no clear meaning unless they are referred to the Church, of which he is recognised to have borne the person in a figure. On this point the illustrious de Dominis rightly says (§23): He is dull who does not see that in certain Gospel passages and in Holy Scripture Augustine strips Peter truly and properly of his own person, and clothes him only with the person of the universal Church, so that he is her type and figure. Therefore Augustine did not understand this as the constitution of a monarch in the case of Peter. For what clearer understanding could there be? But he judged, as we also judge, that Peter represented the Church, to which the power of the keys belongs principally and in the highest degree, formally, in whom it is always preserved. Otherwise their principal bond would have perished, at least for a time, and they would have to hold that it perishes with every Pope and that the source of this power is often dried up. To that extent the keys were promised to Peter only materially, just as Abraham indeed had two sons formally, but not those two peoples. Nevertheless, he also received the keys formally, partly in so far as he was one, indeed the first, of those who were figured, and partly because after the resurrection, together with the other Apostles, when it was said to them, (As the Father sent me, etc.), he received the keys most formally, and first, as Tertullian puts it, imbued the keys. The illustrious de Dominis illustrates the matter with a similar example (l.c. §26), when he says: Just as if someone were to cede to the Doge of Venice the right and dominion of some city or kingdom, the Doge certainly receives that dominion and right, not for himself alone, but indirectly, consequentially and inclusively (in so far as he too is one of the nobles of that republic) (not as monarch), but for the whole Venetian nobility, principally and directly, which he represents as a whole. So Peter received the keys for the whole Church, principally and directly, that is, for all her prelates, and consequentially and indirectly for himself too.

units.la: IX. Quòd autem Petrus acceperit claves tanquam jam Primatum habens istum & ob istum Primatum, illud Bellarminus & gratis fingit, & sibi contrariatur. Gratis illud fingit, neque enim talem primatum involvit, vel illud, quod quis aliorum personam repræsentat, cùm & Judas omnium impiorum personas sine tali primatu Augustino repræsentâsse dicatur; vel illud, quòd quis claves accipit, quod satis patet ex confessione ipsa Monarchicorum, quatenus & Apostolis claves promissas & exhibitas esse fatentur, & quæcunque quoad reges in deditione urbium clavium traditio significet, alia etiam significat, ministerialem nimirum curam, etiam, ubi tamen fundamentum suæ argumentationis quærunt, apud Esaj.XXII. ubi clavis domûs David clavem ærarii sub cura præpositi, ingrediendi & egrediendi liberam potestatem habentis denotat, quem locum de Dominis § 11. non nimis à Monarchicis urgeri vult, ne ex hac ipsius allegoria dicaces occasionem sumant obloquendi, & dicendi, jam Pontificis munus & officium totum in eo consistere, ut confletur pecunia 4. Reg. XXII. siquidem velint Pontificem tenere allegoricè locum præpositi domus Davidis, hoc est, quæstoris, ærariique curatoris. Probandum igitur, potiùs illum regium, quàm verò hunc ministerialem clavium usum designari. Nam si argumentari licet : claves alicubi ita accipiuntur. cipiuntur. E. & hîc; pariter argumentari liceret ex Luc. XI. 52. ubi clavis cognitionis, Petrum tantùm scientiam cum clavibus accepisse. Huic certè ministeriali acceptioni etiam favere videtur, quòd Christus verisimiliter ab illo, quod sub lege fiebat, dum Judæi Magistros suos clavium traditione inaugurabantur, similitudinem hanc clavium mutuatus est; neque etiam ex eo, quòd Christus ad solum Petrum, quem accuratè ante descripserat, sermonem suum direxit, & post ei soli dixit: Vade post me; Nam descriptio personae Petri praeter ea, quae nos ultrò damus, nihil planè involvit: & post ea illud: Vade post me: ex quo, malo suo, eundem personae in utroque loco respectum Monarchici probare annituntur, cùm sic etiam Petro tanquam Monarchae Ecclesiae dictum fuisset: Vade &c. Soli Petro sine figura dictum fuit, quia, quod textus docere videtur, proprio motu & sine collatione cum caeteris Apostolis ante institută, Christo passionem dissuadere ausus sit, cùm talis contra ea, quae, prout ostensum est, nomine communi dixerat, dubio procul praecesserit. Et si in altero etiam nomine omnium locutus fuisset, non minùs procul dubio in altero responsum omnes respexisset.
units.tr: IX. But that Peter received the keys as already holding this primacy, and on account of this primacy, Bellarmine both invents without reason and contradicts himself. He invents it without reason, for the reception of the keys does not involve such a primacy. Neither does the fact that someone bears the person of others, since Judas too is said by Augustine to have borne the persons of all the wicked without any such primacy. Nor does the fact that someone receives the keys, which is clear enough from the very confession of the monarchists, since they admit that the keys were promised and delivered to the Apostles too. Whatever the handing over of keys signifies with regard to kings in the surrender of cities, it also signifies something else, namely a ministerial care. They seek the foundation of their argument in Isaiah 22, where the key of the house of David denotes the key of the treasury, which is entrusted to a steward having the free power of going in and out. Concerning this passage de Dominis (§11) wishes that it not be pressed too hard by the monarchists, lest from this allegory of his the scoffers take occasion to object and say that the whole office and duty of the Pontiff already consists in this, that money be melted down (4 Kings 22), if indeed they wish the Pontiff to hold allegorically the place of the steward of the house of David, that is, of the treasurer and keeper of the coffers. It must therefore be proved that the kingly use of the keys is designated rather than this ministerial one. For if we may argue that the keys are taken in one way somewhere, then here too, we could equally argue from Luke 11:52, where the key of knowledge shows that Peter alone received knowledge together with the keys. Certainly this ministerial sense also seems to be favoured by the fact that Christ probably borrowed this likeness of the keys from what was done under the law, when the Jewish teachers were installed by the handing over of keys. Nor does it follow from the fact that Christ addressed his speech to Peter alone, whom he had described carefully beforehand, and afterwards said to him alone: Go behind me. For the description of Peter's person involves nothing at all beyond what we ourselves freely grant. And as for the saying Go behind me, by which the monarchists, to their own harm, strive to prove that in both places Peter's person is in view, it could just as well have been said to Peter as to the monarch of the Church: Go, etc. It was said to Peter alone without a figure because, as the text seems to teach, he presumed on his own initiative, and without consultation with the other Apostles, to dissuade Christ from his passion, although undoubtedly something contrary to what he had said earlier in the name of all had gone before. And if he had also spoken in the name of all on that other occasion, then beyond doubt in the other case too the reply would have had regard to all.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Et non tantùm res multis ex æquo communis futura uni ob certas causas etiam praesentibus reliquis promitti potest, V. g. Cardinalatus, quem æquè accipiunt, quibus vel nunquam promissus fuit, sed & multò magis id obtinet, ubi promissio & commendatio, vel jam facta est, vel mox fieri debet: Sicut si vinea alicujus Dominus mitteret plures operarios in vineam suam ad operandum, eámque omnibus commendaret in solidum; uni tamen, cui vel maximè sideret, quemque agnosceret officiosum supra omnes & industrium ac indefessum, seorsim diceret: Commendo tibi vineam meam; hoc profectò non illum principem super omnes constitueret, ubi vult ille Dominus omnes in solidum culturam illius vineae applicare; neque ille propterea diceretur ab hoc domino accepisse in illos colonos & in totam vineam ullam jurisdictionem: cùm nihil aliud & ipse sit, nisi unus ex colonis, quamvis praecipuus; Quas duas similitudines illustri de Dominis debemus. Dein & illud, nimirum Petrum propter talem Primatum summum promissionem clavium accepisse, sibi contrariatur; sic enim ipsi promissus fuisset Primatus, quia jam eum habuisset; quod absurdum.
units.tr: Not only can a thing that is common to many equally be promised to one of them for certain reasons, even while the others are present. For example, the cardinalate is accepted equally by those to whom it was never promised, and this holds much more where the promise and commendation have already been made or ought soon to be made. Suppose a lord of a vineyard sent several workers into his vineyard to labour there, and commended the whole vineyard to all of them alike, but then said to one of them in private, whom he especially favoured and recognised as more dutiful and diligent than all the others and untiring: "I commend my vineyard to you." This would certainly not make that man prince over all, when that lord wishes all of them alike to apply themselves to cultivating that vineyard; nor would he for that reason be said to have received from the lord any jurisdiction over those tenants and over the whole vineyard, since he is nothing more than one of the tenants, though a foremost one. We owe these two similitudes to the illustrious Bellarmine. Next, the claim that Peter received the promise of the keys because of such a supreme primacy contradicts itself. For the primacy would then have been promised to him when he already had it, which is absurd.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Videamus jam, quomodo distinctius alibi, & non sub persona unius, Ecclesiae claves regni coelorum promissae sint, ut ex eo adhuc magis apertum fiat, Petrum nullam potestatem accepisse, pisse, quæ non & aliis concessa sit. Locus est evidens Matth.XVIII. 18. ubi Christus, postquam ad interrogationem Petri de gradibus correptionis fraternæ egisset, dixisetque, eum qui Ecclesiam non audituru sit, habepi debere pro Ethnico & publicano, subjungit: Amen dico vobis, quæcunque ligaveritis in terra, ligata erunt in cœlis, & quæcunque solveritis in terra, soluta erunt in cœlis. Quæ verba ad Apostolos, imò fideles omnes & maximè ad Ecclesiasticum cœtum directa eadem plane sunt cum illis, quæ Matth.XVI. habentur, nisi quòd Matth. XVI. præmittitur: Tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum; Ante omnia igitur ostendi debet, hæc verba non distinctam potestatem ab illa, quam sequentia verba promittunt, continere, sed illam per sequentia verba declarari.
units.tr: Let us now see how, elsewhere and not in the person of one man, the keys of the kingdom of heaven are promised to the Church, so that it becomes still clearer that Peter received no power that was not also granted to the others. The passage in Matt. 18:18 is plain.
