There Christ, after answering Peter's question about the steps of fraternal correction, and after saying that whoever will not hear the Church should be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector, adds: Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. These words, addressed to the Apostles, indeed to all the faithful and above all to the ecclesiastical assembly, are exactly the same as those in Matt. 16, except that Matt. 16 begins with: To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven. First, therefore, it must be shown that these words do not contain a power distinct from the one which the following words promise, but that it is explained by the following words.

units.la: XII. Hoc autem ostendere possumus ex ipso Bellarmino, qui rejectis, quas Origeni & Theophylacto tribuit, duabus locis Matth.XVIII. expositionibus, etiam rejicit sententiam Cajetani illam, quæ Maldonati, Stapletoni, Baronii quoque est, quorum ille expresse ait: Non ego eodem sensu, quo Patres, hoc dictum interpretor; Comm. in locum. Hæc nimirum illorum hominum erga Patres religio, & eorum inventis plus scilicet credendum quam Patrum consentientibus testimoniis! quòd non idem sint claves regni cœlorum, & potestas solvendi & ligandi, & quòd illa includant potestatem tam ordinis, quam jurisdictionis, quæ significentur per actiones ligandi & solvendi, & aliquid præterea amplius, cum latius patere videatur, & aperire & claudere, quàm solvere & ligare; ut nimirum sic, saltem per verba: Tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum; peculiarem quandam potestatem promissam esse constet.
units.tr: XII. We can show this from Bellarmine himself, who, having rejected the two interpretations of Matt. 18 which he attributes to Origen and Theophylact, also rejects the opinion of Cajetan, which is also that of Maldonatus, Stapleton and Baronius. Of these, Maldonatus expressly says: I do not interpret this saying in the same sense as the Fathers. (Commentary on the passage.) Such is the reverence of these men for the Fathers, and so much more credit they give to their own inventions than to the agreeing testimony of the Fathers! That the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of loosing and binding are not the same; that the keys include both the power of order and the power of jurisdiction, which are signified by the actions of binding and loosing; and that something more is included, since opening and shutting seem to extend more widely than loosing and binding. The aim, of course, is that by the words To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven alone, it should be established that some peculiar power was promised.

units.la: XIII. Verùm rectissimè judicat Bellarminus, illam Cajetani sententiam subtiliorem quàm veriorem esse, cùm inauditum sit, in Ecclesia esse alias claves, quam verò ordinis & jurisdictionis; (Igitur etiam Bellarmino inauditum erit in Ecclesia, quòd Sixtus Senensis impudentissimè triplicem potestatem clavium finxit, ordinis, Apostolatûs & regni; inauditum, quòd nonnulli argutè distinguunt inter claves cœli, omnibus, & cœlorum soli Petro datas;) & planum sensus illorum verborum: Tibi dabo &c. iste sit, ut primò promittatur authoritas seu potestas designata per claves, deinde & actiones sive officium explicetur per ista vocabula: solvere & ligare, ita ut omninò sit idem solvere & aperire, claudere & ligare; Dominus autem clavium actiones per solvere & ligare, non per claudere & aperire, expressit, ut intelligeremus, esse omnes ista ista metaphoricas locutiones, & tum demum coelum hominibus aperiri, cum homines solvantur à peccatis, quae ingressum in coelum prohibebant. Hactenus Bellarminus & quidem satis commodè; Nam Scripturae solenne est ad significandam plenitudinem rerum spiritualium diversas metaphoras sive similitudines à rebus terrenis desumtas conjungeret; Ut saltem non valde necesse sit de tali clavium genere, quod solvendo & ligando aperiat & claudat, hic cogitare, secundum nuperam Authoris cujusdam de clavibus Dissertationem.
units.tr: XIII. But Bellarmine judges quite rightly that that opinion of Cajetan is more subtle than true, since it is unheard of that there should be other keys in the Church than those of order and jurisdiction. (So it will also be unheard of in the Church, to Bellarmine, that Sixtus of Siena most shamelessly invented a threefold power of keys: of order, of apostleship and of the kingdom; unheard of, that some subtly distinguish between the keys of heaven, given to all, and the of the kingdom of heaven, given to Peter alone.) And the plain sense of those words, "To you I will give," etc., is this: first, the authority or power signified by the keys is promised, and then the action or office is explained by these words, to loose and to bind, so that to loose is altogether the same as to open, and to bind the same as to shut. The Lord, however, expressed the actions of the keys by to loose and to bind, not by to shut and to open, so that we would understand that all these are metaphorical expressions, and that heaven is then at last opened to men when men are freed from the sins which barred the way into heaven. So far Bellarmine, and quite suitably. For it is characteristic of Scripture to combine various metaphors or similitudes drawn from earthly things in order to signify the fullness of spiritual things. So it is not really necessary to think here of such a kind of keys which open and shut by loosing and binding, as in the recent dissertation of a certain author on the keys.

units.la: XIV. Bellarminus igitur concedit, per claves regni coelorum nihil aliud designari, praeter illam ipsam ligandi & solvendi potestatem. Nos inde colligimus aequalitatem Apostolorum in suprema potestate, si enim, teste Bellarmino, idem sunt claudere & ligare, aperire & solvere, & ista omnibus promissa sunt, quid Petro amplius tribui potest? quid amplius habuit, nisi quod coelum aperire & claudere potuit? Vel an illud in singulari; quicquid ligaveris; plus potest, quam alterum in plurali: quaecunque ligaveritis, &c? Colligimus inde, illud, quod Petro Matth.XVI. expressius promissum est, Matth.XVIII. omnibus Apostolis & toti Ecclesiae promitti, & forte etiam exhiberi, quamvis illud Bellarminus neget, ex eo fundamento, quod Apostoli demum in ultima coena Sacerdotes & nonnisi post resurrectionem Christi Episcopi & Pastores facti sint, antea privati fuerint, nec ullam potestatem Ecclesiasticam habuerint; quod tamen salsissimum est, & absurdissimum, eos antea privatos fuisse, cum jam ad Israelis oves perditas missi sint, & sic fingantur Sacerdotes aliquandiu fuisse sine clavibus, jurisdictionem habuisse cum sacerdotio, sed sine ordine, &c. & quod alias etiam dici debeat, potestatem reapse per illa quoque verba: quodcunque ligaveris, &c. exhibitam esse. Ubi autem dispar est ratio, cum ibi promissio de futuro exprimatur: Tibi dabo &c. hic contra Christus tanquam de casu quotidie contingente & praesente interrogatus tanquam de re jam ab illo tempore valitura loquatur: si contra te peccet frater tuus &c. si Ecclesiam non audiat, &c. quaecunque ligaveritis &c. Et forte in illis verbis posterioribus jam priorum complementum sit. Sed sit, promittatur tantum aliquid hic, nihil exhibeatur. Sufficit promissio, quam & impletam esse Bellarminus ait, & claves Apostolis datas Johan.XX.v.23. Nam Joh.XX. cum Dominus dixerit Apostolis: pax vobis, sicut misit me pater, & ego mitto vos; tum eis potestatem, seu clavem jurisdictionis attribuisse, fecisse enim his verbis bis eos quasi legatos & nomine suo gubernatores Ecclesiae. Verbu autem sequentibus: accipite Spiritum S. quorum remiseritis peccata, illis remissa erunt, & quibus retinueritis, illis retenta erunt; dedisse eisdem potestatem ordinis.
units.tr: XIV. Bellarmine therefore concedes that by the keys of the kingdom of heaven nothing else is signified except that very power of binding and loosing. From this we conclude that the Apostles were equal in supreme power. For if, according to Bellarmine's testimony, to shut and to bind are the same, and to open and to loose are the same, and these are promised to all, what more can be attributed to Peter? What more did he have, except that he could open and shut heaven? Or can the singular whatever you bind have more force than the plural whatever you bind, etc.? From this we conclude that what was promised to Peter more explicitly in Matt. 16 is promised to all the Apostles and to the whole Church in Matt. 18, and perhaps even given to them, although Bellarmine denies this on the ground that the Apostles were made priests only at the last supper and bishops and pastors only after Christ's resurrection, that before this they were deprived and had no ecclesiastical power at all. Yet this is most false and absurd: that they were deprived before, since they had already been sent to the lost sheep of Israel. Thus they are imagined to have been priests for a while without keys, to have had jurisdiction along with the priesthood but without order, and so on. And it should be said in other ways too, that power was really conveyed by those words also: whatever you bind, etc. But where the reasoning is different, since there a promise about the future is expressed, To you I will give, etc., here on the contrary Christ speaks as if about an everyday occurrence, which is present, and as if about a matter that would be valid from that time on, when he is asked: If your brother sins against you, etc.; if he does not hear the Church, etc.; whatever you bind, etc. And perhaps in those later words the earlier promise is already fulfilled. But let it be so: here something is promised, nothing is yet given. The promise is sufficient, and Bellarmine says it was fulfilled, and that the keys were given to the Apostles in John 20:23. For in John 20, when the Lord said to the Apostles, Peace be with you; as the Father sent me, so I send you, then he gave them power, or the key of jurisdiction, for by these words he made them twice as it were legates and governors of the Church in his name. But by the following words, Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained, he gave them the power of order.

units.la: XV. Et sic pervenimus duce Bellarmino ad illum locum Joh.XX. ubi promissionis Apostolis & Petro factae complementum narratur, vel, si quis malit, illud quod jam antea habuerant, non sine magno gratiae & Spiritus augmento ad plenarium N.T. etiam inter gentes ministerium dirigitur, & promissio jam antea facta ablato metaphorae crassioris cortice renovatur & nuda proponitur. Ait Bellarminus, de hoc posteriore loco nullam esse difficultatem. Est profecto ipsi & aliis Monarchicis insolubilis. Cum hic in complemento omnino pares inveniantur, quibus promissio quaedam cum aliqua differentia facta videbatur. Sed cur hic nulla difficultas est? Quia per illa verba, respondet Bellarminus, non datur omnis potestas clavium, sed tantum ordinis ad remittenda peccata, ligari autem homines etiam legibus, & retinere peccata minus esse, quam ligare peccatorem, quomodo novum vinculum imponatur per excommunicationem, interdictum, legem, &c. quare etiam Patres dicant, dari hic potestatem remittendi per Sacramenta Baptismi & poenitentiae.
units.tr: XV. And so, with Bellarmine as our guide, we come to that passage in John 20, where the fulfilment of the promise made to the Apostles and to Peter is narrated. Or, if anyone prefers, what they already had is directed, not without a great increase of grace and of the Spirit, towards the full ministry of the New Testament even among the Gentiles, and the promise already made is renewed and set out plainly, with the coarser bark of metaphor removed. Bellarmine says: there is no difficulty in this latter passage. Indeed, it is insoluble for him and for other monarchists. For here, in the fulfilment, we find them altogether equal, between whom a certain promise seemed to have been made with some difference. But why is there no difficulty here? Because by those words, Bellarmine answers, not all the power of the keys is given, but only that of order for remitting sins. To bind men, however, also by laws, and to retain sins, is less than to bind a sinner, as a new bond is imposed through excommunication, interdict, law, etc. Therefore the Fathers also say that the power of remitting is given here through the sacraments of baptism and penance.

units.la: XVI. Ast 1. Posito, per illa verba sola omnem potestatem collatam esse, sufficit, quod per illa immediatè praecedentia: sicut me misit Pater &c. ipso etiam Bellarmino fatente, Apostolis etiam clavis jurisdictionis & plane idem cum illo, quod Petro per verba: Pasce oves meas; collatum fuit. Acceperunt igitur omnem clavium potestatem, per quaecunque jam verba acceperint. Sed 2. omninò etiam in verbis: quorum peccata remiseritis &c. omnis potestas clavium continetur, & omninò etiam de illis magna esse debet Bellarmino & cum ipso sentientibus difficultas. Cum non tantùm potestas illa ordinis ex institutione Christi conjuncta sit cum illa altera jurisdictionis, ita ut illa non sit, ubi non & haec, utraque in sano sensu accepta; quemadmodum etiam Alexander Alensis p. 4. q. 20. m. f. ait: claves dantur aut conferuntur in & cum ordine sacerdotali: neque possunt ab ea separari; Et Scotus clavem commissoriam, quae possit homini committi, sacerdoti dari insuscepitione ordinis in 4. dist. 18. testatur; Et Bonaventura in eundem locum, potestatem clavium promissam fuisse Matth.XVI. datam Joh.XX. accipite &c. Definiente vero Magistro, clavis est potestas ligandi & solvendi quâ Ecclesiasticus judex dignos recipere & indignos excludere debet à regno: Qui & totam hanc potestatem ordinis esse cum omnibus bus suis discipulis docet, & ad peccatum determinari; Sed & remittere & retinere peccata omnia dicat, quæ Matth. XVI. & XVIII. per τὸ solvere, & τὸ ligare dicuntur, quamvis certè nullus horum locorum Pontificium ligare, id est, à Deo permissa & licita illicita reddere, & Pontificium solvere, id est, à Deo non permissa & illicita licita reddere, sive promittat, sive exhibeat, & omninò absurdissimum sit, per ligare, quod necessariò debet ibi triste aliquid & hominibus metuendum significare, intelligere Ecclesiasticarum legum promulgationem; Et peccator, cujus peccata retinentur, vi oppositi & consentientibus Scholasticis omnibus, omninò ligetur, & quatenus admonitionem fraternam spernere præsupponitur, non in statu suo relinquatur, & excommunicatio ad illam retentionem pertineat, Baptismus etiam & pœnitentia, quæ in sensu Pontificio Patribus Sacramentum nunquam fuit, omnes leges, quæ Christianis ferri possunt, respiciant, & omnis potestas in claudendo & aperiendo cœlo consistat, & ipse Bellarminus contra Cajetanum jamjam dixerit, claudi cœlum, si homines ligentur, ligantur autem per retentionem peccatorum, aperiri cœlum, si à peccatis solvantur, solvuntur autem per remissionem peccatorum, quæ & publicè & privatim annunciatur, & applicatur, ut etiam contraria retentio; illam autem τὸ solvere, & hanc τὸ ligare explicare nemo non videt, & nemo non novit, Apostolos reliquos in præcipiendo, excommunicando, &c. minimè Petro inferiores fuisse, cùm & Paulus & Johannes & Jacobus non pauciora utique præcepta dederint, quàm Petrus, & Jacobum confessionem & extremam unctionem præcepisse dicant, & Paulus Satanæ tradiderit, adventum in virga comminatus sit, & penes Ecclesiam sit, facere, ut incorrigibiles habeantur tanquam Ethnici & publicani. Et per consequens Bellarmino non una etiam de hoc loco est difficultas.
units.tr: XVI. But first: granting that all the power was conferred by those words alone, it is enough that it was conferred by the words immediately preceding, as the Father sent me &c., which Bellarmine himself admits. The Apostles too received the key of jurisdiction, and it was entirely the same as that which was given to Peter in the words: Feed my sheep. So they received the whole power of the keys, through whatever words they received it. But second, the whole power of the keys is contained also in the words whose sins you remit &c., and Bellarmine and those who agree with him must surely have a great difficulty with these words as well. For that power of order, as instituted by Christ, is so joined to the other power of jurisdiction that the former does not exist where the latter does not, both being taken in a sound sense. Alexander of Hales also says, p. 4, q. 20, m. f.: the keys are given or conferred in and with the priestly order, and cannot be separated from it. Scotus attests that the commissory key, which can be committed to a man, is given to the priest by the reception of orders, in 4 dist. 18. Bonaventure, on the same passage, says that the power of the keys was promised in Matthew 16 and given in John 20: receive ye &c. The Master [Peter Lombard] defines it: the key is the power of binding and loosing, by which the ecclesiastical judge ought to admit the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy. He also teaches that all this power is of order, and belongs to all his disciples, and is determined to sin; and he says it is to remit and retain all sins, which in Matthew 16 and 18 are called the loosing and the binding [τὸ λύειν, τὸ δεῖν]. Yet surely none of these passages means that the Pope binds, that is, makes unlawful things that God has permitted and lawful, nor that the Pope looses, that is, makes lawful things that God has not permitted and unlawful, whether he promises or exhibits them. And it is utterly absurd to understand by binding the promulgation of ecclesiastical laws, when here it must signify something grievous to be feared by men. A sinner whose sins are retained is, by the opposing view and by the agreement of all the Schoolmen, bound altogether; and insofar as he is presumed to spurn fraternal admonition, he is not left in his state, and excommunication belongs to that retention. Baptism too and penance, which in the Papist sense were never a sacrament to the Fathers, concern all the laws that can be laid on Christians, and all power consists in shutting and opening heaven. Bellarmine himself, against Cajetan, has just said: heaven is shut if men are bound; they are bound by the retention of sins; heaven is opened if they are loosed from sins; they are loosed by the remission of sins, which is announced both publicly and privately and applied, as also its contrary, retention. Everyone sees and knows that the loosing [τὸ λύειν] and the binding [τὸ δεῖν] explain these things. Everyone also knows that the remaining Apostles, in commanding, excommunicating and so on, were in no way inferior to Peter, since Paul, John and James gave no fewer precepts than Peter, and James is said to have enjoined confession and extreme unction, and Paul delivered to Satan, threatened to come with a rod, and it lies with the Church to make offenders who cannot be corrected be regarded as heathens and tax collectors. Consequently, even in this passage, Bellarmine has no small difficulty.

units.la: XVII. Concludimus enim cum Doctissimo du Pin, primò
units.tr: XVII. For we conclude with the most learned du Pin, first,

units.la: Petro promissas esse eas ipsas claves, quæ posteà cæteris concessæ sunt, ac proinde per claves hic non intelligi, ut vult Bellarminus, summam potestatem in omnes Ecclesias.
units.tr: that the very keys which were afterwards granted to the others were promised to Peter, and therefore by the keys here is not understood, as Bellarmine wishes, supreme power over all churches.

units.la: Secundùm, claves istas hic: Matth. XVI. non datas esse Petro, sed promissas; Quod ab initio notavimus.
units.tr: Second, those keys here in Matthew 16 were not given to Peter but promised; this we noted from the beginning.

units.la: Tertium, in persona Petri promissas esse Ecclesiæ & cunctis Apostolis, quibus posteà datæ sunt.
units.tr: Third, they were promised in the person of Peter to the Church and to all the Apostles, to whom they were afterwards given.

units.la: Quartùm, id singulariter dictum Petro, tum ut unitas commendaretur.
units.tr: Fourth, this was said singularly to Peter, partly so that unity might be commended,

units.la: Conclusiones Doct. du Pin. tur, tum quia Primatum inter Apostolos obtinebat, hoc est, primus erat Apostolorum.
units.tr: conclusions of Doctor du Pin, partly because he held the primacy among the Apostles, that is, he was first of the Apostles.

units.la: Itaque ex hoc loco, Petrum inter Apostolos primum fuisse colligi potest, at eum tunc aliquid accepisse, quod caeteris Apostolis datum non sit, inde inferri minime potest.
units.tr: Thus from this passage it can be gathered that Peter was first among the Apostles, but it can by no means be inferred from this that he then received something that was not given to the other Apostles.

units.la: XVIII. Conclusionibus his Doctissimi du Pin addi meretur & illa, nempe si, secundum ipsius & Gallorum reliquorum & tot Patrum aliorumque virorum antehac celebrium & nostram doctrinam hactenus probatam, posterior loci Matth.XVI. pars etiam Apostolos respiciat, & claves Petro etiam tanquam typo Ecclesiae promissae sint, priorem etiam dicti partem de Petra, quatenus per eam homines designentur, pariter non de sola Petri persona, exclusis reliquis, intelligi posse, cum verba haec: Tu es Petrus & super hanc Petram &c. & illa: Tibi dabo claves &c. similiter & non interrupto cursu fluant, & haec posteriora aeque tanquam de una persona enunciata sint, nobisque adeo aeque ac Bellarmino (respectu Cajetani, qui, secundum ea quae dicta sunt, cursum verborum post illa: Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum; inhibuit, illa soli Petro propria, sequentia autem reliquis etiam communia esse dicens;) de sententia Bellarmini aliorumque verba illa: Et super hanc Petram &c. nimis arcte ad Petrum adstringentium, licere, ut dicamus, eam subtiliorem quam veriorem esse.
units.tr: XVIII. To these conclusions of the most learned du Pin should be added also this one: namely, that if, according to his own view and that of the other Frenchmen, and of so many Fathers and other men famous until now, and according to our doctrine hitherto proved, the latter part of Matthew 16 also concerns the Apostles, and the keys were promised to Peter also as a type of the Church, then the former part of the saying about the rock, insofar as through it men are designated, likewise can be understood not of Peter's person alone, to the exclusion of the rest; and the words You are Peter and upon this rock &c. and those I will give you the keys &c. flow on in a similar way without interruption, and these latter words are stated just as if of one person. So for us, as much as for Bellarmine (in regard to Cajetan, who, according to what has been said, interrupted the course of the words after I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, saying that those things are proper to Peter alone but the following are common to the rest as well), it is permissible, in the view of Bellarmine and others who bind those words And upon this rock &c. too tightly to Peter, to say that this view is more subtle than true.

units.la: XIX. Quando vero Doctissimus Vir in quarta sua conclusione rationes reddit, cur tamen Petro singulariter dictum sit: Tibi dabo claves &c. id non inconvenienter fit; rationem aliam & forte praecipuam jam nos dedimus, nimirum, quia nomine caeterorum Christum confessus est. Alias etiam dant Patres, unitatem non tantum Ecclesiae, quae sic significata sit, sed & Apostolorum duplici modo, item figuram & typum Ecclesiae exhibendum, imitationem & consensum fidei cum fide Petri, quae ex illis prolixe ostensa mysteria apud Doctissimum de Dominis l. c. §. 17--32. videre est.
units.tr: XIX. When, however, the most learned man, in his fourth conclusion, gives his reasons why it was nonetheless said singularly to Peter, I will give you the keys &c., this is not done without good reason. We have already given another reason, and perhaps the chief one: namely, that he confessed Christ in the name of the others. The Fathers also give other reasons: the unity not only of the Church, which was thus signified, but also of the Apostles in a twofold way; likewise that Peter was to exhibit a figure and type of the Church, the imitation and agreement of faith with the faith of Peter. These mysteries, which are set out at length from those passages, may be seen in the most learned de Dominis, l. c. §. 17–32.

units.la: XX. Haec autem omnia multum certe absunt ab illo Monarchicorum mysterio, quod solum causam singularis alloquii, cui tandem unice innituntur, esse potuisse fingunt, nimirum quod sic Petrus Monarcha Ecclesiae declaratus sit, & omnes omnium temporum Praesules claves non nisi a Petro habituri sint, nec sine mensura communicatas, Apostolis solum exceptis, qui extraordinaria quadam ratione eas a Christo immediate acceperint, ut Bellarminus loquitur, quos tamen men Apostolos alii non excipiunt. Turrecrem. l. 2. c. 54. Jacobat. de Concil. l. 10. §. judice Doct. Launojo. T. 2. epist. V. in hac discordia multò salsius, sed consequentius, Bellarmino non tam falsò, sed minùs consequenter philosophantes, & expresse docentes, illos quoque à Petro, non immediate à Christo potestatem suam accepisse, expressè sic etiam Scripturæ Joh. XX. contradicentes, ubi Apostoli potestatem suam immediate accipiunt, & quidem antequam secundùm Bellarminum Petrus per verba: pasce oves meas; Ecclesiæ Monarcha constitutus esset. Sed rectè censet de Dominis de hac & aliis jam suprà refutatis distinctionibus Bellarmini & Sociorum. Omnes ista solutiones, distinctiones & interpretationes Monarchicorum sunt ipsorum proprie & singulares nova atque inaudita ante illos, ac nullis ex Patribus cognita, imò ipsis patribus, ut videmus, repugnantes. Quod est signum manifestum novitatis & consequenter falsitatis nuper inventa. Et alibi: quasi verò tamdiu Ecclesia Catholica caruerit verâ illius loci notitiâ, ut nonnisi post mille & ultra annos in illis verbis: super hanc petram &c. Tibi dabo claves &c. Petri Monarchicum primatum agnoverit, & absolutum in Ecclesia principatum. Constat vel ex ipsa Bellarmini confessione, unde potestatem suam Apostoli habuerint, non igitur pependerunt à Petro, constat, quòd aliis potestatem Ecclesiasticam communicaverint, non nomine Petri, eo non consulto.
units.tr: XX. Yet all these things are certainly far removed from that Monarchist mystery, which they imagine could have been the only cause of the singular address, on which they finally rest entirely: namely, that Peter was thus declared monarch of the Church, and that all the prelates of all times were to have the keys from Peter alone, and communicated without measure, except the Apostles only, who by a certain extraordinary method received them immediately from Christ, as Bellarmine puts it, though other writers do not except those Apostles. Turrecremata, l. 2, c. 54; Jacobatius, De Concilio, l. 10, §.; in the judgment of Doctor Launoy, T. 2, epist. V. In this dispute, philosophizing much more wittily but more consistently than Bellarmine, though not so falsely, they expressly teach that those too received their power from Peter, not immediately from Christ, thereby expressly contradicting Scripture in John 20, where the Apostles receive their power immediately, and indeed before, according to Bellarmine, Peter was constituted monarch of the Church through the words feed my sheep. But de Dominis rightly judges concerning this and the other distinctions of Bellarmine and his companions, already refuted above: all these solutions, distinctions and interpretations of the Monarchists are peculiar and singular to themselves, new and unheard of before them, and known to none of the Fathers, indeed contrary to the Fathers themselves, as we see. This is a manifest sign of the novelty and consequently of the falsity of what has lately been invented. And elsewhere: as if the Catholic Church had lacked the true knowledge of that passage for so long, that only after a thousand and more years did it acknowledge in those words, upon this rock &c., I will give you the keys &c., a monarchical primacy of Peter and an absolute principate in the Church. It is clear, even from Bellarmine's own confession, whence the Apostles had their power; therefore they did not depend on Peter. It is clear that they communicated ecclesiastical power to others, not in Peter's name and without his counsel.

units.la: XXI. Absurditates auget, quòd porrò potestatem clavium, quam Petrus acceperit, tam perversè intelligunt; Dictum jam est de Monarchia. At nos & Catholici omnes per claves datas Petro intelligimus summam potestatem in omnes Ecclesias, inquit Bellarminus; Supremum dominium eas significare astruit Baronius, summam & absolutam potestatem regendi, quia hoc sine claves urbium solent Regibus tradi, Tirinus in Matth. XVI.19. Quàm autem hoc falsum est? Videat Doctissimus du Pin, videat Gallia, videant alii in Romana communione viventes, videat Bonaventura, Thomas, Durandus, Scotus, Alexander Ales, & alii Scholastici inter clavem principalem commissariam cum praeeminentia authoritatis & excellentia distinguentes, & hanc solam Petro tribuentes; Videat ipse Catholicorum Magister de suo Catholicismo, qui, ut suprà notavimus, aliter definivit claves, & omnibus communes fecit, & ad remittenda & retinenda peccata determinavit. Nullus hic inter Pontificios consensus est, &, ut Bellarminus plus æquo Papæ tribuit sub isto clavium nomine, respectu Gallorum, ita contrà multò hic inferior manet Canonistis.
units.tr: XXI. He further multiplies their absurdities by understanding so wrongly the power of the keys that Peter received. We have already spoken about the monarchy. But we and all Catholics understand by the keys given to Peter the supreme power over all the churches, says Bellarmine. Baronius asserts that they signify supreme dominion, the highest and absolute power of ruling, because the keys of cities are customarily handed to kings in this way, says Tirinus on Matthew 16:19. But how false this is! Let the most learned du Pin see it, let France see it, let others who live in the Roman communion see it, let Bonaventure, Thomas, Durandus, Scotus, Alexander of Hales and the other Schoolmen see it, who distinguish the principal key, entrusted with pre-eminence of authority and excellence, and who assign this alone to Peter. Let the Catholic master himself see it, who, as we noted above, defined the keys differently in his own Catholicism, made them common to all, and determined them for the forgiving and retaining of sins. There is no agreement here among the Papists. And just as Bellarmine, under this name of keys, grants more to the Pope than is fair with respect to the French, so, on the other hand, he remains far below the canonists here.

units.la: XXII. Verè Catholici autem summam illam Petri unius in omnes Ecclesias potestatem planè negant, negant prærogativas illas planè divinas, quas in hominem impiè conferunt, negant justitiam multiplicis tyrannidis, negant etiam, quòd Petrus concipi debeat tanquam cœli janitor, qui quasi ad ostium stet intromittens & repellens, quia ei datæ sint claves regni cœlorum, quo respectu & olim Rex Angliæ Ofvvi, referente Beda Hist. Eccl. Angl. l. 3.25. circa quæstionem de Paschate, contra Petrum, id est, Papam decernere & decerni noluit, veritus scilicet, quod & verbis protulit, ne ab ipso ea de causa in cœlum non admitteretur, quasi Scriptura per regnum cœlorum beatam in cœlis vitam & non Ecclesiæ, maximè militantis, statum denotet; negant, recte jactatum fuisse, referente Mornæo Myst. iniq. p.238. ab Hildebrando, clavi Romana Reges non minus quàm cateros esse subjectos, quia noverunt, Petrum etiam post acceptas claves omni humana potestati propter Dominum subjectum fuisse, & aliis, ut idem facerent, 1.Ep.II. 13. præcepisse, & 2.Ep. II.10. dominationum contemtoribus & majestatum blasphematoribus grave judicium annunciâsse. Et negant cum Fero, claves regni cœlorum esse claves regni terrarum; Ut etiam negant claves has rectè in clavos, enses, lanceas, sceptra, coronas conflari, & tandem, Petrum claves abyssi in purgatorium, quod illo tempore ignotum, & infernum, ut cum Clemente VI. in Bulla Jubilæi, Angelis Paradisi mandare potuerit; quid de animabus agere & quomodo poenam inferni certis minimè infligere debeant; accepisse. Claves sunt istæ, certè non à Christo, verùm ab infernali potiùs Vulcano fabricatæ, quas tamen à Petro accepisse videri volunt, quibus insignia claves, symbolum jurisdictionis, sicut tiara dignitatis; qui claves dextrâ, minùs gratam crucem sinistrâ gerunt; qui & aliquando claves Regibus dono dederunt; At parùm Petrus de his omnibus intellexisse videtur, parùm cætera discipulorum turba, & parùm promissionis suæ memor fuisse videtur ipse Christus: Discipuli enim postea tribus distinctis vicibus de præeminentia litigârunt acriter; Petrus non ad promissiones sibi factas provocavit, necetiam in litis decisione Christus.
units.tr: XXII. The true Catholics, however, flatly deny that supreme power of one man, Peter, over all the churches. They deny those utterly divine prerogatives which they impiously confer on a man. They deny the justice of their manifold tyranny. They also deny that Peter should be conceived as the doorkeeper of heaven, standing as it were at the door, letting in and shutting out, because the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to him. On this basis, long ago, the king of England, Oswy, as Bede reports (Hist. Eccl. Angl. l. 3.25.), in the dispute about Easter, wished neither to decide nor to be decided against Peter, that is, against the Pope, fearing, as he himself said in words, that for this reason he would not be admitted into heaven by him. As if Scripture by the kingdom of heaven denoted the blessed life in heaven and not the state of the Church, especially the Church militant. They deny that Hildebrand rightly boasted, as Mornaeus reports (Myst. iniq. p.238.), that kings of Rome are no less subject to the keys than others, because they know that Peter, even after receiving the keys, was subject to every human power for the Lord's sake, and that he commanded others to do the same (1 Peter 2:13), and announced a grievous judgment to despisers of dominions and blasphemers of majesties (2 Peter 2:10). They also deny, with Fero, that the keys of the kingdom of heaven are the keys of the kingdom of earth. Likewise they deny that these keys may rightly be cast into nails, swords, lances, sceptres and crowns. And finally, they deny that Peter received the keys of the abyss, to send to purgatory (which at that time was unknown) and to hell, so that, as Clement VI in the Bull of the Jubilee, he could order the angels of paradise what to do with souls and how they must certainly not inflict the punishment of hell. These keys are certainly not from Christ, but rather were forged by the infernal Vulcan. Yet they want it to appear that Peter received them, along with the keys as insignia, the symbol of jurisdiction, just as the tiara is the symbol of dignity. They carry the keys in the right hand and the cross, which is less pleasing, in the left. And at times they have given keys as gifts to kings. But Peter seems to have understood little of all this, the rest of the band of disciples seems to have understood little, and Christ himself seems to have been little mindful of his own promise. For the disciples afterwards quarrelled sharply about pre-eminence on three distinct occasions. Peter did not appeal to the promises made to him, nor did Christ in settling the dispute.

units.la: SECTIO QUINTA,
units.tr: SECTION V,

units.la: In qua, Invaliditas argumentorum Pontificiorum pro Electione Petri ad talem Pontificatum, instituto examine loci Joh. XXI.15.16.17. porrò ostenditur. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which the invalidity of the Papists' arguments for Peter's election to such a Papacy is further shown, by a detailed examination of John 21:15, 16, 17. Summary.

units.la: I. Speciale examen loci Ioh XXI,15.16 17. incipit, atque ejus Metaphora notatur; II. Primò conceditur, aliter licèt interdum loqui visis Patribus nonnullis, Petro & soli Petro dici; Pasce oves meas; III. Quod tamen non probat, sic Monarchiam Petro collatam esse, cùm alia fuerint causa peculiaris alloquii; IV. Varia, juxta Patres, sed præcipua inter eas, quòd Petrus in dignitatem Apostolicam post lapsum gravissimum restitui atque triplici confessione abnegationem triplicem emendare debuit; V. Quod similibus illustratur; VI. Adeòque in verbis est tantùm confirmatio, non nova potestatis collatio. VII. Pascere ibi non denotat potestatem absolutam, licèt, quod Bellarminus urget, Christo tributum eam involvat; VIII. Licèt etiam nonnunquam tribuatur Regibus; IX. Quando autem de Rectoribus Ecclesiæ accipitur, minimè omnium potestatem absolutam denotat, quia multis tribuitur, Apostolis nimirum, ipso fatente Bellarmino, suprema potestas Ecclesiastica; X. Aliis sub Metaphoris æquivalentibus, imò etiam propriis verbis, quæ idem quod pascere denotant; XI. Imò sub illa Metaphora; XII. Quid pascere significet Rectoribus Ecclesiarum tributum, maximè juxta emphasin verbi ποίμνω; XIII. Ex genuina significatione patet, Petrum sic non potuisse constitui talem Pontificem, primò quia Episcopi Romani non docentes populum non pascunt. Refutatur exceptio Bellarmini prima; XIV. Secunda; XV. Tertia & quarta; XVI. Quarta in specie quoad simile de Pro-Rege; XVII. Quoad exemplum Valerii Hipponensis; XVIII. Redarguitur silentium Bellarmini ad ratiunculam, ut vocat, Lutheri, quòd major pars Pontificum non diligat, neque exemplo pascat. Ex qua porrò & secundò patet tales non pascere; Et Petrum talem Pontificem constitui non potuisse; XIX. Tertiò ex eo, quòd Pontifices sub prætextu illo faciunt & sibi tribuunt, quæ Petrus nunquam fecit aut habuit, nempe dominatum absolutum, & potestatem temporalem in Reges & Principes, quæ ex loco à Bellarmino & Becano adstruitur; XX. Explicatur; XXI. Refutatur primò ex eo, quòd non ita pavit Petrus; XXII. Atque vana est exceptio, eum jus quidem habuisse, at vires defuisse, quemadmodum etiam primis Successoribus. XXIII. Secundò ex eo, quòd actus isti, quos exercent, contra Principes, Pastorales scilicet, minùs eum officio pastorali Petro demandato convenire videntur. XXIV. Cujus jam objectum constituuntur, semel agni; bis, oves; non; bis, agni; & semel, oves, uti Bellarminus pertendit. XXV. Cujus hic examinatur mysterium primum; XXVI. Secundum; XXVII. Tertium & quartum. XXVIII. In genere redarguuntur ista mysteria etiam ex de Dominis & Iansenio; XXIX. Non magis objectum Monarchiam Petri in universam Ecclesiam probat ratione vocula; meas; quâ quibusdam Iudai tantùm designari videntur, atque inter eos Doctissimo de Dominis, ex quo sententia proponitur & explicatur, atque XXX. Ab exceptionibus quodammodo liberatur, nec non ejus robur contra Adversariorum sententiam notatur; XXXI. Qua nec juvatur, si per vocula promiscuè Iudai & Gentes designari dicuntur; Propositio enim est indefinita particulari aequipollens; quod similibus illustratur; XXXII. Neque etiam pro ea quicquam valet, quòd Bellarminus dicit; Petro commendatam esse curam ovilis, quod unum sit; quâ occasione quoque de Pastore uno, cujus respectu ovile unum dicitur, aliquid annotatur; XXXIII. Ejusdem farina est cum argumentis reliquis disjunctiva ejusdem; Aut nulla, aut aliqua, aut omnes oves commissa sunt &c. Cui similis argumentatio primò ex Matth. XXVIII 19. opponitur; XXXIV. Secundò specialiùs respondetur; XXXV. Generaliùs ad Patrum testimonia, atque suppeditantur fontes solutionis ex Doctissimo du Pin. XXXVI. Solidum contra adversariorum sententiam argumentum ex eo nectitur, quòd Petrus nec omnes, nec speciatim Apostolos pavit; XXXVII. Quod specialiùs respectu Pauli ostenditur; XXXVIII. Testimonium Chrysostomi vindicatur, ex de Dominis, Apostolos Petri oves non fuisse porrò ostenditur, atque specialissimè ex reprehensione Petri per Paulum Antiochiæ facta; XXXIX. Argumentatio contra adversarios ex vocula; meas; instituitur; XL. Atque tractatio locorum ab adversariis præcipuè allegari soliterum, indicio ulteriori, de eo, quòd parùm in faveant, in obscuritate sensûs in hanc partem, ostenso; clauditur.
units.tr: I. A detailed examination of John 21:15, 16, 17 begins, and its metaphor is noted. II. First it is granted that, though some Fathers have sometimes spoken otherwise, the words "Feed my sheep" were said to Peter and to Peter alone. III. This does not prove that the Monarchy was conferred on Peter in this way, since there were other particular causes for the address. IV. Various causes are given, according to the Fathers, but the chief among them is that Peter, after his very grave fall, had to be restored to the apostolic dignity and to make amends for his threefold denial by a threefold confession. V. This is illustrated by similar cases. VI. So the words contain only a confirmation, not a new conferral of power. VII. To feed there does not denote absolute power, although, as Bellarmine presses, it implies that power given to Christ. VIII. It is sometimes also attributed to kings. IX. When it is taken of the rulers of the Church, it by no means denotes absolute power, since it is given to many, namely to the apostles, to whom, as Bellarmine himself admits, the supreme ecclesiastical power belonged. X. It is also expressed by other equivalent metaphors, and even by proper words, which denote the same as to feed. XI. Indeed, it is expressed under that very metaphor. XII. What to feed signifies when it is ascribed to the rulers of the Churches, especially according to the emphasis of the Greek verb ποιμαίνω [poimainō]. XIII. From its genuine meaning it is clear that Peter could not thus be appointed such a Pontiff, first because the Roman bishops who do not teach the people do not feed them. Bellarmine's first exception is refuted. XIV. The second. XV. The third and fourth. XVI. The fourth in particular, as to the comparison with a vice-king. XVII. As to the example of Valerius of Hippo. XVIII. Bellarmine's silence is rebuked in response to what he calls Luther's little argument, that the greater part of the Popes do not love, nor feed by example. From this, secondly, it is further clear that such men do not feed; and that Peter could not have been appointed such a Pontiff. XIX. Thirdly, from the fact that the Popes, under that pretext, do and claim for themselves what Peter never did or had, namely absolute lordship and temporal power over kings and princes, which is asserted from the passage by Bellarmine and Becanus. XX. This is explained. XXI. It is first refuted by the fact that Peter did not feed in this way. XXII. And the plea that he had the right but lacked the strength, as also with the first successors, is empty. XXIII. Secondly, from the fact that those acts which they perform against princes, pastoral acts forsooth, seem less suited to the pastoral office entrusted to Peter. XXIV. Whose objects, as Bellarmine maintains, are constituted: once lambs; twice, sheep; not; twice, lambs; and once, sheep. XXV. Its first mystery is examined here. XXVI. The second. XXVII. The third and fourth. XXVIII. These mysteries are refuted in general, also from De Dominis and Jansen. XXIX. The object proves the Monarchy of Peter over the whole Church no more by the little word "my", by which some are seemingly designated only as Jews, and among them the most learned de Dominis, from whom the opinion is put forward and explained. XXX. It is in some measure freed from exceptions, and its strength against the opinion of the adversaries is noted. XXXI. Nor is it helped if by the little word Jews and Gentiles are said to be indiscriminately designated; for the proposition is indefinite, equivalent to a particular one. This is illustrated by similar cases. XXXII. Nor does anything avail for it what Bellarmine says, that the care of the fold was committed to Peter, because it is one. On this occasion also something is noted about the one Shepherd, with respect to whom the fold is said to be one. XXXIII. The disjunctive argument of the same kind as the other arguments is: either none, or some, or all the sheep were committed to him, etc. An argument similar to this is first opposed from Matthew 28:19. XXXIV. Secondly, a more specific answer is given. XXXV. More generally, to the testimonies of the Fathers; and sources of solution are supplied from the most learned du Pin. XXXVI. A solid argument against the opinion of the adversaries is connected here, because Peter fed neither all, nor specifically the Apostles. XXXVII. This is shown more specifically with respect to Paul. XXXVIII. The testimony of Chrysostom is vindicated; from de Dominis it is further shown that the Apostles were not Peter's sheep, and most especially from Paul's rebuke of Peter at Antioch. XXXIX. An argument against the adversaries is instituted from the little word "my". XL. The treatment of the passages which the adversaries are especially accustomed to allege is concluded, with further evidence, shown in the obscurity of their sense, that they little favour this side.

units.la: I. PRobavimus hactenus, Petro Pontificatum talem sive Monarchiam non promissam esse; An ei collata sit (quod quidem vel sine promissione prævia fieri potuisset;) jam discipiendum est, & quidem in consideratione posterioris loci, sive textûs, ex duobus, quibus Bellarminus & alii Monarchici tanquam palmariis utuntur, & qui secundùm Cajetanum præcipuè de hoc (Monarchiæ Petri) mysterio expresse loquuntur. Habetur ille Joh. XXI.v.15. 16.17. ubi Christus semel ad Petrum ait: Pasce agnos meos; & bis: Pasce oves meas; præmissâ & inspersâ trinâ de amore Petri erga se interrogatione. Figuratus est & hic locus, & metaphoram continet à Pastore ovium desumptam; uti in priori loco duplicem vel triplicem metaphoram à Petra fundamento ædificii, clavibus & ligatione vel solutione desumi vidimus; ut planè, quoad argumenta ex Scriptura, metaphorica sit illa Petri Monarchia, & tantò magis gis mirandum,quòd Bellarminus Ecclesiae illius Doctor , quae, quando sensus improprius displicet , eum obscuro æquipollere contendit, ita quoad priorem locum ait: Quorum verborum planus & obvius sensus est,ut intelligamus sub duabus metaphoris promissum esse Petro totius Ecclesia Principatum l.1. de Rom. Pont. c.X. ait mirandum magis,Christum, qui aliquoties Apostolis munus suum demandavit, & alia minora saepius inculcavit,non nisi semel & quidem non nisi metaphoricè Monarchicam potestatem, id est, rei Christianae summam Petro tradidisse, nec unquam dixisse: Ego te constituo Monarcham Ecclesia mea, qui possit &c. & cui,cujusque Successoribus, qui erunt Episcopi Romani,omnes omninò Christiani absolutam debent & debebunt obedientiam; altum verò de his in Scriptura silentium, & de hoc loco posteriori speciatim rectissimè ait,quod & verum esse ostendemus,de Dominis l.1. de Rep. Eccl. cap. 8. §. 13. qui solus ac ferme unicus Evangelii locus Petri fundare Ecclesiasticam videbatur Monarchiam ; is omnium maximè & plures & planas fert Catholicas interpretationes à primatu & Monarchia unius abhorrentes. Tantine igitur res momenti adstrui debet locis,si non contrariis, certè ad minimum dubiis, & ad summum vix probabilibus? Optimè profectò dicunt communiter Jurisconsulti, Textum, qui plures habet intellectus, non esse allegabilem, nempe solum & in tantis, & si omninò dubius sit sensus.
units.tr: I. We have so far proved that a Papacy or Monarchy of such a kind was not promised to Peter. Whether it was conferred on him (which indeed could have been done even without prior promise) is now to be discussed; and indeed by considering the latter passage or text, out of the two which Bellarmine and the other Monarchists use as their chief weapons, and which, according to Cajetan, speak expressly of this mystery of the Monarchy of Peter above all. It is found in John 21:15, 16, 17, where Christ says once to Peter: Feed my lambs; and twice: Feed my sheep; with a threefold question about Peter's love for him, placed before and interspersed. This passage too is figurative and contains a metaphor taken from the shepherd of sheep; just as in the earlier passage we have seen a double or triple metaphor drawn from the rock as foundation of a building, the keys, and binding or loosing. So, as far as the arguments from Scripture go, that Monarchy of Peter is plainly metaphorical; and all the more to be wondered at is that Bellarmine, a teacher of that Church which, when an improper sense displeases it, contends that it is equivalent to an obscure one, says of the earlier passage: The plain and obvious sense of these words is that we understand the headship of the whole Church to have been promised to Peter under two metaphors (On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, ch. 10). It is more to be wondered at that Christ, who several times committed his office to the apostles and often inculcated other lesser things, never once, and indeed never except metaphorically, handed over Monarchical power, that is, the sum of Christian affairs, to Peter; and never said: I appoint you monarch of my Church, who may etc.; and to whom, and to whose successors, who will be the Roman bishops, all Christians absolutely owe and will owe absolute obedience. Rather, there is a deep silence about these things in Scripture; and about this later passage in particular Bellarmine says most rightly, which we shall also show to be true, citing de Dominis (On the Commonwealth of the Church, book 1, ch. 8, §13): the only and almost unique passage of the Gospel which seemed to ground an ecclesiastical Monarchy for Peter; it is the one which bears most and plainest Catholic interpretations abhorrent to a primacy and monarchy of one. Should so great a matter, then, be built on passages that are, if not contrary, at least doubtful, and at most scarcely probable? The jurists commonly say very well that a text which has several meanings is not to be cited, namely, in such great matters, and especially if the sense is altogether doubtful.

units.la: II. His praemissis, videbimus, primò cui in textu aliquid dicatur,quâ occasione & quas ob causas Petro dictum sit: Pasce agnos meos,oves meas; ut postmodum de ipsa re eò melius judicari queat. Igitur & Petro hic aliquid dictum fuit; Nulli negamus, & quamvis Patres nonnulli Augustinus cumprimis &, quo ille magistro usus est,Ambrosius hic quoque ad Petrum tanquam ad typum omnium pastorum,& qui totam Ecclesiam repraesentarit, sermonem Christi directum fuisse doceant; Et ille quidem in Joh. tract.46. his verbis: Non in ipso Petro, sed in corpore suo ait; Petre amas me? pasce oves meas. Et serm.24. de Sanctis: Nempe in uno Petro figurabatur unitas Pastorum. Hic autem de dign. Sacerd. l.2. non minùs aperte: Quas oves,inquit, & quem gregem non solùm tunc suscepit B. Petrus, sed & nobiscum eas suscepit & cum illo eas nos suscepimus omnes: Quae verba valdè emphatica sunt, illis enim Ambrosius testatur, non à Petro, sed cum Petro quosvis Pastores & Petrum cum illis suscepisse oves & gregem ; Quamvis,inquam, Patres quidam ,quos etiam doctissimus du Pin in Dissert. sape citata adducit,sic sermonem Christi non solum Petrum respexisse dicant, sed Petrum rursus figuram Ecclesiae faciant, adeoque hic etiam Augustinus saltem, juxta ea quae supra dicta sunt, illustrem intellectum non in Petro, sed in Ecclesia quaerendum esse censeat, & hanc etiam causam, quod nimirum hic etiam personam Ecclesiae gerere debuerit, & ipse Loyolita Otto in Dedic. Rom. Glor. ad Archiep. Salisburg. dicens: Hoc est Pastoris (loquitur generalissime) partes sub supremo Pastore Christo exequi, illudque Domini in Petri persona bis omnibus inculcatum implere: Si amas me; Pasce agnos meos; Petri peculiari alloquio assignet; His tamen insistere nolumus, nec etiam necesse est, quando idoneam rationem ipsa Petri persona suppeditat; Ultro igitur Monarchicis largiemur, & Petro, & soli Petro hic aliquid dici, soli Petro dici: Pasce oves meas; quod Bellarminus integro capite & sex ex Scriptura rationibus, quarum tamen quinta & sexta imprimis nullius plane momenti, probat, quamvis idem, quod hic Petro dicitur, aliis occasionibus & verbis, aliis alibi, quod nobis sufficit, & proin in illo sensu non soli Petro dici; Pasce oves meas; mox demonstraturi simus.
units.tr: II. With these things premised, we shall first see to whom something is said in the text, on what occasion and for what reasons it was said to Peter: Feed my lambs, my sheep; so that afterwards the matter itself may be judged better. Therefore something was said here to Peter too; we do not deny it to anyone. Although some Fathers, above all Augustine, and Ambrose, whom he took as his master, teach that the address of Christ was directed here too to Peter as to a type of all shepherds, and as representing the whole Church, Augustine says in his Tractate 46 on John, in these words: He said not in Peter himself, but in his body: Peter, do you love me? feed my sheep. And in Sermon 24 on the Saints: Indeed in the one Peter the unity of the pastors was prefigured. Ambrose, in On the Dignity of Priests, book 2, says no less plainly: Which sheep and which flock did not only blessed Peter then receive, but he received them with us, and we all received them with him. These words are very emphatic, for by them Ambrose testifies that not by Peter alone, but with Peter, all pastors received the sheep and the flock, and Peter with them received the sheep and the flock. Although, I say, some Fathers, whom the most learned du Pin also cites in the dissertation often cited, say that the words of Christ regarded not only Peter, but make Peter again a figure of the Church; and so here too Augustine, at least according to what has been said above, thinks that the clear meaning is to be sought not in Peter but in the Church; and for this reason too, namely because here also he had to bear the person of the Church; and the Jesuit Otto himself in the Dedication of Roma Gloriosa to the Archbishop of Salzburg, saying: This is the part of a pastor (he speaks most generally) to carry out under the supreme Pastor Christ, and to fulfil that saying of the Lord, inculcated on all in the person of Peter twice: If you love me, feed my lambs; he assigns to Peter's particular address. Yet we do not wish to insist on these things, nor is it even necessary, since the person of Peter himself supplies a suitable reason. We will therefore readily concede to the Monarchists that something is said here to Peter, and to Peter alone, that to Peter alone it is said: Feed my sheep; which Bellarmine proves in a whole chapter, with six reasons from Scripture, of which however the fifth and sixth are especially of no weight at all; although what is said to Peter here is said on other occasions and in other words, and elsewhere, which is enough for us; and therefore in that sense it is not said to Peter alone: Feed my sheep; as we shall soon demonstrate.

units.la: III. Sed an hoc nobis sufficit? An non jam nimium Monarchicis concessimus? Annon ex eo, quod Christus Petro soli in praesentia caeterorum dixit: pasce oves meas; sequitur, eum singulari modo Ecclesiae Christianae Pastorem, summum Pastorem, & a quo caeteri omnes & omnia plane pendere debeant, a Domino constitutum esse? Ita quidem Monarchici putant, imo tandem, quando nimirum ipsis ostendimus, rem communem & aliis multis fuisse & esse, eo adiguntur, ut non amplius in ipsis verbis, sed in ista actione Christi, qua Petrum potius quam alios alloqui voluit, argumentationis suae fundamentum quaerere necesse habeant, quod & illis circa priorem locum accidisse supra notavimus, & hic quoque accidere ex Turrecremata tantum non loco cedente cognoscimus: Non summus argumentati, inquit l. 2. de Eccles. cap. 11. primatum B. Petri ex sola pastoralis cura commissione; sed ex eo, quod praesentibus aliis Apostolis, nulla de illis mentione facta, soli Petro Christus indefinite curam gregis sui commisit. Ast jam satis superque debilem istum argumentandi modum loc. cit. refellimus, ut hic tantum, quia de sapientia Christi non modo praesumimus, aliquam causam hujus singularis alloquii fuisse, sed & per ejus bonitatem, certam hujus rei rationem ex historia facile discimus, rationes aut rationem ostendere debeamus, cur hic etiam potius Petrum quam vero Johannem, em, Jacobum, aut quemcunque alium Christus alloquio suo dignatus sit, quo sic constare possit, Monarchicos pro more à non causa tanquam à causa argumentari, & ex singulari alloquio Christi ad Monarchiam Petri consequentiam non valere.
units.tr: III. But is this enough for us? Have we not already conceded too much to the Monarchists? Does it not follow from the fact that Christ spoke to Peter alone, in the presence of the others, pasce oves meas, that he was appointed by the Lord as the unique shepherd of the Christian Church, the chief shepherd, on whom all the others and everything else must wholly depend? That is what the Monarchists think. Indeed, when we show them that the thing was and is common to many others, they are driven to seek the foundation of their argument not in the words themselves but in that action of Christ by which he chose to address Peter rather than the others. We noted above that this happened to them with the earlier passage, and we see from Turrecremata, who almost gives way on this point, that it happens here too: "The chief one argues," he says, in book 2 of On the Church, chapter 11, "the primacy of St Peter from the mere commission of pastoral care; but from the fact that, while the other Apostles were present, no mention was made of them, Christ committed the care of his flock indefinitely to Peter alone." But we have already refuted this very weak method of arguing, more than enough, in the passage cited above. Here, since we presume not only that Christ's wisdom had some reason for this singular address, but also, through his goodness, we easily learn the certain reason for it from history, we must show what reason or reasons there are why Christ chose to address Peter here rather than John, James, or anyone else. In this way it can be established that the Monarchists, as is their habit, argue from a non-cause as if from a cause, and that the inference from Christ's singular address to Peter's monarchy is not valid.

units.la: IV. Patres praeter jam allegatam rationem, quòd nimirum Petrus totius Ecclesiae personam assumere debuerit; (ad quod ille potiús ob solas donorum & ordinis praerogativas quasdam adhiberi jam potuisset) etiam alias commemorant, unitatem Ecclesiae & collegii Apostolici propius etiam praerogativam laboris inter undecim spectantes; praecipua autem, quam non pauci dant, quorum testimonia alibi videri possunt, & dare quispotest, quámque vel ipsis tacentibus facile ipsimet perspiceremus, haec est; debuisse sic Apostolum, qui per turpissimam eámque trinam abnegationem indignus & exsors tanti muneris factus videri potuisset, & omninò se indignum honore etiam pristino reddiderat, Collegis praesentibus, non tantùm trina confessione trinam illam abnegationem emendare, sed eâ de novo in Apostolatu confirmari, & illustre ac peculiare hocce testimonium perennantis in Christo amoris contra desperationem propriam, & ad certitudinem aliorum accipere, ac vicissim testari, se, quia multùm ei remissum sit, multùm etiam diligere Luc. VII. 47. Insuper etiam de priori animositate & confidentia nimia, quâ, se plus caeteris diligere, temerè jactaverat, in posterum vitanda, vel saltem melius stabilienda, speciatim moneri. Christum quippe negaverat, qui sese negantes apud Patrem negaturum professus erat; χαλεπώτερον τ' ἀλλων αυτῆ τὸ πῶμα; inquit Chrysost. in Matth.28. caeteri fugerant, ille etiam abnegaverat; Oportebat igitur, ut restituatur, & ut trina responsio aboleat trinae negationis errorem, quod & Sedulius lib.5. canit: Hoc terno sermone monens, ut terna negantis Culpa recens parili numero purgata maneret.
units.tr: IV. Besides the reason already cited, namely that Peter ought to have borne the person of the whole Church (for which he could already have been chosen, rather because of his gifts and the privileges of his rank alone), the Fathers also mention other reasons. These concern the unity of the Church and of the Apostolic college, and the privilege of labour, the more closely so as they bear on the eleven. The chief reason, which many give (their testimonies can be seen elsewhere, and anyone can cite them), and which we would easily perceive even if they were silent, is this: it was fitting that the Apostle, who through his shameful threefold denial had seemed unworthy and undeserving of so great an office, and who had made himself unworthy even of his former honour, should, with his fellow Apostles present, not only make amends for that threefold denial by a threefold confession, but also be confirmed in the Apostleship by it. And that he should receive, for the certainty of others, this illustrious and peculiar testimony of the love of Christ that endures against his own despair, and in turn bear witness that, since much had been forgiven him, he also loved much (Luke 7:47). Furthermore, he was to be especially warned to avoid in future, or at least to restrain more firmly, his earlier boldness and excessive self-confidence, by which he had rashly boasted that he loved more than the others. For he had denied Christ, though he had professed that Christ would deny those who denied him before the Father. "The lid is a heavier burden than the rest" [χαλεπώτερον τ' ἄλλων αὐτῇ τὸ πῶμα], says Chrysostom in Matth. 28: the others had fled, but he had also denied. It was therefore necessary that he be restored, and that the threefold answer should wipe out the error of the threefold denial, as Sedulius also sings in book 5: "Admonishing with this threefold speech, so that the threefold guilt of the denier, now cleansed by an equal number, might remain."

units.la: V. An ista negant Monarchici? Non audent. An igitur haec ratio vel sola non sufficit? Vel an Monarchiam involvit? Scilicet ideò Monarcha factus est, quia abnegavit, quia peculiariter restitui debuit! Si imperator ex ducibus aliquem, qui se ante timidiús in praelio gesserat, moneret atque hortaretur, ut nunc fortissimè pro patria pugnaret, an ei idcirco singulare aliquid mandaret? Si Princeps magistratum aut judicem inferiorem, quem audierat, non bene functum esse suo munere, accerseret, eique gravissimis verbis denuntiaret, ut jus diceret sanctè atque integrè; an ideò major ei potestas, an dominium in judices cæteros traderetur? Si Minister aliquis ordinatur, an ei novum munus & supereminens committitur, quod alii non habeant? Non arbitror; Et certè ipse Petrus scopum Domini cognovisse videtur optimè; hinc non, ac si dignitatem eminentem accepisset, lætatur, sed ob trinam interrogationem, lapsûs nimirum sui memor, valdè contristatus fuit.
units.tr: V. Do the Monarchists deny these things? They do not dare. Then is this reason alone not sufficient? Or does it involve a monarchy? Surely he was made monarch because he denied, because he had to be restored in a special way! If an emperor, rebuking and exhorting one of his commanders who had earlier fought too timidly in battle, bade him now fight most bravely for his country, would he thereby entrust him with something singular? If a prince, hearing that a lesser magistrate or judge had not performed his office well, summoned him and warned him in the gravest terms to administer justice soundly and uprightly, would greater power be given him thereby, or lordship over the other judges? If some minister is ordained, is a new and supereminent office committed to him which others do not have? I think not. And surely Peter himself seems to have understood the Lord's purpose very well. Hence, not rejoicing as if he had received an eminent dignity, but mindful of his own fall, he was very greatly saddened by the threefold question.

units.la: VI. Satisfecisse jam Monarchicis videri possumus, quatenus ex singulari alloquio argumentantur; interim tamen, quia plerique ipsam rem, ipsa Domini verba valdè urgent, & in illis constitutionem Petri, ut esset Monarcha Ecclesiæ, inveniri sibi imaginantur, secundò etiam rem istam, verba ista accuratius pensitabimus. Et primò quidem hic se offert consideratio ipsius muneris pastoralis sine respectu multo ad objectum ejus. Dicitur Petro: Pasce; Volunt sic ei plane novum munus impositum &, quod per locum priorem promissum sit, exhibitum fuisse. Id equidem verbum Domini non docet, promissionis complementum jam cum Apostolis reliquis acceperat, per verba: sicut me misit Pater &c. ut diximus, peculiaris confirmatio hic est, non novæ potestatis collatio, & quidem ita confirmatur, ut tantùm de officio admoneatur, quod vel centies pro occasionum diversitate fieri potuisset, sine ullo etiam potestatis augmento.
units.tr: VI. We may seem to have satisfied the Monarchists insofar as they argue from the singular address. Nevertheless, since most of them press the matter itself and the very words of the Lord, and imagine that Peter's appointment to be monarch of the Church is to be found in them, we shall weigh the words themselves more carefully in a second step. First of all, here the consideration of the pastoral office itself presents itself, without much regard to its object. Peter is told: Pasce. They want a wholly new office to have been imposed on him then, and, as the earlier passage promised, to have been given. The word of the Lord does not teach this. He had already received the completion of the promise together with the other Apostles, in the words sicut me misit Pater, etc., as we have said. This is a particular confirmation, not a conferral of new power. And it is confirmed in such a way that he is only reminded of his duty, which could have been done a hundred times, according to the variety of occasions, without any increase of power.

units.la: VII. Dicitur Petro: pasce; An igitur; Monarcha esto, absolutè impera; fer leges pro libitu; subjice Tibi hominum conscientias, opes, regna, imperia? Id certè vocabulum hoc non arguit; Et aliis idem dictum, eodem fere tempore, ejusdem etiam Ecclesiæ Rectoribus. Provocat tamen Bellarminus ad communem usum loquendi, juxta quem hic omnis actus pastoralis intelligi debeat, non tantùm præbere cibum, sed etiam ducere, reducere, tueri, præesse, regere, castigare. Hinc pascere in Scriptura passim accipi pro regere. Psal.2. legi: Reges eos in virga ferrea. Cyrum. Jer.44. Pastorem dici & apud Homerum Agamemnonem ποιμένα λαῶν, pastorem populorum, & Matth.2. per pascere explicari quod Mich.5. dominium dicatur. Quàm belle hæc omnia! Hic intelligitur omnis actus pastoralis. Quis negat? Sed actus pastorales sunt etiam ducere, reducere, tueri, præesse, regere, castigare; Et hoc quis negat? Admittimus, imò postulamus, sed etiam, ut ista convenienter regimini spirituali per servos Christi, & officio communi explicentur. Et dum hoc merito postulare facile videri possupossumus, jam etiam apparere potest, quàm ineptè loca de Christo & Regibus terrenis agentia à Bellarmino producantur. Christus Ecclesiae suae Pastor est, Pastor ille bonus Joh. X. Et quando pascere, quod ei Mich. V. adscribitur, explicat dominium, indicat, quale illud dominium Christi futurum, & quòd ad commodum & salutem suorum dirigendum sit. Christus certè caput & Monarcha Ecclesiae suae & eatenus etiam Pastor unus in ovili uno, princeps Pastor, magnus animarum Pastor & pascit, & imperat, pascit cum imperio & potestate absoluta. Verùm quae illa impudentia est, servo tribuere velle, quae sunt domini, velle Christi ἀνεψηνται sibi vendicare, & nolle de servo & ad servum dicta servorum ad instar accipere? Profectò in nullum haec quadrare possunt, nisi in pastorem aliquem stultum, de quali Zach. XI. 15 seqq. agitur.
units.tr: VII. Peter is told: pasce. So then: Be monarch, rule absolutely; make laws at will; subject to yourself the consciences, wealth, kingdoms and empires of men? Surely this word does not prove that. And the same was said, at about the same time, to other rulers of the same Church. Yet Bellarmine appeals to the common usage of speech, according to which every pastoral act here ought to be understood, not only to provide food, but also to lead, bring back, protect, preside over, rule, and correct. Hence, he says, to feed is everywhere in Scripture taken to mean to rule. In Psalm 2 we read: "Rule them with an iron rod." Cyrus (Jer. 44) is called a shepherd; and in Homer Agamemnon is called poimena laōn [ποιμένα λαῶν], shepherd of the peoples; and in Matthew 2 to feed is explained by what Micah 5 calls dominion. How fine all this is! Here every pastoral act is understood. Who denies it? But pastoral acts also include leading, bringing back, protecting, presiding, ruling, and correcting. Who denies that either? We admit it, indeed we demand it, but also that these be explained in a way fitting to spiritual government through the servants of Christ, and to the common office. And while we can easily see that this is rightly demanded, it can also now be seen how absurdly the passages about Christ and earthly kings are produced by Bellarmine. Christ is the Shepherd of his Church, that good Shepherd (John 10). And when feeding, which Micah 5 ascribes to him, expresses dominion, it indicates what sort of dominion Christ's will be, and that it is to be directed to the benefit and salvation of his own. Christ is certainly the head and Monarch of his Church, and to that extent also its one Shepherd in one fold, the chief Shepherd, the great Shepherd of souls; he feeds and commands, he feeds with authority and absolute power. But what shameless impudence is it to wish to ascribe to a servant what belongs to the Lord, to wish to claim for oneself what Christ alone possesses, and not to accept, as said of a servant and to a servant, the words about servants in the manner of servants? Surely these cannot apply to anyone except a foolish shepherd, of whom Zechariah 11:15 ff. speaks.

units.la: VIII. Quae de Regibus affert, pariter inepta sunt.
units.tr: VIII. What they adduce from the kings is equally absurd.

units.la: Cyrus sanè Jesaj. XLIV. 28. pastor dicitur & pastor Domini, typus nimirum illustris Christi, pastoris illius boni, & ratione beneficiorum, quae populo Dei in recolligendis, remittendis & reducendis in captivitate dispersis, & in aedificando Templo, quod & citato loco exprimitur, praestare debuit. Agamemnon etiam apud Homerum saepè pastor populorum dicitur. Sed quae est illa consequentia? Pascere aliquando Regibus tribuitur; Ergò ille, cui dicitur; pasce; necessariò constituitur Rex, Monarcha. Pascere alicubi involvit potestatem supremam sine socio. E. semper. E. & hic. In Regibus terrae. E. etiam in servo Christi, in uno ex illis, quibus dictum: Vos autem non sic. Et certè etiam, quando de dominantibus in terra sermo est, non tantùm Reges & Monarchae pastores vocantur, sed & illi, qui unà cum aliis aequali potestate praeditis Rempublicam administrant, & duces sunt sine summo imperio, cujus quidem usûs vocis exempla apud Platonem de Rep. l. 4. & Sophoclem in Ajace videri possunt. Ut ne quidem in translatione vocabuli ad potestates mundanas omnes Pastores Monarchae sint; Imò quotiescunque illuc transfertur, potestatem temperat, & tantùm non ad paternas curas & solicitudinem reducit.
units.tr: Cyrus, indeed, is called "shepherd" in Isaiah 44:28, and "shepherd of the Lord," clearly a notable type of Christ, that good Shepherd, and by reason of the benefits he was bound to confer on God's people in gathering, releasing and bringing back those scattered into captivity, and in building the Temple, which the passage cited also expresses. Agamemnon too is often called "shepherd of the peoples" in Homer. But what kind of consequence is this? Feeding is sometimes attributed to kings; therefore he to whom it is said "feed" is necessarily established as king, monarch. To feed somewhere involves supreme power without a colleague. Therefore always. Therefore also here. Among the kings of the earth. Therefore also in the servant of Christ, in one of those to whom it was said: "But you shall not be so." And certainly also, when the discourse is about those who rule on earth, not only kings and monarchs are called shepherds, but also those who govern the commonwealth together with others endowed with equal power, and are leaders without supreme authority; examples of this use of the word may be seen in Plato, Republic book 4, and in Sophocles' Ajax. So not even in the transfer of the word to worldly powers are all shepherds monarchs. Indeed, whenever it is transferred there, it tempers the power and brings it back almost only to paternal care and concern.

units.la: IX. Quod adhuc multò evidentius est in translatione vocis ad Rectores Ecclesiarum: Certè nihil per hanc vocem pasce Petro datum esse dici potest, quod non aliis etiam commune sit, sicut etiam dilectio Christi, de qua Petrus interrogatus erat, omnes servos Christi urget, 2. Cor. V. 14. & Paulo judice, qui Christum non diligunt, gunt, anathema sunt. 1.Cor.XVI.22. ut valde necesse sit fateri, vocabulum illud haud probare Petri Monarchiam, aut statuere myriadas Monarcharum, Paparum & summorum Pontificum in Ecclesia dari eod m tempore, quod posterius, ut absurdum & contradictorium est, ita maxime Monarchicis ingratum foret. Nam primo quidem Bellarminus ipse fassus est, supremam Ecclesiasticam potestatem & authoritatem Apostolis per verba illa: Sicut me misit pater &c. collatam esse. An igitur Petro plus conferri potuit per verbum pascere? Concedi debet saltem viventibus Apostolis verbum hoc non Monarchicam potestatem designare, id est, Petrum Monarchicam potestatem plane nunquam exercuisse, nec etiam Successorum ejus, quos in suprema potestate faciunt, primos. Et si verbum hoc praeter supremam potestatem etiam probat, ordinariam illam & perpetuam in Ecclesia esse debere, quomodo quaeso probat?
units.tr: IX. This is far more evident in the transfer of the word to the rulers of churches. Certainly nothing can be said to have been given to Peter by this word "feed" which is not also common to others, just as the "love of Christ," about which Peter was questioned, presses on all the servants of Christ (2 Cor. 5:14), and in Paul's judgment, "those who do not love Christ are anathema" (1 Cor. 16:22). So it is very necessary to admit that this word does not prove Peter's monarchy, nor establish that myriads of monarchs, popes and supreme pontiffs exist in the Church at the same time; the latter, being absurd and contradictory, would be most unwelcome even to the monarchists themselves. For first, Bellarmine himself confessed that supreme ecclesiastical power and authority were conferred on the Apostles by those words: "As the Father sent me, etc." Could more have been conferred on Peter through the word "feed"? It must be conceded at least that, while the Apostles were living, this word did not designate monarchical power; that is, Peter never exercised monarchical power at all, nor did his successors, whom they make the first in supreme power. And if this word proves, besides supreme power, that such power must be ordinary and perpetual in the Church, how, I ask, does it prove that?

units.la: X. Secundo illud ipsum, quod hic Petro per metaphoram a pastore desumtam injungitur, aliis alibi proprie, vel sub metaphoris aliis aequivalentibus injungi manifestum est. Oporteret ad hoc, quantum fieri posset, probandum, bonam partem Scripturae exscribere, cum omnes actus ministeriales Ecclesiastici huc pertineant. Evangelizare, inquit Bernhard. de consid. lib.4. cap.3. pascere est. Sed lubet paucis apud Apostolos manere. Quam late se extendit illud, sicut me misit Pater, ita & ego mitto vos? Quam illustre est illud; Ite, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes &c. An minus dicunt haec verba, quia propria sunt? Imo plus dicere videri possent, cum generaliora sint, & pastura ad praedicationem maxime respicere videatur. Pascent scientia & intelligentia; dicitur Jerem.III.10.
units.tr: X. Second, it is plain that what is here enjoined on Peter through a metaphor taken from the shepherd is enjoined elsewhere on others, either literally or under other equivalent metaphors. To prove this as far as possible, one would have to copy out a good part of Scripture, since all the ministerial acts of the Church pertain to it. "To evangelize," says Bernard (De consideratione book 4, chapter 3), "is to feed." But let us remain with the Apostles for a few points. How widely does that saying extend: "As the Father sent me, so I send you"? How illustrious is that: "Go, teach all nations, baptizing, etc."? Do these words say less because they are proper? Indeed they might seem to say more, since they are more general, and the feeding seems chiefly to look to preaching. "They shall feed you with knowledge and understanding," it is said in Jeremiah 3:15.

units.la: XI. Sed & tertio sub eadem metaphora pluribus datum idem. An unus Pastor? Unus certe Christus cum imperio & potestate absoluta; Sed hic dedit alios pastores, Eph.IV. alios, non, alium, ipse dedit, non Petrus. Et Spiritus Sanctus posuit Ephesinos Presbyteros Episcopos ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, Act.XX.28. Et Petrus compresbyter presbyteros hortatur, ut pascant gregem Dei, 1.Pet.V.1.2. An autem, ut etiam Papae & Ecclesiae Monarchae sint? Subjungere hic lubet verba Doctissimi du Pin l.c. Quasi vero, inquit, non omnes privilegium olim habuerint Apostoli, & nunc etiam habeant Episcopi omnes, qui dicuntur Ecclesiae, ac proinde ovium Christi pastores. Et paulo post; Idem fuit munus caeterorum Apostolorum omnium, & id ipse Petrus Petrus diserte tradit, Ep.1. cap.5. ubi seniores alloquens ipse consenior; pascite, qui in vobis est, gregem Dei; Eodem sensu Apostoli omnes, imo Episcopi & Presbyteri semper dicti sunt pastores ovium Christi, quod notius est, quam ut probari debeat. Et iterum: Uno verbo, quotidie in Missa de omnibus Apostolis dicitur; quos gregi tuo contulisti, praesse vicarios & pastores.
units.tr: XI. But thirdly, under the same metaphor the same thing is given to many. Is there one shepherd? Certainly one is Christ, with authority and absolute power; but here he "gave some shepherds" (Eph. 4:11): "some," not "another," he gave, not Peter. And "the Holy Spirit placed the elders of Ephesus, bishops, to feed the Church of God" (Acts 20:28). And Peter, a fellow elder, exhorts the elders "to feed the flock of God" (1 Pet. 5:1-2). But is it so that the Popes and the Church's monarchs are such? Here I wish to add the words of the most learned du Pin, loc. cit.: "As if," he says, "the Apostles did not formerly have this privilege, and all the bishops who are called churches do not now have it, and therefore are shepherds of Christ's sheep." And shortly after: "The same office belonged to all the other Apostles, and Peter himself expressly teaches this, 1 Pet. 5, where, addressing the elders as a fellow elder, he says: feed, as far as is in you, the flock of God. In the same sense all the Apostles, indeed bishops and presbyters, have always been called shepherds of Christ's sheep, which is better known than needs proof." And again: "In a word, every day in the Mass it is said of all the Apostles: whom you gave to your flock to be rulers, vicars and shepherds."

units.la: XII. Quid igitur pascere denotat, quando Petro aut aliis Ecclesiarum Rectoribus tribuitur?
units.tr: XII. What, then, does feeding mean when it is ascribed to Peter or to other rulers of the churches?

units.la: Certè ministerium Ecclesiasticum, docere, etiam exemplo, consolari, hortari, redarguere, verbo, illud omne quodam modo, quod Ministris Ecclesiae hinc inde in Scripturis & in Epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum maximè commendatur.
