Praecipuè autem alimentorum cura & praebitio, sive ductio ad pascua Verbi divini, cibi spiritualis, hoc verbo comprehenditur. Pasco à Graeco βόσκω manifeste oritur, quod & in textu vocabulum Graecum bis occurrit, cùm semel tantùm ad Petrum dicatur ποίμαινε; βόσκω autem pasturam respicit sive cibationem, hinc à Fut. βόσω est βόσις cibus, & nunquam Bellarminus, vel post ipsum alius proferet locum, in quo βόσκειν Monarchicam potestatem dicat. Bernhardus Serm.2. de resur. Petrus, inquit; mandatum accepit tertiò pascere gregem Domini: pasce inquit, mente, pasce ore, pasce opere, pasce animi oratione, verbi adhortatione exempli exhibitione. Alii sic ajunt: Pasce pabulo doctrina, exemplo vita, & opum subsidio.
units.tr: Certainly it denotes the ecclesiastical ministry: to teach, also by example; to console, exhort, and rebuke by word; all of that, in a way, which is especially commended to the ministers of the Church here and there in the Scriptures, and in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus. But above all, the care and provision of food, or the leading to the pastures of the divine Word, the spiritual food, is comprehended in this word. The Latin pasco clearly comes from the Greek βόσκω [boskō], and the Greek word itself occurs twice in the text, whereas to Peter it is said only once, ποίμαινε [poimaine]. But βόσκω refers to pasture or feeding; hence from the future βόσω [bosō] comes βόσις [bosis], food. Bellarmine, or anyone after him, will never produce a passage in which βόσκειν [boskein] means monarchical power. Bernard, Sermon 2 on the Resurrection: "Peter," he says, "received the command to feed the Lord's flock three times. Feed, he says, with the mind, feed with the mouth, feed with work, feed with the prayer of the soul, with the exhortation of the word, with the display of example." Others put it this way: Feed with the fodder of doctrine, with the example of life, and with the support of resources.

units.la: XIII. Et quid jam ex eo colligere licet?
units.tr: XIII. And what may we now gather from this?

units.la: Petrum neutiquam constitutum fuisse talem Pontificem, imò per illud verbum, Pasce, ipsi non licuisse, ut talis fieret Pontifex. Mira sanè argumenti Catastrophe! Sed vera tamen & justa. Dictum fuit Petro; Pasce, id est vel maximè, doce. Ast non docent Pontifices hodierni, non docendo pascunt, inde à temporibus Gregorii Magni, quem ex bonis Episcopis Romanis ultimum, ex malis primum fuisse dicunt, paucissimi fuerunt, qui verbum Dei populo annunciaverint, nullius avus, nullius atavus, credo, pabulum hoc ex ore Pontificis gustavit; Praedicari enim, quàm praedicare malunt. Fatetur Bellarminus, plerosque eorum non concionari; Sed non proprie dicitur pascere (est illius exceptio) qui cibum quacunque ratione ministrat, sed qui procurat ac providet alteri cibum. Respondeo. 1. Licet non omnis, qui cibum quacunque ratione ministrat, pascere dicatur, oportet tamen, ut pastor cibum ministret, & qui pastor ad instar Petri esse vult, eodem modo, quo Petrus respectu verborum Christi id sibi faciendum putavit. Ast Petrus, quamvis pro ratione muneris Apostolici, lici, etiam aliis, ut officium facerent, invigilaverit, tamen vel maximè ipse, quod suum erat, fecit, & verbo fideles pavit immediatè, prout etiam in loco, quem Bellarminus allegat, Luc.XII. fidelis dispensatoris esse dicitur, Ἀδόναι ἐν καιρῷ τὸ σιτομέτρεον, ut det in tempore justam cibi mensuram, & in hoc differt Oeconomus à Domino, ut ille præscribat; Hic partiaturic autem non aliis functionem sibi impositam demandare potest, qui post rursus alios bajulos substituant, ut faciunt in Papatu Episcopi, ipsi interea tacentes, ac si mulieres essent, quibus in Ecclesia loqui prohibitum. Si enim tantum de præscribendo aliis ageretur, quomodo Magistratus Politicus hoc respectu Ecclesiæ nutricius, imò quæris muliercula non sufficere hic posset?
units.tr: That Peter was by no means appointed to be such a Pontiff; indeed, by the word Feed it was not even permitted to him to become such a Pontiff. What a remarkable collapse of the argument! Yet it is true and just. It was said to Peter, "Feed," that is, above all, "Teach." But today's Pontiffs do not teach; by not teaching they feed no one. From the time of Gregory the Great, whom they call the last of the good Roman bishops and the first of the bad, very few have announced the Word of God to the people. No grandfather or great-grandfather of anyone, I believe, has tasted this food from the mouth of a Pontiff; they prefer to be preached about rather than to preach. Bellarmine admits that most of them do not preach. "But," he says, "one is not properly said to feed (this is his exception) who supplies food by whatever means, but who takes care and provides food for another." I reply: (1) Although not everyone who supplies food by whatever means is said to feed, it is still necessary for a shepherd to supply food, and whoever wishes to be a shepherd like Peter must do so in the same way Peter thought he had to do it in response to Christ's words. But Peter, although, in accordance with his apostolic office, he also watched over others so that they might perform their duty, nevertheless himself most of all did what was his own and fed the faithful directly with the word. So too, in the passage Bellarmine cites, Luke 12, the faithful steward is described as one who ἀποδοῦναι ἐν καιρῷ τὸ σιτομέτριον [apodounai en kairō to sitometrion], that is, gives the proper measure of food in due time. The steward differs from the Lord in this: the Lord prescribes, while the steward distributes. Yet a steward cannot hand over the office imposed on him to others, who then substitute yet other carriers, as the bishops do in the Papacy, while they themselves remain silent, as though they were women, to whom it is forbidden to speak in the Church. For if the matter concerned only prescribing to others, how could the political magistrate, a nurse of the Church in this respect, not suffice here? Or would you ask whether a mere little woman could?

units.la: XIV. Ast Romani Pontifices alios multos exercent actus pastorales
units.tr: XIV. But the Roman Pontiffs exercise many other pastoral acts

units.la: (est alia Bellarmini exceptio, sive responsio) dum ligant, solvunt, dispensant, controversias judicant, Episcopos creant. Nempe laboriosum Bó oвe refugiunt, quæ dominii speciem habent, tantum affectant, imò plane aliena & verbo Christi contraria agunt. Ligare & solvere per verbi prædicationem & applicationem fieri ostendimus; Dispensatores mysteriorum Dei plures sunt, sed quòd per pecuniarias dispensationes jura humana divinaque violantur, id Petri Successoribus parum convenit, & ejusmodi scelera vel sine summis Pontificibus peragi possent; Controversiarum judicium immeritò, imò impiè ad se rapiunt; Episcopos & Presbyteros creârunt Apostoli quivis, & Dominus messis nusquam dicit, se nonnisi per Papam operarios emissurum. Et quæcunque hic officia prætexantur, minora certè sunt illo prædicationis, quod & Apostoli omnibus aliis anteponendum esse censuerunt, dicentes: Non est bonum, ut nos relinquentes sermonem Dei mensis serviamus Act. VI.v.2.
units.tr: (this is another exception or answer of Bellarmine) while they bind, loose, dispense, judge controversies, create bishops. Indeed they shun the laborious work, which has the appearance of lordship; they merely aim at that, and even act in ways that are wholly alien and contrary to the word of Christ. We have shown that binding and loosing is done through the preaching and application of the word. There are many dispensers of the mysteries of God, but that they violate human and divine law through financial dispensations is hardly fitting for the successors of Peter, and such crimes could be carried out even without the supreme Pontiffs. They wrongly, indeed impiously, seize for themselves the judgment of controversies. Any apostle created bishops and elders, and the Lord of the harvest nowhere says that he will send out workers only through the Pope. And whatever offices are pretended here, they are certainly less than that of preaching, which the apostles also judged should be placed above all others, saying: It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables, Acts 6:2.

units.la: XV. Quod per se concionando non faciunt; Respondet Bellarminus, per alios faciunt.
units.tr: XV. That they do not do this by preaching themselves; Bellarmine answers that they do it through others.

units.la: Quàm benè id faciant, quàm salubria sint ista pascua, vel potiùs quàm venenatis herbis referta, à nostris jugiter ostenditur. Sed & sic concionantur, ut tamen nesciant, quid, quando, quoties aut per quos, & concionando contraria docent, per Jesuitas plerosque, prædestinationem esse ex prævisO bono usu liberi arbitrii; per Dominicanos; Dogma hoc esse Pelagianum; per Jesuitas rursus; se esse supra Concilia & supra Reges, quos regnis suis exuere possint; per Sorbonicos contrà; sententiam hanc esse multis nominibus damnosam & perniciosam, & sic deinceps in aliis etiam maximi momenti articulis. Sed & quaeritur, an ita officium sibi demandatum aliquis relinquere possit aliis? Regula certè juris est: Mandatarius, quod in mandatum accepit, alii mandare non potest. Et aliter etiam ac isti Pontifices verba Christi intellexisse videtur Petrus: Et cur non & caetera per alios fieri possunt? Et quomodo non, qui ipsi per se pascunt, majori jure pastores sunt, quàm ejusmodi Pontifices? Ast ita per illa praecepti verba institutus est principatus, ut tamen potestas collata non pendeat ab observatione praecepti, quemadmodum etiam Pro-Rex non rectè provinciam regens non definit esse Pro-Rex, donec à Rege revocetur; Et quemadmodum Valerius Episcopus Hipponensis & alii nonnulli vel senio vel linguae vitio impediti per suos Presbyteros concionandi munus implebant. Ita tandem excipit Bellarminus. Cui porrò Respondeo. 1. Qualis per illa verba principatus institutus sit, adhuc disquirimus. 2. Frivolum planè illud est, principatum ita institutum fuisse ut tamen potestas collata non pendeat ab observatione praecepti. Volunt probare, Petrum principatum accepisse, quia ipsi dictum sit; Pasce; ajunt tamen eum principatum habuisse, etsi non pavisset! Lepida hominum ingenia! Petrus igitur pastor factus est, ut esset princeps, & non princeps, ut esset pastor? Imò princeps esse potuit & non pastor! Apostoli dignitatem & munus retinuissent, si aut Evangelium omninò praedicare noluissent, aut doctrinam Evangelii pravis erroribus corrupissent! Forte ut Judas proditor factus!
units.tr: How well they do it, how wholesome these pastures are, or rather how full of poisonous herbs, is constantly shown by our people. But they preach in such a way that they do not know what, when, how often, or through whom; and in preaching they teach contrary things: through the Jesuits, for the most part, that predestination is based on foreseen good use of free will; through the Dominicans, that this dogma is Pelagian; through the Jesuits again, that they themselves are above councils and above kings, whom they can strip of their kingdoms; through the Sorbonnists, on the other hand, that this opinion is harmful and pernicious in many respects; and so on in other articles of the greatest importance. But it is also asked whether anyone can thus leave to others the office entrusted to himself. Surely the rule of law is: One who has received a commission cannot commit it to another. And Peter seems to have understood the words of Christ differently from these Pontiffs. Why then can the other things not also be done through others? And how is it that those who feed by themselves are not, by a greater right, shepherds than such Pontiffs? But by those words of precept the principate was so instituted that the power conferred does not depend on the observance of the precept, just as a viceroy who does not govern his province rightly does not cease to be viceroy until he is recalled by the King; and just as Valerius, Bishop of Hippo, and several others, hindered by old age or by a defect of speech, carried out the office of preaching through their elders. Thus at last Bellarmine takes exception. To this I reply: (1) What sort of principate was instituted by those words we are still investigating. (2) That it was instituted in such a way that the power conferred does not depend on the observance of the precept is utterly frivolous. They want to prove that Peter received the principate because it was said to him, "Feed"; yet they say he had the principate even if he did not feed! What charming cleverness of men! So Peter became a shepherd in order to be a prince, and a prince and not a shepherd? Rather, he could have been a prince and not a shepherd! The apostles would have retained their dignity and office if they had either not wanted to preach the Gospel at all, or had corrupted the doctrine of the Gospel with foul errors! Perhaps like Judas, who became a traitor!

units.la: XVI. Quod de Pro-Rege ait, ipsum planè non juvat, & parùm huc facit, cùm non per omnia similis sit ratio Ecclesiasticorum & Politicorum munerum, & Pro-Rex quidem maneat multa malè agens, sed non, officium omninò non agens, ut hîc de Pontificibus, qui omninò non pascunt, prout mandatum est, loquimur, & etiam non maneat rebellis & sub Regis nomine subditos contra Regem armans, imò non maneret ullus non rectè provinciam regens, si Rex sciret, & injustitiae ofor esset, & subditorum amans, tunc certè vastatorem, usurpatorem & Tyrannum rejiceret. Haec autem de Christo praesumere non modò licet, sed & oportet, à quo ejusmodi Pro-Reges primò constitutos esse non probant, & à quo eos non esse constitutos probamus, & qui per quamlibet demonstrationem ex verbo, illos Pro-Reges suos minimè esse, sed in omni emphasi Antichristo, id est, qui quidem pro-Christi esse velint, interim tamen contra Christum sint, manifestum ftum facit attendentibus. Cæterum bene facit Bellarminus,quòd hîc ipse non observationem præcepti, non rectam administrationem provinciæ simpliciter præsupponit.
units.tr: XVI. What he says about the viceroy does not help him at all, and has little bearing here, since the reasoning of ecclesiastical and political offices is not in every respect similar. A viceroy indeed remains while doing many things badly, but he does not remain while not performing his office at all, as we are speaking here of Pontiffs who do not feed at all, as was commanded. Nor does he remain a rebel, arming subjects against the King under the King's name. Indeed, there would be no viceroy who did not govern his province rightly if the King knew, and were not an enemy of injustice and a lover of his subjects; then he would certainly reject a devastator, usurper and tyrant. But this may not only be presumed about Christ, but must be, since we do not prove that such viceroys were first appointed by him, and we prove that they were not appointed by him; and by whatever demonstration from the Word, it makes plain to attentive readers that those viceroys of his are by no means his, but are in every sense Antichrist, that is, men who wish indeed to be for Christ, yet meanwhile are against Christ. Nevertheless Bellarmine does well in that here he does not simply presuppose the observance of the precept, or the right administration of the province.

units.la: XVII. Haud magis Bellarminum juvat, allatum Valerii exemplum, de quo Possidonius in vita Augustini cap.5. refert, eum, cùm homo Græcus fuerit, Latinámque Linguam & literas non calluerit, ideò Augustini operâ in concionando libenter usum fuisse, interim tamen, quoad per ætatem licuerit, suo munere fungi nunquam desitisse. An autem sequitur; hic & alii nonnulli vel senio, vel linguæ vitio impediti, per alios concionabantur, illo tempore, quod Episcopum, qui concionari aut nollet, aut per cognitionis defectum non posset, nullum vidit. E. Papis licet nunquam concionari, cùm per ætatem & valetudinem possent, aut tales possunt eligi, qui tam apti ad concionandum sunt, quàm bos ad volandum, quales certè secula maximè præterita complures dederunt ? Sed molestum est concionari, & insuper impedit pompam & voluptates seculi. Martha Martha; Sollicita es de multis, unum est necessarium! Sed & audiant Gregorium M. Papam & illum : Mercenarius, inquit in Joh.X. quidem est, qui locum quidem Pastoris tenet, sed lucra animarum non quærit, terrenis honoribus inhiat, temporalibus lucris pascitur, impensâ sibi honoris revera latatur.
units.tr: XVII. Bellarmine is no more helped by the example of Valerius, which Possidius reports in the life of Augustine, chapter 5: that he, since he was a Greek and did not have a good command of the Latin language and literature, therefore gladly used Augustine's services in preaching, yet, as far as his age allowed, never ceased to discharge his own office. But does it follow? This man and some others, hindered either by old age or by a defect of speech, preached through others at that time, because they saw no bishop who either would not preach or could not through lack of knowledge. Therefore the Papists may never preach, though they could do so by reason of age and health, or such men can be chosen as are as fit for preaching as an ox is for flying, which the most recent ages have certainly produced in great numbers? But preaching is troublesome, and besides it hinders the pomp and pleasures of the world. Martha, Martha; you are anxious about many things; one thing is needful! But let them also hear Pope Gregory the Great, who says on John 10: He is a hireling who indeed holds the place of a shepherd, but does not seek the gain of souls, pants after earthly honours, is fed by temporal profits, and in truth rejoices in the honour bestowed upon himself.

units.la: XVIII. Addendum hîc videtur, quod Bellarminus inter ratiunculas Lutheri posuit ; Majorem Pontificum partem neque diligere gregem neque etiam exemplo pascere. Sed respondit planè non ad hæc! Ad hanc objectionem, vel objectionis partem mutus ut piscis omninò siluit, nisi verba de non recta administrata provincia & non observatione præcepti huc etiam trahi debeant; Nempe nihil attinebat, hæc specialiùs tangere; Periculosum erat de his loqui, de quibus tamen clamant monumenta seculorum & proclamant, fuisse monstra & propudia generis humani, Apostaticos, Apotacticos; Et difficile erat respondere; Eligebatur igitur de non sanctis sanctum silentium. Licebit tamen nobis loqui, & paucis interrogare; An, si Petro principatus ob magnitudinem amoris, & juxta Cajetanum de R. P. instit. c. 8. persona Petri charitate qualificata, obtigit, verisimile sit, illos etiam, qui Christum non tantùm non plus cæteris hominibus aut Ecclesiarum Rectoribus, sed planè non diligunt, imò contrà eum & oves ejus odio habent & persequuntur, & nec verbo, nec exemplo pascunt, proinde nec pascunt, quia diligunt, neque diligunt, ut pascant, Principatum tamen & dominium in universam Ecclesiam cum Petro ex æquo accepisse. Forsan & hæc objectio sive ratiuncula responsionem aliquam meruisset!
units.tr: XVIII. It seems worth adding here what Bellarmine put among Luther's little arguments: The greater part of the Popes neither love the flock nor feed it by example. But he plainly did not answer this! To this objection, or part of the objection, he kept a complete silence, like a mute fish, unless the words about the province not being rightly administered and the precept not being observed are to be dragged in here as well. Clearly there was no point in touching these matters more specifically; it was dangerous to speak of things of which the records of the ages nevertheless cry out and proclaim that they were monsters and disgraces of the human race, apostates, apotactics; and it was difficult to reply; so a holy silence was chosen about unholy things. Still, we may be allowed to speak and to ask a few questions. If the primacy was given to Peter on account of the greatness of his love, and, according to Cajetan, On the Institution of the Roman Pontiff, ch. 8, the person of Peter was qualified by charity, is it likely that those who not merely do not love Christ more than other men or the rectors of the churches, but plainly do not love him at all, and on the contrary hate him and his sheep and persecute them, and feed them neither by word nor by example, and therefore do not feed them because they do not love, and do not love in order to feed, have nevertheless received the principate and dominion over the whole Church equally with Peter? Perhaps this objection, or little argument, would have deserved some answer!

units.la: XIX. Satis jam ostendimus, Petrum per præceptum Christi; pasce; non constitutum fuisse talem Pontificem, imo per istud præceptum ei non licuisse, ut fieret talis Pontifex, ex eo, quòd illi non faciant, quæ Christi præceptum Petro imposuerat; Idem porro ostendamus ex eo, quòd sub prætextu hujus præcepti & Successionis Petri talia sibi tribuunt, quæ Petrus, cui dictum; Pasce; nec habuit, nec habere potuit, & quæ cum illo; pasce aperte pugnant: Sibi tribuunt Dominatum & quidem absolutum, supremum, sed aliter sonat sermo pastoralis Pauli, & credo eos daturos hic saltem Petri & Pauli paritatem; Non nos prædicamus, inquit, 2. Cor. IV. 5. Sed Christum Jesum Dominum, nos autem servos vestros propter Jesum Christum. Ergo, qui pascere jubetur, dominari prohibetur. Sed audiamus porrò, Pontifices inde ab aliquot seculis, qualia sibi & qualia ipsis alii, & quidem quasi vi hujus præcepti tribuant. Gregorius VII. in excommunicatione Imperatoris apud Platinam allegavit verba: Pasce oves meas. Bellarminus (qui tamen in doctrina de potestate Papæ temporali adeò non satisfecit, dum nonnisi indirectam eam esse docuit, ut parùm abfuerit, quin ideò omnia ejus Scripta, Papismo cæterùm maximè extollendo destinata & nata, à Sixto V. condemnarentur) ita ex præcepto Christi infert; pastori necessariam esse potestatem lupos arcendi omni ratione, quâ poterit, arietes furiosos recludendi & oves pascendi, ita ut convenit eis. Becanus autem magis aperte in controversia sua Anglicana pag.146. Canes quàm diu fidi sunt, inquit, apud se retinet pastor pro tutela & protectione ovium: Sin rabidi aut negligentes, aut ovibus infesti evadunt, mox submovet, & ab officio repellit: Et mox, quasi priora applicans: Igitur hi canes, quàm diu fidi & excitati sunt, Pastori ad manus esse debent. At si languidi & otiosi, si rabidi, si inquieti, si ovibus molesti esse incipiunt, mox à pastore submovendi & à pastore repellendi sunt. Hoc dictat recta ratio. XX. Id igitur hi homines docuerunt & docent, quotquot Papæ potestatem temporalem sive directam sive indirectam adscribunt, vi hujus dicti; pasce; ei competere jus Imperatores, Reges & Principes alios tanquam rapaces lupos ab Ecclesia vi arcendi, partim tanquam arietes furiosos recludendi, partim tanquam rabidos, ovibus infestos, aut saltem languidos & otiosos canes, id est, exexplicantibus id alibi aliis, non satis in exstirpatione haereticorum diligentes, qualis Henricus III. Galliarum Rex caeterum Pontificiae Religionis tenacissimus, à Monacho Jacobo Clemente, Sixto V. ob id plurimùm laudato occisus, fuit, submovendi & ab officio repellendi, id est, testibus iisdem Doctoribus & experientiâ, deponendi, regna illorum primo occupanti donandi, subditos illorum à juramento fidelitatis absolvendi; imò eos, (quod tamen non omnes aperte cum Mariana & aliis profiteri audent, cùm id interim recta ratio aeque dictet; nonne enim & lupi & arietes furiosi aut otiosi occidi possunt?) è medio tollendi; Hæc illis recta ratio dictat, hàc omni ratione pastor, secundùm illos, lupos arcere potest! Hoc illis est, pascere oves prout iis convenit!
units.tr: XIX. We have now sufficiently shown that Peter was not appointed such a Pontiff by Christ's precept, feed; nor was it even lawful for him to become such a Pontiff by that precept, since those men do not do what Christ's precept imposed on Peter. Let us next show the same from the fact that, under the pretext of this precept and of the succession of Peter, they claim for themselves things which Peter, to whom it was said feed, neither had nor could have, and which clearly clash with feed. They claim for themselves dominion, and indeed absolute and supreme dominion; but the pastoral language of Paul sounds otherwise, and I think they will grant here at least the equality of Peter and Paul: We do not preach ourselves, he says, 2 Cor. 4:5, but Christ Jesus the Lord, and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. Therefore, he who is bidden to feed is forbidden to lord it over others. But let us hear further what the Popes, for some centuries now, have claimed for themselves and attributed to others, and indeed as if by virtue of this precept. Gregory VII, in the excommunication of the Emperor, according to Platina, cited the words: Feed my sheep. Bellarmine (who nevertheless in the doctrine on the temporal power of the Pope satisfied so little, while he taught that it is only indirect, that it hardly fell short of making all his writings, aimed at and born for extolling Popery above all else, condemned by Sixtus V) thus infers from Christ's precept: it is necessary for the shepherd to have the power to ward off wolves by every means he can, to drive back furious rams, and to feed the sheep as is fitting for them. Becanus more openly, in his English controversy, p. 146: As long as dogs are faithful, the shepherd keeps them at hand for the protection and defence of the sheep; but if they become rabid or negligent, or hostile to the sheep, he at once removes them and drives them from office. And soon after, applying the former points as it were: Therefore these dogs, as long as they are faithful and alert, ought to be at the shepherd's hand. But if they become languid and idle, if rabid, if restless, if troublesome to the sheep, they must at once be removed by the shepherd and driven from his service. Right reason dictates this.

units.la: XXI. Sed certè non ita pavit oves Petrus, talis Pastor non fuit. Nullam sibi in Reges & Regna terrae potestatem arrogâsse legitur; Imperatores & Reges in Ecclesiam Christianam scelestè grassantes non depositit; mullum eorum vitâ privavit, eorum subditos nunquam à Juramento fidelitatis absolvit; Sed & ipse potestati supereminenti obediens, obedientiam aliis etiam erga difficiles Dominos & patientiam commendavit; adeóque si ita oves pascere convenit, in officio planè negligens fuit, & verbi, pasce; emphasin minimè intellexisse dicendus erit. Quod judicium quoque de omnibus per mille fere annos Episcopis Romanis ferri debet.
units.tr: XXI. But certainly Peter did not feed the sheep in that way; he was not such a shepherd. It is read that he claimed no power for himself over the kings and kingdoms of the earth; he did not depose emperors and kings who raged wickedly against the Christian Church; he deprived none of them of life; he never absolved their subjects from the oath of allegiance. Rather, himself obeying the supreme power, he commended obedience to others, even towards difficult masters, and patience. And so, if it were fitting to feed the sheep in that way, he must be said to have been wholly negligent in his office, and not to have understood the emphasis of the word feed at all. The same judgment should also be passed on all the Roman bishops for almost a thousand years.

units.la: XXII. Quod enim excipiunt; Petrum & caeteros jus quidem ita pascendi habuisse, sed non vires sufficientes, & ideo exercitium potestatis tamdiu abfuisse; illud planè frivolum est, cùm Christus primò, si ita pascere oves convenire, ante mille annorum decursum sufficientibus viribus Ecclesiae Rectores instruere potuisset; Secundò Petro non defuerint vires, qui Ananiam tam facilè sustulit & Sapphiram, & ad cujus praesentiam Deus tot alia miracula operatus est; Tertiò nec vires defuerint Pastoribus, Tertulliani jam tempore, ipso teste, sufficientes & multò magis post; & quartò denique satis sic per istam exceptionem doceant, magis in magnitudine virium, dolo suo & indulgentia principum auctarum fundatum esse illum pascendi modum, quàm verò in verbo Christi: Pasce:
units.tr: XXII. As for what they object, that Peter and the others indeed had the right to feed in this way but not sufficient strength, and that therefore the exercise of the power was absent for so long, that is entirely frivolous. First, if it was fitting to feed the sheep in that way, Christ could have equipped the rectors of the Church with sufficient strength before a thousand years had passed. Second, Peter did not lack strength, he who so easily destroyed Ananias and Sapphira, and in whose presence God worked so many other miracles. Third, the ministers did not lack sufficient strength, which by Tertullian's own testimony was there already in his time, and much more so afterwards. And fourth, finally, by this exception they sufficiently teach that that mode of feeding is founded more on the greatness of their strength, their own craft and the indulgence of princes, than on the word of Christ: Feed:

units.la: XXIII. Et certè mirum est illud; pasce oves meas, id est, macta duces ovium; pasce oves meas, id est, abduc eas à caulis; pasce oves oves meas; id est, dissipa, fuga oves meas, fac ut conculcentur pascua earum, ut turbida fiat aqua illarum, quod ordinarium est consequens excommunicationis & depositionis Principum. Haec pastoralis fistula non dulce canit; mala est haec herba, amarus cibus. Hoc est pascere gladio Mich. V.6. absynthio & succo cicuta, Jerem. IX. 15. Sed nec Pascere tale commendavit Petrus: Pascite gregem, inquit, 1.Epist. v. 2.3.non coacte tanquam dominantes Clero, id est, fidelibus; Nec etiam talis gratia referenda est Ecclesiae nutriciis, tutoribus; ψ̓δὲ Φονικῶς τε καὶ τυραννικῶς, ἀλλ' ἀποστολικῶς τε καὶ πνευματικῶς; Id est, Non per cadem & tyrannice, sed Apostolice & spiritualiter hoc fieri debet, ut Greg. Nazianz. de electione Athanasii verba hic applicemus. Hoc non est bene ... Alia in textu Petro, alia aliis alibi injuncta esse, supra ex Scripturis ostendimus, alia & multum ab hisce diversa. Ut denuò concludere liceat; Petrum per verbum pasce neutiquam constitutum fuisse talem Pontificem, imò per illud verbum; pasce; ipsi non licuisse, ut talis fieret Pontifex. Quantò vero rectius Bellarmino & aliis Benedictus Justinianus in t. Ep. Petri cap. V. scripsit Jesuita & ipse: Qui ex verba pascendi, cum Christus apud Johannem Petro dixit, Pasce agnos, & Pasce oves, colligunt, Petro ejusque Successoribus orbis terrae totius Imperium ac Dominatum fuisse concessum, perperam argumentantur, vitiose que concludunt, & denique Patribus priscis omnibus adversantur. Sed satis jam de illo verbo, & actu pastorali ipso, judicet aequus lector, an recte dixerit Bellarminus: Nobis non difficile erit, ex hac ipsa voce, pasce, demonstrare summam potestatem illi attribui, cui dicitur: pasce oves meas; & cogitet, quam late se extendat illa summa potestas Bellarminiana; Nos autem ad omnes ejus demonstrationes sigillatim respondimus, ne una quidem exceptâ.
units.tr: XXIII. And indeed that is a remarkable thing: feed my sheep, that is, slaughter the leaders of the sheep; feed my sheep, that is, lead them away from the folds; feed my sheep my sheep, that is, scatter and drive off my sheep, let their pastures be trampled and their water made muddy, which is the usual consequence of the excommunication and deposition of princes. This pastoral pipe does not sing sweetly; this is a bad herb, bitter food. This is to feed with the sword (Mic. 5.6), with wormwood and gall of hemlock (Jer. 9.15). But Peter did not recommend such feeding: Feed the flock, he says (1 Pet. 5.2, 3), not by compulsion, as lording it over the clergy, that is, over the faithful. Nor is such favour to be ascribed to the nurses and guardians of the Church: [οὐ φονικῶς τε καὶ τυραννικῶς, ἀλλ' ἀποστολικῶς τε καὶ πνευματικῶς], that is, not murderously and tyrannically, but apostolically and spiritually this ought to be done, to apply here the words of Gregory Nazianzen concerning the election of Athanasius. This is not good... Other things were enjoined on Peter in the text, and other things on others elsewhere, as we showed above from the Scriptures, things quite different from these. So, to conclude once more: Peter was by no means constituted such a Pontiff by the word feed; indeed, by that very word feed, it was not permitted to him to become such a Pontiff. How much more rightly than Bellarmine and others did Benedictus Justinianus, himself a Jesuit, write in the commentary on the Epistle of Peter, chapter 5: Those who gather from the words of feeding, when Christ said to Peter in John, Feed the lambs and Feed the sheep, that dominion and lordship over the whole world was granted to Peter and his successors, argue wrongly, conclude faultily, and in the end oppose all the ancient Fathers. But let the fair reader judge enough about that word and the pastoral act itself, whether Bellarmine spoke rightly: It will not be difficult for us to show from this very word, feed, that supreme power is attributed to him to whom it is said: feed my sheep; and let him consider how far that supreme power of Bellarmine extends. We, for our part, have answered all his demonstrations one by one, not even one excepted.

units.la: XXIV. Considerandum nunc porrò sequitur objectum illius actûs sive officii pastoralis: Semel Petro dicitur: Pasce agnos meos; & bis: pasce oves meas.
units.tr: XXIV. We must now consider the object of that pastoral act or office. To Peter it is said once: Feed my lambs; and twice: feed my sheep.

units.la: Invertit haec Bellarminus, & bis legi vult; agnos meos; semel tantum; oves meas. In quo quidem vulgatam versionem contra omnium codicum fidem & Patrum Graecorum lectionem sequitur, quam ut defendat, & mysteria mox revelanda salva maneant, locum vitio librariorum corruptum esse arbitratur, & facile ipsi fuit unum Iota excidere; nimirum vult legi secunda vice προβάτα pro πρόβατα; oviculas (quae tamen non semper agni, fatente id expresse ipso Bellarmino) non; oves. Sed quomodo probat? bat? Primò testimonio Ambrosii, qui in cap. ult. Luca Petro secundò oviculas, quæ dicantur Græcè ωρεβάπα, commendatas esse ait. Sed posito, eum in Textu Græco quodam sic legisse, an non potiùs sequendi essent tot alii? Verùm non dicit, in Textu Græco se ita legisse, & forte aliquid sibi indulsit mysterium captans, quamvis, ut mox dicetur, à Bellarminiano illo primario diversum. De Maximo, cujus testimonium subjungit Bellarminus, minor est certitudo, eum legisse in textu Græco ωρεβάπα, alias enim dicere potuit serm. de Sanctis Petro & Paulo; Petro commendatas esse oviculas & oves, sive, per oviculas agnos intelligens, quomodo oviculas & agnos idem esse arguit etiam Bellarminus, prima vice commendatas, sive inter oves minores & majores distinguens. Versionis autem vulgatæ, ad quam porrò Bellarminus provocat, authoritas apud nos non est suprema, & facilè hîc per incuriam in secunda vice agnos pro ovibus ponere potuit author, minimè forte cogitans de aliquo, quod hîc subesse debeat, mysterio. Ut etiam, juxta confessionem Bellarmini non satis accuratè vertisset ωρεβάπα agnos, cùm sæpè tantùm oviculæ & agni pro eisdem accipiantur. Sed in eo satis accuratus fuit, quia sic fundavit mysterium.
units.tr: Bellarmine reverses this and wants it read twice as my lambs and only once as my sheep. In doing so he follows the Vulgate against the agreement of all the manuscripts and the reading of the Greek Fathers. To defend this, and to keep intact the mysteries he is about to reveal, he thinks the passage has been corrupted by the errors of scribes, and it was easy for him to suppose that one iota had dropped out. He wants the second occurrence read as [προβάτια] for [πρόβατα], that is, little sheep (which, however, are not always lambs, as Bellarmine himself expressly admits), rather than sheep. But how does he prove this? First, by the testimony of Ambrose, who in his commentary on the last chapter of Luke says that the little sheep, called in Greek [προβάτια], were commended to Peter a second time. But granting that Ambrose so read in some Greek text, should not so many others be followed instead? Yet he does not say that he read it so in the Greek text, and perhaps he indulged himself a little in seeking a mystery, although, as will be said shortly, it differs greatly from Bellarmine's primary one. As for Maximus, whose testimony Bellarmine adds, there is less certainty that he read [προβάτια] in the Greek text. Otherwise he could have said in his sermon on the saints Peter and Paul that little sheep and sheep were commended to Peter, or he meant by little sheep the lambs, as Bellarmine himself argues that little sheep and lambs are the same, commended the first time, or he distinguished between the smaller and the larger sheep. As for the authority of the Vulgate, to which Bellarmine appeals further, it has no supreme authority with us, and the author could easily have carelessly put lambs for sheep in the second instance, perhaps hardly thinking of any mystery that ought to lie hidden here. Likewise, by Bellarmine's own admission, he would not have translated [προβάτια] accurately enough as lambs, since often little sheep and lambs are taken for the same thing. But in this he was accurate enough, because it is on this that he founded his mystery.

units.la: XXV. Quale autem? multiplex.
units.tr: XXV. What sort, then? A manifold one.

units.la: Nam ex latitudine objecti tandem Petro prærogativam Monarchicam cudere volunt, & quia negare non possunt pascere multis demandatum esse, ita effugere conantur, ut dicant, cæteris partem tantùm gregis Dominici commissam esse, & sic Petrum Presbyteros hortari ποίμανε τὰ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον & Θεοῦ, pascite, qui in vobis est; (quamvis Erasmus sine læsione Textûs Originalis vertendum putet; quantum in vobis est,) gregem Dei, 1. Pet. V. 2. Ipsum autem omnibus omnino Christi fidelibus præfectum esse; quare Bellarminus, ut probet per oves meas intelligi universam Ecclesiam, &, quod sibi exploratum certùmque esse ait, omnes omninò Christianos, etiam Apostolos ipsos, Petro tanquam oviculas (en! Apostoli ipsi jam sunt oviculæ, quos tamen mox ab oviculis solicitè distinguet, & in ista distinctione fundamentum argumentationis suæ constituet!) commendari, cùm ei dicitur: pasce oves meas; ut inquam illud probet Bellarminus, toto cap. XVI. satis prolixo omnem movet lapidem, & primò ad mysteria confugit, Ex hac variatione, dum bis agni, semel oves ponuntur, quæ mysterio non videtur carere, probamus. Inquit; Mysterio non carere tantùm videtur, & tamen probat. Sed quid? Petro omnes Christianos esse subjectos. stos. Sufficit hoc probâsse ex variatione, quæ mysterio non videtur carere. Sed quomodo probat? Nam, si per Oviculas intelligamus agnos (si dubitantis est; possunt igitur per oviculas non agni intelligi, id est, potest probatio ejus suo carere fundamento, licet variatio non videatur carere mysterio; jam expressè id fassus est. Egregia probatio ex incerto!) dicemus (quod Patrum nullus dixit), agnos bis repetitos esse, ad significandum duos populos, Judaicum & Gentilem, oves autem semel nominatas significare Episcopos (quibus paulò post Apostolos adjungit) qui sunt veluti matres agnorum; & quorum omnium curam Dominum Petro commisse, addit. Pulchrè, nihil supra! pergit autem Doctor mysticus:
units.tr: For from the breadth of the object they want at last to hammer out a monarchical prerogative for Peter. And because they cannot deny that feeding was committed to many, they try to escape by saying that only a part of the Lord's flock was entrusted to the others, and that so Peter exhorts the elders: feed the flock of God which is among you (1 Pet. 5.2) [ποίμανε τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον τοῦ Θεοῦ], feed, as far as is in you (though Erasmus thinks it should be rendered, without harm to the original text, as far as in you lies); but that Peter himself was set over all the faithful of Christ without exception. Therefore Bellarmine, in order to prove that by my sheep the whole Church is meant, and, which he says is certain and settled for him, that all Christians without exception, even the Apostles themselves, are commended to Peter as little sheep (see! the Apostles themselves are now little sheep, whom nevertheless he will carefully distinguish from the little sheep, and on this distinction he will build his argument!) when it is said to him: feed my sheep; that, I say, Bellarmine may prove, he moves every stone throughout the whole rather lengthy sixteenth chapter, and first has recourse to mysteries: From this variation, when lambs are named twice and sheep once, which does not seem to lack a mystery, we prove it. He says: it seems not to lack a mystery, and yet he proves it. But what follows? That all Christians are subject to Peter. It is enough to have proved this from the variation, which does not seem to lack a mystery. But how does he prove it? For, if by little sheep we understand lambs (if this is said with doubt, then little sheep may be understood as not lambs, that is, his proof may lack its foundation, even though the variation does not seem to lack a mystery; and he has already expressly admitted this), we shall say (which none of the Fathers said) that the lambs are repeated twice to signify the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile, while the sheep, named once, signify the bishops (to whom shortly afterwards he adds the Apostles), who are, as it were, the mothers of the lambs; and the care of all these, he adds, the Lord committed to Peter. Splendid, nothing more! The mystical doctor goes on:

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Si verò per oviculas intelligimus (aliud, Si, mysterium aliud; hic datur mysteriorum optio;) oves parvas, majores agnis, minores perfectis ovibus (igitur oviculæ etiam sunt oves, sed parvæ; Sunt agnis majores; igitur ab agnis diversæ, En! mysterium unum tollit alterum!) dicendum erit cum S. Ambrosio, loco notato, Petro committi agnos, oviculas & oves, id est, incipientes, proficientes & perfectos, ita ut nulli sint in Ecclesia, quantumvis Spirituales, eruditi & Sancti, qui Petro non subsint. Hæc postrema verba Bellarmini glossa sunt. Hodie Petro nec agni, nec oviculæ, nec oves subsunt, cùm non ampliùs pascat, sed pascatur beatitudine. Donec autem in terris pavit, diversi generis, statûs, incrementi homines, incipientes, proficientes & perfectos etiam comparatè sic dictos, pavit omninò post resurrectionem à Domino magister factus non tantùm tenerorum, sed & robustiorum & profectiorum, cùm antea timidus fuisset ipse. Hoc Ambrosius dicit & intendit, ast Petro etiam Apostolos, (quod istis hominibus exploratum certúmque est) qui nullius nisi Christi oves unquam fuerint, licèt istis nonnunquam oviculæ Petro commissæ videantur, & qui omnes auditores diversorum profectuum & oves æquè diversas sibi commissas habuerunt, (ut certè Paulus non tantùm cum carnalibus & infantibus in Christo lacte adhuc opus habentibus, sed & cum adultioribus solidum cibum postulantibus rem habuit, & sapientiam inter perfectos locutus est;) Apostolos, inquam, Petro tanquam concreditas oves unquam subfuisse, non dicit, nunquam dixit, nec ante eum, aut ejus tempore alius, cùm mens ista æquè antiquitati ac Scripturarum veritati sit contraria.
units.tr: If, however, by the little sheep we understand (another "if," another mystery; here we are offered a choice of mysteries) little sheep, greater than lambs and less than full-grown sheep (so the little sheep are also sheep, only small; they are greater than lambs, therefore different from lambs. See! one mystery cancels the other!) we must say, with St Ambrose in the passage noted, that the lambs, the little sheep and the sheep, that is, beginners, those making progress and the perfect, were committed to Peter, so that there is no one in the Church, however spiritual, learned and holy, who is not subject to Peter. These last words are Bellarmine's gloss. Today neither lambs, nor little sheep, nor sheep are subject to Peter, since he no longer feeds but is fed with blessedness. But while he fed on earth, he fed people of different kinds, conditions and growth, beginners, those making progress and the perfect, even those so called in a comparative sense. Certainly, after the resurrection, when he had been made a teacher by the Lord, he fed not only the tender but also the stronger and more advanced, although he had been timid before. Ambrose says and means this. But that Peter had the Apostles (which is established and certain for these men) also committed to him, who were never the sheep of anyone but Christ, although to some of them little sheep committed to Peter sometimes seem to be, and who all had hearers of different degrees of progress and sheep equally diverse committed to them (as Paul certainly dealt not only with the carnal and infants in Christ who still need milk, but also with the more mature who ask for solid food, and spoke wisdom among the perfect), that the Apostles, I say, were ever subject to Peter as sheep entrusted to him, he does not say, and no one ever said, nor did anyone before him or in his time, since this notion is as contrary to antiquity as it is to the truth of Scripture.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Sequitur tertium mysterium; Vel per agnos intelligemus populos, qui nullam habent curam pastoralem, quaque solùm filii sunt, sunt, non parentes: per oviculas accipiemus Sacerdotes minores, id est, Presbyteros & Parochos, qui sic Parentes sunt populorum, ut sint filii Episcoporum (En! argumentum, quod vel solum hoc mysterium ab utilitate commendare posset! probat Presbyteros jure divino Episcopis esse inferiores;) per oves denique interpretabimur Sacerdotes majores, id est, Episcopos, qui & agnis & oviculis praesunt, & tamen etiam ipsi Petro subjiciuntur. Semper loquitur in praesenti, nam Papa & Petrus ipsis jam diu aequipollent; quando autem sic de Petro loquuntur, non est cogitandum de eximio illo Christi Apostolo jam in coelis glorioso & qui ejusmodi dominatum odit ἐως αἰδὸο πύληον; sed de Petro quodam Pontificio, id est, larva quadam & persona Petri, quam ambitioni suae obducunt. Hic parcere videtur Apostolis & apud Episcopos subsistere; illos tamen mox aeque subjicit. Atque huc videtur respexisse (videtur tantum, & rursus) S. Leo, cum 123. serm. de anniversario assumptionis suae dicit, Petrum a Christo esse propositum (praepositum) omnibus gentibus, omnibus Patribus, & omnibus Apostolis. Gentes enim agni sunt, Patres oviculae (sed Episcopi sunt oves, ut jam jam audivimus, hic autem Patres, tanta Ecclesiae fulcra, Episcopi complures, sunt rursus oviculae, crescunt, decrescunt ut Luna; hic autem habemus quartum mysterium, in quo pro Judaeis juxta primum, pro incipientibus, juxta secundum, pro Laicis juxta tertium mysterium gentes, pro Gentilibus, juxta primum, pro proficientibus, juxta secundum, pro Presbyteris juxta tertium mysterium Patres, ponuntur. Adeo mysteriorum omnia sunt plena, & magna est foecunditas, quorum tamen unum alterum destruit, ut vipera matrem, unum alterum devorat, ut vaccae tenues carne vaccas pingues carne! Prout & similiter macida manent prioribus absumptis posteriora mysteria) Apostoli oves magnae atque perfectae. Quibus sic redit debitus honos, dum ex oviculis fiunt oves magnae: & perfectae, sed Petri, & ponuntur pro perfectis, juxta secundum, pro Episcopis juxta tertium mysterium! Leonem autem, licet praepositum Apostolis Petrum dicat, quod sine Monarchica potestate concipi potest, nempe praerogativarum personalium & ordinis respectu, & circa aliquem jam primatum non nihil sibi interdum blanditus sit Leo, & inter primos nimiae praeeminentiae affectatores numerari debeat, tamen de primatu summi & ordinarii pastoris Ecclesiae universalis ac Vicarii generalis Christi ne somniasse quidem, post Illustrem de Dominis l.1. de Rep. Eccl. c.7. §.3. quam persuasissimi sumus.
units.tr: There follows the third mystery: or by the lambs we shall understand the peoples, who have no pastoral care, and who are only sons, not parents; by the little sheep we shall take the lesser priests, that is, the elders and parish priests, who are thus parents of the peoples and sons of the bishops (see! an argument which alone could commend this mystery for its usefulness: it proves that elders are inferior to bishops by divine right); finally, by the sheep we shall interpret the greater priests, that is, the bishops, who preside over both lambs and little sheep, and yet are themselves subject to Peter. He always speaks in the present tense, for the Pope and Peter have long been equivalent to them. When they speak thus of Peter, we must not think of that outstanding apostle of Christ, now glorious in heaven, who hated such lordship until the gates of Hades [ἐως αἰδὸο πύληον], but of some Papist Peter, that is, a certain mask and persona of Peter, which they draw over their ambition. Here he seems to spare the Apostles and to stop at the bishops; yet soon after he subjects them equally. And it seems that Leo looked to this (it only seems, and again) when, in sermon 123 on the anniversary of his assumption, he says that Peter was set (placed before) over all nations, all Fathers and all Apostles. For the nations are lambs, the Fathers little sheep (but bishops are sheep, as we have just heard; here, however, the Fathers, such great pillars of the Church, and many bishops, are again little sheep, they grow and shrink like the moon). Here we have a fourth mystery, in which, according to the first mystery, the Jews stand for the lambs, according to the second, beginners; for the laity, according to the third, the nations stand for the Gentiles according to the first, those making progress according to the second, and for the elders according to the third mystery the Fathers. So full of mysteries is everything, and so great is the fecundity of them, yet one destroys another, as a viper devours its mother, as lean cows eat fat cows, and as, once the former are consumed, the later mysteries remain lean as well. The Apostles are great and perfect sheep. By this the due honour is returned to them, when from little sheep they become great and perfect sheep, but Peter's; and they are placed among the perfect according to the second, and among the bishops according to the third mystery! As for Leo, although he calls Peter set before the Apostles, which can be conceived without monarchical power, namely with respect to personal prerogatives and rank, and although Leo somewhat flattered himself at times about a certain primacy already and ought to be counted among the first seekers of excessive pre-eminence, yet he had not even dreamed of the primacy of the supreme and ordinary pastor of the universal Church and vicar general of Christ, as we are fully persuaded after Illustris de Dominis, book 1 on the Church's government, chapter 7, section 3.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Satis autem est mysteriorum, imò plusquam satis Bellarminianorum deliriorum, quæ in tantum ingenium cadere potuisse, mirari possemus, nisi mala causa, quam sibi defendendam sumpserat, malis mediis agi opus habuisset. Itane in Scripturis divinitùs inspiratis mysteria fingere licet? Quid igitur non licet? Et quid non per agnos & oves intelligere æquè licet? Et qui non Scripturæ dictis simili artificio sensus absurdissimi affingi possunt? Mirum certè est, Bellarminum non etiam mysteria in hoc quæsivisse cum quibusdam, de quibus Augustinus de Civit. Dei l.14. c.7. quòd Christus bis dixit: ἀγαπᾷς με; tertiâ autem vice: φιλεῖς; & non etiam idcirco distinxisse inter amare & diligere, quæ tamen promiscuè sumi, tum ex eo, quòd Petrus molestè tulit, se ter interrogatum esse φιλεῖς με, cùm duplex ἀγαπᾷς με, præcesserit, tum ex eo, quòd Petrus semper, Tu nosti, ὅτι φιλῶ σε, respondit, apparet. Mirum est, eum non etiam mysteria quæsivisse in duplici βόσκε & unico ποίμαιν, & in eo, quod ἀρνία primùm, post πρόβατα ponuntur & in quo non? Rectè de his mysteriis Bellarminianis de Dominis l. c. c. 8. §. VI. Mysteria, quæ alii venerantur in verbis, pasce agnos, sive oviculas & oves, ut Bellarminus, à me contemnuntur in propositâ de principatu Petri quæstione, quoscunque enim significent, sive agni sint, sive oviculæ, sive oves, dummodo denotent homines curâ & institutione ad fidem indigentes, eos omnes indifferenter commendari Petro & reliquis Apostolis, arbitror non posse dubitari, illos tamen probare non possum, qui verbis illis (pasce oves meas) Petro etiam ipsorum Apostolorum curam censent à Christo fuisse commissam. Et (cui lubentius assentiuntur nonnulli) Jansenius in Harmon. Evang. c.147. Quærendum non est in eo mysterium, quòd in prima interrogatione dixerit; agnos meos, in secunda verò & tertia oves meas. Contra Vulgatam bis oves admittit, mysteria autem hîc captanda esse negat. Et sic multis nominibus inepta est prima Bellarmini probatio.
units.tr: There is enough, indeed more than enough, of Bellarmine's mysteries and nonsense; we could only wonder that such a mind could fall into them, were it not that his bad cause needed bad means to defend it. May one then invent mysteries in Scripture, which was inspired by God? Then what is not allowed? And why should it not be equally allowed to read mysteries into sheep and lambs? And can absurd meanings not be attached to the words of Scripture by the same trick? It is surely remarkable that Bellarmine did not also seek mysteries here, as some have done with the passage in Augustine, de Civit. Dei book 14, chapter 7, where Christ asked twice ἀγαπᾷς με; ("do you love me?") and the third time φιλεῖς; ("do you have affection for me?"). Nor did Bellarmine therefore distinguish between amare and diligere, which are used interchangeably. This is clear both from the fact that Peter was distressed at being asked three times φιλεῖς με, when the double ἀγαπᾷς με had come first, and from the fact that Peter always answered Tu nosti, ὅτι φιλῶ σε ("You know that I love you"). It is also remarkable that he did not seek mysteries in the double βόσκε ("feed") and the single ποίμαινε ("tend"), or in the fact that ἀρνία ("lambs") comes first and πρόβατα ("sheep") after it, and why this is not so elsewhere. Rightly does de Dominis say of these Bellarmine mysteries, l. c. c. 8. §. VI. "The mysteries which others revere in the words 'feed my lambs' or 'my little sheep and sheep', as Bellarmine has them, are despised by me in the question proposed about Peter's primacy. For whatever they signify, whether lambs, little sheep or sheep, provided they denote men who need care and instruction in the faith, I think no one can doubt that they are all committed indifferently to Peter and the other Apostles. But I cannot approve of those who, by those words ('feed my sheep'), think that the care of the Apostles themselves was committed to Peter by Christ." And Jansenius (whom some more gladly follow), in Harmon. Evang. c. 147.: "There is no mystery to be sought in the fact that in the first question he said 'my lambs', but in the second and third 'my sheep'." Against the Vulgate, he admits bis oves ("sheep" twice), but denies that mysteries are to be sought here. And so the first proof of Bellarmine is inept in many respects.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Pergit: Aliam rationem eámque insignem nobis suppeditat pronomen illud meas. Ex quo infert, omnes Christi oves Petro committi, quia omnes velint esse oves Christi. Insignis est aut ratio, aut error; si ratio, sola absurditate insignis. Petro commissæ sunt oves Christi. E. omnes oves Christi, quas habuit & habiturus est ex Judæis & Gentibus. Sunt qui dicant, ait Doctissimus du Pin l.c. istud pasce oves meas de Judæis intelligi oportere, quæ speciales dici possunt oves Christi & quarum curam Petrus veluti proprium & sibi specialiter demandatarum datarum ovium habuit: Et certè hæc sententia Doctissimo de Dominis videtur probatissima, quam & prolixè confirmare conatur l.1. de Rep.Eccl. c.8. §.10. Ubi primò ostendit, Israëlitas peculiari ratione oves Christi fuisse, utpote qui se missum esse tantum ad oves perditas domûs Israëlis Matth. X.15. professus erat, & Paulo Rom. XV. minister circumcisionis dicitur. Porrò ostendit, Petrum etiam peculiarem curam Judæorum habuisse (ex quo Bellarminus infert honorificentius ejus munus fuisse quàm Pauli, quia ipse Dominus Judæis prædicaverit; quod etsi ob dispensationem temporum factum sit, nullam tamen Judæis aut Judæorum posthac Apostolo, saltem non magnam prærogativam conciliare potuit; cùm olea ista in oleastrum degeneraverit, & prærogativa, si quæ hic Petri esset, Jacobo & Johanni communis foret, quibus pariter creditum circumcisionis Evangelium, imò magis Jacobo, quem Eusebius Metropolewς Judæorum Episcopum facit, quàm Petro propria, ut etiam Bellarminus parùm sibi & hìc constans alibi Paulo dextram ob præconium inter gentes, quæ Judæis in N.T. præla-tæ sint, concessam esse, suspicatur) illud autem ostendit ita, ut alleget loca, quibus Petro expressè Apostolatus circumcisionis Gal.II. tribuitur, & quàm difficilem se in introitu ad gentes præstiterit Act.X. & quàm solicitum in excusatione illius introitus Act.XI. nimirum timore, ne suos Judæos scandalizaret, & quomodo eodem timore ductus Gentiles conversos Judaizare coegerit Gal.II. narratur. Insuper illam peculiarem curam Petri respectu Judæorum illustrat ex simili peculiari cura Pauli respectu gentium, qui & Doctor gentium & vas electionis ad portandum nomen Christi inter gentes Act.IX. dicatur, & sibi ministerium præputii Gal.II. tribuat, se Apostolatum in omnibus gentibus accepisse Rom.I. ministrum Jesu Christi in gentibus, Apostolum gentium, Rom.XI.XV. & alibi esse testetur. Tandem ait; huic expositioni favere Gregorium Nazianzenum, qui Orat.24. ad Arian. dicat: sit Petri Judaa, Pauli gentium universitas &c. Et magis Ambrosium, qui asserat, primatum ad fundandas Ecclesias in Judaismo accepisse Petrum; primatum vero fundandi Ecclesias inter gentes, Paulum accepisse.
units.tr: He goes on: The pronoun 'my' gives us another reason, and a notable one. From this he infers that all the sheep of Christ are committed to Peter, because all want to be sheep of Christ. The reason is notable, or the error is; if a reason, it is notable only for its absurdity. The sheep of Christ were committed to Peter. Therefore all the sheep of Christ, whom he had and will have from Jews and Gentiles. There are those who say, as the very learned du Pin says in the same place, that the words 'feed my sheep' must be understood of the Jews, who may be called the special sheep of Christ, and whose care Peter had as a charge specially given to him as his own. And certainly this opinion seems to the very learned de Dominis most probable, and he tries to confirm it at length in book 1 of De Republica Ecclesiastica, chapter 8, §. 10. There he first shows that the Israelites were the sheep of Christ in a special way, since he professed that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24), and Paul is called minister of the circumcision (Rom. 15). He further shows that Peter also had a special care of the Jews. From this Bellarmine infers that his office was more honourable than Paul's, because the Lord himself preached to the Jews. Although this was done because of the dispensation of the times, it could nevertheless confer no great prerogative on the Jews or on the Apostle who was later to be sent to them, since those olives had degenerated into wild olives. And if there were any prerogative here for Peter, it would be shared by James and John, to whom the Gospel of circumcision was likewise entrusted, and indeed more by James, whom Eusebius makes bishop of the Jews, than by Peter, as Bellarmine himself, not very consistent with himself, suspects elsewhere that Paul was granted the right hand because of his proclamation among the Gentiles, to which the Jews were preferred in the New Testament. But de Dominis shows this by citing the passages in which the apostleship of the circumcision is expressly attributed to Peter (Gal. 2), and how reluctant he showed himself at the entrance to the Gentiles (Acts 10), and how anxious he was in excusing that entrance (Acts 11), namely from fear that he would scandalise his Jews; and how, driven by the same fear, he compelled the converted Gentiles to Judaize (Gal. 2). Moreover, he illustrates that particular care of Peter towards the Jews by the similar particular care of Paul towards the Gentiles, who is called teacher of the Gentiles and a chosen vessel to carry the name of Christ among the Gentiles (Acts 9), who claims for himself the ministry of the uncircumcision (Gal. 2), who says he received the apostleship among all the Gentiles (Rom. 1), minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, apostle of the Gentiles (Rom. 11, 15), and bears witness to this elsewhere. Finally he says: Gregory Nazianzen favours this interpretation, who in Oration 24 against the Arians says: let Peter's be the Jewish world, Paul's the universality of the Gentiles, etc. And even more so Ambrose, who asserts that Peter received the primacy for founding churches among the Jews, but Paul received the primacy of founding churches among the Gentiles.

units.la: XXX. Et dum his inserit; se ista ita tantùm intelligere, quòd præcipua Petri cura debuerit in Judæos extendi; omnibus illis exceptionibus Bellarminianis de Petri cura etiam inter gentes facilè occurrit, ut etiam illud, quod Doctissimus du Pin contra hanc sententiam affert, minùs stringere videtur. Sed ista interpretatio, inquit, haud videtur
units.tr: XXX. And when he adds to these: I understand these things only in the sense that Peter's chief care ought to extend to the Jews; all those Bellarminian objections about Peter's care among the Gentiles readily come to mind, and so does the point that the very learned du Pin brings against this opinion, which seems to press less. But this interpretation, he says, does not seem

units.la: Quasi sententia quodammodo ab exceptionibus liberatur; detur esse verisimilis, quia Christus nomine ovium & ovilis sui non Judaos tantùm sed omnes, qui sibi credituri erant, intelligit: Habeo, inquit, alias oves, quae non sunt ex hoc ovili, eas oportet me adducere, & fiet unum ovile & unus pastor, nempe Christus, qui pastor est bonus καὶ ἐξο-χλὼ (quae verba ultima contra Monarchicos, qui per pastorem unum Papam intelligi debere contendunt, notari possunt.) Ast videtur sufficere ad expositionem allatam, quòd Judaei peculiari modo oves Christi fuerunt, quod & citata loca evidentissimè ostendunt, & quòd, licèt ex gentibus oves adducendae erant, illae tamen tum temporis nondum de ovili isto, ad quod Christus missus fuerat, fuerunt. Si autem ista expositio valere deberet, ut certè analogiae fidei non est contraria, & verisimilitudinem hanc etiam habet, quòd Christus Dominus, sunt verba de Dominis l. c. sicut ipse nonnisi Judaeis praedicavit, ita ad majorem confusionem post ipsius discessum primum & praecipuum Apostolorum ad ipsos praecipuè destinâsse dicitur; actum jam esset de Monarchia Petri & ejus ex hoc loco probatione & omnibus argutiis Bellarminianis, cùm qualiscunque sic Petro inter Judaeos primatus tribueretur, non minor certè Paulo inter gentes, juxta citata Ambrosii verba, assignandus foret.
units.tr: to free the opinion entirely from the objections, let it be granted that it is probable, since by the name of sheep and fold Christ means not only the Jews but all who were going to believe in him. "I have other sheep," he says, "which are not of this fold; I must bring them, and there will be one fold and one shepherd," namely Christ, who is the good shepherd and καὶ ἐξοχὴν ("and pre-eminently"). (These last words can be noted against the Monarchists, who insist that by "one shepherd" the Pope must be understood.) But it seems enough for the interpretation proposed that the Jews were the sheep of Christ in a particular way, as the cited passages most clearly show, and that, although sheep were to be brought from the Gentiles, they were at that time not yet of that fold to which Christ had been sent. But if this interpretation were to hold, as it certainly is not contrary to the analogy of faith, and as it also has this probability, that Christ the Lord, the words of de Dominis, l. c., just as he preached only to the Jews, so after his departure he is said to have chiefly sent the first and principal Apostle to them, to their greater confusion, then the Monarchy of Peter and the proof from this passage, with all Bellarmine's subtleties, would already be finished. For if Peter were given any kind of primacy among the Jews, an equal primacy would certainly have to be assigned to Paul among the Gentes, according to the cited words of Ambrose.

units.la: XXXI. Sed nec illa expositio, quae oves ex gentibus aeque ac Judaeis in textu Petro committi docet, Monarchicos juvat, aut omnes omnino oves hic Petro demandari, convincit.
units.tr: XXXI. But neither does that explanation, which teaches that the sheep of the Gentiles as well as of the Jews were committed to Peter in the text, help the monarchists, nor does it prove that all the sheep whatever are entrusted to Peter here.

units.la: Quis enim non videt, Bellarminum ab indefinito, quod saepissimè particulari aequipollet, ad universale formare consequentiam pessimè? Æquipollet quidem aliquando universali, ut in illo à Bellarmino citato Joh. X. cognosco oves meas, sed non semper; Nam, quando Christus Matth. XXV. 27. ad inutilem servum dicit; Oportuit te committere pecuniam meam mensariis; exiguam tantùm pecuniae suae partem intelligit; quando Joh. XV. 14. ita discipulos alloquitur: Vos amici mei estis; Patriarchas, Prophetas & alios, eodem etiam tempore viventes, ideò ab amicitia sua non excludit; Et ut exemplum familiarius & propius detur, quando aliquis Pater familiâs diversos greges sub diversis pastoribus habens eorum aliquem antehac negligentiorem in specie compellat: Pasce oves meas; non ideò is omnibus omninò & gregibus & pastoribus cum dominio absoluto praeficitur; Propositio ista, ita rectissimè Doctissimus du Pin censet, est indefinita & in historia, ut à Dialecticis observatur, plerúmque particularis, quemadmodum illa, milites plectentes coronam de spinis. An igitur,quia aliquando ejusmodi propositiones universalibus æqui-pollent, semper æquipollere judicandum est? Imò ipsum illud, quod Bellarminus contra nos adducit, exemplum facile in favorem nostrum transferimus,dum enim Pater moriens, de quo constat,eum bona sua filiis suis relinquere velle sine exceptione omnibus,ut de Christo certissimè constat, eum præfecturam Ecclesiæ Apostolis in genere demandâsse; ad unum ex filiis,occasione certâ natâ, præmissis adhortationibus generalibus, & quando adhuc etiam subjungendæ sunt, diceret: Cave ne dissipes bona mea, sed cura,ut probè illa administres; an id de omnibus omninò Patris illius bonis, etiam de illis, quæ filiis aliis relinquere destinaverat, intelligendum foret? Non equidem puto. Et quando Pater moriens aliquot Tutores liberis suis constituit, & tutorem unum aliquot liberis constituit,eíque injungit: Habe curam liberorum meorum; An ideò omnes omninò liberi huic Tutori committuntur, & annon æquè reliqui Tutores manent? Hoc puto.
units.tr: For who does not see that Bellarmine draws a very bad inference from the indefinite to the universal, when the indefinite is very often equivalent to the particular? It is indeed sometimes equivalent to the universal, as in the passage of John 10 cited by Bellarmine, I know my sheep, but not always. When Christ says to the unprofitable servant in Matthew 25.27, You ought to have committed my money to the bankers, he means only a small part of his money. When in John 15.14 he addresses his disciples thus, You are my friends, he does not thereby exclude from his friendship the patriarchs, the prophets and others living at the same time. And to give an example more familiar and closer to hand: when a householder who has different flocks under different shepherds addresses one of them, who had been rather careless before, with the words Feed my sheep, he does not thereby set that man over all the flocks and all the shepherds with absolute dominion. That proposition, as the most learned du Pin rightly judges, is indefinite, and in historical matters, as the dialecticians observe, is for the most part particular, just as that one: soldiers plaiting a crown of thorns. Therefore, because such propositions are sometimes equivalent to universals, must we judge that they are always equivalent? Indeed we easily turn to our own favour that very example which Bellarmine brings against us. For when a dying father, of whom it is certain that he wishes to leave his goods to all his sons without exception, just as it is most certainly known of Christ that he entrusted the oversight of the Church in general to the Apostles, says to one of his sons, when a particular occasion has arisen, after general exhortations have been given and while more is still to be added: Take care not to squander my goods, but see that you manage them well; should that be understood of all that father's goods without exception, including those which he had intended to leave to his other sons? I certainly do not think so. And when a dying father appoints several guardians for his children, and appoints one guardian for some of the children and enjoins on him, Take care of my children: are all the children therefore committed absolutely to this one guardian, and do the other guardians not remain equally in charge? I think so.

units.la: XXXII. Pergit Bellarminus: Petro commendatur cura ovilis, quod unum est. E. universus grex. Quàm bene! Petro commendatur uni cura ovilis unius. Unde hoc probat Bellarminus? Ex Scriptura contrarium ostendimus; Igitur plures habuerunt curam unius ovilis? Quid obstat? An, verbi gr. Paulo non commissa est cura ovilis,quod unum est? Negare non possunt. An igitur universus grex commissus est soli? Nolent Monarchici. Cæterùm hic notandum est,ovile unum dici ratione pastoris unius illius boni, Joh. X. qui Christus est,qui pro ovibus animam suam posuit, & cujus illa vocem audiunt. Testatus de eo jam est Doctissimus du Pin. Lyranus breviter in locum: Fiet unus pastor,id est,Christus. Augustinus tract.47. in Joan. plenius; Duobus istis gregibus, quasi duobus parietibus factus est (Christus) lapis angularis. Proin solus,dum fideles in eo conjunguntur,unum ovile facit; respectu aliorum autem pastorum multa potius sunt ovilia,id est,cœtus multi, multæ Ecclesiæ,quarum quædam,cùm unus omnibus non sufficiat, Petro commissæ sunt, aliæ aliis.
units.tr: XXXII. Bellarmine goes on: The care of the fold is committed to Peter, which is one. Therefore the whole flock. How well! To Peter alone is committed the care of one fold of one. From what does Bellarmine prove this? We have shown the contrary from Scripture. Therefore several have had the care of one fold? What hinders it? Could not, for example, the care of the fold, which is one, have been committed to Paul? They cannot deny it. Is the whole flock then committed to one alone? The monarchists would be unwilling to say so. Moreover, it must be noted here that the fold is called one with respect to that one good shepherd of John 10, who is Christ, who laid down his life for the sheep and whose sheep hear his voice. The most learned du Pin has already testified to this. Lyra, briefly on the passage: There shall be one shepherd, that is, Christ. Augustine, Tractate 47 on John, more fully: Christ was made the cornerstone of these two flocks, as of two walls. Therefore he alone makes one fold, since the faithful are joined together in him; but with respect to the other shepherds there are rather many folds, that is, many assemblies and many churches. Some of these have been committed to Peter, others to others, since one man is not enough for all.

units.la: XXXIII. Addit Bellarminus: Dominus Petro vel omnes vel aliquas vel nullas oves commendavit, non nullas, quod manifestum, si aliquas, vel definitas, vel indefinitas; Non definitas, quod pariter evidens, sed nec indefinitas, quia non est sapientis Providoris relinquere indefinitam curam, cùm possit eam definire, præsertim cùm certa certa confusio & perturbatio ex illa indeterminatione oriatur, & commendare aliquos, & non indicare quos, idem esse videatur, ac si commendarentur nulla; Quas enim, quaso, pascet, qui gregem suum non cognoscit? E. Omnes. Respondebo; sed velim ut mihi prius Bellarminiani hujus sophismatis admirator respondeat: Quando Matth. XXVIII. 19. Apostolis dicitur: Euntes docete omnes gentes; quae particula omnes; non occurrit in verbis; pasce oves meas; & quando Paulo, Act. IX. dicitur, portabis nomen meum coram gentibus. Apostolis, & inter Apostolos priores v.g. Jacobo, Johanni, postea autem Paulo, aut omnes, aut aliquae, aut nullae Gentes commissae fuerunt. Nullas illis commissas esse, quamvis forte lubenter dicerent, & Apostolis tanquam Apostolis, id est, fatente Bellarmino, supremam potestatem habentibus, nullae committi potuerint, si Petro omnes omnino commissae fuerunt, dicere tamen aperte non audent. Si igitur aliqua, vel definitae, vel indefinitae. Non definita, quod manifestum, sed nec indefinita, ob eadem absurda, quae Bellarminus nobis opponit; Ergo Jacobo, Johanni, Paulo, singulis, omnes omnino Gentes, & per consequens omnes omnino oves Christi commissae fuerunt. Concluditur pessime, sed maxime Monarchicis. Conclusionem igitur nostram rejicimus, sed sub ea conditione, ut & Monarchici suam rejiciant, similibus plane fundamentis innixam. Quem in finem etiam, qualia sint illa absurda, quae Bellarminus, mandatum circa indefinitum sequi, contendit, examinabimus.
units.tr: XXXIII. Bellarmine adds: The Lord committed to Peter either all sheep, or some, or none. Not some, which is manifest; if some, then either definite or indefinite. Not definite, which is equally evident; nor indefinite either, because it is not the mark of a wise provider to leave an indefinite care when he can define it, especially since a certain confusion and disturbance arise from that indeterminacy, and to commit some while not indicating which seems the same as if none were committed. For whom, I ask, will he feed who does not know his own flock? Therefore all. I shall reply; but first I should like the admirer of this sophism of Bellarmine's to answer me this. When it is said to the Apostles in Matthew 28.19, Go and teach all nations, the particle all does not occur in the words feed my sheep; and when it is said to Paul in Acts 9, You shall bear my name before the Gentiles, to the Apostles, and among the Apostles to the earlier ones, for example James and John, and later to Paul, either all, or some, or none of the Gentiles were committed. That none were committed to them, although they might perhaps gladly say so, and that none could have been committed to the Apostles as Apostles, that is, as Bellarmine admits, having supreme power, if all were wholly committed to Peter, they nevertheless do not dare to say openly. If then some were committed, they were either definite or indefinite. Not definite, which is manifest; but not indefinite either, for the same absurdities that Bellarmine opposes to us. Therefore to James, John and Paul, each one, all the Gentiles without exception were committed, and consequently all the sheep of Christ without exception. This is a very bad conclusion, but most welcome to the monarchists. We therefore reject our own conclusion, but on this condition, that the monarchists reject theirs too, which rests on exactly similar foundations. To this end we shall also examine what those absurdities are which Bellarmine contends follow from a command concerning the indefinite.

units.la: XXXIV. Si pascere Apostolicum fuisset pascere Pontificium, id est, si potuissent pascentes, vel to pascere prae se ferentes, se ipsos laute pascere, ut hodierni Episcopi, maxime Romani, & si cum hoc, vel etiam sine hoc ambitiosi fuissent, ut de multis, qui Apostolicam Successionem jactant, praesumere licet; Certe opus fuisset ad evitandam confusionem, perturbationem & seditionem, quae sequi solent, ubi quis alienos fines invadit, cuivis Apostolorum & Petro etiam certos constituere limites; Verum quando non tantum pascere Apostolicum ab hodierno plerorumque plane diversum fuit, sed & Apostoli tales fuerunt, quales fuerunt, ut definitus singulis grex adscriberetur jam ab initio, opus minime fuit, nec in omissione determinationis sapientia defuit, nec etiam, quia non definitae commendatae sunt, nullae commendatae sunt. Nam etiam sine determinatione ista certum erat, neminem sibi plus sumpturum, quam ad se pertineret, sed id acturum quemvis, quod suum esse sciret; Cum eos non ita miserit Dominus indefinitè ad gentes, ut non post etiam direxerit, & quid, quando, ubi, & quibus prædicare debeant, semper significaverit, quod partim singularium occasionum oblatione, partim immediata Spiritus inspiratione, partim visionibus nocturnis (qualia de Paulo Act.XIII.2. XVI.6. 7.10. XVIII. 9. XX.22. leguntur) partim interveniente consilio humano factum, & sic oves antea indefinitas, definitas esse, cognoscimus. Ut in specie Petrus ivit, quò eum Collegium Apostolicum miserat, & unà cum Jacobo & Johanne, Paulo & Barnabæ dextram societatis dedit, ut cum illis in circumcisione prædicaret, hi autem Gentibus Verbum annunciarent, Gal.II. Et sanè existimo, Apostolos sic satis greges suos cognovisse, colligendos, quos Providentia Dei ipsis obtulerat, collectos, qui fidem operibus ostendebant, & utroque respectu homines, mediante peculiari dono discretionis Spirituum, vel saltem ob revelationes Spiritus Dei immediatas frequentes, qualia speciatim in Petro erga Ananiam & Sapphiram & Simonem notari possunt. Melius forte sic cognoverunt greges suos, quàm Pontifices nostrorum temporum, qui cùm omnium omninò ovium Christi pastores esse velint, saltem plerosque ignorant, nec ut eas cognoscant valdè laborant, χειροτονία vera non adhibent, imò oderunt, execrantur.
units.tr: XXXIV. If to feed as an Apostle had been to feed as a Pontiff, that is, if those who fed could, or pretended to feed, feed themselves sumptuously, as the bishops of today do, especially the Roman ones, and if, with this or even without it, they had been ambitious, as one may presume of many who boast of Apostolic succession, then certainly there would have been need, in order to avoid the confusion, disturbance and sedition that usually follow where someone invades another's territory, to set definite limits for each of the Apostles and for Peter too. But since feeding as an Apostle was not only wholly different from what most people do today, but the Apostles were also of such a kind that a definite flock was assigned to each from the beginning, there was no need at all, nor was wisdom lacking in the omission of a determination; nor, because they were not committed definitely, were none committed. For even without such a determination it was certain that no one would take more upon himself than pertained to him, but that each would do what he knew to be his own. The Lord did not send them indefinitely to the Gentiles in such a way as not afterwards to direct them too, and always to signify what they should preach, when, where and to whom. This was done partly by the offering of particular occasions, partly by immediate inspiration of the Spirit, partly by nocturnal visions (such as are read of Paul, Act. 13.2; 16.6, 7, 10; 18.9; 20.22), and partly through intervening human counsel. So we know that the sheep, formerly indefinite, became definite.
