Thus Peter in particular went where the Apostolic College had sent him, and together with James and John gave the right hand of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas, so that he should preach among the circumcision while they announced the Word to the Gentiles, Gal. 2. And I indeed think that the Apostles knew their flocks sufficiently to gather them, those whom the providence of God had offered them, and who had been gathered, who showed their faith by their works. They judged men on both counts by a special gift of the discernment of spirits, or at least by the frequent immediate revelations of the Spirit of God, such as can be noted particularly in Peter's dealings with Ananias and Sapphira and Simon. Perhaps they knew their flocks better than the Pontiffs of our own times, who, while they want to be shepherds of all the sheep of Christ without exception, at least ignore most of them, and labour hard not at all to know them. They do not practise true ordination [χειροτονία]; nay, they hate and execrate it.

units.la: XXXV. Quæ Bellarminus subjungit, Patrum testimonia nonnulla, aut non probant, quod probandum erat, aut si quæ probare videntur, partim sera sunt, partim Pontificum, in quibus Spiritum ambitionis citiùs se exeruisse aliquo modo, haud miramur, cùm eorum Successores occupârit penitùs. Responderunt jam ad ea luculenter alii, & contrà locum hunc ex Patribus vindicârunt. Fontem solutionum egregiè suppeditat Doctissimus du Pin, & quidem his verbis: Cùm Petrus & reliqui Apostoli per totum orbem prædicandi potestatem accepissent, ita ut omnibus & singulis indefinitè per universum orbem oves sint commissæ, dici possunt totius orbis pastores: Sic Chrysostomus Timotheum totius orbis Episcopum dicere non veretur, & Paulum sæpius, præsertim homil. 2. de Pauli laudibus. Itaque Petro totius orbis oves commissæ dici possunt, quia non unius certi cujusdam regni aut loci oves regendas accepit, sed indefinitè totius mundi oves, ad quas ille accederet. Et paulò ante. Ambiguitas latet in verbo, totius: nam si collectivè istud sumatur & definitè, ut omnes omninò comprehendat, quasi Petrus Pastor fuerit universæ omninò Ecclesiæ, sequetur, non alios fuisse proprie pastores quàm Petrum, quod falsum; si vero
units.tr: XXXV. Bellarmine adds some testimonies of the Fathers, but these either do not prove what had to be proved, or, where they seem to prove it, are partly late and partly about Popes in whom, we are not surprised, the spirit of ambition showed itself rather early, since it had entirely taken over their successors. Others have already answered these clearly and defended this passage from the Fathers against them. The very learned du Pin supplies the key to the solutions, and in these words: Since Peter and the other Apostles had received the power of preaching throughout the whole world, so that the sheep were committed to each and every one of them indefinitely throughout the entire world, they can be called shepherds of the whole world. So Chrysostom does not hesitate to call Timothy bishop of the whole world, and Paul often, especially in homily 2 on the praises of Paul. Thus the sheep of the whole world can be said to have been committed to Peter, because he did not receive for governing the sheep of some one particular kingdom or place, but the sheep of the whole world indefinitely, to whom he would come. And a little before: There is an ambiguity in the word "whole". For if it is taken collectively and definitely, so as to embrace absolutely all, as if Peter were the shepherd of the entire Church without exception, it would follow that no one else was properly a shepherd except Peter, which is false; but if

units.la: Fontes solutionis Objectionam ex Patribus vero sumatur indefinitè, ut sumi solent propositiones hujusmodi particula-res, ut sensus sit, si me amas, pasce aliquas oves meas, idem fuit munus cate-rorum &c.
units.tr: Sources of the solution to the objection from the Fathers: it is taken indefinitely, as propositions of this particular kind are usually taken, so that the sense is: "If you love me, feed some of my sheep"; the office of the others was the same, and so on.

units.la: XXXVI. Et certè hæc omnia ita intelligenda sunt, ut ma-neat, Petrum officio fecisse satis. Fecit utique, sed non pascendo omnes; Paverunt etiam Apostoli; certè etiam oves Christi, non aliorum, aut suas; Paverunt & longè plures, plures vel solus Paulus. Excipit Bellarminus. Petrum per Apostolos pavisse, egisse, à quo illi tanquam à capite & imperatore suo pendebant. Bona verba, si modò vera! Unde probat? An hæc dixisse sufficit? Sed Chrysostomus dicit; Fratrum curam Petro commissam esse. De hoc videbimus postea. Jam autem dicimus, nec volam nec vestigium in Scripturis apparere ejus, quòd Petrus per Apostolos paverit, eorum caput & Imperator fuerit, multa extare in contrarium ex parte jam allata, deinceps ex parte afferenda. Clamant omnia, Apostolos à Petro non dependisse, nec in esse, nec in operari. Prius fatetur & jam fassus est, post Cajetanum de instit. Papæ c. 10. Bellarminus, Stapletono gratis fingente, Petrum totum Apostolorum munus, quod soli ab initio incubuerit, in aliorum humeros disperti sse. Sed sic uno tantùm Apostolo opus fuisset, manentibus cæteris ejus Vicariis; Ast plures facti sunt, sine discrimine potestatis, simul, quibus æquè dictum: Eritis mihi testes Act. I. 8. & qui non, stylo hodierno, se Dei & sedis Apostolicæ gratiâ, sive etiam Petri gratiâ tales dixerunt, sed simpliciter Dei, Christi Apostolos & servos. Quoad posterius, ostendat quæ ò vel unum locum, ubi Petrus cæteris mandata dederit, modum agendi præscri-serit, quod certè, si reliqui quasi organa Petri fuissent, sæpissimè fieri debuisset.
units.tr: XXXVI. And certainly all of this must be understood in such a way that it remains true that Peter did his duty. He did, certainly, but not by feeding all. The Apostles also fed; certainly they fed the sheep of Christ, not of others or their own; they fed, and far more, and Paul alone fed more than all. Bellarmine objects: Peter fed through the Apostles, acting through them, on whom they depended as on their head and emperor. Fine words, if only they were true! From what does he prove it? Is it enough to have said it? But Chrysostom says: The care of the brethren was committed to Peter. We shall see about this later. For now we say that neither a wish nor a trace appears in the Scriptures that Peter fed through the Apostles, or that he was their head and emperor. Many things stand in the opposite direction, both from the part already brought forward and from the part still to be brought forward. Everything cries out that the Apostles did not depend on Peter either for their being or for their acting. Bellarmine, following Cajetan (On the Institution of the Pope, ch. 10), admits this first and has already admitted it, while Stapleton idly imagines that Peter had the whole office of the Apostles, which rested on him alone from the beginning, distributed onto the shoulders of others. But if that were so, only one Apostle would have been needed, with the others remaining his vicars. Instead there were several, without any difference of power, all at once, to whom the words apply equally: You shall be my witnesses (Acts 1:8). And they did not, in the style of today, call themselves such by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See, or even by the grace of Peter, but simply apostles and servants of God, of Christ. As for the latter point, let them show at least one place where Peter gave commands to the others and prescribed a manner of acting. Certainly, if the rest had been like instruments of Peter, this would have had to happen very often.

units.la: XXXVII. Utriusque respectu si Paulum consideremus, vocatus fuit non ab hominibus, neque per homines, Gal. I 1. Vidit Petrus cum sociis, ei concreditum esse Evangelium præputii æquè ac sibi & sociis Evangelium circumcisionis, cap. II. 7. Non ergo à Petro illud habuerunt, sed ab alio, eo nempe, qui ei dixerat: Ego te procul ad Gentes mittam, Act. XXII 21. ab eo etiam acceperat, quod Corinthiis tradidit, 1. Cor. XI. 23. ejus, non Petri, exemplum sibi proposuit: Imitatores mei estote, inquit, ut ego Christi. Ei nihil (qui dicit nihil, omnia negat, etiam gubernationem, quâ tandem solâ Petrum majorem fuisse fingunt, sed quâ tamen, præcepta, disciplinam, excommunicationem &c. si respicias, Paulo, Petri authoritate nihil agente, nemo unquam illustrior fuit) contulerunt oi δοκοῦντες,qui videbantur aliquid, inter quos & Petrus; Ast certè capitis est,aliquid conferre membris singulis; sed non est talis capitis,δεξιὰν κοινωνίας,dextram societatis jungere, & absolutè & simpliciter provincias partiri cum membro; non Imperatoris,cum subdito; ita ut ne minimam quidem inæqualitatem suspicari liceat ex narratione. Hæc non arguunt pascere per alium,nisi forte per Paulum Petrus paverit, quando Petrum reprehendit Paulus, & ei in faciem restiit, & velis dicere, sibi restitisse, secum expostulâsse, se reprehendisse Petrum. Quocunque oculos converto, nihil video de isto actu pascendi Petri per Paulum & alios; de actibus gubernationis Pontificiæ, cujus membra hæc sunt,vel esse dicuntur: Creare Episcopos; sed Paulus à Petro creatus non est; dare authoritatem prædicandi; sed eam à Petro Paulus non accepit: Præscribere,quid & quomodo & ubi prædicandum; sed ejusmodi Petrus Paulo præscripsisse nullibi legitur, aut cuiquam Apostolorum; Apostoli autem potiùs per Petrum pavïsse leguntur,non tantùm,quando eum cum Johanne simpliciter & æquè in Samariam misisse leguntur,quemadmodum etiam superiores mitti posse, Bellarminus exemplis allatis probat minimè, sed & quando illorum nomine verba ad populum fecit,os illorum.
units.tr: XXXVII. If we consider Paul in relation to both, he was called not by men, nor through men (Gal. 1:1). Peter and his companions saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to him, just as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter and his companions (Gal. 2:7). So they did not have it from Peter, but from another, namely him who had said to him: I will send you far away to the Gentiles (Acts 22:21). He also received from him what he handed on to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 11:23); he set before himself the example not of Peter but of Christ: Be imitators of me, he says, as I am of Christ. Peter contributed nothing to him. (Whoever says nothing denies everything. Even if you look at governance, by which alone they pretend Peter was greater, or at precepts, discipline, excommunication and the like, no one was ever more distinguished than Paul, while Peter's authority did nothing.) Those who seemed to be something (οἱ δοκοῦντες), among whom was Peter, contributed nothing. But surely it is the mark of a head to contribute something to each of the members; it is not the mark of such a head to join the right hand of fellowship (δεξιὰν κοινωνίας), to join the right hand of fellowship, and to divide provinces absolutely and simply with a member, as an emperor does with a subject. So from the narrative we may not suspect even the smallest inequality. These things do not show that Peter fed through another, unless perhaps Peter fed through Paul when Paul rebuked Peter and withstood him to his face, and you wish to say that he withstood himself, argued with himself, and rebuked Peter. Wherever I turn my eyes, I see nothing of this act of Peter feeding through Paul and others, nor of the acts of Papal governance, of which these things are said to be members: to create bishops; but Paul was not created by Peter. To give authority to preach; but Paul did not receive it from Peter. To prescribe what, how and where to preach; but nowhere is it read that Peter prescribed such things to Paul or to any of the Apostles. Rather, the Apostles are read to have fed through Peter, not only when they are read to have sent him to Samaria simply and equally with John, which Bellarmine by his cited examples does not at all prove, just as superiors can be sent, but also when he spoke to the people in their name, as their mouth.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ast fundamentum ejus,quòd Petrus per Apostolos paverit,in eo ponit Bellarminus,quòd,Chrysostomo teste,ei fratrum cura commissa sit. De eo jam videbimus & dabimus primò,ipsos etiam Apostolos hoc nomine venire; Si illorum etiam curam habuit, ut ei in genere dictum: Confirma fratres tuos,si conversus fueris; habuit curam,ut frater fratrum,ut frater ætate aut dotibus major cæteris,non tantùm bono exemplo,sed & adhortatione atque consiliis prodesse tenetur,imò quivis frater alteri,dono,quod à Deo accepit,qui diversa diversis tribuit pro suo beneplacito. Sic Petro Apostolorum,Apostolis Petri cura commissa,dum ex Magistro audiverunt omnes: Diligite alii alios. Hæc voluit dicere Chrysostomus,non plura,nec etiam potuit de æqualibus. Pascere oves jubetur Petrus,non pastores unâ secum ad idem vocatos, qui unâ secum solius Christi oves erant. Ad quid,obsecro,interrogat rectè de Dominis,Petro tanquam pastori etiam ipsorum Apostolorum curam censent à Christo fuisse commissam? Fortasse ad ipsorum confessiones audiendas? An ad ipsos docendos & instruendos? an ad corrigendos & puniendos? Ego sanè (Gal.II.) Petrum à Paulo instructum & correctum invenio, nullum
units.tr: XXXVIII. But Bellarmine places the foundation of his claim that Peter fed through the Apostles in this: that, according to Chrysostom, the care of the brethren was committed to him. We shall now look into this, and we shall first grant that the Apostles too come under this name. If he had care of them as well, as is said of him in general: Strengthen your brethren, when you have turned back (Luke 22:32), he had care as a brother of brothers, as an elder brother in age or gifts over the others, and is bound to help them not only by a good example but also by exhortation and counsel. Indeed any brother is bound to any other, with the gift he has received from God, who distributes different gifts to different people according to his good pleasure. So the care of the Apostles was committed to Peter, and the care of Peter to the Apostles, since they all heard from the Master: Love one another. This is all Chrysostom meant, and he could not have meant more, nor could he have meant it of equals. Peter is commanded to feed sheep, not shepherds called together with him to the same office, who with him were the sheep of Christ alone. To what end, I beg you, rightly asks the Lords: do they think that the care of the Apostles themselves was committed by Christ to Peter as to a shepherd? Perhaps to hear their confessions? Or to teach and instruct them? Or to correct and punish them? For my part (Gal. 2) I find Peter instructed and corrected by Paul, none

units.la: Chrysostomus vindicatur; Apostolos Petri oves non fuisse, porrò ostenditur, atque specialissimè de repreheníone Antiochena; Ium vero Apostolum a Petro rectum, aut correctum, aut instructum cerno: Et pascere oves, erat hominibus fidem & doctrinam Christi instillare, ac virtutes persuadere; quibus rebus Apostolos indiguisse, ab alio quam a Christo, nemo sanae mentis dixerit. Et certe vel sola memorata illa, Petri correptio a Paulo Antiochiae facta, si attente cum omnibus circumstantiis consideretur, heic Apostolos ab illa pastorali cura Petri eximit, nisi pessime Paulum fecisse dicere velimus pessime; Nec enim debita, quam Bellarminus requirit erga caput & Imperatorem Pauli reverentia in illo actu deprehenditur. Statim & coram omnibus & in faciem resistit Paulus, & sine ulla honoris praefatione objurgat, & sic pessimum parvipendendi capitis & Imperatoris exemplum relinquit, nec praevenit in epistola, aut factum esse sine praejudicio debitae reverentiae monet; Petrus autem patitur, etiam ut chartis haec consignentur. Quis hic pastorem videt Petrum, & ovem sive oviculam Paulum? Cajetanus certe non vidisse videtur, dum ita scripsit: Non sufficit Paulo, monstrasse se aequalem aliis Apostolorum primariis, sed monstrat, se quoque exhibuisse se majorem in actione summo Apostolorum vertice, Petro.
units.tr: Chrysostom is vindicated; it is further shown that the Apostles were not Peter's sheep, and especially concerning the rebuke at Antioch. Indeed I see the Apostle Peter neither corrected, nor rebuked, nor instructed by another. And to feed sheep was to instil into men the faith and doctrine of Christ and to persuade them of virtues; and that the Apostles needed these things from anyone other than Christ, no one of sound mind would say. And surely that one matter alone, the rebuke of Peter by Paul at Antioch, if it is considered carefully with all its circumstances, removes the Apostles here from that pastoral care of Peter, unless we are willing to say that Paul acted very badly. For the due reverence which Bellarmine requires toward the head and emperor is not found in that act of Paul's. At once, before everyone and to his face, Paul resists, and rebukes without any preface of honour, and so leaves the worst example of despising the head and emperor. Nor does he forestall it in his letter, or warn that it was done without prejudice to due reverence. Peter, however, suffers it, even though these things were committed to writing. Who here sees Peter as shepherd and Paul as a sheep or little lamb? Cajetan certainly seems not to have seen it, when he wrote: It is not enough for Paul to have shown himself equal to the other chief Apostles; he shows that he also appeared greater in the action than Peter, the highest summit of the Apostles.

units.la: XXXIX. Non igitur obtinuerunt Monarchici ex vocula meas; quod voluerunt; Superest, ut jam ex illa contra eos argumentemur paucis.
units.tr: XXXIX. The Monarchists have therefore not gained what they wanted from the little word "my". It remains to argue briefly against them from that passage.

units.la: Ita possumus: Christus Petrum jubet pascere, non oves proprias, sed alienas; ei non dicit: Pasce oves, quas tibi dono, meae fuerunt, illas ad tempus ipse rexi, jam tibi illas relinquo, tuae sunt, arbitrii tui, pasce eas. Sed simpliciter: Pasce meas oves. Quando igitur magna est inter herum proprias oves pascentem, & inter servum alieno gregi praefectum differentia, & hic ne lanam quidem inscio Domino ab ovibus sumere jure potest, illius autem in omnibus longe major est potestas: Oporteret pari modo Petrum servum non heri personam hic induere, Petri servi Successores non deberent illam heri personam sumere, absolutam sibi potestatem dominatumque tribuere, sed de ministerio potius & quidem mero cogitare, & memores esse ipsius, cujus Successionem crepant, Petri hortantis: Pascite gregem, non ut dominantes Clero, sed ut sitis exemplaria gregis. Pet. V. 3. Memores etiam verborum Magni Augustini in Joh. tr. 123. Quid est aliud, inquit; si diligis me, pasce oves meas; quam si diceretur; Si me diligis, non te pascere cogita, sed oves meas; sicut meas pasce, non sicut tuas; gloriam meam in iis quaere, non tuam; dominium meum, non tuum; lucra mea, non tua. Ast pariter operam ludunt,
units.tr: We can argue thus: Christ bids Peter feed, not his own sheep but another's. He does not say to him, "Feed the sheep I give you. They were mine; I ruled them for a time; now I leave them to you. They are yours, at your discretion; feed them." He says simply, "Feed my sheep." Since there is a great difference between a master feeding his own sheep and a servant set over another's flock, who may not even take wool from the sheep without the master's knowledge, while the master's power over everything is far greater, Peter's servant should likewise not take on the master's role here. Peter's successors ought not to assume that master's role, claim absolute power and lordship for themselves, but think rather of ministry, and of mere ministry at that. They should remember him whose succession they boast of, when Peter exhorts, "Feed the flock, not as lording it over the clergy, but so that you become examples to the flock." 1 Pet. 5.3. They should also remember the words of the great Augustine in John, tract. 123: "What else, he says, is it: if you love me, feed my sheep, than if it were said: If you love me, do not think of feeding yourself but my sheep. Feed them as mine, not as yours; seek my glory in them, not yours; my lordship, not yours; my gains, not yours." But equally they play at a pointless game: those who look for Peter's feeding among the Papists, and those who want to show the Pope's feeding in Peter.

units.la: Argumentatio contra Adversarios ex vocula meas; instituitur dunt, qui pascere Petri quærunt apud Papas, ac illi, qui pascere Paparum ollendere volunt apud Petrum.
units.tr: An argument against the opponents from the little word "meas" (my) is set up, (not translated) Correction to the line above: [2] An argument against the opponents from the little word "meas" (my) is set up, which is pursued by those who seek Peter's feeding among the Papists, and by those who want to show the Pope's feeding in Peter.

units.la: XL. Ut jam finito satis prolixo examine locorum, quibus Petrum ad talem Pontificatum à Christo electum fuisse, probare conantur Monarchici, & quæ præcipuè expresse de hoc mysterio loqui ajunt, concludere nobis liceat cum Doctissimo du Pin: Itaque ex locis à Bellarmino allatis (quæ & alii omnes palmaria faciunt;) non potest colligi Primatus Petri, ut ipse colligit; Id est, etiam talis, qualem ille colligit; non potest colligi talis Pontificatus Petri, Monarchia talis. Diximus & probavimus, loca Scripturæ hic requiri clara & manifesta; Allata autem loca clarè & manifestè Monarchicis favere, nullus, opinor, sibi unquam persuadere poterit, aut persuaderi patietur, qui ea attentè consideraverit, vel etiam ea, quæ hic annotavimus, sine præjudiciis legerit; Imò contrà unumquemque horum locorum Monarchicis multis modis contrariari intelliget. Licet proin etiam appellare ad Lectorem à studio partium vacuum, annon hæc ita se habeant? Vel, an talem Petri Monarchiam clarè & diserte in istis locis descriptam, promissam, collatam invenerit? Et annon credat, si Christus tantam dignitatem, in qua tantum situm, & à qua credita, aut repudiata æterna tot hominum felicitas aut miseria dependere debet, Petro conferre voluisset, eum multò manifestius istam suam voluntatem declaraturum, & istum suum Pro-Regem, Vicarium & Legatum tabulis longè evidentioribus instructurum fuisse: Præsertim quando in rebus humanis, terrenis, id est, nullius fere in comparatione momenti, tantam quoad hæc diligentiam, idque merito, adhiberi solere omnes norunt? Et quando hic tabulæ unius aliquot centum aliis, primo maximam partem dissimillimis, & qui propriis tabulis fidei suæ cavere non possunt, & qui tanta tamen ab omnibus exigunt, inservire debent, non minus, ac si uniuscujusque nomen quoad syllabas & literas omnes in iis plenissimè & planissimè expressum esset? Certè Christum saltem primo illi tabulis longè evidentioribus, & à quibusvis horum Pro-Regum subditis facile quoad illum sensum intelligibilibus, prospecturum fuisse, judicare, & justitiæ & benignitati Servatoris consentaneum est, & per consequens etiam consentaneum veritati, in locis explicatis ejusmodi Pro-Regem Petrum, Pontificem talem constitutum minimè fuisse.
units.tr: XL. Now that the lengthy examination of the passages by which the Monarchists try to prove that Peter was chosen by Christ for such a Pontificate, and which they say speak expressly of this mystery, is finished, let us conclude with the most learned du Pin: "Therefore from the passages cited by Bellarmine" (which all the others also make their strongest proofs) "it cannot be inferred that Peter had primacy, as he infers it." That is, not even the kind of Peter's Pontificate and Monarchy that he infers can be inferred. We have stated and proved that clear and manifest passages of Scripture are required here. Yet no one who has weighed these passages carefully, or read what we have noted here without prejudice, will, I think, be able to persuade himself, or allow himself to be persuaded, that the passages cited clearly and manifestly favour the Monarchists. Indeed, he will see that each of these passages is in many ways contrary to the Monarchists. The reader, free from partisan zeal, may therefore be asked: are these matters not so? Or will he find such a Monarchy of Peter clearly and expressly described, promised, or conferred in these passages? Will he not believe that, if Christ had wished to confer on Peter a dignity on which so much depends, and on the acceptance or rejection of which the eternal happiness or misery of so many people depends, he would have declared that will far more plainly, and furnished this his Pro-King, Vicar and Legate with far more evident documents? This is especially so since everyone knows that in human, earthly affairs, which are of almost no importance in comparison, such great care is customarily and rightly taken over these matters. Moreover, here a document of one or a few hundred is to serve others, most of them very dissimilar, who cannot secure their own faith by their own documents, and who nevertheless demand so much from everyone, as if each man's name were fully and plainly expressed in them, syllable by syllable and letter by letter. Surely it is consistent with the justice and kindness of the Saviour, and consequently with the truth, to judge that he would at least have provided for the first of these with far more evident documents, easily understood in that sense by any subject of these Pro-Kings. So it is consistent with truth to conclude that, in the passages explained, Peter was in no way constituted such a Pro-King or Pontiff.

units.la: SECTIO SEXTA,
units.tr: SECTION SIX,

units.la: In qua, Quem Petrus, cùm ad talem Pontificatum electus non sit, Primatum habuerit, ostenditur. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which it is shown that Peter, although he was not elected to such a Pontificate, nevertheless held a Primacy. A summary.

units.la: I. Transitio; II. Quales Petri Primatus fuerit; III. Quibus fundamentis innixus; IV. Primatus ille porrò ex Patribus à Doctissimo du Pin citatis atque ipsiusmet judicio declaratur, ordinis tantùm eum fuisse; V. Ostenditur illud specialiùs, quoad appellationem Principis Apostolorum; VI. Ex eo, quòd aliis non minora in Scriptura & apud Patres tributa leguntur; talibus, qui ne quidem Apostoli fuerunt, Episcopis, Cænobiarchis, Diaconis; sed maximè Apostolis; primò Andreæ; VII. Secundò Iacobo & Iohanni; tertiò Iohanni soli; VIII. Quartò Iacobo Alphai filio; cujus prærogativa, cumprimis ex Clemente Alexandrino memorantur; IX. Hujusque dictum porrò explicatur; X. Atque contra exceptiones Bellarminianas;
units.tr: I. Transition; II. What kind of Primacy Peter had; III. On what foundations it rested; IV. That this Primacy is further declared from the Fathers cited by the most learned du Pin, and by his own judgment, to have been one of order only; V. That this is shown more specifically with respect to the title Prince of the Apostles; VI. From the fact that equal or greater things are read of others in Scripture and among the Fathers, namely of men who were not even Apostles: bishops, abbots, deacons; but chiefly of the Apostles: first of Andrew; VII. Secondly of James and John; thirdly of John alone; VIII. Fourthly of James the son of Alphaeus, whose prerogatives are recorded especially from Clement of Alexandria; IX. And his saying is further explained; X. And against the Bellarmine exceptions;

units.la: XI. Defenditur; XII. Specialiùs respectu dignitatis sedis Hierosolymitanæ;
units.tr: XI. It is defended; XII. More specifically with respect to the dignity of the see of Jerusalem;

units.la: XIII. Quæ ejus in Antiquitate ratio habita, & cur non major? XIV. Iacobi prærogativa amplius testimonio Epiphanii & Chrysostomi confirmantur;
units.tr: XIII. What account was taken of it in antiquity, and why not a greater one? XIV. James's prerogative is further confirmed by the testimony of Epiphanius and Chrysostom;

units.la: XV. Atque hoc plenius deducitur; XVI. Qualem Primatum Chrysostomus Petro tribuerit; XVII. Quintò denique Paulo; cujus prærogativa ex Scriptura & Patribus explicata traduntur; XVIII. Elogia ex Patribus enumerantur; XIX. Elogia Epistolarum; XX. Elogia in comparatione cum quibuscunque aliis; XXI. Cum Petro; XXII. Responsiones Bellarmini ad duas, quas sibi format, objectiones examinantur, Prior objectio, Paulum per Antonomasiam Apostolum vocari; XXIII. Respondetur ad responsionem;
units.tr: XV. And this is more fully deduced; XVI. What kind of Primacy Chrysostom ascribed to Peter; XVII. Lastly, fifthly, to Paul, whose prerogatives are set out from Scripture and the Fathers; XVIII. The praises of him from the Fathers are enumerated; XIX. The praises of his Epistles; XX. The praises in comparison with any others whatever; XXI. With Peter; XXII. Bellarmine's replies to the two objections he forms for himself are examined; the first objection: that Paul is called the Apostle by antonomasia; XXIII. A reply is given to that reply;

units.la: XXIV. Objectio altera; Paulum in diplomatibus Pontificum sapiùs pingi solere à dextris, quæ ex Bellarmino & du Pin unà cum hujus responso proponitur; XXV. Quod primò argumentationem, tanquam nostram, continet, quâ nemo unquam usus est;
units.tr: XXIV. The second objection: that Paul is often painted on the right in the diplomas of the Pontiffs, which is put forward from Bellarmine and du Pin together with the latter's reply; XXV. Which first contains an argument, as though it were ours, which no one has ever used;

units.la: XXVI. Secundò frustrà licentia pictoria prætextu ista excusari posse arbitratur; quam quidem licentiam in Ecclesia Pontificia maximam esse ostenditur; XXVII. Sed tum aliàs, tum maximè hoc intolerabilem, atque immeritò allegatam; XXVIII. Incipit examen variarum Bellarmini responsionum. Primò dicit, concessâ majori authoritate Pauli nihil derogari Pontificibus, hujusve quoque Successoribus. Quā jactantia uberiùs declaratur;
units.tr: XXVI. Secondly, he judges that this can be excused in vain under the pretext of artistic licence; which licence is shown to be very great in the Papist Church; XXVII. But this is intolerable at other times, and above all here, and wrongly alleged; XXVIII. The examination of Bellarmine's various replies begins. First, he says that by granting Paul's greater authority nothing is taken away from the Pontiffs, or from their successors either. This boast is set out more fully;

units.la: XXIX. Etiam ex allegata pariter Pauli authoritate & exemplo Iulii II. XXX. Tutissima videtur, quia Petri Successio in dubium vocatur, & vix ab utroque tantam potestatem accipere possunt; Sed admiratione dignum, quòd tamen tantopere in imminutione authoritatis Paulina laborent;
units.tr: XXIX. Also from the similarly alleged authority and example of Paul and of Julius II. XXX. It seems the safest, because Peter's succession is called into doubt, and they can hardly receive so great a power from either; but it is worthy of wonder that they nonetheless labour so greatly at diminishing the authority of Paul;

units.la: XXXI. Verùm non est usque adeò tuta; XXXII. Ostenditur
units.tr: XXXI. But it is not so very safe; XXXII. It is shown

units.la: ditur primò incertitudo illius ipsius Pontificatus Paulini; XXXIII. Atque incertitudo multiplex, quae, eo praesuppositio, oritur; XXXIV. Secundò, praesuppositio eodem, sequitur, Ecclesia Romana gubernationem mutatam esse, cùm tunc fuerit Duumviratus, non Monarchia; XXXV. Et videtur, duos hodienum requiri, quos tamen abominantur; XXXVI. Patet exemplo Sixti V. XXXVII. Tertiò non minùs sequitur, posse esse Pontificem Romanum, qui Primatu careat; XXXVIII. Respondetur ad objectionem Doctissimi du Pin primam; XXXIX. Alteram; XL. Secundò ait Bellarminus, nihil Pontificatum illum simultaneum derogare ipsi Petro; quia hujus ordinaria, Pauli extraordinaria dignitas fuerit; quae examinantur; XLI. Respondetur ad simile Mosis & Aaronis; XLII. Tertia Bellarmini responsio; non semper Paulum ad dextram apparere, examinatur; XLIII. Quarta, lævam Veteribus honorationem fuisse, atque Paulum corpus Petri tegendo obsequium testatum esse; In quo refutatur, XLIV. Locus ex Eusebio allatus ad examen vocatur, ut & ille ex Ambrosio; XLV. An eximperitia Pictorum Paulus dextram occupet, ubi aliquis in medio? XLVI. Annon ob Pauli honorem et dextram datam esse, appareat ex eo, quòd Petrus alias semper & in omnibus praeponatur? XLVII. Bellarminum ipsum minimè de responsionum suarum vi persuasum fuisse, quod partim ex earum diversitate, partim ex dubiis loquendi modis cstenditur; XLVIII. Ad quintam Bellarmini responsionem transitur, in qua dat mysteria, ob quae Paulus cum honore suo dextram occupare potuerit; XLIX. Primum; L. Secundum; LI. Tertium; LII. Quartum; Cum conjecturis aliorum aequè futilibus; LIII. Concluditur, summam esse dignitatem Apostolicam, Petrum nonnisi Primatum aliquem inter aequales habuisse.
units.tr: that firstly the uncertainty of that very Pauline Pontificate; XXXIII. And the manifold uncertainty which arises from that presupposition; XXXIV. Secondly, from the same presupposition it follows that the government of the Roman Church has been changed, since there was then a duumvirate, not a monarchy; XXXV. And it seems that two are required today, whom nevertheless they abominate; XXXVI. It is clear from the example of Sixtus V. XXXVII. Thirdly, it no less follows that there can be a Roman Pontiff who lacks the Primacy; XXXVIII. A reply is given to the first objection of the most learned du Pin; XXXIX. To the other; XL. Secondly, Bellarmine says that that simultaneous Pontificate takes nothing away from Peter himself, because his was the ordinary dignity and Paul's the extraordinary one; which are examined; XLI. A reply is given to the similar case of Moses and Aaron; XLII. Bellarmine's third reply, that Paul does not always appear on the right, is examined; XLIII. Fourthly, that the left was an honour among the Ancients, and that Paul bore witness to his deference by covering Peter's body; in which it is refuted; XLIV. The passage from Eusebius cited is called to examination, as is that from Ambrose; XLV. Whether, through the artists' inexperience, Paul occupies the right where someone is in the middle? XLVI. Does it not appear that the right was given because of Paul's honour, from the fact that Peter is otherwise always and in all things placed before him? XLVII. That Bellarmine himself was by no means persuaded of the force of his own replies, which is shown partly from their diversity, partly from the doubtful modes of speaking; XLVIII. We pass to Bellarmine's fifth reply, in which he gives the mysteries on account of which Paul, with his honour intact, could have occupied the right; XLIX. The first; L. The second; LI. The third; LII. The fourth; with other conjectures equally frivolous; LIII. It is concluded that the Apostolic dignity was supreme, and that Peter had only some Primacy among equals.

units.la: I. SEd videamus jam, postquam Petrum talem Primatum Monarchicum non habuisse ostendimus, qualem igitur habuerit, cùm eum aliquem habuisse jam aliquoties ipsi indigitaverimus, & veri ac legitimi Primatūs Petri consideratio suspicioni de indebito & fictitio adhuc plenius eradicandae aptissima, & nihil nisi demonstrationis coeptae quaedam continuatio, & simul ad praerogativam Bellarminianam, quam ex ordine, quo ab Evangelistis numerantur, format, responsio sit.
units.tr: I. But let us now see, since we have shown that Peter did not hold such a Monarchical Primacy, what kind he did hold, since we have several times already pointed out to them that he had some Primacy. The consideration of Peter's true and lawful Primacy is most apt to root out, more fully still, the suspicion of an undue and fictitious one, and it is nothing other than a certain continuation of the demonstration begun, and at the same time a reply to the Bellarmine prerogative, which he forms from the order in which the Evangelists list the Apostles.

units.la: II. Bellarminus de R. Pont. lib.1. cap.21. ait : Haereticos (quo nomine ab Ecclesia Romana dissentientes ordinariò insignire solerquoscunque:) tantopere vocem Primatūs (inter Apostolos, vel Petri) odisse. Non odimus vocem, quae convenienter Scripturae primo loco Petrum semper ferè (excipiendus enim est locus Gal.II.v.9. ubi Jacobus Petro praeponitur) collocanti, imò etiam expresse πρῶτον primum Matth. X.2. vocanti, adhiberi potest. Quae vox citato loco eo nomine, quòd est ἀναπόδοτος, quippe non sequente δεύτερος, secundus, aut τρίτος, tertius, suspecta videri non debet. Cùm simile exemplum Od. A. 157. occurrat. Et primò quidem notamus, eum Primatum habuisse antequam confessionem illam ederet Matth. XVI. Tu es Christus &c. atque adeò antequam audiret Tu es Petrus, &c. Primatum autem habuit tantùm ordinis, quatenus ordo eam significat rerum dispositionem, quæ confusionem excludit, & quatenus in omni hominum collegio debet aliquis ordo servari, & necesse est, aliquem primum inter plures esse; juxta verba Clarissimi du Pin loc. cit. qui & hic tantùm non noster est; quemadmodum inter Pares Franciæ, quos vel ipsum nomen pares ostendit, olim primus fuit Burgundus. Primatus ille ordinis etiam fuit aliquo modo authoritatis & honoris, quatenus nimirum talis Primatus inter æquales obtinere potest, & honor exhibetur, non intuitu gradus & officii diversi, sed primatus in eodem cum aliis officio & gradu, & etiam propter virtutem personalem, nam Primatus ille ordinis, authoritatis & honoris fundatus fuit in primatu donorum & Zeli, forte etiam ætatis & vocationis.
units.tr: II. Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, chapter 21, says: heretics (by which name the Roman Church usually brands all who dissent from it) hate so greatly the word Primacy (among the Apostles, or of Peter). We do not hate the word, which can fittingly be applied to Peter, who in Scripture is almost always listed in the first place (for the passage Gal. 2:9, where James is placed before Peter, must be excepted), and who is even expressly called first [πρῶτον] in Matt. 10:2. That word, in the passage cited, is unpaired [ἀναπόδοτος], since no second [δεύτερος] or third [τρίτος] follows, and so it should not be thought suspect, since a similar example occurs at Od. A. 157. And first of all we note that he held the Primacy before he made that confession in Matt. 16, You are Christ, etc., and so before he heard You are Peter, etc. But he held a Primacy only of order, in so far as order means that arrangement of things which excludes confusion, and in so far as in every gathering of men some order must be kept, and it is necessary that one be first among several; in the words of the most distinguished du Pin, loc. cit., who in this point too is scarcely not on our side. Just as among the Peers of France, whom the very name peers shows, the first was once the Burgundian. That Primacy of order also had some measure of authority and honour, in so far as such a Primacy among equals can be held, and honour is paid not on account of a different rank and office, but a primacy within the same office and rank as the others, and also on account of personal virtue; for that Primacy of order, authority and honour was founded on a primacy of gifts and zeal, and perhaps also of age and calling.

units.la: III. De quo triplici fundamento Doctissimum du Pin Patrum & suæ sententiæ interpretem audire juvabit:
units.tr: III. On the threefold foundation of this matter, it will be pleasing to hear the most learned du Pin, the Fathers' and his own opinion's interpreter:

units.la: Cur autem hanc prærogativam ipsi Christus concesserit, inquit, loc. cit. nemo certè definire potest. Sunt qui id ei ob ætatem delatum dicant, ut Hieron. lib.1. contra Jovin. Ætati, inquit, delatum, quia Petrus senior erat. Caff. lib.3. de incarnat. Primum, inquit, hunc docuit respondere, ut idem ordo esset responsionis, qui erat honoris, & ipse antecederet confessione, qui antecedebat ætate: Chrysost. Homil.59. in Matth. ait: Didrachma pro Petro solutum, quòd ipse esset primogenitus, ac proinde Andreâ senior, quem tamen Epiph. Petro seniorem esse arbitratur hæresi 51. sed sine fundamento. Alii primatum Petri repetunt ex eo, quòd primus fuerit vocatus. Nam licèt Andreas prior accesserit ad Christum, videtur tamen primus Petrus ad munus electus, cùm dixit ei Christus, Marc.I. Noli timere, ex hoc enim eris homines capiens: Ita Epiph. hæresi 51. Occursus Andreæ primus contigit, postea rursus, quando perfecta renuntiatio facta est, ipse fratrem suum præcessit, & in Ancorat. Ipse Dominus constituit Petrum primum Apostolorum, Cypr. item in lib. testim. ad Quirinum ait, Petrum primum esse, quem Christus elegit. Hil. in Matth. cap.7. Petrus primus credidit, & Apostolatûs est princeps. Greg. Magn. lib.2. super Ezech. Homil.18. & non in memoriam revocat, quòd primus in Apostolatum vocatus sit, & Chrysost. Homil.9. de pœnit. Petrum cùm dico, Petruma nomino primum discipulorum,primum vocatum & primum obedientem. Denique,quod minus ad propositum facit, à nonnullis dicitur primus Petrus esse constitutus, ob eximiam in Christum charitatem,ita Augustt. ferm. 13. de verbis Domini: Petrus in Apostolorum ordine primus,in Christi amore promptissimus. Cyrillus in Joh. lib.12. c.64. Præveniebat, inquit, Petrus alios ardore,namque Christi præcipuè fervens & ad faciendum & ad respondendum paratissimus erat. Illius porrò amoris in Christum multa extant in Scripturis vestigia,quæ hic commemorare non est necesse. Sed nihil interest, qua ratione motus Christus Petrum primum Apostolorum constituerit, sufficit illud extra controversiam posuisse, Petrum inter Apostolos primum locum obtinuisse, vivente Christo &c. Ad quæ duo tantùm notari velim. 1. Concipi vix posse, quomodo ratio à charitate & zelo desumta minùs ad propositum faciat, cum illa & in Scriptura apertè fundata sit, & ita non tantùm, quemadmodum duæ reliquæ,probabilitatem habeat, & Christum etiam facillimè inducere potuerit ad Primatum Petro conferendum. 2. Rationes quæ à Doctissimo Viro tanquam diversæ sententiæ proponuntur, conjungi posse & verisimiliter debere, & à multis conjungi.
units.tr: "Why Christ conferred this prerogative upon him," he says, loc. cit., no one can certainly determine. There are those who say it was granted to him on account of his age, as Jerome, Book 1, against Jovinian: "It was given to age, because Peter was the elder." Cassian, Book 3, On the Incarnation: "First," he says, "he taught him to answer, so that the order of answering might be the same as the order of honour, and he who preceded in age might also precede in confession." Chrysostom, Homily 59 on Matthew, says: the didrachma was paid for Peter because he was the firstborn, and therefore older than Andrew, though Epiphanius thinks Peter was older, Heresy 51, but without foundation. Others trace Peter's primacy to the fact that he was called first. For although Andrew approached Christ earlier, Peter seems nevertheless to have been chosen first for the office, when Christ said to him, Mark 1: "Fear not, for from now on you will be catching men." So Epiphanius, Heresy 51: "Andrew's meeting took place first; afterwards, again, when the full renunciation was made, he went before his brother." And in the Ancoratus: "The Lord himself appointed Peter first of the Apostles." Cyprian likewise, in the book of Testimonies to Quirinus, says that Peter is first, whom Christ chose. Hilary on Matthew, chapter 7: "Peter believed first, and is the prince of the apostolate." Gregory the Great, Book 2 on Ezekiel, Homily 18, and does not recall that he was called first into the apostolate. And Chrysostom, Homily 9 on repentance: "When I say Peter, I name the first of the disciples, the first called and the first obedient." Finally, which bears less on the point, some say Peter was set first on account of his outstanding love for Christ, so Augustine, sermon 13 on the words of the Lord: "Peter, first in the order of the apostles, most ready in the love of Christ." Cyril on John, Book 12, chapter 64: "Peter, he says, surpassed the others in ardour, for being especially fervent in love for Christ, he was most ready both to act and to answer." Many traces of that love for Christ are found in the Scriptures, which need not be recalled here. But it makes no difference by what reasoning Christ, moved as he was, appointed Peter first of the Apostles; it is enough to have placed beyond controversy that Peter held the first place among the Apostles while Christ was living, etc. On these two points only I would like to note: 1. It can hardly be conceived how a reason drawn from charity and zeal bears less on the point, since it is also plainly founded in Scripture, and so has not merely, as the other two do, probability, and could easily have induced Christ to confer the primacy on Peter. 2. The reasons which that most learned man puts forward as different opinions can be combined, and probably ought to be, and by many they are combined.

units.la: IV. Allata jam ex parte docent, qualem Patres Petro Primatum adjudicaverint. De quo tamen amplius inquirendum. Ait idem Doctissimus Vir: De Petri primatu nihil apud Justinum, Irenaeum, Clementem Alexandrinum & alios antiquissimos. Mirum profecto,si tantum olim in Petri Primatu situm fuisset,quantum hodie, Bellarmino judice, in Romani Pontificis Primatu situm est? Itane de summa rei Christianæ prorsus illi tacuerant, & quidem tunc,quando Petrus & Primatus ejus adhuc in recenti memoria esse, & semper tanquam fundamentum Primatus Pontificum illorum temporum, id est,summæ rei Christianæ considerari debuisset! Infelicia tempora,quibus Monarcha Ecclesiæ primus & solus in Scriptura ostensus usque adeò negligebatur; & nihil planè ex hodie identidem decantari solitis; Tu es Petrus &c. Tibi dabo claves &c. pasce oves meas &c. inaudiebatur! Vel potiùs,felicia tempora,quibus genuino verborum istorum sensu contenti erant omnes, illis ad fraudem abutebatur nemo,charitatis,patientiæ & humilitatis Primatum post Apostolum affectabant omnes;Producit Vir Doctissimus prima pro Petri Primatu testimonia ex Origene,quibus tamen men ipse parùm fidere videtur ; Utriusque loci, inquit, αὐτοχεάφον non habemus, & versio Ruffini innumeris ejusmodi additionibus (quis autem addiderit, nisi Pontificiæ potestatis fraudulentus assertor?) scatere creditur. Subjungit Clementis Origene antiquioris ex Eusebio locum: Post Servatoris ascensum[Petrum, Jacobum & Johannem, quamvis Dominus ipsos cæteris prætulisset,non idcirco de honoris gradu inter se contendisse, sed Jacobum cognomine Justum Hierosolymorum Episcopum elegisse; Et ex eo infert ;Vides Petrum, Jacobum & Johannem cæteris Apostolis prælatos, & ex his primum fuisse Petrum. Eum primo loco nominari videmus, cæterùm istos Apostolorum coryphæos æquiparari, & communi operâ Episcopum constituere, quod & Anacletus in epist.2. testatur. Pergit ; Citatur ex Cypriano locus in libro de Unit. Ecclesiæ ; Primatus Petro datur, ut una Christi Ecclesia monstretur ; Sed ἐπιχείρησιν suam sic annectit: Verùm, ut admonet Rigaltius, hæc verba (quæ tamen primatum ordinis simpliciter denotare possent) sunt adscititia, nec habentur in vetustissimis duobus Msc. & à proposito Cypriani aliena plane sunt, quod & agnovit auctor notarum ad calcem editionis Romanæ. Quoad alium Cypriani locum à Bellarmino citatum judicat, eum sensum Cypriani minimè assequutum esse, hunc quidem in Petro Primatum agnovisse, sed non eum quem Bellarminus intendat. Probat illud ex alio loco Cypriani in Epist.70. Nam nec Petrus, quem primum Dominus elegit, & super quem ædificavit Ecclesiam suam; cùm secum Paulus de Circumcisione disceptaret, vindicavit sibi aliquid insolenter, aut arroganter assumsit,ut diceret, se Primatum tenere & obtemperari à novellis & posteris sibi oportere ; id est,teste Rigaltio, non imperium, non dominatum, non potentatum, sed primum locum. Ad illud, quòd Eusebius lib.2. cap.14. Petrum vocat fortissimum, & inter reliquos Apostolos virtutis merito facilè Principem, notat, hunc locum esse de virtutis,non de loci primatu. Optati post verbis abuti ait,qui inde concludere velint, Cathedram Romanam unicam esse in tota Ecclesia. Concludunt autem illud, qui Romanam sedem Magistram omnium Ecclesiarum cum Concilio Tridentino vocant, & qui Episcopos de jure divino esse negant. Post quædam alia testimonia illud etiam Hieronymi lib.1. adversus Pelag. adducit: Ut Plato fuit Princeps Philosophorum,ita Petrus fuit Apostolorum; Ast Plato non erat Dominus Philosophorum,non ab illo pendebant,non illi subjecti erant, contrà cum ipso de Primatu contendentes,eo non inferiores.
units.tr: IV. Having now presented what they teach on this point, let us see what kind of primacy the Fathers assigned to Peter. This must be investigated further. The same most learned man says: "Nothing about Peter's primacy is found in Justin, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and other very early writers." Truly remarkable, if so much was once placed in Peter's primacy as is now, according to Bellarmine, placed in the primacy of the Roman Pontiff! Had they really been silent on the substance of the Christian religion, and at a time when Peter and his primacy were still in recent memory and should always have been considered the foundation of the primacy of the Pontiffs of that time, that is, of the very substance of the Christian religion! Unhappy times, in which the Monarch of the Church, shown first and alone in Scripture, was so neglected, and nothing at all was heard of those words so often sung today: "You are Peter, etc.; I will give you the keys, etc.; feed my sheep, etc." Or rather, happy times, in which all were content with the genuine sense of those words, no one abused them for deceit, and all aspired to the primacy of charity, patience and humility after the Apostle! The most learned man brings forward the first testimonies for Peter's primacy from Origen, though he himself seems to have little trust in them: "We do not have an autograph [αὐτόγραφον] of either passage, and Rufinus' translation is believed to abound in countless additions of this kind" (but who would have added them, unless a fraudulent advocate of papal power?). He adds a passage from Clement, older than Origen, taken from Eusebius: "After the Saviour's ascension, Peter, James and John, although the Lord had set them above the rest, did not on that account contend among themselves for the rank of honour, but chose James, surnamed the Just, as bishop of Jerusalem." And from this he infers: "You see that Peter, James and John were set above the other Apostles, and of these Peter was first." We see that he is named in the first place, but that these leaders of the Apostles are put on a level and jointly appoint a bishop, as Anacletus also attests in his second epistle. He goes on: "A passage is cited from Cyprian's book On the Unity of the Church: 'The primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ may be shown.'" But he attaches his own argument [ἐπιχείρησιν] thus: "But, as Rigaltius warns, these words (which could nonetheless simply denote a primacy of order) are interpolated, are not found in the two most ancient manuscripts, and are plainly foreign to Cyprian's purpose, which the editor of the notes at the end of the Roman edition also acknowledged." As for the other passage of Cyprian cited by Bellarmine, he judges that Cyprian did not grasp that sense, though he did recognise a primacy in Peter, but not the one Bellarmine intends. He proves this from another passage of Cyprian in Epistle 70: "For Peter, whom the Lord chose first, and upon whom he built his Church, when Paul disputed with him about circumcision, did not insolently or arrogantly claim anything for himself, so as to say that he held the primacy and that novices and successors ought to obey him"; that is, according to Rigaltius, not rule, not lordship, not power, but the first place. As for Eusebius, Book 2, chapter 14, calling Peter "most courageous, and easily the leader among the other Apostles by merit of virtue," he notes that this passage concerns the primacy of virtue, not of place. He says that those who wish to conclude from Optatus' words that the Roman See is the only see in the whole Church abuse them. Those who call the Roman See "Mistress of all the Churches" with the Council of Trent conclude that, and those who deny that bishops are of divine right. After some other testimonies he also adduces that saying of Jerome, Book 1 against Pelagius: "As Plato was the prince of philosophers, so Peter was of the Apostles." But Plato was not the lord of the philosophers; they did not depend on him, they were not subject to him; on the contrary, they disputed with him about the primacy and were not inferior to him.

units.la: V. Quæ alia ex Patribus allegat testimonia, Ordinis tantum primatum Petro vendicant, nec etiam aliâ intentione ista allegat. Et certè quæcunque Patres, vel Primatûs hujus legitimi, vel muneris Apostolici, vel utriusque simul spectati, respectu, Petro, satis nonnunquam emphaticè, imò hyperbolicè, tribuunt, talem tamen primatum, qualem nos negamus, neutiquam probant; qualem nec probat illustre Principis Apostolorum, quo eum nonnulli ornant, elogium, quandoquidem, ut mox dicetur, & alii hoc ipso & æquè invidendis elogiis aliis à multis insigniuntur: Et jamjam, Petrum sic Principem Apostolorum fuisse, quomodo Plato fuerit Philosophorum, ex Hieronymo didicimus, & in ista locutione princeps idem est, ac primus, quo sensu frequentem hujus vocabuli usum exemplis probat Forbesius Instruct. Theol. l.XV. c. 1. v. 1. quemadmodum etiam Doctissimus du Pin l. c. §. 3. notanter, quamvis alia agens, ait: Sciunt omnes, istis phrasibus; Princeps Apostolorum &c.) significari tantum super alios præstantiam: Sic cùm Virgilium, Horatium & Ovidium voco Poëtarum principes, hoc unum volo, eos inter Poëtas eminere & cæteris præstantiores esse. Quin etiam fieri posse, imò sæpissimè fit, ut ista appellationes latè sumantur, & nonnunquam primus aliquis vocetur ac Princeps, qui non absolutè primus est, sed insignis tantùm. Sic Cicero dicitur Oratorum Princeps, licèt Demosthenes cum eo de primo gradu contendere possit. Sic Horatium Poëtarum Principem dicere nemo veretur, quamvis Virgilium præferendum esse vix quisquam dubitet. Haud ergo mirum, si nonnunquam Paulus (agit enim de eo, utrum Paulus, primus & Princeps Apostolorum multis dictus, Primatui Ordinis in Petro aliquid deroget:) solus dicatur primus, ac Princeps Apostolorum, non quòd absolutè primus sit, sed quia inter primos & principes numerari potest. Adde, quòd unus dici potest alio prior ac præstantior secundùm aliqua: & sic Paulus Petro præferri potest, &c.
units.tr: V. The other testimonies which he cites from the Fathers claim for Peter only a primacy of order, and they do not cite them with any other intention. Indeed, whatever the Fathers, with regard either to a legitimate primacy, or to the apostolic office, or to both together, sometimes attribute to Peter, quite emphatically, even hyperbolically, they nowhere prove the kind of primacy that we deny; nor does the illustrious epithet "Prince of the Apostles," with which some adorn him, prove it, since, as will shortly be said, others are decorated with this same and equally enviable epithet by many. And we have already learned from Jerome that Peter was thus prince of the Apostles as Plato was of the philosophers, and in that expression prince means the same as first; Forbes, Instructiones Theologicae, Book 15, chapter 1, section 1, proves this frequent usage of the word with examples, just as the most learned du Pin also notes, though he is doing something else: "Everyone knows that by such phrases as 'Prince of the Apostles,' etc., only a superiority over the others is meant." (l. c., §3) So when I call Virgil, Horace and Ovid princes of poets, I mean only this: that they stand out among poets and are more excellent than the rest. Indeed it can happen, and very often does, that such titles are used broadly, and sometimes someone is called first and prince who is not absolutely first, but only distinguished. Thus Cicero is called prince of orators, though Demosthenes might contend with him for first place. No one hesitates to call Horace prince of poets, although hardly anyone doubts that Virgil should be preferred. It is therefore no wonder if sometimes Paul alone "is called first" and prince of the Apostles, though he is called first by many, and this, (for he is speaking of whether Paul, who is said by many to be first and prince of the Apostles, takes anything away from Peter's primacy of order), not because he is absolutely first, but because he can be counted among the first and the princes. Add that one can be called earlier and more excellent than another in certain respects, and so Paul can be preferred to Peter, etc.

units.la: VI. Et si Petro apud Patres magna & multa tribuuntur, profectò non minora & pauciora aliis apud eosdem tributa legimus; Ut enim non multùm dicam de illis, qui Apostolis & tempore & dotibus & munere longè inferiores fuerunt, & quos tamen columnas & firmamenta veritatis, Ecclesiæ, fidei fulcra, supernæ Hierusalem verè metropolitas, universi terrarum orbis præfectos, cornua salutis, lapides angulares, veritatis regulas, habitabilis totius orbis Doctores & lumina, communes orbis portus, omnium vertices, fulcimenta rectitudinis, ora Ecclesiæ, oculos piorum, Patres Episcoporum, columnas Orthodoxiæ vocarunt, Episcopos, non Romanos, cænobiarchas; ut author libri de 7. ordiordinibus Ecclesiæ, qui Hieronymo tribuitur cap. de quinto gradu, ipsos etiam Diaconos columnam & fundamentum veritatis appellare voluit; ut, inquam, de his non multum adferam, quanta quæsò sunt illa, quæ Apostolis aliis tribuerunt? Andreas, qui tamen non fuit ex illis, quos columnas haberi Paulus Gal.II. testatur, Hesychio Presbytero Hierosolymitano, in encomio B. Thomæ in Biblioth. Photii cod. 269. in versione Andreæ Schotti Jesuitæ, audit primus Apostolorum fœtus, prima Ecclesiæ columna, ante Petrum Petra, fundamenti fundamentum, initii primitiæ.
units.tr: VI. And although great and many things are attributed to Peter by the Fathers, we read that no fewer and no smaller things have been attributed to others by the same writers. I will not say much about those who were far inferior to the Apostles in time, gifts and office, and yet were called by the Fathers "pillars and firmaments of the truth, supports of the Church, true metropolitans of the heavenly Jerusalem, rulers of the whole world, horns of salvation, cornerstones, rules of truth, teachers and lights of the whole inhabited world, common harbours of the world, summits of all, props of uprightness, mouths of the Church, eyes of the godly, fathers of bishops, pillars of orthodoxy." They called them bishops, not Roman bishops, abbots. The author of the book On the Seven Orders of the Church, which is attributed to Jerome, in the chapter on the fifth rank, even wanted to call the deacons themselves "the pillar and foundation of the truth." So I will not dwell on these. But how great are the things they have given to the other Apostles? Andrew, who nevertheless was not one of those whom Paul in Galatians 2 testifies to be "reputed pillars," is addressed by Hesychius the Presbyter of Jerusalem, in his encomium on St Thomas, in the Bibliotheca of Photius, codex 269, in the translation of Andreas Schottus the Jesuit, as the first offspring of the Apostles, the first pillar of the Church, a rock before Peter, the foundation of the foundation, the first-fruits of the beginning.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Jam si, quid de duabus illis columnis Jacobo & Johanne dicant Scripturæ & Patres, consideremus, quanta intelligimus? Fuerunt illi cum Petro ex intimis, illis æquè nova nomina sunt indita (qualem primam in Petro prærogativam Bellarminus de Pont. Rom. lib.1. cap.17. integro prosequitur) æquè admissi fuerunt ad αὐτοψίαν illustris illius Metamorphoseos Domini in monte Matth.XVII. (ob quam communem admissionem etiam Joh. Damascenus Orat. de transfigur. tres illos τὰς κορυφαίους τῶν ἀποστόλων, Apostolorum coryphæos vocavit) & gravissimi angoris ejus in horto Gethsemane, Matth.XXVI.37. Johannes Christo in mensa propior & interioris quodammodo admissionis, adeò ut Petrus opus habuerit eo scisciitante proditoris indicium cognoscere, Joh.XIII.23.24. &c. Sicut etiam Cyrillus Alex. cum Synodo Alex. ep. ad Nest. p.1. Conc. Ephes.pag.209. T.2. Conc. Ed. Paris. A.1636. de utroque pronuntiavit: Πέτρος & Ἰωάννης ἰσότιμοι ἀλλήλοις, Petrus & Johannes inter se honore æquales.
units.tr: Now let us consider how much we understand from what the Scriptures and the Fathers say about those two pillars, James and John. They were with Peter among the closest, and they too were given new names (Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, chapter 17, pursues in full the first prerogative of Peter of this kind). They were equally admitted to the eyewitness of that illustrious transfiguration of the Lord on the mount, Matthew 17 (because of this shared admission John of Damascus, in his Oration on the Transfiguration, called those three "the leaders of the Apostles" [τὰς κορυφαίους τῶν ἀποστόλων]), and to his most grievous agony in the garden of Gethsemane, Matthew 26:37. John was nearer to Christ at the table and in a certain sense admitted to a more intimate place, so that Peter needed him to ask who the betrayer was, John 13:23-24, etc. Cyril of Alexandria, together with the Synod of Alexandria, in his letter to Nestorius, part 1, Council of Ephesus, page 209, volume 2, Paris edition of the Councils, 1636, likewise pronounced of both: "Peter and John are equal in honour to one another" [Πέτρος καὶ Ἰωάννης ἰσότιμοι ἀλλήλοις].

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Jacobus alter Alphæi filius, Matth.X.3. frater Domini, Gal.I.19. hoc est, vel cognatus Domini, ut multi volunt, ex Maria, Sorore Matris Domini, vel Josephi ex alia conjuge priore filius, frater etiam Judæ, Jud.v.1. ætatis suæ, cum altero Jacobo, comparatione dictus Μικρὸς minor Marc.XV.40. Epistolæ Canonicæ auctor, suis prærogativis usque adeò non destituitur, ut Bellarminus necessarium judicaverit, integro capite 26. lib. cit. illius respectu Petri primatum studiosè vindicare. Jam eum inter columnas relatum, & ante Petrum nominatum, & in Concilio Hierosolymitano sententiam ferentem vidimus. Factus est urbis illius Episcopus (Non quòd sedi vel Ecclesiæ illi affixus fuerit, quod muneri Apostolico repugnaret) sed quòd ad omnium Ecclesiarum utilitatem promovendam paulò diutiùs ibi ex consilio reliquorum Apostolorum stolorum substiterit) secundùm Clementis Alexandrini verba adducta §. IV. Quæ verba notatu dignissima sunt,licèt non legendum esset, quemadmodum in Basileensi codice versionis Ruffini habetur;Apostolorum Episcopum; quæ lectio forte fundamento prolatorum Codicum haud caret. Non is nostris mos,neque etiam tanta facultas est, codices ut corrumpamus; Si Bellarminus,aut post eum jam alius,quinam corruptionis codicum merito rei peragantur,cognoscere vult, ut vitam Patris Pauli editionis Venetae Italicae pag.90.91. præter alia domestica testimonia plurima, confessionésque domesticas legat, oportet; Apostolorum quodammodo Episcopus est ab Apostolis, in loco, ubi Apostoli degunt,ad peculiarem curam ante quosvis alios destinatus Apostolus; Quod nemo negat, & verbis Clementis consentaneum est.
units.tr: The other James, son of Alphaeus, Matthew 10:3, the brother of the Lord, Galatians 1:19 (that is, either a kinsman of the Lord, as many hold, through Mary, the sister of the Lord's mother, or a son of Joseph by an earlier wife), the brother also of Jude, Jude 1, was called "the Less" [Μικρός] by comparison with the other James, Mark 15:40. He is the author of a canonical Epistle, and he is so far from lacking prerogatives that Bellarmine judged it necessary, in the whole of chapter 26 of the book cited, to defend the primacy of Peter zealously in comparison with him. We have seen him listed among the pillars, named before Peter, and passing judgment at the Council of Jerusalem. He became bishop of that city (not that he was fixed to that see or church, which would have been contrary to the Apostolic office, but because, in order to promote the good of all the churches, he remained there rather longer, by the counsel of the other Apostles), according to the words of Clement of Alexandria quoted above in section 4. These words are most worthy of notice, although it would not be necessary to read them as they stand in the Basel codex of Rufinus' translation: "Bishop of the Apostles". This reading perhaps has some support in the codices produced. It is not our custom, nor do we have such power, to corrupt codices. If Bellarmine, or anyone after him, wishes to know which people are rightly accused of corrupting the codices, he must read the Life of Father Paul, Venetian Italian edition, pages 90-91, along with the many other domestic testimonies and domestic confessions. James was in a certain sense bishop of the Apostles: he was appointed by the Apostles, in the place where the Apostles dwelt, as an Apostle assigned to special care before all others. No one denies this, and it agrees with the words of Clement.

units.la: IX. Quæ etiam plus dicunt,cùm dicunt,tres illos à Domino Prælatos,non de primo honoris gradu inter se contendisse, sed Jacobum cognomine Justum Hierosolymorum Episcopum elegisse. Sunt ibi tres Prælati, & Præləti à Domino, non est unus tantùm,tres illi μὴ ἀπο-δικαίζοντες δόξης, non contendunt inter se de primo honoris gradu,ut optimè Valesius verba omnium codicum vertit,& ex eo du Pin assumsit. Ut immeritò Bellarminus loc.cit. illud etiam jactet,non reperiri nomen primatus. Quid enim est primus honoris gradus nisi primatus? Et certè ipsa verborum series docet, vocabulum δόξης,sive jam gloria, sive primatus, sive primus honoris gradus in versione dicatur, maximam prærogativam significare, hanc illi tres non quæsiverunt, ut Bellarminus vult, non propriam suam gloriam,sed elegerunt, &c. Quomodo hæc connexionis ratio stare potest, si non maximum quid & maximè gloriosum Jacobo Minori collatum dicitur? Non dicitur, non contenderunt illi tres de primo honoris gradu, sed Petro tanquam Monarchae eum omnimodò & de jure divino competere,duo reliqui facile agnoverunt: Sed dicitur; sed Jacobum cognomine Justum Hierosolymorum Episcopum elegerunt.
units.tr: IX. Those who say that these three prelates appointed by the Lord did not contend among themselves for the first rank of honour, but chose James, surnamed the Just, as bishop of Jerusalem, say even more than they intend. There are three prelates, and prelates appointed by the Lord; it is not just one. These three "did not strive [μὴ ἀπο-δικαίζοντες δόξης] for the glory," that is, did not contend among themselves for the first rank of honour, as Valesius rightly translated the words of all the codices, and du Pin followed him. Bellarmine, in the passage cited, undeservedly boasts that the term primacy is not found there. For what is the first rank of honour but a primacy? And indeed the very sequence of the words shows that the word δόξα, whether it is rendered glory, primacy, or first rank of honour, signifies the greatest prerogative. Those three did not seek this, as Bellarmine wants, but chose not their own glory, etc. How can this connection hold unless something very great and most glorious is said to have been given to James the Less? It is not said that those three did not contend about the first rank of honour, while the other two readily acknowledged that Peter, as monarch, belonged to him in every way and by divine right. What is said is: they chose James, surnamed the Just, as bishop of Jerusalem.

units.la: X. Ipse Bellarminus satis aperte judicat,agi de re Jacobo collata,quæ si Petro collata fuisset, gloriam ejus multùm auxisset, dum ita loquitur: Ait (Clemens,) Apostolos præcipuos non quæsivisse gloriam propriam, & ideò non sibi assumsisse Episcopatum omnium eo tempore nobilissimum, sed eum Jacobo minori detulisse. Etsi enim Episcopatus unius Urbis non derogat primatui, tamen non parva gloria erat, fieri Episcopum Hierosolyma eo tempore, quo nullus erat ex particularibus Episcopis
units.tr: X. Bellarmine himself judges quite plainly that the matter concerns something given to James, which, had it been given to Peter, would have greatly increased his glory, when he speaks thus: "Clement says that the principal Apostles did not seek their own glory, and therefore did not assume for themselves the episcopate, the most noble of all at that time, but handed it over to James the Less. For although the episcopate of one city does not detract from the primacy, it was nevertheless no small glory to become bishop of Jerusalem at a time when there was none of the particular bishops who were more noble than that."

units.la: Huiusque dictum porro explicatur;
units.tr: The saying is further explained as follows.

units.la: Atque contra exceptiones Bellarminianas; scopis eo nobilior. Rectissimè ait Bellarminus, non parvam gloriam fuisse, magna fuit, & quæ saltem derogat Primatui, qualem ille fingit, Monarchicæ potestatis & dignitatis. Si Cathedra ulla & Ecclesia honorifica fuit, illa certè, quam antiquitate Ecclesiarum omnium matrem, & multis privilegiis insignem, ob Domini & Apostolorum præsentiam, quam longo tempore habuit, & præcipuè ob mysteria redemptionis nostræ eo loco perfecta & consummata, fuisse ipse Bellar. loc. cit. fatetur, in qua Christus docuit, ex qua lex & verbum Domini exire debuit.
units.tr: And against Bellarmine's objections: he rightly says that it was "no small glory." It was great, and it at least detracts from the primacy of monarchical power and dignity which he invents. If any see or church was honourable, it was certainly that one, which Bellarmine himself, in the passage cited, admits was the mother of all churches in antiquity, distinguished by many privileges, on account of the presence of the Lord and the Apostles, which it had for a long time, and especially because the mysteries of our redemption were there perfected and consummated, the church in which Christ taught and from which the law and word of the Lord had to go forth.

units.la: XI. Respondet Bellarminus, Christum non fuisse Episcopum ullius particularis Urbis, sed fuisse & esse Pontificem, non solùm Hierosolymæ, sed totius Ecclesiæ, neque ullum succedere illi cùm semper vivat. Quis satis miretur hoc initium responsi Bellarminiani! Neminem Christo successisse dicit, cùm semper vivat; quomodo ergo Papa est Successor Christi, quo elogio eum Scriptores Pontificii ornärunt? Quomodo Vicarius generalis, ut eum ipse Bellarminus immediatè post hæc verba vocat? Et Vicarius talis, quo, cùm Christus terras reliquerit, ad gubernationem Ecclesiæ Monarchicam opus sit? Egregium responsum, vel responsi initium, quod totius Papatus fundamentum evertit! Certè Jacobus non ita fuit Episcopus Hierosolymitanus, ut Ecclesiæ illi planè affixus fuerit, sicut dictum, hoc etenim repugnàsset muneri Apostolico, quod involvit curam omnium Ecclesiarum, & propter quod illi quoque dictum: Docete omnes gentes Matth. 18. v. 17. nec alià ratione Hierosolymitanus, quàm quâPetrum Romanum fuisse concedi posset; Si autem Christo succedere, vel certè ejus Vicarius esse potuit Petrus Romæ, quidni etiam Jacobus Hierosolymæ?
units.tr: XI. Bellarmine replies that Christ was not bishop of any particular city, but was and is the High Priest, not only of Jerusalem, but of the whole Church, and no one succeeds him since he always lives. Who could sufficiently marvel at this opening of the Bellarminian reply! He says that no one has succeeded Christ, since he always lives. How then is the Pope the successor of Christ, with which title the Papist writers have adorned him? How is he the vicar general, as Bellarmine himself calls him immediately after these words? And what sort of vicar is it, for whom, since Christ has left the earth, a monarchical government of the Church is necessary? An excellent reply, or at least an opening of a reply, which overturns the whole foundation of Papacy! Certainly James was not bishop of Jerusalem in such a way as to be wholly fixed to that church, as has been said; for this would have been contrary to the Apostolic office, which involves care of all the churches, and on account of which it was also said to him: Teach all nations, Matthew 18:17 (sic). Nor could Peter be granted to have been of Rome in any other way than James was of Jerusalem. If Peter could succeed Christ, or at least be his vicar, at Rome, why not James at Jerusalem?

units.la: XII. Respondet Bellarminus, Vicarium Christi generalem magis decuisse, ut alibi quàm Hierosolymis, constitueretur: quoniam sicut mutabatur per Christi adventum Lex & Sacerdotium, ita etiam decuit, ut locus mutaretur summi Sacerdotis, & fierent verè omnia nova. Atque ideò fortasse templum & Hierusalem brevi eversa & incensa post ascensionem Domini fuerunt. Sed 1. Hypothesis illa de Vicario illo generali & summo Sacerdote sine fundamento, imò, juxta jam jam allata verba Bellarmini, absurda est. 2. Quid deceat Vicarium Christi generalem & summum in Ecclesia Sacerdotem, aut magis deceat, ex verbo cognoscendum est, quod pro se adferre non possunt. 3. Mutato sacerdotio mutatur & Lex; id Paulus dicit. Locum etiam mutari debere, Bellarminus sine ratione dicit. 4. Omnia satis nova. va mutato Sacerdotio, mutatâ lege, mutatâ ad unum locum conveniendi, ab uno loco dependendi necessitate, quam, dum adhuc durare Pontificii fingunt, non omnia nova facta esse potiùs docent. 4. Si locus statim etiam mutari debuisset, Christus non Hierosolymæ docuisset, non Hierosolymâ verbum exire debuisset. 5. Si mutato jam Sacerdotio, mutatâ jam lege, & Christo jam per passiones consummato, imò in cœlos sublato, ad tempus Hierosolymitanus Episcopatus omnium nobilissimus fuit, illi, qui alium locum præter & contra Scripturam eligunt, & ut omnia nova sint, tanquam sedem religionis Universalem, quam habere potiùs deceat, obtrudunt, facto hoc probant, se mutare Sacerdotium & legem Christi. 6. Illud fortasse Bellarmini fundamento caret, cùm quidem ideò Templum & Hierusalem brevi post ascensionem Domini eversa & incensa sint, ut partim ingratitudo populi Judaici puniretur, partim cultus Leviticus plane aboleretur, partim etiam in N. T. sedem religionis unam & Ecclesiam ulli loco affixam non esse, ne quidem illi, ex quo initia sumsit, ostenderetur, non autem ut ideò Roma religionis sedes fieret. 7. Licet Hierosolyma eversa fuerit, semper tamen fuerunt Episcopi Hierosolymitani. Nec Cathedræ Romanæ obesse putant, quòd aliquoties sub N. T. Roma vastata est, & tum aliàs alibi, tum maximè per 70 annos Episcopi Romani Avenione fuerunt, quot annis Christianis Hierosolymitanis cum Episcopo suo Pellæ non mandum erat.
units.tr: XII. Bellarmine replies that it was more fitting that the general vicar of Christ should be set up elsewhere than at Jerusalem, since, just as the Law and the Priesthood were changed by the coming of Christ, so it was fitting that the place of the High Priest should be changed too, and that everything should truly become new. And so perhaps the temple and Jerusalem were overthrown and burned shortly after the Lord's ascension. But: (1) That hypothesis about that general vicar and high priest has no foundation; indeed, according to the very words of Bellarmine just quoted, it is absurd. (2) What befits the general vicar of Christ and the high priest of the Church, or what befits him more, must be learned from the Word, which they cannot produce in their support. (3) "When the priesthood is changed, the law is changed too," Paul says. That the place too ought to be changed, Bellarmine says without reason. (4) Everything was new enough: with the priesthood changed, the law changed, and the necessity of gathering in one place and depending on one place changed, which the Papists, while they pretend these things still endure, rather show were not all made new. (5) If the place ought to have been changed at once, Christ would not have taught at Jerusalem, and the word would not have had to go forth from Jerusalem. (6) If, with the priesthood already changed, the law already changed, and Christ already perfected through his sufferings, and indeed taken up into heaven, the Episcopate of Jerusalem was for a time the most noble of all, then those who choose another place besides and against Scripture, and, so that everything may be new, thrust it upon us as a universal seat of religion, which it would rather befit to have, prove by this act that they are changing the priesthood and the law of Christ. (7) That perhaps of Bellarmine lacks foundation: the temple and Jerusalem were indeed overthrown and burned shortly after the Lord's ascension partly so that the ingratitude of the Jewish people might be punished, partly so that the Levitical worship might be entirely abolished, and partly also to show that in the New Testament there is no one seat of religion, nor a Church fixed to any place, not even to that from which it took its beginning; not so that Rome might thereby become the seat of religion. (8) Although Jerusalem was overthrown, there have always been bishops of Jerusalem. Nor do they think it harms the Roman see that Rome has been laid waste several times under the New Testament, and at other times elsewhere; and above all, for seventy years the Roman bishops were at Avignon, which was no more an obstacle to the Christians of Jerusalem with their bishop at Pella than it was to the Romans.

units.la: XIII. Et licèt Concilii Nicæni tempore authoritas Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ ob respectus maximè seculares, quibus aliæ sedes magis commendabantur, & quia (verba sunt Guicciardini Hist. Pap. lib.4.) religionis sedes Imperii atque armorum potentiam sequi consuevit, multùm jam imminuta fuerit, tamen maximam illam Apostolorum tempore fuisse (quod ad prærogativam Jacobi sufficit:) ipse jam Bellarminus fassus est; interim etiam illius Concilii Patres Canoni suo septimo aperta pristinæ dignitatis indicia inseruerunt, dicentes; consuetudinem obtinuisse & antiquam traditionem, ut Ælia (Hierosolymæ) Episcopus honoretur: quemadmodum etiam seculo adhuc quinto, Cœlestino Papa Romano Primatum affectante, Polychronius Episcopus Hierosolymitanus sanctè affirmavit, si aliquis quærendus esset, illum multis nominibus sua potiùs Ecclesia deberi. Ante oculos, credo, habuit, Jacobi prærogativam. De qua adhuc duo Patrum testimonia audire non inutile erit.
units.tr: XIII. Although at the time of the Council of Nicaea the authority of the Church of Jerusalem had already been greatly diminished, chiefly for secular reasons, since other sees were more highly regarded, and because (the words are Guicciardini's, Hist. Pap. lib. 4) the seat of religion has usually followed the power of empire and arms, Bellarmine himself has admitted that in the time of the Apostles it held the greatest dignity, and this is enough for the privilege of James. Meanwhile the Fathers of that Council, in their seventh canon, also inserted clear signs of its former dignity, saying that custom and ancient tradition had prevailed that the Bishop of Aelia (Jerusalem) should be honoured. So too in the fifth century, when Pope Celestine of Rome was claiming the primacy, Polychronius, Bishop of Jerusalem, rightly affirmed that if anyone were to be sought, he was owed by many titles to his own Church rather than to Rome. He had, I believe, the privilege of James before his eyes. It will not be unprofitable to hear two testimonies of the Fathers on this privilege.

units.la: XIV. Unum est Epiphanii hær.78. §. 7. interprete Dionysio Petavo Jesuita.
