Idem ille, inquit, primus Episcopalem Cathedram cepit, cùm ei ante cateros omnes suum in terris thronum Dominus tradidisset, qui quidem Domini frater est vulgò nominatus. Alterum est Joh. Chrysostomi ab ipso etiam Bellarmino tanquam gravissimum testimoniorum, quæ Jacobi primatui favere videantur, allatum; Ita se habet hom. 3. in Acta. Vide Jacobi Modestiam. Is acceperat Hierosolymis munus, & tamen hic nihil loquitur. Consldera autem & aliorum discipulorum singularem modestiam, quo pacto ei concedunt solium, nec amplius ambigunt disceptantes inter se.
units.tr: XIV. The first is that of Epiphanius, Heresy 78, §7, in the translation of the Jesuit Denys Petavius: This same man, he says, was the first to take an episcopal chair, since the Lord had given him his throne on earth before all others; he is commonly called the brother of the Lord. The second is a passage of John Chrysostom, which Bellarmine himself cites as the weightiest of the testimonies which seem to favour the primacy of James. It reads thus in Homily 3 on Acts: See the modesty of James. He had received the office at Jerusalem, and yet here he says nothing. Consider too the singular modesty of the other disciples, how they grant him the throne and no longer dispute among themselves.

units.la: XV. Juxta hunc posteriorem locum fuit modestia & in Jacobo, quòd tacuit, potuisset enim tanquam Episcopus loqui & cum magna authoritate, & in discipulis, quod non amplius ambigunt disceptantes inter se; Ergo inter primos potuisset esse disceptatio de isto honore, qui proin maximus fuit; (quod & supra memoratus Clementis locus docet) & quòd solium Jacobo concedunt. Ast solium particulare; excipit Bellarminus. Fateor, non enim fuit Hierosolymitana Ecclesia Universa, nec dantur solia Universalia, cùm Ecclesia particularis non sit Universalis, quam absurditatem Pontificiis relinquimus quoad solium Romanum, licet interim tenendum sit illud, Jacobum cœterorum Apostolorum ad instar tanquam Apostolum Universalem fuisse; Sed fuit solium, solium καὶ ἐξοχὴν, ut etiam in priori loco Epiphanii emphaticè θρόνῳ αὐτοῦ, thronus illius, Christi nimirùm dicitur, qui eum Jacobo ante cæteros tradiderit.
units.tr: XV. In accordance with this latter passage, James showed modesty in keeping silent, for he could have spoken as a bishop, and with great authority; and the disciples showed it in that they no longer disputed among themselves. Therefore among the first the dispute could have been about this honour, which was therefore the greatest (as the passage of Clement cited above also shows), and they grant the throne to James. But Bellarmine objects that it was a particular throne. I admit it: the Church of Jerusalem was not the universal Church, and there are no universal thrones, since a particular Church is not a universal one. This absurdity we leave to the Papists in regard to the Roman throne. Still, it must be held that James, like the other Apostles, was an Apostle to the whole world in the manner of the others. But it was a throne by eminence (καὶ ἐξοχὴν), just as in the first passage of Epiphanius it is emphatically called his throne, that is, the throne of Christ, who gave it to James before all others.

units.la: XVI. Cœterùm ultrò damus, etiam Joh. Chrysostomum (quod Bellarminus allegatis locis sibi probandum esse judicavit:) Petro primatum adscribere; Sed negamus, talem eum Petro adscribere, multò magis talem eum illi jure adscribere potuisse, qui fuerit Monarchæ, qualis certè primatus cum loco isto Chrysostomi & cum aliis aliorum nequaquam consistere potest. Habuerit Primatum ordinis Petrus; habuit etiam suas prærogativas Jacobus, & tales, quæ eum æqualem ostendunt, imò si ad sedem certam respicitur, secundùm hactenus dicta, major Jacobi Hierosolymitani quàm verò Petri, ut volunt, Romani prærogativa fuisse videtur.
units.tr: XVI. Moreover, we freely grant that John Chrysostom (which Bellarmine judged must be proved from the passages he cited) ascribes a primacy to Peter. But we deny that he ascribed such a primacy to Peter, and much less could he rightly have ascribed such a primacy to one who was a monarch. Such a primacy certainly cannot stand together with that passage of Chrysostom or with the other passages of others. Peter had a primacy of order; James also had his privileges, and such as show him to be equal to Peter. Indeed, if we look to a fixed see, then according to what has been said so far, the privilege of James of Jerusalem seems to have been greater than that of Peter of Rome, as they claim.

units.la: XVII. Sed jam etiam de Pauli prærogativis distinctius videndum, quas jam supra paucis tetigimus. Quàm verè arbitratus est ipse, se μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων, nihil inferiorem riorem seriorem fuisse summis Apostolis, 2.Cor.XI.v.5. idem, qui alibi se minimum Apostolorum & non dignum tanto munere, habito nimirum ad statum pristinum respectu, vocavit; Factus quippe ex seductore Doctor, ex praedone praeco, quam ob causam Tertullianus contra Marcionem. l.5. judicavit, eum jam olim Genesin (cap.49.) repromisisse, qui ex tribu Benjamin oriturus, & lupi rapacis ad instar ad matutinum comesturus, id est, primâ aetate ut persecutor Ecclesiarum pecora Domini vastaturus; debinc ad vesperam escam daturus, id est, demergente jam aetate ovës Christi ut doctor nationum educaturus sit; qui idem Tertullianus loco eodem censuit, Saulis primò asperitatem insectationis erga Davidem, debinc poenitentiam & satisfactionem pro malis bona recipientis, non aliud portendisse, quàm Paulum in Saule secundùm tribus, & Jesum in David secundùm virginis censum &c. Et quanta quaeso bona pro malis recepit ille? Ipse Dominus, qui vocavit eum σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς vas electum mihi est, inquit, ad portandum nomen meum inter gentes, Reges & filios Israël, Act.IX.v.15. Quis adeò nobili magistro usus est? Quando ex illis salutaribus emersit fluentis, inquit Joh.Chrysostomus hom. in laudem D. Pauli, tanto igne plenus exivit, ut nec necessarium sibi putaret magistrum. Vide Gal.I.v.12.17.II. v.6. Non enim exspectavit Petrum, nec venit ad Jacobum, nec ad alium omninò quenquam: Peculiari ille modo Θεοδίδακτος, à Deo doctus coelitus, imò in coelo edoctus, raptus in paradisum, in tertium coelum, verba ibi accepit ineffabilia, 2.Cor. XII.v.2.
units.tr: XVII. But now we must look more distinctly at the privileges of Paul, which we touched on briefly above. How truly he thought himself to be nothing inferior to the chiefest Apostles [μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων] (2 Cor. 11:5), he who elsewhere called himself the least of the Apostles and not worthy of so great an office, evidently in comparison with his former state. Indeed, from a deceiver he became a teacher, from a robber a herald. This is why Tertullian, against Marcion, book 5, judged that Jacob had long before prophesied of him in Genesis (ch. 49), that he would arise from the tribe of Benjamin and devour like a ravening wolf in the morning, that is, in his early life as a persecutor of the Churches he would ravage the Lord's flock; and that in the evening he would give food, that is, when his age was already declining, he would bring up the sheep of Christ as the teacher of the nations. The same Tertullian, in the same place, held that the harshness of Saul's persecution of David, and afterwards his repentance and satisfaction, by which he received good for evil, portended nothing other than Paul in Saul according to the tribe, and Jesus in David according to the lineage of the virgin, and so on. And what great goods, I ask, did he receive for evil? The Lord himself, who called him a chosen vessel [σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς]: He is, he says, a vessel of election to me, to carry my name among the nations, kings, and the sons of Israel (Acts 9:15). Who was ever so well served by so noble a master? When he came up out of those saving waters, says John Chrysostom in his homily in praise of St Paul, he came out so full of fire that he did not think he needed a teacher. See Gal. 1:12, 17; 2:6. For he did not wait for Peter, nor did he go to James, nor to any other person at all. In a peculiar manner he was taught by God [Θεοδίδακτος], taught from heaven, indeed instructed in heaven, caught up into paradise, into the third heaven, where he heard unspeakable words (2 Cor. 12:2).

units.la: XVIII. Ut jam mirum non fit, tanta de eo praedicari, quòd Ecclesiae nutritor sit, quo elogio eum Augustinus ornat, quòd igne ipso vehementior, quod de eo Chrysost. lib. cit. testatur, quòd ipsi itineris non parvum praemium, urbis Romae conversio proposita sit, ibidem, quòd sol quidam sit hominibus, qui totum prorsus orbem fulgentibus linguae suae radiis illuminârit, quique universas circumeundo gentes cursum omninò solis imitatus sit, ac mundi regiones omnes quasi libero à corpore animo pervolârit, hom.8. de laude Pauli, quòd totum terrarum orbem velut ignis & spiritus percurrerit, percurrendóque purgârit, hom. 1. totum orbem attraxerit, ejus sublimitas omnes coelos transcenderit, ipse Deus eum admiratus sit electum vas vocando, mentem ejus nulla tentatio obnubilaverit, in cap.2. epist ad Rom. quòd omnibus hominibus praestantior, orbis terrarum Doctor, adductor sponsae ad Christum sponsum, Ecclesiae plantator, sapiens Architectus, Apostolis major sit. hom. contra haer. & in petit; matris fil. Zebed. T.5. h.33. pag.209. ed. Savil. quòd totius orbis bis ei cura commissa sit, lingua orbis, lux Ecclesiarum, fundamentum fidei, columna & firmamentum veritatis (al. ecclesiae) fuerit Hom.1. in verbis: Salutate Priscillam, quae est n.47. T. ejusd.
units.tr: XVIII. It is therefore no wonder that such great things are said of him: that he is the nourisher of the Church, a praise with which Augustine adorns him; that he is more vehement than fire itself, as Chrysostom testifies in the work cited; that a great reward for his journey was set before him, the conversion of the city of Rome, in the same place; that he is a kind of sun to men, who has illuminated the whole world with the shining rays of his tongue, and who, going round all the nations, has imitated the course of the sun altogether, and has flown through all the regions of the world as if his mind were free of the body, Homily 8 on the praise of Paul; that like fire and spirit he has run through the whole orb of the earth, and by running has purified it, Homily 1; that he has drawn the whole world to himself; that his sublimity has passed beyond all the heavens; that God himself admired him in calling him a chosen vessel; that no temptation has clouded his mind, on Romans ch. 2; that he is more excellent than all men, the teacher of the world, the one who brought the bride to the bridegroom Christ, the planter of the Church, a wise architect, and greater than the Apostles, homily against heretics, and on the petition of the mother of the sons of Zebedee, vol. 5, homily 33, p. 209, ed. Savile; that the care of the whole world was committed to him twice; that he was the tongue of the world, the light of the Churches, the foundation of the faith, the pillar and firmament of the truth (other reading: the Church), Homily 1 on the words "Salute Priscilla", which is no. 47 of the same volume.

units.la: XIX. Ut jam etiam mirum non sit, tanta de epistolis illius praedicari. Παῦλος πάντων ἐν ἀποστόλοις λόγων δυνατώτατος, νοήματα ἱκανώτατα γεγονώς, Paulus inter omnes Apostolos & verborum apparatu & sententiarum pondere praestantissimus factus, judice Eusebio. Hist. Eccles. l.3.c.24. edit. Valef. Quae Pauli epistola non melle dulcior, non lacte candidior? quaerit Augustinus de sanct. serm. 26. Quotiescunque lego, inquit Hieron. in Apol. pro libris contra Jovin. videor mihi non verba audire, sed tonitrua. Legite Epistolas ejus, & maximè ad Romanos, ad Galatas, ad Ephesios, in quibus totus in certamine positus est, & videbitis enim in testimoniis, quae sumit de veteri testamento, quam artifex, quam prudens, quam dissimulator sit ejus, quod agit. Videntur quaedam verba simplicia & quasi innocentis hominis ac rusticani & qui nec facere, nec declinare noverit insidias: Sed quocunque respexeris, fulmina sunt. Haret in causa, capit omne quod tetigerit, tergum vertit, ut superet, fugam simulat, ut occidat.
units.tr: XIX. Nor is it any wonder that such great things are said of his Epistles: Paul, the most powerful of all the Apostles in words, and most able in his thoughts [Παῦλος πάντων ἐν ἀποστόλοις λόγων δυνατώτατος, νοήματα ἱκανώτατα γεγονώς], Paul having become the most excellent of all the Apostles both in the array of words and in the weight of his opinions, as Eusebius judges, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, ch. 24, Valesius's edition. What epistle of Paul is not sweeter than honey, whiter than milk? asks Augustine, On the Saints, sermon 26. Whenever I read him, says Jerome in Apology for his books against Jovinian, I seem to hear not words but thunderclaps. Read his Epistles, especially those to the Romans, the Galatians and the Ephesians, in which he is wholly engaged in the struggle; and you will see in the testimonies which he takes from the Old Testament how skilled, how prudent, how much a dissembler he is in what he is doing. Some words seem simple, as of an innocent and rustic man who knows neither how to make nor to avoid a trap. But wherever you look, they are thunderbolts. He clings to the cause, seizes everything he touches, turns his back so as to conquer, feigns flight so as to kill.

units.la: XX. Ut jam non magis mirum sit, eum tantum in compa-ratione apparere. Cui te, ô beate Paule, verba sunt Joh.Chrysost. de laud. Pauli hom.8. justorum veteris Testamenti vel novi audeam comparare? Omnium quippe virtutem quasi in arca quadam, sed cum multo prorsus cumulo condidisti. Denique si totum contra te aliquis sigillatim justorum appendat chorum, inveniet trutinam virtutum à tua parte depressam. Paulus enim secundus Abel & alter Noë, Abraham, Isacc, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Phineas, David, Elias, Elisaeus, Ezechiel, Josias, Johannes, Petrus, Gabriel, Michaël, quibus omnibus ita Paulum confert, ut superiorem quodam modo esse ostendat, & Petro quidem, cùm sit non de terra, sed de coelo vocatus ad credendum. Concludit tandem: Etiamsi angelorum, etiamsi justorum hominum circumvolem choros, non invenio comparationem, cui non tamen cumulo meritorum occurrat. Et alibi: Paulo illustrius nihil fuit.
units.tr: XX. So it is no longer surprising that he appears only in comparison. To whom, O blessed Paul, may I dare to compare you among the righteous of the Old or New Testament? For you have stored up the virtues of all of them, as it were in a certain chest, but with a truly great heap. Indeed, if anyone should weigh the whole choir of the righteous against you, one by one, he will find the scale of virtues weighed down on your side. For Paul is a second Abel and another Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, David, Elijah, Elisha, Ezekiel, Josiah, John, Peter, Gabriel, Michael, and he compares Paul with all of these in such a way as to show that he is in some sense superior, and especially to Peter, since Peter was called from heaven, not from the earth, to believe. He concludes at last: Even if I fly around the choirs of angels and of righteous men, I find no comparison to which he does not rise, with a heap of merits. And elsewhere: Nothing was more illustrious than Paul.

units.la: XXI. Comparationem ejus cum Petro in specie quod attinet, idem Joh. Chrysost. Tomo cit. hom.167. (siquidem authentica est) quae de coryphaeis Apostolorum Petro & Paulo agit: Quid enim Petro, inquit, majus? Quid autem Paulo aquale? Et itidem de ambobus; Eorum quidem, quae supra sunt, acceperunt claves, eorum autem, quae infra sunt, solvendi & ligandi potestatem habentes. Ibidem etiam ambos columnas luminas Ecclesiæ, magna orbis luminaria vocat, & ut hom.168. (de qua etiam dubitatur) Apostolos quosvis rectè doctrinâ columnas immotas, Petram Ecclesiæ, regni sceptra, gregis præfectos laudat; ita ibidem denuò ambos Apostolorum coryphæos Paulum ex postremis primum nuncupat. Ambrosius autem Serm.66. de Natali Petri & Pauli, & Augustinus Serm.3, Petri & Pauli, & judiciis & verbis his conveniunt: Eminent super (inter) universos Apostolos & peculiari quàdam prærogativâ præcellunt, verùm inter ipsos, quis cui præferatur, incertum est. Idem Ambrosius lib. de Sp. S. cap.12. Nec Paulus, inquit, inferior Petro, quamvis ille Ecclesiæ fundamentum & hic sapiens Architectus sciens vestigia credentium fundare populorum, nec Paulus, inquam, indignus Apostolorum collegio, cum primo quoque facilè conferendus & nulli secundus; nam qui se imparem nescit, facit æqualem. Et idem Augustinus Serm. 25. de sanctis: Etsi Petrum priorem, tamen ambos donavit honore uno. Maximus Taurinensis hom.5. in natali Apost. eadem dicit, quæ jam jam dixerunt Ambrosius & Augustinus. Et Gregorius I. ipse Papa Dial. cap. ult. Paulus Apostolus Petro Apostolorum primo in principatu frater est. Quibus quatuor postremis locis doctissimus du Pin subjungit: Hinc Petrus & Paulus æquè dicuntur Apostolorum principes, Apostolorum primi, summi Apostoli, ad culmen & apicem Apostolorum subvecti. Paulus non secus ac Petrus totius orbis curam habere dicitur, & omnium orbis Ecclesiarum pastor, quin etiam Paulus sæpe solus dicitur princeps Apostolorum, caput Apostolorum, qui primatum Apostolatûs inter gentes habuerit, quemadmodum Petrus inter Judæos &c. Addi possunt glossæ Nicolai de Lyra ad Gal.II. sequentes, Paulum contrà Apostolis principalibus contulisse aliquid, in eo, quòd nihil illi contulerint, apparere, (quæ ibi Augustini glossa) quòd illis inferior non sit, utrumque æquè principaliter missum fuisse, non ausum fuisse in faciem Petro resistere, nisi se non imparem sensisset. XXII. Cogitâsse saltem de plerisque, quæ hactenus allata sunt, Bellarminum, verisimile est; Quamvis in capite 27. l.1. de Pont. Rom. cui titulus: de comparatione Petri cum Paulo; duo tantùm sibi objiciat, quæ unà cum responsionibus Bellarmini attentiùs etiam considerare operæ pretium erit. Primò sibi objicit; Paulum per Antonomasiam vocari Apostolum. Confirmat illud Augustinus l.3. ad Bonif. c.3. Apostolus, inquit, cùm dicitur, si non exprimatur quis Apostolus, non intelligitur nisi Paulus. Ait Bellarminus; inde sequi videtur, ut ipse potiùs, quàm Petrus Princeps Apostolorum sit. Certè videtur sequi qui ex sententia illorum, qui Paulum sic denotare amant, non minorem Paulum Petro, etiam Apostolorum principem, in nonnullis Petro superiorem, Petrum non Monarcham, à quo cum subjectione tanquam à capite & imperatore Paulus pependerit, non minores Pauli prærogativas fuisse; quemadmodum dum per eandem figuram Oratorem Latinum dico, & Ciceronem; Græcum, & Demosthenem; Poëtam Græcum, & Homerum, Latinum, Virgilium intelligo, eo ipso innuo, Ciceronem, inter Latinos, Demosthenem, inter Græcos Oratores, Homerum inter Græcos, Virgilium inter Latinos Poëtas maximos fuisse.
units.tr: XXI. As far as his comparison with Peter in particular is concerned, the same John Chrysostom, in the cited homily 167 (if indeed it is authentic), which deals with the leaders of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, says: For what is greater than Peter, he says? And what is equal to Paul? And likewise of both: they received the keys of the things above, and they had the power of loosing and binding the things below. In the same place he also calls both the luminous pillars of the Church, the great lights of the world, and, in homily 168 (which is also doubted), he praises the Apostles as rightly the immovable pillars by their teaching, the rock of the Church, the sceptres of the kingdom, the overseers of the flock; so in the same place again he names Paul, as one of the two leaders of the Apostles, first from the last. Ambrose, in Sermon 66 on the Birthday of Peter and Paul, and Augustine, in Sermon 3, on Peter and Paul, agree with these opinions and words: They stand out above (among) all the Apostles and excel by a certain peculiar prerogative, but as to which of the two is preferred to the other, it is uncertain. The same Ambrose, in book on the Holy Spirit, chapter 12: Nor is Paul, he says, inferior to Peter, although the one is the foundation of the Church and the other the wise architect who knows how to lay the foundations for the steps of believing peoples; nor, I say, is Paul unworthy of the college of Apostles, since he can easily be compared with the first and is second to none; for he who does not know that he is unequal, makes himself equal. And the same Augustine, in Sermon 25 on the saints: Although he gave Peter the first place, yet he gave both one honour. Maximus of Turin, in homily 5 on the Apostle's birthday, says the same things that Ambrose and Augustine have just said. And Gregory I, the Pope himself, in Dialogues, last chapter: Paul the Apostle is a brother to Peter, the first of the Apostles in the leadership. To these four last passages the most learned du Pin adds: Hence Peter and Paul are equally called the princes of the Apostles, the first of the Apostles, the highest Apostles, raised to the summit and peak of the Apostles. Paul is said to have the care of the whole world no less than Peter, and to be the minister of all the churches of the world; indeed Paul is often called alone the prince of the Apostles, the head of the Apostles, since he held the primacy of the apostolate among the Gentiles, just as Peter did among the Jews, etc. The following glosses of Nicholas of Lyra on Galatians 2 may be added: that Paul gave something to the principal Apostles, in that they appear to have given him nothing (which is Augustine's gloss there); that he was not inferior to them, since both were sent equally as principals; that he would not have dared to resist Peter to his face, unless he had felt that he was not unequal. XXII. It is likely that Bellarmine has at least considered most of the things adduced so far; although in chapter 27 of book 1 on the Roman Pontiff, which is entitled On the comparison of Peter with Paul, he raises against himself only two points, which it will be worth considering more carefully together with Bellarmine's replies. First, he objects to himself that Paul is called the Apostle by antonomasia. Augustine confirms this in book 3 to Boniface, chapter 3: When it is said "the Apostle", he says, if no one is named, only Paul is understood. Bellarmine says: From this it seems to follow that he himself, rather than Peter, is the prince of the Apostles. Certainly it seems to follow, on the view of those who love to designate Paul in this way, that Paul was not less than Peter, even though Peter was the prince of the Apostles, and that in some respects Paul was superior to Peter; that Peter was not a monarch, from whom Paul depended with subjection as from a head and commander, and that Paul's prerogatives were not less than his. In the same way, when by the same figure I say "the Latin orator" and mean Cicero, "the Greek" and mean Demosthenes, "the Greek poet" and mean Homer, "the Latin" and mean Virgil, I by that very fact imply that Cicero was the greatest orator among the Latins, Demosthenes among the Greeks, Homer among the Greek poets, and Virgil among the Latin poets.

units.la: XXIII. Respondet Bellarminus: Paulum ita vocari, non quia major fuerit Petro potestate vel auctoritate, sed 1. quia plura scripserit, 2. Quia in pluribus locis fidem plantaverit. Repono 1. Rationes etiam ab Augustino allatæ bonæ sunt; Ideo καὶ ἐξοχὴν Paulum Apostolum & nos dicimus, quia plura scripsit & in pluribus locis fidem plantavit, sed hoc ipsum, juxta ea, quæ hactenus dicta sunt. 2. Ejus auctoritatem auxit & principatum inter Apostolos ei peculiarem acquisivit. Sic enim maximè universalis declaratus, sic illustrioribus signis Apostolatus ejus confirmatus, sic demonstratum est, neminem ad majora missum fuisse; quem enim Deus mittit, illum etiam idoneum reddit, illius laboribus etiam benedicit, & si ad majora Petrum misisset, majora ille etiam majoris missionis documenta procul dubio ostendisset, ut etiam apud Deum major labor majorem gloriam post se trahit, quia unusquisque propriam mercedem accipiet secundum proprium laborem, 1. Cor. III. 8. Quoad potestatem vero 3. & Petrus & Paulus & cæteri æquales fuerunt, habuerunt quippe, ipso Bellarmino fatente, summam atque amplissimam potestatem. Et Paulus, consentiente nobis glossa Augustini in c. 1. ad Gal. minor Petro non fuit etiam in jurisdictione, quod ex hactenus dictis, & Excommunicatione incestuosi & aliis patet, ut illorum responsio, qui paritatem inter Petrum & Paulum intelligunt de paritate vitæ & sanctitate conversationis stare nullo modo possit, quam etiam responsionem & interpretationem Gratiani non convenire verbis, literæ probant Ulricus Argentinensis lib. 6. sui operis cap. 23. quoniam redarguere coram omnibus ad officium Ecclesiasticæ dignitatis pertineat, illi peccantem coram omnibus arguant, ut cæteri timorem habeant, juxta sententiam Pauli 1. Tim. V. quod Paulus erga Petrum Gal. II. fecisse legitur. Ita ut jam amplectamur Bellarminum in fine responsionis Responsio ad responsionem; sionis suae dicentem: Paulus dici potest Princeps Apostolorum, quia munus Apostolicum excellentissimè adimplevit. Quomodo Virgilius dicitur Princeps Poëtarum, & Cicero Princeps Oratorum. Excellentissimè adimplevit munus, juxta Bellarminum, etiam summum Ecclesiasticum; ubi igitur Monarchicus Petri primatus? Princeps Apostolorum dici potest, qui non Monarcha Ecclesiae; ubi igitur solidum pro Monarchia Petri argumentum ullum ex eo, quòd plerumque primò nominatur?
units.tr: XXIII. Bellarmine replies: Paul is so called not because he was greater than Peter in power or authority, but 1. because he wrote more, 2. because he planted the faith in more places. I answer, first: the reasons also adduced by Augustine are good; so we too call Paul the Apostle par excellence [καὶ ἐξοχὴν], because he wrote more and planted the faith in more places; but this very thing agrees with what has been said so far. Second, his authority was increased and a principate peculiar to him among the Apostles was acquired for him. For thus he was declared most widely universal, thus his apostleship was confirmed by more illustrious signs, thus it was shown that no one was sent to greater things; for whom God sends, him he also makes fit, and he also blesses his labours; and if he had sent Peter to greater things, Peter would undoubtedly also have shown greater proofs of a greater mission, just as with God greater labour draws after it greater glory, because each shall receive his own reward according to his own labour, 1 Cor. 3:8. As for power, third: Peter and Paul and the others were equal, for they had, as Bellarmine himself admits, the highest and most ample power. And Paul was not less than Peter even in jurisdiction, as the gloss of Augustine on Galatians 1 agrees with us, which is clear from what has been said so far, and from the excommunication of the incestuous man and other things. So the reply of those who understand the equality between Peter and Paul as equality of life and holiness of conduct cannot stand in any way; and the letter itself shows that the reply and interpretation of Gratian do not agree with the words, as Ulrich of Strasbourg shows in book 6 of his work, chapter 23: since it belongs to the office of ecclesiastical dignity to rebuke in front of all, let them accuse the sinning man before all, so that the others may have fear, according to the sentence of Paul, 1 Tim. 5, which we read Paul did towards Peter in Gal. 2. So let us now embrace Bellarmine at the end of his reply, saying: Paul can be called the Prince of the Apostles because he most excellently fulfilled the Apostolic office. As Virgil is called the Prince of the Poets, and Cicero the Prince of the Orators. According to Bellarmine, he most excellently fulfilled even the highest ecclesiastical office; where then is the monarchic primacy of Peter? He can be called the Prince of the Apostles who is not the monarch of the Church; where then is any solid argument for Peter's monarchy from the fact that he is most often named first?

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Prolixior est Bellarminus in respondendo ad alteram objectionem, quam sic format; Accedit, quòd in antiquis sigillis, quibus diplomata summi Pontificis obsignantur, inveniuntur imagines Petri & Pauli, sed hujus à dextris, illius à sinistris. Quod etiam observavit S. Thomas in Epist. ad Galatas lectione prima, & Petrus Damianus in tractatu de hac ipsa re. Hanc ipsam objectionem sibi etiam facit Doctissimus du Pin, quando Diff. IV. cap. 1. 5. 3. ait: Hinc imaginibus Petrus & Paulus velut aequales depingi solent, imò nonnunquam Paulus ad dexteram, Petrus ad sinistram ponitur. Et ad eam brevissimè respondet: Argumentum ex imaginibus repetitum ego nihil moror, nihil enim illo levius; nam ex eo, quòd Petrus & Paulus simul pinguntur, non sequitur, eos esse aequales in Primatu, sed ad summum in Apostolatu: cur verò nonnunquam Paulus dextrum locum occupet, ratio certa reddi non potest praeter pictorum arbitrium, quibus quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas. Responsum hocce certissimum indicium est, Doctissimo Viro multas & operosas Bellarmini responsiones minimè satis fecisse, quemadmodum certè etiam in aliis, etiam juxta porrò dicenda, Bellarminus Doctissimo Viro satis fecit minimè. Sed examinemus primùm, & antequam responsiones Bellarminianas ad examen vocemus, ipsum illud Doctissimi Viri responsum.
units.tr: Bellarminus is more long-winded in answering the second objection, which he frames thus: Moreover, on the ancient seals with which the diplomas of the supreme Pontiff are sealed, images of Peter and Paul are found, but Peter's on the right and Paul's on the left. St. Thomas also observed this in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, lesson one, and Peter Damian in his treatise on this very matter. The most learned du Pin raises this same objection against himself when, in Diss. IV, chap. 1, §5, no. 3, he says: Hence Peter and Paul are usually painted as if they were equals; indeed sometimes Paul is placed on the right and Peter on the left. And he answers it very briefly: I attach no weight to the argument drawn from images, for nothing is lighter than that. For from the fact that Peter and Paul are painted together it does not follow that they are equal in primacy, but at most in apostleship. Why Paul sometimes occupies the place on the right cannot be given a certain reason, except the painters' judgement, who have always had an equal licence to dare anything. This answer is a very certain sign that the many laborious replies of Bellarmine have not satisfied the most learned man at all, just as, in other matters too, as will be said further on, Bellarmine has by no means satisfied him. But let us first examine that very answer of the most learned man, before we call Bellarmine's replies to trial.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Forte deprehendetur argumentum illud non usque adeo leve esse, ut quis illud nihil morari posset Doctor Romanae Communionis. Ex eo, quòd Petrus & Paulus simul pinguntur, inquit Vir Doctissimus, non sequitur, eos esse aequales in principatu, sed ad summum in Apostolatu. De sententia Doctissimi Viri circa primatum Petri & jam nonnulla diximus, & mox plura dicemus. Hic autem cum venia Viri Doctissimi, primò, neminem unquam sic argumentatum esse: Petrus & Paulus simul pinguntur E. sunt aequales. Possunt enim personae diversarum dignitatum simul pingi, Apostoli cum coetu quodam integro. Sed si in diplomatibus Romanorum Pontificum, & ubi
units.tr: Perhaps that argument will be found not so light that a doctor of the Roman communion could make nothing of it. From the fact that Peter and Paul are painted together, says the most learned man, it does not follow that they are equal in principality, but at most in apostleship. We have already said something, and will soon say more, about the most learned man's view of Peter's primacy. Here, however, with the most learned man's pardon, first, no one has ever argued like this: Peter and Paul are painted together, therefore they are equal. For persons of different dignities can be painted together, apostles along with a whole company. But if in the diplomas of the Roman Pontiffs, and where the founders of the Roman Church are to be designated...

units.la: Objectio altera, de situ Pauli in Diplomatibus, & ad eam Doct. du Pin responsio;
units.tr: Second objection, concerning Paul's position in the diplomas, and Doctor du Pin's answer to it.

units.la: Ostenditur, eum nobis affingere argumentationem à nobis alienam; & ubi fundatores Ecclesiæ Romanæ designandi sunt, sine ullo discrimine Petrus & Paulus ponuntur, cæteris paribus, eorum æqualitatem etiam in eo, quod Petrus tanquam Ecclesiæ Romanæ fundator habuisse dicitur, jam ex eo aliquo modo concludi omninò posse sanè videtur, & si præterea in ejusmodi picturis Paulus à dextra, quæ honoratior haberi solet, conspicitur, videtur, etiam inde concludi posse, Paulum honoratiorem fuisse; contrà non videtur sufficere responsum de pictoria licentia.
units.tr: It is shown that he attributes to us an argument that is not ours. Where the founders of the Roman Church are to be designated, Peter and Paul are set down without any distinction; other things being equal, their equality can already be concluded in some way from this, even from the fact that Peter is said to have held the position of founder of the Roman Church. Indeed it seems entirely possible to conclude this. And if moreover in such pictures Paul is seen on the right, which is usually regarded as the more honourable place, it seems that one may conclude from this too that Paul was the more honoured. On the contrary, the answer about the painter's licence does not seem sufficient.

units.la: XXVII. Pictores quidem quidlibet ausi sunt, (ut nihil dicam de iis, quæ religionem non tangunt,) jam olim inter Gentiles.
units.tr: XXVII. Painters have certainly dared anything (to say nothing of those things that do not touch religion), even long ago among the Gentiles.

units.la: Plinius enim, citante Vavassore Jesuita in Tractatu de forma Christi, memorat pictorem, qui amasiarum suarum formas deabus dederit, quod forsan, eodem conjiciente, respexit Justinus Martyr, quando dixit; gentiles adorare amasias pictorum suorum. Pictores quidlibet audent etiam in Ecclesia Pontificia. Ausi sunt olim multa ad veritatis expressionem, quæ fieri debuit per pictores, quando silebant, & male docebant, & male vivebant plurimi Doctores. Exempla hujus habet Clar. Hottingerus, ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις, ὀδηγ. p. 3. p. 31. seqq. Ausi sunt olim & adhuc audent quodlibet ad fucanda mendacia. Ausi sunt, & audent, qui Trinitatem sub senis, juvenis & columbæ formis depingunt, quales tamen, teste Aventino, tanquam Religionis hostes Johannes XXII. Papa comburi curavit, Ausi sunt, qui depinxerunt eandem in forma corporis trium capitum, vel duorum capitum, inter quæ, ad probandam processionem Spiritûs S. ex Patre Filioque, columba; vel trium facierum; vel senis, & crucifixi & columbæ; Loca & testes de illis & aliis plurimis in Ecclesia Pontificia licentiæ pictoriæ effectibus noxiis adducente eodem Cl. Hottingero b. mem. l. c. 43. &c. Audent quidlibet, qui Christum pro lubitu fingunt & pingunt formosissimum, & deformem, qui tamen, ita saltem judicante Vavassore l. c. nec formosus, nec deformis fuit. Audent, qui, referente eodem ibidem, S. Borromaum, licet valde deformis fuerit, formosum depingunt; audent vel Græci vel Latini pictores, apud quos picta Christi & Virginis facies plurimùm differunt; ausus fuit, qui Lauretanam in forma mulieris Æthiopica depinxit; audent, qui in quibusdam locis formosissimas, non semper castissimas congregant, per tirar la modestissima beltà d' una vergine della vaghezza delle putane, ad efformandam modestissima virginis faciem ex vagis meretricum vultibus, quemadmodum ait, cui etiam hæc posteriora exempla debeo, Nobil. Sandis in Relatione eximia sua de statu Religionis.
units.tr: For Pliny, as cited by the Jesuit Vavassor in his treatise on the form of Christ, records a painter who gave the goddesses the features of his mistresses, which perhaps, by the same conjecture, Justin Martyr had in view when he said that the Gentiles worship their painters' mistresses. Painters dare anything in the Papist Church too. Long ago they dared many things in the name of expressing the truth, which ought to have been done by painters, when most teachers were silent, taught badly and lived badly. The illustrious Hottinger has examples of this, ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις, ὀδηγ. p. 3, p. 31 seqq. Long ago and still today they dare anything to disguise falsehoods. Those dare who portray the Trinity under the forms of an old man, a young man and a dove, which forms, according to Aventinus, Pope John XXII had burned as enemies of religion. Those dare who painted the same in the form of a body with three heads, or two heads, between which a dove was placed to prove the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; or three faces; or an old man, a crucified man and a dove. The places and witnesses concerning these and many other effects of painters' licence that are harmful in the Papist Church are cited by the same illustrious Hottinger, of blessed memory, l.c. 43 etc. They dare anything, those who feign and paint Christ at will, most beautiful and deformed, though, at least as Vavassor judges, l.c., he was neither beautiful nor deformed. Those dare who, as the same author reports in the same place, paint St. Borromeo as beautiful, although he was very deformed; Greek or Latin painters dare, among whom the painted faces of Christ and the Virgin differ very much; one dared to paint the Lauretan Madonna in the form of an Ethiopian woman; those dare who in some places gather the most beautiful, not always the most chaste women, so as to draw the most modest beauty of a virgin from the wanton beauty of whores, shaping the most modest face of a virgin from the loose faces of harlots, as says Noble Sandis, to whom I owe these last examples too, in his remarkable Relation on the state of religion.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Interim tamen ista licentia pictoria quoad Religionem non tolerari deberet, saltem in ista communione, in qua imagines pro libris Laicorum venditantur, & in qua nonnunquam ex picturis argumenta formantur, quale quidem pro Regia Magorum dignitate (quam dubiam esse multi ingenuè fatentur Pontificii) formavit Salmero Cham. Pans. T.2. pag.665. Saltem illud, de quo hic agitur, tale est, ut non possit solùm licentiae pictorum tribui; agitur enim de imaginibus in diplomatibus Pontificum, ubi ars pictoria non accedit, vix praevit, & si cum errore praevit, cum errore ad imitationem non duci, sed à Papis, quorum intererat, ut Petro semper constet honos debitus, & ut ansa isto errore ad ejus praejudicium abutendi abscinderetur, corrigi debuisset, cùm contrà jam longo seculorum usu haec consuetudo Pontificia confirmationem acceperit, & non tam dici deberet, pictoribus &c. quàm verò, si quae hic audacia est:
units.tr: Even so, this licence of painters ought not to be tolerated in matters of religion, at least in that communion where images are hawked as books for the laity, and where arguments are sometimes built from pictures, as Salmeron built one for the royal dignity of the Magi (which many Papists frankly admit is doubtful), Cham. Pans. T.2. pag.665. At least the matter under discussion here is of such a kind that it cannot be put down to the licence of painters alone. It concerns images in the papal bulls, where the art of painting is not involved, or scarcely comes in, and if it comes in with an error, that error should not be copied in imitation but corrected by the Popes, whose interest it was that due honour always be paid to Peter, and that the occasion for abusing that error to his prejudice be cut off. On the contrary, this Papal custom has now received confirmation through a long succession of ages, and so it should not be said to painters, etc., but rather, if there is any audacity here: The Papists have always had the power to dare anything.

units.la: Papis Quidlibet audendi semper fuit aqua potestas.
units.tr: The Papists have always had the power to dare anything.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Bellarminum quod attinet, multis modis hanc objectionem solvi posse, ait. Videamus. Ad eam respondet primò. Etiamsi concederet; Sic Pauli majorem auctoritatem adumbrari solere & solitam esse, illud tamen nihil Pontificibus officere, aut Petro. Non Pontificibus, quia ipsi tam Petrum quàm Paulum praedecessorem & parentem agnoscant. Equidem hoc aliquo modo faciunt & omnium tutissimè; Faciunt aliquo modo, assentientibus illis, qui apud doctissimum du Pin Diss.IV.c.1. §. 3. ajunt, Antiquos omnes unanimi consensu tradere, Ecclesiam Romanam à Petro & Paulo fundatam, utrumque Ecclesiae hujus Episcopum fuisse, utriusque hanc fuisse cathedram, Romanos Pontifices non solùm Petri, sed & Pauli Successores esse ac Vicarios, & ab eis authoritatem & Episcopatum accepisse; Quorum causam non ita pridem dedita operâ doctissimus Arnoldus Sorbonista, & plurium etiam S.Patrum testimoniis fretus Baptista Casalius libro de Sacris veterum Christianorum ritibus Romae impresso; denique famosus ille Graeco-Romanus Leo Allatius libro de consensu Orientalis & Occidentalis Ecclesiae, egerunt, & quibus etiam Doctissimus Vir plane adstipulatur, in responsione subjungens: Ad hanc urbem ambo venerunt, ambo Evangelium ibi annuntiaverunt; ambo multos illic ad fidem adduxerunt; ambo hanc Ecclesiam per tempus aliquod rexerunt; ambo sibi Successores ordinarunt, si fides nonnullis habeatur; ambo denique ibi gloriosè vitam pro Christo finierunt: ergo haud immeritò Ecclesiae hujus ambo dicuntur Episcopi scopi (non quòd illi Ecclesia ita fuerint addicti, ut non aliarum etiam curam susceperint) ut verba ejus immediatè præcedentia se habent, & Romani Pontifices iflorum ex æquo Successores esse perhibentur.
units.tr: As for Bellarmine, he says that this objection can be answered in many ways. Let us see. First he replies: Even if one should grant it, it is usual for the greater authority of Paul to be foreshadowed in this way, and that does nothing to harm the Popes or Peter. Not the Popes, because they acknowledge both Peter and Paul as their predecessor and parent. Indeed they do this in a certain way, and most safely of all. They do it in a certain way, with the agreement of those who, according to the most learned du Pin Diss. IV, ch. 1, §3, declare that all the ancients hand down with unanimous consent that the Roman Church was founded by Peter and Paul, that both were bishops of this Church, that this was the chair of both, that the Roman Pontiffs are the successors and vicars not only of Peter but also of Paul, and received authority and the episcopate from them; a cause which the most learned Arnold the Sorbonnist not long ago took up with deliberate care, and Baptista Casalius, relying also on the testimonies of many Holy Fathers, in his book On the Sacred Rites of the Ancient Christians, printed at Rome; and lastly that notorious Greco-Roman Leo Allatius, in his book On the Agreement of the Eastern and Western Church. To these the most learned man plainly gives his assent, adding in his reply: Both came to this city, both there announced the Gospel, both brought many there to the faith, both governed this Church for some time, both appointed successors for themselves, if credence is given to some, and both at last there gloriously ended their lives for Christ. Therefore, not undeservedly, both are called bishops of this Church (not that they were so attached to that Church that they did not also take up the care of others), as the words immediately preceding it have it, and the Roman Pontiffs are said to be equally the successors of both.

units.la: XXIX. Juxta has assertiones non tantùm in diplomatibus Pontificum Petrus & Paulus simul depicti videntur, sed & authoritate Petri & Pauli simul omnia peragere videri volunt; Istam quoq; in locum Pauli Successionem Papa Julius II. egregiè confirmavit, dum nimirùm sinistro de clade accepta nuntio turbatus, abjectis in Tiberim Petri clavibus, Pauli gladium arripuisse & simul dixisse fertur, illis deficientibus hunc auxilio fore, quâ nimirùm & actione & elocutione genuinum se Pauli Apostoli etiam Successorem esse manifestum fecit, siquidem convenientia est inter illud, quòd S. Paulus Apostolus à Magistratu gentili ob fidem Christianam gladio occisus est, &, ut videtur, ideò cum gladio martyrii instrumento (quemadmodum & circa alios Apostolos & Martyres fieri consuevit) pingitur, & inter illud, quòd Julius II. ejus, nisi valdè decipiantur, Successor gladium terrenum ob causas terrenas contra Magistratum Christianum arripuit, sed saltem illud æquè convenienter factum est, ac simile quid à Bonifacio, qui paulò oculatior Julio jam ante illum duos apud solum Petrum gladios vidit, & proin istam Successionem Paulinam allegare non opus habuit, sed verbis Petri Successor Petri altero Jubilæi primi die, Cæsareo habitu (ut primo die Pontificio vestitus erat) sumpto, proclamavit: Ecce duo gladii!
units.tr: XXIX. According to these assertions, Peter and Paul are seen to be depicted together not only in the papal bulls, but they also wish to be seen as carrying out everything together by the authority of Peter and Paul. Pope Julius II also strikingly confirmed this succession in Paul's place, when, troubled by the news of a bad defeat, he is said to have thrown Peter's keys into the Tiber, seized Paul's sword, and at the same time said that with those failing, this one would be of help. By that action and that utterance he plainly showed himself to be the genuine successor also of the Apostle Paul. For there is a correspondence between the fact that St. Paul the Apostle was put to death with the sword by the pagan magistrate for the Christian faith, and is therefore, as it seems, painted with the sword, the instrument of martyrdom (as is customary with other Apostles and Martyrs too), and the fact that Julius II, his successor, unless I am greatly mistaken, seized the earthly sword for earthly causes against a Christian magistrate. Yet something similar was done just as fittingly by Boniface, who, rather more sharp-sighted than Julius, had already seen two swords before him, in Peter alone, and therefore had no need to cite this Pauline succession. Instead, in Peter's words, the successor of Peter, on the first day of the second Jubilee, assuming the imperial dress (as he had worn the pontifical dress on the first day), proclaimed: Behold, two swords!

units.la: XXX. Dixi etiam ad verba Bellarmini, Pontifices Romanos tutissimè omnium tam Petrum, quàm Paulum prædecessorem & parentem agnoscere. Ob duas potissimùm causas. Primò enim dubitari aliquo modo potest de Successione Petri, contra quam dubia equidem multa & graviora suo loco proponenda erunt, juvat igitur, in prædecessione illi comitem adjungere Paulum, qui certè propiori aliqua relatione Romanæ Ecclesiæ unitus videtur, & cui conversionem illius urbis tanquam molesti itineris premium obtigisse, ex Chrysostomo suprà didicimus, ut si Petrus desit, Paulus prosit, vel si unus, sive Petrus, sive Paulus desit, alter prosit. Secundò. Si etiam uterque prosit, utroque etiam eis opus & in utroque nihil plane superflui est. Tanta enim, quemadmodum notissimum est, & ex parte ab initio jam ostendi, de se prædicant & prædicari volunt Papæ, ut junctæ Apostolorum & quidem Apostolici chori coryphæorum
units.tr: XXX. I also said, in response to Bellarmine's words, that the Roman Pontiffs acknowledge both Peter and Paul as their predecessor and parent most safely of all. I gave two main reasons. First, the succession of Peter can be doubted in a certain way, against which many and weightier doubts will be set out in their place; it helps, therefore, to join Paul as a companion to him in this predecessorship, since he certainly seems united to the Roman Church by a closer relation, and since, as we learned above from Chrysostom, the conversion of that city was granted to him as the reward of a troublesome journey. So if Peter is lacking, Paul will profit, or if one of them, whether Peter or Paul, is lacking, the other will profit. Second. If both profit, both are also needed by them, and in both there is nothing at all superfluous. For the Popes, as is very well known, and as I have already shown in part from the beginning, claim and wish to be claimed for themselves so much that, joined together, the leaders of the Apostles, and indeed of the Apostolic chorus,

units.la: Etiam ex allegata pariter Pauli authoritate, & facta Julii II.
units.tr: Also from the authority of Paul, cited in the same way, and from the deed of Julius II,

units.la: Tutissima videtur, sed admirationem pariens; phæorum vires haud immeritò requirantur, & ut suâ uterque inopiâ divitias Papales augeat, Textor rete conficiat, Piscator illud commodè tractet ; Seriò autem judico, si omnes Apostoli omnes suas prærogativas contulissent, & Pontifices Romanos earum ex asse hæredes constituissent, eos tamen nondum istas potestatis divitias possessuros, quas hodie jactant, ut certè non sine causa Bellarminus dicat, omnem etiam Pauli gloriam ad Romanos Pontifices pertinere. Qua tamen occasione mirari subit, cur tanto cum studio Petrum extollere, Pauli contrà authoritatem deprimere conetur! Itáne diversè commune parentes tractandi sunt? Et cur non respondisse sufficerit: Vos hæretici multa nobis de Pauli prærogativis, quæ Petri prærogativis quodammodo majores, saltem non minores sint, ogganitis, sed parùm refert quis major fuerit, uterque noster est; sive Paulus in diplomatibus ad dextram stet, sive Petrus, parùm rursus refert, modò uterque in diplomatibus Pontificum nostrorum stet?
units.tr: It seems most safe, but it causes wonder; the strength of the leaders is not undeservedly sought, and so that each may increase the Papal riches by his poverty, the weaver makes the net, the fisherman handles it conveniently. Yet, seriously, I judge that even if all the Apostles had conferred all their prerogatives, and had made the Roman Pontiffs the heirs of them in full, they would still not possess those riches of power which they boast of today; so that Bellarmine, not without reason, says that all the glory of Paul too belongs to the Roman Pontiffs. Yet on this occasion one is moved to wonder why he strives with such zeal to exalt Peter and, on the contrary, to lower the authority of Paul! Are the common parents to be treated so differently? And would it not be enough to answer: You heretics rant to us at length about the prerogatives of Paul, which are in some ways greater than those of Peter, or at least not less, but it matters little which was the greater; both are ours. Whether Paul stands at the right hand in the bulls or Peter, again it matters little, provided only both stand in the bulls of our Popes?

units.la: XXXI. Sed quàm valdè vereor, ne hic lateat anguis in herba, & causam habeant non unam Scriptores Pontificii ejus, quòd non apertiùs Paulum æquè Pontificem Romanum faciunt
units.tr: XXXI. But I greatly fear that a snake lies hidden here in the grass, and that the Papist writers have more than one reason for not more openly making Paul equally the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: (non enim hactenus videre licuit Scriptorem, qui in texendo Pontificum Romanorum Catalogo, Pauli tanquàm Pontificis, vel primi, vel secundi, vel simultanei rationem habuerit;) quamvis juxta præmissa & Bellarminus & alii, antiquitatis etiam unanimem consensum jactantes, satis aperte Paulum ad istud dignitatis supremæ fastigium evehant. Quibus jam sequentia opponere lubet, Bellarminianis maximè;
units.tr: (For so far I have not been able to see any writer who, in drawing up the catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs, has taken account of Paul as Pontiff, whether first, second, or joint.) Yet, in line with what was said above, both Bellarmine and others, who boast of the unanimous consensus of antiquity, do quite clearly raise Paul to that summit of supreme dignity. To these I now wish to oppose the following, chiefly against the Bellarminians.

units.la: XXXII. Primò incertitudinem, quoad Pontifices Romanos, quæ tamen juxta demonstrationem ab initio factam hic planè abesse, summa contrà pro rei dignitate omnium certitudo haberi deberet, per ejusmodi hypothesis mirum in modum augeri; Jam enim quæritur de evidenti constitutione duorum, cùm ne unius quidem ostendi possit certa designatio.
units.tr: XXXII. First, uncertainty concerning the Roman Pontiffs, which, according to the demonstration made at the beginning, is here wholly absent, and in fact the greatest certainty should be had, befitting the dignity of the matter, is wonderfully increased by such a hypothesis. For now we are inquiring about the evident constitution of two, when not even the certain designation of one can be shown.

units.la: An igitur etiam Paulus (quoad Petrum plura suo loco interrogabimus;) divinitus Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopus constitutus est? Providentiâ quidem Dei Romam captivus pervenit, qualis & ibi biennium mansit, solutum post vinculis Româ discessisse, & Evangelium per aliquot annos alibi prædicâsse, pòst denuo vinctum Romam pertractum, ibidémque martyrio coronatum fuisse, & vetus ex Eulalio in peregrinatione tione Pauli, & Eusebio Hist. Eccles. l.II. 22. traditio est, & docti hodiéque ex 2.Tim.IV.13.16.17.18. non male colligunt; Ut Romam non venerit nisi in vinculis, Romæ, quantum certò constat, non fuerit, nisi quandiu vinculorum necessitas retinebat, qui contrà alibi liberè & per satis magna etiam, pro festinatione Apostolica, temporis spatia, saltem Corinthi, nimirum per undecim menses, commoratus est, & cæterum, cujus testem ipse Bellarminus Hieron. in 5. cap. Amos allegat, non solùm fidem Christi per totum eum longissimum tractum, qui est ab Hierusalem usque ad Illyricum, ut etiam ipse Paulus ait Rom.15. sed etiam à mari rubro usque ad Oceanum, per totum ferè orbem plantavit, ut priùs eum terra defecerit, quàm studium prædicandi. Quid igitur vetat, quò minùs æque alius cujusvis loci, ubi fuit, ubi docuit, Corinthi maximè, Episcopus dicatur, si loci alicujus Episcopus dicendus est? Cur Romani eum prædecessorem & parentem suum majori jure jactabunt? Cur omnis etiam Pauli gloria ad illos pertinebit? Nonne ipsis sufficit gloria Petri? An Paulus ne minimam quidem gloria suæ partem alibi reliquisse dicendus erit? Annon Thessalonicæ, ad cujus urbis fideles scripsit: Vos estis gloria nostra & gaudium nostrum, 1.Thess.II.v.20. Vel an ideò omnis Pauli gloria ad Romanos pertinet, quia ibi ejus gloria quasi cum capite sancti abscissa est, nimirum quoad continuationem gloriosi ministerii? Gloriosa igitur Hierosolyma & ter gloriosa, quia tot Prophetarum & Apostolorum & Apostolicorum Virorum, imò Christi ipsius sanguinem hausit terra illa! Si non potiùs puri sanguinis injustâ effusione impura facta est?
units.tr: Was Paul then also (we will question concerning Peter in its place) divinely constituted bishop of the Roman Church? By the providence of God he came to Rome as a prisoner, and there remained for two years; that he left Rome after being released from his chains, preached the Gospel elsewhere for some years, and afterwards, being bound again, was brought back to Rome and there crowned with martyrdom, is an ancient tradition, drawn from Eulalius on the journey of Paul and from Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 22, and learned men today also reasonably infer it from 2 Timothy 4:13, 16–18. That he came to Rome only in chains, and was in Rome, as is certain, only as long as the necessity of his chains kept him there, while on the contrary elsewhere he stayed freely and for fairly long periods, given the Apostle's haste, at least at Corinth, namely for eleven months; and moreover, of which Bellarmine himself cites the witness, Jerome on Amos chapter 5: he planted the faith of Christ not only through that very long stretch which is from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, as Paul himself says in Romans 15, but from the Red Sea to the Ocean, through almost the whole world, so that the land failed him before his zeal for preaching did. What then forbids that, with equal right, he be called bishop of any other place where he was, where he taught, especially Corinth, if he is to be called bishop of any place at all? Why will the Romans boast with greater right of him as their predecessor and parent? Why will all of Paul's glory belong to them? Does not the glory of Peter suffice for them? Or must it be said that Paul left not even the smallest part of his glory elsewhere? Is not Thessalonica, to whose faithful he wrote, You are our glory and our joy (1 Thess. 2:20)? Or is all the glory of Paul the Romans' because his glory was, as it were, cut off there along with its head, namely as to the continuation of his glorious ministry? Glorious then was Jerusalem, and thrice glorious, because that land drank the blood of so many Prophets and Apostles and apostolic men, indeed of Christ himself! Unless rather it has been made impure by the unjust outpouring of pure blood?

units.la: XXXIII. Si verò tanta est incertitudo quoad constitutionem Pauli; certè non minor est illa, quæ suppositâ illâ constitutione demum nascitur. Demus, Paulum unâ cum Petro fuisse prædecessorem Episcoporum Romanorum.
units.tr: XXXIII. But if there is so great uncertainty concerning the constitution of Paul, certainly no less is that which arises only after that constitution is supposed. Let us grant that Paul, together with Peter, was the predecessor of the Roman bishops.

units.la: Quænam in munere Petri partes, quænam Pauli fuerunt? Quænam fuit Petri dignitas? Quæ Pauli? Utra potior? Annon Pauli, qui ad dextram positus est? Sed sic tollitur prærogativa Petri. Et si Paulus ante Petrum Romæ fuit, ut quidem videtur, an tunc ille Monarcha? Si Petrus post adventum suum, etiam cùm Paulus ibi ageret, alias Ecclesias invisit, ut præsupponunt, an tunc ille Monarcha? Vel an Vicarius Petri? Quod non videtur. Quot ordinârunt Successores? Si Petrus aliquem, cur non etiam Paulus? Si Paulus, quem? Si unus utriusque Successor fuit, & omnes utriusque Successores sunt, cur non ab utroque se vocant? An pudet Pauli?
units.tr: What were the parts of Peter in the office, and what were Paul's? What was Peter's dignity? What was Paul's? Which was the greater? Was it not Paul's, who was placed at the right hand? But so the primacy of Peter is removed. And if Paul was at Rome before Peter, as indeed seems to be the case, was he then the Monarch? If Peter, after his arrival, visited other churches, even while Paul was acting there, as they presuppose, was he then the Monarch? Or was he Paul's vicar? That does not seem so. How many successors did they appoint? If Peter appointed some, why not also Paul? If Paul, whom? If there was one successor of each, and all successors of each are successors, why do they not call themselves from both? Are they ashamed of Paul?

units.la: XXXIV. Secundò Bellarmino & reliquis opponimus: Statum sic pristinum Ecclesiæ Romanæ & quasi naturalem fuisse gubernationem per duos, imò primos Romanos Pontifices non fuisse Monarchas; Duūmviratus fuit Ecclesiæ illius gubernatio, non Monarchia; Quomodo enim Petrus Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopus Monarcha fuit, si Paulus socius, socius ita, ut Prædecessor & Parens & ipse? Vel an Petrus ideò Monarcha, quia simul & aliarum Ecclesiarum curam habebat? Ast certè tunc non depositit solicitudinem pro omnibus Ecclesiis Paulus; Vel an Petrus ideò Monarcha, quia magis Romanorum saluti intentus? Ast plùs apud eos laborâsse Paulus invenitur. Vel an ideò Petrus Monarcha, quia Paulus sub eo? Sed quis hujus rei fidem faciet? Annon, quæ dicta sunt, repugnant? Annon etiam situs ad dextram? Annon etiam Prædecessoris & Parentis, qualis æquè fuerit, apud Bellarminum mentio? Sin duo fuerunt, ut, & quales fuisse dicuntur, cadit regimen Monarchicum, quod tam operosè adstruere voluit Bellarminus, possunt esse & eligi duo Pontifices summi, quod etiam expressè docuerunt Armacanus de quæst. Arm. l. 7. cap. 17. & Occam. in Dial. pag. 3. ad finem. Si duo, cur non etiam 3. 4. &c. opere crescente & onere, contrà deficientibus hominum dotibus? Regimen igitur erit planè Aristocraticum, quemadmodum etiam Linus & Cletus Petro adhuc superstite adjutores Episcopalis officii vocantur, qui quidem Petro non tam, quàm hodierni Clerici Romani Papæ, subjecti fuisse videntur.
units.tr: XXXIV. Secondly, we oppose Bellarmine and the rest: that the original and, as it were, natural state of the Roman Church was government by two, or rather by the first two Roman Pontiffs, and not by a monarch; the government of that Church was a duumvirate, not a monarchy. For how could Peter be a monarch as bishop of the Roman Church, if Paul was a colleague, a colleague in such a way as to be predecessor and parent and himself? Or was Peter a monarch because he also had the care of other churches? But certainly Paul did not then lay down concern for all the churches. Or was Peter a monarch because he was more concerned for the salvation of the Romans? But Paul is found to have labored more among them. Or was Peter a monarch because Paul was under him? But who will vouch for this? Do not the things said contradict it? Does not the seat at the right hand? Is not the mention in Bellarmine of a predecessor and parent, such as he equally was, also contrary to it? But if there were two, and they are said to have been such, the monarchical rule falls, which Bellarmine so laboriously sought to establish; two supreme pontiffs can exist and be chosen, which Armachanus also expressly taught (On the Questions of Armagh, book 7, chapter 17) and Occam (in Dialogue, p. 3, near the end). If two, why not also three, four, and so on, as the work grows and the burden with it, while the endowments of men fail? The rule will therefore be plainly aristocratic, just as Linus and Cletus, while Peter was still alive, are called helpers of the episcopal office, who indeed seem to have been subject to Peter not as the present Roman clergy are subject to the Pope.

units.la: XXXV. Imò his præsuppositis, quæ Bellarminus & alii propinant de duobus Fundatoribus, videtur, debere necessariò duos saltem Episcopos Romanos esse & eligi, & defecisse à longo tempore sedem illam à statu instituto; Non minor est virtus quàm quærere parta tueri; Æquè magno ad conservationem, quàm verò ad fundationem labore opus est, & jam aucta sunt Ecclesiæ Romanæ pomœria, auctus est authoritatem ejus agnoscentium numerus; Nemo Petrum æquat, Paulum nemo. Et videntur ipsi quoque Patres Successores constituisse, de quo plura deinceps. Et sic schismata excusari possent Paparum; Non fuit Papa & Antipapa, non Christus & Antichristus, ut dicere soliti sunt, sed fuit hic Petri, ille Pauli Successor, si duo; duo Petri, unus Pauli Successores, aut vice versa, si tres; cujusvis duo, si aliquando quatuor fuerunt. En Schismata sublata! Sed incidit, hoc posito non tamen etiam lites sublasublatas esse, tunc enim æquè de Primatu pugna fuisset. An ille penes Petrum, an penes Paulum? Tunc demum diplomata & numismata, dextram & sinistram allegâssent. Extra casum Schismatis verò, ut & illud fatear necesse est, hodie non amplius laboriosum esse Episcopatum Romanum, ut simul Petrum & Paulum exigeret. Non is amplius mos est, Episcopi ad populum illi ut verba faciant, nedum ut singulis ferè diebus: Unus multis millibus vel per alios, quid illi loco suo facere debeant, commodè significat, non opus est ad id socio, & quod fieri potest per pauca, non debet fieri per plura. Verè jam Episcopatus ille potestas est, non tantùm spiritualis, sed & terrena, potestas autem socium non vult:
units.tr: XXXV. Indeed, given the presuppositions that Bellarmine and others offer about two founders, it seems that there must necessarily be at least two Roman bishops and that they should be chosen, and that for a long time that see has departed from its founded state. Preserving what has been gained is no less a virtue than seeking it; the labour needed for conservation is as great as that needed for foundation, and now the boundaries of the Roman Church have been enlarged, and the number of those acknowledging its authority has increased. No one equals Peter, no one Paul. And the Fathers themselves seem to have appointed successors, of which more later. And thus the schisms of the Popes could be excused: there was not Pope and Antipope, Christ and Antichrist, as they were wont to say, but this one is the successor of Peter, that one of Paul, if there were two; two of Peter and one of Paul, or the reverse, if there were three; two of anyone, if at some time there were four. Behold, schisms abolished! But it follows that, on this supposition, quarrels are not also abolished, for then the struggle over the primacy would be just as great: whether it lay with Peter or with Paul? Then at last the diplomas and coins would have alleged right and left hand. Apart from the case of schism, however, as I must also admit, the Roman episcopate is no longer so burdensome that it would require Peter and Paul together. That is no longer the custom, that bishops should address the people, much less almost every day. One man can conveniently signify through others what those in his place ought to do; there is no need of a colleague for this, and what can be done through a few should not be done through many. Truly that episcopate is now a power not only spiritual but also earthly, and power does not want a partner:

units.la: Omnísque potestas Impatiens consortis erit.
units.tr: Every power will be impatient of a partner.

units.la: Ait Persius in Satyris. Verè jam regnum etiam mundanum & temporale est. Non capit regnum duos, teste Seneca in Tragœdiis. Unitas est de essentia Pontificis Romani. Mox quidem Bellarminus Mosen & Aaronem typos Pauli & Petri sistet, sed neutrum par intentione eâ memorat, ac si statuat, per paria Ecclesiam etiam hodie administrari debere. Et præstat non habere Fratrem, si vel esset Moses, quàm habere hujus Sacro sanctæ potestatis ex æquo participem.
units.tr: Persius says this in the Satires. Truly, a worldly and temporal kingdom is the same. A kingdom does not hold two, as Seneca says in his Tragedies. Unity belongs to the essence of the Roman Pontiff. Bellarmine soon brings forward Moses and Aaron as types of Paul and Peter, but he mentions neither pair with that purpose, as if he meant that the Church should even today be governed by pairs. It is better not to have a brother, even if he were Moses, than to have a equal sharer in this sacred power.

units.la: XXXVI. Agnovit illud optimè Sixtus V. Quamvis enim, cùm adhuc esset Cardinalis Montaltius, id est, juxta ipsa illius verba, cùm adhuc in terris quæreret claves regni cœlorum, inter alias, quas suo loco commemorabimus, artes huic fini aptas, ad conciliandum in Conclavi sibi favorem Cardinalium Principum, continuò, cœptâ de se negotiatione, illis persuadere voluerit, & etiam facile, adjuvantibus simplicitatis & infirmitatis longo tempore adhibitis artificiosis mendaciis, persuaserit, se non esse tanto oneri ferendo solum, opus habiturum (quod illis quidem in primis votis erat, regnare nimirum sub alieno nomine, teste etiam, quod protinus secutum est; (Lo faremo, lo faremo; Faciemus, faciemus;) ipsorum consiliis, auxilio diésque noctésque, ut gubernent unà secum Statum & Ecclesiam, quomodo si ipsum eleCturi sint, se ipsos sint eleCturi Papas, omnes habituri Papatum, sed divísum, ille titulum, ipsi titulum, ille nomen & speciem, ipsi authoritatem & imperium; ut ii astuti verbis illis fidem habentes jam de futura sua gloria strenuè triumphaverint: quamvis etiam talia identidem ad eos iteraverit, & conscientiam allegaverit, & fidem exegerit illius. illius, quòd electionem suam non in Conclavi finituri, sed majorem ejus partem demum in Vaticano peracturi sint, & subdolè magis adjunxerit: Per l'amor di Dio, non pensate à farmi Papa, se non mi giurate di pigliarne tutto il governo sopra di voi. Per amorem Dei, ne cogitetis de me in Papam eligendo, nisi promiseritis sanctè, Vos omne regimen suscepturos in Vos; Tamen vix visis primo obtutu clavibus tantopere quaesitis (quae dignitatis illius vis transsubstantiativa est!) jam novis linguis loqui coepit, cùm enim pro more coram ligno crucis prostratum Magister Ceremoniarum; Num Papatum acceptare vellet? interrogasset, gravi vultu & Majestatis pleno respondit: Non possumus acceptare, quae jam acceptavimus, sed adhuc alium acceptaremus, si quidem daretur, satis enim virium & vigoris & donorum nos habere cognoscimus, auxiliante Deo, ad regendum duos mundos, & multò magis unum solum Papatum. Quae quidem verba voce alta, ut ab omnibus intelligi possent, prolata, Cardinalem Farnesium moverunt, ut in haec verba proruperit. Domini illi credebant, se facturos Papam, cui pro lubitu imperent, sed video talem eos elegisse, qui omnes habebit pro--Et cùm inter vestiendum recens electus rem multùm promoveret, & robur ostenderet, illud alium Rusticuccium Cardinalem, qui ex delusis non minimus, movit ad dicendum: Sanctissime Pater, Papatus est bona Medicina, faciens Cardinales senes juvenes, agros sanos; Responsum à Papa: Id equidem novimus experientiâ. Cùmque idem cum Alexandrino, ex maximè deceptis altero, quietem posit multas diei molestias suaderet, audivit denuò; Quies nostra maxima erit labor; Et huic subjungere ausō: Sanctitas Vestra aliter loquitur, quàm heri & pridie locuta est; dictum; Tunc non eramus Papa. Sed dura, & dira demum cum aliis quasi honoris causâ ad mensam Pontificiam admissi audire coacti fuerunt; Prima tunc Papae verba dignitatem Pontificiam describebant & magnitudinem honoris, quo Christus Vicarium suum in terris afficiat; Saepe repetebat locum: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, eúmque in hunc modum magnâ cum Spiritus vehementiâ illis explicabat: O quàm profunda sunt divina judicia! Christus unum tantùm Petrum in terris relinquere voluit, unum tantùm Pontificem, unum tantùm Vicarium, unum tantùm caput; Uni tantùm dedit authoritatem pascendi oves suas. Tu es Petrus; Tu, tu solus es Pontifex. Tibi dabo claves Regni coelorum. Tibi tantùm do claves ad aperiendum & ad claudendum omnia pro lubitu tuo. Tibi, tibi do potestatem sustinendi & regendi di meam Ecclesiam. Tibi, Tibi,qui meus es Vicarius, non aliis, qui nonnisi simplices ministri tui sunt. Quæ verba absque alio interprete Cardinalibus istis satis clara erant ad significandum,quòd spes nectere longas hîc multa vetent,interim tamen maximè affligere illos poterant tædiosa repetitiones, & quòd,hoc aut illo vel os aperiente, statim Pontifex sermonem interruperit ad suum semper reversus; Che nella chiesa non doveva essere che un sol commandante;In Ecclesia unum debere esse gubernantem: Cúmque nihilominus auderet semel interfari Rusticuccius, & diceret:Vestra Sanctitas sanè in Conclavi dixerat, impossibile sibi futuram soli Papatûs administrationem, jam verò ne quidem permittit,ut opem ferentis ulla fiat mentio: Responsum tulit: Verum est,diximus,quia tunc ita credebamus,jam non idem dicimus, quia jam non idem credimus, & si vel aliquo mendacio per rationem statûs usi fuissemus, sufficientem jam dare possemus Confessori nostro potestatem nos absolvendi ab omni culpa in eo commissa. Additum: Igitur vos Papam elegistis propter utilitatem vestram, & nos vobis ostendemus, nos Papatum accepisse nostra utilitatis gratiâ. Quam irrisionem Pontificiam Pasquinus etiam facilè imitari novit, narrante hæc omnia fusiùs Gregorio Leti Vita di Sisto V. p.I. l.5. p.365. 429. certè,nisi multùm fallar, aut Sixtus V. aliter intellexit locum: Tu es Petrus &c. & magis sensum ejus perspexit,quàm ipse Petrus; aut Paulus non unâ cum Petro Ecclesiam Romanam fundavit & gubernavit; ut quidem vellent Bellarminus & reliqui.
units.tr: XXXVI. Sixtus V understood this very well. For although, while he was still Cardinal Montalto, that is, in his own words, while he was still seeking the keys of the kingdom of heaven on earth, among other arts suited to this end, which we shall mention in their place, to win the favour of the Cardinal Princes in the Conclave, he at once, having begun to bargain on his own behalf, wished to persuade them, and easily did persuade them, aided by the simplicity and weakness of those men and by artful lies told over a long time, that he would not need a helper to bear so heavy a burden. This was indeed their first wish, namely to rule under another's name, as what immediately followed also shows: (We will do it, we will do it; We will do it, we will do it;) with their counsel and help, day and night, so that they might govern the State and the Church together with him; as if they were electing themselves popes, all of them to hold the papacy, but divided: he the title, they the title; he the name and appearance, they the authority and power; so that those shrewd men, believing these words, already vigorously triumphed in their future glory. Yet he also repeatedly said such things to them, appealed to his conscience, and demanded their trust in him that they would not finish their election in the Conclave but would complete most of it in the Vatican; and more craftily he added: For the love of God, do not think of electing me pope unless you solemnly swear to take the whole government upon yourselves. Yet hardly had he seen the keys so eagerly sought at first glance (what a transubstantiating power that dignity has!) when he began to speak in new tongues. For when the Master of Ceremonies, as is customary, had him prostrate before the wood of the cross and asked whether he wished to accept the papacy, he answered with a grave face full of majesty: We cannot accept what we have already accepted, but we would still accept another, if one were given, for we know that we have enough strength, vigour and gifts, with God's help, to rule two worlds, and much more so one single papacy. These words, spoken in a loud voice so that all could understand them, moved Cardinal Farnese to burst out in these words: Those gentlemen believed they were making a pope whom they could command at will, but I see they have chosen one who will have them all as-- And when the newly elected pope, while being dressed, pressed the matter further and showed his strength, this moved another Cardinal, Rusticucci, who was among the deceived no small figure, to say: Most Holy Father, the papacy is a good medicine, making old cardinals young and sick cardinals healthy; the Pope replied: Indeed, we know this from experience. And when the same Rusticucci, with the Alexandrine, one of the most deceived, advised him to rest from the many troubles of the day, he heard again: Our rest will be our greatest labour; and he dared to add: Your Holiness speaks differently from how you spoke yesterday and the day before; the reply was: Then we were not yet pope. But at last those who had been admitted to the papal table, as if for the sake of honour, along with the others, were forced to hear harsh and dreadful things. The Pope's first words then described the dignity of the papacy and the greatness of the honour with which Christ honours his vicar on earth. He often repeated the passage You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and expounded it to them in this way with great vehemence of spirit: O how deep are the judgements of God! Christ wished to leave only one Peter on earth, only one Pontiff, only one Vicar, only one head; he gave the authority to feed his sheep to one alone. You are Peter; you, you alone are the Pontiff. To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven. To you alone I give the keys to open and to shut everything at your pleasure. To you, to you I give the power of sustaining and ruling my Church. To you, to you who are my Vicar, not to others, who are only your simple ministers. Without any other interpreter these words were clear enough to those Cardinals to signal that many things here forbade them to build long hopes; yet the tedious repetitions could especially distress them, and whenever this or that man opened his mouth, the Pontiff at once broke off the discourse and always returned to his own: In the Church there ought to be only one ruler. And when Rusticucci nevertheless dared once to interrupt and said: Your Holiness certainly said in the Conclave that the administration of the papacy alone would be impossible for you, and now you do not even allow any mention of one who would bring help, he received the answer: It is true, we said it, because we then so believed; now we do not say the same, because we no longer believe the same; and if we had used some lie for reasons of state, we could now give our confessor sufficient power to absolve us of every fault committed in this. It was added: Therefore you elected us pope for your own advantage, and we will show you that we accepted the papacy for the sake of our own advantage. Pasquino also knows how to imitate this papal mockery easily, as Gregorio Leti relates all these things at greater length in Vita di Sisto V. p.I. l.5. p.365. 429. Certainly, unless I am much mistaken, either Sixtus V understood the passage You are Peter, etc. differently and perceived its sense more clearly than Peter himself, or Paul did not, together with Peter, found and govern the Roman Church; as Bellarmine and the others indeed wish.

units.la: XXXVII. Opponimus his illorum hypothesibus tertiò,
units.tr: XXXVII. We set against their hypotheses, thirdly,

units.la: Episcopum Romanum posse esse, qui non habeat Primatum Apostolicum, multò minus Monarchiam etiam Ecclesiæ. Eadem ferè sibi objicit Doctissimus du Pin,loco jam sæpiùs allegato, cùm, præmissâ suâ & aliorum de Episcopatu Petri & Pauli simultaneo sententiâ, ait: Ergò, inquiet aliquis, inde sequetur, aliquem fuisse Episcopum Romanorum, qui primatu caruit, ac proinde dici poterit, Ecclesiam Romanam Primatu caruisse. Differt autem hæc illatio nostra à præcedente. Præsupposuimus enim in præcedente, duos in Ecclesia Romana potestatem supremam habuisse; jam supponimus, Paulum etiam Ecclesiam Romanam, sed secundùm sententiam Bellarmini, du Pin, aliorum, sine Primatu administrâsse. Et certè illatio nostra ex eo bona est. Si enim Paulus (quantum in Ecclesia nomen) sine Primatu, & multò magis sine Monarchica potestate Ecclesiam fundavit & gubernavit; utique Successores ejus (Successores autem sunt, si ille Prædecessor est;)
units.tr: that the Roman bishop could be one who did not hold apostolic primacy, much less monarchical authority over the Church. The most learned du Pin raises almost the same objection against himself, in the work already cited many times. Having first set out his own view and that of others on the simultaneous episcopate of Peter and Paul, he says: "Therefore, someone will say, it follows that there was some Roman bishop who lacked primacy, and so it could be said that the Roman Church lacked primacy." Our inference differs from the earlier one. In the earlier one we assumed that two men in the Roman Church held supreme power. Now we assume that Paul also governed the Roman Church, but, according to Bellarmine, du Pin and others, without primacy. And indeed our inference is sound on this basis. For if Paul (as far as the name of Church goes) founded and governed the Church without primacy, and much more without monarchical power, then surely his successors (and they are successors, if he is a predecessor)

units.la: Tertiò non minùs sequitur, posse esse Pontificem sine Primatu; æque Primatu & Monarchicâ potestate carere poterunt.
