Vel an alii, quos Paulus tot parasangis superat, (ut de decimi & aliorum Seculorum monstris nihil dicam;) tanquam Episcopi Romani Primatum & Monarchicam potestatem habebunt, & necessariò habebunt, cum Paulum ne Primatum quidem habuisse dicant, Ecclesia Romæ fundatorem & gubernatorem?
units.tr: Thirdly, it follows no less that the Pontiff can exist without primacy; they too could be without primacy and monarchical power. Or will others, whom Paul surpasses by so many parasangs (not to mention the monsters of the tenth and other centuries), hold primacy and monarchical power as Roman bishops, and necessarily hold it, since they say that Paul did not even have primacy as founder and governor of the Church at Rome?

units.la: XXXVIII. Respondet Doctissimus du Pin; Non sequi inde, Ecclesiam Romanam aliquando Primatu caruisse.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Doctissimus du Pin replies: "It does not follow from this that the Roman Church was ever without primacy."

units.la: Id quidem sequi omnino videtur, & caruisse dicant oportet, ante adventum Petri; Caruisse dicant oportet, Petro ad alias civitates digrediente, & Paulo solo Romæ relicto, urbis illius Episcopo altero, sed Primatu, secundum suppositiones, destituto; Sequi autem id negat Doctissimus Vir, quia semper Ecclesia Romana dici potuit omnium Ecclesiarum prima; Primò ob urbis illius amplitudinem. Verùm amplitudo urbis hic neminem juvat contrà illud, quòd Ecclesiam Romanam Primatu caruisse, aut carere posse infertur. Urbium enim amplitudinem per se Primatum, imò secundùm Bellarminum Monarchicam Ecclesiæ potestatem determinare, & ad se quasi trahere, primò satis inconvenienter dicitur de Ecclesia Christi, cujus regnum non est ex hoc mundo, Joh. XVIII.36. Scilicet mœnia dilatare, & populos injustâ hominum venatione subigere oportebit, ut Christi in persona Vicarii sui copia fiat. Et quamvis ultrò fatear, regnis & Regibus terræ in Christi potestatem redactis, Regiarum etiam Urbium hac in parte aliquam rationem habitam, & majorem Episcoporum spiritualia eis administrantium authoritatem fuisse, & haberi, & esse posse, (quod tamen tyrannidi & contentionibus in Ecclesiam introducendis haud parùm inservit;) ut etiam semper digniores majoribus Gregibus Pastores quæri debent, nihilominùs ea fuit ab initio Christianismi Urbis Romæ conditio, ut Primatum sibi ob amplitudinem quasi debitum haud poscere potuerit. An enim ob multa fdolorum fana? An quia ibi sedes Draconis, crudelis Tiberii, monstrosi Caligulæ, stulti Claudii, detestabilis Neronis, & pessima omnia, Primatum illum, Monarchicam illam Ecclesiæ potestatem meruit? Et an non potiùs magni fidelium numeri (uti Hierosolymæ statim plura hominum millia Christo sua dederunt nomina, in aliis urbibus etiam amplis, Antiochiæ & Alexandriæ, &c. Christianorum numerus mox in immensum auctus fuit, Romana Ecclesia primò nondum fundata, post in paucioribus consistente;)
units.tr: Indeed it seems altogether to follow, and they must say that it was without primacy before Peter's coming. They must say that it was without primacy when Peter went off to other cities and Paul alone was left at Rome, with another man as bishop of that city, yet destitute of primacy according to the suppositions. The most learned man denies that this follows, "because the Roman Church could always be called the first of all churches." First, he says, "on account of the greatness of that city." But the greatness of the city helps no one here against the inference that the Roman Church lacked, or can lack, primacy. For to say that the size of cities by itself determines primacy, and even, according to Bellarmine, monarchical power over the Church, and draws it to itself, is first of all quite out of keeping with the Church of Christ, "whose kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36). Clearly, the walls would have to be extended and peoples brought under by the unjust hunting of men, so that there might be an abundance of Christ's power in the person of his Vicar. And although I freely grant that, with kingdoms and kings of the earth brought under the power of Christ, some regard was also paid in this respect to royal cities, and a greater authority of bishops administering spiritual things to them existed, and can exist (which nevertheless serves tyranny and the stirring up of contention in the Church not a little, just as always the more worthy ministers ought to be sought for the larger flocks), nevertheless from the beginning of Christianity the condition of the City of Rome was such that it could not claim primacy for itself as, so to speak, owed to it on account of its size. For was it on account of the many temples of idols? Or because it was the seat of the Dragon, of cruel Tiberius, monstrous Caligula, foolish Claudius, detestable Nero, and every sort of wickedness, that it earned that primacy, that monarchical power over the Church? And was it not rather the great number of believers (as at Jerusalem several thousand men at once gave their names to Christ; in other large cities too, Antioch and Alexandria, and so on, the number of Christians soon grew immensely; the Roman Church, not yet founded at first, later stood with fewer members)

units.la: Respondetur ad objectionem Doctissimi du Pin, primam stente;) an,inquam,non potiùs magni fidelium numeri in alia quadam urbe,si Primatus talis habẹri debuisset,ratio habenda,fuit? Porrò si pendet ab urbis amplitudinePrimatus,quis Petrus in minoribus oppidis in exiguis vicis sæpè docens fuit? Si pendet ab urbis amplitudine primatus,quis magnus Paulus in urbe amplissima docens, & annon primus fuit? Anno fuerunt sive Andronicus, sive Junia, inter Apostolos celebres,ante Paulum in Christo, &, ut videtur, primi Evangelii in urbe præcones Rom.XVI.7. vel quicunque alii illuc ad prædicandum profecti? Et si pendet Primatus ab urbis amplitudine,quid accidit & accidere debet, quando aliæ urbes Christianæ ampliores factæ, Imperii sedes aliò translata fuit, Regum potentissimorum,Christianissimi,Catholici,sedes aliæ sunt amplissimæ, & Romæ gloria adhuc magis obscurari potest? Ingratæ sunt istæ,Romanensibus saltem,quæstiones & consequentiæ.
units.tr: Reply to du Pin's objection, the first, standing; whether, I say, rather the great number of believers in some other city ought to have been taken into account, if such a primacy were to be held? Moreover, if primacy depends on the size of the city, who was Peter, who often taught in smaller towns and tiny villages? If primacy depends on the size of the city, who was the great Paul, teaching in a very large city, and was he not first? Were Andronicus and Junia, famous among the Apostles, who were in Christ before Paul and, as it seems, the first heralds of the Gospel in that city (Rom. 16:7), or any others who went there to preach? And if primacy depends on the size of the city, what has happened, and what ought to happen, when other Christian cities have become larger, when the seat of empire has been moved elsewhere, and other seats of the most powerful kings, the most Christian and the Catholic, are very large, and the glory of Rome can be obscured even more? These questions and consequences are unwelcome, at least to Romanists.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Secundò Romanam Ecclesiam,non obstante eo, quòd Paulus Episcopus Primatu caruerit, Primatum tamen ideò semper habuisse,pertendit D. du Pin, quia unus ex ejus Episcopis (Petrum intelligit;) Primatum inter Apostolos habuerit. De eo, an Petrus Romæ Episcopus fuerit, suo loco dicemus. Hic sequentia annotâsse sufficiat. 1. Saltem manere,Episcopum Romanum non semper Primatum necessariò habere. 2. Incertum esse, utrum hodiernus Pontifex sit Petri, an Pauli Successor. Distinctos cuivis obtigisse Successores,homines Catholici, quibus ipse Doctiss. du Pin adstipulari visus est,in præcedentibus dixerunt,si verò Pauli Successor sit,Primatum ex hypothesi non habet,cùm cum Faulus non habuerit, nam , quod quis non habet illud dare, Successori suo relinquere non potest; Nimium autem videtur ex supra dictis,unum hodie Pontificem duobus simul, iisque tantis Apostolis, in omnibus illorum juribus, privilegiis & prærogativis succedere. Sed audiamus denuò Bellarminum, cui hactenus respondimus ad illud, quod dixerat,etiamsi major supponatur Pauli authoritas quàm verò Petri,illud tamen nihil obstare Pontificibus Romanis.
units.tr: Secondly, du Pin maintains that the Roman Church nevertheless always had primacy, even though Paul, as bishop, lacked primacy, "because one of its bishops" (he means Peter) "had primacy among the Apostles." Whether Peter was bishop of Rome we shall discuss in its place. It is enough here to have noted the following. 1. At the very least it remains that the Roman bishop does not always necessarily have primacy. 2. It is uncertain whether the present Pontiff is the successor of Peter or of Paul. Catholic men, with whom the most learned du Pin seemed to agree, said in the preceding passages that distinct successors fell to each; but if he is Paul's successor, he does not have primacy on this hypothesis, since Paul did not have it, for what someone does not have he cannot leave to his successor. But it seems too much, from what has been said above, that one Pontiff today should succeed two Apostles at once, and such great ones, in all their rights, privileges and prerogatives. But let us hear Bellarmine again, to whom we have so far replied regarding what he said: "even if the authority of Paul is supposed to be greater than that of Peter, that nevertheless is no obstacle to the Roman Pontiffs."

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Dicat jam,quomodo illud non obstet Petro, id est, Primatui & Monarchiæ Petri,in quibus adstruendis totus fuit: Nihil etiam, inquit, Petri Pontificatui officeret dignitas & autoritas Pauli, quoniam extraordinaria erat, quanta tandem esset. Quàm solidè! Indignum planè est sydere,malleo hæreticorum,vertice Theologorum, quibus elogiis Bellarminus à Cardinali de Sourdis apud Alegambium in Bibliotheca Scriptorum Soc. Jesu insignitur, ad hunc modum argumentari: Pauli potestas fuit extraordinaria, ergo quantacunque fuerit Petri, qui eodem cum Paulo die martyrio affectus fertur, Pontificatui, Monarchiae & Primatui nihil obstat; Si majorem authoritatem habuit Paulus, eodem tempore vivus Romana etiam Ecclesia fundator & gubernator, illud certè Primatui tali obstat, licèt illa potestas magis quàm Petri extraordinaria fingatur. Quoniam, ut simili rem declarem, Possessor mille florenorum utique ditior est possessore centum, vel, si quis malit, nongentorum nonaginta novem florenorum, & illius divitiae obstant, quin hujus majores sint, licèt illum sterilem concipiam & haerede destitutum, hunc non item. Verùm hos conceptus irregulares jam suprà refutavimus fictitios & Petri primatui non derogantes; Si Doct. du Pin fides habenda est.
units.tr: Let him now say how that does not stand in the way of Peter, that is, of Peter's primacy and monarchy, which he devoted his whole effort to establishing. "Nor," he says, "did the dignity and authority of Paul detract from the pontificate of Peter, since it was extraordinary, however great it may have been." How solidly! It is truly unworthy that Bellarmine, whom Cardinal de Sourdis, as cited by Alegambe in the Bibliotheca Scriptorum Societatis Jesu, honours with the titles "star, hammer of heretics, summit of theologians," should argue in this way: "The power of Paul was extraordinary; therefore, however great Peter's power was, and he is said to have suffered martyrdom on the same day as Paul, nothing stands in the way of the pontificate, the monarchy and the primacy." If Paul had greater authority, living at the same time as the founder and governor of the Roman Church, that certainly stands in the way of such a primacy, even though that power is imagined to be more extraordinary than Peter's. To explain the matter by a similar example: the possessor of a thousand florins is certainly richer than the possessor of a hundred, or, if one prefers, of nine hundred and ninety-nine florins, and his riches stand in the way of the other's being greater, even if I imagine the former as barren and without an heir, and the latter not so. But we have already refuted these irregular conceptions above, as "fictitious and not derogating from Peter's primacy," if the credit of Doctor du Pin is to be trusted.

units.la: XLI. Ast simili quoque Bellarminus utitur; Dicit; Quemadmodum Moses major Aarone, & nihilominus tamen Aaron, verè ac proprie summus Pontifex fuerit, posteris ei in potestate ordinaria succedentibus, ita etiam si admitteretur, Paulum Petro majorem fuisse, non propterea negatum iri, Petrum ordinarium ac summum Ecclesiae Pontificem fuisse. Verùm ad istam comparationem contra Bellarminum notari possunt sequentia. 1. In Ἀρχιερεῦσι occurrunt viri diversi planè ordinis, Moses & Aaron, Moses legislator populi & supremus magistratus, Aaron persona tantùm Ecclesiastica, contrà in Ἀποστόλοις Petrus & Paulus conferuntur, Apostolus Apostolo, Ecclesiae Romanae fundator & gubernator, ut volunt, Ecclesiae Romanae fundatori & gubernatori; In Mose & Aarone quivis videt praerogativas ex officio diversas, in Petro & Paulo non item, proin si Paulus Ecclesiae Romanae fundator & gubernator (illud enim spectatur in Diplomatibus Pontificum) Petro etiam tum major fuit, non tam facilè Petro aliunde satis intuitu istius Ecclesiae, & illius, quod de Rectoribus suis jactant, consuli potest. 2. Minùs tutum est, in comparatione, ubi Petri, non Pauli eminentia quaeritur, hunc Mosi, qui adeò manifestè Aarone major cognoscitur, praeferre. 3. Mosen extraordinarium, Aaronem ordinarium fuisse, diserte ex Scripturis discimus, sed qui eandem differentiam quoad Petrum & Paulum ostendent? Et annon, si ignobilioris foederis Sacerdos Aaron cum Successoribus suis clarissimè constitutus, eorúmque etiam ordinationi peculiariter provisum, & in specie Eleasar, Parentis in officio statim Successor, referente illud Scriptura S. etiam vestibus Parentis, eo nec dum mortuo, indutus est; Paria, si non illustria magis, circa potioris Testamenti Summorum, quales haberi volunt, Pontificum constitutionem merito exspectemus? 4. An Bellarminus, quod circa Petrum & Paulum facit, quoad Mosen & Aaronem inferet; Aaron Successores habuit, aliter ac Moses, E. ipse major Mose fuit? Eum autem ita de Petro & Paulo inferre, & quidem emphaticè valdè, in hoc diversum esse Petrum Ecclesiae Monarcham ab Apostolis, caeterum ipsi aequalibus, & eos superare, quòd ordinarius ille fuit, & Successores habuerit, ex supra allatis ac refutatis certum est. 5. Certè major Pauli authoritas non obstaret Pontificatui Petri simpliciter, ut nec obstat cujusque alius Pontificatui, sed Pontificatui Petri tali, qualem Monarchiam defendit Bellarminus, vel in eodem Pontificatu Monarchico primatui. Sed maluit Bellarminus simpliciter vocem Pontificatus adhibere, quod non sine causa factum, verùm de Primatu & praecellentia inter illos duos quaestio est & erat.
units.tr: XLI. But Bellarmine also uses a similar comparison. He says: "Just as Moses was greater than Aaron, and nevertheless Aaron was truly and properly high priest, his successors following him in ordinary power, so too, even if it were admitted that Paul was greater than Peter, it would not therefore be denied that Peter was the ordinary and supreme pontiff of the Church." But against Bellarmine's comparison the following points may be noted. (1) Among the high priests [Ἀρχιερεῦσι] there appear men of clearly different rank, Moses and Aaron: Moses the lawgiver of the people and supreme magistrate, Aaron only an ecclesiastical person. Here, on the other hand, among the apostles [Ἀποστόλοις] Peter and Paul are compared, apostle with apostle, and (as they claim) the founder and governor of the Roman Church with the founder and governor of the Roman Church. In Moses and Aaron anyone can see prerogatives differing by office; in Peter and Paul this is not so. Therefore, if Paul was the founder and governor of the Roman Church (for that is what is looked for in the diplomas of the Popes), he was greater than Peter as well. Peter cannot easily be vindicated on the basis of that Church, or of what they boast about its rulers. (2) It is less safe, in a comparison where Peter's eminence, not Paul's, is the question, to set Paul before Moses, who is so clearly known to be greater than Aaron. (3) We learn expressly from the Scriptures that Moses was extraordinary and Aaron ordinary; but who will show the same difference between Peter and Paul? And should we not rightly expect, for the constitution of the Supreme Pontiffs of the better Testament, which they wish to be held, the same or, if not more illustrious, at least similar arrangements, seeing that Aaron, the priest of the less noble covenant, was clearly appointed with his successors, and provision was made for their ordination in particular; and Eleazar, the immediate successor of his father in office, is related by Holy Scripture to have been clothed in his father's vestments while the father was not yet dead? (4) Or will Bellarmine infer about Moses and Aaron what he does about Peter and Paul: that Aaron had successors, unlike Moses, therefore Aaron was greater than Moses? But that he infers this about Peter and Paul, and indeed very emphatically, namely that Peter was a monarch of the Church and different from the apostles, who were otherwise equal to him, and that he surpassed them because he was the ordinary one and had successors, is certain from what has been adduced and refuted above. (5) Certainly the greater authority of Paul would not stand in the way of Peter's pontificate simply, as it does not stand in the way of anyone's pontificate; but it would stand in the way of Peter's pontificate of the kind that Bellarmine defends, a monarchical pontificate, or of the primacy within that same pontificate. But Bellarmine preferred simply to use the word "pontificate," which was not done without reason; yet the question is and was about primacy and precedence between those two.

units.la: XLII. Pergit Bellarminus quoad situm imaginum, & tertiò respondet; non semper Pauli imaginem dextram occupare, in iis, quae Romae nunc exstent, modò ad dextram, modò ad sinistram in numismatibus.
units.tr: XLII. Bellarmine goes on regarding the placement of the images, and thirdly replies: "Paul does not always occupy the right-hand place in the images that now exist in Rome; sometimes he is on the right and sometimes on the left in the coins."

units.la: Ad quae noto. 1. Ipsum illud, quòd Paulus aliquando ad dextram collocetur, ejus cum Petro aequalitatem etiam in munere Romano probare, quemadmodum ipse Bellarminus, consultò à veteribus modò unum, modò alterum antepositum esse, ait, nimirum, ut eo modo significarent, hos Apostolos vel pares esse inter se, vel certè ignorari, uter alteri praefer. Sicut etiam post verba Leonis M. Ser. 1. de natali Apostolorum allegat; quibus ille dixerat; Hos gratia Dei in tantum apicem inter omnia Ecclesiae membra provexit, ut eos in corpore, cui caput est Christus, quasi geminum constitueret lumen oculorum: de quorum meritis atque virtutibus nihil diversum, nihil debemus sentire discretum, quia illos & electio pares & similes, & finis fecit aequales. Quibus & alia jam allata testimonia ex Maximo & Gregorio subjungit. Sed parum horum memor est Bellarminus, dum his immiscet, Petrum esse potestate majorem. Quod cum iis, quae hactenus ab ipso etiam Bellarmino allata sunt, nullo modo consistere potest. 2. Verisimile est ex Thoma & Damiano & ipsis etiam Bellarmini verbis; in iis, quae Roma nunc extant &c. Paulum antiquitus semper, vel plerumque saltem dextrum latus occupâsse; prout etiam imagines Pontificum in Diplomatibus prius, quàm in numismatibus expressae sunt. Forsan igitur
units.tr: To these things I note the following. (1) That very fact that Paul is sometimes placed on the right proves his equality with Peter even in the Roman office, just as Bellarmine himself says that "the ancients deliberately placed now one, now the other, in front, namely, so that by this means they might signify that these apostles were either equal to one another or at least that it was unknown which of them was preferred over the other." He also cites, after the words of Leo the Great, Sermon 1 on the Birthday of the Apostles, in which Leo had said: "The grace of God has raised these men to such a height among all the members of the Church that it has made them, in the body of which Christ is the head, as it were two lights of the eyes. Concerning their merits and virtues we ought to feel nothing different, nothing divided, because their election made them equal and similar, and their end made them equal." To these he adds the other testimonies already cited from Maximus and Gregory. But Bellarmine is little mindful of these, while he mixes in with them that "Peter is greater in power." This cannot in any way agree with what Bellarmine himself has adduced so far. (2) It is probable, from Thomas and Damian and from Bellarmine's own words, "in those things which now exist at Rome," etc., that Paul in ancient times always, or at least for the most part, occupied the right-hand side, just as the images of the Popes were expressed in diplomas before they were expressed in coins. Perhaps therefore

units.la: Tertia Bellarmini responsio examinatur; igitur progressu temporis errores animadverterunt, &, quòd situs ille in præjudicium Monarchiæ Petri exponi posset : Et quidni etiam daretur index expurgatorius quoad imagines?
units.tr: The third reply of Bellarmine is examined here; so, with the passage of time, they noticed errors, and that this arrangement could be exposed to the prejudice of Peter's monarchy. And why should there not also be an "expurgatory index" for images?

units.la: XLIII. Quartum responsum daturus Bellarminus, primò probare conatur,lævam veteribus honoratiorem fuisse; Quod apud certos certis temporibus obtinuisse, aut hodienum apud nonnullos obtinere non in controversiam vocabimus. Utitur argumentis Antonii Nebrissensis, & primò quidem versu Ovidii,in quo interior omninò honoratior fuisse videtur; Quòd autem ex Virgilii versu; Radit iter lævum interior, interiorem ad lævam accedentem dici ostendere nititur,me quidem judice,absque ratione fit,cùm in illa navalis certaminis descriptione Cloanthum Gyæ propiorem fuisse tantùm dici videatur; hinc non dicitur: radit iter lævum interius, vel simpliciter interius. Melius forte dicitur, alibi interiorem dici, vel medium, vel eum, qui ambulat propior versùs parietem, vel aliquid parieti simile, qui incedendi mos magis exaltat & à viæ sordibus purior esse solet, & adhuc hodienum inter quosdam honori ducitur.
units.tr: XLIII. Bellarmine, about to give his fourth reply, first tries to prove that "the left side was more honourable among the ancients." We shall not dispute that this prevailed among certain people at certain times, or that it still prevails among some today. He uses the arguments of Antonio de Nebrija, and first of all a verse of Ovid, in which the "interior" seems to have been more honourable. But that he tries to show from a verse of Virgil, "the inner one grazes the left-hand course," that the inner one is meant as the one approaching on the left, seems, in my judgement, to be without reason, since in that description of the naval contest Cloanthus is said only to have been nearer to the turning-post Gyas. Hence it is not said "grazes the left-hand course more inwardly," or simply "more inwardly." It is perhaps better said that elsewhere "interior" means either the middle, or the one who walks closer to the wall or something like a wall, a manner of walking which exalts more and is usually purer from the filth of the road, and which is still held in honour among some people today.

units.la: XLIV. Testimonium Eusebii, quod de suo addere videtur Bellarminus,haud magis eum juvat. Lib.1. de vita Const. cap.19. illud dicitur, Constantinum adolescentem, jam summo in honore apud Imperatores fuisse, & Eusebium quoque eum vidisse, cùm per Palæstinam à Diocletiano transfiret. Addit: Ad cujus dextram assistens, ἑστὼς δεξιὰ πεῤῥησίας cunctis, qui videndi desiderio tenebantur, præstantissimus videbatur; Ad quæ notare lubet. 1.Si incessisset Constantinus ad dextram Diocletiani in visitatione provinciæ,nemine sinistrum ejus latus claudente,pars summi illius honoris fuisset,in quo Constantinum apud Imperatorem fuisse testatur; prout etiam sæpè alias lateris dextri in sedendo honos, maximè personis, quas Reges honorare voluerunt,teste etiam Scriptura,obtigit, peculiaris etiam favoris & æstimationis judicium; & constat, imperaturos aliquando per extraordinaria honoris signa à prædecessoribus populo commendatos fuisse ; quemadmodum illud hic etiam populus ita interpretari, & nullo modo honor ille Imperii Candidato exhibitus in contemptum senioris Augusti cedere potuisset ; Quales respectus autem inter Petrum & Paulum, æquales Apostolos, fingi nulli possunt; proin more ordinario dextra quoad illos honoratior erit. 2. Si ad dextram incessit Constantinus,unde probat Bellarminus,eum solum lum Imperatoris Comitem fuisse, non alium ad sinistram incessiſse, adeóque exemplum illud huc facere? Solius quidem Constantini meminit Eusebius, quòd adstiterit Imperatori, quia solius vitam describit, & ostendere vult, quàm honorificè adhuc adolescens in comitatu Cæsaris habitus fuerit, ad quod sufficit, quòd latus alterutrum ejus texit, aliis procul dubio pro Magnatum more adstantibus, Viris, aut Adolescentibus præcipuæ nobilitatis.
units.tr: XLIV. The testimony of Eusebius, which Bellarmine seems to add of his own, helps him no more. In Book 1 of the Life of Constantine, chapter 19, it is said that Constantine, as a young man, was already in high honour among the emperors, and that Eusebius too saw him when he passed through Palestine with Diocletian. He adds: "standing at his right hand, with freedom of speech" [ἑστὼς δεξιὰ πεῤῥησίας], "he appeared most outstanding to all who were held by the desire of seeing him." On these words it is pleasing to note the following. (1) If Constantine had walked at the right hand of Diocletian during a visitation of the province, with no one closing off his left side, that would have been part of that highest honour in which Eusebius testifies that Constantine was held by the emperor. Likewise, the honour of the right side in sitting, given especially to persons whom kings wished to honour (Scripture also bears witness to this), was a mark of particular favour and esteem. And it is established that emperors sometimes commended to the people, by extraordinary signs of honour, those who had been their predecessors' favourites; just as this people also would interpret it in that way, and that honour shown to the candidate for the empire could in no way have been a contempt for the senior Augustus. But no such respects can be imagined between Peter and Paul, who were equal apostles; therefore, by the ordinary course, the right side will be the more honourable for them. (2) If Constantine walked on the right, from which Bellarmine proves that he alone was the companion of the emperor, and that no one else walked on the left, how does that example serve his purpose? Eusebius mentions only Constantine as standing beside the emperor because he describes only Constantine's life, and wishes to show how honourably he, while still a young man, was held in Caesar's retinue. For this it is sufficient that he covered one or other side of the emperor, while others undoubtedly stood by in the manner of the great men, men or young men of distinguished nobility.

units.la: 3. Non dicit Eusebius in opere, quod apud Bellarminum, non; Constantinum semper ad Augusti dextram incessisse: sed simpliciter: Assistens à dextra præstantissimus apparuit; Augusto forsan sedente; Si stante Augusto; quidni etiam alio quodam stante à sinistra? Ut jam omnino repugnare videatur Bellarmino etiam Ambrosius ab eo pro sinistra sede honoratiori citatus; Saltem ea, quæ de tegendo corpore Petri adducit, minùs cum dignitate Pauli conveniunt. Credibile est, inquit, initio cœpisse depingi Paulum ad dextram Petri, ut juniorem & minorem, ut Petrum præcedat, & fermè totum claudat, quod argumentum obsequii in Paulo, & dignitatis in Petro: Num Petro Paulus junior fuerit, & multò junior, incertum, credo, est, hoc, ut arbitror, falsum; Certum illud est, minorem Paulum non fuisse, ut etiam obsequia testari Petro opus habuerit Petri quasi satelles & latero, vel per contractionem latro, quod nomen imponebatur, ut Bellarminus ex Nebrissensi ait, iis qui dextrum latus nobilium hominum defensionis causa tegebant, (quod etiam concedo, nisi quòd sine causâ ad dextrum latus restringere videtur:) Forsan ideò Paulus Petro hoc officium præstare debuit, quia hodie cum gladio pingitur: Mirum est, Bellarminum non allegâsse morem apud Turcas, ut scribunt, receptum, juxta quem honoratiores lævam tenent, ut in ipsorum potestate sit gladius comiti, sed vix credibile est, Petrum diffidentem erga Paulum, etiam armatum, fuisse.
units.tr: 3. Eusebius, in the work that Bellarminus cites, does not say that Constantine always walked at the right hand of Augustus. He says simply: standing at the right hand, he appeared most distinguished. Perhaps Augustus was seated; or, if he was standing, why could not someone else be standing on the left? Ambrose, whom Bellarminus cites for the more honourable seat on the left, seems wholly to contradict him. At least what Ambrose adds about covering the body of Peter does not agree well with the dignity of Paul. It is credible, he says, that at first Paul began to be painted at Peter's right hand, as the junior and lesser, so that he would precede Peter and almost wholly cover him, an argument of obedience in Paul and of dignity in Peter. Whether Paul was younger than Peter, and much younger, is uncertain; I think it is false. What is certain is that Paul was not the lesser, since Peter needed Paul's obedience as a bodyguard and latero, or by contraction latro, a name given, as Bellarminus says from Nebrissensis, to those who covered the right side of noble men for the sake of defence. I also grant this, except that he seems to restrict it without reason to the right side. Perhaps Paul had to perform this office for Peter because today he is painted with a sword. It is strange that Bellarminus did not cite the custom, which they write is received among the Turks, by which the more honourable hold the left, so that the sword is in the power of the companion. But it is hardly credible that Peter, distrustful of Paul, would have had him armed.

units.la: XLV. Objectionem prævidit Bellarminus hanc; Si Paulus tantùm ad tegendum defensionis causâ latus Petri ad dextram incessit, cur igitur etiam ad dextram pingitur, quando Petrum non tegit, cùm nimirum vel Christus, vel Beata Virgo medium locum tenent. Opportunè respondet, ex imperitiâ factum est, nimirum viderant (boni illi pictores, antea peritissimi ad depingendum vel in diplomatibus Pauli erga Petrum obsequium, jam imperiti planè!) alicubi Paulum ad dextram depictum, nec adverterunt, (miseret me illorum:) sic eum esse ad dextram, ut Petrum tegeret, existimârunt, ob honorem Pauli id fieri (ô pictormu
units.tr: XLV. Bellarminus foresaw this objection: If Paul walked at Peter's right only to cover his side for the sake of defence, why then is he also painted at the right when he does not cover Peter, since evidently either Christ or the Blessed Virgin holds the middle place? He answers opportunely: it happened through lack of skill, namely, the painters had seen (those good painters, formerly most skilled at depicting Paul's obedience towards Peter in the diplomas, now quite unskilled!) Paul depicted at the right somewhere, and did not notice (I pity them) that he was there so as to cover Peter; they thought this was done out of honour for Paul (O the astonishing simplicity of the painters!)

units.la: ˆ storum simplicitatem stupendam! qui prius non adverterant, posterius possimè existimârant!) ac propterea in sedibus quoque, vel cùm inter se multùm distarent, (quàm multa saltem hìc sibi pictores licere putârunt!) dextram partem Paulo tribuerant, ubi tamen nihil plane ad Petri tutelam eo opus fuit.
units.tr: who had not noticed earlier, judged all the more foolishly later!) and therefore, even in seats, or when they were far apart from one another (how much licence the painters thought they had here!) they assigned the right-hand place to Paul, where nevertheless there was plainly no need of it for Peter's protection.

units.la: XLVI. Pergit Bellarminus: Cæterùm non ob Pauli honorem id à Veteribus factum esse, vel inde probari potest, quòd in omnibus aliis rebus semper Petrus Paulo anteponitur; Si nominandi sunt, Petrus præcedit &c. cur igitur in imaginibus ordo iste alioqui perpetuus mutaretur? Petrum primò nominari existimo, quia ante Paulum in Christo, & Apostolus, & Apostolorum primus fuit, cùm Paulus demum post Christi ascensionem Apostolis aggregatus sit, forte etiam addi possit ætatis, secundùm vulgarem opinionem, consideratio, quibus tamen Pauli eminens virtus & dignitas juxta ea, quæ supra allata fuerunt, tantopere à Patribus deprædicata non minuitur, ut Bellarminus certè immeritò dicat, Paulo in omnibus rebus semper Petrum anteponi: Cùm tamen jamjam tanta non solùm Paulo per concessionem præ Petro tribuerit, sed & positivè pronunciârit, Veteres consultò significare voluisse, hos Apostolos vel esse pares, vel nesciri, uter alteri præstet, & Paulo quoque majorem sapientiam ex Maximo adjudicaverit, & æqualitatem egregiè attestantes Patres adduxerit: Et tamen hìc putat, fieri non posse, ut imago Pauli in Diplomatibus honoris causâ ad dextram pingatur; Sed facilè concipit, illud factum esse obsequii causâ!
units.tr: XLVI. Bellarminus goes on: But that this was not done by the ancients out of honour for Paul can be proved from this, that in all other matters Peter is always placed before Paul. If they are to be named, Peter comes first, etc. Why then would this order, otherwise constant, be changed in images? I think Peter is named first because he was before Paul in Christ, and was an apostle and the first of the apostles, since Paul was added to the apostles only after Christ's ascension. Perhaps the consideration of age, according to the common opinion, could also be added; yet Paul's eminent virtue and dignity, according to what was brought forward above, which the Fathers so greatly proclaimed, is not diminished by these things. So Bellarminus certainly says undeservedly that Peter is always placed before Paul in all things. Yet he has just granted by concession that so much was given to Paul over Peter, and has positively declared that the ancients deliberately wished to signify that these apostles were either equals or that it is not known which of them surpasses the other; and he has also awarded Paul greater wisdom from Maximus, and has brought forward the Fathers who clearly attest to equality. And yet here he thinks it impossible that Paul's image in the diplomas should be painted at the right for the sake of honour. But he easily conceives that this was done for the sake of obedience!

units.la: XLVII. Vix tamen puto, eum hac de re planè persuasum fuisse, quid enim tunc opus fuisset, tot responsiones alias fusè commemorare? Cur non, (qui vel minima arripuit, doctissimi du Pin judicio, partim gratis conficta, partim impertinentia, omnia vel percurrenti levissima;) vicesimam nonam Petri prærogativam in eo constituisset, quòd Paulus tanquam satelles, vel latero Petri obsequii causâ ad ejus latus dextrum pingatur? Et certè de tota hac re valdè dubiè loquitur; Et primò quidem; multis modis solvi potest: Deinde; potest etiam responderi; porrò; fortasse consultò Veteres observârunt; Insuper: Tertia quoque responsio adhiberi potest; Amplius; credibile est; Tandem; si hæc aliquibus non probantur, admitti potest &c.
units.tr: XLVII. Yet I hardly think he was fully persuaded of this matter. For what need would there have been then to recount at length so many other answers? Why did he not (he who seized even the smallest, which, in the judgement of the most learned du Pin, were partly invented without grounds, partly irrelevant, all very flimsy to anyone who runs through them) make the twenty-ninth prerogative of Peter consist in this, that Paul is painted at Peter's right side as a bodyguard or latero out of obedience? And certainly he speaks very doubtfully about this whole matter. First: it can be resolved in many ways. Then: it can also be answered. Further: perhaps the ancients observed it deliberately. Moreover: a third answer can also be applied. Again: it is credible. Finally: if these things are not approved by some, it can be admitted, etc.

units.la: XLVIII. Admitti posse dicit, honoris gratiâ Paulum à dextris Petri in signis & imaginibus collocari. Nimirum Bellarminus est, prout vis; accommodat se cuivis, est in sensu propriissimo ambi-dexter, & modò dextram, modò sinistram honoratiorem supponit pro lu-bitu, artificium, quod æquè calluit ejus Amicus & in dignitate Cardinalitia Collega Baronius, qui, quando Imperatores dextram tenuerunt, sinistram, & aliâ occasione rursus dextram honoratiorem facere novit: Bellarminus jamjam impossibile judicavit, ut ob Pauli honorem & non obsequii causâ ei in diplomatibus dextra tributa sit, alius nunc erit, & in situ illo mysteria Paulo honorificentissima ostendet.
units.tr: XLVIII. He says that it can be admitted that Paul is placed at Peter's right in signs and images for the sake of honour. Bellarminus is, as you like: he accommodates himself to anyone. He is truly ambidextrous, and supports now the right, now the left, as the more honourable, at his pleasure. This trick his friend Baronius, his colleague in the cardinal's dignity, knew equally well: when the emperors held the right, Baronius makes the left the more honourable, and on another occasion he knows how to make the right the more honourable again. Bellarminus has just judged it impossible that the right was assigned to Paul in the diplomas for the sake of his honour and not of obedience. Another man will now say, and in that position will show mysteries most honourable to Paul.

units.la: XLIX. Primum est, sic significari, Paulum plurimùm in propagatione fidei laborâsse, & easdem ob causas, alios etiam sanctos ex minoribus ordinibus, magis honorari aliis ex ordinibus majoribus;
units.tr: XLIX. The first is that this signifies that Paul laboured most in the propagation of the faith, and for the same reasons, that other saints from the lower orders are honoured more than others from the higher orders;

units.la: Nolumus immorari tristibus ἐπιγεόσεως consequentiis. De Paulo tantùm dicimus; Si ordinem summum habuit, Apostolus, dignitatem, juxta illos quoque, summam, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Fundator & Gubernator, & majorem insuper diligentiam in munere adhibuit, majorem utilitatem præstitit, utique nomine duplici nulli inferior, Petrum in aliquo saltem inferiorem habuisse videtur. Et certè credo, hic Ecclesiam utilitatis suæ rationem habuisse, & Paulum ideò Veteres ad dextram collocâsse, quia de ipsius in urbe commoratione, & Ecclesiæ Romanæ per ipsum ædificatione certiora habere potuerunt, quàm verò de Petro documenta.
units.tr: We do not wish to dwell on the dismal consequences [ἐπιγεόσεως]. We say only this about Paul: if he held the highest order, that of apostle, and, according to them too, the highest dignity, as founder and governor of the Roman Church, and in addition applied greater diligence to his office and rendered greater usefulness, then, being in both respects inferior to no one, he seems to have been at least somewhat inferior to Peter in some respect. And I certainly believe that here the Church took account of its own advantage, and that the ancients placed Paul at the right because they could have more certain evidence of his sojourn in the city and of the building up of the Roman Church by him than evidence about Peter.

units.la: L. Secundum est, quia Paulus Doctor Gentium præcipuè fuit, Petrus Judæorum, ut igitur significaret Ecclesia, Gentiles Judæis tandem antepositos esse, ab eo, qui dixit: Major serviet minori, Paulum anteposuit Petro; Et hoc admittimus mysterium (quod suo loco movebit dubium; annon Petrus sine fundamento vel ad sinistram in Diplomatibus Romanorum Pontificum collocetur;) & porrò dicimus; Si (convenienter iis, quæ supra posuimus) Paulo æquè ministerium præputii concreditum fuit, & is æquè primatum inter Gentiles obtinuit, & Gentiles præla-ti sunt Judæis, annon forte & Gentilium Apostolus, qui longè plura peregit Judæorum Apostolo, variè, non tantùm in Diplomatibus Pontificum prælatus, & de his quoque dictum fuit; Major serviet minori? Quod quidem contra Monarchiam Petri pugnare aliquo modo videtur.
units.tr: L. The second is that, because Paul was principally the teacher of the Gentiles and Peter of the Jews, the Church therefore wished to signify that the Gentiles were at last placed before the Jews, and that he who said, The greater shall serve the lesser, placed Paul before Peter. We admit this mystery (which in its place will raise the question whether Peter is not placed without foundation even on the left in the diplomas of the Roman Pontiffs). And further we say: if (in agreement with what we have laid down above) the ministry of the uncircumcision was entrusted equally to Paul, and he equally obtained the primacy among the Gentiles, and the Gentiles were preferred to the Jews, is it perhaps not the case that the apostle of the Gentiles, who accomplished far more than the apostle of the Jews, was preferred in various ways, not only in the diplomas of the Pontiffs? And was it not said of these too: The greater shall serve the lesser? Which indeed seems in some way to conflict with the monarchy of Peter.

units.la: LI. Tertium est: Quoniam Petrus à Christo vocatus fuit, adhuc mortali, & quodammodo in sinistrâ constituto, Paulus autem de cœlo vocatus est à Christo immortali, & regnante ac sedente à dextrâ Patris: Addit, Damianum ad S. Thomam eandem rationem attingere. Sed an nom non in illo quoque consistit prærogativa aliqua Pauli satis magna, quòd etiam post ascensionem Christi, regnante jam Petro, neque à Petro, neque, ut Matthias, ab Ecclesia vocatus fuit? An non inde colligi potest, Apostolum Paulum non dependisse à Petro, prout non in esse, ita etiam non in operari? Sanè hîc prærogativam Paulinam, & quidem talem, quâ major & dignior cæteris Apostolis factus sit, vidit Augustinus, cujus glossa super illud Gal.I. neque per hominem, sed per Jesum Christum & Deum Patrem; hæc est: Ut per hoc sit major, qui videbatur esse minor; Cateri enim Apostoli videbantur majores, quia priores per Christum, iste minimus, quia novissimus, sed inde apparet esse dignior, quia priores per Christum constituti sunt adhuc ex parte hominem,id est, mortalem, novissimus verò Paulus per Christum jam totum Deum, id est, ex omni parte immortalem.
units.tr: LI. The third is: since Peter was called by Christ while still mortal, and in some way placed on the left, but Paul was called from heaven by Christ immortal, reigning and sitting at the right hand of the Father. He adds that Damian touches on the same reason in regard to St Thomas. But does not some quite great prerogative of Paul also consist in this, that even after Christ's ascension, when Peter already reigned, he was called neither by Peter nor, as Matthias was, by the Church? Can it not be concluded from this that the apostle Paul did not depend on Peter, and, just as not in being, so also not in acting? Certainly here Augustine saw a Pauline prerogative, and indeed one by which he was made greater and more worthy than the other apostles. His gloss on that verse of Gal. 1., neither through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, is this: so that he who seemed to be the lesser might be the greater through this; for the other apostles seemed greater because they were earlier through Christ, while he was the least, because the last; but from this it appears that he is more worthy, because the earlier ones, established through Christ, are still in part man, that is, mortal, while the last, Paul, through Christ is now wholly God, that is, immortal in every part.

units.la: LII. Quartum Mysterium, sive quartam rationem mysticam, Damianum addere ait, hanc, quòd Paulus ex tribu Benjamin & in Benjamin demonstratus ac typicè in Scripturis expressus sit
units.tr: LII. Damian says he adds a fourth mystery, or fourth mystical reason: that Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin, was shown in Benjamin, and was typically expressed in the Scriptures.

units.la: : qui Benjamin filius dextra à Patre appellatus sit, & à Josepho omnibus prælatus fratribus; Mystici planè sunt hi homines! Paulus ex tribu Benjamin se esse ipse testatur; Tertullianus, in præcedentibus, prædictionem Jacobi de Benjamine Paulo applicuit: Sed quæ ex his consequentia: E. Paulus debet stare ad dextram Petri, à quo, tanquam altero Josepho, fratribus cæteris, id est, Apostolis antepositus est? Si fratribus antepositus est, etiam Petro, id ab eo factum est, qui eum vocavit; Ait, Petrum nihil contulisse sibi. Et an credunt isti Viri, ipsum Benjaminem tanquam filium dextræ ordinarió dextram Josephi, cui in Ægypto dignitatem fere similem cum ea, quam Petrus Romæ habuerit, obtigisse supponunt, occupâsse? Ego non credo, & multo minùs probo mysticas illas conclusiones: Paulus vocatus est à Christo, qui sedet ad dextram Patris: E debuit in Diplomatibus Romanorum Pontificum stare ad dextram Petri: Paulus fuit ex tribu Benjamin, quod nomen significat Filium dextra: E. debuit pingi ad dextram Petri. Forte Petrus ad sinistram pingi solitus fuit ex tribu aut familia alicujus, cui nomen Benschemol, Filius sinistra! Quas jam alii de dextro Pauli loco afferunt, conjecturas æque futiles alias, ut, quod ajunt, id profectum esse à Græcis Pictoribus in Paulum propensioribus, vel à Petri modestia ac humilitate, dextram in Ecclesia sua Paulo deferentis, vel, cum Leone Allatio, ex Eotholarum Basilicarum dispositione à Græcis Romam illata, quibus, quod dextrum est, sit Latinis sinistrum; eæ, cùm tantùm numerum, & cum numero responsionum incertitudinem augeant, ulteriorem considerationem merito non accipiunt.
units.tr: that Benjamin was called the son of the right hand of the Father, and was set above all his brothers by Joseph. These men are plainly mystics! Paul himself testifies that he is of the tribe of Benjamin. Tertullian, in the earlier passage, applied Jacob's prophecy about Benjamin to Paul. But what follows from this? Therefore Paul ought to stand at the right hand of Peter, by whom, as by another Joseph, he is set above the other brothers, that is, the Apostles? If he is set above the brothers, he is set above even Peter, which was done by the one who called him. Paul says that Peter contributed nothing to him. Do these men really believe that Benjamin himself, as the son of the right hand, occupied the right hand of Joseph, to whom, they suppose, a dignity nearly like that which Peter held at Rome had fallen in Egypt? I do not believe it, and I much less accept those mystical conclusions: Paul was called by Christ, who sits at the right hand of the Father; therefore he ought to stand at the right hand of Peter in the diplomas of the Roman Pontiffs; Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin, a name which means son of the right hand; therefore he ought to be painted at the right hand of Peter. Perhaps Peter was customarily painted at the left because he was of a tribe or family whose name is Benschemol, son of the left! The other conjectures that people now offer about Paul's place on the right are equally trifling: that it came about, as they say, from Greek painters who favoured Paul more; or from Peter's modesty and humility in giving Paul the right hand in his Church; or, with Leo Allatius, from the arrangement of the Eastern basilicas brought to Rome by the Greeks, for whom what is right is left to the Latins. Since these only add to the number and to the uncertainty of the answers, they rightly do not receive further consideration.

units.la: LIII. Nam & aliâs prolixior in his fui, quàm ab initio cogitâram; Interim, quia comparationem Petri & Pauli Bellarminianam examinare cœperam, coepto etiam modo pergere placuit; Illud ex prolixitate ista commodum, gustus nimirum aliquis haberi poterit argumentationum Bellarminianarum; Quod superest, concludimus ex dictis & probatis, Apostolicam dignitatem celsissimam fuisse, & Petrum inter Apostolos peculiares quasdam prærogativas, & quendam ordinis Primatum habuisse, sed nec aliis Apostolis, Johanni & Jacobo cumprimis, suas prærogativas, eásque eximias defuisse; De Paulo nihil in Scriptura legi, quod eum Petro inferiorem fuisse probet, nihil in Patribus, multa contrà, & in Scriptura, & in Patribus, quibus Petrum superâsse videatur; Incertum etiam esse, an ille Petri Primatus semper durare, & ad omnes occasiones, etiam respectu Pauli, se extendere debuerit; Videri, huic repugnare ipsum situm Imaginum Apostolicarum in Pontificiis Romanorum Diplomatibus; Certissimum contrà esse illud, Petrum nullam planè potestatem, jurisdictionem, dominatum nullum in cæteros Apostolos habuisse, exercuisse, non fuisse Monarcham Bellarminianum.
units.tr: LIII. Indeed, I have been more lengthy on these matters than I first intended. Meanwhile, since I had begun to examine Bellarmine's comparison of Peter and Paul, I have decided to continue in the same manner as I began. From this lengthiness, some taste, at least, of Bellarmine's arguments may be had, which is useful. As for the rest, we conclude from what has been said and proved that the apostolic dignity was most exalted, and that Peter had certain peculiar prerogatives among the Apostles and a certain primacy of order; but the other Apostles, especially John and James, did not lack their own prerogatives, and these outstanding ones. Nothing is read in Scripture that proves Paul was inferior to Peter; nothing in the Fathers does; much to the contrary, both in Scripture and in the Fathers, by which he seems to have surpassed Peter. It is also uncertain whether that primacy of Peter ought always to last and extend to all occasions, even with respect to Paul. It seems to contradict this that the very arrangement of the Apostolic images in the Papists' Roman diplomas is as it is. What is most certain, on the contrary, is this: Peter had, exercised, and possessed no power, jurisdiction, or dominion at all over the other Apostles; he was not the Bellarminian monarch.

units.la: SECTIO SEPTIMA, In qua Ostenditur, ne quidem Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ cæterùm Pontificiæ, judicio, Petrum ad talem Pontificatum electum esse.
units.tr: SECTION SEVEN, in which it is shown that not even the Gallican Church, let alone the Papist Church, judges that Peter was elected to such a Pontificate.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Transitio & testimonium Doctissimi du Pin ; II. Annotatio ad illud ; III. Malè tamen idem affirmat, Catholicos suos hoc consentire, & ab hæreticis, quos vocat, injustè accusari, quasi Petro Monarchiam absolutam & dominatum in cæteros Apostolos tribuant. IV. Ostenditur, eos neutiquam consentire, ex antithesi doctrinarum ea de re in Ecclesia Romana receptarum ab ipso Doctissimo Viro institutà ; Vbi primò Monarchicorum de Petro & Papa sententiam exponit ; V. Secundò doctrinam Ecclesiæ maximè Gallicanæ
units.tr: I. Transition and testimony of the most learned du Pin; II. Note on it; III. But he nevertheless wrongly affirms that his Catholics agree with this, and that they are unjustly accused by the heretics, as he calls them, of ascribing to Peter an absolute monarchy and lordship over the other apostles. IV. It is shown that they by no means agree, from the antithesis of doctrines received in the Roman Church on this matter, set up by the most learned man himself; where first he sets out the opinion of the Monarchists about Peter and the Pope; V. Secondly the doctrine of the especially Gallican Church

units.la: oppenit; Antithesis prima; VI. Ad quam notatur, inconvenienter Gallos de regimine Monarchico loqui; VII. Quia Petro nonnisi ordinis Primatum concedunt; VIII. Antithesis secunda, cum annotatione; IX. Tertia & quarta; X. Quinta; XI. Cum annotatione; XII. Sexta, Septima, Octava, Nona, & Decima; XIII. Additio Doctiss. du Pin de aliis Privilegiis negatis. Testes ejus. XIV. Themata reliquarum ejus Dissertationum eodem respicientia; XV. Concluditur, heic non consentire Pontificios, nec injuste accusari; XVI. Exceptio: sed nos Galli & quidam alii tantam potestatem Petro non tribuimus; XVII. Ad quam porro respondetur; XVIII. Quam exosa Gallorum doctrina Romanis sit, exemplo Maimburgii ostenditur; XIX. XX. Et XXI. Porro, XXII. Concluditur exinde de dissensu, atque ex omnibus; Petrum non ad talem Pontificatum electum esse.
units.tr: opposes; Antithesis first; VI. To which it is noted that the Gallicans speak improperly about a monarchical government; VII. Because they grant Peter only a primacy of order; VIII. Second antithesis, with annotation; IX. Third and fourth; X. Fifth; XI. With annotation; XII. Sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth; XIII. Addition of the most learned du Pin on other privileges denied. His witnesses. XIV. Themes of his other dissertations bearing on the same; XV. It is concluded that here the Papists do not agree, nor are they unjustly accused; XVI. Objection: but we Gallicans and certain others do not grant Peter such great power; XVII. To which it is further answered; XVIII. How hateful the Gallican doctrine is to the Romanists is shown by the example of Maimbourg; XIX, XX and XXI. Further; XXII. It is concluded from this about the dissent, and from all things, that Peter was not elected to such a Pontificate.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Conclusionis nostrae in Sect. praced. respectu, hodienum Ecclesiam Gallicanam, non minimam certe illorum, qui Romanae communioni adhaerent, partem, magno interim Romanae Curiae taedio & dispendio, & contra Papatum praejudicio, vix diversum a nobis sentire, lectis recentioribus & nobilioribus ex illa gente Scriptoribus, quam persuasissimos sumus. Testem saepe hactenus, etiam quoad hoc, audivimus Doctissimum du Pin; Qui Petro certe nihil tribuit praeter Primatum ordinis simplicissimum, ex eo tantum argumenta formans, quod primus dicatur, & in omni Collegio aliquis primus esse debeat, & plures primi esse non possint, nempe sub eadem ratione. Ut merito hic nobis de consensu gratulemur, & vehementer optemus, ut etiam magis magisque hujus veritatis consequentias nobiscum illi agnoscant, & sedulo attendant, quis ille esse debeat, qui, quando Apostolus Petrus solo ordinis primatu contentus fuit, Monarchiam, Potentatum & Dominatum in fratres omnes tantum non absolutum, originem omnis potestatis Ecclesiasticae, quoad Episcoporum, qui sui tantum sint juris, sibi etiam obedientiam jurare teneantur, missionem, peccatorum remissionem, legislationem, pro lubitu conferendae, sub S. Petri, imo sub sanctissimo Christi nomine sibi tribuit; ut sedulo etiam attendant, ex quo fundamento secula proxime elapsa errorum etiam monstra ad pudorem Christianismi, obstetricantibus, de Regno Ecclesiastico-Politico universali, ambitiosis consiliis, ab una, & hominum superstitione & ignorantia, ab altera parte, enata, acceperint? Annon ex eo fundamento, quod tunc omnibus fere in illa communione creditum, Petri Successorem, fidei esse Magistrum, infallibilem, Legislatorem supremum, fontem omnis gratiae? Quod quidem
units.tr: With respect to the conclusion of our previous section: today the Gallican Church, certainly not the smallest part of those who adhere to the Roman communion, and whom we are firmly persuaded are so, thinks almost the same as we do, to the great weariness and loss of the Roman Curia and to the prejudice of the Papacy, as we have learned from the more recent and more distinguished writers of that nation. Up to now we have often heard the most learned du Pin as a witness, also on this point. He certainly ascribes nothing to Peter beyond the simplest primacy of order, forming his arguments only from this: that he is called first, and in every college someone ought to be first, and several cannot be first under the same respect. So here we rightly rejoice in their agreement, and earnestly wish that they would more and more acknowledge with us the consequences of this truth, and would carefully consider who ought to be the one who, when the apostle Peter was content with the primacy of order alone, claimed for himself a monarchy, a power and a lordship over all the brethren that was virtually unlimited; the origin of all ecclesiastical power; over the bishops, who are of their own right only, he claimed that they must also swear obedience to him; he claimed that the sending out, the forgiveness of sins, and legislation were to be conferred at his pleasure, under the name of St Peter, and even under the most holy name of Christ. And let them also carefully consider on what foundation the centuries just past, with the monstrous errors that disgraced Christianity, obstetrically brought forth, from one side the ambitious plans for a universal ecclesiastical-political kingdom, and from the other the superstition and ignorance of men. Was it not from that foundation, which was then believed by almost everyone in that communion, that the successor of Peter is the teacher of the faith, infallible, the supreme lawgiver, the fountain of all grace? And this foundation, which is built as the shadow of Peter rather than on the rock, is against Peter and against the Rock, and so it is rightly rejected by the Gallican Church. And must not, in consequence, those doctrines, which may appear erroneous at first sight to a man not preoccupied with prejudices about an infallible teacher (and to which, by councils serving some plans of this monarch in clear craft, and deriving their authority from him, and whose authority is refuted just as solidly in those ways, as the Papists' other flatterers also refute it, as they see and grieve over their own monarchical authority of the Pope's primacy being refuted), have been able to add little weight, be subjected to the serious examination of the prudent, in keeping with the dignity of the matter, which ought to help or harm them?

units.la: Transitio, & testimonium Doct. du Pin; quidem fundamentum, ut umbrae potiùs Petri, quàm verò Petrae inaedificatum, & contra Petrum & contra Petram est, ita ab Ecclesia Gallicana haud immeritò rejicitur; Et annon per consequens dogmata illa, quae erronea vel primo Viri praejudiciis de infallibili Doctore non occupati intuitu apparere possunt, (& quibus à Conciliis, quibusdam consiliis hujus Monarchae arte manifestâ inservientibus, & authoritatem ab eo derivantibus, & quorum authoritatem dictis modis potestativam praeter alios ipsi quoque Papae gnathones aequè solidè refutant, ac suam de Primatu Papae authoritatem Monarchicam refutari vident & dolent, parùm ponderis accedere potuit:) pro rei, cui aut prodesse, aut obesse debent, dignitate, serio prudentum examini subjici debeant?
units.tr: Transition, and testimony of Doctor du Pin; (the foundation indeed) which is built as the shadow of Peter rather than on the rock, is against Peter and against the Rock, and so it is rightly rejected by the Gallican Church. And must not, in consequence, those doctrines, which may appear erroneous at first sight to a man not preoccupied with prejudices about an infallible teacher, (and to which, by councils serving some plans of this monarch in clear craft, and deriving their authority from him, and whose authority is refuted just as solidly in those ways by the other flatterers of the Pope, as they see and grieve over their own monarchical authority of the Pope's primacy being refuted) have been able to add little weight, be subjected to the serious examination of the prudent, in keeping with the dignity of the matter, which ought to help or harm them?

units.la: II. Interim tamen, quando in re inter Gallos & nos consensus est, ad verba Doctissimi du Pin & hoc annotandum censuimus; Primatum ordinis ratione temporum & subjectorum variare posse, & licet plures sub eadem ratione primi esse non possint, nihilominus tamen, ob ornamentorum, & donorum personalium, & efficaciae divinae in diversis diversitatem, sub diversa ratione, modò hunc, modò illum, primum in aequalitate potestatis dici, & alteri praeferri, & praerogativarum collationem instituì posse.
units.tr: II. Meanwhile, however, since there is agreement between the Gallicans and us on the matter, we have thought fit to note this on the words of the most learned du Pin: that the primacy of order can vary according to the times and the persons, and although several cannot be first under the same respect, nevertheless, on account of the differing ornaments, personal gifts, and divine efficacy in different people, one may be called first, now this one, now that one, under a different respect, within an equality of power, and be preferred to another; and a bestowing of prerogatives may be established.

units.la: III. Non obstante etiam hoc consensu, in Doctissimo du Pin displicet illud, quòd Catholicos, quos vocat, hic consentire supponit, haereticos, (quod nostrum quoque apud Pontificios elogium est;) injustè Catholicos accusare, contendit. Prius supponere videtur, quando ait: His de primatu Petri praemissis, in illa disputatione celebri de ejus Monarchia non haereo; Nam si Monarcha dicitur is, qui primum obtinet locum, haud dubium est, Petrum hoc sensu fuisse Monarcham. Si verò Monarchatus sumatur pro authoritate absoluta, nec non pro Dominatu, cui nullus sese potest opponere, nego Petrum hoc sensu Ecclesiae Monarcham fuisse, hanc enim Monarchiam à se & suis rejicit Christus, cùm ait: Reges Gentium dominantur iis, vos autem non sic: Et Petrus ipse, scribens: Pascite, qui in vobis est, gregem Dei, non coactè, sed sponte, non dominantes in Cleris, sed forma facti ex animo gregis. Posterius aperte contendit, ita Caput de Petri Primatu claudens; Quod idcirco monui, (nimirum Petri Primatum non fuisse Monarchiam absolutam, aut dominatum in Apostolos caeteros;) quia solent haeretici haec secum invicem confundere, & accusare Catholicos, quasi Monarchiam absolutam & Dominatum in Ecclesiam admittant, quod à veritate alienum
units.tr: III. Notwithstanding this agreement, what displeases in the most learned du Pin is that he supposes these Catholics, as he calls them, agree here, and contends that the heretics, (which is also our title among the Papists), unjustly accuse the Catholics. He seems to suppose the first when he says: With these things about Peter's primacy laid down, I do not hesitate over that famous dispute about his monarchy; for if he is called a monarch who holds the first place, it is beyond doubt that Peter was a monarch in this sense. But if monarchy is taken to mean absolute authority, and also lordship, which no one can oppose, I deny that Peter in this sense was the monarch of the Church; for Christ rejects this monarchy from himself and his own, when he says: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you shall not be so. And Peter himself, writing: Feed the flock of God that is among you, not by constraint but willingly, not lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock from the heart. He contends the latter plainly, concluding thus the chapter on Peter's primacy: I have warned of this because the heretics are accustomed to confuse these things with one another, and to accuse the Catholics, as if they admitted an absolute monarchy and lordship over the Church, which is foreign to the truth.

units.la: Annotatio ad illud; alienum est. Sed Pontificios hic minimè consentire, & accusationes nostras à veritate non alienas esse, patet partim ex allatis ipsius du Pin testimoniis, partim & adhuc multò distinctiùs, ex ea, quam c.II. §.3. in disputatione contra nos, etiam ipse instituere coactus fuit, doctrinarum in Ecclesia Romana ea de re receptarum Antithesi:
units.tr: Note on that: foreign to the truth, indeed. But that the Papists here by no means agree, and that our accusations are not foreign to the truth, is plain partly from the testimonies of du Pin himself which we have cited, and partly, and still much more distinctly, from the antithesis of the doctrines received in the Roman Church on this matter, which he himself was compelled to set up in his disputation against us in chapter 2, section 3.

units.la: IV. Dicit; Callem nobis oppositum plane insistere Theologos Romana Curia placitis nimium addictos, qui, dum Pontificis Primatum defendant, ita eum extollant, ut invidiam ipsi maximam conflent. 1. Igitur ajunt Pontificem Romanum esse absolutum Ecclesiae Monarcham, & ita jure divino constitutum esse; Monarchiam autem hanc Ecclesiae nullâ Aristocratiâ temperatam esse. 2. Dicunt, Pontificem Romanum habere claves & jurisdictionem immediatam à Deo, cateros autem Episcopos à Pontifice Romano accipere. 3. Ajunt, eum esse controversiarum de Religione omnium Judicem supremum, appellationes universae Ecclesiae ipsi jure Divino competere. 4. Eum leges de novo condere posse, quae universam Ecclesiam obligent. 5. Eum non modò praeesse debere Conciliis omnibus, sed etiam supra Concilia omnia esse, & à nemine judicari posse. 6. Idem tribuunt Pontificibus jus ordinandorum ubique, non modò Patriarcharum & Metropolitarum, sed etiam Episcoporum. 7. Romanum Pontificem saltem ex Cathedra loquentem infallibilem esse in judiciis de fide perhibent. 8. Ipsum esse Dominum totius mundi dominio temporali, & habere potestatem deponendorum Regum, fidelium subditorum à Sacramento fidelitatis absolvendorum. Has & alias ejusmodi incredibiles prærogativas Romana Ecclesia ejusque Episcopo deferunt, Turrecremata, Sanderus, Bellarminus, & alii Curiæ Romanæ plus aquo addicti.
units.tr: IV. He says: Theologians devoted too much to the decrees of the Roman Curia have followed a course directly opposed to ours, who, while they defend the primacy of the Pope, so exalt him that they draw the greatest hatred upon him. 1. They therefore say that the Roman Pontiff is the absolute monarch of the Church, and has been so established by divine right; and this monarchy of the Church is not tempered by any aristocracy. 2. They say that the Roman Pontiff has the keys and an immediate jurisdiction from God, while the other bishops receive theirs from the Roman Pontiff. 3. They say that he is the supreme judge of controversies about religion, and that appeals from the whole Church belong to him by divine right. 4. That he can make new laws which bind the whole Church. 5. That he ought not only to preside over all councils, but also to be above all councils, and can be judged by no one. 6. They grant the same to the Pontiffs, the right of ordaining everywhere, not only patriarchs and metropolitans, but also bishops. 7. They hold that the Roman Pontiff, speaking at least from the Chair, is infallible in judgements about faith. 8. That he is the lord of the whole world with temporal dominion, and has the power of deposing kings, and of absolving faithful subjects from the oath of fidelity. These and other such incredible prerogatives the Roman Church and its bishop confer, Torquemada, Sanders, Bellarmine, and others who are more devoted than is right to the Roman Curia.

units.la: V. At cateri Theologi, præsertim Galli, primò statuunt, in Ecclesiæ jure divino esse quandam Monarchiam, hoc est, in ea primum esse Pontificem Romanum; Attamen ajunt, Christum immediatè ac per se claves toti Ecclesiæ collectim sumptæ dedisse, & subjectum, ut loquuntur, immediatum potestatis Ecclesiæ esse non Papam aut Prælatos, sed totam Ecclesiam, ita tamen, ut per Prælatos jus clavium exerceatur, non per solum Pontificem, licèt primus sit inter eos, qui jus illud habent; Hinc ajunt; Statum Ecclesiasticum Monarchicum esse, Regimen Aristocraticum, seu Ecclesiam Monarchiam esse Aristocratico regimine temperatam. Interpositis dein quibusdam de Episcoporum Romanorum Successione, quæ suo loco examinabimus, pergit. Verùm ut majorem his lucem afferamus, distinguenda sunt plura in Romano Pontifice; Primò quòd sit primus Episcoporum; Secundò quòd sit Metropolitanus & Patriarcha; Tertiò quòd aliquas aliquas habeat prærogativas, aliqua jura peculiariter concessa; Quartò quòd habeat potestatem temporalem in patrimonium Sancti Petri: Primum habet præsertim ex institutione Christi: Secundum & tertium habet ex consuetudine & Canonibus ob urbis & Ecclesiæ dignitatem: Quartum partim ex donatione Pipini & Caroli M. partim jure gentium & præscriptionis, more aliorum Principum Politicorum.
units.tr: V. But the other theologians, especially the French, first hold that there is a certain monarchy by divine right in the Church, that is, that the Roman Pontiff is first in it. Yet they say that Christ gave the keys immediately and directly to the whole Church taken collectively, and that the immediate subject of the power of the Church, as they put it, is not the Pope or the prelates but the whole Church. The right of the keys is exercised through the prelates, however, not through the Pope alone, although he is first among those who hold that right. From this they say that the ecclesiastical state is monarchical, but the government is aristocratic, or that the Church is a monarchy tempered by aristocratic government. After some remarks about the succession of the Roman bishops, which we shall examine in their proper place, he goes on: "But to throw more light on these matters, several things must be distinguished in the Roman Pontiff. First, that he is first among the bishops. Second, that he is metropolitan and patriarch. Third, that he has certain prerogatives and rights granted to him in a special way. Fourth, that he has temporal power over the patrimony of St Peter. The first he has chiefly by the institution of Christ. The second and third he has by custom and the canons, on account of the dignity of the city and the Church. The fourth he has partly by the donation of Pepin and Charlemagne, and partly by the law of nations and prescription, like other secular princes."

units.la: VI. Ad quæ, antequam cæteri articuli subjungantur, quædam annotabimus. Faciunt sic, uno verbo, Regimen Ecclesiæ Aristocraticum, quicquid de Monarcha, Monarchia, & statu Monarchico dicant: Siquidem de vocibus non est litigandum, quod verbosi, contentiosi, calumniosi hominis esse, Durandus rectè asseruit; Interim tamen male & inconvenienter plane fit, quòd, offensionis Romanæ metu, statum Ecclesiæ Monarchicum (ratione hominum, Christum enim Ecclesiæ suæ Monarcham esse, & verè talem, id est, unicum, nos contendimus) dicunt, longè diversa, ut attendenti manifestum fit, ab illo, quod hæc verba significant, sentientes; Licet enim in iis, quæ communi Ecclesiæ nomine, & in Rectorum congregationibus geri debent, omninò aliquis primus esse, Primatum quendam ordinis habere, primus loqui debeat, idque non tantùm juris Divini revelati sit, secundùm quod in Ecclesiis omnia ordine & decenter fieri debent, 1.Cor.XIV.40. Sed etiam juris naturalis, quod ordinem aliquem in omni re postulat, tamen, ut ab una parte (prout sequentia id docebunt;) ex eo nondum ad Pont. Rom. valet consequentia, ita ab altera parte, si vel ille primus foret, & semper primus, nondum Monarcha foret, nondum respectu illius Ecclesiæ status Monarchicus, Ecclesia Monarchica. Quid enim est Monarcha, status Monarchicus, Monarchia? Monarchia, & status Monarchicus vi originis, & usûs inter homines recepti, est suprema potestas unius, & Monarcha, qui unus imperium summum habet, cæterisque dominatur omnibus; Certè Bellarminus & cæteri, qui pro Monarchia Papæ tanquam pro aris & focis pugnant, hos sensus vocum istarum retinent & commendant, sicque etiam cum vocum origine & usu probè conveniunt, licèt alienissimi à veritate.
units.tr: VI. Before the remaining articles are added, we shall make some observations on these points. In a word, whatever they say about a monarch, a monarchy and a monarchical state, they make the government of the Church aristocratic. Indeed, as Durandus rightly asserted, one should not quarrel about words, which is the mark of a verbose, contentious and calumnious man. Nevertheless, it is plainly wrong and improper that, from fear of offending Rome, they call the state of the Church monarchical (in respect of men, for we contend that Christ is the Monarch of his Church, and truly such, that is, the only one). Yet, as anyone attending closely can see, their meaning is quite different from what these words signify. For although, in those matters which must be done in the common name of the Church and in assemblies of its rulers, someone must certainly be first, have a certain primacy of order, and speak first, and this is required not only by revealed divine law, according to which all things in the churches ought to be done "decently and in order" (1 Cor. 14:40), but also by natural law, which demands some order in every matter; yet, on the one hand (as what follows will show), it does not yet follow from this that the Roman Pontiff is a monarch. On the other hand, even if that first man were indeed first and always first, he would not yet be a monarch, and the state of that Church would not yet be monarchical, nor the Church monarchical. For what is a monarch, a monarchical state, a monarchy? By the origin of the word and its accepted use among men, a monarchy and a monarchical state is the supreme power of one, and the monarch is the one who holds supreme command and rules over all the others. Certainly Bellarmine and the others, who fight for the monarchy of the Pope as for their altars and hearths, keep and commend these meanings of the words, and so agree well with the origin and usage of the words, although they are most alien to the truth.

units.la: VII. Ast quomodo dici potest, Ecclesiæ statum esse Monarchicum, quatenus in ea aliquis sit, qui primum locum obtineat? Quis status sic non Monarchicus erit? Annon etiam ordo aliquis in statu Aristocratico, Democratico? Annon etiam in utroque primi dantur? An ex eo, quia ubique aliquis primus, statim de Monarchico narchico statu præsumitur? Negant Politici, id fieri debere, sed ex eo potius, ubi potestas suprema consistat, an penes unum, an penes optimates, an penes populum, de statu judicandum esse censent. Quando igitur Galli Theologi cum aliis quibusdam supremam in Ecclesia potestatem legislatoriam, decisivam controversiarum &c. Papis neutiquam tribuunt, sed, ut aperte etiam profitentur, solum ordinis primatum, Protarchia hæc Paparum potestas quodammodo vocari posset, Monarchia vocari nullo modo potest, & ego quidem distinctionem illam inter statum & Regimen, ut ille sit Monarchicus, hoc Aristocraticum, concipere nequeo, cùm videatur, ob Regiminis formam statum modò Monarchicum, modò Aristocraticum, modò Democraticum dici. Ut certè etiam Doct. du Pin Regimen primæ Ecclesiæ Aristocraticum c. 1. §. 3. supra allegatâ, dixerat expressè. Et similiter suo & aliorum nomine, in verbis jam allegatis, subjectum supremæ potestatis Ecclesiasticæ immediatum Ecclesiam facit, quæ eam per Prælatos cæteros æquè ac per Papam exerceat, ut primò Ecclesia in prima possessione potestatis, secundò non solus Papa de Jure Divino sit, prout illud quidem Papæ assentatores pertendunt, sed & quilibet Ecclesiæ Rector, & tertiò illud tantùm præ aliis Papa de Jure divino habeat, quòd sit Episcoporum primus: Et quemadmodum ita multum nobis appropinquant, qui etiam Episcopo Romano, si potiùs Episcopum genuinum, quàm verò defectionis Antistitem & Tyrannum se præberet, primatum aliquem de jure humano concederemus, quæ etiam optimi Melanchthonis in subscriptione Articulorum, Schmalcaldicorum sententia fuit, ita contrà ab illis procul abeunt, qui Pontificem Rom. absolutum Monarcham Ecclesiæ, de jure Divino, sine Aristocratiæ & Democratiæ commixtione secundùm aliter sentientium expressa verba, faciunt. Sed redimus ad theses Gallorum & cum iis facientium.
units.tr: VII. But how can it be said that the state of the Church is monarchical, insofar as there is someone in it who holds the first place? What state would not be monarchical in this way? Is there not also some order in an aristocratic or a democratic state? Are there not also firsts in each of these? Is a monarchical state presumed at once because somewhere someone is first? The politicians deny that this should be done. Rather, they judge that the state should be determined by where supreme power lies, whether with one, with the nobles, or with the people. So when the French theologians, together with some others, do not in any way attribute to the Popes the supreme legislative power in the Church, the power to decide controversies and so on, but, as they openly profess, only a primacy of order (this papal power could in some way be called a protarchy, but it cannot in any way be called a monarchy), then I myself cannot conceive that distinction between state and government, by which the one is monarchical and the other aristocratic, since the same state is called now monarchical, now aristocratic, now democratic, according to the form of government. Certainly Doctor du Pin, in the passage cited above (chapter 1, section 3), had expressly said that the government of the primitive Church was aristocratic. Likewise, in the words already cited, speaking in his own name and that of others, he makes the Church the immediate subject of supreme ecclesiastical power, which it exercises through the other prelates just as much as through the Pope; so that, first, the Church holds the power in its first possession; second, it is not the Pope alone who holds it by divine right, as the flatterers of the Pope maintain, but also every ruler of the Church; and third, the Pope has by divine right only this advantage over the others, that he is first among the bishops. And just as those come very near to us who would also concede some primacy by human right to the Roman bishop, if he showed himself a genuine bishop rather than a leader of defection and a tyrant (which was also the opinion of the excellent Melanchthon in his signature to the Schmalkald Articles), so those are far removed from them who make the Roman Pontiff an absolute monarch of the Church by divine right, without any admixture of aristocracy and democracy, contrary to the express words of those who think otherwise. But let us return to the theses of the French and of those who agree with them.

units.la: VIII. Ex hoc primatu, ait Doctiss. du Pin, secundò fluunt multa prærogativa, quæ ipsi (Papæ) non secus ac primatus jure divino competunt.
units.tr: VIII. From this primacy, says the most learned du Pin, secondly, many prerogatives flow, which belong to the Pope himself no less than the primacy by divine right.

units.la: Enumerat curam observationis Canonum, & in casu contumacia convocationis Concilii generalis: ubi dicit: Verum equidem est, prima Concilia generalia ab Imperatoribus esse convocata, sed sæpè sæpiùs id fecerunt ad preces Romanorum Pontificum, sed in casu imminentis periculi posse Papam ipsummet classicum canere, & Concilia convocare, & eos, qui legitimè vocati adesse renuerint, velut Ecclesiæ desertores excommunicare. Quæ quidem prærogativæ sunt, & majores, quàm sunt, esse videntur, sed in comparatione ejus, quod postulatur, nihil plane sunt, quando & Canonum observationem transgressionum rei jactare, & ad Concilium à Papis provocare, & in Concilio Papam ipsum condemnare, & ab illo vocati, vocationem non legitimam esse, pertendere, & excommunicantem vicissim excommunicare possunt.
