units.tr: He lists the care for observing the canons, and, in the case of contumacy, the convening of a general council, where he says: It is indeed true that the first general councils were convened by the emperors, but very often they did so at the request of the Roman bishops. In a case of imminent danger, however, the Pope himself can sound the trumpet, convene councils, and excommunicate as deserters of the Church those who, though lawfully summoned, refuse to attend. These prerogatives are indeed greater than they are, or seem to be, but compared with what is demanded, they are nothing at all. For the councils can both accuse the Pope of breaking the canons, and appeal from him to a council, and in the council condemn the Pope himself; and, when summoned by him, they can contend that the summons is not lawful, and in turn excommunicate the one who excommunicated them.

units.la: X. Tertiò Romani Pontificis definitiones magni apud omnes momenti esse, & universam spectare Ecclesiam, licet non infallibiles sint, Doctissimus Vir affirmat; Sed examinant, sed, si ingratæ sunt, rejiciunt, experientiâ teste. Quartò Pontifici Romano præcipuas in judicando partes, licet non sit solus omnium controversiarum judex, assignat, & privilegium hoc, quòd nihil in Ecclesia magni momenti definiri possit, quod non ad ipsum referatur, vel de quo non consulatur. Sed hîc per præcipuas partes tantùm primum suffragium intelligunt, multa etiam eo inscio, imò invito, imò maximi momenti, imò contra eum, sæpè definiunt, cùm consulunt, obsequii libertatem sibi semper reservantes. Quintò, ait Doctissimus Vir, Theologi nostri censent, Romanum Pontificem à legibus, à Conciliis etiam generalibus latis sapienter dispensare posse, eo in casu, quo Concilium ipsum dispensaret, nec non agnoscunt, ipsum leges generales posse condere, & toti Ecclesiæ observandas proponere, sed quâ vim (non) habeant, nisi promulgata & recepta communi omnium consensu.
units.tr: X. Thirdly, the most learned man affirms that the definitions of the Roman Pontiff are of great weight with everyone and concern the whole Church, although they are not infallible. But they examine them, and if they are unwelcome, they reject them, as experience bears witness. Fourthly, he assigns to the Roman Pontiff the chief role in judging, although he is not the sole judge of all controversies, and this privilege, that nothing of great weight can be defined in the Church which is not referred to him or on which he is not consulted. But here they understand by chief role only the first vote. Often they also define many things of great weight without his knowledge, indeed even against his will, and against him, while they consult him, always reserving for themselves the freedom of obedience. Fifthly, the most learned man says: Our theologians hold that the Roman Pontiff can wisely dispense from laws, and from general councils that have been enacted, even in the case where the council itself would dispense. They also acknowledge that he can enact general laws and propose them to be observed by the whole Church, but they have no force unless promulgated and received by the common consent of all.

units.la: XI. Sed non permittunt, quod extravagantes Joh. XXII. al. XXIII. postulant, facere ex quadratis rotundum, ex injusto jus, dispensare contra jus gentium, Civile, Decreta, Canones, Concilia, Testamentum Vetus, Evangelia. Quoad dispensationes & Concilia audiantur, qui dans le Journal du Palais disputant; Num Papa possit dispensare in primo gradu affinitatis? Dicitur ibi eâ occasione, Romanorum Pontificum authoritatem non eos superiores reddere jure Canonico aut Conciliis, cumprimis postquam Clerus judicaverit, Papam esse sub Concilio, nec Dominum absolutum disciplinæ; Et si Papa liceret abolere decreta Conciliorum generalium, nullum eorum usum fore, ipsúmque Papam Zozimum dicere: Contra statuta Patrum condere aliquid, vel mutare, nec hujus sedis valet authoritas. Si displicet dispensatio? Non sapienter dispensatum est. Si displicet dispensatio? Concilium hîc non dispensâsseт. Leges Paparum generales demum vim habent promulgata & recepta communi omnium consensu, id est, nullam sine communi consensu vim habent, vim suam inde demum accipiunt, in se nullæ sunt.
units.tr: XI. But they do not allow what the Extravagantes of John XXII (or XXIII) demand: to make a round thing out of a square, to make the unjust just, to dispense against the law of nations, civil law, decrees, canons, councils, the Old Testament, the Gospels. As for dispensations and councils, let those be heard who dispute in the Journal du Palais: Can the Pope dispense in the first degree of affinity? It is said there, on that occasion, that the authority of the Roman bishops does not make them superior to canon law or to councils, especially after the clergy has judged that the Pope is under a council and is not an absolute lord of discipline. And if the Pope were allowed to abolish the decrees of general councils, none of them would have any use; Pope Zosimus himself said: it is not valid for the authority of this see to enact or change anything against the statutes of the Fathers. If the dispensation displeases? It was not wisely dispensed. If the dispensation displeases? The council did not dispense here. The general laws of the Popes finally have force when promulgated and received by the common consent of all. That is, they have no force without common consent; they receive their force only from that, and in themselves they are nothing.

units.la: XII. Sextò, ajunt, πrεεδεῖων in Conciliis ipsi quidem ex convenientia deberi, sed non ex necessitate, quandoquidem tribus primis Conciliis generalibus non præfuit, negant porrò illum esse supra Concilia, aut à nemine judicari posse, quin imò contrarium disertè affirmant, & probant ex ipsorum Pontificum exemplis: Disertè affirmant! Septimò, probavimus in Dissertatione præcedenti (III. de antiqua infligendæ excommunicationis ratione,) jus ordinationum Pontificem non habuisse extra Patriarchatus sui limites. Et hæc verba clara sunt! Octavò, Pontificem infallibilem esse negant & de facto plures errâsse contendunt; Ista quoque intelliguntur sine interprete infallibili! Nonò contendunt, ipsum Oecumenicis Concilius inferiorem esse, & ab ipsis judicari ac deponi posse. Nec illa luce egent! Decimò execrantur illorum sententiam, qui asserunt, Pontificem jus habere deponendorum Regum, & subjectorum à Sacramento fidei absolvendorum, regnorúmque aut transferendorum, aut cuilibet occupanti tradendorum. Execrantur!
units.tr: XII. Sixthly, they say that precedence [πρεσβεῖα] is owed to him in councils, indeed by agreement but not by necessity, since he did not preside over the first three general councils. They further deny that he is above the councils, or that he cannot be judged by anyone; indeed they clearly affirm the contrary, and prove it from the examples of the Popes themselves. They clearly affirm! Seventhly, we have shown in the preceding dissertation (III, on the ancient manner of inflicting excommunication) that the Pope did not have the right of ordination beyond the limits of his own patriarchate. And these words are clear! Eighthly, they deny that the Pope is infallible and contend that many have in fact erred. These things too are understood without an infallible interpreter! Ninthly, they contend that he is inferior to the ecumenical councils, and can be judged and deposed by them. Nor do these need any light! Tenthly, they execrate the opinion of those who assert that the Pope has the right to depose kings, to absolve subjects from their oath of allegiance, and to transfer kingdoms or hand them over to whoever seizes them. They execrate it!

units.la: XIII. Videtur satis dixisse; Sed addit: Sunt & alia quaedam quæ sibi arrogant Romani Pontifices, quæ ex istis NB. fluunt, quæ illi pariter non agnoscunt: ut quòd solus Papa possit deponere Episcopos, quod salsissimum est, & innumeris exemplis refellitur: quòd necesse sit Concilia ab ipso confirmari, ut robur habeant, quod pariter falsum esse docent prima Concilia, quæ à Pontificibus confirmata minimè sunt. Item, quòd solus jus habeat ea convocandi, quod adeò falsum est, ut octo priora Concilia ab Imperatoribus convocata esse constet. Hæc sunt, quæ nostri præsertim Theologi ad primatum Pontificis Romani pertinere negant, vide de his Gersonem in tractatu de potestate Ecclesiæ, de auferibilitate Papæ, de statibus Ecclesiæ, de pace, & in articulis contra Petrum de Luna, Petrum de Alliaco in tract. de Ecclesiæ authoritate, Jacobum Almainum tract. de Dominio naturali, Civili & Ecclesiastico, de authoritate Ecclesiæ, de potestate Ecclesiastica & Laica, Johannem Majorem disput. de authorit. Concilii supra Pontificem & in 4. dist.24. & post hos Richerium tract. de Eccles. & Politica potestate, in Apologia pro Gersone, & in historia octo Conciliorum generalium nuper edita: Simonem Vigorium in responsione Synodali, & in libro Gallicè edito, cui titulus, de l'état & gouvernement de l'Eglise, Joannem Launojum in Epistolis variisque tractatibus, Petrum de Marca in Libro de Concordia, assertiones Parisiensium Theologorum, & censuram eorundem in Vernantium cum ejus assertione, librum de antiquis & majoribus Episcoporum causis, librum Gervasii Doctoris Parisiensis de eodem argumento, & alios. Citationes iltæ tam dignæ sunt,& tam bene de communi interest
units.tr: XIII. He seems to have said enough, but he adds: There are also certain other things which the Roman Pontiffs claim for themselves, which flow from these (NB.), and which they likewise do not acknowledge: that the Pope alone can depose bishops, which is most false and is refuted by countless examples; that councils must be confirmed by him to have force, which the first councils, none of which were confirmed by the Popes, teach is likewise false; likewise, that he alone has the right to convene them, which is so false that it is established that the eight earlier councils were convened by the emperors. These are the things which our theologians especially deny pertain to the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. See on these Gerson, in his treatise on the power of the Church, on the revocability of the Pope, on the states of the Church, on peace, and in the articles against Peter de Luna; Peter d'Ailly in his treatise on the authority of the Church; James Almain in his treatise on natural, civil and ecclesiastical dominion, on the authority of the Church, and on ecclesiastical and lay power; John Major in his disputation on the authority of a council above the Pope, and in book 4, distinction 24; and after these Richer in his treatise on the Church and political power, in his Apology for Gerson, and in the recently published history of the eight general councils; Simon Vigor in the Synodal response, and in the book published in French entitled de l'état et gouvernement de l'Eglise; John Launoy in his letters and various treatises; Peter de Marca in his book on concord; the assertions of the Parisian theologians and their censure of Vernantius, with his assertion; the book on the ancient and greater causes of bishops; the book of Gervase, doctor of Paris, on the same subject; and others. Those citations are so worthy, and so well serve the common interest,

units.la: tex ter Gallos sententia, à Doctissimis Viris jam olim integris tractati-bus strenuè defensa,testantur, ut eas etiam exscribere nullus dubi-taverim,quò sic Lector Benev. plura de his legere cupiens noverit, ubi sitim suam extinguere queat.
units.tr: as the opinion of the Gauls attests, long since vigorously defended in full treatises by the most learned men, so that I have not hesitated to copy them out, so that the kindly reader, wishing to read more on these matters, may know where he can quench his thirst.

units.la: XIV. Addit doctissimus du Pin: Eadem nos post tot graves ac summos Theologos de primatu & prærogativis summi Pontificis asserere non dubitamus, & jam ex illis nonnulla probavimus (nimirum præter III. jam allegatam,in I. Dissertat. de forma & distributione Ecclesiarum, præsertim quarto Seculo, ubi de Patriarchis, Metropolitis,istorumque jure & prærogativis; & in II. ubi de forma judiciorum Ecclesiasticorum, & de appellationibus adversus nuperam Christiani Lupi de illis lucubrationem egit;) cætera fusè deinceps probabuntur: (Dissertationibus nimirum. V. ubi de fictitia Pontificis Romani infallibilitate. V. ubi de Superioritate Conciliorum. VII. ubi contra temporalem potestatem Papæ agere constituerat.)
units.tr: XIV. The most learned du Pin adds: After so many grave and eminent theologians, we do not hesitate to assert the same things about the primacy and prerogatives of the supreme Pontiff, and we have already proved some of them from those (namely, besides the third already cited, in the first dissertation on the form and distribution of the Churches, especially in the fourth century, where he treats of the patriarchs, metropolitans, and their rights and prerogatives; and in the second, where he treated of the form of ecclesiastical judgments, and of appeals against the recent work of Christian Lupus on them); the rest will be proved fully hereafter (namely in the dissertations: the fifth, where he treats of the fictitious infallibility of the Roman Pontiff; the fifth again, where he treats of the superiority of councils; and the seventh, where he had determined to deal against the temporal power of the Pope).

units.la: XV. Jam post allatam hanc sententiarum in Communione Romana antithesin judicandum relinquo; utrùm nos miseri hæretici res diversas confundamus, & à veritate alieni,Catholicos accusemus, quasi Monarchiam absolutam & Dominatum in Ecclesia admittant. Quid igitur? An Turrecremata, an Sanderus, an Bellarminus, an Baronius, an Lupus,an alii Curiæ Romanæ multùm addicti non sunt Catholici? Catholicissimi, quia Curiæ Romanæ addictissimi. Nam (ut egregiè ait Doctissimus Archipræsul Spalatensis in scripto Venetiis relicto, quo profectionis suæ consilium expo(uit, & quod statim post discessum Heidelbergæ primùm, deinde etiam aliis pluribus locis,ac linguis seorsum impressum & publicatum, tandem etiam libris de Republ. Ecclesiast. præpositum fuit;) aliquando quidem fuit articulus fidei, universitatem Ecclesiasticam per totum mundum diffusam, esse Ecclesiam Christi Catholicam,cui Christus ipse perpetuam promisit assisten-tiam, quam Paulus columnam vocat, & firmamentum veritatis; Nunc articulum hunc fidei nostri Romani contraxerunt: ut jam Catholica Ecclesia ipsa Romana Curia intelligatur; atque in ea sola, imò in solo Papa, totum Christi Spiritum residere firmâ fide credendum proponatur. Et quicquid in honorem universitatis Christi Ecclesiæ olim dictum sit, id totum ad solam Curiam Romanam per summam vim & injuriam Ecclesiæ, pertrahatur, & ad fidei articulos Romæ reducantur plurima,quorum nullam à Christo habuimus unquam institutionem: quibusve insuper animæ fidelium miserabiliter decipiuntur: ac consequenter cœci simul cum suis cætis ductoribus in barathrum perditionis ruunt, & praecipitantur. Quia igitur hi Curiae Romanae, id est, Ecclesiae Catholicae addictissimi fuerunt & sunt, etiam maximè Catholici fuerunt & sunt, ut etiam numero inter Catholicos plures fuerunt & sunt, & per consequens non est diversorum confusio, nec etiam à veritate aliena accusatio haereticorum, dum dicunt, Monarchiam absolutam & Dominatum à Catholicis sic dictis in Ecclesia admitti.
units.tr: XV. Now, after this antithesis of opinions within the Roman communion has been set forth, I leave it to be judged whether we wretched heretics confuse different things, and, being alien to the truth, accuse Catholics of admitting an absolute monarchy and dominion in the Church, as if they did. What then? Are Turrecremata, Sanderus, Bellarmine, Baronius, Lupus, and the other men very much devoted to the Roman Curia not Catholics? They are most Catholic, because they are most devoted to the Roman Curia. For (as the most learned archbishop of Spalato excellently says, in the writing he left at Venice, in which he set out the purpose of his departure, and which, immediately after his leaving, was first printed and published at Heidelberg, and then separately in many other places and languages, and finally was also prefixed to his books on the Ecclesiastical Republic): At one time it was indeed an article of faith that the ecclesiastical universality spread through the whole world is the Catholic Church of Christ, to which Christ himself promised perpetual assistance, which Paul calls the pillar and foundation of the truth. Now our Romans have narrowed this article of faith, so that the Catholic Church is now understood to be the Roman Curia itself; and it is proposed that the whole Spirit of Christ resides firmly, and must be believed, in it alone, indeed in the Pope alone. And whatever was once said in honour of the universal Church of Christ is all drawn, by the greatest force and wrong to the Church, to the Roman Curia alone, and many things, of which we have never had any institution from Christ, are brought back to the articles of faith at Rome; and by these the souls of the faithful are miserably deceived, and consequently the blind, together with their leaders, fall headlong into the pit of destruction. Since therefore these men were and are most devoted to the Roman Curia, that is, to the Catholic Church, they were and are also most Catholic, and as many as there were and are among the Catholics, and consequently there is no confusion of different things, nor accusation of heretics, alien to the truth, in saying that an absolute monarchy and dominion is admitted in the Church by those called Catholics.

units.la: XVI. Sed nos Catholici Galli & quidam alii, inquiet Doctissimus Vir, non admittimus. Respondeo 1. Si datur peccatorum alienorum participatio, etiam datur, & multò magis datur, ubi est expressa in religione confoederatio, errorum. Si non admittunt graves hos eósque ex parte execrandos errores, etiam non deberent in communione Ecclesiae, quae illos fovet, & omnibus modis commendat & promovet, manere, deberent contrà ex faストu illo, cui similis non datur, & ex tyrannide illa, eum, qui se effert supra omnia, agnoscere, & obtemperare edicto divino: Exite ex illo, populeemi, ne participetis de peccatis & plagis ejus. 2. Si non admittunt, etiam non accusantur, nam soli admittentes accusantur; Quare & ego certè Doctissimum Virum nunquam accusabo, quòd Monarchiam absolutam & Dominatum respectu Petri aut Pontificis Romani in Ecclesia admiserit; Quia autem caeteri non tantùm numero plures, sed etiam longè acceptiores sunt, eos utique ista, quam ex hac nostra accusatione sibi pollicentur, gloria privare non debemus.
units.tr: XVI. But we Catholics of Gaul, and certain others, will say, the most learned man, do not admit this. I reply: first, if a sharing in other people's sins is allowed, then sharing in errors is also allowed, and far more so where there is an express agreement in religion to hold them. If they do not admit these grave and, in part, execrable errors, then they ought not to remain in the communion of a Church which harbours those errors, fosters them, and commends and promotes them in every way. They ought instead, in view of that pride which has no equal and that tyranny of a man who lifts himself above all things, to acknowledge the divine command: Come out of her, my people, that you have no part in her sins and do not share in her plagues. Second, if they do not admit these errors, they are not accused either, for only those who admit them are accused. So I will certainly never accuse the most learned man of having admitted absolute monarchy and dominion in the Church with respect to Peter or the Roman Pontiff. But since the others are not only more numerous but also far more esteemed, we ought not to deprive them of the glory which they expect from this accusation of ours.

units.la: XVII. Ast distinguimus inter eos, filios dilectos, Benjaminos, & Gallos, filios tolerantiae. Siquidem tolerantia hic est, non potiùs continua inter Patrem & filios, etiam primogenitum, pugna, juxta illud, quod Johannes Major Doctissimo du Pin inter alios etiam laudatus apud Navarrum, super C. novit. not. 3. n. 48. quoad doctrinam de infallibilitate Papae, quam magnam controversi primatus partem esse, ex praemissis intelligitur, ait: Roma nemini permittitur, tenere Parisiensium & Panormitani sententiam: nec rursus Academia Parisiensis patitur, ut contraria opinio asseratur in ea; & juxta illud, quòd, Bellarmino mitissimè ex principiis suis judicante, Gallorum sententia quidem non proprie haeretica (dixisset certè de sententia receptam fidei regulam tollente, si ratio status permisisset) interim tamen & haeresi proxima est, & contrà Gallis, qui plus nonnunquam audent, judicibus, eorum, quos Curia Romana nimis addictos esse censent, sententia, modò nova Jesuitarum haeresis, modò monstrosa Jesuitarum opinio, opinio, modò error non simplex, nec vulgaris hæresis, sed errorum maximorum origo & generalis hæresis, qua totam religionem evertit, modò horrenda impietas & idololatria species est; Ut etiam Doctissimus du Pin in citatis ex præfatione, dedicatione, & tractatione verbis, quamvis aliquantò mitius, non tamen sine duris & diris verbis, facta etiam execrandi dogmatis mentione, de sententia opposita locutus est, & à parte & altera scripta prohibentur, condemnantur, imò etiam comburuntur, authores censuris notantur, à Papa, qui ei præ cæteris infensiores sunt, ex societatibus religiosis, imò, latâ excommunicationis sententiâ, ex Ecclesia tota ejiciuntur.
units.tr: XVII. But we distinguish between those who are beloved sons, Benjamins, and the Gauls, who are sons of toleration. For here toleration means not a continual fight between the Father and the sons, even the firstborn, in line with what John Major, praised among others by the most learned du Pin, says in Navarrus, on C. novit., note 3, n. 48, concerning the doctrine of papal infallibility, which, as is clear from what has been said, is a large part of the controversy over primacy: Rome permits no one to hold the opinion of the Parisians and Panormitanus, nor again does the Paris Academy allow the contrary opinion to be asserted in it. It also means what Bellarmine, judging very gently from his own principles, said: the opinion of the Gauls is not properly heretical (he would certainly have said that of an opinion which removed the accepted rule of faith, if the reasons of state had allowed it), yet nonetheless it is close to heresy. On the other hand, the Gauls, who sometimes dare more, judge the opinion of those whom the Roman Curia thinks too devoted to be now a new heresy of the Jesuits, now a monstrous opinion of the Jesuits, now not a simple error nor a common heresy, but the origin of the greatest errors and a general heresy which overturns the whole religion, now a horrible impiety and a kind of idolatry. So too the most learned du Pin, in the words he cites from the preface, dedication and treatment, though somewhat more mildly, yet not without harsh and dire words, and even with mention of an execrable dogma, spoke of the opposing opinion. On both sides writings are forbidden and condemned, and indeed burned; authors are marked with censures by the Pope, who are more hostile to them than to others; they are expelled from religious orders, and indeed, by a sentence of excommunication pronounced, from the whole Church.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Sed lubeat, quid Romanæ Curiæ addictiores de Gallis his sentiant, famosi Maimburgii exemplo (cujus tractatum de prærogativa Ecclesiæ Romanæ, & Scripta alia Doctissimus du Pin æquè ac multorum aliorum Gallorum similes multos libros, si voluisseт ad quosvis descendere, facilè etiam allegare potuisseт) cognoscere. P. Cœlestinus Sfondrati, Gallia vindicata author, in præfatione ita de eo, vel contra eum loquitur; Nemo veritatem pulchrioribus verbis ac singulisferè paginis professus est, nemo turpioribus factis foedavit; meruit Innocentii XI. approbationem, cui librum de schismate Graecorum (nimirum in his facile est placere) dedicavit; sed hanc laudem corrupit posterioribus libris: in his enim ex industria, quæsitisque minimè necessariis digressionibus, totus est in deflorandā Pontificum authoritate, eáque aut Regibus, aut Episcopis submittenda. Incertum, quid causa fuerit, qua tot titulis Pontifici Romano adstrictum in Vaticanum armavit. An genius Societatis (Jesu scil.) fortunam ac potentiam Gallicam amplexa, sed Pontifici offensa, à quo tot Theologia sua moralis capita, nec sine gemitu pariqué æmulorum gaudio configi viderat, an denique, quòd libros Roma majori encomio, quàm præmio exceperat. Ejus scriptionis commune votum & fama damnavit; nec enim debuit intempestivis ac minimè necessariis quæstionibus (Ast agitur de summa rei Christianæ!) pax inter Ecclesiam regnumque turbari, ac haereticis ridendi (Claudius Hermianus, Cappadociæ sub Severo Imperatore Præses & Christianorum persecutor, à vermibus corrosus, occultans judicium Dei; Nemo sciat, ajebat, ne gaudeant Christiani!) seque obstinandi occasio præberi, quam ex domesticis jurgiis captârunt, Pontificios, qui unitatem tantopere jactant, de rebus maximi momenti maximo cum Zelo invicem tanquam Cadmæos fratres pugnare videntes.
units.tr: But let us learn what those more devoted to the Roman Curia think of these Gauls, from the example of the notorious Maimbourg. (Du Pin, like many other Frenchmen, could easily have cited his treatise on the prerogative of the Roman Church and his other writings, and many similar books, had he wished to go through them all.) Father Celestine Sfondrati, author of Gallia vindicata, speaks of him, or rather against him, thus in the preface: No one has professed the truth in finer words, or on almost every page; no one has defiled it with more shameful deeds. He earned the approval of Innocent XI, to whom he dedicated his book on the schism of the Greeks (in such matters it is easy to please). But he spoiled that praise by his later books. In these, deliberately and with digressions that were in no way necessary, he is entirely bent on undermining the authority of the Roman Pontiff and subjecting it to kings or bishops. It is uncertain what caused him, bound to the Roman Pontiff by so many titles, to take up arms against the Vatican. Was it the genius of the Society (of Jesus, namely), which embraced French fortune and power but offended the Pontiff, from whom it had seen so many heads of its moral theology attacked, not without groans and the joy of its rivals? Or finally, because Rome had received his books with more praise than reward? The common wish and reputation condemned that writing. For peace between the Church and the kingdom ought not to be disturbed by untimely and wholly unnecessary questions (but the matter at issue is the sum of the Christian religion!), and an occasion for the heretics to mock (Claudius Hermianus, governor of Cappadocia under the emperor Severus and a persecutor of Christians, eaten by worms and concealing God's judgment, used to say: Let no one know, lest the Christians rejoice!) and to harden themselves should not be given, which they have seized from domestic quarrels, seeing the Papists, who boast so much of unity, fighting with the greatest zeal over matters of the greatest moment, like the Cadmean brothers.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Vetuit Roma aliquot libros, qui maximè veritatem offenderunt,
units.tr: Rome forbade several books that most of all offended the truth,

units.la: {a} Quàm exosa Gallorum doctrina Romanæ sit, exemplo Maimburgii ostenditur;
units.tr: {a} How hateful the French doctrine is to Rome is shown by the example of Maimbourg.

units.la: Porrò; derunt, id est, Papæ pupillam incautiùs & duriùs attrectârunt;sed eo tantò magis calamum urgente, oblitóque, quid & ipse & Societas tota Romæ & Religioni debèrent; meruit excludi; hæsit tamen adhuc annum in Societate, protegente Rege, tandem excessit, sed irato & minanti similis, & ferè qualis Hannibal ex Italia. Sic enim in præfatione Historiæ Calvinismi: Ainsi n' étant plus Jesuite par l'ordre de N. S.P. & par la permission, que le Roy a donnée de l'executer; je seray de la grace de S. M. tout ce qui luy plaira, pour la servir avec plus d' ardeur & de Zele, & de liberté, que jamais; præstitit. Si nimirum servire Regi est, bellum Ecclesiæ & veritati inferre, fama est, eum 20000. libras reliquisse. Vixit quatuor ab egressu annos, tantillum temporis fluxit fruendi Principis gratiâ, quam tantis laboribus, tantaque omnium offensione, ac forsan æternâ luit pœnitentiâ; (Tantæne cœlestibus animis iræ!) Sed (nisi præponderent ejus in debellandis hæreticis merita:) requiem, quam vivus non habuit, defuncto precor: (Sit divus, modò non sit vivus.) XX. Scripsit infesto æque Catholicis ac Calvinistis, quos vocant, calamo, mediam viam eligendo (quam Doctissimus du Pin tanquam tutissimam circa eadem adeò depræRicat in Diss. de Primatu prælo-quio) effecit, ut (quod neutralistarum fatum est) odia ab utrisque mereretur. Constat enim, eum non veritati, sed Regi scribere, si enim hujus gratiâ Pontificem, quantò magis Calvinum persequeretur? (En Galliæ vindicem, etiam Calvini vindicem! Convenit illud, Romano quodam Pontifice à Romanis veneno sublato, Imperatoris dictum: Ecce non ferunt Romanum, quomodo ferent Germanum?) Nec Religionis causa societatem ac transactiones admittit; impudica est, qua thalamum dividit; una uni, aut tota, aut nulla; Meretricis sunt illa voces, nec mihi, nec tibi, sed dividatur &c. Malè ergo Religioni consuluit, qui illam obtentu pacis (cujus studium Galli præ se ferunt) inter Petrum Calvinumque; (id est, inter Papam & Christi veritatem, cui restituendæ Calvinus unà cum aliis fideliter inserviit, divisit,) nec composuit bellum, sed auxit (dum nimirum nec alii conciliationes ejus admittere potuerunt nondum sufficientes, & ab altera parte grave bellum exortum est;) ferri poterat, si modò bona fide &c. Argumenta eadem cum Calvinianis adhibuit (& merito quidem in causa eadem contra eandem;) Legantur, qua Illyricus de translatione Imperii scripsit, nihil noster novi, præter idioma (nempe sufficiebant illa.) XXI. Non puduit etiam exempla ab hæreticis petere, (ô rem pudenpudendam!) & illa summis laudibus extollere, & Pontifices admonere, ut Lutherum imitentur, religionem Principum voluntati subservientem, (non illud quidem, sed Deo quae Dei, Caesari, quae Caesaris sunt, attribuentem, Christianos Principes à jugo servitutis Pontificiae, quod eorum solla diu graviter presserat, liberos merito pronunciantem, Nutritios Ecclesiae & utriusque Tabulae Custodes non plane à cura Religionis arcentem:) Infinitus sim, si omnia persequar, quae Maimburgium mala fidei accusant, nec ignorantiâ tantùm, sed industriâ peccâsse; forsitan si vita superfuisset, emendâsset (ut piè creditur;) quae odio aut amore peccaverat: nec dubito, nunc ea improbare, quando his affectibus vacuus, ac rerum vanitatem expertus dolet, respuítque forsan praeterita; postquam ei mors alios (libros, quibus priora emendare sc. volebat) paranti, scribendi juxta vivendíque finem indixit, & calamum jam intinctum excussit; Hactenus ille.
units.tr: Further, derunt, that is, they handled the Pope's pupil too carelessly and harshly; but the more urgently and forgetfully he pressed his pen, forgetting what he himself and the whole Society owed to Rome and to Religion, he deserved to be excluded. Yet he still lingered a year in the Society, protected by the King, and at last left it, but like one angry and threatening, and almost like Hannibal leaving Italy. For thus in the preface to the History of Calvinism: "So, no longer being a Jesuit by the order of our Most Holy Father and by the permission which the King has given me to carry it out, I shall be, by the grace of His Majesty, whatever pleases him, to serve him with more ardour, zeal and freedom than ever"; he did this. If indeed to serve the King means to wage war on the Church and on truth, it is said he left 20,000 pounds. He lived four years after leaving; a little time passed in enjoying the Prince's favour, which he paid for with such great labours and such great offence to everyone, and perhaps with eternal penance; (Can such anger exist in heavenly minds!) But (unless his merits in crushing heretics outweigh it) I pray that the rest he did not have while alive be his now that he is dead: (Let him be divine, provided he is not alive.) XX. He wrote with a pen hostile alike to Catholics and to those whom they call Calvinists, choosing a middle way (which the most learned du Pin, in his preface to the Dissertation on the Primacy, commends as the safest on these very matters), he brought it about that (as is the fate of neutralists) he earned hatred from both sides. For it is clear he wrote not for the truth but for the King. For if for the King's sake he pursued the Pope, how much more would he pursue Calvin? (Behold the defender of France, even the defender of Calvin! That saying of an emperor fits here, spoken when a certain Roman Pontiff had been removed by Roman poison: Behold, they do not bear a Roman; how will they bear a German?) Nor does he admit fellowship and compromises for the sake of religion; it is shameless, that which divides the marriage bed: one to one, or all, or none. Those are the words of a harlot: "neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided," etc. He therefore did ill by religion, who under the pretext of peace (the pursuit of which the French put forward) divided (that is, between Peter and Calvin, between the Pope and the truth of Christ, for the restoration of which Calvin faithfully served together with others) and did not settle the war but increased it (since, of course, neither side could accept his conciliations, which were not yet sufficient, and a grave war broke out on the other side); it could have been borne, if only in good faith, etc. He used the same arguments as the Calvinists (and rightly so, in the same cause against the same opponent); let those be read which Illyricus wrote about the transfer of the empire; our author has nothing new, except the idiom (namely, those arguments were sufficient). XXI. He was not ashamed also to take examples from heretics (O shameful thing!) and to extol them with the highest praise, and to admonish the Pontiffs to imitate Luther, who made religion subservient to the will of princes (not indeed that, but ascribing to God what is God's and to Caesar what is Caesar's, rightly declaring Christian princes free from the yoke of Papal servitude, which had long pressed heavily upon them, and not wholly excluding from the care of religion those nurses of the Church and guardians of both Tables:) I would be endless if I pursued all the charges by which Maimbourg is accused of bad faith, and of having sinned not merely through ignorance but through design. Perhaps, had his life continued, he would have amended (as is piously believed) whatever he had sinned through hatred or love. Nor do I doubt that he now disapproves of them, since, free from these passions and having learned the vanity of things, he grieves and perhaps rejects his past; after death, which cut off his preparing other books, by which he wished to correct his earlier ones, put an end to his writing and to his living, and shook out the pen already dipped in ink; So far he.

units.la: XXII. Judicet jam aequus Lector, quando tantopere multis Romani Pontificis Monarchia absoluta & dominatus curae est, ut erga secum sentientes tam rigidi sint, utrum à veritate alienum sit, quod dicimus, non quidem Catholicos, (quomodo enim dogma tale Catholicum esse posset?) sed Pontificios Monarchiam, dominatum admittere; judicet simul ex dictis, utrum bene admittant, utrum bene, vel Petro, talem Monarchiam, talem dominatum tribuant, eum ad talem Monarchiam, & dominatum electum esse dicant, &c. Itaque quid sibi usurpat Romana Ecclesia propter Petrum, quod à Petro remotissimum fuit? merito cum Illustri de Dominis de Rep. Christ. lib. IV. cap. I. §. 1, quaerimus.
units.tr: XXII. Let the fair reader now judge, since so many people are so keen on the absolute monarchy and domination of the Roman Pontiff that they are so harsh toward those who think otherwise, whether what we say is alien to the truth: that the Papists, though not Catholics (for how could such a dogma be Catholic?), admit a monarchy and domination. Let him judge from what has been said whether they admit it rightly, and whether they rightly attribute such a monarchy and such domination to Peter, saying that he was chosen for such a monarchy and domination, etc. What, then, does the Roman Church claim for itself on account of Peter, which was most remote from Peter? we rightly ask, with the illustrious de Dominis, De Republica Christiana, book IV, chapter I, §1,

units.la: Concluditur exinde de dissensu, atque ex omnibus: Petrum non ad talem Pontificatum electum esse.
units.tr: It follows from this, from the disagreement and from all of it, that Peter was not chosen for such a Pontificate.

units.la: DISSERTATIO SECUNDA, In qua, Petrum ad talem Pontificatum Romanum minimè electum esse, cùm, an unquam Romam venerit, valdè incertum, quòd ibi per viginti quinque annos Episcopus fuerit, manifestè falsum sit, porrò ostenditur.
units.tr: SECOND DISSERTATION, in which it is further shown that Peter was by no means elected to such a Roman Pontificate, since whether he ever came to Rome is very uncertain, and it is plainly false that he was bishop there for twenty-five years.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Petrus potestatem, quam nunquam accepit, nusquam exercere, neque certùm Successoribus relinquere potuit; Instituitur tamen disquisitio etiam de loco, ad cujus Episcopatum electus dicitur; II. Posito, Petrum non tantùm Romæ fuisse, sed & peculiarem Ecclesiæ illius urbis curam, ex quo cœperit, constanter habuisse, nondum tamen satis ponitur ad victoriam Monarchicorum;
units.tr: I. Peter could never exercise anywhere the power he never received, nor could he certainly leave it to successors. Still, an inquiry is made into the place whose bishopric he is said to have been elected to. II. Granted that Peter was not only at Rome but also constantly held a special care of that city's church from the time he began, it is still not sufficiently established for the victory of the Monarchists;

units.la: III. Petrum Romæ fuisse, ex Scriptura probari deberet; conantur; IV. Preferunt primò 1.Pet.V.13 ex quo loco argumentatur Bellarminus; V. Respondetur, atque primò accipitur, quod dat Bellarminus, Romam esse Babylonem in Apocalypsi; pro quo etiam Patres, atque Pontificii Authores alii adducuntur; VI. Exceptioni Bellarmini, ad nostram explicationem, Romam in statu præsenti ibi designari, dicentis, Gentilem, qualis Iohannis tempore fuerit, denotari; (cui in transitu aliorum de Roma Gentili, qualis sub finem mundi futura sit, explicatio opponitur;) VII. Occurritur, atque ostenditur, Romam Pseudo-Christianam in Apocalypsi per Babylonem significari.
units.tr: III. That Peter was at Rome ought to be proved from Scripture; they try. IV. They first bring forward 1 Pet. 5:13, from which passage Bellarmine argues. V. It is answered, and first we accept what Bellarmine grants, that Rome is Babylon in the Apocalypse; for this the Fathers and other Papist authors are also cited. VI. Against Bellarmine's objection to our explanation, that Rome is there designated in its present state, and his claim that a Gentile Rome, such as it was in John's time, is meant (to which, in passing, an explanation of the Gentile Rome as it will be at the end of the world is opposed); VII. It is met, and it is shown that Rome as a pseudo-Christian city is signified in the Apocalypse by Babylon.

units.la: VIII. Sed secundò ostenditur etiam, in citato Petri loco Romam non per Babylonem designari; Obstante primò stylo Petri simplici, familiari, epistolari, narratorio; IX. Secundò repugnat causa, ob quam in epistolis nonnunquam loci, ubi scripta sunt, mentio fit. X. Minimè autem Petrus sedem suam ita dissimulare debuisset. Tertiò repugnat exemplum Pauli in epistolis;
units.tr: VIII. But, secondly, it is also shown that in the cited passage of Peter, Rome is not designated by Babylon. First, Peter's style stands in the way: it is plain, familiar, epistolary and narrative. IX. Secondly, the reason for which letters sometimes mention the place where they were written is inconsistent with this. X. Yet Peter ought not to have concealed his see in this way. Thirdly, the example of Paul's letters is inconsistent with it;

units.la: XI. Neque, ut Baronius vult, non usus est proprio Urbis nomine, quia è carcere Hierosol. elapsus, ubi ageret, non ab omnibus percipi voluerit; XII. Neque etiam juvat dicere cum eodem, mutatis nominibus homines sæpe appellari; XIII. Quartò ut allegorica æquè fingi possent omnia in epistola, ita nulla etiam necessitas cogit, ut de impropria Babylone hic cogitemus. Gemina Babylon tum inclyta commodè intelligi potuit, judice etiam Doctissimo de Marca. XIV. Argumentum Baronii & Valesii contra Ægyptiacam refellitur; XV. Contra Chaldaicam; XVI. Contra utramque, non posse ostendi Successionem ibi Petro succedentium. Clauditur testimonio Doct. de Marca pro Chaldaica, & Grotii aliter sentientis, de reditu tamen in partes Babyloniæ loquentis, & conjecturâ Illustris Salmasii, commorationem in Babylonia causam incertitudinis quoad ultima Petri faciendis; XVII. Secundò examinantur loci ex Act. ult. & ex epist. ad Rom. à Bellarmino porrò citati; XVIII. Responsionibus Bellarmini ad prædicatiodicationem ante Petrum ab aliis Romæ, Patribus quibusdam judicibus & Suetonio indice, factam; adeóque Bellarminiana ex locis istis conclusioni contrariam; XIX. Occurritur; respectu narrationis Suetonianæ XX. Testimonii ex Tertulliano; XXI. Orosio; XXII. Libris Recognitionum Clementis, & Dorotheo; XXIII. Argumentatio instituitur contra iter Petri Romanum & commorationem in urbe, saltem ad demonstrandam summam ejus incertitudinem; atque primò ex ipso S. Scriptura silentio;
units.tr: XI. Nor is it true, as Baronius holds, that he did not use the proper name of the city because, having escaped from the prison at Jerusalem, he did not want it perceived by everyone where he was acting. XII. Nor does it help to say, with the same author, that men are often called by changed names. XIII. Fourthly, although everything in the letter could be fabricated as allegorical, there is also no necessity forcing us to think here of the improper Babylon. A twin Babylon, then famous, could conveniently be understood here, as the most learned de Marca also judges. XIV. The argument of Baronius and Valesius against the Egyptian Babylon is refuted; XV. against the Chaldean; XVI. against both, that a succession of those succeeding Peter there cannot be shown. The section closes with the testimony of the learned de Marca for the Chaldean view, and of Grotius, who thinks otherwise yet speaks of a return to the parts of Babylon, and with the conjecture of the illustrious Salmasius that the sojourn in Babylonia was the cause of the uncertainty concerning Peter's last days; XVII. Secondly, the passages from Acts 28 and from the Epistle to the Romans, further cited by Bellarmine, are examined; XVIII. Bellarmine's replies to the claim that the preaching of the gospel at Rome had been done before Peter by others, by certain Fathers as judges and by Suetonius as witness, and so the Bellarmine passages are contrary to the conclusion; XIX. It is met, with respect to Suetonius's narrative; XX. the testimony from Tertullian; XXI. from Orosius; XXII. from the Recognitions of Clement, and Dorotheus; XXIII. An argument is set up against Peter's journey to Rome and his sojourn in the city, at least to demonstrate its great uncertainty; and first from the silence of Holy Scripture itself;

units.la: XXIV. Respondetur exceptioni Bellarminianæ, atque infertur jam, non esse de fide iter illud, commorationem illam, & quæ ex ea sequi dicunt; XXV. Argumento à Scriptura silentio robur accedit, quòd testimoniorum defectus est, ubi testimonia adesse debere, videtur; Idque primò ob rei dignitatem, ex hypothesi; XXVI. In veritate; XXVII. Secundò ob occasionum varietatem, quas habuisset Lucas; XXVIII. Paulus; XXIX. Ipse Petrus; XXX. Secundò argumentatio instituitur ex iis, quæ in Scripturis S. contra istam Petri in urbe præsentiam habentur. Et primò quidem ex serie rerum gestarum; XXXI. Secundò ex peculiari Petri circa Judaos cura, & Epistola ad Galatas; XXXII. Ex Epistolis ad Philippenses, Colossenses, atque ad Timotheum posteriori; XXXIII. Tertiò argumentatio instituitur ex silentio Authorum profanorum, Taciti, Suetonii, Dionis;
units.tr: XXIV. Bellarmine's objection is answered, and it is inferred now that that journey, that sojourn, and what they say follows from it, are not matters of faith. XXV. The argument from Scripture's silence gains strength because testimonies are lacking where they ought to be present. This is seen first from the dignity of the matter, on the hypothesis; XXVI. in truth; XXVII. secondly from the variety of occasions Luke would have had; XXVIII. Paul; XXIX. Peter himself. XXX. Secondly, an argument is set up from what is found in Holy Scripture against Peter's presence in the city. And first, from the sequence of events recorded; XXXI. secondly, from Peter's particular care for the Jews, and the Epistle to the Galatians; XXXII. from the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians, and the later one to Timothy; XXXIII. thirdly, an argument is set up from the silence of profane authors: Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio.

units.la: XXXIV. Patrum ferè omnium consensus aliter sentientibus largiendus; Quem tamen plura hic minus validum pronuntiant; XXXV. Et qui non semper justicit, ipsis etiam Pontificiis; XXXVI. Contra quos mutatin relationibus de itinere & commoratione Petri Romana faciunt; XXXVII. Nos autem porrò ab assensu cohibet multiplex Authorum in istis relationibus discordia; Occurritur exceptioni Bellarminianæ; XXXVIII. Authorum pugna & contradictiones recensentur; XXXIX. In specie quoad mortem Petri;
units.tr: XXXIV. The near-unanimous consensus of the Fathers must be granted to those who think otherwise; yet many here pronounce it of less weight. XXXV. And it is not always just, even by the Papists themselves. XXXVI. Against them, the Papists make changes in the accounts of Peter's journey and sojourn at Rome. XXXVII. But the manifold disagreement of authors in these accounts also restrains us from assent. The Bellarmine objection is met. XXXVIII. The conflicts and contradictions of the authors are recounted; XXXIX. especially concerning Peter's death.

units.la: XL. Posito, Petrum Romæ fuisse, exinde nihil lucrantur Pontificii; nil ex præsentia;
units.tr: XL. Granted that Peter was at Rome, the Papists gain nothing from this; nothing from his presence.

units.la: XLI. Nec plus ex morte, quam ibi obierit; XLII. De Episcopatu igitur videndum; Quomodo dici possint Apostoli Episcopi; XLIII. Non fuerunt Episcopi certorum locorum proprii; XLIV. Applicantur ista ad Petrum, atque ex Irenæo & Ruffino ostenditur, ipsis judicibus, partes Petri in urbe non fuisse Episcopales; XLV. Contra Episcopatum Petri Romanum porrò argumentum nectitur, ex eo, quòd omni rationis & Scripturarum fundamento destituitur. Respondetur ad rationes Bellarminianas, primam, quòd non ostendere possimus, alibi sedisse; XLVI. Alteram, quòd negantes Petrum fuisse Episcopum universalem, concedere debeamus, fuisse particularem;
units.tr: XLI. Nor anything more from his death, than that he died there. XLII. So we must consider the episcopate: how the Apostles can be called bishops. XLIII. They were not bishops of particular places, each proper to them. XLIV. These points are applied to Peter, and from Irenaeus and Rufinus it is shown, by their own judgment, that Peter's role in the city was not episcopal. XLV. Further, an argument is built against the Roman episcopate of Peter, from the fact that it lacks every foundation of reason and Scripture. The reasons of Bellarmine are answered: the first, that we cannot show he had his see elsewhere; XLVI. the second, that those who deny Peter was a universal bishop must concede that he was a particular one.

units.la: XLVII. Urgetur Scripturarum silentium, atque ex Bellarmino illustratur;
units.tr: XLVII. The silence of the Scriptures is pressed, and illustrated from Bellarmine.

units.la: XLVIII. Insuper minus convenit Petri Episcopatus cum quibusdam, quas Monarchici adoptant, antiquorum narrationibus; XLIX. Præterea sic magnâ Petrum contumelia afficiunt, primò Doctorem orbis Episcopum urbis facientes; L. Secundò ei, quòd à patribus solenniter initis iurpiter resilierit, tribuentes; LI. Tertiò pessimorum in Ecclesia, quoad Ecclesiasticas dignitates, abusuum eum primum Authorem facientes, nempe α. translationis ab uno Episcopatu ad alium; LII. Vel β. pluralitatis beneficiorum; cujus nævus detegitur; LIII. Applicatio fit ad Petrum; LIV. γ. Non-Residentia; LV. Quartò ei dimidium saltem Episcopatum tribuentes;
units.tr: XLVIII. Moreover, Peter's episcopate agrees poorly with certain accounts of the ancients which the Monarchists adopt. XLIX. Besides, they do great dishonour to Peter: first, by making the teacher of the world a bishop of a city; L. secondly, by attributing to him that he shamefully withdrew from the agreements solemnly made with the fathers; LI. thirdly, by making him the first author of the worst abuses in the Church concerning ecclesiastical dignities, namely α. the transfer from one bishopric to another; LII. or β. the plurality of benefices, whose blemish is exposed; LIII. the application is made to Peter; LIV. γ. non-residence; LV. fourthly, by attributing to him at least half of an episcopate.

units.la: LVI. Concluditur tractatio de Electione Petri.
units.tr: LVI. The treatment of Peter's election is concluded.

units.la: I. POstquam satis prolixè in Dissertatione prima de prima Electionis Petri parte, sive de eo; Num potestatem Summi Pontificis & Monarchae Ecclesiae acceperit? actum est; sequitur jam ut videamus; Num potestas illa ad eum, quem ostendunt, locum determinata, an nimirum B. Apostolus non modò talis Pontifex, sed & talis Pontifex Romanus constitutus fuerit? Omittere quidem possemus hanc & sequentes disquisitiones alias, ob demonstrationes praecedentes; Quando enim Petrum potestatem talem non accepisse, abundè jam probatum dedimus, quando ita primum catenae, cujus possessionem jactant, annulum, qui eam Christo & Divinae ejus institutioni jungere deberet, deesse, multis ostendimus, de caeteris securi esse possemus, cùm potestatem Petrus, quam accepit & habuit nunquam; certo loco alligare, vel in certo loco exercere, aut certis Successoribus relinquere haud potuerit; Nisi locum, de quo jam dispiciendum, ei potestatem, quam Christus non contulit, contulisse, fingere quis velit, quod tamen Monarchici ipsi rejicere videntur, contendentes magno cum studio, locum à Pontifice hoc sanctificatum esse, ab illo tantae Majestatis splendorem accepisse, Romam, ubi Petrus primò fuerit, secundò mortuus sit, tertiò Episcopum egerit, quartò ad vitae suae finem.
units.tr: I. Since the first part of Peter's election, that is, whether he received the power of supreme Pontiff and Monarch of the Church, has been treated at sufficient length in the first Dissertation, we now proceed to see whether that power was determined to the place they point to; that is, whether the blessed Apostle was constituted not only such a Pontiff but such a Roman Pontiff. We could indeed omit this and the following inquiries, given the preceding demonstrations. For we have already given ample proof that Peter did not receive such power, and we have shown to many that the ring which should have joined the chain they boast of to Christ and his divine institution is missing; so we could be secure about the rest, since Peter could never bind that power, which he received and held, to a certain place, nor exercise it in a certain place, nor leave it to certain successors. Unless someone should wish to imagine that he gave that power, which Christ did not confer, to the place now to be examined. The Monarchists themselves seem to reject this, contending with great zeal that the place was sanctified by this Pontiff, and received from him the splendour of such majesty: Rome, where Peter first was, secondly died, thirdly acted as bishop, fourthly until the end of his life.

units.la: II. Quatuor ista constanter tenent & defendunt acerrimè, ut etiam valdè irascantur, aut unum, aut plura horum, aut omnia in dubium vocantibus; quod tamen mirum videri non potest attendentibus, quantum Monarchicis in unoquoque horum situm sit, & quòd deficientibus istis, Monarchiae Pontificum Romanorum fundamenta deficiant, non equidem sufficientia sola, quod, quae praecessit, Dissertatio docet, interim tamen planè necessaria; Pugnatur igitur ab illorum parte pro aris, quod ajunt; & focis, imò pro fundamentis ararum & focorum, nobis interim in tuto navigantibus, & minori longè cum discrimine, imò sine ullo discrimine nostro veritatem hic propugnantibus, cùm, posito etiam, Petrum non tantùm Romae fuisse, sed & peculiarem Ecclesiae illius urbis curam, ex quo coeperit, constanter egisse, nondum tamen ipse talis Pontifex & Monarcha dicatur, quod ex dictis patet; & multò minùs potestas Monarchica aliis vi successionis tribui debeat, quod deinceps ostendendum erit.
units.tr: II. These four things they hold and defend constantly and most fiercely, so much so that they grow very angry at those who call one or more or all of them into doubt. This cannot seem surprising to those who consider how much of the Monarchists' cause rests on each of them, and that if these fail, the foundations of the Monarchy of the Roman Pontiffs fail too. Not indeed that they are sufficient by themselves, as the preceding Dissertation teaches, though they are plainly necessary. So on their side the fight is for altars, as they say, and hearths, indeed for the foundations of altars and hearths. Meanwhile we sail in safety, and with far less danger, indeed with no danger to ourselves, in defending the truth here. For even granting that Peter not only was at Rome but also constantly exercised a special care of that city's church from the time he began, he is still not called such a Pontiff and Monarch, as is plain from what has been said. And much less should monarchical power be attributed to others by right of succession, which will have to be shown later.

units.la: III. Quomodo autem primò primum probant, nempe Petrum Romae fuisse? An ex Scriptura? Necessarium illud esse proba-tiobationis genus Differt. Sect. I. n. 6. ostendimus; Et quando, Petrum ad talem Pontificatum electum esse, & Petri ipsius & Successorum, quos vocant, respectu ex Scriptura constare debet, eum ad Pontificatum talem Romanum electum esse, & proin Romae etiam fuisse, ob Successores maximè ex eadem ostendi deberet, cum loca, quibus Petrum, aliorum quorundam ad instar, Episcopum quidem Romanum, sed extra necessitatem Romam videndi, fuisse probent, ostendere nec velint, nec possint, & ex praesentia jam de caeteris praesumant: Conantur igitur etiam ex Scriptura probare, Petrum Romae fuisse. Videamus conatum eorum, & post etiam, quid ex Scriptura contra iter Petri Romanum & ejus in urbe per tot annos commorationem maximè faciat.
units.tr: III. But how do they first prove the first point, namely that Peter was at Rome? From Scripture? We showed in Differt. Sect. I. n. 6. that this is the kind of proof that is required. If it is to be established from Scripture that Peter was elected to such a Roman pontificate, and that this holds of Peter himself and of his so-called successors, then it ought to be shown chiefly from the same source that he was elected to such a Roman pontificate and therefore was also at Rome. The passages which prove that Peter was a Roman bishop, like some others, but without any need to have seen Rome, neither will nor can show this, and they simply assume from the presence of the others the rest. So they try to prove from Scripture that Peter was at Rome. Let us look at their attempt, and then also at what Scripture chiefly says against Peter's journey to Rome and his long residence in the city over so many years.

units.la: IV. Proferunt primò (non enim libet denuò attingere nugas mysticas ex Luc. V. 4. quas Differt. I. Sect. III. n. 1. attigimus) locum ex 1.Pet.V.13. Salutat vos, quae in Babylone est, simul electa, & Marcus Filius meus; & contendunt, per Babylonem Romam intelligi debere, proin Petrum Romae fuisse, utpote qui inde Epistolam scripserit. Fundamentum autem hujus, quòd per Babylonem Roma intelligi debeat, in Apocalypsi ex parte quaerunt. Johannes in Apoc. inquit Bellarminus, de Rom. Pont. l.2.c.2. passim Romam vocat Babylonem, ut Tertullianus annotavit l.3. contra Marcionem & lib. contra Judaeos, & aperte colligitur ex cap.17. Apocalypsis, ubi dicitur Babylon magna sedere supra septem montes & habere imperium super Reges terrae. Nec enim alia civitas est, quae Johannis tempore imperium habuerit super Reges terrae, quàm Roma, & notissimum est, supra septem colles Romam aedificatam esse. Nempe ita avidè avent homines hi, Petrum Romae alicubi in Scripturis reperire, potiùs ut Babylonem, ubi Petrus fuit, velint esse Romam, quàm ut Petrus Romae non fuerit.
units.tr: IV. First they bring forward (for I do not wish to touch again the mystical trifles drawn from Luke 5:4, which we touched on in Differt. I. Sect. III. n. 1.) the passage from 1 Peter 5:13, She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, salutes you, and Mark my son. They contend that by Babylon Rome must be understood, and so Peter was at Rome, since he wrote the epistle from there. The basis for taking Babylon to mean Rome they seek partly in the Apocalypse. John in the Apocalypse, says Bellarmine, in De Romano Pontifice, book 2, chapter 2, everywhere calls Rome Babylon, as Tertullian noted in book 3 against Marcion and in the book against the Jews, and it is plainly gathered from chapter 17 of the Apocalypse, where it is said that great Babylon sits upon seven mountains and has dominion over the kings of the earth. For there is no other city which in John's time had dominion over the kings of the earth except Rome, and it is well known that Rome was built upon seven hills. Thus these men are so eagerly desirous of finding Peter somewhere in Scripture at Rome that they would rather make Rome the Babylon where Peter was, than admit that Peter was not at Rome.

units.la: V. Nos autem, quod sic dant, accipimus haud illibenter. Clamamus passim, quod nobis Bellarminus tribuit, Romam esse Babylonem de Apocalypsi, & Lutherum de captivitate Babylonica recte librum inscripsisse arbitramur, & cum Centuriatoribus Apocalypsin ea de causa, quamvis etiam de aliis, recipimus in numerum librorum Divinorum; quòd in eo libro multa adversus Romam, sub nomine Babylonis praedicantur partim jam impleta, partim adhuc implenda. Clamamus, repeto, passim, Romam esse Babylonem de Apocalypsi; Clamamus proin etiam Dei nomine: Exite ex ea, populE mi, ut ne participes sitis delictorum ejus, & de plagis plagis ejus non accipiatis; & dum ita clamamus, vehementer quoque optamus, ut clamori nostro attenderent inf-lices hujus Babylo-nis Amasii. Et quid miri est, nos ita clamare, cum, vel tacentibus nobis, multi clamarent alii, ex veteribus quidem Tertullianus, quem Bellarminus citat, Hieronymus, Augustinus &c, quos ὁμοψήφους allegat Ribera Jesuita, Eusebius, Orosius, Oecumenius, Beda, Victorinus, alii; Ex Pontificiis autem Doctoribus plurimi, Cornelius à Lapide &c, quos ille consentientes inducit, præter Malachiam quendam, Bernhardi συγχέχυον, Viega, Ribera jam nominatus, qui Aretam, Forerium, alios, hanc expositionem, relictâ eâ, quàm priùs defenderant, complexos esse, testis est; Lindanus, Alcasar, qui eandem expositionem in rubricis M SC. antiqui codicis in Bibliotheca S. Laurentii haberi, addit Apringius, Gugnejus, Hes-selius, Thomas, Rizius; imò ipse Bellarminus, qui hanc expositionem ex Apoc. XVII. jamjam urget, aperte colligi posse, & necessariam esse judicavit, argumentis firmavit.
units.tr: V. We, however, take what they give us not unwillingly. We cry out everywhere that Bellarmine is right to attribute to us the view that Rome is Babylon in the Apocalypse, and we think Luther rightly inscribed his book On the Babylonish Captivity; and with the Centuriators we receive the Apocalypse among the books of the divine canon, for this reason among others, that in that book many things against Rome under the name of Babylon are foretold, some already fulfilled, some yet to be fulfilled. We cry out, I repeat, everywhere, that Rome is Babylon in the Apocalypse. We therefore also cry out in God's name: Come out of her, my people, that you be not partakers of her sins, and that you receive not of her plagues. And while we so cry out, we also earnestly desire that these unhappy lovers of this Babylon would heed our cry. And what wonder is it that we so cry out, when, even if we were silent, many others would cry out: among the ancients Tertullian, whom Bellarmine cites, Jerome, Augustine and others, whom the Jesuit Ribera cites as of the same vote, Eusebius, Orosius, Oecumenius, Bede, Victorinus, and others; and among the Papist teachers very many, Cornelius a Lapide and others whom Bellarmine brings in as agreeing, besides a certain Malachias, Bernard's συγχέχυον, Viega, and the Ribera already named, who is witness that Arethas, Forerius and others, abandoning the exposition they had earlier defended, embraced this one; Lindanus and Alcasar; Apringius adds that this exposition is found in the rubrics of an ancient manuscript codex in the Library of St Lawrence; Gugnejus, Hesselius, Thomas, Rizius; indeed Bellarmine himself, who presses this exposition from Apocalypse 17 and has judged that it can be plainly gathered and is necessary, confirmed it with arguments.

units.la: VI. Ast excipit Bellarminus; Babylonem vocari non Romanam Ecclesiam, sed Romam urbem, qualis erat Johannis tempore, caput imperii Ecclesiam persequens, habitatio Daemoniorum, id est, Idololatrica, cujus imperium per Gothos, Wandalos, Hunnos, Longobardos fere ad nihilum redactum sit; quaeque deserenda fuerit corde, non corpore. Novimus certè nonnullos ex citatis Pontificiis authoribus (Patres ante complementum, ante quod omnis Prophetia aenigma est, parùm hîc vidisse, sibi etiam parùm constitisse, nemo jure miratur;) quando eos rei evidentia cogit, ut nobiscum Babylonem in Apoc. Romam dicant, Ecclesiae suae honori consulere volentes, illud de Roma antiqua Gentili cum Bellarmino intelligere, ut eorum alii contra, ad alterum temporis extremum prolabentes, Romam, qualis sub finem mundi & adventum Antichristi futura sit idololatrica rursus & Christiano nomini infesta, sic designari arbitrantur.
units.tr: VI. But Bellarmine objects: Babylon is called not the Roman Church but the city of Rome, such as it was in John's time, the head of the empire persecuting the Church, the habitation of demons, that is, idolatrous, whose power was brought almost to nothing by the Goths, Vandals, Huns and Lombards; and which must be forsaken in heart, not in body. We certainly know that some of the Papist authors cited (that the Fathers, before the fulfilment, before which all prophecy is a riddle, saw little here and were not very consistent with themselves, no one rightly wonders) when the evidence of the matter compels them, as with us, to call Babylon in the Apocalypse Rome, wishing to serve the honour of their Church, they take it of ancient pagan Rome with Bellarmine; while others of them, sliding to the other end of time, think that Rome, as it will be at the end of the world and at the coming of Antichrist, idolatrous again and hostile to the Christian name, is thus designated.

units.la: VII. Cùm autem hîc & rationes aliorum infringendo & absurditates sententiae oppositae ostendendo se invicem solidè refutent; & in specie ipsa argumenta Bellarminiana (quorum hîc solum aliqua ratio habenda) sententiam ejus magis intricent & absurditatis convincant; & in libro prophetico, in quo Johannes de rebus, quae ventura essent, edoctus fuit, status Romae, qualis tum, imò qualis jam antea erat (allegat enim Bellarminus persecutiones sub Nerone) describi non potuerit, maximè sub similitudine Bestiae, quæ nondum erat, sed demùm ex abysso ascensura sit, & meretricis, cum qua Reges terra decem scortaturi sint; Et consideratio urbis tanquam Imperii capitis generalis sit, & persecutio à Bestia mystica, & quæ cornua agnina similia & per Pseudo-Prophetam vim signa faciendi habitura sit, designetur; & habitatio Daemoniorum ac Idololatrica esse nondum desierit, & vastatio quædam ac brevissima per Barbaros excidium illud prædictum finale & gravissimum à Regibus decem, qui cum ea antea scortaturi sint, & quibus Deus illud in corda daturus sit, ita infligendum, ut in mare instar lapidis molaris mittenda nec post unquam invenienda sit, minimè æquet; Cùm inquam hæc ita se habeant, & Roma Pseudo-Christiana contrà, Babylonem illam veterem, sive jam initia, dum utraque ad faciendum nomen & religionis sedem destinata fuit, sive potentiam, quam utraque maximam acquisivit, sive vitia communia, scortationem, idololatriam, crudelitatem, blasphemias, superbiam, veneficia, nundinationem, sive denique judicium finale, Romæ ex parte jam immissum, ex parte adhuc secundum prophetias ad Babylonis similitudinem immittendum; spectemus; exactè referat; (quæ omnia apud Celeberrimum Heideggerum in Mysterio Babylonis Magna latè deducta videri possunt) illam utiq; per Babylonem Apocalypticam denotari, post tot alios, qui à multis seculis hic nobis præiverunt, & ex quibus multorum testimonia idem de Ecclesia Dei meritissimus Vir in Prologo Galeato libri cit. adducit, jure meritóque asserimus, & prorei, de qua agitur, momento, passim clamamus; Babylonem istam deserendam esse primò & maximè corde, interim tamen etiam, quando & ubi ad communionem peccatorum & errorum sollicitat, imò cogit, libertatem Deo soli in Spiritu & veritate serviendi adimit, & crudelissimè fideles persequitur, quoad fieri potest, corpore.
units.tr: VII. Since, however, here they mutually and solidly refute one another, both by overthrowing each other's reasons and by showing the absurdities of the opposing view; and since Bellarmine's own arguments (of which only some account must be taken here) further entangle his opinion and convict it of absurdity; and since in a prophetic book, in which John was instructed about the things that were to come, the state of Rome as it then was, or even as it already had been before (for Bellarmine alleges the persecutions under Nero), could not be described, especially under the likeness of the Beast, which was not yet, but was at length about to ascend out of the abyss, and of the harlot, with whom the kings of the earth were to commit fornication; and since the consideration of the city as the head of the empire is general, and the persecution is designated as by the mystical Beast, which was to have horns like a lamb and, through the false prophet, power to work signs; and since the habitation of demons and idolatry has not yet ceased, and a certain very brief devastation by barbarians is not equal to that final and most grievous destruction foretold, to be inflicted by the ten kings, who were first to commit fornication with her, and to whose hearts God will put it, so that she is to be cast into the sea like a millstone and never found again; since, I say, these things stand thus, and we look at Pseudo-Christian Rome on the other hand, and accurately compare it with that old Babylon, whether in its beginnings, when both were destined to make a name and a seat of religion, or in the power which both acquired to the greatest degree, or in common vices, fornication, idolatry, cruelty, blasphemies, pride, sorceries, trading, or finally in the final judgment, which has in part already fallen upon Rome and in part is yet to fall according to the prophecies, in the likeness of Babylon (all of which may be seen laid out at length in the most famous Heidegger's Mystery of Great Babylon), we assert, with the right and with good reason, that it is that Babylon which is meant in the Apocalypse, after so many others who have gone before us for many centuries, and from whom the most worthy man, in the Galeatus preface of the book cited, adduces the testimonies of many concerning the Church of God on the same point; and on the matter at issue, we cry out everywhere that this Babylon is to be forsaken, first and chiefly in heart, yet also, when and where she solicits or even compels us to share in her sins and errors, takes from us the freedom of serving God alone in spirit and truth, and most cruelly persecutes the faithful, in body, as far as that can be done.

units.la: VIII. Et ita quidem clamamus passim, Romam esse Babylonem de Apocalypsi. Sed an Bellarminus nos unquam audivit clamantes, Romam esse Babylonem de, vel ex epistola Petri? Vel an necessarium est eandem utrobique Babylonem intelligere? Imò an conveniens est? Johannem in libro Prophetico & plane ænigmatico pro veterum & novorum juxta Dei Providentiam & viarum similitudinem convenientia, novis vocabula veterum imponere, jure miratur nemo, cumprimis quando ibidem typi & antitypi paritatem exactè deduxisse, & sub Babylonis ænigmate ita Romam mam quasi digito monstrasse deprehenditur, ut, ipso Bellarmino & tot Doctoribus Pontificiis aliis judicibus, necesse sit de Roma omnia intelligere, idq; aperte colligi possit; Ast Petrum in Epistola sua per Babylonem Romam denotare, an æquè necesse est? An æquè aperte colligi potest? Imò adhuc semel, an conveniens est? An illud patitur simplex, familiaris, cumprimis in calce Epistolæ, ubi salutem impertit, Petri & Epistolaris stylus, ut sine ullo explicationis, & in ea vel conjecturæ vestigio locum mysticè denotasse credi possit, cùm tamen Divus Johannes librum scribens, cujus singuli versus singula sunt mysteria, Ecclesiarum, ad quas scripsit, septem nomina propria expresserit, & ab appellationibus mysticis abstinuerit, in libro alioquin per totum mystico?
units.tr: VIII. And so indeed we cry out everywhere that Rome is Babylon in the Apocalypse. But did Bellarmine ever hear us crying out that Rome is Babylon from, or on the basis of, the epistle of Peter? Or is it necessary to understand the same Babylon in both places? Indeed, is it even fitting? No one rightly wonders that John, in a prophetic and wholly enigmatic book, in keeping with the likeness of old and new according to God's providence and the ways of God, gave new names to old things, especially since there he is found to have set out exactly the parallel of type and antitype, and under the enigma of Babylon so pointed at Rome as if with a finger that, by Bellarmine's own judgment and that of so many other Papist teachers, one must understand everything of Rome, and this can be plainly gathered. But is it equally necessary that Peter in his epistle denotes Rome by Babylon? Can it equally be plainly gathered? Once more: is it even fitting? Does the plain, familiar style of Peter's epistle, especially at its close where he sends greetings, allow it to be believed that he designated a place mystically, with no explanation and without a trace of conjecture in it, when John, writing his book, each verse of which is a mystery, named the seven churches to which he wrote by their proper names, and abstained from mystical appellations in a book otherwise mystical throughout?

units.la: IX. De loco, ubi Epistolæ scribuntur, aliquid subinde monetur, ad fidem eò certiorem Epistolæ conciliandam, si autem sic de loco monere aliquid voluit Petrus, quomodo quæso id facere potuit mysticè? Quomodo Romam sub Babylonis nomine intelligens? An Romam Babylonem esse tunc temporis adeò communiter inter fideles recens conversos sciebatur, quod hodienum scire nolunt nonnulli Doctores Pontificii? Colligit illud Bellarminus ex Apocalypsi, colligunt & probant alii; Verùm quâ ratione illud colligere potuerunt eo tempore, quo Epistola illa scripta fuit, non tantùm diu antequam Apocalypsis scriberetur sub Domitiano, sed, Baronio quidem Judice, tertio Claudii anno, & annis aliquot ante Synodum Hierosolymitanam, adeóque haud longo intervallo à conversione Judæorum Act. II. descripta, quos inter qui per Pontum, Galatiam, Cappadociam, Bithyniam, Asiam dispersi, sed eo tempore, quo Petrum Romæ nec fuisse, nec esse potuisse mox ostendemus?
units.tr: IX. Some remark is made here and there about the place where the Epistles were written, to make the Epistle more credible. But if Peter wished to say something about the place in this way, how, I ask, could he have done so figuratively? How could he have meant Rome by the name Babylon? Was it so commonly known among the recently converted faithful at that time that Babylon meant Rome, a fact that some Papist doctors are now unwilling to acknowledge? Bellarmine infers this from the Apocalypse, and others infer and prove it too. But by what reasoning could they have inferred it at the time when that Epistle was written? That was not only long before the Apocalypse was written under Domitian, but, according to Baronius, in the third year of Claudius, and some years before the Synod of Jerusalem. The Epistle was therefore written not long after the conversion of the Jews in Acts 2, among whom were those scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Bithynia and Asia. Yet at that time, as we will soon show, Peter neither was nor could have been at Rome.

units.la: X. Et cur quæso Petrus sic sedem sui Episcopatus dissimulasset? Et contrà cur non indicâsset, leve saltem & ex Scripturis omnibus unicum illius loci, cui affixa per tot secula, si vera narrant, esse debebat Monarchia, præsentiæ suæ debita, sub nomine suo in omnes omnium temporum & locorum fideles æterno eorum commodo exercenda, & necessariò ab omnibus agnoscenda, daturus indicium? Cur non potiùs locum illum Cathedræ suæ perpetuum, Romam, quam modò quasi Ῥώμλω, robur, modò quasi רום sublimitatem dici volunt, convenientiori certè ad sedem usque adeò sublimem & robustam denotandam vocabulo, & proprie vocâsset? An fortè veritus est, fideles, quod Sybilla Erythraea maluisset, quasi Ῥώμην in quam certatim confluere tandem debeat, quicquid abominationis & superstitionum sit, & futurum sit, dici, cogitaturos esse? Et ideò Babylonis nomen potiùs elegit; quòd plane funestum, & Judæis multis nominibus invisum, Hierosolymæ adhuc tum temporis nimis affixos, licèt ad Christum conversos, à reverentia Sedi Apostolicæ debita magis & æquè ferè ac ipsum inferni nomen alienare facilè potuisset? Et tandem an is mos Paulo fuit, ita in designatione locorum mysteria captare? Aut quorsum Petrus Romam scribens, Romam nominare non est ausus; quam Paulus, cùm inde sex epistolas scriberet, urbem Romam, cives Romanos, & ausus, & nominavit?
units.tr: X. And why, I ask, would Peter have concealed in this way the seat of his episcopate? Conversely, why would he not have given at least a slight indication, drawn from all the Scriptures, of the one place to which, if these stories are true, the monarchy ought to have been permanently attached, a monarchy due to his presence, to be exercised under his name for the eternal benefit of all the faithful of all times and places, and necessarily to be acknowledged by all? Why did he not rather name that place of his chair, Rome, which they now want to be read as if from the Greek for strength [Ῥώμλω, robur] and now as if from the Hebrew for height [רום, sublimitatem], using a word far more suitable for denoting so lofty and strong a see, and call it by its proper name? Or did he perhaps fear that the faithful would think of Rome, as the Erythraean Sibyl would have preferred, as the place into which, whatever abomination and superstition there is or will be, everyone must eventually rush? And so did he choose the name Babylon instead, because it was plainly deadly and hateful to the Jews in many ways, who still at that time were tied to Jerusalem, even though they had been converted to Christ, and it could easily have turned them away from the reverence due to the Apostolic See, almost as much as the very name of hell? And finally, was it Paul's custom to catch at mysteries in this way when naming places? Or why, when Peter wrote from Rome, did he not dare to name Rome, when Paul, who wrote six epistles from there, both dared and did name the city of Rome and the Roman citizens?

units.la: XI. Sed hîc se ingerit Baronius, qui ad an. Chr. 45. n. 17. se non imprudenter dicturum existimat, Petrum non esse usum proprio Urbis nomine, quòd Hierosolymis fugâ lapsus è carcere, ubi ageret, non ab omnibus percipi vellet. Ista autem mysticae appellationis causa 1. gratis & sine fundamento fingitur. 2. Minùs convenit cum Zelo Apostolico imperterrito. 3. Non usque adeò certa sunt, quæ Baronius de tempore scriptæ epistolæ conjicit, incertum sanè est, an statim post liberationem Petri ex carcere & discessum in alium locum epistola scripta sit. 4. Certum autem illud, quod & mox ostendendum, Petrum tam citò Romam non venisse. 4. Certum etiam illud, saltem Chronologis receptum, Herodis mortem subsecutam fuisse anno Claudii IVto, cùm epistolam XImo demùm Claudii anno scriptam esse verisimile sit, quomodo quidem metu Herodis & ob carcerem ante sex aut septem annos relictum Petrum locum commorationis reticuisse, absurdè planè diceretur. 5. Ostensum est, ne fideles quidem sic locum commorationis Petri tunc temporis percepturos fuisse, & allatæ sunt contra mysticam vocis acceptionem rationes aliæ. 6. Scripsit ad fideles, fidelem etiam nactus latorem Sylvanum, illi igitur dubio procul intelligere debuerunt, salutationem ad ipsos directam, si intellexerunt igitur, etiam, venire ab Ecclesia Romana, & proin idem periculum mansit, quod ex aperta loci designatione sibi imaginatur Baronius, cùm ex coetu aliquis æquè facilè mysterium prodere potuisset, ac simplex nomen indicare. Constat igitur, ista quidem non imprudenter dixisse Baronium sic nimirum ὡς ἀπρόσφορα δεῖ λέγειν prudenter satis volentem, sed sine fundamento ullo dixisse, imò contra rei veritatem.
units.tr: XI. But here Baronius intrudes, who, under the year of Christ 45, number 17, thinks that he will not be "unwise" in saying that Peter did not use the proper name of the city, because, having escaped from prison at Jerusalem, he did not want it known to everyone where he was staying. But this invented reason for a figurative name (1) is baseless and made up for the occasion; (2) agrees less well with the fearless zeal of an Apostle; (3) the things Baronius conjectures about the time of the written Epistle are not so certain. It is surely uncertain whether the Epistle was written immediately after Peter's release from prison and his departure for another place; (4) it is certain, as we will soon show, that Peter did not come to Rome so quickly; (4) it is also certain, at least as accepted by the chronologists, that Herod's death followed in the fourth year of Claudius, whereas the Epistle was probably written in the eleventh year of Claudius. It would be plainly absurd to say that Peter, who had left his place of residence six or seven years before because of Herod's threat and the prison, kept silent about that place. (5) It has been shown that even the faithful could not have understood Peter's place of residence in this way at that time, and other reasons have been brought against the figurative sense of the word.
