(6) He wrote to the faithful, and he had a faithful bearer, Silvanus. Without doubt they ought to have understood the greeting addressed to them. If they understood it, they would also have understood that it came from the Roman Church. The same danger would therefore remain that Baronius imagines arising from a plain indication of the place, since someone from the gathering could just as easily have revealed the mystery as simply named the place. It is clear, then, that Baronius said these things "not unwisely", that is, as things that ought to be said as little as possible, wishing to be prudent enough. But he said them without any foundation at all, indeed contrary to the truth of the matter.

units.la: XII. Quodl
units.tr: XII. Quodl[...]

units.la: XII. Quod enim mutatis nominibus homines appellari addit, parùm huc facit, ut & exemplum unicum allatum, quando nimirum Paulus 2. Tim. IV.17. ait, liberatum se esse ex ore Leonis, Neronem intelligens; Locorum enim diversam rationem ostendimus, ex quibus scribitur. 2. Ex antecedentibus & consequentibus, & maximè ex subscriptione, si illa genuina est, patet de Nerone agi, quod hic Romæ respectu non patet. 3. Et periculum ibi manifestius fuit, & honor forte muneri habitus, & convenienter Tyranni furor indigitatus, quid autem attinebat Romam Babylonem vocare, ubi de salutatione fidelium Romanorum agebat Apostolus?
units.tr: XII. For his addition that "people are called by changed names" has little bearing here, not least because the only example offered is that when Paul, in 2 Timothy 4:17, says that he was rescued from the mouth of the lion, meaning Nero. For we have shown that the places from which the letters are written differ in their circumstances. (2) From the context before and after, and above all from the subscription, if it is genuine, it is plain that Nero is meant, which is not plain here at Rome. (3) The danger there was more obvious, the honour perhaps granted to the office, and the fury of the tyrant appropriately indicated. But what was the point of calling Rome Babylon, where the Apostle was speaking of greeting the Roman faithful?

units.la: XIII. Et si allegoricus est locus Babylon, annon & allegorica erit persona Marcus, qui mox sequitur, & forte Linus aut Clemens, aut Cletus, aut alius? Cur non & allegorica omnia? Præstat igitur de Babylone aliqua proprie sic dicta cogitare, cùm sine necessitate gravi sensus proprius semper sit præferendus, quod & ipsi sedulò nobis inculcare non negligunt, ubi tamen non simplex gravis necessitas ad sensum improprium nos vocat. Et hic quidem se offert gemina Babylon tum inclyta (tertia enim Phœniciæ in Batanæa regione à Geographis quibusdam memorata obscurior fuit:) Ægyptiaca una, altera Chaldaica vel Assyriaca. Quæcunque autem eligatur, perinde est, cùm utrobique Judæorum, quorum peculiarem curam Petrus susceperat, magna messis fuerit, paucioribus interim Romæ, imò inde à Claudii edicto nullis aperte degentibus; in quo etiam consentientem habemus Doctissimum Archiepiscopum Parisiensem, Petrum de Marca, cujus de Concord. Imp. p.2. l.6. c.1. n.4. hæc sunt verba: Cùm Petrus destinatus fuisset ad erudiendos Judæos, jamque in Judæa Evangelium prædicâsset, curam suam convertit ad Judæos, tum prima dispersionis, id est, Babylonia, tum secunda, id est, Græcanica. Prout vir ille Doctissimus hic planè nobiscum sentit, nimirum aliam Babylonem, quàm Romam, post Clarissimos ex Pontificia Communione Viros multos alios, intelligens, id est, judice Baronio, nobiscum insigniter delirans, Novator & ipse, molestè accipiens ex Canonicis divinisque scripturis etiam Petri Romam adventum reddi testatum, & ipse, cum tot aliis.
units.tr: XIII. And if Babylon is an allegorical place, will not the person Mark, who immediately follows, also be allegorical, and perhaps Linus, or Clement, or Cletus, or someone else? Why not make everything allegorical? It is better, then, to think of some Babylon properly so called, since a proper sense should always be preferred unless some serious necessity calls us to an improper one. Our opponents do not neglect to press this upon us themselves, though not where a simple, serious necessity calls us to an improper sense. Here there appear two Babylons, both famous: for a third Babylon in the region of Batanaea in Phoenicia, mentioned by some geographers, was rather obscure. One is Egyptian, the other Chaldean or Assyrian. But whichever is chosen makes no difference, since in both there was a great harvest of Jews, whose special care Peter had undertaken, while at Rome there were fewer, and indeed from the edict of Claudius onward none openly lived there. On this point we also have in agreement the most learned Archbishop of Paris, Peter de Marca, whose words in De Concordia Sacerdotii et Imperii, part 2, book 6, chapter 1, number 4, are: When Peter had been appointed to instruct the Jews, and had already preached the Gospel in Judea, he turned his care to the Jews, both of the first dispersion, that is, Babylonia, and of the second, that is, the Greek. That most learned man plainly agrees with us here, understanding a Babylon other than Rome, as do many other very distinguished men from the Papist communion. According to Baronius, they are all remarkably raving innovators like us, and he himself, taking it badly that the arrival of Peter at Rome is attested by the canonical and divine Scriptures, is one of them, along with so many others.

units.la: XIV. Sed ostendere conantur, Babylonem aliquam propriam hic intelligi nullo modo posse, adeóque, (quæ Annalium scriptoris verba porrò sunt;) licèt quis nolit, fateri compelli, per Babylonem esse Romam significatam. Et quidem tribus id ipse, & post eum Doctissimus
units.tr: XIV. But they try to show that some proper Babylon cannot be understood here in any way, and so (these are the words of the writer of the Annals) although one may be unwilling, one must admit that by Babylon Rome is meant. And indeed the author himself, and after him the most learned Valesius, want to prove this on three grounds.

units.la: Altera; Quartò ut allegorica æquè fingi possent omnia; ita commodè Babylon sive Ægyptiaca, sive Chaldaica intelligitur; Argumenta contrà illam; ctissimus Valesius, probare volunt rationibus, quarum prima contra Babylonem Ægyptiacam directa est, quam obscurum planè locum non civitatis nec oppidi dignum nomine fuisse, sed Castellum à Strabone & aliis nominatum esse, nec de Ecclesia ibi collecta ex Annalibus constare, causantur, imò Annalista Petrum hanc Babylonem intellexisse, insignem stultitatem & rem nimium absurdam vocat; Verùm & locum hunc (cui favet, quòd Palæstinæ vicinior fuit, & mittendis ad Judæos Græcanicæ dispersionis literis opportunior, & in eo tractu innumera ferè Judæorum multitudo, & Marcus veterum testimoniis à secundo Claudii ad octavum, vel (juxta Eutychium in Originibus Alexandrinis) ad primum Neronis annum,) satis olim magnum & celebrem fuisse, hodie famosi Cairi partem esse, & à Strabone castrum munitum, ceu insigne Ægypti propugnaculum, & in quo una ex Legionibus præsidiariis fuerit, vocari, & in Actis Concilii Ephesini Cyrum ejus Episcopum inveniri Celeberrimus Spanhemius, cui in hac quæstione multum me debere lubens profiteor, Dissert.III. de Petri itinere Romano §. 17. ex idoneis Authoribus fusè &, ut solet, doctè ostendit.
units.tr: Second, as everything could equally be made up as allegorical, so Babylon, whether Egyptian or Chaldean, is conveniently understood. Arguments against that Babylon: the first is directed against the Egyptian Babylon. They claim that it was a plainly obscure place, not worthy of the name of city or town, but a fort named by Strabo and others, and that it is not established from the Annals that a Church was gathered there. The annalist even calls it remarkable stupidity and a thing too absurd that Peter should have understood this Babylon. But this place (which is favoured by its being nearer to Palestine, by its being more convenient for sending letters to the Jews of the Greek dispersion, and by the almost countless multitude of Jews in that district, and by the testimony of the ancients that Mark was there from the second to the eighth year of Claudius, or, according to Eutychius in the Origines Alexandrini, to the first year of Nero) was once large and famous enough. Today it is part of famous Cairo. Strabo calls it a fortified camp, as a notable bulwark of Egypt, in which one of the garrison legions was stationed. And the most celebrated Spanheim, to whom I gladly confess I owe much on this question, has shown at length and, as is his custom, learnedly, from reliable authors, Dissertation III, on Peter's Roman journey, §17, that a bishop of it, Cyrus, is found in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Secundam rationem ex eo contra Babylonem Chaldaicam sumunt, quòd Caji tempore, Josepho teste, Judæi, qui agebant in Babylone & apud Assyrios, fuerint expulsi, denique trucidati. Sed 1. Non illud dicit Josephus, verùm modò, Anilæum cum suis, Babyloniis impetum in Judæos facientibus, interfectum esse, reliquos autem Judæos coactos Seleuciam vicinam concedere, hinc Ctesiphontem, postea plerosque Nisibim Mesopotamiæ & contermina loca petiisse. Ex quo tamen minimè sequitur, sub Claudio Caji successore, & quidem decimo imperii ejus anno, secundùm verisimilem de tempore scriptionis Epistolæ conjecturam, nullos planè Babylone Judæos fuisse, cùm & furor Babyloniorum, pro ejusmodi tumultuum ratione, brevis esse, & Judæi ex vicinis locis mox reverti potuerint, & quidam sponte Seleuciam recesserint, & , plerosque tantùm Nisibim & Neerdam se recepisse, testatur ἀρχαιολόγ.
units.tr: The second argument they take from this against Chaldean Babylon is that in the time of Caius, according to Josephus, the Jews who were living in Babylon and among the Assyrians were expelled and finally slaughtered. But, first, Josephus does not say that. He says only that Anilaeus and his men were killed when the Babylonians attacked the Jews, and that the remaining Jews were forced to withdraw to the nearby Seleucia, and from there many went to Ctesiphon and later most went to Nisibis in Mesopotamia and neighbouring places. Yet it does not follow from this that under Claudius, Caius's successor, and indeed in the tenth year of his reign, according to the likely conjecture about the date of the letter, there were absolutely no Jews at Babylon. The Babylonians' fury, given the nature of such disturbances, was brief; the Jews could soon return from the nearby places; some withdrew voluntarily from Seleucia; and Josephus attests that most had retreated only to Nisibis and Neerda [ἀρχαιολόγ.].

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Tertiò urget Doctissimus Valesius, si Petrus Babylone sederit, ostendi oportere successionem Episcoporum, qui Ecclesiam illam post Petrum administrarint, proferendos esse fastos illius Ecclesiæ, sicut successiones Episcoporum urbis Romæ, qui post Petrum Apostolum Romanæ Ecclesiæ præfuerunt, ex Irenæo aliisque proferantur. Quasi verò, ubicunque Apostoli Epistolas scripserunt, successores etiam necessariò instituerint, stituerint, & successioni initium dederint partim illustri, partim minimè interruptæ! Quid igitur de Paulo, qui Petro nihil inferior fuit, respectu tot locorum dicemus? An Ephesi, Philippis & Athenis, quia inde Epistolas transmisit, Episcopus sedit? Vel annon rectiùs Doctissimus Vir ad Euseb. l. 3. cap. 21. Petrum & Paulum in Episcoporum ordine fuisse, negat? Et annon Petrus Babylone parvas moras facere, & tamen Epistolam inde scribere potuit: Διερχόμενον δὲ πάντων, omnia loca pertransiens, quod ipsi respectu Palastinæ Act. IX.32. tribuitur? Cùm, quæcunque jam intelligatur Babylon, habuerit sedes in Antiquitate illustres? Quemadmodum etiam, non obstantibus his rationibus, laudatus Doctissimus de Marca l. c. de Babylone Assyriæ verba Petri accepit: Petrus abiit Alexandriam, inquit, quæ Ægypti Metropolis erat, & in qua habitabant Judæi secunda dispersionis, institutóque illic Episcopo Marco Evangelista, Antiochiam profectus est, atque hinc Babylonem, ubi degebat hereditarius Patriarcha Judæorum prima dispersionis. Ea in urbe constitutus scripsit primam Canonicam, ut patet ex subscriptione, salutat vos Ecclesia, quæ Babylone. Tametsi enim veteres existimaverint, D. Petrum vocabulo Babylonis signifi-câsse urbem Romam: probabilis est Scaligeri conjectura, qui ex ipsa Babylone scriptam à Petro putat Epistolam hanc ad Judæos dispersos, qui habitabant in Provinciis, quarum Synagogæ pendebant à Patriarcha Babylonico. Et Eruditissimus Grotius, dum Petrum Româ in Babylonia partes reversum esse, in annot. ad Marcum vult, annon sententiam etiam suam, quòd per Babylonem intelligi Roma debeat, ipse refutat, claréque innuit, jam in illis partibus Petrum fuisse, & nihil scriptioni ex illis partibus obstitisse? Sic etiam non contemnenda videtur illa illustris Salmasii Appar. de Prim. Pap. pag. 15. conjectura, nihil certi de morte Petri Clementis tempore innotuisse, quia in Babylone externi Imperii sede, longissimè à Roma, ubi tum degebat Clemens, dissita, videatur martyrium passus, nec ab ea, id est, ab eo tractu unquam recessisse. Hactenus de loco ex Epistola Petri.
units.tr: Thirdly, the most learned Valesius presses: if Peter sat at Babylon, the succession of the bishops who governed that church after Peter ought to be produced, just as the successions of the bishops of the city of Rome, who presided over the Roman church after the apostle Peter, are produced from Irenaeus and others. As if wherever the apostles wrote letters, they necessarily also appointed successors and gave a beginning to a succession, partly famous and partly not at all interrupted! What then shall we say of Paul, who was in no way inferior to Peter, with respect to so many places? Did he sit as bishop at Ephesus, Philippi and Athens because he sent letters from there? Or is the most learned man on Eusebius, book 3, chapter 21, right to deny that Peter and Paul were in the order of bishops? And could Peter not stay there for a short time and yet write a letter from there, passing through all places [Διερχόμενον δὲ πάντων], which is attributed to him with respect to Palestine, Acts 9:32? Whatever Babylon is understood to be, did it not have seats famous in antiquity? Likewise, despite these arguments, the praised most learned de Marca, loc. cit., has taken the words of Peter about Babylon of Assyria: Peter went away to Alexandria, he says, which was the metropolis of Egypt, and where the Jews of the second dispersion lived; and after setting up Mark the Evangelist there as bishop, he went to Antioch, and from there to Babylon, where the hereditary patriarch of the Jews of the first dispersion dwelt. Established in that city, he wrote the first Catholic letter, as is clear from the subscription: the church that is at Babylon salutes you. For although the ancients thought that the blessed Peter by the word Babylon meant the city of Rome, Scaliger's conjecture is probable, who thinks that this letter was written by Peter from Babylon itself to the Jews of the dispersion who lived in the provinces whose synagogues depended on the Babylonian patriarch. And the most learned Grotius, while in his notes on Mark he wants Peter to have returned from Rome to the parts of Babylonia, does he not himself refute his own opinion, that Babylon must be understood as Rome, and clearly hint that Peter was already in those parts and that nothing stood in the way of writing from those parts? So too the famous conjecture of Salmasius in his Apparatus on the First Popes, p. 15, does not seem to be worthless: that nothing certain about the death of Peter became known in Clement's time, because he seems to have suffered martyrdom at Babylon, the seat of an outlying empire, very far from Rome, where Clement then lived, and never to have withdrawn from that place, that is, from that region. So much for the place in Peter's letter.

units.la: XVII. Secundò probatur hoc (Petrum nimirum Romæ fuisse) ex Act. ult. & ex epistola ad Romanos. Constat enim ex his locis, Romæ multos fuisse Christianos, imò Ecclesiam amplam & florentem, antequam Paulus eò veniret. Peto igitur, quis hos Christianos fecerit, si Petrus non fuit Romæ? Sunt verba Bellarmini. Damus ultrò, quod & Scripturæ postulant, ante Paulum Christianos & Ecclesiam Romæ fuisse; sed negamus ex eo sequi, Petrum illos Christianos Romæ convertisse. tisse, illam Ecclesiam Romæ fundâsse. Quænam est hæc consequentia; Paulus non fundavit. E. Petrus, & quidem Romæ degens? Annon potuerunt Ecclesiæ plantari sine horum Apostolorum præsentia? Quid igitur cum Samaritana Ecclesia, quid cum Antiochena, quam Petri quoque Episcopatum dicunt, factum est? Videatur Act. VIII.4.5. XI.18.19. Petit Bellarminus; Quis hos (Romanos) Christianos fecerit, si Petrus non fuerit Romæ? Quid si responderemus, nos illud nescire; quemadmodum fundationes primas aliarum etiam Ecclesiarum cum Bellarmino ignoramus plures? Sed tamen quoad Romanam Ecclesiam aliquid scimus. Nonne Act.II. etiam memorantur Judæi & Proselyti Romani? Nonne Rom.XVI.7. Paulus de Andronico & Junia Romæ habitantibus testatur, eos ante se in Christo fuisse? Nonne ipse aliquot annis ante iter Petri Romanum, quod tam maturum fingunt, in Christo fuit? Nonne, citato loco, Andronicum & Juniam vocat insignes inter Apostolos? Nonne igitur ex his omnibus quodammodo intelligi potest, quinam primi fundatores Ecclesiæ Romanæ fuerint, etiam ante adventum Petri & Pauli, si quidem ille Romam venit unquam? Certè Romanos illos Pentecostales Petri auditores domum reversos lucem feliciter accensam non sub modio occultâsse, dici debet; Certè Andronicus & Junia non sine causa insigni insignium inter Apostolos elogio ab Apostolo ornantur. Quòd autem Juniam fœminam fuisse Bellarmino certum est, quàm incertum quæsò est, & quàm parùm verisimile de insigni inter Apostolos? Et si vel certum esset, Andronico non obstaret, nec etiam ipsi Juniæ, quando etiam Iberos à fœmina Christiana captiva ad fidem adductos esse, historia Ecclesiastica testatur. Sic, posito etiam, nullum fuisse ausum prædicare Gentilibus, antequam Petrus cœlesti visione admoneretur Act.X. & XI. manet tamen præconium inter Judæos Romanos, quales jam ante Christum multos fuisse, ex Cicerone constat; hoc etiam non impedit, quò minùs alius ante Petrum Romæ Christum etiam Gentilibus annunciaverit, cùm visio illa Act.X. ante tempora Claudii contigerit, imò etiam prædictio Agabi Act.XI.28. de fame sub Claudio futura, sicut etiam demum Act.XVIII.2. de Claudii imperio primus sermo est.
units.tr: XVII. Secondly, this (namely that Peter was at Rome) is proved from the last chapter of Acts and from the letter to the Romans. For it is clear from these passages that there were many Christians at Rome, indeed a large and flourishing church, before Paul came there. I ask, therefore, who made these Christians, if Peter was not at Rome? These are the words of Bellarmine. We readily grant what the Scriptures also require, that there were Christians and a church at Rome before Paul; but we deny that it follows from this that Peter converted those Christians at Rome or founded that church at Rome. What kind of inference is this: Paul did not found it, therefore Peter did, and indeed while living at Rome? Could churches not be planted without the presence of these apostles? What then happened to the Samaritan church, and to the Antiochene, which they also say was Peter's see? See Acts 8:4-5 and 11:18-19. Bellarmine asks: who made these Christians (the Romans), if Peter was not at Rome? What if we answered that we do not know this, just as we are ignorant of the first foundations of many other churches along with Bellarmine? Yet as to the Roman church we do know something. Are not Jews and Roman proselytes mentioned in Acts 2? Does not Paul testify in Romans 16:7 that Andronicus and Junia, who lived at Rome, were in Christ before him? Was he himself not in Christ some years before the journey of Peter to Rome, which they imagine to be so early? Does he not, in the passage cited, call Andronicus and Junia outstanding among the apostles? Can it not therefore be understood in some way from all of these who were the first founders of the Roman church, even before the coming of Peter and Paul, if indeed Peter ever came to Rome? Surely it must be said that those Roman hearers of Peter at Pentecost, when they returned home, did not hide the light happily kindled under a bushel. Surely Andronicus and Junia were adorned by the apostle with the distinguished title of being outstanding among the apostles, and not without reason. But that Junia was a woman is certain to Bellarmine; how uncertain is that, I ask, and how improbable is it that she was outstanding among the apostles? And even if it were certain, it would not stand in the way of Andronicus, nor even of Junia herself, since ecclesiastical history attests that Iberians too were brought to the faith by a Christian woman who was a captive. Thus, even granting that no one dared to preach to the Gentiles before Peter was admonished by the heavenly vision, Acts 10 and 11, there remains the proclamation among the Roman Jews, of whom it is clear from Cicero that there were many even before Christ. Nor does this prevent another, before Peter, from having proclaimed Christ at Rome even to the Gentiles, since that vision in Acts 10 happened before the time of Claudius; indeed even the prophecy of Agabus in Acts 11:28 about the famine to come under Claudius, just as at last Acts 18:2 is the first mention of Claudius's reign.

units.la: XVIII. De Patribus à Bellarmino pro se citatis suo loco videbimus; hîc autem ad allegatorum Scripturæ locorum vindicias etiam ex antiquitate testimonia de prædicantibus Romæ an-
units.tr: XVIII. We shall see the Fathers whom Bellarmine cites for himself in their proper place. Here, however, in support of the Scripture passages alleged, it will be worthwhile to produce and point out also testimonies from antiquity about preachers at Rome before Peter.

units.la: te Petrum producere & indicare operæ erit pretium. Et jam produxit Ulricus Velenus in tractatu de hac quæstione edito, quem sibi maximè refutandum sumsit Bellarminus. Testimonia autem produxit Velenus ex Orosii Lib. VII. Hist. Tertulliani Apologetico, Platina in Vita Christi, & Tranquillo in vita Tiberii, quibus nempe ostendere voluit, statim post passionem Christi adhuc Tiberii tempore coepisse Romae esse Christianos, & proin non demum tempore Claudii à Petro Ecclesiam Romanam accepisse fundamenta. Addit Bellarminus responsurus in gratiam Veleni, (tam gratiosus est Antagonistis;) testimonium Clementis lib. I. Recogn. ubi legatur, Barnabam tempore Tiberii Romae praedicâsse. Quem secutus Dorotheus Tyrensis in Synopsi dixerit; Barnabam esse primum, qui Romae praedicârit.
units.tr: Ulricus Velenus has already produced them in his treatise published on this question, and Bellarmine took it upon himself to refute him above all. Velenus produced his testimonies from Orosius, Book VII of the History; from Tertullian's Apologeticus; from Platina's Life of Christ; and from Suetonius' Life of Tiberius. His purpose was to show that Christians began to be at Rome immediately after Christ's passion, while Tiberius was still emperor, and therefore that the Roman Church did not receive its foundations from Peter only in the time of Claudius. Bellarmine, intending to answer, adds (so gracious is he to his opponents) "in favour of Velenus" the testimony of Clement, Recognitions Book I, where it is read that Barnabas preached at Rome in the time of Tiberius. Following this, Dorotheus of Tyre in his Synopsis says that Barnabas was the first who preached at Rome.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: In Responsione Bellarminus primò quoad Tertulliani & Tranquilli testimonia dicit, Velenum aperte mentiri. Hoc non est in gratiam Veleni! Quomodo autem probat Bellarminus, Velenum apertè mentiri? Tranquillus, ait, in vita Tiberii non meminit Christianorum, sed in vita Claudii, ubi dicit, Judæos Chresto impulsore tumultuantes à Claudio fuisse Româ expulsos. Id quod suæ sententiæ faveat; Sed si Judæi, à quibus tum Christiani non discernebantur, Christo, vel juxta editionem Stephani Chresto (quomodo Servatorem nostrum nonnunquam olim appellatum esse docent Lactantius & Tertullianus;) impulsore tumultuantes, id est, ob Christianam religionem Gentilibus exosi expulsi sunt, verisimile certè est, jam sub finem imperii Tiberii, & certum, ante adventum Petri aliquos saltem Christianos Romae, post paulatim auctos fuisse, ut dicto modo tumultuari, noti et molesti valdè esse, & ad expulsionem Claudium jam ab initio imperii, quod & acta Apostolorum docere videntur, aliquo modo adigere potuerint. Ut omninò tunc tumultuantes Romae Christianos fuisse sententiae Bellarminianae non faveat; Saltem non magis ac oppositae; Christianorum enim aliquot saltem sub finem Imperii Tiberii Romae fuisse, non ideo negatur, potiùs ex incremento & licentia sub Tiberio jamjam commemoranda colligi potest.
units.tr: In his reply, Bellarmine first, regarding the testimonies of Tertullian and Suetonius, says that Velenus openly lies. This is not "in favour of Velenus!" But how does Bellarmine prove that Velenus openly lies? "Suetonius," he says, "in the Life of Tiberius makes no mention of Christians, but in the Life of Claudius, where he says that the Jews, rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, were expelled from Rome by Claudius." He says this "favours his own opinion." But if the Jews, from whom Christians were not then distinguished, were rioting at the instigation of Christ, or (according to Stephanus' edition) of Chrestus (as Lactantius and Tertullian teach that our Saviour was sometimes called of old), that is, if they were expelled because they were hated by the Gentiles on account of the Christian religion, it is certainly probable, and certain, that at least some Christians were at Rome before Peter's arrival, and that they later grew gradually in number, so that by that time they had become known and very troublesome, being able to riot in the manner described, and in some way to force Claudius to expel them, which the Acts of the Apostles also seem to teach, since this happened from the beginning of his reign. So, although the rioting Christians at Rome do not in any way favour Bellarmine's opinion, at least they favour it no more than the opposite view. For that some Christians were at Rome at least towards the end of Tiberius' reign is not denied for this reason; rather, it can be inferred from the growth and licence under Tiberius, which are about to be mentioned.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Tertullianus verò in Apol. ita pergit Bellarminus, potiùs contrarium judicat. Nam dicit, Pilatum ex Palæstina scripsisse Tiberio de resurrectione Christi, & quòd à multis Deus credebatur. Tiberium autem retulisse ad Senatum, an videretur Christus in Deum recipiendus, porrò senatum natum recusâsse, propterea quòd antea cœpisset à Populis Deum habéri, ut Pi-latus scripserat, quàm à Senatu consecratus esset. Ex qua narratione non potest colligi, tunc Romæ fuisse Christianos, sed potiùs non fuisse; si enim fuissent, ex illis priùs Tiberius cognovìsset famam Christi, quàm ex literis Pi-lati. Igitur actum jam est tempore, si vera narrat Tertullianus, Tiberii, Romæ de Christo in Deum recipiendo, quidnî igitur tunc saltem inquisitionem de eo quidam instituere cœpissent, si priùs nulli, ne Judæi quidem Romani ulli, eum cognovìssent? Et sic vi-vente adhuc Tiberio Christiani Romæ oriri potuerunt; Porrò Se-natus Christum rejecit tanquam jam ante consecrationem suam à populis receptum. A populis? Quare igitur etiam non à Roma-nis? Saltem quibusdam, saltem Judæis, saltem post, Tiberio ad-huc imperante? Quomodo igitur contrarium potiùs dicit Tertul-lianus? Quomodo ex illius narratione potest colligi, potiùs tunc Romæ non fuisse Christianos? Quia non ex illis, sed ex literis Pilati ea de re cognovit. Ast unde novit Bellarminus, nihil planè Tiberium de hoc ex aliquot Christianis Romanis cognovìsse? Pilati literæ non testantur. An autem præfecti in Judæa literæ testari debue-runt in specie, quid quidam saltem Judæi crediturì mox & dicturi sint? Quis non videt, Bellarminum hîc argumentari ex silentio, quod aliter se habere non debuit, imò vix potuit, quem argumen-tandi modum merè negativum in nobis mox improbabit falsò no-bis tributum? Et certè aliu de etiam eadem cognoscere potuit, & non referre ad Senatum, potuit referre ad Senatum, id tamen ta-ceri, potuit etiam non cognoscere ex Christianis. Quid enim? An pauci illi & recens conversi ad Imperatorem sponte deferre? An sic proprio judicio se prodere debuerunt, gnari odii, saltem aliorum? An id postea factum est? An talia Imperatori ipsis incumbebat proponere, quando Petrus ipsum commorationis suæ locum tacere potuit? Et annon videtur, quicquid jam de relatione Christianorum sit, literas Pilati & statim secutas, & longè majoris authoritatis, & solùm dignas habitas fuisse, de quibus Senatui communicatur? Sed & Tertulliani locce testimonium lucem mutua-bit à sequentibus, in quibus continuatio tantùm est narrationis ejusdem, & ex quibus adhuc magis apparebit, Velenum saltem non tam aperte mentitum esse.
units.tr: "But Tertullian in the Apologeticus," Bellarmine continues, "rather judges the contrary. For he says that Pilate wrote from Palestine to Tiberius about the resurrection of Christ, and that he was believed by many to be God. Tiberius then referred it to the Senate, whether Christ ought to be received as God; moreover, the Senate refused, because he had begun to be regarded as God by the peoples before he was consecrated by the Senate, as Pilate had written. From this narrative it cannot be gathered that there were Christians at Rome at that time, but rather that there were not; for if there had been, Tiberius would have learned of Christ's fame from them before he learned of it from Pilate's letters." Therefore, if Tertullian tells the truth, the matter of receiving Christ as God was already being dealt with at Rome in Tiberius' time. Why then could not some have begun at least then to make inquiry about him, if none of them had previously known him, not even the Roman Jews, any of them? And so Christians could have arisen at Rome while Tiberius was still alive. Moreover, the Senate rejected Christ as already received by the peoples before its own consecration. By the peoples? Why then not also by the Romans? At least by some, at least by Jews, at least afterwards, while Tiberius was still reigning? How then does Tertullian say the contrary? How can it be gathered from his narrative that rather at that time there were no Christians at Rome? "Because Tiberius learned of this matter not from them, but from Pilate's letters." But how does Bellarmine know that Tiberius had learned nothing at all about this from any Roman Christians? Pilate's letters do not testify to it. Ought the prefect's letters from Judaea to have testified specifically what certain Jews were about to believe and say soon afterwards? Who does not see that Bellarmine is here arguing from silence, which could not, indeed scarcely could, be otherwise, and that this merely negative mode of arguing, which he will shortly censure in us, is falsely attributed to us? Certainly he could have learned the same things, and not reported them to the Senate; he could have reported them to the Senate and kept silent about them; he could also not have learned them from Christians. For what? Did those few and recently converted men voluntarily report to the Emperor? Ought they to have betrayed themselves by their own judgment, aware of the hatred, at least of others? Was this done afterwards? Was it incumbent on them to put such things before the Emperor, when Peter could keep silent about the place of his own sojourn? And does it not seem that, whatever the report of the Christians may be, Pilate's letters and what immediately followed them, and which were of far greater authority and were considered alone worthy, were those on which the Senate was informed? But the testimony of this passage of Tertullian will also receive light from what follows, in which there is only a continuation of the same narrative, and from which it will become still clearer that Velenus, at least, did not so "openly lie."

units.la: XXI. Orosius igitur l. c. addit, Senatum decrevisse, exterminandos ex Urbe esse Christianos.
units.tr: XXI. Orosius, therefore, in the same place, adds that the Senate decreed that the Christians should be driven out of the City.

units.la: Idem plenius dicunt Eusebius & Plati-
units.tr: Eusebius and Platina say the same, more fully.

units.la: Ex Orosio, Platina ; Ille quidem in Chron. an.34. Ex consulto Patrum, inquit, Christianos eliminari urbe placuit, & Tiberius mortem comminatus est Christi accusatoribus. Hic vero l. c. clarissimè omnium;Admonitus Tiberius à Pilato de morte Christi ac dogmate ad Senatum retulit, censuitque, Christum in Deum referendum. Fieri id non modò Senatus vetuit, verùm etiam pellendos urbe totâ Christianos censuit. Proposita sunt accusatoribus præmia, quos Tiberius à tanto scelere minis & morte prohibuit. Sed excipit Bellarminus, id non ita accipiendum esse, quasi tunc in urbe Christiani essent, sed ut non reciperetur ullo modo Christiana religio. Quis non aliter intelligeret illud; exterminandos sive eliminandos ex urbe tota esse Christianos ? Certè in urbe est, qui ex urbe pelli, exterminari, eliminari debet, & secundùm Bellarmini mentem Senatus potiùs decernere debuisset, ex Judæa pellendos, exterminandos, eliminandos esse Christianos, & in urbem minimè admittendos. Videtur etiam aliquid de Christianis jam in urbe degentibus Tiberium retulisse, vel alias Senatum & Tiberium cognovisse. Maximè dum insuper accusatoribus præmia proposita sunt, & Tiberius à tanto scelere minis & morte eos prohibuit; Saltem etiam ex his, præsertim si cum Baronio statim post resurrectionem contigisse, licèt præter necessitatem, supponas, reliquo Tiberii tempore & sub Cajo & Claudio ante adventum Petri, si is contigit unquam, Romæ aliquot Christianos, saltem Judæos fuisse, præsumere licebit.
units.tr: Platina takes it from Orosius. Orosius, in his Chronicle under the year 34, says: "By the consent of the Fathers it was decided that the Christians should be removed from the city, and Tiberius threatened death to the accusers of Christ." Platina, in the same place, states it most clearly of all: "When Pilate informed Tiberius about the death of Christ and his doctrine, Tiberius referred the matter to the Senate, and proposed that Christ be counted among the gods. The Senate forbade this, and further decreed that the Christians be expelled from the whole city. Rewards were offered to the accusers, whom Tiberius, by threats and the penalty of death, restrained from so great a crime." Bellarmine objects that this must not be taken as meaning that Christians were then in the city, but only that the Christian religion was not to be received in any way. Who would not understand the words otherwise: that the Christians were to be driven out, or removed, from the whole city? Surely a person who is in the city is one who must be driven out, expelled, removed from it. On Bellarmine's own view, the Senate ought rather to have decreed that Christians be driven out, expelled and removed from Judaea, and not admitted to the city at all. It also seems that Tiberius reported something about Christians already living in the city, or that the Senate and Tiberius knew of them. Especially since rewards were offered to the accusers, and Tiberius restrained them from so great a crime by threats and death, we may at least suppose, even if it goes beyond what is necessary, that after the resurrection, as Baronius supposes, this happened. Then we may presume that in the rest of Tiberius's reign, and under Caius and Claudius before the coming of Peter (if he ever came), there were at least some Christians, at least Jews, in Rome.

units.la: XXII. Ad exceptionem Bellarmini contra Barnabæ prædicationem Romanam sub Tiberio, illam, nullum facilè ausum fuisse gentilibus prædicare, jam n. 17. respondimus.
units.tr: XXII. Bellarmine's objection to Barnabas's preaching at Rome under Tiberius, namely that "no one would have easily dared to preach to the Gentiles," we have already answered above, at n. 17.

units.la: Quòd autem addit; Libros Recognitionum Apocryphos censeri, illius, quando ex illis contra nos sæpe testimonia adduxit, etiam memor esse debuisset, & memores esse in similibus occasionibus deberent sodales; Sic etiam quoad Synopsin Dorothei, quæ hic similiter à Bellarmino rejicitur, quamvis narratio ficta de Eunucho ex LXX. discipulis in ea non reperiatur, & de Junia, viro jam vindicaverimus; Memores quoque rejectorum testimoniorum esse deberent, quando mox ex similibus, quibus maximam partem narrationes, etiam apertè confictæ, admixtæ sunt, rem totam conficere volent. Quòd autem ad testimonium utriusque authoris porrò excipit, (nam eo tantùm fine dedit, ut rursus auferret, licèt non omni modo posse videatur;) In illis dici, Barnabam post primam Concionem sine fructu habitam in Judaam dam rediisse, adeoque illis Velenum aut parum, aut nihil lucrari; lucrum tamen (praesuppositio, ut Bellarminus praesupponi permittit, vera narrari;) relinquere videtur, cum & alii fructum facere potuerint, & Barnabas verisimiliter sine fructu, id est, sine magno & sperato fructu rediisse dicatur cum illo maxime tempore nullae conciones sine omni plane fructu fuerint, maxime tantorum & Divina Providentia in tam longinquas oras abductorum; Imo si ille fructum praesens non vidit, facile tamen post discessum, cumprimis accedentibus aliis persuasionibus, & scripturarum scrutatione, & auditorum collatione, apparere potuit; Quod etiam sufficit; Et ista, illustrationis ergo tantum, ex antiquitate responsioni ad secundum ex Scriptura argumentum subjunxisse.
units.tr: As for his addition that "the Apocryphal books of the Recognitions are regarded as spurious", he ought to have remembered this when he himself often brought forward testimonies from them against us; and comrades should be mindful of such things on similar occasions. So too with the Synopsis of Dorotheus, which Bellarmine likewise rejects here: although the fabricated story about the eunuch among the Seventy is not found in it, and we have already vindicated the matter of Junia as a man, they too ought to remember the testimonies they have rejected, when they soon want to make up the whole case from similar sources, to which narratives, even ones openly invented, are largely mixed in. As for his further objection to the testimony of each author (for he gave it only so that he might take it away again, although it may not seem possible to do so in every way): "In those writings it is said that Barnabas, after the first sermon, which was fruitless, returned to Judaea; so that Velenus gained little or nothing from them." Yet this seems to leave some gain, if we grant what Bellarmine permits us to assume, that the story is true, since others too could have produced fruit; and Barnabas is said to have returned probably without fruit, that is, without great and hoped-for fruit. At that time there were indeed no sermons at all that were entirely without fruit, especially when they were preached by men carried by divine providence into such distant shores. Indeed, if he did not see the present fruit, it could nevertheless have become apparent afterwards, especially as other persuasions came in, and through the searching of the Scriptures and the comparing of hearers. That is enough. I have added these things from antiquity, only for the sake of illustration, to our reply to the second argument from Scripture.

units.la: XXIII. Plura non habent; Nos igitur jam videbimus, quid contra iter Petri Romanum tale Scripturae nobis suppeditent.
units.tr: XXIII. They have nothing more. We shall now see what Scripture supplies us against Peter's journey to Rome.

units.la: Et primo quidem argumentamur ex ipso Scripturarum, de tali itinere Petri silentio, postquam ex allatis Scripturae testimoniis iter illud probari non posse satis ostendimus, & alibi de eo ne quidem suspicandi causa datur. Hic autem statim excipit Bellarminus, nihil concludi argumentis ab authoritate negative. Nihil certe defectus testimonii unius authoris probat, dum alii ejusdem fidei authoritatis testantur; Nihil etiam testimonii defectus, ubi testimonium dari non debuisset; Ast hic aliter se rem habere ostendemus. Nam primo quidem hic non ex unius authoris silentio argumentamur, aut duorum, aut trium, sed sacrorum omnium, & quando hi omnes tacent, & alii profani authores etiam tacent, & Clemens ipse tacet, quemadmodum ostendemus; in re certe suspecta suspecti, & si unum forte excipias, posteriores Clemente omnes, & Metaphrastes ex Seculo XI. praeter quem neminem, qui describat historiam itineris Petri invenimus, ut Baronius ad An. 44. n. 27. ait, audiri facile non debent; bona est nostra argumentandi ratio, & dissimilis valde illi, cui nostram assimilat Bellarminus: Alioqui, quia Matthaeus non scribit in Evangelio, Christum circumcisum: Marcus non meminit praesentationis, Lucas non meminit stella novae: Joannes non dicit, Christum natum de Maria virgine, ista omnia erunt falsa, quod absurdissimum est.
units.tr: First of all, we argue from Scripture's own silence about such a journey of Peter, since we have shown sufficiently, from the cited passages of Scripture, that the journey cannot be proved, and elsewhere no ground is given even for suspecting it. Here Bellarmine at once objects that "nothing is concluded from arguments drawn from authority in the negative." Certainly the lack of testimony from one author proves nothing, while other authors of the same faith and authority bear witness. Nor does the lack of testimony prove anything where testimony ought not to have been given. But we shall show that the case here is otherwise. For first, we do not argue from the silence of one author, or two, or three, but of all the sacred writers. When all of these are silent, and the other profane authors are silent too, and Clement himself is silent, as we shall show, then in a matter that is itself suspicious, the witnesses are suspect too. Unless you except perhaps one, all the later writers after Clement, and Metaphrastes of the eleventh century, beside whom, as Baronius says at the year 44, n. 27, "we find no one who describes the history of Peter's journey," ought not to be easily heard. Our method of argument is sound, and very unlike that to which Bellarmine compares it: "Otherwise, because Matthew does not write in the Gospel that Christ was circumcised, Mark does not mention the presentation, Luke does not mention the new star, John does not say that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, all these things would be false, which is most absurd."

units.la: XXIV. Absurdissimum hoc est, quia quod ab Evangelistarum uno, aut duobus, aut etiam tribus tacetur, a reliquis, aut quarto, juxta sapientiam & dispensationem Dei supplebitur & traditur ejusdem fidei, authoritatis ejusdem, supremae Divinae, sed, quia de re, quam tractamus, omnes silent, primo omnium illud inferre possumus, eam non esse certam certitudine fidei, non esse de fide, cum in iis, quae aperte posita sunt in Scripturis, teste Augustino de Doctr. Christ. cap.9. inveniantur ea omnia, quae continent fidem moresque vivendi, quod & alibi lib.3. cap.6. cont. Lit. Petiliani plenius & efficacius pronuntiat: Sive de Christo, inquit ,sive de ejus Ecclesia, sive de quacunque alia re quae pertinet ad fidem vitamque nostram, non dicam, si nos nequaquam comparandi ei, qui dixit; licet si nos, sed omnino quod adjecit, si Angelus de coelo annunciarit, praeterquam quod in Scripturis legalibus & Evangelicis accepistis, anathema sit. In quo autem Scripturae loco docetur, Petrum fuisse, esse, aut fore Romae, sive jam Petrus id ipse testetur, sive de eo testentur alii? Et si de fide non est, Petrum fuisse Romae, simul etiam de fide non erit, quicquid huic Petri in urbe Domina praesentiae superstruitur, ibi fuisse Episcopum, Papam esse ejus Successorem, & proin Monarcham Ecclesiae infallibilem, de fide non erit fundamentum totius religionis Pontificiae.
units.tr: XXIV. This is absurd, because what is passed over by one, or two, or even three of the Evangelists will be supplied and handed on by the others, or by the fourth, according to the wisdom and dispensation of God, of the same faith and the same authority, supreme and divine. But since all are silent about the matter we are discussing, we can first of all infer this: it is not certain with the certainty of faith, it is not a matter of faith. For, as Augustine teaches in De doctrina christiana, chapter 9, "in those things which are plainly set down in the Scriptures are found all those things which contain faith and the rule of living"; and he declares this more fully and forcefully elsewhere, in Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, chapter 6: "Whether concerning Christ, or concerning his Church, or concerning any other matter which pertains to our faith and life, I will not say, if we, but altogether what he added: if an angel from heaven should announce anything other than what you have received in the legal and evangelical Scriptures, let him be anathema." In what passage of Scripture is it taught that Peter was, is, or will be at Rome, whether Peter himself bears witness to it or others bear witness about him? And if it is not a matter of faith that Peter was at Rome, then at the same time it will not be a matter of faith that whatever is built upon this presence of Peter in the lady city, that he was a bishop there, that the Pope is his successor, and therefore an infallible monarch of the Church, will not be a matter of faith. The foundation of the whole Papist religion will not be one.

units.la: XXV. Secundo testimoniorum defectus est, ubi testimonia adesse deberent. Quid enim? An res tanti momenti in Scriptura taceret? Annon uno & altero verbo saltem innui debuit, quomodo Petrus Apostolorum Princeps & Ecclesiae Monarcha (loquor ex hypothesibus Pontificiis;) Romam ad sedem Monarchicam & totius Christianismi caput ibi erigendam & aeternum stabiliendam, concesserit? Tot regiones eum in finem peragrârit? Itinere tot & tanta egerit, gentes converterit, provincias salutârit, erexerit, Patriarchatus fundârit? Quàm illustris, quàm tanto duce, regiones, quemadmodum in exercitu, ut Leo Allatius de Perp. Conf. l.1. c.11. loquitur, obambulante, dignus fuerit? An haec omnia res tantae tamque scitu necessariae silentio Scripturarum involvi debuerunt prorsus, quando Scriptores sacri tot alia minoris longe ponderis fusè prosecuti sunt! Certè si homo Pontificius hic vel parùm attenderet, statim ipsi, quaecunque de Petri Monarchia credit, suspecta fieri deberent, & non possunt illa modo ullo cum ipso Scripturarum de Petri profectione silentio conciliari.
units.tr: XXV. Second, there is a lack of testimony where testimony ought to be present. For what? Would a matter of such importance be passed over in Scripture? Ought it not at least to have been hinted at in one word or another, how Peter, the Prince of the Apostles and Monarch of the Church (I speak from Papist premises), granted that Rome should be set up there as the monarchic see and head of all Christianity, and eternally established? Did he traverse so many regions to that end? Did he accomplish so many and such great journeys, convert nations, greet and set up provinces, found patriarchates? How illustrious, how worthy would it have been, with so great a leader, that "the regions, as in an army," as Leo Allatius says in De perpetua consensione, book 1, chapter 11, "were walked through"? Or ought all these things, so great and so necessary to know, to have been wholly hidden by the silence of the Scriptures, when the sacred writers have dealt at length with so many other things of far smaller weight! Certainly if a Papist considered this even a little, all the things he believes about Peter's monarchy would at once have to become suspect, and they cannot in any way be reconciled with the Scriptures' silence about Peter's departure.

units.la: XXVI. Sed & mirum non immeritò videtur, vel sine istis hypothesibus, Scriptores Sacros & Lucam maximè Actorum Apostolicorum auctorem tanti Apostoli tam celebre iter ne verbo quidem attigisse, cùm non tantùm aliorum itinera, longè infra momentum hujus, Philippi Azotum, Caesaream, Saulis Tharsum, Discipulocipulorum in Phœniciam, Cyrum, Antiochiam, Barnabæ & Saulis in varias Syriæ & Asiæ minoris Civitates, sed & Petri Samariam, Lyddam, Joppen, Cæsaream, Hierosolymam, & alia de Petro referrat, conversiones per eum factas, miracula edita, vincula illi injecta, & quæ aliquot post annis, diu autem post tempus, quod itineri Petri Romano assignant, subsecuta sunt? Ut valde frivolum sit illud Baronii & aliorum effugium, Pauli cum primis acta Lucam retulisse.
units.tr: XXVI. It also seems not unreasonably strange that the sacred writers, and Luke above all, the author of the Acts of the Apostles, should not mention in so much as a word so famous a journey of so great an Apostle, even without these hypotheses. They relate the journeys of others, far below the importance of this one: Philip to Azotus and Caesarea; Saul to Tarsus; the disciples of the disciples into Phoenicia; Barnabas and Saul to various cities of Syria and Asia Minor. They also relate Peter's journeys to Samaria, Lydda, Joppa, Caesarea and Jerusalem, and other things about Peter: conversions made through him, miracles performed, chains laid on him, and what followed some years later, and long after the time they assign to Peter's Roman journey. So that evasion of Baronius and others, that Luke chiefly recounted the acts of Paul, is very flimsy.

units.la: XXVII. Testimonia autem adesse debuissent non tantùm ob rei dignitatem, sed & ob occasionum varietatem.
units.tr: XXVII. Testimonies ought to have been present, not only because of the importance of the matter, but also because of the variety of occasions.

units.la: Quot quæsò Lucas habuit? Habuit, ubi de primo cum Simone congressu egit, & facilè addere potuisset, eundem Simonem postea Romæ illustriori longè certamine à Petro victum fuisse. Habuit, dum de Petri profectionibus & aliis locutus est; Habuit, dum præsentem in Concilio Hierosolymitano Petrum Act. XV. induxit, sine ulla reditûs ex urbe & Cathedræ relictæ mentione; Habuit denique maximè in descriptione satis prolixa adventûs Pauli in Urbe, ubi Petrum, fratribus reliquis obviam venientibus, seu ut præsentem tum, seu ut forte ab urbe absentem, inducere potuisset. Sed nullâ earum, non etiam aliis occasionibus usus est.
units.tr: How many occasions did Luke have, I ask? He had one when he described the first encounter with Simon, and he could easily have added that this same Simon was afterwards defeated by Peter at Rome, in a far more famous contest. He had occasions while speaking of Peter's journeys and of other matters. He had one when he introduced Peter as present at the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15, with no mention of any return from the city or of Peter's leaving his chair. He had one, finally and above all, in the fairly lengthy description of Paul's arrival in the City, where he could have introduced Peter as coming to meet the other brothers, either as present at that time or as perhaps absent from the city. But he used none of these occasions, nor any others.

units.la: XXVIII. Quot etiam memorandæ in urbe præsentiæ occasiones Paulus habuit?
units.tr: XXVIII. How many other occasions for mentioning Peter's presence in the city did Paul have?

units.la: Habuit primùm in Epistola ad Romanos, dum enim multus fuit in laudanda Romanorum fide & laudandis, per quos res Christi inter eos strenuè promota erat, operariis, quî tanti fundatoris oblivio subire potuit? Et dum in fine salutem operariis & illustribus in Ecclesia nominatim impertiit, qui Petri, omnium Principis, nullam omninò mentionem fecit? Qui non subinde eos ad reverentiam Petro Episcopo suo debitam & ad doctrinæ ab eo traditæ & tradendæ observationem hortatus est? Imò qui ad eos scribere necesse habuit, cùm Petrus ipsorum Episcopus satis eorum saluti invigilare potuerit? Habuit in omnibus Epistolis Româ datis, in quibus Clementis, Lucæ, Timothei, Marci, Aristarchi, Demæ, Epaphræ aliorúmque opus Domini secum peragentium aliquoties meminit; Petri ne verbo quidem unquam. Abfuisse tunc dicunt; sed dicunt; atque ita semper abfuisse, Episcopo loci parùm convenire potuit; Et si vel semper abfuisset, quid ordinarius aut primarius urbis & orbis Pastor, & ubi ageret, saltem semel indicari debuisset.
units.tr: First, he had them in the Epistle to the Romans. For while he was so full in praising the faith of the Romans, and the workers through whom Christ's cause had been vigorously advanced among them, how could he have forgotten so great a founder? And when at the end he gave greetings to the workers and to the distinguished persons in the Church by name, how did he make no mention at all of Peter, the Prince of all? Did he not repeatedly urge them to the reverence due to Peter their Bishop, and to observing the doctrine taught by him and to be taught? Indeed, why did he even need to write to them, when Peter their Bishop could have watched sufficiently over their salvation? He had occasions in all the Epistles written from Rome, in which he mentions several times Clement, Luke, Timothy, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Epaphras and others working the work of the Lord with him; but never even a word about Peter. They say Peter was absent then; but they say it, and if he was always absent in this way, it would hardly suit the Bishop of the place. And even if he had always been absent, the ordinary or chief minister of the city and the world, and where he was working, ought at least once to have been indicated.

units.la: XXIX. Et quot tandem memorandæ suæ in urbe præsentiæ occasiones ipse Petrus habuit? Habuit, & debuisset ipse saltem, tacentibus Luca & Paulo, in alterutra Epistolarum vel Romæ, vel cathedræ ibi erectæ, vel circumstantiæ alterius meminisse, officium erga se & Successores præscribere, sed facere plane neglexit. Quæ omnia sufficienter jam testantur, argumentationem nostram non à defectu testimoniorum mere negativorum, sed potius privativorum esse, id est, talium, quæ non affirmant, ubi deberent affirmare, si res ita se habuisset. Et hoc genus argumentandi, inquit Medina in Thom. p.3. q.1. a.3. efficacissimum est. Nam hoc genere argumentationis colligitur, tantùm unum mundum esse factum, & solum Filium assumsisse carnem humanam, licet non dicatur in Sacra Scriptura, alios mundos non fuisse factos à Deo, neque verò, quòd alia persona non assumserit carnem humanam; Commune etiam & apud adversarios vel maximè usitatum est.
units.tr: XXIX. And how many occasions for mentioning his own presence in the city did Peter himself have? He had them, and he ought at least, while Luke and Paul were silent, to have mentioned in one of the Epistles either Rome, or the chair erected there, or some other circumstance, and to have prescribed the duty towards himself and his successors. But he plainly neglected to do so. All of these things already sufficiently show that our argument rests not on a lack of merely negative testimonies, but rather on privative ones, that is, on those which do not affirm where they ought to affirm if the matter were so. And this kind of argument, says Medina in Thom. p.3. q.1. a.3., is most effective. For by this kind of argument it is concluded that only one world was made, and that only the Son assumed human flesh, although it is not said in Holy Scripture that other worlds were not made by God, nor that another person did not assume human flesh. It is also common, and most used even among our adversaries.

units.la: XXX. Secundò etiam argumentamur ex iis, quæ in Scripturis Sacris contra istam in urbe Roma Petri præsentiam expressa reperimus. Et primò quidem ex serie rerum illo tempore gestarum. Communis ferè est Pontificiorum opinio, Petrum Romam venisse secundo Claudii anno, & ejus loci per 25. annos Episcopum fuisse; Atqui ex Actis Apostolicis primò indubium est, egisse adhuc in Palæstina Petrum anno Claudii quarto, ante quem etiam ibi constanter mansit, & quo ipso Herodis Agrippæ, consentientibus Chronologis, ultimo anno ab Herode in carcerem conjectus fuisse plane videtur; Quare etiam Doctissimus Valesius; Igitur, inquit Not. ad Euseb. l. 2. c. 16. Petrus ante hunc annum Romam profici non potuit. Rursum Hierosolymis fuit Petrus tempore Synodi Act. XV. quando etiam Pauli Hierosolymitanam illam profectionem, de qua Gal. II 1. factam esse, tum aliunde, tum etiam ex consensu Theodoreti veterumque aliorum, & ex recentioribus, Baronii, Valesii, cognoscimus; Facta autem illa, sicut Apostolus expresse testatur post 14. annos, quos à conversione Pauli numeramus dos esse, & nostri probant, & fatetur ipse Baronius; & quam conversionem, Caligulæ circiter ultimo anno accidisse, æquè probari potest; Ut per consequens Concilii tempore, & Claudii anno ultimo adhuc in Palæstina Petrus fuerit; quin si detur Baronio, Concilium anno Claudii 9. habitum fuisse, porrò constabit ex Gal. II. 12. Petrum Antiochiæ post Concilii celebrationem commoratum esse, quò cum eum demum post Concilium habitum concessisse, Onuphrius & Halloixius Jesuita strenuè defendunt. Posito igitur, quod post alios Illustris Salmasius conjicit, concertationem Pauli cum Petro in annum Claudii 12. incidisse,&, ut ajunt, Petrum per septennium Antiochiae Episcopum sedisse, nec sub Claudio Romam venire, nec ibi p. r 25. annos sedere potuit; {m}mò jam res, Eutychio Alexandrino in Ecclesia istius originibus p.37. quem multi multùm æstimant, confecta erit, ibi enim Petrum sub extrema Claudii occisum esse dicitur. Ut etiam ex Veteribus alii Petri martyrium martyrio Pauli aliquot annis prius faciunt, &, si vel sub Nerone etiam Petrus martyrio affectus esset, ex dictis constare poterit, eum nec secundo aut tertio Neronis anno, quando Paulus ad Romanos scripsit, nec etiam sexto, eo illinc veniente, Romae fuisse, Paulo autem Ecclesiae urbis illius operam suam addicente, causam Petrus nullam habuisset ex Oriente (Babylone etiam eum scripsisse supra docuimus) molestissimis itineribus Romam properandi. Ista autem latius deducta apud Celeb. Spanhemium Diss. cit. §. 27. seqq. videri possunt.
units.tr: XXX. Secondly, we also argue from those things which we find expressed in the Holy Scriptures against this presence of Peter in the city of Rome. And first, indeed, from the sequence of events at that time. The opinion of the Papists is almost universal, that Peter came to Rome in the second year of Claudius, and was Bishop of that place for 25 years. But from the Acts of the Apostles it is first beyond doubt that Peter was still acting in Palestine in the fourth year of Claudius, before which he also remained there constantly; and in the very year in which, by the agreement of the chronologers, Herod Agrippa, in the last year, had put him into prison, it plainly seems that he was cast into prison. Hence also the most learned Valesius: Therefore, he says, Not. ad Euseb. l. 2. c. 16., Peter could not have set out for Rome before this year. Again, Peter was at Jerusalem at the time of the Synod of Acts 15, when we also know that Paul's journey to Jerusalem, of which Gal. 2:1 speaks, took place, both from other sources and from the agreement of Theodoret and other ancients, and from more recent writers, Baronius and Valesius. That journey, however, as the Apostle expressly attests, took place after 14 years, which we count from Paul's conversion, and our writers prove this, and Baronius himself admits it. And that conversion can be equally proved to have happened about the last year of Caligula. So that at the time of the Council, and in the last year of Claudius, Peter was still in Palestine. Indeed, even if Baronius's view be granted, that the Council was held in the ninth year of Claudius, it will further be established from Gal. 2:12 that Peter stayed at Antioch after the Council was held; and that he only withdrew there after the Council, Onuphrius and the Jesuit Halloix vigorously defend. Granting, therefore, what the illustrious Salmasius conjectures after others, that Paul's contest with Peter fell in the twelfth year of Claudius, and, as they say, that Peter sat as Bishop of Antioch for seven years, he could neither have come to Rome under Claudius, nor have sat there for 25 years. Indeed, the matter will by now be settled by Eutychius of Alexandria in his Origines Ecclesiae p.37., whom many value highly; for there it is said that Peter was killed at the very end of Claudius's reign. Thus some of the ancients also place Peter's martyrdom a few years before Paul's, and if Peter had suffered martyrdom even under Nero, it can be established from what has been said that he was not at Rome in the second or third year of Nero, when Paul wrote to the Romans, nor even in the sixth, when he was coming thither; and since Paul was devoting his labour to the Church of that city, Peter would have had no reason to hasten to Rome from the East (we have shown above that he also wrote from Babylon), by the most troublesome journeys. These matters are discussed at greater length by the renowned Spanheim, Diss. cit. §. 27. seqq., and may be consulted there.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Porrò argumentamur ex aliis, quae in Scripturis, Petrum Romae degisse, impugnare videntur. Dissertatione primâ multa de peculiari ejus circa Judaeos cura diximus; Cui se Bellarminus quadantenus opponit, l.1. de R. P. c. 17. dicens, Petrum sic magis Hierosolymae Episcopatus sui sedem ponere debuisse, quàm Antiochiae, aut Romae, quae urbes gentium fuerint. Admitteremus, si de commorationis loco tantùm loqueretur, & illum non Hierosolymis circumscriberet. Rectè ais, Bellarmine, potiùs in aliqua urbe Judaeorum, id est, ubi Judaeorum magna multitudo, commorari debuit Judaeorum Apostolus, quàm Romae (nam, quod Antiochiam attinet, & plures ibi Judaei, & Episcopatum illius loci septennalem quoque negamus;) in urbe gentium, ubi tempore quidem Claudii nullos, aut ferè nullos ex edicto, sed & aliàs paucos fuisse Judaeos, & ex eo, quòd eorum Primores Paulum illuc delatum non sponte convenerunt, triduo post adventum ejus demum evocandi, quidam de secta Christiana parùm etiam edocti; & ex Epistola, in qua Romani Gentibus non semel accensentur, & salutationes originę Graecorum, vel Latinorum occurrunt, & ex aliis, facilè colligi potest, sicut etiam in reliquo Occidente pauciores fuerunt; Jam autem vix concipi potest, quomodo Petrus eo ipso tempore, quo Paulus & Barnabas gentibus inserviebant, in tanta Judaeorum per Graeciam
units.tr: Further, we argue from other passages of Scripture which seem to oppose the view that Peter stayed at Rome. In my first dissertation I spoke at length of Peter's particular concern for the Jews. Bellarmine opposes this to some extent, Book 1, On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 17, saying that Peter ought to have fixed the seat of his episcopate in Jerusalem rather than in Antioch or Rome, which are cities of the Gentiles. We would grant this if he spoke only of the place of residence and did not confine it to Jerusalem. You are right, Bellarmine, that the Apostle of the Jews ought rather to have stayed in some city of the Jews, that is, where there was a great multitude of Jews, than at Rome in a city of the Gentiles. (As for Antioch, we deny both that it had many Jews and that its episcopate lasted seven years.) At Rome, in the time of Claudius, there were either no Jews or almost none because of the edict, and otherwise only a few. That is clear from the fact that its leading Jews did not come to meet Paul of their own accord but were summoned only three days after his arrival, and from the fact that those men knew rather little of the Christian sect. It is also clear from the Epistle, in which the Romans are often counted among the Gentiles, and from the greetings, which are Greek or Latin in origin, and from other evidence. The same was true of the rest of the West, where there were fewer Jews. Now it can hardly be conceived how Peter, at the very time when Paul and Barnabas were ministering to the Gentiles, should, amid so great a number of Jews scattered through Greece,

units.la: Note: Secundo ex peculiari Petri circa Judaeos cura, & epistola ad Galatas. Græciam, Thraciam, Asiam minorem, Syriam, Babyloniam, Ægyptum, Orientem omnem, messe, neglectis suis, seu ex composito, seu ex divina jussione, partibus, longis itineribus Romam adierit, sedem & Cathedram ibi fixurus, nec nisi casu & vi edicti Imperatorii in Orientem reversurus, & illo denuo relicto omnes Occidui orbis partes lustraturus? Quod eo magis mirum, quando accedit, Paulum Petro Judæorum Apostoli elogium tribuisse in Epistola ad Galatas sero satis, & inscriptionum consensu Româ data & missa, ex ea urbe, in qua tum Petrus æquè Gentium ac Judæorum Episcopus, imò convertendis in Occidente Gentibus occupatior sedisset.
units.tr: Note: Secondly, from Peter's particular care for the Jews and from the Epistle to the Galatians. Peter, neglecting his own provinces, whether by agreement or by divine command, would have gone to Rome by long journeys through Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor, Syria, Babylonia, Egypt and all the East, which were his harvest field. He would have done this to fix his seat and chair there, and would have returned to the East only by chance or by the force of an imperial edict, and then, having left it again, would have travelled through all the parts of the Western world? This is all the more remarkable since Paul, in his Epistle to the Galatians, gave Peter the title Apostle of the Jews, and it was written and sent from Rome, from a city in which Peter would then have been equally bishop of the Gentiles and the Jews, or rather more occupied with converting the Gentiles in the West.

units.la: XXXII. Sic impugnare videtur Petri in urbe præsentiam Epistola ad Galatas, sed etiam illa ad Philippenses, in qua Romā
units.tr: XXXII. In the same way the Epistle to the Galatians seems to oppose Peter's presence in the city, and so does the Epistle to the Philippians, in which from Rome

units.la: c.II. 20. testatur, se neminem habere ἰσόψυχον, pari animo praditum erga fideles, cæteris omnibus, quæ sua, & non quæ Christi sint, quærentibus. Posito autem, posterius hoc non de omnibus omninò intelligendum esse, prius tamen arguere videtur, Petrum etiam tunc in urbe non fuisse, utpote qui pari, si non majori affectu, cumprimis si Pastor Universalis fuisset, fideles quoscunque amplecti debuit; Accedit quoque testimonium ex illa ad Colossenses, Romă pariter scripta, in qua tres modò memorat Paulus συνεργούς εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, cooperarios in regno Dei, Aristarchum, Marcum & Jesum; Ast Petrus vel primus horum fuisset, si Romæ; Nec omitti debet, quòd 2.Tim.IV. 16. 17.Omnes se dereliquisse, Paulus conqueritur, id est, explicante Aquinate, omnes discipulos territos & nullum fuisse, qui illum consilio aut ope juvaret; Quod certè Petro tribui non potest, nec proin dici, eum, saltem tunc, Romæ fuisse. Alia tacemus, & concludimus, Scripturam Sacram parùm favere Petri in urbe Roma præsentiæ.
units.tr: Ch. 2, v. 20, he testifies that he has no one like-minded [ἰσόψυχον] towards the faithful, since all others seek their own things, not the things of Christ. Granting that this latter statement is not to be understood of everyone without exception, it still seems to argue that Peter was not in the city at that time, since, having the same or even greater affection, especially if he had been the Universal Minister, he ought to have embraced all the faithful. There is also the evidence of the Epistle to the Colossians, written likewise from Rome, in which Paul mentions only three fellow workers for the kingdom of God [συνεργούς εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ]: Aristarchus, Mark and Jesus. But Peter would have been first among them, had he been at Rome. Nor should it be passed over that in 2 Timothy 4:16-17 Paul complains that all had forsaken him. That is, as Aquinas explains, all the disciples were frightened and there was none who would help him by counsel or by aid. This certainly cannot be attributed to Peter, nor therefore can it be said that he, at least then, was at Rome. We pass over other points and conclude that Holy Scripture gives little support to Peter's presence in the city of Rome.

units.la: XXXIII. Scriptores profani, Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio, qui res sub Claudio & Nerone in urbe gestas commentariis suis tradiderunt, silentio suo ei parùm quoque favere deprehenduntur; Nam & causam & occasionem de Apostolorum Principe, si Romæ tunc versatus fuisset, mentionem injiciendi aliquam omninò habuissent; Tacitus, Christianos sub Nerone introducens; quorum fuisset tum Petrus in urbe ipsa, summum post Christum caput, alter Christus, cathedra Romæ stabilita tantæ authoritatis, ut inter equuleos, cruciatus, tormenta, res illa taceri Neroni & Aulicis potuisset Ex Epistolis ad Philippenses, Colossenses, atque ad Timotheum; Tertiò argumentatio instituitur ex silentio Authorum profanorum; tuisset minimè, nec à Scriptore hoc Christianorum tanti Rectoris, haud semel, nisi fallant Lini, Marcelli acta, vetustique Anastasii Codices, ad Neronem admissi, supplicium publicum tam rarum, causis & circumstantiis tam nobile, planè negligi debuisset. Suetonius autem, qui de Icaro & Tiridate insigni mago retulit, & de Christianorum suppliciis & expulsione unà cum Judaeis sub Claudio, qui Simonem tantum & Neroni carissimum ejusque historiam tacuisset? Qui Dio diligentissimus? De Plinio & aliis ut nihil dicamus.
units.tr: XXXIII. The profane writers, Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio, who related the events in the city under Claudius and Nero in their histories, are also found to give little support to Peter's presence by their silence. For if the Prince of the Apostles had been at Rome at that time, they would surely have had some cause and occasion to mention him. Tacitus, when he introduces the Christians under Nero, would have been bound to name Peter, who would then have been in the city itself, the highest head after Christ, another Christ, with a chair established at Rome of such authority that, amid the racks, torments and tortures, that matter could have been kept quiet from Nero and the court. Thirdly, an argument is set up from the silence of profane authors. Unless the Acts of Linus and Marcellus and the old Codices of Anastasius are mistaken, Peter was admitted to Nero more than once, as the leader of these Christians. Such a public execution, so rare and so notable in its causes and circumstances, ought surely not to have been passed over entirely by this writer. And Suetonius, who related the story of Icarus and of the famous magician Tiridates, and the punishments of the Christians and their expulsion with the Jews under Claudius, would he have kept silent about Simon, who was very dear to Nero, and about his history? And Dio, the most diligent of all? Let us say nothing of Pliny and the others.

units.la: XXXIV. Interim tamen non diffitemur, universae propemodum pro illa praesentia Antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae consensum, ob quem etiam, non tantum praesentiam illam vel negasse, vel in dubium vocasse toti Romanensium choro res delirio propior & Allatio aliisque supremus animam agentis haereseos conatus visus est; Sed & in Protestantium castris de absentia ἐπέχοντες non pauci, praesentiam haud gravatè largientes, fuerunt plurimi, Episcopatum tamen & 2ς. illos annos acriter & constanter nobiscum impugnantes. Ast nihil attinet multum traditionis illius examini post exactissimas tum aliorum ex nostris, tum maximè Celeberrimi Spanhemii, curas immorari; qui Diss.II. & 1. non tantùm in primos ejus Authores studiosè inquirit, sed &, ex Eusebii tantùm fide, Papiae ejus primam originem tribui posse, erudite ostendit, illi σφόδρα σμικρῷ ἢ νῦν, mediocri admodum ingenio pradito, juxta Eusebium, Hist. l.3. cap.39. & qui, eodem ibidem testante, aliis quoque exempla copiosè suppeditantibus, ὡς ἐν τῷ ἀγράφῳ, ut ex traditione non scripta, multa ξένα καὶ μυθικώτερα, nova & fabulis propiora propinavit, & cujus occasione Annalista ad an.Chr.118. n.5. monet, habendum esse in traditionibus delectum; ut non mox, ut quis se aliquid ex majorum traditione accepisse tradat, (ut de Papia acciderit,) fidem illi omnes adhibeant; Insuper Eusebii locum, & aliorum posteriorum, qui, quod usu venire solet, priorum testium fide hic falsa probárint, testimonia accuratè examinat, & occasiones probabiles compositae & continuatae narrationis in Babylone, scriptionis loco, quam propensi in mysticos sensus Romam, lectâ Apocalypsi, crediderint aetate Papiae saltem aliqui, & credito multis Romano Petri cum Simone Mago, quod fictitium esse ostenditur, certamine, & Icaro Suetoniano illuc ineptè traducto, & Romanensium omnia ad augendam suam authoritatem quadantenus apta undiquaque conquirentium & sedulò promoventium citò surgente fastu; diligenter & prolixè commemorat.
units.tr: XXXIV. Meanwhile we do not deny that almost the whole consensus of ecclesiastical antiquity favours that presence. Because of this consensus, the Roman party, a choir nearer to madness, and Allatius and others, the last gasps of a dying heresy, thought it necessary not only to deny that presence but even to call it into doubt. Yet within the Protestant camp, not a few, who suspend judgement about the absence, have been very willing to grant the presence, though they strongly and consistently oppose with us the episcopate and those first two hundred years. But there is no point in dwelling long on the examination of that tradition after the most exact labours of others among us, and above all of the most celebrated Spanheim. In his Dissertations 2 and 1 he not only inquires diligently into its earliest authors, but also shows learnedly that, on the testimony of Eusebius alone, its first origin can be traced to Papias, who was of very small, or rather of quite mediocre, intelligence, according to Eusebius, Hist. book 3, ch. 39. Eusebius also testifies that Papias, as from the unwritten tradition [ὡς ἐν τῷ ἀγράφῳ], put forward many strange and more fabulous things [ξένα καὶ μυθικώτερα], new and closer to fables, and while others also supplied examples in abundance. On this account the annalist, Annals, year 118, n. 5, warns that a choice must be made among traditions, so that not everyone straightway gives credence to whatever someone reports as having received from his elders, as happened with Papias. Moreover, Spanheim carefully examines the passage of Eusebius and of other later writers, who, as usually happens, prove falsely by the faith of earlier witnesses. He also carefully and at length recounts the probable occasions for the composed and continued story of Babylon, put forward as a figure for Rome: some, at least in Papias' age, were inclined to read the Apocalypse in a mystical sense and believed that it referred to Rome. He recounts the widely believed story of the contest of Peter with Simon Magus at Rome, which is shown to be fictitious, and the Icarus of Suetonius carelessly transferred there, and the Romanists, eagerly seeking out and promoting everything that could in some measure enlarge their authority, and the pride that quickly rose up.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Nec certè est, cur nobis hic Pontificii ob rejectas, vel saltem non sufficienter eorum judicio æstimatas tot veterum authoritates tantopere indignentur, quando, juxta præmissa, Scripturæ divinitùs inspiratæ ista de Petro credere & indubitata habere, nobis prohibere videntur. Idem hîc facimus, quod Romanenses respectu Veterum alibi, nunquam forte tot Divinis testimoniis prohibiti; At Patres id ajunt! inquit occasione alia famosus ille Graeco-Romanus Allatius de Perp. Conf. l. 1. c. 5. n. 14. 15. Patres non possunt dicere, quod non fuit? Item; Dictis Patrum solis in hoc negotio inniti, est frustra operam perdere. Sic & præclarè Baronius ad an. Chr. 39. n. 22. Profectò majoris esse fidei Acta Apostolorum, à Luca conscripta, quavis authoritate Majorum, nemo negarit. Atqui nos hunc ipsum Lucam (quem Baronius & alibi cum Bellarmino traditioni, nempe in examinata Ecclesiae Romanae per Barnabam fundatione, opponunt;) & praeterea Paulum, imò ipsum Petrum urgemus. Sin verò omnia admittere deberemus, quaecunque Patres, etiam aliquando magno cum consensu, praeter & contra Scripturarum authoritatem in scriptis suis reliquerunt, quàm bellè cum fide nostra ageretur, & quanta fabularum plaustra nostra faceremus, ab ipsis etiam Pontificiis ex parte repudiata!
units.tr: Nor indeed is there any reason why the Papists should be so indignant with us here, because we have rejected, or at least not weighed sufficiently by their judgment, so many authorities of the ancients. According to what has been said, they seem to forbid us to believe and hold as indubitable what Scripture, divinely inspired, teaches about Peter. We do here what the Romanists elsewhere do with respect to the ancients, though perhaps never prohibited by so many divine testimonies. But the Fathers say so! says that famous Graeco-Roman Allatius on another occasion, in On the Perpetuity of the Confession, book 1, chapter 5, nn. 14–15: The Fathers cannot say what was not? Likewise: To rely only on the sayings of the Fathers in this matter is to waste effort in vain. So too Baronius, excellently, on the year of Christ 39, n. 22: Surely no one will deny that the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke, carry greater authority than any authority of the elders. Yet we press this same Luke (whom Baronius, and elsewhere together with Bellarmine, opposes to tradition, namely concerning the founding of the Roman Church by Barnabas, which is open to examination), and besides him Paul, and indeed Peter himself. But if we were obliged to admit everything the Fathers left in their writings, besides and against the authority of the Scriptures, even sometimes with great consensus, how badly would our faith be served, and what carts full of fables would we be making, many of which even the Papists themselves have partly repudiated!

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Haberent utique praegnantes causas, nisi de fundamento Religionis suae rejiciendo ageretur, & ea, quae de Petri in urbem adventu & ejus commoratione in urbe, in defensione utriusque dicuntur, rejiciendi.
