Multa enim dicuntur & dici debent parùm cum illorum hypothesibus convenientia; Sic Petro honorificentius inter Judaeos praedicandi munus per praeconium tam longi temporis in urbe Gentium eripitur; Sic tot aliis locis, ubi eum Ecclesias fundâsse, Episcopos, Patriarchas constituisse, quibus eum privilegia dedisse, simul adfirmant, gloriosa ejus, ex qua tot & tanta sibi propria vendicant, praesentia communicatur; Sic simultaneus Petri & Pauli Romanus Episcopatus, (quem ipsis tantum nocere Differt. praced. ostendimus) adstruitur; Prout certè Clemens, Petri, ut ajunt, Successor in Epistola sua ad Corinthios magnae meritò authoritatis, ubi ei sermo de Apostolo utroque, de utriusque laboribus & martyrio, de Petro paucissimis defungitur, nec locum designans martyrii, nec profectiones in Occidentem, nec Romanum Episcopatum, minùs, fuisse hunc sibi à Petro ante mortem concreditum; At de Paulo, ut post Petrum sublato, ut laboribus boribus maximo, ut ἐπὶ τὸ ἠρμα τῆς δύσεως ad fines Occidentis, seu Romam delato, ut totius Orbis Doctore, ut sub Imperatoribus, Nerone videlicet, perpessò, sermo illi prolixior & ἐμφατικώτερος. Ex quo non immeritò concludi potest, Clementem hunc ignorâsse Petri ad τὸ ἠρμα τῆς δύσεως profectionem, & totius orbis peragrationem, & martyrii Petrini, fortè in Oriente consummati, locum & cæteras circumstantias; Quemadmodum etiam, quod ex Irenæo producunt, testimonium, utrumque Apostolum pariter saltem Romanam Ecclesiam fundâsse, prima ejus fundamenta jecisse, simul eam administrâsse, pari tandem potestate Lino Episcopatum tradidisse, dicit, primum illud, quod hic Bellarminus Petro tribuit, non habens; Et testes alii Dionysius Corinthius, Cajus, Tertullianus, Origenes, Epiphanius, & omnia utrique communia faciunt, imò aliquando soli Paulo fundationis laudem tribuunt; Sic quoque testis Pseudo-Clemens, Romanam Ecclesiam à tertio, Barnaba nimirum, fundatam, Romæ jam ante adventum Simonis, cui oppugnando Petrus accesserit, collectam Ecclesiam fuisse, & de aliis, quæ Pontificiis suppositionibus parùm congrua sunt, simul testatur; Sic pariter Tertullianus, testis alius, in eodem, ubi de Petro agit, loco, suum & quartum fundatorem addit, Johannem, quem Romæ in oleum primò igneum demersum, & postquam nihil passus esset, in Insulam relegatum fuisse (certo falsitatis indicio) primus omnium tradidit. Et ista quidem præter multa alia Pontificios à credito illo Petri adventu, & commoratione tot annorum recepta abducere deberent.
units.tr: They would certainly have strong grounds, unless the matter concerned rejecting the foundation of their own religion, and what is said about Peter's coming to the city and his sojourn in it, in defence of each, must be rejected. For many things are said, and must be said, that agree poorly with their hypotheses. Thus the honour of preaching to the Jews is taken from Peter and transferred, through a proclamation over so long a time, to a city of the Gentiles. Thus in so many other places, where they affirm at the same time that he founded churches, appointed bishops and patriarchs, and gave them privileges, his glorious presence, from which they claim so many and such great things as their own, is shared. Thus the simultaneous Roman episcopate of Peter and Paul (which we have shown in the preceding Dissertation to be very harmful to them) is asserted. Indeed Clement, said to be Peter's successor, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, which rightly has great authority, speaks of both apostles, of the labours and martyrdom of each, but dispatches Peter in very few words, neither naming the place of his martyrdom, nor his journeys to the West, nor the Roman episcopate, nor that this had been entrusted to him by Peter before his death. But of Paul, as one who, after Peter was taken away, laboured most of all, was brought to the chariot of the west [ἐπὶ τὸ ἅρμα τῆς δύσεως] to the borders of the West, or to Rome, as teacher of the whole world, and suffered under the emperors, namely Nero, his discourse is fuller and more emphatic. From this it can not unreasonably be concluded that this Clement was ignorant of Peter's journey to the chariot of the west, of his traversing the whole world, and of the place of Peter's martyrdom, perhaps completed in the East, and of the other circumstances. In the same way, the testimony of Irenaeus which they produce, that both apostles equally founded the Roman Church, laid its first foundations, governed it together, and at last handed over the episcopate to Linus with equal power, says the first point, which Bellarmine here attributes to Peter, does not hold. And other witnesses, Dionysius of Corinth, Caius, Tertullian, Origen, Epiphanius, make everything common to both, and sometimes give the praise of founding to Paul alone. Likewise the witness Pseudo-Clement attests that the Roman Church was founded by a third, namely Barnabas, and was already gathered at Rome before the coming of Simon, against whom Peter came to fight, and he bears witness at the same time to other things that agree poorly with Papist suppositions. Likewise Tertullian, another witness, in the same place where he speaks of Peter, adds a fourth founder, John, whom he was the first of all to report as plunged into boiling oil at Rome, and, when he suffered nothing, relegated to an island (a sure sign of falsehood). And these things, along with many others, ought to draw the Papists away from the accepted belief in Peter's coming and so many years' sojourn.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Nos autem præter Scripturarum silentium, & ea, quæ in illis Petri in urbe præsentiæ aperte contrariari videntur, & alia jam saltem indigitata, porrò ab assensu retrahit multiplex authorum talia de Petro tradentium in enarrandis circumstantiis discordia. Cui quidem mederi conatur Bellarminus, dicendo, sæpissimè accidere, ut constet de re, & non constet de modo, vel alia circumstantia; Sed frustrà. Nam etiamsi res certa esse possit, cujus modus ignoratur, de cujus etiam circumstantiis nonnullis haud constat, ut ex Scripturis quidem certissimum est, (in quibus exemplis Bellarminus subsidium quæritur;) Christum mortuum fuisse, fuisse Reges Persarum, Saulem, Samuelem, & mundum esse conditum, & impletas esse Danielis septimanas, licèt omnes, temporis etiam, circumstantiæ à Divinis Scriptoribus non recenseantur distinctè, & alii de tempore dissentiant, tamen ubi certitudo de re ipsa ex Scriptura non tantum non habetur, sed potius illa Scripturae manifeste repugnare videtur, quemadmodum illud circa hanc quæstionem hactenus ostendimus, & accedit non tantum de circumstantiis nonnullis quorundam silentium, sed & primorum etiam authorum inter se pugna, certè res talis eò magis rejicienda videtur.
units.tr: But we, besides the silence of the Scriptures and those things which seem clearly to contradict Peter's presence in the city, and the other points already pointed out, are further held back from assent by the manifold disagreement of authors who hand down such things about Peter in relating the circumstances. Bellarmine tries to remedy this, saying that it very often happens that it is established concerning the thing, but not concerning the manner or some other circumstance. But in vain. For even if a thing may be certain whose manner is unknown, and about whose circumstances some are not clear, as is certain from the Scriptures (in which examples Bellarmine seeks help): that Christ died, that there were kings of the Persians, Saul, Samuel, that the world was created, and that Daniel's weeks were fulfilled, although all the circumstances, even of time, are not recounted distinctly by the divine writers, and others disagree about the time, nevertheless where certainty about the thing itself is not only not had from Scripture, but rather that very Scripture seems manifestly to contradict it, as we have hitherto shown concerning this question, and where there is not merely silence about some circumstances on the part of certain writers but also conflict among the earliest authors themselves, surely such a matter seems all the more to be rejected.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ast quot & quantæ hic Authorum in circumstantiis, etiam præcipuis, pugnæ! Contradictiones quoque! Non jam leviora attingam, non in ipsis historiæ circumstantiis præcipuis circumstantiarum minorum inconvenientia & contraria, qualia sine fineferè in solo cum Simone Mago certamine Clarissimus Spanhemius Differt.III. §.20. exhibet; Non magna illa de primis Successoribus dissidia suo loco plenius tradenda. Ex illis tantùm, quæ de adventûs tempore & morte habent Authores, nonnulla diversa, pugnantia adducere lubet. Quoad adventûs in urbem tempus Fastis Siculis anno 18. Tiberii Romæ Petrus Episcopus constitutus dicitur, ut Marcus Alexandriæ, Hierosolymis Jacobus. Sub Cajo Arabes Petrum Romam adiisse volunt. Antiquissimus Codex apud Blondellum, sub Consulatu Vinutii Quartini, id est, annis 12. ante. 2. Claudii, Marcellinus Comes (notante Scaligero) biennio ante tempus assignatum in Latino Eusebii, venisse ait. In Græco Eusebii, quem edidit Joh. Scaliger, legitur, anno Chr.40. Romam ivisse Petrum, qui foret Caji ultimus, ad summum Claudii primus. Orosius certius nihil habens in exordio Imperii Claudii id factum esse testatur simpliciter; Communis est opinio, secundo Claudii anno factum esse; Sed Valesium, Petrum ante quartum annum Claudii Romam proficisci non potuisse, testantem jam audivimus; In quem etiam annum Petri in urbem adventum conjicit post Marianum Scotum Author Fasciculi Temporum; Imò Beda in Act.XV. idem fecit, idem etiam Waldensis T.1. Doctr. fid. l. 1. art.1.c.7. Franciscus autem Horantius l.6.c.12. cont. Calv. Inst. quinto Claudii anno advenisse dicit, dum, advenisse decimo quinto post Christum passum anno. Tardiorem adventum facere videtur Th. Aquinas, in Gal. 2. lect.1. dum decimo quarto post Pauli conversionem anno profectionem Petri tribuit. Passionale verò de Vitis Sanctorum adventum illum in decimum tertium Claudii rejicit. Damasus, aut, si quis malit, Anastasius, in Pontificali demum sub Nerone contigisse, adfirmat; Origenes T. 3. in Genes. vitæ finem Petri innuit. Denuò & hîc addi meretur, ante Concilium, juxta Onuphrium & Halloixium ne quidem Antiochiæ Petrum fuisse. Ut autem supra ne unum quidem horum verisimilitudinem post Scripturarum considerationem habere, ostendimus, ita in specie hîc omnes illos post secundum Claudii annum incipientes numerum 25. annorum destruere notamus,id quod & Bellarminus & omnes agnoscere debent, illo etiam ex eo fundamento Fasciculum temporis & Scotum rejiciente, tanquam sibi & veritati non constantes. Sed quomodo in re tam incerta certi esse potuissent? De 25. annis autem,quot in Chronico Eusebiano etiam Antiochiæ Olymp. CCIII. A.IV. secundum Parisiensem Michaëlis Sonnii & Basilienses editiones tribuuntur, eos Chronico isti ab Hieronymo insertos fuisse, Doctissimus Jos. Scaliger Animadv. in Eus. pag.189. probat, suum ei etiam assensum addente Valesio. Illos autem non minùs tollunt, qui septennalem Episcopatum Antiochenum præponunt ; Immò omnes, qui causam adventûs expugnationem Simonis Magi faciunt, qui, si Romæ fuisset, nonnisi postremis Neronis temporibus victus & oppressus esset, cui intimum fuisse, & propter cujus occisionem Petrum in odium Neronis incurrisse, & in carcerem conjectum, & morte mulctatum esse Hegesippus l.3. c.2. tradit ; quamvis jam sub Claudio sublatum esse, Valesius ex Eusebio l.2.c.15. contendat. Quis autem credat, vel 25. annis ad istam victoriam opus fuisse,aut Petrum nondum debellato Simone tam longinqua & longa itinera suscepturum fuisse? Sed itáne fieri potest ut incertus sit numerus tam mysticus (qui radix quadrata est, extracto ex numero Apocalyptico 666. idemque impariter impar & infaustus) & singulari semper ratione in Romana Ecclesia conspicuus, quemadmodum Franc. Potterus Explic. Num. Bestia ingeniosissimè ostendit; & secundùm quem primitùs 25. Tituli à Marcello instituti, Presbyteri 25. Basilicæ, seu templa Baptismalia 25. Valesio etiam observante, quòd, cùm singuli Presbyteri suas regerent Basilicas, quot fuerunt Presbyteri, totidem Basilicas fuisse dicendum sit. Hinc Paroeciæ 25. imò ex Onuphr. de Tit. & de Civit. Rom. urbis portæ 25. addità ab ipso portâ triumphali ad 24. portas Plinii. Prout etiam nefas est,ullum Papam annos Petri excedere.
units.tr: XXXVIII. But how many and how great are the conflicts of authors here, even about principal circumstances! Contradictions too! I shall not touch on lesser matters, nor on the minor inconsistencies and contradictions within the principal circumstances of the history, of the kind which the most distinguished Spanheim, in Dissertation III, §20, sets out almost endlessly in the contest with Simon Magus alone. Nor on those great disagreements about the first successors, which are to be set out more fully in their place. I wish to adduce only some of the diverse and conflicting points which the authors give concerning the time of his coming and his death. As to the time of his coming to the city, in the Sicilian Fasti, in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, Peter is said to have been made bishop at Rome, just as Mark at Alexandria and James at Jerusalem. Under Caius, the Arabs want Peter to have come to Rome. The most ancient codex, in Blondel, under the consulship of Vinucius Quartinus, that is, in the twelfth year before the second of Claudius, says that Marcellinus Comes (as Scaliger notes) came two years before the time assigned in the Latin of Eusebius. In the Greek of Eusebius, which John Scaliger edited, it is read that in the year of Christ 40 Peter went to Rome, being the last of Caius, at the latest the first of Claudius. Orosius, having nothing more certain, simply testifies that this happened at the beginning of the reign of Claudius. The common opinion is that it happened in the second year of Claudius; but Valesius, who has already been heard testifying that Peter could not have set out for Rome before the fourth year of Claudius, also places Peter's coming to the city in that year, after Marianus Scotus, the author of the Fasciculus Temporum. Indeed Bede did the same on Acts 15, and so did Waldensis, in Doctrina fidei vol. 1, book 1, art. 1, ch. 7. Francis Horantius, in book 6, ch. 12, against Calvin's Institutes, says that he came in the fifth year of Claudius, while elsewhere he says he came in the fifteenth year after Christ's passion. Thomas Aquinas seems to make the coming later, when on Galatians 2, lecture 1, he assigns Peter's journey to the fourteenth year after Paul's conversion. But the Passionale de Vitis Sanctorum puts that coming in the thirteenth year of Claudius. Damasus, or, if anyone prefers, Anastasius, in the Pontificale, affirms that it happened only under Nero; Origen, in vol. 3 on Genesis, hints at the end of Peter's life. Here too it deserves to be added that, according to Onuphrius and Halloix, Peter was not even at Antioch before the Council. But as above we have shown that not one of these has any likelihood after consideration of the Scriptures, so here in particular we note that all of those who begin after the second year of Claudius destroy the number of twenty-five years, which Bellarmine and everyone must acknowledge, while also rejecting the Fasciculus temporum and Scotus on this foundation, as not consistent with themselves or with the truth. But how could they have been certain in a matter so uncertain? As for the twenty-five years, which are attributed to the Chronicle of Eusebius, also of Antioch, Olympiad 203, year 4, according to the Parisian edition of Michael Sonnius and the Basel editions, that these were inserted into that Chronicle by Jerome, the most learned Joseph Scaliger proves in his Animadversions on Eusebius, p. 189, with Valesius adding his assent. But those who put a seven-year episcopate at Antioch remove them no less; indeed all who make the reason for his coming the overthrow of Simon Magus, which, if it had happened at Rome, would have been overcome and crushed only in the last times of Nero, and to whom Peter was intimate, and on account of whose killing Peter incurred Nero's hatred, and was thrown into prison and punished with death, as Hegesippus, book 3, ch. 2, relates; although Valesius, from Eusebius, book 2, ch. 15, contends that it had already been done away with under Claudius. But who would believe that even twenty-five years were needed for that victory, or that Peter, with Simon not yet defeated, would undertake such long and distant journeys? But can it be that the number is uncertain, so mystical (being the square root, extracted from the apocalyptic number 666, and at the same time equally odd and unlucky), and always conspicuous in the Roman Church by a singular reckoning, as Francis Potter ingeniously shows in his Explication of the Number of the Beast? And according to which, originally, 25 titles were instituted by Marcellus, 25 presbyters, 25 basilicas or baptismal churches; Valesius also observes that, since each presbyter governed his own basilica, there must be said to have been as many basilicas as there were presbyters. Hence 25 parishes, and indeed, according to Onuphrius, On the Titles and On the Cities of Rome, 25 gates of the city, the gate by the Triumphal Arch being added to the 24 gates of Pliny. Likewise it is wrong for any pope to exceed the years of Peter.

units.la: XXXIX. Mortem quod attinet, Ambrosius Serm.66. de Petro & Paulo ait,utrumque simul uno die & loco & sub uno judice passos esse; Quod etiam confirmat hymnus Romanus: Quomodo in vita se dilexerunt,ita in morte non separati fuerunt. Linus contrà in lib. de
units.tr: XXXIX. As for the manner of death, Ambrose, in Sermon 66 on Peter and Paul, says that the two suffered together on one day, in one place and under one judge. The Roman hymn confirms this: As they loved one another in life, so in death they were not separated. Linus, on the other hand, in his book on

units.la: Speciatim quoad mortem Petri, de pass. Pet. & Paul. non uno die, nec eodem loco, nec etiam ejusdem Tyranni sententiâ id factum esse adfirmat, ideò à Bellarmino etiam rej.ctus, & omnino rejiciendus cum multis aliis scriptis similibus, quæ primis Papis tribuuntur, sed proin etiam rejiciendus quoad illud, de Episcopatu Petri; Alii cum Hieron. Cat. in Paulo, eundem diem & annum assignant, sed diversa loca & supplicii genera; Alii eundem diem, sed anni vertentis; Si autem Eutychio l. cit. credimus, Petrus sub extrema Claudii, & annis, ante vulgarem opinionem, 13. vel 14. martyrii coronam accepit. Clementem etiam audivimus, qui Petrum præmissum esse præsuppofuit. Ut vetustissimus Patricii author, quasi ex Justino & Irenæo, Paulum iφ' ἑλοις ἑπτα πέντε, totis quinque annis subsecutum esse, tradidit. Fuit autem Petrus, juxta Bellarminum & Genebrardum, annos 87. natus, quando mortuus est, & tamen paulò ante tam multa, & tam molesta, & tam longinqua, & quasi continua itinera confecit! Mortis autem circumstantiæ plurimæ à tertii, quarti, quinti & sequentium seculorum scriptoribus demum repertæ fuerunt. Quoad reliquias se habere utriusque Apostoli corpora dicunt, sed separata & partem dimidiam in Petri, alteram in Pauli templo, libravisse autem Sylvestrum, ut utrobique pars æqualis esset; Interim tamen etiam capita tantum Romæ, dentem unum separatim, ossa ubique fere esse perhibent, Pictavii rursus Petri cum barba mandibulum, Treveris ossa multa, Argentinæ Pauli humerum, Genevæ Petri cerebrum; Calvinus autem de reliquiis ait, pumicem ejus loco repertum esse. Incerta igitur omnia & valdè incerta, ipse etiam in urbem adventus valdè incertus est, si non manifeste falsus. Quod & agnoverunt diversis temporibus ex ipsa communione Pontificia Viri Doctissimi haud pauci, quorum nonnulli velut Joh. Baptista Mantuanus, Michaël Cæsenas, Marsilius Patavinus, Johannes Aventinus, Johannes Lelandus, Carolus Molinæus, dubiâ etiam traditionis fide adducti, B. Petrum unquam Romæ, nedum Ecclesiæ ejus fundatorem & per 25. annos Episcopum fuisse, partim multum ambigunt, partim aperte, productis etiam rationibus minimè contemnendis, inficiantur.
units.tr: Concerning the death of Peter in particular, the book De passione Petri et Pauli asserts that it did not happen on one day, in one place, or under the same tyrant's sentence. For this reason Bellarmine rejected it, and it must be rejected entirely, along with many other writings of this kind that are ascribed to the first popes; and so it must also be rejected on the point about Peter's episcopate. Others, with Jerome in the Catalogue under Paul, assign the same day and year but different places and kinds of punishment. Others assign the same day but in a different year. If we believe Eutychius, loc. cit., Peter received the crown of martyrdom under the end of Claudius, and in the thirteenth or fourteenth year before the commonly accepted date. We have also heard Clement, who assumed that Peter went on ahead. The very ancient author of the Patrician [writing], as if drawing on Justin and Irenaeus, handed down that Paul followed him after five years, in all five years. Yet, according to Bellarmine and Genebrardus, Peter was eighty-seven years old when he died, and shortly before that he undertook so many, so troublesome and so long journeys, almost continuous ones! Moreover, most of the circumstances of his death were first discovered by writers of the third, fourth, fifth and later centuries. As for relics, they say that the bodies of both apostles are present, but separated: half in Peter's temple and the other half in Paul's, and that Sylvester balanced the shares so that each place had an equal part. Meanwhile they also say that the heads alone are at Rome, one tooth separately, and bones almost everywhere: at Poitiers a jawbone of Peter with his beard, at Trier many bones, at Strasbourg a shoulder of Paul, at Geneva the brain of Peter. Calvin, however, says of the relics that a pumice stone was found in their place. Everything, then, is uncertain and very uncertain; even his arrival in the city is very uncertain, if it is not manifestly false. Quite a few learned men within the Papist communion itself have recognised this at various times. Some of them, such as Giovanni Battista Mantuano, Michele Cesena, Marsilio of Padua, Johannes Aventinus, John Leland and Charles Molinaeus, though drawn on by the doubtful reliability of tradition, either greatly doubt or openly deny, partly with reasons that are by no means to be despised, that Blessed Peter was ever at Rome, let alone that he was the founder of its church and bishop there for twenty-five years.

units.la: XL. Sed fuerit Romæ Petrus, aliquoties illuc venerit, multum ibi ad fidelium ædificationem fecerit, ibi etiam mortem gloriosam obierit; Quid inde? Fuit & alibi, Antiochiæ, ut volunt, per septennium, & ante profectionem Romanam mori facile potuisset alibi, mors non nobilitat locum, & sic nobilissima foret Hierosolyma. De præsentia recte ait Baronius, ad an. 39. n. 16. Si præsentia Petri quamlibet Ecclesiam primariam effecisset, tot essent numeranda sedes Patriarchales (Monarchicæ,) quot à Petro fuerunt institutæ; Sed multæ ab ipso institutæ sunt, infinitæ ferè juxta illos, in ipso itinere Romano in Asia, Sicilia, Calabria, ac ditione Neapolitana. Brundusium, sic ait Leo Allatius de Perp. Conf. l. 1. c. 5. n. 11. Hydruntum, Tarentum, Regium, Sicilia, Neapolis, hujus profectionis & prædicationis vestigia non errabunda, sed infallibilia tenent atque inconcussa. Baronius quoque ad an. 44. n. 28. celebrem locorum memoriam celebrat, Neapolis, Liberni, Pisarum, ubi Petrus iter faciens missam celebrásse feratur. Addit tamen: De rebus tam antiquis, tam incertis, quid potissimum affirmare debeamus, non satis constat. Sic etiam post adventum in urbe diversis profectionibus in mediam Hispaniam & tandem ad toto divisos orbe Britannos ultimúmque Occidentem penetrâsse volunt, & Hispaniæ quidem imagines Antiochenas (unde virgo Madrittana de Atocha) intulisse, in Britannia verò longo tempore moratum esse, multas gentes non nominatas ad Christi fidem attraxisse, Ecclesias constituisse, Episcopos, Presbyteros & Diaconos ordinasse, Ecclesiam etiam Westmonasteriensem dedicasse, pari quoad omnia incertitudine. Certa autem illa sunt, utpote in Scripturis divinis consignata, Hierosolymæ, in Judæa, Galilæa, Samaria, Lyddæ, Joppæ, Cæsareæ, Antiochiæ, Babylone, Petrum fuisse; certum illud etiam, jam seculo secundo illâ ipsâ Petri ac Pauli præsentiâ Hierosolymam, Cæsaream, Antiochiam superbiisse, eandem Corinthum jactâsse, & Alexandriam, & Babylonem; uti Marcum, ita Petrum quoque fundatorem prædicantes. Quid igitur? Omnes istæ Regiones & Urbes primatum habebunt, ob Petri præsentiam? Vel annon idem Petrus alibi prædicavit, qui & Romæ prædicásse dicitur? An forte minori cum studio, fide, & diligentiâ opus Domini alibi promovit? Etiam ubi diutiùs substitisse videtur, quàm Romæ? Et unde colligitur, Romam potiùs ex præsentia ista, ut Monarchica sedes fieret, lucratam esse?
units.tr: XL. But suppose Peter was at Rome, came there several times, did much there for the building up of the faithful, and died there a glorious death. What follows from that? He was also elsewhere, at Antioch, as they claim, for seven years; and he could easily have died somewhere else before his journey to Rome. Death does not ennoble a place, or else Jerusalem would be most noble. Baronius rightly says concerning presence, at the year 39, no. 16: If the presence of Peter had made any church the chief one, then as many patriarchal (monarchical) sees would have to be counted as were founded by Peter. But many were founded by him, indeed almost countless ones according to them, on his very journey to Rome, in Asia, Sicily, Calabria and the territory of Naples. Brundisium, as Leo Allatius says in On the Perpetuity of the Confession, book 1, ch. 5, no. 11: Hydruntum, Tarentum, Rhegium, Sicily, Naples keep the traces of this journey and preaching, not wandering but infallible and unshaken. Baronius too, at the year 44, no. 28, celebrates the famous memory of places: Naples, Liburnum, Pisa, where Peter is said to have celebrated Mass while on his journey. He adds, however: It is not sufficiently clear what we ought chiefly to affirm about things so ancient and so uncertain. So too, after his arrival in the city, they want him to have made various journeys into the interior of Spain and finally to have penetrated to the Britons, scattered across the world, and to the furthest West, and to have brought the Antiochene images of Spain (whence the Virgin of Atocha at Madrid), and to have stayed a long time in Britain, drawn many unnamed peoples to the faith of Christ, established churches, ordained bishops, presbyters and deacons, and even dedicated the church at Westminster, with equal uncertainty in all these things. Certain, however, are those things that are recorded in the divine Scriptures: that Peter was at Jerusalem, in Judaea, Galilee, Samaria, Lydda, Joppa, Caesarea, Antioch and Babylon. It is also certain that already in the second century, by that very presence of Peter and Paul, Jerusalem, Caesarea and Antioch took pride, Corinth boasted, and Alexandria and Babylon did too, each claiming its own founder, Mark in the one case and Peter in the other. What then? Will all these regions and cities have primacy because of Peter's presence? Or did the same Peter not also preach elsewhere, although he is said to have preached at Rome? Or did he perhaps promote the work of the Lord elsewhere with less zeal, faith and diligence? Even in places where he seems to have stayed longer than at Rome? And from where is it inferred that Rome gained, by this presence, to become a monarchical see rather than others?

units.la: XLI. Ex morte, ajunt; Primatum Romanorum Pontificum, inquit Allatius de Perpet. l. c. c. 2. n. 7. morte suâ fundavit. Morte? Sed cur & quomodo? Quid si alibi mortuus fuisset Petrus? Si in itinere quodam? Si Româ Ostium, vel Albam, vel Prænestam, vel Spoletum ad supplicium adductus fuisset? Num hinc Pontificatûs supremi jura locis illis data, natáque credidissent antiquitus, aut contendere de Primatu hæc ipsa jure potuissent? Vel, annon potius absurdum censeri debet, locorum dignitatem Ecclesiasticam à persequentium injustitia arcessere? Et si Romanus fuit Petrus, & Romam perpetuò nobilitavit ob mortem, & martyrii cruciatus ibi exantlatos, quid non de aliis locis ubi Apostoli morte suâ Deum glorificârunt, censeri debet? Et ubi Pontifices alii mortui sunt? Et speciatim de Hierosolyma, quæ hîc primas sibi vendicare potest, ex Matth.XXIII.34 &c. Et ubi Christus ipse, magnus animarum nostrarum Pastor, vitam salutari morte clausit! Certè non malè olim Græci ex eo contra Latinos inferebant, Nilus nempe Thessalonicensis, Barlaam Monachus, Macarius Ancyranus, & alii; Si argumentum à loco mortis virorum in Ecclesia illustrium valeret, Hierosolymitanum fore; Τοσῳτον μεἰζονα τῆς Ῥώμης. ὅσον καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ‖ Πέτρου; Tanto majorem Romano, quanto Christus major fuerit Petro.
units.tr: XLI. From his death, they say. Allatius, On the Perpetuity, loc. cit., ch. 2, no. 7, says that the primacy of the Roman pontiffs was founded by his death. By his death? But why, and how? What if Peter had died somewhere else? On a journey? What if he had been led from Rome to Ostia, or Alba, or Praeneste, or Spoleto for execution? Would they have believed that the rights of supreme pontificate were granted to those places and born there in antiquity, or could they have contended about the primacy on this very ground? Or ought it rather to be judged absurd to derive the ecclesiastical dignity of a place from the injustice of its persecutors? And if Peter was Roman, and ennobled Rome forever by his death and the torments of martyrdom endured there, what ought not to be judged about other places where the apostles glorified God by their death? And where other popes died? And especially about Jerusalem, which can claim first place here, from Matthew 23:34 etc. And where Christ himself, the great Shepherd of our souls, closed his life by a saving death! Certainly the Greeks used to argue against the Latins from this, and not badly: Nilus of Thessalonica, the monk Barlaam, Macarius of Ancyra, and others. If an argument from the place of death of men illustrious in the Church were valid, Jerusalem would be the greater: Τοσοῦτον μείζονα τῆς Ῥώμης, ὅσον καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς Πέτρου [So much greater than Rome, as Christ is greater than Peter].

units.la: XLII. Sed Petrus fuit Romanus Episcopus; De eo jam videndum est; Vidimus in præcedentibus de Apostolici muneris ratione nonnulla, nimirum Apostolos universales fuisse, non affirmative, sed negative, id est, nulli Ecclesiae particulari affixos fuisse, & potestatem habuisse omnibus prædicandi habitualem & potentiale, utpote quibus dictum fuerit: Euntes docete omnes gentes &c. Et quidem talibus, etiam extraordinariâ & supremâ potestate prædictis, nullíque certo loco alligatis illo tempore, ut sermo Domini curreret, maximè opus fuit.
units.tr: XLII. But Peter was the Roman bishop; this must now be examined. We have seen in what precedes some points about the nature of the apostolic office, namely that the apostles were universal, not affirmatively but negatively, that is, that they were attached to no particular church, and that they had a habitual and potential power of preaching to all, since it was said to them: Go and teach all nations, etc. Indeed, at that time, when the word of the Lord was to run its course, there was great need of such men, endowed with an extraordinary and supreme power and bound to no fixed place.

units.la: Et ita habuerunt quidem potestatem Episcopalem, id est, verbum Dei prædicandi, & Sacramenta administrandi, & possent eatenus quodammodo vocari Episcopi, quemadmodum etiam de Juda prædictum: Episcopatum ejus accipiat alius Act.I.20. & quia etiam diutius in nonnullis locis quidam commorati sunt, & peculiarem coetuum ibi collectorum curam habuerunt, hinc veteres Jacobum Hierosolymæ, Johannem Ephesi, Petrum ex hypothesi & Paulum Romæ, & Apostolicos Viros, Marcum Alexandriæ, Ananiam Damasci, Zacchæum Cæsareæ, Nicolaum Samariæ, Silam Corinthi, Barnabam Mediolani, & sic deinceps, Episcopos vocârunt; Quæ tamen non ita accurate ab iis, Apostolorum maximè respectu, dicta sunt, & ex parte surgenti Episcoporum fastui debentur, qui cùm Apostolatum sibi arrogare non possent, Apostolis in vocationis modo, munere ipso, authoritate, successione, donis & charismatis longè inferiores, sæculo à Christo alter tero & tertio ipsos jam Apostolos quasi in suum Episcopalem ordinem cogere primò videbantur.
units.tr: And so they indeed had episcopal power, that is, the power of preaching the word of God and administering the sacraments, and in this respect they could be called bishops in some sense, just as it was foretold of Judas: Let another take his bishopric, Acts 1:20. And because some of them stayed longer in certain places and had a particular care of the assemblies gathered there, the ancients accordingly called James bishop of Jerusalem, John of Ephesus, Peter (on the supposition) and Paul of Rome, and the apostolic men Mark of Alexandria, Ananias of Damascus, Zacchaeus of Caesarea, Nicolaus of Samaria, Silas of Corinth, Barnabas of Milan, and so on. These titles, however, were not used by them in so exact a sense, especially with respect to the apostles, and they are owed partly to the rising pride of bishops, who, since they could not claim the apostolate for themselves, being far inferior to the apostles in the manner of their calling, their office itself, their authority, succession, gifts and charisms, first seemed, in the second and third century after Christ, to force the apostles themselves into their own episcopal order.

units.la: XLIII. Accuratè autem loquendo non possunt certorum locorum Episcopi vocari, utpote quorum parœciæ & Diæceses tam latè patebant, quàm latè patet orbis terrarum, imò quorum totus orbis parœcia & diœcesis dici potest. Nisi quòd solicitè caverunt singuli, ne iis locis prædicarent Evangelium, in quibus ab aliis prædicatum jam fuerat, nisi forte vel obiter, vel necessaria de causa. Hinc Paulus Rom.XV.30. testatus est, se φιλοτιμὸσθαι, hoc est, penè ambitiosè studere, ne ædificaret super alienum fundamentum. Et 2.Cor.X.15. de canone suo, suo veluti districtu, sive attributo sibi à Deo spatio, & quasi area, cui Ecclesiam inædificaret, locutus est; Alioqui cap.XI.28. curam omnium Ecclesiarum sibi adscribens, tanquam ex eorum numero, quibus (ut Consulibus Imperii Romani) cura totius incumbebat, quod ad jus attinet, & potestatem, quamvis οἰκονομικῶς inter se operas partirentur, pro eo ac Evangelii propagandi ratio postulabat. Hinc etiam in locis, ad quæ veniebant, ordinarios aut invenerunt, aut statim constituerunt, illis interim cooperantes, vel soli ad tempus operantes, quemadmodum Princeps moras alicubi faciens inferioris Magistratus officium adimplere potest, ita tamen, ut nec ipse inferior fiat, nec inferiorem suo discessu ad dignitatem & potestatem Principis evehat.
units.tr: XLIII. Strictly speaking, the bishops of particular places cannot be called such, since their parishes and dioceses reached as far as the world itself, indeed each one's parish and diocese may be called the whole world. Only, each took care not to preach the gospel in places where others had already preached it, unless perhaps in passing or for some necessary reason. Hence Paul testifies (Rom. 15.30) that he was zealous [φιλοτιμούμενον], that is, almost eagerly anxious not to build upon another's foundation. And (2 Cor. 10.15) he spoke of his "rule," as it were his district, the space God had granted him, and as an area in which he would build the Church. Otherwise (2 Cor. 11.28) he claims for himself "the care of all the churches," as one of those to whom the care of the whole belonged, as consuls of the Roman Empire had charge of the whole, so far as right and power are concerned, although they divided the labours among themselves economically [οἰκονομικῶς], as the manner of spreading the gospel required. Hence also in the places to which they came, they either found or at once appointed ordinary ministers, cooperating with them meanwhile, or working alone for a time. Just as a prince who lingers somewhere can perform the duty of an inferior magistrate, yet in such a way that he himself does not become inferior, nor by his departure raise the inferior to the dignity and power of the prince.

units.la: XLIV. Applicemus jam ea, quæ hactenus de Apostolis in genere dicta sunt, Apostolo Petro; Ubicunque fuit, pro Apostolici muneris authoritate egit, nullibi pastor ordinarius, συμπρεσβύτερος, compresbyter, 1.Pet.V.1. ubique: Si Romæ fuit, ibi verbi divini ministros, quos Paulus Rom.XVI.3.7.9. memorat, aliquot invenit. Linum non infimi ordinis Authores illius Ecclesiæ Episcopum fuisse scribunt; Sic Irenæus l.3. c.3. ait: B. Apostolos (Petrum & Paulum intelligit:) Ecclesiam Romanam fundâsse, sed Episcopatum Lino tradidisse. Ruffinus autem in præfat. Recognit: Clem. ad Gaudent: scribit in hunc modum: Linus & Cletus fuerunt ante Clementem Episcopi in urbe Roma, sed superstite Petro, videlicet, ut illi Episcopatûs curam gererent, ipse verò Apostolatûs implerēt officium. Quis non videt, in his testimoniis Episcopatum ab Apostolatu accuratè distingui? Igitur, si Petrus Romæ fuit, non ibi tanquam Episcopus, tanquam Pastor ordinarius, tanquam Urbi illi addictus fuit & docuit, & extra illam urbem nihil tanquam ejus Episcopus egit, Apostolicam ubique personam gerens.
units.tr: XLIV. Let us now apply what has been said so far about the apostles in general to the apostle Peter. Wherever he was, he acted by the authority of the apostolic office. Nowhere was he an ordinary minister, a "fellow-elder" [συμπρεσβύτερος] (1 Pet. 5.1), everywhere. If he was at Rome, he found there some ministers of the divine word, whom Paul mentions (Rom. 16.3, 7, 9). Authors not of the lowest rank write that Linus was bishop of that church. Thus Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 3, says: "The blessed apostles (he means Peter and Paul) founded the Roman church, but handed over the episcopate to Linus." Rufinus, in the preface to his translation of the Recognitions of Clement, writes in this manner: "Linus and Cletus were bishops in the city of Rome before Clement, but while Peter was still living, so that they had the care of the episcopate, while he himself fulfilled the office of apostle." Who does not see that in these testimonies the episcopate is carefully distinguished from the apostolate? Therefore, if Peter was at Rome, he was not there as bishop, as ordinary minister attached to that city, teaching and ruling it. Outside that city he did nothing as its bishop, but everywhere acted as an apostle.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Qui contra eum Episcopum Romanum faciunt, primò omni rationis & Scripturarum fundamento destituuntur. Rationibus quidem nos convincere vult Bellarminus, dum l. 2. de Pont. Rom. c. 4. ita argumentatur. Si non fuit Petrus Episcopus Romae usque ad mortem, exponant adversarii, ubi Petrus sederit, ab eo tempore, quo reliquit Antiochiam. Respondemus; Petrus nullibi sedit, tanquam loci Episcopus, obambulavit potius tanquam mundi Apostolus, qui unâ cum aliis audire meruit: Ite, docete omnes gentes &c. Porrò non necesse est, ut exponamus, an Petrus Antiochiam reliquerit, ubi relictâ Antiochiâ fuerit, nec enim certè novimus, & aliorum quoque Apostolorum ultima, id de unoquoque interim facilè cogitantes, ubique locorum Domino mittenti fidelem fuisse, necesse autem est, ut illi certioribus documentis exponant, Petrum tam diu Romae tanquam Episcopum sedisse; multo minùs necesse, imò, secundùm praemissa, ne quidem conveniens est, ut Petrus tanquam Episcopus, sive Antiochiae, sive post alibi sederit. Et meritò adversariis reponimus; Si Petrus in iis locis, quibus Evangelium annuntiavit, tanquam Episcopus fuit, exponant, ubi tanquam Episcopus sederit ante illud tempus, quo Antiochiam pervenit; Fuit ibi Ecclesia, antequam illuc veniret Petrus. Fatentur illud ipsimet, fatentur & hoc, tres aut quatuor, Bellarminus, quinque annos effluxisse, antequam particularem aliquam Ecclesiam regendam suscepperit. Si autem illud ante iter Antiochenum non necessarium fuit, quomodo necessarium fuit postea! Et quomodo profin non ineptè argumentatur Bellarminus! maximè quia concedit, potuisse Petrum nunquam particularem Ecclesiam regendam suscipere! Exponant etiam, ubi ipse Jacobus frater Johannis, ubi Andreas, ubi Apostoli alii tanquam Episcopi caeterorum locorum sederint, vel det nobis rationem, cur Petrus certi loci Episcopus esse debuerit, non item alii Apostoli; Si non potest, desinat, tanquam rem absurdam urgere; Num ergò dicemus, Petrum non fuisse ullius loci Episcopum?
units.tr: Those who make Peter bishop of Rome against this first lack every foundation of reason and Scripture. Bellarmine tries to convince us by argument, when in book 2 On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 4, he reasons thus: "If Peter was not bishop of Rome until his death, let our opponents explain where Peter sat from the time he left Antioch." We reply: Peter nowhere sat as bishop of a place. He wandered rather as an apostle of the whole world, who with the others deserved to hear: "Go, teach all nations," and so on. Moreover, it is not necessary for us to explain whether Peter left Antioch, or where he was after leaving it. For we certainly do not know, and, thinking easily meanwhile of each of the other apostles too, we suppose that the last of them was faithful wherever the Lord sent him. But it is necessary that they explain, by more certain evidence, how Peter sat at Rome as bishop for so long. Much less necessary, indeed (according to what has been premised), it is not even fitting, that Peter as bishop sat either at Antioch or elsewhere afterwards. And we rightly reply to the opponents: if Peter was bishop in those places to which he proclaimed the gospel, let them explain where he sat as bishop before the time when he came to Antioch. There was a church there before Peter came. They themselves admit this, and they admit also this: Bellarmine concedes that three or four, even five years, passed before Peter undertook the government of any particular church. But if that was not necessary before the journey to Antioch, how was it necessary afterwards? And how foolishly Bellarmine argues! Especially since he concedes that Peter might never have taken up the government of a particular church! Let them also explain where James, the brother of John, where Andrew, where the other apostles sat as bishops of other places. Or let them give us a reason why Peter must have been bishop of a certain place, but not the other apostles. If they cannot, let them stop pressing it as an absurd thing: "Shall we then say that Peter was not bishop of any place?"

units.la: XLVI. Addit, nos illud dicere non posse, quia velimus Petrum non fuisse Episcopum universalis Ecclesiae, sed alicujus tantùm particularis. Si id vellemus, quodammodo nobis incumberet designare particularem illam Ecclesiam; Sed quis Bellarmino dixit, nos id velle? Volumus contrà, Petrum fuisse universalis Ecclesiae Episcopum, non quidem quasi totam Ecclesiam actu docuerit, aut in totam actu supremam, eámque Monarchicam potestatem exercuerit (quod volunt adversarii:) sed quatenus non peculiari cuidam Ecclesiæ affixus fuit, & prout jam explicavimus, ubique secundùm providentiæ divinæ ductum docere potuit, & hinc etiam nolumus eum alligare Urbi unicæ, valdè interim mirantes, eum unicæ urbi alligari, ejúsque Episcopum vocari ab illis, qui eum vel maximè actu universalem fuisse, ac proin universali peculiare, orbi urbem æquipollere contendunt. Nos certè Petrum particularem Episcopum fuisse credimus, quemadmodum de Johanne & Jacobo, quos particulares fuisse non credimus, & licèt duo isti ob peculiares apud Ecclesias Hierosolymitanam & Ephesinam curas à veteribus non-nunquam illarum Episcopi dicantur, illud tamen, ne cum munere Apostolico pugnet, non ita strictè accipiendum est, ac si non etiam extra illas Ecclesias potestatem & curas habuerint, potestatem extraordinariam, curas Apostolicas, quarum respectu cùm eis alii non successerint, idem de Petro, si vel maximè Romæ fuisset, & peculiarem Ecclesiæ ibi collectæ curam habuisset, dicendum foret; De quo contra, post ea, quæ dicta & probata sunt, neutiquam tenemur indicare, quò, si fuerit Romæ Episcopus, & postea sedem mutârit, eam transtulerit. Non fuit, non mutavit, non transtulit.
units.tr: XLVI. He adds that "we cannot say that," because we wish "Peter not to have been bishop of the universal Church, but only of some particular one." If we wished that, we would in some way be bound to name that particular church. But who told Bellarmine that we wish it? On the contrary, we hold that Peter was bishop of the universal Church. Not indeed as if he actually taught the whole Church, or actually exercised supreme and monarchical power over the whole (which our opponents want), but in so far as he was not attached to any particular church, and, as we have already explained, could teach everywhere according to the guidance of divine providence. For this reason we also do not wish to tie him to the one city, while we marvel greatly that he should be tied to one city, and that his bishop should be called such by those who contend that he was most of all actually universal, and therefore that the city is equivalent to the world, which belongs to the universal. Certainly we believe Peter was a particular bishop, just as we do not believe John and James were particular. Although these two are sometimes called by the ancients bishops of those churches, because of their particular cares for the churches of Jerusalem and Ephesus, that nonetheless, lest it conflict with the apostolic office, must not be taken so strictly as if they had no power and cares outside those churches: extraordinary power, apostolic cares. Since others did not succeed them in respect of these, the same must be said of Peter, even if he had been at Rome and had had a particular care of the church gathered there. Concerning this, on the other hand, after what has been said and proved, we are by no means bound to indicate whither he moved his see, if he was bishop at Rome and afterwards changed it. He was not, he did not change it, he did not transfer it.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Scripturas quod attinet, si juxta præcedentia de adventu Petri in urbem silent, multò magis de ejus in urbe Episcopatu. Adscribit quidem Bellarminus l. c. c. 12. eum modò nutui, modò jussu, modò inspirationi Christi. Sed in Scripturis nequidem de facto constat, multò minùs de facti causis istis; Nutus non satis certus locum remotum, ut erat tum Roma, non satis certò designat; De inspiratione pro Episcopatûs erectione nihil plane constat; Mandatum Divinum expressum ex ipsis Pontificiis non pauci negant expresse; Quod autem l. c. Bellarminus putat, non esse improbabile, Dominum etiam aperte jussisse, ut sedem suam figeret Roma Petrus; illud Scripturæ valdè improbabile reddunt; imò, quemadmodum ostendimus, falsitatis aperte convincunt; Bellarminus modò ut probabile perhibet. Ast certum planè esse deberet, si de fide esse deberet, & quod huic Episcopatui Petri superstruitur; Certum esse deberet ex Scripturis Sacris, in quibus, fatente ipso Bellarmino de Verbo Dei l. 4. c. 11. omnia necessaria & utilia ab Apostolis scripta sunt; Et merito hic adhibemus alia quoque ipsius Bellarmini verba ad probandum, quòd Apostoli non ex mandato ducti scripserint,l. c. c.4. adducta, sed paululùm hìc immutata : Si Christo & Petro fuisset propositum, Episcopatum talem erigendi, inprimis rem tanti momenti Christus certè præcepisset, & Petrus alicubi testaretur, se ex Domini mandato sedem Romæ collocâsse.
units.tr: As for the Scriptures, if they are silent about Peter's coming to the city, they are much more silent about his episcopate there. Bellarmine indeed, in the same place, chapter 12, says that he came now by a nod, now by command, now by the inspiration of Christ. But Scripture does not establish even the fact, much less the causes of the fact. A nod does not sufficiently clearly designate a remote place such as Rome then was. Nothing at all is certain about an inspiration to erect an episcopate. An express divine command, many Papists themselves expressly deny. As for what Bellarmine in the same place thinks, that it is not improbable that the Lord also openly commanded Peter to fix his see at Rome, this makes it highly improbable from Scripture, and indeed, as we have shown, it clearly convicts it of falsehood. Bellarmine presents it only as probable. But it ought to be quite certain, if it were a matter of faith, and if this episcopate of Peter is built upon it. It ought to be certain from the Holy Scriptures, in which, as Bellarmine himself admits, in De Verbo Dei l. 4. c. 11., all things necessary and useful were written by the Apostles. Rightly here we also bring in other words of Bellarmine himself, cited l. c. c. 4. and slightly altered here, to prove that the Apostles did not write under command: If it had been purposed by Christ and Peter to erect such an episcopate, Christ would certainly have commanded first of all a matter of such moment, and Peter would have testified somewhere that he set up his see at Rome by the Lord's command.

units.la: XLVIII. Secundò minùs convenit Petri Episcopatus cum quibusdam, quas Monarchici adoptant, antiquorum narrationibus.
units.tr: XLVIII. Secondly, Peter's episcopate agrees less well with certain accounts of the ancients, which the Monarchians adopt.

units.la: Narrant quippe, Petrum Romam properâsse, ut Simonem Magum ibi debellaret; Occasionem igitur habuit factum Petri ex facto Simonis, nec illum id in animo habuisse, ut vel maximè à Deo jussus Episcopatûs sedem ibi stabiliret, facilè credi debet. Narrant porrò, Christum Petro ab urbe discedenti apparuisse, eique ad interrogationem: Domine, quò vadis? respondisse, se Romam ire, ut ibi denuò crucifigeretur; ex quo Petrus intellexerit, sibi Romam redeundum, ibique moriendum esse. Non igitur Petri mens fuit, Romæ perpetuò manere, multò minùs, eum ibi jam ab initio Episcopalem Cathedram occupâsse, dici potest; Et obliquum Domini mandatum fingunt, non ad eam demum erigendam, sed ad moriendum simpliciter.
units.tr: For they relate that Peter hurried to Rome to defeat Simon Magus there. The occasion of Peter's deed therefore came from Simon's deed, and it is easy to believe that he had no intention, even if commanded by God most of all, of establishing an episcopal see there. Moreover they relate that Christ appeared to Peter as he was leaving the city, and that to his question, Lord, where are you going?, Christ replied that he was going to Rome to be crucified there again; from this Peter understood that he had to return to Rome and die there. So it was not Peter's purpose to remain at Rome permanently, much less can it be said that he had already occupied an episcopal chair there from the beginning. And they invent an indirect command of the Lord, not to erect a see at all, but simply to die.

units.la: XLIX. Tertiò sic Petrum multis modis contumeliâ afficiunt; qui de honore ejus maximè solliciti videri volunt.. Nam
units.tr: XLIX. Thirdly, they dishonour Peter in many ways, though they want to appear most concerned for his honour. For

units.la: 1. Orbis Doctorem ad eas angustias redigunt, ut ex Apostolo Ecclesiae Romanae particularis Pastorem & Episcopum faciant. Id quod in appendice Nili Thessalonicensis de primatu Papæ in initio disceptationis cujusdam Græcum inter & Cardinales Romanos habitæ ipsis etiam valdè exprobratur; Ibi enim, Cardinalibus pertendentibus, Petrum fuisse primum Ecclesiae Romanae Pastorem, respondetur: Si aquis animis audire velitis; id quod vos veluti honoris causâ de coryphæo Apostolorum adfertis, in contrarium potius vergere intelligetis. Primum quidem, quòd totius orbis Doctorem & magistrum, qui prædicationis suæ initium à Judæa fecit, Romæ autem Apostolatûs sui cursum peregit, tali vestra propositione solius Romæ magistrum fuisse statuitis. Atque ita etiam Servatoris ad illum promissionem, quam sancti Patres universaliter de omnibus, qui credidissent & credunt, interpretantur, vos ad solam Romam coarctatis, violentâque interpretatione torquetis. Quo concessso, reliquum est omninò, eam, quæ Roma est tantùm, non autem universam fidelium Ecclesiam sibi adoptâsse Servatorem, ædificationémque hujus tanquam super Petri doctrinam promisisse. At verò qui ita & sentiunt, & lo& loquuntur, qualem honorem Apostolorum Coryphaeo deferant, ipsimet considerate.
units.tr: 1. They reduce the teacher of the whole world to such narrow limits that they make him, from an apostle, the minister and bishop of the particular church of Rome. This is sharply reproached to them in the appendix of Nilus of Thessalonica on the primacy of the Pope, at the beginning of a certain disputation held between a Greek and the Roman cardinals. For when the cardinals contend that Peter was the first minister of the church of Rome, it is answered: If you will listen with calm minds, you will understand that what you bring forward about the coryphaeus of the Apostles, as if for the sake of honour, tends rather to the contrary. First, because by this proposition of yours you establish that he was the teacher only of Rome, when he was the teacher and master of the whole world, who began his preaching in Judea and completed the course of his apostleship at Rome. And so you also restrict the Saviour's promise to him, which the holy Fathers universally interpret of all who believed and believe, and you twist it by a forced interpretation to Rome alone. Granting this, it follows entirely that the Saviour adopted for himself only that church which is Rome, and not the whole church of the faithful, and promised that his building would rest upon Peter's teaching as upon this. But consider for yourselves what honour those pay to the coryphaeus of the Apostles who think and speak in this way.

units.la: L. Secundò Petrum à pactis solenniter initis turpiter resilientem, adeóque fœdisfragum faciunt. Quando enim inter Jacobum, Petrum, & Johannem ab una, Paulum & Barnabam ab altera parte Gal II. ita convenit, ut illi circumcisioni, id est, Judæis, hi vero inter Gentes prædicarent, & fœdus hoc dextrarum porrectione firmatum est, jam Petro id tribuunt isti, ut, quod Paulus tam sollicitè sibi cavendum duxerat, alieno fere semper Canoni inædificaverit, & missō, quod ei ibidem concreditum legitur, Evangelio circumcisionis, Evangelium præputii suum fecerit, in urbe Gentium per 25. annos, ut ajunt, Episcopus, & ex illa urbe gentium in extremo Occidente, ubi, si ulli Judæi, certè tunc temporis rarissimi fuerunt, Doctor & Apostolus Gentium, id est, tituli Paulini usurpator. Et certè mirari subit, quomodo Petrus, si jam ante collationem Antiochenam Divino jussu Episcopus Romæ, id est, juxta Bellarminum, urbis gentium constitutus erat, nihilominus ad Evangelium circumcisionis in pactione ista denuò transfire potuerit, id est, simul & eâdem operâ & contra Divinam institutionem agere, & fidissimis Collegis imponere. Apage autem scelesta in B. Apostolum & sanctissimum Dei conservum convitia!
units.tr: L. Secondly, they make Peter basely break away from covenants solemnly entered into, and so a breaker of faith. For when, according to Gal. 2, it was agreed between James, Peter and John on one side, and Paul and Barnabas on the other, that the former should preach to the circumcision, that is, to the Jews, and the latter among the Gentiles, and this agreement was confirmed by the giving of right hands, these men now attribute to Peter that he built, almost always, on another's rule*, which Paul had been so careful to guard against. Leaving behind the Gospel of the circumcision entrusted to him there, as we read, he made the Gospel of the foreskin his own. For 25 years, as they say, he was bishop in the city of the Gentiles, and from that city of the Gentiles, in the far West, where, if there were any Jews, there were certainly very few at that time, he was teacher and Apostle of the Gentiles, that is, a usurper of the title of Paul. And indeed one is struck with wonder how Peter, if already before the Antiochene conference he had been appointed bishop of Rome by divine command, that is, according to Bellarmine, of the city of the Gentiles, could nevertheless in that agreement pass back again to the Gospel of the circumcision. That is, at the same time and by the same act he would have acted against the divine institution and imposed on his most faithful colleagues. Away with such wicked insults against the blessed Apostle and the most holy fellow-servant of God!

units.la: L. Sic etiam pessimorum in Ecclesia, quoad Ecclesiasticas dignitates, abusuum eum primum authorem faciunt. Nam tertiò hic supponunt translationem ab uno Episcopatu ad alium, & plerique quidem, Petrum ab Episcopatu Antiocheno ad Romanum transisse volunt, Onuphrius contrà, & qui eum sequuntur, transitum ab Episcopatu Romano ad Antiochenum fingunt; Accedit Nicephorus, & l.14.c.39. asserit, Petrum sedem suam Româ Alexandriam transtulisse. Atqui constat Canonibus, ex Apostolicis, quos faciunt, decimo quarto, Niceni Concilii decimo quinto, Antiocheni vicesimo primo, translationes & transitiones ejusmodi vetari. Constat etiam, Formoso Papæ (de quo plura suo loco) à Stephano id vel primo loco vitio datum esse, quòd contra Canones ab una sede nempe à Portuensi ad aliam, ad Romanam videlicet translatus fuerit, & hoc nomine omnes ejus Ordinationes Papales, Stephani quidem judicio, nullas fuisse. Quamvis enim illâ occasione, Canones non ita absolutè accipi debere, Auxilius in libro, quo Ordinationes saltem Formosi defendit, pertenderit, & Nicenum quidem dem per Concilium Chalcedonense explicatum ita esse, ut non quaslibet translationes vetet, dixerit; Apostolicus autem in editione Moguntina ita se habeat: Non est fas Episcopo alienam Parochiam propriâ relictâ pervadere, licèt cogatur à plurimis. Nisi forte quis cum rationabili causa compellat, (forte compellatur) tanquam qui possit ibidem constitutis (forte constitutus) plus lucri conferre & in causa religionis aliquid profecto (forte profectûs) prospicere, & hoc non à semetipso pertentet, sed multorum Episcoporum judicio & maxima supplicatione perficiat; istæ tamen conditiones minùs Petro favere videntur, cùm, si juxta plerosque, primò Antiochiæ Episcopus, in eo sensu, de quo disputatur, fuisset, propriam utique Parochiam reliquisset, alienam contrà sive aliorum primorum fundatorum, sive Pauli, qui Ecclesiæ Romanæ multùm inserviit, & ad cujus Canonem urbs gentium pertinuit, pervasisset, nequidem à plurimis coactus. Et licet videri posset, eum plus lucri Romæ facere potuisse, tamen non in Evangelio circumcisionis, quod ei concreditum erat, ex quo principio in Oriente ei manendum fuisset, lucri autem majoris consideratio sola Romam vocare non potuit contra fidem datam, maximè Paulo ista lucri majoris occasione strenuè utente; Quemadmodum etiam non indicant, quomodo multorum Episcoporum judicio & maxima supplicatione translationem, qualiscunque jam illa fingatur, perfecerit. Planè igitur videtur, idem facere debuisse, ex hypothesibus, Petrum, quod tæste Sozomeno hist. Eccl. l. 2. c. 19. Eusebius Pamphilus fecit, sedem Antiochenam, depósito Eustathio, vacuam recusans, quia lege Ecclesiasticâ vetitum fit, ne ad alium Episcopatum aliquis transfiret. Saltem non debuisset facilè, cumprimis fiducitati Canonis Apostolici Author ex parte, minimùm adprobator, fuisset, vel in speciem contrà facere, & hominum in secuturis seculis ambitioni & avaritiæ prætextum istum satis plausibilem suppeditare, sed potius rectà Romam ad Episcopatum perpetuò cum suprema potestate duraturum erigendum concedere. Neque ipsos juvat, si hic excipere velint, vel Canones tunc temporis nondum factos fuisse, vel Petrum supra Canones fuisse. Non juvat illud, cùm Apostolos sibi ipsis Canones justi & æqui amore ac strictissima ordinis observatione fuisse, & causam disciplinæ corrumpendæ dare noluisse, præsumendum sit. Non hoc, (præsuppositio nempe, Canones Apostolicos jam illo tempore formatos fuisse,) cùm contra Canonum statuta ne Romana quidem sedis, adeóque Ecclesiæ Ecclesia Monarcharum, quales se post Petrum faciunt, valeat authoritas, judice Zosimo Papâ.
units.tr: L. Thus they also make him the first author of the worst abuses in the Church concerning ecclesiastical dignities. For thirdly, they here assume a transfer from one episcopate to another. Most want Peter to have transferred from the Antiochene episcopate to the Roman; Onuphrius on the contrary, and those who follow him, invent a passage from the Roman episcopate to the Antiochene. Nicephorus is added, and l.14.c.39. asserts that Peter transferred his see from Rome to Alexandria. Yet it is established by the Canons, among those Apostolic canons which they cite, the fourteenth, of the Council of Nicaea the fifteenth, and of Antioch the twenty-first, that transfers and transitions of this kind are forbidden. It is also established that Formosus the Pope (of whom more in its place) was first charged with fault by Stephen, because he had been transferred against the Canons from one see, namely from Porto to another, to the Roman see, and on this account all his papal ordinations, in Stephen's judgment, were null. For although on that occasion Auxilius, in the book in which he defended at least the ordinations of Formosus, contended that the Canons ought not to be taken so absolutely, and said that the Nicene canon, as explained by the Council of Chalcedon, does not forbid every transfer, yet the Apostolic canon in the Mainz edition reads thus: It is not lawful for a bishop to invade another's parish, leaving his own, even if he is compelled by very many. Unless perhaps someone compels him with a reasonable cause (perhaps compelled), as one who might (perhaps might be) established there, bring more gain, and certainly foresee something (perhaps of progress) for the cause of religion, and does not undertake this on his own, but accomplishes it by the judgment of many bishops and with the greatest supplication. Yet these conditions seem less favourable to Peter. For if, according to most, he had first been bishop of Antioch in the sense under dispute, he would certainly have left his own parish, and invaded another's, either that of the other original founders, or that of Paul, who served the Roman church greatly and to whose canon the city of the Gentiles belonged, and this without being compelled by very many. And although it might seem that he could have made more gain at Rome, yet this was not in the Gospel of the circumcision, which had been entrusted to him, and from which principle he would have had to remain in the East. But consideration of greater gain alone could not call him to Rome against the faith given, especially since Paul vigorously made use of this occasion of greater gain. Likewise they do not show how he accomplished the transfer, whatever it is supposed to have been, by the judgment of many bishops and the greatest supplication. It seems clear, then, that on their hypotheses he ought to have done what, as Sozomen witnesses, Eusebius Pamphilus did, refusing the Antiochene see, which was vacant after Eustathius was deposed, because it is forbidden by ecclesiastical law that anyone pass to another bishopric. At the very least he should not have done so easily, since the author of the Apostolic canon would have been, at least in part, an approver of it, and would have acted against it, or seemed to, and would have supplied in the ages to come a fairly plausible pretext for the ambition and avarice of men. Rather, he ought to have granted outright that an episcopate should be erected at Rome which would endure forever with supreme power. Nor does it help them, if they wish to make an exception here, either that the canons had not yet been made at that time, or that Peter was above the canons. It does not help that the Apostles, out of love for just and fair canons and the strictest observance of order, must be presumed to have been unwilling to give cause for corrupting discipline. Nor does this help, namely the presupposition that the Apostolic canons had already been formed at that time, since, by the judgment of Pope Zosimus, against the statutes of the canons not even the authority of the Roman see, and thus of the Church, can hold, the Monarchs such as they make themselves after Peter, and so on.

units.la: LII. Si verò dicere velint, Petrum istos Episcopatus simul habuisse, neque localiter ab uno ad alterum transiisse, ut certè Onuphrius, & qui cum eo Petrum Romæ demum Antiochiam venisse & ibi per septem annos sedisse, pòst Romam rediisse, affirmant; aut translationes jamjam impugnatas, exiguo sanè Petri, sic parum sibi constantis, honore augere & eum primò Romæ Episcopum fuisse, post Antiochiæ, tandem rursus Romæ, dicere, similiter etiam 20. annos Episcopatûs Romani ex hypothesibus propriis hac quoque ratione destruere, aut simultaneos in Petro Episcopatus admittere debent; eum quarto Non minoris abusûs, Beneficiorum nempe pluralitatis, vel saltem Beneficiorum unionis Patronum faciunt. Qui certè abusus in Ecclesia Pontificia jam à longo tempore magni sunt. Et Gerson quidem, illustris olim Galliæ Cancellarius tract. de defect. num. 49. testatur, de abominatione, quòd unus teneat ducenta, alter trecenta beneficia Ecclesiastica; & post n.51. Quid est, quærit, quòd hodiernus, utinam mediocriter doctus, tenet 4. 5. 6. aut 8. beneficia Ecclesiastica, quorum uno non est dignus, quibus octo sustentari possent &c. Addit; An potiùs hodie equi, canes, aves & superflua Ecclesiasticorum familia patrimonium Ecclesiæ comedere debent, quàm pauperes Christi? &c. Et in sermone coram Alex. III. Videas alios 9. ordinibus non contentos, non enim 9. beneficiis saturantur, tamdiu novos hiatus pandere, quamdiu vivunt; conjungere domum ad domum, agrum agro copulare, quasi in medio terra soli habitarent; ipsum verò Propheticum: (Esaj. IV. 5.) pro fabula contemnere. Franciscus autem Duarenus de S. Minist. Eccles. & Benef. l. 8. 4. pessimi rem exempli & antiquis Canonibus omninò contrariam vocat, & subjungit; Captatores beneficiorum Romam certatim cursitare, pratextu literaturæ, aut nobilitatis veniam (contra Canones) à Pontifice impetraturos, quæ nemini, quamlibet indigno nebuloni, modò æs numeret, denegari consueverit. Prodigiosam tandem rem vocat hanc beneficiorum cumulationem, nec sibi minùs monstrosos videri ait, qui tot personas in Ecclesia sustineant, quàm Briareum illum, qui centum manus habuerit, ut sit in fabulis; aut Geryonem, quem trium fuisse corporum perhibeant. Unionem verò beneficiorum, de qua priùs dixerat, nonnunquam in gratiam Cardinalis aut Viri alicujus illustris 30. aut 40. beneficia uniri, etiam in diversis orbis Christiani locis sita; S. Polanus Hist. Conc. Trid. l. 2. p. 225. facetè irridet, dicens,sic collatum in specie unum beneficium complura secum trahere, adeóque eum,qui illo gaudeat,posse ad eundem modum peccatum suum: (maxime in officii administratione commissum:) confiteri, quo is, qui patri piaculari (Confessori, Sacerdoti) fassus, se furto abstulisse frenum equi,reticens interim freno huic alligatum fuisse caballum. Cui duplici abusui etiam Concilium Tridentinum,sed,manente penes Papam dispensandi potestate,frustra mederi voluit,Patribus unanimi assensu vetandum censentibus, ne quis cujuscunque conditionis, plura beneficia quam tria obtinere posset, nonnullis autem adjicientibus, quando 2. ex his annuum valorem 400. Philippæorum non attingunt. Ratione etiam sess.7. cap. de reform.2. addità,quòd valdè felix sit ille censendus,cui unam Ecclesiam bene ac fructuosè & cum animarum sibi commissarum salute regere contigerit.
units.tr: LII. If, however, they wish to say that Peter held these bishoprics at the same time and did not move from one to another by place, as Onuphrius certainly maintains, and those who agree with him, that Peter first came to Rome, then to Antioch, where he sat for seven years, and afterwards returned to Rome; or else they must either admit simultaneous bishoprics in Peter, or say that translations, already refuted, increase the slight honour of Peter, who is thus so inconsistent, and that he was first bishop of Rome, then of Antioch, and finally again of Rome. Likewise, by their own hypotheses they must destroy in this way the twenty years of the Roman episcopate. They make Peter the patron of a fourth abuse, no less serious: the pluralism of benefices, or at least the union of benefices. This abuse has certainly been great in the Papist Church for a long time. Gerson, once the illustrious chancellor of France, testifies in his treatise On the Defects (no. 49) to the abomination that one man holds two hundred and another three hundred ecclesiastical benefices. After no. 51 he asks: "What is it that the present-day man, would that he were moderately learned, holds four, five, six or eight ecclesiastical benefices, of which he is worthy of none, and with which eight could be supported, etc.?" He adds: "Should horses, dogs, birds and the superfluous household of the clergy rather eat up the patrimony of the Church than the poor of Christ? etc." And in a sermon before Alexander III: "You may see others, not content with nine orders, since nine benefices do not satisfy them, opening new gaps for as long as they live, joining house to house and field to field, as if they alone lived in the middle of the earth; and they despise the very prophetic word (Isaiah 4:5) as a fable." Francis Duaren, in On the Holy Ministry of the Church and Benefices, book 8, calls this a very bad example and wholly contrary to the ancient canons, and adds: "Hunters of benefices race eagerly to Rome, pretending learning or nobility, to obtain permission from the Pope (against the canons), which is usually refused to no one, however unworthy a scoundrel, provided he pays the money." Finally he calls this accumulation of benefices a monstrous thing, and says that those who support so many persons in the Church seem to him no less monstrous than that Briareus who had a hundred hands, as in the fables, or Geryon, whom they say had three bodies. As for the union of benefices, of which he spoke earlier, that sometimes for the favour of a cardinal or some illustrious man thirty or forty benefices are united, even when situated in different parts of the Christian world, S. Polanus in his History of the Council of Trent, book 2, p. 225, wittily mocks, saying: "A single benefice conferred in name thus drags many others along with it, and so the one who enjoys it may confess his sin (especially one committed in the administration of his office) in the way that one confesses to an expiatory father (a confessor, a priest) that he has stolen a bridle from a horse, while keeping silent that a horse was attached to that bridle." The Council of Trent also wished to remedy this double abuse, but in vain, since the power of dispensation remained with the Pope. The Fathers, by unanimous assent, judged that it must be forbidden for anyone, of whatever condition, to hold more than three benefices; some added: unless two of them do not reach an annual value of 400 Philippine coins. With this there was also added, in session 7, chapter 2 on reform, the reason that he is to be considered very happy to whom it has fallen to rule one church well and fruitfully, and with the salvation of the souls committed to him.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: Jam, si ista Petro applicemus, fateri quidem oportet,minùs lauta cum temporis fuisse beneficia, & forte Petrum Ecclesiæ Monarcham & summum Pontificem satis suum nondum tam largo pede mensum fuisse,ac hodiegregarii in Ecclesia Pontificia Sacerdotes, teste S. Polano l. c. p.223. suum metiri solent, reputantes, non satis esse,quòd non sibi, familiaque è consanguineis, tribus famulis & equo alendo sufficiat; nobili autem (non fuit multùm piscator Petrus;) aut bene docto (satis fuit,si Christum nôsse & Christum amare melius est, quàm omnia scire) eò plus esse largiendum; multò minùs Cardinalium hodiernorum more,quos Curiæ Romanæ sermo quotidianus Regibus æquiparat, eodem teste, nullum apparatum nullúmque reditum nimium æstimásse,nisi qui Regni exsuperet. Forte etiam ab Ecclesia Antiochena,vel Romana ultra annuum valorem 400. Philippæorum non accepisse,cum Paulo,non ea,quæ fidelium, sed fideles eorúmque salutem 2.Cor.XII.14. quærentem, & divitiarum acquisitione suum illud; aurum & argentum non habeo; haud immutantem;quamvis familiam,non quidem consanguineam,sed propriam alendam habuerit,sororem fœminam cum aliquo Ecclesiarum incommodo circumduxerit, & filiam, ut volunt, Petronillam; nec etiam multùm equis, canibus, avibus & superfluis,secundùm Gersonis querelam, insumsisse, neque ultrà tres Episcopatus, quod Concilium Tridentinum permittere videtur,habuisse; neque verisimile esse, Antiochenam aut Romanam Ecclesiam absentem aluisse. Tamen cùm verisimiliter una Antiochena aut Romana Ecclesia eum cum suis alere potuerit,plura autem beneficia, secun-dùm
units.tr: Now, if we apply these things to Peter, one must indeed admit that benefices were less lavish in his time, and perhaps Peter, as Monarch of the Church and supreme Pontiff, did not yet measure out his sufficiency on so generous a scale as the ordinary priests in the Papist Church are accustomed to measure out their own today, as S. Polanus reports, l. c. p. 223, reckoning that it is not enough if it suffices for themselves, for a household of relatives, three servants and a horse to feed; but that for a nobleman (Peter was not much of a fisherman) or a well-educated man (it was enough that to know Christ and to love Christ is better than to know all things) more must be given; much less in the manner of today's Cardinals, whom the daily talk of the Roman Curia, by the same witness, puts on a level with kings, and who judge no equipage and no income excessive unless it exceeds a kingdom. Perhaps also he did not receive from the Antiochene or Roman Church more than an annual value of 400 Philippine coins, along with Paul, who sought not what belongs to the faithful but the faithful themselves and their salvation (2 Cor. 12:14), and who did not change that saying of his, "I have neither gold nor silver", through any acquisition of riches. Peter had a household to feed, not indeed of relatives but his own, and he led about a sister, a woman, with some inconvenience to the churches, and a daughter, Petronilla, as they would have it. Nor did he spend much on horses, dogs, birds and superfluities, according to Gerson's complaint, nor did he hold more than three bishoprics, which the Council of Trent seems to permit. Nor is it likely that the Antiochene or Roman Church supported him while he was absent. Yet since one Antiochene or Roman Church could probably have fed him and his household, while more benefices, according to

units.la: Applica-tio fit ad Petrum; dùm Canonistarum glossam, uni deferenda non sint, nisi quando unum ministro alendo non sufficit; & beneficia ista duo incompatibilia, id est, talia, quæ residentiam postulârint, videantur; &, quod nemo unquam homo antehac vidit, nec potest fieri, tempore uno homo idem duobus locis ut simul sit, etiam de Petro obtineat, satis felice, dum unam Ecclesiam uno tempore bene ac fructuosè & cum animarum sibi commissarum salute, tanquam Episcopus loci, rexit; & Roma atque Antiochia loca nimis longè dissita sint, quàm ut commodè tunc uniri potuerint; asserendum omninò videtur, Petrum non tantùm sui causâ, sed & propter abominationes sequentium temporum, quas ei Spiritus facile revelâsset, noluisse, pessimo & in favorem earum interpretando exemplo, Episcopatus habere simultaneos, quemadmodum quidem eos in favorem suum interpretatus legitur quidam Manasses Arelatensis Episcopus, Hugonis Regis Italiæ cognatus, simul etiam Episcopus Veronensis, Tridentinus, Mediolanensis & Mantuanus.
units.tr: Application to Peter: the gloss of the canonists holds that they should not be conferred on one man unless one is not enough to feed a minister; and these two benefices seem to be incompatible, that is, such as require residence. And, what no man has ever seen before and what cannot happen, that at one time one man should be in two places at once, even if he holds them in Peter's case: it is quite happy enough that, as bishop of the place, he ruled one Church at one time well and fruitfully, and with the salvation of the souls committed to him. Rome and Antioch are too far apart to have been conveniently united at that time. It seems absolutely necessary to assert that Peter was unwilling to hold simultaneous bishoprics, not only for his own sake but also on account of the abominations of later times, which the Spirit could easily have revealed to him, lest he set the worst and most self-serving example. Thus a certain Manasses, bishop of Arles, cousin of King Hugh of Italy, is read to have interpreted such bishoprics in his own favour; he was at the same time also bishop of Verona, Trent, Milan and Mantua.

units.la: LIV. Ex his autem abusibus, quibus ita Petri larvam obducunt, fluit quintò non-Residentia,quam præsentissimum omnium malorum Ecclesiæ fundum esse, in Concilio Tridentino ipse Cardinalis Montanus acriter conquestus est, & ideo Ecclesiam navi comparavit, quæ absente nauclero, cujus sit eam gubernare, facile submergatur, referente S. Polano l. 2. Hist. Conc. p.168. & quam jure Divino prohiberi, major pars Theologorum, ut & Præsules Galli, Hispani, imò & Itali nonnulli in eodem Concilio ad restaurandam Episcoporum autoritatem p.206. contenderunt pag.193. & ex Dominicanis Barth. Caranza & Dominicus Soto, præcipuè ex eo, quòd Episcopi munus à Deo sit institutum tanquam ministerium & opus, adeóque actionem personalem requirat, quam absens præstare non possit, & quòd Christus boni pastoris qualitates describens dicat, eum ponere vitam pro grege, ovium nomina cognita habere & gregi suo præire; productis in eum finem plurimis ex utroque Test. Scripturæ locis, ostenderunt, & simul etiam ex titulis Episcoporum, Decretis Conciliorum, Pontificum & Patrum, & rationibus refutârunt; Facile autem de Petro præsumimus, eum, distinctionem inter beneficia residentiæ, judice Historico, perniciosam & abominandam ignorâsse, & tritum illud; Beneficium datur propter officium; non ita intellexisse, ac si pro reditibus mille, imò decies mille & suprà aureorum, ex precibus horariis Breviarii, quæ officium sint, sumpto in manum libro, paginæ aliquot quot, submissâ voce, properante linguâ, nec ullâ rei, sed solius verborum pronunciationis, habitâ ratione, legi deberent; Interim tamen, si Petrus fuisset Episcopus Romanus, non-Residentiæ, si quisquam alius, reus peragi posset omninò; Et si ex supra allatis aliquid temporis ejus in urbe præsentiæ relinqueretur, quantillum quæsò illud foret, & quàm longè infra 25. annos? Abfuit, ut vult Cortesius, per 18. annos, ut Onuphrius, per 7. ut Bellarminus, per 5. Et, quod negligentiæ Episcopum extremæ magis convinceret, toto illo tempore ad Romanos suos Epistolam non scripsit, verùm duas tantùm ad Judæos ἐν Διασπορᾷ in dispersione. Faciunt igitur Petrum tam longo tempore Episcopum Apostolum, & suis Titularibus similem.
