Neque enim causas absentia diuturna idoneas habuisset; non edictum Claudii, ob quod Gentiles Romanos, majorem gregis partem non deseruisset Apostolus, & quod Aquilæ, Priscillæ, aliis, paucis annis elapsis, redire permisit, Romæ postea in Epistola Paulina salutatis; Petrum autem ob absentiam non salutatum esse, pariter dant nonnunquam; Quomodo autem non vel primus ad gregem rediisset suum, si Episcopus fuisset? Nec etiam causa absentiæ Episcopi idonea fuisset, desiderium aliis quoque prædicandi, quod quidem ab Episcopatu facile Petrum arcere potuit suscipiendo, ast eum susceptum tam diu deserendi causa justa esse potuisset minimè, quando & proxima proximè & maximè curanda sunt, & Romæ satis negotii ad Episcopum retinendum fuit, & Ecclesiæ Monarchæ satis Ministrorum, quos in alias orbis partes delegaret.
units.tr: LIV. From these abuses, by which they thus veil Peter's mask, there follows, fifthly, non-residence, which Cardinal Montanus himself bitterly complained at the Council of Trent is the most present foundation of all the Church's evils; and so he compared the Church to a ship which, when the pilot is absent, whose task it is to steer it, easily sinks, as S. Polanus reports, l. 2 Hist. Conc. p. 168. The majority of theologians, as well as the Gallican and Spanish prelates, and even some Italians in the same Council, contended that it is forbidden by divine law, in order to restore the authority of bishops, p. 206, and p. 193. Among the Dominicans, Bartholomew Carranza and Dominic Soto did the same, chiefly because the office of bishop has been instituted by God as a ministry and a work, and so requires personal action, which an absentee cannot perform; and because Christ, describing the qualities of the good shepherd, says that he lays down his life for the flock, knows his sheep by name and goes before his flock. They produced for this purpose many passages from both Testaments of Scripture, and at the same time refuted the opposing view from the titles of bishops, the decrees of councils, of popes and of the Fathers, and by arguments. We may easily presume about Peter that he did not know the distinction between benefices of residence, which in a historian's judgement are pernicious and abominable, and did not understand that trite saying, "A benefice is given on account of the office", as though it meant that for revenues of a thousand, or ten thousand and more gold pieces, one should read, from the hourly prayers of the Breviary, which constitute the office, a few pages of a book taken in hand, in a low voice, with a hurrying tongue, having regard not to the sense but only to the pronunciation of the words. Meanwhile, if Peter had been Roman bishop, he could fully be convicted of non-residence, as anyone else could be. And if from what has been said some presence of his in the city were left over, how small would that be, I ask, and how far short of 25 years! He was absent, as Cortesius would have it, for 18 years, as Onuphrius would have it for 7, as Bellarmine for 5. And, to convict the bishop of extreme negligence even more, during all that time he wrote no letter to his Romans, but only two to the Jews in the Dispersion [ἐν Διασπορᾷ]. They thus make Peter, a bishop and apostle, so long absent, like their titular bishops. For he would not have had adequate reasons for such a long absence: not the edict of Claudius, on account of which the Apostle would not have deserted the Gentile Romans, the greater part of his flock, and which he permitted Aquila, Priscilla and others to return from after a few years had passed, and who were afterwards greeted at Rome in the Pauline epistle. Nor, while they sometimes also say that Peter was not greeted because of his absence, how would he not have returned first to his flock, if he had been bishop? Nor would the desire to preach to others have been a suitable cause for the bishop's absence. That desire could indeed have kept Peter from taking up the bishopric, but once it was undertaken, it could by no means be a just cause for deserting it for so long, since the nearer matters are to be cared for first and most, and there was enough business at Rome to keep a bishop there, and enough ministers for the Monarch of the Church whom he might send to other parts of the world.

units.la: LV. Sed quàm parùm etiam sexto honori Monarchæ suî consulunt, dum ei dimidium tantùm Episcopatum committunt? Ne dicam quartam tantùm partem, secundùm illa veterum testimonia, quibus superstite Petro Linus & Clemens Episcopi fuisse dicuntur. Potiores & certiores Pauli circa Ecclesiam Romanam curas jam aliquoties occasionibus natis notavimus, & exinde etiam argumentati sumus; Æquales saltem partes ei à veteribus hîc tribui, quoque indicavimus, probavimus. Paucula heic quoad Episcopatum addere lubet à veteribus in sensu latiori Apostolis duobus simul adscriptum. Episcoporum, inquit Epiphanius hæres. 27. in Roma, successio hanc consequentiam habet, Petrus & Paulus (qui simultanei fuerunt, si uno die martyrio affecti;) Linus, Cletus, Clemens &c. Clara hæc sunt; Sed audiamus adhuc Leonem Allatium, apud
units.tr: LV. But how little do they also serve the honour of their sixth Monarch, when they commit to him only half of the episcopate? Not to mention only a quarter, according to those ancient testimonies by which Linus and Clement are said to have been bishops while Peter was still living. We have already several times noted, as occasions arose, Paul's more powerful and certain cares for the Roman Church, and have argued from them; that at least equal parts of the office are assigned to him here by the ancients, we have also indicated and proved. It pleases us to add here a little on the episcopate, which the ancients ascribed to the two Apostles together in a broader sense. Epiphanius, in heresy 27, says of the succession of bishops in Rome that it has this sequence: Peter and Paul (who were contemporaries, if they were put to death on the same day); Linus, Cletus, Clement, etc. These things are clear. But let us hear again Leo Allatius, who in the same place...

units.la: Quarto ei dimidium saltem Episcopatum tribuentes; apud quem de Perp. Conf. l. 1. c. 3. 4. 5. loca Patrum pro simultaneo Episcopatu Apostolorum videri possunt; Ille tandem c. 5. n. 21. ita in summam colligit totius Antiquitatis sententiam: Ut rem in pauca conferam: auctoritates Patrum, Conciliorum & summorum Pontificum, quibus Pontificum Romanorum successio à Petro & Paulo illisque Romana Ecclesia fundatoribus agnoscitur, auctoritas in decernendo Petri & Pauli esse asseritur; Dominium, Principatus, cura & sollicitudo omnium mundi Ecclesiarum communis Petro & Paulo indicatur; Sedes, Thronus & alia dignitatis Pontificia munia astruuntur non minus Pauli esse quàm Petri, ac decernuntur; quas res planas, apertas, minimèque dubias ex una parte si videam, ex altera Ecclesiæ majestatem Monarchicam considerem, Petro soli exhibitam &c. incertum mihi est quid pronunciem: Subdit, rem se committere Sacrosanctæ Inquisitioni, & Innocentio X. qui tum sederat. En! quò isti homines tandem perveniant! Et hæc est illa, quâ Patres prosequi videri volunt, reverentia! Tam planis, tam apertis, minimèque dubiis illorum testimoniis fidem habere, ex illis contra Monarchiam concludere non audent! Sed quis non videt, eam Patribus ignoratam esse, hos Apostolo Petro etiam Episcopatum nonnisi in sensu latiori tribuisse, talem, qui Apostolo, imò Apostolis duobus in eodem loco eodem tempore convenire potuerit, prorsus nobiscum credidisse; Petrum non ad talem Pontificatum Romanum electum esse? Ὀπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι.
units.tr: Fourth, giving him at least half the episcopate; in whom, On the Perpetuity of the Confession, book 1, chapters 3, 4, 5, the passages of the Fathers may be seen in favour of a simultaneous episcopate of the Apostles. Finally, he sums up the opinion of all antiquity in chapter 5, number 21, in these words: To bring the matter into a few words: the authorities of the Fathers, of the Councils and of the supreme Pontiffs, by which the succession of the Roman Pontiffs is acknowledged as coming from Peter and Paul, and from them as founders of the Roman Church, assert that the authority of decision belongs to Peter and Paul; dominion, principate, care and concern for all the Churches of the world are shown to be common to Peter and Paul; seats, thrones and other offices of papal dignity are declared to belong no less to Paul than to Peter, and are decreed accordingly; if on the one hand I see these matters plain, open and by no means doubtful, and on the other I consider the monarchical majesty of the Church, which is shown to Peter alone, etc., I am uncertain what I should pronounce. He adds that he commits the matter to the Most Holy Inquisition and to Innocent X, who then sat in the chair. Behold! Where these men finally arrive! And this is that reverence which they wish to seem to show the Fathers! They do not dare to give faith to such plain, open and by no means doubtful testimonies, nor to conclude from them against the Monarchy! But who does not see that this was unknown to the Fathers, who ascribed the episcopate to the Apostle Peter only in a broader sense, and who believed, altogether as we do, that such an episcopate could belong to one Apostle, or indeed to two Apostles in the same place at the same time; and that Peter was not chosen to such a Roman Pontificate? Which was to be shown.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Atque ita absolvimus tractationem de Electione Petri, Conclave Petri; siquidem hoc ita loqui convenit; Convenit sanè aliquo modo; Petrum enim etiam cum clave, vel potiùs cum clavibus videre contigit. Sed talibus, quæ nobis non aperuerunt Conclave, in quo factam ad talem Pontificatum Romanum B. Apostoli electionem videre licuerit, quod nec aperire nobis potuit, licet omnia tentantibus, certæ cognitionis clavis. Et certè oportet, electionem istam in Conclavi omninò factam esse nondum ad hunc usque diem reserato, Conclave istud non esse ex illorum numero, quali si sono potuto trovare sino à questo giorno, à nemine Apostolorum, qui forte tum Conclavista, aut Cardinales, ex parte Papabiles, scripto, forte quia dolebant de prærogativis alteri collatis, consignatum esse, Ipse autem in eo Papa electus ita statim ingenti negotiorum mole obrutus fuit, ut scriptioni historiae electionis, tempus defuerit; Imò ne quidem audita in conclavi hoc in tectis prædicâsse deprehenduntur. Quæ autem scripserunt & prædicârunt, quàm saŕta sunt, quàm posterioribus seculis dissimilia, & quàm bene se ex omni parte habent. Planè singularis fuit ista electionis forma ab ipso Domino, sine næyis; Consequentia hîc habeas non adorationem &c. sed tantùm sedulitatem in officio & Divinam benedictionem cooperantem. Sancta electio! sine ambitione, sine competitoribus, sine factionibus, sine promissionibus, sine minis, sine schismate, sine aliis vitiis; Benedicta electio! & quam comitabatur larga vocantis gratia! Mira electio! illius, quod in mundo vile erat, ad ea, quæ in pretio, confundenda, paucorum ad mundi totius conversionem, sed paucorum, non unius, omnibus ex hoc Conclavi cum dignitatis augmento exeuntibus, & orbi universo gaudium magnum annunciantibus, nemine deinceps primatum quærente, nisi amoris, laboris & afflictionum pro Christo.
units.tr: Thus we have finished the treatment of the election of Peter, the Conclave of Peter; for so it is fitting to speak; it is fitting in some sense, for we have seen Peter indeed with a key, or rather with keys. But not with keys that have opened for us the Conclave in which the blessed Apostle's election to such a Roman Pontificate could be seen to have been made, which key of certain knowledge could not open for us, although we tried everything. And certainly it must be that this election was made in a Conclave altogether unopened to this day, a Conclave not of the kind such as have been found up to this day, which no one of the Apostles, who perhaps were then conclavists or cardinals, partly papabili, has recorded in writing, perhaps because they grieved over the prerogatives conferred on another; and he himself, elected Pope, was so immediately overwhelmed by the great mass of business that there was no time for writing a history of the election; indeed they are not even found to have preached what was heard in this conclave on the housetops. But how holy are the things they wrote and preached, how unlike the later centuries, and how well they hold up in every respect! Truly singular was that form of election, made by the Lord himself, without blemish; here you may have no adoration etc., but only diligence in the office and the cooperating divine blessing. Holy election! without ambition, without competitors, without factions, without promises, without threats, without schism, without other vices; blessed election! and how abundant grace of the calling accompanied it! Wonderful election! of what was base in the world, to confound what is held in esteem; of a few, for the conversion of the whole world, yet of a few, not of one, all going out from this Conclave with an increase of dignity, and announcing great joy to the whole world, with no one afterwards seeking primacy, except the love, labour and afflictions for Christ.

units.la: DISSERTATIO TERTIA,
units.tr: DISSERTATION THREE,

units.la: In qua De electione Pontificum Romanorum, quatenus per eam Petro succedere dicuntur; agitur. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which the election of the Roman Pontiffs, insofar as they are said to succeed Peter through it, is discussed. A summary.

units.la: 1. Successionis Petri in tali Pontificatu Romano fundamenta jam sunt sublata; Interim tamen de ipsa quoque videndum est, & utrum Pontifices Romani Petro, saltem in omni eo, quod revera habuit, vi Electionis sua succedant. II. De Successione agimus Pontificum, qui proin non secundùm ordinem Melchisedek; Pontificum summorum; qui titulus explicatur; III. Quanti faciant Successionem Pontificum suorum; IV. In quibus Petro eos succedere nolint; V. Iactata Successionis primò jus Divinum impugnatur; quia in Scriptura non asseritur; Respondetur Bozio ad 2. Pet. I 12. 13. 14. 15. & Phil. IV. 3. Bellarmini distinctio in Successionem & successionis rationem; VI. Colligitur atque probatur ex agnito Scripturarum silentio, Successionem istam & illa, qua ei inniti dicuntur, non esse de fide; VII. Distinctio Bellarmini inter esse de fide, & esse de jure Divino; VIII. Confessio ejusdem contra jus Divinum. IX. Consequentia ex defectu Iuris Divini formata; X. Secundò non juvat Monarchicos opinio de necessario in Ecclesia Monarcha; XI. Argumentatio Bellarmini proponitur, atque in responsione ostenditur, primò, quòd convenions forma Regiminis Ecclesiastici non ex absolutè optimo inferri possit; XII. Secundò quòd illam non humana sapientia, sed Divina revelatio prescribere debeat; XIII. Tertiò quòd Regnum Christi, quod quod non est de hoc mundo, in omnibus, & praeter Scripturarum manuductionem quidem ad similitudinem Regnorum hujus mundi componi haud debeat; XIV. Quartò, quòd de optima etiam mundani regiminis forma non satis inter omnes convenit; XV. Quintò, quòd Ecclesia Monarchicum omninò regimen sit, sed respectu Christi; XVI. Sextò, quòd de Monarcha alio Scriptura nihil doceat; XVII. Septimò, quòd illa aliam Regiminis formam aperte tradat; XVIII. Octavò, quòd praecepta illi praxis Ecclesiae primitivae respondeat, dum Christi exemplum Monarchicis non favet, & Episcoporum aequalitas à Patribus saepe inculcatur. XIX. Tertiò demonstratur, Petrum in omni ea, quod revera fuit, Successores non habere, nec habere debere. Fuit enim Apostolus; XX. Effugia Bellarmini tolluntur; XXI. In certo sensu Apostolis omnibus ab Episcopis omnibus aequè succedi; XXII. Observationes circa illam successionem; Prima; Quilibet non uni tantùm, sed omnibus simul succedere dicitur; XXIII. Altera; Non succeditur in praerogativis personalibus, in successione locali; XXIV. Applicantur ista; Successio supponitur, atque primò commendatur etiam successio Pauli; XXV. A Petro nihil habere possunt, quod non alii ab eodem habere possint aequè; maximè Antiocheni, teste Innocentio I. XXVI. Annotationes septem ad testimonium illius; XXVII. Diluuntur objecta à Bellarmino; XXVIII. Respondetur ad appellationem sedis Apostolicae; XXIX. Qua ab initio communis fuit, ut docetur exemplis & testimoniis; XXX. Supposità potestate Monarchicà in Petro, incertitudo manet, & non simul necessariò supponitur successio Episcoporum Romanorum in ea. Fortè plures, fortè dignissimi semper, fortè semper apud sedem Imperatoriam succedere Episcopi debuerunt; XXXI. Inconvenientia in eo, quòd ostendi non potest, quomodo Episcopus Romanus praeter Episcopatum urbis etiam Praefecturam orbis habeat; XXXII. Incertitudo porrò in eo, an semper & omnes Episcopi Romani ista successione gaudere debeant; XXXIII. Argumentum Bellarmini, quòd nullus se ita Successorem Petri vocaverit unquam praeter Episcopum Romanum alius; Cui respondetur primò, jactantiam & praesumptionem non probare possessionem legitimam; XXXIV. Responsionis subsequentis summa; XXXV. Secundò ostenditur, primos Episcopos Romanos ejusmodi successionem ne affectâsse quidem. Testimoniis generalibus. XXXVI. Conatus levis Victoris P. Testimonia Cypriani; XXXVII. Tertiò ostenditur, alios similia affectâsse. Testimonium generale Guicciardini de Episcopis Constantinop & Ravenatibus. Exemplum Iohannis Constantinopolitani ob titulum universalis Episcopi à Gregorio M. reprehensi; XXXVIII. Similia Iohannem illum affectâsse & absolutè à Gregorio damnata; XXXIX. Vitiosa igitur in Bonifacio III. etiam & in successoribus. Causa mutata illius tempore alea atque ei concessi à Phoca tituli, à Iohanne III. etiam rejecti. XL. Contra successionem talem testantur Episcopi singuli; XLI. In Concilio congregati, non vocante Romano, non Praside in Conciliis ordinario; non petentes confirmationem; XLII. Decernentes contraria tali successioni; XLIII. Ostenditur, quo fundamento, sive pratextu, quibus mediis & artibus ad talem totius Ecclesiae Pontificatûs usurpationem venerint, Quò non pervenerunt sola expositione verborum; Tu es Petrus; quae antiquitùs raro in eum finem citabantur; XLIV. Sed multùm ad primatum primò ordinis tantùm contulit primò Politica urbis dignitas & Majestas; XLV. Nec parùm juvit secundò primorum Episcoporum Romanorum Zelus, probitas & Orthodoxia; XLVI. & XLVII. Artes pessima plurima adhibita
units.tr: 1. The foundations of Peter's succession in such a Roman Pontificate have already been overturned. Meanwhile, it must still be considered whether the Roman Pontiffs succeed Peter, at least in all that he really possessed, by virtue of their election. II. We treat of the succession of the Pontiffs, who therefore are not according to the order of Melchizedek; the highest Pontiffs, a title which is explained. III. How highly they value the succession of their Pontiffs. IV. In what respects they do not want them to succeed Peter. V. First, the vaunted divine right of succession is attacked, because it is not asserted in Scripture; a reply is given to Bozius on 2 Peter 1:12–15 and Philippians 4:3. Bellarmine's distinction between the succession and the manner of succession. VI. It is inferred and proved from the acknowledged silence of Scripture that this succession, and those things on which it is said to rest, are not matters of faith. VII. Bellarmine's distinction between what is of faith and what is of divine right. VIII. His own admission against divine right. IX. The consequence drawn from the lack of divine right. X. Secondly, the opinion of the Monarchians about the necessary monarch in the Church does not help them. XI. Bellarmine's argument is set out, and in the reply it is shown, first, that the most suitable form of ecclesiastical government cannot be inferred from what is absolutely best. XII. Second, that it ought to be prescribed not by human wisdom but by divine revelation. XIII. Third, that the kingdom of Christ, which is not of this world, ought not to be constructed in all respects, and beyond the guidance of Scripture, after the likeness of the kingdoms of this world. XIV. Fourth, that there is not sufficient agreement among all people even about the best form of worldly government. XV. Fifth, that the Church is indeed a wholly monarchical government, but with respect to Christ. XVI. Sixth, that Scripture teaches nothing about another monarch. XVII. Seventh, that Scripture plainly hands down another form of government. XVIII. Eighth, that the precept corresponds to the practice of the primitive Church, since the example of Christ does not favour monarchy, and the equality of bishops is often impressed by the Fathers. XIX. Third, it is demonstrated that Peter has no successors in all that he truly was, nor ought to have any. For he was an apostle. XX. Bellarmine's escapes are removed. XXI. In a certain sense all the apostles are succeeded by all bishops equally. XXII. Observations about that succession. First: one is said to succeed not only one, but all at once. XXIII. Second: one does not succeed in personal prerogatives, but in a local succession. XXIV. These things are applied: the succession is presupposed, and first the succession of Paul is also commended. XXV. They can have nothing from Peter which others cannot equally have from the same source, especially the Antiochenes, as Innocent I testifies. XXVI. Seven notes on his testimony. XXVII. The objections of Bellarmine are dissolved. XXVIII. A reply is given to the appeal to the Apostolic See. XXIX. Which from the beginning was common, as is taught by examples and testimonies. XXX. Granted a monarchical power in Peter, uncertainty remains, and the succession of Roman Bishops in it is not necessarily presupposed at the same time. Perhaps several, perhaps always the most worthy, perhaps always the bishops ought to have succeeded at the imperial see. XXXI. The inconveniences in the fact that it cannot be shown how the Roman Bishop, besides the bishopric of the city, also holds the prefecture of the world. XXXII. Further uncertainty, whether all Roman Bishops ought always to enjoy this succession. XXXIII. Bellarmine's argument, that no other than the Roman Bishop ever called himself thus the successor of Peter. To this it is replied, first, that boasting and presumption do not prove lawful possession. XXXIV. Summary of the following reply. XXXV. Second, it is shown that the first Roman Bishops did not even aim at such a succession. By general testimonies. XXXVI. The slight attempt of Victor. The testimonies of Cyprian. XXXVII. Third, it is shown that others aimed at similar things. The general testimony of Guicciardini about the Bishops of Constantinople and of Ravenna. The example of John of Constantinople, rebuked by Gregory the Great for the title of universal bishop. XXXVIII. That John aimed at similar things, and was absolutely condemned by Gregory. XXXIX. Therefore faulty in Boniface III also and in his successors. The cause changed by his time, and the titles granted to him by Phocas, which John III also rejected. XL. Individual bishops bear witness against such a succession. XLI. Gathered in councils, not summoned by the Roman, not presiding as the ordinary president in councils, not seeking confirmation. XLII. Decreeing things contrary to such a succession. XLIII. It is shown on what foundation, or pretext, by what means and arts, they came to such a usurpation of the pontificate of the whole Church, to which they did not arrive by the mere exposition of the words "You are Peter", which in antiquity were rarely cited to that end. XLIV. But the political dignity and majesty of the city first contributed much, first, to the primacy of order only. XLV. Nor did the zeal, integrity and orthodoxy of the first Roman Bishops help little, secondly. XLVI and XLVII. Many very bad arts that were employed are recounted. XLVIII. The help which came over several centuries from the constitution of the political government. XLIX. If all things are conceded with respect to the first Roman Bishops, they would gain nothing at all from those who have existed for several centuries, who are most unlike Peter in everything. L. For they do not succeed him either in office or in doctrine. LI. Local succession indeed is sometimes useful, and was so formerly. LII. But it is not sufficient. LIII. This is confirmed from the ancients. LIV. By reasons. LV. The conclusion is drawn, and the argument of the following treatment is set out.

units.la: commemorantur; XLVIII. Auxilium, quod ex constitutione Regiminis Politici per aliquot secula accessit; XLIX. Si omnia concedantur respectu primorum Episcoporum Romanorum, nihil planè inde lucrarentur, qui ab aliquot seculis fuerunt, sed Petro in omnibus dissimillimi; L. Neque enim ei succedunt in officio, neque etiam in doctrina; LI. Successio autem localis quidem aliquando utilis est & olim fuit; LII. Sed non sufficit; LIII. Quod ex veteribus comprobatur; LIV. Rationibus; LV. Concluditur, & argumentum tractationis sequentis exhibetur.
units.tr: are commemorated; XLVIII. The help that came through the constitution of the civil government over several centuries; XLIX. If everything is granted with respect to the early Roman bishops, they gain nothing at all from it, namely those who have held the office over the last several centuries, who are in every respect most unlike Peter; L. For they do not succeed him in office, nor indeed in doctrine; LI. Local succession, however, is sometimes useful and was so in the past; LII. But it is not sufficient; LIII. This is confirmed from the ancients; LIV. By reasons; LV. Conclusion, and the argument of the following treatise is set out.

units.la: I. DIximus ab initio Dissertationis secundae, omitti potuisse post primam de Petri Monarchico Primatu, disquisitiones alias, quia Petrus potestatem, quam acceperit & habuerit nunquam, certo loco exercere, aut certis successoribus relinquere haud potuerit. De loco tamen Differt. secunda vidimus, utrum nimirum Petrus Romæ, & Urbis Episcopus fuerit, idem jam circa successores facturi, in eos pariter inquisituri. Nempe iubet factum prosequi, quamvis tali jure destituatur, & filum quadantenus erroris sequi, cui solenne ἀσύγκλωστε συγκλώθειν, & adhuc magis detegere non sanctas sub nomine sancto impostura, & ædificationem considerare, quæ sit super cariosum fundamentum, & videre, utrum saltem illius, quod Petrus possedit, ex asse hæreditatem habeant, certissimè interim jam persuasi, non posse bene judicari de omnibus illis, quotquot quasi ex hæreditate Petri possessiones, quibus Petrus caruerat, jactant, cum primis tot & tantas, & eum dedisse sic fingunt, quæ habuerat nunquam.
units.tr: I. We said at the beginning of the second Dissertation that, after the first, other inquiries about Peter's monarchical primacy could have been omitted, because Peter could never exercise at a fixed place, nor leave to fixed successors, a power which he neither received nor possessed. Yet in the second Dissertation we saw whether Peter was at Rome and was Bishop of the City, and we shall now do the same with regard to his successors, and inquire into them equally. Indeed, it bids us follow the deed, although they are destitute of such a right, and to follow somewhat the thread of error, to which belongs the well-known saying, to spin together what cannot be spun together ["ἀσύγκλωστε συγκλώθειν"], and still more to uncover the unholy impostures under a holy name, and to consider what edifice stands upon a rotten foundation, and to see whether they at least have the whole inheritance of what Peter possessed. We are already most certainly persuaded that no sound judgment can be made about all those possessions, however many, which they boast of as if from the inheritance of Peter, and which Peter lacked, especially so many and such great ones, which they pretend he gave, and which he never had.

units.la: II. De successione igitur summorum Pontificum hic loquuntur, quos ita non secundum ordinem Melchisedek esse docent, in quo unus habet ἱερωσύνην ἀπαράβατον sacerdotium non transiens, sed potius ex illorum ordine, quorum πλείονές εἰσι γινόμενοι ἱερεῖς, διὰ τὸ θανάτῳ κωλύεσθαι παραμένειν [?], plures facti sunt, quia morte manere prohibebantur, Hebr. VII. 23. 24. id est, ex ordine Aaronico unà cum Veteri Test. abolito, nisi reductum jam esse velint, aut tertium proprie sic dictorum Pontificum, & quidem etiam summorum fingere; Utimur autem hac appellatione stylum ipsorum imitantes; Postquam enim Episcopi Romani diu satis ita simpliciter, vel Papæ (nomine adhuc seculo sexto aliis quoque Episcopis dari solito) vocati essent, & Patriarchæ titulus, quem seculo etiam sexto, teste Isidoro Hispalensi, P. Hormisda primus ex Romanis à Justino Imp. accepit, tanquam quibusdam aliis præcipuis communis, proin minus distinctivus, haud multum arrideret Monarchiam affectantibus; bus, tandem nomina Papärum & Pontificum summorum, Maximorum sibi appropriârunt, quorum posterius (quod etiam seculo adhuc sexto aliis commune erat) juxta Decr. I. Cap. Clericos: par. Pontifex. dist.21. & libr. sentent. Cap.X. ad exemplum Numæ Pompilii, Regis simul & Sacerdotis Romani, suum fecerunt: Sacerdotes autem Gentiles Romani suos hoc nomine appellabant, quia præter Religionis curam etiam pontis habebant, in quo posita simulachra; Christianis verò Pontifex dicitur, quasi pontem in alteram vitam faciens, si Antonius de Rosellis M. p.1. c. 56. rectè conjicit.
units.tr: II. Therefore they speak here of the succession of the highest Pontiffs, whom they teach are not according to the order of Melchizedek, in which one has "a priesthood that does not pass away" ["ἱερωσύνην ἀπαράβατον"], not passing to another, but rather after the order of those of whom "there were many priests, because they were prevented by death from remaining" ["πλείονές εἰσι γινόμενοι ἱερεῖς, διὰ τὸ θανάτῳ κωλύεσθαι παραμένειν"] [?], "they were made many, because they were prevented by death from continuing", Hebrews 7:23, 24; that is, according to the Aaronic order, together with the Old Testament, which has been abolished, unless they wish it to have been already restored, or else feign a third kind of properly so-called Pontiffs, and indeed of highest ones. We use this name, however, imitating their own style. For after the Roman Bishops had for a long time been called simply "Bishops" or "Popes" (a name still given at the sixth century to other bishops as well), and the title of Patriarch, which, according to Isidore of Seville, Pope Hormisdas first of the Romans received from the Emperor Justin in the sixth century, seemed not very pleasing to those aiming at monarchy, since it was common to certain other principal bishops and therefore less distinctive, at last they appropriated to themselves the names "Popes" and "Highest Pontiffs" and "Greatest". The latter (which was also common to others at the sixth century) they made their own, following the example of Numa Pompilius, king and priest of Rome, according to the Decretum, I, chapter "Clerici", paragraph "Pontifex", distinction 21, and the Book of Sentences, chapter 10. The Gentile priests of Rome called their own by this name, because besides the care of religion they also had charge of the bridge on which the images were placed. Among Christians, however, the Pontiff is so called "as making a bridge into the other life", if Antonius de Rosellis, in his Summa, part 1, chapter 56, rightly conjectures.

units.la: III. Pontifices hi Romani Christiani Petro succedere dicuntur, & ista eorum aliorúmque ab illis dependentium successio ejusque continuatio inter Ecclesiæ veræ notas apud Pontificios numeratur. Quamvis autem hoc, sine respectu ad veram in ore Doctorum doctrinam ex verbo Dei semper examinandam, satis ineptè fiat, cùm & successio continua Seductorum, & Seductorum quidem etiam post Doctores veritatis dari possit & detur, ut Tyrannorum & Usurpatorum post Reges legitimos, latronum post pastores, & Ecclesiæ particulari constans Episcoporum bonorum successio nullibi promissa legatur, universalis autem, non Pontificia istâ successione bonorum Episcoporum, pro diversitate temporum & locorum, plurium aut pauciorum, Verbum Dei pro eadem diversitate magis, minùs purè, semper tamen cum fundamenti retentione, tractantium, sola gaudeat; tamen etiam ex falsa ista hypothesi non exiguum tractationi nostræ pondus accedere liquet, utpote in quo examinandum suscipimus, qualis illa Ecclesiæ nota, utrum digna, & tanta sit, quæ in istum censum venire mereatur, & utrum non potiùs respectu Ecclesiæ Romanæ maximis næвis laboret.
units.tr: III. These Roman pontiffs are said to succeed Peter, and this succession of theirs, and of the others who depend on them, is counted by the Papists among the marks of the true Church. Yet this is done quite foolishly, since it is made without regard to the true doctrine in the mouths of the teachers, which must always be tested by the Word of God. A continuous succession of seducers can exist, and does, even after the teachers of the truth, as tyrants and usurpers follow lawful kings and robbers follow shepherds. No succession of good bishops is promised anywhere in Scripture for a particular Church. The universal Church, however, does not rejoice in the Papists' succession, but in a succession of good bishops, and of those who handle the Word of God more or less purely according to the diversity of times and places, though always while the foundation is kept. Even so, it is clear that from this false hypothesis no small weight accrues to our treatment, since we undertake to examine what sort of mark of the Church this is, whether it is worthy and important enough to be counted in this list, and whether it does not rather labour under very great blemishes with respect to the Roman Church.

units.la: IV. Succedere autem volunt non in lapsu Petri, utpote qui infallibilitatem à longo tempore jactant; nec proin etiam in pœnitentia, quamvis Petrus Danesius Episcopus Vaurensis, referente Thuano in castr. sub Carolo IX. ex Gallia Romam missus illud ita voluisse videatur, qui, cùm non nemo, Guidone Fabro, Regis Legato, Reformationem vehementer urgente, irridendo diceret: Gallus cantat! reposuisse fertur: Utinam Gallicinio Petrus ad resipiscentiam & fletus excitetur! nec etiam in reprehensione per Paulum Gal.II. erga Petrum facta, Nam si Papa (sunt verba apud Gratianum dist.40.) suæ & fraterna salutis negligens deprehenditur, inutilis & remissus in suis operibus, & insuper à bono taciturnus, quod magis officit sibi in omnibus, nihilominus innumerabiles populos secum ducit primo mancipio gehennacum ipso plagis multis in aeternum vapulaturos, hujus culpas isthic redarguere praesumit mortalium nullus, quod cunctos ipse judicaturus, a nemine est judicandus, nisi deprehendatur a fide devius. Quibus tamen postremis verbis etiam remedium invenerunt, statuendo, Papam non posse a fide deviare. Concinunt verba Glossatoris in caput, quando persona. de translatione Episcopi in Decretalibus; quibus Papae tribuit coeleste arbitrium, eumque ideo naturam rerum mutare, substantialia unius rei applicando alii; Et de nullo posse aliquid facere, & de sententia, quae nulla est, facere aliquam: in his, qua vult, ei esse pro ratione voluntatem: nec esse, qui ei dicat: Cur ita facis? posse enim supra jus dispensare & de injustitia facere justitiam, corrigendo jura & mutando: demum, plenitudinem obtinere potestatis. In his Papam aliquando Petro, qui reprehensionem admisit, majorem, nec ejus successorem faciunt; nec etiam in munere concionandi, quod aliis committunt; nec etiam in miraculorum patratione, cujus se incapaces profitentur; nec etiam in sorore foemina circumducenda, quales non tantum non habent, matrimoniali nexu sibi junctas, sed ne quidem aliis permittunt; nec etiam in obedientia Magistratui exhibita, cum contra omnibus mundi Magistratibus imperare velint; nec etiam in piscatione hominum, illam argenti magis amantes; nec etiam in illo: Aurum & argentum non habeo; utroque abundantes; nec etiam in martyrio pro Christo obeundo, cum saltem Innocentius IV. in Concilio Lugdunensi testatus sit, se adveniente Imperatore Friderico II. quem ibi excommunicaverat, statim discessurum, quia nolit fieri Martyr; nec etiam in multis aliis, sed tantum in dignitatibus, & quidem non modo in Episcopatu, quem Petro tribuunt, Romano, sed simul etiam in Monarchia Ecclesiastica, ut Bellarminus in titulo habet, quamvis in ipsa tractatione tantum de Pontificibus, quia vocabulum hoc mitius est, & facilius admittitur; loquatur.
units.tr: IV. They wish to succeed not in Peter's fall, since they boast of his infallibility for a long time, nor therefore in his repentance either, although Peter Danès, Bishop of Vaur, sent from France to Rome under Charles IX, as Thuanus reports in castr., seems to have wished it so. When someone, Guy Fabre, the King's envoy, urging reformation vigorously, mockingly said, "The Gaul sings!" he is reported to have replied, "Would that by the cock's crow Peter might be roused to repentance and weeping!" Nor do they wish it in the rebuke that Paul gave Peter (Gal. 2). For (these are the words in Gratian, dist.40.): "If the Pope is found neglecting his own and his brothers' salvation, useless and slack in his works, and moreover silent about good things, which harms himself most in all things, yet he leads countless peoples with him, destined first for hell, to be beaten with many blows for eternity, no mortal presumes to rebuke his faults here, because he himself is to judge all, and is to be judged by no one, unless he is found to have strayed from the faith." Yet they have found a remedy even in these last words, by laying down that the Pope cannot stray from the faith. The words of the Glossator on the chapter "quando persona", de translatione Episcopi in the Decretals agree with this. To the Pope they attribute a heavenly judgement, and therefore he changes the nature of things, applying the substantial qualities of one thing to another; "and he can make something out of nothing, and out of a sentence which is nothing make some sentence: in those matters which he wills, his will is the reason; nor is there anyone who may say to him, 'Why do you act so?' For he can dispense beyond the law, and make justice out of injustice, by correcting and changing the laws; finally, he holds the fullness of power." In these respects they do not make the Pope the successor of Peter, who admitted rebuke, but greater than him. Nor do they wish it in the office of preaching, which they commit to others; nor in working miracles, for which they profess themselves incapable; nor in leading about a sister as a wife, which they not only do not have, bound to them by marriage, but do not even permit to others; nor in the obedience shown to the magistrate, since they want to command all the magistrates of the world; nor in the fishing of men, since they love silver more; nor in that saying, "I have neither gold nor silver," since they abound in both; nor in dying as a martyr for Christ, since Innocent IV at the Council of Lyons at least testified that, when the Emperor Frederick II, whom he had excommunicated there, approached, he would at once depart, "because he is unwilling to become a martyr." Nor do they wish it in many other things, but only in dignities, and indeed not only in the Roman bishopric, which they attribute to Peter, but at the same time also in the Ecclesiastical Monarchy, as Bellarmine has in his title, although in the treatise itself he speaks only of Pontiffs, because that word is milder and more easily admitted.

units.la: V. De qua successione jam primo dispiciendum, quo jure illam sibi tribuant, aut tribuere possint.
units.tr: V. Concerning this succession, we must first examine by what right they claim it for themselves, or can claim it.

units.la: Certissimum est, in Scriptura nullibi legi; Episcopum Romanum esse successorem Petri. Et juxta praecedentia ne quidem in illa legitur; Petrum Romae fuisse, Romae Episcopum fuisse. Unus (quantum sciamus) repertus fuit Bozius, qui de signis Eccl. l.18.c.3. ex Scriptura, & quidem 2.Pet.III. 12.13.14.15. & Phil.IV. 3. Romanum Episcopum authoritate Apostolica
units.tr: It is most certain that nowhere in Scripture is it read that the Roman bishop is the successor of Peter. And from what has gone before, it is not even read there that Peter was at Rome or that he was bishop of Rome. One man (so far as we know) was found, Bozius, who de signis Eccl. l.18.c.3., from Scripture, and indeed from 2 Pet. 3:12–15 and Phil. 4:3, wished to show more closely that the Roman bishop, by apostolic authority, presides over all.

units.la: {} stolica omnibus præesse, propius ostendere voluerit; sed illud adhuc ita remotum & ineptum est, ut multò plùs lectori locorum laboris impendendum sit, ad conjiciendum, quomodo inde argumentatus sit, quàm verò ad refutandum argumentandi modum, si eum tandem cognoverit. De utroque videri potest Doctiss. Chamierus Panstr. Cath. l. 13. c. 2. integro. Reliqui monent, hic distinguendum esse inter successionem, & successionis rationem; Successionem ipsam esse ex instituto Christi, rationem autem successionis, quâ Romanus Pontifex potiùs quàm Antiochenus, vel aliquis alius succeḋat, esse ex facto Petri. Ut jam quilibet videre possit, eos non audere, successionem Pontificis Romani ex instituto Christi derivare, eos quidem ex instituto Christi derivare successionem alicujus, quisquis jam ille sit, (in quo mox etiam eos refutabimus) sed non successionem Romani Pontificis, de qua præcisè quæritur; unde illa sit? Hinc etiam Bellarminus l. 2. de Rom. Pont. c. 12. ubi de hoc agit, dicit; potuisse Petrum nullam sedem particularem sibi unquam eligere, adeóque successionem Episcopi Romani, quia Episcopus Romanus sit, ex facto Petri ortum habere, non ex prima Christi institutione; Et quamvis (si Petrus jubente Domino (de quo jam vidimus) Romam concesserit) non improbabile sit, Dominum etiam aperte jussisse, ut sedem suam Petrus ibi figeret Romæ, ut Romanus Episcopus absolutè ei succeederet; tamen, quicquid de hoc sit, saltem istam rationem successionis non esse ex prima institutione Pontificatûs, quæ in Evangelio legatur. Hinc etiam bis subjungit; Licèt forte non sit de jure divino, Romanum Pontificem, ut Romanum Pontificem, Petro succedere; Et hinc etiam successionem illam ex traditione arcessit. Hinc etiam vult, ex facto Petri dignitatem Pontificalem localem factam esse. Omnia citato loco.
units.tr: {} See, presides over all. But this is so remote and inept that far more labour must be spent by the reader in guessing how he argued from these texts than in refuting his mode of argument, if he has at last understood it. On both points the very learned Chamier may be consulted, Panstr. Cath. l. 13. c. 2., throughout. Others warn that here one must distinguish between the succession and the manner of the succession. The succession itself is by the institution of Christ, but the manner of succession, by which the Roman Pontiff rather than the Antiochene, or someone else, succeeds, is by the act of Peter. So anyone can now see that they do not dare to derive the succession of the Roman Pontiff from the institution of Christ. They do derive from the institution of Christ the succession of someone, whoever he may be (and we shall refute them on this point shortly), but not the succession of the Roman Pontiff, which is precisely the question: whence is it? Hence Bellarmine too, l. 2. de Rom. Pont. c. 12., where he treats this matter, says: "Peter could never have chosen for himself any particular see, and so the succession of the Roman bishop, because he is Roman bishop, arises from the act of Peter, not from the first institution of Christ." And although (if Peter, at the Lord's command (of which we have already seen), came to Rome) it is not improbable that the Lord also openly commanded that Peter should fix his see there at Rome, so that the Roman bishop should succeed him absolutely; yet, whatever be the case, at least this manner of succession is not from the first institution of the pontificate which is read in the Gospel. Hence he also adds twice: "Although perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff, as Roman Pontiff, succeeds Peter." And hence he also derives that succession from tradition. Hence he also wills that the local pontifical dignity was made by the act of Peter. All in the place cited.

units.la: VI. Ex quibus jam colligimus, successionem Pontificum Romanorum, si vel Petro in Monarchia Ecclesiæ succederent, non esse de jure divino, non esse de fide.
units.tr: VI. From these things we now conclude that the succession of the Roman Pontiffs, even if they succeeded Peter in the monarchy of the Church, is not by divine right and is not a matter of faith.

units.la: Id quod & magis, minùs apertè fatentur adversarii. Expi esse illud docuit Alphonsus adv. Haret. l. 1. c. 9. Docuerunt ab initio hujus seculi, in famosa sua thesi, Jesuitæ, credere Clementem VIII. (qui Pontifex illius anni erat) esse legitimum successorem Petri, non esse ex articulis fidei. Docuit, & concedere coactus est famosus ille Valerianus M. Capucinus, nequicquam propterea à Jesuitis, aliter tunc loquentibus, pulsatus; ut etiam Bellarminus secum pugnans, ubi priora dedit, dixit quoque; Si quis absolutè petat, an jure divino Romanus Pontifex pastor sit & Caput totius EccleEcclesiæ: omninò esse id asserendum, quia ad hoc nihil aliud requiratur quàm ut ipsa successio sit de jure divino; Item; Ad fidem Catholicam pertinere, Romanum Pontificem, ut Romanum Pontificem Petro succedere.
units.tr: Our opponents admit this, though more covertly than openly. Alphonsus adv. Haret. l. 1. c. 9. expressly taught it. At the beginning of this century the Jesuits, in their notorious thesis, taught that to believe that Clement VIII (who was Pope in that year) is the lawful successor of Peter is not one of the articles of faith. The notorious Valerianus Magnus, the Capuchin, also taught this and was forced to concede it, though the Jesuits then, speaking differently, attacked him for it in vain. Bellarmine too, contradicting himself, when he had first given one answer, said also: If anyone asks absolutely whether the Roman Pontiff is by divine right the pastor and head of the whole Church, this must be affirmed, because for this nothing more is required than that the succession itself be by divine right. Likewise: It belongs to the Catholic faith that the Roman Pontiff, as Roman Pontiff, succeeds Peter.

units.la: Sed rectè Bellarmino hæc secum pugnanti tribuimus; tribuimus etiam Bellarmino pugnanti cum sana ratione. Si enim Petrus potuit nullam sedem particularem sibi nunquam eligere, si successio Episcopi Romani ortum habet, non ex prima institutione Christi, sed ex facto Petri, eoque in Scripturis sacris nullibi memorato, & si forte de jure divino non sit, Romanum Pontificem, ut Romanum Pontificem Petro succedere, quomodo jam jure divino Romanus Pontifex Pastor & Caput totius Ecclesiæ vi illius successionis erit? An causa non erit de jure, sed effectum? Certè ad hoc, ut de jure divino Caput Ecclesiæ sit, plus requiritur, vel ipso Bellarmino judice, quàm ut ipsa successio sit de jure divino; requiritur adhuc ista successionis ratio, quá Romanus Pontifex potius quàm Antiochenus, vel aliquis alius succedat, ex Divina quoque institutione & revelatione cognoscenda. Quid enim est Jus divinum? Jus divinum est Thomæ 2. 2. q. 57. art. 1. quod à Deo promulgatur. Ubi autem à Deo promulgatum est, Romanum Pontificem in Monarchia Ecclesiæ universalis esse Successorem Petri? Forte ideo illud à Deo promulgatum, quia à Papa, quem aliquando Deum ab ipsis vocari ostendimus! Porrò; Si forte de jure divino non sit, Romanum Pontificem ut Romanum Pontificem, Petro succedere, quomodo illud ad fidem Catholicam pertinebit?
units.tr: But we rightly attribute these statements to Bellarmine, who contradicts himself; we also attribute them to Bellarmine as he contends against sound reason. For if Peter could have never chosen any particular see for himself; if the succession of the Bishop of Rome arose not from the first institution of Christ but from Peter's act, which is nowhere mentioned in holy Scripture; and if perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff, as Roman Pontiff, succeeds Peter, then how will the Roman Pontiff be, by divine right, the pastor and head of the whole Church by virtue of that succession? Or will the cause not be of right, but only the effect? Certainly, to make him head of the Church by divine right requires more, even by Bellarmine's own judgment, than that the succession itself be by divine right. There is still required that manner of succession by which the Roman Pontiff rather than the Antiochene, or someone else, succeeds, to be known from divine institution and revelation as well. For what is divine right? Divine right is, according to Thomas 2. 2. q. 57. art. 1, that which is promulgated by God. But where has God promulgated that the Roman Pontiff is the successor of Peter in the monarchy of the universal Church? Perhaps that was promulgated by God because it was promulgated by the Pope, whom we have shown elsewhere is sometimes called God by them! Further: If perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff, as Roman Pontiff, succeeds Peter, how will that belong to the Catholic faith?

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Quia non est idem, aliquid esse de fide & esse de jure divino, nec enim de jure divino fuit, ut Paulus haberet penulam, est tamen hoc ipsum de fide, Paulum habuisse penulam; Ita respondet Bellarminus, sed strenuè nugando, & secum porrò pugnando. Paulus certè non de jure divino habuit penulam, id est, Deus non peculiari modo instituit, ut Paulus istam penulam haberet, quod circa illam penulam etiam non necesse fuit, interim tamen jus divinum postulat, ut qui in Scripturis Sacris legit, Paulum penulam habuisse, illud etiam credat; Cur? Legit enim in Scripturis Sacris, & proin est à Deo promulgatum. Ideò etiam Bellarminus vult, hoc esse de fide; Quamvis alibi de verbo Dei l. 4. c. 12. contendat, in Scripturis multa esse, quæ ex se non pertineant ad fidem, cujus generis sint omnes Historiæ Vet. Test. & multa etiam Novi. Ast quando de Successione Pontificum Romanorum quæritur, utrum sit de jure divino & de fide, id est, utrum Deus illam successionem instituerit, & promulgaverit, & tamen institutionem dubiam relinquunt, promulgationem autem ostende-
units.tr: It is not the same thing for something to be a matter of faith and for it to be by divine right; for it was not by divine right that Paul should have a cloak, yet it is a matter of faith that Paul had a cloak. So Bellarmine answers, but trifling vigorously and contradicting himself again. Paul certainly did not have his cloak by divine right, that is, God did not institute in a special way that Paul should have that cloak, which was not even necessary concerning that cloak. Yet divine right requires that whoever reads in Holy Scripture that Paul had a cloak should also believe it. Why? Because he reads it in Holy Scripture, and so it has been promulgated by God. Therefore Bellarmine also wants this to be a matter of faith; although elsewhere De verbo Dei l. 4. c. 12. he contends that there are many things in Scripture which of themselves do not pertain to faith, of which kind are all the histories of the Old Testament and many of the New. But when the question is about the succession of the Roman Pontiffs, whether it is by divine right and a matter of faith, that is, whether God instituted and promulgated that succession, and yet they leave the institution doubtful, while they show the promulgation

units.la: Distinctio Bellarmini inter, esse de fide, & esse de jure Divino; re non possunt, annon exinde concludere fas est, successionem non esse de jure divino, non esse etiam de fide; Esse quidem de fide penulam Pauli, de qua Scriptura loquitur, non item Pallium Pontificale Romanum, de quo Scriptura non loquitur? Et si multa in Scripturis sint, quae ex se ad fidem non pertineant, multo minus ad fidem pertinere successionem illam, quae in Scripturis non est? Quis autem non miretur, Pauli penulam in Scriptura esse, Paparum successionem non esse?
units.tr: Can we not conclude from Bellarmine's distinction between being a matter of faith and being by divine right that the succession is neither by divine right nor a matter of faith? Is it right that Paul's cloak, which Scripture speaks of, is a matter of faith, but the Roman pontifical pallium, of which Scripture does not speak, is not? And if there are many things in Scripture which of themselves do not pertain to faith, is it much less the case that that succession, which is not in Scripture, pertains to faith? Who would not marvel that Paul's cloak is in Scripture, but the succession of the Popes is not?

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Sed quid, si ipse Bellarminus dicit, sedem Romae divino jussu constituram esse, non definiri a Pontificibus (Marcello & Leone, testibus domesticis, illo etiam suppositititio) tanquam rem, quae de fide sit, sed narrari tantum ut historiam. Non esse autem de fide Pontificum narrationes, sed solum decreta? Igitur ad fidem Catholicam pertinebit ista successio, quae tamen nec expresse, nec implicite in Scriptura est, cum Sophistae tamen a nobis postulent, ut ea, quae ad fidem pertinent, ipsis expressis Scripturae verbis demonstremus; ad fidem pertinebit Catholicam; & tamen non erit de fide; Sed nec pertinet ad fidem, nec etiam est de fide, nimirum divina, cujus objectum esse potest nonnisi revelatio divina; Et qualis quaeso fides divina & Catholica est, quae ex facto humano, de quo nihil habet Codex Divinus, pendet? Factis & factorum per homines non θεo- πνεύστος relationibus, probabilitatem tantum aliquam, & nonnisi moralem certitudinem habentibus, circa Petrum, & multo magis circa reliquos, heic omnia inniterentur, proin de fide esse, vel ad fidem pertinere non possunt, nec etiam illis summa, quam aliunde non habent, certitudo a Paparum definitionibus accedere potest, cum ex communi sententia Papae saltem in rebus & quaestionibus facti errare possint, quaestiones autem facti sunt; an Petrus Romae & Episcopus fuerit, sedem ibi ad tot secula collocarit, ipsi ejus Successores sint?
units.tr: But what if Bellarmine himself says that the see at Rome will be established by divine command, but is not defined by the Popes (Marcellus and Leo, domestic witnesses, and that spurious one too) as a matter of faith, but only related as history. Moreover, the narrations of the Popes are not matters of faith, only their decrees? So that succession will pertain to the Catholic faith, though it is neither expressly nor implicitly in Scripture, while the Sophists nonetheless demand that we demonstrate from the express words of Scripture the things that pertain to faith. It will pertain to the Catholic faith, and yet it will not be a matter of faith. But it neither pertains to faith nor is a matter of faith, namely divine faith, whose object can only be divine revelation. And what kind of divine and Catholic faith is it, I ask, that hangs on a human fact about which the Divine Codex has nothing to say? Everything here would rest on facts and on relations of facts handed down by men, not [θεόπνευστος] God-breathed, which have only some probability and merely moral certainty, concerning Peter and much more concerning the rest. Therefore these things cannot be of faith or pertain to faith, and the definitions of the Popes cannot add to them the certainty they do not have from elsewhere, since by the common opinion the Pope can err at least in matters of fact, and these questions are questions of fact: whether Peter was at Rome and was bishop there, whether he established the see there for so many centuries, and whether his successors are the present ones?

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Manet igitur nostra conclusio, successionem Romanorum Pontificum, si vel Petro in Monarchia Ecclesiae succederent, non esse de jure divino, non esse de fide. Et proin, quamvis anxie disputantibus de suprema sua potestate Domesticis Paulus III. ridens dixerit, se possessionem vel solam optimum titulum habere, referente illud Guicciardino hist. Pap. praef. tamen maxime est, cur terreantur Pontifices isti & eorum Gnathones. Sic enim, quod Petrae inaedificatum esse jactant, arenae superstructum deprehenditur, & quod pro certo tradunt, incertitudinis convincitur, non tantum Petri tam immensa potestas, & in urbe præsentia, & per tot annos commoratio, & Episcopatus (quorum etiam ex parte falsitas demonstrata ;) sed insuper quoque successio in ejus jura aliorum: (cujus etiam falsitas jamjam demonstrabitur;) Si autem ista hactenus saltem incerta sunt,incerta sunt (quod heic repeto;) ea quoque omnia,quæ istis superstruuntur,Monarchia, infallibilitas, legislationis potestas, in religione ista omnia!
units.tr: Our conclusion therefore stands: that the succession of the Roman Pontiffs, even if they succeeded Peter in the monarchy of the Church, is not by divine right and not a matter of faith. And so, although Paul III, when his own courtiers disputed anxiously about his supreme power, laughingly said that possession alone is the best title, as Guicciardini reports in hist. Pap. praef., there is still great reason why these Pontiffs and their flatterers should be alarmed. For what they boast is built on rock is found to be built on sand, and what they hold for certain is shown to be uncertain. Not only Peter's immense power, his presence in the city, his long stay there, and his episcopate (the falsity of which is partly demonstrated already), but also the succession of others into his rights (whose falsity will be demonstrated presently) are uncertain. If these things are at least uncertain so far (which I repeat here), then everything built upon them, the monarchy, the infallibility, the power of legislation, all of it in this religion!

units.la: X. Sed ne quidem certitudinem illam humanam, historicam, minorem,istis relinquimus; fictitiam planè & apertè falsam esse illam in Monarchia Ecclesiæ successionem demonstramus. Non quidem hic omnibus modis,eò enim collimat tota nostra tractatio, & maximè illa suo loco secuturà de vitiis Electionum Pontificum. Hic pauca tantùm generaliora & origini propiora attulisse sufficiet. Et primò quidem progredimur ad successionis hujus examen ex ipsa Petri conditione instituendum. Postulant illud, & valdè postulant, dicentes, Petrum fuisse Ecclesiæ Monarcham, talem autem Ecclesiæ omnibus temporibus summè necessarium esse. Sed nos, Petrum Monarcham non fuisse, ostendimus prolixè, & proin merito argumentamur; Si Petri tempore Petrus, aut alius Monarcha non fuit,haud magis nostro tempore tali,sive ille jam Petri Successor esse velit,sive non,opus est: Quando autem in illo argumento de necessario Monarcha tantopere sibi abblandiuntur, & constitutionem talium Pontificum & successionem Episcoporum Romanorum eo potissimùm confirmare nituntur, operæ pretium erit, illud, quamvis post ea, quæ allata sunt, ex superabundanti, proin etiam,nec non ob aliorum in hac materia studium & prolixitatem, paucis considerare.
units.tr: X. But we do not leave even that human, historical, lesser certainty to them. We demonstrate that the succession in the monarchy of the Church is wholly fictitious and plainly false. Not indeed in every way here, for our whole treatment aims at that, and especially the discussion that will follow in its place on the defects of the elections of the Popes. Here it will be enough to have brought forward only a few more general points, closer to the origin. And first we proceed to examine this succession from Peter's own condition. They demand this, and insistently, saying that Peter was the monarch of the Church, and that such a monarch is always most necessary to the Church. But we have shown at length that Peter was not a monarch, and so we rightly argue: if in Peter's time Peter, or another, was not a monarch, then there is no more need for one in our time, whether or not he wishes to be Peter's successor. Since, however, they flatter themselves so greatly with that argument about a necessary monarch, and strive chiefly to confirm the constitution of such Popes and the succession of the Roman bishops by it, it will be worth considering it briefly, although after what has been said it is superfluous, and so also on account of the zeal and length of others on this matter.

units.la: XI. Ajunt cum Bellarmino de Pont. Rom.l.i.c.i. nemini dubium esse posse, quin & potuerit & voluerit Salvator noster Jesus Christus Ecclesiam suam eâ ratione & modo gubernare, qui sit omnium optimus & utilissimus,præstantissimum autem esse Monarchicum.E. Respondeo, nemini omninò dubium esse posse,quin & potuerit & voluerit Salvator noster Jesus Christus Ecclesiam suam eâ ratione & modo gubernare, qui sit omnium optimus,id est,suæ sapientiæ & hominum viatorum statui maximè accommodatus; Nam ita simpliciter optimum & præstantissimum Ecclesiæ militanti attribui nequit, utpote,quam Dominus Jesus gradatim ad perfectionem perducit. Hinc quamvis optima constitutio fidelium sit perfectè amantium, tales tamen in hac vita non reperiuntur. Sic etiam in specie omnes omninò in regimine Ecclesiae suae, quales dari nemo negabit, nævos emendare statim, vel prævenire Spiritus sui gratiâ, si voluisset, potuisset; quod tamen eum noluisse, & sapientiae ejus convenit, & experientia testatur. Non igitur ita absolutè argumentandum est, cùm & Bellarminus in Regimine per Papas facilè nævos deprehendere potuerit, maximos etiam, & regimen sine illis absolutè melius & utilius & praestantius concipere; v. g. sub Monarcha in officio diligente, quàm verò sub ignavis & voluptatibus tantùm ac curis secularibus immersis, quales multi fuerunt; Sub Monarcha sancto, quàm sub monstris, qualia non pauca, secula cumprimis praeterita viderunt; Monarcha infallibili etiam in quaestionibus facti, cùm communior sit sententia, tantùm in quaestionibus juris infallibiles esse Pontifices; sub Monarcha, qui ne quidem tanquam doctor privatus haereticus fieri possit, quod Bellarminus etiam de Pontificibus suis largitur. Et sic deinceps.
units.tr: XI. They say, with Bellarmine (On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, chapter 1), that no one can doubt that our Savior Jesus Christ both could and would govern his Church by that method and manner which is the best and most useful of all, and that the monarchical is the most excellent. I answer: no one at all can doubt that our Savior Jesus Christ both could and would govern his Church by that method and manner which is the best of all, that is, most suited to his wisdom and to the state of wayfaring men. For the best and most excellent cannot simply be attributed to the militant Church, since the Lord Jesus leads it gradually to perfection. Hence, although the best constitution of the faithful is one of perfect love, such people are not found in this life. So also, in particular, in the government of his Church, which no one will deny is of such a kind, he could, if he had wished, have immediately corrected or prevented blemishes by the grace of his Spirit; yet that he did not wish it both agrees with his wisdom and is attested by experience. Therefore we must not argue so absolutely, since Bellarmine too could easily have detected blemishes, even very great ones, in government by Popes, and could conceive of a government without them as absolutely better, more useful, and more excellent: for example, under a monarch who is a diligent officer rather than under ignorant men immersed in pleasures and worldly cares, of which there have been many; under a holy monarch rather than under monsters, of which the past centuries saw not a few; under a monarch infallible even in questions of fact, although the more common opinion holds that Popes are infallible only in questions of law; under a monarch who cannot even become a heretic as a private teacher, which Bellarmine also grants to his Popes. And so on.

units.la: XII. Cùm igitur hic non de absolutè optimo & perfectissimo cogitandum sit, nec etiam humana sapientia, cui in divinis stultescere solenne est, quid Ecclesiae Christi, in terris adhuc imperfectae, & variis modis exercendae, mirisque Providentiae Divinae viis ad culmen perfectionis tandem perducendae, maximè conveniat, temerè definire debeat, missis, quas illa suppeditare posset, argutiis, à benignissimo Servatore potiùs discere debemus, qualem Ecclesiae suae Regiminis formam constituere voluerit, quàm ipsi docere, quid potuerit aut debuerit heic facere; Qualis certè magisterialis in hoc & aliis Deo quasi praescribendi cacoëthes, ut sapientiam primam non exiguâ injuriâ afficit, & religionem eáque quae ad religionem spectant, omni tempore corrupit, ita inprimis post tam luculentam voluntatis divinae expositionem ab hominibus Christianis procul abesse, nec proin quaeri deberet, quale institui debuerit regimen, sed quale institutum sit, cùm, quicquid Deus efficit, ita efficiat, ut optimum sit; ut hominis natura homini optima est à Deo condita, licèt Angelicâ inferior & composita.
units.tr: XII. Since, then, we must not think here of what is absolutely best and most perfect, nor should human wisdom, which is accustomed to play the fool in divine matters, rashly determine what most suits the Church of Christ, still imperfect on earth and to be governed in various ways, and to be led at last to the summit of perfection by the wondrous ways of divine Providence, we ought rather to learn from our most gracious Savior what form of government he wished to establish for his Church, than to teach him ourselves what he could or should have done here. Such a magisterial itch to prescribe to God, setting aside the subtleties that it could supply, does no small injury to the primary wisdom and has always corrupted religion and the matters that pertain to religion. It is especially out of place among Christian men after so clear an exposition of the divine will; nor should it be asked what sort of government ought to have been instituted, but what sort has been instituted, since whatever God effects, he so effects that it is best, just as human nature, though inferior to the angelic and composite, was created by God as best for man.

units.la: XIII. Inprimis autem illud cavendum foret, ne, in quo Monarchici impingunt, Regnum Christi, quod non est de hoc mundo Joh.XVIII. ad similitudinem Regnorum hujus mundi in omnibus, & praeter Scripturarum manuductionem, componendum crederetur, cùm optimum alicui, non ideò etiam optimum alii & in alio, sed penes naturarum & circumstantiarum diversitatem saepe sit convenientiae determinatio, & semper etiam respici debeat, an aliquid bonum sit; qua ratione plurima in mundo splendorem habent, Ecclesiae valde indecora, nec enim est Respublica, quales mundanae, & nonnisi improprie sic dicitur; Hinc qui cum Panigarolla in Lect. Cath.6. pag.1. ex eo argumentantur, quod rerum publicarum sit optima Ecclesia; non absimiles videntur dicentibus; Homo omnium animalium ratione carentium est doctissimum; vel; cancer coelestis est omnium cancrorum maximus: In specie quoad regimen, par conditio esse nequit, cum illius diversa objecta, diversi modi & fines omnibus manifesti sint, & circa illud nemo ignorare possit, Ecclesiae Tyrannidem & hypocrisin & vim conscientiis allatam, quae supremam unius potestatem, experientia etiam teste, facile excipiunt aut comitantur, plurimum nocere, cum contra populus Christi spontaneus esse, nonnisi demonstratione Spiritus trahi, & in regno coelorum nomen humanum audiri non deberet. Et nequidem adversarii volent, in omnibus, eandem quoad regimen mundi & Ecclesiae rationem esse, cum sic sequeretur, Democratiam in Ecclesia etiam esse a Deo, sicut a Deo esse negare non audent respectu mundi, maxime autem differentiam confirmant Galli, qui sub Monarchia maxime absoluta viventes, tamen juxta ea, quae Diss.1. prolixius notavimus, regimen Ecclesiae Aristocraticum faciunt.
units.tr: XIII. Above all, however, care must be taken lest the kingdom of Christ, which is not of this world (John 18), be thought to be constructed in every respect like the kingdoms of this world and beyond the guidance of the Scriptures. For what is best for one thing is not therefore best for another, nor in another; the determination of fitness often depends on the diversity of natures and circumstances, and one must always consider whether something is good at all. By this reasoning, many things in the world have splendor that is very unbecoming to the Church, for it is not a commonwealth like worldly ones, and it is only improperly called that. Hence those who argue with Panigarola (Lect. Cath. 6, p. 1) from the fact that the Church is the best of commonwealths seem not unlike those who say: man is the most learned of the animals that lack reason; or: the heavenly crab is the largest of all crabs. As for government in particular, there can be no equal footing, since its different objects, different methods, and ends are plain to all, and no one can be unaware that the tyranny of the Church, its hypocrisy, and the violence done to consciences, which, as experience also attests, readily accept or accompany the supreme power of one, do great harm. Whereas the people of Christ ought to be willing, drawn only by the demonstration of the Spirit, and in the kingdom of heaven no human name should be heard. Nor indeed will our adversaries want the same reasoning about government in the world and in the Church in all things, since it would then follow that democracy too is from God in the Church, just as they do not dare to deny that it is from God with respect to the world. Indeed the French confirm the difference most strongly: though living under a most absolute monarchy, they nonetheless make the government of the Church aristocratic, in line with what we noted more fully in Diss. 1.

units.la: XIV. Sed nequidem quoad regimen mundi res ita se habet, ut eam quoad Ecclesiam desiderant, & ut inde argumentum pro necessitate Regiminis Monarchici in Ecclesia formari possit. Sunt diversae regiminis formae; De quibus, quaenam sit optima, adhuc sub judice lis est, & ne ipse quidem Bellarminus ausus est aliter praeferre Monarchiam, quam seclusis circumstantiis, in quo minus adversamur, ut &, quando de Monarcha alterius & praestantioris naturae sermo est; quemadmodum optime mundum Deus regit, pastor oves. Sed heic circumstantiae vel maxime considerari debent, & de Monarcha ejusdem naturae quaeritur Nunquam autem vel mundum sub unius Monarchae Regimine fuit, nec forte unquam futurus est. Formae regiminis plerumque sunt mixtae; earum unaquaeque commoda habet & incommoda; Haec huic nationi magis apta est, illa illi; Et si potentissimarum Monarchiarum exempla habemus, non desunt exempla Rerumpublicarum, quae in statu Aristocratico & Democratico diu, potenter & feliciter durârunt, imò constat, ab initio Monarchias nullas constitutas nisi per vim, bella & scelera, contrà verò reliquas formas ex communi consensu, aut omnes, aut plerasque, quod posterius certè naturæ humanæ multò magis accommodum est. Dein in Monarchico Regimine illud eruditissimi Politici præferunt plurimi, quod hæreditario jure devolvitur, quod tamen ea de causa nemo in Ecclesiam introduci cupit.
units.tr: XIV. But the situation regarding the government of the world is not such that it can be used as they wish it to be for the Church, so that an argument for the necessity of a monarchical government in the Church could be built from it. There are different forms of government, and as to which is best the question is still undecided. Not even Bellarmine dared to prefer monarchy outright rather than with circumstances set aside, and there we disagree less, as also when the talk is of a monarch of another and more excellent nature, such as God, who rules the world, or the shepherd, who rules his sheep, does so supremely well. But here circumstances above all must be considered, and the question concerns a monarch of the same nature. Yet the world has never been under the rule of one monarch, nor perhaps ever will be. Forms of government are for the most part mixed, and each has its advantages and disadvantages: this one suits this nation better, that one another. And if we have examples of the most powerful monarchies, there are no lack of examples of commonwealths that have flourished for a long time, powerfully and happily, under aristocratic and democratic forms. Indeed, it is established that from the beginning no monarchies were set up except through force, wars and crimes, whereas the other forms arose from common consent, all or most of them, and the latter is certainly far more agreeable to human nature. Then, among monarchical governments, very many of the most learned political writers prefer the one that passes by hereditary right; yet for that very reason no one wishes it to be introduced into the Church.

units.la: XV. Et quod jam attinet illius regimen, ex revelatione cognoscimus, omninò Monarchicum illud esse, sed respectu Christi, unici capitis, fundamenti, sponsi, debere esse & unam fidem, & unum baptisma, & unum Dominum; Dominum esse illum, qui fideles sanguine suo redemerit, regeneraverit, conservaverit, & adhuc regeneret & conservet Spiritu & verbo suo, & defendat contra hostes quosvis potentiâ suâ; Cujus etiam Ecclesia regnum dicitur, non alicujus hominis; Et proin, cùm gloriam suam alteri dare nec possit, nec velit, & ob ipsum illud, quòd regimen Ecclesiæ Monarchicum esse debet, non Duumviratus, & cùm adhuc vivat & sub se habeat, qui alii cuidam subjecti non sunt, nec esse debent, alius etiam in consortium potestatis supremæ admitti non debet. Vanum enim est, quod contendunt, Monarcham visibiliter præsentem esse debere, cùm nequidem Rex terrenus corpus suum per omnes regni sui angulos circumferre debeat, imò salvo regno constitutis vicariis in exteras regiones proficisci possit; Christus autem, qui corpore suo in cœlos, ut in regni sui meliorem beatioremque partem transiit, non abest ut internus doctor, nec etiam, ut dictum, aliis functionibus regiis, sed tantùm ut doctor externus, quomodo etiam in terris manens non ubique ipse docere potuisset, & ideo quoque constituit Doctores homines, non Monarcham alium.
units.tr: XV. As for the government of the Church, we know from revelation that it is wholly monarchical, but with respect to Christ, the one head, foundation and bridegroom. There must be one faith, one baptism and one Lord: he is the Lord who redeemed the faithful with his blood, regenerated them, preserved them, and still regenerates and preserves them by his Spirit and word, and defends them against all enemies by his power. His Church is also called his kingdom, not the kingdom of any man. Therefore, since he can neither give his glory to another nor wishes to, and because the government of the Church must be monarchical for that very reason, it is not a dual rule; and since he is still alive and has under him those who are not, and must not be, subject to anyone else, no other person ought to be admitted to a share of supreme power. For it is vain for them to contend that the monarch must be visibly present, since not even an earthly king must carry his body through every corner of his kingdom; indeed, with his kingdom secure, he can appoint vicars and set out for foreign regions. Christ, however, who passed with his body into the heavens, as into the better and happier part of his kingdom, is not absent as inner teacher, nor, as has been said, from his other royal functions, but only as external teacher. Even while remaining on earth he could not have taught everywhere in person, and so he also appointed men as teachers, not another monarch.

units.la: XVI. De quo etiam Monarcha altero, sive vice-Monarcha in Scripturis sacris altum silentium; Usque adeò, ut nec nomen ejus occurrat, nec dignitas, nec sedes descripta; nihil dicatur de ejus attributis, signis, functionibus, successione; non memoretur Ecclesiæ erga illum officium; Illud autem prædicitur satis aperte, oriturum esse quendam, qui talem potestatem sub nomine Christi, sed contra Christum affectare debeat. Nec etiam talem necessarium Ecclesiæ faciunt fines, quos prætexunt. Cùm nullibi dictum sit, controversias ex Ecclesia, maximè per ejusmodi Rectorem universalem versalem tolli debere; Imò manent, ubi ejus authoritas agnoscitur, multò maximæ, & quidem circa illum ipsum. Sic etiam sine tali mittente universali Evangelium annunciari potest, cùm Dominus messis varie sine ipso mittere possit operarios; nempe jam itur, quò divina trahit providentia, & saluti proximi consuli potest, coetibus & eorum præcipuis, maximè magistratibus, occasionem & facultatem præbentibus; Communio quoque exercetur Rectorum & Coetuum invicem diversorum fidem æquè pretiosam profitentium communi bono & pro occasionum diversis in locis & temporibus varietate; Datur non minùs aliquando prærogativa quibusdam, observatur aliquis ordinis primatus, sed sine imperio in fratres, multò magis in universam Ecclesiam, absoluto. Cæterùm qui videtur sub tali Monarcha ordo, maxima contra Christum confusio est. Et ille plus sibi sumit quàm præstat, aut præstare potest s curam omnium ecclesiarum, aliter etiam ac Paulus, cùm à se uno omnes omninò Ecclesias pendere velit; dum interim nullas curat, Pauli-num illud de se non valere putans, ut quidem adhuc putavit Gregorius M. hom.17. in Evang. Væ mihi, si non evangelizarem! 1.Cor.IX. 16.17. molestum est & ferè supra vires unius ecclesiæ bonum regimen particularis, id quod Chrysostomus multis libris de Sacerdotio contendit, & nos credemus omnium Ecclesiarum administrationi unum sufficere & quidem promissione destitutum? Nam omnipotentiam Dei non negamus, sed hic & alibi nolumus, ut Deum non in alium finem credant omnipotentem, nisi ut hanc omnipotentiam, cùm ipsi vellent, exsereret; quemadmodum dicunt, seculărem gladium ad nutum sui Monarchæ exserendum esse. Deus certè virtutem Spiritûs dat dimensam, non immensam, nullique uni propriam, sed pluribus communem, unus enim ille est, cui non det Spiritum ἐκ μέτρου ex mensura, Joh.III. reliqui autem accipiunt ex plenitudine ejus gratiam pro gratia, Joh.I. non autem semper maximam isti Monarchæ, sed sæpe minimam, imò nullam; quod aliter se haberet, si toti Ecclesiæ providere deberent; Et rectè Doctissimus suo tempore Wesselus Goese Voet de pœnit. scripsit: Impossibile homini est fines terræ nôsse; quomodo igitur judicabit, quos nôsse non poterit? quomodo judicabit fidem, quorum linguam ignorat? Unitatem igitur sibi Spiritus S. foventdam, vivificandam, conservandam retinuit & augendam, non Pontifici Romano, sæpe non curanti, reliquit; multi Ecclesiæ membra sunt, etiamsi Romam aut Romanum aliquem Papam esse nesciant. Et tamen universales esse volunt, similes magnis illis hominum venatoribus, qui lacrymas fudisse, eguntur audientes, alias adhuc terras esse sibi non subditas; quemadmodum Sixtum V. in Diss.I. introduximus dicentem; si adhuc alius Papatus esset, se illum acceptaturum.
units.tr: XVI. Of this other monarch, or vice-monarch, the Holy Scriptures keep a deep silence. Indeed, his name does not occur, nor his dignity, nor his seat is described; nothing is said of his attributes, signs, functions or succession; the Church's duty toward him is not mentioned. It is foretold quite plainly, however, that someone will arise who is to claim such power in the name of Christ, but against Christ. Nor do the ends they put forward make such an office necessary to the Church, since nowhere is it said that controversies must be removed from the Church, especially by such a universal ruler.
