On the contrary, where his authority is acknowledged, controversies remain in the greatest number, and indeed concerning him himself. So too the Gospel can be proclaimed without such a universal sender, since the Lord of the harvest can send labourers in various ways without him. Indeed, people go wherever divine providence leads, and care for the salvation of their neighbour can be taken, with congregations and their chief men, especially the magistrates, providing the occasion and the means. There is also a fellowship of rulers and congregations which, professing a faith equally precious, exercise it for the common good and according to the variety of occasions in different places and times. Nor, at times, are some given prerogatives, and a certain primacy of order is observed, but without absolute command over the brethren, much less over the whole Church. Moreover, the order that seems to exist under such a monarch is a great confusion against Christ. He claims more for himself than he performs or can perform, undertaking the care of all the churches. He does this otherwise than Paul did, who wished that all the churches depended on himself alone, while in the meantime he cares for none, thinking that the saying of Paul, which Gregory the Great still thought applied to himself, does not hold for him: hom. 17 in Evang.: Woe is me, if I do not preach the gospel! (1 Cor. 9:16-17). Is not the good government of a single particular church burdensome and almost beyond the strength of one man, as Chrysostom argues in his books on the Priesthood? And shall we believe that one man, and moreover one who lacks the promise, is sufficient for the administration of all the churches? For we do not deny the omnipotence of God, but here and elsewhere we do not want them to believe that God is omnipotent for no other purpose than that he should exert this omnipotence whenever they themselves wish, just as they say the secular sword must be drawn at the nod of their monarch. God certainly gives the power of the Spirit by measure, not without measure, and not as a property of any one man, but as something common to many. For he is the one to whom God does not give the Spirit ek metrou [ἐκ μέτρου], by measure (John 3), while the others receive from his fullness grace for grace (John 1). Yet this is not always the greatest measure for that monarch, but often the least, or none at all; it would be otherwise if they were bound to provide for the whole Church. And rightly did the most learned Wessel Gansfort write in his de poenitentia: It is impossible for a man to know the ends of the earth; how then will he judge those whom he cannot know? How will he judge the faith of those whose language he does not understand? The Holy Spirit therefore kept for himself the task of cherishing, quickening, preserving and increasing the unity of the Church, and did not leave it to the Roman Pontiff, who is often careless of it. Many are members of the Church even if they do not know Rome or any Roman pope. And yet they wish to be universal, like those great hunters of men who, as we heard, are moved to tears because there are still other lands not subject to them; as we introduced Sixtus V saying in our first Dissertation: if there were yet another papacy, he would accept it.

units.la: XVII. De ordine autem à Christo constituto ita Scriptura
units.tr: XVII. Concerning the order established by Christ, Scripture speaks thus:

units.la: loquitur; Dedit alios quidem Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores, ad compactionem sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad aedificationem corporis Christi, donec omnes veniamus ad unitatem fidei &c. Eph.IV.11. seq. In quo loco satis expresse dicitur, Ecclesiam ad fines suos sine tali Monarcha posse venire. Et, ut ibi, ita quoque alibi proponitur Ministerium, non Magisterium, & proin minus accurate ac convenienter heic adhibentur ipsa definentia in archia & cratia, ἀρχὴ καὶ κεφαλὴ, principatus & imperium, cum ipsi Apostoli tantum voluerint haberi pro Ministris Christi & Dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei, 1.Cor.IV.1. & talibus, qui non dominentur fidei fidelium, sed tantum cooperarii sint gaudii illorum, 2.Cor.I.24. & Paulus de se testatus sit, quòd à Deo fidus judicatus, & in ministerio positus sit, 1.Tim.I.12. convenienter nimirum praecepto Christi: Reges Gentium dominantur eis, & qui inter eas potestatem habent, vocantur benefici; Vos autem non sic. Sed qui maximus est inter vos, sit sicut qui minimus est; & qui princeps est, sicut qui ministrat, Luc.XXII.25.26.
units.tr: "He gave some to be apostles, and some prophets, and some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, until we all come to the unity of the faith," etc. Eph. 4.11 ff. In this passage it is stated quite plainly that the Church can reach its goal without such a monarch. And, as there, so elsewhere, what is set forth is a ministry, not a magistracy. Therefore the very words for government and rule, ἀρχὴ καὶ κεφαλὴ (principality and headship), are applied here in a way that is neither accurate nor fitting, since the apostles themselves wished to be regarded only as "ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Cor. 4.1), and as those "who do not lord it over the faith of the faithful, but are fellow workers for their joy" (2 Cor. 1.24). Paul testified of himself that he was judged faithful by God and placed in the ministry (1 Tim. 1.12). This agrees with the precept of Christ: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But it shall not be so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves" (Luke 22.25–26).

units.la: XVIII. Respondet etiam praecepto praxis. Et primò quidem, quae Christus in terra obambulans exercuit, ad alium, juxta ea, quae diximus, trahuntur pessimè; Nec bene concluditur, Ecclesiam in ista Regiminis circumstantia haud variare posse; Ipse enim Christus Monarcha perpetuò manet, nec ei succedi saepe dicere audent, quamvis audeant nonnunquam. Supremum igitur semper manet, & omnis mutatio, quae unquam accidit, in subalterno est, cum quo non statim mutatur civitas, ut eadem civitas Romana sub Regibus, sub Consulibus, sub Decem-viris, & Dictatoribus fuit, suprema potestate & Majestate semper penes populum manente. Praeter quod Christus, quatenus in terris docuit, ministrum se potius gessit & vocavit, Luc.XXI.27. Matth.XX.21. & quidem Circumcisionis, Rom.XV.8. Doctor, dum in terris ageret, Judaeorum Matth.X. certè non talis Monarcha, qui sibi potestatem etiam in temporalibus arrogârit. Et quidem dum juxta hypotheses Monarchicorum Pontifex summus Aaronicus adhuc visibilis Monarcha cha esset. Quid statim post Christum secutum sit, nimirum Apo-stolorum tempore, supra jam prolixè notavimus. Sed nec post Apostolorum excessum, & diu post Monarcha Ecclesiæ fuit, & agnitus fuit, quoad nimirum juxta Can. Apostolorum 32. & Nicenum 4. excommunicati ab uno ab alio ad communionem recipi; Et juxta Concilia Africana appellationes trans mare non instituì potuerunt; Et obtinuit constitutus in Concilio Niceno ordo, ut nimirum tandem ad Patriarcham causæ referantur, & eorum quivis suam habeat Ecclesiæ portionem curandam; Quoad creditum cum Cyprian0, ex lib. de unitate Ecclesiæ: Nemo unus Episcopus Monarcha totius Ecclesiæ; Episcopatus unus est, cujus à singulis in solidum pars tenetur; & cum Hieronymo in ep. ad Evagr. Si authoritas quæritur, orbis major est urbe, ubicunque fuerit Episcopus, sive Romæ, sive Eugubii, sive Constantinopoli, sive Rhegii, sive Alexandriæ, sive Tanis, ejusdem meriti est & Sacerdotii. Potentia divitiarum & paupertatis humilitas vel sublimiorem, vel inferiorem Episcopum non facit. Cæterum omnes Apostolorum Successores sunt. Quæ testimonia commentario non indigent, nec illud, nec hoc S. R. E. ut vocant, Cardinalis. Plura dabimus, quando propiùs successionem Pontificum Romanorum in Monarchia impugnabimus.
units.tr: XVIII. Practice also agrees with this precept. And first, what Christ did while he walked on earth is very badly drawn into support of another [monarch], according to what we have said. Nor is it rightly concluded that the Church cannot vary in this form of government. For Christ himself remains the Monarch forever, and they do not dare to say often that a successor is appointed to him, although they sometimes do dare. The supreme authority therefore always remains where it was, and every change that ever happened concerns only a subordinate matter, which does not at once change the state. Thus the Roman state was the same under kings, under consuls, under the decemvirs and under dictators, the supreme power and majesty always remaining with the people. Besides this, Christ, in so far as he taught on earth, conducted himself and called himself a minister (Luke 22.27; Matt. 20.21), and indeed a minister of the circumcision (Rom. 15.8), a teacher of the Jews while he was on earth (Matt. 10). Certainly he was not such a monarch as claimed power even in temporal affairs. And indeed, on the hypotheses of the monarchists, the high priest of Aaron's line was still a visible monarch. What followed immediately after Christ, namely in the time of the apostles, we have already noted at length above. But nor after the death of the apostles, and for a long time afterwards, was there a monarch of the Church, nor was one acknowledged. Thus by the canon of the Apostles 32 and the Nicene canon 4, those excommunicated by one were to be received into communion by another. And according to the African councils, appeals across the sea could not be instituted. The order established at the Council of Nicaea prevailed: namely, that causes were ultimately referred to the patriarch, and each of them had his own portion of the Church to care for. As to the belief of Cyprian, from his book On the Unity of the Church: "No single bishop is the monarch of the whole Church; there is one episcopate, of which a part is held by each individual in its entirety." And with Jerome, in his letter to Evagrius: "If authority is asked for, the world is greater than the city. Wherever there is a bishop, whether at Rome, or at Eugubium, or at Constantinople, or at Rhegium, or at Alexandria, or at Tanis, he is of the same worth and priesthood. The power of wealth and the humility of poverty do not make a bishop either higher or lower. Moreover, all are successors of the apostles." These testimonies need no commentary, nor does the cardinal of the holy Roman church, as they call him, need one, either for this or for that. We will give more when we come nearer to attacking the succession of the Roman pontiffs in the monarchy.

units.la: XIX. Et quando sic patet, successiones in Monarchia Ecclesiæ necessarios haud esse; imò Ecclesiam diu sine tali mero homine, qui potestatem, ut Herodianus lib.1. Imperatoriam vocat, αὐτοκράτορα καὶ ἀκώλυτον in eam habuerit, exercuerit, fuisse; & quidem illo tempore, quo ex angusta augusta fieri & mundus converti debuit; ad quas conversiones, ex hypothesi maximè, mittente Monarchâ opus fuisset. Jam autem dilatatis Ecclesiæ pomœriis, minùs unus orbi sufficit, ut plane ineptus sit Bellarminus, dum contendit, jam magis tali Pontifice uno summo opus esse, cùm Christiani sint plures & pejores; quasi onus magis auctum eò melius unius alicujus humeris imponeretur. Videndum nunc porrò est, utrum Petrus saltem in eo, quod revera fuit, successores habeat, & habere debuerit & quidem Episcopos Romanos. Fuit Apostolus; qualis autem illa potestas fuerit, ex Differt.I. abundè constat, nempe fuit suprema potestas Ecclesiastica, quæ quidem in meros homines unquam cecidit, sed extraordinaria. Quemadmodum etiam in V.T. extraordinariæ personæ fuerunt 12. Patriarchæ, extraordinarii Ministri, Prophetæ, & inter illos quoque Moses legislationis Judaicæ daicæ Minister; in N. T. autem extraordinaria quoque munera fuisse videntur Evangelistarum & Prophetarum, qui post Apostolos Eph.IV.11. nominantur. Et certè quoad Apostolos facilè cognoscimus, eorum planè peculiarem rationem fuisse, etiam quatenus ipsis dictum fuit: Euntes docete omnes gentes &c. Ex quo, etiam lege in medio omnium posità, Jerem.XXXI. 3. & ita confirmatâ, ut aliud verbum & Evangelium aliud annunciari & audiri non debeat, Gal. I.8. concludimus, Apostolos Apostolis succedere non debere, & per consequens nec Pontifices Romanos Petro insuprema universali & Apostolica potestate succedere. Quod & ante nos Nilus Thessalonicensis, de Princ. Papæ lib.2. eodem modo collegit. Nos autem conclusionem nostram contra successionem Episcoporum porrò confirmamus & illustramus ipsis Bellarmini verbis l.4. de Pont. Rom. 25. contra successionem Episcoporum aliorum in hunc modum adhibitis: Nullam habent partem verae Apostolicae authoritatis. Apostoli poterant in toto terrarum orbe prædicare & fundare Ecclesias, ut patet Matth. ult. & Marc. ult. hoc non possunt Episcopi (Romani etiam:) item, Apostoli poterant scribere libros Canonicos, ut omnes fatentur, hoc non possunt Episcopi (Romani etiam:) Apostoli habuerunt donum linguarum & miraculorum, non habent Episcopi (Romani etiam:) Apostoli habuerunt in totam Ecclesiam jurisdictionem, non habent Episcopi (Romani etiam:) Addimus; eos etiam non habere immediatam vocationem, quam habuerunt Apostoli, nec illud, ut sint testes oculati vitæ, mortis & resurrectionis Christi, non eandem copiam Spiritûs, infallibilitatem Doctrinæ, conformitatem gratiæ, plenitudinem scientiæ &c.
units.tr: XIX. And since it is thus clear that successions in the monarchy of the Church are not necessary, indeed that the Church existed for a long time without such a mere man who had and exercised over it power, as Herodian in book 1 calls imperial, autocratic and unhindered (αὐτοκράτορα καὶ ἀκώλυτον), and that particularly in the period when she had to grow from a narrow beginning into the whole world, for which conversions, on the monarchical hypothesis above all, the sending of a monarch would have been needed. But now that the boundaries of the Church have been extended, one man is less sufficient for the world. So Bellarmine is plainly foolish when he contends that there is now more need of one such supreme pontiff, "since Christians are more numerous and worse"; as if a burden made heavier would be better laid upon the shoulders of one man. Next we must see whether Peter, at least in what he really was, has successors, and whether he ought to have them, namely Roman bishops. He was an apostle. But what kind of power that was has been sufficiently established in our first Dissertation: it was the supreme ecclesiastical power, which indeed never fell to mere men, but was extraordinary. Just as in the Old Testament the twelve patriarchs were extraordinary persons, extraordinary ministers, and prophets, and among them Moses too was the minister of the Jewish legislation; so in the New Testament the extraordinary offices appear to have been those of the evangelists and prophets, who are named after the apostles (Eph. 4.11). And certainly with regard to the apostles we easily recognise that their situation was quite peculiar, even in that it was said to them: "Go and teach all nations," etc. From this, together with the law placed in the midst of all (Jer. 31.33), and so confirmed that another word and another gospel ought not to be announced or heard (Gal. 1.8), we conclude that apostles ought not to have apostolic successors, and consequently that the Roman pontiffs ought not to succeed Peter in the supreme universal and apostolic power. Nilus of Thessalonica, in book 2 of On the Primacy of the Pope, had already drawn the same conclusion before us. We, however, further confirm and illustrate our conclusion against the succession of bishops with the very words of Bellarmine, in book 4 of On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 25, where he argues in this manner against the succession of other bishops: "They have no part of true apostolic authority. The apostles could preach throughout the whole world and found churches, as is clear from Matthew's and Mark's last chapters; bishops cannot do this (Roman ones too). Likewise, the apostles could write canonical books, as everyone admits; bishops cannot do this (Roman ones too). The apostles had the gift of tongues and of miracles; bishops do not have them (Roman ones too). The apostles had jurisdiction over the whole Church; bishops do not have it (Roman ones too)." To these we add: they do not have the immediate calling that the apostles had, nor the fact that they were eyewitnesses of the life, death and resurrection of Christ, nor the same abundance of the Spirit, the infallibility of doctrine, the conformity of grace, the fullness of knowledge, and so on.

units.la: XX. Effugia pro more quærit Bellarminus, & primò quidem respectu Pontificum suorum concedit, non esse immediatè ab ipso Deo doctos, nec posse scribere libros Canonicos (& tamen vult cum sociis, omnia eorum effata, saltem ex Cathedra venientia, pari pietatis affectu recipienda, & æquè Canonicam regulam & normam fidei esse, & eos, quod hic aliis denegare videtur, novas revelationes dare posse:) Addere potuisset etiam reliqua, quæ non habeant, aut possint Pontifices Romani, quibus tamen Ecclesiæ constitutionem & fidei propugnationem, ubi antea non fuit, tanquam secundam potestatis Apostolicæ partem tribuit, id est, rem non tantum Episcopis quibusvis, sed & fidelibus quibusvis, datâ occasione, convenientem; docente historiâ Ecclesiasticâ, etiam mulieres novas Ecclesias plantasse,
units.tr: XX. Bellarmine, as usual, seeks escapes, and first, with respect to his own pontiffs, he concedes that they are "not immediately taught by God himself, nor can they write canonical books." (Yet he wishes, with his companions, that all their utterances, at least those coming from the chair, be received "with equal affection of piety," and that they be equally a canonical rule and norm of faith; and that they can give "new revelations," which he seems to deny to others here.) He could also have added the remaining things which the Roman pontiffs do not have, or cannot have; yet he attributes to them, as "a second part of apostolic power," the "establishing of the Church and the defence of the faith where there was none before," that is, a thing suitable not only to any bishops but also to any believers, when the occasion arises, as ecclesiastical history teaches: women too have planted new churches,

units.la: XX. Effugia pro more quærit Bellarminus, & primò quidem respectu Pontificum suorum concedit, non esse immediatè ab ipso Deo doctos, nec posse scribere libros Canonicos (& tamen vult cum sociis, omnia eorum effata, saltem ex Cathedra venientia, pari pietatis affectu recipienda, & æquè Canonicam regulam & normam fidei esse, & eos, quod hic aliis denegare videtur, novas revelationes dare posse:) Addere potuisset etiam reliqua, quæ non habeant, aut possint Pontifices Romani, quibus tamen Ecclesiæ constitutionem & fidei propugnationem, ubi antea non fuit, tanquam secundam potestatis Apostolicæ partem tribuit, id est, rem non tantum Episcopis quibusvis, sed & fidelibus quibusvis, datâ occasione, convenientem; docente historiâ Ecclesiasticâ, etiam mulieres novas Ecclesias plantasse, taffe, & quidem, quas Papa nullo modo miserit apud Ruff.l.1.c.10. ubi & de quodam; Nondum initiatus in sacris fit gentis sua Apostolus; Et de Ædesio & Frumentio Indorum Apostolis apud Theod.l.1.22. Tribuit eis etiam partem tertiam, nempe summam in omnem Ecclesiam potestatem, ea ratione, quia Petro succedant; Et dum, illam potestatem in Apostolatu quoque contineri, asserit 1. Monarchicam esse negat, cum Apostolatum plures habuerint. 2. Pontifices Apostolis quibusvis in nullo superiores facit, cum illis tantum tribuat potestatem, quam hi habuerint; imo inferiores multo, cum illis bonam partem, quam hi habuerunt, tribuere non audeat. 3. Negat etiam, in ea Petro Pontifices succedere, cum in Apostolatu juxta hanc ejus præeminentiam, prout ostensum est, successio non detur. Nec eum hic juvat cantilena ordinaria, succedere Petro, non proprie ut Apostolo Pontifices; sed ut pastori ordinario l.4.c.25. in quo hæc potestas ordinaria fuerit, non delegata, ut in Apostolis cæteris. l.2.cap.12. Nam si Pontifices Petro non proprie ut Apostolo succedunt, nullo modo proprie succedunt, & successio illa tantum impropria est, fortè ironica, quatenus & extra communem Episcopalem potestatem eos succedere fingunt, & Petrus non alius quàm verò Apostolus fuit, Apostolus, juxta Differt.I. ut reliqui Apostoli, non magis ordinarius, æquè delegatus à Christo, ac ipsi, vel ipso Bellarmino judice, dum nimirum contrarium sæpe ex ipso audivimus, immediatè à Christo potestatem habentes, nullo modo delegati Petri; ut, si succedi debeat in summa potestate Ecclesiastica in universam Ecclesiam Apostolis, etiam aliis in ea succedi debeat præter Petrum, quâ ratione infinitos ex hypothesi Monarchas habituri essemus, quos & aliâs vel sola in illa potestate Petri successio daret.
units.tr: XX. Bellarmine, as usual, seeks escapes, and first, with respect to his own pontiffs, he concedes that they are "not immediately taught by God himself, nor can they write canonical books." (Yet he wishes, with his companions, that all their utterances, at least those coming from the chair, be received "with equal affection of piety," and that they be equally a canonical rule and norm of faith; and that they can give "new revelations," which he seems to deny to others here.) He could also have added the remaining things which the Roman pontiffs do not have, or cannot have; yet he attributes to them, as "a second part of apostolic power," the "establishing of the Church and the defence of the faith where there was none before," that is, a thing suitable not only to any bishops but also to any believers, when the occasion arises, as ecclesiastical history teaches: women too have planted new churches, and indeed churches which the Pope in no way sent, as in Rufinus book 1 chapter 10, where someone is said to be "an apostle of his own nation, not yet initiated in the sacred rites"; and concerning Aedesius and Frumentius, apostles of the Indians, in Theodoret book 1, chapter 22. He also grants them a third part, namely "supreme power over the whole Church," on the ground that "they succeed Peter." And while he asserts that this power is also contained in the apostolate, (1) he denies that it is monarchical, since there were several apostles; (2) he does not make the Pope in any respect superior to any apostles, since he grants to them only the power which these had; indeed he makes them much inferior, since he does not dare to grant them the good part which these had. (3) He also denies that the popes succeed Peter in that power, since within the apostolate, according to this his pre-eminence, as has been shown, there is no succession. Nor does the usual song help him here, that the popes succeed Peter "not properly as an apostle," but "as an ordinary pastor" (book 4, chapter 25), in whom this power was ordinary, not delegated, as in the other apostles (book 2, chapter 12). For if the popes succeed Peter "not properly as an apostle," they do not succeed him properly at all, and that succession is only improper, perhaps ironic, insofar as they pretend to succeed him even beyond the common episcopal power. Peter was no other than a true apostle, and as an apostle, according to Dissertation I, like the other apostles, not more ordinary, equally delegated by Christ as they were, by the judgment of Bellarmine himself, since we have often heard the opposite from him: they had power immediately from Christ and were in no way delegates of Peter. So if succession were to be made to the apostles in the supreme ecclesiastical power over the whole Church, succession would also have to be made in it to others besides Peter; by which reasoning we would have infinitely many monarchs on the hypothesis, whom the succession to Peter's power alone would give us even on its own.

units.la: XXI. Cæterùm omninò Petro & Apostolis reliquis succeditur, & successum est ab illis Pontificibus Romanis, qui doctrinam Apostolorum annunciârunt; Sed non ab illis solis, ut nec annuntiârunt soli. Nempe omnes omninò Episcopi, quibus Ecclesiam Christi ex verbo Christi docere contingit, eatenus Apostolorum successores sunt, quomodo etiam in n.18. allegato Hieronymi, & in infinitis prope aliorum Patrum locis, imò ab ipso Concilio Tridentino Sess.23. vocantur, & in potestate Apostolica, ordinaria & perpetua ab extraordinariis & ad tempus tantùm concessis distinguenda sunt, illorúmque illis largienda est successio, cuivis in parte sibi demandata; quod quidem ita adfirmant Patres, ut simul etiam Episcopis scopis supremam in Ecclesiam, & omnem, quæ nimirum inter homines continuare debet, potestatem tribuant, eámque adinstar Apostolorum à Christo immediatè profectam. In quo etiam ex ipsa communione Romana Doctores sine numero, Concilia multa, quædam etiam generalia, verbo, omnes illi, & omnia illa, qui & quæ Conciliorum authoritatem supra Pontificiam evehant, iis adstipulantur. Quemadmodum quoque in Concilio Tridentino Galli maximè & Hispani Episcopi veritatem istam magno cum ardore propugnârunt, ut Synodus tandem in ambigua verborum generalitate & hic remedium quærere coacta fuerit, Papæ nimirum Gnathonibus non minori cum vehementia pro dependentia Episcoporum à Pontifice pugnantibus, dicente non tantùm Lainezzio, Jesuitarum tum temporis Generali: Si statuatur, Episcopos jure divino institutos esse, id est, esse Apostolorum Successores, potestatem à solo Christo habentes, Pontificem non amplius fore caput Ecclesiæ & Vicarium Christi; Sed & Segoviensi palàm jactante, unicam voculam juris divini Papæ fore causam ruinæ. Nempe sic par illorum potestas redditur, quam augere, diminuere, aut tollere Papa nequit, idémque eis conceditur, quod ipse sibi vendicare potest ex successione Apostolica.
units.tr: XXI. Yet succession to Peter and the other Apostles certainly does take place, and it has been carried on by those Roman Pontiffs who announced the teaching of the Apostles. But it is not carried on by them alone, any more than they alone announced it. For all bishops whatever, to whom it falls to teach the Church of Christ from the word of Christ, are to that extent successors of the Apostles. So they are called in the passage of Jerome cited at n.18., in almost countless other places of the Fathers, and even by the Council of Trent itself in Sess.23.. In the Apostolic power they must be distinguished, as ordinary and perpetual, from the extraordinary powers granted only for a time, and succession to the former must be granted to each in the part committed to him. The Fathers affirm this so firmly that at the same time they also attribute to bishops supreme power over the Church, and all the power which must continue among men, and they derive it, like that of the Apostles, immediately from Christ. In this matter countless teachers of the Roman communion itself, many councils, and even some general councils agree with them; in a word, all those men and all those writings which raise the authority of councils above the Pope's. At the Council of Trent too, the French and above all the Spanish bishops defended this truth with great ardour, so that the Synod was at last forced to seek a remedy in the ambiguous generality of its words. The Pope's flatterers fought for the dependence of bishops on the Pontiff with no less vehemence. Not only Lainez, then General of the Jesuits, said: If it is laid down that bishops are instituted by divine right, that is, are successors of the Apostles, holding their power from Christ alone, the Pontiff will no longer be the head of the Church and Vicar of Christ; but Segovia also openly boasted that the single little word of divine right would be the cause of the Pope's ruin. Indeed, in this way their power is made equal, a power which the Pope cannot increase, diminish or take away, and the same is granted to them as he himself can claim from Apostolic succession.

units.la: XXII. Sed lubet circa hanc successionem adhuc in genere notare; Succedi Apostolis non tam loci, (licèt etiam à multis quodammodo loci,) quàm verò doctrinæ & muneris respectu. Et quamvis olim ante magnam illam defectionem & Christianismi confusionem in majori quadantenus, accedentibus maximè ex locorum & Ecclesiarum amplitudine præröogativis, cæteris paribus, existimatione fuerint illi Episcopi, qui præter successionem Apostolorum omnium in doctrina & munere, etiam localiter Apostolis certis succedebant, aut succedere credebantur, illis frequentiùs Apostolicorum, sedibus illorum Apostolicarum elogia data, & illorum successiones in specie ab Apostolis, qui Ecclesiarum, in quibus sedebant, fundatores perhibebantur, derivatæ fuerint, (ex quo quidem infeliciter ambitiosi in Ecclesia dominatûs & detestandæ prælationis primordia nata sunt,) tamen etiam antiquioribus constanter creditum fuit, quoscunque Episcopos, etiam illarum Ecclesiarum, quarum fundatores immediati Apostoli non extiterant, cunctis Apostolis pariter, & proin etiam Petro, imò illi modo peculiari, quatenus in Evangelio aliquoties Ecclesiam & ejus Rectores figurâsse legatur, succedere, quò cumprimis facit Differt.I. allegatus Ambrosii locus, ubi testatur; Episcopos omnes in Petro & simul cum Petro claves accepisse à Domino; & præter innumeros alios evidens ille Hieronymi,epist.1. In quo Heliodoro Clericatum & Episcopatum dissuadere volens,ait: Non est facile stare loco Pauli,tenere gradum Petri; Ut non crediderint successionem illam nonnisi penes eos, qui in eodem loco præsint, nec etiam singulos singulis succedere, & illum quidem Petro,alium Paulo,alium Jacobo,alium Johanni, & sic deinceps, ita ut non etiam succedant reliquis, quod fuisset & esset eandem cantilenam canere cum illis schismaticis Corinthiis, dicentibus: Ego sum Cephæ, ego sum Pauli,ego sum Apollo, 1.Cor.1.1. sed in officio, quod erat Apostolorum commune, succedere omnes omnibus. Quod etiam ex illis Patribus facile confirmatur,qui per analysin ad sua principia, Episcoporum successiones nonnunquam reducunt ad Apostolos in genere, non ad unum aliquem singularem,quod maximè etiam fieri debuit,ubi Apostoli duo aut plures Ecclesiæ alicujus primam curam habuerunt. Ubi autem non docuerunt alii Apostoli, ibi tamen eis succeditur ratione doctrinæ & officii, (quod sufficere potest;) Sed & successum maximè olim fuit,dum ibi docuerunt Apostolici viri alii,aut Episcopi ab Apostolis constituti, aut venientes ab illis.
units.tr: XXII. But it is worth noting further, in general, about this succession: the Apostles are succeeded not so much in place (although by many also in a certain way in place) as in respect of teaching and office. Formerly, before that great defection and confusion of Christianity, those bishops were held in somewhat greater esteem, other things being equal, chiefly because of the privileges of places and the size of the Churches, who, besides succeeding all the Apostles in teaching and office, also succeeded, or were believed to succeed, certain Apostles in place. For this reason the sees of those Apostles were often given the title Apostolic, and their successions in particular were traced back to the Apostles who were said to be founders of the Churches in which they sat. From this, unhappily, the beginnings of ambitious domination in the Church and of detestable pre-eminence arose. Nevertheless, even the more ancient writers held constantly that whatever bishops, even those of Churches whose immediate founders were not the Apostles, succeeded all the Apostles alike, and so also Peter, indeed in a peculiar way, insofar as it is read in the Gospel that he several times figured the Church and its rulers. The passage of Ambrose cited in Differt.I. bears most on this, where he testifies: All bishops received the keys from the Lord in Peter and together with Peter. Besides countless others there is that clear passage of Jerome in epist.1., where, wishing to dissuade Heliodorus from the clerical and episcopal office, he says: It is not easy to stand in the place of Paul, to hold the step of Peter. So they did not believe that succession was only with those who preside in the same place, nor that single men succeed single men, one to Peter, another to Paul, another to James, another to John, and so on, so that they do not succeed the rest. That would have been to sing the same tune as those schismatic Corinthians who said: I am of Cephas, I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, 1.Cor.1.1. Rather, all succeed all in the office which was common to the Apostles. This is also easily confirmed from those Fathers who, by analysis, sometimes trace the successions of bishops back to the Apostles in general, not to some one individual. This especially ought to have been done where two or more Apostles had the first care of a Church. Where other Apostles did not teach, succession is nonetheless made to them by reason of teaching and office, which can suffice. Succession was especially made in former times when other Apostolic men taught there, or bishops appointed by the Apostles, or coming from them.

units.la: XXIII. Quoad successionem localem verò tenendum & succedi Apostolis certis, ut non in prærogativis Apostolatui propriis (quod clarum est & supra ostensum) ita non magis in prærogativis ob dona personalia propriis; Ut ideò honoratior per se censeri non debeat, nedum majori potestate instructus,qui localiter maximo Apostolo succedit, quàm, qui minimo, sed inter Episcopos potestate æquales omnes majori is authoritate jure optimo polleat, quem dona propria personalia maximè commendant; quod tamen non in præjudicium ordinis inter Ecclesias & earum Rectores constituti, & maximè necessarii,litibus aliàs de donorum personalium præcellentia infinitis orituris, dicimus; licèt nonnunquam ex communi consensu & discrimine omnibus manifesto virtutis potius,quàm loci ratio habita fuerit, & haberi possit. Atque ut omninò dona personalia non sunt,(hæreditaria,& neque Ciceronis filius,neque,qui mortui Ciceronis uxorem duxit,Oratores fuerunt, & laudes illas non meruerunt,) ita etiam prærogativæ ob illa haud magis sunt hæreditariæ.
units.tr: XXIII. As for local succession, however, it must be held that the Apostles are succeeded in certain places, but not in prerogatives proper to the apostolate (which is clear and shown above), and no more in prerogatives due to personal gifts. Therefore a man is not to be regarded as more honourable merely because he has greater power, much less because he succeeds in place the greatest Apostle rather than the least. Among bishops who are equal in power, the one whom his own personal gifts especially commend has, by the best right, greater authority. We say this, however, not to the prejudice of the order established among the Churches and their rulers, which is most necessary; otherwise endless disputes would arise about the pre-eminence of personal gifts. Yet sometimes, by common consent and with a distinction manifest to all, the reason of virtue rather than of place has been taken into account, and can be. And just as personal gifts are not hereditary (neither the son of Cicero nor the man who married Cicero's widow were orators, and they did not earn those praises), so the prerogatives due to them are no more hereditary.

units.la: XXIV. Applicemus jam ea, quæ hactenus diximus, porrò ad successionem Apostolicam in Ecclesia Romana. Jactatur ibi successio Petri. Demus, licet memores præcedentium: Imò volumus, ut istam suam gloriationem augeant, & jactent pariter (ut de Johanne & Barnaba nihil dicamus) successionem Pauli, quam paulò potiori & certiori sibi jure tribuere possent. Sed nolunt, cùm & Paulum extraordinariis annumerent Doctoribus, & vel ideò nolunt, ne ipsis sic Monarchia pereat; Sed pereat; Paulus saltem æquè Romanæ Ecclesiæ præfuit pari cum potestate, proin neuter cum potestate Monarchica, nec possunt ostendere rationem, cur uni ex illis succedi debeat, alteri non item; Imò si multis ex ipsis credimus, utrique revera successum est, uterque successores constituerunt, & non tantùm possunt duo summi Pontifices creari & haberi, quod etiam docuerunt ex Scholasticis Armacanus de quæstio. Arm. l. 7. c. 17. & Occam in Dialog. part. 3. ad finem; Sed etiam ad illorum exemplum debent; quorum tamen alter erit Successor Pauli, illius ipsius Pauli, qui in infinitis ferè locis docuit, tot aliis Ecclesiis inserviit, & cujus successionem maximè Corinthiaca Ecclesia jactaverat, imò simul etiam Petri, non trajecturi in Italiam scilicet, nisi Corinthum Achaiæ urbem principem, ac florentem ibi Ecclesiam salutâssest; Hinc quoque nata traditio, quòd in Corinthiis essent illorum traduces, qui se Petrinos olim appellâssent, ut Paulinos alii, & quòd Cephæ meminisset diserte Paulus in Epistola priore. Ut successionis ratione Ecclesia Corinthiaca non minùs sibi tribuerit Romanâ, quoad Petrum pari forte utrobique certitudine. Ast de simultaneo Petri & Pauli apud Romanos regimine, ex hypothesi Dissert. I. & II. prolixiùs, datis occasionibus, egimus.
units.tr: XXIV. Let us now apply what we have said so far to the Apostolic succession in the Roman Church. They boast of the succession of Peter. Let us grant it, though mindful of what has gone before. Indeed, we want them to increase this boast and to claim equally (to say nothing of John and Barnabas) the succession of Paul, which they could claim by a somewhat better and surer right. But they do not want it, since they count Paul among the extraordinary teachers, and for this very reason they do not want it, lest the Monarchy perish for them. But let it perish. Paul at least presided over the Roman Church with equal power, so neither has monarchical power, nor can they show a reason why succession should be granted to one of them and not to the other. Indeed, if we believe many of them, succession has really been made to both, and both have set up successors. Not only can two supreme Pontiffs be created and held, as Armachanus taught from the Schoolmen in quæstio. Arm. l. 7. c. 17. and Ockham in Dialog. part. 3. ad finem also taught, but they ought also, after their example, to be such that one of them is successor of Paul, of that very Paul who taught in almost infinite places, served so many other Churches, and whose succession the Church of Corinth had especially boasted. And at the same time he would also be successor of Peter, not destined to pass into Italy unless he had first greeted Corinth, the principal city of Achaia, and the flourishing Church there. Hence also arose the tradition that there were among the Corinthians those who had once called themselves Petrine, as others called themselves Pauline, and that Paul expressly mentioned Cephas in his first Epistle. So, in respect of succession, the Church of Corinth may claim for itself no less than the Roman Church does, as far as Peter is concerned, with perhaps equal certainty on both sides. But concerning the simultaneous rule of Peter and Paul among the Romans, on the hypothesis, we have treated at greater length in Dissert. I. & II., as occasions were given.

units.la: XXV. Petrum solum quod attinet, quæcunque ab illo habere possunt, multi equidem etiam alii. Omnes illi, qui, sicuti diximus, Apostolorum & Petri etiam successores sunt omni loco & omni tempore Christi in vinea sua operarii; Porrò specialiùs, omnes illi, qui docent, ubi Petrus docuit, in Ecclesiis, quas ille plantavit. Alexandrini præsertim, si, quod Dissert.II. Nicephorus dixit, ibi quoque Episcopus fuit; Antiocheni maximè omnium, quorum, si vera narrant, per septennium Episcopus fuit, & ubi saltem, de quo testatur Scriptura, docuit. Et sanè considerari merentur ipsa Innocentii I. Papæ in epist.18. ad Alexandrum Antiochenum, quæ T.I. Concil. p.463. habetur, verba; Nempe primam Apostoli (Petri) sedem dem vocat,ubi & nomen Christi religio acceperit; & quæ conventum Apostolorum apud se celebrem fieri meruerit, quaque urbis Roma sedi non cederet, nisi quòd illa in transitu meruit, ista suscepturn apud se consummatúmque gaudet.
units.tr: XXV. As far as Peter alone is concerned, many others may indeed also have whatever they can have from him. All those who, as we have said, are successors of the Apostles and of Peter are workers in Christ's vineyard in every place and at every time. More specifically, all those teach where Peter taught, in the Churches which he planted. Especially the Alexandrians, if, as Nicephorus said in Dissert.II., he was bishop there too; the Antiochenes most of all, of whom, if they report truly, he was bishop for seven years, and where at least he taught, as Scripture testifies. Indeed, the words of Pope Innocent I in epist.18. to Alexander of Antioch, which are found in T.I. Concil. p.463., deserve to be weighed. He calls the first see of the Apostle (Peter) where also the religion of Christ's name was received, and which deserved to have the assembly of the Apostles celebrated before it, and to which the see of the city of Rome would not give way, except that the one earned it in passing, while the other rejoices to have received it and to have completed it among itself.

units.la: XXVI. Ad quæ Innocentii I. verba nonnulla annotamus. Et primò quidem probè observari velim,quas Papa recensèt, Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ peculiares prærogativas, quòd prima Apostoli sedes sierit,ibi nomen Christi religio acceperit & conventus celebris Apostolorum factus sit; Tales certè istæ sunt prærogativæ,quibus majores Ecclesia Romana ostendere poterit nunquam, & de quibus,si sibi convenirent omnes,Romani valdè triumpharent.Secundò,quoad communia credita,sedem Petri æquè Antiochiæ ostendit. Quoad præeminentiam autem, quam sibi vendicare studet, tertiò satis inconvenienter transitus dicitur septem annorum commoratio, præsertim si cum Onuphrii ὁμωψήφοις dicamus,Romā venientem Antiochiæ per septem annos sedisse. Quartò suscipit omninò Ecclesia Episcopatum, quo per 7. annos fruitur. Quintò, idem Antiochiam meruisse,dicit. Sextò Petrus ubíque consummatus æquè fuit,nam potestatem Monarchicam jam ante Episcopatum Antiochenum eum habuisse ajunt, proin & Antiochiæ sibi in ea successorem constituere potuit, quemadmodum etiam in Episcopatu, si alibi; Sic & dubio procul æquè consummati fuerunt ex ipsius institutione Antiocheni, quàm Romani. Septimò evidens est, Innocentium partim ex longiori in urbe Roma commoratione argumentari; sed septem annorum Episcopus æquè est Episcopus ac viginti quinque annorum Episcopus, nec potestas annis augetur. Et ex dictis constare potest, diuturniorem saltem commorationem fuisse Antiochenam quàm Romanam; partim ex loco mortis; Sed ex eo hic argumentum formari non posse Dissert.II. demonstravimus, & ipse Bellarminus de Pont. Rom. l.2. c.12. ait; non ideò Romæ esse sedem Pontificalem, quia Petrus Romæ obiit.
units.tr: XXVI. We make some remarks on the words of Innocent I. First, I would like it carefully noted which peculiar prerogatives of the Church of Antioch the Pope lists: that it was the first see of the Apostle, that there the name of Christ first received its religion, and that it became the famous assembly of the Apostles. These are certainly such prerogatives as the Roman Church could never show, and over which the Romans would greatly triumph if all agreed. Secondly, as to the common beliefs, he shows the see of Peter equally at Antioch. As to the pre-eminence he strives to claim for himself, thirdly, it is rather inappropriate to call a seven-year stay a passage, especially if, with Onuphrius, we say that the one coming from Rome sat at Antioch for seven years [ὁμωψήφοις, of equal numerical value]. Fourthly, he certainly receives the bishopric, which he enjoys for seven years. Fifthly, he says that he deserved Antioch. Sixthly, Peter was equally consummated everywhere. For they say he had monarchical power even before the Antiochene bishopric, and so could appoint a successor for himself there, just as elsewhere in the episcopate; so without doubt they were equally consummated at Antioch and at Rome by his appointment. Seventhly, it is evident that Innocent argues partly from a longer stay in the city of Rome; but a bishop of seven years is just as much a bishop as a bishop of twenty-five years, and power is not increased by years. And from what has been said it can be established that at least the stay at Antioch was longer than the Roman one, partly from the place of death. But that no argument can be built on this we have demonstrated in Dissertation II, and Bellarmine himself in De Pont. Rom. book 2, chapter 12 says: the Pontifical see is not at Rome for this reason, that Peter died at Rome.

units.la: XXVII. Quòd autem addit Bellarminus: Sed quia Romanus Episcopus fuit,nec sedem ex Roma unquam alió transtulit; 1. Falsum est 2. Etiam Antiochenus dicitur 3. & aliquoties Romā aliò & aliunde Romam concessisse, quod & de Antiochia ex hypothesi dicere coguntur; ut certè aut insulsè ex mortis loco argumentari debeant, aut fateri, se nescire quoad prærogativas discriminis causam, quia etiam illud, quod Bellarminus contra successionem cessionem distinctiùs excipit,æquè frivolum est,nempe non succedi nisi cedenti locum,vel per mortem naturalem,vel per mortem legitimam,id est,depositionem,vel renunciationem; tum quia eadem inconvenientia Romanos premunt, nam in epist. Clementis ad fratrem Domini Petrus ita loquitur,ac si Clementi tradat cathedram Romanam; Jacobus autem ille Frater Domini sexto Neronis anno, id est, octo annis ante Petrum occisus fertur; ut itaque secundùm Clementem, cum quo Leo II. Successor Agathonis in Decretali apud Marianum Scotum idem docet, Petrus octo annos saltem ante mortem suam se Episcopatu etiam Romano abdicârit, adeóque, si bona est contra Antiochenos Bellarmini argumentatio, etiam ex eo Episcopis Romanis non simul Monarchicam potestatem contulisse dicendus sit. Quin ex Damaso in Pontificali, in Lino,quem Marianus Scotus sequitur,respectu Lini colligi potest, Petrum duodecim annis ante mortem suam se Episcopatu Romano abdicâsse. Igitur primò eadem inconvenientia Romanos premunt; tum quia etiam incertum est,Petrum Romæ mortuum esse, tum quia falsum, aliquid habuisse Petrum, præter extraordinariam potestatem Apostolicam planè non communicandam, quod non antè communicare potuerit; tum quia, si vel Monarchicam potestatem habuisset ad mortem usque retinendam, adhuc quæri posset,cui tunc relinquendam, non enim constat de Romano; noluit enim ex eo argumentari, quòd Petrus ibi obierit; incertum igitur manet, utrum non omnes Ecclesiæ quovis modo succedentes potestatis illius, siquidem communicari debuit, hæreditatem divisam accipere debuerint, vel,si non dividi debuit, utrum non filiæ primogenitæ,id est, Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ concedi debuerit; saltem de his ex Petri testamento non constat; saltem non sequitur; Pater in domo hujus filii occisus est,ergò majorem hæreditatis partem capiet jure; multò minus; ergò totam jure habebit hæreditatem. Hactenus ergò pares.
units.tr: XXVII. As for what Bellarmine adds, But because he was Bishop of Rome and never transferred the see from Rome to another place: (1) this is false; (2) he is also called Antiochene; (3) and several times he withdrew from Rome elsewhere and came to Rome from elsewhere, which they are compelled to say of Antioch too, by their own hypothesis. So either they must argue foolishly from the place of death, or they must confess that they do not know the cause of the difference in prerogatives. Equally trivial is what Bellarmine distinctly makes an exception to succession by cession, namely one succeeds only the one who yields the place, either by natural death or by legitimate death, that is, deposition or renunciation. Then, the same inconveniences press upon the Romans. For in the epistle of Clement to the brother of the Lord, Peter speaks as if handing the Roman chair over to Clement; and that James, the brother of the Lord, is said to have been killed in the sixth year of Nero, that is, eight years before Peter. So, according to Clement, whom Leo II, successor of Agatho, teaches the same with in a decretal cited by Marianus Scotus, Peter gave up his episcopate, even the Roman one, at least eight years before his death. Thus, if Bellarmine's argument against the Antiochenes is sound, it must be said that he did not at the same time confer monarchical power on the Roman bishops. Indeed, from Damasus in the Pontifical, in Linus, whom Marianus Scotus follows, it can be gathered with respect to Linus that Peter gave up the Roman episcopate twelve years before his death. Therefore, first, the same inconveniences press upon the Romans; then, because it is also uncertain that Peter died at Rome; then, because it is false that Peter had anything beyond an extraordinary apostolic power, which by no means could be communicated, and which he could not have communicated earlier; then, because if he had held monarchical power to be retained until death, it could still be asked to whom it was then to be left, for it is not established regarding the Roman see. For he did not wish to argue from the fact that Peter died there. It therefore remains uncertain whether all churches succeeding in any way ought to have received a divided share of that power, if indeed it had to be communicated, or, if it had not to be divided, whether it ought not to have been granted to the firstborn daughter, that is, the Church of Antioch. At least nothing is known of these things from Peter's testament; at least it does not follow: the father was killed in the house of this son, therefore by right he will take the greater part of the inheritance; much less: therefore by right he will have the whole inheritance. Thus far they are equals.

units.la: XXVIII. Nec etiam impares Ecclesias facit, ut quidem Bellarminus l. c. contendit, quia Romani Pontificis sedes Apostolica sedes vocatur.
units.tr: XXVIII. Nor do they make the Churches unequal, as Bellarmine contends in the place cited, because the see of the Roman Pontiff is called the Apostolic See.

units.la: Addimus in ejus gratiam, ut nempe gratiam ab eo supra Veleno factam rependamus, vocari etiam frequenter Petri cathedram, Petri solium, item (quod pro simultaneo Petri & Pauli Rectoratu, si de Petro aliquid veri subsit, adhuc notandum) limina Apostolorum, item Ecclesiam Petri & Pauli; Imò adhuc Romæ cathedram dram ligneam,in qua Petrus sedisse fertur,ostendi, & Festum Cathedrae Petri quotannis celebrari. Sed primò crassum nimis foret, si quis per cathedram Petri,ut facere videntur recentiores, thronum & solium quoddam Regium illius temporis angustiis & furtivis quasi hincinde conventibus minùs conveniens, in quo Petrus ordinariò sedere, & ex quo docere solitus sit,intelligere vellet; Proin etiam ligneam illam cathedram, suppositarum reliquiarum partem esse arbitramur; Per Cathedram Petri autem veteribus,stylo Scripturae Matth.XXIII.2. Act.XVIII.11. nihil aliud significari, quàm Petrum in aliquo loco Evangelium annuntiâsse, sive jam illud sedens, sive stans pro infinitarum fere occasionum & tot locorum conditione fecerit. Cathedra autem Petri veteribus tantopere decantata, Antiochena fuit, in 22.Februarii incidens, & Festo anniversario culta,cùm Romana Petri cathedra, demum ante Seculum, & quod excurrit, à Paulo IV. instituta & in 18.Februarii conjecta fuerit.
units.tr: We add, for his sake, so that we may repay the favour he has done us above. It is also frequently called the chair of Peter, the throne of Peter, likewise the thresholds of the Apostles (which, for the joint rectorship of Peter and Paul, should still be noted, if anything true lies behind Peter), likewise the Church of Peter and Paul. Indeed, even now at Rome a wooden chair is shown in which Peter is said to have sat, and the Feast of the Chair of Peter is celebrated each year. But first, it would be too crude if anyone, as recent writers seem to do, wished to understand by the chair of Peter a throne and a certain royal seat, which would be unsuited to the narrow and furtive, as it were, gatherings of that time here and there, in which Peter ordinarily sat and from which he was accustomed to teach. Therefore we also judge that the wooden chair is a part of the supposed relics. By the chair of Peter, to the ancients, in the style of Scripture (Matth. XXIII.2. Act. XVIII.11.), nothing else was meant than that Peter preached the Gospel in some place, whether he did so sitting or standing, as the circumstances of countless occasions and so many places required. But the chair of Peter so much celebrated by the ancients was the Antiochene one, falling on 22 February and kept with an annual festival, whereas the Roman chair of Peter was at last instituted by Paul IV nearly a century ago and more, and placed on 18 February.

units.la: XXIX. Caeterum nemo, nisi in historia Ecclesiastica planè hospes,ignorat,quemadmodum Roma ipsa Cypriani aetate Cathedra Petri &c. dicta fuerit,ita non minùs Corinthum,Philippum, Thessalonicam, Ephesum (ut de Antiochena, Alexandrina & Hierosolymitana sileamus; nisi quòd verbo monemus,Concil.Const. V. act.1. Clericos & Monachos Apostolici throni,Antiochena magna Civitatis Catholica, sancta Ecclesia Dei,illustri certè titulo, & quo majorem Romanenses ex antiquitate genuina non proferent, memorari;) jam ante à Tertulliano de Praescript. c. 36. nimirum ob praeconium in illis urbibus Apostolicum,non minùs Ecclesias Apostolicas, Cathedras Apostolorum vocatas, & inde quoque honorem praesidentiae illis adscriptum esse; Quemadmodum etiam Augustinus de Doctr.Christ. l.II.cap.8. quàm plurium Ecclesiarum Catholicarum authoritatem in Canonicis Scripturis sequendam esse, suadet,inter quas illae sint,qua Apostolicas sedes habere, & Epistolas accipere meruerint. Et Cathedras Apostolorum dictas fuisse Principales Ecclesias, ab ipsis scilicet Apostolis constitutas, fassus est ad Tertullianum Rigaltius ad cit. Tert. loc. Et Isidorus Hispalensislib.2. de officiis Ecclesiasticis cap.5. ubi Episcopum, seu Superintendentem summum Sacerdotem (l.7.Orig. seu Etymol. c.12. etiam Pontificem Maximum & Antistitem, & primum in ordine Ecclesiae ac supra se nullum habentem) vocat, sicut fuerit Aaron; loquens de Apostolis & eorum Successoribus, ait: Caeteri Apostoli cum Petro par consortium honoris tioris & potestatis acceperunt, qui etiam in toto orbe dispersi Evangelium praedicârunt, quibúsque decedentibus successerunt Episcopi, qui sunt constituti per totum mundum in sedibus Apostolorum. Quibus ipsis verbis etiam Rabanus Maurus l. 1. de Inst. Cler. cap. 4. utitur. Et quando haec de quibusvis Ecclesiis & quarumvis Ecclesiarum Episcopis dicuntur, ita similia testimonia sine numero fere dare possemus, ubi (ob rationes nimirum in praecedentibus memoratas,) Ecclesiae, Apostolica sedes; Episcopi, Apostolici, Apostolici Patres, Apostolici Papae, summi Antistites, Apostolicae dignationes; ipsorum vero dignitates (de quo elogio Bellarminus, quòd in ipso Concilio Chalcedonensi, quod Nilus citat, Act. 1. Romani Pontificis dignitati tribuatur, gloriatur;) Apostolatus dicuntur. Ut iste Monarchicorum Princeps & compilator, (quomodo M. Ant. de Dominis eum vocavit;) praerogativas & proprietates, & quidem tantas, simplicibus ostendere velit in rebus maximè communibus, cùm tamen etiam sine Monarchicae Potestatis fide haud mirum esset, si in Occidente & ab Occidentalibus rariùs aliae, quàm Romana Ecclesia & eorum Episcopi ejusmodi titulis exornati apud veteres fuissent, quando ex Occidentalibus Ecclesiis nulla adeò manifestè immediatam Apostolicam fundationem ostendere potuit; Nobis autem heic denuò concludere liceat: Hactenus ergò pares Ecclesiae & Ecclesiarum Episcopi.
units.tr: XXIX. Moreover, no one who is a complete stranger to ecclesiastical history is unaware that, just as Rome itself was called the chair of Peter etc. in the age of Cyprian, so no less were Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica and Ephesus (not to mention Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem; except that we note in passing that the Council of Constance, Session 5, Act 1 mentions the clergy and monks of the Apostolic throne, the great Antiochene city, the Catholic, holy Church of God, a distinguished title, and one which the Romans will not bring forward from genuine antiquity as greater). Already earlier, Tertullian De Praescriptione, chapter 36, namely because of the apostolic renown in those cities, calls the apostolic Churches, the chairs of the Apostles, and from this the honour of presidency was likewise ascribed to them. Augustine also De Doctrina Christiana, book 2, chapter 8 urges that the authority of many Catholic Churches is to be followed in the canonical Scriptures, among which are those which have merited to have apostolic sees and to receive epistles. And that the chairs of the Apostles were the principal Churches, founded by the Apostles themselves, Rigaltius admitted in his note on Tertullian ad cit. Tert. loc. And Isidore of Seville book 2, De Officiis Ecclesiasticis, chapter 5, where he calls the bishop or superintendent the chief priest (Origines, or Etymologies, book 7, chapter 12), also the chief Pontiff and Antistes, and the first in the order of the Church, having none above himself, just as Aaron was; speaking of the Apostles and their successors, he says: The other Apostles with Peter received an equal fellowship of honour and power, who also, scattered throughout the whole world, preached the Gospel; and when they died, bishops succeeded them, who have been appointed throughout the whole world in the sees of the Apostles. Rabanus Maurus book 1, De Institutione Clericorum, chapter 4 uses these very words as well. And when these things are said of any Churches whatever and of the bishops of any Churches whatever, we could give almost countless similar testimonies, where (for the reasons, namely, mentioned above) the Churches are called apostolic sees; the bishops, apostolic, apostolic fathers, apostolic popes, chief Antistites, apostolic dignitaries; and their dignities themselves (on which Bellarmine glories, because in the Council of Chalcedon itself, which Nilus cites, Act. 1, dignity is ascribed to the Roman Pontiff) are called apostolates. Thus this prince and compiler of the Monarchists (as M. Antonius de Dominis called him) wishes to show prerogatives and peculiarities to the simple, and indeed such great ones, in matters most in common; whereas even without faith in monarchical power it would hardly be surprising if, in the West and among Westerners, other churches than the Roman Church and its bishops, adorned with titles of this kind, were rarer among the ancients, since none of the Western Churches could show so clearly an immediate apostolic foundation. Let us here conclude once more: thus far the Churches and the bishops of the Churches are equals.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Ut praesuppositio etiam, Petrum majorem reliquis Apostolis potestatem habuisse, eámque in Ecclesia perennare debuisse, quod tamen salsissimum, porrò dispiciendum foret, de ejus in hac peculiari potestate, Successore, vel Successoribus; Annon plures esse debuerint eâ potestate praediti, saltem post Petrum & primò fuerint? Quâ ratione lis de primis Successoribus tolli potest. Cum primis crescentibus tanti muneris molestiis, donis contrà manifestè decrescentibus? Et si unus, quis ille tandem? Annon Petro in potestate totam Ecclesiam concernente succedere debuerit, qualem Successorem ultimis verbis Alexander M. designâsse fertur, dignissimus, sive Romae, sive Eugubii, sive Constantinopoli, sive Rhegii, sive Alexandriae, sive Tanis Episcopus? Qua ratione loco Lini, Cleti & Clementis certè in ista plus quàm Apostolica potestate adhuc sub Domitiano superstes Apostolus Johannes succedere debuisset; Sed forte ipsius in ista potestate successioni obfuit absentia, & quia absentium non habetur ratio; nisi potiùs dicere velimus, eum Clementis ad instar tanti muneris onus deprecatum esse, quia se viribus
units.tr: As a further presupposition, that Peter held greater power than the other apostles and that this power ought to have continued in the Church, which is in fact most unsound and must be examined more closely: we must ask who his successor, or successors, in this particular power were. Should there not have been several men endowed with that power, at least after Peter, and first of all? That would settle the dispute about the first successors. For the burdens of so great an office grew at the start, while its gifts plainly declined. And if there was only one, who was he? Should not Peter's successor in a power concerning the whole Church have been (as Alexander the Great is said to have named in his final words) the most worthy bishop, whether of Rome, or of Eugubium, or of Constantinople, or of Rhegium, or of Alexandria, or of Tanis? By what reasoning, in place of Linus, Cletus and Clement, should the apostle John, who was still alive under Domitian, have succeeded to that more than apostolic power? But perhaps his absence stood in the way of his succession to this power, and absent men are not taken into account. Unless we prefer to say that, like Clement, he declined the burden of so great an office, because he felt himself

units.la: {Suppositâ etiam potestate Monarchicâ in Petro, incertitudinem multiplicem manere, ostenditur} bus imparem senserit. Alii certè aliis etiam temporibus potiùs quàm multi Romani Episcopi ob virtutis praeeminentiam succedere debuissent. Vel, si Imperatoriae sedis, aut aliàs potentis Metropoleos in ista successione ratio haberi debeat, quia in magnis urbibus magna sunt vitia, & ex aula omne malum; annon istarum urbium, & Romanis, quamdiu illi ista potestate praediti, Episcopis mensura gratiae manifeste major à Deo in Ecclesiae bonum conferri deberet, & tantò major, quantò major is, qui summus habetur? Et annon ad eò melius omnis malitiae fontem obturandum, saltem majorem malitiam compescendam, Imperatoriâ sede Constantinopolin translatâ, urbis illius Patriarcha (quod ita intellexisse videtur) Successor Petri in ista praecipua potestate haberi debuit, & imperio ad Germanos translato, quilibet in Residentia, ut vocant, Imperatoria Episcopus? Ut ita potestas summa Ecclesiastica Imperatoriam urbem semper ornare debeat, quemadmodum Petrus cum illa potestate eam adiisse fingitur? Vel, si forte non necesse est, ut sedi Imperatoriae semper adhaereat, annon illam sibi aequè ac Roma, potestate temporali per temporales exercenda nudata, vendicare possunt Residentiae, aut Regis Christianissimi: ut apud Primogenitum Filium habitet Pater, aut Catholici, ut jungantur sedes Regis & Episcopi καὶ' ἐξοχὴν Catholicorum?
units.tr: {Even granting a monarchical power in Peter, it is shown that a manifold uncertainty remains} unequal to it. Certainly, at different times, others rather than many Roman bishops should have succeeded on account of their pre-eminence in virtue. Or, if account must be taken in this succession of the imperial see, or of some other powerful metropolis, because great cities have great vices and all evil comes from the court, should not the bishops of those cities, and of Rome for as long as they held that power, have received from God a measure of grace clearly greater for the good of the Church, and all the greater as the one held to be supreme is greater? And should it not have been better, in order to stop up the fount of all wickedness, or at least to restrain greater wickedness, that with the imperial seat moved to Constantinople, the Patriarch of that city (as he seems to have understood it) should have been held Peter's successor in this chief power; and with the empire transferred to the Germans, any bishop in the so-called imperial residence? So that the supreme ecclesiastical power would always adorn the imperial city, just as Peter is imagined to have come to it with that power? Or, if it is perhaps not necessary that it always cling to the imperial see, could not the residences of the most Christian King, stripped of temporal power to be exercised by temporal rulers, claim it for themselves just as Rome does, so that the Father dwells with the firstborn Son, or the Catholic [king], so that the seats of king and bishop are joined as the Catholics' pre-eminent [καὶ' ἐξοχὴν]?

units.la: XXXI. Vel, si Romanus Episcopus praeter Episcopatum Romanum etiam illam Ecclesiae universae Praefecturam habet, quomodo habet? An eo modo, quo Episcopus alicujus loci adjungit sibi alium Episcopatum, vel Canonicatum, aut Abbatiam? Negat Bellarminus. Vel an ita, ut Romana urbis Episcopatum erexerit ad summum orbis terrae Pontificatum, quemadmodum cum Episcopatus simplex erigitur in Archiepiscopatum, vel Patriarchatum, & Archiepiscopus, vel Patriarcha non est bis aut ter Episcopus, sed semel tantùm, ut in hujus rei signum non dari debeat Pontifici summo nisi unum Pallium, etiamsi Episcopus, Patriarcha, & summus Pontifex sit, & haec omnia in eo sint unum actu, & tantùm in potentia multa? Hoc posterius affirmat Bellarminus l.2. de Rom. Pont. cap.12. Sed, quando illud ibi affirmat, ubi probat? Ubi legitur de monstrosa illa commixtione? De illo, quòd Romanae urbis Episcopatus, id est, Episcopatus unius urbis proprius, ad Praefecturam totius Ecclesiae erectus, id est, toti orbi communis factus sit, ut jam particulare & universale, proprium & commune unum sint actu? Nonne qui talia dicunt, ad postpraedicamenta Aristotelis stotelis relegandi essent. Ast etiam Episcopatus in Archiepiscopa-tum vel Patriarchatum eligitur; De illo quidem nihil in Scriptu-ra; sed dum fit, de eo constat ex illorum revelatione, qui id ita con-stituisse dicuntur, de Papa in hoc non ita constat, & dispar quoque est ratio quoad illud, quòd Archiepiscopi aut Patriarchæ non æquè supra Episcopos, ac Papæ supra omnes ponuntur, ita ut omnem ubique potestatem soli habeant, soli ubique verè Episco-pi, dum cæteri ad lubitum suum Vicarii sunt, aut non sunt; quod circa Archiepiscopos aut Patriarchas non obtinet, non enim illis aliquid præter primatum ordinis erga alios tribuitur, nec alii dicuntur juris ipsorum, nec etiam quatenus illi sunt Episcopi urbis primariæ, dicuntur Episcopi minorum diœcesium, aut totius na-tionis, aut Provinciæ, ut Episcopi Romani, quâ tales, orbis; jam au-tem major certè Pallio opus esset ad tegendum simul talem Episco-pum, Archiepiscopum, Patriarcham & summum Pontificem; cur non etiam addit Presbyterum, Diaconum, Subdiaconum, Lectorem, Exorcistam, Acoluthum, & quid non? Si Comes aliquis Imperator eligitur, an quâ Comes Imperator est, & Comitatus ac Impe-rium actu unum sunt? Non puto. Sed talia fingere oportuit, ne in præjudicium cedat primum Episcoporum Romanorum nomen.
units.tr: XXXI. Or, if the Roman bishop, besides the Roman bishopric, also holds that prefecture of the whole Church, how does he hold it? In the way in which a bishop of some place adds to himself another bishopric, or a canonry, or an abbey? Bellarmine denies it. Or in the way that the bishopric of the city of Rome was raised to the supreme pontificate of the world, just as when a simple bishopric is raised to an archbishopric or patriarchate, and the archbishop or patriarch is not a bishop twice or three times but only once, so that as a sign of this only one pallium is to be given to the supreme pontiff, even though he is bishop, patriarch and supreme pontiff, and all these are one in act and only many in potency? Bellarmine affirms the latter in l.2. de Rom. Pont. cap.12. But when he affirms this, where does he prove it? Where is that monstrous mixture read of? Where is it read that the bishopric of the city of Rome, that is, a bishopric proper to one city, was raised to the prefecture of the whole Church, that is, made common to the whole world, so that the particular and the universal, the proper and the common, are now one in act? Should not those who say such things be relegated to the postpredicaments of Aristotle? But indeed a bishopric is also chosen into an archbishopric or patriarchate. Of that, indeed, there is nothing in Scripture; but when it is done, it is established from the revelation of those who are said to have so constituted it. Of the Pope, in this, it is not so established. The reasoning is also different in this respect: archbishops or patriarchs are not placed above bishops as equally as the Pope is placed above all, so that they alone have all power everywhere and alone are everywhere truly bishops, while the rest are vicars at their pleasure or are not. This does not hold for archbishops or patriarchs, for nothing is granted to them beyond primacy of order over the others, nor are the others said to be under their jurisdiction. Nor, insofar as they are bishops of a chief city, are they said to be bishops of the smaller dioceses, or of a whole nation or province, as the Roman bishop, as such, is said to be bishop of the world. Now certainly a larger pallium would be needed to cover at once such a bishop, archbishop, patriarch and supreme pontiff. Why does he not also add presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, reader, exorcist, acolyte, and whatever else? If some count is elected emperor, is he, as count, emperor, and are county and empire one in act? I do not think so. But such things had to be feigned, lest the first name of the Roman bishops suffer prejudice.

units.la: XXXII. Sed posito etiam hoc, supremam illam potestatem per Successionem ad Episcopos Romanos primos derivari debuis-se, quæritur adhuc, an etiam ad ultimos, an ad omnes, an semper Episcopi Romani præ aliis hujus Potestatis successione frui de-beant? Illud certè certò asserere non audent ipsimet Monarchici, nam sicut docent, Bellarminus quidem, potuisse Petrum nullam omni-nò sedem particularem eligere; Scotus autem in 4. dist.24. Cordubensis l. 4. c. 1. Cajetanus de Primatu Papæ, c. 23. & Bannes in 2.2.q.1.a.10. electionem tantùm per accidens, & non Deo jubente, factam esse, ita etiam Bellarminus l.4. de Rom. Pont. c.4. dicit, quamvis sententia, Ro-manam Ecclesiam non posse ita deficere, ut sedes Apostolica alió transfer-ri debeat, sit pia & probatissima, tamen non adeò certam esse, ut contraria dici possit hæretica, vel manifestè erronea, ut rectè doceat Joannes Driedo l. 4. c. 3. part. 3. de Eccles. dogmat. & Scripturis; & quòd non sit omni-nò de fide, à Rom. Ecclesia non posse separari Apostolicam sedem, patere, quia neque Scriptura, neque traditio habeat, sedem Apostolicam ita fixam esse Romæ, ut inde auferri non possit. Et in eodem capite; Etiamsi consta-ret, Christum imperâsse Petro, ut Romæ sedem collocaret, non tamen contì- Insertum non minùs, an semper & omnes Episcopi Romani successione... nàü sequeretur, jussisse,ut eam immobiliter ibi collocaret. Quoniam ergò non constat, quomodo Christus jusserit Petrum, ut Roma sedem collocaret, ideò non esse de fide,divino & immutabili praecepto, Roma sedem constitutam esse ; Igitur & hic in incertitudinis tenebris palpitant, exiguo sanè Romae solatio,sic enim fieri poterit,ut propedi m loco moveatur, quae per accidens tantùm est, sedes Apostolica, Monarchica, quemadmodum fere jam mota videbatur aliquoties,maximè tempore Captivitatis Babylonicae Avinionensis ; Certè autem loco movenda videtur,quando tempore Anti-Christi Roma desolanda & cremanda videtur, ut deducitur ex Apocalypsis c.XVII. licèt prius illud Bellarmino non idem videatur.Quòd enim ait,illud non futurum, nisi in mundi fine,probat saltem,in mundi fine & ante diem judicii sedem alio transferri debere, & cur tunc etiam summus Pontifex, Romanus Pontifex diceretur & futurus esset, licèt Romae non habitaret? Illud certè jam aliquoties accidit, sed cur titulotenus fuerunt & erunt Romani tantùm? Et cur non cogitant,potiùs Christum, si vellet nominetenus Vicariatum suum Romae allegatum, probè curaturum, ut ibi semper tutò & quietè commorari posset?
units.tr: XXXII. But granting this too, that the supreme power should have been derived by succession to the first Roman bishops, it is still asked whether it should also have passed to the last, or to all, or whether Roman bishops should always enjoy this power by succession in preference to others. The monarchists themselves certainly do not dare to assert this with certainty. For as they teach, Bellarmine indeed holds that Peter could have chosen no particular see at all; Scotus indeed in 4. dist.24., Cordubensis l. 4. c. 1., Cajetan de Primatu Papæ, c. 23. and Bañez in 2.2. q.1. a.10. hold that the choice was made only per accidens, and not by God's command. So too Bellarmine l.4. de Rom. Pont. c.4. says that although the opinion that the Roman Church cannot so fail that the apostolic see must be transferred elsewhere is pious and very well approved, nevertheless it is not so certain that the contrary can be called heretical or manifestly erroneous, as Johannes Driedo rightly teaches, l. 4. c. 3. part 3. de Eccles. dogmat. & Scripturis; and that it is by no means of faith that the apostolic see cannot be separated from the Roman Church, since neither Scripture nor tradition holds that the apostolic see is so fixed at Rome that it cannot be removed from there. And in the same chapter: Even if it were established that Christ commanded Peter to place his see at Rome, it would not follow that he commanded him to place it there immovably. [Inserted, no less: whether always and all Roman bishops by succession...] Since therefore it is not established how Christ commanded Peter to place his see at Rome, it is therefore not of faith by a divine and unchangeable precept that the see was established at Rome. Hence here too they flutter in the shadows of uncertainty, a slight comfort indeed to Rome. For thus it may happen that the apostolic, monarchical see, which is so only per accidens, is moved elsewhere, as it already seemed to be moved several times, especially during the Babylonian captivity at Avignon. Certainly it seems it must be moved elsewhere when, in the time of Antichrist, Rome is to be laid waste and burned, as is deduced from Revelation chapter 17, although the former point does not seem the same to Bellarmine. For when he says that this will not happen unless at the end of the world, he proves at least that at the end of the world and before the day of judgment the see ought to be transferred elsewhere. Why, then, would the supreme pontiff be called, and be going to be, the Roman pontiff, even though he did not dwell at Rome? This has certainly happened several times already, but why have they been, and will they be, Romans only in name? And why do they not rather consider that Christ, if he wished his Vicariate to be named as attached to Rome, would have taken good care that they could always dwell there safely and quietly?

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Jam verò quòd Petri dicto modo Successor sit Romanus Pontifex, sic facilè Bellarmino probari potest. Nullus enim est,nec fuit unquam, dicit, qui se Petri Successorem ullo modo asseruerit, vel pro tali sit habitus, praeter Romanum & Antiochenum Episcopum: atqui Antiochenus non successit Petro in Pontificatu Ecclesiae totius, nam &c. (in praecedentibus infinitos ferè Petri Successores ostendimus, & primam rationem cum refutatione dedimus §. XXV. XXVI. XXVII.) Nicaenum Concilium Can. 6. Antiochenum Episcopum tertium Patriarchàm, non primum, nec secundum esse declarat ,sicut fuerat semper, neque unquam Antiocheni Episcopi altiorem locum quaesiverunt. Et cur eo ordine collocati sint Patriarchae,mox videbimus. Reliqua ita ferè sonant: Episcopus Romanus se vocat successorem Petri in Pontificatu Ecclesiae totius. E. est. Lepidum certè argumentandi genus, à praesumptione ad possessionem legitimam ! Adeóne vili pretio Monarchiae acquiruntur, eaeque tantae ! Quis non sic Monarcha statim fiet ! Et quidem heic eò minùs convenit argumentatio à praesumptione & eo, quod praetenditur,quia ,juxta demonstrationes praecedentes, talis Monarchia legitima in rerum natura nunquam fuit, & proin successio in ea dari nullo modo potest, ut, qui sucsuccessionem in ea non jactant, & potestatem ejus non usurpant, eatenus modesti, alieni, imò divini non appetentes, concesso sibi à Deo contenti, ista verò de se præsumentes, usurpatores vani, superbi, injusti, in Deum & Christum ejus maximè injurii, censendi sint; Tantum abest ut hic tanta præ se ferre sufficiat.
units.tr: Now, that the Roman Pontiff is the successor of Peter in the sense just described can easily be proved against Bellarmine. For there is no one, and never has been anyone, he says, who has asserted in any way that he is the successor of Peter, or has been regarded as such, except the Roman and the Antiochene Bishop; but the Antiochene did not succeed Peter in the Pontificate of the whole Church, for etc. (In what precedes we have shown almost countless successors of Peter, and we gave the first argument with its refutation in §§ XXV, XXVI and XXVII.) The Council of Nicaea, Canon 6, declares the Antiochene Bishop to be the third Patriarch, neither the first nor the second, as he always had been; nor did the bishops of Antioch ever seek a higher place. Why the Patriarchs were placed in that order we shall see shortly. The rest runs more or less like this: The Roman Bishop calls himself the successor of Peter in the Pontificate of the whole Church. Therefore it is so. Certainly a charming kind of argument, from presumption to lawful possession! Are monarchies acquired at such a cheap price, and such great ones at that? Who would not become a monarch at once in this way! And indeed the argument from presumption and from what is claimed fits here all the less, because, according to the demonstrations above, such a lawful monarchy has never existed in the nature of things, and so succession to it can in no way be given. Those who do not boast of succession to it, and do not usurp its power, are to be judged modest, not greedy for what belongs to others, indeed not seeking what is divine, and content with what God has granted them; but those who presume these things about themselves are to be judged vain, proud, unjust usurpers, most injurious to God and his Christ. So far is it from being enough for them to flaunt such great claims here.

units.la: XXXIV. Sed præbet nobis Bellarminus hisce suis ineptiis occasionem, in historiam istius successionis, vel potiùs præsumptionis, inquirendi. Infiniti essemus, si omnia illa, quæ contra istam successionem faciunt, ex Antiquitate & historia Ecclesiastica afferre vellemus, sed pauca tantùm delibabimus, breviter ostensuri, ejusmodi Pontificatum, sive Monarchiam totius Ecclesiæ, primos Episcopos Romanos, id est, si istis hominibus credimus, primos Monarchas ne affectâsse quidem, & eos, qui illam temporis progressu aff ectârunt, diu non obtinuisse, aliis interim similia ferè pari vanitate affectantibus, tandem tamen, sed demum seculo undecimo inclinante, adhibitis per aliquot annorum centurias variis artibus, ceu tot mysterii iniquitatis testibus, contradicentibus tamen semper multis, voti ex parte compotes factos esse, adeóque ita se habere istud successionis negotium, ut, quando alii successiones benè fundatæ, quò origini propiores & magis manifestæ sunt, hæc contrà paulatim & nonnihil longo temporis spatio ad suam ἀκμὴν tandem pervenirs deprehendatur.
units.tr: XXXIV. But Bellarmine, by these silly remarks of his, gives us an occasion to inquire into the history of this succession, or rather of this presumption.
