We would be endless if we wanted to bring forward everything from antiquity and church history that tells against this succession, but we shall only touch on a few points, briefly showing that such a Pontificate, or monarchy of the whole Church, was not even aspired to by the first Roman bishops (that is, if we believe these men, the first monarchs). And those who aspired to it in the course of time did not hold it for long; meanwhile others, aspiring to similar things with equal vanity, at length, but only when the eleventh century was already declining, after various arts had been used over several centuries (witnesses, as it were, of the mystery of iniquity), and yet with many always contradicting, attained in part what they wished. The business of succession thus stands in such a way that, whereas other well-founded successions are nearer to their origin and more manifest, this one, on the contrary, is found to have gradually, and only over a long span of time, reached its peak [ἀκμήν] at last.

units.la: XXXV. Pro certo igitur primò haberi debet, primos Episcopos Romanos per secula non pauca ejusmodi successionem in Monarchia seu Pontificatu supremo totius Ecclesiæ ne affectâsse quidem, & legat quis genuinos antiquitatis interpretes à capite ad calcem (non loquor de supposititiis illis primorum Pontificum Epistolis, quorum etiam Doctissimos inter Pontificios pudet;) ne quidem de ejusmodi Pontificatu supremo & ejus successione inveniet, multa contrà & longè plurima figmentum talis successionis planè evertentia. Hinc Æneas Sylvius, postea Papa Pius II. ipse fateri coactus est: Ad Pontifices Romanos ante Nicenum Concilium (an. 324.) aliquis sanè, etsi non magnus respectus fuit. Guicciardinus, homo Italus & Leonis X. Papæ à præfectura militiæ, idem planè testatur, dum Hist. Pap. l. IV. ait, Papæ priores non modò potentiâ Civili & mundanâ penitus nudatos, verùm etiam ab illa vexatos, diu obscuros & ferè ignoratos fuisse, eorum nomine nulla re magis, quàm supplicis & recruciatibus perferendis innotescente. Accedit quoad potestatem tem-poraporalem, ceu alteram hujus, quam praetendunt successionis partem, testis non ignobilis Poëta Adriano IV. ita accinens: Cogitet antiquos primaevi temporis annos Praeteritósque dies; & secula prisca revolvat; Num Petrus? Aut Clemens? Num caetera turba priorum Sceptra Latina dabat? Romanus tempore prisco Pauper erat Praesul, regali munere crevit: Nec tamen ut fasces & Regni jura Latini Vel dare praesumat, vel cuiquam tollere posset.
units.tr: XXXV. It must therefore first be held as certain that the first Roman bishops, for not a few centuries, did not even aspire to such a succession in a supreme monarchy or Pontificate of the whole Church. Let anyone read the genuine interpreters of antiquity from beginning to end (I am not speaking of those spurious letters of the first Pontiffs, whose falsity even the most learned Papists are ashamed of). He will not find even a mention of such a supreme Pontificate and its succession; on the contrary, he will find much, and far more, completely overturning the fiction of such a succession. Hence Aeneas Sylvius, afterwards Pope Pius II, was himself compelled to admit: Among the Roman Pontiffs before the Council of Nicaea (324) there was surely some regard, though not a great one. Guicciardini, an Italian who held the office of military prefect under Pope Leo X, plainly testifies to the same thing when, in Hist. Pap. l. IV., he says: The earlier Popes, not only stripped entirely of civil and worldly power but even harassed by it, were for a long time obscure and almost unknown, their name becoming known by nothing so much as by the supplications and tortures they had to endure. To this is added, as regards temporal power, which is the other part of the succession they claim, the witness of no ignoble poet, who sings thus to Adrian IV: Let him consider the years of the ancient, primeval time, and the days gone by, and let him turn over the early ages. Did Peter? Or Clement? Or did the rest of that crowd of predecessors give the Latin scepter? The Roman prelate was poor in ancient times; he grew by royal gift. Yet he could neither presume to bestow the fasces and the rights of the Latin kingdom, nor could he take them from anyone.

units.la: XXXVI. Et quamvis adhuc seculo secundo Victor Papa Asiaticos, ob dissensum, quod ad tempus celebrationis Paschatis, temerè excommunicare tentaverit, illis cum Polycrate Ephesino fortiter reclamantibus, ideò etiam ab Irenaeo caeterùm ὁμοψηφῶν reprehensus, & sic affectatae cujusdam dominationis primum specimen dederit, & circa medium quarti Basilius M. τῷ δυτικῷ ὀρφνῷ, Occidentalem fastum flagellare, & expresse quoque dicere potuerit: Odi fastum illius Ecclesiae; referente id, & nonnihil stomachante, & Jobi ac Jeremiae navis haec annumerante, Caesare Baronio ad an. Chr. 372. §. 32. tamen non statim ista fidem successionis Monarchicae praesupponebant, & simul cognita simul reprehendebantur, eóque acriùs veritatibus antiquis insistebatur. Hinc, ut dicta hic non repetam, S. Cyprianus ad Stephanum Papam epist. 67. scribere ausus. Etsi Pastores multi sumus, unum tamen gregem pascimus; Et paulò post: Si quis ex Collegio nostro haeresin facere &c. Ubi Papam nec ab haeresi, nec etiam à censuris in Casu haereseos eximit; Prout etiam in Concilio Carthaginensi sub eo habito 85. Episcoporum eos ita allocutus legitur: Neque quisquam nostrum Episcoporum se Episcopum constituit, aut tyrannico terrore ad obsequendi necessitatem Collegas suos adegit, quando habeat omnis Episcopus pro licentia libertatis & potestatis suae arbitrium proprium, támque judicari ab alio non possit, quàm nec ipse potest alios judicare. Sed exspectemus universi judicium Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui unus & solus habet potestatem & praeponendi nos in Ecclesia sua gubernatione, & de actu nostro judicandi. Quibus clarissimis verbis, teste Binio, Stephanum Papam sugillare voluit, ita fecit, ut Papae quoque titulum Episcopi Episcoporum, quem ei Bellarm. in recogn. de Rom. Pont. l. 2. c.31. tribuit, convenire aperte negaverit; Nec parùm horum verborum authoritatem augex, quòd Augustino l. 3. de Bapt. contra Donat. c. 3. nomine mitissimi mitissimi & veracissimi sermonis venerunt,nec ibi honorem Papæ vindicavit ullo modo,ubi tamen verba illa; Episcopum à nemine judicari, & alium judicare non posse; quadantenus improbavit.
units.tr: XXXVI. And although already in the second century Pope Victor rashly tried to excommunicate the Asians on account of their disagreement about the time of celebrating Easter, they strongly protested, together with Polycrates of Ephesus; and for this reason he was also rebuked by Irenaeus, who was otherwise of one accord [ὁμοψηφῶν]. So he gave the first sample of a certain assumed domination. And in the middle of the fourth century Basil the Great could lash the Western pride with the Western darkness [τῷ δυτικῷ ὀρφνῷ], and say expressly: I hate the pride of that Church. Caesar Baronius, reporting this somewhat vexedly and counting it among the troubles of Job and Jeremiah, at the year of Christ 372, §32, nevertheless, these men did not at once presuppose belief in a monarchical succession; and as soon as such claims were known, they were at the same time rebuked, and so the ancient truths were pressed all the more keenly. Hence, not to repeat what has been said here, St Cyprian dared to write to Pope Stephen, Epistle 67: Although we are many ministers, we feed one flock; and a little later: If anyone from our college makes heresy, etc., where he exempts the Pope neither from heresy nor from censures in a case of heresy. Likewise, at the Council of Carthage held under him by 85 bishops, they are read to have addressed him thus: None of us bishops has made himself a bishop, or has driven his colleagues by tyrannical terror to the necessity of obeying, since every bishop has his own free judgement, by the licence of liberty and his own power, and cannot be judged by another any more than he can judge others. But let us all await the judgement of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone has the power both of setting us over the government of his Church and of judging our conduct. By these most clear words, according to Binius, he wished to rebuke Pope Stephen, and he did so in such a way that he plainly denied that the title Bishop of Bishops, which Bellarmine attributes to the Pope in Recognitio de Romano Pontifice, l. 2, c. 31, applies to him. The authority of these words is not a little increased by the fact that Augustine, in l. 3 de Baptismo contra Donatistas, c. 3, calls them the most gentle and most truthful discourse; and yet there he did not in any way defend the Pope's honour, though he partly disapproved of those words: that a bishop is judged by no one and cannot judge another.

units.la: XXXVII. Jam alios similia affectâsse , quod argumentum hoc ab eo , quod prætenditur , porrò infirmat , ostendere proclive est. Ita supra laudatus Guicciardinus l. citato & jam etiam allato,ait : Episcopi Constantinopolitanus & Ravennas, quoniam Religionis sedes Imperii atque armorum potentiam sequi consuevit,cum Romano Episcopo sæpenumerò de principatu disputabant. Multa certè & magna affectârunt, si cum ipso Monarcha de principatu disputârunt. Sed talis tunc nondum erat, interim primi esse ipsi voluerunt & præcipui ; Et ille quidem,Constantinopolitanus nempe, eò usque progressus est,ut,adprobante Imperatore Mauritio, & Romano Episcopo reverentiam erga Constantinopolitanum injungente, Episcopi Universalis titulum assumserit ; Idò etiam Gregorium I. sive Magnum adversarium expertus, qui Epist.l.IV. ep. 30. 32. 34.36. 38. ita fastui Constantinopolitano occurrit, ut titulum Universalis Episcopi novum, profanum, temerarium, superstitiosum, stultum, pompaticum, superbum, nefandum, pestiferum, scelestum, & blasphemia vocabulum esse dixerit, quo cæteris Episcoporum & Patriarcharum nomen derogetur, Ecclesia turbetur, scandalizetur, & scindatur, contra charitatem & communem gratiam agatur , & contra omnium sanctorum exempla, cùm sancti ante legem, sancti sub lege, sancti sub gratia, omnes hi perfidientes Corpus Domini (Ecclesiam) in membris sint Ecclesia constituti, & quorum nemo unquam se universalem vocari voluerit ; & contra exempla Apostolorum, ex quibus Paulus (1.Cor.I.12.) membra Dominici corporis certis extra Christum quasi capitibus & ipsis Apostolis subjici particulariter evitârit, & qui, Petrus Apostolus primum membrum Sancta & Universalis Ecclesia, Paulus, Andreas, Johannes, singularium plebium capita, & tamen sub uno capite omnes membra Ecclesiæ fuerint ; Et contra exempla Episcoporum Romanorum præcedentium, quorum nullus unquam tali vocabulo appellari voluerit ; nullus sibi hoc temerarium nomen arripuerit, ne,si sibi in Pontificatûs gradu gloriam singularitatis arriperet,hunc omnibus fratribus derogâsse videretur ; Contrà in tam perverso vocabulo nonnisi illum imitandum proponi, qui , despectis Angelorum Legionibus ,secum socialiter constitutis , ad culmen conatus sit singularitatis erumpere , ut & nulli subesse, & solus omnibus præesse videretur, qui etiam dixerit : In Cœlum conscendam, supra astra Cœli exaltabo solium meum, sedebo debo in monte Testamenti,in lateribus Aquilonis. Ascendam super altitudinem nubium: similis ero altissimo Jesaj.XIV.13.14. Et contra interdictum Christi; Et Patrem nolite vocare vobis super terram. Unus enim est Pater vester (Matth.XXIII.9.) quid enim ille terribili examine venientis judicis dicturus sit, qui non solum Pater, sed etiam generalis Pater in mundo vocari appetat, qua ratione omnia quae praedicta sint, fiant, Rex superbia prope sit, &, quod dici nefas sit, Sacerdotum esse praeparatum exercitum, quia cervici militent elationis, qui ad hoc positi fuerint, ut ducatum praebeant humilitatis. Quare etiam fidenter dicat, quia quisquis se Universalem Saterdotem vocet, vel vocari desideret, in elatione sua Antichristum praecurrat, quia superbiendo se ceteris praeponat, nec dispari superbia ad errorem duci, quia sicut perversus ille, Deus videri velit super omnes homines, ita, quisquis iste sit, qui solus Sacerdos appellari appetat, super caeteros Sacerdotes se extollat.
units.tr: XXXVII. Now it is easy to show that others aspired to similar things, which further weakens this argument from what is claimed. Thus Guicciardini, cited above, in the book already quoted and already brought forward, says: The bishops of Constantinople and Ravenna, since they were accustomed to follow the seat of religion with the power of empire and arms, often disputed with the Roman bishop about primacy. They certainly aspired to many great things if they disputed about primacy with the Monarch himself. But such a monarchy did not yet exist; meanwhile they wished to be first and pre-eminent. And the former, namely the Constantinopolitan, went so far that, with the Emperor Maurice approving and the Roman bishop enjoining reverence towards the Constantinopolitan, he assumed the title of Universal Bishop. Hence Gregory I, or the Great, as his opponent, who in Epist. l. IV, ep. 30, 32, 34, 36, 38 met the Constantinopolitan pride in such a way that he called the title of Universal Bishop a new, profane, rash, superstitious, foolish, pompous, proud, execrable, pestilent, wicked and blasphemous word, by which the name of the other bishops and patriarchs is detracted from, the Church is disturbed, scandalized and split, charity and common grace are violated, and it is contrary to the examples of all the saints, for the saints before the law, the saints under the law, and the saints under grace, all of whom, forming the Body of the Lord (the Church), are constituted as members of the Church, and none of whom ever wished to be called universal. It is also contrary to the examples of the Apostles, from whom Paul (1 Cor. 1:12) avoided having the members of the Lord's body subjected in particular to certain heads outside Christ, and even to the apostles themselves: Peter the Apostle was the first member of the holy and universal Church, while Paul, Andrew and John were heads of particular peoples, and yet all were members of the Church under one head. It is also contrary to the examples of the preceding Roman bishops, none of whom ever wished to be called by such a title, and none seized for himself this rash name, lest, if he seized for himself the glory of singularity in the degree of Pontificate, he should seem to have detracted from all his brethren. On the contrary, in so perverse a title only the one is set forth for imitation who, scorning the legions of angels associated with him in fellowship, sought to break out to the summit of singularity, so that he might seem both to be subject to none and to preside alone over all; who also said: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven, I will sit on the mount of the covenant, in the sides of the north. I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High (Isaiah 14:13-14). And it is contrary to Christ's prohibition: And call no one father upon earth, for one is your Father (Matt. 23:9). For what will that man say at the terrible examination of the coming judge, who desires to be called not only Father but also general Father in the world? By what reasoning all the things foretold come to pass: the King of pride is near, and, what it is unlawful to say, a prepared army of priests, since they serve as soldiers of the neck of elation, who were appointed to lead the way in humility. Wherefore he may confidently say that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, Universal Priest, runs before Antichrist in his elation, because by his pride he sets himself above the others; nor is he led into error by any unequal pride, for as that perverse one wishes to be seen as God above all men, so whoever he is who desires to be called alone Priest exalts himself above the other priests.

units.la: XXXVIII. Certè si affectare, si praetendere, si magna de se jactare sufficit, maximus & in totius Ecclesiae Pontificatu Successor, si quisquam alius, Johannes ille Jejunator, Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus fuit; judicibus ipsis Monarchicis, qui, ut differentiam inter Monarchas suos, & illum assignare queant, eum ita Episcopi Universalis titulum usurpâsse contendunt, ut unus solus singularis Episcopus, praeter quem alius nemo sit, & cui Episcopi caeteri omnes subsint ut filii, non ut fratres, esse voluerit; Quamvis multum in eo fallantur, & vanum illud κεηνσφύγελον sit. Cùm primò quidem tales etiam Episcopi Universales Episcopi Romani esse velint, dum non quidem reliquis Episcoporum nomen adimunt, sed rem, eósque sibi plane subjiciunt, & sui duntaxat juris esse, à se omnimodè dependere asserant, prout secundò saltem non plùs, sed quod suis Monarchis convenire volunt, supereminentiam prae caeteris, & curam totius Ecclesiae generalem Johannes sibi tribuisse deprehenditur, qui nunquam id sibi arrogavit, quòd solus esset in orbe Episcopus, reliquis sibi Patriarchraum, Metropolitanorum, Episcoporum titulos constanter retinentibus, nam & tunc quoque in ditione Constantinopolitani Episcopi manserunt, & unum ex illis, ubi se universalem, comministrum & Episcopum religiosissimum, quod in Codice Juris Graeco-Romani videri potest, insignivit, & Gregorius Oecumenicum, qualem se Constantinopolitanus haberi velit, talem, qui omnibus dignior appareat, nulli subsit, omnibus praesit solus, Imperatori se praeponat, & omnia Christi membra sibi subjiciat, definivit, qualia Monarchici Universali suo Episcopo ubique vendicant, & testibus Scriptoribus, non uter solus in orbe Episcopus maneret, sed uter caput omnium Ecclesiarum, Princeps omnium Pontificum esset, inter Constantinopolitanum & Romanum tum temporis & postea disceptatum, & idem, quod Mauricius antehac Constantinopolitano concesserat, à Phoca postmodum Romano tributum fuit; Testibus etiam apud Baronium ad an. Chr. 606. n. 2. Anastasio, qui ita in vita Bonifacii P. loquitur: Hic obtinuit apud Phocam Principem, ut sedes Apostolica B. Petri Apostoli esset caput omnium Ecclesiarum, id est, Romana Ecclesia: quia Ecclesia Constantinopolitana se primam omnium Ecclesiarum scribebat; Et Paulo Diacono de Gest. Longobard. l. 1. c. 11. Cujus haec sunt verba: Hic Phocas Imperator, rogante P. Bonifacio, statuit, sedem Romanae & Apostolicae Ecclesiae primam esse, cum prius Constantinopolitana se primam omnium scriberet. Imò ipse Baronius n. 5. in hunc modum rem enarrat; Quid suo edicto contulit Romanae Ecclesiae Phocas? Nihil plane, nisi quod declararit sua sententia, indebitè usurpari ab Episcopo Constantinopolitano Oecumenici nomen, quod Romanae duntaxat conveniret Ecclesiae.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Certainly, if it is enough to aspire to the office, to lay claim to it, and to boast loudly of oneself, then John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople, was the greatest successor in the pontificate of the whole Church, if anyone was. Even the Monarchist judges themselves, who contend that he assumed the title of Universal Bishop in such a way that he wished to be the one single bishop, with no other beside him, and with all other bishops under him as sons, not as brothers, must admit this, so that they may distinguish their Monarchs from him. Yet they are greatly mistaken in this, and that empty [κεηνσφύγελον] claim is worthless. For firstly, such Universal Bishops wish to be the Bishops of Rome as well. They do not take the name of bishop from the rest of the bishops, but the substance of the office, and they plainly subject those bishops to themselves, declaring that they belong only to their own jurisdiction and depend entirely on them. And secondly, at the least, John is found to have claimed for himself not more, but only what his Monarchs want to belong to them: a supremacy above the rest and a general care of the whole Church. He never claimed that he alone was bishop in the world, for the others constantly kept the titles of Patriarch, Metropolitan and Bishop. Indeed, they remained even then within the dominion of the Bishop of Constantinople. Among these, he styled himself Universal, fellow-minister and most religious Bishop, as can be seen in the Code of Greco-Roman Law. And Gregory defined the Oecumenical bishop, which the Constantinopolitan wished to be considered, as one who appears more worthy than all, is subject to no one, rules over all alone, puts himself before the Emperor, and subjects all the members of Christ to himself. These are the things the Monarchists everywhere claim for their Universal Bishop. And, according to the writers, the question at that time and afterwards between the Constantinopolitan and the Roman was not which of them alone would remain bishop in the world, but which of them would be the head of all the Churches and the prince of all the pontiffs. The same privilege that Maurice had earlier conceded to the Constantinopolitan was afterwards granted to the Roman by Phocas. The witnesses include Anastasius, cited by Baronius ad an. Chr. 606. n. 2., who speaks thus in the life of Boniface III: He obtained from Phocas the Prince that the Apostolic See of the blessed Apostle Peter should be the head of all the Churches, that is, the Roman Church, because the Church of Constantinople was writing itself the first of all the Churches. Also Paul the Deacon, de Gest. Longobard. l. 1. c. 11., whose words are these: Phocas the Emperor, at the request of Pope Boniface, decreed that the See of the Roman and Apostolic Church should be first, since before this the Church of Constantinople was writing itself first of all. Indeed Baronius himself, n. 5., relates the matter in this way: What did Phocas confer on the Roman Church by his edict? Nothing at all, except that he declared by his judgment that the name of Oecumenical, which belonged only to the Roman Church, was wrongly claimed by the Bishop of Constantinople.

units.la: XXXIX. Sed juvabit, etiam hic connotare partim causas mutatae sic aleae, & partim, quid ex verbis Gregorii, facto Bonifacii & reliquorum junctis quoad successionem colligi possit, de qua agimus.
units.tr: XXXIX. But it will help to note here, in part, the causes of the changed game, and in part, what can be gathered from the words of Gregory, the deed of Boniface and the rest taken together, concerning the succession with which we are dealing.

units.la: Bonifacius titulum à Phoca Universalis Episcopi & primatum à Constantinopolitano antea usurpatum impetravit, ipso Baronio l. c. n. 2. & 3. illud testante, in odium Cyriaci Constantinopolitani, qui Phocae parricidium in Mauricio patratum adprobare noluit, cum contra Romani non sine invidendis elogiis Parricidae de potestate acquisita statim gratulati sint, & modis omnibus in ejus se insinuârint amicitiam, ipso etiam probè considerante, quanti referat, habere in Occidente Romanos Episcopos, potentia, opibus, & authoritate indies crescentes, amicos. Non igitur factum est evidentia verborum: Tu es Petrus &c. & successionis Episcoporum Romanorum in totiu Ecclesiae Pontificatu indubitatâ certitudine, ut nec Gregorius Johanni ejusmodi opponere ausus est, aut voluit; Qui &c, verbi saltem, longissimè à successionis in totius Ecclesiae Pontificatu præsumptione abfuit, dum Universalem Pontificatum sive Episcopatum non tantùm in Constantinopolitano damnavit, sed & absolutè improbavit, & prægnantibus rationibus refutavit, & talia sibi tribuentem, quisquis iste sit, Antichristi præcursorem vo-
units.tr: Boniface obtained from Phocas the title of Universal Bishop and the primacy, which had earlier been claimed by the Constantinopolitan, as Baronius himself testifies l. c. n. 2. & 3., out of hatred for Cyriacus of Constantinople, who refused to approve the murder of Maurice committed by Phocas. On the other hand, the Romans, not without enviable praises, at once congratulated the murderer on the power he had acquired, and insinuated themselves into his friendship by every means, while also carefully considering how much it mattered to have Roman bishops in the West who were daily growing in power, wealth and authority as friends. Therefore the succession of the Roman bishops to the pontificate of the whole Church did not become a matter of clear words, "You are Peter," etc., nor of undoubted certainty. Gregory did not dare, or did not wish, to oppose John with any such claim. At least in words, he was very far from presuming a succession to the pontificate of the whole Church, since he condemned the universal pontificate or episcopate not only in the Constantinopolitan, but absolutely, and refuted it with weighty reasons. He called whoever assigned such things to himself, whoever he might be, a forerunner of Antichrist.

units.la: Vitiosa igitur in Bonifacio III. ejusque Successoribus vocavit; ut sic, quando Johannes Constantinopolitanus, Antichristi praecursor fuit, Bonifacium & reliquos elationis (quo vocabulo aperte ad ὑπερεχόμενον, sese efferentem supra omne, quod Deus aut venerabile dicitur; alludit:) haeredes (quibus etiam nomen Patris Patrum à Gregorio rejectum, juxta Bellarminum l.2. de R. P. c.31. eisque solis competit;) Antichristorum nomine insigniisse putandus sit; & successionem in ista elatione, non Petri (quem membrum Ecclesia à capite distinctum fecit,) sed Diaboli notârit. Quemadmodum etiam Johanni III. Papae constitutio contra Vigilium Papam tribuitur, neminem summum Pontificem, aut Episcopum Universalem vocari debere.
units.tr: Therefore Gregory called Boniface III and his successors guilty, so that, since John of Constantinople was a forerunner of Antichrist, Boniface and the others should be thought to have been marked with the name of Antichrists, as heirs of this elation (a word which clearly alludes to [ὑπερεχόμενον], exalting itself above everything that is called God or worthy of worship). The title Father of Fathers, which Gregory rejected, belongs to them alone, according to Bellarmine l.2. de R. P. c.31. And he marked the succession in this exaltation not as Peter's, whom the Church made a member distinct from the head, but as the Devil's. In the same way, a decree is attributed to Pope John III against Pope Vigilius, that no one ought to be called chief Pontiff or Universal Bishop.

units.la: XL. Videamus autem in ista successionis hujus inquisitione porrò, quid ex Episcopis singulis; videamus etiam, quid ex congregatis in Concilio pro aut contra habeamus. Episcopi singuli per universam Ecclesiam à Papis aut eorum Vicariis minimè constituebantur, nec etiam in eos exercebatur jurisdictio, qualis hodie ex ista successione derivatur, & quando nonnunquam Papae fimbrias suas dilatare voluerunt, fortiter eis diu resistebatur. Quae quidem singula apud alios prolixè deducta videri possunt; nobis hic tantùm annotâsse sufficiat, quo stylo & quibus titulis in epistolis ad Papas usi sint, nam ex illo de caeteris quodammodo judicium fieri potest, saltem eatenus, quatenus non majora creduntur illis, quae scribuntur, hominibus plerumque ad adulationem propensis, aut aliàs quoque emphaticè loquentibus aut scribentibus; Sed ne quis à nobis exspectet augustos illos saltem titulos, quibus Clemens Papa Jacobum Apostolum insigniisse fertur, in epistola ad eum data, cujus initium: Clemens Jacobo, Fratri Domini, Episcopo Episcoporum, regenti omnes Ecclesias Dei, quae ubique fundatae sunt per ejus providentiam; quale tamen alloquium Petrum & Petri in Pontificatu totius Ecclesiae Successores, & quidem solos, spectare deberet. Ast longè infrà substiterunt candidi, & scapham scapham appellare volentes, & eâdem ratione Episcopos Romanos compellârunt, quâ & ipsi compellandi erant, de aequalitate sic testaturi, & in quavis epistola quasi ingeminantes illud Junonis ad Jovem: Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ Θεὸς εἰμι γάμου δέμοι ἐνθεν ὀθεναί. Cyprianus enim T. I. Concil. p.388. Fratri Cornelio scripsit; Dionysius Corinthius Euf. l. 7. c.59. Stephanum & Sixtum, Papas; Frater; singulos allocutus est, Marcellus Epiph. haeref.2. Julium Comministrum vocavit; Johannes Constantinopolitanus nus T.III. Conc. l.III. Hormisda fratri Epistolam misit; Carthaginenses Conc. T. I. p.788. Innocentium p.841. Bonifacium; Ephesini pag. 1087. Cælestinum, fratres suos, comministros suos simpliciter compellárunt. Qui certè tituli, ut non ex hodiernis libris, quos vocant, titularibus desumpti sunt, ita puritatis omnimodæ fidem faciunt, & non sunt scribentium ad suos Monarchas, nisi valdè fallar, non sunt agnoscentium successionem Petri in Pontificatu totius Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: XL. Let us further look, in this inquiry into the succession, at what we have from the individual bishops, and also at what we have from those gathered in council, for or against. Individual bishops throughout the universal Church were not appointed by the Popes or their Vicars, nor was jurisdiction exercised over them of the kind that is derived today from this succession. And when the Popes sometimes wished to extend their borders, they were strongly resisted for a long time. These matters can be seen set out at length by others. It will be enough for us here to note only the style and the titles they used in their letters to the Popes, for from that one can form some judgment about the rest, at least so far as those things written are not believed to be greater than they are. People are usually inclined to flattery, or otherwise speak or write in an emphatic manner. But lest anyone expect from us those lofty titles at least, with which Pope Clement is said to have honoured the Apostle James in the letter addressed to him, whose opening is: Clement to James, brother of the Lord, bishop of bishops, governing all the Churches of God, which have been founded everywhere by his providence, such a form of address should have pertained to Peter and to the Successors of Peter in the pontificate of the whole Church, and to them alone. But the candid men stood much lower, wishing to call a boat a boat, and on the same principle they addressed the Roman bishops as they themselves were to be addressed, bearing witness to equality in this way, and in every letter repeating almost like an echo that line of Juno to Jove: [Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ Θεὸς εἰμι γάμου δέμοι ἐνθεν ὀθεναί.] For Cyprian wrote to his brother Cornelius, T. I. Concil. p.388. Fratri Cornelio. Dionysius of Corinth, Euseb. l. 7. c.59., addressed Stephen and Sixtus, the popes, individually, as brother. Marcellus, Epiph. haeref.2., called Julius fellow-minister. John of Constantinople sent a letter to his brother Hormisdas. The Carthaginians, Council, T. I. p.788, addressed Innocent, p.841, and Boniface simply as their brothers and fellow-ministers, and the Ephesians, p.1087, addressed Celestine as their brother and fellow-minister. Certainly these titles, not being taken from the so-called titular books of today, make full proof of an unqualified purity, and, unless I am greatly mistaken, they were not written by men who acknowledged the succession of Peter in the pontificate of the whole Church, as they would have to write to their Monarchs.

units.la: XLI. Sed non pauciora nobis suppeditant Episcopi in Conciliis congregandi & congregati; Congregandi antiquitus in Conciliis generalibus non, Episcopis Romanis convocantibus & jubentibus, sed ex Imperatorum mandatis confluebant; Congregatorum non Episcopi Romani, aut eorum Legati ordinarii Præsides erant; fatentibus utrumque ingenuè Gallis, aliisque.
units.tr: XLI. But the bishops, both those to be gathered and those gathered in councils, provide us with no fewer points. In ancient times, bishops came together for the general councils not at the summons and command of the Roman bishops, but at the mandate of the Emperors. Those gathered were presided over not by the Roman bishop or his ordinary legates, as both the Gauls and others frankly admit.

units.la: Quinimò constat, in quinto generali Concilio Constantinopoli anno 558. habito Vigilium Papam, tunc temporis Theodati Gothorum Regis Legatum in urbe degentem, solâ post Constantinopolitanum sedendi repugnantiâ à Patrum conventu, sed malo suo, abfuisse. Quorum forte respectu habito Cardinales quondam confessi sunt, posse Concilium coire, in quo non præsideat Papa, sed fasces submittat & villicationis suæ rationem reddat, apud Guicciardinum l. 9. Tunc quoque Spiritus S. non (prout quidem de Tridentino Concilio notissimum & testatissimum infame illud, ac eo tempore ab ipsis etiam Papistis jactatum proverbium habet) Româ in mantica clausus subinde mittebatur, nec usurpari poterat Romæ respectu, licèt mari interjacente, quod, teste Dudithio in Epist. ad Maximil. II. tabellariis Oraculorum latoribus ob inundationes expeditè non revertentibus, in Tridentina Synodo pariter dici consuevit, Spiritum non super aquas, ut sit in Genesi, ferri posse. Nec etiam Concilia generalia prima (ad quorum exemplum multa post nationalia & provincialia Concilia in omnibus se composuerunt;) confirmationem à Papis, verùm ab Imperatoribus petebant.
units.tr: Indeed, it is clear that at the fifth general council, held at Constantinople in the year 558, Pope Vigilius, who was at that time staying in the city as legate of Theodatus, King of the Goths, was absent from the assembly of the Fathers, though to his own harm, by reason of his refusal to sit after the Constantinopolitan alone. Perhaps with this in mind, the Cardinals once confessed that a council could meet in which the Pope does not preside, but lowers the rods and gives an account of his stewardship, as reported by Guicciardini l. 9. At that time too the Holy Spirit was not, as is well known and widely attested of the Council of Trent, the notorious proverb, bandied about at that time even by the Papists themselves, has it, sometimes sent out shut up in a bag from Rome. Nor could it be exercised with respect to Rome, though the sea lay between, which, according to Dudithius in Epist. ad Maximil. II., was commonly said at the Synod of Trent in the same way: the couriers carrying the oracles did not return quickly because of floods, so that the Spirit could not be carried over the waters, as is in Genesis. Nor did the first general councils (after whose example many later national and provincial councils have arranged everything in their own affairs) seek confirmation from the Popes, but from the Emperors.

units.la: XLII. Si verò modus celebrationis Conciliorum antiquus non favet successioni Episcoporum Romanorum in Pontificatu, sive Monarchia totius Ecclesiæ, ei certè decreta primorum Conciliorum haud magis favere deprehenduntur; Jam suprà innuimus, assignatos fuisse in Concilio Niceno etiam Episcopo Romano, æquè ac aliis, certos limites, certam, ut sic loquar, activitatis Sphaeram, Episcopo Alexandriae, Lybiae & Ægypti primatum concessisse, quandoquidem parilis mos Romano, nempe quoad loca vicina, juxta Rufinum l. 10. suburbiaria, juxta Versionem Arabicam generaliter, ea, quae circa eam; Constantinopolitanum, quia secundum post Romanum locum Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae adjudicavit, parvam apud Monarchicos gratiam promeruit; Iratum ideo Onuphrium etiam quis videre potest in annot. ad Bonif. III. qui & stomachatur quodammodo ob decretum Chalcedonensis Concilii, in quo Patres τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα ἀπένειμαν ᾗ τῆς νέας ῥώμης ἀγιωτάτῳ θεοῦ; aequalia privilegia adjudicarunt sanctissimae sedi nova Romae, id est Constantinopoleos; Cui simile plane Concilium Constantinopolitanum VI. Trullanum dedit, nam ἴσων ἀπολαυεῖν πρεσβείων, paribus privilegiis utrumque Episcopum frui voluit; Prout etiam Anastasius in Joh.VII. testatur, Synodum Constantinopolitanam Quinisextam Trullanam an. 692. fecisse quaedam capitula Ecclesiae Romanae contraria. Quid autem de Africanis Conciliis dicam? Non favent pariter successioni isti Romanorum, illud minimè, in quo supra allata Cypriani verba audita, & fraudes Romanorum in allegatione supposititii Canonis Niceni detectae, &, quod & alias factum, appellationes transmarinae, damnatae sunt. Ubi ridiculè annotat Gratianus; Nisi forte Romanam sedem appellaverint; cùm apertum sit, propter Romanam sedem decretum formatum esse. Quâ ratione autem ista Conciliorum decreta cum successione, quam praetendunt, in totius Ecclesiae Pontificatu conciliari poterunt? Videmus igitur, diu non creditam, jactatam statim omni studio impugnatam fuisse talem praefecturam universalem, successionis istius praetextu tandem quadantenus, Deo id ob varias causas secundum praedictiones permittente, stabilitam.
units.tr: XLII. But if the ancient manner of holding councils does not favour the succession of Roman bishops to the papacy, or monarchy over the whole Church, then the decrees of the first councils are certainly found no more favourable to it. We have already hinted that at the Council of Nicaea definite limits were assigned even to the Roman bishop, as to the others, a fixed sphere of activity, so to speak. The Bishop of Alexandria was granted primacy over Libya and Egypt, since the same custom applied to Rome, namely regarding the neighbouring places: according to Rufinus, book 10, the suburban districts; according to the Arabic version, generally "those which are around it." The Council of Constantinople, because it assigned the Church of Constantinople second place after Rome, earned little favour among the monarchists. Hence Onuphrius too, as anyone can see in his notes on Boniface III, was angry, and somewhat put out by the decree of the Council of Chalcedon, in which the Fathers "granted equal privileges to the most holy see of New Rome" [τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα ἀπένειμαν τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ τῆς νέας Ῥώμης], that is, Constantinople. The Council of Constantinople in Trullo, the Sixth, gave a similar ruling, for it wished both bishops to enjoy "equal privileges" [ἴσων ἀπολαυεῖν πρεσβείων]. As Anastasius also testifies in his life of John VII, the Quinisext Council of Constantinople in Trullo, in the year 692, "made certain chapters contrary to the Church of Rome." But what shall I say of the African councils? They likewise do not favour that succession of the Romans. Above all, the councils rejected the very thing in which the words of Cyprian quoted above were heard, and in which the Roman frauds were exposed in the appeal to the spurious canon of Nicaea; and, as had also happened elsewhere, appeals beyond the sea were condemned. Gratian makes a foolish remark here: "Unless perhaps they appealed to the Roman see", when it is plain that the decree was framed on account of the Roman see. But by what reasoning can these decrees of the councils be reconciled with the succession they claim in the papacy over the whole Church? We see, therefore, that such a universal prefecture, not believed for long, was at once opposed with every effort, and was at length somewhat established under the pretext of that succession, God permitting it for various causes, according to the predictions.

units.la: XLIII. Videndum paucis nunc restat, quo fundamento sive praetextu, quibus mediis & artibus ad talem totius Ecclesiae Pontificatum pervenerint.
units.tr: XLIII. It remains now to consider briefly on what foundation or pretext, and by what means and arts, they came to such a papacy over the whole Church.

units.la: An forte armis hic, ut decuisset, spiritualibus usi sunt tantum? An ex Scriptura desumptis? An sola locorum: Tu es Petrus &c. Tibi dabo Claves &c. Pasce oves meas; explicatione, & genuina pro successione illa in totius Ecclesiae Pontificatu sensus ad omnem conscientiam demonstratione? Neutiquam; Sed rarior in primis seculis horum verborum Christi, quae hodie instar panis quotidiani sunt, & successionis Petri in eum finem, fiebat mentio. Hinc Platina in Bonif. III. secutus in eo veteres, adductis jam
units.tr: Did they perhaps use only spiritual weapons here, as would have been fitting? Did they draw on Scripture? Or was it only by the explanation of the passages, "You are Peter, etc.", "I will give you the keys, etc.", "Feed my sheep", and by a genuine sense of those words supporting that succession in the papacy over the whole Church, demonstrated to every conscience? By no means. Indeed, in the earliest ages there was rarely any mention of those words of Christ, which today are like daily bread, nor of the succession of Peter to that end. Hence Platina, following the ancients in this, as he already has in the life of Boniface III,

units.la: Ostenditur, quo fundamento, sive praetextu, quibus mediis ad talem usurpationem venerint; nonnisi jam pro primatu Romano rationibus Politicis, demum subjurgit; Omitto, quòd Petrus &c. Hinc etiam Zosimus Papa, Africanis primatum suum in dubium vocantibus, non argumentis ex Scriptura occurrit, (quod simplicissimum fuisset, nec tam facilè difficilem in Orientem ad investigationem genuini exemplaris legationem necessariam reddere potuisset;) sed brevi Pseudo-Canonis Niceni allegatione iis imponere voluit. Aliis igitur viis ad istum, quem ab aliquot seculis usurpant, dominatum pervenerunt.
units.tr: It is shown on what foundation or pretext, and by what means, they came to such a usurpation. Only now, in defence of the Roman primacy, does he at last fall back on political reasons: "I omit that Peter, etc." Hence also Pope Zosimus, when the Africans called his primacy into question, did not meet them with arguments from Scripture (which would have been the simplest course, and would not have made it necessary to send a difficult embassy to the East to look for the genuine exemplar), but tried to impose upon them by a brief appeal to the spurious canon of Nicaea. They therefore reached this dominion, which they have claimed for some centuries, by other routes.

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Et primò quidem multùm ad primatum, primò ordinis tantùm, Episcopis Romanis acquirendum contulit politica urbis dignitas & authoritas. Nam religionis sedes Imperii atque armorum potentiam sequi consuevit, ut jam bis ex Guicciardino audivimus. Hinc Primatus, hinc de Primatu lites, hinc istæ tandem lacrymæ, hinc etiam aliæ sedes aliis prælatæ, Patriarchales &c. ut non ideò Patriarchales factæ sint, quemadmodum quidem Bellarminus contendit, quòd ibi Petrus docuerit, quot enim sic Patriarchales enumerandæ forent? Sed ob urbium dignitatem; Alexandria enim & Antiochia illustres in Imperio Romano Metropoles erant, hinc & tertius Antiochiæ locus, non primus, ob majorem Romæ & Alexandriæ Politicam dignitatem, hinc & Hierosolymæ, talibus prærogativis Politicis destitutæ, sedes illas prælatas esse, jam Dissert. I. innuimus. Nec ista diffitentur magis ingenui ex Pontificiis, Galli neutiquam, nec etiam ea, quæ de Roma jam jam dicturi sumus; Sed & narrant post veteres, hanc, consequendi Metropolitani dignitatem, rationem fuisse, quòd ostenderint Episcopi, urbes suas politicè Metropoles esse, aut, ut de novo fierent, ab Imperatoribus impetraverint. Igitur etiam in minoribus Ecclesiasticis prærogativis omnia ad similitudinem temporalium componere voluerunt. Id quod multò magis in maximis factum esse apparet. Cur enim Romæ primus locus competebat? Affirmabant Romani Pontifices, ita Platina l. c. urbem Romam, unde Constantinopolin Colonia deducta est, caput Imperii habendam esse, cùm etiam Graci ipsi literis suis Principem suum, (loquitur de illis, quæ post translationem Imperii acciderunt) τὸν ῥωμαίων αὐτοκράτορα, id est, Romanorum Imperatorem vocent, ipsíque Constantinopolitani, etiam atate nostra ῥωμαῖοι, non Graci vocentur; Et ob hanc Politicam dignitatem Concilia primum locum Romanæ, secundum Constantinopolitanæ sedi de tulerunt; Audiantur 630. Concilii Chalcedonensis Patres, qui Canone 28. testantur; Sedi Veteris Roma, quod urbs illa Imperatrix essèt, merito Patres Primatus dignitatem tribuisse, eademque ratione motos 150. Episcopos (Constantinopolitani primi Concilii) sedi Nova Roma parem primatus honorem attribuisse, consentaneum rationi judicantes, urbem & Regia & Senatu Imperii decoratam, pari etiam cum veteri Regia urbe honoris prærogativa fruentem, in rebus quoque Ecclesiasticis parem atque illa præeminentiam obtinere. Quid ex his discimus? interrogat Nilus Thessalonicensis de Primatu Papæ l. 2. Quidnam aliud, sibi respondet, quàm non ab Apostolis, sed à Patribus datum esse Papæ Primatum aliarum Ecclesiarum, & quidem idcirco, quod scilicet urbs Roma reliquis urbibus imperaret. Si vero, quia caput Imperii urbs illa erat, Primatum obtinet Papa, certè non eo nomine eum est consecutus, quòd sit Successor Petri. Similia etiam affert ex Novella 100. Justiniani. Et recte quoque Barlaam Monachus de Primatu Papæ c.3. Antea (nempe ante Imperatorum conversionem & Conciliorum Decreta) Romanum Episcopum, ut nec cæterorum quenquam, nec primum (nimirum constituto ordine, & latâ lege) fuisse, nec postremum. Qui & c. 4. ex eo, quòd Constantinus atque Justinianus, ut de re sui juris sic promulgârint; Sanctione; decernimus, ut Romanus Episcopus primus omnium Sacerdotum sit; argumentabatur, si Episcopus antea Romanus primus fuisset, orbisque terrarum Pastor à S. Petro constitutus, ista lege minimè opus fuisse, imò impietate sese obstrinxisse videri posse, si Petri potestatem seu jurisdictionem sibi arrogassent, quodque tot ille ante seculis sanxisset, id ipsi decernere præsumpsissent superciliosè.
units.tr: And first of all, the political dignity and authority of the city contributed much to the acquiring of primacy, at first of order only, for the Roman bishops. For "the seat of religion has commonly followed the power of the empire and of arms," as we have already heard twice from Guicciardini. Hence the primacy, hence the disputes about primacy, hence at last those tears; hence also other sees were preferred to others, the patriarchal sees and so on. They did not become patriarchal, as Bellarmine contends, because Peter taught there. For how many sees would then have to be counted as patriarchal in this way? Rather, it was on account of the dignity of the cities: Alexandria and Antioch were illustrious metropolises in the Roman Empire, hence Antioch's third place, not first, because of the greater political dignity of Rome and Alexandria; hence too Jerusalem, lacking such political prerogatives, was passed over, as we have already indicated in the First Dissertation. Nor do the more candid of the Papists deny these things, the French by no means, nor even what we are about to say concerning Rome. Rather, they too relate, following the ancients, that the reason for obtaining the dignity of metropolitan was that the bishops showed their cities to be politically metropolises, or obtained from the emperors that they should become so. Therefore they also wished to arrange even the lesser ecclesiastical prerogatives entirely on the model of temporal ones. This appears to have been done much more in the greatest matters. For why was the first place due to Rome? "The Roman pontiffs affirmed," so Platina says in the passage cited, "that the city of Rome, from which Constantinople was colonized, must be held as the head of the empire, since even the Greeks themselves in their writings call their prince" (he is speaking of what happened after the transfer of the empire) "the Roman emperor [τὸν Ῥωμαίων αὐτοκράτορα], that is, Emperor of the Romans, and the Constantinopolitans themselves, even in our own age, are called Romans, not Greeks." And because of this political dignity, the councils gave the first place to the Roman see and the second to the Constantinopolitan. Let the Fathers of the 630 Council of Chalcedon be heard, who testify in canon 28 that "the Fathers rightly granted primacy to the see of Old Rome, because that city was the imperial city; and that for the same reason the 150 bishops moved (of the first Council of Constantinople) attributed equal honour of primacy to the see of New Rome, judging it consistent with reason that the city, adorned with the royal seat and the senate of the empire, and enjoying an equal prerogative of honour with the old royal city, should also obtain equal pre-eminence in ecclesiastical affairs." What do we learn from this? asks Nilus of Thessalonica in his book on the primacy of the Pope, book 2. He answers himself: "What else, than that the primacy over the other churches was given to the Pope not by the Apostles, but by the Fathers, and indeed for this reason, namely that the city of Rome ruled the other cities. But if the Pope holds primacy because that city was the head of the empire, certainly he has not attained it on the ground that he is the successor of Peter." He also cites similar things from Justinian's Novella 100. And Barlaam the monk rightly says, in his book on the primacy of the Pope, chapter 3: "Previously" (that is, before the conversion of the emperors and the decrees of the councils) "the Roman bishop was neither first nor last among the others, by a fixed order and an established law." In chapter 4 he argues, from the fact that Constantine and Justinian, as they promulgated concerning a matter within their own right, declared in a sanction: "We decree that the Roman bishop shall be first of all priests," that "if the Roman bishop had been first before, and the pastor of the world constituted by St Peter, there would have been no need for that law, and indeed they could seem to have bound themselves in impiety, if they had arrogated to themselves the power or jurisdiction of Peter, and had presumed arrogantly to decree what he had ordained so many centuries before."

units.la: XLV. Porrò non parùm ambitionem posteriorum juvit zelus, probitas & Orthodoxia priorum, authoritati & amplitudini Urbis juncta. Illustre est Divi Pauli in Ep. ad Romanos elogium, de Romanorum fide quæ multùm crescebat posthac, ipso Sancto Apostolo eos oretenus docente, sic etiam fideli, comitum, & aliorum post gloriosum ejus excessum, ad urbem Dominam Evangelii propagandi causâ confluentium, operâ; Convertebantur sub Imperatoribus infidelibus multi ex Magnatibus, & Ecclesiæ illi aggregabantur, cui proin pacis tempore non tantùm optimè prosp.ctum, sed & facile fuit, aliorum necessitatibus varie providere & succurrere; Persecutionum vero tempore splendidam eam in fidelium oculis reddebat fusus illustrium Martyrum, etiam Episcoporum, sanguis. Tempore omni aulæ & urbis magnificentia exteris etiam innotescebat; Dum statu imminente, sive felici, sive infelici, Ecclesias quodam-modo modo edocere poterat;Felix etiam status, nonnunquam, & ex parte,Magnatum in illa fidem profitentium, authoritati & apud Imperatores gratiæ tribuebatur;Sic & quandoque illorum intercessionibus, & Episcoporum ac fidelium cæterorum defensionibus & excusationibus infelicis statûs terminatio ; Orthodoxiam diu sanctè custodiebant, & ortis,in Oriente maximè, hæresibus,consulti ad earum extirpationem multum conferre poterant,sic & in aliis extra partes constituti, & utrâque, ut fieri solet, tertiam in suam sententiam perducere omnibus modis allaborante;Accedebat etiam de illustri per Apostolos,Paulum & Petrum fundatione, quamvis non æquè certa persuasio; Et hinc non potuit non magna esse, & crescere hujus Ecclesiæ authoritas, hinc illi data multa illustria,quæ apud Patres occurrunt, elogia,hinc nonnunquam inter partes litigantes judicium ei delatum fuit, hinc ab aliis damnati sæpè ad illam,ut partim rationibus, partim authoritatibus,partim intercessionibus juventur, confugiebant.
units.tr: XLV. Moreover, the zeal, uprightness and orthodoxy of the earlier Romans, joined to the authority and greatness of the city, helped the ambition of later generations no little. Famous is the praise of the Divine Paul in his Epistle to the Romans, concerning the faith of the Romans, which greatly increased afterwards, the holy Apostle himself teaching them by word of mouth; and likewise through the labour of his companions and others who flocked to the city, the Lady of the Gospel, for the purpose of spreading the Gospel, after his glorious departure. Under unbelieving emperors many of the great men were converted and joined that Church. In time of peace it was not only well situated but also easily able to provide for and help the needs of others in various ways. In time of persecution, the flowing blood of illustrious martyrs, even bishops, made it splendid in the eyes of the faithful. At all times the magnificence of the court and city became known even to foreigners, since it could in some measure instruct the Churches in the imminent state of affairs, whether prosperous or unprosperous. A prosperous state also sometimes, and in part, was attributed to the authority and favour with the emperors of the great men who professed the faith in it. So too, at times, by their intercession, and by the defences and excuses of the bishops and other faithful, an unhappy state came to an end. They kept orthodoxy holy for a long time, and when heresies arose, chiefly in the East, they could contribute much by counsel to their extirpation. So also those placed in other parts, and each (as usually happens) labouring by every means to bring the third party into its own opinion. There was also the belief, not equally certain, about the famous foundation by the Apostles Paul and Peter. Hence the authority of this Church could not but be great and grow; hence many illustrious praises were given to it that occur among the Fathers; hence sometimes judgment between litigating parties was referred to it; hence others, condemned, often fled to it, to be aided partly by arguments, partly by authorities, partly by intercessions.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Sed paulatim bono semini inspersa sunt ambitionis zizania,cœlo sub infidelibus sereno aliquando, quando & aliarum Ecclesiarum simplicitas,humilitas & probitas,juxta Patrum querelas, multùm defecerunt, ut Deus sæpè jacentem fidem, sunt verba Cypriani, & penè dormientem cœlesti censurâ erigere opus habuerit: Maximè etiam,postquam ipsi etiam Imperatores Christo sua nomina dedissent, venenum in Ecclesiam effusum est, tunc incipiebant alii magis, alii minùs (bonis nonnunquam etiam haud malo animo authoritatem sedis suæ plùs æquo promovere studentibus, & humani multùm patientibus;) elogiis superbire,quibus indics indigniores reddebantur; Successionem illustrium Antecessorum jactare, à quorum virtutibus magis magisque degenerabant ; De Martyrum victoriis triumphare, dum ipsi ab ambitione & dominandi libidine pederentim,& quidem in ipsarum victoriarum spiritualium consideratione turpiter se vinci patiebantur; Salvâ adhuc orthodoxiâ charitatis naufragium facere, leviter etiam dissentientibus graves esse, primam non manifeste errandi felicitatem quasi in argumentum necessariæ infallibilitatis trahere, ex prærogativis gratiætela luxuriæ & ambitionis instrumenta formare;nucleoChristianismi neglecto, religionem ad splendorem mundanum componere, hinc superstitioni inservire,ad superstitionem tuendam & augendam etiam dogmata immutare,omnia ad regnum aliquod Politico-Ecclesiasticum fundandum disponere. XLVII. Sed ad hoc præcipuè regiminis mutatione, de qua etiam nunc agimus, opus fuit, hinc elogia antecessoribus & sibi data non tantum in omni emphasi ipsi accipiebant, sed & aliis inculcabant, & eorum augmentum quærebant, facta strenuè in jus, voluntarium in necessarium, maximè quoad appellationes & postulata consilia, commutabant, quosvis fugientes ad se facilè recipiebant, & illis, patrocinio suo animum & aliis addituri, Absolonis corda Israëlitarum ita furantis adinstar, aderant, ultrò se etiam litibus decidendis ingerebant, se apud multos necessarios reddere studebant, inferioribus quasi injustæ dominationis odio, sed revera, ut cuilibet adversarius in promtu sit, & omnia sibi accepta ferantur, & multi sibi devinciantur, contra potentiores suppetias ferebant, multis tanquam Vicariis suis, quæ jure proprio habere potuissent, concedebant, & rursus illorum jurisdictioni alios pro lubitu subducebant; testante de utroque Doctissimo Mezeraeo, illius etiam exemplum præbente in Archiepiscopo Rhemensi, cui, ne pergeret independentiam suam quoad septem provincias asserere, Vicariatum septendecim provinciarum dederunt ; Et ainsi il tenoit d'eux à titre de precaire, ce qu'il eut pû tenir de son chef, & cette superiorité, que son siege lui donnoit sur les 7. provinces, fut absorbée par celle, qu'ils luy donnerent sur toutes les dix sept. Hujus autem respectu ait, eos appellationes ita deamâsse, ut gratiosè receperint etiam à Vicariis suis condemnatos, & à prædecessoribus suis injustitia & scelerum accusatos. Sic omnibus modis extra territorium suum jus dicebant.
units.tr: But gradually the tares of ambition were sown among the good seed. Sometimes the sky was clear for the unbelievers, when the simplicity, humility and integrity of the other Churches, according to the complaints of the Fathers, had greatly declined, so that God often had to raise up the faith lying prostrate, in Cyprian's words, and almost sleeping, by heavenly censure. This was especially so after the emperors themselves had given their names to Christ, for poison was poured into the Church. Then some began, more or less, (some good men, sometimes not with a bad mind, striving to advance the authority of their see beyond measure, and very tolerant of human weakness) to take pride in titles, by which they became less worthy of them. They boasted of the succession of illustrious predecessors, from whose virtues they increasingly degenerated. They triumphed over the victories of the martyrs, while they themselves were gradually overcome by ambition and lust for domination, and indeed in considering those spiritual victories they let themselves be shamefully defeated. While orthodoxy was still intact, they suffered shipwreck of charity, and were harsh even toward those who dissented slightly. They drew the first happy fact of not manifestly erring into an argument for necessary infallibility. From the prerogatives of grace they formed instruments of luxury and ambition. With the kernel of Christianity neglected, they arranged religion for worldly splendour, and so served superstition; to defend and increase superstition they even changed doctrines; they arranged everything to found some politico-ecclesiastical kingdom. XLVII. But this above all required a change of government, which is also what we are now discussing. Hence they not only accepted for themselves, with every show of emphasis, the praises given to their predecessors and to themselves, but also pressed them on others and sought their increase. They changed what was voluntary into what was required by law, especially in matters of appeals and petitions and counsels. They readily received whoever fled to them, and, adding their patronage to the minds of others, they were present, after the manner of Absalom stealing the hearts of Israel. They even forced themselves on others to decide disputes and strove to make themselves necessary to many. As if from hatred of unjust domination toward their inferiors, but in truth so that an adversary might always be at hand, all things be credited to them, and many be bound to them, they gave aid against the more powerful. To many they granted, as their vicars, what those men could have held by their own right, and again they withdrew others from their jurisdiction at will. Of both things the most learned Mezeray is witness, and he gives an example in the Archbishop of Rheims, to whom, lest he continue to assert his independence over seven provinces, they gave the vicariate of seventeen provinces. And so he held of them by a precarious title what he could have held in his own right, and that superiority which his see gave him over the seven provinces was absorbed by the one they gave him over all seventeen. Regarding this, he says that they so loved appeals that they gladly received even those condemned by their own vicars, and those accused of injustice and crimes by their predecessors. Thus in every way they gave judgment outside their own territory.

units.la: XLVIII. Valdè etiam eos juvabat, occasiones quasvis captantes, regiminis Politici per aliquot secula constitutio; Primò quidem translatio sedis Imperatoriæ; Quamvis enim ab una parte quadantenus nocitura videbatur, dum nimirum sic Patriarchis Constantinopolitanis ex præsentia Imperatorum, quam Romani antè habuerant, & Ravennensibus, ubi postmodum Exarchi tanquam Vice-Imperatores residebant, spiritus & animi creverunt, & argumentum ab urbis prærogativis ex parte ereptum, & illis necessitas, in posterum alio armorum genere, hactenus minus usitato, nempe trito illo: Tu es Petrus; magis utendi, imposita fuit; Interim tamen plus commodi ab altera, quàm verò incommodi ab hac parte habere deprehendebantur. Sic enim ὁ κατέχων, ille qui retinebat, 2.Thess.II. Imperator, cujus continua præsentia erectioni talis regni obesse potuisset aliquâ ratione, tanquam severus quidam dam Pædagogus amotus, Pontificibus autem facilius fuit, magnam sibi Romæ,in Italia,imò per totum ferè Occidentem,authoritatem comparare,tandem etiam partem sibi quasi temporali jure subjicere ; Imperatoribus interea temporis in Oriente impeditis, Barbarorum continuis ferè incursionibus & aliis bellis,ac intestinis etiam tumultibus freqventioribus ab Occidente quasi avulsis, & in eo sæpissimè statu positis,ut ad Occidentis reliquiarum conservationem ipsis Pontificum amicitiâ valdè opus fuerit,hinc plurima etiam in illorum gratiam fecerint, dum contrà suâ Tyrannide & ipso Imperii decremento, & errorum violentiâ Patriarcharum Constantinopolitanorum fastus , haud parùm depressus fuit, & multò magis Patriarchæ reliqui non tantùm tantis prærogativarum temporalium ornamentis,quarum præsentiam aut absentiam Ecclesiastico primatui multùm profuisse,aut obfuisse,jam aliquoties notavimus,nudati manserunt, sed & tandem, postquam diu satis illorum Diœceses modò huc, modò illuc inclinantis belli sedes fuissent,in potestatem infidelium pervenerunt; Romanis contrà authoritatem suam , auxiliante etiam superstitione, & crescente ignorantiâ ad eum gradum perducentibus, ut variè illud: Do, ut des; exercere, Occidentis Regibus, Pipinis maximè & Carolis, liberalitatem ex alieno, deposito etiam Childerico, ostendere potuerint, ἀντιδωρεῖν vicissim recipientes pretiosissima, ut Calvinus Inst. c.8. §. 122. loquitur, quemadmodum prædones commune spolium solent partiendo diripere, juxta Sigonii, de Regno Italiæ. l.2. verba autem,rebus pro Ecclesiæ salute & sedis Apostolicæ authoritate non tam piè, quàm prosperè gestis. Imò tandem planè se & simul etiam universam Italiam ab Imperatorum Constantinopolitanorum, quos excommunicare ob Iconomachiam ausi sunt, obedientia subducebant, & à Francis non semel defensi ipsis Imperii Occidentalis possessionem suo etiam calculo confirmabant, statim tamen etiam his defensoribus, & in dignitate Imperatoria Successoribus graves, donec renunciatione jurium, confirmationis Pontificiæ, Investituræ Episcoporum, possessionis Romæ & Italiæ,aliorúmque,nec non concessione,ut Papa omnia pro lubitu ageret,imò etiam juramento ad Papæ defensionem jurari solito, quietem sibi post aliquot seculorum continuos ferè ex resistentia ortos tumultus,seditiones,multiplices excommunicationes, depositiones, variásque contumelias alias,emerunt,& potestatem suam ad augmentum potestatis Pontificiæ, sciæ, & omnium subjectionem impendere cœperunt; Tanta molis erat Romanam condere gentem! Et per tot casus, per tot discrimina rerum ad successionem Petri in tali Pontificatu totius Ecclesiæ ventum est! Nec tamen plane perventum, cùm Ecclesiæ pars non exigua semper Pontificatum hunc supremum rejecerit, & inter eos etiam populos, qui admiserant, Doctissimi Viri reclamantes nunquam defuerint, & maximè à tempore Reformationis futilis iste successionis prætextus examinetur, quem quasi solum sufficere arbitrantur, qui nobis persuadere volunt, succedere Petro Episcopos Romanos in Monarchia, quia ista de se prædicant; Cui ineptæ quidem argumentationi hactenus occurrere, & eâ occasione breve compendium quasi historiæ hujus successionis, vel potiùs auctarum præsumtionum, dare visum fuit.
units.tr: XLVIII. The constitution of the political government over several centuries also greatly helped them, as they seized on any occasion. First, there was the transfer of the imperial seat. Although on one side it seemed likely to do some harm, since the Patriarchs of Constantinople, from the presence of the emperors that the Romans had had before, and the Ravennese, where afterwards the exarchs resided as vice-emperors, grew in spirit and courage, and the argument drawn from the city's prerogatives was partly taken away from them, and they were compelled to use a different kind of weapon, hitherto less common, namely that familiar one: You are Peter. Nevertheless, they were found to gain more advantage from the one side than harm from the other. For thus ὁ κατέχων [ho katechōn], the one who restrains, 2 Thess. 2, the emperor, whose continual presence could in some way have hindered the erection of such a kingdom, was removed like a stern schoolmaster. It was easier for the Pontiffs to acquire great authority for themselves at Rome, in Italy, and indeed through almost all the West, and finally to bring a part under themselves as if by a temporal right. Meanwhile the emperors were hindered in the East by almost continuous incursions of barbarians and other wars, and by more frequent internal tumults, and they were, as it were, torn away from the West and placed in that state so often that they greatly needed the friendship of the Pontiffs to preserve the remnants of the West. Hence they made many concessions for the sake of the Pontiffs. Meanwhile, by their own tyranny and the very decline of the empire, and by the violence of errors, the pride of the Patriarchs of Constantinople was not a little humbled. The other Patriarchs were stripped not only of such temporal prerogative ornaments, whose presence or absence, as we have noted several times already, had greatly helped or harmed the ecclesiastical primacy, but finally, after their dioceses had for a long time been the seats of a war that swung this way and that, they fell into the power of unbelievers. The Romans, on the other hand, with superstition helping and ignorance growing, brought their authority to such a degree that they could, in various ways, practise the principle I give, that you may give, and show the liberality of others to the kings of the West, above all to the Pepins and Charleses, even after Childeric had been deposed. Receiving most precious things in return, [antidōrein], as Calvin says in Institutes ch. 8, §122, as robbers are wont to share and tear apart common plunder; according to Sigonius, On the Kingdom of Italy, book 2, in words about things done not so much piously as successfully for the salvation of the Church and the authority of the Apostolic See. Indeed, at last they fully withdrew themselves and at the same time all Italy from the obedience of the emperors of Constantinople, whom they dared to excommunicate over the Iconoclasm. They were defended more than once by the Franks, and they confirmed by their own reckoning the possession of the Western Empire. Yet immediately afterwards they were burdensome even to these defenders and to the successors in the imperial dignity, until, by the renunciation of rights, the papal confirmation, the investiture of bishops, the possession of Rome and Italy, and other things, and also by the grant that the Pope might do everything at his pleasure, and even by the oath customarily sworn to defend the Pope, they bought quiet for themselves after nearly continuous tumults, seditions, manifold excommunications, deprivations, and various other insults, arising from resistance over several centuries. They began to devote their power to increasing papal power, and to the subjection of all. So great a labour it was to found the Roman race! And through so many chances, through so many crises of affairs, they came to the succession of Peter in such a Pontificate over the whole Church! Yet they did not fully arrive there, since no small part of the Church has always rejected this supreme Pontificate, and among those peoples who had admitted it, most learned men have never been lacking to protest. And especially since the time of the Reformation, this futile pretext of succession, which they think is enough by itself, is examined: the pretext by which those who want to persuade us that the Roman bishops succeed Peter in the monarchy, because they themselves claim such things for themselves. To this foolish argument it has seemed fit to reply so far, and on that occasion to give a brief compendium, as it were, of the history of this succession, or rather of the increasing presumptions.

units.la: XLIX. Sed esto rursus, argumentationem non ineptam, sed bonam, imò optimam fuisse, & Episcopos Romanos Petro in suprema potestate succedere debuisse; quid autem de successione posteriorum Episcoporum Romanorum prioribus usque adeò dissimilium dicendum erit? Utinam essent Petri Successores in omnibus, loquor cum Stephano Wintoniensi Episcopo Anglo, ex oratione ejus, de vera obedientia; quo casu præessent omnibus non dubito, si non eminentiâ potestatis externa, cujusmodi haud dubiè nullam habet, certè admiratione ac ratione interna virtutis, quo nomine etiam ipsis Imperatoribus voluit Christus suos prælucere, ac primatum obtinere. Utpote quibus tanquam legatione pro se fungentibus claves etiam tradidit regni cœlorum; & in iis Petro, qui omnium nomine confessionem primus emiserat tam salutarem, ut Jesum agnosceret Filium Dei vivi. Quam quidem confessionem, ut caro & sanguis non revelârat, ita nec carni in Petro, aut sanguini data est prærogativa, quæcunque data est, sed potiori ejus parti, qui Spiritus erat, nimirum ut uberiore gratiâ in Deo donatus, in virtute ac verbi Dei potentia, regendorúmque affectuum potestate primatum obtineret &c.
units.tr: XLIX. But grant again that the argument was not foolish but good, indeed the best, and that the Roman bishops ought to have succeeded Peter in supreme power. What then must be said of the succession of the later Roman bishops, who are so unlike the earlier ones? Would that they were Peter's successors in all things, I speak with Stephen, Bishop of Winchester, an Englishman, from his oration on true obedience; in which case I do not doubt that they would be over all, if not by external eminence of power, of which they certainly have none, then certainly by the admiration and internal reason of virtue, for which name Christ also wished his own to shine before even the emperors and to obtain the primacy. For to them, as those acting on his behalf by commission, he also gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and among them to Peter, who on behalf of all had first made so saving a confession, that he acknowledged Jesus as the Son of the living God. Indeed, as flesh and blood had not revealed that confession, so neither was the prerogative, whatever it was, given to flesh in Peter, or to blood, but to the better part of him, which was Spirit, namely that he, endowed by God with richer grace, might obtain the primacy in the power of God's virtue and Word, and in the power of governing the affections, etc.

units.la: L. Triplex recensetur in dignitatibus Ecclesiasticis successio. 1. Officii. 2. Doctrinæ. 3. Loci. Videamus circa hæc tria successionis genera paucis, (de successione in sanctitate, quæ in multis pessima, nulla planè fuit, nihil dicturi, cujus tamen occasionem aliquam post habebimus;) quid sibi vendicare possint Episcopi Romani jam ab aliquot seculis, respectu ad Petrum habito. Non succedere eos in officio Petri, ex hactenus dictis liquidò patet, & eos longè alia quasi ex officio facere velle & facere, quàm quæ Petro ex officio incubuerint, quae ille ex officio fecerit. In doctrina Petri, saltem circa Primatum & dominatum suum & Petri, eos cum ipso Petro, Christo & Apostolis plane non consentire, sed contrarium docere, adeoque in ea doctrina, id est, juxta Bellarminianum illud ab initio tractationis nostrae allatum, in summa rei Christianae, Petro non succedere, pariter manifestum fecimus. Sed & in multis aliis, iisque praecipuis fidei Christianae articulis eos a fide Petri defecisse, & ἐπροδιδασκαλῶν, a nostris quotidie ostenditur; Sed nos jam illud non agimus. Constat igitur, Pontifices ultimorum Seculorum ista duo successionum genera essentialia & plane necessaria respectu Petri sibi tribuere non posse, ut jam solum restet dispiciendum, quid ex successione locali (si quidem illa certa praesupponatur post tot in contrarium persuasiones,) sibi promittere possint.
units.tr: L. Three kinds of succession are recognised in ecclesiastical offices: 1. of office, 2. of doctrine, 3. of place. Let us briefly consider these three kinds of succession (I will say nothing about succession in holiness, which in many cases was very bad and in fact was entirely absent, though I shall come back to it later), and ask what the Roman Bishops have claimed for themselves for some centuries now, with respect to Peter. That they do not succeed Peter in his office is clear from what has been said so far. They wish, and do, to perform as if from office many things quite different from those which Peter was bound to do by his office, and which he did. In Peter's doctrine, at least concerning his primacy and his lordship, and Peter's own, they plainly do not agree with Peter, Christ and the Apostles, but teach the opposite. Therefore, in that doctrine, that is, according to the saying of Bellarmine brought forward at the beginning of our treatment, in the sum of the Christian religion, I have likewise shown that they do not succeed Peter. But that they have departed from the faith of Peter in many other, and those chief, articles of the Christian faith, and are [ἐπροδιδασκαλῶν] traitorous teachers, is shown by us every day. Yet we are not now doing that. It is therefore established that the Pontiffs of the latest centuries cannot claim for themselves these two essential and altogether necessary kinds of succession with respect to Peter. So there remains only to examine what they can promise themselves from succession of place (supposing that it is certain, after so many persuasions to the contrary).

units.la: LI.
units.tr: LI.

units.la: Successio localis reliquis successionis generibus juncta quandoque est utilis, & maxime olim fuit contra Scripturae aut doctrinae adulteratores haereticos, quando adhuc ipsa Scripturarum Apostolicarum autographa asservabantur, in iis Ecclesiis, ad quas Scripturae illae missae, vel apud quas depositae erant. Utilis etiam erat contra novorum dogmatum fabricatores, quamdiu palam in illis Ecclesiis illibata permansit doctrinae ab Apostolicis acceptae praedicatio & professio. Quae utilitas hodieque aliquo modo durat, nempe intuitu primorum illorum Seculorum, quorum doctrina & successio utiliter opponuntur citeriorum temporum novitatibus; Serviit etiam olim Orthodoxorum Episcoporum successio adversus Schismaticos alieni muneris usurpatores; Hinc aliquando Patres ad eam provocasse leguntur.
units.tr: Succession of place, joined with the other kinds of succession, is sometimes useful, and was especially useful of old against heretical corrupters of Scripture or of doctrine, when the very autographs of the apostolic Scriptures were still preserved in those Churches to which those Scriptures had been sent, or with which they had been deposited. It was also useful against the forgers of new dogmas, so long as in those Churches the preaching and profession of the doctrine received from the Apostles remained openly unimpaired. This usefulness still lasts in some measure even today, namely with regard to those first centuries, whose doctrine and succession are usefully set against the novelties of later times. The succession of orthodox bishops also once served against schismatics, usurpers of an office not their own; hence we read that the Fathers sometimes appealed to it.

units.la: LII.
units.tr: LII.

units.la: Sed ut non est plane & omni tempore necessaria, id est, ut in eodem loco semper Episcopi sint, non requiritur, quando nunc veri adoratores Patrem, non in certo loco, sed in spiritu & veritate adorant, Joh. IV. 21. 23. 24. & ubi duo aut tres in nomine Christi congregati sunt, ibi in illorum medio est, Matth. XVIII. 20. & mandatum ab ipso: quum persequentur vos in civitate ista, fugite in aliam, Matth. X. 23. & angelo Ephesino comminatio de movendo candelabro Ap. II. 5. 7. communicata fuit, adeoque Ecclesia N. T. nulli particulari civitati, regioni aut gnti alligata est, & ad exemplum multarum Ecclesiarum in Asia, Europa & Africa, ab ipsis Apostolis etiam plantatarum in multis locis Episcoporum successio interrumpi, vel desinere potest, quod & Romae tandem eventurum Pontificii multi afferunt; ita sola inutilis & fallax, iisdem Patribus testibus, est.
units.tr: But although it is not absolutely and at all times necessary, that is, that bishops always be in the same place, it is not required, since now true worshippers worship the Father, not in a certain place, but in spirit and in truth (John 4:21, 23, 24), and where two or three are gathered together in the name of Christ, there he is in the midst of them (Matt. 18:20), and the command from him: when they persecute you in this city, flee into another (Matt. 10:23), and the threat to the Ephesian angel about moving the candlestick (Rev. 2:5, 7) were given. Thus the Church of the New Testament is bound to no particular city, region or nation, and, after the example of many Churches in Asia, Europe and Africa, which were planted by the Apostles themselves, the succession of bishops in many places can be, or has ceased to be, interrupted, which many Papists also assert will one day happen at Rome. So succession of place is, by the testimony of the same Fathers, useless and deceptive alone.

units.la: LIII. Et cumprimis quoad hoc gravia & memoratu digna sunt Hilarii in fine lib. contra Arianos & Auxentium Mediolanensem verba: Unum moneo, inquit, cavete Anti-Christum, male enim vos parietum amor cepit, male Ecclesiam Dei in tectis, adificiisque veneramini, male sub his pacis nomen ingeritis. Anne ambiguum est, in his Anti-Christum sessurum? Montes, mihi & sylva, & lacus, & carceres, & voragines sunt tutiores, in his enim Prophetae aut manentes, aut demersi Spiritu Dei prophetabant. Absistite ab Auxentio Satana angelo, hoste Christi &c. Cui etiam concinit Chrysostomus Homil.33. in Joh.IV. 21. propter locum nulla debet deinceps contentio esse, inquit. Sic quoque in v.23. illos veros adoratores vocat, qui loco divinum cultum non circumscribunt, sed Deum in Spiritu colunt. Etherius autem & Beatus l.1. contra Elipand. in Biblioth. Patr. T.4. non lapidibus consistere Ecclesiam, sed dogmatum veritate, inquiunt. Similiter, Gregorio Nazianzeno Orat.21. in laudem Athanasii teste, Qui eandem doctrinam profitetur, ejusdem quoque throni socius est; qui autem contrariam sententiam profitetur, adversarius quoque quoad thronum censeri debet. Atque hac quidem nomen, illa vero rem ipsam & veritatem habet successionis. Et paulo post, neque qui contraria dogmata tenet, sed qui ejusdem est fidei, Successor ei habendus est. Digna non minus sunt, quae hic exscribantur verba Juris Canonici Dist.49. Non sanctorum filii sunt, qui tenent loca sanctorum; non cathedra facit Sacerdotem, sed Sacerdos Cathedram; non locus sanctificat hominem, sed homo locum; non omnis Sacerdos sanctus, sed omnis sanctus est Sacerdos: qui bene sedet super Cathedram, honorem accipit Cathedra, qui male sederit, injuriam facit Cathedra. Claudat Tertulliani quaestio prascr. adv. haret. Ex personis probamus fidem? An ex fide personas? Quo posterius illud praefert.
units.tr: LIII. And especially in this matter the words of Hilary at the end of his book against the Arians and Auxentius of Milan are weighty and worthy of mention: I give one warning, he says, beware of Antichrist.
