For the love of walls has taken hold of you badly, you revere the Church of God badly in roofs and buildings, you badly bring the name of peace under these things. Is it doubtful that Antichrist will sit in these? For me, mountains, and woods, and lakes, and prisons, and chasms are safer; for in these the prophets, either remaining or sunk down, prophesied by the Spirit of God. Keep away from Auxentius, the Satan-angel, the enemy of Christ, etc. Chrysostom also agrees with this, in his thirty-third homily on John 4:21: because of the place there ought to be no contention from now on, he says. Likewise, on verse 23, he calls those true worshippers who do not confine divine worship to a place, but worship God in Spirit. Etherius and Beatus, in book 1 against Elipandus (in the Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 4), say that the Church does not consist in stones, but in the truth of doctrine. Similarly, according to Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration 21 in praise of Athanasius: He who professes the same doctrine is also a partner in the same throne; but he who professes the contrary opinion ought to be counted an adversary also as regards the throne. The first has the name of succession, but the second has the thing itself and the truth. And a little later: not he who holds contrary doctrines, but he who is of the same faith, is to be regarded as his successor. No less worthy of being copied out here are the words of the Canon Law, Dist. 49: Those who hold the places of the saints are not sons of the saints; the chair does not make the priest, but the priest the chair; the place does not sanctify the man, but the man the place; not every priest is holy, but every holy man is a priest. He who sits well upon the chair receives honour from the chair; he who sits badly does injury to the chair. Tertullian's question in the Prescription against Heretics settles it: Do we prove the faith from persons, or persons from the faith? The latter is to be preferred.

units.la: LIV. Et certe nemo ignorat, non tantum bonos Episcopos, sed & lupos rapaces Act.XX.29. & docentes perversa v.20. & falsos doctores, 2.Pet.II.1. Paulo & Petro succesisse: Nemo ignorat, vel Monarchicis testibus, saltem in plerisque Orientis locis schismaticos, imo haereticos, imo Turcas respectu loci successisse. Nemo ignorat, virtutum nomina vitiis imponi posse & solere, & mutato statu saepe antiquum nomen retineri, cum, Tacito judice, arcanum novi statûs sit nomen antiqui, quod secundùm prædictiones, etiam respectu Anti-Christi accidere non tantùm potuit, sed etiam debuit, quia ille sessurus erat in Templo Dei, & habiturus cornua agni. Nemo etiam ignorat, in natura quoque tenebras luci, tempestatem tranquillitati, mentis alienationem prudentiæ, morbum sanitati, mortem vitæ, hyemem æstati, contraria alia aliis succedere. Ut Pontificii, si aliquid ex successione lucrari velint, successionem doctrinæ, quod in æternum non præstabunt, simul ostendere teneantur. Non enim habent, verba sunt Augustini, l.1. de pœnit. c. 6. Petri hæreditatem, qui fidem Petri non habent. Et fatente Gretsero in defens. Bellarm. l.4. de verbo Dei. c.8. Sine veritate doctrinæ successio pastorum exigui est ponderis. Sine qua Papam Barlaam Monachus de Primatu Papæ cap. 13. Petri successorem dixit, ut sit morbus sanitatis &c. Et qui claves regni cœlorum gerat, non illas, quæ aperiant, sed quæ claudant, nec eorum cuiquam, qui ipsum sequuntur, introire permittant. Nec male supra laudatus Episcopus Wintoniensis, loc. cit. officii maximè respectu dixit: Primus ante alios doceat & prædicet Christum Episcopus Romanus, & tantisper ante alios obtineat ejus functionis primatum. Quàm verò illud ridiculum, ut multis in stadio currentibus, unus quispiam à spectatoribus magno cum ambitu cupiat impetrare, ut ipse ad currendum quidem inter cæteros designatus, cùm jam aut culpâ suâ claudus, aut aliter ad cursum ineptus factus sit, alios tamen omnes etiam tum cursu antevertisse, ac primus omnium metam attigisse dicatur, quum, præterquam quòd vestitu ad cursum adposito prodierit, sederit interim inter spectatores otiosus, nullam aliam precum suarum rationem afferens, quàm quòd ab iis (si diis placet) ortus & prognatus sit, qui olim optimi cursores, atque ideò primi sunt appellati. LV: Atque ita absolvimus consideRationem Electionis Pontificum Romanorum, quatenus per eam Petro succedere dicuntur; absolvimus tractationem, quæ est de constitutione, quam prætendunt, remotiori Romanorum Pontificum, ceu universæ Ecclesiæ Rectorum. In sequentibus constitutio propior & specialior examinanda erit, & videndum, quando, ut hactenus ostendimus, Petrum in Monarchia Ecclesiæ prædecessorem non habent, nec etiam propiorem aliis ad eum relationem, utrum igitur saltem ex propria constitutione & electione Episcopi Romani pro Monarchis Ecclesiæ agnosci possint, vel annon ipsa illa electio Monarchiæ illorum prætextum falsitatis variè convincat, & corruptionis tandem dem secutæ maximæ certissima indicia suppeditet? Quæ eo ordine pertractabimus, ut primò de diversis Electionum Pontificum Romanorum formis; Secundò de multiplicibus nævis ac vitiis; Tertiò de ejusdem consequentibus proximis acturi simus. Quam divisionem tractationis reliquæ non eo animo instituimus, qui formas & consequentia Electionis ipsa nævis & vitiis carere credat, contrà probabimus, ipsas formas & Electionis consequentia, constitutioni Monarcharum Ecclesiæ universæ minùs convenire, & nævis vitiisque suis laborare, sed ideò tantùm, quia in formis & consequentibus nævi & vitia indirectè tantùm & remotiùs apparent, cùm contrà nævi & vitia illa, de quibus distinctè acturi sumus, pro talibus primo intuitu agnoscantur.
units.tr: LIV. And surely no one is unaware that not only good bishops, but also ravening wolves (Acts 20:29), teaching perverse things (v. 30) and false teachers (2 Pet. 2:1), have succeeded Paul and Peter. No one is unaware, even by the testimony of the Monarchists, that in most places of the East schismatics, indeed heretics, indeed Turks, have succeeded in respect of place. No one is unaware that the names of virtues can be and usually are imposed upon vices, and that, when the state has changed, the old name is often retained, since, in the judgement of Tacitus, the name of the old state is the secret of the new. This, according to the predictions, could not only happen, but must happen, even with respect to Antichrist, because he was to sit in the Temple of God and have the horns of a lamb. Nor is anyone unaware that in nature too darkness succeeds light, storm succeeds calm, madness succeeds prudence, sickness succeeds health, death succeeds life, winter succeeds summer, and other contraries succeed other things. So the Papists, if they wish to gain anything from succession, are bound at the same time to show succession of doctrine, which they will never provide. For they do not have the inheritance of Peter, these are Augustine's words (book 1 on repentance, ch. 6), who do not have the faith of Peter. And, as Gretser admits in his defence of Bellarmine, book 4 on the Word of God, ch. 8: Without the truth of doctrine, the succession of ministers is of little weight. Without it, the monk Barlaam, in his On the Primacy of the Pope, ch. 13, called the Pope the successor of Peter, so that he is the disease of health, etc. And he who bears the keys of the kingdom of heaven should not hold those which open, but those which shut, and should not allow any of those who follow him to enter. Nor did the above-mentioned Bishop of Winchester speak badly, loc. cit., chiefly with respect to office: The Bishop of Rome should first, before the others, teach and preach Christ, and so long hold the primacy of that function before the others. But how ridiculous it is, when many are running in a race, that one of the spectators should with great ambition desire to obtain that he, though designated to run among the rest, yet, since he has either through his own fault become lame or otherwise unfit for the course, should nevertheless be said to have outrun all the others and to have reached the goal first of all, when, besides having come out dressed for the race, he has meanwhile sat idle among the spectators, giving no other reason for his prayers than that he is (if it pleases the gods) sprung and descended from those who were once the best runners and therefore called the first. LV: Thus we have finished the consideration of the election of the Roman Pontiffs, insofar as they are said to succeed Peter through it. We have finished the treatment of the more remote constitution, which they put forward, of the Roman Pontiffs as rulers of the whole Church. In what follows, the nearer and more specific constitution will be examined, and it must be seen whether, as we have shown so far, they have no predecessor in the Monarchy of the Church, nor even a closer relation to him than others; whether, therefore, the Bishop of Rome can at least be acknowledged as Monarch of the Church on the strength of his own constitution and election alone, or whether that very election variously convicts their claim to monarchy of falsehood and provides the most certain signs of the corruption that followed. We shall treat these matters in this order: first, the diverse forms of the elections of the Roman Pontiffs; second, their many blemishes and vices; third, their immediate consequences. We have not made this division of the rest of the treatment in the mind of one who believes that the forms and consequences of the election are free from blemishes and vices. On the contrary, we shall prove that the forms themselves and the consequences of the election agree less with the constitution of the Monarchs of the whole Church, and suffer from their own blemishes and vices; but this only because blemishes and vices appear in the forms and consequences only indirectly and more remotely, whereas those blemishes and vices of which we shall treat distinctly are recognised as such at first sight.

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS QUARTÆ, In qua De diversis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum formis agitur,
units.tr: DISSERTATION FOURTH, In which the various forms of the election of the Roman Pontiffs are discussed

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA, In qua Post generales ad Formas Electionum annotationes de tribus primis Electionum Formis per Prædecessores, per Clerum & Populum, & per Imperatores agitur; Breviarium.
units.tr: FIRST SECTION, In which, after general remarks on the forms of elections, the three earliest forms of election are discussed: by the predecessors, by the clergy and people, and by the emperors. A summary.

units.la: I. De Formis Electionis agendum; Monarchia enim est electitia, pro qua Bellarmini rationes adducuntur, atque ad eas aliquid annotatur; II. De formis agendum; diversæ enim sunt, non est unica in Scripturis prascripta; III. Cùm tamen omninò videatur aliquam prascribi debuisse; IV. Christi & Petri electiones, sive Vocationes in Scriptura describuntur, multùm & inter se, & plurimùm ab Electionibus Episcoporum Romanorum differentes; V. Forma diversa, partim respectu Electorum, partim ratione modorum per eosdem. Respectu Electorum storum sunt quatuor; VI. Prima, quâ eligebantur à Prædecessoribus, ut ajunt, Petrus à Christo, Clemens à Petro; VII. Eadem forma postea confirmata fuit decreto Concilii Romani sub Symmacho, & exemplo Bonifacii II. VIII. Similia exempla Electionis per Antecessores alia quoque, præter Romanam, Ecclesia suppeditant; IX. Nec etiam speciè caret ista eligendi forma; maximè quoad Episcopos Romanos; X. Intercedit Bellarminus post alios; XI. Consuetudo in specie quoad Episcopos Romanos abolita, & cur? XII. Responsiones ad exemplum Mosis & reliqua; XIII. Speciatim ad exemplum Clementis; XIV. Parùm sibi hic constant Monarchici; XV. Eorundem hic difficultas; XVI. Concluditur. XVII. Forma secunda per Clerum (quæ vox explicatur populúmque Romanum. Quæ confirmatur ex ipso Bellarmino; XVIII. Ex consuetudine primitiva Ecclesia per secula multa, quoad Episcopos Romanos; XIX. Alios; Ex sacris; XX. Adducuntur testimonia & statuta Ecclesiastica usque ad Concilium Nicenum; XXI. Post Concilium Nicenum; XXII. Temporibus Caroli M. Ludovici Filii, ac sequentibus; XXIII. Nubes testium in Conciliis illorum & sequentium temporum; Pontificum testimonia; XXIV. Confessiones Pontificiorum; XXV. Bellarmini impudentia; XXVI. Consuetudo fuit præter antiquitatem & Apostolicam traditionem perutilis quoque; XXVII. In Ecclesias Reformatas pro occasionum & locorum differentia magis, minùs reducta; XXVIII. Pontificiarúmque hèic à statu pristino defectio; XXIX. Maximè quoad Electiones Pontificum Romanorum; XXX. Ex illa consuetudine contra Monarchicos argumentum nectitur; XXXI. Tertia forma eligendi per Imperatores; quæ exemplis Imperatorum Græcorum & Regum Italiæ illustratur; XXXII. Exemplis Imperatorum Germanorum; XXXIII. Quæ paucis comprehendit Maimburgius; XXXIV. Ius Imperatorum in ejusmodi Electionibus; XXXV. Ex quo patet, malè nullas jam Imperatoribus in Electione Pontificum Romanorum partes relinqui; XXXVI. Electiones ab Imperatoribus factas non Ecclesiæ oppressionem, nec sacrilegium fuisse constat, partim ex Pontificum ea de re decretis, XXXVII. Partim ex eo, quòd tot Pontifices ab Imperatoribus electi leguntur.
units.tr: I. The forms of election must be discussed, for the Monarchy is elective, and Bellarmine's arguments are adduced for it, and something is noted on them. II. The forms must be discussed, for they are diverse; there is not one form prescribed in the Scriptures. III. Yet it seems altogether that some one form ought to have been prescribed. IV. The elections, or calls, of Christ and Peter are described in Scripture, differing greatly from one another and very much from the elections of the Roman bishops. V. The forms are diverse, partly with respect to the electors, partly with respect to the methods used by them. With respect to the electors there are four. VI. The first, by which, as they say, Peter was chosen by Christ and Clement by Peter, was by the predecessors. VII. The same form was afterwards confirmed by a decree of a Roman council under Symmachus, and by the example of Boniface II. VIII. The Church supplies similar examples of election by predecessors, also outside Rome. IX. Nor does this form of election lack a specific character, especially as regards the Roman bishops. X. Bellarmine intervenes, following others. XI. The custom, in particular as regards the Roman bishops, was abolished, and why? XII. Replies to the example of Moses and the rest. XIII. Specifically to the example of Clement. XIV. The Monarchists here are little consistent with themselves. XV. The difficulty for them here. XVI. The conclusion. XVII. The second form, by the clergy (which term is explained) and the Roman people. This is confirmed from Bellarmine himself. XVIII. From the primitive custom of the Church, for many centuries, as regards the Roman bishops. XIX. Others; from the sacred writers. XX. Testimonies and ecclesiastical statutes are adduced up to the Council of Nicaea. XXI. After the Council of Nicaea. XXII. In the times of Charlemagne, his son Louis, and those following. XXIII. A cloud of witnesses in the councils of those and later times; testimonies of the Pontiffs. XXIV. Confessions of the Papists. XXV. Bellarmine's impudence. XXVI. The custom was, besides its antiquity and apostolic tradition, also very useful. XXVII. In the Reformed Churches it was more or less restored, according to differences of occasion and place. XXVIII. The defection of the Papists here from their original state. XXIX. Especially as regards the elections of the Roman Pontiffs. XXX. From that custom an argument is built against the Monarchists. XXXI. The third form of election, by the emperors, illustrated by the examples of the Greek emperors and the kings of Italy. XXXII. By the examples of the German emperors. XXXIII. What Maimbourg sums up briefly. XXXIV. The right of the emperors in such elections. XXXV. From which it is clear that it is wrongly claimed that no part is now left to the emperors in the election of the Roman Pontiffs. XXXVI. It is established that the elections made by the emperors were not an oppression of the Church nor a sacrilege, partly from the decrees of the Pontiffs on that matter, XXXVII. partly from the fact that so many Pontiffs are read of as chosen by the emperors.

units.la: I. GItur juxta ordinem n. ult. Dissert. præced. notatum heic de formis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum acturi sumus. Monarchia enim ista ex illarum genere est, quæ electitiæ vocantur; & proin minùs perfecta ex illorum Celebrium Politicorum opinione, qui hæreditarias præstare aliis arbitrantur, quamvis Hieromonarchici heic perfectissima quævis requirant; quare etiam Bellarminus l.1. de Clericis c.6. longè meliorem esse successionem per electionem, quàm per generationem, ne nimirum Monarchia sua hinc imperfectionis arguatur, contendit, & exinde argumentum ad thesin, quam ibi defendit, nimirum; non decuisse Christianos Sacerdotes carnali successione propagari; probandam ducit. Quam quidem thesin ipso defendentes &, Christianos Sacerdotes, voce in sano sensu accepta, æquè ac Christianos fieri, non nasci debere, statuentes, interim tamen ad primam & tertiam ejus rationem duo notamus. Primum est, eum satis inconvenienter exemplum Melchisedeki pro Christianis, quos proprios fingunt præter Christum, Sacerdotibus, & successione per electionem allegare, cùm Sacerdoti secundùm ordinem Melchisedek successio, sive per electionem, sive per generationem, plané repugnet, & is, juxta Apostolum, ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ, Sacerdotium non transiens habere debeat, quod jam bis notavimus; Secundum est, eum hinc ab exemplo Aaronis & successorum, quod tamen alibi strenuè in sequelam trahit, discedere, & in N. T. Sacerdotibus, quos illi V. T. præfiguraverint, proprie sic dictis nec conjuges, nec successores ex conjugio admittere, atque ita satis docere, quàm imbelle sit suum à Sacerdotibus V. T. pro Monarchia & Monarchica successione etiam hac ex parte argumentum, & quòd non tam facilè ex veteribus ad nova argumentatio præter Scripturam institui debeat.
units.tr: I. Therefore, in accordance with the order noted at the end of the preceding dissertation, we shall here treat of the forms of election of the Roman Pontiffs. For this Monarchy belongs to the class of those called elective, and so, according to the opinion of those well-known political writers who think hereditary monarchies preferable to others, it is less perfect; although the Hieromonarchists here demand every kind of perfection. For this reason Bellarmine too, in book 1, On the Clergy, chapter 6, contends that succession by election is far better than succession by generation, lest his Monarchy be charged with imperfection on this account, and from this he derives an argument for the thesis he defends there, namely that Christian priests ought not to be propagated by carnal succession. Those who defend this thesis themselves, holding that Christian priests, taking the word in a sound sense, ought to be made, not born, just as Christians are, we nonetheless note two points on his first and third reasons. First, he quite inappropriately cites the example of Melchizedek, in favour of Christian priests, whom they imagine to be priests apart from Christ, and of succession by election; for succession, whether by election or by generation, is plainly incompatible with the priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, and such a priest, according to the Apostle, is a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek [ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ], having a priesthood that does not pass to another, which we have already noted twice. Second, he departs here from the example of Aaron and his successors, which elsewhere he nonetheless vigorously pursues in argument, and by admitting neither wives nor successors born of marriage to the priests of the New Testament, strictly so called, whom those of the Old Testament prefigured, he sufficiently shows how feeble his argument from the Old Testament priests is for a Monarchy and a monarchical succession, even on this side, and that one ought not to argue so easily from old things to new without Scripture.

units.la: II. Acturi autem sumus de formis diversis Electionis Pontificum; Non enim una semper fuit (Bellarminus 17. in Electione Pontificum mutationes enumerat;) eáque in Scripturis Sacris præscripta. Una si semper fuisset, certitudo heic adeò necessaria certè hinc aliquatenus augeretur; animadvertentibus illis, quorum interest, à tot seculis Vicarii Christi Electionem uno eodémque modo se habere, nihil hìc à tam longo tempore variare; nec etiam sine causa unitatem, quoad Electionis Pontificum Formam, ostendi quis velit ab illis, qui ad Ecclesiæ unitatem unum supremum ex hominibus Pastorem, unam, & quæ nec quoad subalternos Rectores ullo tempore variet, regiminis formam necessariam esse docent; Quidni ex illorum hypothesibus etiam semper una unius Monarchæ in una Ecclesia Electionis forma necessaria esset?
units.tr: II. We are about to treat of the various forms of election of the Pontiffs. For it has not always been one (Bellarmine, in On the Election of the Pontiff, enumerates the changes), and it is not prescribed in Holy Scripture. If it had always been one, certainty here, which is so very necessary, would surely be somewhat increased by this; for those concerned would notice that for so many centuries the election of the Vicar of Christ has stood in one and the same manner, and that nothing has varied here over so long a time. Nor, indeed, without reason would anyone who teaches that a single supreme human Pastor, and one form of government which never varies even as to subordinate rulers, is necessary for the unity of the Church, rightly demand that unity in the form of the election of the Pontiff. Why, on their own hypotheses, should not one form of election for one monarch in one Church also always be necessary?

units.la: III. Sed quis non miratur, in Sacris Scripturis Electionis istius formam, vel formas non præscribi, imò nullam planè in verbo Dei illarum mentionem fieri! De re tanti momenti, & ex qua summa rei Christianæ pendet, Scriptores Sacros omninò tacere, cùm tamen alia longè, ex hypothesi certè, minora fusè prosecuti sint, alia minora quoque saltem uno & altero verbo innuerint? Eos non occurrere tot circa Electiones Papales dubiis, næv is, vitiis suo loco ex parte enarrandis? Certè nemo contra mirari potest, quòd Monarchici Scripturam imperfectionis accusant, mutam quoad hæc & alia jam ex parte memoramorata; Nec sufficit heic, Scripturam exempla & alia de Electione Ministrorum suppeditare,cùm adeò diversorum diversi etiam, ut revera sunt, eligendi modi tradi deberent, & multò magis Ecclesiae Monarcharum,si Ministrorum simplicium.
units.tr: III. But who does not wonder that in the Holy Scriptures no form, or forms, of this election is prescribed, indeed that no mention of them at all is made in the Word of God! That the sacred writers should be wholly silent about a matter of such importance, on which the whole sum of the Christian cause depends, while they have treated at length other matters, certainly less important on that hypothesis, and have hinted at others, less important still, in at least one or two words? That they do not meet the many doubts, blemishes and faults surrounding the Papal elections, some of which must be partly recounted in their place? Certainly no one can marvel that the Monarchists accuse Scripture of imperfection, since it is silent on these and other matters already partly recalled. Nor is it enough here to say that Scripture supplies examples and other things about the election of ministers, since the diverse modes of election of diverse persons, as they really are, ought to be handed down, and much more so for the Church of Monarchs than for simple ministers.

units.la: IV. Duorum quidem (sed talem fingi alterum,ostendimus) in Scriptura Ecclesiae Monarcharum Electio describitur, Jesu Christi & Petri, Domini & servi, illum misit Pater,hunc Filius,utrumque uterque,modo illustri,sed ab Electionis Pontificum Romanorum revera talium formis omnibus multùm diverso. Illius divina Electio juxta Dissert.I. Sect. I.n. 5. partim Scripturis Propheticis,partim apparitione & descensu Spiritûs,partim voce bis coelitus missâ, partim piorum testimoniis, partim doctrinae praestantiâ,partim signorum efficaciâ, partim plane irreprehensibili vitâ,imò exactissimâ eorum omnium, quae talem decebant, & à tali exspectari poterant, praestatione,hominibus approbata fuit. Hujus electionem Dissert. I. & II. prolixè tractavimus, missionem caeteris communem,immediatam à Domino, conjunctam dationi Spiritûs, confirmatam miraculis. Ille in constitutione tantò major apparet,quantò in officio major fuit; sed frustrà Electionem eorum, quibus par dignitas & potestas dignitati & potestati utriusque tribuitur, saltem hujus electioni parem cognoscere cupias. Jam & hic tantò major apparet in Electione, quantò in officio major fuit; Ne exspectes immediatam eorum,etiam bonorum, vocationem à Christo, ne exspectes ejus confirmationem adeò illustrem; Qualia tamen in Electione Capitis & Monarchae Ecclesiae & tanti Vicarii Christi forte non sine causa exspectes; Minora dabimus, qualia nempe contigerunt, & longè minora.
units.tr: IV. Indeed, the election of the Church's Monarch is described in Scripture in the case of two persons (though we have shown that the other is feigned): Jesus Christ and Peter, the Lord and the servant. The Father sent the former, the Son the latter, each in his own illustrious way, but very different from all the forms of election of the Roman Pontiffs. The divine election of the former, as noted in Dissertation I, Section I, n. 5, was approved by men partly through the prophetic Scriptures, partly through the appearance and descent of the Spirit, partly through the voice sent twice from heaven, partly through the testimonies of the pious, partly through the excellence of his teaching, partly through the efficacy of his signs, and partly through a wholly blameless life, indeed through the most exact performance of all those things that befitted such a person and could be expected from him. We have treated his election at length in Dissertations I and II: a mission common to the others, but immediate from the Lord, joined with the gift of the Spirit and confirmed by miracles. He appears so much greater in his constitution as he was greater in his office; but you would vainly seek an election of those to whom an equal dignity and power is given, at least one equal to his election. Here too he appears so much greater in the election as he was greater in his office. Do not expect an immediate call from Christ of those men, even good ones, nor so illustrious a confirmation of it. Yet such things perhaps you may not without reason expect in the election of the Head and Monarch of the Church and of so great a Vicar of Christ. We shall give smaller things, namely those which in fact happened, and far smaller ones.

units.la: V. Diversae autem eligendi Pontifices Romanos Formae dicuntur, partim respectu diversorum diversis temporibus Electorum, partim respectu diversorum, quos iidem Rectores in eligendo adhibere solent,modorum. Respectu Electorum quatuor potissimùm enarrantur formae diversae. In prima Electores Praedecessores; in secunda Clerus & Populus Romanus; in tertia Imperatores fuerunt,in quarta denique Clerus Cardinalium sunt.
units.tr: V. Different forms of electing Roman Pontiffs are spoken of, partly with respect to the different electors at different times, and partly with respect to the different methods which those same rulers were accustomed to use in the election. With respect to the electors, four different forms are chiefly described. In the first the electors were the predecessors; in the second the clergy and people of Rome; in the third the emperors; and in the fourth, finally, the college of cardinals.

units.la: VI. Primam quam dicimus, tempore talis habetur & antiquissima. Nam & Petrum à Praedecessore suo ad Pontificatum talem electum esse fingunt, qui eum Christi successorem aliquando vocant, omnes, qui Christum primum Ecclesiae Monarcham cham visibilem, Petrum secundum, Petrum Christi vicarium, eâ-dem ratione, quâ sequentes nonnunquam audiunt Vicarii Petri, & Petrum adhuc superstitem Linum, aut Clementem (quam litem jam non examinamus, istam quoad primos Petri successores incertitudinem ad electionis naevos relaturi;) successorem sibi constituisse, quod de Clemente admittunt plerique etiam illorum, qui Linum tamen ante eum sedisse volunt. Et Platina quidem, postquam jam in Petro verba, quae scilicet ad Clementem Petri eum nempe suum in Monarchia Ecclesiae Successorem deligens, fecerit, retulisset, & in Lino dixisset, Petrum Clementi quasi ex Testamento successionis locum tradidisse; in Clemente ex epistola, quae ei ad Jacobum Hierosolymitanum falsò tribuitur, verbis Clementis rem ita enarrat: Simon Petrus, ubi finem vitae suae adesse sensit, in corona fratrum positus, apprehensa manu mea; Hunc, inquit, urbis Episcopum constituo, qui mihi in rebus omnibus, postquam Romam veni, comes fuit. Subterfugiebam ego tamen onus. Tum ille; Tibi tantummodò consules, populum Dei in fluctibus ambulantem deseres, cùm periclitanti subvenire possis?
units.tr: VI. The first, as we call it, is held to be the most ancient and of that time. For they pretend that Peter was chosen for the papacy in this way by his predecessor, whom they sometimes call Christ's successor. All who call Christ the first visible monarch of the Church, Peter the second, and Peter the vicar of Christ, do so by the same reasoning by which later men sometimes hear themselves called vicars of Peter. They say that Peter, while Linus or Clement was still living (we will not examine this dispute now, but will attribute that uncertainty about Peter's first successors to the blemishes of the election), appointed a successor for himself. Most of those who want Linus to have sat before Clement also admit this about Clement. Platina indeed, after he had reported the words spoken in the case of Peter, namely choosing Clement as his successor in the monarchy of the Church, and had said in the case of Linus that Peter had handed the place of succession to Clement as if from a testament of succession, then relates the matter in the case of Clement, from the letter which is falsely attributed to him and addressed to James of Jerusalem, in Clement's own words: "Simon Peter, when he felt that the end of his life was near, placed in the midst of the brothers, having taken my hand". "I appoint this one," he says, "bishop of the city, who was my companion in all things after I came to Rome." "I, however, was fleeing the burden. Then he said: 'Will you alone take counsel for yourself, and desert the people of God walking amid the waves, when you are able to help those in peril?'"

units.la: VII. Et quamvis haec per Antecessores respectu primorum Episcoporum Romanorum non semper adhibita, sed Electio, juxta formam secundam, non raro ab Ecclesia, (quâ conscià & consentiente, etiam Successores à Praedecessoribus lectos esse, praesupponimus;) ut Petrus in corona fratrum positus Clementem elegisse dicitur, demum post Praedecessorum mortem facta videatur, & prima illa omnia densissimis fabularum & incertitudinis tenebris involvantur; tamen in uno ex Conciliis Romanis sub Symmacho P. circa initium saeculi sexti inter alia statuta, illud legimus, quod & dist.79. c. si transitus habetur: Si, quod absit, transitus Papae inopinatus evenit, ut de sui electione successoris, ut supra placuit, non possit ante decernere: Siquidem in unum totius inclinaverit Ecclesiastici ordinis electio; consecretur electus Episcopus. In quo decreto, cui haud dubiè Schisma inter Symmachum & Laurentium occasionem dedit, tanquam res consueta & ordinaria supponi videtur, ut Romanus Episcopus adhuc superstes sibi successorem deligat, saltem, si Symmachum ob peculiares causas peculiariter id ita statuisse, dicatur, inde colligi potest, istam eligendi formam tum temporis pro legitima habitam fuisse; Prout etiam tribus tantùm Papis interpositis Bonifacius II. simili forte Schismatis in Electione sna occasione motus tus vivens adhuc, referente Anastasio in Bonif. II. & Onuphrio in annot. ad Vigil. Vigilium Diaconum in Synodo successorem sibi legit & Electionem hanc Cleri juramento ac Chirographo stabilivit; Etsi eandemipse, iterum congregatâ Synodo, rescideritut mox dicemus. Sed & Greg. VII. narrante Baronio ad a. 1085. n. 21. ante 3. sui obitûs diem rogatus, quid de Rom. sedis post obitum suum ordinatione juberet; hortatus est, ut si quo pacto possent, ipsum Desiderium Pontificem facerent. Qui etiam electus moriturus Cardinales monuit ac jussit, ut, juxta Gregorii Papæ statutum Ottonem Ostiensem Episcopum quàm primùm eligerent & constituerent; ut apud eundem ad a. 1087. n. 16. habetur. Et ad an. 1119. n. 2. de Gelasio, quòd cùm his, qui aderant, Cardinalibus, moriturus coeperit exhortationibus agere, ut Conon eligeretur. Nec non ad an. 1198. n. 2. quòd, dum paulatim ægrotare coepit, convocatis coram se Cardinalibus omnibus præceperit, ut tractarent de Successore, ipse autem nisus sit modis omnibus, ut Dominus Johannes ei succederet. Recentius est exemplum Urbani VIII. de quo Divortium cœleste, quòd sæpe secum deliberârit otiosus, s'il seroit possible de rendre le Pontificat electif, non plus par le Consistoire, mais par la persone de celui, qui regne, afin de le rendre en apres hereditaire à la posterité; Id est: an Papatus ullo modo fieri possit electitius non amplius per Consistorium, sed per Pontificem regnantem, ut illum postea posteritati suæ hereditarium facere posset. De quo propósito Urbani etiam testatur Il Nipotismo l. c. 4. imò etiam de mediis Cardinales absoluto & hæreditario Urbium & Provinciarum dominio in eum finem devinciendi; Adhuc autem recentius est exemplum Innocentii X. qui moriturus, Antonio Cotono l. citando mox, referente ex 4. Cardinalibus Alexandrum VII. ad successionem commendavit.
units.tr: VII. And although these things were not always done by predecessors with respect to the first bishops of Rome, but the election, according to the second form, was often made by the Church (with whose knowledge and consent, we presuppose, successors too were chosen by their predecessors), as Peter is said to have chosen Clement while "placed in the midst of the brothers", and although the matter seems finally to have been done after the death of the predecessors, and all those first things are wrapped in the thickest darkness of fables and uncertainty; nevertheless, in one of the Roman councils under Pope Symmachus, near the beginning of the sixth century, among other decrees we read this, which is also held in dist. 79, c. si transitus: "If, which God forbid, the Pope's passing should come unexpectedly, so that he cannot previously decide on the election of a successor, as has been decided above, then, since the election of the whole ecclesiastical order has inclined to one man, let the elected bishop be consecrated." In this decree, to which the schism between Symmachus and Laurence undoubtedly gave occasion, it seems to be presupposed as a customary and ordinary thing that a Roman bishop still living should choose a successor for himself. At least, if it is said that Symmachus enacted this specially for particular reasons, it can be inferred from this that this form of election was then regarded as legitimate. Just so, with only three popes intervening, Boniface II, moved perhaps by a similar schism over his own election while still living, as Anastasius reports in Bonif. II., and Onuphrius in his notes on Vigilius, chose the deacon Vigilius as successor in a synod and confirmed this election by an oath and written pledge of the clergy; although he himself, when the synod met again, annulled it, as we shall say shortly. But also Gregory VII, as Baronius reports at 1085, n. 21, being asked three days before his death what he ordered concerning the arrangement of the Roman see after his death, urged that, if they could in any way manage it, they should make Desiderius himself pope. Desiderius, also elected and about to die, admonished and ordered the cardinals that, according to the statute of Pope Gregory, they should elect and install Otto, bishop of Ostia, as soon as possible, as is held at 1087, n. 16. And at 1119, n. 2, of Gelasius, that when he began to die, he began to urge with exhortations those cardinals who were present that Conon should be elected. Also at 1198, n. 2, that when he began to fall gradually ill, having summoned all the cardinals before him, he ordered them to deal with a successor, while he himself strove by every means that Lord John should succeed him. A more recent example is that of Urban VIII, concerning whom the Divortium cœleste says that he often deliberated with himself in idleness whether it might be possible to make the papacy elective, not any more by the consistory but by the person of the one who reigns, so that he could afterwards make it hereditary to his posterity. That is: whether the papacy could in any way be made elective, not any more through the consistory but through the reigning pontiff, so that he could afterwards make it hereditary to his descendants. Concerning this design of Urban, Il Nipotismo also bears witness, in the same chapter 4, even about the means by which the cardinals were bound to him, namely an absolute and hereditary dominion over cities and provinces for that end. Even more recent is the example of Innocent X, who, when dying, commended Alexander VII to succession, as four cardinals reported, according to Antonio Coton, who soon follows in the work cited.

units.la: VIII. Similia exempla electionis successorum per antecessores aliæ quoque præter Romanam, Ecclesiæ suppeditant, dum nimirum variè, sed maximè ætatis decrepitæ, & infirmitatis respectu, vel Coadjutores, quibus simul successio confirmata, & qui nonnunquam soli Sacra peragebant, prioribus solo titulo contentis, adsciti, vel Successores simpliciter lecti fuerunt. Exempla Alexandri Hierosolymitani, Gregorii Nazianzeni, Petri Alexandrini, Augustini Hipponensis & plurimorum aliorum à prædecessoribus, quamvis quadantenus cooperante, modò Clero, modò Clero & populo simul electorum, apud M. Ant. de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. l. 3. c. 3. §. 62. seqq. videri possunt.
units.tr: VIII. The Church also supplies similar examples of successors being elected by their predecessors, besides the Roman one. This happened in various ways, but chiefly on account of advanced age and infirmity: coadjutors were taken on, to whom succession was confirmed at the same time, and who sometimes alone performed the sacred duties while the earlier bishops were content with the title alone; or successors were simply chosen. Examples of Alexander of Jerusalem, Gregory Nazianzen, Peter of Alexandria, Augustine of Hippo, and very many others, who were elected by their predecessors, though sometimes with some cooperation from the clergy alone and sometimes from clergy and people together, can be seen in M. Antonius de Dominis, On the Republic of the Church, book 3, chapter 3, §62 and following.

units.la: IX. Nec etiam specie caret ista eligendi forma. Nam quoad Coadjutores necessarios, ut essent proprii Pastores, non mercenarii, Coëpiscopi facti sunt, & destinati successores. Quoad Successores simpliciter, Basilius Cappadociae Metropolitanus Innocentio Episcopo talem postulanti apud Bar. ad an.Chr. 417.n. 9. rescripsit: Prudenter profecto, dum vivus, eum videre cupiens, qui post te electum Domini gregem recturus sit, quod Beatus Moses optavit & vidit. Sic etiam videtur nonnunquam optime Schismatibus & irregularitatibus aliis quaeri posse remedium; Et quoad Episcopos Romanos in specie, quibus infallibilitas a longo tempore a suis tribuitur, convenientissimum hoc videtur, partim illo respectu, partim etiam, ut vidimus, ob exempla primorum, quos faciunt, Ecclesiae Monarcharum, partim etiam, ut potestas illa summa, Papa exspirante, habeat, quo abeat, nec debeat incertis sedibus usque ad novi Monarchae electionem illarum animarum ad instar, quarum corporibus sepultura denegatur, vel quibus aliás Charon vecturam denegat, vagari. Hinc etiam Pontificii Doctores non incelebres Antonius Cotonus Franciscanus, in repudiata summa Diana l.3. cont. 9. c.2. &, quos ille citat, Victoria, Ledesma, Arriaga, formam hanc eligendi probant atque defendunt, in Petro constitutionem Clementis peculiare privilegium fuisse, negantes, exemplum Bonifacii tantum ob electi qualitates vitiosum fuisse, affirmantes, atque dicentes; Videri sibi potestatem istam involvi in potestate Capitis Ecclesiae, atque sic incommoda commode evitari posse, cum non sit metuendum, Papam Augusti ad instar gloriam ex successore malo quasiturum, sed potius praesumendum, cum ad exemplum Alexandri dignissimum substituturum esse; dicentes porro cum Vasquezio in 3. 16. T. 3. disp. 244. c. 3. n.26. Si non posset summus Pontifex successorem sibi eligere, neque etiam lege sua positiva aliis prescribere posset modum electionis, sicut revera praescripsit &c. Et cum Franc. Amico Curs. Theol. t.3. disp.6. sect.6. n. 204. licet videatur jure divino determinatum, ut Pontificis electio ad Ecclesiasticos spectet, modus tamen eligendi non est de jure divino determinatus: ergo ad eum talis determinatio spectabit, cui commissum est supremum Ecclesiae Regimen &c.
units.tr: IX. Nor does this form of election lack some appearance of support. For as regards necessary coadjutors, so that they might be proper ministers and not hired men, they were made co-bishops and designated successors. As for successors simply, Basil, metropolitan of Cappadocia, replied to Bishop Innocent when he asked for this, as cited in Baronius at AD 417, n. 9: "Surely it is prudent, while you are alive and wish to see him who, chosen after you, is to rule the Lord's flock, as the blessed Moses desired and saw." So also it seems that a remedy for schisms and other irregularities can sometimes be sought very well in this way. And as regards the Roman bishops in particular, to whom infallibility has long been ascribed by their own people, this seems most convenient: partly for that reason; partly also, as we have seen, on account of the examples of the first monarchs of the Church, whom they put forward; and partly so that that supreme power, when the pope dies, may have somewhere to go, and not have to wander with uncertain seats until a new monarch is elected, like the souls of those whose bodies are denied burial, or whom Charon otherwise refuses passage. Hence also the Papist doctors of some note, Antonius Coton the Franciscan, in the rejected summary, Diana, book 3, treatise 9, chapter 2, and those whom he cites, Victoria, Ledesma and Arriaga, approve and defend this form of election. They deny that the constitution of Clement in the case of Peter was a special privilege, and they affirm that the instance of Boniface was faulty only on account of the qualities of the one elected, saying: "that this power seems to them to be included in the power of the head of the Church, and so the inconveniences can be conveniently avoided, since there is no need to fear that the Pope would seek the glory of Augustus from a bad successor, but rather it should be presumed that he would substitute the most worthy one, as Alexander did;" saying further, with Vasquez, "In 3, q. 16, disp. 244, c. 3, n. 26: If the supreme pontiff could not choose a successor for himself, nor even prescribe to others by his own positive law the mode of election, as indeed he has prescribed, etc." And with Francisco Amico, Cursus Theologicus, tome 3, disp. 6, sect. 6, n. 204: although it seems determined by divine right that the election of the Pope belongs to the ecclesiastics, the mode of electing is not determined by divine right; therefore such determination will belong to him to whom the supreme government of the Church has been entrusted, etc.

units.la: X. Sed intercedit gravissime Bellarminus & ait l.1. de Cler. cap.9. quoad Pontifices summos, non expedit, ut praedecessor eligat successorem. Sed non solus intercedit, nec etiam primus. Theodoretus sane Paulini Antiocheni factum, quo sibi solus successorem Evagrium constituit & ordinavit, reprehendit, dicens l. V. c. 23. In quare complures simul Canones vitiavit: Siquidem Canones neq; faciunt potestatem cuiquam jam mortem appetituro, quenquam in locum suum sufficere: Atque omnes Provincia Episcopos jubent in unum ad eam rem convocari, quia etiam vetant rursus quenquam absque tribus Episcopis Episcopum constitui. Sed contra ipsam Electionem à Prædecessoribus & quidem Coadjutorum, qui Coëpiscopi sint, solùm pugnare videtur ex antiquis Canonibus Nicenus Octavus, dum nimirum vult, duos Episcopos in una civitate non admitti debere; Quamvis forte contra illam electionem pugnare tantùm videatur, & multorum judicio duos Episcopos primarios cum Schismate & divisione respiciat.
units.tr: X. But Bellarminus objects most gravely, and says (On Clerics, book 1, ch. 9) that as regards the supreme pontiffs, it is not expedient that a predecessor choose a successor. But he is not alone in this, nor the first. Theodoret indeed rebukes the act of Paulinus of Antioch, who alone appointed and ordained Evagrius as his successor, saying (book 5, ch. 23): In doing this he violated several canons at once. For the canons neither give anyone who is about to die the power to put someone in his place, and they order all the bishops of the province to be summoned together for that purpose, and they also forbid anyone to be made bishop without three bishops. But against the election itself by predecessors, and indeed by coadjutors who are co-bishops, the eighth Nicene canon alone seems to speak among the ancient canons, namely in that it wills that two bishops ought not to be admitted in one city. Yet perhaps it seems to fight only against that kind of election, and in the judgment of many it refers to two chief bishops in relation to schism and division.

units.la: XI. Quoad Episcopos Romanos in specie, memoratus n.7.
units.tr: XI. As regards the Roman bishops in particular, as mentioned in n. 7.

units.la: Bonifacius II. ut Anastasius ait, ob reverentiam Sancta sedis electionem successoris sui abolevit, qui & Chirographum antea formatum combussit, & teste Platina in Vita, instituit, ne quisquam sibi in Episcopatu successorem deligeret; Ut jam ante eum Hilarius l. c. a. 461. narrante eodem in Vita, instituit, ne Pontifices deinceps successorem sibi deligerent, quæ institutio ad omnes gradus Ecclesiasticos pertineat; Atque ita Bonifacius II. priori sua constitutione reus transgressionis legis à prædecessore latæ factus est. Sic & Pius IV. referente ex Victorello Joh. Bapt. Casalio de Ritib. Veter. Sacr. Christ. C. 69. p. 404. edit. Francof. in Consistorio, suadente majore Cardinalium numero, & Gambara dicente, declaratum jam olim hoc à Papa in Consistorio, decretóque firmatum, videndúmque quibus verbis constitutio conficienda, decretum non inutile futurum ratus, se declaraturum asseruit, Pontificem non posse Successorem adjutorémve cum futura successione sibi eligere; Imò Baronius ad an. 531. ad exemplum Bonifacii supra allatum sequentia notat: Intelligis, Lector, quantum exhorruerint Romani omnes, inprimis verò iidem ipsi Romani Pontifices, ut aliquis subvivens quovis digno prætextu Pontifex deligat successorem. Et paulò post: Verùm etsi videri potuissent isthæc de eligendo Successore commissa à Bonifacio ab eodem expiata: tamen citò Deus ad aliorum exemplum eum ex hac vita subtraxit. Interim tamen Pontificibus, eodem Casalio l. c. indicante & loca notante, admonitionem hîc aliquam, sed sine prejudicio libera electionis Cardinalium, relinquunt. Quò pars exemplorum quorundam ex allatis spectare videtur; Quamvis admonitio Papalis pro imperio habenda & habita, & proin in præjudicium liberæ Cardinalium dinalium
units.tr: Boniface II, as Anastasius says, out of reverence for the Holy See, abolished the election of his own successor. He also burned the document previously drawn up, and according to Platina in Vita, he ordained that no one should choose a successor for himself in the episcopate. Earlier still, Hilarius, in the year 461 (as the same writer tells in Vita), ordained that popes should not choose successors for themselves in future, and that this ordinance should pertain to all ecclesiastical grades. And so Boniface II, by his earlier constitution, was made guilty of transgressing a law enacted by his predecessor. So too Pius IV, as reported by Victorello, Giovanni Battista Casali de Ritib. Veter. Sacr. Christ. C. 69. p. 404. edit. Francof., in consistory, with the greater number of cardinals urging, and Gambara saying that this had been declared long ago by a pope in consistory and confirmed by decree, and that it must be considered in what words the constitution should be framed, thinking that a decree would not be useless, he asserted that he would declare that a pope cannot choose a successor or helper for himself with future succession. Indeed Baronius, at the year 531, following the example of Boniface cited above, notes the following: You understand, reader, how much all the Romans shrank back from it, above all the Roman pontiffs themselves, that any living pope, under any worthy pretext, should choose a successor. And a little later: But although these matters concerning the choosing of a successor, committed by Boniface, might seem to have been expiated by the same man, nevertheless God quickly removed him from this life as an example to others. Meanwhile, however, as Casali indicates in the same place and notes the passage, they leave the pontiffs some admonition here, but without prejudice to the free election of the cardinals. To this part some of the examples cited seem to relate; although a papal admonition ought to be, and was, taken as a command, and so to the prejudice of the free election of the cardinals.

units.la: Consuetudo speciatim quoad Episcopos Romanos abolita, & cur? dinalium electionis aliquando cessisse quoque videatur in illis. Hinc etiam deliberationes de futuro Pontifice, praecedente adhuc superstite, tantum vetant eo inconsulto factas. Mirum autem esset, quod illam electionis formam primam ita rejecerunt & rejiciunt, nisi de propriis infirmitatibus ex propria eorum confessione constaret, nempe probe animadverterunt, plane futurum esse, ut sic Papalis dignitas, mox haereditaria fieret, & praeda illorum, qui disturi fuissent ex Psal. LXXXII. venite, hereditate possideamus Sanctuarium Dei. Quod & Franc. Amicus l. c. innuit, non eligere Pontifices dicens, etiam ne daretur occasio, ne Pontifices hoc jure uterentur ut proprio & hereditario, qui esset pessimus potestatis abusus. Quandoquidem alias quoque Papae Agnatis & Nepotibus suis haud male etiam de futuro prospicere norunt.
units.tr: Custom, especially as regards the Roman bishops, abolished, and why? The freedom of the cardinals' election seems at times also to have given way in those cases. Hence they forbid deliberations about the future pope, made while the present one is still alive, only when they are made without his knowledge. It would be strange, however, that they rejected and still reject that first form of election in such a way, unless their own weaknesses were evident from their own confession. They plainly foresaw that the papal dignity would soon become hereditary, and the prey of those who, as in Psalm 82, would say: Come, let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance. Franc. Amicus also hints at this in the place cited, saying that popes should not choose, lest an occasion be given that popes should use this right as their own and hereditary, which would be the worst abuse of power. Since, moreover, popes also know well enough how to provide for their agnates and nephews in the future.

units.la: XII. Ad exemplum autem Mosis respondet Antonius de Rosellis Monarch. p.2. c. 8. mandato Dei eum sibi Successorem Josuam elegisse. Quae tamen responsio undiquaque ex V. Test. typos & argumenta captantibus & divinam infallibilitatem Papis suis tribuentibus non sufficit; ut & responsiones ad exempla reliqua cum Monarchicorum hypothesibus minus conveniunt, nam ad exemplum Christi Petrum ad Pontificatum talem, si Diis placet, eligentis respondet, fecisse ex divinitate sibi conjuncta, secundum quam ejus judicium falli non potuerit, quae non sint in Papa & in humano judicio, quia Papae judicium possit fallere & falli, quia Papa sit homo & peccare possit 21. dist. nunc autem. Et ideo propter vitandum hominum fallibile judicium statutum fuisse, ut Papa sibi non eligat successorem; Et ad exemplum Petri Clementem successorem suum constituentis, fecisse Dei voluntate & inspiratione Spiritus Sancti, nec esse istud in argumentum assumendum, nisi ab illis, qui talem sibi substituerint, qualem sibi successorem B. Petrus quaesiverit 8. q. 1. §. his omnibus. Quomodo ex ipsa Paparum lege ostenditur, quod alia habeant, quam quae in Christo & Petro fuerunt, agendi principia, nam & ille addit; Quasi velit ille textus, quod cum hodie non conferatur hoc officium homini sancta vita, sed potius sanguini & consanguinitati, si in Papa solo spectaret electio, ideo opus fuit, quod ratione plurium electio fieri deberet.
units.tr: XII. As for the example of Moses, Antonius de Rosellis (Monarch. part 2, ch. 8) replies that he chose Joshua as his successor by God's command. Yet this reply does not suffice in every respect for those who snatch at types and arguments from the Old Testament and attribute divine infallibility to their popes. The replies to the other examples also agree poorly with the hypotheses of the monarchists. For to the example of Christ choosing Peter for such a pontificate, if it pleases the gods, he replies that he did so from the divinity joined to him, according to which his judgment could not err, which are not in the pope and in human judgment, because the pope's judgment can err and be erred, since the pope is a man and can sin (dist. 21, "Nunc autem"). And therefore, to avoid fallible human judgment, it was decreed that the pope should not choose a successor for himself. And to the example of Peter appointing Clement as his successor, he says that this was done by the will of God and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, nor is this to be taken as an argument, except by those who have appointed such a successor as Blessed Peter sought (8 q. 1, §. his omnibus). How it is shown from the very law of the popes that they have principles of action other than those which were in Christ and Peter. For he adds: As if that text meant that, since today this office is conferred not on holy life but rather on blood and kinship, if the election belonged to the pope alone, it was therefore necessary that the election be made on the principle of a plurality.

units.la: XIII. Lepidum autem est, quod ad constitutionem Clementis porro respondent; Platina in vita Lini ait: Clementem a Petro solenniter & invitum quasi, juxta ipsorum traditionem, sublato etiam excusationis praetextu, ut n. 6. vidimus, constitutum, tanta modestia fuisse, ut Linum ac Cletum (quos ita immodestos faciunt acceptantes, quod alii demandatum esse noverant,) coegerit ante se munus Pontificatus obire, ne posteri hac principatus ambitio (quod tam non ambiens constitutus fuit) perniciosi exempli haberetur; Idem autem, qui supra de Rosellis l.c. dicit; Clementem eam ob causam renuntiasse no. 8. q. 1. Si Petrus: & communi cleri electione voluisse personam Papa eligi debere & determinari, ut ex collatione & plurium concordia talis electio careret errore & mereretur divinam suscipere inspirationem, cum melius judicent plures quam unus l. ita vulneratus in fi. ad I. aquit. quia cum plures, duo vel tres conveniunt in nomine Dei, ideo ipse in medio eorum sit, 24. q. 1. alienus in fi. Qua ratione culpa omnis in Petrum devolvitur, qui scilicet aut minus, perniciosum esse exemplum, praevidit, aut minus, illud praevidens, evitare voluit. Et eximium omnino est, quod priorum exempla ob errores posteriorum perniciosa fieri possunt, & quod hic valere potest illud; Oculi plus vident, quam oculus; alibi quoque applicandum.
units.tr: XIII. It is a charming thing, however, that in reply to the appointment of Clement they go on to say: Platina in vita Lini says that Clement was appointed by Peter solemnly and, as it were, unwillingly, according to their own tradition, even with the pretext of excuse removed, as we saw in n. 6. He was so modest that he compelled Linus and Cletus (whom they make so immodest in accepting, since they knew it had been commanded to others) to discharge the office of the pontificate before him, lest posterity regard this ambition for rule as a precedent for harm, since he had been appointed without any such ambition. The same man who spoke above (de Rosellis, l.c.) says that Clement renounced for that reason (no. 8, q. 1, "Si Petrus"), and by the common election of the clergy wished that the person of the pope should be chosen and determined, so that such an election, from the comparison and agreement of many, should be free from error and deserve to receive divine inspiration, since many judge better than one l. (…wounded at the end, ad I. Aquit.) for where two or three are gathered in the name of God, there he is in the midst of them, 24 q. 1 (alienus in fin.). On this principle all the blame falls on Peter, who either foresaw that the example would be less harmful, or, foreseeing it, wished to avoid it less. And it is altogether remarkable that the examples of earlier men can become harmful because of the errors of later ones, and that this saying may apply here as well as elsewhere: The eyes see more than the eye.

units.la: XIV. Sic quoque parum sibi constant Monarchici, dum ab una quidem parte statuunt, (utimur verbis Panormitani super prima primi in cap. 6. Licet de vitanda) non posse Papam sibi eligere successorem, pro quo citat no. glo. 1. §. his omnibus 8. q. 1. & quod sequitur Joan. aud. hic & Archid. in c. si transitus 89. dist. Qui & addit; Teneri hoc dictum communiter per Doctores, & esse rationem, quia effectus hujusmodi electionis referatur ad tempus, quo non sit futurus Papa 1. eum qui ff. de jurisd. om. judic. rationem aliam etiam afferente de Rosellis l. c. electionem de Clemente a Petro factam non valuisse, quia Papa sit universalis Vicarius Jesu Christi. de transla. praela. c. quanto, sed vicarium non posse illi, qui eum praefecerit, vicarium alium universaliter dare: ut de ossi. vica. & Clericos. & ideo se credere, quod etiam sibi non posset substituere Vicarium, qui omnem haberet sicut Papalem potestatem, ratione praedicta, & ideo bene Clementem renunciasse & voluisse, quod per electionem fieret; Ab altera parte vero; eum posse facere constitutionem, quae admittatur, quia provideat futuris scandalis & in casu, quo alius praeter eum providere non posset. Nam difficultatem, quam hic facit de Rosellis l. c. quod illa constitutio de modo eligendi successoris sit futura fienda post mortem Papae, & proin videatur, non debere posse Papam de illo disponere, per D. eum qui §. fide jurisdi. om. in. illam, inquam, difficultatem non tollit, quando addit; Quaedam esse, quae consummationem & effectum sumant in vita Papae, & durent
units.tr: XIV. In this way the monarchists are also rather inconsistent with themselves. On the one hand they lay down (we use the words of Panormitanus on the first of the first, in ch. 6, "Licet de vitanda") that the pope cannot choose a successor for himself. For this he cites the gloss at 8 q. 1, §. his omnibus, and what follows, John Andreae here, and the Archdeacon on ch. "si transitus," dist. 89. He also adds: "This statement is commonly held by the doctors, and the reason is that the effect of such an election refers to the time when there will not be a pope" (1, "eum qui," ff. de jurisdictione omnium iudicum). De Rosellis, l.c., gives another reason too: that the election of Clement by Peter was not valid, because "the pope is the universal vicar of Jesus Christ" (de translatione praelatorum, ch. "quanto"), "but a vicar cannot give another universal vicar to him who appointed him" (de officio vicarii, and Clerics). "And so I believe that he also could not substitute for himself a vicar who would have all papal power, for the reason stated; and so rightly Clement renounced and wished it to be done by election." On the other hand, Panormitanus holds that he can make a constitution which is admitted, because it provides for future scandals, and in the case where no one but himself could provide. For the difficulty which de Rosellis, l.c., raises here, that this constitution about the mode of choosing a successor is to be made after the death of the pope, and so seems not to be something the pope ought to be able to dispose of (D. "eum qui," §. fide, jurisdi. om., in illam), he does not remove when he adds: There are some things which take their consummation and effect during the pope's life, and endure

units.la: Marginal notes (right): "Parum sibi hic constant Monarchici; Quod ostenditur ex Panormitano & de Rosellis;" & durent etiam post mortem, sicut sint statuta, sententia, contractus & similia, & talem esse constitutionem de futura electione Pontificis, quæ statim sumat vires Papa vivente & ipsam constituente. Sed ipsam electionem futuri Pontificis esse impossibilem, quòd incipiat vires sumere vivente Papa, quia esse non debeant duo Pontifices summi: sed tantùm debere sumere vires & initium post mortem Papæ, & ideo à Papa vivente fieri non posse, quod secus sit in constitutione de eligendo, quæ statim sumat vires, licèt ejus constitutionis exercitium sit de futuro.
units.tr: Marginal note: "The Monarchians are not consistent here; this is shown by Panormitanus and de Rosellis." And they last even after death, just as statutes, judgments, contracts and the like do. Such is the case with a constitution about the future election of a Pontiff: it takes effect at once while the Pope is alive and while he makes it. But the election of a future Pontiff itself is impossible, because it could not begin to take effect while the Pope is alive, since there should not be two supreme Pontiffs at once. It must take effect and begin only after the Pope's death. For this reason it cannot be made by a Pope while he lives, unlike a constitution about electing someone, which takes effect at once, even though the exercise of that constitution concerns the future.

units.la: XV. Monarchicos hic quoque parùm sibi constare, & difficultatibus impediri, quas tollere nequeant, manifestum est. Si enim Papa potest constitutionem facere de modo successionem eligendi, & potestatem eligendi conferre certæ personæ, quæ eam aliâs non habet, quidni etiam posset sibi, maximè conscìis illis, quorum interest, successorem eligere? Annon constitutio de modo eligendi successorem æquè refertur ad tempus quo non est futurus Papa? Annon de multis disponit Papa, quæ referuntur ad tempus, quo non est futurus Papa? Annon æquè potest facere constitutionem de ipso successore, quæ admitti debet, quia providet futuris scandalis & in casu, quo alius præter eum providere non potest? Vel, annon æquè possunt post mortem Papæ providere electores de modo eligendi ac de ipso successore? Et quomodo electio futuri Pontificis est impossibilis superstite prædecessore, etiamsi ponatur, non posse actu simul esse duos? Eo ipso, quòd futurus dicitur, nondum est, & prorsus non sunt duo, interim de successore constitutio fieri potest, designari potest; Et statuta, sententia, contractus & similia eundem planè respectum habent quoad modum eligendi & quoad ipsum successorem, incipiunt vires sumere vivente Papa, id est, fundamentum habent, sed pariter consummationem & effectum demum post ejus mortem habent, & utrobique est constitutionis exercitium de futuro, sive jam successor designatus actu succedat & admittatur, sive verò præscripto modo eligatur. Dum autem electio futuri Pontificis impossibilis & contradictionem involvere dicitur, istius absurditatis rei peraguntur, quicunque sibi successores elegerunt, aut de eligendis cogitârunt, & quidem ex hypothesi, Christus & Petrus; Petrus maximè omnium, qui tot ante mortem annis successores non tantùm designâsse, sed & ad communionem muneris actu admisisse, supponi debet. Ut jam concludere liceat, præsuppositâ tali Monarchicâ potestate, &, si Papæ tales essent, quales esse debe-rent rent,id est,bonum Ecclesiæ magis quàm sua & suorum commoda propria quærentes,primam hanc Electionis Formam, ut prima & antiquissima habetur, etiam commodissimam fore, nec tum opus fuisse, ut aliarum formarum introductione,quod juxta Ant. de Rosellis c.l. eo modo fit,statuS totius universalis Ecclesiæ,qui ab Electione Papæ pendet, innovaretur. Quæ etiam formarum aliarum introductio sine certa revelatione fieri non debuisset,quicquid jam de aliis Ecclesiis earúmque Rectoribus sit.
units.tr: XV. It is plain that the Monarchians are again inconsistent here and are hampered by difficulties they cannot remove. For if the Pope can make a constitution about the mode of electing his successor, and can confer the power of electing on a certain person who does not otherwise have it, why could he not also choose his own successor, especially with those whose interest it is in the know? Does a constitution about the mode of electing a successor not equally refer to a time when he will not be Pope? Does the Pope not decide many things that refer to a time when he will not be Pope? Can he not equally make a constitution about the successor himself, which ought to be admitted, because it provides against future scandals and in a case where no one else can provide? Or can the electors not equally make provision after the Pope's death both for the mode of electing and for the successor himself? And how is the election of a future Pontiff impossible while the predecessor is alive, even if it is granted that two cannot actually exist at the same time? Simply because he is called future, he does not yet exist, and there are in fact not two of them; meanwhile a constitution about the successor can be made and a successor can be designated. Statutes, judgments, contracts and the like have exactly the same bearing both on the mode of electing and on the successor himself: they begin to take effect while the Pope is alive, that is, they have their basis then, but likewise they have their completion and effect only after his death. In both cases there is the exercise of a constitution concerning the future, whether the designated successor actually succeeds and is admitted at once, or whether he is chosen in the prescribed manner. Yet when the election of a future Pontiff is said to be impossible and to involve a contradiction, all who have chosen successors for themselves, or thought about who should be chosen, are charged with this same absurdity, and on their own hypothesis Christ and Peter are among them. Peter above all must be supposed to have not only designated successors many years before his death but also actually admitted them to share his office. So, to conclude: granted such a Monarchical power, and granted that the Popes were such as they ought to be, that is, seeking the good of the Church rather than their own and their people's private advantage, this first form of election, as it is regarded as the first and most ancient, would also be the most convenient. Nor would it then have been necessary, by the introduction of other forms, which according to Antonius de Rosellis in the passage cited is done in this way, to alter the state of the whole universal Church, which depends on the election of the Pope. Nor could the introduction of these other forms have been made without a certain revelation, whatever may now be the case with other churches and their rulers.

units.la: XVI. Sed talis Monarchica potestas,Papæ tales non dantur,Christus optimè solus Apostolos constituere potuit, Apostoli etiam pro plenitudine potestatis suæ Ecclesiis, maximè vix dum plantatis,idoneos Ministros præponere potuerunt,licèt nihil ejusmodi sine consensu fidelium unquam fecisse legantur, Episcopi autem Romani primi, licèt boni viri,fallibiles tamen fuerunt, & si aliquando in persecutionum necessitate successores sibi constituerunt,illud nonnisi Ecclesia cooperante factum est, & extra periculum transmittendæ ad suos dominationis, quia sic constituebant laboris & afflictionum successores; posterioribus, authoritate,opibus & potentiâ auctis, contrà primam fidem & charitatem deserentibus, istam de successore curam relinquere, committere solis,aut etiam primas partes in electione omninò tutum non fuisset. Hinc natæ prohibitiones, hinc semper ferè post mortem eorum demum,quod & ab initio in Ecclesiis aliis obtinuit,Ecclesiæ Rectores ab aliis,& diu à tota Ecclesia eligebantur.
units.tr: XVI. But such a Monarchical power is not given to the Popes. Christ alone could appoint the Apostles in the best way. The Apostles too, by the fullness of their authority, could set suitable ministers over the churches, especially those scarcely planted, although we read that they never did anything of this kind without the consent of the faithful. The first Roman bishops, though good men, were nevertheless fallible; and if at times in the necessity of persecution they appointed successors for themselves, this was done only with the Church cooperating and outside any danger of handing on their rule to their own people, since they appointed successors to labour and afflictions. For later bishops, whose authority, wealth and power had grown, and who had abandoned the first faith and charity, it would not have been at all safe to leave this care of a successor to them alone, or even to let them have the first role in the election. Hence the prohibitions; and hence, almost always, the ministers of the Church were chosen by others, and for a long time by the whole Church, only after the death of their predecessors, as had also been the custom from the beginning in other churches.

units.la: XVII. Et ista fuit secunda electionis Pontificum Romanorum forma per Clerum (quod vocabulum fidelibus quibusvis ab initio & vi significationis,(fortem quippe & hereditatem signifi-cat, qualis populus fidelis Dei est) commune 1.Petr.V.3. laicorum, plebejorum nomine illis etiam inter eos, qui dotibus naturalibus, & spiritualibus & authoritate pollent minùs aptè & minùs statui N.T. convenienter impositio, Ecclesiastorum officiorum administratores sibi appropriârunt,atque ita hac & aliis artibus sensim sine sensu adhibitis effecerunt,ut à longo tempore aliud quasi hominum genus videantur) Populúmque Romanum. Ita Pontifices Romanos complures electos esse,ne ipsa quidem diffitebitur cæterùm huic mori,juxta quem etiam populus ad electionem etiam Pontificum Romanorum eligendo concurrebat, infensa impudentia. Hinc Bellarminus l.1. de Cler. cap.9. de electione Pontificum Romanorum agens, non tantùm secundum per Episcopos eligendi modum, postulato testimonio & consensu Cleri & populi, obtinuisse, & hunc modum antiquissimum satis diu durâsse, affirmat, eúmque testimonio Cypriani l.1. epist.4. tali; Apud nos & fere per universas provincias tenetur, ut ad ordinationes rite celebrandas, ad eam plebem, cui prapositus ordinatur, Episcopi ejus provincia proximi quique conveniant, & Episcopus deligatur plebe presente, qua singulorum vitam plenissimè novit & unius cujusque actum de ejus conversatione perspexit; confirmat; sed & tertium (qui tamen duo modi conveniunt, & confundit Bellarminus ordinationem sive consecrationem cum electione, quarum illa semper ab Ecclesiæ, sive ejusdem, sive vicinarum Rectoribus, hæc à Clero & populo simul peracta fuit) subjungit, quo factum, ut eligeret Clerus & populus Civitatis, qui eligendi modus in usu fuerit tempore Chrysostomi, Ambrosii, Augustini, Leonis, Gregorii, ut pateat ex locis supra citatis.
units.tr: XVII. This was the second form of electing the Roman Pontiffs: by the clergy (a word which, from the beginning and by the force of its meaning, belongs to any faithful persons, since it signifies a lot and inheritance, as the faithful people of God is; compare 1 Pet. 5:3), and by the common people, a name which was rather unsuitably and less agreeably to the state of the New Testament applied to the common people, and which the administrators of ecclesiastical offices appropriated to themselves, even among those who excel in natural and spiritual gifts and authority. By this and other arts, gradually and without anyone noticing, they brought it about that for a long time they have seemed to be a different kind of men. (The Roman people also took part.) Even they will not deny that several Roman Pontiffs were elected in this way; but this custom, according to which the people also gathered for the election of the Roman Pontiffs, was held with unbounded impudence. Hence Bellarmine, book 1 on the clergy, chapter 9, treating the election of the Roman Pontiffs, asserts that not only did the second mode of election, by bishops, obtain, after the testimony and consent of clergy and people had been sought, but that this most ancient mode lasted long enough. He confirms this by the testimony of Cyprian, book 1, letter 4, which runs thus: Among us, and in nearly all the provinces, it is held that, in order to celebrate ordinations properly, the bishops nearest in that province should come together to the people over whom the ordained person is to be set, and the bishop is chosen with the people present, who know the life of each man most fully and have carefully observed each one's conduct. But he also adds a third mode (though these two modes do agree, and Bellarmine confuses ordination or consecration with election, of which the former was always carried out by the rulers of the Church, either of the same church or of neighbouring churches, and the latter by clergy and people together), by which the clergy and people of the city elected. He says this mode of electing was in use at the time of Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Leo and Gregory, as is clear from the passages cited above.

units.la: XVIII. Istum autem per populum etiam eligendi modum non tantùm illo tempore, sed & diu ante & diu post in usu fuisse ex sequentibus patet. De Cornelii quippe electione Cyprianus l.4. ep. 2. & l.3. ep. 13. ait, eum de plebis, qua tunc affuerit, suffragio factum esse. Presbyteri verò Romani ad Honorium Imperatorem, se, participato cum Christiana plebe consilio, acclamatione totius populi ac consensu meliorum civitatis Bonifacium I. elegisse, scribunt. Sic & Honorius idem inter ep. Bonif. lege sanxit, permansurum esse, duobus competitoribus exclusis, quem ex numero Clericorum, novâ ordinatione, divinum judicium & universitatis consensus elegerit. Eodem modo Symmachus in Romano Concilio decrevit, ut, si studia cœperint esse diversa eorum, de quibus certamen emersevit, vincat sententia plurimorum. Pariter Bonifacius III. in Synodo, referente Anastasio in vita & dist.79. c. Nullus 2. constituit; ut tertio die depositionis, adunato clero & filiis Ecclesia, tunc electio fieret, & quem quisque voluerit, haberet licentiam sibi eligendi Sacerdotem. Non minùs, testante Platina in Benedicto II. ad eam nuper electum Constantinus Imperator sanctionem misit, ut quem demceps clerus, populus, exercitúsque Romanus in Pontificem delegisset &c. Cujus quoq; Successor Johannes V. teste Anastasio in vita, à tota generalitate creatus est; Similiter, qui huic successerunt, Conon, Sergius I. Hadrianus II. & alii multi, ut habent Anastasius & Platina. Porrò Florus, qui nona post Christum ætate scribebat ap. Bar. in append. an.
units.tr: XVIII. That this mode of election by the people was in use not only at that time, but also long before and long after, is clear from what follows. Concerning the election of Cornelius, Cyprian, book 4, letter 2, and book 3, letter 13, says that he was made bishop by the vote of the people who were present at that time. The Roman presbyters, writing to the Emperor Honorius, say that they had chosen Boniface I, with the advice of the Christian people taken into account, by the acclamation of the whole people and the consent of the better men of the city. So too Honorius himself, in a law among the letters of Boniface, decreed that the one whom the divine judgment and the consent of the whole body had chosen from the number of the clergy, by a new ordination, should remain in office, the two rivals being excluded. In the same way Symmachus decreed in the Roman council that, if their zeal began to differ on the matter over which the dispute had arisen, the opinion of the majority should prevail. Likewise Boniface III, in a synod, as Anastasius reports in his Life and in Dist. 79, c. Nullus 2, ordained that on the third day after the death, with the clergy and the sons of the Church gathered together, the election should then take place, and each man should have the liberty to choose the priest he wished. No less, as Platina bears witness in the life of Benedict II, the Emperor Constantine sent a sanction to that newly elected Pope, that whomever the clergy, people and Roman army should henceforth nominate as Pontiff, etc. Anastasius, in his Life, testifies that his successor John V was created by the whole body. Similarly those who followed him, Conon, Sergius I, Hadrian II and many others, as Anastasius and Platina record. Moreover Florus, who was writing in the ninth age after Christ, testifies in Baronius in the appendix to the year

units.la: 883. testatur, ex sacrorum Canonum authoritate & consuetudine Ecclesiastica, juxta dispositionem divinæ legis & traditionem Apostolicam, quem communis & concors Cleri & totius Plebis consensus elegerit, locum obtinere, & in Romana Ecclesia usque in præsentem diem solo dispositionis judicio & fidelium suffragio, legitimos Pontifices consecrari. Qua ætate etiam Benedictum III. à Clero & populo electum esse Platina in vita perhibet. Postea autem Lotharius Ludovici filius & locum tenens in reformatione Romæ, circa Papæ electionem mandavit, ut soli Romani, quos antiqua consuetudo firmârat, Papam eligerent; nowturba adventitiorum. Ottonem eâdem ratione Clero & populo electionem reliquisse, ex Platina in Leone VIII. cognoscimus. Nono verò hujus nominis ab Imperatore electo, tradente Platina in Vita, Monachi quidam obvii facti persuaserunt, ut depositio Pontificali habitu Romam privatus ingrederetur, dicentes, ad Clerum populumque Romanum eligendi potestatem pertinere. Ipse quoque Nicol. II. dist.23. cap.1. prædecessorum suorum aliorumque SS. Patrum autoritate statuit, ut Cardinalibus reliquus Clerus & populus ad consensum novæ electionis accedat; qui &, si pravorum atque iniquorum hominum ita perversitas invaluerit, ut pura, sincera, atque gratuita in urbe fieri non possit electio, Cardinales Episcopos, cum religiosis clericis, Catholicisque laicis, licet paucis, jus potestatis eligendi Apostolicæ sedis Pontificem, ubi congruere viderint, obtinere voluit. Præter quos Cardinales Episcopos Petrus Damiani de electione Papæ ap Bar. ad an. 1061. n. 18. Cleri assensum & populi favorem requirit. Ut & Gregorii VII. electio in Regestr. Epistolarum Greg. VII. init. consentientibus etiam plurimis turbis utriusque sexus, diversique ordinis acclamantibus facta perhibetur, cum interrogationibus & responsionibus; Placet vobis? Placet. Vultis eum? Volumus. Laudatis eum? Laudamus; Qui & Robertum Calabriæ Ducem juramento adegit, ut, secundum quod monitus fuerit à melioribus Cardinalibus, Clericis Romanis, & Laicis, adjuvaret, ut Papa eligatur &c.
