Cujus quoque successor Victor III. à Clero & populo factus l.3. c.65. 66.67. Guiberti Antipapæ promotionem l. c. c.71. reprehendens Apostolicæ sedis invasorem effectum esse scribit, contra præcepta Evangelica, contra Prophetarum, Apostolorumque decreta, contra Canonum & Romanorum Pontificum jura: nullo Cardinalium Episcoporum præcedente judicio, nullo Romani Cleri approbante suffragio: nullo devoti populi requisito consensu &c. Hujus autem Successor Urbanus II. juxta Chronici Cassinensis l.4. c.2. à Cardinalibus Episcopis, Abbatibus, Clero & populo populo electionem suam habuit. Et tandem Gelasius II. secundùm Platinam, in Paschali, & Callistus II. secundùm Pandulphum ap. Bar. ad an. Chr. 1119. communi consensu Cardinalium & populi facti sunt Episcopi. Ut sic per undecim secula Romani Pontifices, & non tantùm Chrysostomi &c. ut Bellarminus ait, tempore, à Clero & populo simul, licèt cum aliqua subinde variatione & paulatim tandem decrescente populi potestate electi sint.
units.tr: 883. testifies that by the authority of the sacred canons and ecclesiastical custom, according to the arrangement of divine law and apostolic tradition, whoever is chosen by the common and united consent of the clergy and the whole people holds the place, and in the Roman Church, down to the present day, legitimate Popes are consecrated by the sole judgment of the disposition and the suffrage of the faithful. At that period Platina in his life also reports that Benedict III was elected by the clergy and people. Afterwards, however, Lothair, son of Louis and vicar in the reform of Rome, ordered concerning the election of the Pope that only the Romans, whom ancient custom had established, should elect the Pope, not the crowd of outsiders. From Platina in the life of Leo VIII we learn that Otto left the election in the same way to the clergy and people. When Emperor Nicholas IX of that name was chosen, Platina reports in his Life that certain monks who met him persuaded him to enter Rome as a private man, laying aside the pontifical dress, saying that the power of electing belongs to the clergy and the Roman people. Nicholas II himself, dist. 23, cap. 1, by the authority of his predecessors and of other holy Fathers decreed that the rest of the clergy and people should join the cardinals in consenting to the new election; and he further wished that, if the perversity of wicked and iniquitous men should so prevail that a pure, sincere and free election could not be held in the city, the cardinal bishops, together with religious clergy and Catholic laymen, though few, should obtain the right of electing the Pope of the Apostolic See, wherever they judged it fitting. Besides these cardinal bishops, Peter Damian, on the election of the Pope, ad an. 1061, n. 18 in Baronius, requires the assent of the clergy and the favour of the people. So too the election of Gregory VII is said to have been made in the Register of the Epistles of Gregory VII at the beginning, with very many crowds of both sexes and of various orders acclaiming, with questions and responses: Does it please you? It pleases. Do you want him? We want him. Do you praise him? We praise him. He also bound Robert, Duke of Calabria, by oath that, as he should be advised by the better cardinals, the Roman clergy and the laity, he would help that a Pope be elected, etc. His successor Victor III, made by the clergy and people, book 3, chapters 65, 66, 67, in rebuking the promotion of the antipope Guibert (ibid., ch. 71), writes that he had become an invader of the Apostolic See, against the precepts of the Gospel, against the decrees of the Prophets and Apostles, against the canons and the rights of the Roman Pontiffs: no judgment of the cardinal bishops preceding, no approving suffrage of the Roman clergy, no requested consent of the devout people, etc. His successor Urban II, according to the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, book 4, chapter 2, had his election from the cardinal bishops, abbots, clergy and people. And finally Gelasius II, according to Platina in Paschalis, and Callistus II, according to Pandulf ad an. 1119 in Baronius, were made bishops by the common consent of the cardinals and the people. Thus for eleven centuries the Roman Pontiffs, and not only in the time of Chrysostom, etc., as Bellarmine says, were chosen by the clergy and people together, though with some variation from time to time and with the power of the people gradually declining.

units.la: XIX. Quod & aliorum in sedibus aliis Episcoporum per tot secula exemplis illustrare proclive foret; Sed malumus in exemplis Scripturæ, & quoad reliqua, testimoniis generalibus subsistere, atque ita non tam de facto, quàm verò de facti authoritate & jure dispicere. Scriptura nos docet, fidelibus, de quorum coetu dictum: Dic Ecclesiæ; quibus promissum; Quicquid ligaveritis &c. quibus promissus consolator spiritus, Spiritus veritatis, eos ducturus in omnem veritatem Joh. XVI. 13. à Deo (ad magnum à pusillo) Hebr. VIII. 12. doctis Joh. VI. 45. unctionis participibus 1. Joh. II. 20. Dei viri filius, Rom. IX 26. generi electo, Sacerdotio regali, genti sanctæ, acquisitionis populo, 1. Petr. II. 2. non insciis, sed cooperantibus, Rectores Ecclesiasticos electos esse. Nam simul ac ascendentis in coelos Servatoris triumphali spectaculo animati Apostoli de sufficiendo, qui Judæ locum impleret, cogitârunt, quotquot Christo nomen dederant, ad consilii participationem vocantur, nec Apostoli, qui publicâ jam pro Domino legatione functi erant, Collegam vel elegerunt, vel Deo obtulerunt, sed omnes προσευξάμενοι ἔδωκαν κλήρους, cùm orâssent, sortes jecerunt Act. I. 24. 26. Sic & cùm exorto murmure Apostoli Diaconos septem μαρτυρουμένους bono testimonio ornatos eligendos suaderent, ἤρεσεν ὁ λόγος ἐνώπιον παντὸς τοῦ πλήθους καὶ ἐξελέξαντο &c. placuit sermo coram omni multitudine, & elegerunt &c. Act. VI. 1. 3. 5. Pariter in Ecclesia Antiochena Prophetarum & Doctorum luminibus collustrata de segregandis Barnaba & Paulo Spiritus S. mandatum ad universum coetum directum fuisse, Act. XIII. 1. 3. legimus, & quòd fideles jejunantes, orantes & manus segregatis per praepositos suos imponentes omnes dimiserint illos. Qui & Act. XIV. 23. Presbyteros, χειροτονήσαντες per suffragia Ecclesiis praefecisse dicuntur. Paulus autem 2. Cor. VIII. 19. 23. fratris, qui suffragiis ab Ecclesiis delectus sit peregrinationis suæ socius meminit. A praeceptoris autem praxi non diversam fuisse discipuli Titi, licèt ex Tit. I. 5. cum authoritate electionibus eum praefuisse colligi possit, conveniens est; ut illa
units.tr: XIX. This could also easily be illustrated by examples of other bishops in other sees over so many centuries. But we prefer to rest on the examples of Scripture and, as to the rest, on general testimonies, and so to inquire not so much into the fact as into the authority and right of the fact. Scripture teaches us that the faithful, of whose assembly it is said, Tell it to the Church, and to whom it is promised, Whatever you bind, etc., and to whom is promised the Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who will lead them into all truth (John 16:13), from God (from the greatest to the least) (Heb. 8:11), taught by God (John 6:45), sharers in the anointing (1 John 2:20), the sons of the living God (Rom. 9:26), a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's possession (1 Pet. 2:9), were not ignorant but took part in choosing their ecclesiastical rulers. For as soon as the Apostles, inspired by the triumphant sight of the Saviour ascending into heaven, thought about filling up the place of Judas, all who had given their name to Christ were called to share in the counsel. Nor did the Apostles, who had already discharged a public embassy for the Lord, either choose a colleague themselves or offer one to God; rather, all of them, after praying, gave lots, when they had prayed, they cast lots (Acts 1:24, 26) [proseuxamenoi edōkan klērous]. So too, when a murmur arose, the Apostles advised that seven deacons, men of good report [martyroumenous], should be chosen, and the saying pleased the whole multitude, and they chose, etc. (Acts 6:1, 3, 5) [ēresen ho logos enōpion pantos tou plēthous kai exelexanto]. Likewise, we read that in the Church of Antioch, illumined by the lights of prophets and teachers, the Holy Spirit's command for setting apart Barnabas and Paul was directed to the whole assembly (Acts 13:1, 3), and that the faithful, fasting, praying and laying hands on those set apart, through their leaders all dismissed them. They are also said (Acts 14:23) to have appointed elders by vote [cheirotonēsantes] over the churches. Paul also mentions (2 Cor. 8:19, 23) a brother who was chosen by the votes of the churches as his companion on his journey. That the practice of the disciple Titus was no different from that of his teacher is fitting, although from Titus 1:5 it can be gathered that he presided over the elections with authority; as also

units.la: Alios; Ex Sacris; illa quoque plebis in eligendo potestas ex eo,quòd veros pastores sequi, falsos fugere Joh.X. Episcopus etiam ab extraneis, 1.Tim.III. 7. multò magis ab Ecclesia bonum testimonium habere debet, & Ecclesiæ Minister 1.Cor.XII.21. 1.Petr.V.3. est,fluit. Et Scripturarum evidentiæ intuitu Azorius Jes. p. 2. l. 6. c. 14. fateri coactus fuit, negari non posse,ritum esse ab Apostolis servatum, quo ministros Ecclesiæ præficiebant, populi testimonio approbatos, Act.1. 6.13. &14. Quem ritum & formam Ecclesia diu servârit, quia Apostolorum exemplum sequi voluerit. Quòd autem eosdem Apostolos Episcopos à se creatos nonnunquam ad populos absentes & infideles misisse (quod de Evangelistis extraordinariis quoque Ministris largimur) Bellarminus causatur, ad illud Cardinalis Cufanus l. 2. optimè respondet; Non concladi, (ex eo, quod Apostoli fecerunt erga infideles:) Ecclesiis aliquando provisum sine electione, quia tunc non fuerunt Ecclesia, missi fuerunt ad ædificandas Ecclesias, & ideò electio locum habere non potuit: quia Ecclesia eligens tunc defuit. Unde illi missi gerentes figuram Christi, secundi Adæ,ex costa sua, scilicet divini verbi, sibi Evam ædificârunt, quam desponsaverant: & sic Eva genita posthac non dabatur nisi sponsus desideratus.
units.tr: the others; from the Sacred Writings: that power of the people in choosing is also derived from this, that the true shepherds are to be followed, and the false to be fled from (John 10). A bishop too must have a good report even from outsiders (1 Tim. 3:7), and much more must he have it from the Church, and he is a minister of the Church (1 Cor. 12:21; 1 Pet. 5:3). And by the evidence of the Scriptures, Azor (Institutiones, part 2, book 6, ch. 14) was compelled to confess that it cannot be denied that the custom was kept by the Apostles by which they set ministers over the Church, approved by the testimony of the people (Acts 1:6, 13, 14). That custom and form the Church kept for a long time, because it wished to follow the example of the Apostles. But as to Bellarmine's charge that the same Apostles sometimes sent bishops whom they had created to absent and unbelieving peoples (which we also concede of the extraordinary evangelist ministers), Cardinal Cusanus answers this well in book 2: It does not follow (from what the Apostles did towards unbelievers) that churches were sometimes provided without election, because then there were no churches; they were sent to build churches, and so election could not take place, because the electing Church was then lacking. Hence those sent, bearing the figure of Christ the second Adam, built Eve for themselves out of their side, that is, out of the divine word, to whom they had become betrothed; and so, once Eve was born, a husband was given only when desired.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Sed audiamus etiam testimonia & statuta Ecclesiastica; Primò Petrum,vel illum potiùs, qui in Constitutionibus Apostolicis (quarum authoritas saltem ad hominem est Apostolica, & quæ saltem indicant morem vetustum;) personam Petri assumit; Ita l. 8. c. 2. legimus : Primus igitur ego Petrus dico, Episcopum ordinari debere ab omni populo delectum: quo nominato & approbato, convenientes populus, cum Collegio Presbyterorum & Episcopis, qui adsunt, in die Dominico, præcipuus ex omnibus interroget Presbyteros & plebem, quis sit,quem petant in Rectorem. In quo testimonio etiam observari potest,authorem mirâ subtilitate non distinguere cum Legistis inter electionem, nominationem, postulationem, præsentationem, sed omnia confundere. Pergimus ad Ignatium, qui ad totam Ecclesiam Philadelphensem epist.6. scribit: Decet itaque vos ut Dei Ecclesiam eligere Episcopum &c. Audiatur post illum testis indubitatus & luculentissimus Cyprianus, ad cujus Epist. 68, in annot. Pammelius Pontificius multis de electione per suffragia plebis agit; Ita autem sanctus ille Martyr l. 1. epist. 3. pronuntiat; illum demum esse legitimum Episcopum, qui post divinum judicium, post populi suffragium, post Coëpiscoporum consensum suam Cathedram obtineat; Ibidem eum populi universi suffragio in pace deligi docet; Epist. autem 4. sequentia habet: Nec sibi plebs blandiatur, quasi immunis à contagione esse delicti possit, cum sacerdote peccatore communicans & ad injustum atq; illicitum praepositi sui Episcopatum consensum suum commodans, à peccatore praeposito separare se debet, nec se ad sacrilegi sacerdotis sacrificia miscere, cum ipsa maxime habeat potestatem vel eligendi dignos sacerdotes, vel indignos recusandi. Quod & ipsum videmus de divina authoritate descendere &c. Et postquam loca Act. I. & VI. supra allata citâsset, subjungit: Propter quod diligenter de traditione divina & Apostolica observatione servandum est & tenendum, quod & apud vos quoque & fere per Provincias universas tenetur, ut ad ordinationes rite celebrandas ad eam plebem, cui praepositus ordinatur, Episcopi ejusdem provincia proximi quique conveniant &c. Legat, cui lubet, similia habentem Origenem hom.6. in Lev. quae ponitur 8. quaest.1. cap. licet, & apud Cyrillum l. 6. in Levit. Item hom.22. in Num. Sed omnino hic quoque audiendi sunt Concilii Niceni Patres, qui cap.6. decreverunt; Si communi omnium electioni, quae & rationi consentanea & ex regula Ecclesiastica facta sit, duo vel tres propter suam, quâ delectantur, contentionem contradicunt, vincere debere plurium suffragia. Imò expressius apud Theod. hist. l.1.c.9. ad Episcopos Ægypti scribunt: Unus ex illis modò idoneus videatur, & populus illum eligat, Episcopúsque Alexandria ei suffragetur, atque adeò populi electionem confirmet, in locum succedat demortui. Quemadmodum etiam Constantinus Imperator circa idem tempus, referente Euf. de Vita Const. l.3. cap.58.59.60. populo Antiocheno & Episcopis mandavit, ut loco Eusebii Caesareensis, qui transire noluerat, alium sibi canonicè de more eligerent; Et Athanasius strenuus Christi in Concilio, imò ante & post Athleta Apol.2. ubi ad Ecclesiasticum Canonem & Apostolicam traditionem provocat, & ad Orthod. eundem morem confirmat; Et iidem, qui Niceae antea congregati erant Patres in Concilio Sardicensi, juxta textum Graecum, cap.5. Dist.65. sin. in annot. eundem manifeste suppositerunt; Quod & fecerant prius Romanae Synodi sub Sylvestro, prior c.5. ab omni Ecclesia, nullo de membris intercedente, & omni Ecclesia conveniente, eligendum esse statuens; Posterior decernens, ut, si probatus fuerit dignus, & vota populi & Cleri convenerint, canonicè Episcopus consecretur.
units.tr: But let us also hear the testimonies and ecclesiastical statutes. First, Peter, or rather the one who in the Apostolic Constitutions (whose authority is at least that of a human Apostolic writer, and which at least indicate an ancient custom) assumes the person of Peter. So we read in book 8, chapter 2: I, Peter, therefore first say that a bishop ought to be ordained, chosen by the whole people. When he has been named and approved, the people, gathered together on the Lord's day with the college of presbyters and the bishops who are present, shall have the most eminent of all of them ask the presbyters and the people who it is whom they seek as their ruler. In this testimony one may also observe that the author, with remarkable subtlety, does not distinguish, like the lawyers, between election, nomination, postulation and presentation, but confuses them all. We go on to Ignatius, who writes to the whole Church of Philadelphia, epistle 6: It is fitting therefore that you, as God's Church, choose a bishop, etc. After him let us hear the unquestioned and most lucid witness, Cyprian. Concerning his Epistle 68, in the notes, Pamelius the Papist treats at length of election by the votes of the people. That holy martyr, in book 1, epistle 3, declares: that he is at last the lawful bishop who, after the divine judgment, after the suffrage of the people, and after the consent of his fellow bishops, obtains his chair. There too he teaches that he is chosen by the suffrage of the whole people in peace. In Epistle 4 he has the following: Nor let the people flatter themselves that they can be free from the contagion of sin, when they communicate with a sinful priest and lend their consent to the unjust and unlawful episcopate of their appointed head. They ought to separate themselves from a sinful head, nor mix themselves into the sacrifices of a sacrilegious priest, since the people above all have the power either of choosing worthy priests or of refusing unworthy ones. We see that this too comes down from divine authority, etc. And after citing the passages from Acts 1 and 6 above, he adds: Therefore what has been handed down by divine tradition and observed by the Apostles is to be diligently kept and held, which is also held among you and almost throughout all the provinces: that for the proper celebration of ordinations, the bishops of the same province nearest to that people over which the ruler is ordained should gather together, etc. Let whoever wishes read Origen, who has similar things in Homily 6 on Leviticus, which is cited in Distinction 8, question 1, chapter "licet", and Cyril in book 6 on Leviticus; likewise Homily 22 on Numbers. But here too the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea must certainly be heard, who in chapter 6 decreed: If, in a common election of all, made both in accordance with reason and according to the ecclesiastical rule, two or three contradict out of their own contentiousness, in which they take delight, the suffrages of the majority ought to prevail. Even more explicitly, in Theodoret, History, book 1, chapter 9, they write to the bishops of Egypt: Let one of them now seem suitable, and let the people choose him, and let the bishop of Alexandria give his suffrage to him, and so confirm the election of the people, and let him succeed in the place of the deceased. Just so the Emperor Constantine, at about the same time, as Eusebius reports in Life of Constantine, book 3, chapters 58, 59, 60, commanded the people and bishops of Antioch that, in place of Eusebius of Caesarea, who had refused to move, they should canonically and according to custom choose another for themselves. And Athanasius, the vigorous athlete of Christ, both in the Council and even before and after it, in his Apology 2, where he appeals to the ecclesiastical canon and apostolic tradition, and in the Orthodox work, confirms the same custom. And the same Fathers who had earlier met at Nicaea, in the Council of Sardica, according to the Greek text, chapter 5, Distinction 65, in the notes, clearly presupposed the same practice. The Roman synods under Silvester had also done this earlier: the former, chapter 5, decreeing that a bishop is to be chosen by the whole Church, no member interceding, and with the whole Church assembling; the latter, decreeing that, if he has been approved as worthy, and the wishes of the people and clergy agree, he is to be consecrated canonically as bishop.

units.la: XXI. Jam verò post Concilium Nicenum & ad nostra tempora, eundem perpetuò morem electionis per Clerum & populum obtinuisse, ex Patribus, Conciliis, Juribus & Romanorum Pontificum
units.tr: XXI. Now, that after the Council of Nicaea, down to our own times, the same constant custom of election by clergy and people was maintained could be proved at length from the Fathers, the Councils, the laws, and the decrees and attestations of the Roman Pontiffs,

units.la: Post Concilium Nicenum; tificum decretis atque attestationibus, Pontificiorúmque confessionibus prolixè comprobari posset. Sed pauca tantùm notabimus paucorum ex plurimis. Digna autem sunt, quæ in prima acie ponantur Ambrosii ep.82. verba; Merito vir tantus evasit, de S. Eusebio loquitur, quem omnis Ecclesia elegit, merito creditum, quód divino esset electus judicio, quem omnes postulavissent. Quare etiam vult, ut omninò populi consensus expectetur, nec opera pretium esse, ut quis Episcopus constituatur, si de illo suscipiendo plebs tota non consenserit: Vix enim, inquit, inter consentientes onus Episcopale sustinetur, quantò minùs inter dissentientes sustinebitur: Hinc etiam Vercellensibus tanquam Provinciæ Metropolitanus Episcopum ordinare noluit, nisi prius tota illa Ecclesia in unum consentiret. Ambrosii autem discipulus Augustinus epist.204. populum etiam Episcopos rapere, nedum eligere solere, Donato objicere potuit. Et de illa paulò præcedente, atque mox sequente ætate diligenter notanda omninò est hæc Petri Soti propositio apud Azorium l.2. i.3.c.30. Antiquissimi illi Episcopi, Cyprianus, Augustinus à Rom. Pontifice nihil sibi arbitrabantur in suis diœcesibus commissum esse; electione plebis & ordinatione comprovincialium quasi ministerio quodam putabant se suscipere auctoritatem. Et rectè non minùs Mezeræus Historiographus Gallicus de primis illis seculis: L'election des Prêtres se faisoit par le clergé de leur Eglise & par le peuple; Sacerdotum electio fiebat per Clerum Eccesiæ illorum & per populum. Item: La voix du peuple passoit en cela pour une vocation de Dieu; Vox populi habebatur ad instar vocationis Divinæ.
units.tr: After the Council of Nicaea; of the Pontiffs' decrees and attestations, and from the confessions of the Papists. But we shall note only a few of the very many. Worthy of being placed in the front rank, however, are the words of Ambrose, letter 82: He rightly turned out to be such a great man, he says of St. Eusebius, whom the whole Church chose, rightly believed to have been chosen by divine judgment, since all had asked for him. Therefore he also wishes that the consent of the people be altogether awaited, and that it is not worth while for anyone to be made bishop if the whole people has not agreed to accept him. For, he says, the episcopal burden is scarcely borne among those who agree, much less will it be borne among those who dissent. Hence also he refused to ordain a bishop for the Vercellenses, as their metropolitan, unless first that whole Church agreed as one. Augustine, the disciple of Ambrose, in letter 204, could object to Donatus that the people were accustomed to seize bishops, let alone choose them. And concerning that period, a little before and soon after, this proposition of Pedro de Soto, cited in Azor, book 2, part 3, chapter 30, is certainly to be carefully noted: Those most ancient bishops, Cyprian and Augustine, did not think that anything had been entrusted to them in their dioceses by the Roman Pontiff; they thought they took up their authority by the election of the people and the ordination by fellow provincials, as by a certain ministry. And the French historiographer Mézeray is no less correct about those first centuries: The election of priests was made by the clergy of their church and by the people; the election of priests was made by the clergy of their church and by the people. Likewise: The voice of the people was regarded in this as a vocation from God; the voice of the people was held to be like a divine vocation.

units.la: XXII. Progrediamur ad Caroli M. & Ludovici Filii, ac sequentia tempora; Ita statuerunt Capitul. l.1. c.84. ponitur Dist.63. c. 34. Sacrorum Canonum, ajunt, non ignari, ut in Dei nomine sancta Ecclesia suo liberius potiretur honore, assensum ordini Ecclesiastico prabuimus: ut scilicet Episcopi per electionem Clericorum & populi secundùm statuta Canonum de propria Diœcesi eligantur. Cui Imperiali decreto praxin conformem fuisse ex epistola Hincmari ad Carolum, quæ apud Bar. ad an.813. n. 27. 28. habetur, apparet; Et vel maximè ex Floro satis laudato circa illa tempora Authore, qui ap. Bar. ad an. 813. in append. ait; Manifestum esse omnibus, qui in Ecclesia Dei Sacerdotale officium administrent, quae sint illa, quae in ordinatione Episcopali & Sacrorum Canonum authoritas & consuetudo Ecclesiastica juxta dispositionem Divinæ legis & traditionem Apostolicam jubeat observari, videlicet, ut pastore defuncto & sede vacante, unus de Clero Ecclesiæ, quem communis Temporibus Caroli M. Ludovici Filii, ac sequentibus; munis & concors ejusdem Cleri & totius plebis consensus elegerit, & publico decreto celebriter ac solenniter designârit,legitimo Episcoporum numero consecratus, locum decedentis Antistitis valeat obtinere, nec dubitetur, divino judicio & dispositione firmatum, quod ab Ecclesia Dei tam sancto ordine & legitima observatione fuerit celebratum.
units.tr: XXII. Let us proceed to the time of Charlemagne and his son Louis, and the following times. Thus they decreed in the Capitularies, book 1, chapter 84, which is placed in Distinction 63, chapter 34 of the Sacred Canons: We, not unaware of the sacred canons, have granted our assent to the ecclesiastical order, so that the holy Church might more freely possess its honour in the name of God: namely, that bishops be chosen by the election of the clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, from their own diocese. That practice conformed to this imperial decree appears from Hincmar's letter to Charles, which is found in Baronius at the year 813, nn. 27, 28. And most of all from Florus, an author of those times, sufficiently praised, who in Baronius at the year 813, in the appendix, says: It is manifest to all who administer the priestly office in the Church of God what those things are which the authority of the sacred canons and ecclesiastical custom, according to the arrangement of divine law and apostolic tradition, command to be observed in the ordination of a bishop: namely, that when the pastor has died and the see is vacant, one of the clergy of the church, whom the common and harmonious consent of the same clergy and of the whole people has chosen, and has solemnly and publicly designated by a public decree, may, when consecrated by the lawful number of bishops, be able to obtain the place of the deceased prelate; and let it not be doubted that what has been celebrated by the Church of God in so holy an order and lawful observance is confirmed by divine judgment and disposition.

units.la: XXIII. Accedit nubes testium in Conciliis illorum & sequentium temporum. Nempe adstipulantur Arelatense II. Carthaginense III. & Constantinopolitanum II. Generale, Aurelianense II. & III. Arvernense, Aurelianense V. Canones Græcarum Synodorum, Cabilonense, Quini sexta Synodus, Valentinum, Ticinense, Bellovacense, Rhemense, alia, quæ & plebibus invitis obtrudi noluerunt Episcopos, & potestatem fecerunt insciis ordinatos rejiciendi; Ipsi etiam Pontifices Romani in omnibus tum consentientes Siricius, Bonifacius I. Cœlestinus, Leo, (cujus Dist.62. hæc sunt verba: Nulla ratio finit, ut inter Episcopos habeantur, qui nec à Clericis sunt electi, nec à plebibus expetiti &c. quæ verba etiam dist.23. c. 1. Nicolaus II. Seculi undecimi demum Pontifex de Electione Pontificum agens sua fecit, similibúsque etiam præcipientibus, confirmavit severè, contrariantem perpetuo cum suis Anathematibus, tanquam à liminibus sancta Ecclesia Dei separatum, Antichristum, invasorem & destructorem totius Christianitatis &c. subjiciens;) Hilarius, Gelasius, Hormisda, Agapetus, Stephanus, Pelagius, Gregorius M. moris hujus,quem & sæpè inculcavit, observantissimus, Bonifacius III. cujus hac in re decretum unâ cum Platinæ ἀπαχεί- hic apponi maximè meretur; Voluit nempe, electionem Episcopi à Clero pariter & populo fieri, à Principe verò & Papa approbari. De quo ita judicat Platina. Sancta institutio & pernecessaria, nostris præsertim temporibus, quibus in pejus omnia dilabuntur: Est enim simile vero, Clerum & populum, ac Principem civitatis, si libera suffragia sunt, non alium electuros, quàm qui merito possit & debeat aliis præesse: Nicolaus I. Adrianus II. Johannes VIII. Gregorius VII. Innocentius II. Urbanus II. Alexander III. Innocentius III. qui circa annum 1177. sedit.
units.tr: XXIII. A cloud of witnesses is added from the councils of those and later times. Indeed there support him the Second Council of Arles, the Third of Carthage, and the Second General Council of Constantinople; the Second and Third Councils of Orléans, the Council of Clermont, the Fifth Council of Orléans, the canons of the Greek synods, the councils of Chalon, Quinisext, Valence, Ticino, Beauvais, Reims, and others, which did not wish bishops to be forced upon unwilling peoples, and granted power to reject those ordained without their knowledge. The Roman Pontiffs themselves also, all agreeing: Siricius, Boniface I, Celestine, Leo (whose words in Distinction 62 are these: No reason allows that those be counted as bishops who were chosen neither by the clergy nor sought by the peoples, etc., which words are also in Distinction 23, chapter 1); Nicholas II, the Pontiff of the eleventh century, when he dealt with the election of Pontiffs, adopted these words as his own, and, with similar commands, strictly confirmed them, subjecting the one opposing them, with his perpetual anathemas, as separated from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, an Antichrist, an invader and destroyer of all Christianity, etc.; Hilary, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Agapetus, Stephen, Pelagius, Gregory the Great, most observant of this custom, which he also often impressed; Boniface III, whose decree in this matter, together with Platina's, most deserves to be set down here: He wished, namely, that the election of a bishop be made by the clergy and people alike, and be approved by the prince and the Pope. On which Platina judges thus: A holy and most necessary institution, especially in our times, when all things slide for the worse. For it is like the truth that the clergy and people, and the prince of the state, if the suffrages are free, will choose none other than one who can and ought rightly to preside over others. Nicholas I, Adrian II, John VIII, Gregory VII, Innocent II, Urban II, Alexander III, Innocent III, who sat about the year 1177.

units.la: XXIV. Ex quibus jam patet,ab una parte,quàm non plus æquo nobis largiantur magis ingenui ex Pontificiis partim jam allati, partim adhuc hic adducendi. Cusanus præcipuè Cardinalis,qui sententiam Concilii Basilensis de Concordantia Catholica lib. 2. c. 18. ita interpretatur & suam exponit; Rectores Ecclesiastici per conconsensum jure divino & humano constitui debent; Avitius Papa dixit; Oportet,ut qui omnibus praeesse debet,ab omnibus eligatur Dist.66. Archiep. & quòd nullus detur invitis: quoniam secundùm Leonem, nulla ratio sinit, ut inter Episcopos habeatur non electus. Adhuc enim, ut unum corpus in concordantia constituatur, ex subjectis & praesidente, ratio & naturale jus simul & divinum exigunt, in hac spirituali, matrimoniali unione consensum mutuum, quem ex omnium electione & electi consensu deprehendimus. Episcopus non est, qui non est electus. Plebani etiam & Curati sunt eligendi; Jura ac dicta Sanctorum Patrum loquuntur, nullum ad Praesidentialem curam ordinari debere, nisi electum ab iis, quibus praesidere debet, ut praesidentia originem ab iis habere cognoscat, quibus praeest, & sic absque superbia in amore pascat. Et cap.34. Ex subjectorum electione & consensu radicatur superiorum potestas. Recta regula praerequirit subjectionem liberam Christianorum, cùm ipsi non arctentur extra terminos libertatis; Post quem ponimus Parisienses, qui de Eccles. & Polit. potest. sect.2. ita testantur. Praxi Ecclesiae primitiva & sacris Canonibus exploratissimum est, collationes beneficiorum, sicut nunc eas vocitant, 1400. annis communi jure, hoc est, sacrosanctis electionibus factas. Ratio est, quoniam omnis principatus, quoad vim coactivam ab hominum consensu pendet, ut lex divina & naturalis confirmant. Quibus tandem adjungimus jam supra laudatum Azorium Jesuitam, qui p.2. l.3. c.28. & lib. c. c.14. licèt terminos non satis extendens, fatetur. Veterem ritum ac morem fuisse, Episcopos eligendi, quo plebe praesente imò & ipsius suffragiis aliquando eligebantur: eámque rationem eligendi durâsse usque ad Gregorium I. imò & ad Caroli M. & Ludovici Pii usque tempora perdurâsse. Apostolos praefecisse ministros populi testimonio approbatos: Ecclesiam Apostolorum exemplo, Canones sancivisse, ne Ecclesiarum praefecti eligerentur sine populi suffragio.
units.tr: XXIV. From these things it is now clear, on the one hand, how much more than is fair the more candid Papists grant us, some already cited and some to be adduced here. Cusanus, above all a cardinal, who interprets and sets out the opinion of the Council of Basel in De Concordantia Catholica book 2, chapter 18, puts it thus: Ecclesiastical rulers ought to be appointed by common consent, by divine and human law; Pope Avitus said: It is fitting that he who must preside over all be chosen by all, Dist. 66, Archbishop, and that no one be given to those unwilling; for, according to Leo, no reason allows that one who has not been elected be counted among the bishops. For still, that one body may be constituted in harmony out of subjects and president, reason and natural law together with divine law require, in this spiritual, matrimonial union, a mutual consent, which we discover from the election of all and the consent of the one elected. He is not a bishop who is not elected. Parish priests and curates too are to be elected; the laws and sayings of the holy Fathers speak to this, that no one ought to be ordained to presiding office unless chosen by those over whom he is to preside, so that he may know his authority has its origin in those he presides over, and so may feed them in love without pride. And chapter 34: The power of superiors is rooted in the election and consent of subjects. Right rule requires the free subjection of Christians, since they should not be constrained beyond the limits of liberty. After him we place the Parisians, who in On ecclesiastical and political power, section 2 bear witness thus: By the primitive practice of the Church and the sacred canons it is most thoroughly established that benefices, as they are now called, were conferred for 1400 years under common law, that is, by most sacred elections. The reason is that every principate, as far as its coercive force goes, depends on the consent of men, as divine and natural law confirm. Last we add the Jesuit Azorius, already praised above, who, part 2, book 3, chapter 28, and lib. c. c.14, although not extending the limits sufficiently, admits: that the ancient rite and custom was to elect bishops with the people present, indeed sometimes by their votes; and that this manner of electing lasted until Gregory I, indeed persisted even to the times of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. The Apostles set over the people ministers approved by the people's testimony; following the Apostles' example, the Church's canons decreed that the heads of churches should not be elected without the people's suffrage.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Ab altera verò parte meritò admiramur summam & hîc Bellarmini impudentiam, qui ad fucum Lectori suo faciendum popularem electionem, primò non de jure tantùm, sed & de facto dubiam fecit his verbis: Si quid aliquando in hac re populus potuit; quasi illud non certissimum & evidentissimum esset; secundò loco citato istum eligendi modum ad tempus Chrysostomi, Ambrosii, Augustini, Leonis, Gregorii restringit, quamvis in temporis assignatione etiam sibi contradicere videatur, nam modò docet, paulatim usque ad Leonis & Chrysostomi tempora auctam fuisse populi in electione ne Pastorum potestatem,modò contendit, à Concilio Laodiceno & aliis ante hac tempora, populum ab electione exclusum fuisse. Nos autem contrà probavimus, vel maximè Apostolicis temporibus, quibus insciente populo Pastores electos esse, statuere ausus est, populum suffragiis electiones adjuvâsse, ex illis autem temporibus & ob exemplum Apostolicum secula equidem multa ultra Ambrosii &c. tempus sanctam consuetudinem retinuisse. Tertiò maximam officii popularis circa hæc partem ad testimonium de vita & moribus eligendorum dandum reducit, quod ex allatis clarissimè refutari potest, licèt non difficiteamur, sub finem observati moris, & quia, ut Bellarminus ait, paulatim sublata est populi electio, minorem populi quoad suffragia rationem habitam fuisse. Quartò in quibusdam tantùm locis jus suffragii populum sibi usurpâsse, contendit, cùm contra morem ad provincias fere universas Cyprianus l. c. extendat, & Azorius Jesuita (Tantum Jesuita Jesuita præstat!) l.c. in Africa, Gracia, Hispania & ubique fuisse observatum, doceat, quod & allata testimonia clarissimè ostendunt. Quintò omne illud concessioni & conniventia Pontificum suorum tribuit, forsan eâdem ratione, qua fur aliquis dicere posset, bonorum possessores suâ concessione & conniventiâ antehac hæc aut illa habuisse, & eâdem ratione, qua populus fidelis ante Concilii Constantiensis non-obstantiensia decreta Calicis usum habere potuit. Nempe convenientissima & compendiosissima ad maximas difficultates respondendi ratio est, quam illis porrò commendamus, ut dicant, omnia aliorum jura ante ultima tempora à Pontificum suorum concessione & conniventia orta esse, sic quicquid hodiernis ipsorum moribus & dogmatibus, sic quicquid illorum, quam jactant, absolutæ potestati contrarium & Differt. Præced. contra eam ex antiquitate allatum est, commodè explicare poterunt. Sed ut in illis concessionis & conniventiæ Pontificiæ nec vola, nec vestigium apparet, primi Pontifices eam non prædicârunt, alii eam nunquam agnoverunt; ita & hic, quamvis tandem ad injuriæ populo Dei factæ & faciendæ justificationem ita loqui, & omnia à nutu suo suspendere cœperint, in quo Bellarminus iis assentatur, nihil pro ista concessione & conniventia maximè universalis Ecclesiæ, in qua morem obtinuisse vidimus, deprehendimus, sed plurima in contrarium, talia nempe, quibus consuetudo ista à divina & Apostolica traditione derivata, confirmata, decreta, commendata, & ejus jus varië assertum fuit, ab ipsis etiam, juxta præcedentia, tia, Pontificibus. Qui, si consuetudo tam perversa, rationi, Scripturæ & antiquitati contrarietur, ut Bellarminus cum sociis pertendit, certè eam concedere, & ad eam per tot annorum centurias connivere nullo modo potuissent, sed eam statim pro Pontificiæ authoritatis plenitudine ex tota Ecclesia eliminare debuissent.
units.tr: On the other side, we rightly marvel at the great shamelessness of Bellarmine here, who, to dupe his reader, first made popular election doubtful not only in right but also in fact, with these words: If at any time the people could do anything in this matter; as if that were not most certain and most evident. Secondly, in the passage cited he restricts this manner of electing to the time of Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Leo, Gregory, although in assigning the time he seems even to contradict himself: for now he teaches that the people's share in the election gradually increased until the times of Leo and Chrysostom, and now he contends that from the Council of Laodicea and others before this time, the people had been excluded from the election. We, on the contrary, have proved, above all in apostolic times, when ministers were chosen with the people unaware, and yet he dared to lay down that the people helped elections by their suffrages; and from those times, and because of the apostolic example, many centuries beyond the time of Ambrose etc. kept this holy custom. Thirdly, he reduces the greatest part of the people's duty in these matters to giving testimony about the life and morals of those to be elected, which can be most clearly refuted from what has been adduced, although we do not deny that, toward the end of the observed custom, and because, as Bellarmine says, the people's election was gradually taken away, less regard was had to the people's suffrages. Fourthly, he contends that the people claimed a right of suffrage for themselves only in certain places, whereas Cyprian, loc. cit., extends it, contrary to custom, to almost all provinces, and the Jesuit Azorius (So much does a Jesuit achieve!) loc. cit. teaches that it was observed in Africa, Greece, Spain and everywhere, as the testimonies adduced also very clearly show. Fifthly, he attributes all of that to the concession and connivance of their Popes, perhaps by the same reasoning by which some thief might say that the owners of goods held this or that by their concession and connivance, and by the same reasoning by which the faithful people could have had the use of the cup before the non-obstante decrees of the Council of Constance. Indeed it is the most convenient and most summary way of answering the greatest difficulties, and we commend it to them: let them say that all the rights of others arose, before the latest times, from the concession and connivance of their Popes. So whatever is contrary to their present customs and doctrines, and whatever is alleged from antiquity against that absolute power they boast of, as in the previous Dissertation, they will be able to explain conveniently. But just as in those papal concessions and connivances no wish or trace appears, the first Popes did not proclaim them and others never acknowledged them, so here too: although at last they began to speak thus, to justify the wrong done and to be done to the people of God, and to make everything depend on their nod, in which Bellarmine plays up to them, we find nothing in favour of this concession and connivance of the most universal Church, in which we have seen the custom prevail. We find very many things to the contrary, namely those by which that custom, derived from divine and apostolic tradition, was confirmed, decreed and commended, and its right variously asserted, even by the Popes themselves, as the preceding passages show. If so perverse a custom were contrary to reason, Scripture and antiquity, as Bellarmine with his allies contends, they certainly could not have conceded it and connived at it for so many centuries; they ought rather to have eliminated it at once from the whole Church by the fullness of papal authority.

units.la: XXVI. Sed præter antiquitatem & Apostolicam traditionem, quovis tempore agnitam, perutilis quoque, ut revera est, habita fuit; Id quod jam ex præmissis constare potest, & porrò ex evidenti Azorii Jesuitæ, quod hic subjungere visum est, testimonio. Ex populi electione factum esse l. c. dicit & docet, 1. ne Pastor invitis ovibus præficeretur. 2. ut inter Pastorem & Ecclesiam conjugium spirituale, mutuo amborum consensu contraheretur. 3. ut ab ovibus magis amaretur & coleretur. Non quidem inficias imus, suis & hanc electionis Ministrorum formam incommodis laborare, & abusus ejus, maximè in electione Pontificum, & tot scandalosis Schismatibus, loco suo enumerandis, citò satis notatos, & hinc quoque prætextum immutationi quæsitum esse. Verùm quando humana omnia imperfecta, & aliæ formæ (quod è præcedentibus & sequentibus cognosci poterit) non minoribus incommodis gravantur, & abusus, cui remedium quodammodo inveniri potest, usum Scripturæ & totius antiquitatis exemplis firmatum tollere non debet, vanum illum prætextum, adeóque malè Christianum populum ab electione plane exclusum fuisse apparet. Remedium autem adesse potest, à prudenti Ecclesiasticorum aut Magistratûs fidelis moderamine, & diligenti fidelium de rei, de qua agitur, gravitate, admonitione, inprimis autem à reductione statûs Episcopalis ad pristinam suam formam, quamdiu enim Episcopatus magis onus, quàm honos fuit, quamdiu mundanus fastus abfuit, & mundanarum opum affluxus in ista dignitate ignorabatur, parùm etiam de tot & tantis abusibus inauditum, imò plebi sæpe necessitas impositta fuit, vel invitos trahendi, & cogendi; sed quam primùm venenum divitiarum & honorum terrestrium in Ecclesiam infusum est, potentes certatim ambitione stimulante, animum ad Episcopatus adjecisse & adjicere, mirum non est; ista tolli debent, quoad possunt, non jura populi fidelis.
units.tr: XXVI. But besides antiquity and apostolic tradition, recognized at every time, it was also held, as indeed it is, most useful. This can now be established from what has been said, and further from the clear testimony of the Jesuit Azorius, which it has seemed good to add here. He says and teaches that election by the people was done, loc. cit., (1) so that a shepherd would not be set over unwilling sheep; (2) so that a spiritual marriage would be contracted between shepherd and Church by the mutual consent of both; (3) so that he might be loved and cherished more by the sheep. Indeed we do not deny that this form of electing ministers also labours under its own inconveniences, and its abuses, especially in the election of Popes, and the many scandalous schisms, to be listed in their place, have been noted quickly enough, and hence a pretext for change has also been sought. But since all human things are imperfect, and other forms (as can be known from what precedes and follows) are burdened with no fewer inconveniences, an abuse for which a remedy can somehow be found should not remove a practice confirmed by the use of Scripture and by the examples of all antiquity. That empty pretext therefore appears, and the faithful people has been wrongly excluded from election altogether. A remedy, however, can exist: from the prudent moderation of the churchmen or of the faithful magistrate, from the diligent admonition of the faithful about the gravity of the matter in question, and above all from restoring the episcopal state to its former form. For as long as the episcopate was more a burden than an honour, as long as worldly pride was absent and an influx of worldly wealth was unknown in that dignity, and little was heard of so many and such great abuses, the people was indeed often under the necessity of being dragged and compelled, even against their will. But as soon as the poison of riches and earthly honours was poured into the Church, it is no wonder that the powerful, with ambition spurring them on, eagerly applied, and still apply, their minds to the episcopates. Those things must be removed, as far as they can be; not the rights of the faithful people.

units.la: XXVII. Quæ in Ecclesias nostras populi fidelis jura, cum aliqua tamen, pro diversitate occasionum & locorum, differentia, & magis, minùs perfectè reducta videmus. In multis quippe regionibus gionibus & diversis etiam locorum eorundem coetibus paribus fideles votis & suffragiis concurrunt; Alibi familiarum omnium, alibi praecipuarum Capita; Alibi bonam partem coetus constituentes, saltem subditorum fidelium personam gerentes & simul nomini Nutriciorum Ecclesiae & Custodum utriusque Tabulae & Defensorum fidei respondentes fideles magistratus; Alibi mixta ex personis Politicis & Ecclesiasticis Presbyteria, Consistoria, quae suo modo & Ecclesiae tantum, modo etiam nomine Magistratus agunt, expressam, vel tacitam constitutionem ab Ecclesiis habent, & ut digni atque fidelibus grati praeponantur, curant; Alibi illa ipsa Consistoria duos aut tres, quos dignos judicant, Patrono Ecclesiae, qui ratione certorum beneficiorum terrenorum talis habetur, offerunt, aut ab illo oblatos accipiunt & determinant, aut facit Ecclesia, quae ibi quoque, ubi nonnisi unus praesentatur (quod tamen in paucissimis locis fit) consensu suo confirmat, nec tenetur invita recipere indignum. Fateor, in eo esse differentiam non unam inter magis & minus perfecta, & reperiri Papatus reliquias, maxime in illo, quod vocant, Patronatus jure. Nempe non licuit vetus fermentum expurgare penitus, nec tamen nos reprehendere possunt, ubi non omnia jura fidelibus ubique restituta sunt, qui eis abstulerunt omnia. Caeterum in genere electiones populi consensu firmari dicimus, quamvis omnino credamus, posse etiam Ecclesias suum jus quandantenus in quosdam ex suis transferre, & persuasi simus, Apostolos & Apostolicos & antiquitatem primam reliquam non semper cum tota fraternitate occasionibus similibus consilia miscuisse, sed nonnunquam Seniorum delectum habuisse, nec semper, quando Ecclesia aut fratres ab Apostolis convocati leguntur, ad unum omnes convocatos, aut (quod temporum iniquitas quoque minus saepe permittebat) congregatos fuisse, sed fraternitati jus plenum asseri potuisse, etiam si forte eorum conventui vel Titius, vel Maevius defuerit; prout etiam Ecclesiam primi temporis totam Caelestis Spiritus luce circumvestitam & extraordinariis sermonis, Sapientia, cognitionis, linguarum, interpretationis, virtutum, prophetia, discretionis spirituum, donis Apostolo, 1.Cor.XII. 9.10. Rom.XII.5. & 2.Cor.XIV. teste, insignem huic & aliis regiminis Ecclesiastici partibus magis aptam fuisse, & hodie haud male, donis illis extraordinariis sublatis, ex fidelibus ab illis, vel saltem cum eorum consensu delectos communia tractare, arbitramur; maur; quos tamen, ubi omnes pleno jure gaudent, plane ineptos non deprehendimus, ut de Bestia multorum capitum loquuntur Ekius, Bellarminus, alii; sed idoneorum Pastorum cupidos, sed illos sibi, licet intervenientibus apud quosdam affectibus, licet non sine imperfectione, quae, ut dixi, in humanis negotiis ubique appareret, studiose praeficientes; sed illorum etiam, si fidi sint, valde amantes, quibus proin nec doctrinae puritas, nec divina, (Christus enim promisit, in medio se futurum duorum aut trium in nomine suo congregatorum, Matth. XVIII. 20.) nec publica humana authoritas ullo modo deest, & quorum adeo constitutionem, accedente etiam publica benedictione & consecratione, fieri ordine atque decenter, 1.Cor.XIV.40. & aeque bene ac constitutiones aliorum, melius ac constitutiones multorum, nemo jure negabit.
units.tr: XXVII. We see that the rights of the faithful people in our churches are preserved, though with some difference, depending on circumstances and places, and some are more and some less fully restored. In many regions the faithful, both in the same assemblies and in various gatherings of the same places, come together with equal votes and suffrages. Elsewhere it is the heads of all the households, and elsewhere the heads of the principal families. Elsewhere the faithful magistrates, who make up the greater part of the assembly, represent the persons of the faithful subjects and at the same time answer to the title of nurturers of the Church, guardians of both tables of the law, and defenders of the faith. Elsewhere there are presbyteries and consistories made up of civil and ecclesiastical persons, which act in their own way, sometimes for the Church alone and sometimes in the name of the magistrate. They hold an express or tacit commission from the churches and take care that worthy men who are pleasing to the faithful are put forward. Elsewhere those same consistories offer two or three men whom they judge worthy to the patron of the Church, who is regarded as such by reason of certain earthly benefices, and then either accept and determine the candidate from among those he has offered, or the Church itself does so: even where only one man is presented (which, however, happens in very few places), the Church confirms him by its consent and is not bound to receive an unworthy man against its will. I admit that there is more than one difference between the more and the less perfect arrangements, and that remnants of the papacy are to be found, especially in what they call the right of patronage. Indeed, it was not possible to purge the old leaven completely; yet they cannot blame us where the faithful have not everywhere had all their rights restored, when those who took them away have taken everything from them. In general, however, we say that elections are confirmed by the consent of the people, although we fully believe that churches can also transfer their right in some measure to certain men from among themselves. We are persuaded that the Apostles, and the Apostolic and earliest antiquity, did not always consult with the whole brotherhood on similar occasions, but sometimes chose elders; and that when the church or the brothers were summoned by the Apostles, they were not always all called together, or (which the wickedness of the times also allowed less often) gathered; yet full right could be claimed for the brotherhood even if, perhaps, Titius or Maevius was absent from their assembly. Likewise, we judge, on the testimony of the Apostle (1 Cor. 12:9–10; Rom. 12:5; 2 Cor. 14), that the primitive Church, clothed all over with the light of the Heavenly Spirit and distinguished by extraordinary gifts of speech, wisdom, knowledge, tongues, interpretation, miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, was more fitted for this and the other parts of ecclesiastical government; and today, those extraordinary gifts having been taken away, it is not unreasonable for men chosen from among the faithful, or at least with their consent, to deal with common affairs. Yet where all enjoy full right, we do not find them altogether unfit, as Eck, Bellarmine and others speak of a beast with many heads. Rather, they are eager for suitable pastors, and they set such men over themselves diligently, though some feelings intervene and the choice is not without imperfection, which, as I have said, appears everywhere in human affairs. They also value very highly those pastors, if they are faithful, to whom neither the purity of doctrine nor the divine presence (for Christ promised to be in the midst of two or three gathered in his name, Matt. 18:20), nor public human authority is in any way lacking. And no one will rightly deny that their appointment, with public blessing and consecration added, is made decently and in order (1 Cor. 14:40), and as well as the appointments of others, better than the appointments of many.

units.la: XXVIII. Ecclesia autem Pontificia hic quoque plane a laudabili Apostolicae & reliquae primitivae Ecclesiae consuetudine, quam etiam in tot Pontificum electione adhibitam esse fateri debent, defecisse deprehenditur. Omnis Ministros constituendi potestas ponitur, in Papa originaliter, quam Episcopi respectu inferiorum habeant, sed ab ipso sub certis iisque plurimis reservationibus (quae in Regulis Cancellariis, quarum inventio Sixto IV. debetur, & quales Alexandri VII. Sprengerus Roma nova appendicem fecit, videri possunt;) communicatam. Populi autem Christiani ibi nulla plane habetur ratio, & tanquam bestia, quae montem tangere non debet, licet sub suavi N. T. Oeconomia ab electionis actu arcetur, ut & alias in Ecclesiasticae societatis compage (ceu confusa arefactorum stipitum congeries) sub Clero jacere & ignavi pecoris ἡ συνζυγίκ ἀφωνκ ad instar nunquam non agi, nullas a Christo institutae regiminis partes attingere debet. Nec certe Pontificios hic satis excusat qualiscunque praetextus, & habent in proprio suo Pontificali veteri testimonium contra se tam manifestum, ut Passius Concilio Tridentino illius correctionem & locorum expunctionem suaserit; In ea enim ordinator ait; Non frustra a Patribus institutum, ut de electione illorum, qui ad regimen altaris adhibendi sint, consulatur & populus, quia necesse est, ut facilius ei quis obedientiam exhibeat ordinato, cui assensum prabuerit ordinando. Ridicule autem consulunt, & verba sunt Bellarmini, in ordinationibus petitur populus per Diaconum, an aliquid habeant adversus ordinandos; Simiae potius, quam veri observatores veteris consuetudinis, interim tamen testes ejus, dum Diaconus lingua ignota petit testimonium aut sententiam populi vel absen-tis, vel ne de facie quidem & nomine eos cognoscentis, vel saltem alieni, & nihil eos curantis, & aliquis in angulo stans respondet; Doctus est, dignus est; quod Deo & Ecclesiae illudere est.
units.tr: XXVIII. The Papal Church, however, is found here also to have clearly departed from the praiseworthy custom of the Apostles and of the rest of the primitive Church, which they themselves must admit was observed in the election of so many popes. The power of appointing ministers is placed originally in the Pope, and the bishops have it over their inferiors, but it is granted to them by him under certain and very many reservations (which may be seen in the Chancery Rules, whose invention is owed to Sixtus IV, and of which Sprenger added an appendix in his Roma nova, the kind made under Alexander VII). The Christian people have no consideration here at all; like the beast that must not touch the mountain, they are shut out from the act of election, although under the sweet economy of the New Testament. Thus, as in the framework of the ecclesiastical society (like a confused heap of dry logs), they always lie under the clergy and are driven like a dull flock, [ἡ σύνζυγος ἄφωνος], and they must not touch any part of government instituted by Christ. Certainly no pretext of whatever kind excuses the Papists here sufficiently, and they have in their own old Pontifical testimony so plain against them that Passius advised the Council of Trent to correct it and strike out those passages. For in the ordination the ordainer says: It was not in vain that the Fathers instituted that the people should be consulted about the election of those who are to be admitted to the ministry of the altar, because it is necessary that a man more easily shows obedience to the one ordained, to whom he has given his assent when he is being ordained. But they consult the people ridiculously. These are Bellarmine's words: In ordinations the people are asked through the deacon whether they have anything against the candidates. They are rather apes than true observers of the ancient custom, though they are still its witnesses, while the deacon, in an unknown tongue, asks for the testimony or opinion of the people, who are either absent, or do not even know the men by face and name, or are at least strangers and care nothing for them; and someone standing in a corner answers: He is learned, he is worthy. This is to mock God and the Church.

units.la: XXIX. Maximè autem populo Christiano, ubi minimè deberet, in electione Pontificum Romanorum ab aliquot seculis acclamatur:
units.tr: XXIX. But especially in the election of the Roman Pontiffs, where it ought least to be, the Christian people has for some centuries been made to cry out:

units.la: Procul hinc, procul este profani!
units.tr: Away from here, away, you profane!

units.la: Prorsus immutata est electionis, etiam illo respectu, ratio, &, cum olim totum fere habuerit plebs, nihil habet hodie. Nam Pontifice demum creato, ut suo loco videbimus, ex fenestra audire meretur: Annuncio vobis gaudium magnum, habemus Papam &c. Quod tamen gaudium respectu populi non in eo fundatum esse debet, quòd Episcopus electus aptus est ad docendum, futurus vitae sanctitate typus gregis & aliis requisitis Episcopalibus praeditus, sed quòd, dum caeterum saepe ignotus est, de eo forte praesumi potest, eum clementiâ delectari, tributis Statum non gravaturum, consanguineis damno aliorum non nimis concessurum esse. Quamvis saepissimè etiam contrarium ex certis indiciis timeri possit, hinc gaudium nullum, nedum magnum sequatur, magna contrà ab ipsis primordiis aversio, Papâ tamen aequè manente. Sic frustrà in Conclavi Nicolai V. Barones quidam Romani ad electionem concurrere voluerunt. Sic frustrà Romam optantem, atque mortuo Clemente IX. conquerentem l'Ambasc. di Rom. p.21. audimus: Se pur toccasse à me l'elettione, Bandir potrei dal Cuor ogni Cordoglio, Mà perche mi si vieta un si bel soglio, Dubito non si veda un fier Nerone. Id est:
units.tr: The manner of election has been completely changed, even in this respect; and although the common people once had almost the whole of it, today they have nothing. For only when the Pope has been created, as we shall see in its place, does the people deserve to hear from the window: I announce to you great joy, we have a Pope, etc. Yet this joy on the people's part ought not to be founded on the elected bishop being fit to teach, likely to be a figure of holiness of life to the flock, and endowed with the other episcopal requisites, but on the hope that, since he is often otherwise unknown, one may presume that he delights in mercy, will not burden the state with taxes, and will not grant too much to his relatives at the expense of others. Although very often the opposite may be feared from certain signs, no joy at all follows, much less great joy, but from the very beginning great aversion, the Pope nevertheless remaining the same. Thus in vain, in the conclave of Nicholas V, certain Roman barons wanted to take part in the election. Thus, too, we hear Rome, longing for and complaining after the death of Clement IX, in l'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 21: "If the choice had been mine, I could banish all grief from my heart; but since I am forbidden so fine a throne, I fear that a fierce Nero may be seen." That is:

units.la: Non dolerem, si ipsa eligere possem, sed quia arceor à tam pulchro throno, dubito, num non ibi videre debeam audacem Neronem. Sed & reliqua praeter Cardinales Cleri Romani pars ab Innocentii II. tempore ab electione Pontificum arcetur, ex quo nimirum tempore Cardinales soli Electores sunt, & quoddam Monopolium exercent, & eatenus quoque toti dominantur Clero, ut mox fusiùs ostendemus.
units.tr: I would not grieve if I could choose for myself, but since I am shut out from so fine a throne, I fear that I ought to see there a bold Nero. But also the rest of the Roman clergy, apart from the Roman cardinals, has been shut out from the election of the Popes since the time of Innocent II. From that time on, the cardinals alone are electors, and they exercise a certain monopoly, and in this respect too they entirely rule the clergy, as we shall show more fully below.

units.la: XXX. Sed praesuppositâ jam illâ, quam per secula non pauca obtinuisse ostendimus, Episcopos Romanos per Clerum populumque Romanum eligendi consuetudine, tandem optimè contra Monarchiam Ecclesiae argumentari possumus. Quid enim? An verisimile risimile est, Clerum illum & populum particularem toti orbi Caput, Ecclesiae Monarcham per tot secula dare & constituere debuisse? Unde istas Clerus iste, populus iste praerogativas habere potuit? Elegerunt Episcopos, suos; sed ex quo fundamento totius orbis Rectores soli? Et si ab initio credidissent illam Monarchiam universalem, annon delegati ex & ab universali Ecclesia Episcopi eligere debuissent? Cur Clerus populusque Romanus tantum? Et quodnam ostendi potest conferendae per ipsos tantae potestatis fundamentum? Nullum certe; Et proin multiplex ex secunda etiam Electionis Romanorum Pontificum forma contra hodiernos Monarchicos praejudicium formari potest.
units.tr: XXX. But, with that now presupposed, which we have shown to have held for not a few centuries, namely the custom of the Roman Bishops being elected by the Roman clergy and people, we can at last argue very well against the Monarchy of the Church. For what? Is it likely that that particular clergy and people ought to have given and appointed the Monarch of the Church, the head of the whole world, for so many centuries? Whence could that clergy and that people have had such prerogatives? They elected their own bishops; but on what foundation were they alone the rulers of the whole world? And if from the beginning they had believed in that universal Monarchy, ought not bishops chosen by and from the universal Church to have made the election? Why the Roman clergy and people alone? And what foundation can be shown for conferring such great power by them? None certainly. And therefore a manifold prejudice against today's monarchists can be formed even from this second form of the election of the Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: XXXI. Ad Tertiam nunc progredimur; juxta quam Imperatores nonnunquam Episcoporum Romanorum Electores fuerunt; Adeoque de Electione per Imperatores hic loqui animus est, non de confirmatione, de qua inter Electionis Consequentia videbimus.
units.tr: XXXI. We now come to the Third form, according to which the Emperors were sometimes the electors of the Roman Bishops. Accordingly, I intend to speak here of election by the Emperors, not of confirmation, which we shall consider among the consequences of election.

units.la: Electos autem esse ab Imperatoribus, etiam nonnunquam solis, haud paucos Pontifices, tam evidens est, ut illud non ausus sit negare ipse Bellarminus l. de Cler. c. 9. factum ponens, sed jus, de quo postea videbimus, in dubium vocans. Huc autem primo referimus, quod narrante etiam Baronio ad an. 368. 381. Valentinianus Imperator in Schismate Damasi & Ursicini, illum in sede confirmavit, hunc urbe expulit; Quod & Honorius Imperator inter Eulalium & Bonifacium fecisse apud eundem ad an. 418. 419. legitur, qui etiam posthac, utroque a Pontificatu abstinere jusso, Romanae Ecclesiae ad Pontificalia pro tempore exercenda Episcopum Spoletinum dedit, sed tandem machinationibus Eulalii (cujus caeteroquin causa melior erat) motus Bonifacium confirmavit. Sed quoque Odoacer ex Italiae Regibus, (qui eandem hic cum Imperatoribus sibi potestatem asserebant;) sede ex morte Simplicii vacante, per Basilium Patricium Praetorii Praefectum petiit, ut juxta Simplicii obtestationem non sint Imperatoria consultatione, cujuslibet celebretur electio; de quo in Actis Synodi IV. sub Sym. c. 2. videri potest; Quomodo non novam legem fieri postulavit, ut Binius in notis contendit; sed tantum, ut omnia incolumnia serventur, adeoque secundum morem, qui forte intermitti coepit, agatur; Theodoricus quoque Gothus, & ipse Italiae Rex in Schismate post mortem Simplicii, rejecto, sed tamen ad Episcopatum Nuceriae promoto, Laurentio, Symmacho Romanum confirmavit, narrante Theod. lect. collecta. l. 2. & Platina in Sym. Et quarto post anno tumultibus resuscitatis, perhibente Platina l. c. Petrum Altini Episcopum Romam misit, qui pulso utroque sedem obtineret, defuncto autem Johanne Papa teste Cassiod. l. 8. ep. 15. turbarum praecedentium memor Foelicem Virum Catholicum & in Romano Clero probatissimum Episcopum consecrandum Clero proposuit & obtinuit. Et quia Bonifacius II. juxta n. VII. inscio Rege Athalrico, Diaconum Vigilium sibi successorem elegit, ideo, referente Anastasio in Vita, reum se laesae Majestatis agnovit & electionem rescidit. Justinianus pariter (ut ad Imperatores revertamur) de Vigilii, qui quintam Synodum accipere nolens in exilium actus erat, restitutione compellatus, juxta Anastasium in Vita & Baronium ad an. 554. Archidiaconum Pelagium proposuit; de quo & regesserunt & petierunt, ut post mortem Vigilii Imperatoris praeceptione sibi donaretur.
units.tr: That not a few Popes were elected by the Emperors, and sometimes by them alone, is so evident that Bellarmine himself did not dare to deny the fact (De Clericis, c. 9), though he called the right into doubt, which we shall consider later. Here we may first refer to the fact, related also by Baronius (ad ann. 368 and 381), that the Emperor Valentinian, in the schism of Damasus and Ursinus, confirmed the one in the see and expelled the other from the city. The same is read of the Emperor Honorius between Eulalius and Boniface, in the same author (ad ann. 418 and 419). Afterwards, when both had been ordered to abstain from the papacy, he gave the Bishop of Spoleto to the Roman Church to perform the pontifical duties for the time being; but at last, moved by the machinations of Eulalius (whose cause was otherwise the better), he confirmed Boniface. Odoacer also, one of the Kings of Italy (who claimed for himself the same power as the Emperors in this matter), when the see was vacant on the death of Simplicius, sought through Basilius, Praetorian Prefect and Patrician, that, in accordance with Simplicius's entreaty, the election should not be held without the consultation of the Emperor. This can be seen in the Acts of the Fourth Synod under Symmachus, c. 2. Binius, in his notes, contends that he demanded a new law to be made; but he only asked that all should be kept safe, and so that things should be done according to the custom which had perhaps begun to lapse. Theodoric the Goth, also King of Italy himself, in the schism after the death of Simplicius, rejected Laurentius, though he had been promoted to the Bishopric of Nuceria, and confirmed Symmachus as Roman Bishop, as Theodorus Lector relates (Collectanea, bk. 2) and Platina (in Symmachus). Four years later, when the disturbances had been revived, as Platina reports (loc. cit.), he sent Peter, Bishop of Altinum, to Rome, who, with both driven out, obtained the see. When John the Pope died, Cassiodorus (bk. 8, ep. 15) reports that, mindful of the earlier disturbances, he proposed to the clergy, and obtained, that Felix, a Catholic man and a Bishop most approved among the Roman clergy, be consecrated. And because Boniface II, contrary to what we said in no. VII, chose Vigilius, a deacon, as his successor without the knowledge of King Athalaric, therefore, as Anastasius reports in his Life, he acknowledged himself guilty of treason against majesty and annulled the election. Justinian likewise (to return to the Emperors) was pressed to restore Vigilius, who had been exiled for refusing to accept the Fifth Synod; and, according to Anastasius in his Life and Baronius (ad ann. 554), he proposed the archdeacon Pelagius. Concerning him, they both reported and asked that, after the death of Vigilius, he be granted to them by the Emperor's precept.

units.la: XXXII. Sub Imperatoribus Germanis non minora, sed multo illustriora hujus rei documenta reperiuntur.
units.tr: XXXII. Under the German Emperors, no less but far more illustrious documents of this matter are found.

units.la: Adrianus I. enim Imperatori Carolo M. dist.63. c. Hadrianus &c. in Synodo cum Synodo universa tradidit (declarando) jus & potestatem eligendi Pontifices & ordinandi sedem Apostolicam; Ad cujus exemplum Leo VIII. Ottoni I. Imperatori hujus nominis jus eligendi Romanum Pontificem restituit, vel potius ad Imperatorem pertinere denuo declaravit, vel (ut Platina in vita & Nauclerus Gener.33. volunt, Romanorum inconstantiam pertaesus authoritatem omnem eligendi Pontifi-cem a Clero populoque ad Imperatorem transtulit.Illo autem mortuo (ut habet Regino apud Baronium ad a. 965. n. 4.) Legati Romanorum, Imperatorem pro instituendo, quem vellet, Episcopo adeuntes honorifice excepti & cum 2. Episcopis remissi sunt, & omnes tunc demum Johannem Narniensem creârunt. Gregorium V. similiter, & Sylvestrum II. (cujus Electionis decretum apud Baronium ad an. 1191. videri potest;) ab Ottone III. electos esse constat; Et post Leonis IX. obitum, Henricum II. rogatum Episcopum Aichstetensem dedisse, qui Victoris II. nomen assumpsit, Ostiensis l.2. c.90. docet. Non minus Damasum II. Leonem IX. & nominatum Victorem II. & Stephanum IX. Henrici III. authoritate creatos esse Onuphrius Annot. in Clem. II. ex probatis Authoribus affirmat Quin Nicolaus II. in Concilio generali Lateranensi in decreto de Electione Pontificis, quod Dist.23. c. 1. & apud Baronium ad an. 1059. n. 25. habetur, addidit; salvo debito honore & reverentia dilecti filii nostri Henrici, qui in praesentiarum Rex habetur, & futurus Imperator Deo concedente spe-ratur; Sicut jam sibi concessimus & successoribus illius, qui ab Apostolica sede personaliter hoc jus impetraverint. Astutè sic alieni juris concessionem & quidem personalem facere videri volens; Circa quae paulò aliter loquitur Petrus Damiani in Dialogo inter Advocatum Regium & Defensorem Ecclesiae Romanae, etiam apud Baronium ad an. 1059. n. 22. & 1062. n. 25, 26. nempe ita loquentem Advocatum inducit: Tu hoc negare non potes, quòd Pater Domini mei Regis pia memoria Henricus Imperator factus est Patricius Romanorum, à quibus accepit in electione super ordinando Pontifice principatum. Huc accedit, quod praestantius est, quòd Nicolaus Papa Domino meo Regi privilegium, quod ex paterno jure susceperat, praebuit & per synodalis insuper decreti paginam confirmavit. Cùm ergò privatus quisque à suo decidere jure non debeat, donec ventilato negotio judicialis in eum sententia promulgetur: quo pacto Majestas Regia praerogativam hanc suae dignitatis amisit, quam & ex Apostolica Sedis liberalitate percepit & ex paterno Imperialis fastigii jure suscepit? Nempe conqueritur Advocatus de Henrico puero in Electione Alexandri II. neglecto, quod & Schismati occasionem dedit, eique Defensor nonnisi infantiam Henrici & temporis necessitatem praetexens respondet.
units.tr: For Hadrian I handed over to the Emperor Charlemagne, in a Synod, together with the whole Synod, (declaring) the right and power of electing the Popes and of ordaining the Apostolic See (dist. 63, c. Hadrianus etc., in Synod). In imitation of this, Leo VIII restored to the Emperor Otto I of that name the right of electing the Roman Pontiff, or rather again declared that it pertained to the Emperor; or (as Platina in his Life and Naucler, Generation 33, say) he, weary of the Romans' inconstancy, transferred the whole authority of electing the Pontiff from the clergy and people to the Emperor. When he had died (as Regino has it, cited by Baronius ad ann. 965, no. 4), the Roman envoys, approaching the Emperor to appoint whomever he wished as Bishop, were received with honour and sent back with two Bishops, and then at last they all created John of Narni. Gregory V and likewise Sylvester II (whose decree of election can be seen in Baronius ad ann. 1191) are known to have been elected by Otto III. And after the death of Leo IX, Ostiensis (bk. 2, c. 90) teaches that Henry II, being asked, gave Bishop Aichstetensis, who took the name Victor II. Onuphrius (Annotations on Clement II) affirms from approved authors that Damasus II, Leo IX, the nominated Victor II and Stephen IX were created by the authority of Henry III. Nay more, Nicholas II, in the general Lateran Council, in the decree on the election of the Pontiff, which is found in Dist. 23, c. 1, and in Baronius ad ann. 1059, no. 25, added: "Saving the due honour and reverence of our beloved son Henry, who is at present regarded as King and is hoped by God's grace to become Emperor, as we have already granted to him and to his successors, who shall have obtained this right personally from the Apostolic See." Thus, wishing cunningly to appear to make a concession of another's right, and indeed a personal one. Peter Damian speaks somewhat differently on these matters in his Dialogue between the Royal Advocate and the Defender of the Roman Church, also in Baronius ad ann. 1059, no. 22, and 1062, nos. 25, 26. He introduces the Advocate speaking thus: "You cannot deny that the father of my lord the King, Henry of pious memory, was made Patrician of the Romans, from whom he received the principate in the election in ordaining the Pontiff. Moreover, what is more excellent, Pope Nicholas granted to my lord the King the privilege which he had received by paternal right, and confirmed it besides by the page of a synodal decree. Since therefore no private person ought to be deprived of his right by another, until the matter has been debated and a judicial sentence pronounced against him, in what way has the Royal Majesty lost this prerogative of its dignity, which it both received from the liberality of the Apostolic See and took up by the paternal right of the Imperial dignity?" Indeed the Advocate complains that Henry the boy was neglected in the election of Alexander II, which also gave occasion to the schism; and the Defender, pleading only Henry's infancy and the necessity of the time, answers him.

units.la: XXXIII. Paucis autem haec omnia comprehendit Maimburgius Hist. de la decadence de l'Empire liv. 1. p. 91. 92. 93. dum de Ottone Imp. hujus nominis primo pro valdè certo testatur, qu'il ne manqua pas &c. quòd non omiserit sibi vindicare possessionem trium magnarum praerogativarum, quas Imperatores Graeci & Franci habuerint, & quas Carolus Calvus abjecisse dicatur, ut fratri Imperium eriperet; & tertiam ex his praerogativis vocat le pouvoir d'élire un Pape &c. potestatem eligendi Papam, vel saltem, quod eodem fere recidit, impediendi, ne ullus sine consensu suo eligatur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Maimburg, in his History of the decline of the Empire (bk. 1, pp. 91, 92, 93), comprehends all these things in few words, when he testifies, as something very certain, concerning Otto I of that name, that "he did not fail" to claim for himself the possession of three great prerogatives which the Greek and Frankish Emperors had held, and which Charles the Bald is said to have cast off in order to snatch the empire from his brother. He calls the third of these prerogatives "the power of electing a Pope," or at least, which comes to nearly the same thing, of preventing anyone from being elected without his consent.

units.la: Circa quam praerogativam paulò post addit: Il est certain &c. Certum est, Imperatores, ex eo tempore, quo Justinianus à Gothis Romam & Italiam recuperavit, fuerunt Domini Electionis Paparum, ita ut fieri non potuerit absque illorum permissione, & insuper oportuerit, ut facta jam ab illis confirmaretur. Et licèt Imperatores Franci libertatem electionum restituerint, tamen ex pluribus exemplis patet, praecipuè ex illis Benedicti III. Gregorii IV. & Sergii I. quòd ordinari non potuerint, nisi delegati Imperatoris, qui debuerint assistere consecrationi, judicâssent, electionem Canonicè factam esse, & nisi post princeps consensum praebuisset. Ecce potestatem, cujus possessionem reassumpsit sumpsit Otto, quam & eo usque extendit, ut electionem authoritati sua submiserit, nec eligi voluerit, nisi cum, qui sibi placuisset. Qui & de Ottone III. p.159. testis est, que suivant l'exemple &c. quod ad exemplum Majorum, qui se Dominos Electionis Paparum fecerint, eligi curaverit Brunonem &c. Idem etiam Maimburgius lib. cit. hinc inde exempla ab Imperatoribus & eorum jussu electorum adducit, & argumentis Baronii, quibus contra decreta Adriani & Leonis utitur, p.85. seqq. solide respondet. Nos autem allata pro instituti ratione sufficere posse rati, heic non subjungimus exempla Anti-Paparum, qui habentur, post ea tempora ab Imperatoribus sine successu optato creatorum, de quibus in nævo Schismatum agemus; Nec etiam de depositionibus Paparum & Anti-Paparum, & de Jure Investiturae circa alios Episcopos; quamvis illa hanc eligendi potestatem magis illustrare & confirmare possent; heic agere constitutum est.
units.tr: Concerning this prerogative he adds a little later: "It is certain... It is certain that from the time when Justinian recovered Rome and Italy from the Goths, the Emperors were lords of the election of the Popes, so that it could not be done without their permission, and moreover it was necessary that what had been done should be confirmed by them. And although the Frankish Emperors restored the freedom of elections, yet it is clear from many examples, especially from those of Benedict III, Gregory IV and Sergius I, that they could not be ordained unless the envoys of the Emperor, who were to assist at the consecration, had judged the election to have been canonically made, and unless the prince had afterwards given his consent.
