Here is the power, the possession of which Otto resumed," which he also extended so far that he subjected the election to his own authority, and would not allow anyone to be elected except one who had pleased him. He also bears witness concerning Otto III (p. 159): "following the example... that, after the example of his ancestors, who had made themselves lords of the election of Popes, he took care that Bruno should be elected..." The same Maimburg, in the book cited, adduces here and there examples of those elected by the Emperors and at their command, and he solidly answers Baronius's arguments, by which he uses against the decrees of Hadrian and Leo, pp. 85 ff. But we, thinking that what has been brought forward is sufficient for the plan of our work, do not here add the examples of the Anti-Popes, who are recorded as having been created by the Emperors after those times without the desired success, of which we shall treat in the blemish of the Schisms; nor the depositions of Popes and Anti-Popes, nor the Right of Investiture concerning other Bishops; although those things could further illustrate and confirm this power of electing; it is our purpose to treat of them here.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Debemus autem omnino de jure facti, nempe Electionis per Imperatores; De quo tamen jam quadantenus ex iis, quae n.XXVII. dicta sunt, constare potest, quatenus nimirum Episcopi Romani intra terminos Episcopales spectantur. Sed adhuc magis oportuit, ut in illorum electione primae partes essent Imperatoris, quatenus Episcopi illi extra justos limites evagari & a verorum Episcoporum munere aliena suscipere, jactare voluerunt, tantam nimirum in Spiritualibus & temporalibus authoritatem & potestatem sibi sumentes; Quis enim mirabitur, Imperatores, summos Christianorum Magistratus, solicitos fuisse de Electione summorum (ut credebant) inter Christianos Praesulum, tanta authoritate, potestate tanta pollentium, & curare voluisse, ut dignus ad tantamMajestatem Ecclesiasticam promoveretur, subditis suis communis Pastor praeficeretur? Et quis non aequitatem perspicit illius, quod Imperatores, Episcopis Romanis sua maxime liberalitate ad tantas divitias, urbium, regionum possessiones tantas, licet diu non ἀνυπάλγουας provectis, non sibi negligendum esse putarunt, quinam in istis praerogativis temporalibus succederent? Quidni curassent translationem potestatis sibi tantopere metuendae, quotiescunque in malos cecidit, noxiae, dum nimirum illi Imperatorum jura violarunt, eos excommunicarunt, deposuerunt, cum hostibus saepe colluserunt, idque, omnibus ab illorum nutu pendentibus, saepe non sine successu? Et qui Ottoni vitio vertendum esset,
units.tr: We must also deal fully with the fact of election by the emperors. Something of this can already be gathered from what was said in n. XXVII, insofar as the Roman bishops are considered within their episcopal limits. But it was still more necessary that the emperors should have the first role in their election, since those bishops wished to wander beyond their just limits, to take up and boast of duties foreign to the true bishops, claiming for themselves such great authority and power over spiritual and temporal affairs. For who will be surprised that the emperors, the highest magistrates of the Christians, were anxious about the election of the highest prelates among Christians (as they believed them to be), men so mighty in such great authority and power, and wished to see to it that a worthy man was promoted to such ecclesiastical majesty and set over their subjects as common pastor? And who does not see the fairness of this: that the emperors, who by their own great generosity had advanced the Roman bishops to such great riches and such extensive possessions of cities and regions, though for a long time not without gratitude [ἀνυπάλγουας], did not think they could neglect who would succeed to these temporal privileges? Why would they not have taken care to prevent the transfer of a power so much to be feared, whenever it fell into the hands of wicked and harmful men, since those bishops violated the emperors' rights, excommunicated them, deposed them, and often colluded with their enemies, and did so, with everyone depending on their nod, often not without success? And why should Otto be blamed for the emperors' part in such elections, since he took care that the papacy should not slip into the hands of any Roman, after he had found the fidelity of the Romans suspect and nowhere secure, as we read in Baronius, ad an. 999, n. 2?

units.la: Imperatorum in ejusmodi electionibus; essët, quòd operam dedit, ne Pontificatus in aliquem Romanorum relaberetur, postquam suspectam & nusquam tutam fidem expertus fuerat Romanorum, ut apud Baronium ad an. 999. n. 2. legimus? Accedit consideratio Schismatum, in quibus sæpe nullum, nisi ab Imperatoribus, remedium, quibus non tantùm mederi potuerunt, debuerunt ortis, sed & occurrere verisimiliter orituris, semper personæ determinatione, temporibus maximè tam corruptis. Atque eorum authoritate factiones repressas esse, apud Baronium ad an.1058. n. 10. videri potest.
units.tr: To this is added the consideration of schisms, in which often there was no remedy except from the emperors. They could and should not only heal schisms that had already arisen, but also probably forestall those that would arise, always by determining the person, especially in such corrupt times. That they repressed factions by their authority can be seen in Baronius, ad an. 1058, n. 10.

units.la: XXXV. Ut jam immeritò à forma hac electionis eò usque discesserint, ut nullas à longo tempore Imperatori partes in Pontificum Electione relinquant, certè non alias, quàm, quòd de Cardinalibus nonnullis bene merendo, & ratione dependentiæ personarum, aut familiarum efficere potest, ut non facilè condescendant (quod tamen facere à duabus nonnunquam partibus adiguntur) in personam ei adversam; In quo tamen sæpe alii Principes plùs possunt; Nunquam autem efficere poterit, ut (quod à tempore Adriani VI. impossibile videtur;) saltem à Cardinalibus eligatur Papa saltem Germanus; Imò apertè Monarchici Electiones per Imperatores olim factas illorum vi & tyrannidi adscribere audent; Et digna sunt, quæ de eo adducantur, verba Conclavis Gregorii XIV. Cùm enim Hispaniæ Rex (qui in Pontificum Electione diu plurimùm potuit,) per Legatum VII. nominando, ex quibus Cardinalibus unum eligere liberum esse queat, vellet porre le sue laicali mani nel santuario di Dio, laicas manus suas (stylo ipsorum) inferre Sanctuario Dei, à Cardinalibus factioni Hispanicæ contrariis reclamatum est, inter alia hoc etiam argumento, poiche à Dio era piacuto &c. Id est; Quia Deo placuerit semel liberare Ecclesiam suam à servitute, in quam eam injustè posuerint veteres Imperatores, quoad Creationem Paparum, non debere (Cardinales) consentire, ut in eam denuò reponatur sub durioribus conditionibus, & à principe inferioris dignitatis, quâ ratione etiam occasio daretur Imperatori ipsi, renovandi veteres suas pratensiones, si nimirum videret, illud, quod praterito tempore cum quadam protestatione pratenderit, non tantùm obtentum, sed & cum augmento acquisitum esse à Principe inferiori sine omni ratione. Ex quibus verbis apparet, Cardinales injustam ex parte Ecclesiæ suæ servitutem, proin ex parte Imperatorum tyrannidem, imò expresse sacrilegium vocare etiam minimum potestatis secularis cujuscunque ad Electionem Ex quo patet, malè nullas jam Imperatoribus in Electione Pontificum partes relinqui; ctionem Pontificum Romanorum concursum. Quid igitur dictu-ri fuissent, si de ipsa electione per Imperatores olim facta ibi judica-re voluissent?
units.tr: XXXV. Although they have deservedly departed so far from this form of election that for a long time they have left the emperor no part at all in the election of the Popes, certainly the emperor can do nothing more than this: by deserving well of some cardinals, and by the dependence of persons or families, he can bring it about that they do not readily agree (though sometimes they are forced by two parties to do so) to a person hostile to him. Yet in this other princes often have more power. But he can never bring it about (which seems impossible since the time of Adrian VI) that at least a German is elected pope by the cardinals. Indeed, openly monarchist writers dare to ascribe the elections once made by the emperors to their force and tyranny. And the words of the Conclave of Gregory XIV are worth quoting on this. When the King of Spain (who for a long time had great power in the election of popes) wished, through his legate, to nominate seven, from whom the cardinals might freely choose one, to put his lay hands into the sanctuary of God (in their own style), that is, to lay his lay hands on the sanctuary of God, the cardinals opposed to the Spanish faction protested, among other arguments, with this one: since it had pleased God &c. That is: Because God has been pleased once to free his Church from the servitude into which the ancient emperors unjustly placed it as regards the creation of popes, the cardinals ought not to consent that it be placed again under harsher conditions and under a prince of lower dignity. By this reasoning the emperor himself would be given an occasion to renew his old pretensions, if he saw that what he had claimed in past times with a certain protest had not only been obtained, but had been acquired with an increase by a lower prince, without any reason. From these words it appears that the cardinals call the servitude of their Church unjust and, on the part of the emperors, tyranny, and even expressly sacrilege any, even the least, share of secular power in the election. From this it is clear that it is wrongly said that no part is now left to the emperors in the election of the Popes, that is, the concurrence in the election of the Roman Pontiffs. What then would they have said, if they had wished to judge there about the election itself once made by the emperors?

units.la: XXXVI. Sed electionem ipsam per Imperatores factam non injustam Ecclesiæ oppressionem, non sacrilegium fuisse, par-tim ex dictis constat, partim ex ipsis Monarchicorum hypothesi-bus sic porrò facilè ostenditur. Et primò quidem ex Pontificum ea de re decretis. Jam decreta Hadriani I. & Leonis VIII. adduximus, Juri Canonico inserta, & quæ apud alios contra Baronii exceptio-nes solidè & prolixè vindicata videri possunt. Illis addimus hic Stephani P. decretum, quod dist.63.c.28. ita habetur; Quia Sancta Romana Ecclesia, cui authore Deo præsidemus, à pluribus patitur violen-tias, Pontifice abeunte, quæ ob hoc inferuntur, quia absque Imperiali notitia fit Pontificis consecratio, nec Canonico ritu, nec consuetudine, ab Imperatore directi intersunt Nuntii, qui scandala fieri volent; volumus, ut, cùm instituendus est Pontifex, convenientibus Episcopis & universo Clero, eligatur, præsente Senatu & populo, qui ordinatus est, & sic ab omnibus electis, præsentibus Legatis Imperialibus consecretur. Cui decreto Gra-tianus ista præmittit, Principibus verò atque Imperatoribus electiones Romanorum Pontificum, atque aliorum Episcoporum referendas usus & constitutio tradidit, pro Schismaticorum & hæreticorum dissensionibus, quibus nonnunquam Ecclesia Dei concussa periclitabatur: Contra quos legibus fidelissimorum Imperatorum frequenter Ecclesia munita legitur. Repræsentabatur ergo electio Pontificum Catholicorum Principibus, ut eorum authoritate roborata, nullus hæreticorum, aut Schismaticorum auderet contraire, & ut ipsi Principes, tanquam devotissimi filii in eum consentirent, quem sibi in Patrem eligi viderent, ut ei in omnibus suffragatores exisAt in omnibus suffragatores exisferent &c. Quomodo Gratianus hæc ad usum & constitutionem prægnantibus rationibus innixam refert, ut de meris Pontificum concessionibus heic cum Monarchicis cogitare, vanissimum sit.
units.tr: XXXVI. That the election itself made by the emperors was not an unjust oppression of the Church, nor a sacrilege, is partly clear from what has been said, and partly is easily shown from the monarchists' own hypotheses. And first, indeed, from the decrees of the Popes on this matter. We have already cited the decrees of Hadrian I and Leo VIII, inserted into canon law, which can be seen to have been solidly and fully defended against Baronius's objections by others. To these we add here the decree of Pope Stephen, which stands thus in dist. 63, c. 28: Because the holy Roman Church, over which we preside by God's authority, suffers many violences when a pope dies, which are inflicted for this reason, that the consecration of a pope takes place without the knowledge of the emperor, and neither by canonical rite nor by custom are envoys sent by the emperor present, who wish scandals to occur; we will that, when a pope is to be installed, he be elected by the assembled bishops and the whole clergy, in the presence of the senate and people, who have been ordained for this, and thus be consecrated by all the electors, in the presence of the imperial legates. Gratian prefaces this decree with these words: Custom and constitution have handed down to princes and emperors the referral of the elections of Roman Pontiffs and of other bishops, on account of the dissensions of schismatics and heretics, by which the Church of God was sometimes shaken and endangered. Against these, the Church is often read to have been fortified by the laws of the most faithful emperors. The election of Catholic Pontiffs was therefore presented to the princes, so that, their authority having strengthened it, no heretic or schismatic would dare oppose it, and so that the princes themselves, as most devoted sons, might agree to him whom they saw chosen as their father, so that they should be supporters for him in all things, etc. How Gratian refers these matters to custom and constitution, resting on weighty reasons, makes it most absurd to think here, with the monarchists, of mere concessions of the popes.

units.la: XXXVII. Secundò idem facilè ostenditur ex eo, quòd tot Pontifices, in præcedentibus memorati, ab Imperatoribus ele-cti leguntur; de quibus proin necesse est dicere, aut, non Canoni-cè electos esse, Pseudo-Papas fuisse, successionémque illorum respe-ctu interruptam, invalida eorum statuta, nullas eorum ordinatio-nes, aut, Formam illam Electionis per Imperatores bonam atque legitim m fuisse. Præsertim quando ante concessiones, quas sin-gunt jus conferentes, multa ad electionem contulisse leguntur, ele-ctionésque ctionésque sic factas Ecclesia præter Papas electos tacitis suffragiis confirmavit. Et quæso audiatur, quomodo Gregorius M. vel de sua constitutione judicet. Ita ait l. 1. epist. 5. Serenissimus D. Imperator fieri Simiam Leonem jussit. Et quidem pro jussione illius vocari Leo potest, fieri autem Leo non potest. Unde necesse est, ut omnes culpas ac negligentias meas, non mihi, sed suæ pietati deputet, qui virtutis ministerium vasirmo commisit. Ex quibus verbis apparet Gregorii I. etiam electionem, ipsomet ita censente, ad authoritatem Imperatoriam præcipuè referri debere, non enim obscurè docet, potuisse Imperatorem, ne Papa fieret, intercedere, quod certè (juxta testimonium etiam Maimburgii in præcedentibus) eodem recedit cum forma Electionis tertia per Imperatores. Ut etiam præmissa docent, malè Baronium ad an. 1049. n. 1. distinguere inter deligere (quod Imperatoribus tantùm largitur) & eligere, (quod semper penes Cardinales fuisse, affirmat.)
units.tr: XXXVII. Secondly, the same is easily shown from the fact that so many popes, mentioned above, are read to have been elected by the emperors. Of them it must therefore be said either that they were not canonically elected and were false popes, and the succession with respect to them was interrupted, their statutes invalid and their ordinations null; or that the form of election by the emperors was good and lawful. This is especially so since, before the concessions which the adversaries invent, they are read to have contributed much to the election, and the Church, by its tacit assent, confirmed the elections so made, besides the popes elected. And let us hear, I ask, how Gregory the Great judges even his own appointment. He says thus, Book 1, letter 5: "The most serene lord emperor ordered that an ape be made a lion. Indeed by his command one may be called a lion, but one cannot be made a lion. Hence it is necessary that he attribute all my faults and negligences not to me but to his own piety, who committed the ministry of virtue to a feeble man." From these words it appears that Gregory I also thought that his own election should be referred chiefly to imperial authority. For he does not obscurely teach that the emperor could intercede so that he would not become pope, which certainly (also according to the testimony of Maimbourg, cited above) comes to the same thing as the third form of election by the emperors. As the things set out above also show, Baronius is wrong, ad an. 1049, n. 1, to distinguish between to appoint (which he grants only to the emperors) and to elect (which he asserts was always in the hands of the cardinals).

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECTION TWO.

units.la: In qua De quarta per Cardinales solos eligendi forma, & in antecessum etiam de Cardinalibus agitur; Breviarium.
units.tr: In which the fourth form of election, by the Cardinals alone, is discussed, and first the Cardinals themselves; a summary.

units.la: I. Quarta eligendi forma per Cardinales. Vox Cardinalis unde? Quando prima eorum mentio? II. Quales in primitiva Ecclesia fuerint; III. Sententia Onuphrii & Bellarmini; Illum hic refutavit; IV. Refutatur & ipse; Adoptatur sententia Ant. de Dominis, dici quasi fixos ordinarios; VI. Probatur; VII. Atque inde concluditur, antiquissimum esse ministerium Cardinalitium; VIII. Hodiernis tamen Cardinalibus similes diu ignorati. IX. Cardinales elim in quibusvis Ecclesiis. X Cardinales Romani primi quales; Presbyteri maximam partem fuerunt; Episcopi sunt recentiores; XI. De Titulis Cardinalium ex Ciaconio; XII. Ex Onuphrio; XIII. Numerus; XIV. Diaconi; XV. De mutatione Ministeriorum; XVI. Ex consideratione officii patet, incumbere illis, ut in Titulis curam ordinariam per se ipsos exerceant; Quod tamen non faciunt; XVII. Ut etiam respectu dignitatis differunt ab antiquioribus, qui inferiores erant Episcopis; Ostenditur quoad ipsos Episcopos Cardinales Romanos; XVIII. Quoad Presbyteros & Diaconos; XIX. Imprimis ex subscriptione satis
units.tr: I. The fourth form of election, by the Cardinals. Where does the word "Cardinal" come from? When is it first mentioned? II. What they were in the primitive Church. III. The opinion of Onuphrius and Bellarmine, which I refute here. IV. It is refuted also on its own terms. V. The opinion of Antonio de Dominis is adopted: they are called, as it were, fixed ordinaries. VI. This is proved. VII. And from this it is concluded that the Cardinalitial ministry is very ancient. VIII. Yet the Cardinals of today were unknown for a long time. IX. Cardinals once existed in all churches. X. The first Roman Cardinals: they were mostly presbyters; bishops are more recent. XI. On the titles of the Cardinals, from Ciaconius. XII. From Onuphrius. XIII. The number. XIV. Deacons. XV. On the change of ministries. XVI. From consideration of the office it is clear that it falls to them to exercise the ordinary care of their titles in person; which, however, they do not do. XVII. They also differ in dignity from the older ones, who were inferior to bishops; this is shown with regard to the Roman Cardinal bishops themselves. XVIII. With regard to presbyters and deacons. XIX. Chiefly from a signature, which is rather late.

units.tr: rather late. XX. Also from elsewhere. XXI. It is still said that the Rector of the University of Paris sometimes precedes the Cardinals themselves. XXII. Confessions of the Monarchists on the former precedence of bishops. XXIII. The state has now changed. XXIV. This is further illustrated and refuted. XXV. How greatly they are now placed above everyone; bishops perform base services for Cardinals. XXVI. This is confirmed. XXVII. Bishops are otherwise also treated contemptuously in relation to Cardinals. XXVIII. Of the superiority of the Cardinals. XXIX. The foundations, as set out by Bellarmine. XXX. These are refuted. XXXI. Moreover. XXXII. Further. XXXIII. Cardinals are placed on a level with kings themselves. XXXIV. They want to be placed before princes. XXXV. How they are usually received as legates. XXXVI. Some kingdoms hear them as Protectors. XXXVII. In relation to the Pope they appear base on one side. XXXVIII. This is declared more clearly. XXXIX. It is shown more truly. XL. The means of this contempt. XLI. On this ground the title of Princes of the Church is denied to them. XLII. The causes are shown in three kinds of Cardinals. XLIII. On the other side they appear very honoured and endowed with great power. XLIV. Their dignity and power are declared further. XLV. Whether they can be created or deposed by the Pope without the consent of the Cardinals. XLVI. They have often been deposed in this way. XLVII. units.la: I. Quarta tandem sequitur Electionis Pontificum Romanorum Forma, quae fieri solet à Clero Cardinalium, in suas iterum eligendi formas, quas Sectione sequente exhibebimus, ratione modi eligendi potissimum, ut caeterae ratione eligentium, subdivisa. Prius autem aliquid de nomine, Origine, statu & dignitate horum Electorum dicendum erit. Et primo quod nomen attinet, indubium est, derivari à cardine, sed non ita certum est, quomodo, & cur illi, de quibus agimus, & illi, quorum successionem jactant, à cardine Cardinales dicantur, & dicti sint; Ut & non exiguus Authorum dissensus est de eo, quinam olim & primo ex Ministris Ecclesiasticis hoc nomine vocati fuerint. Non reperitur nomen in Scriptura, neque apud Patres antiquos, ne quidem apud historicos, sive Christianos, sive Gentiles, quos inter maxime occasionem habuisset, qui turbas in Electione Episcopi Romani suâ aetate excitatas memoriae tradidit, Ammianus Marcellinus. Quamvis enim non desint, qui scribant, Marcellum I. P. Cardinales constituisse propter Baptismum & alia, in Actis tamen ejus apud Baronium ad an. 309. n. 4. Cardinalium nomen non comparet; Et quamvis alii, Cardinales institutos esse, vel à Pontiano, vel à Sylvestro I. pertendant, & cum Bellarmino l. de Clericis c. 16. ad sextum Canonem Concilii Romani sub illo Sylvestro provocent; tamen, quando Concilium istud & alia, quæ ex puriori & priori antiquitate heic produci solent, valdè dubia sunt, & ex parte manifestè suppositítia, ut etiam Author Doctissimus tractatûs Gallici de l'Origine des Cardinaux du S. Siege p.9. ex suis, id est, Pontificiis innuit, qui tienent ce Concile pour faux supposè, & en allegnent de grandes raisons, id est, qui Concilium illud falsum & suppositicium esse credant & illud rationibus magni momenti probare studeant; Et in margine ponit le Sieur Vigor Conseiler au grand Conseil en son traité des Conciles chap.4. ubi quoq; errorem Matthei Historici Regii, quem cum Bellarmino communem habet, Chronologicum, dum 300. fere annis Sylvestrum Gregorio M. priorem fuisse dicunt, notat; Et quia variis occasionibus tamen titulus Cardinalium non adhibitus fuit, non immeritò cum Erasmo, dum in Vita Hieronymi fabulam de S.Patris Cardinalatu rejicit, infert: Dubitamus, an illis temporibus Cardinalis Titulus fuerit repertus; quod Spiegelius in Lexico Juris planè negat. Sed demum circa an. Chr. 560. Johannes III. P. dilectis filiis, Cardinalibus Clericis se Ecclesiam certam Titulum Cardinalem constituisse, scribens, primam, quæ fidem meretur, Cardinalium mentionem facit, quorum sæpe post eum, M. Antonii de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. l. IV. c. 5. n. 9. judicio omnium primus (nam allata priora indicia ipsi quoque incerta sunt, dubiaque fidei) meminit Gregorius I. post hunc frequentissimè alii.
units.tr: I. The fourth form of election of the Roman Pontiffs follows at last, which is usually made by the clergy of the Cardinals. It is again divided, as the others are by reason of the electors, mainly by the mode of electing, into its own forms, which we shall set out in the following Section. First, however, something must be said of the name, origin, status and dignity of these electors. And first, as regards the name, it is beyond doubt that it derives from cardo (hinge), but it is not so certain how and why those we are discussing, and those whose succession they boast of, are and have been called Cardinals from the hinge. There is also no small disagreement among authors about who first, among ecclesiastical ministers, were called by this name. The name is not found in Scripture, nor among the ancient Fathers, nor even among the historians, Christian or Gentile, among whom Ammianus Marcellinus, who recorded the disturbances stirred up at the election of the Roman bishop in his own time, would especially have had occasion. For although there are not lacking those who write that Pope Marcellus I appointed Cardinals on account of baptism and other matters, the name of Cardinals does not appear in his Acts as given by Baronius at the year 309, no. 4. And although others claim that Cardinals were instituted either by Pontian or by Sylvester I, and with Bellarmine (De clericis, ch. 16) appeal to the sixth canon of the Roman Council under that Sylvester, nevertheless, since that council and the other things usually produced here from the purer and earlier antiquity are very doubtful, and in part manifestly spurious, as the most learned author of the French treatise On the Origin of the Cardinals of the Holy See, p. 9, hints from his own side, that is, from the Papists, who hold that this council is false and supposititious, and bring great reasons for it, that is, who believe that council to be false and spurious and strive to prove it by reasons of great weight; and in the margin he cites Monsieur Vigor, councillor of the Grand Council, in his treatise On Councils, ch. 4, where he also notes the chronological error of Matthew, the royal historian, which he holds in common with Bellarmine, when they say that Sylvester was earlier than Gregory the Great by nearly 300 years. And since on various occasions the title of Cardinals was nevertheless not used, it is not without reason that, with Erasmus, who in the Life of Jerome rejects the fable of the holy Father's cardinalate, we conclude: We doubt whether the title of Cardinal was in use in those times; which Spiegel in his Lexicon of Law plainly denies. But at last, around the year of Christ 560, Pope John III, writing to his beloved sons, the Cardinal clergy, that he had appointed the Church as a fixed title of Cardinals, makes the first mention of Cardinals that deserves credit; after him, according to the judgment of Marco Antonio de Dominis (On the Republic of the Church, bk IV, ch. 5, no. 9), which is often cited, Gregory I, the first of all (for the earlier indications cited are themselves uncertain and doubtful) makes mention of them, and after him very many others.

units.la: II. Ex quorum locis, quæ apud eundem de Dominis l. c. n.9. seqq. possunt videri, sequentia maximè colligimus; 1. Cardinales non tantum à Papa creari. 2. Nec in Romana tantum, sed in quibusvis aliis Ecclesiis. 3. Clericos alicujus Ecclesiæ non-Cardinales ultimos inter sui ordinis alios stare. 4. Incardinari in alia Ecclesia neminem, qui fuerit in alia cardinatus, nisi priori obligatione solutâ. 5. Plures in eadem Ecclesia Diaconos fuisse Cardinales. Sed & inde colligi potest, quinam tandem in veteri Ecclesia, quomodo & cur Cardinales (habet Adrianus I. Cardinarius; Græcus in Dialogo cum Cardinali satis corruptè Caldenarius; Hispanis autem eadem vox Cardenal etiam vibicem sive livorem ex contusione significat;) dicti sint. Volunt quidam, certos Ministros Ecclesiasticos ita vocari σύνωνύμως, quasi Cardines, majorem sic Italici sermonis quàm Latini rationem habentes, quia sint Cardines ostii Ecclesiæ, super quos versetur & sustentetur, & per quos Ecclesiæ axis volvatur; Alii melius παρωνύμως à Cardine dictos esse judicant, de modo tamen quoque dissentientes; Ubi primò Leo IX. sibi ipsi
units.tr: II. From the passages in the same author, de Dominis, l. c. n. 9. ff., which may be consulted, we chiefly gather the following: (1) cardinals were not created only by the Pope; (2) not only in the Roman Church but in any other churches; (3) the non-cardinal clergy of any church stood last among those of their own rank; (4) no one who had been made cardinal in one church could be incardinated in another unless the earlier obligation had been dissolved; (5) several deacons in the same church were cardinals. But from this it can also be gathered who, in the ancient Church, were then called cardinals, and how and why (Adrian I has Cardinarius; the Greek in the Dialogue with a Cardinal, rather corruptly, has Caldenarius; but in Spanish the same word, Cardenal, also means a weal or bruise from a blow). Some think that certain ecclesiastical ministers are so called synonymously [συνωνύμως], as if they were hinges, showing more regard for the Italian idiom than for the Latin, since they are the hinges of the church door, on which it turns and is supported, and through which the axis of the church revolves. Others judge more correctly that they are named from the hinge paronymously [παρωνύμως], though they too disagree about the manner. Here first Leo IX, to himself

units.la: Quales in primitiva Ecclesia fuerint; ipsi nimiùm blandiens Clericos suos Cardinales vocari ait, tanquam Cardini illi, quo catera mouentur, vicinius adhærentes. Sed illi omnes, ita, maximè de Vniversali Ecclesia, loquentes, præterita præsentibus accommodant, licèt maximè diversa, ne dicam pugnantia. Talia hèic contrà demum locum habent, quæ veteri statui Ecclesiæ cujusvis conveniant.
units.tr: What they were in the primitive Church. Flattering himself too much, he says that his clergy are called cardinals, as those hinges to which the rest are moved, adhering more closely. But all these writers, speaking thus especially of the universal Church, apply what was past to what is present, though the two are very different, not to say contradictory. Such things, on the contrary, hold good only for what fits the ancient condition of any church.

units.la: III. Igitur Onuphrius (verbis utor Bellarmini) in libro de Cardinalium titulis existimat, Presbyteros & Diaconos Cardinales dictos esse eos, qui præerant aliis Presbyteris vel Diaconis ejusdem Ecclesiæ, quasi principales Presbyteri, vel Diaconi in illa Ecclesia; Erant enim plures Presbyteri in eadem Ecclesia, sed Præses tantùm dicebatur Cardinalis. Sed recte eum refutat Bellarminus l. c. 1. ex eo, quòd in eodem titulo plures aliquando erant Cardinales. 2. ex eo, quòd tempore S. Sylvestri 7. tantùm Romæ erant Diaconi, omnes Cardinales (quamvis in hoc dubiis innitatur, si non falsis;) 3. ex eo, quòd sic nulla ratio reddi posset, cur dicerentur quidam Episcopi Cardinales: Cùm non possint dici Episcopi Cardinales, quòd præsint aliis Episcopis suæ diœcesis. Ipse Bellarminus existimat, nomen Cardinalis primùm impositum esse loco, & à loco derivatum ad personas; dictos esse titulos Cardinales quasdam Ecclesias principales, ubi Baptisma conferebatur; & dictas esse Ecclesias vel titulos Cardinales, ad differentiam aliorum locorum Sacrorum minùs principalium; Inde Presbyterum, qui eam Ecclesiam regebat, esse dictum Presbyterum Cardinalem. Pari ratione Diaconias Cardinales fuisse loca quadam principalia in urbe distincta juxta numerum Regionum, & Diaconos, qui in eis residebant, dictos fuisse Diaconos videlicet ab Ecclesia Cardinali quam tenebant; Sic etiam postmodum dictos esse Episcopatus Cardinales & inde Episcopos Cardinales sex illos, qui ad eligendum Pontificem conveniebant, & eidem Pontifici à Consiliis erant, præter cæteros orbis Christiani Episcopos.
units.tr: III. So Onuphrius (I use Bellarmine's words) in his book on the titles of the cardinals thinks that priests and deacons were called cardinals who presided over other priests or deacons of the same church, as the principal priests or deacons in that church; for there were several priests in the same church, but only the president was called cardinal. But Bellarmine rightly refutes him, l. c., (1) because in the same title there were sometimes several cardinals; (2) because in the time of St Sylvester there were only seven deacons in Rome, all cardinals (though he relies here on doubtful, if not false, evidence); (3) because no reason could thus be given why certain bishops were called cardinal bishops, since they cannot be called cardinal bishops on the ground that they preside over other bishops of their diocese. Bellarmine himself thinks that the name cardinal was first applied to a place and was transferred from the place to persons; that the cardinal titles were certain principal churches where baptism was conferred; and that these churches or titles were called cardinal to distinguish them from other less principal sacred places. Hence the priest who ruled that church was called cardinal priest. By the same reasoning, the cardinal diaconies were certain principal places in the city, distinguished according to the number of the regions, and the deacons who resided in them were called deacons of the cardinal church which they held. So too, later, the cardinal bishoprics were called such, and hence the six bishops who gathered to elect the Pontiff, and were his counsellors, were called cardinal bishops, apart from the other bishops of the Christian world.

units.la: IV. Igitur & Onuphrius & Bellarminus Cardinalem Ecclesiasticum virum quasi præcipuum dici volunt, eadem ferè ratione, quâ numeri Cardinales dicuntur, à quibus numerandi fit quædam conversio, ut sunt decem, viginti &c. Virtutes Cardinales quatuor, ad quas cæteræ possunt referri, & quæ quasi anima cæterarum sunt; Venti Cardinales totidem, à quibus nomina accipiunt interpositi; Quomodo etiam Cyprianus librum de Cardinalibus, id est, præcipuis Christi operibus inscripsit. In eo conveniunt Onuphrius & Bellarminus, sed in eo jam dissentiunt, quòd alter præcipuum puum inter multos ejusdem loci, alter quemvis in loco præcipuo constitutum Cardinalem vocari autumat; Onuphrium refutavit Bellarminus, refutandus & ipse; Non enim bona est, quam dat, explicatio, cum non ostendere possit ex antiquitate, Ecclesias alias fuisse cum titulis Cardinalitiis, alias vero cum titulis quidem, sed non Cardinalitiis: Multò minùs ostendere potest, sex illos tantùm, quos innuit, Episcopos Romæ vicinos Cardinales Episcopos fuisse; Imò contrarium hujus ex ipsis Gregorii M. epistolis apparet, ut & ex epistolis Adriani II. & Johannis VIII. ubi nonnunquam Cardinalis Sacerdos Episcopus dicitur, & aliquem in aliqua civitate incardinare, idem est, ac eum ibi Episcopum facere, & Cardinalem constitui in Ecclesia Bituricensi, idem est, quod, ibi Archiepiscopum constitui. Sic etiam ex eo sententia Bellarmini solidè refutatur, quòd in eadem Ecclesia Presbyteri Cardinales & non Cardinales, Diaconi similiter Cardinales & non Cardinales memorantur.
units.tr: IV. So both Onuphrius and Bellarmine wish the ecclesiastical cardinal to be called a principal man, by almost the same reasoning by which cardinal numbers are so called, from which a certain conversion of counting arises, as ten, twenty, and so on; the four cardinal virtues, to which the others can be referred, and which are as it were the soul of the rest; the cardinal winds, equally many, from which the intermediate points take their names. So too Cyprian entitled his book on the cardinal works, that is, the principal works of Christ. Onuphrius and Bellarmine agree on this, but already differ in that the one thinks the principal man among many of the same place, the other thinks that anyone placed in a principal position is called cardinal. Bellarmine refuted Onuphrius, and must himself be refuted. For the explanation Onuphrius gives is not sound, since he cannot show from antiquity that some churches had cardinal titles and others had titles that were not cardinal. Still less can he show that those six bishops he hints at, who were near Rome, were the cardinal bishops. Indeed the opposite appears from the very letters of Gregory the Great, and from the letters of Adrian II and John VIII, where a cardinal priest is sometimes called a bishop, and to incardinate someone in a city is the same as making him bishop there, and to be constituted cardinal in the church of Bourges is the same as being constituted archbishop there. So too Bellarmine's view is solidly refuted by the fact that in the same church both cardinal and non-cardinal priests, and likewise cardinal and non-cardinal deacons, are mentioned.

units.la: V. Placet itaque rejectis sic aliis, sententia in antiquitate Ecclesiastica peritissimi & jam sæpiùs laudati M. Ant. de Dominis, qui lib. & cap. cit. n. 5. ita scribit; Cardinalis mea sententia dictus est olim Episcopus (imò etiam Metropolitanus, jamjam de Archiepiscopo vidimus) sive Presbyter, sive Diaconus, qui non per modum provisionis, aut transcursu, ac fere mutatò & ad tempus; sed qui fixè ac permanenter, uti proprius jam illius Ecclesiæ Minister, ad exercenda ministeria Ecclesiastica illius Ecclesiæ propria, in ea legitimè collocatur & inthronizatur, quæ collocatio, seu inthronizatio etiam incardinatio solet vocari. Atque ita Cardinalis Presbyter, aut Diaconus, vel Subdiaconus etiam (Nam apud Baron. T. 10. an. 963. n. 13. Johannem Subdiaconum Cardinalem invenies à Johanne Papa XII. testium amputatione occisum) (de Subdiacono Cardinali etiam n. 17. ex Gregorio M. & Johanne Diacono allegat testimonia) nunquam poterat esse in Ecclesia, quæ non esset revera titulata; hoc est, ad publica ministeria Ecclesiastica erecta & deputata, nam etiam erant Oratoria ad privatas tantùm orationes seu sepulturas fabricata; Quæcunque igitur Ecclesia facta esset ab Episcopo Parochialis, & publicis, ut dixi, ministeriis Sacramentorum deputata, illa dicebatur titulus Cardinalis. Ibidem etiam talibus Cardinalibus loca à Bellarmino pro sua sententia citata applicat.
units.tr: V. It pleases me, therefore, having set the others aside, to adopt the opinion of M. Antonius de Dominis, most learned in ancient ecclesiastical history and often praised already, who in the book and chapter cited, n. 5, writes thus: In my opinion, a cardinal was formerly called a bishop (indeed even a metropolitan, as we have already seen of an archbishop), or a priest, or a deacon, who was not placed there by way of provision, or in passing, nearly as a temporary substitute, but who was fixedly and permanently, as the proper minister of that church, legitimately placed and enthroned in it to exercise the ecclesiastical ministries proper to that church. This placement, or enthronement, is also usually called incardination. And thus a cardinal priest, or deacon, or even subdeacon (for in Baronius, vol. 10, year 963, n. 13, you will find John, a cardinal subdeacon, killed by the cutting off of his witnesses' parts by Pope John XII; and at n. 17 he cites testimonies from Gregory the Great and John the Deacon concerning a cardinal subdeacon), could never be in a church that was not truly titled; that is, dedicated and appointed to public ecclesiastical ministries. For there were also oratories built only for private prayers or burials. Whatever church, therefore, was made by the bishop a parish church, and, as I said, appointed to the public ministries of the sacraments, was called a cardinal title. In the same place he also applies to such cardinals the places cited by Bellarmine in support of his opinion.

units.la: VI. Sanè prima & maximè propria est hæc vocabuli Cardinalis significatio, ut fixum, ordinarium designet, & eidem cardini constanter annexum: altera autem significatio, juxta quam præcipuum cipuum voce illa designant,demùm ex priori nata est,quia id,quod fixum est,vel ideò præcipuum habetur, quod tanquam mensura est eorum,quæ ad hoc referuntur; Sicut etiam priorem hîc commendant significationem ex parte allatæ voces cognatæ, incardinare, incardinandus, incardinatus, incardinatio, adhibere solitæ in Ministrorum Ecclesiæ constitutione. Quare etiam non immeritò Doctissimus de Dominis testem produxit ipsummet Onuphrium, cujus in interpr. vocum obscur. §. de officio, sive de Magistratu, hæc inter alia verba leguntur: Apud Vitruvium idem est Cardinalis, quod annexus, vel insertus, vel compactus. Hæc vox in eandem fere sententiam frequens est in Registro Gregorii & epistolis Pontificum Romanorum Decretalibus. Quibus & Cardinalis dicitur Presbyter, vel Diaconus, qui certa alicui Ecclesiæ, vel Diaconiæ proprius, & ad certi alicujus tituli sive Ecclesiæ ministerium ordinatus, insertus, annexus, & (ut ipse loquitur) incardinatus est.
units.tr: VI. Certainly the first and most proper meaning of the word cardinal is that which denotes what is fixed and ordinary, and constantly attached to the same hinge. The second meaning, by which they designate the principal, arose only from the first, because what is fixed is regarded as principal in that it serves as the measure of those things that are referred to it. Likewise the cognate words that were customarily used in the appointment of church ministers also commend the first meaning: incardinate, incardinandus, incardinatus, incardinatio. Hence de Dominis, most learned, rightly produced as a witness Onuphrius himself, in whose Interpretation of Obscure Words, section on office, or on the magistracy, these words, among others, are read: In Vitruvius, cardinal means the same as attached, or inserted, or fastened together. This word is frequent in nearly the same sense in the Register of Gregory and in the letters and Decretals of the Roman Pontiffs. By these a priest or deacon is also called cardinal who is proper to some fixed church or diaconate, and ordained to the ministry of a certain title or church, inserted, attached, and (as he himself puts it) incardinated.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Ut omninò constet, ministerium Cardinalitium antiquissimum esse, imò fere cum Ecclesia natum. Non, quòd in Veteri Testamento Moses & 70. Seniores, vel Aaron & Levitæ, in Novo autem Christus & Apostoli, vel Christus & 70. discipuli (ut quidem Papæ Cardinalitiumque gnathones illis, ipsi sibi & aliis persuadere volunt) hodiernum statum probent; de quo rectè jam laudatus Author du Traitte des Cardinaux du S. Siege p. 21.22. judicat; C'est tirer l'origine des Cardinaux de trop loing & faire comme ceux, qui tenoient la ruine de Medée être venue des Forests de Peleon, à cause que d'icelle avoit esté tiré le bois pour edifier la navire de Jason, qui en leva Medée de la maison de son Pere. Id est: Sic è longinquo nimis petitur origo Cardinalium, & similes sunt isti homines, illi, qui exitium Medea ex Sylvis Pelei ortum habuisse tradunt, quia inde ligna petita sint, ex quibus Jasonis, qui Medeam ex paterna domo abduxit, navis ædificata fuerit. Apostolos in specie quod attinet, ut non desunt, qui ipsos Cardinalatûs munere functos esse pertendunt, Petrus de Alliaco Cameracensis de Eccl. Author. par. 1. c. 1. 3. col. 899. ita loquens: Apostoli Petro tanquam Papale officium gerenti assistebant, tanquam Cardinalatûs Ministerium exercentes, de quorum Cardinalatu spiritualiter intelligi possit illud Propheticum (1.Sam.II.8.) Domini sunt cardines terræ, & posui super eos orbem; Et Turrecrem. de Eccles. 1. c. 8. Cardinales amplissimi; In quo etiam illum secutus est Magnus Gerson de statibus Eccl. T. 1. prout Manfredus de Card. c. 6. Cardinales Apostolorum ante-
units.tr: So that it may be fully established that the ministry of cardinals is very ancient, indeed almost as old as the Church itself: not that Moses and the seventy elders in the Old Testament, or Aaron and the Levites, or in the New Testament Christ and the apostles, or Christ and the seventy disciples (as the Popes and their cardinal flatterers wish to persuade themselves and others) prove the present state. The already praised author, du Traitte des Cardinaux du S. Siege, pp. 21–22, rightly judges on this: It is to trace the origin of the Cardinals from too far off, and to do as those did who held that Medea's ruin came from the forests of Pelion, because the wood was cut from there to build Jason's ship, which carried Medea away from her father's house. That is: So the origin of the Cardinals is sought from too far off, and these men are like those who maintain that Medea's destruction arose from the woods of Pelion, because the timber was taken from there from which the ship of Jason, who carried Medea away from her father's house, was built. As far as the apostles in particular are concerned, there are not lacking those who claim that they discharged the office of cardinal. Peter of Ailly of Cambrai, de Eccl. Author. part 1, ch. 1, col. 899, speaks thus: The apostles assisted Peter as one performing the papal office, as exercising the ministry of the cardinalate, and of whose cardinalate that prophetic saying (1 Sam. 2:8) can be understood spiritually: "The pillars of the earth are the Lord's, and he has set the world upon them." And Turrecremata, de Eccles. 1, ch. 8, calls them most distinguished cardinals; in this too he followed Great Gerson, de statibus Eccl. vol. 1, as Manfredus, de Card. ch. 6, calls them the cardinals of the apostles' ante-

units.la: Atque inde concluditur, antiquissimum esse ministerium Cardinalium, quamvis nec illi deditî fuerint Levitæ, Apostoli, aut 70. Discipuli. antecessores vocat. Sed Papa hic etiam Christi Simia, ὁ ἀντὶ ἐξ Χρι-στοῦ, Petrum pro lubitu fingit. Nihil autem minus quàm hodiernis similes fuerunt Apostoli, nec in eos jus Divinum quaerere omisisset Bellarminus, si cum aliqua veri specie jactare illud potuisset; Nihil minùs quoque quàm Cardinales, id est, fixi fuerunt, sed in variis regionibus orbis ipsis Evangelium annunciare incubuit. Sed qui eos, mox exceperunt Ecclesiarum Rectores, certis locis affixi eatenus jam Cardinales fuerunt. Ut res omninò diu ante nomen fuerit hocce, & verum dicerent, (si in vero sensu) qui Cardinales cum Eugenio IV. evidenter à S. Petro & ejus Successoribus (potuisset addere, à reliquis etiam Apostolis & eorum successoribus;) institutos esse, contendunt, nec usque ad originem primam pertingant, qui vel Evaristo, vel Hygino, vel Pontiano, vel Marcello (qui Cardinales & ipsi fuerunt, permanserunt;) institutionem Cardinalium tribuunt; Et catenus recte dixerit Coeffetaeus, Dominicanus & designatus Massilienfis Episcopus; Si primitiva Ecclesia ignorârit, quid essent Cardinales, eam etiam ignorâsse, quid essent Episcopi, Presbyteri, Diaconi, cum illi nil aliud sint. Omninò nihil aliud fuerunt, quàm fixi, ordinarii & constantes Episcopi, Presbyteri, & Diaconi, quos tandem ab extraordinariis, Vicariis quasi hospitibus & Ministris pro tempore talibus, quique non ita arctè certis Ecclesiis alligati erant, distinguere opus fuit.
units.tr: And from this it is concluded that the ministry of cardinals is very ancient, although the Levites, the apostles, or the seventy disciples were not devoted to it; "predecessors" he calls them. But the Pope, here too Christ's ape, [ὁ ἀντὶ Χριστοῦ / ho anti Christou], makes up Peter as he pleases. Nothing was less like the present-day cardinals than the apostles, nor would Bellarmine have failed to claim a divine right for them, had he been able to assert it with any semblance of truth. Nor were they fixed as cardinals are, that is, bound to particular places; rather they took pains to proclaim the Gospel in various regions of the world. But those who soon succeeded them as rulers of churches, fixed in certain places, were by then already cardinals in that sense. So the thing existed long before the name, and they speak truly (if in the true sense) who contend that the cardinals were instituted by Eugenius IV, evidently by St Peter and his successors (he could have added: by the other apostles too and their successors); and those who do not reach back to the first origin, but ascribe the institution of cardinals to Evaristus, Hyginus, Pontian or Marcellus (who were themselves cardinals and remained so), speak rightly. And so Coeffeteau, a Dominican and designated Bishop of Marseilles, spoke correctly: If the primitive Church did not know what cardinals were, it did not know what bishops, presbyters and deacons were, since these are nothing other than them. Quite nothing other than fixed, ordinary and constant bishops, presbyters and deacons; whom it was at length necessary to distinguish from the extraordinary ones, vicars as it were, guests and ministers for the time being, who were not so tightly bound to fixed churches.

units.la: VIII. Sed ne quis ideo Coeffetaeo victoriam contra Illustrissimum Plesslaeum tribuat contendentem, Ecclesiam primitivam Cardinales ignorâsse. Ut etiam apud Amplifs. Sprengerum Instit. Jur. Publ. c. 35. Volateranus eorum institutionem Benedicto IX. c. an. 1131. adscribit, alii eam ad Anastasium III. c. an. 914. referunt, qui prohibitus à Berengario, ne Episcopum Papiensem Archiepiscopum crearet, novo ordine excogitato, praedicto Episcopo mitrae rubrae insignia dederit. Quamvis non satis mirari possim, quomodo subjungere potuerit: Inde Cardinalitia dignitas provenit, quae imperante Phoca sub Bonifacio III. summum gloria fastigium attigit; cùm Bonifacius III. tamen diu ante Anastasium illum III. sub quo dignitas provenisse dicitur, fuerit, & illa tunc tantùm à summo fastigio abfuerit. Quando illud dicunt nostri, id non eo animo dicunt, ac si statuerent, rem primorum Cardinalium non semper in Ecclesia fuisse. Damus hoc ultrò, sed illud negamus, nominis certa vestigia ante seculum sextum reperiri, & rem hodiernam ante mille à Christo nato annorum decursum. De nomine jam vidimus. De re nobiscum sentit jam aliquoties nominatus Author de l'origine des Cardinaux du S. Siege. p,22. postquam retulisset, & quadantenus rejecisset aliorum pro antiquitate dignitatis Cardinalitiæ opiniones, ita scribens; C'est notoirement la rechercher d'un temps, auquel les Prétres & Diacres, voire mesme les Evesques, estoient bien differens des Cardinaux dont nous traittons; desquels la grandeur estoit lors inconnüe : car l'institution en est bien plus recente, & elle n'a commencè à paroistre en France, que sous la troisiesme race de nos Roys, comme nous prouverons cy apres, & non pas en la primitive Eglise; auquel temps il n'y avoit point d' Eglises Cardinales, ny de Ministre Cardinal,ny du temps des Apostres, ny quelques siecles apres, car ce peu de Prestres & de Diacres, qu'il y avoit exerçans le Ministere en des Cavernes, & des lieux secrets, ne souffroit point ceste distinction de Prestres Cardinaux à la difference d'autres Prestres; & cela est arrivé seulement & long temps apres que l'Eglise par sa patience eut vaincu la persecution des Empereurs, & qu'elle ait foulé les Idoles sous les pieds; alors on vit multiplier le nombre des Ministres, & on commença distinguer les lieux principaux des autres, & de moindre consideration. Id est: Sic manifeste origo quaritur ab illo tempore, quo Presbyteri & Diaconi imo ipsi Episcopi multùm differebant à Cardinalibus,de quibus agimus; quorum eminentia tunc ignorabatur: Eorum quippe institutio multò est recentior & apparere in Gallia cœpit demum sub tertia Regum nostrorum stirpe, ut post probabimus, & non in primitiva Ecclesia; quando nulla erant Ecclesia Cardinales, Ministri Cardinales (loquitur tanquam, à præcipuo loco Cardinalem appellari,credens) nulli, nec tempore Apostolorum,nec post aliquot secula,nam dum pauci illi Presbyteri & Diaconi tum temporis ministerium exercebant in speluncis & locis occultis, distinctio illa Presbyterorum Cardinalium ab aliis Presbyteris distinctorum locum habere non potuit. Sed tum demum, & diu postquam Ecclesia sua patientia persecutiones imperatorum vicisset & Idola pedibus conculcâsset; Tunc numerus Ministrorum multiplicabatur, & incipiebant distinguere loca pracipua à minus pracipuis. Rursus loquitur juxta illam hypothesin.
units.tr: VIII. But lest anyone therefore give Coeffeteau the victory over the most illustrious Plessis, who contends that the primitive Church did not know the cardinals. Likewise, in the most distinguished Sprenger, Instit. Jur. Publ. ch. 35, Volaterranus ascribes their institution to Benedict IX, about the year 1131; others refer it to Anastasius III, about the year 914, who, forbidden by Berengar to make the Bishop of Pavia an archbishop, devised a new order and gave the said bishop the insignia of the red mitre. Yet I cannot sufficiently wonder how he could add: From this the cardinalitial dignity arose, which under Phocas, under Boniface III, reached the highest summit of glory; since Boniface III was long before that Anastasius III under whom the dignity is said to have arisen, and at that time it was still far from the highest summit. When our people say this, they do not say it with the intention of holding that the thing of the first cardinals was not always in the Church. We grant this freely, but we deny that certain traces of the name are found before the sixth century, or that the present thing existed a thousand years after the birth of Christ. Of the name we have already seen. Concerning the thing, the author often named above agrees with us, de l'origine des Cardinaux du S. Siège, p. 22, having recounted and in some measure rejected the opinions of others about the antiquity of the cardinalitial dignity, writing thus: It is clearly to seek its origin at a time when priests and deacons, even bishops themselves, were quite different from the cardinals we are discussing, whose eminence was then unknown. Their institution is indeed much more recent, and it began to appear in France only under the third race of our kings, as we shall prove below, and not in the primitive Church; at which time there were no cardinal churches, nor any cardinal minister, neither in the time of the apostles nor for some centuries after, for the few priests and deacons who then exercised the ministry in caves and secret places did not admit this distinction of cardinal priests from other priests. This came about only, and long after the Church by its patience had overcome the persecution of the emperors and trampled the idols underfoot; then the number of ministers multiplied, and they began to distinguish the principal places from those of lesser consideration. That is: So the origin is clearly sought from that time when priests and deacons, indeed the bishops themselves, differed greatly from the cardinals of whom we speak, whose eminence was then unknown. For their institution is much more recent and began to appear in Gaul only under the third line of our kings, as we shall prove later, and not in the primitive Church; when there were no cardinal churches, no cardinal ministers, neither in the time of the apostles nor for some centuries after; for the few priests and deacons who then exercised the ministry in caves and hidden places did not admit that distinction of cardinal priests from other priests. But then, and long after the Church by its patience had conquered the persecutions of the emperors and trampled the idols underfoot, the number of ministers multiplied, and they began to distinguish the principal places from the less principal. Again he speaks according to that hypothesis.

units.la: IX. Dixi jam supra, & ostendi, Cardinales in quibusvis, non tantùm in Romanis Ecclesiis fuisse. Quod, ut manifestum est,ita etiam admittitur ab Onuphrio,qui l. c. ait. Hoc porrò nomen (Cardinalium) omnibus Ecclesiis commune multis adhuc hafit, ut Ravennati, Pisana, Mediolanensi, Compostellana, & aliis, sed potissimùm Romana: mana : quia sicut Romanus Pontifex omnium Episcoporum princeps est, ita & Sacerdotes Romanae Ecclesiae omnium Ecclesiarum Clericos dignitate & honore antecellunt : hinc Cardinales hodie tantum appellari videntur : Nempe idem hic accidit, quod circa alia multa. Communia jura ad se traxit Papa, & quae aliis ademit, sibi addidit, sic dives factus. Quod in specie circa nomina & titulos , Papa , Pontifex Romani , Apostolici &c. accidisse Dissert. III. non semel notatum fuit. Et quia etiam in Clericis suis ab aliis Episcopis distingui voluit, hinc alio etiam nomine eos vocari voluit, cum nominum diversitate simplices ad cogitationes & fidem de rerum, ut & de personarum differentia inducantur.
units.tr: IX. I have already said above, and shown, that cardinals existed in various churches, not only in Roman ones. This, as is manifest, is also admitted by Onuphrius, who in the same place says: This name (of cardinals) still clings in common to many churches, such as Ravenna, Pisa, Milan, Compostela and others, but especially the Roman; because just as the Roman Pontiff is the prince of all bishops, so too the priests of the Roman Church surpass the clergy of all churches in dignity and honour; hence cardinals today seem to be called only so. Certainly the same thing happened here as in many other matters. The Pope drew the common rights to himself, and added to himself what he had taken away from others, and so became rich. That this happened in particular with names and titles, Pope, Roman Pontiff, Apostolic and so on, was noted more than once in Dissert. III. And because he also wished to be distinguished from other bishops among his own clergy, he therefore wished them to be called by another name as well, since by a diversity of names simple people are led to thoughts and belief about a difference of things as well as of persons.

units.la: X. Missis igitur aliarum Ecclesiarum Cardinalibus, quorum nomina paulatim periisse & nonnisi in monumentis antiquis superesse, (nisi, quod in quibusdam Ecclesiis mansisse Onuphrius testatus est;) ex praecedentibus constat; ad solos Romanae Ecclesiae Cardinales, (quorum etiam causa ista omnia diximus;) progredimur distincte considerandos; Fuerunt Clerus proprius & ordinarius Ecclesiae Romanae, illorumque munus fuit munus proprium propriorum Clericorum, ac praesertim Presbyterorum, ut singuli in suis Titulis Sacramenta ministrarent, populum erudirent, essentq; Romani Episcopi, ut in singulis quibusq; Ecclesiis suorum Episcoporum proprii Canonici, Consultores & Adjutores, sed quoad dioecesin Romanam tantum. Ut autem munus illorum maxime fuit Presbyterorum, ita etiam maxime dicebantur Cardinales Presbyteri , praeter quos antiquitus etiam Cardinales Diaconi erant, sed numero pauciores. Episcopo autem Romano hoc nominis non datum legitur, quia semper praesupponebatur fixus. De aliis etiam Ecclesiae Romanae Cardinalibus Episcopis nihil diu sciebatur. Id quod vel ex Onuphrii libro de Episcoporum Tit. & Diac. Card. abunde cognoscimus. Ab initio enim dicit, se in explicandis tribus Clericorum ordinibus temporum ordinem sequi decrevisse ; quum enim primo Presbyteri, mox Diaconi & longo tempore post Episcopi Cardinales appellari coeperint, primo loco de Presbyteris &c. Et post tractationem de Presbyteris, & Diaconis : Novissimum omnium Episcopi (nempe in Ecclesia Romana) Cardinalis cognomen habuerunt , quum apud Veteres inauditum fuerit Episcopum Cardinalem dici (in Ecclesia alterius) quum omnes Episcopi (Patriarchis exceptis) aequalis sint authoritatis, nullúsque ratione alterius Cardinalis dici possit, ut diffusè in libro de Origine Cardinalium disputavi, &c.
units.tr: X. With the cardinals of the other churches set aside, whose names gradually perished and survive only in ancient records (except that Onuphrius testifies they remained in certain churches), it is clear from what precedes that we now proceed to consider distinctly the cardinals of the Roman Church alone, for whose sake we have said all these things. They were the proper and ordinary clergy of the Roman Church, and their office was the proper office of proper clergy, especially of the presbyters: that each, in his own title, should administer the sacraments and instruct the people. They were the canons, consultors and assistants of the Roman bishop, just as each bishop in his own church had his own, but their authority extended only to the Roman diocese. Just as their office was chiefly that of presbyters, so they were chiefly called Cardinales Presbyteri. Besides them, in antiquity there were also cardinal deacons, but fewer in number. The name is not read as having been given to the Roman bishop, because he was always presupposed to be fixed. Nothing was known for a long time about the other cardinal bishops of the Roman Church. We learn this abundantly from Onuphrius's book de Episcoporum Tit. & Diac. Card. For at the beginning he says that he decided to follow the order of time in explaining the three orders of clergy: since presbyters were first called cardinals, then deacons, and after a long time bishops, he treats first of the presbyters, and so on. And after his discussion of presbyters and deacons: "Last of all, bishops (namely in the Roman Church) took the surname cardinal, since among the ancients it was unheard of for a bishop to be called cardinal (in the church of another), since all bishops (patriarchs excepted) are of equal authority, and on no ground can one be called the cardinal of another, as I have argued at length in my book On the Origin of Cardinals, etc."

units.la: XI. Tituli autem distinguebantur Cardinales Romani, quorum originem recte Ciaconius tradit, quatenus dicit, nomina accepisse ab aedificiis & reditibus Ecclesiae liberaliter donatis ab hominibus probis & foeminis divitibus ad victum & amictum Presbyterorum & Diaconorum; Quando quidem certum est, Ecclesiam Romanam divitem factam esse donationibus & liberalitatibus virorum piorum & foeminarum devotarum & divitum, teste etiam Ammiano Marcellino l.27. Ita Presbyteri & Diaconi Cardinales titulos suos acceperunt ab aedificiis Ecclesiae donatis, in quibus habitabant, vel de haereditatibus & aliis reditibus ita donatis, quibus fruebantur; inde nati sunt tituli antiqui Equitii, Vestinae, Pammachii, Lucinia, Julii & Calisti, Damasi Papae, Pastoris, Eudoxia, Aemilianae, Crescentianae, Fasciolae, Tibridae; qui tituli omnes erant certi reditus ex praediis, haereditatibus & aliis possessionibus liberaliter donatis à Viris & foeminis devotis ad nutritionem Ministrorum Ecclesiae; qui modus tamdiu fuit, quamdiu Christiani coacti fuerunt se abscondere in Coemeteriis, aut aliis locis occultis, sive subterraneis, ad administrationem Sacramentorum propter persecutiones Gentilium, sed postquam Ecclesia coepit esse libera sub Principibus Christianis, & permissio obtigit, publicè Templa aedificandi, in illis titulis sive aedificiis Ecclesiae datis, tunc Cardinales inceperunt addere illorum titulis nomina Sanctorum Martyrum, sive Confessorum, ita se appellantes: Laurentius Presbyter Cardinalis Sancti Sylvestri in Exquiliis titulo Equitii; Johannes Presbyter Cardinalis SS. Vitalis, Gervasii & Protasii titulo Vestinae.
units.tr: XI. The Roman cardinals were distinguished by titles, whose origin Ciaconius rightly traces, in that he says they took their names from the buildings and revenues of the church, generously given by upright men and wealthy women for the food and clothing of presbyters and deacons. For it is certain that the Roman Church became rich through the gifts and liberality of pious men, devout women and the wealthy, as Ammianus Marcellinus also testifies in book 27. Thus the presbyter and deacon cardinals received their titles from church buildings given to them, in which they lived, or from inheritances and other revenues so given, which they enjoyed. Hence arose the ancient titles of Equitius, Vestina, Pammachius, Lucina, Julius and Callistus, Pope Damasus, Pastor, Eudoxia, Aemiliana, Crescentiana, Fasciola and Tiburtina. All these titles were fixed incomes from estates, inheritances and other possessions generously given by devout men and women for the support of the Church's ministers. This practice lasted as long as Christians were forced, because of the persecutions of the pagans, to hide in cemeteries or other secret, underground places for the administration of the sacraments. But after the Church began to be free under Christian princes, and permission was obtained to build churches publicly, the cardinals began to add to their titles the names of holy martyrs or confessors, calling themselves thus: "Laurence, presbyter cardinal of St Sylvester on the Esquiline, with the title of Equitius"; "John, presbyter cardinal of SS. Vitalis, Gervasius and Protasius, with the title of Vestina."

units.la: XII. Non tam alte assurgit, qui tamen rem porrò explicat, Onuphrius, dum ita de titulis loquitur: Tituli erant Templa, vel ut nunc dicitur Ecclesiae, sive loca Sacra in Sanctorum honorem aut memoriam erecta, (quatenus nimirum prius memoriam benefactorum & B. Martyrum simpliciter ad honorem Dei sic recolebant, in locis partim ab illis donatis, partim ab his sanguinis sui pro Christo effusione nobilitatis; quod tandem in superstitionem & idololatriam degeneravit;) & per Urbis regiones à Romanis Pontificibus antiquitus distincta, in quibus animarum cura à Presbyteris in eis commorantibus habebatur; Et memorat idem ibidem 28. titulos Presbyterorum à multis seculis fuisse; Cujus numeri causam, quae mysterio non vacet, ita aperit; Fuisse in urbe 5. majores & praestantiores Basilicas, quae Patriarchales Ecclesiae palatiaque illis adjuncta Patriarchia appellata sint. Quas Ecclesias his versibus expressit: Paulus, Virgo, Petrus, Laurentius atque Johannes.Hi Patriarchatus nomen in urbe tenent; Et quarum prima nunc S. Johannis dicitur, olim Salvatoris, & Lateranensis à loco, Constantiana ab authore, & aurea ab ornamentis dicta; Quibus etiam Ecclesiis additae sunt Calisti & S. Crucis in Jerusalem, ac progressu temporis aliae quoque, veluti Anastasii ad tres fontes, S. Mariae annunciatae &c. Factum id, in erectione tot Ecclesiarum Patriarchalium, ideò asserit Onuphrius, (atque in hoc est mysterium) vel ut ex quinque Patriarchis, si Romam venirent 4. advena, quilibet Basilicam haberet; vel, ut sic ostenderetur, alios Patriarchas esse Romano subditos; vel, quam causam tertiam superiori non absimilem ipse ex suo addit, ut Ecclesia Lateranensis universum orbem reliqua 4. Orbis partes designarent. Quae quidem causae, sive mysteria ambitiosè finguntur, nec statui pristino conveniunt; Sed magis, vel à se Patriarcha 5. praecipuas ex urbis suae Ecclesiis, vel & à reliquis etiam 4. tanquam à communis fidei sociis sine subjectione denominâsse, congruum est.
units.tr: XII. Onuphrius, who explains the matter further, does not rise so high when he speaks thus of titles: "Titles were temples, or as they are now called churches, or sacred places erected in honour or memory of saints" (namely, since at first they simply commemorated in this way the memory of benefactors and holy martyrs, for the honour of God, in places partly given by them and partly ennobled by the shedding of their blood for Christ; which at last degenerated into superstition and idolatry), "and distinguished by the Roman bishops in ancient times by the regions of the city, in which the cure of souls was held by the presbyters dwelling there. And the same author records that there were 28 titles of presbyters for many centuries." He explains the cause of this number, which is not without mystery, thus: "There were in the city five major and more outstanding basilicas, which were called Patriarchal churches, and the palaces attached to them were called patriarchia." These churches he expressed in these verses: "Paul, Virgin, Peter, Laurence and John: these hold the name of Patriarchate in the city." Of these, the first is now called St John's, formerly the Saviour's, and is called Lateran from its place, Constantinian from its founder, and golden from its ornaments. To these churches were added St Callistus and Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and in the course of time others too, such as Anastasius at the Three Fountains, St Mary of the Annunciation, and so on. "This was done," Onuphrius asserts, in the erection of so many patriarchal churches, and herein lies the mystery, "either so that, if four strangers came to Rome out of the five patriarchs, each should have a basilica; or so that it might be shown that the other patriarchs are subject to the Roman; or, as a third reason, not unlike the former, which he adds from his own resources, so that the Lateran church might signify the whole world and the remaining four parts of the globe." Indeed these reasons, or mysteries, are contrived with ambition and do not agree with the original state of things. It is more fitting that the Patriarch himself named the five principal churches of his city, and likewise the remaining four as fellow-sharers in the common faith, without subjection.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Addit; In Lateranensi tanquam praecipua 7. Episcopos ex circumvicinis civitatibus suis statis solennibúsque diebus celebrâsse, vel Pontifici celebranti adstitisse, atque ob eam causam postea Episcopos Cardinales appellatos esse, & praecipuum, id est, antiquissimum ex praesentibus in urbe, inde à Paulo IV. Decani nomen habuisse. Qui tamen ab Innocentii II. tempore ad sex (suppresso illo Secunda, sive Sylva Candida) redacti sint. In reliquis autem Basilicis 4. quarum singulae 7. Presbyteros habeant, numerum 28. titulorum haberi, sub 2. in illa S. Mariae majoris & illa S. Petri Archipresbyteris, duobus in illa S. Pauli, & in illa S. Laurentii extra muros Abbatibus Cardinalibus; Quorum omnium omninò Presbyterorum Cardinalium Senior sive antiquior appelletur S. R. E. Archipresbyter Cardinalis; Perdurâsse numerum 28. Presbyterorum usque ad Honorium II. à cujus tempore adeò decreverit, ut aliquando tempus fuerit, in quo nomini duo Presbyteri Cardinales viventes in Collegio essent, ut sub Alexand. IV. obitu, & Creatione Urbani IV. (de quo Papyrius Masso, in Historia Paparum: Sanè cùm dicti fratres à Cardine pauci Essent, his sedem multiplicare placet;) Cujus decrementi causa fuerit, quòd Electione ad Cardinales translatâ, & lege de 2. partibus nondum institutâ, ob Cardinalium multitudinem pleraque schismata in Romanorum Pontificum creationibus orirentur, & Pontifices hoc malum repressuri, Cardinalium numerum paulatim dimidiminuere cœperunt, & qui prius, additis 18. Diaconis, certus & determinatus erat, videlicet 53. sensim dilabi & ad incertum numerum reduci cœpit; primò ex 53. sub Innocent. II. vel Cœlest. II. 40. esse cœpisse, mox 35. deinde 30. postea 25. ad hac 20. post 15. vel 10. postremo ad eam paucitatem redactos esse, ut non essent nisi 7. Cardinales viventes, 3. Presbyteri & 4. Diaconi, cum crearetur Nicolaus III. sed postea sensim augeri cœpisse, ut essent 15. post 20. sub Bonif. VIII. Avinione numerum porrò crevisse, nunquam tamen usque ad Xysti IV. Pontificatum 30. attigisse; praesertim, quum in Concilio Constantiensi cautum fuerit, ne plures quàm 24. Cardinales viventes simul essent, quod & placuit Basileensi;) Primum Xystum IV. nulla habita decreti Concilii ratione, numerum supra omnes Predecessores suos maximè ampliasse, ejusque exemplum Alexand. VI. secutum esse, nullum tamen horum antiquum 53. numerum vel excessisse, vel attigisse; Sed primum, antiqui instituti ratione non habità, magnâ illâ 31. Cardinalium creatione veterem atque à nullo unquam excessum numerum 53. longè superâsse, sub eo enim 65. plus minus Cardinales simul viventes fuisse, quod nunquam aliàs contigerit, ejusque exemplum secutum Paulum III. & (qui tunc vixerat, cùm hæc scriberet Onuphrius) IV. illum quidem ad 63. hunc autem ad 70. auxisse; adeóque novis titulis opus fuisse, quibus etiam ob aliam rationem opus fuerit, quia nimirum abusus inoleverit, ut unus Cardinalis duo aliquando habuerit Sacerdotia Cardinalitia; quod præsertim Episcopi Cardinales fecerint, qui Episcopi facti priorem titulum vel Diaconiam, quam, antequam essent Episcopi creati, habebant, retinuerint, qui abusus, ut pleraque alia, post Eugenii IV. tempora & præsertim sub Xysto IV. originem habuerit. Ab illo tempore numerus ferè idem mansit, & penes Papam esse arbitrantur, illum vel augere vel minuere, interim tamen quidam ex c. septuaginta dist.16. determinare volunt, quòd 70. esse debeant, ad formam 70. discipulorum vel totius orbis terræ linguarum. Qui numerus ex Sixti V. prius mysterium allegantis edicto augeri non debet, imò raro hactenus completus fuit, Papis semper vacuum locum relinquentibus, ut in casu necessitatis præmium conferri possit, vel satisfieri Principis alicujus postulato. Quamvis, ut dixi, augmentum penes Papam sit, & teste authore Cardinalismi p. 2. l. 2. 143. fuerint quidam Pontifices, qui ad centum numerum extendere voluerunt, in quo quidem exemplum Romuli centum Patres constituentis ante oculos habuerunt, certè augere eum commodum habet multarum creaturarum, ut diminutio appropriationis redituum. AugmenAugmentum autem penes Papam esse diserte Cassanæus in Catal. Glor. Mundi p.4. consid.12. 5. licet.his verbis docet: Licèt sit quidem numerus Cardinalium taxatus secundùm numerum discipulorum Christi, ut habetur in locis allegatis,potest tamen summus Pontifex,extra illum numerum,tot, quot voluerit, creare de sua plenitudine potestatis, & omnes tales numerarios facere,si velit. Paulus III. 71. creavit; Pius IV. 76. vidit, narrante Onuphrio.
units.tr: He adds: In the Lateran, as the principal church, the bishops of the neighbouring cities used to gather on fixed and solemn days, or to attend the celebrating Pontiff, and for this reason were afterwards called Cardinal Bishops; and the chief one, that is, the most ancient of those present in the city, has been called Dean since the time of Paul IV. Yet these were reduced to six from the time of Innocent II (the one Secunda, or Silva Candida being suppressed). In the other four basilicas, each of which has seven presbyters, there are said to be 28 titles, two of which are held by archpriests in St Mary Major and St Peter's, two in St Paul's, and in St Lawrence outside the Walls by abbots cardinal. Of all these presbyter cardinals the senior or older is called the Archpriest Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. The number of 28 presbyters lasted until Honorius II, from whose time it so declined that at times only two presbyter cardinals were living in the College, as at the death of Alexander IV and the creation of Urban IV (of whom Papirius Massonus, in his History of the Popes: "Indeed, since the said brothers were few from the Cardinals, it pleases to multiply the seats"). The cause of this decline was that, once election had been transferred to the cardinals, and the law concerning two-thirds not yet instituted, many schisms arose in the creation of Roman pontiffs because of the number of cardinals, and the popes, wishing to repress this evil, began gradually to diminish the number of cardinals; and what had been fixed and determined before, with 18 deacons added, namely 53, began gradually to slip away and be reduced to an uncertain number: first from 53 under Innocent II or Celestine II it began to be 40, then 35, then 30, afterwards 25, then 20, after that 15 or 10, and at last it was reduced to such a paucity that there were only 7 living cardinals, 3 presbyters and 4 deacons, when Nicholas III was created. Afterwards, however, it began to increase gradually, so that there were 15, then 20 under Boniface VIII. At Avignon the number grew further, yet never reached 30 until the pontificate of Sixtus IV, especially since at the Council of Constance it was provided that no more than 24 cardinals should be living at the same time, which also pleased the Council of Basel. First, Sixtus IV, with no regard to the decree of the council, greatly enlarged the number above all his predecessors, and Alexander VI followed his example; yet neither of them exceeded or reached the ancient 53. But first, with no regard to the ancient institution, by that great creation of 31 cardinals he far surpassed the old and never exceeded number of 53; for under him about 65 cardinals were living at once, which had never happened at other times. Following his example, Paul III increased the number to 63 and Pius IV (who was alive when Onuphrius wrote this) to 70. So new titles were needed, and there was also another reason, namely that an abuse had grown up whereby one cardinal sometimes held two cardinalitial offices. This especially Cardinal Bishops did: once made bishops, they retained the earlier title or diaconate which they had held before their consecration. This abuse, like many others, had its origin after the time of Eugene IV and especially under Sixtus IV. From that time the number has remained almost the same, and they think it lies with the Pope to increase or diminish it. Meanwhile some want it fixed at 70, from the chapter Septuaginta (dist. 16), after the pattern of the 70 disciples or of the languages of the whole world. According to the edict of Sixtus V, who appealed to the earlier mystery, this number ought not to be increased, and indeed it has rarely been filled up to now, the popes always leaving a vacant place so that it can be conferred as a reward in case of need, or to satisfy the request of some prince. Although, as I said, the increase lies with the Pope, and according to the author of the Cardinalismus, part 2, book 2, p. 143, there have been some popes who wished to extend the number to a hundred, in which they certainly had before their eyes the example of Romulus appointing a hundred Fathers. Certainly, to increase it is convenient, since it has the benefit of many creations, like the reduction of appropriated revenues. That the increase lies with the Pope Cassanaeus clearly teaches in his Catalogus Gloriae Mundi, part 4, consideration 12, no. 5, in these words: Although the number of cardinals is fixed according to the number of Christ's disciples, as is found in the places cited, nevertheless the supreme Pontiff may, beyond that number, create as many as he wishes by the fullness of his power, and make all of them supernumerary, if he wishes. Paul III created 71; Pius IV saw 76, as Onuphrius relates.

units.la: XIV. Idem etiam Onuphrius tradit; olim 7. Diaconos urbis fuisse,illorum primum vel antiquiorem, cum Episcopi, Cleri, populíque consensu electum Archidiaconum, vel Diaconum Cardinalem primum, principalem, Pontifices antiquos appellari statuisse, postea 14. juxta 14. urbis Regiones factos esse,quorum primus Archidiaconus,vel Diaconus Cardinalis; cæteri istius,vel illius regionis, verbi gratiâ,prima,sexta, decima, vel duodecima dicti sint,demum crescente religione his non sufficientibus, vel ad Ecclesiæ majestatem augendam plures in unaquaque Regione Diaconos creari coepisse, numerúmque illorum etiam indeterminatum factum esse,digniorem autem in quavis regione à cæteris ejusdem Regionis Clericis, vel Romano Pontifice electum Cardinalis nomen habuisse, quibus postea 4. alii additi sint, quorum munus tantùm fuerit,Lateranensi Basililicæ, vel Pontifici Romano ibidem celebranti ministrare, quos & altaris Lateranensis Ministros appellatos fuisse legerit, quem numerum 18. semel solus (quod sciat) excesserit Paulus III. sub quo anno 1545. 19.
