Diaconi Cardinales fuerint,cùm aliquando (ut dictum) tres tantùm fuerint; Loca ab eis Diaconias appellata esse,in Divorum honorem dedicata, à quibus postea ipsi Diaconi Cardinales Regionarii, antiquata Regionis appellatione, cognomina ac distinctiones sortiti sint, hos autem in suis Diaconiis commorantes (quas & Martyria à quibusdam vocari legerit,quòd ibi Martyrum sepulchra essent;) demandata sibi munia in sua regione impigrè fecisse, Pontificíque Romano Sacra facienti præsto adfuisse, Ecclesiæ quoque Romanæ Thesauros custodientes, pecunias plebi inopiâ laboranti, juxta præscriptas sibi rationes in suis regionibus largitos esse, & cætera omnia egisse,quæ in libro,quem de origine Sacrorum Ordinum conscripserit, explicaverit. Diaconiis etiam 18. nunquam mutatis Leonem X. primum unam novam adjunxisse, narrat idem.
units.tr: XIV. Onuphrius also reports: Formerly there were seven deacons of the city. The first or senior of them, elected by the consent of the bishop, clergy and people, was determined to be the Archdeacon or first and principal Deacon Cardinal, and the ancient popes called him so. Afterwards there were fourteen, according to the fourteen regions of the city, of whom the first was the Archdeacon or Deacon Cardinal; the others were called by the names of that or this region, for example the first, sixth, tenth or twelfth. Finally, as religion grew and these were not sufficient, or to enlarge the majesty of the Church, more deacons began to be created in each region, and their number became indeterminate; the worthier one in any region, chosen from the other clergy of the same region or by the Roman Pontiff, had the name of Cardinal. To these four others were later added, whose only duty was to minister in the Lateran Basilica, or to the Roman Pontiff celebrating there; and he records that they were called ministers of the Lateran altar. As far as he knows, Paul III alone once exceeded the number of 18, for in the year 1545 there were 19 Deacon Cardinals, although at times there were only three. The places were called Diaconiae, dedicated to the honour of the saints, and from them the deacons cardinal took the names and distinctions of the regions, the region's old name having been dropped. These deacons, staying in their Diaconiae (which some call Martyria, because the tombs of martyrs were there), diligently performed the duties entrusted to them in their region, attended the Roman Pontiff when he performed sacred rites, guarded the treasures of the Roman Church, and distributed money to the poor in their regions according to the rules prescribed for them; and they did all the other things which he has explained in his book on the origin of the sacred orders. The same author relates that Leo X first added one new Diaconia to the eighteen, which were never changed.

units.la: XV. Apud quem etiam de mutatione ministeriorum sequentia fusiùs habentur; Apud antiquos morem laudabilem fuisse,atque per mille & ducentos continuos annos in Romana Ecclesia usurpatum, ut neque Diaconi Diaconias semel acceptas, neque Presbyteri titulos,neque Episcopi Cardinales Episcopatus suos unquam quam mutarent; Diaconum enim in Diaconatûs ordine manentem semel acceptam Diaconiam nunquam dimittere potuisse, & aliam accipere: similem fuisse rationem Presbyterorum de Titulis, Episcoporum de Episcopatibus, quum autem Diaconus Cardinalis Presbyter fieri voluerit, dimissâ Diaconiâ, quæ Presbyteris non convenerit, titulum cooptâsse, & si ex Presbytero Episcopum Cardinalem fieri accidV erit, tunc dimisso titulo, Episcopatum suscepisse, quem, nisi Papa creatus esset, usque ad obitum retinuerit; Hanc autem consuetudinem usque ad Bonifacium IX. & Alex. V. tempora durâsse. Sed mutandi ejusmodi Sacerdotia tres causas fuisse, quarum duæ priores necessariæ, tertia non solum non necessaria, sed etiam inutilis & mala fuerit. Primam causam necessariam fuisse quòd sub Bonifacio IX. Cardinalitia dignitate ad tempus privati duos priores titulos jam aliis collatos reassumere non potuerint; alteram, quòd post schisma pessimum inter Urbanum VI. & Clementem VII. qui ambo tanquam veri Pontifices multos Cardinales in omnibus fere Episcopatibus, titulis & Diaconiis creârint, Alexander V. titulos mutare necesse habuerit; Tertiam ex secunda ortam, quæque nunc passim frequentetur in Romana Curia, esse, quòd multi Cardinales, videntes, jam manus à Romanis Pontificibus missas esse ad ejusmodi mutationes faciendas, etsi valdè necessarias, coeperunt etiam ipsi titulorum, vel Episcopatuum mutationes à Romano Pontifice procurare, non necessitate aliqua, sed, ut de titulo tenuiori transferrentur ad ditiorem; Quorum omnium primus fuerit Jordan Ursinus Cardinalis creatus ab Innocentio VII. qui sub Alexandro V. quum vidisset, eas fieri necessarias mutationes, petierit & ipse à Pontifice Alexandro, titulum sibi mutari, quod & contra Canones Ecclesiasticos obtinuerit, atque contra antiquam & laudabilem consuetudinem, quæ per 1200. annos observata fuerit, eum primum omnium sine necessitate aliqua titulo suo priore dimisso, quòd tenuis esset, opulentiorem cooptâsse. Cui in omnibus similia exempla subjungit, sed pauca, cùm in his usque ad Xystum IV. temperantes admodùm fuerint Romani Pontifices, qui, nullâ habitâ ratione, non solùm crebris mutationibus omnia confundere & religiosum ordinem evertere cœperit, sed etiam, quod ante id tempus inauditum fuerit, Diaconias Presbyteris pro titulis, &, ut abusus omni ex parte responderet, titulos Diaconis, pro Diaconiis dare coeperit, quæ omnia emendatione digna essent; Adhuc tamen optandi morem nondum plenè inolevisse, arbitrio enim Pontificis usque ad illa tempora, Episcopatus, titulos & Diaconias vel datas, vel mutatas esse, júsque optionis adhuc non integrum, verùm tunc paulatim & sensim exortum esse; non enim videri posse ante Alexandri VI. extremos Pontificatûs annos, vel Julii II. Pontificatum quempiam Cardinalium plùs quam 2. titulos, vel Episcopatus vel Diaconias mutâsse; demum circa finem Pontificatûs Alexandri VI. & initia Julii II. crebram hanc mutandorum titulorum rationem & jus optandi plenè exorta esse, quæ etiam nunc usurpentur; Tum primùm enim sub Julio II. accidisse, ut unus Cardinalis omnes sex Episcopatus Cardinales optârit; in qua optione hæc lex facta sit, ut Cardinales absentes sine legitima causa, ut pro Romanæ Ecclesiæ negotiis, in hisce optionibus nullum jus haberent, ac tanquam mortui haberentur; in optionibus autem Sacerdotium Cardinalium rationem tantùm haberi ditioris, vel opulentioris tituli, Episcopatûs, vel Diaconiæ, atque eos, qui minùs locupletes titulos vel Episcopatus aut Diaconias habent, opulentiores semper optare, si quando vacare contingunt. Ordinem etiam optandi subjungit, &c, Episcopum Ostiensem, qui omnium ditior sit, nullum amplius habere optandi locum; Aliquando tamen Pontifices in hisce Episcopis co-optandis optionis jus infringere pristinâque uti authoritate, atque vacante quâlibet harum Ecclesiarum, Portuensi & Ostiensi exceptis, eas non Presbyteris Cardinalibus senioribus, sed alicui ex antiquis Diaconis Cardinalibus tradere, qui ex Diaconatu, in quo per multos annos permanserint, sine Presbyterii gradu ad Episcopatum ascendant, & quidem aliquando jus suum optandi concedente eo Presbytero Cardinale seniore, qui optare deberet, aliquando autem ex mera Pontificis authoritate; quod nunquam negare solent Pontifices Diaconis, qui eos in creatione sua coronent, quibus in coronationis (ut ita dicat) præmium, aliquam ex his sedibus, si vacare per ea tempora contigerit, tribuant, &c. Quibus crebris mutationibus factum sit, ut Cardinales, titulos sibi quum creati sunt primò commissos, non diligant, tanquam paulo post mutandos, eóque ruere patiantur, neque ullam eorum restituendorum curam habeant, clare factum sit, ut plerique tituli & Diaconiæ partim jam solo æquata, partim ruinæ proxima sint. Cæterùm inter alios abusus etiam hunc inolevisse, qui sub Paulo IV. ex parte sublatus sit; ut Presbyter Cardinalis Episcopus factus titulum sibi priorem retineret tanquam in commenda, quod malè male factum, (ut dixerit) emendatione dignum esset. Dicit autem porrò, in præcedendo jam hunc ordinem esse,ut Decanus cæteros Episcopos, Episcopi Presbyteros, Presbyteri Diaconos præcedant, & ex quovis ordine primus,sive antiquissimus in ordine reliquos.
units.tr: XV. In the same work, the following points about the change of ministries are set out at greater length. Among the ancients, he says, there was a praiseworthy custom, observed in the Roman Church for twelve hundred continuous years, that deacons never changed their diaconies once they had received them, nor presbyters their titles, nor bishops their episcopal sees to become cardinals. A deacon who remained in the deaconate could never give up the diaconate he had received and take another. The same rule applied to presbyters with their titles and to bishops with their sees. But when a deacon wished to become a cardinal presbyter, he gave up his diaconate, which was unsuitable for presbyters, and chose a title. And if a presbyter happened to become a cardinal bishop, he then gave up his title and took up an episcopal see, which he kept until his death unless he was created Pope. This custom, he says, lasted until the time of Boniface IX and Alexander V. But there were three causes for changing such offices. The first two were necessary, and the third was not only unnecessary but useless and bad. The first necessary cause was that under Boniface IX cardinals who had been deprived of their dignity for a time could not take back their former two titles, which had already been given to others. The second was that after the very wicked schism between Urban VI and Clement VII, who both, as if they were true popes, created many cardinals in almost all the episcopal sees, titles and diaconies, Alexander V had to change the titles. The third, which arose from the second and which is now commonly practised in the Roman Curia, was this: many cardinals, seeing that the hands of the Roman Pontiffs had been sent out to make such changes, though these were very necessary, began themselves to seek changes of their titles or sees from the Roman Pontiff. This was not from any necessity, but so that they might be moved from a poorer title to a richer one. The first of all these was Jordan Ursini, created cardinal by Innocent VII. Under Alexander V, seeing that these necessary changes were being made, he himself asked the Pontiff Alexander that his title be changed, and obtained it against the ecclesiastical canons and against the ancient and praiseworthy custom, which had been observed for 1200 years. He was the first of all to give up his former title, without any necessity, because it was poor, and to take a richer one. To this he adds similar examples, though few, since the Roman Pontiffs had been quite restrained in these matters up to Sixtus IV. But then, with no regard for anything, they began not only to confuse everything with frequent changes and to overturn the religious order, and also, which was unheard of before that time, to give diaconies to presbyters in place of titles, and, so that the abuse might answer in every respect, to give titles to deacons in place of diaconies. All these things were worthy of correction. Even so, the custom of choosing had not yet fully taken hold, since until those times the episcopal sees, titles and diaconies were given or changed at the discretion of the Pontiff, and the right of choice was not yet complete. Rather, that right arose then, gradually and slowly. For it cannot be seen that before the last years of the pontificate of Alexander VI, or the pontificate of Julius II, any one of the cardinals changed more than two titles, whether episcopal sees or diaconies. Finally, around the end of the pontificate of Alexander VI and the beginning of Julius II, this frequent manner of changing titles and the full right of choosing arose, and they are still practised today. For it was then, under Julius II, that for the first time one cardinal chose all six cardinal sees. In that choice this law was made: cardinals who were absent without lawful cause, such as on business of the Roman Church, had no right in these choices, and were treated as if dead. In choices of cardinal offices, account was taken only of the richer or more opulent title, see, or diaconate, and those cardinals who had less wealthy titles, sees or diaconies always chose the richer ones whenever any happened to fall vacant. He also sets out the order of choosing, and says that the Bishop of Ostia, who is the richest of all, has no further place of choice. Sometimes, however, the Pontiffs, in choosing these bishops, broke the right of choice and used their former authority. When any of these churches fell vacant, except Porto and Ostia, they gave it not to the senior presbyter cardinals but to some one of the old deacon cardinals, who rose from the diaconate, in which they had remained for many years, to the episcopate without the rank of presbyter. Sometimes this happened with the senior presbyter cardinal, who ought to have chosen, yielding his right of choice; and sometimes it happened by the sheer authority of the Pontiff. Popes never refuse this to deacons who crown them at their creation, to whom they grant, as it were as a reward for the coronation, one of these sees if one happens to be vacant at that time, and so on. By these frequent changes it came about, that cardinals do not care for the titles first entrusted to them when they were created, as if they would soon be changed, and allow them to fall into ruin, and have no concern for restoring them. It has become clear that most of the titles and diaconies are partly already levelled to the ground, and partly close to ruin. Moreover, among other abuses this one too had taken hold, and under Paul IV it was partly abolished: a presbyter cardinal who had become a bishop kept his former title as if in commendam, which was wrongly done, as he said, and worthy of correction. He further says that in precedence the order now is that the Dean goes before the other bishops, bishops before presbyters, and presbyters before deacons, and that within each order the first, that is the most senior, comes before the rest.

units.la: XVI. Ex his, quæ de officio & statu Cardinalium antiquiori hactenus attuli, jam constare potest, incumbere illis,ut in titulis curam ordinariam per se ipsos exerceant, titulis illis propriam; nec immeritò Dominicum Sotum de just. & ju. l.3.quaest.5. art.3. & l.10. q.3. ar. 4. asseruisse, Cardinalatum Romanum habere residentiam necessariam, & lege cautum esse, ne Cardinales Romani ad aliarum Ecclesiarum Episcopatus promoveantur; neque Episcopi Ecclesiarum ad Romanum Cardinalatum, retinentes simul Episcopatum, assumantur, cùm incompatibile sit, ut incardinatus in una Ecclesia, incardinetur etiam in alia ab illa diversa & remota, & contradictorium, ut fixus non sit fixus. Ex quo tamen principio plerorumque hodiernorum Cardinalatus perit,dum nimirum,qui revera officia præstant, Canonici Lateranenses & alii, nomen & dignitatem non habent,qui verò habent, alterius cujusdam à primis generis sunt, origine, formâ,sine diversi, partim extra Romam degentes, & in locis remotioribus, suis nempe Episcopatibus &c. (quod quidem non ratione Cardinalium sex Episcoporum dico, qui non obstantibus Episcopatibus suis potuerunt quodammodo assumi ad Romanum Cardinalatum, & fieri quasi Chorepiscopi Romani, Ecclesiae suae in Romanam incorporari, partim ob viciniam, partim ob exiguam curam illarum propriam;) Partim ibi alia, quàm quæ Episcoporum & Diaconorum sunt, agentes,alia omnia omnes. Ut ex sequentibus magis patebit.
units.tr: XVI. From what I have so far set out about the office and status of the older cardinals, it can now be clear that they were bound to exercise the ordinary care of their titles in person, each title being their own. Not without reason, Dominicus Soto, On Justice and Law, book 3, question 5, article 3, and book 10, question 3, article 4, asserted that the Roman cardinalate requires necessary residence, and that the law provides that Roman cardinals should not be promoted to the episcopal sees of other churches. Nor are bishops of churches to be taken up into the Roman cardinalate while keeping their episcopate at the same time, since it is incompatible that someone incardinated in one church should also be incardinated in another church, distinct and remote from it, and it is contradictory that what is fixed should not be fixed. Yet by this principle most of today's cardinalates are lost. Those who really perform the duties, the Lateran canons and others, have no name or dignity, while those who do have the name are of a different kind from the first, in origin, form and character, partly living outside Rome, in more distant places, namely in their own episcopal sees and so on. (I do not say this of the six cardinal bishops, who, despite their episcopal sees, could in some way be taken up into the Roman cardinalate, and become, as it were, Roman chorbishops, their churches being incorporated into the Roman church, partly because of their nearness and partly because of their small care of their own churches.) Partly they carry out there duties other than those of bishops and deacons, and all of them do all things. As will become clearer from what follows.

units.la: XVII. Sed ut officii respectu differunt hodierni Cardinales à prioribus,ita etiam respectu dignitatis. Priores inferiores erant Episcopis; primò enim,ut ostendi,non erant Episcopi Cardinales Romani à Pontifice distincti, sed tantùm Presbyteri & Diaconi; Presbyteri autem tunc Episcopis ubique inferiores habebantur, & id fieri debere contendunt Pontificii. De Diaconis res adhuc magis manifesta est. Et quando Episcopi Romani Cardinales à Pontifice distincti esse coeperunt, saltem eatenus aliis Episcopis non erant antepositi. Ob eam causam, verba sunt Onuphrii in libello, ex quo jam multa attulimus, neque Patriarchis, neque Metropolitanis, vel Archiepiscopis, neque etiam Episcopis aliarum civitatum, licèt Cardinales non essent, ante se tamen consecratis, digniores erant, nec etiam eos praecedebant, ut demonstravi in libro de Cardinalium origine. Sed eorum praecedentia erat ratione temporis, quo Episcopi creati fuerunt.
units.tr: XVII. But just as today's cardinals differ from the earlier ones in respect of office, so they do in respect of dignity. The earlier ones were inferior to bishops. For first, as I have shown, the Roman cardinal bishops were not yet distinguished from the Pontiff, but were only presbyters and deacons. Presbyters were then regarded as everywhere inferior to bishops, and the Papists contend that this ought to be so. The matter is even clearer for deacons. And when the Roman cardinal bishops began to be distinguished from the Pontiff, at least so far they were not placed before other bishops. For this reason, these are the words of Onuphrius in the little book from which we have already quoted much, neither to patriarchs, nor to metropolitans, or archbishops, nor even to bishops of other cities, although they were not cardinals, were they more worthy, consecrated before them, nor did they go before them, as I showed in the book on the origin of cardinals. But their precedence was by reason of the time when the bishops were created.

units.la: XVIII. De Presbyteris & Diaconis, inferiores fuisse varie ostendi posset; In ipsa Synodo, quam pro Cardinalitii nominis antiquitate allegant, sub Sylvestro, ut volunt, habita, c. 1. ad terga Episcoporum sedentium stetisse leguntur.
units.tr: XVIII. That the presbyters and deacons were inferior could be shown in various ways. In the very synod that they cite for the antiquity of the name "Cardinal," supposedly held under Sylvester, canon 1 reads that they stood behind the seated bishops.

units.la: In Synodis sub Symmacho tertia & quinta, quarum major authoritas tanquam certiorum, so-li Episcopi multi, & nulli Presbyteri, aut Diaconi Cardinales Romani subscripserunt, & inter Episcopos Episcopi, qui nihilominus erant Cardinales Romani, ut Ostiensis, Praenestinus, Albanus, aliis non Cardinalibus Romanis postpositi fuerunt; Sic & inter Legatos Leonis ad Ephesinum Concilium designatos ap. Bar. ad an. 449. n. 36. Episcopus Puteolanus ante Cardinales positus fuit. Et in Carthaginensi, cui etiam Divus Augustinus interfuit, post omnes Episcopos demum Presbyteri & Legati Romani subscripsisse inveniuntur. Ejusmodi subscriptiones possent produci multae aliae etiam tempore multò posteriores, & quae apud M. Ant. de Dominis l. 4. c. 5. n. 27. &c. videri possunt; qui & respondet ad objectionem Baronii ad an. 431. n. 81. de praecedentia Cardinalium.
units.tr: In the synods under Symmachus, the third and the fifth (the greater of which has the greater authority as the more reliable), many bishops subscribed and no presbyters or deacons, and the Roman Cardinals subscribed. Among the bishops, the bishops who were nonetheless Roman Cardinals, such as those of Ostia, Praeneste and Alba, were placed after other bishops who were not Roman Cardinals. Likewise among the legates of Leo designated for the Council of Ephesus (Baronius ad an. 449. n. 36.), the Bishop of Puteoli was placed before the Cardinals. And at the Council of Carthage, which Saint Augustine also attended, the presbyters and Roman legates are found to have subscribed only after all the bishops. Many other subscriptions of this kind could be produced, even from much later times, and they can be seen in Marcus Antonius de Dominis (l. 4. c. 5. n. 27. &c.), who also answers the objection of Baronius (ad an. 431. n. 81.) about the precedence of the Cardinals.

units.la: XIX. Unicam tamen adhuc subscriptionem, quia satis senera & valdè clara est, ex Concilio Rom. sub Paulo I. habito, producam; in illo enim, ut Baronius ad an. 761. n. 11.12. habet, Episcopi omnes ante Cardinales sub scripserunt, ut etiam deficiente loco in eo chartae spatio, quod nomina continebat Episcoporum, adscripta sint haec verba: Et alii, qui capere non possumus; Et mox in medio Cardinalium: Hos sequitur subscriptio trium Episcoporum, qui residui erant, sed defectu charta absque subscriptione praeterierant, Suthi-nius &c. & post hos: Sequitur subscriptio reliquorum Cardinalium. Ex quibus apparet, quàm diligenter tunc adhuc cautum fuerit Episcopali dignitati. XX. Sed veritas haec & aliunde cognoscitur, & tam manifesta est, ut nemo illi se opponere audeat: Aliunde cognoscitur, certè ex eo, quòd 72. testes ad Episcopum convincendum requisiti fuerunt, dum 44. contrà Presbyterum Cardinalem, 27. al. 26. contra Diaconum sufficiebant; non minùs ex eo, quòd Presbyteri Cardinales Romani interdum Abbatias assumserunt Regularium, facti Monachi Abbates, ad Monachorum regimen se contulerunt, retento tamen solo nomine Presbyteri Romani Cardinalis, ut ex Registro Gregorii VII. cognosci potest, & quòd nomine jam introducto, sæpe ne nominari quidem illo voluerunt; sed maximè ex eo, quòd, ut ex vita Gregorii M. cognosci potest, & natio Gallica in Epistolis datis quibusdam Cardinalibus ab ejusdem conclusione appellantibus &c. juxta Catalogum Testium veritatis, expressius testatur; Dudum Cardinales, qui bene servierunt, in eorum remunerationem & pro quiete ipsorum promovebantur ad cathedrales Ecclesias.
units.tr: XIX. I will produce one more subscription, since it is old enough and very clear: from the Roman council held under Paul I. In it, as Baronius (ad an. 761. n. 11.12.) records, all the bishops subscribed before the Cardinals. Because the space on the sheet that held the names of the bishops ran out, the words were added: And others, whom we cannot list. And soon after, in the middle of the Cardinals: The subscription of three remaining bishops follows, who had passed by without signing for lack of paper, Suthinius etc. and after these: The subscription of the remaining Cardinals follows. From these it is clear how carefully the episcopal dignity was then still protected. XX. But this truth is also known from elsewhere, and it is so manifest that no one dares to oppose it. It is known from elsewhere, certainly from the fact that seventy-two witnesses were required to convict a bishop, whereas forty-four sufficed against a presbyter Cardinal, and twenty-six or twenty-seven against a deacon. It is known no less from the fact that presbyter Cardinals of Rome sometimes took over religious abbeys: having become abbots of monks, they devoted themselves to governing the monks, keeping only the name of presbyter and Roman Cardinal, as can be learned from the Register of Gregory VII. And since that name had been introduced, they often did not even want to be called by it. But most of all it is known from what the French nation, as the Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth states more explicitly, testifies in letters given to certain Cardinals who appealed from the conclusion of the same council: Formerly, Cardinals who had served well were promoted to cathedral churches as a reward for them and for their peace.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: In qua natione quoad præcedentiam etiam respectu Cardinalium illud quoque observatu dignißimum, quod Author tract. de l'origi des Card. pag.59. ex Belleforest, qui Cosmographiam Münsteri auctam edidit, capite, de Univers. Paris. &c. commemorat, nempe que la majestè du Recteur de l'Universitè de Paris est si grande en l'Escole, qu'es actes publics de quelque faculté que ce soit, il precede les Evêques, Cardinaux, & sussent ils Pairs de France: & ne souffriroit-on pas, que le Nonce du Pape, ny Ambassadeur d'aucun Prince du monde eust cet avantage de le preceder. Id est; Majestatem Rectoris Universitatis tantam in Universitate esse, ut in actibus publicis cujuscunque facultatis precedat Episcopos Cardinales, etiamsi essent Pares Franciæ, neque concederetur, ut vel Nuncius Papæ, vel Legatus ullius Principis eum precedat.
units.tr: In that same nation, concerning precedence even with respect to the Cardinals, the following is also most worthy of notice. The author of the treatise On the Origin of the Cardinals, p. 59, citing Belleforest, who published the enlarged Cosmography of Münster, chapter on the University of Paris &c., records this: the majesty of the Rector of the University of Paris is so great in the School that in the public acts of any faculty whatever he precedes bishops, cardinals, even if they were peers of France; and would one not permit the Pope's Nuncio, or the ambassador of any prince in the world, to have this advantage of preceding him. That is: The majesty of the Rector of the University is so great within the University that in the public acts of any faculty whatever he precedes bishops and cardinals, even if they were peers of France; nor would it be granted that either the Nuncio of the Pope or the legate of any prince should precede him.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Veritas etiam hæc tam manifesta est, ut nemo illi se opponere audeat. Habemus enim confessiones luculentas ipsorummet Monarchicorum. Et Canonistæ quidem in Praxi Episc. c. Episcopus §. 18. fatentur, quòd Episcopi usque ad Clementem V. & Johannem XXII. fuerint in dignitate supra Cardinales, & quòd ad Bonifacium VIII. usque Episcopi non facti sint Cardinales, ad hoc, ne viderentur descendere à majori ad minorem gradum. Sed maximè audiendus est porrò, quem jam quoque testem in hac re audivimus, Onuphrius: Antiquitùs mos fuit, inquit, qui etiam per mille annorum spatium servatus est, ut Presbyter Cardinalis urbis Romæ, neque Episcopus esset, vel Episcopatum administraret, vel ex Episcopo fieret Presbyter Cardinalis (multò minùs Diaconus;) quum major dignitas tunc fuerit esse Episcopum cujuslibet diœcesis quàm Cardinalem, quod ex Cardinalibus Romanæ Ecclesiæ, secùs quàm nunc observatur, Episcopi diversarum civitatum creati fuerint, ex Cardinalatu enim gradus erat ad Episcopatum, sicut nunc ex Episcopatu ad Cardinalatum, Cardinalisque Presbyter Episcopus factus, esse Cardinalem desinebat, sicut nunc Episcopus Cardinalis factus amplius non appellatur Episcopus, sed Presbyter Cardinalis S. R. E. & Administrator perpetuus illius Episcopatus, (quem nominetenus amicis vel nepotibus resignat, reditus sibi usurpans;) quod se invicem compati non possint esse Presbyterum Cardinalem Urbis Roma & Episcopum alterius Ecclesiae, repugnat enim Presbyter & Episcopus, quod antiquis canonibus cautum fuerit, unum hominem nonnisi uno Sacerdotio potiri posse. Imò ipse Bellarminus hic nobis suffragio suo accurrit, licet tantus praeeminentiae Cardinalitiae defensor, post Cardinalis & ipse: Fateor, inquit, olim Episcopos quoscunque pralatos fuisse Cardinalibus non Episcopis, imò etiam Cardinalatum gradum fuisse ad Episcopatum, ut Onuphrius recte docet in libro de Cardinalibus, & apertissime colligitur ex l.1. c. 7. vita S. Gregorii. Postea tamen mutatus est ordo, & coepti sunt Cardinales Episcopis anteponi &c.
units.tr: This truth is also so manifest that no one dares to oppose it. For we have clear confessions from the Monarchists themselves. The canonists, in the Practica Episcoporum, c. Episcopus §. 18., admit that bishops were in dignity above the Cardinals until Clement V and John XXII, and that until Boniface VIII bishops were not made Cardinals, lest they should seem to descend from a greater to a lesser rank. But above all we must further listen to the witness we have already heard in this matter, Onuphrius: Anciently, he says, there was a custom, which was kept even through a span of a thousand years, that a presbyter Cardinal of the city of Rome was not a bishop, nor administered a bishopric, nor did a bishop become a presbyter Cardinal (much less a deacon), since the greater dignity then was to be bishop of any diocese rather than a Cardinal. Bishops of various cities were created from among the Cardinals of the Roman Church, otherwise than is now observed. For from the cardinalate there was a step to the episcopate, just as now from the episcopate there is a step to the cardinalate; and a Cardinal presbyter made bishop ceased to be a Cardinal, just as now a bishop made Cardinal is no longer called bishop but presbyter Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and perpetual Administrator of that bishopric (which he resigns by name to friends or nephews, while taking the revenues for himself); because a presbyter Cardinal of the city of Rome and a bishop of another church cannot be combined, for presbyter and bishop are incompatible, and the ancient canons provided that one man could hold only one priesthood. Indeed Bellarmine himself, though so great a defender of cardinalitial preeminence and himself a Cardinal, comes to our aid here with his support: I admit, he says, that formerly all bishops were placed above Cardinals who were not bishops, and even the cardinalate was a step to the episcopate, as Onuphrius rightly teaches in his book on the Cardinals, and it is most clearly gathered from book 1, chapter 7, of the Life of Saint Gregory. Afterwards, however, the order was changed, and Cardinals began to be placed before bishops etc.

units.la: XIII. Omninò mutatus est ordo, & coeperunt anteponi Cardinales Episcopis.
units.tr: XIII. The order was altogether changed, and Cardinals began to be placed above bishops.

units.la: Quum Cardinalium majestas cum Romani Pontificis authoritate in dies crescere coepisset, ait Onuphrius l. c. multique Cardinales esse ambirent, postea paulatim usurpatum est, ut ex Episcopis fierent Cardinales, & primò usus fuit, ut ex Episcopis non Cardinalibus fierent Episcopi Cardinales, & non Presbyteri vel Diaconi, post etiam ex Episcopis Presbyteri fieri coeperunt &c. primò enim Cardinales Presbyteri nonnisi ex Monachis vel Abbatibus, Decanis, Archipresbyteris, Archidiaconis, Prioribus & cateris ejusmodi hominibus fiebant; Post Clementem verò III. passim usurpari coeptum est, ut non solùm Presbyteri Cardinales, sed etiam Diaconi ex Episcopis, licèt ante consecrationem, crearentur, qui enim Episcopi ordinati erant, fiebant Presbyteri, qui non, sed adhuc electi, ordinabantur Diaconi; & quoniam, (ut dixi;) Presbyter & Episcopus se invicem pati non possunt, qui ex Episcopis facti sunt Presbyteri Cardinales, perpetui administratores deinceps illorum Episcopatuum, non Episcopi appellati, qui verò Diaconi Cardinales creati sunt, electos se illius Episcopatus nominabant. In qua re usque ad Clementem V. temperantes fuerunt Pontifices Romani. Avinione verò passim, & nullâ habità antiquissimi instituti ratione, observatum est, nullúsque ferè Cardinalis creatus, qui non haberet Episcopatum, vel titulum vel in commendam, vel in perpetuam administrationem, quae omnia nomina Avinione inventa sunt. Hæc autem consuetudo usque ad nostra tempora perduravit, in quibus eò deventum fuerat, ut Cardinalis Presbyter vel Diaconus non unum
units.tr: When the majesty of the Cardinals had begun to grow daily along with the authority of the Roman Pontiff, says Onuphrius in the place cited, and many Cardinals were eager to be made so, it was gradually practised that bishops should become Cardinals, and at first it was the custom that non-Cardinal bishops should become Cardinal bishops, and not presbyters or deacons; afterwards bishops also began to be made presbyters, etc. For at first Cardinal presbyters were made only from monks or abbots, deans, archpresbyters, archdeacons, priors and other such men. But after Clement III, it began to be practised everywhere that not only presbyter Cardinals but also deacons should be created from bishops, even before consecration. Those who had been ordained bishops became presbyters, but those who had not yet been ordained, and were still only elect, were ordained deacons. And since (as I said) a presbyter and a bishop cannot suffer each other, those who were made presbyter Cardinals from bishops became perpetual administrators of their former sees, and were not called bishops; but those who were created deacon Cardinals called themselves elect of that see. In this matter the Roman Pontiffs kept moderation until Clement V. But at Avignon it was observed everywhere, with no regard had to the most ancient institution, and almost no Cardinal was created who did not hold a bishopric, either by title, or in commendam, or in perpetual administration, all of which names were devised at Avignon. This custom lasted down to our own times, in which it had come about that a Cardinal presbyter or deacon held not just one

units.la: Mutatus jam status; unum tantùm haberet in commenda Episcopatum , sed aliquando tres, quatuor vel quinque & aliquando sex. Cui rei modus quidam impositus fuit in Concilio Tridentino &c.
units.tr: The status had now changed: he held not just one bishopric in commendam, but sometimes three, four or five, and sometimes six. A certain limit was placed on this matter at the Council of Trent, etc.

units.la: XXIV. Eadem ferè paulò post repetit prolixè, & addit; (Ex quo colligi potest quid in istis dignitatibus spectari soleat;) Quum semel acceptum Episcopatum Cardinalem,qui acceperat amplius,dimittere non posset, neque inter Episcopatus Cardinales esset ea optio, quae posterioribus temporibus usurpata adhuc viget, saepe usu veniebat, ut vacantibus, Albano, Tusculano, vel Praenestino, qui pauperes erant, Presbyter Cardinalis senior nollet accipere Episcopatum, quòd forte ditiorem titulum, vel Diaconiam haberet, tuncque novis Cardinalibus,vel antiquis,qui tenuiores habebant Titulos aut Diaconias, licet posteriores tempore in Collegio essent, tradebantur &c. Hinc forte non male Author Cardinalismi p.1.l.3. p.289. Perme credo fermamente, che l'inventione de Vescovi e de Prelati di far l'orlo del Capello di color verde,non sia altro che un segno d'ambitione, facendo conquesto conoscere, que loro sperano divederlo cambiato in rosso. Id est; Me quod attinet ,firmiter credo,inventionem Episcoporum & Pralatorum, quâ extremum pilei eorum viride est,esse nonnisi signum ambitionis, dum sic declarant spem suam, de eo in rubrum commutando. Nempe spectari solent divitiae & mundanus fastus, & hinc gradu planè retrogrado de Episcopatu ad Presbyteratum, imò ad Diaconiam descenditur,licèt Concilium Chalcedonense sacrilegum esse asserat, si quis Episcopus in poenam ab Episcopali gradu detractus ad Presbyteralem solùm redigatur. Quantò majus Sacrilegium erit ex hypothesi superioritatis Episcoporum, si quis non in poenam & invitus, sed ex propria voluntate, imò ex mera vanitate,id sibi procuret?
units.tr: XXIV. Almost the same things are repeated at length a little later, with this addition: (From this it can be gathered what is usually looked for in these dignities.) Since a Cardinal who had accepted a bishopric could not give up the one he had received if he accepted more, and since among the Cardinal bishoprics there was not that option which was used in later times and still prevails, it often happened that when Albano, Tusculum or Palestrina fell vacant, the senior Cardinal presbyter, if he was poor, would not accept the bishopric, perhaps because he had a richer title or diaconate. Then it was handed over to new Cardinals, or to old ones who had poorer titles or diaconates, even though they were later in the College in time, etc. Hence perhaps the author of Cardinalismo (part 1, book 3, p. 289) not unreasonably says: As for me, I firmly believe that the invention of bishops and prelates, by which the edge of their hat is green, is nothing but a sign of ambition, since by this they make known their hope of seeing it changed to red. That is: As far as I am concerned, I firmly believe that the invention by which the brim of the hat of bishops and prelates is green is nothing but a sign of ambition, since by it they declare their hope of changing it to red. Clearly wealth and worldly pride are what is looked for, and by a plainly backward step one descends from bishopric to presbyterate, indeed even to diaconate, although the Council of Chalcedon declares it a sacrilege if a bishop, as a punishment, is stripped of episcopal rank and reduced only to the presbyterate. How much greater a sacrilege will it be, on the hypothesis of the superiority of bishops, if someone procures this for himself not as a punishment and against his will, but of his own accord, and indeed out of sheer vanity?

units.la: XXV. Sed & magis expressa habentur testimonia mutati status,dum hodie ipsis Patriarchis Diaconus Ecclesiae Romanae Cardinalis antefertur, & Cardinales Episcoporum, Archiepiscoporum, Patriarcharum judices & Domini habentur, assessores, juxta Eugenii IV. epistolam, summorum Pontificum, summi consiliarii Ecclesiae, primi cives Reipublicae Christianae, partes & membra corporis Pontificum,organa Potentiae illorum, Vicarii Vicariorum Dei, Collaterales & Coadjutores in Monarchia spirituali & temporali simul. Hinc etiam non tantùm dignitatem tantam ambiunt Episcopi, sed&eâ vestitis omni obsequio praestò sunt,illis adulantur,favorem illorum emendicant, pedissequarum ad instar eos comitantur, imò in omnibus,ut habet bet II Cardinalismo p.1. l. 3. p. 283. E divenuto l'ordine Vescovale un Vasallaggio de Cardinalitio, non sdegnando alcuni Cardinali di farsi servire da' vescovi in cose Mecchaniche.
units.tr: XXV. But there are even more explicit testimonies to the changed status, since today a deacon of the Roman Church, a Cardinal, is placed before the very Patriarchs themselves, and Cardinals are regarded as judges and lords of bishops, archbishops and patriarchs, assessors, according to the letter of Eugene IV: the advisers of the supreme Pontiffs, the highest counsellors of the Church, the first citizens of the Christian Commonwealth, the parts and members of the body of the Pontiffs, the instruments of their power, Vicars of the Vicars of God, collaterals and coadjutors in the spiritual and temporal monarchy at once. Hence bishops not only seek so great a dignity, but once clothed in it they are at hand with every obedience, flatter the Cardinals, beg for their favour, accompany them like attendants, and indeed in everything, as Cardinalismo has it (part 1, book 3, p. 283): The episcopal order has become a vassalage to the Cardinalate, some Cardinals not disdaining to be served by bishops even in menial tasks.

units.la: XXVI. Cui hæc incredibilia videntur, audiat Authorem libri, cui titulus: Sacra Ceremonia, sive ritus Ecclesiastici sancta Romana Ecclesiæ; ita l. 3. c. de reverentia Episcoporum erga Cardinales, loquitur: Quòd autem aliqui ex Reverendissimis Dominis Cardinalibus permittant, ut audivi, Episcopos loqui ante se genu flexos, & in mensa, dum manus lavant, similiter mantile ministrare, valde absurdum videtur; & quamvis sæpe apud plerosque Reverendissimos Dominos in Conviviis fuerim, & ante & postquam inter Episcopos indignus adscriptus sum, nunquam tamen id servari vidi. Adscribendum est hoc (pace illorum dixerim,) ignavia & vecordia Prælatorum, qui talia faciunt, supremam in Ecclesia Episcopalem dignitatem non cognoscunt, sive eorum ambitioni atque adulationi, ut qui gratiam Cardinalis aucupentur, dignitatis suæ rationem non habentes, quam serviliter deturpant; Cardinales autem, qui talia, sive ex inadvertentia, sive alia causa patiuntur, in charitate Dei obsecro, ut importunas hujusmodi adulationes rejiciant, & cogitent, summum Pontificem, non alio titulo quàm Episcopali decorari, & cùm is publicè & in re divina lavat manus, non Episcopus aliquis, sed Capellanus suus Auditor Rota mantile subministrat: quod si forte aliquos mei similes tanto fastigio viderint, non-personam, sed sacro sanctam in eis dignitatem revereantur, & operâ illorum utantur, in his rebus, quæ dignitati utriusque conveniunt; decet tamen Episcopos in omnibus publicè & privatè, quantum per dignitates licet, Reverendissimos Dominos Cardinales honorare ac venerari, & eis pro viribus assistere, obsequi & inservire, nec minùs convenit, Cardinales ipsos benignè suscipere Episcopos, & quos summus Pontifex Fratres appellat, non ut servos, sed ut confratres honorare.
units.tr: XXVI. Let whoever finds these things incredible hear the author of the book entitled Sacred Ceremonies, or the Holy Ritual of the Roman Church, who speaks thus in book 3, on the reverence of bishops towards Cardinals: That some of the Most Reverend Lord Cardinals allow, as I have heard, bishops to speak kneeling before them, and at table, while they wash their hands, to hand them the towel, seems quite absurd; and although I have often been at the banquets of very many Most Reverend Lords, both before and after I was unworthily enrolled among the bishops, I have never seen this observed. This must be ascribed (with respect to them be it said) to the cowardice and folly of those prelates who do such things, who do not recognise the supreme episcopal dignity, or to their ambition and flattery, since they seek the favour of the Cardinal and, not considering their own dignity, degrade it in servile fashion. But I beg the Cardinals, in the charity of God, that those who suffer such things, whether through inadvertence or some other cause, should reject these importunate flatteries and reflect that the supreme Pontiff is adorned with no other title than episcopal, and when he publicly washes his hands in a holy rite, it is not some bishop but his own chaplain, the Auditor of the Rota, who hands him the towel. But if they have seen some like me raised to such a height, let them revere not the person but the sacred dignity in them, and use their services in those matters which befit both dignities. Yet it becomes bishops, in all things, publicly and privately, as far as dignities allow, to honour and venerate the Most Reverend Lord Cardinals, to assist them as far as they can, to obey and serve them; and it is no less fitting that the Cardinals themselves receive bishops kindly, and honour those whom the supreme Pontiff calls brothers, not as servants, but as fellow brothers.

units.la: XXVII. Sed frustra hic quoque regulæ præscribuntur, quando teste Authore des Legats p. 178. Les Evesques sont plús mal traittez à Rome, que de simples Capellans en France, ils sont tous jours debout & nüe teste en presence des Cardinaux, & n' ont de place qu' au derriere de leurs chaires; l' indignation du grand Archevéque de Bragne merite d' être oüe sur ce sujet & c.l.2.ch.22. Ita scilicet honoratur Episcopatus, qui secundùm caput Venerabilem de præbendis non dignitas, sed culmen dignitatum. Imò Legati nolunt permittere, ut Episcopi in illorum præsentia thorace aut Capuccio Episcopali vestiti compareant. Ibid. p. 177. Quod author absurdum judicat, cùm erga Reges Regos non fiat, multò minùs erga jurisdictionem peregrinam & emendicatam fieri debeat. Cardinalis Nepos autem nunquam sedere permittit ullum Prælatorum, tractando illos subditorum ad instar, laqual cosa,inquit Author Cardinalismi p. 1. l. 3. p. 320. sente un poco del tyrannico &c. Quod tyrannidem aliquo modo redolet. Digna scilicet res est, ita pergit, videre Prælatum barbâ candidâ post 40. & plurium annorum in Ecclesiâ servitium stare presente indocto Nepotulo Pontificis.
units.tr: XXVII. But in vain are rules prescribed here too, when, according to the author of Des Legats, p. 178: Bishops are treated worse at Rome than simple chaplains in France; they are always standing and bareheaded in the presence of the Cardinals, and have a place only behind their chairs; the indignation of the great Archbishop of Braga deserves to be heard on this subject, etc., book 2, chapter 22. So, clearly, the episcopate is honoured in this way, which according to the chapter Venerabilem on prebends is not a dignity but the summit of dignities. Indeed the Legates are unwilling to allow bishops to appear in their presence wearing the episcopal cassock or cape. Ibid., p. 177. The author judges this absurd, since it is not done before kings for kings, much less should it be done before a foreign and begged-for jurisdiction. A Cardinal nephew, moreover, never allows any prelate to sit, treating them as subjects; a thing which, says the author of Cardinalismo (part 1, book 3, p. 320), smacks somewhat of tyranny, etc. which in some way smells of tyranny. It is indeed a worthy sight, he goes on, to see a prelate with a white beard, after forty or more years of service in the Church, standing in the presence of the unlearned little nephew of the Pope.

units.la: XXVIII. Sed quodnam est illius superioritatis ex parte Cardinalium, & subjectionis ex parte Episcoporum fundamentum? Respondet Bellarminus, citatos à se authores in hoc fere omnes consentire, quòd, si consideremus ordinis potestatem, major sit Episcopus Presbytero, vel Diacono Cardinali.
units.tr: XXVIII. But what is the foundation of this superiority on the part of the Cardinals, and of subjection on the part of the bishops? Bellarmine answers that the authors he cites almost all agree in this, that, if we consider the power of order, a bishop is greater than a presbyter or a deacon Cardinal.

units.la: Nam Episcopus, pergit, ordinat Presbyteros, confirmat baptizatos, aliáque id genus facit, qua Cardinales Presbyteri, vel Diaconi facere non possunt. Quâ etiam ratione summus Pontifex Episcopum se vocat, non Cardinalem, & Episcopos omnes appellat Venerabiles Fratres, Cardinales autem dilectos filios, quomodo vocat etiam Laicos: Pari ratione, si consideremus jurisdictionem in propriam Ecclesiam, id est, Episcopi in suam diœcesin, & Cardinalis in suum titulum, aut Diaconiam, major est ordinarie Diœcesis Episcopi quàm titulus Cardinalis, ac praterea Episcopus in sua Diœcesi amplissimam habet jurisdictionem, tanquam proprius & ordinarius pastor, ferendi leges, dispensandi, puniendi, indulgendi &c. At Cardinalis Presbyter, & Diaconus, cùm in suo titulo sit veluti Parochus Episcopo subjectus, nihil potest nisi quantum Episcopus ei permiserit. At si consideremus regimen Ecclesiæ universalis, major est Cardinalis Presbyter, vel Diaconus Episcopo non Cardinali. Nam Episcopi simplices nunquam adhibentur ad regimen Universalis Ecclesiæ, nisi rarissimè, id est, cùm ad generale Concilium convocantur. At Cardinales quotidie prasto sunt Pontifici, neque ullum negotium majoris momenti sine eorum Concilio peragitur. Et quia hinc fit, ut Episcopi à Cardinalibus & summi Pontificis cooperatoribus judicentur, creentur, deponantur, non autem Cardinales ab Episcopis, propterea absolutè Cardinalis Episcopum non Cardinalem precedit.
units.tr: For the bishop, he goes on, ordains presbyters, confirms the baptized, and does other things of that kind, which Cardinal presbyters or deacons cannot do. For this reason too the supreme Pontiff calls himself a bishop, not a Cardinal, and addresses all bishops as Venerable Brothers but Cardinals as beloved sons, just as he also calls laymen. By the same reasoning, if we consider jurisdiction over one's own church, that is, the bishop's over his diocese and the Cardinal's over his title or deaconry, the ordinary authority of a bishop over his diocese is greater than that of a Cardinal over his title. Moreover, the bishop in his own diocese has very ample jurisdiction, as its proper and ordinary pastor: he may make laws, dispense, punish, grant indulgences, and so on. But a Cardinal presbyter or deacon, since in his title he is like a parish priest subject to the bishop, can do nothing except as far as the bishop has permitted him. But if we consider the government of the universal Church, the Cardinal presbyter or deacon is greater than a bishop who is not a Cardinal. For ordinary bishops are never called upon to govern the universal Church, except very rarely, that is, when they are summoned to a general council. But Cardinals are present with the Pontiff every day, and no matter of greater importance is carried out without their council. And because it happens that bishops are judged, created, and deposed by Cardinals, who are the Pope's co-workers, and not Cardinals by bishops, therefore a Cardinal absolutely precedes a bishop who is not a Cardinal.

units.la: XXIX. Mutationis autem illius, juxta quam Cardinales anteponi cæperint, duas causas assignat. 1. Quòd ad solos devoluta est electio Pontificis summi. 2. Quòd soli caperunt adesse Pontifici Romano in Concilii; (consiliis forte) Nam antea Cardinales neque soli, neque primarii consiliarii Pontificis erant; siquidem primis 600. vel 800. annis summi Pontifices ad graviora negotia Ecclesiæ dijudicanda cogebant Concilia nationalia Episcoporum Italiæ, quibus Conciliis intererant quidem Cardinales Presbyteri, sed tamen primus locus Episcoporum erat. Id cognosci potest ex Tomis Conciliorum, ubi plurima inveniuntur Concilia Romana, sive Lateranensia, celebrata ab anno Domini 300. ad 800. Quocirca non erat ratio, cur eo tempore Cardinales Presbyteri Episcopis anteponerentur, cùm eo tempore non minùs imò magis Pontificem juvarent in Ecclesia Universali regenda Episcopi, quàm Cardinales. At postea creverunt negotia Ecclesiæ Romanæ, præsertim cùm accessisset principatus temporalis tempore Pipini & Caroli M. proinde egebat summus Pontifex consiliariorum ope multò sapiùs quàm antea; Neque poterat tam sæpe convocare Concilia Episcoporum, quàm necesse erat. Concilia enim vix tertio quoque anno cogi poterant. Pontifex autem quolibet anno sapius egebat consilio. Itaque usu docente & necessitate cogente his posterioris annis 600. vel 700. caperunt paulatim omitti Concilia Episcopalia & res tota redigi ad Senatum Cardinalium. Potuisse autem hoc fieri & rectè factum esse, in dubium revocari non potest: nam non tenetur Pontifex hos potiùs quàm illos in consilium adhibere: Deinde, hac ratione multa incommoda consecuta sunt. Primum, quòd habeatur nunc senatus in promtu, alterum sine detrimento Ecclesiarum particularium, quibus absentia Episcoporum in Concilio congregatorum perniciosa est; Tertium, quòd habeat Consiliarios magis instructos & exercitatos &c.
units.tr: XXIX. He assigns two causes for that change by which Cardinals began to be placed before bishops. (1) The election of the supreme Pontiff was devolved to them alone. (2) They alone began to attend the Roman Pontiff in councils (perhaps "consistories"). For formerly the Cardinals were neither the only nor the chief counsellors of the Pontiff. For in the first 600 or 800 years the supreme Pontiffs compelled national councils of the bishops of Italy to decide the more serious matters of the Church; at these councils Cardinal presbyters did indeed take part, but the first place belonged to the bishops. This can be known from the volumes of the councils, where very many Roman, or Lateran, councils celebrated between the year of the Lord 300 and 800 are found. Hence there was no reason why at that time Cardinal presbyters should be placed before bishops, since at that time the bishops helped the Pontiff in governing the universal Church no less, indeed more, than the Cardinals did. But afterwards the affairs of the Roman Church grew, especially when temporal sovereignty had been added in the time of Pepin and Charlemagne; accordingly the supreme Pontiff needed the help of counsellors much more than before. Nor could he convene councils of bishops as often as was necessary, for councils could scarcely be held every third year, while the Pontiff needed counsel more than once a year. Therefore, as experience taught and necessity compelled, in the following 600 or 700 years the episcopal councils gradually began to be dropped and the whole business was transferred to the senate of the Cardinals. Yet that this could be done, and was rightly done, can hardly be doubted. For the Pontiff is not bound to call these rather than those into council. Next, many advantages have followed from this arrangement. First, a senate is now at hand; second, this happens without loss to the particular Churches, to which the absence of bishops gathered in council is harmful; third, the Cardinals are better instructed and experienced counsellors, etc.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: En defensionem Bellarminianam superioritatis Cardinalium satis prolixam! Sed cæterùm qualem? Planè frivolam; Cùm non tantùm omnia salsissimæ illi de universali Papæ Monarchia hypothesi fusè in Dissertationibus præcedentibus refutatæ initantur, sed & talia tanquam ideò necessaria asserantur, quæ ex illa non fluunt, imò ne quidem ex parte cum illa & aliis Pontificiorum hypothesibus & secum consistere possunt. Probè notetur, quantas Episcopis præ Presbyteris & Diaconis Cardinalibus, quâ talibus, prærogativas tribuat, ob quas tamen illos nullo modo præponi videmus; Nunquam Episcoporum pars splendidior Cardinalibus obvertitur; nonnisi inferiores semper apparent, & multò inferiores, imò sordidissimo penè famulitio subditi & mutum sponte facti pecus; Venerabiles Papæ fratres, sed ad pedum oscula abjectissimè prostrati; dum Laicorum nomine appellati Cardinales erecti accipiuntur! Venerabiles Papæ fratres, sed quos filii judicant, creant, deponunt, in quos contrà ipsis nihil planè permittitur!
units.tr: Behold the Bellarminian defence of the superiority of the Cardinals, quite lengthy! But what sort of defence? Plainly frivolous, since not only are all those most salty notions about the universal monarchy of the Pope, which have been fully refuted in the preceding Dissertations, brought in again, but also such things are asserted as necessary which do not follow from that hypothesis, indeed cannot even agree in part with it and with the other hypotheses of the Papists. Let it be carefully noted how great the prerogatives he grants to bishops, as such, over Cardinal presbyters and deacons are, yet we see that the bishops are in no way placed before them. The more splendid part of the bishops is never turned toward the Cardinals; they always appear only as inferiors, and far inferior, indeed subjects in an almost filthy servitude, and a flock made dumb of their own accord. Venerable Brothers of the Pope, yet cast down most abjectly at the kissing of his feet, while the Cardinals, called by the name of laymen, are received as erected! Venerable Brothers of the Pope, yet those whom his sons judge, create, and depose, and against whom they are in no way allowed anything at all!

units.la: XXXI. Causa tantæ quoad dignitatem, honorem & potestatem differentiæ in vanis de Monarchia somniis ostenditur; In eo, quòd Episcopi simplices rarissimè ad regimen Ecclesiæ universalis adhibentur &, licèt per 800. annos adhibiti, magis tunc Papas juvantes in regimine Ecclesiæ Universalis, licèt æquè ac Papa bonus ordinarii etiam decisivè adhibentur consiliarii; rarissimè, id est, cùm ad generale Concilium convocantur (quod rarissimum, quia Papæ periculosissimum) ut & provincialia & nationalia contra morem prædecessorum omittuntur, scilicet ut evitetur detrimentum particularium Ecclesiarum, dum interim paucis illis Purpuratis satiandis Ecclesiæ universæ opes vix sufficiunt, minùs certè ac mille Episcopis luxu carentibus; Illi autem ad Regimen universalis Ecclesiæ adhibentur, quod penes Papam non est, adhibentur bonam partem minùs apti, in Ecclesia Romana peregrini, Consiliarii, sed quorum assentiri, assentari est, sine decisivo suffragio, & tamen decidit Ecclesia Catholica! Ubi species tantùm externáque sola Synodi forma! Adhibentur, loco nimirum prædecessorum, qui tamen Episcopis diu inferiores fuerunt, quod & aperte fateri coactus fuit Pamelius annot. in Cypr. Epist. 46. n. 10. Nempe Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quem Cornelius apud Cypr. l. 3. ep. 11. suum vocat Presbyterium, tunc idem Collegium fuisse ejusdem officii ac authoritatis cum eo, quod nunc sit Cardinalium, & tamen Episcopos quoscunque fuisse hoc Presbyterio superiores; In eo causa porrò ponitur, quòd soli sint Electores, id est, alieni juris raptores, Electores, quales etiam fuerunt Cleri populíque singula membra, sed ideò Episcopis non antepositá; In eo quoque causa ponitur, quòd accessit principatus temporalis, id est, quòd Papa rem sibi minimè convenientem partim rapuit, & quia principatus iste temporalis per eos ex parte administratur, ideò etiam Episcopis tanquam in eodem tamen ordine constituti anteponuntur. Quàm bene! XXXII. Et quantò melius Bracarensis Episcopus in Concilio Tridentino apud Historicum l. 7. p. 534. Necessariam hanc esse cogitationem, (de restituendis Episcoporum Juribus) quòd Episcopalis authoritas ad nihilum redacta esset, introducto ordine Cardinalium Episcopis superiore, Ecclesiæ antiquitùs ignorato. Qui primis temporibus reliquorum Presbyterorum & Diaconorum habiti numero, non ante X. Seculum supra debitum conditioni suæ gradum sese extulere: nec tunc quidem in tantùm, ut se Episcopis adæquare sustinerent, quibus imparès habiti ad annum usque CIↃ CC. Ex eo tempore non modò pari cum Episcopis jure vixere, sed etiam tam longè superiores, ut eos jam in adibus suis pro servis habeant. De Reformatione Ecclesia nihil spei esse reliquum, donec Episcopi & Cardinales ad sibi quisque debitum redierint locum. Et certè non minor est illa confusio, quàm quæ olim in Ecclesia Romana fuit, dum Diaconi Presbyteris Augustini & Hieronymi tempore antepositi fuerunt, quod adhuc Bernhardi tempore perduravit, vel potiùs innovari cœpit. Erant illi dubio procul Diaconi Cardinales Romani, quorum tamen vecordiam, supercilium, superbiam & arrogantiam supra dicti Ecclesiæ Doctores acriter pulsant, & quidem iisdem, quibus hodie Cardinalium fastus innititur, fundamentis innixam, urbis nimirum nobilitati & jactantiæ & numeri paucitati; Contrà illam Hieronymus Epist.85. Ubicunque fuerit Episcopus, sive Roma, sive Eugubii &c. ejusdem meriti, ejusdem est & Sacerdotii &c. Quod Presbyteris quoque Romanis illis commodè applicatur. Hanc quod attinet, constat Cardinalibus quoque emolumento esse, sed haud majori jure. Bernhardus verò de Consid. l.4.c.5. Presbyteris tribuit, quòd ordinata sessione ambiant, Diaconis ad pedes sedere, qui propiores assistunt, ut sint paratiores. Ut videatur, illustres illos Viros parùm de magnificentissimis illis Consiliariis & Universalis Ecclesiæ cum Papa Gubernatoribus cogitâsse. Hieronymus certè minimè omnium de talibus cogitavit, dum totum Clerum Romanum Proam. in lib. Dydimi de Sp. S. Senatum Pharisæorum & imperitia factionem vocavit.
units.tr: XXXI. The cause of so great a difference in dignity, honour, and power is shown in the empty dreams about monarchy. It lies in this: that ordinary bishops are very rarely called upon to govern the Church universal, and, although for 800 years they were called upon, they helped the Popes more then in governing the universal Church; although, like a good Pope, they are also called upon as ordinary counsellors with a decisive vote. Very rarely, that is, when they are summoned to a general council (which is very rare, because it is most dangerous for the Pope), and provincial and national councils are dropped, contrary to the custom of the predecessors, namely so that loss to the particular Churches may be avoided; meanwhile the resources of the universal Church scarcely suffice to satisfy those few purple-clad men, certainly less than they would for a thousand bishops who lack luxury. Yet those who are called upon to govern the universal Church, which does not lie with the Pope, are for the most part less fit, foreigners in the Roman Church, counsellors whose assent is flattery, without a decisive vote; and yet the Catholic Church is decided by them! Here there is only the appearance and the bare external form of a synod! They are called in, that is, in place of the predecessors, who nevertheless were long inferior to the bishops, as Pamelius was also compelled to admit openly in his notes on Cyprian, Epistle 46, n. 10. Indeed, Cornelius, in Cyprian book 3, letter 11, calls the clergy of the Roman Church his presbytery; and he says that this same college then had the same office and authority as what is now that of the Cardinals, and yet that all bishops whatsoever were superior to this presbytery. Furthermore, the cause is laid down in this: that they alone are electors, that is, robbers of rights that belong to others; electors such as also were the individual members of the clergy and people, yet on that account not placed before the bishops. In this too the cause is laid down: that temporal sovereignty was added, that is, that the Pope partly seized a thing not at all suitable to him, and because that temporal sovereignty is administered by them in part, therefore they are also placed before the bishops, although constituted in the same order. How well! XXXII. And how much better did the Bishop of Braga say at the Council of Trent, in the historian book 7, p. 534: "This consideration (about restoring the rights of the bishops) is necessary, because episcopal authority has been reduced to nothing by the introduction of an order of Cardinals superior to the bishops, a thing unknown to the Church of antiquity. In the earliest times they were counted among the rest of the presbyters and deacons, and they did not raise themselves above the grade due to their condition before the tenth century; nor even then so much that they could bear to equal themselves with the bishops, to whom they were regarded as unequal until the year 1200. From that time they not only lived with the same right as the bishops, but rose so far above them that they now treat them in their own houses as servants. There is no hope left of reform of the Church until the bishops and Cardinals return each to the place due to him." And certainly that confusion is no less than that which once existed in the Roman Church, when deacons were placed before presbyters in the time of Augustine and Jerome, which lasted still into the time of Bernard, or rather began to be revived. Those were beyond doubt the Roman Cardinal deacons, whose folly, haughtiness, pride, and arrogance the above-mentioned doctors of the Church sharply assail; and indeed they rested on the same foundations on which the pride of the Cardinals rests today, namely the nobility and boastfulness of the city and the small number. Against that, Jerome, Epistle 85: "Wherever a bishop is, whether at Rome or at Gubbio, etc., he is of the same merit and of the same priesthood, etc." This is conveniently applied also to those Roman presbyters. As far as this goes, it is clear that it is also an advantage to the Cardinals, but not by any greater right. Bernard, however, On Consideration, book 4, chapter 5, assigns to presbyters that "when the session is arranged they strive, while deacons sit at the feet, who stand nearer, so that they may be readier." So it appears that those illustrious men had little thought of those most magnificent counsellors and governors of the universal Church along with the Pope. Jerome certainly, of all men, thought of no such people, when he called the whole Roman clergy the Senate of the Pharisees and a faction of ignorance, in the preface to his book on the Holy Spirit of Didymus.

units.la: XXXIII. Sed quibus non anteponerentur Cardinales, qui Regibus in dignitate æqui parantur Principum æmuli facti, imò ipsi potiùs Reguli? Jam olim Imperatorum se fratres ferebant, sub Papa communi Patre. Vid. Crus. Annales Suev. ad an. 1157. Reges cognatos vocant, vocantur à Regibus cognati, sæpe ex ima plebis fæce oriundi; Sed in Gallia promiscuè demum ex illo tempore, quo Henricus IV. absolutionem Romanam, dont il se seroit bien passé, qua facilè carere potuisset, petiit, cùm antea Cardinales charorum amicorum nomen à Regibus acceperint, nisi Principes, aut peculiariter grati fuissent. Traitté des legats. p.2.p.164. Regibus eos æquiparari, notius est, quàm ut Scriptorum testimoniis confirmari debeat. Legi potest ea de re Apologia Bellarmini Contra Prafationem Jacobi Regis Anglia. Amydemus de stylo Dataria. c.5. §.7.9.18. n. 149. tamen dicit, id fieri quoad dignitatem, non quoad potentiam vel Majestatem.
units.tr: XXXIII. But who are the Cardinals, if not those placed above them? They are put on a par with kings in dignity, and have become rivals of princes, indeed little kings themselves. Long ago they already called themselves brothers of the Emperors, under the Pope as their common Father. See Crusius, Annales Suevici, ad an. 1157. Kings call them cousins, and kings call them cousins, though they were often born from the dregs of the common people. In France, however, this name was used indiscriminately only from the time when Henry IV sought Roman absolution, which he could well have done without, whereas before this Cardinals received the name dear friends from kings, unless they were princes or especially favoured. Treatise on the Legates, p.2 p.164. That Cardinals are placed on a par with kings is too well known to need confirmation from the testimony of writers. One may read on this matter Bellarmine's Apology against the Preface of James, King of England. Amydenus, de stylo Dataria, c.5 §§7, 9, 18, n.149, nevertheless says this happens as to dignity, not as to power or majesty.

units.la: XXXIV. Hinc etiam honorantur ut Reges. Wolsæo Cardinali Anglo, qui sæpe dicere solitus: Ego & Rex meus: Brugis prandenti & cœnanti flexis poplitibus (nempe ad imitationem moris regii) ministratum esse Paraleip. ad Abbat. Urspverg. Annal. Rerum Anglio. testantur, licet quoad honorem à Regibus multis iis delatum verè de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. l. 4. c. 5. n. 32. dixerit: Sapientes interea Principes non defuisse, qui Cardinales in locum satis humilem, verèque suum detruserint, eósque nimium insolescentes repressterint. Hinc etiam Electoribus Imperii, tot quasi Regibus, de præcedentia hodierno Cæremoniali Romano convenienter litem movent, & veruit collegium, quemquam ex suo numero Electoribus, etiam in propria domo, cedere; Nam si Reges, Principes, Archiepiscopis & Episcopis suis, sicut debent, reverenter assurgunt, & eis venerabilem sedem assignant, quod habetur in cap. solicitæ de major. & obed. quantò magis hoc præstare tenentur Cardinalibus? Sed inde occasionem nactus est Celeberrimus Freinshemius quinque doctissimas de Imperii Electorum & Cardinalium præcedentia diatribas conscribere. De Electoribus autem, & de Principibus reliquis graviter Bellarminus Apol. cit. c. 4. pronunciat; Quemadmodum Principes omnes Regibus cedunt, sic etiam cedunt Cardinalibus.
units.tr: XXXIV. Hence they are also honoured like kings. It is attested that Wolsey, the English Cardinal, who often used to say I and my King, was served at Bruges, while dining and supping, with bent knees (namely in imitation of royal custom), in Paraleipomena ad Abbatem Urspergensem, Annales Rerum Anglicarum. Yet concerning the honour that many kings bestowed on them, the author of De Republica Ecclesiastica (l.4 c.5 n.32) rightly said: Meanwhile there were not wanting wise princes who thrust the Cardinals down into a rather humble place, which was truly theirs, and checked them when they grew too insolent. Hence too, according to the present Roman ceremonial, they stir up a dispute about precedence with the Electors of the Empire, who are so many quasi-kings. The college forbids any of its members to yield to the Electors, even in its own house; for if kings reverently rise for their Archbishops and Bishops, as they ought, and assign them a venerable seat, as is found in cap. Solicitae de maior. et obed., how much more ought they to do this for Cardinals? But from this occasion the most famous Freinsheim was moved to write five most learned discourses on the precedence of the Electors of the Empire and of the Cardinals. Concerning the Electors and the other princes, Bellarmine pronounces gravely, in the Apology cited, c.4: Just as all princes yield to kings, so they also yield to Cardinals.

units.la: XXXV. Eódem spectat, quòd Sprengerus l. jam sæpiùs cit. ait; Ut videas, quantum se Cardinales faciant, notabis, quòd etiam Legatos Regum visitantes, nonnisi ad caput scalarum conducant, cùm tamen hi Cardinales usque ad caruccam comitentur. Cardinalis Nepos in tantum super alios eminet, ut nulli extra Legatos Regum sedere in sua camera permittat; Alii quidem etiam Agentibus Regum & Aulicis Nobilibus Cardinalium, Ducum & Legatorum in visitatione sessionem indulgent, ita tamen, ut à dextra, licet Duces sint, qui visitant, locum occupent, primíque secedant. Controversiam autem præcedentiæ inter Principes in Gallia Regii sanguinis & Cardinales Freinshemius Diatr. V. ex Authoribus idoneis ostendit, in illorum favorem decisam esse; De illa etiam inter Cardinales eosdem & Pares Franciæ Ecclesiasticos, vide in tractatu jam sæpe citato de l' Origine des Cardinaux du S. Siege. Strenuè scilicet isti observant præceptum Christi: Vos autem non sic.
units.tr: XXXV. To the same point belongs what Sprenger, already cited many times, says: That you may see how much the Cardinals make of themselves, you will note that even when visiting the legates of kings, they lead them only to the head of the stairs, whereas these Cardinals accompany them as far as the carriage. The Cardinal nephew stands so far above the others that he allows no one except the legates of kings to sit in his chamber. Others indeed grant a seat during a visit also to the agents of kings and to courtly nobles, to Cardinals, dukes and legates, yet in such a way that the visitor, even if he is a duke, occupies the place on the right and leaves first. The controversy over precedence in France between princes of royal blood and the Cardinals, Freinsheim shows in Diatribe V, from reliable authors, was decided in their favour. On that dispute between the same Cardinals and the ecclesiastical peers of France, see the treatise already often cited, de l'Origine des Cardinaux du S. Siege. Certainly they diligently observe Christ's precept: But you shall not be so.

units.la: XXXVI. Sine dubio autem fastus illorum non exigua incrementa sumit ex eo, quòd hodie nonnulli inter eos (multis aliis ad idem munus aspirantibus) Regnorum Protectores audiunt. Quales les Cardinales Protectores pro numero Regnorum, Imperii, Galliae, Hispaniae, Portugalliae (non ita pridem etiam de Protectore Angliae actum est:) quinque sunt, id est, tot miracula, dum nimirum Protectores sunt Protectorum istius Ecclesiae, sine quibus illa subsistere non posset. Nempe debetur hoc usurpationi Paparum, & ambitioni Cardinalium; Illi, id est, confusioni temporalium & spiritualium tali, ut jam Romam translata sint Principum commoda & status ratio; Huic, dum ex magnifico nomine & munere gloriam quaerunt; ambiunt, quando aliae Protectiones contrà implorantur à protegendis; Qui hic insuper minùs juvantur, dum proteguntur cum limitatione, & quatenus licet per commoda Pontificum, nunquam enim Protector talis aliquid contrà Pontificis authoritatem faciet, sed subjectionem potiùs erga communem Ecclesiae Patrem & juris relaxationem suadebit, licet etiam semper ad honorem Regni protegendi, quoad fieri potest, salvandum annitatur. Caeterùm apparet omninò, idem feré esse, ac si Pontifex apud Pontificem Protector foret.
units.tr: XXXVI. Without doubt their pride gains no small increase from the fact that today some of them (many others aspiring to the same office) are styled Protectors of Kingdoms. Such are the Cardinal Protectors, according to the number of kingdoms: of the Empire, France, Spain and Portugal (and not long ago there was talk also of a Protector of England); there are five of them, that is, as many marvels, since they are indeed protectors of the protectors of this Church, without whom it could not subsist. This is owed to the usurpation of the Popes and the ambition of the Cardinals. The former have produced such a confusion of temporal and spiritual affairs that the interests of princes and the reasons of state have now been transferred to Rome. The latter seek glory from the magnificent name and office; they court it when other protections are sought against them by those they are meant to protect. These are helped less here, since they are protected only with limitation, and only so far as it is permitted by the advantage of the Pontiffs. For such a Protector will never do anything against the authority of the Pontiff, but will rather urge subjection to the common Father of the Church and relaxation of law, although he always strives, as far as possible, to preserve the honour of the kingdom he protects. Moreover, it appears altogether that this is nearly the same as if the Pope were Protector in the presence of the Pope.

units.la: XXXVII. Respectu Papae multùm etiam honorati apparent; Non quidem omni respectu; Ut enim Author Cardinalismi docet, plerunque sunt congregati in unum, non già in unum con Christo, mà in unum con il Papa; Id est, In unum non cum Christo, sed cum Papa, volentes servire, non Ecclesiae, sed Pontificibus, non gregi Domini, sed Nepotibus Paparum (quorum mancipia saepe sunt,) hinc etiam dicendi Cardinales Pontificum potiùs, quàm Ecclesia ibidem; & non ineptè responsuri cum quodam, sub Pontificatu Innocentii X. se ire, nella congregatione di Donna Olympia; in congregationem Dominae Olympiae; Atque ita non raro praetextui inserviunt tantùm p.98. Nec audiuntur aliquando bona monentes, & rarae sunt voces, quae ab initio Pontificatùs Alexandri VI. ex ore Cardinalis auditae fuerunt: Dio sia lodato, habbiamo pur trovato un: Pontefice, amico de' buoni consigli; Id est; Deo sit laus, invenimus tandem Pontificem, bonorum consiliorum amantem; Et illae ex ore alius: Sin' hora noi siamo stati suditi de' Pontefici, hora siamo fratelli d' Alesandro; Id est; Hactenus fuimus subditi Pontificum, nunc sumus fratres Alexandri; Quae voces etiam tunc falsae fuerunt, priores ex ore unius, qui engannato di una si fatta apparenza deceptus à specie fucata ita locutus est. Dum nello scotolar del sacco, percosi dire, saccorsero, non esservi altro che polvere. Id est; Dum in sacci evacuatione apparuit, pulverem verem tantùm intùs esse p.105. Adhibentur quidem in consilium, sed tantùm volendo il Papa mostrare, chè gli fà le cose, sunt verba Præla-ti dignissimi ad nobilem, à quo de Cardinalium in Consistorio actionibus interrogatus erat, con il maturo giudicio di tanti Consigliari Porporati, volente sic Papa ostendere, se omnia facere maturo tot Purpurato-rum Consiliariorum judicio.
units.tr: XXXVII. In respect of the Pope they also appear much honoured, though not in every respect. For, as the author of Cardinalismo teaches, they are for the most part gathered together, not into one with Christ but into one with the Pope; that is, gathered into one not with Christ but with the Pope, wishing to serve not the Church but the Pontiffs, not the flock of the Lord but the nephews of the Popes, of whom they are often the slaves. Hence Cardinals are to be called Cardinals of the Pontiffs rather than of the Church there. And not inaptly does one reply with a certain man that under Innocent X he goes into the congregation of Donna Olympia; and thus they often serve only as a pretext. Good counsels are not always heard, and rare were the voices that were heard from the mouth of a Cardinal at the start of the pontificate of Alexander VI: Thank God, we have at last found a Pope who is a friend of good counsels; that is, God be praised, we have at last found a Pontiff who loves good counsels. And that other from another's mouth: Until now we have been subjects of the Popes; now we are brothers of Alexander; that is, hitherto we have been subjects of the Popes, now we are brothers of Alexander. These sayings also proved false then: the former was spoken by one who, deceived by such a counterfeit appearance, said: While shaking the sack, we were struck, they saw there was nothing but dust; that is, when the sack was emptied it appeared that there was only dust inside. They are indeed admitted to counsel, but only because the Pope wishes to show that he does things with them. These are the words of a most worthy prelate to a nobleman, of whom he was asked about the actions of the Cardinals in Consistory: with the mature judgement of so many purpled counsellors, as the Pope wishes to show, he does all things by the mature judgement of so many purple-robed counsellors.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quod etiam ex Frà Paolo Guerra di Paolo V. &c. cognoscimus.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Which we also learn from Fra Paolo Guerra on Paul V, etc.

units.la: Non è cosa posta in dubio dalla corte, inquit, che li voti delli Cardinali sono ricevuti in Consistoro per sola apparenza, imperoche mai non sono informati del negocio che si tratta; Il. che anco la corte dice apertamente usando la figura delle annominationi e mutando la voce latina, assentiri in assentari. Id est; Non dubitat Curia, Consistorialia Cardinalium vota tantùm ad speciem colligi, cùm nihil sciant de re tractanda; quod & Curia aperte dicit paranomasiasticè mutans assentiri in assentari. Quibus planè consentanea habet MSC. Italicum à Clarissimo Fascbio communicatum, causas, quibus Hispani electionem Pontificis non negligere jubentur, exponens, periodo: Hora questo &c. Nam ea Paparum de se opinio est, quam Paulus II. referente Platina in edit. prima in vita Pauli, eodem Platina ad Consistorium Cardinalium, quorum judicio stare velit, provocante, prodidit: Quid mihi de judicio loqueris, inquiebat; An nescis, me omnia judicia & rationes in pectoris mei scrinio reconditas habere? Ego neminem respicio, sum Papa, & mihi licet rumpere & acta aliorum approbare pro lubitu meo. Quibus certè verbis praxis hodierna plerorumque maximè respondet; Non tam stulti sunt, ait author Card. l. c. p. 9. ut dividere velint Monarchiam, quam unicè in manibus suis esse arbitrantur; Cujus etiam Sixtum V. testem luculentum Dissert.I. induxi;
units.tr: It is not something the Curia doubts, he says, that the votes of the Cardinals are received in Consistory merely for show, because they are never informed about the business being discussed.
