The Curia itself also says so openly, using the figure of paronomasia and changing the Latin word assentiri into assentari. That is: The Curia does not doubt that the Cardinals' votes in Consistory are gathered merely for show, since they know nothing of the matter being treated; and the Curia also says so openly, punning by changing assentiri into assentari. The Italian manuscript communicated by the distinguished Fascbio, which sets out the reasons why the Spaniards are ordered not to neglect the election of a Pope, agrees plainly with these things in the sentence: Hora questo &c. For this is the Popes' own opinion of themselves, which Paul II revealed, as Platina reports in the first edition, in the Life of Paul. When Platina urged the Consistory of Cardinals, whose judgment the Pope wished to abide by, Paul said: What do you talk to me about judgment, he said; do you not know that I keep all judgments and reasons stored in the chest of my breast? I respect no one. I am the Pope, and it is lawful for me to break the acts of others and approve them at my pleasure. Today's practice mostly matches these words. They are not so foolish, says the author, Card. l. c. p. 9. as to want to divide the monarchy, which they believe is in their hands alone. I have also brought forward Sixtus V as a clear witness to this in Dissert. I.

units.la: XXXIX. Et sunt quidem liberalissimi nel concedere a' Cardinali ampi privilegi e magnificenze esteriori &c. in concedendo Cardinalibus ampla privilegia & magnificentiam externam; Pracedant Principibus, aquales se gerant Regibus, Prælatos mancipiorum ad instar tractent, multò altiùs dignitate Episcopali ascendant; Hac omnia se bene habent, hac omnia ipsis Pontifices larga manu concedent, imò etiam sub pœna excommunicationis contrarium vetabunt; Mà che però si guardio &c. sed probè tamen sibi caveant, ne manum erario publico admoveant, ne Eleemosyne, ne dicant Papis, quid faciendum, ne commendent populum afflictum & malè habitum, ne Beneficia dignis conferri velint, ne respondeant nisi ad interrogata, ne imperare velint nisi jussi, & tandem ne vel verbulo de latrociniis Nepotum loquantur, altramente &c. alias exulandum ipsis erit ab aula, torvis vultibus aspicientur à Nepotibus, privabuntur officiis, & omninò tractabuntur ut vilissimi subditi, sine ullo Purpura respectu: Qualia exempla nostro tempore, pergit author, non desunt, & possem nominare &c. Egregia sunt in hanc rem verba Innocentii Decimi ad Dominam Olympiam: Cognata, inquit sanctissimus Pater p.97. li Cardinali saranno nostri à loro dispetto, e difenderanno lo stato per loro interesse, benche noi lo volessimo ruinare per lo nostro; Id est; Cognata, Cardinales commoda nostra promovebunt vel inviti, & statum defendent ob commoda sua, licèt nos illum perdere vellemus ob commoda nostra. Idem Author p.1. l.3. p.362. ostendit, quomodo negotia in congregationibus tractentur & retractentur, donec omnia sint ad nutum Pontificis, & quòd Cardinales consultent, Papæ proponant & decernant, semper secundùm Cardinalium consultationes, siquidem convenienter propositioni & decreto Pontificum consultent.
units.tr: XXXIX. The Popes are indeed very generous in granting the Cardinals ample privileges and outward splendour, etc. in granting the Cardinals ample privileges and external magnificence. They may take precedence over princes, behave as equals to kings, treat prelates like servants, and rise far above episcopal dignity. All these things are well and good; the Popes will grant all of them with an open hand, and even forbid the contrary under penalty of excommunication. But let them take care that they do not lay a hand on the public treasury, that they do not speak of alms, that they do not tell the Popes what must be done, that they do not commend a afflicted and ill-treated people, that they do not wish benefices to be conferred on the worthy, that they answer only to what is asked, that they do not wish to command unless ordered to, and finally that they do not speak even a word about the robberies of the nephews; otherwise, etc. otherwise they will be driven from the court, looked at with hostile faces by the nephews, deprived of their offices, and treated altogether like the lowest subjects, with no regard for the purple. Examples of this kind, the author goes on, are not lacking in our own time, and I could name them, etc. The words of Innocent X to Donna Olimpia are striking on this point: Cognata, said the most holy Father, the Cardinals will be ours in spite of themselves, and will defend the state for their own interest, although we would wish to ruin it for ours. That is: Cognata, the Cardinals will promote our interests even against their will, and will defend the state for their own advantage, although we wish to lose it for our own advantage. The same author shows, p. 1, l. 3, p. 362, how affairs are treated and retreated in the congregations until everything is at the nod of the Pope, and that the Cardinals deliberate, the Popes propose and decide, always according to the Cardinals' deliberations, provided that they deliberate in agreement with the Pope's proposal and decree.

units.la: XL. Subjungit p.95. Author pluribus, Nepotes perdere, ut salvent Cardinales, & tamen p.96. Nepotibus semper gloriam benefactorum tribui, Cardinalibus male gesta, etiam qua insciis, imò nonnunquam invitis illis gesta sint p.99. imputari, & sic excusari, quod & exemplis p. 100. seqq. probat, & dicto Pauli V. ad Cardinalem Nepotem p.96. Nepote voi havete posto à mal termine questo negotio, onde per salvar la vostra reputatione, bisogna metterlo trà le mani de' Cardinali, perche se si potrà rimediare, noi con tutto cio faremo applicar l'honore à voi, che l'havete cominciato male, non già à Cardinali che l'hanno finito in bene; Id est; Nepos, male dispositisti hoc negotium, quare ad honorem tuum salvandum oportet illud committere Cardinalibus, nam si remedium inveniri poterit, faciam, ut nihilominus id tibi tribuatur, qui male cepisti, & non Cardinalibus, qui negotium ad finem bonum perduxerunt. Idem etiam p. 140. seqq. diminutionem dignitatis Cardinalitiæ Pontificibus, quos vel pœnituerit nimiæ exaltationis, vel qui, quod verisimile sit, bonum publicum privato proposuerint, duobus mediis, 1 Ignobilium & indignorum promotione. 2. Indigna tractatione adhibitis, tribuit, ut jam p.64. recensuerat, quomodo furono miseramente afflitti e tormentati tutti quei Cardinali, che non vollero consentire alle barbare voglie de' Bastardi d'Alesandro, quali tiranneggiavano il mondo, credendo col timore, e con la violenza di poter rendere rendere il Papato hereditario alla casa Borgia &c. Id est: Quàm miserè afflicti & vexati fuerint omnes illi Cardinales, qui noluerunt consentire barbaris Alexandri VI. filiorum nothorum consiliis, qui tyrannicè mundum rexerint, putantes, se timore & vi effecturos, ut Papatus hereditarius fieret domûs Borgiæ &c. Similia exempla Pauli IV. che lasciò piene d'innocenti Prælati e Cardinali le Prigioni di Roma, qui Romæ carceres innocuis Prælatis & Cardinalibus plenos reliquerit, & Urbani VIII. qui quosdam Cardinales Catholicæ religionis zelo eminentes, & damno, quod Ecclesia ex longo illius Papæ Pontificatu accipere potuit, & revera acceperit, depositione ejus mederi volentes non tantùm verbis; Dove è il nuovo Papa, perche le voglio adorare, Id est; Ubi est novus Papa, ut eum adorem? terruerit, sed & punierit p.65. seqq. retulerat; Et certè Papæ quoque Joh. XII. Bonif. VIII. Urb. VI. Jul. II. Leo X. Pius IV. Nicol. III. Greg. XII. non minùs, incarcerando, oculos effodiendo, in mare præcipitando, fracto gutture suffocando, & aliis modis occidendo, ut apud Celeb. Freinsh. Diatr. V. p. 94. videri potest, absolutam suam potestatem adversantibus fratribus Cardinalibus demonstrârunt.
units.tr: XL. The author adds, p. 95, with many examples, that the nephews are destroyed so that the Cardinals may be saved, and yet, p. 96, the glory of good deeds is always given to the nephews, while the Cardinals are charged with wrongs done even without their knowledge, or sometimes against their will, p. 99, and so are excused. He proves this also by examples at p. 100 and following, and by the saying of Paul V to his nephew the Cardinal, p. 96: You, nephew, have set this business off on a bad footing; therefore, to save your reputation, it must be placed in the hands of the Cardinals. For if a remedy can be found, I will nevertheless have the honour go to you, who began it badly, and not to the Cardinals, who brought it to a good end. That is: Nephew, you have handled this business badly; therefore, to save your honour, it is necessary to commit it to the Cardinals. For if a remedy can be found, I will nonetheless have it credited to you, who began badly, and not to the Cardinals, who brought the business to a good end. The same author also, p. 140 and following, attributes to the Popes, who may repent of excessive elevation, or who, as is likely, have put private gain before the public good, a diminution of the Cardinalate's dignity by two means: (1) the promotion of unworthy and base men, and (2) indignities of treatment. As he had already recounted at p. 64, all those Cardinals who would not consent to the barbarous wishes of Alexander's bastards, who tyrannised the world, were miserably afflicted and tormented, since these men believed they could, by fear and violence, make the papacy hereditary in the house of Borgia, etc. That is: How miserably afflicted and harassed were all those Cardinals who refused to consent to the barbarous counsels of the illegitimate sons of Alexander VI, who ruled the world tyrannically, thinking that by fear and force they would bring it about that the papacy became hereditary in the house of Borgia, etc. Similar examples are given of Paul IV, who left the prisons of Rome full of innocent prelates and Cardinals, and of Urban VIII, who, wishing to cure by deposition a certain Cardinal eminent for his zeal for the Catholic religion and for the harm which the Church could receive, and really did receive, from that Pope's long pontificate, not only frightened but also punished him, p. 65 and following, as he had related. Where is the new Pope, that I may adore him? Certainly the Popes John XII, Boniface VIII, Urban VI, Julius II, Leo X, Pius IV, Nicholas III and Gregory XII likewise showed their absolute power against Cardinal brothers who opposed them, not less by imprisoning, gouging out eyes, hurling into the sea, strangling by breaking the throat, and killing by other means, as can be seen in the notable Freinsheim, Diatr. V, p. 94.

units.la: XLI. Ex quo indignæ tractationis & miseræ subjectionis capite idem Cardinalismi Author Reverendissimis Dominis Cardinalibus titulum Principum Ecclesiæ abjudicat, his, quæ p.76. l. c. occurrunt, verbis: Sono Prencipi quelli, che vengono benespesso trattati peggio di schiavi dal Nepotismo &c? Suntne principes illi, qui sapius pejus tractantur quàm mancipia Nepotismi? Principes illi, qui coguntur à mane ad vesperam servire non vicariis Christi, sed Nepotibus Paparum? Principes Sanctæ Ecclesiæ illi, qui nihil minùs sciunt, quàm ubi sit thesaurus Ecclesiæ? Principes Sanctæ Ecclesiæ illi, qui in sua præsentia sinunt spoliare Ecclesiam? Principes illi, qui sinunt destruere Principatum suum? Quibus respondent illa p.80. E certo, che i Cardinali al presente possedono tanta autorità sopra la chiesa, quanta ne tiene il Rè d'Inghilterra sopra la Francia, ed il Duca di Savoia sopra Cipri, che pure non lasciano di chiamarsi l'uno Rè di Cipri, e l'altro Rè di Francia &c. Certum est, Cardinales hodie tantum authoritatis exercere, quantum authoritatis exercet Rex Angliæ in Gallia, & Dux Savoiæ in Cypro, qui tamen ambo vocantur, hic quidem Rex Cypri, ille verò Galliæ. Ita etiam Cardinales vocantur Principes Ecclesiæ, cujus Papa principatum tenet, facta infecta disponendo pro lubitu, & beneficia conferendo ad placitum, & leges imponendo secundùm arbitrium proprium, dum Consisto-ria. ria, Congregationes & Collegia tantum illi praetextum suppeditant, qui & Cardinales aliquid contra voluntatem suam agere impedit, & acta, prout vult, rescindit, ut certo certius sit, eos simplicem & valde simplicem authoritatem habere; Sed & pag.248. ferè audet, dicens; Sono Rè di nome e--- di fatti, id est Cardinales sunt Reges nomine &--- reapse.
units.tr: XLI. From this head of unworthy treatment and wretched subjection, the same author of Cardinalism denies the title of Princes of the Church to the Most Reverend Lord Cardinals, in these words, which occur p. 76, l. c. Are those princes who are very often treated worse than slaves by Nepotism? Are they princes who are forced from morning until evening to serve, not the vicars of Christ, but the nephews of the Popes? Are those princes of the Holy Church who know least of where the treasure of the Church is? Are those princes of the Holy Church who allow the Church to be plundered in their presence? Are those princes who allow their own principate to be destroyed? To these the following words, p. 80, give answer: Certainly the Cardinals now hold as much authority over the Church as the King of England holds over France, and the Duke of Savoy over Cyprus, who yet do not cease to call themselves, the one King of Cyprus, the other King of France, etc. It is certain that the Cardinals today exercise only as much authority as the King of England exercises in France, and the Duke of Savoy in Cyprus, who nevertheless are both called, the one King of Cyprus, the other King of France. So too the Cardinals are called Princes of the Church, whose principate the Pope holds, doing and undoing matters at his pleasure, conferring benefices at his will, and imposing laws according to his own judgment, while the Consistories, Congregations and Colleges merely furnish him with a pretext; and he also prevents the Cardinals from doing anything against his will, and annuls their acts as he pleases, so that it is more than certain they have a bare and very bare authority. But also at p. 248 he almost ventures to say: They are Kings in name and not in deeds, that is, the Cardinals are Kings in name, but not in fact.

units.la: XLII. Causae verò subjectionis & damnorum inde exoriri solitorum ex tribus Cardinalium generibus, quae Authori Cardinalismi ab Academico Bononiense sic indicata fuerunt, & p.95. memorantur, petendae sunt; Nempe sunt partim Papabiles, partim pauperes, partim Principes; Papabiles ne in periculum adducant spem suam alienis suffragiis suffultam, simulárent, se non videre Turcas, si venirent ad spoliandum statum. Pauperes ita cogitationibus de acquirendis & conservandis Abbatiis & Episcopatibus distrahuntur, ut omnium aliorum oblivíscantur; Principes tantùm ideo purpuram accipiunt, quia id volunt commoda Politica familiarum suarum illustrium.
units.tr: XLII. The causes of the subjection, and of the harms that usually arise from it, are to be sought in the three kinds of Cardinals that the Bolognese academic pointed out and mentioned to the author of Cardinalismus. Some are papabiles, some are poor, and some are princes. The papabiles pretend not to see the Turks, should they come to plunder the state, lest they endanger their hope, which rests on the votes of others. The poor are so distracted by thoughts of acquiring and keeping abbeys and bishoprics that they forget everything else. The princes take the purple only because they want the political advantages of their illustrious families.

units.la: XLIII. Interim tamen & his non obstantibus manet, quod ab initio posui, etiam respectu Papae multùm honoratos apparere Cardinales, & non uno mactari honore; Quemadmodum etiam olim ipsimet, quid sibi deberi credant, ita ad Eugenium, cùm Episcopi Gallicani aliquid in rebus fidei definivissent, referente Ottone Frisingensi de gest. Frid. l 1. c.57. loquentes declarárunt: Scire debes, quòd à nobis, per quos tanquam per Cardines universalis Ecclesia volvitur axis, ad regimen totius Ecclesia promotus, è privato universalis pater effectus, jam deinceps non tuus, sed noster potiùs esse debes: Nec privatas, nec modernas amicitias, antiquis & communibus praeponere, sed omnium utilitati consulere; Romanaque Curia culmen ex officii tui necessitudine curare & observare. Sed quid fecit Abbas tuus, & cum eo Gallicana Ecclesia? Si in Oriente, utpote Alexandria, vel Antiochia coram omnibus Patriarchis hujusmodi tractaretur negotium, nihil firmâ stabilitate solidum, sine nostra definiri valeret authoritate &c. Quomodo ergo isti in nostra praesentia usurpare audent &c. Volumus igitur huic tam temeraria novitati celeriter assurgas, ipsorúmque contumaciam punire non differas.
units.tr: XLIII. Meanwhile, however, and despite these points, what I laid down at the beginning still holds: the Cardinals appear very highly honoured even in relation to the Pope, and are given no small honour. Just as they once believed what was owed to themselves, so when the Gallican bishops had decided something in matters of faith, they declared to Eugenius, as Otto of Freising reports (Gesta Friderici, bk. 1, ch. 57): "You ought to know that you were raised from a private man to the rule of the whole Church, through us, by whom, as by hinges, the axis of the universal Church turns, and that you have become the universal father. From now on you ought to be not yours but ours. Do not put private or recent friendships before ancient and common ones, but look to the good of all. Take care and observe that the Roman Curia is the summit of your office and its duty. But what has your abbot done, and with him the Gallican Church? If such a matter were treated in the East, for example at Alexandria or Antioch, before all the patriarchs, nothing could be firmly settled without our authority... How then do these men dare to presume in our presence?... We therefore wish you to rise quickly against this so rash novelty, and not to delay in punishing their obstinacy."

units.la: XLIV. Convenit cum hoc, quòd plerumque Papae conjunguntur, & unâ cum eo tanquam in actionibus socii nominantur; Saepe Pontifex de fratrum suorum consensu aliquid facere dicitur; Ipsi pars corporis Papae, & membra nobiliora, membra Papae vocantur, Papae invisceràti dicuntur; Ipsis & Papae nonnunquam quadam Identitas tribuitur; (Ex qua causa ego puto, inquit Diana Resol. p.5. tr.2. resol.2. p.41. quod est valde notandum, Cardinales agritudine laborantes non posse sanguinis missionem pati, sine licentia Papae, ubi posset commodè haberi, ut ex Hostiensi docet Perez in Pentateucho fidei tr.2. dub. 3. c. 8. n. 81. & Villadiego de Card. quaest. V. n. 13.) Ipsis quoque collateralium coadjutorum nomen datur, quorum collegio adjuvante Papa agit, ut simul cum Papa Universalem Ecclesiam administrent, bene gesta Papae & universo Cardinalium coetui acceptissima sunt, excommunicatio non magis Papae quàm Romano sacerdotum senatui tribuitur; Mores suos ab Urbano VI. reprehendi tam aegrè tulerunt, ut fuerint increpationes istae intempestivae fomentum schismatis sequentis Theod. à Niem. l.5. Jacob Meyer in Chron. Flandr. ad a.1378. Apud Cardinalem Zarabellam de Schismate Innoc.VII. & Bened. Inter alia magnificè pro Cardinalibus decreta & haec sunt, quòd Papa dicatur omnia posse, intelligi, quando faciat consilio habito cum fratribus, sine Cardinalibus autem non posse concedere (condere) legem generalem de universali statu Ecclesiae; Papa, eorum violatores gravissimè puniendos esse VII. Decretal. l.42. decrevit, & laesae Majestatis reos fieri Ibid. c. seq. Item cap. Felicis de poenis in VI. Loth. de re benefic. q.8. n.44. &c. pronunciavit. Contrà Cardinales septem in appellatione Pisis interposita ad Greg. XII. apud Bzov. Annal. Eccles. 1408. mandati; ne ulterius congregentur in aliquo loco, sine expresso Papae mandato, nullitatem & inaequitatem & injustitiam objiciunt, illud tanquam iniquum & abominabile rejiciunt, ad juramentum pertinere negant. Apud eundem n. 12. Se non tantum posse, sed etiam debere in certis casibus & citra conditionem eligendi Pontificis Concilium convocare, asserunt; Quod jus & exercuerunt; Imò ex Petri Damiani apud Bar. ad an. 1061. n. 11. sententia praeter communem Ecclesiae regulam, super ipsos quoque Pontifices authenticam praevalent servare censuram; Monendi Papam jus ex Concil. Basil. sess.23. ipsis competit.
units.tr: XLIV. This agrees with the fact that the Popes are often joined with the Cardinals, and named together with them as partners in their acts. The Pope is often said to do something with the consent of his brothers. The Cardinals are called part of the body of the Pope, his nobler limbs, the members of the Pope, and are said to be bowels of the Pope. Sometimes a certain identity is attributed to them along with the Pope. (For this reason, says Diana, it is very much to be noted, that Cardinals suffering from illness cannot undergo bloodletting without the Pope's permission, where it could conveniently be had, as Perez teaches from Hostiensis in his Pentateuch of Faith, and Villadiego on Cardinals.) They are also given the name of collateral coadjutors, by whose assisting college the Pope acts, so that together with the Pope they govern the universal Church. The good deeds of the Pope are most welcome to the whole assembly of Cardinals, and excommunication is attributed no more to the Pope than to the Roman senate of priests. They took so badly the rebuke of their conduct by Urban VI that those untimely reproaches became a fuel for the schism that followed (Theodoric of Niem, bk. 5; Jacob Meyer, Chronicle of Flanders, year 1378). In the work of Cardinal Zabarella On the Schism of Innocent VII and Benedict, among other things decreed magnificently in favour of the Cardinals, are these: that the Pope is said to be able to do all things, to be understood when he acts with the advice of his brothers, but without the Cardinals he cannot grant (enact) a general law concerning the universal state of the Church; and that violators of this are to be punished most severely (Seventh Decretal, bk. 42). Also he declared that they become guilty of treason (ibid., next chapter). Likewise he pronounced in the chapter Felix, on penalties in the Sixth Book, and in Loth On Benefices, question 8, no. 44, and so on. On the other side, seven Cardinals, in an appeal lodged at Pisa to Gregory XII (Baronius, Annals of the Church, 1408), were ordered not to gather in any place without an express mandate of the Pope. They object to this as null, inequitable and unjust; they reject it as iniquitous and abominable, and deny that it pertains to their oath. In the same place (no. 12) they assert that they can, and must, in certain cases and without any condition of electing a Pope, convene a council, a right which they have also exercised. Indeed, according to the opinion of Peter Damian (in Baronius, year 1061, no. 11), beyond the common rule of the Church, they are bound to observe a censure that prevails even over the Popes themselves. The right to admonish the Pope belongs to them by the Council of Basel (session 23).

units.la: XLV. Ex iis, quae Zarabella l.c. statuerat, sequeretur, quòd Cardinales possent Papam deponere sine Concilio; Ubi etiam subjungit; Cardinalium Collegium repraesentare universalem Ecclesiam. A quibusdam defenditur; Cardinalem legitimum non esse, qui consensu expresso, aut saltem tacito aliorum Cardinalium non sit creatus. Vide Torcellanum apud de Dominis de Rep. Eccles. l.4.c.5. n.46. seqq. ubi etiam ostendit, idem voluisse Concilia Basileense & Constantiense; sicut è diverso, Cardinalem à Papa sine Cardinalium consilio deponi non non posse, nonnulli contendunt; Quamvis hodie revera Papæ tam facile Cardinalem aliquem instituant, destituant, quàm pyrum vulpes comest; Hinc etiam Gregorius XII. cùm ei hac in re leges ponerentur, responderit; ad se ratione Pontificatus pertinere, quos & quot vellet, Cardinales creare; Niem de schism. 3.14.3.31. Et Doctorum Juris sententia sit, Benicas. de constit. Primc. qu. 7. n. 69. per Jo. And. & doct. in ca. solum Papam etiam Cardinalibus invitis Cardinalem creare posse.
units.tr: XLV. From what Zabarella stated in the passage cited, it would follow that the Cardinals could depose the Pope without a council. He adds there: the college of Cardinals represents the universal Church. Some defend the view that a man is not a lawful Cardinal who has been created without the express, or at least tacit, consent of the other Cardinals. See Torquemada, cited by de Dominis, On the Republic of the Church, bk. 4, ch. 5, no. 46 ff., where he also shows that the Councils of Basel and Constance wanted the same thing. On the other hand, some contend that a Cardinal cannot be deposed by the Pope without the counsel of the Cardinals. Yet today the Popes in fact appoint and dismiss Cardinals as easily as a fox eats a pear. Hence also Gregory XII, when laws were laid down for him in this matter, replied that it pertained to him by the reason of the Pontificate to create as Cardinals whom and how many he wished (Niem, On the Schism, 3.14, 3.31). And the opinion of the teachers of law is that the Pope may create a Cardinal even against the wishes of the Cardinals, as Benincasa (On the Constitution of the Primate, question 7, no. 69) states, citing John Andreae and the doctors on the chapter Solum.

units.la: XLVI. Quoad depositionem autem valeat illud Medeæ:
units.tr: XLVI. As for deposition, the saying of Medea holds true:

units.la: Servare potui, perdere an possim rogas?
units.tr: "I could save you; do you ask whether I can destroy you?"

units.la: Cùm non tantùm supra majores contumelias à Papis Cardinalibus illatas viderimus, sed & nonnunquam apud Bzov. ad an. 1404. p. 293. & Theod. Niem. 3. 32. sub pœna privationis Cardinalatus imperent, & apud Torcellanum de potest. Papæ n. 22. Certum sit, quòd Papa solus posset & possit deponere Cardinalem, etiamsi ab Ecclesia jus eligendi Papam haberet; Quemadmodum etiam à Greg. VII. Clem. VII. Jul. II. &c. depositi leguntur, & causam solùm (quam prætextum verius dixeris, & quam fingi posse, dicunt, etiam sine delicto, ad evitandum scandalum;) non autem aliorum Cardin. consilium requirat in abjiciendo Cardinale Pontifex, ne major observatio in depositione, quàm in creatione requirenda videatur.
units.tr: Since we have seen Popes impose insults far beyond the usual, and sometimes, as in Bzovius ad an. 1404, p. 293 and Theodoric of Niem 3.32, order them under penalty of deprivation of the cardinalate; and since Torcellanus de potest. Papae n. 22 states: "It is certain that the Pope alone could and can depose a cardinal, even if the Church had the right to elect the Pope"; just as Gregory VII, Clement VII, Julius II, and others are read to have deposed cardinals. They allege only a cause (which one would more truly call a pretext, and which they say can be feigned), even without fault, to avoid scandal. Yet the Pope does not require the counsel of the other cardinals in casting off a cardinal, lest greater observance seem to be required in deposition than in creation.

units.la: XLVII. Et quod longè maximum, apud Theodor. à Niem de Schism. 1. 42. defendunt Cardinales multi, Theologi item & egregii quidam ICti, quòd si Papa esset negligens & inutilis ad regendum &c. licere idoneum Curatorem, vel aliquos idoneos Curatores per Cardinalium electionem substituere. Accedit, quòd inter Cardinales præcipuè Cancellarius, teste Cassan. Catal. p. 4. consid. 13. pr. olim de pari contendere voluit cum Papa ex gloria propter excellentiam tanta dignitatis. Quæ unâ cum aliis prolixè habet Clar. Freinsh. Diatr. 4. Addo ex Authore de l'origine des Cardinaux Chap. 8. non juramento Obedientia & fidelitatis Papa obstringi, sed simpliciter jurare, se Papam honoraturos & augmentum authoritatis ipsius & Ecclesiæ pro virili quæsituros esse. Addo etiam constitutionum & regularum Cancellariæ Romanæ ab Alex. VII. editarum titulum illum: quòd Cardinales non comprehendantur sub Regulis faciendis. 70. Item, cùm S. R. E. Cardinales sanctissimo D. N. assistant, ac propterea debeant specialibus prærogativis & privilegiis gaudere; Idem D. N. statuit, ordinavit, decrevit & declaravit, quòd in quibuscunque constitutionibus, & Regulis per Sanctitatem ítitatem suam editis, & edendis non comprehendantur, neque comprehen-si censeantur ipsi Cardinales, nisi illa eorundem Cardinalium favorem concernant, vel constitutiones edenda de eorundem Cardinalium, vel majo-ris partis eorum consilio edita fuerint, seu in eisdem Regulis & Constitu-tionibus facta fuerit ipsorum Cardinalium expressa mentio.
units.tr: XLVII. And, by far the greatest point: in Theodoric of Niem, de Schismate 1.42, many cardinals defend it, as do certain theologians and eminent jurists, that if the Pope were negligent and unfit to govern etc., it is lawful for the cardinals, by election, to substitute a suitable curator or suitable curators. Add that among the cardinals, the chancellor especially, as Cassanus testifies (Catal. p. 4, consid. 13 pr.), once wished to contend on equal terms with the Pope from glory, on account of the excellence of so great a dignity. Clarus Freinshemius Diatr. 4 gives this and much more at length. I add, from the author de l'origine des Cardinaux, chap. 8, that the Pope is bound not by an oath of obedience and fidelity, but simply swears that they will honour the Pope and seek the increase of his authority and that of the Church as far as they can. I add also the title of the rules and constitutions of the Roman Chancery issued by Alexander VII: "that cardinals are not included under the rules to be made. 70. Likewise, since the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church assist our most holy Lord, and therefore ought to enjoy special prerogatives and privileges, the same Lord has ordained, decreed, and declared that they are not included in, nor are considered included in, any constitutions and rules issued or to be issued by His Holiness, unless those concern the favour of the cardinals themselves, or unless the constitutions have been issued with the counsel of the cardinals or of the greater part of them, or unless express mention of the cardinals themselves has been made in those rules and constitutions."

units.la: XLVIII. Quoad ceremonialia vero, Cardinales in Consi-storio & conspectu Papæ tractantes negotium, stant in Cappa purpurea, nudato capite, sine chirothecis, in privata vero audientia sedent clausis scabellis con l'appoggio, tecto capite, super pulvinaribus duobus ex rubro panno. Quantum nulli licet, quamvis Regum Legatis, qui sedent sellis sen-za appogio, nudo capite; alii Legati stant, reliqui geniculabundi conspi-ciuntur; referente Joh. Theod. Sprengero Instit. Juris Publ. l.2.c.35. Papæ pedem tantum in prima audientia exosculari tenentur, & quando per sex menses, aut amplius ab urbe absuerunt, tanquam Legati proficiscuntur, aut reduces facti sunt. Cæterum, ut vidi-mus, in Ceremoniis quasi ut fratres tractantur. Nempe satis honorantur à Papis nisi pupillam oculi, certum aliquod tangere noli, tangant, donec obsequuntur, usque ad aras à Papis pro lubitu po-sitas, ponendas. De Reverentiis, quas Pontifici Romano, qui nemi-ni omninò mortalium assurgendo manifestè, aut caput inclinando seu de-regendo, reverentiam facit Sacr. Cerim. l.3. §1.c.2. & quando non est in Pontificalibus, reverentiam facientibus aliquantulum caput inclinat, tan-quam reverentiam reddens, hoc non ex officio, sed ex laudabili humani-tate facit; exhibent, vide c.3.4.5. Et de illis, quas sibi invicem fa-ciunt, c.6. & de illis, quas ab aliis accipiunt c.9.10.12. ab Episcopis. c.13. Et de illis, quibus Pontifici ministranti assistunt §. 2. c.5. seqq. Et de circulo, quem faciunt ante Papam. §.3. c.9. Et de sermone, quem habent in capella Pontificis c.2. §.4. ubi tamen que-ritur, quòd cùm secundùm antiquas & probatas cerimonias Diaconus Car-dinalis, aut alius quispiam non Prælatus non ibi prædicet, nisi sit Doctor Theologia, hodie non modò inferioris gradùs viri, sed sine dignitate, aut sacro ordine in studiis humanitatis tantùm docti non sine loci & ordinis Pontificalis dedecore onus orandi in totius orbis gravissimo, ac celeberrimo consessu sibi assumant.
units.tr: XLVIII. As for ceremonial matters: cardinals, when they treat business in consistory and in the presence of the Pope, stand in a purple cape, with bare head and without gloves; but in private audience they sit, with closed footstools con l'appoggio, covered head, on two cushions of red cloth. No one is permitted this, not even the legates of kings, who sit on chairs without backs, with bare head; other legates stand, the rest are seen kneeling, as Johann Theodor Sprenger reports in Instit. Juris Publ. 2.35. They are bound only to kiss the Pope's foot at the first audience, and when they have been away from the city for six months or more, they set out as legates, or are made to return. Moreover, as we have seen, in ceremonies they are treated almost as brothers. Indeed they are sufficiently honoured by the Popes, unless one should touch the pupil of the eye: let them touch some point (certain), until they comply, even up to the altars placed by the Popes at will. Concerning the reverences which they pay to the Roman Pontiff, who makes reverence to no mortal whatsoever by plainly rising or inclining or lowering the head (Sacr. Cerim. 3.1.2), and when not in pontifical dress, inclines his head slightly to those making reverence, as one returning reverence, which he does not from duty but from laudable courtesy: see chapters 3, 4, 5. Concerning those which they make to one another, chapter 6; and those which they receive from others, chapters 9, 10, 12, from bishops, chapter 13. Concerning those with which they assist the Pontiff while he ministers, §2, chapter 5 ff. Concerning the circle which they form before the Pope, §3, chapter 9. And concerning the sermon which they give in the Pontiff's chapel, chapter 2, §4, where, however, it is complained that whereas, according to ancient and approved ceremonies, a cardinal deacon, or any other non-prelate, may not preach there unless he is a Doctor of Theology, today men not only of lower rank, but without dignity or sacred order, who are learned only in the humanities, presume to take upon themselves the burden of speaking, in the most solemn and celebrated assembly of the whole world, not without dishonour to the place and to the Pontifical order.

units.la: XLIX. Sed & extra comparationem cum Episcopis, Regibus & Principibus hodiernis, & relationem ad Papam magni apparent Cardinales, & ad altissimum potestatis ac honoris fastigium evecti. Tales apparent in comparatione cum antiquis Romanorum parent;
units.tr: XLIX. But even apart from comparison with present-day bishops, kings and princes, and apart from their relation to the Pope, the cardinals appear great, raised to the highest summit of power and honour. Such they appear in comparison with the ancient Roman magistrates.

units.la: Quomodo in ceremonialibus à Papa tractentur;
units.tr: How they are treated by the Pope in ceremonial matters.

units.la: Extra comparationem talem etiam magni apparent; manorum Magistratibus. Vix enim est in tota Romana dignitate ullus post Imperatorem apex,cui non æquiparentur,dum modò Proconsulum, modò Curatorum sive capitum Regionum urbis Romæ, modò Prætorii Præfectorum, modò Patriciorum & Consulum,modò Senatorum urbis vicem implere dicuntur. Tales apparent etiam extra omnem comparationem, Principes Romanæ Ecclesiæ,saltem titulotenus, eadem ratione, qua, juxta Alphonsum, Arragoniæ Regem, Regum consiliarii Reges erant. Nec sunt, si credere fas est,Principes hi ullis limitibus inclusi: Les flatteurs de ces nouveaux Princes, ait Author tractatûs del origine des Cardinaux du S. Siege c.3. p.33. in margine Auct. Anonym. Sac. Carem. Sive Rit. Ecclesiast. S. Rom. Eccl. l.3. de Reverent. Epis. erga Cardinales, ont fait monter leur presomtion si haut, qu'un Autheur de nôtre temps a osé écrire, qu'un Prelat étant honoré du Cardinalat, est fait Prince d'un Estat,qui n'est borné ny par les mers,ny par les montagnes,& que l'estendüe de sa jurisdiction est telle,que s'il y avoit plusieurs mondes, ils en dependroient aussi bien que celuy cy, & en un autre endroit, que le Cardinal fait partie d' un corps auquel Dieu à donné l'infallibilité &c. Id est: Adulatores novorum istorum Principum ad tam altum præsumptionis gradum ascenderunt,ut quidam Author nostri temporis scribere ausus sit, Prælatum Cardinalatu ornatum factum esse Principem Statûs, qui nec mari, nec montibus terminetur, & tantam esse extensionem jurisdictionis ejus,ut si etiam plures mundi essent, ei subjecti essent æquè ac hic; Et in alio loco. Cardinalem esse partem corporis infallibilis &c:
units.tr: Beyond such a comparison, they also appear great, even to the magistrates. For in the whole Roman hierarchy there is scarcely any rank below the Emperor to which they are not made equal, since they are said at one time to fill the place of the proconsuls, at another of the curators or heads of the districts of the city of Rome, at another of the praetorian prefects, at another of the patricians and consuls, and at another of the senators of the city. The Princes of the Roman Church also appear in this way, beyond all comparison, at least in title, for the same reason that, according to Alfonso, King of Aragon, the counsellors of kings were kings. Nor, if it is right to believe it, are these princes confined within any limits. The flatterers of these new princes, says the author of the treatise On the origin of the Cardinals of the Holy See, ch. 3, p. 33, in the margin: Anonymous author, Sacred Ceremonies, or Ecclesiastical Rites of the Holy Roman Church, bk. 3, on the reverence shown by bishops to cardinals, have raised their presumption so high that an author of our time has dared to write that a prelate honoured with the cardinalate is made a Prince of a State, which is bounded neither by seas nor by mountains, and that the extent of his jurisdiction is such that, if there were several worlds, they would be subject to him just as much as this one; and in another place, that the cardinal is part of a body to which God has given infallibility, etc. That is: The flatterers of these new princes have climbed to such a high degree of presumption that some author of our time has dared to write that a prelate adorned with the cardinalate has been made a prince of a state, which is bounded neither by sea nor by mountains, and that the extent of his jurisdiction is so great that, even if there were several worlds, they would be subject to him as much as this one; and in another place, that a cardinal is part of an infallible body, etc.

units.la: L. Quæ non plùs dicunt,quàm verba Papæ creatos ita alloquentis: Estote fratres nostri & principes mundi; Et speciatim Pii II. primos Cardinales à se creatos sic in eodem sacr. carem. sive Rit. Ecclesiast.S. Rom.Eccl. opere l.1. §.8.c.3. compellantis;Maximâ,dilectissimi filii, & excellentissimâ dignitate donati estis: ad Collegium Apostolicum vocati, consiliarii nostri, & conjudices orbis terrarum eritis: inter sanguinem & sanguinem, inter lepram & lepram discernere vos oportebit. Successores Apostolorum circa thronum sedebitis. Vos Senatores Urbis & Regum similes eritis, veri mundi Cardines, super quos militantis ostium Ecclesia volvendum & regendum est.Sunt Romanæ sedis assentatoribus aliis, veluti Isidoro Moscon. de Majestate milit. Eccl. l.1.p.1.c.5. Vicem gerentes Apostolorum, orbis Cardines; Ecclesiæ capita, columna, Lumina, lucerna ardentes, candelabra lucis,decoris, præstantiæ atque splendoris; Stellæ fixæ in cælo; Patres conscripti in Diademate Principis, Viri VeneraVenerabiles, Reverendissimi, Religiosissimi, splendidissimi, Illustres, superillustres, Illustrissimi, item Maximi, Potentissimi, Seniores Populi, Senatores & Patricii Maximi, Principes, Reges denique; Et quid non?
units.tr: L. These words say no more than the words of the Pope addressing those he has created in this way: "Be our brothers and princes of the world"; and especially Pius II, addressing the first cardinals created by him, in the same work Sacr. Caerim. sive Rit. Eccles. S. Rom. Eccl. 1, §8, chap. 3: "You have been endowed with the greatest and most excellent dignity, beloved sons: called to the Apostolic College, you will be our counsellors and co-judges of the world; you will have to discern between blood and blood, between leprosy and leprosy. You will sit about the throne as successors of the Apostles. You will be Senators of the City and like Kings, the true hinges of the world, upon which the door of the Church militant is to be turned and ruled." There are other flatterers of the Roman See, such as Isidoro Moscon, de Majestate militantis Ecclesiae 1.1.5: "Bearing the place of the Apostles, the hinges of the world; heads of the Church, pillars, lights, burning lamps, candlesticks of light, beauty, excellence and splendour; fixed stars in the heavens; conscript fathers in the diadem of the Prince; venerable men, most reverend, most religious, most splendid, illustrious, most illustrious, most excellent; also greatest, most powerful, elders of the people, senators and greatest patricians, princes, and finally kings"; and what not?

units.la: LI. Maximè Eminentissimi ; Cujus tituli hodie Cardinalibus proprii conceptionem & ortum fusè describit Il Cardinal. p. 1. l.3. 366. seqq. ita ut dicat, primò nimis altum ab ipsis judicatum fuisse illum Fratrum in Domino observantissimorum, hodie à minimis Clericis contemtum, & adoptato ab his Reverendorum titulo, ordinario suo Reverendissimos vocari voluisse, & per 8. secula vocatos esse, post, cùm & ita alii vocari coepissent, Illustrissimos, quo tempore statim alii Clerici, & avidè titulum Reverendissimorum arripuerint, hodie Canonicis ipsis spretum, & à vilissimis Sacerdotibus usurpari solitum ; Cardinales autem satiatos titulo Illustrissimorum visos esse, & revera per 2. secula & amplius fuisse, donec Urbanus VIII. non satiatus, saltem ob Nepotes suos, post varias deliberationes, etiam, ut dicant, aliquot saepe horarum nocturnas, rejecto titulo Altitudinis, de quo ob usum aliquem Principum desperaverit, illum Eminentia & Eminentissimorum felici partu exclusserit, Cardinalibus si non obstetricantibus, saltem aliàs magno cum applausu & multa cum gratiarum actione saetum à Deo datum excipientibus, qui & per non essergli ingrati lo lasciarono far & dissere à suo modo il tesoro della Chiesa, di che se ne risente sino al giorno di hoggi, ad evitandum turpe ingratitudinis crimen, cùm thesauros Ecclesiæ pro lubitu tractare siverint, ita ut id hodienum sentiatur ; Dedisse autem illam tituli mutationem occasionem Principibus secularibus, spreto illo Excellentiæ, novum, quoad multos, Altitudinis assumendi, quod quidem malè habuerit Cardinales, ita se superari putantes, qui etiam conati sint, à procurarne l'impedimento, con la violenza delle parole, titulum illum verborum vi suffocare ; Quare etiam Urbanus, quasi Principatus, tituli & honores à se solo penderent, declarârit, se Principibus non alium praeter antiquum Excellentiæ titulum daturum; Sed illos, se pariter Cardinalibus Eminentiæ titulum in eo casu denegaturos esse, respondisse, & quasdam litteras sine Altitudinis titulo missas remisisse. Primum autem Conclave, in quo Eminentissimi vocantur, est illud Innocentii X. cùm in praecedentibus Illustrissimorum tantùm nomine veniant.
units.tr: LI. Above all, Eminentissimi. Its origin and the history of the title now proper to Cardinals are described at length by Il Cardinal. p. 1. l.3. 366. seqq.. That author says that first the title Fratres in Domino observantissimi (most observant brothers in the Lord), now scorned by the lowest clergy, was judged too lofty by the Cardinals themselves; that, having adopted the title Reverendi, they wished to be called Reverendissimi in the ordinary way, and were so called for eight centuries; that afterwards, when others too had begun to be called so, they were called Illustrissimi. At that time other clergy eagerly seized the title Reverendissimi, which is now despised by the Canons themselves and usually used by the most worthless priests. The Cardinals, however, seemed to have had their fill of the title Illustrissimi, and indeed they had it for more than two centuries, until Urban VIII, not satisfied, at least on account of his nephews, after various deliberations, some of which, they say, lasted many hours through the night, rejected the title Altitudinis (Loftiness), since he despaired of its use by some princes, and with a happy birth brought forth Eminentia and Eminentissimi. The Cardinals, if they did not assist at the birth, at least received it with great applause and much thanksgiving, as a gift from God, and so as not to be ungrateful, let them do and say with the Church's treasure as they pleased, of which it still feels the effect to this day, to avoid the shameful crime of ingratitude, since they allowed the treasures of the Church to be handled at will, so that it is still felt today. That change of title gave secular princes the occasion, having rejected the title Excellentiæ, to assume the new title Altitudinis (for many). The Cardinals were indeed annoyed by this, thinking themselves outdone, and tried to prevent it, with the violence of words, to suppress that title by force of words. For this reason Urban also declared, as if principalities, titles and honours depended on him alone, that he would give princes no other title than the old one of Excellency. But the princes replied that in that case he would likewise deny the title of Eminence to the Cardinals, and sent back some letters that had been sent without the title of Altitude. The first Conclave in which they are called Eminentissimi is that of Innocent X, since in earlier ones they were named only as Illustrissimi.

units.la: LII. Privilegia majora ex dictis maximam partem cognoscuntur; Hoc tamen addo, habere Cardinales ex concessione Pauli II. hi II. semissem omnium reddituum, ut & semissem Annatarum de beneficiis, quæ à Consistorio (ita vocatur conjunctim, item sacrum Collegium) conferuntur ; Minora sunt, quòd privatum carcerem habent, prærogativam aliquam testamentariam, Auditores, & alia, de quibus alii pluribus agunt. Sede vacante, illorum Collegium non habet superiorem Bzov. ad an.1408. n. 15. nonnunquam Vicarium S. R. E. qualis ibi commemoratur Balthasar Cossa ; suum & aliàs habent Camerarium, vulgò Camerlingo, à Camerariatu Pontificis distinctum, de quo II Cardinal. p.1.l.3.380. seqq. suum quoque Secretarium, qui Sede vacante expediat literas subscriptas à tribus Cardinalium primis Diaconis, quique Consistoriis privatis & congregationibus intersit, vestitus toga ex panno rubro confecta cum ejusdem coloris capuccio, uti vocant. Habent & suos Clericos Nationales, Secretarios nimirum destinatos ex præcipuis Europæ nationibus: variantibus officiis, alternando per annum. Habent non minùs suum Computistam, qui rationem habet reddituum Sacri Collegii, & ratiocinia sua illius Camerario exhibet. Et ex ipsis constituuntur præcipui Papæ Ministri, præter dictum Vicarium Papæ, Vice-Cancellarius, summus Pœnitentiarius, Papæ Camerarius, Præfectus signaturæ, gratiæ, Præfectus Brevium, Bibliothecarius &c. De quibus omnibus fusè agit II. Card. p.1.l.3.335. seqq. Fiunt etiam Protectores ordinum Religiosorum (de Protectoribus Regnorum jam dixi;) De qua protectione, & quomodo ad detegenda Monasteriorum scandala, & per consequens ad Monachorum contemptum faciat, & Monasteria bonis spoliet, adeóque valde noxia sit, videri potest idem Author Cardinalismi, p.2.l.1.p.15. 23. Addi potest, quòd juxta Castr. in L. addictos in pr. c. de appell. citante Nordermanno tract. de Jure Princip. §. 6. facinorosus à morte liberatur, si modò Cardinalis ei pileum imponat, imò si modò, ut alii referunt, togam Cardinalis attingat.
units.tr: LII. The greater privileges are for the most part known from what has been said. I add this, however: by a grant of Paul II the Cardinals have half of all revenues, and also half of the annates from benefices conferred by the Consistory (so the sacred College is called collectively). The lesser privileges are that they have a private prison, some testamentary prerogative, auditors, and other things, which other writers treat at greater length. When the see is vacant, their College has no superior (Bzov. ad an. 1408. n. 15.), though sometimes a Vicar of the Holy Roman Church, such as Balthasar Cossa is recorded there to have been. They also have their own Chamberlain, commonly called Camerlingo, distinct from the Pope's chamberlainship (on which see II Cardinal. p.1.l.3.380. seqq.). They have also their own Secretary, who during the vacancy dispatches letters signed by the three first deacons of the Cardinals, and who attends the private consistories and congregations, dressed in a toga of red cloth with a hood of the same colour, as they call it. They also have their own national clerks, secretaries chosen from the chief nations of Europe, whose offices rotate, changing each year. No less do they have their own accountant (Computistam), who keeps the account of the revenues of the sacred College and presents his reckonings to its Chamberlain. From among the Cardinals are chosen the chief ministers of the Pope, besides the said Vicar of the Pope: the Vice-Chancellor, the chief Penitentiary, the Pope's Chamberlain, the Prefect of the Signature and of Grace, the Prefect of Briefs, the Librarian, and so on. All of these are treated at length in II. Card. p.1.l.3.335. seqq.. They also become protectors of religious orders (I have already spoken of protectors of kingdoms). Concerning this protection, and how it serves to uncover the scandals of monasteries, and consequently to bring monks into contempt, and how it despoils monasteries of their goods, and is therefore very harmful, the same author of Cardinalismi, p.2.l.1.p.15. 23. may be consulted. It may be added that, according to Castr. in L. addictos in pr. c. de appell., citing Nordermann, tract. de Jure Princip. §. 6, a criminal is freed from death if a Cardinal merely places a cap on him, or indeed, as others report, if he merely touches the Cardinal's toga.

units.la: LIII. Tunc autem maximè potestate abundant & authoritate pollent, quando Papæ sunt Legati, uti appellant, à Latere, & ad Imperatores, vel Reges mittuntur; Hæc enim est, ex Clar. Sprengeri Inst. Pub. c.35. sententia, quoad nomen inter Legatos Cardinales & non-Cardinales differentia, ut hi simpliciter Nuncii Apostolici, illi Legati à Latere vocentur. De quibus Legatis etiam aliquo modo agit tractatus de l'origine des Cardinaux, in quo c. 3. les arbitres de la chrétienté, arbitri Christianismi insigniuntur c.4. verò CataCatalogus usque ad Philippi pulchri tempora in Galliam missorum texitur; & statim quoad primum observatur, eum catenis aureis ad infringenda jura Ecclesiastica attractum esse; ac valde commode, eâ occasione; aurum, quod Menander dixerit, feras quascunque aperire, imò inferorum etiam portas, juxta illud, quòd Æneas & Virgilius cum virga aurea ad inferos descendisse legantur, nec etiam fundamento carere, qu'on remarque, que les lettres dont le mot ROMA est composé portent enigmatiquement ce proverbe: Radix omnium malorum avaritia; Quòd notatur, literas, quibus vox ROMA constat, anigmaticè illud proverbium continere: Radix Omnium Malorum Avaritia. Qui Author certè non minùs dicere videtur, quàm Lutherus, qui Cardinales illos ep.60, avaritiæ Legatos vocavit.
units.tr: LIII. They abound most in power and are strongest in authority when they are Legates, as they call them, à Latere (from the side of the Pope), and are sent to emperors or kings. For this, according to the view of the distinguished Sprenger, Inst. Pub. c.35., is the difference in name between Cardinal and non-Cardinal Legates: the latter are simply called Apostolic Nuncios, the former Legates à Latere. The treatise de l'origine des Cardinaux also deals with these Legates in some measure, in which, in chapter 3, les arbitres de la chrétienté, arbitri Christianismi (the arbiters of Christendom) are given their titles. In chapter 4 a catalogue is woven of those sent into France down to the time of Philip the Fair; and at once, concerning the first, it is observed that he was drawn into golden chains to break Ecclesiastical rights; and very conveniently, on this occasion, the gold which Menander said opens every wild beast, even the gates of hell, in accordance with what is read of Aeneas and Virgil descending to the underworld with a golden bough, nor is it without foundation that one notes that the letters of which the word ROMA is composed enigmatically carry this proverb: the root of all evils is avarice. It is noted that the letters of which the word ROMA consists enigmatically contain that proverb: Radix Omnium Malorum Avaritia (the root of all evils is avarice). This author certainly seems to say no less than Luther, who called those Cardinals Legates of avarice (ep.60, avaritiæ Legatos).

units.la: LIV. Sed prolixiùs de illis agunt, qui & maximè legi merentur, duo simul an.1670. editi tractatus de Legatis, Gallico quoque Idiomate exarati; Quorum prior primò quasdam observationes generales de Legatis continet, ubi Extraordinarii Papæ nuncii dicuntur, ad tempus cum potestate, ferè Pontificiam adæquante, mitti soliti; ad tempus, ob ipsam potestatis plenitudinem, & ne, si perpetui darentur, viderentur plura in Ecclesiam Capita introduci; Quare etiam Universitas Parisiensis Bullis prorogationis Cardinali d'Amboise datis se opposuerit, quas & Parlamentum diu firmare noluerit, ob clausulam, mansurum, donec Papa placuerit, quæ clausula nova & consequentiarum Ecclesiæ unitati periculosarum fertilis judicata fuerit. Ubi Author etiam optimè ostendit, cur potiùs Nuncii illi Legatorum nomine veniant, quàm verò des Ambassadeurs vocentur, ut ab aliis potestatibus missi; Cujus rei causam partim in singularitatis majorem authoritatem conciliantis affectatione ponit, partim illud ideò fieri affirmat, ut Legati illi eximi possint à Legibus, quæ respiciant les Ambassadeurs. Subjungit Author, vanè distinctionem Legatorum in eo poni, quòd Cardinales sint à Latere, non-Cardinales de Latere, totam potiùs differentiam ex Bullis & potestate concredita agnoscendam esse sine respectu ad Cardinalem, vel non-Cardinalem, à Latere, vel de Latere, cùm quicunque ab ultimis Imperatoribus Romanis, quorum hic etiam æmuli sunt Pontifices, Laterales & de Latere missi dicti sint. Omninò tamen admittendum est, Nuncios & Legatos illos saltem ex usu vocum distingui, & Cardinales tantùm Legatos fieri. Ibidem etiam
units.tr: LIV. But more fully treat of them, and deserve to be read most of all, two treatises on Legates published together in 1670, written also in the French language. The first of these, first, contains certain general observations about Legates, where they are called Extraordinary nuncios of the Pope, which are usually sent for a time with a power nearly equal to the papal one; for a time, because of the very fullness of their power, and lest, if they were given permanently, more heads would seem to be introduced into the Church. For this reason the University of Paris also opposed the bulls of prorogation given to Cardinal d'Amboise, which the Parlement long refused to confirm, on account of the clause that it would last as long as the Pope pleases, a clause judged new and fertile in consequences dangerous to the unity of the Church. Here the author also shows very well why those nuncios are rather called Legates, than indeed Ambassadors as sent by other powers. He ascribes the cause of this partly to the affectation of a singularity that gains greater authority, and partly affirms that this is done so that those Legates may be exempt from the laws that concern ambassadors. The author adds that the distinction of Legates, that Cardinals are à Latere and non-Cardinals de Latere, is vain; the whole difference should rather be recognised from the bulls and the power committed, without regard to whether one is a Cardinal or not, à Latere or de Latere, since anyone sent by the last Roman emperors (whose rivals too are the Popes) was called Laterales and sent de Latere. Yet it must altogether be admitted that those nuncios and Legates are distinguished at least by the usage of the terms, and that only Cardinals become Legates. There too

units.la: Maximè ex duobus tractatibus Gallicu de Legatis. In priori sunt primò quædam observationes generales; ostendit, cum quibus præcautionibus & restrictionibus Legati ejusmodi in Gallia recipiantur.
units.tr: Chiefly from the two French treatises on Legates. In the first there are, first, certain general observations: it shows with what precautions and restrictions Legates of this kind are received in France.

units.la: LV. Secundò de honoribus, quibus in Gallia afficiuntur, agit. Cujus partis initium dignum est, quod hîc exscribatur: Les Papes, inquit, se sont servis de tout temps des Legats pour augmenter leur authorité. Monsieur de Marca dans ses œuvres posthumes de Concord. Sac. & Imp. l. 6. c. 28. n. 11. & c.29. n. 1. monstre, que c'est par ce moyen, qu'ils ont ruiné l'authorité des Evesques & des Conciles, il me seroit facile, si je ne m'estois proposé de parler seulement de ce, qui s'est passé en France, de monstrer, que c'est aussi par leur entremise, que les Papes se sont presque rendus toutes les couronnes de l'Europe sujettes & tributaires; neantmoins comme la France s'est toûjours maintenuë dans l'independence de Rome, les Legats n'y ont pas fait de si grands progres que dans les autres états, car toutes leur entreprises n'ont été, qu'à usurper des honneurs, qui à la verité ne leur estoient pas deus: Mais qui pourtant ne diminuent en rien, ny la majesté du Prince, ny la liberté du pais; Id est; Papa semper usi sunt Legatis ad augendam suam authoritatem. Dominus de Marca in suis operibus posthumis de Concordia Sac. & Imp. 1.6. c.28. n.11. & c.29. n.1. probat, eos sic justulisse authoritatem Episcoporum & Conciliorum; Mihíque facilè esset, si non tantùm de eo, quod in Gallia contigit, mihi agere constitutum esset, ostendere, eos sic etiam sibi obnoxia atque tributaria omnia ferè Europa regna reddidisse; Nihilominùs, quemadmodum Gallia semper independens à Roma mansit, ita etiam Legati ibi non tantùm efficere potuerunt, quantum alibi; Totum enim eorum consistit in usurpatione honorum, qui revera ipsis non debebantur; Et qui tamen non diminuerunt, neque majestatem Principis, neque libertatem Regni. Subjungit; Ante Ludovicum XII. Legatos mediocriter honoratos; Venientes ab Adriano P. à Carolo M. incarceratos, à Benedicto XIII. missos ultimis temporibus Parisiis virgis cæsos fuisse; Ludovicum XI. illustrem Bessarionem Legatum post 3. Mensium solicitationem semel ad audientiam admissum, sine Legationis non obtento, remisisse; Carolum VIII. sine permissione Regnum ingresso, jure Legati denegato, solam promtè redeundi gratiam concessisse, Legationem Alexandri VI. filio tantùm ad tegendum obsidis respectum inserviisse, nolente Papa, ut homines scirent, que sa foy fust si suspecte, qu'il est besoing d'en donner des cautions & des Ostages; sidem suam adeò suspectam esse, ut opus haberet dare obsides. Igitur Ludovici XII. tempore pore demum Legatorum honorem crevisse, Papis artificiosè Regibus gratissimos Legatos facientibus, quorum primus Cardinalis d'Amboise, homo ambitiosus & temerarius magis favore Regis, quàm Legationis dignitate extraordinariis honoribus, quos Papa statim titulo Legati tribuerit, mactatus sit, dum nimirum venienti corpora Parisiensium omnia obvia facta, à Parlamentis & aliis supremis Societatibus præcipui deputati, & Legatus in porta sub Conopeum, portantibus præcipuis ex Magistratu Urbis, unica illa vice receptus sit, Parlamentum intrârit, alios introduxerit, altiores à dextris sedes occupârit, à primo Præside Regis personam gerente orationem adulatione plenam audierit, beneficia contulerit, Regium sic honorem acceperit, ut successoribus tantùm his vestigiis insistere reliquum fuerit; Quare etiam Papæ, ut firment primam exemplis possessionem, successivè alios similes submiserint, qui tamen hoc obtento, ne Legati nimis Regem honorarent, neque argentum in Gallia maneret, secundùm consilium Leoni X. datum, non ampliùs Gallos Legatos eligendos judicaverint; Sub Henrico II. Caraffam, illum ipsum, qui populo benedictionis ergò catervatim accurrente, loco soliti voti semper dixerit; Quandoquidem populus ille vult decipi, decipiatur ergò; ut Parlamentum obviam iret, instanter petiisse &c. Cajetanum tempore Ligistico, quo Papæ Regnum saltem tributarium reddere voluerint, ad orationes paucis respondere solitum esse; poche parole, molti effetti, ben venuti, pauca verba, multa effecta, grata; sicque superbiam prodidisse, & ne in Parlamento Regiam sedem occuparet, à Præside, brachio apprehenso, retrahi debuisse, Cardinalem Placentiæ insuper statibus præsidere voluisse, atque Regis locum temerario ausu occupâsse &c.
units.tr: LV. Secondly, he deals with the honours that they are paid in France. The beginning of this part is worth copying out here: The Popes, he says, have always used Legates to increase their authority. Monsieur de Marca, in his posthumous works on the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, book 6, chapter 28, number 11, and chapter 29, number 1, shows that it was by this means that they ruined the authority of bishops and councils. It would be easy for me, if I had not set out to speak only of what has happened in France, to show that it was also through their agency that the Popes have made almost all the crowns of Europe subject and tributary to them. Nevertheless, since France has always kept her independence from Rome, the Legates have not made as great progress there as elsewhere, for all their undertakings have been only to usurp honours that in truth were not due to them, but which do not in any way diminish either the majesty of the Prince or the liberty of the realm. He adds: Before Louis XII, Legates were moderately honoured. Those coming from Adrian the Pope were imprisoned by Charles the Great; those sent in recent times by Benedict XIII were whipped in Paris. Louis XI admitted the illustrious Bessarion as Legate to an audience only once, after three months of solicitation, and sent him away without the Legation being granted. Charles VIII, who entered the kingdom without permission, was denied the right of a Legate and was granted only the favour of returning quickly. The Legation of Alexander VI served only to cover the concern for a hostage, the Pope being unwilling, so that people would know that his faith was so suspect that it was necessary to give security and hostages; that is, his faith was so suspect that he had to give hostages. Therefore the honour of the Legates grew only in the time of Louis XII, when the Popes cleverly made the Legates very welcome to the kings. The first of these was Cardinal d'Amboise, an ambitious and rash man, who was honoured with extraordinary marks of respect, more by the king's favour than by the dignity of the Legation, which the Pope had immediately granted him under the title of Legate. Indeed, when he came, all the chief bodies of Paris met him, the Parlements and other supreme societies sent their principal deputies, and the Legate was received at the gate under a canopy, carried by the leading magistrates of the city, on that one occasion only. He entered the Parlement, introduced others, occupied the higher seats on the right, heard a speech full of flattery from the first president, who represented the king's person, and conferred benefices. He received such royal honour that for successors it remained only to tread in these footsteps. Therefore the Popes, to confirm the first possession by examples, successively sent others like him. Yet, after this had been obtained, so that the Legates would not honour the king too much and so that silver would not remain in France, following the advice given to Leo X, they judged that no more French Legates were to be chosen. Under Henry II, Carafa, that same man who, when the people ran up in crowds to receive a blessing, always said the usual prayer with the words Since that people wants to be deceived, let it be deceived, asked insistently that the Parlement should come to meet him, etc. Cajetan, in the time of the League, when the Popes wanted at least to make the kingdom tributary, was accustomed to answer speeches with few words: few words, many effects; welcome, few words, many deeds, pleasing. Thus he showed his pride, and so that he would not occupy the royal seat in the Parlement, he had to be pulled back by the president, who seized his arm. Moreover, the Cardinal of Piacenza wanted to preside over the Estates and rashly took the king's place, etc.

units.la: LVI. Tertiò honores, quos Cardinalis Chigius tunc ad Regem, ut Papæ displicentiam ratione injuriæ Legato Regio Romæ à Corsis illatæ testaretur, mittendus, jure postulare queat, explicat.
units.tr: LVI. Thirdly, he explains what honours Cardinal Chigi could rightly demand that be sent to the king, to show the Pope's displeasure at the injury done to the royal Legate at Rome by the Corsicans.

units.la: Cujus partis initium rursus damus: Comme les pretensions des Legats, inquit Author, n'ont point de bornes, & qu'elles vont jusqu' à la persone du Roy, nous commencerons par ce qui le regarde: les Legats pretendent être visités par le Roy devant, que de faire leurs entrées à Paris, & pour raison disent premierement, que puisque le Roy rend les dernieres soumissions à Pape, & jusqu' à luy baiser les pieds, il peut bien sans se faire tort, visiter les Legats, qui ont un pouvoir si ample, qu'il semble, qu'ils soyent le Pape mesme. Id est; Quemadmodum pratensiones Legatorum nullis circumscribuntur limitibus, & se extendunt usque ad personam Regis, incipiemus ab illo, quod eum respicit: Legati volunt visitari à Rege ante introitum Parisiis, atque hanc rationem allegant, quia Rex infimas submissiones reddat Papa, etiam pedes ejus exosculando, eum sine injuria aliqua sua invisere posse Legatos, qui tam amplâ potestate sunt instructi, ut videantur ipsimet Papa. His subjungit vindicias exempli ab Henrico IV. dati, qui Cardinali Mediceo Legato obvius fieri voluerit; Et ante speciale illius examen, dicit; Nihil debere Regem Legato, qui non minus illius, quàm Papa Minister sit, & secundum verba cujusdam in Parlamento Parisiensi Praesidis, ab utriusque latere, ejus jurisdictio precaria, & solo nutu revocabilis; Quare etiam crux in praesentia Regis ante Legatos non portetur, non obstante exemplo Caroli VI. quia tunc universum Regnum cum Rege desipere videbatur; Qua verba sunt Fevreti. Henricum IV. autem obviam factum esse solo amicitiae respectu, hinc per veredarios equos, non cum Regali pompa, secundum Thuanum, & quasi incognito; Unde etiam aliis Legatis non obviam processerit idem, etiam Paparum Nepotibus. Cardinalem Barbarinum voti, ut Rex XIII. annum nondum ingressum inviseret, compotem factum non fuisse, interim tamen Richelieum variis artibus inductum fuisse, ut Regi occursum fratris, & quoad illum, dextrae honorem persuaserit, quod male factum esse, exemplis Hispanicis ostendit, quibus non obstiterit, quòd aliquando Reges Castiliae & Arragoniae Legatis obvii facti sint, & locuti capitibus apertis in praesentia Legatorum capitibus apertis, & ex eo, quòd Cardinalis Infans in Hispania tanquam Cardinalis Senior praecedentiam habuerit; Fratres autem Regis secundum Titulorum d'Altesse & d'Eminence differentiam à Papis ipsis approbatam Cardinalibus majores sint; Et Henricum IV. primum Legatos in ingressu suo Principum sanguinis praesentia honorasse, & quidem in personâ Condaei octo annorum, non cogitantem, consequentias ejusmodi formatum iri; Car on s'imagina, inquit Author, que cette action pourroit passer pour une curiosité d'enfant, au quel on avoit voulu donner le plaisir d'aller au devant du Legat, mais il n'y a point de raillerie avec la cour de Rome, elle prend serieusement toutes les choses,qui luy sont avantageuses,& a fait en sin un devoir de ce,qui n'estoit qu'un jeu d'enfant; Id est: Putabant enim actionem illam agnitum iri pro curiositate infantis, obviam eundi Legato, verùm non est jocandum candum cum Curia Romana, qua serio accipit, quæcunque ei sunt utilia, & tandem debitum constituit ex eo, quod erat nonnisi lusus infantilis. Nam ex illo tempore omnes Legati illo honore potiti sunt, & proin licèt Principes sanguinis olim præcedentiam habuerint, videtur tamen ob exempla novissima hodie illos eâ carere & obviam ire debere, & satis magnum lucrum hâc vice obtineri, si Frater Regis non obviam eat, paulatim enim pristinum ordinem esse reducendum &c.
units.tr: Again we give the beginning of this part: As the pretensions of the Legates, says the author, have no limits, and extend even to the person of the King, we shall begin with what concerns him. The Legates claim to be visited by the King before making their entry into Paris, and for this reason they say first that, since the King makes the lowest submissions to the Pope, even kissing his feet, he can without any injury to himself visit the Legates, who have such ample power that they seem to be the Pope himself. That is: Just as the pretensions of the Legates are bounded by no limits, and extend even to the person of the King, we shall begin with what concerns him. The Legates wish to be visited by the King before entering Paris, and they allege this reason: since the King pays the lowest submissions to the Pope, even kissing his feet, he can visit the Legates without any injury to himself, since they are endowed with such ample power that they seem to be the Pope himself. To this he adds the justification of the example given by Henry IV, who wanted to meet Cardinal de' Medici, the Legate. And before a particular examination of that, he says: The King ought to owe nothing to a Legate, who is no less a minister of his than of the Pope; and, according to the words of a certain president of the Parlement of Paris, his jurisdiction comes from both sides, is held at will, and can be revoked by a nod alone. Therefore the cross also should not be carried before the Legates in the King's presence, notwithstanding the example of Charles VI, because at that time the whole kingdom seemed to be out of its wits along with the King. These are the words of Fevret. Henry IV met him only out of regard for friendship, by means of post-horses, not with royal pomp, according to Thuanus, and almost incognito. Hence he did not go out to meet other Legates in the same way, not even the nephews of the Popes. Cardinal Barberini's wish that the King visit him before the thirteenth year was not granted; meanwhile, Richelieu was persuaded by various arts to advise that the king should meet his brother and offer him the right-hand honour. He shows from Spanish examples that this was wrongly done, and the fact that the kings of Castile and Aragon sometimes met Legates and spoke with heads uncovered in their presence, with the Legates' heads uncovered, did not stand in the way; and from the fact that the Cardinal Infante in Spain had precedence as senior Cardinal. Moreover, the brothers of the King, according to the difference of the titles Highness and Eminence, which the Popes themselves have approved, are superior to the Cardinals. And Henry IV was the first to honour the Legates on their entry in the presence of the princes of the blood, indeed in the person of the Condé boy of eight years old, not thinking that consequences of this kind would be drawn. For people imagined, says the author, that this action could pass for a child's curiosity, as if they had wished to give him the pleasure of going out to meet the Legate; but there is no joking with the Court of Rome. It takes seriously all things that are advantageous to it, and has in the end made a duty of what was only a child's game. That is: For they thought that this action would be taken for the curiosity of a child, to go out to meet the Legate, but one must not joke with the Roman Court, which takes seriously whatever is useful to it, and in the end has made a due of what was only a childish game. For from that time all Legates have enjoyed that honour, and therefore, although the princes of the blood once had precedence, it seems that because of the most recent examples they now lack it and ought to go out to meet the Legate, and that it is a large enough gain on this occasion if the king's brother does not go out, since the former order must gradually be restored, etc.

units.la: LVII. In Tractatu altero Cap.III. ex Balsamone XII. Seculi Authore in Glossa in Conc. C. in Trullo observatur appellatio Legatorum à facie ob vestimenta, quibus Papæ quodammodo sint similes. Ibidem eorum prærogativæ declarantur, quòd 1. ante eos, ut olim ante Proconsules fasces, crux portetur. 2. jurisdictionem voluntariam, rursus Proconsulum ad instar, in itinere, ex. gr. absolvendo excommunicationi ob homicidium in Clerico patratum subjacentes, exercere possint. 3. Illis præsentibus aliorum Legatorum potestas evanescat, imò nequidem Patriarchæ ante se crucis vexillum portari curare possint. 4. Beneficia, quorum præsentationem Patronus Ecclesiasticus habet, conferre. 5. Illa unire. 6. In casibus prohibitis dispensare, & alia secundùm Bullæ tenorem agere queant. Cap.IV. prærogativas Legatorum eatenus exponit, quatenus illorum facta & statuta manent etiam post excessum illorum ex Provincia, imò etiam post obitum Papæ, à quo missi fuerant. Caput V. restrictiones aliquot potestatis Legatorum habet secundùm Jus Canonicum. VI. VII. & VIII. quoad materias beneficiarias, secundùm consuetudines Gallicanas. Et cùm Parlamentum Parisiense sæpè voluerit declarare, se Bullas Legatorum approbare sine approbatione Concilii Tridentini, cujus in illis mentio fiebat. Cap.IX. Author ostendit, in quibus Concilium illud juribus Regiis & Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ libertatibus contrarietur. Tandem narratio Historica Receptionum Legatorum in Gallia, in qua Cap.1. inter alia de Legato d'Amboise, cujus jam suprà mentio facta, & ejus prorogatione compendium sequentium verborum explicatur: Cette prorogation etant expirée, le Cardinal d'Amboise, qui vouloit être un second Pape en France, n'ayant peu être le premier à Rome, fit renouveller son pouvoir usque ad beneplacitum Pontificis, ce qui étant extraordinaire, & ne pouvant être approuvé par le Parlement, quoy que Louys XII. se porta à faire passer cette clause, il arriva sur ce point point une si grande contestation entre le Roy & la cour, que peu s'en sal-lut, qu'on ne vint aux extremités. Id est: Postquam illa prorogatio ex-pirâsset, Cardinalis d'Amboise, qui volebat alter in Gallia Pontifex esse, cùm non potuisset primus Roma esse, potestatem suam renovari curavit usque ad beneplacitum Pontificis, id quod cùm extraordinarium esset, neque à Par-lamento approbari posset, licèt Ludovicus XII. promtus esset ad clausulam illam admittendam, de hoc tanta lis inter Regem & Curiam mota est, ut parùm ab extremitatibus abfuerint. Cap.4. Oppositiones Parlamenti, ob formulam in Bulla Legati, & Cancellarii du Prat; usque ad beneplacitum suum; memorantur. c.12. Cùm Regina sub praetextu pacis vellet Bullas Cardinalis Ferrarae approbatas videre, cum restrictione; Sans prejudice des Edicts & des Concordats &c. sine prejudicio Edictorum & Concordatorum &c. Thuanus Praeses dixisse narratur, que ce mot, sans prejudice, estoit donner un soufflet, sans prejudice de faire mal; Id est, verbum hoc, sine prejudicio, esse, dare alapam, sine prejudicio faciendi malum. Ubi etiam pro receptione ejusdem Regius Consiliarius apud Parlamentum ultima haec verba protulisse dicitur; Que le Roy prioit toute cette compagnie de luy obeir à cela; Regem rogare totam illam societatem, ut sibi in hoc obediat; solummodo adjiciens, qu'il n'y avoit point de plus grande & meilleure priere, que de celuy, qui a puissance de commander: Maximas & optimas esse preces illius, qui possit imperare.
units.tr: LVII. In the second Tractate, chapter III, from Balsamon, a twelfth-century author, in his gloss on the Council in Trullo, we are told of the title Legates à facie ("legates in front"), given because of the vestments by which they somewhat resemble the Pope. In the same place their privileges are set out: (1) a cross is carried before them, as the fasces were once carried before proconsuls; (2) they may exercise voluntary jurisdiction on their journey in the manner of proconsuls, for example by absolving those bound by excommunication for a homicide committed by a cleric; (3) when they are present, the authority of other legates lapses, and not even the Patriarch may have the banner of the cross carried before him in their presence; (4) they may confer benefices whose presentation belongs to an ecclesiastical patron; (5) they may unite benefices; (6) they may grant dispensations in cases where these are forbidden, and act in other ways according to the tenor of the Bull. Chapter IV explains the privileges of legates only so far as their acts and statutes remain valid even after they have left the province, and even after the death of the Pope who sent them. Chapter V sets out several restrictions on the legates' power according to canon law. Chapters VI, VII and VIII deal with matters concerning benefices, according to Gallican custom. And since the Parisian Parlement often wished to declare that it approved the Bulls of legates only without approval of the Council of Trent, which was mentioned in them. Chapter IX: the author shows in what respects that Council is opposed to the royal rights and the liberties of the Gallican Church. Finally, there is a historical account of the reception of legates in France, in which Chapter 1, among other things about the legate d'Amboise, already mentioned above, explains his extension by a summary of the following words: After that extension had expired, the Cardinal d'Amboise, who wanted to be a second Pope in France, since he could not be the first at Rome, had his power renewed until the Pope's pleasure. Since this was extraordinary, and could not be approved by the Parlement, although Louis XII was ready to allow that clause, a dispute so great arose between the King and the Court on this point that they came close to extremes. That is: After that extension had expired, Cardinal d'Amboise, who wanted to be another Pope in France, since he could not be the first at Rome, had his power renewed until the pleasure of the Pope; since this was extraordinary and could not be approved by the Parlement, although Louis XII was ready to admit that clause, a dispute so great arose between the King and the Court that they came close to extremes. Chapter 4 mentions the objections of the Parlement, and of Chancellor du Prat, to the formula in the legate's Bull, until his pleasure. Chapter 12: when the Queen, under the pretext of peace, wished to see the Bulls of Cardinal Ferrara approved with the restriction Without prejudice to the Edicts and the Concordats, etc. (sine prejudicio Edictorum et Concordatorum etc.), it is reported that the president Thou said that this word "without prejudice" is to give a slap, "without prejudice" to doing harm; that is, this phrase, "without prejudice", is to give a slap, without prejudice to inflicting harm. There too it is said that, for the reception of the same, a royal councillor before the Parlement uttered these last words: The King asks this whole assembly to obey him in this; adding only, that there is no greater and better request than that of one who has the power to command. The greatest and best requests are those of one who is able to command.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.
