units.la: Ista adducere volui, ut de honore Cardinalium, etiam quatenus nonnunquam Paparum Legati à latere fiunt, constaret. Ut jam constare potest, eos certè multùm honoratos conspici, & in vicinia specietenus omnipotentiae Pontificiae, ex qua acceperunt gratiam pro gratia, donec ad istud fastigium pervenerunt, tantò prioribus Cardinalibus dissimiles facti, quantò Papae hodierni Papis prioribus, utrobique enim auditur illud; Quantum mutatus ab illo! statu pristino. Sed status Cardinalium ob Papas; Vero è, quomodo Il Cardinalismo p.2.l.1.p.91. loquitur, che i Pontefici si sono affaticati d'aggrandire i Cardinali; ma non già per portare con tal grandezza profitto alla maestà Cardinalitia; ma solo per far servire la maestà Cardinalitia all' augmento della loro propria grandezza; Quel Pontefice, che dichiarò i Cardinali simili a' Rè, non hebbe altro riguardo che alla propria, ambitione, acciò resplendesse tanto più il fasto Pontificio, colesser servito da' Rè. Verum est, quòd Pontifices laborârunt ad Cardinalium Majestatem augendam, non quòd isto augmento gmento Majestatis Cardinalitiæ utilitatem quæsiverint, sed tantùm ut Majestatem Cardinalitiam subservire faciant propriæ magnitudini; Pontifex ille, qui Cardinales Regibus similes esse dixit, nihil aliud voluit, quàm ut eò magis elucesceret fastus Pontificius, à Regibus serviliter cultus.
units.tr: I wished to cite these things so that it might be established how highly Cardinals are honoured, including on those occasions when they are sometimes made Legates a latere of the Popes. As can now be seen, they are certainly regarded as greatly honoured, and in the neighbourhood, in appearance only, of Papal omnipotence, from which they received grace upon grace. Until they reached this height, they became as unlike the earlier Cardinals as the Popes of today are unlike the earlier Popes. On both counts one hears the saying: How changed from that former state! But the status of the Cardinals is owed to the Popes. Truly, as Il Cardinalismo (part 2, book 1, p. 91) puts it, the Popes have laboured to aggrandize the Cardinals, but not so that the Cardinalitial dignity might bring any profit through such greatness; rather, only so that the Cardinalitial dignity might serve the increase of their own greatness. That Pope who declared the Cardinals similar to kings had no other concern than his own ambition, so that the Papal pomp might shine all the more, served by kings. It is true that the Popes laboured to increase the majesty of the Cardinals, not because they sought any advantage for the Cardinalitial majesty from this increase, but only to make the Cardinalitial majesty serve their own greatness. That Pope who called the Cardinals similar to kings meant nothing other than that the Papal pomp, served servilely by kings, should shine out all the more.

units.la: LIX. Sed & notâsse juvabit, Cardinales maximam prærogativarum suarum partem debere Pontificibus, qui Imperatoribus infensissimi fuerunt. Id quod non obscurè ipse Onuphrius libro de Titulis Cardinalium innuit, dicens: Cardinalis Presbyter medius locus erat inter Episcopum & cateros Presbyteros non Cardinales, ab Alexandro autem III. sub quo Romana Ecclesia ad maximum in terris fastigium effecta fuit, Imperatore potentissimo, Friderico Ahenobarbo, eoque Ecclesiæ Romanæ infestissimo hoste, conculcato, (rectè ait, etiam in sensu proprio) victo, pacémque ab Ecclesia petere coacto, tum primùm ex Episcopis versâ vice Cardinales fieri cœpti. Cardinalium enim dignitas cum Ecclesia & Romani Pontificis dignitate semper crevit, tunc autem maxima erat; quâ ratione factum est, ut Episcopi multi eam ambirent dignitatem, quâ tantum (tantus) gradus erat ad maximum Pontificatum.
units.tr: LIX. It will also be worth noting that the Cardinals owe the greatest part of their privileges to those Popes who were most hostile to the Emperors. Onuphrius hints at this not obscurely in his book On the Titles of the Cardinals, saying: The Cardinal Presbyter was a middle rank between the Bishop and the other Presbyters who were not Cardinals. But under Alexander III, under whom the Roman Church was raised to the greatest height on earth, when the most powerful Emperor, Frederick Barbarossa, the most hostile enemy of the Roman Church, had been trampled down (rightly so said, even in the literal sense), defeated, and forced to seek peace from the Church, then for the first time the Bishops began in turn to be made Cardinals. For the dignity of the Cardinals always grew together with the dignity of the Church and of the Roman Pontiff, and at that time it was at its greatest. For this reason it came about that many Bishops coveted that dignity, since it was such a step to the highest Pontificate.

units.la: LX. Idem quoque, nempe Papas Imperatoribus infensissimos augmentum Cardinalitiæ dignitatis promovisse, ex Authoribus distinctionis vestium, quas non immeritò particulari consideratione examinamus, liquere potest. Vestitus Cardinalium non vulgaris partes sunt, Sottana, Rochetto, Cappa cum Cappuzio, Beretta, Mitra, Capello; Mantellettam extra urbem non portant; Sed ubique Mozzettâ supra Rochettum vestiti incedunt. Colore pro temporum diversitate utuntur triplici, rubro, purpureo & medio, quem il color de rose secche vocant, quoq; nonnisi quarta Quadragesimæ, quâ Rosam consecrat Pontifex, & tertiâ Adventus Dominica utuntur; Quoad colores cæteros juxta tempora variant, & quidem singulis diebus Veneris colore purpureo, qui Pavonazzo vulgariter appellatur, vestiuntur, luctûs etiam tempore. Et tunc pannum levem de sajetta, exceptis quibusdam diebus feriatis, nempe Nativitatis, Paschatis, Pentecostes, Corporis Christi, Circumcisionis, Epiphaniæ, Ascensionis, Petri, Pauli, Assumtionis Mariæ, omnium Sanctorum, & anniversario coronationis Papæ, habent; Interim tamen luctûs tempore vestimento & cappa rubri coloris incedere obligantur. Nigrum autem planè sibi indecorum arbitrantur. Materiam quod attinet, pannus vel Camelottum ordinariò est, serico Pontifici, si velit, relicto, ad quod tamen extra urbem, maximè si Legati sint, jus etiam habent. In Consistorio vero semper cappam habent purpuream. In Conclavi Papam electuros vestibus croceis uti omnes, Gregorius XV. Bullâ An. 1621. 16. Nov. vulgatâ jussit. Biretum autem rubrum tam iis necessarium est, ut si absens creatus intra annum cum ornamento hoc ad Curiam se non contulerit, vi decreti à Sixto V. in Bulla An. 1586. d. 3 Dec. editi, dignitate excidat.
units.tr: LX. That the Popes, who were most hostile to the Emperors, likewise promoted the increase of the Cardinalitial dignity can also be made clear from the writers on the distinction of vestments, which we examine with particular care. The garments of the Cardinals, which are not ordinary, are these: cassock, rochet, cape with hood, biretta, mitre and zucchetto. Outside the city they do not wear the mantelletta, but everywhere they go about clothed with the mozzetta over the rochet. They use three colours according to the season: red, purple, and the middle colour which they call the colour of dried roses. This last they use only on the fourth Sunday of Lent, when the Pope blesses the rose, and on the third Sunday of Advent. As to the other colours, they vary them according to the season. On every Friday they dress in purple, which is commonly called pavonazzo, and this also at times of mourning. At that time they wear a light cloth of serge, except on certain feast days, namely Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, Corpus Christi, the Circumcision, the Epiphany, the Ascension, the feasts of Peter and Paul, the Assumption of Mary, All Saints, and the anniversary of the Pope's coronation. Nevertheless, at times of mourning they are bound to go about in a garment and cape of red colour. They judge black to be wholly unbecoming to them. As for the material, it is ordinarily cloth or camlet, though they have the right, outside the city especially if they are Legates, to leave silk to the Pope if he wishes. In the Consistory they always wear a purple cape. In the Conclave, that all who are to elect the Pope should wear saffron garments, Gregory XV ordered by a Bull published in 1621, 16 November. The red biretta is so necessary for them that, if one created Cardinal in absence does not come to the Curia within a year with this ornament, he forfeits the dignity by force of a decree issued by Sixtus V in the Bull of 3 December 1586.

units.la: LXI. Innocentio IV. pileum rubrum (sive, ut Theod. à Niem de Schism. l. 4. 3. vocat, flammeum) debent, qui & eos equites incedere jussit, & cujus cum Friderico II. nota sunt certamina, quam ob causam id de spoliis Friderici factum esse Car. Molinæus apud Wolf. Cent. XVI. ad an.1530. author est; Reliqua ejus ordinis insignia, loquitur Onuphrius, annot. in Innoc. IV. posteriores Pontifices excogitârunt, in his præcipuus fuit Paulus II.
units.tr: LXI. The red pileus (or, as Theodoric of Niem calls it in On the Schism, book 4, chapter 3, the flame-coloured cap) is owed to Innocent IV, who also ordered that they should ride on horseback. Concerning him, Carlo Molinaeus, cited by Wolf in Centuria XVI, under the year 1530, is the authority that this was done from the spoils of Frederick, with whom he had famous struggles. Onuphrius, in his notes on Innocent IV, says that the remaining insignia of this order were devised by later Popes, of whom Paul II was the chief.

units.la: LXII. De quo, formidandâ etiam lege Magistratibus indictâ, Clarissimo, & qui, juxtà Platinam, Pontificatûs Majestatem tum auctoritate, tum armis augere conatus est, ita loquitur in vita Pauli idem: Circa cultum corporis etsi morosus non erat, nequaquam tamen negligens habebatur. Fuere etiam, qui dicerent, eum, dum in publicum prodiret, sibi fucis faciem concinnare. De apparatu Pontificio non est, cui ambigas, majores ab hoc uno superatos, regno præsertim, sive mitram velis appellare, in quam multas opes contulit, coemtis undique ac magnis precibus (preciis) Adamantibus, Sapphiris, Smaragdis, Chrysolitis, Jaspidibus, unionibus, & quicquid gemmarum in precio est, quibus ornatus tanquam alter Aaron formâ humanâ augustiore prodibat. Inspici tum ab omnibus volebat & admirari. Hanc ob rem nonnunquam peregrinos in urbe retinuit, intermissâ ostendendi sudarii consuetudine, quò à pluribus eodem tempore cerneretur. Præterea verò ne solus differre à cæteris videretur, publico decreto mandavit, propositâ pœnâ, ne quis biretam coccineam, (ita appellant capitis tegmen) præter Cardinales ferret; quibus etiam primo Pontificatûs sui anno pannum ejusdem coloris dono dedit, quo equos, vel mulos sternerent, dum equitant. Voluit præterea in decretum referre, ut galeri Cardinalium ex serico coccineo fierent, sed id quò minùs decerneretur, vetuére illi, qui bene sentientes diminuendam esse Ecclesiæ Pompam, non augendam cum detrimento Christianæ Religionis prædicabant. Volaterranus etiam l.22. ita loquitur: Pompa his (prioribus) splendórque comitum & ornatus defuere, quos Innocentius addidit, nostrâ quoque ætate (c. an. 1464.) Paulus (secundus) etiam capitis tegmenta rußata. ruffata. Gregorius XIV. verò demùm Cardinalibus Regularibus, narrantibus Cl. Sprengero. l. c. & Auth. Card. p.1. l. 3. p. 309. Biret-rum rubrum dedit,qui cæterùm incedunt colore ordinis; sed formâ & materiâ cæteris Cardinalibus communi, nunquam Rochettam, neque Sottanam ex panno portantes, & dum alii cappam rubram portant,illi ex Camelotto undarum & sine undis,dum alii eam habent violacei coloris; Galerus & Baretta planè similes sunt. Non tamen desunt, qui vestis purpureæ institutionem Bonifacio VIII. (qui magnus & ipse Magistratûs civilis ofor extitit;) adscribant, nempe incerta & hæc sunt quodammodo, sed nec certò scire juvat; Scitur tamen certò, recentioris esse institutionis; Nam & Baronius ad an. 744. 6. ait; Sub Zacharia cœperunt Presbyteri Cardinales plebi sibi subjecta præclariori veste induti debitum prædicationis persolvere.
units.tr: LXII. Of him, who, by a law to be feared, imposed also on the magistrates, that most distinguished man who, according to Platina, tried to increase the majesty of the Pontificate both by authority and by arms, the same Platina speaks thus in the life of Paul: Although he was not fastidious about care of the body, he was by no means regarded as negligent in it. There were also those who said that when he came out in public he arranged his face with cosmetics. There is no doubt about Papal display: he surpassed the greater ones, especially in the kingdom, if you wish to call it a mitre, upon which he expended great wealth, buying up from everywhere, at great prices, diamonds, sapphires, emeralds, chrysolites, jaspers, pearls, and whatever gems are prized; with these adornments he went forth, like a second Aaron, in a form more august than human. He wished to be seen and admired by all at that time. For this reason he sometimes kept foreigners in the city, omitting the custom of displaying the veil, so that he might be seen by many at the same time. Moreover, lest he should seem to differ alone from the others, he commanded by public decree, under penalty, that no one should wear a scarlet biretta (for so they call the head covering), except the Cardinals. To them, too, in the first year of his Pontificate, he gave as a gift cloth of the same colour, with which they might cover their horses or mules while riding. He also wished to have it recorded in a decree that the galeros of the Cardinals should be made of scarlet silk; but this was prevented from being decreed by those who, thinking well, preached that the Church's pomp should be diminished, not increased, to the detriment of the Christian religion. Volaterranus also speaks thus in book 22: The former (Popes) lacked pomp, splendour of retinue and adornment, which Innocent added; and in our own time (about the year 1464) Paul II also added red-tinted and ruffled head coverings. Gregory XIV at last gave the regular Cardinals a red biretta, as related by the distinguished Sprenger, loc. cit., and the author of Cardinales, part 1, book 3, p. 309: they go about otherwise in the colour of their order, but in form and material common with the other Cardinals, never wearing a rochet or cassock of cloth; and while the others wear a red cape, they wear one of watered and unwatered camlet, while the others have one of violet colour. The galero and biretta are wholly alike. Yet there are those who attribute the institution of the purple garment to Boniface VIII, who was himself a great man of civil power. These matters are in a way uncertain, and it is not profitable to know them for certain; yet it is certainly known that it is of more recent institution. For Baronius, under the year 744, number 6, says: Under Zachary the Presbyters who were Cardinals began to discharge the duty of preaching to the people subject to them, clothed in a more distinguished garment.

units.la: LXIII. De ratione verò varii varie ariolantur.
units.tr: LXIII. Concerning the reason, various writers guess in various ways.

units.la: Joh. Baptista de Rubeis Ration. Div. offic. c. 53. rationem hanc reddit, quòd Cardinales ad effusionem usque sanguinis, ad defensionem Papæ & Ecclesiæ parati esse debent. Cui etiam Onuphrius in Epitome Rom. Pontificum consentit his verbis: Papa Innocentius IV. pileum rubrum Cardinalibus dedit, quo ipso significare voluit, illos, qui in illum ordinem legerentur, paratos esse debere pro libertate Ecclesiastica, (melius dixisset, libidine & licentia Pontificia;) si opus erit, propriam vitam morti exponere. Alii rationem à dignitate & splendore Cardinalium arcessunt, quomodo Platina ex Innoc. IV. illud ordinis bonestandi causa factum esse dicit. Alii alia conjiciunt.
units.tr: Giovanni Battista de Rubeis, in Ration. Div. offic. c. 53., gives this reason: that Cardinals must be ready to shed their blood, even to the point of death, in defence of the Pope and the Church. Onuphrius, in his Epitome of the Roman Pontiffs, agrees with him in these words: Pope Innocent IV gave the red hat to the Cardinals, by which he meant that those who were chosen into that order should be ready for ecclesiastical liberty (he would have done better to say, for papal lust and licence), if necessary, to expose their own lives to death. Others derive the reason from the dignity and splendour of the Cardinals, as Platina says the thing was done by Innocent IV for the sake of adorning the order. Others guess other things.

units.la: LXIV. Si autem mysteria hic quærenda forent, varia afferri possent alia à vario coloris illius usu, mentione varia; Idola olim eorúmque Sacerdotes illo utebantur.
units.tr: LXIV. If mysteries were to be sought here, various other explanations could be offered, from the varied use of that colour and its varied mentions. Idols, and their priests in former times, used it.

units.la: Utuntur quoad pileos Persæ, hinc Turcis Kissulbassæ dicti, item Sophi. Qui de Domitiano judicium Taciti in Agric 45. 4. legerunt, suspicari possent, hac etiam de causa colorem istum placuisse Pontifici, ut quum ejus in gratiam multa turpia facturi passurique essent Cardinales, ab hoc rubro colore contra pudorem se munirent. Forte etiam ad generositatem Laconicam habitus est respectus; Quippe Spartanis, teste Plut. Instit. Lacon. c.8. veteribus militaris vestis fuit colore puniceo, ne sanguis vulneratorum conspectus hosti fiduciam & suis metum adderet. De Cardinalibus autem militibus historiæ loquuntur; Atq; de illis etiam dicere possis, quod de se Cardinalis Ximenes Floresta Esparn.1.2. 5. fumum pulveris tormentorum suaviorem iis thure fuisse. Et quid si non sine Numine id factum est, & sanguinaria Edomitici hujus Senatus Consilia ita adumbrari debuerunt? Quò quidem respexit vates in hunc modum canens: Semiviros quicunque Patres radiante Galero Conspicis, & rubra Syrmata longa toga; Crede mihi nullo saturatas murice vestes, Divite nec cocco pallia tincta vides; Sed quæ rubra vides tantorum cæde virorum, Et mersa insonti tota cruore madent; Aut memor istorum, quæ celet, crimina, vestis Pro Dominis justo tacta pudore madet.
units.tr: The Persians use it for their caps, and so the Turks call them Kissulbassae, and likewise the Sophi. Those who have read Tacitus's judgement on Domitian (Agric. 45. 4.) might suspect that this colour was also chosen by the Pope for this reason: that, for his favour, the Cardinals would do and suffer many shameful things, and so they might protect themselves against shame by this red colour. Perhaps regard was also had for Spartan courage: for the Spartans, as Plutarch testifies (Instit. Lacon. c. 8.), in ancient times wore a military garment of purple colour, so that the sight of the blood of the wounded might give confidence to the enemy and fear to their own. Histories speak of Cardinals as soldiers too, and of them one could say what Cardinal Ximenes said of himself (Floresta Esparn. 1.2. 5.): that the smoke of gunpowder was sweeter to them than incense. And what if this was not done without the will of the Deity, and the bloodthirsty counsels of this Edomite senate had to be foreshadowed in this way? To this, indeed, the poet seems to have looked when he sang in this manner: You see the half-men, the Fathers, whoever they are, with radiant galero, and long red robes over the toga. Believe me, you see garments soaked not with purple dye, nor cloaks tinted with rich scarlet; but what you see red is from the slaughter of such great men, and they are drenched, wholly steeped in innocent blood; or, mindful of the crimes they conceal, the robe, touched by a just shame for their masters, is soaked.

units.la: Quomodo etiam ad illud, quod ex Tacito de Domitiano attuli, respicere videtur. Sed & dici potest, in eo etiam esse complementum proprii sensus Prophetiæ in Apocalypsi c.XVII.v.4. Ubi purpurata meretricis mentio fit, & c.XVIII. v.12. ubi inter merces Babylonis etiam purpura ponitur. Maximè quando ipse etiam Papa recens electus ex Anastasii II. Papæ decreto coccino vestiendus est.
units.tr: It also seems to refer to what I quoted from Tacitus about Domitian. But it may also be said that in this there is the fulfilment of the proper sense of the prophecy in Revelation 17:4, where mention is made of the woman clothed in purple, and Revelation 18:12, where purple is listed among the merchandise of Babylon. Especially since the newly elected Pope himself must be clothed in scarlet by the decree of Pope Anastasius II.

units.la: LXV. Indubium autem illud est, in eo luxum esse, & luxûs causâ potissimùm ejusmodi statuta obtinuisse. Id quod haud difficulter ex iis, quæ ex Platina de institutione Pauli II. suprà huic tractationi inserui, colligitur. Qui vitarum Pontificum Scriptor magis aperte in Greg. IV. de luxu Cleri sui testatur: Nostris temporibus, inquit, in omnem luxum & libidinem sese effundit Ecclesiasticus ordo. Coccinatos & trabeatos nunc inspiceres non homines, quod leve fortasse videretur, sed equos & jumenta. Cœlestinus V. pro sua simplicitate, ob quam Bonifacio Successori ad Papatum ineptus videbatur, primo, postquam Papalem Cathedram ascendisset, Conventu constituit, ut ab eo tempore nec Papa, nec Cardinales cum tanta Pompa solennibus equis uterentur, nec mulis quidem, sed asinis tantùm veherentur, dicens: Jesus Christus Filius Dei, humilis asini dorso vectus est, cujus nos imitatores esse debemus, (& sic testibus Henr. de Erfordia apud Wolf. memorab. Cent. XIV. ad an.1350. & Langio in Chron. Citizenfi ad an.1294. Cardinales, imò etiam Papas ab equis ad asinos promovere voluit) precedente, dum incedunt, magno adolescentum & altero Presbyterorum agmine subsequente, non in asinis, ut Christus nostri dogmatis author & bene vivendi unicum in terris exemplar; sed in equis præferocibus & phaleratis, ac si ex hodie devicto triumphum ducerent. Cùm potiùs apud tales vel maximè valere deberet Cœlestini P. Decret. c.14. Discernendi à Plebe,vel cateris sumus, doctrinâ, non veste; conversatione non habitu; mentis puritate,non cultu. Sed ad purpuram deventum est, quae regii decoris est insigne,ut ait Hieron. in Jef.c.61. sed ad purpuram deventum est, quae Regem, non Sacerdotem facit, juxta verba Ambrosii apud Antonin. Chron. 2. p. tit. 9. c. 8. §. 3. (Cujus etiam,ut aliâs quoque vestitus respectu,omninò Lipsius de Collegio Cardinalium præf. in libr. de magnit. Rom. scribere potuit, Cyneam, si rediret,de Cardinalibus,quemadmodum olim de Senatoribus fecerat, judicaturum, tot Reges esse, Regum similes ab ipso Papa in Confirmationibus declarari solitos,certè contra illud rursus:Vos autem non sic.) Sed ad purpuram deventum est,contra severum Narbonensis cujusdam Concilii apud Bar. ad an.598. n. 32. decretum: Ut nullus Clericorum vestimenta purpurea inducat: quae ad jactantiam pertinent mundialem; non ad religiosam dignitatem; ut sicut est devotio in mente, ita etiam ostendatur in corpore, quae purpura maximè Laicorum potestate praeditis debetur,non religiosis. Provocet jam Baronius ad purpuram V. T. ad majorem gloriam novi,ad peculiarem usum Romanae Ecclesiae,nihil efficit; & erubescere debuisset non minùs in vultu,quàm in cultu. Veteres enim umbrae,carnalia ista transierunt,gloria novi fœderis spiritualis est. Tunc sanè & purpura & aurum (cum Hieronymo epist. 2. loquor) probabantur à Domino,quando Sacerdotes bestias immolabant, & sanguis pecudum erat redemptio: quanquam haec omnia in figura praecesserint; Nunc verò, cùm paupertatem domûs suae pauper Dominus dedicârit, cogitemus Crucem ejus, & divitias lutum putabimus &c. Ut vel hinc constare possit, quantâ injuriâ sanctus ille Vir afficiatur, dum vili semper palliolo contentus & luxûs osor hodiernorum Cardinalium ad instar purpurâ fulgens pingitur, qui nequidem Cardinalis, nedum Romanus, ipso Bellarmino posterius hoc nobiscum negante, fuit, Concilium autem Narbonense manifestè usum purpurae in quocunque Sacerdote reprehendit. Ad cujus etiam exemplum Ludovicus Pius apud Platinam l. c. constituì voluit: Ne Episcopi,Clerici cujusvis gradûs pretiosas vestes sericas coccinei coloris ferrent. Sed mirum non est, bonos illos contrà agere, volunt Regibus æquiparari, illis etiam nonnunquam præferri, quorum olim purpura quasi propria,purpuram sumere, imperium acceptare erat, ut nunc est purpura Cardinalium,color purpureus, il Cardinalesco colore. LXVI. Ad istum luxum etiam pertinet, quòd, ut Sprengerus l. c. & II Card. p. 1. l. 3. p. 311. habent, in signum præeminentiæ ante Cardinales baculus argenteus vel inauratus per Tonsorem domûs, quando Cappam imponunt, portatur, donec autem ad locum pervenitur, & Cappa imponitur, per alium tectus portatur; hæc autem fiunt, quotiescunque cum Cappa exeunt Cardinales, excepto tantùm die Veneris, & quando visitatur Prædicatio Palatii. Apud eundem quoque Cardinalismi Authorem superbæ equitationes, sive Pontificalis, sive privatæ Cardinalium l. c. videri possunt; Ubi etiam, se ex ore Episcopi, Mulæ Cardinalis vestimenta pretiosa invidentis audivisse, testatur: In Roma è meglio d'esser mula d'un Cardinale, che Prelato di Santa Chiesa: Melior Roma conditio Mulæ alicujus Cardinalis, quàm verò Ecclesiæ Prælati. Vide etiam de vestitu Cardinalium Sacr. Cerim. l. 3. §. 3. c. 5. 7.
units.tr: LXV. It is beyond doubt that there is luxury in this, and that such regulations were established chiefly for the sake of luxury. This is not difficult to gather from what I inserted above in this discussion from Platina on the institution of Paul II. The writer of the lives of the Popes testifies more openly, in the life of Gregory IV, to the luxury of his clergy: In our times, he says, the ecclesiastical order pours itself out into every luxury and lust. If you were to look now at those clothed in scarlet and in triumphal robes, you would see not men, which perhaps would seem a small matter, but horses and beasts of burden. Celestine V, because of his simplicity, for which he seemed unfit for the papacy to his successor Boniface, first, after he had ascended the papal throne, decreed in a gathering that from then on neither the Pope nor the Cardinals should use solemn horses with such great pomp, nor even mules, but should be carried only on asses, saying: Jesus Christ, the Son of God, rode on the back of a humble ass, and we ought to be his imitators (and so, according to the witness of Henry of Erfurt, cited in Wolf, Memorab. Cent. XIV. ad an. 1350., and Lange, in the Chronicle of Zwickau, ad an. 1294, he wished to promote Cardinals, and even Popes, from horses to asses), while, as they proceed, a great company of young men and another of priests follow, not on asses, as Christ, the author of our doctrine and the sole pattern of good living on earth, did, but on very proud and decorated horses, as if they were leading a triumph over a foe conquered that day. Yet this decree of Celestine ought especially to have weight among such men: We are to be distinguished from the people, or from others, by doctrine, not by dress; by conduct, not by attire; by purity of mind, not by ornament. But they have come to purple, which is the badge of royal dignity, as Jerome says on Isaiah c. 61; they have come to purple, which makes a king, not a priest, according to the words of Ambrose cited in Antoninus, Chron. 2. p. tit. 9. c. 8. §. 3. (Of this, as of other matters concerning clothing, Lipsius could write in his preface to the book on the greatness of Rome, On the College of Cardinals, that Cineas, if he returned, would judge the Cardinals, as he once judged the senators, that there are so many kings, and that they are usually declared to be like kings by the Pope himself in his confirmations; certainly this is contrary to that saying: But you shall not be so.) But they have come to purple, contrary to the strict decree of a certain Council of Narbonne cited in Baronius ad an. 598, n. 32: That no clergyman shall wear purple garments, which pertain to worldly boasting and not to religious dignity; so that, as devotion is in the mind, so it may also be shown in the body; purple, which is due chiefly to laymen who hold civil power, not to religious men. Baronius now appeals to purple in the Old Testament, for the greater glory of the New, for the peculiar use of the Roman Church; he achieves nothing by this, and he ought to have blushed no less in his face than in his dress. For the old shadows and carnal things have passed away; the glory of the New Covenant is spiritual. Then indeed both purple and gold (I speak with Jerome, Epist. 2.) were approved by the Lord, when priests sacrificed beasts and the blood of cattle was the redemption; although all these things went before in a figure. But now, since the poor Lord has consecrated the poverty of his house, let us think of his Cross, and we shall count riches as mud, etc. So that from this alone it may be clear with how great an injury that holy man is treated, while he, always content with a plain little cloak and a hater of luxury, is painted in the likeness of today's Cardinals, shining in purple; he was not even a Cardinal, much less a Roman, as Bellarmine himself later denies with us; and the Council of Narbonne plainly rebukes the use of purple in any priest whatsoever. Louis the Pious, too, following this example, wished it to be established, as cited by Platina in the passage above, that bishops and clerics of any rank should not wear costly silk garments of scarlet colour. But it is no wonder that these good men act to the contrary: they wish to be made equal to kings, and sometimes preferred to them, whose purple was once, as it were, their own: to take up the purple was to accept imperial power. Just as now the purple of the Cardinals, the purple colour, il Cardinalesco colore, is.

units.la: LXVII. Veniamus jam ad Creationem horum Purpuratorum
units.tr: LXVII. Let us now come to the creation of these purple-robed men.

units.la: Quòd olim ab Episcopo Romano, Clero reliquo & Populo Romano Cardinales genuini constituti fuerint, suprà ex Onuphrio didicimus. Hodierni, ut alii sunt, ita quoque aliter fiunt. Non posse fieri legitimè nisi de consensu expresso aut saltem tacito aliorum Cardinalium, suprà quoque annotavimus. Plùs etiam Concilium Constantiense à Martino V. confirmatum postulâsse, ut nimirum Cardinalium novorum promotio illa demum foret legitima, ad quam etiam Cardinales pro majori parte concurrerent expresso suffragio & subscriptione, testis est Dominicus Venetus Episcopus Torcellanus in tract. de Cardinal. quem sub Calixto III. scripsit, & Doctissimus de Dominis edidit, prop. II. In quo tractatu etiam concursum Cardinalium in creatione Cardinalium probat 1. ex eo, quòd creatio illa sit ex maximè arduis 2. alias Papa posset cum Ecclesiæ deformatione juvenculos, inexpertes, illiteratos & inhonestos ac viles eligere. 3. Decrum Concilii pertineat ad decorum Ecclesiæ. 4. quilibet, etiamsi Papalis dignitatis existat, teneatur obedire Concilio generali. 5. Papa juxta promissionem Bonifacii promittat, se cum Cardinalibus & consilio eorum administrare velle Ecclesiam; Quibus multùm insistere nolit. Ponit autem, 12. propositiones, quarum pleræque respiciunt electionem Pontificis, de quibus infra etiam agendum erit; Solùm decima dicit, Concilium Constantiense legitimum & approbatum esse; Undecima, ita decrevisse. Quia autem decretum illud in actis Concilii lii Constantiensis, prout nunc eduntur, haud reperitur, ex eo haud immeritò suspicatur Doctissimus Vir, fraude sublatum esse. Ingratum enim fuit, & praxi jam aliquot seculorum manifestè contrarium. Cui etiam contrarium est illud Concilii Basileensis Sess.23. Non fiat Cardinalium electio solùm per auricularia vota; sed facto vero scrutinio ac publicato, majorem partem Cardinalium per subscriptionem manûs propriæ constiterit collegialiter consensisse. Desuper etiam Apostolica literæ cum subscriptione Cardinalium conficiantur &c.
units.tr: That Cardinals were once appointed legitimately by the Roman Bishop, with the rest of the clergy and the Roman people, we have learned above from Onuphrius. Today they are made in another way, as other things are. We have also noted above that they cannot be made lawfully without the express or at least tacit consent of the other Cardinals. Moreover, that the Council of Constance, confirmed by Martin V, demanded more, namely that the promotion of new Cardinals should be lawful only if most of the Cardinals also concurred by express vote and signature, is attested by Dominicus Venetus, Bishop of Torcello, in his tract. de Cardinal., which he wrote under Callixtus III and the most learned de Dominis published (prop. II). In this treatise he also proves that the Cardinals must concur in the creation of Cardinals: (1) because that act is among the most weighty; (2) otherwise the Pope could, to the disgrace of the Church, choose young and inexperienced men, the unlettered, the dishonourable and the worthless; (3) the decree of the Council pertains to the dignity of the Church; (4) anyone, even one who holds the papal dignity, is bound to obey a general council; (5) the Pope, according to the promise of Boniface, promises that he will govern the Church with the Cardinals and with their counsel, and he is unwilling to insist much on that. He sets out twelve propositions, most of which concern the election of the Pope, which we shall also have to discuss below. In the tenth he says only that the Council of Constance is legitimate and approved; in the eleventh, that it so decreed. But since that decree is not found in the acts of the Council of Constance as they are now published, the learned man reasonably suspects that it was removed by fraud. For it was inconvenient and is clearly contrary to the practice of several centuries. The Council of Basel, Sess. 23, is also contrary to it: The election of Cardinals shall not be made by whispered votes alone; but, when a true scrutiny has been taken and published, it shall be established that the greater part of the Cardinals have agreed collegially by the subscription of their own hand. Moreover, apostolic letters shall be drawn up with the signatures of the Cardinals, etc.

units.la: LXVIII. Olim quidem secundùm illa Decreta plerumque creationes Cardinalium fiebant.
units.tr: LXVIII. Formerly, indeed, under those decrees, the creations of Cardinals mostly took place as follows.

units.la: Pontifex non eligebat, nisi priùs in Consistorio secreto rationes propositset, cujus vota requirere opus erat, & deficiente majore parte ad electionem non veniebatur, sed votis sufficientibus pro affirmativa collectis, demum Papa nominabat, cum recensione meritorum & commendationum à Principibus. Quo facto secreta Cardinalium vota fiebant, & quibus majora favebant, Cardinales à Papa declarabantur cæteris exclusis. Et certè videtur omninò ita fieri debere electiones Cardinalium, juxta hypothesin, quasi ex jure divino. Postquam enim Judas Apostolus excidisset (reddimus verba italica del Gardinalismo p.1.l.1. p.154 155.) Sanctus Petrus (à quo per successionem se claves accepisse dicunt Pontifices, ut Cardinales Apostolorum Successores faciunt;) non vocavit ad Collegium Apostolicum alium pro lubitu; non motu proprio Successorem elegit, non propriâ authoritate declaravit, &c. sed forte Matthias electus fuit. Theologorum libri non continent hoc caput, ipsi non legunt, Papa non putat, se cum istâ obligatione claves accepisse, sed Acta Apostolorum, ac si malè scripta essent, subvertit. Quod certè ostendit, dum mortuo quâdam Cardinale non convocat Collegium Cardinalium, ut eligat Successorem, sed ipse eligit, pronunciat, creat, format, generat, declarat, parùm curans & cœlum & terram, jus & injustiriam, & Apostolos, & Cardinales, & Apostolica Acta, & Canones Ecclesiasticos. Egregia certè res est, velle claves Petri, sine observatione illius, quod observavit Petrus &c.
units.tr: The Pope did not choose anyone unless he first laid out the reasons in a secret Consistory, whose votes had to be sought. If the greater part did not agree, the election did not go forward; but once sufficient votes for the affirmative had been collected, the Pope at last named the man, with a recital of his merits and of the recommendations from princes. After this, secret votes of the Cardinals were taken, and those whom the greater number favoured were declared Cardinals by the Pope, the others being excluded. And indeed it seems that the elections of Cardinals ought certainly to be carried out in this way, according to the hypothesis, as if by divine right. For after Judas the Apostle had fallen (we give back the Italian words of the Cardinalism, p. 1, l. 1, pp. 154–155), Saint Peter (from whom the Popes say they received the keys by succession, as the Cardinals, the successors of the Apostles, do) did not call another to the apostolic college at his pleasure; he did not elect a successor on his own initiative, nor declare him by his own authority, etc., but by chance Matthias was chosen. The books of the theologians do not contain this chapter; they do not read it; the Pope does not think that he received the keys with this obligation, but overturns the Acts of the Apostles as if they had been badly written. This certainly shows, when on the death of some Cardinal he does not summon the college of Cardinals to elect a successor, but himself elects, pronounces, creates, forms, generates, declares, caring little for heaven and earth, right and wrong, the Apostles, the Cardinals, the apostolic Acts and the Church canons. It is certainly a splendid thing to want the keys of Peter without observing what Peter observed, etc.

units.la: LXIX. Verum quidem est, nonnisi in Consistoriis pronunciari etiam hodie Cardinales, sed pronunciantur, jam voluntate Papæ electi, non proponuntur suffragiis Cardinalium demum eligendi, qui se tantùm instar testium habent, quos aliquando vocat Notarius, ut sint præsentes lectioni alicujus Instrumenti, secundùm Authorem Cardinalismi p.1.l.3.p.295.296. Idem sæpe sine consensu Consistorii siftorii fieri,se vel mille exemplis probare posse,ait. Unum brevi-tatis studio subjicit creati ab Innocentio X. Cardinalis Maldachi-ni, & ita creati,ut Papa nonnihil de eo quasi in transitu in congre-gatione paucorum partim sibi devotorum simpliciter,partim etiam suarum creaturarum, locutus,eum, non exspectato vel illorum ju-dicio, è vestigio Cardinalem cum maxima plùs quàm 40. Cardi-nalium aversatione secuta pronunciârit. Addit etiam,Paulum IV. primum fuisse,qui Consistorio Cardinalium potestatem illam eli-gendi obtulerit , aliquot creando, ne verbo quidem ea de re in Consistorio facto. Cujus vestigiis Successores institerint, maximè Sixtus V. pro suo cerebello Monarchæ absoluti , parvi pendens Consistoria & Cardinales, pro lubitu promovens, & Cardinales ad placita sua qualiacunque adigens,ut jam Pontifices in Consisto-rio promoveant, nominent,eligant, quoscunque velint, absque ul-lo planè impedimento. Quod & eos posse,Marcellus Corcyren-sis Episcopus Sacr. Cerim. l. 1. §. 8. existimat, creare nimirum non tantùm pro more in quatuor temporibus, quod & aliquando fe-cerint,proin quandocunque, sed & quoscunque velint,pro potesta-tis plenitudine.
units.tr: LXIX. It is true that even today Cardinals are declared only in Consistories, but they are declared already elected by the Pope's will; they are not put forward to be chosen by the votes of the Cardinals, who have only the standing of witnesses, whom the Notary sometimes summons to be present at the reading of some instrument, according to the author of the Cardinalism, p. 1, l. 3, pp. 295–296. He says the same thing is often done without the consent of the Consistory, and he says he can prove it with a thousand examples. For the sake of brevity he cites one: Cardinal Maldachini, created by Innocent X, who was created in such a way that the Pope, having spoken of him somewhat in passing in a gathering of a few men, some of them devoted to him and some of them his own creatures, simply declared him Cardinal on the spot, without waiting for even their judgment, to the great aversion of more than forty Cardinals. He adds also that Paul IV was the first who presented that power of electing to the Consistory, creating some without even a word about it made in the Consistory. His successors followed in his footsteps, especially Sixtus V, who, as a monarch absolute in his own little brain, made little of Consistories and Cardinals, promoting whom he pleased and forcing the Cardinals to accept whatever he wished, so that now the Popes promote, nominate and choose in a Consistory whomever they wish, without any real hindrance. Marcellus, Bishop of Corcyra, Sacr. Cerim. l. 1, §. 8, also thinks that they may create, namely not only at the customary Ember times, which they have sometimes also done, but whenever they like, and whomever they like, by the fullness of their power.

units.la: LXX. De modo eligendi ex §. annorum commoratione in urbe, & diligentissima observatione se sequentia habere ait; Si Cardinabiles sint Romæ, vesperâ ante electionis diem à Cardina-le Nepote monentur,ut cras̃tinâ in Palatio horâ solitâ compareant; Pontifex eâdem horâ in Consistorium ingressus secretum,mentem suam & nomina promovendorum aperit, & sine prævio ullo re-sponso aut judicio Cardinalium præsentium, vocatis in illud ipsum Consistorium, atque geniculantibus, Birettam rubram ordine, si plures adsunt,imponit,prolatis ad singulos verbis: Esto Cardinalis! (Ex quorum verborum efficacia aliquando Catholicum in Dispu-tatione cum hæretico serió Divinam Papæ Potentiam probare volentem audiverit, ob similitudinem nempe illorum Creatoris: Fiat lux!) Impositam autem Birettam statim deponunt novi Car-dinales &, osculo Pontificis pedi dato,ad amplexus Cardinalium præsentium tanquam fratrum se conserunt. Sic præstito juramen-to,quod Sprengerus in Instit. Jur. Publ. c.35. habet, & exhibitâ gra-tiarum actione, à Cardinale Nepote, qui & introduxerat, retrodu-euntur.
units.tr: LXX. Concerning the manner of choosing, from the same section on residence in the city, and with the most careful observation, he says the following. If the Cardinals-to-be are in Rome, on the evening before the day of election they are told by the Cardinal Nephew to appear in the Palace at the usual hour the next morning. At that same hour the Pope enters the Consistory in secret and discloses his mind and the names of those to be promoted, and, without any prior answer or judgment of the Cardinals present, who have been called into that very Consistory and kneel, he places the red biretta on each in turn, if there are several, speaking to each the words: Be a Cardinal! (From the efficacy of these words a Catholic, arguing seriously with a heretic who wished to prove the divine power of the Pope, once heard it, namely because of the likeness to the words of the Creator: Let there be light!) The new Cardinals immediately take off the biretta they have been given, and, after giving the Pope's foot a kiss, they turn to embrace the Cardinals present as brothers. After the oath has been taken, which Sprenger has in Instit. Jur. Publ. c. 35, and an expression of thanks has been given, they are led back by the Cardinal Nephew, who had also brought them in.

units.la: LXXI. Alium modum ita idem Cardinalismi Author de-scribit fusiùs. (Omnium enim quasi compendia damus.) Cardina-lis lis Nepos, pronuntiatione in Consistorio facta, juxta acceptum Catalogum per Camerarium suum in essedo suo advehit non diu quaerendos; In cujus domo rasuram Gardinalitiam à Tonsore ejus, qui à singulis 25. scudi accipit, accipiunt, & à Camerae Ministris, quibus vestes priores obtingunt, Cardinalitio habitu vestiuntur, & post solenne convivium ad Papam ducuntur, à quo ter poplite flexo, & pedi osculo dato, similiter Birettam accipiunt, & dimissi cognatos Pontificis invisunt, post domi manentes, Camerâ suâ, licèt accesserint invisentes, (invisendi autem non sunt à Cardinalibus publicè) non egrediuntur, donec cum magna pompa in primo Consistorio publico Galerum rubrum ex manibus Pontificis accipiunt.
units.tr: LXXI. The same author describes another manner more fully. (For we give, as it were, summaries of everything.) After the announcement has been made in the Consistory, the Cardinal Nephew sends for those listed in the catalogue, by his Chamberlain, in his carriage, men not far to seek. In the house of each, they receive the Cardinalitial tonsure from his barber, who takes twenty-five scudi from each, and from the officers of the Camera, to whom their former clothes fall, they are dressed in Cardinalitial habit, and after a solemn banquet they are led to the Pope, before whom they kneel three times, give the kiss to his foot, and likewise receive the biretta. Then, dismissed, they visit the Pope's relatives; afterwards they remain at home in their own chamber, and although they have come to visit, they do not go out (they are not to be visited publicly by Cardinals) until, with great pomp at the first public Consistory, they receive the red hat from the hands of the Pope.

units.la: LXXII. Absentium ea secundùm eundem habetur ratio, ut pronunciatione in Consistorio facta primum de promotione nuncium per Nepotis Cursorem accipiant, quem Papae Camerarius cum Biretta rubra & Brevi Pontificio sequitur donis & honoribus maximis excipiendus.
units.tr: LXXII. According to the same author, the same reckoning is kept for those who are absent: after the announcement has been made in the Consistory, they first receive news of the promotion through a courier of the Nephew, whom the Pope's Chamberlain follows with the red birettas and a papal Brief, to be welcomed with the greatest gifts and honours.

units.la: Post Cursoris adventum statim rasuram à suo Tonsore accipiunt, ut Cardinales vestiuntur, tales se subscribunt, non tamen ante adventum Camerarii sive habitu rubro vestiuntur, sive Birettâ rubrâ teguntur. Galerum autem non imponunt nisi primò ex manibus Pontificis, vel alterius, cui id ex speciali gratia speciali brevi conceditur, acceptum.
units.tr: After the courier's arrival, they at once receive the tonsure from their own barber, they are dressed as Cardinals, and they sign themselves as such; yet they do not dress in red, nor cover themselves with a red biretta, before the arrival of the Chamberlain. They do not put on the red hat unless they have first received it from the hands of the Pope, or of another to whom that is granted by a special brief as a special favour.

units.la: LXXIII. Gratia autem illa rarò conceditur, non quòd traditio Galeri ab ipso Pontifice immediatè sit necessaria ex ordine Ecclesiae, mà solo per l'ambitione del Pontefice, inquit Il. Card. p.1. l.3.313. sed tantùm ex ambitione Pontificis, qui vult gratiarum actionem ex ipso cujusvis recens electi Cardinalis ore audire, & simul cum illo de familiae suae commodis agere, eíque ob oculos ponere obligationem erga cognatos, quâ ratione quibusdam Pontificibus solenne est dicere novis Cardinalibus, se eos ob varios respectus, sed maximè ad instantias Nepotis sui creâsse, licèt in contrarium quandoque res se habeat.
units.tr: LXXIII. This favour, however, is rarely granted, not because the handing over of the hat by the Pope himself is necessary by the order of the Church, but only through the ambition of the Pope, says Il. Card. p.1. l.3.313. but merely from the ambition of the Pope, who wishes to hear the thanks of any newly chosen Cardinal from his own lips, and at the same time to discuss the advantages of his family with him and to set before his eyes his obligation towards his relatives. For this reason it is customary for some Popes to tell the new Cardinals that they created them for various reasons, but chiefly at the urging of their nephew, although sometimes the matter stands otherwise.

units.la: Solet tamen etiam ceremonia & impositio Birettae vel Nuncio, vel Episcopo, vel Principi seculari in loco committi, qui genua flectenti verbis solitis eam imponunt, sed pedis osculum soli Papae debitum tamen non recipiunt. Quae quidem in Ecclesia post Missam simplicem, aut solennem peraguntur: Dum absentes Romam contendunt, verba sunt Sprengeri, in itinere parùm refert, an purpureo, an rubro vestitu incedere malint, juxta temitempora tamen, nisi quòd ultimo itineris die purpureo solùm uti possunt: in splendido ingressu excipiuntur obviam à Cardinale Nepote, altero sive eodem die Consistorium petunt in solenni Cardinalium conductu. Quam primùm ingressus est geniculabundus humiliter Pontificis pedes osculatur, sequente osculo manûs & oris facta salutatione osculi ad Cardinales incipiunt solennia: Insignitur Cappucio à Cardinale Diacono, assistentibus reliquis duobus Diaconis, & Camerario supremo, adigitur ab eodem Cardinali Diacono in juramentum solitum, quo praestito Papa pileum Cardinalitium post brevem orationem imponit Cardinalis capiti, his additis: Cardinalis esto! Fervent solennia, & pileus exhibetur novo Cardinali à Camerario secreto Pontificis, cui datur remuneratorium.
units.tr: Yet the ceremony and the imposition of the biretta are often entrusted in some place to a nuncio, a bishop, or a secular prince, who, when the kneeling man has been addressed in the usual words, place it on him, but they do not receive the kiss of the foot, which is owed to the Pope alone. These things are indeed carried out in the Church after a simple or a solemn Mass. While they make their way to Rome as absent men, are the words of Sprenger, it matters little on the journey whether they prefer to go in purple or in red dress, according to the season; only on the last day of the journey, however, may they use purple. In a splendid entrance they are met on the way by the Cardinal Nephew, and on the same or the next day they seek a consistory in a solemn escort of Cardinals. As soon as they have entered, kneeling humbly, they kiss the Pope's feet; after the kiss, with the greeting of the hand and mouth, the Cardinals begin the solemnities. He is invested with the cappuccio by a Cardinal Deacon, the two other Deacons and the chief Chamberlain assisting, and is put under the usual oath by the same Cardinal Deacon. When this has been taken, the Pope, after a short prayer, places the Cardinal's hat on his head, adding: "Be a Cardinal!" The solemnities are celebrated with fervour, and the hat is handed to the new Cardinal by the Pope's private Chamberlain, to whom a gratuity is given.

units.la: LXXIV. In primo Consistorio secreto, denuò loquitur Author Cardinalismi, post publicum, Papam os claudere novis Cardinalibus, digitum illi imponendo, cum nescio quibus ceremoniis, ita eos loqui & sententiam in Consistoriis & congregationibus ferre, id est, vocem activam & passivam habere prohibens. Ante Pontificatum Pii V. saepè relinquebant in illo statu Cardinales, ad adimendam iis occasionem concursûs ad Papatum aut suffragii, sed fallebantur, mortuo enim Papa statim Collegium Cardinalium gratias faciebat. Pius V. autem decreto an. 1571. declaravit, illam oris occlusionem non secum ferre privationem vocis ullam, verùm simplicem esse ceremoniam, quare etiam in sequenti Consistorio Papa illis os aperiat, annulum illis tradat, Titulum significet; Quod & fit erga absentes. Sprengerus hic annulum cum Sapphiro speciatim memorat, & tunc restare, ut novus Cardinalis accipiat possessionem Ecclesiae, quod quomodo fiat, apud Franciscum Sestini del Maestro di Camera videre possis.
units.tr: LXXIV. In the first secret consistory the author of Cardinalismus speaks again, after the public one, of the Pope closing the mouths of the new Cardinals by laying a finger on them, with I know not what ceremonies, so that they may not speak or give their opinion in consistories and congregations; that is, forbidding them to have an active and a passive voice. Before the pontificate of Pius V. Cardinals were often left in that state, in order to take from them the opportunity of gathering for the papacy or of a vote, but they were deceived, for on the Pope's death the College of Cardinals at once gave thanks. Pius V., however, by a decree of the year 1571, declared that that closing of the mouth carried with it no deprivation of voice, but was a mere ceremony; therefore also in the following consistory the Pope opens their mouths, hands them the ring, and indicates the title. This is done also for those who are absent. Sprenger here mentions especially the ring with a sapphire, and then it remains for the new Cardinal to take possession of the Church; how this is done you may see in Francesco Sestini, del Maestro di Camera.

units.la: LXXV. Sed memoratu sunt dignissima, quae narrationi de occlusione oris subjicit Author Cardinalismi, verba. Con tutto ciò, inquit, bisogna credere, che i Pontefici hanno trovato il vero modo di chiuder la bocca a' Cardinali &c. Id est: Credi tamen debet, Pontifices invenisse optimum modum os Cardinalibus claudendi, eósque ad silentium adigendi; Imò licèt eis Pontifices os aperiant, ipsi tamen sponte denuò illud claudunt, dum se perverso regimini opponere non audent, non dico, perverso regimini Pontificum, sed Nepotum, Ecclesiam pereuntem videre, quàm eam ex officio defendere malentes.
units.tr: LXXV. But the words the author of Cardinalismus adds to his account of the closing of the mouth are most worthy of being recalled: Con tutto ciò, he says, bisogna credere, che i Pontefici hanno trovato il vero modo di chiuder la bocca a' Cardinali, etc. That is: Nevertheless it must be believed that the Popes have found the best way of closing the mouths of Cardinals and forcing them to silence; indeed, although the Popes open their mouths for them, they themselves of their own accord close them again, while they do not dare to oppose a perverse government, I do not say of the Popes but of the nephews, preferring to see the Church perishing rather than defend it as their duty required.

units.la: LXXVI. Quae de muneribus idem habet, hinc inde largâ manu exhibendis, ita ut dona praesentium minimùm quingentis, absentium ultra mille, quae pro Biretta solvere tenentur, trecentis ducaducatis aureis constent, Principes autem creati multò plùs, nem-pe ad quatuor & usque ad sex scutorum millia expendant, præ-ter munera ab omnibus Nepotum Camerae Magistris, item pro Bullis conferenda, quae à Papa & Cardinalibus præsentibus subscriptæ ordinariò plumbo annuli Piscatoris signentur, exceptis Principum & aliorum superioris conditionis Bullis auro signari solitis; Quæ, inquam, de ejusmodi muneribus multis habet; sacram Romanorum auri famem, veritatem nominis ROMA in sensu suprà memorato, & quòd venalia Romæ omnia sint, nihil sine nummis præsentibus detur, Apostolus Petrus olim, si Deo placuit, Papa, aurum & argentum & ejusmodi neque scuta neque tela habens, hodie ne quidem Cardinalis fieri posset; ostendunt. Cæterum non immeritò dolet Author, quòd dari soleant tot dona privatis, nihil detur publico; approbator Consilii, quod & alius Scriptor dederit, & Alexander VII. (sed sine successu, quia forte creaturas suas bono publico gravare noluerit;) agitârit, de tormento magno recens electi sumptibus ad usus bellicos parando. Qui plura de his & alia etiam ceremonialia respectu Cardinalium cognoscere cupit, legat Episcopi Corcyrensis Sacr. Carim. l. 1. §. 8. 9. funebria luxu plena, 1000. pro singulis Missas, & abactionem muscarum hyemali tempore, & cera in convenientem satis, valde importunam & tumultuosam dispensationem, sive potius dissipationem §. 15. c. 1.
units.tr: LXXVI. What he says about the gifts, which are given out with a lavish hand on all sides, so that the presents of those present cost at least five hundred, those of absent men more than a thousand, which they are bound to pay for the biretta, three hundred golden ducats, while newly created princes spend much more, namely four to six thousand scudi, besides the gifts from all the Masters of the Camera of the nephews, and likewise for the Bulls to be conferred, which, signed by the Pope and the Cardinals present, are ordinarily sealed with lead by the ring of the Fisherman, except the Bulls of princes and others of higher rank, which are usually sealed with gold; all this, I say, he says at length about such gifts. He shows the sacred hunger for gold among the Romans, the truth of the name ROME in the sense mentioned above, and that everything in Rome is for sale and nothing is given without present money. If Peter the Apostle, were he Pope now, having gold and silver and such things but neither shields nor weapons, could not even be made a Cardinal today. Moreover, the author rightly grieves that so many gifts are given to private persons, and nothing to the public good; he approves the proposal, which another writer has also put forward, and which Alexander VII. (but without success, perhaps because he was unwilling to burden his creatures for the public good) pursued, that a great engine of war should be prepared at the expense of a newly elected Cardinal. Whoever wishes to know more about these and other ceremonial matters concerning Cardinals, let him read the Bishop of Corfu, Sacr. Carim. l. 1. §. 8. 9. funerals full of luxury, a thousand Masses for each individual, and the driving away of flies in winter, and wax in a sufficiently suitable, but very troublesome and tumultuous distribution, or rather dissipation, §. 15. c. 1.

units.la: LXXVII. Quales autem eliguntur? Quales eligendi sint, constat non tantùm ex aliorum Ministrorum Ecclesiasticorum requisitis in Scripturis Canonicis & apud Patres antiquos proliXè recensitis & satis notis, sed & ex illorum, qui Cardinales, postquam jam à vera antiquorum Cardinalium ratione degenerâssent, in officio & intra certos limites, quos abusus concessit, continere voluerunt, decretis, definitionibus, admonitionibus. Ita Concilium Basileense sess. 23. Necesse est, inquiunt Patres, ut tales instituantur, qui sicut nomine, ita re ipsa Cardinales sint. Sint viri in scientia moribúsque ac rerum experientia excellentes, non minores 30. annis, Magistri, Doctores, seu Licentiati, cum rigore examinis, in Jure Divino, vel humano: sit saltem tertia, vel quarta pars de Magistris aut Licentiatis in S. Scriptura. Inter hos autem 24. (quem numerum definiisse suprà diximus;) esse aliqui poterunt admodum pauci, filii, fratres, aut nepotes Regum, seu magnorum Principum; in quibus cum circumspectione & maturitate morum competens literatura sufficiat. Non fiant Cardinales Quales juxta Canones eligi debeant; nales nepotes ex fratre, vel sorore Romani Pontificis, aut alicujus Cardinalis viventis: non illegitimè nati, non corpore vitiati, nec alicujus criminis aut infamiæ notâ respersi: Prædicto autem numero 24. pro magna Ecclesiæ necessitate, vel utilitate, duo alii, in quibus vitæ sanctitas, vel eximiæ virtutes refulgeant: quanquam memoratos gradus non habeant: ac de Græcis, cùm Romanæ Ecclesiæ uniti fuerint; insignes aliqui viri adjici poterunt. Patres autem Tridentini satis timidè, breviter & generaliter Pontifices, ut lectissimos tantùm Cardinales adscisçant, monent.
units.tr: LXXVII. But what sort of men are chosen? What sort ought to be chosen is clear not only from the requirements for other ecclesiastical ministers, which are set out at length and are well enough known from the canonical Scriptures and the ancient Fathers, but also from the decrees, definitions and admonitions of those who, after the Cardinals had already degenerated from the true practice of the ancient Cardinals, wished to keep them to their office and within certain limits which the abuses had allowed. Thus the Council of Basel, session 23: It is necessary, the Fathers say, that such men be appointed as are Cardinals in fact as well as in name. Let them be men excelling in learning, morals and experience of affairs, not less than thirty years old, masters, doctors or licentiates, examined with rigour in divine or human law; let there be at least a third or fourth part of masters or licentiates in Holy Scripture. Among these twenty-four (the number we said above was fixed) there may be some very few sons, brothers or nephews of kings or great princes, in whom a suitable learning, together with circumspection and maturity of character, is sufficient. Let them not be made Cardinals [as they should be chosen according to the canons]: nephews by a brother or sister of the Roman Pontiff, or of some living Cardinal; not illegitimately born, not bodily defective, nor tainted with any mark of crime or infamy. Beyond the said number of twenty-four, for great need or advantage of the Church, two others in whom the sanctity of life or outstanding virtues shine may be added, although they do not hold the said grades; and as to the Greeks, once they have been united to the Roman Church, some distinguished men may be added. The Fathers of Trent, however, rather timidly, briefly and in general terms, admonish the Pontiffs to admit only the most choice men as Cardinals.

units.la: LXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXVIII.

units.la: Sed an jam tales, requisitis non ad rigorem Evangelii exactis supra positis decorati eliguntur? Contrarium manifestum est, & contemni, rejici à Papis hujusmodi definitiones, admonitiones, & aliter ac censet Torcell. de potest. Papæ n. 5. decreta Conciliorum de ordinatione Cardinalium ab iis propter privatas affectiones & commoditates palàm infringi; Qui & eligendorum respectu multò magis à primitiva puritate defecerunt. Eligebantur enim olim multi inviti, saltem parum honoris cupidi; Olim, non multi nobiles; Olim, plerique digni, & meritorum respectu. Hodie alia omnia. Olim bisognava che i Pontefici &c. Oportebat, inquit Author Cardinalismi, ut Pontifices lacrymis rogarent homines, ut dignarentur habitam Ecclesiasticum recipere, quia tum suâ humilitate & mansuetudine opprobrium erat mundi; hodie more receptum est, ut homines memorialibus, supplicationibus, ut non dicam, nummis, apud Pontifices ambiant vestem Prælati, quando jam humilitas in fastum, mansuetudo in magnificentiam conversa est; Olim & dieci secoli indietro &c. ante decem secula, ita pergit, vix mendici, nedum Mechanici voluerunt relinquere tuguria & officinas, ad imperandum more Principum in Principatu Ecclesiæ, & Pastores maluerunt sudare apud aratrum, quàm regere more Principum Christi Monarchiam. Sed quia il danaro della chiesa &c. denarius Ecclesiæ primò amarus, jam dulcis factus est, & servire Ecclesiæ, imò illud saltem præ se ferre, questus est, nec in orbe aula, quæ magis possit divites, nobiles, illustres reddere familias etiam pauperrimas, vilissimas, beneficiorum, ut vocant, multitudine, hinc est, che desiderando tutti &c. ut desiderantibus omnibus instinctu quodam naturali familiæ suæ augmentum, omnes Romam accurrant, certi, se aliquando obtenturos talem dignitatis gradum, ut major à Principibus expeti haud posset &c.
units.tr: But are such men now chosen, adorned with the qualities set out above and with the requirements of the strict rule of the Gospel? The contrary is plain. The Papists scorn and reject these definitions and admonitions, and, as Torcell. says in de potest. Papae n. 5, they openly break the decrees of the Councils on the appointment of Cardinals for private affections and conveniences. In the matter of those who are chosen they have fallen much further from primitive purity. For formerly many were chosen against their will, or at least had little desire for honour; formerly not many were noble; formerly most were worthy and chosen for their merits. Today everything is otherwise. Formerly, "it was necessary that the Popes beg men with tears to deign to accept ecclesiastical office," as the author of Cardinalismi says, "for then through their humility and gentleness they were a reproach to the world; today it has become customary for men to seek the dress of a prelate from the Popes by petitions and supplications, not to say money, since humility has already turned into pride and gentleness into magnificence." Formerly, "ten centuries ago," he goes on, "hardly beggars, let alone craftsmen, were willing to leave their hovels and workshops to rule in princely fashion in the principality of the Church, and pastors preferred to sweat at the plough rather than rule Christ's monarchy like princes." But because "the money of the Church was at first bitter, but has now become sweet, and it is sought not to serve the Church, or at least not only to display that intention; nor is there any court in the world that can make families, even the poorest and most despised, rich, noble and illustrious, more than the multitude of benefices, as they call them," hence it is that "since all, by a certain natural instinct, desire the increase of their family, all run to Rome, certain that they will one day obtain such a degree of dignity that nothing greater could be sought from princes, etc."

units.la: LXXIX.
units.tr: LXXIX.

units.la: Gradus ille summus, post Pontificiam, est Cardinalitia dignitas, ad quam cæteræ scalarum ad instar habentur; Hinc etiam maximis ambitur desideriis, & quanto profundo sit questo desiderio &c. quàm profundum sit desiderium illud in cordibus Præla-torum, ex eo colligi potest, quòd sæpe pra gaudio moriuntur, videntes se ad istam dignitatem pervenisse,alii pra dolore,videntes se isthuc pervenire non posse; Præter multa millia talium, quibus dulces molestiæ, quas susci-piunt, per 40. sæpe annos,modò huic, modò illi Prælato servientes ; hinc commendationes Regum omnium pro Cardinalatu tam sollicitæ siunt; hinc ipsi Pontifices tantâ curâ & festinatione sibi charissimos atque san-guine conjunctissimos promovere student &c. Hæc autem ordinaria sunt desideria, ambitiosa, avara, licèt non negemus, paucos quos-dam dignitatem non ambire, imò fugere, probè nimirum conside-rantes, quanto vale l'onza, quanti ematur & sit. Sed omninò pauci sunt tales, & vix ex multis millibus unus.
units.tr: The highest rank after the Papacy is the Cardinalate, and the other steps are regarded as rungs of a ladder leading to it. For this reason it is also sought with the greatest longing. "And how deep that desire is, etc." How deep that desire is in the hearts of prelates can be gathered from the fact that they often die of joy on seeing that they have attained this dignity, and others of grief on seeing that they cannot reach it. Apart from the many thousands of such men, who for often forty years endure the sweet troubles they undergo, serving now this prelate, now that one. Hence "the recommendations of all kings for a Cardinalate are made so eagerly", and hence "the Popes themselves study to advance, with such great care and haste, those most dear to them and most closely related by blood, etc." These desires, however, are ordinary, ambitious and greedy. We do not deny that a few men do not seek this dignity, indeed flee from it, clearly considering "how much an ounce is worth, what it costs and what it is." But such men are wholly few, and scarcely one in many thousands.

units.la: LXXX. Non possum autem hic omittere ambitionem ri-diculam Octaviani Raggii, Genuensis, ch'era uno de' più ridicoli sog-getti &c. verba sunt del Card. p.2. l. 2.202.qui fuit ex maximè ridiculis, qui unquam in Collegio visi sunt, simplex, indoctus, ineptus, malignus, qui habitum Cardinalis sibi procuravit, antequam talis esset, & quotidie bis, aut ter in præsentia famulitii sui eo se vestire solebat,ex eo post quarens, an sibi conveniret, responsione; quòd sic; semper prompta. Sed & quadam vesperà in illo habitu ad Urbanum VIII. P. qui eum ob simplicitatem & alia diligebat, se contulit,ad quem post pedis osculum dixit: Sancte Pa-ter, dignare quæsò gaudio afficere bonum illum s.nem, Patrem meum, me Cardinalem creando, quod & ille valde desiderat, & ego plùs quàm ille. Cum eo successu, ut in prima creatione promotus fuerit, & acceptâ Birettâ statim ad agendas Sanct. Sua gratias concesse-rit,amplectendo illam,quasi in ecstasi, modis ex omni parte plùs quàm ri-diculis; ut Pontifex necesse habuerit, amplexus cum doloris commemora-tione deprecari, illo regerente: Son tanto allegro d'esser Cardinale,che vi vorrei mangiare d'allegrezza; Id est : Tanto gaudio sum perfusus, quia Cardinalis creatus sum, ut S. V. pra gaudio devorare cuperem. Subjun-git Author,stultitias & ineptias hujus hominis multas alias insignes suis-se ; quarum unam adhuc addit , dicentis post promotionem ad Nepotem, posthac Cardinalem & illum : Mio Nipote, se voi havete il pensiero &c. Id est: Nepos mi, si speras gradum assequi, quem me vi-des assecutum esse, oportet,ut incumbas studiis, & mea premias vestigia. Quibus verbis & præsentes aulicos & Nepotem ipsum ad risum concitârit.
units.tr: LXXX. I cannot omit here the ridiculous ambition of Octavian Raggi of Genoa, "who was one of the most ridiculous persons, etc." The words are those of the Cardinal (p.2 l.2 p.202): "He was one of the most ridiculous men ever seen in the College, simple, unlearned, inept, malicious, who procured for himself the habit of a Cardinal before he was one, and daily, twice or three times, in the presence of his servants, used to dress himself in it. Afterwards he would ask them whether it suited him; they always replied promptly that it did. Indeed, one evening he went in that dress to Urban VIII, who loved him for his simplicity and other qualities, and after kissing the Pope's foot he said to him: 'Holy Father, deign, I beg you, to give joy to that good gentleman, my father, by creating me a Cardinal, which he desires greatly, and I even more than he.' With such success that in the first creation he was promoted; and having received the biretta, he at once gave thanks to His Holiness, embracing it as if in ecstasy, in ways more than ridiculous in every respect. So that the Pope was obliged to beg him to stop, with a remark about his sorrow, while he answered: 'I am so glad to be a Cardinal that I would like to eat you up with joy.'" That is: "I am so overcome with joy at being created a Cardinal that I would like to devour Your Holiness for joy." The author adds that this man had many other notable follies and ineptitudes, of which he adds one more: when he had been promoted, he said to his nephew, who would later be a Cardinal too: "My nephew, if you have the thought, etc." That is: "My nephew, if you hope to reach the rank I see I have reached, you must apply yourself to your studies and follow in my footsteps." With these words he moved both the courtiers present and his nephew himself to laughter.

units.la: LXXXI. Sed & multi nobiles dignitatem ambiunt, ad eam eliguntur. Ambiunt desiderando &c. ipsi etiam Principes ensem cum toga, & pallium regium cum vili caputio Monachi mutare desiderantes p.257. Et observat, che le prime case &c. praecipuas in Christiano orbe familias multum se honoratas existimare, si possint obtinere pileum, atque praecipuos in orbe Reges gloriari, quando eorum haeredes possint simul conjungere supremas Monarchiae coronas & pileum Romanum rubrum; quia multi fuerunt qui sponte Principatum cum Cardinalatu commutarunt p.288. Et certe Principes creati multum ad augmentum dignitatis mundanae conferunt, & utiles sunt regno mundano, nec Beneficiorum pluralitate fastui Cardinalitio convenienter pauperum adinstar ali debent. Hinc etiam Alexander VII. qui Magnificentiam Alexandri Magni, juxta eundem, ab initio prae se tulerat, atque, se Principes multos creaturum, ea ratione occasionem dedit veteri Aulico ad Amicum Cardinabilem dicendi: Monsignore &c. Domine, credidi hactenus, Vos manere Cardinalatum, quia Cardinales fiebant ex farina communi, sed quia jam Papa nonnisi ex farina alba eos conficere vult, spes vestra nulla est, estis enim ex farina communi. Quamvis inde bono illi nullum periculum fuerit, &, annotante eodem, Principem nullum creârit Alexander.
units.tr: LXXXI. But also "many nobles" seek the dignity and are chosen to it. They seek it "by desiring, etc." Princes themselves, "desiring to exchange the sword for the gown, and the royal mantle for the coarse hood of a monk" (p.257). And he observes that "the leading families, etc." believe they are greatly honoured if they can obtain the red hat, and that the foremost kings in the Christian world glory when their heirs can unite the supreme crowns of monarchy and the Roman red hat, because there have been many who willingly exchanged a principality for a Cardinalate (p.288). And certainly princes who are made Cardinals contribute much to the increase of worldly dignity and are useful to the worldly kingdom. Nor, with the plurality of benefices, should they be fed in a manner suited to the pride of a Cardinal, like the poor. For this reason too Alexander VII, who, according to the same author, had from the beginning displayed "the magnificence of Alexander the Great," and who, because he would create many princes, gave an old courtier the occasion to say to a Cardinal friend: "Monsignore, Lord, I have so far believed that you would remain a Cardinal, because Cardinals were made from common flour; but since the Pope now wishes to make them only from white flour, your hope is nothing, for you are of common flour." Yet, as the same author notes, this gave that man no danger, and Alexander created no prince.

units.la: LXXXII. Creârunt autem alii multi ante eum, quidam etiam post eum, Principes Cardinales, etiam regali prosapiâ ortos; Quorum primus Cisalpinus, omnes ex regio Galliae sanguine, alii ex Hispanico, alii simpliciter tales apud Authorem tractatûs de l'Orig. des Card. Chap.6. videri possunt; quibus addimus, ex Anglis, Cardinalem Polum Regio sanguine satum, & Albertum Austriacum, Rodolphi Imperatoris fratrem. Ejusmodi autem μεγιστᾶνες τῆς γῆς, Magnates terrae, Apoc. XVIII.23. ut non studio Ecclesiam aedificandi, sed ob rationes Politicas & respectus terrenos dignitatem quaerunt, ita etiam plerique ad Ministerium Ecclesiasticum inepti planè sunt, meri, ut ex hypothesi cum M. Ant. de Dominis de Eccl. Rep. l.IV. c.5. n.64. loquar, laici, & nullo sacro ordine initiati, & fortasse nunquam initiandi, nec erubescimus, illos quoque inter Ecclesiae Praelatos numerare; Jam Ecclesia Romana in curiam versa est saecularem.
units.tr: LXXXII. Many others before him, and some after him, have indeed created princes Cardinals, even men of royal lineage. Of these, the first was Cisalpinus, all of the royal blood of France; others were of Spanish royal blood, and others simply such. They may be seen in the author of the treatise de l'Origine des Cardinaux, ch. 6. To these we add, from England, Cardinal Pole, born of royal blood, and Albert of Austria, brother of the Emperor Rudolf. Such "magnates of the earth" (Rev. 18:23, Greek megistanes tes ges) seek the dignity not out of zeal for building the Church, but for political reasons and earthly considerations. Thus most of them are also quite unfit for ecclesiastical ministry, "mere", to speak as Marcus Antonius de Dominis does (de Eccl. Rep. l. IV, c. 5, n. 64), on this hypothesis: "laymen, initiated into no sacred order and perhaps never to be initiated; nor are we ashamed to count them among the prelates of the Church. Now the Roman Church has been turned into a secular court."

units.la: LXXXIII. Sed non soli inepti sunt; alii etiam saepissimè creantur inepti, indigni, nullo meritorum, utpote quibus carent, sed omni alio respectu; Imò, quibus ne tanta quidem aptitudo tudo adest, quanta Principibus Theologicè etiam indoctissimis, interim tamen ad regnum illud mundanum educationis prærogativâ aptioribus. Sed ad Episcoporum, Presbyterorum, Diaconorum, quales titulotenus fiunt, munera quot apti eliguntur? Quot intentionem saltem istis muneribus vacandi habentes? Potiùs, quot primò minorennes contra Canones creati sunt? Exempla ex multis pauca dabo. Paulus III. referente Authore Conclavis Julii III. hà fatto &c. creavit duos Nepotes Cardinales, unum, filium Petri Ludovici 14. amorum, nomine Cardinalis Farnesii insignitum, & alterum parùm ætate maturiorem, quod malevolis occasionem dedit Sanctitatem suam eo nomine traducendi; quibus ut occurreret SS. prudentiâ plena, rumore ad ipsos etiam Lutheranos perlato, paulò post dignam illam Cardinalium promotionem instituit. In genere pronunciat Author Cardinalismi p.r.l. p.287. Papas promotionem sanguine conjunctorum quærere, poco curando &c. parùm curantes annorum difformitatem & meriti carentiam,prout fecit Julius III. qui dedit pileum puerulo, cognato suo, Paulus V. Mauritio Sabaudiæ Principi quatuordecim ferè annos nato, & Ferdinando Hispaniæ Infanti & Philippi III. filio decennî. Clemens VIII. filio cujusdam Nepotis sui, annos 14. nato, & Innocentius X. stupido & ignaro Maldachino, cujus ætatem immaturam annorum 18. patienter tulissent Cardinales, si aliquod meritum habuisset. De quo p.2.l.2. p.205.seqq. porrò testatur, eum creatum esse da gran violenza &c. ob exuberantem vim affectûs Papæ erga Dominam, Dominam Olympiam, fuisse monstrum naturâ, non potuisse pro voto Olympiæ ad Nepotismum erudiri, quia à ventre materno laborârit incredibili stupiditate,quem &statuam, & Phantasma porrò vocat, & Hispanorum Legati de eo, qui contra nationem aliquid locutus dicebatur, voces refert: Voce d'Asino non giunge al Cielo: Voces asininæ cœlum non attingunt. Ut in utroque etiam contra articulos in Conclavi Pii IV. juramento firmatos egerit, quatenus de non eligendo Cardinale per ætatem, aut aliâs incapace agunt.
units.tr: LXXXIII. But they are not only unfit; others too are very often created who are unfit and unworthy, having no merit, which they lack, but being chosen for every other reason. Indeed, some lack even that aptitude which princes possess, even those most untrained in theology, who are nonetheless more apt for that worldly kingdom by the prerogative of their upbringing. But how many are chosen as suitable for the offices of bishop, presbyter and deacon, which are conferred in name only? How many have even the intention of devoting themselves to those duties? Rather, how many have first been created while under age, contrary to the canons? I shall give a few examples out of many. Paul III, according to the author of the Conclave of Julius III, "made, etc.", created two nephews Cardinals: one, the son of Pierluigi Farnese, bearing the name of Cardinal Farnese, and the other somewhat younger in years, which gave malicious men the occasion to slander His Holiness on that account. To meet this, His Holiness, full of prudence, instituted, shortly afterwards, a worthy promotion of Cardinals, the rumour of which reached even the Lutherans. In general, the author of Cardinalismo (p. r. l. p. 287) asserts that Popes seek promotion for their blood relations, "caring little, etc.", that is, caring little about the disproportion of their ages and their lack of merit. Julius III did so, who gave the biretta to a little boy, his kinsman; Paul V to Maurice, Prince of Savoy, about fourteen years old, and to Ferdinand, Infante of Spain, son of Philip III, aged ten. Clement VIII to the son of one of his nephews, aged 14; and Innocent X to the stupid and ignorant Maldachini, whose immature age of eighteen the Cardinals would have endured patiently, had he had any merit. Concerning him the author further testifies (p.2 l.2 p.205 seqq.) that he was created "with great violence, etc." because of the excessive force of the Pope's affection for his lady, Donna Olimpia; that he was "a monster of nature," and could not be trained, as Olimpia wished, for nepotism, because "from the womb he laboured under incredible stupidity"; and he calls him "a statue and a phantom." He also reports the words of the Spanish envoy about him, who was said to have said something against the nation: "An ass's voice does not reach heaven." Thus in both respects Innocent acted against the articles confirmed by oath in the Conclave of Pius IV, which forbid electing a Cardinal who is by age, or otherwise, incapable.

units.la: LXXXIV. Nam & aliâs incapaces, indigni eliguntur.
units.tr: LXXXIV. For they also elect others who are incapable and unworthy.
