units.la: Qualesnam delectos reris; Verba sunt Baronii ad an. 912. ab his monstris (Papis illorum temporum;) Presbyteros & Cardinales fuisse putandum? Quum nihil tam naturâ insitum sit, quàm unumquemque sibi similem generare. Quales fuerunt à Sixto IV. creati? Cognoscimus illud ex fragmento literarum à Cardinali Papiensi ad Cardinalem Vice-Cancellarium in Hispaniis Legatum scriptarum, quod apud Bzovium ad an.1473. n.14. habetur: Majo praeterito,scribit, octo Cardinales creavimus: Hoc Junio eramus pene totidem creaturi, nisi benignitas Dei magis quam nostra diligentia subvenisset. Dilata tantum, non sublata est res. Quo autem ex genere hominum nostrum dedecus paretur, ex aliorum literis plene intelliges. Unum designabo aque cognitum tibi ac mihi: Nosti,quem toties spurium dixisti, quem cavere admonuisti semper: de quo etiam ego in arcanis commentariis Calixti nostri exempla diplomatum reperi sua manu descripta, quibus vitium ortus ad sacerdotia & dignitates Ecclesia tollebatur. Hunc ipsum nunc includere ordini nostro conabatur, qui potest, ac tanto quidem impetu,ut,quonam modo hanc jacturam evaserimus, ipse demirer. Nil tot annorum constans fama,non Patrum nonnullorum dissuasio, nil etiam testificatio mea valere apud precipitem animum poterat: Michaelis Ferrarii fides adhibebatur in medium, petebaturque ad testimonium dicendum, vel evocari huc, vel illius accipiendi curam tibi committi. Neutri est assensum. Nescio an de hoc ipso occulte admoniturus sint Michaelem, & procuraturi literas officiosi mendacii. En quales personas! En qualia apud Pontifices saepe studia! En artes! Quales etiam Alexandro VI. & Leoni X. non displicuisse Guicciardinus l.1. & 12. testatur.
units.tr: What sort of chosen men do you think they were? These are the words of Baronius at the year 912: were the presbyters and cardinals to be thought to have come from these monsters (the popes of those times)? Since nothing is so implanted by nature as for each to beget one like himself. What sort were those created by Sixtus IV? We know from a fragment of a letter written by the Cardinal of Pavia to the Vice-Chancellor, who was legate in Spain, which is found in Bzovius at the year 1473, n. 14. It reads: In May last, he writes, we created eight cardinals. This June we were going to create nearly as many, had not the kindness of God helped more than our own diligence. The matter has only been postponed, not abandoned. You will fully understand from the letters of others what kind of men our disgrace is being prepared from. I will point out one whom you and I both know well. You know the man whom you have so often called spurious, and whom you have always warned us to beware of. I have also found in the secret commentaries of our Calixtus copies of documents in his own hand, by which the defect of his birth was to be an obstacle to priesthoods and dignities in the Church. This very man was now trying to force his way into our order, and with such violence that I myself marvel how we escaped this loss. No fame of so many years' standing, nor the dissuasion of some of the Fathers, nor even my own testimony could prevail with his headlong mind. The trustworthiness of Michael Ferrarius was brought forward, and it was demanded either that he be summoned here to give evidence, or that the care of receiving him be committed to you. We assented to neither. I do not know whether they will secretly warn Michael about this very matter and arrange dutiful letters of white lies. Behold what kind of persons! Behold what arts are often practised with the Popes! Guicciardini testifies in books 1 and 12 that such men did not displease Alexander VI and Leo X.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Et quid judicandum est de illis 12. quos Alexander VI. idem apud eundem Guicciard. l. 5. ad an. 1500. propter pecunias creasse dicitur. Quid de illa promotione Clementis VII. qui,narrante Jovio in Pompejo Columna,expugnata Roma tres galeros purpureos concessit, ut, illis licitantibus, qui foeda ambitione corrupti ad senatoriam dignitatem aspirabant, aurum proferrent, eoque modo ad hastam propositis emtores non defuerunt. De quibus ita Tolosan. de Rep. Certe puto habitos ideo indignos, quod non per ostium, sed per fenestram ingredi vellent tam sanctissimum Senatum; Quomodo etiam Guicciardinus l. 18. de eodem Papa scribit: Creo per danari alcuni Cardinali, persone, la maggior parte, indegne di tanto honore: Id est: Creavit pro argento quosdam Cardinales maximam partem tanto honore indignos. Et quid quaeso de Paulo III. judicabimus, qui, ut ex Henr. Corn. Agrippa Wolf. Cent.XVI.p.127.f. ubi & alia pudenda habet, Roderico a Borgia Hispano, seu Alexandro VI. sororem suam Juliam Farnesiam stuprandam tradidit, ut Cardinalis, & Episcopus Hostiensis fieret? Qua conditione etiam Petrarchae Cardinalitius pileus oblatus in vita ejus legitur.
units.tr: And what must we judge of those twelve whom Alexander VI, according to the same Guicciardini in book 5, at the year 1500, is said to have created on account of money? What of that promotion of Clement VII, who, as Jovius relates in his life of Pompeius Columna, after Rome was captured, granted three red galero hats, so that those who were corrupted by shameful ambition and aspired to senatorial dignity might bid and bring out gold, and in this way buyers were not lacking for the offices put up for auction. Of these men Tolosanus says thus in On the Republic: Surely I think they were judged unworthy for this reason, that they wished to enter so most holy a Senate not through the door but through the window. Guicciardini also writes of the same Pope in book 18: He created for money some cardinals, persons for the most part unworthy of so great an honour. That is: He created for silver some cardinals, the greater part unworthy of so great an honour. And what, I ask, shall we judge of Paul III, who, according to Henricus Cornelius Agrippa in Wolf, Cent. XVI, p. 127, where he also gives other shameful facts, handed over his own sister Julia Farnese to be defiled by Roderic Borgia, the Spaniard, or Alexander VI, so that he might become a cardinal and bishop of Ostia? On the same condition, it is also read that a cardinal's hat was offered to Petrarch in his lifetime.

units.la: Ab Alexandro VI. Clemente VII. Paulo III.
units.tr: By Alexander VI, Clement VII, Paul III.

units.la: LXXXVI. Quid indignius unquam fuit tantâ Principis Ecclesiæ dignitate Innocentio illo juvene, cui Simia nomen, quòd in familia simiæ curam gesserat, retinenti Julius III. narrante Thuano l.6. 40. 181. statim adeptâ dignitate galerum suum, cognomen atque insignia, nefarii amoris seu Bononiæ, uti Suavis, seu Placentiæ, uti Pallavicinus, memorant, exerciti præmium exhibuit? Sed & quid indignius fuit responso à Vicario Christi & Monarcha Ecclesiæ Cardinalibus de promotione indigna querentibus dato: Et vos quid tandem in me meritorum comperistis, quem Christiana Reip. Principem constitueritis? Nec satis digna Pallavicini l.XIII.10.8. omnia, quantum potuit, emollire conantis verba; Pronum eum fuisse ad laxamenta: suum sanguinem deamavisse, variis purpuris inter consanguineos distributis &c.
units.tr: LXXXVI. What was ever more unworthy than the promotion, to so great a dignity of a Prince of the Church, of that young man Innocent, nicknamed Simia, because he had looked after a monkey in a household? When he was retained, as Thuanus relates in book 6, 40, 181, Julius III, immediately after he had obtained the dignity, gave him his galero, his title and his insignia, as the reward of an unlawful love, which some report was practised at Bologna, as Suavis does, and others at Piacenza, as Pallavicini does. But what was more unworthy than the answer given by the Vicar of Christ and Monarch of the Church to the cardinals who complained of the unworthy promotion: And what, pray, have you found in me of merit, that you should have set up a Prince for a Christian commonwealth? Nor are the words of Pallavicini, book 13, 10, 8, which try as much as they can to soften everything, worthy enough: He was prone to indulgence; he had loved his own blood, distributing various purples among his relatives, etc.

units.la: LXXXVII. De Clemente VIII. observârunt nonnulli,
units.tr: LXXXVII. Some have observed concerning Clement VIII,

units.la: juxta Conclave successoris, mortis causam habuisse perturbationem ex ultima Cardinalium creatione ortam, ò perche &c. aut quia viderit majorem ibi partem habuisse Principes, aut quia timuerit judicium mundi, qui videbatur in quibusdam promotis desiderare majus meritum diligentia, virtutis & nobilitatis. Et quis nescit, sæpe pro norma esse verba Nepotis Pontificis, cùm Cardinalismus ederetur, ante 30. annos nondum mortui, qui avunculo de meritis solicito audacter respondit: Ch'esso &c. se non opus habere Cardinalibus nisi in Conclavi, hinc parùm referre, utrum virtute aut eruditione destituti eligantur, modò apti sint ad votum dandum.
units.tr: that near the successor's conclave the cause of his death was a disturbance arising from the last creation of cardinals, oh why, etc., either because he saw that the greater part there belonged to the princes, or because he feared the judgment of the world, which seemed to demand in some of those promoted a greater merit of diligence, virtue and nobility. And who does not know that the words of a Pope's nephew have often served as the rule when cardinals were being created? About thirty years ago, when he was not yet dead, a nephew, anxious about merit, boldly replied to his uncle, That it is not that he has need of cardinals except in the conclave; hence it matters little whether they are chosen lacking virtue or learning, provided they are fit to give a vote.

units.la: LXXXVII. Qualis autem Urbanus VIII. fuit in promotionibus? Siveniva &c. Concludebant, inquit Author Conclavis Alexandri VII. valdè infelicem fuisse Papam hunc in promotionibus, & quòd semper magis inclinationem aut Nepotum, aut suorum, quàm verò meritum promovendorum respexit. Quibus II Cardinalismo p. 2.l.2.243. planè consentit. An Innocentius X. in solo Maldachini aberravit? Non. Cecchini era &c. Cecchini ab Innocentio creatus erat in secunda promotione, quæ prima fuit inter eas, quas vocabant plenas ***. Exprimere non ausus fuit. Aliquantò distinctiùs Il Card.l.4. Nisi Domina Olympia fuisset, tantùm bonos creaturum fuisse, quales, qui ex motu proprio, contrà promotos ad voluntatem Olympiæ, uno aut duobus plurimùm exceptis, numerum, non ornamentum auxisse. LXXXVIII. Nec felicior Alexander VII. fuit, & memoratu dignæ sunt responsiones Authoris Cardinalismi p. 2. l.2. p.258. ad quæstionem de eruditione Cardinalium Romā missæ, dum alius amicorum rescripsit ; Che i letterati &c. Doctos tam raros esse, ut, omni diligentiâ adhibitâ, non potuerit ullum investigare ; Alius ; Che erano &c. Tot Cardinales indoctos esse, ut docti inter eos non possint videri ; Alius, & quidem Sacerdos ; Che non si trovava &c. Nullum esse in Sacro Collegio Cardinalem, qui tantam in scholis literis operam navârit, quantam ipse in investigatione, quantam navârint. Alius, Academicus ille ; Che le lettere &c. Literarum studia in Curia non amplius in usu esse, quia quilibet esse velit doctus, ideò negligere Cardinales sapientiam, quia ipsis videatur nimis communis. Alius denique Romanus ; Che li Cardinali venivano fatti dal Pontefice, e dal Nipotismo, quali curavano molto più di trovar fogetti ricchi che dotti ; Id est : Cardinales creari à Pontifice & Nepotismo, qui magis divites quàm doctos quærant.
units.tr: LXXXVII. What sort of promotions, then, did Urban VIII make? They concluded, etc., says the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII, that this Pope was very unfortunate in his promotions, and that he always looked more to the inclination of his nephews or his own people than to the merit of those to be promoted. The author of Cardinalismus, part 2, book 2, p. 243, fully agrees with these. Did Innocent X go wrong only in the case of Maldachini? No. Cecchini was, etc. Cecchini was created by Innocent in the second promotion, which was the first of those they called full ***. He did not dare to express it. More distinctly, Il Card., book 4: Had not Lady Olympia been there, he would have created only good men; such as, who on their own initiative, against those promoted at Olympia's pleasure, with one or two excepted, increased the number, not the ornament. LXXXVIII. Alexander VII was no more fortunate, and the answers of the author of Cardinalismus, part 2, book 2, p. 258, to the question about the learning of the cardinals, sent from Rome, are worth recording, when one of his friends wrote back: That the learned are so rare that, though every diligence was applied, he could not find any. Another: That they were so many unlearned cardinals that the learned among them could not be seen. Another, and indeed a priest: That there was not to be found any cardinal in the Sacred College who had devoted as much effort to school learning as he himself had to investigation, or as much as they had. Another, that academic: That letters are no longer in use in the Curia, because everyone wishes to be learned, and therefore cardinals neglect wisdom because it seems to them too common. Finally another, a Roman: That cardinals were made by the Pope and by nepotism, who cared much more to find rich subjects than learned ones. That is: Cardinals are created by the Pope and by nepotism, who seek the rich rather than the learned.

units.la: LXXXIX. Quare etiam idem Author ita edoctus p.263.
units.tr: LXXXIX. Wherefore the same author, thus instructed, p.263.

units.la: subjungit: Corrono al presente altre raggioni &c. Id est: Alia jam respiciuntur, dum tam non in Vaticano eruditio prævalet, ut nemo eam audeat urgere, cùm sufficiat pulsare januas Gubernatorum illorum, qui omnia possunt, cum quadam auri crumena, quæ cuivis viam aperire potest. Hinc esse, quòd Sacerdos de causa ignorantiæ Sacerdotum interrogatus respondere potuerit: Sarebbono bestie &c. Id est: Homines essent bestiæ, si studiis incumberent, ut possent fieri Sacerdotes, si Papa Cardinales creat, qui sunt Asini; Atque omnes judicant, si Sacerdos bestia possit obtinere Pileum, multò magis facile fore Seculari Asino, accipere Canonicatum. Hinc etiam Religiosorum, si qui docti essent, spem esse inanem, già che l'ignoranza, e non la dottrina dona i luoghi nel Vaticano. Cùm ignorantia & non eruditio promoveat in Vaticano. Quæ certè inter Cardinales illius temporis eruditionis inopia in seculo tam docto admiratione omni major esset, nisi ex allatis simul conitaret, alia planè in promotionibus respici; Quod distinctiùs idem Author p.257. docet: Li Cardinali ordinari, inquit, ricevono il Capello, perche così lo vuole l'interesse del Nipotismo: li Principi accettano la porpora, perche così lo ricerca la maestà del Christianesmo e la riputatione del sagro Collegio. Id est: Cardinales ordinarii Pileum accipiunt, sic volentibus commodis Nepotum: Principes acceptant Purpuram, id exigente Majestate Christianismi & reputatione S. Collegii.
units.tr: He adds: Other reasons now come to mind, &c. That is: Other things are now taken into account, since learning so little prevails in the Vatican that no one dares to press it, when it is enough to knock at the doors of those governors who can do everything, with a certain purse of gold that can open any road to anyone. Hence a priest, asked why the priests were ignorant, could reply: The men would be beasts, if they devoted themselves to study so that they could become priests, if the Pope creates cardinals who are asses; and everyone judges that if a priest, being a beast, can obtain a cap, a secular ass will much more easily get a canonry. Hence too the hope of the religious, if any of them were learned, is empty, since ignorance, and not learning, gets places in the Vatican. Ignorance and not learning advances men in the Vatican. Indeed, the lack of learning among the cardinals of that time would be a source of the greatest wonder in so learned an age, were it not clear from what has been cited that other considerations are plainly regarded in promotions. The same author teaches this more distinctly, p.257. The ordinary cardinals, he says, receive the hat because the interest of nepotism so wills it; the princes accept the purple because the majesty of Christendom and the reputation of the sacred College require it. That is: Ordinary cardinals receive the cap, as the advantages of nephews wish; princes accept the purple, as the majesty of Christendom and the reputation of the Sacred College demand.

units.la: XC. Illi autem hos numero longè superant, quod Author p.244. querelam expressit: Gran vergogno in vero, &c. Id est: Pudendum sanè, à seculo circiter Pontifices non habuisse in animo, nisi creare creare Cardinales mancipia suorum Nepotum, neglectis Principibus & bene meritis, id est, talibus, qui tanto cum sudore laborárunt, bono non quidem Nepotismi, sed Ecclesiæ. Cur autem Principes plerumque negligantur, & ad eorum creationem Pontifices plumbeis pedibus incedant, ideò fieri judicat, quòd ambulent per certe strade independenti, per quasdam vias independentes, nec patiantur se tirar per il naso dal Nipotismo, à Nepotibus se naso circumduci. Hinc censeatur un voto perso per il Nipotismo, pileum principi datum esse votum Nepotismo perditum; Cùm tamen votis multis ad authoritatis saltem partem conservandam & persecutionem, si quæ à successore oriri posset, eò melius evitandam maximè opus habeant, & in eum finem Cardinalium quasi cohortes creari soleant. Quorum plerique, ut Author Card. dixit, numerum augent, non ornamentum, Qui & l. c. p. 264. judicat, maximè illud in die judicii Papis imputatum iri, di haver rigettata la virtù, e porporata l'ignoranza, quòd virtutem rejecerint, ignorantiam purpurá donaverint; posse melius nomen suum immortale reddere, addit, dignorum creatione, quàm verò auro Nepotibus relinqui solito, quod pereat, bona fama non item, interim illud Pontificibus esse gratius, augere culpam & magnum Cardinalium numerum, & sic duodenos creari, ex quibus nullus eruditus, non havendosi altra mira che la sodisfattione de'proprii interessi; Nihil aliud respicientibus Papis, quàm ut satisfiat commodis suis privatis. Tandem provocat p. 265. ad Historiam Curiæ Romanæ & descriptiones Promotionum, & claudit pessimo Urbani VIII. exemplo, qui post 70. creationem ultimis vitæ diebus doctum, sed non eo intuitu solo, creârit.
units.tr: XC. The princes, however, far outnumber these, which the author p.244. expressed in a complaint: Truly a shameful thing, &c. That is: It is certainly shameful that for about a century the Popes have had no purpose except to make cardinals the tools of their nephews, neglecting princes and those well deserving, that is, men who have laboured with such sweat, for the good not indeed of nepotism but of the Church. As to why princes are for the most part neglected, and why popes move with leaden feet when it comes to creating them, he judges that this happens because they walk by certain independent streets, by certain independent ways, and do not suffer themselves to be dragged by the nose by nepotism, to be led about by the nose by nephews. Hence the cap given to a prince is reckoned a vote lost to nepotism, a vote lost to nepotism; although the Popes have great need of many votes, at least to preserve part of their authority and to avoid, as far as possible, any persecution that might arise from a successor, and it is for this purpose that cardinals are usually created, as a kind of cohort. Most of them, as the author Card. said, increase the number, not the ornament. He also judges, l. c. p. 264., that this will be charged against the Popes most of all on the day of judgment, that they have rejected virtue and clothed ignorance in purple, that they have given ignorance the purple; he adds that they could make their name immortal better by creating the worthy than by leaving gold to their nephews, as is customary, which perishes, whereas good fame does not. Meanwhile, that course is more pleasing to the Popes: to increase the guilt and the great number of cardinals, and so to create twelve at a time, none of whom is learned, since they have no other aim than the satisfaction of their own interests; the Popes, looking to nothing else, than that their private advantages be satisfied. Finally he appeals p. 265. to the history of the Roman Curia and the accounts of promotions, and closes with the very bad example of Urban VIII, who, after the seventieth creation, in the last days of his life created a learned man, but not for that reason alone.

units.la: XCI. Creare autem amant Pontifices eum & alios in fines, hinc læti Cardinale quodam moriente, non minùs ac Cardinalibus mors Pontificis Evangelium esse solet, eodem p.256. annotante.
units.tr: XCI. The Popes also love to create cardinals for other ends too; hence they rejoice when some cardinal dies, and the death of a Pope is usually no less a gospel to the cardinals, as the same author notes p.256.

units.la: Finis autem non minimus est, quello d'empir la borsa, ut impleant crumenam p.245. Quemadmodum de Leone X. refertur, eum magnâ illâ & jam suprà Onuphrii verbis memorata 31. Cardinalium creatione 5000. ducatorum lucratum esse. Cum quo scopo non malè convenit, quod Sprengerus Instit. Jur. Publ. l. 2. c. 35. annotat: Facilior ad talem dignitatem perveniendi modus est, si quis prælaturam Camera emerit, quam si quis relinquere velit, cùm ex hac reditus, ex Cardinalatu verò sapius nihil habeant, (nempe per se, addunt post beneficia beneficiis;) facilè illam dignitatem attingere poterit.
units.tr: The end, moreover, is by no means small: that of filling the purse, that they may fill the purse p.245. As is reported of Leo X, that by his great creation of thirty-one cardinals, already mentioned above in the words of Onuphrius, he gained 5000 ducats. With this aim agrees well what Sprengerus notes in Instit. Jur. Publ. l. 2. c. 35.: An easier way to attain such a dignity is if someone has bought the prelacy of the Chamber, than if someone wishes to give it up, since from the former they have income, but from the cardinalate they often have nothing (namely in itself, they add, after benefices have been given for benefices); one will be able to attain that dignity easily.

units.la: Oo
units.tr: Oo

units.la: XCII. Sed
units.tr: XCII. Sed

units.la: XCII. Sed non negligenda est illa Authoris Cardinalismi p.145. observatio, che mentre si veggono &c. Id est: Dum Pontifices prosperâ valetudine utuntur, ab omni infirmitate remoti, vacuas relinquunt dignitates Cardinalitias, reditúsque interea sibi vendicant, sed appropinquante fine vitae eorum eas implent, ad exemplum Urbani VIII. qui per 7. annos nullum elegit, sed extremis vitae suae diebus simul 15. unâ creatione & aliâ 11. promovit. Sic & Alexander VII. ultimos vitae suae dies expectare voluit &c. Sed & desiderium creandi tam vehemens est, ut juxta authorem del Origine des Card. cap. 1. p. 10. aliquando creent, non cum assignatione tituli, sed sub expectatione tituli postea assignandi. Qualis creationis etiam exemplum subjicit. Scilicet egregius est Cardinalis, id est, fixus, ordinarius, proprius minister, qui ne quidem titulum habet; Sed fere eodem recidit, titulum non habere, &c, quod hodierni titulares faciunt, titulum habere, sed in illo non servire, nisi hoc pejus sit. Quandocunque autem creantur, acceptio pilei, ut Nepos in Conclavi Urbani VIII. loquitur, tantum beneficium est, ut omnium injuriarum memoriam delere, & defectui etiam aetatis mederi deberet.
units.tr: XCII. But the observation of the author of the Cardinalismi (p. 145) should not be neglected: while one sees etc. That is: While the Popes enjoy good health and are far from any sickness, they leave Cardinalate dignities vacant and meanwhile claim the revenues for themselves; but as the end of their life approaches, they fill them, as Urban VIII did, who for seven years created no one, but in the last days of his life promoted fifteen in one creation and eleven in another. So too Alexander VII wished to wait for the last days of his life, etc. Moreover, the desire to create is so strong that, according to the same author (del Origine des Card., ch. 1, p. 10), they sometimes create people without assigning a title, with the expectation of assigning one later. He also gives an example of such a creation. Namely, he is an egregius Cardinal, that is, a fixed, ordinary, proper minister, who does not even have a title. But it comes to nearly the same thing whether one has no title, or, as today's titular Cardinals do, has a title but does not serve in it, unless the latter is worse. Whenever they are created, however, receiving the biretta, as Nepos speaks of it in the Conclave of Urban VIII, is such a benefit that it ought to erase the memory of all injuries and even remedy the defect of age.

units.la: XCIII. Non autem abs re erit, post istum creandi amorem morémque indignos etiam creandi, hic ex eodem Authore c. p.71. seqq. aliquid de celebri illo seculi duodecimi Doctore Bernhardo compendiosè annotare. Nempe quaestionem proponit ad imitationem Ciaconii, qui admirationem suam alicubi expresserit, de eo, quòd Bonaventura & alii, quibus Thomas Aquinas nec eruditione, nec etiam vitae sanctitate inferior fuerit, ad Cardinalitiam dignitatem promoti sint, hic non item, & tandem causam illius differentiae in eo invenit, quòd familia Aquinatis à Gibellinorum, id est, ab Imperatoriis partibus steterit, hinc Guelphis, id est, Pontificiis exosa bono viro, licèt Cardinalatu dignissimo, promotionem intercepit; Idem se in Bernhardo mirari, inquit Author, cur nimirum tantus vir, Secretarius B. Virginis, miraculis clarus, centum & sexaginta Monasteriorum, quae ipso adhuc superstite fundata fuerint, Pater, non etiam ad instar tot Monachorum, Amicorum, discipulorum suorum, qualis ipse Eugenius III. Papa, eo etiam tum diu adhuc superstite fuerit, Cardinalis factus sit. Conjecturam autem de causa omissae sic promotionis hanc subjicit, fuisse libros Bernhardi de consideratione ad Eugenium, courageusement écrits, forti animo scriptos, & le mecontentement, qu'il témoignoit ouvertement à voir des appellations trop frequentes à Rome de toutes parts, &r des dispenses (par luy appellées dissipations de l'Eglise) trop souvent lors accordées ; tristitiam , quam expresserit aperte ob appellationes nimium frequentes Romam undique factas , & dispensationes (quibus nomen dissipationum dabat) aequo saepius concessas ; fuisse Epistolas quibusdam Cardinalibus scriptas, des quels il ne pouvoit approuver les deportemens , quorum inordinatas actiones approbare non poterat; & inter alios Cardinali Jordano, Legato Papæ, qui in itinere per Germaniam , Galliam & Normanniam avoit acquis une fort mauvaise reputation , famam valde malam acquisiverit, id quod Sanctum Virum moverit ad mittendam ei Epistolam 290. ex suis,pleine d'aigreur, acrimonia plenam; Omnes illius sinceras & intrepidas reprehensiones suo judicio causam fuisse sic omissæ promotionis, licèt optimè meritæ; fuisse Bernhardum plenum libertate Gallica, magnóque zelo bonum Ecclesiæ quæsivisse, ut appareat ex 5. libris de consideratione &c. Ut ex utroque exemplo jam mihi post authores illos Pontificios concludere liceat, jam tum veri impatientes Papas fuisse, & in promotionibus in specie ad Cardinalatum magis affectuum quàm virtutis merita secutos esse. Sed addi posset alia quaestio, cur tam pauci eligantur Cardinales Germani? Ad quam Henricus Pantaleon p.2. de Vir. Illust. Germ. ad a. 1444. respondet; Hanc unicam causam esse, quia Sigismundus Imperator noluerit admittere, ut Ecclesias Germanicas pro sua voluntate administrarent. Digna certè & haec causa est, & morem Cardinalium Episcopatus administrandi valde commendat.
units.tr: XCIII. It will not be out of place, after this love of creating and the custom of creating even the unworthy, to note briefly from the same author (c. p. 71 seqq.) something about that famous doctor of the twelfth century, Bernard. He poses a question in imitation of Ciaconius, who somewhere expressed his astonishment that Bonaventure and others, to whom Thomas Aquinas was not inferior in learning or even in holiness of life, were promoted to the Cardinalate dignity, but he was not. In the end he finds the cause of this difference in the fact that the family of Aquinas stood with the Gibellines, that is, with the imperial party; hence the good man, though most worthy of the Cardinalate, was denied promotion, being hated by the Guelphs, that is, by the Papists. The author says that he likewise wonders about Bernard: why, namely, such a great man, secretary of the Blessed Virgin, famous for miracles, father of one hundred and sixty monasteries founded while he was still alive, and not also, like so many monks, friends and disciples of his, was made a Cardinal, even though Pope Eugene III himself, who was still alive for a long time afterward. He offers this conjecture about the cause of the omitted promotion: that there were Bernard's books On Consideration addressed to Eugene, written courageously, with a bold spirit, and the displeasure which he openly showed at the too frequent appeals from every quarter to Rome and the dispensations (which he called "dissipations of the Church") too often granted then; that there were letters written to certain Cardinals, whose conduct he could not approve, whose disorderly actions he could not approve; and among others to Cardinal Jordan, Papal Legate, who on his journey through Germany, Gaul and Normandy had acquired a very bad reputation; which moved the holy man to send him the 290th of his letters, full of bitterness. In the author's judgment, all his sincere and fearless rebukes were the cause of the promotion being omitted, though he had most richly deserved it. Bernard, he says, was full of Gallic frankness and with great zeal sought the good of the Church, as appears from the five books On Consideration, etc. So from both examples I may now conclude, following those Papist authors, that already at that time the Popes were impatient of truth, and in promotions, especially to the Cardinalate, they followed the merits of their passions rather than of virtue. But another question could be added: why are so few German Cardinals chosen? To this Henricus Pantaleon (p. 2, de Vir. Illust. Germ., ad a. 1444) replies: that this is the only cause, namely that the Emperor Sigismund was unwilling to allow the German Churches to be administered at their own pleasure. Surely this reason is worthy, and it strongly commends the custom of Cardinals administering bishoprics.

units.la: XCIV.
units.tr: XCIV.

units.la: Qualis creatio, talis etiam plerunque subsequens est creatorum actio. De qua post illam non multa nobis dicenda restant; Nam facilè de caeteris praesumitur, etiam in omnibus fastu, in vestibus luxu, consideratis. Officium genuinum negligi supra ostendimus; Heic paucis ex Conciliis recentioribus notamus, ne quidem praestare , quae etiam post degenerationes à genuina Cardinalium ratione ab illis expectes. Basileense sess.23. Ecclesiarum, titulorum conservationem, visitationes suorum titulorum, & Cleri in iisdem servientis, curam & vigiliam contra haereses & superstitiones iis commendat. De quibus certè paucissimi soliciti sunt: Sed quis eorum praestat, quod erga Papam injunctum est officium? Si quando Papam, inquiunt Patres, quod absit, negligentem aut remissum, seu agentem, quae statum illius non decent, ipsi Cardinales inspexerint, filiali reverentia rentia & charitate, tanquam Patrem obsecrent, ut officio Pastorali, honorique ac debito suo satisfaciat. Et primò quidem aliquis vel aliqui de per se, deinde, si se non corrigat, omnes collegialiter, accersitis quibusdam notabilibus Prælatis: prædicentes, quòd si non abstinuerit, proximo generali Concilio deferent: nec pro salute ipsius summi Pontificis & bono publico , vel quicquam aliud timeant: dum tamen reverenter & charitativè id agant. Hìc certè obtinere deberent verba Bernhardi ep. 188. Agite pro loco, quem tenetis, pro dignitate, qua polletis, pro potestate, quam accepistis. Sic etiam minùs cum praxi hodierna supra memorata & porrò memoranda conveniunt, quæ Concilium quoad benignam & honorificam pertractationem Prælatorum, minùs conveniunt, quæ de non ditandis agnatis, minùs conveniunt, quæ de familia, mensa, supellectile rerum & equorum tam Papæ, quàm Cardinalium, nec numerositate, nec fastu, aut Pompis, neque aliquo excessu reprehensibili, præscribit.
units.tr: As the creation is, so for the most part is the conduct of those created. Little remains for us to say about this after the creation; for from the rest one can easily presume, once the pride in everything and the luxury in clothing are considered. We have shown above that the genuine office is neglected; here we briefly note from more recent Councils what you could not even expect from them, even after their degeneration from the genuine principle of the Cardinals. The Council of Basel (sess. 23) commends to them the preservation of churches and titles, visitations of their titles, and the care and vigilance of the clergy serving in them against heresies and superstitions. Very few are indeed concerned with these matters. But who among them performs the duty enjoined toward the Pope? If ever, the Fathers say, the Cardinals themselves should see the Pope, which God forbid, negligent or remiss, or acting in ways unbecoming his station, let them beseech him, with filial reverence and charity, as a Father, to fulfil his pastoral office, his honour and his duty. And first indeed one or several of them on their own, then, if he does not correct himself, all together as a college, having summoned certain notable Prelates, warning that if he does not refrain, they will refer the matter to the next general Council; nor should they fear anything for the salvation of the Supreme Pontiff himself or for the public good, provided they act reverently and charitably. Here surely the words of Bernard (ep. 188) ought to hold: Act in the place you hold, by the dignity you possess, by the power you have received. So too the present practice mentioned above, and to be mentioned further, agrees the less with these things: what the Council prescribes concerning the kind and honourable treatment of Prelates agrees the less; what it prescribes concerning not enriching relatives agrees the less; and what it prescribes concerning the household, table, and furnishings, of goods and horses, both of the Pope and of the Cardinals, neither in number, nor in pride, nor in pomp, nor in any blameworthy excess.

units.la: XCV. Minùs etiam conveniunt, quæ præscripsit recentius sub Leone X. Lateranense Concilium Sess. 9. de iisdem ferè, iisdem verbis ferè, nisi quòd prolixiùs est quoad Prælatorum tractationem: Prælatos, decernit cum Concilio Pontifex, ad Romanam Curiam venientes benignè honorificéque, tam publicè quàm privatim tractent: & apud nos & successores nostros gratiosè liberaliterque eorum negotia commendata suscipiant. Præterea ministerium indecorum (quod ex tempore Concilii Basileensis demum irrepserat) Episcoporum Prælatorumque in domibus non habeant, ne cæteris præesse instituti, & sacro charactere insigniti in vilia descendant ministeria: passimque pastoralis officii contemptum inducant. Eos itaque, quos vel nunc habent (in ministerio) vel in posterum sunt habituri, honorificè ut fratres, ac juxta eorum statûs condecentiam tractent &c. Idem etiam titulorum & Ecclesiarum commendatam curam commendat, fastum, luxum & prodigalitatem, sed non Papæ, fugiendam esse dicit, leges vestiarias ponit, Legatis à Latere officium per se, & non per officiales faciendum imponit, & funebres expensas Cardinalium 1500. florenorum summam, (dura lex, nec semper observata. Vide de Pompa funebri Il Card. p. 1. l. 3. p. 364. seqq.) excedere vetat.
units.tr: XCV. Less in agreement still are the things prescribed more recently under Leo X by the Lateran Council (Sess. 9), nearly on the same matters and in nearly the same words, except that it is more prolix concerning the treatment of Prelates: The Pontiff decrees with the Council that Prelates coming to the Roman Curia are to be treated kindly and honourably, both in public and in private; and that their business is to be taken up by us and our successors graciously and generously. Furthermore, the unseemly ministry (which had crept in only since the time of the Council of Basel) of Bishops and Prelates in their households they shall not have, lest those appointed to preside over others and marked with the sacred character should descend to base ministries and everywhere induce contempt for the pastoral office. Therefore those whom they now have, or shall have in future, in ministry, they shall treat honourably as brothers, and according to the propriety of their station, etc. The same Council likewise commends the careful attention to titles and churches; it says that pride, luxury and prodigality are to be avoided, but not by the Pope; it lays down sumptuary laws; it imposes on Legates a Latere that they perform their office in person, and not through officials; and it forbids the funeral expenses of Cardinals to exceed the sum of 1500 florins (a harsh law, and not always observed; see on funeral pomp, Il Cardinale, p. 1, l. 3, p. 364 seqq.).

units.la: XCVI. Sed juvabit ex ipso consilio delectorum Cardinalium & aliorum Prælatorum de emendanda Ecclesia jussu Pauli III. conscripto & exhibito, atque ad finem Hist. Conc. Trid. Petri Sarpii edito, cognoscere, an Cardinales faciant, quod ipsis incumbit; Ita inter alia se habet: Alius etiam abusus invaluit, ut Reverendiss. Card. Card. Episcopatus conferantur, seu commendentur, non unus tantùm, sed plures, quem, Pater Beatissime, putamus magni esse momenti in Ecclesia Dei: primò quidem, quia officium Cardinalatus & officium Episcopi, incompatibilia sunt. Nam Card. est assistere Sanctitati Tuæ in gubernanda universali Ecclesia. Officium autem Episcopi est, pascere gregem suum, quod præstare bene, nec, ut debet, potest, nisi habitet cum ovibus suis, ut pastor cum grege. Præterea Pater Sanct. hic usus maximè obest exemplo. Quomodo namque hac Sancta Sedes poterit dirigere & corrigere aliorum abusus, si in præcipuis suis membris abusus tolerantur? Nec ob id, quòd Cardinales sint, putamus eis magis licere transgredi legem, imò longè minùs. Horum enim vita debet esse aliis lex: nec imitandi sunt Pharisæi, qui dicunt, & non faciunt, sed Christus Salvator noster incepit facere, & postea docere. Amplius hic usus nocet in consultationibus Ecclesiæ, nam hac licentia est fomentum avaritiæ. Ambiunt præterea Card. à Regibus & Principibus Episcopatus, à quibus postea dependent: nec possunt liberè sententiam dicere, imò si possent & vellent, fallerentur tamen passione animi in judicando perturbati. Ideò utinam hic mos tolleretur, & provideretur Card. ut possent honestè pro dignitate vivere, omnibus æquales redditus, quod putamus facilè fieri posse, si vellemus abjicere servitutem Mammonæ, & Christo tantùm servire. Et quibusdam interjectis: Abusus etiam est, quòd tot Reverendiss. Card. absint ab hac Curia, nec aliqua in parte faciant quicquam ejus officii, quod spectat ad Cardinales. Ideo, & si fortasse non omnes, quia expedire existimamus, nonnullos habitare in provinciis suis, nam per illos tanquam per radices quasdam in totum Orbem Christianum sparsas continentur populi sub hac Romana Sede, plurimos tamen esset Sanctitatis Tuæ vocare ad Curiam, ut hic residerent. Hac enim ratione, præterquam quòd fungerentur officio suo Card. provideretur etiam amplitudini Curiæ, suppleretúrque, si quid ei detractum fuisset per recessum multorum Episcoporum, qui ad suas Ecclesias se contulissent.
units.tr: XCVI. But it will be helpful to learn from the very counsel of the chosen Cardinals and other prelates on amending the Church, drawn up and presented at the command of Paul III and printed at the end of Pietro Sarpi's Hist. Conc. Trid., whether the Cardinals are doing what is incumbent on them. It runs thus, among other things: Another abuse has crept in, that the most reverend Cardinals are given, or commended with, not one bishopric but several. Most blessed Father, we consider this to be of great importance in the Church of God. First, the office of Cardinal and the office of bishop are incompatible. The duty of a Cardinal is to assist Your Holiness in governing the universal Church. The duty of a bishop is to feed his flock, which he cannot properly do, nor as he ought, unless he lives among his sheep, as a shepherd lives with his flock. Moreover, Holy Father, this practice is especially harmful as an example. For how can this Holy See correct the abuses of others if abuses are tolerated among its principal members? Nor, because they are Cardinals, do we think they should be allowed to break the law more than others; indeed, far less. For their life ought to be a law to others. They must not imitate the Pharisees, who say and do not do; rather, our Saviour Christ began by doing and afterwards by teaching. Furthermore, this practice does harm to the Church's consultations, for this licence is a breeding ground for greed. Besides, Cardinals seek bishoprics from kings and princes, on whom they afterwards depend, and so they cannot speak their opinion freely. Indeed, even if they could and would, they would be deceived, disturbed in their judgement by the passion of their minds. Therefore we wish this custom were abolished, and that provision were made for the Cardinals to be able to live honourably in keeping with their dignity, with equal revenues for all. We think this could easily be done if we were willing to cast off the slavery of Mammon and serve Christ alone. And after some intervening words: It is also an abuse that so many most reverend Cardinals are absent from this Curia and do nothing of their office, which pertains to the Cardinals. Therefore, although perhaps not all, because we think it expedient, some should live in their provinces, for through them, as through roots spread throughout the whole Christian world, peoples are held under this Roman See. Nonetheless, it would be well to call most of them to the Curia so that they might reside here. For in this way, besides the Cardinals fulfilling their office, provision would also be made for the dignity of the Curia, and what had been taken from it through the departure of many bishops, who had gone off to their own churches, would be made up.

units.la: XCVII.
units.tr: XCVII.

units.la: An post consider ationes has non liceret cum Gallicana natione in Catal. Test. Verit. p.278. concludere, Cardinalium statum nimiùm Ecclesiæ onerosum & non necessarium esse? Licet etiam maximè vitæ, quam plerique vivunt, intuitu. Vita plerunque nihil minùs quàm Apostolica est, cùm tamen Apostolorum, primorum, si bene nomen imponunt, Cardinalium, successores, & potestatis eorum hæredes ex asse esse velint; Et Antonino quidem p. 3. p. 2. tit. 2. Domini sunt isti Cardines terra 1.Sam.II. non tantùm quia sunt Domini Papæ fratres & familiares per eximiam dignitatem, & quia sunt Domini mundi, gubernatores per consultabilitatem; sed etiam quia sunt Domini Dei peculiares per perfectam bonitatem; quemadmodum etiam inter rationes Zecchii pro summa Cardinalium dignitate illud memoratur, quòd habeant majorem erga Deum caritatem omnibus Episcopis; Sed non habent; Imò nequidem faciunt, quæ ultimorum temporum norma requirit. in Concilio citato Lateranensi l. c. hæc habentur. Cùm R. S. E. Cardinales, cæteros omnes in Ecclesia ipsa post summum Pontificem, honore ac dignitate precedant: Conveniens ac debitum est, ut vitæ munditiâ ac virtutum splendore cunctis præfulgeant. Quapropter non modò hortamur eos, ac monemus; verùm etiam statuimus, & ordinamus, ut de cetero quilibet Cardinalium pro tempore existens, juxta doctrinam Apostolicam sobriè, castè ac piè vivat, ut non solùm à malo, sed ab omni specie etiam mali abstinens coram hominibus luceat, Deúmque imprimis operibus honorificet. Sint omnes vigiles, ac divinis officiis missarúmque celebrationibus intenti &c.
units.tr: Having considered these things, could one not conclude with the French nation in the Catal. Test. Verit. p.278. that the state of the Cardinals is excessively burdensome to the Church and not necessary? One might do so even with regard to the life that most of them live. Their life is for the most part anything but apostolic, although they wish to be, in full, the successors of the Apostles, the first (if the name is rightly given) Cardinals, and the heirs of their power. Antoninus, indeed, p. 3. p. 2. tit. 2. says: "They are the lords of the earth's pillars" (1 Sam. 2.), not only because they are the lord Pope's brothers and intimates by their outstanding dignity, and because they are lords of the world, governing by their counsel; but also because they are the peculiar lords of God through perfect goodness. Likewise, among the reasons Zecchi gives for the high dignity of the Cardinals, this is recorded: that they have a greater love for God than all bishops. But they do not have it. Indeed they do not even do what the rule of the latest times requires. In the Lateran Council cited above, l.c., the following is found: Since the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church surpass all others in the Church itself, after the supreme Pontiff, in honour and dignity, it is fitting and due that they should shine above all in purity of life and splendour of virtues. Therefore we not only exhort and admonish them, but also decree and ordain that henceforth each Cardinal who exists at any time should live soberly, chastely and piously according to Apostolic teaching, so that, abstaining not only from evil but from every appearance of evil, he may shine before men and above all honour God by his works. Let all be watchful, and intent on the divine offices and the celebration of Masses, etc.

units.la: XCVIII. Talesne sunt? Itane faciunt? Non sunt, non faciunt plerique, ut ex sequentibus patebit. Quid autem, si norma Bernhardi de Consid. l. 4. c. 4. adhibeatur? In talibus, ut opinor, requiesceret spiritus tuus, qui non attrita frontis, sed verecundi, sed timorati: qui præter Dominum timeant nihil, nihil sperent nisi à Deo. Qui adventantium non manus attendant, sed necessitates. Qui sint compositi ad mores, probati ad sanctimoniam, parati ad obedientiam, mansueti ad patientiam, subjecti ad disciplinam, rigidi ad censuram, Catholici ad fidem, fideles ad dispensationem, concordes ad pacem, conformes ad unitatem, in adversitate securi, in prosperitate devoti, in Zelo sobrii, in misericordia non remissi, in ocio non ociosi, in hospitio non dissoluti, in convivio non effusi, in cura rei familiaris non anxii, aliena non cupidi, suæ non prodigi, ubique & in omnibus circumspecti. Qui legatione pro Christo fungi, quoties opus erit, nec jussi renuant, nec non jussi affectent. Qui Regibus Joannem exhibeant, Ægyptiis Moysen, fornicantibus Phinees, Heliam Idololatris, Helisæam avaris, Petrum mentientibus, Paulum blasphemantibus, negotiantibus Christum; Qui vulgus non spernant, sed doceant, qui Ecclesias non spoliant, sed emendent, qui marsupia non exhauriant, sed corda reficiant. Qui non de dote viduæ, & patrimonio crucifixi se vel suos ditare festinent, gratis dantes, quod gratis acceperunt &c. XCIX. Sed
units.tr: XCVIII. Are they such? Do they act so? Most of them are not, and do not act so, as will be clear from what follows. But what if the standard of Bernard de Consid. l. 4. c. 4. is applied? Among such men, I think, your spirit would rest: men not with brows hardened but modest and fearful of God; who fear nothing but the Lord and hope for nothing but from God; who look not at the hands of those who approach them but at their needs; who are settled in morals, proven in holiness, ready for obedience, gentle in patience, subject to discipline, strict in censure, Catholic in faith, faithful in stewardship, agreeable for peace, conformed to unity, secure in adversity, devout in prosperity, sober in zeal, not lax in mercy, not idle in leisure, not dissolute in hospitality, not lavish at table, not anxious over household affairs, not covetous of what is another's, not prodigal of their own, circumspect everywhere and in all things. Men who serve as legates for Christ whenever needed, who neither refuse when sent nor seek to go when not sent; who present John to kings, Moses to the Egyptians, Phinehas to fornicators, Elijah to idolaters, Elisha to the greedy, Peter to liars, Paul to blasphemers, Christ to traders; who do not despise the common people but teach them; who do not plunder the churches but mend them; who do not empty purses but refresh hearts; who do not hasten to enrich themselves or their own from the dowry of the widow and the patrimony of the crucified, giving freely what they have received freely, etc. XCIX. But

units.la: XCIX. Sed quàm bene vitæ diversas rationes, & ab Apostolorum moribus degenerationes ob oculos posuit Capucinus ille, qui referente Auditore, Authore Cardinalismi 193. in quadragesima Romæ in conventu d'Araceli præsentibus duobus Cardinalibus in illos etiam defixis oculis & præmissis præmitti solitis, sed sine textûs ullius præleEione post breve silentium ita subitò exorsus est: Pazzo san Petro &c. Stultus Petrus, stultus Paulus, stulti Apostoli, stulti Martyres, stulti omnes primitivi sancti Ecclesiæ Jesu Christi Redemptoris nostri. Quibus verbis insolitis Cardinalibus quasi in statuas mutatis, universo populo stupente, & ore aperto exitum initii audire cupiente, post aliquot rursus silentii momenta subjunxit: Prelati, non credete voi salvar vi? Padre sì, sò che me risponderete &c. Pralati an vos salutem consequuturos esse creditis? Ita Pater, mihi respondebitis. Omnis populo (oportuit enim populum immiscere, ne Cardinales de manifesta contumelia querendi facilem occasionem arriperent, & ut malum in aula non manere ostenderetur;) annon certus es de Paradiso? Sine dubio, responsum dabitis. Ita, ego dico vobis, noctem in diem, & diem in noctem in convivis, deliciis, profusionibus commutando? Ita, totum diem in curribus obambulando? totam noctem in Comœdiis stando, purpura & bysso, auro & argento vosmet vestiendo? Ita, caudas sericì per plateas trahendo? Vitam Sardanapali vivendo? Ita, Templa Sacra ad vestiendos muros profanos spoliando, & Christo, quod mundo datis, auferendo? Itane salvari vultis, o Romani? Igitur Apostoli, igitur sancti primitivi, dum potuissent eodem modo salvari, fuerunt stulti, mundum in miseriis obambulando &c. Fallimini, o Romani, Apostoli &c. sancti primitivi fuerunt sapientissimi &c. si nolumus &c. Sed vos estis stulti &c. Postea prælegit textum: Ductus est Jesus in desertum.
units.tr: XCIX. But how well that Capuchin set before our eyes the different ways of life and the degeneracy from the manners of the Apostles, he who, as the Author of Cardinalismi 193 reports on the testimony of a hearer, during Lent in Rome, in the convent of Aracoeli, with two Cardinals present, their eyes fixed upon those whom they usually send ahead, began suddenly, after a brief silence and without reading any text, in these words: Foolish Peter, foolish Paul, foolish Apostles, foolish Martyrs, foolish all the first holy ones of the Church of Jesus Christ our Redeemer. With these unusual words the Cardinals were turned as if to statues, the whole people stood amazed and eager with open mouth to hear the outcome of the beginning. After a few more moments of silence he added: Prelates, do you not believe you will be saved? Father, yes, I know what you will answer, etc. Prelates, do you believe you will attain salvation? So, Father, you will answer me. Everyone (for it was necessary to mix in the people, so that the Cardinals would not seize an easy occasion to complain of open insult, and so that it might be shown that the evil does not remain in the court) are you not certain of Paradise? Without doubt, you will reply. Yes, I tell you, changing night into day and day into night in banquets, delights and extravagances? Yes, passing the whole day driving about in carriages? Spending the whole night at the theatre, clothing yourselves in purple and fine linen, gold and silver? Yes, dragging silk trains through the streets? Living the life of Sardanapalus? Yes, plundering the sacred temples to adorn profane walls, and taking from Christ what you give to the world? Do you, O Romans, want to be saved in this way? Then the Apostles, then the first holy ones, while they could have been saved in the same way, were foolish, wandering through the world in miseries, etc. You are deceived, O Romans, the Apostles, etc. The first holy ones were most wise, etc. if we do not wish, etc. But you are foolish, etc. Afterwards he read the text: Jesus was led into the wilderness.

units.la: C. Facit applicationem non malam Author de Christianis hodiernis quibuscunque, sed de Cardinalibus: Se pur non vogliamo &c. Si nolumus, inquit, includere simul cum illis Pontifices ipsos, prosequitur p.204. Se ne stanno in Roma &c. Roma degunt in deliciis Apollinis, & in Apolline deliciarum, quotidie soliciti de exaltandis Palatiis, quæ cum cœlis quasi altitudine certent, de præparandis hortis ita deliciosis, ut prærogativam quasi eripiant terrestri illi Paradiso omnipotentis Dei manibus fabricato, & de multiplicando famulitio, usque adeò, ut possint superâsse maximorum orbis Monarchiarum aulas &c. Divitiarum & felicitatis Ecclesiæ pluvias avidè hauriunt, & sibi appropriant, quæ etiam intercidunt molestia, laboris, afflictionum gutta, à Dominus Cardinalibus, Sanctissi-
units.tr: C. The author makes a not unfair application, not to Christians in general today, but to the Cardinals: Even if we do not wish, etc. If we do not wish, he says, to include the Popes themselves along with them, he goes on, p.204. They stay in Rome, etc. They live in Rome in the delights of Apollo, and in Apollo's delights, daily anxious to raise palaces that vie with the heavens in height, to prepare gardens so pleasant that they almost snatch away the prerogative of that earthly paradise fashioned by the hands of almighty God, and to multiply their retinues to such an extent that they may have surpassed the courts of the greatest monarchies of the world. They greedily drink in the showers of the Church's riches and happiness and appropriate them to themselves, and these are also mixed with the drops of trouble, labour and affliction, from the Lord Cardinals, most holy

units.la: Quomodo vivant; Ex Concione cujusdam Capucini; Sanctissimis Pontificibus procul esse jubentur; regalia sunt ista pauperum Monachorum, munera ordinis Capucinorum, dona Reverendorum Missionariorum, vel pauperis cujusdam Episcopuli. Subdit, animarum curam aliis plane reliquit infausto sydere natis: mentre i Cardinali se ne spasseggiano in Carozza per Roma &c. dum interea temporis Cardinales in curribus Romam obambulant, dum ad sonum instrumentorum Musicalium prandiunt; dum viriditate hortorum veris tempore delectantur, & dum servitia sibi procurant tanta Majestatis, qua Principibus propria est.
units.tr: How they live: from a sermon of a certain Capuchin. Most holy Popes are bidden to keep away; these things are the royal privileges of poor monks, the offices of the Capuchin order, the gifts of the Reverend Missionaries, or of some poor little bishop. He adds: They have left the care of souls entirely to those born under an unlucky star, while the Cardinals stroll about Rome in carriages, etc. while meanwhile the Cardinals drive about Rome in their coaches, while they dine to the sound of musical instruments, while they delight in the greenery of their gardens in springtime, and while they procure for themselves such a retinue of majesty as belongs to princes.

units.la: CI. Quem luxum post p.206. &c. exaggerat ex Episcoporum & Sacerdotum multorum inopia, quibus jejunandum, & à quibus quasi ostiatim victus necessarius à secularibus emendicandus sit, qualis etiam Episcopi pauperis querelas p.208. subjungit, addi molestias molestiis Episcoporum, divitias divitiis Cardinalium ditissimorum, omnia dari nihil facientibus, nihil dari facientibus omnia. Et suas: Dio sa, quello dicono &c. Deus novit, quid Roma dicant centeni Episcopi mendici, ne dicam, pauperes, videntes, ex reditibus Episcopatuum suorum, id est, ex sudore frontis sua & ex vigiliis tot molestiarum; videntes ex visceribus tot miserarum animarum, qua timent acerbas purgatorii flammas nutriri in stabulis Cardinalium, & in equilibus Nepotum & Pontificum duodenos & centenos caballos, argento fidelium Ecclesia ad nutriendos pauperes dato emptos; imo majoribus Roma gaudere equos Pontificis, & Mulos Nepotis privilegiis pra Episcopis, dum his non conceditur aula gravamina sua aperire, illi subtractiones avena facile produnt, quod forte occasionem dedit non nemini, dicendi; Se malle esse Mulum Papae, quàm verò Episcopum Orvietanum! p.210. Alium Sacerdotem in convivio, cui ipse etiam interfuerit, non inepte, quod res est, dixisse, narrat Author, optando reducta tempora Cibationis multorum panibus paucis; Per supplicare il Signore &c. Ad rogandum Dominum Deum, ut velit Cardinales dignari multiplicatione divitiarum, prout multiplicavit quinque panes hordeaceos, quandoquidem alii non possint habere nisi reliquias Cardinalium. p.212. Confer cum his, quae apud Baronium ad an. 106. c. n. 41. de luxu Clericis interdicto habentur.
units.tr: CI. The author goes on, p.206. etc., to lament the great poverty of many bishops and priests, who must fast, and who must beg their necessary food from laymen almost door to door. He adds also the complaint of a poor bishop, p.208.: that troubles are added to the troubles of bishops and riches to the riches of the very wealthy Cardinals, that everything is given to those who do nothing, and nothing to those who do everything. And his own words: God knows what the hundred beggarly bishops, not to say poor ones, say in Rome, seeing that from the revenues of their bishoprics, that is, from the sweat of their brow and the watches of so many troubles, seeing from the very bowels of so many wretched souls, who fear that the harsh flames of purgatory are being fed, in the stables of the Cardinals and in the stalls of the nephews and Popes, twelve and a hundred horses bought with the money of the faithful, given to the Church to feed the poor; indeed, the horses of the Pope and the mules of the nephew enjoy greater privileges in Rome than the bishops, since the bishops are not permitted to lay their grievances before the court, while the others easily betray their deprivations through the withholding of oats. This perhaps gave occasion to someone to say: that he would rather be the Pope's mule than the Bishop of Orvieto! p.210. The author relates that another priest, who was himself present at a banquet, said, not inappropriately, as is the case, wishing back the times when the many were fed with few loaves: To pray to the Lord, etc. to ask the Lord God that he would deign to multiply the riches of the Cardinals, just as he multiplied the five barley loaves, since others can have nothing but the leftovers of the Cardinals. p.212. Compare with this what is found in Baronius at the year 106, c. n. 41, concerning the luxury forbidden to clergy.

units.la: CII. Sed aliquando generalia sunt ista, & fortè hodierni moris tantùm. Sufficeret equidem nostri temporis iniquitas, verùm non est χρῆς ἡ συνέχρες nata. Testis sit Platina, qui in Stephano III. occasione supplicationis illo tempore indictae in sequentem querelam erumpit: Nunc verò adeò refrixit pietas & religio, non dico, nudi nudis pedibus; sed caligati & cothurnati vix supplicare dignantur. Non flent inter eundum, vel dum sacrificant, ut illi Sancti Patres: sed rident & quidem impudenter; debis & loquor, quos purpura insigniores facit; non hymnos canunt, id enim servile videtur, sed jocos & fabulas ad risum concitandum inter se narrant. Quid plura? Quò quis dicacior est & petulantior, eò majorem in tam corruptis moribus laudem meretur, severos & graves viros reformidat hic Clerus noster. Quid ita? quia in tanta licentia malunt vivere, quàm bene monenti, aut cogenti obtemperare, & ob eam rem Christiana religio quotidie in pejus labitur. Confer cum his, quòd apud Baronium ad an. 1061. joci in ore sacerdotum blasphemia dicuntur.
units.tr: CII. But sometimes these things are general and perhaps only of present custom. Certainly the wickedness of our own time would suffice, yet it was not born yesterday. Let Platina be witness, who, on the occasion of a supplication appointed at that time under Stephen III, breaks out into this complaint: Now piety and religion have so cooled that, I do not say the barefoot (supplicate) with bare feet; but scarcely deign to supplicate even in boots and buskins. They do not weep as they go, or while they sacrifice, as those holy Fathers did; but they laugh, and that shamelessly; I speak of the ones whom the purple makes more distinguished. They do not sing hymns, for that seems servile to them, but among themselves they tell jokes and stories to provoke laughter. What more? The more witty and pert someone is, the greater praise he earns in such corrupt morals; this clergy of ours shuns serious and grave men. Why so? Because in such great licence they prefer to live rather than to obey one who admonishes or compels them well; and for this reason the Christian religion slips daily into worse. Compare with this what Baronius has, at the year 1061, jokes are spoken with blasphemy on the lips of priests.

units.la: CIII. Gloriosissimus Imperator Fridericus Barbarossa jam suo tempore in epistola ad Adrianum Papam, cujus initium: Fridericus Adriano, omnibus illis adhaerere, qua coepit Jesus facere & docere! Sequentia habet de Cardinalibus, quibus reditum in via Regia, ne seditiones excitarent, aut Ecclesias spoliarent, imperaverat, superbè se gerentibus: Cardinalibus utique vestris clausa sunt Ecclesia, & non patent civitates, quia non videmus praedicatores, sed seductores, non pacis corroboratores, sed pecunia raptores, non orbis reparatores, sed auri insatiabiles corrasores. Cùm autem viderimus eos, quales requirit Ecclesia, portantes pacem, illuminantes patriam, adsistentes causa humilium in aequitate, necessariis stipendiis & commeatu eos sustinere non differemus.
units.tr: CIII. The most glorious Emperor Frederick Barbarossa already in his own time, in a letter to Pope Adrian, whose opening is: Frederick to Adrian, to cling to all those things that Jesus began to do and teach! He goes on about the Cardinals, to whom he had ordered a return by the royal road, so that they might not stir up sedition or despoil churches, and who behaved arrogantly: "Certainly your Cardinals have closed the churches, and the cities are not open, because we see not preachers but seducers, not strengtheners of peace but plunderers of money, not restorers of the world but insatiable scrapers together of gold. But when we see them such as the Church requires, bearing peace, enlightening the country, standing up for the cause of the humble in fairness, we will not hesitate to support them with necessary stipends and provisions."

units.la: CIV. Sic quoque jam olim per Anagramma Dicarnales, quasi bis, dupliciter carnales, Conrado Episcopo Moguntino in Chronico apud Wolf. Memorab. Cent. XIII. p. 533. Cardinales audierunt; Verba illius sunt quoque sequentia: O Cardinales, carpinales pacem de terra accepistis, & ut homines se invicem interficiant, vos fecistis &c. Et in Onere Ecclesia ita scriptum legimus: Modò verificatur Hieronymi sententia: quòd singuli superiores per potentiam vindicant totum, quod inferiorum Clericorum est, ac in suos usus redigunt. Mendicat infelix Clericus servili operi mancipatus, quidam stipendia perdit, clamat ad Dominum, & exauditur à Christo: nec differetur divina ultionis sententia, si Cardinales bona pauperis Cleri defraudantes, non reddunt universa.
units.tr: CIV. Thus long ago too, by the anagram Dicarnales, as if bis, twice carnales (carnal), they heard the Cardinals called so by Conrad, Bishop of Mainz, in his Chronicle, cited in Wolf, Memorab. Cent. XIII. p. 533. His words are also these: O Cardinals, you carpinals have received peace from the earth, and you have made men slay one another, etc. And in Onus Ecclesiae we read this written: Now the saying of Jerome is verified, that each superior by power claims the whole of what belongs to the inferior clergy and turns it to his own uses. The unhappy cleric, enslaved to servile work, begs, some lose their stipends, cry out to the Lord, and are heard by Christ; nor will the sentence of divine vengeance be delayed, if the Cardinals, who defraud the poor clergy of their goods, do not restore everything.

units.la: CV. Nicolaus autem Clemangis Archidiaconus Bajacensis de corrupto Ecclesiae statu ita eos depingit: Papa assidentium spiritus, verba tumentia, gestus insolentes, ut si artifex quisque vellet superiorum simulachrum fingere, nulla congruentius ratione illud facere posset, quàm Cardinalis effigiem oculis intuentium objectando; qui ex sortis infimae Clericatu in hanc elationem cum sedis Apostolicae pompatu pervenerunt; nunc vero vero phylacteria sua in tantum dilataverunt, ut non modò Episcopos, sed Patriarchas, Primates, sed Archi-Præsules velut infra se positos despiciant, imò se jam ab illis supplicibus propemodum adorari sinant, quia & Reges æquiparare contendunt. Idem etiam testis est insatiabilis eorum avaritiæ: Quis inquit, c. 10. immensam & extricabilem voraginem ipsorum verbis æquare valeat, nulla prorsus ad hoc verba sufficiunt, nullum ingenium, nulla facundia. Quoniam de re ista plenè differere non nostra facultatis est, pauca solùm summatim attingam ex acervo grandissimo excerpta. Et subjungit, ubi varias eorum artes & pragmaticas Mercuriales an Mammonicas perstrinxit, c. 12. nummularios supremæ tabulæ non incongruenter eos à quibusdam vocatos fuisse; Tandemque queritur, ruinam universalis Ecclesiæ ex dira ambitione horum probo-rum virorum profectam esse. Cui querelæ haud absimile est Machiavelli experientiâ firmatum testimonium de Cardinalibus, causa Factionum Romanarum in versione Gallica de son Prince Ch. XI. subsequens: De sorte, que par là on voit, que les discordes & les seditions naissent de l'ambition des Prelats. Id est: Ita ut exinde videri possit discordiam & seditiones nasci ex ambitione Prælatorum.
units.tr: CV. Nicholas Clamanges, archdeacon of Bayeux, depicts them thus in his account of the corrupt state of the Church: The Pope's attendants have haughty spirits, swelling words and insolent gestures, so that if any craftsman wished to fashion a statue of the superiors, he could do so by no more fitting method than by setting before the eyes of onlookers the figure of a Cardinal; who from the rank of the lowest clergy have risen to such pride along with the pomp of the Apostolic See; but now they have so enlarged their phylacteries that they despise not only bishops but patriarchs, primates, and archbishops, as if placed beneath them, and even allow themselves to be almost adored by those who supplicate them, because they also strive to equal kings. The same witness also testifies to their insatiable avarice: Who, he says in chapter 10, could match in words the immense and inextricable whirlpool of them? No words, no talent, no eloquence suffices for this. Since it is not within my power to treat this matter fully, I shall touch briefly on only a few things, selected from a very large heap. And he adds, where he has touched on their various arts and mercantile, or rather Mammonite, practices, in chapter 12: that they were called by some, not inappropriately, money-changers of the highest table; and at last he complains that the ruin of the universal Church has come from the dreadful ambition of these worthy men. Not much unlike this complaint is the testimony of Machiavelli, confirmed by experience, about the Cardinals, the cause of the Roman factions, in the French version of his Prince, ch. XI, as follows: Thus it is clear from this that discords and seditions are born from the ambition of the prelates. That is: So that from this it can be seen that discord and seditions arise from the ambition of prelates.

units.la: CVI. Sed & paulò ante Reformationem Philippus Burgundus, post Episcopus Ultrajectinus, Legatus, à Maximiliano I. ad Julium II. narrante Gerardo Noviomago in vita ejus Marg. Aust. dedicata, redux factus & , ut Roma placeret? interrogatus non tantùm de Curtisanis scelerum ibi face respondit, minimè placere, sed & sacrificorum, Episcoporum, Cardinalium, Pontificis Maximi, non minùs impudentem, quàm impurum luxum ita execratus est, ut affirmaret, se non dubitare, quin gentiles & pagani castiùs innocentiúsque vixerint, quàm hi, qui nunc Christiano orbi Religionis leges præscribant; Et addidit: Se vidisse Cardinales (quod cum allato Platinæ testimonio valdè convenit) quosdam primi nominis, dum Sacra reliquiæ populo & præcipuè Germanis nostris ostenderentur, exertis linguis ac digitis in turpem modum compositis, nostrorum simplicitati insultâsse. Nihil apud hoc hominum genus sacrum esse præter aurum, & quod vel nominari nefas sit. Præ… dicavit etiam, se hac legatione inter cætera hoc assecutum esse, quòd plurimorum Rom. Pontificum Max. diplomata, leges, decreta, indulgentias, ut meras impostures, ut plùs quàm perniciosa veneficia detestetur. Tantum Romam etiam extra florem, & in maxima corruptione Purparatorum ibi vitam videre juvat!
units.tr: CVI. But even shortly before the Reformation, Philip of Burgundy, afterwards Bishop of Utrecht, who was sent as legate by Maximilian I to Julius II, came home and, as Gerard Noviomagus relates in his life of Margaret of Austria, which he dedicated to her, was asked "How did you like Rome?" He answered that he did not like it at all, not only because of the courtesans of crime there, face and all, but also because he so condemned the luxury of the priests, bishops, cardinals and the Supreme Pontiff, no less shameless than impure, that he declared he had no doubt the heathen and pagans had lived more chastely and blamelessly than those who now prescribe the laws of religion to the Christian world. He added that he had seen cardinals of the first rank (which agrees well with the testimony of Platina cited above) thrusting out their tongues and making obscene gestures with their fingers while the holy relics were shown to the people, and especially to our Germans, mocking the simplicity of our people. Nothing is sacred to this class of men except gold, and that which it is wrong even to name. He also said that among the other things he had achieved by this embassy was this: that he detests the many diplomas, laws, decrees and indulgences of most of the Roman Pontiffs as mere impostures, as more than deadly poisons. How pleasant it is to see Rome, even outside its bloom, living in the greatest corruption of its purple-clad men!

units.la: V. Recentiora autem exempla particularia ad ostendendum, quibus delectentur Cardinales, & quàm ægrè à voluptatibus bus arceantur, duo tantùm subjungam. Cùm Cardinalis Montalto, pòst Sixtus V. in Vita p.1. l. 4. p.308. certo tempore invisere vellet Cardinalem Austriæ, non satis opportunè advectus fuit simulator senectutis & infirmitatis, proin à studiis reliquorum adeò diversus, ut Legatus Moscus p.291. dixerit: Bisogna, che questo Cardinale sia bastardo, non essendo possibile, che sia fratello degli altri, che habbiano sin hora veduto. Id est; Oportet hunc Cardinalem esse spurium, impossibile enim est, ut sit frater aliorum, quos hactenus vidimus. Cùm enim chartis ludenti (Come è ordinario de Cardinali Prencipi, che non perdono mai momento di tempo, mentre quando non hanno altro à fare givocano à Carte; Id est: Quemadmodum ordinarium est Cardinalibus Principibus non negligere tempus, aliis quippe negotiis destituti chartis ludunt; nunciaretur adventus Montaltii, egli rispose in una bona compagnia, che va facendo questo Lazaro quatriduano? respondit inter multos; quid vult Lazarus ille quatriduanus? Ita interruptorem gaudii ingratum hospitem innuens, cùm tamen ex munere primo & institutione, ut volunt, Pontiani Papæ, juxta quem Cardinales etiam mortuorum sepeliendorum curam habere debebant, persona aptior, sepeliendus saltem Lazarus, Cardinalem, cui etiam aleæ lusus præ fratre gratus esse non debuisset, invisere haud potuisset.
units.tr: V. I will add only two more recent particular examples, to show how cardinals take their pleasures and how hard it is to keep them from them. When Cardinal Montalto, afterwards Sixtus V, in his Life, part 1, book 4, p. 308, wished to visit the Cardinal of Austria at a certain time, the pretender to old age and infirmity arrived not very opportunely. He was so unlike the others in his pursuits that the legate Moscus p. 291 said: "This cardinal must be a bastard, since it is impossible that he is a brother of the others we have seen so far." That is: "This cardinal must be a bastard, for it is impossible that he is a brother of the others we have seen so far." For when it was announced that Montalto was coming, while the cardinals were playing cards (as is usual with cardinal princes, who never waste a moment, since when they have nothing else to do they play cards), he replied among a good company: "What is this Lazarus, four days dead, doing?" That is, he replied among many: "What does that Lazarus, four days dead, want?" Thus he hinted that the visitor was an unwelcome guest who interrupted their pleasure. Yet, according to the first duty and institution of Pope Pius, as they say, under which cardinals were also to take care of burying the dead, a person more suited, at least a Lazarus to be buried, could not have visited the cardinal, who should not have been pleased by a game of dice any more than by his brother.

units.la: CVIII. Sed & Cardinalium, juniorum maximè & Principum mores ac studia cognosci possunt ex eo, quod in ipso Leonis XI. Conclavi accidit, Cardinales juniores Dominica sera alli 20. di Marzo, con le loro buggie andorno. Dominica vespera 20. Martii iverunt turmatim personati per Conclave ridendo & jocando, atque expergefaciendo modò hunc, modò illum Cardinalem, ut occasionem dederint Monti eos argutè reprehendendi sub specie distributionis personarum in Comœdia; Ubi Dietrichsteinius, Germanus, Detri Nympha, Pius nummularius, Bevilaqua amans, S. Cesano ancilla, Delphinus Magnificus, erant, & sic concinnè testificati sunt & alii Dominis illis, quàm sanctè in hoc loco se gerere oporteat, & quòd similes strepitus hic nec soliti sint, nec liciti; Hinc abstinuerunt, & alias recreationes quæsiverunt, fra le quali su che facevano corona hora in questa hora in quella cella; quòd convenerunt modò in hac, modò in illa cella. Sed aliquo tempore interjecto juventus Cardinalium rursus reprimi debuit, nam andò girando per il Conclave, allentassero la briglia all' immodestiaca, ivit circumgirando per Conclave & frænum ad immodestiam usque relaxârunt. Secundùm Allobrandini verba: Mà non è dubio, che si acquie tassero gl'humori anco per alcune pasquinate, &c. Sed nullum est dubium, ge-nios nios adhuc delectatos fuisse quibusdam Pasquillis, qua introducta fuerunt intus, quaque celebrata fuerunt Roma, & quibus Aldobrandinus acriter mordebatur. In his recreationibus nocturnis quidam juniores catarrhu af-secti sunt.
units.tr: CVIII. The manners and pursuits of the cardinals, especially the younger ones and the princes, can also be learned from what happened in the very conclave of Leo XI. On Sunday evening, 20 March, the younger cardinals went out with their masks. On Sunday evening, 20 March, they went through the conclave in troops, masked, laughing and joking, and waking now this cardinal, now that one, so that they gave Montalto the chance to rebuke them wittily under the guise of distributing roles in a comedy. There were Dietrichstein the German, the Nymph of Detri, Pius the moneychanger, Bevilacqua the lover, San Cesareo the maidservant, and Delfino the magnificent, and in this way they bore witness, neatly and to the other lords, how holy a manner of behaviour is fitting in this place, and that such noises are neither customary nor permitted here. From this they refrained and sought other recreations, among which was that they gathered in a crowd, now in this cell, now in that one, in this hour or that. But after some time the youth of the cardinals had to be curbed again, for they went wandering through the conclave and loosened the rein on their licentiousness, as Aldobrandini's words run: "But there is no doubt that the humours were calmed also by some lampoons, etc." Yet there is no doubt that these geniuses were still delighted by certain lampoons, which were brought in inside, which were also circulated in Rome, and by which Aldobrandini was sharply bitten. In these nocturnal recreations some of the younger men were afflicted with catarrh.

units.la: CIX. Qui plura & majora his ultimis, id est, magis scan-dalosa de modo vivendi Cardinalium cognoscere vult, legat, praeter alios, saepius citatum Authorem Cardinalismi p. 1. l. 3. p. 325. seqq. p. 331. seqq. p. 386-f. Inveniet conversationes multorum perpetuas cum foeminis, con tutti i piaceri imaginabili, cum omnibus delitiis, quas imaginatio capit, conjunctas, causam abstinentiae nonnullorum spem Papatus, dum alii per sodisfare &c. ut satisfaciant libertati suorum sensuum currant per viam tanta licentia, ut se gloriosos aestiment in voluptatibus, magnos in recreationibus, majestate plenos in luxu, persuasi se saginari in scandalis & saginari, quia credant, in Comoediis eos primum locum occupare, primos ridere de verbis ridiculis; In saltationibus non esse ultimos, in ludis non expectandos esse, ante secundam invitationem currentes; Audiet dicentem, che alcuni &c. quosdam majorem reditvum suorum partem impendere Comoediis domi habendis, quasi decori sint Ecclesiae in Comoediis, etsi Bacchanalium tempore abstineant a turmis Comicorum ad se evocandis, illud facere ideo tantum, ut nummos majoribus scandalis impendant; Quaerentem intelliget: Quante ve ne sono &c. Quot sunt, qui integras noctes consumunt lusum chartarum in manibus habentes? Qui ludunt a mane ad vesperam lusus profanos, oblitti celebrationis illius officii divini, quod exigit Cardinalatus? Testem habebit, che compiacino &c. ipsis placere, ut omnia faciant sine modo, tempus & locum voluptatibus suis accommodantes; Oculatum ejus; Ch'un Cardinale &c. Cardinalem, qui adhuc sit in vivis, tota nocte cum foemina nobili lusisse, sponte ei semper cedendo, ut eo lubentius secum ludere amet; Et sentiet concludentem: Non bisogna &c. Non oportet scandalizari vitio illo, quod quasi decus habetur omnium Ecclesiasticorum Romanorum. Sed & cognoscet denuo ex eodem, che questi &c. Ecclesiasticos illos, si non nutriendos habeant filios, nutriendos habere Nepotes multos, & debere... divites reddere; Quibus tamen expensis abunde provisum sit per proventus eleemosynae, cum certo certius sit, similes esse campanae Manfredoniae, quae hunc sonum proverbio emittere dicatur; Dammi e dotti: dammi e dotti; Indicium quoque accipiet ejus, quod quidam Cardinalium Theologi ad alia incapaces (capaces autem esse rarissimos & lucerna Diogenis quaerendos;) utantur arcano di guadagnar &c. obtinendi favorem Eminentissimorum, quibus serviant, procurando, rando, ut prostituantur inhonestis, & adjuvando eos in aperienda portastmulis sensuum; Exempla specialia ob varios respectus omitti, so-lum specialiùs notari, certum superstitem optimè commendatio-nibus Eminentissimi sui exinde promotum, Lenonem egisse Emi-nentissimi, meretricis & ancillae, quam sibi reservârit, Confessorem.
