Tandem etiam notam deprehendet antiqui moris & decretorum multorum Pontificum, quae Dominis Cardinalibus juvenes famu-los non permittant, quae tamen à quibusdam, qui sciant Papatum non esse sibi paratum, haud observari soleant &c. Atque similia plane quis cognoscere poterit cumprimis ex Statera Cardinalium.
units.tr: CIX. Whoever wishes to learn more, and greater things still, that is, more scandalous ones, about the way of life of the cardinals, let him read, among others, the often-cited author of Cardinalismus, part 1, book 3, pp. 325 ff., p. 331 ff., p. 386 f. He will find that many have constant intercourse with women, joined with all imaginable pleasures, with every delight the imagination can grasp, and that some abstain from hope of the papacy, while others run in such licence to satisfy their senses, so that they think themselves glorious in pleasures, great in recreations, full of majesty in luxury, persuaded that they are fattened on scandals and fatten themselves, because they believe that in comedies they occupy the first place, that they laugh first at the ridiculous words, that they are not last in dances, and that in games they do not wait to be invited a second time, but run ahead. He will hear it said that some devote a greater part of their income to having comedies performed at home, as if they were an ornament to the Church in comedies; and though in carnival time they refrain from summoning troops of comedians to themselves, they do this only so that they may spend their money on greater scandals. He will hear the question: "How many are there who spend whole nights playing cards in their hands? Who play profane games from morning till evening, forgetting that celebration of the divine office which the cardinalate requires?" He will have a witness: that they please themselves, so that they do everything without measure, adapting time and place to their pleasures; and an eyewitness to this: that a cardinal, who is still alive, played cards the whole night with a noblewoman, always yielding to her, so that she might love to play with him all the more gladly. And he will hear the conclusion: "It is not necessary to be scandalised by that vice, which is regarded as an ornament of all the Roman ecclesiastics." He will also learn again from the same source that these ecclesiastics, if they have no sons to rear, have many nephews to rear and to make rich; yet they are amply provided for with the income of alms, since it is most certain that they are like the bell of Manfredonia, which is said to give out this sound in a proverb: "Give me, and gifts! Give me, and gifts!" He will also receive a sign of this, that some theologians among the cardinals, who are unfit for other things (and fit ones are very rare and must be sought with Diogenes' lantern), use the secret of gaining favour, of obtaining the favour of the most eminent men whom they serve, by arranging for them to be prostituted to dishonourable persons and by helping them to open the gates to their senses. Specific examples, for various reasons, are omitted; let it only be noted more particularly that a certain survivor, promoted thereafter by the recommendations of his most eminent master, acted as pimp for his most eminent master, and as confessor of the maidservant and mistress whom he kept for himself. Finally, he will also observe a note of the ancient custom and of many decrees of Popes, which do not permit young servants to the lord cardinals, yet which are usually not observed by some who know that the papacy is not prepared for them, and so on. Anyone can plainly learn similar things, above all from the Statera Cardinalium.

units.la: CX. Sed hic finem facimus descriptioni Cardinalium; Fi-nis non coronat opus, certè non commendat ita viventes; quo-modo tamen aliquos non vivere, imò multos ab ejusmodi scanda-lis majoribus immunes esse, cum Authore facilè supponimus; Dum interim talia ex longo tempore tolerari, & in multis ex ordine il-lo tolerari, toti orbi manifestum est, atque non audere Pontifices aliquando, si tales manere velint, vel hiscere contrà; quemadmodum illud, teste Platina, Urbano VI. aemulum excitavit, quòd semel atque iterum Cardinales vocatos ad se admonuit, ut manus abstinentes haberent, &c. interminatúsque est, se acerrime puniturum in Simonia deprehensos, aut injustas causas agentes; Praterea que ostendit, sibi placere, & ita vel-le, ut Pompam dimitterent tantámque familiarium turbam & equorum, cum id, quod in tales sumptus consumerent Ecclesia Romana perniciosos, pauperibus deberetur &c. Dum de communi etiam fastu, de luxu plerorúmque constat, satis certum jam exinde contra actiones ordinis, maximè tam supereminentes & singulares, ac ferè divinas in Ecclesia praejudicium formari potest, ut etiam formari potest ex dictis omnibus. Quare etiam prolixior esse volui in horum Electorum nomine, origine, statu, &c. describendis, cùm tot & tanta de illis in sequentibus dicenda sint, nec tam facilè notum omnibus sit, quid sit Cardinalis, quàm verò, quid sit Clerus & populus, quid Imperator, penes quos ante Cardinales electio Pontificum Romanorum fuerat. Applicabimus igitur in sequentibus & in tractatione de naevis quodammodo illud Sebae & Zalmunae: Ut vir est, ita & vis ejus Judic. VIII. 21.
units.tr: CX. But here we make an end of the description of the Cardinals. The end does not crown the work, and it certainly does not commend men who live like this. Yet we readily grant with the Author that some do not live this way, and that many are free of such greater scandals. Meanwhile it is plain to the whole world that such things have been tolerated for a long time, and that in many cases the order has tolerated them. Nor do the Popes dare at any time to open their mouths against them, if they want such men to remain. Thus, according to Platina, it stirred up a rival against Urban VI, because he admonished the Cardinals, called to him once and again, to keep their hands clean, and threatened that he would punish most severely those caught in simony or pursuing unjust causes. Moreover he showed that it pleased him, and that he wished it so, that they should give up their pomp and so great a crowd of household servants and horses, since what they spent on such outlays was owed to the poor, which the Roman Church found harmful. Since the common pride and luxury of most of them are established, it can already be fairly certain from this that a prejudice is formed against the actions of the order, especially those so outstanding and singular, and almost divine, in the Church, as it can also be formed from everything said so far. For this reason I wanted to be more lengthy in describing the name, origin, and standing of these Electors, since so many and such great things are to be said about them in what follows, and it is not so easily known to everyone what a Cardinal is, still less what the clergy and people are, or the Emperor, by whom the election of the Roman Pontiffs was made before the Cardinals. Therefore in what follows, and in the treatment of the blemishes, we will apply in some measure that saying about Zebah and Zalmunna: As the man is, so is his strength (Judg. 8:21).

units.la: CXI. Hic autem & in continuatione, vel, si mavis, Lector benigne, in initio tractationis de Electione Pontificum Romanorum per Cardinales, & post tractationem de istis Electoribus, primo
units.tr: CXI. Here, however, and in the continuation, or, if you prefer, kind reader, at the beginning of the treatment of the election of the Roman Pontiffs by the Cardinals, and after the treatment of these Electors, first

units.la: Finis imponitur tractationi de Cardinalibus in genere.
units.tr: An end is put to the treatment of the Cardinals in general.

units.la: In originem Electionis per solos Cardinales. mò notamus, quando primò Cardinales elegerint, & quem Papam. Jam suprà notavimus, primum, exclusò populo & reliquo Clero, à Cardinalibus electum esse Innocentium II. Fecerat quidem diu ante eum, nempe an. 769. in Synodo Romana Stephanus IV. al. III. Occasione Anti-Papæ Constantini ex Laico promoti, decretum, ne Papa nisi ex Cardinalibus legeretur, quod tamen nec perpetuò observatum, nec adhuc conjunctum fuit cum illo, ut Papa à solis Cardinalibus eligeretur, ut ipse etiam Stephanus apud Platinam in vita omnium (in populo) suffragiis suffectus legitur; quod & circa successores ejus multos & diu post ipsum adhuc observatum esse suprà ostendimus. Sic etiam, quòd quidam apud Cajetanum opusc. 2. c. 22. in sexta Synodo datam esse potestatem electivam Cardinalibus contendunt, illam nimirum, quam Nicolaus II. ante Innocentium II. & an. 1059. ad Papatum promotus Dist.23.c.1. explicârit; frustrà omninò fit, cùm neque sexta Synodus aliquid hac in re sanxerit, neque Nicolaus, sive ex Papali authoritate, ut vult Cajetanus, sive authoritate Synodi Lateranensis agens, solis Cardinalibus totam Pontificis Electionem commendârit, sed primas tantùm Cardinalibus in electione partes. Quod ex ipso decreto constat, ubi inter alia ista habentur: Mox Christi Clericos Cardinales adhibeant, sicque reliquus Clerus & populus ad consensum novæ electionis accedat.
units.tr: On the origin of the election by the Cardinals alone. Let us further note when the Cardinals first elected, and whom as Pope. We have already noted above that, with the people and the rest of the clergy shut out, Innocent II was first elected by the Cardinals alone. Indeed, long before him, in the year 769, Stephen IV (or III) had decreed in a Roman Synod, on the occasion of the anti-pope Constantine, who had been promoted from the laity, that the Pope should be chosen only from among the Cardinals. Yet this was neither observed consistently, nor was it yet joined with the rule that the Pope should be elected by the Cardinals alone. Stephen himself is read in Platina as having been installed in the sight of all, by the votes of the people, and we have shown above that this continued to be observed for many of his successors and long after him. Likewise, the claim of some, in Cajetan's Opuscula 2, chapter 22, that electoral power was given to the Cardinals at the Sixth Synod, is entirely vain, since the Sixth Synod decreed nothing on this matter. Nor did Nicholas II, who was raised to the papacy in 1059, before Innocent II, and who explained this in Dist. 23, c. 1, entrust the whole election of the Pope to the Cardinals alone, whether acting by papal authority, as Cajetan holds, or by the authority of the Lateran Synod. He gave the Cardinals only the first part in the election. This is clear from the decree itself, where among other things these words stand: Let the clerics of Christ, the Cardinals, first take part, and so the rest of the clergy and the people may come to consent to the new election.

units.la: CXII. Ut formæ hujus electionis omninò non vetustior assignari possit origo, Clero universo & populo etiam in Electionibus eorum Pontificum, qui Nicolaum II. proximè exceperunt, semper, modò magis, modò, & ultimò quidem, minùs, (Sino bel bel n'esclusero indi à poco Cesare, il Clero e il Popolo Romano; ut Roma canit L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.12.) cooperantibus, illâ, quam jam in Innocentio II. assignavimus; Qui & primus an. 1130. à solis Cardinalibus electus fuit, & ut eodem modo successores eligerentur, decreto constituit. Quòd autem Author Tractatùs de l'origine des Cardinaux c. VII. p.75. 76. constitutionem Alexandro III. qui demum an. 1159. & aliquot post Innocentium II. interpositis Papis, electus fuit, tribuit, illud (ut ex sequentibus magis patebit) non de prima constitutione, sed de primæ constitutionis per Innocentium II. factæ, fortè etiam ab aliis interjacentibus Decretis novis roboratæ, confirmatione intelligi potest & debet; Et fortè illud Viro Doctissimo, si de prima formæ constitutione, ut videtur, locutus est, errandi occasionem præbuit, quòd Alexander ille III. constitutioni prædecessorum occasione schismatis, quod electus, licèt 22. Cardinalium suffragiis, perpessus fuerat, Anti-Papam habens Octavianum à 3. tantùm Cardinalibus creatum, in Concilio Lateranensi par. 1. c. 1. hanc legem adjecit: Ut electio per scrutinium à Cardinalium duabus tertiis sit legitima, & non pluribus; præsuppositâ jam reductione Electorum ad solos Cardinales. Quæ lex hodienum rata habetur, licèt non plane semper, ut in nævis electionum ostendemus, observata fuerit.
units.tr: CXII. Since no earlier origin can be assigned for this form of election, the clergy as a whole and the people also took part, sometimes more and sometimes less, and at the last even less, in the elections of those Popes who immediately followed Nicholas II (Little by little, not long after, Caesar, the clergy and the Roman people were shut out, as Rome sings in L'Ambasciata di Roma, p. 12), in the manner that we have already assigned to Innocent II. He was the first to be elected by the Cardinals alone, in 1130, and by decree he established that successors should be elected in the same way. But as to the Author of the treatise De l'origine des Cardinaux, chapter 7, pp. 75–76, who attributes this constitution to Alexander III, who was finally elected in 1159, with several Popes intervening after Innocent II, it can and must be understood (as will appear more clearly from what follows) not of the first establishment, but of the confirmation of the constitution first made by Innocent II, perhaps also strengthened by other new decrees in between. And perhaps, if that most learned man spoke of the first establishment of the form, as seems to be the case, he gave occasion for error. For that Alexander III, on account of the schism, in which he had suffered, though elected by the votes of twenty-two Cardinals, while the anti-pope Octavian, created by only three Cardinals, was in place, added this law to the constitutions of his predecessors in the Lateran Council, Part 1, chapter 1: that an election by scrutiny is legitimate only if made by two-thirds of the Cardinals, and not by more. This presupposed the reduction of the electors to the Cardinals alone. This law is still held valid today, although, as we will show in the blemishes of the elections, it has not always been observed fully.

units.la: CXIII.
units.tr: CXIII.

units.la: Satis igitur recens est ista electionis per solos Cardinales forma, cùm undecim integris à Christo nato seculis & amplius nunquam adhibita fuerit. Certè hîc non applicari volent: Quod antiquissimum, illud & etiam optimum est. Et haud immeritò mirari subit, non citiùs, sed demum tot seculis elapsis hunc eligendi morem in Ecclesiam introductum fuisse, si nempe tam conveniens, imò, ut Bellarminus ostendere conatur, omnium optimus & solus ferè conveniens est, & nihil juribus populi Christiani & Cleri reliqui derogat. Sed non tam convenientem esse, sed derogare, vel ex ipsa sera institutione cognoscas. Ex qua etiam, quàm serò alterum & præcipuum, Bellarmino, ut suprà vidimus, contendente, prærogativarum Cardinalitiæ apud Romanos dignitatis fundamentum positum fuerit, manifestum est, & per consequens, cùm electio Pontificis per solos Cardinales eorum hodie definitionem tanquam essentiale quid ingrediatur, quàm serò tales Cardinales orti sint, quod & suprà ex aliis capitibus prolixè demonstravimus.
units.tr: This form of electing by the Cardinals alone is therefore quite recent, since it was never used in the eleven full centuries and more after the birth of Christ. Surely they will not want to apply the principle here: What is most ancient is also best. And one cannot help wondering why this custom of electing was introduced into the Church so late, after so many centuries had passed, if it really is so suitable, indeed, as Bellarmine tries to show, the best of all and almost the only suitable method, and if it takes nothing away from the rights of the Christian people and the remaining clergy. But you may learn from its very late institution that it is not so suitable and that it does take something away. From this, too, it is clear how late was laid the other and chief foundation of the prerogatives of the Cardinalate among the Romans, as Bellarmine contends, as we have seen above. And consequently, since the election of the Pope by the Cardinals alone now enters into their very definition as something essential, it follows how late such Cardinals arose, which we have also demonstrated at length above from other chapters.

units.la: CXIV.
units.tr: CXIV.

units.la: Proderit autem etiam cognoscere: Ex qua authoritate, quo jure, vel quâ injuriâ Cardinales ita soli eligere cœperint. Injuria jam satis ex iis patet, quæ suprà de plebe & Magistratu non prorsus excludendis annotavimus. Reliquum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Clerum, qui, quæ Cleri sunt, saltem suo modo, & magis quàm Cardinales, agit, magis proin ex Cardinalibus constat, non sine injuria quoque excludi, est evidens quoque. Sed videamus, annon usurpationis meræ vestigia in ipsa prima per solos Cardinales facta Innocentii II. electione deprehendere possimus. Manifesta deprehendimus. Neque enim Clerus populúsque Romanus, quos legitimos tot suorum usque ad illa tempora Pontificum Electores fuisse admittere tenentur, tunc publicè & solenniter, ut oportuisset, imò nullo modo se jure suo tam antiquo, & tam diuturno, & tam æquo abdicavit, neque etiam,quod,ex salsissima quidem hypothesi Papatûs in Ecclesia universalis, omninò necessarium fuisset, Ecclesia universalis per Rectores suos in Concilio universali congregatos tunc jus eligendi originaliter indubiè suum in Cardinales transtulit; Sed hic Innocentius raptim à nonnullis Episcopis, Presbyteris ac Diaconis Cardinalibus Episcopus factus est. Contra quam electionem Portuensis Episcopus Cardinalis, qui Anacletum post aliam electionem adversus Innocentium consecrárat,ad alios Episcopos partis adversæ apud Malmesb. Hist. Novell. lib.11. ita scribit: Quia igitur neglecto ordine, contempto Canone, spreto etiam ipso à nobis condito anathemate, me inconsulto Priore vestro, inconsultis etiam fratribus, majoribus & prioribus: nec etiam vocatis, aut expectatis,cùm esseris novitii, & in numero brevi paucissimi, facere præsumpsistis, pro infecto habendum esse: & nihil omninò existere, ex ipsa vestra æstimatione potestis advertere: Citò autem nobis Dominus adfuit, & viam, quâ errori vestro contra ire possemus, ostendit. Fratres siquidem vestri Cardinales, quorum præcipua in electione potestas,cum Clero universo,expetente populo, cum honoratorum consensu, in luce,in manifesto, unanimi voto & desiderio delegerunt Dominum Petrum Cardinalem in Romanum Pontificem Anacletum.
units.tr: It will also be useful to know by what authority, by what right, or by what wrong the Cardinals began to elect alone in this way. The wrong is already sufficiently clear from what we noted above about the people and the magistrate, who must not be wholly excluded. That the rest of the Roman clergy, who act in the matters of the clergy at least in their own way, and more than the Cardinals, and who therefore consist more of the Cardinals, are also excluded, not without wrong, is equally evident. But let us see whether we can detect traces of mere usurpation in the very first election by the Cardinals alone, that of Innocent II. We find them plainly. For the clergy and the Roman people, whom they were bound to admit as lawful electors of their Popes down to those times, did not then publicly and solemnly renounce their right, as they ought to have done; indeed, they did not renounce in any way a right so ancient, so long-standing, and so fair. Nor did the universal Church, which on the most mistaken hypothesis of a universal Papacy would have been entirely necessary, transfer its original and undoubted right of electing to the Cardinals through its rulers gathered in a universal council. Rather, Innocent was hastily made Bishop of the Cardinals by certain bishops, presbyters and deacons. Against this election the Cardinal Bishop of Porto, who had consecrated Anacletus after another election against Innocent, writes to the other bishops of the opposing party, in Malmesbury, Hist. Novell. lib. 11.: Since, therefore, you have presumed to act, neglecting the order, despising the Canon, scorning even the anathema that we ourselves enacted, without consulting me, your Prior, or your brothers, the elders and the leaders, and without even calling or awaiting them, while you were newcomers and very few in number, you may yourselves perceive by your own judgment that it must be held as void and that it has no existence at all. But the Lord has quickly come to our aid and has shown us the way by which we could go against your error. For your brothers the Cardinals, whose chief power lies in the election, together with the whole clergy, the people asking for it, and with the consent of the honourable men, have chosen in the light, in the open, with one voice and one desire, Lord Peter the Cardinal as Roman Pontiff, Anacletus.

units.la: CXV. En igitur egregia Electionis per solos Cardinales primordia! Hic initium non coronat opus, non commendat ita eligentes, neglecto ordine contempto Canone, spreto, quod ipsi considerant, anathemate, inconsulto Priore, inconsultis fratribus, novitios numero brevi paucissimos! Verùm equidem est, Innocentium, & non Anacletum obtinuisse; Sed non semper obtinuerunt optimè electi. Et rectè de Dominis de Rep.Christ. l.IV. c.11 n.12. causas ejus rei in eo ponit, quòd Innocentius 1. favorem Lotharii, quem ex Rege Imperatorem fecerat,habuerit. 2. Anacletus animo largitionibus ex relatione Bernhardi Abbatis se ita in sede firmare volens abalienârit. 3. Innocentii partes Bernhardus Clarevallensis, vir eo tempore summæ existimationis, tuendas suscEPERIT, qui tamen non omnimodo electionem ejus anteferre ausus est,ut & acta Anacleti rata manserunt Innocentius autem ita in sede collocatus, cùm Romanos Pontificum in urbe r gimini tamdiu resistere videret, in populum Romanum commotus,eum & anath mate notavit, & tunc primùm ab Electione Pontificis penitùs exclusit, adeóque, inquit Onuphrius, annot. in Innoc. II. Pontificis electio paulatim, Cleri etiam primoprimoribus exclusis, vel in Cardinalium Collegium cooptatis, ad solos Cardinales est redacta. Primus porrò sine ullo populi interventu creatus est mortuo Innocentio secundo, Coelestinus secundus, & sic deinceps alii.
units.tr: CXV. Here, then, are the splendid beginnings of election by the Cardinals alone! This beginning does not crown the work, nor does it commend those who so elected: neglecting the order, despising the Canon, scorning, as they themselves consider it, the anathema, without consulting the Prior, without consulting the brothers, and being newcomers, very few in number! It is true that Innocent, and not Anacletus, gained the upper hand; but those who were elected best did not always win. Marco Antonio de Dominis rightly, in de Rep. Christ. lib. IV, cap. 11, n. 12, places the causes of this in the following: first, that Innocent II had the favour of Lothair, whom he had made Emperor from King; second, that Anacletus, wishing to establish himself so firmly in the see by largesse, alienated the mind of the people, on the report of Abbot Bernard; third, that Bernard of Clairvaux, a man of the highest esteem at that time, took up Innocent's cause, though he did not dare to prefer his election in every respect, so that the acts of Anacletus also remained valid. Innocent, however, once placed in the see, seeing that the Roman Pontiffs had resisted for so long in the city, was moved against the Roman people and marked them with an anathema, and then for the first time he wholly excluded them from the election of the Pope. And so, says Onuphrius, annot. in Innocent II, the election of the Pope was gradually reduced to the Cardinal College alone, the chief men of the clergy also being excluded or co-opted into the Cardinal College. Moreover, the first to be created without any intervention of the people was Celestine II, on the death of Innocent II, and so on with the others.

units.la: CXVI. Continuavit ita forma haec semel introducta, nec tamen nisi diu post in Concilio Constantiensi pro universali habito confirmata. Sed quando constat, morem iniquum esse, & caeterum illud à Monarchicis partim rejici, partim, quod jam supra notavimus, corrupti, parum certè authoritatis huic eligendi modo inde accedere potest. Ut etiam inter ipsos Pontificios non convenit, de modo, quo Cardinales in Pontificum Electione se habeant, & inde aliquando inter Parisienses & Cajetanum grave certamen exortum est; Contendentibus illis cum Gersone de Auferib. Pap. Consid. 16. & Almain de autor. Eccl. c. 9. Papae Electionem ab Ecclesia universali absolutè & in omnibus pendere, tam in deputandis Electoribus, quàm in modo Electionum praescribendo, corrigendo, reformando; hoc verò id totum ad solum Papam Opusc. 1. c. 6. 13. Opusc. 2. c. 22. reducente: Post quem etiam Bellarminus de Cler. l. 1. c. 9. posse Pontificem absolutè illam eligendi rationem mutare, asseruit, licèt c. 10. hanc propositionem posuerit; Si nulla exstaret Pontificia constitutio de Electione summi Pontificis: vel casu aliquo omnes Electores à jure designati, id est, omnes Cardinales simul perirent, jus electionis ad Episcopos vicinos & Clerum Romanum pertinere, cum dependentia tamen aliqua à Concilio generali Episcoporum. In cujus propositionis exegesi etiam producit & conciliare nititur diversas opiniones, statuentium ab una parte, jus eligendi devolvi ad Concilium Episcoporum, ab altera verò, pertinere tunc ad Clerum Romanum. Sed ab una parte non agitur, ut luculenter ostendimus, de electione Monarchae universalis Ecclesiae, ab altera verò omninò Romanis, Clero & populo jus suum non prorsus auferri jure potuit. Sed praesuppositio Papatu universali, optimè omninò ratiocinantur Parisienses pro Ecclesia & Conciliis; Optimè etiam de Dominis l. c. n. 18. huic certamini subjicit: Stulti sunt Papae, qui doctrinam Cajetanicam sequentes, non faciunt Papatum jus Patronatus suae tantum domûs, & suae familiae ac suorum consanguineorum (facere tamen quadantenus valdè velle & in id multùm incumbere, ex dictis & dicendis liquere potest;) siquidem Domini sunt (Cajetano judice) ut possint potestatem electivam conferre & dare (vide Sect 1. n. XV.) quibus volunt. Posset quilibet Papa, si non successorum suorum omnium (quia hac concessio ab alio Papa rescindi potest) ad minimum proximi successoris eligendi potestatem suo Nepoti concedere, aut amico, vel propinquo, imo etiam faeminis; quae sicut Juris Patronatus ita electionis quoque non sint incapaces. Et hujusmodi Nepos, quem penes erit potestas eligendi plenaria, poterit per subornatum, cui vices suas crediderit, procuratorem, curare se eligendum, & ita successive alii nepotuli in infinitum, adeoque fiet Papatus haereditarius. En quò nos, imò quo Papatum pessimi Paparum adulatores sua stultitia perduxerint!
units.tr: CXVI. This form, once introduced, continued, yet it was not confirmed at the Council of Constance, held as a universal council, until long afterwards. But since it is clear that this custom is unjust, and since that matter was partly rejected by the Monarchists, and partly, as we have already noted above, corrupted, very little authority can accrue to this method of electing from it. Nor do the Papists themselves agree about the manner in which the Cardinals stand in the election of the Pope; and from this a serious dispute once arose between the Parisians and Cajetan. The former, with Gerson (de Auferib. Pap. Consid. 16) and Almain (de autor. Eccl. c. 9), contended that the election of the Pope depends absolutely, and in everything, on the universal Church, both in appointing the electors and in prescribing, correcting and reforming the mode of election; but Cajetan (Opusc. 1, c. 6, 13; Opusc. 2, c. 22) reduces all this to the Pope alone. After him Bellarmine (de Cler. l. 1, c. 9) asserted that the Pope may absolutely change that method of electing, although in c. 10 he put forward this proposition: If there were no Papal constitution about the election of the supreme Pontiff, or if by some chance all the electors designated by law, that is, all the Cardinals together, were to perish, the right of election would belong to the neighbouring bishops and the Roman clergy, with some dependence, however, on a general council of bishops. In explaining this proposition he also brings forward and strives to reconcile the different opinions of those who hold, on the one hand, that the right of electing devolves on a council of bishops, and on the other, that it then belongs to the Roman clergy. But on the one side, as we have clearly shown, the matter at issue is not the election of a monarch of the universal Church; and on the other, the Romans, the clergy and the people could not rightly be deprived of their right altogether. But the Parisians reason most excellently for the Church and the councils, on the presupposition of a universal Papacy. Dominis also most excellently subjoins to this dispute (l. c. n. 18): Foolish are the Popes who, following the Cajetanian doctrine, do not make the Papacy a right of patronage of their own house, of their family and of their kinsmen (yet from what has been and will be said it can be made clear that they do, in some measure, very much wish to do so and to labour greatly at it), since they are lords (according to Cajetan) so that they can confer and give the power of electing to whom they will (see Sect. 1, n. XV). Any Pope could, if not for all his successors (since this grant can be rescinded by another Pope), at least grant to his nephew, or to a friend or relative, or even to women, the power of electing the next successor, since they are no more incapable of electing than of the right of patronage. And such a nephew, in whose hands the full power of electing will lie, may, through a suborned proxy to whom he has entrusted his place, arrange to be elected himself; and so, in succession, other little nephews in infinitum, and thus the Papacy will become hereditary. See where the worst flatterers of the Popes, by their folly, have led us, or rather the Papacy!

units.la: CXVII. Cardinalium autem authoritas in eligendo Papa olim non omnino aequalis erat; Sed cum Cardinales eligere coeperunt, primo tractabant inter se Episcopi Cardinales, & deinde alios Cardinales vocabant, ut d. c. in nomine Domini 23. di. Prout certe in genere ante Bernhardum uno, aut altero seculo, veri collaterales & intimi Papae, non erant omnes Cardinales, sed soli illi Episcopi Cardinales. Id quod ex Petri Damiani ad Cadolaum Anti-Papam verbis, quae apud Baron. ad an. 1061. n. 11. colligi potest. Sed hodie ista praerogativa Episcoporum Cardinalium sive in electione Pontificis, sive in aliis non tenetur, dum in tractatibus omnibus omnes habentur pares, Episcopi, Presbyteri, Diaconi.
units.tr: CXVII. Now the authority of the cardinals in electing the Pope was once not wholly equal. But when the cardinals began to elect, the cardinal bishops first deliberated among themselves, and only then summoned the other cardinals, as in the chapter "In nomine Domini," distinction 23. Indeed, in general, before Bernard, one or two centuries earlier, the true colleagues and intimates of the Pope were not all the cardinals, but only those cardinal bishops. This can be gathered from the words of Peter Damian to Cadalus the Antipope, which are cited in Baronius at the year 1061, no. 11. But today that prerogative of the cardinal bishops is not maintained, either in the election of the Pontiff or in other matters, since in all deliberations everyone is regarded as equal: bishops, presbyters, deacons.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA,
units.tr: SECTION THREE,

units.la: In qua Partim de proxime Electionem Pontificis per Cardinales antecedentibus, partim de Conclavi, ceu Electionis per eosdem loco, partim de Conclavistis, ceu Cardinalium, dum Electionis causa congregati sunt, ministris, partim de legibus Conclaviariis, partim denique de variis modis, quibus Cardinales Pontificem sive per scrutinium, sive per accessum, sive per inspirationem, sive per compromissionem eligere solent, modis; agitur. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which is discussed, partly the events that precede the election of a Pope by the Cardinals, partly the Conclave, as the place of the election by them, partly the Conclavists, as ministers of the Cardinals while they are gathered for the sake of the election, partly the laws of the Conclave, and finally the various ways in which the Cardinals are accustomed to elect the Pope, whether by scrutiny, by accession, by inspiration, or by compromise. Summary.

Ex Ceremoniali Gregorii XV. XC. Executores legum; XCI. Conclusio.
units.tr: I. Transition to the history of the form of election that serves this purpose. II. Antecedents: either resignation, or deposition, or death; the circumstances and rites concerning the dying and the one just dead; the change of status brought about by the death of the Pope, with Gregory XV's Constitution kept before our eyes. III. A note on the word Conclave. IV. Their declaration with regard to the dying Pope. V. The joy of many, if he has not loved the Church as he ought; the example of Adrian VI. VI. If he has loved too much, he has been unjust and has indulged his nephews too much; the examples of Boniface VIII, Paul IV and Innocent X. VII. Indeed he is often assailed with the curses of all; the examples of Sixtus IV and Paul IV. VIII. The humbling of nephews, from the Conclave of Leo XI. IX. Of Alexander VII. X. The change with regard to the political and ecclesiastical government. XI. The care and authority of the Cardinals while the see is vacant. XII. Tumult in the city. XIII. The funeral of the Pope. XIV. The practice, from the Conclave of Clement IX, with regard to Alexander VII. XV. The congregations of the Cardinals. XVI. The postponement of the election for ten days. XVII. When these have elapsed, the Pope may be elected even by a very few present, yet those arriving afterwards are admitted. XVIII. The eagerness to come to Rome early. XIX. The institution of the Conclave. XX. Violated on several occasions. XXI. The place of the Conclave. XXII. Questions about it. XXIII. The particular place, the cell. XXIV. Their distribution, the coverings, and the constant possession of them by the same occupants. XXV. The Conclavists enter together, first. XXVI. Their privileges. XXVII. Concerning the privileges, the complaint of the Tridentines. XXVIII. The authority of the Conclavists, the manner of passing the time, and the art of speaking with those who live outside the Conclave. XXIX. Most of the writers on Conclaves are authors whose accounts are imperfect. XXX. Yet they are not of no weight. XXXI. Other companions of the Cardinals in the Conclave who attend them. XXXII. Entry into the Conclave. XXXIII. The freedom of the first day as regards entry. XXXIV. This is followed by the necessity of leaving on the part of those who ought not to be present; nor is it permitted to live or remain near the Conclave. XXXV. The closing of the Conclave and the instrument concerning it. XXXVI. Communication with those who stay outside is forbidden, yet is sometimes arranged and sometimes even prevented. XXXVII. The searching of food. XXXVIII. Leaving before the election is made is not permitted; the custom of leaving on the first day has been abolished. XXXIX. Yet it is permitted for the sick to go out and return. XL. Those who went out before the election, two of them; concerning the departure of many and of all. XLI. Concerning the departure of the Conclavists. XLII. The guards of the Conclave. XLIII. The laws on food. XLIV. How they are observed. XLV. The law on clothing; the peculiarities in matters of dress. XLVI. Transition to the activities within the place: the chapel, in which deliberations and elections take place. XLVII. Among the activities in the Conclave the first is the drawing up of the capitulations for the future Pope. XLVIII. The different methods of election by the Cardinals alone. XLIX. The first, by scrutiny. The acts before the scrutiny. L. The first: the preparation of the ballots. LI. The second: the drawing of the scrutineers. LII. The third: the writing of the ballots. LIII. The fourth: the folding. LIV. The fifth: the sealing. LV. The scrutiny itself; where, first. LVI. The bringing of the ballot, second the taking of the oath; third, the placing of the ballot in the urn. LVII. What is usually observed with regard to the sick. LVIII. The infirmarians. LIX. Fourth, the mixing of the ballots; fifth, the counting. LX. Sixth, the publication of the scrutiny. LXI. Seventh, the threading of the ballots on a string; eighth, their separate deposit. LXII. After the scrutiny. LXIII. The second method, by accession, which is employed when the scrutiny is insufficient. LXIV. What is almost always the case. LXV. The custom of accession from Roman antiquity; the acts in accession. LXVI. The difference between the preliminaries and the first act of accession, and between a simple scrutiny. LXVII. The second, third and fourth acts after the scrutiny, when accession also has taken place and the votes have been counted. LXVIII. The method of examination. LXIX. Signs and seals. LXX. What is usually done if two or more ballots are found with the same signs and seals. LXXI. The fifth act, the counting of the votes. LXXII. The sixth, the recognition by the recognisers. LXXIII. The seventh, the burning of the ballots. LXXIV. The treatment of scrutiny and accession is concluded. LXXV. The third method, by adoration. LXXVI. The difference concerning the number required for adoration. LXXVII. Whether there is one method by adoration and by inspiration. LXXVIII. The dispute about the required number. LXXIX. This method of electing is rarer, and dangerous in electing, if the votes of all are required. LXXX. Dangerous and also high. LXXXI. Adored, yet not elected. LXXXII. Scrutiny after adoration, without prejudice. LXXXIII. What ought to be done if the scrutiny fails after adoration. LXXXIV. The fourth method, by compromise; where the appointment of compromissaries takes place. LXXXV. Election by compromissaries. LXXXVI. When it is used and is usually used. LXXXVII. A peculiar method under Martin V. LXXXVIII. Concerning the sanction of the methods and the perpetual validity enjoined, from the Bull of Pius IV. LXXXIX. From the Ceremonial of Gregory XV. XC. The executors of the laws. XCI. Conclusion.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Pergimus jam ad ipsam historiam Electionis per Cardinales, non Electionum specialium, sed electionis, sive ad antecedentia, locum, leges & formas eligendi; Quæ omnia distincte enarranda sunt, non quasi omnia illa, quæ commemoraturi sumus, in qualibet Electione & omni tempore occurrerint, sed quia omnia paulatim ad hodiernum morem excreverunt legibus Pontificum, maximè Alexandri III. Gregorii X. Clementis V. & VI. Julii II. Pii V. Gregorii XV. stabilitum.
units.tr: We now proceed to the history itself of election by the Cardinals. We are concerned not with particular elections but with election in general: the circumstances that precede it, and the laws and forms of electing. All of these must be set out in order. Not all of the things we are about to mention occur in every election or at every time. But they all gradually grew into the present custom, and were settled by the laws of the Popes, above all those of Alexander III, Gregory X, Clement V and VI, Julius II, Pius V, and Gregory XV.

units.la: II. Antecedentia quod attinet, Electioni viam sternit Prædecessoris vel resignatio, vel depositio, vel mors. Resignâsse leguntur Pontifices Romani quinque, nempe Clemens I. de cujus exemplo ratione Electionis per Prædecessorem pluribus Sect. I. actum est; Cyriacus ex visione S. Ursulæ & 11000. Virginum in fabula comes futurus, juxta Glossam ad c. 1. [?]nuntiat, in 6. de quo tamen, juxta eandem in Codicibus vetustioribus, creditum per Cardinales, quòd non propter devotionem, sed propter oblectamenta Virginum Papatum dimisisset. Quò forte etiam respexit Gomezius apud Limnæum l. 2. c. 11. scribens: Pontificem posse Papatui renunciare, id tamen raro fieri, nisi cum causa, quando videlicet propter oblectamenta Virginum eum dimittat; Marcellinus ob commissum à se Idololatriæ & Apostasiæ crimen; Cœlestinus tenuitatis suæ conscientiâ & suo loco memorandâ Successoris Bonifacii VIII. fraude, qui & memor, quantum inde sit lucratus, atque ad jus suum roborandum, decreto abdicationem lib.6. Decretalium firmavit, indicavitque, fieri posse; Uti etiam Augustinus Triumphus Anconitanus de potest Eccl. quaest. 4. art. 5. decretum contrarium fieri à Papa non posse statuit, eo potissimum argumento nixus, nullum dubitare debere, quin talis posset eligi in Papam, qui nec scientia, nec experientia sufficiens esset ad regendam totam Ecclesiam: sicut aliquando electus est. Unde si sibi renunciare non liceret, faceret contra veritatem suae conscientiae &c. Denique Johannes XXIII. in schismate, de quo suo loco etiam. De Renunciatione Papae autem peculiari tractatu egit Ægidius Columnius Romanus. Atque eam à longè pluribus fieri debuisse, tum ex causa jam jam apposita, tum ex exemplis indignitatis suo loco ponendis patet, patebit; Papas Romanos aliquot depositos esse historia schismatum secutura testabitur; Deponi Papas posse inter Pontificios controvertitur, dependetque haec de Controversia, quae inter eos est, quoad supremae potestatis Ecclesiasticae subjectum. Et hëc quidem modò ajunt, verbis supra allatis, Papas plane non judicari, modò addunt, etiam deponi posse, si sit à fide devius, modò à fide deviare posse negant. De depositione propter crimina, praeter haeresin, haud minus dissentiunt, dum eam alii in eo casu licitam, imò necessariam esse contendunt, alii, maximo numero scelaratos & aperte scandalosos fuisse haud nescientes, male certè, de Sanctitatibus Suis, negant; Optimè autem nos denuò concludimus, longè plures etiam deponi debuisse, indignos renunciare nolentes. Omnes, qui non ante deponunt, nec deponuntur, deponit mors. Mortis Pontificum circumstantiae & ritus in S. Cerem. Rom. l.1. p 155. seq. videri possunt; Ut nempe & à Medicis, & à Confessore in discrimine vitae de illo, & ut voluntati divinae non invitus adhaereat, eáque, quae ad animae salutem pertinent, curet, admoneri ut confiteri, ut plenariam indulgentiam petere, ut ab omnibus, quos forte injuste offenderit, veniam, veniam item, si in administratione offenderit, postulare, ut Sacramenta recipere, ut Cardinalibus valedicere, ut eos de Successore digno eligendo horrari, & unum vel plures, si ei videatur, nominare, ut debita & credita aperire, scripturas & thesauros manifestare, ut testamentum, si velit, condere, ut sepulturam eligere, ut Camerarius cum tribus ex Collegio inventarium facere & custodiam apponere, ut aliquis ex domesticis Praelatis crucem inspiciendam, osculandamque praebere, ut Sacrista commendationem animae, prout in ordinario, facere,
units.tr: II. As to what comes before the election: the way is prepared for it by the predecessor's resignation, deposition, or death. Five Roman Pontiffs are said to have resigned. The first is Clement I, from whose example the election by the predecessor's choice was discussed at length in Section I. Cyriac is said, according to the Gloss on c. 1 [?] in the Sixth Book, to have announced his resignation after a vision of St Ursula and the 11,000 virgins, who were to be his companions in the fable. But, as the same Gloss says in the older manuscripts, the Cardinals believed he had given up the Papacy not out of devotion but out of fondness for the virgins. Perhaps Gomezius, writing in Limnaeus, book 2, chapter 11, also had this in mind when he wrote that a Pontiff can renounce the Papacy, but that this rarely happens, except with cause, namely when he gives it up for the pleasures of the virgins. Marcellinus did so because of the crime of idolatry and apostasy he had committed. Celestine did so from awareness of his own weakness, and because of the fraud of his successor Boniface VIII, who, mindful of how much he had gained from it and wishing to strengthen his own right, confirmed by decree in the sixth book of the Decretals that abdication was possible and declared that it could be done. Augustine Triumphus of Ancona, in On the Power of the Church, question 4, article 5, also held that a decree to the contrary could not be made by the Pope. He relied chiefly on this argument: there is no doubt that someone could be elected Pope who lacked sufficient knowledge and experience to govern the whole Church, as has sometimes happened. So if he were not allowed to renounce, he would act against the truth of his own conscience, etc. Finally, John XXIII during the schism, of whom more in its place. Gilles Colonna of Rome wrote a separate treatise On the Renunciation of the Pope. That it ought to have happened far more often is clear, both from the cause just now mentioned and from the examples of unworthiness that will be set out in their place. History of the schisms will show that several Roman Popes were deposed. Among the Papists it is disputed whether Popes can be deposed, and this depends on the controversy between them about the subject of supreme ecclesiastical power. Some now say, in the words quoted above, that the Pope cannot be judged at all. Others add that he can even be deposed if he departs from the faith, while others deny that he can depart from the faith. They disagree no less about deposition for crimes other than heresy. Some maintain that it is lawful, and indeed necessary, in such a case. Others, not unaware that very many of them were wicked and openly scandalous, deny it, and at any rate speak badly of their Holinesses. We ourselves conclude, most rightly, that far more of them ought to have been deposed, since they were unwilling to renounce when they were unworthy. All those who are neither deposed beforehand nor deposed are deposed by death. The circumstances and rites of a Pontiff's death may be seen in the Roman Ceremonial, book 1, p. 155 and following. Namely: that he is reminded by the doctors and by his confessor, when his life is in danger, to submit himself to the will of God, not unwillingly, and to attend to those things that pertain to the salvation of his soul: to confess, to ask for a plenary indulgence, to ask forgiveness from all whom he may have unjustly offended, and likewise forgiveness if he has offended in his administration; to receive the sacraments; to take leave of the Cardinals; to exhort them to elect a worthy successor, and to name one or more if it seems good to him; to reveal debts and credits, to disclose the papers and treasures; to make a will if he wishes; to choose a burial place; that the Chamberlain, with three from the College, make an inventory and set a guard; that one of the household prelates present a cross to be looked at and kissed; that the Sacristan make the commendation of the soul, as in the ordinary,

units.la: ex Conclavi Gregorii XV. ob oculos posita; cere, ut Pœnitentiariorum circumstans chorus Psalmos pœnitentiales & alia, mortuo Pontifice Officium mortuorum legere, Cardinalium verò mox narrare, & quilibet defunctum absolvere, responsoriúmque cum suis versiculis & orationem pro defunctis dicere, ut Camerarius annulum Piscatoris minutè concidere, & typum Bullarum ex parte illa, ubi nomen Pontificis, frangere, ut mors Pontificis per signum æris Campani aliàs nunquam pulsari soliti è Capitolio populo notificari, ut à Cubiculariis aqua calida cum herbis odoriferis parari, ut à tonsore barba radi, ut corpus in Camera secreta cum optimo vino albo aromatizato & calido lavari, locus spumans quilibet aromatibus, myrrha & aloës nares, & aures musco, & totum corpus balsamo, manibus bene fricatis, impleri, vestibus communibus usque ad rochetum, deinde sacris, ac si esset celebraturus, cum omnibus ornamentis indui, inde super lecticam aureo panno coopertam cum Pontificis & Ecclesiæ armis & cervicalibus ex panno aureo etiam ad pedes cum duobus pileis Pontificalibus in Camera Papali poni, ut ibi à psallentibus custodiri, ut denique horâ competente & quâ pompâ ad Capellam majorem portari debeat. Romano autem Pontifice expirante, status, qui sub eo obtinuit, simul quoque expirat universus, mutantur omnia. Hinc author Conclavis Gregorii XV. ita orditur: Non dica d'essere stato in Roma &c. Non dicat, se Roma fuisse, qui non ibi commoratus est sede vacante, quando enim alio tempore omnia eo ordine incedunt, quem Pontificis viventis authoritas prescribit, tunc omnia ita mutantur, ut ne species quidem priorum remaneat; Tunc altitudines adorata & idololatricè culta ab adulatione aulica omnes cum magna sua mortificatione humiliantur. Ita ut ille, qui prius ostenderat spiritum dominii & superbia & cum primis de præeminentia contenderat, humiliatus se inclinet atque incurvet coram iis, quos paulò ante contempserat; Tunc fastus prioris Magistratûs deponitur, & talis, qui nihili antea æstimabatur, pra se fert, se posse pro lubitu suo claudere aut aperire viam ad sublimitatem Pontificatûs illi, qui se ei antea humanum exhibuerat. Tunc cessat tribunalium authoritas, & cuivis libera facultas relinquitur loquendi & scribendi publicè, quod antea multù de causis reticendum erat. Ille proin felix & sapiens est, qui ita vivit, ut in tali casu non accusari possit &c.
units.tr: as set before the eyes in the Conclave of Gregory XV; that the circle of Penitentiaries recite the penitential Psalms and other prayers; that, once the Pontiff is dead, the Office of the dead be read; that the Cardinals then at once speak the absolution, and each one absolve the dead man, and say the responsory with its versicles and the prayer for the dead; that the Chamberlain cut the Fisherman's ring into small pieces and break the die of the Bulls at the part where the Pontiff's name is; that the death of the Pontiff be announced to the people from the Capitol by the sound of the Campanian bronze, which is otherwise never rung; that warm water with fragrant herbs be prepared by the chamberlains; that the barber shave the beard; that the body be washed in the secret chamber with the best white wine, perfumed and warm; that every part be filled with aromatics, myrrh and aloes for the nostrils, musk for the ears, and the whole body with balm, rubbed well into the hands; that he be dressed in ordinary garments up to the rochet, then in sacred vestments, as if he were about to celebrate, with all the ornaments; and that he then be placed in the Papal Chamber on a bier covered with gold cloth, with the arms of the Pontiff and of the Church, and cushions of gold cloth also at the feet, with two Pontifical caps; that he be watched there by those chanting; and finally that he be carried to the Major Chapel at a suitable hour and with due pomp. When the Roman Pontiff expires, the whole state that held under him expires at the same time, and everything changes. Hence the author of the Conclave of Gregory XV begins thus: Let no one say he has been in Rome, etc. Let no one say he has been in Rome who has not stayed there during the vacancy of the See. For at other times everything goes in the order that the authority of the living Pontiff prescribes, but then everything changes so that not even the appearance of the former things remains. Then the heights, adored and worshipped idolatrously, are all humbled by courtly flattery, to their great mortification, so that he who had previously shown the spirit of lordship and pride, and above all had contended for precedence, bows and bends low before those whom he had just despised. Then the pomp of the former magistracy is laid aside, and one who was thought of as nothing before now declares that he can at his pleasure open or close the way to the high dignity of the Pontificate for the man who had shown himself humane to him. Then the authority of the tribunals ceases, and everyone is given free licence to speak and write publicly, which before, for many reasons, had to be kept silent. He therefore is happy and wise who so lives that in such a case he cannot be accused, etc.

units.la: III. Contendit Author, Roma non fuisse, qui non sede vacante ibi fuerit.
units.tr: III. The author contends that no one was at Rome who was not there during a vacancy of the see.

units.la: Quod paradoxum quodammodo contrariari videtur vulgari verbo: Roma fuit, & Papam non vidit! Hic contrà sentit, Romæ non fuisse, qui Papam semper viderit; Nempe sede vacante Roma est magis Roma, ‘Pῥμη, confluxus sordium omnium, alia Roma à priori multùm diversa. Videamus autem de mutatione illa distinctiùs, quia lucem aliquam tractationi nostræ dare potest, & ex corruptione illa paulatim nova oritur generatio.
units.tr: This paradox seems in some measure to contradict the common saying, Rome has been, and yet has not seen the Pope! Here, on the contrary, he holds that a man was not at Rome who always saw the Pope. Indeed, when the see is vacant, Rome is more truly Rome, Ῥώμη [Rhōmē], the confluence of all filth, a Rome very different from the former one. Let us look more closely at that change, since it can throw some light on our discussion, and out of that corruption a new generation gradually arises.

units.la: IV. Ipse Papa, Vicarius Christi, Caput Ecclesiæ, potentior omnibus, metuendus omnibus, etiam Regibus, præcipuum idolum adoratum, idolum idolorum reliquorum, fundamentum reliquorum jacet, plerunque invitus & malè jacet, non tantùm aliquo modo mortificatus, sed planè mortuus; mortuus, ut moriuntur homines cæteri, sed ejus memoria plerunque non est in benedictione.
units.tr: IV. The Pope himself, Vicar of Christ, Head of the Church, more powerful than all, feared by all, even by kings, the chief idol worshipped, the idol of all the other idols, the foundation on which the rest rest, lies for the most part unwillingly and ill. He is not merely in some way mortified but plainly dead: dead as other men die, yet his memory is for the most part not in blessing.

units.la: V. Sed primò mors gaudium affert; Ut tunc quoque sæpe dici possit: Annuncio vobis gaudium magnum, perdidimus Papam. Pervolgata per Roma la morte d'Innocentio &c. Id est: Publicatâ per Romam Innocentii (X.) morte, gaudere cœpit Civitas, ut solet in ejusmodi casibus. Neque hoc mirum videri debet, quandoquidem gaudet populus ob libertatem, quam habet sede vacante, gaudent Cardinales ob spem cujuscunque, si non directè de Papatu sibi conferendo, saltem de Papa secundùm placitum suum eligendo. Exultant gaudio omnes Cardinalium cognati & amici, sperantes, se mediante promotione eò confecensuros, unde alii descendunt, & tandem gaudent malè contenti, videntes, se liberos à tantis oppressionibus; Sunt verba Abbatis Gualdi Vita di Donna Olympia p.437.438. Gaudium autem aliquando, sed rarius, affert mors Pontificis, si minùs Curiæ fastum amavit defunctus; Cujus exemplum in Adriano VI. Papa Germano, habemus; De quo ita Conclave Successoris Clementis VII. La cui morte intesa &c. Romani, morte ejus intellectâ, incredibili gaudio atque voluptate perfusi sunt, quoniam universaliter toti Curiæ parùm gratus erat, tanquam multùm diversus à pompa & magnificentia & splendore Antecessorum suorum proximorum, quanquam revera magis propinquus bonis illis qualitatibus, quæ quæri atque desiderari solebant in electione Pontificum Ecclesiæ primitivæ. Usque adeò, ut postquam Sanctitati suæ periculum imminuisset à casu supraliminaris portæ Capellæ Pontificiæ, quò mane quodam ibat ad Missam audiendam, ita ut ex casu Lapidis illius occisi sint nonnulli milites præsidiarii Helvetii, & Sanctitas suæ vix salvata fuerit ex illo periculo; & salus facta fuisset, tam parùm multis Prælatis ibi præsentibus grata fuerit, ut quidam illorum in præsentia Cardinalium, dum de periculo Sanctitatis suæ sermo erat, populo insultârit, & fortunæ maledicere ausus sit, & fato, eò quòd à morte eam liberaverit; & , quod maximè mirandum, Prælatus ille non fuit à Cardinale ideò reprehensus ullo modo ob maledica illa verba, sed potiùs laudatus & benignè habitus. Proin sanctus iste vir tanquam parùm regimini mundano aptus multis calumniis laceratus fuit &c.
units.tr: V. But first, death brings joy, so that then too it can often be said: We bring you good tidings of great joy: we have lost the Pope. Once the death of Innocent was spread through Rome, etc. That is: When the death of Innocent X was made known throughout Rome, the city began to rejoice, as usually happens in such cases. Nor should this seem strange, since the people rejoice at the liberty they have while the see is vacant, and the cardinals rejoice at the hope of something, if not of conferring the papacy on themselves directly, at least of electing a Pope according to their own pleasure. All the cardinals' relatives and friends exult, hoping that by means of a promotion they will climb to where others have come down from, and at last they rejoice, glad to be free of such great oppressions. These are the words of Abbot Gualdi, Vita di Donna Olympia, pp. 437–438. Sometimes, though more rarely, the death of a Pontiff brings joy if the deceased loved the pomp of the Curia less. We have an example of this in Adrian VI, a German Pope, of whom the Conclave of Clement VII's successor says: When his death became known, the Romans were filled with incredible joy and delight, since he was generally little liked by the whole Curia, as being very different from the pomp, magnificence and splendour of his immediate predecessors, although in truth he was closer to those good qualities which were usually sought and desired in the election of the Popes of the primitive Church. So much so that when he had escaped danger from the fall of the lintel of the papal chapel's door, through which he was going one morning to hear Mass, so that some Swiss guards were killed by the falling stone, and His Holiness was barely saved from that danger, the outcome was so little welcome to the many prelates present there that one of them, in the presence of the cardinals, while the danger to His Holiness was being discussed, insulted the people, dared to curse his fortune and his fate for having saved him from death. What is most astonishing, that prelate was not in any way rebuked by the cardinal for those abusive words, but rather praised and treated kindly. Therefore this holy man, as being little fit for worldly government, was torn to pieces by many slanders, etc.

units.la: VI. Sed gaudium multò majus, saltem frequentius & quasi ordinarium affert mors Papæ, si ultra modum malus fuit, nimis fastum amavit, Nepotibus nimis indulsit; Neque tantùm, quando Papa gaudii vehementiâ moritur, quod Onuphrius Leoni X. contigisse in vita testari videtur; Bonifacius VIII. quidem mortuus est, secundùm Authorem Cardinalismi p.3.l.1. p.74. di dissipacere, ægritudine mentis; sed grande in vero &c. Magnum revera fuit gaudium, quod accepit Christianus orbis ex morte Pontificis Pontificatu indignissimi, & præcipuè Principes & Cardinales ignibus accensis latitiam testati sunt. Plurima ejusmodi exempla ex seculis remotioribus dare possemus, sed tunc monstra in sede monstrabantur. Propius exemplum in Paulo IV. contueamur, de quo Vita di Sisto V. p.1.l.3, p.181. La sua morte &c. Mors ejus gaudio affecit non tantùm populum Romanum, sed omnes Principes Christiani orbis. Exemplo sit adhuc recentiori Innocentius X. quod ita exhibet Abbas cit. loc. cit. Ma se mai la Città di Roma si trovò in allegrezza &c. Sed si unquam Roma gaudio affecta fuit per mortem Pontificis, certum est, gaudium ex morte Innocentii quodvis aliud superâsse, non tam ipsius Innocentii, quàm verò Domina Olympia tam exosa intuitu. Omnes boni Deum laudabant videntes sic Ecclesiam à tyrannide istius fœmina liberam &c. Ita etiam gaudium illud exhibet Author Conclavis Alexandri VII. ut ipse quoque simul de gaudio ex morte Pontificum quasi ordinario testetur: L'angonia &c. Per angonem decem dierum, inquit, diminuta fuit latitia ex morte ipsius, qua sequi solet ex morte Pontificum diu regnantium; quandoquidem & bonum & malum majora sunt, dum ex improviso obtingunt, utrumque autem longa expectatione diminuitur. Ubi manifestè loquitur de morte Pontificum, tanquam de bono quodam, de nuncio mortis, tanquam de Evangelio.
units.tr: VI. But joy far greater, at least more frequent and almost ordinary, is brought by the death of a Pope if he was excessively bad, loved pomp beyond measure, and indulged his nephews too much. This happens not only when a Pope dies in the violence of his joy, which Onuphrius seems to attest happened to Leo X in his lifetime. Boniface VIII indeed died, according to the author of Cardinalismo, p. 3, l. 1, p. 74, of a disordered mind, a sickness of the mind; but truly great was the joy which the Christian world received from the death of a Pontiff most unworthy of the papacy, and especially the princes and cardinals showed their gladness with lit fires. We could give very many examples of this kind from more remote centuries, but in those days monsters were displayed on the throne. Let us look at a closer example in Paul IV, of whom Life of Sixtus V, p. 1, l. 3, p. 181: His death gave joy not only to the Roman people but to all the princes of the Christian world. An example of more recent date is Innocent X, which the abbot just cited presents thus: But if ever Rome was filled with rejoicing, it is certain that the joy at the death of Innocent surpassed every other, not so much because of Innocent himself as because of Donna Olympia, who was so hated. All good men praised God, seeing the Church thus freed from the tyranny of that woman, etc. In the same way the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII sets forth that joy, so that he himself also testifies at the same time that joy at the death of Popes is almost ordinary: The anguish, he says, of ten days diminished the happiness that usually follows the death of Popes who have reigned long, since both good and evil are greater when they come unexpectedly, and each is lessened by long expectation. Here he speaks plainly of the death of Popes as of some good thing, of the news of death as of the Gospel.

units.la: VII. Indecorum hoc est, lætari de morte Patris, lætari de morte Vicarii Christi, Capitis & Sponsi Ecclesiæ; Ast quid si ei post mortem sæpe maledicitur? Exemplum hic luculentissimum in Sixto IV. ut multa alia taceamus, occurrit. De cujus morte Author Conclavis Innocentii VIII. sequentia habet: Die decimâ Augusti gusti S. D. N. Sixtus Papa IV. visus fuit complicatis manibus in vesperam & multùm tristis. Deinde sequenti die accesserunt ad eum ordines Confœderatorum, putantes forte afferre ei aliquod gaudium, & exposuerunt ei, qualiter conclusa erat pax per totam Italiam, etiam, quòd omnes Potentiæ de Liga & confœderatione reducta erant ad concordiam; de quo ipse multùm obstupuit; & miratus est, quare pax sine eo conclusa esset, attento quòd, ut dicebat, ipse principaliter debuisset intervenire. Et cùm hoc sæpius interrogâsset ab illis, & esset certificatus, quòd dicta pax erat conclusa; adeò quòd non poterat amplius retractari, doluit valde; (Vicarius Principis pacis!) Et causa doloris communi omnium existimatione hæc fuit, quia semper in omnibus suis operibus animum suum ostendit in hunc finem, ut aliquem statum, potentiam, sive dominium acquireret Comiti Hieronymo, (egregia causa pacis inimica!) ut videri potest per exempla. Primò, propter bellum, quod gessit Tudertinis, Spoletanis, Civitati Castelli & Florentinis. Deinde propter confœderationes, quas fecit, primò cum Rege Ferdinando, secundò contra eum cum Venetis, tertiò (horas mutatus in omnes, ut finem memoratum assequeretur;) contra Venetos cum dicto Rege, & in aliis similibus. Putabat modò, in hac pacis conclusione se posse aliquid Comiti Hieronymo acquirere, & ista de causa in tali confœderatione (En dignam rursus causam!) & pecuniam Ecclesiæ expendit, (En eleemosynæ optimum usum!) sed postquam vidit se illusum, (astutus decipitur in astutia sua!) & cecidisse ab hac spe, & pecunias Ecclesiæ expositas perdidisse, nihilque ex bello prædicto acquisivisse, doluit valde; (spes enim improba non satiat;) Itaque tam ex primo dolore, quàm ex novissimo (quem Evangelium pacis attulerat!) infirmatus est ex febre; jacuitque in lecto, & obmutuit, visúsque fuit examinis per aliquod spatium, deinde in se reversus, inflato gutture, duodecimâ Augusti quintâ horâ noctis ab hac vita migravit. Manè sequenti corpus ejus delatum fuit in Ecclesiam Sancti Petri viginti duntaxat cereis in torcitiis (ut non hic opus fuerit lege pompam funebrem restringentes) in quadam antiqua aurea planeta, paucis comitatus hominibus. Erat quidem niger, deformis, & guttur ejus inflatum. Omnes eum maledicebant, nec visus fuit homo, qui de eo bene dixerit, nisi quidam Frater S. Francisci, qui solus illa die corpus non sine magno fœtore observabat. Condita fuerunt in eum multa carmina, fortasse quia literarum & bonos mores habentium semper inimicus fuit, inter quae fuerunt ista: Leno, vorax, Pathicus, Meretrix, Idolater, Adulter, Si Romam venerit, illico Crœsus erit. Quæ quidem eximia & Vicario Christi scilicet digna sunt elogia; cujus tamen sanctissimo imperio soli Platinæ historiam de Vitis Pontificum debemus, ita enim ille in proœmio ad Xystum, vel Sixtum hunc loquitur, Theologorum ac Philosophorum, quibus ibidem adulatoriis vocibus utitur,Principem. Aliud exemplum indigitat Onuphrius, qui Paulo III. in vita tribuit, quod mortuus non adeo probatus fuerit; Aliud in cæteris eminens suppeditat Vita di Sisto V. p.1.l.3.p.185. ubi,quid mortem Pauli IV. immediatè exceperit, significatur: La plebe di Roma &c. inquit Author,Plebs Romana agrè ferens,se usque adeò subjugari tremendo illo Sancti Officii tribunale, mille insolentias exercuit, nam cum magno impetu cucurrit ad flammis consumendum Inquisitionis locum; Sed neque sic contentus furibundus populus porrò caput cum manu dextra amputavit statua marmorea Pontificis magnis sumptibus & à peritissimis artificibus confecta atque in Palatio Conservatorum locata,eam tribus continuis diebus per plateas trahendo,in omnibus civitatis angulis, eámque omni immunditiei genere conspurcando &c. Exempla malè tractatorum post mortem Pontificum, & à Pontificibus quidem,Formosi,in historia Schismatum; Johannis XIV. apud Baron. ad an. 1058. n. 1. 2. videri possunt &c. Sæpissime autem Pontifices post mortem malè audiunt ob insolentiam Nepotum; Hinc Urbanus VIII. L'Amb. di Rom. vectigal, (Papa Gabella) vocatur; p.220. Alex. VII. omne Senensium nomen Romanis abominationi fecisse dicitur &c.
units.tr: VII. It is unseemly to rejoice at the death of a father, to rejoice at the death of the Vicar of Christ, the Head and Bridegroom of the Church. But what if after death he is often reviled? The most striking example of this, to pass over many others, occurs in Sixtus IV. About his death the author of the Conclave of Innocent VIII has the following: On the tenth of August His Holiness Pope Sixtus IV was seen in the evening with his hands folded and very sad. Then on the following day the envoys of the allies came to him, thinking perhaps to bring him some joy, and they told him how peace had been concluded throughout Italy, and that all the powers of the League and confederation had been brought back to concord. At this he was greatly astonished, and wondered why peace had been concluded without him, since, as he said, he should have intervened chiefly. When he had asked this several times and had been assured that the said peace was concluded, so that it could no longer be revoked, he grieved greatly (the Vicar of the Prince of Peace!). The cause of his grief, by the common opinion of all, was this: that in all his undertakings he showed his mind directed to this end, that he might gain some state, power or dominion for Count Girolamo (an excellent cause, hostile to peace!), as can be seen from examples. First, because of the war he waged against the men of Todi, Spoleto, Città di Castello and Florence. Then because of the confederations he made, first with King Ferdinand, second against him with the Venetians, third (changing sides to every party so as to attain the aforesaid end) against the Venetians with the said King, and in other similar things. He thought now that in the conclusion of this peace he might acquire something for Count Girolamo, and for this reason he spent the Church's money on such a confederation (behold a worthy cause again!), (behold the best use of alms!). But when he saw himself deceived (the crafty man is caught in his own craft!), and had fallen from this hope, and had lost the Church's money spent on it, and had gained nothing from the aforesaid war, he grieved greatly (for an impious hope does not satisfy). Therefore, both from the first grief and from the last (which the gospel of peace had brought!), he was struck down by a fever, lay in bed and fell silent, and for some time seemed like a dead man. Then, coming to himself, with his throat swollen, on the twelfth of August at the fifth hour of the night he departed this life. The next morning his body was carried into the Church of St Peter with only twenty candles in torches (so that there was no need here for law to restrict the funeral pomp), in some old golden chasuble, accompanied by few men. He was indeed black, misshapen, and his throat swollen. Everyone cursed him, and no man was seen who spoke well of him, except a certain Franciscan friar who alone that day watched over the body, not without a great stench. Many verses were composed about him, perhaps because he was always an enemy of men who had learning and good morals, among which were these: Pimp, glutton, sodomite, whore, idolater, adulterer; if he comes to Rome he will at once be a Croesus. These are indeed excellent eulogies, and fitting for the Vicar of Christ. Yet to his most holy rule alone we owe Platina's history of the Lives of the Popes, for in his preface to Xystus, or Sixtus this man, he addresses him as the Prince of Theologians and Philosophers, with which flattering titles he speaks of him in the same place, calling him Prince. Onuphrius points out another example, who attributes to Paul III in his life that he was not much approved when dead. Another, outstanding among the rest, is supplied by Life of Sixtus V, p. 1, l. 3, p. 185, where it is indicated what immediately followed the death of Paul IV: The Roman people, taking it badly that they were so subjected to the terrible tribunal of the Holy Office, committed a thousand insolences; for with great fury they ran to the place of the Inquisition to burn it with flames. But the raging people, not content with this, further cut off with their right hand the head of a marble statue of the Pope, made at great expense by most skilled artists and placed in the Palace of the Conservators; dragging it for three continuous days through the streets, in every corner of the city, and defiling it with every kind of filth, etc. Examples of those ill-treated after the death of Popes, and by Popes indeed, such as Formosus in the history of the Schisms, and John XIV, can be seen in Baronius at the year 1058, nn. 1, 2, etc. But very often Popes after death are badly spoken of because of the insolence of their nephews. Hence Urban VIII is called the Gabelle of Rome (Papa Gabella) by the Ambassador of Rome, the tax, p. 220; of Alexander VII it is said that he made the whole name of the Sienese an abomination to the Romans, etc.

units.la: VIII. Nepotes autem vel maximè dicuntur idola adorata; Et quorum mortificatio etiam mortem Pontificum excipere, electionem aliorum præcedere solet. Audiatur de eo omnium loco Author Conclavis Leonis XI. qui,factâ de morbo Clementis VIII. lethali & nuncio Cardinali Aldobrandino allato, mentione, subjungit: Nova, la quale &c. Quod nuncium,quàm amaras reddiderit dulcedines Cardinalis, assueti semper dormire in brachio fortuna, & quàm attonitam reddiderit Curiam, quæ non expectabat tam altum precipitium; hoc omne consideractioni Lectoris relinquo. Angebant stuporem voces populares,quòd per delirium perpetuum Pontificis Aldobrandinus specialiter non potuerit Brevia conficere, ad transferendam dignitatem Camerarii in Sanctum Cesarium,Nepotem suum,ad retinendum pro se summi Pœnitentiarii gradum, ad vendendam dignitatem Thesaurarii, & ad vendicandum sibi alia ambigua; unde novus Pontifex non habere posset occasionem & prætextus legitimos domum Aldobrandinam debilitandi; quam multi assimilabant spelunca illi, in qua Leo se infirmum finxit, animalibus quidem omnibus ingredientibus, sed redeunte nemine, indicare volentes, ibi cum summa parsimonia conservari divitias, collectas cum tanta aviditate &c.
units.tr: VIII. Nephews, however, are especially called idola adorata (idols to be adored), and their mortificatio (mortification) usually follows the death of a pope and comes before the election of another. Let the author of the Conclave of Leo XI be heard on this point. After mentioning the news of Clement VIII's deadly illness brought to Cardinal Aldobrandini, he adds: News, which etc. How bitter that message made the sweetness of the Cardinal, who was always accustomed to sleep in the arms of fortune, and how stunned it left the Curia, which did not expect so high a fall, I leave entirely to the reader's consideration. The popular voices increased the amazement, because during the Pope's continuous delirium Aldobrandini could not draw up the briefs, especially those transferring the office of Chamberlain to Sanctus Caesarius, his nephew, retaining for himself the rank of chief Penitentiary, selling the office of Treasurer, and claiming other doubtful things for himself; so the new pope would have no opportunity or lawful pretext for weakening the Aldobrandini house. Many compared it to that cave in which Leo feigned himself sick, into which all the animals entered but from which none returned, wishing to indicate that riches gathered with such greed are kept there with the greatest frugality, etc.

units.la: IX. Testis non minus luculentus accedit Author Conclavis Alexandri VII. dum narrat, quomodo circa finem Urbani VIII. tractatum fuerit cum Cardinale Capponi de resignatione Archiepiscopatus, che Antonio &c. quem Antonius ad imitationem Petri Aldobrandini (illius ipsius, de quo n. praced. agit) volebat capere, ut habeat, sicut ille, locum refugii, prasagiens jam tum adversitates, qua eum Roma expellere debebant. Sed ille ipse Antonius mortuo Alexandro VII. odio erga Nepotes illius concepto rursus commendatus fuit, quando nimirum cognati recens defuncti Pontificis non potuerunt sfuggire &c. effugere convitia & injurias plebis insolentis, graviter exacerbata; Et faeminae domus Chigiae necesse habuerunt, sine con &c. etiam lachrymis deplorare Satyrica & Pasquinalia continua, qua contra familiam etiam cum honoris lasione quotidie audiebantur, juxta Authorem Conclavis Clementis IX. Tunc enim Antonius ille, che alla morte &c. quem post mortem Urbani maledictis persequebantur se improvisa mutatione elogiis & applausibus ornatum vidit; Quia nimirum Nepos Nepotem commendat, pejor meliorem, vel potius recentior antiquiorem. Tunc enim Marius Chigius defuncti Pontificis frater, referente Il. Cardinal. l. 3. p. 3. p. 365. Equiti Collesio in servitio antehac suo constituto & tantum annuam 90. scutatorum pensionem habenti tanquam avunculo recens electi Pontificis & Fratri Matris Nepotum dextram cedere coactus fuit, che sono, addit Author, le solite metamorfosi della corte di Roma; Id est; quae sunt solita metamorphoses curiae Romanae.
units.tr: IX. An equally clear witness is the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII, when he tells how, near the end of Urban VIII's reign, an arrangement was made with Cardinal Capponi for the resignation of the archbishopric: to Antonio etc., whom Antonio wished to take, in imitation of Pietro Aldobrandini (the very man discussed in the preceding paragraph), so that he might have, as that man did, a place of refuge, foreseeing already the adversities which were to drive him out of Rome. But this same Antonio, after Alexander VII's death, was recommended again, when the relatives of the recently deceased Pope could not sfuggire etc., escape the insults and injuries of the insolent, sharply aroused populace; and the women of the house of Chigi were obliged sine con etc., to lament even with tears the continual satires and lampoons which were heard daily against the family, with damage even to its honour, according to the author of the Conclave of Clement IX. For then that Antonio, che alla morte etc., whom they had persecuted with abuse after Urban's death, saw himself adorned with unexpected changes of tone and applause. For, of course, a nephew commends a nephew; the worse commends the better, or rather the more recent the older. For then Marius Chigi, the brother of the dead Pope, according to Il. Cardinal. l. 3. p. 3. p. 365., was forced to yield the right hand to Equite Collesio, who had previously been in his service and had only an annual pension of ninety scudi, as the uncle of the newly elected Pope and brother of the mother of the nephews. Che sono, the author adds, le solite metamorfosi della corte di Roma; that is, these are the usual metamorphoses of the Roman court.

units.la: X. Quoad regimen, tempore illo sedis vacantis Marescallus sedis, quod officium familiae Savellicae haereditarium est, Reipublicae invigilat, militiam regit, tumultibusque majoribus in civitate avertendis maxime studet. Camerarii etiam tunc magna est authoritas, illi enim cura civitatis quoque incumbit, fabricari monetas suo nomine jubet, & ad necessaria Reipublicae providenda Conclavi libere exire potest. Poenitentiarius autem & ejus officiales ea tantum faciunt, quae ad forum conscientiae pertinent; Interim tamen neque Camerarius, neque Poenitentiarius, neque etiam Collegium Cardinalium in iis, quae ad Pontificem Maximum, mum, dum viveret, pertinebant, ullam omninò potestatem, aut jurisdictionem habent, neque gratiam, neque justitiam faciendi, aut factam per Pontificem mortuum executioni demandandi, sed ea omnia futuro Pontifici reservare tenentur. Datarii verò ministerium per Pontificis obitum omninò expirat, ita ut non solùm datas per eum antea notatas extendendi potestatem minimè habeat: Sed quascunque supplicationes gratiarum & justitiæ, penes eum aut ejus ministros adhuc existentes, etiam si datæ fuerint, Collegio Cardinalium, statim sub sigillo clausas præsentare teneatur futuro Pontifici reservandas; Quod & respectu Cardinalium & Præla-torum signaturæ gratiæ & justitiæ obtinet, dum eorum officia pariter cessare intelliguntur.
units.tr: X. As for government, during that time of vacancy the Marshal of the See, an office hereditary in the Savelli family, watches over the commonwealth, directs the soldiery, and devotes the greatest effort to averting larger disturbances in the city. At that time the Chamberlain also has great authority; for the care of the city falls to him as well, he orders money to be minted in his own name, and he may go freely out of the Conclave to provide for the necessities of the commonwealth. The Penitentiary and his officials, however, deal only with matters that pertain to the forum of conscience. Yet neither the Chamberlain, nor the Penitentiary, nor even the College of Cardinals has any power or jurisdiction at all over matters that pertained to the Supreme Pontiff while he lived, nor may they grant favour or justice, or order the execution of anything the dead Pope had done; they are bound to reserve all these things for the future Pope.
