The office of the Datary, however, wholly expires at the Pope's death, so that he not only has no power to extend the dispensations previously noted by him, but is bound to present to the College of Cardinals, at once and sealed, any petitions for favours and justice still existing with him or his ministers, even if they have been granted, to be reserved for the future Pope. This also holds with regard to the Cardinals and Prelates of the Signatura of Grace and Justice, since their offices are likewise understood to cease.

units.la: XI. Quæ verò, sede vacante, pro defensione terrarum & locorum, status securitate ac provisionibus Conclavis facienda sunt, à Cardinalibus præsentibus per secreta suffragia ordinantur, qui etiam, si opus fuerit, Gubernatores & Officiales pro statûs Ecclesiastici regimine eligunt; Et quorum tunc authoritas ex eo inter alia perspici potest, quòd Alexandro VII. mortuo, referente Authore Conclavis Clementis IX. Ludovicus XIV. Rex Galliæ hodiernus in Congregatione per Legatum fatte le 3. genu fleffioni &c. facta triplice genu flexione, ac si Pontifex ipse præsens esset, præstitit debitum obsequium Eminentissimis Dominis Cardinalibus, atque ita ob oculos posuit devotionem Regis sui erga sedem sanctam, offerens ejus copias ad ejus, & ad S. Collegii defensionem. Quod & paulò post de Legato Regis Hispaniæ innuit.
units.tr: XI. As for what must be done during the vacancy for the defence of the lands and places, and for the security of the state and the provisions of the Conclave, these are decided by the Cardinals present through secret votes; and they also elect, if need be, governors and officials for the administration of the ecclesiastical state. Their authority at that time can be seen, among other things, from the fact that when Alexander VII died, according to the author of the Conclave of Clement IX, Louis XIV, the present King of France, through his Legate in the Congregation, fatte le 3. genu fleffioni etc., made a threefold genuflection, as if the Pope himself were present, paid the due homage to the most eminent Lord Cardinals, and thus set before their eyes the devotion of his king towards the Holy See, offering his troops for the defence of it and of the Sacred College. He hints at something similar shortly afterwards concerning the Legate of the King of Spain.

units.la: XII. Cæterùm civitas illo tempore & dum Roma canit, L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.16. Horche vedova son, ò quanti e quanti con Mascare posticeie e labra fozze Vorreber meco celebrar le nozze! &c. Id est: O quot hypocritæ, dum vidua jam sum, nuptias meas appetunt! variis tumultibus, quod ex dictis jam colligitur, est obnoxia; Dimittuntur incarcerati pro levibus causis à Conservatoribus P. R. cæteris ad arcem Hadriani imminente morte transmissis; Regnant scelera, & mox hinc, mox inde alius insurgit; homicidia sunt frequentia; Verbo, vivitur, sicut sine capite solet, & ferè Saturnalia veterum Romanorum reducuntur; vel potiùs mos obtinet, quem in Persia viguisse ajunt, ubi, mortuo Rege, per triduum cuilibet, quodlibet, liceat. Testis sit αυτοπλης Janus Nicius Erythræus epist. 68. ad Tyrrhenum ita scribens: Civitas (tempore hoc Sedis vacantis) sine ullo jure est, sine dignitate Resp. Tantus Tantus in urbe armatorum numerus cernitur, quantum me alias vidisse non memini. Nulla domus est paulo locupletior, qua non militum multorum praesidio muniatur. Ac si in unum omnes cogerentur, magnus ex eis exercitus inde confici posset. Summa in Urbe armorum impunitas, summa licentia: passim caedes hominum fiunt, nil ita frequenter auditur, quam hic vel ille notus homo est interfectus. Haec inter Romanos tunc aguntur, qui olim ad electionem ipsi statim concurrebant; Sic ad Vicarii Christi regnum praeparantur, in ea confusione saepe diu, pro ratione nimirum morarum in Conclavi, vivere adiguntur.
units.tr: XII. Meanwhile the city at that time, and while Rome sings, L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.16. Horche vedova son, ò quanti e quanti con Mascare posticeie e labra fozze Vorreber meco celebrar le nozze! etc., that is, O how many hypocrites, now that I am a widow, desire to celebrate their nuptials with me!, is exposed to various tumults, as may already be gathered from what has been said. Prisoners are released for trivial causes by the Conservators of the Roman People, while others are sent to the fortress of Hadrian under threat of death; crimes flourish, and now here, now there, another uprising breaks out; homicides are frequent. In short, men live as a body without a head usually does, and something close to the Saturnalia of the ancient Romans is brought back, or rather a custom prevails which they say flourished in Persia, where, when the King died, anyone might do anything whatever for three days. Let Janus Nicius Erythraeus bear witness, epist. 68., writing thus to Tyrrhenus, who is αυτόπτης [eyewitness]: The city (during this vacancy of the See) is without any law, without any dignity of government. Such a number of armed men is seen in the city as I do not remember having seen at any other time. There is no house somewhat wealthy that is not protected by the guard of many soldiers. And if they were all gathered into one place, a great army could be made from them. There is the greatest impunity for arms in the City, the greatest licence; everywhere men are slain, and nothing is heard so often as that this or that well-known man has been killed. These are the things done among the Romans at that time, who once used to gather for the election at once; thus, while they are being prepared for the reign of the Vicar of Christ, in such confusion they are often forced to live for a long time, namely for the sake of the delays in the Conclave.

units.la: XIII. Funebria Pontificis quod porro spectat, de tota pompa Pii IV. & Gregorii XV. Bullis constitutum est, ut exequiae novemdiales (nempe propter associationem in Angelorum novem ordines habentium Chorum, revera autem ad imitationem Centilis ritus a S. Augustino improbati;) fiant, & si quando per observantiam alicujus magni & praecipui Festi Cardinalibus officium exequiarum intermitti debere videretur; dies illi sic intermissi in numerum 9. dierum nihilominus computentur, & impensa, quae in eis pro exequiis facienda esset, inter pauperes Christi distribuatur, utque superfluis quoque sumptibus, qui jam in immensum excreverint, modus imponatur, funus simplicius, quam consueverit, fiat, ita ut illius ratione (praeter Regalia populo Romano praestari solita) decem millium ducatorum summam pannis lugubribus & regalibus tam Camerarii, quam Clericorum, ac aliorum Cameralium, quam aliorum quorumcunque ministrorum & Officialium, ac aliis omnibus computatis, impensa non excedat. Summa autem decem millium hujusmodi, vel, si Collegio visum fuerit, etiam minor, at nullo modo major, per tres Cardinales antiquiores, unum videlicet de quolibet ordine, & Camerarium proportionabiliter pro rata distributionis alias fieri solitae, inter praedictos omnes & singulos dividatur.
units.tr: XIII. As for the funeral of the Pope, as far as the rest goes, it has been established by the Bulls of Pius IV and Gregory XV that the nine-day obsequies are to be held (namely on account of the association with the choir of the nine orders of angels, though in truth in imitation of the Gentile rite disapproved by St Augustine); and if at any time the office of the obsequies seems to have to be omitted for the observance of some great and especial feast, those days so omitted are nevertheless to be counted in the number of nine days, and the expense that would have been incurred for the obsequies is to be distributed among the poor of Christ. Likewise, so that a limit may be set even on superfluous expenses, which have already grown immensely, the funeral is to be made more simply than has been customary; so that on its account (besides the royal gifts customarily given to the Roman people) the sum of ten thousand ducats, computed with all the mourning cloths and royal cloths for the Chamberlain, the clergy and other officials of the Chamber, and all other ministers and officers, shall not be exceeded. The sum of ten thousand of this kind, or even less if the College sees fit, but in no way more, is to be divided among the aforesaid persons, each and all, by three of the senior Cardinals, namely one from each order, and the Chamberlain, in proportion to the share otherwise customarily distributed.

units.la: XIV. Istas autem conditiones, quamvis minime duras, non semper observari, vel ex solo Alexandri VII. in Conclavi Clementis IX. exemplo constare potest, ubi multis narratur, quomodo, morte Cardinali Camerario nuntiata, fuerit nuncius con soliti termini di Cortesia ricevuto &c. solitis terminis civilitatis exceptus & cum doloris testificatione erga suam sanctitatem dimissus, tempus & occasio data consanguineis, reliquam supellectilem transportandi & ad palatia sua cito revertendi, quomodo idem Camerarius veste violina lina inductus, comitantibus eum omnibus Camerae Clericis palliis nigris indutis, Palatium Pontificum ingressus, factis solitis circa cadaver ceremoniis, possessionem nomine Reverendae Camerae Apostolicae universalem occupârit, cadaver apertum & ex usu aliorum Pontificum conditum, & in Ecclesiam S. Petri cum pompa militari transvectum, & Missa quovis die (primo tantùm Pentecostes, in quo in caputiis violinis comparere per Festi solennitatem non licuerit, excepto) per l'anima di Nostro Signore, pro anima Domini nostri (ita absolutè vocant) cantata & magnificum monumentum (quod ibi prolixè describitur, in quo etiam conceptio B. Virginis, quam sine peccato factam esse definierat, depicta dicitur, & cui, praeter sumptus Camerae ordinarios 2. millia scutorum consanguinei impendisse perhibentur;) perfectum, erectum, aquâ benedictâ undiquaque conspersum, simul suffitus factus & oratio in laudem defuncti habita, sicque tandem finitae fuerint solitae functiones à Dominis Cardinalibus, per pregare Requie all'anima del Defonto Pontefice, ad orandam requiem animae defuncti Pontificis; qui tamen ceu Vicarius Christi & aeternae beatitudinis arbiter tot & tantis ceremoniis non opus habuisse videtur! De osculo pedum Cadaveri etiam figi solito, infrà, ubi de osculo pedum, quod adorationis, quae sequitur, pars est, videatur.
units.tr: XIV. These conditions, though by no means harsh, are not always observed. This can be seen from the example of Alexander VII in the conclave of Clement IX alone, where it is recounted at length how, when the death of the Cardinal Camerlengo was announced, the messenger was received "with the usual terms of courtesy, ricevuto &c.", and dismissed "with the usual terms of civility and with a declaration of grief towards His Holiness". Time and opportunity were given to the relatives to carry away the rest of the furniture and to return quickly to their palaces. The same Camerlengo, dressed in violet linen and accompanied by all the clerks of the Camera in black cloaks, entered the Pontifical Palace and, after the customary ceremonies around the body, took possession of it in the name of the Reverend Apostolic Camera as a whole. The body was opened and embalmed according to the practice of other Popes, and carried with military pomp into the Church of St Peter. A Mass was sung every day, except on the first day of Pentecost, when the violet hoods could not appear because of the solemnity of the feast, "per l'anima di Nostro Signore, for the soul of Our Lord" (this is how they absolutely term it). A magnificent monument was completed and erected (it is described at length there, and is said to depict the conception of the Blessed Virgin, which he had defined as made without sin; the relatives are also said to have spent 2,000 scudi on it, besides the ordinary expenses of the Camera). It was sprinkled all round with holy water, incense was burned, and a speech in praise of the deceased was given. Thus at last the customary functions were finished by the Lord Cardinals, "per pregare Requie all'anima del Defonto Pontefice, to pray for rest for the soul of the deceased Pontiff". Yet he, as Vicar of Christ and judge of eternal blessedness, seems to have had no need of so many and such great ceremonies! Concerning the kiss of the feet, which is also customarily given to the corpse, see below, where the kiss of the feet is discussed, since it is part of the adoration that follows.

units.la: XV. Sed mortuum mortuis relinquimus, & ad antecedentia promotionem successoris propiùs spectantia pergimus. Hic autem primò Cardinales in Congregationibus reperimus; qui à tribus Cardinalibus antiquioribus ex quolibet ordine, & à Camerario congregantur, penes quos quatuor etiam proponendi jus est, sed post triduum aliis relinquendum. In Congregationibus autem non tantùm de regimine ad tempus, & de officialibus extra & intra Conclave futuris disponunt, & Legatos Principum audiunt, & de loco Conclavis consultant, sed de ipso etiam successore ordinario inter se tractant; Congregantur autem sic, vestiti cum rochettis & mozzettis sine Cappa, quod est insigne jurisdictionis in qua succedunt. Sunt istae Congregationes quasi Ante-Conclavia, hinc etiam lites Conclavium adumbrant. Nam ita legimus in Conclavi Leonis XI. L'alterationi &c. Alterationes inter Cardinales in congregationibus quasi praeparabant ad discordias futuras. In Conclavi autem Alexandri VII. sequentia habentur: Nelle congregationi &c. In congregationibus, quae quotidie fiebant in Sacello S.Petri, detegebantur termini
units.tr: XV. But we leave the dead to the dead, and pass on to what precedes, the election of the successor. Here we first find the Cardinals in Congregations. These are gathered by the three senior Cardinals from each order, together with the Camerlengo, and they also have the right to propose matters, though this is to be left to the others after three days. In the Congregations they not only make arrangements for the government in the interim and for the officials who are to serve inside and outside the Conclave, hear the envoys of princes, and consult about the place of the Conclave, but also discuss among themselves the successor himself. They gather dressed in rochets and mozzettas without the cappa, which is the mark of the jurisdiction in which they succeed. These Congregations are almost pre-conclaves, and hence they also foreshadow the quarrels of the Conclaves. For we read thus in the conclave of Leo XI: "L'alterationi &c.", that is, the disputes among the Cardinals in the Congregations were in a sense preparing the way for future discord. In the conclave of Alexander VII the following is found: "Nelle congregationi &c.", that is, in the Congregations which were held daily in the Chapel of St Peter, the limits were revealed.

units.la: Congregationes Cardinalium; mini diuturnæ durationis Conclavis futuri, quandoquidem valde clare apparuit discordia opinionum in D. D. Cardinalibus, & constantia jam determinata in factionibus, qua una quaque suam partem prævalere curare voluit. Sunt nimirum ista principia spirationis Spiritus pacis!
units.tr: Congregations of the Cardinals. The conclave to come would be of very long duration, since the discord of opinions among the Lord Cardinals appeared very clearly, and the firmness already settled in the factions, by which each one wished to make his own side prevail. These, surely, are the beginnings of the breathing of the Spirit of peace!

units.la: XVI. Jam verò tempus est, ut plenè spiret, exequiæ novem dierum factæ sunt, satis diu expectavimus Cardinales absentes, illuxit dies undecimus ingressui in Conclave destinatus. Olim quidem etiam primo post mortem prædecessoris die eligebatur aliquando Successor. Vide Baronium ad an. 418. n. 78. & ad an. 1144. n. 1. aliquando ipso mortis die. ad an. 1130. n. 1. Olim quidem etiam, ut distinctione 79. nullus, habetur, per triduum tantùm expectandum erat. Quod & in electione Gregorii VII. factum esse apud Baronium ad an. 1073. n. 22. memoratur; Sed Glossa, per contrariam consuetudinem hoc hodie abrogatum esse, dicit. Expectandum tamen est hodie per decendium, de cujus initio Ant. de Rosellis Monarch. p. 2. c. 8. dubium movet; & decidit, à morte censeri debere, & non à tempore scientiæ, & ibidem dubium proponit, an, si Cardinales absentes sint in locis ita remotis, quod certissimum sit, infra 10. dies venire non posse: an 10. diebus nihilominus sit expectandum; Nimirum repetit dubium, quod Glossa in cap. ubi periculum. in verbis: Decem diebus. movit, & affirmando solvit, ob eam quoque rationem, quòd fortè intellexerant infirmitatem Papæ, unde iter ante mortem inceperunt, & sic intra decem dies poterunt pervenire. Melius tamen ideò affirmat, quia quandocunque veniunt re integra, id est, ante electionem completam, admittendi sunt, juxta d. c. ubi periculum. §. sanè. in fine, possunt autem (ut plerunque accidere infra notabimus) tantùm discordes esse Cardinales in Conclavi, quòd magna temporalia laberentur, ita, quòd possent venire absentes, & à vocibus suis non excludi, & pro hoc tex. in c. comissa de elect. l. 6. conjuncta l. id illa stipulatione si Calendis de verb. obli. & est utilis illa investigatio: quia si ante lapsum 10. dierum Cardinales elegerunt, absentes possent mutare electionem ratione contemptus.
units.tr: XVI. Now indeed it is time that it should fully breathe. The funeral rites of nine days have been performed, and we have waited long enough for the absent Cardinals. The eleventh day, appointed for entry into the Conclave, has dawned. In former times, indeed, a successor was sometimes elected on the first day after the death of the predecessor; see Baronius, ad an. 418, n. 78, and ad an. 1144, n. 1; sometimes even on the day of death itself, ad an. 1130, n. 1. In former times, indeed, as is stated in distinctio 79, nullus, only three days had to be waited. That this was done also in the election of Gregory VII is recorded by Baronius, ad an. 1073, n. 22; but the Gloss says that this has been abrogated today by contrary custom. Nevertheless, today one must wait ten days, about the beginning of which Antonius de Rosellis, Monarch. p. 2, c. 8, raises a doubt. He decides that it should be reckoned from the death and not from the time of knowledge. In the same place he proposes the doubt whether, if the absent Cardinals are in places so remote that it is quite certain they cannot come within ten days, one must nonetheless wait the ten days. Surely he repeats the doubt which the Gloss raised in cap. ubi periculum, in the words "decem diebus", and resolves it by affirming, for the reason also that perhaps they had heard of the Pope's illness, whence they set out before his death, and so could arrive within ten days. Yet he affirms this more correctly because whenever they come with the matter still open, that is, before the election is complete, they must be admitted, according to the same d. c. ubi periculum, §. sanè, at the end. Moreover (as we shall note below is generally the case) the Cardinals in the Conclave may be so divided that great temporal losses would follow, so that the absent could come and not be excluded from their votes; for this, see the text in c. commissa de elect., lib. 6, together with l. id illa stipulatione, si Calendis, de verb. oblig. And this inquiry is useful, because if the Cardinals elected before the lapse of ten days, the absent could change the election on account of contempt.

units.la: XVII. Nempe licet non ultrà 10. dies expectari debeant absentes & sufficiens habeatur electio à præsentibus die undecimo facta, duabus nimirum tertiis, juxta legem Alexandri III. suprà allatam, imò juxta jamjam laudatum de Rosellis l. c. p. 320. n. 40. Si duo tantùm præsentes essent & eligerent, (De quo tamen inter Dianam negantem & Bonacinam affirmantem lis est; ) vel si unus solus; quamvis unum solum non posse seipsum eligere statuat, quia electio
units.tr: XVII. Indeed, although the absent ought not to be waited for beyond ten days, and an election made by those present on the eleventh day is held to be sufficient, namely by two-thirds, according to the law of Alexander III cited above, indeed according to the de Rosellis cited just now, l. c. p. 320, n. 40: if only two were present and elected (about which, however, there is a dispute between Diana, who denies it, and Bonacina, who affirms it), or if only one, although he holds that one alone cannot elect himself, because the election

units.la: Dilatio Electionis per decem dies;
units.tr: Postponement of the Election for ten days;

units.la: Quibus exactis licet etiam pauccissimis præsentibus Papam eligere, {a}stio alicujus non debet habere ortum à se ipso de elec. c. cum in jure &c. per nostras. De jure Patron. & in c. cùm ad nostrum de institu. Et licèt, juxta eundem l. c. p.325. præsentes vocari & admoneri non debeant à duabus tertiis, tamen nemo, etiam post. 10. dies & vel ultimo ante electionem momento accedere volens arceri, sed semper, proponente eodem p.327. nisi voci suæ plane renuntiaverit (nam si propter justam infirmitatem, vel similem causam legitimam renuntiavit, vel causa est dubia, poenitentem tamen admittendum esse judicat ; De quo casu Glossa Decr. VI. l. 1. Tit. Vide elect. ad §. hoc sacro. addit; talem de iis, quæ medio tempore facta in Conclavi, conqueri non posse,) admitti debet. Quare etiam in Conclavi quodam recentiori Cardinalis Austriæ ex itinere recens tempore minimè opportuno, ipso nimirum tempore scrutinii jam coepti advolans, licèt Magistro Ceremoniæ moras brevissimas suadente, tamen, ne de ultimo actu primis diebus ageretur, ex ignorantia diuturnitatis ordinariæ, veritus, pulsare, & de nullitate protestari non destitit, donec intromissus fuit.
units.tr: When these are past, the Pope may be elected even by very few present. A challenge to anyone ought not to arise from himself, de elect. c. cum in jure etc., per nostras, De jure Patron., and in c. cum ad nostrum de institut. And although, according to the same l. c. p. 325, those present ought not to be summoned and warned by two-thirds, nevertheless no one, even after the ten days and even at the last moment before the election, is to be shut out if he wishes to come, but always, as the same author holds at p. 327, he must be admitted unless he has plainly renounced his vote. (For if he has renounced it on account of a just illness or similar lawful cause, or if the cause is doubtful, he judges that he is nevertheless to be admitted as one who repents; on this case the Gloss in Decr. VI, lib. 1, tit. de elect., ad §. hoc sacro, adds that such a man cannot complain about what has been done in the meantime in the Conclave.) Therefore also in a certain more recent Conclave, a Cardinal of Austria, arriving in haste from a journey at a most inopportune time, precisely while the scrutiny had already begun, did not desist from knocking and protesting against the nullity of the proceedings, although the Master of Ceremonies advised a very brief delay. He feared lest the last act be dealt with in the first days, through ignorance of the usual length of the period, until he was admitted.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Ipsi tamen absentes curant, ne diu, quoad locorum distantia permittit, expectari debeant, maturè moniti à præsentibus, qui, si vel incipiat periculosè decumbere Pontifex, statim Creaturis suis per nuntios id significant, eósque (quia sæpe damna in mora vel absentia) ut se ad iter accingant, studiosè hortantur, saltem vix mortuo Pontifice nuntii in varia orbis Christiani loca ad Cardinalium absentium convocationem dilabuntur; Qui etiam mox advolare videntur, & sæpe vi nuncii mortem antecedentis adsunt ante Pontificis mortem. Duo tantùm exempla subjungam. Gregorio XIV. in extremis constituto, juxta Conclave successoris Innocentii IX. Cardinales Sforza, & Monte, ille ex legatione in Romania, hic Florentiâ, adhuc superstite Pontifice, accessere moniti, aliis de meliori Papæ statu in itinere novis acceptis, ad Episcopatus suos redeuntibus. Sed maximè, lethaliter decumbente Alexandro VII. festinationis Cardinalitiæ in casu nostro documenta visa sunt. Narrat quippe Il Cardinalismo p.3. l.3. p. 271. seqq. ob agonem quasi duorum mensium & nova de morte ante mortem in ipsa urbe bis sparsa, Cardinales absentes præcipitâsse, correndo con l'ali ne e' piedi verso Roma, pedibus alatis Romam currentes, & nunquam tantum studium maturè Romam veniendi in Cardinalibus apparuisse, ut inde multi mandata & acres Principum stimulos suspicati sint. Solum Cardinalem Roselli in sede sua Episcopali remansisse, licet de omnium fere Cardinalium praesentia & agone Pontificis probè edoctum, & vel pedem Romam versus movere noluisse, antequam sibi authentica de exequiis fides in loco facta fuerit, gnarum nimirum fraudis prioris & suspicantem redivivas Pontificis artes olim à Nuncio apud Colonienses adhibitas, dum nimirum ad certae resolutionis dilationem tegendam per duos menses agonem simularit, ter viaticum recipere voluerit, plus quatuor vicibus Psalmos pro anima sua cantari curaverit. Nempe veritus est, fabulam Leonis decrepiti, & mortem simulantis hic agi, & forte periculum festinantibus imminere, vel Pontificem saltem animos explorare velle. Qui &, narrante porrò authore, licet revera morti propinquus, adventu praecipiti tot fratrum intellecto, demum ad eos turbandos simulationem, de qua falsa priùs Roselli suspicio, quamvis in contrarium, adhibuit, meliora & augmentum virium praë se ferens, & Barbarino ad quaestionem, come si portasse, quomodo valeat! respondens; come quelli che givocano all'oca, ut illi qui ludunt lusum anseris; ita indigitans, quemadmodum in lusu illo, qui mortem attingat, reverti ad initium teneatur, ad eundem modum, se, qui jam in domo mortis degere visus fuerit, ad vitae initia quasi relapsum esse. Sed, ut dixi, simulatio ista fuit, quam & loquentis infirmitas & mors statim subsecuta detexit, &, ut Author ait, studium Barbarinum mortificandi peperit. Sed pessimum hic est, quòd nonnunquam festinatio festinantibus sanitatem, imò vitam eripit, cujus exemplum Conclave Gregorii XV. in Cardinale Aldobrandino suppeditat, qui ex incommoditate itineris in tempestate, & postquam quatriduo Ravennâ Romam venisset, aeger è Conclavi egressus vitam cum morte commutavit, Paulo V. in statu altero, se magno studio successorem ei vel se ipsum in Papatu designandi, successorem in morte factum esse, nuntiaturus.
units.tr: The absent cardinals themselves, however, take care that they need not be awaited for long, as far as distance between places allows, having been promptly warned by those present. If the Pope begins to fall dangerously ill, the latter at once signal this to their creatures through messengers, and eagerly urge them to set out on their journey, since delay or absence often causes loss. At the very least, as soon as the Pope is almost dead, messengers scatter to various parts of the Christian world to summon the absent cardinals. These too seem to fly to Rome at once, and often, by the speed of the messenger, they are present before the Pope's death. I will add only two examples. When Gregory XIV was at the point of death, before the conclave of his successor Innocent IX, the cardinals Sforza and Monte came, warned while the Pope was still alive. The one came from his legation in Romagna, the other from Florence. On the way they received newer reports of the Pope's better condition, and they returned to their bishoprics. But the greatest evidence of cardinalitial haste in our case was seen when Alexander VII lay mortally ill. The Il Cardinalismo, part 3, book 3, p. 271 ff., relates that, because the agony had lasted almost two months and news of his death had twice been spread in the city before he died, the absent cardinals hurried, correndo con l'ali ne e' piedi verso Roma (racing to Rome on winged feet). Never, it says, had such eagerness to come early to Rome appeared in the cardinals, so that many suspected orders and sharp spurs from princes. Only Cardinal Roselli remained in his episcopal see. Although he had been well informed of the presence of nearly all the cardinals and of the Pope's agony, he refused to move a foot toward Rome until an authentic report of the funeral had been made to him in that place. He knew well the earlier deceit, and suspected that the Pope's old tricks were being revived, tricks once used by the nuncio among the people of Cologne. There, to conceal the postponement of a certain decision, the Pope had feigned agony for two months, had wished to receive viaticum three times, and had Psalms sung for his soul more than four times. Roselli feared that the story of the decrepit Leo who feigns death was being acted out here, and that danger might threaten those who hurried, or that the Pope merely wished to test their minds. And, the author continues, although he was in truth near death, when he learned of the hasty arrival of so many brothers, he at last used a pretence, of which Roselli had earlier had false suspicions, to disturb them. Showing a better condition and an increase of strength, he answered Barbarino's question, "How are you, how do you fare?" with come quelli che givocano all'oca (like those who play the goose game). By this he indicated that, just as in that game a player who reaches death must return to the start, so he, who had already seemed to live in the house of death, had as it were slipped back to the beginnings of life. But, as I said, this was a pretence, which his worsening illness and the death that immediately followed revealed. And, as the author says, it produced studium Barbarinum mortificandi (the Barberini's zeal for mortifying him). The worst part here is that sometimes haste takes health from the hurrying, indeed takes life. The Conclave Gregorii XV. supplies an example in Cardinal Aldobrandini. Because of the discomfort of the journey in a storm, and after he had come from Ravenna to Rome in four days, he left the conclave ill and exchanged life for death. This was to announce that a successor had been made in death, since he had hoped, with great zeal, to designate either a successor to Paul V or himself in the papacy while Paul was in his other state.

units.la: XIX. Olim quoque non inclusi erant in certo Conclavi Electores, sed in diversis locis amplioribus (maximè quoad usque populi suffragia requisita fuerunt;) praecipuè autem post conversionem Imperatorum ad fidem Christianam in Templis majoribus, & Romae quidem vel in illo S. Johannis Lateranensi, vel in S. Petro, extra Romam verò in aliis Ecclesiis Cathedralibus, vel locis spatiosioribus non inclusi eligebant; Sed numero Electorum pedetentim ad paucitatem redudo, & licentiâ veniendi & redeundi electionem saepe retardante, tandem Gregorio X. quem an.
units.tr: XIX. In former times the electors were not shut up in one fixed conclave but in various larger places, especially while the votes of the people were still required. After the emperors' conversion to the Christian faith, the electors were not enclosed in the greater churches, at Rome either in that of St John Lateran or in St Peter's, and outside Rome in other cathedral churches or more spacious places, but they elected there without enclosure. But as the number of electors was gradually reduced to a few, and the freedom to come and go often delayed the election, at last, under Gregory X, who is said to have been elected pope in 1272, the Council of Lyons decided, about 140 years after the introduction of the mode of electing by cardinals alone, to establish a conclave. That is, a place entirely closed and carefully guarded is to be used after the cardinals enter for the election, and once they are in it, they may not leave before the election is made, unless because of a clear common danger or a special illness. In such a place, under the conditions stated, Innocent V was the first to enter, at Arezzo in 1276, and he was elected on the twenty-first day of January, towards evening.

units.la: Sf 1272. ad Pontificatum electum esse ajunt, adeóque elapsis ab institutione modi eligendi per solos Cardinales circiter 140. annis, in Concilio Lugdunensi placuit Conclave instituere, id est, locum undique, post Cardinalium electionis causa ingressum, clausum ac optimè custoditum, ex quo nisi communis periculi manifesti, vel specialis infirmitatis causâ ante electionem factam illis egredi non licet. In quali loco sub conditionibus dictis primus apud Aretinos an.1276. primo ingressus, vicesimo primo Januarii die sub vesperam electus fuit Innocentius V.
units.tr: XX. It is worth noting that those enclosure laws of Gregory X and the Council of Lyons were not observed in continuous order from that time. They were declared void three or four times, and were restored as often. First, Adrian V, the successor of Innocent, who had been created pope in the conclave, in the Lateran atrium, and whose decree had been confirmed by the council regarded as general, soon revoked those conclave laws. Since they had been announced by a man not yet crowned, he held them invalid after his death, whether by suspension or by revocation. His successor John XXIII, who also disapproved of the name of conclave, not only confirmed them as lawfully made by Adrian, but annulled in every way the contrary constitution of Gregory. Thus the popes who next succeeded, Nicholas III, Martin IV, Honorius IV, Nicholas IV and Celestine V, did not come out of conclaves. After them, Gregory's constitution found an avenger in Celestine V, elected in 1294, who, moved by the same reasons as Gregory, made a decree, which his successor Boniface VIII also inserted into the Decretals. From that time no one has been found who acted or decreed against it.

units.la: XX. Notari autem meretur, leges illas Gregorii X. & Concilii Lugdunensis inclusorias ex eo tempore non continuo ordine observatas, sed ter aut quater irritas declaratas, toties etiam reductas fuisse. Et primo quidem Adrianus V. Innocentii successor leges illas Conclaviarias, licet in Conclavi, in Atrio Lateranensi creatus, licet etiam à Concilio, quod Generale habetur, stabilitas mox revocavit; Quam etiam, quòd à nondum coronato pronuntiata esset, invalidam eo mortuo habitam, sive suspensionem, sive revocationem Successor Johannes XXIII. Conclavis nomen parùm quoque probans, non tantùm tanquam legitimè ab Adriano factam confirmavit, sed & constitutionem contrariam Gregorii modis omnibus annullavit; Et sic Pontifices, qui eum propius exceperunt, Nicolaus III. Martinus IV. Honorius IV. Nicolaus IV. & Coelestinus V. non è Conclavibus prodierunt. Post quos constitutio Gregoriana vindicem habuit Coelestinum V. an.1294. electum, qui iisdem cum Gregorio rationibus motus decretum prea fecit, quod & Successor Bonifacius VIII. Decretalibus inseruit, nec ex eo tempore inventus fuit, qui contrà egerit, vel contrà decreverit.
units.tr: XX. It deserves notice that the enclosure laws of Gregory X and the Council of Lyons were not observed in unbroken sequence from that time. They were declared void three or four times and restored as often. First, Adrian V, Innocent's successor, though he had been created in the conclave in the Lateran hall and though the laws had been confirmed by the council regarded as general, soon revoked them. Whether by suspension or by revocation, the successor John XXIII, who also disapproved of the name "conclave," held that the constitution, because it had been pronounced by a man not yet crowned, was invalid once he died. He not only confirmed it as legitimately made by Adrian but annulled Gregory's contrary constitution in every way. And so the popes who followed closely after him, Nicholas III, Martin IV, Honorius IV, Nicholas IV and Celestine V, were not chosen in conclaves. After them Gregory's constitution found an avenger in Celestine V, elected in 1294, who, moved by the same reasons as Gregory, issued a decree in its favour. His successor Boniface VIII also inserted this into the Decretals, and from that time no one has been found who acted or decreed against it.

units.la: XXI. Quoad locum, in quo Conclave ex constitutione Gregorii existere debet, ita Onuphrius annot. ad Greg. X. decretum esse ait: Ut novi Pontificis comitia habeantur loco idoneo, ubi Pontifex precedens cum sua Curia residens, causarúmque & literarum Apostolicarum audientiam habens, mortuus fuerit. Quod si in villa, pago aut oppido obierit, & propterea commodè ibidem comitia haberi nequiverint, in urbe, in cujus diœcesi villa, pagus vel oppidum fuerint, habeantur, nisi interdicta sint. Quo casu in proximiore urbe non interdicta ipsa electio fieri debet. Si vero ipsa audientia alio loco fuerit, tunc non ubi Papa obierit, sed ubi eadem audientia fuerit, futuri Pontificis creatio habeatur. Gregorius X. & Clemens V.
units.tr: XXI. As to the place in which the conclave must be held under Gregory's constitution, Onuphrius, in his notes on Gregory X, says the decree is as follows: "That the assembly for electing a new Pontiff be held in a suitable place, where the preceding Pontiff died while residing with his Curia and holding the hearing of causes and apostolic letters. But if he died in a country house, village or town, and therefore the assembly cannot conveniently be held there, it shall be held in the city in whose diocese the villa, village or town lies, unless that city is under interdict. In that case the election, not under interdict, must be held in the nearest city. But if the hearing itself was held in another place, then the creation of the future Pontiff shall be held not where the Pope died but where that hearing was held." Gregory X and Clement V.

units.la: XXII. Circa hanc constitutionem de loco generaliori quaeritur; Ubi debeat Conclave haberi, si Papa moriatur in mari? Et respondet glossa decret. l. VI. l. 1. Tit. V. ad § Porro. Cardinales in illo casu debere convenire in civitate, per quam locus ille maris distinguatur, & si non distinguatur per aliquam civitatem, debere fieri in viciniori. Secundo quaeritur; Quid de electione judicandum sit, quae facta fuerit in terra interdicta, id est, excommunicationi subjacente? Vel in loco alio, quam à jure requisito. Ubi ante omnia ex Glossatore l. c. notamus, in loco interdicto non posse electionem celebrari, id est, qualemcunque. Et nihilominus locum in electione Pontificis nullo modo, neque quoad illum constitutiones n. prae. memoratas obstare, idem cum aliis statuit. Sed audiamus Antonium de Rosellis ilta, l. c. p. 336. disceptantem. Aie primo, videri, quod ex istis loci irregularitatibus exceptio contra electionem detur, & hoc tenere Gloss. 23. di. in nomine Domini per tex. c. ad haec &c. quod sicut. de elec. & de ap. c. qua fronte. Postea subjungit Archi. tenere, quod in quocunque loco facta teneat, dummodo non in coquina vel lupanari ar. l. pe. de justi. & juris. Ipse etiam tandem judicat, bonam esse, etiam in coquina vel lupanari factam. Ad loci interdicti exceptionem specialiter respondet, etiam ibi valere, quia licet in tali loco sit facta prohibitio celebrationis divinorum, tamen secreta & submissa voce possint nonnunquam divina (ibi) celebrari, ut no. de sen. exco. c. alma. & quia in loco interdicto Clerici sint interdicti quoad locum, non quoad se, ut no. de consue. c. inter vos ita no. glo. in d. c. ubi periculum. §. Porro inversi. interdicta. de elec. l. 6. Tertio idem proponit casum duplicem de exeuntibus sine causa plerisque extra Conclave, vel extra diaecesin illam, & contra eos pro paucioribus remanentibus, imo unico remanente, pronuntiat. Quia autem Gregorius loci idonei mentionem facit, & alii expresse tutum requirunt, adeoque in defectu securitatis, causa supponi potest, ideo quarto & p. 327. primo remanentibus duabus tertiis in loco non tuto, eligendi, in loco tuto autem, dum alter non tutus est, degentibus pluribus, reliquos vocandi, potestatem vocatis obligationem ad obsequium tribuit.
units.tr: XXII. On this constitution, a more general question is raised: Where should the Conclave be held if the Pope dies at sea? The gloss on the decretal, Sext, book 1, title 5, at the paragraph Porro, answers that in that case the cardinals ought to assemble in the city by which that stretch of sea is bounded, and if it is not bounded by any city, the meeting should be held in the nearest one. Second, it is asked: What is to be judged of an election made in an interdicted land, that is, one subject to excommunication? Or in some place other than the law requires? Here, first of all, from the Glossator (ibid.) we note that an election cannot be celebrated in an interdicted place, of whatever kind. Nevertheless, he decides with the others that the place in no way bears on the election of the Pontiff, and the constitutions mentioned above do not stand in the way as far as that goes. But let us hear Antonius de Rosellis (ibid., p. 336) debating. He says, first, that it seems an exception against the election arises from these irregularities of place, and to hold this (Gloss on 23 dist., In nomine Domini, by the text of c. Ad haec etc., as at De electione and De appellationibus, c. Qua fronte). Afterwards he adds that the Archbishop holds that an election is valid wherever it is made, provided it is not in a kitchen or a brothel (last law, De iustitia et iure). He himself finally judges that it is good even if made in a kitchen or a brothel. To the objection about an interdicted place in particular, he replies that it is valid there too, because although a prohibition of celebrating divine services has been made in such a place, nevertheless divine services can sometimes be celebrated there in a secret and subdued voice, as is noted at De sententia excommunicationis, c. Alma; and because in an interdicted place the clergy are interdicted as to the place, not as to themselves, as is noted at De consuetudine, c. Inter vos, thus the gloss on the said c. Ubi periculum, §. Porro, reversed, interdicta, De electione, Sext, book 6. Third, he puts forward the double case of those who leave the Conclave without cause, most of them, or leave that diocese, and he pronounces against them, in favour of the fewer who remain, indeed even of a single one remaining. But since Gregory mentions a suitable place, and others expressly require a safe one, and so a cause may be assumed where there is a lack of security, therefore, fourth, and p. 327. first, he grants the power to elect when two-thirds remain in a place that is not safe, and the power to call the others when more are staying in a safe place while the other is not safe, and an obligation to obey on the part of those called.

units.la: XXIII. Pergimus jam ad ipsam Conclavis specialiorem descriptionem, & legum ac consuetudinum Conclaviariarum explicationem. (Si Romae electio fiat, quod à longo tempore semper factum) in Capella Sixti I. & in Consistorio Salae, ordinario in Vaticano Palatio (quod 5500. habitacula 13000. portas & fenestras
units.tr: XXIII. We now proceed to a more detailed description of the Conclave itself, and an explanation of the Conclave's laws and customs. (If the election is held at Rome, which has always been done for a long time) it is built in the Chapel of Sixtus I and in the Consistory Hall, which is ordinarily in the Vatican Palace (which has 5,500 rooms, 13,000 doors and windows)

units.la: Note at right margin: Quaestiones de co...; Locus specialior; Cellulae. stras habet) (dico ordinariò, vide enim lites de loco alio in conclavi Clementis IX.) & si opus sit, in Sala etiam Regia, ædificantur tot Cellulæ, quot Cardinales vivunt, latitudinem 20. & longitudinem 22. pedum habentes, & singulæ à singulis unico tantùm pede distantes, interjacente exiguo vacuo ; Earum quælibet unâ ex Alphabethi literis, quædam, cùm hodie longè plures sint Cardinales, duplici, quædam triplici notantur. Dividitur etiam Conclave in æstivum & hybernum, quorum illud, uti necesse est, magis aëri expositum est. In Decretalibus tamen LVI. l. 1. tit. 6. c. 4. ubi periculum. habetur, nullo intermedio pariete seu alio velamine omnes in commune unum Conclave inhabitare debere. Onuphrius autem annot. in Greg. X. laneis pannis distinctas cellulas constitutioni tribuit, dum hodie ligneis trabibus discernuntur, juxta constitutionem Pii IV.
units.tr: Note at right margin: Questions about the specific place; the cells. (I say ordinarily; for see the disputes over another place in the Conclave of Clement IX.) And if need be, also in the Royal Hall, as many cells are built as there are cardinals living, each 20 feet wide and 22 feet long, and each set one foot apart from the next, with a small gap between. Each of them is marked with one of the letters of the alphabet, some with a double letter and some with a triple letter, since today there are far more cardinals. The Conclave is also divided into a summer and a winter section, of which the former is, as is necessary, more exposed to the air. Yet in the Decretals Sext, book 1, title 6, c. 4, Ubi periculum it is stated that all should live together in one common Conclave with no intervening wall or other covering. Onuphrius, however, in his notes on Gregory X, attributes to the constitution that the cells are distinguished by woollen cloths, whereas today they are separated by wooden beams, according to the constitution of Pius IV.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Cellæ istæ sorte dividuntur, ita, ut in uno vase nomina Cardinalium schedulis inscripta, in alio Alphabethi literæ ponantur, & singulæ à singulis Cardinalium domesticis extrahantur, atque secundùm eam sortem Cellæ Cardinalium nominibus signentur. Qui & aliquando ex sorte & situ omina formare solent, in Cellas sibi assignatas, lectulam, mensulam, alia utensilia & necessaria transportari curant, ac trabes ligneas telâ aut lanâ subtilissimâ coloris viridis, qui à defuncto creati sunt, violini, reliqui obtegunt. Quamvis quoad hæc variare & nonnunquam rubrum, aliquando etiam album colorem adhibere soleant. Adhibuit colorem ultimò memoratum in Conclavi Nicolai V. Cardinalis Bononiensis mero singularitatis studio, de quo ita Author Conclavis; Solamente il Cardinale Bolognese ordinò, che la sua cella fosse accommodata di color bianco, forse perche la mente sua non era nè più pura, nè più retta degli altri. Id est: Solus Cardinalis Bononiensis voluit, ut cella sua album acciperet ornatum, sed forte ipsius animus non erat purior aut rectior aliorum animis. Cellas autem, juxta Constitutionem Pii IV. nec etiam infirmitatis prætextu mutare licet, aut desuper ædificare, vel illas dilatare: Sed quilibet, etiam Decanus, forte sua contentus esse debet. Hinc cùm in Conclavi Leonis X I. S. Cæcilia febri affectus mutare Cellam desideraret, Aldobrandinus regessit; Che non dovesse sotto pena della scommunica, minaciata della Bolla, che prohibiva la mutatione della Cella, etiandio con pretetto dell' infirmità. Id est: Illud fieri neutiquam debere sub pœna excommunicationis, quam Bulla comminetur, qua prohibeat Cella mutationem, etiam sub prætextu infirmitatis.
units.tr: These cells are divided by lot. Slips bearing the names of the cardinals are placed in one vessel, and letters of the alphabet in another, and each cardinal's servant draws one of each. The cells are then marked with the cardinals' names according to this lot. Some also form omens from the lot and the position of the cells. They have a small bed, a little table and other furnishings and necessities carried into the cells assigned to them, and they cover the wooden beams with very fine cloth or wool of green colour, the cardinals created by the deceased pope covering them with violet and the rest with other colours. Although they are accustomed to vary this, and sometimes use red and occasionally white. The last-named colour was used in the conclave of Nicholas V by the Cardinal of Bologna, from a mere desire for singularity, of whom the author of the Conclave writes thus: Only the Cardinal of Bologna ordered that his cell be furnished in white, perhaps because his mind was neither purer nor more upright than the others. That is: Only the Cardinal of Bologna wished his cell to receive a white decoration, but perhaps his mind was not purer or more upright than the minds of others. Moreover, according to the Constitution of Pius IV, cells may not be changed, nor built over, nor enlarged, not even on the pretext of sickness; but each one, even the Dean, ought to be content with his lot. Hence when, in the conclave of Leo XI, Cardinal Cecilia, suffering from fever, wished to change his cell, Aldobrandini replied: That this should on no account be done, under pain of excommunication, which the Bull threatens, which prohibits changing the cell, even under the pretext of infirmity. That is: It ought by no means to be done under pain of excommunication, which the Bull threatens, by which a change of cell is forbidden, even under the pretext of infirmity.

units.la: XXV. Inter
units.tr: XXV. Among

units.la: Earum distributio, tegumenta, & constans earundem ab iisdem possessio; XXV. Inter illos, qui unâ cum Cardinalibus includi possunt, præcipui sunt Conclavistæ, quos vocant; De quibus ita Decretal. Sext. l.1. lib.6. c.4. ubi periculum §. Hoc sacro. Contenti singuli singulis tantùm modò servientibus Clericis, vel Laicis, prout duxerint eligendum, illis tamen, quibus potens necessitas id suggerit indulgeri, (Glossa habet: Ut forte quia podagras patitur, itaque necesse habet per servientes sustineri & portari, vel alia causa similis) duos haberi permittimus, eisdem electionis arbitrio (juxta Glossam, ut possit habere, vel vult Clericos, vel vult Laicos, vel alterum Clericum, vel Laicum) reservato. Paulò benignior est Bulla Pii IV. quæ singulis duos servientes Clericos, vel Laicos concedit, infirmis autem & graviter affectis à majori parte Collegii per secreta suffragia tertium ad summum indulgeri posse judicat. Quorum etiam qualitates describit: Servientes familiares domestici, subjungit, & continui commensales ipsius Cardinalis & ab anno ante fuisse, & tunc esse debeant, & non mercatores, ministri Principum, Domini temporales & jurisdictionem habentes, neque fratres aut nepotes Cardinalium, etiamsi expensis eorum viverent. Et de qualitatibus Conclavistarum Cardinalium deputati ante Conclavis ingressum diligenter inquisitionem habere, & eos approbare, ac post ingressum denuò diligenter providere debeant. Ex Conclavi Clementis IX. porrò discimus, unum solere esse Ministrum Cameræ ad servitium, alterum Nobilem ad negotiationem, tres etiam concedi Cardinalibus Principibus, quod ultimum olim non usitatum fuerit.
units.tr: Their distribution, their coverings, and the constant possession of them by the same occupants. XXV. Among those who can be shut in with the cardinals, the chief are the so-called Conclavists. Of these, the Sext decretal, book 1, book 6, c. 4, Ubi periculum, §. Hoc sacro, reads: Each cardinal may have only one serving man, whether clerical or lay, as he thinks fit; but to those whom pressing necessity suggests, we allow two to be kept, at the choice of the cardinal (the gloss says: so that perhaps, because he suffers from gout and so needs to be supported and carried by servants, or for some similar reason), reserving to him the choice of having either clerics or laymen, or one cleric and one layman. The Bull of Pius IV is somewhat more lenient, which grants each cardinal two serving men, clerical or lay, while it judges that a third may be granted at most to the sick and gravely afflicted by the secret votes of the majority of the College. It also describes their qualifications: The serving men, it adds, must be household domestics and continual companions of the cardinal, and must have been and be so for a year before, and they must not be merchants, ministers of princes, temporal lords or men holding jurisdiction, nor brothers or nephews of the cardinals, even if they live at their expense. And the cardinals' deputies ought to make a diligent inquiry about the qualifications of the Conclavists before they enter the Conclave, and approve them, and after they have entered, again diligently provide. From the Conclave of Clement IX we further learn that there is usually one Minister of the Chamber for service, another, a nobleman, for business matters, and three are also granted to cardinal princes, which last was formerly not customary.

units.la: XXVI. Conclavistarum horum magna sunt privilegia.
units.tr: XXVI. The privileges of these conclavists are great.

units.la: In Conclavi Leonis X. Conclavisti fecero congregatione, per dimandare l'essentioni, e prerogative, che sono solite concedersi à Conclavisti. In eodem Conclavi ad Capitulorum suorum conscriptionem invitati leguntur, atque illa à Cardinalibus, post statim subscripta reperiuntur. Eorundémque Conclavistarum contractus ibidem memoratur, quo se invicem obstrinxerunt, ut ille, cujus Patronus eligeretur, reliquis ex ejus Camera solveret 1500. ducatos aureos; Cui contractui suo etiam authoritatem Notarii Camerae Apostolicæ conciliârunt. Nec fuit pejor conditio Conclavistarum in Conclavi Urbani VII. in quorum favorem ad instantias Cardinalium Protectorum, quos sibi eligere solent, Cardinales sequentia Privilegia subscripserunt: Nos Episcopi, Presbyteri & Diaconi infra scripti S. R. E. Cardinales Conclavistis nostris, qui intra septa dicti Conclavis nobis famulantur, promittimus, quemlibet nostrum concessurum & in-
units.tr: In the conclave of Leo X, the conclavists held a meeting, to demand the exemptions and prerogatives that are customarily granted to conclavists. In the same conclave, they are read as having been invited to draw up their articles, and these were afterwards found signed by the cardinals. The same contract among the conclavists is also recorded there, by which they bound themselves to each other that whoever's patron was elected would pay the rest of his household 1500 gold ducats. The notary of the Apostolic Chamber also lent his authority to this contract. The condition of the conclavists was no worse in the conclave of Urban VII. In their favour, at the request of the Cardinal Protectors whom they usually choose for themselves, the cardinals subscribed the following privileges: We, the undersigned bishops, priests and deacons of the Holy Roman Church, cardinals, promise to our conclavists, who serve us within the enclosure of the said conclave, that each of us will grant and bestow and-

units.la: Simul intrant primò Conclavistæ;
units.tr: At the same time the conclavists enter first;

units.la: Eorum privilegia; & indulturum omnes & quascunque gratias, concessiones & indulta, tam spiritualia, quàm temporalia alias per fel. record. Sixtum Papam V. eisdem Conclavistis in Conclavi, in quo ipse ad Apostolatus apicem assumptus fuit, existentibus concessas & indultas. Insuper & facultates eisdem Conclavistis concessas transferendi pensiones, vel fructuum reservationes usque ad summam scutorum 100. tendantur & amplientur ad scuta 200. similia. Ac insuper quia de presenti major Conclavistarum numerus existit, promittimus & quilibet nostrum promittit loco 10000. scutorum auri in auro, quæ idem Sixtus Conclavistis prefatis donavit, donare & largiri ducatos aureos de Camera novos 12000. Item quòd dicti Conclavistæ non teneantur ad conservationem constitutionis novissimæ per fel. record. Sixtum V. datæ super habitu & tonsura per Clericos deferendis, & hoc quoad obtinentes pensionem tantùm.
units.tr: Their privileges: and will grant all and any graces, concessions and indults, both spiritual and temporal, which the late Pope Sixtus V of happy memory granted to these same conclavists in the conclave in which he himself was raised to the summit of the apostolate. Moreover, the faculties granted to the same conclavists for transferring pensions or reservations of fruits, up to the sum of 100 scudi, are to be extended to 200 scudi of the same kind. And since there is at present a greater number of conclavists, we promise, and each of us promises, to give and bestow in place of the 10,000 scudi of gold in gold, which the same Sixtus gave to the aforesaid conclavists, 12,000 new gold ducats of the Chamber. Likewise, that the said conclavists are not bound to observe the latest constitution of the late Sixtus V of happy memory, given concerning the dress and tonsure to be worn by clerics, and this only as regards those who hold a pension.

units.la: XXVII. Ex ejusmodi autem privilegiis natæ sunt in ipso Concilio Tridentino graves querelæ: Per id tempus, inquit Historicus l.VI. p.503. Præsules Hispani Legati exhibent petitionem omnium chirographis suscriptam, quâ multis incommodis commemoratis, quæ nascuntur ex immensis gratiis ac privilegiis concessis Conclavistis, revocationem, aut saltem moderationem eorum postulabant. Solens est Cardinalibus, cùm ingrediuntur Conclave, in quod includendi sunt ad electionem futuri Pontificis, ut singuli duos habeant ministros, unum tanquam sacellanum, alterum veluti cubicularium. Hos primùm eligunt, non tam ut Personis Dominorum, quàm ut negotiationibus inserviant, adeoque usu venire solet, ut optimi censeantur in urbe Roma aulici, non minorem in negotiando, ac suffragiis emendicandis, quàm ipsi Domini partem obtinentes. Unde consuetudo inveteravit, ut egressi Conclavi in novi Pontificis familiam adsciscantur, horúmque singuli privilegiis loco ac conditioni cujusvis convenientibus, prout aut Sacerdotes sunt, aut Seculares ornentur. Jam inter privilegia, quæ dari solebant Sacerdotibus, hæc erant, ut, quæ possidebant beneficia, in manus cujuscunque Ecclesiastici ad libitum resignare possent, qui ea conferet in illum, quem ipsi nominabant. Item, ut Sacerdotia sua cum quocunque altero beneficium tenente possent permutare, & ad voluntatem deligere eum, qui in utrumque beneficium conferet; Ab hac facultate adeò, immani & extraordinaria nata est aperta beneficiorum nundinatio: adeò ut Episcopis, quorum in Diœcesi talis aliquis Conclavista erat, necesse esset, Canonicatus, beneficia parochialia, aliáque magno Ecclesiæ scandalo, ad ipsorum arbitrium permutanda permittere. De his Hispanorum erat querimonia, propter recentia, quæ in Catalonia inde inde acciderant, incommoda. Sed Legati respondent, harum ac similium corruptelarum moderationem ad Papam solum spectare, cujus de familia jam agatur; cúmque sæpius antea decretum sit, Papa emendationem aulæ relinquere, æquitati magis consentaneum, suam ei familiam emendandam permittere. De ejus tamen abusùs reformatione (uti receperant) ad Pontificem scripserunt. Ille verò Conclavistarum præcipuos Romæ & apud Cardinales commorari ratus, cæteros verò, qui emendandi essent, & paucos esse, nec magni nominis, qui ab aulico strepitu ad sua se subduxerant: tum per rebus suis commodum aliqua parte Præsulibus Concilii, ac Hispanis potissimùm, satis facere arbitratus, in hoc decrevit iis gratificari, facta mense sequenti multorum privilegiorum illis priùs concessorum revocatione, quam successores tamen ejus sequuti non sunt.
units.tr: XXVII. From privileges of this kind, however, serious complaints arose at the Council of Trent itself. At that time, says the historian, book VI, p. 503: the Spanish prelates, the legates, presented a petition signed by all of them, in which, after mentioning the many inconveniences that arise from the immense graces and privileges granted to the conclavists, they demanded its revocation, or at least its moderation. It is customary for cardinals, when they enter the conclave in which they are to be shut up for the election of the future pontiff, to have two attendants each, one as chaplain and the other as chamberlain. These they choose first, not so much for the persons of their masters as to serve in their business dealings, and so it usually happens that the best of them are considered courtiers in the city of Rome, no less skilled at negotiating and begging for votes than the masters themselves who hold a share. Hence the custom has become established that, when they leave the conclave, they are taken into the household of the new pontiff, and each of them is adorned with privileges suited to his rank and condition, according as he is either a priest or a layman. Now among the privileges that were usually given to priests were these: that they could resign whatever benefices they held into the hands of any ecclesiastic at will, who would confer them on whomever they named. Likewise, that they could exchange their benefices with any other beneficed person, and choose at will the one who would confer on them both benefices. From this faculty an enormous and extraordinary open market in benefices arose, so that bishops, in whose diocese such a conclavist was, were obliged to permit canonries, parish benefices and other things to be exchanged at their pleasure, to the great scandal of the Church. The Spaniards complained of these things because of the recent inconveniences that had arisen from them in Catalonia. But the legates replied that the moderation of these and similar abuses belonged to the Pope alone, whose household was now under discussion; and since it had often been decreed before that the Pope should leave the reform of the court to himself, it was more fitting to equity that he be allowed to reform his own household. Nevertheless, as they had undertaken, they wrote to the Pontiff about the reform of this abuse. He, however, thinking that the chief conclavists stayed at Rome and with the cardinals, and that the others who needed reform were few and of no great name, who had withdrawn from the courtly bustle to their own affairs, judged that he could satisfy the prelates of the Council, and the Spaniards above all, well enough by a certain concession to their interests. In this he decided to oblige them, by revoking, the following month, many privileges previously granted to them; which, however, his successors did not follow.

units.la: XXVIII. Quæ Præsules isti de parte Conclavistarum in negotiationibus non exigua conquesti sunt, omninò ita se habent, & potest, cui lubet, exemplum hujus rei in Conclavi Clementis X. quoad Abbatem Melani, videre, vel supra citatum MSS. Italicum periodo: I Conclavisti; inspicere.
units.tr: XXVIII. What those prelates complained about concerning the part played by conclavists in no small measure in business dealings is entirely true, and anyone who wishes may see an example of this matter in the conclave of Clement X with regard to Abbot Melani, or consult the Italian manuscript cited above, in the passage beginning The conclavists.

units.la: Cæterum quoque juvabit horum rationem tempus in Conclavibus fallendi cognoscere. Uno verbo rid- ent & exagitant sæpissimè actiones Dominorum suorum. In Conclavi Leonis XI. ragionavano, per passare il tempo ironicamente, & temporis fallendi causâ ironicè ratiocinabantur, Baronium eligi debere, eum nempe, cùm sit homo perfectus, observaturum præceptum divinum: Diligite inimicos vestros, & benefacite iis &c. Alii dicebant, Baronium Papam eligi debere, qui, cùm melius omni alio noverit defectus & peccata suorum, posset etiam eos melius quovis alio castigare, atque vesperâ illâ satis multa dixerunt, insigniendo factionem Patronorum suorum Sanctam Unionem, belluam multorum Capitum, hanc Protestantium, illam Catilinarium, & diminuebant cum jocis similibus tædium fatidi illius carceris & laboriosi, dum per majorem diei partem debuerunt portare scabella, & præstare alia magis humilia servitia, ad quæ Patroni Conclavistas admittere solent, ut eos multùm honorent; Stultos aulicos, qui cum dispendio ambiunt molestias corporis, & semet faciunt lubentissimè togatos faciferos, exercentes artem, quæ tanquam singularis reliquis hactenus non est annumerata Romæ, attamen invidiosè expetita ab aliis, & maximè à **** qui Memoriale obtulerunt, quo petiverunt participes reddi privilegiorum, quæ semper promittuntur, raro conferuntur miseris Conclavistis. Ita describit miseriam, sed paulò post redit ad ludibria, nempe, facta exclusionis Baronianæ mentione, subjungit: Conclavi-stii
units.tr: Furthermore, it will also be helpful to learn how these men pass the time in conclaves. In a word, they very often mock and harass the actions of their masters. In the conclave of Leo XI, they were talking, to pass the time, ironically, and in jest they reasoned that Baronius ought to be elected, namely, that man who, since he is perfect, would observe the divine precept: Love your enemies, and do good to them, etc. Others said that Baronius ought to be elected pope, since, knowing the defects and sins of his people better than anyone else, he could also punish them better than anyone. And that evening they said many things, labelling the faction of their patrons the Holy Union, a beast with many heads, this one the Protestants, that one the Catilines; and with similar jokes they lessened the tedium of that dismal and laborious prison, while for most of the day they had to carry stools and perform other humbler services, to which patrons usually admit conclavists, so that they may greatly honour them. Foolish courtiers, who at their own expense seek out bodily discomforts and most willingly make themselves bearers of gowns, practising an art which, as something special, has not hitherto been counted among the others at Rome, yet is envied by others, and especially by those who presented a memorial asking to be made sharers in the privileges, which are always promised and seldom conferred on wretched conclavists. Thus he describes their misery, but shortly afterwards he returns to mockery; having mentioned the exclusion of Baronius, he adds: Conclavists

units.la: Conclavistarum authoritas, tempus fallendi modus, & cum iis qui extra Conclave degunt, loquendi ars; {*}sti se ne prendevano &c. Id est: Conclavista ludibrium eâ occasione habebant, & ob velocitatem nimis audacter vocabant Magistrum cursorum. Addam his lusibus Conclavistarum ænigmaticæ, quâ erga eos, qui extra Conclave degunt, nonnunquam utuntur, loquendi rationis exemplum. In eodem Conclavi narratur, che il Conclavista di Baronio &c. Conclavistam Baronii ænigmate parum ænigmatico voluisse apud rotam significare notis suis, Baronium habuisse 30. vota, atque in eum finem ab illis foris degentibus petiisse 30. Candelas, quod Conclavista alii occasionem dederit, statim subjiciendi: Sic quasò, curate ut mittantur, agitur enim de exequiis Patroni vestri.
units.tr: The authority of conclavists, their way of passing time, and their art of speaking with those who live outside the conclave: they were taking it in turns; that is, the conclavists used that occasion for mockery, and because of the great speed they boldly called the master of the couriers. I shall add to these conclavist jests an example of the enigmatic manner of speaking that they sometimes use towards those who live outside the conclave. In the same conclave it is related that the conclavist of Baronius etc. The conclavist of Baronius, by a not very enigmatic riddle, wished to signify to the Rota by his signs that Baronius had thirty votes, and to that end he asked those outside for thirty candles, since another conclavist had given an opportunity for immediately adding: I beg you, arrange for them to be sent, for it concerns the funeral rites of your patron.

units.la: XXIX. Idem Conclavistæ sunt plerunque Authores Conclavium, quæ habemus in unum volumen compacta & an. 1667. Italicè edita, numero 32. à Clemente V usque ad Clementem IX. non tamen, quoad initium, ordine continuo. Accesserunt his Conclavia Clementis IX. & X. Conjecturæ viri, Aulæ & rerum Romanarum peritissimi, statim post mortem Clementis X. respectu mox futuri Conclavis editæ; Ut autem istas conjecturas ad manus heic non habeo, ita multò magis mihi perfecta Innocentii XI. & Alexandri VIII. Papæ hodierni Conclavia desunt; Ajunt autem, demum post mortem cujusvis Pontificis edi, de transmissione antehac rogati. Jam verò metum severi Inquisitionis Tribunalis prætexunt denuò rogati. Quia autem ex istis quæ ad manus sunt, Conclavibus (quatenus vox sumitur pro iis, quæ in Conclavibus acciderunt) hucusque multa citavimus, plura in sequentibus contra Electiones Pontificum inde prolaturi, ideò haud exiguum operæ pretium erit, si distinctius in Authores & authoritatem illorum scriptorum (ut jam ab initio hujus tractationis polliciti eramus;) hâc occasione inquisiverimus. Eorum nomina ignorari non est mirum, quum omnis ejusmodi scriptio lege sit vetita. Fidem omnium, quæ narrant, præstare non est nostrum; fieri potest, ut quædam aliter narrent, quàm prout contigerunt; verisimile est, eos nonnunquam conjecturas potius suas, quàm verò certam actorum scientiam secutos esse; Et quando diversi eadem Conclavia (Author Cardinalismi testatur, se legisse 5. Conclavia unius Innocentii X.) diversè descripserunt, necessariò in quibusdam ab una aut altera parte error est. Non sine causa idem Author multa Conclavia maximæ confusionis accusat; Quamvis illud quoque negari non possit, impossibile esse, ut res tam confusæ accuratò ordine recenseantur; Haud magis negari potest, profunditates illas negotiationum difficulter, imò à nemi-ne, perfectè penetrari; Tractatus Conclavium esse, juxta eundem Authorem, duplices, secretos & publicos. Non omnes omnium arcanorum esse participes; externam apparentiam sæpe fallere; imagines Conclavium, teste eodem, habere pedes, & non ambulare, oculos, & non videre, aures, & non audire, linguas, & non loqui; multa partim cæcè fieri & sine causa, quæ ex post facto fingatur, partim ex alia causa, quàm quæ sæpe fingitur.
units.tr: XXIX. The same conclavists are for the most part the authors of the conclaves which we have gathered into one volume and which were published in Italian in 1667 as number 32, from Clement V down to Clement IX, though not in continuous chronological order at the beginning. To these have been added the conclaves of Clement IX and X, the conjectures of a man most skilled in the court and in Roman affairs, published immediately after the death of Clement X with regard to the conclave soon to follow. But since I do not have those conjectures to hand here, the complete conclaves of Innocent XI and of the present pope, Alexander VIII, are much more lacking to me; they say, however, that these are published only after the death of each pontiff, and they were asked about the transmission of these before. Moreover, when asked again, they plead the fear of the severe tribunal of the Inquisition. Since, however, from those conclaves which are at hand (insofar as the word is taken for those things which happened in conclaves) we have cited much up to now, and shall bring forward more in what follows against the elections of the pontiffs, it will therefore be no small service, on this occasion, to inquire more distinctly into the authors and the authority of those writers, as we promised from the beginning of this treatment. It is no wonder that their names are unknown, since every writing of this kind is forbidden by law. It is not our task to vouch for the truth of everything they relate; it may be that some of them relate things differently from how they happened; it is likely that they sometimes followed their own conjectures rather than a certain knowledge of the facts; and when different writers have described the same conclaves differently (the author of Cardinalismus testifies that he read five conclaves of Innocent X alone), necessarily in some cases one side or the other is in error. The same author not without reason accuses many conclaves of the greatest confusion; although it cannot be denied that it is impossible for things so confused to be recounted in exact order. Nor can it be denied that those depths of negotiation are with difficulty, indeed by no one, fully penetrated. According to the same author, the proceedings of conclaves are double, secret and public. Not all are sharers in all the secrets; the outward appearance often deceives; the images of conclaves, as he attests, have feet and do not walk, eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear, tongues and do not speak; many things are done partly blindly and without cause, which are afterwards invented, partly from another cause than that which is often invented.

units.la: XXX. Interim tamen non omnem istis Authoribus authoritatem derogari patimur; Quos primò Pontificios, secundò aliquando Cardinales, Conclavistas aliquando, adeóque tertiò negotiationum multarum semper partim actores, partim spectatores fuisse, ambigere neutiquam licet. Ipsosmet audiamus, & primò quidem Authorem Conclavis Gregorii XIV. Ita ille de se loquitur: Jo che son stato &c. Ego, qui fui si non omnium particeps, saltem spectator magnæ istius actionis, & occasionem habui intelligendi & investigandi specialissima etiam eorum, quæ contigerunt &c. Loquatur etiam Author Conclavis Clementis VIII. Ita orditur ille: Con tutto, che jo non sia stato &c. Quamvis non fuerim ex primariis in Conclavi præsente, nihilominùs quia fui curiosus investigator & spectator negotiationum in illo factarum &c. Nec frustrà forte authoritatem operi suo conciliare nititur Author Conclavis Innocentii X. cujus tale exordium: Veramente non si trovò mai &c. Profectò nullum Conclave usque adeò excitavit curiositatem Curiæ, ad investigandas cum omni diligentia artificiosas molitiones, quemadmodum illud, ex quo prodiit Innocentius X. Hinc est, quòd multi Scriptores, ut satisfaciant iteratis precibus amicorum suorum, mundo publicare voluerunt negotia Conclavis illius; Sed, quod pessimum est, multi defectu notitiæ rerum necessariarum, curiosarum & ad substantiam pertinentium, tantùm circumvagati sunt in contemplatione quarundam narrationum, quæ quidem in foro fuerunt, sed non in Conclavi. Illi successus, qui sunt satis reconditi & noti paucissimis Cardinalibus, qui illos integrè publicare nolunt, difficulter ex fundo veritatis accipiuntur, sine lumine, quod ipse dextrè emendicavi à tali, qui certè plenè de omnibus informatus fuit. Et ut possim uti methodo ipsius in rebus, quæ acciderunt &c. Quis præter alios Scriptor Conclavis illius fuerit, ex Conclavi Alexandri VII. cognoscimus, ubi causa inimicitiæ inter Cardinales Spadam & Rapacioli statuitur, quòd hic scripserit Conclave Innocentii; Et ut Author Conclavis Alexandri ab una quidem
units.tr: XXX. Still, we do not allow all authority to be taken away from these authors. They were, first, Papists; second, at times cardinals; and at other times conclavists; and so, third, they were always, in part, actors and, in part, spectators of many negotiations, which cannot be doubted at all. Let us hear them for themselves, and first the author of the Conclave of Gregory XIV. He speaks of himself thus: I, who have been &c. "I, who was, if not a sharer in all of that great business, at least a spectator of it, and had the opportunity of understanding and investigating even the most particular things that happened &c." The author of the Conclave of Clement VIII also speaks. He begins thus: Although I have not been &c. "Although I was not among the leading men present in the conclave, nevertheless, since I was a curious investigator and spectator of the negotiations carried on there &c." Perhaps not in vain does the author of the Conclave of Innocent X seek to win authority for his work, with this opening: Truly there was never &c. "Truly no conclave has ever so stirred the curiosity of the Curia, to investigate with every care the artful manoeuvres, as that from which Innocent X emerged. Hence it is that many writers, to satisfy the repeated entreaties of their friends, have wished to make the affairs of that conclave public to the world. But, what is worst, many, lacking knowledge of the necessary facts, which are curious and pertain to the substance, have wandered only among accounts of certain things that did indeed happen in the forum, but not in the conclave. Those outcomes, which are fairly recondite and known to very few cardinals, who are unwilling to publish them in full, are with difficulty drawn from the ground of truth, without the light that I myself skilfully begged from one who was certainly fully informed on all matters. And so that I may use his method in the things that happened &c." Who else was the writer of that conclave we learn from the Conclave of Alexander VII, where the cause of the enmity between the cardinals Spada and Rapaccioli is stated to be that the latter wrote the Conclave of Innocent. And as the author of the Conclave of Alexander, on the one hand, frankly admits the difficulty of the work, he begins thus:

units.la: Non tamen nullius ponderis; dem parte ingenuè operis difficultatem fatetur,ita exorsus: Quanto è grande &c. Quantò major est curiositas legentis, tantò major est difficultas scribentis accidentia Conclavis. Difficulter veritas reperitur, ubi eam abscondere conantur consilia hominum: In Seraglio Conclavis quidam tantum radii solares, obscura loca illa redduntur, ut sol impediatur &c. Ab altera verò parte amorem veritatis egregiè præ se & Authore illo altero fert, dum occasione illius alterius ait: L'odio &c. Odium & amor sunt venenum historia, sed cadaver est sine veritate, ut aliquis modernorum dixit, amor & odium tollendo ipsam virtutem, eam vita privant. Et paulò post de Cardinale Rapacioli Authore Conclavis Innocentii; male habuisse multos, quòd publicaverit, qua mala ipsorum electionem secuta fuissent; perche quei medesimi &c. quia illi ipsi, qui honores negligunt, volunt tamen iis digni videri; & reperiuntur quidem, qui imperia recusent, sed qui velint incapaces haberi ad illorum administrationem; nequidem Diogenis lucerna investigantur &c. Sed & Author Conclavis Clementis IX. fontes suos ostendit, & ille, qui Conclave Clementis X. scripsit, conatus suos approbat, atque ita omnes isti de se testantur, ut etiam testimoniis exacta plerorumque commemoratione, & ad cognitionem Curiae sæpe iterata provocatione certam fidem faciant, præsertim quando nunquam repertus fuit, qui, ejurato omni pudore, istud, quod tradunt, consiliorum & affectuum humanorum in electione Pontificum regnum aperte negare ausus fuerit; Testatur etiam Lud à S. Carolo l. 2. Bibl. Pont. p. 291. Romæ M SC. aliquot Conclavia in Bibliothecis Vaticana & Barbarina servari; Quibus electiones sanctiores describi haudequidem arbitror. Et quando, ut dixi, & dixerunt ipsimet, omnia exactè penetrare non potuerunt, eò magis ex ungue, qui ab ipsis ostenditur, Leonem cognoscere licet, ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἐκ τὸ φασμα. Sed pergamus ad reliquos in Conclave cum Cardinalibus ingressuros Ministros.
units.tr: Not, however, of no weight; on the other part, he begins thus: How great &c. "The greater the curiosity of the reader, the greater the difficulty for the writer in describing the events of the conclave. Truth is found with difficulty where the counsels of men try to hide it. In the seraglio of the conclave certain rays of the sun make those dark places so that the sun is hindered &c." On the other hand, he displays a love of truth splendidly, and that author of the other, when speaking of the occasion of that other, says: Hatred &c. "Hatred and love are poison to history, but it is a corpse without truth, as one of the moderns has said; love and hatred, by destroying virtue itself, deprive it of life." And a little later, of Cardinal Rapaccioli, the author of the Conclave of Innocent says: that he had offended many by publishing what evils followed their election; because those same &c., "because those very people who neglect honours nevertheless wish to seem worthy of them; and there are indeed some who refuse commands, but who wish to be regarded as incapable of administering them; not even Diogenes' lantern is needed to find them &c."
