But also the author of the Conclave of Clement IX shows his sources, and he who wrote the Conclave of Clement X approves his own efforts; and so all these men bear witness about themselves, so that, with the careful mention of testimonies for the most part, and with the frequent appeal to the knowledge of the Curia, they make sure of credit, especially since no one has ever been found who, having cast off all shame, has dared to deny openly that the kingdom of human counsels and passions in the election of Popes is what they relate. Ludovicus a S. Carolo also testifies, book 2, Bibliotheca Pontificia, p. 291, that at Rome in the year 1650 several conclaves are kept in the Vatican and Barberini libraries; I do not think that elections more holy are described in them. And when, as I have said, and as they themselves have said, they could not penetrate everything exactly, then all the more one may know the lion from the claw that is shown by them [ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἐκ τὸ φασμα]. But let us proceed to the other ministers who are to enter the conclave with the cardinals.

units.la: XXXI. De illis ita loquitur citata Pii IV. Bulla:
units.tr: XXXI. Of these the cited Bull of Pius IV speaks thus:

units.la: Sacrista quoque cum uno Clerico adjutore in officio Sacrista, duo quoque Magistri Ceremoniarum Conclave ingrediantur, Missis celebrandis & aliis, qua ad ipsos pertinent, vacaturi. Adsit præterea unus Religiosus pro Confessionibus audiendis à majore parte Cardinalium per secreta suffragia eligendus, unus Collegii Secretarius, tantum duo Medici, unus Chirurgus, unus aromatarius cum uno, aut duobus servientibus. Item octo aut decem servientes publica utilitati & commoditati omnium, veluti pro lignis portandis, pro verrendo Conclavi & similibus necessariis ministrandis, qui omnes omnes à Collegio Cardinalium, non tamen ex familia alicujus Cardinalis per fabas secretas eliguntur, ita tamen, ut is obtineat, qui plura vota tulerit, & eis salaria de publico persolvantur. Quòd si ultra prafatas personas in Conclavi aliquis inventus fuerit, expelli statim debet. Et si quis uspiam se occultâsse deprehendatur, ignominiosè expellatur, & infamiâ notetur, & officiis atque beneficiis privetur: Consci vero sub eadem pœna illos Collegio revelare teneantur, præmium reportaturi, si indicaverint.
units.tr: The Sacristan also, with one clerk as assistant in the office of Sacristan, and two masters of ceremonies, shall enter the conclave, to be occupied with celebrating Masses and other things that pertain to them. Moreover, there shall be present one religious, to be chosen by the majority of the cardinals by secret ballot, for hearing confessions; one secretary of the College; only two physicians, one surgeon, one apothecary with one or two attendants. Likewise eight or ten servants for the public use and convenience of all, for carrying wood, sweeping the conclave and providing similar necessities; all of whom are to be chosen by the College of Cardinals, not however from the household of any cardinal, by secret ballot, in such a way that he obtains the office who has received more votes; and their salaries shall be paid from public funds. If anyone is found in the conclave beyond the aforesaid persons, he must be expelled at once. And if anyone is caught hiding himself anywhere, he shall be expelled in disgrace, marked with infamy, and deprived of offices and benefits. Those who are aware of such things are bound under the same penalty to reveal them to the College, and they will receive a reward if they have pointed them out.

units.la: XXXII. Ingrediantur jam in locum ita hactenus descriptum, cum comitibus hactenus memoratis. Ingrediuntur, ut dixi, undecimo post mortem Pontificis die, hoc ordine: Primò valedicunt Cardinales Domesticis suis; qui celebrare possunt, Missam dicunt; Mox omnes in Basilica S. Petri conveniunt, ubi Decanus Missam cantat, & , qui non celebrárunt, communicant; Finitâ Missâ, Prælatus, cui id muneris à Camerario impositum est, orationem de eligendo Pontifice recitat. Quibus ita peractis, Clericus Ceremoniarum, loquor ex Ceremoniali Conclavis à Gregorio XV. editi, capit crucem Papalem, & præcedit, quem Cardinales sequuntur, Episcopi primùm, deinde Presbyteri, postremò Diaconi, cum suis cappis & violaceis. Crucem præcedunt familiares Cardinalium, & immediatè Cantores (hymnum; Veni Creator Spiritus; cantantes.) Post Cardinales sequuntur Prælati, atque ita processionaliter procedentes, Conclave ingrediuntur, & cùm ad Capellam S. Nicolai, al Sixti IV. pervenerint, Cardinalium Decanus apud altare dicit orationem (Deus, qui Corda fidelium) quâ finitâ, leguntur & jurantur per Cardinales constitutiones de Rom. Pontificis electione, & speciatim constitutio Gregorii XV. Deinde Cardinales post sermonem habitum per Decanum, quo eos convenientibus verbis ad electionis negotium ritè & rectè peragendum hortatur, ad cellas sorte inter eos, juxta Constitutionem Pii IV. distributas divertunt; Et post prandium omnes simul congregantur, & Officiales Conclavis & alii præstant S. Collegio juramenta consueta.
units.tr: XXXII. Now let them enter the place so far described, with the companions already mentioned. They enter, as I have said, on the eleventh day after the death of the Pontiff, in this order. First the cardinals take leave of their household; those who can celebrate say Mass. Then all gather in the Basilica of St Peter, where the Dean sings Mass, and those who have not celebrated take communion. When the Mass is finished, the prelate to whom this duty has been assigned by the Chamberlain recites a prayer about choosing the Pontiff. When these things have been done, the master of ceremonies (I speak from the ceremonial of the conclave published by Gregory XV) takes up the papal cross and goes before; the cardinals follow, bishops first, then priests, lastly deacons, with their capes and violet vestments. The servants of the cardinals go before the cross, and immediately the singers, singing the hymn Veni Creator Spiritus. After the cardinals follow the prelates, and so, proceeding in procession, they enter the conclave. When they have come to the chapel of St Nicholas, the one of Sixtus IV, the Dean of the cardinals says a prayer before the altar (O God, who hast the hearts of the faithful). When this is finished, the constitutions about the election of the Roman Pontiff are read and sworn to by the cardinals, and especially the constitution of Gregory XV. Then the cardinals, after a sermon given by the Dean, in which he exhorts them with fitting words to carry out the business of the election properly and rightly, turn aside to the cells distributed among them by lot, according to the constitution of Pius IV. And after dinner all are gathered together, and the officials of the conclave and others take the customary oaths to the Sacred College.

units.la: XXXIII. Non tamen statim post ingressum omne commercium cum foris degentibus sublatum est, sed ingrediuntur illi liberè, maxmè Regum Legati, Principes, Prælati & Primores alii, partim animum testaturi, partim etiam expresse pro suis & suis partibus faventibus negotiaturi, ídque in multam usque noctem, & sæpissimè vix tandem à lateribus Cardinalium, interpositis admonimonitionibus, protestationibus, avelluntur; Licèt Gregorii XV. Ceremoniale, quo tempore exire debeant, definiverit, dum ita ibi legimus: Conclave post per jussum Cardinalis Decani personatam campanulam, videlicet prima vice circa primam horam noctis, secundâ circa secundam, & tertiâ circa tertiam, exclusis omnibus, qui in Conclavi remanere non debent, intus & extra claudatur. Sed & accidit, ut nec primo die, nec prima nocte clausum fuerit, nempe in Conclavi Alexandri VII. ob multitudinem Cardinalium, iisque servientium, Quæ moræ ibi Hispanis multùm utiles, Sacchetio contrà valde noxiæ dicuntur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Yet not at once after their entry was all communication with those living outside removed. The envoys of kings, princes, prelates and other nobles freely enter, partly to bear witness to their own feelings, partly also to negotiate expressly for their own parties and their supporters. This goes on until late at night, and very often they are scarcely dragged away from the sides of the cardinals, after warnings, admonitions and protests have been interposed. Although the Ceremonial of Gregory XV has defined at what time they must leave, since there we read thus: After the conclave has been shut, at the command of the Cardinal Dean, with the little bell rung, namely the first time about the first hour of the night, the second time about the second, and the third time about the third, all who ought not to remain in the conclave being excluded, let it be locked inside and outside. But it also happened that it was not closed on the first day nor on the first night, namely in the conclave of Alexander VII, because of the great number of cardinals and their attendants. This delay is said to have been very useful to the Spanish, but very harmful to Sacchetti.

units.la: XXXIV. Tandem tamen omnes, exceptis Cardinalibus & Ministrantibus, exire coguntur, imò omnibus aliis apud Conclave habitare, vel morari prohibitum. De quo ita sonant verba in Bulla Pii IV. Post Conclavis verò ingressum interdicimus & expressè prohibemus sub officiorum & beneficiorum privationis pœna, atque etiam sub alia arbitrio Gubernatoris ad custodiam Conclavis deputari soliti infligenda, ne quis immediatè supra aut infra Conclave, seu à lateribus habitare vel morari possit. Qua loca muris claudi, & à præsidentibus custodia Conclavis & à dicto Gubernatore sapius visitari debeant. Et si qua fraus commissa fuerit, teneatur ipse Gubernator sub perjurii pœna eo ipso incurrenda, & alia arbitrio futuri Pontificis infligenda, delinquentes hujusmodi Cardinalibus pro tempore deputatis revelare, curaréque, ut delinquentes ipsi carcerentur & acriter puniantur.
units.tr: XXXIV. Finally, however, all persons except the Cardinals and their attendants are compelled to leave, and indeed it is forbidden for anyone else to live or stay near the Conclave. On this the words of Pius IV's bull read: After the entry into the Conclave, we forbid and expressly prohibit, under the penalty of loss of offices and benefices, and also under other penalties to be inflicted at the discretion of the Governor who is customarily appointed to guard the Conclave, that anyone live or stay immediately above or below the Conclave, or beside it. These places must be walled up, and they must often be inspected by the presiders over the custody of the Conclave and by the said Governor. And if any fraud is committed, the Governor himself shall be bound, under the penalty of perjury which he incurs by that very fact, and under other penalties to be inflicted at the discretion of the future Pontiff, to disclose such offenders to the Cardinals then deputed, and to take care that the offenders themselves are imprisoned and sharply punished.

units.la: XXXV. Ipsum Conclave optimè undiquaque clauditur quatuor portis, ita muro vallatum, ut nemo introire possit, solummodò fenestrella in foramen rotæ facta ad servitium epularum destinata aperta relinquitur; Et extra tempora tabulæ & intrà & extrà non solùm ferrata, sed & sigillata est, & à certis quibusdam ad hoc destinatis personis custoditur; Quarta ex quatuor portis propriè porta Conclavis est, & quatuor Clavibus aperiri debet. Quarum duas illi, qui foris sunt, habent, unam ad portam, alteram ad Fenestram, duo nimirum præcipui Prælati, Claves verò duas reliquas in Conclavi habent Magister Ceremoniarum, & omnes quatuor ad aperturam concurrere debent. Insuper quoque porta intrinsecus telâ obtegitur, ne fenestrella aperta ab ullo ex intus degentibus videri possit; Cæterùm & intus cuivis Camerae ferè sua fenestrella est. Ubi verò ferratum est Conclave, Ceremoniale Gregorii jubet, ut accensis funalibus tres Cardinales, capita ordinum & Cameramerarius unâ cum Magistro Ceremoniarum latebras & angulos omnes Conclavis diligenter perquirant, ne quis exiis,qui esse in Conclavi prohibentur, intus remanserit. Quâ scrutatione peractâ, in testimonium bona serratura prodit publicum instrumentum à Magistris Ceremoniarum compositum. Post hujusmodi documentum autem, ut habet Cæremoniale Gregorii, etiamsi Conclave in totum, vel pro parte de facto apertum fuisse reperiatur, semper tamen clausum & pro clauso censeri debet ad effectum validitatis electionis, donec de consensu duarum partium Cardinalium præsentium per secreta suffragia apertum esse declaretur. Hac tamen declaratio electioni,qua ante ipsam facta fuerit, nullatenus prajudicare debet, neque ob ipsam declarationem precedens electio impugnari potest.
units.tr: XXXV. The Conclave itself is closed off on every side with great care: it has four doors and is walled round so that no one can enter, and only a small window, made in the turntable for the service of food, is left open. Outside the hours for serving, both the turntable and the window, inside and out, are not only barred with iron but also sealed, and are guarded by certain persons appointed for this purpose. The fourth of the four doors is properly the door of the Conclave, and it must be opened with four keys. Two of these are held by those outside, one for the door and the other for the window, namely the two chief prelates; the remaining two keys are held inside the Conclave by the Master of Ceremonies, and all four must come together for the opening. Moreover, the door is covered on the inside with a cloth, so that the small window, when open, cannot be seen by anyone living inside; and in any case each chamber inside has almost its own little window. Where the Conclave is barred with iron, the Ceremonial of Gregory orders: that, with torches lit, three Cardinals, the heads of the orders and the Chamberlain, together with the Master of Ceremonies, carefully search all the hiding places and corners of the Conclave, lest anyone who is forbidden to be in the Conclave remain inside. When this search is finished, a public instrument drawn up by the Masters of Ceremonies is issued as evidence that the locking is secure. After such a record, however, as the Ceremonial of Gregory has it, even if the Conclave is found to have been opened wholly or in part in fact, it must nevertheless always be considered closed and be regarded as closed for the purpose of the validity of the election, until it is declared open by the consent of two parts of the Cardinals present, by secret votes. Yet this declaration must in no way prejudice the election made before it, nor can a previous election be impugned because of the declaration itself.

units.la: XXXVI. Atque ita intus degentibus omnis occasio cum extra constitutis communicandi abscinditur.
units.tr: XXXVI. In this way every opportunity of communicating with those outside is cut off from those who live inside.

units.la: Colloquia ita vetat Bulla Pii IV. Clauso Conclavi, nulli ad colloquium etiam extra portam Conclavis, etiam Principum Oratores, nisi ex magna & urgenti causa à majori parte Collegii approbanda admittuntur. Et si quis forte (quod absit) clam ipsum Conclave, & aliunde quàm per ostium ingrediatur, omni honore, gradu & officio & beneficio ipso facto privatus existat, & tradatur curiæ seculari acerrimis pœnis puniendus. Qui autem per ostium in certis casibus intromittuntur, illis regressus non datur, quod exemplo etiam in Conclavi Leonis X. nato constat, cùm enim ad secundum ei, qui adhuc Cardinalis Medicæus erat, apostema Chirurgus intromissus esset, non permissum ei fuit rursus exire, licèt petenti. Literas & signa Bulla ita vetat: Literas verò, aut cujusvis generis scripta ad eos,qui in Conclavi erant, seu nuncium, vel votum, aut signum mittere seu recipere, aut contrà, è Conclavi ad eos, qui foris erunt, nullo modo liceat: qui contra fecerint, quacunque dignitate, etiamsi Cardinalatûs honore præfulgeant, pœna excommunicationis latæ sententiæ subjaceant, absolvendi facultate, præterquam in mortis articulo soli Pont. Max. reservata, à quo nihilominus pro qualitate delicti ultra dictam excommunicationis pœnam puniendi erunt. Non autem ita exactè observari commercii colloquiorum omissionem, & tamen nonnunquam impediri, tum ex candelis Baronianis supra memoratis, tum ex exemplo, quod Conclave Leonis X. suppeditavit, apparet.
units.tr: Pius IV's bull forbids conversations as follows: Once the Conclave is closed, no one is admitted to a conversation, even outside the door of the Conclave, not even the ambassadors of princes, unless for a great and urgent cause approved by the greater part of the College. And if anyone (which God forbid) should enter the Conclave secretly, and by some other way than through the door, he shall be deprived by that very fact of all honour, rank, office and benefice, and shall be handed over to the secular court to be punished with the sharpest penalties. But those who are admitted through the door in certain cases are not allowed to go out again. This is shown also by the example in the Conclave of Leo X, when a surgeon was admitted to lance an abscess on the second day for the Cardinal who was still Medici; he was not permitted to go out again, although he asked. The bull forbids letters and signals as follows: It is in no way lawful to send or receive letters, or writings of any kind, to or from those who are in the Conclave, nor a messenger, a vote, or a sign, nor, conversely, to send anything from the Conclave to those who will be outside. Whoever acts against this, of whatever dignity, even if he is distinguished by the honour of the cardinalate, shall be subject to the penalty of excommunication by sentence already passed, the power of absolution being reserved to the Supreme Pontiff alone, except at the point of death; and nevertheless, according to the nature of the offence, they shall be punished beyond the said penalty of excommunication. However, that the omission of commerce and conversations is not observed so strictly, and yet is sometimes hindered, appears both from the Baronian candles mentioned above and from the example which the Conclave of Leo X supplied.

units.la: XXXVII. Sed & epulæ inspiciuntur, ne literæ, notæ vel signa unà cum eis intus Conclave mittantur; Quem in finem ita citata
units.tr: XXXVII. But the food is also inspected, so that letters, notes or signs are not sent into the Conclave along with it. To this end the bull cited above reads thus:

units.la: citata Bulla se habet: Prælati quoque ad custodiam Conclavis deputati sub pœna perjurii & suspensionis à Divinis, maximâ & exquisitâ diligentiâ utantur in inspiciendis ac perscrutandis epulis, & aliis rebus, ac personis Conclave intrantibus & de eo exeuntibus, ne sub rerum earum velamine litera, aut nota, vel signa aliqua transmittantur. Quod si tale quid inventum fuerit, familiares Cardinalium, aut alii delinquentes pœnam privationis officiorum & beneficiorum, ac inhabilitatis ad obtenta & obtinenda incurrant; Et ulterius per Gubernatorem carceribus mancipentur, exinde nisi mandato novi Pontificis minimè relaxandi: sed ejus arbitrio acriùs puniendi, omni facultate Collegio Cardinalium in favorem quorumcunque, qui in præmissis, vel eorum aliquo deliquerint, omninò interdicta. Eidem solicitudini adscribendum, quòd vinum & aqua tantùm in vasibus vitreis intus accipiuntur. Exactæ verò observationis documentum singulare in Conclavi Clementis IX. occurrit; Ubi tamen etiam de epistola non lacerata agitur.
units.tr: The prelates also who are deputed to guard the Conclave, under the penalty of perjury and suspension from divine offices, shall use the utmost and most exact diligence in inspecting and searching the food, and other things, and the persons entering the Conclave and leaving it, lest any letter, note or sign be sent under the cover of those things. If anything of the kind is found, the servants of the Cardinals or other offenders shall incur the penalty of loss of offices and benefices, and of incapacity to obtain and hold them; and further, they shall be handed over to prison by the Governor, not to be released except by the order of the new Pontiff, but to be punished more severely at his discretion; and every power is wholly forbidden to the College of Cardinals to show favour to any who have offended in these matters, or in any of them. To the same care must be ascribed the fact that wine and water are taken in only in glass vessels. A singular proof of exact observance occurs in the Conclave of Clement IX, where, however, there is also question of a letter that was not torn open.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ipsis Cardinalibus (qui omninò, juxta Bullam etiam Pii IV. intrare tenentur, extra casum infirmitatis verò foris manentes constitutionis Gregorii X. pœnam (quæ juxta Decr. 6. l. 4. tit. 6. c. 4. §. Hoc sacro. in eo consistit, quòd ipso minimè requisito, nec in ejusdem electionis negotio ulterius admittendo per alios ad eligendum summum Pontif. liberè proceditur; incurrunt;) extra infirmitatis etiam casum & ante electionem factam egredi minimè permittitur. Solebant quidem Cardinales olim, ut ex Conclavi Gregorii XIII. discimus, primo die exire, neque ante vesperam redire; Verùm, ut ibidem narratur, ob tentatam tunc ab amicis Moronis adorationem ejus, & quia Bulla Pii IV. vult, ut ingredientes sine mora aliqua, omissâ Capitulorum confectione primis diebus fieri solitorum, in electionis negotio procedant, & singulis diebus scrutinium fiat, & in primo scrutinio etiam accedere liceat; quamvis à longo tempore scrutinium primo die nunquam factum sit; tamen in sequente Sixti V. Conclavi memores præteritorum atque potestatis nulli primo die exiverunt, ob novas etiam quorundam molitiones. Quorum quoque in sequente Urbani VII. Conclavi memores perhibentur. XXXIX. Ægris solis exire & redire permittitur. Sic præter alios aliàs ex Conclavi Leonis XI. exiit Cardinalis Sfondrata, quamvis egressum, cùm jam rhedæ & lectica in promptu essent, aliquandiu distulerit, & il pareva &c. Et videbatur, inquit Author, Medicos, sive quia ita persuasi erant ab iis, quorum intererat, sive sive quia viderant mali declinationem, remedium adhibuisse humori peccanti; quare etiam mansit, forte, ut factioni suæ non displiceat, neque utatur ponte aureo, quem ei nimis civiliter fabricare volebant adversarii. Eodem infirmitatis privilegio etiam usus est Cardinalis Spada, ex Conclavi Alexandri VII. egressus, de quo Cardinalis Montalt-tius facetè dixit: Il solo odore &c. Solus odor Papatûs agrum fecit Spadam, quanto igitur malo afficeretur, si cum planè comederet? Si verò Cardinalium in Conclavi degentium proximi etiam, in extremis etiam, jaceant, ipsis tamen ad eos exire non licet, quod exemplo Antonii Card. Barbarini, cui, utut valdè petenti ad matrem moribundam egredi in Conclavi an. 1644. copia nulla facta est.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The Cardinals themselves (who, by the bull of Pius IV also, are bound to enter in every case, and who, if they remain outside apart from the case of illness, incur the penalty of Gregory X's constitution (which, according to Decr. 6. l. 4. tit. 6. c. 4. §. Hoc sacro., consists in this, that, without being asked, and without being admitted any further to the business of that same election, they proceed freely by others to elect the Supreme Pontiff) are not permitted to leave even outside the case of illness and before the election has been made. Indeed, the Cardinals used formerly, as we learn from the Conclave of Gregory XIII, to go out on the first day and not return before evening; but, as is related there, because of the adoration of Moroni that his friends then attempted, and because Pius IV's bull wills that those entering, without any delay, and omitting the drawing up of the chapters which used to be made on the first days, proceed to the business of the election, and that a scrutiny be held each day, and that it be permitted to take part even in the first scrutiny, although for a long time no scrutiny had ever been held on the first day; nevertheless, in the following Conclave of Sixtus V, mindful of past events and of the power of none, they did not go out on the first day, also because of new schemes of certain men. They are also said to have been mindful of these things in the following Conclave of Urban VII. XXXIX. Only the sick are permitted to go out and return. Thus, among others, the Cardinal Sfondrata went out from the Conclave of Leo XI, although, when the carriage and litter were already ready, he delayed the going out for some time, and it seemed, &c., and it seemed, says the author, that the physicians, either because they had been persuaded so by those whose interest it was, or because they had seen the bad tendency, had applied a remedy to the peccant humour; wherefore he also remained, perhaps so as not to displease his faction, and not to use the golden bridge which his adversaries were trying too courteously to build for him. The Cardinal Spada, who went out of the Conclave of Alexander VII, made use of the same privilege of illness, and of him Cardinal Montalto wittily said: The mere smell &c. The mere smell of the Papacy made Spada sick; how much harm, then, would he suffer if he actually ate it? But if the neighbours of the Cardinals living in the Conclave lie even at the point of death, it is nonetheless not lawful for them to go out to them; this is shown by the example of Cardinal Antonio Barberini, who, although he begged very earnestly to go out in the Conclave of 1644 to his dying mother, was granted no opportunity.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Bis Cardinales omnes ante electionem Pontificis egressos esse reperio. Primò post Martini IV. mortem, cui tandem An. 1288. nimirum Nicolaus IV. successit; Egressi autem sunt A. 1287. morborum maximè, (quibus unius septimanæ spatio 5. præcipui Cardinales consumpti fuerunt;) & terræ motuum respectu; sed mense Martio anni sequentis denuò cum fructu congregati sunt. Alterà vice post mortem Benedicti IX. al. XI. discordiæ maximè intuitu Conclave reliquerunt, andandosene &c. abeuntes, ut Author Cardinalismi p.3.l.1.p.77. ait, extra civitatem, hic huc, ille illuc, in loca delitiosa, quarentes gaudia & voluptates, & de omnibus aliis potius quàm de Papa creando cogitantes; Sed populi Perusini armis recollecti tandem Clementem V. qui sedem in Galliam transtulit, elegerunt. De egressu multorum, vel plerorumque jam supra egi. Heic addo judicium de Rosellis: Mon. p. 2. p. 328. de egressu multorum, compellendos videri, dicit, quia juxta legem forte possint alios in suam sententiam pertrahere, & quia ratio, qua omnes compelli debere velit, etiam de multis obtineat; ipse tamen tenet, non esse aliquos compellendos, quia, quo pauciores numerus, hoc major concordia, & invitus ad electionem non cogi, sed voci juxta legem renuuciare possit, & magis scandalum excitaret ingressus, & non dicatur intrâsse, qui non usque in finem steterit, denuò juxta legem. De egressu omnium ita cum eodem de Rosellis p.2. c.8.p.327.25. &c. statuunt: Si notorium aut evidens sit periculum, & impressio vel metus ab altero, quàm à Domino civitatis, in cujus territorio debet fieri electio, tunc ipsum Dominum, si possit, per se debere metum illum reprimere, & si non possit per se, tunc debere convocare brachium & auxilium vicinorum & aliorum, qui tutum facerent, argu.23. quæst. 2. Dominus. Cod. de judi 1. properandum §. sin autem. Et in cap. 1. de brev. & pa. Et si nullo modo possit locum tutum facere, vel non velit, vel metus sit ab ipso Domino loci ipsum inferente, & notorius, tunc, si omnes Cardinales sint concordes, posse concordare de alio loco tuto 78. di. c. Si quis pecuniam. & valere concordationem, quoniam hoc casu ipsi propter periculum, quod imminet, habent jurisdictionem Papæ: Ut in d. decret. ubi periculum & Cle. ne Romani. statuatur. Si autem causa non sit notoria, esse per Dominum temporalem civitatis, ubi fieret electio, ad reintrandum compellandos: & si non sit potens ad compellandum, tunc vicinos Dominos, in quorum dominia aufugerint, debere eos ad loca, ubi electio fieri deberet, remittere, ut no. glo. in d. Cle. ne Romani. in verbo dioecesis. Quæ etiam in constitutionibus Gregorii X. apud Onuph annot. in Greg. X. Plat. fundata sunt.
units.tr: I find that all the Cardinals have twice left the Conclave before the election of a Pontiff. The first time was after the death of Martin IV, to whom at last in 1288 Nicholas IV succeeded. They left in 1287, chiefly because of illnesses (by which five principal Cardinals were carried off within the space of one week), and because of earthquakes; but in the month of March of the following year they were gathered together again, with success. The second time was after the death of Benedict IX (alias XI), when they left the Conclave chiefly because of discord, going away &c., departing, as the author of Cardinalismus says (p.3.l.1.p.77.), outside the city, one here, another there, into pleasant places, seeking joys and pleasures, and thinking of everything rather than of creating a Pope. But the people of Perugia, gathering under arms, at last elected Clement V, who moved the seat to France. I have already treated the departure of many, or most, above. Here I add the judgment of de Rosellis (Mon. p. 2. p. 328.) on the departure of many. He says they seem to be compelled, because by law they might perhaps draw others to their opinion, and because the reason by which all ought to be compelled also holds for many. He himself holds, however, that none should be compelled, because the fewer the number, the greater the concord; one cannot be forced to the election against his will, but may renounce his vote according to law; and entering would cause more scandal, and one is not said to have entered who has not stayed to the end, again according to law. On the departure of all, de Rosellis (p.2. c.8.p.327.25. &c.) with the same authority lays down: If the danger is notorious or evident, and the fear is inflicted by someone other than the lord of the city in whose territory the election must take place, then the lord himself, if he is able, must restrain that fear by his own power; and if he is not able by himself, then he must summon the arm and help of neighbours and others, who would make it safe (argu.23.) Q. 2 Dominus; Cod. de judi. 1, properandum §. sin autem. And in cap. 1 de brev. & pa.: And if he can in no way make the place safe, or does not wish to, or the fear is from the lord of the place himself and is notorious, then, if all the Cardinals agree, they may agree upon another safe place (78 dist. c. Si quis pecuniam), and the agreement is valid, since in this case they have, on account of the imminent danger, the jurisdiction of the Pope. As in the said decretal, where danger and Clement, Ne Romani, are established. But if the cause is not notorious, the temporal lord of the city where the election would take place is to compel them to return; and if he is not able to compel them, then the neighbouring lords, in whose domains they have fled, ought to send them back to the places where the election should be held, as the gloss notes on the said Clement, Ne Romani, in the word dioecesis. These things were also established in the constitutions of Gregory X, cited by Onuphrius in his notes on Gregory X, Platina.

units.la: XLI. De Conclavistis & aliis, præter Cardinales, discedentibus, ita Pii IV. Bulla de Conclavi statuit:
units.tr: XLI. Concerning conclavists and others, besides Cardinals, who leave: thus Pius IV in his Bulla de Conclavi decreed:

units.la: Conclavista verò & quicunque alii servientes, Conclave ex causa infirmitatis manifesta & notabilis, à medicis medio juramento probata, & de consensu deputatorum, quorum etiam conscientiam desuper oneramus, & non aliter exituri, nullo modo reverti possint: Sed eorum loco alii, eodem prorsus tempore, quo infirmi exibunt, ingrediantur. Videtur autem ita ad infirmitatem Conclavistarum & aliorum ministrantium egressus restringi, ut nequidem ob mala facta ejici quis possit; Quod confirmatur exemplo Abbatis Mediolani in Conclavi Clementis X.
units.tr: But a conclavist or any other servants may in no way return to the Conclave once they have left it on account of manifest and notable sickness, proved by physicians under oath, and with the consent of the deputies, whose conscience we also burden in this matter, and who are not to go out otherwise; but in their place others shall enter at the very same time as the sick leave. It seems, however, that the departure of conclavists and other attending servants is so restricted to sickness that one cannot even be expelled for bad conduct. This is confirmed by the example of the Abbot of Milan in the Conclave of Clement X.

units.la: XLII. Ut autem ista omnia observentur, & Cardinales tuti sint, beneficio illorum, qui Conclave custodiunt, fit.
units.tr: XLII. So that all these things may be observed and the Cardinals kept safe, it is done by the help of those who guard the Conclave.

units.la: De quibus ita apud Onuphrium l. c. legitur: Ut locus & porta Conclavis diligentissime custodiantur, Si Roma electio habeatur, primum à Pratorianis, deinde à Regulis & Oratoribus Principum Sacramento prius adstrictis, demum in loco ostio Conclavis proximiore ab Episcopis & Conservatoribus Urbis; Si autem extra Urbem Comitia hæc habentur, à loci ejusdem Dominis temporalibus eodem juramento fidelitatis obligatis. Quorum munus est, Conclave custodire, & diligenter cavere, ne quid Conclavi inferatur, seu exportetur, quo minus legitima suffragia ferri possint, atque singula scrutari, quæ vel cibi, vel alterius rei causa inferuntur ad eos, & providere, ne quid detrimenti patiantur Cardinales, omnibusque ipsorum nutibus præsto esse, ac eligere Pontificem differentes ad maturandum arctare. Milites verò Pratoriani, ac Reguli Romani Conclave ab omni impressione tutum reddere debent. Hodie quatuor sunt Portæ, quarum secundam dicti Conservatores Romæ custodiunt, atque neminem nisi tempore cibo destinato intromittunt ; Apud tertiam eminet sedis Marescallus, Gubernator Burgi, quod officium Familiæ Savellicæ hæreditarium est.
units.tr: Of these the following is read in Onuphrius, l.c.: That the place and the door of the Conclave be most diligently guarded. If the election is held at Rome, first by the Praetorians, then by the Reguli and the envoys of princes already bound by oath, and finally in the place nearest the door of the Conclave by the Bishops and the Conservators of the City; but if these assemblies are held outside the City, by the temporal lords of that same place, bound by the same oath of fidelity. Their duty is to guard the Conclave and carefully take heed that nothing is brought into the Conclave or carried out which might hinder the lawful votes from being cast, and to examine each thing that is brought to them, whether for food or for some other reason, and to provide that the Cardinals suffer no harm, to be at hand at all their nods, and to press those who delay in choosing a Pontiff to hasten. The Praetorian soldiers and the Roman Reguli must make the Conclave safe from every attack. Today there are four gates, of which the second is guarded by the said Conservators at Rome, who admit no one except at the time set for food. At the third the Marshal of the Holy See presides, the Governor of the Borgo; this office is hereditary in the Savelli family.

units.la: XLIII. De cibo quoque leges latæ sunt; Et quidem ita Gregorius X. in Concilio Lugdunensi 6.Decr. l.1. tit.6.c.4. §. hoc Sacro. decrevit : Si (quod absit) intra 3. dies, postquam (ut prædicitur) Conclave præfatum iidem Cardinales intraverint, non fuerit ipsi Ecclesiæ de Pastore provisum : per spatium quinque dierum immediatè sequentium singulis diebus, tam in prandio, quàm in cœna, uno solo ferculo sint contenti, quibus, provisione non factâ, decursis, ex tunc tantummodò panis, vinum & aqua ministratur eisdem, donec eadem provisio subsequatur : Ubi Glossa addit: Not. hic, quòd electores nolentes eligere, possunt cogi etiam tormentis tex. est hic juncta. glo. in Cle. i. de hæreti. Phil. Fonta. (partem quoque hujus dicit Onuphrius annot. in Greg.X. Plat. verbis sequentibus: Ut post triduum ingressûs Conclavis nisi Pontifex renuntiatus fuerit, Episcopi, Reguli Romani, & qui Conclavis custodia præsunt, maximam in epulis & cibis, qui Cardinalibus inferuntur, rationem habeant, & illis nonnisi ferculum unum inferri permittant. Sed adhuc durior est, quoad initium Bulla Pii IV. quæ ita legem cibariam exponit: Cardinales primo ipso die, quo Conclave ingressi fuerint, tam in prandio, quàm in cœna uno solo ferculo, unius speciei tantùm eóque moderato & aliàs juxta constitutionem præfati Clementis VI. (quam ad manus non habeo) qualificato contenti sint & esse debeant, nec quisquam in alterius cella, vel de alterius ferculo vescatur. Rigorem auget, quòd additio 6. Decr. l.1.tit.6. c.4. §. ubi periculum ista habetur: Quid, si unus velit unum ferculum, alius aliud ; puta unus vult carnes bovinas, alius capones, alius perdices. Dicunt Doctores, quòd est administrandum unum solum ferculum omnibus, & non sunt eis administranda diversa fercula, quia aliàs posset fieri fraus. Nam ipsi sibi ipsis ministrarent diversa fercula.
units.tr: XLIII. Laws were also passed about food. Thus Gregory X, in the Council of Lyons, decreed (6 Decr. l.1. tit.6. c.4. §. hoc Sacro.): If (God forbid) within three days after the same Cardinals have entered the aforesaid Conclave, as has been said, the Church has not been provided with a Pastor, then for the space of five days immediately following, each day, at dinner as well as at supper, they shall be content with one single dish; and when the provision has not been made and these days have passed, then from that time only bread, wine and water shall be served to them, until the same provision follows. Where the Gloss adds: Note here that electors who are unwilling to elect may be compelled even by torments, a text here joined with the gloss in Clement I, de haeret., Philippus Fontanus. Onuphrius also cites part of this in his notes on Gregory X, Platina, in the following words: That after three days from entering the Conclave, unless a Pontiff has been proclaimed, the Bishops, the Reguli of Rome, and those who preside over the custody of the Conclave shall take the greatest account of the feasts and foods brought to the Cardinals, and shall permit only one dish to be brought to them. But the Bull of Pius IV is still harsher at the beginning, which sets out the law on food thus: The Cardinals, on the very first day on which they have entered the Conclave, shall be and must be content, both at dinner and at supper, with one single dish, of one kind only, and that moderate, and otherwise qualified according to the constitution of the aforesaid Clement VI (which I do not have at hand), and no one shall eat in another's cell, or from another's dish. The rigour is increased by the addition in 6 Decr. l.1. tit.6. c.4. §. ubi periculum, which reads: What if one wants one dish and another another; say one wants beef, another capons, another partridges? The Doctors say that one single dish is to be served to all, and different dishes are not to be served to them, because otherwise fraud could occur; for they would serve themselves different dishes.

units.la: XLIV. Quoad observationem harum constitutionum Conclavia tantùm sequentia exhibent; In Conclavi Clementis V. supra quoque memorato Perusini præsidium non tantùm posuerunt, ne rursus dilaberentur Cardinales, sed & ad electionem maturandam alio remedio usi sunt, riducendo il lor mangiare &c. reducendo cibum illorum ad modum moderatum, atque iis comminando, si Electionem paucis diebus non absolvissent, se iis nihil prater panem & vinum permissuros esse ; Quod etiam remedium tunc juvisse eventus docuit.
units.tr: XLIV. As for the observance of these constitutions, the Conclaves show only the following. At the Conclave of Clement V, the Perugians, already mentioned above, not only posted a guard so that the Cardinals might not again slip away, but also used another remedy to hasten the election: reducing their food, that is, reducing their food to a moderate amount, and threatening them that if they did not finish the election within a few days, they would allow them nothing but bread and wine. The outcome showed that this remedy also helped at that time.

units.la: Ut post triduum ingressûs Conclavis… (see text above)
units.tr: So that after three days of the Conclave's entry… (see text above)

units.la: In Conclavi Nicolai V. simpliciter consuetudo & constitutio illa innuitur,juxta quam primis quinque diebus Conclavis fosse lecito &c. licitum esset habere omnis generis cibos,atque illis elapsis unum duntaxat ferculum assum vel tostum pro lubitu, & si intra tempus illud non crearent summum Pontificem, ipsis assignata esset nonnisi quaedam portio panis & vini. Quae consuetudo & constitutio à singulis n. praced. allatis differre deprehenditur. In recentiori vero Clementis IX. Conclavi tantum innuitur, constitutionem de solo pane & vino post diem tertium fuisse mitigatam ad patinam unam,qua conficere debeat prandium integrum. Ex quo partim silentio de datis unquam,tot habitis occasionibus,pane & vino tantum, partim mitigationis indicio, satis colligi posse arbitror, durantibus licet per plures dies plerisque, imo multis per unum & alterum mensem, Conclavibus, Bullarum rigorem nunquam observari. Nec etiam videtur illud de eodem omnibus ferculo administrando judicium observari; Quamvis rigor talis multum omnino prodesse & electiones valde maturare posset. Interim tamen constat,in Conclavibus degentes haud parum infra Majestatem alias in hac etiam parte ostendi solitam, & luxum suum subsistere debere.
units.tr: In the Conclave of Nicholas V that custom and regulation is simply implied, according to which during the first five days of the Conclave it was lawful to have food of every kind, and after those days had passed, one roast or toasted dish at choice, and if within that time they did not create a supreme Pontiff, only a set portion of bread and wine was assigned to them. This custom and regulation is found to differ from those cited by the individual preceding notes. In the more recent Conclave of Clement IX it is only implied that the regulation of bread and wine alone after the third day was softened to one dish, with which they should make up a full dinner. From this, partly from the silence about bread and wine alone ever being given, though there have been so many occasions, and partly from the sign of softening, I think it can be sufficiently gathered that the rigour of the bulls was never observed, although for several days in most Conclaves, indeed for one or two months in many, the Conclaves lasted. Nor does it seem that the judgement about serving the same single dish to all was observed; yet such rigour could greatly help and speed up elections. Meanwhile, however, it is established that those living in the Conclaves must not a little go beyond the Majesty, which in this part also has usually been shown, and that their luxury must be kept within bounds.

units.la: XLV. Quod vero attinet ad vestes,sunt verba Caeremonialis Gregorii XV. non solum cum ad electionem Cardinales procedunt, croceis uti debent, sed juxta vetus Caeremoniale, cum aliquid Collegialiter agendum est. Afferam hic 2. vel 3. singularitates, quas apud Authores Conclavium recentiorum reperire datum fuit, vestes respicientes; Unus, ille nimirum, qui Conclave Alexandri VII. scripsit, jam ab initio monet Lectorem, non debere à se expectari minutias quascunque, quae tunc acciderint, le Masthere &c. larvarum per quadragesimam continuationes, cum quibus Cardinales se invicem inviserint. Alter,Scriptor nempe Conclavis Clementis X. solicite Bullionaeum Cardinalem defendit contra illos, che pretendino &c. qui pertendant, eum noctu portasse calceos alla spagnuola; ex hoc fundamento: Nunquam eum sic vidi, ast nunquam ex cella egredi potuit,ut eum non viderim: Semper portabat calceos altos in calcaneo alla Francese, cum rosis alla moda. Idem author Cardinalem Retzium excusare videtur, qui noctu larvam per Conclave portasse dicatur, dicendo,fuisse aliquid larvae simile!
units.tr: XLV. As for clothing, these are the words of the Ceremonial of Gregory XV: The Cardinals must wear saffron not only when they proceed to the election, but, according to the old Ceremonial, whenever something is to be done collegially. Here I shall set out two or three peculiarities, which it has been possible to find in the authors of recent Conclaves, concerning clothing. One, namely he who wrote the Conclave of Alexander VII, warns the reader at the outset that he should not expect from him any trifles whatever that happened then: the Masters, etc., the continuing of masks through Lent, with which the Cardinals visited one another. Another, the writer of the Conclave of Clement X, carefully defends Cardinal Bullion against those who claim, etc., that he wore Spanish-style shoes at night, on this ground: I never saw him so, but he could never leave his cell without my seeing him: he always wore high-heeled shoes in the French fashion, with rosettes in the modern style. The same author seems to excuse Cardinal de Retz, who is said to have carried a mask through the Conclave at night, by saying that there was something like a mask!

units.la: XLVI. Satis jam de loco,de sociis ministrantibus, de commercii cum exteris privatione, de manendi necessitate, de legibus cibariis
units.tr: XLVI. Enough has now been said about the place, the attending companions, the deprivation of dealings with outsiders, the necessity of staying, and the food regulations.

units.la: Lex vestiaria. Singularitates quaedam respectu vestium.
units.tr: The clothing regulation. Certain peculiarities concerning clothing.

units.la: Transitio ad actiones in loco. cibariis & vestiariis diximus; Appropinquemus magis ipsis Cardinalium in loco & statu hactenus memorato actionibus, eligendi rationibus. De loco, unicum adhuc monuisse contenti, nempe deliberationem de Electione hodie regulariter fieri in Capella Paulina, electionem ipsam in Sixtina, in qua super altari monstrari ajunt nobilem illam Michaelis Angeli Bonarottae de judicio supremo picturam; Illam forte, in qua Cardinalis quidam pictori exosus & proin ad sinistram ad vivum depictus juxta votum suum a Pontifice potestatem suam ad infernum se extendere negante liberari ex ignominia non potuit.
units.tr: Transition to the Cardinals' actions in the place, food and clothing we have discussed. Let us come closer to the actions of the Cardinals in the place and condition mentioned so far, and to the methods of electing. Concerning the place, content to have warned of one thing only: that deliberation about the election is today regularly held in the Pauline Chapel, and the election itself in the Sistine, where they say that above the altar is displayed that noble painting of the Last Judgement by Michelangelo Buonarroti; perhaps the one in which a certain Cardinal, hated by the painter, was depicted on the left from life, and as he wished, by the Pope's decision, who refused to free his power to extend to hell, he could not be freed from disgrace.

units.la: XLVII. Post actiones autem, quae ingressum proxime excipientes jam supra a me indicatae sunt, primum est, quod Cardinales praeter capitula, quae ad favorem Conclavistarum spectantia supra quoque notavimus, si opus esse judicent & velint, quaedam capitula alia & quasi leges quasdam futuro Pontifici scribunt, atque adeo unusquisque eorum, in se earum observationem, si forte contingat, ut ipse eligatur, recipit. Quam consuetudinem aliquid juxta voluntatem Collegii juramento confirmandi Vita di Sisto V. p.1.l.5. p.347. a 200. annis, sed modo diverso obtinuisse ait; Et cui Onuphrius quoque annot. in Clem. V. Plat. attestatur: Patres, inquit, Conclave ingressi diem integrum sequentem formandis legibus impendunt, ad sanam Romani Pontificis administrationem maxime necessariis: quibus Patrum quisque subscribens jurejurando votoque promittit, obtemperaturum se illis, si Pontifex fuerit factus. Exempla vide in Conclavi Pii IV. & in Vita Sixti V. l. c. Sed etiam Dissert.VIII. quam parum ejusmodi Capitula & juramenta curent.
units.tr: XLVII. After the actions which immediately follow entry, already indicated by me above, the first thing is that the Cardinals, apart from the chapters which concern the favour of the Conclavists, as we have also noted above, if they judge it necessary and wish, write certain other chapters, and as it were certain laws, for the future Pontiff; and so each of them accepts, for himself, the observance of these, should he happen to be elected. Vita di Sisto V says this custom of confirming something by oath, according to the will of the College, has prevailed for 200 years, though in a different manner. Onuphrius also, in his notes on Clement V in Platina, bears witness to it: The Fathers, he says, on entering the Conclave, spend the whole following day in drawing up laws most necessary for the sound administration of the Roman Pontiff; each of the Fathers, subscribing them, promises by oath and vow that he will obey them if the Pontiff is made. See examples in the Conclave of Pius IV and in the Life of Sixtus V, loc. cit. But see also Dissertation VIII, how little such chapters and oaths are taken care of.

units.la: XLVIII. Perventum jam est ad ipsos electionis actus, sive modos, quorum in forma illa quarta electionis per solos Cardinales quatuor, vel tres sunt. Si quatuor ponimus, per scrutinium, per accessum, per adorationem, sive inspirationem Spiritus S. & per compromissum Papas eligi dicimus; Si vero tres constituimus modos, illum per scrutinium dividere debemus ratione scrutinii simplicis & cum accessu conjuncti. Cumque ista omnino differant, & scrutinii saltem divisio necessaria atque diversa accessus ratio, & quidem accessus nullus sine scrutinio sit, interim tamen nonnunquam per simplex scrutinium electio perficiatur, aliquando etiam vel unico voto in scrutinio recepto, alicui accessus dignitatem conferat, melius quatuor formae sive modi numerari videntur; Quos distindistinctè & juxta ordinem indigitatum enarrabimus, quando priùs notaverimus, posse Cardinales, secundùm supra etiam memorata, electionem, si commodum illis sit, ipso ingressùs die aggredi; imò etiam antequam Conclave petant, sed modico temporis spatio, eligere posse. In Conclavi autem saltem mane sequenti post clausum precedente nocte Conclave, sunt verba ea Caeremonialis Gregorii XV. post solitum Campanula sonum, conveniunt Cardinales in eo praesentes, qui infirmitate non sunt impediti, ad Capellam Paulinam, & ibi concelebratâ consuetâ Missâ & factâ Cardinalium communione, statim ad negotium electionis procedere debent &c.
units.tr: XLVIII. We have now come to the acts of election themselves, or the methods, of which in that fourth form of election by the Cardinals alone there are four, or three. If we posit four, we say popes are elected by scrutiny, by accession, by adoration, or the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and by compromise. If, however, we set up three methods, we must divide the one by scrutiny on the basis of simple scrutiny and scrutiny combined with accession. Since these differ entirely, and at least the division of scrutiny is necessary, and the manner of accession is different, and indeed accession is never without scrutiny, yet sometimes the election is completed by simple scrutiny, and sometimes even with a single vote received in scrutiny one confers the dignity of accession on someone, it seems better to count four forms or methods. These we shall describe distinctly and in the order indicated, after first noting that the Cardinals, according to what has also been mentioned above, can, if it suits them, undertake the election on the very day of entry; indeed, even before they seek the Conclave, but within a short space of time, they can elect. In the Conclave, however, at least on the morning following, after the Conclave was closed the preceding night, these are the words of the Ceremonial of Gregory XV: after the customary sound of the little bell, the Cardinals who are present and not prevented by sickness assemble in the Pauline Chapel, and there, after the customary Mass has been celebrated and the Cardinals have communicated, they must at once proceed to the business of the election, etc.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Et quidem ordinariò ferè solent & primò electionem per scrutinium tentare. De quo scrutinio apparebit, secretum esse, non publicum. Constat autem tota actio tribus partibus 1. Antescrutinio. 2. Scrutinio ipso. 3. Post scrutinio. Ad Antescrutinium pertinere dicuntur actus 5. sequentes: 1. Praeparatio Schedularum 2. Extractio Scrutatorum & Deputatorum pro votis infirmorum per sortem. 3. Scriptio Schedularum. 4. Earum complicatio. 5. Obsignatio.
units.tr: Indeed, they ordinarily try first to make the election by scrutiny. From this scrutiny it will appear that it is secret, not public. The whole action has three parts: 1. the before-scrutiny; 2. the scrutiny itself; 3. the after-scrutiny. Five acts are said to belong to the before-scrutiny: (1) the preparation of the ballots; (2) the drawing by lot of the scrutineers and the deputies for the votes of the sick; (3) the writing of the ballots; (4) their folding; (5) their sealing.

units.la: L. Primus Antescrutinii, sive scrutinium antecedens actus Schedularum nimirum praeparatio ad Magistros caeremoniarum pertinet, qui eas impressas, ubi fieri poterit, alioquin unius manu scriptas secundùm formam infrà ponendam accipiunt, & ponunt in disco, vulgò (bacile) nuncupato, quem in mensa ante Altare collocant, (apud Onuphrium habetur, debere esse calicem, in quo illa die sacra facta sint;) ut inde possint Cardinales, cùm opus fuerit, Schedulas sumere; Sed Vita di Sisto V. p. 1. l. 5. p. 460. ubi de hodiernis electionis formis agit, & Schedularum praeparationem & scriptionem singulis singulorum Cardinalium Conclavistis tribuit vespera praecedente conficiendam. Forma autem Schedulae scrutinii, quod ejus figuram attinet, est altera parte longior, hoc est, plùs longa quàm lata; longitudo ejus ferè palmi, latitudo autem dimidii palmi. Quoad contenta, in anteriori parte, quae facies nominari potest, tria continet. Primò in superiori parte secundùm ejus latitudinem duo haec verba (Ego Card.) cum tanta ab invicem distantia, ut inter ipsa nomen proprium Cardinalis eligentis scribi possit; & paulò inferiùs duos circulos parvos, ad loca sigillorum indicanda. Secundò in medio continet haec verba: Eligo in summum Pontificem Reverendissimum Dn. meum Dn. Cardinalem. Tertiò riò in parte inferiori alios duos parvos circulos ad loca sigillorum similiter demonstranda. En ad meliorem perceptionem exemplum sive figuram anterioris partis, sive faciei Schedulæ talis scrutinii. Ego Card. O O Eligo in summum Pontificem Rever. D. meum D. Cardin. O O
units.tr: L. The first act of the before-scrutiny, namely the preparation of the ballots, belongs to the masters of ceremonies. They take the ballots, printed where that is possible and otherwise written out by hand by one person, in the form given below, and place them on a dish, commonly called the bacile, which they set on the table before the altar. (Onuphrius holds that it should be the chalice in which the sacred rite was celebrated that day.) This allows the cardinals to take ballots when needed. But the Vita di Sisto V, p. 1, l. 5, p. 460, where it treats of the present forms of the election, assigns the preparation and writing of the ballots to the conclavists of each individual cardinal, to be done on the evening before. The form of the ballot for the scrutiny, as to its shape, is longer in one direction, that is, longer than it is wide: its length is about a span and its width about half a span. As to its contents, the front side, which may be called the face, contains three things. First, in the upper part, across its width, are the two words (Ego Card.), spaced far enough apart to allow the proper name of the electing cardinal to be written between them; and a little lower, two small circles to mark the places of the seals. Second, in the middle it contains these words: I elect as supreme Pontiff my Most Reverend Lord, my Lord Cardinal. Third, in the lower part, two more small circles, likewise marking the places of the seals. For better understanding, here is an example, or figure, of the front side or face of such a ballot. I, Card. O O. I elect as supreme Pontiff my Most Reverend Lord, my Lord Cardinal O O.

units.la: In exteriori autem parte, quæ tergum nominari potest, duo sunt imprimendi limbi ex illis, quos ad ornatum librorum impressores adhibent, & vulgari vocabulo fregi nuncupant, quorum primum circa sui medium continet hoc verbum, Nomen, impressum secundum longitudinem ipsius limbi, alterum vero continet hoc verbum, signa, similiter impressum, ut præcedens. Hi autem limbi excogitati sunt ad obscurandum diaphanum paginarum, ne scilicet ad lumen nomina & signa eligentium conspici possint; Ubi vero impressoris copia non fuerit, limborum defectus lineis suppleri poterit. Sed en quoque figuram, sive exemplum tergi Schedulæ: Nomen
units.tr: On the outer side, which may be called the back, two borders are to be printed, of the kind printers use to decorate books and call by the common name fregi. The first of these has, in its middle, the word Nomen, printed along the length of the border; the other has the word signa, printed in the same way as the first. These borders were devised to darken the transparency of the pages, so that the names and signs of the electors cannot be seen against the light. Where there is no supply of printers' borders, the lack can be made up with lines. But here too is the figure, or example, of the back of the ballot: Here is also the figure or example of the back of the ballot: Nomen

units.la: Vu 3
units.tr: Vu 3

units.la: [Framed box containing the device: Signa]
units.tr: [Framed box containing the device: Signa]

units.la: LI. Secundus actus antescrutinii, sive scrutinium antecedens est extractio scrutatorum: quæ extractio, antequam ad scrutinium procedatur, sorte fit ita: In sacculo aut vase publicè ponuntur tot schedæ, vel, si magis placet, sphærulæ ligneæ palàm numeratæ, quot sunt Cardinales præsentes in Conclavi, cum eorum nominibus, deinde per ultimum Diaconum extrahuntur primò scrutatores, qui brevitatis gratiâ infirmarii appellantur. De quorum omnium officio inferius suo loco dicendum erit. Si autem extractione scrutatorum & infirmariorum ac etiam recognitorum, de quibus quoque suo loco dicemus, extracti fuerint Cardinales, qui ob infirmitatem aliudve impedimentum muneribus dictis satisfacere non possunt, alii non impediti eorum loco extrahuntur. Peractâ verò extractione, Schedæ, seu sphærulæ eorum, qui extracti fuerunt, in sacculum sive in vas iterum conjiciuntur.
units.tr: LI. The second act of the before-scrutiny is the drawing of the scrutineers. Before proceeding to the scrutiny, this drawing is done by lot in the following way. Publicly, as many slips, or if you prefer, small wooden balls marked with numbers, are put into a bag or vessel as there are cardinals present in the conclave, each with his name. Then the last deacon draws out first the scrutineers, who for brevity are called the infirmarii. Their duties will be explained in their proper place below. If, when the scrutineers, the infirmarii, and also the examiners (of whom we will likewise speak in their place) are drawn, some cardinals are drawn who, because of sickness or some other hindrance, cannot discharge these offices, others who are not hindered are drawn in their place. When the drawing is finished, the slips or balls of those who were drawn are put back into the bag or vessel.

units.la: LII. Tertius actus antescrutinii, vel scrutinium antecedens est Schedularum scrutinii scriptio, quæ fit hoc modo: Ad duas vel plures parvas mensas, quæ sunt cum atramento & calamis paratæ in loco Capellæ apto, ut, qui scribunt, conspici possint, quid verò scribatur, non possit conspici, accedentes Cardinales per ordinem incipiendo à Decano & ibi sedentes in scabellis paratis, Schedulam quisque suam acceptam priùs ex disco scribit hoc modo. Primo in primâ parte in spatio inter verba, (Ego Card.) scribit nomen proprium; deinde in secundâ parte nomen illius, quem eligit, charactere tamen, quantum fieri potest, alterato, ut manus scribentis cognosci non possit. Attamen Vita di Sisto V. l. c. habet, omnia ordinariò Conclavistas scribere, non Cardinalem ullum (altro che se sapesse contrafare cosi bene lamano) acciò che non sia osservata da altri e riconosciuta, già che in tal caso soglione tutti stare molto oculati, cercando ogni uno di penetrare il disegno dell' altro; che però si fà scrivere detto voto d'un altro, acciò da segreto, non venga poi con la cognitione della mano, farci palese, e dia occasione di odio e di diffidenza agli altri. (Nisi bene nôrit aliam literarum suarum figuram pingere) ne Scriptura ab aliis observetur & agnoscatur, cùm in tali casu omnes oculati esse soleant valde, quovis propositum alterius penetrare studente; hinc votum ab alio scribitur, ne secretum cognità manu palàm fiat, & occasionem diffidentiæ & odii aliis præbeat. Cavere autem quivis debet, ne plures in Schedula scribat, tunc enim suffragium juxta constitutionem Gregorianam nullum foret. In tertia verò parte signa, hoc est, numerum aliquem & dictum aliquod Scripturæ, seu verbum aut aliquid hujusmodi scribit. Quod in collatione cum schedulis accessûs juvat, tum enim sine tali signo semper nomina eligentium ipsa aperire deberent.
units.tr: LII. The third act of the before-scrutiny, or the antecedent scrutiny, is the writing of the scrutiny ballots, which is done in this way. At two or more small tables, prepared with ink and pens in a suitable place in the chapel so that those who write can be seen but what they write cannot, the cardinals approach in order, beginning with the dean, and sit on the prepared stools. Each one, taking his ballot first from the dish, writes as follows. First, in the first part, in the space between the words (Ego Card.), he writes his own name. Then, in the second part, he writes the name of the man he chooses, though with the handwriting altered as much as possible, so that the hand of the writer cannot be recognised. Yet the Vita di Sisto V, l. c. states that ordinarily the conclavists, not any cardinal, write everything (unless he knew how to imitate the hand so well), so that it is not observed and recognised by others. For in such a case they are all accustomed to be very watchful, each trying to penetrate the design of the other. Therefore the vote is written by another, so that it may remain secret and not, through recognition of the hand, become known and give occasion for hatred and distrust among the others. (Unless he knows how to make a different form of his letters.) Let each be careful not to write more than one name on the ballot, for then the vote would be void according to the Constitution of Gregory. In the third part he writes a sign, that is, some number and some saying of Scripture, or a word or something of that kind. This helps when the ballots are compared with the entrance list, for otherwise the names of the electors would have to be opened without any such sign.

units.la: LIII. Quartus actus antescrutinii sive scrutinium antecedens est schedularum complicatio: quae ut expeditiùs à Cardinalibus peragi valeat, à Magistris ceremoniariis, cùm eas præparant, fieri solent in hunc, qui sequitur modum: Binæ fiunt plicaturæ ex utraque parte cujusque schedulæ, ita ut nomen eligentis & signa, quum fuerint scripta, maneant tecta ex utraque parte à limbis; deinde, quod reliquum est, ita complicetur, ut schedula ferè ad latitudinem pollicis redigatur. Cæterùm Magistri Ceremoniarum Schedulas non complicatas, sed explicatas, & cum cera rubra in parvis circulis ponunt in disco, & Cardinales postquàm eas, ut supra scripserunt, eò usque solùm plicant, quò nomen & signa eligenris legantur, reliquas autem plicaturas tunc faciunt, quando schedulas, ut infrà dicetur, obsignârunt. LIV. Quintus actus & postremus antescrutinii est schedularum obsignatio, quae ab unoquoque Cardinali facienda est in tergo schedularum cum sigillo ad hoc parato, in loco parvorum circulorum, ubi cera fuerit posita. Porrò sigillum non est solitum Cardinalis, sed aliud & secretè habitum, & ita simplex, ut faciliùs notari possit, veluti si in sigillo sculpuntur, aut tres numeri, aut tres literæ, vel literæ & numeri, vel una tantùm imago. Hæc de antescrutinio, sive de actibus ipsum scrutinium antecedentibus. Quæ autem respectu infirmariorum, ut vocant, aut aliter impeditorum observari solent, mox quoque dicetur. LV. Actio-
units.tr: LIII. The fourth act of the before-scrutiny, or the antecedent scrutiny, is the folding of the ballots. So that the cardinals may carry it out more quickly, the masters of ceremonies, when they prepare the ballots, usually do it in the following way. Two folds are made on each side of every ballot, so that the name of the elector and the signs, once written, remain covered on either side by the borders. Then the rest is folded so that the ballot is reduced to about the width of a thumb. The masters of ceremonies, however, place the ballots not folded but flat, fixed with red wax in small circles on the dish. After the cardinals have written them as described above, they fold them only so far as the name and signs of the elector can be read. They make the remaining folds only when they have sealed the ballots, as will be said below. LIV. The fifth and last act of the before-scrutiny is the sealing of the ballots. Each cardinal must do this on the back of the ballots, with a seal prepared for the purpose, in the place of the small circles where the wax has been put. The seal is not the cardinal's usual one but another, kept secret, and so simple that it can be easily marked. For example, the seal may be engraved with three numbers, or three letters, or letters and numbers, or just a single image. This is what is said about the before-scrutiny, or the acts that come before the scrutiny itself. What is customarily observed with regard to the so-called infirmarii, or others who are otherwise hindered, will be said shortly as well.

units.la: LV. Actionis secundæ, quæ scrutinium appellari solet, octo sunt actus distincti, videlicet 1. Delatio schedulæ. 2. Juramenti præstatio 3. Positio schedulæ in calicem. 4. Schedularum mixtio 5. Numeratio. 6. Scrutinii publicatio. 7. Schedularum in filum insertio. 8. Earundem depositio seorsim. De quibus actibus singulis nonnulla quoque annotanda sunt.
units.tr: LV. The second action, which is usually called the scrutiny, has eight distinct acts: 1. the delivery of the ballot; 2. the taking of the oath; 3. the placing of the ballot in the chalice; 4. the mixing of the ballots; 5. the counting; 6. the publication of the scrutiny; 7. the threading of the ballots onto a string; 8. the separate depositing of them. Some remarks should be added on each of these acts.

units.la: LVI. Delatio schedulæ, & duo sequentes actus, qui ob eorum connexionem melius simul describuntur, hoc modo fiunt. Quilibet Cardinalis propriam schedulam, postquam illam scripsit, obsignavit & complicavit, duobus primis digitis sumit, ac elevatâ manu palam defert ad altare, penes quod stant scrutatores, & in quo est calix magnus ad recipiendas schedulas paratus, & patera coopertus, ibique genu flectens, aliquantulum orat, deinde surgens, altâ & intelligibili voce jurat in hanc formam, quæ in tabella super altari posità descripta habetur: Testor Christum Dominum, qui me judicaturus est, me eligere quem secundùm Deum judico eligi debere, & quod idem in accessu præstabo. Post hæc schedulam ponit in pateraм, & per pateraм mittit in calicem, quo facto inclinat se ad altare & ad suum locum revertitur.
units.tr: LVI. The delivery of the ballot, and the two following acts, which are better described together because they are connected, are done in this way. Each Cardinal, after he has written, sealed and folded his own ballot, takes it between the first two fingers, carries it openly with his hand raised to the altar, where the scrutineers stand and where a large chalice stands ready to receive the ballots, covered with a paten. There he kneels and prays briefly. Then, rising, he swears in a loud and clear voice in the form written on a tablet placed above the altar: I call Christ the Lord, who is to judge me, to witness that I choose the one whom I judge before God ought to be chosen, and that I will do the same at my approach. After this he places the ballot on the paten, sends it through the paten into the chalice, and then, bowing to the altar, returns to his place.

units.la: LVII. Hactenus recensita observantur, si Cardinalis ad altare pergere posset; nam si ob infirmam valetudinem non posset, & præsens in capella est, ultimus scrutator discum cum schedulis ad eum defert, ex quo Cardinalis infirmus, unam accipiens, eam in loco suo secretè, ut suprà dictum est, conficit; deinde prævio juramento prædicto schedulam obsignatam & complicatam eidem scrutatori tradit, qui eam palàm ad Altare & sine oratione & juramento in patinam ponit, & per eam in calicem mittit, quæ omnia observanda sunt per ultimum scrutatorem erga eos Cardinales, qui in Capellà præsentes ob valetudinem ad Altare pergere non possunt.
units.tr: LVII. The things recounted so far are observed if the Cardinal is able to go up to the altar. If, because of poor health, he cannot do so, but is present in the chapel, the last scrutineer brings a dish with the ballots to him. The sick Cardinal takes one ballot and prepares it secretly in his place, as said above. Then, after the aforesaid oath, he hands the sealed and folded ballot to the same scrutineer, who openly places it on the altar, without prayer or oath, on the paten, and sends it through the paten into the chalice. All these things are to be observed by the last scrutineer for those Cardinals who are present in the chapel but cannot go to the altar because of their health.

units.la: LVIII. Si verò aliqui Cardinales infirmi sunt in suis cellis, tres Cardinales Infirmarii, ut suprà, extracti ad eos accedunt cum capsula altitudine unius palmi, in cujus superiori parte est rima, seu foramen, ejus magnitudinis, ut per illud schedula complicata possit per suam latitudinem intus capsulam transmitti, quam capsulam, antequam scrutatores infirmariis tradant, palàm aperiunt, ut cæteri Cardinales possint eam inanem & vacuam conspicere, deinde claudunt & clavem ponunt super altare; Deinde InfirInfirmarii cum capsula clausa & cum parvo disco tot schedulas continente, quot sunt infirmi Cardinales, ad unumquemque eorum accedunt, & infirmi acceptas ex disco schedulas secretè scribunt, obsignant & complicant, & prævio juramento jam dicto, in capsulam per rimam mittunt. Quòd si infirmi scribere non possunt, alii eorum arbitrio deligendi præstito de secretè servando in manibus Infirmariorum juramento prædicta faciunt; Qui non solùm juramenti illius vinculo servare tenentur secretum, sed etiam, si contra faciant, in excommunicationem latæ sententiæ incurrunt. Hisperactis, Infirmarii ad Capellam cum capsula revertuntur, quam scrutatores aperiunt, & schedulas in ea contentas palàm numerant, & tot repertas, quot sunt infirmi, ponunt sigillatim in patinam & per patinam simul omnes in calicem. Ne autem nimis in longum pertrahatur scrutinii actio, Infirmarii possunt proprias schedulas statim post Decanum conficere & in calicem ponere, deinde dum cæteri Cardinales scrutinium agunt, ad Infirmos pergere ad accipienda eorum suffragia eo modo, quo diximus.
units.tr: LVIII. If some sick Cardinals are in their own cells, three Cardinal infirmarians, chosen as above, go to them with a box one palm high, in the upper part of which there is a slit or opening of such size that a folded ballot can be passed through it by its width. Before the scrutineers hand the box to the infirmarians, they open it openly so that the other Cardinals can see that it is empty, then they close it and place the key on the altar. Then the infirmarians, with the closed box and a small dish containing as many ballots as there are sick Cardinals, go to each of them. The sick Cardinals take a ballot from the dish, write it secretly, seal and fold it, and, after the oath already mentioned, put it through the slit into the box. But if a sick Cardinal cannot write, another, chosen at his discretion, does these things after swearing in the infirmarians' hands to keep the secret. Such persons are bound by the bond of that oath to keep the secret, and if they act against it, they incur excommunication latae sententiae. When this is done, the infirmarians return to the chapel with the box. The scrutineers open it, count openly the ballots found in it, and, as many as there are sick Cardinals, place them one by one on the paten and send them all together through the paten into the chalice. So that the scrutiny is not drawn out too long, the infirmarians may prepare their own ballots and place them in the chalice immediately after the Dean, and then, while the other Cardinals are carrying out the scrutiny, go to the sick to receive their votes in the way we have described.

units.la: LIX. Quartus actus scrutinii est schedularum permixtio: Quæ fit per primum scrutatorem, calice, in quo ipsæ schedulæ positæ fuerunt, patinâ cooperto, pluries agitato. Quintus actus est numeratio schedularum, quæ palàm fit per ultimum scrutatorem, capiendo sigillatim unamquamque schedularum ex calice, eúmque ponendo in alium, qui ad hoc paratus est, calicem vacuum. Quòd si numerus schedularum non respondeat numero Cardinalium, omnes comburendæ sunt, & iterum, id est, secundâ vice ad suffragia statim est deveniendum. Si verò numerus schedularum numero Cardinalium respondeat, prosequendi sunt alii actus scrutinii.
units.tr: LIX. The fourth act of the scrutiny is the mixing of the ballots: this is done by the first scrutineer, who, with the chalice in which the ballots were placed covered by the paten, shakes it many times. The fifth act is the counting of the ballots, which is done openly by the last scrutineer, who takes each ballot singly from the chalice and places it in another empty chalice prepared for this purpose. But if the number of ballots does not correspond to the number of Cardinals, all of them are to be burnt, and at once one must proceed again, that is, to a second vote on the suffrages. If, however, the number of ballots corresponds to the number of Cardinals, the other acts of the scrutiny are to be carried on.

units.la: LX. Sextus actus est publicatio scrutinii, quæ per scrutatores, qui sedent ad mensam ante altare positam, in hunc modum fit. Primus scrutator accipit unam schedam, eámque intactis sigillis explicat, & viso in ea schedula electi nomine, eam tradit secundo scrutatori, qui pariter eodem electi nomine perspecto, eandem tradit tertio, qui illam voce alta & intelligibili prælegit, ut omnes Cardinales præsentes notare possint suffragium in folio impresso, quod penes se habent cum nominibus omnium Cardinalium, notant autem juxta nomen Cardinalis ex schedula recitati. Idem fit de caeteris schedulis in calice positis usque ad ultimum; Quod si in scrutinii publicatione inveniunt scrutatores duas schedulas ita complicatas, ut ab uno tantum datas fuisse appareat, siquidem unus & idem in utraque electus fuerit, schedulae praedictae habentur & notantur pro uno suffragio, si vero diversi fuerint notati, neutrum suffragium juxta Bullam Gregorianam validum est. Scrutinium tamen neutro casu vitiatur. Caeterum suffragia praedicta possunt, finita scrutinii publicatione, a Patribus juxta nomina Cardinalium, qui ea obtinuerunt, in unam summam redigi, vel in separato folio ita notari: Reverendissimus D. Cardinalis A. habet suffragia 20. Reverendissimus D. Cardinalis B. habet suffragia 15. & sic de aliis; Quod fit, ne Cardinales, cum opus est, semper suffragia numerare cogantur, qui juxta nomina Cardinalium notârunt.
units.tr: LX. The sixth act is the publication of the scrutiny, which is done by the scrutineers, who sit at a table placed before the altar, in this manner. The first scrutineer takes one ballot and unfolds it with the seals intact; having seen in it the name of the person elected, he hands it to the second scrutineer, who likewise, having noted the name of the elect, hands it to the third. The third reads it aloud in a clear and intelligible voice, so that all the Cardinals present can mark the vote on the printed sheet they have, which bears the names of all the Cardinals; they mark the vote beside the name of the Cardinal read out from the ballot. The same is done with the other ballots placed in the chalice, down to the last. But if in the publication of the scrutiny the scrutineers find two ballots folded in such a way that they appear to have been given by one and the same person, and if one and the same person has been named in both, the ballots are regarded and noted as one vote. If, however, different persons were named, neither vote is valid according to the Bull of Gregory. Nevertheless, the scrutiny is not vitiated in either case. Moreover, after the publication of the scrutiny is finished, the Fathers may collect these votes into one sum according to the names of the Cardinals who obtained them, or note them on a separate sheet in this way: The Most Reverend Lord Cardinal A. has 20 votes. The Most Reverend Lord Cardinal B. has 15 votes. and so on for the others. This is done so that the Cardinals, when it is needed, are not always forced to count the votes again, since they have marked them beside the names of the Cardinals.

units.la: LXI. Septimus actus scrutinii est Schedularum in filum insertio, quae, ut schedulae ipsae cautius conservari possint, excogitata fuit.
units.tr: LXI. The seventh act of the scrutiny is the threading of the ballots onto a string, which was devised so that the ballots themselves might be kept more securely.

units.la: Haec autem insertio fit per ultimum scrutatorem, inserendo schedulam unamquamque, postquam eam perlegerit, acu cum filo ad hunc effectum parato, ubi est verbum Eligo. Octavus & postremus scrutinii actus est depositio schedularum seorsim, quae similiter fit per scrutatorem ultimum, qui finita insertione schedularum omnium in filum, capita fili nodo jungit, & schedulas omnes ita colligatas in alium vacuum, vel in mensa seorsim ponit.
units.tr: This threading is done by the last scrutineer, who passes each ballot, after reading it through, onto a thread with a needle prepared for this purpose, at the place where the word Eligo is. The eighth and last act of the scrutiny is the separate depositing of the ballots, which is likewise done by the last scrutineer. When all the ballots have been threaded, he ties the ends of the thread together with a knot and places the bound ballots in another empty vessel or sets them apart on a table.

units.la: LXII. Tradenda jam esset tertia totius actionis pars, quae nomine Postscrutinii venit, & cujus actus, si electio per scrutinium secuta fit, tres tantum sunt.
units.tr: LXII. We should now set out the third part of the whole proceeding, which goes by the name of Postscrutiny. If the election is secured by scrutiny, it has only three acts.

units.la: Videlicet 1. Numeratio schedularum 2. Cognitio suffragiorum & 3. Schedularum combustio. Qui tamen optime ex iis, quae de actibus compluribus Accessum proximè excipientibus dicenda erunt, cognosci poterunt.
