units.tr: These are: 1. The counting of the ballots, 2. The reading of the votes, and 3. The burning of the ballots. These can best be understood from what will be said about the several acts that immediately follow the accession (Accessus).

units.la: LXIII. Accessus, secunda per Cardinales solos eligendi forma, sive, si quis malit, scrutinium compositum, multa habet cum scrutinio simplici, quoad schedularum scriptionem, obsignationem, complicationem, delationem, positionem in calicem, numerationem, publicationem, suffragiorum notationem & insertionem in filum ac depositionem seorsum, communia, atque adhiberi solet immediatè post scrutinium, si in eo Papa creatus non fuerit. LXIV. Rarissimè autem in ipso scrutinio electio perficitur. Aliquando quidem adeò felices fuerunt Electores isti, ex gra. quando post Martini V. mortem an. 1421. Cardinales, licet paulò ante respectu duorum aliorum divisi, Conclave cum unanimi sententia, Cardinalem Condulmariam, qui electus nomen Eugenii IV. assumpsit, creandi, ingressi sunt, eúmque etiam in primo scrutinio, tribus tantùm votis alió directis, creárunt. Sic & mortuo Leone X. an.1522. quamvis post longas disceptationes, quibus necessarius Medicæi abitus finem imposuisse in Conclavi dicitur, Adrianus VI. in Cardinalismo p. 3. l. 2. p. 248. 249. & Vita di Sisto V. p. 1. l. V. p. 410. in simplici, sed nono demum scrutinio, quod simplex fuisse, citati Authores, vel citati libri, citatus Author, volunt, delectus fuisse dicitur; sed per accessum electum fuisse Adrianum illum & non in scrutinio simplici, non tantùm ex Conclavi, verùm etiam ex ipso Cardinalismi Authore p.3.l.2.p.157. qui proin quoad illud sibi contradicere videtur, constat, dum cum Conclavi consentiens, Adrianum in ultimo scrutinio 15. Oftiensem autem 14. vota habuisse, sed postea plures Adriano accessisse, tradit. Interim de illa electione Adriani per scrutinium simplex pronunciat Il Card. l. c. Venne ad essere stimata, come una cosa non più successa un puro miracolo. Inaudita res existimabatur & miraculosa. Vita di Sisto V. loc. c. de electione per scrutinium simplex, per dire à vero, questo arriva tanto raramente, che quasi sene perde hormai la memoria. Id est; Ut verum dicam, hoc rarò accidit, ut memoria quasi perierit. Et de electione Adriani in specie: Da molti venne giudicata una cosa più tosto miracolosa che altra opera humana. Id est: A multis existimabatur res potius miraculosa, quàm verò opera humana. Ubi tamen juxta Conclave & ipsum Authorem Cardinalismi l. c. nihil minùs quàm miracula, humana omnia distinctè apparent.
units.tr: LXIII. The accession, the second form of election by the Cardinals alone, or, if anyone prefers, the compound scrutiny, has much in common with the simple scrutiny: the writing, sealing, folding, carrying, placing in the chalice, counting, publishing, noting of votes, and threading and separate depositing of the ballots are the same. It is usually held immediately after the scrutiny, if no Pope has been created in it. LXIV. But the election is very rarely completed in the scrutiny itself. Indeed, the electors were sometimes so fortunate that, for example, after the death of Martin V in 1421, the Cardinals, although shortly before they had been divided between two others, entered the conclave with unanimous agreement to create Cardinal Condulmer, who took the name Eugenius IV on his election; they created him in the first scrutiny, with only three votes going elsewhere. Likewise, when Leo X died in 1522, although after long disputes, which are said to have been ended by the necessary departure of the Medici in the Conclave, Adrian VI was said to have been chosen in a simple scrutiny, but only in the ninth scrutiny; the cited authors, or the cited books, or the cited author, say that this was a simple scrutiny. But that Adrian was chosen by accession and not in a simple scrutiny is clear not only from the Conclave but also from the author of the Cardinalismo himself, p. 3, l. 2, p. 157, who seems to contradict himself on this point. For while agreeing with the Conclave, he reports that Adrian had 15 votes in the last scrutiny and the Cardinal of Ostia 14, but that afterwards several more came to Adrian by accession. Meanwhile, concerning that election of Adrian by simple scrutiny, he says: Il Card. l. c. It came to be esteemed as a thing that had never happened before, a pure miracle. Inaudita res existimabatur & miraculosa. Vita di Sisto V. loc. c. Concerning election by simple scrutiny, to tell the truth, this happens so rarely that its memory is almost lost. That is: To tell the truth, this rarely happens, so that its memory has almost perished. And concerning Adrian's election in particular: By many it was judged a thing more miraculous than any human work. That is: By many the thing was esteemed more miraculous than a true human work. Yet here, according to the Conclave and the author of the Cardinalismo himself, l. c., nothing less than miracles appears; everything is plainly human.

units.la: LXV. Multùm similis est accessus antiquæ Senatûs Romani consuetudini, quâ Senatores nonnunquam, relictâ priori sententiâ, ab alio propositam amplectebantur, & ad significandum hoc vel è loco suo versus Authorem sententiæ à priori sua diversæ ibant, vel simpliciter assurgentes altâ voce dicebant; accedo ad talem, ut etiam fieri solet in Conclavi, unde quoque nata est frequens apud Authores Latinos phrasis; ire in sententiam alicujus. Actus autem accessûs Conclavistici sunt septem, videlicet 1. Accessus ipse 2. Sigillorum & signorum, aperitio. 3. Eorum annotatio. 4. Suffragiorum examen. 5. Suffragiorum scrutinium, vel scrutinii & accessûs numeratio. 6. Eorum recognitio, & 7. Schedularum combustio.
units.tr: LXV. The accession is very like the ancient custom of the Roman Senate, by which senators sometimes abandoned their earlier opinion and adopted one proposed by another. To signify this, they either moved from their place toward the author of the opinion that differed from their former one, or simply rose and said aloud: I accede to such a one, as is also commonly done in the Conclave. From this also comes the frequent phrase in Latin authors, to go over to someone's opinion. The acts of the conclavist accession are seven: 1. the accession itself; 2. the opening of the seals and signs; 3. their noting; 4. the examination of the votes; 5. the scrutiny of the votes, or the counting of the scrutiny and the accession; 6. their recognition; and 7. the burning of the ballots.

units.la: LXVI.
units.tr: LXVI.

units.la: Quoad antecedentia & actum primum sequentes differentiae inter scrutinium simplex & accessum deprehenduntur; Primò quòd Cardinales schedulas pro accessu sumunt ex alio disco sive bacili, quàm ex quo sumserunt schedulas pro scrutinio; Secundò loco verborum in facie sive anteriori parte schedulae scrutinii: Eligo &c. in schedula accessûs, facie sive anteriore parte impressum est vel scribitur: Accedo Reverendissimo Domino meo D. Cardin. Tertiò in schedularum accessûs scriptione, si Cardinalis nemini velit accedere, in media schedulae parte, loco nominis Cardinalis, qui scribendus esset, si ad eum fieret accessus, scribere solet: nemini. Quales nemini in Conclavi Alexandri VII. numero ad tempus constanti viginti & trium Hispani crediti fuerunt, ed havessero il Nemini per segno della loro unione, si che le speranze di Sacchetti cadevano par terra, essendo irremediabile la caduta. Et usi sunt voce Nemini tanquam signo confœderationis suæ, ita ut spes Sacchetti in terram ceciderit, cùm lapsus immedicabilis fuerit. Quem proin Nemo perdidit, vel Nemini. Quartò non potest accessus fieri ad eum Cardinalem, qui in scrutinio saltem unum suffragium non obtinuerit. (Quidam volunt dicere, apud Ant. de Rosellis Mon. p.2. cap.9. quòd accessioni locus sit demum, quando electus habuit saltem majorem partem Cardinalium, per tex. d. c. licet ibi nisi major concordia) Ut debeat esse accessus etiam ratione voti in scrutinio prius obtenti, neque ad eum, qui ab ipsomet Cardinali fuit in scrutinio nominatus; ut olim non dabatur in senatu accessus ad priorem suam sententiam; Sed ut ibi fuit sententiae mutatio, ita & heic esse debet, quamvis temerarium & parum à perjurio remotum videri possit, nullis intervenientibus persuasionibus & majoris dignationis documentis, alium statim, & quidem ferè ordinariò praeferre ei, quem quis paulò ante tanquam optimum eligendum esse censuerat. Quintò, quamvis in accessu non liceat plures nominare, sicut non licet in scrutinio plures eligere sub poena nullitatis suffragii, tam in accessu quàm in scrutinio; licèt A. de Rosellis l. c. p.337. statuat, regulariter Cardinales eligere sub conditione, ut, eligo talem, si talis non erit, eligo talem, vel alternativè, consentio in talem, vel in talem, juxta glo. in c. 2. de elect. 16 in verbo alternativa; non item; eligo, quem eligat talis Cardinalis; nihilominùs licet accedere uni ex pluribus nulliter à se nominatis in scrutinio, dummodò ei ab alio aliquod suffragium, non tamen nulliter, ut praefertur, in ipso scrutinio datum fuerit. Imò necessariò alii, quàm quem quis in scrutinio elegerat, accedendum esse ex dictis patet. Sextò in accessu non præstatur juramentum, de quo supra, quia jam in scrutinio præstitum fuit, per illa verba: Et quod idem etiam præstabo in accessu; subintelleċto, si ad eum devenire necessum sit. Septimò Infirmarii deferunt ad infirmos schedulas accessûs, & simul etiam folium impressum, in quo sit notatus suffragiorum numerus palàm recognitus, quem quisque Cardinalium inscrutinio nominatus obtinuerit. Illud quoque notandum est probè, debere schedulam accessûs scribi & obsignari cum eisdem sigillis & signis schedulæ scrutinii sub pœnâ nullitatis suffragii ipsius accessûs.
units.tr: As to what precedes and the first act, the following differences between the simple scrutiny and the accession are found. First, the Cardinals take the ballots for the accession from a different dish or basin than the one from which they took the ballots for the scrutiny. Second, in place of the words I elect, &c., which are printed or written on the front or upper side of the scrutiny ballot, the front side of the accession ballot has printed or written: I accede to my Most Reverend Lord, Cardinal N. Third, in writing the accession ballot, if a Cardinal does not wish to accede to anyone, he usually writes in the middle of the ballot, in place of the name of the Cardinal who would have been written had the accession been made to him, the word nemini (to no one). Such nemini in the conclave of Alexander VII, when twenty-three Spaniards were counted for a time, were believed to have written nemini as a sign of their union, so that the hopes of Sacchetti fell to the ground, the fall being irremediable. And they used the word Nemini as a sign of their confederacy, so that the hope of Sacchetti fell to the ground, since the fall was incurable. Hence Nemo or Nemini ruined him. Fourth, an accession cannot be made to a Cardinal who has not obtained at least one vote in the scrutiny. (Some wish to say, according to Antonius de Rosellis, Mon. p. 2, cap. 9, that accession has place only when the one elected has had at least a majority of the Cardinals, by the text of the chapter licet, where it says, unless there is a greater agreement.) So that there ought to be an accession also by reason of a vote previously obtained in the scrutiny, and not to the one whom the Cardinal himself nominated in the scrutiny; just as formerly there was no accession in the Senate to one's own earlier opinion. But as there was a change of opinion there, so there should be here, although it may seem rash and not far removed from perjury, when no persuasions or documents of greater weight have intervened, to prefer at once, and indeed almost ordinarily, another to the one whom one had a little earlier judged should be elected as the best. Fifth, although in an accession it is not lawful to nominate several, just as it is not lawful in a scrutiny to elect several under penalty of nullity of the vote, both in accession and in scrutiny; yet Antonius de Rosellis, l. c. p. 337, lays down that Cardinals ordinarily elect under a condition, such as, I elect such a one, if such a one shall not be, I elect such a one; or alternatively, I consent to such a one or such a one, according to the gloss on c. 2, de elect., in the word alternativa; but not: I elect whom such a Cardinal elects. Nevertheless, it is lawful to accede to one of several whom he has nullly nominated in the scrutiny, provided that some other vote, not however null, as has been said, was given to him in that same scrutiny. Indeed, it is clear from what has been said that the accession must necessarily be to someone other than the one whom one elected in the scrutiny. Sixth, in an accession no oath is taken, of which we spoke above, because it was already taken in the scrutiny, by those words: And that I will do the same in the accession; it being understood, if it is necessary to come to that. Seventh, the infirmarians carry the accession ballots to the sick, together with a printed sheet in which is noted the number of votes openly recognized that each Cardinal nominated in the scrutiny has obtained. This also must be carefully noted: that the accession ballot ought to be written and sealed with the same seals and signs as the scrutiny ballot, under penalty of nullity of that accession vote.

units.la: LXVII. Secundus, tertius & quartus actus post scrutinii, accedente & numerato etiam accessu sunt sigillorum aperitio, eorum annotatio & suffragiorum examen:
units.tr: LXVII. The second, third and fourth acts after the scrutiny, once the access has been received and counted, are the opening of the seals, their recording, and the examination of the votes:

units.la: qui actus tum solùm locum habent, quando secuta est electio per scrutinium & accessum, & fiunt hoc modo: Primus scrutator schedulas accessuum, quos obtinuit electus, in ea parte solùm, quæ signa continet, aperit, & inspectis diligenter eorum sigillis & signis, apertas ac in filo, ut erant, insertas tradit secuudo scrutatori, & secundus, eadem inspectione factâ, porrigit tertio, qui altâ & intelligibili voce sigilla & signa prædictarum schedularum enuntiat & annotat in latere sinistro folii impressi ad hunc effectum parati, sub verbis (sigilla & signa Accessuum) quam etiam annotationem faciunt cæteri Cardinales, si velint in simili folio impresso. De quo tamen Vita di Sisto V. p.r.l.5. p.410. notat; Che ogni Cardinale nota i suoi voti, ma non gia quelli del compagno, è per lo piu se ne trovano di quelli, che non hanno la briga di notare; quem-vis Cardinalem sua vota numerare, sed non aliorum, atque plerunque non eos cupidinem notandi urgere.
units.tr: These acts take place only when an election has followed through the scrutiny and the access, and they are carried out as follows. The first scrutineer opens the schedules of the accesses that the elected candidate obtained, only in the part that contains the seals and signs. After carefully inspecting their seals and signs, he hands them, still opened and inserted in the thread as they were, to the second scrutineer. The second scrutineer, after making the same inspection, passes them to the third, who in a loud and clear voice announces the seals and signs of these schedules and records them on the left side of the printed sheet prepared for this purpose, under the words seals and signs of the accesses. The other Cardinals also make this record on a similar printed sheet, if they wish. Yet the Life of Sixtus V, p.r.l.5. p.410., notes on this point: Every Cardinal records his own votes, but not those of his companion; for the most part there are some who take no trouble to record them. Whatever Cardinal wishes may count his own votes, but not those of others, and usually there is no strong urge to record them.

units.la: LXVIII. Deinde primus scrutator, reliquis scrutatoribus inspicientibus, pro accessuum prædictorum examine capit schedulas scrutinii, & incipiens ab uno capite fili, in quo insertę sunt, sigillum primę ejus schedulæ quærit insigillis accessuum notatis, ut supra in folio impresso, & si illud in eo non invenerit, omissâ primâ scrutinii schedulâ, capit secundam ejusque sigillum similiter quærit, quod si etiam non invenerit, capit tertium & deinde sequentes sigillatim, donec sigillum alicujus earum inveniat; eóque invento, scrutinii schedulam in eâ parte, ubi signa sunt, aperit, & si non invenerit signa hujus schedulæ concordare cum signis accessûs, schedulam illam Secundus, tertius & quartus actus post scrutinii, accedente & numerato etiam accessu. Examinatio. illam omittit, & aliam capit, sicut paulò ante de schedulis non concordantibus in sigillo dictum est; si invenerit signa concordare, ostendit illa secundo & tertio, scrutatoribus, qui unà cum ipso, post diligens examen super identitate sigillorum & signorum ambarum schedularum, scrutinii scilicet & accessus, inspiciunt, an idem, vel diversi in utraque schedula sint nominati; & si idem nominatus sit, suffragium accessus nullum censetur; si verò diversi nominati sunt, suffragium accessus pro valido habetur, & hoc casu tertius scrutator sigillum & signa schedulae scrutinii, ac etiam nomen electi, qui in eâ continetur, altâ & intelligibili voce enunciat, & annotat in latere dextro prædicti folii impressi, sub verbis (sigilla & signa scrutinii respondentia accessibus) notat autem ex adverso accessus concordantis in sigillo & signis: quam annotationem caeteri quoque Cardinales, si voluerint, in simili folio impresso faciunt.
units.tr: LXVIII. Then the first scrutineer, while the other scrutineers look on, takes the schedules of the scrutiny for the examination of the aforesaid accesses. Beginning at one end of the thread on which they are inserted, he seeks the seal of the first schedule among the seals of the accesses recorded on the printed sheet. If he does not find it there, he sets aside the first scrutiny schedule, takes the second, and looks for its seal in the same way. If he does not find that one either, he takes the third and then the following ones one by one, until he finds the seal of one of them. When he has found it, he opens the scrutiny schedule in the part where the signs are. If he finds that its signs do not agree with the signs of the access, he omits that schedule and takes another, just as has been said a little earlier about schedules whose seals do not agree. If he finds that the signs agree, he shows the schedules to the second and third scrutineers. Together with him, they examine carefully the identity of the seals and signs of both schedules, that of the scrutiny and that of the access, and see whether the same or different persons are named in each schedule. If the same person is named, the vote of the access is considered null. If different persons are named, the vote of the access is held to be valid. In this case the third scrutineer announces, in a loud and clear voice, the seal and signs of the scrutiny schedule, together with the name of the elected candidate contained in it, and records them on the right side of the aforesaid printed sheet, under the words (seals and signs of the scrutiny corresponding to the accesses). Opposite this he notes the access that agrees in seal and signs. The other Cardinals also make this record on a similar printed sheet, if they wish.

units.la: LXIX. Exemplum hujus actus ad faciliorem intellectum ex Ceremoniali Conclavis Gregorii XV. ex quo etiam pleraque excerpsimus hactenus de scrutinio & accessu dicta, subjungere visum est hocce, in quo Literae Alphabethi, sigilla, verba, Deus &c. Signa sive Symbola indicant.
units.tr: LXIX. To make this act easier to understand, I have thought it fitting to add the following example, taken from the Ceremonial of the Conclave of Gregory XV, from which I have drawn most of what has been said so far about the scrutiny and the access. In it, the letters, seals, words, God and so on, indicate the signs or symbols.

units.la: Sigilla & signa Accessuum. | Sigilla & signa scrutinii Accessibus respondentia. | Cardinales nominati in scrutinio. ACD. 43. Deus, | BRF. 32. Bonitas. | B R F. Bonitas. | Card. S. Eusebii. R G J. 50. Beatitudo. | RGJ.50 Beatitudo. | Card. S. Sixti. NSP. 26. Gloria.
units.tr: Seals and signs of the Accesses. | Seals and signs of the scrutiny corresponding to the Accesses. | Cardinals named in the scrutiny. ACD. 43. God, | BRF. 32. Goodness. | B R F. Goodness. | Cardinal of S. Eusebius. R G J. 50. Blessedness. | RGJ.50 Blessedness. | Cardinal of S. Sixtus. NSP. 26. Glory.

units.la: LXX. Quod si fortasse in ista inquisitione contingat, duas vel plures schedulas scrutinii reperiri cum eisdem sigillis & signis alicujus schedulae accessûs, tunc si in earum aliqua electus nominatus fuerit, in alia verò alius, primus scrutator, reliquis scrutatoribus similiter inspicientibus, scrutinii, schedulas ejusmodi & schedulam accessûs in ea etiam parte, in qua est nomen eligentis & accedentis, aperit, ut constare possit secundùm Gregorianam constitutionem de validitate vel invaliditate accessûs; si verò in aliqua hujusmodi schedularum scrutinii concordantium dantium cum accessu non sit nominatus electus, eæ schedulæ omit-tuntur, & ad subsequentes proceditur.
units.tr: LXX. If it happens in this inquiry that two or more scrutiny schedules are found bearing the same seals and signs as one access schedule, then, if the elected candidate is named in one of them and someone else in another, the first scrutineer, with the other scrutineers likewise looking on, opens these scrutiny schedules and the access schedule in the part that contains the name of the elector and the one elected. In this way it can be established, according to the Gregorian constitution, whether the access is valid or invalid. If, however, the elected candidate is not named in any of these scrutiny schedules that agree with the access, those schedules are omitted and the process moves on to the following ones.

units.la: LXXI. Quintus actus post scrutinii est numeratio suffragiorum, vel scrutinii, vel scrutinii & accessus, quæ fit per scrutatores semper, sive secuta sit electio, sive non: Si quidem secuta non sit electio, ut sciatur, quòd in eo scrutinio, vel scrutinio & accessu, non habetur Papa, si verò secuta sit, ut constet de Canonica Pontificis electione; ita autem fit hæc suffragiorum numeratio: Scrutatores in unam summam redigunt suffragia, quæ quilibet nominatus in Pontificem obtinuit, sive in scrutinio solo, sive in scrutinio & accessu simul, & si invenerint, nullum ex nominatis ad duas tertias partes suffragiorum pervenisse, non habetur Papa in illo scrutinio, sive scrutinio & accessu, si verò invenerint aliquem ex nominatis duas tantùm partes obtinuisse, aperiunt electi schedulam, etiam in ea parte, in qua est nomen eligentis; Et si quidem ex ea apparuerit, electum alii suffragatum fuisse, electio ejus est Canonica; si verò constiterit, sibi suffragium dedisse, ejus electio ex dispositione Gregorianæ constitutionis nulla est ob defectum unius suffragii, si denique plures invenerint, duas tertias partes suffragiorum obtinuisse, vel etiam ultra duas tertias, tunc suffragiorum paritate nullus est electus, in imparitate verò ille est Canonicus Papa, qui superat alium etiam in uno suffragio.
units.tr: LXXI. The fifth act after the scrutiny is the counting of the votes, of the scrutiny alone or of the scrutiny and the access together. It is always carried out by the scrutineers, whether or not an election has followed. If no election has followed, it is done so that it may be known that in that scrutiny, or in that scrutiny and access, there is no Pope. If an election has followed, it is done so that it may be established that the election of the Pontiff was canonical. The counting of votes is done in this way. The scrutineers add up the votes that each named candidate obtained for the papacy, whether in the scrutiny alone or in the scrutiny and access together. If they find that no one named has reached two thirds of the votes, there is no Pope in that scrutiny, or in that scrutiny and access. If, however, they find that one of the named candidates has obtained only two thirds, they open the schedule of the elected candidate, in the part that contains the name of the elector as well. If it appears from it that the candidate gave his vote to another, his election is canonical. If it is established that he gave his vote to himself, his election is null under the provisions of the Gregorian constitution, because of the lack of a single vote. Finally, if they find that several candidates have obtained two thirds of the votes, or even more than two thirds, then, where the votes are equal, no one is elected; where there is inequality, he is the canonical Pope who surpasses the other even by a single vote.

units.la: LXXII. Sextus actus post scrutinii est Recognitio, quæ per Recognitores, sive secuta sit electio, sive non, fieri solet; inspiciendo tam schedulas scrutinii & accessûs, quàm suffragiorum annotationes factas per scrutatores, ut per hujusmodi recognitionem constare possit, an scrutatores sincerè & fideliter muneri suo satisfecerint. Recognitores autem extrahuntur sorte, ut scrutatores & Infirmarii, statim quidem post scrutinium, si secuta sit in eo electio, si verò non sit secuta, post scrutinium & accessum, cùm scilicet scrutatores impleverint numerum per numerationem suffragiorum.
units.tr: LXXII. The sixth act after the scrutiny is the recognition, which is usually carried out by the recognizers, whether or not an election has followed. They inspect the schedules of the scrutiny and of the access, as well as the records of the votes made by the scrutineers. By such recognition it can be established whether the scrutineers have discharged their duty sincerely and faithfully. The recognizers are chosen by lot, as the scrutineers and the infirmarians are. This is done immediately after the scrutiny if an election has followed in it, but if none has followed, after the scrutiny and the access, that is, when the scrutineers have completed the number of votes by counting them.

units.la: LXXIII. Septimus & postremus actus post scrutinii est combustio omnium schedularum, quæ semper, & palàm per scrutatores fit, ac statim post recognitionem, sive Electio sit secuta, sive non. Et hæc omnia, quæ de scrutinii ritibus expositai sunt, servari debent diligenter à Cardinalibus in omnibus scrutiniis, sive fiant manè post Missam, sive vesperè post Hymnum, (Veni creator Spiritus) Spiritus) bis autem in die uno ut fiant, per Bullam Gregorii XV. haud licet, & quidem sub excommunicationis poena illud vetuit.
units.tr: LXXIII. The seventh and last act after the scrutiny is the burning of all the schedules. It is always done openly by the scrutineers, immediately after the recognition, whether or not an election has followed. All these things that have been set out concerning the rites of the scrutiny must be observed carefully by the Cardinals in every scrutiny, whether they are held in the morning after Mass or in the evening after the hymn (Come, Creator Spirit). Gregory XV's Bull does not allow them to be held twice in one day, and it forbids this under penalty of excommunication.

units.la: LXXIV. Ex dictis constat, quàm solicitè ambitionis humanae machinationibus in electione successorum occurrere voluerint Pontifices nonnulli, quàm omnia minima etiam definiri, fraudi undiquaque aditum praecludi necesse fuerit; Interim memoratos eligendi modos naevis adhuc dum in praxi pluribus scatere, fraudes saepe intervenire, quos proin praevenire voluisse frustraneum prorsus fuerit, scrutinium ab una parte simplicem ceremoniam esse, & aliunde plane vim electionis hodie dependere, ab altera tamen parte diuturnitatis Conclavium causam & pertinaciae instrumentum esse, ex sequenti nostra de naevis electionum tractatione patebit, ut spero, luculentissimè. LXXV. Jam autem pergimus ad tertiam per solos Cardinales eligendi formam, quae per adorationem, vel per inspirationem, seu, ut in sacris Canonibus scriptum esse Gregor. XV. in Ceremoniali Conclavis perhibet, quasi per inspirationem. Quas, autem illud hic minimè superfluum esse sequentia docebunt. De illa autem electionis quasi per inspirationem, scilicet Spiritus S. forma sequentia Gregorius idem ibidem habet; in eo consistere, quòd omnes Cardinales, quasi afflati Spiritu S. aliquem unanimiter & vivâ voce summum Pontificem proclamant. Sequentia autem circa istam formam notari debere, monet. Primò posse praedicari solùm in Conclavi & eo clauso. Secundò debere fieri ab omnibus & singulis Cardinalibus in Conclavi praesentibus. Tertiò communiter, & nemine eorum dissentiente. Quartò nullo praecedente de persona speciali tractatu, & per verbum (eligo) intelligibili voce prolatum, aut scripto expressum, si voce non possit proferri; Exemplum autem suppeditant in hunc modum: Si aliquis Patrum, clauso Conclavi, nullo, ut praefertur,) speciali tractatu, diceret: Reverendissimi; perspectâ singulari virtute & probitate Reverendissimi N. judicarem illum eligendum esse in summum Pontificem, & ex nunc ego ipsum eligo in Papam. Deinde si, hoc audito, caeteri Patres, nemine excepto, sequentes primi sententiam eodem verbo (eligo) intelligibili voce prolato, aut si non potest, in scriptis expresso, eundem N. de quo nullus specialis tractatus praecessit, communiter eligerent, ipse N. esset Canonicè electus & verus Papa. Per adorationem autem id fieri dicitur, quia vocem gestus adorationis & profundae inclinationis comitatur, vel statim excipit, quâ tamen appellatione per adorationem Gregorius non utitur.
units.tr: LXXIV. From what has been said it is clear how carefully some Popes have wished to guard against the schemes of human ambition in the election of successors, and how necessary it was to define even the smallest matters and to close every avenue to fraud. Meanwhile, the aforesaid modes of election still abound in practice with many blemishes, and frauds often intervene, and it would be utterly pointless to try to forestall them in advance. On the one hand, the scrutiny is a mere ceremony, while on the other hand the real force of the election today depends elsewhere. Yet on the other hand, the length of the Conclaves and the instrument of obstinacy are at stake, as I hope will be made very clear in our following treatment of the blemishes of elections. LXXV. Now we proceed to the third form of election by the Cardinals alone, which takes place by adoration, or by inspiration, or, as Gregory XV says in the Ceremonial of the Conclave, as it is written in the sacred canons, as if by inspiration. The following will show that this is by no means superfluous here. Concerning this form of election as if by inspiration, namely the form of the Holy Spirit, Gregory himself says the following in the same place: it consists in this, that all the Cardinals, as if inspired by the Holy Spirit, unanimously proclaim someone as supreme Pontiff with a living voice. He advises that the following points should be noted about this form. First, it can be declared only in the Conclave and when it is closed. Second, it must be done by all and each of the Cardinals present in the Conclave. Third, it must be done in common, with none of them dissenting. Fourth, it must be done without any previous special discussion about the person, and expressed by the word (I elect), uttered in an intelligible voice, or written down if it cannot be spoken. He gives an example in this way: if one of the Fathers, with the Conclave closed and with no special discussion, as has been said, were to say: Most Reverend Lords, having observed the singular virtue and integrity of the Most Reverend N., I judge that he should be elected supreme Pontiff, and from now on I elect him as Pope. Then, if the other Fathers, none excepted, following the first one's opinion, were to elect the same N., about whom no special discussion had preceded, in common, by uttering the same word (I elect) in an intelligible voice, or if that is not possible, expressing it in writing, then N. himself would be canonically elected and a true Pope. It is said that this is done by adoration because the voice is accompanied by, or immediately followed by, a gesture of adoration and deep bowing. Gregory, however, does not use this term, by adoration.

units.la: LXXVI. Ex dictis evidenter apparet, juxta Gregorium, per adorationem, sive quasi per inspirationem Papam eligi debere communi omnium & singulorum Cardinalium præsentium consensu, nec hic sufficere duas tertias. Quod & convenit cum verbis Cardinalis Rhotomagensis in Conclavi Pii III. prolatis, cùm enim Author Conclavis, (qui proin Cardinalis etiam fuit, & quidem ex præcipuis) postquam cantâsset Missam Spiritûs S. Cardinalibus diceret, che poiche erano d'accordo, era bene facessero l'elettione per via dello Spirito Santo; Id est; quia concordes sint, commodè adhiberi posse electionem Spiritûs S. respondit ille; Electionem per viam Spiritûs S. esse periculosam, cùm, contradicente vel uno, electio sit nulla, che l'eleggere per via dello Spirito Santo era periculoso, perche contradicendo un solo l'elettione era nulla. Et tamen Onuphrius Annot. ad Clem. V. Plat. adorationem justam 2. partium pronuntiat, & Authores recentiores, nempe Il Cardinalismo p. 3. l. 2. p. 249. 250. & Vita di Sisto V. p. 1. l. 5. p. 411. ita de electione per adorationem loquuntur, ut expressè dicant, sufficere in ea quoque forma duas tertias, & tunc demum electionem talem nullam esse, si aliquis contradicat ex duabus tertiis. Quemadmodum certè etiam exemplum Sixti V. quod Gregorius Læti in vita cit. describit in casu adorationis per omnes & singulos faciendæ Fautoribus impossibile videri potuisset, cùm habuerit aliquo modo inimicos, quidam etiam fraudibus circumventi in Capellam perducti fuerint.
units.tr: LXXVI. From what has been said it is clearly evident that, according to Gregorius, the Pope must be elected by adoration, or as it were by inspiration, with the common consent of all and each of the cardinals present, and that two thirds are not sufficient here. This agrees with the words of the Cardinal of Rouen spoken at the conclave of Pius III. For when the author of the conclave (who was therefore also a cardinal, and indeed one of the leading ones), after he had sung the Mass of the Holy Spirit, said to the cardinals since they were agreed, it would be well for them to make the election by way of the Holy Spirit; that is, since they are of one mind, the election by the Spirit of the Holy Spirit can conveniently be employed, the other replied: an election by way of the Holy Spirit is dangerous, since, if even one dissents, the election is void; to elect by way of the Holy Spirit was dangerous, because if a single one dissented the election was void. Yet Onuphrius, in his Annotations on Clement V, Platina, declares that adoration rightly requires two parts, and the more recent authors, namely Il Cardinalismo, part 3, book 2, pp. 249 and 250, and Life of Sixtus V, part 1, book 5, p. 411, speak of election by adoration in such a way that they expressly say two thirds suffice in this form also, and that such an election is then void only if someone dissents from the two thirds. Indeed, the example of Sixtus V, which Gregorio Leti describes in the work cited, could certainly have seemed impossible in the case of adoration to be performed by all and each of the supporters, since he had enemies in some way, and some men were brought into the chapel having been taken in by fraud.

units.la: LXXVII. Ut verum fatear, ista de numero ad adorationem requisito differentia satis ponderosa mihi jam cogitationes de diversis adorationis & inspirationis formis, adeóque de quinta forma per solos Cardinales suggessit, quia videbam Gregorium, qui omnium & singulorum ad electionem per quasi inspirationem concursum requirit, vocabulo adorationis neque in Bulla, neque in Cæremoniali uti, illos contrà, qui de duabus tertiis hic sufficientibus loquuntur, nominatos authores, nomen inspirationis, vel quasi inspirationis in descriptione non adhibere. Intercessit tamen tandem Author Vitæ Sixti V. his verbis post descriptionem demum positis: Questo modo di eleggere il Papa per via d' improvisa adoratione, se bene da molti anni in dietro era stato chiamato d'alcuni la vera via dell' inspiratione Divina &c. Id est: Hic modus Papam eligendis gendi per improvisam adorationem licet à multis abhinc annis à quibusdam vocatus sit vera via inspirationis Spiritus S. &c. Ubi illi ipsi eligendi per adorationem modo, ad quem duas tertias sufficere jam dixerat, à longo tempore nomen inspirationis divinae tributum fuisse agnovit. Ut & ad cogitationes illas meas supprimendas haud parum juvit, quòd viam adorationis per duas tertias & inspirationis per omnes & singulos à nullo Authorum tanquam diversas tradi incidit.
units.tr: LXXVII. To tell the truth, this difference concerning the number required for adoration weighed on me enough to suggest to me thoughts about the different forms of adoration and inspiration, and hence about a fifth form, by the cardinals alone, because I saw that Gregorius, who requires the concurrence of all and each for election by a kind of inspiration, does not use the term adoration either in the Bull or in the Ceremonial, whereas the authors named, who speak of two thirds sufficing here, do not use the name inspiration, or quasi-inspiration, in their description. Yet the author of the Life of Sixtus V at last intervened, placing these words after the description: This manner of electing the Pope by unexpected adoration, although for many years past it has been called by some the true way of divine inspiration, etc. That is: This mode of electing the Pope by unexpected adoration, although by many for some years past called by some the true way of the Holy Spirit's inspiration, etc. There he acknowledged that the very mode of election by adoration, to which he had already said two thirds suffice, had for a long time been given the name of divine inspiration. And it helped not a little to suppress those thoughts of mine that none of the authors handed down the way of adoration by two thirds and that of inspiration by all and each as diverse.

units.la: LXXVIII. Oportet igitur, ut vel errent Authores isti, vel, Author iste si idem utrumque tractatum, ut verisimile mihi videtur, dederit, dum dicitur duas tertias sufficere, veterem rigorem tempore Sixti V. forte relaxatum, à Gregorio XV. reductum esse, vel hunc diversam ab adoratione, quam dicti libri exhibent, formam tradere. Diversam autem, quae legitima & aliquando exercita sit, tradere, ex dictis vix verisimile relinquitur; Eum, ut & authores illos in assignando necessario numero errâsse, pronunciare non audeo, quando iis moderni Conclavium Authores non obscurè adstipulantur; Cùm enim e. g. in Conclavi Clementis VIII. S. Severina ferè à 35. per adorationem electus esset, unicum votum ad constituendum numerum 36. id est, duarum tertiarum defuisse dicitur, quod ipse S. Severina addere non potuit, già che non haveva potestà, cùm non habuerit potestatem adorandi se ipsum. Igitur si vel unicum votum adhuc accessisset, si accessisset vel unicus adorator, S. Severina à 2. tertiis legitimè per adorationem electus Papa habitus fuisset. Sed etiam pro eodem numero sufficiente facere vident ea, quae jam de periculo electionis per adorationem dicturus sum. Solvat, vel secet nodum, qui potest; Verba Gregorii clara sunt, sed & evidens, diversum tradi ab aliis.
units.tr: LXXVIII. It is therefore necessary that either those authors are in error, or, if this author has given both treatises (as seems likely to me), then while he says two thirds suffice, the old strictness, perhaps relaxed in the time of Sixtus V, was restored by Gregorius XV, or else this author sets out a form different from the adoration which the said books present. Indeed, from what has been said, it scarcely remains probable that he sets out a different form which is lawful and has sometimes been practised. I do not dare to pronounce that he, and those authors too, erred in assigning the necessary number, since the modern authors of the conclaves clearly support them. For example, when in the conclave of Clement VIII Santa Severina had been elected by adoration with almost 35 votes, it is said that a single vote was lacking to make up the number 36, that is, two thirds, which Santa Severina himself could not add, since he had no power, since he did not have the power to adore himself. Therefore, if even one more vote had come in, if even one adorer had come, Santa Severina would have been held to have been lawfully elected Pope by two thirds through adoration. But they also see that the things I am about to say on the danger of election by adoration make for the same sufficient number. Let whoever can untie or cut the knot; the words of Gregorius are clear, but it is also evident that a different form is set out by others.

units.la: LXXIX. Fortè distinctius istum eligendi per inspirationem Spiritus S. modum cognoscer emus, si frequentius adhiberi soleret, sed rarius adhibitus fuit; Onuphrius annot. in Clem. V. Plat. ita Julium III. Marcellum II. & Paulum etiam III. renunciatos esse dicit, inde à facta Gregorii XV. Bulla nunquam adhibita est, nunquam etiam, ut videtur, amplius adhibebitur. Nec ea mea tantùm conjectura est, sed ita de citata sæpiùs Gregorii Bulla Author Conclavis Urbani VIII. loquitur; la nova Bolla haveva à bastanza proveduto che all' improviso, si come aveniva prima per mezzo dell' adoratione, non si poteße fare il Papa. Id est: Nova Bulla satis providit, ne ex improviso, quemadmodum antea eveniebat, mediante adoratione, fieri posset Papa. Providit, non prohibendo, nam in Bulla expressa habentur verba; non improbamus; sed omnium & singulorum ad unius electionem nullo speciali tractatu praevio concursum, qui impossibilis habetur, requisito. Et certè, non immeritò supra Rhotomagensis praesuppositâ talis concursûs necessitate electionem per inspirationem Sp. S. periculosam, eligendo nimirum & eligentibus vocavit.
units.tr: LXXIX. Perhaps we would know this mode of electing by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit more distinctly if it were customarily employed more often, but it has been used rarely. Onuphrius, in his Annotations on Clement V, Platina, says that Julius III, Marcellus II and also Paul III were elected in this way. Since the Bull of Gregorius XV was issued, it has never been used, and never, as it seems, will be used again. Nor is this merely my conjecture, but the author of the conclave of Urban VIII, speaking of the frequently cited Bull of Gregorius, says so: the new Bull had made sufficient provision that the Pope could not be made by surprise, as previously happened by means of adoration. That is: The new Bull has sufficiently provided, lest a Pope could be made unexpectedly by means of adoration, as used to happen before. It made provision not by prohibiting, for the words we do not disapprove are expressly found in the Bull; but it required the concurrence of all and each for the election of one, without any special prior treatment, which is regarded as impossible. And indeed, not without reason, the Rouen cardinal above, presupposing the necessity of such concurrence, called election by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit dangerous, namely for the one electing and for those electing.

units.la: LXXX.
units.tr: LXXX.

units.la: Ut ab altera parte Authores illi, qui duas tertias sufficere arbitrantur, periculosum Ecclesiae esse istum eligendi modum judicant, parùm etiam cum electionis necessaria libertate convenire. Ita enim in Vita di Sisto V. l. c. legitur: Questo modo ogni modo era tenuto per violente e periculoso, perche tre ò quattro Cardinali, spesse volte i più giovani, erano quelli, che ò per potenza, ò per aderenza facendo li Capi degli altri, quidavano e reggevano il Conclave secondo la loro propria ambitione. Che però li Pontefici providero con santissime leggi, ordinando, che l'elettione del Papa si facesse per solo scrutinio, acciò che ciascun Cardinale fosse libero nel dare il voto secundo la sua conscienza, e non gia secondo l'altrui pareri; Id est: Hic modus omnimodo habebatur violentus & periculosus, quia tres aut quatuor Cardinales, saepe maximè juvenes, aut potentiâ, aut adherentium numero se Capita aliorum constituendo, ducebant & regebant Conclave secundùm propriam ambitionem. Quare Pontifices sanctissimis legibus caverunt, ut electio Papae fieret per solum scrutinium, ut quivis Cardinalis liber esset in dando votum suum secundùm conscientiam suam, & non secundùm aliorum opiniones. Passioni, Passiones, habet Conclave Sixti V. unde Authorista exscripsit. Quas autem leges innuant, nescio, nisi ad Bullam ipsam illam Gregorii respiciant talem, qualem innui. Consentit Il Cardinalismo l. c. p.250. dum sequentia habet: L'adoratione si suole tentare da qualche numero di Cardinali ostinati alla promotione di qualche sogetto portato da loro, dubitando, che nello scrutinio segreto possano mancare alcuni, di quelli, che haverano dato ferma parola, come già si è visto mille volte, dove che nell' adoratione, ch' è una cosa publica, non si può ingannare, à chi si sià donato la parola. Id est: Adoratio tentari solet à quibusdam Cardinalibus obstinatis ad promotionem ejus, quem volunt, quando dubitant, de fide quorundam, qui promiserant, in scrutinio secreto, quae vel millies jam defuisse deprehensa fuit, cùm in adoratione, qua publicè fit, non possit decipi, cui fides data. Periculum tamen etiam respectu spectu sui, quem ita eligere volebant amici, praesuppositâ licèt sufficientiâ duarum partium, agnovit in Conclavi Pauli V. Cardinalis Tosco, qui ex improviso adorare volentibus & sufficientem numerum promittentibus obsequi noluit, parendogli questa proposta piena di troppo tomolto e pericolo, id est, quia ei videbatur propositio talis plena tumultu & periculo. Author Conclavis tamen judicat, eum adorationem tunc non admittendo rebus suis male consuluisse, quia revalescente Cardinale Aldebrandino ejus adversario, amicorum numerus diminutus fuerit.
units.tr: On the other side, those authors who think two-thirds is enough judge that this way of electing is dangerous for the Church and scarcely consistent with the freedom that election requires. Thus in Life of Sixtus V, loc. cit. we read: This method was held to be violent and dangerous in every respect, because three or four Cardinals, often the youngest, made themselves the heads of the others by power or by their following, and they guided and ruled the Conclave according to their own ambition. For this reason the Popes provided, by most holy laws, that the election of the Pope should be made by secret scrutiny alone, so that each Cardinal might be free in giving his vote according to his own conscience and not according to the opinions of others. That is: This method was held to be violent and dangerous in every way, because three or four Cardinals, most often the younger ones, setting themselves up as the heads of others by power or by the number of their adherents, led and governed the Conclave according to their own ambition. Therefore the Popes took precautions by most holy laws, so that the election of the Pope would be made by secret scrutiny alone, so that each Cardinal would be free in giving his vote according to his conscience and not according to the opinions of others. Passioni, Passiones, is the reading in the Conclave of Sixtus V, from which the author copied. What laws they mean I do not know, unless they refer to that very Bull of Gregory, of the kind that is hinted at. Il Cardinalismo, loc. cit. p. 250, agrees, where it says the following: The adoration is usually attempted by some obstinate Cardinals in favour of the promotion of someone they have put forward, fearing that in the secret scrutiny some of those who had given their firm word may fail them, as has been seen a thousand times; whereas in the adoration, which is a public matter, one cannot be deceived about the person to whom one has given one's word. That is: Adoration is usually attempted by certain obstinate Cardinals for the promotion of the man they want, when they doubt the loyalty of some who had promised, in the secret scrutiny, which has been caught failing even a thousand times; whereas in the adoration, which is done publicly, one cannot be deceived about the person to whom faith was given. Yet the danger, even with respect to the candidate whom his friends wished to elect in this way, even granting that two-thirds were sufficient, was recognised in the Conclave of Paul V by Cardinal Tosco, who, when suddenly asked to adore him and promised a sufficient number, refused to comply, finding this proposal full of too much tumult and danger, that is, because this proposal seemed to him full of tumult and danger. Nevertheless, the author of the Conclave judges that by not admitting the adoration at that time he ill served his own interests, because with the rise of Cardinal Aldobrandini, his opponent, the number of his friends was reduced.

units.la: LXXXI. Nempe adorati non semel à multis fuêre, qui tamen non obtinuerunt, illi ipsi praeter alios, quorum jam mentionem feci S. Severina & Tosco; Illum adorare voluerunt jam ante discessum Legati Regis Hispaniae, electioni, quam pro certa habebat & ipse, faventis; Et cùm postea cum ipso 36. (qui numerus sufficiens fuisset) eum adoraturi per salam Regiam pergerent, atque Altempsium ad augendum numerum ipse S. Severina corpus ad illum amabiliter amplectendum inclinaret, humanitatem tamen Altempsius ambabus manibus & prolatâ voce: Và via Papa del Diavolo: Id est: Apage Papa Diaboli; rejecit, quam & appellationem parùm honorificam alia occasione mox subsecutâ repetiit, & unâ cum aliis electioni isti intercessit. Hic verò, Tosco nimirum, cùm jam eum complures per adorationem eligere tentâssent, à Baronio à sede Pontificiâ, quam jam penè occupaverat, dejectus fuit, placuit enim Deo, ut ait Author Conclavis, di spiccar la pietra piccola della parola di Baronio, per dar con essa ne' piedi di questa grande statua di Nabuchodonosor e gettar la à terra. Id est; movendi parvum lapidem verborum Baronii, ad allidendum ad statuam Nebucadnezaris (coram qua jam plures procidebant;) & illam in terram projiciendam; Testatus enim est altâ voce Baronius fraude in Capellam perductus, di non voler andar' à quella adoratione, se non in ultimo luogo, che voleva, che fi scrivesse nelli suoi stivali, che egli era stato l'ultimo à concorrere à questa elettione; Id est: Ultimum se adorationi illi accessurum, atque velle, ut inscribatur ocreis suis, se ultimum fuisse. Qui & contrarium sermonis sui profitentibus aliis, & electionem bonam vocantibus, dimenando la mano per il petto e crollando il capo, reprovò questa risposta con igesti con sospiri e parole interotte; Id est; manus per pectus trahendo, caputque movendo, rejecit illam responsionem gestibus & suspiriis & verbis interruptis. Qua ratione etiam animos multorum Adoratorum ad alia conconsilia perduxit, atque, ut irrita esset à multis jam facta adoratio‐heroico planè Zelo effecit. Quid autem de ejusmodi adorationibus judicandum sit, ubi de adoratione electionem consequente acturi sumus, indicabitur.
units.tr: LXXXI. Indeed, many times he was adored, but he never obtained the papacy: besides the others whom I have already mentioned, Santa Severina and Tosco, they wished to adore him before the departure of the Legate of the King of Spain, who favoured the election, which he too regarded as certain. And when afterwards they went with him, thirty-six (which would have been a sufficient number) to adore him through the royal hall, and Santa Severina himself bowed his body to embrace Altemps lovingly in order to increase the number, Altemps rejected this courtesy with both hands and with a loud voice: Go away, Papa del Diavolo! that is, Away, Pope of the Devil! He repeated this not very honourable name on another occasion soon afterwards, and joined the others in opposing that election. Tosco, however, when many had already tried to elect him by adoration, was thrown down from the papal seat, which he had almost occupied, by Baronius; for it pleased God, as the author of the conclave says, to pluck out the small stone of Baronius's word, to strike with it the feet of this great statue of Nebuchadnezzar and throw it to the ground. That is: moving the small stone of Baronius's words, to dash against the statue of Nebuchadnezzar (before which many were already prostrating themselves) and to cast it to the ground. For Baronius declared in a loud voice, having been led into the chapel by a trick, that he did not want to go to that adoration unless in the last place, and he wanted it written on his boots that he had been the last to join in this election; that is: that he would approach that adoration last, and wished it to be inscribed on his boots that he had been the last. When others professed the opposite of his words and called the election a good one, he rejected that reply with gestures, sighs and broken words, drawing his hand across his chest and shaking his head; that is: drawing his hand across his chest and moving his head, he rejected that answer with gestures and sighs and interrupted words. By this means he also led the minds of many adorers to other plans, and with truly heroic zeal he made the adoration, which many had already performed, void. What must be judged about such adorations will be shown when we come to treat of the adoration that follows the election.

units.la: LXXXII.
units.tr: LXXXII.

units.la: LXXXIII. Et quia post adorationem à legitimo numero fratrum Scrutinium aliquando deficere posset,ideo Author Cardinalismi l. c. commodè illud dubium proposuit; quid fieri debeat in tali casu? Respondet; hoc nunquam accidisse hactenus, nec pro- in decisum esse,cùm casuum decisio plerumque casus sequi soleat; se tamen credere, in tali casu aut schisma oriturum, aut accessuros esse adorato. Non autem posse casum accidere, quia adoratione facta scrutinium publicum sit,quod fortè observari soleat ad ipsum schisma evitandum. Verum quidem est,id aliquando observatum esse. Exemplum suppeditat idem p.154. in Paulo III. in cujus scruti- nio adorationem subsecuto missero tutti i Cardinali le lor Polize aper- te,in modo, che Ciascun poteva leggere commodamente tutto quello che scriveva il suo compagno. Id est: Posuerunt omnes Cardinales schedas suas apertas, ita ut quilibet commodè legere potuerit omne illud, quod scribebat ejus socius. Quamvis tunc adhuc Cardinalis Trivultius se ei opponere aliquo modo ausus fuerit, hinc acriter ab ado- rato increpatus, & ad mutuam reconciliationem adactus. Interim tamen verum & illud est, legem Scrutinium tale publicum probantem non dari, quamvis electionem per adorationem pro- bans omnino detur, dentur etiam ita electorum exempla; Insuper constat, Cardinales excludentes ad Scrutinium post adorationem S. Severinae instituendum concurrere noluisse, sentendo,che s'era or- dinato,che si dessero li noti aperti. Id est; Sententes, constitutum esse, ut nota darentur aperta; Sed de nullitate protestatos esse.
units.tr: LXXXIII. And because after an adoration by a lawful number of brothers the scrutiny might sometimes fail, the author of Cardinalismus, in the passage cited, fittingly raised this doubt: what ought to be done in such a case? He answers that this has never happened hitherto, nor has it been decided, since the decision of cases usually follows the cases themselves; he himself believes, however, that in such a case either a schism would arise, or the one adored would be pressed to accept. But the case cannot occur, he says, because once the adoration is made a public scrutiny follows, which is perhaps customarily observed in order to avoid schism itself. It is indeed true that this has sometimes been observed. The same author, at p. 154, supplies an example under Paul III, in whose scrutiny, after the adoration, all the Cardinals sent in their ballots open, so that each could easily read everything his neighbour wrote. That is: All the Cardinals placed their ballots open, so that each could easily read all that his companion wrote. Although at that time Cardinal Trivulzio did venture to oppose him in some way, he was then sharply rebuked by the one adored and forced into a mutual reconciliation. Meanwhile, however, it is also true that there is no law prescribing such a public scrutiny, although a law permitting election by adoration certainly exists, and examples of those elected in this way also exist. Moreover, it is established that the Cardinals who were excluded refused to join in the scrutiny to be instituted after the adoration of Santa Severina, thinking that it had been ordered that the ballots be given open. That is: Thinking it had been decreed that the ballots should be given open; but they protested that it was null.

units.la: LXXXIV. Quarta nunc tandem sequitur electionis per solos Cardinales forma, quae est per compromissum, quam verbo- tim damus, sic ut eam in Caeremoniali Gregorii XV. sequentibus verbis traditam reperimus; Modus per Compromissum est, quan- do scilicet Cardinales ad electionem per hanc formam seu viam procedere volentes committerent aliquibus ex Patribus eligendi potestatem, ut vice omnium Ecclesiae Catholicae provideant de Pastore, cujus forma praxis po- test esse hujusmodi: Primo omnes & singuli Cardinales in Conclavi clauso praesentes,nemine eorum dissentiente,in aliquos ex Patribus compromissum faciunt faciunt e.g. in hanc formam : In Nomine Domini Amen! Anno ab ejusdem &c. mense &c. die &c. Nos Episcopi, Presbyteri & Diaconi S. R. E. Cardinales omnes & singuli in Conclavi existentes videlicet N. N. (& sigillatim omnes nominentur Cardinales) elegimus per viam procedere compromissi: & unanimiter & concorditer, nemine discrepante, elegimus Compromissarios N. N. & N. Cardinales &c. quibus damus plenariam facultatem & potestatem providendi S. R. E. de Pastore sub hac forma videlicet (Hic optimum erit, ut Cardinales compromittentes exprimant modum & formam, secundum quam electus debet censeri verus & legitimus Papa, ut puta, si electi sint tres compromissarii, declarandum est, an ad hoc, ut electio sit valida, prius proponere debeant Sacro Collegio personam vel personas ab ipsis nominandam vel nominandas ad Pontificatum, an vero absolute debeant electionem peragere; an omnes tres debeant convenire in unam personam, an vero sufficiat, quod duo in unam concordent, & an debeant nominare aliquem de Collegio, vel etiam aliquem extra Collegium, & alia his similia :) His autem vel aliis similibus expressis addi compromisso solet tempus, ad quod usque volunt Cardinales potestatem Compromissarios habere eligendi, & postea subjunguntur haec verba : Et promittimus, nos illum pro Romano Pontifice habituros, quem D. D. Compromissarii secundum formam praedictam duxerint eligendum. Vel alia ad formam Compromissariis praescriptam accommodata.
units.tr: LXXXIV. Fourth, now at last follows the form of election by the Cardinals alone, which is by compromise. We give it word for word, as we find it set out in the Ceremonial of Gregory XV in the following words: The manner by compromise is when the Cardinals, wishing to proceed to election by this form or way, entrust the power of electing to certain of the Fathers, so that they may provide, on behalf of all the Catholic Church, a pastor; the practice of this form can be of the following kind: First, all and each of the Cardinals present in the closed Conclave, none dissenting, make a compromise with certain of the Fathers in this form, for example: In the Name of the Lord, Amen! In the year of the same, &c., month &c., day &c. We, the Bishops, Presbyters and Deacons of the Holy Roman Church, all and each of the Cardinals existing in the Conclave, namely N. N. (all the Cardinals shall be named individually), have chosen to proceed by way of compromise; and unanimously and harmoniously, none dissenting, we have chosen as compromisers N. N. and N., Cardinals, &c., to whom we give full faculty and power of providing the Holy Roman Church with a pastor in the following form, namely (Here it will be best for the compromising Cardinals to express the manner and form according to which the elected man ought to be counted a true and lawful Pope; for instance, if three compromisers are chosen, it must be declared whether, in order that the election be valid, they must first propose to the Sacred College the person or persons to be named by them for the Papacy, or whether they must carry out the election absolutely; whether all three must agree on one person, or whether it is enough that two agree on one; and whether they must nominate someone from the College or also someone from outside the College; and other matters similar to these:) When such or similar matters have been expressed, a time is usually added to the compromise, up to which the Cardinals wish the compromisers to have the power of choosing; and afterwards these words are added: And we promise that we shall hold as Roman Pontiff him whom the Lord compromisers, according to the aforesaid form, shall have judged to be chosen. Or other words adapted to the form prescribed for the compromisers.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Secundo, completo hujusmodi mandato, Compromissarii ad partem in aliquo loco separato se conferunt, & de electione facienda tractant, & solet inter eos praemitti protestatio, qui per quamcunque prolationem verborum, suum dare consensum non intelligant, nisi in scriptis illum expresse ponunt. Et haec protestatio videtur necessaria inter Compromissarios, ut verbis humanis & reverentialibus inter se sine praejudicio uti possint. Tertio facta per Compromissarios electione secundum formam ejus praescriptam, & servatis iis, quae Gregorius XV. in sua constitutione jussit, electus per hujusmodi viam Compromissi est Canonicus & verus Papa.
units.tr: Secondly, once this mandate has been completed, the compromissaries betake themselves to some separate place apart and deal with making the election, and it is customary for a protestation to be put forward among them, to the effect that by no kind of utterance of words do they intend to give their consent unless they express it in writing. This protestation seems necessary among the compromissaries, so that they may use human and courteous words with one another without prejudice. Thirdly, when the election has been made by the compromissaries according to the form prescribed for it, and the requirements that Gregory XV. laid down in his constitution have been observed, the one elected by this way of compromise is a canonical and true Pope.

units.la: LXXXVI.
units.tr: LXXXVI.

units.la: Satis ex his constare potest, tota electionis per Compromissum ratio, quae nimirum adhiberi solet, si Cardinales inter se discordes de eligendo vix convenire possent; Habita fuit rarissime & notum est exemplum Cardinalis de Ossa Cadurcensis Galli, qui, cum Clemente V. An. 1314. mortuo, Cardinalibus mire dissentientibus, duorum annorum Inter-Pontificium esset, essel, & eligendi tandem Pontificis arbitrium ei soli deferretur, praeter omnium exspectationem conscenso throno; Ego sum Papa; clamavit, atque sic, Jove scilicet aequo judicans, se ipsum elegit, Johannes XXII. al. XXIII. dictus. De quo exemplo mox in naevis pluribus acturi sumus. Exinde non legitur unquam adhibita, quamvis juxta allata ex Caeremoniali adhuc adhiberi possit.
units.tr: From these points it can be sufficiently established what the whole rationale of election by compromise is, which is naturally employed if the cardinals, disagreeing among themselves, could hardly come to agreement about the choice. It has been employed very rarely. The well-known example is that of Cardinal de Ossa of Cahors in France, who, when Clement V. died in the year 1314 and the cardinals strangely disagreed, was for two years in an interregnum; and when at last the decision about choosing a pope was handed over to him alone, beyond everyone's expectation he mounted the throne and cried, I am Pope; and so, judging as impartially as Jupiter himself, he elected himself, being called John XXII (or XXIII). We shall treat this example in more detail shortly, among the several blemishes. Since then it is never read of as having been used, although, according to what has been reported from the Caeremoniale, it could still be used.

units.la: LXXXVII.
units.tr: LXXXVII.

units.la: Atque hae sunt Electionis per solos Cardinales Formae, constanti ordine semper haec est electio per solos Cardinales inde a prima institutione, sed, ut dictum, varie facta, nisi quod in Concilio Constantiensi, depositis aliis, novus Papa, Martinus V. non tantum a 32. Cardinalibus, sed &, ut omnis scrupulus, & aemulatio Nationum omnis tolleretur, a 30. Nationistis, id est, Viris Ecclesiasticis praecipuis ex 6. Nationibus Christianismi praecipuis simul ibi Conclave ingressis an. 1414. ipsa S. Martini feria post trium duntaxat dierum moras electus fuit. Qui tamen casus peculiaris in peculiari rerum confusione & plane extraordinarius fuit, nec Concilium ea ratione electionem per solos Cardinales sustulit, quam potius decreto suo stabilivit. Ut non opus fuerit ab hoc unico exemplo propriam formam denominare, nec etiam opus sit ejus considerationi diutius immorari.
units.tr: These are the forms of election by the cardinals alone. In a fixed order, this has always been the election by the cardinals alone from its first institution, though, as said, it has been carried out in various ways. The exception was at the Council of Constance, where, after the others had been deposed, the new Pope, Martin V., was elected in the Conclave in the year 1414, on the feast of St. Martin, after only three days' delay, not only by the 32 cardinals but also, so that every scruple and rivalry among the nations might be removed, by 30 Nationists, that is, leading ecclesiastical men from the six chief nations of Christendom, who had entered the Conclave together. Yet this peculiar case occurred in a peculiar confusion of affairs and was plainly extraordinary, and the Council did not by this means abolish the election by the cardinals alone; rather, it confirmed it by its decree. So there is no need to name a distinct form from this single example, nor any need to dwell longer on its consideration.

units.la: LXXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXXVIII.

units.la: Varii varia nugantur disputando, an ista electionis forma sola jam sint legitima, annon alia etiam adhiberi possint, penes quem sit novas introducere &c. Nobis istud tantum adhuc notasse sufficiat, Pontifices certe, qui de hodiernis formis, loco, legibus &c. constitutiones ediderunt, earum perpetuitatem simul imperasse; Decernit Pius IV. in fine Bullae suae aliquoties citatae constitutiones illas suas omnes & singulos Cardinales etiam absentes, praesentes & futuros & alios quoscunque, quorum interest vel interesse possit, ligare, nullamque earum ignorantiam praetendere posse, ac si eis personaliter intimata forent, praemissis, ac aliis constitutionibus & Ordinationibus Apostolicis caeterisque contrariis non obstantibus quibuscunque. Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat, ita pergit, hanc paginam nostrorum definitionis, statutorum, declamationum, prohibitionum, mandatorum, interdicti, praecepti, rogationis, hortationis, & voluntatum (satis bullanter) infringere, vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis autem hoc attentare praesumpserit, indignationem Omnipotentis Dei, ac Beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum ejus (satis severe) se noverit incursurum.
units.tr: Various people babble various things in disputing whether this form of election alone is now lawful, or whether others may also be used, and who has the power to introduce new ones. For our purpose it is enough to have noted this much: the popes who issued constitutions about the present forms, place, laws and so on certainly also commanded that they should last forever. Pius IV., at the end of his Bull, cited several times, decrees that his constitutions bind all and each of the cardinals, whether absent, present or future, and all others whatsoever whom it concerns or may concern, and that no one may plead ignorance of them, as if they had been intimated to them personally, notwithstanding the foregoing, and other apostolic constitutions and ordinances and whatever contrary things there may be. Therefore let it in no way be lawful for anyone, so it goes on, to infringe this page of our definitions, statutes, declarations, prohibitions, mandates, interdicts, precepts, requests, exhortations and wills (quite bullishly), or to contravene it with rash presumption. If anyone should presume to attempt this, he is to know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul (quite severely).

units.la: LXXXIX. Nec indulgentior est sæpius citati à Gregorio XV. editi Ceremonialis Conclavis clausula, quæ ita se habet: Motu itaque proprio, & ex certa scientia nostra, ac de Apostolicæ potestatis plenitudine, omnia & singula in prædicto Ceremoniali ordinata & quomodolibet contenta, tenore præsentium perpetuo approbamus & confirmamus; illisque omnibus & singulis perpetuum & inviolabilis Apostolicæ firmitatis robur adjicimus, eáque à Venerandis Fratribus nostris S. R. E. Cardinalibus omnibúsque & singulis aliis, ad quos spectat & spectare quomodolibet poterit in futurum, omnino observari præcipimus & mandamus, ac Ceremoniale hujusmodi, in totum vel in parte mutari, vel ei aliquid addi prohibemus. Decernentes, sic & non aliter per quoscunque ac eosdem S. R. E. Cardinales, sublatâ eis & eorum cuilibet quavis aliter judicandi, & interpretandi facultate, & authoritate, ubique judicari & definiri debere. Non obstantibus omnibus illis, quae in primò dicta constitutione voluimus non obstare, caterísque contrariis quibuscunque. Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat, &c.
units.tr: LXXXIX. The clause of the Ceremonial of the Conclave, published by Gregory XV. and often cited, is no more lenient, and reads thus: By our own motion, and from our certain knowledge, and out of the fullness of apostolic power, we approve and confirm, by the tenor of these presents, for ever, all and each of the things ordained and in whatever way contained in the aforesaid Ceremonial; to all of them and each of them we add the perpetual and inviolable strength of apostolic firmness, and we strictly command and order that they be observed by our venerable brothers, the cardinals of the holy Roman Church, and by all and each of the others to whom it pertains, or in future may in any way pertain; and we forbid that this Ceremonial, in whole or in part, be changed or anything be added to it. Decreeing that thus and not otherwise it must be judged and defined everywhere by whomsoever, and by the same cardinals of the holy Roman Church, the power and authority of judging and interpreting otherwise being taken away from them and from each of them; notwithstanding all those things which we have willed in the first-mentioned constitution not to stand in the way, and whatever contrary things there may be. Therefore let it in no way be lawful for anyone, etc.

units.la: XC. Nec contentus hisce Pius IV. Executores etiam Bullæ suæ his verbis deputare voluit: Quia verò parùm esset jura tradere, nisi forent, qui executioni ea demandarent; statuimus & ordinamus, ut Prælati, Rectores, Officiales Urbis, ac Principum Oratores, Illustres Viri, quos omnes à Collegio pro custodia Conclavis eligi contingat (eligere autem Collegium debebit eos, qui ad id magis idonei videntur) præmissa omnia plenè ac inviolabiliter ac sine fraude & dolo aliquo observari faciant, de quo corporale juramentum coram ipso Collegio ante ingressum Conclavis, quoties opus fuerit, præstare teneantur; quæ quidem nisi fecerint, vel, si in eis dolum aut fraudem commiserint, prædictas pœnas & cateras in dicta constitutione Gregorii X. contentas incurrant.
units.tr: XC. Not content with these, Pius IV. also wished to appoint executors of his Bull in these words: Since it would be of little use to lay down laws unless there were men to carry them out, we decree and ordain that the prelates, rectors, officials of the city, and ambassadors of princes, illustrious men, whom the College may happen to choose for guarding the Conclave (the College shall choose those who seem most suitable for this), shall cause all the aforesaid things to be observed fully and inviolably, and without fraud or any deceit, and they are bound to give a bodily oath on this before the College itself before entering the Conclave, as often as it is necessary; and if they do not do so, or if they commit any deceit or fraud in these matters, they incur the aforesaid penalties and the others contained in the said constitution of Gregory X.

units.la: XCI. Sed quàm facilè Papa Papæ decreta mutet, corrigat, tollat, notissimum est; Quàm legitima sit praxis, in tractatione de nævis & vitiis Electionis, ad quam jam deventum est, explicabitur; Maximè quoad Moralia, ut sic loquar, constitutionum istarum, quæ hactenus tangere non opus fuit, & quæ in iisdem constitutionibus comprehensa, cum eadem quoque severitate commendata, aliam in Constitutionibus, in praxi aliam, longè aliam habere faciem proximè ostensurus, huic de Electionis Pontificum Romanorum Formis Dissertationi facio finem.
units.tr: XCI. But how easily one pope changes, corrects or abolishes the decrees of another is very well known. How lawful this practice is will be explained in the treatment of the blemishes and defects of the election, to which we have now come; especially as regards the moral side, so to speak, of those constitutions, which up to now it has not been necessary to touch, and which, though commended with the same severity in those very constitutions, will show, as I am about to make plain, one face in the constitutions and quite another face in practice. With this I bring to an end this dissertation on the forms of the election of the Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: DISSERTATIO QUINTA, In qua Partim de nævis & vitiis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum aliquid in genere notatur, partim de iis, quæ personas eligentes propiùs respiciunt, speciatim agitur.
units.tr: FIFTH DISSERTATION, in which some blemishes and faults of the election of the Roman Pontiffs are noted in general, and others, which relate more closely to the electing persons, are treated in particular.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Transitio ad tractationem de nævis; II. Electiones quales esse debeant & qualium ex Vet. Test. III. Ex N. Test. præsertim; IV. In Epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum requisita enarrantur; V. Expositio loci 1. Tim. III.1. VI. De illis, qui oblatum munus accipere refugiunt; VII. Eorum magnus olim numerus; Quatenus appetere liceat; VIII. Navi Electionibus Præconum Veritatis sæpe & variè adhærentes non excusant navis in Electionibus Pontificum; IX. In quibus primò vitiorum & navorum maximus confluxus; X. Vbi tamen nullus esse deberet, Secundò ob rei dignitatem; XI. Cùm peculiare opus Dei & Spiritus S. tertiò vocare soleant; XII. Et quartò successionem heic tantopere jactent, XIII. Quintò omnia quodammodo à dignitate Ministri suspendant, & intentionis necessitatem doceant; XIV. Sextò talium, imò etiam eligentium, potestas sit ἀνυπεύθυνον. XV. Non omnes navi enumerari possunt; XVI. Classes navorum tres; XVII. Respectu eligentium navis primus, quòd de iis nihil plane habet Scriptura; XVIII. Secundus, quòd toties variârunt; XIX. Tertius quòd non habent potestatem, quam conferre dicuntur; XX. Quartus, quòd incertum est, an habeant requisita necessaria; XXI. Quintus, quòd Cardinales Laici interdum eligunt; XXII. Sextus, quòd officium non facientes; XXIII. Septimus, quòd de intentione nihil constat; XXIV. Octavus, quòd non semper duæ tertiæ; XXV. Nonus, quòd feré sola Factionum Capita; XXVI. Decimus, quòd etiam hæretici, excommunicati; XXVII. Undecimus, quòd multi seipsos eligunt; XXVIII. Duodecimus, quòd sæpe sæculari potentiâ armati; XXIX. Decimus tertius, quòd aliquando mulieres infames; XXX. Exempla porrò narrantur; XXXI. Exemplum Dominæ Olympiæ; XXXII. Decimus quartus, quòd Papæ nonnulli propiori Diaboli ope electi fuerunt; Exemplum Sylvestri II. XXXIII. Testimonia de Gregorio VII. XXXIV. Sixto V. XXXV. Conclusio.
units.tr: I. Transition to the treatment of blemishes; II. Elections, what they ought to be, and of what kind they were in the Old Testament; III. Especially in the New Testament; IV. The requirements are set out in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus; V. Exposition of 1 Tim. 3:1; VI. Of those who shrink from accepting the office offered; VII. Their number was once great; how far it is lawful to desire it; VIII. Those who often and variously cling to the elections of the heralds of truth do not excuse the blemishes in the elections of the Popes; IX. Where first the greatest concourse of faults and blemishes; X. Where yet there should be none, secondly because of the dignity of the matter; XI. Since they commonly call it a peculiar work of God and the Holy Spirit, thirdly; XII. And fourthly, they boast so much here of succession; XIII. Fifthly, they make everything depend in some way on the dignity of the minister, and teach the necessity of intention; XIV. Sixthly, the power of such men, indeed even of the electors, is unaccountable (ἀνυπεύθυνον). XV. Not all the blemishes can be listed; XVI. Three classes of blemishes; XVII. With respect to the electors, the first blemish is that Scripture says nothing at all about them; XVIII. The second, that they have varied so often; XIX. The third, that they do not have the power which they are said to confer; XX. The fourth, that it is uncertain whether they have the necessary requirements; XXI. The fifth, that lay Cardinals sometimes elect; XXII. The sixth, that some do not perform the office; XXIII. The seventh, that nothing is certain about the intention; XXIV. The eighth, that two thirds are not always present; XXV. The ninth, that it is almost always only the heads of factions; XXVI. The tenth, that even heretics and excommunicated persons (take part); XXVII. The eleventh, that many elect themselves; XXVIII. The twelfth, that they are often armed with secular power; XXIX. The thirteenth, that sometimes infamous women (take part); XXX. Examples are then related; XXXI. The example of Lady Olympia; XXXII. The fourteenth, that some Popes were elected with the closer help of the Devil; the example of Sylvester II. XXXIII. Testimonies concerning Gregory VII. XXXIV. Sixtus V. XXXV. Conclusion.

units.la: I. NImis multa detecta videri possent Electionis Romanorum Pontificum vitia, jam sunt nævorum omnia plena; Vitium est, nævus est, quòd Apostolo Petro talis Monarchica potestas nunquam collata fuit, quod Dissert. I. ostendimus, proin potestas illa, ad quam tanquam ejus successores eligi volunt, legilegitima non datur; Vitium est, nævus est, quòd valde incertum est, an Petrus unquam Romæ fuerit; Vitium est, nævus est, quòd manifestè falsum est, Petrum Romæ per 25. annos fuisse & ibi Episcopum egisse; (quod Differt.II. docet.)
