Vitium est, nævus est, quòd illa ipsa potestas, quam Petrus habuit, Apostolica in plenitudine sua ad successores ullos transmitti non debuit, & quòd Apostolorum omnes ubique locorum veri Ecclesiarum Rectores in communi ipsis sensu & æquè Apostolorum, proin etiam Petri Successores sunt, & quòd, qui à multis annis eliguntur, Pontifices Romani, partim officium Petri neglexerunt, partim doctrinam ejus corruperunt, ut nulla nisi successio in loco, & illa in tenuissima etiam significatione valdè incerta, sed nullo modo ad hereditatem potestatis sufficiens, ipsis ab ullo concedi possit (quod Dissertationis III. argumentum est,) atque adeò ad potestatem Apostolicam nullo etiam modo eligi queant. Vitium est, nævus est, quòd Electionis forma in Scriptura nullibi tradita est, & quòd tot sunt támque diversæ, & quòd, qui fuerunt per tot secula Electores electioni ad tantam Majestatem primo etiam obtutu impares videntur, (quod ex Differt.IV. jam aliquo modo apparet.) Ut omninò jam vitia in Electione Pontificum Romanorum nimis multa detexerimus, nævorum omnia plena esse ostenderimus, quorum vitium unum, nævus unus jam subvertit omnia, & satis grave est contra Electionem istam præjudicium. Attamen heic demum tractationem de nævis & vitiis incipimus, id est, de manifestioribus, propioribus, & talibus, quæ sub nullo alio respectu ad tractationem nostram pertinent.
units.tr: I. Too many faults of the election of the Roman Pontiffs might seem to have been revealed; now all things are full of blemishes. It is a fault, it is a blemish, that such monarchical power was never conferred on the Apostle Peter, which we showed in Dissertation I; therefore that power, to which they wish to be elected as his successors, is not given by any legitimate law. It is a fault, it is a blemish, that it is very uncertain whether Peter ever was at Rome; it is a fault, it is a blemish, that it is manifestly false that Peter was at Rome for twenty-five years and acted there as bishop (which Dissertation II teaches). It is a fault, it is a blemish, that that very power which Peter had, in its Apostolic fullness, ought not to have been handed down to any successors; and that all the true rulers of the Churches everywhere are, in the common sense and equally, successors of the Apostles, and therefore also of Peter; and that the Roman Pontiffs who have been elected for many years have partly neglected the office of Peter and partly corrupted his doctrine, so that no succession except in place can be granted to them by anyone, and even that in the most slender sense is very uncertain, and in no way sufficient for the inheritance of power (this is the argument of Dissertation III); and therefore they can in no way be elected to Apostolic power. It is a fault, it is a blemish, that the form of election is nowhere handed down in Scripture; and that there are so many and such diverse forms; and that those who have been electors through so many centuries seem, at first glance, unequal to an election to such great majesty (as is already in some measure apparent from Dissertation IV). Although we have now uncovered too many faults in the election of the Roman Pontiffs, and shown that everything is full of blemishes, of which one fault, one blemish, already overthrows everything, and is a sufficiently grave prejudice against that election, nevertheless here at last we begin the treatment of blemishes and faults, that is, of those that are more manifest, closer, and such as pertain to our treatment under no other aspect.

units.la: II. Electiones ad Sacra & Ecclesiastica munia sacræ debent esse & Canonicæ. Veteris Testamenti Sacerdotium à Deo fuit institutum: Οὐχ ἑαυτῷ τις λαμβάνει τὴν τιμὴν, ἀλλὰ ὁ καλούμενος ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Ἀαρών. Nemo sibi ipsi sumit honorem, inquit Author Epistolæ ad Hebræos c.V. v.4. sed qui vocatus à Deo, quemadmodum & Aaron; à Deo vocatus & ipse fuit, & instituta fuit posterorum successio, qui in Oeconomia illa Ceremoniali ad Christi & Christianorum verorum, quos inter eminere debent in muneribus sacris publicis constituti, sanctitatem præfigurandam à nævis etiam corporis liberi esse debuerunt, & quorum etiam filiæ peccantes graviùs & multò graviùs aliis puniri debuerunt, Levit. XXI.17. seqq. & 9. Quemadmodum & aliâs Deus in Oeconomiæ illius decursu sæpe testatus est, ab una quidem parte, grave esse judicium sine missione prophetantium, ab altera parte verò, se maximè abominari vitia Sacerdotum, & velle, ut digni constituantur in sacris muniis, & ab utero Jeremiam sanctificâsse, Jer.I.5.
units.tr: II. Elections to sacred and ecclesiastical offices ought to be sacred and canonical. The priesthood of the Old Testament was instituted by God: "No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was" [Οὐχ ἑαυτῷ τις λαμβάνει τὴν τιμὴν, ἀλλὰ ὁ καλούμενος ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Ἀαρών]. No one takes this honour to himself, says the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 5, v. 4, but he who is called by God, as Aaron also was; he himself was called by God, and a succession of descendants was established, who in that ceremonial economy, appointed to foreshadow the holiness of Christ and of the true Christians, among whom those set in public sacred offices ought to stand out, were required to be free even from bodily blemishes; and whose daughters, when they sinned, were to be punished more severely and far more severely than others, Lev. 21:17 ff. and 9. In the course of that economy God also often testified in other ways that, on the one hand, the judgment is grave for those who prophesy without being sent, and on the other hand, that he most utterly abhors the faults of priests, and wishes that those who are set in sacred offices be worthy; and that he sanctified Jeremiah from the womb, Jer. 1:5.

units.la: III. Maximè autem in N. T. (ad cujus etiam Præcursorem Johannem Baptistam ῥῆμα Θεοῦ ἐγένετο, verbum Dei factum est, Luc.III.2.) docetur, quales esse oporteat electiones eorum, qui in publico munere viam justitiæ aliis ostendere debent; Quia Christianorum Doctores & Ductores etiam ordinarii non per carnalem generationem, sed per electionem ex constitutione succedunt. Et Apostolos quidem Christus ipse vocavit & misit, primò ad perditas Israëlis oves, Matth.X.1. seqq. dein ad omnes gentes c.XXVIII.19. sicut eum Pater misérat, Joh.XX.21. Idem etiam 70. discipulos, Luc.X.1. seqq. Quid autem omni subsequente tempore circa electionem Ministrorum fieri debeat, Apostoli partim exemplo, partim præceptis suis docuerunt, qui & Act.I. Matthiam ex tot fidelibus aptissimum ad Apostolatus communionem receperunt, & Act.VI. viros testimonio ornatos, plenos Spiritu & Sapientiâ Diaconos eligi curârunt, & quorum insuper Acta docent, cap.IX. quomodo Paulus, qui & in epistolis hinc inde ad Divinam suam vocationem provocat, & Rom.I.1. semet ad Evangelium Dei vocat, vas electionis v.15. coelitús vocatus & statim ad docendum & redarguendum aptus factus, cap.XIII.v.3. quomodo idem cum Barnaba Spiritûs Sancti jussu ad opus ministerii à jejuniis & precibus præviis acceptâque manuum impositione separatus fuerit, c.XIV.23. quomodo iidem per suffragia Presbyteros in Ecclesiis quoque precibus & jejuniis constituerint & cap.XVIII.v.24.25 quomodo Apollo potens in Scripturis & edoctus de via Domini & fervens Spiritu docuerit, & magis ab Aquila & Priscilla confirmatus fuerit, & cap.XX.17.28. quomodo Spiritus S. Presbyteros Ephesinos constituerit Episcopos gregis ad pascendum Ecclesiam Dei proprio sanguine redemtam, curam habituros sui ipsorum & illius. Sed & Divina est generalis illa D. Pauli Rom.X.15. sententia: Quomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint; Et notatu dignissima sunt, quæ 1.Cor.XII. & XIV. de charismatibus extraordinariis habet, qui-bus. bus Deus illos, per quos coetum fidelium docere voluerit, instruxerit.
units.tr: III. But especially in the New Testament (to whose forerunner John the Baptist "the word of God came" [ῥῆμα Θεοῦ ἐγένετο], Luke 3:2) it is taught what kind of elections ought to be of those who must show others the way of righteousness in a public office; because the teachers and leaders of Christians, even the ordinary ones, succeed not by carnal generation but by election under an ordinance. And indeed Christ himself called and sent the Apostles, first to the lost sheep of Israel, Matt. 10:1 ff., then to all nations, ch. 28:19, as the Father had sent him, John 20:21. He likewise sent the seventy disciples, Luke 10:1 ff. What ought to be done about the election of ministers in all the following time, the Apostles taught partly by their example and partly by their precepts; they who, in Acts 1, received Matthias out of so many faithful as most fit for communion in the apostolate, and in Acts 6 saw to it that men attested by witness, full of the Spirit and wisdom, be chosen as deacons; and whose Acts further teach, in ch. 9, how Paul, who here and there in his epistles appeals to his divine calling, and in Rom. 1:1 calls himself to the Gospel of God, a vessel of election (v. 15), was called from heaven and at once made fit to teach and to rebuke (ch. 13, v. 3); how the same, with Barnabas, by the command of the Holy Spirit was set apart for the work of the ministry after fasting and prior prayers, and with the laying on of hands (ch. 14:23); how the same, by vote, appointed elders in the churches with prayers and fasting; and in ch. 18, vv. 24–25, how Apollos, mighty in the Scriptures and instructed in the way of the Lord and fervent in spirit, taught, and was more fully confirmed by Aquila and Priscilla; and in ch. 20:17, 28, how the Holy Spirit set the Ephesian elders as bishops of the flock, to feed the Church of God, which he redeemed with his own blood, they being going to have care of themselves and of it. Also divine is that general sentence of St. Paul, Rom. 10:15: How shall they preach, unless they have been sent? And those things are most worthy of note which he has in 1 Cor. 12 and 14 about the extraordinary charismata, by which God equipped those through whom he willed to teach the assembly of the faithful.

units.la: IV. Præprimis verò in Epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum; ubi etiam in genere, 1.Tim.V.22. præcipit : Χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει, μηδὲ κοινώνει ἁμαρτίαις ἀλλοτρίαις; Manus nemini facilè impone, neque te participem redde peccatorum alienorum; requisita non tantùm Episcoporum, sed & Diaconorum recensetur, quòd nimirum esse debeat talis ἀνεπίληπτος, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ, νηφάλιος, σώφρων, κόσμιος, φιλόξενος, διδακτικὸς, μὴ πάροινος, μὴ πλήκτης, μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆς, ἀλλ' ἐπιεικής, ἄμαχος, ἀφιλάργυρος, τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου καλῶς προϊσταμένους, τέκνα ἔχων ἐν ὑποταγῇ μετὰ πάσης σεμνότητος, μὴ νεόφυτος, ἔχων μαρτυρίαν καλὴν καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξωθεν, σεμνὸς, μὴ διλόγος, ἔχων τὸ μυστήριον τῆς πίστεως ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει, δεδοκιμασμένος, ὡς Θεοῦ οἰκονόμος, μὴ αὐθάδης, μὴ ὀργίλος, ἀλλὰ φιλόξενος, φιλάγαθος, σώφρων, δίκαιος, ὅσιος, ἐγκρατής, ἀντεχόμενος τοῦ κατὰ τὴν διδαχὴν πιστοῦ λόγου, ἵνα δυνατὸς ᾖ καὶ παρακαλεῖν ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν, irreprehensibilis, unius uxoris vir (Joh. Chrysost. hom.IV. in 1. ad Tim. cap. 3. non hoc veluti sanciens dicit, quasi non liceat absque uxore Episcopum fieri, sed ejus rei modum constituens. Judæis quippe licitum erat etiam secundo matrimonio jungi, & duas itidem habere simul uxores, saltem mos iste fuit, maximè Gentilium,) vigilans, sobrius, compositus, hospitalis, aptus ad docendum, non vinosus, non percussor, non turpiter lucri cupidus, sed moderatus, alienus à pugnis, alienus ab avaritia, qui suæ domui bene præsit, qui liberos contineat in subjectione cum omni honestate, non novitius, habens bonum testimonium etiam ab extraneis, honestus, non bilinguis, habens mysterium fidei in bona conscientia, probatus tanquam Dei dispensator, non sibi pertinaciter placens, non iracundus, sed bonorum amans, justus, pius, continens, tenax fidelis illius sermonis, qui ad doctrinam facit, ut possit etiam exhortari per doctrinam sanam, & contradicentes convincere,1. Tim.III.2.3.4.6.7.8.9.10. Tit.I.6.7.8.9. talium etiam, oppidatim, sicut præceperat, constituendorum Presbyterorum gratiâ Apostolus Titum in Creta reliquerat v.5.
units.tr: IV. Above all in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus, where he also gives a general precept (1 Tim. 5:22): "Lay hands on no one hastily, and do not share in other men's sins" [Χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει, μηδὲ κοινώνει ἁμαρτίαις ἀλλοτρίαις]. The qualifications he lists are not only those of bishops but also those of deacons. Such a man must be blameless, the husband of one wife, [ἀνεπίληπτος, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ], (John Chrysostom, Homily 4 on 1 Timothy, ch. 3: he does not say this as though it were a law, as if a bishop could not be made without a wife, but as laying down the measure of the matter. For the Jews were permitted to marry again after a second marriage, and likewise to have two wives at the same time; indeed that custom was prevalent, especially among the Gentiles) watchful, sober, orderly, hospitable, apt to teach, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy of base gain, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous; one who rules his own house well, keeping his children in subjection with all dignity; not a novice; having a good testimony even from outsiders; serious, not double-tongued; holding the mystery of the faith in a good conscience; proved as God's steward; not self-willed, not quick-tempered, but a lover of good men, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast the faithful word as taught, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to convict those who speak against it (1 Tim. 3:2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10; Titus 1:6, 7, 8, 9). [νηφάλιος, σώφρων, κόσμιος, φιλόξενος, διδακτικὸς, μὴ πάροινος, μὴ πλήκτης, μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆς, ἀλλ' ἐπιεικής, ἄμαχος, ἀφιλάργυρος, τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου καλῶς προϊσταμένους, τέκνα ἔχων ἐν ὑποταγῇ μετὰ πάσης σεμνότητος, μὴ νεόφυτος, ἔχων μαρτυρίαν καλὴν καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξωθεν, σεμνὸς, μὴ διλόγος, ἔχων τὸ μυστήριον τῆς πίστεως ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει, δεδοκιμασμένος, ὡς Θεοῦ οἰκονόμος, μὴ αὐθάδης, μὴ ὀργίλος, ἀλλὰ φιλόξενος, φιλάγαθος, σώφρων, δίκαιος, ὅσιος, ἐγκρατής, ἀντεχόμενος τοῦ κατὰ τὴν διδαχὴν πιστοῦ λόγου, ἵνα δυνατὸς ᾖ καὶ παρακαλεῖν ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν]. Such men, too, the Apostle had left Titus in Crete to appoint, town by town, as he had directed, for the sake of ordaining elders (v. 5).

units.la: V. Respectu talium quoque pronunciat,1Tim.III.1. Εἴ τις ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται, καλοῦ ἔργου ἐπιθυμεῖ. Si quis Episcopatum appetit, bonum opus desiderat. Nempe, si quis, qui in examine humilitatis, non autem cæci amoris proprii, aptum se aliquo modo, doctrinâ instructum, vitæ inculpatæ amatorem &, quantum per infirmitates tes humanas licet, actorem atque gloriae Divinae Zelo instructum deprehendit, ejusdem gloriae Divinae in aedificatione fratrum promovendae studio magis quàm vitae commodius transigendae desiderio Ministerium aliquod Ecclesiasticum subire cupit, atque voluntatem illam suam iis, penes quos electionis cura est, exponit, non peccat, & non, quae Toftati minùs congrua expositio est, bonum opus male, sed bene desiderat, dum sic desideratur inspectio, visitatio, quae vocis Ἐπισκοπῆς Latina significatio est, officium, munus, labor; Onus potiùs, quàm honos, prodesse potiùs, quàm praesse, juxta Augustinum epist.204. ad Donatum, Episcopatus non Principatûs ac dominationis fastu, verùm curâ regiminis & charitatis affectu, ut Joh. Chrysostomus in loc. commentatur, nam Apostolus ad operis desiderium, non ad honoris ambitum provocat, teste Hieronymo in loc. pariter.
units.tr: V. He also pronounces concerning such men (1 Tim. 3:1): "If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work" [Εἴ τις ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται, καλοῦ ἔργου ἐπιθυμεῖ]. That is, if someone, who on examining himself, in humility and not in blind self-love, finds that he is in some measure fit, instructed in doctrine, a lover of blameless life, and, so far as human infirmities allow, zealous to act for the glory of God, and who desires to undertake some ecclesiastical ministry out of a wish to advance that divine glory by building up the brethren, rather than out of a desire for a more comfortable life, and who makes this desire known to those in whose hands the choice lies, does not sin. Nor does he, as the less suitable exposition of Tostatus has it, desire a good work badly, but well, since such inspection and visitation are desired. That is the Latin sense of the word episcopē: oversight, office, duty, labour; a burden rather than an honour, to serve rather than to rule, according to Augustine (Letter 204 to Donatus): the episcopate is exercised not with the pride of princely power and lordship, but with the care of governing and the affection of charity, as John Chrysostom comments on the passage. For the Apostle calls to a desire for the work, not to an ambition for honour, as Jerome likewise witnesses on the same passage.

units.la: VI. Si quis autem modestiùs de se sentiens & simul operis magnitudinem respiciens sibi diffisus, licèt compellatus (quod hodie inter rarò contingentia) difficulter munus oblatum acceptaptat, nec ille malè facit, sed laudem majoris modestiae meretur, nisi aliis agatur ignaviae, vel etiam dissimulatae superbiae, quae rogari vult, & sic gloriam vanè quaerit, principiis, & nisi se penitùs Ecclesiae necessitatibus subtrahat, & Divinam vocationem parvi aestimet, suae tantùm imbecillitatis, non etiam communis in aliis humanae fragilitatis, non etiam fidelitatis in vocante consideratione. Quibus rationibus fortè multi olim peccârunt graviter ex illis, qui planè inviti & reluctantes rapi & ordinari debuerunt, & nonnunquam, ne Episcopi ordinarentur, membris suis se mutilârunt, qualis Ammonius ille Monachus fuit, de quo Sozom. hist. Eccles. l.VI.28. narrat, quòd, cùm ordinandus esset, auriculam sibi abscideri, minatus, idem se cum lingua facturum, ni desisterent. Quales tamen, si ullo modo capaces fuerunt, ut dixi, graviter peccârunt.
units.tr: VI. If anyone, thinking more modestly of himself and at the same time considering the greatness of the task, distrusts himself and, although called (which today is rarely the case), accepts the office offered with reluctance, he does not act wrongly but deserves praise for greater modesty. This does not hold if the reluctance is sloth, or a pretended pride that wishes to be asked and so vainly seeks glory; nor if he entirely withdraws from the needs of the Church and makes little of the divine calling, considering only his own weakness, and not also the frailty common to other men and the faithfulness of him who calls. On such grounds perhaps many men formerly sinned grievously, those who had to be seized and ordained quite unwillingly and against their will; and sometimes, so that they would not be ordained bishops, they mutilated their own limbs. Such a one was that famous monk Ammonius, of whom Sozomen (Ecclesiastical History 6.28) relates that when he was to be ordained, he threatened that he would have his ear cut off, and would do the same to his tongue, unless they desisted. Such men, however, if they were in any way capable, as I have said, sinned grievously.

units.la: VII. Caeterùm olim, maximè persecutionum tempore numerus eorum, qui inviti ordinabantur, magnus, & ideò vix legitimus habitus fuit Episcopus, nisi multùm rogatus. Hinc nata etiam formula interrogatoria, in Ordinationibus adhiberi solita: Visne Episcopari? cum responsione: Nolo. Quae dum hodienum in Ordinationibus Pontificiis adhiberi solet, plerique strenuè contra mentem suam respondent, nonnisi per commodas reservationes menmentales à mendacio liberandi. Extrema & hic sunt vitanda, sed hodie, quando Ecclesiæ sæpe & in multis locis pace externâ fruuntur, & munera Ecclesiastica plerumque sustentationis satis commodæ adminicula sunt, maximè alterum illud de ambitu. Et quamvis propter numerositatem juventutis in spem Ecclesiæ educatæ & edoctæ, imò etiam propter virtutem & doctrinam in multis sæpè minùs æstimatam, quæ rationes vix nisi desideranti & opem suam offerenti munera concedunt, desiderare & opem suam offerre dicto modo liceat, tamen, si electio sine næviis & vitiis esse debet, probè cavendum est, ne 1. inepti & indigni, vel 2. potiorem propriæ utilitatis aut gloriæ, quàm verò utilitatis communis & gloriæ per eam Divinæ rationem habentes, vel 3. muneribus, promissionibus, adulationibus, importunis item precibus, & aliis malis mediis scopum attingere volentes, hèic aliquid sibi indulgeant. Contrà diligenter studendum est, ut, qui spem istam habet, & in spem istam educatur, quoad studia, mores, & laborum tolerantiam, aptus, dignus, magis magisque appareat, finis non sine mediis necessariis desideretur, atque ita hæc simul desiderentur, ἵνα ἡ προκοπὴ φανερὰ ἦ ἐν πᾶσιν, ut profectus manifestus sit in omnibus, 1.Tim.IV.15. & ut profectus ille sit potissimus desiderium explicandi modus, commendatio potissima; Finis autem porrò desiderandus est, media simul adhibenda sunt ædificationis proximi & gloriæ Divinæ maximè intuitu: ut illius respectu constituendus etiam oves, non lanam quærat, atque ad gregem sibi fortè committendum cum Apostolo dicere queat: Οὐ ζητῶ τὰ ὑμῶν ἀλλ' ὑμᾶς Non vestra quaero, sed vos; 2.Cor.XII.14. Quoad hanc verò ipsius unigeniti Filii vestigia premantur in veritate dicentis: Οὐ ζητῶ τὴν δόξαν μου. Non quaero gloriam meam, Joh.VIII.50. Et iterum: ἐὰν ἐγὼ δοξάζω ἐμαυτόν, ἡ δόξα μου οὐδέν ἐστιν. Si me ipsum glorifico, gloria mea nihil est, v.54. Et fidei servi illius, Paulum intelligo, severè quærentis & pronuntiantis: Ἀρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω, ἢ τὸν Θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ γὰρ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην. An Deum, an homines suadeo? An hominibus placere studeo? Si hominibus placerem, non essem servus Christi, Gal.I.10. His certè animo firmiter impressis ambitus, media illicita omnia aberunt, nec ibit operarius, nisi extrusus à Domino messis, Matth.IX.38. nec praedicabit concionator, nisi missus, Rom.X.15. rursus ad exemplum Christi, qui οὐχ ἑαυτὸν ἐδόξασε γενηθῆναι ἀρχιερέα, non se ipsum glorificavit, ut fieret primarius Sacerdos, Heb.V.5.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, formerly, especially in times of persecution, the number of those ordained against their will was large, and for that reason a man was hardly thought a lawful bishop unless he had been much entreated. Hence also arose the set question used in ordinations: "Do you wish to be made bishop?" with the answer: "I do not wish it." Since this is still customary in Papist ordinations, most men answer vigorously against their own mind, and are freed from lying only by convenient mental reservations. Extremes must be avoided here too. But today, when the Churches often and in many places enjoy external peace, and ecclesiastical offices are for the most part fairly comfortable means of support, the second of those points, that of ambition, is especially pressing. And although, on account of the large number of young people being raised and taught as the hope of the Church, and on account of virtue and learning, which in many places are too little valued, reasons that scarcely grant offices except to one who desires them and offers his help, it may be permitted to desire and offer one's help in the manner described, yet, if an election ought to be free of blemishes and faults, great care must be taken lest 1. the inept and unworthy, or 2. those who have more regard to their own advantage or glory than to the true common good and the glory of God, or 3. those who seek to reach their goal by gifts, promises, flattery, importunate prayers, and other evil means, indulge themselves in anything here. On the contrary, diligent effort must be made that the one who has this hope, and is being trained for it, should appear more and more apt and worthy in his studies, his morals, and his endurance of labour. The end must not be desired without the necessary means, and so both are to be desired together: "that his progress may be manifest to all" [ἵνα ἡ προκοπὴ φανερὰ ἦ ἐν πᾶσιν] (1 Tim. 4:15), and that this progress be the chief way of showing the desire and the chief recommendation. Moreover, the end is to be desired, and the means applied at the same time, chiefly with a view to the edification of one's neighbour and the glory of God, so that with that in view the man to be appointed seeks not the wool but the sheep, and can say with the Apostle to the flock perhaps committed to him: "I do not seek your things, but you" [Οὐ ζητῶ τὰ ὑμῶν ἀλλ' ὑμᾶς] (2 Cor. 12:14). As for the footsteps of the only-begotten Son himself, let them be followed in the truth of his words: "I do not seek my own glory" [Οὐ ζητῶ τὴν δόξαν μου] (John 8:50). And again: "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing" [ἐὰν ἐγὼ δοξάζω ἐμαυτόν, ἡ δόξα μου οὐδέν ἐστιν] (v. 54). And let us understand Paul, the faithful servant of that Lord, asking and declaring sternly: "Am I now persuading men or God? Or am I seeking to please men? If I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ" [Ἀρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω, ἢ τὸν Θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ γὰρ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην] (Gal. 1:10). Certainly, with these things firmly impressed on the mind, all unlawful means of ambition will be far away. No one will go out as a labourer unless he is thrust out by the Lord of the harvest (Matt. 9:38), and no preacher will preach unless he is sent (Rom. 10:15); and so again, following the example of Christ, who did not glorify himself to become high priest [οὐχ ἑαυτὸν ἐδόξασε γενηθῆναι ἀρχιερέα] (Heb. 5:5).

units.la: VIII. Dedimus hanc regulam, quia rectum est quoque mensura obliqui, & quia opposita juxta se posita magis elucescunt, & requisita legitima nævos vitiosæ electionis quodammodo illustrabunt. Non equidem diffiteri possumus, haud raro etiam in Ministerio legitimo Canonem deseri, sæpe electionem etiam Præconum veritatis Evangelicæ non usque quaque se bene habere, non semper optimos eligi, interdum etiam indignos, multos dari, qui se, gloriam suam, utilitatem suam magis quàm Deum, gloriam Dei, utilitatem proximi in Deo spectent, Ministerium appetentes, artes nonnunquam in subsidium vocari indecoras, aliquando secundùm favorem terrenis respectibus innixum munia Ecclesiastica hinc inde conferri; Ut imperfecta sunt omnia, quæ per homines geruntur imperfectos, in Ecclesia, quæ bonis malos mixtos habet, interdum etiam ad gubernacula sedentes; Ut veneni istius in Ecclesiam effusi guttæ quædam, etiam ubi antidota adhibentur, superstunt; Ut tempora nostra undiquaque corrupta apparent, hinc etiam judiciorum Divinorum in Ecclesia etiam, incipientibus illis à Domo Dei, fertilia. Interim tamen nævos & vitia Electionis Pontificum Romanorum ita minimè excusari, nec etiam in communi imbecillitate illis dignum operculum inveniri posse, multis modis ostendere proclive erit.
units.tr: VIII. We have laid down this rule because the straight is also measured by the crooked, and because opposites set side by side show up more clearly, and the lawful requirements will in some measure bring out the blemishes of a faulty election. We cannot deny that the canon is sometimes abandoned even in the lawful ministry, that the election of heralds of the Gospel of truth is not always in good order, that not always the best are chosen, sometimes even unworthy men, that many are admitted who seek the ministry for their own glory and advantage rather than for God's glory and their neighbour's good in God, that sometimes unbecoming arts are called in to help, and that at times ecclesiastical offices are handed out here and there on the basis of earthly favour. Everything done by imperfect men is imperfect, in a Church that has good and bad mixed together, and sometimes even bad men sit at the helm. Some drops of that poison poured into the Church remain even where antidotes are applied. Our times appear corrupt on every side, and hence the judgements of God are also fruitful in the Church, beginning, as they do, at the house of God. Meanwhile, it will be easy to show in many ways that the blemishes and vices of the election of the Roman Pontiffs are in no way excused by this, nor can a fitting covering for them be found in general human weakness.

units.la: IX. Et primò quidem ex sequenti tractatione nostra manifestum fore confido, in Electione Pontificum Romanorum, ex quo plùs cæteris Episcopis esse voluerunt, tantò majorem nævorum & vitiorum confluxum reperiri, quam in cæterorum Episcoporum sive Ecclesiarum Rectorum electionibus, quantò cæteris Episcopis & Ecclesiarum Rectoribus majores esse voluerunt, & quoad usurpationem in spiritualibus, potentiam mundanam atque divitias terrenas revera facti sunt; atque proin ibi inexhaustum nævorum & vitiorum Oceanum esse, & semper esse, dum alibi in comparatione vix parvi rivuli currunt, originem etiam suam ex isto corruptionis Oceanoferè habentes, sæpissimè etiam vel in afflictionum, vel ferventis Zeli Divini æstu tantùm non exsiccati; ut vel hinc satis grave contra electionem istam præjudicium formari possit, quòd jam à multis seculis Conclavia corruptionis aquis iStis inædificantur, quæ & intima eorum pervadunt & inficiunt, nec spirare potest ibi aër nisi ita infectus, veneno puta ambitionis, Simoniæ, & humanorum consiliorum, quibus peritissimi etiam Politici vix suffisufficerent, mundanarum artium in decipiendo, obliquè agendo, quas vel ipse minùs calluit Macchiavellus, scilicet in electione Vicarii Jesu Christi, humilis, abjecti, sanctè simplicis, scilicet in electione Capitis, Sponsi & Monarchae Ecclesiae ipsius, regni istius, quod non est de hoc mundo ! Joh. XVIII. 36.
units.tr: IX. And first, I trust it will be made plain from our following treatment that in the election of the Roman Pontiffs, since they wished to be greater than other bishops, a much greater confluence of blemishes and vices is found than in the elections of other bishops or rectors of churches. For as they wished to be greater than other bishops and rectors of churches, so in fact they have become, in respect of usurpation in spiritual things, worldly power and earthly riches. Therefore there is there an inexhaustible ocean of blemishes and vices, and there always will be, whereas elsewhere, in comparison, only small streams flow, which also have their origin largely in that ocean of corruption, and very often are dried up, if not entirely, by the heat of afflictions or of fervent zeal for God. So from this alone a serious prejudice against that election can be formed: for many centuries now the conclaves have been built with these waters of corruption, which both pervade and infect their innermost parts, and the air there cannot breathe unless it is so infected, with the poison, that is, of ambition, simony and human counsels, and the worldly arts of deceiving and acting by indirect means, with which even the most skilled politicians would hardly suffice, and which Machiavelli himself knew less well. That is, in the election of the Vicar of Jesus Christ, who was humble, abject and holily simple; that is, in the election of the Head, Spouse and Monarch of the Church itself, of that kingdom which is not of this world! John 18:36.

units.la: X. Cùm tamen secundò aquae corruptionis, si vel atria Domûs Dei hîc & nunc alluerent, in Sanctum Sanctorum minùs, imò nullomodo pertingere deberent. Peccetur sanè in electione Cleri inferioris saepe & multis modis, ast quis eadem praesumere audeat de electione summi Pontificis, Vice-Christi, Vice-Dei, & alterius in terris Dei, quas appellationes ab initio Differt. I. vidimus? Sit nonnunquam vitiosa electio Ministrorum ministrantium & exiguâ in exiguo distric-tu potestate praeditorum, ast cui liceat vitiosam credere electionem ipsius Magistri, Domini & Monarchae universa-lis, qui eâdem planè potestate gaudet, jure eodem cum Christo, cu-jus ex asse haeres dicitur, & cujus tam sancta, & tam ab omni nae-vo aliena electio fuit, & cum Petro, extra suam & in longè altio-ri sphaera collocato, cujus etiam modò Successor, modò Vicarius audit, & cujus etiam tam sancta, & tam ab omni nevo aliena electi-o fuit? Laborent interdum electiones vulgarium Praeconum, quorum tot in orbe Christiano millia Gregem Domini pascunt, actiones illae ordinariae & quasi quotidianae naevis suis, ast quomodo idem dicei poterit de electione Pontificum Romanorum, quae senza alcun dubio è la maggiore e la più sublime, la più grave & la più importante attione, che nella Christianità si tratti, anzi che si sacci al mondo ; sine omni dubio est maximè ardua actio, qua in Christiano orbe, imò in toto mundo, fiat, juxta verba Conclavium Sixti V. & Innocentii IX. ab initio Differt. I. pariter citata? Provideatur minùs perfectè necessitatibus minoribus, ast cur non optimè provideatur Papae carentiae, per electionem à vitiis & naevis liberam, quando, ut Glossa Clement. l. 1. Tit. 3. §. Caeterùm. habet, Papa carentia est maxima necessitas?
units.tr: X. Yet, secondly, if the waters of corruption were to wash the courts of the house of God here and now, they ought much less, indeed in no way, to reach the Holy of Holies. Certainly mistakes are made in the election of the lower clergy often and in many ways; but who would dare to presume the same of the election of the supreme Pontiff, the Vicar of Christ, Vice-God, and another God on earth, titles which we saw at the beginning, in Dissertation I? Sometimes the election of ministers who serve, and who have only a little power within a small district, is faulty; but who may believe that the election of the Master, Lord and universal Monarch is faulty, he who enjoys exactly the same power, by the same right as Christ, whose sole heir he is said to be, and whose election was so holy and so free of every blemish? He is placed apart from Peter, in a far higher sphere, and he is now called Peter's successor, now his vicar, and his election too was so holy and so free of every blemish. The elections of common heralds, by whom so many thousands in the Christian world feed the flock of the Lord, sometimes suffer from their blemishes in those ordinary and almost daily actions; but how can the same be said of the election of the Roman Pontiffs, which without any doubt is the greatest, most sublime, most weighty and most important action that is transacted in Christendom, indeed that is done in the world, and which, according to the words of the Conclaves of Sixtus V and Innocent IX, cited likewise from the beginning in Dissertation I, is without doubt the most arduous action that takes place in the Christian world, indeed in the whole world? Let there be less than perfect provision for lesser needs, but why should provision not be made in the best way for the vacancy of the Papacy, through an election free of vices and blemishes, when, as the Gloss in Clement. book 1, title 3, §. Caeterum has it, the vacancy of the Papacy is the greatest necessity?

units.la: XI. Optimè etiam & peculiari modo omninò provideri debet, & providetur tertiò, si verum subest vocibus sequentibus; Ut dicit Barb. Sunt verba Glossae l. c. §. Verum, quia electio Papae est negotium Dei, magis quàm alia electiones c. licet. §. eo idem Bald. in l. 1. Col. IIII. C. de la lib. tol. quamquam Hus & Vicheif per sacras Scriptu-ras dicant, esse negotium Diaboli. Fonta. Quibus consentiunt voces quasi ordinariæ Conclavium Scriptorum ; Ita enim in Conclavi Pauli IV. legimus; Si vedessero li miracoli del Conclave, e come è Iddio veramente quello,che fa il Papa ; Id est: Apparuerunt miracula Conclavis, & quòd Deus revera Papam faciat. Sic & author Conclavis sequentis Sixti V. qui tamen artificia ipsius Sixti in progressu, & quomodo unum ex altero fluxerit, minimè silet, ab initio peculiares in ista electione Dei curas laudat. Cui initio finis Conclavis sequentis Gregorii XIV his verbis optimè respondet, licet minùs veritati: Si è veduto manifestamente, inquit Author, che questa operatione èstata tutta di Dio &c. Id est: Manifestè apparuit, hanc operationem omnem à Deo profectam esse. Fini rursus respondet initium Conclavis rursus immediatè sequentis: A questa si grande attione non è dubio alcuno, inquit Author ille, e per prova manifestamente si vede, che assiste semper lo Spirito Santo &c. Id est: Nullum est dubium, & manifestè apparet, semper magna illi actioni assistere Spiritum S. Qui & totum illud opus Spiritui Sancto adscribi solere docet, dum paulò post narrat, paulò ante lucem, cùm S. Quattro mox eligendus esset, multos per Conclave obambulâsse, non tam, ut ipse credat, ad eum excludendum, quanto per provare, se lo Spirito Santo continuava à dar segno,di voler,che l'elettione cadesse in lui; quàm vero ad videndum, num Spiritus S. adhuc velit,ut ipse eligatur; Quamvis statim ibi subjungat, alios etiam ibi obambulâsse per loro interessi, ob commoda propria. Sicut quoque ex Conclavi sequente Clementis VIII. discimus, immediatam ibi inspirationam nonnunquam exspectari, postquàm enim, referente Authore, Cardinalis Alexandrinus, cùm de S. Severina ageretur, cujus exclusoribus se associabat, per aliquod temporis spatium in genua provolurus fuisset, tandem surgens dixit: Jo ho pregato nostro Signore,che me inspirâsse à far cosa à suo servitio,ma perche non ho sentito ne pur pungermi il Cuore, si deve credere, che questo huomo, non sia data di Dio. Id est: Rogavi Dominum nostrum, ut mihi inspiraret quid ad servitium ejus facere debeam, sed quia ne leviter quidem cor meum pungi sensi, credendum est, hominem istum non à Deo datum esse. Similiter Conclave sequens Leonis XI. testimonium peculiaris in electione Pontificum Regiminis Divini exhibet. Non minùs in Conclavi Clementis X. sperabatur in favorem Odeschalchii,che volendo una volta lo Spirito Santo doppo tanta lunghezza risolvere questa creatione, lo faccia contro ogni Politica humana,velle Spiritum S. tandem & post tam longam durationem decernere vere illam creationem, eámque efficere contra omnem Politicam humanam. Hinc etiam Gregorius XV. in Bulla requirit, ut tota res directioni & gubernaculo Spiritûs Sancti permittatur. Ex eadem certa persuasione Franciscus Lottinus ita Dissertationem suam de Conclavi orditur: Summum Pontificem solo divino nutu creari, eligique, tanquam oculatus testis profiteri & attestari queo &c. Atque ordinaria est acclamatio Pontificis recens electi: A Deo electo; quae similiter de extraordinaria directione intelligenda est. Certè non videtur in negotio, cui Deus tam singulari modo Spiritu suo praeest, (nisi vana sit illa jactantia;) nævos & vitia intervenire posse, videtur saltem, vitia multa intervenire, intervenientia unquam obtinere non posse.
units.tr: XI. It must also be provided for in the best and a peculiar way altogether, and it is provided for, thirdly, if there lies under these following words something true: As Barbosa says. These are the words of the Gloss, l.c., §. Verum: because the election of the Pope is God's business more than other elections, c. licet, §. eo; the same Bald. in l. 1, col. 4, C. de la lib. tol.; although Hus and Wycliffe say from the Holy Scriptures that it is the devil's business. Fonta. The ordinary exclamations of the Conclave writers agree with these. Thus in the Conclave of Paul IV we read: If they had seen the miracles of the Conclave, and how God truly is the one who makes the Pope; that is: The miracles of the Conclave appeared, and that God really makes the Pope. So also the author of the following Conclave of Sixtus V, who nevertheless does not at all keep silent about Sixtus's own devices as the matter proceeds, and how one led from another, praises at the outset the peculiar care of God in that election. The beginning of the Conclave of Gregory XIV that follows answers the end of the previous one very well with these words, though less truthfully: It has been clearly seen, says the author, that this whole operation has been of God etc. That is: Manifestly it appeared that this whole operation proceeded from God. Again, the beginning of the Conclave immediately following answers this end: In regard to this so great action there is no doubt, says that author, and it is clearly seen by proof that the Holy Spirit always assists etc. That is: There is no doubt, and it is manifestly apparent that the Holy Spirit always assists that great action. He also teaches that the whole of that work is usually ascribed to the Holy Spirit, while he relates shortly afterwards that, shortly before dawn, when Cardinal Quattro was about to be elected, many walked about the Conclave, not, as he himself believes, to exclude him, but to prove whether the Holy Spirit was still giving a sign that he wished the election to fall on him; or rather to see whether the Holy Spirit still wished him to be elected; although he at once adds there that others also walked about there for their own interests, for private advantage. As we also learn from the following Conclave of Clement VIII, immediate inspiration is sometimes awaited there. For after, as the author reports, Cardinal Alessandrino, when the matter concerned Santa Severina, whose excluders he joined, had for some space of time been about to throw himself on his knees, at last he rose and said: I have prayed our Lord that he would inspire me to do something for his service, but because I have not felt my heart pricked even slightly, it must be believed that this man is not given by God. That is: I asked our Lord to inspire me what I ought to do for his service, but because I felt my heart not even slightly pricked, it must be believed that this man has not been given by God. Likewise the following Conclave of Leo XI offers testimony of a peculiar divine government in the election of Pontiffs. Nor was it less hoped in the Conclave of Clement X, in favour of Odescalchi, that the Holy Spirit, being willing at last after so long a delay to decide this creation, would bring it about against all human policy: that the Holy Spirit would at last and after so long a delay truly decree that creation and bring it about against all human policy. Hence also Gregory XV requires in the Bull that the whole matter be left to the direction and government of the Holy Spirit. From the same firm conviction, Francesco Lottini begins his Dissertation on the Conclave thus: I can profess and attest, as an eyewitness, that the Supreme Pontiff is created and chosen by the divine nod alone, etc. And the ordinary acclamation of a newly elected Pontiff is: To the God-elected; which likewise must be understood of an extraordinary direction. Surely in a matter over which God presides in so singular a way by his Spirit (unless that boast is empty), blemishes and vices do not seem able to intervene; or at least, if many vices do intervene, they cannot ever prevail.

units.la: XII. Quibus quartò heic viam praecludere deberet frequens de successione, quae per electiones istas oritur, jactantia jam Dissert. III. paucis notata.
units.tr: XII. Fourthly, the frequent boast about succession, which arises through these elections, should cut off my path here. I have already noted it briefly in Dissertation III.

units.la: Successionem Episcoporum notam faciunt Ecclesiae, maximè Romanorum, à quibus & caeteri mittendi sunt, & sine quibus caeteros mitti atque succedere posse negant. Atque de illa Romanorum Pontificum à Christo ad sua tempora continuata successione B. Platinae de vitis Pontificum Romanorum historiae editor Bernardus Gualtherius in epist. dedic. ad Reverendiss. & Illustriss. D. D. Theodorum, Dei & Apostolicæ sedis Gratiâ Episc. Paderb. S. R. J. Principem, Dominum Clementiss. ita loquitur, quòd Catholicos omni censu, praescriptione, authoritate, tabulis & instrumentis instructos esse doceat, cùm ad sua juste possidenda, tum ad hæreticos horum temporum velut injustos Ecclesiae tituli & fundi captatores jure depellendos & profligandos. Oportebit igitur, ut ista Ecclesiae nota non sit vitiosa, ut successio ista sit legitima, continua & non interrupta, proin ut nulli intrusi, invasores, usurpatores, &, ut verbis Gualtherii ipsius utar, injusti Ecclesiae (& universalium Ecclesiae Pastorum;) tituli & fundi captatores, sedem illam occupaverint, uno verbo, ut census justus, praescriptio bona, authoritas sufficiens, tabula certae, instrumenta authentica sint, ne, his deficientibus, injustè non sua, sed aliena ipsimet possideant, jure depellendi & profligandi ipsimet, ne, his deficientibus, vana sit illa etiam & stolidæ jactantia mentis.
units.tr: The Churches, and especially the Romans, make the succession of bishops a mark of the Church. From these bishops all others must be sent, and without them they deny that others can be sent or can succeed. On that unbroken succession of the Roman Pontiffs from Christ down to their own times, Bernardus Gualtherius, editor of Platina's history of the lives of the Roman Pontiffs, speaks in his dedicatory epistle to the Most Reverend and Illustrious Lord Theodor, by the grace of God and the Apostolic See Bishop of Paderborn, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, his most gracious Lord: he teaches that Catholics are furnished with every kind of title, prescription, authority, records and instruments, both to possess justly what is theirs and to drive out and crush by right the heretics of our times, like unjust grabbers of the Church's titles and lands. It will therefore be necessary, for this mark of the Church to be sound and this succession to be lawful, continuous and uninterrupted, that no intruders, invaders or usurpers, and (to use Gualtherius' own words) no unjust grabbers of the titles and lands of the Church (and of the Pastors of the universal Church), have occupied that see. In a word, the title must be just, the prescription good, the authority sufficient, the records certain and the instruments authentic. Otherwise, if these are lacking, they themselves are unjustly holding what is not theirs but another's, and they themselves deserve to be driven out and crushed. Without these, that boast of theirs is empty and foolish.

units.la: XIII. Quintò electiones à vitiis & nævis immunes postulat dogma etiam illud Pontificium, quo omnia, quae in Ecclesia peraguntur & valida esse debent, quodammodò à dignitate Ministri stri suspendunt, quatenus nimirum necessitatem intentionis, saltem faciendi illud, quod facit Ecclesia, asserunt. Quâ ratione adhuc magis opus est dignorum & piorum Pontificum digna electione, nempe habentium bonam intentionem, Ecclesiae utilitatem quaerendi, omnia ad salutem fidelium dirigendi, nec Deum & Divina, quod nonnunquam accidit, ludibrio habentium, quo in casu etiam, quae per tales decernuntur, indulgentur &c. ex hypothesi mala censeri debent. Cùm contra apud nos indignitas electionis & sequens administratio vitiosa quidem gravissimum peccatum habeatur authorum, non tamen in damnum Ecclesiae eatenus redundet, quemadmodum etiam successionem localem non urgemus, illâ officii & doctrinae merito contenti, quomodo minus est Ecclesiae ab electionibus interdum vitiosis periculum.
units.tr: XIII. Fifthly, the Papist dogma also demands that elections be free of faults and blemishes. By this dogma everything carried out in the Church and required to be valid depends, in some measure, on the dignity of the minister, inasmuch as they maintain the necessity of intention, at least of doing what the Church does. For this reason there is all the more need for a worthy election of worthy and pious Popes, who have a good intention, seek the advantage of the Church, direct everything to the salvation of the faithful, and do not make a mockery of God and divine things, as sometimes happens. In that case, even what such men decree, grant indulgences for and so on must be judged bad by their own hypothesis. With us, on the other hand, the unworthiness of an election and the faulty administration that follows are regarded as a very grave sin of those responsible, yet they do not redound to the harm of the Church in that respect. Just as we do not insist on local succession, being content with the merit of office and doctrine, so the Church is in less danger from elections that are sometimes faulty.

units.la: XIV. Gravissimum autem eidem imminueret periculum à parte Pontificum summorum vitiosè electorum, quia Sextò talium, imò quadantenus etiam eligentium, potestas ἀνυπεύθυνος, nemini subjecta fingitur. Si quid apud nos in electionibus peccatur, adest Christianus Magistratus, ad cujus tanquam nutricii Ecclesiæ munus hoc pertinet, & providere debet, ne Respublica Christiana aliquid detrimenti capiat, ne ambitio, & cognata mala in Ecclesia regnent, ne lupi gregem Domini vastent, ut contrà digni praeficiantur Pastores; Et si vel obtinuerit malè electus, re posthac cognitâ, vel patefactis aliâs malis mali introitùs fructibus, coërceri, deponi debet. Similia autem respectu Pontificum Romanorum adhiberi nequeunt; Quippe & Collegium Cardinalium eligentium sede vacante superiorem non habere dicitur, & qui Bullarum juxta Dissert, praced. n. penult. Executores constituti sunt, nec praesentes electioni assistunt, nec etiam Authoritatem ad Cardinales exorbitantes plerosque coercendam habent; & Papa vitiosè licèt electus omnes alios ridet, cùm & malè praesidenti nemo; Quid facis? dicere, nedum eum deponere atque ita infinitis & quotidianis Ecclesiae damnis occurrere audeat.
units.tr: XIV. Moreover, the greatest danger to the Church on this score would come from the Popes who are elected faultily, because, sixthly, the power of such men, and to some extent of those who elect them, is imagined to be unaccountable [ἀνυπεύθυνος], subject to no one. If anything is done wrongly among us in elections, there is a Christian magistrate, to whose office, as nursing father of the Church, this belongs. He ought to take care that the Christian commonwealth suffers no harm, that ambition and the evils akin to it do not reign in the Church, that wolves do not lay waste the flock of the Lord, and that worthy ministers are set over it instead. And if a man has been badly elected and has obtained office, then once the matter is known, or once the evil fruits of his entry have otherwise come to light, he ought to be restrained and deposed. But similar measures cannot be applied to the Roman Pontiffs. For the College of Cardinals, which elects during a vacancy of the see, is said to have no superior. The executors appointed under the bulls, as noted in the penultimate note of the preceding Dissertation, neither attend the election nor have authority to restrain the many Cardinals who go beyond their bounds. And a Pope, however badly elected, laughs at all others, since no one dares to say to one who governs badly, "What are you doing?", much less to depose him, and so meet the endless and daily losses of the Church.

units.la: XV. Ut ita omninò Electio Pontificum Romanorum naevis & vitiis carere deberet; Quibus tamen, ut dixi, & jam ostendam, abundat, atque ita abundat, ut impossibile sit, enarrare omnia; Oceanum merito vocavi inexhaustum; Non datur heic scrutari quasvis profunditates. Ne quis igitur à me perfectam descriptionem exspectet; Supra attuli confessiones ipsorummet Conclavium vium Scriptorum, qui ἀυλόπλω quoad multa fuerunt, & tamen testantur, se partem duntaxat assecutos esse, pauciores ex ipsis Cardinalibus exactam omnium fere habere notitiam, non omnibus licere esse tam felicibus, à se tantùm radios quosdam visos esse; si autem non omnia viderunt, nec quæ viderunt, omnia dederunt, nec ego, quæ dederunt omnia & singula, sed præcipua tantùm ad certas nævorum & vitiorum classes reducta enarrabo, in quantillo respectu illorum, quæ contigerunt, subsistam, facilè colligi poterit, interim tamen facilè etiam denuò cognoscere licebit, ex ungue Leonem, ἡ̈ν ἐκ ξυγραφῆδε τὸ ὑφασμα.
units.tr: XV. So, although the election of the Roman Pontiffs ought to be wholly free of blemishes and faults, it nevertheless abounds in them, as I have said and shall now show. It abounds so greatly that it is impossible to relate everything. I rightly called it an inexhaustible ocean. It is not allowed here to probe every depth. So let no one expect from me a complete description. I have already cited the confessions of the Conclave writers themselves. They were unskilled in sailing [ἀυλόπλω] in many respects, yet they testify that they grasped only part, that few of the Cardinals themselves have almost complete knowledge of everything, that not everyone is allowed to be so fortunate, and that they saw only certain rays. If they did not see everything, nor did they give all that they saw, then neither will I give all and each thing that they gave. I shall recount only the principal faults, reduced to certain classes of blemishes and vices, and I shall rest content with a small sample of those things that have happened. Still, it will be easy to gather from this, and easy too to recognise again, the lion from its claw [ἐκ ξυγραφῆδε τὸ ὑφασμα: from the claw, the lion].

units.la: XVI. Classes nævorum & vitiorum tres constituo, præcipua ad eas reducturus.
units.tr: XVI. I set up three classes of blemishes and faults, and I shall reduce the principal points to them.

units.la: Nempe hac etiam in electione Pontificum Romanorum sunt 1. eligentes, 2. electio & 3. illi, qui eliguntur, consiederandi. Et cùm unum quodque horum trium distincti nævi, vitia distincta propiùs respiciant, hinc etiam nævos & vitia ratione eligentium. 2. ratione electionis ipsius & 3. ratione eorum, qui eliguntur; ob oculos ponere animus est.
units.tr: There are, indeed, in this election of the Roman Pontiffs also: 1. the electors, 2. the election, and 3. those who are elected, to be considered. And since each of these three has its own distinct blemishes and faults, I intend to set before our eyes the blemishes and faults with respect to the electors; 2. with respect to the election itself; and 3. with respect to those who are elected.

units.la: XVII. Nævorum & vitiorum ratione eligentium partem jam supra, ubi de formis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum diversis actum est, habitis occasionibus tetigimus, circa quam proin heic breviores erimus, nonnulla vel indicâsse contenti. Primum autem nævum non immeritò facimus, quòd de eligentibus in electione hac nihil planè habet Scriptura Sacra, nec sine causa quis postularet, illos sibi ex sacris literis ostendi, vel levi indicio ibi memoratos, cùm multa longè minoris, præsuppositio Papatu, momenti enarrent fusiùs, & saltem ex eventu indicium ejusmodi ex hypothesi necessarium appareat, quia de jure illos Ecclesiæ Monarchas eligendi variis temporibus varie à variis litigatum fuit, quibus litibus Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ tam funestis Spiritus Sanctus omninò aliquo modo obviam ivisset, si ejusmodi potestatem ipse instituisset. XVIII. Secundus nævus ratione eligentium sit, quòd illi in hunc usque diem toties variârunt, &, ut prolixè à nobis enarratum est, modò Prædecessores, modò Clerus & populus, modò Imperatores, modò Cardinales, Electores fuerunt; Cùm tamen, ut jam etiam notatum est, mutationes tales in re tanti momenti vix commodè intervenisse videantur; prout etiam singulorum istorum Electorum rationem nævos, partim revera, partim ex hypothesi erronea augere ostendimus; Nec ab uno Electorum genere ad aliud revelatione nova, sed, vel postulante id confusione priori, vel per usurpationem injustam transitum est.
units.tr: XVII. We have already touched on part of the blemishes and faults concerning the electors above, where we treated the various forms of the election of the Roman Pontiffs and the occasions that arose; so here I shall be briefer, content to point out a few things. The first blemish I rightly note is that Holy Scripture says nothing at all about the electors in this election. Nor without reason would anyone demand that they be shown to him from the sacred letters, or at least mentioned there by a slight indication, since it describes at length many matters of far less importance, given the presupposition of the Papacy. And at least from the outcome, such an indication would appear necessary on that hypothesis, because at various times the right to elect these monarchs of the Church was disputed in various ways by various parties. The Holy Spirit would surely have met these quarrels, so destructive to Church and Commonwealth, in some way, if he himself had instituted such a power. XVIII. The second blemish with respect to the electors is that down to this day they have varied so often: as we have related at length, they have been now the predecessors, now the clergy and people, now the emperors, now the cardinals. Yet, as has already been noted, such changes in a matter of such great importance hardly seem to have occurred fittingly. Likewise we have shown that the character of each of these electors increases the blemishes, partly in fact and partly on an erroneous hypothesis. Nor has the passage from one kind of elector to another come about by new revelation, but either because the earlier confusion demanded it, or through unjust usurpation.

units.la: XIX. Tertium vitium in eo ponimus, quod Electores quicunque potestatem, quam per Electionem conferre dicuntur, aliter, ac in aliis Electionibus obtinet, ex hypothesi etiam non habent; Si solos Electores Praedecessores excipiamus; quibus etiam sola favet eaque salsissima hypothesis. Neque enim vel populo & Clero, vel Imperatoribus, vel ipsis etiam denique Cardinalibus immensam illam potestatem Pontificiam tribuunt, sed, ultimo memoratis, etiam, jurisdictionem in spiritualibus supremam denegant. Jam autem quod quis non habet, illud quoque alteri dare non potest.
units.tr: XIX. Third, we count as a fault that all electors whatever do not have, even on their own hypothesis, the power which they are said to confer through election, in the way it holds in other elections; if we except the predecessors alone, for whom alone this most absurd hypothesis is favourable. For they do not attribute that immense papal power either to the people and clergy, or to the emperors, or finally even to the cardinals; indeed, to the last-named they even deny supreme jurisdiction in spiritual matters. Now, what someone does not have, he cannot give to another either.

units.la: XX. Quarto vitium quoad Electores dici potest, quod incertum est in communione Pontificia, an habuerint & habeant requisita necessaria. Requisitum ante omnia & omnibus Electoribus necessarium dubio procul erit baptismus; Illum autem Electoribus revera collatum esse, apud Pontificios non constat, cum & non constet de intentione baptizantis, neque etiam de intentione baptizantem ordinantis, & sic deinceps; & aliquando forte debita baptismi formula, per obstetrices maxime, non adhibeatur, ut exemplum memoratu dignum in certo Cardinale ostenditur, qui, cognito baptismo suo in nomen B. Virginis, ordinationis, celebrationis, & omnia acta sua irrita pronuntiarit. Eadem incertitudo est quoad Episcopalem, Presbyteralem & Diaconi gradus, quos in Cardinalibus Electoribus hodiernis requirunt, & quos a legitimis legitime & cum intentione iis collatos esse, pariter incertum est, ut etiam non constat de ipsa dignitate Cardinalitia, quam cum intentione a digno dignis datam esse, aeque incertum, imo respectu multorum, quoad ultimum hocce, manifeste, juxta ea, quae supra diximus, falsum est.
units.tr: XX. Fourth, a fault with respect to the electors can be said to be that, in Papist communion, it is uncertain whether they have had and have the necessary requisites. The first requisite, and one necessary for all electors, is undoubtedly baptism. But that it has really been conferred on the electors is not established among the Papists, since it is not established concerning the intention of the one baptizing, nor of the one ordaining the baptizer, and so on. And sometimes perhaps the proper form of baptism is not used, especially by midwives; a memorable example of this is shown in a certain cardinal, who, when his baptism in the name of the Blessed Virgin became known, declared his ordinations, celebrations and all his acts void. The same uncertainty attaches to the episcopal, presbyteral and diaconal orders, which they require in the present cardinal electors; and whether these have been legitimately conferred on them by legitimate ministers and with intention is equally uncertain. Nor is it established concerning the cardinalitial dignity itself, whether it has been given with intention by a worthy man to worthy men. This is equally uncertain, indeed, with respect to many, and in regard to this last point it is manifestly false, according to what we said above.

units.la: XX. Quinto respectu Cardinalium eligentium seorsim illud naevo non carere videtur, quod cum Diaconorum saltem gradum habere debeant, interdum tamen tales ex aequo per Dispensationem Pontificiam, & paribus suffragiis concurrunt, qui ne quidem Diaconi, sed meri Laici sunt; Qualis in Conclavi Sixti V. Cardinalis Austriae nondum in Diaconum ordinatus & tamen admissus memoratur; Sed eo magis hic vitiosum illud haberi debet ab iis, qui le laicali mani, manus laicas, ut suprà vidimus, tantopere abominantur electionis operi qualitercunque admotas.
units.tr: XX. Fifth, with respect to the cardinal electors taken separately, this seems not free of blemish. Although they ought to have at least the rank of deacon, yet sometimes such men come in on equal terms, by papal dispensation and with equal votes, who are not even deacons but mere laymen. Such was, in the conclave of Sixtus V, a cardinal of Austria who is recorded as admitted though not yet ordained a deacon. All the more ought this to be regarded as faulty by those who, as we saw above, so greatly abhor the lay hand, lay hands, applied in any way whatever to the work of election.

units.la: XXII. Sextus nævus itidem quoad Cardinales speciatim hic est, quòd respectu officii sui, ut patet ex dictis, multipliciter Canones Ecclesiasticos violant, atque adeò ad Electiones Canonicas eatenus inepti haberi debent.
units.tr: XXII. The sixth blemish, likewise with respect to the cardinals in particular, is that with respect to their office, as is clear from what has been said, they violate the ecclesiastical canons in many ways, and so must be held unfit for canonical elections so far.

units.la: XXIII. Septimò respectu eorundem & quorumvis aliorum Electorum ignoratur, an intentionem habuerint & habeant, Pontificem summum, & quidem hunc aut illum creandi; Imò contrarium, ut ex Differt.VI. manifestum fiet, aliquando scitur. Sed ex intentione agentium & hinc validitatem actionis dependere asserent, si convenienter suis hypothesibus docere volent Pontificii.
units.tr: XXIII. Seventh, with respect to these and all other electors whatever, it is not known whether they have had, and have, the intention of creating the supreme Pontiff, and this or that one in particular. Indeed, the contrary is sometimes known, as will become clear from Differt. VI. But they assert that the validity of the act depends on the intention of the agents, if the Papists wish to teach consistently with their hypotheses.

units.la: XXIV. Octavò Picus Mirandula, qui scripsit nobis Theoremata de fide Theor. 4. suppeditat exemplum Pontificis, cujus electioni duæ tertiæ Cardinalium assensæ non sunt; Quod tamen in electionibus Pontificum legitimis, Pontificum constitutionibus requiri, ex dictis constat. Sic etiam in Decretalibus de electo à minori ⅓ parte agitur; Imò in Clementinis dicitur, electionem uno Cardinalium contradicente fieri non posse; At quàm multis multi contradixerunt?
units.tr: XXIV. Eighth, Pico della Mirandola, who wrote to us the theses concerning faith, Theor. 4., supplies an example of a pontiff to whose election two-thirds of the cardinals did not assent. Yet it is clear from what has been said that the constitutions of the pontiffs require this in legitimate elections of pontiffs. Likewise in the Decretals concerning one elected by a minority, a third part is treated. Indeed, in the Clementines it is said that an election cannot be made if one of the cardinals objects. But how many objected, and how often!

units.la: XXV. Nonò notissimum est omnibus, qui Conclavia legerunt, Capita Factionum, sive jam Principum commoda promovere studeant certorum, sive Nepotes sint defunctorum Pontificum, sive aliàs certum Cardinalium sibi adhærentium numerum gubernent, ferè solos à longo tempore esse Paparum electores, cæteris cæco impetu sequentibus, vel tanquam à torrente abreptis; De quo tamen posthac plura dicenda erunt.
units.tr: XXV. Ninth, it is most well known to all who have read the conclaves that the heads of factions, whether they seek to advance the interests of certain princes, or are nephews of deceased pontiffs, or otherwise govern a certain number of cardinals adhering to them, have for a long time been almost alone the electors of the popes, the rest following with blind impetus, or as if swept away by a torrent. About this, however, more will be said hereafter.

units.la: XXVI. Decimus nævus non immeritò numeratur, quòd etiam excommunicatis, hereticis & notoriè criminosis, ut loquuntur, jus electionis aperte vindicant; Videatur Decretal. l.1. tit. 6. c.39. Illa quotidiana. Item l. 6. c. 9. si quando. Clement. l. 1. c.2. §. caterum. Et, qui pluribus ista tractat Ant. de Rosellis Mon. p.2. c.9. & 10. nec non Onuphr. annot. ad Greg. X. ejus constitutionem de hoc referens; ut & Bulla Pii IV. quæ quoque metui periculi, quod ex conversatione cum excommunicatis talibus oriri posset, occurrit &c. Digna scilicet res est, & probè cum hypothesibus conveniens, quòd, qui non sunt de Ecclesia, dant caput Ecclesiæ, à cujus constitutione fideles & pii Magistratus sub poena sacrilegii procul arcentur, & quòd, qui sunt instar Ethnicorum & Publicanorum, Christi Vicarium & alterum in terris Deum eligere possunt, qui tamen nequidem ad minimam partem communionis Ecclesiasticæ admitti possunt!
units.tr: XXVI. The tenth blemish is rightly counted: that they openly claim the right of election even for excommunicated, heretics and the notoriously criminal, as they say. See Decretal. l.1. tit. 6. c.39. Illa quotidiana. Likewise l. 6. c. 9. si quando. Clement. l. 1. c.2. §. caterum. And Antonius de Rosellis, who treats these things more fully, Mon. p.2. c.9. & 10., as well as Onuphrius in his annot. ad Greg. X., referring to that pope's constitution on this matter; and the Bull of Pius IV., which also meets the fear of danger that could arise from contact with such excommunicates, and so on. It is indeed a worthy matter, and one well agreeing with the hypotheses, that those who are not of the Church give the head of the Church, from whose appointment faithful and pious magistrates are kept far away under penalty of sacrilege; and that those who are like heathens and publicans can elect the Vicar of Christ, and another God on earth, who yet cannot be admitted even to the smallest part of ecclesiastical communion!

units.la: XXVII. Undecimò vitiosum & hoc est, quòd multi se ipsos eligunt. Dici istud potest de omnibus illis, qui stimulis ambitionis acti, partim muneribus, partim promissionibus, partim adulationibus, partim aliis mediis similibus electionem suam procurant, ejusque primarii Authores existunt; Quorum exempla plurima inter electionis ipsius vitia dabo. Sed & formaliter seipsum elegit Differt. præced. memoratus Cardinalis de Offa Johannes XXII. al. XXIII. dictus. Verisimiliter etiam recentior longè Alexand. VII. observante Authore Cardinalissmi p. III. p. 37. communem famam fuisse, quòd voto proprio se adjuverit, utpote tot, uno minùs, suffragiis creatus, quot erant Electores; dissentiebat autem illud Card. Rosetti juxta confessionem ejusdem ad Amicum. Ut autem electio sui ipsius in se manifeste absurda apparet, ita etiam contra legem Decret. p. 2. cauf. 8. q. 1, Can. 10. qui Episcopatum; Et Glossam ibidem; Et, quod maximum, contra legem Divinam, Hebr. V. 4.
units.tr: XXVII. The eleventh fault is this too: that many elect themselves. This can be said of all those who, driven by the goads of ambition, procure their election partly by gifts, partly by promises, partly by flattery, partly by other similar means, and who are the primary authors of it. I shall give many examples of these among the faults of the election itself. But also, formally, the aforementioned cardinal, John XXII (also called XXIII), of Offa, elected himself, Differt. præced. Probably also the much more recent Alexander VII, the author of Cardinalissmi p. III. p. 37. observing, was commonly reported to have helped himself by his own vote, as he was created with one vote fewer than the number of electors; but Cardinal Rosetti, according to his own confession to a friend, dissented. But just as the election of oneself appears manifestly absurd in itself, so also it is contrary to the law, Decret. p. 2. cauf. 8. q. 1, Can. 10. qui Episcopatum; Et Glossam ibidem; and, what is greatest, contrary to divine law, Heb. V. 4.

units.la: XXVIII. Duodecimum nævum voco, quòd sæpe Electores, vel potiùs intrusores fuerunt Tyranni potentiâ seculari armati. Atque huc referre debent & referunt Pontificii, quicquid ab Imperatoribus & Regibus Italiæ extra concessionem, ut meram vocant, Pontificiam in electione Pontificum authoritate Imperatoriâ vel Regiâ factum est. De quo tamen sententiam meam Differt. præced. expressi. Melius autem huc pertinet & trahitur, quod tum aliàs etiam, tum maximè seculis decimo & undecimo à Regulis & Tyrannis Romanis in electione Pontificum violenter actum est. Et quidem exempla sic electorum Baronius habet quàm plurima; Nobis autem unum & alterum generale testimonium ex illo heic partim innuisse, partim adduxisse sufficiet; quando prius tamen innuerimus, Augustino Oldoino Loyolitæ, in Necrologio Romanorum Pontificum jam Marinum sive Martinum II. Comitum Tusculanorum potentiâ factum dici. Sed videatur maximè Baronius, maximè ad an. 897. n. 4. ubi prolixè de illis Tusciæ Marchionibus conqueritur, quia populo Cleróque Romano sive pecuniis, sive armis dominantes in Cathedram Petri, solium Christi intruserint homines mines monstruosos &c. Qui tamen maximam partem pro veris & legitimis Papis habiti fuerunt & habentur, & scilicet fuerunt. Sed & ad an. 900. n. 7. subjungit: Ita quidem omnia Roma tam sacra, quam profana factionibus miscebantur, ut penes illam partem esset promotio ad Apostolicam sedem Romani Pontificis, qua potentior appareret, ut modo Etruria Principes intruderet (intruderent) saeculari potentia, quem vellet, & dejiceret, quem posset, Romanum Pontificem a contraria factione promotum. Qua toto hoc ferme seculo sunt actitata &c. Et tamen sic electi pro veris & legitimis Papis habiti fuerunt & habentur, & scilicet fuerunt! Consentanea ad an. 931. n. 1. habet idem: Ita plane tanta vires Marchionibus Tuscia in urbe erant, inquit, ut pro arbitrio, quos vellent, e Pontificali sede deponerent, & alios intruderent, ut ex eodem hujus temporis Scriptore Luitprando facile intelligi potest. Cum enim occupassent munitionem pontis Hadriani dictam ab Ecclesia in vertice collocata Sanctum Angelum (S. Angeli) dominabantur Urbi; cum & divitiarum potentia Romanos sibi etiam devinxissent. Quamdiu igitur viguit horum tyrannis, infelicissimus fuit in omnibus Rom. Ecclesia status, ut saepe contigerit, eam non habere legitime creatos Pontifices, sed quos saeculares potentia intrusisset. Et tamen hi quoque in ordine Pontificum numerantur non legitime creati, sed tamen legitimi, veri, qui successionem faciunt, & quorum decisiones, ordinationes, acta omnia valida habentur! Ad an. 934. ex Luitprando narrat, Albericum Romae tyrannidem exercentem Joh. XII. Papam, Dominum Apostolicum quasi servum proprium in conclavi tenuisse. Et ad an. 940. n. 1. rursus de ejusdem vi tyrannica in promotione Pontificum loquitur. Similiter ad an. 1033. de alio ejusdem nominis & conditionis refert, quomodo (proh nefas) tyrannide ejus filius puer in Sacrosanctam Petri sedem intrusus, monstrum erectum, portentumque statutum fuerit; Benedictus nimirum IX. de quo tamen n. 7. subjungit; liquere, eum in Christiano orbe cognitum & habitum fuisse absque controversia Romanum Pontificem. Porro ad an. 1044. n. 2. ait: Haec autem (de Schismate post mortem Benedicti) ut quam exactissime cognoscantur, inprimis sciendum est, duas potentissimas factiones tunc temporis viguisse, alteram Tusculanorum Comitum, a quibus intrusum vidimus Benedictum, alteram Ptolomai Romani civis &c. Claudere itaque licet ipsis Baronii ad an. 1033. n. 3. verbis: Quid potuit Rom. Ecclesia durius ac luctuosius contigisse, quam ut, qui tyrannide lupi sunt, de Pastore creando decernant & curent? Quorum illud unicum studium sit, ut praficiatur ciatur ovibus pastor ignavus, quò ipsis liberum sit, cùm velint, in oves ir-rumpere. Et quomodo tales legitimi Papæ fuerunt, atque succes-sionem talem, qualis prætenditur, Vicariorum Christi talium, quales jactantur, probant?
units.tr: XXVIII. I call the twelfth blemish Duodecimum that the electors, or rather the intruders, were often tyrants armed with secular power. The Papists ought to refer here, and do refer here, whatever was done by emperors and kings of Italy outside the so-called pure Papal authority in the election of popes, by imperial or royal power. I have expressed my view on this in the Differt. præced. But what belongs here more properly is that, at other times as well, and especially in the tenth and eleventh centuries, elections of popes were carried out by violence by Roman petty kings and tyrants. Baronius gives very many examples of such elections. For us it will be enough to point out, and to cite, one or two general testimonies from him here, though first we should note that Augustinus Oldoinus the Jesuit says in his Necrologium of the Roman Pontiffs that Marinus, or Martinus II, was already made pope by the power of the Counts of Tusculum. But Baronius should be consulted, above all at the year 897, n. 4, where he complains at length about those Marquises of Tuscany, because ruling over the people and clergy of Rome, whether by money or by arms, they thrust into the chair of Peter, into the throne of Christ, men who were monsters, and so on. Yet most of these were, and are, held to be true and lawful popes, and indeed they were. But at the year 900, n. 7 he adds: Thus indeed all things at Rome, sacred and profane alike, were thrown into confusion by factions, so that the promotion of the Roman Pontiff to the apostolic see lay with whichever party appeared the more powerful. Thus at one time the princes of Etruria would thrust in, by secular power, whomever they wished, and would depose whomever they could, a Roman pontiff promoted by the opposing faction. These things were carried on through almost this whole century, and so on. And yet those so elected were, and are, held to be true and lawful popes, and indeed they were! The same writer says something consistent at the year 931, n. 1: So plainly were the Marquises of Tuscany so powerful in the city, he says, that they would depose from the papal see whomever they wished, at their pleasure, and would thrust in others, as can easily be understood from the writer of this period, Liutprand. For when they had seized the fortress of the bridge of Hadrian, called Sant'Angelo by the Church, placed on the top, they dominated the City, and by the power of their wealth they had bound the Romans to themselves as well. So long as the tyranny of these men flourished, the state of the Roman Church was most wretched in all things, so that it often happened that it did not have lawfully created popes, but those whom secular power had thrust in. And yet these men too are counted in the order of popes, not lawfully created, but still lawful, true popes, who make up the succession, and whose decisions, ordinances and all acts are held valid! Baronius relates from Liutprand, at the year 934, that Alberic, exercising tyranny at Rome, kept Pope John XII as a private slave, like a servant, in a closet. And at the year 940, n. 1 he speaks again of the tyrannical violence of the same man in the promotion of popes. Likewise, at the year 1033, he tells of another man of the same name and condition, how (shameful to say) a boy, thrust by the tyranny of his father into the most holy see of Peter, was set up as a monster and a portent: namely Benedict IX. Of whom, however, at n. 7 he adds: it is clear that he was recognised and held in the Christian world, without controversy, as the Roman Pontiff. Further, at the year 1044, n. 2, he says: But that these matters (concerning the schism after Benedict's death) may be known as accurately as possible, it must first be understood that two very powerful factions flourished at that time: one of the Counts of Tusculum, by whom we have seen Benedict thrust in, the other of Ptolemy, a Roman citizen, and so on. Thus we may close with Baronius's own words, at the year 1033, n. 3: What could have happened to the Roman Church more harsh and more lamentable than that those who are wolves by tyranny should decide and arrange the creating of a shepherd? Whose one aim is that a lazy shepherd be set over the sheep, so that it may be free for them, whenever they wish, to break in upon the sheep. And how did such men prove to be lawful popes, and prove the succession, such as is claimed, of such Vicars of Christ as are boasted of?

units.la: XXIX. Satis vitiosa quidem ista sunt, sed pejora sequuntur, & Decimum tertium ratione eligentium naevum facimus, quòd mulieres, partim scortationibus atque incestibus, partim ambitione infames, partim simili cum violentia, partim vocatis in subsidium artibus pessimis, non semel Pontificum Romanorum Electrices fuerunt. Ut de Theodora Augusta, quae ingressum Vigilii parum legitimum male promovit, nihil dicam; Quoad infames scortationibus atque incestibus violenter agentes rursus Annalistam audire juvabit. Qui ad an. 908. n. 5. probaturus, post vim tyrannicam Sergii P. in Pontificatum invadendo ab autoribus ejus saeculi scriptis proditam, ejusdem vitae turpitudinem, quae ab eisdem tradita posteris magna infamiae nota manifesta reddita fuerit; Luitprandum, qui obscoena ipsa l. 2. c. 13. nota reliquerit, citat his verbis: Theodora scortum impudens, hujus Alberici, qui nuper hominem exuit, avia (quod dictu etiam nefandissimum est) Romana civitatis non inviriliter Monarchiam obtinebat, quae duas habuit natas, Marozziam atque Theodoram, sibi non solum aquales, verùm etiam Veneris exortivo promptiores. Harum una Marozzia ex Papa Sergio, cujus supra fecimus mentionem, Joannem, qui post Joannis Ravennatis obitum S. Rom. Ecclesiae obtinuit dignitatem, nefario genuit adulterio, ex Alberto autem Marchione Albericum, qui nostro post tempore Romanae urbis principatum usurpavit &c. Subjungit: Audisti temporis hujus deploratissimum statum, cùm Theodora senior, nobile scortum Monarchicum (ut ita dicam) obtineret in urbe? Pergit autem n. 6. ita: Sed unde infami mulieri tanta dignitas? Erat ista nobilis Romana femina, Senatoria orta propagine, excellens pulchritudine, ingenio versutissima, consuetudine Adelberti Tuscia Marchionis potentissimi reddita procacissima, ex quo etiam, quas audisti, genuit filias; Sicque adulteri potentia etiam sibi peperit Monarchiam. Nam cùm (ut suo loco inferius dicetur) munitio S.
