Angeli inexpugnabilis reddita ex mole olim Hadriani, Augustorum sepulchro, possideretur ab eodem Tuscia Marchione, qui ea potiretur, Urbi quoque pariter dominari facile posset: haec pessima femina ea arte dominium Urbis est consecuta, possidens arcem, illúdque in posteros propagare curavit, filias prostituens Pontificibus, sedis Apostolicae invasoribus, & Tuscia Marchionibus; ex quibus tantarum invainvaluit meretricum imperium , ut pro arbitrio legitimè creatos dimo-verent Pontifices, & violentos ac nefarios homines illis pulsis intrude-rent; veros tamen & illos,atque (si Diis placet) Petri in Monar-chia Ecclesiæ,Vicariatu Christi hæredes, digna successionis tanto-pere ja&tatæ vincula !
units.tr: XXIX. These things are indeed quite faulty, but worse things follow, and we make the thirteenth blemish, relating to the electors, that women, partly infamous for fornication and incest, partly for ambition, partly by similar violence, partly by calling in the worst arts, were more than once the electresses of the Roman Pontiffs. I will say nothing of the Empress Theodora, who wrongly promoted Vigilius, not very lawfully. As for those infamous for fornication and incest, who acted by violence, it will again be pleasing to hear the annalist. He, wishing to prove that after the tyrannical violence of Pope Sergius in invading the papacy, which was reported by the writers of his age, the foulness of his life, which was handed down by them to posterity, was made manifest as a great mark of infamy, cites Liutprand, who left those obscene matters in book 2, chapter 13, with a note, in these words: Theodora, a shameless harlot, grandmother of this Alberic, who lately stripped off his manhood (a thing most unspeakable even to mention), held the monarchy of the Roman city not unmanfully. She had two daughters, Marozia and Theodora, who were not only equal to her but even more ready for Venus's rising. One of these, Marozia, bore to Pope Sergius, whom I mentioned above, a son John, who after the death of John of Ravenna obtained the dignity of the Holy Roman Church, born by a wicked adultery; and by Alberic the Marquis she bore Alberic, who afterwards in our time usurped the principate of the city of Rome, and so on. He adds: You have heard the most deplorable state of that time, when the elder Theodora, a noble harlot, held a monarchy (so to speak) in the city? He goes on at n. 6 thus: But whence came such dignity to an infamous woman? This Roman woman was of senatorial descent, excellent in beauty, most crafty in mind, made very bold by her intercourse with Adalbert, the most powerful Marquis of Tuscany, from which she also bore the daughters you have heard of. So the power of the adulterer also gained for her a monarchy. For when (as will be said further below in its place) the fortress of Sant'Angelo, made impregnable from the old mausoleum of Hadrian, the tomb of the emperors, was held by the same Marquis of Tuscany, who could easily hold it, he could likewise dominate the City. This most wicked woman, by that art, obtained dominion over the City, holding the citadel, and she took care to hand it down to her posterity, prostituting her daughters to the Pontiffs, invaders of the apostolic see, and to the Marquises of Tuscany. From these harlots the empire of such great power grew so strong that they would remove lawfully created popes at will, and, having driven them out, would thrust in violent and wicked men. Yet these too, and (if it please the gods) heirs of Peter's monarchy in the Church and of Christ's Vicariate, are the bonds of a succession so greatly boasted of!

units.la: XXX. Specialiùs ista ad annum 912. n. 7. prosequitur, & primò narrat, quomodo, juxta Luitprandum l. 2. c. 13. Theodorâ illâ, potentissimo scorto ac impudentissimo agente, Lando Papa Joannem, quem illa turpissimè deperierit, Archiepiscopum Ravennatem fecerit; Et quo-modo,Landone paulò post mortuo,non quieverit,donec eundem Joannem in Cathedram Petri violenter intrusisset. Ubi etiam, duplici causa tantam auctam esse meretricum potestatem testatur, tum quòd ejus (Theodoræ) filia Marozia (ut dictum sit ex eodem authore) fuisset Sergio Pseudo-Papæ prostituta, tum etiam, quòd altera filia Theodora Alberto Marchioni Tusciæ junčta adulterio esset, ex qua Albericus natus sit, qui Patris potentiâ Urbi dominatus fuerit; Hunc statum infelicem Sanctæ Romanæ tunc temporis Ecclesiæ fuisse, ut arbitrio potentissimæ meretricis Theodoræ matris omnia moverentur. Accessisse verò ad potentiam ejus, quòd, defuncto Adelberto Marchione Tusciæ, loco ipsius regnans filius ejus ex Berta conjuge, Wido nomine, Maroziam, Scortum Sergii in uxorem acceperit. Quæ omnia Luitprandus ejus temporis Scriptor narrat. Ipse autem propriam querelam mox n. 8. subjicit: Quæ tunc facies S. Ecclesiæ Rom. quàm fœdissima, cùm Romæ dominarentur potentissimæ ac sordidissimæ meretrices? quarum arbitrio mutarentur sedes, darentur sedes, darentur Episcopi, & (quod auditu horrendum & infandum est) intruderentur in sedem Petri earum amasii Pseudo-Pontifices, qui non sint, nisi ad consignanda tantùm tempora in Catalogo Romanorum Pontificum scripti. Quis enim à scortis hujusmodi intrusos sine lege legitimos dicere posset Romanos fuisse Pontifices? Nusquam Cleri eligentis, vel postea consentientis aliqua mentio, Canones omnes presssi silentio, decreta Pontificum suffocata, proscripta antiqua traditiones, veterésque in eligendo summo Pontifice consuetudines, sacríque ritus & pristinus usus prorsus extincti. Sic vendicaverat omnia sibi libido, sæculari potentiâ freta insaniens, æstro percita dominandi &c. En satis ingenuam Baronii (ast quanti aliâs Ecclesiæ Romanæ adulatoris!) Confessionem! Næwum certè nobiscum notat, satis magnum electionis vitium; Nec ipsi placent tales Electrices; Dederunt, ipsius etiam judicio, Pseudo-Pontifices &c. O Egregiam successionem! ô solidum Papatûs patûs fundamentum! ô eximiam Ecclesiæ notam! Quàm justus ille census! quàm bona ista præscriptio! quàm certæ istæ tabulæ! quàm authentica ista instrumenta, quibus se, continuatæ successionis jure, instructos esse gloriantur, cùm ad sua juste possidenda, tum ad hæreticos horum temporum, velut injustos Ecclesiæ tituli & fundi captatores jure depellendos & profligendos! Et cur non desistunt ita continuam Pontificum inde à Christo potestatem Monarchicam aliis, Ecclesiæ formam, ordine non interrupto conferentium successionem jactare? Cur numerant, si Pseudo-Pontifices fuerunt, nisi quòd alii defuerunt? Si Pseudo-Pontifices fuerunt, quid de eorum decisionibus, ordinationibus, Canonizationibus &c. judicabunt? Quid de ordinationibus ordinatorum ab illis, &, per consequens, de hodiernis omnibus?
units.tr: XXX. Baronius pursues these things more particularly at the year 912, n. 7. First he relates how, according to Liutprand, book 2, chapter 13, that Theodora, a most powerful harlot and most shameless agent, made Lando's John, whom she had utterly lusted after, Archbishop of Ravenna; and how, after Lando died a little later, she did not rest until she had violently thrust this same John into the chair of Peter. There too he testifies that the power of the harlots was increased by a double cause: first, because her daughter Marozia (as was said, from the same author) had been prostituted to Sergius, the pseudo-pope; and then also because the other daughter, Theodora, was joined in adultery to Adalbert, Marquis of Tuscany, from whom Alberic was born, who by his father's power came to dominate the City. This was the unhappy state of the Holy Roman Church at that time, that all things were moved at the will of the most powerful harlot, Theodora the mother. Her power increased, moreover, because, Adalbert the Marquis of Tuscany being dead, his son Guy, by Bertha his wife, reigned in his place, and took Marozia, the harlot of Sergius, as his wife. Liutprand, a writer of that time, relates all these things. He himself then adds his own complaint at n. 8: What a most foul face the Holy Roman Church then had, when the most powerful and most filthy harlots ruled at Rome! At their will sees were changed, sees were given, bishops were given, and (horrible and unspeakable to hear) their lovers were thrust into the seat of Peter as pseudo-popes, who are only fit for marking the times in the catalogue of Roman pontiffs. For who could call Romans lawful popes who were thrust in without law by such harlots? Nowhere is any mention made of the electing clergy, or of their later consent; all the canons are passed over in silence, the decrees of the pontiffs are suppressed, the ancient traditions are proscribed, and the old customs in electing the supreme pontiff, the sacred rites and the former practice are utterly extinguished. Thus lust, swollen with secular power and goaded by the gadfly of domination, claimed everything for itself, and so on. Behold Baronius's fairly frank confession (but how great an adulator of the Roman Church he is elsewhere!). He certainly notes a blemish in the election which is, to us as well, quite great; nor do such electresses please him: by his own judgment they gave pseudo-popes, and so on. O outstanding succession! O solid foundation of the papacy! O remarkable mark of the Church! How just that title! How good this prescription! How certain these title-deeds! How authentic these instruments by which they boast themselves to be equipped, by the right of continuous succession, both to possess their own things justly, and to drive off and destroy the heretics of these times, like unjust grabbers of the Church's title and land! And why do they not cease to boast of a continuous succession of the Pontiffs, conferring on others the monarchic power of the Church, the form of the Church, from Christ onwards without interruption? Why do they count them, if they were pseudo-popes, except that others were lacking? If they were pseudo-popes, what will they judge of their decisions, ordinations, canonisations, and so on? What of the ordinations of those ordained by them, and so, by consequence, of all today's?

units.la: XXXI. Si non castius, saltem cautius idem tentavit longè recentior famosa illa Domina Olympia Innocentii X. dum ille viveret, idolum; Quamvis enim, referente Abbate Gualdi Vita di Donna Olympia p.67.68. parùm abfuerit idololatra ab exclusione, eâ potissimùm de causâ, quòd multi praeviderunt, ipso electo, Pontificatum subjectum iri vili fœminæ dominationi, propter amorem intensissimum valdè radicatum erga hanc Cognatam, absolutam ambitiosissimámque voluntatis ipsius dominam, tamen, ut illa desiderio Cognatum Papam videndi Horoscopium ejus à perito Astrologo sibi consignari curavit p.52. seq. ita etiam Electionem ipsius ad Papatum haud parùm promovit, tum aliis eum commendando, & quidem modò Hispanis affectum ipsius erga eos praedicans, modò Gallis, de quodam occulto ipsius affectu loquens, quo ductus servire posset cey amicus occultus plùs aliis manifestis p.49.50, tum ipsummet ad altissima quævis semper instigando, artémque simulandi ceu Magistra peritissima docendo, p.42. seq. in qua eo usque profecit discipulus bonæ spei, ut spem de illo bonam nocte ante ingressum in Conclave ipsa Magistra valedicens sic, ut dicant, exprimere potuerit; Forsè vi vedrò Papa, ma non gia più Cardinale; Id est: Fortè te videbo Papam, & non amplius Cardinalem; ipso regerente & spem desideratissimi didactri ita blandè civilitérque, ut solent amantes, confirmante: Pur che voi foste Papessa, non mi curarei d'esser Papa. Id est: Modò tu Papissa esses, ut ego Papa sim, mihi perinde esset. Sed & ejusdem, postquam Papissa, de quo suo loco, quamdiu ille Papa, fuisset, in electione Successoris non minimas partes fuisse ex Vita pariter & Conclavi Alexandri VII. constat; Licet enim in illo tunc quoque haud manserit, ibi tamen fuit, & operata est Spiritu suo, & per Creaturas, & alios sectatores suos. Lubeat illud cognoscere ex sequentibus. Cardinalis Sacchetti eligendus erat; La Signora &c. Domina Olympia minus eum, quam alios timens ei conciliavit vota Azolini & Gualterii. De Cardinali Cherubino ista leguntur; Non poteva &c. Non poterat sibi persuadere, Barberinum non suum esse, quando eum desideravit D. Olympia idem cum Barberino sentiens. Idem Barberinus non voleva &c. nolebat Palottum secundario, quia inservire volens D. Olympiae commodis, non potuit consentire in electionem, quam castigatio illius Domina secutura fuisset infallibiliter, offenderat enim Palottum; ut taceam Pontificem Zelo instructum desiderio publico totius Christianismi illud daturum fuisse, omnes enim Olympia adscribebant mala Pontificatus precedentis. Idem Barberinus noluit S.Clementem ob D.Olympiam, laquale &c. quae ut praecipuas in Pontificatu Cognati partes habuit, ita etiam putavit, se debere haeredem esse aeque odiorum ac divitiarum; Timuit etiam vindictam, quam timere potuit de omnibus male locuta, non omissis spurcissimis verbis, & semper cognominibus contemptum ostendendo; caeterum parum novit S. Clementem, eumque credidit furiam incarnatam & tigridem habitu Cardinalis vestitam, quomodo eum saepe Innocentius describserat. Aversionem ejus erga S. Clementem auxit consideratio Principis Rosanensis, nuri ipsius, e il figurare &c. & quia praevidit, se minus illa deinceps aestimatum iri, hinc furia pectus ejus occuparunt, hinc vipera facta est. A Barberino &c. Barberino innitebatur moles spei ipsius praecipua, ille erat scopus felicitatis ipsius. Hic etiam per illam Innocentio antehac conciliatus propter illam S. Clementi se opposuit, licet contrarium simulans. Idem Author suspiciones quorundam recenseт, de eo, quod Cardinalis Spada Conclave egressus apud D. Olympiam pro Cardinali Carpegna tractarit; Et paulo post subjungit; Cardinalem Cecchini Innocentii creaturam ab ea primo multum amatam, postea eidem valde exosam, hinc Barberini favorem obtinere haud potuisse. In cujus favorem nec illud praetermitti debet, quod ultimo defunctus Papa, qui & Innocentii X. suorumque beneficia grato versans animo Innocentius XI. vocari voluit, fortunas suas maximam partem a D. Olympiae fontibus derivatas nosse potuit; Id quod Author Cardinalismi p.2. l 3. p. 138. seqq. docet; Ut enim Praelaturam primo obtinere studens primo Cardinalem Barberinum (quem hactenus stenus cum D. Olympia cor unum & animam unam vidimus) invocare, vel, quæ vocis Italicæ (corteggiare) Emphasis est, favorem ejus more aulico ambire cœpit, con il disegno &c. Clericatum Camera (quam dignitatem bonum ad Cardinalatum perveniendi medium esse suprà diximus;) & non tantùm solutionem anticipavit, sed & subinde donis minoribus memoriam sui renovavit; quemadmodum etiam se ea de causa ad ejus promotionem obstrictum novit, atque Praelaturam contulit, Cardinalatum paulò post collaturus, qui finis principalis Odeschalchii erat; Ita mortuo Urbano, ambitione in pectore ipsius semper crescente, nihil nisi Cardinalatum somnians, sèque satis divitem esse cognoscens, eodem modo favorem Olympiæ ambire cœpit, oblatis subinde extraordinariis donis, atque inter illa utensilibus argenteis pretiosissimis, sicque sibi viam ad Purpuram aperuit, dum D. Olympia liberalitate non vulgari devincta ad evitandum ingratitudinis crimen, atque ad excitandum aliorum studium Odeschalchio pileum obtinuit; Ita ut non frustrà fuerit invocare Sanctam post Sanctum, & illa hæc dederit saltem proximam Pontificiæ dignitatem.
units.tr: XXXI. If not more chastely, at least more cautiously, the far more recent and notorious Donna Olympia tried the same thing, as an idol of Innocent X while he lived. For although, according to Abbot Gualdi (Vita di Donna Olympia p.67.68.), she came very close to being shut out as an idolater, this was chiefly because many foresaw that, once he was elected, the papacy would be made subject to the rule of a worthless woman, on account of his most intense love, deeply rooted, for this kinswoman, an absolute and most ambitious mistress of his will. Nevertheless, just as she had a trained astrologer draw up his horoscope so that she could see her kinsman as pope (p.52. seq.), so she also promoted his election to the papacy no little. She commended him to others, now praising to the Spaniards his affection for them, now to the French, speaking of a certain secret fondness of his, by which he might be led to serve as a secret friend, more useful than the open ones (p.49.50.). She also kept urging him on to the highest goals of every kind, and, like a most skilled mistress, taught him the art of dissembling (p.42. seq.). In this the pupil made such progress, of promising promise, that on the night before he entered the conclave the mistress herself, bidding him farewell, could express her hope of him, as they say, in these words: Perhaps I shall see you pope, but no longer as cardinal. That is: Perhaps I shall see you as pope, and no longer as cardinal. He replied, and with the sweet and courteous manner that lovers use, he confirmed the hope of his most longed-for teacher: Provided you were a female pope, I should not care about being pope. That is: So long as you were a female pope, it would be all the same to me whether I were pope. Moreover, it is clear from the Life and the Conclave of Alexander VII that she herself, after she had become a female pope (of which in its place), played no small part in the election of his successor, as long as he remained pope. For although she did not then remain in the same position, yet she was there, and she worked by her spirit, through creatures, and through her other followers. Let us learn this from what follows. Cardinal Sacchetti was to be elected: The Signora, etc. Donna Olympia, fearing him less than others, gained for him the votes of Azolini and Gualterio. Of Cardinal Cherubino these things are read: He could not, etc. He could not persuade himself that Barberini was not his own man, when Donna Olympia, thinking the same as Barberini, wanted him. The same Barberini did not want, etc. he did not want Palotto as second choice, because, wishing to serve the advantage of Donna Olympia, he could not agree to an election which would infallibly have been followed by that lady's punishment, for he had offended Palotto. Not to mention that the pope, equipped with zeal, would have granted this to the public desire of all Christendom, since everyone ascribed the evils of the previous pontificate to Olympia. The same Barberini did not want St. Clement because of Donna Olympia, the snare, etc. Since she had the chief role in her kinsman's pontificate, so she also thought she ought to be the heir of hatreds as well as of riches. She also feared the revenge which she might fear from those whom she had spoken ill of, not omitting the foulest words, and always showing her contempt by nicknames. Moreover, he knew little of St. Clement, and believed him to be a fury incarnate and a tigress clothed in the habit of a cardinal, as Innocent had often described him. Her aversion to St. Clement was increased by her consideration of the Prince of Rosano, her daughter-in-law, and the figure, etc. and because she foresaw that she would be held of less account in future, her breast was seized with fury, and she became a viper. On Barberini, etc. The chief mass of her hope rested on Barberini; he was the goal of her happiness. Here too, having previously been won over to Innocent by her, she opposed St. Clement on her account, though pretending otherwise. The same author records suspicions held by some, that Cardinal Spada, on leaving the conclave, negotiated with Donna Olympia on behalf of Cardinal Carpegna. And a little later he adds: Cardinal Cecchini, a creature of Innocent, at first much loved by her, afterwards very hateful to her, could not therefore obtain the favour of Barberini. In favour of this man it must also not be passed over that the pope who died last, who, turning over the benefits of Innocent X and his people with a grateful mind, wished to be called Innocent XI, could know that most of his fortunes were derived from the springs of Donna Olympia. This the author of Cardinalismo teaches (p.2. l.3. p.138. seqq.). For, striving first to obtain a prelacy, he began first to invoke Cardinal Barberini (whom hitherto we have seen as one heart and one soul with Donna Olympia), or, as the force of the Italian word (corteggiare) has it, to court his favour in the manner of a courtier, with the design, etc. the Clericate of the Chamber (which dignity, as we said above, was a good means of arriving at the cardinalate), and he not only paid the fee in advance, but from time to time renewed his memory of himself with smaller gifts. In the same way he knew that he was bound to her promotion for this reason, and conferred the prelacy, intending soon to confer the cardinalate, which was the chief aim of Odescalchi. Thus, with Urban dead, his ambition, ever growing in his breast, dreaming of nothing but the cardinalate, and knowing himself to be rich enough, in the same way he began to court the favour of Olympia, offering from time to time extraordinary gifts, and among them most precious silver household utensils; and so he opened for himself the way to the purple, while Donna Olympia, bound by no common generosity, in order to avoid the crime of ingratitude, and to stir up the zeal of others, obtained the cardinal's hat for Odescalchi. So it was not in vain to invoke one saint after another, and she gave him at least the nearest dignity to the papacy.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Mala sunt, quæ mali homines indignè patrant, & sæpe Diabolica talia facta vocantur, qualia etiam dubio procul narratæ cumprimis per tyrannos & infames superiorum seculorum fœminas intrusiones censeri debent, proin nævis & vitiis majoribus fœdatæ; Sed decimò quartò adhuc ex Authoribus Pontificiis cognoscimus, Papas nonnullos propiori Diaboli interventu, ope & auxilio electos fuisse. Quos inter primus Sylvester II. cui ante Papatum Gerberto nomen erat, numeratur; De quo ita Wernerus Rollfink Author Fasciculi temporum loquitur; Sylvester factus est Papa, auxilio Diaboli, cui homagium fecit, ut cuncta ei ad votum succederent. Consentit Platina in Sylv. II. his verbis: Gerbertus ambitione & Diabolica dominandi cupiditate impulsus, largitione primò quidem Archiepiscopatum Rhemensem, inde Ravennatem adeptus, Pontificatum postremò, majore conatu adjuvante Diabolo, consecutus est; hac tamen lege, ut post mortem totus illius esset, cujus fraudibus tantam dignitatem adeptus erat. Sic etiam Nicolaus Lyranus ad 2. Mach. cap. XIV. per Alchimum, qui Demetrio Coronam auream & palmam obtulit, ut per hoc summum Sacerdotium obtineret, significari scribit, ambitiosum in tantum, ut Diabolo faciat Sacrificium, ut per hoc promoveatur ad dignitatem; sicut, inquit, refert Guillermus in Chronico, de quodam, nomine Gerbertus, qui per hoc ascendit ad Archiepiscopatum Rhemensem
units.tr: The evil deeds that wicked men commit unworthily are often called diabolical, and the intrusions of the sort I have recounted, carried out above all by tyrants and by infamous women of earlier centuries, must without doubt be counted among the greater blemishes and faults. But, fourteenthly, we learn from Papist authors that some popes were elected through the closer intervention, power and help of the Devil. Among them the first is Sylvester II, who before his papacy was named Gerbert. Werner Rolevinck, author of the Fasciculus temporum, speaks of him thus: Sylvester became pope with the help of the Devil, to whom he did homage, so that all things would turn out according to his wish. Platina agrees, in his life of Sylvester II, in these words: Gerbert, driven by ambition and a diabolical lust for power, first obtained by bribery the archbishopric of Reims, then that of Ravenna, and at last, with the Devil helping him with greater effort, achieved the papacy; yet on this condition, that after his death he would belong wholly to the one through whose deceits he had gained so great a dignity. So too Nicholas of Lyra, on 2 Maccabees chapter 14, writes that the Alcimus who offered Demetrius a golden crown and a palm, so as to obtain the high priesthood, signifies a man so ambitious that he makes a sacrifice to the Devil in order to be promoted to dignity; as William reports in his Chronicle, of a certain man named Gerbert, who by this means rose to the archbishopric of Reims.

units.la: Decimus quartus, quòd Papa nonnulli propiori Diaboli ope electi fuerunt, Exemplum Sylvestri II. mensem & postea ad Ravennensem & post ad statum Papalem. Non minùs apud Æneam Sylvium,qui & ipse post Papa nomine Pii II. factus est, in Comment. de gestis Concil. Basil. legimus: Nec nos fugit. Marcellinum jussu Cæsareo idolis thurificâsse, alium verò, quod majus & horribilius sit, Diabolicâ fraude Romanum Pontificatum conscendisse; Quibus verbis hunc ipsum certè Sylvestrum designare videtur; De quo etiam Nauclerus, cujus res Pontificias narrantis magna apud Pontificios authoritas,in Chronico,quod ipso Surio Carthusiano obstetricante editum habetur, narrat, quòd illum Diabolus ex lege adjutum devinxerit,ut post mortem suus esset. Qualem ingressum etiam egressus horrendus ab iisdem & aliis memoratus confirmat, dum Romæ in Templo S. Crucis in Hierusalem parùm metuens fraudes & æquivocationes Diaboli, ob quas non immeritò Loxias veteribus audiit, secundùm pacta Hierosolymæ vitam amissurus, à Dæmone interemptus est; Quod mortis genus cum circumstantiis plurimis partim iidem,partim, qui & ingressum confirmant talem, & quos inter aliquot Magiæ simpliciter noxam Sylvestro iniustam ostendunt,plures alii veteres & recentiores testes Pontificii; Benno, qui paulò post vixit,nec hic saltem apertas odii causas habuisse dici potest; Martinus Polonus, Albericus Monachus trium fontium, Vincentius Bellovacensis, Galfridus Malmesburiensis, Antonius Archiepiscopus, Henricus Erphordiensis, Carthusianus, Stella, alii commemorant; Imò apud Laurentium Schraderum Monum. Ital. l. 2. inscriptionem Sacelli à Bernhardino Canajola Cardinale positam, & non obscurè rem totam significantem videre licet.
units.tr: The fourteenth point: that some popes were elected through the closer help of the Devil. The example of Sylvester II, first as archbishop of Reims, then of Ravenna, and afterwards to the papal see. No less in the Commentaries on the Acts of the Council of Basel of Aeneas Sylvius, who himself later became pope under the name Pius II, do we read: Nor is it unknown to us that Marcellinus offered incense to idols at the command of Caesar, and that another man, which is greater and more horrible, ascended the Roman papacy by diabolical fraud. These words seem certainly to point to this same Sylvester. Of him also Naucler, whose account of papal affairs carries great authority among Papists, relates in his Chronicle, published with the midwifery of Surius the Carthusian, that the Devil, having helped him by the agreement, bound him so that after death he would be the Devil's. The dreadful exit confirms the sort of entrance he had: mentioned by these and other writers, he was, while in Rome in the Church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, little fearing the frauds and equivocations of the Devil, for which the ancients rightly heard the name Loxias, slain by a demon, losing his life according to the pact made at Jerusalem. Concerning this manner of death, with many circumstances, several other ancient and recent Papist witnesses, some of the same men who also confirm such an entrance, and among whom some show that the charge of plain magic against Sylvester was unjust, relate the matter: Benno, who lived shortly afterwards, and who cannot even be said to have had clear causes of hatred; Martin of Poland, Albericus the monk of Three Fountains, Vincent of Beauvais, Geoffrey of Malmesbury, Antoninus the Archbishop, Henry of Erfurt the Carthusian, Stella, and others. Indeed, in Laurentius Schrader's Monumenta Italiae, book 2, one may see an inscription of a chapel set up by Cardinal Bernardino Canajola, which quite clearly signifies the whole affair.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Gregorium VII. Episcopi XXX. Anno 1080. Brixinæ Moricæ ex Italia, Gallia & Germania congregati, narrante Trithemio in Chronico Hirsaugiensi, accusârunt, quòd per artem Magicam necromanticam, & Dæmonum suffragio, sedem Apostolicam invaserit. Quem & alii Magiæ reum peragunt, & cui emortualis confessio, quòd,Dæmone suadente,odium & iram contra humanum genus concitârit, tribuitur. Imò & alios Papas illorum & propiùs sequentium temporum, qui Magiæ accusantur, Benedictum IX. Johannem XXI. Felicem V. Alexandrum VI. Paulum III. commercio Diabolico ad hominum animos lucrandos & fastigium dignitatis Pontificiæ eò facilius, Deo permittente, consequendum usos fuisse, haud improbabile est.
units.tr: Gregory VII. In the year 1080, thirty bishops gathered at Brixen from Italy, Gaul and Germany, as Trithemius relates in his Chronicle of Hirsau, accused him of having invaded the Apostolic See by magic necromancy and with the aid of demons. Others too charge him with magic, and to him is attributed a deathbed confession that at the urging of the Devil he had stirred up hatred and anger against the human race. Indeed it is not improbable that other popes of those times and of the following ages, who are accused of magic, namely Benedict IX, John XXI, Felix V, Alexander VI and Paul III, used dealings with the Devil to win men's minds and to reach the summit of papal dignity more easily, God permitting it.

units.la: XXXIV. Recentius exemplum in Papa Sixto V. haberemus, si vera de eo narrâssent, qui forte odii tantùm stimulis impulsi loquebantur, Hispani & Jesuitæ, famam spargentes, Sixtum (quem per Monachum Franciscanum tenui mantili strangulari curâsse dicuntur; ) à Dæmone strangulatum esse, qui & Papæ sublestam fidem exprobranti, quòd septennii regimen pollicitus, quinquennio vix exacto adesset, respondérit: Eum cuidam minorenni ad suspendium damnato (quod certè in Vita ejus legitur; ) annos 2. de suis, ut ceu in justa ætate puniri posset, donâsse. Qua ratione ei ex pacto electionem ad septennium Dæmon promisisset, illam etiam, sed ad quinquennium tantùm, Deo id ita disponente, præstitisset.
units.tr: XXXIV. We would have a more recent example in Pope Sixtus V, if those who spoke of him had reported true things; but they spoke driven only by the spurs of hatred, the Spaniards and Jesuits, who spread the rumour that Sixtus (whom they say had been strangled with a thin cloth by a Franciscan monk) was strangled by the Devil. The Devil, they say, when the pope reproached him for his shaky faith, since he had promised a reign of seven years and was barely in his fifth year, replied that he had given two of his own years to a condemned youth who was to be hanged, so that he might be punished at a just age (which is certainly read in his Life). By this same reasoning the Devil had promised him election for seven years by the pact, and had indeed granted it, but only for five, God so ordering it.

units.la: XXXV. Si ista vera essent, ut Sylvestri II. Gregorii VII. & aliorum quorundam exempla omninò esse videntur, & saltem unum atque alterum nonnisi impudenter impugnantur, saltem omnia à Pontificiis Authoribus affirmata & tradita accepimus, aliis proin ineptè simul atque injustè de hæreticorum, quos vocant, calumniis hîc conquerentibus; certè nonnunquam Spiritus alius, sancto illi, cujus assistentiam perpetuam & planè singularem supra jactârunt, contrarius, peculiari modo non semel in electionibus Pontificum intervenisset & intervenit, quem etiam in fructibus suis, ambitione, simonia, mendaciis &c. quæ in subsidium tunc ordinariò vocari solent, curvarum animarum technis, ibi præsentem & multis modis efficaciter agentem conspiciemus, quando jam, postquam paucis de nævis & vitiis, quæ eligentes propiùs respiciunt, actum est, ad nævos & vitia, quæ convenientiùs ipsius electionis nævi & vitia convocantur, consideranda pro ordinis instituti ratione transimus.
units.tr: XXXV. If these things were true, as the examples of Sylvester II, Gregory VII and certain others seem altogether to be, and if only one or two were attacked, and if we have received everything affirmed and handed down by Papist authors, then others complain here foolishly and unjustly at the same time about the calumnies of heretics, as they are called. Surely another spirit, opposed to that Holy Spirit whose constant and quite singular assistance they have boasted of, has more than once intervened, and still intervenes, in papal elections in a peculiar way. We shall see him present here and working effectively in many ways, in his fruits: ambition, simony, lies, and the tricks of crooked souls, which are ordinarily called in to help. Now that we have said a little about the faults and blemishes that concern the electors more closely, we pass, according to the order we have set, to consider the blemishes and faults which more fittingly belong to the election itself.

units.la: DISSERTATIO SEXTA, In qua De nævis & vitiis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum iis, qui Electionem ipsam propiùs concernunt, agitur.
units.tr: DISSERTATION SIX, in which the defects and vices of the election of the Roman Pontiffs are treated, insofar as they concern the election itself.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA; In qua Partim nævi respectu silentii Scripturarum, multiplicis incertitudinis, atque dilationis exhibentur, partim de propioribus & magis moralibus Electionis vitiis quædam generaliora præmittuntur, partim denique; vitiosa eligendi principia ostenduntur.
units.tr: FIRST SECTION: In which, partly, the defects arising from the silence of the Scriptures, from manifold uncertainty, and from delay are set forth; partly, some more general points are prefaced concerning the nearer and more moral vices of the election; and partly, finally, the vicious principles of electing are shown.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Transitio; II. Primum Electionis vitium in Scripturarum de ea silentio; III. Secundum in multiplici circa Electionem incertitudine; IV. Ad quam etiam pertinet Historicorum obscuritas, silentium, diversitas, imò contrarietas. V. Dissensus ratione ordinis; VI. Exemplum ratione primorum Petri Successorum porrò urgetur; VII. Exceptionibus Baronii occurritur; VIII. Dissensus ratione temporis; IX. Testimonia & exempla ex Baronio; X. Tertium vitium, in dilatione Electionum & Interregnis; XI. Quantus in iis nævus sit, in dilationibus quibuscunque; XII. Longioribus; XIII. Vitia Electionis propiora & magis moralia; Abesse debərent; XIV. Iuxta Constitutiones Pontificum, aliorumque monitiones; XV. Quarum transgressiones non puniuntur; XVI. Vitiosa sunt primò agendi principia; XVII. Respectu Papabilium ambitio; XVIII. Qua olim aberat, nunc frequentissima; XIX. Inviti creati; XX. Cur hodie ambiatur Pontificia dignitas; XXI. Ambitionis exemplum in Vigilio, querela Baronii generalis, & narratio statûs post mortem Cælestini III. XXII. Post obitum Clem. IV. in electione Greg. X. In Conclavibus Clem. V. & Urb. VI. XXIII. Exemplum Ioh. XXIII. Ex Concl. Nicol. V. Cal. III. Pii II. XXIV. Ex Concl. Marc. II. Pauli III. Sixti V. XXV. Gregorii XIV. XXVI. Clementis VIII. Pauli V. Greg. XV. Urbani VIII. XXVII. Innoc. X. Alex. VII. XXVIII. Clem. IX. & X. L'Ambasc. de Rom. XXIX. Principium illud rejectum à Card. Albano; In Synodo Rom. Decretalibus &c. XXX. Principia dominantia alia; Commoda propria; Passiones alia; XXXI. Commodum proprium in Conclavibus Clem. V. Pii IV.
units.tr: I. Transition. II. The first vice of the election lies in the silence of the Scriptures about it. III. The second lies in the manifold uncertainty surrounding the election. IV. To this also belongs the obscurity, silence, diversity, and indeed contrariety of the historians. V. Disagreement concerning the order of succession. VI. The example of the first successors of Peter is pressed further. VII. The objections of Baronius are met. VIII. Disagreement concerning the time. IX. Testimonies and examples from Baronius. X. The third vice, in the delay of elections and interregnums. XI. How great a defect there is in these delays, in whatever form they occur. XII. Longer delays. XIII. The nearer and more moral vices of the election, which ought to be absent. XIV. According to the constitutions of the Popes and the warnings of others. XV. Whose transgressions go unpunished. XVI. The first vicious principles of acting. XVII. Ambition with regard to the papabili. XVIII. Ambition, which was once absent, is now most frequent. XIX. Those created unwillingly. XX. Why the papal dignity is now sought after. XXI. An example of ambition in Vigilius, Baronius's general complaint, and an account of the state of affairs after the death of Celestine III. XXII. After the death of Clement IV, in the election of Gregory X; in the conclaves of Clement V and Urban VI. XXIII. The example of John XXIII. From the conclave of Nicholas V; Calixtus III; Pius II. XXIV. From the conclave of Marcellus II; Paul III; Sixtus V. XXV. Gregory XIV. XXVI. Clement VIII; Paul V; Gregory XV; Urban VIII. XXVII. Innocent X; Alexander VII. XXVIII. Clement IX and Clement X; L'Ambasc. di Rom. XXIX. The principle rejected by Cardinal Albani; in the Roman Synod, the Decretals, etc. XXX. Other dominant principles: private advantage; other passions. XXXI. Private advantage in the conclaves of Clement V and Pius IV.

units.la: XXXII. Sixti V. Greg. XIV. Innoc. IX. Pauli V. Greg. XV. Vrb. VIII. Alex. VII. XXXIII. Clem. IX. & X. L'Ambasc. di Rom. XXXIV. Ambitio adjuvantium maxime; XXXV. Passiones varia; XXXVI. Ex Cardinalismo & Conclavibus; XXXVII. Studium gratitudinis; XXXVIII. Odium; XXXIX. Vindicta studium; XL. Studium contrariandi; XLI. Metus poena.
units.tr: XXXII. Sixtus V; Gregory XIV; Innocent IX; Paul V; Gregory XV; Urban VIII; Alexander VII. XXXIII. Clement IX and Clement X; L'Ambasc. di Rom. XXXIV. Chiefly the ambition of those who assist. XXXV. Various passions. XXXVI. From cardinalship and conclaves. XXXVII. Zeal for gratitude. XXXVIII. Hatred. XXXIX. The zeal for vengeance. XL. The zeal for opposition. XLI. Fear of punishment.

units.la: I. Am supra Differt. nimirùm IV. Sect.II. n. 110. nostra fecimus sequentia Sebæ & Zalmunæ, Regum Midianitarum, verba: Prout vir est, ita etiam est ipsius actio, Judic. VIII. 21. Quod axioma heic non immeritò repetimus, post absolutam de nævis & vitiis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum, quibus personæ eligentes remotiori quodam ad electionem respectu laborant, tractationem, & in isto tractationis de nævis & vitiis, quibus ipsa electio foedari solet, exordio. Non enim difficulter ex iis, quæ hactenus dicta sunt, infertur, electionem eligentibus responsuram, vitiis & nævis ipsam minimè caituram, non aptos Electores etiam non aptè, non bene electuros esse. Id quod ita se habere nunc prolixiùs ostendendum erit.
units.tr: I. As we have set down above, in Dissertation IV, section II, n. 110, the words of Sebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian: "As the man is, so also is his action," Judg. 8:21. We repeat this saying here not without reason, now that the treatment of the defects and vices of the election of the Roman Pontiffs, by which the electing persons are burdened by a certain remoteness from the election, has been completed, and at the beginning of this treatment of the defects by which the election itself is commonly fouled. For it is not difficult to infer from what has been said so far that an election will correspond to the electors: that an election which is not free of vices and defects will itself be made by unfit electors, who will not elect unfitly and not well. This must now be shown at greater length.

units.la: II. Et quidem heic etiam primum nævum in Scripturarum silentio ponimus, atque contra Electionem illam Pontificum Romanorum non leve præjudicium formamus ideò, quia nihil prorsus de ea in Sacris habetur Literis. Itáne res tanti momenti, electio Vicarii Christi, cui obedire sit de necessitate salutis omni creaturæ, plane taceri debuit? Non certè; Sed, si vel Electores silentio involvi potuissent, de ipsa tamen Electione saltem aliquid dicendum fuisset; Non tantùm de formis, (quod supra voluimus) verùm etiam de modo secundùm formas illas agendi, de dubiis, quæ circa praxin oriri, de vitiis, quæ Divini Spiritûs regimen negare videntur, & quomodo illis occurrendum, quid his tam evidenter manifestatis agendum sit. Proin dum Spiritus S. in Scriptura loquens plane ignaros & dubios heic homines relinquit, certum præbet indicium, se speciali atque approbante concursu, ut quidem jactant, quod in Electionibus ad tantam Majestatem agitur, non curare atque providere.
units.tr: II. And here too we place as the first defect the silence of the Scriptures, and we form against that election of the Roman Pontiffs no slight prejudice, for the reason that nothing whatever about it is found in the Sacred Letters. Was a matter of such great moment, the election of the Vicar of Christ, to which every creature must of necessity obey for salvation, to be passed over in complete silence? Certainly not. But even if the electors could have been passed over in silence, something at least about the election itself ought to have been said: not only about the forms (which we wished to deal with above), but also about the manner of acting according to those forms, about the doubts that arise in practice, about the vices which seem to deny the governance of the Divine Spirit, and how these are to be met, and what must be done about things so evidently manifest. Therefore, while the Holy Spirit, speaking in Scripture, leaves men here plainly ignorant and in doubt, he gives a sure indication that he does not, by a special and approving concurrence, as they boast, take care and provide for what is done in elections to so great a Majesty.

units.la: III. Secundum Electionis Pontificum Romanorum nævum ostendemus in multiplici circa eam incertitudine. Atque huc etiam referri posset non unius generis incertitudo de potestate ipsa, ad quam Electio fieri dicitur, de Petri itinere, commoratione & Episcopatu Romano, de successione, formis, eligentibus, eorúm-que que baptismo, ordinatione, promotione ad Cardinalatum, suffi- cienti numero &c. Imò magna jam jam à nobis posita est incer-titudo cum Scripturarum de Electione ista silentio, & quòd fide tantùm humana, historica, minori atque morali certitudine elec-tiones in hunc usque diem factæ, & electiones nobis viventibus factæ cognosci debent, nec etiam signo aliquo extraordinario. (De quo tamen Dissert.VII. adhuc dispiciendum;) tam extraordi-nariæ personæ innotescunt.
units.tr: III. We shall show the second defect of the election of the Roman Pontiffs in the manifold uncertainty surrounding it. To this could also be referred an uncertainty of no single kind: about the power itself to which the election is said to be made; about Peter's journey, sojourn, and episcopate at Rome; about the succession, the forms, the electors, and their baptism, ordination, promotion to the cardinalate, a sufficient number, and so on. Indeed, we have already laid down a great uncertainty, since the Scriptures are silent about this election, and since the elections made up to the present day, and those made in our own lifetime, must be known with only human, historical, lesser, and moral certainty, and not even by some extraordinary sign (about which, however, we must still look into in Dissertation VII) by which such extraordinary persons become known.

units.la: IV. Verùm incertitudinem illam jam satis, imò nimis ma- gnam haud parùm auget fidei humanæ ipsius, quæ heic sola superest, nec vel in suo genere perfecta sufficeret, ulterior atque essentialis imperfectio, historiæ humanæ ipsius, quæ heic sola lucem præbet, obscuritas, atque partim silentium, partim etiam diversitas, imò contrarietas; Cùm tamen videatur, Deum, si in aliis humanas res tenebris involvi permittit, minimè tamen permittere debere, ut constitutio certa Vicariorum suorum tantorum, ad æternæ salutis acquisitionem cunctorum mortalium bono positorum, non certò, saltem quatenus id per hominum non infallibiliter inspiratorum relationes fieri potest, cognoscatur, atque saltem illa monumenta, quæ Electionem eorum & continuam successionem probare, illustrare, atque dubia tollere possent, non omnia habeantur, & per omnia secula conformiter rebus gestis conservantur. Eum tamen ista permisisse, nec majorem hic quàm in quarumcunque rerum profanarum declaratione lucem haberi, ex sequentibus patebit.
units.tr: IV. But this uncertainty, already great enough and indeed too great, is considerably increased by the merely human faith which alone remains here, and which would not be sufficient even in its own kind if it were perfect; and by a further and essential imperfection of human history, which alone gives light here: its obscurity, and partly its silence, partly even its diversity, indeed its contrariety. Yet it seems that God, although he permits human affairs in other matters to be wrapped in darkness, ought by no means to permit the certain institution of his so great Vicars, who are set over the attainment of eternal salvation for all mortals, not to be known with certainty, at least insofar as this can be done through the accounts of men who were not infallibly inspired; and that those records at least which could prove and illustrate their election and continuous succession, and remove doubts, should not all be extant, or be preserved in agreement with the events through all ages. That he has permitted such things, and that there is no more light here than in the explanation of any profane matters, will be clear from what follows.

units.la: V. Ut enim de rebus post electionem gestis maximæ Scriptorum pugnæ reperiuntur (quod ostendere non hujus loci est;) ita etiam summus est Authorum dissensus de eo, quando Electio hujus vel illius facta sit; De dissensu autem quoad Electos Dissert. seq. agendum erit. Summus, inquam, est Authorum dissensus de eo, quando Electio hujus vel illius facta sit. Et quidem in ipso limine jam manus conserunt. Qui enim, juxta Dissert.II. ostendere non possunt, quando Petrus Episcopus Romanus factus sit, & mirè in temporis illius assignatione variant, pariter & vel maximè de primis ejus, quos in plenitudine potestatis Monarchicæ fingunt, successoribus dissentiunt, quando & quo ordine nimirum singulorum electiones factæ sint, quis à Petro primus, quis secundus, quis tertius, quis quartus, & quo tempore factus fuerit. De prima quinque Pontificum successione maxima est, inquit Onuphrius annot. in Vitam B. Petri & 4. seqq. Pont. tum inter Graecos & Latinos, tum inter Latinos ipsos controversia.
units.tr: V. For just as the greatest battles of the writers are found concerning the events after the election (which it is not the place here to show), so too there is the greatest disagreement among the authors about when this or that election took place. Concerning the disagreement about the electees themselves, we shall treat in the following dissertation. I say, the disagreement among the authors about when this or that election took place is very great. And indeed they already join battle at the very threshold. For those who, according to Dissertation II, cannot show when Peter became Bishop of Rome, and differ remarkably in assigning the time, likewise disagree most of all about his first successors, whom they imagine in the fullness of monarchical power: when and in what order the individual elections took place, who was first after Peter, who second, who third, who fourth, and at what time each was made. "Concerning the first succession of the five Popes," says Onuphrius, Annotations on the Life of Blessed Peter and the following four Popes, "there is the greatest controversy, both among the Greeks and the Latins, and among the Latins themselves."

units.la: VI. Est certè; Nam post Petrum (de quo prolixè l. c. egimus) quidam immediatè Linum ponunt & post ipsum Clementem, alii viceversa Clementem Lino praeponunt, alii Lino & Clementi Cletum interponunt, alii rursus loco Cleti Anacletum ponunt, alii unum eundemque Cletum & Anacletum fuisse supponunt. De Clemente adeóque Seculo adhuc decimo tertio canebatur:
units.tr: VI. Indeed it is so; for after Peter (of whom we have treated at length in the passage cited) some place Linus immediately, and after him Clement; others conversely place Clement before Linus; others interpose Cletus between Linus and Clement; others again put Anacletus in place of Cletus; others suppose that Cletus and Anacletus were one and the same. Concerning Clement, even in the thirteenth century there was a verse sung:

units.la: Nutat adhuc mundus, sit quartus sitne secundus;
units.tr: Still the world wavers: is he the fourth, or perhaps the second?

units.la: Imò adhuc nutat, utrum forte sit tertius; Quotus gravissimis inter Pontificios Authoribus est; Qui &, quoniam communem opinionem secuti (prout Dissert. IV. Sect. I. vidimus) ab ipso Petro χειροτονηθέντα ἢ Κλήμεντα, electum & ordinatum Clementem admittunt, in eo tamen sententiae suae, quòd nempe Clemens demum post Linum sederit, fulcrum quaerunt & fingunt, quòd Clemens, (quem cum Cleto Petri coadjutorem & Chorepiscopum fuisse ajunt;) licèt electus, prae modestia usque ad obitum Lini sedere recusaverit; quasi verò verisimile sit, Clementem, quem, si Successor designari meruit, non etiam Coadjutorem & Chorepiscopum Petri fuisse primò miramur, eoúsque modestiam plane incongruam prodidisse, ut, ipso Petro jubente & ordinante, sedere tamen constanter vel post ejus mortem demum noluerit, & contra modestiâ usque adeò caruisse Linum, ut ab ipso Petro ordinati, proin etiam dignissimi, Clementis sedem occupare sustinuerit, quem alii, juxta Dissert. II. ante ipsum Petrum defunctum esse perhibent. Potiùs omnem illam de primis Romanis Pontificibus controversiam, cui simile quid respectu aliorum in praecipuis sedibus primorum Antistitum deprehenditur, inde venire dicendum est, quòd uno eodémque tempore plures in una eadémque urbe Episcopi, sive Presbyteri in verbo laborantes fuerunt. Confer Phil. I. 1. Quâ ratione absurdum illud adoptamus, quod Baronius ad an.69. n.36. rejicit, quaerens: An duos simul sedisse volunt?
units.tr: Indeed it still wavers over whether he is perhaps the third. This is the view of the most serious Papist authors. Following the common opinion (as we saw in Dissert. IV. Sect. I.), they admit that Clement was ordained [χειροτονηθέντα ἢ Κλήμεντα] and appointed by Peter himself, and so they hold that Clement was ordinatum Clementem. Yet on this point they seek and invent a prop for their opinion, namely that Clement, whom they say was Peter's coadjutor and chorepiscopus along with Cletus, refused out of modesty to sit in the chair until the death of Linus, although he had been chosen. As if it were likely that Clement, whom they admit was Peter's coadjutor and chorepiscopus, and whom, if he deserved to be named successor, we would first expect to be Peter's coadjutor, showed such a plainly unsuitable modesty that, although Peter himself commanded and ordained him, he nevertheless steadfastly refused to sit in the chair, even after Peter's death. And, on the other hand, that Linus lacked modesty so completely that, although he was ordained by Peter himself, and so was surely the most worthy, he took the see of Clement, whom others, according to Dissert. II., say died before Peter. Rather, the whole controversy over the first Roman bishops, of which something similar is found in the case of others in the principal sees of the first bishops, must be said to arise from the fact that several bishops, or presbyters labouring in the Word, were in the same city at one and the same time. Compare Phil. I. 1. On this ground we adopt that absurd idea which Baronius ad an.69. n.36. rejects, asking: Do they want two to have sat at once?

units.la: VII. Non autem usque adeò levem illam controversiam esse, vel ex eodem Baronio (cujus animum non mediocris suspicio pulsavit, Clementem quarto post Petrum loco sedisse, licet eum ante Anacletum, adeóque tertio loco ponendum esse verius putârit, ad an.69 n.40. liquet; Ita enim n. 43. concludit: Hac licet pluribus dicta videantur, necessariò tamen tractata, nam si in ordine & tempore primorum Pontificum Romanorum quempiam errare contigerit, in multos alios errores ferri omninò cogetur. Ex dictis autem patet, fundamento carere assertionem ejusdem Baronii hanc: Ex his narratis stabilis firmáque remanet Ecclesia Romana sententia de Petri Successoribus, consensúque antiquorum Patrum tam Græcorum, quàm Latinorum stabilita. Manet contrà, Electionis Pontificum Romanorum in isto dissensu non exiguum esse nævum. Qualis etiam apud Baronium eundem ad an. 158. n. 3. observatur, dum Hygini P. Successorem alios Anicetum, Pium verò illi suffectum, dicere, alios primo loco Pium, ac post eum Anicetum numerare, testatur, atque utrumque sententia haud vulgares assertores haberi.
units.tr: VII. That this controversy is not so trivial is clear even from Baronius himself. A not inconsiderable suspicion troubled his mind, that Clement sat in the fourth place after Peter, although he thought it truer that Clement must be placed before Anacletus, and so in the third place, ad an.69 n.40. is clear. For n. 43. he concludes: Although these matters may seem to have been said at length, they had to be treated, for if anyone should happen to err about the order and time of the first Roman bishops, he will be forced to be carried into many other errors. From what has been said, however, it is plain that this assertion of the same Baronius lacks foundation: From these things narrated the Roman Church's opinion about Peter's successors remains firm and stable, and it was established by the consent of the ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin. On the contrary, it remains that in this disagreement there is no small blemish on the election of the Roman bishops. The same blemish is observed in Baronius himself ad an. 158. n. 3., where he testifies that, while some say that Hyginus was succeeded by Anicetus and Pius was appointed after him, others number Pius first and Anicetus after him, and that both opinions have no mean advocates.

units.la: VIII. Sed & nævus in eo apparet, quòd adeò non de tempore electionis horum & aliorum conveniunt, haud magis atque de ordine; Necessariò autem dissensus de ordine dissensum quoque de tempore secum trahit, & jam facilè intelligitur, Authores, qui de ordine primorum Pontificum non consentiunt, de tempore, quo electiones ipsorum factæ sint, dissentire. Qui & aliàs sæpissimè anno, sæpe annis aliquot, multis nonnunquam variant. Quod per exempla ostendere facile, sed nimis longum foret. Sufficiat igitur testimonia pauca attulisse. De Libro, quem Damasus Papa de Papis conscripsisse dicitur, ita idem Baronius l. c. n. 35. ait; Demonstrabimus, pluribus locis continere repugnantia inter se, feré in unoquoque Pontifice, in annis cujusque consignandis. De eodem n. 37. subjungit: Ex his videas, per quos anfractus, & quanto cum discrimine prodenda veritatis, rerum Ecclesiasticarum narratio ducenda esset, si, quæ in eo scripta sunt libro, absque diligenti pervestigatione quis esse suscipienda contenderet, ut necessario sibi ipso contrario (ipsi contraria) dicere opus esset. Onuphrius autem suum de Platinæ Chronologia Pontificum annot. ad Anacletum judicium tale exponit; Caterùm cùm in singulorum feré Pontificum annis à Platina dissentiam, qui eos longa, difficili & operosa supputatione formavi, & nimis fastidiosum esset, unicuique Pontifici meam sententiam adjungere, in libri fine brevem omnium Romanorum Pontificum Catalogum, cum annorum, quibus unusquisque sedit, numero adjiciam, ex vetustis probatisque auctoribus à me constitutum. Verùm idem de Baronii & Onuphrii supputationibus judicabunt ab ipsis dissentientes; Ut in hoc etiam incerta sint omnia. IX. Fa-
units.tr: VIII. There is also a blemish in this, that they do not agree on the time of the election of these and other men, any more than on their order. Disagreement about the order necessarily brings disagreement about the time with it. It is easily understood that authors who do not agree about the order of the first bishops also disagree about the time at which their elections took place. They also very often vary by a year, often by several years, and sometimes by many. To show this by examples would be easy, but it would be too long. It is enough, therefore, to have cited a few testimonies. Baronius himself says of the book which Pope Damasus is said to have written On the Popes, l. c. n. 35.: We shall show that it contains, in many places, contradictions among themselves, almost for each pope, in recording the years of each. About the same book, n. 37., he adds: From this you may see by what twists, and with how great a risk to the truth, the narrative of ecclesiastical affairs would have to be conducted, if someone undertook to accept as necessary whatever is written in that book without careful investigation, so that he would have to contradict himself. Onuphrius, however, sets out his judgement on Platina's chronology of the popes in his note on Anacletus as follows: But since I differ from Platina in almost the years of the individual popes, which I worked out by a long, difficult and laborious reckoning, and since it would be too tedious to add my opinion to each pope, I will add at the end of the book a brief catalogue of all the Roman popes, with the number of years each sat, drawn up by me from old and approved authors. Yet those who differ from Baronius and Onuphrius will judge the same about their calculations, so that in this too everything is uncertain. IX. Fa-

units.la: IX. Fatetur ex parte ipse Baronius, dum ad an. 80. n. 1. ita scribit: Nos, cùm non appareat, quot diebus (scribere potuisset etiam: mensibus, annis) alicujus Pontificis sedes vacaverit, à die sequenti obitus praecedentis, annos ejus, qui subrogatus est, cogimur numerare. Sicque recensentes Lini annos à die post martyrium Petri, deducentésque annos usque ad diem, qua anniversaria ejus Commemoratio in Ecclesia antiquitus fieri consuevit, non tantùm annos, sed & menses & dies hac ratione tutiùs putamus esse ponendos; cum praesertim diversa à diversis scribantur, nec quicquam certi habeatur, quod omni ex parte subsistat. Idem etiam ad an. 112. n. 1. de communi naufragio Scripturarum quoad historiam Pontificum conqueri necesse habuit. Qui jam porrò exempla differentiae quoad tempus electionum cognoscere vult, Catalogos diversos conferat, in quo labore Doctissimus Hunnius jam praevit & viam ostendit triplici, quem edidit, Romanorum Pontificum Catalogo; Audiat Authorem Fascic. temp. p. 67. conquerentem: Nota, quòd libri satis discordant de tempore horum Pontificum &c. & Genebrardum ad Leonem VIII. Hi & sequentes Pontifices variè ab Historicis collocantur, quin & ante hunc aliqui nominant Benedictum V. Et ad an. 684. confusa sunt admodum istorum temporum historia &c. & Arnoldum Pontacum ad initium Nicolai: Hic mirè variant Historici in adnotatione annorum: & Platinam in Bonif. VI. Quantum in Pontificatu vixerit, magna controversia est. Plùs enim alii, minùs quidam huic tempori adscribunt. Sentio ego &c. Maximè autem Onuphrium ad Nicol. I. Plat. ista annotantem: Sequentes Pontifices, usque ad Clementem II. tempora adeò incerta & obscura habent, ut neque quo loco, neque quo ordine aliquot Rom. Pontificum nomina reponerentur, satis liqueat &c. Sed & videri possunt sequentia apud Baronium loca T.II. an. 167. n. 1. an. 175. n. 2. an. 179. n. 50. an. 253. n. 5.6. an. 260. n. 2. an. 275. n. 1. an. 283. n. 14. T.III. an. 311. n. 40. an. 313. n. 47. an. 335. n. 4. & 58. an. 336. n. 61. T.IV. an. 367. n. 2. T.V. an. 423. n. 1. T.VII. an. 559. n. 1. T.IX. an. 417. n. 1. T.X. an. 910. n. 1. an. 936. n. 4. T.XI. an 1012. n. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. &c. &c. ubi circa tot Pontificum Electiones diversae, quoad annum & annos, sententiae occurrunt.
units.tr: IX. Baronius himself confesses this in part, when he writes ad an. 80. n. 1.: Since it does not appear how many days (he could also have written: months, years) the see of any pope was vacant, we are compelled to count the years of the one who was substituted from the day after the death of the previous one. And so, reckoning the years of Linus from the day after Peter's martyrdom, and carrying the count to the day on which his anniversary commemoration used to be kept in the Church, we think it safer to put down not only years but also months and days in this way, especially since different things are written by different authors, and nothing certain is held which stands on every side. He also had to complain ad an. 112. n. 1. about the common shipwreck of the Scriptures so far as the history of the popes is concerned. Whoever now wishes to know further examples of the difference in the time of the elections should compare the various catalogues. In this labour the most learned Hunnius has already gone before and shown the way, in the threefold catalogue of Roman popes which he published. Let the author of the Fascic. temp. p. 67. be heard complaining: Note that the books differ quite a lot about the time of these popes, etc., and Genebrardus, on Leo VIII: these and the following popes are placed in various ways by the historians; indeed some name Benedict V before this one. And ad an. 684.: the history of those times is very confused, etc.; and Arnoldus Pontacus on the beginning of Nicholas: Here the historians vary wildly in the note of the years, and Platina on Boniface VI: how long he lived in the papacy is a great controversy. For some ascribe more time to him, others less. I myself think, etc. Above all, Onuphrius, annotating on Nicholas I, Platina, says: The following popes, down to Clement II, have such uncertain and obscure times that it is not sufficiently clear in what place or order some of the names of the Roman popes should be put, etc. But the following passages in Baronius may also be consulted: T.II. an. 167. n. 1. an. 175. n. 2. an. 179. n. 50. an. 253. n. 5.6. an. 260. n. 2. an. 275. n. 1. an. 283. n. 14. T.III. an. 311. n. 40. an. 313. n. 47. an. 335. n. 4. & 58. an. 336. n. 61. T.IV. an. 367. n. 2. T.V. an. 423. n. 1. T.VII. an. 559. n. 1. T.IX. an. 417. n. 1. T.X. an. 910. n. 1. an. 936. n. 4. T.XI. an 1012. n. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. etc. etc., where, concerning so many elections of popes, different opinions as to the year and the years occur.

units.la: X. Ad naevos & vitia sic pertinet incertitudo temporis Electionum, sed magis adhuc longior & frequentior dilatio Electionum. Nempe saepe satis diuturna Interregna (ita Baronius nonnisi regia cogitans vocat, quae melius Inter-Pontificia dicuntur,) fuerunt. Et quidem Baronius testatur ad an.102. n. 24. postmortem tem Clementis per complures menses; ad an. 253. n. 6. post mortem Fabiani anno 1. & amplius; (ad an. 304. n. 25. refutare studet inter Pontificium an. 7. m 6. d. 25. in libro de Pontificibus Romanis traditum) ipse vero porrò testatur; ad an. 577. n. 1. post mortem Johannis per m. 10. d. 3. ad an. 638. n. 5. post mortem Honorii an. 1. m. 7. d. 17. ad an. 683. post mortem Agathonis an. 1. m. 7. d. 5. ad an. 767. n. 4. post mortem Pauli I. an. 1. m. 1. sedem Papalem vacâsse. Onuphrius annotat, mortuo Cœlestino IV. sedem an. 1. m. 8. d. 15. vacâsse. Alii referunt, post mortem Clementis IV. quae anno 1270. accidit, per 2. annos Ecclesiam illam capite caruisse, non habendo possuto, sunt verba authoris Cardinalismi p. 3. l 1. p. 50. i Cardinali accordarsi per l'elettione d'un successore; dum non potuerunt Cardinales consentire in Successorem; Mortuo an. 1287. Honorio IV. ob morbos & terrae motus electiones impedientes per 10. menses Pontificem nullum fuisse, atque, satis functo, qui in fine illorum tandem electus fuit, Nicolao IV. per 2. annos & 2. menses Ecclesiam illam ob discordiam Cardinalium viduam mansisse. Sed magis & longè magis diuturna Inter-Pontificia fuerunt, ratione habitâ invasorum, intrusorum, Schismaticorum, de quibus partim jam suprà egimus, partim suo loco amplius agemus. Posterioribus autem Seculis plerunque per mensem, duos, interdum etiam tres menses sedes vacua fuit, & esse solet, atque forte à longo tempore maximè diuturnum fuit Inter-Pontificium, quod electionem Pii IV. antecessit 4. mensium 7. d. De causis autem dilationis longioris, brevioris, quas jam ex parte innuimus, prolixius infrà agendum erit.
units.tr: X. The uncertainty of the time of the elections belongs to the blemishes and faults, but the still longer and more frequent delay of the elections belongs more to them still. Indeed, quite long Interregna (as Baronius calls them, thinking only of kings, though they would better be called inter-papal periods) have often occurred. Baronius himself testifies ad an.102. n. 24. that after the death of Clement the see was vacant for several months; ad an. 253. n. 6. after the death of Fabian for one year and more; (ad an. 304. n. 25. he tries to refute the seven years, six months, twenty-five days handed down in the book on the Roman popes), and he further testifies: ad an. 577. n. 1. after the death of John, for ten months and three days; ad an. 638. n. 5. after the death of Honorius, one year, seven months, seventeen days; ad an. 683. after the death of Agatho, one year, seven months, five days; ad an. 767. n. 4. after the death of Paul I, one year, one month, the papal see was vacant. Onuphrius notes that on the death of Celestine IV the see was vacant for one year, eight months, fifteen days. Others report that after the death of Clement IV, which happened in 1270, the Church was without a head for two years, not having been able (these are the words of the author of the Cardinalism, p. 3. l 1. p. 50., the Cardinals agreeing on the election of a successor) since the Cardinals could not agree on a successor. After the death of Honorius IV in 1287, because of illnesses and earthquakes which hindered the elections, there was no pope for ten months; and after the death of Nicholas IV, who was finally chosen at the end of those months, the Church remained widowed for two years and two months because of the discord of the Cardinals. But the inter-papal periods were much longer still, if one takes into account the usurpers, intruders and schismatics, of whom we have partly already treated above and will treat more fully in their place. In later centuries, however, the see has commonly been vacant for one month, two months, and sometimes even three months, and it is usually so; and perhaps the longest inter-papal period in a long time was the four months and seven days which preceded the election of Pius IV. The causes of longer and shorter delay, some of which we have already hinted at, will have to be treated more fully below.

units.la: XI. Hic autem quantus ille dilationis nævus, vitium quantum sit, paucis monebo.
units.tr: XI. How great this blemish of delay is, and how serious a fault it is, I will show briefly.

units.la: Et primò quidem qualiscunque etiam brevissima mora heic multùm obesse videtur. Ubi enim est, mortuo Pontifice, illa potestas Pontificia, Monarchica? Penes quem, vel ubi residet? Ostendimus Dissert. IV. & V. ex Monarchicorum doctrina eam non esse penes Collegium Cardinalium; Dissert. I. eam non esse penes Ecclesiam universam? Ubi igitur haerebit, & quomodo ad Pontificem futurum derivabitur, quomodo ei conferetur, neque interiit? Respondet Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. l. 1. c. 12. moriente Pontifice claves (per eas autem innuit potestatem illam Pontificiam) non perire, nec tamen remanere formaliter in Ecclesia, nisi quatenus communicatae sunt inferioribus Ministris, sed manere in manibus Christi. Cùm eligitur novus Pontifex, neque adferri ab eo claves, neque illi dari ab Ecclesia, sed à Christo, non nova traditione, sed antiqua institutione. Siquidem Petro eas cùm dedit, omnibus ejus successoribus dedit simili ratione, qua aliquis rex proregem provincia imponens simul subditis potestatem, alium eo mortuo eligendi largiretur. Verùm ab una parte hæc omnia gratis finguntur, atque jam Differt. I. ostensum est, ne quidem Petro talem omnipotentiam Pontificiam concessam fuisse, ita ab altera parte sic non absurdum tollitur, siquidem in allato simili cum determinatione futurorum Pro-Regum simul quoque in subditis esse debet potestas, quam Pro-Regibus, qui ab iis constituuntur, conferre possint, usque ad eorum constitutionem illa præditi, atque illa simul cum determinatione Pro-Regum iis collata intelligitur; neque enim bonus Rex mortuus sine Magistratu & regimine necessario subditos, mortuo ex Pro-Regibus aliquo, relinquit; vivus ipse inferioris defuncti potestatem sua plenitudine compensat, si præsens sit; absens penes alios Pro-Regis illius potestatem constituit, aliter ac in quæstione, qua de agitur, supponitur; supponitur enim, neque Cardinales, neque Ecclesiam universam potestatis Pontificiæ in sua plenitudine capaces esse; Supponitur etiam, Christum Regem caput visibile illa, quæ pro-Regis, capitis visibilis, sint, præstare non posse; Qui certè etiam potestatem tantam, quam per homines non confert, tot monstris, tot indignè electis, immediatè sive nova traditione, sive antiqua institutione contulisse dici nequit.
units.tr: And first, even the briefest delay of any kind seems to do great harm here. For when the Pope has died, where is that papal, monarchical power? In whose hands does it rest, or where does it reside? We showed in Dissert. IV. & V., from the doctrine of the monarchists, that it does not rest with the College of Cardinals; and in Dissert. I., that it does not rest with the universal Church. Where, then, will it remain, and how will it pass to the future Pope? How will it be conferred on him, and will it not perish? Bellarmine answers in de Rom. Pont. l. 1. c. 12.: when the Pope dies, the keys (by which he means that papal power) do not perish, nor do they remain formally in the Church, except insofar as they have been communicated to the lesser ministers, but they remain in the hands of Christ. When a new Pope is elected, the keys are neither brought by him nor given to him by the Church, but by Christ, not by a new handing down but by an ancient institution. For when he gave them to Peter, he gave them to all his successors in the same way as a king who appoints a viceroy over a province and at the same time grants to the subjects the power of choosing another when he dies. But on the one hand all these things are invented without any grounds, and it has already been shown in Dissert. I. that not even to Peter was such papal omnipotence granted. On the other hand, the comparison does not remove the absurdity so easily. For in the comparison cited, when the future viceroys are determined, the subjects must also hold a power that they can confer on the viceroys who are appointed by them, and it is understood that they hold that power until those viceroys are installed, and that this power is conferred on them at the same time as the determination of the viceroys. For a good king who dies does not necessarily leave his subjects without government and rule, if one of the viceroys dies; if he is present, he himself makes up for the lost power by his own fullness; if he is absent, he appoints others to hold that viceroy's power, which is not how things stand in the question under discussion. For it is assumed that neither the Cardinals nor the universal Church are capable of papal power in its fullness; it is also assumed that Christ, the King, cannot provide the things that belong to the visible head in place of the king. Surely such great power, which he does not confer through men, cannot be said to have been conferred immediately, whether by a new handing down or by an ancient institution, on so many monsters, so many unworthy men.

units.la: XII. Secundò difficultatem etiam auget dilationis diuturnitas.
units.tr: XII. Secondly, the length of the delay also adds to the difficulty.

units.la: Semper loquuntur de maxima necessitate Papæ; Quæ tamen tanta non esse, nec ad Ecclesiæ essentiam pertinere potest, si illa tam sæpe & tamdiu sine Papa subsistere potuit & potest; Et certè, si per biennium & amplius aliquando sine Papa substitit, dicendum est, eam longiori etiam temporis spatio sine tali capite subsistere, eòque planè carere posse. Hactenus autem recensita electionis Pontificum Romanorum vitia quodammodo remota generaliora sunt atque minùs in se moralia; Pergamus ad propiora, vitiosum electionis actum specialiùs constituentia, atque etiam in se plùs malitiæ moralis habentia.
units.tr: They always speak of the very great necessity of the Pope; yet this cannot be so great, nor can it belong to the essence of the Church, if the Church has been able and still is able to subsist so often and for so long without a Pope. And certainly, if it has at times subsisted for two years or more without a Pope, it must be said that it can subsist for an even longer span of time without such a head, and so can clearly do without one. But the faults of the election of Roman Pontiffs recounted so far are, in a sense, more remote and more general, and less morally serious in themselves. Let us proceed to the closer ones, which constitute the faulty act of election more specifically and which in themselves contain more moral wickedness.

units.la: XIII. Vix forte induci potes, Lector, ut credas, talia nos in Electionibus Pontificum Romanorum ostendere posse, memor eorum, quæ de sublimitate Majestatis, quam jactant, spiritualis, & de eximiis Vicarii Christi & Monarchæ, Capitis ac Sponsi Ecclesiæ siæ nominibus dicta sunt; memor eorum, de quibus quoad peculiarem Dei & Spiritūs S. in opere isto curam,regimen & assisten- tiam gloriantes introduximus; memor etiam juramenti à Cardinalibus ante singula scrutinia conceptis verbis sequentibus præstari soliti: Testor Christum Dominum, qui me judicaturus est, me eligere, quem secundum Deum judico, eligi debere, & quod idem in accessu præstabo. Quod juramentum etiam in aliis eligendi modis, cum de eodem semper negotio agatur, animum occupare debere videtur; non immemor aliorum, quæ de necessitate optimæ & vitio carentis electionis diximus; Hinc forte præsumens, in negotio hoc semper per lineas rectas procedi, nunquam viis obliquis incedi; ambages omnes ducente Spiritu omitti, Dignissimum statim omnium unicum scopum esse; Spiritus ejusdem fructus heic maximè,imò solùm apparere,charitatem, gaudium, pacem, lenitatem, fidem, mansuetudinem, Gal.V.22. addo,in electione Vicarii Christi, humilis, humilitatem; in electione Vicarii Christi, dolo carentis, simplicitatem; in electione Vicarii Christi, veracis, veracitatem; in electione Vicarii Christi, perfecti, perfectionem omnem,omnia operante eodem Spiritu Christi peculiariter assistente; Hinc forte cogitans;opera carnis fructibus Spiritus, Gal.VI.19.20.21. opposita procul abesse, inimicitias, litem, amulationes, iras, contentiones, dissidia, invidias, cades, & his similia, superbiam superbi Dæmonis filiam; mendacia, sobolem patris mendaciorum; deceptiones, opera Spiritūs seductoris, mala omnia. Hinc forte secundùm Deum heic omnia agi; secundùm Deum, & non secundùm Mammona iniquitatis; secundùm Deum, & non secundùm omnis generis passiones.
units.tr: XIII. Perhaps you can hardly be persuaded, reader, that we can show such things in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs, when you remember what has been said about the sublimity of the spiritual majesty they boast of, and about the outstanding names of the Vicar of Christ, the monarch, head and bridegroom of the Church; when you remember those things about which, in this work, we have introduced them boasting of the particular care, rule and assistance of God and the Holy Spirit; and remember also the oath which the Cardinals were accustomed to take before each scrutiny, in these words: I call Christ the Lord, who is to judge me, to witness that I elect the one whom I judge, before God, ought to be elected, and that I will do the same at the accession. This oath, since it always concerns the same business, ought also to occupy the mind in the other modes of electing; and yet one is not unmindful of the other things we have said about the necessity of the best election, free from fault. Hence, perhaps, one presumes that in this business everything always proceeds in straight lines and never goes by crooked ways, that all circuitousness is omitted under the leading of the Spirit, and that the most worthy man is at once the only aim of all. Here, especially, the fruits of that Spirit appear, or rather appear alone: love, joy, peace, patience, faith, gentleness, Gal. V. 22. I add: in the election of the Vicar of Christ, humility, in the humble; in the election of the Vicar of Christ, freedom from deceit, simplicity; in the election of the Vicar of Christ, truthfulness, truth; in the election of the Vicar of Christ, of the perfect one, all perfection, the same Spirit of Christ working all things and assisting in a special way. Hence, perhaps, one thinks that the works of the flesh, which are opposed to the fruits of the Spirit, Gal. VI. 19, 20, 21, are far away: enmities, strife, rivalries, angers, contentions, dissensions, envyings, murders, and things like these; pride, the daughter of the proud devil; lies, the offspring of the father of lies; deceits, the works of the seducing spirit, all evils. Hence, perhaps, one thinks that here everything is done according to God, and according to God and not according to the mammon of unrighteousness; according to God, and not according to all kinds of passions.

units.la: XIV. Et quidem idem postulant Pontificum quorundam decreta, constitutiones, Bullæ, aliorúmque monitiones.
units.tr: XIV. Indeed, the decrees, constitutions, bulls of certain popes, and the admonitions of others demand the same thing.

units.la: Ita Gregorius X. apud Onuphrium annot. ad Greg. X. Plat. vetat: Ut in comitiis habendis sub anathematis pœna nulli fas sit, aut largitione uti, aut quicquam polliceri, aut prensare, sive animos Cardinalium sibi in nova creatione devincire, Sed non inutile erit, audire ipsas illius voces; In Concilio Lugdunensi, quod Generale habetur, ita loquitur: 6. decr. l. 1. de el. tit. 6. c. 4. ubi periculum §. Caterùm (quia cùm arbitrium vel inordinatus captivat affectus: vel ad certum aliquem obligationis cujusque necessitas adigit, cessat electio,dum libertas adimitur eligendi) Cardinales eosdem obsecrantes per viscera misericordie dia Dei nostri, per aspersionem sui pretiosi sanguinis obtestamur, ut pensantes attentiùs, quid eis imminet: cùm agitur de creatione Vicarii Jesu Christi, Successoris Petri, Rectoris universalis Ecclesiæ, gregis Dominici directoris, omni privata affectionis inordinatione depositâ: & cujuslibet pactionis, conventionis, obligationis necessitate: nec non conditi & intendimenti contemplatione cessantibus: non in se reciprocent considerationis intuitum, vel in suos: non, quæ sua sunt, quærant; non commodis privatis intendant, sed nullo arctante ipsorum in eligendo judicium: nisi Deo puris & liberis mentibus nudâ electionis conscientiâ utilitatem publicam liberè prosequantur: Omni conatu & solicitudine (prout possibilitas patitur) id acturi tantummodo: ut eorum ministerio acceleretur utilis & necessaria totius mundi provifio: idoneo celeriter eidem Ecclesiæ Sponso dato. Qui autem secus egerint: divinæ subjaceant ultioni: eorum culpa (nisi gravi propter hoc peractâ pœnitentiâ) nullatenus abolenda.
