Et nos nihilominus pactiones, conventiones, obligationes, conditta & intendimenta omnia, sive inferens juramenti, sive cujuslibet alterius fuerint vinculo firmitatis annexa: cassamus, irritamus, & viribus decernimus omninò carere: ita quòd nullus ad illa observanda, quomodolibet sit adstrictus: nec quisquam ex eorum transgressione, notam vereatur fidei non servatæ: sed non indignæ laudis titulum potius mereatur: cùm lex etiam humana tetetur, Deo magis transgressiones hujusmodi, quàm jurisjurandi observationes acceptas. Pius IV. vero in Bulla de Conclavi, ita Cardinales obtestatur, stmúlque iis præcipit, transgressoribus minatur: Cardinales autem per viscera misericordiæ Domini Jesu Christi enixè rogamus & hortamur, ac eis nihilominus sub divini interminatione judicii præcipimus & mandamus, ut attendentes magnitudinem ministerii, quod per eos tractatur in dandis suffragiis, ac aliis omnibus & singulis electionem quomodolibet concernentibus, omni dolo, ac fraude, factionibus & animorum passionibus remotis, ac Principum sæcularium intercessionibus cæterisque mundanis respectibus minimè attentis: sed solum Deum pra oculis habentes, sese purè, liberè, sincerè, quietè & pacificè gerere & habere debeant, nec pro ipsius Pontificis electione conspirationes, conditta, actiones, & alios illicitos tractatus inire, signa aut contra signa votorum suorum alteri dare, minasve aliquibus inferre, tumultus excitare, aut alia facere, per quæ electio retardetur, vel minùs liberè suffragia præstentur, per se, vel alium, directè vel indirectè, quovis colore vel ingenio audeant, vel præsumant. Quod si secus fecerint, aut contra prohibita in præsenti constitutione aliquid admiserint, ultra divinam ultionem arbitrio futuri Pontificis pro modo culpæ in eos quandocunque animadverti possit. Merentur, quæ Pontificiis decretis his addantur graviter monentia Jani Nicii Erythræi Ep. ad Tyrrh. p. 178, verba: At ubinam, inquies, hunc, qui sit talis, quærent? Num inter eos, qui sint nobis vel mutuo amicitiæ vinculo juncti, vel arcto cognationis nexu constricti? Minimè quidem. Nam Christus, qui futurus erat Pontifex in æternum, inter cognatos ac notos noluit inveniri. Quamobrem hoc? Quia voluit nobis per hanc rationem insinuare, non eum esse in comitatu cognatorum amicorumque petendum, qui successurus esset Vicarius sui muneris, qui esset alter ipse futurus. Tum ille disertis verbis omnem amicitiam, omnem cognationis necessitudinem respuit præter eam, quam Dei amor ejúsque divinarum legum obedientia cultúsque conjunxit; Nam, qui fecerit, voluntatem patris mei, qui in cœlis est, hic mater mea & frater vocabitur. At, si sola cognationis amicitiæque ratio non debeat eum nobis Pontificem dare, quem quærimus, dabit saltem spes privatæ cujuspiam utilitatis, vel potentiæ vel divitiarum. O semper humi defixas nostras cogitationes! O terrena consilia! Ergo orbis terrarum Imperatoris, Ecclesiæ universæ moderatoris, animarum nostrarum Pastoris, Christianorum omnium magistri ac Domini comitiis utilitatis privatæ ratio dominabitur? Ergo ille magis vel minùs dignus, qui cæteris præsit, habeatur, ille magis vel minùs idoneus, qui Successor Petri, qui summæ potestatis Antistes sit, declarabitur, quem plùs minùs è re nostra sit in tanto dignitatis gradu locari? Ergo illi tutiùs Christianorum omnium salus committi declarabitur, qui utilior ac fructuosior nobis futurus existimetur, contra, in eo omnium fortunas agi, communem salutem periclitari, orbis terræ interitum metui, unde parùm vel nihil sit ad nos lucri redundaturum? Velle autem pluribus verbis demonstrare, quàm hæc partim sint levia, partim intolerabilia, non modò superfluum ac non necessarium, verùm etiam ineptum existimo.
units.tr: So Gregory X, as Onuphrius reports in his annotations on Gregory X in Platina, forbids: that in holding elections it is lawful for no one, under pain of anathema, either to use largesse, or to promise anything, or to canvass, or to bind to himself the minds of the Cardinals in a new creation. But it will not be unprofitable to hear his very words. In the Council of Lyons, which is regarded as general, he speaks thus: 6 Decretals, book 1, On Elections, title 6, chapter 4. where the danger is pointed out: § But (since the free choice of electors is taken away when either an inordinate affection captivates them, or the necessity of some obligation binds each one to a certain party, the election ceases), we earnestly beseech the same Cardinals through the bowels of the mercy of our God, and we solemnly charge them by the sprinkling of his precious blood, that weighing more carefully what hangs over them, since it is a matter of creating the Vicar of Jesus Christ, the Successor of Peter, the Ruler of the universal Church, the director of the Lord's flock, they should put off every private inordinate affection, and the necessity of any pact, agreement, or obligation, and, setting aside also the consideration of any condition or intention, should not turn the gaze of their consideration upon themselves or their own; they should not seek what is their own, nor aim at private advantages, but, with no constraint upon their judgement in choosing, they should freely pursue the public good, with pure and free minds and a clear conscience before God alone. Let them act with all effort and care (as far as possibility allows) only so that, by their ministry, the useful and necessary provision for the whole world may be speedily secured by giving a suitable spouse to the same Church. Those who act otherwise shall be subject to divine vengeance, and their guilt (unless it is atoned for by grave repentance) is in no way to be wiped away. And we, nonetheless, quash, annul, and by our authority decree to be entirely without force all pacts, agreements, obligations, conditions and intentions, whether they are bound to the firmness of an oath or of any other tie, so that no one is bound to observe them in any way, and no one should fear from their breach the mark of faithlessness, but rather deserves the title of praise not unworthy of him, since even human law holds that God accepts such breaches more than the keeping of oaths. Pius IV, however, in the bull on the Conclave, so entreats the Cardinals, and so charges them, and threatens transgressors: "We earnestly request and exhort the Cardinals through the bowels of mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ, and nonetheless we command and order them under threat of divine judgement, that, attending to the greatness of the ministry which is handled through them in giving votes and in all and each of the other matters concerning the election in any way, all deceit and fraud, factions and passions of mind being removed, and with no regard for the intercessions of secular princes or other worldly considerations, but keeping God alone before their eyes, they ought to conduct and comport themselves purely, freely, sincerely, quietly and peaceably; and they must not dare or presume, by themselves or through another, directly or indirectly, under any pretext or contrivance, to enter into conspiracies, agreements, actions and other unlawful negotiations concerning the election of the Pontiff, to give signs or counter-signs of their votes to another, to threaten anyone, to stir up tumults, or to do other things by which the election is delayed or the votes are given less freely. But if they act otherwise, or admit anything against what is forbidden in the present constitution, then, besides divine vengeance, they may at any time be punished in proportion to their fault at the discretion of the future Pontiff." The following words of Janus Nicius Erythraeus, in his letter to Tyrrhus, page 178, deserve to be added to these papal decrees as a serious warning: But where, you will ask, will they seek such a man? Among those who are joined to us by the bond of friendship or bound by the close tie of kinship? Certainly not. For Christ, who was to be the Pontiff forever, chose not to be found among kinsmen and acquaintances. Why so? Because he wished to show us by this that the one who is to succeed as Vicar of his office, who is to be another himself, is not to be sought in the company of relatives and friends. Then he rejects in plain words all friendship and all the claims of kinship, except that which the love of God and obedience to his divine laws have joined; for whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is called my mother and my brother. But if the reason of kinship and friendship ought not to give us the Pontiff we seek, will the hope of some private advantage, of power or riches, give him? O our thoughts, always fixed to the earth! O earthly counsels! So shall the reason of private advantage rule the assembly of the Emperor of the whole world, the governor of the universal Church, the shepherd of our souls, the master and Lord of all Christians? So shall he be declared more or less worthy to preside over others, he be declared more or less fit to be Successor of Peter, the Bishop of supreme power, whom it is more or less to our interest to place in so high a rank of dignity? So shall the salvation of all Christians be declared safer to entrust to him who is thought likely to be more useful and profitable to us, while on the contrary the fortunes of all are put at stake, the common safety endangered, the ruin of the world feared, from which little or nothing of gain would flow back to us? To wish to demonstrate in more words how light, and partly intolerable, these things are, I consider not only superfluous and unnecessary but even absurd.

units.la: XV. Impossibile fortè judicas, Lector, ut graves ejusmodi admonitiones planè negligantur, & summorum maximè Pontificum præceptiones nihili æstimentur, simúlque & perjurii crimen committatur, & anathematis pœna transgressione multiplici attrahatur; Maximè quia Bullæ de electionibus ante electiones singulas legi solent. Verùm totum hoc non tantùm possibile esse, sed & ordinariò fieri, ex sequentibus patebit. In Conclavia te introducam reserata, Lector, ubi contraria omnia Pontificum admonitionibus & præceptionibus, inversa omnia videbis, non aliter ac si contrarium Pontifices suasissent, præcepissent ejus, quod suaserunt, ferunt, præceperunt; non aliter ac si anathematis loco (in quod multis modis plerosque semper incurrere, atque proin, juxta dicta, ad electionem ineptos fieri & habere debere, sequentia docebunt;) transgressoribus præmia amplissima constituissent. In qua tamen transgressionum multitudine de animadversione arbitraria futuri Pontificis pro modo culpæ institutæ nihil plane auditur. Gaudet præsentibus ipse, forte ejusmodi artibus prohibitis promotus, quas proin in authoribus punire ingratitudinis speciem haberet; Contrà recens electi in his etiam se Clementes ostendunt. Exemplo sit Urbanus VI. à quo, finito sermone Inaugurali Cardinales petierunt plenariam Indulgentiam omnium suorum peccatorum, & dispensationem super quibuscunque Irregularitatibus, quas ipsi quacunque occasione, vel causa forsitan incurrissent, quod etiam Papa libenter concessit, & subsequenter quilibet eorum Confessorem elegit, per quem in forma Ecclesiæ se absolvi fecerunt, juxta Conclave ejusdem. Sed & jam diximus Differt. I. quàm indulgens sibimet Sixtus V. ratione mendaciorum in Conclavi forte prolatorum esse voluerit.
units.tr: XV. Perhaps you judge it impossible, reader, that serious admonitions of this kind should be utterly neglected, and the precepts of the greatest Pontiffs held as nothing; and that at the same time the crime of perjury is committed and the penalty of anathema is incurred by manifold transgression; especially since the bulls on elections are customarily read before each individual election. But that all this is not only possible but ordinarily happens will be clear from what follows. I shall lead you, reader, into the Conclave laid open, where you will see everything contrary to the admonitions and precepts of the Pontiffs, everything turned upside down, just as if the Pontiffs had advised the contrary of what they advised, or had commanded the opposite of what they commanded. It is as if, instead of an anathema (into which, as what follows will show, most men in many ways always fall, and therefore, according to what has been said, ought to be and are unfit for the election), they had set the most generous rewards for transgressors. Yet in this great multitude of transgressions nothing at all is heard about punishment at the discretion of the future Pontiff in proportion to the fault. The one who is present rejoices, perhaps having been promoted by just such forbidden arts, whom it would therefore seem a kind of ingratitude to punish in those who made him; on the contrary, the newly elected show themselves merciful even in these matters. Let Urban VI be an example, after whose inaugural sermon the Cardinals asked for a plenary indulgence of all their sins, and a dispensation from whatever irregularities they might perhaps have incurred on any occasion or for any cause, which the Pope also granted willingly, and afterwards each of them chose a confessor, through whom they had themselves absolved in the form of the Church, according to the same Conclave. But we have already said, in Dissertation I, how indulgent Sixtus V was willing to be toward himself with respect to the lies perhaps uttered in the Conclave.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Fidem dictis facturi, in consideratione ulteriori næ- vorum & vitiorum Electionum Pontificum Romanorum primo principia, secundùm quæ in Electionibus istis operatio instituitur, secundo media, quibus scopum consequi studeant, & tertio adjuncta quædam, quæ ex principiis & mediis talibus fluunt, ob oculos ponemus. Prius autem illud monendum putamus, nos non eo animo vitiosa ista ostendere velle, qui omnes Electores eorum ex æquo participes credat; contrà persuasissimi sumus, non paucos ex erronea quidem opinione, quòd Papatus sit Divina institutio, Viros honestos sæpe intervenire, ex principiis honestis, licitorum, facta hypothesi, mediorum usu, bonum Papam eligere modis omnibus studentes, quales etiam tractatio sequens subinde ostendet; sed & ex illa constabit, longè majorem esse numerum ex aliis principiis aliter alió collimantium, illósque ab his ordinario torrentis cujusdam violentiâ in sequiorem partem abripi, imò etiam quosdam, quos extra Conclave ab omni fuco alienos crederes, latus multùm diversos apparere, atque occasionibus datis, tentationibus auctis, detractâ etiam larvâ, morbo communi infectos. Hâc premissâ monelâ jam ad rem ipsam &, juxta ordinem jam jam positum, primo ad considerationem Principiorum agendi vitiosorum progredimur.
units.tr: To make good what I have said, in the further consideration of the blemishes and faults of the elections of the Roman Pontiffs, I will set before your eyes first the principles on which the operations in these elections are founded, second the means by which they strive to reach their goal, and third certain circumstances that flow from such principles and means. But first I think this must be said: I do not wish to show these faults with the intention of suggesting that all their electors share them. On the contrary, I am quite convinced that not a few men of honour, moved by a mistaken belief that the papacy is a divine institution, often take part, and that, granting the hypothesis, they use lawful means from honest principles and try in every way to choose a good Pope, as the following discussion will sometimes show. But it will also be clear that the far greater number are aiming at different goals from different principles, that they are dragged by the usual violence of a sort of torrent into the worse course, and that even some men whom you would believe free of all pretence outside the Conclave appear quite different, and, when occasions are given and temptations increased, with the mask removed, are infected with the common disease. With this preface, we now proceed to the matter itself and, following the order just laid down, first to the consideration of the principles of wrongful action.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Sect. I.
units.tr: Sect. I.

units.la: XVII. Ad ea autem distinctius cognoscenda distinguimus statim inter Cardinales Papabiles,id est, eos qui aliquam spem Papatum consequendi habere possunt, & Non-Papabiles, distinctionem adhibentes apud Conclavium scriptores usitatissimam. Sunt enim certa Papabilium plerorumque principia, ex quibus omnia reliqua pendent. Est ambitio & cupiditas se ad sublime Petri solium evehendi. Haec principia si Papabiles non haberent, media vitiosa quaelibet intermitterentur, frustra etiam alii vitiosa principia foverent. Hinc, quamvis ambitionem illam, tanquam vitium eorum,qui eliguntur, demum Dissertatione sequente spectare possemus commodè,tamen,quia est Roma etiam Radix Omnium Malorum Ambitio,heic non minùs commodè inter principia vitiosa electionis eam, tanquam primum aliquod movens,considerabimus.
units.tr: XVII. To know these things more clearly, we at once distinguish between the Cardinals who are Papabiles, that is, those who can have some hope of obtaining the papacy, and the Non-Papabiles, a distinction very commonly used by writers on the Conclave. For there are certain principles that most of the Papabiles share, on which all the rest depend. There is ambition and the desire to raise oneself to the lofty throne of Peter. If the Papabiles did not have these principles, no wrongful means would be employed, and others would be fostering wrongful principles in vain. Hence, although we could fitly consider that ambition later, in the following Dissertation, as the vice of those who are elected, nevertheless, because "ambition is the root of all evils" [Rome is also the root of all evils, ambition], we will consider it here, no less fittingly, among the wrongful principles of the election, as a first moving cause.

units.la: XVIII. Olim quidem non erat sic, sed non ambientes, imò etiam inviti constituebantur Episcopi Romani,aequè ac aliarum Ecclesiarum,in quorum ore veritas erat suprà indigitatum illud: Nolo Episcopari; Quamdiu nimirum Episcopus Romanus intra Episcopi particularis limites se continebat, quamdiu persecutio vigebat,quamdiu nondum ad istam potentiam mundanam, ad istas divitias terrenas, ad luxum istum deveniebatur. Imò, ut unus & alter quasi anticipando ambivit, ita quoque postea non defuerunt, qui, si historiae fides est habenda, onus recusârunt, quamvis rariores illi fuerint; & rariores indies facti sint, usque adeò, ut à longo tempore non ambiens miraculi ad instar haberi potuisset, atque albo corvo rarior hic fuerit. Id quod ex sequentibus manifestum fiet.
units.tr: XVIII. Formerly it was not so, but the Bishops of Rome, like those of other Churches, were appointed without seeking it, even against their will, and in their case the saying was true: I do not wish to be made a bishop. Namely, as long as the Bishop of Rome kept within the limits of a particular bishopric, as long as persecution raged, as long as they had not yet come to that worldly power, those earthly riches, that luxury. Indeed, just as one or another sought the office, as though getting ahead of things, so afterwards there were not lacking those who, if the account of history is to be believed, refused the burden, although such men were rarer; and they became rarer day by day, to such a degree that for a long time a man who did not seek the office could have been regarded as a kind of miracle, and as rare as a white crow. This will become clear from what follows.

units.la: XIX. Non tamen possumus non,quia opposita juxta se posita magis elucescunt,aliquid porrò de abstinentia &moderatione priori afferre. Illustre est, quod Cornelio c. an. 254. electo S. Cyprianus ep. 52. ad Antonianum apud Bar. ad an. 254. n. 43. testimonium perhibet: Tum deinde Episcoparum nec postulavit, inquit, nec voluit, nec, ut cateri, quos arrogantia & superbia sua tumor inflat, invasit, sed quietus & modestus, & quales esse consueverunt,qui in hunc locum divinitus eliguntur,pro pudore virginalis conscientia sua & pro humilitate ingenita sibi & custodita verecundia, non ut quidam vim fecit,ut Episcopus fieret. sed ipse vim passus est, ut Episcopatum coactus exciperet, &c. Sed & de Gregorio I. ex Martyrol. Rom. d. 3. Sept. apud eund. ad an.590. n. 3. similia paucis occurrunt: Romae ordinatio,verba sunt Martyrol. incompincomparabilis viri S. Gregorii M. in summum Pontificem, qui onus illud subire coactus e sublimiori throno clarioribus sanctitatis radiis in orbe refulsit. Exemplum serius idem ad an. 1086. n. 3. in Victore III. exhibet.
units.tr: XIX. Nevertheless, since opposites shine more brightly when placed side by side, I cannot refrain from adding something further about the earlier abstinence and moderation. It is a famous testimony that St Cyprian gives concerning Cornelius, who was elected in the year 254: Ep. 52 to Antonianus, cited in Baronius at the year 254, no. 43: "Then, he says, he neither sought the bishopric, nor wished it, nor did he, like others whom the swelling of arrogance and pride puffs up, seize it; but he was quiet and modest, as those usually are who are chosen by God for this place, out of the modesty of his virginal conscience and the humility and reverence innate and preserved in him; not, as some have done, did he force his way to become bishop, but he himself was forced, so that he was compelled to accept the bishopric, etc." Also, concerning Gregory I, from the Roman Martyrology, 3 September, cited in the same place at the year 590, no. 3, similar things are found in brief: "At Rome the ordination," say the words of the Martyrology, "of the incomparable man St Gregory the Great as supreme Pontiff, who, compelled to undertake that burden, shone in the world from the higher throne with brighter rays of holiness." The same author gives a later example at the year 1086, no. 3, in Victor III.

units.la: XX. Causam mutati paulatim status & subsecutæ cupiditatis , quam jam quoque n. 18. innuimus, non male pandit Author Conclavis Sixti V. qui, postquam de suprema Pontificis dignitate & potestate egisset, mox subjungit: Effendo il Papato &c. Id est; Cùm Papatûs tanta fit dignitas & authoritas, mirum non est, naturâ ad alta aspirantes homines eum ambire atque quarere; Sed mirum est, illos, quos non Zelus pro honore Divino, sed ambitio perversa & desiderium injustum agit, eum propter commoda vel acquirere vel aliis procurare.
units.tr: XX. The author of the Conclave of Sixtus V explains not badly the cause of the gradually changed state and of the desire that followed, which we have already hinted at in no. 18. After discussing the supreme dignity and power of the Pope, he immediately adds: Since the papacy, etc. That is: "Since the papacy is of such great dignity and authority, it is no wonder that men, who by nature aspire to high things, seek and desire it; but it is a wonder that those whom zeal for the divine honour does not move, but perverse ambition and unjust desire, should seek to acquire it, or to procure it for others, for the sake of advantages."

units.la: XXI. Ita autem contingere jam ostendemus. Et quidem sine dubio cupiditatis heic stimulis pulsantur, qui (quod de plurimis mox declarandum erit;) varii generis malis artibus promotionem suam quærunt; Sed & habemus manifestiora atque propiora in exemplis sequentibus indicia. De Vigilio P. cujus posthac etiam prolixiorem mentionem facturi sumus, Baronius ad an.540. n. 5. testatur, quòd consueta summi honoris prurigine exagitatus, ut eum tuto consequi posset, nec unquam inde ejici ob delicta patrata, certam sibi viam aperiendam curaverit. Ad an. 900. n. 3. vehementer & in genere declamat contra Principum secularium manus in Rom. Pontificum electionem immittentium pessimos suasores, quos hostes Ecclesiæ Rom. infensissimos, procos impudentissimos & procacissimos, nefarios, avidissimos & audacissimos competitores vocat, qui turpis assentationis lenocinio ad Cathedram Petri sibi accessum parent. Idem Baronius ad an.1198. ex Rogerio illius temporis Scriptore ita statum post Cœlestini III. P. obitum exprimit: D. Ostiensis Episc. Cardinalis nitebatur, ut ipsemet Papa fieret; Similiter D. Jordanus de Fossa nova, similiter D. Gratianus, & cateri omnes nitebantur, unusquisque pro posse suo, ut ipse fieret summus Pontifex.
units.tr: XXI. We shall now show that this happens in this way. And undoubtedly those driven here by the goads of desire, who (as will soon be made clear for most of them) seek their advancement by evil arts of various kinds, but we also have clearer and more direct signs in the following examples. Concerning Pope Vigilius, of whom we are also going to make a fuller mention later, Baronius at the year 540, no. 5, testifies that, driven by the usual itch for the highest honour, he took care to open for himself a sure way of attaining it, so that he could never be cast out because of crimes committed. At the year 900, no. 3, he vehemently and generally declaims against the wicked advisers of secular princes who thrust their hands into the election of the Roman Pontiffs, whom he calls the most bitter enemies of the Roman Church, most shameless and insolent suitors, impious, most greedy and most audacious competitors, who prepare for themselves access to the Chair of Peter by the enticement of base flattery. The same Baronius, at the year 1198, from Roger, a writer of that time, expresses the state of affairs after the death of Pope Celestine III in this way: "Lord Bishop of Ostia, the Cardinal, strove that he himself might become Pope; similarly Lord Jordan of Fossanova, similarly Lord Gratian, and all the others strove, each one as far as he could, that he himself might become supreme Pontiff."

units.la: XXII. Parallelum plane exemplum habet Il Cardin. p. 3. l. 1. p. 51. Ubi de Cardinalibus post obitum Clementis IV. congregatis ista habentur: Tutti &c. Omnes se credebant dignos Papatu, & quod maximum est, electione in longum protractâ, quilibet pro se negotiabatur, nullam aliorum competitorum mentionem faciendo, hinc impossibile erat, ut 18. competitores iidemque Electores aliquid concluderent. rent. Eadem fere Platina in Greg. X. qui tandem electus fuit, verba habet. Porrò in Conclavi Clementis V. legimus, I pensieri &c. cogitationes aliorum Cardinalium tendebant ad exaltationem propriam. Sic etiam Card. de Ursinis in Conclavi Urbani VI. Papatum, ut credebatur, aspirabat.
units.tr: XXII. Il Cardinale, part 3, book 1, page 51, has a clearly parallel example. There, concerning the Cardinals gathered after the death of Clement IV, the following is recorded: "All of them believed themselves worthy of the papacy, and what is greatest, with the election drawn out at length, each one canvassed for himself, mentioning no other competitor; hence it was impossible for eighteen competitors, who were also the electors, to conclude anything." Platina has almost the same words about Gregory X, who was at last elected. Further, in the Conclave of Clement V we read: "The thoughts of the other Cardinals tended to their own exaltation." So also the Cardinal de' Orsini in the Conclave of Urban VI was aspiring to the papacy, as was believed.

units.la: XXIII. De Johanne XXIII. al. XXIV. cujus electionem certo ambitionis indicio à se ipso profectam bis jam tetigimus, ita Platina in vita & ex eo forte Il. Card. p. 3. l. 1. 93. loquitur: Constat, eum ad dignitatem Pontificiam semper aspirâsse; Nam cum adolescens esset, ac Bononiae aliquot annis juri civili operam dedisset, assumpto (ut nunc fit) doctrinae gradu Romam iter instituit. Interrogatus autem ab amicis, quò proficisceretur; Ad Pontificatum; respondit; Quàm egregiis autem, scilicet, mediis ad desideriorum suorum complementum usus sit, suo loco dicemus. In Conclavi Nicolai V. miraculum Il Card. l. c. p. iii. hocce accidisse testatur, quòd nimirum semel electus fuerit Papa aliquis, che non ambiva, qui non ambiebat Papatum. De reliquis Conclave ipsum habet: Quelli &c. Illi, qui omni studio Papatum ambiebant, repulsam ferebant &c. Sequens Conclave Calixti III. habuit molti pretendenti, multos ambientes gradum dignitatis illius. Ipse Calixtus, sede vacante, omnibus affirmavit, se Papam futurum, &, referente Platina etiam, nondum Papa, tanquam Papa promisit. Et in subsequente Pii II. potentiores omni studio aut se, aut amicos promovere studuisse dicuntur; ne mancavano &c. neque deerant, qui, depositâ omni modestiâ, lequebantur pro se ipsis, & se dignos Papatu judicabant, ita &c. Sed inter hos periculosissimè communi ambitionis morbo laborabat & tandem moriebatur Cardinalis Rhotomagensis, cui sequentia pro se verba tribuuntur: Jo sono &c. Fui Cardinalis ante eum (Æneam) atque jam novistis, me non esse inconsideratum, neque stultum, neque doctrinae respectu Papatu indignum, sum ex stemmate regio, neque mihi desunt amici, neque facultates, neque divitiae &c. addebat preces, minas, se non amplius Simoniacum futurum &c. Ad Æneam, cùm votum Calici injicere vellet, humili prece idem dixisse fertur: Enea &c. Ænea miserere mei, & me habe recommendatum, recordare mei; Cúmque tamen Æneam vicisse videret, repentina miser morte abreptus fuit. XXIV. Ex Conclavi Marcelli II. pauca ista tantùm excerpsimus: Gli Card. &c. Cardinales omnes volebant eligi, aut alium eligere ad modum suum. Testatur etiam Conclave Pauli III. de ipso Paulo, lo, cum ante electionem Clementis VII. orationem habuisse, quâ se ipsum tectè ad Papatum commendârit, & eum, sede Clementis vacante, astutiorem Clemente fuisse, dum praetente Imperatore Concilium, forse per tenere ingelosito il Papa, forte ut amulationem in Papa foveat, timuerit, neque timorem, occultare potuerit, Paulus contrà hic Imperatore post mortem Clementis petitionem iterante, forse per tenere à freno il Papa, forte ad fraenum Papa injiciendum, de Concilio habendo locutus sit, ut nimirum Episcoporum Germania & Caesaris favorem eo facilius obtineret. In Conclavi Sixti V. praeter Card. Cesis aliorum pratendentium mentio fit, Farnesiusque introducitur incapricciato &c. pertinaci, flagrante & incredibili Papatum consequendi desiderio actus; Cui etiam tribuitur, quòd Torresium decrepitum promovere voluerit, ut postea ipse succedere posset, amulo illo sublato. Ipsius Sixti immoderatum ad Papatum perveniendi desiderium partim jam Differt. I. & IV. expressimus, partim porrò, quatenus in Conclavi & Vita ejus, sic etiam in Cardinalismo artes adhibitae memorantur, suis quamvis locis declarabimus; Artes, inquam, Sixti, qui vix à porcorum grege abductus & habitu Monastico primùm indutus jam de Papatu & cogitabat, & loquebatur; Atque sermones illos qualibet occasione resumebat, propiori semper applicatione factâ, & clariùs expresso suo desiderio.
units.tr: XXIII. Concerning John XXIII (or XXIV), whose election, a certain sign of ambition proceeding from himself, we have already touched on twice, Platina speaks thus in his life; and perhaps from him Il Cardinale, part 3, book 1, page 93: "It is established that he always aspired to the papal dignity; for when he was a young man and had devoted some years at Bologna to civil law, having taken up (as is now done) the degree of teaching, he set out for Rome. When his friends asked where he was going, he replied: 'To the papacy.'" By what excellent means he used to complete his desires, we shall say in its place. In the Conclave of Nicholas V, Il Cardinale, loc. cit., part 3, reports this miracle, namely that once some Pope was elected who did not seek it, who did not aspire to the papacy. About the rest of the Conclave he says: "Those who, with all zeal, aspired to the papacy were rebuffed," etc. The following Conclave of Callixtus III had many claimants, many who sought the rank of that dignity. Callixtus himself, while the see was vacant, assured everyone that he would be Pope, and, as Platina also reports, promised as if he were already Pope, though he was not yet. And in the following Conclave of Pius II, the more powerful are said to have striven with all zeal to advance either themselves or their friends; there were not lacking men who, laying aside all modesty, spoke for themselves and judged themselves worthy of the papacy, and so on. But among these the Cardinal of Rouen laboured most dangerously under the common disease of ambition, and at last died of it; to him the following words are attributed for himself: "I am," etc. "I was a Cardinal before him (Aeneas), and you already know that I am not thoughtless, nor foolish, nor unworthy of the papacy in respect of learning; I am of royal lineage, nor do I lack friends, resources or riches," etc. He added prayers, threats, and that he would no longer be a simoniac, etc. It is reported that when he wished to cast his vote for the chalice to Aeneas, he said with humble entreaty the same thing: "Aeneas, etc. Aeneas, have mercy on me, and hold me in your recommendation, remember me"; and when he saw that Aeneas had nevertheless won, the wretch was snatched away by sudden death. XXIV. From the Conclave of Marcellus II we have chosen only these few extracts: "All the Cardinals wished to be elected, or to elect another according to their own wishes." The Conclave of Paul III also testifies about Paul himself that, before the election of Clement VII, he delivered an oration by which he commended himself covertly for the papacy; and that, with the vacancy of Clement's see, he was more shrewd than Clement, since, when the Emperor was pressing for a council, he feared lest perhaps it would keep the Pope jealous, or perhaps foster rivalry in the Pope, and could not hide his fear; Paul, on the other hand, when the Emperor after Clement's death repeated the request, spoke about holding a council perhaps to keep the Pope in check, or perhaps to put a bridle on the Pope, namely so that he might more easily obtain the favour of the German bishops and of the Emperor. In the Conclave of Sixtus V, besides Cardinal Cesi, mention is made of other claimants, and Farnese is introduced as obstinate, persistent, driven by a burning and incredible desire of attaining the papacy. To him is also attributed that he wished to promote the decrepit Torres, so that afterwards he himself might succeed, his rival having been removed. We have already partly expressed the immoderate desire of Sixtus himself to attain the papacy in Dissertations I and IV; partly, further, as far as the arts used in the Conclave and his Life, and so also in his Cardinalate, are recorded, we shall make clear in their proper places. The arts, I say, of Sixtus, who, scarcely led away from a herd of swine and first clothed in monastic habit, already both thought and spoke about the papacy; and he took up those discussions on any occasion, always making them more directly applicable and expressing his desire more clearly.

units.la: XXV. In Conclavi Gregorii XIV. primò fit mentio difficultatum, quae circa respectu sui ipsius occurrerint.
units.tr: XXV. In the Conclave of Gregory XIV, first mention is made of the difficulties that arose concerning each man's own standing.

units.la: Subjungitur tristis querela Cardinalis Columnae, che havendo &c. quòd post multa & diuturna Hispaniae praestita servitia, jam non commemoratus sit inter competitores à Rege approbatos, atque sibi praeferri videat multos de Rege minùs meritos. Additur conatus Card. Madruccii, quòd, postquam aliquam prosè negotiationem instituì curâsset, non obstantibus Sforza in contrarium conatibus, nihilominus Montaltium rogârit, ut illuc concurreret &c. Triste est, quod sequitur ibidem traditum, nempe Montaltius dixit Albano, ut laetaretur, se eum Papam facturum; quo sono bonus senex gaudio repletus, ad ostendendum, quòd non sit tam decrepitus & debilis, ut non possit onus illud sustinere, cella exire & aliquot passus ambulare voluit, sed humi procidit tali percussione, ut inde vita jacturam fecerit. Tantùm huic etiam nocuit solum Papatûs desiderium! Quod saltem non profuit Card. Paleotto, qui in eodem Conclavi, cùm paucorum accessus deesset, ut ipse sibi in tali occasione omni adjumento possibili non deesset, rogavit Comum, qui sibi vicinus erat, ut Columnam
units.tr: Next comes the sorrowful complaint of Cardinal Colonna, that, having &c., after many long services rendered to Spain, he was no longer named among the competitors approved by the King, and he saw many less deserving of the King preferred to himself. The attempt of Cardinal Madruzzo is added: that, after he had carried on some private negotiation, Sforza's efforts to the contrary notwithstanding, he nevertheless asked Montalto to come over there &c. It is sad what is related next, namely that Montalto told Albano to be glad, for he would make him Pope; at which news the good old man, filled with joy, wanted to show that he was not so decrepit and feeble as to be unable to bear that burden, so he left his cell and tried to walk a few steps, but fell to the ground with such a blow that he lost his life. Only the desire for the papacy harmed this man! Paleotto did not benefit either, who in the same Conclave, since the approach of a few was lacking, and so that he would not lack every possible help on such an occasion, asked Como, who was near him, to urge Colonna

units.la: Gregorii XIV. mnam & Aragoniam ad dandum sibi accessum, sed nemine ideò surgente, hortaretur.
units.tr: and Aragon to give him access; but since no one rose for this, Como urged them in vain.

units.la: XXVI. Ex Conclavi Clementis VIII. jam vidimus, quàm inhumanè S. Severinæ amplexus, verbis: Va via Papa del Diabolo; Id est; Apage Papa Diaboli! rejectus fuerit, & quàm parùm eum suum, senza mio pregiudicio, sine meo præjudicio; cùm scrutinium post adorationem à multis tentaretur, juverit. Sed nec Conclave Pauli V. desiderantibus caruit; novi era &c. Non ibi fuit senex aut media ætatis, qui non sperárit. Ipse Borghesius mox eligendus, cognitâ de se coeptâ negotiatione, Aldobrandino gratias egit. Inter rationes autem, ob quas Borghesius Nepos in sequente Conclavi Gregorii XV. Camporam nondum decrepitum promovere studuit, numeratur & illa, quòd, illo sedente, ipse maturus ad Papatum fieri & Cardinales interea temporis pro lubitu suo disponere voluerit. Campora idem jam habitus à multis piu da Papa,che da qual ch'era, potiùs pro Papa, quàm pro Cardinali; Ipse etiam jam spe Papatum devorârat totum, hinc jam quoque pollicitus, qualem se certo certiùs præstiturus sit. Meliori successu Barberinus in Conclavi, ex quo ipse Papa Urbanus VIII. exiit, se commendâsse & omnia ad electionem suam disposuisse, cæterùm etiam honoris imminutionem in casu repulsæ (quam eum multi cum reputatione jactura certò passurum esse in ipso ingressu ad electionem adhuc affirmabant;) timuisse dicitur; Qui etiam ad Borghesium de bono successu diffidentem dixisse fertur, che col fondamento &c. se cum favoris ipsius fundamento procurare velle mane illo feliciter eventurum; sperare finem responsurum medii tam bene ordinatis.
units.tr: XXVI. In the Conclave of Clement VIII we have already seen how inhumanly Cardinal S. Severina was rejected when he embraced [the Pope], with the words Va via Papa del Diabolo; that is, Away with you, Pope of the Devil! and how little his senza mio pregiudicio, without prejudice to me, helped him, when many attempted a scrutiny after the adoration. Nor did the Conclave of Paul V lack men who desired the office: new ones &c. There was no old man or middle-aged man there who did not hope. Borghese himself, soon to be elected, when the negotiation begun about him became known, thanked Aldobrandini. Among the reasons why Borghese's nephew, in the following Conclave of Gregory XV, tried to advance the not yet decrepit Campora, is also counted this: that, while that man sat, he himself wanted to become ripe for the papacy and in the meantime arrange the Cardinals as he pleased. Campora himself was already regarded by many as more like a Pope than whatever he was, more for a Pope than for a Cardinal. He himself had already devoured the whole papacy in hope, and so he also already promised what sort of Pope he would certainly prove to be. With better success Barberini, in the Conclave from which Pope Urban VIII himself emerged, is said to have commended himself and arranged everything for his election, but also to have feared a diminution of honour in case of rejection (which many still asserted he would certainly suffer, with loss of reputation, at the very entrance to the election). He is also said to have told Borghese, who doubted a good outcome, that with the foundation &c. that he wished to bring it about, on the foundation of his favour, that the matter would turn out happily by morning; he hoped the end would answer to means so well arranged.

units.la: XXVII. In Conclavi Innocentii X. sermo est de multis, che pretendevano &c. qui pratendebant Papa fieri, tam in illo, quàm in futuro Conclavi. Similiter Conclave Alexandri VII. ægrotantes exhibet, & primò quidem Card. Saccherium, qui Neppotem in Hispaniam misit, ut favorem impetraret, & ostenderet, neminem se utiliorem Hispanis Papam fore. Paulò post 22. Cardinales memorantur, che aspiravano &c. qui simul aspirabant ad Papatum, & quorum major pars illuc pervenire studiosè contendebat. Quivis illorum se proponi sinebant à Capitibus factionum, neque ullus erat, qui non speràrit, se præ aliis diligi. Ex illis Cherubinus non poteva &c. credere non poterat, Barberinum se nolle &c. Idem risum totius Conclavis excitavit, coram crucifixo dicere auditus: Domine, si populo tuo sum necessarius, non recuso laborem. Barberino autem non videbatur longa Conclavis duratio displicere. plicere,quia ipse tandem eligi cupiebat,quò & collimârunt verba Conclavistæ &c. qui & amicos sibi argento comparare voluit, qui gratitudine moti eum evehere possent,quò tantopere aspirabant desideria ejus.
units.tr: XXVII. In the Conclave of Innocent X there is talk of many who claimed &c., who were claiming to become Pope, both in that Conclave and in the future one. Likewise the Conclave of Alexander VII presents the sick, and first of all Cardinal Sacchetti, who sent his nephew into Spain to obtain favour and to show that no one would be more useful to the Spanish as Pope. A little later 22 Cardinals are mentioned, who aspired &c., who together aspired to the papacy, and of whom the greater part eagerly strove to reach it. Each of them let himself be put forward by the heads of the factions, and there was none who did not hope that he would be preferred to the others. Of these, Cherubini could not &c.; he could not believe that Barberini did not wish &c. The same excited the laughter of the whole Conclave, when he was heard to say before the crucifix: Lord, if I am necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labour. But the long duration of the Conclave did not seem to displease Barberini, because he himself wished at last to be elected; to this also the words of the Conclavist aimed &c., who also wished to buy friends for himself with money, who might be moved by gratitude to raise him up, to which his desires so greatly aspired.

units.la: XXVIII. Clementis IX. Conclave pariter conceptiones multorum memorat. Ante ingressum Cardinali Chigio, cùm de eligendis Officialibus ageretur, niun' Card. &c. Nullus Cardinalis displicere voluit,ne perderet commoda sua respectu Conclavis futuri. Eius sibi ipsi non deerat &c. Barberino variis modis procurare voluit l' elettione &c. electionem aut in persona sua, id quod maximè probabile est &c. Similia habet quoad sedem, tunc, imò ex parte nondum, vacantem. Il Card. p.3. l.3. p.274. seqq. Non è credibile, inquit Author, quàm superbas dederint Cardinales Papabiles (Legato Hispaniæ eos invisenti) recreationes,maximè Farnesius,de quo pra aliis agebatur,qu isi inclusiones Regnorum per gulam trahi debeant. Non desisle-bant, pergit idem, conciliare sibi animum & affectionem ambarum partium, licèt ad praesumtionem meriti sui sive veri, sive putatitii non vilem reddendam, simularint, se longius ire. Tunc quoque Facchinetti si racommando &c. se commendavit modestè, declarando, pratensionem suam exiguam esse in Conclavi pleno dignissimis aliis; sed cùm soleat sape turbidum quid atque litigiosum accidere, Hispanos & amicos sucs rogavit, ut sint memores essent; sed turbidum illud nunquam venit &c. Eodem tempore veniva &c. Palotta ponebatur in Catalogo Pretendentium. Ibidem mentio fit spei Odeschalchii &c. Cardinalis Ginetii che cominciò &c. qui coepit ipse negotiationem de persona sua. Adiit eum in finem Barberinum, rogans eum, ut ei cura cordíque essent commoda sua &c. In Aphorismis Politicis autem Cardinalis Azzolini (De quo vide L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 25.120. 165.) annotatur, Hispaniæ Legatum in Conclavi Gregorii XIV. alterâsse animos totius Conclavis, septem tantùm nominando, per vederfi &c. sic enim reliqui omnes semet voce passiva privatos videbant. Tandem in Conclavi Clementis X. studium D. Bonvisii pro Avunculo, de quo spes ipsi facta erat inanis, apud Legatum Galliæ memoratur,quo petiit,che S. E. &c. duabus lineis Card. Gallos moneret de ultima manu admovenda, sic agnitum iri fortunas Avunculi ab Ea profluere. Tunc etiam Roma vidua de procis suis ita L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.16. cecinit: Horche vedova son, ò quanti e quanti. Id est; Jam dum vidua sum, ô quot & quot &c. Vide Dissert.IV. Sect.III. n. 12.
units.tr: XXVIII. The Conclave of Clement IX likewise records the schemes of many. Before Cardinal Chigi entered, when the appointing of officials was being discussed, no Cardinal &c. No Cardinal wished to give offence, lest he lose his advantages with a view to the future Conclave. Of this there was no lack in himself &c. Barberini wished to procure, by various means, the election &c., either in his own person, which is most probable &c. He has similar things concerning the see, then still, indeed in part not yet, vacant. Il Card. p.3 l.3 p.274 seqq. It is not credible, says the author, how haughty the entertainments were that the Cardinals who were papabili gave (when the Legate of Spain visited them), especially Farnese, of whom more was spoken than of the others, as if the kingdoms were to be drawn in by the gullet. They did not cease, the same author goes on, to win over the mind and affection of both parties, although they pretended to go further, so as not to make small the presumption of their merit, whether real or supposed. Then too Facchinetti si racommando &c. commended himself modestly, declaring that his claim was slight in a Conclave full of most worthy others; but since something troubling and contentious is wont often to happen, he asked the Spanish and his friends to be mindful of him; but that trouble never came &c. At the same time veniva &c. Palotta was put on the list of candidates. There is also mention of the hope of Odescalchi &c. Of Cardinal Ginetti che cominciò &c. who began a negotiation about his own person. To this end he approached Barberini, asking him that his interests be a care and concern to him &c. In the Political Aphorisms of Cardinal Azzolini (on whom see L'Ambasc. di Rom. pp. 25, 120, 165) it is noted that the Legate of Spain, in the Conclave of Gregory XIV, changed the minds of the whole Conclave, naming only seven, per vedersi &c., for thus all the others saw themselves deprived of the passive voice (of being chosen). Finally, in the Conclave of Clement X, the zeal of D. Bonvisi for his uncle, of whom the hope given him was empty, is recorded with the French Legate, whom he asked che S. E. &c. to warn the French Cardinals, in two lines, about the final touch to be applied, so that the uncle's fortunes would be seen to flow from Her Excellency. Then too Rome, a widow, sang of her suitors thus: Horche vedova son, ò quanti e quanti. That is: Now that I am a widow, oh how many and how many &c. See Dissert. IV, Sect. III, n. 12.

units.la: XXIX. Hi
units.tr: XXIX. These

units.la: XXIX. Hi omnes & multi alii certè diversa principia habuisse videntur à principiis Albani in Conclavi V. cui multi vitio verterunt,quòd sibi gratiam Alexandrini & aliorum capitum procurare non allaboraverit, ò fosse &c. sive ideò illud factum sit, quòd nimium de se confidenter præsumpserit, sive indignum atque illicitum duxerit,ut Cardinalis aliquis Papatum ambire præsumat,aut eum procurare arte & simulatione; atque solebat respondere iis, qui tunc ei consulebant,ut incedat communi corrupti moris via,Cardinalem non debere ambire aut ita procurare Papatum, sed ita vivere & operari, ut à bonis omnibus dignus Papatu judicari queat &c. Sed neque multùm hi omnes & multi alii curâsse videntur severas Symmachi P. leges in Synodo Romana latas: Si,ut fieri solet, (ergò jam tunc solebat fieri!) studia coeperint esse diversa eorum,de quibus certamen emerserit. Sacerdotio careat,qui captus promissione,non recto judicio,de electione decreverit. Item: Propter occultas fraudes & conjurationum secretas insidias eorum,qui de Pontificali ambitu egerit, & rationabili probatione convicerit, particeps actionis non solùm purgatus sit, sed etiam remuneratione sublevetur. Nec etiam approbâsse videntur illam verborum: Si quis Episcopatum &c. quæ in Decr. p.2. cauf.8.q.1.c.10. habetur, explicationem: Episcopatus nomen est operis, non honoris &c. ut intelligat,non se esse Episcopum,qui præesse dixerit,non prodesse &c. Locus superior, sine quo regi populus non potest,etsi ita teneatur,atque ministretur, ut decet, tamen non decenter appetitur &c. negotium justum suscipit necessitas charitatis: quam sarcinam, si nullus imponat, percipienda atque intuenda vacandum est veritati: Si autem imponitur,suscipienda est propter charitatis necessitatem; sed nec sic omnimodo veritatis dilectio desideranda est,ne subtrahatur illa suavitas, & opprimatur justa necessitas. Nec etiam credidisse cum Jano Nicio Erythræo Epist. ad Tyrrhenum p.178. circa eandem Pontificis Electionem: Nullum bene imperaturi signum est majus,quàm si imperare recusset; Vel parùm certè bonum imperium curâsse. Ambiunt locum non quia sanctus habetur,sed quia summus est; Et multò magis recedunt à rigore Evangelii, & exemplis Christi atque sanctorum suprà memoratis, qui sibi honorem non sumpserunt; Nam quando secundùm principia suae ambitionis agunt, illorum classem constituunt, quos suprà quasi se ipsos eligere diximus; Tales etiam, ut diximus, ambitione sua locum, quem aliâs non haberent, dant vitiosis aliorum principiis, propriisque, quibus unus ad alterius commodum vel incomincommodum pro occasionibus natis trahitur, passionibus. De quibus jam quoque agendum erit.
units.tr: XXIX. All these men, and many others, seem certainly to have held principles different from those of the Albani in the Conclave V., whom many blamed for not labouring to win the favour of Alexander and the other chiefs, whether because he presumed too confidently on himself, or because he thought it unworthy and unlawful for any Cardinal to presume to ambition the Papacy or to procure it by art and pretence; and he used to answer those who then advised him that he should walk in the common way of a corrupt custom, that a Cardinal ought not to ambition or so procure the Papacy, but to live and act in such a way that he may be judged worthy of the Papacy by all good men &c. But these men and many others do not seem to have cared much for the severe laws of Symmachus the Pope, enacted in the Roman Synod: If, as is usually done (so it was already then usual to do!) their zeal begins to differ on the matter about which the contest has arisen, let him who, won by a promise and not by sound judgement, has decided about the election be deprived of the priesthood. Likewise: Because of the hidden frauds and secret plots of conspirators of him who has carried on the canvassing for the Papacy, and has been convicted by reasonable proof, let the participant not only be cleared but also be relieved by a reward. Nor do they seem to have approved the explanation of that saying: If anyone desires the episcopate &c., which is found in the Decretum, part 2, cause 8, question 1, chapter 10: Episcopate is the name of a work, not of an honour &c., so that he who has said he rules, not that he serves, understands that he is not a bishop &c. A higher place, without which a people cannot be governed, though it is held and administered as it ought to be, is nevertheless not fittingly sought &c. Necessity of charity takes up a just task; if no one lays this burden on him, he must give himself to the truth and attend to it; but if it is laid on him, he must accept it on account of the necessity of charity; yet not even so is the love of truth to be wholly desired, lest that sweetness be withdrawn and that just necessity be oppressed. Nor did they believe, with Janus Nicius Erythraeus, Letter to Tyrrhenus, p. 178, concerning the same election of the Pope: There is no greater sign of one who is going to rule well than if he refuses to rule; or at least they certainly cared little for ruling well. They ambition the place not because it is held to be holy, but because it is highest; and they depart far more from the rigour of the Gospel and from the examples of Christ and of the saints mentioned above, who did not take honour to themselves. For when they act according to the principles of their ambition, they form the class of those whom we said above are, as it were, electing themselves. Such men, as we said, by their ambition give a place to the vicious principles of others, and to their own passions, by which one man is drawn to another's advantage or disadvantage, as occasions arise. These we must now also treat.

units.la: XXX. Vitiosa sunt; Nequis igitur expectet, ut principia in Electionibus Ecclesiasticis genuina multis commemoremus, quorum ab aliquot Seculis in Electionibus Pontificum rarissima nonnisi & obscurissima vestigia apparent, studii nimirum praecipuè Ecclesiae ad Dei gloriam, sepositis affectibus humanis, in Electionibus istis serviendi. Contraria studia atque principia dominantia Scriptores exponunt unanimiter, commoda propria, passiones varias. De quibus primò in genere aliquid dicendum erit; Cognosci autem jam aliquomodo possunt ex sequentibus testimoniis varia simul complectentibus, atque ex parte ad nullum certum Conclave restrictis. Sic conjungit Lottinus Differt. de Concl. invidiam, conspirationes, privatos affectus &c. Author vero Card p.3.l.2.p.249. dicit, adorationes favere Cardinalem alteri, per amicitia, &c. vel ex amicitia, vel ex conscientia, vel per aliquod commodum particulare; Idem testatur l.3.p.268. Tra li &c. Inter Cardinales quidam sunt, qui neq; Dei sunt, neq; Diaboli, alii unicè suis commodis intenti, alii obligati ad sequendas partes Nepotismi, alii Gallia, alii Hispania, quidam promittunt aliquid lingua alicui, & corde alteri; imò tales etiam dantur, quibus volupe est omnes excludere, ut negotia intricent &c. Sed & Conclave Leonis XI. diversa Cardinalium eligentium principia enumerat. De creaturis Aldobrandini ita author ait: Altre &c. Alii fame laborabant, alii offensi erant, alii Principum mancipia, alii obligati pecuniae propria, alii ducti à Spiritu S. Et forte hi, quemadmodum ultimò locantur, paucissimi erant; Ipsius autem Aldobrandini principium erat, di conservare &c. Conservare illud dominium Ecclesiasticum in forma pristina, id est, dependente à se, cùm divino atque humano jure Aristocraticum esse debeat & commune iis, qui Zelo & caritate ad regimen apti sint. Sed alia omnia credentem Sixtum V. jam Differt. I. exhibuimus. Atque etiam non pauca cumulavit in Conclavi Gregorii XIV. Montaltius, dum ex 7. ab Hispanis propositis aliquem electurus cumulavit atque invicem comparavit commoda, respectus, difficultates, & promissiones, quae in singulis concurrebant; hinc plenus erat dubiis atque ambiguitatibus, dum desideravit simul placere Magno Duci, & Duci Mantuae, satisfacere Altempsio & Sforza & Columnis, removere periculum Paleotti, se approbare suis creaturis, certa reddere sua commoda, & promissa praestare singulis; hinc nesciebat, quò se velit vertere ad omnes istos fines consequendos; dos ; distinguere autem, quodnam horum minùs noxium aut magis desi-derandum sit, difficillimum erat, ut non dicam, impossibile. Similia ferè habentur in Conclavi Clementis IX. ubi de alienis Chigii & Rospigliosii, Nepotum, animis agitur. Sed ista & reliqua omnia commodè ad commodum proprium & passiones varias reduci possunt.
units.tr: XXX. They are vicious. Let no one, therefore, expect that we shall mention many genuine principles in ecclesiastical elections, of which, for some centuries, only the rarest and most obscure traces appear in the elections of Popes, namely the chief aim of the Church to serve God's glory in these elections, setting aside human affections. The writers unanimously set out the contrary aims and dominant principles: private advantages, various passions. Of these we must first say something in general; they can now be known in some measure from the following testimonies, which embrace various matters together and are partly restricted to no certain Conclave. Thus Lottinus, in his Dissertation on the Conclave, joins envy, conspiracies, private affections &c. But the author of the Cardinal, p. 3, l. 2, p. 249, says that Cardinals favour another through friendship, &c., or from friendship, or from conscience, or through some particular advantage. The same author attests in l. 3, p. 268, Tra li &c.: Among the Cardinals there are some who belong neither to God nor to the devil; some intent only on their own advantages; some bound to follow the party of nepotism; some to France, some to Spain; some promise something with the tongue to one and with the heart to another; indeed there are even such men to whom it is a pleasure to exclude everyone, so that they may tangle affairs &c. But the Conclave of Leo XI also lists the different principles of the Cardinals who elect. Of the creatures of Aldobrandini the author says: Others &c. Some were suffering hunger, some were offended, some were slaves of princes, some were bound by money, some were led by the Holy Spirit. And perhaps these, as they are placed last, were very few; but the principle of Aldobrandini himself was to preserve &c. to preserve that ecclesiastical dominion in its former form, that is, dependent on himself, when by divine and human right it ought to be aristocratic and common to those who are fit to rule by zeal and charity. But we have already set out, in Dissertation I, all the other things believed of Sixtus V. Montaltius also heaped up not a few things in the Conclave of Gregory XIV, when, about to choose one of the seven proposed by the Spaniards, he heaped up and compared with one another the advantages, considerations, difficulties and promises which concurred in each; hence he was full of doubts and ambiguities, since he wished at once to please the Grand Duke and the Duke of Mantua, to satisfy Altemps, Sforza and the Colonna, to remove the danger from Paleotti, to approve himself to his own creatures, to make his own advantages secure, and to fulfil promises to each; hence he did not know to which side to turn in order to attain all those ends; and to distinguish which of these is less harmful or more to be desired was most difficult, if not impossible, to say. Similar things are found in the Conclave of Clement IX, where the minds of the Nephews, Chigi and Rospigliosi, are discussed as alien. But all these and the rest can conveniently be reduced to private advantage and various passions.

units.la: XXXI. Commodum proprium relationem maximè habet ad promissiones & Simoniam, de quibus suo loco, ubi proin etiam hoc-ce principium magis declarandum erit ; Respicit autem partim divitias, partim honores; Atque utroque respectu heic principium esse solet, ut sequentia docebunt. Accipe primò, Lector, generale ex libello, cui titulus: L' anima di Ferrante Pallavicino, & cujus Author Joh. Franc. Loredanus creditur, de communi hodie in hoc negotio commodi proprii studio verba Latinè versa p.84. Res mira & deploranda est, videre nos creari Pontifices, non judicatos ex meritis, sed secundùm eas qualitates, quas factiones sibi proficuas reputant, atque hæ non tergiversarentur in creando ipso etiam Diabolo, modò illis prodesse vellet. Quid enim in Conclavi Clementis V. quærebatur? Commodum proprium: Subito si mostrorno &c. Subitò se ostendebant inter eos potius inimici, quàm amici, & odio habentes, quàm bene affecti, omnibus se pro commodis propriis defatigantibus; qui & tandem studio placendi Regi Galliæ, utque fautorem haberent, Episcopum Burdegalensem Regi familiarem elegisse dicuntur; Prout quoque Cardinalis Columna, electione peractâ, statim ad Regem profectus est, accio &c. ut eo mediante posset habere quandam partem gratiæ apud Sanct. suam, asserens, non alio fine electionem in longum protractam esse, quàm ut nihil contrà voluntatem & beneplacitum Regis fieret &c. Imò addit Author, multos credidisse, Cardinalem promissionem favoris Pontificii à Rege obtinuisse. Quò tendebant vota in Conclavi Pii IV? Ad commodum proprium; Omnia quisque faciebat, secondo che pensava &c. prout putavit maximè artificiosè juvare causam propriam.
units.tr: XXXI. Private advantage is chiefly related to promises and simony, of which in their place; and there this principle too will need to be explained more fully. It concerns partly riches and partly honours; and with each of these aspects this is usually the principle here, as the following will show. First take, reader, a general statement from the little book entitled The Soul of Ferrante Pallavicino, whose author is thought to be Giovanni Francesco Loredano, on the study of private advantage, which is common today in this business, rendered into Latin, p. 84: It is a strange and lamentable thing to see us creating Popes not judged by their merits, but according to those qualities which their factions consider useful to themselves; and these factions would not hesitate in creating even the Devil himself, provided he wished to serve them. For what was sought in the Conclave of Clement V? Private advantage: Suddenly they showed themselves &c.: among them there appeared at once enemies rather than friends, and men who hated rather than were well disposed, each wearing himself out for his own advantages. These men, too, at last, from a desire to please the King of France, and so as to have a patron, are said to have chosen the Bishop of Bordeaux, a familiar of the King. So also Cardinal Colonna, once the election was over, went at once to the King, so that through him he might have some part of favour with His Holiness, asserting that the election had been drawn out for a long time for no other end than that nothing should be done against the will and pleasure of the King &c. Indeed the author adds that many believed that the Cardinal had obtained a promise of papal favour from the King. To what did the votes aim in the Conclave of Pius IV? To private advantage. Each man did everything as he thought best, so as most artfully to help his own cause.

units.la: XXXII. Sic etiam Conclave Sixti V. loquitur de procurare volentibus aliis Papatum per interessi, per commoda; In eodem introducuntur pro Sixto vota quærentes, che giudicavano &c. quae judicabant facilius acquiri posse, ò per interessi aut per dependentias, id quod feliciter successit. Qualia etiam in Conclavi Gregorii XIV. inveniuntur quasi venalia vota Neutralistarum, che aderivano &c. qui adhærebant modò huic, modò illi parti, secundùm ductum conscientiæ, aut comcommodi. Non minùs in Conclavi Innocentii IX. jam ſupra often-dimus obambulantes per loro intereffi,propter commoda ſua. In Concla-vi autem Pauli V. jam ab initio dicitur: L'oggetto &c. Scopus omnium idem erat,qui in Conclavi precedente, promovendi proprium commodum in promotione amicorum & remotione inimicorum. Imò totam Curiam Romanam ab utilitatis propriæ ſtudio quasi animari,ex Conclavi Gregorii XV. discimus,dum eam Author vocat,una radunanza &c. confluxum personarum, quæ omnes propriam conditionem meliorem reddere unicè ſtudent. In Conclavi Urbani VIII. quemvis ſecutum eſſe privatam opinionem, e lo privato interesse, & proprium commodum cognoscimus. Eosdem duces Conclave Alexandri VII. habuit. Quia enim proprium commodum quæritur, ideò Ogn'uno vuol &c. quivis vult videri author creationis novi Pontificis & negat se alium promovere voluisse ; Quod Author generaliter affirmat. In eodem Conclavi ægrè ferebat Hispaniæ Legatus, quòd Cardinales Medicæi proprio commodo intenti erant, non, quòd nihil aliud respici hîc voluerit præter Dei gloriam & commodum Ecclesiæ, sed, quòd trà gl'interessi &c. inter commoda Hispaniæ etiam respicerent ad proprium, & quia judicavit, omnia hîc sacrificari debere, non Deo,sed,utili Principis sui , æmulatione urgebatur ob ſolam apparentiam habiti cujusdam ad proprium commodum reſpeſtûs. In eodem occasionem habuit Author dicendi: E cosa incredibile &c. Incredibile est,quàm facile sit cuivis decipi ab utilitate propria ; hæc arbitrum agit affectuum humanorum,neque ullus est, sapiens licet,qui non cedat vanis ejus apparentiis.
units.tr: XXXII. So also the Conclave of Sixtus V speaks of those wishing others to procure the Papacy through self-interest, through advantages. In the same, votes are introduced for Sixtus that were sought, which they judged could be acquired more easily, either through self-interest or through dependencies, which succeeded happily. Such are found also in the Conclave of Gregory XIV, as if the votes of the Neutralists were for sale: who adhered now to this party, now to that, according to the guidance of conscience or of advantage. No less in the Conclave of Innocent IX, as we have already shown above, men wander about through their own self-interest, on account of their own advantages. In the Conclave of Paul V, at the very beginning it is said: The aim of all was the same as in the preceding Conclave: to promote one's own advantage in the advancement of friends and the removal of enemies. Indeed we learn from the Conclave of Gregory XV that the whole Roman Curia is, as it were, animated by the zeal for its own profit, when the author calls it a gathering, a gathering of persons who all strive solely to make their own condition better. In the Conclave of Urban VIII we learn that each man followed a private opinion, private interest and his own advantage. The Conclave of Alexander VII had the same leaders. Because their own advantage is sought, everyone wants to appear the author of the creation of the new Pope, and denies that he wished to promote another; which the author affirms in general. In the same Conclave the Spanish Legate was displeased that the Medici Cardinals were intent on their own advantage, not that he wished that nothing else be regarded here besides God's glory and the advantage of the Church; but because among the advantages of Spain they also looked to their own, and because he judged that everything here ought to be sacrificed, not to God, but to the advantage of his Prince, he was driven by rivalry, merely because of the appearance of a certain regard for their own advantage. In the same Conclave the author had occasion to say: It is incredible how easily anyone may be deceived by his own advantage; this drives the judgement of human affections, and there is no one, however wise, who does not yield to its empty appearances.

units.la: XXXIII. Cessit Cardinalis Rupertus in Conclavi Clementis IX.
units.tr: XXXIII. Cardinal Rupert withdrew in the Conclave of Clement IX.

units.la: cujus regula ostenditur negl intereffi bisognevoli della sua ca-sa, in commodis necessariis familiæ suæ; Cessit Cardinalis Chigius in eodem Conclavi negotiando pro Elcio , che per la parentela &c. quem ob cognationem, Purpuræ obligationem , communem patriam, & familiarum amicitias,maximè sibi proficuum fore putavit ; Cesse-runt, quibus ſub novo Papa regnare volentibus Rospigliosius non convenire videbatur, habens in familia Nepotem futurum magnorum negotiorum capacem. Cesse-runt in Conclavi Clementis X. multi; Medicæus, che in primo luogo &c. qui primò ſpeſtabat utile ſuæ familiæ ; Et cujus re-ſpeſtu magna confusio in illo Conclavi oriebatur,quia ne alcun altro &c. nemo plane potuit ſcopum ejus perſpicere , quem primò quidem familiæ ſuæ commodis inservire voluit ; Cesse-runt Medicæi ſemper, mentre &c. experientia ſemper teſte, eadem ſemper primò loco quærentes. Cesserunt tunc Cardinales complures alii, ut tandem necesse habuerit Legatus Hispaniae in ultima audientia nomine Regis sui Cardinale> exhortari, che posposti &c. ut Eminentia sua postpositis omnibus commodis privatis & particularibus, spectent ad electionem Pastoris Sancti &c. se esse scandalizatum moris, qua inde orta dicantur, quòd quidam nomine turma (lo squadrone) commodis privatis aptum reperire nequeant. Cessit Chigius, che pareva &c. qui videbatur ambiguus circa Electionem Altieri, incertus, utrum favorem Palutiorum, seu praecipuorum cognatorum ejus habiturus sit De omnibus istis canit L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.80. Chi non vede aperto e chiaro,che ciascun qual Molinaro Tira l'acque al suo molino. Id est; Quis non manifeste videt, Molitores hos aquam ad molam suam dirigere.
units.tr: His rule is shown in he neglects the needs of his household, in the necessary advantages of his family; Cardinal Chigi withdrew in the same Conclave while negotiating for Elcio, because of kinship, the obligation of the purple, a common homeland and friendships between families, which he thought would be especially advantageous to himself; those withdrew who, wishing to reign under a new Pope, did not think Rospigliosi suitable, since he had a nephew in his family who would be capable of great affairs: under a new Pope who wished to reign. Many withdrew in the Conclave of Clement X. The Medici, who in the first place etc., looked first to the advantage of their family, and because of them great confusion arose in that Conclave, since no one else etc. no one could clearly see the aim which they first wished to serve for the advantage of their family. The Medici always withdrew, while etc., experience always bearing witness that they always sought the first place for themselves. Then several other Cardinals withdrew, so that the Spanish Legate, in his final audience, had to exhort a Cardinal in the name of his King, that, having put aside etc., His Eminence should, with all private and particular advantages set aside, look to the election of a holy Pastor etc.; he said he was scandalized by the custom, from which, it is said, some in the name of a faction (lo squadrone) found that they could not find suitable private advantages. Chigi withdrew, who seemed etc., who seemed ambiguous about the election of Altieri, uncertain whether he would win the favour of the Paluzzi, or of his chief kinsmen. The Ambassador of Rome sings of all these things, p. 80: Who does not see plainly and clearly that each, like a miller, draws the water to his own mill? That is: Who does not see plainly that these millers direct the water to their millstone?

units.la: XXXIV. Ambitio in adjuvantibus maximè & speciaIius in Conclavi Sixti V. ostenditur, dum enim Medicaeus ad exaltationem Montaltii, qui Cognati sui Ursini inimicus erat, concurrere voluit, potè più in lui &c. plùs in eo potuit ambitio & desiderium excludendi Farnesium & Torresium, quàm verò beneficium & respectus cognati. Quod testimonium respectus inter se saepe pugnantes exhibet terrenos, vitiosos omnes.
units.tr: XXXIV. Ambition among helpers is shown especially in the Conclave of Sixtus V. For when Medici wished to concur in the exaltation of Montalto, who was an enemy of his kinsman Orsini, ambition and the desire to exclude Farnese and Torres prevailed more in him than the benefit and regard of a kinsman. This testimony shows that worldly regards, which often fight among themselves, are all vicious.

units.la: Quomodo ambitione sua commoti primarii Authores Electionis Sixti V. fuerint, jam Differt.I. expositum est, de eo enim, juxta Conclave cogitabant, eum non habere nepotes magnis aptos, se sub eo regnaturos esse. Et paulò post dicit Author de iisdem: Tirati &c. Eousque igitur desiderio dominandi inducti pro Montaltio negotiabantur. Ad ambitionem commodè etiam referimus gloria studium, quod in Card. Montaltio Conclave Greg. XIV. ostendit: Voleva &c. Voluit, ut quemadmodum determinatio faciendi Papam & Personae electio ab eo profecta erat, ita etiam gloria totius operis sua esset; Id quod Madruccius aegrè ferebat factum.
units.tr: How the primary authors of the election of Sixtus V were moved by their ambition has already been set out in Differt. I. For they were thinking of the Conclave in this way, that he did not have nephews fit for great things, under whom they would reign. And a little later the author says of the same men: Drawn etc.; so far, therefore, led by the desire to dominate, they were negotiating for Montalto. We also rightly count as ambition the zeal for glory, which Cardinal Montalto showed in the Conclave of Gregory XIV.: He wanted etc.; he wished that, just as the decision to make a Pope and the choice of the person had come from him, so also the glory of the whole work should be his own; which Madruzzo took badly.

units.la: XXXV. Diximus n. XXX. praeter commodum proprium etiam varias passiones principia in Electionibus Pontificum Rom. dominantia esse.
units.tr: XXXV. We said in n. XXX that, besides private advantage, various passions are also dominant principles in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: Est quidem studium commodi proprii ex passionibus latiùs sumptis, sive jam pecunia, sive honor, sive utrumque quaeratur, vitiosae sunt istae passiones, atque omnes omninò passiones commodum proprium quodammodo respicere videntur; Interim tamen alia quaedam χίνης est; Et passiones quidem in genere latiorem aliquem conceptum praebent atque saepe commodo proprio contrariari videntur, passio autem haec vel illa commodum proprium sub certa forma contuetur, vel enim commodum dum proprium ab alio promotum est, & tunc oritur desiderium gratitudinis, vel læsum, & tunc odium & vindicta studium; vel lædendum timetur, & tum adest metus &c. Quæ omnia inter causas in Electionibus Pontificum præcipuè moventes esse, jam ostendendum erit, & quidem primò generaliter aliquid de dominio passionum & affectuum in istis electionibus dicemus.
units.tr: There is indeed the pursuit of private advantage, taking passions in a broad sense, whether money, honour, or both are sought; these passions are vicious, and all passions seem in some way to look to private advantage. Yet there is also something different: passions in general offer a rather broad concept and often seem to conflict with private advantage, whereas this or that passion views private advantage under a certain form. For either the advantage is promoted by another, and then the desire for gratitude arises; or it is injured, and then hatred and the zeal for vengeance; or it is feared that it will be injured, and then there is fear, etc. All these things, which are among the most powerful causes in the elections of the Pontiffs, will now have to be shown; and first we shall say something in general about the dominion of passions and affections in these elections.

units.la: XXXVI. De quo Author Cardinalismi tanquam de re notissima atque pro certo præsupponenda loquitur: Ogni uno sà &c. Nemo nescit, inquit p. 1. l. 3. p. 326. in electionibus Pontificum regnare passiones terrenas.Non tamen inutile erit, dominium illud testimoniis Conclavium non nullorum probare. Primum ex iis, quæ habentur, Clementis V. innuit, quòd Cardinales ob discordiam ex Conclavi egressi all' instanza &c. Urgente populo (Perusino) profecti redierint ad locum electioni destinatum, sed non sine passionibus prioribus; Quas in Conclavi Pii V. ipsi Cardinali Borromæo dominatas esse cognoscimus: Fece conoscere &c. Omnibus, inquit Author, notum fecit, passiones & ambitionem mundanam non plane ex animo suo pulsas esse, quemadmodum hinc inde prædicabat atque illud aperte profitebatur.
units.tr: XXXVI. The author of the Cardinalism speaks of this as a most well-known matter, to be presupposed as certain: Everyone knows etc.; no one is ignorant, he says, p. 1, l. 3, p. 326, that in the elections of Pontiffs earthly passions reign. Yet it will not be useless to prove this dominion by the testimonies of some Conclaves. First, from what is recorded of Clement V., he hints that the Cardinals, having left the Conclave because of discord, at the instance etc.; urged by the people (of Perugia), went and returned to the place appointed for the election, but not without their earlier passions. We know that these passions dominated even Cardinal Borromeo himself in the Conclave of Pius V.: He made it known etc.; he made it known to all, says the author, that passions and worldly ambition had not been plainly driven out of his mind, as he proclaimed here and there and openly professed.

units.la: XXXVII. Si commodum proprium promotum est, sequitur studium gratitudinis. Sic in Conclavi Leonis X. Baronium Borromæus, & Paravicinus volebant cum prætextu, quòd ejus discipuli fuerint. Cùmque Monopoli respectu ejusdem vacillaret, exprobrato illi beneficio, quòd opera hujus ex Monasterio liberatus esset, non sine resistentia & quasi lacrymans condescendit ad votum ei dandum. In Conclavi Clementis X. mandatum fuit Gallis, di assister &c. ut assisterent particulariter Rospigliosio per affectum gratitudinis, &c. Quamvis Palleotto in Conclavi Clem. VIII. respectum gratitudinis rejecerit, & urgente Montaltio in causa Severinæ, atque argumentum ab auxilio, quod Severina antehac Paleotto præstiterit, desumptum adhibente, eidem responderit: Quando si tratta di conscienza, non si guarda à gratitudine. Id est: Ubi de conscientia agitur, gratitudo non respicitur. Quamvis etiam in Conclavi Clem. X. Chigii ingratitudo notetur, & Conclave Leonis XI. axioma tale suppeditet: Ingratitudo pecunia est, quam vilis, vel superbus animus pro acceptis magnis beneficiis reddit.
units.tr: XXXVII. If private advantage has been promoted, the zeal of gratitude follows. Thus in the Conclave of Leo X., Baronio, Borromeo and Paravicino wanted him with the pretext that they had been his disciples. And when Monopoli wavered out of regard for the same man, the benefit being thrown in his face, namely that by this man's work he had been freed from the monastery, he yielded, not without resistance and as if in tears, to give him his vote. In the Conclave of Clement X. the French were instructed to assist etc., that they should assist Rospigliosi particularly through affection and gratitude, etc. Although Paleotti in the Conclave of Clement VIII. rejected the regard of gratitude, and when Montalto urged it in Severina's cause, using the argument from the aid which Severina had previously given Paleotti, he answered him: When it is a matter of conscience, gratitude is not considered. That is: where conscience is at issue, gratitude is not regarded. Although also in the Conclave of Clement X. the ingratitude of Chigi is noted, and the Conclave of Leo XI. supplies this maxim: Ingratitude is the money which a base or proud mind pays back for great benefits received.

units.la: XXXVIII. Si commodum proprium læsum est, odium oritur & vindicta studium. Odium prodidisse in Concl. Pii V. dicitur CardiCardinalis Borromæus erga Montepulcianum, cujus promotioni obstitit, ostinato &c. obstinatus in conatibus suis, mediante humido melancholico, quod manifestè in eo dominabatur; Sibi autem jam ante ingressum proposuit, eum non debere eligi, e la cagione &c. cujus hanc causam assignant, factum esse odio erga Thomam Marinum, de quo firmiter credebat, Montepulcianum Papam factum amicum illum suum protecturum esse.
