In Concl. Sixti V. non multùm agebatur de Savello, quia Colonna & Cesis inimici ejus aperti erant. In eodem Concl. observatum fuit; non essere &c. Nihil magis pestiferum atque electioni Cardinalis alicujus contrarium esse, quàm si habeat Cardinales inimicos; Ibidem Medicaum malè habuit, & fronti sudorem expressit, quòd exclusionem Torresii invenire non potuit, quo non excluso, Farnesium immediatè dominaturum esse prævidit. Medicæum autem tunc ad exaltationem Montaltii compulit desiderium Farnesium & Torresium excludendi. Odio quoque satis in Concl. Innoc. VIII. indulsisse videtur Vice-Cancellarius, qui, cùm Cardinalis Arragonensis ei diceret; Si volebant simul facere unum Pontificem ad votum eorum, respondit; dummodò disturbaretur electio S. Marci, quem solum odio habebat, atque etiam sub ista conditione consensit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. If private advantage has been injured, hatred arises and the zeal of vengeance. Hatred is said to have revealed itself in the Conclave of Pius V. in Cardinal Borromeo toward Montepulciano, whose promotion he opposed, obstinate etc.; obstinate in his attempts, through a moist melancholic humour, which clearly dominated in him. He had also resolved before entering that Montepulciano should not be elected, and the cause, they assign, etc., the cause being hatred toward Thomas Marinus, about whom he firmly believed that Montepulciano, once made Pope, would protect that friend of his. In the Conclave of Sixtus V. not much was done about Savelli, because Colonna and Cesi were his open enemies. In the same Conclave it was observed: nothing is more pestilential or more contrary to the election of any Cardinal than if he has Cardinal enemies. There too the Medici was distressed, and sweat broke out on his brow, because he could not find a way to exclude Torres, without whose exclusion he foresaw that Farnese would immediately dominate. The Medici was then driven to the exaltation of Montalto by the desire to exclude Farnese and Torres. The Vice-Chancellor also seems to have indulged his hatred sufficiently in the Conclave of Innocent VIII., who, when the Cardinal of Aragon said to him: If they wished to make one Pope at the same time to their liking, replied: provided the election of St Mark is disturbed, whom alone he hated, and he even consented on this condition.

units.la: XXXIX. Vindicta studium notatur in Concl. Sixti V. respectu Altempsii, qui Montaltio accessit, ut in Farnesio ulciscerentur exclusionem Sirleti. Quid de vindicta in Concl. Julii III. à Farnesio erga Imperatorem ob consensum in mortem Petri Ludovici exercenda consultum fuerit, videri potest apud Authorem Card. p. 3. l. 2. p. 171. Sic etiam in Concl. Clem. X. Medicæi vendetta transversale, vindicta transversa & animus passione occæcatus aliquoties observatur, qui & eandem exercere valde studuit. Ibidem, quid Sforza in Medicæo digerere haud potuerit, & quales inimicos hic expertus sit, commemoratur. L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 223. eundem Sforzam ex vindictæ studio Celsio obstiturum innuit. In Conclavi rursus non minùs Rospigliosius introducitur memore de' disgusti sofferti, injuriarum acceptarum memor; Introducuntur Squadronistæ abalienati à Chigio, frustrà posthac adhibito reconciliationis studio; Introducitur Barberinus, cui à Pio, promotionem Altierii quærente, tempus non datum fuit respondendi, che non (con) questo &c. quòd cum eo diu litigârit in causa ardua coram Rota, & quòd eum ad solutionem adegerit, S. E. proin hic se excusatum habere debere.
units.tr: XXXIX. The zeal of vengeance is noted in the Conclave of Sixtus V. with respect to Altemps, who joined Montalto so that they might avenge on Farnese the exclusion of Sirleto. What was advised about vengeance to be exercised in the Conclave of Julius III. by Farnese against the Emperor, on account of his consent to the death of Pietro Luigi, can be seen in the author, Card. p. 3, l. 2, p. 171. Thus also in the Conclave of Clement X. the Medici's vendetta transversale, indirect vengeance and a mind blinded by passion is observed several times, and he also strove greatly to exercise the same. There too what Sforza could not digest in Medici, and what kind of enemies he experienced here, is recalled. The L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 223 hints that the same Sforza, out of zeal for vengeance, would oppose Cesi. In the Conclave, again, Rospigliosi is introduced no less, mindful of the displeasures suffered, mindful of the injuries received; the Squadronists estranged from Chigi are introduced, with the zeal for reconciliation applied in vain afterwards; Barberini is introduced, to whom, when Pio sought Altieri's promotion, no time was given to reply: that not with this etc., because he had litigated long with him in a difficult cause before the Rota, and because he had forced him to payment, His Eminence should therefore consider himself excused here.

units.la: vindicta studium
units.tr: the study of revenge

units.la: XL. Ad odium & vindictæ studium pertinet studium contrariandi. Sic in Concl. Pauli V. Aldobrandinus excludebat tacitè omnes Montaltianos, e si dichiarò &c. atque se expressè declarabat contrà Sauli, gnarus enim, quanto cum ardore Collegiati & omnes alii ejus exaltationem quærerent, necessarium judicabat respectum deponere, atque se manifestè contra eum declarare; cujus odii plures erant causa, atque inter alias, quòd Sauli procuraverat olim exclusionem Clementi, suo avunculo; quia insuper erat creatura dilecta Montaltii, neque tantum se inimicum exhibebat, verùm etiam aperté declarabat, quicquid contra eum in præcedente Conclavi factum sit, sua dispositione factum esse, atque adeò implacabilis erat, ut licèt infinitis officiis & artificiis eum mitigare conati sint, nunquam tamen illud evincere potuerint. Contrà multi ex amicis Sauli ejus promotionem à malgrado di Aldobrandino, rumpantur licèt ilia Aldobrandino; sperâsse. Contrariandi studium tale emphaticè atque generaliter innuit Author Vita D. Olympia p.59.60. postquam verba Olympiæ responsoria ad dicta quorundam, obstare Cognato inimicitiam Barbarinorum, sequentia attulisset: Igitur ob hanc ipsam rationem obtinebit, cùm tam exosi sint Barbarini; ita paucis interjectis pergens: Sit Papabilis aliquis Diabolus, sed Gallorum inimicus, eum proponere non intermittent Hispani; Sic etiam Galli facilè adclamabunt Dæmoni, si sit Hispanorum inimicus; Nepotésque Pontificis defuncti, qui in tali Electione oculos valde apertos habent, omnibus viribus adjuvant Antichristum, si sit ipsorum Amicus. Consentiunt, quæ p.442.443. de Conclavi Alex. VII. habet: Cardinales D. Olympia inimici, ut eam perderent, votum suum daturi fuissent vel ipsi Dæmoni, & multò magis Cardinali nullius pretii, si modò ejus inimicus fuisset, amici autem ejus non dubitassent vel Sanctum excludere, si modò ei se contrarium ostendisset; quod experientia testata est. Eadem Olympia ab eodem p.445. cùm aliter non posset, tantum exclusioni maximè manifestorum inimicorum suorum invigilasse dicitur. Simili etiam contrariandi studio in eodem Conclavi Alexandri VII. agebatur Barbarinus Olympiæ hyperaspistes, che non haveva &c. qui ideò tantùm Carpegnam noluit, quia eum voluerunt adversarii. Quod & variè notatur in Concl. Clem. X. ubi Medicæus cum Chigio contrà Barberinum conspirasse dicitur, etiam per le ruggini &c. propter offensas veteres, quæ facta fuerunt vulnera incurabilia; Huic autem Galliæ Legatus servire noluit per la novità &c. propter novitatem, quòd eum cum Hispanis associatum videri: Ille porrò Retzio exclusionem Cardinalis Delci annuncianti, con con gran calore,magno ardore respondit: Se dunque &c. Si Galli excludunt Delcium, nos Hispani excludemus Vidonium. Qui & cum Pio Legatum Hispaniae ad exclusionem per jus talionis faciendam movere conatus est. Atque huc quoque pertinet invidia, quâ Cardinales in genere abripi Il Card. p. 3. l. 2. p. 182. testatur, exemplum autem speciale p 183. subjungit.
units.tr: XL. The study of opposition belongs to hatred and revenge: the study of opposing. Thus in the Conclave of Paul V, Aldobrandini tacitly excluded all the Montaltians, and declared himself, and openly declared himself against Sauli, for, knowing how eagerly the Cardinals and all the others sought Sauli's elevation, he judged it necessary to set respect aside and to declare himself plainly against him. The causes of his hatred were several, among them that Sauli had once procured the exclusion of Clement, his uncle. Moreover, since Sauli was a creature beloved of Montalto, Aldobrandini not only showed himself an enemy but also openly declared that whatever had been done against him in the previous Conclave was done by his arrangement; and he was so implacable that, although they tried to soften him by countless services and stratagems, they never could win him over. On the other hand, many friends of Sauli hoped for his promotion in spite of Aldobrandini, even if that should break Aldobrandini. The author of the Life of Donna Olympia, pp. 59–60, hints at such a study of opposition in emphatic and general terms, after setting out Olympia's answer to those who said that the enmity of the Barberini stood in the way of her kinsman. He continues, a few words later: So for this very reason he will obtain it, since the Barberini are so hated; Let there be some Diabolus who is papabile, but an enemy of the French; the Spaniards will not cease to propose him; So too the French will readily acclaim the Devil himself, if he is an enemy of the Spaniards; and the nephews of the deceased Pontiff, who have their eyes very wide open in such an Election, support Antichrist with all their might if he is their friend. What pp. 442–443 says of the Conclave of Alexander VII agrees with this: The Cardinals hostile to Donna Olympia would have given their vote even to the Devil himself, to ruin her, and much more to a Cardinal of no worth, if only he were her enemy; her friends would not have hesitated to exclude even a Saint, if only he had shown himself opposed to them; which experience has attested. The same Olympia, according to the same p. 445, since she could not do otherwise, is said to have watched only over the exclusion of her most manifest enemies. With a similar study of opposition, in the same Conclave of Alexander VII, Barberini, Olympia's champion, acted that he had not etc., and for this reason alone did not want Carpegna, because his adversaries wanted him. This is noted in various ways also in the Conclave of Clement X, where Medici is said to have conspired with Chigi against Barberini, even through the rust etc., on account of old offences, which made incurable wounds. The French Legate, however, would not serve this because of the novelty etc., because of the novelty, since he seemed to be associated with the Spaniards. That man, when Retz announced the exclusion of Cardinal Delci, with great heat, with great ardour, replied: So then etc. If the French exclude Delci, we Spaniards will exclude Vidoni. He also tried to move the Spanish Legate to make an exclusion by the law of retaliation. To this belongs also the envy by which the Cardinals in general are carried away, as Il Card. p. 3, l. 2, p. 182 testifies, and he adds a particular example at p. 183.

units.la: XLI. Si commodum proprium timetur ab alio laedendum, ex isto metu ex. gr. poena agitur; Qui etiam inter causas numeratur, ob quas Aldobrandinus, ut n. prec. dictum est, tantopere se promotioni Sauli opposuit: Erat &c. Erat Sauli homo politicus, ingenio acuto, aptus & dispositus ad praeterita revidenda, atque jam nimis liberè confoederati nonnulli spargebant, se Papam facturos, qui castiget Aldobrandinum; & statim post haec dicta proponebant Sauli; Quam causam ipse Aldobrandinus allegavit, cùm quidam ex eo causam exclusionis Sauli instanter cognoscere cuperet. Contrà in Conclavi Greg. XV. secundùm quosdam proxima causa, ob quam Borghesius promotionem Camporae quaerebat, fuit, acciò non &c. ne reviderenter actiones praeteritas, quae fortè alii Pontifici non placiturae fuissent. Simili planè modo D. Olympia, in Concl. Alex. VII. temendo meno &c. minùs timens Sacchetium, quàm multos alios, ipsi acquisivit Azolinum & Gualterium. Contrà Barberinus Paleotto tunc noluit, timens abeo castigationem Olympia; Quae ipsa rursus vindictam à S. Clemente timebat &c. In Concl. Clem. IX. idem metus exclusiones dirigebat, dum nimirum & Rospigliosius intuitu Ravizzae & Chigius pro se Farnesium noluerunt, uterque come (di) persona &c. tanquam de persona severa metuebat vindictam, & ita non videbatur difficilis ejus exclusio. Sic etiam Card. Bonelli obstitisse dicitur, la parentela &c. cognatio Imperialis, cujus dominium apud eum respectu praeteritorum terribile videbatur. Secundùm recensitas & alias passiones semper Papam facere volunt à lor' modo, modo suo, quod supra ex Concl. Marc. II. notavimus.
units.tr: XLI. If one's own advantage is feared to be harmed by another, then from this fear, for example punishment, arises. This is also counted among the causes for which Aldobrandini, as said in the preceding number, so strongly opposed Sauli's promotion: Erat etc. Erat Sauli was a politic man, of sharp wit, apt and inclined to revise past things; and already some confederates were spreading abroad that they would make a Pope who would punish Aldobrandini; and immediately after these words they proposed Sauli. Aldobrandini himself gave this as the reason, when someone was eager to learn from him urgently the cause of Sauli's exclusion. On the other hand, in the Conclave of Gregory XV, according to some, the immediate cause for which Borghese sought the promotion of Campora was so that past actions, which perhaps would not have pleased another Pontiff, should not be reviewed. In exactly the same way Donna Olympia, in the Conclave of Alexander VII, fearing Sacchetti less than many others, won Azzolino and Gualterio for herself. On the other hand Barberini then did not want Paleotti, fearing from him the castigation of Olympia; who herself in turn feared vengeance from St. Clement etc. In the Conclave of Clement IX the same fear directed the exclusions, since both Rospigliosi, on account of Ravizza, and Chigi, on behalf of himself, did not want Farnese; each, as of a person etc., as from a severe person, feared vengeance, and so his exclusion did not seem difficult. Thus Cardinal Bonelli is also said to have stood in the way, the Imperial kinship, whose lordship over him, in respect of past things, seemed terrible. According to these and the other passions just listed, they always want to make the Pope after their own fashion, in their own way, which we noted above from the Conclave of Marcellus II.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA,
units.tr: SECTION TWO,

units.la: In qua
units.tr: In which

units.la: De factionibus, quas, ut secundùm vitiosa principia commodè agere possint, erigunt, nec non de artificiosis, quas in Factiones certas coeuntes adhibent, molitionibus in genere, agitur.
units.tr: Concerning the factions which they set up so that they can act conveniently on their vicious principles, and concerning the artful schemes which they employ in forming certain factions, is treated in general.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Transitio; II. Factiones triplicis potissimùm generis; Capita necessaria; III. Sua authoritate libertatem Electionis multis modis infringunt. IV. Quam eorum authoritatem etiam probant nomina Capitum & Creaturarum. V. Hinc est, quòd jam ante ingressum in Conclave aliquid quoad Electionem futuram conjicitur; VI. Quibus modis circumscripta sit Capitum authoritas; VII. An valde ei obsit scrutinium secretum; VIII. Qualis authoritas ipsis conveniat; IX. Capitum plerorumque qualitates augent vitium ex authoritate illorum; X Factiones Nepotum; XI. Nationum, sive Principum; XII. Concursum Principum quantum aliàs abominentur; XIII. Porrò idem ostenditur; XIV. Quid de Concursu Principum sit judicandum; XV. Quid Principes hîc spectare soleant; XVI. Concursus vitiosus probatur ex Concl. Clem. V. quoad Regem Gallia, Reges alios atque Barones Romanos; XVII. Hispania quantùm potuerit ostenditur ex Nobil. Sandis; XVIII. Ex Concl. Greg.XIII. XIX. Sixti V. XX. Greg.XIV. respectu Magni Ducis Hetruria; XXI. Vbi rursus magna etiam Hispanorum partes, proposito S. Severina; XXII. Nominatis nonnisi sex aliis quoque, exclusis reliquis; XXIII. Oppositiones factæ; XXIV. Quantum potuerint in Concl. Innoc.IX. nominantes unicum Madruccium; XXV. Quod porrò declaratur; Ex Concl eodem; XXVI. Leonis XI. Testimonio etiam Grammondi de Baronio; XXVII. Ex Conclavi Vrbani VIII. MSC. Epistola Regis Gallorum respectu Electionis Innoc. X. & Vita D. Olympia. XXVIII. Concl. Alex VII quoad Concursum promiscuum; XXIX. Ex Cardinalismo; XXX. Concl. Clem IX. XXXI. Clem.X. etiam respectu Legati Venetorum; L'Ambasc. di Rom. XXXII. Quæ omnia Electionis libertati contrariantur, etiam respectu Regina Suecia; Hinc metus offendendi Reges, major respectu Regis Hispania; Quod etiam ostenditur ex Anonymo Gallo & MSC. Italico; Concursus tamen Nepotum multò efficacior; Hinc Regibus consulta abstinentia; XXXIII. Quibus contraria hîc consulit Lottinus, & primò quidem, ut utilitatis suæ rationem probè habeant; XXXIV. Secundò, ut liberales sint erga Cardinales, etiam in pensionum assignatione; XXXV. Factiones Neutralistarum, sive Turma volantis, ex Authore Card. XXXVI. Ex Conclavibus; XXXVII. Termini Conclaviarii partim nautici, sed maximè militares; XXXVIII. Bellum quorundam Cardinalium, bellum amoris; XXXIX. Sequitur modus agendi, secundùm principia, in Factionibus; XL. Per artificiosas molitiones, declaratus ex Conclavibus Clem. V. Cal III. Pii II. Pauli IV. Pii IV. XLI. Pii V. Sixti V. Greg. XIV. XLII. Vrb. VII. Innoc. IX. Clem. VIII. IX. & X. XLIII. Incipiunt Papa adhuc superstite, sed non deberent; XLIV. Contra molitiones, Exclusiones.
units.tr: I. Transition; II. Factions of three main kinds; the necessary chiefs; III. They undermine freedom of election in many ways. IV. Scripture names and the names given to chiefs and creatures also confirm their authority. V. Hence, even before entering the Conclave, something is guessed about the coming election. VI. The ways in which the authority of the chiefs is limited. VII. Whether the secret ballot greatly hinders them. VIII. What kind of authority belongs to them. IX. The qualities of most chiefs increase the evil of their authority. X. Factions of nephews. XI. Factions of nations, or of princes. XII. How much they condemn, at other times, the concurrence of princes. XIII. The same is shown further. XIV. What is to be judged about the concurrence of princes. XV. What princes usually look to here. XVI. Vicious concurrence is proved from the Conclave of Clement V with regard to the King of France, other kings, and the Roman barons. XVII. How much Spain could do is shown from the Nobile Sandis. XVIII. From the Conclave of Gregory XIII. XIX. Of Sixtus V. XX. Gregory XIV, with regard to the Grand Duke of Tuscany. XXI. Where again the Spanish too had a large part, in the proposal of S. Severina. XXII. Only six others named, the rest excluded. XXIII. Objections raised. XXIV. How much they could do in the Conclave of Innocent IX, when they nominated only Madruzzo. XXV. What is further declared; from the same Conclave. XXVI. By the testimony of Leo XI, also Grammond on Baronius. XXVII. From the Conclave of Urban VIII, the manuscript letter of the King of the French concerning the election of Innocent X, and the life of D. Olympia. XXVIII. The Conclave of Alexander VII concerning the mixed concurrence. XXIX. From Cardinalism. XXX. The Conclave of Clement IX. XXXI. Clement X, also with regard to the Venetian envoy; L'Ambasciatore di Roma. XXXII. All these things are contrary to freedom of election, also with regard to Queen Christina of Sweden; hence the fear of offending kings, greater with regard to the King of Spain; which is also shown from an anonymous Frenchman and an Italian manuscript; yet the concurrence of nephews is much more effective; hence abstention is advised to kings. XXXIII. Lottini advises the contrary here, and first indeed that they should properly consider the reckoning of their own advantage. XXXIV. Secondly, that they be generous towards the Cardinals, even in the assignment of pensions; XXXV. The factions of the Neutralists, or the flying squadron, according to the author Card. XXXVI. From the Conclaves. XXXVII. The terms of the Conclave, partly nautical but chiefly military. XXXVIII. The war of certain Cardinals, a war of love. XXXIX. Follows the manner of acting, according to the principles, in factions. XL. Through artful schemes, shown from the Conclaves of Clement V, Callixtus III, Pius II, Paul IV, Pius IV. XLI. Pius V, Sixtus V, Gregory XIV. XLII. Urban VII, Innocent IX, Clement VIII, IX and X. XLIII. They begin while the Pope is still alive, though they ought not to. XLIV. Against the schemes, exclusions.

units.la: I. Vitiosa sunt, quæ hactenus à nobis visa sunt, Cardinalium eligentium principia, juxta quæ non minùs vitiosè agunt. Ut autem eò melius agere possint atque pro voto suo felicius, certas societates ineunt, sive Factiones constituunt. In quibus diversi partim communi patriâ, partim creatione ab eodem, partim aliâs quadam scopi convenientiâ, partim etiam merâ necessitate conjunguntur; Neque enim putandum est, simplici consensu, amore & votorum identitate societates ejusmodi iniri. Non sempre &c. Non semper homines se conjungunt per benevolentiam, inquit Author Concl. Leonis XI. sed sæpe vel invidia, vel timor, vel aliud quid animos caterùm dissonantes atque contrarios ad aliquam harmoniam reducere possunt. Neque raro accidit, ut in ejusmodi societatibus, sive factionibus quot membra, tot sensus. Quod etiam ex sequentibus patebit.
units.tr: I. The principles of the electing Cardinals which have so far been seen by us are vicious, and according to them they act no less viciously. But so that they may act better in this and more happily according to their wish, they enter into certain associations, or form factions. In these, various men are joined partly by a common homeland, partly by creation by the same man, partly by some other agreement of purpose, and partly even by sheer necessity; for it should not be thought that associations of this kind are entered into by simple agreement, love, and identity of wishes. Non sempre &c. Men do not always join together out of goodwill, says the author of the Conclave of Leo XI, but often envy, or fear, or something else can bring minds that are otherwise discordant and opposed into some harmony. It is not rare for it to happen that in such societies, or factions, there are as many opinions as members. This will also be clear from what follows.

units.la: II. Triplicis generis plerunque & à longo tempore sunt istæ Factiones, vel Nepotum, vel Nationum, Hispanicæ olim maximè, sed & jam à multis annis æquè Gallicæ (Imperatoris ab aliquo tempore etiam nonnulli commoda observant, quæ tamen cum commodis Hispanorum arctè conjuncta sunt;) vel Neutralista. Quarum Factionum quælibet à certo Capite, illa à Nepote, ista à primario Nationis, vel Nationi addicto, vel fidissimo habito, hæc à quodam magnæ authoritatis Cardinale regitur. Et quidem Capita habentur necessaria; Non illud quidem agnoscere voluerunt multi Neutralistæ, qui cùm in Concl. Alex. VII. à Principe Pansilio monerentur, ut se certo Capiti subderent, responderunt: Che havevano &c. Se habere caput proprium, & pedes proprios. Interim tamen, præsuppositò isto hodierno agendi modo vitioso, omninò necessitas magna est societatis ineundæ & constituendi capitis. Audiatur testis Jo. Franc. Lottinus, homo Italus, & qui non diversus videtur, ab illo Volaterrano, cui Marcellus II. P. unum suosuorum trium, quæ hactenus obtinuerat, Sacerdotiorum, Onuphrio teste, concessit. Ejus in Dissert. de Concl. hæc sunt verba: Neque verò admirentur, quòd ferè semper Principum & Capitum mentio interseratur, neque peculiares cuilibet Cardinali regula adscribantur, cùm præsertim dici soleat, quemlibet Cardinalem in Conclavi tantundem posse; nam eo tempore, cùm unusquisque cognoscat, se unum parùm proficere posse, necessariò adhaeret alteri, sicque diversis de causis & respectibus diversas ineunt amicitias. Quod si, v. gr. boni sunt & Reip. studiosi cum similibus conjunguntur, si utilitatis alicujus gratiâ ducuntur, cum iis, qui eòdem respiciunt, congregantur & conspirant. Ideòque cùm dicitur, cum tot Capitibus & sententiis agendum esse, non est verum: nam statim atque aliquis ambit, semper ab eo regitur, qui illius ambitus Caput esse potest, cùm inter multos oportet aliquem aut authoritate, aut prudentia cæteris præcellere: quibus rationibus Caput & Princeps ille ferè semper suas ipsius utilitates respicit promovétque.
units.tr: II. These factions are usually of three kinds, and have been for a long time: either of nephews, or of nations, formerly chiefly Spanish, but for many years now equally French (for some time now some also observe the advantages of the Emperor, which nonetheless are closely bound up with the advantages of the Spanish); or neutralists. Each of these factions is ruled by a certain chief: the first by a nephew, the second by the leader of a nation, or one devoted to or regarded as most faithful to the nation, and the third by a certain Cardinal of great authority. And indeed the chiefs are held to be necessary. Many neutralists were unwilling to acknowledge this; when, at the Conclave of Alexander VII, they were advised by Prince Pamphili to submit themselves to a certain chief, they replied: Che havevano &c. They had a head of their own, and feet of their own. Meanwhile, however, granted this present vicious manner of acting, a great necessity certainly exists for forming an association and appointing a chief. Let the witness be Giovanni Francesco Lottini, an Italian, who seems not to differ from that man of Volterra to whom Pope Marcellus II, according to Onuphrius, granted one of the three benefices which he had hitherto held. His words in the Dissertation on the Conclave are these: Nor should they be surprised that mention is almost always made of princes and chiefs, nor that particular rules are not assigned to each Cardinal, since especially it is commonly said that each Cardinal in the Conclave can do as much as any other; for at that time, since each one knows that he can achieve little on his own, he necessarily attaches himself to another, and so for different causes and considerations they form different friendships. If, for example, they are good men and zealous for the commonwealth, they join with like-minded men; if they are led by some advantage, they gather and conspire with those who look to the same thing. Therefore, when it is said that one must deal with so many chiefs and opinions, it is not true; for as soon as anyone seeks support, he is always ruled by the one who can be the head of that canvassing group, since among many someone must surpass the rest in authority or prudence; and for these reasons that chief and prince almost always looks to and promotes his own advantages.

units.la: III. Capita autem libertatem electionis multis modis infringunt; Testem habemus Authorem Concl. Pii V. qui, postquam occasione multitudinis Cardinalium tunc præsentium dixisset, multos putâsse longiùs duraturum esse, opinionem illam quasi refutans subjungit: In questi Conclavi &c. In his Conclavibus, quæ hactenus fuerunt, semper Papa à Capitibus factionum creati fuerunt, & Cardinales alii, in quocunque numero fuerint, fecerunt, quod his Capitibus placuit, sive ratione obligationis, sive ratione timoris alicujus, sive quia conjuncti se eò fortiores viderunt, quàm si soli mansissent; atque dum scrutinium in isto tempore tantùm prætextui inserviit, quod certò credi potest, aperte cognoscitur diuturnitatem aut brevitatem Conclavis nasci non ex multitudine aut numero Cardinalium, sed ab obstinata, vel prompta resolutione Capitum &c. Sed & Capitum authoritas quodammodo apparet ex eo, quòd in Conclavi Pauli V. de Cardinali Aldobrandino narratur, eum nimirum creaturas suas Cardinales interrogâsse, an secundùm promissionem datam unum ex suo numero vellent, atque respondentibus cunctis, quòd sic; inclinando se versus Borghesium dixisse; Ecco il Papa! Ecce Papam! Nec non ex Concl. Greg. XV. ubi dixisse fertur Borghesius Nepos, se Conclave ingredi cum Papa facto; licèt illud nocuerit divulgatum; Et in quo Creaturæ Aldobrandinianæ, cùm ad electionem irent, maximam partem nesciverunt, quo ducerentur. In Concl. Alex. VII. dicitur: Ogn' uno &c. Vide sect. prec. n. 27. Ibidem aliquis Charon dictus, perche tum tutti imbarcava al Papato,quia omnes instar Charontis,animabus in alterum mundum transvehendis destinati,cymba imponebat,ductas ripæ ulterioris amore. Capitum quoque authoritatem libertati votorum contrariam atque proin vitiosam probant verba ex Concl. Clem. IX. sequentia, quibus in judicio de Card. Bonvisio obstaculum recensetur respectu Chigii Nepotis,non quoad ipsum Bonvisium plurimùm semper à Chigio amatum,sed ob Nepotem,qui,si non esset, cum honore egrederetur facilè, atque de eo, quemadmodum etiam de Rospigliosio,dici potest; Si non eligetur,Chigius eum noluit. Sed ibidem etiam Ravizzæ Conclavistæ tribuitur, quòd dirigat voluntatem Chigii.
units.tr: III. The chiefs, moreover, undermine freedom of election in many ways. We have a witness in the author of the Conclave of Pius V, who, after mentioning, on the occasion of the large number of Cardinals then present, that many had thought the Conclave would last longer, adds, as if refuting that opinion: In these Conclaves which have been held hitherto, the Pope was always created by the heads of the factions, and the other Cardinals, however many there were, did what pleased these heads, either from a sense of obligation, or from some fear, or because, joined together, they saw themselves stronger than if they had remained alone; and while the ballot at that time served only as a pretext, it is clearly recognised, as can certainly be believed, that the length or brevity of the Conclave arises not from the multitude or number of Cardinals, but from the stubborn or ready resolution of the chiefs etc. But the authority of the chiefs also appears in some measure from the fact that, in the Conclave of Paul V, it is related of Cardinal Aldobrandini that he asked his own creatures, Cardinals, whether they wished to choose one from his number according to the promise given, and when all replied that they did, he bowed towards Borghese and said: Ecco il Papa! Behold the Pope! And likewise from the Conclave of Gregory XV, where it is reported that Borghese the nephew said he was entering the Conclave with the Pope already made; although this, once divulged, did harm; and in which the Aldobrandini creatures, when they went to the election, for the most part did not know where they were being led. In the Conclave of Alexander VII it is said: Every one &c. See the preceding section, number 27. There too someone called Charon, because then everyone was embarking for the Papacy, since all were like Charon, appointed to ferry souls to the other world, he loaded them into his boat, led by love of the further shore. The authority of the chiefs, too, which is contrary to freedom of votes and therefore vicious, is proved by the following words from the Conclave of Clement IX, in which an obstacle is listed in the judgment on Cardinal Bonvisi with regard to the nephew Chigi: not as far as Bonvisi himself is concerned, who was always greatly loved by Chigi, but on account of the nephew, who, if he were not there, could easily leave with honour; and of him, as also of Rospigliosi, it can be said: If he is not elected, Chigi does not want him. But in the same place it is also attributed to the Conclave-attendant Ravizza that he directs the will of Chigi.

units.la: IV. Eandem Capitum authoritatem & potestatem confirmant vel ipsa, quibus illi, & quibus reliqui insigniuntur nomina; Capita dicuntur ipsi; Capitis autem est corpus regere, corporis, sequi Capitis ductum. Reliqui vocantur Creatura ; creaturæ autem multis modis à Creatore,vel creatoris Vicario utique dependent. Atque sic dici arbitror omnes sub Capitibus, Nepotibus maximè, constitutos;Sunt illi creati & ad dignitatem Cardinalitiam promoti (nec inconveniens est creationis appellatio,si voces: Esto Cardinalis ; juxta Differt.IV. vim creatricem similem illi,quæ in Deo est,in Papis probant; ) à Papis,quorum Nepotibus subsunt, atque his quasi testamento relinquuntur, ut commoda eorum in Conclavibus observantes gratitudinem pro dignitare collata, cui gratitudinem nullam sufficere suprà dixerunt,testentur.
units.tr: IV. The same authority and power of the Heads is confirmed by the very names by which they and the others are distinguished. They are called Heads, and it belongs to the head to rule the body and to the body to follow the head's lead. The others are called creatures, and creatures in many ways depend on their Creator, or at least on the Creator's vicar. So I think all who are placed under the Heads, especially the Nephews, are subject to them. They are created and promoted to the dignity of cardinal (and the word "creation" is not out of place, if we take the words Be a cardinal as, in line with Differt. IV., proof that the Popes possess a creative power like that which is in God). They are raised by the Popes, whose Nephews they serve, and are left to these as a kind of legacy, so that by watching over the interests of their patrons in the conclaves they may bear witness to their gratitude for the dignity conferred on them. Earlier they said that no gratitude is enough for that.

units.la: V. Ab ejusmodi autem Factionibus & Capitibus certo Cardinalium numero quasi imperantibus maximè venit, quòd jam ante ingressum in Conclave aliquid quoad electionem futuram conjici potest; Exclusionem Factiones singulæ sæpe habent, id est, possunt, si aliquis à Factionibus contrariis proponatur ingratus, per unam tertiam Cardinalium præsentium partem & unum atque alterum amplius ei Papatum eripere, si cohæreant, nonnunquam etiam aliis ex aliis factionibus cum ipsis ad exclusionem alicujus ob peculiares respectus, concurrentibus, &, si non habeant antea ultra unam tertiam numerum,isto majorem efficientibus; quo in casu propositus,utpote numero sufficiente ⅔ destitutus excludi dicitur. Nunquam autem (quod sciam,atque etiam consentit Il. Card. p.3.l.3.p.383.) factio aliqua sola inclusionem habuit, id est, sola sufficienti ⅔ numero constans aliquem ad Papatum provehere vehere potuit. Considerantur igitur diligenter Cardinales Papabiles, & studiosè examinatur, quo animo erga singulos Capita maximè Factionum sint, & quinam ad singulorum vel exclusionem, vel inclusionem cooperatuti sint, atque secundùm illa jam ante electionem de electione cum quadam verisimilitudine judicium fertur. Hinc n. 3. introduximus Borghesium ob numerositatem Creaturarum suarum & fiduciam de nonnullis aliis gloriantem, se Conclave ingredi cum Papa jam facto. Hinc aliàs etiam vota jam ante ingressum numerata fuerunt; Jam ante ingressum in Concl. Clem. VIII. li fautori &c. Amici Severina palam dicebant, se habere ultrà quinque vota superflua. Nec minor fuerat de ista votorum sufficientia ipsius Legati Hispaniæ persuasio; quippe post negotiationem pro S. Severina ultimus è Conclavi egressus; l haveva &c. eum tam certò Papam credidit, ut nonnulli affirmârint, quòd, dum intus valediceret; quia ultra incerta habuerint 37. vota firmissima columnarum stabilium adinstar, atque Fautores peterent, ut ante egressum Sua Excell. adoratio institueretur, noluerit, ne praesentia authoritatis sua videretur Cardinales coegisse, adeò securus erat, enim aliàs proximo mane Papam futurum. Similiter ante ingressum in Concl. Clem. IX. differo &c. Cardinalem Imperialem jam pro Bonellio collegisse 40. vota quod si fuisset, 4. duntaxat adhuc defuissent.
units.tr: V. From these Factions and their Heads, who rule as it were by a fixed number of cardinals, it largely follows that something about the coming election can be guessed even before entry into the conclave. Each Faction often has exclusion, that is, if some candidate is put forward who is unwelcome to the opposing Factions, they can, if they hold together, snatch the papacy from him by one third of the cardinals present plus one or two more. Sometimes other Factions also join them in excluding someone, for particular reasons, and if they did not already have more than one third, they make up that larger number. In that case the candidate put forward is said to be excluded, since he lacks the sufficient two thirds. But no single Faction has ever had inclusion, as far as I know (and the author Il. Card. p.3.l.3.p.383. agrees), that is, no single Faction, consisting only of the sufficient two-thirds number, has been able to advance anyone to the papacy. So the Papabili are carefully considered, and it is closely examined what attitude the Heads of the Factions have toward each one, and who cooperates in excluding or including each. On the basis of this, a judgement about the election is formed with some likelihood even before the election. Hence, at n. 3., we introduced Borghese, who, boasting of the number of his creatures and his confidence in several others, said that he would enter the conclave with the Pope already made. Hence on other occasions too the votes were counted even before entry. Before entry into the conclave of Clement VIII, the partisans, friends and followers of Severina openly said that they had more than five surplus votes. The Spanish Legate's conviction that the votes were sufficient was no less: indeed, after negotiating for Severina he was the last to leave the conclave. He had so certainly believed him to be Pope, that some affirmed that, when he was saying farewell inside, because he had 37 very firm votes, like the stable pillars, and his followers were asking that an act of homage to His Excellency be arranged before he left, he would not allow it, lest it seem that by the presence of his authority he had compelled the cardinals. He was so confident that otherwise he would be Pope the next morning. Similarly, before entry into the conclave of Clement IX, a certain imperial cardinal had already gathered 40 votes for Bonelli; if that had been so, only 4 would still have been lacking.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Fateor quidem, spem hos fefellisse, & alios aliàs similiter al tavolino i conti senza l'hoste, apud mensam rationem sine hospite, ut ex Conclavi Clem.X. loquar, iniisse. Fateor, non absolutam esse istam Capitum authoritatem & potestatem, neque creaturas ipsis in omnibus omnes semper obsequentes esse. Atque valdè probo, quae apud Authorem Card. p. 3. l. 3. p. 336. lego: Per me stimo &c. Ego quidem, inquit, parùm astimo tot Factionum uniformitatem, cùm prater titulum nihil aliud habeat, & quandam speciem exiguam, cùm sapiùs in una Factione 4. aut 5. sententiae sint, singulis à duobus aut tribus Cardinalibus receptis; id quod electionem difficilem reddit, si enim Factionistae sequerentur voluntatem Capitum, Papa in momento factus esset, sufficeret etiam duo tantùm Capita accommodare, sed aliter res se habere deprehenduntur, dum in Conclavi quot Cardinales, tot Factiones, quot Factiones, tot Capita, quot Capita, tot Papae sunt; Ita semet confundunt, dum uniuntur, dum disjunguntur, multùm facientes, & nihil tamen. Proin etiam valde aptam judico comparationem apud eundem p. 337. seqq. ab Abbate Romano, qui Conclavi Innocentii X. interinterfuerit, institutam. Narrat, quomodo viderit exerceri milites inexercitatos à Capitaneis inexercitatis : I Capitani &c. Duces, inquit, imperabant obediendo, & milites obediebant imperando ; quidam currebant, quò non erant vocati, alii nolebant ire, quò eundum fuisset. Quidam dux vocabat. 2. vel. 3. Cohortis sua, & veniebant 5. ex cohorte alterius ; quando ordo aliquis duplicandus erat, caput & cauda deerant ; anteriores enim, quibus standum fuisset, retrocedebant, posteriores in tantùm anteriora petebant, ut ibi soli manserint; Murmurabant duces de inobedientia militum, hi maledicebant ducibus, eò quòd imperare nescirent, sicque facti erant duces milites, milites duces. Et subjungit ridentis, dum spectator esset, Abbatis judicium, che non li pareva &c. sibi exercitium illud Conclavi Cardinalium parùm dissimile visum esse &c. cùm non potuerit meliorem ordinem in D. D. Cardinalium negotiationibus observare &c. Atque speciatim iste obedientiæ universalis defectus nocet Nepotibus, quatenus inter suos habent subditos hujus & illius Regis, quorum commoda specialia in Conclavibus spectari solent. De quibus ita Author idem p. 334. 335. Trà le fattioni &c. In Factionibus multi sunt, qui tanquam dependentes aut subditi Regum, non aliter se Capitibus subjicere possunt, nisi quatenus de Regi grato agitur. Et revera, licèt tantum dicatur de Factionibus, Hispanica & Gallica, illarum tamen Cardinales non Capiti à Regibus deputato subsunt (Id tamen sæpe respectu quorundam, saltem Cardinalibus Nepotibus se non subjicientium, sed unicè, ab illo, cui secretum Regni concreditum est, dependentium, contingit; ut omnes semper, si vel in aliis factionibus membra sint, illius sententiam sequi tenentur, atque eo respectu nos Capita etiam Factionum Nationalium jam suprà commemoravimus;) sed ex prudenti politica dividuntur hinc inde, & sufficit Regibus, si ipsis serviatur, melius autem servitur ipsis, dum Cardinales suos sub Capitibus aliarum Factionum habent, quàm si proprias Factiones erigunt (nempe dispersis in aliis Factionibus, quid agatur, communicatur, atque dispersis, qui proin minùs notantur & magis occultè agere possunt, eò minùs resistitur;) hinc Cardinales Regii potiùs Nationista, quàm Factionista vocandi essent, in colloquiis particularibus convenientes &c.
units.tr: I admit indeed that these hopes have deceived them, and that others on other occasions have likewise entered into reckoning the accounts at the table without the host, to speak as the conclave of Clement X does. I admit that this authority and power of the Heads is not absolute, and that the creatures do not always and in all things obey them. And I strongly approve what I read in the author Card. p. 3. l. 3. p. 336.: I, for my part, think little of the uniformity of so many Factions, since it has nothing beyond the title and a certain small appearance, since often within one Faction there are four or five opinions, each held by two or three cardinals. This is what makes the election difficult. For if the members of the Factions followed the will of the Heads, the Pope would be made in a moment; it would suffice to win over only two Heads. But it is found otherwise: in the conclave there are as many Factions as cardinals, as many Heads as Factions, and as many Popes as Heads. Thus they confound themselves, when they unite and when they separate, doing much and yet nothing. Accordingly I also judge very apt the comparison drawn by the Roman abbot who had been present at the conclave of Innocent X, found at the same author, p. 337 ff. He tells how he saw untrained soldiers drilled by untrained captains: The captains, he says, commanded by obeying, and the soldiers obeyed by commanding. Some ran where they were not called, others refused to go where they ought to have gone. One leader called two or three of his cohort, and five from another cohort came. When some rank had to be doubled, head and tail were missing; the front ranks, where they should have stood, fell back, and the rear ranks pressed forward so far that they alone remained there. The leaders grumbled about the disobedience of the soldiers, and the soldiers cursed the leaders because they did not know how to command; so the leaders became soldiers and the soldiers leaders. And the abbot, while watching, adds with a smile his judgement, that it seemed to him this drill was not very unlike the business of the College of Cardinals, since he could not observe better order in the negotiations of the most eminent cardinals. In particular, this general lack of obedience harms the Nephews, since among their own subjects they have men belonging to this or that king, whose special interests are usually considered in the conclaves. Of these the same author writes thus, p. 334-335: Among the Factions there are many who, as dependants or subjects of kings, cannot submit to the Heads except insofar as the king's favour is concerned. And indeed, although this is said only of the Spanish and French Factions, their cardinals are nevertheless not subject to a Head appointed by the kings (yet this often happens with respect to some, at least to those cardinals who are not subject to the Nephews but depend solely on the one to whom the secret of the kingdom has been entrusted; so that all of them, even if they are members of other Factions, are bound always to follow his opinion, and in that respect we have already mentioned above the Heads even of the National Factions), but through prudent policy they are divided here and there, and it is enough for the kings that they are served. They are served better when their cardinals are under the Heads of other Factions than if they set up Factions of their own (namely, because what is being done is shared with those dispersed among other Factions, and because those dispersed are less noticed and can act more secretly, so there is less resistance), hence the royal cardinals ought rather to be called Nationalists than Factionists, meeting in private conversations etc.

units.la: VII. Sic etiam authoritati Capitum obstare videtur scrutinium secretum, in quo videtur, cuivis liberum esse, cui votum suum dare velit. Atque huc respicit Author Concl. Urb. VIII. qui inter tres causas, ob quas stimava &c. omnes putabant, Conclave illud multò praecedentibus diuturnius, difficultatibus atque contentionibus plenius nius fore ; primam facit il modo &c. modum electionis in Bulla Greg. XV. praescriptum, per quam libertas Electoribus constabat, mediante suffragio secreto; credebatur, ita pergit, communiter, quando quivis propria opinione & propriis commodis regatur, difficulter sufficientem numerum habitum iri. Verùm primò tantùm in modo eligendi per scrutinium libertas electionis quodammodo constat; Secundò demum ita a tempore Gregorii XV. Ergò antehac, quod etiam Author satis innuit, libertas electionibus legitimis adeò essentialis imminuta erat. Tertiò tantùm ex illo tempore & vi Constitutionis Gregorianae quodam, & non omni modo salva est. Capita enim, quemadmodum audiemus, variis modis Creaturas obligare nôrunt, síque scrutinium non respondeat, instare, suspiciones formare, dubios magis obligare, imò etiam nonnunquam signum & contra signum postulare &c. Imò & aliàs nonnunquam scitur, cujus suffragium in scrutinio defit ; Exemplum Concl. Clem. IX. suppeditat.
units.tr: VII. In the same way the authority of the Heads seems to be hindered by the secret ballot, in which it seems to be free to each person to give his vote to whomever he wishes. The author of the Conclave of Urban VIII has this in view. Among the three causes for which everyone thought that that conclave would be longer than the earlier ones, and fuller of difficulties and disputes, he puts first the method of election prescribed in the bull of Gregory XV, by which freedom was secured for the electors through a secret vote. It was believed, he goes on, generally, that when each is governed by his own opinion and private interests, it would be difficult to attain a sufficient number. But, first, freedom of election is secured only in some measure by the manner of electing by ballot. Secondly, this has been so only since the time of Gregory XV. Therefore, before that, as the author also sufficiently hints, freedom, which is so essential to lawful elections, had been diminished. Thirdly, only since that time, and by the force of the Gregorian Constitution, is it preserved in a certain way, and not in every way. For the Heads, as we shall hear, know how to bind their creatures in various ways. So if the ballot does not match their wishes, they insist, form suspicions, bind the doubtful more firmly, and even at times demand a sign and a counter-sign, and so on. Indeed, at other times it is also sometimes known whose vote is missing from the ballot. The conclave of Clement IX supplies an example.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Sed nec magis quàm Scrutinium Secretum ea, quae dicta sunt, authoritatem Capitum tantam, quanta aequalitati votorum & libertati electionum contrariatur, plane tollunt. Licèt enim non semper obsequantur Creaturae, saepe tamen; licèt non in omnibus, in multis tamen; licèt non omnibus, tamen quibusdam Capitibus magis regimini aptis ; Si non Nepotibus, sub quibus Nationistae quidam esse solent, tamen Capitibus Nationum, simpliciter ob Nationum commoda, quod non minùs vitiosum, aequè ac illud, quòd multi commune Factionis, vel Capitis commodum, non Ecclesiae, sed suo, & mendaciter quidem, aliquando perjurè postponunt; Ut & obedientia, quà suffragia ad nutum Capitis dare tenentur, & inobedientia talis, utraque naevos habeat. Saepiùs tamen saltem à plerisque jurata quasi praestatur obedientia, exiguo ad gloriam Dei in Ecclesiae commodis respectu habito ; Hinc Capita pro se & aliis promittunt, se cum tot Electioni tali accedere velle. Hinc Aldobrandinus Nepos in Concl. Leonis XI. irrisione quidem, deficientibus nonnullis, in quadam schedula hinc inde per Conclave sparsa citabatur à compa-rire &c. ad comparendum termino tot dierum, ad Creaturas suas vendendas, instantibus Avila & Marchione Viglienensi, aliàs &c. quae Author exprimere non fuit ausus. Et quamvis ab initio quilibet sibi Papam fingat atque eligendum praesumat commodis suis utilissimum, mum, interim tamen, quia tandem videt vota sua, imò etiam conatus suos deficere, tandem etiam, si aliter fieri non possit, plerisque ex Factione, atque adeò Capiti sese accommodare cogitur, & quasi à torrente unà cum aliis abripitur. Sed & idem Author Concl. Urb. VIII. qui per Constitutiones Gregorianas restitutam esse libertatem votorum dicere videbatur, & porrò dicit; Nova Bulla tribuebatur, di haver &c. quod rem eò deduxerit, ut ne consentientia quidem Factionum Capita Papam facere queant; idem, inquam, rationibus, quibus necessitatem Capitum declarat, & difficultatem voti occultandi ostendit, & quasi impossibilitatem, poiche sono &c. quando tantopere commoda cujusvis ventilata sint, & tam exacta habeatur notitia dependentiarum, naturarum & morum, & tantum sit studium gressus aliorum observandi; Salvam manere Capitum authoritatem probat; Atque ideò Il. Card. p.3.l.2. p.167. pronuntiat: Jam, id est, à centum circiter annis vota Cardinalium non sunt amplius libera, ultimi precedunt primos, & primi cedunt ultimis.
units.tr: But the things said above do not entirely remove the authority of the Heads (Capita), which is great enough to conflict with the equality of votes and the freedom of elections, any more than the Secret Scrutiny does. For although the Creatures do not always obey, they often do; although not in all matters, yet in many; although not all Heads, yet some who are better suited to rule: if not Nephews, under whom some Nationalists are wont to stand, then at least the Heads of the Nations, simply for the advantages of the Nations. This is no less vicious, just as it is that many, sometimes mendaciously and even perjuriously, put the common advantage of the Faction or of the Head ahead of the Church's, and their own. So both obedience, by which they are bound to give their votes at the Head's nod, and such disobedience, each has its blemishes. Yet more often at least, obedience is rendered by most as if sworn, with little regard to the glory of God and the advantages of the Church. Hence the Heads promise for themselves and for others that they will come to such and such an election. Hence Aldobrandini, the nephew in the Conclave of Leo XI, cited in mockery, when some were lacking, a notice scattered here and there through the Conclave: to appear, etc., to appear within so many days, to sell off his creatures, with Avila and the Marquis of Viglienense pressing, otherwise etc., which the author did not dare to spell out. And although at the start each person imagines a Pope for himself and presumes to elect the one most useful to his own interests, yet meanwhile, because in the end he sees his votes, even his efforts, fail, at last too, if it cannot be otherwise, he is compelled to accommodate himself to most of the Faction, and so to the Head, and is swept away along with the others as if by a torrent. But also the same author, in the Conclave of Urban VIII, who seemed to say that freedom of votes was restored by the Gregorian Constitutions, goes on to say: a new bull was ascribed, to have..., which has brought the matter to such a point that not even the agreeing Heads of the Factions can make a Pope. The same author, I say, by the reasons with which he declares the necessity of the Heads and shows the difficulty of concealing a vote, and as it were an impossibility, since sound, etc., when the advantages of each are so thoroughly weighed, and such exact knowledge of dependencies, natures and morals is had, and such is the zeal for watching the steps of others, proves that the authority of the Heads remains intact. And therefore Il. Card. p.3 l.2 p.167 pronounces: Now, that is, for about a hundred years the votes of the Cardinals are no longer free; the last go before the first, and the first give way to the last.

units.la: IX. Vitium autem illud, quod Electionibus Pontificum ex Capitum authoritate accedit, eò majus est, quia non gravissimi atque dignissimi ex Cardinalium Collegio Factionum Capita existunt, sed plerunque juvenes, qui exiguam de Ecclesiæ bono & Dei gloria curam gerunt, sed commodis suis, si non unicè, saltem maximè intenti sunt, atque rursus à passionibus suis abripiuntur; Quales plerosque Nepotes esse nemo negare audit. Quod autem Capita Nationum attinet, rursus non dignitas & Zelus pro gloria Dei, sed Regni commodum speciale in iis constituendis spectari solet, item authoritas, item prosapiæ splendor; Prout ex Concl. Clem. X. discimus, Hispaniæ factionis semper, si quidem detur, Cardinalem Medicæum esse solere, solere autem etiam commodorum suorum præter Hispanica rationem habere, jam notatum est. Sed audiamus unum & alterum testem de Capitum hisce qualitatibus. Primus sit Author Concl. Sixti V. qui de hac re circa finem ita loquitur: Trè ò quattro &c. Tres aut quatuor Cardinales soli, sæpe omnium juniores vel potentiâ, vel sequacium numero Capita aliorum ducunt & regunt Conclave, secundùm voluntatem & ambitionem suam. Cui adstipulatur secundus Jo. Fr. Lottinus Dissert. de Concl. Inter Capita Principésque Conclavis, inquit, quidam aliquando sunt, qui etsi virtute, quæ ipsos deceret, destituuntur, tamen aliorum duces existunt propter authoritatem. Quod ideò fit, vel quia Nepotes sunt sunt prateriti Pontificis,atque ideò multos habent addictos sibi Cardinales; vel quia Italorum Principum, quorum plerique summam rationem habent, ministri existunt &c. Tertius ita canit: Primo capo à Pretendenti Si fa un huomo pazzo e furioso Inimico del riposo Amator d'abjette genti &c. Id est:
units.tr: IX. The vice that accrues to Papal elections from the authority of the Heads is all the greater because the leaders of the Factions in the College of Cardinals are not the most serious and most worthy, but for the most part young men who take little care for the good of the Church and the glory of God, and are intent on their own advantage, if not solely, at least chiefly, and are in turn carried off by their own passions. Nearly all Nephews are such, as no one denies. As for the Heads of the Nations, again it is not dignity and zeal for God's glory, but the special advantage of the kingdom that is usually looked to in appointing them; likewise authority, likewise the splendour of birth. As we learn from the Conclave of Clement X, the Spanish faction, if indeed it can have one, is always wont to have the Cardinal de' Medici, and it has already been noted that they are wont to have regard for their own advantages beyond the Spanish reason. But let us hear one or another witness about these qualities of the Heads. The first is the author of the Conclave of Sixtus V, who speaks thus about this matter near the end: Three or four, etc. Three or four Cardinals alone, often the youngest of all, either by power or by the number of their followers, lead and rule the Heads of the others and the Conclave, according to their own will and ambition. To this the second, Jo. Fr. Lottinus, in his Dissertation on the Conclave, adds: There are sometimes certain men who, though lacking the virtue that would befit them, are nonetheless leaders of others on account of their authority. This happens either because they are nephews of the previous Pope, and so have many Cardinals attached to them, or because they are ministers of Italian princes, most of whom have great weight, etc. The third sings thus: In the first place, the head of the Pretenders is made a man foolish and furious, an enemy of rest, a lover of abject folk, etc. That is:

units.la: Primum caput pratendentium constituitur homo stultus & furiosus, quicunque inimicus,abjectorum hominum amator &c.
units.tr: The first head of the pretenders is constituted a stupid and furious man, whoever is an enemy of quiet, a lover of abject men, etc.

units.la: X. Sed juvabit jam Factiones & illarum Capita speciatim quoque consideraře; In qua speciali consideratione primi occurrunt Nepotes cum creaturis suis. Quorum Factiones maximè à tempore Pauli III. potentes fuerunt, æquè ac illæ nationum, sive regnorum; Atque usque ad Paulum III. non è stato &c. superficies tantùm fuit commodorum Politicorum Curia. Post ejus mortem aperte introductæ fuerunt Factiones Nepotismi & Regnorum, ut Author Card. p.3.l.2.p.165. testatur simul,ubi sic magis diuturnam atque difficilem,id est, magis mundo annexam electionem factam esse,nec non, prævalere Factionem illam Nepotum, asserit; Subjungit, eam causam fuisse,quòd post mortem Urbani & Innocentii, Cardinalibus discordibus per plures septimanas & menses in Conclavi manendum fuerit; quia nimirum prævaleant commoda Nepotum præ commodis Nationum, cùm tamen hæc prævalere deberent. Ecce jam, sic pergit, libertatem Cardinalium mutatam in servitutem Nepotum! Ecce superbiam Nepotismi dominantem libertati Ecclesiæ! Igitúrne præcedat oportet juventus senectutem? Igitúrne Ganymedes præstabunt Jovi similibus? Igitúrne fas est, ut excludantur,qui merito ingeminarent: Quadraginta annis proximus fui generationi huic; ad includendos illos,qui vix cæperunt canere: Introibo in domum tuam Domine? Igitúrne Cardinalis aliquis Papatu dignissimus eo carebit, quia non est creatura Papæ recens defuncti? Ita certè fit,quia ita volunt, sed non ita fieri deberet. Verissima est Authoris querela atque optimè fundata,námque is primò Nepotum scopus est,(quod ostendimus,ubi de metu pœnæ egimus;) ut rationem reddere non debeant,neque aliquid à novo Pontifice timere; Secundò haud raro juniores promovere student, ut ipsi interim maturi fiant; Tertiò tandem ipsi succedere volunt. Et quidem successere aliquot, Paulus II Alexander VI. Pius III. Julius II. Clemens VII. Et dum non succedunt, à lor modo eligere volunt, atque que interdum eligunt. Hinc Card. Albicius, referente il Card. p. 3. l. 3. p. 341. cùm Chigius aperte testaretur, imò etiam juraret in praesentia majoris partis Cardinalium, se nonnisi Creaturam suam eligere velle, dixit ad multos collegas: Signori &c. Domini Eminentissimi, volumus nos Papam facere, jam est factus, Alexander quippe cum hereditario jure Creaturas suis reliquit. Eundem Chigium in Concl. Clem. IX. supra vidimus omni contradictionis periculo in congregationibus exemptum, dependendo &c. quia ab illo, qui exclusionem certam habet, bona electionis pars dependet.
units.tr: X. But it will now be helpful to consider also the Factions and their Heads one by one. In this particular consideration, the Nephews with their Creatures come first. Their Factions have been most powerful since the time of Paul III, as equally those of the Nations or Kingdoms have been. And up to Paul III, there was no such thing as...; the Curia's political advantages were only a surface. After his death the Factions of Nephews and of Kingdoms were openly introduced, as the author of Card. p.3 l.2 p.165 testifies at the same time, where he asserts that the election was made more long-drawn-out and difficult, that is, more bound to the world, and that the Faction of those Nephews prevailed. He adds that the cause of this was that after the deaths of Urban and Innocent, with the Cardinals at odds, they had to remain in the Conclave for several weeks and months, because surely the advantages of the Nephews prevailed over those of the Nations, when these ought to have prevailed. Behold now, he goes on, the freedom of the Cardinals changed into the servitude of Nephews! Behold the pride of Nepotism ruling over the freedom of the Church! Must youth therefore go before old age? Must Ganymedes rank above those like Jove? Is it right that those be shut out who might rightly cry out: For forty years I was grieved with this generation (Ps. 95); and that those be shut in who have scarcely begun to sing: I will come into thy house, O Lord (Ps. 5)? Must therefore some Cardinal most worthy of the Papacy go without it, because he is not a creature of the Pope lately dead? Thus it surely happens, because they wish it so, but it ought not to be so. The author's complaint is most true and well founded. For, first, the aim of Nephews is (as we have shown where we treated of fear of punishment) that they need not give an account and need fear nothing from the new Pope; secondly, they often strive to promote juniors, so that they themselves may meanwhile mature; thirdly, at last they themselves wish to succeed. And indeed several have succeeded: Paul II, Alexander VI, Pius III, Julius II, Clement VII. And when they do not succeed, they wish to elect in their own manner, and sometimes they do elect. Hence Cardinal Albizzi, as il Card. p.3 l.3 p.341 reports, when Chigi openly testified, and even swore in the presence of the greater part of the Cardinals, that he would elect nobody but his own Creature, said to many colleagues: Gentlemen, most eminent Lords, we wish to make a Pope; he is already made: Alexander, of course, left his Creatures to his successors by hereditary right. The same Chigi, as we saw above in the Conclave of Clement IX, was exempted from every danger of contradiction in the congregations, since the good part of the election depends on him who holds certain exclusion.

units.la: XI. Factiones Nationum, sive Principum jam sequuntur.
units.tr: XI. The Factions of the Nations, or Princes, Now Follow.

units.la: Ab initio neque illae erant, non erat sic. Non si sarebbono &c. Non tanto cum Zelo se immiscuissent tractationibus Conclaviariis, inquit Il Card. p. 3. l. 2. p. 165. Si Pontifices manere voluissent Vicarii Christi in regimine animarum, quia autem commodum judicârunt adjungere gladium cruci, Principes rationem gladii habituri, crucis quoque rationem habere debuerunt; Hinc in quantum Pontifices magni facti sunt in temporalibus & potentes populorum imperio, in tantum etiam Reges, quibus à Deo mundi obtigit regimen, necesse habuerunt istis temporalibus, quae spiritualia sibi eripuerant, invigilare. Cùm adhuc pauperes essent Pontifices, atque tantùm Claves Petri, id est, spiritualia haberent, Pontificatûs negotiis se immiscebant Principes sive Zelo pro Ecclesia, sive odio veritatis, sed postquam divites facti sunt, & gladium Petri manibus tenent, hujus gladii curam habent, ne statibus, imò personis suis noceat, ut ordinarió Pontifices nocent personis. Olim Zelus Dei eligebat atque commodum Ecclesiae, nunc commodum Regnorum, Politica mundi atq; ratio statûs, quae, si non absolutè eligit, saltem praevalet rationibus Dei & Ecclesiae, atque certè persuasus sum, paucos Cardinales, conscientiâ salvâ, contrarium affirmare posse &c.
units.tr: From the beginning they were not like this either: it was not so. They would not have &c. They would not have mixed themselves into the conclave dealings with such zeal, says the Cardinal, p. 3, l. 2, p. 165. If the Popes had wished to remain the Vicars of Christ in the government of souls, but since they judged it advantageous to add the sword to the cross, and the princes would take account of the sword, they ought also to have taken account of the cross. Hence, to the extent that the Popes became great and powerful in temporal affairs and in dominion over peoples, to that same extent the kings, to whom God gave the government of the world, were obliged to watch over those temporal things which had snatched the spiritual from them. When the Popes were still poor and had only the keys of Peter, that is, spiritual things, princes meddled in papal affairs, whether from zeal for the Church or from hatred of the truth; but after they became rich and hold Peter's sword in their hands, they take care of this sword, lest it harm their states or even their persons, as the Popes ordinarily harm persons. Formerly the zeal of God chose, and the advantage of the Church; now it is the advantage of kingdoms, worldly policy and the reason of state, which, if it does not choose absolutely, at least prevails over the reasons of God and the Church. And I am certainly persuaded that few cardinals, with their conscience intact, could affirm the contrary &c.

units.la: XII. Variae Regum & Principum, ex eo, quo colla sua Christo subdiderunt, in electione Pontificum partes fuerunt, datae, sumptae, legitimae, illegitimae. De Electione per Imperatores Dissert. IV. actum est. Intrusiones Tyrannorum & Regulorum Romanorum Dissert. V. consideravimus. Confirmationem Imperatoriam ad tractationem de Consequentibus reservare visum fuit. Qualemcunq; secularium concursum heic Hiero-Monarchici valdè improbare reperiuntur. Hinc istae apud Baronium maximè lacrymae, saepe fusae, querelae aliquoties iteratae. Nonnihil ex illis adhuc adnotabimus. Ad an. 900. n. 3. ait, cuncta, quae olim Ecclesia passa sit sub gentilibus Imperatoribus, vel quae ab haereticis, sive Schismaticis, aliisve quibuscunque persecutoribus aestimanda esse lusus quodammodo puerorum, imò referenda in lucrum Note at right margin: Natio-num, sive Princi-pum; Concur-sum Princi-pum quantum aliàs abo-minentur. lucrum & computanda in certum emolumentum &c. comparata cum eo,quòd Seculi X. Principes quantumvis Christiani,hac tamen ex parte dicendi tyranni sævissimi, arrogaverunt sibi tyrannicè electionem &c. n. 4. addit ; Nihil penitus Rom. Ecclesia contingere posse funestius,tetrius nihil atque lugubrius,quàm si Principes sæculares in Rom. Pontificum electionem manus immittant &c. n. 5. adhortatur; qui verò eidem S. Sedi bene cupiunt atque consultum volunt impertita ipsi per Petrum à Christo divinitus libertati, & Zelo exæstuant paternarum legum : cùm quid hujusmodi fieri viderint (quod nunquam videri contingat!) magno animi vigore & fortitudine semper ex adverso consurgant, omníque conatu resistere, obsistéréque Sacerdotali constantia non formident ; robustóque & obstirmato pectore objiciant se pro muro domui Israël, atque etiam, si opus sit, lucroso vita dispendio velocès occurrant,ne castissima atque sanctissima Mater nostra, princeps omnium Ecclesiarum, ipsa Romana Ecclesia prostituatur Principibus sæcularibus pro ipsorum arbitrio abutenda, sed Christi sanguine partam, defensámque sanguine, sanguine pariter sibi statuant conservandam semper illam auream ejusdem Ecclesiæ libertatem. Hæc licèt obiter dicta, perpetuò tamen maneant uti in anea fusum columna de incolumitate sancta Romana Ecclesia adversus infestiores hostes jugiter conservanda, semper loquens,imò clamans, indelebile monumentum posteris profuturum &c.
units.tr: XII. The various parts played by kings and princes in the election of Popes, since they bowed their necks to Christ, have been given, taken, lawful and unlawful. The election by the emperors was dealt with in Dissert. IV. The intrusions of tyrants and Roman chieftains we considered in Dissert. V. It seemed good to reserve the imperial confirmation for the treatment of the consequences. Hiero-Monarchists are found to disapprove strongly of any kind of concourse of secular powers here. Hence those tears in Baronius especially, often shed, and complaints repeated at times. We shall note some of them. At the year 900, n. 3, he says that all that the Church once suffered under the pagan emperors, or from heretics, schismatics or any other persecutors, is to be reckoned as somewhat of a children's game, nay, to be counted as gain and reckoned as a certain profit &c. (Marginal note: Of nations, or of princes; the concourse of princes, however much they are otherwise abhorred.) compared with the fact that in the tenth century the princes, however Christian, yet in this respect to be called most cruel tyrants, arrogated to themselves the election tyrannically &c. n. 4. he adds: nothing more deadly, more foul or more mournful could befall the Roman Church than if secular princes were to lay their hands on the election of the Roman Pontiffs &c. n. 5. he exhorts: but those who wish well to this same Holy See and desire its good, and who burn with zeal for the paternal laws, granted to it by Christ through Peter, when they see anything of this kind happening (which may it never be seen!), should always rise up against it with great vigour and courage, and not fear with priestly constancy to resist and oppose it with every effort; and with a firm and steadfast breast, let them set themselves as a wall for the house of Israel, and even, if need be, rush forward at the cost of their lives, lest our most chaste and holy Mother, the Church of Rome, the princess of all the churches, be prostituted to secular princes to be abused at their pleasure, but let them resolve that that golden liberty of the same Church, won by the blood of Christ and defended by blood, be kept forever by the same blood. These things, though said in passing, let them remain fixed like a column cast in bronze, for the safeguarding of the holy Roman Church against more hostile enemies, always to be preserved; always speaking, nay crying out, a lasting monument to profit posterity &c.

units.la: XIII. Eandem cantilenam querulam canit ad an. 1024. n. 4. Rursum monstra nobis peperit potentia secularis,procul facienda semper ab electione Romanorum Pontificum,ut ne vel auditu percipi omninò valeat : tractent Sacra Deo Sacri, non profani, ab his procul arcendi &c. Et ad an.1033. n. 3. Quid potuit Romana Ecclesia durius ac luctuosius contigisse, quàm ut, qui tyrannide lupi sunt, de pastore creando decernant & curent ? quorum illud unum studium sit,ut præficiatur ovibus pastor ignavus,quò ipsis liberum sit,cùm velint,in oves irrumpere. Nunquam audiatur amplius tyrannis ista in Ecclesia Dei , ut Pontificem cogatur accipere à Principibus.
units.tr: XIII. He sings the same querulous tune at the year 1024, n. 4: Again secular power has brought forth monsters for us, to be kept always far from the election of the Roman Pontiffs, so that they may not even be heard of at all: let holy things be handled by the holy servants of God, not by the profane, and let these be kept far off &c. And at the year 1033, n. 3: What could have happened more harshly and more sorrowfully to the Roman Church than that those who are wolves by tyranny should decree and take care about creating the shepherd? Their one aim is that an idle shepherd be placed over the sheep, so that it may be free for them to break in upon the sheep whenever they wish. Let such tyranny never again be heard of in the Church of God, that the Pontiff be compelled to accept from princes.

units.la: XIV. Nec certè frustra ita abominabatur concursum qualemcunque Regum & Principum in electionibus Pontificum Romanorum sibi usque adeò fatalem, & causam unicam, quæ eum sublime Petri solium scandere prohibuit. Cæterùm probè hic distinguendum esse inter legitimum Magistratûs Christiani in electionibus Ecclesiæ rectorum & violentas violentorum Tyrannorum intrusiones, ex Dissert. IV. & V. constare potest. Concursum sum verò Principum Secularium in electionibus Pontificum Romanorum à seculo, & quod excurrit, maximè vigentem planè obliquum, authoritati, promissionibus, minis, muneribus, familiarumque necessitatibus innitentem, atque pro scopo commoda Politica tantùm habentem, inter nævos & vitia electionum Pontificum Romanorum haud immeritò à nobis numerari, ex sequentibus patebit. Quæ secundùm ordinem Conclavium dabimus.
units.tr: XIV. Nor indeed was that kind of concourse of kings and princes in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs abhorred in vain, since it was so fatal to them and the only cause which kept them from mounting the lofty throne of Peter. Moreover, it can be shown from Dissert. IV and V that a clear distinction must here be made between the lawful authority of the Christian magistrate in the elections of the church's rulers and the violent intrusions of violent tyrants. But the concourse of secular princes in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs, which has flourished most strongly since the century and beyond, is plainly oblique, resting on authority, promises, threats, gifts and the needs of families, and having only political advantage as its aim; that it should rightly be counted by us among the blemishes and vices of the elections of the Roman Pontiffs will become clear from what follows. We shall set these out in the order of the conclaves.

units.la: XV. Aliquid tamen de scopo, quem Principes quoad Electiones Pontificum habent, ex Joan. Fr. Lottini Dissert. de Concl. præmittemus: Quantumvis, inquit, Catholicæ Religionis sint studiosissimi, magis tamen propriæ utilitatis respectu moventur, idcirco Pontificem plerique malunt, qui animo timido sit & sollicito, quàm prompto ac vehementi, ut bonis Ecclesiasticis, quæ in ipsorum sunt ditionibus, tanto liberius uti, frui possint. Quòd si vel Rex Franciæ, vel alius quis Princeps Pontificem desiderent, qui animo magno sit & elato, non equidem ideo faciunt, quòd sedis Apostolicæ dignitatem auctam cupiant, sed ut eorum consiliis ad res in Italia novandas utantur. Hispaniarum quidem Rex aliique Principes, qui ditiones suas pacificè possident, Italiæ quieti unicè student; ac propterea iis, qui illustri prosapia magnisque opibus subnixi inquieto sunt animo, minùs favent: quod idem sine dubio Rex Franciæ, si tantum terrarum in Italia possideret, facturus esset. Quoniam verò quietis in Italia conservanda præcipuum momentum in tali Papa est positum, qui humilis sit conditionis, ac nullis factionibus deditus, solent iidem omnium hujus farinæ Cardinalium favorem, quibus possunt, officiis sibi conciliare eósque obnoxios sibi facere.
units.tr: XV. Yet we shall first set out something about the aim which princes have in regard to the elections of the Pontiffs, from Giovanni Francesco Lottini's Dissertation on the Conclave: However zealous they may be for the Catholic religion, says he, they are yet moved more by regard for their own advantage; for this reason most of them prefer a Pontiff of a timid and anxious mind rather than one who is ready and vehement, so that they may use and enjoy more freely the ecclesiastical goods which lie within their dominions. But if either the King of France or some other prince desires a Pontiff of great and lofty spirit, they do not indeed do so because they desire the dignity of the Apostolic See increased, but so that they may use him for their counsels in stirring up affairs in Italy. The King of Spain indeed, and other princes who peacefully possess their dominions, are solely eager for the quiet of Italy; and therefore they favour less those who, supported by illustrious lineage and great wealth, have restless minds; which the King of France would undoubtedly do likewise, if he possessed so much land in Italy. But since the chief importance in keeping Italy quiet lies in such a Pope as is of humble condition and devoted to no factions, they are accustomed to win for themselves, by whatever services they can, the favour of all Cardinals of this sort, and to make them obligated to themselves.

units.la: XVI. In Concl. Clem. V. quod primum est ex iis, quæ hodie habentur, Card. Petrus persona assai prudente &c. prudens & astutus, videns rem isthuc deductam, atque memor, Philippum Franciæ Regem cum Bonif. VIII. inimicitias exercuisse, familiæ autem suæ amicissimum esse, per literas eum certiorem reddidit de deliberatione Cardinalium, atque quasi promisit, se electionem in longum protracturum, rogans Majest. ejus, ut tanti negotii plenam curam haberet, eique simul supra fidem suam promittens, se nonnisi ea facturum, quæ ei placitura essent, atque nunquam à mandatis ejus recessurum. Rex cogitans, quantum sibi electio contraria nocere posset, literis credentialibus Cardinali gratias egit, aurum & dona misit, magna ei promisit, eúmque exhortatus est, ut diligenter cum aliis negotiaretur, quò finis optatus obtineri possit; neque quiesceret, donec tam arduum negotium effectum sit, se ista non minùs quoquocunque alio curare, atque reipsa ostensurum etiam deinceps, quomodo officium praestitum agnoverit. Cardinalis splendidi Regis promissionibus motus, & gaudio plenus, unicè corrumpendis, quos auri cupidos sciebat, intentus, eos insuper promissionibus lectis auditisque pavit &c. Atque adeò turbulenta fuit ista electio, ut ipsi etiam Principes seculares manus immittere voluerint; Quare etiam Carolus Neapolitanus Rex in illam civitatem concessit — studuit inservire amicis. Alii primarii Barones Romani cum variis mundi Regibus, laborabant, ut Papa non fieret, putantes in tanta diversitate locum habitura vota peregrinorum &c. Cúmque tandem Cardinales discordes de extraneo loquerentur, conosciuta &c. Cognitâ hac deliberatione Petrus & Jacobus Columna, antehac à Bonifacio depositi, & desiderio Regi placendi acti nullam occasionem arripuerunt, experti etiam, quanti referat Papam inimicum habere. Scientes igitur Episcopum Burdegalensem in Gasconia Regi carum esse, atque ab ipsa juventute familiarem, cum amicis locuti sunt, & diligentissimè eum eligere laborârunt &c. Eóque electo, in un subito &c. Subito Petrus equo ad Regem avolavit, ut, eo mediante, apud S. Sanct. aliquam gratiam habere posset, asserens, adeò tantùm in longum se protraxisse electionis negotium, ut nihil accidat placito ipsius contrarium. Opinio multorum fuit, addit Author, Cardinalem Regi intimum, ante electionem secretè nova promissa perpetua Pontificis in omni casu gratia à Rege obtinuisse &c. Subjungit tandem: Electione ita perfectâ universalem tristiam apparuisse. En sanctam ex interventu quoque regio electionem!
units.tr: XVI. In the Conclave of Clement V, which is the first of those held today, Cardinal Peter, a very prudent person &c., being prudent and astute, and seeing the matter brought to this point, and mindful that Philip, King of France, had carried on enmity with Boniface VIII, but was most friendly to his own family, informed him by letter of the deliberation of the cardinals, and as good as promised that he would prolong the election a long time, asking His Majesty to take full care of so great a business, and at the same time promising him on his faith that he would do nothing but what would please him and would never depart from his commands.
