The King, considering how greatly the election could harm him if it went against him, thanked the Cardinal by letter of credence, sent gold and gifts, promised him great things, and exhorted him to work diligently with the others so that the desired end might be attained; and that he should not rest until so arduous a business was accomplished, and that he would show in fact, in the future too, how he recognised the service rendered, no less in the other matters too. The Cardinal, moved by the splendid promises of the King and full of joy, intent solely on bribing those whom he knew to be greedy for gold, fed them besides with the promises read and heard &c. And so turbulent was that election that the secular princes themselves wished to lay their hands on it. Wherefore also Charles, King of Naples, went into that city, and strove to serve his friends. Other leading Roman barons, with various kings of the world, laboured that there should be no Pope, thinking that in so great a division the wishes of foreigners would have room &c. And when at last the cardinals, divided, were speaking of someone from outside, having learned &c. When this deliberation became known, Peter and James Colonna, previously deposed by Boniface, and moved by desire to please the King, seized on no opportunity, having also learned how much it matters to have a Pope as an enemy. Knowing therefore that the Bishop of Bordeaux in Gascony was dear to the King, and familiar to him from his very youth, they spoke with their friends and laboured most diligently to elect him &c. And when he was elected, suddenly &c. Peter flew on horseback to the King so that, through him, he might gain some favour with His Holiness, asserting that the business of the election had been so prolonged that nothing turned out contrary to his wishes. It was the opinion of many, the author adds, that the Cardinal, intimate with the King, had secretly before the election obtained from the King new promises of perpetual favour from the Pope in every case &c. He adds at last: The election being thus completed, universal sadness appeared. Behold the holy election, by the intervention of the king as well!

units.la: XVII. Galliae Reges heic primò se immiscuisse vidimus.
units.tr: XVII. Here we first see the Kings of France meddling.

units.la: Nascitur jam occasio de Hispanis quoque loquendi. Quorum certè partes in electionibus Pontificum potiores fuerunt, usque adeò, ut Ministri quidam Regii (narrat Nobil. Sandis Relat. de Statu Relig. c. XI.) pro superbia gentis (quae per Regem jurare coeperit;) aperte Collegio exposuerint spem suam, fore nimirum, ut Rex Papa propediem 6. proponat Cardinalitio pileo sine ulla repulsa donandos, & Papa quoque non alius eligatur, praeter nominatum à Rege. Subjungit idem ibidem, quàm astutè Hispani, quorum nempe auxilio Papa ad restitutionem Spiritualium uti voluerint, quosdam Papas circumduxerint. Assertioni quoad Pontificum Electionem sequentia fidem facient.
units.tr: The occasion now arises to speak of the Spanish too. Their influence in papal elections was certainly greater, to such an extent that certain royal ministers (the noble Sandys reports in his Relation of the State of Religion, ch. XI) openly told the College their hope, namely that the King would shortly propose six men to receive the cardinal's hat without any objection, and that no pope would be chosen except the one named by the King, out of the pride of the nation (which has begun to swear by the King;) The same author adds how cunningly the Spanish, whose help the Pope wanted in order to restore the spiritual matters, led several popes about. The following will confirm the assertion concerning papal elections.

units.la: XVIII. In Concl. Greg. XIII. Card. Granvellanus Farnesio significat, che sua Maestà &c. Majestatem suam desiderare & eum rogare, ut desistere velit à cogitando de se, quia quadam Familia Italica & Ger-
units.tr: XVIII. In the conclave of Gregory XIII, Cardinal Granvelle signifies to Farnese that his Majesty etc. desires his Majesty's wish and asks him to stop thinking about himself, because a certain Italian and German family

units.la: Ex Concl. Greg. XIII. & Germanica eum nolint, quibus S. Majestas deesse non posset, proin, si persistere velit, oppositionem possibilem imminere &c. Quod nuntium eò magu Farnesium perculit, quia improvisum, sed recollectis spiritauum suorum reliquiis &c. dixit, se mox bonum Pontificem electurum, atque ea de re cum amicis locuturum. Regessit Granvellanus, che era &c. aquum esse, ut tantam in Collegio partem habens etiam electionis particeps sit &c. Atque sic Farnesium ad nominationem trium adegit, quâ intellectâ, apud Alexandrinum statim verbis altis & imperantibus dixit, si non omni opera Papam Regi amicum & certa fidei, idque quàm primùm creare velit, Regem illud agrè laturum, atque adeò ei 3. illos significavit, ex quibus unus eligendus sit; electus autem fuit Buoncompagno.
units.tr: (from the conclave of Gregory XIII) and German do not want him, and His Majesty could not do without them; therefore, if he persists, a possible opposition threatens, etc. This message struck Farnese all the harder because it was unexpected, but gathering up the remnants of his spirits etc. he said that he would soon choose a good pope, and would speak about the matter with his friends. Granvelle replied that it was etc. fitting that he, who held so large a part in the College, should also share in the election etc. And so he forced Farnese to nominate three men. When this was understood, he at once spoke to Alessandrino in high and commanding words, saying that if he did not by every effort want to create a pope friendly to the King and certain of his faith, and that as soon as possible, the King would take it badly; and so he indicated to him three men, from whom one was to be chosen; the one actually elected was Buoncompagni.

units.la: XIX. In sequente Concl. Sixti V. Madruccio haveva &c. habebat arcanum Regis Catholici, habebat quoque, multorum judicio, nominationem Regiam 4. Papabilium, ex quibus etiam fuit electus; Arcanum autem idem in seqq. etiam Conclavibus saepe occurrit. In eod. Concl. Legatus Hispaniae cum Cardinale Austriae simul protestatus est. Ibidem mentio fit Factionum Hispanicae & Gallicae, Ministrorum Regiorum, & utilitatis pro Montaltio, ex eo, quòd promotores favore Regis Catholici gavisi sint. Tunc quoque in sparsis de Torresio ad deterrendos Papabiles reliquos vocibus circumferebatur, che stava &c. Farnesium Promotorem favorem & auxilium ex Hispania & Gallia expectare, atque ad Creaturas illas cursores missos esse, speciatim autem Regi Gallia servitia domûs Farnesia ob oculos posuisse. XX. Concl. Greg. XIV. novum electionis arbitrum sistit, Magnum Hetruriae Ducem, quo de ita Author loquitur: Era trà &c. Erat inter Principes alios M. Hetruria Dux, cujus ob territorium suum statu Ecclesia circumdatum quasi, multùm interest, ut Papam amicum & faventem habeat; semper magna cum vigilantia in id incubuit, ne Papa aliquis sine auxilio suo crearetur &c. atque sibi in illa Curia tantam authoritatem conciliavit, ut communiter inter praecipuos Conclavis arbitros numeretur. Qualem se quoque in isto Concl. praestitit, atque, Papa subitò mortuo, ad conciliandum Regis Hispania minùs faventis amorem, cursorem ad eum misit, se cum omnibus suis amicis, & omnibus suis viribus ei offerens, quemcunq; jam velit, S. Quattro excepto, quem privata commoda unà cum pragnantibus causis aliis excipiendum dictabant. Ab una parparte Regi satisfacere, ab altera vero hunc excludere, & tamen partem in electione habere voluit.
units.tr: XIX. In the following conclave of Sixtus V, Madruccio had etc. the secret of the Catholic King; he also had, in the judgment of many, the King's nomination of four papabili, from whom one was also elected. The word Arcanum however often recurs in the following conclaves too. In the same conclave the Spanish ambassador protested together with the Cardinal of Austria. In the same place there is mention of the Spanish and French factions, of the royal ministers, and of the advantage for Montalto, because his promoters enjoyed the favour of the Catholic King. Then too, in scattered rumours about Torres, to frighten off the remaining papabili, it was passed around that he was etc. that Farnese, the promoter, was expecting favour and help from Spain and France, and that couriers had been sent to those creatures, and that the services of the house of Farnese had been put before the eyes of the King of France in particular. XX. The conclave of Gregory XIV introduces a new arbiter of the election, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, of whom the author speaks thus: There was etc. Among the other princes was the Grand Duke of Tuscany, whose territory surrounds the State of the Church, as it were, and who has a great interest in having a pope who is friendly and favourable; he has always laboured with great vigilance to ensure that no pope is created without his help etc. and he secured for himself in that Curia such authority that he is commonly counted among the chief arbiters of the conclave. He showed himself the same in this conclave as well, and, when the Pope died suddenly, to win the affection of the King of Spain, who was less favourable, he sent a courier to him, offering himself with all his friends and all his strength, whomever he now wished, except Santi Quattro, whom private advantages together with other pressing reasons dictated he should exclude. He wanted to satisfy the King on the one hand, and on the other to exclude him, and yet to have a share in the election.

units.la: XXI. Hispaniam quod attinet, Comes Olivares, resolute &c. animum suum inducens omni studio & vi S. Severinam & amicum intimum, & qui semper res Gallicas secundum Hispanorum vota intelligere visus fuit, ad Papatum perducere, declaravit, hunc primum a Rege nominatum esse, atque aperte pro eo negotiatus est, non sine multorum opinione, quod hac faciat propriis inductus commodis atque praeter voluntatem Regis; Rationes subjungit Author a promotore & genio S. Severinae desumptas; Sciebatur enim, eum prodiisse ex Schola Pauli IV. cui principium exaltationis sua debebat, & credebatur, quod iisdem principiis agatur, eo magis, quia erat amator praeeminentia Sedis Apostolicae & libertatis Ecclesiasticae Zelator, qui ceu talis improbarat postulata Hispanorum respectu Monarchiae Sicula, & lo exequatur respectu Regni Neapolitani; & erat insuper animo alto, atque novis magnisque consiliis gravido &c.
units.tr: XXI. As for Spain, Count Olivares, resolutely etc., setting his mind with every effort and force on advancing Santa Severina, an intimate friend who always seemed to interpret French affairs according to the wishes of the Spanish, to the papacy, declared that he was the first named by the King, and openly negotiated on his behalf, not without the opinion of many that he did this led by his own advantages and against the King's will; The author adds reasons drawn from the promoter's and Santa Severina's character: For it was known that he had come out of the school of Paul IV, to whom he owed the beginning of his elevation, and it was believed that matters would be handled by the same principles, all the more because he was a lover of the pre-eminence of the Apostolic See and a zealot for ecclesiastical liberty, who, as such, had disapproved of the Spanish demands regarding the Sicilian monarchy, and so on regarding the Kingdom of Naples; and he was moreover of a lofty mind, pregnant with new and great plans etc.

units.la: XXII. Interim tamen 6. alios quoque nominaverat Legatus ante ingressum, se bene &c. licet nominationem quadantenus restringere ad tres primos, tanquam Regi gratiores & magis desideratos, sed nominationi illi post annexa fuit prohibitio expressa erga Madruccium & alios fide certa addictos, nullum alium admittendi. Caeteri igitur omnes excludebantur, e quesita esclusione &c. atque ista exclusio tam ampla & generalis, inquit Author, non minorem occasionem murmurandi dedit Curia & magna Collegii parti, eo, quod nominationem daret cum annexa supradicta prohibitione; nempe non minus injusta & ratione destituta, quam insolita visa fuit, dum enim Rex antehac 2. vel 3. plurimum, saepe nullum excluserat, jam exclusi videbantur 30, Cardinales, imo dici potest, praeter 7. reliquos omnes tanquam inimicos & Regi suspectos exclusos fuisse; illud autem maxime mirum videbatur, quod Mendovius exclusus fuit, dignissimus & a Cardinalatus initio Papa creditus, subditus bonus, mediocris familia, devinctus Duci Sabaudiae, Regis genero, jam nominatus, sine cognatis, servus fidus, & de domo Austriaca bene meritus, Pensionarius Regis &c. Dicebant, quia Navarrae Regi servierit olim, Sixti V. in negotiis Gallicis Consiliarius fuerit, a Navarristis desideretur. Quae obstacula Author removet, & concludit: Era necessario &c. Necesse igitur erat credere, exclusionem istam a Legatis & non a Rege profectam esse, qui in Conclavi precedente in hoc forte decepti eum non nominantes, jam vindictam metuentes, vel, se non erraâsse ostendere volentes, eum eum exclauerunt. Ut nonnunquam Legatorum affectus & errores Conclave dirigant!
units.tr: XXII. Meanwhile, however, the legate had nominated six others before the entry into conclave, well etc. although he restricted the nomination somewhat to the first three, as more pleasing and more desired by the King, but to that nomination was annexed an express prohibition against Madruccio and the others firmly attached to the Spanish faith, admitting no other. All the others were therefore excluded, by the exclusion sought etc. and this exclusion, so wide and general, says the author, gave no small occasion for grumbling to the Curia and to a large part of the College, because he gave the nomination with the aforesaid prohibition attached; which seemed no less unjust and devoid of reason than unusual. For whereas the King had before excluded two or three at most, and often none, now thirty cardinals seemed excluded; indeed it may be said that, apart from seven others, all were excluded as enemies and suspected by the King. But the thing that seemed most surprising was that Medici was excluded, the most worthy, and from the beginning of his cardinalate believed to be a future pope, a good subject, of modest family, bound to the Duke of Savoy, the King's son-in-law, already nominated, without relations, a faithful servant, and well deserving of the House of Austria, a pensioner of the King etc. They said that, because he had once served the King of Navarre and had been a counsellor to Sixtus V in French affairs, he was disliked by the Navarrists. The author removes these obstacles and concludes: It was necessary etc. It was therefore necessary to believe that this exclusion came from the legates and not from the King, who, deceived in this perhaps in the previous conclave, when they did not nominate him, now fearing revenge, or wishing to show that they had not been mistaken, excluded him. How often the feelings and errors of the legates direct the conclave!

units.la: XXIII. Quoad nominationem septem-Viralem, Madrucius aliquanto post sece gagliarda instanza &c. instantias vehementes formavit apud Montaltium, ut unum ex 7. assumeret, sic desiderium Regis, conscientiam & reputationem, salva mansura omnia, cum sic electio ab ipso utique profectura sit. Sed jam concluserant Creaturae Montaltii, ch'era necessario &c. Necesse esse, ut se opponant sedulò, ne nominatio ista effectum consequatur, utpote non tantum contraria libertati Ecclesiasticae, quae in ista electione debeat secundùm Canones & Concilia intacta atque illaesa manere, sed quae etiam faciat Papam jus Patronatûs Hispaniae, quia enim Hispani magis diligentes sint in retinendo & augendo eo, quod semel acquisiverint, quàm verò negligentes in eo perdendo, ideò eos, si consequerentur, quod jam consecuti sint in Concl. Urb. VII. in hoc etiam, Regi possessionem hujus nominationis firmaturos esse, qua deinceps ad numerum multò minorem restringi posset, atque adeò Cardinales adactum iri, unum ex nominatis eligendi, reclamante licèt conscientiâ. Addehant, talem nominationem multò pejoris conditionis esse, quàm verò praesentationem, quam ei sedes Apost. merâ concessione respectu tot Ecclesiarum indulgeat, non tantum ob praeeminentiam Pontificatûs, sed & ideò, quia praesentatus inhabilis à Papa recusari possit, quod hîc Cardinalibus non permittatur. Dicebant porrò &c. Vide Dissert.IV. Sect.I. n. 35. Carolum V. & ipsum Regem Philippum quidem aliquando nominâsse, sed non semper, atque potiùs commendâsse amicis, quàm verò nominâsse toti Collegio; neque tam magnum numerum, neque prohibitum illis ipsis fuisse, alium praferendi, modò non expressè exclusus fuerit; Imò Conclavia Julii III. Marcelli II. & Pauli IV. docere, non tantùm frustraneas fuisse nominationes, sed & illos ipsos ob exclusionem electos fuisse. Subjungebant, oppositionem eò magis faciendam, quia verisimile sit, nominationem non à Rege, sed à Ministris tantùm profectam esse, cùm Rex pius sit, religiosus & haberi velit acerrimus S.Sedis defensor, à qua & insignem titulum acceperit, non igitur praesumi posse, eum velle Laicas suas manus admovere sanctuario Dei, & turbare & retardare simul cum tanto Religionis Catholica & totius Christianismi dispendio, liberam electionem Vicarii ipsius, simúlque foedare bonam & sanctam, quam orbis de eo conceperit, opinionem. Regerebant, si Rex id faciat studio & Zelo Religionis, bonum esse finem, mala media, cùm cura ista praecipuè spectet ad Papam, & post ipsum ad Cardinales, Capita & membra ad fundendum pro eo sanguinem devincta; Curam igitur istam relin-
units.tr: XXIII. As for the nomination of seven, Madruccio, some time later, formed vehement entreaties with Montalto, that he should take one of the seven, so that the King's wish, his conscience and his reputation would all remain safe, since the election would certainly proceed from him. But Montalto's creatures had already concluded that it was necessary etc. It was necessary that they oppose diligently, lest this nomination achieve its effect, as being not only contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, which in this election ought to remain untouched and unharmed according to the canons and councils, but also one that would make the Pope the right of patronage of Spain, because the Spanish, being more diligent in retaining and increasing what they have once acquired than negligent in losing it, therefore, if they obtained what they have already obtained in the conclave of Urban VII, they would also in this confirm the King's possession of this nomination, which could afterwards be restricted to a much smaller number, and so the cardinals would be compelled to choose one of those named, though their conscience cried out. They added that such a nomination was of much worse condition than a presentation, which the Apostolic See grants by mere concession in respect of so many churches, not only on account of the pre-eminence of the Pontificate, but also because a presented man who is unfit can be rejected by the Pope, which is not permitted here to the cardinals. They further said etc. See Dissertation IV, Section I, n. 35. Charles V and King Philip himself had indeed sometimes nominated, but not always, and rather recommended to friends than nominated to the whole College; nor was the number so great, nor was it forbidden to them to prefer another, provided they were not expressly excluded; indeed the conclaves of Julius III, Marcellus II and Paul IV show that the nominations were not only fruitless, but that those very men were elected because of the exclusion. They added that opposition should be made all the more, because it is likely that the nomination came not from the King but only from the ministers, since the King is pious, religious, and wishes to be regarded as the most zealous defender of the Holy See, from which he also received a distinguished title; it cannot therefore be presumed that he would wish to lay his lay hands on the sanctuary of God, and to disturb and delay at the same time, with such great loss to the Catholic religion and to all Christendom, the free election of his Vicar, and at the same time to stain the good and holy opinion that the world has formed of him. They replied that if the King does this out of zeal for religion, the end is good but the means are bad, since that care belongs chiefly to the Pope, and after him to the cardinals, the heads and members bound to shed their blood for it; therefore they should leave this care

units.la: Oppositiones factae relinqui debere hominibus, quibus ea à Deo demandata sit, non autem illis auferri debere, & sibimet appropriari, sed siquid ad votum suum fieri posset, Cardinalibus id quidem significet, sed ita, ut arbitrium relinquat, neque illorum conscientias ad passiones & commoda sua trahat. Concludebant, ita omnes non nominatos offendi, quasi non digni essent dignitatis gradu illo, cum tamen multi, si non superiores, saltem aequales nominatis sint; sic quoque totius Collegii judicium improbari, quasi Rex absens & Ministri ejus melius scirent, quisnam aptus sit ad onus illud sustinendum; tandem sic Cardinales subditos & mancipia togata reddi, non tantum Regis, sed & Ministrorum, ad procurandum nimirum, ut etiam nominentur, cum aliàs eligi non possint. His atque aliis rationibus inductus Montaltius Principem opponentium, quamvis frustra, egit; Unum quippe ex nominatis tandem eligere coacti fuerunt.
units.tr: The objections raised ought to be left to the men to whom God has entrusted this task, and not taken from them and appropriated to oneself. If anything could be done to suit their wishes, it should indeed be signified to the cardinals, but in such a way as to leave them their free judgment, and not to draw their consciences into one's own passions and interests. They argued that in this way all the men not named would be offended, as if they were unworthy of that rank, although many of them, if not superior, are at least equal to those who were named. In this way too the judgment of the whole College would be disparaged, as if the absent king and his ministers knew better who was fit to bear that burden. Finally, in this way the cardinals would be made subjects and gowned slaves, not only of the king but also of his ministers, namely to ensure that they too are named, since otherwise they could not be elected. Moved by these and other arguments, Montalto, the leader of the objectors, pressed his case, though in vain; for in the end they were compelled to elect one of the named.

units.la: XXIV. In Concl. Innoc. IX. narratur, quomodo, Papa adhuc superstite, Hispani con tutto &c. cum omni suo calido ingenio & authoritate, ut non perderent acquisitum honorem, sibi addictum, à se nominatum eligendi, & ut adhuc magis in ista electione authoritatem suam augerent, non solum talem eligere omnibus viribus annisi sint, sed & nominationem ad solum Madruccium restringere voluerint; verum animadvertentes tandem, hoc non successurum, tanquam in mala vita homine, Ultramontano & nimis Hispanizante, ei adjunxerint S. Severinam & S. Quattro, in casu necessitatis adhuc in Comum & Columnam consentire volentes.
units.tr: XXIV. In the Conclave of Innocent IX it is related how, while the Pope was still alive, the Spaniards, with all their hot wit and authority, so as not to lose the honour they had gained, of electing a man devoted to them and nominated by them, and so as to increase their authority even more in this election, not only strove with all their might to elect such a man, but also wanted to restrict the nomination to Madruccio alone. Yet, realising at last that this would not succeed, they joined to him, as a man of bad life, an Ultramontane and too Spanish-leaning, Santa Severina and Santi Quattro, being willing in case of necessity still to agree to Como and Colonna.

units.la: XXV. Ingressus ipso die Legati in Concl. adhuc praesentes si adoperavano &c. negotiabantur pro diversis, pro exclusionibus etiam diversorum; atque visitationibus in cellis absolutis, cum omnibus Cardinalibus tractabant, respectibus & verbis diversis, quarta autem & dimidia nonis hora discedebant; Hispanis relinquentibus post se nonnisi displicentiam & murmur, ob numerum septenarium ad solum Madruccium restrictum; quemadmodum etiam Montaltium etiam atque etiam rogaverant, ut in Regis gratiam eum Papam faceret. Qui se etiam non, ut in praced. Concl. fecerat, amplius opponere voluit; E opinione &c. Opinio est, inquit Author, causam hujus fuisse, vel quia 50000. scutorum reditus in ditione Hispanica habuerit, praeter statum Celani nuper in Regno pro Michaele fratre emptum, vel quia promissionem acceperit, proxime creaturam suam nominatum iri, seque cum familia semper ab Hispanis peculiari modo protectum iri, vel (quod maxime verisimile) quia cum tam potente adversario non amplius litigandum esse censuerit — desperans igitur de rebus suis statim se Hispanis dedit.
units.tr: XXV. On the day the legate entered the conclave, while the cardinals were still present, they were busy with various candidates and also with various exclusions; they made the rounds of all the cardinals' cells, paying visits with varied courtesies and words, and left at the fourth and a half hour after None. The Spaniards left behind them nothing but displeasure and murmuring, because the number of seven had been restricted to Madruccio alone, and they had also begged Montalto again and again to make that man pope for the king's favour. He did not, as in the preceding conclave, wish to oppose it any further. It is the opinion, says the author, that the cause of this was either that he had an income of 50,000 scudi in the Spanish dominions, besides the estate of Celano recently bought in the kingdom for his brother Michele; or that he had been promised that his own creature would soon be nominated, and that he and his household would always be protected by Spain in a special way; or (which is most likely) that he judged he should not dispute any longer with so powerful an adversary. Despairing therefore of his affairs, he at once gave himself up to the Spaniards.

units.la: XXVI. In Concl. Leon. XI. Avila maluit annum degere
units.tr: XXVI. In the Conclave of Leo XI, Avila preferred to spend a year

units.la: priùs,quàm permittere alcun pregiudicio al suo Re &c. damnum aliquod Regi suo. In eod. significatum, electionem Baronii, quem Hispania nolebat, post se tracturam schisma ò almeno guerra, aut minimùm bellum. Imò in eodem per Hispanos actu exclusus fuit à prima sede, ad quam, inquit Grammondus Hist. Gal. l.1. p. 10. virtute & suffragiis vocabatur. Adeò lubricum est, subjungit, scribere de Regum potestate, de Imperio & ditione ipsorum, ut regnant, & jure vel injuria possident. In eod. la volontà &c. voluntas & commodum Hispania merum erat vocabulum & nomen sine realitate imaginarium, quod larva ad instar erat effectis quibusdam, qua confiteri quemvis pudebat. In eod. rursus Leonis XI. Conclavi Gioiosa Gallus non haveva &c. unicum hunc scopum habuit, ut cum honore ex tenebroso illo carcere egredi posset.
units.tr: rather than permit any prejudice to his King, etc., some damage to his king. In the same place it is indicated that the election of Baronio, whom Spain did not want, would drag after it schism, or at least war, or at the very least a battle. Indeed, in the same event, by the action of the Spaniards, he was excluded from the first see, to which, says Grammond, Hist. Gal. l. 1, p. 10, he was called by virtue and by votes. So slippery is it, he adds, to write about the power of kings, their empire and dominion, as they reign and possess, by right or by wrong. In the same place, the will, etc.; the will and advantage of Spain was a mere word and name, an imaginary thing without reality, which served as a mask for certain effects that anyone would be ashamed to confess. In the same place again, in the conclave of Leo XI, the Frenchman Gioiosa had, etc.; had this one aim, that he might leave that dark prison with honour.

units.la: XXVII. In Concl. Urb. VIII. cùm ageretur de Card. Araceli, Hispaniae Legatus aperte professus est, se habere in hoc ordini precisi, mandatum expressum, nimirum se opponendi. In eod. senes Barberinum promoveri nolentes ad Hispanos dixerunt, non convenire Regia Majest. ut Legatus in Gallia eligatur, cùm seniores adsint Legatione in Hispania functi. Ex Concl. Innoc. X. aliquid afferemus, ubi de mutatione Pontificum agendum erit. Heic tantùm innuimus, visam nobis esse MSC. epistolam Regis Galliarum ad Marchionem Chamontium Legatum suum à Celeb. D. Faeschio, Basileensi Professore, comunicatam, in qua Rex multis declarat, quemadmodum Barberinus Nepos, Rege ad juvandam Panfilii exclusionem vocato atq; permoto, eo tamen inscio, imò mendacium ab eo literarum praetextu, eundem promoverit, & ob infames istas actiones protectione Galliae, Regnique insignibus è vestigio privari debeat. Ut eundem Panfilium cognata Olympia utriusque Regni Ministris commendârit, infrà, ubi de simulationibus Conclaviariis, dicemus. Hic autem referenda duximus saltem verba Authoris vitae Olympiae p.55. de concursu Regum generalia: Donec ingrediuntur Cardinales Conclave, inquit, ponderantur & trutinantur Roma à Factionibus utriusque Regni omnes inclinationes, morésque Cardinalium pratendentium, vel potiùs pratendere judicatorum; Et si unquam Legati pra se ferunt Zelum pro partibus Dominorum suorum, tunc certè eum vel maximè pra se ferunt. XXVIII. In Concl. Alex.VII. primò dicitur, ob notas odii causas suffecisse amorem Ducis Modena ad Hispanorum odium excitandum. Secundò tractatus pro & contrà concursum Principum editi memorantur.
units.tr: XXVII. In the Conclave of Urban VIII, when Cardinal Araceli was under discussion, the Spanish legate openly professed that he had an express and precise mandate in this matter, namely to oppose it. In the same place, old men unwilling to see Barberini promoted said to the Spaniards: it is not fitting for His Royal Majesty that a legate be elected in France, since there are elders present who have served as legate in Spain. We shall bring forward something from the Conclave of Innocent X, where we shall have to treat of the change of popes. Here we only hint that we have seen a manuscript letter of the King of France to his legate, the Marquis Chamont, communicated by the celebrated Faesch, professor at Basel. In it the King declares at length how Barberini the nephew, the King having been summoned and moved to help exclude Pamfili, yet without his knowledge, indeed by a lie under the pretext of letters, promoted him; and that on account of these infamous actions he ought to be deprived at once of the protection of France and the insignia of the kingdom. That the same Pamfili was commended by his cousin Olimpia to the ministers of both kingdoms, we shall say below, where we speak of conclave simulations. Here, however, we thought fit to cite at least the words of the author of the Life of Olimpia, p. 55, on the general concourse of kings: While the cardinals enter the conclave, he says, all the inclinations and manners of the cardinals who are aspiring, or rather who are judged to be aspiring, are weighed and balanced in Rome by the factions of both kingdoms; and if ever the legates display zeal for the cause of their lords, then they display it most of all. XXVIII. In the Conclave of Alexander VII, first it is said that, because of well-known causes of hatred, the love of the Duke of Modena was enough to stir up hatred of the Spaniards. Second, the treatises for and against the concourse of princes that were published are mentioned.

units.la: Concl. Alex.VIII. respectu Concursus tur. In uno asserebatur,che nissun &c. nullum plane Principem secu-larem sine gravi peccato, & obligatione restitutionis damnorum privato-rum & publicorum se opponere posse exaltationi ullius Cardinalis; atque mortaliter peccare Cardinales,qui intuitu Regis,aut Principis cujuscunque, suffragium dent alicui, quo dignior tamen sit. In altero pertendeba-tur,Che i Card. &c, Cardinales neque posse neque debere Papam facere eum, qui à Magno aliquo Rege Christiano manifeste exclusus sit. Tertiò mentio fit literarum Regis Galliae ad Collegium,in quibus perten-debat,necessarium esse bonum Caput Ecclesia intestinis Catholicorum bel-lis afflicta — Papam non debere esse Simoniacum,quemadmodum non fue-rit Pontifex mortuus. Verbo, inquit Author, non tam exhortari voluit quàm redarguere, atque Gallos ideo tam irreverenter locutos esse de Ponti-fice defuncto,ut ostendant,non se poenitere debere, quòd Innoc. X. ipsis re-nitentibus electus sit. Addicti etiam Papa illi agre ista tulerunt, neque ve-ritas tantum in iis potuit, quantum amor potuit. Quartò ibi videmus renovationem negotiationis pro Chigio, postquam Mazarini literis appro-batus esset.
units.tr: In the Conclave of Alexander VIII, with respect to the concourse [of princes]. In one treatise it was asserted that no secular prince can oppose the exaltation of any cardinal without grave sin and an obligation to make restitution for private and public damages; and that cardinals sin mortally who, out of regard for a king or any prince, give a vote to someone, even though he is more worthy. The other argued that the cardinals neither can nor ought to make pope one who has been manifestly excluded by some great Christian king. Third, mention is made of letters of the King of France to the College, in which it was maintained that it is necessary for a good Head of the Church, afflicted by the internal wars of Catholics, … that the Pope ought not to be a simoniac, just as the dead pontiff was not. In a word, says the author, he wished not so much to exhort as to refute; and the French spoke so irreverently of the dead pontiff in order to show that they ought not to regret that Innocent X was elected against their wishes. Those attached to that Pope also took these things badly, and truth in them could not prevail as much as affection could. Fourth, we see there the renewal of negotiation for Chigi, after he had been approved by letters of Mazarin.

units.la: XXIX. Post Alexandri mortem celerrimus Cardinalium in urbem sine simili antehac festinatione adventus apud Auth. Card. p. 3. l. 3. p.272. tribuitur mandato severo Regum. Eadem sede vacante, Legatus Hispaniae urbem ingressus Chigio promisit la protettione &c. protectionem tantopere desideratam, sed brevi innotuit, politice id factum,ut Papa Hispanizans eligeretur. Illa ipsa vespera Excell. suam inviserunt Chigius & Sforza,in quam, licet brevis fuerit audientia, multa tamen de Electione dispositæ creduntur. Legatus tamen omni-bus diebus,non obstantibus continuis pluviis, sine intermissione invise-bat. Subjungitur de recreationibus supra memoratis mentio. Du-rante Pontificis morbo,quod tempus quasi Conclavis erat, Gabriel Pa-pa credebatur, usque adeo,ut excommissa (à Pio IV. in Bulla severè vetitæ) fierent; Credebatur, eum ab Hispanis commendari, à Gallis non recusatum iri. Sed falsò amici sperabant, primò quia Galli nunquam concurrissent ad instantias Cardinalis recens creati ad promotionem homi-nis,qui se subinde Hispanizare prodiderat; Imò ipsi Hispani,qui eum pro-tegebant & fovere videbantur, eum noluissent, utpote nondum optimè co-gnitum,damnis à Paulo IV. & Sixto V. acceptis tandem sapientes. Erat Albicius abominationi Hispanis tanquam cerebrum profundum & ple-num &c. Alii credebant, hac ipsa de causa Gallis gratum fuisse, sed pru-denter eum omiserunt. Idem fere Farnesium impedivit,contrà quem. maxima exceptio, exclusiva Hispania, cui suspectus multum erat, ob optimas suas qualitates. Tales nunquam vult Hispania, inquit Author, licèt etiam Madridi nati essent. Littæ Archiep. Mediolanensi pariter Hispani obstiterunt, sed maximè Gubernator Mediolanensis, qui professus est, si res illi in favorem successuras arbitraretur, Romam se velocissimè perrecturum ad illum excludendum. Hactenus Author & loc. cit. à p.272--321.
units.tr: XXIX. After the death of Alexander, the very rapid arrival of the cardinals in the city, with a haste unlike any before, is attributed by the author (Card. p. 3, l. 3, p. 272) to a severe order of the kings. While the see was vacant, the Spanish legate, on entering the city, promised Chigi the protection so much desired, but it soon became known that this was done cunningly, so that a Pope favouring Spain would be elected. That very evening Chigi and Sforza visited His Excellency, and although the audience was brief, it is believed that much was arranged concerning the election. The legate nonetheless visited him every day, despite continual rains, without interruption. Mention is made of the recreations mentioned above. During the Pope's illness, which time was almost like a conclave, Gabriel was believed to be pope, to such an extent that excommunications (severely forbidden by Pius IV in a bull) were carried out; it was believed that he would be commended by the Spaniards and would not be refused by the French. But his friends hoped in vain, first because the French would never have come together at the urging of a newly created cardinal to promote a man who had shown himself to be a Spanish partisan from time to time; indeed the Spaniards themselves, who seemed to protect and foster him, would not have wanted him, since he was not yet well known, and had become wise through the losses suffered under Paul IV and Sixtus V. Albicius was an abomination to the Spaniards, as a deep and full brain, etc. Others believed that for this very reason he was pleasing to the French, but they prudently passed him over. Much the same prevented Farnese, against whom the greatest objection, the Spanish exclusion, was raised; he was much suspected by them because of his excellent qualities. Spain never wants such men, says the author, even if they were born at Madrid. The Spaniards likewise opposed Litta, Archbishop of Milan, but especially the Governor of Milan, who declared that if he judged the business would succeed in his favour, he would most swiftly set out for Rome to exclude him. So far the author, and the passage cited, from p. 272 to 321.

units.la: XXX. In ipso Clem. IX. Concl. sequentia legimus, Cardinales quosdam se pro Hispania declarâsse ; Pro Rospigliosio autem Cursorem, communi opinione, ad impetrandum Regis assensum missum esse, de quo tamen assensu dubitari posset ob Nunciaturam à Card. in Hispania exercitam.
units.tr: XXX. In the Conclave of Clement IX we read the following: some cardinals declared themselves for Spain; but a courier was sent for Rospigliosi, by common opinion, to obtain the King's assent, though that assent could be doubted because of the nunciature the cardinal had held in Spain.

units.la: XXXI. In Conclavi Clementis X. fuit observatum; non esser soliti Francesi negotiar con flemma; Negotiationes Gallorum calidas esse; Qui cùm moras viderent, decreverunt à chariche &c. Id est; urgente, ut dicebant, etiam conscientia, principium dandum esse Conclavi, atque ita post 50. dies aperte declarari coepit exclusiva Regis respectu Delcii. Contrà Cardinalibus Medicæo & Pio studio vindictæ Vidonium à Legato Hispaniæ excludi desiderantibus, eóque sine expresso Curiæ mandato id facere non audente, sed illis continuò idem urgentibus, ordinò l'Ambasciatore &c. Id est: Legatus schedulam misit, ut Vidonius desisteret, ob difficultates, neque mentio fiebat exclusiva, licèt fama fuerit, schedulam continuisse exclusivam apertam, quam etiam ore ferebant. Laborabat idem Medicæus, Magno Duci Hetruriæ nuncio misso, nomine totius factionis, ut alius in Galliam mittatur, & exclusio Cardinalis Delci co' l supposto che dà Parigi non sia venuta, suppositione, quòd Parisiis non venerit, revocetur. Sed exclusio à Rege nimis manifesta erat. Quoad eundem Delci literis ex Hispania recens missis à Legato & Cardinalibus Factionariis exigebatur, il dare giustificationi &c. Id est; Ut se justificarent respectu negotiationum pro Delcio, qua non placeant Madridi, neque proin Liga cum Chigio, neglecto Barberino bene merito. In eodem Conclavi de Bonvisio præsumebatur, che concurrendo &c. Id est; Quòd concurrentibus ad ejus promotionem Chigio & Medicao, id est, Hispanis & Gallis, indubitatò Papa futurus sit. In eodem Conclavi novus negotiator apparuit, Legatus Venetorum: Sarà il primo &c. Cùm nullus Antecessorum se manifestè negotio immiscuerit, sed neutrales fuerint; quemadmodum etiam ei objectum, novitatem Reipublica haud placituram esse. Optimum est, quod Cardinalis Retzius nomine Regis Galliarum ultimò & post tam longas moras ad Cardinalem Sforzam protulisse fertur; Il mio Rè, ajebat, non è di quelli &c. Id est; Rex meus non vult quemadmodum alii regulas prescribere de electione Paparum, sed Collegio Apostolico libertatem relinquere, imò ceu Primogenitus Ecclesia eam defendere. Vide judicium de omnibus in illo Concl. Factionibus L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.216. 217. ubi etiam ad Gallicam multi Squadronistarum Regia liberalitate devincti pertinere dicuntur. Hinc Cardinales metu exclusionum Reges offendere metuunt, magis tamen Hispanum; Car il y a une remarque &c. inquit Author Anon. Gallus, Gallos esse aque ad condonandum faciles, ac Hispani sint ad oblivionem injuriarum difficiles; Hinc &c. Vide etiam MSC. Italicum de causis, cur Hispani se immiscere debeant. §. Non vi è stato mai &c. Id est; Nullus est Papabilis, qui non Hispanum se profiteatur, vel saltem Hispanis placere modis omnibus studeat &c.
units.tr: XXXI. In the Conclave of Clement X it was observed that the French do not usually negotiate with phlegm; the negotiations of the French are hot-blooded; and they, seeing the delays, decided to act at once etc. That is: conscience also urging, as they said, a beginning had to be made in the Conclave, and so after 50 days an open exclusion on the King's part concerning Delci began to be declared. Against the cardinals Medici and Pio, who, eager for revenge, wanted Vidoni excluded by the Spanish Legate, and he did not dare do so without an express mandate from the Curia, but they kept urging the same, the ambassador ordered etc. That is: the Legate sent a note that Vidoni should desist, because of difficulties; and no mention was made of exclusion, although rumour had it that the note contained an open exclusion, which they even announced by word of mouth. The same Medici, having sent a messenger to the Grand Duke of Tuscany in the name of the whole faction, laboured for another man to be sent to France and for the exclusion of Cardinal Delci on the supposition that he has not come to Paris, a supposition that he did not come to Paris, to be revoked. But the exclusion by the King was too plain. As for the same Delci, the Legate and the faction's cardinals demanded, by letters lately sent from Spain, that they give justification etc. That is: that they justify themselves concerning the negotiations for Delci, which do not please at Madrid, nor the league with Chigi, while Barberini, who deserved well, was neglected. In the same Conclave Bonvisi was presumed to be sure to become pope, with Chigi and Medici concurring etc. That is: with Chigi and Medici, that is, Spaniards and French, concurring in his promotion, he would undoubtedly be pope. In the same Conclave a new negotiator appeared, the Legate of the Venetians: he will be the first etc. Since none of his predecessors had openly meddled in the business, but had remained neutral, it was also objected to him that the new Republic would not be pleased. The best is what Cardinal Retz is reported to have finally conveyed to Cardinal Sforza, on behalf of the King of France, after such long delays: My King, he said, is not one of those etc. That is: My King does not wish, like others, to prescribe rules for the election of popes, but to leave the Apostolic College its freedom, and indeed, as firstborn of the Church, to defend it. See the judgement on all the factions in that Conclave in L'Ambasciatore di Roma, pp. 216, 217, where many of the Squadronisti, bound by royal liberality, are also said to belong to the French party. Hence the cardinals, fearing exclusions, dread offending kings, and the Spanish more than the others; for there is a remark etc., says the anonymous French author, that the French are as easy to pardon as the Spanish are hard to forget injuries; hence etc. See also an Italian manuscript on the reasons why the Spanish ought to meddle. §. There has never been etc. That is: no one is papabile who does not declare himself Spanish, or at least strive in every way to please the Spanish etc.

units.la: XXXIV. Patet itaque ex dictis, non semper libertatem Collegio Cardinalium relinqui, non in Conclavi tantùm, sed & alibi, Madritti maximè & Parisiis Papas eligi; Hinc de Carafa etiam Roma lugens L'Ambasc. di. Rom. p.26. canit: Mensam meam ornaturus esset, atque ibi sine vitro bibere posset, sed nemo eum ibi sessurum censet, nisi Hispania dispenset. Ibidem p.27. licet suprà mulam pedi podagrico innitenti atque manum ad collum habenti, omnis spes praescinditur, quia non sappar ballar la Spagnoletta, non Hispano more globis ludere fingitur; Ibidem p.83. Delsino, utut ei tribuatur ingenium liberale, tamen lo non Hispanizare objicitur tanquam peccato capitale. Ibidem p.247. Monarcha Iberi odium simul Litta, Viscontio & Homodeo forte meritum honorem eripere dicitur. Imò ibidem p.230. 243. ipsi etiam Suecię Reginae partes quędam in electione, protectio certorum Cardinalium, commendatio, odium tribuuntur. His verò præsuppositis, præsuppositio etiam, quod tam sæpe inculcant, laicas manus huic operi non admovendas esse, præsuppositio haud minùs, Cardinales solos liberè & ex motu proprio Pontificem eligere debere, iste Regum interventus non sine magno vitio erit. Licèt, quod nunc quoque monendum, minùs heic possint Reges quàm Nepotes; judicio certè Abbatis Romani apud Authorem Cardinalismi, qui p. 3. l.2.p.168. 169. ita loquitur: Nell' elettione, &c. In electione Pontificum minimè omnium pravalent commoda Principum &c. Tantùm de Nepotismo agitur, tur, cui Principes adinstar pratextus inserviunt. Credo, tandem Principes id agnituros & Romam Cardinalibus, Cardinales Roma relicturos, quorum quivis se spoliatum videns divitiis, quas Principes, ut commodorum suorum ratio habeatur, expendunt, alta voce exclamabit: Quid faciam miser, quia Dominus meus aufert à me villicationem? Tunc etiam majorem partem in electione habebunt, quae jam valde exigua est, si non nulla.
units.tr: XXXIV. It is plain, then, from what has been said, that the college of cardinals is not always left free, and that popes are elected not only in the Conclave but also elsewhere, at Madrid above all and at Paris. Hence the Roman lamenting Carafa also sings, L'Ambasciatore di Roma p. 26: he would adorn my table, and there he could drink without glass, but no one thinks he will sit there unless Spain dispenses. In the same place, p. 27, although he is set above a mule, leaning on a gouty foot and with his hand on his neck, all hope is cut off, because he cannot dance the Spanish dance, he does not play at bowls in the Spanish manner, it is pretended. In the same place, p. 83, Delsino, though a generous disposition is attributed to him, is nevertheless charged with not being Spanish as with a deadly sin. In the same place, p. 247, the Spanish monarch is said to snatch away, through hatred, the honour perhaps deserved by Litta, Visconti and Homodei. Indeed, in the same place, pp. 230, 243, even a certain part in the election is ascribed to the Queen of Sweden herself: protection of certain cardinals, recommendation, hatred. Given these presuppositions, the presupposition too, which they so often urge, that lay hands must not be laid on this work, the presupposition that the cardinals alone ought to elect the Pontiff freely and of their own motion, this intervention of kings will not be without great fault. Although, as must also be warned now, kings can do less here than nephews; certainly in the judgement of the Roman abbot, in the author of Cardinalismus, who speaks thus, pp. 3, 168, 169: In the election, etc. In the election of popes the advantages of princes least of all prevail etc. The matter concerns only nepotism, to which princes serve as a pretext in the manner of a cloak. I believe that at last the princes will acknowledge this, and that the cardinals will leave Rome, and each of them, seeing himself stripped of the riches which the princes spend in order to have their own advantages considered, will cry out aloud: What shall I do, wretch, because my lord takes the stewardship from me? Then they will also have a greater part in the election, which is now very small, if any at all.

units.la: XXXV. Sic ille Regibus consulit; sed aliter Joan. Fr. Lottinus in Differt. de Concl. Qui duo cumprimis suadet; Primum est, ut utilitatis suae rationem habeant.
units.tr: XXXV. Thus that writer advises kings. Joan. Fr. Lottinus, however, takes a different line in his Dissertation on the Conclave. He recommends two things above all. The first is that they should take account of their own advantage.

units.la: Hanc diligentiam, inquit, ipsi Cardinales, qui Principum alicui vel obligati sunt, vel propinquitate conjuncti, adhibere debent, ut, si rebus ipsorum conducat Pontificem habere mitem & humilis prosapia, talem, cujuscunque sit factionis, vel à quocunque is propositus sit, & commendatus, acceptent. Idem faciant, si magnanimum aliquem & novandis rebus opportunum Pontificem res ipsorum desiderent: neque dubitent, quia cum quocunque alio Principe diversa factionis se conjunxerint, postquam quis factus sit Papa, is statim ad eum, quem rebus suis maximè arbitratur opportunum, se se sit applicaturus. Ac propterea fuerunt nonnulli, qui aliquibus suffragari noluerant, eò tantùm, quòd ab adversariis fuissent propositi: atque ita passionibus suis indulgere, quàm commodi alicujus, quod ipsi consequi non poterant, causâ, amulis gratificari maluerunt.
units.tr: The cardinals themselves, he says, who are bound to some prince or related to him by blood, ought to take care that, if it suits that prince's interests to have a gentle pope of humble birth, they accept such a man, whatever his faction and whoever has proposed and recommended him. They should do the same if the prince's interests call for a magnanimous pope suited to upheaval. Nor should they hesitate: even if they have allied themselves with a prince of another faction, once someone has been made pope, they will immediately attach themselves to the man they judge most suited to their affairs. For this reason there have been some who refused to support certain candidates simply because those candidates had been proposed by their opponents. They preferred to indulge their passions and gratify their rivals rather than secure some advantage that they themselves could not obtain.

units.la: XXXVI. Alterum est, ut Reges erga Cardinales benefici sint, eisque pensiones exhibeant; Postquam enim de liberalitate Papabilibus necessaria egerat, statim subjungit: Idem faciendum est cunctis Principibus, qui amicos in Conclavi habere volunt; qui immeritò alioqui conquerentur, dolebúntque, eam sui rationem habitam non fuisse, quam magnitudo sua postulare videbatur. Quod tantò magis ipsorum auget culpam, quia praecipua Ecclesia membra, quae sunt Cardinales, beneficiis suis non cohonestantes merito ingrati animi arguuntur, cùm ab eadem Ecclesia facultatem reddituum Ecclesiasticorum dispensandorum impetraverint. Neque verò adversatur, quòd nonnulli asserunt, provincialia beneficia & sacerdotia in eos conferenda, qui sunt ejusdem provinciae: nam hac lex potiùs ob utilitatem provincialium Principúmque sancita est, quàm propter Zelum religionis; nam aequum est, ut qui ipsis provinciis praesunt, quales sunt Cardinales, saltem per modum pensionis iisdem Commodis perfruantur; Adeò ut, si Principes aliquando videntur amicis carere, id ipsis sit imputandum. An verò amicis indigeant, ipsi bene norunt; nôrunt; cùm experimentis plurimis non ignorent, quantum beneficio aut detrimento eorum Pontifex malè vel bene erga eosdem animatus efficere possit. Si verò dicant, Pontificem nobis conciliabimus post ipsius creationem, fallitur sæpe hoc axioma, præterquam quòd longè utilius est providisse, & hujusmodi incommodo occurrisse.
units.tr: XXXVI. The second recommendation is that kings should be generous to the cardinals and pay them pensions. After he had spoken of the liberality necessary toward the papabili, he at once adds: The same must be done by all princes who want friends in the Conclave. Otherwise they will rightly complain and grieve that their standing has not been given the consideration that their greatness seems to demand. This adds all the more to their fault, since the principal members of the Church, namely the cardinals, who have been granted by that same Church the power to dispense its revenues, are rightly accused of ungrateful spirit if they do not honour the Church's benefices with their own. Nor does it count against this that some claim that provincial benefices and priestly offices should be conferred only on men of the same province. That rule was enacted for the benefit of the provinces and their princes rather than out of zeal for religion. It is fair that those who preside over the provinces, such as the cardinals, should at least enjoy the same advantages by way of a pension. So if princes sometimes seem to lack friends, they have only themselves to blame. Whether they need friends, they know very well; they cannot be unaware, from many experiences, how much a pope who is ill or well disposed toward them can do for good or ill. But if they say, "We will win over the pope after his creation," that maxim often fails, quite apart from the fact that it is far more useful to have provided beforehand and to have met such an inconvenience in advance.

units.la: XXXVII. Præter factiones Nepotum & Regum hactenus recensitas etiam dantur Factiones Neutralistarum, qui in ultimis Conclavibus nomine Turmæ volantis (Squadrone volante) uniti fuerunt; Quod nomen ideò elegisse videntur, quia modò huic, modò illi Factioni, neque Nepotibus, neque Regibus mancipati copias auxiliares ad exaltationem dignissimorum in subsidium mittere videri volunt. Neminem autem novi, qui de illis melius & prolixius agat Authore Cardinalismi p. 3. l. 3. p.341. seqq. Cujus proin verbis ibi positis in Factionis hujus Squadronariæ descriptione utemur; Postquam de duabus Factionibus in Conclavi Clementis IX. egisset, Barbariniana & Chigiana, atque insuper monuisset, Hispanos & Gallos obligatos fuisse, di aderire a gli ordini ricevuti dalle loro Corone, obsequendi mandatis, qua à Regibus acceperint; & duos Cardinales Venetos a gli ordini della Republica, jussibus Reipublica; tandem subjungit: La terza fattione &c. Tertia factio erat Turma volantis, qua tantùm habebat exclusivam, erantque maximam partem Creatura Innocentii X. nec mediocriter voluntatibus juncti. In Conclavi precedente erat Turma volans sine Capite &c. In hoc Cardinali Imperiali se submittebant &c. Galli ægrè ferebant erectionem hujus Turma volantis, maximè quia regebatur à Capite parùm ipsis favente; interim ferebant, quod auferre non poterant. Et certè vel solum nomen Turmæ volantis nationibus exosum erat in Conclavi precedente, sed magis reddebatur in hoc; poterant excludere pro lubitu, erantque parati ad exclusionem cujuscunque, qui non placebat &c. Imò Politicis & Ecclesiasticis omnibus displicebat Turma, qui ritè rem examinarunt, quamvis enim protestati essent manibus pectori admotis, oculisque in Cœlum erectis, se non nisi promotionem dignissimi quærere, tamen ipsa eorum unio, & quòd cum aliis tractare nollent, eos suspectos reddebat, dum sic videri voluerunt quasi electionis arbitri, cùm quivis sine Factionibus ejusmodi ad conscientia dictamen dignissimum promovere potuisset &c.
units.tr: XXXVII. Besides the factions of nephews and kings recounted so far, there are also the factions of the Neutralists, who in the last conclaves were united under the name of the Flying Squadron (Squadrone volante). They seem to have chosen this name because they wished to send auxiliary forces to help promote the most worthy candidate, now to this faction and now to that, being bound neither to the nephews nor to the kings. I know of no one who treats them better or more fully than the author of Cardinalismo, p. 3, l. 3, p. 341 ff. I shall therefore use his words in describing this squadron faction. After discussing the two factions in the conclave of Clement IX, the Barberini and the Chigi, and having further remarked that the Spanish and the French were bound to adhere to the orders received from their crowns, to obey the commands they had received from their kings, and that two Venetian cardinals were bound to the orders of the Republic, to the commands of the Republic, he finally adds: The third faction etc. The third faction was the Flying Squadron, which alone had the power of exclusion. Its members were for the most part creatures of Innocent X and were not slightly bound together in their wills. In the previous conclave there was a Flying Squadron without a head, etc. In this one they submitted themselves to the imperial cardinal, etc. The French bore with difficulty the setting up of this Flying Squadron, chiefly because it was led by a head not very favourable to them; for the time being they put up with what they could not prevent. Indeed the mere name of the Flying Squadron was hateful to the nations in the previous conclave, and it became more so in this one. They could exclude whom they pleased, and they were ready to exclude anyone who was not to their liking, etc. Indeed the whole Flying Squadron was displeasing to all the politicians and churchmen who examined the matter carefully. For although they protested, hands pressed to their breasts and eyes raised to heaven, that they sought only the promotion of the most worthy man, their very union, and their refusal to deal with others, made them suspect. They wished to appear as the arbiters of the election, although anyone without such factions could have promoted the most worthy man as his conscience dictated, etc.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ipsum Conclave de Squadroniistis narrat, quòd in congregatione epistolam quasi à Rege Poloniæ missam atq; à Cardinale Protectore Ursino Collegio exhibitam legi impedive-rint; In eodem inter prærogativas Bonelli recensetur, che su por-tato dal Squadrone volante. Turmam volantem eum promovere studuis-se; In eodem factio illorum composita dicitur di qualcuno de' Pan-filiani, e de i mal contenti delle altre, ex quibusdam Pamphilianis, & male contentis ex aliis Factionibus. Vota 10. habens. De iisdem Con-clave Clementis X. narrat, quomodo Medicæus voluerit Fabricar-si &c. erigere sibi magnum triumphum cum Squadronistis, qui ideò tantùm quòd Medicei defuncti violenter Carpegnam promovere voluerunt,in Conclavi Alex.VII. sub isto nomine coaluerunt, atque Medi-caos Alexandrum eligere adegerunt. Author L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.213. alio etiam nomine eos Acephalos vocat, atque præter eos Fa-ctionis Romana, id est, Cardinalium ex statu Ecclesiæ mentionem, sed cum timore abortûs conjunctam facit. P.252. exiguæ Squadro-nitarum laudi notat,eos nolle un huom' da bene, hominem probum. Sed & jam in Concl. Greg.XIV. mentio facta fuit Neutralistarum sim-pliciter,qui modò huic,modò illi Factioni adhæserint,prout com-modum, vel conscientia postulârit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The Conclave itself describes the Squadronists as having prevented, at a congregation, the reading of a letter apparently sent by the King of Poland and presented to the College by Cardinal Protector Ursino. In the same work, among the prerogatives of Bonelli, it is recorded that he was carried in by the Flying Squadron. The Flying Squadron strove to promote him. In the same work, their faction is said to have been formed of some of the Pamphilians and of the malcontents of the other factions, having ten votes. Concerning the same people, the Conclave of Clement X relates how the Medici wanted to build themselves up, to win a great triumph for themselves with the Squadronists, who, because the late Medici had violently wished to promote Carpegna, banded together under this name in the conclave of Alexander VII and forced the Medici to elect Alexander. The author of L'Ambasciatore di Roma, p. 213, calls them by another name, Acephali, and, besides them, mentions the Roman faction, that is, the cardinals concerned with the state of the Church, though he couples this with a fear of abortion. On p. 252 he notes, to the small credit of the Squadronists, that they did not want un huom' da bene, that is, an honest man. But already in the conclave of Gregory XIV mention was made simply of Neutralists, who attached themselves now to this faction and now to that, as advantage or conscience required.

units.la: XXXVII. Sunt isti termini; turma volans, Squadronista, factio Squadronaria,Neutralista, militares, adeóque minùs videntur convenire Conclavi,in quo Spiritus Pacis debet eligere Vicarium Principis pacis.
units.tr: XXXVII. These are the terms: flying squadron, Squadronist, squadron faction, Neutralist. They are military terms and seem therefore hardly suited to a conclave, in which the Spirit of peace ought to choose the vicar of the Prince of peace.

units.la: Ast non hi soli sunt termini militares in Concla-vibus & à Conclavium scriptoribus adhiberi soliti. Bellum ali-quod tibi describi putares,Lector,ob terminos bellicos,sicut etiam discordiam bellicam ibi obtinere mox ostendemus. Utuntur qui-dem etiam Metaphoris aliunde desumptis, ex. gr. à re nautica. Atque huc pertinet terminus imbarcare,nomen Charontis,de qui-bus suprà. Heic autem addimus locutionem Metaphoricam simi-lem. In Conclavi Gregorii XIV. ad exclusionem Mondovii Hi-spani duos Gregorianos Lancellotum & Cajetanum lucrati dicun-tur, spe ipsis de Papatu facto, cùm tamen illum Rex exclùserit, hunc non nominârit; Tanto è potente, subjungit Author, una debo-lissima, benche facilissima aura di speranza, che in qual si voglia modo fossi à favore di chi naviga nel Pelago del Pontificato. Id est: Tam po-tens est maximè debilis, sed maximè facilis aura spei,qua quocunque modo faveat naviganti in pelago Pontificatûs. Sed maximè Conclavium scriptoribus militares termini placuerunt, hi maximè idonei ad gesta in Conclavibus describenda judicati sunt. Hinc inter Con-
units.tr: But these are not the only military terms that are customarily used in conclaves and by writers on them. You would think, reader, that some war was being described, because of the warlike terms, and we shall soon show that a warlike discord prevails there too. They also use metaphors drawn from elsewhere, for example from seafaring. To this belongs the term to embark, the name of Charon, mentioned above. Here we add a similar metaphorical expression. In the conclave of Gregory XIV, when the Spanish had excluded Montalto, the two Gregorians Lancellotti and Caetani are said to have been won over by the hope of the papacy being conferred on them, though the king had excluded the one and not named the other. So powerful, the author adds, is a very weak, though very easy, breeze of hope, which in whatever way favours the one sailing on the sea of the Pontificate. That is: So powerful is a most weak but most easy breeze of hope, which in whatever way favours the one sailing on the sea of the papacy. But military terms have pleased the writers on conclaves most of all, and these have been judged most suitable for describing the deeds done in conclaves. Hence among the

units.la: Termini Conclavarii partim nautici, sed maximè militares; clavistarum jocos Differt. IV. Sect. 3. n. 28. recensuimus, quòd Patronorum suorum factionibus nomina di Sta Unione, &c. S. Unionis, Bellua multorum Capitum, Protestantium, Catilinaria; imposuerunt. Duces sunt Capita, milites Creaturæ. Primus conflictus, sive, juxta authorem Conclavis Alexandri VII. il principio di battaglia il primo scrutinio, initium prælii primum scrutinium; notabile robur paucorum, sed Veteranorum. Sic in Conclavi Leonis XI. Anti-Aldobrandiniani fecero l'esclusione sedatamente & con tal franchezza di animo, che pareva fusse guidata da Veterani, e veramente, secondo che disse uno di loro, erano &c. Id est: exclusionem sedatè fecerunt, & tanta cum confidentia, ut apparuerit à Veteranis directam fuisse, atque verè, quemadmodum dixit unus, erant exigui numero; sed bello vivida virtus; Idem dicunt sequentia in eodem Conclavi verba; assimiglian- dose &c. Se ipsos assimilantes civitati bene munita, sed obsessa ab exercitu malè ordinato, qui exiguo tempore diffluere debeat; Addebant, puguare jam numerum cum valore, atque adversarios esse exercitum cuniculorum, vulpe duce, sed cujus artes detecta sint. In bello dantur velitationes & prælia magna. Velitatio in eodem Conclavi fuit negotiatio pro Panfilio, mà su una Scaramuccia (Scharmützel) si leggiera, che si senti à pena, velitatio tam levis, ut vix quisquam eam senserit. Opponit author impetum majorem, Non si può però dire ita pergit, che gagliardissimo &c. Id est; Neque tamen dici potest, impetum non fuisse validissimum venientem ab Aldobrandinianis solis die sequente in favorem Baronii. Bellum in genere & prælia magna ita proponit Author idem. La libertà Ecclesiastica &c. Id est: Libertas Ecclesiastica oppressa fuisset, si non contra Aldobrandinum defensa fuisset ab istis generosis Ducibus, qui tam fortes erant, ut, quemadmodum Avila ad eos animandos secundùm rei veritatem dixit, fortissimorum propugnaculorum & turrium adinstar firmi in omni impetu manserint, dum contrà Adversarii tormenta & machinas omnes relinquere debuerint. Delfinus se vocabat Nestorem apud Agamemnonem Aldobrandinum, atque admittebatur ad consultationes maximè arcanas, satisque audacia pra se ferebat, tanquam Venetus; Continuò apud Joyosam Gallorum caput, quorum partes non exiguae erant in isto prælio; Et de quibus cogitatum fuit, eos, si independentes mansissent, prudentia & authoritatis majoris titulum acquisituros fuisse, cùm contrà subitò se declarantes ex Ducibus milites vulgares facti sint. In Conclavi Alexandri VII. post exclusionem Sacchetti quasi in proverbium abiit bellica quoque locutio; L' hanno sacchettato. tato. Telo eum percusserunt. Sic in Conclavi Clementis X. ut supra diximus, Medicæus Turmam volentem quasi triumpho circumducere voluit. Neque verò mirum cuiquam esse debet, ita describi Conclavium historiam, quando Spiritus Bellicosi aliâs quoque in Conclavibus se produnt. Id quod pluribus posthac, ubi de discordia & violentia agendum erit, enarrabimus. Hîc autem unicum exemplum dabimus ex eodem Conclavi. In quo Avila & Aldobrandinus ferè à verbis ad verbera venerunt; atque post ille in præsentia octo creaturarum hujus apertè professus est, pentirsi &c. pœnitere se, quòd non cum baculo responderit, (dicenti nimirum ad Avilam Aldobrandino, hoc verum est, non quod dicis, nihil metuo; siquę miles esset, se eum castigaturum fuisse, & qua verba alia senilis iracundia suggesserat, qua, juxta Philosophum, nunquam à ratione derivatur. Tempore isto multis impossibile videbatur, quæsta &c. ista fundamento caruisse, licèt quidam, ad discordiam conciliandam, affirmârint, Dominos illos, linguas, in quibus locuti sint, non bene intell gentes non intellexisse significationem aut emphasin verborum, multitudo autem præsens ea credidit, quæ ei credita necessaria videbantur, atque vespera illa satis turbulenta erat, nondum enim mediatores viam reconciliationis invenerant. Cogitabatur bonum hoc electionis principium, cùm corruptio generationem præcedere soleat, ista etiam confusio & secretorum publicatio opportuna judicabatur, ad confundendos Aldobrandini conatus, saltem ad fovendam aliquam umbram, sive suspicionem inter Creaturas ejus, unde deinceps dividantur. Reconciliati sunt in Camera Dietrichsteinii febricitantis, perche essendo &c. quia vespera precedente ad testimonium vocatus languidi sui sermonis in narratione auditorum usu defatigatus fuit, atque dicebat, se esse Cavalliere di natura & non di Birreta; Id est, nobilem naturâ & non Birettâ. Ibi se rursus salutârunt, dicente Dietrichsteinio, che gl' ire &c. Iras amantium augere amorem. Sed neque illi unquam amantes erant, inquit Author, neque iræ illorum jocosæ &c.
units.tr: Conclave terms are partly nautical, but mostly military. We have already noted in Differt. IV, Sect. 3, n. 28, the jokes of the conclavists, who gave their patrons' factions names such as of the Holy Union, etc.; Holy Union, Beast of Many Heads, Protestant, Catilinarian. The leaders are the heads, and the creatures are the soldiers. The first clash, or, according to the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII, the beginning of the battle is the first scrutiny, initium prælii, primum scrutinium, is a notable force of a few, but veterans. So in the Conclave of Leo XI the anti-Aldobrandini carried out the exclusion calmly, and with such assurance of mind that it seemed to be guided by veterans, and indeed, as one of them said, they were etc. That is: they carried out the exclusion calmly, and with such confidence that it appeared to have been directed by veterans; and truly, as one said, they were few in number, but in war courage is vigorous. The same author's following words in that Conclave say much the same: comparing themselves to a city well fortified but besieged by a badly ordered army, which ought to dissolve in a short time. They added that they were now fighting with numbers against strength, and that their opponents were an army of miners, with a fox as leader, but whose arts had been detected. In war there are skirmishes and great battles. In the same Conclave the negotiation for Panfilio was a skirmish, but so light a skirmish that hardly anyone felt it. The author sets a greater attack against it: Yet it cannot be said, he goes on, that it was not very strong, etc. That is: Yet it cannot be said that the attack, coming from the Aldobrandini alone on the following day in favour of Baronius, was not very strong. The same author describes the war in general and its great battles thus: Ecclesiastical liberty etc. That is: Ecclesiastical liberty would have been crushed, had it not been defended against Aldobrandino by those noble leaders, who were so brave that, as Avila said to encourage them, in truth they remained in every assault like the strongest bastions and towers, while their opponents had to abandon all their siege engines and machines. Delfino called himself Nestor to Aldobrandino's Agamemnon, was admitted to the most secret consultations, and bore his audacity openly, like a Venetian. Moreover, at Joyeuse, the head of the French, whose party was not small in this battle. And it was thought of them that, had they remained independent, they would have gained the title of prudence and greater authority; but by declaring themselves suddenly they became common soldiers instead of leaders. In the Conclave of Alexander VII, after the exclusion of Sacchetti, a military expression passed into a proverb: They have sacked him. They struck him with a weapon. So in the Conclave of Clement X, as we said above, Medici wished to lead his troop about as if in triumph. Nor should anyone find it strange that the history of the conclaves is described in this way, since warlike spirits reveal themselves in conclaves on other occasions too. We shall recount these more fully later, when we come to discord and violence. Here, however, we shall give one example from the same Conclave. In it Avila and Aldobrandino came nearly from words to blows, and afterwards Avila openly professed in the presence of eight creatures of his to repent that he had not answered with a staff (namely, when Aldobrandino said to Avila: this is true, not what you say; I fear nothing; if he were a soldier, I would have chastised him, and other words which senile anger had suggested, and which, according to the Philosopher, never come from reason). At that time many thought it impossible that these things lacked foundation, although some, to bring about discord, affirmed that those lords, not understanding well the languages in which they spoke, had not understood the meaning or emphasis of the words; but the crowd present believed what seemed necessary to believe. That evening was quite turbulent, for the mediators had not yet found a way of reconciliation. It was thought that this good beginning of the election, since corruption usually precedes generation, was also judged an opportune confusion and publication of secrets, to confound the attempts of Aldobrandino, or at least to foster some shadow or suspicion among his creatures, from which they might afterwards be divided. They were reconciled in the room of the feverish Dietrichstein, because, the previous evening, having been called as a witness, and wearied by the use of his languid speech in narrating to his listeners, he said that he was a cavalier by nature and not by biretta. That is, noble by nature and not by biretta. There they greeted each other again, Dietrichstein saying: che gl' ire etc., anger increases the love of lovers. But neither of them were ever lovers, says the author, nor were their angers playful etc.

units.la: XXXVIII. Amantes tamen erant in Conclavi Clementis X. Retzius & Sforza, eorum iræ, iræ amantium, eorum bellum, bellum amantium. Ille enim, cùm ad scrutinium irent Cardinales, arreptâ hujus manu ambos à reliquis, amborum pugnas à pugnis reliquorum ita distincturus dixit; Il nostro è bellum amoris. Fortè in eodem sensu, in quo Archiepiscopus Parisiensis in vita Henrici IV. pariter loquitur de la guerre des amoureux, de bello amantium.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Yet in the Conclave of Clement X Retz and Sforza were lovers; their anger was the anger of lovers, their war the war of lovers. For when the cardinals went to the scrutiny, Retz took Sforza's hand, separating the fights of the two from the fights of the others, and said: Ours is the war of love. Perhaps in the same sense in which the Archbishop of Paris, in the life of Henry IV, likewise speaks of the war of lovers, de bello amantium.

units.la: XXXIX. Hactenus de causis belli, sive de principiis ad bellum moventibus & in bello regentibus, nec non de militibus ipsis, & contrariis sub contrariis Ducibus, exercitibus actum est.
units.tr: XXXIX. So far we have treated the causes of the war, that is, the principles that move to war and govern it, as well as the soldiers themselves, and the opposing armies under opposing leaders.

units.la: Sequitur jam, ut ipsum pugnandi modum cominus spectemus, stratagemata, sive artes bellicas notemus, atque alia accidentia hujus belli enumeremus; (Vel, terminis his bellicis Cardinalibus & Conclavistis relictis) ut demonstremus, quomodo ex vitiosis illis Principiis, post initas illas factiones vitiosas, sub vitioso illo Ducum regimine, in electionibus Pontificum Romanorum vitiose agant Cardinales, atque adeo ex illa etiam parte vitiosæ electiones exístant.
units.tr: We now come to consider the manner of fighting itself at close quarters, to note the stratagems or the warlike arts, and to list the other incidents of this war (or, leaving aside these military and conclavist terms), so as to show how cardinals, from those faulty principles, after those faulty factions were formed, under that faulty rule of the leaders, act faultily in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs, and so from that side too the elections become faulty.

units.la: XL. Hic autem primo modus ille negotiandi per artificiosas molitiones, quas Græco vocabulo Itali prattiche, Germani Practiken vocant, in genere declarandus erit.
units.tr: XL. Here, first, the manner of doing business through crafty schemes, which the Italians call prattiche and the Germans Practiken, must be explained in general terms.

units.la: In primo ex Conclavibus, quæ habentur, Clementis V. I Cardinali gagliardamente &c. Id est: Cardinales artificiosè negotiabantur cum finibus humanis. Ex eodem collusionem Cardinalis Columnæ cum Rege Galliæ jam supra adduximus. Sic quoque tempestatem, da quella su sbattuta la nave di Pietro, quâ Petri navis jactata fuerit, innuimus. In Conclavi Calixti III. furono mosse gagliarde prattiche; artificiosa negotiationes institutæ fuerunt. In Conclavi Pii II. era veramente &c. revera magnus inter eos tumultus fuit, nulla neque noctu, neque interdiu quies. In Conclavi Pauli IV. Cardinalis Perusinus senes col pratticare alla scoperta, aperte negoriando exacerbâsse dicitur. In Conclavi Pii IV. non sù cosa &c. nihil intentatum relinquebatur, dum quivis prudentia, aut simulatione, aut authoritate, aut meritis suis & suorum usus est, prout putavit, sic causam propriam maxima arte promoveri posse, ita ut hactenus nulli eorum (tam cordati fuerunt;) labi, sed aliorum contrà lapsus in iram, in odium, in timorem & affectus alios cum quibus negotiatio sine consilio & ratione est, promovere sustinuerint; Cogitantes, hac ratione res suas promoveri posse, ita, ut non minor spes locata fuerit in confusione quàm in ordine, firmiter credentes, utrinque electionem Papa venire posse; Unde clare cognoscitur, animo præsente esse, suis occasionibus invigilare & adversariis suas eripere, semper & omni hominum generi prodesse, in Conclavi verò, ubi occasiones tam citò, in tanto numero, tam velociter pratereuntes habentur, maximè omnium juvare.
units.tr: In the first of the Conclaves recorded, that of Clement V, we read The Cardinals were dealing craftily with worldly ends. Above I have already cited from the same source the collusion of Cardinal Colonna with the King of France. Likewise we hint at the storm, the ship of Peter tossed by that tempest. In the Conclave of Callixtus III vigorous intrigues were set on foot; artful negotiations were begun. In the Conclave of Pius II there was truly great tumult among them, with no rest by night or by day. In the Conclave of Paul IV, the Cardinal of Perugia is said to have embittered the old men by practising openly, negotiating in the open. In the Conclave of Pius IV nothing was left untried. Each man used whatever prudence, pretence, authority or merit he had, as he thought, so that his cause could be advanced by the greatest art. Yet so far none of them, wise as they were, fell, but on the contrary others endured to promote their dealings through anger, hatred, fear and other passions, with which negotiation has no counsel or reason. They reasoned that their affairs could be advanced this way, and placed no less hope in confusion than in order, firmly believing that the election could come from either side. From this it is clearly known that presence of mind is needed to watch over one's opportunities and snatch them from one's adversaries, a help always and to every kind of man; but in the Conclave, where opportunities pass so quickly, in such numbers and so swiftly, it helps most of all.

units.la: XLI. In Conclavi Pii V. Borromæus tutto infiammato &c. totus inflammatus in Conclavi circumibat studiosissimè contrà Montepulcianum
units.tr: XLI. In the Conclave of Pius V, Borromeo, all aflame, went around the Conclave most zealously, totally inflamed, working against the man from Montepulciano.

units.la: tianum operando. In Conclavi Sixti V. quidam coeperunt trattare alla gagliarda la prattica diSirleto &c. artificiosè trattare de promotione Sirleti &c. In eodem Conclavi de Capitibus Torresium promovere studentibus dicitur, lo portarano con bella e segreta stratagemma trà loro &c. eum promovere studebant eximio & secreto inter se stratagemate (En rursus terminum bellicum!) Conclave Gregor.XIV.
