Authoris judicio fuit uno de' più belli, de' più savii, e de' più digni di consideratione &c. ex pulcherrimis, artificiosissimis & consideratu dignissimis,non tantùm accidentium per 2. quasi menses varietate, sed etiam Factionum, atque sectarum multitudine, finiúmque in singulis contrarietate, & magno Cardinalium numero, tandem ob difficultates quasi insuperabiles, quas singuli respectu sui & suorum amicorum invenerunt &c. Accedit,quòd prae aliis Conclavibus in hoc maximè occasio obtigit,detegendi animos,genios, & fines majoris Principum partis,imò passionum, finium & commodorum omnium quasi Cardinalium,quae omnia primò tecta,multùm diversa credita fuerunt ab eo,quod detectum fuit; Brevi,in hoc nova regula eaque contraria prioribus formata, atque cum successu contrà observationes precedentes negotiationes instituta fuerunt. In eodem Conclavi Comes Olivaræus faceva le prattiche &c. aperte pro S. Sever. negotiabatur. In eodem ita ultima verba sonant; A Deo esse electionem, se bene non può &c. Id est; licèt negari non possit, partem in ea habuisse discursum & prudentiam civilem.
units.tr: Working against him. In the Conclave of Sixtus V some began to pursue the intrigue for Sirleto vigorously, to negotiate artfully for the promotion of Sirleto. In the same Conclave, it is said, those who strove to promote Torres among the heads of the factions carried it through between themselves by a fine and secret stratagem. (Here again is a military term!) The Conclave of Gregory XIV, in the author's judgement, was one of the most beautiful, wisest and most worthy of consideration, not only for the variety of events over about two months, but also for the multitude of factions and sects, the opposition of their aims in each case, and the large number of Cardinals, and finally for the difficulties, almost insuperable, which each man found with respect to himself and his friends. In addition, more than in other Conclaves, here an occasion arose of uncovering the minds, dispositions and aims of the greater part of the Princes, indeed the passions, aims and advantages of almost all the Cardinals, all of which were at first hidden and were believed to be very different from what was afterwards revealed. Briefly, a new rule, contrary to the earlier ones, was formed here, and negotiations were instituted with success against previous practice. In the same Conclave Count Olivares was making intrigues openly for San Severino. In the same place the last words read: The election is from God, but one cannot... That is, although it cannot be denied that prudence and worldly wisdom had a part in it.

units.la: XLII. In Conclavi Urbani VII. Negotiatio primò pro Columna benche scorgessero &c. licèt multa difficultates apparerent, illas tamen superare sperabant huic soli negotio omne studium destinaturi atque Petram illa obsidione quasi capturi. (En iterum terminum militarem!) In Conclavi Innocentii IX. memorantur factae ante mortem Papae molitiones aperta, prattiche scoperte, & in Conclavi prattiche gagliarde, che se fecero contra Madruccio; Studiosa negotiationes contra Madruccium.
units.tr: XLII. In the Conclave of Urban VII the negotiation was first for Colonna, although they saw many difficulties; yet they hoped to overcome them, devoting all their zeal to this one business and as if about to capture a fortress by siege. (Again a military term!) In the Conclave of Innocent IX are recorded schemes made before the Pope's death, open intrigues, open practices, and in the Conclave vigorous intrigues that were made against Madruzzo: zealous negotiations against Madruzzo.

units.la: Sed & generale testimonium exhibetur; Che lo Spirito S. &c. Id est. Spiritum S. permittere,ut jam magnam partem provisiones & commoda Factionistarum prævaleant, inde displicentia & discordia oriantur,qua saepe manifesto cum periculo Conclave prolongant. In Conclavi Clementis VIII. si fecero &c. multa erant molitiones pro Camerino, sed plurima pro Tosco. In Conclavi Clementis IX. Tentò più fissamente &c. Chigius magis quàm unquam Magno Duci persuadere voluit molitionum Elciavarum approbationem, sed videns tandem, Factionum Capita ne quidem de eo audire quicquam velle,remittere studium & molitiones tiones omittere cœpit. In Conclavi Clementis X. sequentia legimus: Si vedrà &c. Id est: In hac Scena Hispanus Gallum, Gallus Hispanum aget. Quique ibi sunt, satisfactionem quandam debent, si enim non poterunt perdere, poterunt saltem aliquo modo impedire molitionem aliquam forte prætextibus displicentiæ & responsionibus, incipiendo à capite, quomodo in infinitum iretur. In eod. tutti pretendono &c. omnes prætendunt, debere tenere bacile ad barbam non tantum aliis factionibus, sed & superare omnes. In eod. Legatus Galliæ Bonvisio & Ravizzæ gloriantibus, se habere S.Collegium in pugno; vidisse machinas suas magna cum infamia in terram projectas.
units.tr: But a general witness is also brought forward: that the Holy Spirit... That is, that the Holy Spirit permits that now for the most part the provisions and advantages of the factions prevail, from which displeasure and discord arise, which often prolong the Conclave with manifest danger. In the Conclave of Clement VIII they made... there were many schemes for Camerino, but most for the Tuscan. In the Conclave of Clement IX he tried more steadily... Chigi wanted to persuade the Grand Duke more than ever to approve the schemes of the Elciavari; but seeing at last that the heads of the factions would not so much as hear anything of it, he began to relax his zeal and to drop his schemes. In the Conclave of Clement X we read the following: It will be seen... That is: In this scene the Spaniard will play the Frenchman, the Frenchman the Spaniard. Those who are there must receive some satisfaction; for if they cannot destroy a scheme, they can at least in some way impede it, perhaps by pretexts of displeasure and evasive replies, beginning at the head, so that it would go on to infinity. In the same, everyone claims that they must hold the shaving basin under the beard, not only for the other factions but to surpass them all. In the same Conclave the French Legate, with Bonvisi and Ravizza boasting that they had the Sacred College in their fist, saw their machines thrown to the ground with great disgrace.

units.la: XLIII. Initium harum molitionum non demum ab ingressu in Conclave arcessendum est; Diu ante suscipiuntur. Recenset quidem Author Concl. Greg. XIII. Borromæum Nepotem Pio V. in extremis constituto noluisse vel in minimis sibi gratiam comparare Magni Hetruriæ Ducis, e questo dicono &c. quod fecisse dicitur, quia Bulla quadam sub pœna excommunicationis negotiationes de Papatu, Papa superstite, vetabant. Et certè talis lex exstat. Sed neque secundùm ejus exemplum ordinariò vivitur, neque Lex æquè curatur ab aliis. Dico dunque &c. Dico igitur, inquit Author Concl. Greg.XIV. notum esse, quibus Curia nota est, majorem temporis Pontificatûs partem impendi constitutioni successoris, quia negotium tot difficultatibus plenum, tòtque accidentibus obnoxium, necessariò diu ante disponi debet ab eo, qui aliquem heic juvare, quemadmodum etiam ab eo, qui ei nocere vult, ut quandocunque mors Papæ contingat, res digesta, dispositæ media, materia præparata sint, faciléque tunc sit, diu ante propositæ executioni mandare. Subjungit; Hac tunc obtinere ob brevem Urbani VII. Pontificatum non potuisse. Consentit Author Concl. Urb.VIII. Gl'aparecchi &c. Præparationes, inquit, illius, quod ibi tractari debuit, diu ante cœperunt, & ultimò sede vacante renovatæ sunt diligentissimè. Sic & Author Concl. Alex. VII. testatur: Sei mesi &c. Sex menses ante mortem Innocentii penetrabantur molitiones Sacchettianæ. Eadem confirmat Author Concl. Clem. IX. qui 2. causas brevitatis Conclavis illius videri potuisse dicit, primam magnum æstum; Secundam res ob mortem Pontificis diu prævisam jam digestas; licèt illa ipsa mora, ita subdit, quæ locum dederunt molitionibus, etiam dederint contra-molitionibus. Idem de exclusione Farnesii agens eandem veritatem exemplo ita probat; Fu adunque &c. Fuit igitur exclusio ista magis renovata, quàm determinata in Conclavi. Quam alio etiam exemplo sic illustrat: Furono &c. Fuerunt illo die (qui quartus erat à morte Pontificis;) detecta & intercepta à Cardinalibus Gallis molitiones pro assumtione Bonelli facta &c. quem & jam 40. vota habuisse dicebant. Similiter Author Concl. Clem. X. narrat, Chigium Florentia nuncium de morbo lethali Pontificis accepisse, quò profectus fuerit, ad deliberandum de Pontifice futuro, de quo eò magis deliberaverint, nuncio illo accepto, atque conceptus suos firmârint. Bonum itaque est, quòd excommunicati etiam eligere possunt, alias ob tractationes tales praematuras multi jure isto excidérent!
units.tr: XLIII. The beginning of these schemes is not to be traced only from entry into the Conclave; they are undertaken long before. The author of the Conclave of Gregory XIII indeed recounts that Borromeo, nephew of Pius V, when Pius lay at the point of death, did not wish to win the favour of the Grand Duke of Tuscany even in the smallest things, and they say this was done because a certain bull, under penalty of excommunication, forbade negotiations about the papacy while the Pope was alive. And indeed such a law exists. But men do not ordinarily live by its example, nor is the law equally observed by others. I say therefore, says the author of the Conclave of Gregory XIV, that it is known to those who know the Curia that the greater part of a pontificate is spent on arranging the successor, because a business so full of difficulties and so liable to accidents must necessarily be arranged long beforehand, by the one who wishes to help someone here, as also by the one who wishes to harm him, so that whenever the Pope's death comes, the matter is settled, the means are arranged, the material is prepared, and it is then easy to carry out what was proposed long before. He adds: These things could not be obtained then because of the brief pontificate of Urban VII. The author of the Conclave of Urban VIII agrees: The preparations, he says, for what was to be dealt with there began long before, and at the vacancy were renewed most diligently. So too the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII bears witness: Six months before Innocent's death the Sacchetti schemes were being pushed through. The author of the Conclave of Clement IX confirms the same, who says that two causes of the brevity of that Conclave might seem to be: first, the great heat; second, matters already settled, foreseen long before because of the Pope's death; although, he adds, that very delay which gave room to schemes has also given room to counter-schemes. Dealing with the exclusion of Farnese, the same author proves the same truth by example: So the exclusion was renewed in the Conclave rather than decided. He illustrates it by another example: On that day, the fourth from the Pope's death, the schemes made for the election of Bonelli were detected and intercepted by the French Cardinals, who were said already to have had forty votes. Similarly the author of the Conclave of Clement X tells that Chigi received news in Florence of the Pope's deadly illness, and went there to deliberate about the future Pope, and that they deliberated all the more about him after receiving that news and firmed up their plans. It is good, therefore, that even the excommunicated can elect; otherwise, through such premature dealings, many would forfeit that right!

units.la: XLIV. Rectè dixit Author Concl. Clem. IX. occasionem molitionum esse etiam contra-molitionum. Quamprimùm enim vel minima suspicio est, moliri quosdam promotionem amici sui, statim contraria factio ad arma conclamat, ac si Hannibal ante portas esset, vixque de inclusione cogitatur, & jam exclusio paratur; Quare etiam qui seriò & prudenter pro alicujus electione laborant, id, quoad fieri potest, rectè faciunt; ut contrà (quemadmodum inter artes speciales videbimus) molitionibus apertis aliquando exclusio studiosè quaeri solet. Hinc etiam saepe, ut Author Concl. Alex. VII. loquitur, nissun voleva &c. nemo volebat publicè proponi, dum quivis scivit, sic spes suas praecipitatum iri. Quòd autem de spei praecipitatione loquitur, illud porrò declarandum est. In Concl. Pii V. Card. Ferrara rogatus, ut Card. Medicaeum absolveret ab obligatione excludendi Moronem, pro quo jam apertas molitiones coperant, respondit: Spatio 24. horarum illum per se liberum esse posse some quello &c. quia scivit exclusum per 24. horas in illo Conclavi semper manere exclusum, quia semel aperte contradicentes metu vindicta à promoto contradicere pergant. In Concl. quidem Clem.VIII. fautores adhuc spem habebant pro S. Severina jamjam exclusò; sed obstabant 2. regulae 1. Che un &c. quia Cardinalis est irretractabilis (adeóque Sp. S. nonnisi primâ vice est exorabilis;) che è &c. quia facilius excludere sine proportione, quàm includere. Sed & plerunque exclusi spes praecipitata est, quoad Conclavia sequentia omnia. Quod bonus ille Sacchetti una volta sacchettato, semel telo percussus (Et quomodo hoc non sufficeret!) magno suo damno experiri debuit; Rursus quidem proponebatur in Concl. Alex VII. instabant amici, omnémque pro ejus electione lapidem movebant; Sed frustrà; Rationem dat Author: E constante opinione &c. Constans est opinio, quòd semel exclusus, semper exclusus. Sic Hispani Sacchet-tium tium semper impedivissent, cessantibus etiam exclusionis praeter metum vin-dicta causis. Tantæne animis cœlestibus iræ? Subjungit quidem Author exceptionem in Aldobrandino, atque etiam hinc redivivas Sacchetti spes, cum studio postplacentiæ, & quòd per Nepotem ea de causa in Hispaniam missum amicitiam quidem cum Mazarino non dissimulârit, cæterùm tamen persuadere conatus sit, non esse &c. neminem se in Pontificem electo Hispanis utiliorem fore &c. Sed rursus frustrà, altâque manebat mente repostum judicium latum spretæque injuria formæ!
units.tr: XLIV. Rightly did the author of Conclave Clementis IX say that the occasion of plots is also counter-plots. For as soon as even the slightest suspicion arises that certain men are plotting the promotion of their friend, the opposing faction at once cries to arms, as if Hannibal were before the gates. Scarcely is exclusion thought of before it is already being prepared. Therefore even those who labour seriously and prudently for someone's election do well, as far as possible, to keep their work quiet. Conversely (as we shall see among the special arts), once the plots are openly made, exclusion is sometimes eagerly sought. Hence also often, as the author of Conclave Alexandri VII puts it, nissun voleva (nobody wanted) to be publicly proposed, while everyone knew that their hopes would thus be dashed. But as to his saying that hopes are dashed, this must be further explained. In Conclave Pii V, Cardinal Ferrara was asked to release Cardinal Medici from the obligation of excluding Morone, for whom open plots had already begun. He replied: Within 24 hours he can by himself be free, as he is that one, etc., because he knew that one excluded for 24 hours remains excluded in that Conclave forever, since those who have once openly opposed continue to oppose out of fear of vengeance from the one promoted. In Conclave Clementis VIII indeed, the supporters still had hope for Santa Severina, who was already as good as excluded. But two rules stood in the way. The first: that one, etc., because a cardinal is irretractable (and so the Holy Spirit is only persuadable the first time). The second: that is, etc., because it is easier to exclude without proportion than to include. But also, generally, the hope of the excluded is dashed for all the conclaves that follow. That worthy Sacchetti had to experience to his great loss: once bagged, once struck by the weapon (and how could this not be enough!). Again he was proposed in Conclave Alexandri VII. His friends pressed on and moved every stone for his election, but in vain. The author gives the reason: From the constant opinion, etc. It is a fixed opinion that once excluded, always excluded. Thus the Spaniards always prevented Sacchetti, even when the causes for exclusion, apart from the fear of vengeance, had ceased. Can there be such anger in heavenly minds? The author does add an exception in the case of Aldobrandini, and here too Sacchetti's hopes were revived, given his zeal for the post-placentia, and because the nephew sent to Spain for this purpose did not hide his friendship with Mazarin, yet tried to persuade them that it was not, etc., that no one would be more useful to the Spaniards in an elected pope, etc. But again in vain. The judgment passed stayed fixed in their minds, and the wrong done to a spurned beauty was not forgotten!

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA, In qua De vitiosis Regulis, quas Pontificii Authores Pontificum Electoribus præscribunt, agitur. Breviarium.
units.tr: SECTIO TERTIA, In which the faulty rules that Papist authors prescribe to the electors of popes are discussed. Summary.

units.la: I. Molitionum artificiosarum, de quibus hactenus in genere actum est, certa dantur Regula; II. Inter Regulas proprias ambientibus, est, ut Virtutes suas ostendant; III. Ut navos contrà celare studeant; IV. Tegere etiam studeant Spiritus altos; V. Amicitias nimis arctas cum Nepotibus non contrahant; VI. Inimicitias fugiant; VII. Nemini irascantur, saltem iram suam dissimulent, injuriásque tolerent; VIII. Contrà, occasiones benefaciendi captent; IX. Idque ante mortem Pontificis; X. Sed non ita, ut studium Papatum consequendi nimis aperte prodant. IX. Præstat, se commendare per alium liberalitate atque beneficiis devinctum; XII. Ne tamen interim otiosi sint ambientes; XIII. Papabiles propiores & remotiores diversis viis incedant; XIV. Remotissimi etiam spem ne abjiciant; XV. Neque abjiciat, cui minùs favet initium; XVI. Exclusus tamen ab Amicis ne pergat instare XVII. Regula Capitibus sive Principibus Factionum qualibusque communes. Eorum requisita; XVIII. Illis opus est Administris; XIX. Maximè si ipsi virtute destituantur; XX. Non tamen omnia omnibus revelare debent; XXI. Duo agere nec esse habent. XXII. Certa sit exclusio Creaturarum; XXIII. Curent, ne vel Amicus promoveatur, ipsis haud consentientibus; XXIV. Spem faciant omnibus; XXV. Suos omnes quomodo porrò tractare debeant; XXVI. Contrariarum factionum consilia explorent; XXVII. Semper invigilent; XXVIII. Temporum momenta cognoscant; Aliquando nimis citò proposuisse nocuit; XXIX. Sed & aliquando nocuit non citius proposuisse; XXX. Non differenda est propositio & electio, si media probè sint dispositi. XXXI. Tempore minùs aliàs opportuno tuno proposuisse nocuit. XXXII. Tempus vel maximè opportunum est, quando Electores sibi invicem contrarii timent Electionem sibi noxiam; XXXIII. Quando diu pugnatum est pro aliis & contra alios, ex improviso commodè producitur, de quo antea nulla facta erat mentio; XXXIV. Proponere juvat adversarium adversario; XXXV. Item alium, si obstinati sint, eiusdem factionis ut dividantur; XXXVI. Proponendi quoque sunt saepe quinque, ita ut absco datur sextus; XXXVII. Proponendum aliquando talis, quem altera factio ex benigna voluntate, cùm quasi sine ea eligi potuisset, propositum fuisse sentiat; XXXVIII. Nonnunquam prudenter in Caput oppositum Electionis authoritas transfertur; XXXIX. In Propositionibus autem & Consiliis non semper eadem via calcanda est. XL. Quid faciendum sit, si difficultas in tractatione orta sit; XLI. In magna difficultate novam Legem proponant; XLII. Maxima difficultas oritur, si caput de propria exaltatione cogitet; XLIII. Ne suam exaltationem quaerentes Principes Factionum nimis Conclave prolongare studeant; XLIV. Quibus artibus Capita contraria se opponere debeant? XLV. Nunquam se vinci patiantur a studio vincendi nimio. XLVI. Neque etiam a timore. XLVII. Sed neque se nimis opponant merenti. XLVIII. Regula Nepotibus propria, ut non proponant nisi probè cognitam creaturam. XLIX. Regula pro Capitibus Nationum, sive Principum; Ne nimis apertè velint excludere & includere. L. Ambientes Papatum ipsimet, & dubitantes, num Reges, quibus sese subdiderunt, ipsi causa ipsorum exclusionis; non intelligere se isthoc simulent &c. LI. Regula Cardinales quosvis, licèt nonnulla rursus magis Papabiles & Capita concernentes; Ne se nimis subdant Capiti, quod neque exclusionem, neque magnam de ea spem habet; LII. Alios bene cognoscere studeant; quod ab una parte difficile; LIII. Ab altera verò facile redditur; LIV. Consideradum quoque est, qualis sit futurus, qui eligi debet & quales Agnatos habeat; LV. Ne putetur, beneficii intuitu facilem futurum; LVI. Studendum, ut noscantur illi, cum quibus est tractandum; cum diversis enim diversimodè tractandum est; LVII. Ita nonnulli obsideri debent, ut eis tempus ad consultationes in contrarium non concedatur. LVIII. Non facilè fidendum est votum unum & alterum speciosum & honoris gratiâ emendicantibus, neque simulatio tunc limites excedere debet; LIX. Omnium ratio habenda est, timeri debent omnes; LX. Ut in bello, ita hic quoque bis peccare non licet; LXI. Vitanda quoque affectuum vehementia & festinatio; LXII. Absint inconstantia atque torpedo animi, item negligentia. LXIII. De Regulis judicium.
units.tr: I. There is a fixed rule for the artful schemes of which we have treated so far in general. II. Among the particular rules for candidates is that they should show off their virtues. III. On the contrary, they should take care to conceal their vices. IV. They should also take care to hide their lofty aspirations. V. They should not form overly close friendships with nephews. VI. They should avoid enmities. VII. They should be angry with no one, or at least conceal their anger and tolerate injuries. VIII. On the contrary, they should seize opportunities to do good. IX. And this before the death of the Pope. X. But not in such a way as to reveal too openly their desire to attain the papacy. XI. It is better to recommend oneself through another person who is bound by liberality and benefits. XII. Yet candidates should not be idle in the meantime. XIII. Those who are papabili, nearer and more remote, should proceed by different ways. XIV. Even the most remote should not abandon hope. XV. Nor should he abandon hope to whom the beginning is less favourable. XVI. Though excluded by his friends, he should not cease to press on. XVII. A rule common to the heads or leaders of factions and to any others: their requirements. XVIII. They need agents. XIX. Especially if they themselves lack virtue. XX. Yet they must not reveal everything to everyone. XXI. They should not try to pursue two aims at once. XXII. The exclusion of rivals should be certain. XXIII. They should take care that not even a friend is promoted without their consent. XXIV. They should give hope to all. XXV. How they ought to treat all their followers from now on. XXVI. They should explore the plans of opposing factions. XXVII. They should always be watchful. XXVIII. They should know the moments of the times: sometimes it has harmed to propose a candidate too early. XXIX. But sometimes it has also harmed not to propose him sooner. XXX. The proposal and the election should not be deferred if the means are rightly arranged. XXXI. It has sometimes also harmed to propose a candidate at a less suitable time. XXXII. The most favourable time is when electors who are opposed to one another fear an election harmful to themselves. XXXIII. When a long struggle has been waged for some and against others, a candidate who was not mentioned before may conveniently be brought forward unexpectedly. XXXIV. It helps to propose one adversary against another. XXXV. Likewise, if they are obstinate, to propose one from within the same faction, so that they are divided. XXXVI. Often five should also be proposed, so that a sixth is given as a choice. XXXVII. Sometimes one should be proposed whom the other faction, out of goodwill, will feel was put forward when he could almost have been elected without their help. XXXVIII. Sometimes the authority of the election is wisely transferred to the opposing head. XXXIX. In proposals and counsels, however, the same path should not always be trodden. XL. What must be done if difficulty arises in the negotiation. XLI. In great difficulty they should propose a new law. XLII. The greatest difficulty arises if the head thinks of his own exaltation. XLIII. Leaders of factions, seeking their own exaltation, should not strive to prolong the conclave too much. XLIV. By what arts should opposing heads oppose themselves to one another? XLV. Let them never allow themselves to be overcome by an excessive zeal for winning. XLVI. Nor by fear. XLVII. But neither should they oppose a deserving candidate too strongly. XLVIII. A rule proper to nephews: they should propose only a candidate who is well known to them. XLIX. A rule for the heads of nations or princes: they should not wish too openly to exclude or to include. L. Those who aspire to the papacy themselves, and who doubt whether the kings to whom they have submitted are themselves the cause of their exclusion, should pretend not to understand this, and so on. LI. A rule for all cardinals, although some are again more papabili and concern the heads: they should not subject themselves too much to a head who has neither hope of exclusion nor great hope from it. LII. They should strive to know the others well, which is difficult on one side. LIII. On the other side, however, it is made easy. LIV. It must also be considered what sort of man will be, who ought to be elected, and what kinsmen he has. LV. He should not be thought likely to be easy because of favours. LVI. Care must be taken that those with whom one is to deal are known, since one must deal with different people in different ways. LVII. Some must be so closely watched that they are not allowed time for consultations on the other side. LVIII. One should not easily trust a vote, one or another, given as a show of respect and begged for the sake of honour, nor should the pretence then exceed its limits. LIX. Regard must be had for all; all must be feared. LX. As in war, so here too it is not permitted to err twice. LXI. The vehemence of the passions and haste should also be avoided. LXII. Let inconstancy and sluggishness of mind be absent, and likewise negligence. LXIII. Judgement on the rules.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Hactenus de mediis Electionis, id est, de artificiosis molitionibus & contra-molitionibus in genere; Sequitur, ut eas jam specialius proponamus. Proponemus itaque primò Regulas quasdam speciales de ratione instituendae negotiationis; Secundò Praxin Regulis conformem; Regulas certè vitiosas, nonnisi à Spiritu mundi dictatas, Praxin ex omni parte naevis scatentem. Regulas autem dabimus non à nobis excogitatas, sed à peritis in arte Conclaviaria Viris acceptas, ex multis, imò infinitis (in hunc modum innumera colligi possent documenta, prudentibus cognitu haud difficilia, inquit Joh. Fr. Lottinus Dissert. de Conclavi;) præcipuas, ordine tantùm quodam à nobis dispositas, ordine sequenti: Dabimus primò Regulas speciales ambientibus; Secundò communes Capitibus; Tertiò proprias Nepotibus; Quartò proprias Capitibus Nationum; Quintò communes omnibus.
units.tr: So far I have treated the means of the Election, that is, the artful manoeuvres and counter-manoeuvres in general. It follows that we now set them out more particularly. First, then, we will set out certain special rules for conducting the business, and secondly the practice that conforms to those rules. The rules are indeed faulty, dictated by nothing but the spirit of the world, and the practice is blotted with flaws in every part. We will give the rules not as things we have devised ourselves, but as received from men skilled in the conclave art, drawn from many, indeed countless, sources (innumerable instances could be gathered in this way, not difficult for prudent men to know, says Johann Franz Lottini in his Dissertation on the Conclave). We have arranged the chief ones in a certain order of our own, as follows: first we will give the special rules for those who canvass; secondly the common rules for the Cardinals; thirdly the rules peculiar to the Nephews; fourthly the rules peculiar to the Cardinals of the nations; fifthly the rules common to all.

units.la: II. Inter Regulas speciales ambientibus primo loco ponimus fidam Joh. Franc. Lottini Dissert. sæpe cit. monelam: Qui aliquid in se ipsis deprehendant, quod ad Pontificatum consequendum adjumento ipsis esse possit, operam dare debent, ut id augeatur potius, quàm minuatur: Itaque semper vitam omnésque suas actiones instituant, ac si omnium oculi in ipsos sint defixi, & ex quovis vel minimo facto de voluntate homines sint facturi judicium. Solent enim, qui opinione sua frustratos se vident, amorem in odium erga eos, à quibus decepti sunt, mutare.
units.tr: II. Among the special rules for those who canvass, we place first the faithful advice of Johann Franz Lottini in the Dissertation often cited: Those who find in themselves anything that could help them to obtain the papacy should take pains to have it increased rather than diminished. So they should always order their life and all their actions as if the eyes of everyone were fixed on them, and as if men were going to judge their will from every least deed. For those who see themselves cheated of their hopes are wont to turn love into hatred towards those by whom they were deceived.

units.la: III. Contrà, defectus suos Papabiles tegere omnibus modis studeant, ex Consilio Cardinalis Azzolini Afor. Polit. facti anno 1667. Ita ille de hoc studio: Se è vero &c. Si verum est dictum Aristotelis; Magistratus Virum ostendit; qui gravidus est Papatu & cognoscit malum suum naturale, sive superbiam, sive severitatem, sive aliud quicquam, fugiat, dum Cardinalis est, illa officia, in quibus non posset occultare imperfectiones dictas, quia omnes in hunc modum argumentari solent: Qui non potest freno regere ejusmodi passiones in minoribus officiis, neque spe Pontificatús, neque timore amulorum, quomodo illas regere poterit in Pontificatu, ubi non amplius spei aut timori locus est? Subjungit exempla.
units.tr: III. On the other hand, let them study to hide their defects by every means, following the counsel of Cardinal Azzolini in his Political Aphorisms of the year 1667. He speaks thus of this study: If it is true, etc. If the saying of Aristotle is true, the magistrate shows the man. Whoever is pregnant with the papacy and recognises his natural fault, whether pride, severity, or anything else, should avoid those offices in which he could not conceal the said imperfections, because everyone is accustomed to argue in this way: He who cannot curb such passions in the lesser offices, neither through hope of the papacy nor through fear of rivals, how will he be able to curb them in the papacy, where there is no longer any place for hope or fear? He adds examples.

units.la: IV. Tegere etiam studeant Spiritus altos; Fà di mestiere, inquit idem, ad un Cardinale &c. Conveniens est Cardinali, qui Spiritus altos habet & ferventes, eos non ostentare neque cognoscendos sistere ei, qui juvare aut nocere potest, sed potius eos occultare sub cineribus modesta prudentia, ut tempore suo cum majori vigore & robore prodi possint.
units.tr: IV. Let them also study to hide high spirits. It is the business, says the same author, of a Cardinal etc. It suits a Cardinal, who has high and fervent spirits, not to display them nor to present them to be known by one who can help or harm him, but rather to hide them beneath the ashes of modest prudence, so that they may be brought forth in their time with greater vigour and strength.

units.la: Exempla subdit.
units.tr: He adds examples.

units.la: V. Quoad Amicitias, ne nimiam contrahat cum Cardinale Nepote, ex Ejusdem consilio: La seconda eccettione &c. Secunda exceptio, inquit, esse solet, si quis valde familiaris est Cardinalibus, qui antea Pontificatum administrârunt, maximè si regimen illorum exosum fuerit, dum enim dubitare solet Collegium, an non continuaturum sit illud ipsum dominium, nunquam induci poterit ad illorum Amicos promovendos.
units.tr: V. As to friendships, let him not form too close a bond with a Cardinal Nephew, according to the same author's counsel: The second exception etc. The second exception, he says, is usually this: if someone is very intimate with Cardinals who previously governed the papacy, especially if their rule was hateful, then, since the College is wont to doubt whether that same domination will not continue, he can never be brought to promote their friends.

units.la: Exempla & hic subjicit.
units.tr: He adds examples here too.

units.la: VI. Quoad
units.tr: VI. Concerning

units.la: VI. Quoad Inimicitias, fugiat illas, maximè in Conclavi, juxta monita ejusdem: Fugga à tutto studio &c. Fugiat omni studio, inquit, Cardinalis in Conclavi occasiones ruptura, ne, si una vice se inimicum declaret, tam fervidi vindicta Spiritus cor occupent, ut aliud cogitare haud possit, quàm ut adjuvet talem, qui nocere possit adversario, potius quàm sibi prodesse. Rursus exempla habet.
units.tr: VI. Concerning enmities, let him avoid them, especially in the conclave, following the same author's warnings: Let him flee with all zeal etc. A Cardinal, he says, should flee with all zeal from occasions of quarrel in the conclave, lest, if he once declares himself an enemy, the spirit of a fervent desire for vengeance should so possess his heart that he can think of nothing but how to help the man who can harm his adversary, rather than how to benefit himself. Again he gives examples.

units.la: VII. Imò nemini irascantur, saltem iram suam dissimulent & injurias tolerent, pro eo quod Joh. Fr. Lottinus Diss. cit. monet, Ambientes Papatum, inquit, etiamsi à Capitibus suis apertè recusentur, non ideò debent iis irasci, & inimicitias indicere, & si, qui ambiunt, Illustris sanguinis essent, & dubitarent; Num ipsi Reges, quibus sese subdiderunt, causa sint ipsorum exclusionis; Imò non intelligere simulent, & Regis voluntatem Cardinalibus abscondant, ne, qui Regibus addicti sunt, difficiliores ad ipsos promovendos efficiantur. Quamobrem consultius est, sive Illustris sit sanguinis, sive non, ut simulet ea se credere, quae minùs credit; nam hoc modo, qui contradicturi sunt, lentiùs id agunt, & Amici poterunt facilius adjuvare. Adeò, ut nunquam expediat se abalienare ab iis, qui nobis contradixere, tametsi alium elegerant; etenim iterum favere poterunt &c. Quia forte hac fastidium pariunt &c. dico, Papabiles eò minùs irasci debere, quò majores sunt occasiones, quibus mutantur voluntates hominum: proinde fit sapenumero, ut, qui infenso animo respuebatur, is paulò post, vel deterioris formidine, vel alterius ladendi causâ promoveatur: Et in Conclavi minima offensio, vel gratificatio magis moveat, quàm summa antehac beneficia, sive injuriae. Adeò ducuntur homines magis sensu praesentium rerum, quàm praeteritarum memoriâ ac futurarum providentiâ &c. Et statim ab initio Dissertationis: Necesse est, ut, qui Pontificatum expetit, pectus bene adversus omnes odii ac malevolentiae insultus muniat, neque cum quoquam ob quamcunque injuriam etiam ab amicissimis in se profectam simultatem sibi suscipiendam putet.
units.tr: VII. Indeed let them be angry with no one, or at least let them hide their anger and tolerate injuries, as Johann Franz Lottini advises in the Dissertation cited: Those who canvass for the papacy, he says, even if they are openly refused by their Cardinals, ought not on that account to be angry with them or declare enmity. And if those who canvass are of illustrious blood and have doubts, let them ask whether the Kings themselves, to whom they have submitted, are the cause of their exclusion. Indeed, let them pretend not to understand and conceal the King's will from the Cardinals, lest those who are devoted to the Kings become more difficult to promote. Therefore it is more advisable, whether of illustrious blood or not, to pretend to believe what they do not believe; for in this way those who are going to oppose them act more slowly, and friends can more easily help. So much so that it is never expedient to alienate oneself from those who have opposed us, even though they have chosen another; for they may favour us again etc. Because perhaps this causes disgust etc. I say that the candidates for the papacy ought to be the less angry the greater the occasions by which men's wills are changed. Hence it very often happens that the man who was rejected with hostile mind is promoted a little later, either from fear of someone worse or for the sake of injuring another. And in the conclave a very small offence or favour moves more than the greatest benefits or injuries received before. So much are men driven more by the feeling of present things than by the memory of past ones or the providence of future ones etc. And right at the beginning of the Dissertation: It is necessary that he who seeks the papacy fortify his breast well against all the assaults of hatred and ill will, and that he not think he must take up a quarrel with anyone, on account of any injury, even one done to him by his closest friends.

units.la: VIII. Contrà, captent occasiones benefaciendi, obsequentes eidem; Attentam, inquit, ac vigilantem esse oportet, ut occasiones benefaciendi capiantur; quia per modicam moram perduntur, neque reversurae sunt; Nullis parcant, si ex potentioribus orti familiis divitias possideant, muneribus, suadente eodem: Quamvis plerique omnes (Cardinales,) inquit, honestiùs sint orti natalibus, minor tamen est numerus eorum, qui è potentibus ac Illustrissimis Familiis genus ducunt. Tametsi autem hi prae caeteris multa Pontificatûs consequendi habeant adjumenta; Sape tamen ipse sua & votis excidere eos videmus. Id inde fit, quòd, cùm varii variis officiis, quorum ob divitias & autoritatem amplissima iis suppetit materia, reliquorum sibi studia adjungere facile possent, existimant tamen, quemadmodum in vita communi propter generis splendorem omnibus illis libenter cedunt, ita hoc quoque, licet maximum in terris munus suæ authoritati & præeminentiæ deberi. Interim verò ipsi quoque in varias scinduntur factiones, neque illud cogitant, id maximè tempus à Cardinalibus humilioris conditionis expectari ac captari ad ulciscendas potentiorum injurias & in excludendis illis miro quodam modo hos satagere. Sic enim existimant, quum antea tam insolentes eos ac parùm gratos & beneficos experti sint, multò eosdem ad summum fastigium evectos insolentiores ac iniquiores futuros, facultatésque ad quemvis alium potiùs usum, quàm ad tenuiorum Cardinalium, quorum operâ jam non amplius egent, necessitates sublevandas collaturos. Sed & hoc idem tanto minus facturos eos credibile est, quòd Apostolicæ sedis opes non adeò magnæ sunt, ut sumptibus in Rempubl. faciendis multum superfit. Quocirca erga Cardinales ejusmodi merito illud usurpari potest, quod Maherbal ad Annibalem dixisse fertur; Non omnia uni à Deo data esse; Siquidem, cùm his favoris & opum abundè sit, iis tamen uti nesciunt. Idque tanto minus in ipsis ferendum est, quanto, si rectè uterentur iis, non solùm bonam Christianæ Reip. operam navare, verùm etiam reliquorum Regum ac Principum studia & conatus in eligendo Pontifice facilius eludere ac impedire possent; reliquorum Cardinalium animis, ex collatis priùs in se beneficiis in majoris libertatis spem erectis.
units.tr: VIII. On the other hand, let them seize opportunities of doing kindnesses, and be obliging to everyone. One must be attentive and watchful, he says, so that opportunities of doing good are seized, for they are lost through the slightest delay and will not return. Let them spare no expense, if they possess wealth from the more powerful families, in gifts, as the same author urges: Although most of them (the Cardinals), he says, are of more honourable birth, yet the number of those who trace their descent from the powerful and most illustrious families is smaller. Although these have many aids for obtaining the papacy above the others, yet we often see them fall from their own hopes and wishes. This happens because, while various men could easily attach to themselves the zeal of the rest through various offices, for which they have ample material owing to their wealth and authority, they nonetheless think that, just as in common life they readily yield to all those men on account of the splendour of their family, so this too, though the greatest office on earth, is owed to their authority and pre-eminence. Meanwhile they themselves are torn into various factions, and do not consider that this is precisely the time when the Cardinals of humbler condition wait for and seize their chance to avenge the wrongs of the more powerful, and labour with a wonderful ingenuity to exclude them. For they reckon that, since they have found them so insolent, so little grateful and beneficent before, once they are raised to the highest eminence they will be far more insolent and unjust, and will bestow their resources on any use rather than on relieving the needs of the poorer Cardinals, whose services they no longer need. But it is credible that they will do this all the less, because the resources of the Apostolic See are not so great that much is left over for expenses on the Commonwealth. Wherefore, as regards Cardinals of this kind, what Maherbal is said to have told Hannibal may rightly be applied: that not all things are given by God to one man. For, since they have abundance of favour and wealth, yet they do not know how to use them. And this must be borne in them all the less, because if they used them rightly they could not only render good service to the Christian Commonwealth, but could also more easily frustrate and impede the efforts and endeavours of the other Kings and Princes in electing the Pope, and raise the minds of the other Cardinals, who have been lifted by earlier benefits conferred on them, to the hope of greater liberty.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Sed caveant & valde caveant, ne istam liberalitatem suam ad mortem usque Pontificis differant, quod reprehendit idem verbis sequentibus: Qui non ante ad Pontificatum sibi viam sternunt, sed usque dum sedes vacat, expectandum sibi putant, vehementer errant, ac sæpe suâ ut plurimùm frustrantur. Tum enim amicos habere, non jam demum facere oportet: omnésque magis grati pro acceptis beneficiis animi declarandi desiderio quàm incerta remunerationis spe ducuntur. Quid quòd illa ipsa officia, quæ tum conferuntur, cùm eorum remunerandorum tempus tam propinquum sit, & parùm grata sint, & vix bonâ conscientiâ acceptari possint? Necesse ergo est, ut eorum maximè, qui præcæteris magno sunt animo, & quorum magna apud reliquos Cardinales est authoritas animi priùs disponantur, & benevolentiâ & favore nobis devinciantur. Cujus quidem rei consequendæ nunquam deest occasio, modò quis ea uti velit. Et hic quidem sæpe sola gratificandi voluntas, quàm ipsum beneficium, gratior est & acceptior, & benevolentiam interdum majorem jorem (oblatum) acceptum conciliat beneficium, quàm præstitum, apud potentiores præsertim; Quibus illud satis est, si sentiant se amari & magni fieri, & futuri officii spe beneficium à se requirì gaudent. Ratione vero caret illorum excusatio, qui dicunt, à tali ambitione se abstinere, ne viventem offendant Pontificem: neque enim illud potest displicere Pontifici, ut de amicis quìs bene mereri studeat. Imò vero id unumquemque decet &c.
units.tr: But they should take care, and take great care, not to postpone this generosity until the Pope's death, which the same author criticises in the following words: "Those who do not first pave their own way to the papacy, but think they must wait until the see is vacant, are greatly mistaken, and most often, for the most part, they are disappointed. For then it is too late to make friends; and everyone is moved more by the desire to show gratitude for benefits received than by the uncertain hope of reward. Moreover, those services which are offered when the time for repaying them is so near are seldom welcome and can scarcely be accepted with a good conscience. It is therefore necessary that they first dispose of those who stand out above the rest, and whose authority is great among the other Cardinals, and bind them to us by goodwill and favour. The opportunity for achieving this never fails, provided someone wishes to use it. Indeed, often the mere willingness to do a favour is more pleasing and acceptable than the benefit itself, and a benefit offered wins goodwill more than one already conferred, especially among the more powerful, for whom it is enough to feel that they are loved and esteemed, and they are glad to have a favour asked of them in the hope of future service. The excuse of those who say they refrain from such ambition so as not to offend the Pope while he lives has no reason behind it: for it cannot displease the Pope that someone should strive to do good to his friends. Indeed, this befits everyone, etc."

units.la: X. Interim tamen ista & reliqua non ita agant, ut nimis aperte studium Papatum consequendi prodant, quod dissuadet Cardinalis Azzolini Afor. Polit. Si quardi ogni Cardinale &c. Caveat quilibet Cardinalis, inquit, in Conclavi, ne predat animum suum de Papatu sibi consequendo; Sic enim viam parabit mille deceptionibus illius, qui os aperit & cor occultat, & quemadmodum sermones ejus nunquam sinceri habebuntur, sic etiam nunquam sibi favorem acquiret. Exemplo & hunc Aphorismum confirmat. XI. Præstat se commendare per alium liberalitate atque beneficiis devinctum, docente Lottino l. c. Amici hisce modis quaesiti, inquit, ii sunt, qui in Conclavi procurant pro Candidatis: cùm præsertim minimè conveniat, cum, qui ambit Papatum, de se ipso ea prædicare, quæ cæteros ad illum eligendum movere queant.
units.tr: X. Yet they should not act in such a way, in these and other matters, as to reveal too openly their desire to obtain the papacy. Cardinal Azzolini advises against this in his Aphorisms of State: "Let every Cardinal take care," he says, "in the Conclave, not to betray his mind about obtaining the papacy for himself. For in this way he will open the path to a thousand deceptions by one who opens his mouth and hides his heart; and just as his words will never be taken as sincere, so he will never win favour." He confirms this aphorism with an example. XI. It is better to recommend oneself through another, bound by generosity and benefits, as Lottini teaches in the passage cited: "Those friends won in this way," he says, "are the ones who in the Conclave work on behalf of the candidates, especially since it is not fitting for the man who seeks the papacy to speak of himself in ways that could move others to elect him."

units.la: XII. Absit autem, ut ista sinistrè intelligantur, ita nimirum, ac si Candidatus omnia aliorum curis permittere, ipse interim otiosus spectator, manibus in sinu jacentibus sedere, atque Papatum vel ori suo ab aliis ingerendum, expectare debeat. Opportunè & gravissimè intercedit idem: Etsi autem qui eligi cupiunt, inquit, non ideò per se ambire oportet: debent nihilominus gratis modis cos suscipere, qui colloquii causâ ad ipsos accedunt, & quandam modestiam præse ferentes, quæcunque de Pontificatu evenient, alienæ humanitati, non suis meritis attributuros se profiteri. Ostendunt præterea, quodcunque auxilium maximi fore momenti, sibíque charissimum. Etenim omnis homo naturâ hominem juvare desiderat, illúdq; adjumentum, quod præstiterit sibi, cupit aliquam parere grati significationem animi ab eo, in cujus utilitatem procuratum est. Idcirco dies atq; noctes ad alloquia promtissimos, sempérq; januis apertis esse oportet, imò aperto etiam vultu ac fronte, prabendáq; benignitatis & officii nimia expectatio. Ejus verò, cum quo sermo habetur, natura ac vota exploranda sunt, eidémq; magnæ insinuanda spes ad ejus desideria promovenda, nam qui spe lactantur, multò officiosiores esse solent cæteris multóq; diligentiores. Hac verborum humanitas incredibile est, quantum quantum prodesse soleat: neq; defuerunt pleriq; eorum, qui eam aut negligentes, aut nescientes, occasiones non amplius rediturac amiserunt.
units.tr: XII. Yet let no one understand these things wrongly, as if the candidate were to leave everything to the care of others, sitting idle as a mere spectator with his hands folded in his lap, and waiting for the papacy to be thrust upon him by others. The same author intervenes wisely and most seriously: "Although those who wish to be elected," he says, "need not seek it for themselves in person, they should nevertheless receive graciously those who come to them to talk, and, showing a certain modesty, profess that whatever comes of the papacy they will attribute to the kindness of others rather than to their own merits. Moreover, they should show that any help given is of the greatest importance and most dear to them. For every man by nature desires to help a man, and wishes that the help he has rendered be met with some sign of gratitude from the one for whose benefit it was undertaken. Therefore they ought to be ready for conversation day and night, with doors always open, indeed with an open face and brow, and must hold out the expectation of great kindness and service. But the nature and wishes of the man with whom they speak must be explored, and great hope must be given him to advance his desires, for those who are buoyed by hope are usually more obliging than others and much more diligent. It is incredible how much this courtesy of speech is usually worth; and there have been not a few who, neglecting such opportunities or not knowing them, lost chances that never returned."

units.la: XIII. Cæterum quivis videat, ex quo genere Papabilium sit, alii enim propius, juxta eundem, alii longius à Pontificia dignitate absunt, qui etiam diversas ad Papatum vias habent.
units.tr: XIII. Moreover, anyone can see to which class of papabili a man belongs, for some, according to the same author, are closer to the papal dignity and others further away, and they also have different routes to the papacy.

units.la: tate absunt, qui etiam diversas ad Papatum vias habent. Hos illis, præsertim Factionum Principibus servitium & operam saltem ostentare oportet: nam hoc casu non modò ipsorum gratiam lucrabuntur, sed eorum etiam, qui propositi fuerunt; Qui profectò, ubi se à Papatu exclusos viderint, libentius illis favebunt, quos sibi Fautores experti fuerunt. Verùm illi, qui magnam alunt spem, ii non facilè adduci debere videntur, ut prompte adjuvent alios ad Pontificatum, ideóque amicis suis inservire difficiliùs queunt. Sed ex alia parte inofficiosi esse non debent, nam uno eodemque tempore, & eos, qui propositi sunt, & eos, qui proponunt, à se abalienarent. Ad hanc difficultatem accedit alia, quòd, cùm in principio Conclavis pleraq; fiant exclusiones, rogabuntur forte, ut iisdem oppugnationibus, sive exclusionibus aggregent sese: quam rem si fecerint, certi sint, eum, quem excluserunt (si modò humani sensûs aliquid habuerit) nunquam erga eos bene affectum esse posse; Si verò non fecerint, Capita principésq; exclusionum abalienant. Et hæ difficultates adeò difficulter explicari possunt, ut non modò bonum in iis judicium, sed bona etiam fortuna requiratur. Judicium illud adhibendum est, ut, quoad fieri potest, mentem dissimules: quod si tamen cogaris studia tua declarare, ad favorem Principum in Conclavi potentiorum inclines. Verùm profectò ii Candidati, qui ob egregias dotes Papatum merentur, à Principibus Factionum tali circumspectione atq; judicio tractandi essent, ut ne in difficultates inciderent. Deberént q; iidem Principes omnem malevolentiam causam ab iis amovere, sibíque potius eam attribuere, & ambitum eo pacto instituere, ut Candidati possent sua suffragia cæteris Papatu dignis concedere absque lasione Principum; nisi tamen obstaret justa aliqua ratio vel ob gratificandum Principibus, quibus manifestè devincirentur, vel propter privatas alias causas, quibus legitimè se excusare possent; deberent & persuadere, cùm negant ex ipsis repulsam non provenire, sed ex necessitate, qua illos cogat invitos.
units.tr: It is fitting for these men, especially the leaders of factions, to show at least service and effort to those others. For in this case they will win the favour not only of those men, but also of those who were put forward; and these, once they see themselves shut out from the papacy, will more willingly favour those whom they have found to be their supporters. But those who nurse a great hope do not seem easily persuaded to promptly help others toward the papacy, and so they are less able to serve their friends. Yet on the other hand they ought not to be unobliging, for at one and the same time they would alienate both those who are put forward and those who put them forward. To this difficulty another is added: since many exclusions are made at the start of the Conclave, they will perhaps be asked to join in the same attacks, or exclusions; if they do so, let them be sure that the man they have excluded (if he has any human feeling) can never be well disposed towards them; but if they do not, they alienate the leaders and chief movers of the exclusions. And these difficulties are so hard to resolve that not only good judgement but also good fortune is required. That judgement must be exercised so that, as far as possible, you conceal your mind; but if you are nonetheless forced to declare your inclinations, incline to the favour of the princes most powerful in the Conclave. Yet truly those candidates who deserve the papacy because of outstanding gifts ought to be handled by the princes of the factions with such caution and judgement that they do not fall into difficulties. And these same princes ought to remove every cause of ill will from them, and attribute it rather to themselves, and conduct the canvassing in such a way that the candidates may give their votes to others worthy of the papacy without injury to the princes; unless some just reason stood in the way, either to gratify princes to whom they were manifestly bound, or on account of other private causes by which they could lawfully excuse themselves; and they ought also to persuade them, when they deny that the rejection comes from themselves, that it does not arise from their own will, but from a necessity that compels them against their wishes.

units.la: XIV. Remotissimi etiam spem abjicere non debent, ut docet idem: Solent autem Cardinales de eligendo Pontifice cogitare, vel ante Conclave, vel postquam illud ingressi sunt. Primo modo nondum apparentibus iis impedimentis, quæ plerunque postea incidere solent, cùm Papam creare cogitant, de quo maximam sibi benevolentiam pollicentur. Altero modo si consilium mutare necesse sit, ei plerunque studeat, quem, si non amicissimum sibi, saltem iniquum minùs fore arbitrantur. Qua-propter nemo Cardinalium, etiamsi multa sibi obstare animadvertat, si quicquam habeat in se tali munere dignum, spem ejus consequendi abjicere debet. Nam quemadmodum ob summam in loquendo libertatem, quà omnes sede vacante utuntur, nullius vitia & defectus latere possunt; ita saepe res circa eligendum Pontificem eò redigitur, ut vitia & defectus ejusmodi non æstimentur: sive, quòd, qui ab aliis propositi sunt, majoribus laborent; sive, quòd is, qui ab alio commendatur, tametsi melior, parùm tamen amicus, vel rebus aliorum opportunus fore credatur. Nullum quidem tantum est vitium, quod non tolerabile aliquando existimetur & pro minùs malo accipiatur, ita suadente scilicet rerum statu, & tempore sive occasione: quæ quidem in conficiendo quolibet negotio utramq;, quod dicitur, paginam implet. Periculum facere an aliquis de suis Cardinalibus evehi possit, etsi effectus non sequatur, haud improbandum est.
units.tr: XIV. Nor should even the most remote men abandon hope, as the same author teaches: Cardinals usually think about electing a Pope either before the Conclave or after they have entered it. In the first way, before those obstacles appear which generally arise afterwards, they think of creating as Pope the man from whom they promise themselves the greatest goodwill. In the second way, if it is necessary to change their plan, they usually aim at the man whom they judge will be, if not their closest friend, at least less hostile to them. Therefore no Cardinal, even if he notices that many things stand in his way, ought to abandon the hope of attaining it, if he has anything in himself worthy of such an office. For just as, because of the great freedom of speech which everyone uses while the see is vacant, no one's faults and defects can remain hidden, so it often happens in the choosing of a Pope that faults and defects of this kind are not weighed: either because those who are put forward by others labour under greater ones, or because the man commended by another, though better, is thought to be less friendly or less suited to the affairs of others. There is indeed no fault so great that it is not sometimes thought tolerable and accepted as the lesser evil, the state of affairs and the time or occasion so suggesting; and this, as is said, fills both pages in the conduct of any business. To make trial whether one of their own Cardinals can be raised up, even if the outcome does not follow, is not to be condemned.

units.la: XV. Neque etiam, quibus initium parùm favere visum fuit: Est enim, indice eodem, primus in Conclavi impetus sive ingressus Cardinalium acerrimus: quem qui sustinuerit, neq; vel indignatione vel nimiâ festinatione spes suas corruperit, quàm plurimos modos promovendi desiderii poterit comminisci ac reperire.
units.tr: XV. Nor should those whose beginnings seemed unpromising lose heart. According to the same author, the first onset or entrance of the Cardinals into the Conclave is the fiercest. Whoever endures it, and does not ruin his hopes through indignation or excessive haste, will be able to devise and discover very many ways of advancing his desire.

units.la: XVI. Si autem quis se videat exclusum ab Amicis, ne instare tunc pergat. Consilium est Cardinalis Azzolini: Chi si vede &c. Qui se videt exclusum ab Amicis ex fundamento ratione non destituto, ne fortunâ invitâ causam suam protegere studeat: sed cedat ad tempus & prolonget spes cogitando subitò, sine offensæ indicio, de promotione alterius, qui placeat; Sic enim effugere poterit lapsum, qui ei semper nociturus esset, alet confidentiam amicorum, & illos devinciet tempore magis opportuno ad satisfaciendum ei, eligendo eum, quem ipse proposuerit, & tandem elogium acquiret hominis prudentis; quod ipsi prodesse poterit alio tempore in Electione aut sui ipsius, aut amici. Exemplis & hoc declaratur.
units.tr: XVI. If someone sees that he has been shut out by his friends, he should not press on at that point. This is the counsel of Cardinal Azzolini: Chi si vede &c. Whoever sees himself shut out by his friends, for a reason that is not without foundation, should not strive to defend his cause against the wishes of fortune. He should yield for the time being and keep his hopes alive by suddenly, and without any sign of offence, speaking of the promotion of another man whom people like. In this way he can avoid a slip that would always harm him, he will nourish the confidence of his friends, and he will bind them to himself so that at a more opportune time they will satisfy him by electing the man he himself has proposed. In the end he will win the reputation of a prudent man, which can benefit him at another time in an election, either his own or a friend's. This is also illustrated by examples.

units.la: XVII. Hactenus Regulæ Papabilibus, sive Candidatis respectu molitionum & negotiationum suarum propriæ. Sequuntur secundò Capitibus, sive Principibus Factionum qualibuscunque communes. De eorum requisitis primò ita Lottinus l. c. Qui ambitum dirigere debent, inquit, eos oportet præteritorum Conclavium habere exactam notitiam, & reipsa perspexisse præcipuas causas, unde quis repulsus fuerit à Papatu, aut ad eum sublatus. Proinde non ignorent tempora distinguere ac dijudicare, in quo statu olim, & in quo præsenti tempore sese res habeant; noscant mores ac præcipua non modò Cardinalium omnium omnium, sed etiam eorum, qui ipsis famulantur, studia ac desideria; scrutentur amicitias, quas vicissim habent, & qua de causa; Et quousque favor exterorum Principum, eorúmve, qui Principes in Conclavi referunt, iis profuturus aut præsto futurus sit. Præter hanc notitiam oportet eos ad negotium aptos & ad explicanda animi sensa efficaces esse, ut ea persuadere queant. Sæpe enim accidit, aliquem perspicacem in rebus intelligendis, at in iis eloquendis rudem esse: Quod perinde est, ac si non intelligerent. Sed & necesse est eos audaces esse: nam quadam nonnunquam contingunt, in quibus ille superior evadit, qui contrà audentior iverit. Et quamvis huiusmodi audacia naturæ debeatur; tamen oportet eam ab egregio aliquo stemmate destitutam non esse, vel à factione assectarum numerosa, vel ab excellente virtute: nam quicunq; absq; aliquo harum rerum subsidio audentior esse vellet, profecto deluderetur potius & rem turbaret, quàm audiretur, rémve emendaret.
units.tr: XVII. So far, the rules for the papabiles, or candidates, concerning their own schemes and negotiations. Next, I shall set out the rules common to the heads or leaders of any factions. First, concerning their requirements, Lottinus says, in the passage cited: Those who must direct the canvass, he says, ought to have an exact knowledge of past conclaves, and to have truly grasped the chief reasons why someone was rejected from the papacy or raised to it. Accordingly, they should not be ignorant of how to distinguish and judge the times, in what state affairs once stood and in what state they now stand. They should know the characters and chief studies and desires not only of all the Cardinals but also of those who serve them. They should examine the friendships which the Cardinals have with one another, and their cause; and how far the favour of foreign princes, or of those who represent princes in the Conclave, will be of use to them or be at hand. Besides this knowledge, they must be fit for the business and effective in expressing their feelings, so that they can persuade. For it often happens that someone is sharp in understanding things but clumsy in putting them into words, and this is the same as if they did not understand. But they must also be bold, for in certain circumstances it sometimes happens that he prevails who has gone further in daring than the others. And although such boldness is owed to nature, yet it ought not to be without some distinguished lineage, or without a numerous body of followers, or without outstanding virtue. For whoever wished to be bolder than the rest without some support of these kinds would surely be mocked rather than heard, and would throw the business into confusion rather than set it right.

units.la: XVIII. Capitibus etiam talibus opus est Administris; Oportet Principes & Capita partium, inquit idem, pluribus Administris uti: sciántq; si onera & officia distincta habuerint, id ad totius negotii salutem fore: & Caput, sive Principem illum, qui vel ob ambitionem, vel propter parvam intelligentiam ex se ipso omnia facere, vel suis assectis artificiosè uti vult, semper futurum causam confusionis.
units.tr: XVIII. Heads of this kind also need agents. The leaders and heads of the parties, he says again, ought to use several agents, and they should know that if they have separate burdens and offices, this will serve the welfare of the whole business. A head or leader who wishes to do everything himself, either from ambition or from little understanding, or who wishes to use his followers cunningly, will always be the cause of confusion.

units.la: XIX. Maximè autem Administris & consilio opus habent, si ipsi virtute destituantur. Hujusmodi homines, ait idem de Capitibus, sive Principibus; Si virtute destituti sint, & se destitutos esse animadvertant, ab iis, quos inter suos sapientiores cognoscunt, consilium mutuò accipiant: At si sufficientes sese putaverint, neq; tamen fuerint, ut plurimùm errare conspiciuntur, neq; eos quicquam juvat, moneri à quopiam sive doceri.
units.tr: XIX. They need agents and counsel most of all if they themselves lack virtue. Of such men, the same author says of the heads or leaders: If they lack virtue, and notice that they lack it, let them take counsel in turn from those whom they know to be wiser among their own people. But if they think themselves sufficient when they are not, they are seen to err for the most part, and it does them no good to be advised or taught by anyone.

units.la: XX. Quæ verò de Administris & Consilio dicta sunt, non ita intelligi debent, ac si omnibus Creaturis arcana omnia communicanda essent, contrà quod idem ita præscribit: Capita Factionum oportet suffragatores multos habere, nec non ministros, qui eorum voluntatem exsequantur, singulis verò cura peculiaris demandetur &c. Sunt deinde sui distribuendi, ut singuli suum munus exsequi sciant, & ubi jubentur, convenire possint: Nam quotiescunque aliquem propositum intelligent, quem ipsi nolint, statim remedium reperietur, quò is repulsam patiatur; Ad quæ suis amicis utendum est; Nam fides fidem parit, & unusquisq; gaudet Capiti suo utilis esse, & aliquid cum honore suo alicubi elaboravisse. Sed rerum summa iis tantùm committenda est, qui dotibus prædictis insigniuntur. XXI.
units.tr: XX. What has been said about agents and counsel should not be understood as if all secrets were to be communicated to all the creatures, contrary to what the same author prescribes: The heads of the factions ought to have many supporters, as well as ministers who carry out their will, and to each one a special charge should be entrusted, etc. Then their people must be distributed, so that each knows how to carry out his task and can come together when ordered. For whenever they perceive some proposal which they themselves do not want, a remedy will at once be found by which that proposal suffers defeat. To this end their friends must be used, for faith begets faith, and each man rejoices to be useful to his head and to have laboured somewhere with credit to himself. But the sum of affairs must be committed only to those who are marked out by the aforementioned gifts. XXI.

units.la: Sect. III.
units.tr: Sect. III.

units.la: XXI. Duo autem agere debent Capita ; Primò suffragia disponere ; Secundò disposita ordinare. Id quod ex eodem discimus. In ambitu agendo, inquit, duabus oportet insignitos esse Conditionibus; altera in suffragiis disponendis, altera, postquam disposita sunt, in iis ordinandis ad peragendam electionem.
units.tr: XXI. Heads ought to do two things: first, to arrange the votes; second, to order the votes once they are arranged. We learn this from the same author. In conducting the canvass, he says, they must be distinguished by two qualities: one in arranging the votes, the other, once they have been arranged, in ordering them to carry through the election.

units.la: XXII. Suffragia ita disponenda atq; ordinanda sunt, ut quilibet semper securus esse possit de exclusione non-Creaturarum, vel, juxta verba ejusdem, illorum, qui extra eorum Factionem Papatum ambiunt. Quod si inter suos illam exclusionem non habuerint, quaerenda erit inter alios. Etenim multos invenient, qui contra aliquem conspirabunt, vel qui nolentes tam facile Pontificatūs spem deserere, in omni exclusione diu inservient. Imò hoc studium quaerenda exclusionis aliquando in causa est, ut, qui antea adversabantur, simul versando amici fiant, unde exoritur Pontificis Electio, adeóque amicantur invicem cum iis, à quibus opem acceperunt, ut, si forte casus ita ferat, per inconsultam beneficentiam ille fiat Papa, de quo antea nunquam cogitatum fuerat. Verùm quia excluduntur aut inimici, aut amici, ne scilicet ob jus imperii aut aliam ob causam amicitia in inimicitiam convertatur; prima exclusiones palàm tractantur; alia maximè cauta esse debent, ne suâ sponte, sed ex accidenti, aut ob difficultatem facta esse videantur; Cúmq; celari affectus non potest, & periculum prope adesse cognoscitur, ne amici abalienentur, decet pratermittere exclusionem & electionem divertere, eligendo aliquem Factionis, qui eodem damno te afficere nequeat, quo alter ille amicus potuisset. Ea sunt potissima exclusiones, nam qua fit procrastinando & providendo, ut nihil incogitatum accidat, ea suspensio potiùs quàm exclusio dicitur; quemadmodum ea, quae unius causâ fit, pertinacia est, quae frequenter cum damno pertinacis infringitur. Exclusio, quae fit propter Reip. respectum, quia, excepto uno aut altero, non tollitur, quin Papa singulis momentis creari possit.
units.tr: XXII. Votes must be so arranged and ordered that each man can always be secure against the exclusion of non-creatures, or, in the words of the same author, of those who seek the papacy outside their own faction. If they do not have that exclusion among their own people, it must be sought among others. For they will find many who will conspire against someone, or who, unwilling to abandon their hope of the pontificate so easily, will serve for a long time in any exclusion. Indeed this zeal for seeking an exclusion is sometimes the cause that those who were formerly opposed become friends by working together; from this the election of the pontiff arises, and they become friends with those from whom they received help, so that, if chance so brings it about, through an ill-considered kindness that man becomes pope of whom no one had ever thought before. But since either enemies or friends are excluded, lest friendship be turned into enmity for the sake of the right of rule or some other cause, the first kind of exclusion is handled openly; the other must be especially cautious, lest it appear to be done of its own accord but by chance, or because of difficulty. And since feelings cannot be concealed, and the danger is recognised as close at hand that friends may be estranged, it is fitting to pass over the exclusion and turn the election aside, choosing someone of the faction who cannot inflict on you the same harm that the other friend could have done. These are the chief kinds of exclusion. For an exclusion that is brought about by delaying and by arranging that nothing unforeseen happens is called a suspension rather than an exclusion; likewise, that which is made for the sake of one man is obstinacy, which is often broken to the obstinate man's loss. An exclusion made out of regard for the commonwealth is not removed, except by one or two, for the pope can be created at any moment.

units.la: XXIII. Imò etiam curare debent, ne ex amicis aliquis promoveatur, sine ipsorum consensu. De quo ita loquitur idem: Caput factionis ita praparare se debet, ut, cùm Adversarii Papam aliquem creare voluerint ex illis, quos probat, eum creare nequeant, nisi ipse creationem foverit, ne derisui habeatur, eíque necesse sit cum multitudine accurrere omnium rerum ignarus. Etenim exploratum est, quoties Cardinales coguntur incognito alicui electione consentire, electum, etsi olim amicissimum, nihil ei debere.
units.tr: XXIII. Indeed they must also take care that no one is promoted from among their friends without their consent. The same author speaks of this as follows: The head of the faction must so prepare himself that, when the adversaries wish to create as pope someone from those whom he approves, they cannot create him unless he himself has encouraged the creation, lest he be held up to ridicule, and he be obliged to hasten with the crowd, ignorant of all the facts. For it is well known that whenever Cardinals are forced to consent to the election of someone unknown to them, the one elected, though once very dear to them, owes them nothing.

units.la: XXIV. Cúmq; quaelibet factio habeat ambientes Papatum, sunt verba ejusdem, Princeps Factionum illos in eo affectu nutrire debet, nam si eos inhabiles declararet, videretur illos contemnere, & contemptus au-daciam gignit, unde res novas atq; periculosas tentant: quòd si audacia addatur authoritas, vel singularis aliqua utilitas, maximas turbas ciet. Ideò Capita faveant suis, & desiderium ipsis inserviendi ostentent, effi-ciántq;, ut per alios, vel per negotium ipsum illis contradicatur: nam qui etiam jure contradicit alicui, is contradictione animum alterius nunquam non lædit.
units.tr: XXIV. And since every faction has men who aspire to the papacy, the same author's words are: The leader of the factions must nourish them in that desire, for if he declared them unfit, he would seem to despise them, and contempt breeds boldness, whence they attempt novel and dangerous things. If to this boldness is added authority or some particular advantage, they stir up the greatest disturbances. Therefore the heads should favour their own people and display a desire to serve them, and they should bring it about that opposition to them comes through others, or through the business itself; for he who opposes someone even with right on his side always wounds that person's spirit by the opposition.

units.la: XXV. Suos omnes ut sequenti modo tractent, exigit iterum Lottinus: Amici non minori diligentiâ tractandi sunt, inquit, & officiosè tractandi, quàm alieni conciliandi: ideóq; singulorum necessitates atq; cupiditates exploranda. Eósq; ita Principes illectent, ut aliunde spes eorum non dependeant, quàm à Capite suo: Sapiúsq; cum iis differendum, & reddenda ratio eorum, qua ad adversarios pertinent; Nam de intimis suis cogitationibus cum iis tantùm tractandum est, quos magis addictos esse sibi cognoverint, vel minùs de suis utilitatibus cogitantes. Cum suis Amicis dexterrimè agant, aquè se illos promovere velle profiteantur, ostendántq; ex difficultate negotii potiùs, quàm ex defectu voluntatis eos non promoveri; alioquin animis alienabuntur, & se contemptos putabunt. Vide Vita di Sisto V. p.2. 352. XXVI. Ut contraria partis consilia explorentur, idem postulat, quem Cardinalem cogitet promovere, quibus suffragiis, quanam sit suffragantium firmitudo, qua causa favendi; invenienturq; nonnulli, qui nihil fautorum habere putabantur, & re ipsa plurimos habent, & alii plurimùm authoritatis habere videntur, qui nihil possunt. XXVII. Semper autem invigilare eos vult idem, atq; nullumferè utilius documentum pro Capitibus Principibúsq; Factionum in Conclavi afferri posse; nunquam non attendant; nam si diu duraturum est Conclave, varias induit formas, eorúmq; sagacitas atq; industria multas inde utilitates colligere potest. XXVIII. Ante omnia quoq;, juxta eundem, convenit, ut temporum momenta cognoscant, & opportunè capere non ignorent. Aliquando nimis citò proposuisse nocuit. Certè nimis citò proponi nocuit in Conclavi Sixti V. Sirleto. Hinc Altempsius, qui primarius Sirleti promotor videri volebat, ab amicis hujus accusatus fuit, di troppa presumtione &c. nimia præsumptionis negotiationem illam suscipiens in primo Conclavis impetu, in quo bulliunt & fervent spes Cardinalium prætendentium, desiderante quovis negotiari pro sese; quæ causa est, quòd in prima illa tractatione facilia fiunt difficilia; Si igitur Altem- Suos omnes quomodo porrò tractare debeant; Contrariarum Factionum consilia explorent; Semper invigilent; Temporum momenta cognoscant; Aliquando nimis citò proposuisse nocuit; Altempsius dissimulâsset desiderium suum, aliis spopondisset, & expectâsset exclusionem competitorum, potuisset cum fundamento sperare felicem votorum suorum eventum, sed nimius ejus calor atq; nimia credulitas eum unâ cum amico perdidit &c. Fuerunt tamen qui crediderunt, Altempsium simulâsse tantùm, se præcipuè Sirleto favere, proposuisse tantùm, qualiscunq; satisfactionis ergò, revera autem Vercelli promotionem quasivisse. Quod æquè confirmat Cardinalis Azzolini, in Aphorismis sæpiùs cit. qui, postquam hunc Aphorismum proposuisset; Si hâ da passare per sospetto di simulatione &c. In suspicionem simulationis veniet Caput Factionis, à quo in primo impetu & magno cum ardore aliquis proponitur &c. Illud ipsum Sirleti & Altempsii exemplum subjicit.
units.tr: XXV. Lottinus again requires that they handle all their own people in the following way: Friends must be handled with no less diligence, he says, and handled dutifully, than outsiders are won over. Therefore the needs and desires of each one must be explored. And the Princes should so entice them that their hopes depend on nothing other than their Head. It is wiser to delay with them and to give an account of what concerns the adversaries. For the innermost thoughts must be discussed only with those whom they have known to be more devoted to them, or less concerned with their own advantages. Let them deal most skilfully with their friends, professing that they wish equally to advance them, and showing that they are not promoted because of the difficulty of the business rather than a lack of will. Otherwise they will be alienated in spirit and will think themselves despised. See Vita di Sisto V. p.2. 352. XXVI. That the plans of the opposing party be explored, he likewise demands: whom he intends to promote as Cardinal, by what votes, how firm the supporters are, and for what reason they favour him. Some will be found who were thought to have no supporters yet in fact have very many, and others who seem to have great authority can do nothing. XXVII. He wants them always to keep watch, and nothing is almost more useful as a lesson for heads and princes of factions in the Conclave; they should never stop attending. For if the Conclave lasts long, it takes on various forms, and their shrewdness and industry can gather many advantages from it. XXVIII. Above all, according to the same author, it is fitting that they know the moments of the times and not fail to seize them opportunely. Sometimes proposing too early has done harm. Indeed, proposing too early did harm in the Conclave of Sixtus V with Sirleto. Hence Altempsi, who wished to appear the chief promoter of Sirleto, was accused by Sirleto's friends of "di troppa presumtione" [of too much presumption], etc., undertaking that business with too much presumption in the first rush of the Conclave, when the hopes of the Cardinals who aspire are boiling and seething, each one wishing to negotiate on his own behalf. This is why, in that first handling, easy things become difficult. If therefore Altempsi had dissembled his desire, had promised it to others, and had waited for the exclusion of his rivals, he could have hoped with good reason for a happy outcome of his wishes. But his excessive warmth and excessive credulity ruined him together with his friend, etc. Yet there were some who believed that Altempsi only pretended to favour Sirleto especially, that he proposed him only for the sake of some kind of satisfaction, and that in truth he was seeking the promotion of Vercelli. The Cardinal Azzolini, cited often in the Aphorisms, equally confirms this, who, after proposing this aphorism, "Si hâ da passare per sospetto di simulatione" etc. [if it is to pass as suspicion of pretence], says: The head of a faction, by whom someone is proposed at the first onset and with great ardour, will come under suspicion of pretence. He appends the very example of Sirleto and Altempsi.

units.la: XXIX. Aliquando etiam & vice versa nocuit, non satis citò proponi & constanter posthac urgeri; Id quod malo suo expertus est Cardinalis Papabilis Sauli in Conclavi Pauli V. Li amici suoi &c.
