Amici ejus polliciti sunt, se tentare velle inopinatam adorationem in favorem ejus, quam feliciter successuram sperabant ob commercium, quod habebant cum multis ex ipsis Aldobrandinianis, qui sine dubio commotus fuisset motu usq; adeò inopinato, & fortè cum aliis ipse etiam occurrisset; noluit Sauli, quia hoc ipsi videbatur plenum tumultu & periculo &c. Cosi nuoce spesso &c. Ita sape nocet, inquit Author, non prosequi certos impetus, qui fundamento cum ratione innituntur, licèt difficiles videantur in executione.
units.tr: XXIX. Sometimes it has also harmed the other way round, not to propose early enough and not to press constantly afterwards. The Cardinal papabile Sauli learnt this to his cost in the Conclave of Paul V. His friends promised that they wished to attempt an unexpected acclamation in his favour, which they hoped would succeed happily because of the dealings they had with many of the Aldobrandini, who would undoubtedly have been moved by a movement so unexpected, and perhaps would have joined him with others. Sauli did not want this, because it seemed to him full of tumult and danger, etc. Cosi nuoce spesso [thus it often harms], etc. So often it harms, says the author, not to pursue certain impulses that rest on a sound foundation, although they seem difficult to carry out.

units.la: XXX. Non differenda est propositio & electio, si media sint bene ordinata. Monet Cardinalis Azzolini ita: Maturata che si sia &c. si secura sit inclusiva facta, malè non statim executioni datur; Semper vel minimum temporis spatium timeri debet, præcipuè si pars contraria aut numero, aut authoritate aut experientiâ multùm valentes habeat; Cùm enim in his desperatio animum addere possit, illi de ardore suo inclusivo remittere possint, etiam breve tempus excludentes victores facere valet. Exempla nec hîc desunt.
units.tr: XXX. A proposal and election should not be postponed if the means are well arranged. Cardinal Azzolini advises thus: "Maturata che si sia" [once it has been ripened] etc. If the inclusive arrangement is secure, it is not wrong to put it into execution at once. Always some least space of time should be feared, especially if the opposing party has men who are strong in number, authority or experience. For since despair can add courage to these men, they can relax their inclusive ardour, and even a brief time can make the excluded men victors. Examples are not lacking here either.

units.la: XXXI. Tempore autem aliâs minùs opportuno proponi aliquando nocuit. Atque ejusmodi inopportuna propositio Authori Conclavis Innocentii X. sequentia verba expressit: Notate qui per vita vestra &c. Notate heic per totam vestram vitam, quantum nocere possint in Conclavi amici tales, & quantò melius sit Cardinali Seni, ut homines adeò imprudentes potiùs inter inimicos quàm verò inter amicos numerentur.
units.tr: XXXI. Yet to propose at a time less suitable has sometimes done harm. The author of the Conclave of Innocent X expressed such an inopportune proposal in these words: "Notate qui per vita vestra" [note here all your life], etc. Note here, throughout your whole life, how much such friends can harm in a Conclave, and how much better it is for the Cardinal of Siena that men so imprudent be numbered among enemies rather than among friends.

units.la: XXXII. Tunc autem vel maximè est tempus opportunum, quando Electores sibi invicem contrarii timent electionem sibi noxiam. De quo casu Aphorismus Cardinalis Azzolini sequens habetur: Giova à maraviglia &c. Plurimum juvat Caput authoritate pollens, si producit, & proponit quem habet, dum Electores contrarii sunt in magna animi angustia, timentes futuram electionem sibi exosam: Timor enim mali praesentis, qui eos occupavit, non permittit, ut videant, aut examinent malum futurum, quod e longinquo tantum apparet, & omnia amplectentur avidi, ut tantum ex praesenti liberentur labyrintho. Exempla & hic Aphorismus habet ab Authore annexa.
units.tr: XXXII. But the most opportune time is especially when the Electors who are opposed to one another fear an election harmful to themselves. Concerning this case the following aphorism of Cardinal Azzolini is found: "Giova à maraviglia" [it helps wonderfully], etc. It greatly helps if a Head mighty in authority brings forward and proposes the man he has, while the opposing Electors are in great anguish of mind, fearing an election that will be hateful to them. For the fear of the present evil that has seized them does not allow them to see or examine the future evil, which appears only from afar, and eager, they will embrace everything, so that they may be freed at once from the present labyrinth. This aphorism also has examples attached by the author.

units.la: XXXIII. Item, quando diu pugnatum est pro aliis & contra alios, ex improviso commodè producitur, de quo antea nulla facta erat mentio, ex consilio ejusdem tali: E buona regola &c. Bona est regula Captibus Factionum, semper in pectore unum aliquem occultare, qui placeat, neque illum nominare, nisi tempore tumultus & discordia, ut, quando tempus illud adest, & Factiones longo certamine lassi atque destituti spe sua sunt, inopinatò proponatur, atque adhibitis, quot haberi possunt, votis omnibus audacter ad adorationem procedatur; Animi enim diuturnis pugnis lassati atque ita ex improviso & cum tanta vehementia oppugnati cum consilio perdunt & vires. Quod & exemplo docet.
units.tr: XXXIII. Likewise, when long fighting has been waged for some and against others, a candidate is conveniently brought forward unexpectedly, of whom no mention had been made before, following the counsel of the same author to this effect: "E buona regola" [it is a good rule], etc. It is a good rule for heads of factions always to keep hidden in their breast someone who is acceptable, and not to name him except at a time of tumult and discord, so that when that time has come, and the factions, wearied by a long contest, are deprived of their hope, he may be proposed unexpectedly, and with all the votes that can be had, they may boldly proceed to the acclamation. For minds worn out by long battles, and so attacked suddenly and with such vehemence, lose both counsel and strength. He teaches this also by example.

units.la: XXXIV. Proponere juvat adversarium adversario: Si tal' hora, inquit idem, persevera ostinata &c. Si aliquando obstinata manet factio quadam in studio exaltandi minùs tibi gratum, bene facies ad eum irretiendum, si in scrutinio tuo oppones ex maximis ejus adversariis aliquem, ut sic timor efficiat, quod non licet amori. Stratagematis hujus quoque exempla largitur.
units.tr: XXXIV. It is useful to propose one adversary against another. "Si tal' hora" [if at some hour], says the same author, "persevera ostinata" [persists obstinate], etc. If at some time a certain faction remains obstinate in its zeal to exalt someone less pleasing to you, you will do well to ensnare them by opposing in your scrutiny one of their greatest adversaries, so that fear may accomplish what love does not allow. He also supplies examples of this stratagem.

units.la: XXXV. Item alium, si obstinati sint, ejusdem factionis, ut dividantur; Aliter enim, inquit idem, è troppo malagevole rompere il filo d'una ostinata congiura nell' Elettione d'un soggetto, quando la parte è ponderosa. Atque hanc artem adhibitam plerunque feliciter successisse, verbis docet, exemplo confirmat.
units.tr: XXXV. Likewise, if they are obstinate, one may propose another man from the same faction, so that they are divided: "Aliter enim" [for otherwise], says the same author, "è troppo malagevole rompere il filo d'una ostinata congiura nell' Elettione d'un soggetto, quando la parte è ponderosa" [it is too difficult to break the thread of an obstinate conspiracy in the election of a subject, when the party is weighty]. He shows in words, and confirms by example, that this art, when applied, has for the most part succeeded happily.

units.la: XXXVI. Proponendi quoque sunt saepe quinque, ita ut abscondatur sextus. Consilium hocce est ex Aphorismis ejusdem, & quidem de tali sexto, che piu si desira nel suo cuore, qui maximè desideratur. Ita enim, pergit, devinciuntur animi propositorum, atq; occasio praebetur aliis, credendi, non insistere proponentem firmiter finibus particularibus, non esse obstinatum, non superbum; neq; etiam talis proponens timere debet inclusionem unius ex propositis quinq;, utpote qua facilè postmodum impediri potest. Atq; si tandem desistit à quinq; illis, sextúmq; hactenus occultatum, sed maximè desideratum proponit, non tamen men alienatos inveniet quinq; illos, quos per propositionem priorem lucratus est. Dicit, hoc artificii in Conclavi Pii V. factionum Capitibus ad votum successisse.
units.tr: XXXVI. Often five men should also be proposed, so that a sixth is kept hidden. This counsel is taken from the same Aphorisms, and indeed concerning such a sixth: "che piu si desira nel suo cuore" [which is most desired in his heart], that is, the one who is most desired. For thus, he continues, the minds of the supporters are bound, and an opportunity is given to others of believing that the proposer does not firmly cling to particular ends, is not obstinate, is not proud. Nor should such a proposer fear the exclusion of one of the five proposed, since that can easily be remedied afterwards. And if at last he drops those five and proposes the sixth, hitherto kept hidden but most desired, yet he will not find those five, whom he gained by the earlier proposal, alienated in mind. He says that this artifice succeeded according to wish for the heads of factions in the Conclave of Pius V.

units.la: XXXVII. Proponendus aliquando talis, quem altera Factio ex benigna voluntate, cùm quasi sine ea eligi potuisset, propositum fuisse sentiat: Suadet idem Capiti magna authoritatis respectu alterius (quando non sia però di gran capitale & esperienza; Si tamen non nimium possit, neq; valde magna sit ejus experientia;) atque docet; Sic ab una parte amorem conciliari, timorem ab altera parte utiliter injici, atque ita Gregorium XIII. electum esse.
units.tr: XXXVII. Sometimes one should propose a candidate whom the other faction, believing it could have elected him without them, feels was put forward out of goodwill. The same author advises that the head of the faction, with respect to the great authority of the other (provided he is not of great standing and experience; if however he cannot do very much, nor has very great experience;) and teaches that in this way love is won from one side, and fear is usefully instilled from the other, and that thus Gregory XIII was elected.

units.la: XXXVIII. Imò nonnunquam prudenter in Caput oppositum electionis authoritas transfertur. E ottimo mezo, optimum medium est eidem, adhibendum maximè, là dove le Fattioni sono già stanche e poco meno che disfingannate delle loro forze; id est ubi Factiones jam sunt lassæ & viribus suis frustrata. Atque hoc profuisse Marcello II. & Sixto V. obfuisse contrà Cardinali Sforzæ in Conclavi Pii V.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Indeed, sometimes the power of election is prudently transferred to the opposing head. It is an excellent means, optimum medium est, to be used above all where the factions are already weary and little short of disillusioned about their own strength; that is, where the factions have already grown tired and been frustrated in their own strength. This has helped Marcellus II and Sixtus V, and harmed Cardinal Sforza in the conclave of Pius V.

units.la: XXXIX. In propositionibus autem & Electionibus non semper eadem calcanda via est. Contrarium præcipit Lottinus: In Conclavi, inquit, non possunt ea Consilia, quæ extra Conclave cœpta sunt, constanter retineri: nam res nova cogunt hominem eo pacto se defendere, quo lacessitur, & adversarium ab ea parte ferire, quâ intectum atq; inermem se ostendit; Idcirco illic plura consilia, modósq; plures agendi habere oportet &c.
units.tr: XXXIX. In proposals and elections, however, one must not always tread the same path. Lottini prescribes the opposite: In the conclave, he says, those plans which were begun outside the conclave cannot be consistently kept up, for new circumstances compel a man to defend himself in the way he is attacked, and to strike the adversary on the side where he shows himself uncovered and unarmed; therefore there ought to be more plans and more ways of acting there, etc.

units.la: XL. Si difficultas in tractatione orta sit, ante omnia, ex consilio ejusdem, perpendendum est, an difficultas exsequendi sua optata nascatur ex suo errore, an ex adversariorum potentia. Si ex errore & inexperientia sua proficiscitur & corrigi potest, corrigatur; Verùm si ex adversariorum opera manaverit, itaq; bene rem gesserint, tunc opinio mutanda & minus malum eligendum est. Quod semper consequetur, si modo cuncta prævideantur, & rei status consideretur, & æquitati congrua propositiones minimè refellantur; Quæ conditiones ab aliis Factionum Principibus dubio procul semper accipientur, antequam certam conceperint spem creandi Pontificis, quam præ omnibus ipsimet exoptant, ut effugiant periculum, quod Conclavis ambiguitas secum affert, ubi quotiescunq; mediocre aliquid hodie obtineri possit, non est procrastinandum, ut melioribus potiamur, quia nullus usquam locus atq; ille insolitis & incogitatis rebus æquè variatur.
units.tr: XL. If a difficulty has arisen in the negotiation, one must first of all, on his advice, weigh whether the difficulty in attaining his desired aims arises from his own error or from the power of his opponents. If it proceeds from his own mistake and inexperience and can be corrected, let it be corrected; but if it has come from the work of the opponents, and they have therefore managed the matter well, then the opinion must be changed and the lesser evil chosen. This will always follow, provided everything is foreseen, the state of affairs is considered, and proposals that are fair are not rejected. These conditions will undoubtedly always be accepted by the other leaders of the factions, before they conceive a firm hope of creating a pope, which above all they themselves desire, so that they may escape the danger that the uncertainty of the conclave brings with it, where, whenever something moderate can be obtained today, it should not be put off in the hope of getting better things, because nowhere is there a place equally subject to change through unusual and unforeseen events.

units.la: XLI. In
units.tr: XLI. In

units.la: Quid faciendum sit, si difficultas in tractationibus orta sit.
units.tr: What should be done if a difficulty arises in the negotiations.

units.la: XLI. In magna difficultate novam Legem proponat; Consilium dat Cardinalis Azzolini, rebusferè desperatis, tanquam non malam artem ad distrahendos adversarios; sed Legem tunc proponi vult, ch'habbia ò sembianza di zelo, ò speranza d'interessare e giovare altrui; quæ habeat aut Zeli speciem, aut spem attrahendi & juvandi alios. Sic rumpi filum negotiationum præcedentium, sic animos antea contrarios uniri posse ad propositæ Legis observationem; Sic in Conclavi Pii IV. propositâ Lege, ut nullus amico votum suum revelet, multorum animos & vota Cardinali Caraffæ, contra quem etiam ars ad inventa, alienata fuisse.
units.tr: XLI. In great difficulty he should propose a new law. Cardinal Azzolini gives this advice when affairs are almost desperate, as not a bad art for dividing the adversaries; but he wants the law then proposed which has the appearance of zeal, or the hope of benefiting and helping others; which has either the look of zeal or the prospect of attracting and aiding others. Thus the thread of the preceding negotiations can be broken, and minds previously opposed can be united in observing the proposed law. Thus in the conclave of Pius IV, with a law proposed that no one should reveal his vote to a friend, the minds and votes of many were estranged from Cardinal Carafa, against whom the device had also been turned.

units.la: XLII. Semper autem cogitandum, sic monet iterum Lotinus, maximas difficultates orituras, si Caput de Electione propria cogitet. Quotiescunq; Capita, inquit, authoritate pollent, sed nihilominus velint Pontificatum sibi vendicare, in magnas sese implicant difficultates: nam tanta magnitudinis cupiditas omnem superat cupiditatem; proinde nunquam videntur eos libenter audire, qui diversas à Consiliis suis conditiones proponunt, exceptis iis, à quibus opem aliquam sperant. In quo desiderio magis ac magis immorantur, quia cateri ad Pontificatum aspirantes, qui diversa sunt factionis, ut eorum studia lucrifaciant, sua ipsis offerunt suffragia: quæ nihilominus pleriq; actu ipso denegarent, si ea ambienti profutura suspicarentur. Veruntamen ejus interim spem lactant, neq; sinunt alio mentem convertere.
units.tr: XLII. Moreover, one must always bear in mind, as Lottini again warns, that the greatest difficulties will arise if the head thinks about his own election. Whenever heads, he says, are powerful in authority yet nonetheless wish to claim the papacy for themselves, they entangle themselves in great difficulties: for so great is the desire for such a dignity that it overcomes every other desire; therefore they seem never willingly to listen to those who propose conditions different from their own plans, except those from whom they hope for some help. In this desire they linger more and more, because the others aspiring to the papacy, who belong to different factions, offer their votes to them in order to win over their zeal; which nevertheless most of them would in fact refuse, if they suspected it would profit the one canvassing. Yet meanwhile they feed his hope and do not allow him to turn his mind elsewhere.

units.la: XLIII. Ne nimis suam exaltationem quærentes Principes Factionum prolongare studeant Conclave: Pontificatum ambire & cupere, inquit idem, bonum est, simulitérq; dare operam, ut Conclave differatur parumper, usq; quò res sua componantur, bene est: Sed exploratis voluntatibus eorum, qui fautores sese profitebantur, non debet Princeps pertinaciter suam opinionem defendere, eósq; audire, qui propter eandem ambitionem Conclavis diuturnitatem desiderant; Nam propter ejusmodi pertinaciam illuc devenit, ut Pontifex absque eorum consensu declaretur, vel, ut impetu multorum oppressus subita consentiat atq; inopinata Pontificis Electioni. Qui quidem Pontifex putaturus est, se electum fuisse non ob probitatis opinionem, sed ex opportunitate quadam ac necessitate eligentibus inevitabili. Profitebuntur quidem omnes, ejusdem bonitatis gratiâ ad eum eligendum consensisse, eóq; prætextu timorem honestabunt, itidémq; adversarii eodem prætextu intimam animi molestiam obtegent, & utraq; pars se conscientia sua satisfecisse prædicabit: Sed Cardinalis ille, qui ex his controversiis emersit Pontifex, rem totam optimè percipiet, piet, & pro tanto beneficio civilem solummodo obligationem quandam debebit: neq; ideo illos tanquam bonos & Reipubl. amantes existimabit, sed pro re comperta, si malitia conatus eorum adjuvare potuisset, ipsius etiam, nedum solius virtutis, ope usuros fuisse.
units.tr: XLIII. Lest the leaders of the factions, seeking too much their own exaltation, strive to prolong the conclave: to desire and canvass for the papacy, he says, is good, and at the same time to take care that the conclave be deferred a little, until their affairs are arranged, is well; but once the wills of those who professed themselves supporters have been explored, the leader should not stubbornly defend his own opinion, nor listen to those who, on account of the same ambition, desire the conclave to last a long time; for through such obstinacy it comes about that a pope is declared without their consent, or that, overwhelmed by the sudden onslaught of many, one consents suddenly and unexpectedly to the election of the pope. Such a pope will think that he was elected not for the sake of his reputation for integrity, but from a certain opportunity and necessity unavoidable for the electors. All will indeed profess that they consented to elect him for the sake of his goodness, and they will dignify their fear with this pretext; likewise the adversaries will conceal their inner vexation under the same pretext, and each side will declare that it has satisfied its conscience. But that cardinal who has emerged as pope from these disputes will perceive the whole matter very well, and and for so great a benefit he will owe only a certain civil obligation; nor on that account will he regard them as good men and lovers of the commonwealth, but, knowing the fact, if their malice could have aided their attempts, they would have used his help as well, not merely his virtue.

units.la: XLIV. Quibus artibus Capita contrariarum Factionum se opponere atque exclusionem minus gratorum promovere debeant, jam n. XXII. ubi de suffragiorum dispositione actum, ex Lottino ostendimus.
units.tr: XLIV. By what arts the heads of opposing factions ought to resist one another and promote the exclusion of less welcome candidates, we have already shown from Lottini at no. XXII, where the arrangement of votes was discussed.

units.la: XLV. Nunquam se vinci patiantur à studio vincendi nimio: Auvenga che l'ardor di vincere &c. Ardor vincendi, inquit Cardinalis Azzolini, ita solet turbare judicium, ut quis victoriæ cupidine ductus, quid è re sua sit, animadvertere non possit, quod tamen vel maximè animadverti deberet. Sic Paulum IV. à quibusdam solo Imperiales vincendi studio exaltatum, ardore isto posthac extincto, tanquam adversarium prævisis malis sibi ab eo imminentibus terribilem iisdem apparuisse.
units.tr: XLV. Let them never allow themselves to be conquered by an excessive zeal for conquering: Although the ardour to conquer etc. The ardour of conquering, says Cardinal Azzolini, is accustomed to disturb judgment in such a way that a man led by desire for victory cannot notice what is to his own advantage, which yet ought above all to be noticed. Thus Paul IV, raised up by some of the imperialists solely by their zeal for victory, when that ardour was afterwards extinguished, appeared terrible to the same men as an adversary, the evils threatening them from him having been foreseen.

units.la: XLVI. Neque etiam à timore, siquidem habeant authoritatem & exclusivam, monente eodem, atque rursus exemplum in Electione Pauli IV. ostendente, quæ Imperialibus Gallos nimis timentibus facta sit.
units.tr: XLVI. Nor should they act from fear, since they have authority and the power of exclusion, as the same author warns, again showing by example the election of Paul IV, which was made by the imperialists who feared the French too much.

units.la: XLVII. Sed nec se nimis opponant merenti; Quod dissuadet idem, quia à Spiritu S. regantur Conclavia. De quo tamen dicta & dicenda testari possunt! Imò vel ipsum, quod subjungit, Pauli IV. exemplum, parùm convenit ejusmodi peculiari Spiritûs S. assistentiæ. Cæterùm nonnunquam omninò accidere solet, ut quibusdam nimis commodis suis inhiantibus, aliquis, qui remotissimus videbatur, sedem occupet; Cujus rationes quoque infra dabimus.
units.tr: XLVII. But neither should they oppose the deserving candidate too much; the same author advises against this, because conclaves are governed by the Holy Spirit. Yet what has been said, and what can be said, bears witness against this! Indeed, even the example of Paul IV which he adds agrees poorly with such a special assistance of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, it does sometimes happen altogether that, while some men are too eager for their own advantages, someone who seemed most remote occupies the see. We shall give the reasons for this below as well.

units.la: XLVIII. Atque istæ sunt Regulæ præcipuæ Capitibus qualibuscunque communes. Regulam Capiti Nepoti propriam nonnisi unam damus hanc: ut non proponat nisi probè cognitam creaturam; Cautelam heic quoque suadente Cardinale Azzolini in Aphorismis, ne nimirum Nepotem spes sua fallat, damno & pœnitentiâ æquali. Cujus exemplum in Sixto V. suppeditat, qui alius plane apparuerit, quàm Cardinalis Alexandrini vana spes credederat.
units.tr: XLVIII. These are the chief rules common to any heads whatever. We give only one rule peculiar to the nephew-head, this one: that he should propose only a creature he knows well. Cardinal Azzolini also advises this caution in his Aphorisms, lest the nephew's hope deceive him, with equal loss and repentance. The example of Sixtus V supplies this, who plainly turned out to be another man from what the vain hope of Cardinal Alessandrini had believed.

units.la: XLIX. Cardinales, qui sunt Capita Nationum & observant commoda Principum, sequentia maximè notare debent. Primò ne nimis apertè excludere velint & includere. In quibus moderationem eis commendat Cardinalis Azzolini, ne aliâs, numero adversariorum aucto, in præceps ruant.
units.tr: XLIX. Cardinals who are heads of nations and look after the interests of princes should especially note the following. First, not to wish to exclude and include too openly. On this point Cardinal Azzolini commends moderation to them, lest otherwise, the number of adversaries having grown, they rush headlong.

units.la: L. Secundò, ambientes Papatum & dubitantes, num Reges, quibus sese subdiderunt, ipsi causæ sint eorum exclusionis, non intelligere simulent & Regis voluntatem Cardinalibus abscondant &c. Est Consilium Lottini.
units.tr: L. Secondly, those aspiring to the papacy, and doubting whether the kings to whom they have submitted themselves are themselves the cause of their exclusion, should pretend not to understand, and conceal the king's wishes from the cardinals, etc. This is the advice of Lottini.

units.la: LI. Regulæ Cardinales quosvis, licet nonnullæ magis Papabiles & Capita concernentes, sequentes ferè sunt. Primò, ne se nimis subdant Capiti, quod neque inclusionem, neque magnam de ea spem habet; Prohibet Cardinalis Azzolini, atque damnum Contrarii exemplo ex Conclavi Marcelli II. declarat.
units.tr: LI. Cardinals should observe certain general rules, though some of them concern the more papabile candidates and the heads of factions. These are mostly as follows. First, they should not subject themselves too much to a head, who has neither the power of exclusion nor much hope of it. Cardinal Azzolini forbids this and illustrates the harm of the opposite course by the example of the conclave of Marcellus II.

units.la: LII. Secundò alios bene cognoscere studeant; Quod ab una parte difficile, ab altera verò facile redditur; Difficile ob simulationem. Virtutes enim requiri solita, secundùm Lottinum, vel à natura insita sunt, ut altissimas in animo radices egisse, & in alteram naturam transisse quasi videantur, vel ab ipsis hominibus ad tempus modò simulantur, quò id, quod volunt, facilius consequantur &c. Quum enim intimi hominum sensus difficillimè cognosci possint, fucus sæpe tanto artificio est obtectus, ut vera etiam sagacibus alioqui virtus videatur. Et simulatum quidem nihil est diuturnum: at naturam expellas furcâ, tamen usq; recurrit. Ut verò naturam hominis atq; ingenium pernoscamus, actiones ejus observare necesse est. Ex. gr. si scire velimus, an liberalis quis sit, observabimus, an & quibus donaverit, utrum iis, à quibus rursus beneficium expectârit: quod si hoc, fœneratio illa magis, quàm liberalitas censenda est.
units.tr: LII. Second, they should take care to know others well. This is hard on one side but easy on the other. It is hard because of pretence. For the virtues usually required, according to Lottinus, are either inborn in nature, so that they seem to have struck the deepest roots in the mind and passed into a second nature, or they are only pretended by men for a time, so that they may more easily obtain what they want, and so on. Since the inner feelings of men can very hardly be known, a deception is often covered with such skill that it looks like true virtue even to the otherwise shrewd. Pretence, indeed, lasts for no time at all, but you may drive nature out with a pitchfork, and yet it always comes back. To know a man's nature and character, we must observe his actions. For example, if we wish to know whether someone is generous, we shall observe whether he gives, and to whom, and whether he gives to those from whom he afterwards expects a favour. If so, that should be counted as usury rather than generosity.

units.la: LIII. Facilem autem quadantenus aliorum notitiam reddit, atque, juxta eundem, affectiones singulorum illic scire non est difficile, quia unusquisq; libenter amicorum merita aut defectus enarrat, & vires adversariorum examinat. Modò adsit audiendi patientia, quæ quidem rerum agendarum fundamentum est: nam quicunq; magis differre cupit, quàm audire, is magis docet, quàm discit.
units.tr: LIII. Knowledge of others is made somewhat easier, and, according to the same author, it is not hard to learn the dispositions of individuals there, because everyone gladly recounts the merits or faults of his friends and examines the strength of his opponents. Only let there be patience in listening, which is indeed the foundation of acting well. For whoever wants to talk more than listen teaches more than he learns.

units.la: LIV. Sed, juxta eundem, non solùm qualis is jam sit, qui in Pontificem eligendus est, sed etiam, qualis post futurus sit, considerandum est. Quamprimum enim quis Pontificatum adipiscitur, statim ad aliorum Principum mores accommodare se, suáq; studia & actiones unicè ad Reip. utilitatem dirigere oportet. Verum quidem est, unumquemq; hic diversam ingredi viam, pro suo quemque ingenio & natura: ad retinendum tamen Pontificis favorem nullum est vinculum efficacius, quàm sua ipsorum cognatiocognatio: nec ulla offensa tanta, quam non imperii ac Reip. obliteret respectus. Itaq; sæpe suæ plerique omnes frustrantur Cardinales, qui existimant, amorem, quo is, qui factus est, antea ipsos complexus fuerat, plùs apud istum valiturum, quàm propria aut suorum utilitatis respectum. Quocirca iidem eò allaborant, ut eum faciant Pontificem, in quo duo hæc, Utilitas & Amor concurrant. At, si alterutrum omittendum sit, præcipua utilitatis ratio habenda est, quæ ipsa amorem facilè conciliat. Huc illud quoq; pertinet, ut eos, qui ingenio & moribus nobis similes sunt, suffragiis nostris juvemus. Vix enim quicquam ad benevolentiam conciliandam aptius est, quàm studiorum & morum similitudo. Quod si Cardinalis quispiam longè alia studia sectetur, quàm Pontifex: vix est, ut consuetudine ejus & amicitia diu uti possit, nisi naturam ac vitæ instituta jam inveterata mutare velit: quod durissimum est & quasi impossibile. Sed hanc morum ac vitæ dissimilitudinem perspicere non minùs difficile, quàm rara prudentia est. Cognatorum quoq; (quod ex dictis fluit, & ab eodem inculcatur;) & amicorum futuri Pontificis ratio habenda est; qui plerunq; liberalitatis Pontificia cursum vel sistunt, vel ad se derivant. Equidem novi, inquit, qui hanc unam ob causam eum, cui ceteroqui optimè favebant, suffragiis suis destituerint.
units.tr: LIV. But, according to the same author, one must consider not only what sort of man the one to be elected Pontiff already is, but also what sort he will be afterwards. For as soon as someone attains the papacy, he must at once adapt himself to the ways of other princes, and direct his pursuits and actions solely to the good of the state. It is true that each man enters this path in his own way, according to his own talent and nature. Yet for keeping the Pontiff's favour there is no tie more effective than ties of kinship, and no offence so great that the regard for empire and state does not wipe it out. So very many cardinals are often disappointed, since they think that the affection with which the new Pontiff had embraced them before will count for more with him than the consideration of their own advantage or that of their relations. Therefore they labour to make such a Pontiff as will unite these two things, usefulness and affection. But if one of the two must be set aside, the chief consideration should be usefulness, which itself easily wins affection. To this also belongs that we should help with our votes those who are like us in talent and character. For there is hardly anything more suited to winning goodwill than similarity of pursuits and manners. But if some cardinal follows pursuits quite different from those of the Pontiff, he can hardly enjoy his company and friendship for long, unless he wishes to change his nature and long-established way of life, which is very hard and almost impossible. But to see this difference of manners and life is no less difficult than it is rare to have prudence. We must also take account of the Pontiff's relatives and friends (as follows from what has been said, and is impressed again by the same author), since they often either check the flow of papal generosity or divert it towards themselves. Indeed, I know, he says, of men who for this one reason withdrew their votes from one whom otherwise they had very well favoured.

units.la: LV. Ne putetur beneficii intuitu benevolum futurum:
units.tr: LV. Let it not be thought that he will be well disposed because of a benefit received:

units.la: Chi sta macchiato di conscienza &c. qui malam habet conscientiam, inquit Cardinalis Azzolini in Aphorismis, fallitur, si adjuvat promotionem Papabilis zelo praditi, sub spe, beneficio benevolum redditum iri, atque naturam eatenus mutaturum esse; beneficium enim statim excidit ex natura recipientis, qui eo non amplius indiget, natura autem mutatur nunquam. Subjungit; id expertum esse à sue spese, malo suo Cardinalem Moronem, qui suspectus Inquisitioni, Paulum IV. sibi propitium fore speravit, si omni operâ ad ejus promotionem concurreret, qui tamen posthac eum in Castello S. Angeli malamente prigioniero, in custodia dura tenuerit.
units.tr: He who is stained in conscience, etc., who has a bad conscience, says Cardinal Azzolini in his Aphorisms, is mistaken if he helps the promotion of a papabile endowed with zeal, in hope that he will become well disposed through a benefit, and will thereby change his nature. For the benefit is at once forgotten by the nature of the recipient, who no longer needs it, and nature is never changed. He adds: Cardinal Morone found this to his cost, who, though under suspicion by the Inquisition, hoped that Paul IV would be favourable to him if he worked with all his effort for his promotion. Yet afterwards Paul kept him in harsh custody in the Castel Sant'Angelo, where he was badly held prisoner.

units.la: LVI. Studendum verò quoque est, ut quis cognoscat illos, cum quibus tractare debet;
units.tr: LVI. One must also take care to know those with whom one has to deal;

units.la: Cum diversis enim diversè quoq; tractandum est; postulat Lottinus, ut obsideantur Cardinales, qui authoritatem habent, aut confidentiam, quòsq; magis nôrint, (obsidentes) ut facilius eos ad timorem, aut ad spem allicere iisque persuadere possint; Nam quemadmodum non omnes Cardinales cum quolibet Cardinale conveniunt, ita varianda sunt rationes; Gl' inconstanti &c. Inconstantes, inquit Card. Azzolini, persuadeantur, electionem jam certam esse, ne tempus habeant consultandi atque se mutandi. Quod etiam in Conclavi Sixti V. respectu Cardinalis S. Sixti feliciter successisse docet.
units.tr: For with different men one must deal differently, Lottinus demands, so that the cardinals who have authority or confidence are besieged, and especially those whom one knows better (the besiegers), so that they can more easily be drawn to fear or hope and persuaded by them. For just as not all cardinals agree with every cardinal, so the methods must be varied. The inconstant, etc. The inconstant, says Cardinal Azzolini again, should be persuaded that the election is already certain, so that they have no time to deliberate and change their minds. He shows that this also succeeded happily in the conclave of Sixtus V with respect to Cardinal San Sisto.

units.la: LVII. Atque ita nonnulli obsideri debent, ut eis tempus ad consultationes in contrarium non concedatur. Fù stimata gran sagacità quella &c. Magna sagacitatis illud æstimabatur, inquit denuò Card. Azzolini, quo usi sunt Fautores Marcelli II. ad certam reddendam ejus electionem, occultè conjunxerunt se magis certi, & luserunt, chartas in manibus tenentes, numerando & considerando Cardinales, quos allici posse sperabant, sufficientem numerum constituentes; Postea elegerunt ex se quosdam majoris authoritatis, & Marcello maximè familiares, qui hinc inde seorsim, quos sperabant, acquirere studuerunt, eis ob oculos ponendo spem, quam inde concipere possint, acquisitos autem è conspectu nunquam dimiserunt, donec, de novo calculo votorum facto, sine induciis & subitò ad adorationem ventum est. Quod artificium tantâ dexteritate adhibitum fuit, ut felicissimè optatum pepererit effectum.
units.tr: LVII. And so some must be besieged in such a way that they are not granted time for deliberations to the contrary. That was esteemed great sagacity, etc. It was judged great sagacity, says Cardinal Azzolini again, which the supporters of Marcellus II used to make his election certain. They secretly joined together, being more certain, and played with cards in their hands, counting and considering the cardinals whom they hoped could be won over, and so fixing a sufficient number. Afterwards they chose from among themselves some of greater authority and especially close to Marcellus, who strove to win over those whom they hoped for, each separately, setting before their eyes the hope they might conceive from it, and never let go of those already won out of their sight, until, after a new count of the votes had been made, they came without delay and suddenly to the adoration. This device was used with such skill that it brought forth the desired result most happily.

units.la: LVIII. Non autem facilè fidendum votum unum & alterum speciosos & honoris causâ quærentibus, neque simulatio tunc limites excedere debet: Nam sub petitionibus ejusmodi, ut idem docet, tal hora vi si nascondono scogli non pensati già mai; nonnunquam latent scopuli, de quibus nunquam cogitâsses. Sic in Conclavi Pii IV. Cardinali Torresio fere Papatum, 32. vota in Scrutinio, multa in eodem Cardinali Pisano acquisita fuisse testatur.
units.tr: LVIII. Nor must one easily trust a vote or two given to those who seek them for show and for the sake of honour, nor should pretence then exceed its limits. For under petitions of this kind, as the same author observes, "there are at times hidden rocks never thought of"; sometimes reefs lie hidden of which you never thought. So he testifies that in the conclave of Pius IV nearly the papacy went to Cardinal Torres, who had 32 votes in the scrutiny, and that many votes were won for the same Cardinal Pisano.

units.la: LIX. Omnium ratio habenda est, timeri debent omnes, ex consilio Lottini: Nunquam satis admonetur, inquit, quod nunquam non animadvertendum est, & raro animadvertitur: hoc autem est: In Conclavium omnium habendam rationem, & quemlibet timendum esse, & efficiendum, ut ambitus ita à principio ad finem ordinentur, ne invitis Principibus Factionum Pontifex creari possit. Hinc siquidem dignoscitur, quantum ista præmeditatio atq; ordo possit, quia in principio Capita cum sequacibus suis conjuncta possunt celebriores ac meliores Candidatos excludere, quales sunt, qui futuri Pontifices populari voce acclamantur. Quod, cùm ita se habeat, tantò credibilius est, eodem ordine ac conspiratione minores Candidatos excludi posse, & à Pontificatu, quem plerumq; consequuntur, arceri: & nihilominus, vel quia, unde non valde timetur, ibi minor cura collocatur, vel quia homines perpetuò vigilare & omnibus horis bene prospicere nequeunt, semper imparati, vel coguntur Candidatum propositum, quem nollent, minoris dedecoris ergò, approbare, vel cum periculo subitam exclusionem machinari.
units.tr: LIX. All must be taken into account; everyone must be feared, according to Lottinus's counsel: "It is never sufficiently reminded," he says, "what must always be noticed and is rarely noticed. This is: that account must be taken of all in the conclave, that everyone must be feared, and that the canvassing must be arranged from beginning to end so that the Pontiff cannot be created against the wishes of the leaders of the factions." For from this one may see how much such forethought and order can do. At the start the heads, joined with their followers, can exclude the more famous and better candidates, such as those whom the popular voice hails as future Pontiffs. Since this is so, it is all the more credible that by the same order and conspiracy the lesser candidates can be excluded and kept from the papacy, which they usually attain. And nevertheless, either because less care is given where little is feared, or because men cannot keep watch continually and look well ahead at every hour, they are always unprepared; or they are compelled to approve a candidate put forward whom they would not want, for the sake of less disgrace, or to plot a sudden exclusion at risk.

units.la: LX. Ut in bello, ita hic quoque, peccare bis, vix licet, judicio ejusdem; Cúmq; adversarius praparatus & urgens atq; instans habeatur, & qui errores alienos in victoriam sui convertere festinat, hinc fit, ut parvi errores in Conclavi commissi gravissimi evadant, minimaq; voluntatum, sive propitia sint, sive adversa, mutationes maximos pariant effectus: quippe Papatum valent donare aut auferre: Et ratio est, quia amici statim juvari, inimici vero statim offendi possunt. Una offensiuncula, addit Anonymus consentiens in Dissert. de Creatione Pontificum; una Cardinalium creatio, unus vel levissimus casus rem omnem perturbare, consilia omnia evertere, spem omnem praecidere solet.
units.tr: LX. As in war, so here too, it is hardly permitted to err twice, according to the same judgement. Since the rival is regarded as prepared, pressing and at hand, and whoever hastens to turn the errors of others into his own victory, it comes about that small mistakes made in the Conclave turn out to be most serious, and the slightest changes of will, whether favourable or hostile, produce the greatest effects, since they are able to bestow or take away the papacy. The reason is that friends can be helped at once, while enemies can be offended at once. A like-minded anonymous author, in his dissertation on the Creation of Popes, adds: a single slight offence, a single creation of cardinals, or one very trivial mishap is wont to upset the whole affair, overturn all plans and cut off all hope.

units.la: LXI. Vitanda quoque affectuum vehementia & festinatio: Propensiones, inquit idem, incitantur a plerisque adeo, ut partim ex affectu suo, partim ex aliorum persuasione, eo temporis momento nihil aliud perspiciant, quàm quod sibi suggeritur a timore, vel obstinatione seu ambitione, aut desiderio vindicta, sive quocunq; illorum affectuum, qui omnes hominum cogitationes brevis horae spatio evertunt. Dúmq; affectus ille urget, adéstq;, etsi rerum futurarum status ob oculos versetur, statim cogitant, quod communiter similibus in rebus cogitatur, hoc est, magnitudinem beneficii, quo electus in Pontificem afficitur, posse damnis quibuscunque occurrere, quam ratio in contrarium adduxerit. Idcirco apertè cernimus, quotiescunq; consilium capitur, vel nimium festinando, vel nimio affectu, semper in errorem incidi: nam festinatio tempus eripit ea conquirendi, quae ante conclusionem rei consideranda fuerant; affectus autem impedit occupatque animum, ut nihil sinat cognoscere, nisi quod eo momento angit & urget.
units.tr: LXI. The vehemence of the passions and haste must also be avoided. Inclinations, the same writer says, are stirred up in most people so much that, partly from their own feeling and partly from the persuasion of others, at that moment they see nothing except what is suggested to them by fear, obstinacy, ambition, the desire for revenge, or whichever of those passions drives all human thoughts out in the space of a short hour. And while that passion presses and is at hand, even if the state of future things is set before their eyes, they at once think what is commonly thought in similar cases, namely, that the greatness of the benefit by which the one elected is raised to the pontificate can meet any losses whatever, whatever reason may argue to the contrary. Hence we clearly see that whenever a decision is taken, either by hasty action or by excessive passion, men always fall into error: for haste snatches away the time needed to seek out those things which ought to have been considered before the matter was concluded; passion, on the other hand, hinders and occupies the mind, so that it allows it to know nothing except what troubles and presses it at that moment.

units.la: LXII. Abesse tandem debent inconstantia atque torpedo animi, item negligentia, duae res non minus ac festinatio & vehementia affectuum noxiae. Etenim inveniuntur, teste eodem, nonnulli, qui, etiamsi ab affectibus immunes existant, satisq; temporis habent ad res examinandas: nihilominus propter ista nihil unquam boni efficere posse videntur. Atque equidem hac quatuor hominum genera (comprehendit adhuc etiam illos, qui affectibus abripiuntur, aut festinant;) Si conquerantur, quòd negotia votis suis minimè respondeant, summá injuriâ conqueruntur; Oportebat enim ab se nihil eorum, quae facienda erant, praetermitti; deinde si ex animi sententia res non successisset, tum justius conquererentur; Verum nunquam admiratione dignum est, si quis, vel incogitanter, vel stolido quodam modo, vel affectu aliquo obcaecatus, vel nimiâ festinatione aliquid aggressus fuerit, quòd negotium illud exiuum minùs nùs prosperum sortiatur : imò inter miracula collocandum erit, si bene suc-cesserit &c.
units.tr: LXII. Finally, inconstancy and sluggishness of mind must be absent, likewise negligence, two things no less harmful than haste and the vehemence of the passions. For, according to the same writer, there are found some who, even if they are free from the passions and have enough time to examine matters, nevertheless seem never able to achieve anything good because of these faults. And indeed, if these four kinds of men (this also includes those who are carried away by the passions or act in haste) complain that their affairs have not answered to their wishes, they complain with the greatest injustice. For nothing of what had to be done ought to have been left undone by themselves; then, if the matter had not turned out according to their mind, they would have had more justice in complaining. But it is never a thing to wonder at if someone, whether thoughtlessly, or in some foolish manner, or blinded by some passion, or by excessive haste, has undertaken something and it meets with a less successful outcome; indeed, if it turns out well, it will have to be counted among the miracles, etc.

units.la: LXIII. Hactenus Regulæ Papabilibus, Capitibus & Cardinalibus reliquis præscriptæ ab iis, qui ita Electionis optimè instituendæ suasores videri volunt,cùm tamen pleraeque in se vitiosæ,injustæ,fraudulentæ appareant; Reliquæ,quæ monita Politica, cæterum salubria continent, hic saltem de ambitione, partim eorum, quibus, partim eorum, contra quos Regulas ejusmodi præscribi necesse fuit,testantur. Nævis certè & vitiis scatere debent Electiones, quarum bene, ut putant, ordinandarum Regulæ ipsæmet vitium partim continent,partim propius ostendunt! Sed Praxin multò magis vitiosam esse sequentia docebunt.
units.tr: LXIII. Thus far the rules prescribed for the papabili, the heads, and the remaining cardinals by those who wish to appear the best advisers for conducting an election well, although most of them appear vicious, unjust and fraudulent in themselves. The remaining rules, which contain otherwise wholesome political warnings, here at least bear witness to ambition, partly of those for whom, and partly of those against whom, such rules had to be prescribed. Surely elections ought to abound in blemishes and vices, when the very rules meant to order them well, as they think, partly contain the vice and partly point more closely to it! But the following will show that the practice is far more vicious.

units.la: SECTIO QUARTA, In qua De vitiosa vitiosarum Regularum applicatione, artibus electionem promoventibus indignis, precibus nimiis, promissionibus, contra-promissionibus, comminationibus, simulationibus, dissimulationibus, mendaciis, calumniis, fraudibus injustis, Simonia, Vi, Discordia, pertinacia, hincque oriri solitis diuturnis in Conclavi moris, tædiis, inopinatorum promotionibus, incertitudinibus respectu promovendorum electionem antecedentibus, verbo; de artificiosissimis, sed ordinario vitiosis Electionibus agitur;
units.tr: SECTION FOURTH, in which the faulty application of faulty rules is discussed: arts that promote an election but are unworthy of it, excessive entreaties, promises, counter-promises, threats, pretences, dissemblings, lies, calumnies, unjust frauds, simony, force, discord, obstinacy, and the lengthy customs of the conclave that usually arise from these, weariness, unexpected promotions, and uncertainties about those to be promoted that precede the election. In short, the most artful, yet ordinarily faulty, elections are treated.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.tr: I. A transition from the rules to practice, which first deals with entreaties, threats and promises. II. Promises and counter-promises create obligations to render help. III. No one can place much trust in them. IV. Deceitful promises. V. Pretences; specifically that of Sixtus V. VI. Also outside the conclave. VII. Of others. VIII. Real pretences and dissemblings. IX. Lies. X. Calumnies. XI. When an unwelcome truth is published out of hatred and a desire to harm. XII. Other unworthy arts; for in proposals not everyone acts in earnest, nor in giving votes. XIII. Not only the young. XIV. Often discord within the opposing party is also sought. XV. Frauds. XVI. Nocturnal dealings. XVII. Haste in the proceedings and fraud in the form of election. XVIII. Simony. XIX. How far it extends, according to Damiani. XX. Even the strictly so-called kind is in use. XXI. Examples: Stephen VI, the case of Formosus; Platina's general complaint about Sergius III, and Stella's about Romanus I; the tyrants of the ninth and tenth centuries. Examples also of Boniface VII, John XVII. XXII. Sylvester II. XXIII. Benedict IX. Sylvester III. XXIV. Gregory VI. XXV. Sylvester III again; and Platina's more general complaint; Gregory VI once more. XXVI. Clement II. XXVIII. Damasus II. XXIX. Benedict X. Eugenius III. XXX. From the conclave of Clement V. XXXI. The example of John XXIII. XXXII. From the conclave of Pius II. XXXIII. Innocent VIII. XXXIV. The author's wish, on that basis, for Innocent. XXXV. The example of Alexander VI. XXXVI. From the conclave of Pius III and cardinalism. XXXVII. From the conclave of Julius II. XXXVIII. Leo X. XXXIX. Leo XI. XL. Gregory XV. XLI. Innocent X. XLII. Alexander VII. XLIII. Clement IX. XLIV. How great the fault of simony is in papal elections, apart from Scripture, is evident. XLV. From the canon of the Apostles and of Chalcedon. XLVI. From the letter of Athalaric and the example of Dioscorus. XLVII. From the decree of Pelagius. XLVIII. From the Roman council under John XII. XLIX. From Damiani's letter and poem. L. From his special testimony. LI. From the Roman council under Gregory VII. LII. From the case of Victor II. LIII. From Gregory VII's admonition to the Emperor Henry. LIV. From the admonitions of Urban VI to the cardinals. LV. From the admonitions of Gregory XII. LVI. Finally it is shown in various ways that simonists have no power at all and accomplish nothing well. LVII. There follows the way of fear: force brought against predecessors. The example of Vigilius, Pelagius, Leo V (by Christopher), Clement II (by Stephen), Benedict VI (by Boniface), and others removed by others, most of all by poison. LVIII. Force applied in other ways, as is shown by many examples. LIX. Force arises from discord and produces discord; not every harmonious election, however, was also good. LX. But many were also highly discordant. LXI. Discord is the daughter of obstinacy. LXII. Both draw out the business of the election at length. LXIII. But the long duration of the conclave produces weariness. LXIV. Weariness often (affects) the Pope. LXV. Often the unexpected. LXVI. Therefore, he does not argue for a peculiar assistance of the Holy Spirit in papal elections. LXVII. Rather, he argues, among other things, a lack of the qualities required for the most artful elections. LXVIII. Which is also confirmed by the testimony of an anonymous writer. LXIX. Who also, from the same principle, judges a certain prediction of the person to be elected impossible. Why promises concerning the future Pope are forbidden. LXX. All that we have said proves, and the testimonies also bear out, concerning bad arts in general, that the elections of the Roman Pontiffs are many, most, and today all, bad. LXXI. Conclusion.

units.la: I. QUalis jam, post considerationem Regularum, praxis sit, respectu artificiosarum molitionum supra terminis generalibus generaliter expositum est, quae jam artificiosae molitiones, media vitium habentia, porrò atque specialiùs recenseri debent. Ubi nobis primò preces, promissiones, minae occurrunt. In Conclavi Pii II. non cessavano di rogare, di promettere, & insieme di minacciare: non cessabant rogare, promittere, & minari. In Conclavi Gregorii XIV. Tentavano tutta via di Spagnuoli e di fuori con minaccie e di
units.tr: I. What the practice is, after consideration of the rules, has been set out in general terms with respect to artful schemes; now the artful schemes themselves, which involve faulty means, must be listed more fully and specifically. Here first come to us entreaties, promises and threats. In the conclave of Pius II they did not cease to ask, to promise and at the same time to threaten: non cessabant rogare, promittere, & minari. In the conclave of Gregory XIV they kept trying, with threats from the Spaniards and from outside, and with entreaties from within,

units.la: Gregorii XIV. Tentavano tutta via di Spagnuoli e di fuori con minaccie e di dentro con prieghi &c. In Conclavi Pii V. Boromæus, Como & Altemps concluserunt, che per via de cortesia &c. civilitate nihil apud Florentinos effici posse, proin timoris viam esse eligendam. Cùm in Conclavi Pauli V. Gioiosa ad Toscum transfire vellet, amplexando & precibus violentis intercedebant adversarii & promissionibus maximis. In Conclavi Gregorii XV. varia variis promissa, etiam quæ Ecclesiæ statum diminuissent, Montaltio à Borghesio spes facta, se post mortem Camporæ jam promovendi eum aut Creaturarum aliquam certo certius promoturum esse. In Conclavi Leonis XI. ipsi Medici promissionibus inducti credebantur ad persuadendum ægro commorationem in Conclavi ulteriorem. In eodem tanto cum studio Dietrichsteinii votum ambiebatur, che rassemblava la bella Elena, per cui guerreggiorno i Greci e Trojani, qui similis erat (verba sunt Authoris) Helena, de qua tamdiu pugnabant Græci & Trojani. In Conclavi Urbani VIII. visus fuit Cardinalis Nepos Ludovisius, deporre il fasto e descendre ad ogni sorte di humiliatione, e vili preghiere, fastum deponere, & ad omnis generis humiliationes precésque viles descendere. Borghesius autem non s'astenne di prorompere in querele e minaccie : in querelas & minas prorumpere sustinuit. Et quando per disporre gli huomini in questo modo ad acconsentire in alcuna cosa, pare che vi siano due strade l'amore o il timore : hominibus vel amore, vel timore aliquid persuadetur, juxta Conclave Clementis X. Cardinalis Chigius, con le aperte dichiarationi contre le Squadrone &c. postquam se aperte contrà Squadronistas declarâsset, amorem deseruit &c. atque ab illis haud magis amatus, multò minùs timore eos convincere potuit.
units.tr: Gregory XIV. They kept trying with threats from the Spaniards and from outside, and with entreaties from within, etc. In the conclave of Pius V, Borromeo, Como and Altemps concluded that by courtesy and civility nothing could be achieved with the Florentines, and therefore the way of fear had to be chosen. When in the conclave of Paul V Gioiosa wished to pass over to Tuscus, the opponents intervened with embraces, violent entreaties and very great promises. In the conclave of Gregory XV various things were promised to various people, even things which would have diminished the state of the Church, and Montalto was given hope by Borghese that, after the death of Campora, he would certainly promote him or some one of his creatures. In the conclave of Leo XI the Medici themselves were believed, induced by promises, to persuade the sick man to stay on in the conclave. In the same conclave, Dietrichstein's vote was sought with such zeal that he was like the beautiful Helen, for whom the Greeks and Trojans fought (these are the author's words), Helen, over whom Greeks and Trojans so long fought. In the conclave of Urban VIII the cardinal nephew Ludovisi seemed to lay aside his pride and stoop to every kind of humiliation and base entreaty. Borghese, however, did not refrain from breaking out into complaints and threats. And since to dispose men in this way to agree to something, there seem to be two roads, love or fear: men are persuaded of something either by love or by fear, according to the conclave of Clement X. Cardinal Chigi, after he had openly declared himself against the Squadroni, lost love; and, not loved by them, he could much less, by fear, win them over.

units.la: II. Pariunt preces, promissiones & minæ obligationes sive contra-promissiones de auxilio præstando, voto dando, prout etiam sæpè aliàs alteri auxilium suum & suorum promittitur; Licèt illud contra memoratas Pontificum constitutiones fiat. In Conclavi Pii V. Cardinalis Ferrara rogatus fuit, ut Cardinalem Medicæum absolveret ab obligatione excludendi Moronem. In Conclavi Gregorii XIV. ciascuna di 2. fattioni dato parola di non pigliar mai Cremona; Utraque factio promisit, se nunquam Cremonam electuras. In Conclavi Pauli V. Aldobrandinus promisit Farnesiis exclusionem quorundam & isti Aldobrandino promotionem creaturæ suæ. Idem Aldobrandinus, postquam interrogâsset creaturas, an vellent secundùm promissiones sibi factas unam ex Creaturis, Papam creavit. In Conclavi Clementis VIII. jactantia Severinistarum de superfluis fluis etiam plùs quàm quinque votis: & in Conclavi Gregorii XV. Camporistarum, se ingredi cum Papa jam facto; non sine præviis promissionibus & obligationibus esse potuit. In eodem Conclavi Altempsio contra Severinam loquenti tribuitur : O qualche revelatione da Dio &c. aut quadam revelatio divina, aut certa promissio humana de rebus, quæ postea contigerunt; Quorum utrum probabilius sit, judicet Lector. In Conclavi Leonis XI. si sece professione di fede contro Baronio: conjurârunt contra Baronium. In eodem Conclavi obligationes pro Baronio emta memorantur.
units.tr: II. Entreaties, promises and threats produce obligations, or counter-promises, to render help and to give a vote, just as very often, at other times too, help for oneself and one's own is promised to another, although this is done contrary to the aforesaid constitutions of the Popes. In the conclave of Pius V Cardinal Ferrara was asked to absolve Cardinal Medici from the obligation of excluding Morone. In the conclave of Gregory XIV each of the two factions gave its word never to take Cremona; each faction promised that it would never choose Cremona. In the conclave of Paul V Aldobrandini promised the Farnese exclusion of certain men, and to these Aldobrandini a promotion of his own creature. The same Aldobrandini, after he had asked the creatures whether they wished, according to the promises made to them, one of the creatures to be made Pope, created the Pope. In the conclave of Clement VIII the boasting of the Severini about surplus votes, even more than five, and in the conclave of Gregory XV the boasting of the Camporesi that they would enter with a Pope already made, could not have happened without prior promises and obligations. In the same conclave, to Altemps speaking against Severina is attributed the words: Or some revelation from God, etc., or a certain divine revelation, or a certain human promise, concerning things that later came to pass. Which of these is more probable, let the reader judge. In the conclave of Leo XI, if they made a profession of faith against Baronius: they conspired against Baronius. In the same conclave, obligations bought for Baronius are recorded.

units.la: III. Interim tamen & illud tenendum est, ejusmodi obligationibus & promissionibus neminem multùm fidere posse; cùm nihil frequentius in Conclavibus sit datæ fidei fractione. Le parole fallaci per l'ordinario in tutti gli huomini in ogni tempo, inquit Author Conclavis Gregorii XIV. ma fallacissime ne i Cardinali in Conclave &c. Id est: Promissiones sunt ordinariò fallaces, sed maximè in Conclavi, ubi exiguus motus, minimum idque sæpè inopinatum accidens omnibus horis res & cum rebus voluntates mutant, non obstantibus etiam promissionibus &c. Atque usque adeò fallaces sunt promissiones Conclaviariæ, ut etiam in proverbium abierint. Cùm enim in Conclavi eodem aliquis datam à se fidem prætexeret, paucis ei responsum fuit: essere parole, come si suol dire, di Conclave, esse fidem, ut dici soleat, Conclaviariam, & cùm contrà in Conclavi Gregorii XV. Madruccio promissio data pro Campora objiceretur, similiter paucis respondit: E vero, che l'ho promesso, ma nuovi accidenti mi liberano di questa promessa: certè promisi, sed nova accidentia me liberant. De similibus autem fidefragis Cardinalis Ascanius, che venne in qualche sospitione, che da molti non li fusse osservata la fede, suspicans, fidem datam sibi à multis non servari, graviter in Conclavi Urbani VII. conquestus, atque auditus est ad aliquem Cardinalem dicens: Si esset in iis fides (sunt verba Ciceronis) in quibus summa esse deberet, non laboraremus. Laborantes certè & repulsam passi, quorum jactantiam §. praced. innuimus, eandem querelam ingeminare potuissent. Exemplum quoque simulatæ promissionis suppeditat Il Card. p.3.l.3.353. ubi promisit Legatus Hispania Chigio protectionem tantopere desideratam, sed simulando, ut supra visum est.
units.tr: III. Meanwhile, it must also be held that no one can put much trust in such obligations and promises, since nothing is more frequent in conclaves than the breaking of given faith. "The deceitful words of men in general, at every time," says the author of the Conclave of Gregory XIV, "but most deceitful among the cardinals in conclave, etc." That is: promises are usually deceitful, but most of all in conclave, where a slight movement, and often the smallest unexpected accident, changes things and wills at every hour, notwithstanding promises, etc. Conclave promises are so deceitful that they have even passed into a proverb. When someone in the same conclave pleaded the faith he had given, he was briefly answered: these are conclave words, as people say; it is conclave faith, as it is commonly called. And when, in the conclave of Gregory XV, the promise Madruccio had given on behalf of Campora was thrown at him, he likewise answered briefly: It is true that I promised it, but new accidents free me from this promise: I did promise, but new circumstances release me. As for similar breakers of faith, Cardinal Ascanius, who came under some suspicion, that by many his given faith was not kept, complained bitterly in the conclave of Urban VII, and was heard saying to a certain cardinal: If there were faith in those in whom it ought to be supreme, we would not be in trouble (these are the words of Cicero). Those who were in trouble and had suffered rejection, whose boasting we hinted at in the previous section, could have repeated the same complaint. The Spanish legate also supplies an example of a feigned promise, when he promised Chigi the protection he so greatly desired, but by pretence, as was seen above.

units.la: IV. Neque ista datæ fidei fractio adscribenda est ordinariò Pontificum constitutionibus, quæ promissiones & obligationes nes
units.tr: IV. Nor should this breaking of given faith ordinarily be ascribed to the constitutions of the Popes, which declare promises and obligations null and void.

units.la: Mmm mes irritas declarant, nam, ut ostensum est, parvi habitis illis con-stitutionibus promittunt, se tenẽri credunt, absolvi volunt, cau-sas alias desertionis allegant, imò tales etiam dantur non pauci, quod jam ostendam, qui planè mendaciter promittunt, neque un-quam animum habent satisfaciendi, præstandi. Talem sistit Au-thor Conclavis Pauli V. Cardinalem Nepotem Aldobrandinum, che escludeva &c. qui excludebat tacitè Montaltianos omnes, licèt se amicum Camerini, & Montelpazi simulàrit, atque insuper spem aliis fecerit, ita ut senex nullus fuerit, cui non promiserit, se eum Papam facturum. Si-milem habuit Conclave Urbani VIII. Cardinalem Nepotem Borg-hesium, de quo, ancor che di parole e dimonstrationi fosse largo ad ogn' uno &c. licèt verbis & demonstrationibus erga quoscunq; liberalis, tamen suffragiis atque reali favore parcissimus habitus erat; senibus spem faciebat, ne accederent Ludovicio. In Conclavi Alexandri VII. Ogn' uno di loro (22. Cardinali, che aspiravano al Papato) si lasciava imbarcare da Capi di fattione, ne vera che non havesse speranza déssere il più amato da quelli; Id est. Ex 22. Cardinalibus aspirantibus singuli proponi volebant, atque spem, se pra aliis à Capitibus amari habebant. Barberinus ingre-diebatur cum proposito, omnes suas creaturas excludendi, tribus tantùm exceptis, interim omnes eum sibi promittebant, prestando fede alle sue promesse; fidem habentes verbis ipsius. Per Principem Palestinæ signifi-cavit ante ingressum cuivis, ch'egli non haveva altro intento, che di promovère la sua persona, ricordava egli gli obblighi, che diceva d'havere, parlava della convenienza: Id est, sibi tantùm propositum esse illum eligere, obligationes commemorabat, quas se habere dicebat, loquebatur de convenientia. Quomodo Chigii suffragium in Conclavi Clementis IX. & scrutinio in favorem Rospigliofii contra datam fidem defuisse deprehensum fuerit, jam supra indicavimus. Ante-ingressum in Conclave istud: Gli Spagnuoli escludivano Celsi, referente Authore Cardinalisimi, p. 3. l. 3. p. 329. con tutte le viscere del cuore, mà non già con le parole della lingua &c. Hispani Celsium ex toto corde excludebant, sed non lingua: verùm ei promittebant, se per mariæ & montes, ad ei serviendum ituros, sed differebant illud iter semper, neque itineris instrumenta invenire poterant. In eodem Conclavi putabatur, Bar-berinum & Chigium ad electionem Rospigliofii decernendam & ordinandam congregatos fuisse, ma però non havevano intentione ne l'uno, ne l'altro à far da senno; Sed neuter serio agebat, commiserunt tamen negotium Cardinali Azzolini, qui & omni studio vota con-quirebat, quirebat,mà quelli steßi che promessero il voto ad Azzolino per Rospiglio- si in publico,lo negarso forse per Azzolino in segreto à Rospigliosi; sed illi ipsi qui publicè promiserunt votum Azzolino pro Rospigliosio, Rospigliosio illud fortè propter Azzolinum non dederunt secretò. In Conclavi Clementis X. eodem quatuor Legato Hispaniæ proponente, lui per complimento e gala approvogli, con la mira più in tutti gli altre, che in Bonvisi: ipse per complementum eos approbavit, sed quemvis alium reverà malens, quàm Bonvifium, qui erat unus ex illis. Idem Chigius haveva negoziato &c. Jam negotiatus erat bonis verbis & bonarum intentionum promissionibus, cum Gallis, qui ei fidem habuerunt. Idem semper credidit, se Gallos ligâsse humanis literis Parisios missis. In eodem Conclavi; ardiscono di porre in speranza &c. Id est, omnibus Papabilibus spem fecerunt, ne ob commoda propria aliò concurrerent, licèt spes falsa fuerit. Communem autem morem exprimunt denuò supra jam allata Lottini verba, in casu ambientium Pontificiam dignitatem Principum; Cateri ad Pontificatum adspirantes, inquit, qui diversa sunt factionis, ut illorum studia lucrifaciant, sua ipsis offerunt suffragia, quæ nihilominùs actu ipso denegant, si ea ambienti profutura suspicarentur. Sic omnia simulationibus atque mendacibus promissionibus ab hac parte plena.
units.tr: For, as has been shown, the cardinals, having made little of those constitutions, promise, believe themselves bound, wish to be released, and allege other reasons for their desertion. Indeed, there are not a few who promise quite falsely, and never have any intention of keeping or performing, as I shall now show. The author of the Conclave of Paul V presents Cardinal Nephew Aldobrandini, who excluded, etc., who tacitly excluded all the Montalto men, although he pretended to be a friend of Camerino and Montalpazi, and moreover gave hope to others, so that there was no old man to whom he did not promise that he would make him pope. The Conclave of Urban VIII had a similar figure in Cardinal Nephew Borghese, of whom it is said: although he was generous with words and displays to everyone, etc.; although he was liberal in words and displays toward whomever, he was yet held most sparing in votes and real favour; he gave hope to the old men so that they would not join Ludovisi. In the Conclave of Alexander VII, each one of them (the 22 cardinals who aspired to the papacy) let himself be embarked by the heads of factions, nor was there one who did not hope to be the most loved by them. That is: of the 22 cardinals aspiring, each wanted to be proposed, and each had hope that he was loved above the others by the heads. Barberini entered with the purpose of excluding all his creatures except three; meanwhile all promised him, trusting in his promises, having faith in his words. Through the Prince of Palestrina he signified to each before entering that he had no other aim than to advance his person; he recalled the obligations he said he had, and spoke of convenience. That is: it was only his purpose to elect him; he recalled the obligations which he said he had, and spoke of convenience. How Chigi's vote and ballot in favour of Rospigliosi, contrary to his given faith, was found to be lacking, I have already indicated above. Before entering the conclave, that saying: the Spaniards excluded Celsi, according to the author of the Cardinalismo, p. 3, l. 3, p. 329, with all the bowels of their heart, but not with the words of their tongue, etc. The Spaniards excluded Celsi from their whole heart, but not with their tongue; but they promised him that they would go to serve him through the seas and mountains, yet they always postponed that journey, nor could they find the means of travelling. In the same conclave it was thought that Barberini and Chigi had met to decide and arrange the election of Rospigliosi, but neither of them had any intention of acting in earnest; yet they entrusted the business to Cardinal Azzolini, who sought votes with all zeal, but those very men who publicly promised their vote to Azzolini for Rospigliosi, perhaps denied it to Rospigliosi secretly in favour of Azzolini. In the conclave of Clement X, when the Spanish legate Quatuor proposed the same candidate, he approved him out of compliment and courtesy, with his aim more on all others than on Bonvisi; he approved them out of politeness, but in truth preferred any other to Bonvisi, who was one of them. The same Chigi had negotiated, etc.; he had already negotiated with the French, who trusted him, with fair words and promises of good intentions. He always believed that he had bound the French by letters sent to Paris. In the same conclave: they dare to put in hope, etc.; that is, they gave hope to all the papabili, so that they would not run elsewhere for their own advantage, although the hope was false. Moreover, the words of Lottini already quoted above express the common custom, in the case of princes canvassing for the papal dignity: the others who aspire to the papacy, of differing factions, so as to gain their pursuits, offer their votes to them, which nevertheless in fact they deny, if they suspected that they would benefit the canvasser. Thus everything on this side is full of pretences and lying promises.

units.la: V. Sed non minimi tunc simulatores atque dissimulatores sunt Cardinales Papabiles, sive Candidati, quorum commune symbolum: Qui nescit simulare, non poterit regnare. De simulatione Sixti respe&tu auxilii necessarii jam Differt.I. Se&t.VI. n.36. actum est, & de simulatione morborum atque senectutis agemus, ubi de nævis respe&tu eorum, qui eliguntur, & in specie de senectute decrepita. Simulationes varias à regulis permittit, imò per regulas commendari, præcedentia docent. Nonnulla tamen & hic quoad praxin secundùm regulas referenda erunt. Maximus & maximè artificiosus simulator, quem homines unquam aspexerint, fuit, antequam, & ut Papatum consequeretur, jam sæpiùs memoratus Sixtus V. vel, quomodo tunc vocabatur, Cardinalis Montaltius. Simulandi artem jam calluit exercuitque in Conclavi Gregorii XIII. Lubeat illud cognoscere ex Vita, p.I. l.4.276. seqq. Factis Pii V. exequiis, Cardinales Conclave ingressi sunt, sed Montaltius licèt inter eos fuerit, non tamen inter eos esse videbatur, non majori cum strepitu in Conclavi versando, quàm pauper Monachus in cella sua, ex sua non egrediebatur, nisi ad Missam celebrandam, singebat se planè ignarum omnis generis negotiationum, & ut ostenderet, se nulli parti adhærere, allicere volentibus respondere solebat, verbis simplicitatem tantùm spirantibus, dicendo; se quidem paratum esse, di tener &c. sequi præeuntes, sed quia nunquam in Conclavi fuerit, nolle se errorem aliquem per ignorantiam committere, quem alii experientia sua evitare queant, atque his similibúsque sermonibus occurrebat semper omnibus, qui eum in partes pertrahere voluerunt. Ille autem procedendi modus, tantopere contrarius vitæ anteactæ, manifestum indicium continebat, ficta esse omnia, atque affectata, ut mansuetudine res suas promoveret, quod & agnovisse videtur Cardinalis Gambara Brefciano, qui dum vesperà quàdam cum Montaltio de instante electione verba misceret, atque eum ad Factionem suam perducere non valeret, tandem dixit: Monsignore &c. Mi Domine, differ istam Methodum Eremiticam, jam non de te agitur. Alii similiter judicabant de fictionibus, ille tamen pergebat, nec aliud ex ore ejus audire poterant, quàm che in conscienza &c. se nescire in conscientia sua, cui votum dare debeat, cùm omnes capaces & idoneos inveniat: desiderare igitur, ut tot vota habere possfet. Quod cùm Farnesio nuntiatum esset, dixit; Chi vi crede, è un gran balordo; Hic certè stultus est. Electione facta, ignarus erat Montaltius omnium, donec in Capellam ad adorationem conduceretur, transibant enim propè Cameram ejus, atque Alexandrinus, pulsatâ portâ, ei dicebat: Mon Signore, venite, il Papa è fatto: id est: Domine, veni, Papa factus est.
units.tr: V. But the cardinals who are papabili, or candidates, are no small pretenders and dissemblers, whose common motto is: He who does not know how to feign will not be able to reign. The pretence of Sixtus regarding the necessary help has already been dealt with in Difference I, Section VI, n. 36, and we shall deal with the feigning of illnesses and old age, where we treat of the blemishes in respect of those who are elected, and in particular of decrepit old age. The preceding passages show that the rules permit various pretences, indeed recommend them through the rules. Yet some matters must also be referred to the rules as regards practice here. The greatest and most skilful pretender whom men have ever seen was the often-mentioned Sixtus V, or, as he was then called, Cardinal Montalto, before and in order that he might obtain the papacy. He had already learned and practised the art of feigning in the conclave of Gregory XIII. Let it be known from his Life, part I, book 4, p. 276 ff. After the funeral rites of Pius V were completed, the cardinals entered the conclave, but Montalto, although he was among them, did not seem to be among them, moving about in the conclave with no more noise than a poor monk in his cell, going out of it only to celebrate Mass. He pretended to be wholly ignorant of every kind of negotiation, and to show that he adhered to no party, he used to answer those who wished to draw him in with words breathing only simplicity, saying: that he was indeed ready to hold, etc., to follow those who go before, but since he had never been in a conclave, he was unwilling to commit any error through ignorance, which others by their experience could avoid; and with these and similar speeches he always met all who wanted to draw him into a party. That manner of proceeding, so contrary to his former life, gave clear evidence that everything was feigned and affected, so that he might advance his affairs by mildness. This Cardinal Gambara of Brescia seems also to have recognised, when one evening he was talking with Montalto about the imminent election and could not bring him over to his faction; at last he said: Monsignore, my lord, put off this eremitic method; it is no longer about you. Others likewise judged his pretences, yet he persisted, and nothing else could be heard from his mouth but that in conscience, etc., that he did not know in his conscience to whom he ought to give his vote, since he found all capable and fit; he therefore wished to have as many votes as possible. When this was reported to Farnese, he said: Whoever believes it is a great fool. After the election was made, Montalto was ignorant of everything, until he was led into the chapel for adoration; for they passed near his chamber, and Alessandrino, knocking at the door, said to him: My lord, come, the Pope is made, that is: Lord, come, a Pope has been made.

units.la: VI. Sed & extra Conclave & ex quo Cardinalis factus est, simulare novit.
units.tr: VI. But he also knew how to dissemble outside the Conclave, and from the time he became a Cardinal.

units.la: Narrat idem p.275. seqq. Non si tosto &c. Quamprimùm Cardinalis factus est, cœpit ambulare per viam, quæ ducit ad Papatum, armavit se humilitate incredibili & patientiâ inaudita, usque adeò, ut simulârit, se ne aquam quidem turbare posse, sepeliendo interiori viscerum suorum ebullientes Spiritus, quos à natura habebat; verbo totus mutatus ab illo apparebat, in vestibus, in gestibus, in sermonibus, in verbis, in actionibus: Hinc multi dicebant: Montalto vuol esser Papa; Montaltius vult fieri Papa. Docet, quantum gaudium ob electionem Gregorii XIII. præ se tulerit, quantopere se coram agnatis ejus humiliatus sit, quod forte ob illas ipsas fictiones Gregorius P. diligere non potuerit, per che odiava al maggior segno gli animi finti, quia simulatores maximo odio prosecutus sit; quomodo seorsim cum familia habitârit modestè, eleemosynas largè distribuerit, pauperes peregrinos grinos visitârit, Religiosos sui ordinis in domum suam receperit, in Confessionibus audiendis assiduus fuerit, quod bonam populi Romani de eo opinionem haud parùm auxerit,il quale suoli pascersi per lo più di si fatte esteriorita, qui ordinariò ejusmodi externis pascatur; quomodo ob simulationem homo piger, vilisque anima à Papa creditus sit,alius in Consistorio,Montaltio absente, dixerit : Il suo voto vale tanto vicino che longhi, votum ipsius tantum valet prope, quantum è longinquo. Hic, reditibus à Papâ ademtis,quoque simulârit, item interemto à Sicariis Nepote suo, quodam Prælato dicente : Questi son frutti,che ricerca il Papato.
