Ita agere solent, qui Papatum quaerunt; Quomodo simulatione suâ & Legatis Moscis imposuerit, quomodo rursus tempore famis pauperes adjuverit, illis de eo prædicantibus : Che Montalto,che viveva d'elemosyne, dava dell' elemosine agli altri, è gli altri Cardinali,che mangiavano il bene della chiesa mostravano à poveri la strada dell Hospitale. Id est : Montaltium Elemosynâ viventem eleemosynas dare, reliquos verò Cardinales bona Ecclesiae consumentes pauperibus viam ad Xenodochium ostendere. Quomodo mortuo Gregorio XIII. se gesserit; Caeteri per decem exequiarum dies pro se aut amicis laborabant, ipse verò non videbatur quicquam curare, extrinsecus nempe, intrinsecus autem nemo ardentiùs de Papatu cogitabat; certè viâ peculiari incedebat, quam nemo animadvertebat, nemo ita benè fingere sciebat, aut pauci de ejus promotione somniabant; Quidam de eo non cogitabant ob simplicitatem, quae ignorantia videbatur, hinc & in congregationibus & Consistoriis l'asino della Marca, asinus ex Marca vocabatur, quod se partim non intelligere, partim non curare simulabat &c. Quis credidisset, inquit Author, Cardinales daturos fuisse Papatum, cui nonnisi magna virtus par est,homini,quem ipsimet saepiùs asinum canonizarunt? &c. Astutis tamen viis promovebat occulta sua desideria, & anchoram figebat, quando eum plenis velis in longinquas oras ferri putabant; Media,quibus utebatur,multùm diversa erant à mediis reliquorum, ille res suas promovebat alios laudando, se contemnendo, hi alios contemnendo, se laudando; Multos invisebat ante ingressum in Conclave, in specie etiam Cardinalem Farnesium,contemptorem omnium Cardinalium pauperum,maximè Montaltii,quem non tantùm saepiùs Asino della Marca, sed & bestiam Romanam vocare solitus erat, & cum multa submissione ad eum tanquam Decanum Joqui videri volebat,eoque hortante ad ingresingressum, à quo se dispensari velle præ se ferebat, respondit, che la speranza d'ajutar sua Signora illustrissima col suo voto, gli dava volon-tieri l'animo di andar all' in contro della morte isteßa; Id est; spem, quam habeat Illustrissimam Dominationem suam juvandi, sibi animum addere, quo vel in mortis occursum tendere queat. Atque excipiente Farnesio; Monsignore, ajutate pure li vostri interessi, per che non vi credo essente della volonta d'esser Papa. Id est: Domine, promovete tantùm commoda vestra, quia vos desiderio Papatus etiam agi suspicor: Subjunxit: Bisognarebbe, che i Cardinali fossero dell' tutto ciechi, di levare il Papato ad un sogetto di tanto merito, e esperienza; per darlo ad uno, che n'è dell' tutto indegno, non havendo che una buona volontà di servire i suoi padroni e amici. Id est: Cardinales caci essent, si Papatum homini tantorum meritorum, tantaque experientia ereptum, indigno atque nihil prater solam fautoribus & amicis serviendi voluntatem habenti, conferrent. Idem dicebat aliis, quos invisebat Papabiles & alios, Capita factionum maximè, omnes laudans, omnibus se devinctum esse profitens, ídque cum omni submissione, cœlum testem implorando conscientia sua, ardorem magnum ostentabat, omnibus serviendi; sibi tantùm displicere, quod non tot vota haberet, quot essent Cardinales, (quam cantilenam jam in Conclavi Gregorii XV. canebat) ut unumquemque adjuvare posset. Verbo, cuivis Papabili dicebat; Che la chiesa haurebbe ricevuto gran torto, s'egli non riusceva Pontefice: Ecclesia magnam injuriam illatum iri, si ipse non Papa futurus sit.
units.tr: The same author narrates at p. 275 ff.: As soon as he was made Cardinal, he began to walk along the road that leads to the Papacy. He armed himself with incredible humility and unheard-of patience, so much so that he pretended he could not even stir the water, burying within himself the boiling spirits he had from nature. In a word, he appeared completely changed in his clothes, gestures, conversation, words, and actions. Hence many said: "Montalto wants to be Pope"; Montaltius wants to become Pope. He shows how much joy he displayed at the election of Gregory XIII, and how far he humbled himself before that Pope's kinsmen. Perhaps for this very pretence Gregory XIII could not love him, for he hated feigned minds to the highest degree, since he pursued dissemblers with the utmost hatred. He lived modestly apart with his household, gave alms generously, visited poor pilgrims, received Religious of his order into his house, and was assiduous in hearing confessions, which greatly increased the good opinion of the Roman people about him, who is usually fed mostly by such outward things. On account of his dissembling, the Pope believed him a lazy and base-spirited man. Another man, in the Consistory, with Montalto absent, said: His vote counts for as much nearby as from afar. Here, when his revenues were taken from him, he also dissembled. Likewise, when his nephew was killed by assassins, a certain prelate said: These are the fruits that the Papacy demands. Those who seek the Papacy are wont to act in this way. He also deceived the Moscovite legates by his dissembling. Again, in a time of famine, he helped the poor, while people said of him: Montalto, who lives on alms, gives alms to others, while the other Cardinals, who consume the goods of the Church, show the poor the road to the hospital. That is: Montaltius, living on alms, gives alms, while the other Cardinals, consuming the Church's goods, point the poor to the almshouse. He also behaved in a particular way when Gregory XIII died. The others laboured for themselves or their friends through the ten days of the funeral rites, but he seemed to care for nothing outwardly; inwardly, however, no one thought more ardently about the Papacy. Certainly he walked by a peculiar path that no one noticed. No one knew how to feign so well, and few dreamed of his promotion. Some did not think of him because of his simplicity, which seemed like ignorance; hence in both the congregations and the Consistories he was called the ass of the Marche, because he pretended partly not to understand and partly not to care, etc. Who would have believed, says the Author, that the Cardinals would give the Papacy to a man to whom only great virtue is fitting, and whom they themselves had so often canonized as an ass? etc. Yet by cunning ways he advanced his hidden desires, and he cast anchor when they thought he was being carried with full sails to distant shores. The means he used were very different from those of the others. He promoted his own affairs by praising others and despising himself, whereas they despised others and praised themselves. Before entering the Conclave he visited many, especially Cardinal Farnese, a despiser of all the poor Cardinals, and above all of Montalto, whom he was accustomed to call not only the ass of the Marche but also the Roman beast. Yet with much submissiveness Montalto wished to seem to speak with him as with the Dean. When Farnese urged him to enter the Conclave, from which he professed he wished to be excused, he replied: that the hope of helping your most illustrious Lordship with my vote gives me the courage to go willingly to meet death itself; that is: the hope which your Most Illustrious Lordship has of helping me gives me courage, so that I could hasten even to meet death. And Farnese answered: Monsignore, by all means promote your own interests, for I do not believe you are of a mind to become Pope. That is: Sir, only promote your own advantages, for I suspect you are also driven by desire for the Papacy. He added: The Cardinals would have to be utterly blind to take the Papacy from a man of such merit and experience and give it to one wholly unworthy, who has nothing but a good will to serve his masters and friends. That is: Cardinals would be blind if they conferred the Papacy, snatched from a man of such great merit and experience, upon one unworthy, who has nothing but the will to serve his patrons and friends. He said the same to others he visited, both the papabili and the rest, especially the heads of factions. He praised everyone, professed himself bound to all, and with the utmost submissiveness, calling heaven to witness his conscience, he displayed a great ardour to serve everyone. He was only displeased that he did not have as many votes as there were Cardinals (a tune he was already singing in the Conclave of Gregory XV), so that he could help each one. In short, to every papabile he said: The Church would suffer a great wrong if he did not become Pontiff. That is: The Church would be gravely wronged if he were not to be Pope.

units.la: In Conclavi se plane negligentem & neglectum fingebat, atque omni humano auxilio destitutum, ad instar illius ægroti ad piscinam, qui expectabat aliquem, qui eum aquæ commotæ committeret, rarò è cella sua egrediebatur, ídque sive ad Missam, sive ad scrutinium, tanquam nihil curæ habens, & ignarus, utrùm Papa factus sit, vel non. Haud tamen omittebat modis solitis negotia sua promovere, quando enim aliquem Cardinalem S. Sixto faventem offendit, paucis incepit dicere; Cardinales debere ad nutum illius Papam eligere, quia id mereatur optimis suis qualitatibus & respectu ad Avunculum Gregorium XIII. habito, qui tanto cum Zelo Ecclesiam rexerit; Ita etiam obvius factus cuidam ex familiaribus Farnesii, eum usque ad cœlum extollebat laudibus, admirationem præ se ferens, quòd tam diu electionem ejus differrent. Sic quoque erga domesticos Medicæi eum ita laudabat, ut æstimetur admirator virtutum ejus; Alios laudabat similiter, sed maximè tres illos potentiores atque miminùs sibi propitios. Semper gratiam ambiebat Cardinalium potentium miris modis, eos honorando, iis serviendo, eos nunquam non laudando, atque testando, se iis omnem satisfactionem atque exaltationem vovere &c. In Congregationibus & Consistoriis submissus atque mansuetus erat, opinionem alterius nunquam vincere volebat, sed se facilè vinci patiebatur, atque voto suo, modò hunc, modò illum sequebatur &c. læto vultu calumniatoribus gratias agebat cum magna humilitate de favore & gratia accepta, gratiam injurias interpretatus, ad exemplum illorum Pontificum, quibus tribuitur, quòd injurias ferendo atque gratiam faciendo Papatum consecuti sint &c. Si de Principibus eorúmque negotiis agebatur, eos magnâ prudentiâ aut defendere aut excusare allaborabat, sine præjudicio tamen dignitatis & jurisdictionis sanctæ Sedis, cujus semper acerrimum Protectorem se gerebat &c. humanitatem exercebat erga Monachos, qui eum odio semper habuerant, ut hinc occasionem nacti sint dicendi: Veramente il Cardinal Montalto, o è un grande huomo da bene, o un gran Semplicione, per che si non ricorda, che noi gli siamo stati nemici. Certè Montaltius, aut valde probus, aut valdè simplex est, quòd non memor est inimicitia nostra. Publicè privatímque prædicabat obligationem, quam habebat Alexandrino, dicendo; Si Dominus mille mundorum esset, non posse solvere minimam partem ei debitorum, ob immensos honores & beneficia incredibilia accepta ex sancta manu Pii V. & ab ipso, & ab omnibus suis &c. Maximè autem simulationibus suis deceperat Hispanos, qui magis stultos & simplices, quàm verò astutos & speculativos Papas desiderant. In Conclavi nunquam ambitionem manifestam ostendebat, simpliciter & in genere omnibus promittens, se ea beneficia esse præstiturum, quae tempus & locus datura essent. Altempsio infinitam obligationem ipso ingressùs die testabatur, & quòd omnem gratiam, quam in hoc mundo recepturus sit, quasi ex manibus suis recepturus sit, quâ ratione eo magis ad servitium ei præstandum incitabatur, dicúntque, eum dixisse; non mancara par mio voto à farvi Papa, per me Papa eris; atque Montaltium respondisse, Chiamo Iddio in testimonio, se ha ambitione di desiderare una cosa, della quale me ne conosco indegno, ne altra cosa mi stimolarebbe à desiderarla, se non, che la volontà di far cognoscere agli amici, ed alle persone di merito come Vostra Signoria Illustrissima, la stima che ne faccio: Deum testem invoco, si dignitatem, quâ me indignum profiteor, ambio, nisi solo amicis amicis atque bene meritis, qualis vestra Illustrissima Dominatio est, æstimationem, quâ eos prosequor, ostendendi desiderio. Eadem civilitate contra Madruccium, qui Secretum Hispaniæ habebat, utebatur. Simulationes Montaltii etiam efficiebant, ut tandem Farnesius interrogârit Cardinalem S. Sixti: Perche si fosse risoluto di concorrere in Montalto: Cur Montaltium promovere vellet? Hicque respondérit: à causa che lo cognosceva d'una natura molto humana ed inclinato à lasciar fare ogni cosa agli altri; Quia eum valdè humanum noverit, atque talem, qui omnia aliis agenda relinqueret; atque ille exceperit: Oh bene, ancora io dirò lo stesso, perche mi pare, che non ha Spirito à far del male, ne giudicio à far del bene; Sic est, illud ipsum credo, eum nempe, neque ingenio pollere ad malefaciendum, neque judicio ad benefaciendum. Eadem breviùs narrantur in Conclavi.
units.tr: In the Conclave he made a show of being wholly negligent and neglected, and deprived of all human help, like that sick man at the pool who waited for someone to put him into the stirred water. He seldom left his cell, whether for Mass or for the scrutiny, as if he had no concern and did not know whether he had become Pope or not. Yet he did not neglect to advance his affairs by the usual means. When he met a Cardinal favourable to Sixtus, he began briefly to say: The Cardinals ought to elect a Pope at his nod, because he deserves it by his excellent qualities and in view of his uncle Gregory XIII, who ruled the Church with such zeal. Likewise, when he met one of Farnese's household, he extolled him to the skies, showing admiration that they delayed his election so long. He also praised the Medici household so much that he seemed an admirer of their virtues. He praised others similarly, but especially those three more powerful and less favourable to him. He always courted the favour of powerful Cardinals in remarkable ways: honouring them, serving them, never ceasing to praise them, and protesting that he vowed to them all satisfaction and exaltation etc. In the Congregations and Consistories he was submissive and mild. He never wished to defeat another's opinion, but allowed himself to be easily defeated, and followed now this man's vote, now that one's, etc. With a cheerful face he thanked his detractors with great humility for their favour and kindness, and interpreted their injuries as kindness, after the example of those Popes to whom it is credited that by bearing injuries and showing kindness they attained the Papacy etc. When matters concerning princes and their affairs came up, he laboured with great prudence either to defend or to excuse them, yet without prejudice to the dignity and jurisdiction of the Holy See, whose most fierce Protector he always professed himself to be, etc. He showed kindness to the Monks, who had always hated him, so that they seized the chance to say: Truly, Cardinal Montalto is either a very good man or a great simpleton, because he does not remember that we have been his enemies. Certainly Montalto is either very upright or very simple, because he does not remember our enmity. He proclaimed publicly and privately the obligation he had to Alessandrino, saying: If the Lord had a thousand worlds, he could not repay the smallest part of what he owes him, because of the immense honours and incredible benefits received from the holy hand of Pius V, and from him and from all his people, etc. He deceived the Spaniards especially by his dissembling, since they desire Popes who are more foolish and simple than shrewd and far-seeing. In the Conclave he never showed open ambition, but promised everyone simply and in general that he would grant those favours which time and place would allow. On the first day of the Conclave he testified to Altemps that he was infinitely obliged to him, and that he would receive as from his own hands every favour he might receive in this world, by which he was the more incited to render him service. They say he told him: I will not fail to make you Pope with my vote; you will be Pope through me. And Montalto replied: I call God to witness that if I desire a thing of which I know myself unworthy, I am moved by nothing else than the wish to show my friends and persons of merit, such as your Most Illustrious Lordship, the esteem in which I hold them. Against Madruzzo, who held the secret of Spain, he used the same courtesy. Montalto's dissembling even brought it about that at last Farnese asked the Cardinal of Sixtus: Why was he willing to join in promoting Montalto? He replied: Because I know he is of a very humane nature and inclined to leave everything to others. And the other answered: Oh well, I will say the same too, for it seems to me he has neither the spirit to do evil nor the judgement to do good. The same things are told more briefly in the Conclave.

units.la: VII. Verùm quoque alii Papatûs consequendi gratiâ simulâsse dicuntur. Julii III. ante Papatum curam præcipuam, ut bene undique audiret; vide apud Onuphrium in vitâ. Ubi etiam de virtutibus ab eo affectatis agit. Qui non minùs haud obscurè Pii IV. simulationes prævias in vita innuit, imò eidem tribuit, quòd cuiuslibet rei, quæ ignorari suâ interesset, simulator ac dissimulator fuerit. In Conclavi Pii V. pariter creditum, civilitatem Card. Moronis affectatam fuisse, ut obtineret animi superbi desiderium. De Baronio observavano alcuni, inquit Author Concl. Leonis XI. ch'egli di zotico, tozzo, malinconico, & astretto, era divenuto affabile, civile, mansueto & galant huomo, salutava volentieri, rideva con ligiovani, caminava ondegiante per tutto il Conclave: Id est; Observabant quidam, Baronium rusticum, inhumanum, melancholicum, abstractum, affabilem, civilem, mansuetum, urbanum factum esse; ridebat cum juvenibus, lubenter salutabat, in Conclavi circumcursitabat: Tanta Conclavibus vis transsubstantiativa inest! Similiter D. Olimpia, referente in Vita p. 42. seqq. Abbate Gualdi, docuit Cardinalem Panfilium, postea Innocentium X. artem simulandi, utut ipse jam diu in Curia Romana fuerit, ubi præcipuè studetur simulationibus. Audivi egomet, ita subjungit Author, Cognatam aliquando ita ad Cardinalem loquentem: Cognate, quantas Tua mihi purpura in corde gaudii flammas excitet, non facile dici potest, verùm id ipsemet, cùm clavem affectuum meorum teneas, facile colligis. Merito Tuo, non affectui Urbani debes Cardinalatum, neque enim negari potest Prælato Ecclesiæ tam utili. Sed meritum promovet ad Cardinalatum, non ad Papatum, heic alia requiruntur. Neque mihi videtur ad hunc eligi probos, bos, sed qui videntur; Externa, non interna Papas faciunt. Cardinalis loqui debet cum omnibus, negotiari cum omnibus, & familiaris esse omnibus, sed Papabilis contra loqui parum, minus negotiari, nemini familiaris esse. Non virtutem respiciunt Cardinales eligendi, virtus tunc consistit in collo torto. Historiae docent, testatúrque experientia Urbani, Pontifices mutare naturam, dum enim Cardinales sunt, naturam habent, non ostendunt. Ad cumulum felicitatis domûs Panfiliæ mearúmque deliciarum nihil restat, nisi ut videaris sedens in throno Vaticani. Eadem fortuna, qua tot alios vocavit ad hanc dignitatem sine meritis & sine spe, etiam te illuc vocare poterit, cùm eam expectare possis aliquo Tuo merito. Sixtus V. qui erat Doctissimus, finxit se esse indoctum simplicémque, quamdiu Cardinalis fuit, gnarus fictam simplicitatem plùs valere ad obtinendum hunc gradum, quàm scientia valeat speculativa. His exhortationibus, subjungit, subjunxit alias, quæ, ut verum fatear, indignæ mihi videntur calamo viri Ecclesiastici, prater quod etiam opus esset simul commemorare, quæ oculis vidi, id quod Deus nolit. Sufficit scire, quòd D. Olimpia in omnibus unicè cognato invigilaverit, eidémque interdiu noctúque semper morum dissimulationem suaserit ab ea vocari solitam Portiera del Pontificato, Viam ad Pontificatum: Neque frustranea fuerunt, subjungit porrò, ista monita; Cardinalis quippe, utut malitiosus natura, simplex insuper, ne dicam ignarus certarum regularum Aulicarum, Romæ plùs alibi abundantium, gnarus tamen, cognatam suam unicè spectare exaltationem, personámque propiorem non habens, cum ea sæpe diu sermones miscebat de novo Pontificatu, quem ob decrepitam Urbani ætatem mox vacaturum vero simile erat. Sicque factus est bonus Cardinalis Magister in simulando omnia, amorem Cognatæ si excipias, simulabat quippe in congregationibus mansuetum, in conversationibus humilem, in Templis devotum, sed impossibile ei erat abscondere amorem erga D. Olympiam. Eam quippe amabat & pro idolo habebat palàm & clam, omnibus valdè mirantibus, Cardinalem Papabilem, quamvis è longinquo, tam apertè deditum esse amiciiæ mulieris, utut cognatæ. Difficile est, subjungit ultra, ut magni abscondant defectus suos, in omnium, alta spectare solitorum, conspectu existentes. Tandem p.49.50. subjungit, ut ipsamet eum in simulando juverit; Quotiescunque occasionem habuit loquendi cum quodam Factionis Hispanicæ, sive Cardinale, sive Ministro Politico, ei ob oculos posuit ingentem cognati erga illud Regnum affectum. Contrà cum quodam Factionis Gallicæ loquens, ei significavit; Cognatum habere occultum quendam erga Gallos affectum, eúmque occasione datâ melius serviturum ceu amiamicum occultum aliis manifeste id agentibus. Eâdem ratione in Con-clavi Clementis IX. Elci non mancava à se stesso &c. Id est: Elcius sibi nequicquam deerat, Cardinales invisendo, cum exhibitionibus, submissionibus, civilitatibus, vilem se reddebat &c. De ejusmodi simulationibus maximè L'Ambasc. di Rom. agit. Vid. p. 16.17. omnes species recensitas, atque conclusionem de Bacchanalium simililibus larvis, Comœdorum personis, Camaleontibus & Proteis. Item p.21.81. nec non p.103. 113. sed pag.235. dicit: Si Petrus umbrâ corporis sui corpora sanaverit, ejus Cathedram solo desiderio (quod quasi umbra animi sit) animos sanare, atque exemplum in Vidonio, quem solum Papatûs desiderium ab avaritia lethali febri, specietenus saltem, sanârit, ostendit. p.239. Bona abstractiones inefficaces pronuntiat, propter experimenta fictionum in tot ante eum Monachis, ad Papatum evectis. p.224. In Albicio simulationis defectum promotionis impedimentum vocat. Contra Raspponi p.245. Fachinetti p.255. simulatores introducuntur, & Barberinus. 294.
units.tr: VII. Yet others are said to have feigned in order to win the Papacy. Before his pontificate, Julius III's chief concern was to be well spoken of on all sides; see Onuphrius in his life, where he also treats of the virtues Julius affected. Onuphrius hints no less plainly at the prior pretences of Pius IV in his life, and even ascribes to him that he was a feigner and dissembler in whatever matter it was his interest to keep hidden. In the Conclave of Pius V it was likewise believed that the courtesy of Cardinal Moroni was affected so that he might obtain the desire of a proud spirit. Of Baronio, the author of the Conclave of Leo XI says: some observed that from being rustic, rough, melancholy and aloof he had become affable, courteous, gentle and a fine gentleman; he greeted people willingly, laughed with the young men, and walked about the whole Conclave swaying: that is, some observed that Baronio, once rustic, inhuman, melancholic, aloof, had become affable, civil, gentle and urbane; he laughed with the young, greeted gladly, and ran about the Conclave. So great is the transubstantiating power that Conclaves have! Similarly, Donna Olimpia, as reported in the Life, p. 42ff. by Abbot Gualdi, taught Cardinal Panfili, later Innocent X, the art of pretence, although he had long been in the Roman Curia, where pretences are especially practised. The author adds: I myself heard a kinswoman once say to the Cardinal: "Cousin, it is not easy to say what joyful flames your purple kindles in my heart, but since you hold the key to my feelings, you can easily gather it for yourself. You owe your cardinalate to your merit, not to Urban's affection, for no one can deny that you are so useful a prelate to the Church. But merit advances a man to the cardinalate, not to the Papacy; other things are required here. Nor does it seem to me that the good are chosen for this, but those who seem good. Popes are made by outward, not inward, qualities. A cardinal must speak with everyone, do business with everyone and be friendly to everyone, but a papabile must speak little, do less business and be friendly to no one. Cardinals who are to be elected do not regard virtue; virtue then consists in a twisted neck. The histories teach, and Urban's experience attests, that Popes change their nature: while they are cardinals they have a nature, but they do not show it. To crown the happiness of the house of Panfili and my own delights, nothing remains but that you should be seen sitting on the throne of the Vatican. The same fortune that has called so many others to this dignity without merit and without hope can call you there too, since you may expect it by some merit of yours. Sixtus V, who was most learned, pretended to be unlearned and simple as long as he was a cardinal, knowing that feigned simplicity counted for more in gaining this rank than speculative learning. To these exhortations, the author adds, she added others which, to tell the truth, seem unworthy of the pen of an ecclesiastic; besides, it would be necessary to mention what I saw with my own eyes, which God forbid. It is enough to know that Donna Olimpia watched over her kinsman alone, and by day and night always urged him to dissemble his manners, a practice she customarily called the gateway to the Papacy, the road to the Pontificate. Nor, the author goes on, were these warnings in vain: the Cardinal, malicious by nature yet simple, and I shall not say ignorant of certain courtly rules that flourish more in Rome than elsewhere, knew nonetheless that his kinswoman sought his exaltation alone, and since he had no closer confidant, he often spent long conversations with her about the new Pontificate, which was likely to fall vacant soon because of Urban's decrepit age. And so he became a good master of pretence in all things, except his love for his kinswoman, for he pretended in congregations to be gentle, in conversation humble, in churches devout; but it was impossible for him to hide his love for Donna Olimpia. He loved her and openly and secretly held her as an idol, to the great astonishment of all, a cardinal who might be papabile being so openly devoted to a woman's friendship, though his kinswoman. It is hard, the author adds further, for great men to hide their defects when they stand in the sight of all who look up to them. Finally, at pp. 49-50, the author adds that she herself helped him in pretending: whenever he had occasion to speak with someone of the Spanish faction, whether a cardinal or a political minister, she set before his eyes her kinsman's great affection for that kingdom; but speaking with someone of the French faction, she signified that her kinsman had a hidden affection for the French, and that he would serve them better, given the chance, as a secret friend while others openly did so. In the same way, in the Conclave of Clement IX, Elci did not fail himself, etc. That is: Elci was never wanting to himself; by visiting the cardinals with displays, submissions and courtesies he made himself contemptible, etc. On such pretences, above all, L'Ambasciatore di Roma treats, see pp. 16-17, listing all the kinds and concluding with masks like those of the Bacchanalia, the roles of comic actors, chameleons and Proteuses. Likewise at pp. 21, 81, and also p. 103, 113; but at p. 235 he says: If Peter by the shadow of his body healed bodies, so the desire of his Chair alone (which is as it were the shadow of the mind) heals minds, and he shows this by the example of Vidonio, whom the mere desire for the Papacy cured, at least in outward appearance, of a deadly fever of avarice. At p. 239 he declares good withdrawals ineffective, on account of the experience of so many monks before him who were raised to the Papacy by pretences. At p. 224, concerning Albizzi, he calls a defect of pretence an impediment to promotion. Against Raspponi (p. 245) and Fachinetti (p. 255), pretenders are introduced, and Barberini (p. 294).

units.la: VIII. Præter autem istas simulationes & dissimulationes, ut sic loquar, personales, solitæ sunt adhuc in Conclavibus reales. Talis placuerat in Conclavi Sixti V. Torresii Fautoribus: Questi Capi, che lo portavano, inquit Author, con bella e secreta stratagemma tratoro &c. Id est: Amici ejus eum Papam facere volebant, dum Conclave ingrederetur, occasione revera accommodata & opportuna, dum ingrediente aliquo Cardinalium omnes ad eum honorandum porta appropinquant, quâ improvisâ ratione ipsorum conatus perfici potuissent. Huc etiam referri debet, quòd in Conclavi Pauli V. quidam Cardinales Aldobrandini Amici impedire volentes exclusionem S. Clementis ad eum in finem congregatos accesserunt, quasi temporis fallendi gratiâ nugas agentes, atque firmiter credentes, in sua præsentia negotium intermissum iri. Qualis simulatio aliis fautoribus, nempe Barbarini, aliâs, nimirum in Conclavi Urbani VIII. feliciter cessit, dum interventu suo consultationem contra eundem abrumpere potuerunt. Sed & evidens, licèt breve de simulationibus omnis generis in Conclavi exerceri solitis testimonium in Conclavi Alexandri VII. Tutto ciò, inquit Author, che s'opra traquelle pareti è coperto della simulatione. Id est: Omne illud quod intra istos parietes fit, simulatione tegitur;
units.tr: VIII. Besides these personal feignings and dissemblings, so to speak, real ones have also been customary in Conclaves. Such a one was tried in the Conclave of Sixtus V by the supporters of Torres: these leaders, who were carrying him, says the author, were devising by a fine and secret stratagem, etc. That is: His friends wished to make him Pope while he was entering the Conclave, the occasion being truly suitable and opportune, when, as a cardinal entered, all approached the door to honour him, by which unexpected device their efforts might have been carried through. To this should also be referred what happened in the Conclave of Paul V: some cardinals, friends of Aldobrandini, wishing to prevent the exclusion of St Clement, came together to that end, as if passing the time with trifles, and firmly believing that the business would be dropped in their presence. A similar pretence by other supporters, namely the Barberini, succeeded happily at another time, namely in the Conclave of Urban VIII, when by their intervention they were able to break off the deliberation against him. But there is also clear, though brief, testimony to the kinds of pretence customarily practised of every sort in Conclaves, in the Conclave of Alexander VII: All that is done within those walls, says the author, is covered by pretence. That is: Whatever is done within those walls is covered by pretence.

units.la: IX. Simulationes excipiunt mendacia, à quibus illæ vix differunt. In Conclavi Sixti V. Cardinalis Riario sequente stratagemate tagemate usus est; quia chiragra laborabat, portari se curavit ad Cardinalem S. Sisto & asseveravit,jam jam instare electionem Montalti (post Sixti,) oppositionémque omnem fruftraneam futuram, atque opponentem semet perdituram esse, necessarium cum amore admitti debere. Idem ratione eadem Guastavillanum tunc decepisse legitur. In Conclavi Pauli V. iisdem quoque armis pugnatum est. Cardinalis Aldobrandinus Fautor S. Clementis apud ægrotantem S. Marcellum effecit, ut in locum electionis veniret, mentiendo, agi de electione Tosci, cujus ille erat amicus, sed quærebat Aldobrandinus electionem S. Clementis, de qua etiam, sed frustra agebatur. Cumque in eodem Conclavi dictus Tosco eligendus esset, simili ratione Baronius in Capellam productus fuit, sub prætextu, nemi-nem ibi de electione locuturum esse &c. Similibus artibus Urbanus VIII. promotus fuit, nam cum adhuc Cardinalis Barberinus, statimque eligendus esset, coeptâ negotiatione apud Borghesium primo se commendavit, hinc ad Borghesium concedens, multaque subticens idem fecit, & hinc ad Ludovisium apud quem, ex pacto, diffidentiam erga Borghesium præ se tulit, & id tantùm, che gli pareva opportuno, quod ipsi opportunum videbatur, protulit, apud quem etiam decretum, ut ad evitandam quasi sinistram Borghesii opinionem, per tertium ageret. In eodem Conclavi in una cella studiosè falsum prolatum fuit, utin altera intelligeretur. In Conclavi Clementis IX. imò jam ante ingressum Cardinalis Imperialis sece un giorno &c. Id est; Quodam die per totam Romam spargebat, se habere 40. vota certa, atque proin Bonelli Papam facere posse, isto artificio utens ad ora excludentibus obturanda, atque ad reconciliationem, ne Papam inimicum experiri debeant, ius extorquendam. Tunc quoque Galli, qui artificiosè præ se ferebant, se neminem excludere velle, nihilominus sub aqua aquam à mola, quò fluebat, alió flectere studebant. In Conclavi Clementis X. Bonvisiani fecero precorrer voce &c. Spargebant, cursorem ex Gallia venisse, Creaturas Rospigliosii, eo etiam invito, illuc ire velle, & pro capite Acciacoli habere, qui id ipsum Rospigliosio detexerit; Spargebant insuper, Barberinianos multos illuc concurrere velle. Sed & Author Conclavis Alexandri VII. rursus dicit de mendacio, quod jam dixit de simulatione; Tutto cio che s'opra trà quelli pareti è coperto tal hora anco della menzogna. Omne illud, quod intra parietes istos (Conclavis) fit, insuper mendacio tegitur.
units.tr: IX. Lies follow pretences, from which they scarcely differ. In the Conclave of Sixtus V Cardinal Riario used the following stratagem: because he suffered from gout, he had himself carried to Cardinal St Sisto and asserted that the election of Montalto (as Sixtus's successor) was at hand, that all opposition would be in vain, and that whoever opposed would ruin himself; it was necessary to admit him with affection. It is read that Guastavillani was then deceived by the same device, for the same reason. In the Conclave of Paul V the same weapons were used. Cardinal Aldobrandini, a supporter of St Clement, persuaded the sick St Marcellus to come to the place of election by lying that the election of Tosco was under discussion, whose friend he was; but Aldobrandini was seeking the election of St Clement, which was also being discussed, though in vain. And when in the same Conclave the said Tosco was to be elected, Baronio was brought into the chapel by a similar device, under the pretext that no one would speak there of the election, etc. Urban VIII was promoted by similar arts. For while he was still Cardinal Barberini and was about to be elected at once, after beginning negotiations he first commended himself to Borghese; then, going over to Borghese, he did the same thing, keeping silent about much; then he went to Ludovisi, to whom, by agreement, he displayed distrust of Borghese, and he put forward only what seemed fitting to him, as it seemed fitting to them; and to Ludovisi a decision was also made that he should act through a third party, to avoid what was, as it were, Borghese's unfavourable reputation. In the same Conclave, something false was deliberately spoken in one cell so that it would be understood in another. In the Conclave of Clement IX, even before the entry of Cardinal Imperiale, one day he gave it out all over Rome that he had 40 certain votes, and therefore could make Bonelli Pope, using this trick to stop the mouths of those who excluded him and to extort, by way of reconciliation, the right not to have a hostile Pope. Then too the French, who artfully pretended that they wished to exclude no one, nevertheless strove secretly to turn the water of the mill elsewhere, away from where it was flowing. In the Conclave of Clement X the Bonvisi spread the word, etc. They spread it that a courier had come from France saying that the creatures of Rospigliosi, even against his will, wished to go there, and that they had Acciaioli as their leader, who had revealed this very thing to Rospigliosi; they further spread that many Barberini wished to come there. And the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII again says of lying what he has already said of pretence: All that is done within those walls is sometimes covered by lying as well. All that is done within those walls (of the Conclave) is moreover covered by lies.

units.la: X. Mendacium, si famam proximi lædat, dicitur calumnia; quæ quoque est ex artibus Conclaviariis. Neque enim tantùm extra Conclave & ante ingressum arte ista aliquando utuntur Regii Ministri, Electioni isti se immiscentes, de quibus Author Vita D. Olympia p. 55. Publicano cento vitii &c. Centum vitia spargunt de eo, quem nolunt, & contrà cumulum virtutum colligunt in favorem sibi adhærentium. Sed saltem respectu quarundam partium, Calumnia quoque infectus erat in Concl. Leonis X. sermo Cardinalis Veronæ contra Cardinalem Baronium, à Cardinali Spinelli ei propositum; responsum quippe fuit; Che egli era inetto à questo peso &c. Id est: Eum ineptum esse oneri ferendo, neque Theologum, neque Legistam; descripsisse 4. historias, esse scriptorem aculeatum, atque tantum abesse, ut Ecclesiam universalem regere possit, ut dubitare liceat, utrùm regere possit particularem. Idem ferri potest judicium de fama contrà Cardinalem Papabilem Sauli, cùm de ejus electione ageretur, sparsa; Non manco, chi andasse seminando Zizanie molto grani per ruinare questo soggetto &c. Id est: Non defuerunt, qui Zizanii grana multa ad eum perdendum seminarent; Sparserunt, eo Authore impressionem Operum Baronii prohibitam fuisse, dum Legato consuluerit, ut occulta cum Gallis consilia iniret; Avum ejus stipendiatum Caroli VIII. fuisse; imò quidam addiderunt, eum liberos habere: Et quia nesciebatur, unde ista? Statim à malo aliquo Spiritu dictum fuit, venire ex domo Pinelli; quod mentitus est, ut hunc odio fautorum Sauli objiceret. Paulò ante ingressum in Conclave Clementis IX. furono publicate, referente Il. Cardin. p. 3. l. 3. 312. alcune scritture satiriche &c. Id est: Publicata fuerunt quædam scripta Satyrica, contra S. Susannam, quæ multi ex domo Farnesii prodiisse credebant, qui Papabilis præ aliis, ut solus in equo maneret, cateros dejiciendos putavit. Qui & paulò post idem Celsio accidisse narrat, con scritture poco confacevoli &c. Id est: Cum scriptis parùm decoro Ecclesiastico atque honestati convenientibus, de quibus non sine fundamento supponebatur, venire ex eadem domo, quare etiam se ad jus talionis erga eundem exercendum adactos viderunt.
units.tr: X. If a lie injures a neighbour's reputation, it is called calumny. This too is one of the Conclave arts. Nor do the royal ministers use this art only outside the Conclave and before entering it, when they meddle in the election. The author of the Life of Donna Olimpia, p. 55, says of them: They spread a hundred faults about the man they do not want, and on the other hand they gather a heap of virtues for those who favour them. But at least in some parties, calumny also tainted the Conclave of Leo X. The Cardinal of Verona's remark against Cardinal Baronius, put to him by Cardinal Spinelli, was of this kind. The reply was: He is unfit to bear this burden; he is neither a theologian nor a lawyer; he has written four histories; he is a stinging writer; and he is so far from being able to rule the universal Church that one may doubt whether he could rule even a particular one. The same kind of judgment can be made about the report spread against Cardinal Sauli, a papabile, when his election was under discussion: There were not lacking those who went about sowing many seeds of tares to ruin this man. That is: there were some who sowed many seeds of tares to destroy him. They spread the report that, on his advice, the printing of Baronius's works had been forbidden, since he had counselled the Legate to enter into secret plans with the French; that his grandfather had been a paid soldier of Charles VIII; and some even added that he had children. Since no one knew where these things came from, it was at once said, by some evil spirit, that they came from the house of Pinelli. This was a lie, so that he might expose Sauli's supporters to hatred. Shortly before the entry into the Conclave of Clement IX, some satirical writings were published, as Cardinal Il. reports, p. 3, l. 3, 312. That is: some satirical writings were published against St Susanna, which many believed had come from the house of Farnese. He, being the most papabile of all, thought the others should be cast down so that he alone might remain on the horse. The same author relates that a little later the same thing happened to Celsi: with writings little fitting to ecclesiastical decorum and honesty, which were not without ground supposed to come from the same house. For this reason they saw themselves driven to exercise the law of retaliation against him.

units.la: XI. Calumnia quoque vocatur, quando veritas odiosa ex odio & nocendi studio contra proximum publicatur.
units.tr: XI. Calumny is also the name given when an odious truth is published against a neighbour out of hatred and a desire to harm.

units.la: Accidit id saltem in Conclavi Pii V. quando ipse Borromæus Cardinalis, obstinato nell' imprese che pigliava &c. Id est; Obstinatus in suo proposito, atque jam ante ingressum in Conclave ad excludendum Montepulcianum se convertens sparsit, eum causam omnium gravaminum atque tributorum sub Pio IV. fuisse, cum tamen constituerit, quam parva ejus tunc authoritas fuerit.
units.tr: This happened at least in the Conclave of Pius V., when Cardinal Borromeo himself, obstinate in the enterprises he undertook, etc., being obstinate in his purpose and already, before entering the Conclave, turning to the exclusion of Montepulciano, spread the report that he was the cause of all the burdens and taxes under Pius IV., although he knew how slight his authority then had been.

units.la: Sic quoque in Conclavi Pauli V. cum tractatio de Bellarmino coepta esset, su rinovata &c. renovata atque sparsa fuit memoria digressus Bellarmini à Sixto V. injuncti, qui ei prohibuerit impressionem Operis de Potestate Papæ. Eandem fortunam expertus est in Conclavi Leonis XI. Baronius Bellarmino amicissimus, etenim era dichiarato dissidente di Spagna, declarabatur hostis Hispaniæ, quia sæpe Catonis adinstar locutus sit, & in suis Annalibus liberè scripserit, ac si in primitiva Ecclesia viveret, non in corrupto hoc seculo. Lecta epistola Proregis Siciliæ altera ad Collegium, & altera ad Papam, le quali accusavano &c. Id est: Quibus Baronius accusabatur, atque petebatur prohibitio librorum ejus, tanquam mendaciis plenorum, maximè autem in prajudicium Regis respectu Monarchiæ Siciliæ cedentium. Ob eandem causam Baronio soggetto aborrito, abominationi ; atque judicante Avila, non era soggetto tanto eminente &c. Id est; non adeò excellebat, ut multùm alios superârit, atque meliores erant, cum quorum injuria anteferebatur. Contrà Baronium allegavano S. Thomaso &c. Allegabant S. Thomam 2. 2. q. 181. art. 3. ubi statuit, ejusmodi homines inertes, utut caterùm innocentes, & virtute praditos, si inde scandala & bella sequi possint, non debere promoveri ad dignitates eminentes, multò minùs hunc, qui cum multa affectatione contra Sicilia rationes scripserit, atque meruerit inimicus declarari; Commemorabant etiam sinistra officia alia, occasione Jurisdictionis Mediolanensis, & tandem contra S. Jacobum, qui Apostolus Hispaniæ credatur, atque pro tali colatur. Asserebatur quoque, Baronium in regimine propria domûs semper agrestem, difficilem, iracundum & quasi tyrannicum se prabuisse. Ita quoque in Conclavi Alexandri VII. Spada de Rapaccioli circumferebat, chegli &c. Id est; Eum in Diœcesi suâ Deum invocari curâsse, ut ignoscere velit peccatis Dæmonis cujusdam in corpore Diœcesani cujusdam; Nempe Diabolus interrogatus, pœnitentiam suam, sed quæ non prosit, professus intercessioni occasionem dedit, quamvis aliter scripto rem narrârit contra illud Spada edito, tamen multi omnia credentes hinc de ignorantia, crassisque adeò corpori, vultuique similibus Cardinalis conceptibus conceptus formârunt.
units.tr: So also in the Conclave of Paul V., when the discussion of Bellarmine had begun, it was renewed, etc., and the memory was spread of Bellarmine's departure from Sixtus V., who had forbidden him to print his work on the Power of the Pope. Baronius, Bellarmine's closest friend, met the same fate in the Conclave of Leo XI., for he was declared to be dissenting from Spain, that is, declared an enemy of Spain, because he had often spoken like Cato and had written freely in his Annals, as if he were living in the primitive Church and not in this corrupt age. The letter of the Viceroy of Sicily, one to the College and another to the Pope, was read, which accused, etc.: that is, by them Baronius was accused, and the prohibition of his books was sought, as full of lies, and above all to the prejudice of the King with regard to the Monarchy of Sicily. For the same reason Baronius was called a hated subject, an abomination; and Avila, judging him not such an eminent subject, etc., said that he was not so excellent as to surpass others by much, and that those better men were the ones wronged when he was preferred. On the other side, they cited St Thomas against Baronius, they alleged St Thomas, etc., citing 2. 2. q. 181 art. 3, where he decided that such men, however otherwise innocent and endowed with virtue, if scandals and wars could follow from them, ought not to be promoted to eminent dignities, much less this man, who with great affectation had written against the reasons of Sicily and had deserved to be declared an enemy. They also recalled other unkind offices, on the occasion of the jurisdiction of Milan, and finally against St James, who is believed to be the Apostle of Spain and is venerated as such. It was also asserted that Baronius, in governing his own household, had always shown himself rustic, difficult, irascible and almost tyrannical. So too in the Conclave of Alexander VII., Spada of Rapaccioli circulated the story that he took care, etc.: that he had seen to it that God was invoked in his diocese, that He might be willing to forgive the sins of a certain demon in the body of a certain diocesan. Namely, when the devil was questioned, he professed his penance, but one that does not profit, and so gave occasion for intercession. Although Spada related the matter differently in writing, in his edited reply, many believed everything, and from this formed conceptions of the Cardinal's ignorance and gross mind, fitting his body and his face.

units.la: XII. Sed & multæ aliæ artes indignæ exercentur. Primùm in propositione & adjumento per suffragium. Quis cogitet, ibi vel minimam obliquitatem intervenire posse post juramentum tam grave, tam severum! Sed multiplex intervenit. Ne quis putet, serio tunc agere Cardinales omnes. Quidam jocantur, alii politicè, saepè etiam ex odio ejus, cui votum dant, agunt, minimè exaltationem ejus desiderantes, alia omnia cupientes. Certè nonnisi joco quidam in Conclavi Adriani VI. tredecim Cardinalibus simul voto adfuit. Ita etiam in Conclavi Leonis XI. Bellarminus, con fidò con alcuni &c. communicavit confidenter quibusdam, se scandalizatum esse, quòd Bullis & honore Dei Benedicti Cardinales ad electionem dignissimorum obligantibus, simul eligant juvenes 15. annorum, jocando tractantes illud, quod cum respectu infinito tractandum esset, atque dixit, eos mortaliter peccare. In eodem Conclavi accade, che su dato &c. Votum datum fuit Monopoli, cujus barba vix crescere coeperat, atque simul tribus imberbibus; quod quemadmodum rubore suffudit illum, ita displicuit iis, qui putabant, negotium tale, quod à Deo sit, magis devotè tractari debere. Neque certè à talibus valdè seria expectari possunt, & qui ita in Conclavi ipso se gerunt, quemadmodum Dissert. IV. Sect. 2. n. 108. notatum est.
units.tr: XII. But many other unworthy arts are also practised. First in the proposing and supporting of candidates by vote. Who would think that the slightest crookedness could intervene there, after so grave and severe an oath! Yet it intervenes in many forms. Let no one suppose that all the Cardinals then act in earnest. Some joke, others act politically, and often out of hatred for the man to whom they give their vote, wanting by no means his exaltation, but everything else. Certainly some, in jest only, in the Conclave of Adrian VI., thirteen Cardinals together took part in the vote. So also in the Conclave of Leo XI., Bellarmine confidently communicated to some that he was scandalised that the Cardinals, bound by the bulls and the honour of God to elect the most worthy, were at the same time electing youths of fifteen years, treating jokingly a matter that ought to be treated with infinite respect; and he said they sinned mortally. In the same Conclave it happened that a vote was given for Monopoli, whose beard had scarcely begun to grow, and at the same time for three beardless men. This made him blush, and it displeased those who thought that such a matter, which comes from God, ought to be treated more devoutly. Certainly nothing very serious can be expected from such men, and from those who conduct themselves in this way in the Conclave itself, as is noted in Dissert. IV, Sect. 2, n. 108.

units.la: XIII. Ast sunt haec juventutis vitia; Quid igitur juventus ad Cardinales? Forte castius rem adeò arduam tractant seniores.
units.tr: XIII. But these are the vices of youth. Why then bring the young men into the matter of the Cardinals? Perhaps the elders handle so arduous a business more chastely.

units.la: De omnibus id non admitti posse, docebunt sequentia, atque parùm à joco abest, si quis proponat, & tamen eligere vel eligi talem nolit, imò valde repugnet. In Conclavi Urbani VI. elegerunt quidem Galli eum, verùm post, alio substituto, se excusârunt, d'essere stati sforzati &c. se ad illam electionem à Populo Romano coactos fuisse, caterùm nunquam intentionem fuisse suam, ut Italum eligerent. In Conclavi Clementis VII. ipse Ursinum se promovere velle simulabat, ideò tantùm, ut juratus ejus hostis Columna eò facilius in Electionem suam condescenderet. In Conclavi Pauli V. Bellarminum proponebant, & sperabant etiam consensum Aldobrandini, sed isto non accedente, maximè alienationem Bellarmini ab eo in favorem Sauli; cùmque Baronius etiam Aldobrandino Bellarminum commendâsset, ille ad hunc misit, & nunciari curavit, non serio rem agere omnes, qui à partibus ejus stare videantur, esse artes quorundam. In Conclavi Urbani VIII. postquam invisisset Borghesius Borromaeum, ex instinctu huic sequente die vota data, eum solum in finem, ut Borghesius Hispanis suspectus fieret, che se ne dolsero seco, qui de eo apud illum conquesti sunt, neque suspicionem deposuerunt, donec iis hostium artificium vel manu palpandum ob oculos posuerit. Nonnunquam aliquos quos proponi ideò tantùm, ut aliquid agatur, & interim negotiationes alia bene disponuntur, ex eodem Conclavi discimus, in quo Barberinus totus licet Papatûs desiderio flagrans, fautores tamen rogavit, ut differretur negotiatio, donec prius propositi forent adhuc quidam seniores, quos non promotum iri pro certo sciebat. Similiter in Conclavi Innocentii X. à Barberino, che reputo &c. id est: qui cogitavit, periculosum esse, statim de Panfilio loqui, alius propositus legitur, quasi exercitii gratiâ & ut videre possit affectus, & interim cogitare de modo agendi, quoad Sacchetti, aut Panfilium. Cúmque post Sachetti negotiatio vigeret, ejus causam egerunt, qui eum semel pro semper excludi voluerunt, & quidem hi vehementissimè, alii simpliciter hoc modo gratiam Barberini quaesiverunt Papabiles ipsi, qui se manus dare simularunt, con professione &c. profitentes se illud facere conscientia stimulis, obligationibus, & qua alia tenerrima expressiones erant. In Conclavi Alexandri VII. Charontem dictum, quòd omnes proponeret, serió cum omnibus, tanquam dignissimis, id egisse, nemo sibi persuadebit. In eodem Conclavi nemo proponi voluit, quia notum erat, se nonnisi spes suas praecipitare. Et cùm in eodem Medicaei se Spadam non abhorrere præ se ferrent, sic tantùm animum Barberino addere voluerunt, ut occasio daretur eum semel pro semper excludendi. In Conclavi Clementis IX. Barberinus Spadam proponebat & commendabat per dar solo satisfattione à detto Spada, sapendo per altro, che non era per riuscire; Id est: Tantùm ad satisfaciendum ei, gnarus caterùm, rem non successuram, qui & aliàs eum Rospigliosio non anteposuisset, referente Auth. Card. p.3. l.3. p.318. qui & de Farnesio sequentia p.318. subjicit: Vi furono alcuni &c. Erant quidam, qui propius observarunt Politicam Gallorum, & eos ideò tantùm pro Farnesio laborare, ut Hispanis iratum penitùs suum facerent; gnari, quò magis pro eo laboraturi essent, eò magis Hispanos restituros atque exclusionem effecturos, atque ea de causa Farnesium con quell suo cervello risentitivo, cum suo genio ad iram pronissimo odium contra eos suscepturum esse; ma questi più pratici è più fini ne gli interessi di Roma de Francesi isteßi, seppero salvarela capra ed i cavoli: Ill. vero magis exercitati & astuti in negotiationibus Romanis, quàm Galli erant, opportunè periculum evitârunt. Respetu Rospigliosii finis Barberini erat, che si proponesse &c. ut proponeretur, non promoveretur, sed creatura Chigiana dividerentur, atque ad alium, forte se ipsum, quod probabilius, eligendum adigerentur. In Conclavi Clementis X. mentre che Raggi &c. dum Raggii barba raderetur, cum Conclavista loquens, dixit, negotiationem institui pro electione Spinola, quo ille cognito, statim advolavit, atque per amorem Dei rogavit, ne Eminentia sua jactura honoris sui occasionem daret, cum talia sperare ipse non audeat. Huc tandem etiam referimus sequentia ex eodem Conclavi verba: Si auvera &c. Creditum, de Vidonio agi, tantum, ut Chigius metuat, & in Scyllam incidat volens vitare charybdim. Ita tractantur illi, quorum amici videri volunt; Redeamus ad negotiationis rationem cum adversariis.
units.tr: That this cannot be admitted of all men will be shown by what follows, and it is scarcely far from a joke if someone puts forward a candidate and yet is unwilling, indeed strongly opposed, to elect or be elected such a man. In the Conclave of Urban VI., the French did indeed elect him, but afterwards, another having been substituted, they excused themselves, that they had been forced, etc.: that they had been compelled by the Roman people to that election, but that it had never been their intention to elect an Italian. In the Conclave of Clement VII., he himself pretended that he wished to promote Ursini, only so that his sworn enemy Colonna would the more easily agree to his election. In the Conclave of Paul V., they proposed Bellarmine and hoped also for the consent of Aldobrandini, but since that did not come, especially because of Bellarmine's estrangement from him in favour of Saul; and when Baronius had also commended Bellarmine to Aldobrandini, the latter sent to him and had it announced that not all who seemed to stand on his side were acting seriously; these were the tricks of certain people. In the Conclave of Urban VIII., after Borghese had visited Borromeo, votes were given the next day on his prompting, with the sole aim that Borghese might become suspect to the Spaniards; those who complained about him to them did not lay aside their suspicion until the enemies' trick was set before their eyes to be felt with the hand. Sometimes we learn from the same Conclave that some are proposed only so that something may be done, while meanwhile other negotiations are well arranged. In that Conclave Barberini, although wholly burning with desire for the Papacy, asked his supporters that the negotiation be postponed until some elders had first been proposed, whom he knew for certain would not be promoted. Similarly in the Conclave of Innocent X., Barberini, who thought it, etc.: since he judged it dangerous to speak at once of Panfilio, another candidate was put forward, as if for practice and so that he could see people's feelings, and meanwhile he could consider how to proceed with regard to Sacchetti or Panfilio. And when afterwards the negotiation for Sacchetti was in progress, they pleaded his cause, those who wished him excluded once and for all, and indeed these most vehemently; others simply sought Barberini's favour in this way. The Papabili themselves, who pretended to give their hands, professing with, etc., declared that they did it from the promptings of conscience, obligations, and other most tender expressions. In the Conclave of Alexander VII., that Charontes was said to propose everyone; no one will persuade me that he did it in earnest with all of them as most worthy. In the same Conclave no one wished to be proposed, because it was known that they would only be throwing away their hopes. And when the Medici in the same Conclave professed that they did not abhor Spada, they wished only to encourage Barberini, so that an occasion would be given to exclude him once and for all. In the Conclave of Clement IX., Barberini proposed and commended Spada only to give satisfaction to the said Spada, knowing otherwise that it would not succeed: that is, only to satisfy him, though aware that the matter would not succeed; for he had not otherwise preferred him to Rospigliosi, as the Author Cardinal reports (p. 3, l. 3, p. 318), who also adds the following about Farnese at p. 318: There were some, etc. There were some who observed the French policy more closely, and who said that they laboured for Farnese only so that they might make the Spaniards thoroughly angry, knowing that the more they laboured for him, the more they would restore the Spaniards and bring about the exclusion; and for this reason Farnese, with his resentful head and his temperament very prone to anger, would take up hatred against them. But these more practical and subtle men, in the interests of Rome itself and of the French, knew how to save the goat and the cabbages. The Illustrious men, being more practised and shrewd in Roman negotiations than the French, opportunely avoided danger. With respect to Rospigliosi, the aim of Barberini was that he be proposed, etc.: that he be proposed, not promoted, so that the creatures of Chigi would be divided and forced to elect another, perhaps himself, which is the more probable. In the Conclave of Clement X., while Raggi's beard was being shaved, speaking with a conclavist, he said that a negotiation was being set up for the election of Spinola. When Spinola learned this, he at once flew to him and begged, for the love of God, that His Eminence not give occasion for the loss of his honour, since he himself did not dare to hope for such things. Here finally we also refer the following words from the same Conclave: If it is true, etc. It was believed that the matter concerned Vidonio, only so that Chigi might be afraid, and fall into Scylla while wanting to avoid Charybdis. Thus are those treated whose friends they wish to seem. Let us return to the method of negotiating with adversaries.

units.la: XIV. Sæpè in tractatione quaritur & fovetur, quidem secundùm Regulam, discordia corum; quâ arte Barberinus in Conclavi Clementis IX. referente Il Cardin. p. 3. l. 3. 344, 345. usus est, cùm enim factionem suam valdè infirmam cognosceret, audava distornando l'acquâ &c. Aquam, ut dici solet, à mola avertere & confusionem atque discordiam inter Creaturas Chigianas seminare studebat, quod facilè fieri posse videbatur, quia illa facile videbant prater mentem suam Chigium quarere Papam à suo modo.
units.tr: XIV. Often in negotiation discord among them is sought and fostered, as the rule itself prescribes. Barberini used this art, as the Cardinal reports in the Conclave of Clement IX, p. 3, l. 3, pp. 344, 345. For when he knew that his faction was very weak, he was diverting the water, etc. He aimed, as the saying goes, to divert the water from the mill and to sow confusion and discord among the Chigian creatures. This seemed easy to do, because they readily saw that Chigi was seeking to make a Pope in his own way.

units.la: XV. Variis adversarios fraudibus ultra simulationes & mendacia simplicia cirmcumvenire sæpè solent. Levius forte illud est, (quamvis nec illud cum familiaritate & sinceritate fraterna satis conveniat,) quòd in Conclavi Pii V. Altempsius & Como, veniente ad Borromæum, in cujus cella tres simul negotiabantur, Pacecco, alterius Factionis negotiatore, retrò lectum se abscondiderunt, unde ille tandem, sermones prolongante Pacecco, præ impatientia prodiit Sed graviora sequuntur. Detestabili cumprimis fraude Pontificatum consecutus legitur Bonifacius VIII. fraude & magnâ iniquitate, ut ait Stella, ergà prædecessorem ipsum adhibitâ, quâ eum, ut Stella rursus, se abdicare quasi coegit. Simplici Cœlestino V. à Cardinalibus quibusdam, referente Platina in Cœlest. V. maximè verò Benedicto Caetano (fuit is postea Bonifacius VIII.) Viro in jure Civili & Canonico peritissimo vafróque, qui primum locum apud Pontificem tenebat, persuasum fuit, ut se Pontificatu abdicaret, vehementer instabant, ut id quàm primùm agat, proposito Reip. Christianæ discrimine, quod suâ ignoratione imminere omnium cervicibus ostendebant, affirmantes, omnia mala tum accidentia, die judicii sibi imputatum iri. Imò Bonifacium, quem non sine ambitionis crimine ad Pontificatum pervenisse, & à Cardinalibus quibusdam apud Reges Principes & nationes accusatum fuisse de ambitione, quòd contrà jus, fásque Pontificatûs sedem occupâsset, rejecto fraudibus Cœlestino, eodémque in carcerem conjecto; Platina in Bonif.VIII. testatur; Idem ibidem, hac fraude usum, esse, qui scribant, docet: Immisit subornatores clanculum quosdam, qui noctu, dimissâ quasi coelitus voce in cubiculum Coelestini, ei persuaderent, ut Pontificatum dimitteret, si salvus fieri vellet. Sed & aliâs fraudibus ceu occultioribus machinationibus ex improviso nocere, atque absque reliquorum scitu negotium conficere voluerunt. Factum illud in primo ex Conclavibus, quae habentur, Clementis V. in quo artes Columnarum demum post electionem cognita dicuntur. In Conclavi sequente Urbani VI. Cardinalis de Ursinis, qui, ut credebatur, ad Papatum aspirabat, videns, in Barensem sufficientes adfuturos, conabatur, ut creditur, impedire, unde hac, vel similia verba protulit: Domini mei, differamus istam electionem, ut possimus deludere istos de populo Romano, & vocemus ad nos unum fratrem minorem, eique imponamus cappam & mitram Papales, & fingamus, nos eum elegisse, & sic recedamus, & alium alibi eligamus. In Conclavi Innocentii VIII. recensetur, quomodo Cardinales eum fraudulenter elegerint: Superveniente nocte Cardinales omnes iverunt dormitum: quibus dormientibus, praedictus Cardinalis S. Petri ad vincula unà cum dicto Vice-Cancellario tractaverunt cum omnibus Cardinalibus, ut darent voces eorum Cardinali Melphitensi; promittentes illis se multa daturos; & hoc modo tractârunt cum omnibus Cardinalibus, praeterquàm cum sex de senioribus & principalibus &c. qui Cardinales dormiebant in eorum cubiculis. Itaque caeteri dederunt vota sua, & elegerunt Pontificem; Manè autem facto, vocaverunt illos dormientes, dixerúntque illis; Venite, Papam fecimus: at illi dixerunt, quem? responderunt; Cardinalem Melphitensem; Dixerúntque illis: quomodo? responderunt, hâc nocte dum dormivistis (zizania seminavimus) congregavimus omnes voces, praeterquam vestrum dormientium. At illi videntes, quòd erant 18. v.19. qui consenserant, & quòd ipsi tanquam pauciores non poterant actum disturbare, consenserunt. Deinde die sequenti detectum fuit, &c.
units.tr: XV. Adversaries often try to get round us by frauds beyond simple pretences and lies. Perhaps the lesser case (though even this does not fit well with brotherly familiarity and sincerity) is that in the Conclave of Pius V, when Altempsius and Como came to Borromeo, in whose cell three men were negotiating at once, Pacecco, a negotiator for the other faction, hid himself behind the bed. Eventually he came out of it, impatient, as Pacecco prolonged the talk. But more serious things follow. Boniface VIII is read to have obtained the papacy by a detestable fraud, with great iniquity, as Stella says, practised against his predecessor himself. By this he forced him, again as Stella says, to abdicate as it were. Celestine V was persuaded by certain cardinals, as Platina reports in the life of Celestine V, but especially by Benedict Caetani (who later became Boniface VIII), a man most expert and crafty in civil and canon law, who held the first place with the Pope. They pressed him vehemently to abdicate the papacy as soon as possible, given the danger to the Christian commonwealth which they showed was hanging over everyone's necks through his ignorance, affirming that all the evils that then befell would be imputed to him on the day of judgement. Indeed Boniface, whom, as Platina testifies in his life of Boniface VIII, certain cardinals accused before kings, princes and nations of having reached the papacy not without the crime of ambition, and of ambition in that he had occupied the seat of the papacy contrary to law and right, Celestine having been rejected by fraud and thrown into prison; Platina also teaches, in the same place, that those who write say he used this fraud: He secretly sent certain suborners who, at night, with a voice let down as if from heaven into Celestine's bedchamber, would persuade him to resign the papacy if he wished to be saved. But they also wished to harm by other frauds, as more hidden machinations, unexpectedly, and to finish the business without the knowledge of the rest. That happened in the first of the conclaves that are extant, that of Clement V, in which the arts of the Colonna are said to have become known only after the election. In the following conclave of Urban VI, the Cardinal of Ursini, who, as was believed, aspired to the papacy, saw that sufficient votes would come to the Barese. He tried, as is believed, to prevent this, and so he uttered these or similar words: My lords, let us postpone that election, so that we can fool those of the Roman people. Let us call to us one lesser brother, put on him the papal cope and mitre, pretend that we have elected him, and so withdraw, and elect another elsewhere. In the conclave of Innocent VIII it is recounted how the cardinals elected him fraudulently: Night having come, all the cardinals went to sleep. While they slept, the aforesaid Cardinal of St Peter ad Vincula, together with the said Vice-Chancellor, treated with all the cardinals to give their votes to the Cardinal of Melfi, promising them many things; and in this way they dealt with all the cardinals except six of the senior and principal ones, etc., who were sleeping in their chambers. So the others gave their votes and elected the Pope. In the morning, having called those sleeping, they said to them: Come, we have made a Pope. But they said: Whom? They answered: The Cardinal of Melfi. And they said to them: How? They answered: This night while you slept (we sowed tares), we gathered all the votes except yours who were sleeping. But they, seeing that there were 18 or 19 who had consented, and that they themselves, being fewer, could not disturb the act, consented. Then the next day it was discovered, etc.

units.la: XVI. Sed & aliâs nocturnae tractationes placuerunt; De negotiatione pro Sixto V. ita Author Conclavis loquitur; Quella pratica su fatta piu di notte che di giorno. Id est, Negotiatio illa magis nocturna, quàm diurna fuit; Quod negotiationis tempus in alio casu Bellarmino non conveniens fuit; Cùm enim Borghesius 7. noctis horâ Camporam Papam facere vellet, & ob id Bellarminum molestaret, regessit iratus: Non son &c. Non jam tempus est Papam faciendi; sed opera tenebrarum, permittite, ut quiescam. Cui hujus responso sponso simile fuit,ut etiam similis importunus interpellator fuit, illud Cardinalis Montaltii Nepotis,in Conclavi Pauli V. nam Sfondrata se jam jam coenaturum ad exclusionem Comi,forte ut avocaret (est conjectura Authoris) à Bellarmino, cujus tunc ibi negotium agebatur,evocanti respondisse dicitur: Tratti si di che si fia, che io voglio cenare: De quocunque agatur, jam coenam sumam. Alexandro VII. in agone constituto & ante ingressum in Conclave, domus Cardinalis Albizii Conclave videbatur, mentre si raunavano di notte tempo molti Cardinali edanco alle volte di giorno ; Id est, quia noctu ibi congregabantur multi Cardinales, imo etiam interdiu aliquando.
units.tr: XVI. But other nocturnal negotiations have also been popular. About the negotiation for Sixtus V the author of the Conclave speaks thus: That business was done more by night than by day. That is, the negotiation was more nocturnal than diurnal. This time of negotiating did not suit Bellarmine in another case. When Borghese at the seventh hour of the night wanted to make Campori Pope, and therefore troubled Bellarmine, Bellarmine replied angrily: No... It is not now the time for making a Pope, but for the works of darkness. Allow me to rest. A similar importunate interrupter was the nephew of Cardinal Montalto in the Conclave of Paul V, a reply resembling this one. Sfondrata, who was about to dine at once, is said to have answered the man calling him, perhaps (this is the author's conjecture) to draw him away from Bellarmine, whose business was then being conducted there: Whatever it is about, I want to dine; whatever is being treated, I will now take my supper. In the time of Alexander VII, when the contest was set and before the entry into conclave, the house of Cardinal Albizzi seemed to be a conclave, while many cardinals gathered there at night, and sometimes even by day. That is, many cardinals gathered there at night, and sometimes even by day.

units.la: XVII. Nempe saepe urgetur opus & cum festinatione proceditur, non relicto adversariis sufficiente ad contra-molitiones tempore. Sic senibus in Conclavi Pauli V. non concessum fuit satis temporis,ad consulendum contrà. Atque hûc quoque pertinent, quae in Conclavi Gregorii XIII. quibusdam primo die egressis atque absentibus peragi debuissent, & in sequentibus quoque Conclavibus Cardinales aliàs egressuros retinuerunt, & jam suprà plu-ribus sunt enarrata. Quae omnia hactenus tribus S. recensita eò magis vitiosa sunt, quia aliàs electio vel cum contemptu unius facta rejicitur. Praeterea quoque fraus in eligendi forma intervenisse legitur. In numeratione schedularum Scrutinii,in qua scrutatorum unus schedulam abscondidisse in Conclavi quodam visus fuit, quod ad evitandum scandalum non manifestari debuit. Sic etiam in numeratione adorantium, dum in Conclavi Clementis VIII. Decanus exclusioni S. Severinae favens sufficientem numerum praesentium indicare noluit, semper & per 3. horas ad initium regressus, vix 5. numeratis,atque causâ in continuos praesentium motus & quòd confuse stent,rejecta.
units.tr: XVII. Indeed the work is often pressed and carried on in haste, with no sufficient time left to the adversaries for counter-manoeuvres. Thus the old men in the Conclave of Paul V were not granted enough time to take counsel against it. Here also belong the things that, in the Conclave of Gregory XIII, ought to have been done with some who went out and were absent on the first day. In the following conclaves too, they held back cardinals who would otherwise have left, as has been related above in several places. All these things, recounted so far, are the more faulty because otherwise an election made with contempt for one is rejected. Moreover, fraud is read to have intervened in the form of the election. In the counting of the ballot papers of the scrutiny, one of the scrutineers seemed, in a certain conclave, to have hidden a ballot, which, to avoid scandal, ought not to be made known. Likewise in the counting of those who did homage, when in the Conclave of Clement VIII the Dean, favouring the exclusion of S. Severina, refused to report a sufficient number of those present. He always went back to the start for three hours, scarcely five having been counted, and the count was rejected on account of the continual movements of those present and because they stood about in confusion.

units.la: XVIII. Artibus his & Papatûs consequendi mediis vitiosis adnumeranda jam venit Simonia; quam heic locum habere posse, nemo inficiatur, licèt enim multi Papae gnathones negent, cum Simoniam committere posse,cùm sit Dominus beneficiorum, nemo tamen negat, aliquem Papatum Simoniâ consequi posse; imò ex propriis Romanensium testimoniis ostendemus,multos ita Papatum revera consecutos esse.
units.tr: XVIII. Among these arts and wrongful means of obtaining the papacy, simony must now be counted. That it can have a place here no one denies. For although many of the Pope's flatterers deny that a Pope can commit simony, since he is the lord of benefices, nobody denies that someone can obtain the papacy by simony. Indeed, from the Papists' own testimonies we shall show that many have really obtained the papacy in this way.

units.la: XIX. Prius tamen ex Petri Damiani ad Fratres Cardinales epistola, quae apud Baronium ad an. 1057. p.24. seqq. habetur, cognocognoscere lubeat, quàm latè se extendat Simonia; Agit n.29. de illis, qui ad consequendas dignitates Ecclesiasticas molestum servitium potentioribus præstant. De talibus dicit: Facilioris exitus fuerat, si pro honoribus venaliter acquirendis pecuniam semel appenderent, quàm tot laborum, tot pressurarum molestias sustinerent. Nam cùm Propheta (Jesaj XXXIII.) de vero justo dicat: quia excutit manus suas ab omni munere; quis eum à munerum præstatione defendat, qui & se ipsum aliena servitutis imperio subjugat, & insuper in diuturna expeditionis impensas facultatum suarum lucra profligat. Planè Prophetica illa sententia sic exponitur, ut tria dicantur esse munerum genera, scilicet munus à manu, munus ab obsequio, obedientia subjectionis; munus à lingua, favor adulationis. Et cùm ab unaquaq; harum manus excutiendas Propheta denuntiet: Omnibus his manus implicâsse convincitur, qui nanciscenda dignitatis ambitu potestatum sublimium castra sectatur &c. Quam ergò sui afferent excusationem, qui licèt verbis non contraxerint venalis pacta commercii, operatione tamen, non uno, sed omnibus his probantur laqueis irretiti? Veruntamen jactant se & eo gloriantur, se innoxios, quia nullam talenti summam pro suscipiendis (pro suscipiendis) honoribus se pepigére daturos. Sed dic mihi, o Clerice, quisquis es, si redempto quolibet aureo vase vel prædio, distractor exigeret, ut retenti apud te vice pretii hujusmodi sibi sedulitatis impendium exhiberes: Nunquid non postmodum constanter assereres, te, quod acceptum est, justo pretio comparâsse? Non videlicet, quia pecuniam persolvisti, sed quia servitium præstitisti. Diceres enim, & non hoc fortassis impudenter astrueres, charius emi, dum tanto me labore vexarem, dum toties facultatum mearum sumptus expenderem, quàm si semel præfixæ quantitatis pecuniam numerarem. Nequaquam ergo sibi innocentiam spondeant, & à Simoniacæ hæreseos maculis se mundos esse confidant, qui licèt metalla vibrantia non appendunt, pretium tamen pro suscipiendis honoribus per subjectionis ei obsequium quædam quasi talenta persolvunt.
units.tr: XIX. First, however, let us learn from Peter Damian's letter to the Brethren, the Cardinals, which is found in Baronius at the year 1057, p. 24 ff., how widely simony extends. At n. 29 he treats of those who render troublesome service to the more powerful in order to obtain ecclesiastical dignities. Of such people he says: It would have been an easier outcome if, to acquire honours venally, they had once weighed out the money, rather than endure the troublesome burdens of so many labours and pressures. For since the Prophet (Isaiah XXXIII) says of the true just man: "who shakes his hands from every bribe"; who will defend from the rendering of bribes him who both subjects himself to the rule of another's servitude and, moreover, in a long campaign squanders the profits of his resources on expenses? Clearly that prophetic sentence is explained so that three kinds of gifts are named: a gift from the hand, a gift from obedience, which is the obedience of subjection; and a gift from the tongue, which is the favour of flattery. And since the Prophet declares that the hand must be shaken from each of these, he is convicted of having entangled his hands in all of them, who, in seeking to obtain dignity through ambition, follows the camps of the high powers, etc. What excuse, then, will they offer who, although they have not contracted venal pacts of commerce in words, are yet proved, by their actions, to be caught in not one but all of these snares? Yet they boast and glory that they are innocent, because they have agreed to give no sum of talents for receiving honours. But tell me, O clerk, whoever you are: if, on buying some golden vessel or estate, a seller demanded that you, in place of the price, render him such a service of diligence, would you not afterwards firmly assert that you had bought what was received at a just price? Not because you had paid money, but because you had rendered service. For you would say, and perhaps would not shamelessly maintain, that I was bought more dearly, since I was vexed with so much labour and so often spent the costs of my resources, than if I had once counted out money of a fixed amount. In no way, then, let those promise themselves innocence, and let them trust that they are clean of the stains of simoniacal heresy, who, although they do not weigh out ringing metals, nevertheless pay, as it were, certain talents of price for receiving honours through the obedient service of subjection.

units.la: XX. Opportunè hæc ad Cardinales jam sui temporis scripsit.
units.tr: XX. He wrote these things at a fitting moment, addressing the Cardinals of his own time.

units.la: Quænam autem ex vitiosis illis artibus & mediis hactenus recensitis non simul Simoniæ vitio infecta est, juxta latiorem vocis istam acceptionem? Quot juxta eam post secula prima Pontifices non Simoniacè electi fuerunt? Sed ostendemus, multorum electiones etiam in sensu strictissimo Simoniâ contaminatas esse. Dubitare quis audeat, quando inter Pontificios non desunt, qui Simoniacè Papatum esse quærendum suadere fuerunt ausi: En sin un puissant moyen,inquit, Anonymus, pour l'affoiblissement des adver-saires, seroit d'avoir de l'argent à distribuer sous main à beaucoup de Cardinaux pauvres, ou de leur asseurer secrettement des pensions. Id est: Tandem potens medium adversariorum partes debilitandi esset, si quis sub manu multis Cardinalibus pauperibus argentum distribuere posset, vel iis occultè assignare pensiones. Similia vide, ubi de liberalitatis simulatione agitur. Vide etiam Regulas suprà allatas, & consilium à Lottino Regibus datum. Jam verò pergimus ad exempla.
units.tr: But what is there among the corrupt arts and means reviewed so far that is not also tainted by the vice of Simony, taking the word in its wider sense? How many popes after the first centuries were not elected simoniacally, by this standard? We shall show that the elections of many were defiled by Simony even in its strictest sense. Who would dare to doubt it, when among the Papists there have been some who ventured to advise that the papacy be sought by simony? Behold a powerful means, says the anonymous author, for weakening the adversaries would be to have money to distribute under the table to many poor Cardinals, or to secretly assure them pensions. That is: At last a powerful means of weakening the adversaries' side would be if someone could distribute money under the hand to many poor Cardinals, or secretly assign them pensions.
