See similar passages where the pretence of generosity is discussed. See also the Rules cited above, and the advice Lottino gave to kings. But now we proceed to examples.

units.la: XXI. Odii, quo Stephanus VI. erga Formosum I. fereba-tur, immanis causam Platina in Vita illius ambitionem facit; hinc odium esse, quo etiam in mortuum Stephanus saevierit, testatur, quòd ei antea (Formosus) impedimento fuisset, quo minùs optata sede potiretur, cùm jam eo devenissent Ecclesiastici, ut non coacti, ut antea, sed sponte & largitionibus Pontificum munus obirent. Exemplum paulò ante in ipso etiam Formoso dederat, qui largitione potiùs, quàm virtute ad Pontificatum assumtus fuerit: Consentit Stella, atque ita canit Janus Vitalis: O si formosus factis, Formose, fuisses; Non auro emisses Pontificale decus.
units.tr: XXI. Platina, in his Life of Stephen VI, attributes the monstrous hatred that Stephen bore toward Formosus to ambition. He testifies that this was hatred, since Stephen raged even against the dead man, because Formosus had earlier stood in his way and kept him from the see he desired; by then the clergy had come to the point where they took up the office not, as before, under compulsion, but willingly and through the bribes of the popes. Formosus himself had given an example a little earlier, for he was raised to the papacy by largesse rather than by virtue. Stella agrees, and so Janus Vitalis sings: "O Formosus, had you been handsome (formosus) in deeds, you would not have bought the papal glory with gold."

units.la: Sed Platina in Sergio III. ad generaliorem querelam redit: Vide quaso, inquit, quantum isti degeneraverint à majoribus suis; Illi enim utpote viri sanctissimi, dignitatem ultrò oblatam contemnebant, orationi & doctrina Christiana vacantes: hi verò largitione & ambitione Pontificatum quaerentes, & adepti, posthabito divino cultu, inimicitias non secus ac saevissimi quidam Tyranni inter se exercebant; suas voluptates postea securiùs implebant, cùm nullibi extarent, qui eorum vitia coërcerent. Cui querelae Platinae respondet simillima Stellae in Romano I. ubi tanquam rarum quid memorat, quòd non, ut multi sui temporis, ambitione aut largitionibus, sed de more Petri Pontificatum adeptus sit. De Seculi IX. & X. Tyrannis Baronius ad a.597. n.4. testatur, eos etiam pecuniis populo Cleróque Romano dominantes homines monstruosos in Cathedram Petri intrusisse. De Bonifacio VII. ita Platina in vita: Initio Magistratu, conspirantibus simul bonis civibus, relinquere urbem coactus, pretiosissima quaque è Basilica Petri subtrahens, Constantinopolin confugit: ubi tamdiu substitit, quoad divenditis, quae sacrilegè abstulerat, magnam vim pecuniarum comparâsset, quibus tanquam adminiculis occupandae tyrannidis fretus urbem repetit, cives Romanos largitione corrupturus. Obstabant conatibus suis viri boni, maximè verò Joannes Diaconus Cardinalis, dinalis, quem captum, adjuvantibus quibusdam perniciosis hominibus, oculis statim privavit &c. Subjungit mox querelam pro more: Vide quaso quantum degeneraverint hi Pontifices à majoribus suis, qui hanc rempublicam Christianam tam amplam, tamque magnificam suo sanguine nobis reliquere. Pontifex Romanus sacrorum Pater & Rex, sacra ipsa abstulit furto, & qui vindicare sacrilegia debuerat, tanti sacrilegii factus est Author. Hoc autem contingere in quavis Rep. consuevit; quando plus malorum ambitio & avaritia valet, quàm bonorum virtus & gravitas. In Clerum igitur deligendi essent, quorum vita & doctrina probata sit; non autem hi, qui, cùm virtutis & religionis nil habeant, ambitione & largitione sibi potentiam quarunt. De Gregorii V. (quem ob affinitatem à Cæsare electum esse, Platina in vita testatur) æmulo; cujus nomen quidam inter Pontifices supprimunt, utpote minùs legitimè creatum, (creati,) aliis Johannem XVII. vocantibus, quòd populi clericque Romani consensu, ad quos electio spectârit, Pontificatum iniiisset; ita Platina in Gregorio V. Romani Crescentium denuò cum summa potestate Consulem decernunt, qui statim Joannem quendam natione Graecum, Episcopum Placentinum non minùs pecuniosum quàm doctum, Pontificem creat. In ipsâ hujus vitâ, quem jam Johannem XVIII. vocat; potentiâ Crescentii Romani Consulis fretus, quem pecuniâ corripuisse (corrupisse) creditum est, tempore Gregorii V. per factionem Pontificatum occupat. Tantum enim pecuniarum ex Constantinopoli ad urbem secum detulerat, ut constantes etiam suâ largitione ad maleficium impelli potuissent, nedum Crescentius homo avarissimus & regnandi cupidus. Miror ego, historicos Johannem ipsum inter Pontifices numerâsse, cùm vivente adhuc Gregorio sedem occupâsset, nisi forte in conscribendis Pontificum vitis ita faciendum censent, ut in perpetua historia fit. Nam & Tyrannorum perversè facta, optimorum Principum rebus gestis annumerantur, ut quantùm inter se boni & mali dissideant, à legentibus cognosci possit, quò malorum exemplo à vitiis deterreantur, & bonorum exemplo ad virtutem impulsi, vitam ducant in terris felicem & beatam: quâ quidem beatitudine Johannes caruit, fur certè in Pontificatu & latro: non enim, ut par fuerat, per ostium intravit. Moritur autem, atque cum ignominia quidem, decimo usurpati Pontificatus mense. Usurpati Pontificatûs mense? Et tamen Scriptores numerant, ipse Platina, qui id in aliis miratur, numerat, fur & latro fuit, & mansit, non bis electus fuit.
units.tr: But Platina, on Sergius III, returns to a more general complaint: Look, I beg you, he says, how far these men have degenerated from their ancestors. For those, being most holy men, despised the dignity offered to them unsought, devoting themselves to prayer and Christian teaching. But these, seeking the papacy by largesse and ambition, and having obtained it, neglected divine worship and carried on enmities among themselves no less than the cruellest tyrants; afterwards they indulged their pleasures more securely, since nowhere were there any left to restrain their vices. To this complaint of Platina a very similar one by Stella responds, in his life of Romanus I, where he records as something rare that he, not, like many of his time, by ambition or largesse, but in the manner of Peter, obtained the papacy. Concerning the tyrants of the ninth and tenth centuries, Baronius, at the year 597, no. 4, testifies that they also, ruling the people and the Roman clergy by money, thrust monstrous men into the Chair of Peter. Of Boniface VII Platina writes thus in his Life: At the beginning of his magistracy, when good citizens conspired together, he was forced to leave the city. Carrying off the most precious things from the Basilica of Peter, he fled to Constantinople, where he stayed so long that, by selling what he had sacrilegiously taken, he gathered a great sum of money. Relying on this as a support for seizing tyranny, he returned to the city, intending to corrupt the Roman citizens with largesse. Good men opposed his attempts, above all John, the deacon and cardinal, whom, having seized him with the help of certain pernicious men, he at once deprived of his eyes, etc. Then, as is customary, he adds a complaint: Look, I beg you, how far these popes have degenerated from their ancestors, who left us this Christian commonwealth so large and so glorious with their own blood. The Roman pontiff, Father and King of sacred things, stole the holy things themselves, and he who ought to have avenged sacrileges became the author of such a great sacrilege. This usually happens in any commonwealth when the ambition and avarice of the wicked prevail over the virtue and dignity of the good. Therefore those should be chosen for the clergy whose life and teaching have been tested, not those who, having no virtue or religion, seek power for themselves by ambition and largesse. Concerning Gregory V's rival (whom Platina, in his Life, says Caesar elected on account of kinship), whose name some suppress among the popes as less lawfully created, while others call him John XVII, because he had entered the papacy by the consent of the people and the Roman clergy, to whom the election belonged; so Platina, in his Life of Gregory V: The Romans again appoint Crescentius consul with full power, who at once creates a certain John, a Greek by birth, bishop of Piacenza, no less wealthy than learned, as pope. In his own life, which he now calls John XVIII, relying on the power of Crescentius the Roman consul, who is believed to have been bribed with money, he seized the papacy by faction in the time of Gregory V. For he had brought so much money with him from Constantinople to the city that even steadfast men could have been driven to wickedness by his largesse, not to mention Crescentius, a most avaricious man and eager to rule. I marvel that the historians have counted John himself among the popes, since he seized the see while Gregory was still alive, unless perhaps they think the lives of the popes should be written as in a continuous history. For the wicked deeds of tyrants are recorded alongside the achievements of the best princes, so that readers may learn how far good and bad differ, in order that they may be deterred from vices by the example of the wicked and impelled to virtue by the example of the good, and lead a happy and blessed life on earth. John lacked that blessedness; he was certainly a thief and a robber in the papacy, for he did not enter by the door, as was proper. He died, moreover, and that in disgrace, in the tenth month of his usurped papacy. Of the usurped papacy's month? And yet the writers count him, and Platina himself, who marvels at this in others, counts him: he was a thief and a robber, and remained so, and he was not elected twice.

units.la: XXII. De Silvestro II. cujus jam Differt. V. §. 32. prolixior mentio facta est, testatur, quòd diabolum secutus,cui se totum tradiderat, ambitione & Diabolicâ dominandi cupiditate impulsus largitione primò quidem &c. consecutus sit.
units.tr: XXII. Of Silvester II, of whom a fuller mention has already been made in Differt. V. §. 32., he testifies that having followed the devil, to whom he had wholly given himself, he was driven by ambition and by a diabolical lust for domination and obtained the papacy at first indeed by largesse, etc.

units.la: XXIII. Benedicti IX. electionem describens Baronius ad an. 1033. n. 5. seqq. Simoniacam quoque fuisse ita testatur: Quae non audet furore percita dominandi libido? Quae non tentat flagrans praefectura cupiditas? Non parcit legibus, quas caeca non videt, non timet Deum, quem non considerat; non reveretur homines, quos omnes spernit. Ad facinus implendum parat pecuniâ infelix pater infeliciori filio viam; Romanos, quos novit potentiores aggreditur, quos expugnatos auro sibi devincit, quorum emptione suffragiorum, quam conceperat, parit iniquitatem, dum filium in thronum provehit &c. Ingemuit ad aspectum Catholicus orbis haud mediocre passus in electione adeò illegitima scandalum. Post ex Glabro, tunc superstite, ista vidente, scribente ac detestante, inter alia dicit, intercedente thesaurorum pecuniâ electum fuisse. De eodem Benedicto IX. ad an. 1044. n. 1. ex Hermanno ait; seipsum privavit & alium pro se ob avaritiam contra Canones ordinavit. Et n. 2. Contrariam factionem Sylvestrum subrogâsse qui & malis artibus, nempe collatâ pecuniâ, ad sedem Petri sibi ascensum paraverit. Quod ex Leone Ostiensi porrò confirmat, Joannem nempe, cui Sylvestri nomen impositum esset, non tamen gratis, in Romanum Pontificem subrogatum esse.
units.tr: XXIII. Baronius, describing the election of Benedict IX, at the year 1033, no. 5 and following, likewise testifies that it was simoniacal: What lust for domination, stirred up by fury, does not dare? What flaming desire for rule does not attempt? It spares no laws, which it does not see with blind eyes; it does not fear God, whom it does not consider; it does not respect men, whom it despises all. To accomplish the crime the unhappy father prepares, by money, a way for his even unhappier son; he approaches the Romans whom he knows to be more powerful, binds them to himself by gold once they are won over, and by buying their votes, which he had conceived, he gives birth to iniquity, while he advances his son to the throne, etc. The Catholic world groaned at the sight, having suffered no little scandal from such an utterly illegitimate election. Afterwards, from Glaber, who was still alive, seeing these things, writing and denouncing them, he says among other things that he was elected through the intervention of money from the treasuries. Concerning the same Benedict IX, at the year 1044, no. 1, he says from Hermann: He deprived himself, and out of avarice ordained another in his place contrary to the canons. And no. 2: the opposing faction had substituted Silvester, who by wicked arts, namely by money paid, prepared his ascent to the see of Peter. He further confirms this from Leo of Ostia: John, namely, who had been given the name Silvester, was made Roman pontiff not for nothing.

units.la: XXIV. N. 5. Postquàm jam n. 2. de tribus tunc pseudo-Pontificibus egisset, subjungit. Ad (At) quodnam primum remedium fuerit adhibitum ad extinguendam tricipitem bestiam hanc, portis inferis emergentem, videamus. Illi planè simile excogitatum remedium est, quod in extinguendo Cerbero illo fabuloso finxere Poëta, nempe piceâ offâ implendo fauces, dando illis mandatum aliquid, ut à latratu omninò cessarent. Quis autem istud paraverit, ex Ottone Freisingensi post declarat. Gratianum nimirum, quem alii vocant Johannem, eis à sancta sede cedere pecuniâ persuasisse, Benedicto redditibus Angliæ, quia majoris videbatur authoritatis esse, relictis; Ob ea cives eum elegisse eúmque mutato nomine Gregorium VI. vocâsse. N. 6. addit: Hæc sunt, quæ loco Simoniæ Gregorio objecta fuere. Sed an emptio sedis, vel redemptio potiùs vexationis transactio ista adeò necessaria ad pellendos intrusos Pontifices fuerit, periti Canonum omnes facilè judicabunt. Unum hoc liquet, eundem Gregorium VI. verè germanum atque legitimum Pontificem habitum esse &c.
units.tr: XXIV. No. 5. Having already spoken at no. 2 of the three pseudo-popes of that time, he adds: But let us see what first remedy was applied to extinguish this three-headed beast, emerging from the gates of hell. The remedy devised is very like that which the poets invented for quelling that fabulous Cerberus, namely stuffing its jaws with a pitch-cake and giving it a command so that it would cease barking altogether. Who devised this, he declares afterwards from Otto of Freising: namely Gratian, whom others call John, persuaded them to resign the holy see for money, the revenues of England being left to Benedict, since he seemed to have greater authority. On this account the citizens chose him and, changing his name, called him Gregory VI. N. 6. adds: These are the things objected to Gregory in place of Simony. But whether the purchase of the see, or rather this transaction of redeeming the vexation, was so necessary for driving out the intruding popes, all experts in the canons will easily judge. This one thing is clear, that the same Gregory VI was regarded as a true and lawful pope, etc.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: XXV. Nobis & hoc liquet, electionem illam valde suspe- ctam esse, vixque à Simonia abfuisse; Cur enim ipse pecuniam dare debuit? Cur non cogitavit, electionem suam à Simoniæ suspicione neutiquam liberam esse posse? Videtur certè alios pellendo sibi locum comparâsse, utrumque iisdem armis effecit, pecuniâ. Sed & Platina testatur Benedictum IX. huic ipsi, ut quidam affirment, Pontificium munus vendidisse. Quam ob rem merito ab omnibus Benedictus ipse accusatus sit, & judicio divino damnatus. Subdit apparitionem simulacri ejusdem admodum monstrosi, & plus feritatis, quam humanitatis in se habentis. Et denique: Moritur; nec vacâsse tunc sedes dici potest, cùm Pontificatum vendiderit; Si vendidit, & Gratiano vendidit, Gratianus emit.
units.tr: XXV. We also see clearly that this election was very suspect and scarcely free of simony. For why did he himself have to give money? Why did he not consider that his own election could in no way be free of suspicion of simony? He seems to have secured his place by expelling others, and he achieved both by the same means, money. Platina also testifies that Benedict IX sold the papal office to this very man, as some affirm. For which reason Benedict himself was rightly accused by all and condemned by divine judgment. He adds the appearance of an image of the same man, very monstrous, having more savagery than humanity in him. And finally: He dies; nor can the see be said to have been vacant then, since he had sold the papacy. If he sold it, and sold it to Gratian, then Gratian bought it.

units.la: XXVI. In vita Silvestri supra dicti, nomine III. idem auctor est, Cardinalem Sabinum Pontificem creatum, non dicere se, à Collegio Patrum, quod tolerabilius fuisset, sed largitione, ut quidam tradunt; merito pulsum esse, cùm non per ostium sed per posticum intrâsset, ut fur & latro. Habet ibidem rursus querelam suam: Eò tum Pontificatus devenerat, inquit, ut qui plùs largitione & ambitione, non dico sanctitate vitæ valeret, sed tantum modò dignitatis gradum, oppressis & rejectis aliis, obtineret, quem morem utinam aliquando non detinuissent nostra tempora. En eadem Platinæ tempore contigerunt! Imò pejora imminere vidit, nam addidit: sed hoc parùm est, (si hoc hoc parùm est, quid multùm est?) pejora, ni Deus caveat, visuri aliquando sumus. Ita Ecclesia Romana quotidie in melius proficit. Et sunt hodie cautiores quidam, sed non castiores, ut sequentia docebunt. Ipse autem Gratianus, sive Gregorius VI. ut apud Baronium ad an.1046. n.1. Hermannus narrat, convictus (Simoniæ nimirum, cujus eum Baronius quoque tunc postulatum esse n.3. ait) baculo pastorali ab Imperatore Henrico in Synodo Sutrina privatus fuit; Atque inanes sunt Baronii contra istam depositionem querimoniæ. Ut & Stella de eo narrat, quòd à multis homicida & sanguinis humani effusor potentissimus habitus, nec non à Cardinalibus omnibus facinorosus prædicatus sit.
units.tr: XXVI. In the life of Silvester mentioned above, under the name III, the same author says that Cardinal Sabinus was created pope, not, he says, by the college of Fathers, which would have been more tolerable, but by bribery, as some relate; and he was rightly thrown out, since he had entered not by the door but by the back, like a thief and robber. There again he has his complaint: To such a point had the papacy come, he says, that whoever prevailed more by bribery and ambition, I do not say by holiness of life, but merely obtained the rank of dignity, others being crushed and rejected; a custom which would that our times had at some time not kept. Behold, the same things happened in Platina's time! Indeed he saw worse threatening, for he added: but this is too little (if this is too little, what is much?) we shall one day see worse, unless God forbid. Thus the Roman Church daily makes progress for the better. And some are more cautious today, but not more chaste, as what follows will show. Moreover Gratian, or Gregory VI, as Hermann narrates in Baronius at the year 1046, n.1, being convicted (of simony, of course, for which Baronius also says he was then accused, n.3) was deprived of the pastoral staff by the Emperor Henry in the Synod of Sutri. Baronius's complaints against that deposition are empty. Stella also relates of him that he was regarded by many as a most powerful murderer and shedder of human blood, and was proclaimed a criminal by all the cardinals.

units.la: XXVII. In Clemente II. Platina hanc Imperatorii concursûs causam allegat; Videbat Imperator, eò licentiæ factiosum quemque & potentem, quamvis ignobilem, devenisse, ut corruptis suffragiis tantam dignitatem consequeretur; quæ certè nisi sanctitate & doctrinâ bene meritis volente Deo demandari cuipiam non deberet.
units.tr: XXVII. In the case of Clement II, Platina gives this reason for the imperial intervention: The Emperor saw that licence had reached such a point that any factious and powerful man, however ignoble, could by corrupt votes obtain so great a dignity, which certainly ought not to be committed to anyone unless he were well deserving through holiness and learning, God willing.

units.la: XXVIII. In Damaso II. sequentia habet ; Adeo inoleverat hic mos, ut jam cuique ambitioso liceret Petri sedem invadere. Sed obstitit Deus justus vindex, ut is cateris exemplo esset, ne quod virtus dare consuevit, ambitione & largitione quaereretur. Nam 23. Pontificatus sui die moritur. Censent nonnulli, hunc inter Pontifices nequaquam numerandum esse, cum non recte Pontificatum adeptus sit.
units.tr: XXVIII. Concerning Damasus II he has the following: This custom had so taken root that now any ambitious man could invade the seat of Peter. But the just God, the avenger, stood in the way, so that he might be an example to the rest, lest what virtue usually gives should be sought by ambition and bribery. For on the 23rd day of his pontificate he dies. Some judge that he should by no means be counted among the popes, since he did not rightly obtain the papacy.

units.la: XXIX. De Benedicto X. testatur, ab Hildebrando Pontificatu pulsum, quod non per ostium, quemadmodum dicebant, sed per vim & largitionem intrasset. Et Onuphrius in Annot. Hic Benedictus legitimus Pontifex non fuit, cum Simoniace per vim & metum contra canones & juramenta Pontificatum occupavit. Quod diserte in epistola quadam refert Petrus Damiani Episcopus Ostiensis, qui hoc tempore vixit. Unde merito alio subrogato, exactus est, quare in numeri nota ejus ratio habenda non esset. Vide Authores Hermannum Contractum, Lambertum Schafnaburgensem, Leonem Episc. Ostiensem, Hist. Cassinen. l.2.c.102. Ad Eugenium P. Bernhardus de Consid. l. IV. 2. ita scripsit: Quem dabis mihi de tota maxima urbe, qui te in Papam receperit, pretio, seu spe pretii non interveniente?
units.tr: XXIX. Of Benedict X he testifies that he was driven from the papacy by Hildebrand, because he had entered not through the door, as they said, but by force and bribery. And Onuphrius in the Annotations: This Benedict was not a lawful pope, since he occupied the papacy simoniacally, by force and fear, against the canons and oaths. Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who lived at this time, clearly says so in a certain letter. Hence, with another put in his place, he was rightly expelled, so that his reign need not be counted in the numbering of the popes. See the authors Hermann the Lame, Lambert of Schafnaburg, Leo bishop of Ostia, Hist. Cassinen. l.2.c.102. To Pope Eugenius, Bernard de Consideratione l. IV. 2. wrote thus: Whom will you give me from the whole great city who received you as pope for a price, or without the intervention of hope of a price?

units.la: XXX. In Conclavi Clementis V. ejusdem electio Simoniaca satis aperte traditur. Rex Galliae Philippus oblatione officiorum Columnae usurus ad eum mando un suo con oro & con presenti, &c. aliquem ex suis misit cum auro & argento & donis, magna ei insuper promittens, atque dicens, se alias quoque testaturum, quanti officium illud faciat. Hic etiam mosso dalle speranze &c. motus spe a splendido Rege falsa, gaudio plenus, omni studio corrumpere coepit eos, quos auri cupidos noverat, eos insuper quoque pascens promissionibus, quos literis confirmatos viderat, atque etiam ex ore Nuncii Regii audiverat. Cumque eo cognati desiderosi a compiacere il Re, elegerunt & eligi curarunt charum, amicum & familiarem Regi.
units.tr: XXX. In the conclave of Clement V his election is set out quite openly as simoniacal. King Philip of France, wishing to use the offices of the Colonna, sent to him one of his men with gold and with gifts, etc. He sent someone of his with gold and silver and gifts, promising him great things besides, and saying that he would also show on other occasions how much he valued that service. Moved too by the hopes, etc., moved by hope from the splendid but false king, full of joy, he began with every effort to corrupt those whom he knew to be greedy for gold, feeding them besides with promises, whom he had seen confirmed by letters and had also heard from the mouth of the royal messenger. And with him his relatives, eager to please the King, chose and took care that there be elected one dear to, a friend and intimate of the King.

units.la: XXXI. Sed & Joannes, Platinae XXIV. eodem referente, post mortem Alexandri V. largitione usus, maxime vero erga Cardinales a Gregorio creatos, pauperes adhuc, Pontifex creatus est.
units.tr: XXXI. But also John, according to Platina XXIV, the same authority reporting, after the death of Alexander V, having used bribery, especially toward the cardinals created by Gregory, still poor, was created pope.

units.la: XXXII. Ut in Conclavi Pii II. promissiones non defuerunt, & Rhotomagensis divitiarum jactantia se commendare studuit, quibus pauperi Ecclesiae subveniri posset, e se alcuno voleva dire &c. Et quia aliquis objicere potuisset, quod ob Simoniam suam non posset obtinere Pontificatum, quia sic omnia beneficia venalia futura essent; ipse non negavit, se hactenus illo crimine foedatum fuisse, sed pro certo affirmavit & jurajuravit, se deinceps ab illo purum futurum. Ita in suo favore era &c. Ipsi favebat Cardinalis Avignonensis homo audax & sordidus & avarus, qui eum omnibus viribus juvabat. Non tam quia Gallus erat, sed quia à promotione ejus infallibiliter sperabat & Ecclesiam Rhotomagensem, & Palatium ejus Romæ, & Vice-Cancellariatum, multi attracti erant magnis promissis & capti muscarum ad instar ab esca &c. Quamprimùm ipsi aliquem noverat, statim ei beneficia & officia promisit, imò insuper munera in diversis Provinciis &c. Videbatur, eum jam habere 11. vota, neque dubitabant duodecimum certò accessurum, cùm in tali casu non deesset, qui dicat; Et ego quoque Te Papam facio; ad acquirendam electi gratiam &c.
units.tr: XXXII. In the conclave of Pius II promises were not lacking, and the Archbishop of Rouen tried to commend himself by boasting of his riches, by which the poor Church could be helped, as someone would say, etc. And since someone could object that because of his simony he could not obtain the papacy, since thus all benefices would be for sale, he did not deny that he had until then been defiled by that crime, but firmly affirmed and swore that he would thenceforth be free of it. Thus in his favour, it was, etc. The Cardinal of Avignon, a bold, sordid and greedy man, favoured him, and helped him with all his strength. Not so much because he was French, but because from his promotion he infallibly hoped for the church of Rouen, and his palace in Rome, and the vice-chancellorship. Many were drawn in by great promises and caught like flies by bait, etc. As soon as he knew anyone, at once he promised him benefices and offices, and indeed gifts in various provinces, etc. He seemed now to have eleven votes, and they did not doubt that a twelfth would surely come, since in such a case there would not be lacking someone who says: "And I too make you pope," to win the favour of the elect, etc.

units.la: XXXIII. In Conclavi Innocentii VIII. vel maximè Simonia regnavit.
units.tr: XXXIII. In the Conclave of Innocent VIII, simony above all reigned.

units.la: Nam modus creationis fuit iste: videlicet, quia cùm die Sabbathi in hora vespertina starent Cardinales in scrutinio, qui erant omnes numero 25. causâ faciendi Pontificem, Cardinalis S. Petri ad vincula, ut fertur, dixit Cardinali S. Marci, qui illo tempore habebat XI. voces, si volebat promittere domum suam Cardinali Aragonensi filio Regis Ferdinandi & ipse promittebat se daturum ei tres alias voces, ita quod essent 14. At ille respondit, se minimè hoc facturum; Nam si hoc fecisset, non esset canonicè, ut decet, electus. Item quia domus sua fortiter prejudicabat Castro S. Angeli, unde si hoc fecisset, fuisset forte causa disturbationis urbis & totius fidei Christianæ: Nam posset de facili ibi Rex venire & facere se Dominum urbis, & disturbare statum Ecclesiæ. Deinde prædictus Cardinalis S. Petri ad Vincula accessit ad Vice-Cancellarium, dixitque ei, si volebant facere simul unum Pontificem ad votum eorum. At ille, dummodo disturbaretur Electio S. Marci &c. tractaverunt cum omnibus Cardinalibus, ut darent voces eorum Cardinali Melphitensi; promittentes illis, se multa daturos: & hoc modo tractârunt cum omnibus Cardinalibus, praeterquam cum sex senioribus & principalioribus. Deinde die sequenti detectum fuit, quòd pro habendis vocibus multa bona Ecclesiæ promiserant, quæ, ut fertur, sic distributa fuerunt. Primò Cardinalis Sabellus habuit Castrum, quod dicitur Monticelli in partibus Insulæ: Item legationem Bononiensem; Cardinalis Columnensis, Castrum Ceperani & Legationem Patrimonii, & pro restauratione domûs combustæ, & damnorum 25. m. ducatorum; & fuerunt illis promissa beneficia quàm primùm vacantia pro 7000. mille ducatis. Ursinus habuit legationem Marchiæ, quæ fuit ademta Camerario: Item castrum Cerveteris, Marisanensi castrum Capranica, & Episcopatum Avenionensem; Filio Regis Ferdinandi fertur fuisse concessum Pontem Corvum: Item data fuit domus, vel Palatium, quod fuefuerat Domini Papæ, dum erat Cardinalis, videlicet S. Laurentii in Lucina, Cardinali Parmensi Palatium sancti Johannis della Magliana cum omni ejus ædificio; Cardinali Mediolanensi, Archi-presbyteratum S. Johannis Laterani, & Legationem Avenionensem; Cardinalis S. Petri ad vincula & præfectus Urbis, ejus frater, habuerunt fanum cum quinque aliis terris circumstantibus, promisitque facere dictum Præfectum ejus fratrem Generalem Capitaneum Ecclesiæ. Qui Cardinalis S. Petri ad vincula continuè residet, & manet cum ipso summo Pontifice; & omnia quæ gesta sunt & gerentur, cum suo consilio, sive potius ad suum velle fiunt, & aliqua, quæ per eum inadvertenter & insscio dicto Cardinali fiunt, illico revocantur &c.
units.tr: The manner of the creation was this. On the Sabbath, in the evening hour, while the Cardinals, twenty-five in number, were sitting in scrutiny to make a Pope, the Cardinal of S. Peter ad Vincula, as is reported, said to the Cardinal of S. Mark, who at that time had eleven votes, that if he wished to promise his house to the Aragonese Cardinal, son of King Ferdinand, he himself would promise to give him three other votes, so that there would be fourteen. But he replied that he would by no means do this, for if he had done so, he would not have been canonically elected, as is proper. Also, because his house greatly prejudiced the Castle of S. Angelo, if he had done this it might perhaps have caused disturbance to the city and to the whole Christian faith, for the King could easily come there and make himself lord of the city and disturb the state of the Church. Then the aforesaid Cardinal of S. Peter ad Vincula approached the Vice-Chancellor and told him that they could, if they wished, make one Pope to their liking. But he, provided the election of S. Mark was disturbed etc., they negotiated with all the Cardinals that they should give their votes to the Cardinal of Melfi, promising them that they would give much. In this way they negotiated with all the Cardinals, except the six eldest and chief ones. Then on the following day it was discovered that, in order to obtain votes, they had promised many goods of the Church, which, as is reported, were distributed thus. First, Cardinal Sabellus had the castle which is called Monticelli in the region of the island; also the Bolognese legation. Cardinal Colonna had the castle of Ceperano and the legation of the Patrimony, and for the restoration of the burnt house and for damages 25,000 ducats; and benefices were promised to them as soon as they fell vacant, for 7,000 thousand ducats. Ursini had the legation of the March, which was taken from the Chamberlain; also the castle of Cerveteri, the castle of Capranica of Marisano, and the bishopric of Avignon. To the son of King Ferdinand it is reported that Ponte Corvo was granted. Also the house or palace which had belonged to the Lord Pope while he was Cardinal, namely S. Lorenzo in Lucina, was given to the Cardinal of Parma; the palace of S. John della Magliana with all its buildings to the Cardinal of Milan; the archpriesthood of S. John Lateran and the legation of Avignon. The Cardinal of S. Peter ad Vincula and the prefect of the City, his brother, had a temple with five other surrounding lands, and he promised to make the said prefect, his brother, General Captain of the Church. This Cardinal of S. Peter ad Vincula constantly resides and stays with the Supreme Pontiff himself, and all things that have been done and will be done are done with his counsel, or rather at his will; and any things which are done by him inadvertently and without the knowledge of the said Cardinal are immediately revoked etc.

units.la: XXXV. Hinc necesse habuit Author Conclavis illud sequente voto claudere:
units.tr: XXXV. Hence the author of the Conclave was obliged to close with the following wish:

units.la: Deus concedat sibi gratiam rectè vivendi & administrandi, quod difficile videtur, attenta ejus præterita vita, cùm sit juvenis Genuensis, & ex pluribus mulieribus septem filios inter mares & feminas habeat: & attentâ etiam qualitate electionis, quæ deterior fuit electione Sixti: Adeò quòd omnes quodammodo uno ore tam Romani, quàm alienigenæ, & Curiales, de ejus futura vita & gubernatione Imperii & Civitatis per maximè suspicantur, faciúntque super eo diversa judicia.
units.tr: May God grant him grace to live and govern rightly, which seems difficult, given his past life, since he is a young Genoese who has seven children, male and female, by several women; and considering also the quality of the election, which was worse than the election of Sixtus, so that all, as with one mouth, both Romans and foreigners and Curialists, greatly suspect what his future life and government of the Empire and the City will be, and form various judgments about him.

units.la: XXXV. Successor ejus Alexander VI. apud Platinam in vita nonnullorum Cardinalium cacà ambitione & avaritiâ corruptorum operâ tantam dignitatem diciturr esse assecutus, qui postea in ingrato Pontifice perfidiam maximam experti, debitas scelerati venalisque suffragii pœnas dederint: Horum princeps fuit, ita pergit, Ascanius Sforzia, emptus procul dubio profusissimâ largitione, ut hic omnium ejus ordinis deterrimus pro optimo Pontifex renunciaretur. De quo etiam Author Conclavis: Adoperò ogni industria & arte &c. Omni industria & arte immoderata sua ambitioni satisfacere studuit, atque ideò animos Cardinalium potentissimorum omnibus modis licitis & illicitis sibi conciliavit. Antequam altare conscenderet, Sforzam Vice-Cancellarium creavit, secundùm promissionem in Conclavi factam. XXXVI. Pius III. qui hunc excepit, haveva promesso &c. promiserat iis (Cardinalibus Eautoribus) multa, si se sint facturi Papam. Sic & aliâs in illo Conclavi erano &c. multa divisiones & sententiæ inter Cardinales, quas taceo propter absurditatem & Simoniam, quæ sine ullo pudore aut rubore in iis sequebantur. Vocat Il Card. p.3. l.2. p.149. le più infami e detestabili Simonie del Mondo: maximè infames & detestabiles Simonias, quas unquam in mundo fuerint.
units.tr: XXXV. His successor, Alexander VI, according to Platina in the life of some Cardinals corrupted by blind ambition and avarice, attained so great a dignity through their work; these men afterwards, experiencing great treachery from the ungrateful Pope, paid the due penalties for their wicked and venal votes. The chief of these, he goes on, was Ascanio Sforza, bought without doubt by most lavish largesse, so that this worst of all that order was proclaimed the best Pope. Of him the author of the Conclave also says: "He spared no effort or skill" etc. With every effort and every skill, he strove to satisfy his immoderate ambition, and therefore by all lawful and unlawful means he won over to himself the minds of the most powerful Cardinals. Before he mounted the altar, he created Sforza Vice-Chancellor, in accordance with the promise made in the Conclave. XXXVI. Pius III, who succeeded him, had promised etc. he had promised them (the Cardinals who favoured him) many things, if they would make him Pope. So also at other times in that Conclave there were etc. many divisions and opinions among the Cardinals, which I pass over on account of their absurdity and simony, which followed among them without any shame or blushing. He calls them the most infamous and detestable simonies that have ever been in the world: maximè infames & detestabiles Simonias, quas unquam in mundo fuerint. Il Card. p.3. l.2. p.149.

units.la: XXXVII. Conclave Julii II. memorat sequentia: Il Cardinale &c. Card. S. Petri in Vincula (fuit is ipse Julius) locutus est in Vaticano cum Duce Valentino, & Cardinalibus Factionis ipsius, Hispanis ibi praesentibus, concluserúntque cum Capitulis, quorum multa indicari nequeunt, inter alia, eundem S. Petrum debere Ducem, si ejus opera creetur Pontifex, facere Generalem Ecclesia pro suis creaturis, & contrà ipse etiam multa Papa promisit, atque promiserunt etiam & juramento se obligârunt Creatura, se Petrum illum electuras. Ipsi autem Conclavistae, sive Authori Conclavis, cùm ei instantis promotionis nuncium afferret, promisit la Chiesa d'Orti e la sua mula con li fornimenti, la cappa & il Rochetto; Id est: Ecclesiam Orti, mulam suam cum Ornatu, Rochettum & Cappam.
units.tr: XXXVII. The Conclave of Julius II records the following: "The Cardinal etc., the Cardinal of S. Peter ad Vincula (this was Julius himself), spoke in the Vatican with the Duke of Valentinois and with the Cardinals of his faction, Spaniards being present there, and they agreed on terms, many of which cannot be disclosed; among other things, that the same S. Peter, if he were created Pope through his work, should make the Duke General of the Church for his creatures; and on the other hand the Pope himself also promised many things, and the creatures also promised, and bound themselves by oath, to elect that Peter." But when a messenger brought him news of his impending promotion, he promised the Conclavists, or the author of the Conclave, "the church of Orte and his mule with its harness, the cope and the rochet"; that is, "the Church of Orte, his mule with its trappings, the rochet and the cope."

units.la: XXXVIII. In Conclavi Leonis X. lecta fuit Bulla Julii II.
units.tr: XXXVIII. In the Conclave of Leo X the Bull of Julius II was read.

units.la: la quale trattava della Simoniaca elettione de Pontefici, de Simoniaca Pontificum electione. In eodem Conclavi: Si aboccarono &c. Collocuti sunt S. Georgius & Medicaeus, & publicè consultabant ultra horam, nemo tamen cognovit, quid tractârint; Alii autem Cardinales judicârunt, agi de Papatu alterutri conferendo, finaliter cùm totum negotium bene praeparatum esset, Medicaeus Papa declaratus est.
units.tr: which treated of the simoniacal election of popes, of the simoniacal election of popes. In the same conclave: They conferred and consulted publicly for more than an hour, Saint George and Medici; yet nobody knew what they discussed. Other cardinals judged that they were treating of conferring the papacy on one of them; finally, when the whole business had been well prepared, Medici was declared Pope.

units.la: XXXIX. In Conclavi Leonis XI. Fautores Baronii se ne promettevano Vittoria, quasi che certa &c. Victoriam quasi certam sibi promittebant &c. atque postea innotuit distributio praemiorum à fautoribus Baronii inter se facta, Pansilio obtingebat Poenitentiaria, Duci Aqua Spartensi, Card. Cesis fratri Avignonum, Spinellio Archiep. Neapolitanus, alii Orvietum, alii Aversa. Aldobrandinus tantùm petebat, ut ratio de praeteritis reddi non debeat, & ipse Ecclesiastica dirigere possit: Bardino promittebatur Legatio, alii hoc, alii illud. Gallis promotio numerosa, & jam post molestias Conclavis recreatio Frascati habenda destinabatur, &c. In eodem Conclavi mentio fit pontis aurei, quem adversarii, ut ager Sfondrata exiret, praeparaverint. In eodem le Creature &c. Creatura Aldobrandiniana pauperiores magis particulariter obligata erant dono 1000. ducatorum singulis dato, licèt id ob Aldobrandini naturam auri tenacem impossibile multis visum sit; praeter quòd etiam cella eorum sumptibus illius confecta atque ornata fuerunt; adjungebantur promissiones de pensionibus perpetuis, ex parte redituum, qui ad Ecclesia decus singulis statim conferri debuissent; atque nullum mihi est dubium, eum à singulis coutra signum postulâsse, non sine tadio multorum, quibus hoc tyrannicum videbatur, larga praemia & participatio regiminis promittebantur.
units.tr: XXXIX. In the Conclave of Leo XI, the supporters of Baronius promised themselves victory, as if it were certain, etc. Afterwards it became known how the rewards had been divided among the supporters of Baronius: Pansilio was to have the Penitentiary, the Duke of Acquasparta, Cardinal Cesi's brother, Avignon, Spinelli the Archbishop of Naples, others Orvieto, others Aversa. Aldobrandini asked only that no account be demanded of his past conduct and that he himself be allowed to direct ecclesiastical affairs. Bardino was promised a legation, one man this, another that. For the French a large promotion was arranged, and a recreation at Frascati was planned after the troubles of the conclave, etc. In the same conclave mention is made of a golden bridge, which the adversaries had prepared so that Sfondrata's party might withdraw. In the same, the creatures, etc. The poorer creatures of Aldobrandini were bound more particularly by a gift of 1000 ducats to each, although to many this seemed impossible, given Aldobrandini's miserly nature with gold. Besides this, their cells were furnished and decorated at his expense. Promises of perpetual pensions were added, drawn from revenues which should immediately have been conferred on each for the honour of the Church. And I have no doubt that he demanded a sign of agreement from each, not without the distaste of many, to whom this seemed tyrannical; large rewards and a share in government were promised.

units.la: XL. In Conclavi Gregorii XV. narratur, quantum Campora Cardinali Estio Papatûs consequendi gratiâ promiserit; Subjungit Author. Non pareva però &c. Non tamen rationi conveniens aut verisimile videbatur, fore, ut ista, licèt scripto & juramento promissa fuissent, observarentur, tanquam nimis indigna Pontifice, cui incumbit augere, & non diminuere statum Ecclesiæ; In memoriam sibi ea propter revocabant exemplum multorum Pontificum, che con l'isteße arti &c. qui iisdem artibus promissionum Papatum consecuti sunt, & ne Simoniâ fœdarentur, contrarium illius, quod promiserunt, præstiterunt. Qui quidem malè promissa pejus præstare noluerunt, malè tamen promiserunt, & Simoniacis artibus Papatum consecuti sunt. In eodem Conclavi tentorno &c. Estium per proprium Conclavistam convertere studuerunt, promisso ei Canonicatu S. Petri; Sed Conclavista, indigna proponi videns, & digné respondens, abiit.
units.tr: XL. In the Conclave of Gregory XV it is related how much Campora promised Cardinal Estius in order to obtain the papacy. The author adds: It did not seem, however, reasonable or likely that these things, although promised in writing and under oath, would be kept, as being too unworthy of a Pope, whose duty is to increase and not to diminish the state of the Church. For they recalled to mind the example of many Popes who, by the same arts of promising, obtained the papacy, and, so as not to be defiled by simony, did the opposite of what they had promised. Those who indeed were unwilling to perform badly what they had promised badly, nevertheless promised badly and obtained the papacy by simoniacal arts. In the same conclave they tried to win over Estius through his own conclavist, promising him a canonry of St Peter's; but the conclavist, seeing the proposal to be unworthy, and answering worthily, went away.

units.la: XLI. In Conclavi Innocentii X. multis narratur, quantum Gallis promiserint in favorem Cardinalis Pansilii, Nepotes obsides favoris in Galliam mittendos, promotionem Principis Mazarini; quantum Legato Galliæ per fratrem Marchionem S. Viti, qui & nuncium cum promissionibus Pansilianorum in Galliam misit, æstimans ben rilevanti l' offerte &c. oblata non exigui momenti atque digna, quæ in Gallia acceptentur felicésque responsiones pariant, & pro quo Frater dixit, che per conto di lui &c. quòd quia pro se reditus Ecclesiasticos expetere non possit, numerari ei debeant nummi satis multi. Qui tamen & fratrem monuit, che vacando la chiesa d'Imola &c. Quia Ecclesia Imolensis vacet, posse eum de illa disponere pro se; Quæ & occasionem præbuerunt inquisitioni, se l'indurre l'Ambasciadore &c. Utrum si Legatus promissionibus prædictis ad consensum moveatur, electio maculetur, vel conscientia promittentis, maximè quoad nummos destinatos? Atque notatum fuit, sic non acquiri vota Cardinalium Gallorum, qui aliàs obligati sint, & quibus nec opus haberent, sed tantùm simplicem Legati & per consequens Gallia acquiescientiam, quæ non sit de essentia electionis, adeóque tantùm dari temporale pro temporali; Fundamentum quoque quæsitum in more antiquo certam pecuniæ summam pro confirmatione Imperatoriâ solvendi; Additur, quoad Ecclesiam Imolensem, dictum Cardinalis Rapaccioli ad Cardinalem Theodulum, qui Ecclesiam illam à Papa recens facto obtinuerat ;mi rallegro, che la chiesa d' Imola sia la vostra, perche per altro à mio credere credere Immolatus eras; Gaudeo Ecclesiam Imolensem Tuam esse, quia quantum ego credo aliàs immolatus eras.
units.tr: XLI. In the Conclave of Innocent X it is related at length how much they promised the French in favour of Cardinal Pansilio: nephews were to be sent to France as hostages for his favour, and the promotion of Prince Mazarin. How much was offered to the French legate through the brother, the Marquis of St Vitus, who also sent a messenger to France with the promises of the Pansilians, judging that the offers were of no small weight and worth, and that they would be accepted in France and bring about favourable replies; and about whom the brother said: that on his account, etc., since he could not himself seek ecclesiastical revenues, a fairly large sum of money should be counted out to him. Yet the brother also warned him that, since the church of Imola was vacant, etc., that he could dispose of it for himself. These things also gave occasion for the inquiry: whether, if the legate were moved to consent by the aforesaid promises, the election would be tainted, or the conscience of the one promising, especially as to the money designated? And it was noted that thus the votes of the French cardinals, who are otherwise bound and who do not need it, are not obtained, but only the simple acquiescence of the legate and consequently of France, which is not of the essence of the election; and so only a temporal thing is given for a temporal thing. A ground was also sought in the ancient custom of paying a certain sum of money for the imperial confirmation. It is added, concerning the church of Imola, the saying of Cardinal Rapaccioli to Cardinal Theodulus, who had obtained that church from the newly made Pope: I rejoice that the church of Imola is yours, because otherwise, as I believe, you were to be sacrificed (Immolatus). I rejoice that the church of Imola is yours, because, as I believe, you were otherwise to be sacrificed.

units.la: XLII. In Conclavi Alexandri VII. epistola Regis Galliarum voluit,che il Papa doveva &c. Id est: Papam debere esse alienum à Simonia, quemadmodum defunctus Pontifex. In eodem dicitur, Barberinum incitatum fuisse contra S. Clementem quoque calidissimis Jesuitarum instantiis, quibus opus habuerit ad recuperandos reditus Ecclesiasticos in Regno Neapolitano; non avaritiâ motus, sed ut ex Mammone iniquitatis sibi amicos eos parare posset, i quali per motivo di gratitudine lo potessero sollevare, dove tanto aspirano i suoi desiderii; qui studio gratitudinis eum eveherent, quò tantopere aspirabant desideria ipsius.
units.tr: XLII. In the Conclave of Alexander VII, the letter of the King of France wished that the Pope ought, etc. That is: the Pope ought to be free from simony, as the late Pontiff was. In the same place it is said that Barberini was incited against St Clement also by the most urgent entreaties of the Jesuits, for which he had need in order to recover the ecclesiastical revenues in the Kingdom of Naples; not moved by avarice, but so that from the Mammon of unrighteousness he might make those men his friends, who by motive of gratitude could raise him up, where his desires so strongly aspire; who, from a desire for gratitude, would exalt him, to which his desires so eagerly aspired.

units.la: XLIII. In Conclavi Clementis IX. similiter Simoniacarum considerationum, quibus Chigius moveri debuisset, fit mentio. L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.220. p.233. Elcii tunc Papabilis artes Simoniaca indicantur. Ante ingressum, imò Pontifice adhuc superstite, furono gran promesse fatte al Cardinal Caraffa, facta erant magna promissiones, referente Il Card. p. l.3. p.276. Tunc quoque Cardinalis Albicius & cum Gallis, & cum Hispanis negotiabatur, unde era entrato per questo, inquit idem p.278. in Concetto di buono Suizzero &c. Id est: Hinc pro Helvetio bono habebatur, utpote illorum servus, qui plus dabant. Quamvis sic reverà non ex bonis fuerit! Eodem tempore sù consigliato &c. Id est: Consultum fuit à quibusdam Barberino, ut pratensiones suas edificet super divitias suas, ad detestabile Alex. VI. exemplum; atque nonnulli talem perniciosum & abominabilem mercatum jam conclusum putabant; excusat tamen Author Cardinalem; de quo nihilominùs refert (quod Simoniacum videri possit etiam) eum plùs quàm unquam bonum videri voluisse, con la moltiplicata dell' opere pie col raddoppiar l'elemosine solite, che faceva prima a' poveri &c. auctis operibus piis, duplicatis eleemosynis &c.
units.tr: XLIII. In the Conclave of Clement IX likewise mention is made of simoniacal considerations, by which Chigi ought to have been moved. The Ambassador of Rome, p. 220, p. 233. The Papabili of that time are shown to have used simoniacal arts. Before the entry, indeed while the Pope was still alive, great promises were made to Cardinal Caraffa, great promises had been made, as the Cardinal, p. 3, p. 276, reports. At that time Cardinal Albizzi also was negotiating both with the French and with the Spaniards, whence he had entered on this account, says the same author, p. 278, in the reputation of a good Swiss, etc. That is: for this reason he was regarded as a good Helvetian, being in effect the servant of those who gave more. Although in truth he was not one of the good ones! At the same time it was advised, etc. That is: some advised Barberini to build his pretensions upon his riches, after the detestable example of Alexander VI; and some thought such a pernicious and abominable bargain was already concluded. The author, however, excuses the Cardinal; yet he nevertheless reports of him (which might also seem simoniacal) that he wished to appear good more than ever, with the multiplied pious works and doubled the alms which he used to give to the poor before, etc.

units.la: XLIV. Sed ex dictis patet, non omnes æquè facilè excusari posse, plurimos Simoniacis artibus Papatum quæsivisse, multos obtinuisse. Quarum jam artium vitium magis detegendum est; Patebit, magnum esse, sic electos malè electos esse, illegitimos, usurpatores, adulteros esse, etiam Pontifices; patet ex Scriptura, & maximè illo: Gratis accepistis &c. Apostolorum; nec non Simonis Magi exemplo, qui voluit emere, ut rursus vendere posset, Act.VIII. Sed patebit etiam ex Antiquorum, Pontificum, Pontificiorum testimoniis.
units.tr: XLIV. But from what has been said it is clear that not all can be excused equally; that very many sought the papacy by simoniacal arts, and many obtained it. The vice of these arts must now be exposed further. It will be shown that it is a great thing that those so elected are wrongly elected, illegitimate, usurpers, adulterers, even when they are Popes. This is clear from Scripture, and above all from that saying of the Apostles: Freely you have received, etc. It is clear also from the example of Simon Magus, who wished to buy in order to be able to sell again (Acts 8). But it will also be clear from the testimonies of the ancients, of the Popes, and of the Papists themselves.

units.la: XLV. Est inter Canones Apostolicos 30. mus qui & habetur Chalced. Conc. c. 2. Act. 8. si quis Episcopus aut Presbyter, aut Diaconus per pecunias obtinuerit hanc dignitatem, dejiciatur & ipse, & ordinator ejus, & à communione modis omnibus abscindatur, ut Simon Magus à Petro. Non hic excipiunt dignitatem Episcopi Romani, nec eum Romanenses excipi velle puto.
units.tr: XLV. Among the Apostolic Canons is the thirtieth, which is also found in the Council of Chalcedon, canon 2, Act 8: If any bishop, presbyter or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let him be deposed, both he himself and his ordainer, and be cut off from communion in every way, as Simon Magus was by Peter. Here they do not except the dignity of the Roman bishop, nor do I think the Romanists wish him to be excepted.

units.la: XLVI. Athalaricus Rex ad Johannem Bonifacii Successorem Romanum Pontificem scribens, apud Baron. ad an. 530. n. 4. qui ex Cassiod. l. 9. ep. 5. adducit, haec inter alia narrat: A tempore sanctissimi Papae Bonifacii, cum de talibus prohibendis suffragiis P. C. senatus-consultum nobilitatis sua memores considerant: Quicunque in Episcopatu obtinendo, sive per se, sive per aliam quamcunque personam aliquid promisisse declaratur, ut execrabilis contractus cunctis viribus evacuaretur. Baronius legendum putavit, efferretur. Qui etiam subjungit, Dioscorum, testante edicto Justinianeo, quod T. 1. Conc. vet. edit. in Joann. Pap. extat, ob causam pecuniariam post mortem fuisse anathematizatum. Agitur hic de Simonia in ambiendo Papatu.
units.tr: XLVI. King Athalaric, writing to John, the successor of Boniface, Roman Pontiff, in Baronius, ad an. 530, n. 4, who takes it from Cassiodorus, book 9, letter 5, relates among other things: From the time of the most holy Pope Boniface, when the Conscript Fathers, mindful of their nobility, considered by a senatorial decree how such votes were to be prohibited: whoever is declared to have promised anything, whether by himself or through any other person, in order to obtain a bishopric, let that accursed contract be annulled with all their strength. Baronius thought it should be read efferretur. He also adds that Dioscorus, as the edict of Justinian attests, which is extant in the first volume of the old edition of the Councils, under John the Pope, was anathematized after his death on account of money. The matter here is simony in canvassing for the papacy.

units.la: XLVII. Pelagius Papa statim ab initio Pontificatus sui, referente ex Anastasio Baronio ad an. 555. n. inter alia in conventu populi id protulit: Peto ut petitionem meam confirmetis, ut si quis ille est qui promovendus est in sancta Ecclesia apud Ostiarium usque ad gradum Episcopatus, neque per aurum, neque per alias promissiones proficiat (vos enim omnes scitis, quia hoc Simoniacum est) sed si quis ille est doctus in opere Dei, bonam vitam habens, non per datione m, sed per conversationem, inhibemus eum usque ad primum gradum venire. Modus ille praescribitur Papabilibus, hoc inhibetur Papabilibus.
units.tr: XLVII. Pope Pelagius, right at the start of his pontificate, according to Anastasius Baronius ad an. 555. n., declared among other things in an assembly of the people: I ask that you confirm my request: that if anyone is to be promoted in the holy Church, from the doorkeeper up to the grade of bishop, he shall gain nothing by gold or other promises (for you all know that this is simony), but if he is learned in the work of God and has a good life, not by a gift but by his conduct, we forbid him to rise to the first grade. That method is prescribed for the papabiles; this is forbidden to the papabiles.

units.la: XLVIII. In Concilio Romano sub Joan. XII. cujus Acta apud Baron. ad an. 964. n. 6 seqq. habentur: Piissimus atque sanctissimus Papa (erat is Johannes XII.) dixit: Potest aliquis vendere suum Ecclesiasticum gradum cuiquam, annon? S. Concilium respondit: Minime, quoniam neque vendi, neque emi ab aliquo potest. Non emi potest Ecclesiasticus gradus; neque igitur Papatus, de quo maxime agebatur.
units.tr: XLVIII. In the Roman Council under John XII., whose acts are found in Baronius ad an. 964. n. 6 seqq., the most pious and most holy Pope (this was John XII) said: Can anyone sell his ecclesiastical grade to someone else, or not? The holy Council replied: By no means, since it can be neither sold nor bought by anyone. An ecclesiastical grade cannot be bought; therefore neither can the papacy, which was the chief matter under discussion.

units.la: XLIX. Petrus Damiani apud Baronium ad an. 1033. n. 8. ad N. Archi Episcopum, de Romano Pontifice per Simoniam tunc intruso agens, ita inter alia scribit: Ille nimirum (in quantum mihi videtur) absque ulla simulatione Simoniacus est, quia vobis omnibus ejusdem Urbis Cardinalibus Episcopis reclamantibus, obsistentibus, & terribiliter anaanathematizantibus, nocturno tempore cum armatorum turbis undique tumultuantibus & furentibus inthronizatus est. Dehinc ad marsupiorum patrocinia funesta concurritur, pecunia per Regiones, andronas, vel angiportus in populos erogatur; B. Petri venerabilis arca pervaditur: Sicque per totam urbem, velut officinam male fabricantis Simonis factam, vix aliud quàm (ut ita loquar) malleorum & incudinum tinnitus auditur: Et ô scelus & ferale prodigium! Petrus cogitur nundinas Simonis ex sua quantitate persolvere, qui Simonem cum omni suo commercio cognoscitur perpetuâ maledictione damnâsse. Et in fine ei libuit hac plangere:
units.tr: XLIX. Peter Damian, in Baronius ad an. 1033. n. 8., writing to N., Archbishop, concerning the Roman Pontiff who had then been forced in by simony, writes among other things as follows: He is, as it seems to me, undoubtedly a simoniac without any pretence, because he was enthroned at night, with armed mobs raging and rioting everywhere, while all of you, the cardinal bishops of that same city, protested, resisted, and terribly anathematized him. Then people rush to the deadly patronage of purses; money is poured out to the people through the districts, alleys and lanes; the box of St. Peter the venerable is ransacked. And so throughout the whole city, like the workshop of a badly working Simon, scarcely anything is heard but (so to speak) the clanging of hammers and anvils. And, O crime and deadly portent! Peter is compelled to pay the fairs of Simon out of his own substance, he who is known to have condemned Simon and all his trade with perpetual curse. And at the end he chose to lament these things in verse:

units.la: Heu sedes Apostolica. Orbis olim gloria Nunc prohdolor efficeris Officina Simonis. Terunt incudem mallei, Nummi sunt tartarei; Justo Dei judicio Fit ista conditio: Ut quisquis Apostolicam Sedem semel comparat Redimere non desinat, Donec male pereat &c.
units.tr: Alas, apostolic see, once the glory of the world, now, alas, you have become the workshop of Simon. The anvil is worn by the hammer, the coins are of Tartarus; by the just judgment of God this condition arises: that whoever once buys the apostolic see should not cease to redeem it, until he perishes wretchedly, etc.

units.la: In Epistola ad Cadolaum Anti Papam, quae apud eundem Baron. ad an. 1061. n. 7. seqq. extat, in hunc modum loquitur: Unum te non lateat, quia quisquis Ecclesia per venalitatem semel irrepserit, donec illi praefuerit, redimere non cessabit. Justo Dei judicio agitur, ut quisquis regimen Ecclesia nundinatus aggreditur, quietis vel opulentia commodum, quod speraverat, de suo commercio non lucretur: Sed sedens in Cathedra pestilentia fabriles semper malleos versat, ut immunda praelationis rivus per sordida convexa ruens, unde funestus oboritur, suo semper fonti respondeat. Enim vero cùm religiosus quisque Vir subire tam laboriosae sedis onus abhorreat: illícque constitui vix ullis hominum precibus acquiescat: Cur tu onus onerum (ut sanctus Leo Papa dicebat) non modo non paras aufugere, sed ultrò etiam preces & pretium offerendo anxiè te conaris intrudere? ut liquidò videatur tibi sententia illa congruere, quam per Ezechielem adversus Jerusalem divinus sermo pronunciat: (Ezech. XVI.) omnibus meretricibus dantur mercedes, tu autem dedisti mercedes cunctis amatoribus tuis. In eo enim, quòd dedisti mercedes, & mercedes non accepisti, factum est est in te contrarium. En quantopere & sic improbet Simoniam in ambiendo Papatu.
units.tr: In his letter to Cadalus the anti-pope, which is found in the same Baronius ad an. 1061. n. 7. seqq., he speaks in this manner: Let this one thing not escape you: whoever has once crept into the Church by venality will not cease to buy it back for as long as he presides over it. By the just judgment of God it comes about that whoever takes up the government of the Church by trading gets no profit from his business of the comfort or wealth he had hoped for; but sitting in the chair he keeps turning over the hammers of his forge, so that the unclean stream of promotion, flowing down through foul channels, from which it arises deadly, always answers to its own source. Indeed, when every religious man shrinks from undertaking the burden of so laborious a see, and scarcely yields to any entreaties to be installed there, why do you not only not take care to flee the burden of burdens (as holy Pope Leo used to say), but also eagerly strive to thrust yourself in, offering both prayers and price? So that the sentence which the divine word pronounces through Ezekiel against Jerusalem may plainly seem to fit you: (Ezek. XVI.) gifts are given to all harlots, but you have given gifts to all your lovers. For in that you gave gifts and did not receive gifts, the opposite has happened in you. See how greatly he condemns simony in the pursuit of the papacy, in this way too.

units.la: L. Sed adhuc specialiùs exaggerat idem ad eundem scri-bens Simoniam in studio consequendi Pontificatum apud Baron. ad an. 1062. n. 7. his verbis : Enim verò sicut per auxesin dicitur, Sancta Sanctorum, & Cantica Canticorum : Sic Romanam Ecclesiam venaliter distrahi, peccatum est utique peccatorum; Quamlibet quippe Ecclesiam redimens, Simoniacus est; qui autem Romanam Ecclesiam ad taxationem pecunia redigit, quid aliud quàm omnes per orbem terrarum Ecclesias, quibus illa prælata est, venaliter usurpare contendit ? Sanè sicut 30. denarii Judas Iscarioth Dominum vendidit : ita triginta numero maledictiones ejus reperiuntur in Psalmo (CXVIII.) quem adversus eum Propheta conscripsit &c. Si ergo juxta peccati modum maledictionis sive damnationis ponderatur elogium : quanta perditioni Romana Ecclesia mercator erit obnoxius, qui, dum unam negotiatur, omnes simul Ecclesias comparare convincitur ? Videant igitur, quantum ex hypothesi sua scelus sit, Simoniacè Papatum quærere.
units.tr: L. But the same writer, writing to the same man, exaggerates even more particularly simony in the pursuit of the papacy, in Baronius ad an. 1062. n. 7., in these words: Indeed, just as by an augmentative figure we say the Holy of Holies and the Song of Songs, so for the Roman Church to be sold for money is certainly the sin of sins. For whoever buys any church is a simoniac; but whoever reduces the Roman Church to a price, what else does he strive to do than to usurp by sale all the churches throughout the world over which it has been set? Surely, as Judas Iscariot sold the Lord for thirty pieces of silver, so thirty curses of his are found in the Psalm (CXVIII.) which the Prophet wrote against him, etc. If therefore the sentence is weighed according to the measure of the sin, or of the curse or damnation: how deeply liable to destruction will the merchant be who, while he trades in one, is shown to be buying up all the churches at once? Let them see, then, from his own hypothesis, how great a crime it is to seek the papacy by simony.

units.la: LI. Contra Simoniacos talem sententiam in Concilio Romano latam esse Gregorius VII. Præses ad Patriarcham Aquileiensem scribens, & decreta Concilii, imò etiam Conciliorum aliorum præcedentium compendiosè significans apud Baron. ad an. 1075. n. 15. testatur: Qui verò Simoniacè, videlicet per interventum pecunia, sunt promoti, ut absque ulla spe recuperationis deponantur, Apostolica censurâ statuimus. Pseudo-Papæ igitur fuerunt atque deponendi fuissent omnes ita Simoniacè electi, idem enim debet esse judicium parvo & magno, & generale est pronunciatum.
units.tr: LI. Gregory VII, the president, writing to the Patriarch of Aquileia, and briefly indicating the decrees of the Council against simoniacs, and indeed of other earlier Councils too, in Baronius ad an. 1075. n. 15., testifies that such a sentence was passed in the Roman Council against simoniacs: We decree by apostolic censure that those who have been promoted simoniacally, that is, through the intervention of money, shall be deposed without any hope of recovery. Therefore all those so elected by simony were pseudo-popes, and ought to have been deposed; for the judgment must be the same for small and great, and the pronouncement is general.

units.la: LII. Atque sententiam hanc jam ante Gregorium executioni mandavit Victor II. qui apud Platinam in Vita multos Episcopos etiam Simonia causa Episcopatu privasse dicitur. Ita privandi fuissent multi Episcopatu Romano.
units.tr: LII. And Victor II already before Gregory carried this sentence into execution, who, according to Platina in his Life, is said to have deprived many bishops of their see, even for simony. So many would have had to be deprived of the Roman see.

units.la: LIII. Gregorius jamjam memoratus apud eundem Platinam in vita, Henricum Imperatorem admonet, ne deinceps largitione corruptus, episcopatus & beneficia alicui per Simoniacam cupiditatem committat, aliter se usurum censurâ in se & delinquentes censuris Ecclesiasticis; multò magis adhibendis in Clericis, imò Papabilibus, imò Papis crimini, quod hic Laico objicitur, obnoxiis.
units.tr: LIII. Gregory, already mentioned, in the same Platina in the Life, admonishes the Emperor Henry not to commit any bishopric or benefice henceforth to anyone corrupted by bribery through simoniacal greed, otherwise he will use censure against himself and against offenders with ecclesiastical censures; much more to be applied against clerics, and indeed against papabiles, and indeed against popes, who are liable to the crime which is here objected to a layman.

units.la: LIV. Apud eundem Urbanus VI. in vita, semel atque iterum ad se vocatos Cardinales admonuit, ut manus abstinentes haberent, non dona dona aliqua,non munera acciperent,dum causas agunt, dum patrocinium suum beneficia petenti præstant. Interminatúsque est se acerrimè punitururum in Simonia deprehensos. Ejusdem hoc quoque inter alia elogium est monumento inscriptum : Omne Simoniacum tanto sub Patre tremebat. Interdixit Simoniam Cardinalibus, in genere, tanto magis vitandam in negotio sanctissimo electionis Vicarii Christi. Tremebat omne Simoniacum, nec igitur stare coram ipso potuissent Antecessores & Successores Simoniaci. Sed ita Cardinales offendit atque Schismati occasionem dedit,illâ suâ severitate, testantibus Authoribus.
units.tr: LIV. In the same work Urban VI, in his Life, admonished the cardinals, summoned to him once and again, to keep their hands clean, not to accept any gifts or presents while they were conducting cases, while they were granting patronage or benefices to one who sought them. And he threatened that he would punish most severely those caught in simony. This also is among the other praises of his inscribed on his monument: Every simoniac trembled under so great a Father. He forbade simony to the cardinals in general, the more so to be avoided in the most holy business of electing the Vicar of Christ. Every simoniac trembled; therefore the predecessors and successors who were simoniacs could not have stood before him. But by that severity of his he offended the cardinals and gave occasion for a schism, as the authors attest.

units.la: LV. Similiter Papa Gregorius XII. sæpè Cardinales admonuit,ut honestè ac sanctè viverent, atque à Simoniacâ pravitate caverent, aliter se in eos graviter animadversurum. Hâc ratione prohibita, hâc ratione vituperata fuit Simonia, etiam & vel maximè in Cardinalibus, etiam, & vel maximè in electione Pontificum.
units.tr: LV. Similarly Pope Gregory XII often admonished the cardinals to live honourably and holily, and to beware of simoniacal depravity, otherwise he would deal with them severely. By this method simony was prohibited, by this method it was condemned, and especially and above all among cardinals, and especially and above all in the election of popes.

units.la: LVI. Operæ autem pretium erit ampliùs ostendere, quòd nihil bene atque legitimè agere soleant Simoniacè electi. Testimonia luculenta suppeditat rursus Baronius, suum, Damiani quoque ad an. 1058. n. 16. ita loquitur: Quod ad Benedictum Pseudo-Papam pertinet, hoc tempore,quo sedit,nihil boni ab eo factum reperitur, sed malum illud, dignum homine, qui pecuniâ vi aperuissset sibi viam ad sedem capessendam. Apud eundem ad an. 1061. n. 12. Petrus Damiani in Epistola jam citata,ita Cadolaum monet: Fac itaque, frater, juxta vocem Prophetæ, dicentis : Redite prævaricatores ad cor. Discute obsecro, conscientiam tuam & prudenter examina, qua quiete, quo refrigerio potitus es, postquam te huic periculoso negotio,tanquam Scyllæa voraginis fluctibus,immersisti. Dilapidantur æra cupidinis, exhauriuntur folles diversi generis metallo turgentes ; profligantur in cuneos militum erogandæ pauperibus Ecclesiæ facultates. Cunctis subjectus obtemperas,ut cunctis dignitate præcellas, & ambitio dominationis juri te mancipiat servitutis. Unum te non lateat,quia quiquis Ecclesia per venalitatem semel irrepserit; donec illi præfuerit, redimere non cessabit. Idem dicit in carmine suprà posito. Recentiora autem de Simoniaca Pontificum electione judicia suppeditant Decret. l. VII. l. 1. tit. 3. capita tria priora Concilii sub Julio II. coepti Lateranensis contra Pontifices Simoniacos decreta exhibentia. Lemma sive Epitome primi est. Electio Pont. Max. Simoniaca nundinatione inducta est nulla nulliusque potestatis, adeò ut sic electus exauthoretur ab omnibus officiis & dignitatibus, cum
units.tr: LVI. It will be worth the while to show further that simoniacally elected men are accustomed to do nothing well and lawfully. Baronius again supplies clear testimonies; Damian too, in ad an. 1058. n. 16., speaks thus: As regards Benedict the pseudo-pope, at the time when he sat, nothing good is found to have been done by him, but only that evil thing, worthy of a man who by money and force had opened for himself the way to seize the see. In the same place, ad an. 1061. n. 12., Peter Damian in the letter already cited admonishes Cadalus thus: Do this, brother, according to the voice of the Prophet, who says: Return, transgressors, to the heart. I beg you, examine your conscience and weigh it prudently: with what quiet, what refreshment you have enjoyed since you immersed yourself in this dangerous business, as in the waves of the Scylla whirlpool. The bronze of greed is squandered, the bellows swollen with metal of every kind are emptied; the resources to be spent on the poor of the Church are dissipated on troops of soldiers. You submit to all, so that you may surpass all in dignity, and the ambition for domination binds you by the law of slavery. Let this one thing not escape you: whoever has once crept into the Church by venality will not cease to buy it back for as long as he presides over it. He says the same in the verse set out above. More recent judgments on the simoniacal election of popes are provided by Decret. l. VII. l. 1. tit. 3., the first three chapters of the Council of the Lateran begun under Julius II, setting out decrees against simoniacal popes. The summary or epitome of the first is: An election of the Pope Maximus brought about by simoniacal bargaining is null and of no force, so that the person so elected is stripped of all offices and dignities, together with

units.la: sim suis sequacibus & complicibus Cardinalibus. Secundi : Pontifici Simoniacè electo, nemo tenetur obedire, illiusque authoritati detrahere licet omnibus, & novâ electione is è solio Pontificio deturbandus est. Tertii: Simoniacæ electionis conscii, proxeneta & Mediatores ad instar reorum majestatis subjiciantur pœnis activis & passivis, Cardinalibus verò novum Pontificem eligendi æquiori tramite conceditur potestas. Idem dicit carmine suprà posito. Ut jam judicari possit, quales fuerint Simoniacè electi Pontifices, Simonis, non Petri, ut L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.12. vocantur, Successores, quales fuerint eorum actiones, cur Simoniacè agant tam multi, juxta illud.
units.tr: with his followers and accomplices, the cardinals. Second: No one is bound to obey a Pontiff elected by simony; anyone may detract from his authority, and by a new election he is to be cast down from the Pontifical throne. Third: Those who knew of a simoniacal election, brokers and go-betweens, are to be subjected to active and passive penalties, as if they were guilty of treason; but the cardinals are granted the power to elect a new Pontiff by a fairer course. He says the same in the verse set out above. So it may now be judged what sort of Pontiffs were elected by simony, what sort of successors of Simon rather than of Peter they were (as L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.12. calls them), what their actions were, and why so many act simoniacally, according to that line:

units.la: Vendit Alexander claves, altaria, Christum:
units.tr: Alexander sells the keys, the altars, Christ;

units.la: Vendere jure potest, emerat ille prius.
units.tr: he may sell them by right, for he bought them beforehand.

units.la: Quàm magnum sit electionis vitium Simonia.
units.tr: How great a defect simony is in an election!

units.la: LVII Pertinet illa adhuc ad viam amoris, sequitur via timoris, ipsa vis, ceu medium ad Papatum consequendum sæpiùs adhiberi solitum. Vis illata primò Pontificibus Prædecessoribus. Et primò quidem Baronius, ad an.535. n. 1. non prætermittendum censuit, Pelagium Diaconum ductum esse in suspicionem illatæ mortis Vigilio: De ipso Vigilii simili scelere vide ea, quæ de Schismatibus Dissert. VII. sequuntur; id enim Anastasius tradit, cùm agit de Pelagii ordinatione, qui etiam apud eundem, n. 10. dicit : multitudo religiosorum, sapientum & nobilium subtraxerunt se à communione ejus, dicentes: quia in morte Vigilii Papa se immiscuit, ut tantis pœnis affligeretur; & narrat, quomodo Pelagius tenens Evangelium & crucem super caput suum in ambonem ascenderit, & sic satisfecerit cuncto populo & plebi, quia nullum malum peregisset contra Vigilium. Apud Platinam in Leone V. narratur, quòd Pontificatum adeptus à Christophoro ejus familiari dominandi cupido (cupidine) captus & in vincula conjectus sit: quod quidem sine magna seditione & multorum interitu fieri non potuerit. Christophorus itaque sedem occupavit. Leonem ego pra dolore animi paulò post periisse crediderim, quòd ab eo potissimùm honore spoliatus fuisset; quem ipse ut lupum domi aluerat: ut illud Theocriti: Enutrito lupos, qui te comedant. Stellae in vita, sicut Pontificatum malis artibus adeptus est, ita & male amisit, & mensuram, quam Leoni Domino suo mensus fuerat, & ipse recepit, quia septimo mense Pontificatu dejectus, monasticam vitam obire coactus fuit. Apud Platinam. In Clem. II. scribunt authores, venenum ipsum in hos usus à Stephano paratum, qui ei (Clementi II.) in Pontificatu succesit. Benedictum VI. à Bonifacio cognomento Francone Romano mano Ferrutii filio, Diacono Cardinale, scelestissimo viro violentâ manu captum in carcerem detrusum & ibi strangulatum esse, ipsum verò Bonifacium VII. sedem Apostolicam violenter invasisse, testis est Baronius ad an.974. n. 1. Eundem nefandum Apostolicæ sedis invasorem, qui necato Pontifice, & expilatâ Basilicâ Vaticanâ Constantinopolim fugerit, ubi res innovatas accepisset, decessisse nimirum Benedictum VII. qui eum sede expulerat, & Ottonem Imper. esse defunctum, cujus patrocinio fovebatur, qui Benedicto successerat, Johannes Papa, Romanam sedem iterum invasurum suorum studiis roboratum rediisse, ut, quam reliquerat Petri Cathedram, occuparet; Venisse sceleratum atque sacrilegum, suorúmque factione potentem, quem sedentem in Pontificio throno, Joannem invenerit, inde violenter exturbâsse, vinculísque alligatum in Sancti Angeli munitionem detrusisse: ubi fame perire miserum tanquam truculentis (truculentus) prado coegerit duorum Pontificum crudelissimus interfector, invasámque iterum Petri Cathedram pro nefas! tenuisse Tyrannum &c. Unde parùm consulunt, ita Baronius subjicit, n. 1. Ecclesiæ dignitati, minúsque pietati, qui hunc inter Romanos Pontifices referunt, annumerandum potiùs inter famosos latrones, & potentissimos grassatores, atque Patriæ proditores, Syllas atque Catilinas, horúmque similes, quos omnes superaverat sacrilegus iste turpissimâ nece duorum Pontificum. Sed & quicunque violentâ morte perierunt, veneno maximè, Pontifices, (Vide Exemplum Pii III. & Leonis X. apud Onuphrium, & quæ Differt. VIII. de misero Pontificum statu dicenda erunt;) Successorum ferè, vel succedere volentium culpâ perierunt.
units.tr: LVII It still belongs to the way of love; there follows the way of fear, namely force itself, which is often employed as a means of obtaining the Papacy. Force was first inflicted on the Pontiffs who came before him. And first of all Baronius, at the year 535, n. 1, thought it not to be passed over that Pelagius the deacon was brought under suspicion of having caused the death of Vigilius: On Vigilius's own similar crime see what follows in Dissertation VII on Schisms; for Anastasius hands this down when he treats of the ordination of Pelagius, who also, in the same place, n. 10, says: a multitude of the religious, the wise and the nobles withdrew from communion with him, saying that because he had meddled in the death of Pope Vigilius he deserved to be afflicted with such punishments; and he relates how Pelagius, holding the Gospel and the cross over his head, ascended the pulpit and so satisfied the whole people and commons, because he had done no wrong against Vigilius. In Platina, under Leo V, it is related that he had obtained the Papacy, but was seized by the lust for power of Christopher, his familiar, and was cast into chains; which could not have happened without great sedition and the death of many. Christopher therefore occupied the see. I believe Leo died shortly afterwards from grief of mind, because he had been stripped of that honour above all by the man whom he had reared at home like a wolf, as in that saying: "You have reared wolves, which will devour you." He, as he had obtained the Papacy by evil arts, so also lost it wickedly, and received back the measure that he had meted out to his lord Leo, since he was deposed after seven months of the Papacy and was forced to end his life as a monk. In Platina. Authors write of Clement II that the poison for this purpose was prepared by Stephen, who succeeded him in the Papacy.
