That Benedict VI was seized by violent hand by Boniface, surnamed Franco, a Roman, son of Ferrutius, a deacon cardinal, a most wicked man, thrown into prison and strangled there, and that Boniface VII himself violently invaded the Apostolic see, is attested by Baronius at the year 974, n. 1. That same unspeakable invader of the Apostolic see, who, after the Pontiff was killed and the Vatican basilica plundered, fled to Constantinople, where he learned of the changed situation (namely that Benedict VII, who had expelled him, had died, and that Emperor Otto, under whose protection John, Benedict's successor, the Pope, was sustained, had also died), returned to Rome, strengthened by the partisans of his faction, to seize again the Chair of Peter that he had left. He came, the wicked and sacrilegious man, powerful through his faction, and found John sitting on the Pontifical throne; from there he violently drove him out, bound him in chains and thrust him into the fortress of Sant'Angelo, where the cruellest murderer of two Pontiffs forced the wretched man to die of hunger; and, alas, he held the invaded Chair of Peter again, the tyrant, &c. Whence they consult the dignity of the Church too little, and piety less, who count him among the Roman Pontiffs; rather he should be numbered among famous robbers and most powerful brigands, and traitors to the fatherland, Sullas and Catilines and their like, all of whom that sacrilegious man surpassed by the most shameful murder of two Pontiffs. But also, whoever perished by a violent death, Pontiffs especially by poison (see the examples of Pius III and Leo X in Onuphrius, and what will be said in Dissertation VIII on the wretched state of the Pontiffs), mostly perished through the guilt of their successors or of those wishing to succeed.

units.la: VIII. Sed & vis aliâs adhibita legitur. De quo, ut & de aliis, nonnulla dicta sunt, quando de intrudentibus Tyrannis & fœminis egimus. Plura dicenda erunt in vitiis ratione Schismatum. Formosi electionem tumultuariam fuisse, apud Baron. ad an.89. n. 3. Luitprandus testatur. Bonifacium à Stephano VI. al. VII. intrusum ab intruso, (quem & ad an. 900. n. 6. invasorem vocat, qui ut fur & latro ingressus sit;) pulsum esse, atque ista omnia per vim & metum extorta, maximam sanctæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ ignominiam irrogâsse, idem ad an. 897. n. 1. adfirmat, ubi quoque eorum, qui tyrannicè sedem sint adepti, mentionem facit Ad a. verò 907. n.2. tempora illa inopiâ scriptorum obscura & tyrannide sedem Apostolicam invadentium tetra vocat. Atque ad an. 908. n. 1. quomodo Sergius,Christophoro ejecto, sedem invaserit. n.2. quomodo ab omnibus non legitimus Pontifex,sed iuvasor compellatus fuerit, narrat. Ad an. 931, n. 1. qualiter Ecclesia Romana deformiter à Joh.XI. (quem & Stella, quòd Petri sedem vi occupâsse dicatur, è sede statim dejectum inter Pontifices connumerari non merere testatur;) tanto monstro invasa, conculcata fuerit & sæpe contigerit, eam non habere legitimè creatos Pontifices, sed quos sæcularis potentia intrusisset; Ad an.955. n. 1. quâ ratione Johannes XII. invaserit, n.4. abortivum illum tunc parturiisse Roma tyrannidem vi pollentem, armis omnia miscentem, omnia audentem atque subvertentem, ut nullo pacto dicendus tunc fuerit legitimus Pontifex, in cujus electione lex nulla sit suffragata, sed omnia vis & metus impleverit; ad an. 960. n 5. quòd idem male conscius de sua intrusione, sic liberationem Romanæ Ecclesiæ ab Ottone, quem vocaverit, exoptárit, ut tamen antea voluerit sibi esse consultum, ne sui Pontificatûs quoquo modo jacturam pateretur; quia innatum sit à natura latronibus, ut omnes semper timeant, etiam socios, atq; adjutoribus non se credant. Ad an. tamen 693. n. 18. hariolatur, Joanni illi de intrusione ab Ottone in Synodum nullum factum negotium, idque non humanitatis gratiâ esse donatum, sed magno artificio pratermissum, quia si fuisset Joannes electio offensa nulla, aquè Ottonis imperium, quod à Joanne acceperat, illegitimum declaratum fuisset, utpote ab eo collatum. Ad an. 975. n. 1. quâ ratione Benedictus ex Albericis proveniens, exagitans, urgénsque Bonifacium tyrannum, invasorem Apostolicæ sedis abire coëgerit. Benedictus V. Johannis XII. Successor Ottoni Loyolitæ quidem legitimè, sed Cranzio per tumultum, Stellæ ab his, qui Johanni factione & cognatione fuerant conjuncti, Fasc. Temp ita, ut inde pateat, malum principium rarò habere bonum finem; electus fuit. In hujus Successore Leone VIII. Stella notat, quòd ad reprimendam Romanorum malitiam, qui suos passim intrudebant, eligendi potestatem ad Imperatorem transtulerit. Clemens II. Martino Polono invasor per vim Papatum habuit. Platina in Damaso II. testatur, eum Pontificatum per vim occupâsse, nullo Cleri populique consensu. His temporibus, inquit Genebrardus generaliori testimonio, cuique licebat in sedem Petri irrepere. Ad an.1058. recensèt rursus Baronius, quomodo mortuo Imperatore, cujus reverentiâ atque timore oborta factiones reprimi consueverint electioni Pontificum inhiantes, & Apostolicæ sedis invasioni, sive essent ex Comitibus Tusculanis, sive Ptolomæorum, Gregoriorum, sive Crescentiorum familiis, aliisque, armis, divitiisque potentibus: audita summi Pontificis morte, rursus nullo habito respectu eorum, qua Pontifice vivente ab eo omnibus consentientibus statuta fuerint, armis irruperint, Ecclesiam vi publicâ invaserint, & quem cuperant, illum in Apostolicum thronum attulerint, rursúmque sumque maledictionibus suis Deo odibilem, hominibus execrabilem alium Benedictum constituerint. Quod & ibidem ex Leone Ostiensi confirmat. Et quem Platina quoque factione quorundam nobilium creatum esse, in Bened. X. ait, eique in accusatione Hildebrandi introitum non per Ostium, sed per vim quoque tribuit. Quare Onuphrius in annot. etiam eum Pontificem fuisse negat, similiter ob vim. Sed & Platina denuo in Honorio II. eum ambitione quorundam electum esse testatur. In Urbano VI. notans, Cardinales Gallos in eum invectos esse ut falsum Pontificem, quod dicerent, hominem vi creatum, vi etiam coronam Pontificatus accepisse, cum electio illa & coronatio in loco minime tuto sit habita, in qua libera deberent esse hominum voluntates, libera suffragia, cum contra a populo Romano coacti sint Italicum potius quam Gallicum eligere, quod & in Conclavi ejusdem traditur, una cum vocibus in platea tumultuose clamantium. Romano lo volemo. Id est: Romanum volumus. In Joanne XXIV. inducens scribentes, Balthasarem Cossam violenter Bononia esse electum, quod & Legatus Bononia esset, & armatos milites tum in urbe, tum in agris pro statione habuerat, ut si precario id obtinere non posset, minis & armis tandem consequeretur. In Pio III. similiter referens, mortuo Alexandro VI. Caesarem Borgiam statim pecuniis & pretiosis quibuscunque correptis, Vaticanum, quod 12. armatorum millibus tenuerit, & Hadriani molem operibus muniisse eo consilio, ut patres in eodem loco veteri instituto cogendos ad novum creandum Successorem in sua vota cogeret. In Concl. Clem. VIII. cum Rovereus quasi in carcerem duceretur, Altempsius alta voce dixit: Se jo fussi sano mi farei ben mantener la parola, e se altro non potessi, farci alli pugni. Id est: Si sanus essem, fidem mihi haberi curarem, quod, si verbis illud efficere non possem, pugnos adhibere vellem. Quae verba ita animum illius percusserant, ut causa mortis proximae fuerint. In eod. Concl. Card. Columnae ab iis, qui ex Capella exire volentem omni studio retinere conabantur, totum quasi Rochettum discissum memoratur; Ad quem strepitum accurrentes 2. alii magna voce clamabant, vim Cardinalibus non esse inferendam; Excludentes vero omnes, qui Columnam Apostatam osculando se satiare haud potuerunt; Victoria, Victoria, haec actiones dignae sunt Baronibus Romanis, clamabant, & cum reliqui, ne alii Columnam sequerentur, portas clauderent, rursus de violentia protestati sunt. Poenitentiam Avilae in Conclavi Leonis XI. quod non cum baculo Aldobrandino responderit, & quam etiam Epistola Card. Perronii, ubi Conclave aliquod historice describitur, bitur, habet, suprà annotavimus. Tumultus in Conclavi Pauli V. non exiguos fuisse vel sequentia arguunt; In illo tumultu, inquit Author, & in illa pressione Vicontius in terram projectus, Serafinus brachio lasus fuit. De quibus etiam Il Card. p.3. l.3. p.224. narrat: L'insolenza di questo giorno &c. Insolentia istius diei magna fuit ab utraque parte; Singulis Cardinales in partes suas perducere studentibus, non tantum verborum persuasione, sed & vi verberum. Hinc etiam apud eundem quidam dixit: Nollem vel ipsum Petrum sic Papam facere; Tunc quoque per urbem sparsum fuit; Cardinales se invicem verberibus multis excepisse, atque etiam baculis feriisse. In Conclavi Clementis IX. de Estio & Farnesio, molti vociferano esser state con le parole anco congiunte le mani; multi dictitabant, verbis verbera conjuncta fuisse.
units.tr: VIII. But force of another kind is also recorded. Some things have been said about this, as about other matters, when we dealt with intruding tyrants and women, and more will be said about the faults that arise from schisms. That Formosus's election was tumultuous is attested by Luitprand, cited in Baronius ad an. 89, n. 3. The same author, ad an. 897, n. 1, affirms that Boniface, intruded by Stephen VI (or VII), was driven out by the intruder, and that all these things, extorted by violence and fear, brought the greatest disgrace upon the holy Roman Church. There, too, he mentions those who seized the see tyrannically. Ad an. 907, n. 2, he calls those times, obscure for want of writers and foul with the tyranny of men who invaded the Apostolic see. And ad an. 908, n. 1, he tells how Sergius, after Christopher was ejected, seized the see; at n. 2 he relates how he was called not the lawful Pope but an invader by everyone. Ad an. 931, n. 1, he tells how the Roman Church was disgracefully invaded and trampled by such a monster as John XI (whom Stella also testifies should not be counted among the Popes, since he is said to have seized Peter's see by force and was at once thrown out of it), and how it often happened that the Church did not have lawfully created Popes but men whom secular power had thrust in. Ad an. 955, n. 1, he tells by what means John XII seized the see; at n. 4 he says that Rome then gave birth to that abortive tyranny, mighty by force, throwing everything into confusion with arms, daring everything, and overturning everything, so that on no terms could he then be called a lawful Pope, since no law had supported his election, but violence and fear had filled the whole business. Ad an. 960, n. 5, the same man, conscious of his own intrusion, prayed for the liberation of the Roman Church by Otto, whom he had summoned, yet first wished to be provided for so that he would suffer no loss of his Pontificate in any way, because it is innate in robbers by nature that they always fear everyone, even their accomplices, and do not trust their helpers. Yet ad an. 963, n. 18, he guesses that no business was made in the Synod about that John's intrusion by Otto, and that this was granted not out of kindness but passed over with great cunning, because if John's election had been an offence, the empire which Otto had received from John would equally have been declared illegitimate, as having been conferred by him. Ad an. 975, n. 1, he tells how Benedict, of the Alberici family, harassing and pressing Boniface the tyrant, the invader of the Apostolic see, compelled him to leave. Benedict V, successor to John XII, was chosen lawfully, according to Crantz, but through a tumult, according to Stella, by those who were joined to John by faction and kinship, as the Fasciculus Temporum shows, so that it is plain that a bad beginning rarely has a good end. In the case of his successor Leo VIII, Stella notes that to curb the malice of the Romans, who everywhere thrust in their own men, the power of electing was transferred to the Emperor. Clement II had the papacy by violence, as an invader, in the case of Martin of Poland. Platina, in Damasus II, testifies that he seized the papacy by force, with no consent of clergy or people. In those times, says Genebrard, citing a more general witness, anyone could creep into Peter's see. Ad an. 1058, Baronius again recounts how, when the Emperor died, whose reverence and fear had usually held down the factions that coveted the election of Popes and the invasion of the Apostolic see, whether they came from the Counts of Tusculum, or from the families of the Ptolemies, the Gregories, the Crescentii, or others powerful in arms and wealth, then, at the report of the Supreme Pontiff's death, they rushed in again with arms, with no regard for what had been agreed by all while the Pope was alive; they seized the Church by public violence, brought in the man they wanted to the Apostolic throne, and then, hated by God and detested by men, set up another Benedict with their curses. He confirms this in the same place from Leo of Ostia. And Platina also says that Benedict X was created by the faction of certain nobles, and ascribes to his accusation of Hildebrand an entrance not through the door but through violence. Therefore Onuphrius, in his notes, denies that he was even a Pope, likewise on account of the violence. Platina again, in Honorius II, testifies that he was elected by the ambition of certain men. Noting in Urban VI that the French Cardinals inveighed against him as a false Pope, saying that the man had been created by force and had by force also taken the crown of the Papacy, since that election and coronation were held in a place by no means safe, where men's wills ought to be free and their votes free, whereas they were forced by the Roman people to choose an Italian rather than a Frenchman; this is also reported in the Conclave of the same, together with the voices of men shouting tumultuously in the square: Romano lo volemo, that is, We want a Roman. Introducing the writers on John XXIII, he says that Balthasar Cossa was elected violently at Bologna, since he was both Legate at Bologna and had kept armed soldiers on guard in the city and in the countryside, so that if he could not obtain it by request he would finally get it by threats and arms. Similarly, referring to Pius III, he says that after Alexander VI died, Caesar Borgia immediately seized money and whatever precious things he could, fortified the Vatican, which he held with 12,000 armed men, and the Mole of Hadrian with works, with the aim of forcing the Fathers, who were to be gathered in the old customary place to create a new successor, to his own wishes. In the Conclave of Clement VIII, when Rovere was being led as if to prison, Altemps said in a loud voice: If I were well, I would take care that my word was kept, and if I could not do it with words, I would use my fists. Those words so struck his spirit that they were the cause of his approaching death. In the same Conclave, it is recorded that Cardinal Colonna, while those who tried with all their zeal to hold him back were trying to leave the Chapel, had his whole rochet, as it were, torn to pieces; two others, running up at the noise, shouted loudly that violence was not to be done to the Cardinals; but shutting out all who could not satisfy themselves by kissing the apostate Colonna, they cried, Victory, victory! These are deeds worthy of the Roman barons, and while the rest closed the doors so that others would not follow Colonna, they again protested about the violence. That Avila did penance in the Conclave of Leo XI because he did not answer with Aldobrandini's staff, and the letter of Cardinal Perron, in which a certain Conclave is described historically, which I have noted above, shows the same. Tumults in the Conclave of Paul V were not small, as the following events also show: In that tumult, says the author, and in that crush, Visconti was thrown to the ground, and Seraphinus was wounded in the arm. Of these things the Il Cardinale also tells, p. 3, l. 3, p. 224: The insolence of this day, etc. The insolence of that day was great on both sides, each Cardinal striving to lead others to his own party, not only by persuasion of words but also by violence of blows. Hence in the same work someone said: I would not wish even Peter himself to be made Pope in such a way. It was also spread throughout the city that the Cardinals had met one another with many blows and had even struck each other with staves. In the Conclave of Clement IX, concerning Estes and Farnese, many shouted that words had even been joined with hands; many kept saying that blows had been joined to words.

units.la: LIX. Vis nascitur ex discordia, atque discordiam facit. Hæc autem ordinariò cum Cardinalibus Conclavi includitur, atque illis pomum Eridis statim ostenditur; quod & ante Conclavis institutionem in medium Electorum sæpè projici solet. Non quidem Concordia in electione semper legitimam ejus rationem probat. Potuerunt enim apud Baronium, ad an.1130. n. 25. Fautores Anacleti, qui Pseudo-Papa habetur, cives Romani de sua in ejus electione concordia in Epistola ad Imperatorem gloriari. Nos unanimi spontanea omnium Cardinalium voluntate & concordi electione Clericorum omnium Dominum Papam Anacletum elegimus; inquiunt; in cujus promotione, ita pergunt, tantam Cleri & populi concordiam vidimus, ut verè in omnium mentes Spiritus S. mirabiliter venisse credatur &c. Et de electione Alexandri VI. pessima notat: Il Card. p.3. l.2. p.147. Non sera mai inteso &c. Id est: Nunquam Papa sanctus cum tanto applausu electus fuit, quanto impostor ille, concurrentibus ad ipsius electionem ipsis etiam probis viris &c. Interim tamen quando discordia observatur in electionibus Pontificum, discordia magna & quasi ordinaria, non leve illud quoque esse potest contra electiones ejusmodi præjudicium. Observatur autem in Schismatibus maximè, de quibus mox seorsim agemus; sed & in sequentibus.
units.tr: LIX. Violence arises from discord, and it also produces discord. This is ordinarily shut up in the Conclave with the Cardinals, and the apple of Eris is at once shown to them. It is also often thrown into the midst of the electors even before the Conclave was instituted. Concord in an election, to be sure, does not always prove its legitimacy. For in Baronius, ad an. 1130, n. 25, the supporters of Anacletus, who is regarded as the pseudo-pope, the Roman citizens, could boast in a letter to the Emperor of their concord in his election: We have elected Lord Pope Anacletus by the unanimous and spontaneous will of all the Cardinals and by the harmonious election of all the clergy, they say; in whose promotion, they go on, we saw such great concord of clergy and people that it is truly believed the Holy Spirit wonderfully came into the minds of all, etc. And concerning the election of Alexander VI he notes wicked things: Il Card. p.3 l.2 p.147. It will never be understood, etc. That is: Never was a holy pope elected with such applause as that impostor, with even upright men coming together for his election, etc. Meanwhile, however, when discord is observed in the elections of Popes, a great and almost ordinary discord, this too can be no slight prejudice against such elections. It is observed especially in Schisms, of which we shall treat separately soon, but also in the following cases.

units.la: LX. Et primò quidem discordia, quam antea magnam fuisse sæpè, etiam à Baronio, ad an. 1160. 6. discimus, Conclavi originem dedit, ne discordantibus frequenter huc illuc delabentibus electiones nimis tardarentur, Electores ejusmodi carceri includi debuerunt. De quo Onuphrii annot. ad Greg. X. testimonium Dissert. IV. audivimus. Nempe Conclave introductum esse, quia Cardinales nales aliquando per biennium, aliquando fere per triennium discordantes in unum aliquem consentire haud poterant; quod quidem non semel contigerat. Maximè autem post mortem Clementis IV. ut tandem Joannes Episcopus Cardinalis Portuensis videns Cardinalium pertinaciam, iis in Comitio existentibus & Spiritum S. invocantibus, narrante eodem, publicè dixerit: Domini, discooperiamus tectum camera hujus, quia Spiritus S. nequit ad nos per hac tecta ingredi. Addunt alii, eum porrò dixisse. Oporteret ut singuli proprium Spiritum S. haberent, quia nullus vult alteri consentire, Spiritus S. descendit super Apostolos, cùm concorditer unâ congregati essent, sed quomodo nos eum expectare possumus, cùm sumus usque adeò divisi? Cúmque tandem consensissent in Gregorium, idem electionem non à Spiritu Concordiæ profectam esse satis innuit, sequenti disticho. Papatûs munus tulit Archi Diaconus unus, Quem Patrem Patrum fecit discordia fratrum.
units.tr: LX. And first, the discord which we often learn from Baronius, ad an. 1160, 6., was great even earlier, and it gave rise to the Conclave, so that the electors of this kind had to be shut up in a prison, lest elections be delayed too long by discordant men frequently drifting hither and thither. On this matter we heard the testimony of Onuphrius, annot. ad Greg. X., in Dissert. IV. Namely, the Conclave was introduced because the Cardinals, sometimes for two years and sometimes for nearly three years, discordant, could not agree on any one man; which indeed had happened more than once. Especially after the death of Clement IV, when John, Bishop and Cardinal of Porto, seeing the obstinacy of the Cardinals, who were in the assembly and invoking the Holy Spirit, is reported by the same writer to have said publicly: Gentlemen, let us uncover the roof of this chamber, because the Holy Spirit cannot enter to us through these roofs. Others add that he further said: Each one would need to have his own Holy Spirit, since no one wishes to agree with another. The Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles when they were gathered together in concord, but how can we expect him when we are so divided? And when they had at last agreed on Gregory, the same writer hints sufficiently that the election did not proceed from the Spirit of Concord, in the following distich: One Archdeacon took the office of the papacy, whom the discord of the brothers made Father of Fathers.

units.la: Sed & post Gregorium, qui tunc electus Conclave instituerat, institutione ad tempus, ut suo loco diximus, rursus abolitâ, discordia haud evitari potuit. Narrat enim Platina, in Nicolao IV. post ejus mortem Cardinales rem discordiis intestinis biennio menséque tertio in longum deduxisse. Ipsum Carolum Regem Neapolitanum ideò ad eos profectum eos sæpius ad concordiam adhortatum esse; Nec id quidem facere destitisse virum insignem, nisi acriter reprehensus esset à Benedicto Cajetano, quòd instando acerbè nimium ipsis Cardinalibus vim afferre videretur, quorum suffragia libera esse deberent. Sed nec reducta post Conclavis forma discordiam excludere potuit. In primo enim ex Conclavibus, quæ hodienum habentur, Clementis V. Cardinales ex eo discesserant ad tempus discordes; De quo ita Bzovius Col.241. XI. Clemente Pontifice, inquit, extincto, tres & viginti Cardinales Conclave ingressi dissensionibus laborârunt, neque quenquam nominare potuerunt. Intra Conclavis secreta dissentientibus Patribus, etiam domestici eorum in urbe vehementius tumultuabantur. Cúmque aliâ ratione Cardinales vel ad concordiam reducere, vel discordes è Palatio elicere nequirent, multam materiam pinguem & aridam vicinis Palatio adibus famuli suppositam incendunt. Ardebat nemine extinguente domus electioni destinata, & illi potiùs re infectâ discedere, quàm communibus suffragiis Pontificem renunciare maluerunt. In id tantùm consenserunt, ut præscripto tempore in locum designatum pro Antistite eligendo convenirent. Caterùm auctis ultro citróque per malevolentium studia odiis, stato die non redierunt, sed in civi-
units.tr: But even after Gregory, who had then instituted the Conclave, the institution, abolished again for a time as we said in its place, discord could not be avoided. For Platina relates, in Nicholas IV, that after his death the Cardinals drew out the matter over two years and three months by intestine discords. King Charles of Naples went to them and often urged them to concord; nor did that distinguished man cease from this, except that he was sharply rebuked by Benedict Caetani, because by pressing them too harshly he seemed to use force upon the Cardinals themselves, whose votes ought to be free. But even after the Conclave was restored in form, it could not exclude discord. For in the first of the Conclaves which are still held today, that of Clement V, the Cardinals had withdrawn from it for a time in discord. Bzovius writes of this thus: Col. 241, XI. When Pope Clement died, twenty-three Cardinals entered the Conclave and were troubled by dissensions, and they could not nominate anyone. While the Fathers disagreed within the secrets of the Conclave, their household servants in the city also raged more violently. And since the Cardinals could not otherwise either bring them back to concord or draw the discordant ones out of the Palace, they set fire to a great quantity of fat and dry material placed by their servants in the houses next to the Palace. The house appointed for the election burned, with no one putting out the fire, and they preferred to leave with the matter undone rather than to proclaim a Pontiff by common votes. They agreed only on this, that they would meet at the appointed time in the place designated for choosing a Bishop. But, with hatreds increasing on both sides through the zeal of ill-wishers, they did not return on the appointed day, but in the cities

units.la: — civitatibus Narbonensis Provincia loco & proposito disjuncti, non sine maximo Reipublica Christiana detrimento permanserunt, quanquam sancti & Principes viri non deessent, ut eos ad comitia ineunda perurgerent. Duos annos integros Inter-Pontificium Ecclesiam universam tenuit. Quae etiam Massonus in Ludovico nomine insanarum factionum innuit. Imo quando tandem redierunt, illud factum est, non rimettendo delle proprie passioni, ita ut retinuerint passiones pristinas, juxta Authorem Conclavis. Quem secutus Author Conclavis Innocentii IX. testatur de discordiis, che souvente tirano in longo il Conclave, qua sape prolongent Conclave. Neque dissensus simplex esse solet; Odia interveniunt; Sape fit, inquit, Joh. Fr. Lottinus differt. de Conclavi, ut qui arctissima, antea amicitia erant conjuncti, capitalibus fere odiis se mutuo persequantur. Et quando ira atque odium longissime abesse videntur, saepe tamen adsunt. Hinc cum in Conclavi Leonis XI. Cardinalis Aldobrandinus semper hilari vultu incederet, un Conclavista hebbe occasione di dire, &c. Conclavista occasionem habuit dicendi; considerate di gratia, come questi Signori si vogliono male allegramente. Id est; Considerate quaso, quam late hi Domini sibi invicem male velint. Sed non semper tam bene celant affectus; In Conclavi Urbani VIII. tra Ludovisio e Borghese &c. inter Ludovisium & Borghesium ira eo usque creverant, ut non tantum non simul tractarint, sed vix se salutarint. Hinc quidam, cum animos jungere non possent, scandalum saltem tollere allaborarunt. Sic & in Conclavi, Clementis X. passorono &c. inter Rezium & Sforzam non leviter pungentia verba dicebantur in eadem Scrutinii Capella atque occasione motus ad schedularum subscriptionem. Sed & pleraque praecedentia jam satis superque de discordia quasi ordinaria testantur.
units.tr: — in the cities of the Narbonne province they remained separated in place and purpose, not without the greatest detriment to the Christian commonwealth, although holy men and princes were not lacking who urged them vigorously to hold the assembly. For two whole years the Interpontifical period held the entire Church. Massonus also hints at these things under the name of insane factions in his Life of Louis. Indeed, when they at last returned, it happened not by laying aside their own passions, so that they retained their earlier passions, according to the author of the Conclave. Following him, the author of the Conclave of Innocent IX testifies about the discords, which often draw out the Conclave for a long time, that often prolong the Conclave. Nor is the disagreement usually simple; hatreds intervene. It often happens, says Johann Franz Lottinus in On the Conclave, that those who were before joined by the closest friendship pursue one another with almost mortal hatreds. And when anger and hatred seem to be far away, they are often nonetheless present. Hence, when in the Conclave of Leo XI Cardinal Aldobrandini always walked about with a cheerful face, a Conclavist had occasion to say, etc. The Conclavist had occasion to say: Consider, I beg you, how these Gentlemen cheerfully wish one another ill. That is: Consider, I beg you, how greatly these Gentlemen wish each other ill. But they do not always conceal their feelings so well. In the Conclave of Urban VIII, between Ludovisi and Borghese, etc., anger between Ludovisi and Borghese had grown so far that they not only did not deal together but scarcely greeted one another. Hence some, since they could not join their minds, at least labored to remove the scandal. So also in the Conclave of Clement X, they passed, etc., between Rezzonico and Sforza, not mildly stinging words were spoken in the same chapel of the scrutiny, and on the occasion of the motion to sign the ballots. But also most of the preceding cases already testify more than enough to a discord that is almost ordinary.

units.la: LXI. Discordia autem conjuncta esse solet cum pertinacia, dum neutra pars alteri vult cedere. Id quod constare potest ex vocibus & testimoniis sequentibus. In Conclavi, ex quo Gallorum fraude Martinus IV. prodiit, Cardinales tam Galli, quam Itali, stavano tutti saldi &c. persistebant, ut unus ex factione sua eligeretur, firmiter praesumentes in Conclavi clausi manere, donec ex una aut altera parte numerus quidam moreretur, quo mortuo factio altera fortior fiat. In Conclavi Pauli II. ne quidem cum jam Papa electus esset, Cardinalis Mela cedere voluit de sua obstinatione, neque voluit ordine debito ei pedem exoscular. In Conclavi Sixti IV. memoratur firma Cardinalium quorundam resolutio moriendi citius, quam alium praeter Rovereum
units.tr: LXI. Discord, moreover, is usually joined with obstinacy, while neither side wishes to yield to the other. This can be established from the following sayings and testimonies. In the Conclave, from which Martin IV came forth by the deceit of the French, the Cardinals, both French and Italian, remained all firm, etc., they persisted that one from their own faction be elected, firmly presuming that they would remain shut up in the Conclave until a certain number from one side or the other died, and with that death the other faction would become stronger. In the Conclave of Paul II, not even when the Pope had already been elected, Cardinal Mela was unwilling to yield from his obstinacy, nor was he willing to kiss the foot of the new Pope in the proper order. In the Conclave of Sixtus IV is recorded the firm resolution of certain Cardinals to die sooner than to have anyone elected other than Rovere

units.la: Discordia Comes pertinacia; reum eligendi. In Conclavi Clementis VII. Cardinalis Ursinus ad scrutinium, qualia ultra 25. frustra facta sunt, vocatus respondisse scribitur: Che vogliano andar scrutinando &c. Id est: Quid scrutari volumus: Idem manemus, nulla tractatio superest, Columna dura non cedit Medico, Medicus obstinatus hanc medicinam non vult dare Columna; tempus perdimus scrutinando. In Conclavi Leonis XI. disse Avila &c. Avila dixit, se malle annum in Conclavi transfigere potius, quam permittere, ut aliquid damno Regis sui contingat. Aldobrandino replico &c. regessit, se certo certius 2. annos ibi morari quam vero concedere velle, ut Pontificatus alii prater creaturas suas obtingat. In eodem Conclavi, disse Doria &c. Doria dixit Aldobrandino, se ideo Romam venisse, ut plane contrarium faceret. In Conclavi Pauli V. Aldobrandino era tanto implacabile &c. tam implacabilis erat, ut impossibile fuerit, infinitis etiam officiis & artificiis eum mitigare. In eodem, cum in una & altera Capella degerent una & altera factio, lecti & cibi afferri debuerunt, pro nolentibus egredi, nisi victores evasissent. In Conclavi Urbani VIII. hortabantur nonnulli Borghesium, che protestasse alla scoperta &c. ut publice protestaretur, se citius cum omnibus suis creaturis in Conclavi moriturum, quam permissurum, ut extra illas aliquis eligeretur. In Conclavi Innoc. X. teste Abbate Gualdi Vita di D. Olimpia p 62. erano risoluti &c. Firmum erat Nationistarum Hispanorum propositum, vel Innocentium eligendi, vel in Conclavi moriendi; In eodem tamen etiam respondit Barbarinus in ejus gratiam rogatus, jurasse se, quod ei votum suum dare nolit. In Conclavi Alex. VII. teste eodem lb. p. 449. 450. D. Olympia multos quidem excludebat, tres autem cum tanto ardore, ut declararit, se citius moriturum, quam passuram, ut unus ex illis Papa fieret. In eodem Conclavi Alexandri VII. eandem cantilenam canebant, li Factionarii volanti &c. Factionarii volantes, qui potestabantur contra, solum velle Sacchettium, & semper in ore habebant, se alias in Conclavi mori velle. In eodem Conclavi sequens pertinaciae Cardinalis Nepotis Barbarini perhibetur testimonium: Vuol secondare il genio suo &c. Id est: Genium suum servare vult, licet inde coelum & terra perire deberent. Imo sequens pertinaciae utriusque factionis: Era digia trascorso &c. Id est: Jam media quadragesima transierat, neque tamen notari poterat vel minimus ad electionem apparatus, imo talis rerum status erat, ut perierit spes unquam caput Ecclesiae creandi &c. ne quidem de creando Papa loquebantur, dua factiones contraria erant obstinata, spes magis magisque peribat. In Conclavi Clementis IX. difficile aestimabatur, ut aliquis eligeretur, extra Creaturas Chigii, per li sentimenti del Cardinale &c. Quia Cardinalis unicè Creaturis suis, quas æquè amavit, & quas fida ipsi videbantur, intentus erat, electionem non Creatura permittere nolens, si vel 10. annos in Conclavi manendum,imò ibidem moriendum fuisset, quod fidissimis suis professus est; non sine fundamento ita se jactans, dum ad exclusionem cujuscunque superflua vota habuit. Idem Chigius in Conclavi Clementis X. haveva concettato &c. propositum habebat,vel Creaturam eligendi, vel in Conclavi moriendi. In eodem Conclavi mutatæ cogitationes Chigii ejusdem & Medicai dicuntur,non circa personam, sed circa modum eligendi, primò rectâ incedebant,sed motu quodam notato, modum mutarunt, nempe Delcium reservandi, cùm priùs omnes alios in terram dejicere voluerint, hinc 50. dies otiosissimi transierunt, volebant enim delassando,qua verba Chigii & Barberini fuerunt, vincere, & intus comedere alter cerasa, ficus alter. In eodem Conclavi sequentia habentur, per esse esclusè &c. quia exclusa erant Creatura Chigii, & de quovis Papabili cogitabatur, de novo obscurabatur cœlum, nullâ Stellâ favente apparente; Si Barberinus non contrà naturam cedit &c. Atque si quis causam hujus pertinaciæ nôsse velit,est, ut plurimùm commodi proprii, est reputationis,ut vocant, æstimatio; Nam cùm in Conclavi Gregorii XV. tractatio Camporæ non succedere vellet, rogatus Borghesius caput promotionis à confidente, annon alios haberet proponendos, se habere, sed proprium interesse hunc postulare, & jam reputationem implicitam esse; respondit; optimè scilicet!
units.tr: Discord is accompanied by obstinacy, and the one who is to be elected is made to bear the blame. In the conclave of Clement VII. Cardinal Ursini, when called to a scrutiny, of which more than 25 had been held in vain, is written to have answered: "What do you want to keep scrutinising, &c.?" That is: "What do we want to scrutinise? We remain as we were; no negotiation is left. The hard column does not yield to the physician, and the obstinate physician will not give this medicine to the column; we are wasting our time scrutinising." In the conclave of Leo XI, Avila said, &c. Avila said that he would rather spend a whole year in the conclave than allow anything to happen to the loss of his King. To Aldobrandini he replied, &c., that he was more certain than certain that he would stay there two years, rather than consent to let the papacy fall to anyone other than his own creatures. In the same conclave, Doria said, &c. Doria told Aldobrandini that he had come to Rome precisely in order to do the opposite. In the conclave of Paul V, Aldobrandini was so implacable, &c., that he was so unyielding that it was impossible to soften him even with endless courtesies and stratagems. In the same conclave, when one faction and the other were lodged in one chapel and the other, meals and beds had to be brought in for those who refused to leave unless they had come out as victors. In the conclave of Urban VIII, some urged Borghese, "that he should protest openly, &c.," that he should publicly declare that he would sooner die in the conclave with all his creatures than permit anyone to be elected from outside them. In the conclave of Innocent X, according to Abbot Gualdi, Life of Donna Olimpia, p. 62, "they were resolved, &c." It was the firm resolve of the Spanish nation either to elect Innocent or to die in the conclave; yet in the same conclave Barberini, when asked on his behalf, also answered that he had sworn not to give him his vote. In the conclave of Alexander VII, according to the same author, Lib. pp. 449, 450, Donna Olimpia excluded many, but three with such ardour that she declared she would sooner die than suffer one of them to become Pope. In the same conclave of Alexander VII they sang the same tune: "The factions flying, &c." The flying factions, who were able to oppose, wanted only Sacchetti, and always had on their lips that they wished to die in the conclave otherwise. In the same conclave the following testimony of the obstinacy of Cardinal Nephew Barberini is recorded: "He wishes to follow his own inclination, &c." That is: He wishes to keep to his own inclination, even though heaven and earth should perish because of it. Moreover, the obstinacy of both factions followed: "It was now late, &c." That is: Already half of Lent had passed, and yet not the smallest preparation for an election could be seen; indeed the state of affairs was such that all hope of ever creating a head of the Church had perished, &c. They did not even speak of creating a Pope; the two factions were stubbornly opposed, and hope kept on perishing more and more. In the conclave of Clement IX it was thought difficult that anyone should be elected outside the creatures of Chigi, through "the feelings of the Cardinal, &c." For the Cardinal was intent solely on his own creatures, whom he loved equally and who seemed faithful to him, and he was unwilling to allow an election by someone not his creature, even if the conclave had to last ten years, indeed even if they had to die there; this he declared to his most faithful followers. He boasted of this not without foundation, since he had many superfluous votes for the exclusion of anyone at all. The same Chigi, in the conclave of Clement X, had planned, &c. He had the purpose either of electing his own creature or of dying in the conclave. In the same conclave, the thoughts of Chigi and of Medici are said to have changed, not concerning the person but concerning the manner of electing; at first they proceeded straight, but after a certain movement was noticed they changed their method, namely to reserve Delci, whereas before they had wanted to cast all the others to the ground. Hence fifty very idle days passed, for they wanted, in the words of Chigi and Barberini, to conquer by tiring out the other side, and to eat cherries inside, one of them, and figs, the other. In the same conclave, the following are found: "they are excluded, &c., because the creatures of Chigi were excluded, and whatever Papabile was considered, the sky was again darkened, no star appearing in its favour; 'If Barberini does not yield against nature, &c.'" And if anyone wishes to know the cause of this obstinacy, it is mostly the pursuit of private advantage, and of what they call reputation. For when, in the conclave of Gregory XV, the negotiation over Campori would not succeed, Borghese was asked by a confidant whether he had no others to propose, and he replied: "I have others, but this man's interest demands it, and my reputation is already involved;" he answered, "Very well indeed!"

units.la: LXII. Ob istam autem discordiam & pertinaciam in longum protrahitur electionis negotium.
units.tr: LXII. Because of this discord and obstinacy, the business of the election is drawn out to great length.

units.la: Jam suprà dictum est,de inter-regno sive inter-Pontificio; sed non semper interregnum, sive inter-Pontificium diuturnum ex discordia atque pertinacia Electorum ortum fuit; aliæ nonnunquam causæ fuerunt. Saltem in genere tunc innuimus, quasi ordinariò duos, aliquando etiam tres menses ipsi electionis negotio impendi; quod huic discordiæ atque pertinaciæ tribuendum, heicque porrò, sed paucis, declarandum est. Post mortem Gregorii IX. sedes uno & viginti mensibus vacavit, juxta Platinam. Nicolaus III. juxta eundem in vita electus est tandem, protractâ in sex menses electione, non sine magnâ Cardinalium contentione. Ibidem ita scribit: In morte Nicolai vacâsse Pontificatum quinque mensibus ferunt; causam diuturnitatis ostendit in inimicitia Ursinorum & Hannibaldensium,atque subjungit,illis absentibus (urbe pulsis) Gallos suffragiis Italos superantes Gallum (bene scili-
units.tr: It has already been said above concerning the interregnum, or inter-pontificate; but a long interregnum has not always arisen from the discord and obstinacy of the electors. Other causes have sometimes been at work. At least in general, we here note that the business of the election usually took two, and sometimes even three, months; this must be attributed to the discord and obstinacy, and is to be explained here further, though briefly. After the death of Gregory IX the see was vacant for twenty-one months, according to Platina. Nicholas III, according to the same author, was at last elected in his lifetime, the election having been protracted for six months, not without great contention among the Cardinals. In the same place he writes thus: After the death of Nicholas the papacy is said to have been vacant for five months. He shows the cause of the delay in the enmity of the Orsini and the Annibaldi, and adds that while they were absent (having been driven from the city), the French, outnumbering the Italians in votes, elected a Frenchman (of course,

units.la: Vtraque in longum protrahit electionem; scilicet, non tantùm contemptis, sed & vi expulsis quibusdam) elegisse. Post mortem Nicolai IV. eodem narrante, Cardinales electionis negotium discordiis intestinis biennio, menséque tertio in longum deduxere. In Conclavi Clementis V. commoda privata usque adeò imped别 verunt publica, ut Cardinales ultra 2. menses tempus disputando & strepitus toti Christiano orbi scandalosos, infidelibus contrà gratos movendo consumpserint. In eodem Conclavi erant, qui studio prolongationem Conclavis quæsiverunt. In Conclavi Clem. VII. Cardinalium dissidiis non sine summa conventione interregnum ad m. 2. d. 4. fuit productum. In Conclavi Pii III. juxta Onuphrium longa & diuturna contentio fuit. In Conclavi Leonis XI. sequentia legimus: In quesło &c. In isto inordinato & deformi Chaos timoris, & spei & reciproca pertinacia, omnes affirmarunt, Conclave diu duraturum. In Conclavi Urbani VIII. tria erant, quæ diu duraturum Conclave præsignificabant. 1. Bulla Gregorii de scrutinio secreto, si credeva communemente &c. quia quivis proprio commodo & propriâ opinione agatur, difficilem fore suffragiorum sufficientium combinationem. 2. Contrarietas factionum Borghesia & Ludovisiana. 3. Multitudo Papabilium. In Conclavi Clementis X. legimus: Al sequito &c. post 76. dies quadam negotiatio moveri cœpit, ut sentiri posset favor erga Celsium. Et alibi: Complebantur 80. dies in memoriam revocantes illos Alexandri, qui tunc nimii videbantur, sed jam vix negotium cœptum dici potuit. Eodem etiam die aculeati Retzii & Sforzæ sermones suprà memorati in ipsa scrutinii capella auditi dicuntur. Atque hæc exempla pleraque post institutionem Conclavis contigerunt, de qua ita Card. de Luca Relat. Rom. Cur. Forensis p.24. Proficuam adeò fuisse inventionem Conclavis, quo mediante praxis non tribuat illas diuturnas & scandalosas sedis Apostolicæ vacationes, quas Chronica narrant. Quantas igitur moras tracturi fuissent discordes, si nostris temporibus haud inclusi essent?
units.tr: Both protracted the election at length: namely, not only by scorning but also by forcibly expelling certain men) elected. After the death of Nicholas IV, according to the same narrator, the Cardinals drew out the business of the election for two years and three months by intestine discords. In the Conclave of Clement V, private advantages so impeded public business that the Cardinals spent more than two months in disputes and in uproar scandalous to the whole Christian world and pleasing to unbelievers. In the same Conclave there were some who sought to prolong the Conclave on purpose. In the Conclave of Clement VII, by the dissensions of the Cardinals, not without great contention, the interregnum was extended to two months and four days. In the Conclave of Pius III, according to Onuphrius, there was a long and protracted contention. In the Conclave of Leo XI we read the following: In this disordered and deformed chaos of fear and hope and mutual obstinacy, all affirmed that the Conclave would last long. In the Conclave of Urban VIII there were three things which foreshadowed a long Conclave. 1. The bull of Gregory on secret scrutiny, which was commonly believed to make it difficult to combine sufficient votes, since each man acts from his own advantage and his own opinion. 2. The rivalry of the Barberini and Ludovisi factions. 3. The multitude of Papabili. In the Conclave of Clement X we read: The following, etc.: after 76 days some negotiation began to stir, so that favour towards Altieri could be perceived. And elsewhere: The 80 days were completed, recalling those of Alexander, which then seemed excessive, but now the business could scarcely be called begun. On the same day the stinging sermons of Retz and Sforza, mentioned above, are said to have been heard in the very chapel of the scrutiny. Most of these examples occurred after the institution of the Conclave, concerning which Cardinal de Luca says (Relat. Rom. Cur. Forensis p. 24): The invention of the Conclave was so beneficial that, by its means, practice no longer allows those long and scandalous vacancies of the Apostolic See which the chronicles relate. How long, then, would the discordant men have delayed if they had not been shut in in our times?

units.la: LXIII. Ex quo enim tempore includi cœperunt, ex diuturnitate nasci solet tædium Conclavis.
units.tr: LXIII. For from the time they began to be shut in, weariness of the Conclave usually arises from its length.

units.la: In Conclavi Leonis XI. tædium oriebatur & erano alcuni giovani, che sospirayano chi la Donna, altri il giardino; Id est: Et erant quidam juvenes, qui suspirabant, hi post virginés, alii post hortos. Tædium autem præprimis in Conclavi Alexandri VII. magnum fuit: In quo molti &c. præcipuè Conclavista maledicebant horæ, in qua in carcerem hunc ingressi erant, oculi erant tenebris delassati, aures non amplius poterant tolerare communes strepitus in cellis omnibus somnium & quietem interdiu noctúque impedientes; odoratus pliæ plùs reliquis sensibus omnibus patiebatur, quia carnes & reliqua odorem intolerabilem emittebant. Attamen ne verbum quidem de Papa creando audiebatur &c. Sed non minùs fuit tædium, ubi longior mora fuit, in Conclavi Clementis X. quod pareva gravido &c. gravidum videbatur sine ulteriori patientia ullius; Senes zelum præ se ferentes continuò diuturnitatem Conclavis prædicabant, scandalum inde ortum, querelas populi de diuturnitate illa, quæ commercium impediebat. Et paulò post exclamat Author: Ecco il Conclave &c. Ecce Conclave subitò mutatum in ludum mutorum, nemo loquebatur de Papa, quilibet cogitabat, alterum operari; Senes vellent liberari ex istis carceribus; Juvenes reguntur à suis Præceptoribus. Et quantò quæso majus tædium ex tantis moris oriretur, si Illustrissimi Domini Cardinales, paucis in Conclavi diebus exactis, solo pane & aquâ secundùm constitutiones vitam sustentare deberent! Forte tunc non necesse foret, ut aliunde tædium oriretur, nisi dicere velimus, quòd, omnia vincit amor, honorum, ambitio; commodorum terrenorum aliorum, avaritia.
units.tr: In the Conclave of Leo XI weariness arose, and there were some young men who sighed, some for a woman, others for the garden. That is: And there were some young men who sighed, some after girls, others after gardens. Weariness, however, was greatest in the Conclave of Alexander VII. In it many, especially the Conclavists, cursed the hour in which they had entered this prison; their eyes were worn out by the darkness, their ears could no longer bear the common noise in all the cells, which hindered sleep and rest by day and night; the sense of smell suffered more than all the other senses, because the meat and other things gave off an intolerable odour. Yet not a word was heard about creating a Pope, etc. But weariness was no less, where the delay was longer, in the Conclave of Clement X, which seemed burdensome, which seemed burdensome without any further patience on anyone's part. The old men, showing their zeal, kept proclaiming the length of the Conclave; scandal arose from it, and the people complained of that length, which hindered commerce. And a little later the author cries out: Behold the Conclave, etc. Behold the Conclave suddenly turned into a game of mutes; no one spoke of the Pope, each thought the other was working. The old men wished to be freed from those prisons. The young men were ruled by their tutors. And how much greater weariness, I ask, would arise from such delays, if the most illustrious lord Cardinals, after a few days in the Conclave had passed, were obliged to sustain life on bread and water alone, according to the constitutions! Perhaps then there would be no need for weariness to arise from elsewhere, unless we are to say that love conquers all, and that ambition for honours, and avarice for other earthly advantages, conquer too.

units.la: LXIV. Tædium hoc atque diuturnitatis consideratio sæpè facit Papam; In Conclavi sciens Aldobrandinus, quanto perniciosa &c. Id est: Quàm sit Conclavis diuturnitas noxia Nepotibus, & quanto eos odio subjiciat &c. Agebat hic & eligebat tandem, ne sibi damno esset Conclavis diuturnitas. Quoad tædium inspici possunt maximè illa Conclavia, quæ n. præced. citavimus; deprehendetur, ex tædio Papam factum esse commodissimum rebus ita stantibus atque minimis contradictionibus obnoxium, sed quem aliàs voluisset nemo. LXV. Ita sæpè fit, ut duobus vel etiam pluribus inter se litigantibus, tertius, alius quicunque tanquam hæres gaudeat. Testatur Il Card. p.3. l.2. p.211. Cardinales eligentes semper in procinctu esse, ò di cadere in scilla per evitare Carridi, ò in pericolo di cadere &c. ut incidant in Scyllam, dum velint vitare Charybdim, vel ut incidant in periculum cadendi &c. Narrat Platina in Eug. III. quòd, cùm inter Cardinales haud satis constaret, quem potissimùm è numero suo deligerent, Eugenium elegerint. Onuphrius autem annot. ad Urb. IV. annotat, quomodo cùm esset Hierosolymitanus Patriarcha, Cardinalibus inter se discordantibus extra eorum Collegium Romanus Pontifex renuntiatus fuerit. Platina rursus, in Nicol. IV. & Cœlest. V. memorat, Cardinales, postquam rem ipsam discordiis intestinis biennio menséque tertio in longum deduxissent, tandem in anachoretam Petrum Moronem consensisse. sensisse. In Clem. V. author Conclavis, eum, cum pars neutra alteri cedere vellet, extra Collegium creatum esse. Quod idem de Urbano VI. Platina in vita testatur. Recentiora exempla maximè sunt illa Sixti V. & Pauli V. post cujus electionem cum Baronius, competitor & ipse, Annalium suorum Tomum XII. absolvisset eidem dicatum, in fine, nempe ad an. 1198. append. μ�] πολλῆς φαντασίας, cum multa ostentatione Conclavis illius tempestatem, Schismatis naufragiique metum, & quomodo ipse violentis, licet amicis flatibus abreptus in Syrtes, è quibus haud facilis fuisset emergendi facultas, latus sit, describit, tandemque unà cum universa, sc. Ecclesiâ Catholicâ feliciter &c. acclamat: Paulo V. à Deo electo.
units.tr: LXIV. This weariness and the consideration of the length often makes a Pope. In the Conclave Aldobrandini, knowing how harmful, etc. That is: How harmful the length of the Conclave is to the Nephews, and how much it subjects them to hatred, etc. He acted here and at last chose, lest the length of the Conclave should be a loss to him. As to weariness, those Conclaves which we cited in the preceding section may be examined especially; it will be found that, from weariness, a Pope was made who was most convenient when matters stood thus and who was subject to the fewest objections, but whom nobody would otherwise have wished. LXV. So it often happens that, when two or more are quarrelling among themselves, a third, anyone else, rejoices as a kind of heir. Il Cardinale, book 3, page 211, bears witness that the electing Cardinals are always on the point of falling into Scylla while they try to avoid Charybdis, or in danger of falling, etc.; that they fall into Scylla while they wish to avoid Charybdis, or into the danger of falling. Platina relates, in the life of Eugene III, that, since the Cardinals were not agreed on whom to choose chiefly from their number, they elected Eugene. Onuphrius, however, in his notes on Urban IV, observes how, since he was Patriarch of Jerusalem, the Roman Pontiff was proclaimed from outside their College, when the Cardinals disagreed among themselves. Platina again, under Nicholas IV and Celestine V, records that the Cardinals, after they had drawn out the business by intestine discords for two years and three months, at last agreed on the hermit Peter Morone. In Clement V the author of the Conclave says that he was created from outside the College, since neither party would yield to the other. Platina, in the life of Urban VI, bears witness to the same thing. More recent examples are especially those of Sixtus V and Paul V. After Paul's election, Baronius, himself a competitor, finished the twelfth volume of his Annals, dedicated to him, and at the end, namely in the year 1198, appendix, with great show, he describes the storm of that Conclave, the fear of schism and shipwreck, and how he himself, carried off by violent but friendly winds into the Syrtes, from which there was no easy means of escape, was glad, and at last, together with the whole Catholic Church, happily etc., he acclaims: Paul V, chosen by God.

units.la: LXVI. Et quotiescunque id fit, Conclavium aliíque Pontificii ad exemplum Baronii scriptores, peculiarem Dei nutum jactant, & assistentiam Sp. S. singularem depraedicant; semper crepantes, sic Deum ostendere, se facere Papam; Atque istud argumentum habent pro directione divina tantopere jactari solita unicum, quòd nimirum aliquando praeter opinionem initii aliquis tandem eligitur; cum aliàs documenta operationis divinae specialis nulla, neque modum agendi Deo & Dei vicario ullâ ratione dignum ostendere possint, contraria sint omnia. Sed certè & hoc argumentum nullius planè ponderis, sed vanissima illa quoque jactantia est. Nulli equidem dubitamus, providentiam Dei, quae etiam ad minima, etiam ad pessima se extendit, in Electionibus Pontificum Romanorum, etiam post introductam Apostasiam, partes quoque suas habere; per eum Reges regnant & Principes dominantur; Principes etiam infideles, & Heterodoxi in regnis etiam atq; Principatibus, quorum violentae atque injustae origines extiterunt; proin omnino asserendum judicamus, Papam tanquam Principem secularem magnę ditionis eatenus etiam hodie populis divinâ dispensatione atque ad eorum bonum, vel castigationem modò politicè bonum, modò sic malum praefici, aliorum quorumcunq; Principum ad instar; quamvis simul quoque persuasissimi simus, dominium ejusmodi temporale cum professione Vicarii Christi in Ecclesia & Successoris Petri minùs convenire; Imò ulterius progressi quoque affirmamus, divino nutu Papam, qui ratione usurpationis Ecclesiasticae authoritatem & potestatem habet in mundo, ad majorem vel minorem Ecclesiae verae ratione Papae injuriam, sed ratione Dei, justam atque salutarem castigationem, modò talem,
units.tr: LXVI. And whenever this happens, the Conclavists and other Papists, following the example of Baronius, boast of a peculiar nod of God and extol a singular assistance of the Holy Spirit, always crying out that God thus shows that he makes the Pope. And they have this argument, the only one for the divine direction so much boasted of, namely that sometimes, contrary to expectation at the beginning, someone is at last elected. Yet all the other evidence cannot show any special operation of God, nor any manner of acting worthy of God or of God's vicar, but everything is contrary. Indeed, this argument has no weight whatever, and that boast is most vain. We do not doubt that the providence of God, which extends even to the smallest and even to the worst things, has its part also in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs, even after the introduction of the Apostasy; by him kings reign and princes rule. Even unbelieving princes and heterodox men rule in kingdoms and principalities whose origins were violent and unjust. Therefore we judge that it must be asserted altogether that the Pope, as a secular prince of great dominion, is also today set over peoples by divine dispensation, and to their good or for their chastisement, now politically good, now evil, like any other princes; although at the same time we are fully persuaded that such temporal dominion agrees less with the profession of Vicar of Christ in the Church and Successor of Peter. Indeed, going further, we also affirm that by the divine nod the Pope, who by usurpation has ecclesiastical authority and power in the world, is chastised, to a greater or lesser degree, not as an injury to the true Church or to the Pope, but justly and for salutary ends by God, now with such a one, now with another.

units.la: Qui probat non arguit peculiarem Sp. S. assistentiam. lem,modò alium obtingere. Sed in electionibus Pontificum Romanorum peculiarem Dei curam atq; Sp. S. assistentiam atq; talia intervenire,quę electionis negotium tanquam ad electionem Vicariorum Jesu Christi in Ecclesia & Successorum Petri in Monarchia spirituali suscptum commendarc,atque Papis electis tanquam talibus aliquam authoritatem conciliare queant, hoc est, quod negamus atque pernegamus,&c, ut vel praecedentia satis superque arguunt,multis de causis negamus,illud etiam per inopinatum hujus atque illius electionem probari posse, æquè negamus. Atque negationes nostras jam porrò modo sequenti confirmamus:
units.tr: Whoever proves this does not prove a special assistance of the Holy Spirit: that one such man, and at another time another, should come to be chosen. But that in the elections of the Roman Pontiffs there is a special care of God and an assistance of the Holy Spirit, and that such things intervene, which can commend the business of the election as undertaken for the election of the Vicars of Jesus Christ in the Church and of the Successors of Peter in the spiritual monarchy, and which can lend some authority to the Popes so elected as such: this is what we deny and utterly deny, etc. As the preceding arguments sufficiently and more than sufficiently show, we deny it for many reasons. We equally deny that it can be proved by the unexpected outcome of this or that election. And we now confirm our denials in the following way:

units.la: LXVII. Manifestum jam esse potest, artificiosissimas esse istas electiones; hactenus enim illud multis modis demonstravimus; Ut non quilibet inibi actorem agere possit; neque sufficiat nôsse,qualis Papa esse debeat,atque quales sint illi,ex quorum numero eligendus est. Notitia insuper artium Conclaviariarum hactenus recensitarum requiritur, eaque juxta consilia eorum, qui ea de re scripserunt,partim ex lectione Conclavium partim ex experientia hauriri atque haberi debet; Sed neque illa notitia sufficit,si absit prudentia in rebus agendis maxima. Volunt nôsse,quâ ratione Papa sibi maximè prodesse possit, & quis ille sit ex Collegio; Sed multi ab una parte utiles apparent,noxii ab altera,videntur multi æquè utiles, vel æquè noxii; Hinc facilis est transitus ab uno ad alium, à studiosiùs quaesito ad inopinatum,necessitate praesertim simul trahente; Lectio sola non sufficit atque notitia illa theoretica; imò theoretici maximè obstinatione sibi nocent; casus variant, & vel minima circumstantia discrepans aliam tractationem postulat; neque idem est nauclerus in portu de tempestate loquens & in tempestate constitutus; ubi etiam affectus prudentiam notitiámque obnubilant.
units.tr: LXVII. It can now be plain that these elections are most artful. For we have hitherto demonstrated this in many ways: not just anyone can act as a player in them, nor is it enough to know what sort of Pope ought to be chosen, and what sort those are from whose number he is to be chosen. Moreover, a knowledge of the conclave arts recounted so far is required, and this ought to be drawn and gained, according to the counsels of those who have written on the matter, partly from reading about conclaves and partly from experience. But even that knowledge is not enough if great prudence in managing affairs is lacking. They wish to know by what means a Pope can be most useful to himself, and who in the College is such a man. But many appear useful on one side and harmful on the other; many seem equally useful or equally harmful. Hence the transition from one to another is easy, from what was sought with more zeal to what was unexpected, especially when necessity draws them along at the same time. Reading alone is not enough, nor that theoretical knowledge. Indeed the theorists especially harm themselves by their obstinacy. Cases vary, and even the smallest differing circumstance calls for a different handling. Nor is the pilot who speaks of a storm in harbour the same as the one who is in a storm, where feelings also cloud prudence and knowledge.

units.la: Experientia utilis quidem est, atque hic necessarii sunt esperti Maestri del givoco experti in ludendo Magistri, ut in Conclavi Clementis IX. quidam vocantur; quibus in Conclavi Leonis XI. opponuntur: Giovani inesperti,Juvenes inexperti,quibus dicitur, cur timeant? item: Che li paperi non hanno da menare à bere l'oche; Id est: aves non duci à pullis suis ad bibendum; imperfecta tamen est experientia,neque sufficiens ob rationes ex parte easdem. Difficultatem quoque tractationis istius bene exprimit IlCard. p. 3. l.3. 345. Non si tratta, inquit, nel Conclavi di sette o sei voti, ma di sessanta &c. Non agitur in Conclavi de septem,
units.tr: Experience is indeed useful, and here the experienced masters of the game, skilled in playing are necessary, as some are called in the Conclave of Clement IX; against them, in the Conclave of Leo XI, are set young inexperienced men, to whom it is said, why should they fear? Likewise: the ducks must not lead the geese to drink; that is, the birds are not to be led to drink by their chicks. Yet the experience is imperfect, and not sufficient for the same reasons. Il Cardinal, p. 3, l. 3, 345, expresses the difficulty of this business well: Non si tratta, he says, nel Conclavi di sette o sei voti, ma di sessanta, etc. It is not a matter, in the conclave, of seven or six votes, but of sixty, etc. Not a matter of seven

units.la: Potius arguit defectum vel imperfectionem, quae ad artificiosissimas electiones requiruntur; ptem, aut sex, sed de sexaginta suffragiis. Inter illos autem, qui ea dant, quidam neque Dei neque Diaboli sunt, alii unicè propriis commodis inhian-tes, alii partes Nepotum sequi tenentur, alii Galliæ, alii Hispaniæ; quidam promittunt huic linguâ, alteri animo, sed & tales dantur, qui omnes ex-cludere amant, ut in longum negotium protrahant, Cardinales Doctissi-mi minimè valent, & maximè Politicè successibus carent; ignaros juvat animus eorum obstinatus, verbo, ita nonnunquam res cadunt, ut illi ipsi, qui negotiantur, videantur sæpè causam modi ita negotiandi nescire &c. species Conclavis habent pedes & non ambulant, aures & non audiunt, lin-guas & non loquuntur; Multos Papas creant Galli, erga Hispanos simulan-tes, se cogitare de iis, de quibus minimè cogitant. Vide etiam L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.168. un Sonetto sopra il Conclave, ubi novus infernus dicitur, immensa solicitudines & obstinatio clavem gerens memorantur, p.169. Il festino del Conclave; ut & seqq. nec non p.218. ubi de artificiosis ne-gotiationibus, & quomodo alius alium ad fines suos eò facilius obtinendos inescare soleat, legitur. Quid miri igitur, quando nonnunquam, qui, quid sibi magis, minùs prosit, obsit, & quinam magis sibi, mi-nùs utiles, noxii sint non satis norunt, quibus lectio non sufficit, experientia non adest, vel adest rursus insufficiens, quando, in-quam, tales ab affectibus atque necessitate communi illuc abripiun-tur, quo prius non respexerant? Quando à talibus eligūtur tales, qui non primi summè placuerunt, sed vel ideò salvi manserunt tanquam non primo impetu expositi, sed tamen artibus tandem suis, quales certè Sixtus maximè adhibuisse legitur, prorumpunt, an in eo miraculum poni debet? Vel, quid hic est, quod non in re-bus humanis accidat quotidie? In electionibus quibuscunque? Ni-si quòd reliquæ omnes minùs vitii habere deprehenduntur.
units.tr: Rather, it argues a lack or imperfection of what is required for the most artful elections; but of six, and of sixty votes. Among those who give them, some belong neither to God nor to the Devil; others, gaping only for their own advantages, are bound to follow the parties of the nephews, some of France, some of Spain; some promise with the tongue to one side and with the mind to another. And there are also those who love to exclude everyone so as to drag out the business at length. The most learned Cardinals are by no means strong, and especially lack political success. Their obstinate spirit pleases the ignorant; in a word, sometimes things fall out so that those very men who are doing the business seem often not to know the reason for handling it in such a way. Conclaves have the appearance of feet that do not walk, eyes that do not see, tongues that do not speak. The French create many Popes, pretending towards the Spaniards to be thinking about those about whom they least think. See also L'Ambasciatore di Roma, p. 168, a Sonnet on the Conclave, where it is called a new hell, where immense anxieties and obstinacy bearing the key are recorded; p. 169, Il festino del Conclave, and following; and also p. 218, where we read of artful negotiations, and how one is accustomed to lure another the more easily to obtain his ends. What wonder, then, when sometimes those who do not know well what is more or less advantageous or harmful to themselves, and who are more or less useful or harmful to themselves, not having reading enough, nor experience, or having experience that is again insufficient, when, I say, such men are swept there by feelings and by common necessity, to where they had not previously looked? When such men choose such men, who at first were not much liked, but who remained safe for that very reason, as not exposed at the first onset, but who at last break out with their arts, the sort Sixtus is certainly read to have used most, should a miracle be placed in this? Or what is here that does not happen daily in human affairs? In any elections whatever? Except that all the rest are found to have less fault.

units.la: LXVIII. Melius certè de repudiatione maximè Papabi-lium & de electione minùs talium ratiocinatur Anonymus,
units.tr: LXVIII. The Anonymous author reasons more soundly about the rejection of the most prominent candidates for the papacy, and about the election of men less of that sort,

units.la: in Dissert. de creatione Pontificum, verbis sequentibus: Quòd si periculum aliquod in eo esse viderit, si in Pontificem quis eligatur, (ast in quo non aliquod periculum apparet?) facilè conjunctis animis & sententiis remedium afferunt: eoque fit, ut qui præcipua inter eos sunt dignationis & qui præ cæteris eligendi videbantur, sæpe sua plerumque frustrentur; Quoniam verò eadem diligentia adhiberi non potest in omnibus, si forte contingat, ut ejus fiat mentio, de quo ipsi non cogitârunt, & de quo cogitandi vel deli-berandi spatium non habent, videas eos quasi symphalos agi, & certatim hunc In quo adstipulatur Anonymus. hunc illum antevertere : atque inde eum Pontificem renunciari, quem renunciatum iri vix quisquam fuerit suspicatus.
units.tr: in his Dissertation on the Creation of Popes, in the following words: If he sees some danger in it, should anyone be chosen as Pope (but in whom does some danger not appear?), they easily supply a remedy by joining their minds and opinions. And so it comes about that those who are the most distinguished among them and seemed most fit to be chosen are often disappointed of their own hopes. Since the same care cannot be applied in every case, if it happens that the name is mentioned of someone they had not thought of, and they have no time to think or deliberate, you may see them driven about like a herd, each eagerly trying to get ahead of this one [In this the Anonymous author concurs.] and that one, and so he is proclaimed Pope whom hardly anyone would have suspected would be proclaimed.

units.la: LXIX. Hinc etiam est, & ex infinitis istis artibus dependet, & quia judicium certum catenam integram postulat, facilè autem annulus unus & alter deest, ut, cui etiam eventus attestatur, quis Papa futurus sit, ordinariò & certò pronunciari nequeat; vix est,ut idem ait, ut quicquam, non dico pronunciare, sed etiam certâ conjecturâ assequi quis possit, ob continuam rerum Romanarum mutationem &c. Et in fine: Sic, ut qui dicere velit, quis futurus sit Pontifex, divinare potius quàm conjecturare sit existimandus. Imò Proverbium Romanorum est in Conclavi Nic. V. memoratum; Che colui esce di Conclave Cardinale, che vi entra Papa; Id est; Illum Cardinalem è Conclavi egredi, qui Papa habeatur in ingressu. An igitur res adeò mira est, si quis in divinatione sua nonnunquam fallatur? Non equidem arbitror. Isti tamen incertitudini qualicunque forte tribuas, quòd hîc ne quidem divinare omnibus modis per Pii IV. Bullam licet; Quatenus nimirum in ea sponsiones de futuro Pontifice prohibentur. Tribuas etiam opinioni, quam de Papa divinitùs & non secundùm hominum judicia eligendo habent & haberi volunt. Quamvis incertum sit, annon ideò potiùs ista prohibitio facta sit, ne Cardinales in Conclavi cum respectu ad Sponsiones dolosè factas eligant.
units.tr: LXIX. From this too, and from those endless arts, it follows that, since a sound judgment requires a complete chain, and one or another link is easily missing, it cannot be announced reliably and with certainty, even when the outcome itself bears witness, who will be Pope. As the same author says, it is hardly possible for anyone to achieve, I will not say to pronounce, but even to reach by a certain conjecture, anything of the kind, on account of the constant change in Roman affairs, etc. And at the end: So that whoever wishes to say who will be Pope should be thought to prophesy rather than to conjecture. Indeed, there is a Roman proverb recorded in Conclave of Nicholas V.: He comes out of the conclave a cardinal who went in as Pope. That is, that cardinal comes out of the conclave who is regarded as Pope when he goes in. Is it then so strange if someone is sometimes wrong in his prediction? I certainly do not think so. Yet you may perhaps ascribe to this uncertainty, of whatever kind, the fact that here one may not even prophesy by any means, even though Pius IV's Bull allows it, inasmuch as, of course, wagers about the future Pope are forbidden in it. You may also ascribe it to the opinion which they hold, and wish to be held, that they elect the Pope by divine inspiration and not according to human judgments. Although it is uncertain whether this prohibition was not rather made so that cardinals in the conclave would not elect with regard to wagers made by fraud.

units.la: LXX. Sed illud contrà exploratissimum jam haberi potest, electiones istas ordinariò malas atque vitiosas esse, ne illis quidem paucissimis, ubi planè inopinati eliguntur, ordinariò exceptis. Non possunt subsistere ullo modo ad rigorem veteris Ecclesiæ canonum examinatæ; vitia habent, næuis laborant maximis, ordinariis. Quorum ubi unus abest, alter adest, imò adsunt multi alii, si vel tantùm ad ea, quæ Romanæ communionis homines communicant, respicimus; Quanta autem justus judex tandem in lucem proferet hactenus occulta! Sed & præter illas talium narrationes de hoc & illo vitio speciali habemus testimonia de vitiosis electionibus generalia. Qualia certè sunt, quando tot, malis artibus ad Pontificatum pervenisse dicuntur. Vigilius apud Baronium ad an. 540. n. 4. ubi artes & crimina, quibus deturpatus sit, enumerantur; Simoniaca labes, conniventia cum hæreticis, pactis conventis conscripta juratáque ipsorum defensio & Antibini restitutio, Sylverii insuper prædecessoris expulsio, ejusdémque necis cooperatio, atque demum, quòd post anathema in ipsum ipsum à Silverio irrogatum sedit nihilominus tanquam verus in Ecclesia Pontifex. & ad an. 555. n. 2. ubi in genere malis artibus Pontificatum parâsse dicitur. Cujus etiam ingressum parùm legitimum & prater Ecclesiasticas regulas fuisse,Onuphrius in Vigil. annotat. Et de quo Janus Vitalis ita cecinit: Artibus cur malis Vigil inter ovilia Christi Repis? ob id pretium proditionis habes.
units.tr: LXX. But on the other hand this can now be held as thoroughly established: such elections are ordinarily bad and faulty, even if, in the very few cases where men are chosen quite unexpectedly, they are ordinarily excepted. They cannot stand at all when examined by the strict standard of the canons of the ancient Church; they have faults, and suffer from the greatest blemishes, as a rule. Where one of these is absent, another is present, indeed many others are present, if we look only at those things which men of the Roman communion share with one another. And how much will the just judge at last bring to light that has so far been hidden! Moreover, besides those accounts of this or that particular fault of such men, we have general testimonies to faulty elections. Such indeed are those in which so many are said to have reached the papacy by evil arts. Vigilius, in Baronius at the year 540, n. 4, where the arts and crimes by which he was disgraced are listed: the stain of simony, collusion with heretics, a bargain made in writing and sworn to, their defence of Antibinus and his restoration, moreover the expulsion of his predecessor Silverius, and cooperation in his death, and finally that after the anathema pronounced against him by Silverius, he nonetheless sat as the true Pope in the Church; and at the year 555, n. 2, where he is said in general to have obtained the papacy by evil arts. Onuphrius, in his notes on Vigilius, observes that his entry was rather irregular and contrary to ecclesiastical rules. And Janus Vitalis sang of him thus: Why, Vigilius, do you creep among the flock of Christ by evil arts? For that you have the reward of betrayal.

units.la: Christophorus I. Bonifacius VII. Sylvester II. (quem & Baronius ad an. 999. n. 2. hominem astutum & in gratiam se Principum insinuandi maximum artificem tantâ sede indignissimum vocat) Honorius II apud Baron. rursus Joh.XX. qui ad an.1024. n. 3. non legitimè à Deo vocatus, sed malis artibus ad sedem ascendisse, eam occupâsse, indignè atque tyrannicè dicitur, & ad an. 1033. n. 3. malis artibus in Cathedram Petri angelis reverendam intrusus similiter dicitur.
units.tr: Christopher I, Boniface VII, Sylvester II (whom Baronius also calls, at the year 999, n. 2, a crafty man and the greatest artist at winning the favour of princes, most unworthy of so great a see), Honorius II, in Baronius again, John XX, who, at the year 1024, n. 3, is said to have ascended to the see not lawfully called by God, but by evil arts, to have occupied it unworthily and tyrannically, and at the year 1033, n. 3, is similarly said to have been thrust by evil arts into the Chair of Peter, which is to be revered by angels.

units.la: LXXI. Claudimus itaque hanc Dissert. exemplo,quod Nobilissimus Sandis Relat. dello stato della Relig. c. 31. suppeditat; Postquam dixisset; In electione Pontificum Romanorum esse artificiosissimas in toto orbe molitiones; Subjungit; se in Italia degentem fando accepisse, fuisse quendam Cardinalem Siculum, quem eruditio & sanctitas promoverit,(quales nonnulli studio aliquando eligantur,) qui Conclave cum fratribus ingressus,expectaverit,che per incessanti prieghi,come nelli tempi antichi &c. ut continuis precibus, quemadmodum in Ecclesia primitiva, praeuntibus, revelatio quadam quasi digito monstraret Vicarium Christi, sed prater molitiones & tentationes & comminationes, contractus & combinationes, quibusdam nonnisi ad exclusionem promovendam proponentibus, atque sic viam ei,quem ad ultimum alea jactum reservandum putárant,sternentibus, quando spe diminutâ & irâ cessante, oppositionum vis cesset similiter; Brevi cùm ipse etiam urgeretur omnibus modis, atque modò ab his, modò ab illis duceretur, bonus homo stupore plenus, tanquam in casu opinioni suæ pristinæ plane contrario, dixit: Ad hunc modum fiunt Episcopi Romani? Atque posthac Romam redire noluit; Nempe inepti sunt ad ejusmodi electionem viri minùs fucati, quemadmodum Author Conclavis Leonis XI. narrat,Manticam & Bellarminum sæpè antepositae la verita &c. veritatem gratiæ, commodis & larvis fucatis vitæ aulicæ, & proin in Conclavi non multum fiduciæ in illos collocatum fuisse. Et Author Conclavis Pauli V. Aldobrandinum timuisse de rigida conscientia Baronii,fugisse Bellarminum tanquam Jesuitam scrupulosum. Inepti sunt,inquam,ad electiones, in quibus conscientia & Sp. S. sæpè
units.tr: LXXI. We therefore close this dissertation with the example which the most noble Sandys supplies in Relation of the State of Religion, c. 31. After saying that in the election of the Roman Pontiffs there are the most artful schemes in the whole world, he adds: I have heard, while living in Italy, by report, that there was a certain Sicilian cardinal, whom learning and holiness had advanced (such men are sometimes chosen for their reputation), who entered the conclave with his brothers and waited that, by continual prayers, as in the ancient times, a certain revelation, as if by a finger, would point out the Vicar of Christ, as in the primitive Church; but beyond the schemes, temptations and threats, contracts and combinations, some proposing certain men only for the purpose of exclusion, and thus preparing the way for the one whom they had thought to keep for the last throw of the dice, when hope is diminished and anger ceases, the force of opposition likewise ceases; When soon he himself was pressed in every way, and now led by these, now by those, the good man, full of astonishment, as if in a case entirely contrary to his former opinion, said: "Is this how Roman bishops are made?" And afterwards he refused to return to Rome.
