Clearly men who are less disguised are unfit for such an election, as the author of the Conclave of Leo XI relates, saying that Mantica and Bellarmine, often preferred to others, la verita etc., the truth of grace, with the advantages and disguises of court life, and therefore little trust was placed in them in the conclave. And the author of the Conclave of Paul V says that Aldobrandini feared the rigid conscience of Baronius, and that he fled from Bellarmine as a scrupulous Jesuit. They are unfit, I say, for elections in which conscience and the Holy Spirit

units.la: Conclusio. sæpè prætextui tantùm inserviunt; Excusabant se, inquit Author Conclavis Leonis XI. cum conscientia, atque ipsis instar scuti erat Sp. S. imò in quibus conscientiam & Sp. S. sincerè prætexere vix licitum est; Non admittebant, in eodem Conclavi, excusationes conscientiæ, quam locum topicum vocabant, ex quo, tanquam ex gravida pharetra, quisquis pro lubitu suo argumenta in utramq; partem promat. Non possunt non vitiosæ esse tales electiones, in quibus boni rarò concurrunt, si qui concurrant, inepti habentur; qui semel se ineptos deprehendunt, posthac manum operi admovere nolunt, de Conclavi cogitantes, quod fabula de spelunca leonis habet; at nos vestigia terrent. Nempe, quid Conclave sit, cogitant, & quales in Conclavi actiones obtineant, juxta allegata & probata, & juxta hymnum Italicum etiam, quem ex L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.168. heic coronidis loco apponere visum fuit, ita autem sonat: O Pelegrini, e dell' Europa erranti, Fuggite. Ah nò fermate in Roma il piede, Hor che di Papa è vuota la sua sede, Prestate gli occhi à dolorosi pianti: Ecco quel stuol di Porporati manti Che con voci sommesse al ciel richiede Di Dio lo Spirito, e pura senza fede, Oprano da Demoni, e non da Santi; Mille inganni per hora, e mille imbrogli Ogni momento mutansi in Conclave, Finte promesse ogni uno scrive in fogli; Chi meglio sa ingannar meglio si stima Onde ciascun spinge il compagno à scogli Cercan tutti la chiave Nonso se del Diavolo, ò di Christo Basta che un tale abisso io non ho visto D'ogni nequitia misto Hor ecco di qual seme il Vice Dio Nasce a la terra. Ah tacì pensier mio.
units.tr: Conclusion. They often serve only as a pretext. They excused themselves, says the author of the Conclave of Leo XI, with conscience, and the Holy Spirit was for them like a shield; indeed, in elections in which it is scarcely lawful to put forward conscience and the Holy Spirit sincerely as a pretext. In the same conclave, they did not admit the excuses of conscience, which they called a topical argument, from which, as from a quiver full of arrows, anyone may draw arguments at will for either side. Such elections cannot but be faulty, in which good men rarely meet, and if some do, they are thought unfit; those who once discover that they are unfit do not wish afterwards to put their hand to the work, and think about the conclave as the fable of the lion's den has it: but the footprints frighten us. Indeed, they consider what the conclave is, and what kind of actions take place in it, according to what has been alleged and proved, and also according to the Italian hymn, which, from L'Ambasciatore di Roma, p. 168, it seemed fitting to add here as a conclusion, and which sounds thus: O pilgrims wandering through Europe, flee! Ah, do not set foot in Rome now that its papal seat is empty; turn your eyes to bitter weeping. Behold that troop of purple-robed men who with hushed voices call on heaven for the Spirit of God, yet, without faith and pure, they work by demons, not by saints. A thousand deceits for the hour, a thousand tricks change every moment in the conclave; each writes out feigned promises on paper. Whoever knows best how to deceive is thought best; so each pushes his companion onto the rocks. All seek the key. I do not know whether it is of the Devil or of Christ; it is enough that I have not seen such an abyss, mixed with all wickedness. Behold from what seed the Vicar of God is born on earth. Ah, be silent, my thought.

units.la: Id est: O Peregrini, & Europæi errantes, fugite! Ah non Roma manete sede vacante; Adhibete oculos planctibus luctuosis. Ecce Purpurati illi, qui voce submissa Dei Spiritum ex cœlo petunt, Dæmonum non sanctorum ad instar agunt! Mille tunc fraudes, mille artificia singulis in Conclavi momentis mutantur; Promissiones mendaces quilibet scribit; Qui melius novis decipedecipere, meliorem se æstimat, hinc quivis socium in scopulos conjicit; Omnes clavem quærunt, nescio num Diaboli, num Christi, sufficit, me non vidisse similem abyssum nequitiæ mixtæ. Ecce igitur, ex quo semine Vice-Deus terræ nascatur! O sile cogitatio mea! Nostra vero non sileat: Valet enim illud: ἐνδὲ διχοστασίη καὶ ὁ πόγχαχ& ὅμμωρε πυρῆς. Atqui jam concludere licet, vix miraculo fieri posse, ut optimus eligatur, ea vitia cum adsint singula, nedum omnia. Et quid de præsenti dicemus necessitate? Non tam optimo, quàm τῷ τυχόντι rerum habenas dat in manus; Quemadmodum Herodianus l. 4. testatur, mortuo Antonio, & Audente imperium recusante, Martinum electum; Οὐχ ὥτως εὐνοίας καὶ πίστει τῶν στρατιωτῶν ὡς ἀνάγκῃ καὶ χρείας ἢ παρόντι. Id est: Non tam benevolentia fideque militum, quàm necessitate penuriaque præsenti. Sed quales illi sint, qui eligantur, plenius in Dissertatione proxima videndum erit.
units.tr: That is: O pilgrims and wandering Europeans, flee! Ah, do not remain in Rome while the see is vacant. Turn your eyes to these lamentable laments. Behold those purple-clad men, who with lowered voices ask for the Spirit of God from heaven, yet act like demons rather than saints! Then a thousand frauds and a thousand tricks change from moment to moment in the Conclave. Each one writes lying promises. He who knows best how to deceive is thought the better man; hence each one pushes his fellow onto the rocks. All seek the key, I know not whether it is the Devil's or Christ's; it is enough that I have never seen such an abyss of mixed wickedness. Behold, then, from what seed the Vice-God of the earth is born! O be silent, my thought! But let our own voice not be silent: that saying holds true, [ἐνδὲ διχοστασίη καὶ ὁ πόγχαχ& ὅμμωρε πυρῆς]. And indeed we may already conclude that it can hardly happen by a miracle that the best man is chosen, when those vices are present, each one, let alone all of them. And what shall we say of the present necessity? The reins of affairs are placed not in the hands of the best man but of whoever happens along, as Herodian testifies in book 4, when on the death of Antoninus, and Audens refusing the empire, Martinus was chosen: [Οὐχ ὥτως εὐνοίας καὶ πίστει τῶν στρατιωτῶν ὡς ἀνάγκῃ καὶ χρείας ἢ παρόντι], that is, not so much by the goodwill and loyalty of the soldiers as by the present necessity and want. But what sort of men are chosen will have to be seen more fully in the following dissertation.

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS SEPTIMÆ, In qua De Vitiis & Nævis Electionum Pontificum Romanorum illis, qui personas eligi solitas propiùs respiciunt, agitur;
units.tr: DISSERTATION VII, In which the faults and blemishes of the elections of Roman Pontiffs are treated, as far as they concern the persons who are usually chosen.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA, De Vitiis & Nævis respectu Quantitatis, sive Numeri, quatenus incertum est, quot, certum, quòd aliquando duo, aut plures simul electi fuerunt; Breviarium.
units.tr: SECTION I, On the faults and blemishes with respect to quantity, or number, insofar as it is uncertain how many were elected, though it is certain that sometimes two or more were elected at the same time. Summary.

units.la: I. Ex præcedentibus constat, vitia, de quibus hic agendum, non exigua esse; II. Nævus ratione eorum, qui eliguntur, primò est respectu numeri, quando nescitur, quot ad hodiernum usque diem & qui electi fuerint, & quando duo aut plures simul fuerunt aut electi fuerunt; Quod accidit in schismatibus, quorum; III. Primum fuit inter Cornelium & Novatianum ex Cypriano, Baronio & Onuphrio descriptum, addità epicrisi. IV. Schisma vicesimum secundum inter Benedictum X. & Nicolaum II. Benedictus intruditur atque detruditur; LII. Nicolaus eligitur. Schismatis navi indicantur; LIII. Schisma vicesimum tertium inter Alexandrum II. & Cadolaum, sive Honorium II. ubi Electio utriusque. LIV. Schismatis diuturnitas; Sectatores Cadolai, atque armorum vis; LV. Schismatis ambiguitas. LVI. Proponitur causa schismatis atque Gregorii depositio in Conciliis Moguntino & Brixino facta; LVII. Conciliare decretum; LVIII. Historia schismatis ex Baronio traditur; LXVIII. Bernhardi de Anacleto judicium; LXIX. Quae pro Anacleto scripta sint; LXX. Anacletus Innocentium cum sequacibus excommunicat, Cardinales creat, epistolas ad varios scribit, atque scribuntur epistolae ab aliis in favorem ejus, Pontificalesque functiones alias varias exercet, moritur atque Successor se subjiciens finem ambiguo schismati facit. LXXI. Vicesimum octavum inter Alexandrum III. ab una, Victorem IV. ejusque Successores Paschalem III. Calixtum III. & Innocentium III. ab altera parte. Electio utriusque, atque hujus accusatio; LXXII. Litera Apologetica; LXXIII. Cardinalium cum illo sentientium; LXXIV. Concilium Papiense; LXXV. Lecta in eo pro Victore Canonicorum Romanorum litera; LXXVI. Actio Synodi, epistola Synodalis, subscriptiones, epistolae aliae; LXXVII. Gallum promovere studuerunt, atque nihilominus inter se discordes in Italum primo consenserunt; quod ex Conclavi Urbani VI. docetur atque; LXXXIII. Hujus electio describitur; LXXXIV. Benedictus XIII. succedit Clementi VII Bonifacio IX. Innocentius VII. Et qualis ille fuerit; CI. Succedit ei Gregorius XII. eo tempore, quo de schismate tollendo frustra apud Benedictum agebatur; CII. Sub qua conditione Gregorius electus fuerit, & quomodo conditiones atque promissiones uterque Papa irritas fecerit; CIII. Utroque ideo in Concilio Pisano depositio, Alexander V. substituitur. Depositi non cedunt, Benedictus Galliam relinquit; CIV. Alexandri historia; CV. Successor Balthasar Cossa Iohannes XXIII. al. XXIV. qualis ille fuerit & quid primò egerit; CVI. Concilio Constantia habendo consentit a que illuc, dissuadentibus nonnullis, proficiscitur; CVII. Gravissimorum criminum reus deponitur; CVIII. Abdicatio Gregorii; CIX. Benedicti depositio & Martini V. electio; CX. Qui frustra Benedictum ad abdicationem rursus invitat; CXI. Concilium Constantiense ob schisma aliorum Conciliorum tempora prescribens dissolvitur; CXII. Cardinales à Benedicto deficientes honorificè excipiuntur; Idem accidit Iohanni, licèt res novas moliri visso, se dedenti, sed moerore animi mox consumpto; CXIII. Ex eiusdem dubiis in casu schismatis ; CXXX. Occurritur exceptionibus Loyolitæ Ottonis.
units.tr: I. From what has gone before it is clear that the faults to be treated here are not small; II. The blemish in respect of those who are elected is first of all one of number, when it is not known how many have been elected up to the present day, and when two or more were or have been elected at the same time; this happens in schisms, of which III. the first was between Cornelius and Novatian, described from Cyprian, Baronius and Onuphrius, with a critical discussion added. IV. The second was between Liberius and Felix, whose history is handed down, and the uncertainty is shown from various authors. V. The third was between Damasus and Ursicinus, which, together with its evils is described, and the occasion in the wealth and pomp of the Roman Pontiffs is shown from Ammianus Marcellinus and St Jerome; VI. The occasion or cause of schisms in general is further explained from the author of Cardinalism, and a judgment is passed on this schism in particular. VII. The fourth, between Boniface and Eulalius, is set out more fully, together with the laws made on that occasion, and the author illegible, ~6 letters. VIII. The fifth, between Laurence and Symmachus, is variously shown as to what it was like. IX. The sixth, between Boniface II and Dioscorus, is set forth. X. The seventh, between Silverius and Vigilius. The election of Silverius was faulty; XI. the invasion by Vigilius was most wicked; XII. Baronius's testimonies on the very bad state of Vigilius at that time; XIII. on the gravity of this schism, from the same author; XIV. Silverius's letter to Vigilius, in which he refuted and condemned him, together with Baronius's exclamations; XV. the fiction of a new election of Vigilius after the death of Silverius is examined; XVI. that new election is nonetheless invented and described by Baronius as most wicked; XVII. Vigilius was then made an illegitimate pontiff; XVIII. Baronian trifles about the change of Vigilius are put forward; XIX. they are refuted. XX. The eighth schism, between Peter and Theodore. XXI. The ninth, between Theodore and Paschal. XXII. The tenth, between Paul I and Theophylact. XXIII. The eleventh, between Stephen IV (also called III), Constantine and Philip; where there is the intrusion of Constantine; XXIV. his deposition; the appointment of Philip and Stephen, and likewise Philip's removal; XXV. the reordination of those ordained by Constantine, and the fault of the schism, also on Stephen's side. XXVI. The twelfth schism, between Eugenius II and Zosimus (called Zinzinus). XXVII. The thirteenth, between Benedict III and Anastasius. XXVIII. The fourteenth, between Formosus and Sergius. Here first on the succession of bishops of that time, and what the election of Formosus was like; XXIX. what happened with the corpse of the deceased; XXX. this deed is further confirmed, and its nature is shown from the authors; XXXI. on the reordinations then carried out; XXXII. the crime itself is further denounced; XXXIII. here what Stephen was like is declared from Baronius himself. XXXIV. The fifteenth schism, between John IX and Sergius III. XXXV. The sixteenth, between Leo V, Christopher I and Sergius III, in which Christopher expelled Leo, and was himself expelled a little later in the same way. XXXVI. Sergius seized the see, illegitimately by Baronius's own admission; XXXVII. the same author's testimony on the very bad administration of Sergius and others, and on the boast of obedience nonetheless shown to Sergius by the Northerners of that time; XXXVIII. the reply to this; XXXIX. the manifold fault in that schism is shown. XL. The seventeenth, between John XII and Leo VIII. XLI. The eighteenth, between Benedict V (called VI), Boniface VII, Benedict VI (called VII) and John XIV, whose history is handed down, and XLII. its fault is noted. XLIII. The nineteenth schism, between Gregory V and John XVI (also called XVII or XVIII), which is recounted, and XLIV. its fault is shown, together with the uncertainty in it. XLV. The twentieth schism, between Benedict VIII and a certain Gregory. XLVI. The twenty-first, between Benedict VIII (called IX), Silvester III and John XXII. Benedict's intrusion is described in Baronius's words, and the complaint of the so-called Novatians against him is set out, together with Baronius's reply; XLVII. but it is defended. XLVIII. The intrusion of Silvester III is set out at length from the same author; XLIX. the similar invasion of John XXII is explained, and Otto of Freising is introduced as a witness to these three monsters; L. how they ceased, and how great the fault in that schism was. LI. The twenty-second schism, between Benedict X and Nicholas II. Benedict is intruded and deposed; LII. Nicholas is elected. The navigations of the schism are indicated; LIII. The twenty-third schism, between Alexander II and Cadalus, or Honorius II, where the election of each. LIV. The long duration of the schism; the adherents of Cadalus, and the force of arms; LV. the ambiguity of the schism. LVI. The twenty-fourth schism, between Gregory VII and his successors Victor III, Urban II and Paschal II on one side, and Clement III on the other. The cause of the schism is set out, and Gregory's deposition at the councils of Mainz and Brixen; LVII. the conciliar decree; LVIII. the election of Clement III, his adherents, administration, death and successors; LIX. the very bad yet ambiguous account of the schism; LX. The twenty-fifth schism, between Gelasius II and Gregory VIII, is described, and LXI. its fault and ambiguity are declared. LXII. The twenty-sixth schism, between Honorius II and Celestine II, is set out from Baronius and Pandulf. LXIII.–LXIV. The new election of Honorius, said to have taken place, is described. LXV. Its fault is noted. LXVI. The twenty-seventh schism, between Innocent II and Anacletus II, and Anacletus's successor Victor IV, whose persons, electors and the elected by them, the cardinals, are set out. LXVII. The history of the schism is handed down from Baronius; LXVIII. Bernard's judgment on Anacletus; LXIX. what has been written for Anacletus; LXX. Anacletus excommunicates Innocent with his followers, creates cardinals, writes letters to various people, and letters are written by others in his favour; he performs various other pontifical functions, dies, and his successor, submitting himself, brings an end to the ambiguous schism. LXXI. The twenty-eighth between Alexander III on one side, and Victor IV and his successors Paschal III, Callistus III and Innocent III on the other. The election of each, and the accusation of this one; LXXII. an apologetic letter; LXXIII. of the cardinals who agreed with him; LXXIV. the Council of Pavia; LXXV. the letter of the Roman canons for Victor, read there; LXXVI. the proceedings of the synod, the synodal letter, the signatures, and other letters; LXXVII. the growth of Alexander, the death of Victor, the substitution of Paschal; LXXVIII. the wars that followed, and Alexander's final triumph; LXXIX. the silence of Platina and Baronius about Innocent. Many evils in the schism, and great uncertainty. LXXX. The twenty-ninth schism, between John XXI (called XXII) and Nicholas V, is recounted, and LXXXI. its ambiguity is further declared. LXXXII. The thirty-fifty-year schism had this occasion: when Gregory XI died, the French cardinals strove to advance a Frenchman, yet, divided among themselves, they agreed at last on an Italian; this is taught from the conclave of Urban VI, and LXXXIII. his election is described; LXXXIV. the publication of the election was postponed; the pope was personated; LXXXV. the fear of the cardinals. Congratulations were offered to the elect by the officials and cardinals present; LXXXVI. the elect enquires into his own election, the cardinals answering as he wished, and absent ones also coming forward and confirming the election; LXXXVII. a speech delivered after the election was confirmed, acceptance of the papacy and enthronement; LXXXVIII. the petitions of three cardinal promoters were approved; LXXXIX. Urban shows himself as pope in everything; XC. he sharply admonishes the cardinals; XCI. the beginning of disobedience; XCII. Urban sets himself sharply against it; XCIII. the Transalpine cardinals, having left on leave, openly dissent from the pope and elect Clement VII; XCIV. the gravest evils of the schism are briefly recounted; XCV. Clement goes to France; Urban excommunicates, creates new cardinals, punishes those who sought peace to his own loss, creates many others, suffers persecutions until death, and why? XCVI. For what reason these things ought to have been related more fully; XCVII. things consistent with the conclave are brought from Platina and Onuphrius, testifying to Urban's inept severity and rusticity; XCVIII. his death without mourning, an inept epitaph, the abbreviation of the jubilee, and the number of cardinals he created; XCIX. Boniface IX succeeds. What he was like, from Onuphrius and Platina; C. Benedict XIII succeeds Clement VII, Boniface IX, Innocent VII, and what he was like; CI. Gregory XII succeeded him at the time when efforts to end the schism with Benedict were in vain; CII. on what condition Gregory was elected, and how each pope made the conditions and promises void; CIII. therefore both were deposed at the Council of Pisa, and Alexander V was substituted. The deposed did not yield, and Benedict left for France; CIV. the history of Alexander; CV. his successor Balthasar Cossa, John XXIII (also XXIV): what he was like and what he first did; CVI. he agreed to hold the Council of Constance and went there though some advised against it; CVII. deposed as guilty of most grave crimes; CVIII. the abdication of Gregory; CIX. the deposition of Benedict and the election of Martin V; CX. he invites Benedict again, in vain, to abdicate; CXI. the Council of Constance, prescribing times for councils because of the schism, is dissolved; CXII. the cardinals who deserted Benedict are honourably received. The same happened to John, though he had plotted novelties, submitted himself, but was soon consumed by grief of mind; CXIII. the Council of Siena, when the King of Aragon was working there for Benedict, was dissolved, and a council at Basel was ordered to be held after seven years; CXIV. Benedict having died, Clement VIII, substituted, submitted himself to Martin and put an end to the schism; CXV. his many faults and very great uncertainty are set before our eyes. CXVI. The thirty-first and last schism, arising from the quarrels between Eugenius IV and Nicholas V on one side and Felix V on the other. It had its cause in that Eugenius did not wish to come to the Council of Basel, and on the contrary strove in every way to dissolve it; CXVII. he is deposed, and Felix is elected; CXVIII. Platina's judgment on Eugenius; CXIX. his successor Nicholas V, while still a legate of Eugenius before his pontificate, laboured much to remove the schism; CXX. at last he sees it removed and creates Felix a cardinal and legate; CXXI. it is shown that this also was a doubtful and dire schism. CXXII. Observations on the number of schisms; CXXIII. A note on the Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs of Onuphrius, whose author sought to lessen the schisms and reduce their number; CXXIV. it is refuted. CXXV. Something similar to a schism happened in the conclave of Clement VIII, as the author of the Life of the Fathers Paul testifies. Why no more schisms in so long a time? CXXVI. the faults of schisms in general are noted, chiefly from the testimony of Damian in Baronius; CXXVII. from the fact that the anti-popes with their followers are held to be heretics; CXXVIII. from the judgment of Antonio de Roscillis; CXXIX. from his doubts in the case of a schism; CXXX. the objections of Otto the Loyolite are met.

units.la: I. QUando negotio non sufficiens in eo peragendo à legitimis agendi rationibus porrò deflectit, facile est judicare de effectu, nempe malum ordinariò futurum mali malè agentis; Atque specialiùs, minùs idoneum ordinariò à minùs idoneis & malè insuper eligentibus electum iri; Præsertim quando illud ipsum, ad quod eligitur, malum est, injustitia est, mera usurpatio est, plena fraude atque violentia. Ut, consideratis hactenus in Pontificum Rom. Electione Eligentium Differt. V. atque Electionis ipsius Differt. VI. vitiis, jam constare queat, neque pauca, neque parva occurrere in ista Electione ratione eorum quoque, qui eligun-tur, vitia; Neque immeritò heic usurpemus jam Differt. IV. Sect. 2. n. 84. citata Baronii ad an. 912. de creatione Cardinalium per Pontifices malos verba paululùm mutata & ad creationem Pontificum per Cardinales plerunque non bonos, saltem tantæ actioni impares atque insuper vitiosè agentes, inflexa; Quales nam delectos reris ab his, hoc modo agentibus, quum nihil tam natura insitum sit, quàm unumquemque sibi similem generare, neque facilè in via mala boni reperiantur?
units.tr: I. When someone who is not sufficient for a task turns away from the lawful methods of carrying it out, it is easy to judge the outcome: the evil will ordinarily fall on the one who acts badly. More specifically, a less suitable person will ordinarily be chosen by less suitable men who also choose badly. This is especially so when the very thing to which the person is chosen is itself an evil, an injustice, a mere usurpation, full of fraud and violence. Once the faults of the electors in the election of the Roman Pontiffs (Differt. V.) and of the election itself (Differt. VI.) have been considered, it should now be clear that the faults in this election, in regard to the men who are chosen, are neither few nor slight. Nor shall we hesitate to apply here what Baronius said at the year 912 (already cited in Differt. IV, Sect. 2, n. 84), about the creation of Cardinals by bad Popes, with the words slightly altered so that they refer to the creation of Popes by Cardinals who are for the most part not good, or at least unequal to so great an act and additionally acting in a faulty way. For, since nothing is so naturally inborn as for each to generate one like himself, and since good men are not easily found on a bad path, what sort of men do you suppose are chosen by those who act in this way?

units.la: II. Antequam autem eorum,qui eligi solent,nævos & vitia producamus,agendum est de nævo ratione eorum illo,qui numerum simpliciter respicit,atque duplex est; Dum primò quidem adhuc sub judice lis est, quinam ad hunc usque diem electi sint, & non paucos alii numerant, alii expungunt; Quod ordinis atque temporis incertitudinem, de qua Differt. praced. actum est,porrò confirmat: Et ex iis,quæ in Johanna de numeri diversitate dicemus,amplius confirmabitur. De Anacleto jam suprà monitum, eum quibusdam cum Cleto eundem,aliis ab eo diversum esse. Onuphrius ad Nic.I. Plat. annotat:Quidam etiam novi irrepserunt Pontifices, ut post Marinum Agapitus, & post Hadrianum III. Basilius,quos Sigebertus in Chronicis prodidit. Quibus, stante maximè historia veritate, & temporum ratione,locus in hac serie esse non potest. Hi enim vel idem,nominibus mutatis, cum aliquot aliis Pontificibus, vel schismatici fuerunt, vel omninò nunquam exiterunt. Unumquodque autem horum afferere dubium est, & incertum. Eosdem etiam Marianus habet. Quærit de iisdem Blondellus de Johanna p.66. & de aliis porrò: Unde inter Benedictum III. & Nicolaum I. medius Godefrido, Gregorio Hierosolymitano, no, & compilationi Chronologica decantatus Paulus? Unde Fabianus,quem Vigilio ante Pelag. I. successisse eadem fabulatur farrago? Otto Loyo-lita in Roma Gloriosa p. 315. annotat, Romanum & Theodorum II. à Chronologiis quibusdam omitti. Ipse omittit Bonifacium VII. quotum planè non habet. Inter Benedictum VII. & Gregorium V. Fasciculus temp. & alii habent 3. Johannes, ipse nonnisi duos. Bellarminus in Chronol. sua de Johanne XXI. ait: Mirum, cur iste Papa dici voluerit XXI. cùm nullus præcesserit XX. Paulus II. Platinæ est CXX. Onuphrio CXV. sed & secundò næyus ratione numeri est, quatenus duo aut plures aliquando simul vel fuerunt, vel etiam electi fuerunt Pontifices. Næwus in eo utique est atque notissimum & vel ex Dissert. I. Sect. 6. n. 35. 36. evidens, nonnisi unum eodem tempore Pontificem ex hypothesi eligi & esse debere. Scriptum est in Lege eorum, quòd electio duorum ad eandem dignitatem in una persona non valeat. Sic & in Glossa decr. p. 2. c. 7. q. 1. c. 12. quæstio hæc tractatur, atque unus Pontifex ad id refertur, contra quod dispensari non potest. Praterea, inquit Glossator, quia una est Catholica Ecclesia & unum caput, & tamen plures fuerunt Imperatores, legimus XXI. dist. nunc autem. Sed hoc non est ita, quia offenderetur illa regula, unam, sanctam, Catholicam &c. dist. XXIII. qui Episcopus. Vitiosum igitur omninò erit, quòd toties in Schismatibus, quæ vocantur, duo aut plures Pontifices simul partim fuerunt, partim etiam electi fuerunt.
units.tr: II. Before we set out the blemishes and faults of those who are usually elected, we must deal with the blemish that concerns their number, which is twofold. First, the dispute is still before the judge over who have been elected up to the present day: some count many, others strike them out. This further confirms the uncertainty of order and time, which was discussed in the preceding Differt., and it will be confirmed still more by what we shall say about Joan concerning the diversity of numbering. We have already noted about Anacletus that some hold him to be the same as Cletus, and others to be different from him. Onuphrius, on Nicholas I in Platina, observes: "Certain new Pontiffs have also crept in, such as Agapitus after Marinus, and Basil after Hadrian III, whom Sigebert recorded in his Chronicles. Since historical truth and the order of the times stand firmly against them, they cannot have a place in this series. For these were either the same men under changed names as some other Pontiffs, or they were schismatics, or they never existed at all. Each of these is doubtful and uncertain to assert." Marianus also includes the same men. Blondel asks about them, and about others besides: "How did Paul, the man celebrated in Godfrey, Gregory of Jerusalem, and the chronological compilation, come to be placed between Benedict III and Nicholas I? How did Fabian, whom the same nonsense makes to have succeeded Vigilius before Pelagius I?" Otto the Jesuit, in Roma Gloriosa p. 315, observes that Romanus and Theodore II are omitted by certain chronologies. He himself omits Boniface VII, of whom he has no account at all. Between Benedict VII and Gregory V, the Fasciculus temporum and others have three (John); he himself has only two. Bellarmine, in his Chronology, says of John XXI: "It is strange why this Pope wished to be called XXI, since no XX preceded him." Platina makes Paul II the 120th, Onuphrius the 115th. Secondly, the blemish concerning number lies in the fact that two or more Pontiffs have sometimes been, or even been elected, at the same time. The blemish in this is very great and very well known, and is clear from Dissert. I, Sect. 6, nn. 35 and 36: on the hypothesis, only one Pontiff can be elected and can exist at the same time. It is written in their law that "the election of two to the same dignity in one person is not valid." Likewise in the Gloss on Decretum, part 2, causa 7, q. 1, c. 12, this question is treated, and "one Pontiff" is referred to, "against which no dispensation can be given." Moreover, says the Glossator, "because there is one Catholic Church and one head, and yet there have been several Emperors," we read in dist. 21, "but now." "But this is not so, because that rule, 'one, holy, Catholic,' etc., would be offended," dist. 23, "qui Episcopus." It will therefore be altogether faulty that so often in the so-called Schisms two or more Pontiffs were at the same time, some of them actually in office, some also elected.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Primum in Ecclesia Romana Schisma exortum fuit A. Chr. 254. post mortem Fabiani & biennale Inter-Pontificium inter Cornelium & Novatianum, (qui malè cum Novato, cujus hæresi favit, atque auxilio ut & sociorum promotus fuit, confunditur;) Et quidem Cornelii causa melior erat, ejusque electio à S. Cypriano in epistola ad Antonianum valde commendatur, maximè ab eo, quòd invitus, & quòd de clericorum penè omnium testimonio, de plebis, quæ tunc adfuit, suffragio, cùm nemo ante se factus esset, creatus fuit; Novatianus autem Presbyter Romanus in Cornelio communionem cum pœnitentibus vituperans, & multa Cornelio calumniosè, ut Cyprianus tradit, imputans, aliis quoque, Confessoribus etiam in partes suas pertractis, Episcopum tandem se creari passus est; Quo intellecto, Africani Episcopos duos Romam misere, qui, sunt verba Baronii ex Cypriano, dissidentes conciliarent, si possent: si non possent, cujusnam essent potiora jura, in Africam scriberent; ut communicationem. tionem, quam interea suspenderant, cuinam impertituri forent, cunctis li-quidò innotesceret. Licèt autem Africani pro Cornelio contra Novatianum pronuntiârint, hic tamen à coepto haud destitit, sed, missis ad diversos Legationibus & Literis, ut praevaleret, annisus, & magna ista, Baronio judice, Ecclesiæ tentatio fuit, omnes pene,ut ait apud eum Cyprianus, ob Confessorum pro Novatiano epistolas,perturbata sunt Ecclesiæ: & complures ex eis errore decepta, cogitantes, se errare non posse, si eorum affectarentur vestigia, qui Christum toties magna gloria confessi essent, eadem ipsa in errore manserunt, donec iidem, qui sic lapsi fuerant Confessores, facti poenitentes ad Ecclesiam redierunt. Novatianus autem, teste etiam Onuphrio in annotat. ad Cornel. diu in schismate contra Cornelium & ejus Successores Romae Episcopus fuit, &c. atque ejus Successores in Episcopatu usque ad Coelestini Papae Pontificatum permansérunt, à quo deinceps publicè Episcopum habere prohibiti sunt, ut auctor est Socrates lib.VII. c.XI. historiae Ecclesiasticae. En grave schisma, duobus se simul pro Pontificibus Romanis legitimè in locum unius ejúsdemque electis gerentibus! Romani fluctuabant Pastorem verum vix dignoscentes, exteri quoque, dubitantes, cum quonam communionem Ecclesiasticam exercere debeant; Cornelius graviter de multis & speciosè accusabatur, pro Novatiano Confessores stabant, invitum se pariter electum esse testabatur; Si ob Heterodoxiam indignus fuit; fidelibus, an pro Episcopo Romano se gerens veram doctrinam annuntiet, inquirendum est.
units.tr: The first schism to arise in the Roman Church was in the year of Christ 254, after the death of Fabian, and it was a two-year interregnum between Cornelius and Novatian (who is wrongly confused with Novatus, whose heresy he favoured, and who was promoted with the help of Novatus and his associates). Indeed, the cause of Cornelius was the better, and his election is strongly commended by St Cyprian in his letter to Antonian, chiefly because he was created unwillingly, and with the testimony of almost all the clergy and the vote of the people then present, when no one before him had been made in this way. Novatian, however, a Roman presbyter, found fault with Cornelius for his communion with penitents and, as Cyprian relates, made many slanderous charges against Cornelius; he also drew others into his party, including confessors, and at last allowed himself to be created bishop. When this became known, the bishops of Africa sent two men to Rome who, in the words of Baronius from Cyprian, were "to reconcile the dissenters if they could; if they could not, they were to write to Africa about whose rights were the stronger, so that it would be clearly known to whom they should grant the communion which they had meanwhile suspended." Although the Africans pronounced for Cornelius against Novatian, Novatian nonetheless did not desist from what he had begun, but, sending embassies and letters to various places and striving to prevail, he made this "great trial of the Church," in Baronius's judgement. Almost all, as Cyprian says in his letter, were disturbed on account of the letters of the confessors in favour of Novatian, and the Church was thrown into confusion; many were deceived by error, thinking that they could not err if they followed the footsteps of those who had confessed Christ so often with great glory. They remained in the same error until the same confessors, who had so fallen, returned to the Church as penitents. Novatian, however, as Onuphrius also testifies in his notes on Cornelius, was for a long time bishop of Rome in schism against Cornelius and his successors, and so on. His successors in the episcopate continued until the papacy of Pope Celestine, from whom afterwards they were forbidden to hold a public bishop, as Socrates writes in book VII, chapter 11 of his Ecclesiastical History. Behold a grave schism, with two men at the same time acting as Roman Pontiffs, lawfully elected in place of one and the same man! The Romans wavered, scarcely recognising the true pastor; outsiders too, uncertain with whom they ought to exercise ecclesiastical communion. Cornelius was gravely and plausibly accused of many things, the confessors stood for Novatian, and Cornelius likewise testified that he had been elected against his will. If he was unworthy on account of heterodoxy, it must be inquired of the faithful whether he, acting as Roman bishop, proclaimed true doctrine.

units.la: IV. Secundum in Ecclesia Romana Schisma fuit inter Liberium & Felicem, quod An. Chr. 355. coepit, Liberio nimirum ob Orthodoxiae constantem professionem atque S. Athanasii defensionem à Constantio Imperatore in exilium ire jussó, ab Arianis, juxta plerosque, vel à Concilio Sacerdotum, juxta librum de Pontificibus Rom. Damaso adscriptum, etiam, quod aliter, narrante Baronio ad an. 355. n. 57. legitur, procurante Liberio, Felix II. Romanae Ecclesiae antehac Diaconus suffectus fuit; Ipse etiam, Arianus nonnullis, negantibus aliis, atque non tantùm in Episcoporum legitimorum, sed & Sanctorum Catalogo Felicem hunc ponentibus. Tandem verò exilii pertaesus Liberius adversus ὁμοούσιον & Athanasium subscripsit, atque restitutus fuit, Felice, verba sunt Onuphrii in annot. ad Felicem II. à populo & senatu notato, & urbe pulso; qui nihilominùs Sacerdotii jura in Schismate, dum vixit, contra Liberium modò in urbe, modò extrà in alia civitate annos X. menses III. & dies XI. retinuit. uuit. Grave & hoc Schisma fuit inter Sanctum & Sanctum; Liberius in exilio munere fungi non potuit; dicitur à quibusdam; à Concilio Sacerdotum; dicitur, procurante Liberio, Felicem electum esse, licet Arianum fuisse dicat Socrates hist. Eccl. l. II. c.19. studiose tamen vindicatur ab aliis; Contrà Liberius,ut sedem recuperaret, haeresin amplexus est atque damnavit innocentem, uterque autem diu (licet non tam diu post restitutionem Liberii,morte Felicis intercedente;) mansit; Unius autem Ecclesia, inquit Baronius ad an. 355. n. 56. occasione illa ipsa, unum tantum esse caput oportet; cui si alterum addas,horrendum monstrum profectò erit, & n.57. unius corporis duo capita turpiter eminebunt. Atque Felicem Platina non tantùm à Catholicis subrogatum esse, sed & nulla in re Orthodoxa fidei defuisse, ac postremò ab adversariis captum una cum multis secum bene sentientibus interfectum esse testatur, propter seditionem à Liberio motam, quem Damasum secutus, licet immeritò inter Pontifices numeraverit; De quo etiam Baronius ad an. 357. n. 56. Ex Sozom. hist. Eccl. l. IV. c. 14. quòd Episcopi Sirmii congregati ambos pariter sedem Apostolicam administrare,communique consensu & concordia Sacerdotio illo fungi voluerint; sed & n. 57. multos à Liberio deficientes, Felici Catholica fidei vexillum extollenti sese junxisse, atque coepisse tunc Felicem legitimum ab illis haberi Pontificem,existim atúmque esse Liberium — à communione Catholicorum prorsus extorrem: impossibile esse judicantibus cunctis, eundem Liberium communicare posse haereticis atque Catholicis. Cùm igitur adeò manifestè constaret de ejus communione inita Sirmii cum haereticis; ex eo ipso necessariò videbatur exclusus à communione Catholica, atque ob id etiam à Pontificatûs functione penitus alienus; Sic etiam n. 58. loquitur de persecutione excitata à Magistratibus adversus eos,qui non parerent literis Imperatoris pro Liberii restitutione conscriptis. Contra n. 59. seqq. Martyrium Felicis exponit, & n. 63. agitur de controversia non levi, temporibus Pontificatûs Gregorii XIII. expungendus ne esset Felix ob vitiosum ingressum ejus,vel absque martyrii titulo relinquendus; déque his dìu multúmque altercatum esse,séque in eam sententiam pedibus ivisse,ut expungendus esset; sed,veluti Divino miraculo Felicis tunc reliquias,cum Titulo: Corpus S. Felicis Papae & Martyris,qui damnavit Constantium; repertas esse,atque eum sic opportunè visum fuisse admiratione omnium redivivum comparuisse, per se ipsum suam causam acturum,cùm jam valdè stylo contradicentium esset oppressus,atque in magna de ejus meritis disceptatione ob innumeras contrarias assertiones causâ cadere videretur. Contrà Onuphrius in annot. ad Felicem eum absolutè rejicit; Neque enim, inquit, Liberius unquam Arianus fuit, neque Felix legitimè Pontificatum adeptus est, aut quid contra Constantium gessit, vel ab eo capite est cæsus. Et paulò post; Felix, cùm Schismaticus fuerit, nulla ratione inter legitimos Romanos Pontifices numerandus esset: duo enim simul Papæ esse non possunt. In quo quidem Onuphrius Veteres nonnullos sequitur, in eo nempe, quòd malè electus sit Felix, ita enim S. Athanasius apud Doctiss. Launojum Epist. 7. p. 9. seq. in epistola ad solitarios scribit: Constantius incredibile facinus designavit, & quod verè referat imaginem Antichristi, ut qui in locum Ecclesiæ Palatium suum succedere voluerit pro conventu populi & jure comitiorum. 3. Eunuchos præsentes esse voluerit, tresque itidem καπηλεῖς καπηλεῖς , id est, malis artibus imbutos exploratores, (non enim eos dixeris Episcopos;) ut ipsi Felicem quendam Episcopum in Palatio crearent, dignum profectò talibus suffragatoribus. Caterùm populi omnes, cognitâ Hæreticorum pravitate, non permisere eos Ecclesiam intrare, procùlque ab iis recesserunt. Quid igitur hic, quod Antichristi (non) sit, omisit? Similiter Marcellinus & Faustinus in præfatione Libelli precum ad Imperatores ajunt, se jurâsse cum cateris de altero Pontifice, vivente Liberio nullo habendo; Sed Clerum contrà fas, quod minimè decuerit, cum summo perjurii scelere, Felicem Archid. in locum Liberii suscepisse, quod factum universo populo displicuerit & se ab ejus processione suspenderit. Idem habet Hieron. in Chronico. Et tamen Felicem Pontificiis multis valdè probari vidimus; Et tamen Bellarminus citat Epistolam Athanasii ejusdem ad eundem Felicem, sub titulo: Domino Beatissimo & honorabili S. Patri Felici, Sanctæ sedis Apostolicæ Urbis Romæ; ad stabiliendam nimirum authoritatem Papalem. Verùm Doct. Vir l. c. optimè infert, suppositititiam esse illam Epistolam à Bellarmino citatam. Nos autem inferimus ex dictis in causa Liberii & Felicis, quòd Pontificiis incerta hic etiam sint omnia, atque huic Liberius, illi Felix magis placeat, uterque iisdem modò placeat, modò displiceat, modò legitimus, modò illegitimus habeatur, electione nonnisi unâ unius factâ, atque schismate vix ac ne vix quidem morte Felicis sublato.
units.tr: IV. The second schism in the Roman Church was between Liberius and Felix. It began in the year of Christ 355, when Liberius was ordered into exile by the Emperor Constantius because of his steadfast profession of orthodoxy and his defence of St Athanasius. Most accounts say he was sent away by the Arians, while the book on the Roman Pontiffs attributed to Damasus says it was by a council of priests. There is also a third version, which Baronius reports at the year 355, n. 57, as the reading: with Liberius procuring it, Felix II, who had previously been a deacon of the Roman Church, was substituted. Felix himself is counted by some as an Arian, though others deny it, and he appears not only in lists of lawful bishops but also in the catalogue of saints. In the end, however, Liberius, weary of exile, subscribed against the homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] and against Athanasius, and was restored. Felix, in the words of Onuphrius in his notes on Felix II, was marked by the people and the senate and driven from the city; nevertheless, while he lived, he kept the rights of the priesthood in the schism against Liberius, sometimes in the city and sometimes outside it in another town, for ten years, three months and eleven days. This was a grave schism, between a saint and a saint. Liberius could not perform his office in exile. Some say that Felix was elected by a council of priests; others say that he was elected with Liberius procuring it. Socrates, in his Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 19, says that Felix was an Arian, yet others eagerly defend him. On the other side, Liberius, to recover his see, embraced heresy and condemned the innocent man. Both men lasted a long time, though not so long after Liberius's restoration, since Felix's death came in between. Baronius, at the year 355, n. 56, says that on that very occasion there ought to be only one head of the one Church; if you add a second, it will surely be a horrible monster, and at n. 57, the two heads of one body will stand out in a disgraceful way. Platina testifies that Felix was not only put in place by Catholics, but also was in no point lacking in the orthodox faith, and at last was captured by his adversaries and killed along with many who thought as he did, on account of a sedition stirred up by Liberius, whom Platina, following Damasus, counted among the Pontiffs, though undeservedly. Baronius also writes about him at the year 357, n. 56, from Sozomen, History of the Church, book 4, chapter 14, that the bishops gathered at Sirmium wished both men to administer the Apostolic see together and to hold that office by common consent and agreement. At n. 57 he adds that many who deserted Liberius joined themselves to Felix, who raised the banner of the Catholic faith, and that from then on Felix began to be held by them as the lawful Pontiff, and that Liberius was thought to be completely cast out from the communion of Catholics, since all judged it impossible that the same Liberius could communicate with both heretics and Catholics. Since it was so plainly established that he had entered into communion with heretics at Sirmium, it seemed necessarily to follow that he was excluded from Catholic communion, and therefore wholly unfit for the function of the Pontificate. So too, at n. 58, he speaks of the persecution raised by the magistrates against those who would not obey the Emperor's letters written for Liberius's restoration. On the other hand, at n. 59 and following, he sets out the martyrdom of Felix, and at n. 63 he discusses a controversy of no small weight in the time of Pope Gregory XIII, over whether Felix should be struck out because of his faulty entry, or left without the title of martyr; and much was argued about this for a long time, and they went on foot toward the opinion that he should be struck out. But as if by a divine miracle, the relics of Felix were then found bearing the title Body of St Felix, Pope and Martyr, who condemned Constantius. So it seemed fitting that he should appear as if returned to life, to the amazement of all, and plead his own cause, since he was already much overwhelmed by the pen of his opponents, and in the great dispute over his merits, because of the countless contrary assertions, he seemed likely to fall. On the contrary, Onuphrius, in his notes on Felix, rejects him outright: For Liberius was never an Arian, nor did Felix obtain the Pontificate lawfully, nor did he do anything against Constantius, or was he beheaded by him. And a little later: Felix, since he was a schismatic, ought not in any way to be numbered among the lawful Roman Pontiffs; for two popes cannot exist at the same time. In this Onuphrius follows some of the ancients, namely in holding that Felix was wrongly elected. For so St Athanasius, in his letter to the solitary monks, cited from the very learned Launoy, Epistle 7, pp. 9 following, writes: Constantius devised an incredible crime, which truly bears the image of Antichrist, by wishing his palace to take the place of the Church, and the assembly of the people and the right of elections to be replaced by his court. He wished the eunuchs to be present, and three of the same kind, kapēleis [καπηλεῖς], that is, spies steeped in evil arts (for you could not call them bishops), so that they might create a certain Felix as bishop in the palace, a man truly worthy of such supporters. But all the people, once they knew of the wickedness of the heretics, did not allow them to enter the Church, and withdrew far from them. What, then, did he leave out here that is not Antichrist? Likewise Marcellinus and Faustinus, in the preface to their petition to the Emperors, say that they had sworn with the others that no other bishop should be held while Liberius lived; but the clergy, contrary to right and in a manner least fitting, with the greatest crime of perjury, took Felix, the archdeacon, in place of Liberius, which act displeased the whole people, and they withdrew from his procession. Jerome has the same in his Chronicle. Yet we have seen Felix greatly approved by many Papists. And yet Bellarmine cites a letter of the same Athanasius to the same Felix, under the title To the most blessed lord and honourable holy father Felix, of the holy Apostolic see of the city of Rome, plainly to establish papal authority. But the learned man, in the passage cited, rightly infers that the letter Bellarmine cites is spurious. We, however, infer from what has been said about the case of Liberius and Felix that for the Papists here too everything is uncertain. Liberius pleases some, Felix others; each at one time pleases and at another displeases the same people; each is held now lawful, now unlawful; the election was made only once, and the schism was ended scarcely, if at all, by Felix's death.

units.la: V. Tertium secutum est inter Damasum & Ursicinum;
units.tr: V. The third schism followed between Damasus and Ursicinus;

units.la: Mortuo enim Liberio, an. 366. al. 367. al. 368. loquitur Onuphrius, annot. ad Fel. Presbyteri aliquot & Diaconi S. R. E. Liberiana partis statim Ursicinum Diaconum Pontificem constituunt, & à Paulo Episcopo Tiburtino ordinari faciunt; Hi verò, qui Felici adhaserant, Damasum in schismate etiam
units.tr: For after Liberius died, in the year 366, or 367, or 368, Onuphrius speaks, in his notes on Felix. Some presbyters and deacons of the Liberian party of the Roman Church at once set up Ursicinus, a deacon, as pontiff, and had him ordained by Paulus, bishop of Tibur. Those who had clung to Felix, however, were also in schism against Damasus

units.la: Tertium inter Damasum & Ursicinum, quod unâ cum malis suis etiam ipsi Pontificem Romanum renuntiant, atque ita pessimum schisma & civilis seditio urbem vexare coepit, qua eò usque populo in duas factiones divisò, successit, ut in Basilica Sicinii, armatis unà concurrentibus, ad CXXXVII. Interfecti sint. Quod cùm Imperator Valentinianus cognovisset, seditionis Urbanæ, schismatisque tollendi causâ, Damaso in Pontificatu confirmato, Ursicinum urbe expulit anno primo & mense secundo ordinationis ejus, atque ita solus Damasus Præsul Apostolicæ sedis permansit.
units.tr: The third schism, between Damasus and Ursicinus, was that each side, along with its own bad men, also proclaimed its own man Roman pontiff. So the worst schism and civil sedition began to trouble the city. The people were divided into two factions, and it came to such a pitch that, at the Basilica of Sicinius, armed men of both sides met in combat, and as many as 137 were killed. When the emperor Valentinian learned of this, in order to end the urban sedition and the schism, he confirmed Damasus in the pontificate and expelled Ursicinus from the city in the first year and second month after his ordination. So Damasus alone remained as prelate of the apostolic see.

units.la: Subjungit etiam Authores, & tandem: Hac igitur ratione schismata duo fuerunt brevi tempore sub quatuor Pontificibus ferè continuata. Neque immeritò pessimum hoc schisma vocat; Tunc enim, inquit Baronius ad an. 367. n. 6. quæ olim cœperat in Clero Romano dissensio ex substitutione Felicis latenter serpens, novi Pontificis electionis occasione recruduit; Tunc, sunt verba Ammiani Marcellini apud eundem n. 7. Damasus & Ursicinus supra modum ad rapiendam sedem Episcopalem ardentes scissis studiis asperrimè conflictabantur, ad usque mortis vulnerumque discrimina adjumentis utriusque progressis; Tunc, ut narrat idem ibidem, efferata diu plebs agrè postea delinita; Imò anno demum 369. teste Baronio ad eundem n. 2. Ursiciniani, licèt manu militari compressi—nequaquam tamen acquieverunt, atque penitus cum Damaso communicare abhorruerunt, cùmque intra Urbem conventus agere non liceret, in suburbiis, in cryptis arenariis, aliisque privatorum locis Ecclesiam congregârunt &c. Atque sic res non suffragiis tantùm, ut Platina in Damaso loquitur, sed vi & armis tractabatur; Facta est tanta seditio, imò verò tanta bella coorta sunt, loquitur Ruffinus apud Bar. ad an. 367. n. 16. alterutrum defendentibus populis, ut replerentur humano sanguine orationum loca. Atque causam ambitionis eoúsque furentis rectè notat Ammianus Marcellinus apud eundem n. 8. Neque ego, inquit, abnuo, ostentationem rerum considerans urbanarum, hujus rei cupidos, ob impetrandum, quod appetunt, omni contentione laterum jurgari debere: Cùm id adepti futuri sint ita securi, ut distentur oblationibus matronarum, procedántque vehiculis insidentes, circumspectè vestiti, epulas curantes profusas, adeò ut eorum convivia regales superent mensas. Qui esse poterant beati revera, si magnitudine Urbis despecta, quam vitiis opponunt, ad imitationem Antistitum quorundam provincialium viverent, quos tenuitas edendi potandique parcissimè, vilitas etiam indumentorum, & supercilia humum spectantia, perpetuo numini verisque ejus Cultoribus ut puros commendant & verecundos. Quò etiam collimavit apud eundem n. 10. ex Hieron. epist. 61. Præextextatus ille nobilissimus
units.tr: He also adds authorities, and finally: So by this reasoning there were two schisms, which lasted almost continuously for a short time under four pontiffs. He rightly calls this the worst schism. For then, says Baronius at the year 367, no. 6, the dissension which had long been creeping in the Roman clergy since the substitution of Felix broke out again on the occasion of the new election of a pontiff. Then, in the words of Ammianus Marcellinus, cited by the same author at no. 7, Damasus and Ursicinus, burning beyond measure to seize the episcopal see, fought most bitterly with divided zeal, and their efforts went as far as the peril of death and wounds, on both sides. Then, as the same author relates in the same place, the plebs, long enraged, was afterwards with difficulty calmed. Indeed, in the year 369, according to Baronius at the same no. 2, the Ursinians, though restrained by military force, by no means gave in, and utterly refused to communicate with Damasus; and since it was not lawful for them to hold assemblies within the city, they gathered the Church in the suburbs, in sand-pits and other private places, etc. And so the matter was handled not only by votes, as Platina says of Damasus, but by violence and arms. Such great sedition arose, indeed such great wars broke out, says Rufinus, cited by Baronius at the year 367, no. 16, while the peoples defended each side, so that the places of prayer were filled with human blood. And Ammianus Marcellinus, cited in the same place at no. 8, rightly notes the cause of ambition, which raged to such a pitch: Nor do I deny, he says, considering the display of urban affairs, that those who desire this office ought to contend with all their strength to obtain what they seek, since, once they have gained it, they will be so secure that they are supported by the offerings of matrons, ride about in carriages, dress lavishly, provide sumptuous feasts, so that their banquets surpass royal tables. They could truly be blessed if, disdaining the greatness of the city, which they set against the vices, they lived in imitation of certain provincial prelates, whom the meagreness of their food and drink, the plainness of their clothing, and their eyes fixed on the ground commend, as pure and modest, to the eternal deity and its true worshippers. Hieronymus also aimed at this in his letter 61, cited by the same author at no. 10: that most noble Praetextatus,

units.la: Ex Hieron. epist. 61. (marginal notes: describitur, & cum occasione sive causa, fastu nempe & divitiis Pontificum.) lissimus Romanorum, Proconsul in Oriente, ac post Urbanâ Præfectură aliisque magistratibus auctus, qui solebat ludens B. Damaso dicere : Facite me Romana Urbis Episcopum & ero protinus Christianus; frustra luxum excusare conante ibidem Baronio.
units.tr: From Jerome, letter 61 (marginal notes: described, and with the occasion or cause, namely the pride and riches of the pontiffs). Most noble of the Romans, proconsul in the East, and afterwards raised to the urban prefecture and other magistracies, who used to say to blessed Damasus in jest: "Make me bishop of the city of Rome and I will at once become a Christian"; while Baronius there tries in vain to excuse the luxury.

units.la: VI. Hinc etiam tam serò schismata in Ecclesiam Romanam immissa fuerunt, nempe demum postquam venenum divitiarum in eam effusum esset; Consentit atque optimè rem declarat Il Cardin. p.3. l.1. p.21. seqq. Cessò la santità &c. cessavit sanctitas Ecclesiæ (loquor de sanctitate Electionum Pontificum) inquit Author,quia sub Constantino cessavit persecutio. Ecclesia Constantinus pacem dedit, pacem corporis, sed forte tormentum animarum; dum enim divitiæ Ecclesiasticis donata sunt, dum ædes commodâ, imò dominationes urbium assignatæ, caritas refrixit, Zelus evanuit, devotio periit, & qui ante pœnitendo, jejunando cœlum quæsiverant, cœperunt quærere thesauros, postulare Abbatias, ambire Episcopatus, atq; cum his Mundanam gloriam. Cum divitiis introducta sunt schismata, & hæreses, dum introduceretur superbia in corda ante humilium atque dignitates primò fugientium. Atque Papatus ille, qui olim fugiebatur, tanquam furori Tyrannorum exponens, ab omnibus ambiri cœpit, quam primùm perventum est à timore ad securitatem, à fuga ad quietem, à tormentis ad felicitatem. Quos enim ante Pontificatûs paupertas Tyrannis subjecit, hi tandem putabant, se cum Pontificatûs divitiis martyres reddere posse ipsos Tyrannos. Initium hujus ambitionis in hoc schismate notabile apparuit; Duo enim priora magis religionum diversitati deberi ex dictis liquet. In hoc autem inter Damasum & Ursicinum ambitio manifestiùs dominata est, hæc arma utrinque in manus dedit, hæc cædes, quæ utriusque sexûs fuisse dicuntur, promovit, quibus sola Imperatoria authoritas finem imponere potuit, judicio pro Damaso lato An autem fortior & cui violentiæ majorem culpam nonnulli tribuunt, obtinere debuit, idque authoritate & jussu Imperatoris?
units.tr: VI. Hence also schisms were introduced into the Roman Church so late, namely only after the poison of riches had been poured out into it. The author agrees and states the matter very well: Il Cardin. p.3. l.1. p.21. seqq. Holiness ceased, etc., the holiness of the Church ceased (I speak of the holiness of papal elections), he says, because persecution ceased under Constantine. Constantine gave the Church peace, peace of body, but perhaps a torment to souls. For while riches were bestowed on the ecclesiastical order, while convenient buildings and even dominion over cities were assigned to it, charity grew cold, zeal vanished, devotion perished, and those who had earlier sought heaven by repentance and fasting began to seek treasures, to demand abbeys, to ambition bishoprics, and with these worldly glory. With riches came schisms and heresies, as pride was introduced into hearts that had before shunned humility and dignities. And that papacy, which was once avoided as exposing its holder to the rage of tyrants, began to be sought by all as soon as men passed from fear to security, from flight to rest, from torments to happiness. For those whom poverty under the papacy had once handed over to tyrants now thought that, with the wealth of the papacy, they could make the tyrants themselves into martyrs. The beginning of this ambition appeared notably in this schism. For the two earlier schisms are clearly due more to differences of religion, as has been said. In this one, however, ambition ruled more openly between Damasus and Ursinus. It put weapons into the hands of both sides, and it brought about the slaughter, which is said to have involved both sexes. Only the imperial authority could put an end to this, by a judgment given in favour of Damasus. But was it the stronger man, whom some blame for the greater violence, who ought to have prevailed, and that by the authority and command of the Emperor?

units.la: VII. Quartum Schisma A. Ch.418. magnâ, ut Stella in Bonif. habet in Clero seditione cœpit inter Bonifacium & Eulalium, atque hujus quidem, si fides est habenda Symmachi literis, longè melior causa fuit, interim tamen, quia, lite ad Imperatoris & Episcoporum tribunal vocatâ, atque interea temporis Episcopali munere Romano Achilleo Episcopo Spoletino demandato, Eulalius in urbem contra Imperatoris voluntatem regressus ibi tumultui occasionem præbuit, Bonifacius ei ab Imperatore irato prælatus, & con-
units.tr: VII. The fourth schism began in the year 418 with great sedition in the clergy, as Stella has it, in Bonif., between Boniface and Eulalius. If we may trust the letters of Symmachus, Eulalius had by far the better cause. Nevertheless, the case was called before the tribunal of the Emperor and the bishops, and in the meantime the episcopal office in Rome was entrusted to Achilleus, bishop of Spoleto. Eulalius returned to the city against the Emperor's will and there gave occasion for tumult. Boniface was preferred to him by the angry Emperor, and was confirmed in office.

units.la: Qua etiam occasio sive causa schismatum in genere porrò declaratur atque de schismate judicium fertur. & confirmatus fuit, qui & posthac Imperatorem, (Honorius is erat) de tollendo in Romanorum Pontificum Electione ambitu rogavit, atque ita effecit, ut sequens ab Imperatore decretum, quod apud Baronium ad an. 419. n. 41. habetur, atque in Jure Canonico decr. p. 1. dist. 79. c. 8. si duo ; prodierit : Si duo contra fas temeritate certantes fuerint ordinati; nullum ex his futurum penitus Sacerdotem : Sed illum solum in sede Apostolica permansurum, quem ex numero Clericorum nova ordinatione divinum judicium & universitatis consensus elegerit. Unde id observandum est, ut omnes tranquillam mentem & pacificos animos ex serenitatis nostra admonitione custodiant, nec aliquid, seditiosis conspirantibus, tentare conentur : Cum certum sit, nulli partium sua studia profutura; Juxta quod decretum nonnulli ex sequentibus Papatu carere debuissent ; Dubium etiam habet Glossator, quis judex esse debeat de hoc, an electio sit contra fas ? Maxime Pontificiis vitiosum esse debet, quod Bonifacius solo Imperatoris nutu Eulalio, cui major pars adhaerebat, praelatus fuit.
units.tr: This occasion, or cause, of schisms is further set out in general, and a judgment is passed on the schism. Boniface also afterwards asked the Emperor (Honorius was he) to remove ambition from the election of the Roman bishops. And so he brought it about that the following decree of the Emperor was issued, which is found in Baronius at the year 419, no. 41. and in the Canon Law Decretum part 1, distinction 79, chapter 8, si duo: If two men have been ordained, contending rashly against divine law, neither of them shall remain a priest at all. But he alone shall remain in the apostolic see whom the divine judgment and the consent of the whole body shall choose from the number of the clergy by a new ordination. Hence this must be observed: that all keep a calm mind and peaceable spirits in accordance with our admonition of serenity, and that they do not attempt anything at the urging of seditious conspirators, since it is certain that their partisan zeal will profit no one. In accordance with this decree, some of those who followed should have been without the papacy. The glossator also doubts who ought to be the judge of this, whether an election is against divine law? It must be an especially serious fault in the eyes of the Papists that Boniface was preferred to Eulalius, to whom the greater part of the people adhered, by the mere nod of the Emperor.

units.la: VIII. Quintum Schisma fuit Symmachi & Laurentii, facta est horum electio, teste Platina, in Symmacho, non sine magna discordia, parte Cleri illum, parte altera hunc in locum demortui Anastasii sufficiente, atq; seditio ingens in senatu ac populo Romano bifariam diviso orta est, tanta ut multi tum ex Clero, tum ex populo passim caderentur, nec sacris virginibus parcerent, nec finis tantae caedis factus fuisset, ni Faustus Consul Clericos miseratus, contra Probinum tanti mali auctorem arma sumpsisset.
units.tr: VIII. The fifth schism was that of Symmachus and Laurentius. Their election, according to Platina in the life of Symmachus, was not made without great discord, one part of the clergy choosing the former and the other part the latter, to succeed the deceased Anastasius. A huge sedition arose in the senate and the Roman people, who were divided into two factions, so that many of both clergy and people were killed here and there, nor were the holy virgins spared. And there would have been no end to such slaughter had not Faustus, the consul, pitied the clergy and taken up arms against Probinus, the author of so great an evil.

units.la: Quae Anastasius in Symmacho apud Bar. ad an. 502. n. 12. susius persequitur, quod nempe sexus foemininus denudatus, omni die pugna contra Ecclesiam gesta sit, multi Sacerdotes occisi fuerint, ita ut nulli esset securitas die & nocte de Clero in Civitate ambulare. In schismate hoc pernicioso & atroci, ut Onuphrius annot. ad Sym. vocat, praeter caedes etiam rapinas & alia innumera mala commemorat apud Baronium Theodorus Lector l.2. collect; atque, eodem indice, usque ad triennium propagata fuisse docet, ambobus quidem Ravennam ad judicium Regis Theodorici, verba sunt Anastasii Bibliothecarii, pergentibus, a quo Symmachus Episcopus Romanus declaratus fuit; ad an. 477. n. 5. Idem etiam Baronius n. 6. titulum facit ; Schisma ambiguitate perplexum; quod verbis sequentibus declarat: Turbulentissimus quidem hoc anno fuit status Romana Ecclesia, cum & Clerici inter se mutuo scissi certarent, & Senatores amplissimi ordinis magno periculo totius perdenda Urbis inter se invicem obstinatis animis conflictarent: illud autem nutrie-bat bat incendinm, quòd res nequaquam eo statu reposita essent, ut palàm omni-nò de alterius legitima electione constaret, quò de alterius inclusione certum quid patensque affirmari valuerit; adeò ut, cujus essent potiora jura, videri potuisset aliquamdiu excusabilis ignorantia; atque venialis fuerit culpa, magis Laurentio studere, quàm Symmacho usque ad Synodi decretum: quo causa Symmacho adjudicata fuit. Quis enim in re tanta acquiescere judicio sacularis Principis ejusdémque Ariani cogi posse, sibi videri poterat?
units.tr: Anastasius, in his life of Symmachus, as cited by Baronius at the year 502, n. 12, sets out these events at greater length: that the female sex was stripped bare, that battle was waged against the Church every day, that many priests were killed, so that no one of the clergy could walk the city by day or by night in safety. In this pernicious and atrocious schism, as Onuphrius calls it in his notes on Symmachus, Theodorus the Lector, book 2 of the Collectanea, as reported in Baronius, mentions, besides murders, robberies and other countless evils; and by the same account he shows that it spread over three years, both parties proceeding to Ravenna for the judgment of King Theodoric, in the words of Anastasius the Librarian, from whom Symmachus was declared Bishop of Rome; at the year 477, n. 5. Baronius himself, at n. 6, gives the heading: A schism entangled in ambiguity; which he explains in the following words: This year the state of the Roman Church was indeed most turbulent, when the clergy, split among themselves, fought one another, and the most distinguished senators of the order, with the whole city in grave danger, clashed with obstinate minds. But what fed the fire was that matters were by no means so settled that it was plainly certain on either side who had been lawfully elected, or that anything clear and open could be affirmed about the exclusion of the other; so much so that for some time ignorance might seem excusable, and it was a venial fault to favour Laurentius rather than Symmachus, until the decree of the Synod, by which the cause was adjudged to Symmachus. For who could think that in so great a matter he could be compelled to abide by the judgment of a secular prince, and an Arian one at that?

units.la: Sed neque uno anno terminatam fuisse litem idem quoque verbis expressis n. 5. docet: Haud unius anni, inquit, sed plurium fuit ejusmodi in Romana Ecclesia certamen; quod sæpè consopitum, vehementiori eruptione recruduit. Ubi etiam ambiguitatem porrò ita declarat: Parti quidem Laurentii addita vires vehementer ex eo fuerunt, quòd idem habuit promotorem Paschasium Sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ Diaconum, Virum, qui tum ex doctrina, tum etiam ex vita sanctitate summam sibi gloriam comparârat; quò populus perfacilè commoveri posset. Quem Paschasium quoque n. 7. & 8. pœnis Purgatorii ideò mancipatum, atque ex iis tandem liberatum introducit. Ut & ad a. 499. n. 3. seqq. à Symmacho per Theodoricum confirmato celebratum Concilium describit, ut Episcopalem ambitum & confusionis incertum vel popularem tumultum, quem per subreptionem Diaboli usurpatione aliquorum, tempore creationis meæ (loquitur Præses ad Patres) constat exortum, communicato pariter tractatu in futurum possimus robustè ac vivaciter amputare; Cujus acta jam supra dedimus. Causa autem continuati schismatis fuit, quòd adversarii Symmachum adulterii, ut Baronius ex Anastasio ad an. 499. n. 34. narrat, accusantes Visitatorem, sive inquisitorem criminum ad an. 500. n. 3. Petrum Albinæ civitatis, à Rege impetrârunt. En rursus Schisma ambiguum, cædibus, rapinis atque innumeris malis fœdissimum, & quod Authoritate Regis Ariani tandem terminari opus fuit.
units.tr: But that the dispute was not ended within one year, the same author also teaches in express words at n. 5: This contest in the Roman Church, he says, was not of one year but of many; it was often quieted, and broke out again with greater violence. There too he further explains the ambiguity thus: The party of Laurentius was greatly strengthened by the fact that it had as its champion Paschasius, deacon of the holy Roman Church, a man who had won great glory both for his learning and for the holiness of his life, so that the people could be very easily stirred. This Paschasius, at nn. 7 and 8, he also introduces as being therefore handed over to the punishments of Purgatory, and at last released from them. He likewise describes, at the year 499, nn. 3 ff., the council held with Symmachus confirmed by Theodoric, so that by discussing together we might be able to cut off vigorously and effectively, for the future, the episcopal ambition and the uncertain confusion or popular tumult which, as is known, arose at the time of my election (the president says to the Fathers) through the subtle work of the Devil and the seizure of power by certain men; whose proceedings we have already given above. The cause of the continued schism was that the opponents of Symmachus, as Baronius tells from Anastasius at the year 499, n. 34, by accusing him of adultery, obtained from the King a visitor, or inquisitor of crimes, at the year 500, n. 3, namely Peter of the city of Albina. Behold again an ambiguous schism, most foul with murders, robberies and countless evils, which at last had to be ended by the authority of the Arian King.

units.la: IX. Sextum Schisma fuit Bonifacii II. & Dioscori; Cujus hanc causam fuisse conjicit Baronius ad an. 530. n. 3. quòd conanti Athalarico Regi aliquem consecrandum delegere Sacerdotem, parte Cleri illi consentiente, reliqui adversati alium ex adverso creaverint Romanum Pontificem. Sublatum illud mox morte Dioscori, quem defunctum damnari voluit Chirographo Bonifacius, cui tamen, sunt verba Anastasii apud eundem n. 3. in Episcopatu nullus subscripsit, dum plurima multitudo fuisset cum Dioscoro. Morte igitur alterius hoc tolli debuit, Anti-Papæ, cum quo plurima multitudo fuerat.
units.tr: IX. The sixth schism was that of Boniface II and Dioscorus. Baronius, at the year 530, n. 3, conjectures its cause to have been this: when King Athalaric was trying to have someone consecrated, and some of the clergy agreed to his choice of a priest, others opposed him and set up another as Roman Pontiff. It was ended soon after by the death of Dioscorus, whom Boniface wished to be condemned after his death by a written declaration; yet, in the words of Anastasius, cited by the same author at n. 3, no one subscribed to it in the episcopate, since a very great multitude had been with Dioscorus. It had to be ended, therefore, by the death of the other, the Antipope, with whom a very great multitude had been.

units.la: X. Septimum Schisma fuit inter Silverium & Vigilium. Et Silverius quidem procurante Theodato Gothorum Rege Pontificatum adeptus est; Theodato jubente, inquit Platina in Silverio; cujus mina plùs valuerunt; Mortem enim his clericis minatus est, qui nomina sua non subscriberent in creatione Silverii; Eadem, imò plura habet Anastasius apud Baronium ad an. 536. n. 120. his verbis: Theodatus corruptus pecuniæ dato, talem timorem indixit Clero, ut, qui non consentirent in ejus ordinatione, gladio punirentur. Sacerdotes quidam non subscripserunt in eum secundùm morem antiquum, neque decretum confirmaverunt ante ordinationem. Jam autem ordinato Silverio sub vi & metu, propter adunationem Ecclesiæ & religionis, postmodum subscripserunt Presbyteri. En eximiam electionem unius minis & violentiæ hominis Ariani debitam!
units.tr: X. The seventh schism was between Silverius and Vigilius. Silverius obtained the papacy through the influence of Theodatus, King of the Goths; at Theodatus's command, says Platina in his life of Silverius; whose threats prevailed more; for he threatened death to those clergy who would not sign their names at the creation of Silverius. Anastasius, cited by Baronius at the year 536, n. 120, has the same and even more, in these words: Theodatus, bribed with money, put such fear into the clergy that those who did not agree to his ordination were punished by the sword. Certain priests did not subscribe, after the ancient custom, nor did they confirm the decree before the ordination. But afterwards, when Silverius had been ordained under force and fear, for the sake of the unity of the Church and of religion, the elders subscribed. Behold the splendid election, owed to the threat and violence of one Arian man!

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Videamus de electione alterius: An. Ch. 538. quod Baronius n. 5. ex Procopio narrat, oborta suspicione, Silverium defecturum ad Gothos, in Graciam transmissum fuisse. Sed non tantùm Platina in Silverio subornatis à Vigilio testibus id tribuit, verùm etiam Baronius l. c. Silverium excusat, dolosa fraudis prætextum vocando suspicionem: ejusmodi enim, inquit, velamento obtegebatur, quod impia Theodora (ut dictum est ex Liberato Diacono) cum Vigilio ab Urbe Constantinopolim accersito molita fuerat: nempe se effecturam, ut ipse Pontifex, expulso Silverio, crearetur, dummodo, quod spoponderat insana cupiditate flagrans & ambitione Vigilius, Anthimum ab Agapeto (prædecessore) damnatum in Constantinopolitanam sedem restitueret. Quod etiam prolixè ex Anastasio n. eod. & 6. confirmat, maximè quoad falsos testes, qui urgente jussione exierunt, addens, quomodo Silverius, ab Antonina Patricia Belisarii uxore, cui id commiserat maritus, ut huic Theodora Augusta, condemnatus, atque à Subdiacono Regionario Regionis prima Monachicâ veste indutus, à Vigilio Archidiacono in sua quasi fide susceptus, & in exilium ad Pontianas missus, & sustentatus fuerit cum pane tribulationis & angustia.
units.tr: Let us look at the election of the other one. In the year of Christ 538, Baronius (n. 5) relates from Procopius that a suspicion having arisen that Silverius would defect to the Goths, he was sent across to Greece. But Platina does not only ascribe this to the witnesses suborned by Vigilius against Silverius; Baronius too (l. c.) excuses Silverius and calls the suspicion a pretext of deceitful fraud. For, he says, it was concealed under such a veil, which the impious Theodora (as was said from Liberatus the deacon) had contrived with Vigilius, summoned from the City to Constantinople: namely, that she would bring it about that the Pope himself, with Silverius expelled, would be created, provided that Vigilius, burning with mad greed and ambition, restored to the Constantinopolitan see Anthimus, who had been condemned by Agapetus (his predecessor), as he had promised. Anastasius confirms this at length (n. eod. and 6), especially concerning the false witnesses who went out under urgent command, adding how Silverius, condemned at the instance of Antonina the patrician, wife of Belisarius, to whom her husband had entrusted the matter, so that Theodora Augusta might be served, was clothed in monastic dress by the regional subdeacon of the first region, received by Vigilius the archdeacon as it were into his own faith, and sent into exile at Pontia, and sustained with the bread of affliction and distress.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Quam Baronius n. 9. magnam atque horribilem in Ecclesia Romana tempestatem vocat à furente hæretica fœmina excitatam, ab ambitioso Diacono procuratam, per Belisarium autem impiè admodùm consummatam &c. n. 12. autem ex Liberato Diac. in Breviar. cap.22. narrat, quomodo Vigilius ita ordinatus atque à Bellisario, implere promissionem suam, quam Augusta promiserat, ut sibi redderet duo aurei centenaria promissa compulsus, timore Romanorum & avaritiâ patrocinante. nante, sponsiones suas implere noluerit: cujus n. 14. epistolam impiam, quam tamen n. 15. ejus non fuisse contendit,ut & blasphemias,quas n. 16. habet, Vigilii nomine scriptas,de quo tamen n. 17. ait: Quid reliquum esse potuit stalis infatuati, nisi ut conculcaretur ab omnibus, & projiceretur in haeresium sterquilinium? Putorem namque contraxit haeretica pravitatis ex consuetudine inita cum haereticis. En in quod barathrum infelicem hominem conjecit ambitio! in quantam eum insaniam & infamiam adegit gloria vana cupido! cujus causa cogatur & in ipso portu pati naufragium,in Petra petra scandalum esse, atque in sede videri mobilem, & in fide infidelem haberi. Ita plane sententia Domini judicatur a fide excidere, qui gloria mancipium se constituit, ipso dicente (Jo.V.) Quomodo potestis credere, si gloriam ab invicem accipitis? & de hujus simili Joannes (3 Joh.9.) Diotrephes, qui amat primatum gerere in eis,non nos recipit. Et n. 18. quòd jam temporibus Bonifacii,ut ab eo vivente subrogaretur in sedem, contra leges omnes Ecclesiasticas atque morem impudens pertentârit,atque ita plane pondere scelerum pragravatus,dum sursum ascendere meditatus sit,deorsum una cum iis & ab iis,qui in coelo principatum superbè appetierint, demersus fuerit,eadem cum illis consilia mente volvens: In coelum conscendam &c. ex Jef XIV. &c. Et n. 19. quòd undique contra eum sacrilegia clament, & n. 20. aliena sedis emptorem & invasorem,quae negari non possint,fuisse, neque mirum videri debere, ut perditus homo addiderit ad schisma haeresin quoque—lupus gregem invadens,fur & latro,non per ostium, sed aliunde in ovile ovium conscendens, pseudoepiscopus—ac denique Antichristus.
units.tr: Baronius (n. 9) calls this a great and horrible storm in the Roman Church, stirred up by a raging heretical woman, procured by an ambitious deacon, and carried through impiously enough by Belisarius, etc. (n. 12). From Liberatus the deacon in his Breviarium (chap. 22) he relates how Vigilius was so ordained and compelled by Belisarius, who was to fulfil his promise which the Augusta had promised, to pay him the two hundred pounds of gold promised, out of fear of the Romans and with avarice as his advocate, he was unwilling to keep his pledges.
