Of him he (n. 14) relates an impious letter, which yet he (n. 15) contends was not his, as also the blasphemies which he (n. 16) has, written in the name of Vigilius; of him, however, he says (n. 17): What could remain for a man of infatuated stool, except that he be trampled underfoot by all and cast onto the dunghill of heresies? For he contracted the stench of heretical depravity from the habit he formed with heretics. Behold into what unhappy abyss ambition has cast the man! To what madness and infamy has empty desire for glory driven him! Because of it he is compelled to suffer shipwreck even in the harbour itself, to be a stumbling block in the Rock, a rock of offence, and to be seen as unstable in the see and held faithless in the faith. Thus, plainly, by the sentence of the Lord he is judged to fall from the faith, who makes himself a slave of glory, the Lord himself saying (John 5): "How can you believe, who receive glory from one another?" And concerning one like him, John (3 John 9): Diotrephes, who loves to have the pre-eminence among them, does not receive us. And (n. 18) that already in the times of Boniface, that he might be substituted in the see while he was alive, he shamelessly attempted this against all ecclesiastical laws and custom, and so, plainly weighed down by the burden of his crimes, while he planned to rise upward, was sunk downward together with, and by means of, those who had superbly sought the principality in heaven, turning over in his mind the same plans as they: "I will ascend into heaven," etc. (Isaiah 14, etc.). And (n. 19) that on all sides sacrileges cry out against him, and (n. 20) that he was a purchaser and usurper of another's see, things which cannot be denied, and that it ought not to seem surprising that the lost man added heresy to schism as well: a wolf invading the flock, a thief and a robber, climbing into the sheepfold not by the door but from elsewhere, a pseudo-bishop, and finally Antichrist.

units.la: XIII. Subjungit: Superat ejusmodi scelus quodlibet id genus antea perpetratum: cedit huic Novati (Novatiani) impietas, pertinacia. Ursicinii, Laurentii praesumptio,ac denique aliorum omnium Schismaticorum Antistitum superbia, arrogantia atque facinorosa temeritas; siquidem nemo sicut iste,tanta impudentia in viventis Pontificis sedem in siliit, ut talibus perfidia praemissis 'anteambulonibus sacrilegiis eam occupârit, tantoque periculo ex pactis conventis cum haereticis obtinuerit; cùm ejusmodi improbo facto janua aperta videri potuisseт, per quam in Romanam Ecclesiam (proh scelus!) haereses cum haereticis se immitterent,atque cuncta Apostolica dogmata pessum darent. Nullum hactenus schisma extitit, ex quo in tantam ignominiam inducta sit ipsa Pontificis sacrosancta majestas, cùm datur laico homini, absque Concilio, ullóque Sacerdotum assensu damnare primae sedis Antistitem; víque pellere expoliatúmque sacerdotalibus indumentis procul ejicere in exilium, & restitutum licèt sententia Imperatoris,
units.tr: XIII. He goes on: Such a crime surpasses any of this kind committed before: the impiety and obstinacy of Novatus (Novatian) yield to this, the presumption of Ursicinus and Laurentius, and finally the pride, arrogance and criminal rashness of all the other schismatic prelates; for truly no one, like this man, with such impudence leapt into the see of a living Pope, so that, with treachery sent ahead as forerunners, with sacrileges, he seized it, and obtained it with such great peril through agreements made with heretics, since by such a wicked deed a door seemed to have been opened through which heresies, along with heretics, might insinuate themselves into the Roman Church (O the crime!) and overthrow all the apostolic doctrines. Hitherto no schism has arisen by which the sacrosanct majesty of the Pontiff himself has been brought into such dishonour, since it was given to a layman, without a council and without any assent of the priests, to condemn the bishop of the first see, to drive him out, and to cast him stripped of his priestly vestments far off into exile, and, although restored by the sentence of the Emperor, nevertheless to relegate him to an island and force him to die.

units.la: De schismatis hujus gravitate, ex eodem. peratoris, nihilominus in insulam relegare, morìque cogere: Et n. 21. spu-rium atque penitus illegitimum, qua tamen Pontificii muneris essent, exe-qui minimè præterm isse dicit, atque seqq. prolixè ex Epistolis ad va-rios ab eo datis ostendit.
units.tr: Concerning the gravity of this schism, from the same author: by the Emperor's sentence, nevertheless, to relegate him to an island and compel him to die. And (n. 21) he says that he has not at all omitted to carry out what was spurious and wholly illegitimate, though they were the duties of the papal office; and so on, at length, he shows this from the letters he sent to various people.

units.la: XIV. Sed & ad an. 539. n. 283. sequentem Silverii ad Vigi-lium epistolam inserit:
units.tr: XIV. But also at the year 539, n. 283, he inserts the following letter of Silverius to Vigilius:

units.la: Silverius Episcopus Vigilio.
units.tr: Silverius, Bishop, to Vigilius.

units.la: Multis te transgressionibus irretitum Sacerdotalis jam dudum novit genera-litas. Et quia cruentis humano sanguine manibus, decessoribus nostris per-vicaciâ tuâ subripiens, Leviticis præsumpseris excubare ministeriis, pleri-que noverunt fidelium. Nam quia contra jura Canonica, temporibus san-ctæ memoriæ Bonifacii Papæ, ipso vivente, Successor ejus designari conaba-ris, nisi tibi amplíssimi Senatus obviâsset justitia: tunc providentiâ pasto-rali ac Pontificali auctoritate, tua execranda jam debuerant auspicia de-truncari. Sed, dum parvum vulnus in te neglectum est, insanabile accre-vit apostema; quod nisi ferro altiùs abscindatur, fomentorum sentire non potest medicinam. Quippe qui nequissimi Spiritûs audacia, ambitionis phrenesim concipiens, in illius Apostolici medici, cui animas ligandi solven-díque collata & concessa potestas est, versaris contumeliam, novúmque sce-lus erroris in Apostolica sede rursus niteris inducere; & in morem Simonis, cujus discipulum te ostendis operibus, datâ pecunia méque repulso, qui, sa-vente Domino, tribus jam jugiter cmensis temporibus ei præsideo, tempora mea niteris invadere. Habeto ergò cum his, qui tibi consentiunt, pœna da-mnationis sententiam: Sublatúmque tibi nomen & munus ministerii sa-cerdotalis agnosce, sanctí Spiritûs judicio & Apostolicâ à nobis auctoritate damnatus. Sic enim decet fidem sanctorum Patrum in Ecclesia servari Ca-tholica; ut, quod habuit, amittat, qui improbabili temeritate, quod non ac-cepit, assumpserit. Data octavo Kalendas Julii, Principe Basilio, pro quo aliam lectionem Belisario Patricio habere, Baronius annotat. Qui & n. 4. ex epistola in vinculis nitentem Pontificiam potestatem ma-gnificis verbis extollit, utpote quâ ostensum sit orbi universo, illum, qui fastigium Apostolici throni ruiturus ascendit, séque pro Pontifice gerit, non referre Simonem Petrum, sed magum, neque Vicarium Christi esse, sed Antichristum. n. 9. commemorat, quomodo auctis adversariorum odiis, arctiori Silverius custodiæ traditus, ac denique consumi inediâ coactus fue-rit; Sed id quidem sensim, non statim violenterque. ad an. 540, autem n. 2. mortem ejus martyrium vocat.
units.tr: Long ago the general body of priests came to know that you are entangled in many transgressions. Since you snatched the hands of our predecessors, bloody with human blood, out of their obstinacy, and presumed to keep watch in the Levitical ministries, most of the faithful know it. For while you tried, against the canon law, to have yourself designated as his successor during the lifetime of Pope Boniface of holy memory, unless the justice of the most illustrious Senate had stood in your way, your execrable beginnings should already have been cut off by pastoral foresight and papal authority. But because a small wound was neglected in you, an incurable abscess has grown; unless it is cut out deeper with the knife, it cannot feel the remedy of poultices. For you, who, conceiving through the audacity of the most wicked spirit a frenzy of ambition, insult that physician of the Apostolic see to whom the power of binding and loosing souls was given and granted, and you again strive to bring in a new crime of error into the Apostolic see; and, in the manner of Simon, whose disciple you show yourself to be in your deeds, having given money and having been rejected by me, who, with the Lord's favour, have presided for three full periods of time, you strive to invade my position. Therefore, with those who agree with you, have the sentence of damnation: and know that the name and office of the sacerdotal ministry has been taken from you, condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by our Apostolic authority. For thus it is fitting that the faith of the holy Fathers be kept in the Catholic Church: that he who with improper rashness has assumed what he did not receive should lose what he had. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Basilius; Baronius notes that for this others read Belisarius the patrician.

units.la: Silverii ad Vigilium epistola; unâ cum Baronii epiphonematibus.
units.tr: The letter of Silverius to Vigilius, together with Baronius's exclamations.

units.la: XV. Lepidus verò plane est, quòd n. 3. & 4. ex solis Ana-stasii verbis: Cessavit Episcopatus (Silverii) dies sex ; abdicationem Vigilii considerantis, minimè se legitimum fore dicendum Pontificem, quem tot crimina deturpâssent, cùm præter Simoniacam labem, redargue-rent ipsum conniventia cum hæreticis, paētis conventis conscripta juratá-que ipsorum defensio, Anthimi restitutio, Silverii insuper prædecessoris ex-pulsio ejusdémque necis cooperatio, atque demum, quòd post damnationem & anathema in ipsum à Silverio irrogatum sedisset nihilominus tanquam verus in Ecclesia Pontifex; atque electionem novam. Quæ tamen ab una parte ex verbis Anastasii inferri nequit; sunt enim primò Ana-stasii, secundò solius, cùm de abdicatione illa atque nova electione alia atque vetustiora documenta adesse deberent ; tertiò, cessatio, quæ pro more ab Anastasio additur, respicere potest tempus accepti nuncii, quo Vigilius, sublato æmulo, solus atque securus in sede sedere cœpit.
units.tr: XV. It is indeed a charming thing that he takes from the words of Anastasius alone, n. 3 and 4, that Vigilius, considering his own abdication, would say that he could not be called a lawful Pontiff, since so many crimes disgraced him: besides the stain of simony, they convicted him of connivance with heretics, agreements drawn up and sworn to in writing, the defence of them, the restoration of Anthimus, the expulsion of his predecessor Silverius and the cooperation in his death, and finally that, after the condemnation and anathema pronounced against him by Silverius, he nevertheless sat as the true Pontiff in the Church; and then a new election. Yet this cannot be inferred from the words of Anastasius, for first they are the words of Anastasius, second they are his alone, whereas other and older documents ought to exist for that abdication and new election; third, the "vacancy" (cessatio) which Anastasius adds as is his custom can refer to the time when news arrived that Vigilius, with his rival removed, began to sit alone and secure in the see.

units.la: XVI. Ab altera autem parte talem electionem novam Ba-ronius n. 4. seqq. non tantùm sine teste fingit, sed & prolixè, fictis pariter circumstantiis, describit, quæ & ipsa vitiosa sine dubio cen-seri debet; Quòd ipse id fecerit, semet abdicans tanquam repræsenta-turus in scena Comœdiam, non ex animo, sed ut quoquo modo eliceret de sua electione Cleri Romani consensum : inde mihi facilè persuadeo, inquit, dum non, ut par erat, pœnitere scelerum patratorum, omnem penitus con-ceptam de sede Pontificia spem abjecit, séque ea prorsus judicavit indi-gnum, reliquum vitæ tempus (ut ab eo exigebant gravissima criminum pondera) in lacrymis sibi transigendum indixit; sed consuetâ summi ho-noris prurigine exagitatus, ut eum consequi tutò posset, nec unquam inde ejici ob perpetrata delicta, hujusmodi sibi vafer viam aperiendam curavit; Cùm præsertim securus de Belisarii voluntate, cujus studiis ex Theodoræ Au-gustæ mandatis foret totius Cleri extorquendus assensus, haud dubiam ja-ceret aleam, cùm scirent eandem, quam vellet, faciem reddituram.
units.tr: XVI. On the other side, Baronius, n. 4 and following, not only invents such a new election without any witness, but also describes it at length with circumstances equally made up, which must undoubtedly also be judged faulty. That he himself did this, abdicating himself as if he were going to perform a comedy on the stage, not from sincere feeling but so that by some means he might draw from the Roman clergy their consent to his election: from this I am easily persuaded, he says, that since he did not, as was fitting, repent of the crimes he had committed, he abandoned every hope he had conceived of the papal see, and judged himself utterly unworthy of it, and resolved to spend the rest of his life in tears (as the very grave weight of his crimes demanded of him); but, driven by the usual itch for the highest honour, in order that he might attain it safely, and never be cast out from it because of his committed offences, he cunningly arranged for such a way to be opened for himself; especially since he was confident about Belisarius's will, from whose efforts, by the orders of the Empress Theodora, the consent of the whole clergy was to be extorted, so he was staking a sure throw, since they knew it would turn out whatever face he wished.

units.la: XVII. Verùm, ut dixi, de nova Electione utut tam vitio-sam fuisse dicant, nihil habetur, atque insuper etiam præsupponi debet, anathema à Silverio Vigilio denuntiatum nunquam ab illo revocatum esse ; & modis omnibus vitiosa hujus electio apparet, vitiosum regimen, tam malis artibus promoti, à Silverio, judice Baronio, jure meritóque excommunicati. Quem proin idem etiam ridiculè post mortem Silverii, quia nimirum alius tunc deerat, tan-quam legitimum & optimum Pontificem commendat, atque di-vinitûs vinitûs inspirato consilio n. 8. electionem tribuit, quæ nutu Dei facta n.11 divino consilio permissa & insigne miraculum sit, atque certum indicium, Ecclesiam Romanam à portis inferi semper illasam permanere.
units.tr: XVII. But, as I have said, although they call that new election so faulty, nothing is established by it, and moreover it must be presupposed that the anathema which Silverius pronounced against Vigilius was never revoked by him; and in every way this election appears faulty, and the rule of one so promoted by such wicked arts is faulty, excommunicated by Silverius, as Baronius judges, rightly and deservedly. Yet the same Baronius, after Silverius's death, because indeed there was no other at that time, ridiculously commends him as a lawful and excellent Pontiff, and attributes the election to a divinely inspired counsel (n. 8), which, made by the will of God (n. 11), was permitted by divine counsel, and is a remarkable miracle and a certain indication that the Roman Church remains forever unscathed by the gates of hell.

units.la: XVIII. Prout quoque ineptè ibi de mutatione Vigilii atque Pontificum in melius loqui incipit, Romanam Ecclesiam mirificâ quadam transformatione, quos iniquos acceperit, solere mox reddere sanctos, ut iidem fixè mox ipsi inhærentes sacræ petræ, super quam Christus suam fundavit Ecclesiam, instar polypi ipsius colorem accipiant, & quod majus sit, ejusdem quoque consequantur robur & firmitatem; Deum Ecclesiam suam haud dereliquisse, sed, cùm ipse eidem præsideret Antistes, mala cuncta obstantia convertere scivit in bonum, ipsósque lupos in gregem irruentes in optimos mutare pastores: ut omnes intelligerent, esse Deum, qui regat Israël; n. 11. permissam hæc ideò esse, ne quis contemnendum putet, si quem viderit, non meritis, sed nomine tantùm referentem Petrum sedere super Apostolicam sedem Pontificem; memor & umbra Petri à Deo præstitam esse immensam virtutem: nam etsi quid mane esse umbra prorsus appareat, corpus tamen ipsum sole illustratum ostendit: sicque ex Divina Petro facta promissione, qui umbra tantùm ejus corporis sua imbecillitate videri possent creati Pontifices, eosdem tamen non esse Apostolica virtutis expertes.
units.tr: XVIII. Likewise, he there foolishly begins to speak of the change of Vigilius and of the Popes for the better: that the Roman Church, by a certain wonderful transformation, is accustomed soon to make holy those whom it received as wicked, so that they, clinging firmly to the sacred rock upon which Christ founded his Church, take on its colour, like a polyp, and, what is greater, obtain also its strength and firmness; that God did not abandon his Church, but, since he himself presided over it as chief, knew how to turn all the evils that stood in the way to good, and to change the wolves rushing into the flock into the best shepherds, so that all might understand that there is a God who rules Israel; n. 11. this was permitted so that no one should think it contemptible if he sees a Pope sitting on the Apostolic see who represents Peter not by merits but only by name; mindful too that the shadow of Peter was given by God immense power: for although the shadow may appear to be nothing in the morning, the body itself, illumined by the sun, shows itself; and thus, from the divine promise made to Peter, the popes who are created, who can be seen by their weakness only as shadows of that body, are nevertheless not without apostolic power.

units.la: Et paulò post: Vigilius (quod magna admiratione dignum est) statim ubi legitimâ electione Petri thronum conscendit, Sacerdotale robur accepit, & Constantiam induit Pontificiam. Et n.13. sed jam audi grandi miraculo novâ hominem loquentem linguâ, ubi Pontifex coepit esse germanus: ut secundùm vetus proverbium illud: Num & Saul inter Prophetas? acciderit, momentóque temporis, ubi in sancta Ecclesia sede verè Vigilius constitit, novam formam acceperit, novas voces ediderit, & consona sanctis Patribus prophetârit, mutatus mirâ transformatione in virum alterum, nempe ex hoste in defensorem, ex persecutore in prædicatorem, ex blasphemo in confessorem, atque demum in omnibus ex perfido in fidelem.
units.tr: And a little after: Vigilius (which is greatly to be admired) immediately, when he mounted the throne of Peter by lawful election, received priestly strength and put on papal constancy. And n. 13. But now hear of a great miracle: a man speaking in a new tongue, where the Pontiff began to be genuine; so that, according to the old proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?", it came about, and in a moment of time, when Vigilius truly stood in the holy see of the Church, he took on a new form, uttered new voices, and prophesied in agreement with the holy Fathers, changed by a wonderful transformation into another man: from enemy to defender, from persecutor to preacher, from blasphemer to confessor, and finally in all things from faithless to faithful.

units.la: XIX. Miri certè de mira transformatione triumphi! In quibus igitur tam mirè transformatus fuit? Ambitiosus fuit antehac; non amplius se ita ostendere poterat postea, cùm jam optatis potitus, cum jam æmulus sublatus esset; sed tamen adhuc ostendit, quando Synodo Constantinopolitanæ interesse noluit, ne post Constantinopolitanum sedere deberet. Officium egit deinceps; Sedex Baronio jam jam audivimus, cum, cùm adhuc spurius, illegitimus, mus, Simon Magus, Antichristus, Pseudepiscopus, fur & latro esset, quae Pontificii muneris essent, exequi minimè praetermisisse; Orthodoxum se tandem ostendit; sed, quòd Heterodoxis adulatus est, à cupiditate Pontificatûs profectum esse, manifestè Baronius docet, quo igitur obtento, simulare amplius non habuit opus, imò si haeresin defendendam suscepisset, id eum apud Occidentales in calamitates conjicere potuisset, & jam cùm secunda vice adhuc eligendus esset, Romani, fingente Baronio n. 8. agnoverunt, eum esse hominem revera Catholicum, imò posthac non usque adeò se Constantem in doctrina exhibuit, dum Capitula tria modò approbavit, modò damnavit, iteratis vicibus. Ubi igitur mira illa transformatio? Annon potiùs mira est Baronii gloriatio? Mirè sunt ejus triumphi de nihilo? Mansit Vigilius, qualis erat, semel tantum electus erat, male, male & aemulus ejus Silverius, ut hi etiam duo vitium in se contineant.
units.tr: XIX. Truly wonderful, indeed, is this wonderful triumph of transformation! In what, then, was he so wonderfully changed? He was ambitious before; he could not show himself so afterwards, since he had now gained his desire and his rival had been removed; yet he still showed it when he refused to attend the Synod of Constantinople, lest he be obliged to sit after the Constantinopolitan. He afterwards performed his office; but we have already heard from Baronius that when he was still spurious, illegitimate, Simon Magus, Antichrist, false bishop, thief and robber, he did not at all omit to perform what belonged to the papal office; at last he showed himself orthodox; but that he flattered the heterodox arose, Baronius plainly teaches, from his desire for the papacy. What, then, once he had obtained it, did he have no further need to pretend? Indeed, if he had undertaken to defend heresy, he could have brought calamities upon it among the Westerners. And now, when he was to be elected a second time, the Romans, as Baronius feigns (n. 8), acknowledged that he was in truth a Catholic man; indeed afterwards he did not show himself so steadfast in doctrine, since he approved the three Chapters now, and now condemned them, again and again. Where, then, is that wonderful transformation? Is it not rather Baronius's boasting that is wonderful? Are his triumphs wonderful when they come from nothing? Vigilius remained what he was; he was elected only once, and badly, badly; and his rival Silverius likewise, so that these two also contain a fault in themselves.

units.la: XX. Octavum Schisma fuit &, Anastasio testante non minima contentio An. 686. inter Petrum Archipresbyterum, cui clerus, & Theodorum Presbyterum, cui exercitus adhaerebat; Et clerus quidem adunatus, inquit Anastasius apud Bar. ad an. 686. n. 2. ante fores Basilicae Constantinianae sustinebat, eo quòd qui missi fuerant de exercitu ad custodiendas regiae Basilicae valvas, observabant & neminem ingredi permittebant. Exercitus autem omnes in Basilica Sancti Stephani Protomartyris similiter fuerant adunati, & neque illi Clero consentiebant, neque Clerus exercitui acquiescebat, pro supradictis Presbyterorum personis. Sed dum missa ab utrisque partibus responsa irent diutiùs & redirent, & nihil proficerent ad concordiam, tandem clerus tertium elegit, Connonem, qui & exercitui placuit, gaudens ex lite duorum, quorum unus ab universo jam clero electus erat.
units.tr: XX. The Eighth schism was, as Anastasius testifies, no small contention in the year 686 between Peter the Archpriest, whom the clergy supported, and Theodore the Presbyter, to whom the army adhered. And indeed the clergy, gathered together, says Anastasius in Baronius at the year 686, no. 2, held out before the doors of the Constantinian basilica, because those who had been sent from the army to guard the doors of the royal basilica watched and allowed no one to enter. But all the army had likewise gathered in the basilica of Saint Stephen the First Martyr, and neither did they agree with the clergy, nor did the clergy acquiesce in the army, on account of the aforesaid presbyters. But while the replies sent from each side went back and forth for a long time and achieved nothing toward concord, at last the clergy chose a third, Conon, who also pleased the army, rejoicing in the dispute of two men, one of whom had already been chosen by the whole clergy.

units.la: XXI. Nonum Schisma fuit, mortuo Conone, inter Theodorum Presbyterum & Paschalem Archidiaconum, quem Platina semel Archipresbyterum vocat; Et hic quidem thesauri, ut idem Platina in Conone I. habet, Pontificii dispensator regnandi cupidus, cùm Conon post initum Pontificatum statim in valetudinem incidisset, Joannem Exarchum pecuniâ sollicitavit, ut ejus suffragiis post mortem Cononis Pontificatus sibi decerneretur. Accepit pecuniam Exarchus: quanquam nihil eorum, quae promiserat, deinceps praestiterit. Non erat certè alio praemio quàm frustratione dignus, homo avarus & imperandi cupidus, qui thesaurum Ecclesiae, quem mandato Cononis, tum in eleemosynas pauperum, tum in restitutionem templorum erogare debuerat, in largitionem effuderit,
units.tr: XXI. The Ninth schism came, after Conon's death, between Theodore the Presbyter and Paschal the Archdeacon, whom Platina once calls the Archpriest. Platina, in the life of Conon I., says that this man was a steward of the treasure, a Papist eager to rule, and that when Conon fell ill soon after taking up the pontificate, he tried to win over the exarch John with money, so that by his votes the pontificate might be awarded to himself after Conon's death. The exarch took the money, though he afterwards performed none of what he had promised. Certainly this avaricious man, eager to command, deserved no reward other than frustration: he poured out in largesse the treasure of the Church, which by Conon's command he ought to have spent both on alms for the poor and on the restoration of churches. Nothing could be more detestable than this, especially in an ecclesiastical man.

units.la: Nonum inter Theodorum & Paschalem; rit, quo nihil potest esse, in viro praesertim Ecclesiastico, detestabilius. Anastasius autem legati ab ipso aegrotante atque tandem mortuo Pontifice clero & monasteriis relicti, cum nondum persolutum esset, promissionem apud Bar. ad an. 687. n. 1. narrat, qui etiam de ipso Schismate apud eundem n. 2. ita loquitur: Ut fieri assolet, Romanus populus in duas partes divisus est; — Theodorus Archipresbyter cum populo, qui ei favebat, praveniens interiorem partem Patriarchii tenuit; Paschalis vero exteriorem partem ab Oratorio S. Silvestri & Basilica domus Julia, quae super campum respicit, occupavit. Cumque unus alteri locum non cederet, sed utrique immaniter perdurarent, ut unus alium superaret &c. & cum ibi, narrante plenius Platina in Sergio I. tanta altercatio & rixa esset, ut de pugna non ambigeretur, cum alter alteri cessurus non viderentur nisi vi & armis pulsus, principes civitatis, cleri, militiaeque Romanae, pergit idem, unum in locum secedentes, atque, quid maxime fieri oporteret ad seditionem tollendam, consultantes, neutri eorum, qui ob ambitionem tantos motus concitaverant, demandandum Pontificatum censuerunt, sed tertium rursus, Sergium, elegerunt, quem & e media turba humeris tollentes, primo in oraculum Caesarii martyris, mox in Lateranensem Episcopatum detulerunt, refractis vi foribus, repulsisque his, qui locum occupaverant, atque ita illa pars, quia validior erat, sunt verba Anastasii, praevaluit & ingressa est. Quare etiam Theodorus humiliavit se: Paschalem vero nullo modo cordis duritia id facere sinebat, donec coactus & confusus, volens, nolens suum Dominum & electum ingressus salutaret. Hic tamen clanculum, loquitur rursus Platina, Joannem Platinam Exarchum Ravennatum literis, nuntiis & pollicitationibus adeo concitavit, ut, quae antea pollicitus fuerat, largitione corruptus tandem praestaret, ut idem Joannes Romam confestim veniret, nullis praemissis nuntiis, quo negligentes & incautos opprimeret. Verum uti intellexit, Sergium, omnium consensu Pontificem declaratum, insta rétque, ut, quae Paschalis pollicitus fuerat, sibi praestarentur, adversante Sergio, quod tantam largitionem improbaret, donaria quaedam ex Basilica sustulit. Verum Paschalis tanti mali causa, magices accusatus & convictus, ut sortilegus Archidiaconatu privatur: in monasteriumque poenitentiae causa retruditur: ubi quinquennio post eadem semper pertinacia usus, moritur. Subjungit Baronius n. 5. plane apparuit, haud levem esse eam S. R. E. Apostolicaeque sedis persecutionem, quam a domesticis pati consuevit. Duo male electi fuerunt, tertius vi obtinuit, cui cessit unus, alter non valde, sed se ad vitæ usque finem Pontificem esse credidit, nec certò constat de iis, quæ ita oppressis post imputari solent.
units.tr: The ninth schism between Theodore and Paschal. Anastasius, however, in Baronius at the year 687, no. 1, relates the promise made to the envoys left by the Pontiff himself, while he was sick and at last dead, to the clergy and the monasteries, when it had not yet been paid. Concerning the schism itself, he speaks thus in the same place, no. 2: As is usually the case, the Roman people was divided into two parties; Theodore the Archpriest, going ahead with the people who favoured him, held the inner part of the Patriarchium; but Paschal occupied the outer part from the oratory of Saint Silvester and the basilica of the Julian house, which looks onto the Field. And since neither would yield the place to the other, but both persisted fiercely, so that each might overcome the other, etc. And since there, as Platina relates more fully in the life of Sergius I, there was such altercation and brawling that a fight was not in doubt, since neither seemed about to yield to the other except by force and arms, the princes of the city, of the clergy and of the Roman militia, the same writer continues, withdrawing to one place and considering what ought chiefly to be done to put an end to the sedition, judged that the pontificate should not be entrusted to either of those who by ambition had stirred up such great commotions, but they chose a third, Sergius, again, whom lifting him on their shoulders out of the middle of the crowd, they carried first to the oratory of the martyr Caesarius and soon after to the Lateran bishopric, the doors being broken open by force and those who occupied the place being driven out, and so that party prevailed, because it was the stronger, and entered, these are Anastasius's words. Therefore Theodore also humbled himself; but Paschal, with the hardness of his heart, would not allow him to do so, until, compelled and confounded, he entered, willing or unwilling, and saluted his Lord and elect. Yet he secretly, Platina writes again, stirred up the exarch John of Ravenna by letters, messengers and promises, so that John, corrupted by largesse, at last made good what Paschal had earlier promised, and the same John came straight to Rome without sending any messengers ahead, so that he might crush the careless and unwary. But when he understood that Sergius had been declared pontiff by the consent of all, he urged that what Paschal had promised should be given to him; and when Sergius opposed this, since he disapproved of such great largesse, he took certain gifts from the basilica. But Paschal, accused and convicted of magic as a sorcerer, was deprived of the archdeaconate, and was thrust into a monastery for the sake of repentance, where, after five years, still persisting in the same obstinacy, he died. Baronius adds at no. 5: It was plainly evident that the persecution which the Holy Roman Church and the apostolic see is accustomed to suffer from its own members is no light one. Two were badly chosen, a third prevailed by force; one gave way, the other not much, but believed himself pontiff until the end of his life, nor is it certain what is usually imputed afterwards to those so oppressed.

units.la: XXII. Decimum Schisma fuit inter Paulum I. Stephani II. prædecessoris Fratrem, Diaconum, & Theophylactum Archidiaconum; Cùm enim Stephanus ad extremum pertingeret vitæ, inquit Anastasius in Paulo: illicò & populus hujus Romanæ Urbis divisus est, & alii Theophylactum Archidiaconum tenentes, in ejus domo congregati residebant: Alii verò beatissimo concordabant Paulo Diacono, plurima pars judicum & populi cum eo tenentes, quàm cum prædicto Theophylacto Archidiacono. Et paulò post: populi congregatio, quæ cum Paulo tenebat, quoniam validior & fortior erat, eum in Pontificatûs culmen elegerunt. Post hæc hi, qui cum præfato Archidiacono congregati erant, dispersi sunt, atque ita Theophylactus post longam contentionem, inquit Platina in Paulo I. explosus, coactus, ut ait Onuphrius in Indice, abdicavit. Quis non & hic plebis vim prævaluisse videt?
units.tr: XXII. The Tenth schism was between Paul I, brother of his predecessor Stephen II, a deacon, and Theophylact the Archdeacon. For when Stephen drew near the end of his life, says Anastasius in the life of Paul, at once the people of this Roman city was divided, and some, holding Theophylact the Archdeacon, gathered and remained in his house. Others, however, agreed with the most blessed Paul the Deacon, the greater part of the judges and of the people holding with him rather than with the aforesaid Theophylact the Archdeacon. And a little later: the assembly of the people, which held with Paul, since it was the more powerful and the stronger, chose him to the height of the pontificate. After this, those who had gathered with the aforesaid Archdeacon were dispersed; and so Theophylact, after a long contention, says Platina in the life of Paul I, driven out, forced, as Onuphrius says in the Index, abdicated. Who does not see here too that the force of the common people prevailed?

units.la: XXIII. Undecimum Schisma fuit A. Ch. 767. Indice Onuphrio in Indice, maximè turbulentum, inter Stephanum IV. nonnullis III. Constantinum, & Philippum. Cùm enim Paulus Papa in agritudine positus nondum adhuc Spiritum exhalaret; inquit Anastasius in Stephano, illico Toto quidam Dux, Nepesina civitatis dudum habitator cum suis Germanis, Constantino Passino & Paschale (Desiderii Regis Longobardorum juxta Platinam, voto satisfacturus, qui eum hortabatur, ut Constantinum fratrem vi etiam, quando largitione & ambitione fieri non possit, Pontificem deligat;) aggregantes tam ex eadem Nepesina civitate quàm ex aliis Tuscia civitatibus multitudinem exercitus atque catervam rusticorum—in domo ante dicti Totonis armati adsistentes legere ibidem subitò Constantinum fratrem ejusdem Totonis laicum existentem; favenstibus, ut Platina ait, quibusdam amicis largitione & pollicitationibus corruptis. Constantinum autem à Gregorio Prænestino Episcopo coacto sacris initiatum, sicque universum populum sibi Sacramentum præbere fecit, inquit Anastasius, & adveniente die Dominico, rursus cum multitudine armatorum exercituum in Basilicam B. Petri properans, Pontifex ab eodem—& aliis duobus Episcopis—consecratus est, & per anni spatium & mensem unum sedem Apostolicam invasam detinuit;—fecit ordinationem Presbyterorum & Diaconorum, Presbyteros octo, Diaconos quatuor ordinans, sed & Episcopos in ipsius anni circulo & unius mensis fecit per diversa loca numero octo.
units.tr: XXIII. The Eleventh schism was in the year of Christ 767, according to Onuphrius in his Index, most turbulent, between Stephen IV, called by some III, Constantine and Philip. For when Pope Paul, lying sick, was not yet breathing his last, says Anastasius in the life of Stephen, at once a certain Toto, a leader, a former resident of the city of Nepi, with his Germans, Constantine Passinus and Paschal (to satisfy the vow of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, according to Platina, who urged him to choose Constantine his brother as pontiff, even by force, when it could not be done by largesse and ambition), gathering a multitude of army and a band of peasants both from the same city of Nepi and from other cities of Tuscany, standing armed before the house of the said Toto, suddenly chose there Constantine, brother of the same Toto, being a layman, with some friends favouring him, as Platina says, corrupted by largesse and promises. Constantine, however, was initiated into the sacred orders by Gregory, bishop of Praeneste, who was compelled to do so, and thus he made the whole people give him the sacrament, says Anastasius, and on the coming of the Lord's day, hastening again with a multitude of armed troops into the basilica of Saint Peter, he was consecrated pontiff by the same man and two other bishops, and for the space of a year and one month he held the apostolic see which he had seized; he made ordinations of presbyters and deacons, ordaining eight presbyters and four deacons, and he also made bishops, in the course of that same year and one month, to the number of eight in various places.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: XXIV. Idem Anastasius prolixè post exponit, quomodo Christophorus Primicerius & Consiliarius ejúsque filius Sergius tunc Sacellarius à Constantino sub simulatione, se Monachicum habitum in Monasterio Salvatoris suscepturos esse, dimissi & impetrato à Desiderio (qui animum mutâsse dici debet,) auxilio in urbem regressi, Totonem quidem in pugna interfecerint, Passino fratre Constantini alio in Patriarchium ad Constantinum fugiente; quomodo item paulò post Philippus Presbyter curante Waldiperto Presbytero electus, & cum gaudio vocibus acclamantibus exceptus, aliquandiu etiam pro Pontifice habitus ab eodem Christophoro Primicerio, qui jure jurando omnibus Romanis affirmabat, se Româ minimè egressurum, quousque Philippus Presbyter de Lateranensi non fuisset expulsus, Patriarchio expulsus per scalam, quæ ducit ad balneum descendens, cum magna reverentia ad suum monasterium reversus, alia verò die, procurante eodem Christophoro, Stephanus electus sit, quo electo, quidam comprehendentes Theodorum Episcopum & Vicedominum Constantini (quod dici impium sit) eruerint oculos, & linguam ei crudeliter amputârint, sed & Passini similiter oculos eruere nisi sint, & tantam impietatem in eos monstraverint, ut nec in proprias domos eos deportari permiserint, ut illis cura à suis hominibus exhiberi deberet; sed ablatis omnibus eorum rebus atque familiis, atque possessionibus, unum ex eis, Theodorum scilicet Episcopum in Monasterium Clivi, Scauri retrudi fecerint, ubi fame & siti cremans, clamánsque aquam ita exhalârit spiritum; Passinum verò in monasterium S. Sylvestri deduxerint; Constantinum ipsum verò in medium deductum, magna pondera in ejus adhibentes pedibus, in sella muliebri super equum sedere fecerint, & in monasterium deportari curârint; qui porrò ante unam diem ordinationis Stephani degradatus sit, & cui quidam postea oculos eruerint, eúmque cæcum in platea reliquerint, qui & Gracili Tribuno fautori Constantini oculos eruerint & linguam abstulerint, item dicto Waldiperto; In Constantinum autem in Synodo collecta supplicem atque dicentem, vim se in populo pertulisse, atque per brachium populi fuisse electum, nihil durius statutum fuisse, sed alia die respondentem, nihil novi se fecisse, quia & Sergius Archiepiscopus Ravennatium Laicus existens effectus sit, & Stephanus Neapolitana civitatis & ipse Laicus repente Episcopus consecratus sit, iratos Sacerdotes alapis ejus cervicem cadere facientes, eum extra eandem Ecclesiam ejecisse; Tunc combustis omnibus ejus actionum gestis, simul & consilium illud, quod in scriptis de ejus quasi confirmatione editum fuerit, combussisse in medio Presbyterii ipsius Ecclesia; Hoc facto Papam se in terram cum universis Sacerdotibus & populo Romano projecisse, clamantésque kyrie eleyson, cum ingenii fletu peccâsse se omnes confessos esse, pro eo, quòd de manibus ipsius Constantini communionem suscepissent, sícque ex hoc omnibus indictam esse pœnitentiam; Tunc allatis sacratissimis Canonibus, eísque liquido perscrutatis, prolatam esse sententiam ab eodem Sacerdotali Concilio sub Anathematis interdicto, ne ullus unquam præsumat laicorum, neque ex alio ordine, nisi per distinctos gradus ascendens, Diaconus vel Presbyter Cardinalis factus fuerit, ad Sacri Pontificatûs honorem possit promoveri.
units.tr: XXIV. Anastasius then relates at length how Christopher, the Primicerius and counsellor, and his son Sergius, at that time Sacellarius, were dismissed by Constantine under the pretence that they would take the monastic habit in the monastery of the Saviour. Having obtained help from Desiderius (who must be said to have changed his mind), they returned to the city, and in the fighting they killed Totho, while Passinus, Constantine's brother, fled to Constantine in the Patriarchium. He also relates how, shortly afterwards, Philip the presbyter was elected through the efforts of Waldipert the presbyter and was received with joy and acclamations, and for some time was even regarded as pope by the same Christopher the Primicerius. Christopher had sworn an oath to all the Romans that he would not leave Rome at all until Philip the presbyter had been expelled from the Lateran Patriarchium. Philip was expelled by the staircase that leads down to the bath, and returned with great reverence to his own monastery. On the following day, through the efforts of the same Christopher, Stephen was elected. After his election, some men seized Theodore the bishop and the vice-dominus of Constantine (a thing impious to say), tore out their eyes, and cruelly cut out his tongue. They did the same to Passinus, tearing out his eyes, and they showed such impiety towards them that they did not allow them to be taken to their own houses, where their own people ought to have cared for them. Instead, after all their goods, households and possessions had been taken away, they had one of them, namely Bishop Theodore, shut up in the monastery of Clivus Scauri, where, burning with hunger and thirst and crying out for water, he breathed his last; they took Passinus to the monastery of St Sylvester. Constantine himself they led into the middle of the crowd, and, fastening heavy weights to his feet, they made him sit on a woman's saddle on a horse, and they had him carried off to a monastery. He was degraded one day before Stephen's ordination. Some men later tore out his eyes and left him blind in the street. They also tore out the eyes and cut out the tongue of Gracilis the tribune, a supporter of Constantine, and likewise of the aforesaid Waldipert. When Constantine, in a gathered synod, pleaded as a suppliant and said that he had suffered violence from the people and had been elected through the arm of the people, nothing harsher was decreed against him. But on the next day he replied that he had done nothing new, since Sergius, Archbishop of the Ravennates, had been a layman and had been made so, and Stephen, of the city of Naples, was himself a layman and was suddenly consecrated bishop. The angry priests, making him fall by blows to the neck, had thrown him out of that same church. Then, after all the records of his acts had been burned, the counsel that had been published in writing concerning his so-called confirmation was also burned in the middle of the presbytery of that church. After this was done, the Pope cast himself to the ground with all the priests and the Roman people, crying kyrie eleison, and all confessed with weeping of heart that they had sinned in receiving communion from the hands of Constantine; and so repentance was imposed on all for this. Then the most sacred canons were brought forward and carefully examined, and the sentence was pronounced by the same priestly council under the interdict of anathema: that no layman, nor anyone from another order unless he had risen through the distinct grades and become a deacon or a cardinal presbyter, should ever presume to be promoted to the honour of the sacred pontificate.

units.la: XXV. In eodem quoque Concilio promulgatum esse, tradit: Ut qui Episcopi ex Presbyteris sive Diaconibus ab eo ordinati fuerant, in pristinum honoris sui gradum reverterentur, & si placibile fuisset omni populo civitatis sua, denuò facto decreto electionis more solito, cum clero & plebe ad Apostolicam venissent sedem &c. Presbyteri verò illi & Diacones simili modo in illum, in quo existebant, habitum reverterentur &c. ut sic omnia, quæ Constantinus egit, iterari debuerint præter Baptisma ac sanctum Chrisma. Monet tamen de Episcopis Baronius, non iterum consecratos fuisse, sed accepisse tantùm, more majorum, benedictionis mysterium, ritus illos solennes adhiberi solitos in reconciliatione schismatici vel hæretici. Sed tanquam de reordinatione loquitur Anastasius, neque prima ordinatio legitima esse potuit ab Antichristo & Pseudepiscopo facta, neque etiam ab eo baptisma ac Chrisma bene administrari potuerunt. Quid autem judicandum erit de illis, quos ordinati à Constantino ordinârunt, baptizârunt, de aliis, quæ egerunt? Cæterùm certè mala fuit electio Constantini, sed anno integro & amplius alius Papa non fuit, subsecutam autem Stephani Electionem quoque haud nævis suis caruisse, ex dictis patet & rebus violenter gestis, & quæ contra Constantinum gesta atque decreta sunt, etiam aliis profectò haud parùm nocent. Omnia verò nævum in electione duorum multiplicem ostendunt.
units.tr: XXV. He also reports that in the same council it was proclaimed: that those who had been ordained bishops by him from among the presbyters or deacons should return to their former rank of honour; and, if it pleased all the people of their city, a fresh decree of election should be made in the usual way, and they should come with clergy and people to the Apostolic See, etc. Those presbyters and deacons should likewise return to the status in which they had been, etc. So that everything Constantine had done had to be repeated, except baptism and the holy chrism. Baronius, however, remarks that the bishops were not consecrated again, but received only, after the manner of their elders, the mystery of blessing, the solemn rites customarily used in the reconciliation of a schismatic or heretic. But Anastasius speaks as of a re-ordination. Indeed, a first ordination performed by Antichrist and a pseudo-bishop could not be lawful, nor could baptism and chrism be properly administered by him. What, however, must be judged concerning those whom Constantine ordained and baptized, and concerning his other acts? Moreover, Constantine's election was certainly faulty, but no other pope was appointed for a full year and more. It is clear from what has been said that the subsequent election of Stephen also was not free of its own faults, and the violent deeds done and the decrees made against Constantine certainly also did no small harm to others. Indeed, all these things show that the fault in the election of the two was manifold.

units.la: XXVI. Duodecimum Schisma fuit A. Ch. 824. Onuphr. 827. inter Eugenium II. & Zosimum, Onuphrio Zinzinum, duo enim, inquit Anastasius, per contentionem populi electi fuerunt, Eugenius tamen, vincente nobilium parte, subrogatus est, alter verò non longè post, ut Onuphrius in Indice ait, abdicavit. Ejusmodi autem Schisma, cujus sic breviter auctor meminit, haud levis fuisse momenti, significant, judicio, Baronii ad a. 824. n. 12. ea, quæ post electum probatúmque Eugenium remansisse, subjiciuntur, nimirum rum ob Romanorum implacabiles dissensiones ab eo, quibus cum universa urbs flagraret, opus fuisse Ludovico Imperatori, ad has componendas mittere Lotharium filium suum. Etenim Pontifex ab altera parte populi postulatus, ab altera haud adeo libenter acceptus erat, ut se ipsi in omnibus crederet, ut qui à parte adversariorum stare sibi persuaderet. Ad has igitur sedandas haud levioris momenti discordias, Lotharius, ut dictum, mittitur à Ludovico in Urbem &c.
units.tr: XXVI. The twelfth schism was in A.D. 824 (Onuphrius, 827) between Eugenius II and Zosimus (Onuphrius Zinzinus), for, as Anastasius says, two were elected through the contention of the people, but Eugenius was put in place by the party of the nobles, while the other not long afterwards, as Onuphrius says in his Index, resigned. That this schism, which the author mentions so briefly, was of no small importance is shown, in the judgement of Baronius (A.D. 824, n. 12), by what is added after Eugenius had been elected and approved, namely that because of the implacable dissensions of the Romans, by which the whole city was aflame, the Emperor Louis had to send his son Lothair to settle them. For the pontiff was demanded by one part of the people and was not very willingly accepted by the other, so that he could not trust himself in everything, since he was persuaded that he stood on the side of his opponents. Therefore, to quell these discords, which were of no small importance, Lothair, as has been said, was sent by Louis into the City, etc.

units.la: XXVII. Decimum tertium schisma fuit A. Chr. 855. inter Benedictum III. & Anastasium;
units.tr: XXVII. The thirteenth schism took place in A.D. 855, between Benedict III and Anastasius.

units.la: Hic enim, ut Baronius ad an. 855. n. 36. ait atque n. seqq. partim ex Anastasio prolixius ostendit, factione iuniorum, qui usi sunt ad flagitium operâ Legatorum Imperatoris intrusus fuit olim Presbyter tituli S. Marcelli excommunicatus; verum resistente magnâ constantiâ Clero Romano, populóquo Anastasio Schismatico renitente, ejectus, atque in sedem suam iterum Benedictus restitutus fuit. Atque illud etiam Schisma non leve fuit, dum Anastasio Anti-Papæ Clerus (cujus pars quoque ante ei se adjunxerat) atque Romana plebs ac proceres obviârunt pariter n. 41. atque ille in solio resedit, contra Benedictus Pontificalibus spoliatus, multisque injuriis verberibusque repletus fuit, ut quidem Anastasius ibi narrat; Sed tandem ipsi etiam Imperatoris Legati Benedictum suscepere.
units.tr: For here, as Baronius says at the year 855, n. 36, and in the following numbers, and as he shows at greater length, partly from Anastasius, Anastasius, once a priest of the title of St Marcellus and excommunicated, was thrust in by a faction of the younger men, who used the services of the Emperor's legates for this outrage. But, with the Roman clergy and people stoutly resisting and the schismatic Anastasius refusing to yield, he was ejected, and Benedict was restored to his see. That schism was no small one either, since the clergy of the anti-pope Anastasius (part of whom had earlier joined him) and the Roman commons and nobles alike opposed him, as at n. 41. Anastasius then sat on the throne, while Benedict was stripped of his pontifical vestments and filled with many insults and blows, as Anastasius himself relates there. In the end, however, even the Emperor's legates received Benedict.

units.la: XXVIII. Decimum quartum Schisma An. Ch. 891. inter Formosum & Sergium.
units.tr: XXVIII. The fourteenth schism, in A.D. 891, between Formosus and Sergius.

units.la: Ortum illud est, mortuo Stephano VI. atque reprehendit Baronius ad an. 891. n. 1. eos, qui Formosum ante hunc Stephanum collocant, atque etiam Stephano huic absurdè nimis facinus in cadavere Formosi patratum tribuunt, nisi intelligant de Stephano illo nequissimo septimo, dicto sexto. Prout etiam ibi alios, qui Pontifices imaginarios illi tempori tribuant Agapetum atque Basilium, redarguit. De Formoso diversimodè judicant Authores Pontificii, atque de ejus electione. Baronio quidem laudatissimus est, sed Platina longè alium perhibet, narrat enim in vita ejus, quòd aliquando Joannis Pontificis severitatem veritus, Episcopatum suum deserens, in Gallias aufugerit. Verùm cùm revocatus redire abnueret, anathemate notatus Romam veniens omni Ecclesiastica dignitate privatus, profana indumenta simul cum moribus assumpserit. Cujus nonnulli hanc causam arbitrentur, quòd ejus conjurationis conscius & auctor fuerit, quâ Joannes captus & in vincula conjectus sit; coutumelià motum Formosum ab urbe discedentem jurejurando affirmâsse, se nunquam postea vel Romam, vel ad Episcopatum rediturum. At verò Martinum Joannis successorem hominem nem postea juramento solutum in patriam & pristinam dignitatem restituisse, unde ad Pontificatum non ita multò post largitione potius, quàm virtute, contradicentibus quibusdam, assumptus fuerit. Idem in Formoso observat: Nescio quo facto accidisse dicam, ut unà cum industria Imperatorum, simul etiam Pontificum virtus & integritas defecerit: quae quidem tempora infelicissima esse arbitror, cùm authoritate Platonis tales soleant esse reliqui cives, quales sunt in Republica Principes. Assumptionis ejus diem ut & obitus praedecessoris, & tempus sedis vacantis tutò affirmari non posse, auctor est Baronius l. c. n. 3. Caeterum tumultuariam ejus fuisse electionem, elevante se contra eum Sergio Diacono, ex Luitprando ostendit, quem Romanorum pars quaedam sibi elegerit, sed quem ea, quae Formosi partibus favebat pure, cum non mediocri tumultu & injuria ab altari expulerit, & Formosum Papam constituerit. Observat Onuphrius annot. ad Form. Formosum primum omnium Romanorum Pontificum ex aliena dioecesis Episcopo Romanum Pontificem esse factum, cùm ante ipsum nonnisi ex Presbytero, vel Diacono Cardinalibus factus fuisset Romae Papa. Erat enim antehac Portuensis Episcopus.
units.tr: It arose on the death of Stephen VI. Baronius, at the year 891, n. 1, rebukes those who place Formosus before this Stephen, and who also absurdly attribute to Stephen the outrage committed on the corpse of Formosus, unless they understand the most wicked Stephen, the seventh of that name, who is called the sixth. In the same place he also refutes others who assign to that time the imaginary popes Agapetus and Basil. Papist authors judge Formosus and his election in different ways. Baronius indeed praises him highly, but Platina reports quite otherwise, for he says in his life that, fearing the severity of Pope John, he deserted his bishopric and fled to Gaul. But when he refused to return when recalled, he was marked with anathema, came to Rome, was deprived of all ecclesiastical dignity, and took up secular clothing along with a secular manner of life. Some think the cause of this was that he had been aware of and an author of the conspiracy by which John was seized and thrown into chains, and that Formosus, moved by the insult, swore an oath as he left the city that he would never return to Rome or to his bishopric. But Martin, John's successor, absolved him from the oath and restored him to his homeland and former dignity, from which he was raised to the papacy not long afterwards, more by largesse than by virtue, though some objected. Platina makes the same observation about Formosus: "I know not by what chance it came about that together with the diligence of the emperors the virtue and integrity of the popes also failed; these times I judge most unhappy, since, on Plato's authority, such are usually the remaining citizens as the princes are in the commonwealth." Baronius, in the place cited, n. 3, states that the day of Formosus' accession, the day of his predecessor's death, and the length of the vacancy of the see cannot be affirmed with certainty. Moreover, that his election was a tumultuous one, with Sergius the deacon standing against him, Luitprand shows: "whom a certain part of the Romans had chosen for themselves, but whom the party that wholly favoured Formosus drove from the altar with no small tumult and violence, and then set up Formosus as pope." Onuphrius observes in his note on Formosus that Formosus was the first of all the Roman popes to be made Roman pontiff from the bishop of another diocese, since before him the popes had been made by the cardinals only from presbyters or deacons of Rome. For he had previously been bishop of Porto.

units.la: XXIX. Quae cum cadavere defuncti acciderint ad an. 897. n. 2.
units.tr: XXIX. What happened to the dead man's corpse, at the year 897, n. 2.

units.la: ita enarrat: Hoc anno contigere illa nefanda, quae Luitprandus (l. 1. c. 8.) & alii recensent, sed male: retribuunt Sergio, quae Stephano VII. Synodalia adscribunt Acta, quibus fides major jure sit adhibenda. Lapsum verò memoria Luitprandum horum auctorem oportuit, ut adscripserit Sergio Papae, quod factum per Stephanum liquet. Sed audiamus, quae narrat ipse Luitprandus: Formoso, inquit, defuncto atque Arnulpho in propria reverso, is qui post mortem Formosi Papa constitutus est, expellitur, Sergiúsque Papa per Adelbertum constituitur. Quo constituto, ut impius doctrinarúmque Sanctarum inscius, Formosum è sepulchro extrahere, atque in sedem Romani Pontificatûs, Sacerdotalibus indumentis indutum collocare praecepit. Cui & ait: Cùm Portuensis esses Episcopus, cur ambitionis Spiritu Romanam universalem sedem usurpâsti? His expletis, sacratis mox exutum vestimentis, digitisque tribus abscissis: quibus benedicere moris est, in Tyberim jactare praecepit, cunctósque, quos ipse ordinaverat, gradu proprio depositos iterum ordinavit. Ista quidem Onuphrius annotat ad Form. fabula magis quàm vero similia esse contendit, atque id ex scriptorum in hoc diversitate atque repugnantia facilè liquere arbitratur. Non autem tam facile Luitprando digno illius temporis & aliis scriptoribus quaedam relationum diversitas fidem adimere
units.tr: Baronius recounts it thus: "In this year those abominable things occurred which Luitprand (book 1, ch. 8) and others record, but wrongly: they attribute to Sergius what the Synodal Acts ascribe to Stephen VII, and to these Acts greater faith ought rightly to be given. But Luitprand, as an author, must have slipped in memory, so that he ascribed to Pope Sergius what is clear to have been done by Stephen." But let us hear what Luitprand himself relates: "Formosus, he says, having died, and Arnulf having returned to his own land, he who was made pope after the death of Formosus is expelled, and Pope Sergius is set up through Adalbert." When he had been installed, being impious and ignorant of the holy doctrines, he ordered Formosus to be dragged out of his tomb and placed on the throne of the Roman pontificate, clothed in priestly vestments. And he said to him: "When you were bishop of Porto, why did you usurp the universal Roman see out of a spirit of ambition?" When this was done, the dead man was stripped of the consecrated vestments, three fingers were cut off, those with which it is customary to bless, and he ordered them thrown into the Tiber, and all whom he himself had ordained were deposed from their rank and ordained again. Onuphrius, in his note on Formosus, maintains that these things are "more like a fable than the truth," and he thinks this can easily be seen from the diversity and contradiction of the writers on the matter. Yet this diversity of accounts cannot so easily take away the credit of Luitprand, who was worthy of that time, and of other writers.

units.la: Qua cum cadavere defuncti acciderint. potest; De eo, quòd nonnulli Sergio tribuunt factum, jam ex parte respondit Baronius & porrò respondet n. 3. Luitprandum Sergio ad-scribere, quòd ipse fuerit ad illud perpetrandum antesignanus & auctor. Caterùm graviorem culpam Stephani Papæ fuisse &c. Idem etiam non malè ex Synodis ibidem factum in dubium vocantes refutari posse arguit, quia nimirum Stephanus nefarium scelus, impium & detestan-dum Synodo collecta probaverit, quæ rescissa postea ignique tradita fuerit à Joanne IX. cùm ista omnia per Stephanum Papam Synodicè acta, Joan-nes postea convocato ad hæc Concilio (ut testentur ipsa Acta ejusdem Ro-mani Concilii) penitùs aboleverit, ex quibus, ita pergit, erroris arguuntur, qui ista de Formoso negant & confiƈta putant.
units.tr: What happened to the dead man's corpse. Baronius has already answered in part the claim that some attribute the deed to Sergius, and he goes on to answer it at n. 3: Luitprand ascribes to Sergius that he was the leader and author of carrying out that deed. "But the greater guilt was that of Pope Stephen, etc." The same author also argues, not badly, that those who call this into doubt, and think it fabricated, can be refuted from the synods in the same place. For Stephen, in a synod gathered for the purpose, approved the "nefarious crime, impious and to be detested," which was afterwards rescinded, burned, and handed over to the fire by John IX. Since all these things were done synodically by Pope Stephen, John afterwards, having called a council for this purpose (as the Acts of that same Roman council attest), utterly abolished them. Those who deny these things about Formosus and think them fabricated, he says, are convicted of error by these facts.

units.la: XXX. Factum quoque Platina in Stephano VI. confirmat, atque ex Martino (Polono) recenset, ejusque causam in maximo odio Stephani erga Formosum; odii causam in eo ostendit, quòd tunc jam eò devenissent Ecclesiastici, ut non coacti, ut antea, sed sponte largitionibus Pontificum munus obirent, atque Formosus Stephano antea impedimento fuisset, quò minùs optata sede potiretur; Imò inde derivat consuetudinem pessimam, quæ postea ferè semper servata fit, ut acta priorum Pontificum sequentes aut infringerent, aut omninò tollerent. Quod hactenus certè ab optimis illis Pontificibus, quorum vitam conscripsimus, inquit, alienum fuit. Sic quoque quò minùs Paulus II. Formosi nomen obtinuerit, ei tribuit, quòd eum deterruere Cardinales quidam historia non ignari, ne post mortem id acciderët, quod olim Formoso. Quale autem illud factum fuerit, facilè colligitur tanta rabie, ut Platina loquitur, in cadaver sævientis, & jam Baronius culpam ibi majorem atque minorem agnovit, atque non parvam fuisse ex indigitato à Baronio Concilio sub Joanne IX. habito constat; Sed & Baronius porrò n. 2. Furore percitus homo, non quod jure liceret, sed, quod ex-æstuans rabies suasit, implevit: addit tamen: non fuit error in fide, sed violenta tyrannis in facto. Sufficit, quis enim monstro usque adeò sævienti infallibilitatem in fide tribuat? Sed & abrogavit Stepha-nus, teste etiam Platina, in genere decreta Formosi, res gestas ejus rescidit, atque doctrinarum sanctarum nescium damnavit, reclamantibus, (ut Sigebertus ait) qui aderant. Atque quascunque hic partes amplectantur Pontificii, hærent; Aut enim Formosus illegitimus fuit, atque erronea Concilii sub Joanne IX. constitutio; Aut Sergius illegitimus fuit, Stephanus & Concilium sub Stephano pessimè ab-errā-
units.tr: XXX. Platina also confirms the deed in the life of Stephen VI, and recounts it from Martin the Pole. He gives the cause of it as Stephen's greatest hatred of Formosus, and he shows the cause of the hatred to be that the clergy had by then reached the point of undertaking church offices by bribery, not, as before, under compulsion but of their own accord; and that Formosus had earlier been an obstacle to Stephen, preventing him from obtaining the desired see. Indeed, Platina derives from this the very bad custom, which has since been almost always observed, that later popes either overturned or wholly annulled the acts of their predecessors. "This certainly," he says, "has been foreign to those excellent popes whose lives we have written." He also ascribes to this the fact that Paul II did not obtain the name of Formosus, since "certain cardinals, not ignorant of history, deterred him lest after his death what had once happened to Formosus should happen to him." What kind of deed that was may easily be gathered from the phrase Platina uses, "with such rage" against the corpse of the man who raged against him. And Baronius has already recognised both a greater and a lesser guilt there; and it is clear that the guilt was not small, from the council held under John IX, which Baronius has pointed out. But Baronius further says, at n. 2, that the man, "stirred by fury, did not do what was lawful, but what his raging passion urged"; he adds, however: "it was not an error in faith, but a violent tyranny in action." That is enough, for who would ascribe infallibility in faith to a monster so savage? Yet Stephen, as Platina also testifies, in general abrogated the decrees of Formosus, rescinded his acts, and condemned him as "ignorant of sacred doctrines," with those present protesting (as Sigebert says). And whichever side the Papists take here, they are caught: either Formosus was illegitimate, and the constitution of the council under John IX was erroneous; or Sergius was illegitimate, and Stephen and the council under Stephen were gravely in error. From what has been said, the faults of both parties are plain; the blemishes in these ordinations, or re-ordinations, or in both, are plain.

units.la: Quod factum porrò firmatur & quale fuerit, ostenditur. errârunt. Sed patent ex dictis vitia utriusque partis; Patent nævi in istis ordinationibus aut reordinationibus aut utrobique.
units.tr: This deed is further confirmed, and its nature is shown. They erred. But the faults of both parties are plain from what has been said: the blemishes are plain in these ordinations, or reordinations, or in both.

units.la: XXXI. Contra has ita Luitprandus; Hi,qui à Juda Domini nostri Jesu Christi proditore ante proditionem salutem, seu benedictionem Apostolicam perceperant, ea post traditionem propriique corporis suspensionem minimè sunt privati, nisi quos improba forte fœdaverant flagitia. Benedictio siquidem,quæ ministris impenditur, non per eum,qui videtur, sed qui non videtur, Sacerdotem infunditur. Neque enim qui rigat est aliquid; neque qui plantat,sed qui incrementum dat Deus 1.Cor.III. In hunc modum quidem contrà Sergii,vel Stephani reordinationes argumentatur,minùs tamen convenienter hypothesibus Pontificiis,contrà illas etiam reordinationes Baronius n.3. vetustissima acta apponit, triginta objectiones & denfensiones totidem continentia, quibus etiam ista Sacrilegia à Stephano perpetrata continentur. Ipse autem de iis judicat, ad scelus eum addidisse impietatem.{}
units.tr: XXXI. Against these, Luitprand argues thus: Those who had received the blessing or salvation of the Apostle from Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, before the betrayal were not at all deprived of it after the handing over and the suspension of his own body, unless perhaps wicked crimes had defiled them. For the blessing that is bestowed on ministers is poured in not through him who appears, but through him who does not appear, the Priest. For neither is he who waters anything, nor he who plants, but God who gives the increase (1 Cor. 3). In this way, indeed, he argues against the reordinations of Sergius or Stephen; but it fits the Papist hypotheses less well. Baronius (n. 3) also sets out the most ancient records against those reordinations, containing thirty objections and as many defences, in which these sacrileges committed by Stephen are recorded. He himself judges concerning them that he added impiety to crime.

units.la: XXXII. Illud autem defensio ex indigitatis trigesima ita declarat: Sicuti bellua humanitatis immemores, quomodo intellexerunt, ita etiam operati sunt; Miserrimi ubi hæc didicerunt? Præsertim cùm Dominus non dixerit, quæcunque ligaveris sub terra, vel sub flumine; sed ait; quæcunque ligaveritis super terram, erunt ligata etiam in cœlo. De talibus enim ait Apostolus: Quidam habent Zelum Dei,sed non secundùm scientiam. Proh scelus! saltem Poeticam attendere debuerunt sententiam: Parce pias scelerare manus, jam parce sepulto. Veruntamen si ejusmodi de sede ad sedem translatio quodammodo illicita fuissef,nonne Ecclesiasticâ pietate tolerare, & non inauditis crudelitatibus exaggerare debuerant? &c.
units.tr: XXXII. The Defence declares the following from the aforesaid thirtieth point: Like beasts forgetful of humanity, as they understood, so also they acted. Wretched men, where did they learn this? Especially since the Lord did not say, whatever you bind under the earth or under the river, but he said, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven. For of such men the Apostle says: Some have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Alas, the crime! They should at least have heeded the poetic sentiment: Spare, now that he is buried, spare to defile pious hands. Yet if such a transfer from see to see had been in some way unlawful, ought they not to have borne it with ecclesiastical piety, and not have magnified it with unheard-of cruelties? etc.

units.la: XXXIII. De omnibus autem porrò ita judicat Baronius n. 6. Stephanum non auderem inter Romanos Pontifices numerare,nisi id factum à majoribus invenissem,utpote tanto indignum nomine,qui primus & solus nefando & inaudito Sacrilegio Petri sedem adeò deturpavit. Ipse siquidem (ut habent Acta Concilii sub Joanne Papa IX.) vi summâ collecto conventiculo Episcoporum, simúlque Presbyterorum Cardinalium sibi similium, Sergio &c. Diaconis etiam &c. hominibus perditissimis,violatoribus Pontificiæ sepultura, Formosi venerandum cadaver effossum, è sepulchro extractum &c. Intentatum hactenus scelus, quod non Christianorum tantùm aures exhorreant, sed & avertat quoque inhumanos & feros barbaros ab auditu, à fide revocet, & præ sui immanitate fiat omnibus incredibile. Adjecit perfidus, ut omnes à Formoso Sacris ordinibus initiatos exauctoraret. Execrati autem sunt, proh nefas, & lapides tale portentum &c. Ecce egregios Electionis malæ, Electionis duorum fructus!
units.tr: XXXIII. Baronius also judges all these matters thus (n. 6): I would not dare to number Stephen among the Roman Pontiffs, unless I had found that the deed had been done by his elders, as being a man unworthy of so great a name, who first and alone so defiled the see of Peter by an abominable and unheard-of sacrilege. For he himself (as the Acts of the Council under Pope John IX have it), having gathered by main force a conventicle of bishops, and likewise of cardinal elders like himself, with Sergius, etc., and deacons, etc., most depraved men, violators of the papal burial, dug up the venerable corpse of Formosus, drew it out of the tomb, etc. This crime, unattempted until now, which not only the ears of Christians shudder at, but which also turns inhuman and savage barbarians away from hearing it and calls them back from the faith, and by its monstrousness becomes incredible to all. The treacherous man added that he would strip of their sacred orders all who had been ordained by Formosus. But, alas, the crime! They were cursed, and stones... such a portent, etc. Behold the splendid fruits of a bad election, the fruits of a double election!

units.la: XXXIV. Decimum quintum Schisma fuit a.897. Onuphrio indice, qui tamen illud appendicem decimi quarti facit, licet à præcedente tempore disjunctum sit, inter Joannem IX. & Sergium III. Benedicti filium, Romanum, ex Comitibus Tusculanis, Presbyterum in Schismate iterum creatum, sed qui coactus iterum abdicavit, & in exsilium actus est. De quo tamen Schismate neque apud Baronium, neque apud Platinam aliquid reperire contigit.
units.tr: XXXIV. The fifteenth schism was in the year 897, according to the index of Onuphrius, who, however, makes it an appendix to the fourteenth, although it was separated from the preceding time, between John IX and Sergius III, son of Benedict, a Roman, of the Counts of Tusculum, an elder, created again in the schism, but who was forced to abdicate again and was driven into exile. Yet nothing about this schism can be found in Baronius or in Platina.

units.la: XXXV. Decimum sextum Schisma fuit inter Leonem V. Christophorum I. & Sergium III. A.907. seqq. quorum ille, narrante Platina in vita, à Christophoro familiari dominandi cupidine captus & in vincula conjectus fuit: quod quidem fieri sine magna seditione & multorum interitu non potuit; Quanta enim auctoritatis Pontificatus tum esset vitio priorum Pontificum, inquit, ex hoc vel maximè comprehendi poterit, quòd à viro privato tanta dignitas vi & factione uno fere momento occupata est. Verum est certè, quod dici solet: Plus auctoritatis dignitates ex hominibus capere, quàm ex dignitatibus homines; ut in Censura Romana apparuit, quæ primò ut exiguus Magistratus posthabita est: Verùm ubi civitatis optimates obire munus illud dignati sunt, tantam ei auctoritatem tribuere, ut inter optimates infelix haberetur, qui Censoriam dignitatem consecutus in vita non fuisset. Christophorus itaque, pergit, sedem occupat 40. Leonis in Pontificatu die: quem ego pra dolore animi paulò post periisse crediderim, quòd ab eo potissimum honore spoliatus fuisset, quem ipse ut lupum domi aluerat: ut illud Theocriti; Enutrito lupos, qui te comedant. Christophorus autem Pontificatum malis artibus adeptus, malè amisit, inquit idem Platina in Christoph. septimo enim mense dignitate ac merito quidem ejectus, monasticam vitam, unicum calamitosorum refugium obire cogitur. In monasteria enim tanquam in insulas Clerici malè de Ecclesia Dei meriti tum relegabantur. Ejectus fuit, atque Ecclesia Romana, verba sunt Baronii ad an.908. n. 1. rursum pravorum turbis & factionibus, invasionibus & graffationibus tyrannorum vehementer perturbata.
units.tr: XXXV. The sixteenth schism was between Leo V, Christopher I and Sergius III, in 907 and following. Of these, the first, as Platina tells in his life, was seized by Christopher, his intimate, out of a passion for domination, and cast into chains; which indeed could not happen without great sedition and the deaths of many. How great the authority of the Pontificate then was, through the fault of earlier Popes, he says, can be grasped above all from this, that so great a dignity was seized in almost one moment by a private man through violence and faction. It is certainly true, as is commonly said: Offices take more authority from men than men from offices; as appeared in the Roman censorship, which was at first despised as a petty magistracy. But when the nobles of the state deigned to undertake that office, they gave it such authority that whoever had not attained the censorship in life was thought unfortunate among the nobles. Christopher, therefore, he goes on, took the seat on the fortieth day of Leo's pontificate; whom I believe died of grief shortly afterwards, because he had been stripped of that honour most of all, which he himself had reared at home like a wolf, as in that line of Theocritus: You nourished wolves that will devour you. Christopher, however, having obtained the Pontificate by evil arts, lost it badly, says the same Platina in the life of Christopher: for in the seventh month he was thrown out of office and merit, and was compelled to take up the monastic life, the one refuge of the wretched. For into monasteries, as into islands, clerics who had deserved badly of the Church of God were then banished. He was ousted, and the Roman Church, these are Baronius's words (at the year 908, n. 1), was again greatly disturbed by the uproars and factions of wicked men, and by the invasions and raids of tyrants.

units.la: XXXVI. Exurgit rursus, ita pergit n. 2. Sergius ille nefandus, quem audisti in Formosum Papam ita saevisse. Potens iste armis Marchionis Tusciæ Adelberti, homo vitiorum omnium servus, facinorosissimus omnium, omnium, qua intentata reliquit? Invasit iste sedem Christophori, non Formosi, (ut memoria lapsus asseruit Luitprandus) quem quidem constat post malum ingressum, deteriorémque progressum, pessimum demum esse consecutum egressum. De quo etiam ex Sigeberto habet, eum latenter Romam ingressum, Papatum invasisse & Romanos minis & terroribus perpulisse, ut omnes Ordinationes Formosi irritas haberent &c. Caterum, inquit, ab omnibus non legitimus Pontifex, sed conclamatur invasor, ut non mireris, si ordinationes Formosi repulit, sed parum istud, nisi alias superinduxisset ordinationes. Et n. 3. sunt haec infelicissima illa tempora, cum alter alterius res gestas, intrusus quisque Pontifex aboleret. Quae damnans & execrans huius temporis auctor Auxilius nomine suo prosequutus est stylo. Addit post ex Sigeberto: Scripsit Dialogum sub persona Infensoris & Defensoris, divinis & Canonicis exemplis munitam, contra intestinam discordiam Romanae Ecclesiae, scilicet de ordinationibus, exordinationibus & superordinationibus Romanorum Pontificum & ordinatorum ab eis exordinationibus & superordinationibus. Perpetrata sunt ista, ita pergit, ab invasoribus & intrusis in Apostolicam sedem Pontificis nomen usurpantibus & illegitime thronum Apostolicum invadentibus. Verum legitime creati Romani Pontifices (ut Joannes IX.) ista vehementer sunt execrati.
units.tr: XXXVI. Up he rises again, and so he goes on (n. 2): that nefarious Sergius, whom you have heard raged against Pope Formosus. He was powerful through the arms of Adalbert, Marquis of Tuscany, a slave of every vice, the most criminal of all men. What did he leave untried? This man seized the see of Christopher, not of Formosus (as Luitprand mistakenly claims in his memory), and it is certain that after an evil entrance and a worse progress, he at last came to a most wretched exit. Of him he also has from Sigebert that he entered Rome secretly, seized the Papacy, and drove the Romans by threats and terrors to hold all the ordinations of Formosus void, etc. But, he says, by all he was not called a lawful Pontiff but proclaimed an usurper, so you need not wonder if he rejected the ordinations of Formosus; but that would have been little, had he not also introduced other ordinations. And (n. 3) these were those most unhappy times, when each intruded pontiff abolished the deeds of the other. The author Auxilius, condemning and cursing this age, pursued it in his own name with his pen. He adds afterwards, from Sigebert: He wrote a Dialogue under the persons of an Accuser and a Defender, fortified with divine and canonical examples, against the internal discord of the Roman Church, namely concerning the ordinations, reordinations and superordinations of the Roman Pontiffs and of those ordained by them through reordinations and superordinations. These things were perpetrated, he goes on, by usurpers and intruders who assumed the name of Pontiff and unlawfully invaded the Apostolic see. But the lawfully created Roman Pontiffs (such as John IX) most vehemently execrated these things.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Caterum, ita porro n. 4. loquitur, cum huiusmodi invasores Sedis Apostolicae invaluere, quid adeo mirandum sit, si inconcessa Sacris legibus ab illis tentata fuerint & usurpata? At ab istis quis justa legitimaque requirat? At quod mirandum est, isti, licet tales fuerint, tamen eo honoris & reverentia cultu fideles omnes praesertim longe positi Boreales populi prosequebantur Romanam Ecclesiam, ut quemcunque in ea sedentem audirent nominetenus Pontificem; eundem, mirum dictu, nulla habita discussione ejus ingressus, ut Petrum colerent &c. cum tamen eosdem sedis Apostolicae invasores, non Apostolicos, sed Apostaticos esse dicendos, Ecclesiastica bene dispositia (Dist. 79. c. 1. & 9.) censuit disciplina.
units.tr: Moreover, he goes on in n. 4 to say: when such invaders have prevailed over the Apostolic See, why should it be so surprising if they attempted and seized what the sacred laws do not allow? But who would demand what is just and lawful from such men? What is truly astonishing is that these men, although they were such, were still honoured with such reverence and respect by all the faithful, especially the far-off peoples of the north, that they heard anyone sitting in that Church named Pontiff and, strange to say, without any examination of his entry, gave him the honour due to Peter, etc. Yet the ecclesiastical discipline, well ordered (Dist. 79, c. 1 and 9), has judged that these invaders of the Apostolic See are not to be called Apostolic but Apostate.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.
