units.la: Nempe revocare vult Boreales nostri temporis ad similem caecam sane erga sedem Romanam obedientiam, quam in illius temporis Borealibus frustra miratur simplicibus, atque quid Papa sit, parum saepe advertentibus, licet aliquando fucum notasse sequentibus, sed Reformationem praecedentibus temporibus, atque Romanae Tyrannidi haud raro contradixisse legantur; Causam autem, cur Boreales olim, non obstantibus illegitimo ingressu, pessimaque Romanorum Pontificum vita tamen eos valde venerati nerati sint, Baronius ex parte exponit, dum vocat longè positos Boreales, quibus certè parùm de Pontificum ingrediendi & vivendi modis constare potuit. Forte minor veneratio illa fuisset Romæ habitantium, atque ejusmodi abominationes cominus intuentium!
units.tr: Indeed, he wants to recall the northern peoples of our own time to the same blind obedience towards the Roman See, which he marvels at in vain among the simple northerners of that age, who seldom paid attention to what a Pope is. It is read that they sometimes noticed the deception and later followed it, but in the earlier times of the Reformation they often contradicted the Roman tyranny. As for the reason why the northerners of old greatly revered the Popes, despite their illegitimate entry and the worst life of the Roman Pontiffs, Baronius explains it in part when he calls the northerners "far off", for of course they could hardly have known much about the manner in which the Popes entered and lived. Perhaps that veneration would have been less among those who lived at Rome and saw such abominations at close range!

units.la: XXXIX. Sed jam quærere lubet, annon vitiosum sit atque valdè vitiosum, quòd ita plures eodem tempore, non dicam electi, sed invasores, invasor Christophorus ab aquè invasore Sergio an.907. n.2. ejectus fuit? Quid si jam qualitates invasorum, quid si invadendi rationem accuratiùs pensitaremus? Sed id hic datâ operâ non agimus, in numeri duntaxat consideratione occupati. Tres hic nobis ostendunt Pontifices, unum in carcere, dum alter, qui incarceravit, solium Petri conscendit; illum ipsum in Monasterio, dum tertius in vacuam sic sacrilegio suo sedem irrumpit. Ast quid dico; Pontifices ostendunt? Largiuntur, neque secundum, neque tertium Pontifices fuisse, sed invasores, sed intrusos, sed Apostaticos. Ut dum plures æquo videri visi simus Pontifices, nullum viderimus, & quando in schismatibus aliis alterutrum legitimum pronuntiant, hìc utrumque condemnent. Istámne successionem tantopere jactant? Itane annuli in catena, cujus possessionem crepant, cohærent? Quid de actionibus talium judicandum, ab istis quis juxta & legitima requirat? quærit Baronius. Quid judicare possumus de istis, quas Baronius ex Sigeberto, Sigebertus, ex Auxilio commemorant, continuis rerum ab alio gestarum abolitionibus, ordinationibus, exordinationibus, & superordinationibus Romanorum Pontificum, & ordinatorum ab eis exordinationibus & superordinationibus? Annon merito idem Baronius ad an.907. n.2. tempora hac tyrannide sedem, quam Apostolicam vocat, invadentium tetra appellat? Perginus autem nos ad
units.tr: XXXIX. But now I should like to ask whether it is not faulty, and very faulty, that so many at the same time, I will not say elected, but invaders, were thrown out, invasor Christopher by the equally invading Sergius, in the year 907, n. 2? What if we weighed more carefully the qualities of the invaders and the manner of their invasion? But we are not doing that here on purpose, being occupied only with considering the number. Here the Popes show us three: one in prison, while the other, who imprisoned him, climbs the throne of Peter; and the same man in a monastery, while the third bursts into the empty see by his sacrilege. But why do I say "the Popes show us"? They concede that neither the second nor the third were Popes, but invaders, intruders, apostates. So, while we seem to have seen more Popes than is right, we have seen none, and when in other schisms they declare one or the other to be lawful, here they condemn both. Do they boast so much of this succession? Do the rings of the chain, whose clinking they make so much of, hold together in this way? What judgement should be made of the acts of such men, and who would demand from them what is just and lawful? asks Baronius. What can we judge of those things which Baronius recalls from Sigebert, and Sigebert from Auxilius, namely the continual abolitions of acts done by another, the ordinations, the exordinations and the superordinations of the Roman Pontiffs, and of the exordinations and superordinations made by them of those ordained? Does not the same Baronius rightly call the sees of those invaders, which he calls Apostolic, in those times of this tyranny, foul at the year 907, n. 2? But let us move on to

units.la: XL. Schisma decimum septimum inter Johannem XII. & Leonem VIII. atque mortuo illo, inter hunc & subrogatum illi Benedictum V. quod A.Ch.96?. coepit. Joannes XII. al. XIII. vel ipsâ in negando impudentiâ fatente, imò docendo, monstrum & sedis in ætate juvenili invasor gravissimorúmque criminum reus atque Imperatori manifestè perjurus, cùm ad Synodum Romanam venire atque objecta diluere semel atque iterum rogatus, juxta verba Platinæ, judicium bene sentientium refugiens nollet, depositus successorem nactus est Leonem VIII. unanimi consensu electum, qui
units.tr: XL. The schism of the seventeenth between John XII and Leo VIII, and after the death of the former, between the latter and Benedict V, who was substituted for him, began in the year 96?. John XII, also called XIII, showing even in denying it a shameless impudence, indeed teaching it, a monster in the see, an invader in his youthful age, guilty of most grave crimes and manifestly perjured towards the Emperor, when he was asked once and again to come to the Roman Synod and answer the charges, refused, avoiding, in the words of Platina, the judgement of those who thought well of him. Deposed, he got a successor, Leo VIII, elected by unanimous consent, who

units.la: Vitium multiplex in illo Schismate ostenditur.
units.tr: The manifold fault in that schism is shown.

units.la: Decimum septimum inter Ioannem XII. Leonem VIII. & Benedictum V. qui tamen, Romanis perjurium Papæ imitantibus atque Johanne revocato, ad Imperatorem aufugere necesse habuit, & in alia Synodo depositus fuit; Cùm autem paulò post Johannes sive à Diabolo, ut quidam, sive à marito adulterae, ut alii referunt, percussus esset, Romani, sunt verba Luitprandi, non modicè metuentes Imperatoris adventum, Benedictum quendam, Romana Ecclesia Diaconum, fidei & electionis Domini Imperatoris immemores, eligunt & ordinatum sedi Apostolicæ imponunt, idque, jam loquitur Platina, ab Imperatore, quitum Spoleti erat, confirmari contendunt. At Imperator iratus, non solùm Romanos, utpote iniqua postulantes, à se repulit, verùm etiam eosdem armis coegit, abrogato Benedicto, Leonem suscipere; qui etiam paulò post in Germaniam rediens secum Benedictum ipsum duxit, de quo Onuphrius in annot. parùm accuratè illius in numeri ejus nota rationem haberi, cùm schismaticus fuerit contra Leonem VIII. Papam legitimè creatum, per vim, & ut Platina habet, in seditione renuntiatus. Duo autem simul legitimi Papæ esse non possunt. Ille germanus & verus Pontifex semper censetur, cujus in Ecclesia successivo exstat, quæ quidem Leonis VIII. non Benedicti V. pro quo etiam authores citat Contra Baronius Leonem VIII. Schismaticum, Johannem XII. & Benedictum V. semper legitimos fuisse contendit, cui etiam Benedictus in exilio moriens Martyr audit. Tam bene inter hos de Pontificibus suis convenit! Atque Baronio legitimi Pontifices sunt monstra, invasores, in seditione, per vim, perjuri & perjurio electi, non item admittit in Synodo liberè atque à Clero populóque Romano creatum, vita irreprehensibilem! Hoccene est judicare justum judicium?
units.tr: The seventeenth schism is between John XII, Leo VIII and Benedict V, who, however, the Romans imitating the Pope's perjury and John having been recalled, had to flee to the Emperor, and was deposed in another Synod. When shortly afterwards John was struck, either by the Devil, as some report, or by the husband of an adulteress, as others report, the Romans, these are the words of Liutprand, greatly fearing the coming of the Emperor, forgetful of the faith and election of the Lord Emperor, choose a certain Benedict, a deacon of the Roman Church, and set him, once ordained, on the Apostolic See; and they contend, now Platina speaks, that this be confirmed by the Emperor, who was at Spoleto. But the Emperor, angry, not only repulsed the Romans from himself, as men making unjust demands, but also compelled them by arms to take back Leo, with Benedict set aside. Who also shortly afterwards, returning to Germany, took Benedict himself with him. Of him Onuphrius says, in the notes, too little accurately, that account of his number should not be taken, since he was a schismatic against Leo VIII, a lawfully created Pope, and was proclaimed by force, and, as Platina has it, in a sedition. Yet two legitimate Popes cannot exist at the same time. He is always reckoned the true and genuine Pontiff whose succession exists in the Church, which is that of Leo VIII, not of Benedict V. For whom also Baronius cites authorities. He contends that Leo VIII, the schismatic, and John XII and Benedict V were always lawful; Benedict also, dying in exile, is heard as a martyr. So well do they agree among themselves about their Popes! And to Baronius the lawful Popes are monsters, invaders, in sedition, by force, perjured and elected by perjury, while he does not admit, as lawful, one who was freely created in the Synod and by the clergy and people of Rome, and who was blameless in life! Is this to judge a just judgement?

units.la: XLI. Schisma decimum octavum fuit inter Benedictum V. dictum VI. Bonifacium VII. & Benedictum VI. al. VII. & Joannem XIV.
units.tr: XLI. The eighteenth schism was between Benedict V, called VI, Boniface VII, and Benedict VI, also called VII, and John XIV.

units.la: Anno enim Christi 974. juxta Baronium, n. 1. Benedictus Papa VI. ubi sedisset annum unum, menses tres & dies aliquot, à Bonifacio cognomento Francone Romano Ferrutii filio, Diacono Cardinale scelestissimo Viro violentâ manu capitur, in carcerem detruditur, ubi & strangulatur. Platina tamen id omne Cinthio praepotenti Civi Romano (qui fortè Bonifacii adjutor & promotor fuit, quod & Onuphrius in Indice innuit, dicens, jussu Bonifacii factum esse à Cinthio,) adscribit, atque Cusentinum referre ait, fame in carcere mortuum esse. Idem subjungit: Vereor, ne talia fuerint Benedicti merita, quale præmium à Cinthio consecutus est. Ponit etiam inter Benedictum VI. & Bonifacium VII. Donum II, cui tamen nulla gesta, mortem primo Pontificatus anno tribuit,atque forte contrà Bonifacium invasorem à Benedicti fautoribus electus fuit. Adeò confusa sunt, querela est Platinæ in Johanne XIII. & perturbata hæc tempora, scriptorum negligentiâ & incuriâ. Ipse verò Bonifacius, loquitur rursus Baronius ad an.974. n.1. Sedem Apostolicam violenter invasit, quam tenuit annum unum ac mensem,dictúsque Bonifacius VII. verum uti tyrannus ab antiquioribus non numeratur inter Romanos Pontifices. Eum sequenti anno, narrante eodem, Benedictus Romanus ex Albericis proveniens, exagitans urgénsque tyrannum invasorem Apostolicæ Sedis abire coegit. Qui nefandissimus homo, truculentus prædo, quomodo sacra ornamenta secum Constantinopolim abduxerit, ibi divenderit, atque, dum interea temporis Benedictus ille, juxta Baronium l. c. electus atque Johannes XIV. eo mortuo subrogatus esset, reversus pecuniâ denuò sedem invaserit, ubi de Simonia egimus, ex Platina fusiùs indicatum est. Idem in Bonif.VII. porrò narrat, quòd obstantibus conatibus suis bonis viris, maximè Joanne Diacono Cardinale, captum adjuvantibus quibusdam perniciosis hominibus oculis statim privârit; Atque ipse tantorum malorum auctor, glisçente majorem in modum seditione sive timore, sive pœnitentiâ patrati sceleris turpiter vitam finiverit. Ipsum autem Johannem Papam narrante Baronio ad an.985. n.1. sceleratus atque sacrilegus à Pontificio throno violentus exturbavit, vinculisque alligatum detrusit in munitionem S. Angeli,quæ detinebatur à suis: ubi 4. detentum mensibus fame perire tandem truculentus prædo coegit duorum Pontificum crudelissimus interfector, invasámque iterum Petri Cathedram, proh nefas! tenuit tyrannus,mensibus 4. qui nec pilum habuisse dici potest Romani Pontificis, sive spectes ingressum, sive progressum, resque ab eo gestas. Unde parùm consulunt veritati,minúsque pietati, & S. R. E. dignitati,qui hunc inter Romanos Pontifices referunt, annumerandum potiùs inter famosos latrones & potentissimos grassatores, atque patriæ proditores Syllas & Catilinas,horúmque similes,quos omnes superavit Sacrilegus iste turpissimâ nece duorum Pontificum. Mortem idem n. 3. nefandi parricida Deo ultori tribuit, à quo morte repentina percussus sit. Atque ibidem ex veteri Pontificum Vaticano codice refert, quomodo post mortem casus à suis & lanceis vulneratus atque per pedes nudato corpore tractus, projectúsque fuerit.
units.tr: For in the year of Christ 974, according to Baronius, n. 1, Pope Benedict VI, after he had sat for one year, three months and some days, was seized with a violent hand by Boniface, surnamed Franco, son of Ferrutius the Roman, a most wicked Deacon Cardinal. He was thrust into prison, where he was also strangled. Platina, however, ascribes all this to Cinthius, a powerful Roman citizen (who was perhaps Boniface's helper and promoter, which Onuphrius also hints, saying the deed was done by Cinthius at Boniface's command). He says that Cusentinus reports Benedict died of hunger in prison. The same author adds: "I fear that Benedict's merits were of such a kind as the reward he received from Cinthius." He also places between Benedict VI and Boniface VII a Donus II, to whom however no deeds are attributed. He assigns his death to the first year of his pontificate, and perhaps he was chosen by Benedict's supporters against the invader Boniface. So confused are these times, Platina complains, and so disturbed, in John XIII, through the negligence and carelessness of writers. Baronius speaks again about Boniface himself, ad an. 974, n. 1: He violently invaded the Apostolic See, which he held for one year and a month, and Boniface VII, called a tyrant by the older writers, is not counted among the Roman Pontiffs. In the following year, according to the same author, Benedict, a Roman coming from the Alberici, harassing and pressing the tyrant and invader, forced him to leave the Apostolic See. This most wicked man, a savage robber, carried the sacred ornaments away with him to Constantinople and sold them there. Meanwhile that Benedict, according to Baronius l. c., had been elected, and John XIV had been substituted after his death. Boniface returned and again invaded the see with money. We have discussed this under Simony, and Platina has been cited there at greater length. The same author further narrates of Boniface VII that although his attempts were opposed by good men, chiefly John the Deacon Cardinal, and with some pernicious men helping, he at once deprived the captive of his eyes. And he himself, the author of such great evils, as the sedition grew greatly, either from fear or from repentance for the crime committed, ended his life shamefully. Of Pope John himself, Baronius, narrating ad an. 985, n. 1, says: the wicked and sacrilegious man violently drove him from the Pontifical throne, and, bound in chains, thrust him into the fortress of St Angelo, which was held by his men. There, after he had been detained for four months, the most cruel murderer of two Pontiffs, the savage robber, at last compelled him to perish by hunger. The tyrant held the Chair of Peter again, alas the wickedness, for four months, and he cannot be said to have had even a hair of a Roman Pontiff, whether you look at his entry, his progress, or the deeds done by him. Hence those who count him among the Roman Pontiffs, rather than among the notorious robbers, the most powerful marauders, and the traitors to their country, the Sullas and Catilines and those like them, care little for the truth and less for piety and the dignity of the holy Roman Church. This sacrilegious man surpassed all of them by his most shameful murder of two Pontiffs. Baronius, n. 3, attributes his death to God the avenger of the wicked parricide, by whom he was struck down with sudden death. And in the same place, from the old Vatican codex of the Pontiffs, he reports how, after his death, he was wounded by his own men with spears, and dragged by the feet with his body naked, and thrown out.

units.la: XLII. En igitur rursus eandem ferè cum ea, quam supra exhibuimus, scenam, mutatis tantùm personis, imò fœdiorem. Quatuor hîc occurrunt, si Platinæ Donus II. addatur, quinq; Pontifices. Primus Primus capitur, incarceratur, strangulatur, vel fame moritur, dum secundus invadit, saevit, imperat; Tertius interea etiam eligitur, non tamen diu superstes. Secundus abire cogitur, atque Constantinopoli Thesauros divendit; dum quartus invadit, eligitur dominatur; Quintus eligitur, contra quem secundus vim auro paraturus redit, & redux factus vim auro paratam exerit, saevit, quintum tollit. Ut auctus fuerit plus aequo & hic Pontificum simultaneorum interventu numerus, pessime auctus invasione ex parte pessimorum, quorum unum aperte deserunt, atque talium, quorum in ore conveniens sermo fuisset:
units.tr: XLII. Here, then, is almost the same scene again as the one we set out above, with only the persons changed, and even fouler. Five Pontiffs appear here, if Platina's Donus II is added. The first is seized, imprisoned, strangled or dies of hunger, while the second invades, rages and rules. The third is meanwhile also elected, but does not survive long. The second is forced to leave and sells the treasures at Constantinople, while the fourth invades, is elected and rules. The fifth is elected, against whom the second returns, intending to procure force with gold; and on his return he uses the force he had procured with gold, rages, and removes the fifth. Since the number of simultaneous Pontiffs has grown more than is fitting in this way too, it has grown most badly through the invasions of the worst men, one of whom they openly abandon, and of others whose speech in the mouth would have been fitting:

units.la: Nos numerus sumus & populum consumere nati.
units.tr: We are a number, and born to consume the people.

units.la: XLIII. Schisma Decimum nonum An. Chr. 996. fuit inter Gregorium V. & Joannem XVII. al. XVI. Platinae XVIII. Mortuo enim Joanne XV. al. XVI. al. XVII.
units.tr: XLIII. The nineteenth schism, in the year of Christ 996, was between Gregory V and John XVII, also XVI, in Platina XVIII. For when John XV, also XVI, also XVII, had died,

units.la: Otto illico imperiali usus praecepto quendam suum consanguineum, sunt verba Glabri Radulphi Monachi Cluniacensis l. 1. c. 4. his temporibus proximi apud Bar. ad an. 996. n. 7. cujus Ducis filium (ut Platina in Greg.V. habet, ob affinitatem) delegit atque ex more in sede Apostolica sublimari mandavit. Quod utique dum sine mora peractum esset, pragrandis calamitatis occasio extitit; Erat enim quidam Crescentius Romanorum civis praepotens, qui (ut illorum mos est) quantum onerosior est pecunia, tanto proniús servit avaritia. Hic autem non plane partisavebat Ottonis: nam ipsum Pontificem, quem, ut diximus, ordinari Otto jusserat, idem Crescentius destitutum honore a sede expulit alterumque procaciter in ejus locum subrogavit. Quomodo autem argento corruptus Joannem suum promoverit, ex Platina, ubi de Simoniacis electionibus egimus, ostensum a nobis est. Sed promoto Imperator, cum pervenisset ad Urbem, juxta eundem Glabrum, manus quasi Sacrilegas amputari, deinde aures abscindi atque oculos evelli praecepit. Crescentium quoque promotorem morte punivit, Gregoriumque restituit. In Actis tamen S. Nili Abbatis atque conterranei Johannis, quae apud Baronium ad an. 996. n. 16. seqq. ex parte extant, de Successore Johannis, qui paucos post dies vi pulsus & excaecatus, mortuus etiam ac sepulturae mandatus sit, mentio ingeritur, quae cum Gregorio V. diu superstiti haud conveniant, Baronius n. 19. necesse esse judicat, ut dicamus, vel duos successive ista tunc passos esse Pontifices, vel, quod falsum audierit Nilus.
units.tr: Otto at once, using imperial authority, ordered a certain kinsman of his (these are the words of Glaber Radulphus, Cluniac monk, book 1, chapter 4, who lived in these times, cited by Baronius ad an. 996, n. 7) whose son (as Platina has it in his life of Gregory V, because of affinity) he chose and ordered to be raised to the Apostolic See in the usual way. When this had been done without delay, it became the occasion of a very great calamity. For there was a certain Crescentius, a most powerful Roman citizen, who (as is their custom) the more burdensome his money, the more readily he served avarice. This man did not entirely favour Otto's party. For he drove the Pontiff himself, whom Otto had ordered to be ordained, as we have said, from the see, deprived him of his honour, and boldly put another in his place. How he was corrupted by silver and promoted his John has been shown by us from Platina, where we discussed simoniacal elections. But when the Emperor, on arriving at the City, according to the same Glaber, ordered his hands, as if sacrilegious, to be cut off, then his ears to be sliced away and his eyes torn out. He also punished Crescentius, the promoter, with death, and restored Gregory. Yet in the Acts of St Nilus, abbot and fellow countryman of John, which are partly extant in Baronius ad an. 996, n. 16 and following, there is mention of John's successor, who, a few days later, was violently driven out and blinded, and died and was given to burial. Since these things do not agree with Gregory V, who survived for a long time, Baronius, n. 19, judges it necessary to say either that two Pontiffs suffered these things one after another, or that Nilus heard something false.

units.la: XXX
units.tr: XXX

units.la: XLIV. Sufficit, unum id passum esse, jam electo altero, electum. Legitimum habent Gregorium, sed ex illorum hypothesibus vix legitime electum ab Imperatore, consanguineum ob affinitatem, parvoque habito cleri populique respectu, quod ex eo colligi potest, quod, Platina referente, alii Joannem probant atque XVII. vocant, quod populi clerique Romani consensu, ad quos electio spectabat, Pontificatum atque adeo ex ea parte legitime iniisset, cujus tamen Simoniacam constitutionem ex altera parte uno omnes ore execrantur, eum illa non obstante aliorum adinstar probaturi, si successionem ab eo ostendere possent, aut novam Gregorii electionem, qui diu posthac solus in sede superfuit, Joanne in Germaniam relegato.
units.tr: XLIV. It is enough that one suffered this, and that another was elected after him. They hold Gregory to be legitimate, but by their own hypotheses he was scarcely legitimately elected, being chosen by the Emperor, a kinsman because of affinity, with little regard for the clergy and people. This can be gathered from the fact that, as Platina reports, others approve John and call him XVII, because he had entered the Pontificate by the consent of the Roman people and clergy, to whom the election belonged, and so legitimately on that side, although on the other side they all curse his simoniacal appointment with one voice. They would approve him, notwithstanding that, like the others, if they could show a succession from him, or a new election of Gregory, who afterwards survived alone in the see for a long time, John having been banished to Germany.

units.la: XLV. Schisma Vicesimum fuit inter Benedictum VIII. & alium quendam, cujus nomen Onuphrius invenire non potuit, sed quem Baronius ad an. 1012. n. 6. Gregorium vocat, ubi de hoc Schismate ita loquitur: Fuit autem Schisma in Ecclesia Romana in Benedicti hujus creatione, cum adversus eum contra Sacros Canones crearetur Gregorius, qui pollens potentia Romanorum, expulit ab Urbe Benedictum, qui ad Henricum Regem se contulit &c. atque ista ex Dithmaro confirmat; ad an. autem 1013. n. 4. narrat, quomodo Benedictus ab Henrico restitutus fuerit. Faciunt hic adulterinum Pontificem Gregorium, sed nec Benedictum ex omni parte benedictum fuisse constat, si vera sunt, quae nonnulli apud Platinam in vita de eo referunt, Episcopum quendam die in solitudine vidisse Benedictum equo nigro insidentem, cumque interrogasse, quid causa esset, cur mortuus equo nigro veheretur: Tum Benedictum hominem rogasse, ut pecunias, quas occultaverat (locum indicat) pauperibus suo nomine erogaret: qua antea data fuerant eleemosynarum nomine, nil ei profuisse, quia ex rapinis partas constabat.
units.tr: XLV. The twentieth schism was between Benedict VIII and another man, whose name Onuphrius could not find, but whom Baronius, ad an. 1012, n. 6, calls Gregory, where he speaks of this schism thus: There was a schism in the Roman Church at the creation of this Benedict, when Gregory was created against him contrary to the sacred canons. He, powerful in the strength of the Romans, expelled Benedict from the City, who betook himself to King Henry, etc. He confirms this from Dithmar. Ad an. 1013, n. 4, he tells how Benedict was restored by Henry. Here they make Gregory an adulterine Pontiff. But it is not established that Benedict was blessed in every respect, if what some report about him in his life in Platina is true: that a certain bishop one day saw Benedict riding alone on a black horse, and asked him why he was being carried, dead, on a black horse. Then Benedict asked the man to distribute to the poor in his name the money he had hidden (he indicates the place), since the alms given before had done him no good, because it was known that they had been gained by robbery.

units.la: XLVI. Schisma vicesimum primum fuit inter Benedictum VIII. dictum IX. Silvestrum III. & Johannem XXII. Mortuo enim Johannis XX al. XIX. al. XXI. Benedictus IX. subrogatus est: De qua electione ita Baronius ad an. 1033. n. 3. conqueritur. Cum (prohnefas) tyrannide Alberici Comitis Tusculani ejus filius puer in SS. Petri sedem intrudtur, monstram erigitur, statuitque portentum. Cum enim morte duorum Germanorum Pontificum, Benedicti atque Joannis, e domo sua Pontificatum, diu retentum egredi agro animo ferret: ne id fieret, cum alium non haberet, filium, quem habebat, aetate puerum, malis artibus in Petri Cathedram Angelis reverendam idem Albericus intrusit &c. Atque n. 4. eâ occasione Novatores, quos vocat, introducit vociferantes, apparere ex iis factis, in Ecclesia Romana stigmata Antichristi. Respondet: Facitne ista Ecclesia ipsa Romana, an patitur, cùm in eam indignus intruditur, & monstrum aliquod sæculari potentiâ in Sacrosanctam illam sedem projicitur atque occultatur &c.
units.tr: XLVI. The twenty-first schism was between Benedict VIII, called IX, Silvester III and John XXII. For after the death of John XX, alias XIX, alias XXI, Benedict IX was put in his place. Baronius complains of this election at the year 1033, n. 3, in these words: When (shameful to say) by the tyranny of Alberic, Count of Tusculum, his son, a boy, was thrust into the seat of St Peter, a monster was raised up and a portent set in place. For when Alberic was vexed that the papacy, which had long been kept in his house, was leaving it after the deaths of the two German pontiffs, Benedict and John, then, so that this should not happen, since he had no other, he thrust into the chair of Peter, which ought to be revered by angels, his son, though a boy in age, by wicked arts, and so on. And at n. 4, on that occasion, Baronius brings in what he calls the Innovators, crying out that from these deeds the marks of Antichrist are seen in the Roman Church. He replies: Does that Roman Church itself do these things, or does it suffer them, when some unworthy man is forced into it, and some monster is thrust into that most holy see by secular power and hidden there, and so on?

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Sicque putat, se planè silentium imponere posse adversariis suis, dicendo, Ecclesiam Romanam ista non fecisse, sed passam esse. Sed quid intelligit per Ecclesiam Romanam? Certè non omnes & singuli semper tales elegerunt Romani, aut Romani Pontificis authoritatem agnoscentes æquo majorem. Interim tamen Romani complures, præcipui, ipsi Clerici, illi, penes quos tunc electionem fuisse ajunt, ita sæpe corrumpentes, corrupti elegerunt, & tales, omnes eligi, intrudi passi sunt, in communione talium manserunt, Vicariorum Christi, Capitum Ecclesiæ. Talia capita corpori impositâ & fuerunt, capita, quæ cum corpore ordinarió confundunt, sæpissimè per Ecclesiam Papam intelligentes, talis igitur Ecclesia data est & fuit, & tamen successionem horum Episcoporum jactant, continuam, legitimam, nunquam interruptam, dignitatis & potestatis Monarchicæ, atque in fundamentum prærogativarum suarum unicum eam converterunt, dignum sane. Istane eorum Ecclesia ita pati debuisset, quam semper puram, semper Virginem depræAdicant, contrà quam portæ inferorum prævalere non debuerunt, atqui certè prævalere visæ sunt, quoties talia monstra, inferorum mancipia, Satanæ instrumenta ejus Domini, Capita, Monarchæ absoluti fuerunt, atque pro talibus agniti fuerunt, corpus illud animârunt. Qui autem notârunt, improbârunt talia, atque execrati sunt merito, illud altâ voce clamârunt, quod & largiri coguntur de temporibus illis hodierni: Non habemus Pontificem legitimum, successio interrupta est, fures & latrones nobis dominantur; quæ querela eò tristior fuisset, si, prout causam ejus habuissent, simul de corrupta in ore Doctorum istorum doctrina prolata fuisset. Sed pergimus; De Electione enim hujus pueri & jam, ubi de intrusionibus & Simonia, actum est, egimus & porrò, ubi de ætatis nævo acturi sumus, agendum erit.
units.tr: And so he thinks he can fully silence his opponents by saying that the Roman Church did not do these things, but suffered them. But what does he mean by the Roman Church? Certainly not all and each of the Romans have always chosen such men, or have recognised the authority of the Roman pontiff as more than equal. Yet several Romans, the chief ones, the clergy themselves, by whom they say the election was then held, often corrupting and being corrupted, chose such men, and allowed all such men to be elected and thrust in, and remained in communion with such men, the Vicars of Christ, the heads of the Church. Such heads were set upon the body, heads which they commonly confuse with the whole body, understanding by the Church the Pope. Such a Church was therefore given and was so; and yet they boast of an unbroken, lawful succession of these bishops, never interrupted, of a monarchical dignity and power, and they have turned this single thing into the foundation of their prerogatives, and very worthily so! Ought their Church to have suffered such things, which they proclaim always pure and always a virgin, against which the gates of hell ought not to prevail? And yet they have certainly seemed to prevail whenever such monsters, slaves of hell, instruments of Satan, were made absolute lords and heads and monarchs, and were acknowledged as such, and breathed life into that body. But those who noted these things, condemned them, and rightly cursed them, cried out in a loud voice that which even the present-day men are forced to concede about those times: We have no lawful pontiff, the succession is broken, thieves and robbers rule over us. This complaint would have been all the sadder if, as they had reason to, they had at the same time spoken of the corrupt doctrine that came from the mouth of those teachers. But let us go on. For we have already dealt with the election of this boy, where we treated of intrusions and simony, and where we are about to treat of the blemish of his age, that will have to be treated there.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Unicum illud tamen adhuc ex Baronio hic notamus: Porrò in Christiano orbe, inquit n. 7., cognitum fuisse & habitum ipsum Benedictum absque controversia Romanum Pontificem liquet. Controversiam ei movisse videri possunt Romani, qui hominem ignavum, vum, sunt verba Platinæ in Bened. IX. & nullius precii perosi, è sede dejiciunt, in ejúsque locum sufficiunt Joannem Sabinum Episcopum, Silvestrum tertium appellantes; atque ita, ut Baronius ad an. 1044. n.1. loquitur, novo Schismate Romana Ecclesia scinditur; qui & n. 2. specialius de eo agit. Et primò quidem de duabus potentissimis tunc temporis factionibus. Subjungit: Benedicti igitur turpitudinem ubique decantatam, à bonis omnibus deploratam haud diutius ferre valentes Romani, ante oculos ipsam habentes (tam bene vixit tam bene electus, legitimus tamen Baronio absque controversia) haud veriti sunt potentiam Comitum Tusculanorum, quâ urbi imminentes, terrori civibus esse solerent, sed favore aspirante Consulis Ptolomaei, Benedictum rejecerunt & Silvestrum subrogârunt—qui & malis artibus, nempe collatâ pecuniâ ad sedem Petri sibi ascensum paravit, dignus Benedicti æmulus, qui, Silvestro pulso, mox Romanam sedem iterum occupavit.
units.tr: We note only this one thing still from Baronius here: Moreover, in the Christian world, he says at n. 7, it is clear that Benedict himself was known and regarded without controversy as the Roman pontiff. The Romans may seem to have raised a controversy about him, the Romans who, hating a man idle and of no worth, these are Platina's words about Benedict IX, cast him from the see and put in his place John, bishop of Sabina, calling him Silvester III; and so, as Baronius says at the year 1044, n. 1, the Roman Church was split by a new schism; and he treats of it more specifically at n. 2. And first indeed of the two most powerful factions of the time. He adds: The Romans, therefore, no longer able to bear the baseness of Benedict, which was sung about everywhere and deplored by all good men, and having it before their eyes (he lived so well, was so well elected, and yet was lawful, without controversy, to Baronius), did not fear the power of the Counts of Tusculum, by which they used to hang over the city and be a terror to its citizens, but with the favour of the consul Ptolomy's help they rejected Benedict and put Silvester in his place, who also prepared his own ascent to the see of Peter by wicked arts, namely by paying money, a worthy rival of Benedict, who, when Silvester was driven out, soon occupied the Roman see again.

units.la: XLIX. Sed & tertius accessit, Johannes, quem supra innuimus, atque illud scitu dignum, judice Onuphrio in annot. ad Greg. VI. à Platina. Omissum, quòd—Benedictus restitutus secum ordinari fecit alium Pontificem nomine Joannem. Atque ita tres Pontifices Romanam sedem vexabant eamque occupaverat: Monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum; tergeminus Pontifex. De quibus Otto Frisingensis apud Baronium a. c. n. 2. Circa idem tempus pudenda confusio Ecclesiæ Dei in Urbe Roma fuit, tribus ibi invasoribus, quorum unus Benedictus dicebatur, sedem illam simul occupantibus, atque ad majoris miseriæ cumulum, divisis simul reditibus, Patriarchiis uno ad S. Petrum, altero ad S. Mariam Majorem, tertio, id est, Benedicto, in Lateranensi sedente, flagitiosam & turpem vitam, ut egomet in Urbe, Romanis tradentibus, audivi, duxere. Subjicit Baronius: Hæc de tribus Pseudo-Pontificibus simul Romæ sedentibus Otto, nempe Benedicto, Silvestro atque Joanne. Ergò omnes tres fuerunt Pseudo-Pontifices; Ergò etiam fuit Benedictus, quem jamjam pro legitimo absque controversia habitum esse dixerat; Errârunt igitur, qui pro vero habuerunt, verus per tot annos non fuit. Pergit Baronius n. 3. Sed quanta ex his orta mala fuerint, quis numerare sufficiat? Etenim Pseudo-Pontifices, ut ad se allicerent homines, quæque injusta petita libenter eisdem concedebant. Ut fecisse noscitur Benedictus &c.
units.tr: XLIX. But a third also came, John, whom we hinted at above, and this is a thing worth knowing, in the judgement of Onuphrius in his notes on Gregory VI, from Platina. It is passed over that Benedict, when restored, had another pontiff, named John, ordained with him. And so three pontiffs were harassing the Roman see and had occupied it: a horrible monster, shapeless, huge, whose light had been taken away, a three-headed pontiff. Otto of Freising speaks of them in Baronius, ibid. n. 2: At about the same time there was a shameful confusion of the Church of God in the city of Rome, with three invaders there, one of whom was called Benedict, occupying that see together, and, to heap up greater wretchedness, with the revenues divided, one at the Patriarchate of St Peter, another at St Mary Major, and the third, that is Benedict, sitting at the Lateran, they led a shameful and foul life, as I myself heard in the city from the Romans. Baronius adds: These things are said of the three pseudo-pontiffs sitting at Rome together, according to Otto, namely Benedict, Silvester and John. Therefore all three were pseudo-pontiffs; therefore Benedict too was one, whom he had just said was held without controversy to be lawful. Those who held him to be true were therefore wrong, he was not a true one for so many years. Baronius goes on at n. 3: But who could count up how many evils arose from these things? For the pseudo-pontiffs, in order to attract men to themselves, gladly granted them whatever unjust things they sought. As Benedict is known to have done, etc.

units.la: L. Cesserunt tamen tandem omnes tres, vel cessit, ut Baronius n. 1. vocat, triceps bestia. Remedium, argentum nimirum à Gratiano, qui post Gregorius VI. datum, vidimus, ubi de Simoniæ vitio
units.tr: L. All three, however, gave way in the end, or one gave way, as Baronius at n. 1 calls it, a three-headed beast. The remedy was money, given by Gratian, who came after Gregory VI, as we saw where we treated of the vice of simony,

units.la: Ioannis XXII similis invasio exponitur, atque Otto Frising. de tribus illis monstris testis introducitur;
units.tr: the similar usurpation of John XXII is set out, and Otto of Freising is introduced as a witness about those three monsters;

units.la: Quomodo cesserint, & quantum vitio egimus, simul quoque de Simoniaca IVti hujus electione, atque merita depositione. Multa paucis complectitur Sabellicus, dum narrat: Cæsar Benedictum, qui Pontificatum vendidit, Gregorium, qui emit, & Sylvestrum, qui largitione per paucos dies infestavit, tanquam tria monstra aversatus, coegit se dignitate abdicare. Nimirum abdica-vit etiam eos, qui sponte cesse-rant, ne resumerent. Cur autem in specie Benedictus cesserit, (de omnibus, acceptæ pecuniæ amore factum esse constat,) Ostiensis apud Baronium n. 2. ita exponit: Papatu tradito, ipse cupiditates suas liberius executurus, in paternam se recepit domum. En igitur & hic optionem Pontificum, sed, judice Baronio, Pseudo-Pontificum & monstrorum tricipitem bestiam constituentium! De quibus Eremita ad Imperatorem: Imperator Henrice omnipotentis vice, Virgo Sunamitis nupsit tribus maritis: Dissolve connubium & triforme dubium.
units.tr: how they gave way, and how much we have dealt with the vice, at the same time also about this simoniacal election of Gregory VI, and his deposition, which he deserved. Sabellicus sums up much in few words when he narrates: The emperor compelled Benedict, who sold the papacy, Gregory, who bought it, and Silvester, who troubled it for a few days by bribery, as three monsters, to abdicate their dignity. Indeed he also removed from office those who had given it up of their own accord, so that they could not resume it. But why Benedict in particular gave way (it is agreed that in all of them it was done from love of the money received) the Ostiensis explains in Baronius n. 2 thus: Once the papacy was handed over, he, about to indulge his desires more freely, withdrew into his father's house. Here then is the choice of pontiffs, but, in the judgement of Baronius, of pseudo-pontiffs and the three-headed beast of monsters! Of them a hermit said to the emperor: Emperor Henry, in place of the Almighty, the Virgin of Shunem married three husbands: dissolve the marriage and the threefold doubt.

units.la: LI. Schisma vicesimum secundum fuit inter Benedictum X. & Nicolaum II. Cujus origo à decreto Stephani X. P. quod apud Bar. ad an. 1058. n. 4. extat, arcessenda est, quo, cùm Hildebrandus tunc Subdiaconus ob negotia ad Imperatricem Agnetem mitteretur, constituere voluit, ut, si ipse ante hujus reditum moreretur, sedes, usque ad reditum, etiam hujus, intacta vacaret ejus demum ordinanda consilio. Mortuo paulò post Pontifice, mortuo etiam Imperatore, cujus reverentiâ & timore obortæ factiones reprimi consueverunt, sunt verba Baronii ad an. eund. n. 10. quæ inhiarent electioni Romanorum Pontificum, & Apostolicæ sedis invasioni, sive essent ex Comitibus Tusculanis, sive Ptolomæorum, Gregoriorum, sive Crescentiorum familiis, aliisve, armis, divitiisque potentibus: Ubi audita est mors summi Pontificis, rursus nullo habito respectu eorum, quæ Pontifice vivente ab eo omnibus consentientibus statuta fuêre; irrumpunt armis, invadunt Ecclesiam vi publicâ, quem cupiunt, illum in Apostolicum thronum attollunt, rursúmque maledictionibus suis Deo odibilem hominibus execrabilem constant alium Benedictum, fuit is antehac Episcopus Velitrensis Joannes, Mincius postea cognominatus. Atque de ejus electione etiam, ubi de Simonia egimus, agere necesse fuit. Hoc tempore, quo sedit, inquit Baronius n. 16. (mansit namque in Pontificatu totum, quod fuit reliquum anni hujus usque ad Januarii mensem) nihil boni ab eo factum reperitur, sed malum illud, dignum homine, qui pecunia vi aperuisset sibi viam ad sedem capessendam: nempe, ut qui pretio sedem emisset, pretio pariter sedes distrahe-ret ret & invasor ipse faveret sui similibus invasoribus. Accipe de his exem-plum &c. Verùm Hildebrandus rediens, sunt verba Platinæ in Bene-dicto X. cum Gerardo Episcopo Florentino, in omnes acerbissimè invectus est, tum vel maximè in eos qui fidem dederant, se ejus adventum expectaturos. At verò cùm hac de re magna contentio esset, probarént͏ q; nonnulli Benedi-ctum ipsum, ut optimum Virum & sapientissimum, contrà autem eam ele-ctionem plerique magnis clamoribus improbarent, utpote minùs Canonicè & legitimè factam, tandem plurimorum consensu, Hildebrando instante, Gerardus vir tanto Magistratu dignus ejecto Benedicto Pontifex creatur. Sunt tamen, qui scribant, hanc electionem Senis factam, cùm libera suffra-gia Romæ ob factionem quorundam potentum haberi non potuerint; Benedi-ctus itaque mense nono, die XX. Pontificatu dejectus, Velitras exulatum abiit. Atque in annotationibus pariter Onuphrius eum rejicit, addens; quare in numeri nota ejus ratio habenda non esset.
units.tr: LI. The twenty-second schism was between Benedict X and Nicholas II. Its origin must be traced to the decree of Stephen X, which is found in Baronius at the year 1058, n. 4, when Hildebrand, then subdeacon, was sent on business to the Empress Agnes, and Stephen wished it settled that if he himself died before Hildebrand's return, the see should remain vacant until his return, so that it might be filled by his counsel. When the pontiff soon died, and the emperor too had died, by whose reverence and fear the factions that aspired to the election of the Roman pontiffs and the invasion of the apostolic see used to be restrained, whether they were from the families of the Counts of Tusculum, or of the Ptolemies, Gregories, Crescentii, or others powerful in arms and wealth, these are the words of Baronius at the same year, n. 10: When the news of the death of the supreme pontiff was heard, again, with no regard for what had been decreed by all, with the pontiff still living, they burst in with arms, invade the Church by public violence, raise up whom they desire to the apostolic throne, and again by their curses make another Benedict, hateful to God and cursed by men; this was previously the bishop of Velletri, John, afterwards surnamed Mincius. And we had to treat of his election too, where we dealt with simony. In the time he sat, says Baronius at n. 16 (for he remained in the papacy for the whole rest of this year, until the month of January), nothing good is found to have been done by him, but that evil, worthy of a man who had opened for himself a way to seize the see by money: namely, that he who had bought the see for a price should in the same way sell the sees, and that the usurper himself should favour his fellow usurpers. Take an example of these things, etc. But Hildebrand, returning, these are Platina's words on Benedict X, with Gerard, bishop of Florence, inveighed most bitterly against all, and most of all against those who had pledged themselves to wait for his arrival. But when there was great dispute about this matter, some proved that Benedict himself was a very good and wise man, but most, with great outcries, condemned that election on the grounds that it had been made less canonically and lawfully; at last, by the general consent of many, with Hildebrand pressing, Gerard, a man worthy of so great an office, was created pontiff, Benedict being removed. There are, however, those who write that this election was made at Siena, since free votes could not be had at Rome on account of the faction of certain powerful men; so Benedict, deposed from the papacy in the ninth month, on the twentieth day, went into exile at Velletri. Likewise Onuphrius in his notes also rejects him, adding: wherefore his name should not be counted in the list of numbers.

units.la: LII. Gerardus Nicolaus II. dictus fuit ab Imperatore de-signatus, juxta Lamberti apud Baronium n. 15. verba, ait enim:
units.tr: LII. Gerard, called Nicholas II, was designated by the Emperor, according to the words of Lambert in Baronius, n. 15, for he says:

units.la: Romani Principes satisfactionem ad Regem mittunt, se scilicet fidem, quam Patri dixissent, filio quoad possent servaturos, eóque animo vacanti Romana Ecclesia Pontificem usque ad id tempus non subrogâsse, ejus magis super hoc expectare sententiam: Orántque sedulò, ut quem ipse velit, transmit-tat, nihil ejus ordinationi obstare, si quis non per legitima ordinationis ostium, sed aliunde ascendisset in ovile ovium. Rex habitâ cum primoribus deliberatione, Gerardum Florentinum Episcopum, in quem & Romanorum & Teutonicorum studia consenserant, Pontificem designat, Romámque per Godefridum Marchionem transmittit &c. Hoc igitur schisma minùs perplexum fuit aliis, interim nec suis naevis caret, eo ipso dum schis-ma &, cùm de electione Nicolai ageretur, magna contentio fuit, dum Benedictus prior electus fuit, Vir optimus & sapientissimus, modo me-liori, saltem non pejori, quàm quo aliàs electi sunt multi, qui ta-men pro legitimis habentur, imò in subsecuto Concilio Sutrino se vim perpessum esse asserere potuit, habitus fuit tam diu pro Episcopo, tam diu solus fuit. Contrà nimiæ in electione Nicolai partes Hil-debrandi fuisse videntur, nimiæ, ex hypothesi Pontificia, forte etiam Regis, tandem & illud heic denuò noto, omnia magis in favorem ejus, qui obtinuit, scriptis consignari.
units.tr: The Roman princes send a pledge to the King, namely that they would keep faith with the son as far as they were able, as they had promised the father; and with that intention they had not appointed a Pope to the vacant Roman Church up to that time, preferring to await his judgment on the matter. They earnestly beg that he send whomever he himself wishes, and that nothing hinder his appointment, even if someone had climbed into the sheepfold not through the lawful door of ordination but from somewhere else. The King, after deliberating with the leading men, designates Gerard, Bishop of Florence, on whom the wishes of both Romans and Germans had agreed, as Pope, and sends him to Rome through Godfrey the Marquis, etc. This schism was therefore less confused for others, yet it is not free from its own blemishes, in that the schism itself, and when the election of Nicholas was discussed, there was great contention, while Benedict had been elected earlier, a man very good and very wise, by a better method, or at least not a worse one, than many others who were elected otherwise and yet are held to be lawful; indeed, in the later Council of Sutri he could assert that he had suffered violence, he was held as bishop for so long, and he was alone for so long. On the other hand, the role of Hildebrand in the election of Nicholas seems to have been excessive, excessive by the Papal hypothesis, and perhaps also that of the King. Finally, I note here again that everything was recorded in writings more in favour of the one who prevailed.

units.la: LIII. Vicesimum tertium Schisma fuit inter Alexandrum II. & Cadolaum, quem Onuphrius in annot. ad Alex. ex antiquo diplo-mate in Pontificatu suo Honorium II. vocatum esse, tradit. Mortuo enim NicoNicolao II. Cardinales Anshelmum Lucensem Episcopum, patria Mediolanensem, elegerunt, atque Alexandrum II. vocârunt. At vero Cisalpini Episcopi, verba sunt Platinæ in Alex. II. arbitrati ob dignitatem provinciæ suæ par esse, ut è suo numero aliquis eligeretur, atque Ministri Regis, juxta Baronium ad an. 1061. n. 1. indigno animo ferentes, quòd scilicet non ex Regis electione creatus Pontifex esset, mox habito, ut Platina loquitur, Concilio, convocatis, juxta Hermannum, omnibus Italiæ Episcopis, elegerunt & eligendum curárunt Cadalum, quem alii nominant Cadaloum, alii Cadalaum Parmensem Episcopum. Baronius etiam n. 2. legationem Procerum Romanorum, qui Comites dicebantur, & aliorum commemorat, quâ cum, juxta verba Hermanni, interpellárunt pro eligendo summo Pontifice; movit etiam Regios, quòd, referente Damiano, apud Bar. n. 3. Legati asserebant, Nicolaum statuisse decretis suis, quòd nullus deinceps haberetur Romanus Episcopus, nisi priùs à Cardinalibus eligeretur, cui postea accederet consensus Regis.
units.tr: LIII. The twenty-third Schism was between Alexander II and Cadolaus, whom Onuphrius, in his notes on Alexander, reports to have been called Honorius II in his pontificate, according to an ancient diploma. For when Nicholas II had died, the cardinals elected Anselm, Bishop of Lucca, a Milanese by birth, and called him Alexander II. But the Cisalpine bishops, in Platina's words on Alexander II, judged it fitting, on account of the dignity of their province, that someone should be chosen from their number; and the King's ministers, according to Baronius at 1061, n. 1, bearing it with indignant spirit, because the Pope had not been created by the King's election, straightaway, as Platina puts it, a council having been convened, with all the bishops of Italy summoned according to Hermann, they elected and caused to be elected Cadalus, whom some call Cadalous and others Cadalaus, Bishop of Parma. Baronius also records, at n. 2, the embassy of the Roman nobles, who were called Counts, and of others, by which, according to Hermann's words, they petitioned for the election of a supreme Pontiff. He also stirred the royalists, because, as Damian reports, in Baronius n. 3, the legates asserted that Nicholas had decreed by his decrees that no one thereafter should be held as Roman bishop unless first elected by the cardinals, to whom the consent of the King should afterwards be added.

units.la: LIV. Schisma duravit annis aliquot, & Cadalao quidem, narrat Platina, Cisalpini omnes obtemperavêre præter Mithildim optimam faminam & cum Ecclesia Romana bene sentientem. Superveniente deinde Cadolo ab his, qui Alexandro adversabantur, ac cito in pratis Neromianis sub radicibus aurei montis grave prælium committitur, in quo multi utrinque cecidere, Alexandro & Gotifredo Mithildis Viro sese ad ædes Lateranensium continentibus.
units.tr: LIV. The schism lasted some years. And indeed, Platina relates, all the Cisalpine bishops obeyed Cadalus except Mathilda, an excellent woman who was well disposed toward the Roman Church. Then Cadalus, having come up with the support of those who opposed Alexander, a fierce battle was quickly joined in the Neroman meadows at the foot of the Golden Mountain, in which many fell on both sides, while Alexander and Godfrey, Mathilda's husband, kept themselves at the Lateran palace.

units.la: Incerti enim erant, quibus potissimum se committerent, adeò omnia infida & fluxa videbantur. Sunt qui scribant, Alexandrum ante prælium commissum, Lucam profectum, vitanda cædis causâ, eóque loci quieté aliquandiu vixisse. Repulsus tandem ab urbe Cadolus, non diu in provincia quievit, accitus enim à Romanis quibusdam, comparato majori exercitu, quàm ante Romam venit, ac urbem Leoniam Ecclesiamque B. Petri vi occupat. At vero erumpentibus Romanis cum Gotfredi copiis, tantus terror repente hostes invasit, ut & effusâ fugâ omnes abierint, & paulum abfuerit, quin Cadolus caperetur à suis derelictus, quem Cincius Romani Præfecti filius, facto cum suis cuneo, per media civium agmina agrè in arcem Hadriani perduxit, ubi aliquandiu obsessus, cùm nullam liberè abeundi subesse spem videret, 300. argenti libris ab his se redimens, qui arcem obsidebant, conscenso strigosissimo equo inde solus aufugit.
units.tr: For they were uncertain to whom they should commit themselves most, so entirely faithless and unstable did everything seem. Some write that Alexander, before the battle was joined, went to Lucca to avoid bloodshed, and lived quietly there for some time. Cadolus, driven from the city, did not rest long in the province, for, summoned by certain Romans, he came before Rome with a larger army than before and forcibly seized the city of Leonina and the church of St Peter. But when the Romans sallied out with the forces of Godfrey, such great terror suddenly seized the enemy that all of them departed in headlong flight, and it lacked little that Cadolus, abandoned by his own men, should be captured. Cincius, son of the Roman prefect, with his men formed into a wedge and through the midst of the crowds of citizens, with difficulty led him into the castle of Hadrian. There, besieged for some time, and seeing no hope of leaving freely, he ransomed himself for 300 pounds of silver from those who were besieging the castle, and mounting a very lean horse, fled alone from there.

units.la: LV. Tandem in Concilio Mantuano pro Alexandro pronuntiatum est, cujus certè electionem parùm commendat, quòd contrà morem pristinum contempto Rege soli Cardinales negotium peregerint, atque hinc speciem certè habuit electio Cadolai
units.tr: LV. Finally, at the Council of Mantua, judgment was given for Alexander. Certainly this does not much commend his election, that, contrary to the old custom, with the King disregarded, only the cardinals had carried the business through, and hence the election of Cadolaus certainly had the appearance of...

units.la: {a} Schismatis disturbantur; Sectatores Cadolai, atque armorum vis. à tot Episcopis procurante Rege in Concilio facta; In genere autem pessimum illud notatur, quòd in diuturno Schismate pro Vicariatu Christi tanquam pro regno mundano armis mundanis acerrimè variáque fortunâ pugnatum est.
units.tr: {a} The disturbances of the schism; the followers of Cadolaus, and the force of arms. The council was held by so many bishops, the King arranging it. In general, however, this is noted as the worst thing: that in the long schism, for the vicariate of Christ, as for a worldly kingdom, they fought with worldly arms, very fiercely and with varying fortune.

units.la: LVI. Vicesimum quartum Schisma fuit inter Gregorium VII. & ejus successores Victorem III. Urbanum II. & Paschalem II. ab una, atque Clementem III. ab altera parte, judice Onuphrio, pessimum. Notæ sunt controversiæ inter Gregorium VII. Sanctum Damiano apud Baronium ad an. 1061, n. 30: Satanam; & jam sub præcedentibus eidem n. 34. Dominum Papam adoratum & Henricum IV. Imperatorem summâ cum violentiâ à parte & altera agitatae atque eò tandem deductæ, ut Imperator ob investituram Episcoporum à Papa miserrimè exagitatus, atque semel iterumque excommunicatus, excitato quoque sibi æmulo Rodolpho, sed à se mox armorum vi domito, Episcopis non paucis ex Italia Germaniáque sibi accedentibus in Comitiis Wormi dejectum in Concilio Mogunti no novendecim; post in Brixino triginta Episcoporum primùm Gregorium depositurit, post alium quoque eligi curârit. An. D. 1080. inquit Bar. ad an. illum n. 29: cùm apud Brixiam Noricam 30. Episcoporum conventus, nec non & optimatum exercitus non solùm Italia, sed & Germania jussu Regis Henrici congregaretur; Factus est omnium consensus adversus Hildebrandum P. cognomento Gregorium VII. quem, Pseudo-Monachum, totiúsque vesania pestiferum Principem, & præcipuè sanctæ Romanæ Sedis invasorem, affirmantes ab Apostolica sede depellendum, quamvis absentem dijudicabant, & Vuigbertum (Gibertum; cujus etiam in schismate præcedente non minimæ partes fuerunt, dum adhuc Regis Cancellarius esset; factus tamen Rege rogante ab Alexandro II. Archiepiscopus;) Ravennensem Archiepiscopum ipsi surrogandum elegebant.
units.tr: LVI. The twenty-fourth Schism was between Gregory VII and his successors Victor III, Urban II and Paschal II on one side, and Clement III on the other, and according to Onuphrius it was the worst. The controversies between Gregory VII are well known: Sanctum, as Damian calls him, and in Baronius at the year 1061, n. 30: Satan; and already under his predecessors, the same at n. 34, the Lord Pope, worshipped. Henry IV the Emperor, with the greatest violence on each side, was driven to such a point that the Emperor, most miserably harassed by the Pope over the investiture of bishops, was excommunicated once and again. Rudolf was also raised up as his rival, but was soon subdued by his own armed force, and with not a few bishops from Italy and Germany joining him, he was deposed at the Diet of Worms by nineteen bishops, and at the Council of Mainz, afterwards at Brixen, thirty bishops first deposed Gregory and afterwards caused another to be elected. In the year of our Lord 1080, Baronius says at that year, n. 29, when at Brixen in Noricum an assembly of thirty bishops, as well as an army of nobles, not only from Italy but also from Germany, was gathered by the command of King Henry: a unanimous consensus was reached against Hildebrand the Pope, surnamed Gregory VII, whom they called a pseudo-monk, a prince pestilent with all madness, and especially an invader of the holy Roman See, affirming that he must be driven from the apostolic see, and they judged him in his absence; and they elected Wibert (Guibert, whose part in the preceding schism was by no means small, while he was still the King's chancellor, but who was made archbishop by Alexander II at the King's request) archbishop of Ravenna to be put in his place.

units.la: LVII. Hujus decreti conclusio hæc est: Quia illum constat, non à Deo electum, sed à se ipso, in fraude ac pecuniâ impudentissimè objectum (vitiosa etiam dicebatur electio, quòd eo ipso, quo præde cessor sepultus fuerat; die; contrà Canones, qui per triduum expectandum esse censent; Cardinalibus, ut Benno Cardinalis narrat; ideò subscribere nolentibus, à Laicis electus fuit, & quòd, juxta authorem Vitæ Henrici; Romanam sedem olim abjuratam insedit, quia ad eam, dum Archidiaconus esset, adhuc vivente Domino suo per ambitionem aspirare voluerit, quod quidem ille in dubio relinquere videtur;) Qui Ecclesiasticlesiasticum subvertit ordinem; Qui Christiani Imperii subvertit Regnum; Qui inter concordes seminavit discordiam, inter pacificos lites, inter fratres scandala, inter conjuges divortia (Clericorum enim conjugia dissolvere modis omnibus annitebatur atque ideo etiam Episcopi nonnulli partes Imperatoris contra Hildebrandum tuendas existimarunt) & quicquid quieté inter pie viventes stare videbatur, concussit; Nos, auctore Deo, congregati in unum, Legatis ac literis freti decem & novem Episcoporum, die sancto praterita Pentecostes Moguntia congregatorum, contra eundem Hildebrandum procacissimum, Sacrilegia ac incendia praedicantem, perjuria homicidia defendentem (accusatio probatur etiam per rebellionem Rodolphi à Papa excitatam atq; nutritam.) Catholicam & Apostolicam fidem de corpore & sanguine Domini in quaestionem ponentem, haereticí Berengarii antiquum discipulum, (quae causa sola certè eam Episcopatu non indignum fecisset, verè, si vera dicunt, Apostolicae doctrinae post Berengarium sectatorem) divinationum ac somniorum cultorem, manifestum necromanticum, pythonico spiritu laborantem, & idcirco à vera fide exorbitantem, judicamus Canonicè deponendum & expellendum: & nisi ab ipsa sede, his auditis, descenderit, in perpetuum condemnandum. Facta sunt autem haec Septimo Kalend. Julii feria Indict. tertia: Quae quidem apud Urspergensem habentur, Bennonis Cardinalis narrationibus consentanea.
units.tr: LVII. The conclusion of this decree is this: Since it is established that he was elected not by God but by himself, most shamelessly put forward through fraud and money (the election was also said to be faulty, because it took place on the very day the predecessor had been buried, contrary to the canons, which hold that one must wait three days; and since the cardinals were unwilling to sign, he was elected by laymen, as Cardinal Benno relates; and because, according to the author of the Life of Henry, he occupied the Roman see, which he had once renounced, since while he was archdeacon, and while his lord was still alive, he wished to aspire to it through ambition, which he seems to leave in doubt); who has subverted the ecclesiastical order; who has subverted the kingdom of the Christian empire; who has sown discord among the harmonious, strife among the peaceable, scandals among brothers, divorces among spouses (for he strove by every means to dissolve the marriages of the clergy, and for this reason some bishops also thought they should defend the Emperor's side against Hildebrand) and has shaken whatever seemed to stand quietly among the devout. We, gathered together by God's authority, relying on the legates and letters of nineteen bishops who met at Mainz on the holy day of last Pentecost, against that most insolent Hildebrand, preaching sacrileges and arson, defending perjuries and murders (the accusation is also proved by the rebellion of Rudolf, stirred up and nourished by the Pope) putting in question the Catholic and Apostolic faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord, an old disciple of the heretic Berengarius (a cause which alone would certainly have made him unworthy of the episcopate, if indeed, as they say, he was a follower of Berengarius rather than of apostolic doctrine) a practitioner of divinations and dreams, a manifest necromancer, laboring under a Pythonic spirit, and therefore straying from the true faith, we judge that he must be canonically deposed and expelled; and unless he descend from the see itself, these things having been heard, he is to be condemned forever. These things were done on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction. These things are indeed found in the Urspergensis, in agreement with the accounts of Cardinal Benno.

units.la: LVIII. Electus autem Papa sumpto Clementis III. nomine à Rege & suis constanter agnitus atque missis ad Christianos Principes Legatis, aliis quoque commendatus, Romae autem ad an.1083. referente Baronio ad S. Petrum n.1. consecratus, per 28 annos, quibus Schisma contra Gregorium atque dictos ejus successores ab hisque vicissim contra Clementem, Regem atque suos successores bellis, pugnis, incendiis, insidiis, continuatum fuit, sedit, fecitque, numerante Onuphrio in Chronico, Cardinales XIX. Episcopos V. Presbyteros X. & Diaconos IV. Obiit verò tandem Romae, narrante eodem ibidem, in arce S. Angeli, post Kal. Septemb. anno 1101. sepultus Ravennae in Cathedrali Ecclesia, & non longè post Corpus ejus exhumatum, jussu Paschalis II. combustum est. Tribuit ei Domnizo apud Baronium ad an.1100. n. 16. annos viginti tres, quos tamen hic n.17. non ad tempus, quo sederit, sed ex quo facto schismate à Gregorio desciverit, referendos esse ait, cùm demum ab anno 1080. sederit. Mortuus, juxta eum, anno, 100. Subjungit n.18. nequaquam unà cum Anti-Papa obitu extinctum fuisse Schisma vivente adhuc, qui foveret illud, Henrico Imperatore, cujus operâ tres post Guibertum subrogati sint sibi invicem succedentes Pseudo-Pontifices, Albertus, Theodoricus & Maginulphus &c. quos tamen Paschalis vi tandem & armis domuit: Ille, referente Onuphrio in Chronico, captus à militibus Paschalis, quum coactus abdicâsset, in monasterio S. Laurentii Aversa perpetuo carceri relegatus est. Iste Captus ab ejusdem praesidiis, & Sacerdotio privatus in Monasterium S. Trinitatis Cavensis trusus, Monachus factus, ibi Anachoreticam vitam diu duxit. Hic Latio fugatus & monasterio suo expulsus, animi dolore haud ita multò post mortuus est.
units.tr: LVIII. The elected pope took the name Clement III and was constantly acknowledged by the king and his followers. Legates were sent to the Christian princes, and others also recommended him. He was consecrated at Rome in St Peter's in 1083, according to Baronius (n.1). For 28 years he sat and acted, while the schism was kept up by wars, battles, fires and ambushes, first against Gregory and his successors and then, in turn, from their side against Clement, the king and his successors. Onuphrius, in his Chronicle, counts 19 cardinals, 5 bishops, 10 presbyters and 4 deacons. He died at last at Rome, as the same writer relates in the same place, in the castle of St Angelo, after 1 September in the year 1101; he was buried at Ravenna in the cathedral church, and not long after his body was dug up and burned by order of Paschal II. Domnizo, in Baronius at 1100 n.16, gives him twenty-three years. Here at n.17, however, Baronius says these should be counted not from the time he sat, but from when he broke away from Gregory by making the schism, since he really sat only from 1080. According to Domnizo he died in the year 100. At n.18 Baronius adds that the schism did not end with the death of the anti-pope, since it was still alive and being fostered by Emperor Henry. Through Henry's efforts three pseudo-popes succeeded one another after Guibert: Albert, Theodoric and Maginulf, and so on. Paschal nonetheless at last subdued them by force and arms. The first, as Onuphrius relates in the Chronicle, was captured by Paschal's soldiers and, when he had been forced to abdicate, was consigned to perpetual imprisonment in the monastery of St Lawrence at Aversa. The second was captured by the same garrisons, stripped of the priesthood, and thrust into the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Cava. There he became a monk and led an anchorite's life for a long time. The third was driven out of Latium and expelled from his monastery, and died not long afterwards of grief.

units.la: LIX. Ut facilè jam colligi possit, quàm multiplex ex tam diuturno atque pessimo Schismate contra Ecclesiam Romanam praejudicium formari queat, & contrà electiones Pontificum, dum per tot annos Ecclesia illa inter simultaneos Pastores summos fluctuavit, multis millibus ab hac & illa parte semper stantibus, neque hominibus facilè, uter potior esset, dijudicantibus, Gregorii quippe injuria sanctis conjugiis illata, atque Tyrannis erga Imperatorem exercita manifesta erat, sed nec exigua erant partis alterius vitia. Utrobique verò pessimas quasvis artes, atque infinitas hominum caedes mediorum adinstar fuisse, testantur auctores. Testantur, miracula Schismaticos jactâsse, Cassinates apud Bar. ad an. 1130. n. 65. miraculosè Ecclesia fores apertas à se inventas fuisse; Testantur, apud eundem ad a. 1136. n. 7. Schismaticum Papam de felici rerum successu & infelici contra adversantium exitu, quae notae veritatis apud Pontificios, gloriatum esse. Ipse Schismaticus Anti-Papa Guibertus exultans ac insultans pariter, quòd tres ipso vivente atque in Petri Cathedra considente, Deo vindice, essent extincti Pontifices. Sed & Otto Frisingensis pessimi Schismatis rationem, atque ex illo Nauclerus Generat. 37. exponunt: Quanta tum mala, inquiunt, quot bella bellorumque discrimina inde subsecuta sint, quoties Roma miserè obsessa, capta, vastata, quòd Papa super Papam, sicut Rex super Regem positus fuerit, tædet memorare, denique tot mala, tot schismata, tot tam animarum, quàm Corporum pericula hujus tempestatis turbo involvit, ut solus ex persecutionis immanitate ac temporis diuturnitate ad humana miseria infelicitatem sufficeret comprobandam: Unde bene densissimis Ægypti tenebris comparatus &c. Claudit Matth. Paris. Hist. Angl. p.8. his verbis: Nullius haeresis tempore Sancta Ecclesia graviori Schismate fuit scissa.
units.tr: LIX. From this it can now easily be gathered how many prejudices against the Roman Church, and against the elections of popes, could be formed from so long and most wicked a schism. For over so many years that Church wavered between rival supreme ministers, while many thousands always stood on one side or the other, and men could not easily judge which was the stronger. The wrong done to holy marriages by Gregory was plain, and so was the tyranny exercised against the Emperor, but the faults of the other party were no small matter either. Writers testify that on both sides the worst arts of every kind, and endless slaughter of men, were practised as if by common consent. They testify that the schismatics boasted of miracles: the Cassinates, in Baronius at 1130 n.65, claimed that church doors had been miraculously found open by them. They testify, in the same author at 1136 n.7, that the schismatic pope gloried in a happy outcome of affairs and an unhappy end for his opponents, which the Papists regard as marks of the truth. The schismatic anti-pope Guibert himself exulted and jeered alike, because three popes had been put to death, while he lived and sat in the chair of Peter, by God's vengeance. Otto of Freising, and Naucler from him (Generation 37), also set out the nature of this dreadful schism: "How many evils, they say, what wars and what dangers of war followed from it, how often Rome was miserably besieged, captured and laid waste, because one pope was set up above another pope, just as one king above another king, I am ashamed to recall. Finally, the storm of this time has involved so many evils, so many schisms, so many dangers both to souls and to bodies, that the savagery of the persecution and the long duration of the time alone would be enough to prove the unhappiness of human misery. Hence it is fairly compared to the thickest darkness of Egypt, etc." Matthew Paris ends his account, History of England, p.8, with these words: "At no time of any heresy was the holy Church torn by a graver schism."

units.la: LX. Vicesimum quintum Schisma fuit inter Gelasium II. & Gregorium VIII. Gelasio námque electo, Conventus Patrum à Centio Frangipane, qui à partibus Henrici Imperatoris stabat, vi solutus, tus, ipse Papa male aliorum ad instar tractatus, atque ab illo domi incatenatus, sed seditione civium facta haud multo post libertati redditus fuit; Sed non diu securus mansit, oborto enim de Henrici Imperatoris adventu rumore cum suis aufugere necesse habuit, persequentibus eos Alemannis, & nonnisi juramento, Papam evasisse, interposito, a persecutione desistentibus, quo sic revera tandem elapso alius Mauritius Burdinus, Hispanus Archiepiscopus Bracarensis ab Imperatore electus fuit, narrante haec fusius Baron. ad an. 1118. n. 6. seqq. statutumque, ita pergit n. 12. quasi novum simulachrum in loco Papae. Ecce recidivo vulnere recidimus in typum antiquum; Sed Imperator cum frustra aliquandiu in obsidione cujusdam Castelli haesisset, resumente Papa vires, atque auctis ejus auxiliatoribus, in Alemanniam redit, idolo, quod plasmaverat, in urbe relicto; Papa tamen regressus atque cantando proditus denuo in pericula incidit, sui jacula mandata remandant, ensis atteritur ense, lancea retusa retundit; hic pedites, illic milites cadunt, undique strati, undique pugna gravis; sed Papa tandem Gelasius solus, quantum equus poterat, fugere rursus de fuga consultavit: Fugiamus, inquiebat, Sodomam, fugiamus Aegyptum, fugiamus novam, juxta verbum Propheticum Babyloniam, civitatem sanguinum fugiamus; in exilio etiam anno sequenti, in monasterio Cluniacensi mortuus est. Cui post aliquot dies Guido natione Francus Archiepiscopus Viennensis & Cardinalis successor datus est, huicque nomen Callisti II. impositum, quo in urbem anno sequente adventante, Burdinus sperans se ab ipso Imperatore fovendum, apud Sutrium confugium fecit, eiusque munitione se continuit, qui tamen anno sequente nimirum 1121. ibi a Callisto magno cum exercitu obsessus, expugnato castello captus, atque Camelo ex adverso, data ei pro fraeno in manibus cauda, impositus & pilosa pelle vervecis proclamyde rubea indutus, sic omnibus eum blasphemiis incessentibus, in urbem introductus, inde in arcem Fummonis primum, inde vero in monasterium Cavense ad poenitentiam translatus fuit, sed in sua rebellione, inquit Pandulphus, permansit incautus (Bar. in cunctis) qui & in his Papae Clementiam laudat.
units.tr: LX. The twenty-fifth schism was between Gelasius II and Gregory VIII. For when Gelasius was elected, the gathering of the Fathers was violently broken up by Centius Frangipane, who stood on the side of Emperor Henry. The pope himself was treated badly, much as the others had been, and was chained up at home by him. But after a revolt of the citizens he was restored to liberty not long afterwards. He did not remain safe for long, however, for when a rumour arose of Emperor Henry's coming, he had to flee with his followers. The Germans pursued them, and they stopped the pursuit only on the oath that the pope had escaped. Once he had in fact been got away, another, Maurice Burdinus, the Spanish Archbishop of Braga, was elected by the Emperor. Baronius relates this more fully at 1118 n.6 and following, and he goes on at n.12: "as if a new image had been put in the place of the pope. Behold, with a recurring wound we are relapsing into the old type." But the Emperor, after having stuck for some time in vain at the siege of a certain castle, while the pope regained strength and his supporters increased, returned to Germany, leaving the idol he had made in the city. The pope, however, came back, and having been betrayed by singing, fell again into danger. Their missiles returned their orders, the sword was worn down by the sword, the lance was blunted by blunting. Here foot-soldiers, there knights, fell; everywhere men lay low, everywhere the fighting was grim. But at last Gelasius alone, as far as his horse could carry him, again considered flight: "Let us flee," he said, "to Sodom, let us flee to Egypt, let us flee to the new Babylon, according to the prophetic word; let us flee the city of blood." He died in exile the following year, in the monastery of Cluny. Some days later Guido, a Frenchman, Archbishop of Vienne and Cardinal, was given as successor, and he took the name Callistus II. When he came to the city the following year, Burdinus, hoping to be protected by the Emperor himself, took refuge at Sutri and kept himself under its fortifications. Yet in the following year, 1121, he was besieged there by Callistus with a great army. The castle was taken and he was captured. He was set on a camel facing backwards, with a tail given him in his hands as a bridle, and clothed in a red cloak made of shaggy sheepskin. Thus, with everyone pouring blasphemies on him, he was led into the city. From there he was first taken to the citadel of Fumone, and then to the monastery of Cava for penance. "But in his rebellion," says Pandulf, "he remained unrepentant" (Baronius, in cunctis). Pandulf also praises the clemency of the pope in this matter.

units.la: LXI. Atque ita tandem & hoc Schisma sublatum fuit, quod quasi continuatio prioris erat, de quo proin etiam ex iisdem causis, simili vi, partium simili studio, similique Christianorum incertitudine idem ferri debet judicium. Atque sub Callisto demum, docente cente Onuphrio annot. in Calist. inter Imperium & Sacerdotium insignis illa pax & concordia facta est, anno plus minus quinquagesimo, ex quo inter Gregorium VII. & Henricum IV. discordia ingens ob Sacerdotiorum collationes excitata fuerat. In qua Episcoporum & Abbatum electiones, quae ad Imperatorem & Reges hactenus pertinuerent, Clero & Monachis restituta sunt. Qui & in hanc rem pictD0ram antiquam allegat, cum elogio:
units.tr: LXI. And so at last this schism too was ended. It was a continuation of the earlier one, and for the same reasons, with similar violence, similar partisan zeal and similar uncertainty among Christians, the same judgment ought to be passed on it. And under Callistus, as Onuphrius teaches in his note on Callistus, that remarkable peace and concord between Empire and Priesthood was made, about fifty years after the great discord that had been stirred up between Gregory VII and Henry IV over the conferring of priesthoods. By this settlement the elections of bishops and abbots, which had until then belonged to the Emperor and the kings, were restored to the clergy and the monks. He also cites an ancient picture on this matter, with an inscription:

units.la: Ecce Callistus Patriae decus, honor imperialeNequam Burdinum damnat, pacemque reformat.
units.tr: Behold Callistus, the glory of the fatherland, the honour of the empire. He condemns the wicked Burdinus and restores peace.

units.la: Sed brevis illa fuit, eo enim mortuo statim exortum est
units.tr: But that peace was short. For on his death a new schism at once arose

units.la: LXII. Schisma Vicesimum sextum inter Honorium II. & Cœlestinum II.
units.tr: LXII. The twenty-sixth schism, between Honorius II and Celestine II.

units.la: Cujus historiam ex Baronio, atque, ex quo sua confirmat, Pandulpho Subdiacono, qui etiam inter fuit, dabimus. Ita ille ad an. 1124. n. 7. Ubi autem sepultus est Callistus Papa, de electione Successoris agi coeptum, sed non sine formidine, cum Cardinales memores essent tyrannidis Frangipanum, quam adversus Gelasium ante septennium tanto Apostolicae Sedis opprobrio exercuissent, quorum adhuc vigere vires, animositatemque magis magisque incaluisse cognoscerent. Sed etsi perditissimus ille malorum auctor animum non mutavit, viam (viam) tamen aliam aggressus est, nimirum ut non violentia, sed dolo atque fallaciis ageret, paratus etiam, si opus esset, agere violentia, si suo ipsius conatui, qui resisterent, invenisset.
units.tr: We shall give its history from Baronius, and from Pandulf the subdeacon, who was himself present and whose words Baronius uses to confirm his own account. Thus he writes under the year 1124, no. 7: When Pope Callistus was buried, the election of a successor began to be discussed, but not without fear, since the cardinals remembered the tyranny of the Frangipani, which they had exercised against Gelasius seven years earlier to the great shame of the Apostolic See, and they perceived that the strength of that family was still alive and its animosity growing ever hotter. But although that most depraved author of evils did not change his purpose, he took up another way: to act not by violence but by trickery and deceit, and to be ready to use violence as well, if he should find anyone resisting his attempt.

units.la: LXIII. Atque ista porro sequentibus Pandulfi verbis confirmat:
units.tr: LXIII. And he further confirms these points with the following words of Pandulfus:
