units.la: Lambertus Ostiensis Episcopus de mediocri plebe Comitatus Bononiensis genitus, bene tamen litteratus, a Domino Papa Paschali receptus est, & in Episcopum Velitrensem promotus. Religiosa autem memoria Callisto Papa defuncto, omnes Patres de Curia Cardinales, & alii, praesertim vero Petrus Leonis, & Leo Frangipanis pariter condixerunt, ut usque ad diem tertium una simul juxta scita sacrorum Canonum pertractarent, interim de electione nulla mentio haberetur. Hoc idcirco potissimum Leo Frangipanis condixerat, ut intra datum spatium, quod de Lamberto diutius cogitaverat, aliquando quiete perficeret: nam totus populus Saxonem (legendum putavit Baronius; Saxium; Sed & Platina habet; Saxonem) Anagninum S. Stephani in monte Caelio Cardinalem Papam fieri petebat: quos ut deciperet idem Leo Frangipanis, itidem velle simulabat. In sero autem praesenti idem Leo per nuntios unumquemque seorsum de Capellanis Cardinalium pramonet, ut mane summo diluculo cum pluviali rubeo, sub cappa nigra venirent, & ita non ignorante Domino, eundem suum dominum introducerent. Istud vero propter hoc ingenium adinvenit, nit, quatenus singulos pro accipiendo de manibus ejus Papatu attentiores redderet, & sic saltem absque timore venirent; Etenim quod est factum Gelasio, recordantes, convenire timebant. Tandem in castrum ita illecti Papam facturi conveniunt ad B. Joannis Basilicam & in Ecclesia Oratorium, quod S. Pancratii dicitur, intrârunt. Ubi post aliquot verba, Jonathas Sanctorum Cosmi & Damiani Diaconus Cardinalis, collaudantibus omnibus, ipso etiam Domino Lamberto Episcopo, Theobaldum Cardinalem Presbyterum S. Anastasia Cappa rubea induit, & Coelestinum appellat, ut coelitus missum. Non patitur Coelestinus (ego nescio cur aliquandiu noluerit) inceptum est: Te Deum laudamus, cani gaudenter, Lamberto Episcopo Ostiensi pariter nobiscum canente. Non tamen dimidiato adhuc, Robertus impius Frangipanis verti fecit in luctum Citharam. Etenim ipse cum quibusdam consentaneis suis, & aliquibus de curia Lambertum Ostiensem Episcopum Papam acclamârunt. Deinde in Simiis, qua ante Oratorium beati Sylvestri sita sunt, sine mora eum composuerunt. Unde licet maxima discordia & tumultus emergeret, tamen postea pacificationibus & ad concordiam redactis, Lambertus Cardinalis Ostiensis in Honorium Papam sublimatur.
units.tr: Lambert, Bishop of Ostia, was born of the common people of the County of Bologna, but he was well educated. Pope Paschal received him and promoted him to the bishopric of Velletri. When Pope Callistus of pious memory had died, all the Cardinals of the Curia, and others, but especially Peter Leo and Leo Frangipane, agreed together that they would deal with the matter jointly until the third day, according to the decrees of the sacred canons, and that in the meantime no mention would be made of an election. Leo Frangipane had agreed to this chiefly so that within the period given he might quietly bring to completion what he had long planned concerning Lambert. For the whole people were demanding that Saxo (Baronius thought it should read Saxius; but Platina also has Saxo) of Anagni, Cardinal of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, be made Pope. Leo Frangipane pretended that he too wished this, so as to deceive them. But that same evening, Leo sent messengers to each of the chaplains of the Cardinals separately, warning them to come very early in the morning, in a red cope under a black cloak, and so, with their lord not knowing, to bring in their master. He devised this scheme so that he might make each of them more eager to receive the papacy from his hands, and thus they would come without fear. For, recalling what had been done to Gelasius, they were afraid to assemble. At last, thus enticed, they met to make a Pope in the castle, and they entered the Basilica of St John and the oratory in the church called St Pancras. There, after some words, Jonathas, Deacon Cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, with everyone praising it, Lambert the Bishop himself included, clothed Theobald, Cardinal Priest of St Anastasia, in a red cope and named him Celestine, as one sent from heaven. Celestine did not permit it (I do not know why he was for some time unwilling), and the singing was begun: "We praise you, O God," sung joyfully, with Lambert, Bishop of Ostia, singing along with us. But before it was half finished, the impious Robert Frangipane turned the harp to mourning. For he himself, with certain of his associates and some from the Curia, acclaimed Lambert, Bishop of Ostia, as Pope. Then, without delay, they set him down among the apes, which stand in front of the oratory of blessed Sylvester. Hence, although the greatest discord and tumult arose, afterwards, once pacifications had been made and concord restored, Lambert, Cardinal of Ostia, was raised to the papacy as Honorius.

units.la: LXIV. Addit n. 8. ex Codice Vaticano: Sed quia electio Honorii minùs Canonicè praecesserat; post septem dies, nempe 28. Decembris, in conspectu fratrum sponte mitram & mantum refutavit, atque deposuit.
units.tr: LXIV. Note 8 adds, from the Vatican manuscript: But because the election of Honorius had proceeded less canonically, seven days later, namely on 28 December, in the sight of the brethren, he of his own accord renounced and laid down the mitre and the mantle.

units.la: Fratres tam Episcopi, quàm Presbyteri & Diaconi Cardinales videntes ipsius humilitatem, & prospicientes in posterum, ne in Romanam Ecclesiam aliquam inducerent novitatem, quod perperam factum fuerat, & in melius reformârunt, & eundem denuò advocantes ad ejus vestigia prociderunt, & tanquam Pastori suo, & universali Papa consuetam obedientiam exhibuerunt.
units.tr: The brethren, both bishops and presbyter and deacon Cardinals, seeing his humility, and looking ahead, lest they introduce any novelty into the Roman Church, corrected what had been done wrongly and reformed it for the better. Calling him back again, they fell at his feet and rendered him the customary obedience, as to their own minister and universal Pope.

units.la: LXV. En igitur rursus electionem duorum! Alter, qui non obtinuit, legitimè atque prior ab Anti-Papa quoque electus fuisse deprehenditur; alter, juxta Codicem minùs Canonicè, & sua existimatione, judice Baronio n. 7. turpissimam notam inussit, quòd post alterius electionem se eligi & Pontificalibus indui passus sit, & non adeò laudatur, docente Platina, qui & quoad specialia consentanea habet, in vita, ejus ingressus, cùm ambitione quorundam potiùs quàm omnium bonorum consensu Pontificatum inierit; ambitione nimirum perditissimi omnium malorum auctoris dolo atque fallaciis agentis, vim adhibere parati; ita ut Cithara in luctum versa fuerit; Neque quae de electione altera adjiciunt, legitimam fuisse docent; cùm facilè colligi possit. sit, eodem, quo Vigilius rursus electus fingitur, animo, hunc se eligi denuò passum esse, sive potiùs curâsse, reliqui enim in loco certè non tuto atque metu Frangipanum, ipse etiam ante electus cessisse facilè agnoscuntur; sed septimo demum die aliter electus fuit Honorius, per aliquot igitur dies illegitimus atque Idolum, quamvis, ut patet, non per aliquot duntaxat dies.
units.tr: LXV. Behold, then, the election of two men again! The first, who did not obtain the papacy, is shown to have been lawfully and earlier elected even by the Anti-Pope. The second, according to the manuscript, was elected less canonically and, by his own judgment and that of Baronius (note 7), branded himself with a most shameful mark, in that after the other's election he allowed himself to be elected and clothed in the pontifical vestments. Nor is he much praised, as Platina teaches, who in his life also says that he entered the papacy more through the ambition of certain men than through the consent of all good men: that is, by the ambition of him, the most desperate author of all evils, who acts by guile and deceit, and who was ready to use force; so that the harp was turned to mourning. Nor do those who add the other election teach that it was lawful, since it can easily be gathered that Vigilius is feigned to have been elected again with the same intention, that he allowed himself to be elected again, or rather arranged it. For the rest, in a place certainly not safe and out of fear of Frangipane, were easily seen to have given way, and he himself had earlier been elected and had withdrawn. But Honorius was at last elected otherwise, on the seventh day; therefore for some days he was an unlawful man and an idol, though, as is clear, not only for some days.

units.la: LXVI. Schisma vicesimum septimum fuit inter Innocentium II. & Anacletum II, hujusque successorem Victorem IV.
units.tr: LXVI. The twenty-seventh schism was between Innocent II and Anacletus II, and Anacletus's successor Victor IV.

units.la: Mortuo enim Honorio, pars Innocentium, sive, ut antea vocabatur, Gregorium Joannis Guidonis filium de Papa, de regione Transtyberim Canonicum regularem Lateranensem, Romanum, Priorem Diaconorum S. Angeli ab Urbano II. factum, pars Anacletum, sive, nomine quoque priori, Petrum Petri Leonis filium, ex Diacono Cardinale S. S. Cosmae & Damiani à Paschali II. facto, Presbyterum Cardinalem tit. S. Mariae Transtyberim à Calisto II. ordinatum, elegerunt, & quidem, teste Onuphrio, 17. Cardinales Innocentium, 21. verò Anacletum. Ut jam eatenus melior appareat causa Anacleti, quia more & constitutionibus antiquis in electionibus major numerus vincit.
units.tr: For when Honorius had died, one party elected Innocent, or, as he was formerly called, Gregory, son of John Guido, of the Papa family, of the Transtiberine region, a Roman regular canon of the Lateran, made Prior of the Deacons of St Angelo by Urban II. The other party elected Anacletus, or, under his earlier name, Peter, son of Peter Leo, formerly Deacon Cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, made by Paschal II, and ordained Cardinal Priest of the title of St Mary across the Tiber by Callistus II. And indeed, according to Onuphrius, 17 Cardinals elected Innocent, but 21 elected Anacletus. So far, then, the cause of Anacletus appears the better, because by ancient custom and constitutions in elections the greater number prevails.

units.la: LXVII.
units.tr: LXVII.

units.la: Proponemus autem Schismatis maximè confusi historiam ex ipso Baronio. Oborta sunt, inquit ad an. 1130. n. 2. factiones, studia, simultates, conspirationes, ira, rixa, contentiones, cùm in eos, qui jure contradicerent, vis publica ministraret arma bellica. Tunc enim plebs Classico excitata potentium eò properat, quò fures vocat ambitio, & provocat spes avida lucri. Sicq; ejus, cujus scirent horrea esse oppleta, nummis arcas refertas, promptuaria plena eructantia ex hoc in illud, favent electioni, quam labantem nec subsistentem clamoribus obnixè sustentant, minis roborant terroribúsque stabiliunt, ut nemo palam Papam alium vel nominare praesumeret, praeter eum, quem factiosa tyrannis evexerat, ac metus retinere compelleret &c. En Tibi, Lector, populi Romani genium, qui certè & aliâs se prodidit, atque malos dedit Pontifices ita malè electos! Populóne ejusmodi Deus per tot secula electionem Vicarii sui universalis commisisse dicendus est? Pergit Baronius n. 3. Hoc statu miserando collocata erat tunc temporis Romana Ecclesia, in qua triumphans Antichristus, cogeretur verus Christi Vicarius exulare, in templo Sancto, in Petri throno abominatione sedente. Hoc igitur Romae accidere potest! Subjungit, de depraedationibus Templorum per Anacletianos factis, itcm de largitionibus, violentia, atque fuga Innocentii; inocentii; Et tandem n. 5. Perfacile erat cuique intelligere, quis legitimus, quis verò spurius esset Papa; quis Successor Petri, quis Synagoga Satanæ Antichristus, quis pastor, quis verò fur & latro, qui non nisi ut perdat & macted, in ovile ovium intrat. Verùm id non tam facilè fuisse intelligere, ex sequentibus patebit, ex eo nimirum quòd sceleris puri esse voluerunt, omnia legitima jactârunt, similiter accusârunt, complures fuerunt, víxque licuit absentibus maximè, quibus tamen æquè obedire alterutri, alterutrum quoque execrari incumbebat, dignoscere, uter potior esset.
units.tr: We shall set out the history of this most confused schism from Baronius himself. Factions, rivalries, hatreds, conspiracies, anger, quarrels and contentions arose, he says at the year 1130, no. 2, when public force supplied weapons of war against those who lawfully opposed the election. For then the common people, roused by the trumpet call, hurried to where ambition summons thieves and eager hope of gain provokes them. And so, knowing where the granaries were stuffed, the chests crammed with money and the storerooms bursting with produce, they favoured the election, which was wavering and not standing firm. By shouts they vigorously upheld it, by threats they strengthened it and by terrors they made it secure, so that no one dared openly to name any other pope except the one whom factious tyranny had raised up, and fear compelled them to hold back, etc. Behold, reader, the character of the Roman people, which has certainly revealed itself on other occasions too, and has given us wicked popes so badly elected! Must we say that God committed the election of his universal Vicar for so many ages to a people of this kind? Baronius goes on at no. 3: In such a wretched state the Roman Church was then placed, in which triumphant Antichrist forced the true Vicar of Christ into exile, while the abomination sat in the holy temple, on Peter's throne. So this can happen at Rome! He adds an account of the plundering of churches carried out by the Anacletians, likewise of the bribery, violence and flight of Innocent; and finally, at no. 5: It was perfectly easy for anyone to understand which was the lawful pope and which the spurious one; who was the successor of Peter and who the synagogue of Satan's Antichrist; who was the shepherd and who the thief and robber, who enters the sheepfold only to destroy and slaughter. But that it was not so easy to understand, as will become clear from what follows, namely because they were determined to be wholly guilty, each claimed everything lawful for himself and each similarly accused the other, there were many of them, and it was hardly possible, especially for those who were absent, to discern which of the two had the better claim, although it was incumbent on them to obey either equally and likewise to execrate the other.

units.la: LXVIII. Atque illa insuper ipsa scissio vitium habuit. De Anacleto Baronius n. 6. porrò narrat, quòd Bernhardus eum abominationem stantem in loco sancto vocârit, eúmque semel atque iterum Antichristo, Bestiæ Apocalypticæ comparârit, atque de eodem ad Episcopos Aquitaniæ ep. 126. scripserit: Velimus, nolimus, impleri quandoque necesse est veritatem. Spiritu prænuntiata legitur in scripturis discessio: sed væ homini, per quem erit. Quis verò ille, nisi homo peccati, qui super electum à Catholicis Catholicum & Canonicè, locum sanctum invasit? Quem tamen non quia sanctus, sed quia summus est, affectavit. Invasit inquam, invasit armis, igne, pecunia, non vitæ merito vel virtutum pervenit, in quo stat, & stat, in quo pervenit. Nam illa, quam jactat, juratorum suorum, non electio, sed factio, umbra tantùm fuit & occasio & velamentum malitiæ. LXIX. Hæc quidem & alia habet pro Innocentio contra Anacletum, sed & pro Anacleto contra Innocentium epistolas ad Principes & Episcopos, quarum unicam tantùm heic apponere visum fuit, ut ex ea de cæteris judicium ferri possit, atque, nec alteram partem sibi defuisse. Petrus Portuensis Episcopus Anacleti promotor quatuor Episcopis Cardinalibus partis Innocentii in hunc modum scripsit: Quanta sit pro vobis tribulatio cordis mei, ille solus novit, qui omnia novit. Vobis quoque meis literis cognitum saltem ex parte fuisset, nisi Ecclesia sententia & communis auctoritas prohiberet. De Commendatione, seu vituperatione personarum, de quibus nunc sermonum varietas agitatur, non est hujus temporis judicare, est qui quærat & judicet. Si tamen quisquam præsto fuerit accusare: præsto erit & qui debeat respondere: præsertim, cùm in vestro & meo, imò in totius Ecclesiæ conspectu uterque sapienter vixerit & honestè, & quæ officii sui erat, plena hucusque exercuerit libertate. Abstinere vos potiùs convenit à sermonibus otiosis & verbis præcipitationis. Si de rumoribus agitur: longè se aliter habent res, quàm vestra vestra apud me protestantur litera. Adhæc si verba, quæ posuistis, sic ordinis rationem attenditis (ut salvâ reverentiâ vestrâ loquar) factionem illam vestram quâ confidentiâ, quâ fronte electionem vocare præsumitis? Cur illum vestrum dicitis ordinatum, cùm prorsus in causa ejus ordo non fuerit? Siccine didicistis Papam eligere? In angulo, in abscondito, in tenebris, & umbra mortis? Si mortuo Papa vivum succedere volebatis: cur mortuum vivere prædicabatis? Multò melius erat, mortuo humanitatem impendere & sic de vivi solatio cogitare. Sed ecce dum de mortuo solatium vivo requiritis; & vivum & mortuum pariter suffocatis. Postremò nec vestrum, sicut nec meum, fuit eligere; sed potius electum à fratribus spernere vel approbare. Quia igitur &c. vide Differt. IV. Sect. 2. n. 114. Hanc ego electionem Canonicè celebratam conspexi &, auctore Deo, confirmavi. Hunc Ecclesia suscipit & veneratur: hunc per Dei gratiam Episcopi, & Abbates, Principes, Capitanei & Barones, quidam per se ipsos, quidam per nuncios suos, videntibus nobis frequentant. Depradationem illam & crudelitatem, quam prætenditis, non videmus. Quicunque ad eum pro responsis, seu negotiis suis veniunt, benignè suscipiuntur, benigniùs revertuntur. Redite jam, redite ad Cor. Nolite Schisma in Ecclesia facere ad animarum subversionem, nolite ulterius laborare, teneat vos timor Domini, non pudor sæculi. Numquid qui dormit, non adjiciet ut resurgat? Desistite mendaciis, in quibus impii spem suam ponere consueverunt &c. Hæc fuit sententia mea, ut nonnisi sepulto Papa, de successoris persona mentio haberetur. Unitatem Ecclesiæ tenui & tenebo; veritatis & justitiæ adhærere curabo, confidenter sperans, quòd justitia & veritas liberabit me.
units.tr: LXVIII. Moreover, that very split was itself a fault. Baronius, no. 6, goes on to relate that Bernard called Anacletus an abomination standing in the holy place, and more than once compared him to Antichrist, the beast of the Apocalypse, and wrote about him to the bishops of Aquitaine, ep. 126: Whether we wish it or not, the truth must sometime be fulfilled. The division was foretold by the Spirit in the Scriptures, but woe to the man through whom it comes. Who, then, is that man, if not the man of sin, who has invaded the holy place, which was lawfully and canonically chosen by Catholics, and who has aimed at it not because he is holy but because he is highest? He invaded, I say, he invaded with arms, fire and money; he did not attain it by the merit of his life or his virtues; he stands where he has got to, and he stands in it. For that election which he boasts of, made by his own sworn men, was not an election but a faction, only a shadow, an occasion and a veil of malice. LXIX. These and other things he holds for Innocent against Anacletus, but he also holds for Anacletus against Innocent letters to princes and bishops, of which only one has been thought fit to set out here, so that a judgement may be formed from it about the others, and so that it may be seen that the other side was not lacking in its own case. Peter, bishop of Porto and promoter of Anacletus, wrote to four cardinal bishops of Innocent's party in this manner: How great is my heart's distress over you, he alone knows who knows all things. Even to you, by my letters, this would have been made known at least in part, were it not for the judgement of the Church and her common authority forbidding it. To commend or to disparage persons, about whom there is now such a variety of talk, is not for this time to judge; there are those who will inquire and judge. Yet if anyone is ready to accuse, there will also be someone ready to answer, especially since in your sight and mine, indeed in the sight of the whole Church, each of them has lived wisely and honourably, and has exercised the freedom proper to his office, full and unbroken until now. It becomes you rather to abstain from idle talk and hasty words. If it is a matter of rumours, things stand quite otherwise than your letter, which you say is addressed to me, declares. Moreover, if you pay such attention to the order of procedure (with respect to you, let me say it), with what confidence and what face do you presume to call that faction of yours an election? Why do you say that he was ordained by you, when in his case there was no order at all? Is this how you learned to elect a pope? In a corner, in secret, in darkness and the shadow of death? If you wanted a living successor to a dead pope, why did you proclaim that the dead man was alive? It would have been far better to pay the dead man the due of humanity and then think of comfort from the living. But look, while you seek comfort from the living for the dead, you suffocate both the living and the dead alike. Finally, it was neither yours nor mine to elect; it was rather for the brothers to elect and then to reject or approve. Because therefore etc. See Dissertation IV, section 2, no. 114. I have seen this election canonically celebrated and, God helping, I have confirmed it. The Church receives him and venerates him; by the grace of God, bishops and abbots, princes, captains and barons, some in person and some through their envoys, visit him, as we ourselves have seen. That plundering and cruelty which you allege we do not see. Whoever comes to him for answers or for their business is kindly received and returns more kindly still. Come back now, come back to your heart. Do not create a schism in the Church to the ruin of souls; do not labour any further; let the fear of the Lord hold you, not the shame of the world. Will he who sleeps not add that he may rise again? Give up the lies in which the wicked are wont to put their hope, etc. This was my judgement: that mention of a successor should be made only after the pope had been buried. I have kept and will keep the unity of the Church; I will take care to hold to truth and justice, confidently hoping that justice and truth will set me free.

units.la: LXX. Proximo Paschate, pergit Baronius n. 12. Anacletus solemni ritu excommunicavit Innocentium & ei adhærentes Cadinales, dignitatéque privavit & alios plurimos, sed & novos in veteribus titulis substituit Cardinales; ordinationibus aliquot, ait Onuphrius, Cardinales X. Presbyteros V. & Diaconos V. Subjungit Baronius n. 12. seqq. epistolas pro Anacleto alias Dei beneficio, ut n. 6. dixerat, hactenus conservatas, ut nimirum ex illis constare posset, partem Anacleti se suâque æquè defendere contrariámque partem accusare potuisse, imò, quod ex epistola supra posita liquet, de mendaciis conquestos esse; quod docet, non nimium fidendum esse accusationibus contrà eum institutis, maximè cùm tandem loco cedere debuerit, atque semper in gratiam obtinentium scribi soleat. Epistolas autem subjungit ad Lotharium Regem Innocentii, in qua conqueritur, quosdam de fraudibus, loco & tempore vitiosos, & paucissimos numero, quorundam perfidorum blandis astutiis suffocatos, aliud altare eligere &c. Cardinalium unâ cum aliis universóque Clero Romano & Episcopis ad eundem; rursus Anacleti ad eundem, ad Reginam; Magistratus & plebis urbis ad Lotharium denuò, Anacleti ad Regem Francorum, ad alios binas, Legationem Gregorii Card. Diac. in Galliam; epistolas ad Cluniacenses, ad universam Aquitaniae Ecclesiam; ad Imperatorem Constantinopolitanum & Regem Hierosol. cum nunciis; Idem, referente Baronio n. 49. Pontificalibus quoque functionibus apparere Pontifex affectavit: utpote qui celebravit Romae Concilium ex sibi cohaerentibus Episcopis, creavit mox Cardinales, excommunicavit &c. Sed & imitatione praedecessorum, praesertim verò Callisti secundi, qui plura in Urbe consecravit altaria, ipse voluit eadem laude digna peragere. Dedicata nàmque legimus Romae nonnulla ab eo & consecrata fuisse altaria, & eorum in curià servatas adhuc inscriptiones, quas delendas curavimus &c. Eidem n. 51. Rogerius Dux atque Calsi-nenses conjuncti fuisse dicuntur; ille juxta n. 52. ab eodem Rex creatus fuit, atque adeò, volente Baronio n. 53. Auctor Siculae Monarchiae extitit; sed anno 1138. homo peccati, loquitur. Baronius n. 1. invasor Apostolicae Sedis Petrus Leonis Pseudo-Papa, Deo vindice, ex hac vita divulsus ad supernum horrificum tribunal judicandus atque condemnandus adducitur, accepturus cruciatum aeternum; postquam sedisset, ut idem ibidem ex Falcone illius temporis scriptore in Chronico Beneventano subjicit, annis septem, mensibus undecim, & diebus viginti duobus. Sepultus fuit, juxta Onuphrium, Laterani; Successorem nactus est Gregorium Presbyterum Cardinalem in Basilica XII. Apostolorum à Cardinalibus illius partis electum, qui tamen mox Innocentio se subjecit, & qualis ante erat, mansit. Jam verò ex dictis constare potest, hoc etiam schisma ambiguitate suâ perplexum atque naevis valdè scatens fuisse. Anacletus autem vindicatus apud M. Ant. de Dominis videri potest. Ipse Onuphrius l. 2. p. 107. Innocentio tribuit, quòd suffragia sua pecuniâ emerit, adeóque artibus Simoniacis sedem Romanam invaserit.
units.tr: LXX. At the next Easter, Baronius goes on at no. 12, Anacletus solemnly excommunicated Innocent and the cardinals who adhered to him, and deprived them of their dignity, and also many others; and he substituted new cardinals in the old titles: with several ordinations, says Onuphrius, ten cardinals, five presbyters and five deacons. Baronius continues at no. 12 and following with other letters written for Anacletus, which, as he said at no. 6, had been preserved until now by God's kindness, so that it might be clear from them that his side could defend itself and its cause equally well, and accuse the other side; indeed, as the letter set out above makes plain, they complained of lies, which shows that the accusations brought against him should not be trusted too much, especially since in the end he had to give way, and since what is written is usually written in favour of whoever holds power. He adds a letter to Lothair, the king, from Innocent, in which he complains that a few men, few in number and vitiated by their fraud, place and time, have been stifled by the smooth cunning of certain traitors, and have chosen another altar, etc. There is a letter from the cardinals, together with the others and the whole Roman clergy and bishops, to the same king; again one from Anacletus to the same king, and to the queen; a letter from the magistrates and the people of the city to Lothair again; letters from Anacletus to the King of the Franks and to others, two in number; the legation of Gregory, cardinal deacon, into Gaul; letters to the Cluniacs and to the whole Church of Aquitaine; and to the emperor of Constantinople and the King of Jerusalem, with messengers. The same man, according to Baronius at no. 49, was eager to appear in the pontifical functions too, as one who celebrated a council at Rome of bishops adhering to him, and soon created cardinals, excommunicated, etc. But also in imitation of his predecessors, especially Calixtus II, who consecrated many altars in the city, he wished to perform the same praiseworthy acts. For we read that some altars were dedicated and consecrated at Rome by him, and that their inscriptions are still preserved in the curia, which we have taken care to have erased, etc. At no. 51 Roger, duke, and the men of Calabria are said to have been joined with the same man; by no. 52 Roger was made king by him, and so, as Baronius wishes at no. 53, he became the author of the Sicilian monarchy; but in the year 1138 he speaks of the man of sin. Baronius, at no. 1: Peter Leonis, the usurper of the Apostolic See, the pseudo-pope, is torn from this life by God's avenging hand and led to the dread heavenly tribunal to be judged and condemned, to receive eternal torment; after he had sat, as Baronius himself adds there from Falco, a writer of that time, in the Chronicle of Benevento, for seven years, eleven months and twenty-two days. He was buried, according to Onuphrius, at the Lateran; he was succeeded by Gregory, presbyter cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, elected by the cardinals of that party, who nevertheless soon submitted to Innocent and remained as he had been before. Now it can be gathered from what has been said that this schism too was entangled in its own ambiguity and was very full of blemishes. Anacletus may be seen vindicated by Marcantonio de Dominis. Onuphrius himself, book 2, p. 107, charges Innocent with having bought his votes with money, and so having invaded the Roman see by simoniacal arts.

units.la: LXXI. Schisma vicesimum octavum fuit inter Alexandrum III. ab una, Victorem IV. ejusque successores Paschalem III. Calistum III. & Innocentium III. ab altera parte.
units.tr: LXXI. The twenty-eighth schism was between Alexander III on one side and Victor IV, together with his successors Paschal III, Callistus III and Innocent III, on the other.

units.la: Mortuo enim Hadriano IV. cum quo graves lites Imperator Fridericus Barbarossa exercuerat, major Cardinalium pars Rolandum, Cancellarium, Senensem, cujus jus hostilis erga Imperatorem animus jam sub Hadriano patebat, elegit eique nomen Alexandri III. imposuit, reliquis novem in Octavianum, Presbyterum Cardinalem tit. S. Clementis, Romanum, Caesaris amicum sub nomine Victoris IV. consentientibus, qui etiam consecratus fuit, atque à suis adoratus. Ipse verò, inquit Auctor Actorum Alexandri apud Baron. ad an. 1159. n. 33: Antichristi tempora praefigurans, usque adeò erectus est super se, ut in Templo Dei sederet tanquam sit Deus, umbrâ Papali ostendens se, tanquam sit verus Papa.
units.tr: When Hadrian IV died, with whom Emperor Frederick Barbarossa had waged bitter disputes, the greater part of the cardinals chose Roland, the chancellor, a Sienese whose hostile feeling towards the Emperor had already been evident under Hadrian. They gave him the name Alexander III. Nine of the others, with the consent of the remaining cardinals, chose Octavian, a Roman priest and cardinal of the title of St Clement, a friend of the Emperor, under the name Victor IV. He was also consecrated and was adored by his followers. He himself, says the author of the Acts of Alexander, cited by Baronius at the year 1159, no. 33, foreshadowing the times of Antichrist, so exalted himself that he sat in the Temple of God as if he were God, showing by a papal shadow that he was the true Pope.

units.la: LXXII. Dedit etiam indicante Baronio n. 41: literas ad Imperatorem, & omnes Orthodoxos Episcopos, atque junctim ad Patriarchas, Archiepiscopos, Abbates, Duces, Marchiones, Comites & cateros Principes, & egregiam familiam Imperialem in sacratissima Curia Domini Friderici Serenissimi ac invictissimi Romanorum Imperatoris commorantes,
units.tr: LXXII. Baronius, at no. 41, indicates that he also sent letters to the Emperor and to all the orthodox bishops, and jointly to the patriarchs, archbishops, abbots, dukes, marquises, counts and other princes, and to the distinguished imperial household staying at the most sacred court of the lord Frederick, the most serene and invincible Emperor of the Romans.

units.la: in quibus ultimis literis se Deo auctore, ad dignitatem tantam conscendisse ait, Imperatorem commonendo rogari vult, quatenus Imperio sibi à Divina Clementia commisso, & Ecclesiae Dei Sponsae Jesu Christi, cujus Advocatus & defensor est divinitus constitutus, providere & subvenire non tardet, ne in tanta discordia adversariorum malitia nequiter pravalere, navicula B. Petri procellis & tempestatibus suo tempore quassari, & decus Imperiale valeat aliquatenus obnubilari. Insuper, inquit, Universitati Vestrae duximus intimandum, qualiter ad Apostolatús officium, Domino concedente, vocati fuerimus. Felicis memoriae Hadriano Pradecessore nostro viam universae carnis ingressso & in B. Petri Basilica tumulato, convenimus omnes de electione summi Pontificis tractaturi. Post longam verò collationem, & diutinam deliberationem, divinâ tandem inspirante clementiâ, electione Venerabilium fratrum nostrorum Episcoporum, Presbyterorum S. R. E. Cardinalium, Cleri quoque Romani petitione, ejusdem populi assensu, etiam Senatoriae dignitatis honoratorum, insuper Capitaneorum, ad summum Pontificatum, annuente Deo, Canonice sumus electi & in sede Apostolica collocati, ac deinde primâ Dominicâ mensis Octobris benedictionis consecrationem & nostri officii accepimus plenitudinem. Quocirca universitatem vestram humiliter deprecamur, quatenus nos apud ipsum precibus adjuvetis, à quo omnis est potestas & honor dignitatum. Si autem ex parte illius Rolandi quondam Cancellarii, per conspirationem & Conjurationem contra Ecclesiam Dei & Imperium Willelmo Siculo astricti, qui die duodecimâ post electionem nostram se fecit intrudi (quod à saeculis non est auditum) ad vos scripta provenerint, tanquam mendacio plena, & à schismatico & haeretico destinata respuatis, & aures vestras nequaquam illis ullatenus prabeatis.
units.tr: In these last letters he says that he had been raised by God's authority to so great a dignity, and he wishes to admonish the Emperor and request that he not delay to provide for and assist the empire committed to him by divine mercy, and the Church, the Bride of Jesus Christ, of which he has been divinely appointed advocate and defender, so that the malice of his adversaries in such great discord may not prevail wickedly, the little ship of St Peter may not in its time be shaken by storms and tempests, and the imperial glory may not be somewhat obscured. Moreover, he says, we thought it right to inform your community how, by the Lord's permission, we were called to the office of the apostolate. When our predecessor Hadrian of happy memory had entered the way of all flesh and been buried in the basilica of St Peter, we all met to deal with the election of the chief Pontiff. After a long consultation and lengthy deliberation, at last, with divine mercy inspiring, by the choice of our venerable brothers the bishops and the cardinal presbyters of the holy Roman Church, at the request also of the clergy of Rome, with the assent of the same people, and of those honoured with senatorial rank, and besides of the captains, we were canonically elected by God's will to the supreme Pontificate and placed in the apostolic see. Then, on the first Sunday of October, we received the blessing, the consecration and the fullness of our office. Therefore we humbly beseech your community that you help us with your prayers before him from whom comes all power and the honour of dignities. But if letters should come to you from the side of that Roland, formerly chancellor, who was bound by conspiracy and plot against the Church of God and the Empire to William of Sicily, and who on the twelfth day after our election had himself forced in (which has not been heard of in ages), reject them as full of lies and sent by a schismatic and heretic, and do not lend your ears to them in any way at all.

units.la: LXXIII. Similiter Cardinales ab Octaviano vel Victore IV. stantes ad Patriarchas &c. literas dederunt; in quibus Cardinales partis adversæ accusant, quòd in præsentia Hadriani manifestâ Conspiratione Willelmi fautores Sacramento firmaverint, personam Imperatoris excommunicationi subjiciendam; & ex tunc in antea ejus honori & voluntati usque ad mortem immutabiliter contraire; & si contingeret, Dominum Papam vitâ decedere, neminem se, nisi de illis, qui conjuraverant, in Pontificem eligere, circumpositos insuper Episcopos, ne alicui electo, nisi in quem Siculi secta consentiret, in consecratione manus imponerent, juramento nihilominus constrinxerunt. Ibidem etiam conjuratos quatuordecim, se novem numero fuisse atque Octavianum virum utique religiosum & honestum, ad regimen Apostolica sedis & ad concordia & pacis unitatem inter Ecclesiam & Imperium reformandam ac conservandam dignum & utilem esse cognoscentes, elegisse; tradunt; & quomodo adversa pars contra pacta sine communi consensu suum immantare voluerit atque tandem in Castro nomine Cisternam execraverit, narrant. Tandem Deum testem invocant, qui falli non potest, & si Angelus de cœlo aliud Evangelizaret, inquiunt, à veritate penitus aberraret; exhortantur etiam in Domino, quatenus neque per sermonem neque per epistolam à suo sensu moveantur, sed in veritate secum firmi & immobiles permaneant. LXXIV. Imperator verò ancipiti malo novi Schismatis permotus, loquitur Radevicus apud Bar. n. 49. consilio Principum, decrevit dare operam, ne quid exinde seu status Ecclesiæ, seu Respublica Imperii detrimenti caperet. Audiens itaque utrumque electum, in Episcopatûs ordinem consecratum, alterum ab altero excommunicationis sententiâ condemnatum: sine judicio Ecclesiæ controversiam terminari posse non putavit. Auctoritatem autem congregandi Concilii exemplo antiquorum Imperatorum, verbi causâ, Justiniani, Theodosii, Caroli sibi congruere putans, litisque decisionem legitimam esse non posse, nisi partibus hinc inde congregatis, considerans, utrumque per Legatos & literas vocavit; cùm autem Alexander (cui Imperator tanquam Cardinali scripserat) comparere nollet, in Concilio Papiensi anno sequenti habito, residentibus Episcopis, & Clero universo, rursus loquitur Radevicus apud Baronium ad an. 1160. n. 3. septem diebus causa ventilata est: tandemque Domino Octaviano, qui cùm præsens advenisset & haberet, qui partem suam defenderent, cessit litis victoria, & pro ipso Concilium sive curia dedit sententiam, condemnato Rolando & reprobato. Qui citatus legitimè Concilio se præsentare, contumaciter abnuisse dicebatur. Auctor tamen ille liberum Lectori de tota re judicium relinquendum putavit.
units.tr: LXXIII. Likewise the cardinals who stood with Octavian, or Victor IV, sent letters to the Patriarchs etc. In these letters the cardinals of the opposing party are accused of having, in the presence of Hadrian, by open conspiracy with the supporters of William, bound themselves by oath that the person of the Emperor should be subjected to excommunication, and that from then on they would unchangeably oppose his honour and will until death; and if it should happen that the lord Pope died, they would elect no one as Pontiff except from among those who had conspired; moreover, they also bound the surrounding bishops by oath not to lay hands on anyone chosen in consecration, unless it were the one to whom the faction of the Sicilian agreed. In the same place they hand down that the conspirators were fourteen in number, of whom nine, recognising Octavian as a man altogether religious and honourable, and worthy and useful for governing the apostolic see and for reforming and preserving the unity of concord and peace between Church and Empire, chose him; and they relate how the opposing side, contrary to the agreements and without common consent, wished to change its position, and at last cursed the Cisterna in the castle of that name. Finally they call God to witness, who cannot be deceived, and say that if an angel from heaven should preach otherwise, he would utterly wander from the truth; they also exhort them in the Lord that, neither by word nor by letter, they be moved from their opinion, but remain firm and unshaken with them in the truth. LXXIV. The Emperor, moved by the double evil of the new schism, as Radevicus speaks in Baronius at no. 49, by the counsel of the princes, resolved to take care that nothing of harm should come from it either to the state of the Church or to the commonwealth of the Empire. Hearing therefore that each of the two elected had been consecrated to the order of bishop, and that each had been condemned by the other with a sentence of excommunication, he did not think the controversy could be ended without the judgment of the Church. Thinking that the authority to summon a council fitted him, following the example of the ancient emperors, for instance Justinian, Theodosius and Charles, and considering that a lawful decision of the dispute could not be made unless both sides were gathered from either direction, he summoned both parties through legates and letters. But when Alexander, to whom the Emperor had written as to a cardinal, refused to appear, at the council held at Pavia the following year, with the bishops in attendance and the whole clergy, Radevicus speaks again, in Baronius at the year 1160, no. 3: the cause was debated for seven days. At last the victory of the case went to the lord Octavian, who had come in person and had men to defend his side; and the council or court gave sentence in his favour, Roland being condemned and rejected. It was said that he, having been lawfully summoned, obstinately refused to present himself before the council. That author, however, thought the reader should be left free to judge the whole matter.

units.la: LXXV. In Synodo quoque recitata epistola Canonicorum S. Petri pro Octaviano, quæ n. 4. seqq. In qua convenienter iis, quæ suprà ex epistolis aliis apposuimus, narratur, & conjuratio Alexandrinianorum & pactum de non eligendo nisi communi omnium consensu, & facta à saniori & meliori parte Cardinalium ex parte Dei omnipotentis & B. Principum Apostolorum Petri & Pauli atque totius Ecclesiæ auctoritate, dum Rolandum immantare vellent, prohibitio, & Cleri clamor: Dominum Octavianum eligite, per quem solum Ecclesia pacem potest habere; & silentium consensui æquipollens adversæ partis, electione Octaviani factâ, & Cardinalium, Judicum, Scriniariorum, Senatorum populíque Romani acclamatio: Papa Vittore, S. Pietro l'elegge; Id est; Papa Victor S. Petro electus. Alluditur etiam ad nomen loci supra memorati, in qua pars adversa ad tempus fuerit. Juste Cisternam adierunt, inquiunt, quia dereliquerunt fontem aquæ vivæ & foderunt sibi cisternas dissipatas, quæ continere non valent aquas. Provocatur denique ad Legatos Imperatoris, qui statum verum ipsi viderint; Testimonium vivæ vocis ex ordine suo missorum commendatur; Sermo ad Episcopos consecratos dirigitur, & tandem hocce clauditur: Omnipotentis sapientia Patris, qui novit & potest unire vota & voluntates omnium, doceat vos omnes & uniat ad confusionem Babylonicam destruendam, & Simoniam de Ecclesia propellendam, & pacem toti mundo desiderabilem in integrum reformandam.
units.tr: LXXV. In the synod also was read the letter of the canons of St Peter for Octavian, which is at no. 4 and following. In it, in agreement with what we have set out above from other letters, the conspiracy of the Alexandrians is related, and the agreement not to elect anyone except with the common consent of all; and the prohibition, made by the wiser and better part of the cardinals in the name of almighty God and of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, and by the authority of the whole Church, when they wished to change Roland's position; and the shout of the clergy: Elect the lord Octavian, through whom alone the Church can have peace; and the silence, equivalent to consent, of the opposing side when Octavian was elected, and the acclamation of the cardinals, judges, notaries, senators and people of Rome: Pope Victor, St Peter elects him; that is, Pope Victor, elected by St Peter. There is also an allusion to the name of the place mentioned above, where the opposing side had been for a time. They rightly went to the Cisterna, they say, because they forsook the fountain of living water and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water. Finally an appeal is made to the Emperor's legates, who saw the true state of affairs for themselves; the testimony of the living voice of those sent in their order is commended; an address is directed to the bishops who were consecrated, and at last it closes thus: May the wisdom of the almighty Father, who knows and is able to unite the wishes and wills of all, teach you all and unite you to destroy Babylonian confusion, to drive Simony out of the Church, and to reform in full the peace desired by the whole world.

units.la: LXXVI. Epistolæ subjicit Radevicus apud Bar. n.10. actionem Concilii, ubi legitima Victoris electio describitur, & testes longè plurimi pro ea introducuntur. N. 16. seqq. autem epistola Synodalis encyclica ex eodem Radevico apponitur, in qua gesta narrantur, sententia declaratur, item honor Victoris, & excommunicatio adversæ partis; atque idem Victor commendatur ad obedientiam, subscribentibus Patriarcha Aquilejensi, Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, Abbatum verò & Archipresbyterorum multitudine innumera, Longobardorum inæstimabili multitudine, Principibúsque Imperii Romani tam Tutonici, quàm Italici, Regibus item Angliæ, Hungariæ, Boemiæ, Daniæ consentientibus. N.20. seqq. epistola Imperatoris ad Episcopos Germaniæ, qui Synodo non interfuerant. N. 23. 24. epistola Eberhardi Babenbergensis ad Archiepiscopum scopum Salzburgensem. N.25. seqq. Henrici Præpositi ad eundem. Subsecuta sunt edicta Imperatoris de recipiendo Octaviano, quæ n.31. innuuntur.
units.tr: LXXVI. Radevicus, in Baronius at no. 10, appends to the letter the proceedings of the council, in which the lawful election of Victor is described and very many witnesses are brought forward in its favour. At no. 16 and following, the encyclical synodal letter is set out from the same Radevicus, in which the events are narrated, the sentence declared, the honour of Victor set forth, and the excommunication of the opposing party; and the same Victor is commended to obedience. It was signed by the patriarch of Aquileia, the archbishops and bishops, an innumerable number of abbots and archpresbyters, an incalculable multitude of Lombards, and the princes of the Roman Empire, both German and Italian; the kings of England, Hungary, Bohemia and Denmark also consented. At no. 20 and following is the Emperor's letter to the bishops of Germany who had not been present at the synod. At nos. 23 and 24 is the letter of Eberhard of Babenberg to the archbishop of Salzburg. At no. 25 and following is that of Henry the Provost to the same. Then followed the Emperor's edicts about receiving Octavian, which are hinted at in no. 31.

units.la: LXXVII. Sed postquam Alexander anno sequenti Eduardum Angliæ Regem Canonizâssęt, primùm etiam ab Anglia receptus fuit,quem paulatim & alia quædam Regna receperunt,& pro quo a.1163. Concilium Turonense habitum; Anno autem 1164. Victor mortuus est, atque infelicis memoriæ hæresiarcha, ut extat in Actis Alexandri apud Bar. ad an. istum n. 27. impœnitens & excommunicatus de hoc mundo migravit ad inferos. Sed mox Paschalis III. substitutus,juravitque Imperator ore proprio, sic eadem Acta narrant, super sancta Evangelia, quòd eum, ejúsque successores haberet Catholicos Papas; Alexandrum verò ac successores ejus semper schismaticos teneret.
units.tr: LXXVII. But after Alexander canonized King Edward of England the following year, he was first received in England, and certain other kingdoms gradually received him too. A council was held at Tours for him in 1163. In 1164, however, Victor died, and, as the Acts of Alexander in Baronius for that year, n. 27, record, that heresiarch of unhappy memory died impenitent and excommunicated and went down to hell. But Paschal III was soon substituted, and the Emperor swore with his own mouth, so the same Acts relate, upon the holy Gospels, that he would hold him and his successors as Catholic popes, and would always hold Alexander and his successors as schismatics.

units.la: LXXVIII. Eodem tamen anno Venetorum studio, Verona aliæque civitates contra Imperatorem pro Alexandro fœdus ineunt. Anno 1166. Concilium Herbipolense pro Paschali celebratur, Imperator in Italiam venit, Anconam obsidit, confœderatis interim pro Alexandro laborantibus. Anno 1167. Imperator Romam obsidet, Willelmo Siculo Papæ suppetias ferente, Alexander aufugit, Imperator Italiam, peste urgente, deserere cogitur, à Paschale revocatus ab eodem unâ cum Imperatrice coronatur, Paschalíque à Romanis, juramento interposito, recepto, rursus à peste vexatur. Anno 1168. ab Alexandro in Concilio Lateranensi excommunicatur & imperio exauctoratur, atque à Mediolanensibus clade afficitur; Anno 1170. mortuo Paschali III. Calistus III. substituitur; Imperator tamen Legatos ad Alexandrum pro pace mittit. Anno 1172. Romani Alexandrum in urbem recipere nolunt. Anno 1174. Imperator quintam expeditionem in Italiam suscipit, atque Alexandriam diu frustra obsidet, frustra etiam cum Legatis Papæ de pace tractat. Anno 1176. expeditionem renovat, à Mediolanensibus denuò vincitur, mittit Legatos ad Papam, tentat Corcyram; Annus autem 1177. Baronio n.1. verè placabilis est, quo pax exul annis 18. tandem suo decore est postliminio restituta, & dirum Schisma cessavit. Nempe Imperator, capto Filio, tandem Papæ se Venetiis famosâ illa humiliatione, subijcere necesse habuit.
units.tr: LXXVIII. In that same year, however, through the zeal of the Venetians, Verona and other cities made a league against the Emperor in support of Alexander. In 1166 a council was held at Würzburg for Paschal, and the Emperor came into Italy and besieged Ancona, while the confederates labored on Alexander's behalf. In 1167 the Emperor besieged Rome, with William of Sicily bringing aid to the Pope. Alexander fled, and the Emperor, pressed by plague, was forced to abandon Italy. Recalled by Paschal, he was crowned with the Empress by him, and Paschal was received by the Romans, after an oath had been given, but again he was afflicted by plague. In 1168 he was excommunicated by Alexander in the Lateran Council and deprived of the empire, and he suffered defeat at the hands of the Milanese. In 1170, after Paschal III died, Calixtus III was substituted; the Emperor nevertheless sent envoys to Alexander to seek peace. In 1172 the Romans refused to receive Alexander into the city. In 1174 the Emperor undertook his fifth expedition into Italy and besieged Alessandria for a long time in vain, and he likewise negotiated for peace with the Pope's legates, also in vain. In 1176 he renewed the expedition, was again defeated by the Milanese, sent envoys to the Pope, and attempted Corfu. The year 1177, which Baronius (n. 1) rightly calls a year of peace, was the year in which peace, an exile for eighteen years, was at last restored to its honor, and the dire Schism ceased. Indeed, the Emperor, having taken his son prisoner, was at last forced to submit to the Pope at Venice in that famous humiliation.

units.la: LXXIX. Verùm notari meretur, Baronium & Platinam de quarto Anti-Papa Innocentio III. nihil habere, sed in abdicatione Calisti III. Schismatis finem notare; Quod tamen nihilominùs, nùs, ut Onuphrius in Chronico vocat, qui & quatuor Anti-Papas commemorat, maximum fuisse, ex dictis constare potest, simúlque, originem Schismatis ex discordia inter Fridericum Imperatorem & Hadrianum IV. Papam petendam esse, calamitatesque subsecutas ei deberi, quòd Imperatori manifestè exosus à majori Cardinalium parte electus fuit, & de quo facilè præsumi poterat, eum ab Imperatore nunquam sponte receptum iri, cùm tamen hodie vel Regibus illud tribuant, ut ab aliquo manifestè rejectum vix eligant, aut eligi debere, si Schisma oriturum putetur, judicent; Et præter id, quòd hic rursus ipsum Schisma, mala subsecuta gravissima, tot millium cædes, urbiúmque vastationes, maximè autem, quòd tot millia ab utraque parte tam diu steterunt, vitium in se continent, haud pauca insuper occurrunt, quæ Schisma illud quoque ambiguitate sua perplexum reddere potuerunt. Multa quidem de Electione Victoris illegitima sparsa fuerunt, sed & de Electione Alexandri, non tantùm enim se strenuè in citatis defendere, sed & in adversarios illegitimæ electionis imputationem retorquere noverunt Victoriani, & quidem graviter ac speciosè, in testium multitudine. Imò Papiense Concilium haud parvum contrà Alexandrum præjudicium excitare potuit; Comparere noluit, cùm tamen præcipua Schismatis tollendi ratio à Conciliis dependeat, quæ à neutro litigantium convocari possunt aut debent; Damnatus etiam fuit in Concilio, à tot gravibus Episcopis aliisque personis Ecclesiasticis, quæ, si tam manifesta fuissent, quæ Octaviano objecta fuerunt, nunquam certè omnes in eum consensissent; Et si ipsi causam meliorem dignoscere non potuerunt, qui potuit Christiana in toto orbe plebs, quæ diu in eximiis Europæ partibus Victori & successoribus Pseudo-Papis irreparabili tot millium æternæ salutis dispendio adhæsisse dici debet? Quorum seditionibus, ajunt Platina in Alex.III. & Genebrardus ad an. 1180. Romana Ecclesia fere subversa est.
units.tr: LXXIX. It is worth noting, however, that Baronius and Platina say nothing of a fourth antipope, Innocent III, but mark the end of the Schism at the abdication of Calixtus III. Yet that the Schism was nonetheless, as Onuphrius calls it in his Chronicle, which also mentions four antipopes, a very great one, can be established from what has been said. At the same time it can be seen that the origin of the Schism must be sought in the discord between the Emperor Frederick and Pope Hadrian IV, and that the calamities which followed are owed to this: Alexander was chosen by a majority of the cardinals although he was plainly hateful to the Emperor, and it could easily be presumed that he would never be received by the Emperor of his own accord. Yet today men attribute to kings the view that they scarcely choose a man who has been plainly rejected by someone, or that they ought not to choose him if they judge that a schism is likely to arise. Besides this, that the Schism itself, with its very grave evils, the slaughter of so many thousands, the devastation of cities, and above all that so many thousands on each side stood by for so long, carries its own defect, there are not a few other points which could make that Schism even more perplexed by their ambiguity. Many things were indeed spread about concerning the illegitimate election of Victor, but the Victorians knew how not only to defend themselves vigorously in the cited matters but also to turn the charge of illegitimate election back upon their opponents, and that both gravely and plausibly, in the multitude of witnesses. Indeed, the council of Pavia could raise no small prejudice against Alexander. He refused to appear, although the chief means of ending a schism depends upon councils, which neither party to the dispute can or ought to convene. He was also condemned in the council by so many grave bishops and other ecclesiastical persons, which certainly would never all have agreed against him if the charges brought against Octavian had been so manifest. And if they themselves could not discern the better cause, how can it be said that the Christian people throughout the whole world, who for a long time in the chief parts of Europe clung to Victor and his successors, the pseudo-popes, must have done so to the irreparable loss of the eternal salvation of so many thousands? By their seditions, say Platina on Alexander III and Genebrardus at the year 1180, the Roman Church was nearly overthrown.

units.la: LXXX. Schisma vicesimum nonum fuit inter Joannem XXI. dictum XXII. Caturcensem Gallum anno 1316.
units.tr: LXXX. The twenty-ninth schism was between John XXI, called XXII, a Frenchman of Cahors, in the year 1316.

units.la: Lugduni post longam viginti trium Cardinalium altercationem, inquit Platina in vita electum, & Nicolaum V. Reatinum, Ordinis Fratrum Minorum, anno 1327. auctore Ludovico Bavaro creatum. Cùm enim Papa Johannes (sunt verba Hervvarti, Cancellarii Bavarici, in Ludovico IV. defenso, Bzovio injuriarum postulato, quòd in mendosissimis suis Annalibus Eundem
units.tr: At Lyons, after a long dispute among twenty-three cardinals, says Platina in his Life, he was chosen, and Nicholas V of Rieti, of the Order of Friars Minor, was created in 1327 by the authority of Ludwig of Bavaria. For when Pope John (these are the words of Hervart, chancellor of Bavaria, in Ludwig IV Defended, Bzovius being called to account for injuries, because in his most faulty Annals he

units.la: tandem triumphi. Eundem Imperatorem gravissimis calumniis onerârit, ad an.1327. n.19.) eúmque ab imperio arceret; (accedente etiam ejus lite gravissima cum Fratribus ordinis Minorum, quos hæreticos declaravit, affirmantes, Christum vel discipulos nihil proprii habuisse, quod certè, inquit Platina, non multùm cum S. Scriptura convenit, quæ multis in locis testatur, Christum ejúsque discipulos ac veros imitatores nil proprii habuisse, quorum etiam de numero multos damnavit & exussit paupertatis hostis juratus, qui etiam in Thesauris moriens, quantum nullus ante se Pontifex, nempe 25. milliones reliquit;) atque Fratrum causam cum sua conjungeret pro conservatione Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ut idem Hervvartus ibidem testatur, novum Pontificem creandum putavit, qui ei præsens præesset ac prodesset, Johannes enim in Gallias aberat & non tam in Ludovicum, quàm plurimos Italorum bella anathemate gerebat; atque etiam dictum Nicolaum Cleri populíque, ut idem n.17. testatur, atque alibi probat, instinctu, depósito Johanne, instituit; hominem quidem, inquit Platina, humili loco natum, sed doctum & ad res agendas aptissimum, Onuphrio, Bona fama usque ad id tempus existentem; Nillano, Antehac virum bonum, sanctaque vitæ habitum; Ciaconio adhuc magis laudatum, qui etiam ab Imperatore & his, qui tum cum eo aderant, inquit Platina, ut verum Christi Vicarium consalutatus, Cardinales & Episcopos homines sui consimiles creavit; Factum id, quando jam Ludovicus Joannem adeò irritâssेt, ut, verba sunt Bzovii, in publico Patrum consessu, eum veluti divinæ pontificiaque potestatis contemptorem, hæretiçâ labe pollutum, hæreticorum schismaticorúmque fautorem, Imperii Romani invasorem, Ecclesiaque universæ persecutorem & hostem anathemate damnârit, omni dignitate exuerit, omnes juramento fidelitatis ei astrictos exsolverit, potestatem in personam & res illius omnibus usurpare volentibus permiserit.
units.tr: at last triumphed. He burdened the same Emperor with the most grievous calumnies, at the year 1327, n. 19, and kept him from the empire. (His most serious quarrel with the Friars Minor, whom he declared heretics, also came into it, as he affirmed that Christ and the disciples had nothing of their own. This, says Platina, certainly does not agree much with Holy Scripture, which in many places testifies that Christ and his disciples and true imitators had nothing of their own. He condemned many of these friars and burned them, being a sworn enemy of poverty; and dying, he left in his treasuries more than any pontiff before him, namely twenty-five million.) He joined the friars' cause to his own for the preservation of the Roman Church, as the same Hervart testifies in the same place, and he thought a new pontiff should be created, who would be present to preside over him and help him. For John was in Gaul and was waging war with anathema not so much against Ludwig as against very many Italians. And the said Nicholas was instituted, as the same Hervart says at n. 17 and proves elsewhere, by the impulse of the clergy and people, John having been deposed. He was, says Platina, a man of humble birth, but learned and most apt for conducting affairs. According to Onuphrius, he had a good reputation up to that time. According to Niellus, he was formerly a good man, of holy life. Ciaconius praises him even more, saying that he was greeted by the Emperor and by those who were then with him as the true Vicar of Christ, and he created cardinals and bishops, men like himself, says Platina. This happened when Ludwig had already so provoked John that, in the words of Bzovius, in a public assembly of the Fathers he condemned him, polluted with heretical stain, as a despiser of divine and papal power, a supporter of heretics and schismatics, an invader of the Roman Empire, and a persecutor and enemy of the whole Church, with anathema; he stripped him of all dignity, released all those bound to him by oath of fidelity, and permitted his person and goods to be seized by all who wished to usurp them.

units.la: LXXXI. Et tamen idem Bzovius n.19. Cardinales &n.2. Canonicos urbis complures commemorat, qui à partibus Ludovici & Papæ sui steterint, licèt idem Bzovius n.2. §.4. sibi satis manifestè contradicens, dixerit; Non tamen Principi Clero persuadere potuit, ut sacra præsente Bavaro peragerent, aut Ecclesiastica mysteria communicarent. Johanni 18. crimina objecta ab ipso Bzovio enumerata, nec refutata, sed potiùs, ut Hervvartus ad an. 1328. n.37. seqq. pertendit, & ostendit, confirmata. Et publicè quidem facta est Petri Corbarii electio, nemine Johannem defendere sustinente, agnitus, cultus fuit à plurimis, donec abeunte in Germaniam Bavaro, narrat Platina in vita, re omni infecta ad Imperium spectante, Bonifacius Pisanus Comes rem gratam Pontifici facturus, Anti-Papam Avenionem perduxit: ubi in carcerem conjectus, vitam cum morte commutavit. Cui plura de hoc Schismate cognoscere lubet, laudatum Hervvartum legat; Inveniet Ludovicum atque Nicolaum defensos, Johannem in multis iniquissimum; Inveniet Johannem post legitimi Imperatoris petulantem atque injustam excommunicationem Pontificis nomine indignum, aliâs quoque pessimè, etiam quoad visionem Dei animabus ante resurrectionem negatam, errantem; Cui proin haud immerito ab Imperatore, populo Pastore destituto flagitante, alius substitutus fuit; Substitutus haud immeritò præ Johanne agnitus; Immeritò à Johanne in malitia perseverante incarceratus.
units.tr: LXXXI. And yet this same Bzovius, at n. 19, mentions several cardinals and at n. 2 several canons of the city who stood on the side of Ludwig and their Pope, although the same Bzovius, at n. 2, §4, contradicting himself quite plainly, said: Yet he could not persuade the clergy, who were devoted to the Bavarian, to perform sacred rites or to share in ecclesiastical mysteries. The crimes charged against John 18 by Bzovius himself, enumerated but not refuted, were rather, as Hervart insists at the year 1328, nn. 37 ff., and shows, confirmed. And indeed the election of Pietro Corvara was made publicly, no one daring to defend John; he was acknowledged and honored by very many, until, says Platina in his Life, when Bavaria departed for Germany and everything relating to the empire was undone, Boniface of Pisa, a count who wished to do a favor to the Pontiff, brought the anti-pope to Avignon, where he was thrown into prison and exchanged his life for death. For one who wishes to learn more about this Schism, let him read the Hervart already praised. He will find Ludwig and Nicholas defended, and John in many respects most unjust. He will find John, after his unjust excommunication of the lawful Emperor, unworthy of the name of Pontiff, and also in other respects, even concerning the sight of God denied to souls before the resurrection, in error. Therefore, not undeservedly, when the people were left without a shepherd and demanded it, another was substituted by the Emperor. The substitute was not undeservedly acknowledged in preference to John; he was not undeservedly imprisoned by John, who persevered in malice.

units.la: LXXXII. Schisma trigesimum, ut Onuphrius ait; omnium pessimum & diuturnius in Ecclesia Romana, quod quinquaginta annos perduravit, exortum est A. Chr. 1378. quando nimirum præter & post Urbanum VI Clemens VII. electus fuit.
units.tr: LXXXII. The thirtieth schism, as Onuphrius calls it, the worst of all and the longest in the Roman Church, which lasted fifty years, broke out in the year of Christ 1378, when, namely, Clement VII was elected after and in place of Urban VI.

units.la: Ideò autem exortum est, quia Cardinales plerunque Galli mortuo Gregorio XI. qui sedem Avinione Romam iterum transtulerat, Gallium, cives Romani Italum desiderârunt. Et Romani quidem, juxta Conclave Urbani VI. variis rationibus Romanum eligendum esse contendebant, quibus Cardinales non satis ad votum responderunt; Italos juvabat Gallorum discordia, Lemovicensium ex una, & reliquorum ex alia parte, reliqui enim Galli, qui non erant Lemovicenses, concordarunt cum Cardinalibus Italicis de habendo potius Italicum, quàm unum Lemovicensem, dicentes aperte, quòd totus mundus admodum erat attediatus de Lemovicensibus, qui tanto tempore Papatum possederant, quasi hereditarium; Lemovicenses vero Cardinales intelligentes, tam Cardinales Italicos, quàm reliquos sibi adversari, deliberaverunt, & inter se conclauserunt, quòd, ubi non possent habere sufficientem numerum Cardinalium ad faciendum unum de ipsis, vel saltem, Dominum Vivariensem eorum sequacem; eligerent potius Italicum; sed extra Collegium, & nominabant unum Archiepiscopum Barensem, qui Urbanus VI. postea dictus est; & ratio, quare in istum Archiepiscopum vota sua dirigebant, potissimum erat, quia sperabant, Cardinales Italicos in istum Italicum potius, quàm in alium Gallum dibere consentire, credebant itaque, quòd alii Cardinales Ultramontani in hunc concurrerent, quoniam Archiepiscopus Barensis erat homo valdè scientificus, practicus, doctus & instructus in stylo curiæ, & Cancellariæ, & antiquo antiquo familiaris socius & Capellanus familiaris & Domesticus Cardinalis Pampilonensis, Vice-Cancellarii, qui & ipse erat natione Lemovicensis, & dum Gregorius venisset ad Italiam, ipsum Dominum Barensem Archiepiscopum tanquam benevolum, & de quo Dominus Cardinalis Pampilonensis plurimùm considebat, posuit ad regendum Cancellariam loco ipsius Pampilonensis Cancellarii, tum etiam quia ipsi Cardinales habebant & reputabant ipsum Dominum Barensem tanquam unum Ultramontanum, & ipsorum moribus conformem, ex eo quòd multo tempore fuerat cum D. D. Cardinalibus Ultramontanis conversatus in Avenione; tum etiam quia Dom. Barensis erat de Regno Sicilia, & Civitate Neapolitana oriundus, cujus Regni & Civitatis erat Domina Serenissima Joanna, quae fuerat & est S. R. E. devotissima & ipsis Cardinalibus valde grata & accepta. Etiam ante ingressum Conclavis erat quasi patefacta haec Cardinalium Lemovicensium voluntas & dispositio, ita ut diceretur à multis, quòd Dominus Archiepiscopus Barensis esset futurus Papa, imò & aliqui ex ipsis D. D. Cardinalibus, ut ferebatur, se sibi verbis placidis commendârunt, sperantes, eum in summum Pontificem assumi debere. In ejus electione, teste Authore, omnium impressione cessante, scilicet Conclavi bene custodito, progressi sunt, licet fuerint aliqui de populo in platea ante Palatium foris, nullam tamen violentiam vel comminationem facientes, sed incautè clamantes; Romano lo volemo; & expectantes potiùs, publicatâ electione Romani Pontificis, currere ad domum electi, spoliare in signum gaudii, quàm volentes aut valentes aliquam impressionem facere; sicut inveritate postmodùm, alio quàm Romano electo, non fecerunt. Cúmque de Ursinis, qui ad Papatum, ut credebatur, aspirabat, videns vota Dominorum directa & concurrentia ad eligendum in Papam Dominum Barensem, conaretur ipsum negotium electionis Domini Barensis divertere, & differre, & , ut creditur, impedire; quòd Dominus Barensis non eligeretur atque praeter fraudem Dissert. VI. Sect. 4. n. 15. memoratam atque ab eo commendatam persuaderet D. D. aliis Cardinalibus, quòd eligerent Dominum S. Petri Romanum, ei fuit responsum per D. Cardinalem Lemovicensem; quòd licèt D. S. Petri foret homo bonus & sanctus, duo tamen obstant; primò quia Romanus erat, ne forte diceretur Papa factus ad clamorem populi; secundò obstat, quia erat nimis debilis & infirmus, nec posset sufficere ad onera Papatus &c. His dictis Cardinalis ipse Lemovicensis, praesentibus & audientibus omnibus dictis aliis Cardinalibus, & coram eis ibidem omnibus existentibus, in Papam & Romanum Pontificem elegit Dominum Bartholomeum Archiepiscopum Barensem, utendo verbis verbis istis in effectu: Ego purè & liberè eligo, & assumo in Papam, D. Bartholomeum Barensem Archiepiscopum, illicóque sine aliquo temporis intervallo, cæteri omnes Cardinales in numero sufficienti, facientes & constituentes multò majorem partem duarum partium ipsorum Cardinalium in Conclavi existentium purè & liberè eundem Barensem Archiepiscopum similiter in Romanum Pontificem elegerunt; Cardinalis Florentinus videns quòd duæ partes & plures Dominum Archiepiscopum Barensem elegerunt, accessit ad eundem Archiepiscopum, & purè & liberè eundem elegit; & electio fuit sic celebrata.
units.tr: This arose because the cardinals, most of whom were French, desired a Frenchman after the death of Gregory XI, who had moved the seat from Avignon back to Rome, and the Roman citizens desired an Italian. The Romans indeed, according to the Conclave of Urban VI, contended by various arguments that a Roman should be elected, and the cardinals did not respond sufficiently to their wish. The Italians were helped by the discord of the French, the Limousins on one side and the rest on the other, for the other Frenchmen, who were not Limousins, agreed with the Italian cardinals that they should rather have an Italian than one Limousin, saying openly that the whole world was thoroughly wearied of the Limousins, who had held the papacy for so long, as if it were hereditary. The Limousin cardinals, understanding that both the Italian cardinals and the rest were against them, deliberated and resolved among themselves that, if they could not have a sufficient number of cardinals to make one of their own, or at least Lord Vivarais as their follower, they would choose an Italian instead. But they looked outside the college and named one Archbishop of Bari, who was afterwards called Urban VI. The reason they directed their votes to this archbishop was chiefly that they hoped the Italian cardinals would agree to this Italian rather than to another Frenchman, and they believed the other Transalpine cardinals would also converge on him, since the Archbishop of Bari was a very learned, practical, skilled man, experienced in the style of the curia and chancery, and a familiar companion and domestic chaplain of Cardinal Pamplona, the vice-chancellor, who was himself a Limousin by nation. When Gregory came to Italy, he placed the Lord Archbishop of Bari, as a kindly man in whom Lord Cardinal Pamplona greatly trusted, in charge of the chancery in place of Pamplona himself as chancellor. Also, the cardinals themselves held and regarded Lord Bari as one of the Transalpines, conformed to their manners, since he had spent a long time with the Transalpine cardinals in Avignon. Also, Lord Bari was born in the kingdom of Sicily and the city of Naples, of which kingdom and city the most serene Lady Joanna was, and is, most devoted to the Holy Roman Church and very pleasing and acceptable to the cardinals themselves. Even before the conclave was entered this will and disposition of the Limousin cardinals was, as it were, made known, so that many said the Lord Archbishop of Bari would be pope; indeed some of those lord cardinals, as was reported, commended themselves to him with gentle words, hoping he would be taken up as supreme pontiff. In his election, according to the author, with every pressure removed, namely the conclave being well guarded, they proceeded. Although some of the people in the square outside the palace were present, they made no violence or threat, but shouted carelessly, "We want a Roman!", and expected, once the election of the Roman Pontiff was published, to run to the house of the elected man and plunder it as a sign of joy, rather than wishing or being able to bring any pressure to bear; as in truth they afterwards did not do when someone other than a Roman was elected. And since Orsini, who was aspiring to the papacy, as was believed, saw the votes of the lords directed and converging on electing the Lord Archbishop of Bari as pope, he tried to divert and postpone the business of Lord Bari's election and, as is believed, to prevent it, so that Lord Bari would not be elected. Beyond the fraud mentioned and commended by him in Dissert. VI. Sect. 4. n. 15, he persuaded the other lord cardinals to elect Lord St Peter, a Roman. It was answered by Lord Cardinal of Limoges that, although Lord St Peter was a good and holy man, two things stood in the way: first, because he was a Roman, lest it be said that he had been made pope by the clamour of the people; second, because he was too weak and infirm and could not bear the burdens of the papacy, etc. With these things said, the Limousin cardinal himself, all the other cardinals present and hearing, and everyone being there before them, elected Lord Bartholomew, Archbishop of Bari, as pope and Roman Pontiff, using in effect these words: "I purely and freely elect and take Lord Bartholomew, Archbishop of Bari, as pope." Immediately afterwards, without any interval of time, all the other cardinals, in sufficient number, making up by far the greater part of two parts of the cardinals present in the conclave, likewise purely and freely elected the same Archbishop of Bari as Roman Pontiff. The Florentine cardinal, seeing that two parts and more had elected the Lord Archbishop of Bari, came to the same archbishop and purely and freely elected him too; and thus the election was celebrated.

units.la: LXXXIV. Electione peractâ & Conclave adhuc bene & ex omni parte clauso & firmato existente, Cardinales publicationem ad tempus pomeridianum differre voluerunt, quia tunc Dominus non erat in Palatio, & si dicta publicatio facta fuisset, antequam electus ipse venisset ad Palatium & ad ipsos Cardinales, dubitari poterat, quòd aliqua sinistra in via eidem electo possent occurrere, eo quòd ipse electus non erat Romanus, & Romani libenter habuissent natione Romanum &c. Unde pro majori securitate ipsius Barensis electi, & ne aliquis posset suspicari, vel præsumere, ipsum esse electum; Domini Cardinales miserunt pro nonnullis Prælatis Italicis, qui moram trahebant Romæ, ut ad eos venirent pro nonnullis arduis Romanæ Ecclesiæ negotiis, inter quos fuit Barensis electus &c. qui omnes, prout vocati exiterint, accesserunt ad Palatium, non tamen Conclave intraverunt; sed seorsim ab ipsis Cardinalibus pransi sunt; sumpto autem prandio, ad majorem expressionem liberæ voluntatis, & liberi consensûs eorum, & ad majorem etiam cautelam in prædictum Barensem Archiepiscopum iterum purè liberè & concorditer, ac unanimiter, omni prorsus impressione cessante, & Conclavi adhuc bene custodito remanente, consenserunt & eum Papam elegerunt. Subjungit Author, quomodo populum ad tempus placaturi Dominum S. Petrũ Romanum induxerunt ut Papam, & populus tunc ei tanquam Papæ, credentes eum esse Papam, reverentiam exhibuerunt; qui tandem hæc verba protulerit: In effectu ego non sum Papa, nec volo esse Anti-Papa, sed melior me est in Papam D. Archiepiscopus Barensis.
units.tr: LXXXIV. The election being completed, and the conclave still well and on every side closed and sealed, the cardinals wished to defer the publication until the afternoon, because the lord was not then in the palace. If the said publication had been made before the elected man came to the palace and to the cardinals themselves, it could be feared that some misfortune might befall the same elected man on the road, since he was not a Roman and the Romans would gladly have had a Roman by nation, etc. Hence, for the greater safety of the said elect Bari, and lest anyone suspect or presume that he had been elected, the lord cardinals sent for several Italian prelates who were lingering in Rome, to come to them about some arduous business of the Roman Church. Among them was the Bari elect, etc. All of them, as they had been summoned, came to the palace but did not enter the conclave; they were dined separately by the cardinals themselves. When the dinner was over, for a greater expression of their free will and free consent, and also for greater caution, they again, purely, freely, agreeably and unanimously, with all pressure entirely ceasing and the conclave still remaining well guarded, consented to and elected the said Bari archbishop as pope. The author adds how, to placate the people for the time being, they induced Lord St Peter the Roman to be pope, and the people then showed him reverence as pope, believing him to be pope; he at last uttered these words: "In effect I am not pope, nor do I wish to be an anti-pope, but a better one than I is pope, the Lord Archbishop of Bari."

units.la: LXXXV. Narrat etiam Author, quomodo Cardinales sibi ob hanc deceptionem timentes nonnulli ædes suas dereliquerint, quidam etiam Urbem, cæteris sine aliqua lasione vel violentia remanentibus; Item quomodo consultum fuerit electo, quòd pro eo, quòd non erat Romanus, ne ei aliquid sinistri posset occurrere, benefaceret pro securitate personæ suæ, & statu universalis Ecclesiæ. clesia, exire de Palatio, & se in aliquo loco tuto recipere, & noluerit, dicente Domino S. Petri, quòd ipse erat verus Papa, & securè manere ibi poterat; Nec non, quomodo electio Domini Barensis intimata sit Officialibus urbis, qui de electione hujusmodi remanserunt, & fuerunt valde contenti, & voluerunt accedere & accesserunt ad Dominum electum ad exhibendam ei reverentiam exhiberi solitam summis Pontificibus, qui noluit sibi talem reverentiam fieri per dictos Officiales, nec per alium quempiam, dicendo inter catera; quòd pro nunc nolebat nominari, nisi Archiepiscopus Barensis. Et quomodo accesserint Cardinales ipsi, qui in domibus suis remanserunt, ad dictum electum congratulandum de sua concordi electione, & humiliter supplicando, quatenus dignaretur & vellet acceptare.
units.tr: LXXXV. The author also relates how some cardinals, fearing this deception, abandoned their houses, and some even the city, while the others remained without any harm or violence. Likewise, how it was advised to the elect, because he was not a Roman, that for the sake of his personal safety, and the state of the universal Church, lest anything untoward befall him, he should leave the palace and withdraw to some safe place; but he refused, the lord St Peter saying that he himself was the true pope and could stay there safely. Likewise, how the election of Lord Bari was announced to the officials of the city, who had remained for this election and were very pleased, and wished to approach, and did approach the elected lord to pay him the reverence customarily shown to the supreme pontiffs. He did not wish such reverence to be paid to him by the said officials, nor by anyone else, saying among other things that for now he did not wish to be named except as Archbishop of Bari. And how the cardinals themselves, who had remained in their houses, approached the said elect to congratulate him on his unanimous election, and humbly begged that he would deign and be willing to accept.

units.la: LXXXVI.
units.tr: LXXXVI.

units.la: Similiter refert author, quomodo electus volens in sua conscientia esse securus, interrogârit omnes Cardinales, & unumquemque de per se, utrum revera ipse sincerè, purè, liberè & Canonicè per omnes Cardinales in Conclavi fuisset electus in Papam, qui responderunt, quòd pro certo ita purè, liberè, sincerè & Canonicè fuerat electus in Papam, sicut aliquis Canonicè eligi potuisset, persuadentes, quòd nullo modo recusaret, vel differret electioni de se factæ consentire propter periculum longæ vacationis Papatûs; quod posset occurrere pro eo, quòd dicti Cardinales cum magna difficultate iterato possent congregari &c. Cardinales vero absentes dederunt per publicum instrumentum plenam & liberam potestatem illis quinque circa intronizationem ipsius electi omnia faciendi, quæ ipsimet personaliter facere possent.
