Qui tamen Cardinales ipsi post ac etiam accesserunt, à Senatore & aliis officialibus moniti, quoniam in nullo habebant dubitare, quia erant in loco tuto libero & securo, & licèt ipsi non elegissent Papam Romanum, de electione tamen Domini Barensis Romanus populus remanserat contentus, pacificus & quietus, atque sic omnes in Capella convenientes iterum & ad cautelam prædictum D. Barensem in Papam elegerunt, vel ut electus esset, consenserunt, purè, liberè, concorditer & unanimiter. LXXXVII. Habuit tunc orationem Florentinus nomine caterorum proponens illud Apostoli Pauli: Talis decebat, ut esset nobis Pontifex impollutus videlicet — requisivítque electum ipsum, ut consentiret electioni de se factæ; quâ resquisitione factâ, ipse electus verba illa assumpsit Divina Scriptura; Timor, fremor venerunt super me, & contexerunt me tenebræ; Et cùm prosecutus fuissei ad finem, ut videbatur, volens se excusare in sarcina tanti oneris, vel saltem velle tempus ad deliberandum; Cardinalis Florentinus & alii Cardinales tunc dixerunt, quòd Oratio post confirmationem, Papatûs acceptatio atque intronizatio. quòd profecutionem autoritatis per eum proposita pro tunc omitteret,quia non erat de more, cùm alium ipse haberet, facere eis sermonem. Cúmque iteratò requisiverunt, quòd eis responderet, & electioni de se facta in nomine Domini consentiret; ipse verò electus ipsorum precibus & instantiis diutiùs tandem cum timore & tremore animi dicta electioni humiliter consensit. Sic Te Deum cantârunt, eum intronizârunt,nomen ei dederunt,honorem exhibuerunt, & pronuntiatio facta est.
units.tr: The author likewise relates how the elect, wishing to be secure in his conscience, asked all the Cardinals, each one individually, whether he had truly, sincerely, purely, freely and canonically been elected Pope by all the Cardinals in the Conclave. They replied that he had certainly been elected Pope purely, freely, sincerely and canonically, as validly as anyone could have been canonically elected. They urged him not to refuse or delay consent to the election made of him, for fear of a long vacancy of the Papacy, which might follow because the said Cardinals could be assembled again only with great difficulty, and so on. The absent Cardinals gave, by public instrument, full and free power to those five to do everything concerning the enthronement of the elect that they could have done in person. Afterwards those Cardinals also came, having been warned by the Senator and other officials, since they had no cause for doubt, because they were in a safe, free and secure place; and although they had not elected a Roman Pope, the Roman people had nevertheless remained content, peaceful and quiet with the election of the lord of Bari. And so all, gathering again in the Chapel, and as a precaution, elected the said lord of Bari as Pope, or consented that he be elected, purely, freely, harmoniously and unanimously. LXXXVII. Then Florentinus gave a speech on behalf of the others, citing the words of the Apostle Paul: "Such an high priest became us, holy, harmless, undefiled", and he asked the elect to consent to the election made of him. When this request had been made, the elect himself took up those words of Holy Scripture: "Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me." And when he had gone on, as it seemed, to the end, wishing to excuse himself from the burden of so great an office, or at least to ask for time to deliberate, Cardinal Florentinus and the other Cardinals then said that he should omit the continuation of the speech he had prepared for that moment, since it was not customary for him to make a speech to them when another was to do so. When they asked him again to answer them and to consent in the name of the Lord to the election made of him, the elect himself, at last, after long entreaty and pressure from them, humbly consented to the said election with fear and trembling of mind. So they sang the Te Deum, enthroned him, gave him a name, paid him honour, and the proclamation was made.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Eâdem die tres ex dictis Cardinalibus — recesserunt ad partem in dicto Palatio cum prafato D. Papa in loco studii, & inter catera dixerunt eidem,quòd fuerunt ipsi tres causa sua promotionis, & supplicaverunt pro executione Testamenti D. Gregorii XI. & quòd fratres suos & de gente sua haberet commendatos, & præcipuè dignaretur præstare certum subsidium pro redemtione D. Rogerii fratris ipsius D. Gregorii in Anglia captivi, & quòd in prima Creatione Cardinalium, quam faceret,dignaretur assumere unum eorum consanguineorum, quem D. Gregorius facere intendebat, filium scilicet Domini Hugonis de Rupe militis nepotem dicti Gregorii. Petierunt etiam,ut dignaretur in suum Cubiculurium retinere D. Joannem de Baro eorum consanguineum,qui etiam fuerat Cubicularius præfati D. Gregorrii; quibus omnibus D. Urbanus benignissimè respondit, & in suum Cubicularium D. Joannem prædictum retinuit.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. On the same day three of the said Cardinals withdrew to a side room in the said Palace, into the study, with the aforesaid lord Pope, and among other things said to him that they three were the cause of his promotion. They asked that he carry out the will of Pope Gregory XI, and that he keep their brothers and kinsmen in his favour; and especially that he would deign to provide a certain subsidy for the ransom of Lord Roger, brother of the same Gregory, held captive in England. They also asked that at the first creation of Cardinals which he made, he would deign to raise to the purple one of their relatives whom Gregory had intended to make, namely the son of Lord Hugh de Rupe, a knight, and nephew of the said Gregory. They asked too that he would deign to retain as his chamberlain Lord John of Bari, their kinsman, who had also been chamberlain of the aforesaid Gregory. To all of these requests Lord Urban replied most kindly, and retained the aforesaid John as his chamberlain.

units.la: LXXXIX. Porrò enarrat Author, quomodo Papa apud S. Petrum præsente populo à Canonicis reverentiam acceperit, Missam submissa voce audiverit,populo benedictionem dederit,sermonem Cardinalibus fecerit, atque Indulgentiam plenariam rogatus iisdem concesserit, Dominicâ verò in Palmis ramos Olivarum pro more exhibuerit, exequias porrò pro prædecessore peregerit; usque ad diem Jovis in Coena Domini populo & peregrinis Indulgentias dederit, ipso die Jovis ad fulminandum processum exiverit,in die sancta Pascha Coronatus sit, Cardinalibus omnibus numero 16. assistentibus & sic fieri volentibus, ipsíque D. Urbano ministrantibus; Omnes enim, inquit Author, dicti D. Cardinales numero 16. qui in electione,puréque & liberè consenserunt, & 4. illi Cardinales,qui ab urbe recesserunt,jam fuerant ad urbem reversi, ubi omnes dicti Cardinales steterunt ipsi D.Urbano assistendo & Ministrando, Consistoria & alia per Cardinales summis Pontificibus consueta faciendo, usque quod dicti D. Cardinales, seu eorum aliqui de ipsa Urbe, & de licentia dicti Domini Urbani ad Anagniam se contulerunt, & durante tempore dictorum trium mensium d. D. Cardinales semper tractârunt & habuerunt D. Urbanum pro vero, unico & indubitato Summo Pontifice, eum honorando, visitando, gratias petendo, annulos & alia pretiosa jocalia ei largiendo. In Missis quoque ipsorum tam submissâ voce, quàm in cantu celebratis, orationem illam dicendo, seu dici faciendo: Deus omnium fidelium: & pro ipso D. Urbano tanquam pro summo & vero Pontifice, divinum auxilium implorando ad felix & prosperum regimen Ecclesiae suae sanctae; Legatum etiam reducem recepit, qui pede Papae deosculato & ore, P. Urbano Papalem exhibuit reverentiam; Die ascensionis Missam publice celebravit, ministrantibus & praesentibus Cardinalibus; Fecit quoque in Consistorio secreto multas Praelatorum Promotiones & Translationes: tenuitque etiam multa Consistoria publica, causas comm sit Cardinalibus praedictis, super quibus definitivas sententias tulerunt; Pro se etiam & familiaribus suis dispensationes & gratias impetraverunt, ad diversos Mundi Principes sponte & liberè scripserunt, se D. Barensem in verum & indubitatum Pontificem elegisse, ipsis etiam consultantibus, assentientibus & consentientibus, & quòd non adhiberetur fides alicui, qui contrarium asserere, vel super his dubitare vellet, & coram pluribus honestis & gravibus personis saepissimè asseruerunt, ipsum D. Urbanum verum & indubitatum fore R. Pontificem, ipsisque etiam consultantibus, assistentibus & consentientibus D. Urbanus electionem Illustr. Principis D. Vencislai in Regem Romanorum electi confirmavit; Cardinalem quoque Episcopum Hostiensem creavit, & per idem tempus, quo Cardinales praedicti in Urbe fuerunt, continuè absque ulla violentia, & molestatione, omni prorsus metu seclusò, habitârunt, & steterunt in Urbe.
units.tr: LXXXIX. The author next recounts how the Pope, at St Peter's, in the presence of the people, received reverence from the canons, heard Mass said in a low voice, gave the people his blessing, preached a sermon to the Cardinals, and at their request granted them a plenary indulgence; on Palm Sunday he displayed olive branches as was customary; then he performed the funeral rites for his predecessor; up to Maundy Thursday he granted indulgences to the people and to pilgrims; on that Thursday he went out to pronounce the process of excommunication; on holy Easter Day he was crowned, with all sixteen Cardinals present and willing to attend, and ministering to Urban himself. For, says the author, all the said Cardinals, sixteen in number, who had consented to the election purely and freely, together with the four Cardinals who had withdrawn from the city, had now returned to the city, where all the said Cardinals remained, assisting and ministering to Urban and performing the consistories and other duties customary for Cardinals to perform for supreme Pontiffs, until the said Cardinals, or some of them, went from the city to Anagni with the licence of the said Lord Urban. And during those three months the said lord Cardinals always treated Lord Urban as the true, sole and indubitable Supreme Pontiff, honouring him, visiting him, asking favours of him, and giving him rings and other precious jewels. In their Masses too, both those said in a low voice and those sung, they recited, or caused to be recited, the prayer "God of all the faithful", and for Lord Urban, as true and supreme Pontiff, they implored divine help for the happy and prosperous government of his holy Church. He also received back the legate who had returned, and this man, having kissed the Pope's foot and mouth, paid Pope Urban papal reverence. On Ascension Day he celebrated Mass publicly, with the Cardinals present and ministering. He also made many promotions and translations of prelates in secret consistory, and he held many public consistories, hearing causes committed to the said Cardinals, on which they gave definitive sentences. For himself and his household he obtained dispensations and favours. He wrote freely and willingly to various princes of the world that he had elected the lord of Bari as true and indubitable Pope, the Cardinals also advising, assisting and consenting; and that no credence should be given to anyone who wished to maintain the contrary or to doubt these things. Very often, before several honourable and serious persons, they asserted that Lord Urban was the true and indubitable Roman Pontiff. With the same Cardinals also advising, assisting and consenting, Urban confirmed the election of the illustrious Prince Lord Wenceslas as King of the Romans. He also created a Cardinal, the Bishop of Ostia; and throughout the whole time that the aforesaid Cardinals were in the city, they lived and stayed there continually, without any violence or molestation, with all fear entirely shut out.

units.la: XC. Unà autem dierum D. Urbanus, convocatis ad se Cardinalibus omnibus, multas eis admonitiones fecit pro bono Regimine Curiae Romanae, & pro bono exemplo de se ipsis Populo tribuendo; Monuit enim, ut abstinerent & manus suas excuterent ab omni munere &c. monuit etiam eos de honestè vivendo, cùm ipsi essent Cardinales Ecclesiam militantem sustentantes, & tanquam signi positi ad sagittam, debebant de se normam, & exemplum aliis bene vivendi dare & praebere; detestans superfluos sumptus, & numerosam familiam, equorum quoque & vestium & convivantium superfluitatem; asserens, haec omnia cedere ad gravamen potiùs, quàm ad relevationem honoris Curiae Romanae & Ecclesiae: multas quoque eleemosynas propter hos sumptus pauperibus deperire, affirmabat; Dixitque praeterea, sua intentionis fore, quòd justit a ministretur, omnibus petentibus absque aliqua personarum acceptatione, & addidit, quòd cum dispositione divina Romana sedes esset in Urbe collocata, intentio sua erat in Urbe residere,
units.tr: XC. One day Urban, having summoned all the Cardinals to him, gave them many admonitions for the good government of the Roman Curia, and for setting a good example to the people through their own conduct. He urged them to abstain, and to shake their hands free of every bribe, and so on. He also admonished them to live honourably, since they were Cardinals sustaining the Church Militant, and, like a mark set up for an arrow, they ought to give and offer others a rule and example of living well. He denounced superfluous expenses, numerous households, and excess in horses, clothing and banquets, declaring that all these things were a burden rather than an ornament to the honour of the Roman Curia and the Church. He also declared that many alms for the poor were lost because of these expenses. He said further that it was his intention that justice should be administered to all who asked, without any acceptance of persons; and he added that, since by divine disposition the Roman see had been established in the city, it was his intention to reside in the city, and there to live and die.

units.la: Cardinales severè admonet; dere, ibíque & vivere & mori, quódque, si aliter faceret, crederet, se malè agere & Deum offendere.
units.tr: He sternly admonishes the Cardinals: that he would stay there, live and die there, and that if he acted otherwise he would believe he was doing wrong and offending God.

units.la: XCI. Hac dum sic agerentur, Archiepiscopus Arelatensis, qui fuerat Camerarius D. Gregorii XI. & penes quem erant omnia jocalia pretiosa, quae fuerant D. Gregorii XI. per mensem post D. Urbani Coronationem, de urbe absque licentia recessit & ivit ad Anagniam; secúmque asportavit dicta jocalia, & inter catera Thiaram pretiosam, cum qua consueverunt nonnulli R. Pontifices coronari & cum qua ipse D. Urbanus fuerat coronatus; Propter quae D. Urbanus commotus mandavit tribus D. D. Cardinalibus, qui & ipsi erant Anagnia, ut dictum Episcopum arrestarent. Eodem tempore, cùm requireret Papa Castellum S. Angeli ad manum suam, Castellanus se rebellem constituit, socium, ut ferebatur, habens Cardinalem Montis Majoris.
units.tr: XCI. While these things were happening, the Archbishop of Arles, who had been Camerlengo of Pope Gregory XI and in whose keeping were all the precious jewels that had belonged to Gregory XI, left the city without permission about a month after Urban's coronation and went to Anagni. He took the said jewels with him and, among other things, the precious tiara with which several Roman pontiffs have been crowned and with which Urban himself had been crowned. Moved by this, Urban ordered three of the cardinals, who were also at Anagni, to arrest the said bishop. At the same time, when the Pope demanded that the Castle of St Angelo be handed over into his hand, the castellan declared himself in rebellion, having as his accomplice, so it was said, the Cardinal of Montmajour.

units.la: XCII. Cùm hoc ad D. Urbani notitiam pervenisset, reprehendit acerrimè Cardinalem Montis Majoris, eíque comminatus fuit, quòd contrà ipsum procederet, & de eo justitiam faceret juxta formam, & tenorem Processuum felicis recordationis Joannis Papae XXII. contra talia perpetrantes promulgatorum; similiter reprehendit, & comminatus est Dominus Ambianensis Cardinali pro eo, quòd favebat D. Francisco de Vico, Almae Urbis Praefecto, qui occupat civitatem Viterbiensem, quae ei nullo modo pertinet, & est de dominio Romanae Ecclesiae, fuerátque etiam D. Urbanus informatus, quòd Cardinalis S. Eustachii quasdam occultas practicas, & Conventiones tenebat, & fecerat cum Britonibus, in damnum ipsius D. Papae; imò ferebatur, quòd Cardinalis praedictus sibi certas pecunias retinuisset, quas Papa ei dederat ad finem recuperationis Castri S. Angeli, unde etiam huic communicatus (comminatus) est, quòd contra cum faceret Justitiam; fuerat praterea D. Urbanus advisatus, quòd Cardinalis S. Eustachii per suas virtutes & subtiles tractatus, ac deceptoria verba & falsas ac dolosas inductiones sollicitaverat ipsum D. Urbanum, ad dandum societati Britonum magnas pecuniarum summas; Quibus receptis, ipsi Britonenses se hostiliter opposuerunt ipsi D. Urbano, & quòd earum Machinationum conscii erant, & Authores exiterant Cardinalis Gebbenensis &c. & nonnulli alii Cardinales Ultramontani in Italia commorantes, ipsíque Cardinales bene sciebant D. Urbanum de his omnibus habere notitiam, unde propter jam dicta & quia D. Urbanus denegaverat aliquas gratias concedere ipsis d. D. Cardinalibus Ultramontanis, credebatur, eos de sua sanctitate non contentari; imò erigere velle cornua contrà eum, prout tandem fecerunt.
units.tr: XCII. When this came to Urban's attention, he rebuked the Cardinal of Montmajour very sharply and threatened that he would proceed against him and do justice on him according to the form and terms of the decrees issued by Pope John XXII of happy memory against those who commit such things. He likewise rebuked and threatened the Cardinal of Amiens because he favoured Francis de Vico, Prefect of the City of Rome, who occupied the city of Viterbo, which in no way belongs to him but is part of the dominion of the Roman Church. Urban had also been informed that the Cardinal of St Eustache held certain secret dealings and agreements with the Bretons to the Pope's own detriment. Indeed, it was said that this cardinal had kept back certain sums of money which the Pope had given him for the purpose of recovering the Castle of St Angelo, and for this he too was threatened that justice would be done against him. Urban had further been advised that the Cardinal of St Eustache, by his cunning schemes and subtle negotiations, deceitful words and false and crafty inducements, had persuaded Urban himself to hand over large sums of money to the company of Bretons. When they had received these, the Bretons turned hostilely against Urban; and the Cardinal of Geneva, etc., and several other Transalpine cardinals staying in Italy were privy to these machinations and were their authors. The cardinals themselves knew well that Urban had notice of all these things. Hence, for the reasons already given, and because Urban had refused to grant certain favours to the said Transalpine cardinals, it was believed that they were not content with his holiness; indeed they were willing to raise their horns against him, as in the end they did.

units.la: XCIII.
units.tr: XCIII.

units.la: Nam circa finem Janii anno D. 1370. nonnulli ex ipsis D. Ultramontanis in Urbe existentes Cardinales, videlicet &c. ipsi & eorum quilibet supplicârunt & supplicare fecerunt de habendo licentiam recedendi de Urbe, & eundi ad Anagniam, pretendentes in Urbe nimiam Caliditatem, & aëris intemperiem, & Anagnia erat aër temperatior & Clementior, unde D. Urbanus volens eis complacere concessit eis licentiam abeundi, qui prout ante conceperunt, recesserunt, & ipse de Roma venit Tibur. Dum Papa esset Tibure & Cardinales in Anagnia, jam in apertum dissidium inter Papam & Cardinales res vergere coeperunt, jam affirmantibus Cardinalibus, quòd D. Urbanus non esset verus Papa, nec Canonicè electus, quia per impressionem, & quòd electio non fuit celebrata in loco tuto, propterea Cardinales ipsi, intelligentes se cum Principe Fundi, illuc accesserunt, & tanquam Apostolica sedes vacaret, Conclave intraverunt, D. Robertum Gebernensem Cardinalem in summum Pontificem, seu in idolum potiùs erexerant, qui vocari voluit Clemens VII. Circa cujus electionem valde notabilis est fraus ad trahendos in partes etiam tres Cardinales Italos adhibita; Spem fecerunt Galli datis literis singulis, se illos eligere velle, postulato tamen à singulis, ad evitandam aemulationem reliquorum scilicet, silentio. Quâ quidem ratione inescati singuli mox adfuerunt, sed mox etiam singuli se delusos esse senserunt, Theodorico à Niem l. 1. c. 9. & ex eo Maimburgio Hist. du grand. Schism. rem narrantibus. Atque adeò alter violentiâ, fraude alter electi fuerunt! XCIV. Unde in Dei Ecclesia, ita pergit Conclave Urbani VI. ortum est ingens Schisma, & quod multorum malorum causa fuit. Nam Principes Christiani dividi coeperunt, & quidam Urbano, quidam verò Gebernensi ad haeserunt; Urbano enim adhaesit natio Italica, excepto Comite Fundi, & Praefecto de Vico, tota natio Germanica, Regnum Portugallia, Anglia tota; Gebernensi adhaeserunt, Natio Gallica, tota fere Hispania citerior, & ulterior, sicque subsequuta sunt difficultates & errores plurimi in Populo Christiano, & quod unus ligabat, alter solvebat, fiebantque hinc processus, privationes & anathematizationes in magnum Ecclesia & Christianitatis vilipendium; eadem propterea Ecclesia dabatur duobus, & vi armorum quandoque dirimebatur lis, unde sequebantur hominum occisiones, depopulationes Agrorum & plurimorum strages. Propter quod secutum est famosum bellum, quod commissum est inter Ducem Burgundia & Leodienses; in quo, ut fertur, 30000. hominum interempta sunt prope Leodium, Imò vi excommunicationum mutuarum, inde secuta sunt & alia bella, cladesque maximæ, & cædes innocentium Ultramontanorum Romæ jussu Urbani, & publicatum hinc inde bellum sanctum sub indulgentiis ab utraque parte plenariis, conflatis etiam in nummos sanctorum statuis aureis & argenteis, ut melior tunc conditio fuerit sanctorum ligneorum! Suspendio ideò necata fuit in carcere Johanna Regina Neapolitana ab agnato hærede, tuncque datum Gallicis in illud Regnum funestis cursionibus initium, imò infinita inde mala nata sunt, quæ apud Theodoricum à Niem & Maimburgium videri possunt.
units.tr: XCIV. Near the end of January in the year of our Lord 1370, some of the said Transalpine cardinals who were in the city, namely etc., they themselves and each of them petitioned, and had others petition, for leave to depart from the city and go to Anagni, alleging the excessive heat in Rome and the unhealthiness of the air, whereas Anagni had a more temperate and milder air. So Urban, wishing to please them, granted them leave to depart; and they left as they had earlier planned, and he himself came from Rome to Tivoli. While the Pope was at Tivoli and the cardinals at Anagni, matters began to tend toward open discord between the Pope and the cardinals; the cardinals now asserted that Urban was not a true pope nor canonically elected, because the election had been made under duress and had not been celebrated in a safe place. Therefore those cardinals, understanding that they had the support of the Prince of Fondi, went there and, as if the apostolic see were vacant, entered a conclave, and they set up Cardinal Robert of Geneva as supreme pontiff, or rather as an idol, who wished to be called Clement VII. Concerning this election a very notable fraud was employed to draw even three Italian cardinals into their party. The French promised each of them by letter that they would elect him, provided however that each kept silence, to avoid rivalry with the others. Lured by this scheme, each came at once, but soon each perceived that he had been deceived, as Dietrich of Niem (book 1, ch. 9) and after him Maimbourg (History of the Great Schism) relate. And so one was elected by violence, the other by fraud! XCIV. Hence in the Church of God, as the Conclave of Urban VI went on, a huge Schism arose, which was the cause of many evils. For Christian princes began to be divided, and some clung to Urban, others to the Genevan. The Italian nation adhered to Urban, except the Count of Fondi and the Prefect de Vico; the whole German nation, the Kingdom of Portugal and all England likewise. The French nation adhered to the Genevan, and almost all of Spain, both Hither and Further. Thus many difficulties and errors followed among the Christian people, and what one bound, the other loosed; hence processes, deprivations and anathemas followed, to the great contempt of the Church and of Christianity. The one Church was therefore given to two, and sometimes the dispute was settled by force of arms, whence followed the killing of men, the devastation of fields and the slaughter of very many. On account of this there followed the famous war waged between the Duke of Burgundy and the people of Liège, in which, as is reported, 30,000 men were slain near Liège. Indeed, by the force of mutual excommunications other wars followed, and very great disasters, and the slaughter of innocent Transalpines at Rome by Urban's command; a holy war was proclaimed on each side under full indulgences, and golden and silver statues of saints were melted down into coins, so that the wooden saints were then in a better state! Therefore Joanna, Queen of Naples, was strangled in prison by her nearest male heir, and then the baleful Gallic raids on that kingdom began; indeed infinite evils were born from this, which may be read in Dietrich of Niem and Maimbourg.

units.la: XCV. Cardinales, qui idolum erexerant, sic pergit Conclave, vel novum Pontificem secundùm eos, de Italia unà cum electo suo recesserunt, & ad Avenionem se contulerunt; D. autem Urbanus videns, quod actum fuerat, fecit in continenti unam ordinationem 12. Cardinalium lectissimorum hominum, & magnæ commendationis, fecitque Processus & privavit Cardinales, qui erant in Anagnia, vel in Fundis, unà cum eorum pretenso Pontifice, eos anathematizando & ipsos & ipsorum bona occupando, concedendo; fecit etiam Processus contra Principes Fundium, & contra Franciscum de Vico Almæ Urbis Præfectum, qui Viterbium occupavit, & e contra ille Gebernensis, contrà D. Urbanum, & ejus sequaces Processus fulminavit, sicque tota Christianitas hac peste Schismatis involuta annis 45. & ultra laboravit usque ad tempus, & tempora S. Concilii Constantiensis. Urbano sic cum Gebernensi contendente, Cardinales noviter creati, viri Zelantes honorem Ecclesiæ, & pacem populi Christiani, attediati etiam meribus Urbani, cujus nimia severitas potiùs, quàm injustitia tituli Papatus, revera fecerat Cardinales, à quibus creatus erat, ab eo discedere, & Schisma conflare, secreto modo inter se agere cœperunt; de dando D. Urbano Coadjutore, & tractare cum Cardinalibus obedientibus D. Gebernensi; (Imò ut Gobelinus Urbani Domesticus ait, comburere eum voluerunt ceu hæreticum;) quod percipiendo Urbanus captivavit septem ex ipsis, & 4. ex eis, dum esset Januæ, fecit in tetro carcere strangulare, & ad parandum sibi amicitias plurimarum Civitatum & Dominorum, Romæ in S. Maria trans Tiberim existens, fecit unam ordinationem 29. Cardinalium; inter quos multi de Civitate sua Neapolitana connumerati erant &c. Passus est hic Pontifex graves persecutiones & obsessus est per aliquantulum temporis in arce Nuceria in Regno; fertur tamen omnium persecutionum ipsum potissimam causam extitisse, propterea quòd homo ultra quàm decebat, severus erat, & sui capitis, & sibi magis, quàm cateris credens; tandem liberatus ab obsidione, in sede propria Roma residens moritur, & in Ecclesiam S. Petri in Vaticano sepelitur.
units.tr: XCV. The cardinals who had set up the idol, or the new pontiff as they called him, as the Conclave goes on, withdrew from Italy together with their elect and betook themselves to Avignon. Pope Urban, seeing what had been done, at once made a promotion of twelve most select men of great repute as cardinals, and carried out processes against the cardinals who were at Anagni or at Fondi, together with their pretended pope, deprived them, anathematized them, and granted both them and their goods to be seized. He also carried out processes against the princes of Fondi and against Francis de Vico, Prefect of the City of Rome, who had occupied Viterbo; and in turn that Genevan hurled processes against Urban and his followers. And so all Christendom, entangled in this plague of Schism, laboured for 45 years and more, until the time and the days of the Council of Constance. While Urban contended thus with the Genevan, the newly created cardinals, zealous men concerned for the honour of the Church and the peace of the Christian people, and also wearied by Urban's ways (whose excessive severity, rather than any injustice in his papal title, had indeed caused the cardinals who created him to desert him and to foster a schism), began to act secretly among themselves: about giving Urban a coadjutor and about treating with the cardinals obedient to the Genevan. (Indeed, as Gobelinus, Urban's household servant, says, they wished to burn him as a heretic.) When Urban perceived this, he captured seven of them, and four of these, while he was at Genoa, he had strangled in a foul prison. To win for himself the friendship of many cities and lords, while staying at Rome in S. Maria trans Tiberim, he made a promotion of 29 cardinals, among whom many from his own city of Naples were included, etc. This pontiff suffered grave persecutions and was besieged for some time in the fortress of Nocera in the Kingdom. It is said, however, that the chief cause of all the persecutions was that he was a man more severe than was fitting, trusting himself and his own judgement more than others. At last, freed from the siege, he died while residing in his own see at Rome, and was buried in the church of St Peter in the Vatican.

units.la: XCVI.
units.tr: XCVI.

units.la: Longa Verborum serie hujus Pontificis assumptio narrata est propterea, quòd Schisma subsequutum longi temporis fuit & multorum malorum causa, & ex gestis in electione ejusdem intelligi possit justitia tituli Papatus sui, quamvis longè aliter à Cardinalibus, qui recesserunt ab eo, positus extiterit, prætendens (prætendentibus,) metum, qui cadere poterat in constantem virum in actu electionis inter venisse; quem in tribus mensibus, quibus continuò fuerunt cum D. Urbano, nunquam allegaverunt, sicut revera allegare non poterant, & per variam positionem casus necesse fuit varia peritorum consilia hinc inde emanare, qua fuit causa, ut schisma hoc diutius duraret, qualibet parte prætendente, se justitiam fovere, & aliam verè schismaticam dici posse. Atque ista nos, omissis, vel contractis iis, quæ ad rem minus facere videbantur, ex Conclavi Urbani VI. de schismatis gravissimi atque diuturni Origine, ipsis Authoris, licèt satis barbaris, verbis heic inserere voluimus, quia satis accuratè, satis etiam ingenuè initia malorum ob oculos ponere, simulque etiam ipsa mala subsecuta compendio exhibere videtur.
units.tr: The long account of this pontiff's election is given because the schism that followed lasted a long time and caused many evils. From the proceedings at his election one can also understand the justice of his title to the papacy, although the Cardinals who withdrew from him described his position quite differently, alleging (as they claimed) that a fear which could fall upon even a steadfast man had come over them during the act of the election. In the three months during which they were continually with Urban, they never raised this plea, as indeed they could not have done. And because the situation varied, it was necessary for varied opinions of experts to come forth on each side. This was the reason the schism lasted so long, since each party claimed to uphold justice and could be called truly schismatic. We have chosen to insert these matters here in the author's own words, the Conclave of Urban VI on the origin of the most grievous and long-lasting schism, though they are rather crude. We have omitted or shortened those parts which seemed less relevant to the matter. The account seems to set before our eyes, quite accurately and quite candidly, the beginnings of the evils, and at the same time to present in brief the evils that followed.

units.la: XCVII.
units.tr: XCVII.

units.la: Consentanea autem apud Platinam in Urbano VI. reperiuntur, de quo insuper testatur; Urbanus, inquit, non intentus componenda paci inter Christianos, ut par erat, sed injurias à Joanna regina acceptas (eâ enim favente, Gebennensis electus erat) ulcisci cupiens, Ludovicum Ungariæ Regem impulit, ut Adreasii fratris mortem se adjuvante ulcisceretur &c. Et nonnullis interjectis: Tum verò Urbanus terrore Gallico liberatus, Neapolin se conferens à rege petit, ut sibi liceat creare Nepotem suum Campanum Principem, quod cùm impetrare nequivisset, homo sub specie justi & honesti minùs Urbanus ac nulli gratus ad minas conversus, eò iracundiâ regem compulit, ut custodiis adhibitis per aliquot dies prodire in publicum nequiverit. Verùm dissimulatâ ad tempus injuriâ, Nuceriam ad vitandos æstus, ut ipse dicebat, cum bona Regis venia profectus, communitâque firmis præsidiis urbe, & novos Cardinales creat &c. Præterea verò & processum, ut istorum more loquar, contra Regem inchoavit, missâ de more citatione, qui brevi venturum se Nuceriam respondit, diluiturúmque objecta crimina, non verbis modò, verùm etiam armis. Nuceriam itaque cum satis magno exercitu veniens urbem obsidet &c. (cùm que Raimundi Balciani ope cum tota Curia triremibus impositus Genuam deferretur liber, ex 7. Cardinalibus Nuceriæ captis 5. saccis involutos in mare demersit. Eidem etiam ab Authore hoc hoc tribuitur; desiderio, ut ipse dicebat, videndi Neapolim, Ferrentium usque proficiscitur: eâ mente revera, ut Ladislaum admodum puerum & Joannem Caroli filios, hereditate paternâ deturbaret. Ista, qualis Urbani illius genius fuerit, declarantia atque suprà de causa schismatis allata haud parùm illustrantia ideo quoque apponere visum fuit.
units.tr: Platina's account of Urban VI agrees with this, and he further testifies of him: Urban, he says, was not concerned to settle peace among Christians, as he ought to have been, but, wishing to avenge the injuries he had received from Queen Joanna (for it was with her support that the Genevan was elected), he prompted Ladislaus, King of Hungary, to avenge the death of his brother Andrew with his help, and so on. And after some intervening matter: Then Urban, freed from fear of the French, went to Naples and asked the king for permission to create his nephew, the Prince of Campania. When he could not obtain this, the man, who under the appearance of justice and honesty was less Urban and pleasing to no one, turned to threats. So angry was he that he drove the king to take guards, and for some days the king could not appear in public. But, pretending to overlook the injury for the time being, Urban set out for Nocera, with the king's kind permission, to escape the heat, as he himself said. He fortified the town with strong garrisons and created new Cardinals, and so on. Moreover, he began a legal process against the king, as they say, sending a summons in the usual way. The king replied that he would soon come to Nocera and would refute the charges not only with words but also with arms. Coming to Nocera with a fairly large army, he besieged the town, and so on. (When, with the help of Raimund Balciano, he was carried off on triremes with the whole Curia to Genoa, and set free, he sank in the sea, wrapped in sacks, five of the seven Cardinals captured at Nocera. The same author also attributes to him the following. Out of desire, as he himself said, to see Naples, he set out as far as Ferrento, with the real intention of stripping Ladislaus, a mere boy, and John, sons of Charles, of their paternal inheritance.) It also seemed fitting to add these accounts, which show what kind of genius Urban was, and which throw no little light on the cause of the schism mentioned above.

units.la: XCVIII. De morte Platina ita loquitur: Pontificatus sui infeliciter acti anno II. mense 5. Romae moritur, (A. Ch. 1389.) paucis admodùm mortem ejus, utpote hominis rustici & inexorabilis, flentibus. Sepulchrum adhuc visitur cum epitaphio satis rustico & inepto, quod Onuphrius adponit, aptum viro inepto. Jubilaeum à quinquagesimo ad trigesimum annum reduxit. Creavit Cardinales 54. Anti Papa 24. mortuus anno 1394.
units.tr: XCVIII. Platina speaks thus of the death of Urban: He died at Rome in the second year and fifth month of his unhappily conducted pontificate (A.D. 1389), with very few weeping at his death, since he was a rustic and inexorable man. His tomb is still visited, with a rather rustic and foolish epitaph, which Onuphrius gives, fitting for a foolish man. He reduced the jubilee from every fiftieth year to every thirtieth. He created 54 Cardinals and 24 anti-popes. He died in 1394.

units.la: XCIX. Urbano successor, cùm Cardinales suam quisque electionem sperantes Schisma cum Urbano sepelire noluerint, obtigit Petrus cognomento Tomacellus, sub nomine Bonifacii IX. juxta Platinam 30. Onuphrium verò, qui Platinae errorem notat, 45. annorum, magni animi, & qui primus populi Romani vim omnem in Pontificem transtulit, Platina & Onuphrio testibus. Ei, Platina judice, ad summam gloriam nil defuisset; nisi affinium & cognatorum affinitatibus obtemperans aliquam notam contraxisset. Multa enim crimina per Simoniacam pravitatem committebantur, petentibus contrà jus fasque omnia tum fratribus, tum cognatis, quorum magna multitudo quaestûs gratiâ Romam venerat. Indulgentia verò & quidem plenaria ita passim vendebantur, ut jam vilesceret Clavium & literarum Apostolicarum auctoritas. Revocare haec omnia Bonifacius conatus, cognatorum precibus eò identidem redire cogebatur, unde melius actum cum Ecclesia Dei censerem, si Pontifices, rejectis affinibus & cognatis, vel saltem in mediocri fortuna collocatis, Pontificiae dignitati potius quàm carni & sanguini consulerent. Ladislao suprà memorato adhuc puerulo Regnum Neapolitanum, eodem indice, restituit, patremque Carolum fato functum Urbani 6. diris absolvit. Cardinales creavit sex, & 5. ab Urbano privatos restituit, mortuus decimoquarto Pontificatus sui anno, Christi autem 1404.
units.tr: XCIX. Urban's successor was Peter, surnamed Tomacelli, under the name of Boniface IX, since the Cardinals, each hoping for his own election, were unwilling to bury the schism with Urban. According to Platina he was thirty years old; but Onuphrius, who notes Platina's error, says he was forty-five, a man of great spirit, who first transferred all the power of the Roman people to the pontiff. These are the witnesses, Platina and Onuphrius. In Platina's judgment nothing would have been lacking to him for the highest glory, had he not contracted a stain by yielding to the importunities of his relatives by marriage and blood. For many crimes were committed through simoniacal depravity, as everyone, both brothers and kinsmen, sought things contrary to law and right, and a great crowd of them had come to Rome for gain. Indulgences, even plenary ones, were sold everywhere so freely that the authority of the keys and of the apostolic letters was already becoming cheap. Boniface tried to revoke all this, but he was repeatedly driven back to these things by the prayers of his kinsmen. I would judge that it would have been better for the Church of God if the popes, rejecting their relatives by marriage and blood, or at least settling them in moderate fortune, had consulted the dignity of the papacy rather than flesh and blood. To Ladislaus, mentioned above, still a little boy, he restored, by the same account, the Kingdom of Naples, and he absolved from the curses of Urban VI his father Charles, who had died. He created six Cardinals, and restored five who had been deprived by Urban. He died in the fourteenth year of his pontificate, in the year of Christ 1404.

units.la: C. Clemens autem Anti-Papa dolore ex propositionibus pacis mortuus successorem habuit Petrum de Luna, Arragonem Hispanum, Diaconum Cardinalem S. Mariae à Gregorio XI. factum, atque Benedictum XIII. vocatum, Anno 1394. sub conditione juramento firmata depositionis, quandocunque aliis lubeat, creatum, bis Pontificatu privatum, primùm in Concilio Pisano, secundò in Constantiensi. Non tamen paruit perjurus, successorem etiam nactus, quem mox nominabimus. Cardinales creavit XXVII. Ab altera parte Innocentius VII. Bonifacii IX. successor, antea Cosmatius Melioratus dictus, Presbyter Cardinalis & sub Bonifacio Legatus pro pace inter dissidentes bello Principes & res publicas componenda, dum adhuc Cardinalis esset, inquit Platina, carpere negligentiam & timiditatem priorum Pontificum consueverat, quòd diceret, eorum socordiâ factum, ne schisma Ecclesiæ Romanæ, totiúsque Reip. Christianæ pernicies, hactenus exstinctum & sub latum esset. Verùm ipse Pontificatum adeptus, secutúsque in quibusdam Urbani & Bonifacii vestigia, quos privatus carpebat, non modò quod tantopere laudabat, (non) effecit, verùm etiam iniquo animo ferebat, si quis apud se ea de re verbum ullum fecisset. Praterea verò adeò tumultuosè omnia gubernabat, ut cùm semel Romani restitui in libertatem, reddíque sibi Capitolium, pontem Milvium & arcem Hadriani peterent, instarentque item, ut schisma rem perniciosi exempli de Ecclesia tolleret, bella exstingueret & seditiones, rege Gallorum ad eam rem conficiendam operam suam pollicente: at Petro Lunæ Anti-Papa nequaquam tantam concordiam abnuente, Romanos ipsos Pontifex ad Ludovicum Nepotem divertentem apud hospitale S. Spiritûs in Saxia, tanquam ad certum Carnificem, miserit. Undecim enim cives, Reip. suæ labenti in negligentia Pontificis consulturi, statim necantur, è fenestrisque dejiciuntur, quòd diceret, eo modo tolli seditiones & schisma non alio quidem posse &c. Electus est tumultuante tota Italia, qualis etiam fuit ipso sedente, cùm enim & vero Pontifice & optimo Imperatore carerent Itali, unicuique scelerato peccandi licentia data fuit; ait Platina in vita. Mortuus est An. Ch. 1406. anno Pontificatûs secundo, creatis Cardinalibus XI.
units.tr: C. Clement, the anti-pope, died of grief at the proposals for peace. He had as successor Peter de Luna, an Aragonese Spaniard, made deacon Cardinal of St Mary by Gregory XI, and called Benedict XIII. He was created in 1394 under the condition of a sworn promise of resignation whenever others should wish it. He was twice deprived of the pontificate, first at the Council of Pisa and secondly at Constance. Yet, being perjured, he did not obey, and he also found a successor, whom we shall name shortly. He created 27 Cardinals. On the other side was Innocent VII, successor of Boniface IX, formerly called Cosmatius Melioratus, a presbyter Cardinal, and under Boniface legate for settling peace among princes and states at war with one another. While he was still a Cardinal, says Platina, he was accustomed to blame the negligence and timidity of the earlier popes, because, he said, through their sloth the schism of the Roman Church, and the ruin of the whole Christian commonwealth, had not been extinguished and brought to an end until now. But when he himself had obtained the papacy, and followed in some of the footsteps of Urban and Boniface, whom he had blamed as a private man, he not only did not accomplish what he had so greatly praised, but he even took it ill in his heart if anyone said a word about it to him. Moreover, he governed everything so tumultuously that when the Romans, once restored to liberty, sought to recover the Capitol, the Milvian Bridge and the citadel of Hadrian, and likewise urged that he remove the schism, a matter of dangerous example, from the Church, and put an end to wars and seditions, the King of the French promising his help to accomplish this, but Peter de Luna, the anti-pope, by no means agreeing to so great a concord, the pontiff sent the Romans themselves to Louis his nephew, who was staying at the hospital of the Holy Spirit in Sassia, as to a certain executioner. For eleven citizens, who had come to consult about their commonwealth, slipping into neglect under the pontiff, were at once put to death and thrown from the windows, because he said that seditions and the schism could not be removed in any other way, and so on. He was elected while all Italy was in tumult, and it was so even during his reign. For since Italy lacked both a true pontiff and a good emperor, a license to sin was given to every wicked man, says Platina in his life. He died in the year of Christ 1406, in the second year of his pontificate, having created 11 Cardinals.

units.la: CI. Eum autem in Pontificatu excepit Gregorius XII. Venetus, Angelus Corrario, ex Patriarcha Constantinopolitano titulari Presbyter Cardinalis tit. sancti Marci; Et illo quidem tempore creatus fuit, quo de schismate tollendo valde Principes nonnulli laborabant, cùm enim schisma in Ecclesia Dei longiùs protraheretur, inquit Platina, in Greg. XII. cum pernicie Christiani nominis, Principes Galliæ, Duces scilicet, Bituricensis, Burgundus, & Aurelianus, qui tum ob valetudinem Regis Galliæ gubernabant, Calamitatem Ecclesiæ tandem miserati, Avinionem ad Petrum Lunam, Benedictum XIII. appellatum pervenirunt: hominémque rogantes, ut collabenti Ecclesiæ tandem consulat, etiam si ab si abdicare se Pontificatu necesse esset, quemadmodum in Conclavi se facturum promiserat, jure jurando interposito, dum Pontifex creabatur. Spondent praeterea, alterum Pontificem, qui tum Roma crearetur, post mortem Innocentii idem facturum. Ita enim inter hos Principes, & qui in Italia erant Reipublica Christiana amantissimi, convenerat, ut abrogatis duobus de Pontificatu contendentibus, quorum alter Gallica, alter Italica factionis haberetur, unus aliquis postea deligeretur omnium nationum Pater & Pontifex. Respondet Benedictus, se quidem graviter Deum offensurum, si Ecclesiam Dei desereret, cujus Patronus & publicus pater, consensu bonorum, non furtim, sed publice adscriptus esset, nolle se indubium ponere, quod justis suffragiis sibi demandatum fuerat. Quod dicerent, sublato schismate de concordia agendum esse, sibi admodum placere, modo id in loco fieret libero: ne coactus quispiam potius, quam sponte aliquid facere videretur. Unum tamen se polliceri, idque jurejurando affirmare, si aliter tolli schisma non posset, depositurum omnem Pontificiam dignitatem, modo idem eodem tempore ab altero Anti-Papa statim fieret. Principes itaque cognita hominis voluntate, consultare inter se coeperunt, quonam modo Benedictum in sententiam suam perducerent, quorum Colloquia & Consultationes Benedictus veritus Pontificias aedes armis & commeatu optime munivit: in quibus aliquot menses obsessus, tandem, paratis adsugam triremibus, per Rhodanum in Cataloniam, unde Oriundus erat, adnavigavit. Sunt autem, qui scribant, Principes Gallos id molitum in Benedictum esse, instantibus Cardinalibus Gallicis, qui eum oderant, quod alterius nationis esset & non Gallica. Nam cum post mortem Clementis de creando Pontifice Gallico inter eos non convenire t, hunc post longam altercationem crearunt, ut virum bonum & Reip. Christiana amantissimum: qui eos saepe admonuit, ut honeste ac sancte viverent, utique a Simoniaca pravitate caverent, aliter se in eos graviter animadversurum. Hujus itaque mores ferre nequuntes, Principes Gallos in Virum optimum & Constantis vitae concitasse.
units.tr: CI. He was succeeded in the pontificate by Gregory XII of Venice, Angelo Corraro, formerly Patriarch of Constantinople in title, a presbyter Cardinal of the title of St Mark. He was created at a time when some princes were working hard to end the schism. For, as the schism in the Church of God dragged on, to the ruin of the Christian name, says Platina, under Gregory XII the princes of France, namely the Dukes of Bourges, Burgundy and Orléans, who were then governing because of the illness of the King of France, at last took pity on the calamity of the Church and came to Avignon to Peter de Luna, called Benedict XIII, begging him to take thought for the collapsing Church, even if he had to abdicate the pontificate, as he had promised in the Conclave, under oath, when he was created pontiff. They also promised that the other pontiff, who was then being created at Rome, would do the same after the death of Innocent. For it had been agreed among these princes, and among those in Italy who were most devoted to the Christian commonwealth, that both contenders for the papacy should be set aside, one being regarded as the French faction and the other the Italian, and that afterwards some one man should be chosen as Father and Pontiff of all nations. Benedict replied that he would indeed greatly offend God if he deserted the Church of God, whose patron and public father he had been declared, with the consent of good men, not secretly but publicly; he was unwilling to cast doubt on what had been committed to him by lawful votes. As to their saying that, once the schism was removed, concord should be settled, he very much approved, provided it took place in a free place, so that no one should seem to do something under compulsion rather than of his own accord. He promised one thing, however, and affirmed it with an oath: if the schism could not otherwise be ended, he would lay down the whole papal dignity, provided the other anti-pope did the same at the same time. The princes, therefore, having learned the man's will, began to consider among themselves how they might bring Benedict to their opinion. Fearing their meetings and consultations, Benedict fortified the papal residence well with arms and supplies. Besieged there for some months, at last, with galleys made ready for the purpose, he sailed down the Rhône into Catalonia, whence he was a native. Some writers, however, say that the French princes planned this against Benedict at the urging of the French Cardinals, who hated him because he was of another nation and not French. For after the death of Clement, when they could not agree among themselves to create a French pontiff, they elected him after a long dispute, as a good man and one most devoted to the Christian commonwealth; but he often admonished them to live honourably and holily, and above all to beware of simoniacal depravity, otherwise he would proceed against them severely. Unable, therefore, to bear his manners, the French princes stirred up the French against this most excellent man of constant life.

units.la: CII.
units.tr: CII.

units.la: At vero Cardinales, qui post mortem Innocentii Romae erant, & cognita trium priorum Pontificum in tollendo schismate negligentia, cognitoque etiam discrimine, in quo Resp. Christiana ubique terrarum, maxime vero in Gallia versabatur, in unum convenientes, Conclavi ad S. Petrum in Vaticano habito, jurarunt singuli, maximis exsecrationibus interpositis, abdicaturos se statim Pontificatu, si sibi deligi ad tantum Magistratum contigisset, hac conditione tamen, ut id quoque ab Anti-Papa fieret. Venerat autem in hanc sententiam, ut & nationi Gallicae satisfaceret, qua ob impotentiam creandi Anti-Papa consuetudinem introduxerat, a quo removeri
units.tr: But the cardinals who were in Rome after Innocent's death, having learned of the negligence of the three earlier popes in ending the schism, and having also learned of the peril in which the Christian commonwealth stood everywhere, and especially in France, came together in one place, the conclave being held at St Peter's in the Vatican. Each of them swore, with the most solemn curses added, that he would resign the papacy at once if he were chosen to so great an office, on this condition however: that the Anti-Pope should do the same. They had come to this view so as to satisfy also the French nation, which, because it could not create an Anti-Pope, had introduced the custom of... by whom he was to be removed.

units.la: Conditiones, sub quibus Gregorius electus, ab eo & Anti-Papa irrita redduntur; removeri non sine ignominia videbatur, nisi id quoque ab Italis fieret: utque in sententiam Benedicti venirent, qui hac unâ ratione, non aliâ, sanari Ecclesiam posse dicebat. Quod si sibi contigisset, utrunque abrogari, unum verum Pontificem omnium, qui tum erant, Cardinalium consensu creandum esse, cui omnes Reges & Principes ob temperarent. Creatus itaque Gregorius — statim, quod ante Pontificatum promiserat, se facturum, scripto, adhibitis etiam notariis & testibus confirmavit, suâque manu scripta tabellionum notavit.
units.tr: The conditions under which Gregory was elected are made void by him and by the Anti-Pope. It seemed that removal would not be without disgrace unless this too were done by the Italians, and that they should come round to the opinion of Benedict, who said that the Church could be healed in this one way and no other. But if it had happened that both should be abrogated, and that one true Pope should be created, with the consent of all the cardinals then existing, to whom all kings and princes should submit. Thus, Gregory having been created — immediately, he confirmed in writing, with notaries and witnesses also present, that he would do what he had promised before the papacy, and he marked it with the notaries' signs in his own hand.

units.la: CIII.
units.tr: CIII.

units.la: Cùm verò de eligendo loco, quò sine discrimine uterque venire posset, mentio haberetur: neque ea de re satis inter eos conveniret, collusores & fœdifragi ab utroque Cardinalium conventu sunt habiti: qui Pisas hinc Româ, hinc Avinione adnavigantes uno consensu Gregorium & Benedictum tanquam pertinaces, schismaticos, hæreticos dignitate Pontificiâ privârunt, consentientibus in tam gravem sententiam, Bzovio etiam approbatam, omnibus nationibus præter Hispaniam citeriorem, Regem Scotiæ, Comitem Armeniaci, qui Benedicto favebant. Inita deinde creandi novi Pontificis ratione, qui bene ac sanctè sine ulla seditione Ecclesiam Dei gubernaret, venère in hanc sententiam, ut Alexandrum V. crearent; Natione, ita Platina in Alex. V. habet, Cretensem, Petrum antea vocatum, Ordinis Minorum Fratrem, Archiepiscopum Mediolanensem. Hanc ob rem Gregorius in Austriæ civitatem profectus, quasi profugus de Concilio generali mentionem fecit. Verùm, cùm eo in loco nequaquam se tutum arbitraretur, Ariminum profectus à Carolo Malatesta perbenignè & splendidè est habitus. Benedictus autem post habitum in Perpiniano Concilium, quò tutior esset, ad Castellum Panischolà, locum munitissimum confugit, ubi diutius immoratus est. Uterque autem licèt in Pisano Concilio exauctorati essent, tanquam veri Pontifices, Cardinales creârunt, maximè verò Gregorius: qui, dum Lucæ esset, de Consensu Cardinalium, qui nondum ab eo discesserant, Gabrielem Condelmerium Cardinalem creat: qui postea in Pontificem electus Eugenius IV. appellatus est.
units.tr: When the choice of a place to which both could come without danger was discussed, and they did not sufficiently agree on this, the cardinals' two assemblies regarded each other as colluders and oath-breakers. Sailing to Pisa, one from Rome and the other from Avignon, they with one accord deprived Gregory and Benedict, as obstinate, schismatic heretics, of the papal dignity. All nations agreed to so grave a sentence, which Bzovius also approved, except Hither Spain, the King of Scotland and the Count of Armagnac, who favoured Benedict. Then, having settled on a way of creating a new pope who would govern the Church of God well and holily without any sedition, they came to the opinion that they should create Alexander V; by nation, as Platina has it in his life of Alexander V, a Cretan, formerly called Peter, a friar of the Order of Minors, Archbishop of Milan. For this reason Gregory went to a city of Austria, and as a fugitive he made mention of a general council. But since he did not think himself safe in that place, he went to Rimini, and was received very kindly and splendidly by Carlo Malatesta. Benedict, after the council held at Perpignan, fled for greater safety to the very strongly fortified castle of Peñíscola, where he stayed a long time. Both, although they had been deposed at the Council of Pisa, as true popes created cardinals, Gregory most of all: who, while he was at Lucca, with the consent of the cardinals who had not yet left him, created Gabriel Condulmer a cardinal; he was afterwards elected pope and called Eugene IV.

units.la: CIV.
units.tr: CIV.

units.la: Alexander verò, soluto Concilio, Bononiam proficiscitur: cui civitati tum præerat Balthasar Cossa S. Eustachij Cardinalis: quem Alexander in Legatione confirmavit, quòd ejus industriâ ac præsidiis Pisanum Concilium habitum fuisset, quódque etiam vir erat, qui per commodè tyrannis ac rem Ecclesiasticam occupare conantibus, objici quovis tempore posset. In homine tamen plùs ferociæ, plúsque audaciæ & secularitaris (ut ita dicam) erat, quàm ejus professio requirebat. Militaris propè habebatur ejus vita, mili-tares mores, adeò ut multa etiam, quæ loqui fas non est, sibi licere arbitraretur. tur. Cùm verò Alexander graviter agrotare cœpisset, nosséque, mortem prope instare, Cardinales ad se venientes ad concordiam, ad pacem, ad tuendam Ecclesiæ dignitatem adhortatur. Testatus præterea est, per eam mortem, quam ante oculos se continuò cernere dicebat, nec reformidare, conscientiâ bene actæ vitæ motus, se existimare & credere, quæ in Concilio Pisano decreta fuissent, & rectè atque integrè facta esse omnia sine dolo malo fraudeve. Cum hæc dixisset, lacrymantibus omnibus, qui aderant, illud salvatoris verbum ægrè proferens: Pacem meam do vobis, pacem meam relinquo vobis; statim moritur, Pontificatûs sui mense 8, &c. A. Ch. 1410.
units.tr: Alexander, however, with the council dissolved, set out for Bologna. Over that city then presided Balthasar Cossa, Cardinal of St Eustace, whom Alexander confirmed in the legation, because it was by his diligence and protection that the Council of Pisa had been held, and because he was a man who could at any time be set against tyrants and against those who tried to seize church affairs. Yet in the man there was more ferocity, more audacity and worldliness (so to speak) than his profession required. His life was almost that of a soldier, his manners military, so much so that he thought himself allowed many things which it is not right to speak of. When Alexander had begun to be gravely ill, and knew that death was nearly at hand, he urged the cardinals coming to him towards concord, peace and the defence of the Church's dignity. He testified besides that, with that death which he said he now saw continually before his eyes, and not fearing it, moved by a conscience of a well-spent life, he judged and believed that what had been decreed at the Council of Pisa was right and whole, and that everything had been done without evil intent or fraud. When he had said this, with all who were present weeping, and with difficulty uttering the Saviour's word, "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you," he died at once, in the eighth month of his pontificate, etc. A.D. 1410.

units.la: CV. Successorem habuit dictum Balthassarem Cossam, de quo & de ejus electione, partim jam jam, partim verò Dissert. VI. ubi de ambitu & violentia & largitione ad consequendum Pontificatum adhiberi solita egimus, nonnulla dicta sunt.
units.tr: CV. He had as successor the aforesaid Balthasar Cossa, concerning whom and his election some things have been said, partly just now and partly in Dissertation VI, where we discussed the ambition, violence and bribery usually employed to obtain the papacy.

units.la: De eo porrò Onuphrius in Joh. XXIII. al XXIV. (Johannes enim ejus nomen Pontificale erat) ita loquitur: Vir fuit bello & armis, quàm religioni aptior, utpote qui nullam neque fidem nôrat, neque religionem, rebus profanis magis quàm divino cultui accommodatus. Creatus, referente Platina in vita, Oratores statim ad Electores imperij misit, eos oratum, ut Sigismundum Lucimburgum Ungariæ & Bohemiæ Regem, Imperatorem crearent, virum strenuum (ut ipse dicebat) & ad omnia fortiter agenda promptissimum. Hac enim ratione hominis gratiam occupabatur: (occupabat:) Ubi vero hoc ei ex sententia accidit, cùm in conventu Pisano constitutum esset, ut ad certum tempus Concilium haberetur, ne alibi transferretur, celebraturum se id Romæ prædixit: & quò liberiùs eò proficisci omnibus liceret, pacare Italiam conatus est &c.
units.tr: Onuphrius speaks of him at John XXIII (alias XXIV, for John was his papal name) as follows: He was a man more fit for war and arms than for religion, since he knew neither faith nor religion, and was better suited to profane affairs than to divine worship. Once created, as Platina reports in the life, he at once sent envoys to the electors of the empire, asking them to make Sigismund of Luxemburg, King of Hungary and Bohemia, emperor, a man vigorous (as he himself said) and most ready to act boldly in all things. For by this means he was seeking the man's favour. When this turned out as he wished, since at the Pisan assembly it had been decided that a council should be held at a fixed time and not moved elsewhere, he declared in advance that he would hold it at Rome; and so that everyone might go there more freely, he tried to pacify Italy, etc.

units.la: CVI. Tandem verò, quum schisma ob ejus creationem (loquitur Onuphrius) non sedatum, sed auctum esse videretur, tribus jam sepræ Pontificibus gerentibus, quò solus in Pontificatu, cæteris rejectis, confirmaretur, suasu Sigismundi Imperatoris Concilium generale Constantiæ indixit.
units.tr: CVI. Finally, when the schism, because of his creation (Onuphrius says), seemed not to have been quelled but increased, with three popes now holding office, so that he alone might be confirmed in the papacy, the others being rejected, at the urging of the Emperor Sigismund he proclaimed a general council at Constance.

units.la: Eum autem consensu omnium nationum ad Concilium citatum fuisse, Platina testis est, qui & narrat, quosdam proficisci volentem Pontificem admonuisse, ne id faceret, quòd vererentur, ne cùm Pontifex accederet, privatus reverteretur.
units.tr: That he was summoned to the council with the consent of all nations, Platina is a witness, who also relates that some warned the pope, who was preparing to set out, not to do so, because they feared that when he arrived as pope he would return as a private man.

units.la: CVII. Idem Platina narrat; Cum quibusdam Viris in omni genere doctrinæ præstantibus præsentem diu multúmque Germanos disputationibus incertos & ambiguos tenuisse, quid potissimùm decernerent.
units.tr: CVII. The same Platina relates that the Germans, long present and uncertain and divided in their disputations, had held in doubt, together with certain men outstanding in every kind of learning, above all what they should decide.

units.la: Verùm, ita pergit, Superveniente Sigismundo, factaque omnibus dicendi, quod liceret, potestate, multa crimina & quidem gravissima Pontifici objecta
units.tr: But, he goes on, when Sigismund arrived, and everyone was given the freedom to speak as they wished, many crimes, and indeed most grave ones, were charged against the pope.

units.la: Successor Ioannes XXIII. al. XXIV. qualis & quid primò egerit.
units.tr: The successor, John XXIII (alias XXIV): what sort of man he was and what he first did.

units.la: Concilio Constantia habendo consensit, atque illuc proficiscitur.
units.tr: He agreed to the council being held at Constance, and set out there.

units.la: Gravissimorum criminum reus deponitur. jecta sunt: quorum caussa, mutato habitu familiáque, clanculum Scaphu-sam se contulit, veritus, ne quid gravius in se consuleretur; Erat Scaphusa Frederici Austriæ Ducis civitas, quò etiam plerique Cardinales à se creati fugà pervenêre. Verùm his postea Concilii auctoritate revocatis, Joannes Scaphusâ Friburgum confugit, iturus inde, si tutò fieri posset, ad Burgundiæ ducem, sed curante Concilio, Joannes capitur & (in) insula S. Marci prope Constantiam in carcerem conjicitur, Pontificatûs sui anno 4. m. 10. Caussam fugæ disquirere Concilium tam cœpit, certásque judices Viros gravissimos & doctissimos delegit, qui crimina Joanni objecta discuterent, eadémque Concilio ex ordine refert (referrent.) Ad quadraginta Capitula & eo amplius contrà hominem probata sunt; quorum aliqua, quum in eo minimè immutari possent, adeò erant inveterata, contrà fidem judicata sunt, aliqua verò Christianis omnibus, si non damnarentur, Scandalum paritura. Venientibus itaque omnibus in eandem sententiam, Joannes meritò è Pontificatu dejectus, sententiam in se latam comprobat. Traditus postmodùm fuit in custodiam Ludovici Bavari, qui cum Gregorio XII. sentiebat; Ferunt autem, inquit porrò Platina, abrogatum Joanni Pontificatum ab his tantùm, qui cùm eo ante senserant; Nondum enim, qui cum Gregorio & Benedicto sentiebant, convenerant. Hi igitur, ut abrogationem à se factam veram & integram judicarent, omnes Synhodicum decretum promulgárunt, quo affirmabant, Concilium generale legitimè congregatum habere statim à Christo potestatem. Hoc quidem fundamento concesso, ipsum etiam Pontificem Concilio subjiciebant.
units.tr: Accused of the gravest crimes, he is deposed. ...were charged against him. On account of these, changing his dress and household, he secretly betook himself to Schaffhausen, fearing that something more serious would be decided against him. Schaffhausen was a city of Duke Frederick of Austria, whither many of the cardinals created by him also fled. But these, afterwards recalled by the authority of the council, John fled from Schaffhausen to Freiburg, intending to go from there, if it could be done safely, to the Duke of Burgundy. However, the council took care, and John was captured and thrown into prison on the island of St Mark near Constance, in the fourth year and tenth month of his pontificate. The council began to inquire into the cause of the flight, and chose certain very grave and learned men as judges, who were to examine the crimes charged against John and report them to the council in order. About forty chapters and more were proved against the man; some of these, since they could not be altered in him, were so ingrained that they were judged contrary to the faith, and some would be a scandal to all Christians if they were not condemned. All therefore came to the same opinion, and John, rightly deposed from the papacy, approved the sentence passed against him. Afterwards he was handed over to the custody of Louis of Bavaria, who sided with Gregory XII. They say, moreover, Platina goes on, that the papacy was taken from John only by those who had agreed with him before; for those who had sided with Gregory and Benedict had not yet come together. These therefore, so that they might judge the abrogation made by them to be true and complete, all published a synodal decree, by which they affirmed that a general council lawfully assembled has power at once from Christ. Granting this foundation, they also made the pope himself subject to the council.

units.la: CVIII. Quare Gregorio necesse fuit, suadente etiam Imperatore Sigismundo, unum aliquem ad Concilium mittere, cùm ipse proficisci recusaret, qui suo nomine Concilii sententiam approbaret. Missus itaque Carolus Malatesta, vir certè insignis, cùm videret omnes in hanc sententiam venire, ut Gregorius quoque Pontificatu se abdicaret, in publicum prodiens, ac in sede Gregorii non aliter exstructa, si ipse adesset, collocatus, perlectâ renunciandi facultate, Gregorium Pontificatu abdicat: quem statim Conventus omnis pro tam libera abdicatione, agri Piceni Legatum creat. Is itaque non multò post Recanati moritur, dolore animi (ut ajunt) propter subitam abrogationem ante constitutum tempus à Carolo factam. In longum enim re (rem) protrahi volebat, in mora spem aliquam ponens. Mortuus itaque ante Martini Pontificatum, in Recanatensi Ecclesia sepelitur.
units.tr: CVIII. Therefore Gregory had to send one man to the council, at the urging of Emperor Sigismund as well, since Gregory himself refused to go; this man was to approve the council's decision in Gregory's name. Accordingly Carlo Malatesta was sent, certainly a distinguished man. When he saw that everyone was coming round to the view that Gregory too should give up the papacy, he came forward in public. Seated in Gregory's place, which had been set up just as if Gregory himself were present, he read out the authority to resign and then renounced the papacy on Gregory's behalf. The whole assembly at once appointed him legate of the March of Ancona, for so free an abdication. He did not die long afterwards at Recanati, of grief of mind (as they say) over the sudden renunciation that Carlo had made before the appointed time. For Gregory wanted the business drawn out at length, placing some hope in delay. So he died before the pontificate of Martin and was buried in the church of Recanati.

units.la: CIX. Sublatis duobus Pontificibus, tertius, in quo abrogando major difficultas inerat, restabat, Petrus Luna Benedictus XIII. (ut antea dixi) vocatus.
units.tr: CIX. With two popes removed, the third remained, in whose case there was greater difficulty in removing him: Peter de Luna, called Benedict XIII (as I said before).

units.la: CCCC vocatus Ut autem is etiam nolens abdicare se Magistratu cogeretur, Sigismundus Imp. unà cum Oratoribus Concilii ad Franciæ & Angliæ Reges pervenit, eósque adhortatus est, ut pro salute Christiani nominis jam ob schisma periclitantis, in abrogando Benedicto, sublatis aliis duobus, ejus sequerentur sententiam. Graio autem responso accepto, inde Narbonam properat ad Ferdinandum Aragonum Regem, cujus populi magna ex parte Benedicto obtemperabant. Quo cum inter alia Capitula hoc pactus est, ut Benedictum moveret rationibus ea facere, qua Gregorius & Joannes in Concilio Constantiensi egissent. Id vero si recusaret, populos cogeret ab eo ad Concilium Constantiense deficere. Benedictus autem in Castello Panischola loco munitissimo se continens, moveri persuasionibus à sententia sua non poterat, quòd diceret, & se verum Christi Vicarium esse, & Constantiam non esse locum libertati Ecclesiasticæ convenientem, cùm Joannes XXIII. ab his etiam abdicare se Pontificatu coactus fuerat, qui partes suas antea sequebantur. Tùm verò Principes Hispaniæ cernentes pertinaciam Benedicti, Concilii opinionem secuti, in reliquorum sententiam venere. Gerebantur res in Concilio quinque nationum suffragiis, Italica, Gallica, Germanica, Hispanica & Anglica. Quicquid verò harum nationum suffragiis decernebatur, id ita ratum erat, si omnium consensu postea confirmatum fuisset. Quâ quidem auctoritate Benedictus, discussâ aliquandiu re, Pontificatu tandem privatur, absentibus rejectisque nationibus, quæ cum eo sentiebant, maximè verò Scotis & Comite Armeniaci &c. Electus in Concilio fuit Otho Columna Romanus Princeps, S. Georgii ad vellus aureum Diaconus Cardinalis, qui Martinus vocari voluit, quòd ea electio in Martini celebritate habita fuisset, cùm jam quadriennio, inquit Platina idem, vero Pontifice caruisset Ecclesia. Balthasar Cossa autem, referente Onuphrio in vita; quadriennio fere in carcere asservatus, ad extremum, magnâ pecuniæ summâ persolutâ, dimittitur, Martino jam creato atque Florentiæ agente; ad quem Balthasar accedens Episcopus Cardinalis Tusculanus creatur &c.
units.tr: CCCC called. But when he too, refusing to give up his office, was to be compelled to abdicate, Emperor Sigismund went with the envoys of the council to the kings of France and England. He urged them that, for the sake of the salvation of the Christian name, now endangered by the schism, they should follow the council's opinion in deposing Benedict, with the other two set aside. Having received a cool reply, he hurried from there to Narbonne, to Ferdinand, king of Aragon, most of whose people obeyed Benedict. There, among other terms, it was agreed that Ferdinand would try to move Benedict by reasons to do what Gregory and John had done at the Council of Constance. If Benedict refused, Ferdinand would compel his peoples to desert him in favour of the Council of Constance. Benedict, however, shut up in the castle of Peñíscola, a very strongly fortified place, could not be moved from his opinion by persuasion. He said both that he was the true Vicar of Christ, and that Constance was not a place suited to ecclesiastical liberty, since John XXIII had also been forced to give up the papacy there, he who had formerly followed Benedict's side. Then indeed the princes of Spain, seeing Benedict's obstinacy, followed the opinion of the council and came over to the view of the rest. Affairs in the council were conducted by the votes of five nations: Italian, French, German, Spanish and English. Whatever was decreed by the votes of these nations was valid only if it was afterwards confirmed by the consent of all. By this authority, after the matter had been discussed for some time, Benedict was at last deprived of the papacy, the nations that sided with him being absent and rejected, especially the Scots and the Count of Armagnac, etc. Otto Colonna, a Roman prince and cardinal deacon of St George at the Velabrum, was elected in the council. He wished to be called Martin, because the election had been held on Martin's feast day, since, as Platina the same author says, the Church had already been without a true pope for four years. Balthasar Cossa, however, according to Onuphrius in his life, was kept in prison for almost four years and was at last released when a large sum of money had been paid, Martin having already been created and being at Florence. Balthasar, going to him, was created cardinal bishop of Tusculum, etc.

units.la: CX. Martinus idem, cùm restare adhuc caput renascentis hydræ cerneret, sunt verba Platinæ in Martino V; Benedictum Lunam cum aliquot Cardinalibus & Prælatis Panischolæ tanquam in arce Schismatis secontinentem, quibusdam Arragoniæ populis, in utram partem incinarent, adhuc titubantibus, approbante Concilio Alemanum Ademarium Virum Doctissimum — S. Eusebii Presbyterum Cardinalem Legatum è Laterensi suo in Arragoniam mittit, qui sub Pœnis & Censurâ Ecclesiasticâ Petrum admoneret, ut se Pontificatu abdicaret. Cardinales autem, qui cum Petro sentiesentiebant, intelligentes ultimam Concilii & Pontificis sententiam, Petrum ipsum adeunt rogántque, ut de Ecclesia Dei tandem omne schisma tollat, quo jam multis annis Christiana Resp. magnis calamitatibus afflicta erat. Id autem ob salutem labentis Ecclesiæ, à Gregorio & Joanne factum esse. Respondit Petrus Cavillationibus quibusdam, id sibi nequaquam integrum esse, sibi autem cum Martino conventurum, si vera essent, quæ de hominis integritate & humanitate dicerentur, sinerent sibi id negotii, nec amplius ea de re solliciti essent. Ex 4. verò Cardinalibus 2. pertinaciam hominis inspicientes, ab eo ad Martinum statim defecêre. Qui autem in fide manserê, Anti-Cardinales sunt habiti; quorum alter Carthusiensis fuit, alter verò Julianus Dobla appellatus est. Martini quoque auctoritatem Hispania omnis statim secuta est. Idem fecere non multò post Scoti & Armeniaci. Atque ita omnis Resp. Christiana, unâ duntaxat Pansschola exceptâ, Martini auctoritatem secuta est.
units.tr: CX. Martin, seeing that the head of the renewed hydra was still standing (these are Platina's words on Martin V), while some peoples of Aragon were still wavering as to which side to incline towards, and Benedict Luna, with some cardinals and prelates, was holding out at Peñíscola as in the citadel of the schism, sent, with the council's approval, Ademarius, a most learned man, presbyter cardinal of St Eusebius, as legate from his Lateran palace into Aragon. Under penalties and ecclesiastical censure, the legate was to admonish Peter to resign the papacy. The cardinals who sided with Peter, understanding the final judgment of the council and of the pope, approached Peter himself and begged him to finally remove from God's Church the whole schism, by which the Christian commonwealth had for many years been afflicted with great calamities. This, they said, had been done by Gregory and John for the salvation of the failing Church. Peter replied with certain quibbles that this was by no means in his power, but that he would meet with Martin if the things said of that man's integrity and humanity were true. They should let him handle the business and no longer be anxious about it. Of the four cardinals, two, seeing the man's obstinacy, at once deserted him for Martin. Those who remained faithful were regarded as anti-cardinals; one of them was a Carthusian, the other called Julian Dobla. All Spain at once followed Martin's authority, and the Scots and Armagnac did the same not long afterwards. And so the whole Christian commonwealth, with only Peñíscola excepted, followed Martin's authority.

units.la: CXI.
units.tr: CXI.

units.la: In Concilio tandem quia schisma ex parva re antea ortum fuerat, sunt verba ejusdem Platinæ ibidem; duriusque cum magna calamitate Christiana Reipubl. duraverat — decretum — fuit, ut à fine Concilii Constantiensis non nisi ad quinquennium usque Concilium denuò celebraretur: atque à quinquennali in septennium aliud transferretur; ab hoc verò in decennium res protracta, legis haberet locum, ut singulis quibusvis decenniis Concilium Generale idoneo haberetur loco, ubi de rebus omnibus ad fidem & Rempubl. Christianam pertinentibus, mentio fieret &c. Martinus autem omnia decreta ante Pontificatum suum in schismate facta, nisi ad fidem & bonos mores pertinerent, omninò sustulit; Atque Concilium dissolvit.
units.tr: Finally, at the Council, since the schism had arisen earlier from a small matter and had lasted longer, to the great calamity of the Christian commonwealth, a decree was made that after the end of the Council of Constance the Council should not be reconvened until five years had passed. Then it was to be postponed from five years to seven, and from seven to ten, so that by law a General Council would be held at a suitable place every ten years, at which all matters pertaining to the faith and the Christian commonwealth would be discussed, and so on. Martin, however, completely annulled all the decrees made during the schism before his pontificate, except those that pertained to faith and good morals, and he dissolved the Council.

units.la: CXII.
units.tr: CXII.

units.la: Quatuor illi Cardinales, qui olim cum Petro Luna senserunt, cum magno & honorificentissimo comitatu publico Consistorio suscepti, dignitatum suarum titulos retinuêre — Balthassar Cossa verò in Italiam veniens, magnam injecit omnibus suspicionem, ne rursum schisma innovaretur. Erat enim vir magni animi sagacissimíque, & qui privatam vitam nequaquam pateretur. Non deerant praterea, qui hominis audaciam ad res novas moliendas concitarent, adeò tum rebus novis studebatur. At agnoscens Martinum dolore animi, ut putatur, (ferre enim vitam privatam non poterat) aliquot post menses Florentia moritur.
units.tr: The four cardinals who had formerly sided with Peter de Luna were received by a public consistory with great and most honourable retinue, and they kept the titles of their dignities. But Balthasar Cossa, when he came into Italy, aroused great suspicion in everyone that the schism might be renewed. For he was a man of great spirit and shrewdness, who by no means could endure a private life. Nor were there lacking others who urged on the man's boldness for attempting revolutions, so eager for novelties were people at that time.
