But, recognising Martin's power, he died at Florence a few months later, of grief of mind, as is supposed, since he could not bear a private life.

units.la: CXIII.
units.tr: CXIII.

units.la: Et cùm statuto Constantiæ tempore Papiæ primò & post, volente Pontifice, Senis ad Concilium conventum esset, Alphonsus Aragonum Rex Martino infensus, qui titulum Regni Siciliæ & Neapolis habere nequiverat, datum Alouisio Regis Ludovici Filio, Oratorem ad Concilium mittit: quid (qui) & Concilium in longum duceret, & caussam Petri Lunæ adhuc in Paniscbola superstitis restitueret, Largitione, pollicitationibus ambiendo unumquemque ex his, quid (qui) in Concilio authoritatem haberet (haberent.) Hanc ob rem Martinus — mandavit Concilium statim dissolvi, approbatis decretis Concilio habitis, quæ ad fidem pertinebant. Et ne superfugere conventum Christianorum videretur, in sequens septennium Concilio adjudicavit, quod in Basilea celebraretur. Atque hoc modo Schismatis & discordiarum semina à quibusdam in Concilio Senensi jacta & sparsa, sublata hominis prudentiâ & astu sunt &c.
units.tr: When, according to the decision made at Constance, the Council had been convened first at Pavia and afterwards, at the Pontiff's wish, at Siena, Alphonsus, King of Aragon, hostile to Martin and unable to obtain the title of the Kingdom of Sicily and Naples, which had been given to Louis, son of the King of France, sent an envoy to the Council. He wanted to prolong the Council and to restore the cause of Peter de Luna, who still survived at Peñíscola, and he courted each of those who had authority in the Council with largesse and promises. For this reason Martin ordered the Council to be dissolved at once, after the decrees made by the Council that pertained to faith had been approved. And so that it should not seem that he was fleeing the assembly of Christians, he assigned to the Council for the following seven years a meeting to be held at Basel. And in this way the seeds of schism and discord, which had been sown and scattered in the Council of Siena by certain persons, were removed by the man's prudence and cunning, etc.

units.la: CXIV.
units.tr: CXIV.

units.la: Sed mortuo (A. Ch. 1424.) Petro Luna in Paniscbola (ubi sex post mortem annis corpus incorruptibile & optimè olens repertum atque aliò translatum fuit, miraculo non minùs cæteris, quæ jactant Pontificii Benedictum ex hypothesi damnare coacti, insigni, ipsíque etiam Maimburgio ad annotandum digno viso;) ne aliquid deesset, quod Ecclesiam vexaret, duo illi Anti-Cardinales, Alphonso Martini honeste (hoste) adhortante, Ægidium cognomento Munionis, Canonicum Brachinonensem, genere nobilem Pontificem deligunt, Clementémque VIII. appellant; qui statim & Cardinales creavit, & fecit, quæ à Pontificibus fieri consueverunt. Verùm cùm Martinus in gratiam cum Alphonso rediisset, eò statim Petrum de Fuxo Cardinalem misit Apostolicæ sedis Legatum: in cujus manus, jubente Alphonso Panischolæ Domino, Ægidius omnia Pontificatus jura depositi: erga quem hac benignitate Martinus postea usus est, ut eum Majoricensem Episcopum declaraverit; Cardinales autem ab Ægidio creati sponte Cardinalatu se abdicârunt. Illi autem duo, quos à Petro Luna creatos diximus, in suâque pertinacia mansisse, cùm Pontifici Romano parere nollent, in carcerem à Legato conjiciuntur, atque hoc modo Martini Pontificis sapientiâ & industriâ omne schisma undique sublatum est. Factum illud demum anno 1428. adeò, ut (quod ab initio dictum) schisma ab anno 1378. quo Clemens VII. contrà Urbanum VI. electus fuit, per 50. annos durârit; Cujus sic historiam ad finem usque perduximus;
units.tr: But after the death (in the year of Christ 1424) of Peter de Luna at Peñíscola (where, six years after his death, his body was found incorrupt and very sweet-smelling and was moved elsewhere, a miracle no less remarkable than the others the Papists boast of, which they were forced to regard as a remarkable thing even by Maimbourg, who is worth noting), so that nothing should be lacking that might trouble the Church, those two anti-cardinals, Alphonsus, Martin's enemy, urging, chose Giles, surnamed Munión, a canon of Barcelona of noble birth, as Pontiff, and called him Clement VIII. He at once created cardinals and did whatever the Pontiffs are accustomed to do. But when Martin had returned into favour with Alphonsus, he at once sent Peter of Foix, a cardinal and Apostolic Legate, to whose hands, at the command of Alphonsus, lord of Peñíscola, Giles laid down all the rights of the Pontificate. Martin afterwards treated him with such kindness that he declared him Bishop of Majorca; the cardinals created by Giles voluntarily renounced their cardinalate. But the two whom we said were created by Peter de Luna, who had remained in their obstinacy and refused to obey the Roman Pontiff, were thrown into prison by the Legate; and in this way, by the wisdom and industry of the Pontiff Martin, the whole schism was removed everywhere. That event finally took place in the year 1428, so that the schism, which (as was said at the beginning) began in the year 1378, when Clement VII was elected against Urban VI, lasted for fifty years. We have now brought its history down to its end.

units.la: CXV.
units.tr: CXV.

units.la: In qua certè historia infiniti ferè nævi occurrunt, vitia electionis Pontificum Romanorum plurima. Duo fuerunt eodem tempore, tres simul, diu tot fuerunt; quilibet clamabat: Hic est Christus, ibi est Antichristus, vel ejus præcursor! Ego sum bonus Pastor, illi sunt fures & latrones; Quis quovis tempore legitimus fuit? Difficile dictu. Conclave quidem Urbani VI. meliorem ejus successorumque causam facit, sed & impressionis metúsque que Cardinalium eligentium, & quomodo idem metus post electionem etiam manserit, haud levia vestigia exhibet, certa autem pessimi atque inepti in Urbano animi indicia tum idem Conclave, tum Platina & Onuphrius habent. Imò scriptis à parte & altera editis, quorum nonnulla hodienum supersunt, Viri Docti causam modò hujus, modò illius defenderunt, neque certè integra regna cuilibet adhaesissent, si facilè de meliori causa constare potuisset. Multùm autem intererat, ut de ea planè constaret, est enim de necessitate salutis, (definivit, pronuntiavit & declaravit Bonifacius VIII.) omni creaturæ, subjicere te Pontifici Romano; Pontifici Romano, non Anti-Papæ, non Pseud-Episcopo, non Invasori, non Antichristo, non Idolo, non Hæretico, non Tyranno, non Schismatico, non Proditori, non Improbo, non Zizaniorum seminatori, non Filio Belial, non denique furi & latroni, quibus hi se invicem elogiis ornabant; Quid igitur judicabunt de tot Christianorum myriadibus in communione schismaticorum per 50. annos defunctorum? Æternis Cruciatibus eos, vel eo solo nomine addicere debent, nisi contrà hypotheses suas agere velint, qui tamen etiam in singulis obedientiis apud Maimbourg. Hist. du grand Schisme l. 1. Sanctos revelationibus & miraculis claros viros ostendunt, necessariò tamen multos ex hypothesi fundamentali damnandos! Ridiculè enim Maimburgius ait, utramque partem credidisse, se legitimo Papæ adhærere; Quos enim damnabit, si bona fides ejusmodi sufficit? Sed quid si nullus diu verus Pontifex fuit? Jam largitus est illud Platina de quadriennio. Ast depositis in Concilio duobus, omne jus ad tertium jam tum devolutum esse dici omnino debet, cujus tamen successor illud, si accepit unquam, amisisse statim dici debet. Si accepit unquam, adeò illegitimè electus; Amisit, aut nunquam accepit, ex Pontificiis relationibus, haereticus, imò planè Atheus; Vel an Concilium non habet Pontificem deponendi potestatem? Certè non habere volunt hodierni Monarchici; sed tunc neque Concilium Constantiense habuit, Martinus Anti-Papa fuit, sunt ejus successores; moxque dicendum erit, expirâsse veram Ecclesiam cum Petri de Luna duobus Cardinalibus in carcere; Neque enim à dedentibus se Anti-Papis jus mutuari voluit Martinus. Quanta autem vitia latent in illis, quas Author Conclavis Urbani VI. memoravit, constantibus, sed contrariis ligationibus, solutionibus, processibus, privationibus, anathematizationibus, Ecclesiarum earundem distributionibus diversis factis? Quanta in armorum vi, qua quandoque lis dirime-batur, in hominum occisionibus, agrorum depopulationibus, plu-rimorum strage, bello famoso, aliis? Denuò notetur, durasse tot mala per annos quinquaginta. Ubi tunc Ecclesia? Quomodo tunc verum caput ejus dignoscere, illique se subdere potuerunt Chri-stiani. Recte potius, dum schisma cresceret, Wenceslaus in Episto-la: Etsi benedictus Dei filius multa & dura passus sit per viros Synagogicos, adhuc multò duriora patitur per nostros sacerdotum Principes. Recte Author Fasc. temp. p. 86. de hoc ipso schismate; Adeo perple-xum fuit, ut etiam doctissimi & conscientiosi viri non valerent discutere, cui magis esset adhærendum; Et ideò ab isto Urbano VI. usque ad Martinum V. nescio quis fuerit Papa. Recte etiam Gerson Serm. de Sign. ruin. Eccl. Ecclesia – dubitavit, apud quam partem vera sedes – nisi forsitan Deus alicui revelâsset, aut Salomonis judicium de vera aut falsa matre alicui persuaderet.
units.tr: In this history there occur almost countless blemishes, very many faults in the election of the Roman Pontiffs. There were two at the same time, at times three together, for so long a time; each one cried out: "Here is Christ, there is Antichrist, or his forerunner! I am the good Shepherd; they are thieves and robbers!" Who was at any time the lawful one? That is hard to say. The conclave of Urban VI certainly makes his cause and that of his successors better, but both the pressure and the fear of the electing cardinals, and how the same fear remained after the election, show no slight traces; and the same conclave, along with Platina and Onuphrius, provides certain signs of Urban's very bad and foolish mind. Indeed, with writings put out by one side and the other, some of which survive to this day, learned men defended now this cause, now that one, and whole kingdoms would certainly not have adhered to either if it could have been easily agreed which cause was the better. It mattered greatly that this should be plainly agreed, for it is altogether necessary for salvation (Boniface VIII defined, pronounced and declared) that every creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff: to the Roman Pontiff, not to an anti-pope, not to a pseudo-bishop, not to an usurper, not to an antichrist, not to an idol, not to a heretic, not to a tyrant, not to a schismatic, not to a traitor, not to a wicked man, not to a sower of tares, not to a son of Belial, not, finally, to a thief and robber, which epithets these men heaped on one another. What then will they judge concerning so many myriads of Christians who died in communion with schismatics over fifty years? They must consign them to eternal torments on that ground alone, unless they wish to act against their own hypotheses; and yet they show, in the individual obediences, in Maimbourg, History of the Great Schism, book 1, men holy and renowned for revelations and miracles, yet they must necessarily condemn many of them on their fundamental hypothesis! For Maimbourg says ridiculously that both parties believed that they adhered to the lawful Pope. For whom will he condemn, if such good faith is sufficient? But what if no one was a true Pontiff for a long time? Platina has already conceded this regarding the four years. But after the two had been deposed at the Council, it must be said that all right had at once passed to the third, although his successor, if he ever received it, must be said to have lost it immediately. If he ever received it, he was so unlawfully elected; he lost it, or never received it, according to the Papist accounts, being a heretic, indeed a plain atheist. Or does a Council not have the power to depose a Pontiff? Certainly today's monarchists want to deny it; but then the Council of Constance did not have it, Martin was an anti-pope, and his successors are likewise; and soon it will have to be said that the true Church had expired together with the two cardinals of Peter de Luna in prison, for Martin did not wish to borrow a right from the anti-popes who had surrendered to him. And what great faults lie hidden in those things which the author of the conclave of Urban VI recorded, namely the constant but contrary bindings and loosings, proceedings, deprivations, anathemas, and the various distributions of the same churches made by each side? What of the violence of arms, by which the dispute was sometimes settled, of the killing of men, the laying waste of fields, the slaughter of very many, the infamous war, and other things? Let it be noted again that such evils lasted for fifty years. Where was the Church then? How could Christians then recognise its true head and submit themselves to him? Rather, as the schism grew, Wenceslaus rightly said in his letter: Although the blessed Son of God has suffered many hard things at the hands of the synagogue men, he suffers even harder things now at the hands of our princes of the priests. The author of the Fasciculus temporum rightly speaks, on page 86, of this very schism: It was so perplexed that even the most learned and conscientious men could not decide which side ought to be adhered to; and therefore from this Urban VI to Martin V I do not know who was Pope. Gerson also rightly doubted in his sermon on the signs of the ruin of the Church, in which party the true seat was, unless perhaps God had revealed it to someone, or the judgment of Solomon concerning the true and false mother persuaded someone.

units.la: CXVI. Trigesimum primum atque ultimum totale schisma
units.tr: CXVI. The thirty-first and last total schism

units.la: fuit inter Eugenium IV. & Nicolaum V. ab una & Felicem V. ab altera parte. Ille enim Martini V. successor anciputi curâ distractus & quod bellis (Italicis) undique premeretur, narrat Platina in vita, & quòd Basileense Concilium jam ante inchoatum Martini decreto augeri indies cerneret, concurrentibus eò Hispania, Gallia, Germania, Pannoniaque Principibus, qui communem Reip. Christiana causam in arbitrio Concilii reponebant: ad tollendum Concilium versus, illud quidem primò ex Basilea Bononiam transtulit, Cardinalium omnium, qui secum aderant, consensu; Sed Imperator aliique Principes & Prælati, qui tum Basilea erant, non modò Pontifici non obtemperârunt, verùm etiam eum bis terque monuerunt, ut Basileam idoneum à Martino celebrandi Concilii locum delectum unà cum Cardinalibus proficisceretur, aliter se in eum acturos ut in prævaricatorem & contumacem. Motus igitur istorum verbis Eugenius Basileense Concilium literis etiam Apostolicis confirmavit, factâ uniuique eundi ad Concilium potestate. Adeò enim bello undequaque vexabatur, ut vix ei respirandi facultas daretur — Post tamen publico consistorio Basileense Concilium, quod ante approbaverat, Ferrariam transfert, quòd diceret, Græcos cum Ecclesia Romana in fide conventuros, eundem locum sibi delegisse. Instabant contrà Concilii Basileensis Præsides, & precibus ac pollicitationibus Græcos hortabantur, ut omisso Eugenio ad se proficiscerentur. Neque hoc contenti, abrogaturos se Eugenium prædicabant, nisi ipse quoque eò proficisceretur. Substitit aliquandiu Eugenius animi dubius, quid potissimum mum decerneret, missô tamen eò Legato Jo. Fr. Capitelista ICTO, Patavinóque Equite, qui ejus causam tueretur; Verùm mortuo Sigismundo — à quo Basileense Concilium incrementa habuerat — Ferrariense — inchoavit, eò ipse profectus, quòd adventare Imp. Constantinopolitanum Jo. Palaeologum intellexerat — Verùm cùm pestis Ferraria inolevisset — Florentiam transferre Concilium placuit.
units.tr: was between Eugenius IV and Nicholas V on one side and Felix V on the other. Eugenius, Martin V's successor, was distracted by anxious care, and because he was pressed on every side by the Italian wars, as Platina relates in his Life. He also saw that the Council of Basel, begun by Martin's decree, was growing daily, as the princes of Spain, France, Germany and Hungary flocked there and placed the common cause of the Christian commonwealth in the judgment of the Council. To remove the Council, he first transferred it from Basel to Bologna, with the consent of all the cardinals who were with him. But the Emperor and the other princes and prelates who were then at Basel not only refused to obey the Pope, but warned him two or three times that he should go to Basel, the place Martin had chosen for the Council, together with the cardinals, or else they would act against him as a prevaricator and a contumacious man. Moved by their words, Eugenius confirmed the Council of Basel by apostolic letters, granting each man the power to go to it. For he was so harassed by war on every side that he was scarcely given a chance to breathe. Afterwards, however, in a public consistory, he transferred the Council of Basel, which he had earlier approved, to Ferrara, saying that the Greeks would meet with the Roman Church there in matters of faith, and that he had chosen that place for them. The presidents of the Council of Basel opposed this and, by prayers and promises, urged the Greeks to come to them and leave Eugenius aside. Not content with this, they declared that they would depose Eugenius unless he too went there. For a while Eugenius hesitated in doubt over what to decide most importantly, yet he sent thither as legate John Francis Capitelista, a jurist, and a Paduan knight, to defend his cause. But when Sigismund had died, from whom the Council of Basel had gained its strength, he began the Council of Ferrara, going there himself because he had learned that the Emperor of Constantinople, John Palaeologus, was coming. But when the plague had taken hold in Ferrara, it was decided to transfer the Council to Florence.

units.la: CXVII.
units.tr: CXVII.

units.la: Interim Philippus Genuæ antea Dominus Italius potentissimus, agrè ferens, Florentinos adjuvante Eugenio atque adhortante, Franciscum Sforziam Venetis (cum quibus ei tunc inimicitiæ intercedebant) auxilio misisse, cum his agit, qui in Basileensi Concilio erant, ut Eugenium citarent, fecere illi quidem bis terve. Verùm, cùm id ex sententia ei non cederet, eò dementia, inquit Platina, eos pepulit, ut abrogato Eugenio Amedeum Sabaudia Ducem socerum suum, qui Eremitanam vitam Ripalia cum quibusdam nobilibus ducebat, Pontificem crearent, Felicémque appellarent. Hinc magnæ seditiones in Ecclesia Dei exortæ sunt, cùm Christiana Resp. trifariam divisa, aut Felicem, aut Eugenium sequeretur, essentque, qui Neutrales vocarentur, quòd neutri obtemperarent — Eugenius verò, ut partes suas augendo, Basileense Concilium infirmaret, eodem tempore Consistorio publico 18. Cardinales creavit — Romam regressus Concilium generale in Laterano se habiturum omnibus denuntiat; — hac enim ratione infirmari ac tolli omninò Concilium Basileense volebat.
units.tr: Meanwhile Philip, formerly the most powerful lord of Genoa, took it badly that the Florentines, with Eugenius' help and encouragement, had sent Francis Sforza against the Venetians, with whom he was then at enmity. He dealt with those who were in the Council of Basel, that they should summon Eugenius; and they did so, twice or three times. But since this did not turn out as he wished, he was driven by madness, says Platina, to the point of deposing Eugenius, creating as Pope Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, his father-in-law, who lived a hermit's life at Ripaille with some noblemen, and calling him Felix. From this great seditions arose in the Church of God, since Christendom was divided into three parts, following either Felix or Eugenius, and there were those called Neutrals, because they obeyed neither. Eugenius, however, in order to increase his own party and weaken the Council of Basel, at the same time created eighteen cardinals in a public consistory. Returning to Rome, he announced to everyone that he would hold a general council in the Lateran, for in this way he wanted the Council of Basel to be weakened and altogether abolished.

units.la: CXVIII.
units.tr: CXVIII.

units.la: De eo ita tandem judicat Author: Vir certè in vita varius. Principio enim Pontificatûs sui malis consiliis ductus divina humanáque omnia perturbavit. Nam & populum Romanum ad arma excivit, & Concilio Basileensi, unde infinita mala orta sunt, auctoritatem dedit, approbatis eorum per litteras Apostolicas decretis. Verùm postea ad se ipsum rediens &c. Mortuus est Pontificatûs sui anno 16. Ch. 1446.
units.tr: The author finally judges him thus: "Certainly a man variable in his life. For at the beginning of his pontificate, led by evil counsels, he threw everything, divine and human, into confusion. For he both roused the Roman people to arms and gave authority to the Council of Basel, whence infinite evils arose, by approving its decrees through apostolic letters. But afterwards, coming back to himself, etc." He died in the sixteenth year of his pontificate, in the year of Christ 1446.

units.la: CXIX.
units.tr: CXIX.

units.la: Successor ejus Nicolaus V. jam sub Eugenio, ut Platina in vita narrat, in Germaniam ad tollendum Basileense Concilium neutralitatémque (Neutrales enim ideò Germani sunt dicti, quòd neque Eugenii, neque Felicis dictis obtemperarent) missus cum Joanne Garvagialla, — Ecclesia enim Dei multas & maximas calamitates incurrebat, cum imminutione Majestatis Pontificiæ — Difficile quidem erat removere Germanos ab opinione sua, falsa præsertim; Difficile item videbatur Eugenii Oratoribus, ut Postulatis Germanorum obtemperarent. Tandem verò, delinitâ orationibus nimiâ Oratorum severitate, & castigatis Germanorum postulatis, schisma & neutralitatem rem quidem Romanæ sedi perniciosissimam mam sustulerant, si stare promissis,inquit Platina,voluissent; Redux in itinere cùm socio Galerum accepit.
units.tr: His successor Nicholas V, already under Eugenius, as Platina relates in his Life, was sent into Germany with John Carvajal to remove the Council of Basel and the neutrality (the Germans were so called because they obeyed neither Eugenius' nor Felix's decrees). For the Church of God was incurring many great calamities, with a lessening of papal majesty. Indeed, it was hard to draw the Germans away from their opinion, especially a false one; and it also seemed hard for Eugenius' envoys to comply with the demands of the Germans. At last, however, the excessive severity of the envoys was softened by speeches, and the demands of the Germans were corrected, so that they had abolished the schism and the neutrality, a matter most ruinous to the Roman see, if they had wished to keep their promises, says Platina. On the journey back he received the cardinal's hat in company with his fellow envoy.

units.la: CXX. Pontifex factus tandem schisma sublatum vidit, compulit enim Fredericus Imperator, instante Pontifice, Felicem, ut se Pontificatu abdicaret, quòd cerneret tantam seditionem & tam diuturnam Ecclesia Romana perniciosam esse. Usus tamen hac benignitate erga Amadeum Nicolaus est, ad hominem namque Galerum Cardinalatus misit: eundémque legatum Germaniæ fecit, ne omninò sine dignitate viveret. Venere & in arbitrium Pontificis Cardinales illi, quos Amadeus creaverat. Factum illud A. Ch. 1449. Pontificatûs sui anno 3. inde ab exorto schismate 10.
units.tr: CXX. When he became Pope, he at last saw the schism ended. For the Emperor Frederick, at the Pope's urging, compelled Felix to abdicate the papacy, since he saw that such a great and long-lasting sedition was ruinous to the Roman Church. Nicholas, however, used this kindness towards Amadeus: for he sent him the cardinalate, and made him legate of Germany, so that he should not live altogether without dignity. Those cardinals whom Amadeus had created also came under the Pope's judgment. That happened in the year of Christ 1449, in the third year of his pontificate, counting from the outbreak of the schism as the tenth.

units.la: CXXI. Quod non immeritò Onuphrio dirum, acerrimum vocatur, atque valdè dubium fuit, cùm Concilium Basileense, prout in Concilio Constantiensi statutum erat, indictum, ad ejus exemplum Papam semel atque iterum vocatum & comparere tamen nolentem deposuerit; Viro ei vitæ, ut multi volunt, laudatissimæ suffecto. Ei, qui ab initio Pontificatûs sui Divina humanáque omnia, teste Platina, perturbârat, temporibus Ecclesiæ undiquaque periculosissimis. Atque sic alterum, ejus, quòd Papa à Concilio deponi possit, ostendebatur exemplum; Nesciebant miseri, utrum Concilium, vel an & quem Papam potiùs sequi debeant, aliis huic, illi aliis adhærentibus, multis neutri accedentibus, utroque autem tamdiu Cardinales creante atque alia, quæ muneris Pontificii esse putârunt, agente. Vitium igitur & hëic multiplex notari potest ratione numeri eorum, qui eliguntur, in schismate hoc totali haftenus ultimo atque trigesimo primo.
units.tr: CXXI. Onuphrius rightly calls it dire and most bitter, and it was very doubtful, since the Council of Basel, as had been decreed at the Council of Constance, was convened and, on that model, summoned the Pope once and again, and deposed him when he refused to appear; a man of, as many say, most praiseworthy life was put in his place. He who, from the beginning of his pontificate, had, as Platina testifies, thrown everything, divine and human, into confusion, in times most dangerous to the Church on every side. And so another example was shown that a Pope can be deposed by a council. The wretched people did not know whether they ought to follow the Council or whichever Pope, or rather which Pope; some adhered to one, some to another, many to neither, while each side kept creating cardinals and doing other things which they thought belonged to the papal office. Hence the fault in this total schism, the last and thirty-first so far, can be noted in many ways, from the number of those who were elected.

units.la: CXXII. Quot certè in nulla alia Ecclesia schismata notantur, nimirum oportuit, ut, quandoquidem Ecclesia Romana fa-stûs mundani prærogativam habet, etiam illa divisionum, quæ inde sequuntur, non tantùm magnitudine, sed & numero, præsul-geret. Onuphrius quidem tantùm triginta enumerat, quia nimirum decimum quartum & decimum quintum nostrum minùs accuratè conjungere voluit, quæ tamen consideranti diversa apparent.
units.tr: CXXII. Indeed, so many schisms are noted in no other Church; it was surely necessary that, since the Roman Church has the prerogative of worldly pomp, the divisions that follow from it should stand out not only in their magnitude but also in their number. Onuphrius lists only thirty, because he chose to join the fourteenth and fifteenth of ours less exactly, though to one who considers them they appear different.

units.la: CXXIII. Imò etiam nimia visa sunt triginta ab Onuphrio enumerata víxque nomen Schismatum quædam eorum merentia non nemini, auctori nimirum annotationis in Chronicon Romanorum Pontificum sequentis: Enumerat divus Onuphrius schismata aliquot (triginta) in Romana Ecclesia, circa qua notandum est, pleraque eorum tantùm tantùm fuisse controversias & dissidia de Romano Pontifice inter electores aut electos, quæ nonnisi impropriè Schismata dici possint. Quando autem secundùm Ecclesiasticam Phrasin fuit veri nominis schisma propter Pontificatum, ut in Novatiano, hoc non fuit schisma in Ecclesia, sed ab eo, qui extra Ecclesiam erat, contra caput Ecclesiæ. Unde & hic est impropr etas sermonis, dum tale schisma ponitur in R. S. E.
units.tr: CXXIII. Indeed, the thirty listed by Onuphrius even seemed excessive to some, and some of them scarcely deserved the name of schisms, as the author of the annotation on the Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs that follows says: "The divine Onuphrius lists several schisms (thirty) in the Roman Church, concerning which it should be noted that most of them were only controversies and disputes about the Roman Pontiff between electors or the elected, which can be called schisms only improperly. But when, according to ecclesiastical usage, there was a true schism concerning the papacy, as with Novatian, this was not a schism in the Church, but one made by a man outside the Church against the head of the Church. Hence this too is an improper way of speaking when such a schism is placed in the Roman See."

units.la: CXXIV. Ita quidem ille schismata Onuphriana elevare studet, qualia autem illa fuerint ex dictis patet, ex parte quoque ex ipsis Onuphrii testimoniis.
units.tr: Thus he tries to play down the Onuphrian schisms. What those schisms really were is clear from what has been said, and partly also from Onuphrius' own testimonies.

units.la: Pleraque eorum tantùm fuerunt controversiæ & dissidia de R. P. inter electores aut electos. Sed quid quæsò aliud sunt schismata in Ecclesiis ratione Episcoporum? Dividuntur electores atque in diversas partes planè abeunt; nonne hoc Schisma est? Dividitur unitas & cùm unus eligi deberet, duo aut tres eliguntur, nonne hoc Schisma est? Schisma, id est, divisio? Schisma proprìè dictum? Imò constat ex præmissis, utrumque semper sibi abhærentes habuisse, etiam præter eos, qui ad electionem concurrerunt, quando non omnes concurrerunt; plerunque Schismata diu anathematibus, armis, &c. continuata esse. An igitur pleraque — non nisi impropriè Schismata dici possunt? Quid igitur ad Schisma proprìè dictum amplius requiritur? Porrò, ita loqui deprehenditur Auctor, ac si præter leves controversias & dissidia, quæ impropriè tantùm Schismata dici possint, schismata nulla in Ecclesia Romana fuerint, sed ab eo, qui extra Ecclesiam erat, contra caput Ecclesiæ. Quænam illa impudentia? Reclamant omnia. An enim Anti-Papæ non in Ecclesia fuerunt, dum eligebantur? Imò, an etiam constabat omnibus, uter esset caput Ecclesiæ? An capiti Ecclesiæ omnes & singuli in Ecclesia adhærebant contrà Invasores? An non in ipsa Ecclesia partes fuerunt, scissiones, divisiones, quid nì etiam Schismata in Ecclesia, Romana nimirum, sine improprietate sermonis? Exemplum Novatiani allegat, sed unicum, & cui nullum planè simile. An autem sic classis schismatum constituitur non in Ecclesia, præter quæ omnia sint impropriè tantùm Schismata? Ast ne quidem Novatiani Schisma dici potest non fuisse in Ecclesia, sed ab eo, qui contra caput Ecclesiæ extra Ecclesiam erat, adeóque Schisma per improprietatem sermonis tantùm in Ecclesia Romana. Neque enim Novatianus, dum eligeretur, extra Ecclesiam erat, errore quidem infectus erat, sed nondum ab Ecclesia damnato, sed minùs in ipso notato. An enim alias & si extra Ecclesiam fuisset, Confessores ei adhæsissent? An magna ista, juxta Baronium Ecclesia tentatio fuisset? An omnes pene Ecclesia, ut Cyprianus ait, perturbata fuissent? An opus fuisset, ut Ecclesiae Africanae legatione solenni in potiora jura inquirerent? Minimè; Sed simpliciter omnes capiti Ecclesia contra eum, qui extra Ecclesiam erat, adhaesissent, atque sine magna tentatione. Quod autem etiam in Ecclesia Romana aliqui, multi, Confessores Novatiani partes secuti sunt, nonne illud satis superque docet, schisma illud quoque, licet satis singulare, sine improprietate sermonis in Ecclesia Romana & ratione eligentium & ratione electorum, & ratione omnium, poni posse? Si non ratione electorum, (licet non fuerit ab initio excommunicatus, proin adhuc in Ecclesia fuerit,) saltem sine improprietate sermonis, respectibus manentibus reliquis, poni posse? Et an non omnia docent, annotationem istam pessimam atque à vero alienissimam esse? Sed male habuit hominem istum, & male habet alios, quòd in Catalogo Pontificum suorum à divo suo exarato tot Schismata occurrunt, quae modis omnibus pallare, fucare, atque sic ad interiora non penetrantes decipere studeant, dum intus & in ore magis ingenuorum ex suo ordine, tetra, dira, truculenta, maximè turbulenta, pessima, omnium pessima, diuturna, maxima, acerrima & quidnon? intus etiam ossibus mortuorum plena sunt.
units.tr: Most of them were only controversies and dissensions about the Roman Pontiff among the electors or the elected. But what, I ask, are schisms in the Churches with regard to bishops, if not this? The electors are divided and go over completely to different sides. Is this not a schism? Unity is divided, and when one ought to be elected, two or three are elected. Is this not a schism? A schism, that is, a division? A schism properly so called? Indeed, it is clear from what was said above that each side always kept adherents to itself, even apart from those who came together for the election, whenever not all came together; and for the most part these schisms continued for a long time with anathemas, arms, and so on. So are "most of them ... can only be called schisms improperly"? What, then, is further required for a schism properly so called? Moreover, the author is found to speak as if, apart from slight controversies and dissensions, which can only be called schisms improperly, there were no schisms in the Roman Church, but only one from him who was outside the Church, against the head of the Church. What shameless claim is this! Everything cries out against it. Were the antipopes not in the Church while they were being elected? Indeed, was it not known to all who was the head of the Church? Did all and each adhere within the Church to the head of the Church against the usurpers? Were there not parties, splits and divisions in the Church itself? Why, then, should there not also be schisms in the Church, namely the Roman one, without impropriety of speech? He cites the example of Novatian, but a single one, and one to which nothing at all is similar. Or is such a class of schisms constituted not in the Church, apart from which all others are only schisms improperly? But not even the schism of Novatian can be said not to have been in the Church, but from him who, outside the Church, was against the head of the Church, and so a schism only by an improper use of speech in the Roman Church. For Novatian, while he was being elected, was not outside the Church. He was indeed infected with error, but he had not yet been condemned by the Church, only less marked in himself. For otherwise, if he had been outside the Church, would the confessors have adhered to him? Would this have been a great trial of the Church, as Baronius puts it? Would almost the whole Church, as Cyprian says, have been thrown into confusion? Was there any need for the Church of Africa to inquire into the weightier rights by a solemn embassy? By no means. Rather, all would simply have adhered to the head of the Church against him who was outside the Church, and without great trial. But the fact that in the Roman Church too some, many, confessors followed the party of Novatian: does that not sufficiently and more than sufficiently show that this schism too, though quite singular, can be set down in the Roman Church without impropriety of speech, both with regard to the electors and to the elected, and with regard to all? If not with regard to the elected (although he was not excommunicated from the beginning, and so was still in the Church), can it at least be set down without impropriety of speech, the other respects remaining? And do not all things teach that this annotation is very bad and most alien to the truth? But it has troubled that man, and troubles others, that in the catalogue of popes drawn up by his divine (pope) so many schisms occur, which they strive in every way to pale over, disguise and so deceive those who do not penetrate within; while inside, and in the mouths of more candid men of their own order, they are foul, dire, truculent, very turbulent, wicked, the most wicked of all, long-lasting, very great, most bitter, and what not? Inside, indeed, they are full of the bones of the dead.

units.la: CXXV.
units.tr: CXXV.

units.la: Possemus his Schismatibus totalibus atque majoribus, addere, quòd aliquando duo Papae electi fuerunt, sine schismate in Ecclesia subsecuto, quod tamen ad tempus fuit ratione eligentium & electorum. Fuit ejusmodi schisma in Conclavi Clementis VIII, ubi etiam schisma, sive scissionem vestium non defuisse, alibi notavimus; Notavimus etiam, fere Papam ibi fuisse S. Severinam, imò, si Decani in numerando fraus abfuisset, illum verè Papam ex isto Conclavi prodituram fuisse, non alium. Confirmatur idem in Vita Patris Pauli Veneti p. 63. Santa Severina, inquit Author, in Roma sotto Clemente sapeva, quanto fosse stato vicino al Papato, è che non era totalmente estinto il dubio, se la sua elettione fosse valida; però Clemente pasceva l'humore del Cardinale col lasciargli fare, ciò che voleva. Id est: Sancta Severina Roma sub Clemente (VIII.) sciebat, quàm propinquus Papatui fuerit, & quòd non prorsus extinctum sit dubium, num electio sua valida fuerit; quare etiam Clemens multùm huic Cardinali indulgebat eique pro lubitu quidvis agere permittebat. Tunc & saepe aliàs (etiam in Concl. Pauli V. ubi S. Clemens per 6. horas Papa creditus 5. aut 6. vota superflua habebat;) inde ab ultimo
units.tr: We could add to these total and greater schisms that sometimes two popes were elected without a schism following in the Church, which nevertheless existed for a time with regard to electors and elected. A schism of this kind occurred in the conclave of Clement VIII, where we have noted elsewhere that there was also a schism, or a tearing of garments. We noted too that Santa Severina was almost pope there; indeed, had the dean's fraud in counting been absent, he would have come forth from that conclave as the true pope, and no other. The same is confirmed in the Life of Father Paolo Veneto, p. 63: "Santa Severina," says the author, "in Rome under Clement knew how near he had come to the papacy, and that the doubt whether his election was valid had not been wholly extinguished; therefore Clement fed the cardinal's humour by letting him do whatever he wished." That is: Sancta Severina at Rome under Clement (VIII) knew how near he had been to the papacy, and that the doubt whether his election was valid had not been wholly extinguished; wherefore Clement also greatly indulged this cardinal and allowed him to do whatever he pleased. Then also often at other times (even in the conclave of Paul V, where St Clement, believed to be pope for six hours, had five or six superfluous votes), from the last

units.la: Schismatis simile quid contigit in Conclavi Clementis VIII. Cur nulla amplius ex tam longo tempore Schismata? ultimo Schismate Onuphriano parùm à schismatibus erumpentibus abfuerunt Cardinales in Electionibus Pontificum ; Et quòd nulla ex illo tempore eruperunt, non certè ambitionis, quam semper eandem esse ostendimus, defectui tribuendum est, sed partim nocumentis praeteritorum schismatum, quae recentioribus quodammodo documenta facta sunt, partim Conclavium institutioni, postquam rariora statim esse coeperunt schismata, partim multiplicatis ad schisma impediendum constitutionibus aliis, partim etiam separationi Ecclesiarum à Romana merito factae, quâ factâ, schisma in Electione tanto magis nociturum facile vident. Quemadmodum Reformatio in aliis quoque scandalis eos Cautiores, si non Castiores, fecit. Satis autem Scandala Romanam Ecclesiam foedârunt in schismatibus Seculorum praeteritorum recensitis, quorum jam vitium adhuc paucis atque generaliùs notâsse juvabit.
units.tr: Something similar to a schism happened in the conclave of Clement VIII. Why have there been no more schisms in so long a time? Since the last schism, the Onuphrian one, the cardinals in papal elections were scarcely distant from schisms breaking out. That none has broken out since then must be attributed not, certainly, to any lack of ambition, which we have shown to be always the same, but partly to the harm of past schisms, which have in some measure become lessons for later times; partly to the institution of conclaves, after which schisms began at once to be rarer; partly to the many other constitutions multiplied to prevent schism; and partly also to the separation of the Churches from the Roman one, rightly made. Once that was done, they readily see that a schism in the election would harm them all the more. Just as the Reformation has made them more cautious, if not more chaste, in other scandals too. But the scandals have sufficiently defiled the Roman Church in the schisms of past centuries recounted above, the vice of which it will now help to note briefly and in more general terms.

units.la: CXXVI.
units.tr: CXXVI.

units.la: Cognosci jam potuit ex dictis in speciali schismatum consideratione, ex ipsa scissione, ex electorum conditione, ex incertitudine, ex adjunctis & consequentibus, ex testimoniis, ex elogiis, sive potiùs pessimis schismaticorum titulis; Quibus hic addimus appellationes, portenti ex inferorum portis prodeuntis, quomodo Novatianus vocatur; Cathedra pestilentia, quae Constantino tribuitur. Testimonia quoque vitium in genere notantia habemus praeter allata: Audiatur Petrus Damiani apud Baronium ad an. 1061. n. 16. vel ex Grammatica Cadalaum convincere studens; Porrò autem, inquit, sicut Diabolus Divino Nomini pluralem numerum indidit, ut diceret mulieri: Eritis sicut Dii &c Ita tu Grammaticorum regulis novum aliquid addidisti, ut in declinatione jam pueri dicant, Papa, Papae rum: Per te itaque senex jam mundus addiscit, quod hactenus ignoravit. (Sed jam schismata multa fuere ante hoc; ) & sicut juxta Pauli vocem: Summus Pontifex in Sancta per annos singulos ingrediebatur in sanguine alieno; Sic & tu nunc miserorum hominum, velut parcorum succidium, succidium facis, & sanguinem fundis, ut ad B. Petri sanctuarium cruentus ingrediaris. Idem ad eandem apud eundem ad an. 1062. n. 5. O scelus inauditum! Pilati milites inconsutilem Domini non praesumunt scindere tunicam: & tu in duos Papas Catholicam partiris Ecclesiam. Illi pendentis in cruce Salvatoris ossa non frangunt &c. Captam bello Arcam Dei Israel Philistaeorum Principes temerare non audent &c. Si Oza moritur, qui humerum supponit, ne Arca Domini corruat, quid illi merito fiet &c. Idem contra eundem epitheta pessima coacervat apud eunden ad an.1064. n.19. Sentiat, inquit, sentiat teterrimus Draco, Cadalous scilicet, perturbator Ecclesia, eversor Apostolica disciplina, inimicus humanæ salutis; sentiat radix peccati, praeco Diaboli, Apostolus Antichristi; Et quid plura dicam! Sagitta producta de pharetra Satanæ, Virga Assur, filius Belial, filius perditionis, qui adversatur & extollitur super omne, quod dicitur Deus, aut quod colitur, vorago libidinis, naufragium castitatis & Christianitatis opprobrium, ignominia Sacerdotum, genimen viperarum, fœtor orbis, spurcitia scorti, dedecus Universitatis ( attexantur adhuc epitheta Cadalai, Catalogus videlicet nominis tenebrosi ) serpens lubricus, coluber tortuosus, stercus hominum, latrina criminum, sentina vitiorum, abominatio cœli, projectio Paradisi, pabulum tartari, stipula ignis æterni. Sentiat iste &c. Eadem fere epitheta cumulavit ad Coloniensem Archiep. scribens, apud Bar. ad an.1062. n.20. ubi etiam Anti-Papæ tribuit, quòd adulterinum sedis Apostolicæ concubitum quærat, & tanquam petulans adulter suam explere libidinem in Ecclesia Romana violatione medullitùs inardescat. Adde his sequentia ex Theodorico de Niem. de Privil. & jure Imp. Quia Papatûs officium non est vi rapiendum, verùm cum oratione & devotione & timore Dei suscipiendum; Nun est mirum, si tunc mundus inquietatur totus & conturbatur, quando Rom. Ecclesia, in qua est principalitas correctionis universa Christianitatis, obtinetur schismate, & turpitudine quomodo libet confunditur: quia tunc confestim accidit, membra sibi subdita à capitis dolore etiam passibiliter debilitari. Et cùm caput taliter est contritum, continuò membra læsa sunt, quia cùm caput ægrotat, cætera membra dolent.
units.tr: What has been said in the special consideration of schisms can now be recognized from the split itself, from the condition of the electors, from the uncertainty, from the accompanying and resulting circumstances, and from the testimonies and epithets, or rather the worst titles, given to schismatics. To these we add the names a portent coming forth from the gates of hell, as Novatian is called, and a pestilential chair, which is attributed to Constantine. We also have testimonies, besides those already cited, that note the vice in general. Let Peter Damian be heard, as quoted by Baronius at the year 1061, n. 16, where he tries to refute Cadalus by means of grammar: Moreover, he says, just as the Devil gave the plural number to the divine Name, when he said to the woman: You shall be like gods, etc., so you have added something new to the rules of grammar, so that now even boys in their declensions say Pope, of the Pope, of the Popes. Through you, therefore, the old world is learning what it has hitherto not known. (But many schisms had already occurred before this.) And, as the words of Paul say: the High Priest entered into the Holy Place every year in the blood of another; so you now, like butchers of wretched men, as of sheep for slaughter, make a slaughter and pour out blood, so that you may enter bloody into the sanctuary of St. Peter. The same writer, in the same work at the year 1062, n. 5: O unheard-of crime! The soldiers of Pilate did not presume to tear the seamless tunic of the Lord, and you divide the Catholic Church into two Popes. They did not break the bones of the Saviour hanging on the cross, etc. The princes of the Philistines did not dare to violate the Ark of God taken in war, etc. If Uzzah died, who put his shoulder under the Ark so that the Ark of the Lord would not fall, what will rightly happen to those men, etc. The same writer, against the same man, piles up the worst epithets in the same work at the year 1064, n. 19: Let the most foul Dragon feel it, namely Cadalus, the disturber of the Church, the subverter of apostolic discipline, the enemy of human salvation; let the root of sin, the herald of the Devil, the apostle of Antichrist feel it. And why should I say more! An arrow drawn from the quiver of Satan, the rod of Assur, the son of Belial, the son of perdition, who sets himself against and exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshipped, the whirlpool of lust, the shipwreck of chastity and the disgrace of Christianity, the shame of priests, the brood of vipers, the stench of the world, the filth of a harlot, the dishonour of the Universal Church (more epithets of Cadalus are added here, that is, the catalogue of a shadowy name) a slippery serpent, a twisting viper, the dung of men, the sewer of crimes, the sink of vices, the abomination of heaven, the castaway of Paradise, the fuel of Tartarus, the straw of eternal fire. Let him feel it, etc. He heaped up nearly the same epithets when writing to the Archbishop of Cologne, cited by Baronius at the year 1062, n. 20, where he also charges the Anti-Pope with seeking the adulterous embrace of the apostolic see, and, like a wanton adulterer, burning inwardly to satisfy his lust by violating the Roman Church. Add to these what follows from Dietrich of Niem, On the Privileges and Right of the Emperor: Since the office of the Papacy is not to be seized by force, but to be received with prayer, devotion and the fear of God, it is no wonder if the whole world is then disturbed and thrown into confusion, when the Roman Church, in which lies the principal power of correcting all Christendom, is held by schism and is somehow disgraced by shameful conduct; for then, at once, the members subject to it are weakened by the pain of the head. And when the head is so bruised, the members are at once injured, because when the head is sick, the other members suffer.

units.la: CXXVII. Huc etiam pertinet, quòd Anti-Papas cum suis pro hæreticis habent.
units.tr: CXXVII. This also pertains to the fact that they hold the Anti-Popes and their followers to be heretics.

units.la: Hinc formula schisma abdicantium in Concilio Lateranensi an Ch. 1179. præscripta: Ego N. anathematizo & rejecto omnem hæresin extollentem se adversus Romanam Ecclesiam, præsertim verò schisma Octaviani, Guidonis & Johannis &c. Hinc etiam Octavianus ipse ad Imperatorem &c. scribens in literis n.72. citatis Scripta Alexandri tanquam – à schismatico & hæretico destinata respui vult. Qui tamen rursus Octavianus in Actis Alexandri n.77. citatis infelicis memoria hæresiarcha audit. Nec minùs huc pertinet, quòd non tantùm de Anti-Papis passim, quod ibi de Octaviano, judicant, eos de hoc mundo migrare ad inferos, sed &, quod dicta & dicenda probant abundè, eorum asseclis salutem æternam aperte aliquan-
units.tr: Hence the formula prescribed for those renouncing schism at the Lateran Council in the year 1179: I, N., anathematize and reject every heresy that sets itself up against the Roman Church, and especially the schism of Octavian, Guido and John, etc. Hence also Octavian himself, writing to the Emperor etc. in the letters n. 72 cited, wants the writings of Alexander as sent by a schismatic and heretic to be rejected. Yet the same Octavian is called a heresiarch of unhappy memory in the Acts of Alexander n. 77 cited. Nor does it pertain less here that they not only judge, everywhere, the Anti-Popes, as they judge Octavian there, to migrate from this world to hell, but also, as the things said and to be said abundantly prove, that they plainly deny eternal salvation to their followers to some extent

units.la: Exco, quod Anti-Papas cum asseclis pro hæreticis habent. aliquando abjudicant. Vide etiam de Schismaticorum dignitatibus Bar. ad an. 964. n. 8. seqq.
units.tr: Exco, that they hold the Anti-Popes with their followers to be heretics; sometimes they deny them salvation. See also Baronius on the dignities of schismatics, at the year 964, n. 8 ff.

units.la: CXXVIII. Fusiùs idem Pontificiis schismatis eíque adhærentium crimen prosequitur Ant. de Rosellis Monarch. p.2. c.16. seqq. Et c.16. equidem Format,quæstionem: An propter schisma Papa deponi possit? Ubi inter argumenta pro affirmativa ponit,delictum schismatis videri gravius omni delicto, etiam gravius delicto haresis 24. q. 1. c. non afferamus;in fine. Imò prolabi Schismaticum in haresin, quia veniat contrà mentem articuli;dicentis, quòd una sit Ecclesia,sponsa Christi pura &c. fidémque non esse in Schismate, quia si forte teneatur erga Deum, non teneatur erga Ecclesiam &c. &c. duos contendentes videri constituere in Ecclesia duo Capita,tanquam monstrum &c. Videri Ecclesiam corrumpere,ei duos viros attribuendo &c. ad alteram sic facere, à Christi compagne semetipsos abscindere,Christum in eorum cordibus non habitare, nec Deum eos Patrem habere,sed societatem fraternitatis commaculare, & Deum iterum prodere &c. jurisdictionalia perdere, & inter Antichristos numerari debere &c. &c. Atque hinc orta sunt memorata de Schismaticis judicia,Schismaticorum elogia.
units.tr: CXXVIII. The same writer pursues the crime of schism and of those adhering to it among the Papists more fully: Antonius de Rosellis, Monarchy, part 2, ch. 16 ff. Indeed, in ch. 16 he poses the question: Can the Pope be deposed on account of schism? Among the arguments for the affirmative he sets down that the offence of schism seems graver than every offence, even graver than the offence of heresy (24 q. 1, c. non afferamus, at the end). Moreover, a schismatic falls into heresy, because it runs against the sense of the article saying that there is one Church, the pure bride of Christ, etc., and that there is no faith in schism, because if one holds to God, one does not hold to the Church, etc., etc. Two contenders seem to set up two heads in the Church, like a monster, etc. They seem to corrupt the Church by ascribing two husbands to it, etc. In doing so for the one or the other, they cut themselves off from the body of Christ, Christ does not dwell in their hearts, nor do they have God as Father, but they stain the fellowship of brotherhood and betray God again, etc. They lose their jurisdictional rights and ought to be numbered among the Antichrists, etc., etc. From this have arisen the aforesaid judgements on schismatics and the epithets of schismatics.

units.la: CXXIX. Magnitudo quoque criminis in Schismate atque Christianorum tunc incertitudo cognosci potest ex iis, quæ idem Author subjungit c.17. & 18. An & quomodo Papa Schismaticus fieri possit? C. 19. Pontifex de Pontificatu cum alio contendens, vel alius secum contendens de schismate,vel duo etiam non Pontifices inter se de Pontificatu contendentes: an dici Schismatici debeant, & an deponi propter hoc possint? C. 20. 21. 22. Quando plures sint contendentes,quis judex esse debeat? C. 23. & 24. Perplexitatem quandam indissolubilem & aliud dubium majus habet; Si Concilium judicare debeat, quis illud convocare & aucta rare debeat? C. 25. Cæsarem,vel Cardinales, qui fortè crediderint uni ex istis Pontificibus litigantibus,non posse ab ipso se separare,& conscientiâ salvâ convocare Concilium; Sed quid hoc casu possint vel debeant facere,vel subditi? An liceat ipsis à suo,quem reputant Pontificem,separare sine discrimine & peccato; quod & c. 28. tractat C. 26. An Cardinales possint ante sententiam Concilii in casibus praditis ad electionem alterius procedere? C. 29. An subditi debeant servare praecepta,vel timere censuras & excommunicationes.quas eisdem suus Pontifex facint in casu,quo recedant,vel Concilium convocent? Omnia ista nævos Schismatum inter Pontifices magis ostendunt fusè & quodlibeticè ab Auctore tractata; Legat,cui nugas legere vacat. Facilè vel simpliciter proposita agnoscuntur absurda ex falsis hypothesibus ad earum destructionem fluentia.
units.tr: CXXIX. The magnitude of the crime in schism, and the uncertainty of Christians at that time, can also be recognized from what the same author adds in ch. 17 and 18: Can and how can a Pope become a schismatic? Ch. 19: a Pope contending with another, or another contending with him over schism, or two who are not Popes contending with each other over the papacy: ought they to be called schismatics, and can they be deposed for this? Ch. 20, 21, 22: when there are several contenders, who ought to be the judge? Ch. 23 and 24: a certain indissoluble perplexity and another greater doubt he has; If a Council ought to judge, who ought to convene it and increase it? Ch. 25: the Emperor or the Cardinals, who perhaps believed that they could not separate themselves from one of these contending Popes and, with a clear conscience, convene a Council; but what can or ought they or the subjects to do in this case? Whether it is lawful for them to separate from the one they regard as Pope without danger and sin; which he also treats in ch. 28. Ch. 26: whether the Cardinals can proceed to the election of another before the sentence of the Council in the cases stated? Ch. 29: whether subjects ought to keep the precepts, or fear the censures and excommunications which their own Pope issues against them in the case where they withdraw or convene a Council? All these matters show more clearly the blemishes of the schisms among the Popes, treated by the author at length and in a quodlibetical manner. Let whoever has time to waste on trifles read them. Absurdities are easily recognized, whether they are stated plainly or simply, flowing from false hypotheses in order to destroy them.

units.la: CXXX. Neque etiam vitium numeri in Electione Pontificum tollunt dicentes, cum Loyolita Ottone Roma Gloriosa p. 554. 555. eum esse sequendum, cui major & melior Ecclesia pars adhæreat, & (verba ejus Germanica verto) quemadmodum interdum tres Soles in cœlo conspiciantur, & à simplicioribus revera tot credantur, probè interim doctis scientibus, unum tantum solem, duas umbras, sive Parelios esse; ita sæpe à simplicioribus quidem creditum fuisse, tres Papas in Ecclesia sedere, quando sapientes noverint, unum tantùm Papam esse, duos reliquos Antiumbras sive Antipapas citò evanescentes, caterùm legitimo Papa solis ad instar, semper manente. Quemadmodùm etiam in Regno aliquo Mundano duo nonnunquam Regis utantur titulo, quorum tamen unus Tyrannus modò sit, ita idem in Ecclesia accidere posse; atque adeò Schismatibus Ecclesiam non magis contemptibilem, sed magis illustrem reddi, ob singularem Dei in ejus, illis non obstantibus, conservatione providentiam, dum Anti-Papa semper nebularum ad instar citius, serius à semper perpetuo, semperque immutabili sole dispulsi fuerint. Non, inquam, vitium numeri in Electione Pontificum sic tollitur. Neque enim primò constitit, majorem semper partem sequendam esse, cùm contrà Divina cautela suadeat, multitudinem ad malum non esse sequendam, & Christi grex parvus, futurúsque parvus atque ab adorantibus Bestiam in apostasia communi sæpe vincendus præfiguretur; Neque secundò semper constitit, utra pars major esset, integris ab unoquoque Papa interdum regnis stantibus, & modò hoc, modò illo majorem populi partem post se trahente; Neque tertiò semper constitit, utra pars melior, quavis sibi justæ causæ prærogativam vindicante, atque illâ in obscuro positâ. Atque, si interdum de majori & meliori parte præsentibus, sapientibus, doctis quodammodò constare potuit, qui semper absentibus, simplicioribus, & quorum æquè æternæ salutis causâ legitimum Papam sequi intererat, de uno & altero constare potuit? Sed jam audivimus voces judicium certum etiam sapientioribus & doctioribus aperte abjudicantium. Quales etiam sunt sequentes Naucleri Gen. 47. p. 260. de schismate Urbani VI. & Clementis VII. Utraque obedientia habuit religiosissimos Viros, &, quod majus est, etiam miraculis fulgentes, nec unquam potuit quæstio hæc decidi, quin manserint apud plurimos dubia. Quibus planè consentaneas Bzovius an an. 1381. n. 13, habet. Quæ proin satis similia dissimilia de Pareliis & Tyranno inepta esse declarant; Ut taceam, non tantum in vero aut falso de Pareliis, aut Tyranno judicio, neque tot hominibus positum esse; Quod docet, certitudinem hêic majorem haud immerito requiri. Sique ex eventu facta notanda putat, cui quaesò rei ante eventum & per tam longam annorum seriem saepe innitendum fuit? Et an legitimus haberi debuit, qui vi atque armorum potentiâ tandem obtinuit? Et an ideò legitimus haberi debuit, qui, quae quorundam Anti-Papārum manifesta praerogativa erat, adversario forte suo supervixit? Caeterùm, quam jactat, Divinam providentiam, cum quibusvis aliis etiam infidelibus Regnis Papatus communem habet, quae saepe etiam, sic turbatâ licèt legitimorum successione, absque finali tamen ruina intùs collisa historia seculorum exhibet; Siquè Papatus hêic singularia habet, in eo, juxta Scripturas, habet, quòd justo Dei efficaciam erroris mittentis & eos, qui veritatem in injustitia detinuerant, severè punientis judicio, ad longius verè fidelium patientiae fideique exercitium Regnum Antichristianum emergere atque durare (licèt non leviter interdum divisum, suadente semper reconciliationem terreno, qui ex Regni hujus conservatione pendebat, pendet, affectu, aut etiam vi partem oppositam tollente;) debuit, debet. Quis autem inferorum portas nunquam praevaluisse jure dicat coetui, qui fundamentis injustitiae, licèt sub justitiae praetextu, in aedificatus, saepe apertam vim atque in justitiam usque adeò admisit, ut ejus Domini, fundamenta, capita, artifices sibi invicem contrarii in solo ambitionis suae modis omnibus & per omne nefas conservandae conatu consenserint, omnes interdum, id supra ultrò largientibus, quos ei addictissimos fuisse constat, teterrima monstra fuerint; Boni, legitimi tam necessarii nulli saepe diu fuerint. Siquè in eo Ecclesiae splendor situs est, eum certè Romanae degeneri non invidemus; Sed magis ingenuè prae Loyolita alii, Pontificii &
units.tr: CXXX. Nor do those who say, with Loyolita Otto in Roma Gloriosa pp. 554-555, that one should follow "the one to whom the greater and better part of the Church adheres," remove the defect of number in the election of Popes. (I translate his German words.) "Just as sometimes three suns are seen in the sky, and are truly believed by simpler folk to be that many, while learned people know well that there is only one sun, with two shadows or parhelia, so the simpler folk have often believed that three Popes sit in the Church, when the wise know there is only one Pope, the two others being anti-shadows or antipopes, which quickly vanish, while the legitimate Pope, like the sun, always remains. Just as in some worldly kingdom two men sometimes use the title of king, of whom one is then a tyrant, so the same can happen in the Church. Thus schisms make the Church not more contemptible but more illustrious, on account of God's singular providence in preserving it despite those schisms, since the Anti-Popes, like clouds, have always been dispelled sooner or later by the perpetual and ever unchanging sun." No, I say, the defect of number is not removed in the election of Popes in this way. For, first, it has not been established that the greater part is always to be followed, since divine caution rather advises that the multitude is not to be followed into evil. Christ's flock is foreshadowed as small, and as destined to remain small and often to be overcome by those who worship the Beast in common apostasy. Nor, second, has it always been established which side was the greater, since kingdoms have sometimes remained intact under each Pope, and now this one, now that one, has drawn the greater part of the people after himself. Nor, third, has it always been established which side is the better, since each claims the prerogative of a just cause, and that cause lies in obscurity. And if at times it could be somewhat established, among the present, wise and learned, which party was the greater and better, how could it be established about one or the other among the absent, the simpler folk, for whom it was equally a matter of eternal salvation to follow the legitimate Pope? But we have already heard voices openly denying a certain judgment even to the wiser and more learned. Such are also the following words of Naucler, Gen. 47, p. 260, on the schism of Urban VI and Clement VII: "Each obedience had most religious men and, what is greater, men shining even with miracles, nor could this question ever be decided without many remaining in doubt." Bzovius, Ann. 1381, n. 13, agrees entirely with these. Accordingly, these things show that the comparisons with parhelia and the tyrant are similar only in part, and silly. Not to mention that the judgment about what is true or false in the matter of parhelia or the tyrant does not rest on so many people, which shows that greater certainty is rightly required here. And if he thinks things should be noted from the outcome, I ask: on what should one have relied before the outcome, and across so long a series of years? Ought he to be held legitimate who at last prevailed by violence and the power of arms? And ought he to be held legitimate because he happened to outlive his rival, which was the manifest advantage of certain Anti-Popes? Moreover, the divine providence he boasts of the Papacy shares in common with any other kingdoms, even unbelieving ones; history over the ages shows that these have often been shaken from within, even when legitimate succession was thrown into confusion, without final ruin. If the Papacy has something singular here, namely, that according to the Scriptures, by the just judgment of God, who sends the efficacy of error and severely punishes those who held the truth in unrighteousness, the Antichristian kingdom has risen up and endured to give a longer exercise to the patience and faith of true believers (although at times it has been divided, not lightly, since the earthly affection that depended on the preservation of this kingdom always urged reconciliation, or else removed the opposing party by force), then it ought to have done so. Who, indeed, may rightly say that the gates of hell have never prevailed against an assembly that, built upon the foundations of injustice, though under the pretext of justice, has so often admitted open violence and injustice, that its lords, foundations, heads and craftsmen, mutually opposed, have agreed in every way and through every wickedness in the sole effort to preserve their ambition, and that at times all of them, as it is established were most devoted to it, have been most abominable monsters, while good and legitimate ones were often for long none at all? And if the splendour of the Church lies in this, we certainly do not envy the degenerate Roman one. But rather, more frankly than Loyolita, others, Papists and

units.la: illi, in Schismatibus fidem turpissimè laceratam, scandala horrenda, incertitudinem summam supra notârunt.
units.tr: those, have noted above that in the schisms faith was most shamefully torn, horrible scandals arose, and the greatest uncertainty prevailed.

units.la: SECUN-
units.tr: SECOND-

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA,
units.tr: SECOND SECTION,

units.la: In qua, De nævis & vitiis eorum, qui eliguntur, respe- ctu qualitatis generaliùs & levi indicio eorum requisi- torum, quæ minùs considerari merentur, agitur. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which the faults and blemishes of those who are elected are discussed with respect to quality in general, and the slight indications of the requisite qualities, which deserve less consideration. Summary.

units.la: 1. Sequuntur vitia respectu qualitatis, vel qualitatum. Quarum respectu primò illud desideratur, quòd de necessariis eligendo Pontifici qualitatibus Scriptura plane taceat; II. Qua tamen loquitur de requisitis Episcoporum, Diaconorum atque Viduarum; III. In quo silentio navus, quia signis atque miraculis eligendi Pontifices non ostenduntur. IV. Neque enim sufficiunt omina quae jactant; V. Quorum vanitas notatur, generaliùs; VI. Specialiùs in exemplis, ratione situs Cellæ; VII. In exemplo Urbani VIII. quod recensetur; VIII. Ad quod respondetur, atque concluditur, hic non ex signis extraordinario modo datis, sed ex qualitatibus judicium ferri atque illas hoc spectari. IX. Communes illa saltem Episcoporum virtutes in eligendis esse debent Pontificibus, atque debere in majori gradu. X. Quibus certè primi Episcopi Rom. prafulgebant. XI. Neque ab initio alia spectabantur; XII. Quando Electiones etiam aliàs optima. XIII. Et quando multi inviti eligebantur. XIV. Exempla & testimonia generalia; XV. Non est cur glorientur Pontificii de bonis primorum Episcoporum qualitatibus. XVI. Hodie primò homo esse debet eligendus, licèt multi monstra fuisse dicantur, atque Benedictum IX. post mortem in forma ferina apparuisse apud Platinam referatur. XVII. Homo esse debet Physicè atque ratione membrorum corporis ad functiones necessarias non plane ineptus, sed habere debet ex. gr. pedes, qui ambulent, juxta Conclave Alexandri VII. & aures, qua audiant, quod colligitur ex Conclavi Leonis XI. XVIII. Non debet eligi nimis debilis, aut semper ager. XIX. Recensentur alia requisita, qua minorem considerationem merentur.
units.tr: 1. The faults with respect to quality, or qualities, follow. With respect to these, first, it is lacking that Scripture is entirely silent about the qualities necessary for electing a Pontiff; II. although it speaks of the requirements for bishops, deacons and widows; III. and in this silence there is a blemish, because the elected Pontiffs are not shown by signs and miracles. IV. For the omens they boast of are not enough; V. the vanity of which is noted, in general terms; VI. more particularly in examples, with respect to the location of the cell; VII. in the example of Urban VIII, which is recounted; VIII. to which an answer is given, and it is concluded that here judgment is passed not on signs given in an extraordinary way, but on qualities, and that these are what should be considered. IX. Those common virtues of bishops, at least, ought to be present in the elected Pontiffs, and to a greater degree. X. Which indeed the first bishops of Rome shone forth in. XI. Nor were other things looked at from the beginning; XII. when elections were otherwise also very good. XIII. And when many were elected against their will. XIV. Examples and general testimonies; XV. There is no reason for the Papists to boast of the good qualities of the first bishops. XVI. Today the one to be elected must first of all be a man, although many are said to have been monsters, and Benedict IX is reported by Platina to have appeared after death in the form of a beast. XVII. He must be a man, physically and in the arrangement of his bodily members, not wholly unfit for the necessary functions, but he ought to have, for example, feet to walk with, according to the Conclave of Alexander VII, and ears to hear with, which is gathered from the Conclave of Leo XI. XVIII. He ought not to be elected if too weak, or always ill. XIX. Other requirements are listed, which deserve less consideration.

units.la: I. HActenus vitia & nævi eorum, qui ad Pontificatum Romanum eliguntur, ratione qualitatis, sive numeri, sequuntur eorundem vitia respectu qualitatis. Ubi primò respectu qualitatum Pontifici Romano necessariarum vitiosum illud censeri omninò debet, quòd qualitates illæ in S. Scriptura non enarrantur, atque in ea de illis, æquè ac de cæteris ad Electionem Pontificum Romanorum spectantibus, prout jam ex parte ostendimus, altum est silentium; Quale quidem speciatim quoque ratione quantitatis, sive numeri observatur; ratione cujus tamen statim constare potuisset, non nisi unicum eligi debere, si Monarcham eligi debere universalem indicâsset; Ast non indicâsse, similiter ostensum est. Quis verò non miretur, Scriptores Sacros, Petrum, Paulum, Marcum, Lucam, alios, nihil plane de qualitatibus eligendo in summum Romanum Pontificem necessariis habere? Quis non miretur, eos, ne unico quidem verbo, secutura secula maximis, ex hac etiam parte, periculis atque damnis obnoxia futura de requisitis Capitis Ecclesiæ non exiguo hominum commodo atque solatio præmonere voluisse? Eos indicare noluisse, ex quo statu ad illud dignitatum Ecclesiasticarum culmen aliquis commodè promoveri possit? Quænam, quando non omnis fert omnia tellus, Paparum ferax futura sit? In qua ætate Pontifices eligi debeant? Quodnam sit ex illorum requisitis palmarium? An pietas morúmque sanctitas? An Eruditio? An prudentia secularis? Quænam porrò requirantur attributa? Quomodo explorandi, unde agnoscendi sint? Quid agendum sit, si omni bona qualitate destitutus eligatur nonnunquam? Quid, si uno & altero ex primariis requisitis privatus &c? De his omnibus altum plane in S. Scripturis Silentium esse, quis non miretur?
units.tr: I. Hitherto the faults and blemishes of those who are elected to the Roman Pontificate have been considered with respect to quality, or number. Next come their faults with respect to quality. Here, first, with respect to the qualities necessary in a Roman Pontiff, it must be judged wholly a fault that these qualities are not set out in Holy Scripture, and that Scripture is silent about them, just as about the other matters pertaining to the election of Roman Pontiffs, as we have already shown in part. This silence is observed in particular also with respect to quantity, or number; yet from this it could have been plainly established that only one ought to be elected, if Scripture had indicated that a universal monarch ought to be elected. But that it did not indicate this has similarly been shown. Who, indeed, would not marvel that the sacred writers, Peter, Paul, Mark, Luke and the others, have nothing at all to say about the qualities necessary in electing the supreme Roman Pontiff? Who would not marvel that they, not even with a single word, wished to forewarn the coming ages, which would be exposed to the greatest dangers and losses in this respect too, about the requirements for the Head of the Church, for the no small benefit and comfort of men? Did they not wish to indicate from what station someone could conveniently be promoted to that summit of ecclesiastical dignities? What land, since not every soil bears every crop, will be fruitful in Popes? At what age ought Pontiffs to be elected? Which of their requirements is the chief one? Is it piety and holiness of life? Is it learning? Is it worldly prudence? What further attributes are required? How are they to be tested, and how recognised? What is to be done if someone is sometimes elected who lacks every good quality? What if he is lacking one or another of the principal requirements, and so on? Who would not marvel that there is a deep silence about all these things in the Holy Scriptures?

units.la: II. Scriptores quidem Sacros studiosè, quales Episcopi, imò etiam quales Diaconi, imò etiam quales Viduæ ad Ministerium Ecclesiæ eligi debeant, inculcâsse deprehendimus. Verùm non ideò docuerunt, quales Ecclesiæ summi Monarchæ eligendi sint, cùm plane diversa ad munera plane diversa attributa requirantur, neque magis vidua ab Episcopo (utriusque tamen traduntur speciatim virtutes;) differat, quàm Romanus Pontifex, tanquam talis Monarcha, ab Episcopo. Speciale munus specialem eligendorum ad illud descriptionem requirere omninò videtur, cum primis tantum munus, in tanta celsitudine positum, tam latè patens. Vel, an Scriptura docere debuit, quales esse debeant inferiores Rectores paucorum, & non, quales esse debeant summi Rectores omnium? Quales esse debeant Episcopi, Pastores Ovium, & non, quales esse debeant Domini Pastorum? Quales eligi debeant viduæ, & non, quales eligi debeant summi Pontifices? Quorum, etsi ex plenitudine gratiæ scire possent, vel tacente Scriptura, quomodo se in tantæ dignitatis altitudine gerere debeant, requisita tamen Electoribus ob oculos poni debuissent, ut rem bene acturum eligerent atque ad plenitudinem gratiæ, gratiæ jam beneficio, dispositum; Nisi perinperinde fit, qualiscunque eligatur, atque Electio omnibus æquè plenitudinem gratiæ atque donorum conferat; quod non apparet; & qua ratione omnium pessimi atque omnium maximè inepti eligendi forent feliciter sic immutandi; aut omnes, qualescunque jam sint, æquè rem bene agant; cui experientia reclamat.
units.tr: II. We find, indeed, that the sacred writers have carefully inculcated what kind of men bishops ought to be elected, and even what kind of deacons, and even what kind of widows, for the ministry of the Church. But they did not therefore teach what kind of men the supreme monarch of the Church ought to be elected, since for quite different offices quite different attributes are required, and a widow differs from a bishop (although the particular virtues of each are handed down) no more than the Roman Pontiff, as such a monarch, differs from a bishop. A particular office seems entirely to require a particular description of those to be elected for it, especially when the office, placed at so great a height, is so widely extended. Or ought Scripture to have taught what kind of lesser rulers of a few ought to be, and not what kind of supreme rulers of all ought to be? What kind bishops, shepherds of sheep, ought to be, and not what kind the lords of the shepherds ought to be? What kind of widows ought to be elected, and not what kind of supreme Pontiffs ought to be elected? Even if they could know, from the fullness of grace, how they ought to conduct themselves in the height of so great a dignity even without Scripture saying so, nevertheless the requirements ought to have been set before the electors, so that they would choose one who would act well and who was disposed to the fullness of grace, already by the benefit of grace. Unless it simply happens that whoever is elected, whatever sort he is, and the election confers the same fullness of grace and of gifts on all alike; which does not appear; and by what reasoning would the worst of all and the most unfit of all be happily changed in this way when elected; or else all, whatever they now are, would equally do the job well; to which experience cries out in protest.

units.la: III. Quod Scripturarum de requisitis Pontificum Romanorum talium silentium, grave contrà eos præjudicium ideò interpretamur, quòd non aliunde quàm ex qualitatibus certis, quinam eligi debeant, constare potest; non v. gr. ex certis miraculis atque signis cœlitùs extraordinario planè modo datis; quomodo quidem omnes designari debere omninò videtur, ut in hac etiam prærogativa Christo succedant, qui plenissimam ejus potestatem sibi tribuunt, & fiant ἀνδρες ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ εις ἡμᾶς ἀποδεδειγμένοι — σημείοις, viri à Deo ad nos demonstrati signis, qualiter certè Apostoli demonstrati sunt; ast quanto, si istis hominibus credamus aliquando, Pontificibus Romanis minores! ad necessariam Christianorum certitudinem.
units.tr: III. We interpret this silence of Scripture about such requirements for Roman Pontiffs as a grave prejudice against them, because it cannot be known who ought to be elected from any source other than from certain qualities; not, for example, from certain miracles and signs given by heaven in a wholly extraordinary way. Indeed, all ought entirely to be designated in this way, so that they may succeed Christ also in this prerogative, who claims for himself his fullest power, and become [men shown to us by God by signs] [ἀνδρες ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰς ἡμᾶς ἀποδεδειγμένοι — σημείοις], men demonstrated to us by God with signs, as indeed the Apostles were demonstrated. But how much less are the Roman Pontiffs, if we ever believe these men, for the necessary certainty of Christians!

units.la: IV. Ast non ita demonstrantur Pontifices Romani eligendi. Ajunt quidem apud Eusebium Hist. Eccl. l. VI. c. 22. Fabianum columbæ capiti insidentis indicio A. Ch. 238. designatum fuisse. Sed ajunt; adeóque ex rumore incerto ista accepit Eusebius; Atque similia omina, quæ vocantur, alii in quorundam aliorum electionibus ostendunt. Sed rarissima; sed vel magis ex Authorum fide incerta; sed ex parte minoris longè claritatis, propinquitatis, singularitatis; sed talia, quibus similia in quocunque alio, etiam profanorum, statu, multa reperias, & ex quibus proin specialem, atque gratiosam certi statûs approbationem frustrà concludas, quinam quocunque tempore Pontifices eligendi sint, non agnoscas.
units.tr: IV. But Roman Pontiffs are not shown in this way to be elected. They say, indeed, in Eusebius, Church History, book VI, chapter 22, that Fabian was designated in the year of Christ 238 by the sign of a dove sitting on his head. But they say; and so Eusebius received these things from an uncertain rumour. Other similar omens, as they are called, appear in the elections of certain others. But they are very rare; or they rest on the uncertain word of authors; or they concern persons of much lesser fame, closeness or distinction; or they are of such a kind that you may find many like them in any other state, even a profane one, and so from them you will vainly conclude a special and gracious approval of a certain state, by which you would recognise who ought to be elected Pontiffs at any time.

units.la: V. Prout certè in genere nihil omnibus, quæ dicuntur, fallacius esse solet; Ut enim de fraude taceam; multa solent indifferentia, quando aut spes, aut metus adest, atque de certo negotio agitur, vel ante eventum, (quando etiam actiones sæpe juxta talia diriguntur;) vel etiam ex post facto, ut sic loquar, in omina converti; quæ, nisi spes aut metus adesset, nisi de arduo negotio ageretur, vel res ita contigisset, statim certè atque planè negligerentur; Quod etiam, dum in infinitis eventus omnium, quod esse putabamus, non respondet, accidere solet, neque itaque mirum esse debet, nonnunquam inter res div. rsi generis, sed ejusdem fere temporis, quand m convenientiam notari.
units.tr: V. Indeed, in general nothing is usually more deceptive than all the things that are said.
