For, to say nothing of fraud, many indifferent things are often turned into omens, when either hope or fear is present and a certain business is at stake, either before the outcome (when even actions are often directed by such things), or even after the event, so to speak. These things, unless hope or fear were present, unless a difficult business were at stake, or unless the thing had turned out in this way, would certainly and plainly be immediately neglected. This also usually happens while in countless cases the outcome of everything does not correspond to what we thought would be; and so it ought not to be surprising that sometimes some agreement is noted between things of a different kind, but almost of the same time.

units.la: VI. Atque, quando v. g. omen vocatur, dum cuipiam, qui post eligitur, in Conclavi cella vel inter officiales praecipuos, vel in vicinia Capellae Electionis forte obtingit, quoties quaesò in vicinia vel officialium, vel Capellae cellam inhabitâsse deprehenditur, qui Papa factus haud est? Quo in casu omen non omen atque saepissimè plane non notatum fuit.
units.tr: VI. And when, for example, an omen is called such, since it happens by chance to someone who is afterwards elected that he had a cell in the Conclave, or among the chief officials, or in the vicinity of the Chapel of the Election; how often, I ask, is it found that someone who did not become Pope had lived in the vicinity of the officials or of the Chapel, or in a cell there? In such a case the omen is no omen, and very often it was not noticed at all.

units.la: VII. Majus videtur, quod in Conclavi Urbani VIII. acci-disse fertur atque ab Authore Conclavis circa finem ita effertur: Non mi pare di tralasciare, inquit, che essendo alcuni giorni avanti l' elettio-ne concorsa nel Palazzo Vaticano dalla parte di Toscana, quantità gran-dissima d' Api, un sciame si pose nella parte della fenestra, dov' era la cella del futuro Pontefice, il che se fosse fatto, subjungit Author, à caso, si può raccontare per notabil' incontro, che poco avanti l' assontione al Pontificato d' un Toscano, il quale per Armi fà l' Api, sia venuta di Toscana un sciame à posarsi nel Conclave sopra la cella di lui, mà se sù fatto à particolar di-spositione della Providenza Divina, laquale, come vuole. S. Giovanni Da-masceno, si serve alle volte delle cose naturali per annunziar' alcun' eventi, che quelle per se stesse non sono atte à significare; Diremo questo segno esser stato inviato da Dio, per dimostrare, che si doveva eleggere, è per aprire qualche luce à gl' Elettori, nel mezzo di tanta caligine de' privati Inte-ressi e dissentioni. Id est; Non mihi praetermittendum videtur, quòd con-volantibus aliquot ante Electionem diebus ad Vaticanum, quâ Hetruriam respicit, in maxima copia apibus, agmen aliquod parti fenestra, ubi cella futuri Pontificis erat, se applicuit; quod si casu factum est, subjungit Au-thor, notabilis casus videri potest, quòd paulò ante assumtionem ad Ponti-ficatum Tusci, cujus insignia apes ostendunt, ex Tuscia venerit agmen ad in-sidendum in Conclavi cella ejus, sed si peculiari Divina Providentia dispo-sitione illud factum est, quae prout vult S. Johannes Damascenus, interdum utitur rebus naturalibus, ad significandos quosdam eventus, ad quos significandos per se non sunt apta, Dicemus, signum hoc immissum à Deo fuisse, ad demonstrandum illum, qui eligi debeat, & ad aperiendam aliquam Ele-ctoribus lucem, in medio tanta caliginis privatorum commodorum atque dissensionum.
units.tr: VII. The more significant matter, which is said to have happened in the conclave of Urban VIII and which the author of the Conclave reports near the end, runs as follows: "I do not think I should omit that, a few days before the election, a very great number of bees came to the Vatican Palace from the direction of Tuscany, and a swarm settled at the window, where the cell of the future Pontiff was. If this was by chance," the author adds, "it may be recorded as a notable coincidence that shortly before the elevation to the Papacy of a Tuscan, whose arms show bees, a swarm came from Tuscany to settle in the conclave above his cell. But if it was done by the special disposition of divine Providence, which, as Saint John Damascene holds, sometimes uses natural things to signify certain events, for which they are not in themselves fitted, we will say that this sign was sent by God, to show who ought to be elected, and to shed some light for the electors in the midst of such darkness of private interests and dissensions." That is: "It seems to me not to be passed over that, with many bees gathering at the Vatican some days before the election, on the side facing Tuscany, a swarm settled at the window where the cell of the future Pontiff was; if this happened by chance," the author adds, "it may seem a notable coincidence that shortly before the assumption to the Papacy of a Tuscan, whose insignia are bees, a swarm came from Tuscany to settle on his cell in the conclave. But if it happened by a special disposition of divine Providence, which, as Saint John Damascene says, sometimes uses natural things to signify certain events for which they are not in themselves suited, we will say that this sign was sent by God, to show who ought to be elected, and to shed some light on the electors in the midst of such darkness of private interests and dissensions."

units.la: VIII. Sed posito, rem ita contigisse, neque dolo malo con-tigisse, sive jam apes, sive fuci fuerint, vix credo, eos odore Papae, licèt conterranei (de quo tamen non constat, an nimirum ex Hetruria venerint; quinam enim itineris comites perpetui fuerunt? ) eos attractos fuisse. Speciale quidem ibi fuit, quòd Cardinalis Barbe-rinus rinus apes in insignibus habuit, (neque tamen etiam credo, insignia ante fenestram posita imaginum similitudine apes attraxisse, quasi similes quaerentes similes, tam artificiosè picti, quàm uvæ Parrhasianæ, quibus praetervolantes aves accessisse dicunt, quasi partes inde decerpturas; Sed & notatur, maximam apum quantitatem advolâsse, quod forte & aliàs contigit, quando non agebatur de Papæ electione; atque partem duntaxat fenestræ illi adhæsisse, aliis aliis aliorum forte adhærentibus, qui tamen electi non fuerunt. Síque Electores peregrino volatu moti fuissent, sine signi caelitus dati ratione moveri potuissent; Verùm non apparet ex historia Conclavis, Electoribus aliquam lucem ex apium agmine obscurante potiùs accessisse; quod nec idoneum Papatûs emblema constituere potuit, nisi significari debuerit, Christianos undiquaque ad Urbanum dulcedinem aurei melis sui transmittere debere; Certè non apes, sed aves, sive faustæ, sive infaustæ, negotium promovebant, politicis (prout hinc inde ostendimus;) non physicis aut mysticis inducti rationibus homines, ut per apes licuisset semper haerere in tanta privatorum commodorum atq; dissidiorum caligine. Tandem, concesso etiam, signum fuisse, bonum an malum, approbatorium an improbatorium, Divinum an Diabolicum fuerit, adhuc in ambiguo relinquitur, atque ex officii ratione & administratione dignosci debet. Omninò igitur videtur, hic non ex signis caelitùs extraordinario modo datis, sed ex qualitatibus judicium ferri debere. Videamus, quales illæ sint atque requirantur.
units.tr: VIII. But granting that the thing happened in this way, and did not happen by evil design, whether they were bees or drones, I can hardly believe that they were drawn by the smell of the Pope, even if they were from his own country (though it is not certain that they came from Tuscany at all; for who were their constant companions on the journey?). There was indeed one peculiar thing here: Cardinal Barberini had bees in his arms. (Yet I do not even think that the insignia, painted in front of the window, drew the bees by their likeness to the images, as if like seeks like, just as the Parrhasian grapes, so skilfully painted, are said to have drawn passing birds to peck at them.) It is also noted that a very great quantity of bees flew in, which perhaps happens at other times too, when there is no question of electing a Pope; and that only a part of the window was covered, the bees clinging to it one after another, though none of those who clung there was elected. And if the electors had been moved by a flight of foreign origin, they could have been moved without any reason of a sign given from heaven. But it does not appear from the history of the conclave that any light came to the electors from the obscuring swarm of bees. Nor could it have been a fitting emblem of the Papacy, unless it were meant to signify that Christians from every quarter ought to send the sweetness of their golden honey to Urban. Certainly it was not bees but birds, whether of good or of bad omen, that advanced the business, men being moved by political reasons (as we have shown here and there), not by physical or mystical ones, so that through the bees it would always have been possible to remain "in such darkness of private interests and dissensions." Finally, even granting that it was a sign, whether good or bad, approving or disapproving, divine or diabolical, it is still left in doubt, and must be recognised from the reason and administration of the office. It seems altogether right, then, that judgment here should be made not from signs given from heaven in an extraordinary manner, but from qualities. Let us see what those qualities are and what is required.

units.la: IX. Facilè, credo, largientur Pontificij, licèt nihil in Scriptura de Pontificis sui requisitis specialibus habeatur, tamen communia illa Episcoporum Dissert. V. Sect. I. n. III. à nobis enarrata eligendum quoque commendare debere; Jmò ipsimet fortè contendent, requisita illa etiam & vel maximè ad ostendendum aptum Pontificatui hominem exposita esse. Assumimus (licèt non sufficere attributorum illorum communium designationem jam ostenderimus;) atque addimus; igitur etiam & vel maximè in eligendo Pontifice attributa illa adesse atque spectari debere, ibi in gradu eò majori, quò major Episcopis ab Apostolo notatis habetur, vel haberi debet electus. Cujus quidem Te, Lector, memorem esse velim, etiam quando ad vitiosorum atque planè vitiosorum Electiones deventum erit.
units.tr: IX. The Papists, I believe, will readily grant that, although nothing in Scripture is said about the special requirements of their Pontiff, nevertheless those common qualities of bishops, which I set out in Dissertation V, Section I, number III, ought to be commended also in the one to be elected. Indeed they will perhaps themselves contend that those requirements have been laid down especially to show a man fit for the Papacy. I grant this (though I have already shown that naming those common qualities is not enough); and I add: therefore those qualities are also present and must be looked for, and above all in the choice of a Pope, and to a greater degree in proportion as the elect is held, or ought to be held, to be greater than the bishops marked out by the Apostle. Of this, Reader, I would have you be mindful, even when we come to the elections of the vicious, and of those who are wholly vicious.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: De primis per aliquot secula Episcopis Romanis ultrò nos largimur, Viros, sine ulla fere exceptione, optimos fuisse atque virtutibus Episcopalibus ornatissimos, prout etiam nihil aliud fuerunt, aut haberi voluerunt quàm Episcopi Urbis Romæ, qua-les erant alij urbium aliarum. Aurei obtigerunt Ecclesiæ, juxta verissimum Bonifacij M effatum, etiam Romanæ, Episcopi, quoad usque ligneos habebat calices. Et quando, teste Guicciardino Hist. Pap. l. IV. non modò potentiâ civili & mundana penitùs nudati, verùm etiam ab illa vexati, diu obscuri ac fere ignorati fuere: eorum nomine nulla re magis quàm supplicijs & cruciatibus perferendis innotescente, Sic tamen satis innotuit; addo; etiam vitæ sanctitate, doctrinæ puritate, Zelo, orationibus, jejuniis, adhortationibus populo fideli quotidie quasi factis, amore Christi, amore fratrum. Talibus jam valde pollentes Ministrorum Jesu Christi genuinis dotibus eligebantur, hinc etiam quotidiana in talibus incrementa habebant, atque hinc etiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ inter Christianos authoritatem incrementa magna sumpsisse, quòd nimirum tales ejus ab initio Rectores fuerunt atque electi fuerunt, jam Dissert. III. n. 46. à nobis annotatum est.
units.tr: We freely grant that the first Roman bishops over several centuries were men of almost unbroken excellence, most adorned with episcopal virtues. They were nothing other than, and wished to be nothing other than, bishops of the city of Rome, just as other bishops were of their own cities. Golden bishops, with wooden chalices, came to the Church, even the Roman Church, according to the most true saying of Boniface M. And when, as Guicciardini witnesses (Hist. Pap. bk. IV), they were not only stripped entirely of civil and worldly power but were also harassed by it, and for a long time were obscure and almost unknown, their name becoming known by nothing so much as by enduring punishments and torments, they nevertheless became sufficiently known. I add: also by holiness of life, purity of doctrine, zeal, prayers, fasting, exhortations to the faithful people almost daily, love of Christ, and love of the brethren. Already very strong in these genuine gifts of the ministers of Jesus Christ, they were chosen. Hence they also grew daily in such gifts, and hence the authority of the Roman Church among Christians grew greatly, because such men were its rulers and were chosen from the beginning. We have already noted this in Dissert. III, n. 46.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Neque etiam alia tunc, præter attributa illa Episcopalia in Electionibus Romanorum Pontificum sive Episcoporum spectari solebant. Sù il principio di questa Monarchia Pontificia, inquit Author Vitæ Sixti V. p. 1. l. 1. p. 8. che lo spirituale surpassava digran lunga al temporale, e che gli Ecclesiastici metteuano maggior cura nel reggere le conscienze de' fideli, che nel governare la Signoria de' Popoli, si inalzauano ad una tal dignità personaggi dotati d' un integrità di costumi, ed auezzi à consumar l' hore del giorno in orationi, meditationi, ed altre opere sante, con le quali i tiravano sotto il vessillo della croce di Christo le migliaia della Provincie e città; Id est; Ab initio hujus Monarchia Pontificia (imò quando nondum incipiebat, nondum Monarchiam vel quærebant; &) quando adhuc spirituale multùm prævalebat temporali (temporale negligebatur;) & Ecclesiastici majori curâ (imò unicè;) invigilabant regimini conscientiarum fidelium, quàm dominio populorum; ad talem dignitatem (quæ tum onus magis quàm honos, neutiquam dignitas mundano fastu præfulgens erat;) evehebantur Viri sanctis moribus instructi, atque gnari diem consumere in Orationibus, meditationibus, & aliis sanctis operibus, quibus ad vexillum Crucis Christi attrahebant millenas Provincias atque civitates (saltem ipsi, multa animaanimarum millia;) Nel principio della chiesa nascente, inquit author Cardinalismi p. 3. l. 1. p. 16. non si domandava altro di Roma, che le preghiere, le orationi, le prediche, e l' amministratione de' Sacramenti, perche Roma non vi cercava da' Fedeli, che il zelo della conscienza, la salute dell' anima, e la frequenza delle funtioni Sagre. Id est; Ab initio nascentis Ecclesiæ Roma nihil requirebatur praeter preces, Orationes, conciones & Sacramentorum ad ministrationem, quia Roma nihil requirebat à fidelibus prater Zelum conscientiæ, salutem animarum & frequentiam functionum Sacrarum. Et quibusdam interiectis p. 17. Per alcuni secoli se nestette Roma spogliata di tutti quei inveluppi, che s' aggirano nello stato temporale, contentandosi solo di condurre al pascolo le pecorelle con le bastone pastorale, cioè con le sole armi spirituale. Id est; Per aliquot secula Roma carebat omnibus illis statûs temporalis involucris, oves baculo pastorali, id est, solis armis Spiritualibus ad pascua ducere contenta. Hinc Adrianus VI. secundùm requisita hodierna minùs aptus judicatus in Conclavi successoris dicitur più propinque à quell buone qualità che si sogliono ricercare & desiderare nell' elettione de' Pontefici ne' tempo manco lontani della primitiva Chiesa. Id est; Propior bonis illis qualitatibus, quæ requiri & desiderari solebant in Electione Pontificum in temporibus multum distantibus Ecclesiæ primitivæ.
units.tr: Nor, at that time, were any qualities other than those episcopal ones looked for in the elections of Roman Pontiffs or bishops. "At the beginning of this Papal monarchy," says the author of the Life of Sixtus V (p. 1, bk. 1, p. 8), "the spiritual far surpassed the temporal, and the clergy took greater care in governing the consciences of the faithful than in ruling over peoples. To such a dignity were raised men endowed with integrity of morals, accustomed to spend the hours of the day in prayers, meditations, and other holy works, by which they drew thousands of provinces and cities under the banner of the Cross of Christ". That is to say: From the beginning of this Papal monarchy (indeed, when it was not yet beginning, they did not yet seek a monarchy or wish for one; and) when the spiritual still greatly prevailed over the temporal (the temporal was neglected), and the clergy watched over the government of the consciences of the faithful with greater care (indeed, with exclusive care) than over the rule of peoples; to such a dignity (which then was more a burden than an honour, by no means a dignity shining with worldly pomp) were raised men of holy morals, skilled in spending the day in prayers, meditations, and other holy works, by which they drew thousands of provinces and cities to the banner of the Cross of Christ (at least they themselves drew many thousands of souls). "At the beginning of the nascent Church," says the author of Cardinalism (p. 3, bk. 1, p. 16), "nothing was asked of Rome except prayers, orations, sermons, and the administration of the sacraments, because Rome did not seek from the faithful anything but zeal for conscience, the salvation of souls, and the frequency of sacred functions." That is to say: At the beginning of the nascent Church, nothing was required of Rome beyond prayers, orations, sermons, and the administration of the sacraments, because Rome required nothing of the faithful except zeal of conscience, the salvation of souls, and the frequency of sacred functions. And a little further on (p. 17): "For some centuries Rome remained stripped of all those wrappings which belong to the temporal state, content only to lead the little sheep to pasture with the pastoral staff, that is, with purely spiritual arms." That is to say: For some centuries Rome lacked all those wrappings of the temporal state, content to lead the sheep to pasture with the pastoral staff, that is, with spiritual arms alone. Hence Adrian VI, judged less fit by present standards, is said in the conclave of his successor to have been "closer to those good qualities which are usually sought and desired in the election of Popes in the less distant times of the primitive Church." That is to say: Closer to those good qualities which were usually required and desired in the election of Popes in the times of the primitive Church, which are far removed from us.

units.la: XII. Finibus his apti quærebantur, apti etiam Martyrio, ad quod serie longâ eâque continuâ vocabantur, pro Christi nomine sustinendo. Prout etiam in cæteris Electiones illæ meliores erant Electionibus sequentium Seculorum, atque multò meliores: L' elettioni, inquit idem idibem, non uscivano dagli interessi de' Prencipi, e da' capricci de' Nepoti, come escono al presente, mà da un' ardente Zelo, che s' aggirava nelle viscere degli Elettori, quali solevano raunarsi, hora in un luogo, ed hora in un altro, e bene spesso ne' boschi, così obligati dalla crudeltà di quei Tiranni, che invidiavano il riposo de' Fedeli. Non vi erano voti segreti, perche l' interiore di quei primi servi del Signore corrispondeva con il Zelo esteriore dell' opere buone &c. Id est; Electiones non veniebant ex commodis Principum & vana voluntate Nepotum, hodiernarum ad instar, sed ex ardente Zelo, qui occupabat viscera eligentium, qui convenire solebant modò hèic, modò alibi, sæpe etiam in Sylvis, ob crudelitatem mimirum Tyrannorum quietem fidelibus invidentium. Tunc non erant suffragia secreta, quia internum primorum illorum Domini servorum conveniebat cum Zelo externo bonorum operum &c.
units.tr: XII. Men fit for these ends were sought, men also fit for martyrdom, to which they were called in a long and unbroken succession, to bear witness to the name of Christ. In the same way those elections were better than the elections of later centuries, and much better. "The election," says the same author, ibid., "did not come from the interests of princes or the whims of nephews, as they do now, but from an ardent zeal that burned in the hearts of the electors, who used to gather now in one place and now in another, very often even in the woods, compelled by the cruelty of those tyrants who begrudged the faithful their rest. There were no secret votes, because the inner life of those first servants of the Lord corresponded with the outward zeal of good works etc." That is to say: Elections did not come from the advantages of princes and the vain will of nephews, as they do today, but from the ardent zeal which filled the hearts of the electors, who used to meet now here, now elsewhere, often even in the woods, on account of the cruelty of the tyrants who envied the faithful their quiet. There were then no secret votes, because the inward state of those first servants of the Lord agreed with the outward zeal of good works etc.

units.la: XIII. Que-
units.tr: XIII. Que-

units.la: XIII. Quarebantur; atque dum non vi aut blanditiis se ingerebant indigni, meliores atque digniores studiosè quæri, inventi ordinari poterant.
units.tr: XIII. They were sought after; and so long as the unworthy did not thrust themselves forward by force or flattery, the better and more worthy were eagerly sought out and, once found, could be ordained.

units.la: Non si cercava, inquit idem p.19. mà si fuggiva da gli Ecclesiastici il Pontificato, perche il Pontificato à Pontefici costava la vita. Chi non si conosceva dotato d' un animo bastante à soffrire il Martyrio, rinunciava il Papato col Confessare la debolezza della sua natura; Ed in fatti chi haurebbe mai ricevuto, non che cercato un' officio, che non portava seco altra rendita, che la persecutione de' Tiranni? Hor quali imbrogli, hor quali intrighi, hor quali differenze potevano regnare nella creatione de' Pontefici? hor quali voti bisognavano per fare un Martyre, se non che i voti del Cielo? Id est; Non quarebant, sed fugiebant Pontificatum Ecclesiastici, quia Pontificatus Pontificibus vitam auferebat. Qui non animum ad martyrium sibi adesse sentiebat, Papatui renuntiabat confessus natura sua infirmitatem; Et certè quis accepisset, non dico, quæsivisset munus, cujus soli reditus erant persecutiones Tyrannorum? Et quanam molitiones, quanam machinationes, quanam dissensiones regnare poterant in Creatione Pontificum illius temporis? Quanam vota requiruntur ad martyrium prater cæli vota? Subjungit Author; Sanctam atque felicem hodienum futuram Ecclesiam, si i Pontefici fossero chiamati alla poverta e non all oro, à martyrij & non à piaceri; alla cura della chiesa, e non de' Magistrati; Si Pontifices vocarentur ad paupertatem & non ad aurum; ad martyria & non ad delitias; ad curam Ecclesiæ, & non Magistratuum. Certè tunc ambitio dominans multùm imminueretur Olim plane aberat, & qui Episcopatum, etiam Romanum, lubentes accept bant, illud zelo Divini Nominis faciebant, parati vel sanguinem pro Christo effundere; Tunc, in qui bat jam suo tempore, ni fallor, Hilarius, non minori cum studio ambiebantur Martyria, quàm hodie ambiri solent Episcopatus. Cæteri sibi diffidentes in viti ordinari debuerunt.
units.tr: "They were not sought," says the same author on p. 19, "but the churchmen fled from the Pontificate, because the Pontificate cost the Pontiffs their lives. Whoever did not know himself to have a spirit strong enough to endure martyrdom renounced the Papacy by confessing the weakness of his nature. And indeed, who would ever have accepted, let alone sought, an office that brought no other income than the persecution of tyrants? Now what schemes, what intrigues, what disputes could reign in the creation of Popes? What votes were needed to make a martyr, except the votes of heaven?" That is: "They did not seek the Pontificate of the Church; they fled from it, because the Pontificate took away the lives of Popes. Whoever felt that the courage for martyrdom was not in him renounced the Papacy, confessing the weakness of his nature. And surely who would have accepted, let alone sought, an office whose only rewards were the persecutions of tyrants? And what manoeuvres, what machinations, what dissensions could reign in the creation of Popes of that time? What votes were required for martyrdom, except the votes of heaven?" The author adds: "The Church would be holy and happy today if the Popes were called to poverty and not to gold, to martyrdoms and not to pleasures, to the care of the Church and not of the magistrates. Certainly then the dominating ambition would be greatly diminished." Formerly it was plainly absent; those who gladly accepted the episcopate, even the Roman, did so out of zeal for the Divine Name, ready to shed even their blood for Christ. "Then, in what was already his own time, unless I am mistaken, Hilary, martyrdoms were sought with no less eagerness than episcopates are usually sought today." The others, distrusting themselves, had to be ordained against their will.

units.la: XIV. Quales temporibus illis multos & ubique locorum ordinatos fuisse, jam Dissert. V. innuimus, atque de repugnantia illa judicium nostrum exposuimus. Ita etiam Dissert. VI. occasione ambitionis hodiernæ non nihil de Episcopis Rom. qui inviti ordinati fuerunt, diximus. Sic ex primis Cletus, teste Platina; Sic multi sine dubio ex primis seculis alij; Sic serius Bonifacius, ut Presbyteri Romani in libello supplici ad Honorium apud Baronium ad an. 459. n 8. testantur, quod eum magis ornabat, invitus. Sic Platina & aliis narrationibus, Gregorius I. Sic ex recentioribus adhucNicolaus I. referente eodem Platina; Sic etiam ex paulò prioribus, atque etiam exc
units.tr: XIV. We have already noted in Dissertation V that many were ordained in those times, and in many places, against their will, and we set out our judgement on that reluctance. Likewise in Dissertation VI, on the occasion of today's ambition, we said something about the Roman bishops who were ordained against their will. Thus, among the first, Cletus, according to Platina; thus no doubt many others from the earliest centuries; thus later Boniface, as the Roman presbyters testify in their supplication to Honorius, reported by Baronius at the year 459, n. 8, "which honoured him more, against his will." Thus Gregory I, according to Platina and other accounts. Thus from more recent times Nicholas I, again according to Platina; thus also from somewhat earlier times, and even exc

units.la: reprinex posterioribus (quidam eorum forte simulantes) ordinati fuerunt. Verae autem repugnantiae primorum temporum jam ambitionem seculorum sequiorum tanquam vitiosarum Electionum principium oppositimus. Oppositum autem diu ante nos etiam Gabriel Baraletta Praedicatorij Ordinis Monachus in Sermonibus A. 1414. editis ita A tempore Petri usque ad Sylvestrum fuerunt 32. Papae, qui per Martyrium fere translierunt. Unde post Sixtum diu vacavit Papatus, & nullus eum affectaviti ratione mortis, quia Papae primi erant. 2. ratione paupertatis, sed postquam Ecclesia dives facta per Constant. M. Imperatorem, nullus reperitur, qui illum renuat. Imo per mille vias quaeritur.
units.tr: The reprobate (some of them perhaps feigning it) were ordained later. But we set against the ambition of the later centuries, as the source of corrupt elections, the genuine reluctance of the earliest times. The same opposite view was held long before us by Gabriel Baraletta, a Dominican monk, in his Sermons, published in 1414, where he says: From the time of Peter down to Sylvester there were 32 popes, who almost all passed through martyrdom. Hence after Sixtus the papacy stood vacant for a long time, and no one aspired to it, on account of death, because the popes were the first; on account of poverty. But after the Church became rich through the Emperor Constantine the Great, no one is found who refuses it. Indeed, people seek it by a thousand routes.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Minime autem est, cur de Electionibus sanctis primorum sanctorum Pontificum, sive Episcoporum, ut quidem faciunt, glorientur Pontificij. Alij illi primi erant atque toto genere diversi, non dominatum universalem sibi attribuentes, quod Disert. III. ostendimus. Contrariam quoque (quod alias demonstramus) doctrinam profitebantur atque docebant. Quod cum sit, & cum hodierni insuper officium non faciunt, cum longe alia (quod infra probabimus;) hodie in eligendis requirantur, cum plerique bonis illis qualitatibus, quae in primis requirebantur, quae primos ornabant, plane destituti (quales inferius pariter magno numero exhibebimus) reperiantur, ex eo certe omnimoda defectio inferri potest, atque quo meliores fuerunt priores, eo pejor est posteriorum turpiter degenerantium conditio, ut optimi vini, quod vulgo dicitur, acetum pessimum. Sed missis prioribus, ad posteriores nos convertimus, quales jam a longo tempore eligendorum qualitates sint atque requirantur, visuri.
units.tr: There is by no means any reason for the Papists to boast of the holy elections of the first holy Pontiffs, or bishops, as indeed they do. Those first men were quite different in every respect; they did not claim universal dominion for themselves, as we showed in Dissertation III. They also professed and taught the contrary doctrine, as we demonstrate elsewhere. Since this is so, and since they do not even perform the office of today, for far different qualifications (which we shall show below) are now required in those who are elected, and since most of today's electors are found utterly lacking in those good qualities which were chiefly required, and which adorned the first Popes (as we shall likewise show below in great numbers), a complete decline can certainly be inferred from this. The better the earlier men were, the worse is the condition of the later men, who have degenerated shamefully, like the proverbial vinegar of the finest wine, which is the worst of all. But, leaving the earlier men aside, let us turn to the later ones, to see what qualities are now required and demanded in those to be elected.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Hoc primum est, quod eligendus homo esse debet: Licet enim tot monstrorum sive Electiones, sive intrusiones commemorentur, talia tamen fuerunt atque describuntur electi Pontifices, non physice atque ratione membrorum corporis bestiarum similitudinem referentes, quatenus hominibus dissimiles illae sunt, sed moraliter atque ratione foedissimorum morum, turpissimorumque vitiorum. Quod etiam ex Benedicti IX. exemplo apud Platinam in vita constat, cujus simulacrum admodum monstruosum apparuit interrogatumque, quid illa horrida imago prae se ferret, cum antea Pontifex fuisset, respondit: Quia in vita sine lege & ratione vixi, ideo volente Deo & Petro, cujus sedem omnibus probris foedavi, Simulacrum meum plus feritatis, quam humanitatis in se habet. Ubi manifeste ad turpes in vita mores respicirespicitur ejus, cujus simulacrum admodùm monstruosum demum post mortem visum fuit. Homo igitur esse debet eligendus, atque homines fuerunt omnes.
units.tr: This is the first requirement: the man who is to be chosen must be a human being. Many monsters, whether elections or intrusions, are recorded, and the elected popes were of such a kind and are so described. They are not described as resembling beasts physically, in the make-up of their bodily members, insofar as those differ from men. They are described morally, in terms of their most foul morals and most shameful vices. This is clear also from the example of Benedict IX in Platina in the Life, whose image appeared quite monstrous. When he was asked what that horrid likeness showed, since he had been pope before, he replied: Because in life I lived without law and reason, therefore, with God and Peter willing it, whose see I defiled with every disgrace, my image has more of savagery than of humanity in it. Here he plainly refers to the shameful morals of his life, the man whose very monstrous image was seen only after death. The man to be chosen must therefore be a human being, and all of them were men.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Homo esse debet physicè atque respectu membrorum corporis non planè ad functiones necessarias ineptus; Debet enim, aliter atque Idola Psalmi CXV. alitérque ac de Papa portari solito necessarium videri posset, habere pedes, qui ambulent. Hinc in Conclavi Alexandri VII. Cardinali Caraffa, cæterùm valde Papabili, qui tandem in Conclavi ex apoplexia obiit, obstitisse dicitur primò l' impedimento de' piedi assato inutili al caminare, nè pareva conveniente, quando bene non ostasse alla dispositione de' Canoni, che si facesse un Papa nè pure habile à fare la prima funtione e celebrar messa una volta; Id est; Primò impedimentum pedum planè inutilium ad ambulandum, neque conveniens videbatur, licèt non obstitisset Canonum Authoritas, Papam eligere, qui ne quidem aptus sit ad primam functionem & Missam vel unicâ vice celebrandam. Quamvis etiam circa Seculi septimi finem Sisinnius Papa, referente Joh. Stellâ in vita podagrâ adeò laborârit, ut non modò non ambulare, verum nec cibum per se sumere potuerit. Debet etiam habere aures, quæ audiant. Hinc in Conclavi Leonis XI. Cardinalis Taruggius Papabilis & ille introducitur inhabile per mancamento di udire, ineptus ob defectum auditûs. De cæteris ex his judicium ferri potest, debere nimirum esse hominem physicè atque respectu membrorum corporis non planè ad functiones necessarias ineptum.
units.tr: The man must be physically, in respect of the members of his body, not wholly unfit for the necessary functions. He must have feet that walk, as the idols of Psalm 115 do not, and as is customarily thought necessary for the pope to be carried. Hence, in the Conclave of Alexander VII, Cardinal Caraffa, otherwise a strong candidate for the papacy, who died of apoplexy in the conclave, is said to have been held back first by the impediment of his feet, useless for walking. It seemed unsuitable, even if it did not conflict with the canons, to make a pope who was not even fit to perform the first function and celebrate Mass once. That is: First, the impediment of feet entirely useless for walking; and it seemed unsuitable to elect as pope a man who is not even fit to perform the first function and celebrate Mass even once. Again, near the end of the seventh century, Pope Sisinnius, as John Stella reports, suffered so badly from gout in the Life that he could not only not walk but could not even take food by himself. He must also have ears that hear. Hence, in the Conclave of Leo XI, Cardinal Taruggio, a candidate for the papacy, is brought forward as unfit because of a lack of hearing, ineptus ob defectum auditus. Judgment on the rest may be formed from these: the man must be, physically and in respect of the members of his body, not wholly unfit for the necessary functions.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Neque etiam aliâs nimis debilis, aut semper æger. Senem eligi posse, imò à longo tempore non nisi senem, inferiùs indicabitur. Sed requiritur, ut nonnullæ vires supersint. Id quod hinc inde ex Conclavibus discimus; Vide Sect. I. n. 83. Neque etiam plane valetudinarius ullo colore eligi atque populis salvâ Majestate Pontificiâ ostentari posset; Neque facilè consentiunt Cardinales, ut Electus statim sit merum alienæ ambitionis & tyrannidis ludibrium. Neque è re Ecclesiæ suæ putant, ut vix ex Conclavi egressi in illud statim regrediantur, maximè quia plerique Papâ per aliquot annos vivente spes & res suas ad successionem disponere gestiunt.
units.tr: Nor should he be too weak in other respects, or always sick. That an old man may be chosen, indeed that for a long time only an old man has been chosen, will be shown below. But some strength must remain to him. We learn this from the conclaves here and there; see Sect. I, n. 83. Nor could a man who was in any way plainly infirm be chosen and shown to the peoples while the papal majesty is preserved. Nor do the cardinals readily agree that the elect should at once become a mere plaything of another's ambition and tyranny. Nor do they think it to the advantage of their Church that a man who has barely come out of the conclave should at once return to it, chiefly because most of them, while the pope is still living for some years, are eager to arrange their hopes and affairs for the succession.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Sunt & alia multa requisita, quæ breviorem nonnisi consideratione merentur; (potiora suis locis exhibebimus.) Et quamvis multùm, juxta Authores, interest, quis proponat, in eo tamen
units.tr: There are also many other requirements, which deserve only a brief mention; we shall set out the more important in their places. And although, according to the authors, it matters much who proposes a candidate, it also matters greatly how candidates are proposed in respect of many qualities and relations.

units.la: Ffff. tamen quoque haud parùm situm est, quales respectu multarum qualitatum & relationum proponantur. Dico, etiam respectu relationum; Nam, quod sequentia docebunt, externaferè sunt, quæ aliquando maximè impediunt, eaque impedimenta maximam partem Politica, quæ in Conclavi Urbani VIII. cumprimis enumerata videri possunt, & jam quadantenus ex regulis Disput. præced. cognoscuntur. Neque enim tantùm quærunt, an eligendus debeat esse de gremio Ecclesiæ, sed & absentes difficulter eligi docent, & temporibus turbulentis, Hispani omni tempore, quietum postulant; & spiritus altos cum Cardinale Azzolino in Aphorismis Politicis occultare jubent, & severum nolunt, Hispani in Conclavi Leonis XI. Baronium, per haver à guisa di Catone molte volte parlato, quia sape tanquam Cato locutus est; & avarum rejiciunt, Ginettum in Conclavi Alexandri VII. quia fuit poco meno ch' avaro, quasi avarus; & minùs splendidum similiter; ut post displicuit Adrianus VI. per essere stata S. Beat. molto diversa di quella grandezza, magnificenza & splendore, quale havevan' tenuto i suoi più vicini antecessori nel loro Pontificato; Id est; Quia fuit Beatitudo sua, loquitur Author Conclavis Successoris, multùm diversa à majestate, magnificentia & splendore, quem ostendebant in Pontificatu suo proximi ejus Antecessores; Et nimis dependentem à Principibus: Neutralis esse debet Papabilis; E questa virtù, inquit Author Conclavis Pauli III. di neutralità molto gli e giovata, perche in effetto il non dependere da alcun Prencipe, e cosa propria del Papa, ch' è Padre universale; Et virtus ista neutralitatis multùm eum juvit, quia revera non dependere à Principe ullo proprium est Pontificis, qui est Pater universalis; quam etiam neutralitatem Papa Pius IV. electus juramento confirmare debuit, ut in Conclavi habetur; Et contrà Castagno in Conclavi Sixti V. non potuit eligi, per esser troppo favorito da Spagna; quia nimis Hispania placebat. Et tandem etiam exosum Principibus, vel Principum præcipuorum alicui. Sic allegabant in Conclavi Leonis XI. contrà Baronium S. Thomas nella 2. 2. q. 181. art. 3. dove sostenta, che simili persone inerte, ancorche per altro innocenti & virtuose, quando ne possono seguire scandali & guerre non debonsi promovere alla dignità grandi, tanto meno costui, che havendo scritto contro le raggioni di Sicilia con molta affertatione haveva meritato d' esser dichiarato nemico & rimemoravano gl' altri officii sinistri fatti da lui per occasione delle giuriditioni di Milano e sin contro S. Giacomo stimato Apostolo della Spagna & per tale venerato in Spagna; Id est; S. Thomam 2. 2. q. 181. art. 3. ubi sustinet, similes personas inertes, licèt caterùm innocentes & virtute præditas, si inde possent sequi scandala & bella non debere promoveri ad dignitates magnas, multò minùs hunc debere, qui, quia scripserit contrà rationes Siciliæ cum multa assectatione, meritus sit, ut inimicus haberetur, & commemorabant alia sinistra facta ejus occasione Jurisdictionis Mediolanensis & tandem contrà S. Jacobum Apostolum Hispaniæ creditum & pro tali etiam in Hispania cultum. Atque etiam prævaluerunt contrà Baronium, (cujus Annalium Tomus undecimus ob dictam causam respectu Siciliæ publicè carnificis manu exustus, venditórque ad remos damnatus est;) hæ & similes Hispanorum atque Hispani tantum voces; Quas etiam primogenituræ Ecclesiæ derogatione meruit, Gallicissimus in omnibus, hinc quoque Galliarum Regi à Perronio commendatus. Ut contrà Paulum V. major prudentia & abstinentia juvit, & quòd, cùm esset Cardinalis addictus Gallis, Consilio tamen Clementis VIII. Papæ, ne sibi aliquando suffragia ad Papatum deessent, Hispanorum annuam largitionem callidus admisit; eadémque juvit recentiorem Innocentium XI. quòd à nullo Principum dependens omnibúsque placere studens, Hispanus licèt subditus, nulli etiam Principum exosus fuit.
units.tr: Ffff. It matters greatly also what qualities and relations they are proposed with. I say, also in respect of relations. For what follows will show that they are mostly external, and these sometimes hinder most; these hindrances are for the most part political, which can be seen listed especially in the Conclave of Urban VIII, and are already in some measure known from the rules of the previous Disputation. For they do not ask only whether the one to be elected must be from within the bosom of the Church; they also teach that absent men are chosen with difficulty, and in turbulent times the Spanish always demand a quiet man; and they order that high spirits be hidden, with Cardinal Azzolino in the Political Aphorisms, and they do not want a severe man. The Spanish in the Conclave of Leo XI rejected Baronius, because he had often spoken like a Cato, since he often spoke like Cato. They rejected the greedy man, Ginetti, in the Conclave of Alexander VII, because he was a little less than greedy, almost avaricious, and likewise the less splendid; thus Adrian VI was later displeasing, because his Holiness was very different from the majesty, magnificence and splendour which his nearest predecessors had maintained in their pontificate. That is: Because his Beatitude was, the author of the Conclave of the Successor says, very different from the majesty, magnificence and splendour which his nearest predecessors displayed in their pontificate. And a candidate who is too dependent on princes is rejected. The candidate must be neutral. And this virtue, says the author of the Conclave of Paul III, of neutrality greatly benefited him, because in fact not to depend on any prince is proper to the pope, who is the universal father. And this virtue of neutrality greatly helped him, because in truth not to depend on any prince is proper to the Pontiff, who is the universal Father. Pope Pius IV, when elected, had to confirm this neutrality by oath, as is recorded in the conclave. On the other hand, Castagna could not be elected in the Conclave of Sixtus V, because he was too favoured by Spain; for Spain was too pleased with him. And finally, a candidate may be hateful to princes, or to one of the chief princes. Thus, in the Conclave of Leo XI, they argued against Baronius from St Thomas, in the 2nd 2nd q. 181 art. 3, where he maintains that such persons, inert, although otherwise innocent and virtuous, should not be promoted to great dignities if scandals and wars might follow from it; much less should this man be promoted, who, because he had written against the rights of Sicily with much affectation, had deserved to be regarded as an enemy; and they recalled other sinister acts done by him on the occasion of the jurisdiction of Milan, and even against St James, the Apostle believed to be of Spain and venerated as such in Spain. That is: St Thomas, 2nd 2nd q. 181 art. 3, where he maintains that such persons, inert, though otherwise innocent and endowed with virtue, should not be promoted if scandals and wars could follow from it; much less should this man, who, since he wrote against the reasons of Sicily with much affectation, deserved to be regarded as an enemy; and they recalled his other sinister acts on the occasion of the Milanese jurisdiction, and finally against St James the Apostle, believed to be of Spain and worshipped as such also in Spain. And indeed these voices of the Spanish, and of the Spanish alone, prevailed against Baronius, whose eleventh volume of the Annals, for that reason, was publicly burned by the hand of the executioner in respect of Sicily, and he was condemned to the galleys. Such voices, too, earned him the derogation of the Church's primogeniture, he who was most Gallic in all things, and for this reason was also commended to the King of France by Perron. Whereas greater prudence and abstinence helped against Paul V, and because, though he was a cardinal attached to the French, he cunningly admitted the yearly largesse of the Spanish, on the advice of Pope Clement VIII, lest votes for the papacy ever be lacking to him. The same things helped the more recent Innocent XI, because, depending on no prince and eager to please all, he, though a Spanish subject, was hateful to none of the princes.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA, In qua De Nævis & Vitiis Electionum Pontificum Romanorum ratione sexûs eorum, qui eliguntur, sive de famosa Johanna Papissa agitur.
units.tr: SECTION THREE, in which the blemishes and defects of the elections of the Roman Pontiffs are discussed with regard to the sex of those elected, or the infamous Pope Joan.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: 1 Ratione Sexus, è virili esse debet Papa eligendus. II. Sed fœmina electa fuit & sedit Iohanna VIII. cujus historia compendium exhibetur. III. Nobis quidem parùm decederet atque plus quàm satis argumentorùm restaret in refutanda, quam jactant, successione, si fabula narrata esset. IV. Pontificios contrà grave urget ex veritate historia præjudicium, idque partim intuitu qualitatum electa, & turpitudinis facti; V. Partim intuitu illius, quòd Ordinis incapax est ex Pontificiorum ipsorummet doctrina fœmina quavis. Licèt præjudicium contrà se hinc formari posse negent, Antoninus Episcopus Florentinus, & VI. Baronius; VII. Quibus occurritur, atque multiplex navus cum successionis interruptione ostenditur. VIII. Et quòd exinde multis grave salutis prejudicium fuerit IX Vera autem est historia, non obstante, quod urgent, primorum scriptorum silentio, cujus etiam causa traduntur. X. Sed neque cortum est silentium; Authores interierunt, corrupti fuerunt. XI. Qua Authorum corruptio sive mutilatio hic vel maximè locum habere potuit. XII. Fraudis indicia adsunt quoad codices Anastasianos mutilos. XIII. Hodiernos supposititios esse non frustrà conjicitur. XIV. Caterùm in quibusdam Anastasii Codicibus etiam habetur historia Iohanna. XV. Ad aliorum, quorum pratexunt, Authorum silentium respondetur. XVI. De Radulphi Flaviacensis testimonio. XVII. Testimonium Mariani Scoti, quem testari revera, ostenditur. XVIII. Testimonii authoritas exponitur; XIX. Testimonium Sigeberti Gemblacensis. XX. Godefredi Viterbiensis; ubi etiam ad silentium Ottonis Frisingensis provocantibus respondetur. XXI. Martini Poloni testimonium; XXII. Testimonia plurimorum ex omnibus ferè Nationibus. XXIII. Virorum magnorum, Pontificum & Authorum Papis inscriptorum, privilegiis munitorum. XXIV. Platina, Poetarum magni nominis; XXV. Quorum testimoniis diu nemo contradixit. XXVI. Argumentum ex eo, quòd Concilium Constantiense in Iohanne Husso assertionem non damnavit. XXVII. Ex eo, quòd occasio Occamo nata Ecclesiam hinc erroris arguendi. XXVIII. Ex eo, quòd post Reformationem Authores factum adsirmârunt. XXIX Conclusiones ex his testimoniis & argumentis. XXX. Argumentum ex Imaginibus XXXI. Statua Romana. XXXII. Blondelli de ea testimonium. XXXIII. Effugia aliter sentientium præcidun-tur. XXXIV. Statua Senensis, XXXV. De ea testimonium Launoji. XXXVI. Sella perforata. XXXVII. Argumentum hoc confirmatur & illustratur. XXXVIII. Exceptiones aliter sentientium de alio sella usu, & quòd non ad explorandam virilitatem adhibita fuerit, & quòd sic alii quoque explorari debuissent prater Pontifices XXXIX. Cur consuetudo explorandi in desuetudinem venerit. XL. Argumentum ex anfractuosis Pontificum ab illo tempore processionibus. XLI. Exceptionibus occurritur. XLII. Objectio prima de circumstantiarum in diversis diversorum narrationibus diversitate, & primò quidem de nominum & numeri diversitate. XLIII. De diversitate in assignatione temporis. XLIV. In Pontificatûs duratione. XLV. In assignatione Patria. XLVI. Narrationem porrò absurditatis convincere student ptimò ex eo, quòd cùm mox post mortem Leonis Benedictus electus dicatur, Pontificatui Iohanna nullum tempus reliquum sit. XLVII. Secundò ex eo, quòd electionis Benedicti Decretum ad Lotharium perferri haud potuerit. XLVIII Argumentum simile Leonis Allatii à temporis ratione. XLIX. Tertiò ex eo, quòd posthabitis gradibus ignota promoveri vix potuerit, Decretum Electionis Iohanna non habeatur, atque Schisma Anastasii demum post Electionem Benedicti exortum sit. L. Quartò ex eo, quòd Iohanna Athenas concedere haud potuerit. LI. Quintò ex eo, quòd Romæ literas cum applausu docere non potuerit. LII. Sextò ex eo, quòd minùs verisimile, demum in Pontificatu gravidam, neque tamen id observatum fuisse. LIII. Septimò ex eo, quòd æquè probabilitate careat, gravidam publicè incedere voluisse. LIV. Octavò ex eo, quòd Pontifices non in Vaticano habitârint. LV. Nonò ex eo, quòd host es hostes Ecclesia Romana ea de re tacuerint. LVI. Decimò ex eo, quòd Leo IX. talia Graecis exprobrare ausus fuerit. LVII. Undecimò ex Epistolis illo tempore scriptis. LVIII. Duodecimò ex eo, quòd nihil extet de rebus gestis Iohanna. LIX. Examinantur tandem sex Origines, quas Antagonista fabula, qua vocatur, assignant. LX. Ab ipsa Romana sede assignant quadruplicem. Primam à Iohanne VIII. sive IX. LXI Secundam à Iohanne X. LXII. Tertiam à Iohanne XII. LXIII. Quartam à Iohanne XXII. LXIV. Extra Romanam sedem duplicem quaesiverunt Originem. Priorem in sede Constantinopolitana. LXV. Posteriorem in Thiota Prophetissa Moguntina. LXVI. Consultatio tractationis de Iohanna.
units.tr: 1. By reason of sex, the Pope to be elected must be a man. II. But a woman was elected and sat as John VIII, whose history is set out in summary. III. For our part, little would be lost, and there would remain more than enough arguments for refuting the succession they boast of, even if the story were false. IV. The history, if true, presses a grave prejudice against the Papists, partly with regard to the character of the one elected and the baseness of the deed. V. Partly with regard to the fact that, by the very teaching of the Papists themselves, any woman is incapable of Orders. Although Antoninus, Bishop of Florence, and VI. Baronius deny that a prejudice can be formed against them from this; VII. To these objections an answer is given, and the manifold absurdity, together with the interruption of the succession, is shown. VIII. And that from this a grave prejudice to salvation has followed for many. IX. The history, however, is true, notwithstanding what they urge, namely the silence of the earliest writers, for which causes are also given. X. But the silence is not certain; the authors perished, they were corrupted. XI. The corruption or mutilation of the authors could have taken place here above all. XII. There are signs of fraud in the mutilated Anastasian codices. XIII. It is not without reason conjectured that the present ones are spurious. XIV. Moreover, in some codices of Anastasius the story of Joan is also found. XV. An answer is given to the silence of the other authors whom they put forward. XVI. On the testimony of Radulph of Flavigny. XVII. The testimony of Marianus Scotus, who is shown really to bear witness. XVIII. The authority of the testimony is explained; XIX. The testimony of Sigebert of Gembloux. XX. Of Godfrey of Viterbo; where also an answer is given to those who appeal to the silence of Otto of Freising. XXI. The testimony of Martin of Troppau; XXII. The testimonies of very many from almost all nations. XXIII. Of great men, Popes and authors, who are inscribed among the Popes, and fortified by privileges. XXIV. Platina, and poets of great name; XXV. To whose testimonies for a long time no one contradicted. XXVI. An argument from the fact that the Council of Constance did not condemn the assertion in John Hus. XXVII. From the fact that an occasion arose for Ockham to charge the Church with error on this point. XXVIII. From the fact that after the Reformation the authors affirmed the deed. XXIX. Conclusions drawn from these testimonies and arguments. XXX. An argument from the images. XXXI. The Roman statue. XXXII. Blondel's testimony concerning it. XXXIII. The evasions of those who think otherwise are cut off. XXXIV. The Sienese statue, XXXV. On it, the testimony of Launoy. XXXVI. The perforated chair. XXXVII. This argument is confirmed and illustrated. XXXVIII. The objections of those who think otherwise, about another use of the chair, and that it was not employed to test virility, and that on this reasoning others too ought to have been examined besides the Popes. XXXIX. Why the custom of testing fell into disuse. XL. An argument from the winding processions of the Popes from that time. XLI. The objections are met. XLII. The first objection, concerning the diversity of circumstances in the different accounts of different men, and first of all concerning the diversity of names and numbers. XLIII. On the diversity in the assignment of time. XLIV. In the length of the pontificate. XLV. In the assignment of the homeland. XLVI. They further strive to convict the narrative of absurdity, firstly from the fact that, since Benedict is said to have been elected soon after the death of Leo, no time is left for Joan's pontificate. XLVII. Secondly, from the fact that the decree of Benedict's election could scarcely have been carried to Lothair. XLVIII. A similar argument from the chronology, by Leo Allatius. XLIX. Thirdly, from the fact that, with the ranks passed over, someone unknown could hardly have been promoted, no decree of Joan's election is extant, and the schism of Anastasius arose only after Benedict's election. L. Fourthly, from the fact that Joan could not have taught at Athens. LI. Fifthly, from the fact that she could not have lectured in letters at Rome with applause. LII. Sixthly, from the fact that it is less likely that she was pregnant only in the pontificate, and yet this was not noticed. LIII. Seventhly, from the fact that it is equally improbable that she wished to walk about publicly while pregnant. LIV. Eighthly, from the fact that the Popes did not reside in the Vatican. LV. Ninthly, from the fact that the enemies of the Roman Church kept silent on this matter. LVI. Tenthly, from the fact that Leo IX dared to reproach the Greeks with such things. LVII. Eleventhly, from the letters written at that time. LVIII. Twelfthly, from the fact that nothing is extant about the deeds of Joan. LIX. Six origins which the opponent assigns to the fable, as it is called, are finally examined. LX. They assign a fourfold origin from the Roman see itself. The first, from John VIII or IX. LXI. The second, from John X. LXII. The third, from John XII. LXIII. The fourth, from John XXII. LXIV. Outside the Roman see they sought a twofold origin. The former in the see of Constantinople. LXV. The latter in Thiota the Mainz prophetess. LXVI. A consultation on the treatment of Joan.

units.la: I. SEXUM quod attinet, Papa eligendus è virili esse debet; Licèt enim ex non Diacono hodie quoque, interveniente Dispensatione eligi possit atque aliquoties electus sit, tamen postea Ordinem suscipere tenetur, neque heic Dispensatio in promptu est; Ordinis autem mulieres incapaces esse ajunt; Atque si ex hoc fundamento Gradus Doctoratus Theologici Patavii haud ita pridem Virgini Italae Eruditissimae denegatus fuit, multò magis praesupponendum est, ideò faeminas ad Pontificatum ineptas pronunciari, γυναικοκρατίαν heic improbari, de Papatu non minùs ac de Regno Gallico enunciari posse, qu' il ne tombe pas en quenouille; non in colum cadere, atque Lege quidem expresse non latâ, faeminas heic quoque excludi, quemadmodum in Insula Borneo contrario more mares excludi dicuntur; Effaeminatos quidem multos (de quibus postea) Papatum tenuisse, faeminas nullas planè ad illud dignitatis Ecclesiasticae culmen evehi debere.
units.tr: I. As for sex, the Pope to be elected must be a man. For although, even today, one who is not a deacon may be elected by dispensation, and has sometimes been elected, yet afterwards he is bound to receive Orders, and no dispensation is at hand here. They say, however, that women are incapable of Orders; and if on this foundation the doctorate in theology was lately refused at Padua to an Italian virgin, most learned, much more must it be presupposed that women are unfit for the papacy, that female rule (gynaikokratia) is here disapproved, and that it may be said of the papacy no less than of the kingdom of France that it "does not fall to the distaff" (qu'il ne tombe pas en quenouille; non in colum cadere). And although no law has been expressly passed, women are excluded here as well, just as, by a contrary custom, men are said to be excluded in the island of Borneo. Many effeminate men (of whom later) have held the papacy, but no women at all ought to be raised to that height of ecclesiastical dignity.

units.la: II. Ad illud tamen quaedam evecta legitur, famosa illa Johanna VIII. quam Moguntiâ oriundam, sexum virilem mentitam atque Athenis, ubi studiis aliquandiu operam dederat, reducem, postquam Romae sibi singularis eruditionis famam comparâssel, ad Pontificatum promotam fuisse eúmque ab anno Ch. 853. per biennium & amplius tenuisse, factámque à familiari gravidam in processione ad Lateranensem Basilicam ex partu obiisse, Authores perhibent.
units.tr: II. Yet the writers report that one of this kind was in fact raised to it, that famous John VIII, a native of Mainz, who, having pretended to be a man and returned from Athens, where she had for some time devoted herself to studies, after gaining a reputation for singular learning at Rome, was promoted to the papacy; that she held it from the year of Christ 853 for two years and more; and that, having become pregnant by a familiar, she died in childbirth during a procession to the Lateran basilica.

units.la: III. Nobis quidem & causae nostrae parùm decedit, etsi Johannae hujus historia in dubium vocetur, sive etiam negetur. Alia habemus eáque longè graviora contrà successionem Rom. Pontificum tanto cum clamore jactari solitam, argumenta, alia Electionum Rom. Pontificum, etiam respectu eorum, qui eliguntur, vitia. Sufficerent nobis monstra, sufficerent effaeminati, sufficerent Faeminae minæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ atque Pontificibus Romanis, nec non per hos aliis dominantes, item cum his impudenter scortantes; atque adeò fæmina hac lasciva Pontificatûs duplici modo usurpatrice, ad ostendendam Ecclesiæ Romanæ deformitatem, nobis planè non opus esset.
units.tr: III. For our part, little bears on our cause, even if the history of this Joan is called in doubt, or even denied. We have other arguments, and far weightier ones, against the succession of the Roman Pontiffs, which they are accustomed to boast of with such clamour: other defects of the elections of the Roman Pontiffs, even with respect to those who are elected. Monsters would suffice for us, effeminate men would suffice, women would suffice as a threat to the Roman Church and to the Roman Pontiffs, and through these to others whom they dominate, and to those with whom they shamelessly fornicate; so that, to show the deformity of the Roman Church, we would have no real need of this lascivious woman who usurped the papacy in a twofold way.

units.la: IV. Contrà, si talis Fæmina sedem Romanam invasit atque habuit, Ecclesiæ Romanæ probra Carcinomate isto atque dehonestamento illius haud parùm aucta deprehenduntur. Et quomodo quæsò cum peculiari, de qua gloriantur, Dei pro Ecclesia Romana cura convenit, quòd impudica mulier ejus Caput atque Domina immediata etiam, malis, ut Platina in vita loquitur, artibus facta est? Vel, quòd ei Capitis atque Vicarii Jesu Christi, Monarchæ Universalis, summi Legislatoris atque Judicis loco fuit, & quòd mater illa scortationum in ipso partu, in solenni processione, omnium oculis expósita vitam scelecтam finiit? Hinc certè & ab ista rei gestæ deformitate factum est, quòd Paparum Gnathones interdum ex illa ipsa deformitate atque abominatione, contrà historiæ veritatem argumentari voluerunt: Non est existimandum, inquit Onuphr. annot. in Joh. VIII. Deum tulisse, ut sedem Petri — famina polluisset.
units.tr: IV. On the contrary, if such a woman invaded and held the Roman see, the disgraces of the Roman Church are found to be greatly increased by this cancer and this dishonouring of it. And how, I ask, does this agree with the special care of God for the Roman Church, of which they boast, that an unchaste woman, through what Platina in his life calls evil arts (malis artibus), became its head and even its immediate mistress? Or that she took the place of the Head and Vicar of Jesus Christ, the universal Monarch, the supreme Lawgiver and Judge, and that this mother of harlotries, in the very act of giving birth, in a solemn procession, exposed to the eyes of all, ended a wicked life? Certainly from this very disgrace of the deed it has come about that the flatterers of the Popes have sometimes wished to argue, against the truth of history, from that same deformity and abomination: It is not to be thought, says Onuphrius in his notes on John VIII, that God permitted the see of Peter to be polluted by a woman.

units.la: V. Imò etiam contrà successionem ipsam historia illa argumenta propiora suppeditat; Licèt aliter videatur Papatûs promachis. Postquam enim Antoninus Episcopus Florentinus in numerum Sanctorum A. Ch. 1523. relatus in Summa sua historica tit. 16. c. 1. §. 7. recitatis Martini Poloni verbis, iisque fidem adhibens exclamâsset: O altitudo sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei, quàm incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus! ei statim subjungere visum fuit: Etsi fuit verum, nulli tamen ex hoc salutis prejudicium, quia nec Ecclesia tunc fuit sine Capite, quod est Christus, unde influxum gratiæ percipit. Atque porrò; Nec ultimi effectus Sacramentorum, quæ illa conferebat, deficiebant iis, qui devotè ab ea accipiebant, scilicet gratiæ: licèt illa, sicut nec aliæ Fæminæ, sint susceptibiles Caracteris alicujus Ordinis, nec conficere Eucharistiam, etiam de facto ordinatæ possint, nec absolvere à peccatis. Unde ordinati ab ea erant iterum ordinandi, quia nihil ab ea acceperant; Gratiam tamen Sacramentorum Christus supplebat in recipientibus digné, ignorantiâ facti invincibili eos excusante à culpa.
units.tr: V. Indeed, that story supplies arguments even more pertinent against the succession itself, although the champions of the Papacy see it otherwise. After Antoninus, Bishop of Florence, who was enrolled among the saints in 1523, had in his Summa historica tit. 16, c. 1, §7 recited the words of Martin of Poland and, giving them credence, exclaimed: O the height of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how incomprehensible are his judgments!, he at once thought fit to add: Even if it was true, no harm came from it to salvation, because the Church was not then without a Head, which is Christ, from whom she receives the influx of grace. And further: nor did the final effects of the sacraments which she conferred fail those who devoutly received them from her, namely grace; although she, like other women, was not capable of the character of any Order, nor could she consecrate the Eucharist, even if she had been ordained in fact, nor absolve from sins. Hence those ordained by her had to be ordained again, because they had received nothing from her. Yet Christ supplied the grace of the sacraments to those who received them worthily, the invincible ignorance of the fact excusing them from guilt.

units.la: VI. Baronius autem ad an. 853. n. 63. ante pugnam pro more triumphans, insolenter satis, quod tamen & ipsum ei solenne fuit, ait: Sed in ipso limine Controversia rideas inane studium pugnacium Novatorum aerem verberantium, dum anxio & infatigabili animo eam fabulam suadere conantur, ut ex eo continuatam hactenus Successionem Rom. Pontificum, jam esse succisam & interruptam ostendant. Sed frustra. Quid enim? Fingamus esse, quod nunquam fuit, eam electam esse faeminam in Pontificem. Nunquid Pontifex illa fuerit? Nemo adeo imprudens & vacors erit, qui affirmet, resistentibus legibus omnibus, potuisse faeminam revera, quorumvis suffragiis accedentibus, esse Pontificem Maximum; imo nec minoris Ordinis Clericatu initiatam &c. Et paulo post: Nihil ex ea termiseri Novatores, qui veram asserunt fabulam, lucri capiunt, nisi, ut dici possit, duobus illis annis & mensibus, sedem Pontificiam legitimo vacuam fuisse Pastore; non tamen ob eam causam Successionem a Christo per Petrum in posteros continuatam fuisse succisam, nam & aliàs accidit, ut majori etiam temporis spatio sedes Pontificia, dilatâ per discordias eligentium electione, vacârit, nec tamen successionem desiisse, quis unquam ausus est dicere, quod nec dici potuit, sed tantùm esse dilatam, nullo fere modo sublatam. Vides igitur omne penitùs evanescere, quod ex re inani inane captant lucrum vanissimi Novatores.
units.tr: VI. But Baronius, ad an. 853, n. 63, triumphing before the battle as is his custom, and insolently enough (which was also customary for him), says: "But at the very threshold you may laugh at the empty effort of the quarrelsome Novatians, who beat the air, while with an anxious and tireless mind they try to persuade us of that fable, so that they may show that the succession of the Roman Pontiffs continued until now has been cut off and broken. But in vain. For what? Let us suppose what never happened, that a woman was elected as Pontiff. Would she then have been Pontiff? No one will be so imprudent and foolish as to affirm that, with all the laws resisting, a woman could really have become the Supreme Pontiff by whatever votes came to her; nor even that she could have been initiated into the clerical rank of the lowest Order, etc." And a little later: "The Novatians, who assert the story is true, gain nothing from it, except that, so to speak, for those two years and months the Pontifical see stood vacant of a lawful Pastor; yet this is no reason why the succession continued from Christ through Peter to posterity should be said to have been cut off. For it has also happened at other times that the Pontifical see stood vacant for a much longer span of time, the election being deferred by the discords of the electors, and yet no one ever dared to say, nor could it be said, that the succession had ceased; it was only delayed, and hardly removed in any way at all. You see, therefore, that everything the most vain Novatians catch at, from an empty matter, as empty gain, vanishes completely."

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Verùm non ita effugient, in ista ab una parte Mysterii Iniquitatis profunditate, ab altera verò sapientia atque scientia Dei altitudine, qui justo suo judicio impuri coelibatûs fructus, ibi maximè, unde ille violentâ Lege obtrusus prodiit, ostendere, qui fastum Romanorum Pontificum osculum pedum à Valentino An. 827. invectum exigentium, tanto dedecore punire, qui suorum solatio fallacem successionis praetextum tam variè támque bene confundere novit, ut nos jam pugnaces atque termiseri, vanissimíque Novatores neque anxio animo, neque inani studio ex re inani inane lucrum captantes aerem verberemus, neque etiam eatenus ridendi simus. Contenditis, facta hypothesi, Antonine! Baroni! Johannam verum Pontificem neutiquam fuisse; Probamus utroque pollice, atque, cùm id ob naevum in electi fieri haud potuisse dicatur, exinde, naevos in aliis pariter legitimo eorum Pontificatui obfuisse, inferimus, in multis aliis. Sed cur hic nullus naevus est? Cur successio interrupta non est? Quòd sedes aliàs diu vacavit, majori etiam spatio dilatâ per discordias eligentium Electione; in eo haud exiguus naevus est, quem suo loco jam tetigimus. Hoc similem largiuntur; sed major est, neque enim tunc sedes vacabat; Papa electus erat, agnoscebatur sine exceptione ab omnibus; omnia, quae Pontificis esse dicuntur, perageb-bat. bat, Deus autem ista omnia permittebat, sed an Spiritus S. cui Electiones ejusmodi tribuunt, ita aberrare potuit? Ergò non tantùm diu nullus legitimus Pontifex esse potest, atque diutiùs non esse potuisset, sed & illegitimus sedere potest, atque diutiùs sedere potuisset; Dilata fuit successio, nullo verò modo sublata ; id est, interrupta erat, sed non in perpetuum, totaliter quidem, sed non finaliter ; An igitur non interrupta atque succisa est? Vel an non successionem à Christo per Petrum continuatam jactant? Vel quid ergò jactant? Quid hoc est; dilata fuit successio? Et quoties quaesò ita dilata fuit, id est, interrupta? Quoties interrupta fuit, aliquo licèt sedente, sed cui leges resistebant? Et quoties non idem timeri debet, nempe illum, qui se sine socio etiam pro vero Pontifice venditat, quod Johanna fecit, esse nihilominus illegitimum ; esse nihilominus successionem dilatam, id est, interruptam? Tantum nocet, quòd nemo tam imprudens atque vacors est, qui affirmet — potuisse faminam — revera esse Pontificem maximum.
units.tr: Yet they will not escape so easily. In that depth of the Mystery of Iniquity on one side, and on the other the height of the wisdom and knowledge of God, who by his just judgment knows how to display the fruit of impure celibacy precisely where that pope, forced on by a violent law, came forth; who with such disgrace punishes the pride of the Roman Pontiffs demanding the kiss of the feet, a custom introduced by Valentinian in 827; who knows how so variously and so cleverly to confound the fallacious pretext of succession by the comfort of their own people, that we, now quarrelsome and wretched, most vain Novatians, neither beat the air with an anxious mind, nor catching at empty gain from an empty matter with empty zeal, nor are we to be laughed at to that extent. You contend, the hypothesis being granted, Antoninus! Baronius! that Joan was by no means a true Pontiff. We approve this with both thumbs, and since it is said that this could not happen because of a blemish in the one elected, we infer from it that blemishes equally harm the lawful Pontificate of others, in many other cases. But why is there no blemish here? Why is the succession not interrupted? Because the see was at other times vacant for a long time, the election being deferred by the discords of the electors for a longer span; in this there is no small blemish, which we have already touched upon in its place. They grant a similar thing here; but the one in our case is greater, for then the see was not vacant; a Pope had been elected and was acknowledged without exception by all; he performed all the things that are said to belong to the Pontiff. God indeed permitted all those things, but could the Holy Spirit, to whom they attribute such elections, go so far astray? Therefore not only can no lawful Pontiff be for a long time, and could not have been for longer, but also an unlawful one can sit, and could have sat for longer. The succession was delayed, but in no way removed; that is, it was interrupted, but not forever; wholly indeed, but not finally. Is it then not interrupted and cut off? Or do they not boast of the succession continued from Christ through Peter? Or what then do they boast? What is this: the succession was delayed? And how often, I ask, was it so delayed, that is, interrupted? How often was it interrupted, with someone sitting, however, but to whom the laws resisted? And how often must the same fear not arise, namely that the one who sells himself, even without a companion, as a true Pontiff, as Joan did, is nevertheless unlawful; that the succession is nevertheless delayed, that is, interrupted? So much harm is done by the fact that no one is so imprudent and foolish as to affirm that a woman could—really be the Supreme Pontiff.

units.la: VIII. Quomodo autem nulli ex inde salutis præjudicium fuit? Non fuit susceptibilis characteris alicujus Ordinis, non potuit conficere Eucharistiam, nec absolvere à peccatis. Ordinati ab ea erant iterum ordinandi, quia nihil ab ea acceperunt. Non potuit quorumvis suffragiis esse Pontifex Maximus, sive Maxima, nec minoris Ordinis Clericatu initiata.
units.tr: VIII. But how was there no harm to salvation from it? She was not capable of the character of any Order; she could not consecrate the Eucharist, nor absolve from sins. Those ordained by her had to be ordained again, because they received nothing from her. She could not by whatever votes be the Supreme Pontiff, whether male or female, nor initiated into the clerical rank of the lowest Order.

units.la: Quomodo exinde nulli salutis præjudicium fuit? A peccatis non absolvebat, omnia ligata relinquebat. Quomodo hinc nulli salutis præjudicium fuit? Ordinati ab ea non erant ordinati ante reordinationem, siquidem ulla secuta fuit. Quid igitur de eorum ante reordinationem actionibus, & de actionibus atque statu baptizatorum vel ordinatorum ab eis, & sic quasi in infinitum judicari debet? Et quomodo exinde nulli salutis præjudicium fuit? Nihil ab ea acceperant; igitur etiam nihil aliis dare poterant. Christus tunc Ecclesia Caput fuit, ab illo influxum gratia percepit; inquit Antoninus. Omninò; atque semper Ecclesiam fidelium à Christo, sine Capite alio, sine Papa, sive is jam Scortum, sive scortator sit, influxum gratiæ percipere posse dicimus; Proin tali Papa, per quem influxus gratiæ Christi ad omnes Christianos derivetur, planè opus non est, adeóque Antoninus propria vineta caedit, atque hypothesium, de successionis externæ, ordinis externi, intentionis, maximè autem illam de Pontificis Summi necessitate, absurditatem vel invitus declarat; atque eâdem operâ, magna habere historiam Johannæ Papissæ
units.tr: How, then, was there no harm to salvation from this? She did not absolve from sins; she left everything bound. How then was there no harm to salvation from it? Those ordained by her were not ordained before the reordination, if indeed any followed. What then must be judged about their actions before reordination, and about the actions and state of those baptized or ordained by them, and so on, as it were, to infinity? And how was there no harm to salvation from it? They had received nothing from her; therefore they could give nothing to others either. Christ was then the Head of the Church, from whom she received the influx of grace, says Antoninus. Quite so; and we say that the Church of the faithful can always receive the influx of grace from Christ, without any other head, without a Pope, whether she be now a whore or a whoremonger. Therefore there is really no need for such a Pope, through whom the influx of Christ's grace is conveyed to all Christians; and so Antoninus cuts his own vines, and, though unwillingly, declares the absurdity of the hypotheses of external succession, external order, intention, and above all that concerning the necessity of the Supreme Pontiff; and by the same stroke he has great prejudice against the Romanists from the history of Pope Joan.

units.la: Et quòd exinde multis grave salutis præjudicium fuerit; pissæ contrà Romanenses præjudicia. Quod & clarè docet Abbas Gualdi Vita di D.Olimpia p.406.quamvis contrà nos ostensurus eandē explorationis sexûs in inferioribus Pontificatu gradibus necessitatem: Che farebbe &c. Quid fieret,inquit, de tot Sacerdotibus ab electa ad Pontificatum fœmina ante Pontificatum ordinatis,de tot Parochis,Sacramenta ministrantibus,de tot animabus,qua inde peccatorum absolutionem acceperunt, de tot concessis indulgentiis,de tot Canonicatibus, Dispensationibus & Synodis in Diœcesi habitis? p. 408. ait, Sacerdotes, à tali Episcopo ordinatos comburendos esse. Sed ad ipsum historiæ examen, his ita præmissis, jam progredimur.
units.tr: And that from this great harm to salvation came to many, which the Romanists themselves clearly teach, although the Abbot Gualdi, Vita di D. Olimpia p. 406, wishing to prove against us the same necessity of examining the sex even in the lower grades of the Pontificate, says: Che farebbe &c. What would become, he says, of so many priests ordained before the Pontificate by a woman elected to the papacy, of so many parish priests administering the sacraments, of so many souls who thence received absolution from sins, of so many indulgences granted, of so many canonries, dispensations and synods held in the diocese? p. 408. He says that priests ordained by such a bishop must be burned. But, these things having been thus premised, we now proceed to the examination of the history itself.

units.la: IX. De Authoribus primis, qui eam tanquam veram proposuerint, minimè inter omnes convenit; Atque contendunt ii, qui fabulis narrata adnumerant, neminem ex coætaneis illa scripto consignâsse,certissimúmque in eo falsitatis indicium esse.
units.tr: IX. Concerning the first authors who presented it as true there is by no means full agreement among all; and those who count the story among fables contend that none of the contemporaries recorded it in writing, and that this is a most certain sign of falsehood.

units.la: Ponamus silentium istud; Verum sit,neminem planè ex Scriptoribus illius temporis Johannæ Papissæ mentionem fecisse. Quid inde? An ideò sequitur; Ergò talis Johanna Papissa nunquam in rerum natura fuit? Vix equidem arbitror,quando prægnantes silentii causæ adsunt; Adsunt autem; Res erat omnibus cognita atque in conspectu quasi totius mundi facta,proin à scriptoribus illius temporis paucissimis eò minùs notata,quòd simul turpissima,execranda,atque æterni silentii velo tegenda esset; Neque decebat haud degeneres Romanæ Ecclesiæ filios,quales certè videbuntur Scriptores illi,quorum silentium maximè urgetur,pudenda matris retegere, tanta ejus probra in scriptis suis perennantia optare,Scandala tam gravia secuturis Seculis communicare: quod non nisi cum magno contrà Pontifices suos apud omnes præjudicio fieri posse facilè prævidebant,atque ab aliis saltem posthac factum esse evidentissimè ex præcedentibus patere potest; Atque si Herostrati nomen à Græciæ Scriptoribus ob facinus in Templo Ephesino patratum memoriæ prodi non debuit,certè non minùs Johanna illa,quæ ignem lasciviæ suæ ipsi quasi sancto sanctorum Romanæ Ecclesiæ intulit, perpetuò tacenda illis videbatur. Et si Baronio, ad an. 882. n.8. referente, res (Johannis VIII. sive IX.) gesta desiderantur apud Anastasium (cujus loco Gulielmum ejus Continuatorem ponere debuisset) fortasse prætermissa ob odiosam restitutionem Photii; quid igitur de Johanna tali fœmina dici debet?
