Quid verò magnæ Historiarum parti accideret, si ex silentio Scriptorum coætaneorum ad narrationis falsitatem argumentatio valeret? Quid ipsi Petri, ut pertendunt, Romam institutæ profectioni? Contrà cujus certitudinem non ex qualicunque Scriptorum coætaneorum silentio argumentamur, sed ex silentio divinorum maximè Scriptorum, sed ex silentio, cujus nulla causa assignari posse videtur (dum hic contrarium obtinet;) sed ex silentio, quod contrà multis de causis rumpi debuisset; sed ex silentio, quod iidem Divini Scriptores contrariis facto assertionibus confirmare plané videntur; quæ omnia Dissert. II. prolixè probavimus. Cumprimis autem heic silentium priorum minùs curari deberet, quando posteriores, atque contrà quos exceptio nulla valet, ejus causam dedisse videntur; Quam certè dedisse videtur Sigebertus Gemblacensis (de quo mox) Quare, inquit post turpis facti narrationem, eam inter Pontifices non numerant quidam, ideò nomini (Blondellus; nomine) numerum non facit; Dedisse videtur Martinus Polonus (cujus testimonium etiam paulò post examinabimus) his verbis in Codice excuso: Nec ponitur in Catalogo Summorum Pontificum propter mulieris sexum; Quæ in Codice M. SC. Bibliothecæ Heilbronnensis Cl. Wagenseilius, cui communicatus erat, Dissert. de Pont. Germ. ita extare affirmat: Nec ponitur in Catalogo Sanctorum Pontificum propter muliebris sexûs deformitatem; Dedisse videtur Petrarcha; Non ponitur, inquit in Chronico A. 1487. Florentiæ Italicè excuso, ad an. 855. in Catalogo Pontificum, quia fuit fæmina; Dedisse videtur in eodem sæculo Ranulphus Hygden Polychronici l. 5: dum à nonnullis ob deformitatem facti omissam fuisse notat; Dedisse tandem videtur Guilhelmus Jacobus Egmondensis, prope Alcmariam Monachus, in libro membraneo, qui ante 200. annos scriptus videtur, in rythmis de Johanna ita quoque scribens:
units.tr: Let us grant that silence: suppose that no writer of that time made any mention at all of Pope Joan. What follows from that? Does it follow that such a Joan never existed in the world? I hardly think so, since there are weighty reasons for the silence. And there were such reasons. The affair was known to everyone and had taken place, as it were, in full view of the whole world. For that reason few writers of that age noted it, because it was at once most shameful and loathsome, and ought to be covered by the veil of eternal silence. Nor was it fitting for the sons of the Roman Church, who would certainly appear degenerate, the very writers on whose silence so much weight is placed, to uncover their mother's shame, to wish her great disgraces to endure in their writings, or to hand on such grave scandals to the ages to come. They easily foresaw that this could not be done without great prejudice in the eyes of all against their own Popes, and it is clear from what has gone before that later writers did in fact do this. If the name of Herostratus was not to be handed down to memory by the Greek writers for the crime he committed in the Temple at Ephesus, then surely that Joan, who set fire to her own lust, as it were, to the very holy of holies of the Roman Church, seemed to them to be one who must be passed over in perpetual silence. And if, as Baronius reports at the year 882, number 8, the deeds of John VIII or IX are missing in Anastasius (whom he ought to have put in place of his continuator William), perhaps passed over because of the hateful restoration of Photius, then what should be said about a woman like Joan? And what would happen to the great part of history if an argument against the truth of a narrative could be drawn from the silence of contemporary writers? What of Peter's journey to Rome, which they insist upon? Against its certainty we do not argue from the silence of any contemporary writers at all, but from the silence of the divine Scriptures above all; from a silence for which no cause seems to be assignable (since here the opposite holds); from a silence which in many ways ought to have been broken; from a silence which these same divine writers seem plainly to confirm by contrary assertions. All these points we proved at length in the second Dissertation. Above all, the silence of the earlier writers ought to count for less here, since the later writers, against whom no exception holds, seem to have given the reason for it. Sigebert of Gembloux (of whom more shortly) certainly seems to have given it: after narrating the shameful event, he says, Therefore some do not count her among the popes; for this reason she does not make up a number (Blondel reads "name" for "number"). Martin of Poland seems to have given it too (his testimony we shall also examine a little later), in these words in the printed codex: Nor is she placed in the catalogue of the supreme Popes on account of her sex. In a manuscript of the Heilbronn library, which the learned Wagenseil, to whom it had been communicated, affirms in his Dissertation on the German Popes to read thus: Nor is she placed in the catalogue of the holy Popes on account of the deformity of the female sex. Petrarch seems to have given it too: She is not placed, he says in his Chronicle, printed in Italian at Florence in 1487, at the year 855 in the catalogue of the Popes, because she was a woman. In the same century Ranulf Higden seems to have given it, in book 5 of his Polychronicon, where he notes that by some she was left out on account of the deformity of the deed. Finally, William James of Egmond, a monk near Alkmaar, seems to have given it too, in a parchment book which appears to have been written some 200 years ago, writing in verses about Joan in the same way:

units.la: Quam vis inter spatia Pontificum ponatur, propter sexum.
units.tr: Although he is placed among the popes' list, on account of his sex.

units.la: Nempe idem de Johanna cogitabant omnes, quod alii de Barbarii Philippi Prætoris Romani, de quo l. 3. ff. de off. Præt. quasi successore, cùm homo servilis conditionis verus esse & jure Præturam sustinere haud potuerit. Insuper non erant ex eorum censu Romani ad hoc ævi (verba sunt Doct: Blondelli fabulam quidem esse credentis;) ὧν ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ αἰῶνι αὐτῶν, atque ipsis sempiternâ oblivione delendum nefas dictabat pudor. Cæterùm quoque ex tribus illis coætaneis quasi, quorum silentium in argumentum convertitur, Rhegino PrumienPrumiensis historiam consignare non debuit, utpote qui & alios Pontifices praetermisit, rebus Francorum recensendis unicè intentus. De aliorum silentio vide Blond. Ἀνάγκη. crassiorum Ramundiana tractationis navorum 9. -- 30.
units.tr: Indeed, everyone thought about Joan as others did about Barbarius Philippus, the Roman praetor, mentioned in the third book of the Digest, De officiis praetorum, as if he were a successor, though a man of servile condition could not truly be a praetor nor rightly hold the office. Moreover, the Romans of that age were not, by their own reckoning, of this sort (these are the words of Dr. Blondel, who believes the story is indeed a fable), whose fame lay in their own age [ὧν ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ αἰῶνι αὐτῶν], and shame dictated that the wicked deed should be blotted out by everlasting oblivion. Besides, of those three contemporaries whose silence is turned into an argument, Regino of Prüm should not have been expected to record the history at all, since he also passed over other popes, being intent solely on the affairs of the Franks. On the silence of others, see Blondel, Necessity [Ἀνάγκη], the Ramundian treatise, the thicker part, 9.–30.

units.la: X. Neque tamen adeò certum est, omnes plane tacuisse. Quid enim? Annon admitti debet, aliquot saltem ex scriptoribus illius aevi temporum injuriis atque infortuniis interiisse? Quorum unus & alter forte rem exposuit. Et, an ea senectutis nostrae decrepitae felicitas est, ut omnium, quae in virili aetate, vel initio senectutis gesta, imò etiam scripto consignata sunt, certam ex primis scriptis etiamnum superstitibus notitiam habere queamus? Non certe, atque nobis non licet esse tam felicibus ob hominum malitiam, atque injustitiam, quibus, quando res ab Authoribus vetustis expósita minus cum Ecclesiae suae hypothesibus convenire, ejusque authoritatem atque dignitatem laedere videtur, eam calamo deletorio obscurare, scriptores sic mutilare, castrare, non tantum solenne, sed & pium est & fuit, atque è piis fraudibus, aequè ac fingere, addere ea, quae τῆ ὑπόθεσει δυνάμεν atque finibus suis apta esse judicant atque judicârunt. Neque indignus est, qui de his impiis potiùs impostur is, quàm verò piis fraudibus audiatur in Communione Pontificia de Fratribus maximè suis loquens Author Vitae Patri Pauli Sarpii in editione Italica Venetiis in 12 mo excusa p.90. 91. In tutti i secoli &c. In omnibus seculis, inquit, non defuerunt similes Scriptores pestiferi, qui, ut servirent Curiae (Romanae,) fecerunt tot tractatus sub nomine celebrium Scriptorum & S. Patrum, corruperunt veras narrationes, produxerunt legendas fabulosas, & maximè infecerunt orbem impostur is & infamationibus illorum, quorum opera neque extinguere neque refutare potuerunt. Sed postquam suscitata fuerunt illa ipsa Religiones magis addicta commodis Curia, licentia ista alterandi, corrumpendi, mentiendi, fingendi, calumniandi eò excrevit, ut omnia secula & omnes secta in comparatione eatenus non modò excusari, sed & pro sanctis haberi queant. Subjungit: La confutatione &c. Refutatio difficillima est, & prolixas narrationes requirit; Atque paulò post; talibus propositá esse gran premii & attetamenti, magna pramia & incitamenta; Et quibusdam interjectis; esse tales secundùm verbum vetus, gnaviter impudentes. Patet autem ex circumstantiis manifestissimè, eum per recentiores corruptores, mutilatores, Scriptorum suppositititorum Authores atque calumniatores Loyolitas intelligere; Quos veteribus quibusvis longè pejores pronunpronunciat, sed à quibus p. 197. ad veteres denuò ascendit : Con-fessò, inquit, che quelli essempii &c. Confiteor, ista exempla adeò recentia mihi magna dubia movere de alterationibus & corruptionibus tot narrationum praeteritorum saeculorum, & occultatorum atque tantò post publicatorum, quando soli Fautores Factionum Ecclesiasticorum commoditatem Typographiarum admanus habuerunt, & sine ullo scrupulo commendárunt, aut vituperárunt tot magnos Viros, non studio veritatis, sed tantum, quantum aut faventes aut contrarii fuerunt commodis suis mundanis. Atque de Jesuitis etiam Laurentius Bochellus Advocatus Parlamenti Parisiensis Pontificius in Praefat. Decret. Eccles. Gallic. exclamat: Quis falsationes fraudulentorum istorum hominum commemoret? Dies me deficiet potius, quàm exempla. Quin per versitatem suam produnt Romanenses atque authoritate etiam muniunt, Indicum Expurgatorum, sive Romanorum, sive Hispanorum, editionibus, qui uno nunc volumine comprehenduntur, & Apocalypsin Mysterii Iniquitatis manifestam continent, quáque declarant, nullum veri honestíque amorem apud se superesse, seque incorrigibiles aliàs, corrigere nunc atque tanquam falsa dissimulare, constanter olim credita.
units.tr: X. Yet it is not so certain that they all kept silent. For what? Must we not admit that at least some writers of that age perished through the injuries and misfortunes of the times, and that one or another may have set the matter forth? And is our present decrepit old age so fortunate that we can have certain knowledge, from the earliest writings still surviving, of everything that was done in manhood or at the beginning of old age, or even committed to writing? Certainly not. Nor are we permitted to be so fortunate, because of human malice and injustice. For when a matter related by ancient authors seems less in agreement with the hypotheses of their Church, and seems to damage its authority and dignity, it has been not only customary but also thought pious to obscure it with an erasing pen, to mutilate and castrate the writers in this way, and, among pious frauds, equally to invent and add whatever they judge and have judged suitable to their hypothesis and aims. Nor is the author who speaks of these impious impostures rather than pious frauds in the Papal communion, speaking above all of his own brethren, unworthy of a hearing: the author of the Life of Father Paolo Sarpi, in the Italian edition printed at Venice in duodecimo, pages 90 and 91. In tutti i secoli &c. In all ages, he says, there were never lacking pestilent writers of the same kind who, to serve the Court (of Rome), produced so many treatises under the names of famous writers and Holy Fathers, corrupted true narratives, brought forth fabulous legends, and above all infected the world with the impostures and defamations of those whose works they could neither extinguish nor refute. But after those very religious orders became more devoted to the conveniences of the Court, this licence of altering, corrupting, lying, inventing, and slandering grew to such a degree that, in comparison, all ages and all sects can not only be excused but even be held to be holy. He adds: La confutatione &c. Refutation is most difficult, and requires long narratives; and a little later: for such men there is set out great reward and encouragement, great prizes and incitements; and after some intervening words: such men are according to the old saying, boldly shameless. It is clear from the circumstances that he means by the recent corruptors, mutilators, forgers of spurious writings and calumniators the Jesuits of Loyola. He pronounces them far worse than any of the ancients, yet from these he climbs back again to the ancients, at page 197: I confess, he says, that those examples, so recent, raise in me great doubts about the alterations and corruptions of so many narratives of past ages, and of those hidden away and published much later, when only the partisans of ecclesiastical factions had the convenience of printing presses at hand, and praised or disparaged so many great men without any scruple, not from a zeal for truth, but only as far as they were favourable or hostile to their worldly interests. And about the Jesuits too, the Papist Laurent Bochel, advocate of the Parisian Parlement, in the Preface to the Decrees of the Gallican Church, cries out: Who could recount the falsifications of those fraudulent men? The days would fail me sooner than the examples. Indeed, the Romanists betray themselves by their own publication, and even lend it authority, in the editions of the Index of Prohibited Books, both Roman and Spanish, which are now comprehended in a single volume, and which contain a plain Apocalypse of the Mystery of Iniquity. In it they declare that no love of truth or honesty survives among them, and that they now correct, and dissemble as false, what they constantly believed in the past, though otherwise incorrigible.

units.la: XI. Quis autem neget, & non potiùs, juxta praecedentia, credat, etiam Spiritum Jesuiticum in aliquo saltem inferiori gradu alios ante Jesuitas agitâsse? Et quis non credat, Monarchiae Papalis erectores atque confirmatores primos in mala sua causa etiam ad Authorum, quoad ejus fieri poterat (multùm autem ob temporum injurias, ignorantiam, negligentiam, Typographiae defectum, atque contradicentium in Occidente paucitatem ignobilitatémque, Deo permittente, fieri poterat;) corruptionem delapsos esse? Atque in specie etiam multa, quae prae caeteris odiosa erant atque expungi poterant, expunxisse? Quis non videt, multa nos ipsis odiosa nunc nescire debere, saltem quatenus à primis Authoribus tradita fuerunt? Et quis non videt, inter ista odiosa historiam de Johanna Papissa vel primo loco collocari debere?
units.tr: XI. Who would deny, or rather, in view of what has gone before, who would not believe, that even before the Jesuits some spirit of Jesuitry was at work, at least in a lesser degree? And who would not believe that the first founders and defenders of the Papal monarchy, in their bad cause, corrupted the authors as far as they could? (This was possible, by God's permission, largely because of the troubles of the times, ignorance, carelessness, the lack of printing, and the scarcity and obscurity of opponents in the West.) And who would not believe that they removed many things that were especially offensive and could be removed? Who does not see that we ought now to be ignorant of many things that are offensive to us, at least insofar as they were handed down by the first authors? And who does not see that, among these offensive matters, the story of Pope Joan must be placed first of all?

units.la: XII. Sed & fraudis certa indicia adsunt, saltem quoad Anastasii Codices, (de Adone Viennensi mox respondebimus;) dum ipso Doctissimo Blondello, qui hac in quaestione in Pontificiorum castra transiit, vel, ut nonnulli (ex. gr. Cl. Hofmannus in Lexici T. I. sol. 841. 6.) volunt, ingenii exercitandi gratiâ se transisse simulavit, p. 45. teste, vetustiores Manuscripti in Galliae, Germaniae, Italiae, Hispaniae, Britanniae, Belgii &c. Bibliothecis reconditi Codices dices omnes circa finem Leonis IV. mutili reperiuntur. Quæ certè mutilatio Codicum tam universalis in Monasteriis, aliísque Bibliothecis Pontificiis servatorum, nisi ipsius sedis Romanæ authoritate perpetrari non potuisse videtur; Neque desunt, qui Gregorium VII. Criminis reum peragant.
units.tr: XII. There are also clear signs of fraud, at least as regards the Codices of Anastasius (we will answer about Ado of Vienne shortly). The most learned Blondel, who in this question went over to the Papist camp, or, as some (for example, the honourable Hofmann in his Lexicon, vol. I, col. 841, no. 6) think, pretended that he had gone over for the sake of exercising his wits, testifies at p. 45 that the older manuscript codices kept in the libraries of France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Britain, Belgium and elsewhere all break off near the end of Leo IV. Such a universal mutilation of codices preserved in monasteries and other papal libraries seems impossible to have been carried out except by the authority of the Roman see itself. Nor are there lacking those who charge Gregory VII with the crime.

units.la: XIII. Ut neque desunt, qui, an non plures Anastasii in unum constati sint, qualis ille fuerit, ubi cœperit, ubi desierit, cum Cl. Maresio Papiss. restit. p. 28. seqq. dubitant, neque, qui historiam illam Anastasii ex editione Jesuitarum Moguntinensium A. Chr. 1602. hodie extantem, atque A. Chr. 1649. Lutetiæ recusam, scriptum suppositititium esse arguunt, utpote quod multa omittit, quæ in aliis Codicibus habentur, quod idem Cl. Maresi. l. c. p.30.31. ostendit; sed ex stylo potissimùm cum Anastasiano, qualis in genuinis ejus scriptis appareat, minimè conveniente, minùs etiam cum elogio Anastasii, quòd, testibus Sabellico Ennead. 9. l. 1. p. 327. & Trithemio de Script. Eccles. Græcè & Latinè impensè doctus, Græco & Latino multùm peritus eloquio fuerit; & cum munere à Papa Nicolao ei demandato, ut nimirum viam Johannis Eleemosynarii Græcè scriptam in Idioma Latinum verteret; conveniente; cùm contrà ipsi Jesuitæ in opere à se edito Præf. ad Lect. non semel stylum rudem & agrestem notent, atque se loco movisse barbarismos & solæcismos, qui citra Cachinnum legi non poterant.
units.tr: XIII. Nor are there lacking those who doubt how many Anastasii there were, whether they were combined into one, what he was like, where he began and where he ended, following the honourable Maresius in Papiss. restit., p. 28 ff.; nor those who argue that the history of Anastasius now extant in the Jesuits' edition of Mainz of 1602, and reprinted at Paris in 1649, is a spurious writing, since it omits much that is found in other codices, as the same honourable Maresius shows in l. c. p. 30, 31. They argue this chiefly from its style, which does not agree well with the genuine writings of Anastasius, and still less with the praise of Anastasius, that he was, as Sabellicus in Ennead. 9, l. 1, p. 327 and Trithemius testify, thoroughly learned in Greek and Latin, and much skilled in the Greek and Latin tongue, nor with the task Pope Nicholas entrusted to him, namely to translate John the Almoner's work from Greek into Latin. For the Jesuits themselves, in their own edition, in the Preface to the Reader, more than once note the rude and rustic style, and admit that they had altered barbarisms and solecisms, which could not be read without laughter.

units.la: XIV. Cæterùm in nonnullis Codicibus Anastasii Johannæ historiam reperiri extra dubium esse debet, postquam illud Viri Doctissimi à parte altera stantes ingenuè fassi atque testati sunt. Vidit talem Codicem Lutetiæ in Bibliotheca Regia antiquissimum Maresius, ut ipse refert Refut. Apol. Curcell. p. 223. neque inficias it Blondellus, licèt non ex illa parte nostrer p,47. seqq. ἀναχρ. Quæst. Famos. De nonnullis largitur quoque Launojus I. V. Epist. ult. Atque jam ab aliis proditum est, quomodo Illustris Salmasius Eruditissimo Bœclero, qui de his Comment de rebus Sec. IX. & X. agit, atque ipse etiam narrat, fuerit testatus; se Heidelbergæ agente atque in comparabili, qualis tunc ibi erat, Bibliothecæ operam dante, Jesuitas Moguntinos Anastasium ediuros duos Codices MSS. à Serenissimo Electore petiisse, accepisse, atque remissis aliquot exemplaria Editionis suæ, in quibus Johannæ Historia bonâ fide expressa fuerit, adjunxisse, eâ tamen in aliis exemplaribus omissâ. Ait quidem Doctiss. Launojus l. c. esse illos Codices Anastasianos, qui de Johanna agant, recenti manu scriptos; plane aliis tales Codices dari negantibus; atque vidisse se exemplar testatur tempore Concilii Constantiensis scriptum; verùm non ideò, cùm nemo ostendere queat, ad exemplaria vetustiora Codices illos non effórmatos fuisse, omnis illis deneganda est authoritas, atque, juxta ea, quæ dicta sunt, facilius concipitur, è multis Codicibus antiquis erasam fuisse, quàm verò in aliis sine antiquiorum manuductione, additam; facilius concipitur, Martinum Polonum aliósque sua ex Anastasio contexuisse, cùm fere eadem cum Anastasio, quæ exhibentur, verba retinuerit, quibusdam, quæ ex aliis antiquis instructissimæ Vaticanæ Bibliothecæ Codicibus habere potuit, additis; ac ex Martino Polono (quod Blondellus p. 51. pertendit; ) in Anastasium hanc historiam fuisse translatam. Ado Viennensis autem, si ipse siluit, idem cum Anastasio, si & ipse siluit, eum secutus ex eadem causa fecisse dici debet; Ast optimè Cl. Maresius l. c. p. 25. seqq. & Cl. Megerlinus l. c. arguunt, eum ad. annum 840. tantùm opus suum perduxisse, atque adeò verba de Leone & Benedicto Continuatoris cujusdam esse debent.
units.tr: XIV. Moreover, it must be beyond doubt that the story of Joan is found in some codices of Anastasius, since the most learned men on the other side have freely confessed and testified this. Maresius saw such a codex at Paris in the Royal Library, as he reports in Refut. Apol. Curcell., p. 223; Blondel does not deny it, though he does not take our side in p. 47 ff., ἀναχρ., Quaest. Famos. Launoy also grants it in part, in I. V, Epist. ult. And it has already been reported by others how the illustrious Salmasius, when he was testifying to the most learned Boecler, who treats these matters in his Comment. de rebus Sec. IX. & X. (and he himself narrates it), said that while he was working at Heidelberg, in the library there, which was then remarkable, the Jesuits of Mainz, who were about to publish Anastasius, asked the most serene Elector for two manuscript codices, received them, and, after returning some copies of their edition, added them, with the story of Joan faithfully printed in them, though it was omitted in other copies. Indeed, the most learned Launoy in the same place says that those Anastasian codices which deal with Joan were written by a recent hand, while others deny that such codices exist at all; and he testifies that he saw a copy written at the time of the Council of Constance. But it does not follow that, since no one can show that those codices were not copied from older exemplars, all authority must be denied them. According to what has been said, it is easier to conceive that the story was erased from many ancient codices than that it was added in others without the guidance of older ones. It is easier to conceive that Martin of Poland composed his work from Anastasius, since he kept almost the same words that Anastasius gives, adding some things he could have had from other ancient codices in the well-stocked Vatican Library, and that this history was translated from Martin of Poland into Anastasius (which Blondel contends at p. 51). As for Ado of Vienne, if he himself was silent, and followed Anastasius, who was also silent, he must be said to have done so for the same reason. But the honourable Maresius, in l. c. p. 25 ff., and the honourable Megerlin, in l. c., rightly argue that he brought his work down only to the year 840, and therefore the words about Leo and Benedict must belong to some continuator.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Præter tres allatos primis ducentis annis Johannæ quoque mentionem facere debuisse volunt, ex Orientalibus quidem Cedrenum, Curopalatem, Zonaram, quos tamen suis rebus occupatos Pontificum Romanorum successionem neglexisse nemini mirum videri deberet; Ex Occidentalibus autem Hermannum Contractum atque Schafnaburgensem; Sed qui eandem cum Anastasio & reliquis tacendi causam habuerunt, atque insuper ex illius Chronico, cujus exemplaria plurimùm discrepant, facilè etiam Johanna eradi potuit, cui tamen locus, saltem juxta exemplar Coloniense, superest; De quo vide Mares. Pap. Restit. p. 39. seqq. Schafnaburgensis autem Pontifices non seriatim recensuit, sed & alios omisit.
units.tr: Besides the three already cited, they want her to have been mentioned in the first two hundred years as well: among the Orientals, Cedrenus, Curopalates and Zonaras. It should surprise no one that these men, being occupied with their own affairs, neglected the succession of the Roman Pontiffs. Among the Westerners they name Hermannus Contractus and the Schafnaburgensis. But these had the same reason for silence as Anastasius and the rest. Moreover, from his Chronicle, whose copies differ greatly, Joan could easily have been erased, though a place for her remains, at least in the Cologne copy. On this see Maresius, Pap. Restit. p. 39 ff. The Schafnaburgensis did not list the Pontiffs in order, and he also omitted some of them.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Afferri quidem solet ex ducentis illis annis Radulphus Flaviacensis, Benedictini Ordinis Monachus, Vir, elogio Joh. Trithemii, in Divinis Scripturis eruditissimus & in omnibus literis humanitatis suo tempore Doctissimus, qui, eodem Trithemio de Script. Eccles. p. 259. notante, atque Bellarmino aliísque adstipulantibus, jam circa an. 910. floruit, juxta hanc calculationem 60. tantùm annis Johannâ recentior; Verùm, si ipsius est Commentarius in Leviticum libris 20. comprehensus, ut ipsius esse dicitur & apud Genebrardum dum Chronol. sua l. 4. ex l. 29. c. 1. constare, quòd decimo seculo floruerit; Sique ipsius quoque sunt verba omnia lib. 18. c. 1. sequentia: Antichristus de Regibus triumphabit, hoc est, pedibus suis subjiciet eos: testis Ludovicus II. Imperator & Edelvvolphus Rex Anglorum à Johanne VIII. coronati, & Fridericus ( Barbarossa nimirum ) quem pedibus calcavit alius Papa; demum seculi decimi tertii, aut decimi quarti Scriptor fuit, cùm Edelvvolphus quidem & Ludovicus Johannae coaetanei fuerint, Fridericus vero ille demum Seculo XIII. imperárit.
units.tr: It is commonly alleged from those two hundred years Radulph of Flavigny, a monk of the Benedictine Order, a man whom Johannes Trithemius praises as most learned in the Divine Scriptures and the most learned of his time in all the humane letters. According to Trithemius (De Script. Eccles. p. 259) and with the support of Bellarmine and others, he flourished about the year 910, which by this reckoning is only sixty years later than Joan. But if the Commentary on Leviticus in twenty books, which is said to be his and which is included in Genebrardus' Chronology, book 4, is his, then from book 29, chapter 1 it is clear that he flourished in the tenth century. And if all the following words in book 18, chapter 1 are also his: Antichrist will triumph over kings, that is, he will subject them to his feet; witnesses are Ludwig II, Emperor, and Edelwolf, King of the English, crowned by John VIII, and Frederick (Barbarossa, of course) whom another Pope trampled underfoot, then he was a writer of the late thirteenth or fourteenth century. Edelwolf and Ludwig were contemporaries of Joan, but that Frederick reigned only in the thirteenth century.

units.la: XVII. Certa autem est, licet aliquanto minor dicatur authoritas, certum quoq; testimonium Mariani Scoti, Monachi quoque Benedictini Ordinis. Vixit seculo XI. natus, ut ipse in Chronico refert A. Chr. 1028. Sunt autem ejus verba sequentia: Anno DCCCLIII. Leo Papa obiit Kal. August. Huic successit Johanna mulier, annis II. mensibus V. diebus IV. Ut male Onuphrius, atque, qui eum sequitur, Bellarminus, dicant, primum Martinum Polonum, qui quadringentis annis post tempora Johannae assignari solita vixerit, fabulae auctorem esse. Licet enim Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. l. 3. c. 24. pertendat, verba haec in antiquissimis manuscriptis non reperiri: & satis constare, auctores illos corruptos fuisse; non tamen est, cur quisquam eo moveatur. Expressa enim exemplaria, Johannis Pistorii, Niddani, atque Basileense, quod ad imitationem illius est, quod ex libraria Collegii S. Bartholomaei Francofurtensis, Episcopi Moguntini jussu prodiit; non tam facile fidem suam amittere possunt, sola Codicum, quos aliter habentes exhibere non possunt, jactantia, nudaque, quòd Editores, aut alii Auctorum verba interpolaverint & corruperint, sine testibus, vel argumentis ( cur enim ullus id fecisset, haud liquet; ) adsertione, neque etiam ulla ex Editionibus impressis aliter habet, neque ullam ex fide manuscripti alicujus quasi emendare audent, atque eo modo certè omnem historiam dubiam reddere possent. Certè Baronius, qui suum X. Annalium, diu post Bellarmini primum Controversiarum Tomum edidit, Mariano Scoto memorationem Johannae abjudicare ausus non fuit, licet, ut authoritatem testis quodam saltem modo elevaret, ad an. 853. n. 60. dixerit, in scripto Codice, ex quo prodierit prima editio, aliter legi, nempe Johannes, qui, ut asseritur, fuit mulier. Quaë tamen Martini Poloni verba sunt; sed, posito, Mariano quoque suam erga sedem Romanam reverentiam, quam certè maximam fuisse constat,ista aliquo modo dubitantis verba extorsisse,nondum tamen ideò ejus testimonium de re cum omnibus temporis circumstantiis consignata,nullum erit. Verùm nec Codices,qui illud; ut asseritur; habeant, exhibentur, nec etiam concipi potest,cur Editores verba in exemplari, quod secuti dicuntur, addita,non etiam addidissent,cùm Martini Poloni Editor addiderit,quia in Codice suo invenit.
units.tr: XVII. The testimony of Marianus Scotus, also a Benedictine monk, is certain, though its authority is said to be somewhat lesser. He lived in the eleventh century, born, as he himself reports in his Chronicle, in the year 1028. His words are as follows: In the year 853 Pope Leo died on the Kalends of August. He was succeeded by the woman Joan, for two years, five months and four days. Onuphrius, and Bellarmine, who follows him, wrongly say that Martin of Poland, who is usually assigned to a time four hundred years after Joan, was the author of this fable. For although Bellarmine (De Rom. Pont. bk. 3, ch. 24) contends that these words are not found in the most ancient manuscripts, and that it is well established those authors were corrupted, there is no reason for anyone to be moved by this. The printed editions of Johannes Pistorius, of Nidda, and the Basel edition, which follows it, and which was published by order of the Bishop of Mainz from the library of the College of St Bartholomew at Frankfurt, cannot easily lose their credibility. The mere boast of manuscripts, which they cannot produce when they hold otherwise, and the bare assertion, without witnesses or arguments, that editors or others have interpolated and corrupted the words of the authors (for why anyone should have done so is not clear), cannot be believed. No printed edition has a different reading, and they dare not correct it from any manuscript; in that way they could make every doubtful history suspect. Certainly Baronius, who published his tenth volume of the Annals long after the first volume of Bellarmine's Controversies, did not dare to deny Marianus Scotus the mention of Joan. Yet to weaken the witness's authority somewhat, he said at year 853, no. 60, that in the written codex from which the first edition came, it was read otherwise, namely John, who, as is asserted, was a woman. These, however, are the words of Martin of Poland. But even granting that Marianus, out of his well-known and very great reverence for the Roman See, was forced into these words of doubt, his testimony about a matter recorded with all the circumstances of the time will not for that reason be void. Yet neither are the codices which contain as is asserted produced, nor can it be conceived why the editors, who are said to have followed a copy, would not themselves have added the words, since the editor of Martin of Poland added them because he found them in his codex.

units.la: XVIII. Mariani autem hac in parte magna apud omnes esse debet authoritas; Fuit teste Trithemio,ut ex eo habet Guilhelmus Eisengreinius Scriptor Pontificius,qui Marianum etiam Sancti elogio insignit,in Catal.testium Veritatis; Vir omni doctrinarum genere clarus,Philosophus insignis,Poëta gravis,Historicus celeberrimus,Theologorum illa ætate nulli secundus; teste Sigeberto Gemblacensi in Chron ad an.1061. Chronographus antiquus & clarus; Scripsit, judice Bellarmino de Script. Eccl. ad an 1083. historiam universalem satis diligenter; De eruditione autem præter Chronicon etiam testatur Commentarius in Psalmos; & de tali quidem eruditione,quæ longè ultra seculi,quod sui asperitate ac boni sterilitate Ferreum,malíque exundantis deformitate Plumbeum,atque inopia Scriptorum, teste Baronio ad an.900. n.1. appellari consuevit obscurum,genium, ut eò minùs mirari quis jure posset, si hic primus in ista Scriptorum inopia & rerum omnium confusione atque obscuritate Johannæ meminisset; Neque etiam odio in sedem Papalem,cui ubique addictissimus apparet,hæc scripsisse dici potest,neque scripsisse sine fundamento atque tanquam araneus ex sese confinxisse circumstantias etiam temporis,sed in tribus Benedictinorum contubernìis, Colonien si, Fuldensi, & Moguntinensi vivens, ex vetustissimis illorum & aliorum Cœnobiorum libris, qui fallere non possunt,suum Chronicon collegit,prout etiam in vestibulo operis sui recensét,ex quorum monumentis illud congesserit, talibus nempe, quæ vel temporum hominúmque injuriâ interiere,vel alicubi pulvere operta & à blattis arrosa latent; Atque in Fuldensi maximè tunc instructissima Bibliotheca,Codices hodie non amplius extantes invenire potuit, & sine dubio secutus est.
units.tr: XVIII. The authority of Marianus in this matter should be great with everyone. According to Trithemius, as Guilielmus Eisengrein, a Papist writer, reports from him in his Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth, which also honours Marianus with the title Saint, he was a man distinguished in every kind of learning, a notable philosopher, a grave poet, a most famous historian, second to no theologian of his age. According to Sigebert of Gembloux in his Chronicle, at the year 1061, he was an ancient and famous chronographer. He wrote, according to Bellarmine's judgment in De Script. Eccl. at the year 1083, a universal history with sufficient care. Besides the Chronicle, his Commentary on the Psalms also attests his learning. And he belonged to that learned age, which, by the testimony of Baronius at the year 900, no. 1, is commonly called obscure on account of its harshness, its barrenness of good, its leaden deformity of overflowing evil, and its poverty of writers. So no one could rightly wonder that he was the first to mention Joan in that poverty of writers and that confusion and obscurity of all things. Nor can it be said that he wrote this out of hatred for the Papal See, to which he everywhere appears most devoted, nor that he wrote without foundation, or invented the circumstances, even of time, like a spider out of himself. Living in three Benedictine houses, at Cologne, Fulda and Mainz, he gathered his Chronicle from the very ancient books of those and other monasteries, which cannot deceive. In the introduction to his work he lists the records from which he compiled it, namely those which have perished through the injury of time and men, or lie hidden somewhere covered with dust and gnawed by bookworms. And at Fulda, which then had a very well-stocked library, he could find codices no longer extant today, and without doubt he followed them.

units.la: XIX. Eodem cum Mariano Scoto seculo XI. nimirum, sed circa finem floruit Sigebertus Gemblacensis,Vir,judicio Trithemii I. cit. p. 270. multùm eruditus atque in saecularibus literis nulli suo tempore Leodiensium territorio secundus; hic in Chronico ad an.854. & quidem in Editione Parisiensi anni 1513. adeóque triennio antequam Lutheri tanquam Reformatoris nomen in orbe auditum fuisset, facta Johannæ etiam meminit. Cùm verò eadem contrà Sigebertum excipiant, quæ contrà Marianum, eædem quoque hunc jam vindicârunt responsiones.
units.tr: XIX. In the same century as Marianus Scotus, the eleventh, though towards its end, flourished Sigebert of Gembloux, a man, according to Trithemius (loc. cit. p. 270), very learned, and in secular letters second to none in his time in the territory of Liège. In his Chronicle, at the year 854, and indeed in the Paris edition of 1513, and so three years before the name of Luther had been heard in the world as a Reformer, he also mentions Joan. But since the same objections are raised against Sigebert as against Marianus, the same answers have already vindicated him.

units.la: XX. Seculo XII. vixit Godefridus Viterbiensis Presbyter, qui peregrinatione XL. annorum, in qua omnes ferme excussit Bibliothecas, magnam sibi eruditionem paravit. Hic quoque in suo Chronico Universali, quo nominis sui famam longè diffudit, ipsi Urbano III. Pontifici dicato Papissam nominat & admittit, sed inter Pontifices non numerandam esse ait, propter facti ignominiam. Sub medium illius seculi quoque scripsit Otto Frisingensis, ad cujus silentium pariter provocant, cùm tamen nec ille omnes Pontifices enumeret, atque Catalogus libro VII. subjunctus pro Editorum arbitrio variare deprehendatur, atque alicubi in lib. 8. Johanna numero VII. habeatur.
units.tr: XX. In the twelfth century lived Godfrey of Viterbo, a priest, who by a pilgrimage of forty years, in which he searched almost all the libraries, acquired great learning. He too, in his universal Chronicle, which spread the fame of his name far and wide, names and admits Joan as Papess, dedicating it to Pope Urban III; but he says she is not to be numbered among the Popes, on account of the shamefulness of the fact. In the middle of that century Otto of Freising also wrote, and they likewise appeal to his silence, although he too does not enumerate all the Popes, and the catalogue appended to his seventh book is found to vary according to the editors' judgment; and somewhere in book 8 Joan is counted as the seventh.

units.la: XXI. Sequenti Seculo XIII. extitit Martinus Polonus, Cistertiensis Monachus, Consentinus Archiepiscopus, & Innocentii IV. Pœnitentiarius, quem quidem Martinum Polonum Bellarminus, tanquam Virum Simplicissimum & fabularum (hujus quoque primum) Scriptorem traducit; quales Archiepiscopos atque Pœnitentiarios creari quis credidisset? Sed is Chronicon, Bibliothecâ Vaticanâ tanquam Pœnitentiarius instructus, in quo res gestas Pontificum & Imperatorum breviter ad sua usque tempora prosequitur, doctissimè collegit, in quo etiam Johannæ historiam graphicè & latè depingit. Cùm tamen nec ille causas, maximè cum tanto circumstantiarum numero rem fingendi, aut facilè credendi habuisse videatur. Quòd autem nonnulli sive dubitant, sive negant, vel Martinum aliquid de Johanna scripsisse, sed à posterioribus, hæreticis ut Leoni Allatio Comment. de Johanna visum fuit, Martiniano Chronico totum hoc, quod displicet, innexum esse, hinc antiquissimum Romæ Codicem Martinianum nullam plane Johannæ mentionem habere; illud non tanti æstimandum videtur; Quando enim Pontificii vetustiores & ex recentioribus plurimi indubitatâ fide crediderunt & pro certo tradiderunt, Martinum vel primum, vel post alios Johannæ mentionem facere, dubium esse nequit, quin illis temporibus, quæ Reformationem præcesserunt, Manuscripta Martini historiam hanc habuerint; quam & edita exemplaria habent bent ad unum omnia, & proin nemo nisi profligati pudoris reus,sunt verba ipsius Blondelli Αναχεφαλαιωσεως p. 14. negaverit; undecunque decantata Manuscriptorum Codicum corruptela manasse dicantur, Protestantibus longè postquam in ipso Romana Ecclesia sinu à summa dignationis viris publicè recepta, publico patrocinio defensa sunt, natis, ac deinceps à maxima Bibliothecarum parte exclusis, nequaquam eas imputari nisi per summam injuriam posse. Sed neque ab aliis, Pontificiis nimirum ante Reformationem, Codices, quoad insertam Johannæ historiam, corruptos esse, ullo modo verisimile est; atque, quando tum ex iis, quæ n. 19. à nobis dicta sunt, tum etiam ex iis, quæ Eruditissimus Naudæus contrà Benedictinos circa libros de Imitatione Christi scripsit, constat, quàm parum Manuscriptis, quæ in Papatu vulgò jactantur, deferendum, & quàm Monachis, Jesuitis maximè, familiare sit, quælibet in rem suam vel fingere, vel interpolare; neque nobis desunt Codices antiquissimi etiam Martiniani, qui Johannæ historiam habent. Dicendum potiùs, unum illum, qui Romæ ostentatur, Codicem à cæteris omnibus dissentientem malâ malorum fraude corruptum atque quoad illam partem supposittitium esse.
units.tr: XXI. In the following thirteenth century arose Martin of Poland, a Cistercian monk, Archbishop of Cosenza and penitentiary of Innocent IV. Bellarmine presents this Martin of Poland as a most simple man and a writer of fables (the first of them, indeed). Who would have believed that such men were made archbishops and penitentiaries? But he, equipped with the Vatican Library as penitentiary, compiled very learnedly a Chronicle, in which he briefly follows the deeds of the Popes and Emperors down to his own times, and in which he also paints the history of Joan vividly and at length. Yet he does not seem to have had any reason for inventing or easily believing a thing, especially with so many circumstances. As for some who either doubt or deny that Martin wrote anything about Joan, and who think that this whole part which displeases was attached to the Martinian Chronicle by later heretics, as Leo Allatius thought in his Commentary on Joan, and who therefore hold that the most ancient Martinian codex at Rome has no mention of Joan at all: this does not seem worth much. For when the older Papists, and many of the more recent ones, believed with undoubted faith and firmly handed down that Martin mentioned Joan, either first or after others, there can be no doubt that in the times which preceded the Reformation the manuscripts of Martin contained this history; and all the printed copies have it without exception. Hence no one but a defendant of abandoned shame, these are the words of Blondel in his Anacephalaiosis p. 14, would deny it. Whatever is said of the widely sung corruption of manuscript codices, it cannot be imputed to the Protestants, who were born long after the work was publicly received and defended under public patronage by men of the highest dignity in the very bosom of the Roman Church, and who were afterwards excluded from the greatest part of the libraries, without the greatest injustice. Yet it is by no means probable that the codices were corrupted with regard to the inserted history of Joan by the other Papists before the Reformation. Since it is established both from what we have said at no. 19, and from what the most learned Naudé wrote against the Benedictines concerning the books On the Imitation of Christ, how little credit should be given to the manuscripts which are commonly boasted of in Papacy, and how familiar it is to monks, especially Jesuits, to invent or interpolate whatever they please for their own purposes. Nor do we lack most ancient codices, even Martinian ones, which contain the history of Joan. It must rather be said that the one codex displayed at Rome, which differs from all the others, was corrupted by the evil fraud of wicked men and is spurious in that part.

units.la: XXII. Cum Martino & post Martinum per secula sequentia eandem historiam non tantùm quoque crediderunt, sed & scriptis consignârunt, innumeri ferè, & non, ut Ludovicus Richeomius Jesuita sub persona Florimundi Ræmundi Senatoris Burdegalensis, (de quo cæterùm Burdegalæ & in tota Gallia jactabatur; Judicat sine conscientia, libros scribit sine scientia, ædificat sine pecunia;) in libello, cui titulus: Popularis error de Johanna Papissa c. 17. §. 5. impudenter mentitus est; Soli Germani Johanna meminerunt, nulli Franci, Hispani, Angli, Itali, Graeci, Judaei in partes veniunt &c. Sed præter Germanos & Francos & Itali & Hispani & Angli & Scotus & Belga & Polonus & Ungarus & Judæi & Græci; atque ex his Barlaam Monachus, qui c. an. 1300. floruisse, licet de ætate ejus non constet, nonnullis dicitur, homo (elogio Boccatii) corpore pusillus, pragrandis tamen scientiâ & Græcis eruditissimus de Prim. Pap. c. 14. τὴ ἀχολάσει γυναικὶ τῇ γενομένῃ πάπᾳ impudica illius muliercula, qua Papa facta fuit, mentionem faciens; nec non Laonicus Chalcocondylas, qui ad an. 1460. refertur, lib.7. de rebus Turcicis, à Conrado Clausero, Tigurino, Latinitate donatus, cujus pericopam illam non ut Ræmundus & Baronius clamant, Interpretis fraude in textum Latinum irrepsisse, partim ex Textu Græco, qui
units.tr: XXII. Not only did Martin, and after Martin through the following centuries, believe this same story, but they also committed it to writing. Almost countless writers did so, and not only in the way that Ludovicus Richeomius the Jesuit did under the name of Florimundus Raemundus, a senator of Bordeaux. (About that Raemundus it was said in Bordeaux and throughout all of Gaul: "He judges without conscience, writes books without knowledge, and builds without money.") In a little book titled Popular Error concerning Pope Joan, ch. 17, §5, he shamelessly lied: Only the Germans remember Joan; no French, Spanish, English, Italians, Greeks or Jews come into it, etc. But besides Germans, French, Italians, Spanish, English, Scots, Belgians, Poles, Hungarians, Jews and Greeks, there is also the monk Barlaam, who is said by some to have flourished around 1300, although his date is not certain. In On the First Popes, ch. 14, he is described (in Boccaccio's praise) as a man small in body but very great in learning, and the most learned of the Greeks, and he mentions "the shameless little woman who became pope" [τὴ ἀχολάσει γυναικὶ τῇ γενομένῃ πάπᾳ]. There is also Laonicus Chalcocondylas, who is dated to the year 1460, in book 7 of On Turkish Affairs, translated into Latin by Conrad Clauser of Zurich. Raemundus and Baronius cry out that his passage crept into the Latin text through the translator's fraud, but it is in part supported by the Greek text, which

units.la: Testimonia plurimorum ex omnibus ferè Nationibus, co,qui habetur, partim etiam ex eo,quòd, vindicante à calumnia corruptionis pro existentia Johannæ Clauserum ipso Blondello, l. c. p. 75. sciens prudens,qua in Graco exemplari displicebant, tanquam sedi Romanæ nimis ignominiosa,vertendo resecuit. Ut ex omni fere gente historia hæc testes habeat, quorum magnam partem apud ipsum Doctiss. Blondellum Avaxe. p. 3. seqq. Wolfium Lect. Memorab. cent. 9. à p. 176-189. Gerhardum in Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. part. 1. c. 4. p. 629. seqq. & apud Clar. Maresium Pap. Restit. p. 11. & apud Clar. Megerlinum Comment. Chronol. in Tab. Matth. Hist. c. 13. videre est;
units.tr: is extant. It is also supported partly by the fact that Blondel himself, defending Clauser against the charge of corruption in favour of the existence of Joan, admits that the translator knowingly and deliberately cut out, in translating, what displeased him in the Greek copy as too disgraceful to the Roman see. So this history has witnesses from almost every nation. A great many of them can be seen in the most learned Blondel, Avaxe, p. 3 ff.; in Wolf, Lect. Memorab., cent. 9, pp. 176–189; in Gerhard, Confess. Cath., l. 2, spec. part 1, c. 4, p. 629 ff.; in the distinguished Maresius, Pap. Restit., p. 11; and in the distinguished Megerlin, Comment. Chronol. in Tab. Matth., Hist. c. 13.

units.la: XXIII. Testes non tantùm inferioris, ut ajunt, subsellii, sed clara inter Eruditos, magna inter Ecclesiasticos nomina; Testes ipsos Pontifices,illos certè omnes tacitos,qui dum fabula,quam faciunt alii,tanta cum ordinis sui ignominia, tanto cum scandalo pro re verè gesta publicè & ab omnibus narraretur, non tamen publicè contradixerunt,tacitos & illos,qui libros rem gestam narrantes in omnium manibus volitare permiserunt,etiam sibi,ut jam jam dicemus, inscriptos ; Sed & testem loquentem Johannem XXI. quo de Bellarmino Cardinali mirum, cur Papa dic: voluerit vicesimus primus, cùm sine Johannæ interpositu vicesimus demum fuisset, & de quo Ciacconio, ab his,qui fabulosam & commentitiam Joannam fæminam numero Pontificum interserunt,vicesimum primum dictum fuisse,certum est ; Testes etiam,qui Papis, præter n. XX. allegatum, qui Urbano III. Raphaelem Volateranum in Commentariis,qui Julio II. & Stephanum Blank de Romæ Urbis mirabilibus,qui Alexandro VI. qui Imperatoribus, ut Carolo V. Don Piero di Mexia in Selva di varia lettione p. 1. c. 9. hanc historiam se in authenticis reperisse testatus; qui Monasteriorum Præsulibus, ut Præsuli Fuldensis Monasterii Valentinus Muntzerus in Chronographia ex illius Monasterii Bibliotheca collecta; sua dedicârunt; Testem,cujus liber à Cæsare atque Regibus Hispaniarum & Galliarum privilegiatus, quique testatus est, se historiam contexuisse ex illis,qui rectiùs exactiúsque scripserint.
units.tr: XXIII. The witnesses are not only from the lower bench, as they say, but include famous names among scholars and great names among churchmen. The witnesses include the popes themselves, all of whom were surely silent. While a fable which others invented was publicly narrated as a real event, to the great disgrace of their office and with such scandal, and while everyone spoke of it, they did not publicly contradict it. Silent too were those who allowed books narrating the event to fly about in everyone's hands, even books dedicated to themselves, as we shall say presently. There is also John XXI, who speaks as a witness. Concerning him, Cardinal Bellarmine says it is strange why the pope wished to be called the twenty-first, when without the interposition of Joan he would only have been the twentieth; and Ciaconius says it is certain that he was called the twenty-first by those who insert the fabulous and invented woman Joan into the number of popes. There are also witnesses who dedicated their works to popes, besides the one cited in no. XX: to Urban III, Raphael of Volterra in his Commentaries; to Julius II, Stephen Blank in On the Marvels of the City of Rome; to Alexander VI, and others. Witnesses also dedicated works to emperors, such as Charles V, to whom Don Pedro de Mexía, in Selva di varia lettione, part 1, ch. 9, testified that he had found this history in authentic sources. Others dedicated their works to the heads of monasteries, such as the abbot of the monastery at Fulda, to whom Valentinus Muntzerus dedicated his Chronography, compiled from that monastery's library. And there is a witness whose book was privileged by the Emperor and by the kings of Spain and France, and who testified that he had woven his history out of those who had written more correctly and more exactly.

units.la: XXIV. Testem ipsum Platinam,qui tamen,ne Pontifices offendat,memor tetri carceris, è quo sub Paulo II. vix emerserat, ita finire voluit: Hæc, inquit, qua dixi, vulgò feruntur, incertis tamen & obscuris auctoribus; qua ideò ponere breviter & nudè instituì,ne obstinatè nimiùm & pertinaciter omisisse videar, quod fere omnes affirmant.
units.tr: XXIV. The witness Platina himself, who nevertheless, so as not to offend the popes, mindful of the foul prison from which he had barely emerged under Paul II, chose to end thus: "These things which I have said are commonly reported, but on uncertain and obscure authorities. I have therefore set them down briefly and plainly, lest I seem to have obstinately and stubbornly omitted what almost everyone affirms."

units.la: Virorum magnorum etiam, Pontificum etiam, & Pontificibus jua dicantium;
units.tr: Also of great men, even of popes, and of popes who themselves pronounced justice.

units.la: Platina, Poetarum; Erremus etiam nos hac in re cum vulgo. Quanquam apparet, ea quae dixi, ex his esse, quae fieri posse creduntur. Testem alium quendam Martinum Familiae Minoritarum, in Chronico, cui titulus; Flores temporum; & quod pertingit usque ad Carolum IV. ubi etiam nova circumstantia; narrat enim Papissam aliquando in adjuratione Daemoniaci interrogasse, quando Daemon recedere vellet, atque versificum sequens responsum tulisse:
units.tr: Platina, of the poets. Let us also err in this matter with the common crowd. "Yet it appears that the things I have said are among those which are believed possible." Another witness is Martin, of the Franciscan family, in his Chronicle titled Flowers of the Times, which runs down to Charles IV. There is also a new detail: he relates that Joan once asked a demon, during the exorcism of a demoniac, when the demon wished to depart, and that the demon gave the following answer in verse:

units.la: Papa Pater Patrum, Papissa pandito partum;Et Tibi tunc edam, de corpore quando recedam.
units.tr: Pope, Father of fathers, Joan has disclosed her childbirth; and then I will tell you when I shall depart from the body.

units.la: Quod Chronicon Latine Scriptum, sed & Ulmae An. 1486. Germanice impressum est. Testem etiam Bapt. Mantuanum, qui l. 3. Alphonsi in topothesia Tartari, ibi pendentem facit Johannam, juxta versus:
units.tr: This Chronicle was written in Latin and was also printed in German at Ulm in 1486. There is also Baptista Mantuanus, who in book 3 of Alphonsus, in his Topothesia of Tartarus, makes Joan hang there, in the following verses:

units.la: Hic pendebat adhuc sexum mentita virilem:Famina, cui triplici Phrygiam Diademate mitram,Extollebat apex & Pontificalis adulter.
units.tr: Here she still hung, who had falsely claimed the male sex: the woman whom the peak of the papal office raised with the Phrygian mitre and its triple crown, the adulteress of the pontificate.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Testes, quibus per 700. fermè, si ad ipsum Anastasium, per 500. fermè, si ad Marianum Scotum tantùm ascendimus, nemo unquam contradixisse deprehenditur; Primus enim, quod sciamus, Johannes Aventinus (de Aenea Sylvio respondet Cl. Mar. Pap. refut. 2. 3), Bellarmino App. de summo Pont. c. 10. author parum probata fidei, qui An. 1534. mortuus est, historiam falsitatis palam accusare & fabellam appellare atque levi admodum opera aggredi ausus est, quem Onuphrius majori conatu, hunc alii exceperunt; Atque observat ingenuéque agnoscit Doctiss. Launojus Epist. p. IV. Epist. ult. Caeterùm ab adversa ibidem parte stare visus; duo vel tria secula fuisse, in quibus de Famina hujus Pontificatu, nec fortassis uspiam dubitaretur; ubi juxta dicta & allegata melius duo & tria, imò plura secula dixisset.
units.tr: The witnesses, by whom for about 700 years if we go back to Anastasius himself, or for about 500 years if we go back only to Marianus Scotus, no one is found ever to have contradicted the story. For the first person, so far as we know, was Johannes Aventinus (Cl. Mar. replies to Aeneas Sylvius on this point, Pap. refut. 2. 3). Bellarmine calls him an author of little proven faith. He died in 1534, and he dared to accuse the history openly of falsehood, to call it a fable, and to attack it with very little effort. Onuphrius made a greater effort against it, and others took up his cause. The most learned Launoy observes and frankly acknowledges this. He seems, however, to stand on the opposing side. He says that there were two or three centuries in which, concerning this woman's pontificate, perhaps no one anywhere doubted. By the things said and cited, he would have done better to say two and three, indeed many more centuries.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Sic etiam Patres Concilii Constantiensis (Exemplum ipse Launojus l. c. allegat;) qui maxima, minima in libris Hussii occurrentia ad ejus damnationem corrad-bant, sive, ut invita ejus habetur, ingentibus odiis nonnullos articulos ex libris ejus truncatim & Syncopatim extrahebant, fictósque articulos & mendosos contra eum componebant, ad eum finem, ut, omni caritate seclusà, eundem de statu & vita sua ejicere valerent, neutiquam tamen dicam illi impegere, quòd in libro de Ecclesia, quo nullus alius rigidiori censurae subjectus fuit, semel cap. 7. atque iterum cap. 13. Johannam perstrinxerat. XXVII. Et quia sic universaliter atque diu creditum fuit in Johannam Papissam, hinc Guilelmo Occamo in opere 90. dierum contrà Joh. XXIII. c. 124. occasio nata arguendi, Ecclesiam Romanam esse errori obnoxiam, quòd aliquando erraverit, faeminam venerando pro Papa. Neque aliter id excusavit Æneas Sylvius, postea Pius II. l. 1. Epist. 140. quàm dicendo, ignorantiam esse neque fidei, neque juris, sed ignorantiam facti. At talem hanc ignorantiam facti esse, ex qua successio Romanorum Pontificum (Religionis apud ipsos fundamentum) laesa fuerit, ex praecedentibus constare potest, proin eâdem operâ, ignorantiam hanc Ecclesiae Romanae, salvis hypothesibus, neutiquam convenire potuisse.
units.tr: So too the Fathers of the Council of Constance (Launoy himself cites this example in the passage above), who gathered together the greatest and the smallest things found in Hus's books for his condemnation. Or, as his opponents hold, with huge hatreds they extracted some articles from his books in truncated and syncopated form, and composed false and faulty articles against him, with the aim that, all charity set aside, they might remove him from his position and his life. Yet I will by no means say that they charged him with this: that in his book on the Church, which no other book was subjected to stricter censure, he had touched on Joan once in chapter 7 and again in chapter 13. XXVII. And because it was thus universally and long believed about Joan the Female Pope, the occasion arose for William of Ockham, in his Work of Ninety Days against John XXII, chapter 124, to argue that the Roman Church is liable to error, because it once erred in venerating a woman as Pope. Aeneas Sylvius, afterwards Pius II, excused this in no other way than by saying that it was an ignorance neither of faith nor of law, but of fact (Epist. 1.140). But that this ignorance of fact was of such a kind that the succession of the Roman Pontiffs (the foundation of their religion) would have been harmed by it can be seen from what has gone before. Therefore, by the same reasoning, this ignorance could not have applied to the Roman Church while its hypotheses stood.

units.la: XXVIII. Ex qua etiam post tempora Reformationis non pauci rem adfirmârunt. Exempla brevitatis studio omittimus, id tantùm monentes, ipsos Romanos in libello de Indulgentiis Romae anno 1525. edito scribere atque asserere, Angelum huic Papissae uterum gestanti apparuisse, ipsíque optionem eligendi poenam, aut temporalem, aut aeternam, dedisse. Illam verò pudorem temporarium elegisse; Atque haec omnia, Romae adhuc in ore esse omni populo, exceptóque Clero, è civibus haud facilè quempiam reperiri, qui non de certitudine illorum sit persuasissimus.
units.tr: XXVIII. Some have also affirmed this matter after the time of the Reformation. For the sake of brevity we omit the examples, noting only that the Romanists themselves, in a little book on Indulgences published at Rome in 1525, write and assert that an angel appeared to this Papess while she was pregnant, and gave her the choice of punishment, either temporal or eternal. She, they say, chose temporary shame. And all these things are still on the lips of every people at Rome; apart from the clergy, scarcely anyone among the citizens could be found who is not fully persuaded of their truth.

units.la: XXIX. Ut ridiculum planè sit, quòd Papolatrae heic tantùm Novatores, Novatores adversarios suos crepant, & maximè ab una parte Ecclesiae Romanae honori consulant, qui pro vero habent, quod illa unâ cum capitibus suis multis tam constanter credidit; contrà in eam valde injurii sint, qui non tantùm historiam negant, sed & stultissimè excogitatam atque deforme mendacium esse, inanitate, vel levitate, sicut & falsitate alias fabulas omnes superare, non veritate tantùm, sed verisimilitudine etiam omni carere, asserere cum Baronio ad an. 853. n. 56. 62. 64. 66. atque tandem n. 70. Quis ista considerans & manu tangens, locum aliquem fabulae vel per somnium dabit? interrogare non erubescunt, de eo, quod illa & in illa ingens emunctioris naris graviúmq; Virorum cohors tamdiu extra omnem dubitationis aleam posuit. Atque forte, si Reformatio & cum Reformatione Scandalorum Antichristianorum uberior manifestatio non subsecuta fuisset, hodie adhuc, aequè ac per aliquot secula, in ipsa Romana Ecclesia communiter crederetur, Johannam Papissam fuisse.
units.tr: XXIX. It is plainly ridiculous that the Papist idolaters here cry out against their opponents as innovators, and that they especially defend the honour of one part of the Roman Church, holding as true what it, together with many of its heads, believed so constantly. On the other hand, those are very unjust to it who not only deny the history but also assert, with Baronius (ad an. 853, nn. 56, 62, 64, 66), that it is a most stupidly devised and shameful lie, surpassing all other fables in emptiness or frivolity and in falsity, and lacking not only truth but even verisimilitude; and who finally, at n. 70, ask: Who, considering these things and touching them with his hand, will allow any place for a fable, even in a dream? They are not ashamed to ask this about something that such a large and weighty company of keener-nosed men had for so long placed beyond all chance of doubt. And perhaps, if the Reformation, and with the Reformation a fuller exposure of the Antichristian scandals, had not followed, it would still today, as for several centuries before, be commonly believed in the Roman Church itself that Joan was a Pope.

units.la: XXX. Quam & in rerum natura fuisse multa alia praeter nuda Authorum testimonia arguunt. Et primò quidem Imagines eam repræsentant, statuæ ejus memoriam diu renovârunt. Imago habetur in amplo, pulcro & pretioso Codice historico Norinbergæ An. 1493. excuso cum Imaginibus Imperatorum & Pontificum, in quo etiam ad narrationem de Johanna apposita videtur effigies fœminæ Pontificialiter quidem coronatæ, sed pro trabea Pontificiali stolam muliebrem ab humeris pro tricruciato Sceptro infantem in ulnis gestantis. Sic etiam Johannes Boccatius, Petrarchæ ob ingenii, studiorum & morum similitudinem intimus & alter ipse, in libro de Claris mulieribus etiam spectabilem picturam partûs Pontificii circumstantibus Cardinalibus, & Episcopis obstetricantibus, etiam in versione Germanica Ulmæ An. 1473. impressa, atque Ducissæ Austriæ nuncupata, habet. Præter imagines autem has in libris exhibitas multas alias etiam in locis Sacris positas alii urgent.
units.tr: XXX. That she really existed, apart from the bare testimony of authors, many other things also show. First, images represent her, and statues have long kept her memory alive. An image is found in the large, fine and costly historical codex printed at Nuremberg in 1493 with pictures of the Emperors and Popes. In it, beside the account of Joan, there appears the figure of a woman crowned in papal fashion, but who, instead of the papal vestment, has a woman's stole hanging from her shoulders, and who holds a child in her arms in place of the triple-cross sceptre. So too Giovanni Boccaccio, the intimate of Petrarch on account of their similarity of talent, studies and character, and a second self, in his book On Famous Women, has a striking picture of the papal childbirth, with Cardinals standing around and Bishops acting as midwives. It is also in the German translation printed at Ulm in 1473 and dedicated to the Duchess of Austria. Besides these images shown in books, others also urge that there are many more placed in sacred buildings.

units.la: XXXI. Statua multò vetustior multò majoris etiam authoritatis esse debet. Atque duplex ab Authoribus commemorari videtur; Romana, de qua fragmentum de Schola Romæ Græca apud Wolf. Lect. Memorab. Cent. 9. p. 176. Edidit Filium suum primogenitum prope templum pacis in urbe, ut adhuc vetus statua marmorea illic posita figurativè monstrat. De qua etiam Stephanus Blank Passavianus in Mirabilibus urbis Romæ his verbis; Ibi loci adhuc recumbit Saxum quoddam referens sculptam ipsius & infantis ejus imaginem. Sic quoque M. Antonius Coccius Sabellicus, Vir, judice Erasmo, in historia splendidè versatus Ennead. IX. l. 1. quoddam Signum Sculpturæ marmoreæ in via, ubi contigerit, ob hujus rei memoriam positum fuisse, memorat.
units.tr: XXXI. A far older statue, of far greater authority, ought to exist. Authors seem to mention two. One is Roman, concerning which a fragment about the Greek school at Rome is found in Wolf. Lect. Memorab. Cent. 9, p. 176: She put out her firstborn son near the temple of peace in the city, as an old marble statue still placed there figuratively shows. Stephanus Blank of Passau also speaks of it in his Marvels of the City of Rome, in these words: In that place there still lies a stone representing a carved image of her and her child. So too Marcantonio Coccio Sabellico, a man, in Erasmus's judgment, splendidly versed in history, records in Ennead IX, book 1, a certain marble sculpted sign, placed on the road where the event occurred, in memory of this matter.

units.la: XXXII. De statua illa Romana ita Blondellus Avaxq. p. 70. Fieri potuisse, (ut poneretur talis statua) jure nemo negaverit & nihil absurdi commenti sunt, qui statuam, quæ figurativè factum monstraret, positam senserunt: utut quod cogente publica indignationis impetu sub omnium oculis ad famam erectum primùm putabatur, nonnulli posteà sempiternâ oblivione delendum censuerint; Si Nemausus triforme Geryonis Simulachrum usque nunc ostentare non dedignatur; Si post eversum A. D. 389. Serapeum, comminutáque ac fusa Alexandrinorum Idololatrarum simulachra, ne quis eorum, procedente tempore, se Simiam Deum adorâsse negare auderet, (Socr. lib. 5. c. 16.) jure meritóque Theophilus ἐν ἀγαλμα τῶ δὲ τῶ Θεῶ ἀχώνσλον τηςεὶ ἀντ κεκλέσας δημοσίᾳ ἀπέίσηδεν quantò quantò justiùs acri recentis injuria sensu lancinata Romana Ecclesia, infulata illius Scrofa, qua Cleri populíque cultu per biennium, & quod excurrit, conservata dicitur, publicè positâ statuâ detestandam memoriam protestari, altâque mente repositam ob nuper admissum nefas δυσμένειαν in perpetuum profiteri decrevisset?
units.tr: XXXII. Concerning that Roman statue, Blondel says in his Avaxq., p. 70: No one can rightly deny that such a statue could have been set up to show the thing figuratively. Those who thought that a statue had been placed there which showed the deed by a figure were not foolish inventors, although some afterwards judged that it should be destroyed by everlasting oblivion, what was at first thought to have been erected to fame under the eyes of all by the impulse of public indignation. If Nemausus does not disdain to display to this day the triple image of Geryon; if, after the Serapeum was overthrown in A.D. 389, and the images of the Alexandrian idolaters were broken and melted down, lest anyone, as time went on, dare to deny that he had worshipped a monkey as God (Socrates, book 5, ch. 16), Theophilus rightly and justly [ἐν ἀγαλμα τῶ δὲ τῶ Θεῶ ἀχώνσλον τηςεὶ ἀντ κεκλέσας δημοσίᾳ ἀπέίσηδεν] ... how much more justly would the Roman Church, torn by the sharp sense of a recent injury, have decided to protest publicly, by a statue placed in view of all, against that detestable memory, the Church having kept her wrapped in her mitre, with the worship of clergy and people maintained for two years and beyond, and to declare in her deep mind a lasting abhorrence of the crime lately committed?

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Ajunt quidem, Statuam hanc Sacerdotem Ethnicum cum praecedente famulo repraesentâsse, ibíque puerum natu grandiorem formâ faemininae simileм praecessisse. Verùm & quia solus Bellarminus heic se oculatum testem jactitat contrà tot vetustiores, atque magis extra partes constitutos, & quia statuam supressisse atque in Tiberim projecisse dicuntur, Johannae statuam nihilominùs vindicamus. De qua Statuae abolitione ita rursus Doct. Blondellus, Avaxε. 72.73. Nescio autem, an non, quod proximè elapso seculo profunda prudentia Vir, si Pasquini statua in Tiberim abjiceretur, futurum conjectabat, ut nimirum mersus profundo, ranarum more fieret vocalior; post deturbatas, confractásque sive Pii V. (Elias Hasenmuller hist. Jesuit. ord.) sive Sixti V. sive (Raemund. c.22. 23.) Clementis VIII. jussu, Romae Senisque, qua Johannam repraesentare videbantur, statuas evenerit: Stabat Romana sub dio, scabris jam dudum vitiata dentibus aevi, lentâ paulatim (ut catera omnia ejus generis) morte consumenda, ac simul ex animis hominum emovenda. At nunc stat, stabítque (nî fallor) in concertantium monumentis, perennitati quodammodò consecrata: nec video, quo ingenio Viri Docti dilemma eludere liceat (Morton. Apol. Catholi. c. 19.) In statua illa vel ea fuit faminae puerperae similitudo, ut historiae fidem assereret, vel alia fuit, ut fabulam convinceret: Si hoc, cur verum mendacii argumentum è loco publico sublatum esse voluistis? Si illud, cur antiquae repugnatis veritati? Aut igitur imprudens admodùm statuae ablatio fuit, aut impudens formae negatio. Hucusque Vir Doctus ille. Et certè meritò idem Blondellus in fine Scripti sui Gallici de eadem re ita loquitur: Quicunque cognoscet curam adhibitam, in abolenda nota publica, qua vulgò sumebatur pro speciali monumento Papissa Johanna, facilè confirmabitur in ea opinione, quòd illius occasione erecta fuerit. Idem eadem octogesimum sextum crassiorum Ramundiana tractationis naevorum facit, quòd Cap. 23. §. 6. effugium quaesiturus ait: Decantatam Caligulae Pyramidem Sixtus V. pristino loco restituit. Ad quae p. 127. specialiùs respond t: Ipsa Vetus Obelisci inscriptio, Divi Caesari, Divi Julii Filio, Augusto Tiberio Caesari, Divi Caesaris Filio Augusto Sacrum fuisse, RamunRamundúmque temerè quicquid (vel per somnium) in mentem venit, chartis illevisse, docet. Vide ad finem libelli inscripti Ritratto di Roma antica.
units.tr: They say, to be sure, that this statue represented a heathen priest with the attendant who went before him, and that a boy, older by birth, in the form of a woman, went in front. But since Bellarmine alone boasts here of being an eyewitness, against so many older writers who stood more outside the parties, and since the statue is said to have been suppressed and thrown into the Tiber, we nonetheless claim the statue of Joan. Concerning the abolition of this statue, Dr. Blondel speaks again thus: Avaxε. 72.73. I do not know whether it was not foreseen by a man of deep prudence in the last century that, if the statue of Pasquino were thrown into the Tiber, it would become more vocal, like frogs sunk in the depths. After the statues at Rome and Siena, which seemed to represent Joan, were pulled down and broken, either by order of Pius V (Elias Hasenmuller, History of the Jesuit Order), or of Sixtus V, or (Raymond c. 22, 23) of Clement VIII, the Roman statue stood in the open air, already long ago marred by the rough teeth of age, to be consumed slowly by death (as all other things of that kind) and at the same time removed from men's minds. But now it stands, and will stand (unless I am mistaken) in the monuments of the disputants, dedicated in some way to perpetuity. Nor do I see by what cleverness a learned man may be allowed to elude this dilemma (Morton, Apology for the Catholics, c. 19.) In that statue there was either the likeness of a woman in childbirth, to confirm the truth of the story, or there was another, to refute the fable. If the former, why did you want the true evidence of the lie removed from a public place? If the latter, why do you contradict the ancient truth? Therefore either the removal of the statue was exceedingly imprudent, or the denial of its form was shameless. So far that learned man. And certainly Blondel rightly speaks thus at the end of his French writing on the same matter: Whoever shall know the care taken in abolishing the public mark which was commonly taken as a special memorial of Pope Joan will easily be confirmed in the opinion that it was erected on her account. The same man, in the eighty-sixth of the thicker blemishes of Raymond's treatise, since in chapter 23, §6 he seeks an escape, says: Sixtus V restored to its former place the much-sung pyramid of Caligula. To this he replies more particularly at p. 127.: The old inscription of the obelisk itself, that it was sacred to the divine Caesar, to the divine Julius's son Augustus Tiberius Caesar, to the divine Caesar's son Augustus, shows that Raymond rashly scribbled on paper whatever came into his mind, even in a dream. See at the end of the booklet entitled Ritratto di Roma antica.

units.la: XXXIV. Altera Statua Senensis jam unà cum priori verbis Blondelli memorata fuit, quoad abolitionis rationem nimirum. Ab eadem idem ad Romanam p. 70. ita argumentatur: Quod Senis ante annos fere ducentos in seculi feliciori majore luce factum fatentur omnes, Roma, incumbente sequiorum temporum caligine, fieri potuisse, jure nemo negaverit. Sed & octogesimum quintum inter crassiores Ramundiana tractationis nævos in verbis Ræmundi personati sequentibus p. 126. ostendit: Nondum anni ducenti effluxere, ex quo Senensis Trulli prima fundamenta jacta sunt: exinde Michael Angelus, qui pulcherrimis Italia ædibus aliquam excellentis penicilli, calive notam ac testificationem relinquere voluit, eum marmoreis Paparum statuis ditavit, inter quas muliebrem illam collocavit, cap. 23. §. 3. & rursus §. 4. Si quis humanarum rerum spiritibus æterna felicitate fruentibus sensus restat, quantum ex pudore ruboris magnus ille Pontifex Pius II. qui Æneæ Sylvii nomen illustravit, bonúsque, & si quis pius alius, Pius tertius, contrahere debent, mulieris hujus inter decessorum Iconas, imaginem stare passi? Quibus reponit: Atqui Pius II. anno 1464. Septembris 15. solido ante Michaelis natalem decennio, tertius anno 1503. Octob. 17. labente 29. Michaelis anno obdormivit; quo vix (qui postea aquavos omnes superavit) ullum inter artifices nomen sortitus erat. Decessit enim Michael Angelus, Bonarota, nonagenarius, A. D. 1564. prout ex Benedicti Varchii & Georgii Vasarii lucubrationibus adnotavit Vir Illustris memoria Jac. Aug. Thuanus, hist. lib. 35. verum litibus assueto, quique secum consentire nequeat, Ramundo cum aliis parum convenire, nemo mirabitur.
units.tr: XXXIV. The second statue at Siena was mentioned already together with the first, in Blondel's words, namely as to the reason for its abolition. From the same, the same man argues against the Roman one: That at Siena, nearly two hundred years ago, in the greater light of a happier age, it was done, all admit; that Rome, with the darkness of later times settling over it, could have been done, no one would rightly deny. But he also shows, in the eighty-fifth of the thicker blemishes of Raymond's treatise, in the following words put into Raymond's mouth, at p. 126.: Not yet two hundred years have passed since the first foundations of the Sienese cathedral were laid. Thereafter Michelangelo, who wished to leave some mark and testimony of his excellent brush to the most beautiful buildings of Italy, enriched it with marble statues of the Popes, among which he placed that female figure, chapter 23, §3, and again §4. If any sense remains to the spirits of departed men who enjoy eternal happiness, how greatly, from the shame of blushing, should that great pontiff Pius II, who made the name of Aeneas Sylvius illustrious, and the good, and if there is any other pious one, Pius III, have had to draw back, to suffer that image of this woman to stand among the likenesses of their predecessors? To which he replies: But Pius II died on 15 September 1464, a full decade before Michelangelo's birth, and Pius III on 17 October 1503, when Michelangelo was 29 years old; at that time he (who afterwards surpassed all the artists of his age) had scarcely any name among craftsmen. For Michelangelo Buonarroti died at the age of ninety, in the year of our Lord 1564, as the illustrious man of memory Jacques-Auguste de Thou noted from the works of Benedetto Varchi and Giorgio Vasari, Histories, book 35. But that no one will be surprised that Raymond, a man accustomed to quarrels and unable to agree with himself, does not agree with others.

units.la: XXXV. Eadem Senensis statua etiam apud Doctiss. Laun-ojum T. IV. Epist. ult. testimonium habet: Insuper, inquit, quo tempore Pius, hoc nomine secundus, Romanam administravit Ecclesiam (serius id factum esse jam jam Blondellus notavit;) Basilica Senensis Major laquearibus fuit ornata, in quorum parte inferiori Pontificum Romanorum, qui sibi invicem successerunt usque ad Pium Statuæ umbilicotenus eminentes adspectantur, ubi etiam Johannes, ceu Johanna inter Leonem & Benedictum collocatur, quod certum est inveterata persuasionis judicium, ita ut Æneas Sylvius, Vir acris cateroquin ingenii, ausus non fuerit ab illa persuasione omnino recedere &c. Platina, licet non minus eminentis in erroribus notandis, Æneam tamen imitatus est &c. His etiam e medio
units.tr: XXXV. The same Sienese statue also has the testimony of the very learned Launoy, vol. IV, last letter: Moreover, he says, at the time when Pius, the second of that name, governed the Roman Church (that this happened later, Blondel has already noted), the greater cathedral of Siena was adorned with coffered ceilings, in the lower part of which the statues of the Roman Pontiffs who succeeded one another, down to Pius, are seen standing up to the navel; where also John, as Joan, is placed between Leo and Benedict. This is the certain judgment of an long-standing persuasion, so that Aeneas Sylvius, a man otherwise of keen wit, did not dare to depart from that persuasion at all, etc. Platina, though no less eminent in noting errors, nevertheless imitated Aeneas, etc. Having these also

units.la: Statua Senensis; — De ea testimonium Launoji. medio sublatis vetus sine ulla haesitatione per severavit opinio &c. Et paulò post: Manifestum est ex his omnibus, neminem vel certè perpaucos dubitasse, quin Faemina sedem occupaverit Romanam.
