Ut certè omninò, nisi universaliter recepta atque firma fuisset de Johanna Papissa fides, minimè passi fuissent Pontifices tot reliquíque Clerici, ut ejus modi statuae non modò fierent, sed & tanto Ecclesiae Romanae probro altera illa in Templo collocaretur, diu ibi toleraretur atque quotidie ab in colis & peregrinis aspiceretur: In cujus animum cadere potuit, interrogat Differt. de Brunonis secessu; admirabundus Launojus, cogitatio, in loco hocce Sancto sedem potuisse mendacium tam pudendum (quale illud existimasse videtur) invenire passuros tamdiu fuisse Sapientissimos Academiae Senensis Doctores, qui insita pietatis adfectu, in celeberrimum hujus urbis Templum crebrò concurrunt, illámque Johanna statuam vel imaginem intuentur, ita sibi, Scholasticis ac toti Clero & populo imponi, Commento tam atroci, (ita vocare placuit) nec monituros fuisse religiosissimos Ecclesiae celeberrimae Sacerdotes tam perniciosa fictionis obducenda? Quin etiam inscriptionem habuit statua illa hanc: Faemina Angla; De qua idem Petrus Mexia, Hispanus l. c. atque alii testari reperiuntur.
units.tr: Sienese statue; — Launoy's testimony concerning it. With these also removed from the midst, the old opinion persisted without any hesitation, etc. And a little after: It is clear from all these things that no one, or certainly very few, doubted that a woman occupied the Roman see. Indeed, altogether, unless the faith concerning Pope Joan had been universally received and firm, the popes and the rest of the clergy would by no means have allowed such statues not only to be made, but also that other one, to the great disgrace of the Roman Church, to be placed in the temple, to be tolerated there for so long, and to be looked at daily by residents and strangers. Into whose mind could it have fallen, asks the Dissertation on Bruno's retreat; Launoy, wondering, the thought that the most wise doctors of the Academy of Siena, who from innate devotion often gather in the most famous temple of this city and look upon that statue or image of Joan, could have let themselves be so imposed upon, by Scholastics and by the whole clergy and people, by so atrocious a fiction (as it has pleased them to call it), and that the most religious priests of that most celebrated church would not have warned against drawing over so pernicious a fiction? Indeed that statue also bore this inscription: Englishwoman; concerning which Pedro Mexía, the Spaniard, loc. cit., and others are found to testify.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Statuis apponimus Sellam, ut vocant, perforatam, in libro Pontificalium Ceremoniarum, Stercorariam, in qua sedens, vel quasi jacere visus recens electus Pontifex à tempore Johannae virilitatis suae explorationem admittere debuit ab infimo Diacono instituendam, quâ feliciter succedente idem adstantibus acclamare solitus est: Habet; sive; Mas nobis est Dominus. Atque huic mori testimonium perhibent praeter Graecum Laonicum Chalcondylam supra laudati Authores Pontificii Latini, Brevvinus, Malléolus, Sabellicus, Nauclerus, Stella, Blank, &c. Janus item Pannonius, Episcopus Quinquecclesiensis, sequente carmine: Petre tuâ quaedam fuit ausa sedere cathedrâ, Orbi terrarum jura ferenda dedit; Haec compressa quid m multos latuisset in annos, Facta foret partu ni manifesta novo. Posthaec Roma diu simili sibi cavit ab astu, Pontificum arcanos quaerere sueta sinus; Nec poterat quisquam reserantes aethera claves Non exploratis sumere testiculis.
units.tr: We place in the statues the so-called perforated chair, in the book of Pontifical Ceremonies, the dung chair, on which the newly elected Pontiff, seated or nearly lying, was obliged to submit to an examination of his manhood, to be carried out by the lowest deacon. When it succeeded, those standing by were accustomed to shout: He has it; or The Lord is a man to us. Besides the Greek Laonicus Chalcondyles, the Latin Papist authors cited above, Braunius, Malleolus, Sabellicus, Naucler, Stella, Blank, etc., also bear witness to this custom. Janus Pannonius, Bishop of Quinque-Ecclesiae, likewise, in the following verses: "A certain woman dared to sit on Peter's chair and gave laws to the whole world. Had she been hidden in silence for many years, she would not have been revealed unless by a new birth. Afterwards Rome for a long time took care against a similar trick, accustomed to search the secret recesses of the Pontiffs. Nor could anyone take up the keys that unlock heaven without first testing the testicles."

units.la: XXXVII. Crassum hoc quidem putidúmque prævcavendi erroris commentum vocat Blondellus? addit tamen, nemini Romanorum, quos nunc avitæ supinitatis pudeat, Patrum memoriâ persuasum non esse, perforatas in Laterano sedes probando Paparum sexui destinatas fuisse. Sed optimè hanc consuetudinem illustrat Cl. Megerlinus l. c. exemplo Methodii, qui An. 842. Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus factus est, & cùm stupri reus esset, ut se insontem probaret, æquè putidâ fœdáque ratione judicibus arefacta genitalia, testibus Zonara & Cedreno, ostendit; quod hodie ne vilissimus quidem Cerdo admitteret. Hinc etiam esse non nemo observat, quòd in Papatu sæpe numerò Sacrificulum genus membrum virile facetâ antonomasiâ Pontificalia appellare audiverit.
units.tr: XXXVII. Does Blondel call this a crude and foul invention to avoid error? He nevertheless adds that no Roman, who is now ashamed of his ancestral stupidity, is unaware from the memory of the Fathers that the perforated seats in the Lateran were destined for the sex of Popes. But the learned Megerlin, in the work cited, illustrates this custom well by the example of Methodius, who became Patriarch of Constantinople in the year 842. When he was accused of fornication, to prove his innocence he showed the judges his genitals dried up, a method as foul and disgusting, as Zonaras and Cedrenus testify; something not even the lowest tradesman would accept today. Hence, someone also observes that in Papacy the priestly class often hears the male member called, by a witty antonomasia, the pontificals.

units.la: Platina quidem, qui Sellam unâ cum usu jam tradito commemorat, atque post eum alii, Bellarminus maximè, alium finem comminiscuntur, nimirum sedem illam ob id paratam esse, ut qui in tanto Magistratu constituitur, sciat se non Deum, sed hominem esse, & necessitatibus naturæ, utpote egerendi, subjectum esse, unde meritò stercoraria sedes vocetur. Vel, ut Bellarminus habet; ut recens creato Papæ per eam ceremoniam, eum de loco humillimo ad locum summum ascendere, significetur, indéque elevantes canere illud 1. Reg. II. 6. Suscitat de pulvere egenum, & de stercore elevat pauperem. Ast subordinata non pugnant; Authores testantur, sellam explorandæ virilitati destinatam fuisse, Authores veteres, graves atque Pontificii. Fieri cæterum omninò potuit, ut, vel simul ab initio, vel temporis progressu etiam humilitatem Pontifices ex instituto & dicto modo docere debuerit, quam & aliâs exploratio virilium docere potuisset; Forte etiam, quando virilia attrectare porrò noluerunt, usum alterum illum substituerunt. Neque magis rem tollit alia Abbatis Gualdi Vita di D. Olimpia p. 406. seqq; exceptio, quòd sic alii etiam præter Pontifices explorari debuissent; Quando facilè concipi potest, illud factum esse in Pontificibus tantùm 1. occasionaliter, quod satis docetur 2. ob ipsorum in dignitate præeminentiam, majúsque ab ipsis, si forte viri non essent, periculum.
units.tr: Platina indeed, who mentions the chair together with the custom already handed down, and after him others, especially Bellarmine, devise another purpose: namely, that the chair was prepared so that the one who is placed in so great a magistracy should know that he is not God but a man, and subject to the needs of nature, such as evacuation, whence the chair is rightly called the dung chair. Or, as Bellarmine has it, so that by that ceremony the newly created Pope is signified to ascend from the lowest place to the highest, and therefore, lifting him up, they sing that verse from 1 Kings 2:8: "He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung." But subordinate purposes do not conflict. Authors, ancient, grave and Papist, testify that the chair was destined for the examination of manhood. It could well be that, either from the beginning or as time went on, the Pontiffs were also meant, by the established rite and words, to be taught humility, which the examination of the male organs could also have taught in other ways. Perhaps also, when they no longer wished to handle the male organs, they substituted that other practice. Nor does the other objection, from the Life of Donna Olimpia by Abbot Gualdi, pp. 406 ff., remove the matter, namely that in this way others besides the Popes would have had to be examined. For it can easily be conceived that this happened only occasionally in the case of Popes: first, because of the occasion, which is sufficiently shown; second, because of their eminence in dignity and the greater danger from them if perchance they were not men.

units.la: Nempe fatemur, Ceremoniam illam virilitatem explorandi in desuetudinem jam abiisse, atque licèt Interpretes, ceu vocantur, Romanarum Antiquitatum, peregrinis, accepto pretio, res in urbe notabiles commonstrantes, & verbis declarantes etiam in Lateranensis Basilicæ porticu sellam perforatam, cum commemora-
units.tr: Indeed, we admit that the ceremony of testing virility has now fallen into disuse. Although the so-called interpreters of Roman antiquities, who for a fee show foreigners the notable sights of the city and explain them in words, still point out, even in the portico of the Lateran Basilica, the perforated chair, together with the mention

units.la: {y} Argumentum hoc confirmatur & illustratur; moratione explorati Sexûs, hodienum ostendant; tamen non amplius explorari solet, vel, ob rationem, quam suprà laudatus Pannonius aliique dant, Sic enim ille in Carmine citato pergit;
units.tr: {y} This argument is confirmed and illustrated: they still point it out, with mention of the examined sex; nevertheless it is no longer usually carried out, either for the reason which the Pannonian quoted above and others give. For he goes on thus in the poem cited:

units.la: Cur igitur nostro mos hic jam tempore cessat?
units.tr: Why then has this custom now ceased in our time?

units.la: Ante probat quòd se quilibet esse marem.
units.tr: Because it was proved beforehand that anyone was a man.

units.la: Atque de Paulo II.
units.tr: And concerning Paul II.

units.la: Pontificis Pauli testes ne Roma requiras;
units.tr: Do not ask Rome for witnesses to Pope Paul;

units.la: Filia, quam genuit, sat docet esse marem.
units.tr: the daughter he begot is proof enough that he was a man.

units.la: Sanctum non possum, Patrem te dicere possum,
units.tr: I cannot call you holy, but I can call you father,

units.la: Quum video gnatam, Paule secunde, tuam.
units.tr: when I see your daughter, Paul II.

units.la: Marcellus verò de Innocentio VIII.
units.tr: But Marcellus concerning Innocent VIII.

units.la: Quid quaeris testes, sit mas an femina Cibo?
units.tr: Why do you ask for witnesses whether Cibo was male or female?

units.la: Respice natorum, pignora certa, gregem.
units.tr: Look at the children, the sure pledges, the flock.

units.la: Octo Nocens (pro Innocentius) pueros genuit totidemque puellas;
units.tr: Octo Nocens (for Innocentius) begot eight boys and as many girls;

units.la: Hunc merito poteris dicere Roma Patrem.
units.tr: Rome may rightly call him Father.

units.la: Vel potiùs & citra jocum, quia eos tandem pudere coepit foedae explorationis, atque tristem turpitudinis memoriam renovare toties porrò noluerunt, quia etiam non, sicuti seculis antiquis, imberbi Juveni Petri Cathedram ampliùs conscendere datur, sed solùm, cujus mentum cana barba vestit, vetus, vietus, veternosus senex admittitur.
units.tr: Or rather, and without joking, because at last they began to be ashamed of the foul examination, and they were unwilling to renew again and again the sad memory of the disgrace; because also it is no longer granted, as in earlier ages, for a beardless youth to mount Peter's chair, but only an old, worn-out, senile man, whose chin is covered with grey beard, is admitted.

units.la: XL. Testimonium porrò Johannae perhibent anfractuosae Pontificum processiones, qui, quando ex Vaticano ad Lateranum pergunt, hanc, in qua peperisse dicitur Johanna, declinare solent viam, aliàs compendiosiorem, idque unicè ob detestationem facti fieri Pontificii gravissimi Authores plurimi, veteres atque recentiores magno consensu tradunt; Ipse Blondellus, hujus facti exemplum in vico scelerato Romae veteris ob calcatum à Tullia paternum Cadaver ostendit, atque subdit; Cui igitur mirum videatur, si ob violatum per inauditum antea scelus ab impurissimo prostibulo Pontificium, tantâ Clerus urbanus indignatione exarsisse dicatur, ut execrandum posteris, imò ne visu dignum, incredibilis Seculis prioribus piaculi locum duceret? Idem p. 107. Scripti sui Gallici censet; Romam ex quo ad se rediit, id est, me quidem interprete, ex quo delendam omninò esse Johannae memoriam judicavit, sua causa vehementer praejudicâsse, non minùs ac statuarum abolitione, de qua suprà, dirutâ eâ platea, in qua Johanna peperisse ferebatur: Etsi enim dicatur, inquit, Sixtum V. illum dirui curâsse, ut dilataretur, & recta fieret, attamen, qui ex peregrinis & indigeindigenis Romanis considerabunt, pompam Papalem, sive processionem, etiamnum hodie perseverare in transeundo per aliam plateam, quae nec- latior est, & iter processionis prolixius facit, non poterunt sibi imaginari, quòd per hos anfractus procedat, alia de causa, quàm in memoriam, addi-mus, detestationem, in famis accidentis suae Johannae; ratione non ab-simili illi, quâ Pontifex Capitolium nullus ascendere scribitur, quia ibi Papa Johannes aliquis occisus.
units.tr: XL. Further, the winding processions of the Pontiffs bear witness to Joan. When they go from the Vatican to the Lateran, they are accustomed to avoid this street in which Joan is said to have given birth, although it is the shorter way; and that solely out of detestation of the deed. Many grave Papist authors, ancient and recent, hand this down with great agreement. Blondel himself shows an example of this deed in the wicked street of old Rome, because of the father's corpse trampled by Tullia, and adds: To whom then would it seem strange, if on account of a sin of unheard-of kind committed by the most impure prostitute, the Papist clergy of the city were said to have been so inflamed with such indignation that they considered that place an incredible expiation for later ages, cursed to posterity, and not even worth seeing? The same author, p. 107 of his French writing, thinks: Since Rome returned to him, that is, in my reading, since he judged that the memory of Joan must be completely wiped out, it greatly prejudiced his cause, no less than by the abolition of the statues mentioned above, the street in which Joan was said to have given birth having been demolished. For although it is said, he says, that Sixtus V had it demolished so that it might be widened and made straight, yet those who consider it among foreigners and native Romans will not be able to imagine that the Papal procession, that is, the procession, still continues today to pass through another street, which is not wider, and makes the route of the procession longer, for any reason other than to add to the memory and detestation of the misfortune of Joan; on a reasoning not unlike that by which it is written that no Pontiff ever ascended the Capitol, because Pope John was killed there.

units.la: XLI. Excipiunt quidem Adversarii, viam istam, quâ Jo-hanna dicatur peperisse, esse angustam & anfractuosam, Pontifica-lique Comitatui in commodam. Sed ita non facile, judice ipsomet Blondello Avaxe: p. 73. fidem invenient; Nam primò comitatum Pontificium non, ut aciem, in latum, sed, ut in processionibus fieri amat, in longum ex porrigi putamus; angustiam itaque loci transituris obstare haud temerè crediderimus. Secundò neque facilius crediderimus, Auctores fabulae, quam vocant, tam simplices fuisse, ut Johannam Pontificialiter incedentem in platea peperisse dicerent, per quam ob angustiam comitatus Pontificius transire non possit. Tertiò ipse Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. l. 3. c. 24. sui forsan oblitus, vult, non deesse Pontifices, qui non semel per hanc ipsum viam iter fecerint. Quod alii fecerunt, cur non etiam Johanna facere potuit? Quartò Blondellus testatur, testantur, qui urbem inviserunt, testantur etiam typi Urbis maximè post mutatum à Sixto V. locorum situm, viam, quam declinare solent Pontifices, & compendiosiorem & æquè latam esse; Ut quintò post tot Authores gravissimos Pon-tificios, nobis quoque asserere liceat, fieri unicè ob detestationem facti, saltem fieri solitum esse, atque Pontifices primò eo animo declinâsse, & hodienum etiam, forte ne in transitu per locum toties iterato, toties etiam memoria facti pudendi, videntibus renovetur, in declinatione monumentum Johannae Papissae extare debere; Non autem bene concludere Abbatem Gualdi Vita di Donna Olimpia p. 405. Si quis Pontifex per plateam illam transiret, ex Historia fabulam facere posset, atque haud melius jactare; Si tot esse deberent Johannae, quot platea Romanae, per quas non transeunt Pontifices, Pseudo-Historicis nostris plurima scr. bendi materia essent.
units.tr: XLI. The Adversaries indeed object that the road by which Joan is said to have given birth is narrow and winding, and not convenient for the Papal retinue. But, as Blondel himself judges in his Avaxe, p. 73, this will not easily find belief. For first, we think the Papal retinue does not extend across, like a battle line, but, as it likes to do in processions, lengthwise; so we would not rashly believe that the narrowness of the place stands in the way of those passing. Second, we would not more easily believe that the authors of the so-called fable were so simple as to say that Joan gave birth in the street, through which the Papal retinue could not pass because of its narrowness, while she was walking as a Pontiff. Third, Bellarmine himself, perhaps forgetting himself, in On the Roman Pontiff, book 3, chapter 24, wants it to be that there were Pontiffs who did not once make their journey by this very road. If others did this, why could Joan not have done it too? Fourth, Blondel testifies, and those who visited the city testify, and the maps of the City also testify, especially since the arrangement of the places was changed by Sixtus V, that the road which the Pontiffs are accustomed to avoid is both shorter and equally wide. So fifth, after so many very grave Papist authors, we too may assert that it is done solely out of detestation of the deed, or at least that it was customary to do so, and that the Pontiffs first avoided it with that intention; and even today, perhaps so that by passing through the place so often, the memory of the shameful deed may not be renewed in the sight of onlookers, there ought to be a monument of Pope Joan in the place of avoidance. But Abbot Gualdi does not conclude well in his Life of Donna Olimpia, p. 405: If any Pontiff passed through that street, he could make a story out of it, and boast of it no less; if there ought to be as many Joans as there are Roman streets through which the Popes do not pass, our pseudo-historians would have very much material for writing.

units.la: XLII. Multa equidem heic nobis praeter Authorum quorundam silentium, ad quod jam supra occasione utentes respondimus, objiciuntur. Objiciunt primò circumstantiarum diversitatem atque repugnantiam. Diversitatem maximè urget Baronius ad an. 853. an. 853. n. 67. Primò respectu nominis. Audi inprimis,ait,quanta in- ter eos confusio in conficta famina nomine. Alii enim ipsam Johannam nominatam antea Agnetem dixere, quæ ab alio reperitur appellata Gilberta; rursum verò ab alio Isabella, ab alio autem Margarita; Juttam insuper aliquis, aliquis verò Dorotheam nominavit — Rursus quanta diversitas in nomine, quod confinxerunt, Pontificis, vel leviter crediderunt, Papissæ Joan-ne ? Nam alii eam vocant Joannem VII. al. VIII. al. IX. cùm tamen fuerint iidem legitimi Ecclesiæ Romanæ Pontifices, Joannes Septimus, Octavus & Nonus. Ast primò quoad nomina Johannæ ante Pontificatum, tantam alii eorum copiam, quantam Baronius, reperire non possunt; Qui Isabellam, Margaretam, Juttam, Dorotheam, nominaverit, inquit Blondellus p. 13. ( quicquid Ramundi audaciâ freti Baronius Card. Binius &c. asseverare ausint,) sive ex Protestantibus, sive ex Romanæ Ecclesiæ communicatoribus, hactenus innotuit nemo. Germani quidem fœmininum Johannis in lingua sua non habentes Juttam vocandam esse censuerunt. Sic etiam Agnes vel ex Belgico Janke vel ex Italico Janetta, vel ex Gallico Janette originem habere videtur. Nomen Gilbertæ forte habuit à Parentibus impositum. Cæterùm quis nescit, eandem etiam personam sæpe uno atque altero, modò hoc, modò alio nomine appellari ? Et quando Johanna ante mendacium sexûs verisimiliter in diversis locis fuit, in diversis etiam regionibus, diversis, secundùm regionum consuetudines, nominibus quoque appellari, imò unum fingere potuit, quæ post sexum mentita est. In Pontificatu autem Johannam, detectâ fraude, Johannam posthac appellatam fuisse, omnes consentiunt. S. Catharina Alexandrina Cosli Regis filia, modò Catharina, modò Dorothea, modo Hecaterina à diversis appellatur, neque tamen eam ideò fictitiam esse volunt hagiolatræ. Et quòd Baronius secundò ex numeri diversitate argumentatur, inconvenienter quoque ab illo fit, cùm nemo ignoret, ejusmodi variationi Pontifices hujus, imò & aliorum nominum obnoxios esse, atque similiter ex. gr. Johannem eundem al. XVI. al. XVII. al. XVIII. audire, Benedictum XI. XIII. vocari, Felicem IV. V. dici, Paulum multis I. II. appellari, Honorium II. aliis III. nominari &c. Similiter etiam Stephanorum numerum variare; Vide de Johannis nomine ipsum Bar. ad an. 1003: 10. Cæterùm Frisingensis (de quo supra) & Sabellicus, quod sciamus, soli Septimum vocant. Qui IX. crediderit, Blondello l. c. hactenus innotuit nemo. Omnes Octavum faciunt; qui numerus, si fæmina hîc numerum faceret, recte subdu-ctus est.
units.tr: XLII. Many objections are raised against us here, apart from the silence of certain authors, to which we have already replied on that occasion above. They first object the diversity and conflict of circumstances. Baronius presses the diversity most of all, at the year 853, n. 67. First, with respect to the name. Hear first, he says, how great is the confusion among them about the invented woman's name. For some have said that Joan was earlier called Agnes, whom another finds called Gilberta; again another calls her Isabella, another Margaret; someone named her Jutta, someone else Dorothea — Again, how great is the diversity in the name of the pontiff whom they invented, or whom they lightly believed to be Pope Joan? For some call her John VII, or VIII, or IX, although they were the same legitimate popes of the Roman Church, John the Seventh, Eighth and Ninth. But first, as to the names of Joan before her pontificate, others cannot find as great an abundance of them as Baronius does. Whoever named her Isabella, Margaret, Jutta, Dorothea, says Blondel p. 13 (whatever Baronius, Cardinal Binius and others dare to assert, relying on the audacity of Raymond), whether among the Protestants or among those in communion with the Roman Church, no one has come to light so far. The Germans, indeed, since their language has no feminine of John, have thought she should be called Jutta. Agnes likewise seems to derive either from the Dutch Janke, or from the Italian Janetta, or from the French Janette. The name Gilberta she perhaps received from her parents. Moreover, who does not know that the same person is often called by one name or another, now this, now that? And since Joan before her deception of sex was probably in various places, and in various regions, she could also have been called by various names, according to the customs of the regions; indeed she could have invented one for herself after she feigned her sex. But that after the fraud was detected Joan was called Joan from then on, everyone agrees. St Catherine of Alexandria, daughter of King Costus, is called now Catherine, now Dorothea, now Hecaterina by different writers, and yet the worshippers of saints do not therefore want her to be fictitious. And as for Baronius's second argument from the diversity of numbers, this too is made without good reason, since no one is unaware that popes of this kind, and indeed of other names, are liable to such variation: thus, for example, John is heard as the Sixteenth, Seventeenth or Eighteenth, Benedict is called the Eleventh or Thirteenth, Felix is said to be the Fourth or Fifth, Paul is often called the First or Second, Honorius is named the Second by some and the Third by others, and so on. Likewise the number of the Stephens varies. On the name John see Baronius himself at the year 1003, n. 10. But Frisingensis (mentioned above) and Sabellicus, so far as we know, alone call her the Seventh. Whoever believed her to be the Ninth, says Blondel l. c., no one has come to light so far. All make her the Eighth; a number which, if a woman were making a number here, would be reckoned correctly.

units.la: XLIII. Diversitatem porrò Baronius objicit in assignatio-ne temporis; alii hoc monstrum ponunt, inquit, An. 853. alii 854. alii 857. al. 904; præter eos, qui ponunt eam post Martinum I. anno 653. Alii post Johannem V. An. 686. Sed Auctores omnes, quos nostris inspicere datur, constanter inter Leonem IV. & Benedictum III. in anno 853. vel sequente Johannam collocant. Qui anno 857. collocârit præter Bergomatem, qui in annis reliquis, Doct. Blondello l. c. hactenus rursus innotuit nemo. Diversitatem autem cæteroquin in assign-ando Pontificibus antiquioribus tempore & magnam & quasi ordi-nariam esse, supra ostendimus.
units.tr: XLIII. Baronius further objects to a diversity in the assignment of time: Some place this monster, he says, in the year 853, others 854, others 857, others 904; besides those who place her after Martin I, in the year 653, and others after John V, in the year 686. But all the authors whom we are allowed to inspect consistently place Joan between Leo IV and Benedict III, in the year 853 or the following one. As for whoever placed her in the year 857, apart from Bergomas, in the other years, Blondel l. c. again says that no one has come to light so far. Moreover, we have shown above that a diversity in assigning the time of the earlier popes is both great and almost ordinary.

units.la: XLIV. Diversitatem quoque jactat in Pontificatûs dura-tione: Alii, inquit, eam sedisse tradunt anno uno & mense uno, & die-bus 4; alii annis 2. totidémque mensibus & diebus 4; alii 2. annis cum dimidio; 2. tantùm annis alii, alii verò 4. tantùm mensës. Ad quæ eadem respondemus. Nempe primò iterum soli Baronio constitit de tanta & hîc diversitate, quam disertissimè Onuphrius, qui multa legit, & circumstantiis quoque contrà nos, quantum posse sibi vi-debatur, usus est, refutat: Omnes, inquit, qui de ea meminerunt auctores, Joannis fœmina Pontificatum annorum 2. mensium 5. & dierum 3. insuper menstruam vacationem sedis inter Leonis IV. & Benedicti III. Sa-cerdotium (præter unum tantùm mendosum indicem in fine Septimi libri Ottonis Frisingensis collocatum) interponunt. Ast secundò quanta etiam est quoad durationem Pontificatûs antiquiorum aliorum Pontifi-ciorum differentia? Tanta certè, ut paucis dies sui tanto consensu adsignati deprehendantur. Atque si similiter quoad alios ex di-versitate Authorum respectu nominum, temporis, & annorum Pontificum argumentari vellent, multos profectò alios præter Jo-hannam ex Pontificum Catalogo expungere deberent. Cæterum hîc nobis liceat Bellarmini verba nostra facere: Sæpissimè constat de re, & non constat de modo, vel alia circumstantia. Atque ipsa illa in cir-cumstantiis quædam apud Authores diversitas, quæ tamen salvâ rei substantiâ est, arguit, non ab uno omnes descripsisse.
units.tr: XLIV. They also boast of a diversity in the length of the pontificate: Some, he says, hand down that she held the see for one year, one month and four days; others for two years and as many months and four days; others for two years and a half; some for only two years, others for only four months. To these same points we reply as follows. In the first place, again only Baronius has held to so great a diversity here, which Onuphrius, who read widely, refutes most clearly; and he too made use of the circumstances against us as far as he could see: All the authors, he says, who have mentioned her, place the woman John's pontificate at two years, five months and three days, and in addition an interval of one month's vacancy of the see between Leo IV and Benedict III (apart from one faulty index placed at the end of the seventh book of Otto of Freising). But in the second place, how great is the difference, too, in the length of the pontificates of other, earlier popes? So great indeed that the days assigned to a few of them are found with no such agreement. And if they wished to argue in the same way about the other popes from the diversity of authors with respect to names, times and years, they would surely have to strike many others from the catalogue of popes besides Joan. But here let me use the words of Bellarmine in our favour: It is very often agreed about the thing, and not agreed about the manner or some other circumstance. And that very diversity among the authors in certain circumstances, which nevertheless leaves the substance of the matter intact, shows that they did not all copy from one source.

units.la: XLV. Circumstantiarum repugnantiam atque contradi-ctionem in eodem authore vocant, quòd eadem Johanna, simul & Anglica & ex Moguntiaco oriunda, dicitur. Quam tamen contradi-ctionis speciem tollit Wernerus Rolfink scribens: Iste Johannes, AngliAnglicus cognomine, vel ab amasio, vel à commoratione, forte etiam ratione majorum habità, gente, sed natione Moguntinus; vel, Anglicus simulatione, Moguntinus secundum rei veritatem. Cæterùm de aliorum quoque patria litigatur.
units.tr: XLV. They call it a conflict and contradiction of circumstances in the same author that the same Joan is said to be both English and a native of Mainz. Werner Rolfinck, writing on this, removes this kind of contradiction: This John, surnamed the Englishman, either from a lover, or from a residence, or perhaps also from the descent of his ancestors, was of the Englishman's race, but by birth a Mainzer; or, English by pretence, Mainzer according to the truth of the matter. Moreover, the homeland of others is also disputed.

units.la: XLVI. Sed & aliàs narrationem absurditatis convincere student. Primò ex eo, quòd, cùm mox post mortem Leonis Benedictus electus sit, Pontificatui Johannæ nullum tempus superfit. Sed 1. constat, nihil esse incertius Chronologiâ Pontificum, maximè etiam circa illa tempora. 2. Onuphrius in suo Pontificum Chronico Platinæ subjuncto, nonnullis Johannam partim præcedentibus, partim sequentibus menses, imò annos addit apud Marianum non repertos, è quibus biennium Johannæ facilè conficiatur. 3. Cunradus à Lichtenau, Abbas Ursperg ensis An. 1215. creatus, Johannam omittens, Benedictum, cui alii 2. annos cum dimidio tribuunt, eodem, quo Pontificatum inierit, decessisse affirmat: quâ ratione etiam Johannæ tempus aliquod superesset. 4. Si Anastasius, ad quem hoc maximè provocant, Johannam omittere voluit, aut si alius Johannam ex Anastasio erasit, necessariò etiam Chronologia ita mutari debuit, ut Leo IV. & Benedictus III. cohaereant. Atque hoc pro nobis utimur Canone Philosophico, quem Doct. Launojus nobis hac in causa objicere voluit: Qui dat esse, dat etiam Consequentia ad esse.
units.tr: XLVI. But they also try to prove the story absurd on other grounds. First, from the fact that, since Benedict was elected soon after the death of Leo, no time remains for Joan's pontificate. But, 1. it is agreed that nothing is more uncertain than the chronology of the popes, especially about those times. 2. Onuphrius, in his chronicle of popes appended to Platina, adds to some popes, partly to those who went before Joan and partly to those who followed her, months and even years not found in Marianus, from which a two-year span for Joan can easily be made up. 3. Conrad of Lichtenau, Abbot of Ursperg, created in the year 1215, omitting Joan, affirms that Benedict, to whom others assign two and a half years, died in the same year in which he entered the pontificate; by which reckoning some time would also remain for Joan. 4. If Anastasius, to whom they appeal most of all, wished to omit Joan, or if someone else erased Joan from Anastasius, then the chronology must necessarily also have been altered so that Leo IV and Benedict III fit together. And for this we use against them the philosophical canon which Doctor Launoy wished to throw at us in this cause: He who gives the being, also gives the consequence to the being.

units.la: XLVII. Secundò (quod rursus tempus respicit,) ex eo, quòd interposità Johannâ Decretum Electionis Benedicti ad Lotharium Imp. qui anno Ch. 855. mortuus sit, quemadmodum Anastasius testetur, perferri haud potuerit. Quod argumentum Doct. Launojo ἀπόδεικτον (forte dicere voluit, ἀπόδεικτον) est. Verùm omninò videtur de Benedicto narrari, quod de Johanna narrandum fuisset. Ut enim non desunt Authores, qui electionem Benedicti in annum 856. rejiciunt, ita Ado Viennensis, sive ejus continuator, Electionem Benedicti defuncto jam Lothario accidisse, verbis conceptis testatur; quemadmodum etiam Acta publica desunt, in quibus Benedicti ceu Pontificis nomen occurrat. 2. Si hic scrupulus est, ut revera juxta istos Codices est, ad Anastasium pertinet, qui si redivivus orbi redderetur, rationem reddere teneretur hujus suæ narrationis. 3. Si hic scrupulus est, referri debet ad Chronologiam Pontificum in multis aliis quoque irreformabilem.
units.tr: XLVII. Secondly (which again concerns the time), from the fact that, with Joan interposed, the decree of Benedict's election could not have been carried to the Emperor Lothar, who, as Anastasius testifies, died in the year of Christ 855. This argument is demonstrative [ἀπόδεικτον] for Doctor Launoy (perhaps he meant to say demonstrative [ἀπόδεικτον]). But in truth it seems to be said about Benedict what ought to have been said about Joan. For just as there are not lacking authors who put Benedict's election in the year 856, so Ado of Vienne, or his continuator, attests in express words that Benedict's election took place after Lothar had already died; just as public records are also lacking in which the name of Benedict as pope occurs. 2. If this is a scruple, and indeed it is, according to those manuscripts, it belongs to Anastasius, who, if he were restored to life and returned to the world, would be bound to give an account of this narrative of his. 3. If this is a scruple, it must be referred to the chronology of the popes, which in many other matters too is not reformable.

units.la: XLVIII. Ad-
units.tr: XLVIII. Ad-

units.la: XLVIII. Adjungimus hîc argumentum à temporis ratione similiter desumptum Leonis Allatii, qui ex libello Græco Anonymi adversus Photium A. D. 891. scripto ista proferat; Photium à primo Leonis ad primum Formosi per 45. annos à 9. Rom. Pontificibus anathemate percussum fuisse, quorum annis si biennium Johannæ adderetur, 47. numerandi essent. Verùm ipse Doct. Blondellus respondet, veteres, quos detestandi scorti memoriam refricare puduerit, productis ad libitum Leoniani Benedictiníque Pontificatûs annis, lacunam explevisse. Accuratiores autem Chronologiæ Papissæ vindiciæ apud Cl. Maresium & Cl. Megerlinum l. c. videri possunt. XLIX.
units.tr: XLVIII. Here we add an argument drawn in the same way from chronology, which Leo Allatius sets out from an anonymous Greek pamphlet against Photius, written in A.D. 891: Photius was struck with anathema from the first Leo to the first Formosus, over 45 years, counting from the 9th Roman pontiff. If two years of Joan were added to those years, they would have to be counted as 47. But the learned Dr. Blondel himself replies that the ancients, who were ashamed to revive the memory of that detestable harlot, filled the gap by stretching the pontificates of Leo and Benedict as they pleased. More accurate defences of the Papist chronology can be seen in Maresius and Megerlin, l. c. XLIX.

units.la: Tertiò ex eo, quòd de Benedicto referatur, quemadmodum ex infimo gradu ad summum promotus sit; de Johanna nihil tale reperiri ajunt, víxque credibile esse, sub viri specie ignotam ad Pontificatum promotam fuisse; Sic etiam Electionis Benedicti Decretum ad Imperatorem commemorari, non item Johannæ; Et post Benedicti Electionem statim schisma Anastasii exortum esse, qui sub Leone IV. in Synodo excommunicatus sit, neque tamdiu Schisma distulisset. Ita primam, secundam, tertiam, quartam, (ad quintam jam jam respondimus) sextam & septimam (quæ ultima est) Doctissimi Launoji argumentationes conjungimus, tales certè, támque leves, ut vix credibile sit, virum acutissimum seriò rem egisse, sed potiùs in gratiam amicorum ista scripsisse, præsumi debeat. Nam 1. Si in Benedicto promotio per gradus in Ecclesia Romana acceptos contigit, idem in multis aliis Hispanis, Dalmatis, Thracibus, Afris, Syris &c. ante eum factum esse, nescitur, in quibusdam, Telesphoro, qui ex Anachoreta, Dionysio, qui ex Monacho Pontifices creati fuerunt & aliis, non factum esse, scitur. 2. Non sequitur; In Vita Johannæ non traditur, eam per gradus ascendisse; E. non ascendit per gradus; cùm compendiosior ejus historia exhibeatur, atque in ea res majoris momenti tantùm spectentur. 3. Si non per gradus ascendit, in eo laudanda videtur Ecclesiæ Romanæ consuetudo, quòd non habitâ graduum ratione, eruditioni tanto fastigio dignæ atque modo tam extraordinario comprobatæ præmium statim conferre voluit, maximè in defectu aliorum æquè dotibus instructorum; quod etiam in Promotionibus Politicis sæpissimè accidere solet. 4. Si Anastasius in Electione Benedicti etiam consensûs Senatûs Populíque Romani mentionem facit, neque tamen inde colligere volunt, consensum istum ad consue-
units.tr: Thirdly, they say that it is reported of Benedict how he was advanced from the lowest rank to the highest, but nothing of the kind is found about Joan. They add that it is hardly credible that she, unknown under the appearance of a man, was promoted to the papacy. Likewise, the decree of Benedict's election is mentioned as sent to the emperor, but not Joan's. And straight after Benedict's election, the schism of Anastasius arose, who was excommunicated under Leo IV in a synod, and it would not have delayed so long. Thus we join together the arguments of the most learned Launoy: the first, second, third, fourth, (we have already answered the fifth), the sixth and seventh (which is the last). They are certainly so weak and so slight that it is hard to believe that so keen a man treated the matter seriously, but should rather be presumed to have written these things to please his friends. For: 1. If Benedict's promotion through the grades accepted in the Roman Church happened, the same is unknown to have happened before him in many others, Spaniards, Dalmatians, Thracians, Africans, Syrians and so on; it is known not to have happened in some, such as Telesphorus, who was made pope from a hermit, Dionysius, who was made pope from a monk, and others. 2. It does not follow: the life of Joan does not record that she ascended through the grades; therefore she did not ascend through the grades; since her history is presented in a more compendious form, and in it only matters of greater moment are looked at. 3. If she did not ascend through the grades, the custom of the Roman Church is to be praised in this, that, without regard to the order of grades, it wished to confer at once a reward on learning worthy of so high a dignity and proved in so extraordinary a manner, especially in the absence of others equally endowed with gifts; which also very often happens in political promotions. 4. If Anastasius also mentions the consent of the Senate and the Roman people in Benedict's election, yet they do not wish to infer that this consent is to be referred to the apostolic custom; certainly they can no more refer the ascent through the grades to that. 4. The decree sent to the emperor you will seek in vain in any election whatever, nor does it follow that it did not happen because it is not related.

units.la: Ex Pagi Dissert. Hypatica. consuetudinem Apostolicam referri debere, certè haud magis ascensionem per gradus illuc referre possunt. 4. Electionis Decretum ad imperatorem missum frustra in quavis cujusvis Electione quæras, neque, dum id non narratur, non contigisse sequitur. Atque prudenter sæpe omiserunt Authores, ne nauseam perpetuâ repetitione Lectoribus crearent, maximè in exemplis rarioribus omittere potuerunt, quale Johannæ fuit. 6. Anastasium non Johannæ æmulum factum esse (si non factus est, quod forte contigit;) sed demum Benedicti, dicendum est, quia à Leone in Synodo excommunicatus nondum animos ad Pontificatum disposuerat, cùm adhuc in recenti memoria esset ejus Excommunicatio.
units.tr: ...ought to be referred to apostolic custom, from Pagi's Dissertatio Hypatica; but they certainly cannot refer the ascent through the grades to that custom any more than they can refer it there. (4) You will look in vain, in any election whatever, for the decree of election sent to the emperor, and it does not follow that something did not happen merely because it is not related. Authors have often and wisely left such things out, so as not to cause their readers nausea through constant repetition, and they could especially omit them in rarer cases, such as Joan's was. (6) It must be said that Anastasius did not become a rival of Joan (if he did not become one, which perhaps happened), but only of Benedict, because, having been excommunicated by Leo in a synod, he had not yet inclined his mind towards the papacy, since his excommunication was still fresh in memory.

units.la: I. Quarto ex eo, quòd Johanna, ut in fabula habeatur, Athenas studiorum gratiâ concedere haud potuerit, cùm neque Athenæ eo tempore fuerint, neque fuerit in iis amplius ullum Gymnasium. Athenas tunc non fuisse magno magnus alioquin historicus Onuphrius errore asserit, atque proin inter illos est, quibus Cl. Blondellus p. 54. succensetque, quòd nimirum Athenas, quarum in hanc usque diem rudera supersunt, ne Johannam unquam hospitali sinu fovisse fateri cogantur, Sæculo nono nullas fuisse cum Hardingo præfatè contendant; & jure quidem illis succensèt, cùm adhuc post captam Constantinopolim, teste Laonico Chalco condyla de Reb. Turc. l. 9. suprà laudato, urbis arcisque magnificentia admirationi esse potuerit. Sed neque exiguus Onuphrii aliorumque error est, ibi tunc Gymnasium nullum fuisse. Quod quidem Bellarminus ex Synesii, qui paulò post Basilium & Nazianzenum vixit, epistola ad fratrem probare annititur. Cùm tamen 1. tantùm testetur, non usque quaque sibi jam multùm erudito Athenas placuisse, quemadmodum ab initio haud magis placuerant Basilio 2. Si vel plane nullum Synesii tempore Athenis Gymnasium fuisset, esse tamen potuisset diu post, atque tempore Johannæ. 3. Quòd Bellarminus ex Cedreno & Zonara Bardam Cæsarem, qui posterior paulò Johannâ fuit, restauratorem literarum facit, illud de Constantinopoli, ubi opus erat, propter eorum, qui cum imperio erant, inscitiam atque barbariem intelligi debet; Sique Blondello p. 74. Scripti sui Gallici referente, circa annum 855. studium literarum etiam Athenis refloruisset, ex eo ipso sequeretur, ibi quidem antea languisse, non autem penitus extinctum fuisse; Atque licèt Michael bonarum literarum contemptor esset, ejus tamen Parens Theophilus à contrario affectu laudatur; ejúsque tempore eruditi Græci commemorantur, tempore illo ipso, quo Johanna ab
units.tr: I. Fourthly, from the fact that Joan, as the story goes, could not have gone to Athens to study, since neither was Athens in existence at that time, nor was there any longer a university there. The great historian Onuphrius, otherwise a great man, asserts by mistake that Athens did not then exist, and so he belongs to those whom Blondel p. 54. rebukes, because they claim that Athens, whose ruins survive to this day, was never forced to confess that it harboured Joan in its hospitable bosom, since in the ninth century there were no Athens at all, as Harding contends; and Blondel rightly rebukes them, since even after Constantinople was captured, as Laonicus Chalcocondyles testifies in De rebus Turcicis book 9, cited above, the magnificence of the city and its citadel could still be an object of admiration. But Onuphrius and others are also wrong in saying that there was then no university there at all. Bellarmine tries to prove this from the letter of Synesius to his brother, who lived shortly after Basil and Gregory Nazianzen. Yet, first, Synesius merely testifies that Athens did not please him, now that he was already very learned, just as it had not pleased Basil at the beginning. Second, even if there had been no university in Athens at all in Synesius' time, there could have been one long afterwards, at the time of Joan. Third, when Bellarmine makes Bardas Caesar, who was a little later than Joan, a restorer of letters on the testimony of Cedrenus and Zonaras, that must be understood of Constantinople, where it was needed, on account of the ignorance and barbarism of those who held power. And if, as Blondel p. 74. reports from his French writing, about the year 855 the study of letters flourished again even at Athens, it would follow from this that it had indeed languished there before, but had not been wholly extinguished. And although Michael was a despiser of good letters, his father Theophilus is praised for the opposite inclination; and in his time learned Greeks are mentioned, in the very time when Joan is read to have been taken to Athens by her lover, and when the admirably learned Photius arose, as also Boethius, a Roman, devoted himself to letters at Athens after Synesius. At the least, the opponents will also concede that Greek learning flourished at Athens then. For, says Blondel p. 69., suppose there was a literary…

units.la: {K}Kkkk Amasio Athenas deducta fuisse legitur, quoque multiplici eruditione admirabilis Photius exortus est, quemadmodum etiam Boethius, homo Romanus, post Synesium Athenis operam literis dedit. Saltem etiam concedent Adversarii, tunc Græcam linguam Athenis floruisse; Fac enim, inquit Blondellus p. 69. literarium splendorem tunc temporis tota Græcia deliquium passum, quid Latinum hominem addiscenda saltem linguæ spe in Orientem profecisci vetuisset? Quis vel Græce locutos Athenienses, vel Græci sermonis studio Occidentales aliquot teneri olim potuisse negaverit prudens? Sed & Blondellus Episcopi Athenensis, qui tum fuerit, mentionem facit p. 55. Reliquiæ igitur Atheniarum facile alicere potuerunt curiosum & discendi cupidum animum in tanta Occidentis barbarie, ut Antagonistæ incredibile judicent, Johannam eruditionis thesauro divitem atque Athenis reducem, Romæ Auditores atque æstimatores qualescunque reperire potuisse. Ad quam jam exceptionem progredimur.
units.tr: {K}Kkkk and in which Photius arose, admirable for his manifold learning, just as Boethius, a Roman man, also devoted himself to letters at Athens after Synesius. At least the opponents will concede that the Greek language then flourished at Athens. For, as Blondel says at p. 69: "Suppose that the splendour of letters had then fallen into a swoon throughout all Greece; what would have prevented a Latin man from going to the East, at least in the hope of learning the language? Who, being sensible, could deny that the Athenians then spoke Greek, or that some Westerners could once have been drawn by a zeal for the Greek tongue?" But Blondel also mentions the Bishop of Athens who was then in office, at p. 55. The remains of Athens could therefore easily have attracted a curious and eager mind, in such great barbarism of the West, so that the opponents judge it incredible that Joan, rich in the treasure of learning and returned from Athens, could have found hearers and admirers of some sort at Rome. To this objection we now proceed.

units.la: LI.
units.tr: LI.

units.la: Quinto enim historiam Johannæ ex eo absurditatis convincere volunt, quod Romæ bonas literas publice profiteri haud potuerit, quod ejus temporis hominibus (sunt verba Onuphrii) nihil minus cura esset, quam ut in urbe quispiam doceret. Quæ certe egregia Ecclesiæ Romanæ Pontificumque illorum temporum laus est, quod nimirum tam strenuè bonarum literarum studium tam utile ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem támque necessarium medium promoverunt! Sed quo major tunc Romæ præsupponitur insciitia, eo gratior tunc, quibusdam saltem institutio Johannæ, eo facilius ad consequendam dignitatem instrumentum esse potuit, atque quando Athenæ tunc de pristino splendore multum amiserunt, aliquam saltem Johannæ eruditionem admisisse concipi queunt Romani plane rudes. Quemadmodum etiam Doct. Blondell. confessione p. 68.69. nihil absurdi commenti sunt, qui tanto felicis ingenii acumine studiorumque gloria inclaruisse volucrunt, ut publice Rhetoricam, Logicam doceret, dignaque consentiente urbe Cleri populique suffragio censeretur, quæ post Leonis excessum Pontificale solium conscenderet. Id quod etiam exemplis quarundam doctarum fæminarum confirmat & ad illud Marcellæ ob singularem Theologicam cognitionem Romæ circa explicationem Scripturæ locorum non nunquam judicis electæ annotat: Si Sexum infirmitatemque professas tanto cultu prosecuta est Roma, ut supremos (ita dicere liceat) in sacris judices agnosceret, quid mulieri, quam
units.tr: Fifthly, they try to show from this that the story of Joan is absurd, because she could not have publicly taught good letters at Rome. (These are Onuphrius's words:) Nobody of that time cared less than that someone in the city should teach. Surely this is a fine praise of the Roman Church and of its pontiffs of that time, that they so vigorously promoted the study of good letters, a means so useful and so necessary for building up the Church! But the greater the ignorance they assume for Rome at that time, the more welcome, to at least some people, Joan's instruction would have been, and the easier it could have been for her to use it to gain the dignity. Since Athens had by then lost much of its former splendour, the Romans, who were quite uneducated, can be imagined to have admitted at least some learning of Joan's. Doctor Blondel, in his admission on pages 68 and 69, likewise shows that those who wanted her to have become famous for the sharpness of her gifts and the glory of her studies, so that she publicly taught rhetoric and logic and, with the agreement of the city and the vote of clergy and people, was judged worthy to climb the papal throne after Leo's death, have invented nothing absurd. He confirms this also with examples of certain learned women, and, noting the case of Marcella, who for her singular theological knowledge was sometimes chosen as judge in explaining passages of Scripture in Rome, he writes: If Rome, professing the sex and its weakness, honoured her with such devotion that it acknowledged her as, so to speak, supreme judge in sacred matters, what would be denied to a woman whom

units.la: Quinto ex eo, quod Romæ literarum applausu docere non potuerit; quam Virorum doctissimum credidisse volunt, reverentia dignationisque denegare potuisset?
units.tr: Fifthly, from the fact that she could not teach in Rome to the applause of letters: what would be denied of reverence and esteem to a woman whom they wish to have been believed the most learned of men?

units.la: LII. Sextò urget Onuphrius: Hæc mulier nonnisi in Papatu impragnatur! Et quæ diu ante Pontificatum amatorem habuerat sine partu aliquo, nunc senex, ut verisimile est, Papa ingravidata peperit! Nonne ante partum uterum intumescentem præ se ferebat? Et nemo ex tot familiaribus, ex tot aulicis, qui Romanum Pontificem comitari semper solent, rem tam claram animadvertit? Sed, ut Doct. Blondello p.67.68. judice, nihil absurdi commenti sunt, qui læve Johannæ mentum diu Romanos fallere potuisse crediderunt: quandoquidem totis nono, decimo &c. Seculis rasos maxima ex parte Italos fuisse testantur Icones; atque viri passim propemodum imberbes, nonnulla eccontra mulieres pilosa quotidie occurrunt; Et multæ aliæ (quarum exempla quædam producit) Sexum constanter dissimulare potuerunt; De more autem Viros radendi ita Joh. Pierius Valerianus Italus Doctissimus, in oratione pro Sacerdotum Barbis ad Cardinalem Hippolytum Medicem habita atque cum Clementis VII. mox privilegio emissa, inter alia loquitur; Eò aliquando nostrorum delicia processerunt, ut hujus rasitationis ergò confusa quodammodo Specie difficulter vir à fœmina internosceretur. Hinc accidit ut mulier, si vera esset, quæ per omnium ora fabula (à fando vocat sine veritatis, quod ex usu & circumstantiis patet, negatione) circumfertur, in sempiternum Sacro Sancti ordinis opprobrium, ad solii Pontificii Majestatem eveheretur; in cujus facti memoriam &c. His positis, quidni, quærit Blondellus, Moguntina mulier, Germanis suis imò Romanis habitu mutato imponere potuerit? Et eodem judice, nihil etiam absurdi commenti sunt, qui assumptâ virili veste longinquas peregrinationes suscepisse finxere; cùm Christianæ mulieres primitivæ aliquot, quarum exempla refert, idem fecerint; Quod enim in priscis Christianis mirabunda Roma celebravit, cur Seculi IX. hominibus vitio verteret? Ita faciles etiam sunt ad objectam ab Onuphrio ingravidationem, ut sic loquar, celandi difficultatem responsiones. 1. Quis dixit Onuphrio, Johannam tunc primùm & concepisse & peperisse? 2. Quis verisimile illud certum facit, jam senem fuisse? Notum est, atque mox ostendemus, tunc etiam juvenes, tunc promiscuè Viros nondum provectæ ætatis Pontifices creatos fuisse. 3. Verisimile æquè est, Johannam rerum naturalium peritam medicamentis aliquando conceptum prohibuisse vel abegisse, quod forte tandem fiduciâ ætatis ad Senilem vergentis facere neglexit. 4. Deo volente flagitium
units.tr: LII. Sixthly, Onuphrius presses: This woman was made pregnant only in the papacy! And she who had had a lover long before the pontificate, without any offspring, now, as is likely, an old man, bore a child as pope, having become pregnant! Did she not carry a swelling belly before the birth? And did none of so many intimates, so many courtiers, who always accompany the Roman pontiff, notice a thing so plain? But, in the judgment of Doctor Blondel on pages 67 and 68, those who believed that the smooth chin of Joan could long deceive the Romans have invented nothing absurd, since images testify that the Italians, for the most part, were shaven throughout the ninth, tenth and following centuries, and beardless men and, on the other hand, women with hairy faces appear almost everywhere every day; and many others (of whom he produces some examples) could constantly conceal their sex. Concerning the custom of shaving men, the learned Italian Giovanni Pierio Valeriano, in his oration on the beards of priests, delivered to Cardinal Ippolito de' Medici and soon published with the privilege of Clement VII, speaks among other things thus: Our men have at times gone so far in their delight that, by the confused appearance of such shaving, a man could hardly be told apart from a woman. Hence it happens that a woman, if the tale that is carried on everyone's lips were true (from fando, he calls it, a tale without the denial of truth, as is clear from usage and the circumstances), would be raised to the majesty of the papal throne, to the everlasting disgrace of the holy and sacred order; in memory of this deed etc. Given these points, why, asks Blondel, could the woman from Mainz not have deceived her Germans, or even the Romans, by changing her dress? And by the same judgment, those who pretended that she undertook long journeys in male clothing have invented nothing absurd, since several early Christian women, whose examples he cites, did the same; for why should it be held against people of the ninth century what marvelling Rome celebrated in the early Christians? So too the replies to the difficulty of concealing pregnancy, as I may put it, that Onuphrius raises, are easy. 1. Who told Onuphrius that Joan first conceived and first gave birth then? 2. Who makes it certain that she was already old, which that likely claims? It is known, and we will soon show, that then young men, and men not yet of advanced age, were made popes indiscriminately. 3. It is equally likely that Joan, skilled in natural things, once prevented or aborted the conception with medicines, which perhaps, trusting in her age now drawing toward old age, she neglected to do at last. 4. God willing, the crime

units.la: Sextò ac constitutione gravida gitium tandem detegi debuit. 5. Quotidie usu venire solet, ut mulierculæ arte & vafricie Johannâ longè inferiores ad ipsum usque partûs tempus uterum celent 6. Atque heic multùm juvare Johannam potuit, quòd Sexum mentita erat, quis enim Vir, vel quæ Virum artificiosè simulans & Pontifex maximus in talem suspicionem facilè adduceretur? 7. Juvare etiam potuerunt vestes Pontificales. 8. Exempla recentia probant, Pontifices non semper quosvis propiùs admittere. 9. Johanna ne admitteret, peculiares causas habuit.
units.tr: Sixthly, and her pregnancy would at last have to come to light. 5. Every day it happens that little women, far inferior to Joan in skill and cunning, hide a pregnancy right up to the time of delivery. 6. And here Joan's disguise as a man could greatly have helped her, for who, or what woman pretending to be a man, would easily be brought under such suspicion by the supreme pontiff? 7. The papal vestments could also have helped. 8. Recent examples prove that popes do not always admit just anyone close to them. 9. Joan had particular reasons for not admitting anyone.

units.la: LIII. Septimò instat Bellarminus : Nullam habet probabilitatem, quòd mulier uterum gerens jam tot mensesl, tunc maximè voluerit procedere, quando maximè periculum erat, ut detegeretur. Respondemus. 1. Quis dicit, tunc maximè procedere voluisse? Et aliàs processit. 2. Quis probat, jam tot menses uterum gessisse? Si de plenario mensium numero verba accipiantur. Verisimillimum est atque etiam ex obitu puerperæ apparet, fœtum tempore parum congruo & justo maturiùs editum esse, ut casum Consilio prævertere fœmina alioquin vaferrima nequiverit. 3. Quis nescit judicium Dei, quo urgente nihil profuit versutæ sua versutia, sed venit summa dies & ineluctabile malum? 4. Quem latet, quasdam esse festivitates, atque occasiones alias, quibus Pontifex, si per Sanitatem ullo modo liceat, adesse nunquam facilè omittit? 5. Cui non constat incertitudo temporis pariendi, ob quam ita denuò pronunciat Doct. Blondellus p. 70. Nihil absurdi commenti sunt, qui in media platea puerperii doloribus oppressam vulgárunt: Quis enim momentum quo partum fusura mulier, vel pranoscat, vel certò statuat? Quàm multas quotidie imparatas, alio intentas, uteri propemodum oblitas, occupat partitudo? Quam etiam exemplis Cl. Maresius Pap. Reflit. p. 201. confirmat; Imò & ego, inquit, puer olim vidi mulierem, ex eorum grege, qui Zingari appellantur, in media platea parturientem; Novi & rusticam, quæ in messe occupata cum viro, dum pressa partitudinis doloribus, vult domum redire, in itinere peperit sola; fœtúmque involvit panniculo, quem ex suo indusio laceravit, & eum ita in suis ulnis domum detulit? LIV. Octavò dicunt, Pontifices tunc non habitâsse in Vaticano, ut inde ad Lateranum pergens parere potuerit. Ast 1. Martinus Polonus, qui hanc loci circumstantiam annotavit, non dicit, è Palatio Vaticano in Lateranum iviße, sed; quum de S. Petro, è Templo scilicet, ubi statio fuerat & Sacra celebrata erant, in Lateranum tende- Septimò ex eo, quòd æquè probabilitate careat, gravidam publicè incedere voluisse. Octavò ex eo, quòd Pontifices tunc non in Vaticano habitarint. tenderet; Fæminæ autem Rempublicam quidem, sed non amasium Sexum celantis partus æquè in regressu, quàm in egressu accidere potuit. 2. Posito, etiam domum aliquam in vicinia S. Petri intelligi, imò posito, per unum atque alterum diem Johannam in ea commoratam esse, nihil tamen absurdi ponitur atque eadem semper responsio valet. 3. Doctissimo Blondello iterum nihil absurdi commenti sunt, qui ex Vaticano ad Lateranensem Basilicam ad Litanias profectam dixerunt: ut enim statum Papārum domicilium Lateranense Patriarchium fuisse demus; post munitum à Leone IV. Vaticanum potuere nonnulli ibidem aliquamdiu harere; imò facile potuisset è Laterano progressa mulier in reditu parturitionis torminibus intercipi. Quamvis idem Blondellus alibi profectionem hanc tanquam improbabilem rejiciens sibi contrarietur.
units.tr: LIII. Seventhly, Bellarmine insists: There is no probability that a woman carrying a child now so many months along would have wished to go forth just when there was the greatest danger of being found out. We reply. 1. Who says she wished to go forth then especially? She also went forth at other times. 2. Who proves that she had already carried the child for so many months? That is, if the words are taken as full months. It is most probable, and it also appears from the death of the woman in childbirth, that the foetus was born earlier than the proper and fitting time, so that this very cunning woman could not otherwise forestall the danger by planning. 3. Who does not know the judgment of God, under whose pressure her cunning was of no use to her, but the great day came and an unavoidable evil? 4. Who does not know that there are certain festivals and other occasions at which the pope, if he is in health in any way, never easily fails to be present? 5. Who is not aware of the uncertainty of the time of delivery, on account of which Doctor Blondel again pronounces, on page 70: Those who spread the report that she was overtaken by the pains of childbirth in the middle of the street have invented nothing absurd. For who can know beforehand, or fix with certainty, the moment when a woman is about to bring forth? How many women every day are seized by labour pains while unprepared, busy with something else, almost forgetful of the womb? Cl. Maresius also confirms this with examples in his Papal Reflections, page 201: Indeed, he says, I once saw, as a boy, a woman of that group called Gypsies giving birth in the middle of the street. I also know a country woman who, busy at the harvest with her husband, when pressed by labour pains wanted to return home, and gave birth alone on the way, and wrapped the infant in a rag which she tore from her underskirt, and so carried it home in her arms?

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: Nonò pertendit Baronius, si ista revera contigissent. Photium Pseud-Episcopum Constantinopolitanum atque Michaelem Imperatorem, hostes Romanæ Ecclesiæ infensissimos, quique tota conviciorum plaustra in eam ejusque Antistites congesserint, de iis minimè tacituros fuisse. Ꝑ. 1. Cum Doctiss. Blondello ad vicesimum quintum ex crassioribus Tractationis Ræmundianæ nævis: Quid ad nos? An quisquis adversus Romanam sedem bellum suscipit, hoc ipso probra ejus omnia conquirere necesse habet; nec sibi satis cavere dicendus est, si propriam sine aliorum contumelia causam tueatur? Atque specialius de Episcopis Germanis: Cùm Nicolaum unum stylo suo fodicare aggressi nihil in Romanam sedem — moliti sint; quis prudens ab eis exigat, ut quicquid seu verè, seu in specie Romanorum famam dignitatémque pessundabat, in protestationis sua breviculum converherent? 2. Photii scripta à Basilio Michaelis successore Romam missa atque ibi in cineres redacta sunt; Verisimile autem est, bilem Pontificibus Nicolao I. & Hadriano II. vel maximè movisse objectam Johannæ historiam, maximè quando posthac alii Græci eandem producere non omiserunt; Certum autem illud est, non posse igitur, ex silentio Photii argumentum necti; cujus silentii & 3. causa fuisset, quòd ipse Photius Eunuchus palàm fuit & per veteres Canones irregularis, nihilominùs ad Episcopatum Constantinopolitanum promotus, & ex Laico Eunucho sextidui spatio Patriarcha factus & consecratus, ut ex Niceta refert Baronius ad an. 818. n. 5. Sed vitio carere debet, qui paratus est dicere in alium, œimque suæ irregularitatis sibi hac in parte Photius bene conscius fuerit,
units.tr: Ninthly, Baronius argues that if these things had really happened, Photius, the pseudo-bishop of Constantinople, and the Emperor Michael, the bitterest enemies of the Roman Church, who heaped whole carts of insults upon it and its bishops, would not have kept silent about them. (1) With the most learned Blondel, at the twenty-fifth of the grosser blemishes of Ramundus's treatise: What is that to us? Is anyone who takes up war against the Roman see bound by that very fact to hunt out all its disgraces? Or is he to be said not to have taken enough care if he defends his own cause without insulting others? And more particularly about the German bishops: Since they set about stabbing Nicholas alone with their pen and attempted nothing against the Roman see, what prudent person would require of them that they turn into a little protest everything that, whether truly or in appearance, cast down the reputation and dignity of the Romans? (2) Photius' writings were sent to Rome by Basil, Michael's successor, and burned there to ashes. It is likely, however, that the story of Joan objected to them especially stirred the bile of the popes Nicholas I and Hadrian II, the more so since afterwards other Greeks did not hesitate to bring it forward. It is certain, therefore, that no argument can be built on Photius' silence. (3) The cause of that silence might also have been that Photius himself was openly a eunuch and by the ancient canons irregular, yet was nevertheless promoted to the see of Constantinople, and was made patriarch and consecrated after being a lay eunuch for six days, as Baronius reports from Nicetas at the year 818, n. 5. But he ought to be free from fault who is ready to say such a thing against another; and if Photius was well aware of his own irregularity on this point,

units.la: Kkkk 3 fuerit, vix potuisse videtur se mi Vir mulierem objicere Romæ, quin illud audiret illico, Cæcus in lusco. Ad silentium Michaelis 4. respondemus cum Blondello rursus l. c. Michaelis scripta omnia perierunt (Ramundo ipsamet teste;) ut frustra se rursus torqueant, qui rursus de non entibus sibi judicium sumunt. Quamvis idem ejusdem Ramundi naevum crassiorem non agnoscimus sextum faciat, quod Michaelis epistolam reperiri dixit; eumque ex Baronio ad an. 865. § 75. refutet, ubi tradita igni dicitur; quare etiam subdit: Sed eas (literas) forte (Phænicis instar) in favillas resolutas è medio rogo postlim nio excitavit Ramundus noster, ut Romam Burdigalam in sinum ejus evolarent. 5. Eodem judice, quibus Joannam Romæ sedisse persuasum e I facile porro regerent; Michaelem (Nicolao Papa epist. 8. fatente) ab injuriis & convitiis epistolam inchoasse, in Nicolaum ipsummet pr mamque & magistram Ecclesiarum omnium locutum, ad Ecclesiæ Romanæ injuriam, ad ipsius privilegiorum imminutionem, ad sedis Apostolicæ Præsulum derogationem scripsisse; Epist. 70. 39. Michaelem protospatharium cum epistola injuriis plena Romam direxisse: Nicolaum vero injurias suas non curasse, ad nonnulla, quæ in ipsa superfuerunt epistola, nihil respondisse, sed potius philosophando contempsisse, cum plena essent omni pravitate & blasphemia, & contra ipsam dispositionem Dei venena diffunderent: Quo probabile ipsis fiat, nasutum Pontificem pudenda quædam, quibus eluendis imparem se sentiret (verbi gratia Joanna Papatum, stuprum, partum) consulto prætermisse; quódque factum negat Allatius, factum insinuasse.
units.tr: Kkkk 3 he could hardly have seemed able to throw a woman in Rome in a man's face without hearing at once, a blind man among the one-eyed. To Michael's silence we reply again with Blondel, l.c. Michael's writings all perished (as Ramundus himself testifies), so that those who once more pass judgment on non-existent things may torment themselves in vain. Yet the same Ramundus's grosser blemish, the sixth, is not acknowledged, which says that a letter of Michael's was found; and Baronius refutes this at the year 865, § 75, where it is said to have been given to the fire. Hence he also adds: But perhaps these letters, dissolved into ashes like the phoenix, were raised by our Ramundus from the middle of the pyre after a long interval, so that they might fly to Bordeaux, into his bosom, from Rome. (5) By the same judge, those who are persuaded that Joan sat in Rome could easily answer that Michael (as Pope Nicholas admits in epistle 8) began the letter with injuries and insults, speaking against Nicholas himself, the head and teacher of all the Churches, and wrote to the injury of the Roman Church, to the diminishing of its privileges and to the disparagement of the Prelates of the Apostolic see; (epistle 70, 39) that Michael the protospatharius sent to Rome a letter full of injuries; but that Nicholas did not care about his injuries, and made no reply to the particular points that remained in that letter, but rather despised them with philosophical airs, since they were full of all wickedness and blasphemy and spread poisons against God's very ordinance. From this it becomes probable that the keen-scented Pontiff consciously passed over certain shameful matters, which he felt himself unable to wash away (for example, Pope Joan, the fornication, the childbirth); and what Allatius denies to have happened, he suggested had happened.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Decimo ita argumentatur Baronius; Si ista revera contigisset Leonem IX. minime ausurum fuisse Constantinopolitanis exprobrare, quod in illorum Ecclesia aliquando fæmina in sede Pontificum sublimata sit. Quæ ratio Genebrardo ineluctabilis est; Cui tamen reponimus. 1. Neminem nobis fidem facere posse, Leonis IX. epistolam manifeste falsa continentem non esse multarum aliarum ad instar supposititiam. 2. Inter Johannam & Leonem IX. esse annos ducentos, ut Leo Johannam aut in memoria non habere, ut scire potuerit, monumenta de Johanna Græcis antecessorum suorum industria subtracta esse atque aliás etiam ejus memoriam apud Græcos intercidisse. 3. Forte astu Politico impudenter usus est Leo, Constantinopolitanis id, quod sibi imputandum erat, imputans, idque varias ob causas a. Ne Eunuchos Constanti-
units.tr: Tenth, Baronius argues thus: If these things had really happened, Leo IX would certainly not have dared to reproach the Constantinopolitans that once in their Church a woman had been raised to the papal throne. This argument is unanswerable to Genebrard; yet we reply to it. (1) No one can convince us that Leo IX's letter, which plainly contains falsehoods, is not spurious like many others of the kind. (2) Between Joan and Leo IX there are two hundred years, so that Leo either had no memory of Joan or could not have known of her; the records about Joan had been removed by the diligence of the Greeks' predecessors, and in any case her memory had perished among the Greeks. (3) Perhaps Leo, using a political trick shamelessly, charged the Constantinopolitans with what was really to be imputed to himself, and he did so for various reasons: a. lest, reproaching the eunuchs of Constanti-

units.la: a Decimo exeo, quod Leo IX. Græcis talia exprobrare ausus sit. stantinopolitanos exprobrantem feriat facilis de fæmina Romana retorsio: simili fere ratione, quâ manticularii in foro primi furem conclamare solent, ne ipsi facinoris authores habeantur: & mulier mali commatis rixando cum alia, ei statim objicit adulteria & artes meretricias, ut in antecessum eludat, quæcunque istius generis novit sibi objici posse, & quò, si objiciantur, pro muliebribus recriminationibus habeantur & minùs fidei reperiant. β. Ut indirecte insinuet, virilitatis explorationem Romanam non tam deberi famæ de Papissa, quàm verò detestationi Eunuchorum Constantinopolitanorum. γ. Ut tam Græcos obligaret ad nihil credendum de Johanna, ac ipse dicebat, nolle se credere famæ de muliere Constantinopolitana. 4. Impudentia Leonis jam ex eo constat, quòd salsissima Constantinopolitanis affingere ausus fuit; neque enim fortasse, ut Baronius conjicit, respexit ad Cynædos ludicros Imperatorij Michaëlis in aula Pontificis; (atque ne quidem illa ratione fundamentum accusatio habuisset justum) cùm illud ante 200. tunc annos contigerit; atque sub ipsis Johannæ temporibus, quibus certè, qui Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ tunc præerant, Ignatius atque ei postea oppositus Photius, uterque magni nominis, suspicionem de fæmina illorum temporum Patriarcha facilè excluserunt. 5. Si nunc exstaret Michaëlis ad Leonem responsum, forte ex illo deprehenderemus, hanc vafriciem Leonis, uti debuit, à Michaële castigatam fuisse.
units.tr: a. On the tenth point, that Leo IX dared to reproach the Greeks with such things. nople, an easy retort about a Roman woman might strike him: much as market-porters in the forum usually shout "thief!" so as not to be taken for the authors of the crime themselves; and a woman who, quarrelling with another in a shrill exchange, at once throws at her adulteries and whorish arts, so as to forestall whatever of that kind she knows can be thrown at her, so that, if such things are thrown, they may be taken as womanly recriminations and find less credence. (b) So that he might indirectly insinuate that the Roman examination of virility is owed not so much to the story of Pope Joan as to the detestation of the Constantinopolitan eunuchs. (c) So that he might oblige the Greeks to believe nothing about Joan, just as he himself said he was unwilling to believe the story about a woman of Constantinople. (4) Leo's shamelessness is already plain from the fact that he dared to ascribe the most false things to the Constantinopolitans. For he perhaps did not, as Baronius conjectures, look to the ludicrous catamites of the Emperor Michael at the Pontiff's court (and not even on that ground would the accusation have been just), since that happened two hundred years earlier; and in the very times of Joan, those who then presided over the Church of Constantinople, Ignatius and Photius, who was afterwards set against him, both men of great name, easily excluded any suspicion of a woman patriarch of those times. (5) If Michael's reply to Leo still existed, perhaps from it we would discover that this crafty trick of Leo was rebuked by Michael as it deserved.

units.la: LVII. Undecimò pugnat cum Epistolis aliis illo tempore, ut ait, scriptis.
units.tr: LVII. Eleventhly, he argues against the other letters written at that time, as he says.

units.la: Dicit, Lupum Abbatem Ferrariensem in epistola ad Benedictum eum Successorem Leonis vocare, neque pro zelo suo ullam sceleris mentionem facere; Nicolaum autem, qui post 5. annos Benedicto successerit, in epistolis duabus inter præde cessores suos Johannam non numerare, neque annos ejus duodecim annis quibus Ignatium Patriarcham sedisse dicat, adjungere; atque Photium simul cum Imperatore severè reprehendere, quòd ille ex Laico Episcopum se ordinari passus sit. Atque istæ sunt reliquiæ argumentorum Baronianorum, quibus ita occurrimus. 1. Dat epistolas Baronius ex scriniis suis forte supposititias, forte idem ex parte mutilationis infortunium expertas. 2. Non dat Epistolarum verba ipsamet dum integras, quas etiam hastenus mihi videre atque proin ex circumstantiis judicium perficere haud contigit. Sed posito, omnia ita contigisse atque scripta esse. 3. Quando Benedictus nedictus Leonis Successor vocatur, atque in enarrandis ejus prædecessoribus Johannæ ratio nulla habetur; id & verè & decorè fit. Verè, cùm omninò Benedictus Leonis Successor fuerit, licèt non immediatus, quemadmodum omnes Successores Petri haberi volunt, & interdum Romani Pontifices, utor verbis Papirii Massoni de Urbis Episc. l. 5. in Cœlest. 3. sol 212. apud Alex. Cookium Dial. p. 119, non solùm eos, qui proximi Episcopi fuere, sed plerosque disjunctissimos, illo nomine (Prædecessores) complectuntur; Imò etiam immediatus fuit, quatenus Johanna inter legitimos Pontifices, maximè ex illorum hypothesibus, locum habere minimè potuit. Decorè etiam fit, quia detestandæ fœminæ ratio haberi non poterat, neque à Lupo, qui ita Benedictum dehonestàsset; neque à Nicolao, qui Benedictum & se. 4. Nemo vel Lynceis oculis præditus perspicere poterit, quomodo duodecennis Patriarchatus Ignatii apud Baronium sive Johannæ, sive annorum ejus mentionem requirat ullam. 5. Potuit fieri, ut Lupus sciverit quidem Benedicti electionem, sed nondum, cùm scriberet, audità itatim Benedicti electione, pro certo compertum habuerit, quis qualisve fuisset Johannes, quo cum nihil familiaritatis, ut cum Leone habuerat, ater an albus, mas an fœmina; nec primis rumoribus credendum censuerit. 6. Neque necesse fuit, ut conquereretur Lupus de Johannæ turpitudine, alia tunc agens; maximè autem præsupponere debuit, si jam certò factum cognovit, Benedictum mala domestica & optimè nòsse, & vehementer de iis dolere. 7. Quidnì potuerit Nicolaus Photium reprehendere, vel posito Johannæ casu? An igitur, eo posito, omnes Pontificum reprehensiones & quidem in perpetuum cessare debuissent? Majus certè scandalum (si ullum in promotione Photii, quatenus ex Laico ordinatus erat, fuit;) & multò majus fuit, quòd sedem Romanam fœmina occupaverat; interim tamen per deceptionem illud admissum fuit, atque Johannam saltem per unum atque alterum gradum promotam fuisse verisimile est, ut non se illo exemplo excusare potuisset Photius, ut & aliàs crimine alterius stultè excusatur.
units.tr: He says that Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières, in his letter to Benedict, calls him the successor of Leo, and makes no mention of any crime, despite his zeal. He says that Nicholas, who succeeded Benedict five years later, does not count Joan among his predecessors in his two letters, and does not add her years to the twelve years in which he says Ignatius sat as Patriarch. He also says that Photius, together with the Emperor, sharply rebukes Nicholas for allowing a layman to be ordained as bishop. These are the remains of Baronius's arguments, and this is how we answer them. (1) Baronius gives these letters from his own archives; perhaps they are spurious, or perhaps they have suffered the misfortune of being mutilated. (2) He does not give the words of the letters in full, and I have not yet been able to see them, so I cannot form a judgement from the circumstances. But let us suppose that everything happened as they say and was written as they say. (3) When Benedict is called the successor of Leo, and no account is taken of Joan in the list of his predecessors, this is both truthful and fitting. It is truthful, since Benedict was certainly the successor of Leo, even if not his immediate one, as all successors of Peter wish to be regarded; and, to use the words of Papirius Masso, On the Bishops of the City, book 5, on Celestine 3, page 212, cited by Alexander Cook in his Dialogue, page 119, "Roman pontiffs sometimes embrace under that name (predecessors) not only those who were their nearest bishops, but many who were quite remote." Indeed, Joan was not even his immediate predecessor in such a way that she could possibly have a place among the lawful pontiffs, especially on their own hypotheses.
