It is also fitting, since no account could be taken of a detestable woman, neither by Lupus, who would thereby have dishonoured Benedict, nor by Nicholas, who would have dishonoured both Benedict and himself. (4) No one, even with eyes as sharp as a lynx's, could see how the twelve-year Patriarchate of Ignatius in Baronius requires any mention of Joan or of her years. (5) It is possible that Lupus knew of Benedict's election but, when he wrote, had not yet heard of it; or, having heard of it, he did not yet know for certain who or what sort of man Joan had been, with whom he had no familiarity, as he had with Leo, whether dark or fair, male or female; and he judged that the first rumours should not be believed. (6) Nor was it necessary for Lupus to complain of Joan's disgrace, since he was then busy with other matters; but, if he had already learned the fact for certain, he must have presupposed that Benedict knew of the domestic scandal very well and grieved greatly over it. (7) Why could Nicholas not rebuke Photius, even granting the case of Joan? Would all the rebukes of the pontiffs, then, have had to cease for ever? The scandal would certainly have been greater (if there was any scandal in the promotion of Photius, insofar as he was ordained from the laity), and it would have been much greater that the Roman see had been occupied by a woman. Yet meanwhile that was admitted through deception, and it is likely that Joan had been promoted at least one or two grades, so Photius could not have excused himself by that example, just as he foolishly excuses himself, on other occasions too, by another's crime.

units.la: LVIII. Duodecimò tandem Labbeus objicit, quòd nec ipsa Johanna in biennio suo quicquam egerit, nullum diploma scripserit, nullam epistolam emiserit, ac pro famosa sua eruditione proculdubio consulta, nihil responderit; nec alius quisquam Imperator vel Rex &c. aliquid gesserit, quo ejus memoria commendaretur. Verisimile autem est, quod & even-
units.tr: LVIII. Twelfthly and finally, Labbe objects that Joan herself did nothing in her two years, wrote no decree, sent out no letter, and, despite her famous learning, answered no consultation, which would undoubtedly have been made; nor did any other emperor or king, and so on, do anything by which her memory might be commended. It is likely, however, that both the event...

units.la: Duodecimò ex eo, quod nihil extet de rebus gestis Iohanna. & eventus docuit, illam genio suo indulsisse, ac licet (ut in quibusdam Codicibus Martini Poloni extare dicitur) primo post Ambrosium multas praefationes Missarum composuerit, eas modo omnes esse interdictas; quod etiam de epistolis ejus abolitis intelligendum est. Si vero omnes, de quorum rebus gestis nihil nobis constat, ex Catalogo Pontificum essent expungendi, multi certe expungendi essent. Quemadmodum etiam ex. gr. Nicolaus I. licet alias plus satis strepere, in primo tamen biennio nihil publicavit, neque ejus in Actis publicis per illud biennium ullamentio reperitur. Interim tamen Radulphus Flaviacensis supra laudatus citato l. Ludovicum II. Imperatorem & Edelvolphum Angliae Regem ab ea coronatos esse tradit. Sic etiam ab hoc dona accepisse & decrevisse dicitur, privilegia Sedis Romanae per 100. annorum praescriptionem non infirmari. De rebus aliorum, quae nimirum, Johanna sedente, contigerint, scribit Platina in Vita; esse, qui dicant hujus temporibus B. Vincentii Corpus e Valentia citerioris Hispaniae civitate, a quodam Monacho in pagum Albiensem ulterioris Galliae deportatum; item, Lotharium jam grandem natu, sumpto Monachorum habitu, filium Ludovicum Imperatorem reliquisse &c. Quae Sabellicus tunc contigisse, satis constare Rapsod. Histor. Ennead. 9. l. 1. asserit.
units.tr: Twelfthly, from the fact that nothing is extant concerning the deeds of Joan, and the outcome has shown that she indulged her own disposition. And although (as is said to be found in some manuscripts of Martin of Poland) she composed many prefaces for Masses after Ambrose, these have all since been forbidden, and the same must be understood of her letters, which were abolished. But if all those whose deeds we know nothing of were to be struck from the catalogue of pontiffs, many would certainly have to be struck out. Thus, for example, Nicholas I, although otherwise making more than enough noise, published nothing in the first two years, and no mention of him is found in the public records for that period. Meanwhile, Radulphus Flaviacensis, cited above in the passage mentioned, reports that Louis II, Emperor, and Edelwulf, King of England, were crowned by her. It is also said that she granted and decreed privileges to them, and that the privileges of the Roman See are not weakened by prescription of one hundred years. Concerning the deeds of others which, of course, happened while Joan was sitting, Platina writes in the Life: "There are those who say that in her time the body of Saint Vincent was carried from Valentia, a city of Hither Spain, by a certain monk to a village of the Albigeois in farther Gaul; likewise that Lothair, already advanced in years, took the habit of monks and left his son, Emperor Louis, and so on." Sabellicus asserts that these things happened at that time, and that this is "sufficiently established" in Rapsodia historiarum, Ennead 9, book 1.

units.la: LIX. Aliud jam, postquam historiam Johannae veram esse probavimus, atque ad objectiones Antagonistarum, quotcunque videre contigit, respondimus, restare non potest, quam ut eorundem de origine fabulae, quam vocitant, varias opiniones proponamus, atque ad breve examen vocemus; varias, inquam, opiniones; sex tuplicem enim (quantum quidem ego sciam) assignant conjiciendo originem diversi, atque ita a se invicem dissentiunt. Et quadruplex quidem origo ab ipsa sede Romana derivatur, duplex aliunde petitur. Qui a sede Romana originem derivant vel a Johanne VIII. qui, si in numero quoque Johannae ratio habeatur, IX. fuit; vel a Johanne IX. qui tum X. vel a Johanne XXII. eam arcessunt.
units.tr: LIX. Now that we have proved the history of Joan to be true, and have answered the objections of her opponents, as many as I have been able to see, there remains only to set out the various opinions of these same men on the origin of what they call the fable, and to bring them to a brief examination. I say various opinions; for (as far as I know) they assign six or more different origins by conjecture, and so they disagree among themselves. Four of these origins are derived from the Roman See itself, and two are sought elsewhere. Those who derive the origin from the Roman See derive it either from John VIII, who, if Joan is also counted, was the ninth of that name, or from John IX, who was then the tenth, or they bring it from John XXII.

units.la: LX. A Johanne VIII. sive IX. arcessit, qui & aliam alibi, ut mox indicabimus, tradit originem, minus hic quoque sibi constans Cardinalis Baronius, dum ad an. 879. n. 5. de nimia animi facilitate Johannis illius loquitur, qua nescivit resistere Photio Eunucho; sed, cum victus sit ab hoc semiviro, ipsum non Virum, sed faeminam potius nuncupandum fuisse; & sic nomen contumeliae in opinionem veritatis transfiisse &c. Verum frigidam conjecturam ipse Blond. Ilus refellit, atque optime respondet; haec ita quidem (suppositâ narrationis falsitate) non improbabiliter dici, si inter Romanos praecipuè male audiffet Johannes ; sed eo forte nomine Germanis (apud quos audita primum Johanna mentio) (loquitur ex hypothesi negantium) invisus fuit, quòd calcatâ scripti à Ludovico II. Imp. in gratiam Ludovici patrui consobrinorúmque Germaniae regum testamenti religione,Caroli Calvi temere partes secutus,legitimos haeredes Ludovicum, filiósque, Carolomannum, Ludovicum & Carlitum (qui postea Crassus dictus est) Italiâ exclusit; In quo se certè plùs quàm Virum,licèt malum,praestitit. Contrà nihil vel apud Germanos,vel apud Francos occurrit, neque vel minimum indicium,hunc Pontificem unquam dictum esse faeminam. Quibus addimus,Johannem illum 60. annis Johannâ Papissâ secundùm communem calculum, posteriorem esse, atque ideò potiùs in illud tempus rejici debuisse, imò etiam multos alios potiori jure faeminarum nomine appellandos fuisse;neque Johannem hunc, qui per integrum decennium sedit, cum exiguo Pontificatûs Johannae tempore convenire, neque aliquid commisisse,ut puerum peperisse dici posset. Adde,quòd nullius Baronii conjectura testimonio nititur, & multis aliâs laudibus hic Papa à Platina & Onuphrio oneratur; nec tanti fuit,consensisse in restitutionem Photii Viri Doctissimi totius Orientis voto & assensu factam.
units.tr: LX. Those who trace it to John VIII or IX, and who also give another origin elsewhere, as we shall soon point out, include the Cardinal Baronius, who is less consistent here too. At the year 879, n. 5, he speaks of the excessive softness of mind of that John, by which he did not know how to resist Photius the eunuch; "but, since he was conquered by this half-man, he ought rather to be called not a man but a woman; and so the name of insult passed into the opinion of truth," and so on. But Blondel himself refutes this cold conjecture and answers very well: "These things could indeed be said, supposing the falsity of the narrative, not improbably, if John had been especially ill spoken of among the Romans; but perhaps he was hated by the Germans (among whom the mention of Joan was first heard) (he speaks on the hypothesis of those who deny it) because, trampling underfoot the sacred character of the will written by Emperor Louis II, in favour of his uncle Louis and his cousins, the kings of Germany, he rashly followed the party of Charles the Bald and excluded from Italy the lawful heirs, Louis, and his sons, Carloman, Louis and Charles (who was afterwards called the Fat)." In this he certainly showed himself more than a man, though an evil one. On the other hand, nothing occurs, either among the Germans or among the Franks, not even the slightest indication that this pontiff was ever called a woman. To these we add that this John, by the common reckoning, came sixty years after Pope Joan, and so ought rather to be placed in that time; indeed, many others would have had a much better right to be called by a woman's name; nor does this John, who sat for a full decade, agree with the brief pontificate of Joan, nor did he do anything for which it could be said that he bore a child. Add that the conjecture of Baronius rests on no testimony, and that this pope is burdened with many other praises by Platina and Onofrio; nor was it of such weight that he consented to the restoration of Photius, a most learned man, a thing done by the wish and assent of the whole East.

units.la: LXI. Aliam Johannae originem pandit Joh. Aventinus Annal. Bojor.lib.4.
units.tr: LXI. Joh. Aventinus gives another origin of Joan, Annals of Bavaria, book 4.

units.la: ita scribens: Albertus locupl etissimus Etruria Princeps, Ravennam, Bononiam, Romam in potestate habuit; cujus Socrus Theodora scortum nobile atq; imperiosum Romae dominabatur, Joannémq; nonum amatorem suum Bononiensibus primò, deinde Ravennatibus, postremò Romanis primariúmq; Sacerdotem creavit; unde fabellam ortam crediderim, quae temerè vulgárit, hisce temporibus fuisse Sacerdotem maximam, faeminam, quae appellata sit Joannes. Ad quę verba rectè Doct. Blondellus annotat p.61. praeter errores Aventini in Theodora, Adelberto & numero Joannis IX.(cùm de decimo agatur) 1. Cur probrosum Theodora dominatum opportuniorem otiosis cudenda fabellae occasionem subministrâsse demus,quàm Marosia,quae postquam maternas delicias Joannem X. A. D. 929. è medio sustulit, proprium dedecus, Joannem scil. alium spurium Sergio Papa prognatum,Romanis per summam nefas obtrusit? 2. Qui factum,ut faemina Pontifex, quae de Theodora nomine Theodorus Papa dici debuit, à Johanne Amasio
units.tr: writing thus: Albert, the very wealthy prince of Etruria, held Ravenna, Bologna and Rome in his power. His mother-in-law Theodora, a noble and domineering courtesan, ruled at Rome and made John, her lover, first bishop of Bologna, then of Ravenna, and finally chief priest at Rome. Hence I believe the fable arose which was rashly spread about, that in these times there was a chief priest, a woman, who was called John. On these words Dr. Blondel rightly remarks p. 61. that, apart from Aventinus's errors about Theodora, Adalbert and the number of John (since it is the tenth John who is in question): 1. Why should we grant that the shameless rule of Theodora supplied a more convenient occasion for inventing the story than Marozia, who, after her mother's lover John X had been removed in 929, forced on the Romans, by the greatest wickedness, her own disgrace, namely another John, a bastard born to Pope Sergius? 2. How is it that a female pope, who ought to have been called Theodorus after Theodora, was called John, from her lover John X, and was called John the Eighth rather than the Tenth?

units.la: Secunda à Johanne X. Amasio denominationem sortita, Johannes non decimus, sed octavus dicta sit. Addimus rursus temporis differentiam eámque hìc majorem, & conjecturæ tum novitatem tum incertitudinem, nemine Authorum præeunte, atque tunc Romanos de Johanna Papissa locutos esse, indicante.
units.tr: The second [origin], which took its name from John X, her lover, but was called John the Eighth, not the Tenth. We add again a difference in time, and a greater one here, and a novelty and uncertainty in the conjecture; no author went before, and it indicates that the Romans then spoke of Pope Joan.

units.la: LXII. Ad Johannem XII. currit Onuphrius, qui Annot. in Joh.VIII. ita scribit; Sed quoniam omnia insignia mendacia ab aliqua veritate originem habent, hanc fabulam ex Johannis Papa XII. Viri impuri vita manasse crediderim. Is Joannes per vim, Patris Alberici Romani Principis potentia adhuc pene adolescens Papa factus, aliquot concubinas, ut Luitprandus Ticinensis illorum temporum Scriptor l. 6. c. 6. & 7. tradit, habuit: in his praecipuè erant, Joanna, Raineria, & Stephania. Ex Joanne igitur Papa & ejus item Scorto Joanna, ad cujus forte arbitrium tanquam Papa omnia Romae pendebant, Joannis, femina Papa fabula manavit, quae processu temporis aucta, in historia auctoritatem imperiti alicujus Scriptoris operâ paulatim irrepsit. Valde quidem sibi hanc Panvinii opinionem placere, ait Abbas Gualdi Vita di Donna Olimpia p. 416. postquam p. 398. seqq. retulisset, quâ ratione sex ante Innocentii X. mortem mensibus quidam tempore nocturno in omnibus fere tam sacris quàm profanis locis, ubi Innocentii Papae nomen fuerit, eo eraso, Dominae Olympiae, (quam sub Cognato titulari Papatum revera administrasse dicta & dicenda evincunt;) atque verbis: INNOCENTIUS X. PONTIFEX MAXIMUS: partim illa: OLIMPIA PRIMUS PONTIFEX MAXIMUS; in ipsa etiam S. Johannis Lateranensi Basilica: partim illa: OLIMPIA PRIMA PAPESSA: substituerint, id quod per mensem durárit, quia restitutione in pristinum statum alicubi facta, alibi statim contraria inscriptio & semper apparuerit, donec omnibus locis, in quibus nomen Innocentii, custodiae appositae exploratoresque multiplicati fuerint; Quomodo tamen authoritati Pontificiae nondum satis cautum fuerit, iisdem Authoribus hinc inde in Urbe posthac schedulas seminantibus cum verbis impressis: OLIMPIA PRIMUS PONTIFEX NON MAXIMUS. Quales schedulas ipse Luna Paschatis ultra quatuor in Ecclesia S. Mariae Majoris invenerit, duásque Nobili Germano rogatus dederit. Subjungit p. 417. seqq. Non dubitandum esse, quin ante duorum seculorum decursum mundus creaturus sit, fuisse in Ecclesia Papissam Olimpiam, sepulto plane Innocentii decimi nomine, propter nimis absolutum dominium; quod is Cognatæ tradiderit, tantúmque, ut plenius ipsa desiderare non potuerit. Verùm, quando (ut Onuphrio primò respondeamus;) non constat, ad concubinarum arbitrium tanquam Papæ Romæ omnia pependisse; & ad Joannæ magis quàm cæterarum arbitrium; imò quando Luithprandus l. c. inter Johannis concubinas Johannæ nullam, sed pudendam tantùm Raineræ, Stephánæ viduæ, Annæ viduæ, neptísque memoriam exprimit, adeóque Onuphrium hic (velit, nolit) judice Doct. Blondello, ejus, quem laudat, auctoritas destituit; & Johannes XII. centum & aliquot annis Johannâ Papisså posterior fuit; Jiquet, (sepósito etiam Anastasii testimonio) Chronologiam Papissæ conjecturam hanc adhuc magis refutare; quam & refutant quædam alia ex iis, quæ contrà præcedentem originem allata sunt, sed quæ hèic repetere nihil attinet. Quod autem attinet Vitæ D. Olimpiæ Scriptorem, ut in tollenda Johanna, præter ea, quæ jam tetigimus, in eo etiam errat, quòd p. 402. majorem Protestantium partem hic dubiam facit, ibidémque argumentatur ex anathemate, quo Pontifices notent Historicos suæ Religionis cum tanta licentia ejusmodi res, ut sic loquatur, imaginarias tangentes, dum non verisimile sit, Deum benedictum permissurum fuisse, ut Ecclesia in hoc articulo erraret, & quòd p. 407. arbitratur, fabulam hanc meram esse hæreticorum inventionem, p. 499. nunquam in Ecclesia Romana creditam; satis per jam dicta in eo refutatus, ita certè haud minus errat æstimans insuper, Olimpiâ suâ Johannam tolli posse. Neque enim facilè continget, ut, quod in seculo tam illustri, scriptorúmque fertili in totius Christiani Orbis oculis accidit, ante duorum seculorum decursum, usque adeò perversè narretur, neque id, credo, permittent, si durabunt, Pontificii, ut Olimpia planè in locum Innocentii substituatur, haud ullo contradicente; quod respectu Johannæ tamen in ipsa Ecclesia Romana diu juxta allata obtinuit, de qua etiam, quod jam agimus, nemo verisimilitudinem aliquam proferre potest in assignanda alia præter rei, quemadmodum narratur, veritatem origine; prout quidem videtur, facilè occurri posse & occursum iri post duo vel tria secula dicenti, nullum seculo nostro Innocentium X. fuisse, sed Olimpiam sexum ementitam Papatum tamdiu administrâsse. Ubi vel levissimum est Innocentii alicujus in historia Johannæ vestigium, cui quis insistere posset? Et unde contra tot támque speciales non tantùm de regimine, sed & de sexûs mendacio, de partu aliis circumstantiæ? Utut obscuriora fuerint illa tempora, facilè tamen orienti fabulæ statim reclamari debuisset & debuisset ob eandem rationem, quâ reclamaturi essent, si quis similia de Olimpia proferre vellet. Cæterùm dum tam similem Johannæ Olimpiam sistunt, dedecus infeliciter augent, necessitatemque nobis nullam esse ad Johannam, si nolimus exemplum etiam vetus, recurrendi (quod jam n. 3. innui;) recentioris hujus etiam exempli evidentiâ ipsimet ostendunt? Parùm quippe interest inter Johannam solam in Pontificatu regnantem, Innocentióque nonnisi pro larva virili abutentem.
units.tr: LXII. To John XII. turns Onuphrius, who writes thus in Annotations on John VIII.: But since all notorious lies have some grain of truth at their root, I believe this fable arose from the life of John XII, an impure man. This John, made pope by force through the power of his father Alberic, prince of Rome, while still almost a youth, had several concubines, as Liutprand of Cremona, a writer of those times, relates in book 6, chapters 6 and 7. Among these were especially Joanna, Raineria and Stephania. From John the pope, and from his courtesan Joanna, by whose judgment all things at Rome then depended, as if she were pope, the fable of Pope Joan arose, which, as time went on, grew, and little by little crept into history on the authority of some unskilled writer. Abbot Gualdi, in his Life of Donna Olimpia, p. 416., says that Panvinio's opinion pleases him very much. After relating p. 398. seqq. how, in the six months before the death of Innocent X, some people at night, in almost all the sacred and profane places where the name of Pope Innocent stood, erased it and substituted, partly, the words OLIMPIA PRIMUS PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, and even in the basilica of St John Lateran, partly OLIMPIA PRIMA PAPESSA (which, as the facts show, was the rule of Donna Olimpia, who was said and proved to have truly administered the papacy under the title of her brother-in-law); and that this went on for a month, because, when the original state was restored in one place, a contrary inscription would at once appear elsewhere, until guards were posted in all the places where Innocent's name was, and spies were multiplied; yet, he adds, the papal authority was still not sufficiently safeguarded, since the same authors afterwards scattered placards about the city with the printed words OLIMPIA PRIMUS PONTIFEX NON MAXIMUS. Such placards, Luna Paschatis says, he himself found in more than four places in the church of St Mary Major, and at the request of a German nobleman he gave him two. He adds p. 417. seqq.: There is no doubt that before two centuries have run out, before the world is to be created, there will be a Pope Olimpia in the Church, with the name of Innocent X completely buried, on account of his excessively absolute dominion, which he handed on to his relative, and which she could not have desired more fully. But, to answer Onuphrius first: it is not established that all things at Rome depended on the judgment of the concubines as if they were pope, nor that they depended more on Joanna's judgment than on the others'. Indeed, since Liutprand l. c. mentions among John's concubines no Joanna, but only the shameful Raineria, Stephania the widow, Anna the widow, and his granddaughter, Onuphrius here (whether he likes it or not), in the judgment of Dr. Blondel, has lost the authority of the very writer he cites; and John XII was more than a hundred years later than Pope Joan, if (even setting aside the testimony of Anastasius) the chronology of the papess makes this conjecture even more refuted. Certain other points, brought forward against the earlier origin, refute it too, but there is no point in repeating them here. As for the writer of the Life of Donna Olimpia, in removing Joan he errs in this too, besides what we have already touched on: p. 402. he makes the greater part of the Protestants doubtful here, and in the same place argues from the anathema with which the popes mark the historians of their religion, who, to put it so, touch such matters with such license, as if they were imaginary, since it is not likely that the blessed God would have allowed the Church to err on this article; and because p. 407. he judges this fable to be a pure invention of heretics, never believed in the Roman Church, p. 499., he is sufficiently refuted by what has been said. So, certainly, he errs no less in thinking further that Joan can be removed by means of his Olimpia. For it will hardly happen that what occurred in so famous an age, and so fertile in writers, before the eyes of the whole Christian world, will be so perversely narrated before two centuries have passed; nor, I believe, will the Papists, if they last, permit it, that Olimpia should be put completely in place of Innocent, with no one contradicting. Yet in respect to Joan, this story has held its place for a long time in the Roman Church itself, according to what has been brought forward; and about it, as we are now discussing, no one can offer any probable origin other than the truth of the matter as it is related. It seems, indeed, that someone saying, after two or three centuries, that there was no Innocent X in our century, but that Olimpia, having feigned her sex, administered the papacy for so long, could easily be met and will be met. Where is even the slightest trace of some Innocent in the history of Joan, which one might follow? And whence, against so many and such particular circumstances, not only of the rule but also of the lie about her sex, of the childbirth and other details? However obscure those times were, the story should readily have been contradicted at its first appearance, and for the same reason that people would protest if anyone wished to tell similar things about Olimpia. Moreover, while they set up an Olimpia so like Joan, they unhappily increase the disgrace; and do they not show, by the very evidence of this more recent example, that we have no need to have recourse to Joan, if we do not want an ancient example too (which I already hinted at in n. 3.)? For there is little difference between Joan, reigning alone in the papacy, and Innocent, who abused only a male mask.

units.la: LXIII. Ulterius atque usque ad Johannem XXII. progreditur Sorberius quidam Medicus apud Cl. Maresium Pap. Resit. p. 21. in libello, quo reddit rationes transitûs sui ad Pontificios, & in quo inter alia ait, Ranulpho ab Higeden, qui primus circa annum 1343. fabulæ auctor fuerit, occasionem fingendi suggessisse, quod circa illa tempora contigerat in Schismate excitato per Ludovicum Bavarum, ad Minoritarum instantiam, maximè Occami adversus Johannem XXII. cui oppositus fuerit Minorita Monachus, Petrus Rainalutius de Corbaria, qui Nicolai V. nomen assumpsit, & Romæ sedit ultra triennium. Hic autem Corbarius (narrante Spondano ad an. 1328. n. 6. & 7.) Cùm priùs vixisset in conjugio cum Johanna Matthæi de Corbario filia, ipsâ invitâ Monachatum ingressus fuerat, in quo vixerat cum opinione sanctitatis, unde facilior ei fuit gradus ad Papatum: quo cum fungeretur, ejus uxor oblato libello Episcopo Reatino, cui suberat, eum tanquam maritum suum repetiit, utpote qui se invitâ Monachatum subiisset, ac obtinuit sententiam in sui favorem: quæ tamen ad fuerit unquam executioni mandata, non liquet. Hinc factum vult Sorberius, ut vulgò diceretur, hujus negotii tempore, Johannem quidem Papam Avenione sedere, sed Johannam Papissam, uxorem scilicet Corbarii, qui se Papam Nicolaum V. vocabat, in Italia esse. Sed 1. gratis fingitur, id jactatum tunc vulgò fuisse. 2. Omnes ante Ranulphum testes suprà vindicati fictioni contradicunt. 3. Injuria ei fit, ac si, occasione hujus dicterii suo tempore usurpati, totum hoc drama confinxisset, & ad Leonis IV. successorem 500. annis ante sua tempora retrotraxisset. 4. Ranulphus ipse testem suum laudat Martinum Polonum antiquiorem. 5. Jam ante Corbarium, fama Johannæ ita publicè obtinebat, ut Occamus l. c. inde probet Quarta à Johanne XXII. Ecclesiam Romanam errare posse, quòd olim fæmina in Rom. Pontificem eligi potuerit. 6. Si Avenione Petri uxor sub nomine Johannæ Papissæ traducta fuisset, id potiùs argueret veritatem historiæ Johannæ nostræ, quam & arguit Johannis XXII. appellatio suprà indigitata. Interim ad recensitas in sede Romana ipsa quæsitas origines adhuc in genere notamus, parùm honorificas esse & maximam partem summè pudendas; Nempe ad Ecclesiæ suæ decus vindicandum ajunt; Non fœminam Caput habuisse, sed Capita, effœminatos, quibus non natura, sed partim animi imbecillitas, partim vitiorum sordes fœminarum nomina imposuerint.
units.tr: LXIII. Further, and up to John XXII, goes a certain Dr. Sorberius, a physician, cited by Maresius in Papal Resistance, p. 21., in a little book in which he gives his reasons for passing over to the Papists. Among other things he says that Ranulf of Higden, who was the first author of the fable around the year 1343, suggested the occasion for inventing it from what had happened about that time in the schism stirred up by Ludwig of Bavaria, at the urging of the Minorites, especially of Occam, against John XXII. Opposed to him was a Minorite monk, Peter Rainalucci of Corvara, who took the name Nicholas V and sat at Rome for more than three years. This Corvarius (as Spondanus relates ad an. 1328. n. 6. & 7.), when he had earlier lived in marriage with Joanna, daughter of Matthew of Corvara, had entered a monastery against her will, and there lived with a reputation for holiness, whence his step to the papacy was easier. While he was in that office, his wife, presenting a petition to the bishop of Rieti, under whose jurisdiction she was, claimed him back as her husband, since he had taken up the monastic life against her will; and she obtained a sentence in her favour, but whether it was ever carried into effect is not clear. Hence Sorberius holds that the common talk at that time was that John was indeed pope at Avignon, but that Pope Joan, that is, Corvarius's wife, who called himself Pope Nicholas V, was in Italy. But: 1. It is baselessly asserted that this was talked of commonly at that time. 2. All the witnesses before Ranulf, cited above, contradict the fiction. 3. It is unfair to him, as if, on the occasion of this slander used in his own time, he had made up this whole drama and carried it back to the successor of Leo IV, five hundred years before his own time. 4. Ranulf himself cites as his witness the older Martin the Pole. 5. Even before Corvarius, the report of Joan was so publicly current that Occam l. c. uses it to prove that the Roman Church, in the fourth place after John XXII, can err, since once a woman could have been elected Roman pontiff. 6. If Peter's wife had been brought to Avignon under the name of Pope Joan, that would argue more for the truth of our history of Joan, which the appeal to John XXII, pointed out above, also argues. Meanwhile, we note in general about the origins sought within the Roman see itself, as recounted, that they are little to their credit and for the most part extremely shameful. Indeed, they say that to defend the honour of their Church, it was not a woman who had the headship, but heads: effeminate men, to whom not nature, but partly the weakness of their spirit and partly the filth of their vices, gave women's names.

units.la: LXIV. Sed duplex etiam quæsita fuit extra sedem Romanam figmenti, quod æstimatur, origo. Nonnulli eam quærunt in sede Constantinopolitana, Bellarminus atque Baronius, qui jam aliam originem assignavit. Nempe volunt hic, quòd exortâ famâ de fœmina Patriarcha Constantinopolitana, id omne ex malevolorum odio sedi Romanæ applicatum sit. Verùm optimè subjungit Doct. Blondellus p. 62. Itane verò ludicram divinatoriam exercere juvat; ut quicquid in buccam venit pro libidine efflare audeamus? ut non repetamus ea, quæ suprà de epistola Leonis IX. diximus, Michaelis flagitium, in quo fundamentum rumoris Leoniani de fœmina Constantinopolitana quærunt, Martino, quem quidam primum fabulæ authorem faciunt, quadringentis, Leonis IX. epistolâ ducentis annis antiquius fuit. Quæ quidem Mariani Scoti, quem alii primum authorem esse ajunt, ætate scripta fuit, sed quis id, quod, nisi à Cedreno & Curopalata proditum esset, ignoraretur, Mariano Monacho inclusò narravit ante 200. annos perpetratum? Atque quâ quæsò vertigine Baronius è re ludicra rem seriam, è viro Cinædo fœminam, è Gryllo (nomen Cinædi erat,) Johannam, è personato Patriarcha Constantinopolitano serium Romanum Pontificem fecit, annos menses & dies Pontificatûs assignavit? Quando igitur, quasi rem acu tetigisset, exclamat; quis non intelligit? merito addimus; conjecturam hanc ejus scythica glacie frigidiorem, vel juxta verba Blondelli, leviorem & dignam esse, quæ in spongiam incumbat?
units.tr: LXIV. But the origin of the invented story, which is judged to be twofold, has also been sought outside the Roman see. Some look for it in the see of Constantinople, Bellarmine and Baronius among them, and Baronius has already assigned a different origin. They claim that when a rumour arose about a woman Patriarch of Constantinople, all of it was applied to the Roman see out of the hatred of ill-wishers. But the learned Blondel rightly replies (p. 62): Is it really so pleasant to practise this silly guesswork, that we dare to blurt out whatever comes into our mouth? I need not repeat what I said above about the letter of Leo IX and the crime of Michael, on which they base the origin of the Leonine rumour about a woman in Constantinople. That crime was committed about two hundred years before Leo IX's letter, and four hundred years after Martin, whom some make the first author of the fable. That letter was written in the time of Marianus Scotus, whom others name as the first author. But who, unless Cedrenus and Curopalates had reported it, would have known, and who told Marianus the monk that it had been done two hundred years earlier? And by what dizziness, I ask, has Baronius turned a serious matter into a ridiculous one, a sodomite man into a woman, Gryllus (which was the name of the sodomite) into Joan, the masked Patriarch of Constantinople into a true Roman Pope, and assigned years, months and days to his pontificate? So when he cries out, as if he had hit the nail on the head, who does not understand? we rightly add that his conjecture is colder than Scythian ice, or, in Blondel's words, too light, and fit only to be soaked up by a sponge?

units.la: LXV. Sextam tandem originem Leo Allatius Comment. de Johanna divinatoriâ abjectâ certiora spondens assignat, in Thiota Prophetissa Moguntina illius temporis. Sed quam idem Doctiss. Blondellus cæterarum ad instar solidè refutat, dum Moguntiacam tiacam nemini dictam fuisse, dum jam anno 847. vel 848. prophetasse docet, & concludit: quare quod Allatio in animo certum est, nec ambiguum,in ambiguo hæreat necesse est. Et certè quid talis ad Papissam cum talibus circumstantiis? Quoad omnes origines notari meretur, Pontifices justam conquerendi causam habuisse, atque, sive Metaphoricis locutionibus, sive aliunde institutis ad sedem Romanam derivationibus omni studio se opponere debuisse atque etiam se opposituros fuisse, si paulatim atque sine idoneo fundamento talis rumor exortus fuisset; Verùm rei evidentia & contradictionem exclusit, & Confessionem, juxta prac. nonnullis expressit.
units.tr: LXV. Finally, Leo Allatius in his Commentary on Joan sets aside the guesswork and, promising more certain grounds, names as the sixth origin Thiota the prophetess of Mainz of that time. But the same most learned Blondel refutes it solidly, as he did the others. He shows that Thiota was called Mainz by no one, and that she had already prophesied in the year 847 or 848, and he concludes: so what is certain to Allatius is in his mind, and not ambiguous, in the ambiguous must needs cling. And indeed, what has such a woman to do with a Papess in such circumstances? As regards all these origins, it deserves notice that the Popes had a just cause for complaint, and ought to have opposed with every effort, whether by metaphorical expressions or by derivations to the Roman see devised in some other way, and would indeed have opposed it, if such a rumour had arisen gradually and without a sound foundation. But the plain evidence of the matter has excluded it, and it has forced a confession from some, according to prac.

units.la: LXVI. Ut historiae proin, qualis fides & probabilitas plerisque rerum inter homines gestarum narrationibus, maximè ex obscurioribus seculis tribuitur, quoque tribuenda sit. Loquor de probabilitate; Historica enim ita comparata sunt, ut non nitantur omnia certitudine penitùs infallibili, & quae ad evidentiam accedant, sed in plerisque probabilitate contentos esse fas est, quam vel ipse D. Blondellus historiae largitur, dum tandem concludens fatetur, præmissis saepe in speciali circumstantiarum examine verbis: Nihil absurdi commenti sunt, qui &c. p 72 singulas hujus (ut loquitur) fabulae circumstantias verisimilibus insistere fundamentis, nec facilè vel ex ratione, vel ex historia petitis argumentis posse convelli &c.
units.tr: LXVI. Hence it must be considered what faith and probability should be given to the accounts of history, as they are given to most narratives of events among men, especially from the more obscure centuries. I speak of probability. For historical matters are so constituted that not all of them rest on utterly infallible certainty, or come close to evidence; in most cases it is permissible to be content with probability. Even the learned Blondel grants this to history, when at last he concludes, having often said in his detailed examination of the circumstances: They have invented nothing absurd, who &c. (p. 72) that each of the circumstances of this fable, as he puts it, rests on probable foundations, and cannot easily be overturned by arguments drawn from reason or from history &c.

units.la: SECTIO QUARTA, In qua, De nævis & vitiis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum ratione Patriæ & Familiæ eorum, qui eliguntur, agitur.
units.tr: SECTION FOUR, in which the blemishes and faults in the election of the Roman Pontiffs are discussed, concerning the country and family of those who are chosen.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Olim ex omni populo Pontifices Romani eligebantur; II. Et rejectus fuit Nationum respectus; III. Qui tamen notatur in Electione Iohannis XXII. IV. In Conclavi Urbani VI. V. Excluduntur Ultramontani; VI. Graci; VII. Ex Occidentalibus Germani; VIII. Germania Fautores; IX. Galli; X. Hispani; XI. Hispanis grati vel addicti; XII. Itali esse debent; XIII. Sed non omnis terra Italica aquè Paparum ferax est; Excluduntur, qui olim maximè pratendebant, Longobardi; XIV. Neapolitani; XV. Venseti; XVI. Alii ex Italia; XVII. Senenses; XVIII. Genuenses; XIX. Lucenses; XX. Pedemontani, Sabaudi; XXI. Ex quadam regione Hypocritarum orti; XXII. Romanus quondam unicè expetebatur; XXIII. A longo tempore tales ferè esse debent aut Hetrusci; XXIV. Familiarum respectus in exclusione Caraffarum &c. XXV. In eo, quod nobiliores vix admittuntur; XXVI. Sed genus humile commendat; XXVII. Ob causas parùm convenientes; XXVIII. Obstaculum quòd Innocentius XI. ex parte Patria habuit; XXIX. Sed superavit, & quomodo; XXX. Vitium in illo Nationum respectu notatur; XXXI. Ut & vitium in illegitimo nonnullorum ortu.
units.tr: I. Formerly the Roman Pontiffs were chosen from every people; II. and regard for nations was rejected; III. yet it is noted in the election of John XXII; IV. in the conclave of Urban VI; V. Ultramontanes are excluded; VI. Greeks; VII. among Westerners, Germans; VIII. supporters of Germany; IX. the French; X. the Spaniards; XI. those pleasing to or devoted to the Spaniards; XII. they ought to be Italians; XIII. but not every Italian land is equally fruitful in popes; the Lombards, who once claimed the most, are excluded; XIV. Neapolitans; XV. Venetians; XVI. others from Italy; XVII. Sienese; XVIII. Genoese; XIX. Lucchese; XX. Piedmontese and Savoyards; XXI. those sprung from a certain region of hypocrites; XXII. a Roman was once sought exclusively; XXIII. for a long time such men ought to be almost always either Tuscans; XXIV. regard for families in the exclusion of the Caraffas, etc.; XXV. in that the more noble are scarcely admitted; XXVI. but humble birth commends; XXVII. for causes not very fitting; XXVIII. the obstacle that Innocent XI had on his father's side; XXIX. but he overcame it, and how; XXX. a fault is noted in that regard for nations; XXXI. and likewise the fault in the illegitimate birth of some.

units.la: I. HActenus de sexu Papabilium; Sequitur tellturis, quae masculos, quales esse debent, proferre debet, consideratio. Olim quidem Deo, qui non est personarum acceptor, ex quavis gente acceptus erat etiam ad Episcopatum Urbis Romae consequendum timens eum atq; operans justitiam, Act. X. 34. 35. Hinc in Catalogis Romanorum Pontificum antiquiorum praeter ingentem Italorum numerum, Afri, Syri, Dalmatae, Siculi, Sardi, Cretenses, Thraces, Angli, Hispani, Lusitani, Germani etiam (quos peculiari Dissertatione Clarissimus Wagenseilius sistit & quorum aciem Johanna ducit;) & inprimis Galli, occurrunt.
units.tr: I. Hitherto we have considered the sex of those who may be elected. It follows that we consider the land which ought to produce the men, such as they must be. Indeed, formerly, with God, who is no respecter of persons, one who feared him and worked righteousness was acceptable from any nation, even for obtaining the bishopric of the city of Rome, Acts 10:34, 35. Hence in the catalogues of the older Roman Pontiffs there appear, besides a huge number of Italians, Africans, Syrians, Dalmatians, Sicilians, Sardinians, Cretans, Thracians, Englishmen, Spaniards, Portuguese, and also Germans (whom the most distinguished Wagenseil presents in a special dissertation, and whose line Joan leads), and above all the French.

units.la: II. Atque eandem respectu Nationum indifferentiam praese tulerunt Cardinales à Romanis post mortem Gregorii XI. rogati, ut Italum eligerent, sed respondentes; Sibi cura fore, ut Virum Optimum deligerent, qui Ecclesia Dei praeesset, nullàpersonarum aut nationum acceptione habitâ, ad imitationem Salvatoris, qui ad Apostolatum Viros ex omni natione delegerit; narrante Platina in Urbano VI. atque addente Authore Conclavis: Prout Deus inspirabit & conscientia nostra videbitur, & non aliter.
units.tr: II. The cardinals, when after the death of Gregory XI they were asked by the Romans to choose an Italian, showed the same indifference toward nations, answering that it would be their care to choose an excellent man who would preside over the Church of God, with no regard to persons or nations, in imitation of the Saviour, who chose men for the apostolate from every nation. So Platina reports in the life of Urban VI, and the author of the Conclave adds: "As God shall inspire and as our conscience shall judge, and not otherwise."

units.la: III. Verum ab aliquot seculis magnus Nationis respectus notatur. Cùm de Electione Johannis XXII. Lugduni ageretur, viginti tres erant Cardinales, inquit Author Cardinalismi p. 3. l. 1. p. 79. ex quibus duodecim erant Galli & undecim Itali, hi volebant Papam ò puramente Italiano, ò pure di qualche altra Natione, mà che prometesse di rendere la sede all' Italia. Li Francesi poiche si vedevano in maggior numero ed in Francia stimolari tutti i giorni da' loro amici e parenti stavano fermi e risoluti di non voler altro che un Papa Françese; aut simpliciter aut saltem ex quadam alia Natione, sed qui promittat, sedem restituere in Italiam. Galli autem, videntes numero se superiores, & in Gallia inciincitati singulis diebus ab amicis & cognatis suis plane in animo habebant nullum nisi Gallum eligere.
units.tr: III. But for some centuries a great regard for nation has been noted. When the election of John XXII was being held at Lyons, there were twenty-three cardinals, says the author of the Cardinalism, p. 3, l. 1, p. 79, of whom twelve were French and eleven Italian. The latter wanted a pope who was purely Italian, or at least from some other nation, but one who would promise to restore the see to Italy. The French, since they saw themselves in greater number, and were being urged every day in France by their friends and relatives, stood firm and resolved that they would have no one but a French pope, either simply or at least from some other nation, but one who would promise to restore the see to Italy. The French, seeing that they were superior in number, and being urged every day by their friends and kinsmen, were fully resolved to elect no one but a Frenchman.

units.la: IV. Vestigia etiam hujus respectus in illa ipsa jam jam citata Urbani. historia apud Platinam & in Conclavi deprehenduntur; Rogant enim Romani Cardinales, ut unum aliquem Virum praestantem deligant e natione Italica——Italum autem requirebant, ne, si Gallus deligeretur, Romana Curia iterum migrare ultra montes necesse esset. In Conclavi contentio ex eo orta erat, quòd Galli Gallum, Itali Italum promovere conabantur; Gallis quibusdam Lemovicensibus nimirum nonnisi Lemovicensem volentibus, aliis reclamantibus atque dicentibus, quòd totus mundus admodum erat attediatus de Lemovicensibus, qui tanto tempore Papatum possederunt quasi hæreditarium. In eodem Conclavi Cardinalis de Ursinis deludendos suasit istos de Populo Romano, qui voluerunt Romanum. Huc etiam pertinent voces prope Conclave, dum de Electione ageretur, clamantium: Romano lo volemo, id est, Romanum volumus.
units.tr: IV. Traces of this regard are also found in the history of Urban just cited, in Platina and in the Conclave. For the Roman cardinals asked that they choose some outstanding man from the Italian nation, ... they were demanding an Italian, lest, if a Frenchman were chosen, the Roman Curia would again be obliged to migrate beyond the mountains. In the conclave the contention arose because the French tried to advance a Frenchman and the Italians an Italian; some of the French from Limoges, namely, wanted only a man from Limoges, while others objected and said that the whole world was utterly weary of the men of Limoges, who had held the papacy for so long as if it were hereditary. In the same conclave, Cardinal Orsini advised that they should mock those of the Roman people who wanted a Roman. Here also belong the voices shouted near the conclave while the election was going on: "We want a Roman," that is, "We want a Roman."

units.la: V. In genere excluduntur, qui sunt Italis Ultramontani. In Conclavi Gregorii XIV. in Sans, per essere Oltramontano, non accadeva pensare; de Cardinali Sans nemo cogitavit, quia Ultramontanus erat. Et cùm in Conclavi Innocentii IX. Hispani Madruccium promovere vellent, prattiche gagliarde se li fecero contra per esser Oltramantano, summo studio & omni arte iis resistebant alii, quia Ultramontanus erat. Hinc etiam Febo Vaticinante l' Ambasc. di Romolo a' Romani p. 249. ita canit: E voi, che nati oltre l' Italia siete Scusate pur se qui di voi non canto. Doletevi, ch'il Cielo nemico havete, Che non spira voi lo Spirito Santo: Fan nel Vostro Terren Cavoli, e Rapi Mà non è buon' à produr poi de' Papi. Id est:
units.tr: V. In general, those who are Ultramontanes are excluded by Italians. In the conclave of Gregory XIV, "Sans, because he is an Ultramontane, was not to be thought of; no one thought of Cardinal Sans, because he was an Ultramontane." And when in the conclave of Innocent IX the Spaniards wanted to advance Madruzzo, strong schemes were set up against him on the ground that he was an Ultramontane; others resisted him with the greatest zeal and every art, because he was an Ultramontane. Hence also Phoebus prophesying in L'Ambasciata di Romolo a' Romani, p. 249, sings thus: "And you who were born beyond Italy, pardon me if I do not sing of you here. Lament that you have heaven as your enemy, that the Holy Spirit does not breathe upon you. In your land they grow cabbages and turnips, but they are no good for producing popes." That is:

units.la: Et vos, qui ultra Italiam nati estis, excusate solùm, si hîc de vobis non cano; Dolete, quòd Cœlum inimicum habetis, quòd non spirat de vobis Spiritus Sanctus; Crescant equidem in regionibus vestris brassica & Rapa, sed non bona sunt, ut ibi producantur Papa.
units.tr: And you who were born beyond Italy, pardon me alone if I do not sing of you here; lament that you have heaven as an enemy, that the Holy Spirit does not breathe upon you. Cabbages and turnips indeed grow in your regions, but they are not good for producing popes.

units.la: VI. Excluduntur Graci; Quando enim in Conclavi Calixti III. furono mosse gagliarde prattiche, fuerunt suscepta studiosa negotiationes pro Cardinale Bessarione Græco, poi che lo giu di cavano fra tutti lo più atto à reggere e governare questo si gran peso del Pontificato; quia judicabatur batur aptissimus ad regendum & gubernandum tam grave Papatus onus, neque dubium ullum oriri poterat, quin dua Cardinalium partes in eum consensura sint, & jam ipsi particulariter commendati erant status Principum, & unus hoc, alius aliud ipsum rogaverat; atque id nunciatum esset, à parti contrariæ studentibus, factioni contrariæ; omnes & maximè Avignonensis Cardinalis hinc inde suos mittebant, rogando modò hunc, modò alium, ut desisterent ab electione tali, atque ipse Avignonensis ita loquebatur intrepidè; Concederemo noi dunque alla chiesa santa Latina un' huomo Greco? E porremo nell' eccelso loco del Pontificato un' huomo Neofito? E chi vi sa certi che la conversione sua sia vera? Sarà nostro Pastore quello, che poco tempo sa oppugnava la fede Cattolica? E possibile, che la chiesa nostra Latina sia posta in tal necessità, che in essa non si trovi un' huomo degno & atto per reggere e governare la Gregge di Dio? Illustrissimi Signori svegliatevi, e non permettete un tanto scandalo nella chiesa di Christo, per che tale elettione io non approvo come anco tutti li altri, che alle parole mie prestaranno fede, mai non consentiranno, che tale persona sia eletta in Vicario di Christo, & habbia à governare la gregge sua con tanto sospetto e pericolo di tutto il Christianesimo. Id est; Concedemus igitur nos Ecclesia Sancta Latina hominem Graecum? Et ponemus in excelso Pontificatus loco hominem Neophytum? Et quis nos certos facit, ejus conversionem veram esse? Eritne Pastor noster, qui paulo ante oppugnavit fidem Catholicam? Possibile ne est, Ecclesiam nostram Latinam in tali necessitate positam esse, ut in illa non reperiatur homo dignus & aptus ad regendum & gubernandum Gregem Dei? Illustrissimi Domini, evigilate, neque permittite tantum scandalum in Ecclesia Christi, quandoquidem talem electionem non approbo, neque omnes alii, qui verbis meis fidem habebunt, unquam consentirent, ut talis eligatur Vicarius Christi; & gubernare debeat ejus gregem cum tanta suspicione & tanto periculo totius orbis Christiani.
units.tr: VI. Greeks are excluded. For when strong schemes were set afoot in the conclave of Callixtus III, eager negotiations were undertaken for the Greek Cardinal Bessarion, since he was judged to be the man among all most fit to bear and govern so great a burden of the papacy; and no doubt could arise that the two parts of the cardinals would consent to him, and already the rulers of states had individually recommended him, one having asked for him, another for someone else. When this was announced to those working for the opposing side, the opposing faction, all, and especially the Cardinal of Avignon, sent their men here and there, now asking this one, now that one, to withdraw from such an election; and the Cardinal of Avignon himself spoke fearlessly thus: "Shall we then concede to the holy Latin Church a Greek man? And shall we place in the lofty seat of the papacy a neophyte? And who assures us that his conversion is true? Will he be our shepherd, who a little while ago attacked the Catholic faith? Is it possible that our Latin Church should be placed in such necessity that no man worthy and fit to rule and govern the flock of God can be found in it? Most illustrious lords, awake, and do not permit so great a scandal in the Church of Christ; for I do not approve such an election, nor will all the others who give faith to my words ever consent that such a man be chosen as Vicar of Christ and govern his flock with such suspicion and such danger to the whole Christian world."

units.la: VII. Sed & Occidentales, sive Latinæ Ecclesiæ; vi originis etiam, filii excluduntur multi; Germani. Octo quidem exhibet Cl. Wagenseilius Dissert. cit. quorum ultimus Adrianus VI. fuit. Licèt stirpis Odeschalcicæ (quæ Innocentii IX. nuperi fuit;) propaginem Norinbergam superiori seculo concessisse, ibique se diffudisse, idem Clar. Vir, l. c. etiam ex monumento ostendat. Hodie certè, quos Germanos esse constat, eo ipso non possunt esse Papabiles. Hinc in Conclavi Urbani VIII. Madruccius Germanus omni studio originem celare voluit, sed frustrà: Se bene usava, inquit quit Author Conclavis, ogni industria per esser amesso frà i Cardinali Italiani, nondimeno non vi era, che lo ricevesse, che per Tedesco? Id est; Licèt adhibuerit omnem diligentiam, ut admitteretur inter Cardinales Italos, tamen omnes eum pro Germano habuerunt. Hinc etiam sentinella fatta nel Conclave, da Pasquino e Marforio; Ambasc. di Rom. p.266. ita de Germanis colloquentes Pasquinum & Marphorium introducit: Mar : Ecco della Germania un ferra ferra E Lantgravio frà tutti il Caporale O questa volta sì, ch' andiamo à terra. Pas. Si vede ben, che sei qualche stivale, Che s' alla Nave egli s'accosta in torno Rompare ben li voglio li suo boccale. Id est:
units.tr: VII. The Occidentals, that is, the sons of the Latin Church, are also excluded by reason of their origin, and many of them: the Germans. The distinguished Wagenseil, in the dissertation already cited, lists eight, the last of whom was Adrian VI. Although he shows from a monument that the Odescalchi family (to which Innocent XI of recent memory belonged) had sent a branch to Nuremberg in the previous century and spread out there, today those who are known to be Germans cannot for that very reason be Papabiles. Hence in the Conclave of Urban VIII the German Madruccio tried by every means to conceal his origin, but in vain. "He used every effort," says the author of the Conclave, "to be admitted among the Italian cardinals, yet no one would receive him except as a German." That is, although he took the greatest pains to be admitted among the Italian cardinals, all of them nevertheless regarded him as a German. Hence too the sentry set up in the Conclave by Pasquino and Marforio, Ambassador of Rome, p. 266, who introduce Pasquino and Marforio talking about the Germans in this way: Marforio: "Here comes a German, a clumsy fellow, and above all the Landgrave, the corporal; now at last we are going to the ground." Pasquino: "It is plain that you are some sort of boot; if he comes close to the ship, I will smash his jug." That is:

units.la: Mar. Ecce! de Germania turba venit, & Landtgravius inter omnes antesignanus est. O si nunc, ut in terram procidamus Pasq. Facilè apparet, adesse quandam ocream. Si Navi appropinquat, poculum ipsi frangam. Seriò magis magnas agit nugas Anconitanus de potest. Eccl. qu. 102. art. 4. p. 5. rationem, cur ex Germania ne Cardinales quidem adsciscì debeant, ita reddens: Quia de Alemannia consuetum est, ut eligatur Imperator, qui est minister Ecclesia, ne secreta Ecclesia suis ministris pandantur, & ne, quos oportet esse subjectos, habeant in Ecclesia ex sua patria vel genere dominos vel judices defendentes, ideò non consuevit Ecclesia de Alemannia Cardinales vocare. Ob quam rationem dum Imperatores fuerunt Itali, Itali Cardinales Papæ creari non debuissent.
units.tr: Marforio: "Look! A crowd has come from Germany, and the Landgrave is the vanguard of them all. Oh, now we will fall down to the ground!" Pasquino: "It is easy to see that some greave is there. If he comes near the ship, I will break his cup." More seriously, the Anconitan, in On the Power of the Church, question 102, article 4, p. 5, gives the more trivial reason why not even cardinals should be taken from Germany, rendering it thus: "Because it is customary in Germany to elect an emperor, who is a minister of the Church, so that the Church's secrets are not laid open to its ministers, and so that those who ought to be subject do not have, within the Church, lords or judges defending them from their own country or kin; for this reason the Church of Germany has not been accustomed to call cardinals." By this reasoning, while the emperors were Italians, Italians ought not to have been created cardinals of the Pope.

units.la: VIII. Imò etiam Fautores Germaniæ, & qui diu apud Germanos commorati sunt, eò minùs Papabiles sunt. Che havete da fare voi con Enea, dicebat in Conclavi Pii II. Cardinalis Rotho magensis modò ad hunc, modò ad illum, perche lo riputate degno del Papato &c? Quid est in Ænea, quod eum dignum Papatu reddat. Poco fà è venuto di Germania, che sappiamo noi, che per aventura non trasferischi la corte inquelle parti? Nuperrimè ex Germania venit, quàm facilè illuc sedem transferre posset.
units.tr: VIII. Indeed, even the partisans of Germany, and those who have lived for a long time among the Germans, are the less eligible. "What business do you have with Aeneas?" the cardinal of Rothenburg said in the Conclave of Pius II, now to this one, now to that one, "that you think him worthy of the papacy, etc.? What is there in Aeneas that makes him worthy of the papacy? He has only lately come from Germany; who knows whether by chance he will not transfer the court to those parts? He has just come from Germany; how easily he could transfer the seat there."

units.la: IX. Excluduntur à longo tempore vel maximè Galli, quorum tamen Papatus diu quasi hæreditaria possessio erat. In Conclavi Pii IV. il Cardinal Torone (cavatone quel timore, ch'era restato nell'anim' à gl' Italiani, che la corte Romana, come sù già altre volte, non fosse di nuovo trasportata in Avignone, sempre che un Francese fosse stato Papa) era dignissimo del Papato. Cardinalis Torone (dempto timore, qui animos Italorum occupaverat, Romanam Curiam denuò Avignoniam, ubi erat antea, translatum iri; quotiescunque Gallus eligeretur) dignissimus erat Papatu. In Conclavi Pauli V. Author, probaturus, omnes etiam remotiores sperâsse, ait: Serafino istesso, che è pur nato Francese- haveva gran speranza. Seraphinus ipse, licet Gallus origine —— multum sperabat. Sic etiam Pasquinus l. cit. canit: Metlienfi quanto voglion' in Arnese Softenere vogl'io l'orrenda guerra, Non hà da entrar quà dentro il mal Françese. Id est;
units.tr: IX. The French have been excluded for a long time, most of all, although the papacy was for a long time almost a hereditary possession of theirs. In the Conclave of Pius IV, "Cardinal Torone (for that fear which remained in the minds of the Italians, that the Roman court, as had happened once before, would again be carried off to Avignon whenever a Frenchman was pope, had been removed) was most worthy of the papacy." Cardinal Torone (the fear that had taken hold of the minds of the Italians being removed, that the Roman Curia would again be transferred to Avignon, where it had been before, whenever a Frenchman was elected) was most worthy of the papacy. In the Conclave of Paul V, the author, wishing to prove that even the more remote candidates had hopes, says: "Seraphinus himself, though born a Frenchman, had great hopes." Seraphinus himself, although French by origin, was hoping greatly. So too Pasquino, in the passage cited, sings: "Whatever Metz wants to be in the harness, I will support the horrible war; the French disease must not enter here."

units.la: Adhereant quotcunque velint Arnesio; Bellum horrendum sustinere volo: Non huc intrare debet morbus Gallicus.
units.tr: Let as many as wish cling to Arnesio; I am ready to sustain a horrible war: the French disease must not come in here.

units.la: X. Sed & excluduntur Hispani; Barberinus Cardinalis quidem in Conclavi Alexandri VII. Lugo Hispanum atque ab Hispanis promovendum se promovere velle præ se tulit, idque in honorem Nationis, è qua inde ab Alexandro VI. nullus electus sit: Sed notat Author, eum ista suasisse certum de impossibilitate, quod alii ostenderint; e che Lugo non haveva ne pure un Goffio di quel aura, che si ricerca à far vela al Papato, & Lugo non habere vel minimam particulam aura, qua vela ad Papatum secundare queat. Hinc quoque L'Adolorata Roma L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 28. ira queribunda canit: Tutto lindo Aragon senza Capello Humile mi vuol far la riverenza E per esser Spagnol prende licenza, Di rubbare alla grande il mio mantello. Id est;
units.tr: X. The Spaniards are also excluded. Cardinal Barberini, indeed, in the Conclave of Alexander VII, showed that he wished to promote Lugo, a Spaniard, and to be promoted by the Spaniards, in honour of the nation from which no one had been elected since Alexander VI. But the author notes that he advised this while knowing for certain that it was impossible, as others had shown: "and because Lugo did not have even a breath of that breeze which is needed to set sail for the papacy," and Lugo had not even the smallest breath of wind that could fill the sails toward the papacy. Hence too the Sorrowful Rome, in The Ambassador of Rome, p. 28, sings complainingly: "All the Aragonese, without a hat, wants to make me a humble bow; and because he is a Spaniard, he takes the liberty of stealing my cloak in grand style."

units.la: Plane tacitus Aragon sine pileo humiliter me salutare vult; Et quia Hispanus est, licentiam petit magnificè furandi meum Pallium.
units.tr: Quite silently the Aragonese wants to salute me humbly without a hat; and because he is a Spaniard, he asks leave to steal my cloak magnificently.

units.la: XI. Imò similiter nocet nimis vel Hispanis gratum, vel Hispanis addictum esse; Illud nocuit in Conclavi Sixti V. Cardinali Castagna, nempe l'esser troppo favorito da Spagna; quòd fuit in nimio favore apud Hispanos; Hoc in Conclavi Innocentii IX. Madruccio, nempe l'esser troppo spagnuolo, quòd nimis Hispanis addictus fuit.
units.tr: XI. Likewise, it does harm to be too pleasing to the Spaniards or too devoted to them. The former harmed Cardinal Castagna in the Conclave of Sixtus V, namely "being too much favoured by Spain," since he was in too great favour with the Spaniards; the latter harmed Madruccio in the Conclave of Innocent IX, namely "being too much a Spaniard," since he was too devoted to the Spaniards.

units.la: XII. Itali esse debent. Jam supra in Electione Johannis XXII. Itali Italum volebant; & in Conclavi Urbani VI. Romani Italum à Cardinalibus petebant, Italum Cardinales Itali promovere studebant: Hinc & in præcedentibus Italu, Madruccius haberi voluit, & non-Italis spes omnis præcisa fuit.
units.tr: XII. The pope must be an Italian. Already above, at the election of John XXII, the Italians wanted an Italian; and in the Conclave of Urban VI the Romans demanded an Italian from the cardinals, and the Italian cardinals strove to promote an Italian. Hence also in the preceding conclaves Madruccio wished to be regarded as an Italian, and all hope was cut off for the non-Italians.

units.la: XIII. Sed non omnis terra Italica æquè Paparum ferax est. Cum post mortem Nicolai II. de eligendo novo Papa agere-tur, tur, Longobardorum Episcopi congregati, referente ex Nicolao Aragonensi Baronio ad a. 1061. n. 3. & talem personam eligendam duxerant, quæ infirmitatibus eorum compateretur & condescenderet, & non aliunde quàm de Paradiso Italiæ (ita Longobardiam nominabant;) sed hodie est alius Paradisus Italiæ, extra quem, in ipsa licèt Italia, arbor scientiæ boni & mali Pontificalis vix crescit. Contrà Longobardi non admittuntur; Hinc Pasquinus L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 265. ita canit: Lombardi miei Signori, questa tana Non è fatta per voi, havi pacienza, Papi vi voglio fan della Dogna. Id est;
units.tr: XIII. But not every Italian land is equally fertile in popes. When, after the death of Nicholas II, the choice of a new pope was being debated, the bishops of Lombardy gathered, and, as Baronius of Aragon reports from Nicholas, under the year 1061, number 3, they had decided that such a person should be chosen "as would sympathise with their weaknesses and condescend to them, and not from anywhere but from the Paradise of Italy" (so they called Lombardy). But today there is another Paradise of Italy, outside which, even within Italy itself, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil of the papacy scarcely grows. On the contrary, the Lombards are not admitted. Hence Pasquino, in The Ambassador of Rome, p. 265, sings: "Lombards, my lords, this den is not made for you; have patience. I will make you popes of the customs house."

units.la: Longobardi, Domini mei, hæc spelunca non est pro vobis, patienter expectate, Papæ eritis in domo mercium.
units.tr: "Lombards, my lords, this cave is not for you; wait patiently; you will be popes in the merchants' house."

units.la: XIV. Excluduntur Neapolitani, qui jam sub nomine Hispanorum exclusi sunt tanquam eorum subditi; Pessimum autem est, quòd ipsi etiam Hispani Neapolitanos subditos suos promovere nolunt, atque in Conclavi Alexandri VII. obstitit l'esser Neapolitano, Neapoli oriundum esse; Timebant enim Hispani, Neapolitanum Papam Patriam sedi subjecturum esse. Hinc in Vaticinio de Purpuratis L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 255. de Brancaccio Papabili legimus: Brancaccio è dotto, e a prima vista pare Sogetto al sin di non andare in vano, Mà riflettendo, ch' è Neapolitano, Convien pur anche questo rifiutare. Id est;
units.tr: XIV. The Neapolitans are excluded, who were already shut out under the name of Spaniards as their subjects. The worst of it is that the Spaniards themselves do not want to promote their own Neapolitan subjects, and in the Conclave of Alexander VII being "a Neapolitan, born at Naples" stood in the way; for the Spaniards feared that a Neapolitan pope would subject the See to his homeland. Hence in the prophecy about the purple-clad men, The Ambassador of Rome, p. 255, we read of Brancaccio as a possible pope: "Brancaccio is learned, and at first sight seems suited to the chance of not going in vain; but on reflection, since he is a Neapolitan, this too must be rejected."

units.la: Brancaccio est doctus & primo intuitu eligendus videtur, sed quando Neapolitanus consideratur rejectaneus est.
units.tr: "Brancaccio is learned and at first sight seems the one to be chosen, but when he is considered as a Neapolitan he is to be rejected."

units.la: XV. Excluduntur etiam Veneti. Sic in eodem Conclavi Patriæ consideratio Cardinali Bragadino Veneto obstitisse conjicitur, e la memoria d'Eugenio I. e Paolo II. impediva l'aura del Cardinale Bragadini, perche l'uno con la violenza & con l'uso d'un'arbitrio troppo libero, & l'altro con la vanità de' pensieri e con l'odio essercitato contro de' letterati, sece formare concetto, che più tosto à difendere la libertà della patria, che à governare la greggia di Christo fosse habile; & memoria Eugenii I. & Pauli II. impediebat auram Cardinalis Bragadini, quia alter violentia & arbitrii nimis liberi usu, alter conceptuum vanitate & odio in literatos exercito, ansam dederunt cogitandi, esse magis aptum ad liberlatem patria defendendam quàm verò ad gubernandum Christi gregem. Atque planè perversam Romae de Venetis Cardinalibus opinionem conceptam esse, ex Colloquio rursus Pasquini & Marphorii L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.266. discimus; Ita loquuntur: Mar: Mi hanno rotta la testa, e notte e giorno Se ne vengon da me li Venetiani Per farsi del Triregno il Crine adorno. Pas. Dare non voglio nelle loro mani Questi si belli, e nobili bocconi Che saressimo tutti Luterani. Id est:
units.tr: XV. The Venetians are excluded too. Thus in the same Conclave the consideration of country is conjectured to have stood in the way of Cardinal Bragadino, a Venetian: "and the memory of Eugene I and Paul II hindered the favour of Cardinal Bragadini, because the one, by violence and the exercise of an overly free will, and the other, by the vanity of his thoughts and by hatred exercised against men of letters, gave the impression that he was fitter to defend the liberty of his homeland than to govern the flock of Christ." And from the dialogue of Pasquino and Marforio again, in The Ambassador of Rome, p. 266, we learn that a thoroughly false opinion of the Venetian cardinals had been formed at Rome. They speak thus: Marforio: "They have broken my head; night and day the Venetians come to me, to adorn the crest of the triple crown. Pasquino: "I do not want to let these fine and noble morsels fall into their hands, or we would all be Lutherans." That is:

units.la: Mar. Mihi caput ruperunt diu noctúque, si abeunt à me Veneti, ut comam Regno sive coronâ triplici ornent.
units.tr: Mar. They have worn my head down day and night, if the Venetians leave me, to adorn the crown of the Triple Crown with hair.

units.la: Pas. Nolo iis dare hac tam pulchra & tam delicata frusta. Essemus omnes Lutherani.
units.tr: Pas. I do not want to hand over these fine, delicate morsels to them. We would all become Lutherans.

units.la: Sic videtur, Pasquinus Nationis vitium denotâsse, sed personalia longe pejora sequuntur: Mar. Eccoli Barbarigo & Ottoboni Uno di questi la Dataria haveva Pas. Ammettere non vuò questi Ladroni. Id est.
units.tr: So it seems that Pasquin pointed to a national failing, but personal attacks follow that are far worse: Mar. Here are Barbarigo and Ottoboni, one of whom had the Dataria. Pas. I do not want to admit these thieves.

units.la: Mar. Ecce eos Barbarigum & Ottobonum, quorum hic Dataria praefectus erat. Pas.. Non admittam hos fures. Quicquid autem de his fuerit, quorum alter jam admissus est, communiter Veneti minùs grati sunt, quia patriae magis quàm Ecclesiae addicti habentur, atque minùs ambiunt etiam pro concivibus suis Venetis incrementi nimii familiae Pontificiae, periculíque hinc libertati suae imminentis timore; Imò etiam suasum fuit eisdem, ut ne purpuram quidem nobilibus suis indulgeant, eâ Papae magis quàm Patriae devinciendis, atque exinde Patriae minùs fidis futuris. Verùm non desunt etiam suasiones & rationes in contrarium aliquando efficaces.
units.tr: Mar. Here are Barbarigo and Ottoboni, of whom the first was prefect of the Dataria. Pas. I will not admit these thieves. Whatever the case with these men, of whom one has already been admitted, the Venetians as a body are less welcome, because they are considered more devoted to their homeland than to the Church, and they are less eager, even on behalf of their fellow Venetians, for the excessive growth of the papal household, since they fear the danger to their liberty that arises from it. Indeed, it has even been urged on them that they should not grant the purple even to their own nobles, so that the Pope rather than the homeland might bind them to himself, and so that they would be less loyal to their homeland in future. Yet arguments and persuasions to the contrary are not lacking, and at times they have been effective.

units.la: XVI. Terras tunc steriles alias, licèt Italicas, simul brevi Oratione complexus est in Conclavi Urbani VII. Cardinalis Lemovicensis, qui vertendo se ad Dominum Florentinum, dixit; Vos verò estis de Florentia, qua est terra inimica Roma, & ideò non eligemus vos; Dominus autem Cardinalis Mediolanensis est de terra Barnabonis; qui semper fuit contrà Ecclesiam, Dominus Cardinalis de Ursinis similiter est Romanus partialis &c.
units.tr: XVI. In the conclave of Urban VII, the Cardinal of Limoges, in a brief speech, also took in the other barren lands, though they were Italian. Turning to the Florentine lord, he said: You are from Florence, which is a land hostile to Rome, and therefore we will not elect you. The Lord Cardinal of Milan is from the land of Barnabas, who has always been against the Church. The Lord Cardinal Orsini is likewise a partisan Roman, etc.

units.la: XVII. Senenses ferè excluduntur; Hinc in Conclavi Clementis IX. Elcio nocuit l'esser egli Senese, quòd Senensis fuit. Deodem Febo Vaticinante, L'Ambasc. di Romolo. p.242. ita canit;
units.tr: XVII. The Sienese are almost entirely excluded. Hence, in the conclave of Clement IX, Elci was harmed by the fact that he is a Sienese, because he was a Sienese. On the same subject, Phoebus the prophet, in L'Ambasciata di Romolo, p. 242, sings thus:

units.la: Aliiex Italia.
units.tr: Others from Italy.

units.la: Senenses.
units.tr: The Sienese.

units.la: Elci in van' t' affatichi, e speri in vanoGiunger di Pietro à calpestar 'il soglioChe Imperante mirarsi in VaticanoPiù non vogliono i Rè Senese orgoglio;S' oppone à tuoi discgni anch' il Romano,E Chigi trovera più d'uno scoglioHor' ch'il mondo gustò miglior vivandaTornar non vuole à pastur la ghianda. Id est:
units.tr: Elci, you labour in vain and hope in vain to climb to the throne of Peter. Kings no longer want to see Sienese pride ruling in the Vatican. The Roman opposes your designs as well, and Chigi will put more than one rock in your path. Now that the world has tasted better food, it does not want to go back to eating acorns.

units.la: Elci in vanum laboras & frustra speras Petri conscendere solium, nolunt Reges amplius in Vaticano imperantem videre fastum. Etiam Romani sibi opponunt. Et Chigius tibi scopulos objicit. Et postquam mundus melioribus cibis assuetus est, glandes negligit.
units.tr: Elci, you labour in vain and hope in vain to ascend the throne of Peter. Kings no longer want to see pride ruling in the Vatican. The Romans too oppose you. Chigi throws rocks in your way. And since the world has become used to better food, it scorns acorns.

units.la: De eodem Roma per la verità p.188. Ch'al primo noce l' essere Senese, Roma già si stufo de' finti artieri. Id est.
units.tr: On the same subject, Rome through the truth, p. 188: Being a Sienese harms the first candidate; Rome is already sick of pretending artisans.

units.la: Primò nocet, quòd Senensis est. Roma jam odit simulantes artifices.
units.tr: First, he is harmed because he is a Sienese. Rome already hates pretending artisans.

units.la: Similia occurrunt de nominetenus simili Delci p. 88. Li pretend. del Papato: Delci poi di questa Torta Non ne mangia in questo mese Dio ne guardi da Senese Se ben fan la Gatta morta. Id est:
units.tr: Similar things occur about Delci, who bears a similar name, in The Pretenders to the Papacy, p. 88: Delci will not eat of this cake this month; God keep us from the Sienese, even if they play dead like a cat.

units.la: Delcius etiam de hac placenta in hoc mense non edet, Deus nos custodiat à Senensibus, licèt felim mortuam simulent. Maximè eos excludit Magnus Hetruriæ Dux, timens, ne sic Senensibus sub Papa conciye suo animi ad recuperandam libertatem crescant.
units.tr: Delci will not eat of this cake this month either. May God keep us from the Sienese, even if they pretend to be a dead cat. The Grand Duke of Tuscany excludes them most of all, fearing that the Sienese, under a Pope of their own, will grow bolder in their courage to recover their liberty.

units.la: XVIII. Vix admittuntur Genuenses. Nam in Conclavi Clementis IX. Cardinali Duraccio nocuit la fatale compositione d'essere Genouese, fatalis compositio, quòd fuit Genuensis; Id quod Author Cardinalismi p. 3. l. 3. p. 299. non picciolo impedimento; non parvum impedimentum & il peggio che v'era in lui, pessimum, quod in eo erat; vocat: Sic & Romaper laVerità, Ambasc. di Rom. p.188. Bonellum impedire, quòd sit di razza Genouese, origine Genuensis; pronunciat. Et Pasquinus p. 264. canit: Genouese mi pare ogni Soldato Ameter non può già sti tartaglioni Che cangiarian la sedia in un mercato. Id est: Genuenses mihi videtur omnis miles, non admittam balbos hos, mercatum ex sede facerent.
units.tr: XVIII. The Genoese are scarcely admitted. For in the conclave of Clement IX, Cardinal Duraccio was harmed by the fatal composition of being a Genoese, a fatal composition, because he was a Genoese. The author of Cardinalismus, p. 3, l. 3, p. 299, calls this a not small impediment, and the worst thing that was in him. Rome through the Truth, Ambassador of Rome, p. 188, says the same: that Bonelli is hindered because he is of Genoese stock, of Genoese origin. And Pasquin, p. 264, sings: Every soldier seems to me a Genoese. I will not admit these stammerers, who would turn the chair into a marketplace. I think every soldier is a Genoese. I will not admit these stammerers; they would make a market of the seat.

units.la: XIX. Obstat, Lucam patriam habere. Hinc Author Cardinalismi p.3.l.3.p 310.311. memorat, Magnum Hetruriae Ducem, magnum etiam Conclavis Arbitrum minùs Sanctae Susannae, sive Spadae fayisse, ob duas causas, la prima era, l'essere egli Lucchese, cioè cittadino bene merito d'una Republica, che il Gran Duca guarda con l'occhio della misericordia, e che al sicuro la vorrebbe meglio tenere tra le sue mani, che nel mezo del suo stato, Id est: Prima erat, quod fuit Lucensis, id est, civis bene meritus Reipublica, quam Magnus Dux oculis misericordia intuetur, & certè mallet in sua potestate, quàm verò aliàs in medio ditionis sua habere. Idem de eodem in Conclavi Clem. X. degente L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.230. occurrit: Al Gran Duca sarà sempre sospetto à causa della Patria, punto che dara in ogni tempo l'esclusiva à Lucchesi. Id est: Magno Duci semper respectu Patria suspectus erit, quia semper excludet Lucenses. Hinc etiam de Bonvisio Roma canit: Ambasc. di Rom. p.26. Bonvisi se ne stà tutto affamato E da Lucca mi manda una Staffetta, Mà per esser di RaZZa maledetta Sarà da tutti quanti mal trattato; Id est:
units.tr: XIX. Being from Lucca is an obstacle. Hence the author of Cardinalismus, p. 3, l. 3, pp. 310–311, reports that the Grand Duke of Tuscany, the great arbiter of the conclave too, failed to obtain Santa Susanna, or the Sword, for two reasons. The first was that he was a Lucchese, that is, a citizen well deserving of a republic, which the Grand Duke regards with an eye of mercy, and which he would certainly prefer to hold in his own power rather than in the middle of his dominions. The first was that he was a Lucchese, that is, a citizen well deserving of the Republic, whom the Grand Duke regards with an eye of mercy, and he would certainly rather have him in his own power than elsewhere in the midst of his domain. The same appears about the same man in the conclave of Clement X, in L'Ambasciata di Roma, p. 230: The Grand Duke will always be suspicious of him because of his homeland; he will always give the exclusion to the Lucchesi. The Grand Duke will always be wary of him on account of his homeland, since he will always exclude the Lucchesi. Hence Rome also sings about Bonvisi, in L'Ambasciata di Roma, p. 26: Bonvisi sits there starving, and sends me a courier from Lucca, but because he belongs to a cursed race, everyone will treat him badly. Bonvisi, almost dead of hunger, writes to me from Lucca, but because his origin is accursed, everyone will treat him badly.

units.la: Bonvisius fame propemodum enecatus Lucâ ad me scribit, sed quia origo ejus maledicta est, omnes eum male tractabunt.
units.tr: Bonvisi, almost starved to death, writes to me from Lucca, but because his origin is cursed, everyone will treat him badly.

units.la: XX. Impediuntur Pedemontani sive Sabaudi. Impedivit sanè Patria bonum Bonam. De quo L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.239. legimus, eum gratum fuisse Gallis, tanquam Pedemontanum, sed eo ipso nomine ab Hispanis expertè excludendum, oltre che il gran Duca, inquit Author, non permetterà mai, che il Duca di Savoia habbia un Papa alla sua divotione, e molto meno i Cardinali di Genoa: si che il parlar di lui, ciò è un perdere il tempo. Id est; Ut taceam, Magnum Ducem nunquam permissurum ut Dux Sabaudiæ habeat Papam sibi addictum, & multò minùs permissuros esse Cardinales Genuenses: ut tempus perderet, qui de eo loqui vellet.
units.tr: XX. The Piedmontese or Savoyards are hindered. Their homeland certainly hindered the good Bona. Of him we read in L'Ambasciata di Roma, p. 239, that he was pleasing to the French as a Piedmontese, but by that very name he was openly to be excluded by the Spaniards: besides which, the author says, the Grand Duke will never permit the Duke of Savoy to have a Pope devoted to him, and much less will the Genoese cardinals permit it; so whoever wished to speak of him would be wasting his time. To say nothing of the fact that the Grand Duke will never allow the Duke of Savoy to have a Pope devoted to him, and far less will the Genoese cardinals allow it. Whoever wished to speak of him would waste his time.

units.la: XXI. Quæ Patria fuerit Facchinetti & Albergati, nescio; illud ex Febo Vaticinante L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.246. disco, cam illis impedimento fuisse; ita enim canit Phoebus: Facchinetti e Albergati hanno di fuori Quel ch' appar tutto buono, e tutto santo, Mà l' esser del Paese, ove hanno i Cuori Varii dal volto, à lor fa danno tanto Si come di Rettorici colori Sia sol di fuori effigiato il manto, Dentro poi vive il Lupo; e s'è ben visto Altre volte gabbato, e Pietro e Christo. Id est.
units.tr: XXI. What country Facchinetti and Albergati came from I do not know. I learn from Phoebus the Prophet, L'Ambasciata di Roma, p. 246, that their origin was an impediment to them.
