Thus Phoebus sings: Facchinetti and Albergati have on the outside what appears entirely good and entirely holy, but being from the country where the heart varies from the face, it does them great harm; just as rhetorical colours show only the outside of the cloak painted, while inside lives the wolf. And we have often seen both Peter and Christ cheated by such tricksters.

units.la: Facchinettus & Albergatus extrinsecus præse ferunt sanctitatem; sed quia orti sunt è regione, in qua cor vultui non respondet; tantum inde damnum accipiunt, ac si Rhetoricorum istorum pallium sit tantùm extrinsecus pictum, sed intus vivat Lupus. Atque sic sæpe & Petrum & Christum, si nimirum hypocritæ tales Successores essent, deceptos vidimus.
units.tr: Facchinetti and Albergati outwardly display holiness; but because they are born in a region where the heart does not match the face, they suffer that much harm, as if the cloak of these rhetoricians were painted only on the outside, while the wolf lives within. And so we have often seen both Peter and Christ deceived, if such hypocrites were their successors.

units.la: XXII. Romanus olim in Conclavi Urbani VI. unicè à Romanis expetebatur; Licèt enim tunc Italus electus esset, tamen ideò etiam publicationem differre usque ad electi adventum (erat enim extra Collegium;) voluerunt, quia dubitari poterat, quòd aliqua sinistra in via eidem electo possent occurrere, eo quòd ipse electus non erat Romanus, & Romani libenter habuissent natione Romanum.
units.tr: XXII. Formerly, in the conclave of Urban VI, a Roman was sought by the Romans alone. Although an Italian was then elected, the Romans nevertheless wanted the proclamation put off until the arrival of the one elected (he was outside the college), because it could be feared that some misfortune might befall the elected man on the road, since he was not a Roman, and the Romans would gladly have had a Roman by nationality.

units.la: XXIII. Hodie atque à longo tempore in ipsa Italia, vix alibi, quàm in Hetruria, & statu, ceu vocant, Ecclesiastico, homines nascuntur, albæ Gallinæ filii, quibus concessum est eniti in Pontificiæ dignitatis culmen. Atque verè scripsit Gallus Anonymus: On void que le Pontificat est en ce temps destiné seulement a un Cardinal, ou de l'Estat du Pape, ou de l'Estat de Toscane; le reste des Nations étant ou par naissance ou par accidens eloignéz de cette esperance. Id est. Apparet, Pontificatum hodie destinatum esse solùm Cardinali, aut ex statu Papæ, aut ex Hetruria; Reliquis Nationibus vel per nativitatem vel per accidens aliquod procul ab hac spe positis. Bene etiam causas detegere videtur ita pergens: La neutralité, que le Pape & le grand Duc de Toscane garde soigneusement, & dans laquelle ils peuvent se conserver plus que tout autre Prince, par la situation de leurs Etats & la possession, ou ils sont, fait, que leur sujets seuls ont cette prerogative d' être Papables à l'exclusion des autres Nations: Id est: Indifferentia, quam Papæ & Magnus Hetruriæ Dux sollicitè observant, & in qua se præ aliis Principibus conservant, adjuvante Regionum situ, & possessio, in qua sunt, facit, ut eorum subditi soli prærogativâ Papabilitatis, exclusis Nationibus aliis, gaudeant.
units.tr: XXIII. Today, and for a long time now, the Papal throne is hardly ever reached from anywhere except Tuscany and the so-called Ecclesiastical State in Italy itself. Men are born there, sons of the white hen, who are allowed to climb to the summit of the Papal dignity. The anonymous Frenchman wrote truly: One sees that the Papacy at this time is destined only for a Cardinal, either of the Pope's State or of the State of Tuscany; the rest of the nations, whether by birth or by circumstance, being far from this hope. That is: It appears that the Papacy is today destined only for a Cardinal, either from the Pope's State or from Tuscany; the other nations being placed far from this hope, either by birth or by some accident. He also seems to uncover the causes well, when he goes on: The neutrality which the Pope and the Grand Duke of Tuscany keep carefully, and in which they can preserve themselves more than any other Prince, owing to the situation of their States and the possession they hold, means that their subjects alone enjoy this prerogative of being Papabili, to the exclusion of the other nations. That is: The indifference which the Pope and the Grand Duke of Tuscany observe with care, and in which they keep themselves above other Princes, aided by the situation of the regions and by the possession they hold, causes their subjects alone to enjoy the prerogative of being Papabili, other nations being excluded.

units.la: XXIV. Imò etiam Familiarum respectus aliquando obest; Obfuit in eodem Conclavi, referente Authore Cardinalismi p. 3. l. 3. p. 322. Cardinali Caraffæ, d'haver sopra di sè il peccato originale della memoria poco propitia a gli Spagnuoli di Paolo IV. qual ostacolo è grande, e sło per dire impossibile; essendo sì già radicato ne' Conclavi con l'esclusione data dagli Spagnuoli, à tanti altri Cardinali della Casa Caraffa: senza questo potrebbe far passa in qualche Conclave, havendo qualità proprie al Papato &c. Id est: quòd laboravit peccato originali memoria parum propitia Hispanis Pauli IV. quod obstaculum magnum est & quasi impossibile, quia jam radicatum in Conclavibus, exclusis per Hispanos tot ex domo Caraffarum Cardinalibus: Absque hoc promoveri potuisset in quodam Conclavi, cùm qualitatibus Papatui propriis instructus sit &c. Similiter jam in Conclavi Urbani VI. n. XV. obfuisse Cardinali de Ursinis, diximus, quòd fuit partialis Romanus.
units.tr: XXIV. Indeed, regard for families also sometimes stands in the way. It stood in the way in the same Conclave, according to the author of the Cardinalismus, p. 3, l. 3, p. 322, in the case of Cardinal Carafa, because he carries upon himself the original sin of a memory not very favourable to the Spaniards of Paul IV, which obstacle is great, and as it were impossible, since it is already so rooted in the Conclaves by the exclusion given by the Spaniards to so many other Cardinals of the house of Carafa. Without this he could have made his way in some Conclave, having qualities proper to the Papacy, etc. That is: that he laboured under the original sin of a memory little favourable to the Spaniards of Paul IV, which obstacle is great and almost impossible, since it is already so rooted in the Conclaves, with so many Cardinals of the house of Carafa excluded by the Spaniards; without this he could have been promoted in some Conclave, since he is endowed with qualities proper to the Papacy, etc. Likewise, in the Conclave of Urban VI, n. XV, we said that Cardinal de Ursinis was harmed because he was a partisan Roman.

units.la: XXV. Is etiam Familiarum respectus obtinet, ut vix è præcipuis atque Nobilioribus Familiis eligantur, id quod Lottinus Dissert. de Conclavi docet, & Phœbus Vaticinans Ambasc. di Rom. p. 249.
units.tr: XXV. The respect for families also prevails, so that popes are scarcely chosen from the principal and more noble families, as Lottinus teaches in his Dissertation on the Conclave, and Phoebus Vaticinans in Ambasciata di Roma (p. 249).

units.la: Principi Porporati homai sapete: Che non tocca più à voi vestir quel manto &c. Id est: Principes Purpurati, nunc cognoscite, quòd non amplius vestiri vobis contingit hoc pallio &c.
units.tr: Principi Porporati homai sapete: Che non tocca più à voi vestir quel manto &c. That is: Purple-clad princes, now you know that it no longer falls to you to wear that mantle, etc.

units.la: Olim quidem ex Illustribus interdum Familiis electi fuerunt; In media cumprimis ætate. Ab initio enim obtinuit in genere illud: Pauci nobiles &c. Et quia plerunque ad Martyria, ad paupertatem vocabantur, defuit magnatibus mundi ambitionis occasio.
units.tr: Formerly, indeed, popes were sometimes chosen from illustrious families, especially in the middle ages. For from the beginning the general rule held: Few nobles etc. And because they were for the most part called to martyrdom and poverty, the magnates of the world lacked occasion for ambition.

units.la: XXVI. Hodie, licèt aliquando Æneæ Sylvio in Conclavi objectum: Come potrà egli povero & infermo soccorrere & souvenire alla chiesa povera e debole? Id est: Quomodo ipse pauper & infirmus succurrere atque subvenire poterit Ecclesiæ pauperi & debili? pauperiorum tamen prærogativa est, neque tantum eligitur persona alle volte nata dell' ultima plebe, nata interdum ex ultima plebe, ut Conclave Innocentii IX. habet, Urbanus IV. veteramentarii sutoris, Benedictus XII. pistoris, Adrianus VI. secundùm quosdam aulæorum textoris, secundùm plerosque coctoris cerevisiæ ministri, Sixtus V. bubulci in Conclavi d'un povero contadino, pauperis rustici filius, quique sæpe solitus jactare, se in illustri, id est, undiquaque patente domo natum, ut in vita narratur; Et ante hos ex inferiori plebe plures; Sed & genus humile commendat, ut in Conclavi Gregorii XV. Borghesio Camporam.
units.tr: XXVI. Today, although it was once objected against Aeneas Sylvius in the conclave: Come potrà egli povero & infermo soccorrere & souvenire alla chiesa povera e debole? That is: How can he, poor and infirm, succour and help a poor and weak Church? nevertheless the poor have the advantage, and persons are chosen not only from the highest rank: alle volte nata dell' ultima plebe, nata interdum ex ultima plebe, as the conclave of Innocent IX records; Urban IV was the son of an old-clothes cobbler, Benedict XII of a baker, Adrian VI, according to some, of a weaver of hangings, according to most, of a servant who brewed beer; Sixtus V of a herdsman in the conclave, d'un povero contadino, the son of a poor peasant, who often used to boast that he was born in illustri, that is, in a house open on every side, as is recounted in his life; and before these, several from the lower commons. Humble birth also recommends, as in the conclave of Gregory XV, Borghese of Camporae.

units.la: XXVII. Non quidem quòd à divitiis & fastu mundi alie- na jam sit Pontificia dignitas, ut olim fuerat. Sed nullibi jam di- vitiarum & mundani fastûs ostentationem majorem esse, patet o- mnibus. Interim tamen, ne Principes electi nimiâ liberalitate thesauros, ut vocant, Ecclesiæ exhauriant, ne Agnatorum potestati magis magisque augendæ unicè studeant, ne ad Imperium nati Italiæ Principibus contentiones & rixas moveant, ne de Papatu ipso hæreditario reddendo cogitationes, quales de conjungendo Imperio & Papatu Maximilianus I. habuisse dicitur, suscipiant, ne facilè Cardinalibus noceant, & ad Imperium educati minùs laborum sociis tribuant eosdémque contemnant, & quæ rationes aliæ sunt, quàm male eligendis fidant, arguentes; hinc Principes raro Papabiles habentur, & quos ad ordinis decus Cardinales creant, ob periculum potestatis ulteriùs non evehunt, facilius ad infimæ plebis homines, ubi de eligendo Papa agitur, condescendentes.
units.tr: XXVII. Not indeed that the papal dignity is now alien from riches and worldly pomp, as it once was. But it is plain to all that nowhere is there a greater display of riches and worldly pomp. Meanwhile, however, lest elected princes drain the so-called treasuries of the Church by excessive generosity, lest they strive ever more to enlarge the power of their own kin, lest princes born to empire stir up contentions and quarrels with the princes of Italy, lest they entertain thoughts of making the papacy itself hereditary, such as Maximilian I is said to have had about joining the empire and the papacy, lest they easily harm the cardinals, and, being educated for empire, give little reward to their companions in labors and despise them, and, arguing for other reasons besides, lest they trust to the badly chosen: for these reasons princes are rarely held to be papabile, and those whom the cardinals create to the honor of their order they do not advance further for fear of the power, more readily stooping to men of the lowest commons, where the choice of pope is concerned.

units.la: XXVIII. Posito autem Nationum & Patriæ impedimento, monstri propemodum loco videri queat, quòd is, qui nuper Petri claves tenuit, ac pro Christi Vicario se gessit, Innocentius XI. Pontifex extra Papæ & Hetrusci Ducis ditiones, quippe Comi in Insubria ad Larium Lacum atque sic Hispaniarum Regi subjectione obnoxius in lucem editus fuit; atque Divos admodùm faventes habuit, quòd difficultatem gravissimam, quam ista nascendi conditio objiciebat, eluctari illi feliciter licuit. Enim verò accidit hoc præter opinionem tum multorum, tum præcipuè Viri Aulæ rerúmque Romanarum peritissimi, qui simul ac Clemens X. fato concesserat, congregatis in Conclavi Patribus Purpuratis interea temporis hariolationes de consiliis eorundem edidit, & omnium illic congregatorum genium vivis coloribus delineans, ostendit, quantum quisque Papabilium spei foveat, & quibus contrà incommodis urgeatur; Et qui de Innocentio, tunc adhuc Benedicto Odeschalchio, inter alia ita ratiocinabatur: Il n'y a autre chose, qui luy fasse tort, que d'être Milanois sujet du Roy d'Espagne. Cependant ayant été proposé dernierement dans le dernier Conclave à Monsieur le Duc de Chaunes Ambassadeur Extraordinaire de S. M. T. il n'y s'y opposa pas, & il dit seulement à celuy, qui luy en fit la proposition, qu'il luy déplaisoit, que ce Cardinal n'eut pas le bonheur d'être connu du Roy T. C. son Maître; ne faisant aucune expression, qui peut marquer de l'ombrage du lieu, ouil étoit né. Cela nuira ne antmoins à l'exaltation d'Odeschal-chi, sur tout à cause de la jalousie entre les couronnes, qui sont animées l'une contre l'autre, en cette presente guerre. Il faut encore ajouter, que les Espagnols n'ont pas de penchant à faire des Milanois ou des Napolitains Papes, de crainte, qu'ils ne s'accordent avec la France pour les chasser d'Italie, ou ils ont trop de pied & par reflexion aux pretensions du S. Siege e de la France sur le Royaume de Naples & sur l' Etat de Milan respectivement, dont ils ont l'exemple d'Alexandre VI. Espagnol de la Maison Borgia, qui s'accorda avec la France, à les chasser de Naples. Id est; Nihil ipsi obstare potest, nisi quod est Mediolanensis, subditus Regis Hispania. Interim tamen, cùm nuper & in ultimo Conclavi proponeretur Duci Chaunesio Legato Extraordinario Regis Christianissimi, non se opposuit, sed tantùm dixit; dolere se, quòd Regi ignotus sit, nullo indicio dato suspicionis ex loco nativitatis concepta. Hoc tamen nocebit Odeschalchio, maximè ob æmulationem regnorum inimicitias in bello presenti invicem exercentium. Addo, Hispanos non usque quaque faciles esse in promovendis ad Papatum Mediolanensibus aut Neapolitanis, timentes, ne se conjungerent cum Gallis, ad eos Italia pellendos, ubi nimis potentes sunt; Sic etiam intuitu pretensionum Galliæ & sanctæ sedis quoad Regnum Neapolitanum & Ducatum Mediolanensem respectivè; Cujus quidem exemplum habent in Alexandro VI. Hispano ex domo Borgia, qui cum Gallis fœdus inierat ad Hispanos Neapoli pellendos.
units.tr: XXVIII. Yet, setting aside the obstacle of nation and homeland, it may seem almost a monstrosity that Innocent XI, who recently held the keys of Peter and acted as Vicar of Christ, was born outside the dominions of the Pope and the Tuscan Duke. He was born at Como in Insubria, on Lake Como, and so was subject to the rule of the King of Spain. He had very favourable gods, for he was able to overcome happily the very grave difficulty which this condition of birth raised. Indeed this happened contrary to the expectation of many, and especially of a man most skilled in the Court and in Roman affairs, who, as soon as Clement X had yielded to fate, while the Purple Fathers were gathered in the Conclave, meanwhile published guesses about their counsels. Painting in lively colours the character of everyone gathered there, he showed how much hope each of the Papabili cherished and by what disadvantages each was burdened. Speaking of Innocent, who was then still Benedetto Odescalchi, he reasoned among other things thus: Nothing else harms him except that he is a Milanese, a subject of the King of Spain. Yet when lately, in the last Conclave, he was proposed to the Duke of Chaulnes, Extraordinary Ambassador of His Most Christian Majesty, he did not oppose it, and he only said to the one who made the proposal that it displeased him that this Cardinal did not have the good fortune to be known to the Most Christian King his Master; making no remark which could show suspicion of the place where he was born. That is: Nothing can stand in his way except that he is a Milanese, a subject of the King of Spain. Yet recently, and in the last Conclave, when he was proposed to the Duke de Chaulnes, Extraordinary Legate of the Most Christian King, he did not oppose it, but only said that he was sorry that he was unknown to the King, giving no sign of suspicion conceived from the place of his birth. Nevertheless this will harm Odescalchi, chiefly because of the rivalry of the kingdoms, which are waging enmity against one another in the present war. I add that the Spaniards are not altogether ready to make Milanese or Neapolitans Popes, fearing lest they join with the French to drive them out of Italy, where they are too powerful. Thus also, with regard to the claims of France and the Holy See respectively over the Kingdom of Naples and the Duchy of Milan, of which they have the example in Alexander VI, a Spaniard of the Borgia family, who made an alliance with France to drive the Spaniards out of Naples.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Non tamen nocuit Innocentio suum peccatum, ut vocant, Originale, atque eo ipso, quia Hispanis non omni ex parte placere atque eorum metum planè excludere poterat, facilius à Gallis admissus fuit, qui sine dubio parti utrique placere atque omnem de se suspicionem delere semper studuit, ut jam supra eum etiam pecuniâ saltem ad Cardinalatum consequendum rem egisse ostendimus. Interim tamen Galli, si futurorum gnari fuissent, forte non tam facile in ejus Electionem consensuri fuissent.
units.tr: Yet Innocent's sin, as they call it, original sin, did him no harm. Because he could not please the Spaniards in every respect or wholly remove their fear, he was more readily admitted by the French, who certainly always wanted to please both sides and to remove all suspicion of himself. As we have already shown above, he had also worked to obtain the cardinalate, at least with money. Still, if the French had known the future, they perhaps would not have agreed so easily to his election.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: An autem nullum est in ordinario illo, & qui jam à longo tempore obtinuit, Nationum respectu vitium? Est certè, quòd nempe, dum in Christo Jesu neque Judæus, neque Græcus Gal. V. 28. neque proin ulla Nationum distinctio, sed tota terra Domini atque æquè sancta, nullâque de Pontifice ex hac potiùs quàm ex illa Natione, imò provincia eligendo, Prophetia aut jussio facta est; nihilominùs in Vicario, si credere fas est, Jesu Christi & Græcus & Germanus & Gallus & Neapolitanus & Venetus & Florentinus & Longobardus & Senensis & Genuensis & Lucensis & Pedemontanus,imò & Ursinus & Caraffa, & dives & pauper & nobilis & ignobilis & quales non ? dantur, plerique suis temporibus ad Pontificatum planè inepti, licèt aliâs (ex hypothesi) aptissimi,aptiores aliis; Dum interim soli Itali,imò soli Romani atque Hetruriæ incolæ sine peccato originali eatenus concipi dicuntur; Atque ita communis totius, ut ajunt,Universalis Ecclesiæ Parens,Parens æque Americanarum ac Romanæ Ecclesiæ ex solius quasi Romanæ gremio prodire potest. Quod certè est,veterem distinctionem, ut in aliis quoque, reducere atque turpissimum Papatûs universalis,etiam in sensu passivo,monopolium exercere,nec non exemplis primorum seculorum,ut & verbis Cardinalium n. II. de nulla personarum aut nationum acceptione, imò, juxta illos ibidem,ipsius Christi exemplo strenuè contraire. Quasi verò Spiritus S. specialiter eligens ex illo tantùm distric̄tu Papas producere, solam illam terram tam nobili semine imprægnare,nec qui olim super aquas ferebatur, ultra mare jam vel ultra montes ad idoneum Ecclesiæ Pastorem adducendum pergere possit!
units.tr: But is there no fault concerning nations in that ordinary practice, which has long held sway? There certainly is. In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek (Gal. 3.28), and so no distinction of nations. The whole earth belongs to the Lord and is equally holy. No prophecy or command was given that the Pope should be chosen from this nation rather than that, or even from this province. Yet, if it is lawful to believe it, the Vicar of Jesus Christ has been a Greek, a German, a Frenchman, a Neapolitan, a Venetian, a Florentine, a Lombard, a Sienese, a Genoese, a Lucchese, a Piedmontese, and even Orsini and Carafa, rich and poor, noble and base, and whatever kinds there are. Many of them were quite unfit for the papacy in their own times, although on the same hypothesis they were most suitable, more suitable than others. Meanwhile only Italians, indeed only the inhabitants of Rome and Tuscany, are said to be conceived without original sin. So the parent of the whole, as they say, universal Church, the parent of the American Church as much as of the Roman Church, can come forth only from the bosom of Rome, so to speak. This certainly brings back the old distinction, as in other matters, and exercises the most shameful monopoly of universal papacy, even in its passive sense. It also contradicts, in the strongest way, the examples of the first centuries and the words of the cardinals on no respect of persons or nations (n. II.), and indeed, according to them, in the same place, the very example of Christ himself. As if the Holy Spirit, choosing specially, could produce Popes only from that one region, and could impregnate only that land with such noble seed, and the Spirit who once moved upon the waters could not go beyond the sea or beyond the mountains to bring in a fit Pastor for the Church!

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Quando autem (quod & in dignitatibus Ecclesiasticis multò minoribus requiritur) saltem ex legitimo conjugio orti eligi debent, vitiosum & illud merito censetur,quòd, præter incertitudinem communem, de quibusdam,spurios fuisse constat, & ex impuris,imò incestis amoribus genitos. Quò pertinent Paparum filii Papæ post prima secula & ipsi jam memorati & deinceps memorandi. Neque heic reticeri debet,quòd Clemens VII, ipso Platina in vita narrante, Patri Juliano Medicæo natus est ex parùm certa,neque propalam legitima uxore — filius post- humus — non modò lineamentis oris, sed toto corpo- ris habitu patri simillimus.
units.tr: Moreover, they ought to be elected at least from a lawful marriage, as is required even for much lesser ecclesiastical dignities. Rightly, this too is counted a fault: apart from the general uncertainty, it is certain that some were bastards, begotten from impure and even incestuous loves. To this belong the sons of the Popes after the first centuries, who have already been mentioned and will be mentioned again. Nor should it be passed over here that Clement VII, as Platina tells in his Life, was born of a not very certain, and not openly lawful, wife, a posthumous son, most like his father Giuliano de' Medici not only in the features of his face but in the whole habit of his body.

units.la: Ecclesiæ Romanæ Decani ad Episcopatum tandem provehebantur,sed non fuerunt orde sire dicta,dum non- nisquam nullo plane sacro ordine initiati, munere publico deputati tandem ad Episcopatum evecti fuerunt.
units.tr: The deans of the Roman Church were at last promoted to the episcopate, but they were not ordained in what is called orders. Some were initiated into no holy order at all, and after being appointed to public office were at last raised to the episcopate.

units.la: SECTIO QUINTA, In qua, De nævis & vitiis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum, ratione antecedentis dignitatis Ecclesiasticæ, item Ordinis Religiosi & Cœlibatûs, agitur.
units.tr: SECTION FIVE, in which the blemishes and faults in the election of the Roman Pontiffs are treated, with respect to the preceding ecclesiastical dignity, and likewise to the religious order and celibacy.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: I. Respectu dignitatis antecedanea ab initio plerunque ex Diaconis eligebantur, non semper; II. Progressu temporis ex Presbyteris; III. Quamvis subinde ex Laicis promoti sint, contrà constitutionem subsecutam; IV. Cui atiam exempla subsecuta contrariantur. V. Ut & Constitutionibus in Iure Canonico de Episcopis in genere, VI. Qua ad Romanos applicantur; VII. Tandem ex Episcopis &c. VIII. Olim etiam non Cardinales; IX. Quales jam lege requiruntur, sub pratextu; X. Qui examinatur; XI. Recensentur incommoda restrictionis ad solos Cardinales; XII. Quibus non obstantibus Cardinales esse debent, & diu ante ad Cardinalatum promoti; XIII. Quæ omnia vitium habent; XIV. Respectu Ordinis Religiosi, Monachi in genere primò vix admittuntur; XV. Sed maximè in Electionibus sibi contriantur Iesuita & Dominicani, exemplis Lugo & S.Clementis; XVI. S.Clementis Dominicani elogium; XVII. Machinationes Iesuitarum contrà eum per Barberinum; XVIII. Calumnia eorundem contrà eundem; XIX. Dominicanorum artes similes contrà Iesuitam; XX. Conclusiones ex his; XXI. Impedimenta speciatim Iesuitis occurrentia; XXII. Eligendi malè cœlibes esse jubentur; XXIII. Quod malè fieri porrò ostenditur; XXIV. Casus ex Antonio de Rosellis, si fertè conjugem habeat electus.
units.tr: I. With respect to the preceding dignity: at the beginning they were usually, though not always, chosen from among the deacons; II. As time went on, from among the presbyters; III. Although from time to time men were promoted from among the laity, contrary to the constitution that followed; IV. Examples that followed also run against it. V. And so too the constitutions in canon law on bishops in general; VI. How they are applied to the Romans; VII. Finally, from among the bishops, etc.; VIII. Formerly, not even cardinals; IX. What qualifications are now required by law, under pretext; X. Who is examined; XI. The disadvantages of restriction to cardinals alone are listed; XII. Notwithstanding these, they must be cardinals, and have been promoted to the cardinalate long before; XIII. All these things have a fault; XIV. With respect to the religious orders: monks in general are at first scarcely admitted; XV. But above all the Jesuits and Dominicans are opposed to each other in elections, with the examples of Lugo and St Clement; XVI. The eulogy of St Clement the Dominican; XVII. The machinations of the Jesuits against him through Barberini; XVIII. Their slander against the same man; XIX. The similar tricks of the Dominicans against the Jesuit; XX. Conclusions from these; XXI. Obstacles that particularly confront the Jesuits; XXII. Those to be elected are ordered to be unmarried; XXIII. It is further shown that this is done badly; XXIV. A case from Antonio de Rosellis, if perhaps the elected man has a wife.

units.la: I. Egimus de ortu Papabilium; Sed non sufficit sola natalium felicitas; multi in dictis locis ex Familiis approbatis modo legitimo nascuntur, qui tamen ad Papatum nunquam eliguntur, quia & alia requiruntur. Ab initio quidem erat sic: Ut plurimùm Ecclesiæ Romanæ Diaconi ad Episcopatum tandem provehebantur, sed non semper ordo iste observabatur, dum nonnunquam nullo planè antehac in Ecclesia ministerio publico defuncti Episcopi fiebant, quod vel solis jam allegatis Fabiani, Telesphori, atque Dionysii exemplis constare posset. Nimirum donorum exuberantia atque internus gratiæ ordo aliquando ordinem externum turbandum esse sualit.
units.tr: I. We have discussed the birth of those who may be Pope. But the happiness of noble birth alone is not enough: many who are born in the said places, from approved families and in lawful wedlock, are never elected to the papacy, because other things are also required. At the beginning it was indeed so: the deacons of the Roman Church were usually promoted in the end to the episcopate; but this order was not always observed, since sometimes men who had hitherto held no public ministry in the Church at all became bishops. This could be established from the examples of Fabian, Telesphorus and Dionysius, which we have already cited. Clearly the abundance of gifts and the inner order of grace sometimes thought fit to disturb the external order.

units.la: II. Sed introducta statim Episcoporum atque Presbyterorum inæqualitate, ex Presbyteris sæpe creabantur. Sic Cyprianus ad Antonianum Ep.52. in Cornelio laudat, quòd non subito ad Episcopatum perven(er)it, sed per omnia Ecclesiastica officia promotus & in Divinis administrationibus Dominum sæpe promeritus, ad sacerdotii sublime fastigium cunctis religionis gradibus ascend(er)it.
units.tr: II. But once the inequality between bishops and presbyters had been introduced, men were often created from among the presbyters. Thus Cyprian, in his letter to Antonianus (Ep. 52), praises Cornelius because he did not come to the episcopate suddenly, but, having been promoted through all the ecclesiastical offices and often having deserved well of the Lord in the divine administrations, he ascended to the lofty summit of the priesthood through all the grades of religion.

units.la: III. Hinc etiam Platina in Valentino I. admirabundus commemorat, tanta virtutis & sanctitatis fuisse, ut nondum Presbyter, sed Diaconus summum Pontificatus gradum meruerit. De Constantino Laico, ubi de Schismatibus egimus, atque de lato ea occasione decreto, nequisquam laicus nisi per gradus Ecclesiasticos ascendens Pontificatum occupare auderet sub anathematis poena, ut Platina in Stephano III. loquitur. Qua quidem ratione aliquot ex sequentibus anathemati subjecisse videtur.
units.tr: III. Hence also Platina, admiring, mentions in the life of Valentinus I that his virtue and holiness were so great that, not yet a presbyter but a deacon, he earned the highest grade of the pontificate. Concerning Constantine the layman, where we treated of the schisms, and of the decree issued on that occasion, that no layman should dare to seize the pontificate unless he ascended through the ecclesiastical grades, under penalty of anathema, as Platina says in the life of Stephen III. Indeed, for this reason he seems to have subjected several of those who followed to anathema.

units.la: IV. Prout etiam Leoni VIII. quòd neophytus electus esset, apud Baron. ad an. 964. n. 8. seqq. objectum fuit; atque Benedicto VIII. ad an. 1024. n. 4. vitio vertitur; nefas dictu, ait Baron. post verba Glabri, ex Laico transformatus est in Papam. Johannes XXI. inquit Platina——Episcopus Portuensis, ut quidam volunt, ut aliis placet, nullis sacris ante initiatus, Pontificium munus suscepit. Amadeus quoque Felix V. dictus ex Laico ipsius Basileensis Synodi decreto creatus est. Sic per dispensationem Pontificiam hodie etiam interdum Laicis atque non-Diaconis vox etiam passiva conceditur.
units.tr: IV. Likewise Leo VIII was objected to, because he was elected while still a neophyte, as is recorded in Baronius at the year 964, n. 8 and following; and Benedict VIII is blamed at the year 1024, n. 4. Baronius, after the words of Glaber, says: it is an unspeakable thing that he was transformed from a layman into a Pope. John XXI, says Platina, bishop of Porto, as some say, though others think otherwise, took up the papal office without having been initiated into any sacred order. Amadeus also, called Felix V, was created from a layman by a decree of the Synod of Basel. So by papal dispensation today, even laymen and non-deacons are sometimes granted the passive voice.

units.la: V. Quæ omnia contrariantur 36. Dist. Ca. Qui Ecclesiasticis disciplinis per ordinem non est imbutus & temporum approbatione Divinis stipendiis non est eruditus, nequaquam ad summum Ecclesiæ Sacerdotium aspirare præsumat: & non solùm in eo ambitio inefficax habeatur, verùm etiam ordinatores ejus careant eo ordine, quem contrà præcepta Patrum crediderant præsumendum; Atque 61. Dist. Ca. Nullus in Episcopatum eligatur, nisi in Sacris Ordinibus religiosè vivens fuerit inventus; Sacros autem ordines dicimus Diaconatum & Presbyteratum, hos siquidem solos primitiva legitur habuisse Ecclesia.
units.tr: V. All these things are contrary to Distinction 36, chapter: Let him who has not been trained in the ecclesiastical disciplines in order, and has not been instructed in the divine offices by the approval of time, by no means presume to aspire to the supreme priesthood of the Church; and not only is ambition in this matter regarded as ineffective, but also its ordainers lack that order which they had believed, contrary to the precepts of the Fathers, ought to be presumed. And also Distinction 61, chapter: No one is to be elected bishop unless he is found to have lived piously in the sacred orders; now we call the sacred orders the diaconate and the presbyterate, for these alone are read to have been held by the early Church.

units.la: VI. Quæ de Episcopis in genere dicta eò fortiùs respectu Romanorum stringunt, atque etiam eorum, qui ex Diaconis immediatè eliguntur, electiones vitiosas declarare videntur, præsertim quia ordo sæpe non ob necessitatem, aut virtutis excellentiam turbari solet; Quod certè præter exempla jam allata etiam in multis aliis etiam respectu non Diaconorum in invasionibus & intrusionibus maximè contigit.
units.tr: VI. What is said of bishops in general binds even more tightly with respect to the Romans, and seems to declare void the elections of those who are chosen directly from among the deacons, especially since the order is often disturbed not from necessity or from excellence of virtue. Certainly, apart from the examples already cited, this has also happened in many other cases, even with respect to non-deacons, in invasions and intrusions.

units.la: VII. Per aliquot secula non nisi ex Presbyteris & Diaconis, si ex initiatis, eligebantur, nulli ex Episcopis, atque primus ex Episcopo Portuensi Formosus factus est, post quam per varias aetates varii etiam ex peregrinis Episcopatibus ad Romanum assumebantur, imò etiam ex Archiepiscopatibus & Patriarchatibus, quia Romanus Episcopatus tandem multò caeteris dignitatibus Ecclesiasticis quibusvis praestare creditus fuit. Ordinarium autem, saltem frequens, introductis Cardinalibus Romanis Episcopis est, ut ex istis Pontifex eligatur, quod si non contingit, atque adhuc vel Diaconus, vel Presbyter, vel Laicus est, statim ordines accipit electus.
units.tr: VII. For some centuries they were chosen only from among presbyters and deacons, if from among the ordained, and none from among bishops; and the first to be taken from the bishopric of Porto was Formosus. After that, through various ages, various bishops from foreign sees were also received into the Roman see, even from archbishoprics and patriarchates, because the Roman bishopric was at last believed to excel all other ecclesiastical dignities. The usual practice, at least a frequent one, since the Roman cardinals were introduced, is that the Pope is chosen from among them; but if this does not happen, and the man is still a deacon, a presbyter or a layman, he receives the orders immediately after his election.

units.la: VIII. Ex Cardinalibus hodie semper eliguntur atque eligi debent, licèt olim etiam extra Conclave Pontifices quaeri potuerint, atque multi sic quaesiti inventíque fuerint. Ita post mortem Hadriani IV. juxta Epistolam Canonicorum pro Victore ad Fridericum apud Baronium ad an. 1160. n. 5. inter Cardinales convenit tandem contentione crescente, ut concordem electionem facerent de aliquo Cardinalium. Quod si non possent, quaerent extraneam personam. Imò in legibus Gregorii X. Conclaviariis apud Onuphrium. annot. ad Greg. expresse habetur: Ut non solùm Cardinales, sed & omnes cujusvis ordinis & conditionis homines in Romanum Pontificem creari possint. Juxta quas leges etiam sino al Pontificato di Paolo II. inquit Author Cardinalismi p. 3. l. 2. p. 140. che successe à Pio II. venne concesso a' Cardinali di cercare i fogetti fuori del Conclave. Id est; Usque ad Pontificatum Pauli II. qui successit Pio II. permissum fuit Cardinalibus quaerere eligendos extra Conclave.
units.tr: VIII. Today the Pope is always chosen, and must be chosen, from among the cardinals, although formerly popes could also be sought outside the Conclave, and many were sought and found in this way. Thus after the death of Hadrian IV, according to the letter of the canons for Victor to Frederick, in Baronius at the year 1160, n. 5, the cardinals at last agreed, with the contention growing, that they should make a unanimous election of one of the cardinals. But if they could not, they should seek a person from outside. Indeed, in the laws of Gregory X on the Conclave, in Onuphrius (notes on Gregory), it is expressly stated: that not only cardinals but men of every order and condition may be created Roman Pontiff. According to these laws, too, the author of Cardinalismo says (p. 3, l. 2, p. 140) that until the pontificate of Paul II, who succeeded Pius II, it was granted to the cardinals to seek their candidates outside the Conclave. That is to say: until the pontificate of Paul II, who succeeded Pius II, it was permitted to the cardinals to seek those to be elected outside the Conclave.

units.la: IX. At Paulus iste II. qui an Ch. 1464. electus erat, lege cavit, ne in posterum alius quàm Cardinalis in Pontificem evehe- retur. Causabatur in speciem, accidere omninò, ut, quando Candidatus Cardinalibus plerisque haud familiariter notus (quales quoscunque qui extra illorum numerum existunt, esse necesse sit;) in Conclavi proponitur, nimium teratur temporis, priusquam de illius vita emendata, moribus sanctis ac eruditione eximia singulis fides fiat. Interim, sub hoc praetextu, id revera agebat, ut Cardinalium authoritatem in immensum augeret, Regésque & Principes tantò magis ad eos colendos adigeret, si praeter arbitrium eligendi Pontificis, illud ampliùs tenerent, ne eligi posset quisquam nisi ex ipsis.
units.tr: IX. But this Paul II, who was elected in the year 1464, by law forbade that in future anyone other than a cardinal should be raised to the papacy. He pretended that it could happen that, when a candidate who is not very well known to most of the cardinals (as must be the case with all who exist outside their number) is proposed in the Conclave, too much time is wasted before a reliable account of his reformed life, holy character and outstanding learning is given to each. Meanwhile, under this pretext, he was in fact aiming to increase the authority of the cardinals beyond measure, and to bind kings and princes all the more to court them, if, besides the right of electing the Pope, they might keep this further right, so that no one could be elected except from among themselves.

units.la: X. Certè omninò oportet, ut nonnisi probè notus eligatur; sed neq; Cardinales, quorum multi raro Romæ & in aliorum societate sunt, pauci, si nonnulli, ministeria Ecclesiastica Romæ ordinariò obeunt, requisitorum respectu tam bene noti, sed alii sæpe, maximè in universa Ecclesia constanti famâ clari, quales tantùm eligi debent, multò melius cogniti sunt, atque cognosci possunt, neque etiam requisita illa tantopere curantur, aut magis in electis ex illo tempore conspiciuntur.
units.tr: X. Certainly it is essential that the one elected be well known; but neither are the cardinals, many of whom seldom are in Rome and in the company of others, and few, if any, regularly discharge ecclesiastical ministries in Rome, so well known with respect to the requisites; whereas others, often famous for a constant reputation throughout the whole Church, who alone ought to be elected, are much better known and can be known, nor are those requisites so greatly attended to, or more evident in those elected since that time.

units.la: XI. Contrà sua secum tulit Paulina ista constitutio incommoda, eodem ibidem Authore testante; Ne' Conclavi, inquit, non lasciavano d'entrare le stesse passioni di prima, e forse maggiori, perche i Cardinali ingelosendosi uni con gli altri, allungavano l'elettioni per invidia, non volendo alcuno cedere al compagno; moltiplicandosi gli odii e divenendo da fratelli nemici: trovando ciascuno maggior difficoltà di cedere ad un Cardinale pretendente nel Conclave, che ad un' altro soggetto non intercessato nelle concorrenze. Id est: Eadem tamen, quæ antea, imò forte majores passiones in Conclavia ingrediebantur, quia Cardinales, unus alterius æmulus, per invidiam Electiones in longum protrahebant, nemine alteri cedere volente; multiplicatis odiis & fratribus in inimicos mutatis: & quovis difficilius Cardinali in Conclavi Competitori cedere, quàm vero cuidam alii negotationis partem nullam habenti.
units.tr: XI. Moreover, this Pauline constitution brought with it its own inconveniences, as the same author attests in the same place: "In the conclaves the same passions as before, and perhaps greater ones, still came in, because the cardinals, becoming jealous of one another, prolonged the elections out of envy, since no one would yield to his companion. Hatreds multiplied, and brothers became enemies. Each found it harder to give way to a cardinal who was a candidate in the conclave than to some other person who had no part in the rivalry." That is: The same passions as before, or perhaps even greater ones, entered the conclaves, because the cardinals, each a rival of the other, drew out the elections through envy, no one being willing to yield to another; hatreds multiplied, and brothers were turned into enemies; and it was harder for any cardinal to yield to a competitor in the conclave than to someone who had no share in the bargaining.

units.la: XII. Interim tamen ab illo tempore obtinuit, ut nonnisi Cardinales eligerentur; Atque decreta in eum finem Pontificum habentur 79. Distinct. Ca. Oportebat. Ca. nullus unquam. Et Ca. si quis. Verùm non tantùm Cardinales esse debent, sed etiam Cardinales diu ante creati: La seconda eccettione &c. Secunda exceptio est nimia juventus——Cardinalatûs, per eminente che il soggetto si sia di talento e di merito, licèt persona dotibus & meritis multùm emineat, quia amicos offendit, quòd brevis servitus & fidelitas paucorum dierum nominati, diuturna & experimento cognita sua ante ponatur. Inimicis autem facile tunc est vivis rationibus exacerbare animos proponenti adhærentium, imò quilibet in Collegio sub specioso de non facienda tot in Conclavi Senibus & per annos bene meritis injuria, prætextu, negare audebit. Exempla aliquot subjungit idem, atq; habet etiam exemplum Conclave Leonis XI. in quo contrà Baronium dicebant; meliores dari, etiam inter creaturas S. Sixti, alle quali si faceva ingiuria anteponendo à loro quelli, che apena s'erano ancora accommodata la barretta rossa in testa; quibus injuria fiat, si iis anteponantur illi, qui vix assueti sint pileo rubro in Capite.
units.tr: XII. Meanwhile, from that time on it became established that only cardinals should be elected. The decrees issued to this end by the Popes are found in D. 79, cc. Oportebat, Nullus unquam and Si quis. But they must not only be cardinals; they must also have been created cardinals long before. "The second exception, etc. The second exception is the too great youth of the cardinalate, however much the man may be of talent and merit; for even a person who greatly excels in gifts and merits offends his friends, since the short service and faithfulness of a few days of the one nominated is set above the long-standing and proven service of the others. Then it is easy for enemies, with plausible arguments, to inflame the minds of those who are attached to the proposed candidate; indeed, anyone in the College, under the specious pretext of not doing such an injury in the conclave to old men who have deserved well over the years, will dare to refuse." The same author adds several examples, and he also gives the example of the conclave of Leo XI, in which they said that better men were available, even among the creatures of Sixtus, "to whom an injury was done by putting before them those who had scarcely yet got the red hat on their heads." That is: An injury is done to them if those are placed before them who are scarcely accustomed to the red hat on their heads.

units.la: XIII. Quodvis autem horum vitium in Electionibus arguit: Ab initio non eligebantur Episcopi, quia Episcopi alii ejusdem habebantur dignitatis; Primo tempore non Presbyteri, quia iidem erant Romani Presbyteri & Episcopi; si autem necesse est, ut per ordines Diaconatus & Presbyteratus ascendatur ad Episcopatum, & multi ex primis, & multi ex omnibus aetatibus minus bene electi sunt, & inconveniens est Papalis de voce passiva non Diaconorum, quales contemptu fere dignitatum Ecclesiasticarum manent, dispensatio; Ut etiam in conveniens est, quòd Cardinales inter se Papatus Monopolium exercent, atque nonnisi Cardinalibus primò fere creatis dignitatem conferunt, nulla habitâ meritorum in contrarium ratione. Certè hoc est angustos Spiritui S. limites ponere!
units.tr: XIII. Each of these faults shows a defect in the elections. At first bishops were not chosen, because the bishops were considered to hold the same dignity. At the earliest period presbyters were not chosen either, since the Roman presbyters and bishops were the same people. But if it is necessary to ascend to the episcopate through the orders of deacon and presbyter, then many of the first men, and many from every age, have been chosen less well; and the papal dispensation, by which non-deacons are eligible for election, is inconvenient, since such men remain almost in contempt of ecclesiastical dignities. It is likewise inconvenient that the cardinals exercise a monopoly of the papacy among themselves and confer the dignity almost only on those first created cardinals, with no regard had to merit to the contrary. Surely this is to set narrow limits to the Holy Spirit!

units.la: XIV. Quales etiam Eidem ponunt, dum Monachos vix admittunt; Docet Itin. della Corte di Roma p. 2. p. 751. 752. sequentibus verbis; Tengono poco meno &c. Id est: Seculum fere excurrit, ex quo Cardinales Monachos in Vaticano venerari nolunt, atque videtur, Sixtum V. iis ultimam benedictionem elargitum esse — subjungit, che l'humore &c. naturam horum (Pii V. & Sixti V.) nimis severam & nimio Zelo exorbitantem fuisse esse. Et tandem concludit, nullos eligi, non tam quia id inconveniens putent Cardinales, quàm quòd Monachi Cardinales nulli dentur, atque miraculi ad instar futurum, si septuaginta Sacerdotes in unum Monachum consentirent. Aemulantur nimirum, atque hinc ne Cardinalatu quidem Monachi honorantur, severitas eorum timetur, imò etiam, ut ex iis, quae Differt. praeced. notavimus, simulatio.
units.tr: XIV. The same author also sets such limits, since they hardly admit monks. He teaches this in Itinerary of the Court of Rome, part 2, pp. 751–752, in these words: "They hold little less..." That is: It is nearly a century since the cardinals have been unwilling to honour monks in the Vatican, and it seems that Sixtus V granted them their last blessing. He adds: "the humour etc.", that the nature of these men (Pius V and Sixtus V) was too severe and exorbitant in its zeal. And at last he concludes: No monks are elected, not so much because the cardinals think this inconvenient, as because no monk cardinals are given; and it would be like a miracle if seventy priests agreed upon one monk. They are, of course, rivals, and for this reason monks are not even honoured with the cardinalate; their severity is feared, and indeed, as we noted in the preceding Dissertation, even pretence.

units.la: XV. Maximè autem in Religionibus, ut vocant, suis Electiones sibi invicem difficiles faciunt Jesuitae & Dominicani. Exempla habet Conclave Alexandri VII. In quo Lugo (Giesuita) era più contrario di tutto, levatone Montalto per rispetto della religione, già che compenendo hormai la religione di S. Domenico e la compagnia del Giesù, per la maggioranza nel sapere e vantaggio nell altre prerogative, ciascheduna di loro procura tutti quei mezzi, che possono assicurare da prerogativa. Sono, ò si stimano d'essere queste 2. religioni nella chiesa di Dio quali una volta nel mondo furono le 2 republiche, Roma e Carthagine, ogn' una di loro aspirava alla maggioranza ed al Dominio del Sacro Imperio. Un Papa dell' ordine de' Predicatori ingelosia i Giesuiti più che non animava i Domenicani, quelli è temevano ò mostravano di temere, che S. Clemente (Domenicano) non alterasse i loro privileggi, che non facesse cesse qualche dechiaratione contro le loro dottrine; Quelli sapendo che S. Clemente, hà sempre più potuto l'interesse della conscienza, che quello dell'ordine, non speravano che fatto Papa, ò Capo Universale della chiesa di Dio fosse per fare cosa à favore loro, che all' altre membre poteva recare pregiudicio. In Lugo erano tanquam in Capite i voti de' Giesuiti, e gli rappresentava tutto il corpo della compagnia tutta favellava nella sua lingua. Id est; Lugo (Jesuita) magis contrarius erat prater Montaltium, quàm omnes alii, idque Religionis intuitu, quia enim Dominicanorum Ordo & Societas Jesu æmulantur prærogativam eruditionis & alias, quaslibet Religio omnia illa media studiosè querit, quæ prærogativas illas sibi vendicare queunt. Sunt vel haberi volunt duæ istæ Religiones in Ecclesia Dei tales quales olim in mundo fuerunt duæ Respublicæ Roma & Carthago, quarum qualibet aspirabat ad præeminentiam & Dominium Sacri Imperii. Papa ex Ordine S. Dominici magis ad æmulationem provocabat Jesuitas, quàm verò Dominicanos animabat; Illi aut timebant aut timere videbantur, S. Clementem (Dominicanum) mutaturum sua privilegia & facturum quandam contra suas doctrinas declarationem; Hi gnari apud S. Clementem semper plus potuisse conscientia, quàm verò ordinis commodum, non sperare poterant, quòd Papa sive Caput Universalis Ecclesiæ Dei factus in favorem suum quicquam facturus sit, quod reliquis membris damno esse possit. Ad Lugo tanquam ad Caput concurrebant Jesuitarum vota, & ipse repræsentabat totam societatem, tota loquebatur linguâ ipsius.
units.tr: XV. But especially within their own orders, as they call them, the Jesuits and the Dominicans make elections difficult for one another. The Conclave of Alexander VII provides examples. In it, "Lugo (the Jesuit) was more opposed to everyone, except Montalto, out of regard for the religious orders. For since the order of St Dominic and the Society of Jesus, for superiority in learning and advantage in other prerogatives, are each striving for supremacy, each of them pursues all those means which can secure that prerogative. These two orders are, or are thought to be, in the Church of God, what once in the world were the two republics, Rome and Carthage: each aspired to supremacy and dominion over the Holy Empire. A Pope from the Order of the Preachers provoked the Jesuits to rivalry more than he encouraged the Dominicans; the Jesuits feared, or seemed to fear, that St Clement (a Dominican) would alter their privileges and make some declaration against their doctrines. They, knowing that St Clement had always put the interest of conscience above the advantage of his order, could not hope that, once made Pope or universal head of the Church of God, he would do anything in their favour that might harm the other members. Votes of the Jesuits converged on Lugo as on a head, and he represented the whole society; the whole society spoke through his tongue." That is: Lugo, the Jesuit, was more opposed than all others except Montalto, and that out of regard for religion; for since the Order of St Dominic and the Society of Jesus rival each other in the prerogative of learning and in other respects, each religion eagerly seeks all those means which can claim those prerogatives for itself. ... Votes of the Jesuits converged upon Lugo as upon a head, and he represented the whole society; the whole society spoke in his language.

units.la: XVI. Laudat non mediocriter Author Dominicanum S. Clementem: La bonta della vita, inquit, non si contraslava, perche era noto come egli non haveva mai disimparato il rigore della disciplina Claustrale ed era vissuto da Frate ne' palazzi senza mai contaminarsi dalle mense di Babilonia. Id est: Vita eum commendabat, siquidem notum erat, eum nihil unquam remisisse de disciplina Monastica, & vixisse Monasticè in Palatiis non contaminandose mensis Babylonia.
units.tr: XVI. The author praises the Dominican St Clement not a little: "The goodness of his life," he says, "was not disputed, for it was well known that he had never relaxed the rigour of claustral discipline, and had lived as a friar in palaces without ever being defiled by the tables of Babylon." That is: His life commended him, since it was known that he had never relaxed anything of monastic discipline, and had lived as a monk in palaces, not defiling himself with the tables of Babylon.

units.la: XVII. Sed cui nullum à vita præjudicium accedere potuisse dicitur, huic præjudicium invidiosè creabant Jesuitæ; Barberinum enim etiam contrà S. Clementem incitârunt calidissima Jesuitarum instantia, quibus opus habebat etiam ad recuperandos reditus in regno Neapolitano, non avaritiâ motus, sed ut ex Mammone iniquitatis sibi amicos comparare possit, i quali per motivo di gratitudine lo potessero sollevare dove tanto aspirano i suoi desiderii; id est, qui gratitudine moti eum evehere queant, quò tantopere tendunt desideria ejus.
units.tr: XVII. But against one to whom it is said no prejudice could be attached from his life, the Jesuits maliciously created a prejudice. For they stirred up Barberini also against St Clement, with the most urgent insistence of the Jesuits, whose help he needed to recover revenues in the kingdom of Naples. He was moved not by avarice, but so that from the Mammon of unrighteousness he might make friends who, moved by gratitude, could raise him to where his desires aspire so strongly; that is, who, moved by gratitude, could promote him to the height to which his desires so eagerly tend.

units.la: XVIII. Nec tamen ipsi Iesuitæ interim otiosi sedebant atque tacebant Barberinum contrà S. Clementem auxiliatorem nacti. Loquebantur, atque ad alcuni dispiaque assai ciò che disse Lugo da S. Clemente; Se ciò fosse, la chiesa di Dio sarebbe rovinata, volendo significare, che da lui sarebbe deciso à favore di coloro, che tengono la Vergine Marie essere stata nella sua concettione macchiata della colpa di Adamo; ed in favore ancora di Giseniisti, le dottrine dequali haveva in alcune propositioni condennato Innocentio. Ciò, dico, dispiaque a' Cardinali che sanno esse il sommo Pontefice sicuro di non poter errare quando parla in Cathedra, e che percio se veramente La Vergine è stata concepita senza colpa Originale, quando bene salisse su' foglio di Pietro un' Atheista non potrebbe mai decidere il contrario. Tanto più furono scandalose le parole ch'e sapeva la sua dottrina essere grande, e che per ciò favellando per interessi privati voleva mischiare la causa del cielo per afferdargli. Haveva fatto imbere questi senzi all' Ambasciatore di Spagna; unde etiam statim dictum, Literis Regis, quos tamen minimè ostendebant, S. Clementem excludi. Id est: Quibusdam valdè displicuit, quod Lugo de S. Clemente dixit, si futurum sit illud, ut nimirum eligeretur, Ecclesiam Dei perditum iri, significans eum decisurum pro illis, qui Virginem Mariam statuunt in sua concept one maculatam culpâ Adami; sic etiam in favorem Janseni-starum, quorum doctrinas in quibusdam propositionibus Innocentius condemnaverat. Hoc, inquam, displicuit Cardinalibus, qui noverunt summum Pontificem non posse errare in Cathedra loquentem, & proin, si revera Virgo sine peccato originali concepta sit, si vel Atheus Petri thronum occupaaret, eum non posse contrarium decidere. Atque isti sermones eo magis scandalosi habebantur, quia nota erat eximia ejus eruditio, & quòd proin loquendo pro commodis privatis, ut eis satisfiat, velit in periculum adducere commoda cœli. Et quidem propinabant etiam ejusmodi cogitationes Legato Hispaniæ &c.
units.tr: XVIII. Yet the Jesuits themselves were not idle or silent in the meantime, since they had gained Barberini as an ally against St Clement. They talked, and some were very displeased by what Lugo said about St Clement: "If that were to happen, the Church of God would be ruined," meaning that he would decide in favour of those who hold that the Virgin Mary was stained in her conception by the guilt of Adam; and also in favour of the Jansenists, whose doctrines Innocent had condemned in certain propositions. This, I say, displeased the cardinals, who knew that the supreme Pontiff cannot err when he speaks from the Chair, and therefore that, if the Virgin was indeed conceived without original sin, even if an atheist were to mount Peter's throne he could never decide the contrary. These words were all the more scandalous because his learning was known to be outstanding, and because, by speaking for private advantage in order to satisfy it, he was willing to put the advantages of heaven in danger. And indeed they also put such thoughts into the ambassador of Spain, and so on. Whence it was also said at once, "Letters from the King, which however they did not show, exclude St Clement." That is: "It greatly displeased some that Lugo said of St Clement that, if it were to happen that he was chosen, the Church of God would be ruined, meaning that he would decide for those who hold that the Virgin Mary was stained in her conception by the guilt of Adam; likewise in favour of the Jansenists, whose doctrines Innocent had condemned in certain propositions. This, I say, displeased the cardinals, who knew that the supreme Pontiff cannot err when speaking from the Chair, and so, if the Virgin was indeed conceived without original sin, even if an atheist were to occupy Peter's throne he could not decide the contrary. These words were regarded as all the more scandalous, because his outstanding learning was well known, and because by speaking for private advantage, so as to satisfy it, he was willing to bring the advantages of heaven into danger. And indeed they also communicated such thoughts to the ambassador of Spain."

units.la: XIX. Sed si Lugo loquebatur, & peros ejus loquebantur Iesuitæ omnes; haud magis tacebant Dominicani. Dicebant; che questo, sarebbe il fare un Papa molti Giesuiti, che lo governano à loro talento, privandolo dell' uso del proprio arbitrio in qual si voglia ben che minima risolutione. Che i Cardinali non erano tanti pazzi che volessero sotto porsi ad un giogo tanto pesante, quanto sarebbe il dominio de' P. P. Giesuiti, che dalla innocenza della vita e dalla letteratura si fanno strumento à regnare, non aspirando ad altro che à dar leggi dovunque sono, e maneggiare à loro talento i governi Politici de' Prencipi, non meno secolari che EccleEcclesiastici; Id est; si Lugo eligeretur Papa multos Jesuitas electum iri, qui eum pro lubitu regant, privando eum usu proprii arbitrii in quavis etiam minima resolutione; Cardinales non tam stultos esse, ut velint se subjicere tam gravi jugo, quale futurum esset Dominium Patrum Jesuitarum, qui vita innocentia & eruditione utantur tanquam instrumentis regnandi, nihil aliud quarentes quam imperium, ubicunque existant, & legislationem & Regiminis Politici Principum, quocunque velint, inflexionem, Principum aeque secularium ac Ecclesiasticorum; Bellarminum non potuisse eligi, multo minus hunc eligi posse.
units.tr: XIX. But if Lugo was speaking, and all the Jesuits were speaking through his mouth, the Dominicans were no less vocal. They said that this would mean making a Pope of many Jesuits, who would govern him as they pleased, depriving him of the use of his own judgement in any decision, however small. That the cardinals were not so mad as to put themselves under so heavy a yoke as the dominion of the Jesuit Fathers would be, who use innocence of life and learning as tools for reigning, seeking nothing but power wherever they exist, and who would manage the political governments of princes, secular and ecclesiastical alike, and bend them to whatever they wished. Ecclesiastici; that is: if Lugo were elected Pope, many Jesuits would be elected who would rule him at their pleasure, depriving him of the use of his own judgement in any decision, however minor; the cardinals were not so foolish as to submit to so grievous a yoke as would be the domination of the Jesuit Fathers, who use innocence of life and learning as instruments for ruling, seeking nothing but empire wherever they are, and the legislation and the political direction of princes, whatever they wish, the bending of princes, as much secular as ecclesiastical; Bellarmine could not have been elected, and much less could this man be elected.

units.la: XX. En Tibi, Lector, in compendio humilitatem Monachalem, qua ad supremos honores tanto cum Zelo prorumpunt! Charitatem Fratrum invidiae oestro percitorum! Pugnas Cadmaeas! Artes Calumniandi! Romae mensas Babyloniae! Consensum in Religione! Jesuitarum artes! Leve eorum jugum! Finem ultimum! Passiones in Conclavi! Infallibilitatem Papae ex una parte ab ipsis Jesuitis eorumque assectis negatam, dum veriti sunt, ne Papa electus decretis suis de controversiis fidei factis Ecclesiam perderet, falsum decideret! Ubi fides vestra, ἀλιγόπιστοι; En etiam infallibilitatem Papae ex altera parte ab Authore & Cardinalibus quibusdam stulte assertam, quasi vero vel Atheus Cathedrae isti impositus Enthusiastico afflatu & quasi ex Tripode voces infallibiles necessario proferre deberet, nulla de eo promissione extante, atque plane contra rationales atque amicabiles Spiritus S. ductus. Has omnes observationes debemus obicibus, quos sibi invicem in Conclavibus ponunt Dominicanorum atque Jesuitarum societates; Utra sit Roma, utra Carthago, parum refert, modo se invicem destruant, modo semper veniat Hannibal ante portas, veniat & intret, intret & destruat.
units.tr: XX. See here, reader, in brief, the monastic humility with which they burst forth so zealously toward the highest honours! The charity of brothers goaded by the gadfly of envy! Cadmean battles! Arts of calumny! Babylonian banquets at Rome! Agreement in religion! The arts of the Jesuits! Their light yoke! Their ultimate end! Passions in the conclave! The infallibility of the Pope, denied on the one side by the Jesuits themselves and their adherents, since they feared that a Pope once elected would destroy the Church by his decrees on controversies of faith and decide falsely! Where is your faith, O ye of little faith [ὀλιγόπιστοι]? See also the infallibility of the Pope, foolishly asserted on the other side by the author and certain cardinals, as if even an atheist placed in that Chair must by some enthusiastic inspiration, as from a tripod, necessarily utter infallible words, when no such promise exists, and when it is plainly contrary to the rational and friendly guidance of the Holy Spirit. We must attribute all these observations to the obstacles which the societies of Dominicans and Jesuits place in each other's way in the conclaves. Whether it is Rome or Carthage matters little, provided that they destroy each other; provided that Hannibal always comes before the gates, let him come and enter, and having entered, let him destroy.

units.la: XXI. Obices similes, & quod speciatim Jesuitis ponantur, ex Conclavi quoque Pauli V. addiscimus. In eo se Bellarmino, de quo jamjam, opposuerunt praecipue li Cardinali Frati, che mal volentieri vedeano l'essaltatione d'un Giesuita, massime per l'interesse della controversia de auxiliis, e per altri rispetti; Cardinales Monachi, qui non libenter videbant exaltationem Jesuitae maxime ob controversiam de auxiliis, & ob alios respectus. In eodem eidem amorem apud multos diminuisse dicitur, l'esser Giesuita, quod fuit Jesuita. Obices quidem ponere Jesuitis hac in parte minime opus esset, si sincera esset eorundem de alieno suo a dignitatibus suscipiendis animo saepe fa&ta protestatio. Ipse enim societatis fundator Loyola literis ad Regem Ferdin. datis apud Orlandinum in Hist. Societ. l. 6. p. 177. testatur: Vita professionis nostræ sincerè ac fideliter prosequendæ ita adversari honores persuasum habemus, ut plane, deque animi nostri sententia pronunciemus, si cogitatione fingendum sit, qua nam ratione posset hic ordo everti, nescire nos quicquam excogitare, Episcopatuum receptione deterius. Et paulò post: Intelligere aperte licet, quanta nobis pestis Episcopatibus recipiendis impendeat. Et paucis interjectis: Vestræ nos fidei, vestro patrocinio dedimus, orantes, obsecrantesque per Jesu Christi sanguinem, ut quoniam certum habemus hinc impendere societati nostræ exitium, vestra Majestas pro sua benignitate ac religione talia à nobis propulset, arceatque discrimina. Subjungit rationes quatuordecim, quibus Jesuitæ persuasi sint, sibi non licere capessere primarias in Ecclesia dignitates. Carolus quoque Grobendonquius de ortu & progr. Spir. Politici Præfat. §. 3. p. 93. seqq. nihil adeò Societati profuisse docet, quod, de quo exempla profert, ab oblatis Episcopatibus Cardinalitiisque honoribus refugerit, dum paucis, quibus renitentibus obtrusi sint, magno fuerint oneri. Eodem spectat famosi Cottoni, cum ei Henricus IV. Archiepiscopatum Aquensem pileumque Cardinalitium offerret, responsum ex vita ejusdem par le P. Joseph d'Orleans conscripta Politica Jesuitica p. 53. in sertum: Que la Compagnie avoit fait un nouveau vœu de n' accepter jamais aucune dignité dans l'Eglise, sans un commandement expres du Pape. Id est: Societatem novum votum fecisse nunquam ullam dignitatem Ecclesiasticam sine expresso Papæ mandato acceptandi. Non tamen serio semper bonos id Patres agere, atque votis ejusmodi votorumque indiciis tum rei, prout diximus, nonnunquam apparentem difficultatem, tum fictam humilitatem occasionem interdum præbere, tum ex iis, quæ Disput. VIII. Sect. 2. n. 9. de Bellarmino porrò dicturi sumus, tum ex aliis facilè constat; Et quando Athanasio Kirchero, liberioris phantasiæ Jesuitæ, desperatè decumbenti jucundum de se in summum Pontificem electo, & ingenti inde lætitia perfuso, atque Principum Christianorum legationes, congratulationes, omniumque populorum applausus excipiente, tum variarum nationum ac gentium in Urbe Collegia ac Templa ædificante, aliáque multa fidei Catholicæ propagandæ causâ constituente somnium unâ nocte sanitatem attulit; Caspáro Schotto Phys. Curiosa l. 3. c. 25. p. 524. id referente; Atque adeò Kircherus non minorem inde utilitatem consecutus est, quàm Dominicanus ille à parte hostili alterà, tera, quo de Niderus, Dominicanus & ille, Formicarii l. 2. c. 3. narrat, quòd eum fratres tempore Concilii Constantiensis, tribus depositis Papis, de sua ad Pontificatum assumtione planè non dubitantem, ne, electo Martino V. in rabiem planè ageretur, Bacchanalium tempore ludicrum, sed unius tantùm diei, Papam creârint. Si, in quam, Kirchero somnium de Pontificatu tam salutare fuit, ut contrà in præcedentibus Spada Cardinalis solo Papatûs odore æger factus legitur, si eum vel Kircherus, vel alius, vigilantes habere potuissent, quantam inde salutem loco exitii, quod suprà timuit Fundator, quæsò consecuti fuissent? Tantam, ut suspicio jam diu multos tenuerit, fore in illo casu, ut ea amplius carere nollet. Valde enim tenaces isti Patres, à suis etiam fidei sociis describuntur rerum acquisitarum. De immensa eorum avaritia, id est, habendi retinendique cupidine ex domesticis Scriptoribus vide la Politique des Jesuites p. 212. seqq. Ut jam eadem cum Papa sibi vindicent, regimen universale absolutum, infallibilitatem atque similia, idem ex iisdem prolixè narrat Author. Eos Papatum vix dimissuros esse semel acquisitum sic jam vaticinatus est expressis verbis Josephus Scaliger: Si les Jesuites peuvent une fois avoir le S. Siege, ils le tiendront tous jours. Id est. Si Jesuitæ semel S. Sedem obtinebunt, semper tenebunt. Consentit sequens ex Vaticano languente p. 2. p. 128. judicium ex Italico Latinè versum: Ego existimarem, optimum remedium esse introductionem Jesuitarum in Vaticanum, nam ipsi tandem exturbarent Nepotismum, ablegarentque S. Petrum in Indiam, ad peragendam Missionem aliquam, cum baculo in manu, & cruce ad latus suspensâ; atque sic postea tanto facilior ipsis redderetur via, ut faciant ex Vaticano feudum hæreditarium Societatis Jesu. Ista timent socii, votumque Regulæ ipsorum particulare, quo Polit. Jes. p. 51. promittunt, que s'ils sont elevés aux premiers dignités de l'Eglise, c'est à dire, à celle du Cardinalat ou de la Papauté même, ils ne feront rien que de l'avis de leur General, ou de quelcun de la Compagnie deputé par luy pour cet effet; Id est; quòd ad primarias Ecclesiæ, id est, Cardinalitiam vel ipsam Papalem dignitatem elati nihil suscipere velint nisi ex consilio Generalis vel illius ex societate, quem ipse ad eum finem ordinârit. Hinc infert: Quid igitur contingeret, si ipsis liceret esse tam felicibus, ut videre possent aliquando Jesuitam in Sede Petri, Collegiumque Cardinalium ex meris Jesuitis conflatum? Tunc sine dubio Generalis eorum novum planè mundum conficeret, in quo Prælati & Beneficiarii quicunque, omnes etiam Principes ab ipso dependeant, pendeant, sintque omnes Christiani vel actu, vel in votis Jesuita. Tunc Domini fierent omnium Cathedrarum & Confessionum, scirentque omnium familiarum aularumque, omnia secreta, esséntque arbitri summorum inter Christianos negotiorum, dicérentque jam omnia secundùm praedictiones mundi regna Jesu Christo esse subjecta, utpote caeca obedientia dedita, ferulaque Generalis ipsorum subdita. Ista timent socii, jam parte istorum gravati; Si verè dixit, quicunque dixit eorum Moral. Pratique des Jesuites Vol. 1. apud eundem ibidem Generalis ad nobilem Gallum: Veda il Signor di questa Camera, di questa Camera io governo, non dico Parigi, ma la China, non già la China, ma tutto il mondo, senza che nissuno sappia, comme si fa. Id est: Vide, Domine, ex hoc Conclavi ego guberno, non dicam Parisios, sed Chinam, non Chinam, sed totum mundum, ut nemo tamen sciat, quomodo illud fiat. Sed, ut ipse innuit, paulò occultius est hoc regimen, mallent magis apertum, sed obicem ponunt dicta timentes socii.
units.tr: XXI. Similar obstacles, and the fact that they are placed specifically against the Jesuits, we also learn from the conclave of Paul V. In it they opposed chiefly Bellarmine, of whom more shortly: the cardinal friars, who were reluctant to see a Jesuit exalted, especially on account of the controversy de auxiliis and for other reasons; the cardinal monks, who were not willing to see the exaltation of a Jesuit, especially because of the controversy de auxiliis and for other considerations. In the same conclave, it is said, being a Jesuit, which was being a Jesuit, diminished his popularity with many. Obstacles would hardly need to be placed against the Jesuits in this matter if their repeated professions of a sincere mind, indifferent to accepting dignities, were genuine. The founder of the society, Loyola, testifies in a letter to King Ferdinand, given in Orlandinus Hist. Societ. l. 6. p. 177.: We are persuaded that the honours are so opposed to the life of our profession, which we ought to pursue sincerely and faithfully, that we plainly declare, and this is our considered opinion, that if one were to imagine by what means this order could be overthrown, we could devise nothing more ruinous than the acceptance of bishoprics. And a little later: It is clearly evident what a plague hangs over us if we receive bishoprics. And after a few intervening words: We have given ourselves to your faith and your protection, praying and beseeching you through the blood of Jesus Christ, that since we are sure that ruin hangs over our society from this quarter, your Majesty, in your kindness and piety, would ward off and keep away such dangers from us. He then adds fourteen reasons by which the Jesuits are persuaded that they may not take up the chief dignities in the Church. Carolus Grobendonk too, de ortu & progr. Spir. Politici Præfat. §. 3. p. 93. seqq., teaches that nothing has done the society so much good as the refusal, in the examples he gives, of offered bishoprics and cardinalate honours, while the few who were forced upon them against their will became a great burden. To the same point belongs the famous Cotton, when Henry IV offered him the archbishopric of Aix and the cardinal's hat. The reply, inserted from his life written by Père Joseph d'Orléans, Politica Jesuitica p. 53., is: that the Company had made a new vow never to accept any dignity in the Church without an express command of the Pope. That is: the Society had made a new vow never to accept any ecclesiastical dignity without the express mandate of the Pope. Yet these Fathers do not always act seriously in this, and by such vows and signs of vows they sometimes provide an occasion, now for an apparent difficulty of the matter, as we have said, now for feigned humility, and this is easily established from other things, and from what we shall presently say of Bellarmine, Disput. VIII. Sect. 2. n. 9. And when a dream brought comfort to Athanasius Kircher, a rather free-spirited Jesuit, who lay despairing in sickness, the dream being that he himself had been elected supreme Pontiff and was overwhelmed with great joy, receiving embassies and congratulations from Christian princes and the applause of all peoples, and building colleges and churches in the City for the various nations and peoples, and establishing many other things for the propagation of the Catholic faith, and the dream restored his health in a single night, as Caspar Schott reports Phys. Curiosa l. 3. c. 25. p. 524., then Kircher gained no less advantage from it than that Dominican on the opposite side did, of whom Nider, a Dominican too, tells in Formicarii l. 2. c. 3., that during the Council of Constance, when three popes had been deposed, the brothers, lest Martin V, once elected, should be driven into utter madness, because the friar was quite certain of his own elevation to the papacy, made him pope for a single day, as a sort of Bacchanalian game. If the dream about the papacy was so beneficial to Kircher, whereas in earlier times Cardinal Spada is read to have been made ill by the mere smell of the papacy, what great salvation, I ask, would they have gained from that place of ruin which the Founder feared above, if Kircher or someone else had been able to have them awake? So great, that for a long time a suspicion has held many that in that case they would not want to be without it any longer. For these Fathers are very tenacious, and even their fellow members of the faith describe them as covetous of acquired things. On their immense avarice, that is, their desire to have and to keep, see from their domestic writers la Politique des Jesuites p. 212. seqq. The same author narrates at length from the same sources how they claim for the Pope universal absolute rule, infallibility and similar things. Josephus Scaliger prophesied in express words that they would scarcely ever let go of the papacy once acquired: Si les Jesuites peuvent une fois avoir le S. Siege, ils le tiendront tous jours. That is: If the Jesuits once obtain the Holy See, they will always hold it. The following judgment, translated into Latin from the Italian, agrees: I would think the best remedy is the introduction of the Jesuits into the Vatican, for they would at last drive out nepotism and send Saint Peter off to India to carry out some mission, with a staff in his hand and a cross hanging at his side; and thus afterwards the way would be made so much easier for them that they would turn the Vatican into a hereditary fief of the Society of Jesus. The Society fears these things, and its particular rule-vow, by which Polit. Jes. p. 51. they promise, that if they are raised to the first dignities of the Church, that is, to that of the cardinalate or the papacy itself, they will do nothing except by the advice of their General, or of someone of the Society deputed by him for this purpose; that is, that when raised to the primary dignities of the Church, that is, the cardinalate or the papal dignity itself, they wish to accept nothing except by the counsel of the General or of that member of the Society whom he has appointed for that end. From this he infers: What then would happen if they were allowed to be so fortunate as to see a Jesuit one day on the seat of Peter, and a college of cardinals made up entirely of Jesuits? Then without doubt their General would fashion a wholly new world, in which all prelates and beneficed men, even all princes, would depend on him, and all Christians would be, in deed or in wish, Jesuit. Then they would be masters of all the chairs and confessionals, and would know all the secrets of all households and courts, and would be arbiters of the greatest affairs among Christians, and they would at last say that, according to their predictions, all the kingdoms of the world were subject to Jesus Christ, being given over to blind obedience and subject to the rod of their General. The Society fears these things, already burdened by some of them. If he who was the author of the Moral. Pratique des Jesuites Vol. 1. spoke truly, the General said to a noble Frenchman, as recorded in the same work ibidem: Veda il Signor di questa Camera, di questa Camera io governo, non dico Parigi, ma la China, non già la China, ma tutto il mondo, senza che nissuno sappia, comme si fa. That is: Behold, sir, from this chamber I govern, I do not say Paris, but China, not China only, but the whole world, without anyone knowing how it is done. But, as he himself hints, this government is somewhat more hidden; they would rather it were more open, but the fearful companions place an obstacle in the way of what has been said.

units.la: XXII. Igitur non omnes facilè admittuntur coelibes, imò qui coelibatum voverunt; Sed tamen omnes, qui admitti volunt, coelibatum vovisse oportet. Illorum proin respectu superfluum planè aestimari debet illud Apostolicum de Episcopo effatum: Oportet eum esse μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνδρα, unius Uxoris Virum; Cùm velint ipsi esse debere nullius uxoris virum, atque unius esse non posse. Neque etiam permittunt, ut matrimonium honestum inter omnes, etiam honestum sit inter Papas; Neque etiam permittunt, ut exemplo Petri, cui & filiam Petronillam tribuunt, aliquis eligatur conjugatus & conjugatus manet; vel, ut quis insistat exemplis quorundam in ipsa Romana Ecclesia Episcoporum, qui forte, licèt ob persecutionum vehementiam rariores, conjugati fuerunt; aut exemplo honesti etiam Clericis matrimonii vindicet legitimos ortus sive Felicis III. & Agapeti I. qui Presbyteros, sive Silverii, qui Episcopum, sive Deus dedit, qui sub Diaconum, sive Theodori I. qui Episcopum rursus Patres, saltem Platina in vitis indice, habuisse comperiuntur.
units.tr: XXII. Therefore not all are readily admitted as celibates, indeed not all who have vowed celibacy; yet all who wish to be admitted must have vowed celibacy. With respect to them, therefore, that Apostolic saying about the bishop must be considered quite superfluous: he must be a husband of one wife [μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνδρα]; since they wish their men to be husbands of no wife, and cannot be husbands of one. Nor do they permit honorable marriage among all men, not even honorable marriage among popes.
