Sixtum & in Convivio dicta fuerunt, Et quid si moribundi Papæ fiunt? atque subjunxit; se non credere prolongationem notabilem vitæ suæ; cùm quadam stomachi imbecillitas sibi quotidie halitum præcludat; Cúmque S. Sixtus: Stomachum remediis calidis corroborandum esse, diceret, excepit: Che li speciali davano per l'ordinario rimedi, non anni; Medicos ordinariò dare remedia, non annos.
units.tr: Of the things said before the banquet at Sixtus's and during the banquet: And what if dying men become Popes? He added that he did not believe his life would be notably prolonged, since a certain weakness of the stomach cut off his breath every day. When Sixtus said that the stomach must be strengthened with warm remedies, he answered: The apothecaries usually give remedies, not years.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Cùm autem intelligeret desperatam Pontificis & ultimam valetudinem, societates, quantum potuit, evitare studuit, domi semper manendo, ut Cardinalibus persuaderet, se mox Pontificem secuturum in alterum mundum; Cúmque Pontifex restitutus esset, non tamen ipse, sed semper de misero suo statu conquestus est, qui ne horam quidem quietis indulgeret; atque ita modis omnibus sanitatem suam abscondere novit, ut ipsi ejus domestici fraudem non observare potuerint; hinc sæpe in urbe prædicabant; Che era un gran miraculo, ch'egli potesse vivere sì lungamente; Id est. Miraculi ingentis instar esse, quòd tamdiu vivere posset. Id quod Montaltio apprimè placuit, utpote unicè quæsitum, qui &c, quando congregationibus & Consistoriis interesse noluit, per aliquem ex suis Cardinalibus morbum suum nunciari curavit, dicente aliquando non nemine; haveremo ben presto un luogo vuoto nel Consistoro, per che Montalto se ne va all' altro Mondo à gran passi. Id est: Habebimus mox locum vacuum in Consistorio, quia Montaltius magnis passibus ad alterum Mundum festinat.
units.tr: Since he understood that the Pope's illness was desperate and his last, he tried as much as he could to avoid company, always staying at home, so as to persuade the Cardinals that he would soon follow the Pope into the other world. And when the Pope recovered, he himself nonetheless never stopped complaining of his wretched condition, saying he would not allow himself even an hour of rest. In every way he knew how to hide his health, so well that his own household servants could not detect the deceit. Hence they often proclaimed in the city: That it was a great miracle that he could live so long. This pleased Montalto greatly, since it was just what he wanted; when he did not wish to attend the congregations and Consistories, he took care to have his illness announced through one of his Cardinals. Someone once remarked: We will soon have an empty place in the Consistory, because Montalto is hurrying to the other world with great strides.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Mortuo Pontifice, cùm Montaltius cum alio quodam in via esset ad invisendum moribundum vocatus, atque hic diceret, nuntio de morte accepto, se non vederemo il Papa vivo, lo contemplaremo morto; Id est; si non videbimus Papam vivum, eum contemplabimur mortuum. Sic ad continuationem itineris hortari volens; ipse respondit: Per me, me ne ritorno &c. Id est; Me quod attinet, revertor ad habitationem meam, ut cogitem de rebus meis, certus enim sum, me eum mox secuturum esse. Eundem Pontificem nonnunquam equum cum agilitate summa ascendere videns, aliquando dixit: Piacesse al Cielo, che, io potesse farne tanto; Id est; Utinam ego tantum facere possem! Et certè planè se ista agilitate privatum esse finxit, nunquam ferè equo vehi volens, quasi ob imbecillitatem, & quando gravi necessitate adactus debuit, semper dimidium horæ spatium stare, atque auxilium suorum expectare solitus fuit, dicens aliquando præsentibus, ho più bisogno d'esser portato d'huomini alla sepoltura, che d'un Muletto intorno alla Mura; Plùs necesse est ut ab hominibus bus ad sepulturam porter, quàm verò à mulo circa muros. Et aliâ vice: La Bara m' è più propria che il cavello. Feretrum mihi magis aptum est equo. p.306—323.
units.tr: When the Pope had died, Montalto was on the road with another man, summoned to visit the dying Pope. When the news of the death was received, the other man said, If we do not see the Pope alive, we shall gaze upon him dead. Wanting to urge him to continue the journey, Montalto replied: As for me, I am turning back to my lodging to attend to my affairs, for I am certain I shall soon follow him. Seeing the Pope sometimes mount a horse with great agility, he once said: Would to heaven I could do as much! Indeed he feigned that he was entirely deprived of such agility, rarely willing to ride a horse, as if from weakness; and when driven by serious necessity, he was accustomed always to stand for half an hour and wait for the help of his people, saying once in the presence of others, I need more to be carried to the grave by men than to be carried on a mule around the walls. And on another occasion: A bier suits me better than a horse. pp. 306–323.

units.la: XXII. Libro quinto p.339. primò dicit Author; quosdam ideò non credidisse Montaltium Papam futurum, quia tantis infirmitatibus obnoxius visus sit, licèt revera maximè sanus omnium Cardinalium & inter competitores natu minimus fuisset, utpote tantùm 64. annos natus, quos tamen fictionibus suis ita auxit, ac si 70. essent.
units.tr: XXII. In the fifth book, p. 339, the author first says that some did not believe Montalto would become Pope because he seemed so subject to infirmities, although in truth he was the healthiest of all the Cardinals, and among the competitors the youngest by age, being only sixty-four years old, years which, however, he had increased by his pretences as if they were seventy.

units.la: Hora, inquit Author—chi mai &c. Id est; Jam, quis unquam credidisset, Papam factum iri eum, qui videbatur singulis momentis casurus per plateam incedens, & qui difficulter pedes suos regere videbatur? Et tamen maxima, quae videantur diversa à rationibus Pontificatus fecerunt Papam Montaltium. Sede vacante ad Decanum dixit: Si sciret Conclave diu duraturum, se non ingressurum, cùm probè noverit infirmitates suas vitae suae finem ante electionem completam acceleraturas esse, (atque ista dicens tussiebat pessimè.)
units.tr: Now, says the author, who would ever have believed that he would become Pope, he who seemed about to fall at every moment as he walked through the street, and who seemed to have difficulty controlling his feet? And yet the greatest things, which seem quite contrary to the principles of the Papacy, made Montalto Pope. During the vacancy he said to the Dean: If he knew the Conclave would last long, he would not enter it, since he knew well that his infirmities would hasten the end of his life before the election was completed (and while saying these things he coughed dreadfully).

units.la: XXIII. In Conclavi Capitibus de promotione sua loquentibus sermonemque finientibus, statim tussire coepit, quasi jam jam simul Spiritum redditurus, post, compositâ ad imbecillitatem voce, subjungens; che per lui &c. se quidem fore Papam paucorum dierum, quia sua infirmitates sibi halitum intercludant, & multò magis, quia se ineptum noverit ad tantum onus sustinendum. p.—370.
units.tr: XXIII. In the Conclave, when the Cardinals were speaking about his promotion and ending their discussion, he at once began to cough, as if he were about to give up his spirit then and there; afterwards, with his voice adjusted to feebleness, he added that for him it would be a Papacy of a few days, because his infirmities cut off his breath, and much more because he knew himself unfit to bear so great a burden. p. 370.

units.la: XXIV. P. 371. loquitur Author de barba inordinata, ut magis videri possit senex, & æger; atque ex relatione conterranei Sixti, qui eum sæpe inviserit, fratre ibi ministrante, quomodo certos moribundi actus facere noverit, maximè tribus aut duobus ante Pontificatum annis, in quibus raro neque unquam sine baculo, & collo torto egressus sit, quasi jam jam casurus. Provocat idem Author ad Scriptores atque testes alios. p.371—373.
units.tr: XXIV. P. 371. The author speaks of his untidy beard, so that he might appear more old and sickly; and, from the report of a fellow-countryman of Sixtus who often visited him, with a brother serving there, how he knew how to perform the actions of a dying man with precision, especially in the three or two years before his Papacy, during which he rarely, and never without a staff and with a twisted neck, went out, as if he were about to fall at any moment. The same author appeals to other writers and witnesses. pp. 371–373.

units.la: XXV. Jam supra ex eodem Authore indicavimus, quomodo Monaltius electus robustam statim naturam prodiderit studio, altâ voce; Te Deum, intonando, baculum abjiciendo, atque Papatum bonam Medicinam agnoscendo. Idem p.418. seqq. indicat, in quantum populus in primo Papæ conspectu mutationem admiratus fuerit subitò factam, semper ingeminando: Dove è il Papa? Dove è il Papa? Ubi est Papa? Ubi est Papa? quasi non amplius eum cognoscentes, atque etiam invicem dicendo: Non è questo &c. Id est; Nonne esthic Cardinalis ille, qui languidus per urbis plateas incedebat quasi jam jam jam casurus? Nonne ille est, qui videbatur non posse pedibus stare? Nonne ille est, qui capite demisso, & collo ad humerum unum pendente incedebat? Sed quomodo jam erectus & Majestate plenus incedit tanquam alter Aaron? Neque admirationem frustrà fuisse docet Author, perchè &c. Id est; quia hactenus nunquam tam improvisa metamorphosis & mutatio similis in ullo alio homine apparuit. Idem p. 419. introducit Medicaeum, cùm ad adorandum Papam accederet, dicentem: Vostra Santità ha un altro garbo di quel che haveva da Cardinale; Id est; Sanctitas V. aliam nunc speciem prae se fert ab illa in Cardinalatu, atque Sixtum respondentem: Mentre noi summo Cardinale &c. Dum Cardinalis fuimus, humeris demissis incessimus, quaerentes in terra clavescoeli, sed quia nunc illas invenimus, in coelo servamus, quia non amplius opus habemus ullius in terris. Loquitur p. 423. de obambulatione Papae con un passo sollecito, &c. Id est; passu sollicito & leve pede, extra consuetudinem, cùm nunquam obambulare solitus sit, sed tantum stare corpore curvo, hinc multiplicatus fuit stupor in oculis & animo suorum familiarium &c.
units.tr: XXV. We have already shown above, from the same author, how Monaltius, once elected, at once revealed a robust nature: eagerly, in a loud voice, intoning Te Deum, throwing away his staff, and acknowledging the Papacy a good medicine. The same author, p. 418 ff., shows how the people, amazed at the sudden change they saw in the Pope at first sight, kept repeating: Where is the Pope? Where is the Pope? Ubi est Papa? Ubi est Papa?, as if no longer recognising him, and also saying to one another: Is this not ... That is: Is this not that Cardinal who used to totter through the city squares as if about to fall at any moment? Is this not the man who seemed unable to stand on his feet? Is this not the man who walked with his head bowed and his neck hanging on one shoulder? But how he now walks upright and full of majesty, like another Aaron! The author teaches that this amazement was not without cause, because, etc. That is: because until then such an unexpected metamorphosis and change had never appeared in any other man. The same author, p. 419, introduces Medici, approaching to adore the Pope, saying: Your Holiness now has a different bearing from what you had as a Cardinal. That is: Your Holiness now shows a different appearance from the one you had in the Cardinalate. And Sixtus replies: While we were a Cardinal, we walked with drooping shoulders, seeking the keys of heaven on earth; but since we have now found them, we keep them in heaven, because we no longer have need of anything on earth. He speaks, p. 423, of the Pope's walking about con un passo sollecito, etc. That is: with a brisk step and light foot, unlike his custom, since he had never been accustomed to walk about, but only to stand with a bent body; hence the astonishment in the eyes and minds of his household was multiplied, etc.

units.la: XXVI. Hactenus simulationes Sixti respectu Senii atque adversae valetudinis. Quem tamen non solum simulasse constat, quamvis non omnibus successus simulationis idem responderit; Non certè Celso, de quo in Vatic. supra i Porpor. L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.253. legimus: Celso s'inganna à simular vecchiaia. Id est; Celso frustra senectutem simulat. Vide etiam, quae supra innuimus Simulationes autem istas parit promotio senum atque languidorum. Sed causa causae jam ex dictis constare potest. Addimus tamen majoris confirmationis ergò, testimonia, unum atque alterum. Unum Joh. Fr. Lottini in Dissert. de Conclavi; Senectus, inquit, ei, qui ad Pontificatum aspirat, sine dubio magnum adfert adjumentum, per naturam enim senes diu vivere non possunt: quod non ii tantùm, qui & ipsi honorem hunc ambiunt, sed omnes etiam ferè Cardinales in eligendo Pontifice specture solent. Siquidem novi Pontificis creatio semper eis aliquid affert emolumenti. Consentit Anonymus in Dissert. de Creatione Pontificum. Ad Pontificatum adipiscendum, inquit, provecta atas multùm juvat, non solùm eorum respectu, qui ad eandem dignitatem aspirant, sed eo etiam, quòd Pontificis mutatio omnibus & singulis aliquo modo sit fructuosa. Atque idem etiam confirmat illustris atque ingenuus Thuanus lib. 134. ita scribens: Nihil magis in votis habet populus in urbe, & Cardinales in Conclavi, quàm ut brevis aevi Pontifex creetur, dum hi ad illud fastigium aspirant, & crebra mutatione in spem ejus adipiscendi eriguntur: PopnPopulus autem, qui œdium direptionibus gaudet, cum aliquis ex Collegio plerúmque falsò Pontifex renuntiatur, id quotidie evenire exoptat. Nobil. Sandis Relat. dello stato della relig. cap. 31. his verbis: Ætas aut infirmitas maximè commendat Cardinalibus, acciò il luogo tosto resti vuoto di nuovo per l'acquisto del quale sempre si fanno pratiche e disegni immediatamente doppo la nuova elettione. Id est; Ut locus citò denuò fiat vacuus, ad cujus acquisitionem semper molitiones & propositá suscipiuntur immediatè post novam electionem. Addo; commendare etiam Principibus, quorum interest, ut Italia maximè pacata maneat facilius Juvenili fervore turbanda, dum quieta magis senum mens est, atque aliis ordinariò curis occupata, quamvis etiam in allegatis Hispani semel tot atque tam citò se invicem excipientium mutationum pertæsi minùs provectum maluisse visi sint.
units.tr: XXVI. Thus far the pretences of Sixtus with regard to old age and ill health. It is certain, however, that he did not only pretend, although the pretence did not succeed equally for everyone. Certainly not for Celsus, of whom we read in Vatic. above, Porpor. L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 253: Celso s'inganna à simular vecchiaia. That is: Celsus vainly pretends to be old. See also what we hinted above. But such pretences are produced by the promotion of old and infirm men. The cause of this cause can now be established from what has been said. For the sake of greater confirmation, however, I add one or two testimonies. The first is that of Joh. Fr. Lottini in Dissert. de Conclavi: "Old age," he says, "undoubtedly brings great help to one who aspires to the Papacy, for by nature old men cannot live long; and not only those who themselves seek this honour, but almost all the Cardinals, are accustomed to look to this in electing a Pope. For the creation of a new Pope always brings some advantage to them." The Anonymous author agrees in Dissert. de Creatione Pontificum: "Advanced age greatly helps to attain the Papacy," he says, "not only with regard to those who aspire to the same dignity, but also because a change of Pope is in some way profitable to all and each." The illustrious and frank Thuanus also confirms this, writing thus in lib. 134.: "Nothing is more desired by the people in the city, and by the Cardinals in the Conclave, than that a Pope of short life should be created, since these aspire to that summit and are raised up by the frequent change in hope of attaining it." The people, moreover, who delight in the plundering of houses, wish this to happen every day, whenever someone from the College is declared Pope, mostly falsely. The Noble Sandis, Relat. dello stato della relig. cap. 31, says in these words: "Age or infirmity especially recommends Cardinals, so that the place may soon become vacant again, for the acquisition of which schemes and plans are always made immediately after the new election." That is: So that the place may quickly become vacant again, for the acquisition of which schemes and proposals are always undertaken immediately after the new election. I add that they also recommend themselves to princes whose interest it is that Italy remain especially at peace, since it is more easily disturbed by youthful fervour, while the mind of old men is quieter and occupied with its usual cares; although in the cited instances, too, the Spaniards, weary of so many and so quick changes following one another, seemed to prefer a less advanced man.

units.la: XXVII. Atque hanc quoque senum electionem Monarchiæ Pontificiæ quodammodo utilem dicas.
units.tr: XXVII. And this election of old men too you may call in some way useful to the Papal Monarchy.

units.la: Sic Author Vita Sixti V. p. 1. l. 1. p. 9. ait: Come l'altre Monarchie &c. Id est: Quando alia Monarchia debiles facta sunt, quando in potestatem juvenum & inexpertorum pervenerunt, hac (Pontificia) aucta fuit, quia ad eam regendam quaeruntur homines maturi, non tantùm annis, sed & judicio & prudentiâ.
units.tr: Thus the author of Vita Sixti V. p. 1. l. 1. p. 9. says: Come l'altre Monarchie &c. That is: When other monarchies have become weak, when they have fallen into the power of young and inexperienced men, this one (the Papal) has been increased, because men are sought to govern it who are mature not only in years but also in judgement and prudence.

units.la: XXVIII. Ab altera verò parte quoque incommodum notari videas.
units.tr: XXVIII. On the other hand, you may also see a disadvantage noted.

units.la: Statuit enim Nobil. Sandis l. c. c. 9. Politiam Romanam magno hoc defectu laborare, quem ambitio incorrigibilem faciat, quòd senes ex diversis familiis, imò & nationibus (quod rarissimè nunc respectu magnarum nationum accidit) eligantur, sícque accidere, ut rarissimè successor antecessoris placita confirmet, sed invidè potiùs subvertat, saltem humori suo convenientia substituat, sicque etiam duplex ibi sit mutatio regiminis, obstaculum nondum obtenta in omnes absoluta potestatis. Idem, ubi de Paparum divitiis agit, atque ad quæstionem, cur sæpe Papa pauperes sint, parùm argenti in thesauris habentes? hanc secundam causam assignando respondet: Fieri propter il peggio governo d'Italia, pessimum Italiæ regimen, cujus causa frequens Paparum mutatio habeatur, & desiderium agnatos promovendi, quomodo &c. Consentanea habet Macchiavellus Princip. c. XI. verf. Gallic. ita existimans: Tout ce, que pouvoit faire &c. Id est: Omne illud quod Papa aliquis decem annorum spatio facere posset; (ordinariò enim non ultra (in Papatu) vivunt;) consistit in æquandis suæ partis cum illis adversa viribus, sufficiente reliquo vita tempore ad exterminandam Ligam contrariam.
units.tr: Nobleman Sandys, in the place cited (ch. 9), holds that the Roman polity labours under a great defect, which ambition makes incurable: old men are elected from different families and even different nations (which, with respect to the great nations, very rarely happens now). So it comes about that a successor very rarely confirms the plans of his predecessor, but rather overturns them out of envy, or at least substitutes things that suit his own temper. Thus there is also a double change of government, and an obstacle to the absolute power not yet attained by anyone. The same author, where he deals with the riches of the Popes and asks why Popes are often poor, with little silver in their treasuries, gives this second cause in answer: it happens because of the worse government of Italy, the worst government of Italy, from which frequent changes of Pope arise, and the desire to advance one's kinsmen, and so on. Machiavelli, in The Prince, chapter 11, in the French version, holds views consistent with this, thinking as follows: whatever a Pope could do in the space of ten years (for they do not usually live longer in the papacy) consists in equalising his own party's forces with those of the adversaries, leaving enough of his lifetime to exterminate the opposing League.

units.la: XXIX. Nempe habent sua commoda atque incommoda istæ sénum electiones: Et quatenus & quando prudens atque expertus juvenilíque ardore destitutus, cautus in omnibus, neque jam ab ingenio derelictus deligitur, hinc causa Pontificia multùm juvatur; Sed quatenus & quando eligitur sive jam repuerascens, atque alienæ tantùm libidini prætextum præbens, aut mox præbiturus, sive cæco erga Nepotes amore ad eos exiguo temporis spatio ditandos actus, & quatenus frequens mutatio non tantùm periculosa, sed & noxia est, noxia thesauris, ut vocant, Ecclesiæ, noxia in frequentior: Vi consiliorum mutatione; hinc non exigua ab istis senum electionibus damna manant.
units.tr: XXIX. Indeed these senior elections have their advantages and their disadvantages. Insofar as and when a man who is prudent and experienced, free of youthful ardour, cautious in all things, and not yet deserted by his wits, is chosen, the Papal cause is greatly helped. But insofar as and when one is chosen who is already, or soon will be, grown childish again, offering a pretext merely for another's lust, or who is driven by blind love for his nephews to enrich them in a short space of time; and insofar as frequent change is not only dangerous but harmful, harmful to the treasures, as they call them, of the Church, and harmful still more through the change of counsels, a considerable loss arises from these elections of old men.

units.la: XXX. Sed vel maximè indignæ atque vitiosæ apparent: Dum, prout dictum est, non tantùm ab ambitionis vehementia procedunt, atque nævum ambitio quoque incorrigibilem facit; Sed dum porrò immenso Papatûs Cœlo non digni Atlantes, sed infantes sufficiuntur, bis pueri vel jam, vel mox futuri, futuri pariter alienæ ambitionis ludibria, non sine ingentibus, quæ jam innuimus, damnis.
units.tr: XXX. But they appear most unworthy and faulty: since, as has been said, they proceed not only from the vehemence of ambition, and ambition makes the blemish incurable as well; but further, since men not worthy to bear the immense heavens of the Papacy like Atlases are substituted, they are in fact children, twice children, now or soon to be, equally the playthings of another's ambition, and not without the huge losses which we have already hinted at.

units.la: SECTIO SEPTIMA, In qua, De vitiis & nævis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum ratione pietatis, probitatis agitur.
units.tr: SECTION SEVEN, in which the vices and blemishes of the election of Roman Pontiffs are discussed with respect to piety and uprightness.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.tr: I. How far virtue is required; II. Which virtues are chiefly required; III. That the simulation of virtues is approved; IV. That it is openly rejected, whose conscience they presuppose to be delicate; V. That virtue is often an obstacle; VI. That sometimes some did strongly oppose the wicked and prevented their election; VII. But very often the worst are chosen, which is proved partly by the wicked morals of many before the Pontificate, and partly by the great vices of very many during the Pontificate; VIII. More generally; IX. More specifically, and indeed from the sixth century, the example of Vigilius; X. From the seventh century, the example of Sabinian; XI. From the ninth century, the example of Joan, and the testimonies of Genebrard, Aventinus, and Genebrard again; XII. Wernher Rolfinck and Baronius; XIII. The example of Nicholas I, Genebrard's judgement that he was a saint, and Hadrian II; XIV. Martin II, placed among the same praised men; the testimony of Platina on Formosus, Stephen VI and his example; the complaints of Baronius; and the example of Boniface VI. XV. XVIII. The example of Sergius; and the more general testimonies of Baronius and Platina; XIX. likewise the testimony of Cranz, Onuphrius and Rolfinck. XX. Alexander VII and Clement IX, where there is also a remark about Clement X and others. LXXII. Innocent XI and Alexander VIII, where there is also a remark about Innocent XII. LXXIII. It is clear, therefore, that for many centuries very many who were not sufficiently upright, and many who were plainly wicked, have been elected; contrary to the example of the first centuries. LXXIV. After this, a few upright men, from the testimony of Wessel, the anonymous writer and Guicciardini. LXXV. That this is so is established by Papist authors and by the lives that are customarily written in a flattering manner. LXXVI. More general testimonies about the corruption of Rome are brought forward, from Mantuanus. LXXVII. It is shown that the city today has the same face. LXXVIII. [?] The statements about the dishonesty of the Popes are confirmed from the embassy of Romulus to the Romans. LXXIX. From the proverb about the uprightness of the Popes, the testimony of Guicciardini, and the distinction between goodness and the Pope. LXXX. The wickedness of the Popes is magnified from the Decretals, etc. LXXXI. With what impudence the Jesuit Otto, author of Roma Gloriosa, is refuted. LXXXII. But they ought to be holy and to be chosen. LXXXIII. Nor can the wicked in any way be excused, not by their small number. LXXXIV. Nor by the sharing of merits. LXXXV. Nor have they made the Roman Church glorious and illustrious, as is boasted. LXXXVI. Nor can they be excused by the smallness of their faults. LXXXVII. Nor are the excuses of Baronius sound, or that drawn from the priests, scribes and Pharisees of the Old Testament. LXXXVIII. Nor do they remove evil from evil, but rather increase it, by saying that they were not well elected. LXXXIX. They increase it also when they do not count the wicked. XC. Lastly, the evil is increased because corrupt morals also infect faith and government.

units.la: I. PErgimus à senectute ad alia requisita; Neque enim senem esse satis est; inquit Joh. Fr. Lottinus Disser. de Concl. De virtutibus primorum Episcoporum Romanorum jam diximus. Mutato jam statu, alia etiam atque longè plura requiri videmus. Quamvis bona requisita & antiqua satis retineat Onuphrius in Paulo III. dicens: Legendus, qui aetate, prudentia, rerum diuturno usu, inveterata virtute & praecellentibus litteris pra omnibus emineat. Tres verò qualitates praecipuae in Conclavi Urbani VIII. enumerantur; bontà di vita, litteratura e prudenza esperimentata in ogni sorte di negotii. Id est: Vita probitas, eruditio & prudentia experimento cognita in omni negotiorum genere. Initium faciamus à prima, Vitae nimirum probitate: Primò probitas requiritur, inquit Lottinus l. c. cujus amor nec natura pravitate, nec educationis vitio in hominum animis ita obliterari atque extingui potest, quin aliquod ejus studium atque desiderium remaneat: unde fit, ut boni ab improbis etiam honorentur atque magni fiant. Idem dicit Anonymus in Disser. de Creatione Pontificum: Sed & virtutis magnam vim hic esse, non negandum est; neque enim quisquam tam malus est, quin natura quodam instinctu & desiderio ad bonum feratur. Hic autem notari meretur, quàm tenuiter de probitate post alia requisita loquantur: Neque senem esse satis est; sed & virtutis magnam vim &c. Neq; etiam adhibent vel sanctitatis veraeq; pietatis nomina. Atque quasi praeveniunt & praeoccupant objectionem, quomodo ab Electoribus talibus virtutis ratio haberi possit, cùm plerique minùs virtute praediti sint; respondéntque, id provenire à communi etiam malis instinctu virtutem amandi. Cui addi posset persuasio, probos viros minùs nocere, benefacere magis, atque probos viros ros magis authoritati Pontificiae conservandae aptos esse; quod & Author Vitae Sixti V. agnoscit, exemplarem vitam & bonitatem spectari tantum, quia ad humana prudentia molimina sit necessaria. Nam, ut larvatus Mozambano recte c. 8. p. III. ait, Majestas istius Principatus sanctimonia potissimum opinione stat. Sed & sequentia docebunt, eos vix umbram virtutis requirere atque invenire. Non requiunt certè, si vera sunt Papirii Massoni l. 6. de Episc. Urbis in Jul. III. verba : Sanctitatem in Pontificibus nemo hodie requirit, optimi putantur, si vel leviter boni sunt, vel minùs mali, quàm caeteri mortales esse soleant; Sique vera dixit D. Olympia Vit. p. 42. ad Fratrem paulò post eligendum: Meritum potest promovere ad Cardinalatum, sed non ad Papatum, hic aliis opus est. Et iterum: Non respiciunt Cardinales ad virtutem in Electione Pontificis p. 43. Et consentiens libri Author p. 59. Meritum personarum non ingreditur Conclave, neque qualuates bonas pretendentium considerant Cardinales. Et p. 445. rursus: Si quidem bonitas vitae respiceretur in Conclavibus, ob eam honore illo dignus esset. Card. Franc. Barbarinus.
units.tr: I. WE proceed from old age to other requisites. It is not enough to be old, says Johann Franz Lottinus, Dissertation on the Conclave. We have already spoken of the virtues of the first Bishops of Rome. Now that the state has changed, we see that other and far more numerous qualities are required. Although Onuphrius, on Paul III, still retains the good and ancient requisites, saying: He is to be chosen who excels all others in age, prudence, long experience of affairs, long-established virtue and outstanding learning. Three particularly important qualities are listed at the conclave of Urban VIII: goodness of life, learning and prudence tested in every kind of business. That is: uprightness of life, learning, and prudence proved by experience in every kind of business. Let us begin with the first, namely uprightness of life. First, uprightness is required, says Lottinus, loc. cit., whose love can be so little obliterated and extinguished in men's minds, whether by natural depravity or by a fault of upbringing, that some zeal for it and longing for it does not remain; whence it comes about that good men are honoured even by the wicked and become great. The anonymous author of the Dissertation on the Creation of Popes says the same: But it cannot be denied that virtue has great force here too; for no one is so wicked that he is not carried by a certain natural instinct and desire towards the good. It deserves note here how faintly they speak of uprightness after the other requisites: It is not enough to be old; but also virtue has great force, etc. Nor do they even use the names of holiness or true piety. And they almost forestall and anticipate the objection of how account can be taken of virtue by such electors, since most are endowed with little virtue; and they answer that this arises from the instinct, common even to the wicked, of loving virtue. To this could be added the persuasion that upright men do less harm, do more good, and are better suited to preserving papal authority; which the author of the Life of Sixtus V also acknowledges: an exemplary life and goodness are regarded only because they are necessary to the human contrivances of prudence. For, as the so-called Mozambano rightly says, c. 8, p. III: The majesty of that principate rests chiefly on the opinion of holiness. But what follows will show that they scarcely require, or find, even a shadow of virtue. They certainly do not require it, if the words of Papirius Masson, book 6, on the Bishops of the City, on Julius III, are true: Nobody today requires holiness in Popes; they are thought best if they are slightly good, or less bad than other mortals usually are; and if D. Olympia spoke truly, Life, p. 42, to a brother shortly to be elected: Merit can promote to the cardinalate, but not to the papacy; here something else is needed. And again: Cardinals do not look to virtue in the election of a Pope, p. 43. The author of the same book agrees: p. 59: The merit of persons does not enter the conclave, nor do the Cardinals consider the good qualities of those who aspire. And again, p. 445: If indeed goodness of life were regarded in conclaves, he would be worthy of that honour because of it. Cardinal Francesco Barberini.

units.la: II. Cùm verò plures sint Probitatis, sive virtutis partes, ita tamen pergit Lottinus, ea Pontifici futuro magis necessaria existimantur, quae aliorum serviunt utilitatibus & commodis: ut sunt, Beneficentia, Comitas, sive Affabilitas, Justitia & similes. Parsimonia enim, Temperantia, Continentia & alia, quibus homo se ipsum regit, laude quidem dignissimae sunt virtutes, at multò magis in Principe ea desiderantur, quibus magnitudo ejus aliis quasi communicatur. Et alter ille: Sed quarum à Cardinalibus ratio habetur, virtutes illae sunt, quae alteri prosunt, ut Justitia, Affabilitas, Mansuetudo, Beneficentia, Facilitas in communicanda sua cum aliis dignitate, similésque. Apparet, nullam hic internae sanctitatis veraeque pietatis rationem haberi; nihil de sincero Dei, veri cultûs, Evangeliique amore, nihil de zelo pro veritate, nihil de studio conversionis fratrum auditur: Nullae aliae virtutes requiruntur, quàm quae cuivis Principi seculari aequè necessariae sunt, ab illo aequè requiruntur, ut & verbis expressis quid in Principe maximè desideretur, hic exponitur, tali nempe, non, Vicario Jesu Christi, non, Successore Petri, non, supremo Ecclesiae Universalis Pastore; Ecclesiae, quae non sit regnum aliquod mundanum. Imò nullae aliae virtutes requiruntur, quàm quae Electores commodorum suorum avidos allicere atque ad Electionem hujus prae alio movere queant.
units.tr: II. Although there are many parts of integrity, or virtue, Lottinus goes on to say that those qualities are thought most necessary for a future Pope which serve the advantage and convenience of others, such as beneficence, courtesy or affability, justice and the like. Thrift, temperance, continence and the others by which a man governs himself are indeed most worthy of praise, but in a prince those qualities are much more to be desired by which his greatness is, as it were, shared with others. And that other writer: But the virtues which the Cardinals take into account are those which benefit others, such as justice, affability, gentleness, beneficence, readiness to share his dignity with others, and the like. It is clear that no regard is had here for inner holiness or true piety: nothing is heard about sincere love of God, of the true worship and the Gospel, nothing about zeal for the truth, nothing about eagerness for the conversion of brothers. No virtues are required other than those equally necessary for any secular prince, and these are required of him just as equally. Here is set out, in express words, what is most desired in a prince, namely in a prince, not in the Vicar of Jesus Christ, not in the Successor of Peter, not in the supreme Pastor of the Universal Church, which is not any worldly kingdom. Indeed no virtues are required other than those which can attract the Electors, greedy for their own advantages, and move them to elect this man rather than another.

units.la: III. Sed & satis aperte vel harum umbratilium virtutum simulatio probatur. Quoniam autem,inquit idem Lottinus,dicta virtutes homini vel a natura insita sunt, ut altissimas in animo radices egisse & in alteram naturam quasi transiisse videantur; vel ab ipsis hominibus ad tempus modo simulantur, quo id, quod volunt, facilius consequantur: Optandum equidem fuerit, ut, si non omnes illæ virtutes, Beneficentia saltem & comitas Pontificis naturales sint, non ficta aut assumpta. Quum enim intimi hominum sensus difficillime cognosci possint; fucus sæpe tanto artificio est obtectus, ut vera, etiam sagacibus alioqui virtus videatur &c. En quàm in arctum tandem virtutes Vicarii J. Ch. contrahantur! Optandum quidem fuerit, ut saltem Beneficentia & Comitas ejus non ficta aut assumpta sint; Optandum quidem fuerit!
units.tr: III. But the simulation of even these shadowy virtues is shown quite plainly. Since, however, says the same Lottinus, the said virtues are either implanted in man by nature, so that they seem to have struck the deepest roots in the mind and to have passed, as it were, into a second nature; or they are only feigned by men for a time, so that they may more easily obtain what they want. It would indeed be desirable that, if not all those virtues, at least the beneficence and courtesy of the Pope be natural, not feigned or assumed. For since the innermost feelings of men can very hardly be known, the pretence is often covered with such skill that true virtue appears, even to otherwise shrewd men, etc. See how narrowly the virtues of the Vicar of Jesus Christ are at last drawn together! It would indeed be desirable that at least his beneficence and courtesy be not feigned or assumed; it would indeed be desirable!

units.la: IV. Quin aperte rejicitur, cujus conscientiam delicatam esse supponunt. Sic in Conclavi Pauli V. Aldobrandino temeva dalla rigida consciența di Baronio——fuggiva Bellarmino come Giesuita scropoloso &c. Aldobrandinus timebat rigidam conscientiam Baronii——Bellarminum fugiebat tanquam Jesuitam scrupulosum &c. In eodem Conclavi de Bellarmino dicitur; L'esser Giesuita & di conscienza delicata lo rendevano poco amabile; Id est. Quia Jesuita & conscientia ejus delicata erat, ideo parum gratus erat. Nempe talem boni illi viri cum Episcopis Longobardis supra citatis expetunt, qui infirmitatibus eorum compateretur & condescenderet.
units.tr: IV. Nay, they openly reject the man whom they suppose to have a tender conscience. Thus, in the Conclave of Paul V., Aldobrandini was afraid of the strict conscience of Baronius; he fled from Bellarmine as a scrupulous Jesuit, etc. In the same Conclave it is said of Bellarmine: Being a Jesuit and of a tender conscience made him little loved. That is: because he was a Jesuit and his conscience was tender, he was therefore little welcome. Indeed such men as these good fellows seek, along with the Lombard bishops cited above, are men who would sympathise with their weaknesses and make allowances for them.

units.la: V. Hinc non tantùm nimia præcisitas, quæ nonnunquam per conscientiam delicatam denotatur, sed ipsa virtus impedimento esse dicitur: Illud longè maximum ac pessimum est,inquit Lottinus l. c. quòd Virtus, quos promovere ad Pontificatum debebat, iis sæpe obstare deprehenditur; sive aliorum invidia aut conspiratione, vel privato quodam affectu, nullâ habitâ publica utilitatis ratione; Et quibusdam interjectis fatetur; difficile esse bonum reperire, sed repertum ad Pontificatum evehere longè difficilius esse.
units.tr: V. Hence it is said that not only excessive strictness, which is sometimes marked by a tender conscience, but virtue itself is an obstacle. That is by far the greatest and worst evil, says Lottinus in the passage cited, that virtue, which ought to promote men to the Papacy, is often found to stand in their way, whether through the envy or conspiracy of others, or through some private affection, with no regard had for the public good. And after some intervening remarks he confesses: it is difficult to find a good man, but far more difficult to raise him to the Papacy once found.

units.la: VI. Non equidem aliquando defuerunt in Conclavibus, qui votis suis ad bonorum electionem ferri videbantur, atque etiam omni nisu malorum quorundam electionem impedire studebant, atque revera impediebant. Sic in Conclavi Pii II. cùm, consentientibus fere sufficientibus, Cardinalis Rhotomagensis jam Papa factus haberetur, atque Æneas Sylvius, ut ei similiter accedat, monueretur, hujus zelo aculeatáque Oratione (in qua Simoniacum impurum, lupum, membrum Diaboli, Demonium Rhotomagensem vocavit, cavit, cujus electione Ecclesia spelunca latronum futura sit &c.) esse ctum fuit, ut pessimus homo non plane promotus sit. Sic etiam in Conclavi Pauli V. cum similiter Tosco, che non haveva altero pianeto retrogrado, che le opposizioni che li venivano fatte da alcuni scropolosi; qui non habebat alium planetam retrogradum praeter oppositiones quorundam scrupulosorum; ob morum nimirum vitaeque defectus, jam ad adorationem duceretur, Baronius & Tarugius Professori di Conscienza timorata; Professores conscientiae timoratae consentire noluerunt, ille fortiter etiam contradixit, sicque il Signore Dio, inquit Author Conclavis haveva dal monte altissimo della sua providenza risoluto dispiccar la pietra picola della parola di Baronio per dar con essa ne' piedi di questa grande statua di Nabuchodonosor e gettarla a terra; Id est; Dominus Deus voluit de monte altissimo sua providentia devolvere exiguum lapidem verborum Baronii, ut eo pedes hujus magna statua Nebucadnezarii pulsaret eamque in terram projiceret.
units.tr: VI. To be sure, there have never been lacking in the Conclaves those who seemed to be borne by their votes toward the election of good men, and who even strove with every effort to prevent the election of certain bad men, and actually did prevent it. Thus, in the Conclave of Pius II., when the Cardinal of Rouen was held to be already Pope, with almost all the votes sufficient, and Aeneas Silvius was advised to come over to him in the same way, through his zeal and stinging speech (in which he called the Rouen man a simoniac, impure, a wolf, a member of the Devil, a demon, and warned that the Church would become a den of thieves under his election, etc.), it was brought about that the worst man was not promoted at all. Likewise in the Conclave of Paul V., when the Tuscan was being led toward adoration, he had no other retrograde planet than the objections of certain scrupulous men, namely because of defects of character and life; Baronius and Tarugi refused to agree, being Professors of a Conscience Fearful of God; Baronius in particular spoke out strongly against it. And so the Lord God, says the author of the Conclave, had resolved from the highest mountain of his providence to hurl the small stone of Baronius's word, so that by it he might strike the feet of this great statue of Nebuchadnezzar and cast it to the ground. That is: The Lord God willed from his highest mountain of providence to send down the small stone of Baronius's words, so that it might strike the feet of this great statue of Nebuchadnezzar and throw it to the ground.

units.la: VII. Sed non semper ejusmodi oppositiones factae sunt, aut factae non ita semper praevaluerunt. Utque pauciores boni sunt, ita etiam rarius eliguntur; Et quando ex Dissert. VI. constare potest, quam varia & quam communiter vitiosa sint Electionum principia, fere per accidens tantum atque per consequens etiam rarius, nonnunquam in bonum virum vota consentire evidens quoque esse debet; Ut, quod de bonis Regibus dici solet, omnium eorum nomina in exiguo annulo scribi posse, magis Romanis bonis per aliquot Secula Pontificibus aptari queat. Quando etiam historia teste, in nullo Regno Christiano tot tamq; enormia improbitatis dominantium exempla fuerunt, quot & qualia Pontificum Romanorum, ex quo Anti-Christiani nobis audiunt, (neque enim ad manentes in terminis Episcopalibus primos ascendendum est;) series exhibet; Et certe, quando post Electionem complures tam mali, tamque omnis generis vitiis immersi apparuerunt, dicendum est, aut, omnes artem simulandi optime calluisse, atque exercuisse, quae tamen, si Spiritus S. Electionum Praeses & Arbiter esset, nihil juvaret, aut, perspecta licet eorum malitia, nihilominus ab hominibus pessimis ob respectus pessimos pessime electos fuisse, aut, quod longe pessimum foret, Pontificiam dignitatem, quos oves acceperit, in Lupos, Angelos Lucis in Spiritus tenebrarum commutasse.
units.tr: VII. But such objections were not always made, or when made did not always prevail. And just as there are fewer good men, so they are also rarely chosen. And when it can be established from the sixth Dissertation how varied and how commonly corrupt the principles of elections are, it must also be plain that the votes only rarely, and sometimes by chance and as a consequence, agree on a good man. So what is commonly said of good kings, that the names of all of them could be written on a small ring, might rather be applied to the good Roman Popes over some centuries. Moreover, as history attests, in no Christian kingdom have there been so many and such monstrous examples of wickedness in rulers as the series of Roman Popes presents, from the time we have heard of the Antichrists (for we need not go back to the bishops who kept within their episcopal bounds). And certainly, when after their election so many bad men, so steeped in every kind of vice, have appeared, one must say either that all of them had mastered and practised the art of pretending very well, which art, however, would be of no help if the Holy Spirit were the President and Arbiter of the elections; or, though their wickedness was plain, nonetheless the most wicked men, moved by the most wicked considerations, elected the worst; or, which would be far worse, the papal dignity has changed the sheep it received into wolves, and the Angels of Light into spirits of darkness.

units.la: VIII. Quot autem Historia Paparum monstra, quot apostaticos atque Apostaticos, quot profanos Atheos, quot impios Magos, quot injustos Simoniacos, quot impuros scortatores, quot turpissimos adulteros, quot execrabiles incestuosos, invictu & amictu luxuriosos, quot detestandos Sodomitas, quotquot tamen etiam avaros, quot suis inditandis, evehendis unicè intentos, quot crudeles, quot seditiosos, turbulentos, pacis hostes quasi juratos, quot perjuros, quot blasphemos, quot superbos, quot, uno verbo, bipedum nequissimos exhibet? Exhibet Magiae ultra viginti quinque partim convictos, partim accusatos, superbos quasi omnes, ipsâ immensae potestatis usurpatione tales exigente, invictu & amictu luxuriosos quasi omnes, ipso dignitatis mundanae splendore opúmque affluentia occasionem praebente; Exhibet historia ab Authoribus Pontificiis, Clericis, Monachis, Romanis Bibliothecariis, aliis Viris coætaneis, ex parte abominationum spectatoribus, rerum Romanarum maximè gnaris & magnâ cæteroquin Pontifices reverentiâ prosequentibus jam olim consignata, posteriorumque Cardinalium & aliorum in Ecclesia Romana Illustrium Virorum testimoniis, Confessionibus confirmata, & recentioribus etiam exemplis à fide dignis Scriptoribus aucta; atque ita tales exhibet Pontifices, ut de multis simul testentur, pro talibus, cùm eligerentur, aut intruderentur, aut invaderent, jam agnitos fuisse. Lubeat attendere sequentibus.
units.tr: VIII. But how many monsters the history of the Popes presents: how many apostates, how many atheists, how many impious magicians, how many unjust simoniacs, how many impure fornicators, how many most foul adulterers, how many accursed incestuous men, lecherous in food and dress, how many detestable Sodomites, and as many covetous men, intent solely on enriching and advancing their own, how many cruel, how many seditious, turbulent men, as if sworn enemies of peace, how many perjurers, how many blasphemers, how many proud men, and, in a word, how many the most wicked of bipeds? It presents men convicted of magic, some convicted and some accused, nearly all of them proud, since the very usurpation of immense power demanded such pride; nearly all of them lecherous in food and dress, since the very splendour of worldly dignity and the abundance of wealth offered the occasion. The history has been recorded long ago by Papist authors, clerics, monks, Roman librarians and other men of their own time, who witnessed part of these abominations, who knew Roman affairs very well and otherwise paid the Popes great reverence; it has been confirmed by the testimony of later Cardinals and other illustrious men in the Roman Church, by confessions, and has been enlarged by more recent examples from trustworthy writers. And it presents such Popes that their testimony concerns many at once: that they were already recognised as such when they were elected, or intruded themselves, or seized the office. Let the reader give heed to what follows.

units.la: IX. De Vigilio Seculi VI. Pontifice
units.tr: IX. On Vigilius, Pope in the sixth century

units.la: (ante eum jam multos non optimos electos fuisse, ex historia Schismatum supra expositá, nomine Babylonis ab Hieronymo Romae, ejusque Clero impositó, ambitionis documentis plurimis, atque Imperatoris contrà luxum illius maximè Cleri legibus; constare potest.) Sed de Vigilio, inquam, ita Baronius ad an. 540. n. 5. judicat, eum debuisse scelerum patratorum poenitentem, omnem penitus de Sede Pontificia conceptam spem abjicere, séque ea prorsus indignum judicare, reliquúmque vitae tempus (ut ab eo exigebant gravissima criminum pondera) in lacrymis sibi transfigendum indicere, curâsse tamen, ut Pontificatum consequi posset, nec unquam inde ejici ob perpetrata delicta...
units.tr: (That many unworthy men had already been elected before him is clear from the history of the schisms set out above, from the name "Babylon" that Jerome gave to Rome and its clergy, from the many proofs of ambition, and from the emperor's laws against the luxury of the clergy in particular.) But of Vigilius, I say, Baronius judges thus at the year 540, n. 5: he ought, as a penitent for the crimes he had committed, to have abandoned all hope of the papal See that he had conceived, and to have judged himself wholly unworthy of it, and to have declared that the rest of his life (as the heavy weight of his crimes demanded of him) should be spent in tears; yet he took care that he might attain the papacy, and that he should never afterwards be cast out on account of the offences he had committed...

units.la: X. Seculo VII. Sabinianus
units.tr: X. Seventh century. Sabinian

units.la: (primus illaudatus Ottoni Jesuitae in Roma Glor. sed Stellae, (cujus inter diversos primus ignoratur, & cui Anastasius II. Monothelita, divino nutu morbo correptus, effusisque in latrina intestinis, ut habetur in Canon. XIX. dist. c. Anastasius, ceu alter Arius mortuus, secundus numeratur tertius infamis,) obscurus loco, obscurior moribus, (quibus eum elogiis Platina ornat) electus fuit, qui rebus gestis Gregorii Viri sanctissimi adversatus est. Paululum lulùm etiam abfuit, inquit idem, quin libri ejus comburerentur, adeò in Gregorium irâ & invidiâ exarserat homo malevolus. Hinc etiam eum Gregorius, narrat Sigebertus apud Bar. ad an.605. n.8. per visum ter pro culpa tenacia & hujus derogationis increpatum, quòd non resipisceret, etiam quarto horribiliter increpans & comminans in capite percussit. Qua ille dolore vexatus, non multò post mortem obiit. Cadaver autem ipsius, ut Stella in Vita tradit, veluti infamis ad pontem Milvium delatum in quadam Basilica Petri sepultum fuit, ipséque judicio trium Pontificum habitus est, qui culpabili morte damnatus sit.
units.tr: (The first, unpraised by Otto the Jesuit in Rome, glorious in name but a star (among the various accounts the first is uncertain, and Anastasius II the Monothelite, struck by illness by the divine will, with his bowels poured out in the privy, as is recorded in Canon XIX, dist. c. Anastasius, is counted as a second Arius dead, and the third is infamous), obscure in place, more obscure in character (Platina praises him with these commendations), was elected; he opposed the deeds of Gregory, a most holy man. Platina says of him: it was but a little short of the case that his books were burned, so fiercely had that malevolent man flared up in anger and envy against Gregory. Hence also, Sigebert relates in Baronius at the year 605, n. 8, that Gregory rebuked him three times in a vision for his obstinate fault and for his refusal to retract, and, rebuking and threatening him terribly a fourth time, struck him on the head. Racked with pain, he died not long afterwards. His corpse, as Stella reports in his Life, was carried as that of an infamous man to the Milvian Bridge and buried in a certain basilica of Peter, and he himself was judged by the verdict of three popes to have been condemned to a guilty death.)

units.la: XI. Seculi IX. (quod Genebrardus infelix dictum esse, testatur, exhaustum hominibus ingenio & doctrina claris, sive etiam Claris Principibus, in quo nihilferè dignum memoriâ posteritatis gestum sit. Unde ferant, tunc repertum fuisse quoddam monstrum capite leonino & cæteris membris humanis, quod statum illius temporis mirificè referret;) Seculi, inquam, hujus IX. Johannam jam suprà prolixè descripsimus & vindicavimus. Ejus Prædecessores in fine Seculi VIII. & initio IX. non valdè bonos fuisse, ex Aventini l. 4. Annal. verbis liquet, apud quem, electo A.824. in Schismate Eugenio II. missus à Ludovico Imperatore Lotharius Filius, statum Reip. quem superiorum Pontificum ambitio immodica, insatiabilis avaritia, versutiáque improba conturbârat, componit, intercepta direptáque fraude à Flaminibus antiquis possessionibus reddidit. Quales autem post Johannem IX. al. VIII. Pontifices fuerint electi, Gilberti Genebrardi (quo iniquiorem & maledicentiorem hostem Protestantes vix unquam sunt experti) verbis primò in genere declarabimus: Per annos ferè 150, inquit Chronogr. l. 4. sub initium Seculi X. Pontifices circiter quinquaginta, à Johanne scilicet octavo, qui Nicolao primo & Hadriano secundo, sanctis Pontificibus, successit, ad Leonem nonum usque, à virtute majorum prorsus defecerunt, apostatici apostaticive potiùs quàm Apostolici--Etanto Pontificum numero quinque modò & satis tenuiter laudantur Martinus II. Agapetus II. Johannes XVII. Sergius IV. Gregorius VI. En eximium de Pontificibus simul 50. hominis Pontificii testimonium!
units.tr: XI. The ninth century (which Genebrardus testifies was an unhappy age, drained of men distinguished in talent and learning, or even of distinguished princes, in which almost nothing worthy of the memory of posterity was done. Whence they say that a certain monster with a lion's head and other human limbs was then found, which wonderfully represented the state of that time). Of this ninth century, I say, we have already described and vindicated Joan at length above. That his predecessors at the end of the eighth and the beginning of the ninth century were not very good is clear from the words of Aventinus, Annals, book 4, where, after Eugenius II was elected in the schism of 824, Lothair, the son sent by the Emperor Louis, settled the state of the commonwealth which the immoderate ambition, insatiable greed and wicked trickery of the earlier popes had thrown into confusion, and restored to the ancient Flamines the possessions that had been seized by fraud and plundering. But what kind of popes were elected after John IX (or VIII), we shall first declare in general in the words of Gilbert Genebrardus (than whom the Protestants have hardly ever met a more unfair and slanderous enemy). In his Chronography, book 4, near the beginning of the tenth century, he says: For nearly 150 years, from John VIII, who succeeded Nicholas I and Hadrian II, holy popes, down to Leo IX, some fifty popes wholly failed in the virtue of their forebears, being apostates rather than apostolic... and among so many popes only five are praised, and that rather meagrely: Martin II, Agapetus II, John XVII, Sergius IV, Gregory VI. Behold the remarkable testimony of a Papist, concerning fifty popes at once!

units.la: XII. Testatur non minùs Wernh. Rolfink. dum Chronologia illius Seculi incertitudinem tribuit scandalis & intrusionibus, quæ in utroque statu fiebant; Et paulò post exclamat: Heu, heu, Domine, Domine, quomodo obscuratum est aurum! mutatus est color optimus! Qualia contigisse circa hac tempora in Sancta etiam sede Apostolica, quam usq; hac tanto Zelo custodisti, legimus scandala! Quales contentiones & amulationes, secta,
units.tr: XII. Wernher Rolfinck bears witness no less, when, in his Chronology of that century, he ascribes the uncertainty to the scandals and intrusions that happened in both states. And shortly afterwards he cries out: Alas, alas, Lord, Lord, how the gold has become dim! the finest colour has changed! What scandals we read of having happened about this time even in the holy Apostolic See, which you have guarded with such zeal until now! What quarrels and rivalries, factions,

units.la: Ex Seculo IX. testimonio Genebrardi, Aventini, & Genebrardi iterum.
units.tr: From the testimony of the ninth century: Genebrardus, Aventinus, and Genebrardus again.

units.la: Wernheri Rolfinki & Baronius à. stiḊa, invidia, ambitiones, intrusiones? O tempus pessimum, in quo defecit sanctus & diminuta sunt veritates a filiis hominum. Et itrum: Isti octo Pontifices successivè (à Sergio & Formoso) sequentes brevi tempore sederunt. Nescio notabile aliquid de ipsis dicere, quia nonnisi scandalosa de ipsis reperi propter inauditam in sancta sede Apostolica contentionem, unus contra alterum & simul contra se mutuo &c. Cum quo idem plane docet ipse Baronius ad an. 899. At hic finis seculi hujus, inquit, multis ex causis universa Ecclesia ærumnosi; Romanæ vero potissimùm laboriosi &c. Cujus præter alias causam in eo ponit, quòd intestina eædemque implacabilia bella in ipso sinu ejusdem Ecclesiæ Romanæ agitari cœpta; ceteris lugubrius est redditum atque funestius, & sterterunt omnes, quibus ad regimen sucrat invigilandum, imò ii ipsi, ut Apostolica navis fluctibus obruta penitùs mergeretur, curarunt. Hinc & ad an. 897. n. 5; ait, interdum deforme valde, turpéque contigisse apponi Ecclesia caput.
units.tr: Wernher Rolfinck and Baronius: envy, ambitions, intrusions? O most wretched age, in which the holy man failed and the truths were diminished among the sons of men! And again: These eight popes, succeeding one another (from Sergius and Formosus), sat for a short time. I do not know anything notable to say about them, because I have found nothing but scandalous things about them, on account of the unheard-of contention in the holy Apostolic See, one against another and all against themselves, etc. With him, Baronius himself plainly teaches the same thing at the year 899: At this end of the century, he says, the whole Church was troubled for many reasons, but the Roman Church especially was labouring etc. Among other causes he puts this: that internal wars, and those implacable, began to be waged in the very bosom of the same Roman Church; this made things more mournful and deadly than before, and all those who had been appointed to watch over the government stood by, or rather took care, so that the Apostolic ship, overwhelmed by the waves, should be utterly sunk. Hence also at the year 897, n. 5, he says that it sometimes happened, very shamefully and foully, that a head was set upon the Church.

units.la: XLIII. De eodem tamen, cui ceu sancto Pontifici degeneres successisse, Genebrardus testatur, Nicolao I. cui ab Anastasio ipso, quòd victoriosus & per dominium imperârit, tribuitur, qualis fuerit, ex Epistola egregia Episcoporum inferioris Germaniæ ad eum, colligere licet; Ita post enumerationem privilegiorum Ecclesiæ concessorum scribunt: Quæ beneficia tu, veluti latro, intercipis, Templo Domini praripis in téque transfers atque lupus factus es ovibus, vivos occidis, fortes superis detrahis, vulneribus ad inferos extrudis, gladium melle litum condis, mortuis per te reviviscere non licet; Tu Pontificis quidem personam præ fers, at tyrannum agitas, sub cultu & habitu Pastorum lupum sentimus. Titulus Parentem mentitur, in te factis Jovem ostentas: Cùm sis servus servorum Dei, Dominus dominantium esse contendis. Atque juxta disciplinam Christi Servatoris nostri infimus es omnium ministrorum Templi Dei. Tu verò libidine dominandi in præceps abis, quicquid tibi libet, licet: fucus factus es Christianis. His de causis nos cum collegiis nostris neque edictulis tuis stamus, neque vocem tuam agnoscimus, neque tuas bullas tonitruáque timemus; Tu eos, qui SCTis impiis non parant, impietatis condemnas, iisdem sacrificiis indicis. Nos tuo te ense jugulamus, qui edictum Domini Deíque nostri conspuis, concordiam Collegii discindis, pacem immortalem cœlestis Principis tesseram violas. Spiritus S. author est omnium Ecclesiarum, quâ longissimè orbis terrarum porrigitur, Civitas Dei nostri, cujus municipes summus, ad universos Cardines pertinet, major est urbe, quæ Babylon à S. Vitibus appellatur, ut quæ Divinitatem usurpat, cœlo se æquat, æternam se fore jactitat, perinde as si esset Deus, immortalisque sapientia, neque unquam errasse. râsse, neque errare posse mendaciter gloriatur. De simili Adriani II. successoris erga supremos Magistratus in juria, adeóque etiam de similis superbia severe conquerentes præcipuos in Gallia Ecclesiastici & seculária ordinis Viros, vide apud Bochellum Decr. Eccl. Gall. l. 2. t. 2. c. 2. p. 317. in Epistola Hincmari; imò ipsum, quem injuriâ afficiebat; Regem Carolum Calvum in Epistola ab ipsomet etiam responsi loco scripta, in qua inter alia, Quis hanc inversam legem Infernus evomuit? Quis Tartarus de suis abditis & tenebrosis cuniculis eructavit? Contra quam literis Sacris nobis ostensa est via, quam sequamur &c.
units.tr: XLIII. Concerning the same man, to whom, as to a holy pope, Genebrardus testifies that degenerate men succeeded: from Nicholas I, to whom it is ascribed by Anastasius himself that he ruled as a victor and through dominion, one may gather what kind of man he was from the outstanding letter of the bishops of Lower Germany to him. After listing the privileges granted to the Church, they write thus: These benefits you snatch away like a thief, you seize for yourself the Temple of the Lord and transfer it to yourself, and you have become a wolf among the sheep: you kill the living, you drag down the strong from above, you thrust men to hell with wounds, you hide a sword smeared with honey, and it is not allowed for the dead to be revived through you. You indeed bear the person of a pope, but you act the tyrant; under the appearance and dress of shepherds we perceive a wolf. Your title falsely claims the name of father; you display Jove in your deeds. Although you are the servant of the servants of God, you contend that you are lord of lords. And according to the discipline of Christ our Saviour you are the lowest of all the ministers of the Temple of God. But you, driven by the lust to dominate, rush headlong; whatever pleases you, you allow; you have become a drone among Christians. For these reasons we neither stand with your edicts and our colleges, nor acknowledge your voice, nor fear your bulls and thunderbolts. You condemn as impious those who do not prepare your impious decrees, and you hand them over to the same sacrifices. We will cut your throat with your own sword, you who spit upon the edict of the Lord our God, who tear apart the concord of the college, and who violate the immortal peace, the token of the heavenly Prince. The Holy Spirit is the author of all the Churches, which stretch far across the world; the City of our God, whose chief citizen is the one who belongs to all the corners of the earth, is greater than the city called Babylon by the seven hills, since she usurps divinity, equals herself to heaven, boasts that she will last for ever, as if she were God and immortal wisdom, and falsely glories that she has never erred and cannot err. Of a similar pride, and of a similar injustice towards the supreme magistrates, the leading men of the ecclesiastical and secular order in Gaul severely complained against Adrian II, his successor; see in Bouchel, Decrees of the Gallican Church, book 2, title 2, chapter 2, p. 317, in the letter of Hincmar, and indeed against King Charles the Bald himself, whom he wronged; in a letter that Hadrian himself wrote in reply, among other things: What Hell has vomited forth this inverted law? What Tartarus has belched it out from its hidden and dark tunnels? Against which the way that we should follow has been shown to us in the Sacred Letters, etc.

units.la: XIV. De eodem etiam, quem inter laudatos ponit Genebrardus, Martino II. apud Platinam sunt, qui scribant, (scribit inter alios Onuphrius) ejus fraude Johannem Pontificem ita exagitatum fuisse seditionibus, ut ei invincula conjecto aufugere necesse fuerit; Addit ipse: Martinus malis artibus Pontificatum adeptus brevi moritur, nil dignum memoriâ gerens; vel quòd Dei nutu malis artibus principatus acquisiti, veram gloriam, unicum optimi Principis cibum amittunt. De Formoso jam & alterâ vice egimus, atque simul Platinæ observationem de deficientum Pontificum virtute & integritate exhibuimus, ut & Stephani VI. (quem Baronius ad an. 900. n. 6. hominem facinorosum appellat, quique ut fur & latro ingressus sit in ovile ovium;) historiam, in qua Platina quoque ignaviæ Pontificum mentionem facit; Et Baronii ad an. 897. n. 4. querelam de intrusis in Cathedram Petri, solium Christi, hominibus monstruosis, vita turpissimis, moribus perditissimis, usque quaque sœdissimis; Cui similes alibi quoque habet, nempe ad an. 900. n. 1. de abominatione desolationis in templo loquens, n. 3. persecutiones à Gentilibus, susum quodammodò puerorum, respectu illius, quod Ecclesia Seculo X. invasionibus & vita turpitudine passa sit, vocans; atque tandem quærens: Quot tunc proh pudor! proh dolor! in eandem sedem Angelis reverendam visu horrenda intrusa sunt monstra? Quot ex eis oborta sunt mala consummata tragœdia? Quibus tunc ipsam sine ruga & sine macula contigit asperg i sordibus, putoribus infici, inquinari spurcitiis, ex hisque perpetuâ infamiâ denigrari? Ottoni Loyolitæ Bonifacius VI. Formosi successor illaudatus est, neque dignum æstimat, qui inter Vicarios Christi numeretur; numerat tamen ob exemplum aliorum & numerum & ne putetur, malòs omitti. Ante Pontificatum tam sceleratus, ut bis dignitatem Ecclesiasticam amiserit.
units.tr: XIV. Concerning the same Martin II, whom Genebrardus lists among the praised, Platina (citing Onuphrius among others) writes: there are some who write that through his treachery Pope John was so harassed by seditions that he had to flee after being thrown into chains. Platina adds himself: Martin obtained the papacy by evil arts, died soon after, and achieved nothing worth remembering; or because, by the will of God, principates acquired by evil arts lose true glory, the only proper food of an excellent prince. We have already spoken of Formosus on another occasion, and at the same time we presented Platina's observation about the virtue and integrity of the Popes who failed. We also presented the history of Stephen VI (whom Baronius, at the year 900, n. 6, calls a wicked man who entered like a thief and a robber into the sheepfold), in which Platina also mentions the laziness of the Popes; and Baronius's complaint at the year 897, n. 4, about monstrous men, most vile in life, most depraved in morals, utterly foul, thrust into the Chair of Peter, the throne of Christ. He has similar things elsewhere: at the year 900, n. 1, speaking of the abomination of desolation in the temple; and n. 3, calling the persecutions by the Gentiles a kind of child's play compared with what the Church suffered in the tenth century from invasions and the filthiness of its life. Finally he asks: How many, alas! for shame! for sorrow! horrible monsters, terrible to see, were thrust into that seat which angels should revere? How many evils arose from them, consummated in tragedy? By which the Church, which had been without wrinkle or spot, was then befouled by filth and stench, infected with dirt, and blackened with perpetual infamy? Bonifatius VI, successor of Formosus, is unpraised by Otto Loyolita, who does not think him worthy to be numbered among the Vicars of Christ; yet he numbers him for the sake of example, both to make up the number and so that the bad are not thought to be left out. Before the papacy he was so wicked that he twice lost his ecclesiastical dignity.

units.la: SSSSS 3; XV. Pla-
units.tr: SSSSS 3; XV. Pla-

units.la: XV. Platina autem rursus in Romano I. occasione abrogatorum & improbatorum Stephani decretorum & actorum, sequentem observationem ab Onuphrio in Vita confirmatam dat: Nil aliud hi Pontifices cogitabant, quàm & nomen & dignitatem majorum suorum exstinguere, quo nihil potest esse pejus & angustioris animi; qui enim his artibus niuuntur, nulli virtute muniti, eo de loco abradere bene merentes conantur, quod ipsi ob ignaviam & malitiam attingere non possunt. Neminem siquidem unquam invenies aliena fama invidere, nisi qui omnibus probris contaminatus, desperat suum apud posteros celebre nomen aliquando futurum. Hi sunt, qui fraude, malitiâ, dolo, maledicentiâ de humano genere bene meritis mordent, lacerant, accusant, concordant, tanquam ignavi canes & inutiles, nec feris sese objicientes ob timiditatem, sed vinctus & Caveis inclusi mordentes. Commemorare tamen hujus Pontificis nomen libuit, quia de more sedem Petri obtinuit.
units.tr: XV. Platina, again on Romanus I, on the occasion of the abrogated and disapproved decrees and acts of Stephen, gives the following observation, which Onuphrius confirms in his Life: These Popes thought of nothing but to extinguish both the name and the dignity of their predecessors, which can be nothing worse and nothing narrower in spirit. For those who rely on such arts, lacking any defence in virtue, try to scrape away from that place those who deserve well, because they cannot reach what they lack through laziness and malice. You will never find anyone who envies another's good reputation unless he is stained with every disgrace and despairs that his own famous name will ever live among posterity. These are the men who, by fraud, malice, deceit and slander, bite, tear, accuse and dispute with those who have deserved well of the human race, like lazy and useless dogs, who do not throw themselves at wild beasts out of timidity, but bite while bound and shut in their kennels. I have nonetheless wished to mention the name of this Pope, because he obtained the seat of Peter in the customary way.

units.la: XVI. Successori Theodoro idem Platina testimonium perhibet, vestigia seditiosorum secutum esse; Stella, in eorum vis ambulasse nullâ virtute praditum, postposito Dei timore atque honore; atque in Successore hujus Johanne X. al. IX. notat, ideò abolitiones istas decreorum praedecessorum accidisse, quia Pontifices ipsi à Petri vestigiis discesserant &c. Stella, nihil aliud memoriâ dignum gessisse, nisi quòd sedi ioncs prope extinctas renovaverit & suscitaverit. Similiter in Benedicto IV. qui huic successit, Platina notat: Verum est certè, quod Crispus ait: Quae orta sunt, occidunt, quae aucta senescunt. Imperium ipsum magnum habuit incrementum; verùm postea Principum ac populi Romani ignaviâ splendor ille Romani Nominis in obscuras tenebras conversus est, tum vel maximè, ubi remissâ exercitatione virtutis, voluptatibus se & thermis ad effœminanda corpora inventis tradidere. Idem etiam accidisse Pontificali dignitati dicere possumus. Sanctitate enim & doctrinâ, quae nonnisi magnis laboribus consummatáq, virtute comparantur, Pontificum decus sine ullis opibus primò quidem auctum est inter tot hostes & obstinatos Persecutores Christiani Nominis: mox verò, ubi cum ipsis opibus lascivire coepit Ecclesia Dei, versis ejus cultoribus à severitate ad lasciviam, peperit nobis tanta licentia peccandi, nullo principe flagitia hominum tum coercente, haec portenta, à quibus ambitione & largitione sanctissima Petri sedes occupata est potius quàm possessa. Accidit illi aetati, inquit Joh. Stella in eodem Benedicto, quòd omnis virtus, tam in Capite, quàm in membris ex hominum ignavia consumpta fuerit. Ibidem miratur, quòd Benedictus in tam corruptis Pontificum moribus vitam sine infamia nota perducere potuerit.
units.tr: XVI. The same Platina bears witness to the successor Theodore, that he followed the footsteps of the seditious; Stella says he walked in their strength, endowed with no virtue, with the fear and honour of God set aside. And in the successor of this man, John X (or IX), he notes that those abolitions of the decrees of his predecessors happened because the Popes themselves had departed from the footsteps of Peter etc. Stella says: he did nothing else worth remembering except that he renewed and revived the nearly extinct sees. Similarly, of Benedict IV, who succeeded him, Platina notes: It is certainly true, as Crispus says: what has arisen perishes, what has grown grows old. The empire itself had great growth; but afterwards, through the laziness of the princes and the Roman people, that splendour of the Roman name was turned into obscure darkness, especially when, with the exercise of virtue relaxed, they gave themselves over to pleasures and to baths, invented for the softening of bodies. We can say the same happened to the papal dignity. For sanctity and learning, which are acquired only through great labour and perfected virtue, first increased the glory of the Popes without any wealth, amid so many enemies and obstinate persecutors of the Christian name; but soon, when the Church of God began to revel in wealth itself, its worshippers turned from severity to lasciviousness, and such great licence for sinning was produced for us, with no prince then restraining the crimes of men, that these monstrosities, by whose ambition and largesse the most holy see of Peter was seized rather than possessed. "That age," says John Stella of the same Benedict, "was such that all virtue, in the head as well as in the members, was consumed by human laziness." In the same place he marvels that Benedict could lead his life without known infamy amid such corrupt morals of the Popes.

units.la: XVII. Successit Benedicto Leo V. atque in eo, vitio priorum Pontificum authoritatem Pontificatus multùm diminutam fuisse, notatur. Successor Christophorus I. lupus ille à Leone enutritus, ut eum comederet, Pontificatum malis artibus adeptus male amisit; Pontificum, qui ante fuere, brevis vita, quos tanquam monstra quaedam e medio brevi Deus sustulit. Quemadmodum certè in illo Seculo X. plures quàm in quovis alio Papæ numerantur, & quando Seculum I. 4. II. 11. III. 15. IV. 12. V. 10. VI. 14. VII. 21. VIII. 13. IX. 18. XI. 21. XII. 17. XIII. totidem. XIV. 11. XV. 14. XVI. 15. XVII. hactenus 9. habuerunt; Xmo 30. atque solis Ludovici IV, qui per 12. annos imperavit, temporibus, octo fuerunt. Ut Loyolita Otto in calculo suo fallatur, in septimo plurimos fuisse, tradens, in quo tamen tantùm 20. numerat. De Seculo illo X. ita judicat Wernerus Rolfink in Fasc. temp. Tempus erat effoeminatum. Et erat Sacerdos, sicut populus. Horror est audire, scribit Nauclerus Praepof. Tubing. in Chron. Col. cum append. Laurentii Surii edito, quàm multa perperam per 28. ferè Pontifices sint admissa. Sed & juxta Bellarminum de R. P. l. IV. c. 12. seculo illo decimo in doctius aut infelicius nullum fuit. Nempe in eo infeliciùs continuatum fuit, quod in praecedenti infeliciter, juxta Genebrardum, coeptum. Sed jam in praecedente Pontificum virtus & integritas (annotat ad an. 899.) coepit deficere.
units.tr: XVII. Leo V succeeded Benedict, and in him it is noted that, through the vice of the earlier Popes, the authority of the papacy was much diminished. His successor, Christophorus I, that wolf nurtured by Leo so that he might devour him, obtained the papacy by evil arts and lost it badly; the Popes who had gone before had short lives, which God in a brief time removed from the midst as certain monsters. Indeed, in that tenth century more Popes are counted than in any other age, and while the first century had 4, the second 11, the third 15, the fourth 12, the fifth 10, the sixth 14, the seventh 21, the eighth 13, the ninth 18, the eleventh 21, the twelfth 17, the thirteenth as many, the fourteenth 11, the fifteenth 14, the sixteenth 15, and the seventeenth so far 9, the tenth had 30; and in the time of Ludovicus IV alone, who reigned for 12 years, there were eight. Otto Loyolita is wrong in his count when he says there were very many in the seventh, though he counts only 20 there. Werner Rolfink judges that century X thus, in the Fasciculus temporum: "The time was effeminate. The priest was like the people. It is horrible to hear." Nauclerus, provost of Tübingen, writes in his Chronicle, published with the appendix of Laurentius Surius, how many things were wrongly admitted through about 28 Popes. But also, according to Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, book IV, chapter 12, no century was more unfortunate or more unhappy than that tenth one. Indeed, what was begun unhappily in the preceding century, according to Genebrardus, was continued more unhappily in that one. But already in the preceding century (he notes at the year 899) the virtue and integrity of the Popes began to fail.

units.la: XVIII. Christophorum à Pontificatu dejecit Sergius ille nefandus, verba sunt Baronii ad an. 908. n. 2. homo vitiorum omnium servus, facinorosissimus omnium, quae intentata reliquit? Eum constat postea malum ingressum, deteriorémque progressum, pessimum demum consecutum esse egressum. Sunt haec infelicissima tempora, ita pergit n. 3. cùm alter alterius res gestas, intrusus quisque Pontifex aboleret &c. Et n. 4. Eosdem Sedis Apostolicae invasores, non Apostolicos, sed Apostaticos esse dicendos, Ecclesiastica bene dispositia censuit disciplina. Et n. 5. Praeter vim tyrannicam turpitudo quoque vitae Sergii ab auctoribus ejus Seculi tradita posteris magna infamia nota est reddita manifesta. Subjungit ex Luitprando, qui obscoena ista nota reliquit, Maroziam (de qua jam Differt. V.) ex Papa Sergio Johannem, qui post Joannis Ravennatis obitum S. R. Rom. Ecclesia obtinuit dignitatem, nefario genuisse adulterio. N. 6. De Theodora, nobili scorto, quòd filias, una erat Marozia, Pontificibus prostituerit Sedis Apostolicae invasoribus & Tuscia Marchionibus. Et n 7. Quis ista considerans non obstupescens, scandalúmque patiens putárit, Deum oblitum Ecclesiae suae, quam meretricum arbitrio permiserit infamari? &c. In eo-dem dem Sergio Platina notat: Vide quaso, quantum isti degeneraverint a majoribus suis &c. posthabito divino cultu, inimicitias non secus ac saevissimi quidam tyranni inter se exercebant: suas voluptates postea securius expleturi, cum nullibi exstarent qui eorum vitia coercerent.
units.tr: XVIII. Sergius, "that nefarious man", in Baronius's words at the year 908, n. 2, a man, slave of all vices, the most criminal of all, who left nothing untried, drove Christophorus from the papacy. It is agreed that he afterwards entered upon an evil course, advanced to worse, and at last came to the worst end. These are the most unhappy times, he continues n. 3, when each intruded Pope annulled the deeds of the other, etc. And n. 4: The ecclesiastical discipline judged well that these invaders of the Apostolic See should be called not Apostolic but apostate. And n. 5: besides the tyrannical violence, the baseness of life of Sergius, handed down by the writers of his age, has been made known to posterity with great and manifest infamy. He adds from Liutprand, who left this foul record, that Marozia (of whom already in Dissertation V) by Pope Sergius bore an adulterous son, John, who obtained the dignity of the Holy Roman Church after the death of John of Ravenna. N. 6: of Theodora, a noble harlot, who, since she had daughters, one being Marozia, prostituted them to Popes, invaders of the Apostolic See, and to the Marquises of Tuscany.
