N. 7: Who, considering these things, would not be astonished and, suffering the scandal, think that God had forgotten his Church, allowing it to be defamed at the will of harlots? etc. On the same Sergius Platina notes: Please see how far they have degenerated from their ancestors, etc.; neglecting divine worship, they carried on enmities no differently from the most savage tyrants, the more securely to satisfy their pleasures later, since nowhere were there any who might restrain their vices.

units.la: XIX. Conqueritur etiam Cranzius Sax. l. 2 eadem occasione, Romanos Pontifices velut ebrios, furiosos jactatos esse. De Anastasio III. vero Panvinius ait: Hunc Pontificem hac una in re laudare possumus, quod neminem eorum, qui ante se in Pontificatu fuerunt, aliqua notaverit ignominia, vel maledicentia prosecutus sit; Addit Stella; Prater Pontificum sui temporis morem. Sed & Fasciculus temporum in descriptione hujus aetatis sequentia habet: Monstrum habens caput caninum, & cetera membra sicut homo, praesentatur Ludovico; Et bene potuit monstruosum statum signare hujus temporis, ubi homines sine capite quasi canes latrando hinc inde vacillabant.
units.tr: XIX. Cranzius also complains on the same occasion, in Saxonia book 2, that the Roman Pontiffs were tossed about like drunkards and madmen. Of Anastasius III, Panvinius says: We can praise this Pontiff in one respect only: he did not attack any of those who had been Pontiffs before him with disgrace or slander. Stella adds: Except for the custom of the Pontiffs of his own time. The Fasciculus temporum, describing this age, also has the following: A monster with a dog's head and the other members like a man's is presented to Louis. It could well have signified the monstrous state of this time, when men without a head wavered this way and that, barking like dogs.

units.la: XX. De Joannis X. al. XI. Electione, sive potius intrusione supra actum est. Platina ei spiritus militares magis quam religioni deditos tribuit. Si juxta Platinam Sergii P. & Marozae filius fuit, quod nefandum & inauditum, aviae suae Theodorae Concubinarius fuit. Baronius ea occasione atq; ad a. 912. n. 8. notat; arbitrio foedidissimarum meretricum intrusos fuisse in sedem Petri earum amasios Pseudo-Pontifices, qui non sint nisi ad consignanda tantum tempora in Catalogo Romanorum Pontificum. Quis enim a scortis hujusmodi intrusos sine lege legitimos dicere posset fuisse Romanos Pontifices &c. Author vero Fasciculi temporum exclamat: Eja Deus aeterne, quam disparēs illi sunt Pontificibus prioribus! Atq; subjicit: Nescio aliquid notabile de illis dicere, quia nonnisi scandalosa de illis reperi, propter inauditam in S. Sede Apostolica contentionem. Unus contra alium & simul contra se mutuo aque pariter omnes & singuli contra Deum & Christianam Ecclesiam. Et alibi: Sanctitas Papae dimisit, & ad Imperatores accessit, sicut clare apparet. Sed & Albertus Cranzius, Canonicus Hamburgensis Sax. l. 2. exclamat: o Petre, Line, Clete, Clemens! ad quid pervenit vestro sanguine, imo Christi cruore partus principatus!
units.tr: XX. We have already said above that John X (or XI) was intruded into office, or rather forced in. Platina ascribes to him military spirits rather than devotion to religion. If, according to Platina, he was the son of Sergius and Marozia, which is unspeakable and unheard of, then he was the lover of his grandmother Theodora. On this occasion Baronius, at the year 912, n. 8, observes: By the will of the most foul harlots, their lovers were thrust into the seat of Peter as pseudo-Pontiffs, who are good only for marking the years in the catalogue of Roman Pontiffs. For who could say that men intruded without law by such whores were lawful Roman Pontiffs? The author of the Fasciculus temporum cries out: O eternal God, how unlike those earlier Pontiffs they are! And he adds: I do not know what remarkable thing to say about them, because I have found nothing about them but scandals, on account of the unheard-of contention in the Apostolic See. Each one against another, and at the same time all and each equally against themselves, against God and the Christian Church. And elsewhere: The holiness of the Pope has been put aside, and he has gone over to the emperors, as is clearly apparent. Albert Crantz, canon of Hamburg, also cries out in Saxonia book 2: O Peter, Linus, Cletus, Clement! To what has the principality come, born of your blood, nay, of Christ's blood!

units.la: XXI. Johannes XI. Plat. XII. Baronio ad an. 931. n. 1. tantum monstrum est; Et ad an. 936. n. 4. Sedis Apostolica inquinator potius quam Rector. Post eum Stella in Leone VI. priorum Pontificum temeritatem atque stultitiam notat. Septimum vero ejus nominis remissum virum, qui nil memoria dignum post se reliquerit, vocat. Johannem XII. Plat. XIII. Trithemius in Chronico vocat omnium bipedum equissimus mum, imò ipsius Diaboli mancipium. Platina ab adolescentia omnibus probris ac turpitudine contaminatum, venationibus magis, si quid temporis à libidinibus supererat, quàm Orationi deditum atque omnium, qui unquam ante se in Pontificatu fuere, perniciosissimum & sceleratissimum fuisse. Qualem eum Baronius atque Onuphrius fuisse doceant, ex parte suprà vidimus. Idem ad an. 963. n. 4. ex Luitprando narrat, quòd perjurus se Adelberto conjunxerit. n. 5. vero Romanorum accusationem contra Johannem institutam ex Luitprando ita enarrat:
units.tr: XXI. John XI (Platina XII) is such a monster, according to Baronius at the year 931, n. 1; and at the year 936, n. 4, he is a polluter of the Apostolic See rather than its ruler. After him Stella, speaking of Leo VI, notes the rashness and folly of the earlier Pontiffs. He calls the seventh of that name a remiss man who left nothing worth remembering behind him. John XII (Platina XIII): Trithemius in his Chronicle calls him the most unjust of all two-footed creatures, indeed a slave of the Devil himself. Platina says he was from youth stained with every disgrace and baseness, devoted more to hunting, and to prayer only if any time was left over from his lusts, and the most destructive and wicked of all who had ever been Pontiffs before him. That he was such a man, Baronius and Onuphrius teach, as we have seen in part above. The same Baronius, at the year 963, n. 4, relates from Liutprand that he perjured himself by joining with Adelbert. At n. 5, he sets out from Liutprand the accusation brought by the Romans against John, thus:

units.la: Non dispar videtur ratio, cur Joannes Papa Sanctissimum Imperatorem, suum scilicet ex manibus Adelberti liberatorem & Diabolus oderit Creatorem. Imperator, quemadmodum re ipsa experti sumus; ea, quae Dei sunt, sapit, operatur, diligit, Ecclesiastica & saecularia negotia armis tutatur, moribus ornat & legibus emendat: Joannes Papa his omnibus adversatur. Non clam est quod fatemur; Testis est Rainera (al. juxta Baronium, Rainerii) sui ipsius militis vidua, quam caeco captus igne, multis praefectam urbibus, Sacro-Sanctis B. Petri donavit aureis Crucibus atque Calicibus. Testis & Stephana ejus amica, quae in effusione, quod ex eo recens conceperat, recens hominem exuit. Quod si cuncta taceant, Lateranense palatium, Sanctorum quondam hospitium, nunc prostibulum meretricum, non silebit amicam conjugem, Stephanae Patris concubinae sororem. Testis omnium gentium, praeterquam Romanorum absentia mulierum, quae Sanctorum Apostolorum limina orandi gratia timent invisere, quum nonnullas ante dies paucos hunc audierint conjugatas, viduas, virgines vi oppressisse. Testes sunt Sancta Apostolorum Ecclesia, quae non stillatim pluviam, sed totum intrinsecus, supra ipsa etiam Sacro-Sancta altaria, imbrem admittunt &c. Testes sunt non solùm juncearum curatura, sed & quotidianarum formarum mulieres, cui eadem sunt, & silices pedibus, quae conterunt, & quae magnorum subeuntur adjutorio jumentorum. Atque hoc rei est, quòd tanta ei cum Imperatore sancto discordia est, lupus & agnus quanta sortitò obtigit. Illi hoc ut impune liceat, Adelbertum sibi tutorem & defensorem parat.
units.tr: There seems to be no less reason why Pope John should hate the most holy Emperor, his own liberator from the hands of Adelbert, than why he should hate the Creator. The Emperor, as we have learned from experience, savours and does the things that are of God, loves them, defends ecclesiastical and secular affairs by arms, adorns them with morals and reforms them by laws. John the Pope opposes all of these things. What we say is no secret; Rainera is a witness (Baronius has Rainerius), the widow of his own soldier, whom, seized by blind fire, he presented to the most holy shrines of blessed Peter, with golden crosses and chalices, after placing her in charge of many cities. Stephana, his mistress, is a witness, who, when she had recently conceived by him, was rid of the human being in the act of miscarriage. And if all else were silent, the Lateran palace, once a guesthouse of saints, now a brothel of harlots, would not be silent about his mistress-wife, the sister of Stephana, the concubine of his father. Every nation is a witness, except for the Roman women, who, out of fear, do not dare visit the thresholds of the holy Apostles to pray, since they have heard that a few days ago he forced married women, widows and virgins. The holy church of the Apostles is a witness, which admits the rain not drop by drop but in full, inside, even above the most sacred altars, and so on. The women are witnesses, not only of the courtesans but also of the daily prostitutes, to whom the same things belong, and whose feet wear down stones, and who are carried by the help of great beasts. This is the reason why there is such great discord between him and the holy Emperor, as wolf and lamb. He prepares Adelbert as his guardian and defender, so that he may do these things with impunity.

units.la: En eximium Romanorum de suo, imò universalis Ecclesiae Pastore testimonium! N. 6. affert judicium Imperatoris Ottonis suprà allatum de puero in melius mutando. N. 7. exhibet promissionem Joannis de mutatione in melius per legatos, ex eodem, haud mirum esse, si hactenus juventutis igne devictus quid puerile gesserit; jam tempus instare, cùm alieno cuperet vivere more. N. 9. quomodo Imperatorem subdolè suis versutiis deludere studuerit. N. 17. accusationes in Concilio factae feruntur; Postquam enim testati essent Romani Pontifices (Episcopos Cardinales intelligere videtur;) & Cardinales Presbyteri ac Diaconi cum universa plebe, Joannis scelera nec Ibericos, nec Babylonicos, nec Indicos incolas latere, neque eum esse de illis, qui veniunt in vestimentis ovium, intus autem sunt lupi rapaces, eum ita aperte sævire, ita aperte Diabolica negotia pertractare, ut nihil circuitione utatur; Atque Imperator postularet, ut accusationes nominatim exprimantur. Tunc consurgens Petrus Cardinalis Presbyter, se vidisse illum missas celebrâsse & non communicâsse, testatus est. Joannes Episcopus Narniensis, & Joannes Cardinalis Diaconus, se vidisse illum Diaconum ordinâsse in equorum stabulo non certis temporibus sunt professi. Benedictus cum cæteris Condiaconis & Compresbyteris dixit, se scire, quòd ordinationes Episcoporum pretio fecerit, & quòd annorum 10. Episcopum in Tudertina civitate ordinârit. De sacrilegio non esse necesse percontari dixit, quia plùs videndo quàm audiendo scire potuissemus. De adulterio dixerunt, quòd oculis non viderunt, sed pro certo scirent, viduam Rainerii & Stephanam Patris concubinam & Annam viduam cum nepte sua abusum esse, & Sanctum palatium lupanar & prostibulum fecisse. Venationem dixerunt publicè exercuisse. Benedictum Spiritualem Patrem suum lumine privâsse, & mox mortuum esse. Johannem Cardinalem Subdiaconum virilibus amputatis occidisse; ense accinctum galea & lorica indutum fuisse testati sunt. Diaboli in amorem vinum bibisse, omnes tam Clerici quàm Laici acclamârunt. In ludo alea, Jovis, Veneris caterorumque dæmonum auxilium popposcisse dixerunt. Matutinas & Canonicas horas cum non celebrâsse, nec signo Crucis se munivisse professi sunt. N. 20. & 21. ex eodem obtestationem Imperatoriam, ne quis per calumniam aliquid affingeret, subjungit; N. 22. Virò: Tum Episcopi, Diaconi, Clerus & cunctus Romanorum populus, quasi Vir unus dixerunt: Si non & quae per Benedictum Diaconum lecta sunt, hisque turpiora & ampliora Joannes Papa indigna commisit facinora, non nos à peccatorum vinculis absolvat Apostolorum Princeps B. Petrus, qui verbo cælum indignis claudit, justis aperit. Sinus anathematis vinculo innodati, atque in die novissima in sinistra parte positi cum eis, qui dixerunt Domino Deo: Recede à nobis, scientiam viarum tuarum nolumus. Quod si fidem nobis non adhibetis, exercitui Domini Imperatoris saltem debetis credere, cui ante 5. dies ense accinctus, clypeo, galea, lorica indutus occurrit. Solus Tiberis, qui interfluit, ne sic ornatus ab exercitu caperetur, impedivit. Mox Sanctus Imperator dixit: Tot sunt hujus rei testes, quot sunt nostro in exercitu bellatores. In epistola, quâ eum ad causam dicendam vocabat, inter alia scripsit: Talia de vobis tàmque obscenas proprotulerunt, ut, si de histrionibus dicerentur, vobis verecundiam ingererent; — Si cuncta nominatim exprimere cuperemus, dies nobis non sufficeret unus. Noveritis igitur, non à paucis, sed ab omnibus, tam vestri, quàm alterius ordinis, vos homicidii, perjurii, Sacrilegii, & ex propria cognatione, atque ex duabus Sororibus incesti crimine esse accusatos &c. Eo autem comparere nolente, atque sceleratissimo homine, vel monstro potius, sunt verba Platinæ, judicium bene sentientium reformidante; audità Imperatoris propositione, Romani Pontifices, reliquûsque Clerus & cunctus populus dixerunt: Inauditum vulnus inaudito est cauterio exurendum: Si corruptis moribus sibi soli, & non cunctis obesset, quoquomodo tolerandus esset. Quot priùs casti, facti sunt hujus imitatione incesti? Quot prob hujus exempli conversationis sunt reprobi? Petimus itaque magnitudinem Imperii vestri, monstrum illud nullâ virtute redemtum à vitiis, à S. Rom. Ecclesia pelli &c. Factum est, eique substitutus, ut suprà diximus, Leo VIII. contrà quem tamen Joannem, licet objecta crimina negare minimè ausus, Baronius, licet etiam secùs sentiente Onuphrio, doctrinam infernalem de non deponendo Papa, utut omnium sceleratissimo producens, defendit, uti etiam in Synodo sub Johanne congregata nihilominùs pissimus & coangelicus, quasi ἰοχγελ vocari meruit! Sed & mors vitæ generi respondit; Divinitùs periit, secundùm Platinam; cum uxore cujusdam se oblectans à Diabolo percussus ac sine viatico domini-co mortuus est, Sigeberto Gemblacensi & Luitprando narrantibus. Janus Vitalis autem in elogiis Pontificum Bononiæ ante 100. annos impressis ita canit: Pontifices inter celebres dicere Johannes; Ut sunt in mediis sæpe aconita rosis.
units.tr: Behold the outstanding testimony of the Romans concerning their own, nay, the universal Church's, Pastor! N. 6 gives the judgment of the Emperor Otto, cited above, about the boy who was to be changed for the better. N. 7 presents John's promise, through envoys, of change for the better, from the same source: It is no wonder if hitherto, overcome by the fire of youth, he did something boyish; now the time was coming when he would wish to live by another's manner. N. 9 shows how he tried to deceive the Emperor craftily with his tricks. N. 17 reports the accusations made in the Council. After the Roman Pontiffs (he seems to mean the bishops and cardinals) had given testimony, and the cardinal presbyters and deacons, together with the whole people, said that John's crimes were known not only to the Iberians, the Babylonians and the Indians, and that he was not one of those who come in sheep's clothing while inwardly they are ravening wolves, he was raging so openly and handling devilish business so openly that he used no circumlocution. When the Emperor asked that the accusations be stated by name, then Peter, cardinal presbyter, rose and testified that he had seen him celebrate Mass and not communicate. John, bishop of Narni, and John, cardinal deacon, declared that they had seen him ordain a deacon in a horse stable at no fixed times. Benedict, with the other co-deacons and co-presbyters, said that he knew he had sold ordinations of bishops for money, and that he had ordained a bishop in the city of Todi ten years ago. They said it was not necessary to ask about sacrilege, because we could know more by seeing than by hearing. About adultery they said they had not seen it with their eyes, but they knew for certain that Rainerius's widow, and Stephana, his father's concubine, and Anna, a widow, had been abused along with her niece, and that the holy palace had been made a brothel and a bawdy-house. They said he openly practised hunting. They said that he deprived Benedict, his spiritual father, of his sight, and that he died soon after. They testified that John, a cardinal subdeacon, was killed after his genitals were cut off; they said he was girded with a sword and wore a helmet and breastplate. All, both clergy and laity, cried out that he drank wine to the love of the Devil. They said that while playing dice he had asked for the help of Jupiter, Venus and the other demons. They professed that he had not celebrated Matins and the canonical hours, nor armed himself with the sign of the cross. N. 20 and 21, from the same source, add the Emperor's solemn warning that no one should invent anything by calumny. N. 22: Then the bishops, deacons, clergy and the whole Roman people, as if one man, said: If the things read out through Deacon Benedict, and worse and greater crimes that Pope John has committed unworthily, are not true, may the Prince of the Apostles, blessed Peter, who with his word shuts heaven to the unworthy and opens it to the just, not absolve us from the chains of sin. May we be bound in the bond of anathema, and placed in the last day on the left side with those who said to the Lord God: Depart from us, we do not want the knowledge of your ways. If you do not give us credit, you should at least believe the army of the lord Emperor, which five days ago came to meet him girded with a sword, clothed with shield, helmet and breastplate. Only the Tiber, which flows between, prevented him from being taken by the army while so equipped. Soon the holy Emperor said: There are as many witnesses of this matter as there are fighters in our army. In the letter by which he summoned John to answer the charges, he wrote among other things: They brought forward such shameful things about you, so obscene, that if they were said about stage actors they would bring shame upon you. If we wished to state everything by name, one day would not be enough for us. Know therefore that you are accused, not by a few but by all, of both your own order and the other, of homicide, perjury, sacrilege, and of incest with your own relative and with two sisters. He, however, was unwilling to appear, and, that most wicked man, or rather monster, as Platina says, dreading the judgment of those who think well. When the Emperor's proposal was heard, the Roman Pontiffs, the rest of the clergy and the whole people said: An unheard-of wound must be burned with an unheard-of cautery. If his corrupt morals harmed only himself and not all, he would have to be tolerated somehow. How many chaste men have been made incestuous by his example? How many reprobates are there from the conduct of this example? We therefore ask your greatness that this monster, redeemed by no virtue from his vices, be driven out from the Holy Roman Church. It happened, and Leo VIII was substituted in his place, as we said above; against him, however, John, although he did not dare deny the crimes laid to his charge, was defended by Baronius, who, though Onuphrius thought otherwise, put forward the infernal doctrine of not deposing a Pope, however wicked he might be; just as in the synod gathered under John he nevertheless deserved to be called most pious and angelic, as if equal to the angels [ἰσάγγελος]! But his death matched his life: he perished by divine judgment, according to Platina; while enjoying himself with the wife of a certain man, he was struck by the Devil and died without the Lord's viaticum, as Sigebert of Gembloux and Liutprand relate. Janus Vitalis, moreover, in his eulogies of the Pontiffs printed at Bologna about 100 years ago, sings thus: Among the famous Pontiffs, I must name John; as there are often aconites among the roses.

units.la: XXII. In Bonifacio VII. quem Theodoricus à Niem insatiabilem voraginem, cui in avaritia nullus similis, Baronius ad an. 974. n. 1. scelestissimum virum; Ad an. 975. n. 1. tyrannum, invasorem, nefandissimum hominem, truculentum prædonem vocat & cui Stella tribuit, quòd malis artibus Pontificatûs munus adeptus, malè vixerit, & pessime turpitérque vitam finiverit; Platina annotat: Vide quæso, quantùm degeneraverint ii Pontifices &c. Sacrorum Pater & Rex Sacra ipsa furto abstulit, & qui vindicare Sacrilegia debuerat, tanti Sacrilegii factus est auctor &c. In Clerum deligendi essent, quorum vita & doctrina probata sit: non autem hi, qui, cùm nil virtutis & religionis habeant, ambitione & largitione sibi potentiam quærunt. Ipsius Baronii de eo judicium Differt. VI. Sect. 4. n. 57. exposuimus. Joannis XVI. Plat. XVII.
units.tr: XXII. Of Boniface VII. Theodoric of Niem calls him an insatiable whirlpool, to whom none is similar in greed; Baronius, at the year 974, n. 1, calls him a most wicked man, and at the year 975, n. 1, a tyrant, an usurper, a most nefarious man, a savage plunderer. Stella ascribes to him that having obtained the Pontificate by evil arts, he lived badly, and ended his life most wretchedly and shamefully. Platina remarks: See, I beg you, how far those Pontiffs degenerated, etc. The Father of sacred things and King of holy things himself stole the sacred things, and he who ought to have avenged sacrilege became the author of so great a sacrilege, etc. Those should be chosen for the clergy whose life and teaching have been tested, not those who, since they have no virtue or piety, seek power for themselves by ambition and bribery. Baronius's own judgment of him we set out in Dissertation VI, section 4, n. 57. John XVI, Platina XVII.

units.la: Exemplo Bonifacii VII. Querelâ Platinæ; Exemplis Iohannis XVI. & XVII. mum suo loco exhibebimus, contenti hic ex Platina notâsse, superbiam & rapacitatem Pontificis contemtumque Dei & hominum, malorum illius temporis, eo quidem judice, causas; & ex Stella, quòd merito non modò ab ipso Clero, sed & ab omnibus populis odiosus habitus & erroribus ac rapacitatibus involutus, Deo sic volente & non sustinente, quarto mensis mortuus est. Joannes XVII. Plat. XVIII. ideò, judicio hujus, numeratur, qui a & tyrannorum perversa facta, optimorum principum rebus gestis annumerantur, ut, quantum inter se boni & mali desideant, à legentibus cognosci possit. Fuit, eodem indice, fur in Pontificatu & latro, atque beatitudine caruit, cum ignominia mortuus decimo usurpati Pontificatus mense. Stellae Johannes XVII. & XVIII. adulterini Pontifices.
units.tr: We shall present the example of Boniface VII and Platina's complaint, and the examples of John XVI and XVII, in their proper place; here we are content to have noted from Platina that the pride and rapacity of the Pontiff, and contempt for God and men, were the causes of the evils of that time, in his judgment; and from Stella that he was rightly held hateful not only by the clergy themselves but by all peoples, and involved in errors and rapacities; God, so willing and not enduring it, he died in the fourth month. John XVII (Platina XVIII) is therefore, in his judgment, counted among those whose perverse deeds of tyrants are reckoned with the deeds of the best princes, so that, as far as good and bad differ from each other, may be recognised by the readers. He was, by the same judge, a thief and robber in the Pontificate, and lacked blessedness, dying in disgrace in the tenth month of his usurped Pontificate. Stella calls John XVII and XVIII counterfeit Pontiffs.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Certè mirum jam esse non potest, quòd Gerbertus, postea Sylvester II. circa finem hujus Seculi Epist ad Steph. R. E. Diaconum scripsit: Romanorum mores mundus perhorrescit. Et quòd idem coram Synodo Rhemensi inter alia ita locutus est: O Lugenda Roma! quae nostris majoribus clara Patrum lumina praebuisti, nostris temporibus monstruosas tenebras futuro Seculo famosas offudisti &c. Quid sub hæc tempora non vidimus? Vidimus Joannem cognomento Octavianum, in volutabro libidinum etiam contrà eum Ottonem, quem Augustum creaverat, conjurâsse. Quo fugato, Leo Neophytus in Pontificem creatur. Sed Ottone Caesare Roma discedente, Octavianus Romam redit, Leonem fugat, Joannem Diaconum naso dextrisque digitis ac linguâ mutilat, multaque cade primorum in urbe debacchatus brevi moritur. Cui Benedictum Grammaticum, cognomento Diaconum Romani substituunt. Eum quoque Leo Neophytus cum suo Caesare non longè post aggreditur, obsidet, capit, deponit, perpetuóque exilio in Germaniam dirigit; Succedit Ottoni Caesari Otto. Succedit Romae in Pontificatu horrendum monstrum Malefacius (Bonifacii jam jam descripti hoc elogium est;) cunctos mortales nequitiâ superans, etiam prioris Pontificis sanguine cruentus &c. Num talibus monstris hominum ignominia plenis, scientiâ humanarum & divinarum rerum vacuis innumeros Sacerdotes Dei per orbem terrarum scientia & vita merito conspicuos subjici decretum est?
units.tr: Certainly it cannot now seem strange that Gerbert, afterwards Sylvester II, near the end of this century, wrote in a letter to Stephen, deacon of the Roman Church: the world shudders at the morals of the Romans. And that the same man, speaking among other things before the Synod of Rheims, said: O Rome to be mourned! You who offered to our forefathers the bright lights of the Fathers, in our times you have spread monstrous darkness, infamous for the coming age, etc. What have we not seen in these times? We have seen John, surnamed Octavian, conspiring in the mire of lusts even against Otto, whom he himself had made Augustus. With him put to flight, Leo the Neophyte was created Pontiff. But when Caesar Otto left Rome, Octavian returned to Rome, drove out Leo, mutilated John the Deacon of his nose, right-hand fingers and tongue, and, raging with much slaughter of the leading men of the city, shortly died. In his place the Romans set up Benedict the Grammarian, surnamed Deacon. Leo the Neophyte, with his Caesar, soon after attacked him too, besieged him, captured him, deposed him, and sent him into perpetual exile in Germany; Otto succeeded Otto as Caesar. In Rome there succeeded in the Pontificate a horrendous monster, Malefacius (this is the description of Boniface just given), surpassing all mortals in wickedness, bloodied even with the blood of the previous Pontiff, etc. Has it been decreed that countless priests of God throughout the world, rightly conspicuous for learning and life, should be subjected to such monsters, full of infamy and empty of knowledge of human and divine things?

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Seculum XI. merito obscurum & tenebricosum vocaretur, ut Ditmarus ferreum dixit. Quale etiam fuit ob pessimos Pontifices. His temporibus, inquit Bellarm: in Chronol. ad Sec. XI. Pontifices Romani à pietate veterum degenerârunt. Quàm tunc deplorratus fuerit status Ecclesiæ, inquit Genebrard. ad an. 1009. & ferme monstro simillimus, cernere licet apud Sigebertum Vicent. & Anton. Magnae simulsimultates inter Imperatorem & Pontificem. Sacerdotes erant moribus depravatissimis, & propterea ipsi & res Sacra populo contemptibiles &c. De Pontificibus etiam aevi illius ita apud Baronium Ottonis III. in Donatione sua conqueritur: Confusis Paparicis legibus & jam abjectâ Ecclesiâ Rom. in tantum quidam Pontifices irruerunt, ut maximam partem Imperii nostri Apostolatui suo conjungerent: Jam non quarentes, qua & quanta suis culpis perdiderunt, non curantes, quanta ex voluntaria vanitate effuderunt, sed sua propria utpote ab illis ipsis dilapidata dimittentes, quasi culpam suam in Imperium nostrum retorquentes, ad aliena, id est, ad nostra & nostri Imperii maxime migraverunt.
units.tr: The eleventh century would rightly be called obscure and gloomy, as Thietmar called it iron. It was so also because of the very worst Pontiffs. In these times, says Bellarmine in the Chronology at the eleventh century, the Roman Pontiffs degenerated from the piety of the ancients. How deplorable the state of the Church then was, says Genebrard at the year 1009, and almost most like a monster, can be seen in Sigebert of Vicenza and Antonius; great were the quarrels between Emperor and Pontiff. The priests were of most depraved morals, and therefore both they and sacred things were contemptible to the people, etc. Concerning the Pontiffs of that age too, Otto III complains thus in his Donation, as cited by Baronius: With the Papal laws confused, and the Roman Church now cast down, certain Pontiffs rushed so far that they joined the greater part of our empire to their apostolate; not now seeking what and how great things they lost through their faults, not caring how much they poured out through voluntary vanity, but leaving their own things, as if squandered by those very men, turning their guilt back upon our empire, they migrated to alien things, that is, especially to ours and our empire's.

units.la: XXV. De Sylvestro II. Diaboli adjutorio promoto jam Dissert. V. egimus. Benedicti VIII. equum nigrum, cui, teste Platina, post mortem insidere visus, quoque innuimus. Similiter triplex monstrum, Benedicto IX. Joanne quodam, atque Sylvestro III. se simul pro Pontificibus gerentibus & flagitiosam turpemque vitam, ut Otto Frisingensis, qui l. 6. c. 32. scripto consignavit, ipse in urbe, Romanis tradentibus, audivit, ducentibus; supra ostendimus. Et Benedictum quidem sola pecunia auri & argenti, teste Baronio ad an. 1033. n. 5. plus comendavit quam aetas & sanctitas; Fuit, Platina teste, homo ignavus & nullius pretii, judice Volaterrano, probrosus & infamis, Leone Ostiensi judice, Papatum tradidit, cupiditates suas liberius exsecuturus; Atque probante ex libellis domi ejus inventis Bennone, Sacris daemoniorum fuit deditus & in sylvis ac montibus mulieres post se currere fecit, quas artibus magicis ad sui amorem coegit. Sylvestri II. ut Benno vult, cum Laurentio discipulus fuit, narrante eodem, a Diabolo tandem in sylva suffocatus. De conditione ipsius post mortem aeternum desperata & apparitione in forma bestiali multis agit Petrus Damiani Epist. 5. ad Fratres Eremi ex relatione Humberti Episcopi de sylva Candida c. 3. Bibl. Patrum T. 3. Omnes tres Platinae etiam tria teterrima monstra vocantur.
units.tr: XXV. Of Sylvester II, promoted with the devil's help, we have already treated in Dissertation V. We have also hinted at Benedict VIII's black horse, on which, according to Platina, he was seen to ride after death. Similarly the threefold monster: Benedict IX, a certain John, and Sylvester III, who simultaneously acted as Pontiffs and led a shameful and foul life, as Otto of Freising records in writing in book 6, chapter 32, he himself heard in the city, the Romans relating it; we showed this above. And Benedict indeed, by sheer money of gold and silver, according to Baronius at the year 1033, n. 5, commended himself more than age and holiness. He was, according to Platina, an idle man of no worth; in the judgment of Volaterranus, disgraceful and infamous; according to Leo of Ostia, he handed over the Papacy, about to pursue his desires more freely. And Benno proves, from little books found in his house, that he was given to demonic rites, and made women run after him in the woods and mountains, whom he forced by magic arts to love him. Sylvester II, as Benno would have it, was a pupil of Laurentius, the same author relating that he was at last suffocated in a wood by the Devil. Concerning his condition after death, eternally despaired of, and his appearance in bestial form, Peter Damian treats at length in Epistle 5 to the brothers of the hermitage, from the report of Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, chapter 3, in the Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 3. All three are called by Platina also three most hideous monsters.

units.la: XXVI. In Clemente II. Platina notat: Videbat Imperator, eo licentiae factiosum quenque & potentem quamvis ignobilem, devenisse, ut corruptis suffragiis tantam dignitatem consequeretur: quae certe, nisi Sanctitate & doctrina bene meritis volente Deo demandari cuipiam non deberet.
units.tr: XXVI. Of Clement II, Platina notes: The Emperor saw that through such license each factious and powerful man, however ignoble, had come to obtain so great a dignity by corrupt votes; which certainly ought not to be committed to anyone unless well deserving through holiness and learning, God willing.

units.la: XXVII. Tandem Leo IX. Si Genebrardo fides habenda, primus a Deo vocatus velut alter Aharon, antiquam Pontificum integritatem e coelo in Sedem Apostolicam revocavit. Sane hoc ipsum sibi ipsi in epistolastola ad Constantinum Monomachum Imperatorem Græcorum, decessoribus suis damnatis, haud obscurè tribuit: Quia, inquit, abundante iniquitate & refrigescente caritate S. R. Ecclesia & Apostolica sedes nimium diu obsessa fuit à mercenariis & non Pastoribus, à quibus sua, & non, quæ sunt Jesu Christi, quaerenibus devastata jacebat miserabiliter haćtenus; divinum consilium voluit meam humilitatem suscipere tanta cathedræ pondus. In ejus vita Platina: Fecerunt vitia quorundam Pontificum, ut merito ipsi Clero sublata potestas videretur Dei judicio, quò in melius eorum mentes flagitiis contaminata aliquando verterentur, ne Resp. Christiana malis Rectoribus commissa perderetur. Idem tamen Leo miles fuit, licèt infelix utpote ab hoste captus.
units.tr: XXVII. Finally Leo IX. If we trust Genebrard, first called by God, like another Aaron, he restored the ancient integrity of the Pontiffs from heaven to the Apostolic See. Indeed he himself, in his letter to Constantine Monomachus, Emperor of the Greeks, condemning his predecessors, not obscurely ascribed this to himself: Because, he says, with iniquity abounding and charity growing cold, the holy Roman Church and the Apostolic See were too long besieged by mercenaries and not shepherds, and lay miserably devastated until now by those who sought their own things and not the things of Jesus Christ; the divine counsel willed that my humility should take up so great a weight of the chair. In his life Platina says: The vices of certain Pontiffs made it so that the power seemed rightly taken away from the clergy by God's judgment, so that their minds, stained with shameful deeds, might at some time be turned to better things, lest the Christian commonwealth, committed to bad rulers, be lost. Yet this same Leo was a soldier, though unfortunate, since he was captured by the enemy.

units.la: XXVIII. Qualis post eum Gregorius VII. fuisse dicatur, jam supra ex parte annotatum est.
units.tr: XXVIII. What sort of man Gregory VII was after him has already been noted in part above.

units.la: Ambitionem sub quatuor Pontificibus Prædecessoribus prodidit à Damiano Dominus Papa dictus, & sequenti alloquio invocatus: Papam rité colo, sed te prostratus adoro, Tu facis hunc Dominum, te facit ipse Deum.
units.tr: Damian reported the ambition of the four popes who had preceded him. He was addressed as "Lord Pope" and invoked in this address: "I duly honour the Pope, but I adore you prostrate. You make him Lord; he himself makes you God."

units.la: Dæmoniacas artes ei non unus Cardinalis Benno, sed triginta Episcopi ex Italia, Gallia & Germania Brixinæ Noricæ congregati, tribuerunt, ut certè dæmoniacarum doćtrinarum ab Apostolo sic dićtarum acerrimus propugnator erat. Injustus in Imperatorem & rebellionum fomes manifestè fuit; Dićtatibus suis supra Deum & omne quod Deus dicitur, se extulit, Gemblacense narrante, tandem confessus est, se Diabolo suadente odium & iram contrà humanum genus concisse. Cætera in schismate ejus videantur. Antichristiana ipsius manifestè talis superbia, præsumptio, & usurpatio, in Deum & Christum ejus, Christianos Christianorúmque Magistratus injuria multiplex omnes sequentes sine ulteriori deductione jam satis damnaret, utpote strenuè in eodem tramite pergentes. Ejus atque successorum proximorum vitia quoque respiciunt verba Anonymi, qui Henrici IV. vitam scripsit: Hic velim, inquit, abrumpere stylum. Nam ventum est ad factiones, ad fraudes, ad scelera, de quibus vera scribere periculosum, falsa, crimen est; hàc lupus, hàc canis urget. Quid igitur faciam? Eloquar an sileam? Manus incipit & dubitat, scribit & renuit, notat & dolet, ut penè ignorem, quid velim. Sed turpe est, inceptam materiam mutilatam relinquere, & caput absque manibus pinxisse. Pergam igitur, ut cœpi.
units.tr: Diabolical arts were attributed to him not by Cardinal Benno alone but by thirty bishops from Italy, France and Germany who met at Brixen in Noricum. He was indeed the fiercest champion of what the Apostle calls diabolical doctrines. He was plainly unjust toward the emperor and a source of rebellions. In his Dictates he exalted himself above God and everything that is called God. As the Gemblacensis relates, he finally confessed that "at the Devil's urging I stirred up hatred and anger against the human race." The rest may be seen in his schism. His Antichristian pride, presumption and usurpation against God and Christ, and his manifold injuries to Christians and Christian magistrates, would condemn him and all who follow him, even without further argument, since they walk vigorously in the same path. The words of an anonymous writer who wrote the life of Henry IV also refer to his vices and those of his immediate successors: "Here I would gladly break off my pen. For we have come to factions, to frauds, to crimes, about which to write the truth is dangerous, to write falsehoods is a crime; here the wolf and the dog press in. What then shall I do? Shall I speak or be silent? My hand begins and hesitates, writes and refuses, marks and grieves, so that I hardly know what I want. But it is shameful to leave a begun subject mutilated and to paint a head without hands. I will go on, then, as I began."

units.la: XXIX. Urbani II. (qui aliis Turbanus dictus, ob turbas in eodem Schismate excitatas) studia ita Aventinus l. V. Annal. descripsit: Dum alteri alteros quovis modo vincere volunt; Urbanus criminando Imperatorem, plebem Christianam exagitat occulte largiendo, indulgendo, pollicitando magis incendit, ita ipse clarus, potens factus ex libidine sua victoria utitur, plusque sibi ac successoribus spinarum ac potentiae, quam pietatis atque amoris comparavit; sub titulo Christi pro sua magnitudine amplitudineque laboravit &c. Idem fecerunt successores strenuè in bellis sanctis non sanctis per mille fraudes summamque, cui Christianorum myriades vano falsóque praetextu objecerunt, crudelitatem.
units.tr: XXIX. Urban II (called Turbanus by others, because of the disturbances stirred up in the same schism). Aventinus, in book 5 of his Annals, describes his doings thus: "While the parties wish to overcome each other by any means, Urban, by accusing the emperor, stirs up the Christian people; secretly bribing, indulging and promising, he inflames them the more. So he himself, made famous and powerful, uses his victory according to his lust, and has gained for himself and his successors more of thorns and power than of piety and love; under the title of Christ he laboured for his own greatness and extension, etc." The successors did the same vigorously, in wars both holy and unholy, through a thousand frauds and with the greatest cruelty, to which they exposed myriads of Christians under a vain and false pretext.

units.la: XXX. Successoris Paschalis II. non vulgaris fuit erga Henricum V. Imperatorem perfidia, dum hostiâ in duas partes divisâ, atque parti Imperatori exhibita ad testandum, à Christo divisum atque separatum iri, qui foedus rupturus esset, tamen illud impiè rupit.
units.tr: XXX. The treachery of Paschal II toward Henry V, the emperor, was no ordinary one. A host was divided into two parts, and one part was given to the emperor as a pledge that whoever broke the covenant would be divided and separated from Christ. Yet he impiously broke it himself.

units.la: XXXI. Seculo XII. Joannes Sarisburiensis, Episcopus Anglus illustris atque Hadriani IV. P. familiaris, ei ad quaestionem: Quid de me dicunt homines? respondisse fertur: Dicunt, te omnibus Ecclesiae bonis satiari non posse, semper plura appetere & de paupertate queri. Idem in Polycrate: Sedent in Ecclesia Rom. Scriba & Pharisaei ponentes onera importabilia——Pontifex magnus omnibus gravis ac pene intolerabilis est. Ita de bacchantur ejus legati, ac si ad Ecclesiam flagellandam egressus sit Satan à facie Domini——Nocent saepius & in eo sunt Diabolo persimiles, apud eos judicium nihil est, nisi publica merces; quaestum omnem reputant pietatem; Justificant pro muneribus impium, adflictas gravant conscientias, argento & auro mensas ornant & exultant in rebus pessimis. Siquidem pecca a populi comedunt, eis vestiuntur & in eis luxuriantur &c.
units.tr: XXXI. In the twelfth century John of Salisbury, the distinguished English bishop and friend of Pope Adrian IV, is said to have answered his question, "What do people say of me?", thus: "They say that you can never be satisfied with all the goods of the Church, that you always seek more and complain of poverty." The same man, in the Policraticus: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in the Roman Church, laying down intolerable burdens... The great Pontiff is burdensome to all and almost unbearable. So raging are his legates, as if Satan had gone forth from the face of the Lord to scourge the Church... They harm very often and are very like the Devil in this: among them judgment is nothing but public gain; they count all profit as piety; they justify the wicked for bribes, they burden afflicted consciences, they adorn their tables with silver and gold, and they exult in the worst things. Indeed they eat the sins of the people, are clothed by them and live in luxury by them, etc."

units.la: XXXII. Testis quoque de perversitate Pontificum illius temporis Bernhardus: Heu, heu! exclamat Serm. 1. de converf. Paul. Domine, Domine, quia ipsi sunt in persecutione tua ii, qui videntur in Ecclesia tua primatum diligere, gerere principatum——De animarum salute novissima cogitatio. An verò Salvatori animarum gravior ulla esse poterat persecutio? Iniquè agunt & caeteri contrà Christum, multique sunt nostris temporibus Antichristi——Egressa est iniquitas à Senioribus, judicibus, Vicariis tuis, qui videntur regere populum tuum. Sic & alibi luxum & superbiam Cleri Romani reprehendit, Pontificem verò Antichristum vocat, ejusque luxum de Consider. l. 4. fusè proscribit.
units.tr: XXXII. Bernard also bears witness to the perversity of the popes of that time: "Alas, alas!" he cries, in Sermon 1 on the Conversion of Paul. "Lord, Lord, those who seem to love the first place in your Church, and to hold the chief rule, are the very ones who are in persecution of you... The last thought is about the salvation of souls. Indeed, could any persecution be more grievous to the Saviour of souls? Others too act wickedly against Christ, and in our times there are many Antichrists... Iniquity has gone forth from the elders, judges, your vicars, who seem to rule your people." He likewise rebukes elsewhere the luxury and pride of the Roman clergy, and calls the Pope Antichrist, and at length condemns his luxury in the book On Consideration, book 4.

units.la: XXXIII. Sed neque puros Pontifices illius temporis relinquunt versus Bernhardi Morlinensis Cluniacensis l. 3. de contemptu Mundi:
units.tr: XXXIII. But they do not spare even the blameless popes of that time, in the verses of Bernard of Morlaix, a monk of Cluny, from his book On Contempt of the World:

units.la: Fas mihi scribere, fas mihi dicere, Roma peristi,Obruta moenibus, obruta moribus, occubuisti;Urbs ruit inclyta tam modo subdita, quam prius alta,Quo prius altior, hoc modo pressior & labefacta;Fas mihi scribere, fas mihi dicere, Roma ruisti;Sunt tua moenia vociferantia; Roma peristi.
units.tr: It is lawful for me to write, lawful for me to say: Rome, you have perished, / overthrown in your walls, overthrown in your morals, you have fallen. / The renowned city falls, now made as subject as she was once high, / and the higher she was before, so much the more crushed and shaken now. / It is lawful for me to write, lawful for me to say: Rome, you have fallen; / your walls cry out; Rome, you have perished.

units.la: Neque carmen Hildeberti Cenomanensis Episcopi, quod hoc disticho (quod in Lilii Giraldi quinto de Poetis Dialogo Hispani Censores ferre non poterant,) concludit:
units.tr: Nor do they spare the poem of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, which ends with this couplet (which the Spanish censors could not bear, as Lilio Giraldi reports in the fifth dialogue On the Poets):

units.la: Urbs felix, si vel Dominus urbs illa careret,Vel Dominus esset turpe, carere fide!
units.tr: Happy city, if that city lacked its Lord, or if its Lord were shameful to lack faith!

units.la: Neque etiam Dialogus Honorii de Praedest. & lib. arb. in quo Romam Babylonem depingit, ut & aliàs ista appellatio apud veteres frequentissima Pontificum quoque corruptionem ac pessimam vitam involvit.
units.tr: Nor does the Dialogue of Honorius, On Predestination and Free Will, spare them, in which he depicts Rome as Babylon. This name, which was very frequent among the ancients, also implies the corruption and wicked life of the popes.

units.la: XXXIV. Ex eodem Seculo detestandam Alexandri III. superbiam jam supra innuimus; Quâ etiam non minor fuit Antecessoris Adriani IV. Imperatori Friderico ob stapedem sinistrum & praepositum in Epistola nomen irati, & Coelestini III. Coronam Imperialem pede imponentis atque rursus dejicientis, & Inocentii III. qui Matthaeo Parisio supra omnes mortales ambitiosus & superbus, pecuniaq; sititor insatiabilis, & ad omnia scelera pro praemiis datis vel promissis cereus & proclivis audit, Mezeraeo autem mitius partem horum efferenti fuit un Prelat de grand Courage, de rare merite, & qui étant dans la force de son age, agissoit par tout & se mêloit de tout, poussant les choses avec hauteur, quand il trouvoit du foible & de la division. Ambitionem prodidit simúlque perfidiam, dum Philippo Imperatori auxilium sub conditione matrimonii inter Nepotem & Filiam Philippi, dotísque possessione totius ferè Italiae non minoris contrà juramentum antehac Ottoni praestitum promisit. Utque in eo etiam avaritia, sic & eam redoluit, quòd erga Thomam Aquinatem, praesente magna auri signati summa, teste Corn. à Lap. Act. c. III. jactavit, non se quiritare posse cum Petro: Aurum & argentum non habeo; responsum ab Aquinate accipiens, neque etiam dicere posse cum Petro: Surge & ambula. Crudelitatis insuper & impietatis convincit cit eundem institutum ab ipso delegatæ Inquisitionis Officium.
units.tr: XXXIV. From the same century we have already hinted at the detestable pride of Alexander III. Nor was that of his predecessor Adrian IV less, who, toward the emperor Frederick, because of his left stirrup and the name of "irate," placed in an epistle a name... and of Celestine III, who placed the imperial crown under his foot and then threw it down again; and of Innocent III, whom Matthew Paris calls "more ambitious and proud than all mortals, an insatiable thirster after money, and wax-like and prone to every crime for rewards given or promised." Mezeray, who reports part of this more mildly, calls him "a prelate of great courage and rare merit, who, being in the vigour of his age, acted everywhere and meddled in everything, pushing matters with arrogance when he found weakness and division." He revealed his ambition and at the same time his treachery, when he promised aid to the emperor Philip on condition of a marriage between his nephew and Philip's daughter, and the possession as dowry of almost all Italy, no less than what he had earlier promised to Otto under oath. And as he was also greedy, so he showed it in this too: in the presence of a large sum of coined gold, as Cornelius a Lapide reports on Acts chapter 3, he boasted to Thomas Aquinas that he could not say with Peter, "Silver and gold I have not"; and receiving the answer from Aquinas, he could not say with Peter, "Rise and walk." Moreover, the office of the Inquisition, instituted by him and delegated to it, convicts him of cruelty and impiety.

units.la: XXXV. De Pontificum Seculi XIII. aliorum (quos inter etiam Honorius III. Matthæo Parisio Leo feritate, sanguisuga al orum avaritiâ,) injustitia ita apud Fazellum l.9. hist. sic Fridericus Imperator hujus nominis II. queritur: Quousque tandem patientia mea abutetur Pontifex? Quomodo ambitioni sua modum statuet? &c. Ubi enumerat regiones sibi injustè ablatas. Idem apud Petrum de Vineis l.1. op. 1. ita ad Gregorium IX. successorem Honorii scripsit: Iste Pater Patrum, qui dicitur Servus Servorum Dei, omni prorsus exclusâ justitiâ factus est aspis surda, non admittens Romani Principis adlegata, & velut lapis, qui de funda mittitur, sic emisit subitò verbum malum — Petrus relictis omnibus & rete, sequi, Christo vocante, voluit vitæ viam, qui tanquam omnia possidens & nihil habens ad thesaurum cœlestis patriæ semper ardentius aspirabat. Tu enim nihil prorsus habens, omnia autem possidens, quaeris semper, quid devores & deglutias; nec sedare aliquando potest totus mundus Tui ventris ingluviem, quia tibi non sufficit orbis terra. De cœlo, si benerecolis, descendit linteum super Petrum, cui: Surge, macta & manduca, dictum est, dum oraret, qui tamen immunda nolunt manducare, durâ quamvis esset esurie stimulatus. Tu verò ad hoc vivis, ut comedas, in cujus vasis & scyphis aureis inscriptum: Bibo, bibis; cujus verbi præteritum sic frequenter in mensa repetis, & post cibum & quasi raptus ad 3. cœlum Hebraicè & Græcè loqueris & Latinè. Postquam autem impleta vino ventris ingluvies & stomachus usque ad summum, tunc super pennis ventorum astimas te sedere: tunc tibi Romanum subest imperium: tunc adferunt tibi munera Reges terra: tunc vinum mirabiles facit exercitus: tunc tibi serviunt omnes gentium nationes. Ploret igitur mater Ecclesia, quòd Pastor gregis dominici factus est lupus rapax. Fuit ille ipse Gregorius, qui, scribit Urspergensis p. 324. tanquam superbus primo anno Pontificatûs sui cœpit excommunicare Fridericum Imperatorem, pro causis frivolis & falsis, & postpositio omni ordine judiciario &c. Idem etiam Urspergensis ad an. 1228. Pontificiæ perfidiæ & collusionis cum Turca testis est; Papa, inquit, captatâ occasione de absentia Imperatoris, copiosum exercitum destinavit in Apuliam, & terras Imperatoris in servitio Christi demorantis, quod nefandissimum est dicere, abstulit & sibi subegit, & crucesignatos, ne transfretarent, omni studio prohibuit, tam in Apulia, quàm in Lombardia. Quis talia facta rectè considerans, non deploret & testetur, quæ indicium videntur & quoddam portentum & prodigium ruentis Ecclesiæ? Sed & alii de iisdem testantur Papæ cum Turcis contrà Imperatorem rem collusionibus & paratis apud eosdem insidiis, quæ certè non virtutis fuerunt, sed summæ & impietatis & ingratitudinis: Primus enim Fridericus II. Aventino l. 7. p: 672. teste, Papis tanta donavit, ut per ea ipsi nocere potuerint; prout etiam Lehmannus in Chronico Spirensi l. 5. p.92. testatur, omne male illius temporis à Papa manâsse, qui insidiis & bello Fridericum aggressus sit, atque Principes contrà eum instigarit. Fecerunt, judice Aventino l. 7. p. 670. ex ambitione, quæ Germanum Imperium magis florere, quàm ipsis expediret, videre non poterat; Fecerunt maximo cum scandalo: Tunc enim, scribit Matt. Par. p.488. cæpit scandalum oriri per totius mundi latitudinem. Sed & aliquando repulsam tulerunt à Principibus, quos instigârunt, Francis nimirum, Papa ille, qui abdicato Friderico, Robertum Regis fratrem, ut ejus favorem obtineret, constituit, nempe responderunt Franci Matt. Par. p.500. Quo Spiritu vel ausu temerario Papa tantum Principem, quo non est major, imò nec par inter Christianos, non convictum, vel confessum de objectis sibi criminibus exhaeredavit & ab apice Imperiali præcipitavit——De transgressionibus suis, non est hostibus suis fides adhibenda, quorum Papa dignoscitur esse Capitalis. Nobis adhuc insons &c.——tantùm religionis in Papa non invenimus; Imò qui eum debuit promovisse & Deo militantem protexisse, eum conatus est absentem confundere & nequiter supplantare &c. si eum per nos & alios devicerit, omnes Principes conculcabit, sumens cornua jactantia & superbia &c.
units.tr: XXXV. Concerning other popes of the thirteenth century (among whom Honorius III, in Matthew Paris, is called "a lion in ferocity, a leech in the greed of others"), their injustice is described by Fazellus in book 9 of his History. Thus the emperor Frederick II complains: "How long at last will the Pope abuse my patience? How will he set a limit to his ambition? etc." There he lists the regions unjustly taken from him. The same man, in Peter de Vinea, book 1, letter 1, thus wrote to Gregory IX, successor of Honorius: "That father of fathers, who is called servant of the servants of God, has become, with all justice excluded, a deaf asp, not admitting the pleas of the Roman prince, and like a stone thrown from a sling he has suddenly uttered an evil word... Peter, when Christ called him, left all, net and all, and chose to follow the way of life, who, as one possessing all things and having nothing, always aspired more ardently to the treasure of the heavenly homeland. But you, having nothing at all and possessing all things, always seek what you may devour and swallow; nor can the whole world ever satisfy the gluttony of your belly, since the whole earth is not enough for you. From heaven, if you rightly recall, a sheet came down to Peter, to whom it was said: 'Rise, kill and eat,' while he prayed, though he, pressed by hard hunger, did not want to eat unclean things. But you live only to eat, you on whose golden vessels and cups is written: 'I drink, you drink'; this past tense of the word you so often repeat at table, and after food, as if rapt to the third heaven, you speak Hebrew and Greek and Latin. But once the gluttony of your belly and your stomach is filled to the brim with wine, then you think you sit upon the wings of the winds; then the Roman empire is subject to you; then the kings of the earth bring you gifts; then the wonderful army makes wine for you; then all the nations of the peoples serve you. Let mother Church therefore weep, because the shepherd of the Lord's flock has become a ravening wolf." That was the very Gregory who, as Urspergensis writes on page 324, as a proud man began in the first year of his pontificate to excommunicate the emperor Frederick, for frivolous and false causes, and setting aside every judicial order, etc. The same Urspergensis, at the year 1228, is also a witness to papal treachery and collusion with the Turk: "The Pope, seizing the occasion of the emperor's absence, which was made while he remained in the service of Christ (it is most wicked to say it), sent a large army into Apulia and took the emperor's lands and subjected them to himself; and he strove with all zeal to prevent the cross-bearers from crossing over, both in Apulia and in Lombardy. Who, considering such deeds rightly, would not deplore them and bear witness, since they seem to be a sign and a kind of portent and prodigy of a falling Church?" But others too bear witness that the popes, in collusion with the Turks, prepared plots against the emperor, which were certainly not of virtue but of the greatest impiety and ingratitude. For, as Aventinus attests in book 7, page 672, the emperor Frederick II first gave the popes so much that by these gifts they could harm him. Likewise Lehmann in the Speier Chronicle, book 5, page 92, testifies that all the evil of that time flowed from the Pope, who attacked Frederick with plots and war and incited the princes against him. According to Aventinus, book 7, page 670, they acted out of ambition, since they could not bear that the German empire should flourish more than suited them. They acted with the greatest scandal, for, as Matthew Paris writes on page 488, "then a scandal began to arise throughout the whole breadth of the world." But they also sometimes met with rebuff from the princes whom they had incited, namely the French, when that Pope, having deposed Frederick, set up Robert, the king's brother, to gain his favour. The French answered, as Matthew Paris reports on page 500: "With what spirit or what reckless daring has the Pope disinherited so great a prince, than whom there is none greater, nor even an equal among Christians, not convicted nor confessing of the crimes laid against him, and cast him down from the imperial summit? ... Concerning his transgressions, no faith is to be given to his enemies, of whom the Pope is known to be the chief. We find in the Pope as yet no sincerity of religion... Indeed he who ought to have promoted him and protected him while fighting for God, has tried to ruin him in his absence and wickedly supplant him... if he defeats him through us and others, he will trample all princes underfoot, taking up the horns of boasting and pride, etc."

units.la: XXXVI. Innocentium IV. odii erga Imperatorem hæredem, neque commendat fructus Concilii Lugdunensis sub eo habiti illeqnod, qui 3. aut 4. in urbe prostibula invenerant, unum tantùm discedentes post se reliquerunt, sed continuatum ab Orientali porta civitatis usque ad Occidentalem, quod Cardinalis Hugo in Oratione valedictoria felicitatem urbis ex præsentia Papæ declaraturus, teste Matth. Parisiensi in Henr. III. jactare ausus est.
units.tr: XXXVI. Innocent IV's hatred of the heir of the Emperor does not commend him, nor does the outcome of the Council of Lyon held under him, where (as they put it) they found three or four prostitutes in the city, and when they left, only one remained behind; yet the city was continuous from the eastern gate to the western. Cardinal Hugh dared to boast of this in his farewell oration, when he was about to declare the city's happiness from the Pope's presence, as Matthew Paris reports under Henry III.

units.la: Et erat, inquit Author, verbum offensionis in auribus omnium mulierum, quum infinita multitudo mulierum sermoni adsidebat; Neque etiam, quòd de morte Conradi Friderici Filii Veneno procurata lætari atque parricidæ Manfredo favere visus fuit; Neque elogium Antichristi à Roberto Lincolniensi, Viro, ipsis Cardinalibus eum sic excusantibus, pio & vera dixerit; acceptum; Neque duplex illud effatum ab eodem prolatum.
units.tr: And there was, the author says, a word of offence in the ears of all the women, since an infinite crowd of women sat by to hear the discourse. Nor does it commend him that he seemed to rejoice at the death of Conrad, son of Frederick, procured by poison, and to favour the parricide Manfred. Nor is the title "Antichrist" given him by Robert of Lincoln, a man whom the cardinals themselves excused by saying he spoke piously and truly, to be accepted; nor is that twofold saying, uttered by the same man, to be accepted either.

units.la: Ejus avaritia totus non sufficit orbis;
units.tr: His avarice the whole world does not suffice;

units.la: Ejus luxuria meretrix non sufficit omnis. Neque etiam visio, referentibus eodem in Henr. III. p. 868. & Aventino, Cardinali, illâ ipsâ septimanâ, quâ mortuus erat, facta, & in qua matrona honesta Ecclesiam manu tenens Innocentium coram Deo accusavit, quòd eam reddiderit 1. ancillam vilissimam; 2. mensam nummulariorum. 3. fecerit fidem & mores vacillare, sustulerit justitiam; veritatem obumbrárit; Quam accusationem sententia lata excepit: Vade, & pro meritis tuis mercedem ad prehende; Et sic ablatus est. Cui visioni similis etiam de Successore Alexandro IV. narratur, Neque etiam eum commendat, quòd moriens ad circumstantes dixit: Quid lacrymas funditis? Nonne omnes divites atque bene nummatos relinquo? Quid vultis amplius? Neque tandem elogium à dicto successore apud Matth. Par. p. 875. datum venditoris Ecclesiarum. Quemadmodum neque Alexandri IV. Successorem Clementem IV. consilium, quod in MSC. Italico vocatur empio e men Christiano, impium & minùs Christianum de nece Conradini omnibus nota commendat.
units.tr: His luxury, every harlot does not suffice. Nor does the vision commend him, as related by the same author under Henry III, p. 868, and by Aventinus, a cardinal, which occurred in the very week in which he died. In it an honest matron, holding the Church by the hand, accused Innocent before God because he had made her 1. a most vile maidservant; 2. a moneychangers' table; 3. had made faith and morals waver, had removed justice, had overshadowed truth. To this accusation a sentence was given in reply: Go, and take your wages for your deserts. And so he was taken away. A vision similar to this is also told of his successor, Alexander IV. Nor does he commend himself by saying, as he was dying, to those standing about: Why do you shed tears? Do I not leave behind all the rich and well-moneyed? What more do you want? Nor finally does the epithet given to his successor in Matthew Paris, p. 875, seller of churches, commend him. Nor does Clement IV, successor of Alexander IV, commend himself by his counsel, called in an Italian manuscript impious and less Christian, concerning the killing of Conradin, which is known to everyone.

units.la: XXXVII. Johannis XX. al. XXI. Plat. XXII. refert hic morum inaequalitatem & inverecundiam.
units.tr: XXXVII. John XX, or XXI, Platina XXII: here his inconsistency and shamelessness of character are noted.

units.la: Idem sibi, referente ex Stella & Valerio Delrione l. 4 c. 3. q. 2. longam vitam Astrologia superstitiosa confisus, fato spem non implente, promisit. De successore Nicolao III. scribit Platina, suos ita eum amâsse, ut aliunde raperet, quod eis daret &c. Imò & regna rapere voluit, in animo habens duos ex sua familia Reges creare, in Hetruriâ alterum alterum in Longobardia, indice Macchiavello in Historia Florentina.
units.tr: The same man, as reported from Stella and Valerius Delrio, bk. 4, ch. 3, q. 2, trusting in superstitious astrology for a long life, promised himself a long life, but fate did not fulfil his hope. Of his successor Nicholas III, Platina writes that his own people loved him so much that he snatched from elsewhere what he might give them, etc. Indeed he wanted to seize kingdoms too, intending to make two kings from his own family, one in Etruria and the other in Lombardy, as Machiavelli indicates in his Florentine History.

units.la: XXXVIII. De hujus successore Martino IV. referunt alii,
units.tr: XXXVIII. Concerning his successor, Martin IV, others report:

units.la: eum licet minùs antecessori aequum, ejus tamen concubinam retinuisse, atque, ne quod illi contigerat, sibi quoque ursinae speciei infantem pareret, omnia Ursinorum insignia è palatio sustulisse. De eodem Nicolaus Biberacensis Theologus Erfordiensis testatur, quòd, cùm adhuc puer Romae esset, Martinus ipso Sodomiacè abuti voluerit. Eidem in libro occultus Epitaphium sequens posuit: Hic jacet ante chorum submersor Teutonicorum, Pastor Martinus, extrà qui totus ovinus, Et lupus introrsus, cui nulla redemptio prorsus; Sed sit ad inferna detrusus ab arce superna.
units.tr: that he, though less fair than his predecessor, kept his concubine, and, so that she might bear him an infant of the Ursine stock as had happened to him, he removed all the Orsini insignia from the palace. Of the same man, Nicholas of Biberach, an Erfurt theologian, testifies that when he was still a boy in Rome, Martin wanted to abuse him sodomitically. In his book Occultus he placed the following epitaph on him: Here lies before the choir the drowner of the Teutons, Shepherd Martin, outwardly all sheep, and inwardly a wolf, for whom there is utterly no redemption; but let him be thrust down to hell from the high citadel.

units.la: Submersorem Teutonicorum vocat, saepiùs Germaniae submersionem optare solitum.
units.tr: He calls him drowner of the Teutons, since he was often accustomed to wish for the drowning of Germany.

units.la: XXXIX. Cùm in eodem Seculo decimo tertio Germanus Constantinopolitanus ad communionem, vel potiùs ad subjectionem invitaretur, rescripsisse fertur: Mentibus nostris scrupulum generat offendiculi, quòd terrenis tantùm inhiantes possessionibus undecunque poteßis abradere, aurum & argentum congregatis, discipulos tamen ejus esse velle dicitis, qui dixit: Aurum & argentum non habeo. Regna vobis tributo subjicitis——actibus dedocetis, quod ore praedicatis. Moderetur vos temperantia, ut sitis nobis & omni mundo exemplum & exemplar.
units.tr: XXXIX. When in the same thirteenth century the Constantinopolitan Germanus was invited to communion, or rather to submission, he is said to have replied: It causes a stumbling-block to our minds that you, gaping only after earthly possessions and scraping together gold and silver from wherever you can, yet want to be disciples of him who said: I have no gold or silver. You subject kingdoms to tribute; you unteach by your deeds what you proclaim with your mouths. May temperance moderate you, so that you may be an example and model to us and to the whole world.

units.la: XL. Pii etiam non fuerunt Pontifices, qui illo ipso Seculo pessimis suis actionibus Ferdinando Hispaniae Regi de veritate Religionis Christianae dubitandi occasionem praebuerunt. Impius planè fuit Bonifacius VIII. de quo jam supra; Magna porrò ingratitudinis eum accusat Platina in Caelest. V. saevitiam, superbiam atque crudelitatem idem memorat, vitaeque ipsius historiam ita claudit: Moritur autem hoc modo Bonifacius ille, qui Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus, nationibus, populis terrorem potiùs quàm religionem injicere conabatur, aurum undique conquisitum, plùs, quàm dici potest, sitiens. Discant itaque hujus exemplo Principes omnes tam religiosi, quàm saeculares praeesse Clero & populo non superbè & contumeliosè, ut hic, de quo loquimur, sed sanctè & modestè, ut Christus Rex noster, ejúsque discipuli & veri imitatores: & malint amari, quàm timeri, unde tyrannorum pernicies meritò oriri solet. Sunt qui scribant, hunc quoque discordias inter Italos aluisse: maximè verò inter Genuenses & Venetos &c. Scribit etiam Stella, & insuper, quòd arrogantissimus homo omnes ferè contemnere caeperit. Notum est Epitaphium:
units.tr: XL. There were also no pious Pontiffs who, in that same century, by their wicked actions gave King Ferdinand of Spain occasion to doubt the truth of the Christian religion. Boniface VIII was clearly impious, as already noted above. Platina accuses him of great ingratitude towards Celestine V, and recalls his savagery, pride and cruelty, and closes the account of his life thus: Boniface died in this way, who tried to strike terror rather than religion into emperors, kings, princes, nations and peoples, thirsting for gold gathered from everywhere more than can be said. Let all princes, religious as well as secular, learn from his example to rule clergy and people not haughtily and insolently, as he did, but holily and modestly, as Christ our King and his disciples and true imitators did; and let them prefer to be loved rather than feared, whence the ruin of tyrants is usually rightly derived. There are those who write that he also fed discords among the Italians, especially between the Genoese and the Venetians, etc. Stella also writes, and moreover that the most arrogant man began to scorn nearly everyone. The epitaph is well known:

units.la: Intravit ut vulpes, regnavit ut Leo, mortuus ut Canis.
units.tr: He entered like a fox, reigned like a lion, died like a dog.

units.la: Quod concentaneum est verbis Joachimi Abbatis, judicio Cardinalis Bonae, Spiritûs Prophetici Viri, sic eum in vaticiniis suis compellantis: Fraudulenter intrâsti, potenter regnâsti, gemens morieris.
units.tr: This agrees with the words of Joachim the Abbot, in the judgment of Cardinal Bona a prophetic man of the Spirit, addressing him thus in his prophecies: You entered fraudulently, you reigned powerfully, you will die groaning.

units.la: XLI. Seculi XIV. Pontifex Benedictus XII. corruptor faeminini sexûs, concubinarius, Petrarchae sororem à fratre Petrarchae, ipso postulatum, conjunctum licèt cum promissione Pilei Cardinalitii, abominante, argento emit ad impudicitiam. Qualis fuerit, etiam ex Epitaphio, quod Bzovius ad an. 1342. n. 2. habet & à nonnullis Benedicto XI. tribuitur, liquere potest. Ita sonat:
units.tr: XLI. In the fourteenth century, Pope Benedict XII, a corrupter of the female sex and a whoremonger, bought from Petrarch's brother, who himself requested it, Petrarch's sister, though she was joined in marriage, for the purpose of lewdness, with the promise of a cardinal's hat, and with silver, while the brother abhorred it. What sort of man he was can also be made clear from the epitaph which Bzovius has at the year 1342, no. 2, and which some attribute to Benedict XI. It runs thus:

units.la: Hic situs est Nero, Laicis mors, vipera Clero,Dezius à vero, cupa repleta mero.
units.tr: Here lies Nero, death to laymen, viper to clergy, Dezius far from the truth, a cask filled with wine.

units.la: XLII. De Paparum eodem seculo humilitate testantur status Imperii, qui, cùm post mortem Ludovici Imperatoris absolvendi essent, sed sub istis Conditionibus, ut agnoscant, Papam non posse deponi ab Imperatore, & contrarium docentes esse haereticos; se Imperatori obedire haud posse nisi à Papa confirmato; noluerunt, sed reclamárunt: Usque adeóne servus ille servorum fastu libidinéque dominandi fuerit, insanit, atque in praeceps abit, ut omnium saevissimorum tyrannorum, quos unquam fuisse legimus, superbiam vincere propalam perfricatâ fronte contendat? XLIII. Clem. ntem V. neque calumniae & crudelitas contrà Templarios, neque venenicidium Henrici Luzelburgensis, qui juxta Chronicon Archiepiscoporum Magdeburgensium pius erat in moribus, probus in armis, prosequens jura Imperii; valde commendant; Joannis XXII. Plat. XXIII. in Schismate qualitates enarravimus, quem etiam ad vivum descriptum in Imperatoris Ludovici edicto Comitiorum Reginoburgensium consensu vulgato sistit Aventinus, ubi Joannes ille saevissimi lupi, sanguinem Christianorum sitientis, discordiae seditionumque semina serentis, auro corrumpentis, Antichristi, Sathanae, Haeresiarchae &c. elogiis ornatur. XLIV. Urbanus VI. (cujus mores jam supra ex parte descripsimus) tam superbus fuit, ut Ducem Brunsuicensem adgeniculantem coram se jussu suo viderit, donec à Cardinale quodam dictum: Sanctissime Pater, tempus est bibendi. De eodem Theodoricus à Niem testatur, ante eum crudeliorem atque sanguinem magis sitientem Papam nullum fuisse, Deúmque crudelem malitiam in ipso & familia funditus eversa ultum esse. Eum etiam tam avarum nummorum, sed prodigum indulgentiarum fuisse referunt, ut purgatorium planè evacuare visus sit; Lucro quidem suo, cùm ex sola Anglia exiguo temporis spatio 2500000. libras attraxerit. Addimus ex MSC. Italico jam aliquoties citato, quòd ibi ad probandum, Papas noluisse Reges Neapolitanos, qui non essent eorum mancipia, notatur, quanti mali inventor fuerit contrà Regem antehac sibi amicissimum, ea sola de causa, quòd non potuerit divitem familia sua statum obtinere, hinc indignus declaratus, incapax & usurpator Regni maledictus, excommunicatus, indignus & Paradiso privandus. XLV. Aemulo autem Urbani Clementi VII. Bzovius ad an. 1318. n. 8. ex Nicolao de Clemangis sequens testimonium perhibet: Quid Clemente nostro, quoad vixit, miserabilius? Qui ita se servum Galli-
units.tr: XLII. The states of the Empire bear witness to the humility of the Popes of the same century. When, after the death of Emperor Louis, they were to be absolved, but on these conditions, that they acknowledge the Pope cannot be deposed by the Emperor, and that those teaching the contrary are heretics, and that they could not obey the Emperor unless confirmed by the Pope, they refused and protested: Has that servant of servants gone so far in pride and lust for domination, has he so lost his mind and rushes headlong, that he openly strives with brazen face to surpass the arrogance of all the most savage tyrants we have ever read of? XLIII. Neither the calumny and cruelty against the Templars nor the poisoning of Henry of Luxemburg, who, according to the Chronicle of the Archbishops of Magdeburg, was pious in morals, upright in arms, and pursued the rights of the Empire, greatly commend Clement V. We have described the qualities of John XXII in the Schism (Platina XXIII). Aventinus also portrays him to the life, in the edict of Emperor Louis published with the consent of the Diet of Regensburg, where that John is adorned with the titles of the most savage wolf, thirsting for Christian blood, sowing seeds of discord and sedition, corrupting with gold, Antichrist, Satan, heresiarch, etc. XLIV. Urban VI (whose morals we have partly described above) was so proud that he saw the Duke of Brunswick kneeling before him at his command, until a certain cardinal said: Most holy Father, it is time to drink. Of the same man, Theodoric of Niem testifies that there was no Pope before him more cruel or more thirsty for blood, and that God punished his cruel malice by utterly overthrowing him and his family. They also report that he was so greedy for money, yet so prodigal with indulgences, that he seemed to empty purgatory altogether, though for his own profit, since in a short space of time he drew 2,500,000 pounds from England alone. We add from the Italian manuscript already cited several times that there it is noted, to show that the Popes did not want Neapolitan kings who were not their creatures, how much evil the author was against the king, once his dearest friend, for this sole reason, that he could not obtain a rich state for his family; hence declared unworthy, incapable, a usurper of the kingdom, cursed, excommunicated, unworthy, and to be deprived of Paradise. XLV. Bzovius, at the year 1318, no. 8, from Nicholas of Clamanges, gives the following testimony concerning Urban's rival, Clement VII: What was more wretched than our Clement, as long as he lived? He had made himself so much a slave to the French princes

units.la: cipiis cis Principibus adjecerat——juvenibus nitidis & elegantibus, quorum maximè consortio gaudebat, singulos ferè vacantes Episcopatus caterásque præcipuas dignitates impendebat &c.
units.tr: ...the French princes. To young men of fashion and elegance, in whose company he took especial delight, he gave almost every vacant bishopric and the other chief dignities, and so on.

units.la: XLVI. Sub Bonifacio IX. teste Platina, multa crimina per Simoniacam pravitatem committebantur, petentibus contrà jus fasque omnia tum fratribus, tum cognatis: quorum magna multitudo quæstus gratiâ Romam venerat. Indulgentia verò & quidem plenaria ita passim vendebantur, ut jam vilesceret Clavium & Litterarum Apostolicarum authoritas. Quod & Cranzius l. 2. c. 12. ita confirmat: Gratias & indulgentias fecit inauditas, & quàm facilè dedit, tam leviter revocavit; fabulas excitans in orbe Christiano, quod auro expleri non posset. Et Paulus Langius in Chronico: Erat pecuniæ avidus, ad quam colligendam plures Legatos per diversas mundi partes ad negotiandum cum indulgentiis misit: fuit maximus Simoniacus & Simoniæ cultores multis dignitatibus sublimavit &c. Juxta excerpta ex vetustioribus Authoribus Bibl. Univers. T. XI. p. 16. 17. 18. 243. 244. semper plùs offerenti Beneficia vendidit, licèt jam alii vendita, nec dubium unquam erat de signatura obtinenda, aut litterarum expeditione facienda, si impetrans non defecit in pecunia expendenda, qui plùs solvit Papæ, Episcopatum obtinuit; Ipse etiam sæpe dicebat, utinam non adipisceatur possessionem Ecclesiæ aut Monasterii, ad quod eum promovi, ut iterum de alio, sicque recentes pecunias extorqueret; Ecclesiasticos spoliabat idem adhuc in agone constitutos, gratias & indulgentias revocabat, tantùm ut de novo emantur, dispensabat insuper non tantum contrà Apostolum, sed etiam contra Evangelium. Nam Ladislao Regi Siciliæ, seu Napolis, indulsit, quòd ipse abdicatâ à se uxore sua legitima, jam multis annis cum eo commorante aliam superinduxit, uxorem. Ejusdem animum unicè divitiis corradendis intentum Il Nipot. p. 2. p. 378. similiter describit, & quòd præsentibus frui amaverit, ab exactoribus singulis noctibus usque ad medias sæpè expectando, argentum diei præcedentis exegerit, somnum aliàs haud magis capere gnarus, quàm si omnia perdidisset. Atque illuc etiam spectant ejusdem proverbia ibidem expòsita; che amava meglia un picciol pesce melle mani, che un gran Delfino in alto mare; se plùs amare parvum in manibus piscem, quam magnum in mari Delfinum. Item; ch'era meglio l'ovo la matina, che la Gallina la sera; Id est; Ovum mane præstare Gallina, quæ sub vesperam veniat.
units.tr: XLVI. Under Boniface IX, according to Platina, many crimes were committed through simoniacal corruption. Everyone, whether brothers or kinsmen, sought benefices contrary to law and right, and a great crowd of them came to Rome for profit. Indulgences, and plenary ones at that, were sold everywhere, so that the authority of the keys and of the apostolic letters grew cheap. Cranzius confirms this in book 2, chapter 12: "He granted unheard-of graces and indulgences, and gave them so easily, and revoked them just as lightly, spreading fables throughout the Christian world that could not be satisfied with gold." Paulus Langius also says in his Chronicle: "He was greedy for money, and to collect it he sent many legates through various parts of the world to trade in indulgences. He was a great simoniac and raised the promoters of simony to many dignities, etc." According to excerpts from older authors in the Bibliotheca Universalis, vol. 11, pp. 16, 17, 18, 243, 244, he always sold benefices to the highest bidder, even when they had already been sold to someone else. There was never any doubt about obtaining a signature or having letters expedited, provided the applicant did not run short of money: whoever paid the Pope most obtained the bishopric. He himself often said, "I hope the candidate does not obtain possession of the church or monastery to which I have promoted him, so that I can sell it again to someone else and extort fresh money." He also plundered ecclesiastics even when they lay dying, revoked graces and indulgences merely so that they could be bought again, and dispensed not only contrary to the Apostle but also contrary to the Gospel. For he granted King Ladislaus of Sicily, or Naples, a dispensation to put away his lawful wife, with whom he had lived for many years, and take another wife in her place. The same author, in Il Nipote, part 2, p. 378, describes the man's mind as wholly set on amassing wealth, and says that he loved to enjoy the present, so that he exacted the previous day's money from his collectors, often waiting until midnight, and knew no more how to sleep than if he had lost everything. To this also refer his proverbs, set out there: "He loved a small fish in the hand better than a great dolphin in the deep sea," and "An egg in the morning was better than a hen in the evening."

units.la: XLVII.
