Eodem Seculo Nicolaus Orem, vir doctus, in Gallia, & Papam vehementer aliàs impugnavit, & nomine Lucifera epistoepistolam, quâ gratias pro præstitis sibi officiis agens introducebatur, conscripsit atque Avignonensi Palatio teste Alberto Argentinensi, affigi curavit, quæ apud Wolf. T. I. Lect. Mem. Cent. XIV. p. 654. legi potest.
units.tr: XLVII. In the same century Nicolaus Orem, a learned man in France, attacked the Pope with great vehemence on other grounds. Under the name Lucifer he wrote a letter in which Lucifer is introduced giving thanks for services rendered to him, and he saw to it that it was posted on the palace at Avignon, as Albert of Strasbourg testifies. It can be read in Wolf, vol. 1, Lectionum Memorabilium, century 14, p. 654.

units.la: XLVIII. Eodem Seculo vixit Theodoricus Uric vel Urias, Monachus Augustinianus, & juxta Wolfium, Episcopus in Croatia, cujus sequentes sunt apud Langium in Chronico Citizensi Versus:
units.tr: XLVIII. In the same century lived Theodoricus Uric, or Urias, an Augustinian monk, and, according to Wolf, a bishop in Croatia. The following verses of his are quoted by Langius in the Citizen Chronicle:

units.la: Papa stupor mundi cecidit, secúmque ruere Cœlica templa Dei, membra simúlque caput. Papa dolor, mundíque pudor per crebra patescit Crimina, terrarum notus ubique viris. Heu! Simon regnat, per munera quæque reguntur, Judiciúmque pium gaza nefanda vetat. Curia Papalis fovet omnia scandala mundi, Delubra sacra facit perfiditate forum. Ordo sacer, baptisma Sacrum cum Chrismate Sacro Venduntur turpi conditione fori. Dives honoratur, pauper contemnitur, atque Qui dare plura valet munera, gratus erit. Aurea quæ quondam fuit, hinc argentea Papæ Curia procedit deteriore modo. Ferrea facta de hinc dura cervice quievit, Tempore non modico sed modo facta lutum. Postque lutum, quid deterius solet esse? Recordor Stercus; & in tali curia tota sedet.
units.tr: Pope, the wonder of the world, has fallen, and with him the heavenly temples of God fall too, the members and the head together. The Pope is a grief, and the shame of the world is shown through frequent crimes, known to men everywhere on earth. Alas! Simon reigns; all things are ruled by bribes, and accursed treasure bars righteous judgment. The Papal Court fosters every scandal in the world and turns the sacred shrines into a marketplace of perfidy. Holy orders, holy baptism, and holy chrism are sold on the shameful terms of the marketplace. The rich are honoured, the poor despised, and whoever can give the most gifts will be the favourite. The Papal Court, once golden, now proceeds in silver, and in a worse manner. Then it turned to iron and rested in a hard neck; not for a short time, but now it has become mud. And after mud, what is worse? I recall: dung; and in such a court all of them sit.

units.la: XLIX. Petrarcha Avignonem, ubi, vi promissionis à Clemente V. Galliæ Regi, ut votis Gallorum etiam eligi posset, factæ, ad tempus Papæ (ingenti Galliæ utilitate, si juxta Mezeræum dans lalvie de Philippe le Bel inde accepit trois grandes desordres, la Simonie &c. Tria magna vitia, Simoniam, luxús & impietatis filiam, litigandi consuetudinem, & execrabile crimen, quod vel nominare nefas; & certo, Papæ Curiam Sanctam, ipsum Sanctitatem suam esse, indicio) sedebant, vocat Babylonem ad Rhodanum, exiguam moenibus, magnam vitiis, matrem scortationum, sedem avaritiæ, Judam cum 30. argenteis ibi gratum futurum, pauperi Christo januam clausum iri.
units.tr: XLIX. Petrarch, when the Papal court sat at Avignon, by virtue of the promise made by Clement V to the King of France that he could also be elected according to the wishes of the French, called it, for a time, Babylon on the Rhone (to the great advantage of France, if we may trust Mézeray, in the life of Philip the Fair, who took from it three great disorders, simony, etc.: three great vices, simony, the daughter of luxury and impiety, the custom of litigation, and an execrable crime which it is wrong even to name; and, surely, the Holy Court of the Pope, which is itself his holiness, is the sign). He calls it a small place in walls but great in vices, a mother of harlotries, a seat of avarice, where Judas with his thirty pieces of silver would be welcome, and where the door would be shut against poor Christ.

units.la: Et Epist. XIV. T. 2: Novi expertus, quòd ibi nulla sit pietas, nulla charitas, nulla fides, nulla Dei reverentia, nullus timor, nihil sancti, nihil justi, nihil aqui; aequi, nihil pensi, nihil denique vel humani. Amor, pudor, decor, Candor inde exulant, de veritate quidem sileo; Nam quis unquam vero locus, ubi omnia mendacium plena sunt, aer, terra, domus, turres, vici, atria, porticus, vestibula, aula &c. Pontificum sedes? In Epistola autem XVI. de universa Pontificis aula ita pronuntiat: In Babylone Regno avaritia futura vita spes inanis quaedam fabula: & quae de inferis narrantur, fabulosa omnia: Et resurrectio carnis, & mundi finis, & Christus ad judicium venturus, inter nanias habentur. Et Epist. IX. Una spes salutis in auro esset, auro placaretur Rex ferus, auro immane monstrum vinceretur, auro trifis janitor emolliretur, auro caelum panderetur, auro Christus venderetur.
units.tr: And in Epistle 14 of volume 2: I have learned by experience that there is no piety there, no charity, no faith, no reverence for God, no fear, nothing holy, nothing just, nothing equitable, nothing considered, nothing finally even human. Love, shame, grace, and candour are banished from there. Of the truth I say nothing; for what place is there where truth is ever found, when everything, air, earth, houses, towers, villages, courts, porticoes, vestibules, halls, etc., is full of lies, the seat of the Popes? In Epistle 16 he pronounces thus on the whole papal court: In Babylon, avarice reigns; hope of a future life is some empty fable; and what is told about the underworld is all fabulous. The resurrection of the flesh, the end of the world, and Christ's coming to judgment are regarded as nonsense. And in Epistle 9: Hope of salvation would lie only in gold; by gold a ferocious king would be appeased, by gold a monstrous beast would be overcome, by gold a gloomy doorkeeper would be softened, by gold heaven would be opened, by gold Christ would be sold.

units.la: L. Eodem Seculo Brigitta à Bonifacio IX. in Catalogum Sanctarum adscripta, docuit; Papam commutasse X. praecepta in unum: Da argentum; Et cum clamare deberet: Ascendite ut quietem inveniatis pro animabus vestris, clamare: Ascendite & videte gloriam atque pompam meam, & evacuate crumenas vestras, ut inveniatis perniciem pro animabus vestris. Eadem in Revelationibus suis maturo (inquit Cardinalis Bona in Notitia Scriptorum) Theologorum judicio approbatis Pontificem Clementem VI. vocat; animarum interfectorem, ovium Jesu Christi dispersorem & laceratorem, abominabiliorem Judaeis, inimiciorem Juda, injustiorem Pilato, pejorem Lucifero, sedem ejus demergendam esse, sicut lapidem ponderosum: Affectores suos arsuros in igne sulphureo & inextinguibili. De Gregorio IX. vero Christus ipse apud eandem ita judicat; Gregorius Papa est similis Paraclyto, qui non movet manus ad operandum, nec pedes ad ambulandum. Tenet eum quasi impeditum immoderatus amor sanguinis sui & frigus tepiditatis ad me.
units.tr: L. In the same century Bridget, enrolled among the saints by Boniface IX, taught that the Pope had reduced the ten commandments to one: Give money. And where he ought to cry out, "Come up, that you may find rest for your souls," he cried, "Come up and see my glory and my pomp, and empty your purses, that you may find destruction for your souls." In her Revelations, approved by the mature judgment of theologians (as Cardinal Bona says in his Notice of Writers), she calls Pope Clement VI a murderer of souls, a scatterer and mangler of the sheep of Jesus Christ, more abominable than the Jews, more hostile than Judas, more unjust than Pilate, worse than Lucifer; his seat is to be sunk like a heavy stone, and his followers will burn in sulphurous and unquenchable fire. But of Gregory IX Christ himself judges thus in the same book: Gregory the Pope is like the Paraclete, who does not move his hands to work or his feet to walk. An immoderate love for his own blood and the cold lukewarmness toward me hold him as if he were hindered.

units.la: LI. Seculum XV. si inspiciamus; In eo occurrit Gregorius XII. de quo Scriptum affixum, in quo dictum, Diabolum eum à juramento absolvisse, quod 4. ex cognatis ad Cardinalitiam dignitatem evehendo non observarat. De eodem, ut & de Anti-Papa Petro de Luna, simul ob pervicacem ambitionem & collusionem depositis ita Theodoricus à Niem l. 3. scripsit: Si quis fraudes, machinationes Errorii (Gregorium intelligit) & Petri per singula describere vellet, vix charta & atramentum huic sufficerent. Veruntamen clarum est, quod cauteriatas habent suas conscientias, dicentes, se esse simplices, cum sint astutia Diabolica impleti. Et pro opere pietatis dixerunt, & dicunt, se utique voluisse & velle unionem facere, quod tamen in eorum cordibus non habebant nec habent. Quid igitur erit in tam lamentabili Schismate finaliter? De his duobus Senioribus Babylonis, Petro & Errorio, major progressa gressa est iniquitas & passim progreditur in universam terram, quàm unquam ante nostra tempora ab aliquibus de Papatu contendentibus emanavit—Fides Catholica obnubilatur. Omnis Religio naufr gium patitur, bella & alia calamitates multæ pullulant, Dei timor & hominum verecundia & & virtutes à plerisque regnantibus——in longum abierunt——in universali Ecclesia à capite usque ad plantam pedis non est sanitas. Sed neque Epitaphium Uladislai Hungariæ Regis hujus Seculi Pontifices commendat ita sonans: Romulidæ Cannas, ego Varnam clade notavi; Discite mortales non temerare fidem. Me nisi Pontifices jussissent rumpere fœdus, Non ferrent Scythicum Pannonis ora jugum.
units.tr: LI. If we look at the fifteenth century, Gregory XII appears, of whom a written notice was posted, saying that the devil had released him from the oath by which he had not kept his promise to raise four of his kinsmen to the cardinalate. Theodoric of Niem, book 3, wrote of him, and of the antipope Peter de Luna, who were deposed together for stubborn ambition and collusion, thus: If anyone wished to describe in detail the frauds and machinations of Errorius (he means Gregory) and Peter, paper and ink would hardly suffice. Yet it is clear that they have cauterised consciences, saying that they are simple, when they are full of diabolical cunning. And they have said, and still say, that for the sake of piety they wanted, and want, to effect union, which nevertheless they neither had nor have in their hearts. What, then, will be the final outcome of so lamentable a schism? Of these two elders of Babylon, Peter and Errorius, a greater iniquity has advanced and spreads everywhere over the whole earth than ever arose before our times from any of those who contended for the papacy. The Catholic faith is obscured. All religion suffers shipwreck; wars and other calamities multiply; the fear of God and the modesty of men, and the virtues of most rulers, have gone away for a long time; in the universal Church, from head to sole of the foot, there is no health. Nor does the epitaph of Uladislaus, King of Hungary, of this century, commend the Popes, reading thus: Romulids, I marked Cannae with defeat, I marked Varna with slaughter. Mortals, learn not to violate the faith. Unless the Popes had ordered me to break the covenant, the Pannonian would not have borne the Scythian yoke.

units.la: Neque quod Panormitanus de Alphonso Prudente, Rege Arragoniæ & Siciliæ l. de factis & dictis Alfonsi habet: Non jam amplius insulas illas incolunt Harpyæ, uti Poeta fabulati sunt, sed ex insulis migrârunt in Curiam Romanam, ibique domicilium jam constituerunt.
units.tr: Nor should I omit what Panormitanus says of Alfonso the Prudent, King of Aragon and Sicily, in his book on the deeds and sayings of Alfonso: The Harpies no longer inhabit those islands, as the poets have fabled; they have migrated from the islands to the Roman Curia and have there already established their home.

units.la: LII. Joannis XXIII. Plat. XXIV. virtutes, ubi Schisma, quod continuavit, exposuimus. De Eugenio IV. etiam, ubi de Schismatibus, egimus. Idem apud Stellam præter Pontificis dignitatem mirum in modum bella amâsse fertur. Secundus Successor Calixtus III. immensas argenti summas & ipse sub belli sancti prætextu ad suum successorumque luxum immensum corrasse legitur. Successori proximo Pio II. sequens ex vetusto quodam codice Joh. Baleus de Rom. Pont. Actis l. 6. Epitaphium collocavit: Frigida membra Pii retinet lapis iste loquacis, Qui pacem moriens attulit Italiæ. Summe Deus, quantum mortalibus alme dedisti, Fulmine cùm tetigit hoc caput æq̃ a manus? Vendiderat pretio gentes, & crimina multa Virtutis specie gesserat ille Pius. Impius hic fuerat, quamvis sub nomine Pulchro, Crediderit falsis posse juvare fidem. Nunc fidi comites, sceleratáque turba clientum Ingenuere Pium: nam scelus orbis erat.
units.tr: LII. We have set out the vices of John XXIII in Plat. XXIV, where we discussed the schism he continued. We have also dealt with Eugenius IV, where we discussed the schisms. In addition to the dignity of the Pontiff, he is said to have loved wars in a remarkable way, as Stella reports. Calixtus III, the second successor, is also read to have amassed, under the pretext of a holy war, immense sums of silver for his own and his successors' immense luxury. To the next successor, Pius II, John Bale in On the Acts of the Roman Pontiffs, book 6, attributes the following epitaph, taken from an old codex: This stone holds the cold limbs of Pius, the talkative one, who brought peace to Italy as he died. Highest God, how much you gave to mortals, when this head was struck by a thunderbolt from your hand! He had sold nations for a price and committed many crimes, and under the appearance of virtue he had carried on as "Pius." He was impious, though under a fair name, and he believed he could support false faith with lies. Now his faithful companions and a wicked crowd of clients have made him "Pious," for his crime was the world's.

units.la: Unâ cum Conclusione: Impius hic situs est, crudelis, raptor, iniquus, Æneas fatua, quem genuere Sena.
units.tr: Together with the conclusion: Here lies the impious man, cruel, a robber, unjust, a foolish Aeneas, whom Siena produced.

units.la: Neque crimen simplex, sed genium insuper in excusando scorta-tionis rionis peccato satis improbum Epist. XV. ad Patrem prodidit ipse metu, ita scribens: Ait dolere te meum crimen, quòd ex peccato genueram filium. Nescio, quam de me tibi finxeris opinionem. Certè nec lapideum, nec ferreum genuisti filium, cùm esses tu carneus. Scis, qualis tu gallus fueris. At nec ego castratus sum, nec ex frigidorum numero. Nec sum hypocrita; ut videri bonus, quàm esse malim. Fateor ingenuè meum erratum, quia nec sanctior sum Davide Rege, nec Salomone sapientior. Antiquum & vetus est delictum, nescio quis eo careat. Late patet haec pestis, (si pestis est, naturalibus uti) quamquam non video, cùm natura, quae nihil perperam operatur, omnibus ingenuerit animantibus hunc appetitum, ut genus continuaretur humanum. En voti coelibatûs observationem! En egregium futurum legis illius latorem, qui tamen nihil horum, quò minus fieret, obstitit.
units.tr: Nor did he show only a simple sin, but in excusing his fornication, a sin quite shameful in its own right, he revealed a disposition of his own, writing himself in Letter XV to his Father, as follows: You say that you grieve over my sin, because I begot a son out of sin. I do not know what opinion of me you have imagined. Surely you did not beget a stone or iron son, since you yourself were of flesh. You know what sort of cock you were. But I too am not castrated, nor one of the cold men. Nor am I a hypocrite, wanting to seem good rather than to be so. I frankly confess my error, since I am neither holier than King David nor wiser than Solomon. The fault is ancient and old; I do not know who is free of it. This plague spreads widely (if it is a plague, to use natural things), although I do not see why nature, which does nothing amiss, should have implanted this appetite in all living creatures, so that the human race might be continued. Behold the observance of the vow of celibacy! Behold the distinguished future proposer of that law, who yet did nothing to prevent these things from happening.

units.la: LIII. De Pauli II. (qui apud Platinam Iacrymandi etiam dono Papatum consecutus dicitur;) ubi de vestibus Cardinalitiis, actum est; Exercita autem ab eo erga multos crudelitas, apud Platinam, expertum Robertum, videri potest. Genebrardus etiam virtutis inimicum vocat. Vanitatem ejus maximam digne reprehensam videat, qui volet in Epistola Jacobi Papiensis, Cardinalis apud Doctiss. Launojum Epist. p. IV. ep. penult. Neque certè in eo laudem meretur, quòd in Bulla Leonis X. quae l. VII. Decretalium habetur, Author Montium pietatis, potiùs impietatis, perhibetur, ut apud Platinam alias quoque Simoniacus; dignitatumque omnium avarus, posthabitis bonis qualitatibus, venditor.
units.tr: LIII. Concerning Paul II (who, according to Platina, is said to have obtained the papacy even by the gift of tears): we have treated the cardinals' vestments there. His cruelty exercised against many people, as shown in Platina, may be seen in the case of Robert, who was tested. Genebrard even calls him an enemy of virtue. Whoever wishes to see his great vanity, rightly censured, may consult the letter of James of Pavia, the cardinal, in Launoy, the very learned author, Epist. p. IV, second last letter. Nor does he certainly deserve praise for the fact that in the Bull of Leo X, which is found in book VII of the Decretals, he is presented as the author of the Monti di pietà, rather of impiety; and, as Platina says elsewhere, he was also a Simoniac, avaricious of all dignities, a seller who set aside good qualities.

units.la: LIV. Sixti IV. vitia, ubi de odio erga Papas recens defunctos actum est, ob oculos posuimus. Idem Cornelio Agrippa & aliis testibus, lupanar aedificavit, ex quo annuatim 20000. florenos & amplius habuit. Mensibus Junio, Julio & Augusto quibusdam Cardinalibus impuritates quasvis, etiam Sodomiticas, verbis; Fiat, ut petitur; permisit; turpissimas (de quo Wesselus de potest. Eccles. c. 1. eum accusat) dispensationes & Bullas plumbatas de plenitudine & in abusu potestatis Apostolicae emisit; Vestibus semper auro intextis usus & auro intextis lecti tegumentis, & aureis ad excrementa sua excipienda vasibus, dilectâ quoque sua Teresiâ gemmis ornatos calceos dono dedit. Videri quoque potest Baptista Mantuanus. Onuphrius, in vita, suorum amantissimum ac indulgentissimum omnium judicio existimatum fuisse, ait. Quorum causst multa praeter fas jusque egisse & concessisse vitia illi datum est. Idem atrox scelestumque Consilium de Mediceis intersiterficiendis commemorat; Eidem primus dicitur, qui officia vendidit, quum nonnisi pecunia hac munera parentur, quae antea gratuito doctis & probis viris tribui solebant.
units.tr: LIV. We have set before the eyes the vices of Sixtus IV, where we treated his hatred toward the Popes who had recently died. According to Cornelius Agrippa and other witnesses, he built a brothel from which he had more than 20,000 florins a year. In the months of June, July and August he permitted certain cardinals to commit any impurities whatever, even sodomitical ones, by the words: Let it be done as requested. He issued most shameful dispensations and leaden Bulls out of the fullness and abuse of apostolic power (for which Wessel accuses him in On the Power of the Church, ch. 1). He always used garments woven with gold, and beds with covers woven with gold, and vessels of gold for receiving his excrement; he gave his beloved Teresa shoes adorned with gems as a gift. Baptista Mantuanus may also be consulted. Onuphrius, in his life, says that he was judged by everyone's opinion to be most fond of his own people and most indulgent. Many things beyond divine and human law were done for their sake, and he was given to permit vices. The same writer mentions his atrocious and wicked plan to murder the Medici. He is also said to have been the first who sold offices, since these gifts were obtained for money, which had formerly been given freely to learned and upright men.

units.la: LV. De Innocentio VIII. quoque hinc inde jam protulimus
units.tr: LV. We have already brought forward here and there what concerns Innocent VIII.

units.la: {a}heic non repetenda; Addimus tamen versus sagacissimi Sannazarii de sedecim Innocentii liberis: Innocuo priscos aequum est debere Quirites; Progenie exhaustam restituit patriam.
units.tr: {a}not to be repeated here. Yet we add the verses of the very shrewd Sannazaro on Innocent's sixteen children: It is right that the ancient Romans owe thanks to the harmless one; he restored the fatherland, drained of its offspring.

units.la: Et quidem liberos, teste Stella, ex damnato coitu suscepit. Annotavimus quoque sinistrum Authoris Conclavis de ejus regimine omen, attenta ejus praeterita vita. Quale autem regimen illud fuerit, ex parte docet querela Scriptoris noti: O Petre, non tibi Christus dixit: Mulge, aut tonde, sed pasce; Et ultima pars Epitaphii: Spurcities, gula, avaritia atque ignavia deses Hoc, Octave, jacent, quo tegeris, tumulo.
units.tr: Indeed, according to Stella, he begot children from a condemned union. We have also noted the ominous remark of the author of the Conclave concerning his government, given his past life. What kind of government that was is shown in part by the complaint of a well-known writer: O Peter, Christ did not say to you: "Milk, or shear, but feed." And the last part of the epitaph: Filth, gluttony, avarice and idle sloth lie buried in this tomb, Octavius, in which you are covered.

units.la: LVI. Alexander VI. supra quoque nobis memoratus, cui,
units.tr: LVI. Alexander VI, already mentioned by us above, to whom,

units.la: teste Guicciardino, non sinceritas, non verecundia, non veritas, non religio ulla aderat, sed insatiabilis avaritia, ambitio immensa, crudelitas plus quam barbara, ardensque spurios per fas & nefas exaltandi libido, omnium ejus ordinis deterrimus pro optimo Pontifex renuntiatus fuit, ut Onuphrius loquitur. Fuere tum aliqui in Comitio Patres, qui Hispanum occulta iniquitatis, summaque simulationis hominem stultissime Pontificem creatum, exitio tandem cunctis futurum non falsi vates denuntiarunt. Idem recenset Divinam in Electoribus vindictam. Similiter Ferdinandum Neapolitanum Regem ferunt, audita Electione, non sine lacrymis, a quibus tamen in funeribus liberorum etiam abstinuerit, ad Reginam dixisse, Papam hunc Italiae, imo toti Christiano orbi interitum procuraturum esse. Imo, teste Guicciardino, omnibus probis horrori & abominationi fuit ejus electio: Filius spurius Caesar Borgia jactare solebat, se probe nosse quid faciat, aut facere debeat, Patre permittente, qui Spiritu S. regatur. Quot in ejus vita ab Onuphrio descripta verba, tot fere vitia. Omnibus iniquus erat, ut filios ditaret. Caesar adhuc Cardinalis, quo sibi totius Ecclesiasticae ditionis Imperium compararet, regulis omnia aggredi coepit, quum pater omnes suas rationes & consilia ad id unum convertisset, ut nothos suos magnis opibus & potentia extolleret. In hunc finem arma venena &c. frequenter adhibita, Idem Caesar fratrem interfecit; connivente prorsus ad immane patris idui scelus patre Pontifice, qui & ipse sibi vim afferri ab efferato filio procul dubio metuebat. Rursus testatur Author: Pontificem totum in eam incubuisse curam, ut ingentes filio opes, maximæque imperii facultates, vel summa cum omnium injuria pararet. Docet, omnia venditata, nihil pecuniæ negatum fuisse—Cardinales multos pretio crearit. Hæc quoque, cum ingentibus sumptibus non sufficerent, inopiæ metu rapax, atque immani ingenio savus, opulentissimum quemque in aula Sacerdotem & in his aliquot Cardinales cæteris ditiores veneno tollendos constituit, ut eorum opibus in fiscum redactis potitus profusissimè largiretur, inexplebilemque filii cupiditatem expleret, haud dubiè in reliquos aulæ sacerdotiis atque divitiis insignes hereditatis spe saviturus, nisi mirabili Dei providentiâ, homo ad Italiæ exitium natus, quum animo adhuc majora de filio conciperet, diuturnámque sibi vitam polliceretur, fatali pincerna errore, sibi mortem, supremam verò Cæsari filio calamitatem peperisset, hilariorem scilicet in cœna, dum ad umbrosum Vaticani ruris fontem venenum bibunt, medicata Falerni vini lagena pocillatoris errore commutata, quam dira fraude ad opulentiorum aliquot Senatorum, qui convivio aderant, exitium honoris specie paravisset. Cæsar, qui dilutiùs biberat, exquisitis antidotis, vel ipso vivente robore veneni vim sustinente, atrocissimo quidem, sed non lethali morbo correptus est—At Pater Pontifex—est extinctus. Inter virtutes ejus numerat eloquentiam, sed quæ multis exitio fuit &c. Inter vitia ponitur, perfidia plusquam Punica, sævitia immanis, avaritia immensa ac rapacitas, inexhausta parandi filio imperii per fas & nefas libido. Si quando negotiis non premeretur, omni se jucunditatis genere sine discrimine dedit. Mulieribus maximè addictus, ex quibus 4. filios & 2. filias tulit. Omnium præcipua fuit Vannocia Romana, quam à forma venustate & morum illecebris miràque demum fœcunditate minor fortuna legitima propè uxoris loco habuit. Comœdias Plautinas, cæterâque ludicra libenter spectavit, frequentérque in Hadriani molem, ventitabat, ut palam personatos hilaribus festis, ac per omnes dies celebres, si quid elegantius in hominum genere per viam præteriret, propius adspiceret. In filia nuptiis—equestres ludos & venationem in Vaticano extra ordinem dedit. In urbe gladiatorum & sicariorum nunquam licentia major, nunquam populo Rom. libertas minor, delatorum ingens numerus, brevissimo maledicto poena mortis erat. Grassatorum insuper omnia plena, nec nocta tutum per urbem iter, nec interdiu extra urbem, Roma gentium profugium & asylum, omnibusque sæculis populorum omnium tutissima arx, jam carnificina facta erat, qua quidem omnia suorum causa, quibus omnia omnia indulserat, permittebat. Quos etiam ut magnis Clientelis subleva-ret, dominationis praesidia in eo quoque iis paravit, ut ad 43. Cardinales variis lectionibus, in his 18. Hispanos creaverit &c. Sed & societatem pessimi viri amavisse nocuit, Carolus quippe VIII. frater Ludovici XII. referente Thuano, infelix fato cessit, quòd tam arctam cum Alexandro VI. affinitatem contraxisset, & impuri Patris omnique scelerum genere cooperti filii crudelitatem, libidinem, fortunas denique fovisset. Romani illius tempore apud Authorem Nepotismi p. r. l. 2 p. 124. dicebant; Imperatores Tyrannidem docuisse, Pontifices eam exercere. Item, eum Romam Spurii, Hispaniam meretricibus implevisse. Audiamus vero adhuc de homine, vel potius monstro Abbatem Gualdi Vita di D. Olympia p. 90. Papa avarus atque in acquirendo insatiabilis fuit, & usque adeo suis ditandis deditus, ut lubens se P. moni daturus fuisset, si sibi Principatum pro suis promisisset. Bonae fidei testimonium habemus insuper apud ipsum Macchiavellum; Ita ille cap. 18. de Principe: Alexander VI. Papa nihil, quam hominum deceptorem egit; ad nihil, quam ad omnem malitiam & fraudem, quo hominum genus falleret, mentem suam exercuit. Nemo in adseverando quid magis fuit efficax, nemo majore jurejurando aliquid adfirmavit, & minus praestitit. Nihilosecius doli nunquam non commodè et cesserunt, qui fallendi artem & hosce mores hominum probè callebat. Notari porrò meretur ejus apud Janum Vitalem elogium: Nomine magnus eras, sed major, Borgia, factis, Cujus dextra enses strinxerat una duos.
units.tr: according to Guicciardini, sincerity, modesty, truth and every religious feeling were absent, but insatiable greed, immense ambition, a cruelty more than barbaric, and a burning lust to raise his bastards by right or wrong, he was proclaimed the worst of all that order to be pope, as the best, as Onuphrius says. There were then some Fathers in the assembly who foolishly declared that the Spaniard, a man of hidden wickedness and the greatest pretence, had been made pope, and that he would at last be the ruin of all, and they were not false prophets. The same writer records the divine vengeance on the electors. Likewise, they report that Ferdinand, King of Naples, on hearing of the election, said to the queen, not without tears, though he refrained from them at the funerals of his own children, that this pope would bring about the ruin of Italy, indeed of the whole Christian world. Indeed, according to Guicciardini, his election was a horror and an abomination to all good men. His bastard son Caesar Borgia used to boast that he knew well what he was doing, or ought to do, with his father permitting, who is governed by the Holy Spirit. There are almost as many vices as there are words in the account of his life given by Onuphrius. He was unjust to all, so that he might enrich his sons. Caesar, while still a cardinal, began to attack by fixed methods, so that he might gain for himself dominion over the whole ecclesiastical territory, when his father had turned all his plans and counsels to this one end, that he might raise his bastards with great wealth and power. To this end arms, poisons and so on were frequently used. The same Caesar killed his brother, the pope his father quite conniving at this monstrous crime, the pope who doubtless feared that violence would be done to himself by his savage son. Again the author testifies: the pope devoted himself wholly to this care, that he might procure for his son great riches and the very greatest resources of empire, even at the greatest cost to everyone. He shows that everything was put up for sale, nothing of money was refused—he made many cardinals for a price. These things too, since they did not suffice for his vast expenses, greedy from fear of poverty and savage in his monstrous nature, he decided to have the richest priest in the court, and some cardinals richer than the rest, poisoned, so that, having seized their wealth by confiscation to the treasury, he might lavish it most profusely and satisfy his son's insatiable greed, no doubt intending to rage against the others distinguished in the court by their priesthoods and riches, in hope of inheritance; had not, by a marvellous providence of God, the man born for the ruin of Italy, while he still conceived greater things for his son and promised himself a long life, by a fatal mistake of the cupbearer brought death on himself, and the supreme calamity on his son Caesar; namely, while they were drinking poison at the shady spring of the Vatican garden during a more cheerful supper, the poisoned flask of Falernian wine was exchanged by the cupbearer's error, which with dire treachery he had prepared under the appearance of an honour for the destruction of some of the richer senators who were present at the banquet. Caesar, who had drunk more diluted, having recourse to exquisite antidotes, and with his own strength withstanding the force of the poison, was seized by a most atrocious but not fatal sickness—but the father, the pope, died. Among his virtues he counts eloquence, but which was the ruin of many, etc. Among his vices is set down a treachery more than Punic, monstrous cruelty, immense greed and rapacity, an inexhaustible lust to get empire for his son by right or wrong. When he was not hard pressed by business, he gave himself without restraint to every kind of pleasure. He was especially devoted to women, of whom he had four sons and two daughters. The chief of them was Vannozza of Rome, whom her beauty and charm of manners, and at last her remarkable fruitfulness, and a lesser fortune, almost held in the place of a lawful wife. He gladly watched Plautine comedies and other plays, and often went to the mole of Hadrian, so that he might look more closely at whatever more elegant person in the human race passed by on the road, masked on festal holidays and on all the days that were celebrated. At his daughter's wedding he gave equestrian games and a hunt in the Vatican out of the ordinary. In the city, licence for gladiators and assassins was never greater, the liberty of the Roman people never less, the number of informers was huge, and the penalty for the briefest slander was death. Moreover, all places were full of brigands, nor was it safe to travel through the city by night, nor outside the city by day; Rome, the refuge and asylum of the nations, and in all ages the safest stronghold of all peoples, had already become a slaughterhouse, which indeed he allowed for the sake of all his own people, to whom he granted every indulgence. Also, that he might raise them up with great clienteles, he provided for them, in this too, a means of domination, so that he created about forty-three cardinals by various elections, among them eighteen Spaniards, etc. But even associating with a most wicked man did him harm: Charles VIII, brother of Louis XII, according to Thuanus, unhappily met his end, because he had contracted so close a marriage alliance with Alexander VI, and had cherished the cruelty, lust and finally the fortunes of an impure father and a son covered with every kind of crime. In that man's time, according to the author of Nepotismus p. r. l. 2 p. 124, the Romans used to say: that emperors had taught tyranny, and popes practised it. Likewise, that he had filled Rome with bastards and Spain with harlots. But let us hear further about the man, or rather monster, from the Abbot Gualdi, Vita di D. Olympia p. 90. The pope was greedy and insatiable in acquiring, and so given over to enriching his own that he would gladly have given himself up to the Turks, if they had promised him a principality for his people. We have further the testimony of good faith in Machiavelli himself; thus he, ch. 18 of The Prince: Pope Alexander VI did nothing but deceive men; he applied his mind to nothing but every malice and fraud by which he might trick mankind. No one was more effective in asserting anything, no one affirmed anything with a greater oath, and performed less. Nevertheless his deceits never failed to succeed, for he knew well the art of deceiving and these habits of men. Further, his epitaph by Janus Vitalis deserves to be noted: You were great in name, Borgia, but greater in deeds, whose right hand had drawn two swords together.

units.la: Quo spiritus militares ejus obliquè perstrinxit. De quibus etiam testatur Caroli VIII. Manifestum contra Papam; Imò Jovius de Legato ejus ad Turcas contra Gallos misso loquitur. II Nipot. 2. p. 242. judicat, cùm apud alios Papas & Nepotes in magnis malis scintilla quadam boni fuerit, in Alexandro & Nepotismo ejus ne minimum quidem radium: boni fuisse inter mala futuris seculis deplorANDA, & multò magis populis, qui sentire debuerint, gravia. Hinc quibusdam creditum, Alexandrum juràsse, & suos ad jurandum etiam adegisse, dì non far mai bene alla chiesa, de non promovendo unquam Ecclesiae commodo. Aliis & longè aliis cum operam dedisse, docet Epitaphium quoque Lucretiae Filiae, Pontano Authore: Hic jacet in tumulo Lucretia nomine, sed re Thais, Alexandri filia, Sponsa, nurus.
units.tr: By this he obliquely hits off his military spirit. Of these things too the Manifesto of Charles VIII against the pope bears witness; indeed Jovius speaks of his legate sent to the Turks against the French. In II Nepotismus 2 p. 242 he judges that, while among other popes and nephews there was some spark of good in great evils, in Alexander and his nepotism not the least ray: the good there was among evils is to be lamented in future centuries, and much more the peoples, who had to suffer grievous things. Hence it was believed by some that Alexander had sworn, and had even made his people swear, the oath "never to do good to the Church," that he would never promote the advantage of the Church. That others, and very different ones, he worked for, the epitaph of Lucrezia, his daughter, by the author Pontanus also teaches: Here lies in the tomb Lucretia by name, but in fact a Thais, daughter of Alexander, bride, daughter-in-law.

units.la: Docet & Epitaphium ipsiusmet Alexandri, à Sannazario compositum: Fortasse Fortasse nescis cujus hic tumulus sit, Adsta Viator, ni piget. Titulum, quem Alexandri vides, haud illius Magni est, sed hujus, qui modò Libidinosa sanguinis captus siti Tot civitates inclytas Tot regna vertit, tot duces letho dedit, Ntos ut impleat suos. Orbem rapinis, ferro & igne funditus Vastavit, hausit, eruit: Humana jura nec minùs cœlestia Ipsósque sustulit Deos. Ut scilicet liceret, heu scelus! Patri, Nata sinum permingere, Nec exsecrandis abstinere nuptiis, Timore sublato semel. Et tamen in urbe Romuli hic vel undecim Præsidet annis Pontifex. I nunc, Nerones & Caligulas nomina, Turpeis vel Heliogabalos, Hoc sat, Viator: Reliqua non finit pudor, Tu suspicare & ambula.
units.tr: The epitaph of Alexander himself, composed by Sannazaro, also teaches: Perhaps you do not know whose tomb this is. Stop, traveller, if it does not trouble you. The title you see is not of that Great Alexander, but of this one, who, now seized with a lustful thirst for blood, overturned so many famous cities and so many kingdoms, gave so many leaders to death, that he might fill his sons. He laid waste, drained and tore out the world with plunder, sword and fire; he took away human laws and no less the heavenly ones, and the gods themselves. That it might be allowed, alas the crime! for a daughter to pour into her father's bosom, and not to abstain from accursed marriages, fear once removed. And yet in the city of Romulus here a pope presides for eleven years. Go now, name Neros and Caligulas, and the shameful Heliogabaluses; this is enough, traveller: shame does not allow the rest. You suspect, and walk on.

units.la: Æquè ac alterum ab eodem:
units.tr: Just as much as the other one by the same author:

units.la: Sævitia, insidiæ, rabies, furor, ira, libido, Sanguinis & diri spongia dira sitis: Sextus Alexander jaceo hic: jam libera gaude Roma tibi quoniam, mors mea vita fuit.
units.tr: Savagery, treachery, rage, fury, anger, lust, and the cruel sponge of bloody thirst: I, Sextus Alexander, lie here. Now rejoice, Rome, free at last, since my death was your life.

units.la: Neque aliter etiam, teste Guicciardino, inde lætata est. Ex quibus omnibus patet, Onuphrium non sine causa in Paulo III. de dira ac prope exsecrabili Alexandri VI. memoria loqui; neque sine causa Paulum Langium in Chron. Citiz. ex Volaterrano testari, Romam tunc carnificinam factam atq; tunc Roma omnia sacra venalia fuisse.
units.tr: Nor was it otherwise, according to Guicciardini, that Rome rejoiced at it. From all these things it is clear that Onuphrius does not speak without reason of the dreadful and almost accursed memory of Alexander VI in his account of Paul III; nor does Paulus Langius, in his Chronicle of Citizen, testify without reason, following Volaterranus, that Rome was then made a slaughterhouse, and that all sacred things in Rome were then for sale.

units.la: LVII. Seculo XVI. Julius II. ante Pontificatum narrat denuò Onuphrius in vita, filiam tulit, eodem referente, sed cæterùm nimis laudante, contumeliarum insolens & contumacibus implacabilis extitit, à nonnullis parùm probatus, quòd armis magis, quàm Sacrosanctum Pontificem decéret, deditus esse videretur, hinc etiam à Paulo Langio in Chronico Citizensi testimonium habens, quòd non tam Apostolicæ Sedis flaviger quàm armiger fuerit; Ut certè irreverenter satis arrepto Pauli gladio claves Petri in Tiberim projecit; irreverenter satis objicienti dictum Christi: Reconde gladium tuum in vaginam; respondit: Id imperatum ei, post factam percussionem; indecenter satis se valse valse in Bologna de' Turchi, Bononia Turcarum in bello ope usus est, quod in vita Pauli Sarpii legimus. Liberius Guicciardinus restatur: Omnes eum ante Papatum morosissimum, intolerabilem, truculentum & quietis impatientem, quique in eximios quosque Viros immanes jam inimicitias exercuisset, noverant. Cum ad eum Philippus Burgundus, postea Episcopus Ultrajectinus, missus esset, redux testatus est, se credere, Gentiles multos multo melius vixisse, quam qui nunc Christiano orbi leges ferant. Caetera ejus verba D Ssert. IV. Sect. II. n. 106. videri possunt. Idem Julius Ludovico XII. Galliarum Regi, cujus auspiciis tanquam Simoniacus, moribus corruptus, fax divisionis & bellorum, & scandalum Europae, hinc plane incapax ad Papatum accusatus fuit, occasionem dedit in Moneta dicendi: Perdam Babylonis nomen. Idem Maximiliani I. judicio parum probabatur. Deus aeterne, aliquando dicebat, nisi vigilares, quam male esset mundo, quem regimus nos, ego miser venator & ebriosus ille ac scelaratus Julius. Neque etiam eidem probabantur alii ante eum: In veritate dicere possum, inquiebat, nullum Pontificem mihi per vitam meam fidem servasse, atque etiam spero, Deo volente, hunc (Leonem X.) ultimum fore. Occasionem quoque tales eidem Maximiliano dederant de Papatu cum Imperio conjungendo cogitandi, ad exemplum veterum Imperatorum, qui etiam Pontifices dicebantur; prout quoque non ita pridem Vir doctus tractatum edidit, de attrito per Papas Imperio, deque Pontificatu ab Imperatore-Caesare Ecclesia Reique publicae causa capessendo. Ad Julium ut redeamus, ipsi Macchiavello Principis c.25. in omnibus suis actionibus impetuosam violentiam ostendit: Sic etiam Galli, eidem tribuunt des procedes violens, del' animosite & des emportemens contre la France, hinc une memoire fort odieuse dans la Republique Chrestienne. Arrest. du Parl. sur la Bulle du Pape concernant les Franchises p.9. Refut. de la Rep. a la Protest. de Mr. Lavardin: p.10. Totus, quantus fuse describitur in Dialogo, cui titulus: Julius, a viro eruditissimo post mortem Julii ob frustra ab eo pulsatas coeli fores composito, & publicato.
units.tr: LVII. In the sixteenth century, Onuphrius again relates in his life of Julius II before his pontificate that he carried off a daughter, on the same authority, though he praises him too much otherwise. He was intolerant of insults and implacable toward the contumacious, and was not much approved by some, because he seemed more devoted to arms than a holy pontiff should be. Hence Paulus Langius, in his Chronicle of Citizen, also bears witness that he was less the standard-bearer of the Apostolic See than its armour-bearer. Certainly, with rather irreverent haste, he seized Paul's sword and threw Peter's keys into the Tiber. When objected to, quite irreverently, with Christ's words, Put your sword back into its sheath, he replied: That was commanded him after the blow had been struck. Indecently enough, he availed himself of the Turks at Bologna in war, as we read in the life of Paolo Sarpi. Guicciardini protests more freely: All knew him before his papacy to be most morose, intolerable, truculent, and impatient of quiet, one who had already carried on monstrous enmities against all the outstanding men. When Philip of Burgundy, afterwards Bishop of Utrecht, was sent to him, he reported on his return that he believed many Gentiles had lived much better than those who now make laws for the Christian world. His other words may be seen in D Ssert. IV. Sect. II. n. 106. The same Julius gave occasion, in a medal, to Louis XII, King of France, under whose auspices he was accused, as a simoniac, corrupt in morals, a firebrand of division and wars, and a scandal to Europe, and so plainly incapable of the papacy, of saying: I will destroy the name of Babylon. The same man was little approved in the judgment of Maximilian I. Eternal God, he sometimes said, unless you were watching, how bad it would be for the world which we rule: I, a wretched hunter and drunkard, and that scoundrel Julius. Nor were others before him approved by him either: I can truly say, he said, that no pontiff has kept faith with me in my whole life, and I hope, God willing, that this one (Leo X) will be the last. Such men also gave Maximilian himself occasion to think of joining the papacy with the Empire, after the example of the ancient emperors, who were also called pontiffs. Likewise, not long ago a learned man published a treatise on the Empire worn down by the Popes, and on the Pontificate to be taken up by the Emperor-Caesar for the cause of the Church and the commonwealth. To return to Julius: Machiavelli, in The Prince c. 25, shows him in all his actions a headlong violence. So too the French ascribe to him violent proceedings, animosity and outbursts against France, hence a very odious memory in the Christian Republic. Arrest du Parl. sur la Bulle du Pape, p. 9; Refut. de la Rep. a la Protest. de Mr. Lavardin, p. 10. The whole of it, described at length, is in the Dialogue entitled Julius, composed and published after Julius's death by a most learned man, about the heaven's gates he knocked on in vain.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: Leo X. ille ipse fuit, de quo in Vaticiniis Johannis Abbatis Venetiis initio hujus Seculi cum Privilegio & Licentia superiorum editis, praedictum: Veniet Leo sub pelle Agni, & devorabit Oves. In ejus coronatione tantum fastum fuisse, quidam narnarrant, ut uno die 100000. aureorum expenderentur. Onuphrii in vita judicio quietus & voluptatibus contra decessoris morem dedi-tus fuit, &, eo quidem paulò post judice, id un m ei datum, quòd vo-luptatibus, venationibus, aucupiis effusè dedit us, luxui & splendidissimis con-viviis, musicaque magis, quàm tantum Pontificem deceret, totus impenderet. Sed & ei datum ab aliis, quòd injustè avarus fuerit: Patrio more, inquit Langius συγχέον in Chron. Citiz. ad an. 1513. Leo auri sitien-tissimus est, nimirum cùm ad Romanorum Avaritiam Florentinorum accessit cupiditas, aurique Sacra fames creverit in immensum, crescitque usque modò amor nummi, quantum ipsa pecunia crescit; savior que ignibus Ætna ardet amor habendi, quemadmodum & Naso inquit: Creverunt & opes & opum furiosa libido; Quò mage sunt potæ, plùs sitiun-tur aquæ. Hinc, ipso narrante Onuphrio, 31. Cardinales partim pretio creavit, simul officia quadam venalia excogitavit, pecunia quarenda causa, quum multa tum ædificiis, tum effusis largitionibus & bellorum usi-bus absumpsisset. Sed, cùm Cardinalibus creatis pretii 50000. aureorum restitutionem promisisset, eámque aliter præstare non posset, eodem Langio porrò narrante, sub prætextu belli Turcici & ædificationis, ad quam tamen Julius ingentem pecuniæ summam reliquerat, Indulgentias indicendo, & Gazas inter suos distribuendo Reformationi occasionem dedit, qui & aliis modis injustam avaritiam prodidit, hinc iterum Langius conquestus est: Amore equidem auri & nunc Romæ omnia sunt venalia, auro mediante Simonia toleratur &c. Et iterum: Per prædicta & similia, quæ ex Curia Romana manant, gravamina per orbem Christianum, ruina, destructiones & aerumnæ oriuntur &c. Hinc etiam de Leone Vir in Germania ex præcipuis: Turcam profligare Vultis? Laudo propositum, sed vehementer vereor, ne erretis in nomine. In Italia quarite, non in Asia—Hic ubique grassatur & sanguinem miserorum sitit. Hunc Cerberum nullo modo sedare potestis, nisi aureo fluvio &c. Ostultam & superstitiosam opinionem credentium, cœleste numen omnia æquis oculis intuens ad nutum Florentinorum flecti, reflecti, irasci non danti & rursum largienti placari. Templum Domini—Clamant—sed non est Templum Domini. Quin de illis ipsis Romanensibus idem Langius pronuntiat: Ast nunc eorum incuriâ, fraude & Avaritiâ assiduè Turcarum vires crescunt; Et narrationem suam tandem ita concludit: Quæ utinam vera non essent, utinam mendaces in hac parte essemus omnes, ut vitiis eliminatis Romæ sanctitas ipsa & morum integritas, Justitia & Veritas, ad salutem totius orbis & fidei robur inveniretur, destrueretúrque ceu falsum & injuriosum illud vulgatissimum etiam etiam Laicorum dicterium, quo dicunt, Romæ propiores Christianos esse deteriores; &, Curiam Romanam non quærere ovem sine lana. Imò & illud Leoni datum, quòd securo de Numine animo fuerit; quod, ut & ejus de animarum immortalitate mentem, sequentia ostendunt. Aliquando (uti recusat. Synod. Trid. p.2. cauf. 8 p. 266. probatur;) personatos Philosophos duos, ceu moriones mensæ suæ assistere atque de animarum immortalitate disputare jussos illam definitâ sententiâ controversiam dirimens allocutus est: Etsi tu, affirmans, pulchras & bonas rationes habeas, tamen ego sententiam hujus negantis probo, ceu firmiorem & quæ faciat bonum vultum. Et cùm eidem Bembus, Vir apprimè doctus & postea Cardinalis in privato Colloquio locum ex Bibliis proferret, Pontifex ægrè id ferens: Quid, inquit, mihi narras istam de Christo fabulam? Atque hanc relationem nostram non fabulam esse, ex Joh. Pico, Mirandulani Comitis ex Fratre Nepote, colligas, qui in quæstione: Utrum Concilia vel Pontifices errare possint? inter alia de Leone ita loquitur: Meminimus Pontificem creditum & adoratum, qui nullum Deum credens, omne infidelitatis (quam Atheismum vocare licet) culmen excederet: pessimáque ejus opera in coemendo Pontificatu, in omnigenis sceleribus exercendis, id ipsum testabantur, sed & pessima quoque dicta confirmabant. Námque fassum eum affirmabatur, nullum se Deum aliquando, etiam dum Pontificiam sedem teneret, credidisse. Lib. de fide & ordine credendi Theor. 4. p.259.260. Sed & ipse Cardinalis Pallavicinus Histor. Conc. Trid. l.1. c. 2. omnia suo quoque calculo probare videtur. N.2. ad objectionem Suavis, Leonem magis in literis profanis versatum, quàm in Sacris & ad Religionem pertinentibus esse, concedit, vix pueritiam egressum, cùm se in supremo Ecclesiæ Senatu collocatum cerneret, suo plane officio defuisse, neglectâ in literarum studio parte non solùm nobiliore, sed suæ magis congruâ dignitati. Gravior, inquit, apparuit deformitas, quando 37. ætatis anno Præses ac Magister Religionis constitutus, non continenti solùm studio profanarum literarum curiositati se totum impendit, sed in Regiam ipsius Religionis majori curâ eos accersivit, quibus essent perspecta Græcorum fabula, Poetarúmque delicia, quàm Ecclesiæ historia ac Patrum doctrina &c. Non æquè Theologorum ac Poetarum consuetudine est delectatus, nec juxta Sacram eruditionem promovit, ac profanam. Similiter n. 4. & 5. Suavi objectanti, Leoni haud magnæ curæ pietatem fuisse, largitur, in eo, cùm Pontifex electus est, tantam curam pietatis non eluxisse, quantam celsitudo illa pene Divina postulârit. Nam, inquit, ut ea præteream, quæ sub famæ suspiciosuspicione magis, quàm affirmatione delitescunt; Constat, venationes, facetias, pompas adeo frequentes, fuisse in Leone vitia partim Seculi, partim potentia, partim etiam ingenii, nec tamen exigua in eo inter mortales fastigio, cui nihil par esse potest, nisi summa perfectio. Et n. 6. ait, Leonem in sede Romana collocatum passum esse se dementari ab ea specie, quae magnificum cum bono confundit, plausumque multitudinis cum Reip. emolumento. Claudat seriem testium de Leone Sannazarius de fine Leonis eleganter ita canens: Sacra sub extrema, si forte requiritis, hora Cur Leo non poterat sumere: Vendiderat.
units.tr: Leo X was the very one of whom, in the Prophecies of John the Abbot, published at Venice at the beginning of this century with privilege and licence of superiors, it was foretold: Leo will come under the skin of a lamb, and will devour the sheep. Some relate that at his coronation there was such display that 100,000 gold pieces were spent in one day. By the judgment of Onuphrius in his life, he was quiet and given to pleasures, contrary to his predecessor's custom; and, by the same judge a little later, this was held against him: that he gave himself up lavishly to pleasures, hunting, fowling, luxury, most splendid banquets and music, and spent himself wholly on these more than such a pontiff should. But he was also charged by others with unjust avarice: After the paternal manner, says Langius, Leo is most thirsty for gold; namely, since Florentine greed was added to Roman avarice, the sacred hunger for gold has grown immensely, and the love of money grows as money itself grows; and the love of having burns fiercer than Etna, as Naso also says: Wealth grew, and the furious lust for wealth; the more they drink, the more they thirst for water. Hence, as Onuphrius relates, he created thirty-one cardinals, some for a price, and at the same time devised certain offices for sale, to seek money, since he had used up much both on buildings and on lavish gifts and the needs of wars. But when he had promised the cardinals created for a price restitution of 50,000 gold pieces, and could not otherwise make good on it, Langius again relates that, under the pretext of a Turkish war and of building (for which Julius had nevertheless left a huge sum of money), by proclaiming indulgences and distributing the treasures among his own, he gave occasion to the Reformation; and he betrayed his unjust avarice in other ways too. Hence Langius complained again: Indeed, from love of gold everything at Rome is now for sale too; through gold simony is tolerated, etc. And again: Through the aforesaid and similar grievances, which flow from the Roman Curia, ruin, destruction and miseries arise throughout the Christian world, etc. Hence also a man of note in Germany, among the chief ones, on Leo: Do you want to crush the Turk? I praise the purpose, but I greatly fear you may err in the name. Seek in Italy, not in Asia. Here he rages everywhere and thirsts for the blood of the wretched. You cannot in any way calm this Cerberus unless with a river of gold, etc. A foolish and superstitious opinion of believers, that the heavenly power, regarding all things with equal eyes, is bent and turned and angered at the nod of the Florentines, and is placated again when they give. They cry, "The Temple of the Lord"; but it is not the Temple of the Lord. Indeed, the same Langius pronounces about those very Romans: But now, through their carelessness, fraud and avarice, the strength of the Turks grows constantly. And he finally concludes his account thus: Would that these things were not true, would that we were all liars in this matter, so that, with vices removed, holiness itself and integrity of morals, justice and truth might be found at Rome for the salvation of the whole world and the strength of the faith; and that that most common saying, even among laymen, which they utter, that Christians nearer Rome are worse, and that the Roman Curia does not seek a sheep without wool, might be destroyed as false and injurious. Moreover, it was also given to Leo that he had an untroubled mind about the Deity; as the following shows, and also his mind about the immortality of souls. Once (as the Council of Trent relates, p. 2, cause 8, p. 266) he had two masked philosophers, like jesters, stand by his table and dispute about the immortality of souls; and settling the controversy with a definite judgment he said: "Although you, affirming, have fine and good reasons, yet I approve the opinion of this man, denying, as firmer and one that gives a good face." When Bembo, a most learned man and afterwards a cardinal, in a private conversation brought forward a passage from the Bible, the Pontiff, taking it badly, said: Why do you tell me that fable about Christ? That this account of ours is no fable you may gather from John Pico, nephew of the Count of Mirandola, who, in the question Whether Councils or Popes can err?, speaks among other things of Leo thus: We remember a Pontiff who was believed and adored, who, believing in no God, exceeded every height of unbelief (which one may call Atheism); and his worst works in buying the Pontificate and in committing crimes of every kind bore witness to the same thing, and his worst sayings confirmed it. For he was affirmed to have confessed that he had never at any time, even while he held the Papal see, believed in any God. Book On the Faith and the Order of Believing, Theor. 4, pp. 259–260. But Cardinal Pallavicini himself, in his History of the Council of Trent, l. 1, c. 2, also seems to approve all these things by his own reckoning. In n. 2, replying to Soave's objection that Leo was more versed in profane letters than in sacred ones and those pertaining to religion, he concedes that he had scarcely left boyhood when, finding himself placed in the supreme senate of the Church, he plainly failed in his duty, neglecting in the study of letters the part not only nobler but more fitting to his dignity. The deformity appeared graver, he says, when in the thirty-seventh year of his age, set up as President and Master of Religion, he devoted himself wholly not only to continual study of profane letters and their curiosity, but summoned to the royal court of religion, with greater care, those by whom the fables of the Greeks and the delights of the poets were thoroughly known, rather than the history of the Church and the doctrine of the Fathers, etc. He did not delight equally in the company of theologians and of poets, nor did he promote men according to sacred learning as he did according to profane. Similarly, in nn. 4 and 5, to Soave's objection that Leo had little serious care for piety, he grants that in him, when he was elected Pontiff, there did not shine so much care for piety as that almost divine loftiness demanded. For, he says, to pass over those things which lie hidden under suspicion of rumour rather than assertion: it is established that hunting, jests and pomps were so frequent in Leo, vices partly of the age, partly of his power, partly also of his talent; and yet in him there was no small height among mortals, to which nothing can be equal except supreme perfection. And in n. 6 he says that Leo, placed in the Roman see, allowed himself to be dazzled by that appearance which confuses the magnificent with the good, and the applause of the crowd with the advantage of the commonwealth. Sannazaro, closing the series of witnesses about Leo's end, sings elegantly: If perhaps you ask, at the last hour, why Leo could not receive the sacred things: he had sold them.

units.la: LIX. Adriano VI. tribuitur, quòd Demetrio Mago Graeco concesserit, Sylvestrem Taurum Diis Gentilibus sacrificare.
units.tr: 59. Adrian VI is charged with having granted to Demetrius Magus the Greek that Sylvester Taurus should sacrifice to the heathen gods.

units.la: Ab illicito venere victus & ipsius Sodomiae, juxta judicium cujusdam Batti in Memorabilibus Wolfii, suspectus fuit. Quàm exosus Romanis fuerit, Dissert. IV. Sect. 3. n. 5. dictum est, atque ex eo etiam colligi potest, quòd eidem applicârunt illud: A sexto semper diruta Roma fuit. Bene & secus gesta ab Onuphrio in Vita recensentur: Veneni ipsi propinati suspicionem non plane rejicit; quod ut familiares ejus constanter asserere non velint, ita nec inficiari ausint. Et certè severior fuit, quàm Romana Curia ferre posset. Constat id, & constat, quales Antecessores ipsius judicio fuerint, ex instructione Cheregato Legato data, in qua ingenuè fatetur; eam rerum perturbationem nihil aliud esse, quàm supplicium à Deo inflictum noxis praecipuè Sacerdotum ac Praesulum, ac proinde (ut observavit Chrysostomus in eo, quod Christus egit in Urbe Hierosolyma) flagellum à Templo incepisse, cùm prius Capiti, quàm caeteris infirmi corporis membris mederi par esset. In eam sedem aliquot jam annos vitia quaedam irrepsisse, abusus in rebus Sacris, in legibus violationes, in cunctis denique perversionem. Mirum non esse, si morbus à capite reliquas in partes defluxerit, nimirum à summis Pontificibus ad Antistites minores; eos omnes peccasse. statutum sibi esse, Curiam reformare, ut inde sanitas duceret initium, unde morbus inceperat. se cervices submisisse Dignitati, quò deformatam Sponsam reformaret. Nemi-nem mirari tamen debere, si tam cito perfectam emendationem haud cerneret; cùm enim inveterato morbo variisque malis conflato mederi opus esset, pedetentim ac lente agendum &c.
units.tr: Overcome by unlawful desire, he was suspected of sodomy itself, according to the judgment of a certain Battus in the Memorabilia of Wolf. How hateful he was to the Romans has been said in Dissert. IV, Sect. 3, n. 5, and this can also be gathered from the fact that they applied to him the saying Rome has always been ruined by a sixth. His good and bad deeds are recounted by Onuphrius in his Life. He does not altogether reject the suspicion that poison was given to him, which, as his intimates constantly assert, they do not wish to deny, and do not dare to deny. He was certainly stricter than the Roman Curia could bear. This is established, and it is also established what kind of predecessors he had, from the instruction given to the legate Cheregato, in which he frankly confesses that this disorder of affairs is nothing other than a punishment inflicted by God, chiefly for the faults of priests and prelates; and therefore (as Chrysostom observed of what Christ did in the city of Jerusalem) the scourge began at the Temple, since it was right to heal the head before the other members of the weak body. Some years now certain vices have crept into that see: abuses in sacred matters, violations of the laws, and in short a perversion of everything. It is no wonder if the disease has flowed from the head into the remaining parts, namely from the supreme pontiffs down to the lesser prelates; all of them have sinned. He had resolved to reform the Curia, so that health might begin where the disease had begun. He had bowed his neck to the dignity, so that he might reform the disfigured Bride. Nobody, however, should be surprised if he did not see a perfect correction so quickly; for since the disease was long rooted and compounded of many evils, it was necessary to proceed gradually and slowly, &c.

units.la: LX. Sed & testimonium praebet vitiis Pontificum illorum maximè & proximè praecedentium temporum decantatus liber, cui nomen Onus Ecclesiae, Coloniae An. 1531. editus; in quo Sect. V. Ecclesiastica modò sublimitas multifariam est lacerata. Hoc in Apocalypsi ostendiostenditur in Sigilli sexti apertione, id est, moderni temporis nostri, quando Sol, qui est Spiritualis Potentatus, factus est niger, quia non serenum cælum, sed tetrum infernum aperit. Propterea perversus Pontifex nuncupatur Angelus Abyssi. Et Sect. VIII. heu, sicut olim in Imperio Romano, sic hodie in Curia Romana est vorago divitiarum turpissima. Crevit avaritia, periit Lex à Sacerdote ac Visio de Propheta & Consilium à Senioribus. Claves Ecclesiæ sunt in abusu & servitute ambitionis & Simonia. Vitia enim ferme Curialium celari negarique vix possunt. Roma quasi gurges flagitiorum. Sect. XV. vero: Ecce Roma nunc est vorago & Mammona inferni, ubi Diabolus totius avaritiæ Capitaneus residet vendens patrimonium Christi, quod suâ passione promeruit, qui nobis præcipit, ut gratis demus, quod gratis accepimus. Id modo versum est in Proverbium: Curia Romana non petit ovem sine lana: Dantes exaudit, non dantibus ostia claudit.
units.tr: LX. But the much-praised book entitled Burden of the Church, published at Cologne in 1531, also gives testimony to the vices of the popes of the most recent and immediately preceding times. In it, Sect. V: the ecclesiastical loftiness has now been torn in many ways. This is shown in the Apocalypse in the opening of the sixth seal, that is, of our modern time, when the Sun, which is spiritual power, has become black, because it opens not a serene sky but a foul hell. Therefore the wicked Pontiff is called the Angel of the Abyss. And Sect. VIII: alas, as once in the Roman Empire, so today in the Roman Curia there is a most shameful whirlpool of riches. Avarice has grown, law has perished from the priest, vision from the prophet and counsel from the elders. The keys of the Church are in abuse and in the servitude of ambition and simony. For the vices of courtiers can hardly be hidden or denied. Rome is like a whirlpool of crimes. Then Sect. XV: Behold, Rome now is a whirlpool and the Mammon of hell, where the Devil, captain of all avarice, sits selling the patrimony of Christ, which he earned by his passion, who commands us to give freely what we have received freely. This has now been turned into a proverb: The Roman Curia does not seek a sheep without wool; it hears those who give, and shuts its doors to those who do not give.

units.la: LXI. In Clemente VII. Ouuphrius notat, ex parum certa, neque propalam legitima uxore natum esse. Et porrò: Inusitatâ (alibi; fatali) avaritiâ adeò omnium hominum odia in se concitârat, ut nemo esset, qui vicem ejus tam fœdè & prater Sacramenti fidem oppressi doluerit.
units.tr: LXI. Concerning Clement VII, Onuphrius notes that he was born of a not very certain wife, and not openly a lawful one. And further: by his unusual avarice (elsewhere: fatal) he had so stirred up the hatred of all men against himself, that there was no one who grieved for his fate, so shamefully and beyond the faith of the sacrament was he oppressed.

units.la: Eodem notante, ad hastam tres pileos Cardinalitios vendidit. Avaritiæ documentum in eo II Nipot. p. 2. p. 380. exhibet, quòd Legato Imperatoris fœdus contrà Turcam petenti & ad silentium dicenti: V. S. non dice niente; Sanctitas Vestra nihil dicit; respondit: Non, perche voi ci consigliate à spender danari, e noi pensiamo al modo di guadagnarle; Id est; Nihil; quia vos consulitis, ut argentum expendam, cùm ego de modo colligendi sim sollicitus. Sermones providentiam, cùm in mole Adriani obsideretur, negantis exhibet Dux Cæsareanus Fronsbergius l. VI. p. 120. Genium magis Suavis ad a. 1534. declarat: Etsi, inquit, quibusdam dotibus, naturali gravitate, parsimoniâ exemplari ac dissimulatione insigni multorum in se admirationem concitârit: ob avaritiam tamen, austeritatem & crudelitatem, quas semper exercuit, sed in morbo plus solito manifestavit, multò pluribus erat odiosus. Et Pallavicinus ipse quoque, qui eum Hist. Conc. Trid. III. 16. 8. dotibus animos conciliantibus, beneficentiâ & humanitate caruisse, creditúmque caput Pontificatus ejus revera solùm dextrum extitisse, mortémque tanto, quanto erat electio, gaudio exceptum fuisse testatur. Et Jovius tandem Hist. l. 32. ita de eo scribens: Neminem plane oderat, cùm neminem adamaret, præterquam ab occultiore causa conciliatos. His certè unis adeò favit intemperanter, ut ad summos honores, ut ad summum auctoritatis locum stabilesque divitias nullo promoveret pudore; multorum vero
units.tr: Noting the same, he sold three cardinals' hats at auction. As evidence of his avarice, in II Nipot. p. 2, p. 380, he gives the following. When the Emperor's legate sought an alliance against the Turk and said, Your Holiness says nothing; Your Holiness says nothing, he replied: No, because you advise us to spend money, and we are thinking how to earn it. That is: nothing; because you advise me to spend money, while I am concerned with how to gather it. The Caesarean commander Fronsberg, l. VI, p. 120, records the words of one who denied providence, when he was besieged in the Mole of Hadrian. Suavis at the year 1534 sets out his character more fully: Although, he says, by certain gifts, by natural dignity, by an exemplary frugality and by a notable dissimulation, he won the admiration of many; yet because of his avarice, his severity and his cruelty, which he always practised, and which in his illness he showed more than usual, he was far more hateful to very many. Pallavicini himself too, Hist. Conc. Trid. III, 16, 8, testifies that he lacked the gifts that win hearts, namely kindness and humanity; that the head of his pontificate had in truth been only the right one; and that his death was received with as much joy as his election. And Jovius, finally, writing of him in Hist. l. 32, says: He plainly hated nobody, since he loved nobody, except those won over by some hidden cause. Certainly, to these alone he showed such unrestrained favour that he promoted them to the highest honours, to the highest seat of authority and to lasting riches, without any shame; of many, indeed,

units.la: Exemplum Clementis VII. verò constanter oblivisceretur, qui ab optimis literarum studiis, veteríque obsequio commendationem & præmia meruissent. Hos quidem blandè appellarat, ut imagine gratiæ delineret, sed occultè oderat tanquam creditores. De eo atque aliis Pauli III. decessoribus Cardinales atque Prælati, in Consilio, quod jussu hujus conscripserant, ajunt, eos sibi coacervâsse Doctores ad desiderium suum, non, ut ab eis discerent, quod facerent, sed ut eorum callidate inveniretur ratio, quâ liceret, id quod liberet. Quod quidem eximium scilicet est de probitate illorum testimonium.
units.tr: he constantly forgot the example of Clement VII, who had earned commendation and rewards from the best literary studies and long-standing service. He had indeed addressed these men kindly, so as to paint an image of favour, but secretly he hated them as creditors. Concerning him and the other predecessors of Paul III, the cardinals and prelates, in a Consilium which they wrote at his command, say that they heaped up teachers for their own desire, not so that they might learn from them what to do, but so that by their cunning a method might be found by which whatever pleased might be permitted. This is indeed, of course, a remarkable testimony to their probity.

units.la: LXII. Successor Paulus III. (juxta libellum Italicum, titulo Bernhardini Ochini, sed ab aliis, uti creditur, compositum atque Ascanio Columnæ dedicatum, ex quo pluscula Sleidanus ad an. 1549. excerpsit) non una labe contaminatus & deformis fuit.
units.tr: LXII. The successor, Paul III (according to an Italian booklet under the title of Bernardino Ochino, but composed by others, as is believed, and dedicated to Ascanio Colonna, from which Sleidan excerpted several things under the year 1549), was not stained and disfigured by a single blemish.

units.la: Sequentia enim aliàque horrenda de eo narrantur. Quòd, ut Cardinalis fieret, Alexandro VI. sororem Juliam stuprandam dederit; Quòd Anconæ Legatus existens & unius è nobilibus Legati schema induens, puellam nobilem paßti matrimonii colore vitiaverit, quæ agnito errore in insaniam feré incideret; Quòd ex eo contubernio Petrum Aloysium, monstrum hominis potiùs quàm hominem, atque tandem ob intolerabilem tyrannidem à nobilibus suis Placentiæ trucidatum, de muro suspensum, pugionibus confossum, pedibus impetitum & in fossam præcipitatum genuerit; Filiam suam Constantiam jam Pontifex in deliciis habuerit, atque, ut ea liberiùs potiretur, maritum ejus Bosium Sforziam veneno sustulerit; Sororem suam contaminatam priùs toxico interemerit; Matrem item & Nepotem, ut omnis ad se confluerent Farnesiorum hæreditas; Quòd in tabulis 45000. meretrices numeratas habuerit, atque ex illarum quæstu menstruum censum exegerit; Quòd cum Laura Farnesia Nepte sua, sed Nicolai Quercæi uxore congrediens ab hoc vulnus, cicatrice ad mortem usque manente, acceperit; Quòd Magicæ Astrologiæ addictus Dionysium Servitam ejus artis nomine celebrem Cardinalem fecerit, & Gauricum Lusitanum ac Cæcium Marcellum in ea superstitione peritos socios ac familiares semper habuerit, ut sua ac nothorum suorum fata in horoscopis & siderum domiciliis inquireret; Prout etiam Dæmon ei ex antica nummi parte obscurè conjuratores indicâsse dicitur; Et Thuanus Hist. l. 4. testatur, cum Divinationem Astrologicam judiciariam palàm adamâsse, exercuisse & per eam cuncta sua negotia direxisse, ejus denique mystam Lucam Gauricum in sinu suo fovisse, & Episcopatu Civitatensi donâsse. Superbiam prodidit,dum in vita Sixti V. p.1.p.71. Lucæ à Carolo V. ter visitatus semel tantùm respondit. Eidem nonnulli tribuunt,quòd moriturus dixerit, se jam experturum veritatem trium quæstionum,de quibus semper dubitârit,videlicet; an sit 1. anima rationalis. 2. Deus. 3. infernus.
units.tr: For the following and other horrible things are told of him. To become a cardinal, he gave his sister Julia to be debauched by Alexander VI. While legate at Ancona, and assuming the guise of a legate of one of the nobles, he violated a noble girl under the colour of a promise of marriage; when she realised the error, she nearly fell into madness. From that cohabitation he begot Pier Luigi, a monster of a man rather than a man, who, because of his intolerable tyranny, was finally slaughtered at Piacenza by his own nobles, hung from the wall, stabbed with daggers, kicked, and thrown into a ditch. He kept his daughter Costanza as a pleasure while he was pope, and, so that he might enjoy her more freely, he removed her husband Bosio Sforza by poison. He killed by poison his sister, who had been defiled earlier; likewise his mother and his nephew, so that the whole Farnese inheritance would flow to him. He had 45,000 prostitutes entered on his lists and exacted a monthly tax from their earnings. Dealing with Laura Farnese, his niece but the wife of Niccolò Quercia, he received from her a wound which remained as a scar until death. Given over to magical astrology, he made Dionysius the Servite, famous in that art, a cardinal, and always kept as companions and intimates Gauricus of Portugal and Cecco Marcello, skilled in that superstition, so that he might inquire into his own and his bastards' fates in horoscopes and the houses of the stars. As well, a demon is said to have obscurely pointed out conspirators to him from the front of a coin. And Thuanus, Hist. l. 4, testifies that, since he openly loved, practised and through it directed all his affairs, judicial astrological divination, he finally cherished in his bosom his initiate Luca Gaurico and gave him the bishopric of Civitate. He showed pride when, visited three times by Charles V, as recorded in the Life of Sixtus V, p. 1, p. 71, he replied only once. Some attribute to the same man that, when about to die, he said he would now experience the truth of three questions about which he had always doubted, namely: 1. whether the rational soul exists; 2. God; 3. hell.

units.la: LXIII. Cùm de eligendo Successore Julio III. ageretur, Cardinalis Guisius ad Legatum Galliæ scripsit,ut significaret Regi,quanto indegnamente detto Monti essercitasse il Sacerdotio,quàm indignè Cardinalis de Monte (ita vocabatur in Cardinalatu) exercuerit Sacerdotium; Idem tamen ad ejus Electionem tandem concurrit. Sed & Onuphrius in vita testatur,id ante Pontificatum ei vitio datum fuisse,quòd nimiis indulgeret voluptatibus, quæ tamen res, dum privatus sub alieno imperio fuit, cum minimè à publicis muneribus avocabat; Atque tandem in fine monet:Si vita, quam privatus egit,institutum, Pontificatum quoque adeptus constanter servâsset,multa, quæ eo tempore depravata erant,in meliorem haud dubiè formam essent restituta. Qui namque occupationibus totus intentus Cardinalis veluti furtim voluptates sequebatur,Ponntifex factus votorum jam omnium compos,abdicatâ rerum curâ, hilaritati & genio suo nimium indulsit, usque adeò homines, ita pergit, præmii spe potius ad virtutem amplectandam,quam ipsamet virtutis pulchritudine accenduntur. Eidem II Nipot. p.2. p.239. tribuitur, quòd unicè cum suis conviviorum gaudia secutus parùm de Ecclesia sollicitus fuerit. Tandem ei apud eundem Onuphrium vitio datum, quòd tanta potestatis oblitus omniam maximi muneris dignitatem parùm animadvertens,levibus & inanibus verbis suam aliquando majestatem non sine audientium rubore aut risu minuerit. Quàm piè in conviviis suis se gesserit,arguunt verba ejus blasphema apud Baleum de Pap.l.7 p.517.518. Affer ferculum, al dispetto di Dio; & sequentia eódem recidentia,cùm ob pavonem non appositum irato Cardinalis moderationem in re tantilla suaderet,effusa: Si voluit Deus usque adeò propter unum pomum irasci, ut ejecerit primos parentes ex Paradiso,cur non liceat mihi,qui sum ejus Vicarius, irasci propter pavonem, cùm multò major res sit pavo quàm pomum? Quàm autem prodigiosæ libidinis Julius fuisse non sine causa videatur Dissert.IV. Sect.II. n. 86. notatum est; Ubi quoque exhibuimus ingenuam Pontificis de se confessionem ad Cardinales dicentis:Et vos quid tandem in me meritorum comperistis, quem Christianæ Reip. Principem constitueretis? Ipse rursus Pallavicinus licet omnia quàm mollissimè proferens, corruptioni hominis testimonium monium perhibet, palàm l.43. 10. 8. confessus, pronum eum fuisse ad laxamenta: suum sanguinem deamavisse, æstimatione tenui, nec majori benevolentia mortuum esse, quandam ipsius libertatem ac familiaritatem, qua ipsi privatam gerenti personam amorem inter æquales conciliaverant, in excelso postea Principis gradu venerationem minuisse; ipsius vitia majora quidem quoad speciem fuisse, quàm virtutes, sed non fortasse quoad pondus. Levitatem ejus nudè quasi cum Cardinalibus obambulantis, his ad quæstionem; Quid de nobis dicerent homines? respondentibus: Judicarent, nos esse nebulones & conjicerent in nos rudera atque lapides; illo inferente: Ergò, quòd non habemur pro nebulonibus, id acceptum ferre debemus nostris vestibus. Quantum igitur, ô fratres, debemus illi nostris vestibus! Cel. Heideggerus ex vita MSC. & Ven. Bullingero Hist. Pap. n. CLXXVII. enarrat. Onuphrio autem sunt, qui constanter affirment, Julium sibi ipsi mortem intulisse, dum nimirum languorem fingens atque ea de causa solitis cibis abstinens, eòsque parcius ac in solidos ægroto scilicet aptos sumens ex ea vita ratione ludibrio commutata, morbum serió contraxit, qui eum jam senem brevissimè absumpsit.
units.tr: LXIII. When the successor to Julius III was being chosen, Cardinal Guise wrote to the Legate of France that he should tell the King how unworthily the said Monti exercised the priesthood, and how unworthily Cardinal de Monte (that was his name as a cardinal) exercised the priesthood. Yet the same man nonetheless joined in electing him. Onuphrius, in his Life, also testifies that he was faulted before his pontificate for indulging his pleasures too much, though while he was a private man under another's rule this did not draw him away from public duties. Finally he warns at the end: If the life he lived as a private man, together with the discipline he had adopted, had been constantly kept up after he gained the pontificate, many things that were corrupt at that time would undoubtedly have been restored to a better form. For the cardinal, wholly absorbed in his duties, followed his pleasures as if secretly; but once made pope and in possession of all he had longed for, he set aside care for affairs and gave himself too freely to cheerfulness and his own inclinations, so that men, he goes on, are kindled to embrace virtue more by the hope of reward than by the very beauty of virtue. The second Nipot. ascribes to him, p.2 p.239, that following only the pleasures of his banquets, he was little concerned about the Church. Onuphrius, in the same place, also faults him for forgetting how great was his power, and, paying little attention to the dignity of his very great office, sometimes diminished his majesty by light and empty words, not without the blushes or laughter of his hearers. How piously he conducted himself at his banquets is shown by his blasphemous words reported by Bale, de Pap. l.7 p.517.518: Bring in the dish, in spite of God! and the words that follow, spoken in the same spirit when, angry because a peacock had not been served, he was urged to moderate his anger over so trifling a matter: If God was so angry over one apple that he cast our first parents out of Paradise, why should it not be lawful for me, who am his Vicar, to be angry over a peacock, since a peacock is a much greater thing than an apple?
