That Julius was not without reason thought to have been monstrously lustful has been noted in Dissert. IV, Sect. II, n. 86, where we also set out the pope's candid confession about himself, spoken to the cardinals: And what, pray, have you found in me that merits making me the prince of the Christian commonwealth? Pallavicini himself, though he presents everything in the mildest terms, nonetheless bears witness to human corruption, openly confessing l.43 10.8 that he was prone to indulgence; that he loved his own blood with little esteem and was no more kindly disposed toward his kin when dead; that a certain freedom and familiarity he had shown when a private person, which had won him friendship among his equals, lessened the reverence owed to him once he rose to the lofty rank of prince; and that his vices were greater in kind than his virtues, though perhaps not in weight. His levity, when he walked about openly with the cardinals, is recorded by Cel. Heideggerus from the manuscript Life and by Ven. Bullinger, Hist. Pap. n. CLXXVII. When they answered his question, What would men say of us? with They would judge us to be scoundrels and would throw rubble and stones at us, he replied: Then, since we are not taken for scoundrels, we must thank our clothes for it. How much, then, brothers, we owe to our clothes! Some firmly assert, as Onuphrius reports, that Julius brought about his own death: feigning illness and for that reason abstaining from his usual food, and eating sparingly and only what was suited to an invalid, he turned his way of life into a mockery of himself, and so seriously contracted a disease that it carried off the old man within a very short time.

units.la: LXIV. Paulum IV. Julii Successorem ita sollicitè commendat Onuphrius in Vita, ut dicat:
units.tr: LXIV. Onuphrius so earnestly commends Paul IV, Julius's successor, in his Life, that he says:

units.la: Si quid à Rom. Pontificibus Paulo & Julio, sub quibus Cardinalem gessit, forte referretur quod non ita ex Apostolica sedis (cujus unius commodum ante omnia propositum sibi habere dicebat) dignitate esse censeret, vel consilio aberat, vel, si interesset, non assentiebat. Cujus rei plura & maximè memorabilia exempla exstant &c. Idem tamen nimiam severitatem ejus, imò maximam erga innocuos multos sibi injustè delatos crudelitatem, bellum item Hispanis sine causa & ex veteri odio motum, nec non odium populi & statuæ probra, de quibus Dissert. IV. Sect. III. n. 16. commemorat. Vitio ex hypothesi non caruit illud, quòd hæreticorum ex hypothesi in bello opera usus est; Rhætorum nimirum in ipsa Urbe, che chiama-va, narrat Author Vitæ Patris Pauli p.154. Angeli da Dio mandati gli à diffesa; quos vocavit Angelos sibi à Deo in auxilium missos. Superbiam summam Oratione ad Oratores his maximè verbis prodidit, se Regibus cunctis esse superiorem, nolle se arctam cum quovis familiaritatem: sibi concessam regnorum immutandorum potestatem. Avaritiæ documentum est, quòd juxta narrationem Authoris Nepotismi, cùm profundè cogitans Cardinali Campeggio astaret, cur id fiat, interrogatus, respondit; Se cogitare, num ille ditior sit futurus, si illi sibi succedere forte contingeret. Omnia paucis complectitur Joannis Abbatis deeo Oraculum: Intrabit velut Draco, sedebit velut alter Leo, immitis in populo. Quod & turbis in orbe excitatis complevit.
units.tr: If anything were reported of the Roman pontiffs Paul and Julius, under whom he served as cardinal, which he judged not to be in keeping with the dignity of the Apostolic See (whose advantage alone he said he had always set before himself above all), he was either absent from the counsel, or, if he was present, he did not consent. Many examples of this, especially memorable ones, survive, etc. Yet the same writer records his excessive severity, indeed his very great cruelty toward many innocent men falsely denounced to him, the war against the Spanish, begun without cause and out of an old hatred, and also the people's hatred and the reproaches hurled at his statues, of which Dissert. IV, Sect. III, n. 16 speaks. He was not free of a vice, on his own hypothesis, in that he used the services of heretics in war, namely the Rhaetians in the very City, who were called, as the author of the Life of Pope Paul relates, p.154, Angels sent to them by God for their defence; he called them angels sent to him by God as help. He betrayed his great pride in an address to the ambassadors, especially in these words: that he was superior to all kings, that he did not wish to be on close terms with anyone, and that the power to change kingdoms had been granted to him. A sign of his avarice is that, according to the account of the author of Nepotismus, when he stood deep in thought beside Cardinal Campeggio, and was asked why he did so, he answered: I was considering whether he would become richer if it should happen that he succeeded me. Joachim the Abbot's prophecy sums up everything briefly: He will enter like a dragon, will sit like another lion, fierce toward the people. And he fulfilled this by stirring up upheavals throughout the world.

units.la: LXV. Qui post Paulum IV. praefuit, Pius IV. Pontifex creatus à nonnullis sequentes voces gratulatorias accepit: Impius es tu, Pater tuus latro erat, mater tua meretrix, quomodo huc intrâsti? De quo videri potest Marnixii Alvear. Rom. p. 6. c. 3. Idem Paulo IV. minus gratus fuit, qui in illum publicè in Consistorio & aperte invectus fuerat, quòd ex non bonis artibus Archiepiscopatum Mediolanensem procurâsse diceret. Quod narrat Onuphrius. Coronationis ejus die, juxta eundem, circiter 18. homines eâ turbâ necati, supra 40. luxati & elisi, quod miserabile spectaculum fuit, ac à quibusdam ad ipsius Pontificis res gestas pro omine relatum. Initio Pontificatu statim alienam personam, alienos mores induisse visus est. Nam qui hactenus humanus, patiens, beneficus, gratus, mitis, pecuniæ minimè cupidus existimatus fuerat, derepente naturam mutâsse apparebat &c. Vel eorum memor, quæ in suî contumeliam Cardinalis Carafa in Conclavi dixerat, vel Ducis Paliani regia pro Ducatu Paliani compensatione (ut fama fuit) pro sororis filio inhians, aut (quod ipse ajebat) ut Rom. Pontificum propinquis salutare exemplum præberet, Cardinalem & Gubernatorem Carafas judicio plerorumque eo tempore ICtorum iniquè strangulari curavit. Hæc omnia Onuphrius in vita: De qualitatibus vitiosis ejus ita loquitur: Erat verbis & scommatibus acutus, cibi viníque avidus, sed in prandio profusus, in Cœna parcus, involuptates pronus, palam iracundus, occultè invidus, ad audiendum impatiens & difficilis, in responsis aliquando acerbus, dominandi cupidus, vafer, cujuslibet rei, quæ ignorari suâ interesset, simulator ac dissimulator, timidus, audax tamen ad occultandam audacia specie formidinem, parùm gratus est habitus. Patres, & eos præsertim, quorum operâ Pontificatum & alios honores obtinuerat, neglexit. Pecuniæ cupidus, ac ad aurum excipiendum etiam cum alieno detrimento attentus, ad servandum verò parum cautus. Nam quæ excepit, cuncta pene liberalissimè absumpsit. Ferunt enim, eo Pontifice H.S. bis millies haustum. Amicitias non ex re, sed ex commodo æstimabat. In propinquorum amore varius, nam sororum filiis nimis indulsit: Fratrem verò Augustum Marchionem Melenianî, cui ex privatis odiis infensus erat, nunquam dilexit, ita ut eximias ejus virtutes non mediocres defectus observare viderentur. Subjungit post felicitatem in aliis positam: Miserum fuisse quis inficiabitur, si aviditatem, iracundiam, in Rep. administrandu impatientiam æstimabimus: ita ut difficile sit, perfectum illum Principem invenire, qui illustri virtutum temperamento mento vitæ suæ cursum instituens, eum usque ad extremum integrum inla-súmque perducat. Videri etiam potest iisdem fere in describendis Pontificis qualitatibus verbis utens Thuanus lib. 38 maximè de pronitate ad voluptates; Et apud eundem l.35. Caroli IX. adversus Pontificis hujus diploma querelæ vitium in actionibus notant & probant; Ut & in actionibus Pontificum priorum, quòd nimirum nonnisi summo Ecclesiæ dedecore, & quietis publica detrimento in Germania & alibi Principes Regnis exuerint & de eorum possessi-nibus pro arbitrio statuerint. Quæ autem de ingratitudine testa est Onuphrius, ea etiam calculo suo confirmat Author Conclavis Pii V. dum nimirum ei in causa Carafarum tribuit un atroce ingratitudine sotto pretesto di giustitia, atrocem sub justitiæ prætextu ingratitudinem, eámque erga Pontificem Prædecessorem. Vanitatem notat idem qui suprà Thuanus sequentibus l. 26. verbis: Roma, inquit, novus Pontifex jam renudato animo de re publica ferè securus, tantùm privatis commodu & caritatibus indulgebat, & quoniam fraterna vanitatis æmulatione nomen & insignia Medicea gentis usurpaverat, ut quanti Cosmum familiæ Principem faceret, re testaretur, ante omnia Joannem, ipsius secundum filium, vix XIV. egressum, in Cardinalium Collegium cooptavit. Mors detestanda ex nimio Veneris abusu fuit; hinc de eo dictum, quòd per eandem partem vitam effuderit, per quam acceperat. Quæ etiam modesto Thuani l. cit. 38. testimonio confirmantur. Pontifex, ait, ex morbo ex vita intemperanter acta contracto, tandem octavo agritudinis die decessit. Et paulò post: In victu cibi viníque profusus, & in voluptates pronus, qua ei supremum diem accelerâsse credunmr.
units.tr: LXV. Pius IV, who came after Paul IV, was created pope, and some greeted him with these cheering words: You are a wicked man; your father was a robber, your mother a whore. How did you get in here? On this one may consult Marnix, Alvear. Rom. p.6 c.3. The same man was less pleasing to Paul IV, who had openly attacked him in consistory and in public, saying that he had obtained the archbishopric of Milan by dishonest means. Onuphrius reports this. On the day of his coronation, according to the same writer, about eighteen men were killed in the crush and more than forty were crippled and crushed, a miserable spectacle, which some took as an omen for the deeds of the pope himself. At the start of his pontificate he seemed at once to have put on another person and other manners. For he who had hitherto been thought humane, patient, beneficent, agreeable, gentle, and not greedy for money, suddenly appeared to have changed his nature, etc. Whether mindful of the insults Cardinal Carafa had uttered against him in the conclave, or longing, as rumour had it, for the royal fief of the Duchy of Paliano as compensation for his sister's son, or, as he himself said, so that he might offer a salutary example to the kinsmen of the Roman pontiffs, he saw to it that the Cardinal and Governor Carafa was unjustly strangled, in the judgment of most jurists of that time. Onuphrius records all this in the Life. He describes his vicious qualities thus: He was sharp in words and jests, greedy for food and wine, lavish at lunch but sparing at supper, prone to pleasures, openly quick to anger, secretly envious, impatient and hard to deal with in listening, at times harsh in his replies, eager to dominate, crafty, a pretender and dissembler in whatever matter it was his interest to keep hidden, timid, yet bold in covering his fear with a show of audacity. He was held to be little grateful. He neglected the Fathers, and especially those by whose work he had obtained the pontificate and his other honours. He was greedy for money and, in collecting gold, intent on it even at another's loss, but careless in keeping it. For what he received he almost wholly spent very lavishly. They report that under this pope H.S. was spent two thousand times over. He valued friendships not by their worth but by their profit. He was fickle in his affection for kinsmen, for he indulged his sisters' sons too much; but he never loved his brother Augustus, Marquis of Melegnano, against whom he was hostile from private hatreds, so that his outstanding virtues seemed to be marked by no small defects. After describing his good qualities, Onuphrius adds: Who could deny that it was unhappy that he was greedy, quick to anger, and impatient in governing the commonwealth? So that it is hard to find that perfect prince who, setting out on the course of his life with a splendid mixture of virtues, carries it through to the end whole and unstained. The same sort of description of the pope's qualities is given by Thuanus, lib. 38, especially as to his inclination to pleasures. And in the same author, lib. 35, the complaints of Charles IX against this pope's edict note and prove faults in his conduct; as they do in the conduct of earlier popes, who, to the great dishonour of the Church and the public harm, stripped princes of their kingdoms in Germany and elsewhere, and decided their possessions at will. What Onuphrius has said about his ingratitude, the author of the Conclave of Pius V also confirms, since he ascribes to him in the case of the Carafas a monstrous ingratitude under the pretext of justice, and that toward his predecessor the pope. The same Thuanus, in the following words, notes his vanity: At Rome, he says, the new pope, his mind now stripped of concern for the commonwealth and almost free of care, indulged only private advantages and affections; and since, out of a brotherly rivalry in vanity, he had taken the name and insignia of the Medici family, to show by deed how much he valued Cosimo, the head of the family, above all he admitted to the college of cardinals John, Cosimo's second son, scarcely fourteen years old. His death was detestable, the result of excessive abuse of Venus; hence it was said of him that he poured out his life through the same part through which he had received it. This is confirmed by the moderate testimony of Thuanus, l. cit. 38: The pope, he says, died on the eighth day of his illness, a sickness contracted from a life lived intemperately. And a little later: He was lavish in food and wine, and prone to pleasures, which are believed to have hastened his last day.

units.la: LXVI. Pium V. multò multis meliorem atque Beatorum posthac Catalogo adscriptum non sine ingentibus nævis fuisse sequentia probant. Ejus enim jam tum defuncti apud Thuanum Hist. l. 39. ad an. 1566. hæc sunt elogia: Pontifex creatus jurisdictionem, quam sub aliis tantâ severitate exercuerat, & ipse severissimè exercuit, & per alios, cum magna nec toleranda multorum vexatione, exercendam curavit, populo ad ejus electionis famam fremente & indignante, nam injuriarum tenacissimus erat. Et l.51. ad an.1572. Negligentiâ suâ & difficilis ad querelas accessu effecit, ut dum Reip. parùm gnarus minimè ad eam attendit, suorum, quos, more aulæ illi insito, rerum gubernaculis admoverat, rapacitati porta aperta sit, qui avarè & insolenter sub eo impunè grassati sunt diu. Quibus addi potest ipsius Pontificis nota de se confessio fio : Religiosus cùm essem, bene de salute mea speravi, Cardinalis creatus extimui, factus Pontifex pone desspero. Idem Veritatem ejúsque Confessores gravissimè persecutus est, non paucos Romæ de Inquisitione liberiùs loquentes vivicomburio punivit, turbas ob Religionem excitavit, auxit; ut & Successor Gregorius XIII. de horribili Laniena Parisiensi publicè tum aliis signis, tum etiam Monetâ, in cujus altera parte: Hugonotorum Strages; indignè & Antichristianè laetatus est.
units.tr: LXVI. Pius V, though far better than many and later enrolled among the Blessed, was not without great blemishes, as the following show. The elogies of him, already dead, in Thuanus, Hist. book 39, under the year 1566, are these: The Pontiff, once created, exercised the jurisdiction which he had exercised under others with such severity, and he himself exercised it most severely, and through others saw to its exercise, with great and intolerable vexation of many, while the people murmured and were indignant at the news of his election, for he was most tenacious of injuries. And book 51, under the year 1572: By his negligence and by being hard to approach with complaints, it came about that, while he, little acquainted with the affairs of the state, paid no attention to them, a door was opened to the greed of his own men, whom he had raised to the helm of affairs in the courtly manner ingrained in him, and who acted avariciously and insolently under him with impunity for a long time. To these may be added the Pontiff's own confession about himself: When I was a religious, I hoped well of my salvation; when I was made Cardinal, I feared; now that I am Pontiff, I despair. The same man most grievously persecuted the Truth and its Confessors; he punished by burning alive not a few at Rome who spoke rather freely about the Inquisition, and he stirred up and increased disturbances on account of religion. So too his successor Gregory XIII rejoiced publicly, unworthily and unchristianly, over the horrible slaughter in Paris, both by other signs and even by a coin, on one side of which was inscribed: The Slaughter of the Huguenots.

units.la: LXVII. Sixti V. vita à Gregorio Leti descripta atque à nobis sæpe hactenus citata, non dissentiente, quoad usque se extendit, Onuphrii narratione, hominem à porcorum grege usque ad culmen Pontificatûs solâ ambitione eâque plane extraordinariâ animatum exhibet.
units.tr: LXVII. The life of Sixtus V described by Gregorio Leti, and cited by us often hitherto, does not dissent, as far as it extends, from the narrative of Onuphrius. It presents the man as one who rose from a herd of swine to the summit of the papacy, driven by ambition alone, and that quite extraordinary ambition.

units.la: Exhibet hominem profanum, sermonibus variis quoque pro tali proditum; Qualis ille occasione separationis Anglicæ ob divortium Regis à Paulo III. non approbatum factæ prolatus; Pontificis parùm interesse, an Reges fœminas pro meretricibus, an meretrices pro fœminis habeant; Atque ille, quotiescunque ei aliquid adversi contingeret, atque eum pœniteret, quòd non cum 2. aliis, Monasterio derelicto, in Galliam, ubi Religionem mutârunt, concessisset: Sia maledetto quel giorno, che non mi seppe risolvere ad andarmine in Francia. Id est: Maledictus sit dies, quo non in Galliam aufugere apud me decernere potui; Quem sermonem, qui sæpiùs audiverant, heretico d'imaginatione, hereticum in imaginatione Sixtum vocârunt, atque ei diffidere coeperunt. Nec non hic egredientis ex Monasterio Anconitano: Il Diavolo mi porti, se verrò più in questo convento. Id est; Diabolus me auferat, si amplius in hoc Monasterium ingressus fuero. Et alius, cùm non potuisset eligi Provincialis Marcæ, & postea illuc tamen ire deberet: Che sarebbe andato più tosto nell' inferno, che nella Marca. Id est; Se potius ad inferos, quàm in Marcam iturum fuisse. De castitate Monachali notandum, che in breve devienne tanto acciecato d'amore (erga Beatricem meretricem, quæ ad irretiendos Monachos frequenter accedere solebat;) Che un giorno la condusse nel Coro, mà non potè farlo tanto segreto, che il superiore non lo coglielle nel fatto. Id est; eum brevi adeò amore Beatricis occaecatum fuisse, ut eam aliquando in Chorum duxerit, quod tamen non tam occultè facere potuit, ut non à superiori in ipso facto deprehensus sit. Qualia illa sint, quæ Author Vitæ à Secretario Secretorum Montaltii participe, postquam ab eo discessisset, sparserit, Lectori conjiciendum relinquo. Si diede, inquit quit Author, a parlar di cento materie, che non voglio scriverle per honestà. Id est: Loqui coepit de mille rebus, quas scripto consignare pudore deterreor; Relinquo etiam in dubio, num verae fuerint suspiciones atque accusationes Fratrum Monachorum ob juvenem continuò lateri adhaerentem, & in cellam saepe contrà mandatum introductum. Quàm gratus suis fuerit, vel ex eo cognosci potest, quòd, cùm Provincialis eligi vellet, multi fuerunt, che haurebbono dato il voto più tosto al Demonio, qui suffragio suo potius Diabolum ipsum juvissent: Certè Monachus sine obedientia fuit, omnibus contrarius, contrariantibus haud minùs omnibus illi. Simulationes ejus atque dissimulationes plane impias atque cum profanatione Divini Nominis saepiùs iterata conjunctas suis locis exhibuimus. In Pontificatu usque ad crudelitatem severum se praestitit, quod & ipsa quoque ejus natura quasi testata est, aliquando enim, teste Thuano l. 32: lachrymas cruentas fundere & sanguinem pro sudore toto corpore emittere visus fuit. Quemadmodum etiam apud eundem Thuanum l. 95. superbo seni petulantia exprobratur, qui censura iniquissima fulmine in immerentem Henricum III. vibrato, funestissimam tragoediam in Gallia excitâssèt, & nunc, laudato parricidio in eo commisso, jacenti summâ impietate insultaret, & ipse lepus mortuo Leoni barbam velleret. Multa contrà Religionis Pontificiae hypotheses & dixit & fecit. Sanguinem Principum immaniter sitiit. In auro atque argento corradendis totus fuit; Prout etiam Il Nip. p. 381. docet, eum maximam diei partem curis istis impendisse, atque creditum fuisse, morientem adhuc talibus detentum fuisse, cùm à Ministro Veneto duobus ante mortem diebus interrogatus; quomodo valeat? respondVerit: Mi portarei meglio, s'havessi più danari da spendere: Melius valerem, si haberem plus argenti ad sumptus faciendos. Vindictae cupidissimus atque in ea exercenda acerrimus. Et si Hispanis (quibus Regnum Neapolitanum eripere volebat;) atque Jesuitis (quibus tanquam nimis divitibus 20000. coronatos abstulit, & de quibus, cùm Confessorem Jesuitam Sixto dare vellent, dixit; Che sarebbe meglio per l'a chiesa, che i Giesuiti si confessassero al Papa, che non già il Papa a' Gesuiti. Id est; Melius atque Ecclesia utilius fore, si Jesuita Papa confiterent, quàm si Papa confiteretur Jesuitis;) fides habenda, il Diavolo, col quale tenne il Navarrista intelligenza, venne e lo portò via, Diabolus cum quo communionem habuit Navarrista (ita, quia post recriminationes Henrici, tum Navarrae Regis & datum nebulonis elogium. gium, minùs se ei deinceps adversum exhibuit ab Hispanizantibus tum Jesuitis vocatus) venit & eum abstulit, quae Nobilissimi Sandis in Relatione de statu Religionis verba sunt. Videatur de his etiam Bartholomæus Morisolus Divionensis ICtus Vita Henrici M. c. 17. ubi quoque meminit, librum de ejus vita scriptum fuisse, typisque mandatum, ubi scelera omnia, quibus Alexander VI. aspersus fuerit, Author & invenerit & exaggeraverit. Sic etiam post eum libellis editis Clemens VIII. omnis generis criminum praeter ortus vitium, veneficii, homicidii, Simoniae, Sodomiae, perjurii, scortationis, plagii, sacrilegii, Magiae &c. reus factus est. De eodem Galli in refutatione libelli Italici contra Protestationem Lavardini editi p. 10. Les Brefs de Clement VIII. pour exhorter les Ligueurs à elire un Roy à la place de Henry IV. ne feront jamais l'eloge de ce Pape, mais ils rendront odieux à toute la posterité l'usage pernicieux de cette puissance sans bornes, que nous ne connoissons point en France.
units.tr: It presents a profane man, also shown by various sayings, such as the one he uttered on the occasion of the English separation over the King's divorce, which was not approved by Paul III: It matters little to the Pontiff whether kings take women for whores or whores for women. And whenever something adverse happened to him and he regretted that he had not, like two others, left the monastery and gone to France, where they changed their religion, he would say: Cursed be that day on which I could not make up my mind to go off to France. That is: Cursed be the day on which I could not decide to flee to France. Those who had often heard this saying called Sixtus a heretic in imagination, a heretic in imagination, and began to distrust him. Likewise this one, leaving the monastery at Ancona: The devil take me if I ever enter this convent again. That is: May the devil take me if I ever enter this monastery again. And another, when he could not be elected Provincial of the Marches, yet afterwards had to go there: That he would sooner go to hell than to the Marches. That is: that he would sooner go to the infernal regions than into the Marches. Concerning monastic chastity it should be noted that he soon became so blinded by love (for Beatrice, a whore who was accustomed to come often to ensnare the monks) that one day he led her into the choir, but could not do it so secretly that the superior did not catch him in the act. That is: he was soon so blinded by love for Beatrice that at one time he led her into the choir, yet he could not do this so discreetly that he was not caught in the act by his superior. What the author of the Life, who became a sharer in the secrets of Montalto after leaving him, scattered about such things, I leave to the reader to conjecture. He began, says the author, to talk of a hundred matters, which I do not wish to write down out of decency. That is: he began to speak of a thousand things which I am restrained from committing to writing by shame. I also leave in doubt whether the suspicions and accusations of the Brother Monks were true, concerning the young man who constantly clung to his side and was often brought into the cell, contrary to the order. How agreeable he was to his own people may be known even from this, that when he wished to be elected Provincial, there were many who would sooner have given their vote to the Devil, who would have helped him more with their suffrage. Certainly he was a monk without obedience, opposed by all and in turn opposing all. We have set out in their places his simulations and dissimulations, quite impious and often repeated together with the profanation of the Divine Name. In the papacy he showed himself severe even to cruelty, which his very nature seems to have borne witness to, for at times, according to Thuanus, book 32, he was seen to shed bloody tears and to send out blood instead of sweat over his whole body. Likewise in the same Thuanus, book 95, the proud old man is reproached for his wantonness, since he had hurled the most unjust censure like a thunderbolt at the undeserving Henry III, stirred up a most deadly tragedy in France, and now, praising the parricide committed in him, insulted the fallen man with the greatest impiety, and like a hare pulled the beard of the dead lion. He both said and did many things contrary to the principles of the Papist religion. He thirsted immensely for the blood of princes. He was wholly absorbed in gathering gold and silver, as the Il Nip. p. 381. also teaches, that he spent most of the day on these cares, and it was believed that he was still occupied with them even while dying, for when the Venetian Minister asked him two days before his death how he was, he answered: I would be better if I had more money to spend. He was most eager for vengeance and most fierce in exacting it. And as for the Spaniards, from whom he wished to snatch the Kingdom of Naples, and the Jesuits, from whom, as if they were too rich, he took 20,000 crowns, and about whom, when they wished to give him a Jesuit as confessor, he said: It would be better for the Church if the Jesuits confessed to the Pope than if the Pope confessed to the Jesuits. That is: it would be more useful for the Church if Jesuit confessed to the Pope than if the Pope confessed to the Jesuits. Let this be believed: the Devil, with whom the Navarrist had an understanding, came and carried him off. The words the Devil with whom the Navarrist had fellowship (so called by the Spanish-minded and Jesuits, because after the recriminations of Henry, then King of Navarre, and the title given him of scoundrel, he showed himself less hostile to him from then on) are those of the most noble Sandys in his Relation on the state of Religion. On these matters see also Bartholomew Morisolus, a civil lawyer of Dijon, Life of Henry the Great, ch. 17, where he also mentions that a book about his life was written and printed, in which the author found and exaggerated all the crimes with which Alexander VI was smeared. So too, after him, by pamphlets published, Clement VIII was made accused of every kind of crime except incest, poisoning, homicide, simony, sodomy, perjury, fornication, kidnapping, sacrilege, magic, etc. Of the same man the French, in the refutation of an Italian pamphlet against the Protestation of Lavardin, p. 10: The Briefs of Clement VIII to exhort the Leaguers to elect a king in place of Henry IV will never bring praise to this Pope, but will make the pernicious use of this unlimited power, which we do not know in France, hateful to all posterity.

units.la: LXVIII. Pauli V. Vice-Dei, quosipse titulos admisit superbia tumens, Christiana Republica Monarcha invictissimi, Pontificiae omnipotentia conservatoris acerrimi, genius ex sequentibus, quae Author Vita Patris Pauli, & ipse Guerra di Paolo V. &c. l.1. p.7. habet, cognosci potest, non usque quaque mitem Christum atque Christianum à Divinationibus alienum animum referens:
units.tr: LXVIII. Of Paul V, Vicar of God, a title he himself admitted while swelling with pride; Monarch of the Christian Republic, most unconquered, and most fierce defender of Papal omnipotence. His character can be recognised from the following passages, which the author of the Vita Patris Pauli, and he himself in Guerra di Paolo V. &c. l.1. p.7., report, showing a mind by no means gentle, Christian, or averse to divinations.

units.la: La natura, inquit ipse, del Pontefice inclinata e solita à prestar fede alle divinationi, la quale da ogni cosa pigliava alimento per il suo timore——licentiò per questa cosa il cuoco suo——se qualche persona bassa & non conosciuta da lui nell' andare per la città li porgeva memoriali, temeva per quello esser avvelenato & bene spesso li lasciava cader in terra &c. Id est. Genius Pontificis proni ad Divinationes & iis fidem adhibere solentis, qui undiquaque materiam metus arripuit——Dimisit ea de causa coquum suum——Si aliquis humilis conditionis & ignotus ei per Urbem iter facienti Memorialia porrexit, statim sic veneno infici timuit, atque saepe porrecta in terram cadere sivit &c. Qui autem Vitam Patris scripsit p.77. causas ortae inter Pontificem & Venetos litis sequentes enarrat: O perche nel tempo, che su Auditore della Camera, haveva preso grand' inclinatione, à fulminar censure, ò perche fosse poco bene affetto alla Serenissima Rep. di Venetia, ò perche fosse instigato da alcuni Religiosi (come io tengo da certo e n'ho argumenti chiari) ch' à guisa di vipera stracciano e auvellevano il petto del stato, che gli nudrisce &c. Id est: Vel quia, dum esset Auditor Camera, ingens fulminandi censuras desiderium concepit, vel, quia male
units.tr: The nature, he says, of the Pontiff, inclined and accustomed to give credence to divinations, which took nourishment from everything out of fear; he dismissed his cook for this reason; if some person of low condition and unknown to him, as he walked through the city, handed him petitions, he feared he would be poisoned by it, and very often let them fall to the ground, etc. That is: the disposition of a Pontiff prone to divinations and accustomed to give them credence, who seized material for fear from every quarter. He dismissed his cook on that account. If some humble man unknown to him offered him memorials as he made his way through the City, he at once feared poisoning and often let the papers fall to the ground, etc. The author who wrote the Life of the Father, p. 77, relates the following causes of the dispute between the Pontiff and the Venetians: Either because, when he was Auditor of the Camera, he conceived a great inclination to hurl censures, or because he was poorly disposed towards the Most Serene Venetian Republic, or because he was instigated by certain religious (as I hold for certain, and have clear proofs), who, like vipers, tear and rend the breast of the state that nourishes them, etc. That is: Either because, while he was Auditor of the Camera, he conceived a huge desire to thunder censures, or because he was ill-disposed towards the Venetian Republic, or because he was incited by certain religious men (he means the Jesuits), which is most certain to me from clear arguments, who like vipers tear and poison the breast of the state that feeds them. Whatever the cause (and they may well have been combined), it was an evil thing and a proof of an unjust father.

units.la: Ex Secu-lo XVII. Pauli V. male Serenissimæ Venetorum Reip. affectus fuit; Vel, quia instigatus fuit à quibusdam Religiosis, (Jesuitas intelligit) (quod mihi certissimum est ex argumentis claris) qui viperarum ad instar disrumpunt atque inficiunt pectus flatûs,qui eos nutrit. Quæcunque causa fuerit (conjunctæ autem esse potuerunt) mala fuit atque injusti Patris argumentum.
units.tr: From the seventeenth century. Paul V was ill-disposed towards the Most Serene Venetian Republic. Or, he was instigated by certain religious men (he means the Jesuits), which is most certain to me from clear arguments, who tear apart and poison the breast of the state that nourishes them, like vipers. Whatever the cause (and they may well have been combined), it was an evil thing and a proof of an unjust father.

units.la: LXIX. Urbani VIII. vitium ingens eadem Patris Pauli vita ostendit, cùm enim in Gallia & adhuc Maffeus Barberinus, atque Nuntius Pontificis esset, con amplificationi Poetiche (habetur p.137.) gridava, ch'era (il Padre Paolo) peggio di Lutero e di Calvino, e' che conveniva ammazzarlo; cum amplificationibus Poeticis clamavit, esse Patrem Paulum pejorem Luthero & Calvino, atque occultè eum occidi debere. Et p.179. Creato Cardinale l'an. 1606. haveva fatto dimostrationi d'un odio implacabile, anco con maniere poco degne di Christiano, e con inventioni assai vile e Chimeriche, che si tacciano per riverenza e per non far credere che la petulanza del dir ò publicar il falso & di calommiar, cosa attaccata à gl'ossi de gli Ecclesiastici moderni, sia arrivato al capo. Id est: Cardinalis factus anno 1606. prae se tulerat odium implacabile erga Patrem Paulum, utens agendi modis Christiano parùm dignis, & inventionibus satis vilibus & Chimæricis, qua tacentur per reverentiam & ne occasio detur credendi, petulantiam falsum dicendi & publicandi & calumniandi ossibus hodiernorum Ecclesiasticorum arctè adhærentem, ipsum Caput attigisse. Quàm non dignos ad Cardinalatum promoverit, Disser. IV. Sect. II. n. 87. dictum est. Nepotismum non sine magno ejus vitio vitiosum suo loco exhibebimus. Meritorum neglectum, unicum Domum Austriacam destruendi conatum, summum l'amato Luigi nel trono Imperiale, dilectum Ludovicum in throno Imperiali collocandi studium & similia allegatum MSC. Italicum pluribus prodit.
units.tr: LXIX. The same life of Father Paul shows the great vice of Urban VIII. For when Maffeo Barberini was still in France and was the Pontiff's nuncio, he cried out with poetic amplification (see p. 137) that Father Paul was worse than Luther and Calvin, and that he ought to be killed; with poetic amplifications he clamoured that Father Paul was worse than Luther and Calvin, and that he ought to be secretly put to death. And on p. 179: Created Cardinal in 1606, he displayed an implacable hatred, even by means unworthy of a Christian and by very base and chimerical devices, which are passed over out of reverence and so as not to give the impression that the petulance of saying or publishing falsehoods and of slander, a thing clinging to the bones of modern churchmen, had reached the head. That is: Created Cardinal in 1606, he showed an implacable hatred towards Father Paul, using modes of action little worthy of a Christian and inventions quite base and chimerical, which are passed over in silence out of reverence and so that no occasion is given for believing that the petulance of telling and publishing falsehoods and of calumny, which clings to the bones of modern churchmen, had reached the head. How unworthy the men he promoted to the Cardinalate were has been stated in Disser. IV, Sect. II, n. 87. We shall set out in its proper place his nepotism, which was faulty to a great degree. The neglect of merit, his sole attempt to destroy the House of Austria, and his great zeal to set his beloved Luigi on the Imperial throne, and similar matters, are shown in more detail in the cited Italian manuscript.

units.la: LXX. Innocentii X. qualitates (blasphemiæ, quas ante Pontificatum ex nomine Pamphilii, quo vocabatur, admisit, notæ sunt;) (Vindicativus Authori MSC. Italici, dum adhuc Cardinalis esset, visus est;) tum ante Pontificatum, tum in illo Pontifice planè indignas fusè descriptas exhibet: Vita di Donna Olympia Authore Abbate Gualdo (de quo primæ editionis præfatio: Egli amava &c. Veritatem amabat ultra modum, factúsque fuisset Cardinalis, si pro more Curiæ Romanæ adulari potuisset, & qui edit. sec. p.4. licentiam petit de certitudine Historiæ suæ utendi verbo Apostolico: Quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, & manus nostræ contrectaverunt, annunciamus tiamus vobis; paulò post subjungens, se non nisi ea traditurum, quæ in Theatro Romano per viginti quinque annos oculis propriis sui exposita fuerint;) consignata, atq; post ejus mortem in Italia publici juris facta, & cujus universale Compendium apud Celeb. Heideggerum Hist. Pap. n. CCLVI. videri potest; Nos heic tantùm eorum, quæ huc propiùs pertinent, indicem exhibemus. Narrat Author ille, ut Domina Olympia Innocentii fratri nupta, eúmque anno conjugii circiter decimo aversata, totáque in amorem affinis rapta, ejusdem in Conclavi alibíque lateri gravi apud omnes incestorum amorum suspicione individua comes hæserit; ut ille abeadem simulandi & dissimulandi, præter alia ad Papatum consequendum adhiberi solita, artificium, quod januam ad Papatum esse crebrò ei inculcaverat, edoctus, omnia quidem simulare, dissimulare noverit, excepto erga Olympiam amore, quem ut tegeret, induci nunquam potuerit; ut idem γυναικοκρατ plane, vel illa potiùs sub nomine ejus pessimè pessima agendo, procurando, permittendo, indignos promovendo, innocuos puniendo, & pecuniam undiquaque corradendo; dona la chiave della memoria locale, clavem memoriæ localis vocare solita, imperárit; ut, domicilio in Vaticano, proximè Pontificis Conclave sibi ex Consilio Panziroli denegato, singularum dierum appropinquante vespera Pontificem inviserit, & ad seram usque noctem cum eo subinde moram traxerit; ut tandem Pontifex Olympiæ suæ delinificis verbis persuaserit, quò interdiu saltem, ob sinistras omnium interpretationes, domi se contineret, & ab aditu Vaticani sibi temperaret, concessâ interim licentiâ, noctu, quoties luberet, accedendi & quidlibet transfigendi; ut tamen, Panzirolo mortuo, Olympia pristinæ libertati restituta, interdiu iterum adeundi Pontificem licentiam nacta fuerit; Ut, Pontificis conclamatâ valetudine, in aula accita ægrotanti indivulsa astiterit, & circa lectum velis abstrusa, Legatorum propositiones audiverit, & prorumpens subinde ad eas responderit, pro Pontifice cuncta gesserit, & morienti oculos clauserit, ut denique, eâ ab Alexandro Innocentii successore relegatâ atque epidemiâ luce extinctâ, hæredes ejus Alexandro placando millionem auri ejusdem Nepotibus erogare compulsi fuerint, eáque ratione juxta Cardinalis Sforzæ παρρησίαν, pars facultatum per Simoniam inauditam ab Olympia collectarum à latrone ad latronem transiverint; utque sequiora de Pontificis cum Olympia familiaritate ejusdem plùs quàm virili dominatione, judicia tum Italorum, tum exterorum fuerint, à quibus etiam nummus aureus recens cusus una parte Olympiam comâ Papali redimitam & Claves Petri manu prensantem, altera verò Pontificem cum implexa muliebri more coma & manu colum tractantem repræsentabat; Cui Celeberrimus Vir addit ludum scenicum in Innocentii & Olympiæ nuptias Londini ab Italis lusum, & acre Imperatoris Ferdinandi dicterium, quo Innocentii Nuncium, Melzi contrà Pacem cum Sueco initam murmurantem excepit, tale: Papa verò non desunt otium & delitia, cui Olympia Caput demulcet, ut suaviter dormire possit; atque haud immeritò tandem miratur, hunc ipsum Innocentium, Magnum, Oraculum saeculi, Miraculum totius Mundi, Mortalium portentum, coram Deo, coram Mundo Innocentem, Sixti Guardini Ferrariensis impudentiâ adulatoriâ insigniri; De cujus animo in rebus agendis planè irregulari Dux Parmensis II Nipot. p 2. p. 312. ita locutus fertur, cb'era più facile di accommodar' un letto ad un cane, che di conoscere l'humore d'Innocentio. Id est, esse facilius lectum cani praeparare, quàm verò genium Innocentii cognoscere. Qui author etiam regimen Urbani regimini hujus longè antefe-rendum censet ob perversum cum Principum Legatis tractandi modum, ordinariam petitionum qualiumcunque repulsam, pejoris amorem, virtutis qualiscunque suæ ad utilitatem suorum tantùm applicationem, vitiis suis Ecclesiæ & Romæ multùm interea nocentibus, degenerationem etiam ab æquitate initio ostentata, illusionem per Nepotem nulla potestate instructum, solâ relationis promissione solantem, timidè proponentem, responsum ordinariò consiederationis fallacis ferentem; voluntatis omnibus momentis mutationem, eorundem modò exaltationem, modò depressionem, propriæ tantùm utilitatis cum damno Ecclesiastici statûs æstimationem verbis etiam seqq. ad Dominam Olympiam declaratam: Cognata, non temete di nulla, li Cardinali saranno nostri à loro dispetto e difenderanno lo Stato Ecclesiastico per loro proprio interesse, benche noi volessimo ruinarlo per lo nostro. Id est: Cognata, noli timere, Cardinales etiam inviti nostri erunt, & statum Ecclesiasticum defendent ex proprii sui commodi amore, licèt nos eum perdere vellemus ob commodum nostrum. Videatur à p. 312–337.
units.tr: LXX. The qualities of Innocent X (the blasphemies he admitted before his pontificate under the name Pamphili, by which he was called, are well known; he seemed vindictive to the author of the Italian manuscript while he was still a Cardinal) are set out at length, both before the pontificate and in that Pontiff, as entirely unworthy. The source is Vita di Donna Olympia by the Abbot Gualdo. The preface to the first edition says of him: He loved &c. He loved the truth beyond measure, and would have become a Cardinal had he been able to flatter, as is the custom of the Roman Curia. The second edition, p. 4, asks leave to use the apostolic words for the certainty of his history: What we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, and what our hands have handled, we declare to you; and shortly after he adds that he will hand down only those things that were exposed to his own eyes in the Roman theatre for twenty-five years. These were recorded and, after his death, published in Italy. A general summary of them can be seen in the learned Heidegger, Hist. Pap. n. CCLVI. Here we give only an index of those things that bear more closely on this matter. That author relates that Donna Olympia, the wife of Innocent's brother, after about the tenth year of their marriage turned away from her husband and was caught up wholly in love of her brother-in-law, and remained his inseparable companion in the Conclave and elsewhere, under the grave suspicion of all of incestuous love. That he, taught by her the art of pretending and dissembling, which was often used for attaining the Papacy and which she had frequently impressed on him as the door to the Papacy, knew how to feign and conceal everything, except his love for Olympia, which he could never be induced to hide. That she ruled as a woman in every way, or rather she, under his name, acted most wickedly in everything, managed, permitted, promoted the unworthy, punished the innocent, and gathered money from every quarter; she gave the key of the local memory, which she was accustomed to call the key of the local memory, and ordered it. That, with her home in the Vatican, and since she had been refused the right to enter the Conclave next to the Pontiff on the advice of Panciroli, she visited the Pontiff on each evening as it drew near and stayed with him until late at night. That at last the Pontiff persuaded his Olympia with soothing words to keep at home by day at least, because of the unfavourable interpretations of everyone, and to refrain from entering the Vatican, while granting her leave to come at night, as often as she pleased, and to transact anything. Yet when Panciroli died, Olympia was restored to her former freedom and gained licence again to approach the Pontiff by day. That when the Pontiff's illness was openly announced, she was summoned to the hall and stood unseparated beside the sick man, and, hidden behind curtains round the bed, heard the proposals of the legates, and bursting out from time to time replied to them, and did everything on the Pontiff's behalf, and closed his eyes when he was dying. Finally, when she had been banished by Alexander, Innocent's successor, and the light of her favour had been put out, his heirs were compelled to pay a million in gold to the nephews of Alexander to appease him, and in this way, according to the frankness of Cardinal Sforza, part of the property gathered by Olympia through unheard-of simony passed from thief to thief. The more recent judgments, both of Italians and of foreigners, were about the Pontiff's intimacy with Olympia and her domination more than manly. A freshly struck gold coin also circulated, which on one side showed Olympia with a papal crown on her hair and grasping the keys of Peter in her hand, and on the other showed the Pontiff with his hair plaited in womanly fashion and holding a distaff in his hand. To this the very famous man adds the comic play performed in London by the Italians on the marriage of Innocent and Olympia, and the sharp jibe of Emperor Ferdinand, with which he answered the nuncio of Innocent who was grumbling about Melzi's peace concluded with the Swede, in these words: But the Pope lacks no leisure and pleasure, as Olympia strokes his head so that he can sleep sweetly. And not undeservedly he wonders at last that this very Innocent, the Great, the Oracle of the age, the Miracle of the whole world, the Wonder of mortals, Innocent before God and before the world, was decorated with flattering impudence by Sixtus Guardinus of Ferrara. Of his character in managing affairs, which was quite irregular, the Duke of Parma is reported to have said, in the second part of his Nipot., p. 312, that it was easier to make a bed for a dog than to know the temper of Innocent. That is: it was easier to prepare a bed for a dog than to know the disposition of Innocent. The same author also judges that the government of Urban was far preferable to this one, on account of the perverse manner of dealing with the legates of princes, the ordinary rejection of petitions of whatever kind, the love of the worse, the application of whatever virtue he had solely to the advantage of his own people, while his vices did great harm to the Church and to Rome in the meantime; the degeneration from equity shown at the beginning, the deception through a nephew invested with no power who consoled with the mere promise of a report, timidly putting forward proposals and ordinarily giving a reply of deceptive deliberation; the change of his will at every moment, now exalting, now depressing the same men, and valuing only his own advantage to the loss of the ecclesiastical state. This he also declared to Donna Olympia in these words: Cognata, do not fear anything; the Cardinals will be ours in spite of themselves and will defend the ecclesiastical state for their own interest, although we would wish to ruin it for our own. That is: Cognata, do not be afraid; the Cardinals, even against their will, will be ours and will defend the ecclesiastical state out of love for their own advantage, although we wish to destroy it for our advantage. See pp. 312–337.

units.la: LXXI. De Alexandri VII. Electione ita quidem Author Conclavis triumphat: Se altre volte ha permesso lo Spirito S. che siano stati esaltati huomini più tosto atti à discreditare che ad honorare la Sede di San Pietro, l'ha fatto per opera delle nostre colpe — hora è mitigato lo sdegno divino, mentre ha dato per Capo della Christianità, che da nemici della chiesa era riputato per la sua Santità meritevole di reggere il mondo. Id est: Si aliàs Spiritus S. permisit, ut eligerentur homines potius apti ad contemptui subjiciendam, quàm verò ad honorandam S. Petri Sedem, fecit propter peccata nostra — Jam verò ira Dei mitigata est, quia dedit Caput Christiano Orbi, quod etiam ab inimicis Ecclesia habitum erat ob sanctitatem suam dignum regimine totius Orbis. Hinc etiam ei exoptat, ut Deus prosperet l'intentione, che probabilmente nutrisce nel cuore, intentionem, quam probabiliter (sed hoc tenue nimis in capite Ecclesiae tantopere laudato) nutriat in corde. Sic etiam ejusdem apud eundem Authorem Nepotismi p.1. p.166. 167. invidendum planè habetur elogium, quòd ab initio Pontificatûs cibos cinere condire voluerit, lecto Capucini usus sit, divitias, fastum, gloriam, pompam odio habuerit, Legatos quasi in monte Calvaria & in conspectu feretri audiverit, & vitam verè Evangelicam duxerit. Sed virtuti radices defuisse, sequentia arguunt. Quamprimùm, inquit idem p.168.169. Nepotismus Romam ingressus erat, Pontifex naturam mutavit, humilitatem in fastum, afflictiones in Commoditates, lectum Capucini in mollissimas plumas, mortuorum thesauros in Adamantes, cogitationes de morte in illas de vita perpetua, aequitatem in ambitionem, mundi contemptum in vanitatem mundanam, & tandem implevit feretrum vacuum auro, quasi vitam redempturus. Regimen quale fuerit, ex eo liqueat, quòd ante Clementem IX. Roma dicitur fuisse.
units.tr: LXXI. Of the election of Alexander VII, the author of the Conclave triumphs thus: "If at other times the Holy Spirit has allowed men to be raised up who were more fit to bring the See of St Peter into contempt than to honour it, He did so on account of our sins. Now the divine anger is softened, since He has given as head of Christendom a man who, even by the enemies of the Church, was held worthy by his holiness to rule the world." That is: "If at other times the Holy Spirit has permitted men to be chosen who were better fitted to bring the See of St Peter into contempt than to honour it, He did so on account of our sins. But now the wrath of God is softened, because He has given the Christian world a head who, even in the eyes of the enemies of the Church, was worthy by his holiness to govern the whole world." Hence he also wishes that God would prosper the intention which he probably nourishes in his heart, the intention which he probably (but this is too slight a thing in the head of the Church so greatly praised) nourishes in his heart. Likewise, in the same author's Nepotismo, p. 1, pp. 166-167, there is a eulogy that is plainly to be envied: from the beginning of his pontificate he wished to season his food with ashes, used a Capuchin's bed, hated riches, pride, glory and pomp, heard the legates as if on Calvary and in the sight of the bier, and lived a truly Evangelical life. But that he lacked the roots of virtue the following passages show. As soon as, says the same author, pp. 168-169, Nepotismo entered Rome, the Pontiff changed his nature: humility into pride, afflictions into comforts, the Capuchin's bed into the softest feathers, the treasures of the dead into diamonds, thoughts of death into those of perpetual life, equity into ambition, contempt of the world into worldly vanity, and at last he filled the empty bier with gold, as if about to buy back his life. What sort of government it was may be gathered from the fact that it is said that Rome was before Clement IX.

units.la: Spota molt' anni
units.tr: Sposa molti anni

units.la: Di Tiranno marito. Id est:
units.tr: Of a tyrant husband. That is:

units.la: Multis annis Sponsa Tyranni Mariti. L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.20. Plura habet Syndicatus Alexandri VII. Habet etiam citatus Author Legationis Romuli ad Romanos, hinc inde de Clem. IX. Successore Alexandri non pauca, p.562.563. Epitaphium sequens: Hic jacet Clemens Papa, in numero nonus, ut à numero octavo & decimo regularetur, nempe OTTOBONO & DECIO AZZOLINO. Imperio tamen semper Nonus. Simulatione Maximus, Nepotibus optimus, Pistorii natus, ut oculis & capite laboraret, penè adultus jam adulter & quando plures habuit filias, tunc communis evasit Pater. JULII nomen ante Pontificatum potius, ne Julium quidem cum ipse interitum Camera Apostolica relinqueret. In juventute Lunam effoeminatus semper coluit; Mertò in senectute Lunam Ottomanam supprimere nequivit, (ob Candiam sub ipso amissam) licèt Religiones oppresserit. Tandem
units.tr: For many years the bride of a tyrant husband. L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 20. The Syndicatus Alexandri VII contains more of the same. The cited author also has, in the Legatio Romuli ad Romanos, many things here and there about Clement IX, Alexander's successor, pp. 562-563. The following epitaph: "Here lies Pope Clement, the ninth in number, so that he might be corrected from the eighth and the tenth, namely OTTOBONO and DECIO AZZOLINO. Yet always ninth in government, most ninth in dissimulation, best of nephews, born at Pistoia, so that he laboured with his eyes and head; almost grown up, already an adulterer, and when he had several daughters, then he became the common father. Before his pontificate he was named Julius rather than Julius, nor did he even leave the Apostolic Chamber in Julius's time. In youth, being effeminate, he always worshipped the Moon; in old age he was unable to suppress the Ottoman Moon (because of Crete, lost under him), although he oppressed the religious orders. At last"

units.la: etiam observatio de Clemente X. & aliis. dem die Luna anno 1669. morbo Lunari interfectus est. Viam salutis aeterna credere sibi parâsset, nisi Paulus Strada (qui nomine ipsius regnavit) deviâsset. Similia regimen spectantia pag. 614. occurrunt. De Clemente X. noni successore monuisse sufficiat, plus quàm octogenarium adeóque maximè inter electos omnes aetate provectum electum, demum anno aetat. octogesimo octavo, Christi 1676. mortuum fuisse. Nemo miretur, tam provectae aetatis senes quosdam juventutis virilisque aetatis naevis non usque adeò conspicuos fuisse. Quales etiam in inferiori Senectute alii non fuerunt ob Pontificatús brevitatem, ob quam etiam nonnulli in improborum Catalogum hîc referri haud potuerunt, aliis rursus aliâs bene sibi honorique suo & dignitatis caventibus paucioribus.
units.tr: also the observation about Clement X and others: on the same day, the moon of 1669, he was struck down by a lunar disease. He would have prepared for himself the way of eternal salvation to believe, had not Paolo Strada, who reigned in his name, led him astray. Similar things concerning the government appear on p. 614. It is enough to note of Clement X, the successor of Clement IX, that he was more than eighty years old, and thus the oldest of all those elected, and at last, in the eighty-eighth year of his age, in the year of Christ 1676, he died. Let no one wonder that some old men of such advanced age were not so conspicuous for the blemishes of youth and manhood. Others likewise, in their lesser old age, were not such, because of the brevity of their pontificates, on account of which some could not be listed here among the wicked, while others, on the other hand, took care of themselves, their good name and their dignity, and were fewer.

units.la: LXXII. Innocentius XI. Clementis X. Successor multis, ut videbatur, melior, in multis tamen ante Pontificatum non semper virtutis semitam secutus est, si partim chartis ludendo, partim emendo dignitates Ecclesiasticas praeparatorias obtinuit; Siquè post mortem Clementis IX. Papatús competitores describens ratè Poeta L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 90. cecinit:
units.tr: LXXII. Innocent XI, successor to Clement X, seemed in many ways better, yet in many things before his pontificate he did not always follow the path of virtue, since he obtained ecclesiastical dignities as preparatory steps, partly by playing cards and partly by buying them. And so, describing the rivals for the papacy after the death of Clement IX, a poet, in the L'Ambasciata di Roma, p. 90, sang:

units.la: Odescalchi quel grandone Va sperando ne' Conclavi: Mà non toccano le Chiavi A chi fà del Bacchettone. Id est: Vegrandis ille Odeschalchius sperat in Conclavibus: Sed pietatis speciem affectantibus non contingit potiri clavibus.
units.tr: "That great lump Odescalchi hopes in the conclaves, but the keys will not come to the man who plays the devout." That is: "That great fellow Odescalchi hopes in the conclaves; but it does not fall to those who affect the appearance of piety to get hold of the keys."

units.la: Inter qualitates Papabilis illud etiam p. 231. habetur, quòd non tanto buon Frate e niente buon Prencipe, debole le forze del suo speculativo cervello, non tam bonus Episcopus quàm verò bonus Monachus, sed nullo modo bonus Princeps, debiles vires speculativi sui cerebri; ipse huomo poco attivo, tutto contemplativo e diferente troppo à suoi Ministri, homo parùm activus, plane contemplativus & nimium suis Ministris tribuens fuerit. Neque bona, si Gallis, maximè in Decreto Parlamenti contrà Bullam Papae quoad Immunitatem Hospitiorum, ubi & ingratitudinis & seductionis, factiosis, & pertinaciae, & injustae vehementiae, & nimiae dominandi cupidinis, & novitatis scandalosae, & iniquorum conatuum & actionum plane irregularium, ratione carentium, injustarum & monstrosarum & immoderati fervoris & studii partium & affectationis Gallia, offendendi, & erroris præcipitii & usurpationis, & animi curæ & humanitati Apostolicæ contrarii, & amicitiæ cum Jansenistis damnatis, & stupiditatis & lethargiæ respectu Quietistarum; accusatur, fides habenda, agendi principia & acta fuerunt; Neque etiam usque adeò bonum fuit sub ipso regimen Civitatis; Ipse enim, teste Celeberrimo nunc Angliæ Episcopo Burneto in Itinerario suo, Romam suis exactionibus usque adeò perdere perexit, ut sub eo quarta pars incolarum emigrârit, dixeritque Vir in Ecclesia Romana eminens ad D. Burnetum habitu Ecclesiastici incedentem, necessariò horribiliter scandalizare orbem Christianum, quòd Roma magis tyrannicè imperent Papa quàm Turca Constantinopoli, neque videri, illos esse Vicarios J. Ch. vel veram Religionem ibi, ubi regula justitia & æquitatis nulla sint. Qualis ante Pontificatum & cùm adhuc Petrus Ottobonus esset, Alex. VIII. qui Innocentio XI. successit, fuerit, & quomodo sub Clem. IX. unâ cum Cardinale Azzolino præcipuè regnârit, & ipse quidem Datariam exercuerit, malim, ut quis ex L'Ambasciata di Rom. p.22. 33. 90. 92.114 163. seqq. 199. 266.283. 305. 318.365.375.seqq. 393. seqq 436. seqq.438. 646. seqq. cognoscat; Parùm commendare debuissent, quæ ibi occurrunt, nisi quòd aptitudinem ad regimen tale ostendunt. Pontificatûs brevitas autem & hîc nihil nobis præter summam nonnisi Agnatos ditandi, exaltandi studium, successu pro temporis brevitate minimè destitutum, ob oculos posuit, & confessionem moribundi simul in novis publicis de erroribus in regimine commissis. Quæ de eo sufficiunt. Qualis, qui eum nuper post semestre fere Inter-Pontificium exceperit, Innocentius XII. sit atque futurus sit, tempus docebit. Recentiora omnia de artibus indignis testantur adhuc æquè vigentibus, de discordia & pertinacia eligentium, de factionibus, de gaudente tertio in discordia duorum, urgente cumprimis æstu, de decrepito quasi in spem successionis mox secuturæ, quando aliter rebus consuli haud potuit, electo. Quòd autem nuper & Venetus & Neapolitanus admissi sunt, confusioni illud & majoribus, qui alios removerunt, naevis tribuendum est, & quoad Neapolitanum ætati provectæ, in qua timor abest eorum, quæ Neapolitanos aliâs impediunt & suprà à me indicata sunt. Síque melior quorundam nostri Seculi conditio, illud non certè muneri, quod tot monstra tulit, fecit, sed hodiernæ necessitati, ut hypocrisi maximè decipiatur & in errore retineatur mundus, & sapientiæ post damna, & temporibus, quæ tam apertè indignos non amplius ferre possent, plenè planéque adscribi debet.
units.tr: Among the qualities of a papabile this too is set down, p. 231: that he is "a good enough friar but no good prince, weak in the powers of his speculative brain," "not so good a bishop as a good monk, but in no way a good prince, weak powers of his speculative brain; a man of little action, wholly contemplative, too different from his ministers," "a man little active, plainly contemplative, and too generous to his ministers." Nor, if the French are to be believed, especially in the Parliament's decree against the Pope's Bull concerning the immunity of embassies, where he is accused of ingratitude and seduction, of factiousness, obstinacy, unjust vehemence, excessive lust for domination, scandalous novelty, wicked endeavours and actions wholly irregular, lacking reason, unjust and monstrous, of immoderate zeal and partisanship, of a hostility toward France, of a headlong error and usurpation, of a spirit contrary to care and Apostolic humanity, of friendship with the condemned Jansenists, and of stupidity and lethargy toward the Quietists: the principles and acts of his conduct are not to be trusted. Nor was the government of the city under him so very good either. For he himself, according to the most celebrated Bishop Burnet, now of England, in his Itinerary, pressed on so far with his exactions that under him a fourth part of the inhabitants emigrated; and a man eminent in the Roman Church, meeting Dr Burnet walking in ecclesiastical dress, said that it must necessarily be a dreadful scandal to the Christian world that Rome was governed more tyrannically by the Pope than Constantinople by the Turk, and that those there could not seem to be the Vicars of Christ, nor the true religion to exist there, where there is no rule of justice and equity. What Alexander VIII, who succeeded Innocent XI, was before his pontificate, when he was still Pietro Ottoboni, and how he chiefly reigned under Clement IX along with Cardinal Azzolino, and how he himself held the office of Datary, I would rather let the reader learn from the L'Ambasciata di Roma, pp. 22, 33, 90, 92, 114, 163 ff., 199, 266, 283, 305, 318, 365, 375 ff., 393 ff., 436 ff., 438, 646 ff. Those things which occur there should scarcely have commended him, except that they show his aptitude for such government. The brevity of his pontificate, moreover, set before our eyes nothing here but his zeal, not at all lacking in success for so short a time, for enriching and exalting his own kin; and his confession on his deathbed, made at the same time, of the errors committed in his government. These things suffice concerning him. What Innocent XII, who received him after an interpontifical period of nearly six months, is and will be, time will show. All the more recent reports testify to unworthy arts still flourishing equally: to the discord and obstinacy of the electors, to factions, to a third party rejoicing in the discord of two, especially with the heat of the season pressing on, and to an aged, almost decrepit man chosen in hope of a successor who would soon follow, when affairs could not otherwise be provided for. But that both a Venetian and a Neapolitan have lately been admitted must be ascribed to the confusion and to the greater blemishes of those who removed the others, and, as regards the Neapolitan, to his advanced age, in which the fear is absent of those things which otherwise hinder the Neapolitans and which I have indicated above. And if the better condition of some in our age is due to anything, it is certainly not to that office which bore so many monsters, but must be fully and plainly ascribed to the present necessity: that the world is most of all deceived by hypocrisy and kept in error, and that, after the losses to wisdom and the times, men who could no longer bear such openly unworthy men have had to submit.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Ex recensitis tamen satis superque patet, cujus generis plerique à multis Seculis Pontifices, & quòd multi minùs probi, multi planè improbi & impii electi fuerint. Dico, à multis Seculis; Primos enim, ut alii doctrina & officio fuerunt, moribus etiam longè diversos, posteriores proin planè & in vita quoque degeneres esse constat. Et Romanis primis speciatim applicari potest, quod in confutatione Primatus Papæ ante annos penè ducentos scripta Gregorius Heymbuigensis J. U. D. & Norimbergensis Syndicus de primis quibusvis Sacerdotibus dixit: Sacerdotum gloria fuit non purpura, non divitiæ, non equus albus, non fastus, non dominatus; sed: Ecce, nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus Te, Domine. Verissimè etiam Florimundus Ræmundus personatus in fabula Job. c. 20. sic primorum Pontificum humilitatem depinxit; Prioribus illis Seculis, & multorum annorum fluxu Pontifices martyrii sacri laureâ contentos fuisse, quam omni diademate & sceptro potiorem habebant, reliquisque ornamentis ducebant superiorem, nemo ignorat. Prima illa ætate, gloria eorum erat ignominia; Majestas, humilitas; felicitas, tyrannorum ira; quies, supplicium; vita, mors ipsa. Cum humilitate verò & mundani fastûs vitæque contemptu tanquam radicibus habebant etiam virtutes reliquas.
units.tr: From what has been reviewed, however, it is clear enough what sort of men most Popes have been for many centuries: many were less upright, and many were plainly wicked and impious when they were elected. I say "for many centuries," because it is established that the earliest Popes were, like the others, distinguished by learning and office, and also by morals far different from those of their successors, who were in life as well as in character degenerate. This can be applied especially to the first Roman bishops, what Gregory of Heimburg, Doctor of Both Laws and Syndic of Nuremberg, said of the earliest priests of every kind in his Refutation of the Primacy of the Pope, written nearly two hundred years ago: The glory of the priests was not purple, not riches, not a white horse, not pride, not lordship; but: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you, Lord." Florimond de Raemond, writing under a pseudonym in his fable on Job, chapter 20, also described the humility of the first Popes most truthfully: No one is unaware that in earlier centuries, and through the passing of many years, the Popes were content with the laurel of sacred martyrdom, which they held more precious than any diadem or sceptre, and which they counted superior to all other ornaments. In that first age, their glory was disgrace; their majesty, humility; their happiness, the anger of tyrants; their rest, punishment; their life, death itself. Along with humility and contempt for worldly pomp and life, they also had the other virtues as their roots.

units.la: LXXIV.
units.tr: LXXIV.

units.la: Sed Seculo post Christum VII. & sequentibus ob defectionem magnam Ecclesiæ illius infelicibus boni certè: Apparent rari nantes in gurgite vasto;
units.tr: But in the seventh century after Christ and those that followed, through the great defection of that Church, unhappy and certainly few good men appeared: Here and there a few swimmers appear in the vast whirlpool.

units.la: Atque proin non injusta fuit Wesseli Gansfoetii, Groningensis (qui vulgò Lux mundi dictus est, & An. Chr. 1489. obiit;) querela, in Farrag. rerum Theol. p. 32: Valde, ajebat, periclitaretur vita justi, si penderet ex vita Papæ, Summorum enim Pontificum plerique pestilenter erraverunt &c.
units.tr: And so the complaint of Wessel Gansfort of Groningen (commonly called Light of the World, who died in the year of Christ 1489) was not unjust, in his Farrago of Theological Matters, p. 32: The life of a righteous man, he said, would be in great danger if it depended on the life of the Pope, for most of the highest Popes have erred in a deadly way.

units.la: Neque occasione destitutus Poeta cecinit: Papa Pius V. moritur, res mira tot inter Pontifices tantùm quinque fuisse pios.
units.tr: Nor did a poet lack an occasion when he sang: "Pope Pius V has died; a marvel, that among so many Popes there have been only five pious ones."

units.la: Atque quasi nimium largitus esset, priora corrigens: Fallor ego: nam nemo pius re, nomine tantùm Pontifices constat quinque fuisse pios.
units.tr: And as if he had been too generous, correcting his earlier line: "I am mistaken; for it is established that no one, in deed but only in name, has been a pious Pope, only five."

units.la: Ut certè non omnes Pios pios fuisse ex dictis constat. Degenerânunt illi & alii dignitate & pompa mundana elati: His igitur fundamentis, inquit Guicciardinus Hist. Pap. l. IV. & modo ad terrenam potentiam elati, ac sensim animarum salutis divinórumque præceptorum obliti, atque ad mundana imperia omni cogitatione conversi, nec divina auctorita{s}floritate alio, quàm quasi telo & instrumento rerum fragilium abutentes, principes potius gentium, quàm rerum sacrarum Pontifices videri coeperunt. Horum cura &c. Et iterum: Hinc factum est, ut Pontifices sibi indies plura majoráque arrogantes, terrorémque armorum cœlestium in res terrenas caducas vertentes, jus sibi in Imperatores, quasi Christi in terris vices gerentes, assumpserunt &c.
units.tr: Thus it is certainly clear from what has been said that not all the pious were pious. Others degenerated, lifted up by dignity and worldly pomp. On these foundations, says Guicciardini in the History of the Popes, book IV, and now lifted up to earthly power, and gradually forgetful of the salvation of souls and of divine precepts, and turned in every thought to worldly empires, and abusing the divine authority as if it were a weapon and tool of fragile things, they began to appear princes of the nations rather than Popes of sacred things. Their concern etc. And again: Hence it came about that the Popes, daily arrogating more and greater things to themselves, and turning the terror of heavenly arms against transitory earthly things, assumed for themselves a right over the emperors, as though they bore the place of Christ on earth etc.

units.la: LXXV. Constat de his distinctiùs ex vitis, vel earum descriptionibus, quales habemus, & habemus ab Authoribus Pontificiis. Si autem tales nobis descripserunt Pontifices, quales fuisse credendum est? Cùm mitius omnia interpretari soleant addictissimi, cùm multa reticere, nolentes cum Chamo revelare nuditatem Patrum, imò nonnulli adulatoriè scribentes, cujus documentum certissimum in conclusione Operis sui de Vitis ac Gestis Pontificum Joh. Srella ingenuâ Confessione suppeditat: Denum R. D. tuae (scribit ad Ant. Surianum Patriarcham Venetiarum;) innotescat, me de industria plura praetermisisse, pericula undique praecaventem: maximè in his novissimis temporibus gesta, quae sine quorundam nota scribi non potuissent: potissimùm cùm praesentia discrimina Scriptores elanguescere plerumque faciant, cùm sint plurimi, qui veritatem aequo animo audire nolint. Posteris autem cætera sunt relinquenda, qui apertius sine motu & nota suas historias scribere poterunt. Documentum etiam in vita Urbani VIII. quae historiae Platinae adponi solet, exhibet Il Nipot. p.2. p.291. Reperiet Lector, inquit, cumulum tot bonorum operum, ut sanctissimum, mortuum etiam & jam in pulverem redactum credere necesse esset; Sed qui praejudiciis non obcaecatus leget, ridebit non tam de Pontifice, quàm verò de Scriptore. Imò ipse Alexander VI. (ast quàm foedum monstrum!) in quorundam Scriptis pulcherrimus habetur. De quo idem audiri meretur: Omne commodum, inquit p.244. quo Ecclesiam affecit, in eo consistit, quòd liberalis fuit Scriptoribus & Doctis Viris omnium ordinum, non quidem naturali iustinctu, sed eo tantùm fine, ut bona de se & suis Scripto relinquerent. Quomodo certè non defuerunt quidam infames (ita mihi eos vocare liceat) Scriptores, qui regnum ejus cum regno Alexandri comparârunt & virtutum parallelismum instituerunt. Atque ex illis unus librum scripsit, cui titulus: Le glorie del Pontificato d'Alessandro Sesto, e Casa Borgia. Deus, ita pergit, mille malis afficiat tales Scriptores, qui adulando mentiuntur, id est, qui pro lubitu faciunt ex daemonibus malis angelos bonos & ex Tyrannis Sanctos!
units.tr: LXXV. This is established more clearly from the lives, or their descriptions, such as we have, and we have them from Papist authors. But if the Popes have described such lives for us, what sort of men must we believe they were? Since the most devoted authors are accustomed to interpret everything more gently, and to pass over many things, unwilling, like Ham, to reveal the nakedness of the Fathers; indeed some write in a flattering way. The most certain proof of this is given by John Stella, in the ingenuous confession at the end of his work On the Lives and Deeds of the Popes, where he writes to Antonio Suriano, Patriarch of Venice: Let it be known to Your Reverence that I have deliberately omitted many things, guarding against dangers on every side, especially in the deeds of these most recent times, which could not be written without the disgrace of certain men; especially since present dangers commonly make writers faint, since there are very many who are unwilling to hear the truth calmly. But the rest must be left to posterity, who will be able to write their histories more openly, without offence or disgrace. The evidence is also found in the life of Urban VIII, which is usually appended to Platina's history, where the Nipote (p. 2, p. 291) shows: The reader will find such a heap of good works that one would have to believe him most holy, even dead and already reduced to dust; but he who reads without being blinded by prejudice will laugh, not so much at the Pope as at the writer. Indeed Alexander VI himself (but what a foul monster!) is held to be most beautiful in the writings of some. Concerning him the same may be heard: Every advantage that he bestowed on the Church consists in this, that he was generous to writers and learned men of every rank, not indeed from natural instinct, but only with the aim that they should leave behind good things about him and his in their writings. Thus certainly there were some infamous writers (allow me to call them so), who compared his reign with the reign of Alexander and drew up a parallel of virtues. And from among them one wrote a book titled: The Glories of the Pontificate of Alexander VI and the House of Borgia. May God afflict such writers with a thousand evils, who lie in their flattery, that is, who at their pleasure make evil demons into good angels and tyrants into saints!

units.la: LXXVI. Sed tamen etiam Dæmones incarnatos vidimus, Tyrannos ob oculos positos habuimus. Et supersunt generaliora testimonia & sanctitatis Pontificiæ indicia pauca ex multis adhuc addenda. Si Roma funditùs corrupta, certè Dominus Urbis & Pastor (qualis enim Rex, talis grex;) non valde bonus erit. De perditis autem ejus moribus unum Mantuanum audiamus; Ita Poeta suo tempore Celeberrimus Fastor. l. 2. in Febr. de carnisprivio canit: I pudor in villas, si non patiuntur easdem Et villa vomicas, Urbs est jam tota lupanar.
units.tr: LXXVI. But still, we have seen even incarnate demons, and we have had tyrants set before our eyes. There remain more general testimonies, and a few indications of Papal holiness, to be added from among many others. If Rome is utterly corrupt, certainly the Lord of the City and its Pastor (for as the king is, so is the flock) will not be very good. Let us hear one Mantuan on her depraved morals; thus the poet, most celebrated in his time, sings in the Fasti, book 2, on February, concerning the carnival: Shame has gone into the villages, if they do not suffer the same, and the villa is a sore; the city is now altogether a brothel.

units.la: Ita eidem ea de causa valedicit idem: Roma vale, vidi, satis est vidisse, revertar, Cum Leno, meretrix, scurra, Cynædus ero.
units.tr: For the same reason the same poet bids farewell: Farewell, Rome; I have seen, it is enough to have seen; I shall return when I am a pimp, a whore, a jester, a catamite.

units.la: Et testatur rursus in Epigram. ad Falcon. in Colloquio inopum T. 2. p. 144. b. Obtinet expulsâ probitate pecunia Romam, Nec Deus in tota possidet urbe locum. Quot sunt Romæ homines, tot eunt per compita fures, Quosve Canes speras, experiere lupos. Omnibus esse lupos licet in regione luporum; Inter Pygmæos non pudet esse brevem.
units.tr: And again he testifies in his epigram to Falco, in the Colloquy of the Poor, vol. 2, p. 144b: Money, with honesty driven out, holds Rome, and God possesses no place in the whole city. As many men as there are in Rome, so many thieves go through the crossroads; and whatever dogs you hope for, you will find wolves. Everyone may be a wolf in the land of wolves; among pygmies it is no shame to be short.

units.la: Atque fugam tandem suadet Sylva l. 2. T. 3. p. 168. a. Vivere qui sanctè cupitis, discedite: Roma Omnia cùm liceant, non licet esse bonum.
units.tr: And at last he urges flight in the Sylvae, book 2, vol. 3, p. 168a: You who wish to live holily, depart: in Rome, though all things are permitted, it is not permitted to be good.

units.la: LXXVII. Ast Romæ eandem semper faciem esse, testantur, qui viderunt. Nobilissimus Sandis Relat. de statu Relig. cap. 28. testatur, vulgato dicterio Italorum pessimos Romanos perhiberi. Sic etiam Arcani Politici de Principi d'Italia p. 5. legimus: Si dice in proverbio, che il Papa hà i più cattivi sudditi e i megliori Soldati del mondo; perche veramente i popoli di alcune provincie di quello stato tengono poco buon nome trà le nationi d'Italia. Id est: In proverbio dicitur, Papam habere pessimos in orbe subditos & milites optimos; ut revera populi quarundam provinciarum statûs illius malâ famâ laborant inter nationes Italia.
units.tr: LXXVII. But those who have seen it testify that Rome always has the same face. The most noble Sandys, in his Relation of the State of Religion, chapter 28, testifies that by a common saying the Romans are called the worst of the Italians. So also we read in the Political Secrets concerning the Prince of Italy, p. 5: It is said in a proverb that the Pope has the worst subjects and the best soldiers in the world; for truly the peoples of some provinces of that state have a poor reputation among the nations of Italy. That is: It is said in a proverb that the Pope has the worst subjects in the world and the best soldiers; as in truth the peoples of certain provinces of that state suffer a bad reputation among the nations of Italy.

units.la: LXXVIII. Verùm non lubet indirectis testimoniis diutiùs immorari. Verè cecinit, quicunque nomine Romæ, cecinit L'Ambrose di Rom. p. 12. Numera son da secoli più addietro Di questo mio gran male i primi Autori Tutto, l'un doppo l'altro Successori Di Simone si ben,non gia di Pietro. Mentre costor con mill' inganni e frodi Di pietà finta e santità servile, Per strade oblique al sin gionti al Ovile, Ne son lupi rapaci e non custodi. Id est:
units.tr: LXXVIII. But it is not pleasing to linger longer on indirect testimonies. Whoever sang in the name of Rome sang truly, as L'Ambrose sang in Di Roma, p. 12: "Count, from the centuries further back, the first authors of this great evil of mine. All, one after another, the successors of Simon, not of Peter. While these with a thousand deceits and frauds, of feigned piety and servile holiness, reach the fold by crooked paths, they are rapacious wolves and not guardians." That is:

units.la: Sunt à Seculis retrò multùm actis hujus magni mali mei primi Authores, omnes, unus post alterum, Simonis, non Petri Successores. Dum hi mille deceptionibus & fraudibus pietatis fictitiæ & servilis sanctitatis, vis obliquis tandem ad Ovile perducti in eo lupi rapaces sunt, & non custodes.
