Et p.14. sistit ex face pessima & spuma vilissima Roma Principatum habentes, intrusos in Papatum suum,séque pejorem Scytha & Geta Di tutti i morbi idolatrar la lue Dar' à un Porco gl' Incensi, à un Hirco, à un Bue Al Brachier d'un Pedante, ò d'un Poeta;
units.tr: The first authors of this great evil of mine, long ago, were all, one after another, successors of Simon, not of Peter. While these men, by a thousand deceits and frauds of feigned piety and servile holiness, are led at last by crooked paths to the fold, they are ravening wolves in it, and not guardians. And on p. 14 Rome, holding the principate, rising from her most foul face and vilest foam, intruded into their Papacy and made herself worse than the Scythian and the Getae: Of all diseases, she worships the plague of idolatry, offering incense to a pig, a goat, an ox, to a pedant's or a poet's arm-bearer.

units.la: Idololatricè colere omnium morborum pestem, suffitu porcum, hircum, bovem: & pradam esse hor di Papi Tiranni, hor di Papesse, n.odò Paparum Tyrannorum, modò Papissarum.
units.tr: To worship idolatrously the plague of all diseases, offering incense to a pig, a goat, an ox; and to be the prey, now of Papal tyrants, now of Popesses, at one time of Papal tyrants, at another of Papesses.

units.la: Ut sæpe etiam cani potuerit: Caro San Pier se dir ti deggio il vero, Ti vedo questa volta in mal partito Tu sei di Cardinali si mal fornito Che di far Papa un buon' hormai dispero. Id est:
units.tr: So that it could often be said even to a dog: Dear Saint Peter, if I must tell you the truth, I see you are in a bad way this time. You are so poorly furnished with Cardinals that I despair of ever making a good Pope now.

units.la: Chare Sancte Petre, si verum tibi dicere debeo, malè jam tibi provisum, & tam malè Cardinalibus instructus es, ut desperem, unquam bonum Papam creatum iri. Quod & inductione Papabilium, inter quos Clemens X. Innocentius XI. & Alexander VIII. etiam probatur. Et si quando melior fuit, ibidem: O fato Maledetto, Ch'accertar far il gran proverbio prisco Sempre ad un buon è successore un tristo. Id est:
units.tr: Dear Saint Peter, if I must tell you the truth, you have been provided for badly, and you are so badly equipped with Cardinals that I despair of a good Pope ever being created. This is also shown by the list of the papabili, among whom are Clement X, Innocent XI and Alexander VIII. And if at any time there was a better one, the same author adds: O cursed fate, which makes good the old proverb: a bad man always succeeds a good one.

units.la: O fatum maledictum, quod confirmat vulgatum illud vetus; Semper bono malum succedere.
units.tr: O cursed fate, which confirms that old saying: a bad man always succeeds a good one.

units.la: Et querela opportuna fuerit p.250. In tempo, che sourasta un si gran male, Ch'al Diavol soffi, e non Vicario à Dio;
units.tr: And the complaint would be timely: In a time when such a great evil holds sway that it breathes for the Devil and not as God's Vicar;

units.la: In tempore, quo tantum malum imminuit, ut Diabolo, non Deo Vicarius sub-
units.tr: In a time when so great an evil prevailed, that a vicar, not of God but of the Devil, was sub-

units.la: Legatione Romuli ad Romanos; substituendus fuerit ; Et septuaginta illi Apostoli voluerint per Pastore Un che somiglia à Giuda traditore; Pastorem Juda traditori similem; Et semel, Vidonem, ch'altro Dio non conosce, ch'il formaggio; Cui prater caseum nullus Deus. Turma autem volans juxta p.252. non vuol-un huom da bene,non vult Virum probum.
units.tr: (as in the embassy of Romulus to the Romans) was to be substituted. And those seventy apostles wished "a pastor who resembles Judas the traitor"; and once, Vidone, "who knows no god but cheese." The flying throng, moreover, "does not want an honest man."

units.la: LXXIX. Imò in proverbium abiit Pontificum probitas; Proditum enim Nobilissimo Sandis Relat. de statu Relig. c. 28. che tanto fosse essorbitante l' iniquità della lor prima seggia, che facesse nascer frà loro questo detto ,fra gli altri registrato nelli lor libri proprii, cioè, che trà tutti i Christiani in Italia i peggiori sono i Romani,che degli Romani i Preti sono i più cattivi, i peggiori Preti sono inal zati ad esser Cardinali & che il pessimo de i Cardinali s'elegge Papa. Id est; adeò exorbitantem esse iniquitatem prima sedis illorum,ut ratum sit inter eos proverbium, quod & prater alios in propriis eorum libris occurrit,nempe, inter omnes Christianos in Italia pessimos esse Romanos, Romanorum pessimos esse Sacerdotes, Sacerdotum pessimos eligi in Cardinales, Cardinalem pessimum Papam fieri. Papa autem,Guicciardino διxεἰω teste, tum boni censentur,cùm bonitas eorum aliorum hominum malitiam non superat. Joh.Stella Sacerdos Venetus præfat. de Vit. ac Gest. sum. Pontif. ad Dominicum Grimanum Patriarcham Aquilegiensem & Cardinalem scribit,sperare se, eum vitæ suæ sanctimoniâ, ac castigatissimis moribus multiformes omnes Pontificum vivendi ritus esse superaturum. Diversi tamen sunt, & diversi bonitatis ipsorum gradus: sic,juxta Nobil. Sandis c. 32. quelli,che più sottilmente vedono le distintioni di bontà,dirano,che Pio V. era buon prelato,mà prencipe non buono,cheSisto V.era buon prencipe,mà non buon prelato,Gregorio XIII. buono e prencipe e prelato,mà non huomo buono. Clemente VIII. buon' huomo, buon' prencipe e buon prelato. Id est: Illi,qui subtiliùs observant distinctiones bonitatis dicent; Pium V. fuisse bonum Episcopum,sed non bonum Principem; Sixtum V. bonum principem,sed non bonum Episcopum; Gregorium XIII. bonum & principem & Episcopum, sed hominem non bonum; Clementem VIII. juxta illos quidem,bonum & hominem & Episcopum & Principem. Prout etiam à diversis creantur: Hinc Cardinali Sforzæ post mortem Alex. VII. referente Il Cardin. p.3.p.378. interroganti,quis Papa futurus sit, à Cardinale N. responsum:Signor Cardinale,io credo,che se faranno il Papa i Francefi,sarà il Cardinal Farnese, se gli Spagnoli, il Cardinal Rospigliosi, se il Popolo Romano, il Cardinal Barbarino: Se il S. Spirito, il Cardinal Odescalco: se il Diavolo, ò vostra ò vostra Eminenza, ò io. Id est: Domine Cardinalis, credo, si Papam facient Galli, futurum Farnesium; Si Hispani, Rospigliosium; si Populus Romanus, Barbarinum: Si Spiritus S. Odescalchium: si Diabolus, aut Vestra Eminentia, aut ego.
units.tr: LXXIX. Indeed, the probity of the Popes has passed into a proverb. For it is reported by the most noble Sandys, Relation on the State of Religion, ch. 28, that the iniquity of their first see was so excessive that it gave rise among them to this saying, recorded among others in their own books: that among all Christians in Italy the worst are the Romans; that among the Romans the worst are the priests; that the worst priests are raised to be Cardinals; and that the worst of the Cardinals is chosen Pope. That the iniquity of their first see is so excessive that there is a settled proverb among them, which also occurs in their own books, namely: among all Christians in Italy the Romans are the worst; among the Romans the priests are the worst; among the priests the worst are chosen as Cardinals; the worst Cardinal becomes Pope. The Popes, however, as Guicciardini bears witness, are then considered good when their goodness does not surpass the wickedness of other men. John Stella, a Venetian priest, in the preface to his On the Lives and Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, writes to Domenico Grimani, Patriarch of Aquileia and Cardinal, that he hopes that by the holiness and most chaste morals of his life he will surpass all the manifold ways of living of the Popes. They differ, however, and their degrees of goodness differ too: so, according to the noble Sandys, ch. 32, those who more subtly discern the distinctions of goodness will say: Pius V was a good bishop but not a good prince; Sixtus V a good prince but not a good bishop; Gregory XIII good both as prince and bishop but not a good man; Clement VIII, according to them, good man, bishop and prince. As they are also created by different people. Hence, when Cardinal Sforza, after the death of Alexander VII, was asked by a certain Cardinal N. who would be Pope, he is reported to have answered: Lord Cardinal, I believe that if the French make the Pope, it will be Cardinal Farnese; if the Spaniards, Cardinal Rospigliosi; if the Roman people, Cardinal Barberini; if the Holy Spirit, Cardinal Odescalchi; if the Devil, either your Eminence or I.

units.la: LXXX. Ut certè non semper de meliori sit electio, de quo in Decretalibus quaeritur; sed saepe abominatio in loco antea sancto sederit, quod Baronius in Pseudo-Papis accidisse aliquando docet; Et si, quod Lottinus Dissert. de Conclavi ait, ad poenam malus obtingit, saepe Ecclesia illa gravissimè punita sit; Imò Seculo IX. Caput Ecclesiae visibile, ex hypothesi, nullum fuerit, quod ex Paulo Sarpio de Materiis Benefic. p.72. discimus; Et, quae Gregorii XV. in Bulla de Conclavi modesta de se vox est, plerisque sine ullo merito Ecclesia commissa sit; Et plerunque, qui infirmitatibus condescenderet, electus sit; quod Baronius ad an. 1061. n. 26. factum esse dicit; Et, juxta Stapletonum T. 1. Cent. 1. q.5. art.3. p.597. edit. Paris. 1620. Vix ullum peccatum cogitari posse, (solâ haresi, quam immeritò excipit, exceptâ, ) quo illa Sedes turpiter maculata non fuerit, maximè ab an. 800. & infra. Quamvis alii criminum Pontifices consortesque in criminibus convinci posse negent, quod rursus alii de consortibus tantùm stultè largiuntur, subtiles nimirum apud Pileum Modiensem q. 44. argumentatores ita inferentes: Sed adhuc est fortior ratio pro Rosella, (quae cum R. Pontifice adulterium commisisse dicebatur) non potest probari adultera, ergo nec damnari. Quòd non possit convinci, subtili ratione probatur: Impossibile est, Rosellam cum Pontifice adulterium commisisse, quòd Pontifex idem non commiserit cum Rosella. E. non potest probari, adulterium commisisse cum Pontifice Rosellam, quin probetur, Pontificem commisisse cum Rosella, sed hoc probari est impossibile. E. & illud. Tantùm cum Pontifice peccâsse juvat!
units.tr: LXXX. Certainly the choice is not always "of the better," as the Decretals ask; but often "an abomination has sat in a place formerly holy," as Baronius teaches happened at times among the pseudo-popes. And if, as Lottinus says in his Dissertation on the Conclave, "the bad man falls to the punishment," the Church has often been most severely punished. Indeed, in the ninth century there was, on their hypothesis, no visible head of the Church at all, as we learn from Paolo Sarpi, On the Matters of Benefices, p. 72. And what Gregory XV modestly says of himself in his Bull on the Conclave, that the Church was committed to many men "without any merit," is true; and that very often one was chosen who "condescended to weaknesses," as Baronius says happened in the year 1061, n. 26. And, according to Stapleton, Vol. 1, Cent. 1, q. 5, art. 3, p. 597, ed. Paris 1620: scarcely any sin can be imagined (heresy alone, which he unjustly excepts, aside) by which that See was not foully stained, especially from the year 800 onwards. Although other writers deny that Popes and their partners in crime can be convicted of crimes, and still others foolishly grant this only for the partners, the subtle arguers in Pileus of Modena, q. 44, infer thus: But there is a still stronger reason for Rosella (who was said to have committed adultery with the Pope): she cannot be proved an adulteress, therefore neither can she be condemned. That she cannot be convicted is proved by subtle reasoning: it is impossible that Rosella committed adultery with the Pope unless the Pope also committed it with Rosella. Therefore it cannot be proved that Rosella committed adultery with the Pope without it being proved that the Pope committed it with Rosella; but this is impossible to prove. Therefore that too. It is enough to have sinned with the Pope!

units.la: LXXXI. Maximè autem ex dictis vana tum aliorum, tum Loyolitae Ottonis in Roma Gloriosa de Paparum Sanctitate jactantia convinci potest; Jam in dedicatione plerosque omnes tales vocat, qualthat formát Apostolus in suâ ad Titum; qui sine crimine erant, utpote Dei Dispensatores, non superbi, non iracundi, non vinolenti, non percussores, non turpis lucri cupidi; benigni, sobrii, justi, sancti, continentes, amplectentes eum, qui secundum doctrinam est, fidelem sermonem, ut potentes essent exhortari in doctrina sana, & eos, qui contradicunt, arguere. Et paulò post: Plerosque omnes dixi; non dixi; Omnes. Fuere enim inter illos — quidam non continentes, sed ex ex tanto numero paucissimi; aliqui etiam parùm justi; Sed qui vix numerum faciant: non benigni, non hospitales nonnulli &c. Sed qui in tanto horum summorum Præsulum Populo vix agnoscantur. In ipso autem opere p.6. Inveniemus (ô magnam gloriam Ecclesiæ Romanæ!) non decimam, imò non vigesimam partem ex vitiosis Pontificibus constare. Et iterum in margine: Plùs quàm quarta pars sanctis constat, cæteri aliàs laude digni sunt. Pag.9. in Seculo sexto, omnes partim Martyres, partim Confessores, partim bonos fuisse. Pag.11. In Seculo IX. omnes partim bonos, partim sanctos, tribus tantùm exceptis. Pag. 12. In Seculo X. 25. reperiri omnes bonos, paucis exceptis. Pag.13. In Seculo XI. exceptis duobus omnes bonos & laudatos. Pag.14. In Seculo XII. & XIII. omnes bonos & laudatos, nullo excepto. Pag.16. In Seculo XIV. tribus; In XV. duobus; Pag.17. In XVI. uno, qui aliquo modo reprehensibilis. Pag. 18. In XVII. nullo excepto. In universum 77. sanctos incomparabili Romani Papatûs honore fuisse. Ex dictis, inquam, jactantiæ istius vanitas meridiana luce clariùs patet, patet tot improborum exemplis, vel ipsa Pontificiorum Scriptorum Confessione talium.
units.tr: LXXXI. Above all, from what has been said, the empty boasting of others, and of the Jesuit Otto in Roma Gloriosa, about the holiness of the Popes can be convicted. In the dedication he calls most of them such as the Apostle describes in his letter to Titus: men who were without crime, as stewards of God, not proud, not angry, not drunkards, not strikers, not greedy of base gain; but kindly, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word which is according to the teaching, that they may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to convict those who gainsay. And a little later: I said most of them; I did not say all. For among them there were some who were not self-controlled, but of so great a number very few; some also were little just; but these hardly make up a number: some were not kindly, not hospitable, etc. But these are scarcely to be recognised among the Popular crowd of such supreme Prelates. In the work itself, p. 6, we shall find (O great glory of the Roman Church!) that not a tenth, nay not a twentieth part, consists of wicked Popes. And again in the margin: More than a quarter consists of saints; the rest are otherwise worthy of praise. p. 9: in the sixth century, all were partly martyrs, partly confessors, partly good. p. 11: in the ninth century, all partly good, partly holy, with only three excepted. p. 12: in the tenth century, 25 are found all good, with few excepted. p. 13: in the eleventh century, all good and praised except two. p. 14: in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, all good and praised, none excepted. p. 16: in the fourteenth century, three; in the fifteenth, two; p. 17; in the sixteenth, one who is in some way blameworthy. p. 18: in the seventeenth, none excepted. In all, 77 saints were honoured with the incomparable honour of the Roman Papacy. From what has been said, I say, the vanity of this boasting is plainer than the noonday light, plain from so many examples of wicked men, and from the very confession of the Papist writers about such men.

units.la: LXXXII. Sed pii esse & eligi deberent & virtute præditi. Si Episcopi simplices, certè multò magis & in gradu multò majori Episcopi Episcoporum; & qui Sanctissimi audiunt, eorúmque quivis sua sanctitas appellatur, & quorum Curia, exigente Joh. Gerfone T.1. Serm. de Circumc. Dom. consid.3. ad similitudinem Hierarchiæ Angelicæ ordinanda esset & replenda viris caritate fervidis & contemplatione suspensis, ut Seraphim, Viris sapientiâ divinâ splendidis, ut Cherubim, viris æquitate firmissimis, ut throni, nec mutanda in curiam peccantium, ita ut, qui nutriri debent in Croceis, amplexentur stercora, id est, temporalia. Deberent omnes fulgere illis virtutibus Episcopalibus, quas Scriptura recenset, & omnes tales esse, quales format Apostolus, & quales plerosque fuisse Loyolita jactat, imò maximè tales esse deberent; Síque in Lege etiam ipsorum, sine crimine & gravi peccato ordinandus dicitur; Si Ecclesiam ingredi, juxta eam fornicatoribus non licet; Si Clericus matronarum domicilia frequentans, eadem jubente, deponendus esset; Si a lulter in Monasterium detrudendus; Sanè ex his ipsis, quàm certa quámque perfecta Pontificum Sanctitas esse debeat, facilè colligitur; Síq; Papa, de ejusdem Legis imperio, debet esse humilis, & semper præsuper bonus; Si in peccatum non potest in cidere, quod apud Baronium ad an.963. n. 40. habetur; Si rectè quæsivit Rodericus Zamorensis l.2. p.263. Quis Sanctum esse dubitet, quem apex tanta dignitatis extollit? Quod ipsum etiam Dist. 40. c. Non vos, habetur, ubi simul Petrus
units.tr: LXXXII. But the popes ought to be pious, to be chosen, and endowed with virtue. If bishops, plainly, then much more, and to a far greater degree, the bishops of bishops, who are called Most Holy, and each of whom is styled his holiness, and whose Curia, as Johannes Gerson demands (T.1. Serm. de Circumc. Dom. consid.3.), should be ordered after the likeness of the angelic hierarchy and filled with men burning with love and absorbed in contemplation, like the Seraphim; with men shining with divine wisdom, like the Cherubim; with men most firm in justice, like the thrones; and should not be turned into a court of sinners, so that those who ought to be nourished on the saffron cakes embrace dung, that is, temporal things. All of them ought to shine with those episcopal virtues which Scripture lists, and all ought to be such as the Apostle describes, and such as the Loyolite boasts that most of them have been; indeed they ought to be such above all. If, in their own Law too, a man is to be ordained without crime and grave sin; if fornicators are not permitted to enter the Church according to it; if a cleric who frequents the houses of matrons were, by the same command, to be deposed; if one were to be thrust into a monastery by force, then from these very things it is easily gathered how certain and how perfect the holiness of the popes ought to be. And if, by the authority of the same Law, the pope must be humble and always the best; if he cannot fall into sin (as is found in Baronius ad an. 963, n. 40.); if Rodericus Zamorensis rightly asked (l.2. p.263.): who would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity exalts? This is also found in Dist. 40, c. Non vos, where at the same time Peter is said to have left to his successors a perpetual gift of merits and an inheritance of innocence. [Text continues in unit 2.]

units.la: Sed pii esse & eligi deberent Petrus Successoribus suis perpetuum meritorum donum & hereditatem innocentiæ reliquisse dicitur ; ut præsumptiones fundamentum habeant & assertiones veræ maneant, gravibus saltem peccatis Papa foedari non debet ; Sique potius qui peccavit & pœnituit, quàm qui nunquam peccavit, eligendus est, quod dictat Lex eadem ; Saltem qui peccatis manifestis impœnitens occupatur, thronum Pontificium nullo jure conscendit. Etenim pietatis quoque Successio requiritur, & ut aliquis sit ἐκ ἡτῆον Διατάξεως ἡ τῆς Θεολογίας Ἀλέξανδρος non minùs pietatis, quàm præsidentiæ Successor, ut Nazianzenus Orat.21. quæ est in laudem Athanasii, de eo loquitur. Nam de genere conversationis, ut Tertullianus de Præscript. c. 43. loquitur, qualitas fidei æstimari potest : & doctrina index disciplina est ; & Irenæus quoque cum sermone sano conversationem sine offensa conjunxit ; Contrà illos, qui dum Doctores & summi & infallibiles Doctores & Ecclesiæ Capita Christique Vicarii audire volunt, non tantùm in gravissimorum scelerum cœno se volutant, sed & reprehendi nolunt id facientes, & non tantùm exemplo peccare docent, verùm etiam ex hoc capite disciplinam negligunt, imò doctrinam corrumpunt & propter traditiones suas præceptum Dei irritum faciunt, & doctrinas dæmoniorum amantes sub castitatis specie impuritati portam aperiunt, & superba vanitatis loquentes inescant per carnis cupiditates & lascivias, libertatem pollicendo, cùm ipsi servi sint corruptelæ, ex fructibus suis cognoscendi. Si rectè scripsit Episcopus Verdensis, Theodoricus à Niem, ubi de depositione Johannis : Oportet, Papam esse modestum, pacificum, scrutatorem, pium, justum & æquum & mundum. Nam quomodo immodestus modestos, immundus mundes efficere valebit? Qui si pacem oderit, quomodo pacificabit? Aut, si quis habuerit manus sordidatas, quomodo sordes alterius inquinati tegere poterit? Quia scriptum est ; Si cæcus cæcum duxerit, ambobus fovea patebit ; Et juxta dictum Catonis : Turpe est Doctori, si culpa redarguit ipsum. Si rectè non minùs scripsit multò recentior, atque etiam propiùs ad dignitatem Pontificiam, Janus Nicius Erythræus Epist. 78. ad Tyrrhenum p.178. Senatus (Cardinalium) si suum officium facere velit, non eum in tanto dignitatis gradu constituet, qui unum aliquod afferat, ut juris scientiam, aut aliquem Reip. usum, aut solam castitatis virtutem ; sed eum, qui sit virtutum omnium Princeps. Nam quamvis, ut in cæteris rebus, sic etiam virtutibus, alia species sit alia formosior atque illustrior, non tamen intra unius vel alterius virtutis terminos compellendus est ille, qui excurrere per omnes debeat : non præsiniendum est, quatenus progredi in bonorum operum progres- sn si debeat, cui pro viribus danda opera sit, ut unusquisque ita directum illud ad omnes virtutes iter teneat, ut earum perfectionis metam attingat. Quid multis moror? Omnibus virtutibus excellat oportet, qui omnibus specimen esse jubetur; Deo quàm simillimus judicetur necesse est, qui sit in loco, Deo in terris proximo, constituendus. Non potest id, quod dicimus, tam diserta oratione cujusquam explicari, quàm est à Deo ipsa ad vivum expressum. Qui Deus, daturus populo suo Regem, repudiatis omnibus aliis, Saulem potissimum, quem eo fastigio dignißimum arbitrabatur, Regem elegit. Qui eâ corporis formâ atque staturâ fuisse traditur, ut altior esset omni populo ab humero & sursum. In humero probitas, Sophonia voce, designatur; qui de populis Deo subjiciendis ait: Servient ei humero uno, hoc est, pari probitate atque justitiâ. Itaque cùm de Pontifice in demortui locum subrogando consulitur, ille præferendus est cæteris, qui altior sit omni populo, hoc est, qui communem usitatámque caterorum hominum probitatem & sanctitatem excedat, qui rerum divinarum ac cœlestium contemplatione sese cæteris altius extollat. Si rectè rursus & paulò post idem de peccato in electionem mali Pontificis consentientium: Hinc licet intelligere, quanto se peccato alligent, quantum in se hominum odium struant ii, ad quos Principis eligendi jus redit, si fasces indigno detulerint. Magnum irarum irritamentum, magna odii fax est, Principis non boni electio. Hoc enim inter parentem atque electorem Principis interest, quòd ille natura vitio, hic judicio peccet. Ille si minùs ut lem Reip. filium genuit, non continuò id ipsi vitio datur, non continuò civium odio premitur; quoniam non est in potestate nostra, nobis liberos ex animi sententia gignere; imò nemo est, quin filios quàm optimos velit: at, qui malè elegit, quia omnis in ipso culpa resident, cùm bene potuerit; illicò omnium divûm atque hominum odium incurrit, illicò diris & imprecationibus omnibus expetitur, exagitatur, laceratur. Accedit, quòd non est eadem ratio ejus, quem parens minùs feliciter genuit, ejusque, quem intemperans eligentium cupiditas, vel temperarius favor principem declaravit; quod ipsum æquiore homines animo ferunt, quoniam talis erat habendus, hunc perpeti ac tolerare nullo modo possunt, quòd hominum improbitate atque nequitia contigerit, ut sub malo principe essent. Quid si novi Principis comitia inc dant in id tempus, quo rebus afflictis ac perditis succurrendum sit maximè, quantam in se culpam concipientii, quibus ejusmodi electio commissa est, si non, quantum student & quantum possunt conferunt ad communem salutis voluntatem, si non omni studio sibi entendum putent, ut talis rebus afflictis ac perditis moderator existat, qui eas consilio sublevare, operâ recreare, sapientiâ reparare ac resicere valeat? &c. Sique Ecclesia Sancta Romana semper sine macula suit & sine ruga, quod ei Nicolaus teste Esthio in locum, tribuit, in Capite etiam talis ut fuerit, necesse est; Et si Innocentius VI. domi noluit nisi viros probatissimos: Idem ut facerent Cardinales, accerrimo edicto mandavit, dictitans, suam ac omnium Ecclesiasticorum vitam caeteris exemplo esse debere, ad imitationem Salvatoris nostri, cujus tota vita ad institutionem humani generis respiciebat; Id quod Platina de eo in vita narrat. Et tandem si, quantum interest, an optimus eligatur, Lotinus Differt. de Conclavi recte docet, docent etiam orationes contra indignos supra indigitatas; ex his omnibus sequitur, maxime necessarium esse, ut Papae pii sint & eligantur.
units.tr: But the popes ought to be pious and to be chosen, so that the presumption has a foundation and the assertions remain true; at least the pope must not be defiled by grave sins. And rather the one who has sinned and repented should be chosen than the one who has never sinned, as the same Law dictates. At the least, one who is held in manifest and unrepentant sin takes the papal throne by no right. For succession in piety is also required, so that one may be a successor not less in piety than in presidency, as Gregory Nazianzen says of Athanasius in his Oration 21, in praise of Athanasius: [ἐκ τῆς διατάξεως ἢ τῆς θεολογίας Ἀλέξανδρος]. For, as Tertullian says in de Praescript. c. 43, the quality of faith can be judged from the kind of conduct, and teaching is the index of discipline; and Irenaeus too joined sound speech with blameless conduct. Against those who, while wishing to hear their teachers called the highest and infallible teachers, Heads of the Church and Vicars of Christ, not only wallow in the mire of the gravest crimes but also do not want to be reproved for doing so, and not only teach sin by example but also neglect discipline on this ground, and indeed corrupt doctrine and make void the command of God for the sake of their traditions; and who, loving the doctrines of demons, open the door to impurity under the appearance of chastity, and who, speaking proud vanities, entice with the lusts and lasciviousness of the flesh, promising liberty while they themselves are slaves of corruption, to be known by their fruits. Rightly did Theodoricus à Niem, bishop of Verden, write when speaking of the deposition of John: The pope ought to be moderate, peaceable, searching, pious, just, fair and clean. For how can an immoderate man make others moderate, or an unclean man make others clean? If he hates peace, how will he make peace? Or if he has soiled hands, how can he cover the filth of another who is defiled? For it is written: If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit; and according to the saying of Cato: It is shameful for a teacher if he is rebuked for his own fault. Rightly too, not less, wrote a much more recent author, one even closer to the papal dignity, Janus Nicius Erythraeus (Epist. 78 ad Tyrrhenum, p. 178): If the Senate (of Cardinals) wishes to do its duty, it will not place in so high a rank of dignity one who has only some single thing, such as knowledge of law, or some practical experience of public affairs, or the sole virtue of chastity; but one who is the prince of all the virtues. For although, as in other things, so also in virtues, one form is more beautiful and more illustrious than another, yet he who ought to run through all of them must not be confined within the limits of one or another virtue; nor must it be determined how far he ought to advance in the progress of good works, to whom effort is to be given according to his powers, so that each person keeps that straight path towards all the virtues so as to reach the goal of their perfection. Why do I linger over many words? He must excel in all virtues who is set before all as an example; he must be judged most like God who is to be placed in a position nearest to God on earth. This cannot be explained by the speech of anyone so fittingly as it has been expressed to the life by God himself. God, about to give his people a king, rejected all others and chose Saul above all, whom he judged most worthy of that height. He is said to have been of such bodily form and stature that he was taller than all the people from the shoulder upward. The shoulder designates uprightness, in the voice of Zephaniah, who says of the peoples to be subjected to God: They shall serve him with one shoulder, that is, with equal uprightness and justice. Therefore, when a pope is to be consulted for the substitution of one who has died, let him be preferred to the rest who is higher than all the people, that is, who surpasses the common and usual uprightness and holiness of other men, who raises himself above others by contemplating divine and heavenly things. Again, rightly, and a little later the same author, on the sin of those who consent to the election of a bad pope: From this one may understand how much they bind themselves to sin, how much hatred of men they heap upon themselves, those to whom the right of electing a prince returns, if they have conferred the fasces on an unworthy man. The election of a prince who is not good is a great provocation of anger and a great torch of hatred. For there is this difference between a parent and the elector of a prince: the one sins by nature's fault, the other by judgment. If the parent has begotten a less than fitting son for the commonwealth, this is not at once put down to his fault, nor is he at once oppressed by the hatred of the citizens, since it is not in our power to beget children as we wish; indeed, no one would not wish his sons to be as excellent as possible. But he who has chosen badly, since all the blame lies in him when he could have chosen well, at once incurs the hatred of all gods and men, at once is sought out with curses and imprecations, harassed and torn to pieces. Moreover, the case of one whom a parent begot less happily is not the same as that of one whom the intemperate desire of the electors, or the careless favour of the voters, has declared prince; and men bear the former with a more equal mind, since such a one had to be regarded as such, but they cannot in any way endure the latter, since it has happened through the wickedness and villainy of men that they should be under a bad prince. What if the assembly for electing a new prince falls at a time when the afflicted and ruined state most needs help? How great a guilt do those incur to whom such an election has been entrusted, if they do not contribute as much as they strive and as much as they can to the common will for salvation, if they do not think they must devote every effort to ensuring that there should exist such a governor for afflicted and ruined affairs as may be able to relieve them by counsel, restore them by labour, and repair and set them right by wisdom? etc. And if the Holy Roman Church has always been without spot or wrinkle, as Nicholas, according to Esthius in loc., ascribes to her, then the head too must necessarily be such. And if Innocent VI wished to admit to his house only the most approved men; and he commanded the Cardinals by a most stringent edict to do the same, declaring that his own life and that of all ecclesiastics ought to be an example to others, in imitation of our Saviour, whose whole life looked to the instruction of the human race; which Platina relates of him in his Life. And finally, if it matters greatly whether the best man is chosen, Lotinus rightly teaches in his Differt. de Conclavi, and the speeches against unworthy men mentioned above also teach it; from all these things it follows that it is most necessary that the popes be pious and be chosen as such.

units.la: LXXXIII. Neque ullo modo excusari possunt mali; Non paucitate sua, de qua Ottonem Loyolitam gloriantem supra vidimus & denuo introducimus: Primo autem, inquit Rom. Glor. p. 5. ultro lubensque fateor, me nolle Romanam nostram Ecclesiam coelo anteferre, in quo licet tertia Angelorum pars mala fuerit, coelum tamen coelum & Regnum Dei mansit. Sic etiam si tertia Romanorum Pontificum pars defectuosa, scelerata & vilis deprehenderetur, tamen Ecclesia Romana Regnum Dei, coelum terrestre, & communio Sanctorum maneret, proin rebus sic stantibus nullus sapiens causam separationis ab illa inveniret. Ita etiam p. 347. 348. multis gloriabundus urget; In Schola Christi Judam, in Collegio Diaconorum Nicolaum, occasionem saltem haereseos Nicolaitarum, inter Sacerdotes V. T. Aaronem Idololatram, Annam & Cajaphan Deicidas fuisse. Sed 1. Quis ei dixit, tertiam praecise Angelorum partem lapsam esse? 2. Falsam esse de non vigesima sceleratorum parte jactantiam, imo plus quam tertiam Pontificum, ex quo in fide defecerunt (priores enim ut fide, ita etiam vita a posterioribus multum diversos vereque Evangelicos fuisse, ipsimet contendimus) partem malam fuisse, ex allatis Scriptorum Pontificiorum testimoniis patet, & multo magis, cum veritatis laesione a Loyolita dictum, plerosque omnes ad Paulinam regulam formatos, non continentes ex tanto numero paucissimos fuisse, parum justos vix numerum facere, non benignos, non hospitales nonnullos &c. (quos sic latere jubet) in tanto horum summorum Praesulum Populo vix agnosci. Sed & alias simile claudicat; Nam 3. Angeli, qui defecerant, non in Coelo manserunt & cives Regni gloriae, sed in tartarum detrusi & catenis caliginis traditi, damnationi servantur 2. Pet. II. 4. Contra Pontifices defectores, etiam dum tales fuerunt, Capita Ecclesiae, non praevalentibus contra eos inferorum portis, supponuntur, neque in alio statu Ecclesiae Capita supponuntur; Ut, quando Coelum Coelum esse non desiit, quia Angeli defectores ex eo statim praecipitati sunt, contra inferre oportheat, teat, Ecclesiam Romanam Ecclesiam non mansisse, quia praeter doctrinae corruptionem etiam corruptos tales passa est, & Dominos absolutos passa est, imò summopere coluit. 4. Angeli simul defecerunt, simul puniti; Sed Pontifices corrupti Ecclesiam illam per plura secula infecerunt, & tamen Successio talium jactatur, quae certe respectu Angelorum defectorum coelo constanter dominantium bona tribui non posset. 5. Judas & Nicolaus (si vera sunt, quae huic tribuuntur;) in Collegio Apostolorum & Diaconorum, dum pro talibus agniti sunt, non manserunt, ut Pontifices mali & nonnisi mali plurimi fuerunt & manserunt. 6. Aaronis actus quasi unus ad defensionem habituum malorum in Pontificibus malis trahi non debet. 7. Bene faciunt, quòd Pontifices suos malos Annae & Cajaphae assimulant, à quibus tamen ratione muneris horum à Deo instituti differunt. 8. Et Aaron, Idololatriam committens summus Sacerdos, & Annas & Cajaphas in errores inciderunt, documento, quid multò magis Romanis accidere possit. 9. Neque in Juda jam proditore, neque in Nicolao haeresiarcha successionem ullam continuatam volent, neque etiam in Anna & Cajapha legitimam legitimorum Sacerdotum, dum hi male intrusi pejus Deicidae facti sunt. Ut mox fatentes audiemus, malos suos male electos fuisse, numerari non debere. 10. Cum Juda proditore fuerunt undecim Apostoli boni, cum Nicolao haeretico dicto sex Diaconi fuissent boni, nulli cum Pontificibus malis boni Pontifices. Cúmque 11. fateantur, & Judae & Nicolao ex hypothesi & Cajaphae & Annae portas inferorum praevaluisse, idem de Pontificibus non melioribus fateantur, necesse est.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The wicked cannot be excused in any way, not by their small number, which we have already seen Otto the Loyolite boasting about and which we bring up again. First, I freely and gladly admit, that I am unwilling to place our Roman Church before heaven, in which, although a third part of the Angels became evil, heaven nonetheless remained heaven and the Kingdom of God. So too, even if a third part of the Roman Pontiffs were found defective, wicked and base, the Roman Church would still remain the Kingdom of God, an earthly heaven, and the communion of the Saints; therefore, with things standing thus, no wise man would find a cause for separation from her. (Roman Glory, p. 5.) He presses the same boast, with many flourishes, on pp. 347 and 348: In Christ's school there was Judas, in the college of Deacons Nicolas, the occasion at least of the Nicolaitan heresy; among the priests of the Old Testament there was Aaron, an idolater, and Annas and Caiaphas, murderers of God. But: (1) who told him that precisely a third part of the Angels fell? (2) The boast about not a twentieth of the wicked is false. Indeed, more than a third of the Pontiffs, from the time they fell away in faith, were the evil part (for we ourselves contend that the earlier ones were very different from the later ones, truly Evangelical in life as well as in faith). This is clear from the testimonies of the Papist writers quoted above, and even more so from the Loyolite's statement, made with a violation of the truth, that most of them were formed on the Pauline rule, that of so great a number very few were not continent, that scarcely a few were just, that some were not kind or hospitable, etc. (which he bids us overlook) and that among so great a people of these highest Prelates these virtues can scarcely be recognised. But in other respects the comparison also limps. For (3) the Angels who fell did not remain in heaven as citizens of the Kingdom of glory, but were cast down into hell, delivered into chains of darkness, and kept for judgment (2 Pet. 2:4). On the contrary, the Pontiffs who fell away, even while they were such, are presented as the Heads of the Church, against whom the gates of hell did not prevail; and in no other state are Heads of the Church presented. So, just as heaven did not cease to be heaven because the Angels who fell were at once thrown down from it, so one must conclude, against him, that the Roman Church has not remained the Church, because, besides the corruption of doctrine, she has suffered such corrupt men and has suffered absolute lords, indeed has greatly honoured them. (4) The Angels fell together and were punished together; but the corrupt Pontiffs infected that Church for many centuries, and yet the succession of such men is boasted of, which certainly could not be credited as a good thing, in respect of the fallen Angels, who constantly rule in heaven. (5) Judas and Nicolas (if the things attributed to them are true) did not remain in the college of Apostles and Deacons once they were recognised as such; whereas the evil Pontiffs were, and remained, evil, and very many of them. (6) The single act of Aaron should not be drawn to defend the evil habits of the evil Pontiffs. (7) They do well to liken their evil Pontiffs to Annas and Caiaphas, from whom, nevertheless, they differ in the office they held by God's institution. (8) Aaron, the high priest who committed idolatry, and Annas and Caiaphas fell into errors, a warning of what could happen far more readily to the Romans. (9) Neither in Judas, now a traitor, nor in Nicolas, the heresiarch, will they want any continued succession, nor in Annas and Caiaphas a lawful succession of lawful priests, since these, unlawfully thrust in, became worse murderers of God. As they will soon be heard confessing, their evil men were badly chosen and should not be counted. (10) Along with the traitor Judas there were eleven good Apostles; along with Nicolas, called a heretic, there would have been six good Deacons; but with the evil Pontiffs there were no good Pontiffs at all. (11) Since they admit that the gates of hell prevailed, on their own hypothesis, against Judas and Nicolas, and against Caiaphas and Annas, they must likewise admit the same of Pontiffs who were no better.

units.la: LXXXIV.
units.tr: LXXXIV.

units.la: Neque etiam dici potest, quod dicunt tamen, malos esse participes meritorum, quibus boni eminuerint. Dicunt, cum Ennodio nimirum, Ticinensi vel Papiensi Episcopo, qui Symmacho Pontifici adulaturus Centur. Magdeb. Cent. VI. c. 8. p. 233. a. sesquipedalia haec protulit verba: Etiam Papa malus suorum majorum, ac Sacro-Sanctae Sedis Romanae, meritis & dignitate sublevatur. Nam ista sedes aut Sanctos accipit, aut efficit. Quae ipsa etiam, & quòd sufficiant Papae in defectu propriorum merita Antecessorum communicata. Dist. 40. c. Non vos Et apud Rodericum Zamorensem l. 2. p. 263. habentur. Sed absurde ista dici, sequentia probant; Nam 1. cuivis pietatem necessariam esse & singulis dicta demonstrant. Ut & 2. illud, non singulos actu pietatis successionem accepisse, & istam sedem, quos nam Sanctos acceperit, Sanctos effecisse. Neque 3. imputationem merimeritorum humanorum urgere possunt, qui imputationem meritorum Christi Anathemate notant; qui insuper nôrunt, vel ex Platinæ testimonio suprà allato, dignitatem à possidentibus auctoritatem habere, modò auctam, modò diminutam; qui nôrunt, malis malam quoque electionem vel succedendi rationem tribui; qui nôrunt denique, justum, ut fide suâ vivet, ita secundùm fidem & opera sua etiam Deo vel gratum vel abominationi esse & meredem reportaturum. Ut 4. concludere liceat, pessimis illis ab aliis nihil addi posse, quo ad Successionem continuandam apti efficiantur.
units.tr: Nor can it be said, as they nevertheless do say, that the wicked share in the merits by which the good have stood out. They say this, with Ennodius, namely the Bishop of Pavia or Ticinum, who, wishing to flatter the Pontiff Symmachus, Centur. Magdeb. Cent. VI. c. 8. p. 233. a. uttered these high-sounding words: Even a wicked Pope is raised up by the merits and dignity of his predecessors and of the Most Holy Roman See. For that See either receives saints or makes them. And the merits of his predecessors, communicated to him, suffice for the Pope in the absence of his own. Dist. 40, c. Non vos; and they are also found in Rodericus Zamorensis, l. 2. p. 263. But that these things are absurd, the following shows. For (1) it is shown both in general and in particular that piety is necessary for everyone. Likewise (2) that the succession was not received by each one in an act of piety, and that this See made saints of whomever it received as saints. Nor (3) can they press the imputation of human merits, when they brand as anathema the imputation of the merits of Christ. They also know, even from the testimony of Platina quoted above, that dignity draws its authority from its holders, now increased, now diminished; they know that to evil men an evil election or manner of succession is ascribed; and they know finally that the righteous man, who lives by his faith, is by his faith and works also either pleasing to God or an abomination to him, and will receive his reward accordingly. So (4) we may conclude that nothing can be added by others to those wicked men which would make them fit to continue the succession.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Pari ratione absurdum & illud est, quòd, malos Pontifices excusaturi porrò ajunt, illos bonis mixtos Ecclesiæ ornamento fuisse. Tantum verò abest, inquit Loyolita in Dedic. Rom. Glor. ut atræ hæ maculæ paucorum Ecclesia Romana faciem defœdârint, stigmáve inusserint, ut pulchriorem etiam reddiderint & gloriosiorem. Umbræ pulchritudinem addunt pictura, non adimunt, & Carbunculi nunquam pretiosius, splendidiúsve, quàm è densioribus tenebris elucent. Sic etiam Franciscus Carriere ad Johannis X. spurii per matrem intrusionem annotat: Deus hanc Ecclesiæ suæ maculam inuri permisit ad majorem ejus splendorem, more mulierum, quæ ad innati candoris argumentum muscas & nigredines sibi in facie adpingunt. Absurdum, inquam, & hoc est, his etiam similitudinibus turpiter claudicantibus. I. Enim constat, atras maculas non paucorum, sed plurimorum fuisse; nemo autem formosam faciem & eo formosiorem vocabit, quòd atris maculis majorem partem ejus occupantibus pulchri aliquid interpositum sit, ut pauciores ad Regulam Apostolicam formatos & atris maculis destitutos Pontifices inde à defectionis tempore fuisse ostendimus. II. Verum quidem est, aliquando fœminas stultè superbas atras maculas in facie hinc inde disponere, eum in finem, ut sic pulchritudo albedinis faciei magis elucescat; sed cùm aliter longè de faciei pulchritudine judicent sapientes, aliter etiam ac ille, qui de artificiosa pictura rogatus; ut placeat? respondit; ideò non placere, quia nihil in ea reperiat, quod censura suâ notare possit; judicent nimirum, faciem eam esse pulcherrimam in qua nullæ prorsus maculæ, & quæ non opus habeat, mediocritatem suam oppositorum appositione commendare; cùm etiam Ecclesia Christi sit sine ruga & macula, quod Pontificios visibili suæ sub Capite visibili applicare suprà notavimus, jam ex eo manifestus est comparationis tionis eatenus etiam duplex defectus. III. Neque color ater, neque umbratilis in picturis in se aliquid foedi continet, ut de peccato sceleribusque certum est, Deo & piis per se & semper abominationi esse, atque proin plane inconveniens, dicere, sic faciem Ecclesiae Romanae pulchriorem reddi & gloriosiorem, Capitibus nimirum plane monstrosis IV. Neque atrae maculae faciei appositae, neque tenebrae, in quibus fulget Carbunculus, ad faciem pertinent, aut ad Carbunculum, ut monstra hominum Ecclesiae Romanae Capita fuerunt. V. Neque atrae maculae eo aliquid dignitatis consequuntur, quod sua, si quam habent, ut habere supponuntur, deformitate formositatem faciei facilius observandam praebent, neque tenebrae eo, quod in iis Carbunculus fulget; Et proin haud magis indigni Pontifices a dignis dignitatem sufficientem accipiunt. VI. Atrae maculae & facies pulchra simul in oculos incurrunt, simul & eodem tempore praesentes, sed dum Pontifices fuerunt atrae maculae, nulli fuerunt faciem pulchram constituentes, & quia saepe & diu priores fuerunt, diu nulla plane in facie, imo in Capite integro pulchritudo, sed summa fuit deformitas, & per consequens interrupta Pontificum faciem pulchram & gloriosam, qua fideles delectentur, infideles alliciantur, faciem constituentium successio. Sic etiam dum longiori temporis spatio nullus in Ecclesia Romana, seu caput, Carbunculus fulsit, merae tunc fuerunt tenebrae, & Pontifices illi tenebriones atque tenebricosi posteriores haud magis continuarunt successionem priorum, qui (quod ab omnibus fidelibus exigit Apostolus Phil. II. 15) splendidi fuerunt, ut lumina mundi, in generatione perversa & improba, quam in tenebris est successio lucis, sed pertinent ad generationem perversam & improbam; sunt tenebrae, non Capita Ecclesiae, cujus membra quaevis sunt filii lucis, lumina mundi.
units.tr: In the same way it is absurd when they go on to excuse their wicked Popes by saying that these were mixed with good men and were an ornament to the Church. The Loyolite says, in Dedic. Rom. Glor., that far from these black stains of a few men having disfigured the face of the Roman Church or branded it, they have made it more beautiful and more glorious. Painting gains beauty from shadow, not loss, and a carbuncle never shines more precious or more brightly than when it gleams out of thick darkness. So too Franciscus Carriere, commenting on the intrusion of John X, the son of a harlot, writes: God allowed this spot to be burned into His Church for her greater splendour, in the manner of women who paint flies and dark marks on their faces to show off the whiteness of their natural complexion. This too is absurd, I say, and these comparisons limp shamefully. First, it is established that the black stains were not of a few but of very many. No one would call a face beautiful, and more beautiful for it, because a fair part of it is covered by black stains and something lovely has been set among them. We have shown above that there were fewer Popes formed according to the Apostolic rule and free of black stains from the time of the falling away. Second, it is true that foolish, proud women sometimes put dark marks here and there on their faces, with the aim that the beauty of the whiteness of the skin should shine out more; but wise people judge quite differently about the beauty of a face, as did the man who, when asked about a painting, whether it pleased, replied: it does not please, because I find nothing in it that I can censure. They judge, namely, that that face is most beautiful in which there are no blemishes at all, and which needs no mediocre quality to be commended by the addition of opposites. Since the Church of Christ is without spot or wrinkle, which we noted above that the Papists apply to their visible Church under her visible Head, the comparison is doubly defective on this point as well. Third, neither black colour nor shadow in paintings contains in itself anything foul, as it is certain that sin and crimes are in themselves and always abominable to God and the pious. It is therefore quite unfitting to say that the face of the Roman Church is made more beautiful and more glorious in this way, namely by heads that are plainly monstrous. Fourth, neither the black stains set on a face nor the darkness in which the carbuncle shines belong to the face, or to the carbuncle, as the monstrous men who were heads of the Roman Church did. Fifth, black stains do not gain any dignity from the fact that, through their deformity (if they have any, as they are supposed to have), they make the beauty of the face easier to notice; nor does darkness gain it from the fact that a carbuncle shines in it. Therefore the unworthy Popes do not receive sufficient dignity from the worthy any more than they otherwise would. Sixth, black stains and a beautiful face come into view together and are present at the same time. But while the Popes were black stains, none of them made up a beautiful face. And because these were often and long the earlier ones, for a long time there was plainly no beauty in the face, indeed none in the whole head, but the greatest deformity. Consequently the succession of Popes that makes up a beautiful and glorious face, in which the faithful take delight and unbelievers are drawn, was interrupted. In the same way, while for a long stretch of time no carbuncle shone in the Roman Church, or in her head, there was nothing but darkness. Those later Popes, darkeners and men of darkness, did not continue the succession of the earlier ones, who (as the Apostle requires of all the faithful, Phil. 2:15) were bright as lights of the world, in a crooked and perverse generation. The succession of light is in darkness, but these belong to a crooked and perverse generation. They are darkness, not the heads of the Church, whose members are all sons of light and lights of the world.

units.la: LXXXVI. Neque etiam Pontifices suos excusare possunt naevorum parvitate; Conantur quidem; nam loquentem jam audivimus Loyolitam de non continentibus, parum justis, non benignis, non hospitalibus; tenuiter satis, & negatione virtutis, non vitii positione.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Nor can the Popes excuse themselves by the smallness of their blemishes. They try to, for we have already heard the Loyolite speaking of men not continent, not very just, not kind, not hospitable. This is rather a thin way of speaking, which denies a virtue rather than asserts a vice.

units.la: Quemadmodum etiam p.20. testatur, se non Angelorum historiam scribere, alios nimis somnolente interdum rem egisse, alios consanguineis plus aequo indulsisse, eosque nimis promovisse, modo nimis parcos, modo nimis liberales fuisse, & qui alii sint navi hominum dominantium &c. sic tamen manere in numero bonorum hominum, sic etiam Pontificum. Et
units.tr: As he also testifies on p. 20, he is not writing the history of angels, some had been too sleepy at times in their work, others had indulged their relatives more than was fitting and promoted them too much, some had been too stingy and others too generous, and there are other men of the ruling kind, and so on. Yet they remain in the number of good men, and so do the Popes.

units.la: P.348. p.348. Ex 6. Papæ malis Seculi X. nullum superbiâ Luciferum, proditione Judam, abominatione & injustitiâ Cajaphām; ratione permissæ Idololatriæ Aaronem, ratione impuritatis & hæresis introductæ Nicolaum fuisse. Similiter apud Dianam de Ador. Pont. Rom. Caramuel de ingenium vitiorum confluxu ita loquitur: Non omnes Papæ à sinceritate laudantur &c. Bellarmini hic præf. ad libros de Summo Pont. sermo est: Permisit ad extremum Deus, ut etiam quidam parum probi Pontifices aliquando hanc sedem tenerent & regerent. Ne autem vel hic sermo offendat: Si vera sunt, quæ de eorum vita & rebus gestis apud Historicos eorum temporum scripta leguntur.
units.tr: p.348. Six wicked popes of the tenth century: that Lucifer fell through pride, Judas through betrayal, Caiaphas through abomination and injustice, Aaron through tolerating idolatry, and Nicolaus through the introduction of impurity and heresy. Similarly, Caramuel, in Diana's On the Adoration of the Roman Pontiffs, speaks thus about the convergence of many vices: Not all the Popes are praised for their sincerity, etc. Here is Bellarmine's statement in the preface to his books On the Supreme Pontiff: God finally permitted some Popes of little integrity to hold and govern this see at certain times. Lest even this statement give offence: If what is read in the historians of their times about their life and deeds is true.

units.la: LXXXVII. Neque etiam rectam defensionis viam ingreditur Baronius, dum ad an.897. n. 9. primò quidem ait: Ut Deus significaret, suam Ecclesiam nequaquam esse humanum figmentum, sed plane divinum inventum: oportuit ostendisse, eam nequaquam pravorum Antistitum operâ perdi posse, & ad nihilum penitus redigi &c. Secundò soli & lunæ Ecclesiam suam comparat; Et tertiò concludit: Recogites verum tu adeò austerus exactor, quòd, cùm Christus non dedignatus sit adeò scelestos atque adeò impios in sua genealogia habere prædecessores: quid adeò mirandum & indecens, ipsum etiam habere passum esse successores hujusmodi homines peccatores, licet nunquam impios sicut illos? In prima enim defensione partim præsupponit, Ecclesiam Romanam esse veram, quod maximè est in quæstione, partim insuper ex malis Pontificibus ejus veritatem probat, quod quidem pessimè facit; si enim mirum est, Ecclesiam Romanam sub malis aliquando Antistitibus perseverare & divinæ originis argumentum; multò magis mirum erit, Inferorum Regnum sub Antistitibus tantùm malis diutiùs substitisse, & sic vel ipsis Inferis Divinam originem attribuere quis posset potiori jure. An ignoravit autem Annalista humana Regni sui Pontificii fulcra? An nescivit Divinam longanimitatem, & divina de defectione magna diu duratura vaticinia? Annon eadem Regnorum Politicorum (quod negat) diuturnitas sub malis aliquando Principibus? Imò major aliquando sub talibus potentia. Et an regnum iniquitatis iniquitate citò debet destrui? Et si per malos Antistites salva maneret Ecclesiæ Romanæ veritas, quomodo Antistitum legitimorum salva maneret successio? Dum verò in secunda defensione Soli comparat & Lunæ Romanam suam Ecclesiam, sibi necessitatem imponit probandi præter alia, Ecclesiam illam ratione Solis semper in se, etiam respectu Capitum, quibus Ecclesia
units.tr: LXXXVII. Baronius does not take the right path of defence either. At ad an. 897, n. 9 he first says: That God might show that his Church is by no means a human fabrication but plainly a divine invention, it was necessary to show that it could not be destroyed by the work of wicked prelates and reduced utterly to nothing, etc. Secondly, he compares his Church to the sun and the moon. And thirdly he concludes: Consider, you who are so stern an exactor: since Christ did not disdain to have such wicked and impious men among his predecessors in his genealogy, what is so very surprising or unseemly that he should also have had successors of this kind, sinful men, though never impious as those were? In the first defence he partly presupposes that the Roman Church is true, which is precisely the point in question, and partly proves its truth from its wicked Pontiffs, which he does very badly. For if it is remarkable that the Roman Church has persisted under wicked prelates at times, and that this is a proof of divine origin, it will be much more remarkable that the kingdom of Hell has lasted so long under prelates who were only wicked, so that anyone could with better right attribute a divine origin even to Hell itself. But did the annalist not know the human props of his Papal kingdom? Did he not know of divine long-suffering, and of the divine prophecies that a great apostasy would last a long time? Is it not the same with the lasting of political kingdoms (which he denies) under wicked princes at times, and indeed sometimes with greater power under such princes? And must the kingdom of iniquity be destroyed quickly by iniquity? And if the truth of the Roman Church remained safe through wicked prelates, how would the succession of lawful prelates remain safe? But in the second defence, where he compares his Roman Church to the sun and the moon, he imposes on himself the necessity of proving, among other things, that that Church was always bright and shining in itself by the reason of the sun, even with respect to the heads whom the Church represents and in whom it is said to be contained as in a foundation; and that, by the reason of the moon, the comparison was made with respect to spots, and that the spots in the moon have the same cause as those in the Pontiffs, many of whom, being alone, had nothing but spots, by whom the Church

units.la: Ecclesia clesia repræsentari, & in quibus ranquam in fundamento contine-ri dicitur, splendidam, lucidam fuisse; Et ratione Lunæ, comparationem respectu macularum institutam, & macularum in Luna eandem rationem esse, quæ in Pontificibus, quorum multi soli existentes nil præter maculas habuerunt. Dum vero de Ecclipsibus loquitur, successionem talem, qualis ad fidei certitudinem & omnium fidelium salutem à subjectione Pontificibus debita pendentem requiritur, manifeste tollit, ut & aliorum propriamque de civitate semper in monte gloriosa & Ecclesia sine ruga & macula jactantiam. Neque eum in defensione tertia magis juvant Majores Christi secundum carnem p joris notæ; Quis etenim non videt, posse quidem Christum secundum carnem ex Majoribus quibusdam malis descendere, Pontificem Sanctissimum in Spiritual officio ex vocatione Spirituali Successores Vicarios in fid. i morumque doctrina infallibiles, & Ecclesiæ suæ, quæ sine ruga & macula, quæque casta est, Capita & Sponsos impurissimos, plane impios habere non posse? Quod enim Baronius sui oblitus, peccatores quidem, sed non impios fuisse unquam, ait, in eo juxta præcedentia & testimoniis propriis & sociorum & veritati historicæ impudenter contradicit. Quemadmodum etiam non juvantur alii quorundam Vet. Test. Sacerdotum vitiis, & Pharisæorum Scribarumque à Christo subinde notata hypocrisi; Nam 1. ex comparatione longè major longè plurium apparet Romanorum Pontificum præ illis Vet. Test. in longè longiori horum, maximè si defectionis in doctrina apud recentiores illos originem spectes, serie improbitas, quæ proin non tam ordinarium & simile dignitatum quarumvis, quàm verò Spiritus reprobationis in Papatu regnantis consequens. 2. Nec tanta habuerunt, nec tanta sibi tribuerunt Vet. Test. Sacerdotes, proin nec tanta in pauciorum ex eis minori improbitate fuit inconvenientia, & mira Spiritus infallibilis veritatis & summæ impietatis combinatio, maximè si Oeconomiæ diversitatem insuper respicias. 3. Differentia in eo etiam haud exigua est, quòd fere sub finem demum V. T. Doctores, Scribæ & Pharisæi, degenerârunt, quando munus ipsorum prope fuit, ut aboleretur, ad eò magis secundùm Providentiæ Divinæ ductum de instante mutatione & amplectendo Evangelio erudiendos Israelitas, dum contrà in ipso Christianismi, juxta Pontificios, vigore, ingenti infidelium fidelíumque scandalo, ista Rom Ecclesiæ probra vel maximè
units.tr: ...represented by the Church, and in which it is said to be contained as in a foundation, was splendid and bright. And by the analogy of the Moon, the comparison was drawn with respect to spots, and the spots in the Moon bear the same relation as those in the Pontiffs, many of whom, being alone, had nothing but spots. When he speaks of eclipses, he plainly removes the kind of succession that is required for the certainty of faith and for the salvation of all the faithful, which depends on the submission owed to the Pontiffs, as well as the boast of the other city, glorious always on its mountain, and of the Church without spot or wrinkle. Nor do the ancestors of Christ according to the flesh help him much in his third defence, since they were of a notorious sort. For who does not see that Christ could indeed descend according to the flesh from certain wicked ancestors, but that the Most Holy Pontiff, in his spiritual office, by spiritual calling, successors and vicars infallible in matters of faith and moral doctrine, cannot have as the heads and spouses of his Church, which is without spot or wrinkle and is chaste, men who are most impure and plainly impious? For Baronius, forgetting himself, says that they were indeed sinners, but were never non impios...unquam; in saying this he contradicts, shamelessly, both the preceding facts and the testimonies of his own side and of historical truth. Likewise, the Papists are not helped by the vices of certain priests of the Old Testament, or by the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and scribes that Christ from time to time pointed out. For (1) by comparison it appears that far more Roman Pontiffs than those of the Old Testament were wicked, and over a much longer series, especially if you look to the origin of the defection in doctrine among those more recent men; so this wickedness is not the ordinary and similar consequence of any dignities whatever, but rather of the Spirit of reprobation reigning in the Papacy. (2) The priests of the Old Testament neither had such great powers nor claimed such great powers for themselves; therefore, even in the lesser wickedness of a few of them, there was no such incongruity, and no such wonderful combination of the Spirit of infallible truth and the greatest impiety, especially if you also consider the difference in the economy. (3) The difference here is also not small, in that the teachers, scribes and Pharisees of the Old Testament degenerated only near the very end, when their office was almost due to be abolished, and when, according to the guidance of Divine Providence, Israelites had to be instructed about the impending change and the embracing of the Gospel; whereas, on the contrary, in the very vigour of Christianity, according to the Papists, these disgraces of the Roman Church appeared most of all, to the great scandal of unbelievers and believers alike.

units.la: maxi-mè mè apparuerunt. 4. Hypocrisis potiùs quàm externa cunctisque manifesta improbitas fuit,quam Christus in Scribis & Pharisæis reprehendit, superbia, ambitio & avaritia, quibus non obstantibus, manebat quædam honestas externa populíque etiam per austeritatem maximorum Doctorum ædificatio,qualia quis in Papis plurimis,seculorum præteritorum cumprimis monstris, manifestè impiis, frustrà requisiverit.
units.tr: most of all appeared. 4. The sin that Christ rebuked in the Scribes and Pharisees was hypocrisy rather than open and manifest wickedness in every respect: pride, ambition and greed. Despite these faults, a certain outward decency remained, and the people were edified by the austerity of the great teachers. Such decency one would search for in vain in most of the Papists, especially the monsters of past centuries, who were manifestly impious.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Neque etiam malum tollunt, sed augent potiùs,quando malos non legitimè electos fuisse docent. Sic Loyolita Otto jam aliquoties citatus in Dedic. Roma-Glor. iterum: Ad hæc, inquit, talibus vitiis ac sordibus, illorum plane neminem commaculatum fuisse,audenter pronuntio,qui legitimè in Pontifices electi,Petri Cathedram inierunt,sed eorum tantùmodò aliquot,qui auro,quàm Tbolosanum sit,multò nocentiore succollante,irruperunt non semel,atque in altum sublati sunt, ut casu recidèrent graviori. Sic etiam Platina in Bonif.VII. Pontificum illius temporis degenerationem prævalenti malorum in eligendo ambitioni & avaritiæ tribuit. Nec minùs L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.14. ex face pessima intrusi vocantur. Augent sic malum omninò, & dum illi argumentantur à mala vita ad Electionem malam; Genebrardus & Baronius ab Electione mala ad vitam malam: Nihil mirum, inquit ille Chronol. l. 4. ad an. 913. si isti Pontifices prodigiosi essent. Nam non more Majorum eligebantur, sed à Cæsaribus intrudebantur. Hic verò ad an.908. n. 4. quærit: At ab istis (Pontificibus intrusis) quis justa legitimáque requirat? Et Loyolita Otto ista etiam de non continentibus, parùm justis,non benignis, non hosp. talibus &c. affirmat; Et Janus Nicius Erythræus Epist. cit. dicens: Nullum bene imperaturi signum est majus,quàm si imperare recusset; ambitiosorum perversum regimen è contrario probat. Et constat, talium, imò monstrorum fœdissimorum, tantam multitudinem fuisse; constat etiam ex præcedentibus,tot malè,tum verè,tum ex hypothesi, quoad Electiones Cæsarum, electos esse; jam & ob reciprocum istud,multò major pars & mala fuit, & malè electa fuit; id est, & non à Deo vocata fuit, & in honore,quem sibi sumpserunt ipsi,pessimè versata fuit. Qualis autem est talium successio? An religionis fundamentum,firmamentum fidei?
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Nor do they remove the evil; rather they increase it when they teach that the wicked were not lawfully elected. Thus Loyola's Otto, already cited several times, says again in the Dedic. Roma-Glor.: Moreover, he says, I boldly declare that none of those who were lawfully elected to the Pontificate and entered the Chair of Peter was stained with such vices and filth. Rather, only some few of them, who burst in more than once, with gold far more harmful, as Tolosan gold is, lending them support, and were raised on high, so that they fell by a heavier fall. Likewise Platina, in Bonif. VII., ascribes the degeneracy of the Popes of that time to the prevailing evil of ambition and greed in the election. No less does L'Ambasc. di Rom. p. 14. ex face call them the most wicked intruders. In this way they increase the evil altogether. And while they argue from a bad life to a bad election, Genebrardus and Baronius argue from a bad election to a bad life. Nothing is surprising, says the former, Chronol. l. 4. ad an. 913., if those Popes were monstrous. For they were not elected according to the custom of their elders, but were forced in by the Caesars. Here indeed, ad an. 908. n. 4., he asks: But from such intruded Popes, who would seek what is just and lawful? Loyola's Otto also affirms this about men who were not self-controlled, not very just, not kind, not hospitable, and so on. Janus Nicius Erythraeus, in the letter cited, saying Nothing is a greater sign of a man who will rule well than that he refuses to rule, proves the perverse government of the ambitious by the contrary. And it is established that there was so great a multitude of such men, indeed of the most foul monsters. It is also established from what has gone before that so many were elected badly, whether truly or hypothetically, as regards the elections of the Caesars. Now, by this reciprocal argument, a much greater part were both wicked and badly elected: that is, they were not called by God, and they conducted themselves most badly in the honour they took for themselves. What, then, is the succession of such men? Is it the foundation of religion, the firmament of faith?

units.la: LXXXIX. Augent etiam malum,quando malos non numerant, quando dicunt,esse tantùm ad connotanda tempora; non numerari nisi ob Chronologiam, & nonnisi ad exemplum aliorum, quosdam dam, quâ formulâ etiam Loyolita Otto utitur, se pro Pontifice gessisse; Ita enim & quid de aliis non melioribus judicari debeat, quòd nimirum neque illi Pontifices fuerint, & numerandi sint, indicant; plurimos in Pontificum Catalogo expungendos esse docent, & successionem variè interruptam nulliúsque momenti ipsimet ostendunt; licèt ab altera parte cum Baronio ad an. 969. n. 37. statuant, hæreticum esse, statuere, ob peccata auferri Papatum, hæretici ipsimet, dum propter peccata non numerant, judicio proprio.
units.tr: LXXXIX. They also increase the evil when they do not count the wicked, when they say that the names are only there to mark the times, that they are numbered only for the sake of chronology and only as an example of others. This formula Loyola's Otto also uses, saying that he acted as Pope. In this way they also indicate what should be judged about others who were no better: namely, that those men were not Popes and should not be counted. They teach that very many must be struck from the Catalogue of Popes, and they themselves show that the succession was variously broken and of no weight. Yet on the other side, with Baronius, ad an. 969. n. 37., they affirm that it is heretical, and they affirm that the Papacy was taken away on account of sins, the heretics themselves, since they do not count them on account of sins, by their own judgement.

units.la: XC. Augetur & aliâs malum à malis, quòd mali mores etiam doctrinam corrumpunt, maximè in Doctoribus summis, infallibiliter ex hypothesi & ad obsequium sine examine docentibus, sine reprehensione & coercitione tam fœdè támque variè peccantibus. Ut enim veritas secundùm pietatem est salutaris, ita etiam sororius est ab altera parte heterodoxiæ & impietatis nexus. Ὥσπερ γὰρ, inquit Joh. Chrysost. Serm. 20. in verba: Nolo vos ignorare. T. 5. p. 304. a. δόγματα πονηρὰ βίον ἀκαθαρτον εἰσάγειν εἴωθεν· ὅτω καὶ διεφθαρμένῳ βίῳ πονηρίαν δογμάτων πολλάκις ἔτεκεν. Id est: Sicut enim mala dogmata impuram inducere consueverunt vitam, ita & vita perversa sæpe parit perversitatem dogmatum. Atque rectè infert Nilus Episcopus Thessalonicensis: Ἐι σφάλλεται καὶ κακῶν πολλὰ ὡς τὴν συνείδησιν, ἐνδέχεται καὶ ὡς τὴν πίστιν ναυάγιον ὑποστῆναι. Id est: Si fallitur & ille in multis quoad conscientiam, sequitur, eum etiam in iis, quæ fidem concernunt, naufragium facere posse. Quis etenim à mancipio Diaboli unicè commodis regni hujus promovendis intento, veritatem secundùm pietatem & quidem tanquam à judice infallibili & unico fidei Magistro expectet? Et quî non passionum suarum servus in doctrina formanda iis aliquid indulgebit, vel, quâ quæsò violentiâ retinebitur? Qui ab una parte portæ inferorum ei prævalebunt penitùs, & ab altera tam vicina planè extra periculum constitutus erit? Sique mentiri ad mores pertinet, moribus undiquaque corruptissimus & ex mendaciis cæterùm quasi confutus, cur non falsa etiam docendo mentiri poterit? Sed non opus est, ut ista circa Romanos Pontifices inferamus, cùm satis superque experientia testetur & dogmatum hodiernorum consideratio, Pontificum corruptionem ipsam quoque communionis illius fidem lethaliter infecisse, verùmque ad hoc saltem Hobbesii de Homine c. 12. p. 62. verbum esse: Cessante Pastorum sanctitate, populi cessavit, corrupta est, fides; quin etiam didicisse Papas à crimine non puros, magnis, duplici nomine, peccatoribus adulari, indulgere. De quo Vide de Nouv. lettr. de l'Auth. de la Crit. lettr. 19. p. 617.618. neque in favoris sui incremento & decremento alia, quàm potentiam felicitatémque externam hîc crescentem, illic decrescentem respicere. Quo de ex Testt. Polit. Card. Richel. vide Nouv. de la Republ des lettr. T. VIII. p.1316. Atque ita eâdem operâ probavimus, & malos fuisse, & malos electos fuisse & male electos fuisse, & in Catalogo Pontificum expungi debere, non-Pontifices successionémq; minimè continuantes, & erroribus obnoxios fuisse Pontifices dictos plurimos, & illos non immeritò etiam personaliter, quando cæteri ratione officii, impii & hominis peccati nomine 2. Thess. II.3. venire, neq; posse, qui vel Neronės, Caligulas, Sardanapalos & Heliogabalos superant, saltem æquant, pro talibus Jesu Christi Vicariis, Ecclesiæq; verę Monarchis, haberi, contrà vel ex hoc solo Capite Antichristianismum Romanæ Ecclesiæ satis superque agnosci posse Spiritui Evangelii verïque Christianismi in ipsis supremis talibúsque Ecclesiæ illius Rectoribus è diametro oppositum, non obstantibus Papis minùs malis, quorum, si quę ultra minoris malitię gloriam virtutes, (quemadmodum in ipsis etiam Gentilium Rebuspublicis honesti probíque & in sede Draconis, id est, imperio Gentili non minùs tales fuerunt,) in defectu à tot seculis eximia raráque virtute præditorum, atque certis divinæ electionis notis insignium externæ, humanæque nonnisi fuerunt, eò magis tamen observatæ & æstimatæ, quia minùs in illa sede ordinariæ, atpue nonnisi partim indoli, partim educationi, partim Politicæ tum humanæ, tum Diabolicæ, quâ transformatio in Angelos lucis & fucatæ virtutis deceptio necessaria judicatur, ut pro Vice-Christo haberi volenti certè est, debitæ, dum cæterùm vera virtus, crescente ambitione & usurpatione, exemplis ex ignorantia plùs æquo sibi tribuentium bonorum paulatim deficientibus, paulatim etiam in ista sede expirâsse deprehenditur, illúdque singulari Divinâ providentiâ secutum est, ut ea ceu mater abominationum post defectionem plenariam ex hoc etiam capite à fidelibus æstimari queat.
units.tr: XC. The evil is also increased in other ways by evil men, since wicked morals also corrupt doctrine, especially in the highest teachers, who teach infallibly by hypothesis, and who, to obedience without examination, teach men who sin so foully and so variously without rebuke or restraint. For just as the truth according to godliness is salutary, so on the other hand there is a sister bond between heterodoxy and impiety. For just as [Ὥσπερ γὰρ], says John Chrysostom, Serm. 20., on the words I would not have you ignorant, T. 5, p. 304 a: Wicked doctrines are wont to bring in an impure life; so too a perverse life has often brought forth the wickedness of doctrines [δόγματα πονηρὰ βίον ἀκαθαρτον εἰσάγειν εἴωθεν· ὅτω καὶ διεφθαρμένῳ βίῳ πονηρίαν δογμάτων πολλάκις ἔτεκεν]. And Nilus, Bishop of Thessalonica, rightly infers: If he too is often deceived in many matters regarding conscience, it follows that he can also suffer shipwreck in those matters which concern the faith [Ἐι σφάλλεται καὶ κακῶν πολλὰ ὡς τὴν συνείδησιν, ἐνδέχεται καὶ ὡς τὴν πίστιν ναυάγιον ὑποστῆναι]. For who would expect the truth according to godliness from a slave of the Devil, who aims solely at advancing the interests of this kingdom, and indeed from one who is held to be an infallible judge and the sole Master of faith? And who, a slave of his own passions, will not indulge them somewhat in forming doctrine? Or by what violence, I ask, will he be restrained? He who on one side has the gates of hell utterly prevailing against him, and on the other side is so near them, will surely not be placed altogether outside danger. And if to lie pertains to morals, one utterly corrupt in morals and, besides, refuted by his own lies, why will he not also be able to lie by teaching falsehoods? But there is no need for us to draw these conclusions about the Roman Pontiffs, since experience sufficiently and more than sufficiently testifies, and the consideration of today's doctrines too, that the corruption of the Popes has also infected the faith of that communion fatally. And to this extent at least the saying of Hobbes, On Man, c. 12, p. 62, is true: When the holiness of the pastors ceased, the faith of the people ceased and was corrupted. Indeed, the Popes have learned to flatter and indulge sinners who are not pure of crime, great sinners, in a twofold sense. On this see Nouv. lettr. de l'Auth. de la Crit. lettr. 19, p. 617-618, and they regard in their favour nothing other than external power and prosperity, growing here, declining there. On this matter, from the political testaments of Cardinal Richelieu, see Nouv. de la Republ. des lettr. T. VIII, p. 1316. And so by the same work we have proved that they were wicked, were wicked and badly elected, must be struck from the Catalogue of Popes, since they were not Popes and did not continue the succession, and that very many so-called Popes were liable to errors, and that they were not unjustly regarded personally, when the others by reason of their office, under the name of the impious one and the man of sin in 2 Thessalonians 2:3, come forward. Those who surpass, or at least equal, Nero, Caligula, Sardanapalus and Heliogabalus cannot be held as such Vicars of Jesus Christ and true Monarchs of the Church. On the contrary, from this head alone the Antichristianity of the Roman Church can be sufficiently and more than sufficiently recognised, being diametrically opposed to the Spirit of the Gospel and of true Christianity in the highest and such Rulers of that Church. This holds despite the existence of less wicked Popes, whose virtues, if any beyond the glory of lesser wickedness (just as among the Gentile commonwealths there were honest and upright men, and in the seat of the Dragon, that is, the Gentile empire, they were no less such), were rare, outward and merely human, in the lack, over so many centuries, of men endowed with outstanding and rare virtue and marked by the certain signs of divine election. Yet they were all the more observed and esteemed because they were less common in that seat, and because they were due only partly to disposition, partly to education, partly to politics, both human and diabolical, by which transformation into angels of light and deception by feigned virtue is judged necessary for one who wishes to be held Vicar of Christ. Yet since true virtue, as ambition and usurpation grew, was found to be gradually failing, through examples of men who, from ignorance, attributed to themselves more goods than was right, it also gradually expired in that seat. And it followed by singular divine providence that, after complete defection, the faithful could esteem that seat from this very head as the mother of abominations.

units.la: SECTIO OCTAVA,
units.tr: SECTIO OCTAVA,

units.la: In qua, De vitiis & nævis Electionis Pontificum Romanorum ratione Eruditionis & prudentiæ agitur, atque tractatio de nævis quibuscunque clauditur. Breviarium.
units.tr: In which the defects and blemishes in the election of the Roman Pontiffs are discussed with respect to learning and prudence, and the treatment of all kinds of blemishes is brought to a close. A summary.

units.la: I. Requisitum Eruditionis declaratur ex S. Scriptura, & Iure Canonico, respectu Episcoporum & Sacerdotum quorumvis; II. Ostenditur, Eruditionem multo magis & in gradu multo majori Episcopo Romano necessariam esse; III. Probatur varie, multos Episcopos Romanos Eruditione summe necessaria caruisse. IV. Idem probatur ex ignorantia Seculorum superiorum. V. Ostenditur, eruditionem debitam ne quidem valde amplius requiri; VI. Dum maxime respicitur aptitudo ad regimen mundanum & Legista: Theologo longe ante fertur. VII. Idem declaratur exemplis Formosi, Iohannis XII Gregorii VI. Urbani II. Benedicti XII. VIII. Pii II.
