Gregorii XIII. Urbani VIII. Innocentii X. & Alex VII. IX. Imo literarum osores maximi Pontifices nonnulli fuerunt; X. Neque omnes sufficienter prudentes fuerunt; Quod varie atque etiam ostenditur exemplis Gregorii VI. Antecessorum Gregorii VII. XI. Iohannis XXI. XII. Coelestini V. Iohannis XXII. Bonifacii IX. XIII. Adriani VI. ex hypothesi; XIV. Illustratur exemplo Clementis VIII. post electionem ratione privati; XV. Confirmatur exemplis Gregorii XV. & Innocentii X. XVI. Ostenditur, valde prudentes non facile promoveri. XVII. Concluditur in genere, Electiones Pontificum Romanorum ordinario esse vitiosas; XVIII. Probatur, male electos pro nullis habendos esse.
units.tr: I. The requirement of learning is set out from Holy Scripture and from canon law, with respect to bishops and priests of every kind. II. It is shown that learning is necessary for the Roman Bishop much more, and to a much greater degree. III. It is proved in various ways that many Roman Bishops lacked learning, which was greatly needed. IV. The same is proved from the ignorance of earlier centuries. V. It is shown that even the learning due is not required much beyond the ordinary. VI. While fitness for worldly rule and for law is chiefly regarded, theology is put far behind. VII. The same is made clear by the examples of Formosus, John XII, Gregory VI, Urban II, and Benedict XII. VIII. Of Pius II, Gregory XIII, Urban VIII, Innocent X, and Alexander VII. IX. Indeed, some of the Supreme Pontiffs were haters of learning. X. Nor were all of them sufficiently prudent; this is shown in various ways, and also by the examples of Gregory VI, the predecessors of Gregory VII, XI. John XXI, XII. Celestine V, John XXII, Boniface IX, XIII. Adrian VI, on a hypothesis; XIV. It is illustrated by the example of Clement VIII after his election, in a private capacity; XV. It is confirmed by the examples of Gregory XV and Innocent X. XVI. It is shown that very prudent men are not easily promoted. XVII. It is concluded in general that the elections of the Roman Pontiffs are ordinarily defective. XVIII. It is proved that those elected badly must be regarded as not elected at all.

units.la: I. HActenus de requisito primo, nimirum de virtute; Pergimus ad secundum, nempe ad Eruditionem. Requiritur enim in Conclavi Urbani VIII. supra citato etiam litteratura, Eruditio. Scriptura etiam ab Episcopo quovis requirit, ut sit διδα-κτικὸς, aptus ad docendum, 1.Tim.III. 2. 2.Tim.II.24. & tenens fidelis illius sermonis, qui ad doctrinam facit, ut possit & exhortari doctrinâ sanâ & contradicentes convincere, Tit.I.9. Timotheo injungit Paulus, ut ejus profectus manifestus sit inter omnes, 1.Tim.IV.15. Ut sibi ipsi & doctrinæ attendat v.16. ut expressam formam teneat sanorum sermonum, 2.Epist.I.13. ut audita à se committat fidelibus hominibus, qui sint idonei ad alios quoque docendos c.II.2. ut seipsum studeat probatum sistere Deo operarium, qui non erubescat, & qui recte sermonem veritatis secet v.15. ut cum lenitate erudiat eos, qui contrario animo sunt affecti v.25. ut maneat in iis quæ didicerit cap.III. 14. utpote qui à puero sacras literas noverit, v.15. quæ perfectum reddant hominem Dei ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructum, v.17. ut prædicet sermonem, arguat, objurget, exhortetur cum omni lenitate & doctrina; Tito; ut seipsum per omnia prabeat exemplar bonorum operum, in doctrina integritatem, gravitatem, sermonem sanum, qui damnari non possit, Tit.II.8. atque id omnibus dictum Apostolis: Prædicate, docete Matth.XXVIII. 19. 20. Marc.XVI. 15. & dedit Dominus alios quidem Apostolos: alios verò Prophetas: alios autem Evangelistas: alios autem Pastores & Doctores; Ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad ædificationem corporis Christi; Donec evadamus omnes in unitatem fidei, & agnitionis Filii Dei, in virum adultum, ad mensuram statuæ adulti Christi; Ut ne simus amplius pueri, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quovis vento doctrina, in hominum alea, per veteratoriam ad insidiosè fallendum astutiam, Eph.IV.11.12.13.14. Hinc etiam Apollo dicitur potens in Scripturis, Act.XVIII.24. Et Apostolos, qui antecedentis vitæ generis & œconomiæ ratione nonnisi tenuem habebant rerum cœlestium cognitionem, ut subitò fierent orbis Doctores, immediatè ad præconium sapiens & efficax erudivit ipse Sanctus Spiritus extraordinariâ ratione & mensurâ communicatus. Ex Monarchicorum jure autem Can. LV. dist. c. pœnit. discimus, constituisse Hilarium P. ut nullus literarum inscius in Clericum ordinaretur.
units.tr: I. So far I have spoken of the first requirement, namely virtue. We proceed to the second, namely learning. For learning, too, is required in the Conclave of Urban VIII, cited above, but also learning, erudition. Scripture requires this of every bishop, that he be διδακτικὸς [didaktikos], apt to teach (1 Tim. 3:2; 2 Tim. 2:24), and hold fast the faithful word which accords with the teaching, so that he may both exhort with sound doctrine and convict those who contradict (Tit. 1:9). Paul enjoins Timothy that his progress be manifest to all (1 Tim. 4:15); that he take heed to himself and to the teaching (v. 16); that he hold fast the pattern of sound words (2 Tim. 1:13); that what he has heard from him he commit to faithful men who are fit to teach others also (2 Tim. 2:2); that he study to present himself approved to God, a workman who need not be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth (v. 15); that he instruct with gentleness those who are opposed (v. 25); that he continue in what he has learned (2 Tim. 3:14), since he has known the holy letters from childhood (v. 15), which make the man of God perfect, thoroughly furnished for every good work (v. 17); that he preach the word, reprove, rebuke, and exhort with all gentleness and teaching (Titus). To Titus: that he show himself in all things a pattern of good works, in doctrine integrity, gravity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned (Tit. 2:8). And this was said to all the Apostles: Preach, teach (Matt. 28:19, 20; Mark 16:15). And the Lord gave some indeed as Apostles, and some as Prophets, and some as Evangelists, and some as Pastors and Teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ; until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ; that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by the cunning craftiness of men, in the deceitful scheming (Eph. 4:11–14). Hence Apollos too is called mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). And the Apostles, who by the manner of their former life and their way of living had only a slight knowledge of heavenly things, were instructed so that they might at once become teachers of the world; the Holy Spirit himself, communicated in an extraordinary manner and measure, taught them immediately for a wise and effective preaching. From the law of the monarchists, moreover, we learn from Canon 55, dist. (c. pœnit.), that Pope Hilary ordained that no one ignorant of letters be ordained as a cleric.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Hîc autem rursus, quod in Episcopo & Sacerdote quovis & simplice etiam esse debere ostendimus, multò magis & in gradu multò majori debet esse in Episcopo Episcoporum; quod in Doctore particulari, multò magis & in gradu multò majori in Doctore universali, quod in Doctore fallibili, multò magis & in gradu multò majori in Doctore infallibili, in supremo controversiarum judice, & cuju dictatibus omnes omninò Christiani fidem debent & assensum illimitatum & obsequium sine exceptione; Quíque apud Augustinum de Ancona de Potest. Eccles. q. 18. etiam quoad cognitionem Angelis ante fertur; Et de quo cum Gerberto Rhemensi Archiepiscopo, posthac sub nomine Sylvestri II. Romano Episcopo, quærere atque judicare licet: Quid hunc—in sublimi solio residentem, veste purpureâ & auro radiantem: quid hunc, inquam, esse censetis? Nimirum si charitate destituitur solaque scientiâ inflatur & extollitur, Antichristus est, in Templo Dei sedens & se ostendens, tanquam sit Deus: si autem nec charitate fundatur, nec scientiâ erigitur, in Templo Dei tanquam quam statua, tanquam Idolum est, à quo responsa petere, marmora consulere est. Quò ergò consultum ibimus? &c. Et paulò post: Cùm hoc tempore Româ nullus pene sit, (ut fama est) qui literas didicerit, sine quibus, ut scriptum est, vix ostiarius efficitur, quâ fronte aliquis docere audebit, quod minimè didicit? Ad comparationem quidem Romani Pontificis in aliis Sacerdotibus ignorantia utcunque tolerabilis est; in Romano autem, cui de fide, vita, moribus, disciplina Sacerdotum, déque universali Ecclesia Catholica judicandum est, intolerabilis videri potest. — Sed ô infelicissima tempora! quibus patrocinio tanta frustrantur Ecclesia; ad quam deinceps urbium fugiemus, cùm omnium gentium dominam humanis & divinis destitutam subsidiis videamus?
units.tr: Here again, what we have shown must be in a bishop and in any priest, even a simple one, must be much more, and to a much greater degree, in the Bishop of Bishops; what must be in a particular teacher must be much more, and to a much greater degree, in the universal teacher; what must be in a fallible teacher must be much more, and to a much greater degree, in an infallible teacher, in the supreme judge of controversies, to whose decisions all Christians without exception must give faith and unlimited assent and obedience without exception. And he who, in Augustine of Ancona, On Ecclesiastical Power, q. 18, is placed even in knowledge above the angels, is put forward; and concerning whom it is lawful to inquire and judge, together with Gerbert, Archbishop of Reims, afterwards as Bishop of Rome under the name of Sylvester II: What do you think this man is, who sits on his lofty throne, clothed in purple and shining with gold? What, I say, do you think him to be? Surely if he is destitute of charity and is puffed up and exalted by knowledge alone, he is Antichrist, sitting in the Temple of God and showing himself as if he were God; but if he is founded neither on charity nor raised up by knowledge, then in the Temple of God he is like a statue, like an idol, from which to seek answers is to consult marble. To whom then shall we go? etc. And a little later: Since at this time there is almost no one at Rome (so the report goes) who has learned letters, without which, as it is written, one can scarcely become a doorkeeper, with what brazenness will anyone dare to teach what he has least of all learned? In comparison with other priests, ignorance is somewhat tolerable; but in the Roman Pontiff, to whom judgment belongs concerning faith, life, morals, the discipline of priests, and the universal Catholic Church, it can seem intolerable. — But O most unhappy times! In which the Church is thwarted of such patronage; to which we shall flee in future, since we see the mistress of all nations destitute of human and divine aids?

units.la: III. Sed vel hæc ipsa ultima, ut & præcedentia: Quid sub hac tempora non vidimus?
units.tr: III. But these last points, like the preceding ones: what have we not seen in these times?

units.la: Num talibus monstris hominum ignominiâ plenis, scientiâ humanarum & divinarum rerum vacuis innumeros Sacerdotes Dei per orbem terrarum scientia & vita merito conspicuos subjici decretum est? Gerberti & Synodi Rhemensis verba apud Baronium ad an. 992. n. 25. docent, non semper eruditos, non semper aptos ad docendum Papas fuisse; Quod de pueris & juvenibus infra ætatem legitimam electis, item de senibus (de quibus suprà, bis pueris priorum oblitis, memoriâ debilitatis) facilè largientur; Nec non de illis, qui Neophyti & Laici nonnunquam electi sunt. Sed & constat, non prædicare verbum Papas ab aliquot seculis & multos ex eorum numero tam aptos fuisse ad docendum, quàm bos est ad volandum. De quo officii neglectu & aptitudinis defectu Dissert. I. Sect. V. n. 13. seqq. egimus. Addimus hîc famosi Maimburgii dans son Histoire du Pontificat de saint Leon le Grand, observationem occasione ejus, quòd Leonem M. concionatum esse contrà Sozomenum, cui Cassiodorus astipulatur, negat, consignatam; C'est que l'innocence de vie dans un Evêq; sans capacité pour pouvoir precher, nuit autant par le silence necessaire, que l'ignorance lui impose, qu'elle edifie par ses bons exemples; & qu'une sainte rusticité n'est utile, qu'à soy même. Id est. Quòd in Episcopo vita innocentia tantum noceat respectu silentii per ignorantiam necessarii, quantum adificet respectu bonorum suorum exemplorum, & quòd sancta rusticitas sibi tantùm prosit. Quibus verbis ipsum etiam tum temporis sedentem Innocentium XI. Leonis M. post alios successorem notâsse Authori des Nouvell. de la Republ. des Lettr. T. VII. p. 445. creditur ——Mansit enim alta mente repostum Judicium Paridis spretaque in injuria forma. Quid autem de Pontificibus illis, quibus neque ædificans vitæ innocentia & bonum exemplum, neque ulla ad concionandum aptitudo ad fuerunt, sed contraria omnia, & si rusticitas, non sancta quidem. Sed & in Electionibus Pontificum vel ex parte eligentium, vel ex actûs & modi eligendi ratione vitiosis, quales utiq; plurimas fuisse ex Dissert. V. & VI. plûs quàm manifestum esse potest, plerunque etiam defectum hujus loci, supinam nimirum rerum Divinarum & humanarum ignorantiam, adfuisse facili labore colligitur.
units.tr: Must it be decreed that innumerable ministers of God, conspicuous across the world for their learning and their lives, be placed under such monsters, full of human shame and empty of knowledge of human and divine things? The words of Gerbert and of the Synod of Reims, reported by Baronius at the year 992, n. 25, show that the popes were not always learned, nor always apt to teach. The same can easily be granted of boys and youths elected before the lawful age, likewise of old men (of whom we spoke above, who were twice children, having lost their memory through weakness), and also of those who were sometimes elected while still neophytes and laymen. It is also established that for some centuries the popes have not preached the Word, and that many of them were as fit to teach as an ox is to fly. We treated this neglect of duty and lack of aptitude in Dissertation I, Section V, n. 13 and following. To this I add the observation of the notorious Maimbourg in his Histoire du Pontificat de saint Léon le Grand, where, occasioned by the fact that he denies that Leo the Great preached (against Sozomen, to whom Cassiodorus agrees), he writes: "It is that innocence of life in a bishop who lacks the ability to preach harms as much through the silence that his ignorance forces upon him as it edifies through his good example; and a holy rusticity is useful only to himself." That is: in a bishop, innocence of life does as much harm, with respect to the silence necessitated by ignorance, as it edifies with respect to his good examples; and holy rusticity profits only himself. It is believed that the author of the Nouvelles de la République des Lettres, T. VII, p. 445, noted these words as applying also to Innocent XI, who was then sitting on the throne, as a successor of Leo the Great among others: "For the judgement of Paris remained deep in his mind, and the beauty despised in the wrong." But what of those popes who had neither an edifying innocence of life nor a good example, nor any aptitude for preaching, but all the opposite, and a rusticity that was not even holy? Moreover, from Dissertations V and VI it is more than evident that the elections of the popes were vicious, either on the part of the electors or by the manner and procedure of electing; and from this it is easily gathered that, for the most part, the same lack of learning was present, namely a crass ignorance of divine and human things.

units.la: IV. Neque dubitari potest, Pontificum in crassa superiorum seculorum ignorantia haud infimas partes fuisse, quando jam suo tempore & dum anno 593. Dialogos scriberet, Gregorius Magnus epist. ad Narsetem, conqueri debuit, se Græca nescire, nec esse Constantinopoli, qui Latina Græcè convertere posset, & temporis successu atque per 400. an. teste Melchiore Cano Loc.Com. p.59. ipsi Theologi Scholastici non habuerunt Linguam Græcam & Hebraicam peritiam; & juxta Doctiss. Claudium Espensæum com. in 1.Tim. III. Græcè nosse suspectum fuit, Ebraicè propè hæreticum; Et multi cum Remigio, teste Lud. Viv. com. in Aug. de Civ. Dei l.z. c.21. nesciverunt, quo idiomate Paulus scripserit. Et multi fuerunt, teste Rod. à Tostign. in Dictionar. Paup. etiam insignes & præstantissimi Theologi, qui vix integra Biblia perlegerunt; Et non pauci, teste Erasmo Roterod. Rat. Ver. Theol. p.87. si quid iis deponendum fuisset ex Paulo, sibi visi sunt prorsus in alium orbem translati; Et permulti Theologi, Doctores, teste Gerard. List. Notis ad Erasmi Mor. ante 50. annum nondum evolverant omnes Epistolas Paulinas; Et Carolstadius Actis Academiæ sufficientissimus habitus Theologiæ Doctor, octavo demum à promotione anno animum ad Scripturas S. appulit; Et teste Roberto Stephano quidam ex Sorbona plùs habuit, quàm 30. annos, quòd nescirret, quid esset N.T. & Archiepiscopus Moguntinus de Sacro Codice pronuntiavit: Nescio quid hoc libri sit; apud Sixt. Ama Atibarb. Bibl p.78. & teste Wolphg. Musc. L.C. p.385. n. innumeris Sacrificis & Pastoribus ne visa quidem fuerant unquam Sacra Biblia.
units.tr: IV. There can be no doubt that ignorance held no small place among the popes in the crude centuries past. Already in his own time, when he was writing his Dialogues in 593, Gregory the Great, in his letter to Narses, epist. ad Narsetem, had to complain that he did not know Greek, and that there was no one in Constantinople who could translate Latin into Greek, and, as time went on and for 400 years, according to Melchior Cano, Loc. Com. p. 59, the Scholastic theologians themselves did not have knowledge of the Greek and Hebrew languages; and according to the most learned Claudius Espencaeus, Comm. on 1 Tim. III, to know Greek was regarded as suspicious, and Hebrew almost heretical. And many, with Remigius, as Ludovicus Vives testifies, Comm. on Augustine, De Civitate Dei, bk. 2, ch. 21, did not know in what language Paul had written. And, as Rodericus à Tostigno testifies, in his Dictionary, there were many, even distinguished and outstanding theologians, who had hardly read through the whole Bible. And, as Erasmus of Rotterdam testifies, Ratio Verae Theologiae, p. 87, not a few, if anything had to be taken from Paul, seemed to themselves to have been transported into another world. And, as Gerardus Listrius testifies, in his notes to Erasmus's Moriae Encomium, very many theologians and doctors had not yet read through all the Pauline Epistles, even fifty years earlier. And Carlstadt, held to be most sufficient as a Doctor of Theology in the Acts of the Academy, only turned his mind to the Holy Scriptures in the eighth year after his promotion. And, as Robert Estienne testifies, a certain man of the Sorbonne had for more than 30 years not known what the N.T. was, and the Archbishop of Mainz pronounced of the Holy Codex: I do not know what this book is; as reported by Sixtus Amama, Antibarbarus Biblicus, p. 78; and, as Wolfgang Musculus testifies, Loc. Cit., p. 385, the Holy Bible had never even been seen by innumerable priests and pastors.

units.la: V. Indubium autem magis erit, multos eruditionis debitæ defectu laborantes in Pontifices eligi, quando constabit, eruditionem debitam in rebus Divinis amplius ne quidem valde requiri, sed potius prudentiam civilem & peritiam rerum mundanarum. Nempe quod in illa communione respectu Episcoporum in genere obtinet, illud etiam de Romanis accipi debet: Sed jam olim MarsiMarsilius Patavinus part. 2. c. 24. Defensor. scripsit: Quibus de plenitudine potestatis conceduntur majores Ecclesiæ dignitates, & qui ad has gubernandas sufficientes putantur, causidici sunt. Hos enim tanquam utiles dignificat Romanus Pontifex, ut Ecclesiæ defensores, qui pro temporalibus conservandis, vel amplius usurpandis contendere nôrunt, Sacra verò Theologia Doctoribus tanquam inutilibus rejectis. Et non ita pridem celebris in Italia Apostata, editâ sub ficto Alphonsi de Vargas, Toletani nomine Relatione ad Reges & Principes Christianos, graviter questus est: Palam est, majorem eorum partem, qui hodie vel maximis in Ecclesia dignitatibus præsunt, & unctissimis Episcopatibus atque Sacerdotiis fruuntur, quantulacunque juris ac legum notitiâ tinctos ad eos honores opésque pervenisse; cæterum Hebraicè, Græcè & Latinè indoctissimos, tum sacrarum literarum non magis, quam Scythici aut Japonici sermonis intelligentes esse. Quamvis enim S. Paulus eum, qui velit esse Episcopus, Doctorem esse jubeat, qui scilicet, aut ab infantia literas didicerit, aut saltem in lege dies ac noctes meditetur: tamen eò res hodie rediit, ut qui Theologiæ Doctor sit, vix nomen inter Episcopatuum Candidatos profiteri audeat. Atque plane coincidunt, quæ Author Vitæ Sixti V. p. I. ab initio habet, de maximè nunc requisita alta prudenza per lo maneggo delle cose mondane, alta prudentia in negotiationibus rerum mundanarum; Quam etiam prudentiam, magis quam sanctitatem ipsam requiri, Cardinalis Pallavicinus in Adriano VI. pertendit.
units.tr: V. It will be even more certain that many labouring under a lack of due learning are elected popes, once it is clear that due learning is not even greatly required in divine things, but rather civil prudence and skill in worldly affairs. What holds in that communion with respect to bishops in general must also be understood of the Roman popes. Marsilius of Padua wrote long ago, in Defensor Pacis, part 2, ch. 24: "Those to whom the greater dignities of the Church are granted by the fullness of power, and who are thought sufficient to govern them, are advocates. For the Roman Pontiff honours these as useful men, as defenders of the Church, who know how to contend for preserving or extending temporal goods, but rejects the teachers of sacred theology as useless." And not long ago a notorious apostate in Italy, publishing under the false name of Alphonsus de Vargas of Toledo, a Relation to the Kings and Christian Princes, complained bitterly: "It is plain that most of those who today preside over the greatest dignities in the Church and enjoy the richest bishoprics and priesthoods have risen to those honours and riches tinged with only a slight knowledge of law; but in Hebrew, Greek and Latin they are most unlearned, and understand the sacred letters no better than the language of the Scythians or the Japanese." For although St Paul bids that whoever wishes to be a bishop be a teacher, that is, one who either has learned letters from infancy or at least meditates on the law day and night, yet matters have come to such a pass today that one who is a Doctor of Theology hardly dares to profess his name among the candidates for bishoprics. And what the author of the Life of Sixtus V, part I, at the beginning says about the highly required "deep prudence in the management of worldly affairs" fully agrees with this; Cardinal Pallavicino, in his life of Adrian VI, maintains that this prudence is required even more than holiness itself.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Hinc Farnesius Cardinalis in Conclavi Pii V. Sirleto, Cardinali Papabili illud præcipuè objecit, ch'essendo stato sempre occupato nelle lettere non haurebbe niuna cognitione di governi del mondo, affirmando, che uscirebbe con poco honore dal Conclave con una elettione così debole; quòd quia semper in literarum studio occupatus fuerit, non habeat ullam cognitionem regiminum mundanorum; affirmans, exiguo cum honore cum electione tam debili exitum ex Conclavi futurum: Et licet præter la prudenza esperimentata in ogni sorte de negotii, prudentiam in omni negotiorum genere exe citatem in Conclavi Urbani VIII. alia etiam requiri viderimus, tamen, quando quæritur etiam de genere cognitionis, an præstet habere Theologum, vel Legistam, ut in Conclavi Leonis XI. ea de re quæsitum, & dictum ab una parte quidem, che meglio era per un Papa di Professione Theologo, che Legista, poiche li Signori Theologi non s'intendono di governo & necessariamente gli participano con gli altri--dove, che i Legisti presumendo se di sapere governare il mondo, riescono bastardi e riducono la dominatione all' unità &c. Id est; melius esse, habere Papam Theologum, quàm Legistam; cùm Domini Theologi, ceu regimini parùm apti, necessariò ad ejus participationem alios admittere debeant; Cùm contrà Legista, putantes, se mundum regere posse, fallant & dominationem ad unitatem reducant &c. Hæc quidem ex animo propriorum commodorum & regiminis simultanei cupidissimo; Interim tamen ex non meliori regni litigiosi & mundani principio Legista Theologo, ut prudens secundùm mundum apparenter piè docto, antefertur; Ut in illo ipso Leonis XI. Conclavi Promotoribus ab Antagonistis vitio datum, che tentavano essaltare un' huomo uscito hieri dal Chiostro, il quale nel secolo haveva fatta prima vita & professione pedantesca e Papa haurebbe bisogno similmente di pedante; id est, quòd tentarent eligere hominem pridie è Monasterio egressum, qui, sicut antea vitam & professionem Pedanticam secutus, ita etiam Papa factus Pedante opus habiturus sit. Et in Conclavi Gregorii XIV. Cremona, qui tamen obtinuit, licèt humanissimus, nihilominùs, quia non habebat cognitionem aut experientiam rerum Curiæ, multò minùs mundi, parùm aptus judicatus fuit. Et generale habetur apud Frà Paolo, de benef. §. 9. effatum; exceptis locis, qui in vicinia infidelium, praestare, ut Episcopus sit bonus Legista, quàm verò ut sit bonus Theologus.
units.tr: Hence Cardinal Farnese, in the conclave of Pius V, objected above all to Sirleto, a leading papabile, that since he had always been occupied with literature, he would have no knowledge of the governments of the world, and he asserted that the election would end with little honour if so weak a man were chosen. Although we have seen that in the conclave of Urban VIII prudence proved in every kind of business was also required, when the question concerns the kind of knowledge, whether it is better to have a theologian or a lawyer as pope, the matter was raised in the conclave of Leo XI. On one side it was said: it is better for a pope to be a professed theologian than a lawyer, since the gentlemen theologians do not understand government and must necessarily share it with others, whereas lawyers, presuming they can govern the world, come to grief and reduce domination to unity, etc. That is: it is better to have a pope who is a theologian than a lawyer, since theologians, being poorly suited to government, must necessarily admit others to share it, whereas lawyers, thinking they can rule the world, are mistaken and reduce domination to unity, etc. These things were said from the mind of men most eager for their own advantage and for a share in government. Meanwhile, from an equally poor principle of a litigious and worldly kingdom, the lawyer is preferred to the theologian as one who appears prudent by worldly standards, and the theologian is pious and learned. In that same conclave of Leo XI, the promoters were charged by their opponents with this fault: they were trying to exalt a man who had come out of the cloister the day before, who in the world had led a life and profession of a pedant, and a pope would likewise need a pedant; that is, they were trying to elect a man who had left the monastery the day before, who, having followed a pedantic life and profession before, would as pope also have need of a pedant. In the conclave of Gregory XIV, Cremona, who nevertheless obtained the office, although most cultivated, was judged nonetheless not to have knowledge or experience of the affairs of the Curia, much less of the world, and so was judged poorly suited. And Fra Paolo has a general saying, in De benef. §9: except in places near the unbelievers, it is better that a bishop be a good lawyer than a good theologian.

units.la: VII. Neque verò præter testimonia, generalius Eruditionis debitæ in Pontificibus eligendis defectum probantia, exempla, quibus idem in iisdem defectus probetur, desunt. Formosum suprà condemnatum vidimus tanquam doctrinarum Sacrarum insciium. Ubi Episcopus Verdensis & antea Secretarius Pontificis de Privil. & Jur. Imper. depositionem Johannis XII. probat, inter alia dicit: Oportet, Papam esse—doctum, ——Nam quomodo indoctus doctos efficere valebit? De Gregorio VI. scribit Rolf. Carthus. p. 72. a. quòd cùm esset rudis literarum, alterum Papam ad Ecclesiastica officia exequenda secum consecrari fecerit. Sic Urbanus Papa, in Concilio Bari in Apulia anno 1098. uniendæ cum Romana Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ ergò habito, cùm de processione Spiritûs S. disputaretur, explicare se satis, nisi Anselmus ex Anglia evocatus adfuisset & responsionis partes sustinuisset, non potuisset, narrantibus factum Calvisio & Baronio. Cœlestinus V. apud Stellam in Vita literarum ignarus perhibetur. Sed & ingenuam ignorantiæ suæ confessionem edidit Benedictus XII. qui Papa electus Cardinalibus Electoribus dixisse fertur: Scitè fecistis, quòd asinum elegistis.
units.tr: VII. Nor are there lacking examples showing the same defect in the same men, beyond the testimonies that prove a general lack of the learning required in electing popes. We have seen Formosus condemned above as ignorant of sacred doctrines. Where the bishop of Verden, formerly secretary to the pope, proves the deposition of John XII in De privilegiis et iure imperii, he says among other things: the pope must be learned, for how can an unlearned man make others learned? Of Gregory VI, Rolf of Carthusia writes, p. 72a, that since he was unlettered, he had another pope consecrated with him to perform the ecclesiastical offices. So Pope Urban, at the council held at Bari in Apulia in 1098 for the sake of uniting the Roman and Constantinopolitan churches, when the procession of the Holy Spirit was debated, could not explain it sufficiently, had not Anselm, summoned from England, been present and taken up the part of the reply, as Calvisius and Baronius relate. Celestine V, according to Stella in Vita, is said to have been ignorant of letters. Benedict XII also made a frank confession of his ignorance; having been elected pope, he is reported to have said to the cardinal electors: You did well to choose an ass.

units.la: VIII. Alii
units.tr: VIII. Others

units.la: VIII. Alii docti fuerunt, sed non in Sacro Theologiæ Studio. Sic Pio II. in Conclavi objectum: Che lettere ha egli? Porremo noi nella sedia di San Pietro un Poeta? Governaremo la chiesa con statuti e leggi de' Gentili? Quâ eruditione pollet? Poetámne in S. Petri solio collocabimus? Ecclesiámne statutis & legibus Gentilium gubernabimus? Atque hic ipse tamen Pius fuit, de quo Urbanus VIII. inter familiares, (ceu Clariss. Wagenseilus præf. ad tela ignea Satanæ p.35. Romæ à viris fide dignis accepit;) jactare solitus fuit, se neminem omnium antecessorum doctrinâ superiorem, parem, vix ullum, præter Pium II. civem suum (insigni certè modestiâ & magnâ eruditionis Antecessorum laude;) agnoscere. Hic ipse tamen etiam Urbanus fuit, cujus æquè ac Innocentii, (de quo plura sequuntur;) & Alexandri VII. eruditionem per quam levem fuisse Joh. Ad. Osiander in specimine Jansenismi p. 26. ostendit. Sic Gregorius XIII. juris humani quidem consultissimus, at Divini ignarissimus fuit; Sic jam jam indigitati Innocentii X. in Conclavi per sex septimanas ne mentio quidem ulla incidit, etiam propter ingenium ejus à literarum, Sacrarum inprimis, studiis alienum, nonnisi causis dicendis assuetum; Quod & Author vitæ D. Olimpiæ confirmat, quòd eum nempe quidam exceperint ob aspectum Satyricum, Saturnalem, deformem turpissimúmque, ex quo contumaciam hominis quidam conclusserint, dicentibus etiam nonnullis, indignum esse Patris universalis honore tam deformem, ut filii vel solo ejus aspectu terrefieri possent; omni alii ob D. Olympiam, alii videntes eum spoliato d'ogni scienza &c. scientia destitutum literisque, & unicè legum studio immersum, quamvis & viam illius studii deserere coeperit, hincque concludentes, parùm Literatis eum faviturum, quibus tamen Ecclesia tantopere opus habeat, & certè eo Pontifice Ecclesia repleta fuit hominibus ignorantibus. Ignorantiam Theologicam ipse etiam satis prodidit, dum in causa Jansenistica, ut ipse eam cognosceret, rogatus, ne quidem scripto sibi oblata legere voluit, dicens: Non e la mia professione; oltre che son vecchio, non ho mai studiato in Theologia; Id est: Non est mea professio: præter quàm quòd Senex sum, nunquam studui in Theologia. Vel, ut Pater Ubaldinus Journal de S. Amour part. 3. c. 12. 18. loquitur: Il Papa non e Theologo: non e la sua professione: e Legista. Id est: Papa non est Theologus: non est ejus professio: est Legista.
units.tr: VIII. Others were learned, but not in the study of sacred theology. Thus against Pius II, in the conclave, it was objected: What letters has he? Shall we put a poet in the chair of St Peter? Shall we govern the Church by the statutes and laws of the Gentiles? Yet this same Pius was the one of whom Urban VIII, as Clarissimus Wagenseil (preface to Tela ignea Satanae, p. 35) reports having heard from trustworthy men at Rome, used to boast that he acknowledged no one of all his predecessors superior to himself in learning, hardly any equal, except Pius II, his own fellow citizen (with notable modesty and high praise of his predecessors' learning). Yet this was the same Urban, whose learning, like that of Innocent (of whom more follows) and of Alexander VII, John Adam Osiander in Specimen Jansenismi, p. 26, shows to have been rather slight. So Gregory XIII was most learned in human law, but most ignorant of divine law. So too Innocent X, mentioned above, was not even mentioned in the conclave for six weeks, partly because of a temperament alien to literary study, above all sacred study, and accustomed only to pleading cases. The author of the life of Lady Olympia confirms this, for certain men rejected him because of his satirical, saturnine, deformed and most unsightly look, from which some concluded the man's obstinacy, some also saying that it was unworthy of the honour of universal father to be so deformed that his sons might be terrified by the mere sight of him; others, because of Lady Olympia; others, seeing him stripped of all learning, etc., destitute of learning and letters, and wholly immersed in the study of law, although he had begun to abandon the path of that study, and concluding from this that he would show little favour to the learned, whom the Church nonetheless so greatly needs, and that under that pope the Church was certainly filled with ignorant men. He himself also revealed his theological ignorance well enough, when, asked in the Jansenist affair to look into it himself, he would not even read the papers offered to him, saying: It is not my profession; besides, I am old and have never studied theology. That is: It is not my profession; besides, I am an old man and have never studied theology. Or, as Father Ubaldini says in the Journal of St Amour, part 3, ch. 12, 18: The pope is not a theologian; it is not his profession; he is a lawyer. That is: The pope is not a theologian; it is not his profession; he is a lawyer.

units.la: Pii II. Gregorii XIII. Urbani VIII. Innocentii X. & Alexandri VII.
units.tr: Pius II, Gregory XIII, Urban VIII, Innocent X and Alexander VII.

units.la: IX. Imò, cùm saltem literatis favere pulchrum sit, fuerunt Pontifices, qui ex professo inimicitiam cum bonis literis suscepisse visi sunt. Paulus II. Genebrardo etiam virtutis & literarum inimicus, juxta verba Platinae in Vita, humanitatis studia ita oderat & contemnebat, ut ejus Studiosos, uno nomine, haereticos appellaret. Hanc ob rem Romanos adhortabatur, ne filios diutius in studiis literarum paterentur, satis esse, si legere & scribere didicissent. Wicelius in Epit. Rom. Pont. hinc ei crudelem persecutionem omnium doctorum & proborum, spoliationes in bonis, incarcerationes, tormenta, uno verbo Phalaridis potius quàm S. Pauli actiones, juxta exempla etiam Platinae & Mylvertonis Provincialis Angli, Carmelitae, tribuit. Et Successor Antecessori nequaquam dissimilis, Sixtus IV. in Conclavi Innocentii VIII. hoc elogio ornatur, quòd literarum & bonos mores habentium semper inimicus fuerit. Eò usque igitur Pontifices degenerare potuerunt, ut non tantum non virtute praediti & humanitatis atque literarum studiis ornati, sed & virtutis & literarum inimici fuerint? Tantùm abest, ut electio semper sit de doctiori, de quo in Decretalibus quaeritur, vel etiam de satis docto.
units.tr: IX. Indeed, although it is fitting at least to favour the learned, there have been popes who were seen to have openly taken up hostility towards good letters. Paul II, as Platina says in his Life, was an enemy of virtue and letters, and so hated and despised the study of humane letters that he called its students, by a single name, heretics. For this reason he urged the Romans not to let their sons remain longer in literary studies, it being enough if they had learned to read and write. Wicelius, in the Epitome of the Roman Pontiffs, therefore attributes to him a cruel persecution of all the learned and upright: plunder of goods, imprisonment, torments; in a word, deeds more like those of Phalaris than of St Paul, following the accounts of Platina and of Mylverton, the English provincial of the Carmelites. And his successor, by no means unlike him, Sixtus IV, is honoured in the conclave of Innocent VIII with this praise: that he was always an enemy of those who had letters and good morals. So far, then, could popes degenerate that they were not only not endowed with virtue and adorned with the study of humanity and letters, but were even enemies of virtue and letters? So far is it from the case that the election is always of the more learned, as the Decretals ask, or even of one sufficiently learned.

units.la: X. Licèt autem prudentiam in omni negotiorum genere exercitatam supra requiri vidimus, & magis quàm pietatem atque eruditionem requiri, non tamen omnibus prudentia illa, imò ne communis quidem & vulgaris omnibus adfuit. Non certè major illa, rursus saepe iis, qui pessimè electi fuerunt, rarò Neophytis & Laicis, nunquam pueris & juvenibus infrà aetatem legitimam electis, nunquam senibus bis pueris. Gregorius VI. qui alterum Papam ad Ecclesiastica officia exequenda secum consecrari fecit, dubio procul etiam prudentiae, ut scientiae defectu laboravit. Et quatuor illos, sub quibus Gregorius VII. nondum Papa socius Papae, secundùm Platinam, & Dominus Papae, juxta Damianum fuit, insufficienter prudentes fuisse, haud difficulter colligi potest.
units.tr: X. Although we have seen that prudence, exercised in every kind of business, is required above all and more than piety and learning, that prudence, or even the common and ordinary prudence, was not present in all of them. Certainly the greater prudence was not present in many of those who were most badly elected, and rarely in neophytes and laymen, never in boys and young men elected below the lawful age, and never in old men who were twice children. Gregory VI, who had another Pope consecrated with him to carry out ecclesiastical offices, without doubt suffered from a lack of prudence, as he did from a lack of knowledge. And that those four men, under whom Gregory VII, while not yet Pope, was "partner of the Pope" according to Platina and "Lord of the Pope" according to Damian, were insufficiently prudent, can be gathered without difficulty.

units.la: XI. Johannes XXI. al. XX. Plat. XXII. teste Platinâ, ignoratione rerum gerendarum, & morum inaequalitate, plùs detrimenti, quàm honoris & emolumenti Pontificatui attulit. Multa enim stoliditatem & levitatem prae se ferentia egit——Usus tamen consilio Joannis Cajetani, cujus nutu omnia tum agebantur, quòd ipsius auxilio & suffragiis Pontifex creatus fuerat &c. Pollicebatur sibi homo stolidus longam vitam, & diu se victurum omnibus praedicabat: quippe cujus vita & mores omnibus patebant, adeò erat inverecundi & secordis ingenii. Narrat porrò Platina, quoQuomodo ex camerae novae ruina, dum hanc stultitiam omnibus praedicabat, mortuus & Vir parum prudens sepultus fuerit. Atque tandem occasione ista infert: Nescio quo pacto compertum est, ut viri quidam admodum literati, ad res agendas parum idonei videantur. Nescio quo pacto, dixi, cum mirum potius omnibus videri debeat, ut, qui contemplatione delectatur, idem etiam rebus terrenis animum applicet. Praeter Platinam vero etiam Author Fasciculi temporum Johannem stolidum vocat; Nauclerus iisdem fere cum Platina verbis utitur. Johannes Stella, sine multa naturali prudentia atque in rebus agendis fractum & timidum fuisse, docet.
units.tr: XI. John XXI, alias XX, in Platina XXII, according to Platina's testimony, by his ignorance of affairs and the inconsistency of his conduct, brought more harm than honour or advantage to the Papacy. For he did many things that displayed stupidity and levity. Yet he acted on the advice of John Cajetan, at whose nod everything was then being done, because it was through his help and votes that the Pope had been created, and so on. The stupid man promised himself a long life and kept proclaiming that he would live for a long time, since his life and conduct were open to all, so shameless and foolish was his nature. Platina then relates how, while he was proclaiming this folly to everyone, he died from the collapse of the new chamber and was buried as "a man of little prudence." And at last he draws this conclusion from the occasion: "I know not how it has come about that certain men, very learned, seem little fitted for managing affairs. I know not how, I say, since it ought rather to seem strange to everyone that one who delights in contemplation should also apply his mind to earthly things." Besides Platina, the author of the Fasciculus temporum also calls John "stupid," and Naucler uses almost the same words as Platina. John Stella teaches that he was "without much natural prudence and, in conducting affairs, broken and timid."

units.la: XII. Coelestinus V. Platinae rebus agendis parum idoneus fuit, Eidem simplex, Stellę experientia rerum carens, hinc & eidem dicitur; quasi per indignationem & derisum Pontifex creatus, & parum utilis Reipubl. adjudicatus. Johannes XXII. al. XXI. Plat. XXIII. non fine imprudentia, simplices Episcopatus, juxta Platinam, bifariam divisit, ac divisos in unum redegit: & abbatias in Episcopatus & Episcopatus in Abbatias vicissim transtulit; Novas dignitates, nova Collegia in Ecclesiis constituit, ac constituta prius in aliam formam transtulit; Neque sine imprudentia Bonifacius IX. teste Cranzio l. 2. c. 12. quam facile dedit, tam leviter revocavit.
units.tr: XII. Celestine V was, according to Platina, "little fitted for managing affairs"; to the same author he was "simple," and according to Stella, "lacking experience of affairs," and for this reason too he is said by the same writer to have been created Pope "as if by indignation and mockery," and to have been judged "of little use to the Republic." John XXII, alias XXI, in Platina XXIII, not without imprudence, according to Platina, divided the "simple" bishoprics into two parts and then merged the divided ones into one; he transferred abbeys into bishoprics and bishoprics into abbeys in turn; he set up new dignities and new colleges in the churches, and transferred those previously established into another form. Nor without imprudence did Boniface IX, according to Cranzius, book 2, chapter 12, revoke as lightly as he had granted.

units.la: XIII. Adriano VI. imprudentiam & ineptitudinem illi tribuunt, qui Romanae Curiae sunt & fuerunt addictissimi. Onuphrio quidem in quibusdam nonnihil officio defuisse visus est, atque Hieronymo Balbo apud eum, cunctando rem Romanam, atque adeo universam Europam perditurus. Idem, Platina narrante, scurram mensae admovit; Eidem idem non quidem omnibus horis sapuit, interim tamen, si qua in re aliter se gessit, quam fortassis plerisque sapientum probatum fuerit, id tamen nec a sciente factum esse, nec de industria, confidenter dicit; Atque ita excusat, ut partim dicat, divinum potius quam humanum esse, ita ad omnia perpetuo vigilare, ut non alicubi tibi excidas, praesertim in tantis occupationibus, & apud homines tam astutos &c. partim eo, quod sedis Apostolicae functio operosior, quam imperitis rerum, & in otio, quieteque agentibus prima specie videatur. Tandem vero defendit contra quendam, qui in libro, quem de pseudibus inscripsit, de Adriano prodiderit, hominem, sicuti in administranda Rep. hebetis ingenii, vel depravati judicii, ita in esculentis insulsissimi gustus fuisse. Sed & nuperius Doctiss. Launojus, in Epist. I. V. 7. cujus inscriptio ita habet: Adrianus defenditur adversus Pallavicinum & alios Aulae Sectatores, qui Adrianum ad regendam sedem Apostolicam minus idoneum fuisse, calumniantur; opus habuit Adrianum vindicare, re, & verbis Masenii, Germani Jesuitae, in Anima historiarum hujus temporis: Hac simplicitate, qua Germanis se aperiebat, & diffidentia, quâ minùs se credebat Italis, reconditi magis animi sensúsque hominibus displicuit; sua haec opponere: In Episcopalis officii non bene gesti suspicionem venit apud eos, qui seculari potiùs, quàm religiosâ prudentiâ regendam esse Ecclesiam praese ferunt. Quemadmodum & rectè causas accusationis in vita doctrinae conformi, in recto de pluralitate beneficiorum sensu & in desiderio Reformationis, respectu Adriani, respectu Pallavicini, indesiderio Curiae blandiendi, ostendit, atque eâdem operâ, malè prudentiam secularem in Pontifice tantopere requiri.
units.tr: XIII. Those who are and have been most devoted to the Roman Curia ascribe imprudence and incompetence to Adrian VI. Onuphrius indeed thought that "he was somewhat lacking in duty in certain matters," and Girolamo Balbi said of him that "by delaying he would ruin the Roman affair, and indeed all Europe." The same Pope, according to Platina's account, "admitted a jester to his table." Of the same Pope the same writer says confidently that "he did not always show good sense, yet if in some matter he behaved otherwise than most wise men would have approved, yet this was done neither knowingly nor deliberately." And he excuses him in such a way that partly he says it is "more divine than human to watch over everything constantly, so that you do not slip somewhere, especially amid such great occupations and among men so cunning," and partly because "the function of the Apostolic See appears at first sight more laborious than it seems to those who are inexperienced in affairs and act in leisure and quiet." Finally he defends him against "a certain man who, in a book he entitled On Pseudo-, has described Adrian as, in governing the Republic, of a dull wit or depraved judgement, and in food of the most insipid taste." But more recently the most learned Launoy, in his Epistle 1, V. 7, whose title reads: "Adrian is defended against Pallavicini and other followers of the Court, who calumniate him as less fit to rule the Apostolic See," was obliged to vindicate Adrian in fact and in words. Masenius, a German Jesuit, in his Anima historiarum huius temporis, wrote: "By that simplicity with which he showed himself to the Germans, and by that distrust with which he trusted the Italians less, he displeased men of more hidden mind and feeling." Against this he sets his own words: "Suspicion of having ill-performed the episcopal office came upon him among those who profess that the Church ought to be governed by secular rather than religious prudence." And just as he rightly shows the grounds of accusation in his conformity of life to doctrine, in his correct sense on the plurality of benefices, and in his desire for Reform, with respect to Adrian and with respect to Pallavicini, and in his lack of desire to flatter the Court, so by the same means he shows how wrongly so much secular prudence is required in a Pope.

units.la: XIV. In Clemente VIII. Author Conclavis Leonis XI. exhibet exemplum non quidem parùm prudentis tempore electionis, sed tamen annotat, quosdam considerando quello gran Prencipe, che stimavano sapientissimo — si maravigliavano fortemente dell' occulto giuditio di Dio, e che con una repentina privatione della memoria & dell' intelletto l'havesse ultimamente privato della vita &c. id est, considerantes magnum illum Principem, quem sapientissimum aestimabant — miratos esse valde occultum judicium Dei, & quod post repentinam memoriae & intellectûs privationem eum etiam tandem vita privârit.
units.tr: XIV. Concerning Clement VIII, the author of the Conclave of Leo XI offers an example of a man not at all lacking in prudence at the time of his election. But he notes that some, "considering that great Prince whom they thought most wise... were greatly amazed at the hidden judgement of God, and that after a sudden privation of memory and understanding it had at last deprived him of life," etc. That is: "considering that great Prince whom they esteemed most wise, were greatly amazed at the hidden judgement of God, and that after a sudden privation of memory and understanding He had at last deprived him of life."

units.la: XV. Ex posterioribus Pontificibus prudentiam illam majorem in omni negotiorum genere exercitatam non habuisse censendi sunt, qui se faeminis vaferrimis totos regendos permiserunt. Sic Gregorio XV. adhaesit faemina quinquagenaria, versipellis & negotiorum peritissima, cujus consiliis virilibus universum ferè Papatum, effoeminatus ipse, administravit. Sic etiam Innocentius X. de quo in Conclavi diu mentio nulla facta fuerat ideò etiam, quòd, mancipium eum esse libidinis alienae, Olympiae, constaret omnibus; Sed ejusdem Olympiae artibus promotum omnia pro arbitrio ejus egisse, supra, ubi de virtutibus Pontificum egimus, annotatum est. De Urbano VIII. medio inter utrumque, MSC Italicum habet, Cardinalem Crescentium, postquàm jam electus esset, publicè atque ipso etiam Pontifice conscio, dictitâsse, stultum electum esse; juxta quem proin fuisset supra memorata de propria eruditione stolidae jactantia mentis.
units.tr: XV. Among the later Popes, those who have allowed themselves to be entirely governed by most crafty women are to be judged not to have had that greater prudence exercised in every kind of business. Thus a woman of fifty, a turncoat and most skilled in affairs, clung to Gregory XV, and, he himself being effeminate, governed almost the whole Papacy by her manly counsels. So too Innocent X, of whom no mention had been made in the Conclave for a long time, partly because it was clear to all that he was the plaything of another's lust, that is, of Olympia. But, as was noted above where we treated the virtues of the Popes, he, promoted by the arts of this same Olympia, did everything at her discretion. Concerning Urban VIII, midway between the two, an Italian manuscript records that Cardinal Crescenzi, after he had already been elected, said publicly, and with the Pope himself aware, that "a fool has been elected." By his judgement, therefore, the foolish boasting of a mind about its own learning, mentioned above, would have been present.

units.la: XVI. Prout etiam ex iis, quae n. VI. de Electione Theologorum diximus, constat, & amplius jam ostendi debet, valdè prudentes à Cardinalibus non facilè promoveri. Hinc L'Ambasc. di Rom. p.236. inter qualitates Papabilis Cardinalis Rasponi ponitur, quòd
units.tr: XVI. As we have said of the election of theologians in n. VI, and as should now be shown further, it is clear that men of great prudence are not easily promoted by the Cardinals. Hence in L'Ambasciatore di Roma, p. 236, among the qualities of Cardinal Rasponi as a papabile, it is listed that

units.la: Cccccc 3 quòd sit huomo di talenti mediocri, quale appunto desiderano, per interesse proprio i Prencipi, che sia il Papa, di genio rimesso &c. Id est; homo dotibus mediocribus instructus, qualem Papam Principes jam ob commoda propria expetunt, genio remisso &c. Hinc etiam de Cardinali Barberino Phœbus Ibidem p.242. ita canit: V' è Barberino, che per l'età presume Esser nel Mondo il Successor di Piero, Mà perche tropp' è noto il suo costume, Atto al Governo, ei non si stima un zero. Id est;
units.tr: he is "a man of mediocre talents, such as the princes themselves, for their own advantage, desire the Pope to be, of a slack disposition," etc. That is: "a man furnished with mediocre gifts, such as the Princes now desire in a Pope for their own advantages, of a remiss disposition," etc. Hence also Phoebus, ibid., p. 242, sings thus of Cardinal Barberini: "There is Barberini, who, on account of his age, presumes to be the successor of Peter in the world; but since his conduct is too well known, fit for government, he does not count himself a zero."

units.la: Ibi est Barberinus, qui ratione ætatis præsumit, esse se successorem Petri; sed quia nimis notus est genius ejus regiminí aptus, in nullo loco est.
units.tr: There is Barberini, who by reason of his age presumes that he is the successor of Peter; but because his disposition is too well known to be suited to rule, he is in no place at all.

units.la: XVII. Concludimus jam, postquam requisita, quæ breviorem nonnisi consideHationem merentur, Sect.II. n. XVI. XVII. XVIII. XIX. exhibuimus, Electionem Pontificum Romanorum (in qua Gregorius XV. in Bulla de Conclavi, magna diligentia, cura, prudentia & precibus opus esse, tanquam in electione Pastoris Universalis, dixit, ut non prædominentur in ea affectus aut humana sapientia;) & ratione eligentium, & ratione modi eligendi, & ratione personarum eligi solitarum valde vitiosam esse, & (quod M. Ant. de Dominis l. IV. c.12. de Roma ipsa enuntiavit;) primùm (manentibus nimirùm in vocatione sua Episcopis illis;) sanam, post valetudinariam, tandem ægram factam fuisse, sive (quod Pii IV. Bulla habet) ubi, quantum in electione ista situm sit, quoque enarrat, semper in deterius processisse; Ordinarió autem (quod ex Onuphrio in Pio V. ubi bonam viam alieniorem viam & paucorum vocat, colligimus;) malam esse. Et proin tantùm abest, ut ex Electione pateat, (quemadmodum Jesuita Otto Rom. Glor. p.120. gloriatur) Papismum non esse Anti-Christianum, ut potiùs vel maximè in Electionibus Mysterium Iniquitatis reveletur, & specie non caruerit, quòd conjurati in Vita Sixti V. dixerunt, se Papam occidere voluisse, ut meliùs melior eligeretur; Quando enim digni, digne, dignum, dignum scientia, moribus, ætate & legitimo matrimonio eligere debent; & consentientes in indignum potestate privantur; & electio contempta minori parte, imò vel uno facta cassatur; cassatur etiam propter Simoniam &c. quæ omnia in Lege illorum Scripta reperimus; paucorum certè à multis Seculis electio manet integra.
units.tr: XVII. Having now set out, after the requisites, which deserve only a brief consideration, as we did in Sect. II, nn. XVI, XVII, XVIII, XIX, we conclude that the election of Roman Pontiffs (in which Gregory XV, in the Bull on the Conclave, said that "great diligence, care, prudence and prayers are needed, as in the election of a Universal Pastor, so that feelings or human wisdom do not prevail in it") is very faulty, both with respect to those who elect, and with respect to the manner of electing, and with respect to the persons usually chosen. And (as Marcantonio de Dominis, book 4, chapter 12, stated of Rome itself), it was first sound (namely while those bishops remained in their calling), then became sickly, and at last sick. Or (as the Bull of Pius IV has it), where it describes how far this election has been carried, it "has always gone from bad to worse." And as we gather from Onuphrius on Pius V, where he calls the good way "a stranger way of the few," it is ordinarily bad. And so far is it from being evident from the election, as the Jesuit Otto boasts in Roma Gloriosa, p. 120, that Papism is not Antichristian, that rather, especially in the elections, the Mystery of Iniquity is revealed, and it has not lacked a show of appearance, as the conspirators in the Life of Sixtus V said, that they had wished to kill the Pope so that a better one might be elected. For when the worthy ought to elect worthily, a worthy man for a worthy office, one worthy in knowledge, morals, age and lawful marriage; and when those who consent to an unworthy man are deprived of power; and when an election is annulled if the lesser part has been despised, or even if it was made by one vote; and when it is annulled also on account of simony, etc., all of which we find written in their own law, indeed the election has remained intact for many centuries only for a few.

units.la: XVIII. Sed qui malè electi sunt, nulli sunt; Papa non legitimè electus (inquit Baldus ICtus vetus Italus in l. 2. c. sententiam rescindi rescindi non posse;) est Diabolus in terris & Apostata, & ideò non habet Claves Cœli, sed inferni. Imò Nicolaus II. in Concilio Romano, sequens Decretum, quod apud Gratianum Dist. 23. ab initio aliquantò prolixiùs exhibet, sed à Caranza in Summa ita contractum legitur,edidit: Si quis pecuniâ aut gratiâ humanâ,aut populari, militari-rive tumultu, sine concordi & Canonica Electione Cardinalium fuerit in Throno Petri collocatus,is non Apostolicus, sed Apostaticus, id est, à ratione deficiens merito vocetur, liceatque Cardinalibus, Clericis & Laicis Deum colentibus illum ut prædonem anathematizare, & quovis auxilio humano à Sede Apostolica propellere,ac quovis in loco,si non liceat in urbe, Catholicos hujus rei causâ congregare. Quibus in citato jure additur: Quod si quis contra hoc decretum, Synodali sententiâ promulgatum, per seditionem, vel præsumptionem,aut quolibet ingenio electus,aut etiam ordinatus seu intronisatus fuerit, authoritate Divinâ & Sanctorum Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, perpetuo anathemate cum suis authoribus, fautoribus & sequacibus, à limine Sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ separatus abjiciatur, sicut Antichristus,invasor & destructor totius Christianismi &c. Similiter, indoctos indignè promotos,Simoniacos nullam potestatem habere,de Dominis l.II.c.4. probat. Talium ordinationes nullas esse,ex Baronio ad an. 963. n. 5. seq. discimus; Eos nihil bene agere,apud eundem ad an.908. 4. asseritur. Quales ergò fuerunt plerique? Quænam habetur de omnibus certitudo? Quid judicandum est de actionibus plurimorum? Rectè verò de Dominis I.IV.c.10. p.100. pertendit, etiam admisso Romanæ Ecclesiæ Papatu in genere,nullam certitudinem posse in individuo haberi; Et merito cum eo concludentes canimus:
units.tr: XVIII. But those who have been badly elected are no one at all. A pope not lawfully elected (says Baldus, the old Italian jurist, in l. 2 c. that his sentence cannot be rescinded) is the Devil on earth and an apostate, and therefore does not hold the keys of heaven, but of hell. Indeed Nicholas II, in the Roman council, issued the following decree, which Gratian gives at Dist. 23 at its beginning somewhat more fully, but which is read in Caranza's Summa in abbreviated form: If anyone has been placed on the throne of Peter by money or human favour, or by popular or military tumult, without the united and canonical election of the cardinals, let him be called not Apostolic but Apostatic, that is, deservedly one who falls short of reason; and let it be lawful for the cardinals, clergy and laity who worship God to anathematize him as a robber, and to drive him from the Apostolic See by any human aid, and to gather Catholics for this purpose in whatever place, if it is not permitted in the city. To this, the law cited adds: If anyone, contrary to this decree promulgated by synodal sentence, has been elected by sedition or presumption, or by any device, or even ordained or enthroned, let him be cast out by the divine authority and that of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, separated with a perpetual anathema, along with his authors, supporters and followers, from the threshold of the holy Church of God, like Antichrist, the invader and destroyer of all Christianity, etc. Similarly, Dominis, Book 2, c. 4, proves that the unlearned, the unworthily promoted and the simoniacs have no power. From Baronius, at the year 963, n. 5 following, we learn that their ordinations are null; the same author, at the year 908, n. 4, asserts that they accomplish nothing well. What sort of men, then, were most of them? What certainty is there about all of them? What is to be judged of the actions of very many? Dominis rightly contends, Book 4, c. 10, p. 100, that even if the Roman papacy is admitted in general, no certainty can be had about any individual; and rightly, concluding with him, we sing:

units.la: Omnia Papicolis tenui pendentia fîlo.
units.tr: All things hang by a slender thread for the Papists.

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS OCTAVÆ, In qua, De iis, quæ Pontificis Electionem proximè consequi solent, agitur.
units.tr: DISSERTATION EIGHT, in which we treat of those things that usually immediately follow the election of the Pontiff.

units.la: SECTIO PRIOR, In qua, De Ceremoniis, quæ Pontificis Electionem proximè excipiunt, agitur.
units.tr: FIRST SECTION, in which we treat of the ceremonies that immediately receive the Pontiff after his election.

units.la: Breviarium
units.tr: Summary

units.la: I. Transitio ad consequentia; II. Inter Ceremonialia primum est, quòd assensus electi requiritur; III. Sequitur congratulatio; Qua fit adoratione; IV. Adorantur Pontifices; V. Tum aliàs. VI. Tum maximè in electione, consecratione, & coronatione. VII. Aliàs adorandi potantur; VIII. Adorationis signum inter alia osculum pedum. IX. Vitium adorationis notatur multiplex; X. Origo adorationis illius detegitur. XI. Vitium in osculo pedum notatur, ejusdémque origo detegitur, unà cum mysterio & ignominia crucis in crepidis Pontificis; XII. Portandi ritus refellitur; XIII. Vestitum dein mutat electus; XIV. Annotationes ad vestitum Pontificis rubrum & purpureum; XV. Urbani VIII. de vestibus Pontificiis judicium; XVI. Vestes & bona electi, quæ sunt in cella, cedunt Conclavistis. XVII. Sequitur nominis mutatio, cujus origo investigatur; XVIII. Annotationes ad illa, quæ in investigatione tali reperta sunt; XIX. Quidam morem mutandi non observárunt; XX. Quanam in mutatione illa respiciantur; XXI. Nominibus egregiis persona non respondent; XXII. Sequitur Confirmatio Capitulorum &c. quæ tamen negligitur; XXIII. Electio populo annunciatur; Ædes electi diripiuntur; XXIV. Conclave aperitur, diripitur; Processio ad S. Petrum; XXV. Quid fieri soleat, si electus sit absens; XXVI. Consequens Electionis olim etiam erat Confirmatio Imperatoria; quæ unà cum ortu & causis declaratur; XXVII. Exemplis variis; XXVIII. Cessatio consuetudinis; XXIX. Quid agat, & non agat Pontifex simpliciter electus; XXX. Ventilatur quæstio; utrum electus ante Coronationem habeat potestatem, atque ex utraque parte Pontificiorum difficultates insuperabiles ostenduntur; XXXI. Ordinationem & Consecrationem Pontificis nôsse juvat; Potest electus Laicus uno die omnes ordines percurrere; XXXII. Papa fit Subdiaconus; XXXIII. Fit Diaconus; XXXIV. Fit Presbyter; XXXV. Quomodo inferiores Ordines suscipiat; XXXVI. Consecrationis Episcopalis præparatio; XXXVII. Consecratio ipsa, ut sola fieri solet; XXXVIII. Consecrationis, quæ qua simul cum benedictione & Coronatione fit, antecedentia; XXXIX. Consecratio ipsa; XL. Benedictio &c. XLI. Coronatio; XLII. Ejus origo; XLIII. Corona pretium; XLIV. Mysterium; XLV. Refectio ante Processionem & Processio ad Lateranum ipsa; XLVI. Qua apud Lateranum agantur, XLVII. Pompa haec coronationis magni constat, & aliquando infelix est; XLVIII. Parallelismus inter Processiones Christi & Petri ab una, Pontificum vero ab altera parte; XLIX. Convivium Coronationis die tandem institui solitum; L. Annotationes breves ad illud Convivium, & tractationis de consequentibus Ceremonialibus Conclusio.
units.tr: I. Transition to the consequences. II. The first of the ceremonial matters is that the consent of the one elected is required. III. Congratulation follows, which is made by adoration. IV. Pontiffs are adored. V. Otherwise too. VI. Especially in the election, consecration and coronation. VII. At other times the adored are carried about. VIII. Among other signs of adoration is the kissing of the feet. IX. The fault of adoration is noted in several respects. X. The origin of that adoration is uncovered. XI. The fault in the kissing of the feet is noted, and its origin is uncovered, together with the mystery and disgrace of the cross on the Pontiff's slippers. XII. The rite of carrying is refuted. XIII. Then the one elected changes his clothing. XIV. Notes on the Pontiff's red and purple vestments. XV. Urban VIII's judgment on Papal vestments. XVI. The vestments and goods of the one elected, which are in the cell, go to the conclavists. XVII. There follows the change of name, whose origin is investigated. XVIII. Notes on those things which were found in such an investigation. XIX. Some did not observe the custom of changing. XX. What is considered in that change. XXI. Names do not correspond to persons of distinction. XXII. There follows the confirmation of the chapters, etc., which is nevertheless neglected. XXIII. The election is announced to the people; the house of the one elected is plundered. XXIV. The conclave is opened and plundered; the procession to St Peter's. XXV. What is usually done if the one elected is absent. XXVI. The former consequence of the election was also the imperial confirmation, which is explained together with its origin and causes. XXVII. Various examples. XXVIII. Cessation of the custom. XXIX. What the Pontiff simply elected may and may not do. XXX. The question is debated, whether the one elected has power before the coronation, and from both sides of the Papists insurmountable difficulties are shown. XXXI. It is helpful to know the ordination and consecration of the Pontiff; a lay person elected may run through all the orders in one day. XXXII. The Pope becomes a subdeacon. XXXIII. He becomes a deacon. XXXIV. He becomes a presbyter. XXXV. How he receives the lower orders. XXXVI. Preparation for episcopal consecration. XXXVII. The consecration itself, as it is usually done alone. XXXVIII. Of the consecration which is done together with the blessing and coronation, the preceding things; XXXIX. The consecration itself; XL. The blessing, etc. XLI. The coronation; XLII. Its origin; XLIII. The price of the crown; XLIV. The mystery; XLV. The refreshment before the procession and the procession itself to the Lateran; XLVI. What is done there at the Lateran; XLVII. This pomp of the coronation is costly, and sometimes unlucky; XLVIII. A parallel between the processions of Christ and Peter on the one side, and those of the Pontiffs on the other; XLIX. The banquet of the coronation, which at last was customarily instituted on the day; L. Brief notes on that banquet, and the conclusion of the treatment of the subsequent ceremonies.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: SEquuntur tandem ea, quae Electionem Pontificum proxime à multo tempore. Talia autem sequuntur, quae ka praecedunt, pleraque vitiosa atque Pontifice summo, Vicario Jesu Christi in terris unico plane indigna; Ut continuata potius, quam vere finita prolixa de naevis tractatio videri possit; Quippe, Ceremonias si spectemus, superstitione infectae, quaedam idololatria insuper foedatae; pleraque fastum typhumque secularem unice spirantes, & tamen (quod longe pessimum,) omnes cum profanatione Divini nominis dignissimi conjunctae statim apparent. Si consequentia moralia, alia, quam quae summo Ecclesiae Christi Monarchae convenire queant; sunt omnia. Ceremonias primo videamus.
units.tr: Now at last follow those things which in a long period have immediately followed the election of the Pontiffs. Such things as follow are for the most part faulty, and altogether unworthy of the supreme Pontiff, the unique Vicar of Jesus Christ on earth; so that the lengthy treatment may seem rather a continuation of blemishes than a true conclusion. For if we look at the ceremonies, they are infected with superstition, some further defiled by idolatry; most of them breathe nothing but worldly pride and haughtiness, and yet (what is by far the worst) they all appear at once joined with the profanation of the most worthy name of God. If we consider the moral consequences, they are all such as could not befit the supreme Monarch of the Church of Christ. Let us first look at the ceremonies.

units.la: II. Pontifice electo, primum est, quod assensus ejus requiritur; Qui quidem ad omne Ministerium Ecclesiasticum necessarius est, tanquam ad conjugium aliquod spirituale. Ex primis Pontificibus multos invitos electos esse atque ab ipsis assensum vix tandem impetrari potuisse, supra visum est, ubi de ambitione seculorum recentiorum. Faciles hodie sunt, & quaecunque interdum brevis recusatio est, sub persona prompta acceptatio est. Tales enim dignitatem in terris seculari judicio maximam & cum veneratione Idololatrica, potentiae praerogativa, divitiarum splendore, & luculenta se suosque ditandi, & omnibus modis ad dignitatum, qua secularium, qua Ecclesiasticarum, quas vocant, culmina promovendi occasione conjunctam non ambabus, ut ajunt, ulnis amplecti non possunt, nisi, quod paucissimorum sapientum est, in quiete quam in honorato tumultu vivere malint; Atque ridiculum esset, tandem acceptare nolle tanto studio, tot artibus expetitum, quaesitum Papatum. Omnium fere est animus promptus, eadem mens, si non idem sermo, quem Sixti V. de acceptatione rogati fuisse jam Dissert. I. Sect. VI. n. XXXV, indicavimus: Non possumus acceptare, respondit, qua jam acceptavimus, sed adhuc alium acceptaremus, si quidem daretur &c.
units.tr: II. When the Pontiff has been elected, the first thing is that his consent is required. This is indeed necessary for every ecclesiastical ministry, as for some spiritual marriage. That many of the first Pontiffs were elected against their will, and that their consent could scarcely at last be obtained from them, has been seen above, where we spoke of the ambition of later ages. Today they are easy, and whatever brief refusal there is, is a ready acceptance under a mask. For such men cannot, as they say, embrace with both arms the dignity which in earthly secular judgment is the greatest, and which is joined with idolatrous veneration, the prerogative of power, the splendour of riches, and the opportunity of enriching themselves and their own, and of advancing by every means to the summits of dignities, both secular and ecclesiastical as they call them; unless, which belongs to very few wise men, they prefer to live in quiet rather than in honoured tumult. And it would be ridiculous at last to refuse to accept the papacy, sought with such eagerness, desired by so many arts. The mind of almost everyone is ready, and the same attitude, if not the same words, which we have already indicated was that of Sixtus V when he was asked about accepting, in Dissert. I. Sect. VI. n. XXXV: We cannot accept, he replied, what we have already accepted, but we would accept another, if indeed one were given, etc.

units.la: III. Assensu impetrato, omnes surgunt primò ad congratulan-dum,ut Sacr. cerim. l 1. §. 1. & 2. habet. Quæ congratulatio aliquando ante electionem facta & acceptata legitur, imò aliquando, quod triste est, ubi electio secuta non est. Congratulatio autem ista fit adoratione, quâ etiam nonnullos eligi Differt. IV. ostendimus. Heic igitur conveniens est locus tractationi de Adoratione Pontificum; quam tamen brevissimam dabimus, tum quia tantùm tanquam de consequente Electionis hcic agimus, tum quia jam alii fusiùs adorationem hanc prosecuti sunt; Inter quos etiam est ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις Johannes Müllerus S. Theologiae, dum viveret, in Lycéo Tigurino Professor Celeberrimus, in opere, quod ex parte tantùm lucem vidit hactenus.
units.tr: III. Once consent has been obtained, everyone first rises to offer congratulation, as Sacr. cerim. l. 1. §. 1. & 2. has it. This congratulation is sometimes read as having been made and accepted before the election, and indeed sometimes, which is sad, where no election followed. This congratulation, moreover, is made by adoration, by which we showed in Differt. IV. that some were also chosen. Here therefore is a fitting place for a treatment of the Adoration of Pontiffs; which, however, we shall give very briefly, both because we treat it here only as a consequence of the Election, and because others have already pursued this adoration at greater length; among whom is also ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις [the now among the saints] Johannes Müllerus, while he lived a most celebrated Professor of Holy Theology in the Zurich Lyceum, in a work which has so far seen the light only in part.

units.la: IV. Pontifices adorari & ingenua Pontificiorum confessio, & editi ab adulatoribus Curiae Romanae de Adoratione Pontificum integri tractatus, & praxis multiplex dubitare sinunt neminem; Adorationis verò cultum non pati eos tantùm, sed & ab omnibus omninò mortalibus, Regibus, Imperatoribus etiam, tanquam debitum exigere, imò aliquando absentes ad honoris debiti confessionem publicis Instrumentis confirmandam juxta Sacr. Cerim. l. 1. Sect.5. adigere, indubium quoque est. Prout etiam l. c. l. 3. Sect.1. omnibus mortalibus & præsertim Christi fidelibus, cujuscunq; sint dignitatis, & præeminentiæ, injungitur, ut cùm primùm in conspectum Pontificis adveniunt, distantibus spaciis ter ante illum genu flectant.
units.tr: IV. Neither the frank confession of the Papists, nor the complete treatises on the Adoration of Pontiffs published by the flatterers of the Roman Curia, nor the manifold practice, allow anyone to doubt that Pontiffs are adored; and it is also undoubted that they do not merely accept the worship of adoration, but demand it as due from all mortals, from kings and emperors too, and even sometimes compel absent persons, according to Sacr. Cerim. l. 1. Sect. 5., to confirm the confession of the honour owed by public instruments. Just as also, l. c. l. 3. Sect. 1., it is enjoined on all mortals, and especially on the faithful of Christ, of whatever dignity and pre-eminence, that as soon as they come into the sight of the Pontiff they should bend the knee three times before him at a distance.

units.la: V. Adorantur autem Pontifices sæpissimè; In Missa, in Jubilæo, in Processionibus suis Pontificalibus quibuscunque, in Conciliis, in Imperatorum coronationibus, eorundem receptionibus, Sanctorum, Cardinalium, Episcoporum, Legatorum creationibus, in variis, quas vocant, benedictionibus, in omnibus ferme Festis, in Concionibus, in urbium ingressibus, in epistolis, denique etiam post mort. m; Imò in omni, juxta n. praced. primo occursu; Et quando non? Vide haec omnia apud Marcellum, &, si non copia est libri, apud Clarissimum Müllerum, qui pleraque ex eo excerpsit fideliter.
units.tr: V. Pontiffs are adored very often: at Mass, at the Jubilee, in all their Pontifical processions, in Councils, at the coronations of Emperors, at their receptions, at the creations of Saints, Cardinals, Bishops and Legates, at various so-called blessings, on almost all feast days, in sermons, at entries into cities, in letters, and finally even after death; indeed, according to the preceding paragraph, at the first meeting in every case. And when not? See all these things in Marcellus, and, if there is no copy of the book, in the most distinguished Müllerus, who has faithfully excerpted most of them from him.

units.la: VI. Maximè verò adorationis cultu afficiuntur in electionis, consecrationis & coronationis solennitatibus, de quibus heic agendum. Vide Marcellum saepe citatum l. 1. Sect.1. & Cl. Laurentium Bank, in Roma Triumphante ritus electionis & coronationis Innocentii X. cujus αὐτόπτης fuit, p.160. seqq.238. seq. 275. seqq. 297. 315. seqq. 377. seqq. enarrantem; Vide utrumque saltem apud Clar. Müllerum de Ador. Pont. Disp. 2. c. 3. ubi & Antoninus Diana adorationis voce pariter utens adducitur; Atque notari potest, Pontificem adorandum altari sancto, in quo Sacro-Sanctæ reliquiæ, Apostolorum, ut credunt, aliquando corpora sunt, tunc imponi. Singularis vero illa in Alexandro VII. vel modestia, vel hypocrisis fuit, quòd noluit præcedentium Paparum more in altaris medio collocari, sed vehementer institit, ut in angulo quodam altaris relinqueretur, indignum se professus eo loco, quem cæteri Pontifices tenuissent; & ubi corporis & sanguinis Domini consecratio administretur atque perficiatur. De quibus omnibus præter alia, Conclavia etiam antiquiora testantur luculentissimè, prout quoque de illo, quòd adoratio statim post electionem ter fieri soleat.
units.tr: VI. They are, however, especially honoured with the worship of adoration in the solemnities of election, consecration and coronation, of which we are to treat here. See Marcellus, often cited, l. 1. Sect. 1., and the distinguished Laurentius Bank, in Roma Triumphante, describing the rites of the election and coronation of Innocent X, of whom he was eyewitness [αὐτόπτης], p. 160 ff., 238 f., 275 ff., 297, 315 ff., 377 ff.; see at least both of them in the distinguished Müllerus, de Ador. Pont. Disp. 2. c. 3., where Antoninus Diana, likewise using the word adoration, is also cited. It may also be noted that the Pontiff is then placed to be adored at the holy altar, on which, as they believe, the most sacred relics, sometimes the bodies of the Apostles, are. That singular modesty, or hypocrisy, in Alexander VII was indeed remarkable: he would not be placed in the middle of the altar in the manner of his predecessors, but insisted strongly that he be left in a certain corner of the altar, professing himself unworthy of the place which the other Pontiffs had held; and where the consecration of the body and blood of the Lord is administered and completed. Of all these things, besides others, the older Conclaves also bear the clearest witness, as they also do concerning that which is customary, that the adoration is made three times immediately after the election.

units.la: VII. Aliàs ut eò melius à pluribus adorari possit, sæpe portatur humeris. Quod seculo nono primus admisit Stephanus III. al. II. qui, referente Platina, humeris omnium in Basilicam Salvatoris deportatus est, atque inde in Patriarchatum Lateranensem. Quem ritum, sic pergit Polydorus Vergilius de Inv. rerum l. 4. c. 10. deinceps servârunt successores. Adeò semper veterum honorum ac pomparum, magis quàm morum tenax est posteritas. Hîc autem à portandi officio, juxta Sacr. Cerim. l. 1. Sect. 2. & exempla ne ipsi quidem Imperatores, Reges & Principes immunes sunt.
units.tr: VII. At other times, so that he may be adored more conveniently by many people, he is often carried on men's shoulders. Stephen III (also called II) was the first to permit this in the ninth century. According to Platina, he was carried on the shoulders of all men into the Basilica of the Saviour, and from there to the Lateran Patriarchate. Successors have kept this rite, as Polydore Vergil continues in De inventoribus rerum book 4, chapter 10: so tenacious is posterity always of the old honours and pageants, rather than of good morals. Here, according to Sacr. Cerim. book 1, section 2, not even emperors, kings and princes are exempt from the duty of carrying him, and the examples show it.

units.la: VIII. Adoratio ab accedentibus etiam fit osculo, pedi etiam Pontificis figi solito.
