Quod seculo octavo primi accipere meruerunt, Paulo Diacono tradente, pedes Constantini Papæ ab Imperatore Justiniano II. modis omnibus Papam demulcere, & honoribus cumulatum sui beneficii facere conante. Ad cujus exemplum omnis Romanorum senatus Valentini an. 824. electi pedes osculatus est. Quod idem hodienum præstare tenentur etiam Reges & Imperatores, quibus in præsentiam Papæ venire contingit. Atque licèt in Concilio Florentino Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus putârit, sufficere, si Papam ætate majorem salutet tanquam patrem, coætaneum amplectatur tanquam fratrem, juniorem tractet ut filium, tamen, referente Sylvestro Sguropulo in Hist. Conc. Sect. 4. c. 19. p. 92. ab Angario, quem Imperator Græcus ad eum miserat, audire debuit: Expectat Papa R. ἵνα ἡ μεγάλη ἁγιωσύνη σὲ ἐλθὼν προσκυνήσῃ καὶ ἀσπάσῃ καὶ λάβῃ τὸ πόδα αὐτῆς, ut magna Sanctitas Tua veniat, adoret, ejusque pedem sculetur. Imperator autem de tuo honore anxius toto triduo hoc animo agitavit, ne id tua sanctitas admittat. Maluit etiam publicè non accedere, quàm admittere. Vehemens autem de hoc contentio apud eundem c.20.21.22: videri potest. Et Sect. 6. c. 22. p. 176. quomodo Legati Burgundici, Papæ Ministrum secuti, nullum Imperatori Constantinopolitano præsenti reverentiæ signum exhibuerint, appropinquantes verò Papæ, οσοι ... πάντες τὸν πόδα, cunctis adorârint & pedem osculati sint. Profert etiam Josephi Stevani Valentini, Doctoris Theologi de Osculatione pedum Romani Pontificis liber Gregorio XIII. inscriptus & Coloniæ an. 1580. impressus. Qui inter alia hanc osculationis pedum prærogativam passivam soli Papæ propriam esse, ex dictatibus Hildebrandinis docet, quorum nonus ita se habet: Quòd solius Papæ pedes omnes Principes deosculentur. Est autem hæc osculatio calceamentorum potius, & ad quam idiotæ raro aut nunquam admittuntur. Quibus tamen aliquando pedes defuncti exosculari exemplo Sixti V. & aliorum conceditur.
units.tr: VIII. Those who approach also adore him with a kiss, which is customarily placed on the Pope's foot. The first to receive this honour were the feet of Pope Constantine in the eighth century, as Paul the Deacon reports, when the Emperor Justinian II tried in every way to win over the Pope and to lay him under obligation by heaping honours on him. Following this example, the whole Roman senate kissed the feet of Valentine, elected in the year 824. Kings and emperors who happen to come into the Pope's presence are still bound to do the same today. Although at the Council of Florence the Patriarch of Constantinople thought it enough to greet the Pope, if older, as a father, to embrace him, if of his own age, as a brother, and to treat him, if younger, as a son, nevertheless, as Sylvester Syropoulos reports in his History of the Council, section 4, chapter 19, page 92, he had to hear from Angarius, whom the Greek Emperor had sent to him: The Pope of Rome waits for your great holiness to come and worship him, embrace him and take hold of his foot [ἵνα ἡ μεγάλη ἁγιωσύνη σὲ ἐλθὼν προσκυνήσῃ καὶ ἀσπάσῃ καὶ λάβῃ τὸ πόδα αὐτῆς], so that your Great Holiness might come, adore him, and kiss his foot. The Emperor, however, anxious about your honour, was troubled in this mind for three whole days, lest your holiness should admit it. He preferred not to appear publicly at all rather than to admit it. The fierce dispute on this matter can be seen in the same work, chapters 20, 21 and 22. Also section 6, chapter 22, page 176, shows how the Burgundian envoys, following the Pope's minister, gave no sign of reverence to the Emperor of Constantinople who was present, but when they approached the Pope, all of them adored and kissed his foot. Josephus Stevanus Valentinus, Doctor of Theology, also produces his book On the Kissing of the Feet of the Roman Pontiff, dedicated to Gregory XIII and printed at Cologne in 1580. Among other things he teaches that this privilege of having one's feet kissed belongs to the Pope alone, from the Hildebrandine Dictates, the ninth of which reads: That all princes shall kiss the feet of the Pope alone. Yet this kissing is of the shoes rather than the feet, and ordinary people are rarely or never admitted to it. Still, the feet of the dead are sometimes allowed to be kissed, by the example of Sixtus V and others.

units.la: IX. Sed qualis hæc est adoratio? Consequens hoc Electionis quale? Idololatrica est adoratio, maximè vitiosum consequens. Neque immeritò Idololatriæ hëic Papicolas reos agimus, dum eos cultum Religiosum atque Divinum creaturæ tribere constat. Fatemur equidem, & voces & ritus externos aliquando de & in cultu civili usurpari. Verùm quando adoratio in N. T. & apud Veteres nonnisi cultum Religiosum denotat; Latinum verbum adorandi ferè non est in usu (hodie) inquit Loyolita Pererius, neque apud Theologos, neque in vulgari Christianorum sermone, nisi in veri soliusque Dei cultu; Est autem vel maximè in cultu Papæ. Etidem est aliquid adorare, & id pro Deo habere; quando modestiores Pontificii à se adorari sanctos imagines negant, ne Divinum iis honorem tribuere magis videantur; quando omnes Imperatores, Reges aliósque Principes summo quidem honore civili afficiendos, sed non adorandos esse, sibi contrà, licèt Politica ratione longè inferioribus, adorationis cultum deferre debere contendunt; quando apud Orientales ferè tantùm adorationis, sive incurvationis ritus civilis obtinuit, Occidentales verò ceremoniarum harum parciores fuêre, atque apud eos συγκύνησις adoratio nonnisi in sacris usitata, neque aut admissa, nisi ab iis, quibus tyrannidis insolentia mentem mutâssset; aut delata fuit, nisi ab iis, qui servilem in modum potentioribus adulari sueverunt; quando in N. T. Petrus & Angelus adorationem sibi, licèt neutri ut Deo, delatam improbârunt; Ex quo Antoninus: Sum. par.3.tit.22.c.5. sect.4. infert, Papam Angelis esse superiorem; Augustinus de Ancona, de Eccles. Pot. q.9. art. 4. p. 65. majorem Papa honorem exhiberi, quàm Angelis; Æque autem concludere possent respectu Petri, atque similiter à facto ad jus procedendo convincere, & Nebucadnezaris statuam, & Diabolum, & Antichristum, qui supra omne venerabile colitur, Angelis, imò ipso Deo vero à multis contrà neglecto, superiores esse; quando Papa & in reliquis Divinitatem affectat, atque Divina sibi θεοπνεύματα vendicat, ab eo adorato maxima quoq; & Divina sibi beneficia adoratores promittunt; quando ejus adulatoribus, eum ut Deum adorandum esse, non semel excidit; quando omninò ut Pro-Deus, Pro-Christus, Ecclesiæ Monarcha, religionis vertex, adoratur, neque tamen honor ille delatus Papæ in honorem Dei atque Christi vergit, cùm Legatus non eum, qui mittenti tantùm debetur, honorem accipere jure queat, Papa autem honorem osculi pedum accipiat ab eo, qui in Palmis Christi personam refert, honorem, qui Christo, secundùm quod Deus est, debetur, ipsimet Pontificiis nonnullis fatentibus, accipiat, imò majorem in Missa & solenni processione, & nominatione; quemadmodum Paulus Sarpius Guerra di Paolo V. &c. Ii. 24. notat, Nuncium Papæ coràm Senatu Veneto perorantem atque pietatem affectantem, nominato nomine Domini nostri Papæ, caput aperuisse, Deo; non item; Legatus autem Christi non sit, neque ab eo constitutum, ut ita honoretur ille; quando in Papæ adoratione tunsio cordis & incensatio, præter sessionem in altari supra memoratam adhibentur; quando Papæ cultus Sanctorum & Angelorum cultu major, Deiparæ, crucis, Eucharistiæ, imaginis Christi, reliquiarum, & illo, quem olim arcæ fœderis delatum esse dictitant, non inferior insinuatur, qui tamen cultus omnis, ipsis fatentibus, asserentibus, religiosus fuit; & quod nos inde ex religionis objecto & cultûs ratione colligimus, Divinus; imò cultus Papæ à cultoribus manifestè modò ad duliam, modò ad hyperduliam, modò ad duliam & latriam simul referTur; quando jam olim complures in ipsa communione Romana Papæ adorationem cultum religiosum atque divinum esse, viderunt; (quæ argumenta prolixius deducta apud Celeb. Heidegger in Myst. Bab. T. I. Diss. X. Sect. II. n. 38. seqq. videri possunt;) quando (quod addimus) praxis & hic Theoria multò pejor, & ratione simplicium, ex propriis Pontificiorum hypothesibus, in ista adoratione, quę καὶ' ἐξοχὴν Italis talis dicitur, planè inexcusacusabilis est; quando, qui loco Papæ adoratur, Idolum constituitur; Sive jam sit Schismaticus, quales omnes Idola vocare solenne est; Ut Albertus Cranzius in Metrop. l. 9. c. 1. p. 271. hæc habet: Cardinales Gallici — cum suo Idolo (Clemente VII.) in Gallias redierunt, ubi summus Pontifex à Gallis appellatur &c. Sive nec charitate fundetur, nec scientia erigatur, qualis Arnulpho Rhemensi pud Bar. ad an. 992. n. 22. in Templo Dei tanquam statua, tanquam idolum est &c. sive tandem personam Papæ ad tempus edoctus gerat; Ut in Conclavi Urbani VI. Cardinalis de Ursinis hæc vel similia verba locutus: Domini mei, differamus istam electionem; ut possimus deludere istos de populo Romano, qui volunt Romanum, & vocemus ad nos unum fratrem minorem, eique imponamus cappam & mitram Papales, & fingamus, nos eum elegisse, & sic recedamus, & alium alibi eligemus: Isthoc responsi tulit à Lemovicensibus & aliis sequacibus Certè hoc non faciemus, quia nolumus populum facere Idololatram &c. In quo Conclavi tamen, electo jam Urbano VI. timentes Ultramontani, induxerunt Dominum S. Petri, ut contentaretur indui tanquam Papam ad placandum populum, sicque est inductus ut Papa, & populus tunc ei tanquam Papæ, credentes, eum esse Papam, reverentiam exhibuerunt; quando denique Christus & Petrus, quorum Vicarii & successores esse volunt, tam ab omni fastu civili alieni fuerunt, humiles & humilitatis suasores diligentissimi, & in cultu etiam civili facilis est ad Idololatriam Politicam, de qua Filesacus, Sorbonicus Doctor egregiè scripsit, μετάθεσις; concludere licet, Pontifices hic etiam Christi & Petri, aliorúmque Sanctorum hominum & Angelorum potiùs, quàm verò Hamanis, coram quo Mardochæus procidere noluit, timens, ne honorem Dei sui transferret ad hominem, & ne quenquam adoraret, excepto Deo suo. Addit. Esth. XIII. 12. 13. 14. & Herodis, qui populum sibi tanquam Deo acclamantem tulit, Act. XII. 22. 23. & insanientium gentilium Dominorum, divinos sibi honores deferri patientium, jubentium, vestigia premere debuisse, atque iis modo suprà memorato neglectis, non tantùm superbiam detestandam prodere, sed & semet in Idola erigere, atque adeò eorum adorationem omninò idololatricam, consequens hoc electionis eorum maximè vitiosum esse.
units.tr: IX. But what sort of adoration is this? And what sort of consequence of election is it? It is idolatrous adoration, the most vicious consequence of all. Nor do we rightly accuse the Papists of idolatry here, since it is clear that they give religious and divine worship to a creature. We admit that words and external rites are sometimes used of civil honour as well. But when adoration in the New Testament and among the ancients denotes only religious worship, then, as the Jesuit Pererius says, the Latin word for adoring is hardly in use (today), neither among theologians nor in the common speech of Christians, except in the worship of the true and only God. And it is above all in the worship of the Pope that it is used. It is one thing to adore something and to regard it as God. The more moderate Papists deny that holy images are adored by them, so that they may not seem to give divine honour to them. Others contend that all emperors, kings and other princes should be given the highest civil honour, but not adored; on the contrary, they say the worship of adoration must be paid to the Pope, though he is far inferior in political rank. Among Eastern peoples the rite of adoration, or civil bowing, has almost alone prevailed, while Westerners have been more sparing of these ceremonies, and among them adoration by prostration [συγκύνησις] was used only in sacred settings, and was neither admitted except by those whose minds the arrogance of tyranny had changed, nor offered except by those who were accustomed to flatter the more powerful in a servile manner. In the New Testament, Peter and the angel rejected adoration offered to them, though neither wanted it as to God. From this, Antoninus infers in Summa part 3, title 22, chapter 5, section 4, that the Pope is superior to the angels; and Augustinus de Ancona, in On Ecclesiastical Power, question 9, article 4, page 65, says that greater honour is given to the Pope than to the angels. They could draw the same conclusion with respect to Peter, and in the same way, arguing from fact to right, could prove that Nebuchadnezzar's statue, the Devil, and Antichrist, who is worshipped above every object of reverence, are superior to angels, indeed to the true God himself, whom many neglect. The Pope also claims divinity in other respects, and claims divine inspirations for himself; his worshippers promise that the one adored will grant them the greatest and even divine benefits. More than once his flatterers have let slip that he is to be adored as God. Altogether he is adored as Pro-God, Pro-Christ, Monarch of the Church, summit of religion, and yet that honour given to the Pope does not turn to the honour of God and Christ, since a legate cannot rightly receive the honour that is owed only to the one who sent him; but the Pope receives the honour of kissing his foot from one who represents the person of Christ in Palm Sunday, the honour that is owed to Christ as he is God. Some Papists themselves admit that he receives it, indeed a greater honour in the Mass, in the solemn procession and in the naming of his name. Paolo Sarpi, in his War of Paul V, book 2, page 24, notes that the papal nuncio, speaking before the Venetian Senate and feigning piety, uncovered his head when the name of our Lord the Pope was spoken, which he would not have done for God. Yet he is not Christ's legate, nor appointed by him, to be honoured in this way. In the adoration of the Pope, beating the breast and burning incense are used, besides the sitting on the altar mentioned above. The worship paid to the Pope is greater than the worship of saints and angels, and is not inferior to that of the Mother of God, the cross, the Eucharist, the image of Christ, relics, and that which they claim was once given to the Ark of the Covenant. All this worship, as they themselves admit and assert, is religious; and what we gather from the object of religion and the manner of worship is that it is divine. Indeed the worship of the Pope is clearly referred by his worshippers now to dulia, now to hyperdulia, now to dulia and latria at once. Many men even within the Roman communion have long seen that the adoration of the Pope is religious and divine worship. (These arguments, drawn out at greater length, can be found in the learned Heidegger, Mysterium Babylonis, volume 1, dissertation 10, section 2, numbers 38 ff.) And, as we add, the practice and theory here is much worse, and by the plain reasoning of simple people, from the Papists' own hypotheses, this adoration, which the Italians call by that name in a special sense, is utterly inexcusable. Whoever is adored in place of the Pope is made an idol, whether he is a schismatic, as it is customary to call all such idols; as Albertus Cranzius says in Metropolis book 9, chapter 1, page 271: The French cardinals returned to France with their idol (Clement VII), where he is called supreme Pontiff by the French, etc. Or whether he is one who is founded neither on charity nor raised up by knowledge, like the man whom Arnulf of Rheims described, in the temple of God as a statue, as an idol, etc. (Baronius, year 992, n. 22). Or finally whether he plays the part of the Pope for a time, as a cardinal did in the conclave of Urban VI, speaking these or similar words: My lords, let us postpone this election, so that we can deceive those people of Rome who want a Roman, and let us call to us one lesser brother, and put on him the papal cope and mitre, and pretend that we have chosen him, and so let us depart, and elect another elsewhere. The Limousin and other followers gave this answer: Certainly we will not do this, because we do not want to make the people idolaters, etc. Yet in that same conclave, after Urban VI had already been elected, the fearful Ultramontanes brought in the Lord of St Peter, so that he would be content to be dressed as Pope to placate the people; and so he was brought in as Pope, and the people, then believing him to be the Pope, showed reverence to him as Pope. Finally, Christ and Peter, whose vicars and successors they wish to be, were so far from all civil pomp, humble and most diligent advocates of humility, and it is easy to slide from civil worship into political idolatry, about which Filesac, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, has written excellently, metathesis. So we may conclude that these Popes, in this respect too, are rather like the followers of Christ and Peter, of other holy men and of angels, than like Haman, before whom Mordecai refused to bow down, fearing lest he should transfer the honour of his God to a man, and lest he should adore anyone except his God (Esther 13:12–14, Additions), and like Herod, who accepted the people shouting to him as to a god (Acts 12:22–23), and like the mad heathen lords who allowed divine honours to be paid to them and ordered that they be trodden upon. Those who neglect the custom just mentioned not only show a detestable pride, but also set themselves up as idols; and so their adoration is altogether idolatrous, and this consequence of their election is most vicious.

units.la: X. Quando verò dictis Scripturæ Psalm. LXXII. 11. Jesaj. XLV. 23. Jer. XLIX. 7. hanc adorationem Idolorum suorum paliare conantur, dictis illis, Christo Deo tributa creaturis meris vendicando, blasphemè abutuntur. Neque in aliis dictis fundata est, quàm in illo Dan.III.4.5.6. ubi de adoranda Nebucadnezaris statua agitur; Et in illo 2.Thess.II.4. ubi sermo est de illo, qui sese opponit & effert adversus, quicquid dicitur Deus, aut numen: adeò ut in Templo Dei tanquam Deus sedeat, præ se ferens, se esse Deum; Et in illo Apoc.XIII.11. 15. ubi dicitur, Bestiæ, quæ cornua duo similia Agni habeat, sed loquatur, ut Draco, datum esse, ut faciat, quicunque non adorârint imaginem bestiæ, ut occidantur; Et in similibus. Diabolicus adoratio hæc fœtus est, qui loquitur Johannes Gerson, consolatorius, Christianissimus Doctor vulgò vocatus serm.1. de Angelis, M. tanto studio ab hominibus extorsit, & extorquere non cessat, ut adoraretur, sicut Deus: immo ut extollatur super omne, quod dicitur Deus. Etiam homines utique mortales, id est, erumnis subditos hæc portentuosa rabies invasit. Patuit in Nabuchodonosor, in Cosdroe, & communiter in Persarum Principibus. Et verendum est, proh dolor, ne in Prelatos quosdam se hujusmodi insanie virus infuderit &c.
units.tr: X. But when they try to cloak this adoration of their idols with the words of Scripture (Ps. 72:11; Isa. 45:23; Jer. 49:7), they blasphemously abuse those words, claiming for mere creatures what belongs to Christ, who is God. Nor is the practice founded on any other texts than Dan. 3:4-6, which deals with the adoration of Nebuchadnezzar's statue; 2 Thess. 2:4, which speaks of him who opposes and exalts himself against everything called God or an object of worship, so that he sits in the temple of God as God, displaying that he is God; and Rev. 13:11, 15, where it is said of the beast which has two horns like a lamb but speaks like a dragon, that it was given power to cause whoever would not worship the image of the beast to be killed; and similar passages. This diabolical adoration is the offspring of what Johannes Gerson, the most consolatory and most Christian teacher, commonly so called, says in his first sermon on the angels: that it has been extorted from men, and never ceases to be extorted, with such zeal, that one should be adored as God, indeed exalted above everything called God. This monstrous frenzy has invaded even mortal men, that is, those subject to miseries. It was evident in Nebuchadnezzar, in Chosroes, and generally in the princes of the Persians. And it is to be feared, alas, lest the poison of this madness has poured itself into certain prelates, etc.

units.la: XI. Osculum pedis quod attinet specialiùs; frustrà ex Psal LXVIII.24.XCIX.4.5. Esa.LX.14. Matth.XXVIII.9. Luc.VII.38. XXIV.52. Deut.XXXIII.2. 3. quæ loca de Deo & Christo agentia pari temeritate ad Papam σρεξλγ̃σι, defendi, sine ulla refutatione liquet consideranti. Ut aliunde merito indignissimum idololatriæ suæ ritum derivent. Et alii quidem morem æmulatione gentilium, Divorum suorum pedes aut manus osculantium, introductum esse, non improbabiliter divinant; Alii eum à Regibus Persarum & Imperatoribus Romanis deducunt; Morem illum Lipsii Pontificii Elect. lib.II.6. judicio turpem & plusquam servilem; A Cajo Caligula maximè, in quo ritum Seneca paganus homo de Benef. l.II 12. ceu superbiam magnæ fortunæ & stultissimum malum exclamando d testatus est; Qui tamen semel tantùm supplici pedem osculandum præbuisse legitur, minùs in hisce Papâ insolens. Et quando tamen insolentiam ejus Maximinus junior & Diocletianus imitati sunt sæpiùs, contrà Maximinus senior & Trajanus ab ea alienissimi describuntur, quemadmodum etiam Imperatores Romani sequentes. Ut renovationem turpis & plùs quàm servilis ritùs in Occidente Papæ debeamus. Quos Cuspinianus etiam, Maximiliano Imp. à consiliis, de Diocletiano agens, sic exagitat: Divinos sibi (Diocletianus,) nquit, usurpavit honores, veluti in eo esset Cœlestis Majestas, voluit adorari more Regum Persarum, pedésq; exosculandos omnibus sine discrimine gentis exhibuit, idque edicto sanxit; Quemadmodum hodie nostri Sancti Pontifices faciunt, Caligulam imitantes, qui calceamenta auro auro, gemmis & margaritis exornavit. Quibus plane consentanea habet Aventinus Annal. Bojor. lib. 2. & quòd Pontifices Romani morem istum adorandi pertinacissimè æmulentur. Apud quem etiam Ludovicus Bavarus in Edicto, Comitiorum Reginoburgensium consensu vulgato, de Joh. XXII. queritur: Sathana spiritum sibi sumit, se similem Altissimo facit, se adorari, quod tamen Angelus sibi à Johanne fieri prohibuit, pedes sibi osculari, more Diocletiani atque Alexandri, crudelissimorum tyrannorum permittit. Cùm Christus manceps, Divinitatis Dominus, & Deus noster pedes comitum suorum, piscatorúmque, laverit. Qui contrà nullibi ejus pedes deosculati legúntur, quod Cardinales, Apostolorum, ut ajunt, successores, Papæ primò facere tenentur; ut illud, ita Joh. Stevanus de osc. ped. R. Pont. p.117. ineptit, Job. IX. oraculum haberet firmitatem; Sub quo curvantur, qui portant orbem. Pessimum autem est, quod Polydorus Vergilius de Invent. rer. l. 4. cap. 13. prioris originis intuitu dicit, Pontifices nempe, qui osculum suis pedibus sigi patiantur, sese quoque homines tantùm esse non perpendere, moréque illum à Romanis Pontificibus (Gentilibus) institutum, & antiquitùs à Deorum etiam cultoribus observatum, refert. Dignè scilicet post hos Romani Pontifices talia exigunt, id est, humilis Christi Vicarii, & quando olim pedibus Imperatorum advolvi necesse habuerunt, jam insigni metamorphosi Imperatores ad vilíssima pedum suorum oscula damnant; Imò nonnunquam ergo eosdem, vel colla eorum conculcando, vel coronas capitibus eorum impositas dejiciendo, ingentia in suis calcibus iniquitatis mysteria prodiderunt, atque superbiam, quà omnibus modis, S. Augustino in Psal. XLVII. 4. contrarii, Christianos pedibus suis subjiciunt; quam & produnt, crepidis suis crucis figuram (de qua Imperatoris Justiniani L. Unic. c. Nemini &c. Christiana constitutio: Cùm sit nobis cura diligens per omnia supremi Numinis religionem tueri; signum Salvatoris nemini licere vel in solo, vel in silice, vel in marmoribus humi positis (eadem autem fere ratio crepidarum Pontificiarum) insculpere vel pingere, sed quodcunque reperitur, tolli, gravíssimâ pœnâ multando eum, qui contrarium statutis nostris tentaverit, specialiter imperamus;) impressam gerentes; Cujus ineptum mysterium Jos. Stevanus l. c. p.110. sic prodit: Pontificis maximi pedibus crux est impressa, ut gressus nostros in viam pacis duceret atque muniret. Qui cùm totius gregis Christiani ductor atque præceptor sit, oportebat sanè, ne pedes aliquò allideret, neve errore aliquo devios traheret, ne temerè ipse Dux omnium lapsus, in gravíssimos erro-res res populum Christi præcipitem ageret. Ad quod Clar. Mayerus Comment. de Elect. R. Pont. p. 193. annotare voluit: Si quis cavillari vellet, posset regerere; Si idcò Pontificis pedes signo crucis muniantur, ne ad lapidem offendant, partes quoque eidem ad sedendum à natura tributas sacro signo esse præservandas, quod consimilis ratio & ipsa quoque ex Psalmo Davidico suppetere videatur, ne forte Pontifex aliquando sedeat in subselliis irrisorum. Ast ibi non esse posset, quemadmodum in crepidis, ad locum osculi demonstrandum. Vide de hoc pedes osculandi ritu, ejusque imposita necessitate præter alios etiam M. Ant. de Dom. Rep. Eccl. l. 4. c. 7. p. 422.
units.tr: XI. As for the kissing of the foot more specifically: the passages Ps. 68:24; Ps. 99:4-5; Isa. 60:14; Matt. 28:9; Luke 7:38; Luke 24:52; Deut. 33:2-3, which speak of God and Christ, are in vain cited by the Papists in defence of the proskynesis [προσκύνησις] of the Pope, with equal rashness; anyone who considers them will see this without any refutation. So they rightly derive the most unworthy rite of their idolatry from elsewhere. Some not improbably suppose that the custom, of kissing the feet or hands of their divinities, was introduced by emulation of the Gentiles; others derive it from the kings of the Persians and the Roman emperors. Lipsius, the Papist, in Elect. lib. II, 6, judges that custom shameful and more than servile, and it is chiefly traced to Caius Caligula, against whose rite the pagan Seneca, de Benef. l. II, 12, cried out as the arrogance of great fortune and a most foolish evil. Yet he is read as having offered his foot to be kissed by a suppliant only once, less insolent in this than the Pope. And when the younger Maximinus and Diocletian imitated his insolence more often, the elder Maximinus and Trajan are described as most remote from it, as also the Roman emperors who followed them. Thus we owe the renewal of this shameful and more than servile rite in the West to the Pope. Cuspinianus, councillor to the Emperor Maximilian, also castigates them thus, speaking of Diocletian: He, it says, assumed divine honours for himself, as if the heavenly majesty were in him; he wished to be adored after the manner of the kings of Persia, and offered his feet to be kissed by all people of every rank without distinction, and sanctioned this by edict; just as our holy Pontiffs do today, imitating Caligula, who adorned his shoes with gold, gems and pearls. Aventinus, Annal. Bojor. lib. 2, agrees plainly with these, and says that the Roman Pontiffs most stubbornly emulate that custom of adoration. There too Ludwig of Bavaria complains, in the edict on John XXII made public by the consent of the Diet of Regensburg: He takes to himself the spirit of Satan, makes himself like the Most High, allows himself to be adored, though an angel forbade John to do this, and allows his feet to be kissed after the manner of Diocletian and Alexander, most cruel tyrants. Yet Christ, the author, Lord of the Godhead, and our God, washed the feet of his companions and fishermen. On the contrary, nowhere is it read that they kissed his feet, which the Cardinals, as they say the successors of the Apostles, are first bound to do for the Pope. Joh. Stevanus, de osc. ped. R. Pont. p. 117, absurdly argues from Job 9, that the oracle might have firmness, under which those who bear the world are bowed. Worst of all is what Polydore Vergil, de Invent. rer. l. 4, cap. 13, says with regard to the earlier origin: that the Popes, who allow their feet to be kissed, do not consider that they are merely men too, and report that this custom was established by the Roman Pontiffs (pagans) and was observed of old even by worshippers of the gods. Worthily, then, the Roman Pontiffs demand such things, that is, the humble Vicar of Christ; and whereas once they were obliged to fall at the feet of emperors, now, by a remarkable metamorphosis, they condemn emperors to kiss their feet, the most vile of kisses. Indeed, sometimes by trampling on their necks, or by knocking down the crowns placed on their heads, they have displayed the vast mysteries of iniquity in their heels, and their arrogance, by which in every way, as Augustine says on Ps. 47:4, they subject Christians to their feet, which is contrary to them. They also betray it by bearing on their sandals the impressed figure of the cross (concerning which the Christian constitution of the Emperor Justinian, L. Unic. c. Nemini, says: Since it is our careful concern to preserve the religion of the supreme Deity in all things, we especially command that no one be permitted to carve or paint the sign of the Saviour, either on the ground, or on flint, or on marble placed on the ground (the reason for the Papal sandals is almost the same), but that whatever is found be removed, punishing most heavily the one who attempts something contrary to our statutes.) Joh. Stevanus, l. c. p. 110, reveals the absurd mystery of this thus: The cross is impressed on the feet of the highest Pontiff, so that it might lead and guard our steps in the way of peace. Since he is the leader and teacher of the whole Christian flock, it was surely necessary that he not strike his feet against anything, nor lead them astray by any error, lest the Leader of all, stumbling rashly into the most grievous errors, drive the people of Christ headlong. To which the illustrious Mayer, Comment. de Elect. R. Pont. p. 193, wished to add a note: If someone wished to cavil, he could retort: If the feet of the Pontiff are protected by the sign of the cross, lest they strike against a stone, then the parts also given to him by nature for sitting ought to be safeguarded by the sacred sign, since a similar reason seems to arise also from the Davidic Psalm, lest perhaps the Pontiff one day sit in the seat of the scornful. But this could not be done there, as it can on the sandals, to show the place for kissing. On this rite of kissing the feet, and the necessity imposed by it, see, besides others, also M. Ant. de Dom., Rep. Eccl. l. 4, c. 7, p. 422.

units.la: XII. Portandi extra casum necessitatis ritum, haud magis apte ex Scriptura probant.
units.tr: XII. The ritual of being carried, outside cases of necessity, is not proved any more aptly from Scripture.

units.la: Quòd enim Esaj. XLIX. 22. verbis illis: Et afferent filios tuos in ulnis, & filias super humeros portabunt; præditum eum esse, Stevanus, Diana, aliique pertendunt, frivolum planè est; Quando ibi de vocatione Gentium, promptáque Filiorum & Filiarum per parentes ad Ecclesiam adductione sermonem esse & textus loquitur, & non inepti in Papatu Doctores fatentur. Agitur ibi etiam de filiis, non de Pontificibus Patribus, (nisi sint filii perditionis 2. Thess. II. 3.) de filiis in ulnis afferendis, quales si Pontifices sint, cur non ita afferantur, mirari licet; Et si filię super humeros portandæ, ad Papas hoc, Johannâ exceptâ, planè non spectat. Pro n convenientius multò locos Jes. XLVI. 6. 7. Jer. X. 5. Amos. V. 26. Act. VII. 43 Baruch. VI. 3. allegâssent; Et insuper Canonem V. Concilii Bracarensis III. A. Chr. 675. celebrati, quo fastus quorundam Episcoporum, qui se portari voluerunt, ceu detestanda præsumptio pulsatur. Rectius omninò sic ad exempla Idolorum, de quibus loca citata agunt, & quæ à cultoribus portari solebant, atque adhuc à Mexicanis, Japonicis, Sinensibus, aliis solenniter portari solent, origo gestationis Pontificiæ referretur; Vel cum Polydoro Vergilio de Invent. rer. l. 4. c. 10. ad morem prædivitum ac primariorum virorum apud Romanos lectică à servis gestatâ vehi solitorum; quorum tamen fastum Pontifices tantum superarent, quantum Imperator, vel alius Princeps servo est major; Vel cum Diana Resol. 10. p. 11. ad pompam Regis apum graphicè simul cum pompa Pontificis descriptam apud Virgilium l. 4. Georg.
units.tr: For that Stevanus, Diana and others maintain that Isaiah 49:22 (And they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders) hints at this is entirely frivolous. The text speaks of the calling of the Gentiles and of the ready bringing of sons and daughters to the Church by their parents, as the context shows and as the learned teachers within the Papacy themselves admit. The passage also concerns sons, not Popes as fathers (unless they are sons of perdition, 2 Thess. 2:3), and it concerns sons to be carried in arms. If Popes are such sons, one may wonder why they are not carried in that way. And if daughters are to be carried upon shoulders, this does not apply to the Popes at all, except to Joan. They would have done far better to cite Isaiah 46:6-7, Jeremiah 10:5, Amos 5:26, Acts 7:43 and Baruch 6:3. Besides, there is the fifth canon of the Third Council of Braga, held in 675, in which the pride of certain bishops who wished to be carried is condemned as a detestable presumption. It would be far more fitting to trace the origin of the Papal carrying to the idols, of which the cited passages speak, which were customarily carried by their worshippers and are still solemnly carried by the Mexicans, the Japanese, the Chinese and others. Or one could follow Polydore Vergil (On the Invention of Things, bk. 4, ch. 10), who says it was the custom among the Romans for the very wealthy and leading men to be borne in litters carried by slaves. Yet the Popes would surpass that pride as far as an emperor or some other prince is greater than a slave. Or one could follow Diana (Resolution 10, p. 11), who vividly describes, alongside the Papal pomp, the pomp of the king of the bees in Virgil (Georgics bk. 4):

units.la: ——— Illum admirantur, & omnes Circumstant fremitu denso, stipántque frequentes, Et sæpe attollunt humeris ——— Sed his ad Apiarium Romanum remissis, ad alia Electionis Pontificum Romanorum consequentia Ceremonialia pergimus:
units.tr: They marvel at him, and all stand round him with a dense murmur, crowding in great numbers, and often they lift him on their shoulders. But having sent these matters back to the Roman beehive, let us proceed to the other ceremonies that follow the election of the Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: XIII. Post congratulationem adoratione fieri solitam electum, sic pergit Sacr. Cerim. l. 1. c. 2. exuunt crocea, & caputio parvo, & sic cum suo rocchetto faciunt illum sedere super ornata sede, quam locant ante mensam, ubi priores sedebant. Imponunt illi angulum Piscatoris &c. Et paulo post: Ducitur electus in sacrarium, & a Diaconis Cardinalibus exuitur vestimentis communibus, quae ex antiqua consuetudine cedunt Clericis cerimoniarum, induiturque Papali habitu, toga scilicet lana albi coloris: caligis rubeis aurea cruce ornatis, cingulo rubeo cum aureis fibulis, birreto etiam rubeo, & denum mundo nitidoque rocchetto, deinde imponunt ei amictum; albam longam, cingulum, & stolam ornatam cum perlis pendentem a collo, si est Presbyter aut Episcopus; Si autem esset Diaconus, stola sit super humerum sinistrum in formam Diaconi, si sit Subdiaconus, vel infra, non ponatur ei stola &c. Et paulo post: Imponunt novo Pontifici pluviale rubeum preciosum, & mitram auro & gemmis ornatam &c. Haec sunt, quae de vestibus Pontificis habet, corona excepta, quam paulo post specialius considerabimus.
units.tr: XIII. After the congratulation, which is customarily made by adoration, the elected man is treated as follows, according to the Sacred Ceremonies, bk. 1, ch. 2: They take off his saffron-coloured garments and small cap, and, in his rochet, they make him sit on an adorned chair, which they place before the table where the former ones used to sit. They put on him the fisherman's ring, etc. And a little later: The elected man is led into the sacristy, and the cardinal deacons strip him of his ordinary garments, which by ancient custom go to the clerks of ceremonies, and he is dressed in papal attire, namely a woollen toga of white colour, red hose adorned with golden crosses, a red girdle with golden clasps, also a red biretta, and a clean, bright rochet. Then they put on him an amice, a long alb, a cincture, and a stole adorned with pearls hanging from the neck, if he is a priest or a bishop. If he were a deacon, the stole is to be placed over the left shoulder in the manner of a deacon; if he is a subdeacon or lower, no stole is put on him, etc. And a little later: They put on the new Pontiff a precious red cope, and a mitre adorned with gold and gems, etc. These are the things it lists concerning the Pontiff's vestments, except the crown, which we shall consider more specifically shortly.

units.la: XIV. Patet ex his, vestitus Pontificii partem maximam rubri coloris esse. Ruber color, inquit Author idem l. 3. f. 5. c. 5. praecipue ad Papam pertinet. Sed & l. 3. f. 4. testatur, in nocte Nativitatis uti solere Pontificem cappa purpurea, pellibus armillinis duplicata, quam primus Bonifacius IX. invenerit. Addit, duobus Papam uti coloribus albo & rubro, utroque in pluviali &c. Ita rubro colore Idola vestiebantur. Atque, ut Simon Majolus Dier. Canic. Tom. II. p. 42. ex variis Authoribus ostendit, coelestibus Diis purpurei colores placuerunt. Baronius ad an. 324. n. 79. Privilegia Gentilium Sacerdotum, qui purpuram induebant, Christianis Sacerdotibus tributa esse asserit. In ficta Donatione Constantini Papis chlamys purpurea, atque tunica coccinea; & omnia Imperialia indumenta concediuntur. Paschali II. authori alii referunt, quod Papa electus coccinea chlamyde statim ornatur, atque sic in dignitate confirmatur. Sed & Pius II. Perusiam equo candidissimo vectus, duodecim eodem candore purpurâ stratis, sine sessore, frœnis aureis praecedentibus, Magistratibus purpuream & auro intextam umbellam, sub qua ipse candida sindone, stola aurea & purpureo superbus galero vehebatur, praeferentibus, Wolphio Memor. Lect. Tom. II. p. 457. narrante, ingressus est. Vide de hoc colore purpureo, quae Disser. IV. Sect. 2. n. 63.
units.tr: XIV. From these things it is clear that the greater part of the Papal vestment is of red colour. Red colour, says the same author (bk. 3, sec. 5, ch. 5), belongs especially to the Pope. But he also testifies (bk. 3, sec. 4) that on the night of the Nativity the Pope usually wears a purple cape, doubled with ermine furs, which Boniface IX first devised. He adds that the Pope uses two colours, white and red, both in the cope, etc. Thus idols were clothed in red colour. And, as Simon Maiolus (Dies Caniculares, vol. 2, p. 42) shows from various authors, purple colours pleased the heavenly gods. Baronius (at the year 324, n. 79) asserts that the privileges of the pagan priests who wore purple were transferred to the Christian priests. In the forged Donation of Constantine, a purple cloak and a scarlet tunic, and all imperial garments are granted to the Popes. Other writers report of Paschal II that the elected Pope is at once adorned with a scarlet cloak, and thus confirmed in his dignity. But also Pius II, as Wolf (Memorable Readings, vol. 2, p. 457) relates, entered Perugia mounted on a most white horse, with twelve horses covered in the same white and purple cloth, without a rider, with golden bridles going before, while the magistrates carried over him a purple umbrella woven with gold, beneath which he himself was borne, proud in a white linen cloth, a golden stole and a purple hat. On this purple colour, see what we said at Dissertation IV, Section 2, n. 63.

units.la: 64. 65. 64. 65. diximus. Vide etiam Apoc. XVII. 4. ubi meretrix purpura coccóque induta sistitur ; Nec non cap. XVII. 16. ubi inter merces Babylonicas byssus & purpura, & sericum & coccum memorantur.
units.tr: 64. 65. 64. 65. we have said. See also Revelation 17:4, where the harlot is presented clothed in purple and scarlet; and also Revelation 18:16, where among the Babylonian wares fine linen and purple, silk and scarlet are mentioned.

units.la: XV. Cæterum quando Urbanus VIII. recens electus hoc vestitu, & quidem subtilissimo Rocchetto ornatus fuit, Authore Conclavis narrante, ad circumstantes conversus dixit, che quella sot-tilissima tela &c. illam subtilissimam telam ponderosiorem sibi esse, quàm ut verbis illud exprimere queat; Sic miserum Pontificum statum innuens, de quo etiam infrà pluribus agendi locus erit.
units.tr: XV. Moreover, when Urban VIII, newly elected, was adorned with this vestment, and indeed with a very fine rochet, the author of the Conclave relates that he turned to those standing around and said: that fine cloth, etc., that is, that this very fine cloth was heavier for him than he could express in words. Thus he hinted at the wretched state of the Popes, of which there will be occasion to speak at more length below.

units.la: XVI. Dictum est, vestes electi communes ex antiqua consuetudine cedere Clericis ceremoniarum. Cedunt etiam Conclavistis in genere, quæcunque in cella sua habet; Quam proin electione cognita statim spoliant. Hinc qui de electione sua præsumunt, sibi charissima & arcana in cellas alias jam ante electionem transferri curant. Hinc etiam Conclavistæ Cardinalis illius, qui eligi debet, argentum suum in aliam cellam transferunt. Triste autem fuit, quod in Conclavi Clementis VIII. Cardinali S. Severinæ accidisse legitur. De ejus electione jam suprà egimus; Antagonistarum stratagematibus irrita facta est; In scrutinio defecerunt vota, postquam jam ut Pontifex salutatus esset, numerum habuissent, ei Imperium & Regna commendâssent, multa ab eo petiissent. Cardinales eo solo in Capella relicto, discesserunt; solus in locum suum redire necesse habuit; sed cameram gressus eum scopis mundatam invenit; Quod ita ejus afflictionem auxit, ut lachrymas tum fudisse dicatur; Solatio autem fuit, quòd ei statim restituta sunt ablata omnia.
units.tr: XVI. It has been said that the ordinary garments of the elected man, by ancient custom, go to the clerks of ceremonies. Also whatever the Conclavists in general have in their cell goes to them; so as soon as the election is known, they strip the cell. Hence those who presume upon their election arrange for their most precious and private things to be transferred to other cells even before the election. Hence also the Conclavists of the cardinal who is to be elected transfer his silver to another cell. But it was a sad affair, which is read to have happened to Cardinal of Santa Severina in the Conclave of Clement VIII. We have already treated his election above; it was made void by the stratagems of his opponents. In the scrutiny the votes failed him, although after he had been saluted as Pope, had obtained the number of votes, had been committed the empire and kingdoms, and had been asked for many favours by others. The cardinals departed, leaving him alone in the Chapel; he alone had to return to his place. But he found the chamber swept with brooms. This so increased his distress that he is said to have shed tears at that time. Some comfort, however, was that all that had been taken away was at once restored to him.

units.la: XVII. Post vestium quarundam depositionem exquirunt, quo nomine electus velit nuncupari. Nempe à longo tempore electi Pontifices nomina sua mutare solent. De cujus moris origine non inter authores convenit. Platinæ in Sergio II. sunt, qui Sergium primo quidem os porci appellatum fuisse dicant, & ob turpitudinem cognomenti, Sergii nomen sumpsisse, eámque consuetudinem ad nostros manâsse, ut qui Pontifices crearentur, suo omisso, majorum nomina sibi inderent, licèt ab omnibus non sit observatum. Verùm ad ista Platinæ verba annotat Onuphrius: Quæ hîc Platina ex Martino tradit, Sergium II. primum fuisse, qui nomen mutaverit, apud neminem veterum auctorum inveni, immo ex Anastasio Bibliothecario, qui hoc tempore vixit, contrarium magis elicitur, eum scilicet etiam ante Pontificatum Sergium vocitatum esse. Fortè Sergii praenomen semper habuit, Osporci vero cognomen; Pontifex vero factus, cognomen, praenomine tantum retento, omisit. Sed ista nec sic concinnata mihi quadrant. Joannem XII. ego primum inveni, qui priscum nomen Papa creatus mutarit, cum ante Pontificatum Octavianus diceretur, ut infra ostendam. Infra autem & ad Joannem XII. Plat. XIII. ostendit: Joannem hunc — primum esse inveni, qui nomen in Pontificatu mutarit. Nam cum antea Octavianus vocaretur, ut Guillelmus Bibliothecarius scribit, gentili nomine omisso, tanquam parum majestati & religioni Pontificiae idoneo, se Joannem appellavit. Cujus exemplum sequentes Pontifices, qui deforme & parum conveniens tanto magistratui nomen habuere, sensim & paulatim sequuti, levem consuetudinem tanquam in legem perpetuam transtulerunt. Caeterum hanc rem Romani Pontifices, & maxime ex Germania lecti, Bruno, Gerebertus, Suidegerus, Poppo, alius Bruno, Geberardus, Fridericus, Gerardus, Cadolus, Anselmus, Hildebrandus, & similes maxime confirmarunt, barbarorum nominum deformitate commoti. Baronius vero de hisce ita judicat ad an. 844. 1. Quos delectat fabulas verus intexere, hunc primum fuisse tradunt Romanum Pontificem, qui creatus Papa, nomen sibi mutavit; eo quod nomen indecens tanto Sacerdotio visus esset se habere. Sed scias, id factum in Sergio III. neque id accidisse ob turpitudinem nominis, sed reverentiae causa: cum enim ille Petrus vocaretur, indignum putavit, Principem eodem se vocari nomine, quo Christus primum ejus Sedis Pontificem Apostolorum ex Simone Petrum nominaverat. Verum id factum primum ab Octaviano, qui vocatus est Joannes XII. alii tradunt, ut suo loco inferius dicetur. Dicit inferius de Joanne ad an. 955. 4. Hic autem revera primus inventus, qui mutavit sibi nomen, ut qui ex Octaviano voluerit nominari Joanns, pro mutata, non exuta tyrannide: nam qui dictus est a patre ob temporale Urbis dominium Octavianus, ob spirituale, nomen Joannes appellari idcirco voluit, vel quod eo nomine ejus patruus, Joannes XI. Papa sit appellatus, vel ut in nomine saltem bene posset audire in adulatoriis acclamationibus, quibus male usurpatum proferri soleret sacrum illud eloquium (Joan. I.) Fuit homo missus a Deo, cui nomen erat Joannes. Sed ad an. 1009. n. 3. verbis Dithmari l. 6. prope finem de Sergio IV. dicit; qui vocabatur Bucca porci. Ad an. 1012. vero ex ejusdem Epitaphio verba haec quoque affert:
units.tr: XVII. After the removal of certain garments they ask by what name the elected man wishes to be called. For indeed for a long time elected Popes have been accustomed to change their names. Authors do not agree on the origin of this custom. Platina, in Sergius II, says there are those who report that Sergius was at first called Hog's Snout, and that, because of the baseness of that nickname, he took the name Sergius; and that this custom spread to our people, so that those who were created Popes, setting aside their own name, took the names of their predecessors, although it was not observed by everyone. But Onuphrius annotates these words of Platina: What Platina here relates from Martin, that Sergius II was the first to change his name, I have found in no ancient author. Indeed, from Anastasius the librarian, who lived at this time, the opposite is rather deduced, namely that he was called Sergius even before his papacy. Perhaps he always had the forename Sergius, but the surname Hog's Snout; but once made Pope, he dropped the surname, retaining only the forename. But these explanations do not fit together well for me. I first found John XII, who, once created Pope, changed his former name, when he was called Octavian before his papacy, as I shall show below. Below, too, Platina in the life of John XII shows: I found that this John was the first to change his name in the papacy. For although he was previously called Octavian, as William the librarian writes, he dropped his family name as too unfitting for the majesty and religion of the Papacy, and called himself John. The following Popes, who had a name that was ugly and not fitting for so great an office, followed his example, and gradually, step by step, they turned this light custom into a perpetual law. Moreover, the Roman Popes, and chiefly those elected from Germany, namely Bruno, Gerebert, Suidger, Poppo, another Bruno, Gebhard, Frederick, Gerard, Cadolus, Anselm, Hildebrand and similar men, greatly confirmed this practice, moved by the ugliness of barbarous names. Baronius, however, judges these matters thus at the year 844, n. 1: Those who delight to weave true tales say that this was the first Roman Pontiff who, when created Pope, changed his name, because the name seemed unbecoming for so great a priesthood. But know that this happened with Sergius III, and not because of the baseness of the name, but out of reverence: since he was called Peter, he thought it unworthy to be called by the same name as the Prince, whom Christ had named Peter from Simon, the first Apostolic Pontiff of that See. But it was first done by Octavian, who was called John XII, as others relate, as will be said in its place below. He says further below, on John at the year 955, n. 4: Yet this man was in truth the first found to change his name, since he who was called Octavian by his father, on account of the temporal dominion of the City, wished to be called John for the spiritual [authority], either because his uncle John XI had been called Pope by that name, or so that at least in name he might be able to hear, in the flattering acclamations, that sacred saying (John 1), which was commonly and wrongly applied to him: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. But at the year 1009, n. 3, on the words of Thietmar, book 6, near the end, concerning Sergius IV, he says that he was called Hog's Snout. At the year 1012 he also brings forward these words from the epitaph of the same man:

units.la: Post summum ducitur ad solium,
units.tr: After the highest office he is led to the throne,

units.la: In quo mutato permansit nomine praesul
units.tr: In which, the name changed, the prelate remained

units.la: Sergius ex Petro, sic vocitatus erat.
units.tr: Sergius, from Peter, as he was called.

units.la: XVIII. Mirum, quòd non à Petro, quem primum Papam fingunt, nominis mutari soliti originem deducant communiter, qui tamen ex mutatione, quam jactant, nominis Petri peculiarem prærogativam Pontificiam cudunt; quamvis non tam Petri nomen mutatum, quàm cognomen, & quidem jam ante collatam, vel promissam dignitatem Monarchicam, neque etiam soli inter Apostolos additum fuerit? Mirum haud minùs, cùm tot nomina tot assumserint, nullum Pontificem recens electum Petri nomine vocari voluisse; mirum adhuc magis, Sergium, qui Baronio modò tertius, modò quartus est, judicio ejus, sed cui contradixit in suprà allatis, primum, qui nomen mutárit, sic & Johannem XIV. Benedictum XIII. (hinc Gregorio XII. Anti-Papæ Ἀντιπάπας, vel quia electionem damnans nomen quoque non mutandum fuisse censuit, vocitatum; ) imò etiam non ita pridem defunctum Alexandrum VIII. aliàs Petrum Ottobonum, cùm antea Petri vocati fuissent, dignitate Pontificia assumptâ, Sergium, Johannem, Benedictum, Alexandrum, deinceps appellari maluisse; Cùm tamen & Platinæ & Onuphrii & Baronii jam jam citata verba illud docent, deforme, saltem parùm conveniens tanto magistratui nomen mutari solere; Ast quodnam minùs deforme, & magis magistratui conveniens nomen esse potuit, nomine Principis Apostolorum, primi Papæ, & quod ex illorum hypothesibus Papæ facti demum acceperunt? Factum illud, ita nobis occurrit Baronius l. c. reverentiæ causâ— & quòd indignum se putavit eo nomine vocari, quo Christus primum——nominaverat. Sed annon mira hæc, Baroni! modestia? Et quam forte non imitatus fuisses, Papa factus, qui tuum Clementem VIII. Petrum semper appellásti, tuopte judicio adulator, eíque admittenti immodestiæ occasionem præbens. Miram modestiam voco, quòd Apostoli nomen usurpare veriti sunt, Dei Opt. Max. nomina & axiomata dolorum ad instar sustinentes, & quòd indignos se nomine Petri putárunt, non indignos dignitate, impares nomini, pares oneri! Petri vocari noluerunt, sed esse, Vicarii Petri, Successores Petri, sibi tribuentes omnia Petri, potestatem omninò æqualem? Petri vocari noluerunt, Episcopi Romani, sed Albanus, sed locorum aliorum; non indigni sunt sacerdotes, imò plebeii infimi, sunt Pontifices summi! Sed quàm verè vereor, & nomine & onere, & officio & dignitate planè indignos, nec nomine, nec omine, vel re Petros esse, quod & Dissert. III. ostensum dedimus, & am-
units.tr: XVIII. It is strange that they commonly derive the custom of changing names not from Peter, whom they imagine to have been the first Pope, even though they coin a peculiar Papal prerogative from the so-called change of Peter's name. Yet perhaps it was not so much Peter's name that was changed as a surname, and one that had been given before the monarchical dignity was conferred or promised, and not to him alone among the Apostles. It is no less strange that, though they have assumed so many names, no newly elected Pope has wished to be called by the name of Peter. It is stranger still that Sergius, who by Baronius's judgement is now the third, now the fourth, but whom Baronius contradicts in the passages cited above, was the first to change his name. So too John XIV, Benedict XIII (hence called anti-pope to Gregory XII, [Ἀντιπάπας], either because he condemned the election and thought the name ought not to be changed either), and even Alexander VIII, who lately died, formerly Peter Ottoboni: when earlier Popes had been called Peter, these men, on assuming the Papal dignity, preferred to be called Sergius, John, Benedict, Alexander. Yet the words of Platina, Onuphrius and Baronius just cited teach that it is customary to change the name, because a name unsightly, or at least not very fitting for so great a magistracy. But what name could be less unsightly and more fitting to the magistracy than the name of the Prince of the Apostles, the first Pope, which they themselves received on their own hypotheses when made Popes? That deed, so Baronius puts it to us, l. c., for reverence's sake, and because he thought himself unworthy to be called by that name by which Christ had first named [him]. But is this not a remarkable modesty, Baronius! And perhaps you would not have imitated it, had you been made Pope, you who always called your Clement VIII Peter, an adulator by your own judgement, providing him with an occasion of immodesty in admitting it. I call it a remarkable modesty that the Apostles were afraid to take the name, bearing the names and titles of God, Best and Greatest, as if they were burdens of sorrow; and that they thought themselves unworthy of the name of Peter, not unworthy of the dignity, unequal to the name, equal to the burden! Did they refuse to be called Peter, yet want to be Vicars of Peter, Successors of Peter, claiming for themselves all that was Peter's, a power wholly equal to his? They refused to be called Peter, Bishop of Rome, but they are Alban, or of other places. They are not unworthy priests, but lowly commoners; they are the highest Pontiffs! But I truly fear that, both in name and burden, in office and dignity, they are wholly unworthy, neither Peters in name, nor by omen, nor in reality, as we showed in Dissertation III., and am-

units.la: Annotationes ad ea, quæ in investigatione illa reperta sunt; ampliùs, respectu constantiæ in confitendo, atque ædificationis in Christo Petra, ostendi posset; atque adeò solâ indignitatis suæ conscientiâ, & ne à Petris Petrina expectentur, Petros vocari nolle, dignitatis plùs quàm Petrinæ usurpatores, sic contrà successionem quoque suam testantes, & quòd (quam causam Molinæus de Nov. Pap. L. 1. c.37. assignat) vita sua exemplo Petrino minimè omnium respondeat, & quòd, ne, compellatione istâ acceptatâ, eò magis Petrinum illud: sit tecum pecunia tua in perditionem: piis fraudibus divitibus eò sæpiùs occurrat, timeant, vel quòd ex prophetia Malachiæ Hiberni, qui Petrum II. (rectè ob immodestiam) ultimum Papam fore prædixit, pertimescant; Quos tamen in nominum mutatione mystica, ejus, quam ipsimet ostendunt, origo, sive jam à Sergio II. vel III. vel IV. quorum aliquem os porci, vel Buccam porci dictum fuisse dicta arguunt, sive à Johanne XII. quem bipedum nequissimum ipsi etiam vocant, petatur, parùm certè commendat; maximè quando tanquam in legem perpetuam transiit; Haud certè magis illa origo commendat, quàm si à veteribus Babylonis Regibus, juxta Scaligerum de Emend. temp. l. 6. p. 580. nomina in accessu ad imperium mutare solitis, ut Bel-adan in imperio Nabonassar ex. gr. vocatus fuit, eam repetere atque ceu novi Babylonii dicere vellent:
units.tr: Annotations on those things found in that investigation could be shown further, with respect to constancy in confessing and to edification in Christ the Rock. And so, from the sole consciousness of their unworthiness, and so that Petrine things may not be expected from them, they are unwilling to be called Peters. They are usurpers of more than Petrine dignity, thus testifying also against their own succession. And they fear, either because (a reason Molinaeus assigns in de Nov. Pap. L. 1. c. 37.) their life by its example least of all corresponds to Peter's, or lest, having accepted this designation, they should the more often meet with that Petrine saying, let your money perish with you, through pious frauds on the rich; or because, from the prophecy of Malachy the Irishman, who foretold that Peter II (rightly, because of immodesty) would be the last Pope, they dread it. Yet the origin of this mystical change of name, which they themselves show, is sought either from Sergius II, III or IV, one of whom they argue was called pig's mouth or pig's cheek, or from John XII, whom they themselves call the most wicked of bipeds. This certainly commends it little, especially since it has passed as a perpetual law. That origin commends it no more than if one were to derive it from the ancient kings of Babylon, who, according to Scaliger de Emend. temp. l. 6. p. 580., were accustomed to change their names on accession to the empire, as Bel-adan, for example, was called under Nabonassar, and wished to repeat it, as if they were new Babylonians, saying:

units.la: Magnos magna decent: Papas sic nomina Regum.
units.tr: Great names befit the great: thus the names of kings for Popes.

units.la: XIX. Transiit consuetudo tanquam in legem perpetuam, sed tanquam.
units.tr: XIX. The custom passed as a perpetual law, but as if.

units.la: Atque nonnulli eam haud observâsse leguntur. Quales post cœptum morem fuerunt Clemens V. Adrianus VI. Marcellus II. (qui de mutando nomine compellatus: Marcellus eram, ero Marcellus: nec nomen mutabit, neque mores meos Pontificatus; respondisse fertur;) & alii. Sed & duo priores minùs sedi Romanæ commodi fuerunt, & tertio brevis 22. dierum duntaxat Pontificatus ob intermissam nominis mutationem obtigisse dicitur.
units.tr: And some are read not to have observed it. Such after the custom began were Clement V, Adrian VI and Marcellus II, who, when urged to change his name, is reported to have replied: I was Marcellus, I shall be Marcellus; neither the name nor my ways will the Papacy change. And others. But the first two were less advantageous to the Roman See, and the third is said to have had a brief pontificate of only 22 days, because he omitted the change of name.

units.la: XX. Varia autem in nominis mutatione respici solent.
units.tr: XX. In changing the name, various considerations are usually taken into account.

units.la: Et vel Præceptoris, vel Creatoris, vel Patroni, vel Cardinalis Nepotis, qui electionem dirigit, vel Papæ ex eadem regione, civitate, familia, vel, ut vocant, Religione, vel Papæ, quem electus præ aliis felicem censet, & imitari cupit, vel virtutis præ aliis affectatæ, vel aliorum, ratio habetur. Quomodo Joannes XII. quem primum nomen mutâsse volunt, Scripturæ loco abusus fuerit, non à Deo missus, à Patre malis artibus, ipsismet narrantibus, intrusus, suprà ex Baronio audivimus. Singulare quoque illud est, quòd, Platina in FormoFormoso referente, parùm abfuit, quin Paulus II. Venetus ejus tempe-state Formosi nomen (ut fit) sibi inderet, quòd id nomen ei maximè con-venire videretur, propter proceritatem corporis & majestatem. Quò mi-nùs autem id faceret, deterruere eum Cardinales quidam historiæ non igna-ri, ne post mortem id accideret, quod olim Formoso. Tulit id agrè Paulus, quia nil ei praeter hoc nomen ad summam felicitatem deesse videbatur. Quo-modo quidem illi simplicem superstitionem, hic vanitatem ma-gnam utrinque prodiderunt. Vanitatem hic etiam patriæ respe-ctu prodidisse videtur, dum, priori nomine rejecto, Marcus vocari voluit; Sed nec nomen illud posterius Cardinalibus placuit; quasi verò Papa non habeat nomen sibimet imponendi facultatem; Con-senserunt tamen tandem in illud Pauli II. Pauli igitur esse audent, qui non Petri? Non autem mira videri debet ista Cardinalium in admittendo novo Pauli II. nomine difficultas, quando eandem Cosmus de Sulmone, qui Clemens audire praeoptaverat, Innocen-tii nomen potiùs admittere coactus, ob invisa tunc Clementium nomina, expertus esse legitur. Quin ipsos etiam Electores Grego-rii VII. & Urbani VI. nomina imposuisse reperimus, exiguâ certè cum superioritate Pontificia (quando superiorum est nomina in-dendi potestas) convenientiâ.
units.tr: Regard is commonly given to a teacher, a creator (the one who ordained him), a patron, a cardinal nephew who directs the election, or a pope from the same region, city, family, or, as they call it, religious order. It may also be a pope whom the one elected judges happier than others and wishes to imitate, or a virtue he prizes above others, or other people's names. How John XII, whom they say first changed his name, abused a Scripture passage, having been thrust in not by God but by his father through wicked arts, as they themselves relate, we have heard above from Baronius. This too is remarkable: Platina, reporting in FormoFormoso, says that Paul II, a Venetian, at that time almost took the name Formosus for himself, as people do, because that name seemed to suit him best on account of his tall stature and majesty. What stopped him from doing so were some cardinals, not ignorant of history, who warned him that what had happened to Formosus might happen after his death. Paul took this badly, since nothing seemed to him to be lacking for his supreme happiness except this name. Both showed their own kind of folly: the one simple superstition, the other great vanity. Here he also seems to have shown vanity out of regard for his homeland, when, rejecting the former name, he wished to be called Mark. But the cardinals did not like this latter name either, as if the pope did not have the power to impose a name on himself. In the end, however, they agreed on the name Paul II. Do they then dare to be of Paul and not of Peter? This difficulty of the cardinals in admitting the new name of Paul II should not seem strange, since Cosmas of Sulmona, who had wished to be called Clement, is recorded to have been forced to take the name Innocent instead, because the names Clement were then hated. We also find that the electors themselves imposed the names of Gregory VII and Urban VI, though this agreement with papal superiority is certainly slight, since it is the superior who has the power of naming.

units.la: XXI. Nomina sunt egregia! Sed an conveniunt illis no-mina sumpta sibi? Raro. De Johanne XII. mutationis primo au-thore supra Baronii testimonium attulimus, quòd cum nomine mutârit, non exuerit tyrannidem, & nomine saltem bene audire voluerit. Eadem aliorum mens est & fuit. Primus honos, inquit Polydorus Vergilius, Scriptor jam ante Reformationem Pontificius, de Invent. rer. l. 4. c. 10. p. 342. Romano Pontifici habetur, ut si minùs pulchro hone-stetur nomine, ei statim creato licear illud mutare. Verbi gratiâ, non extra jocum dictum sit, si homo maleficus antea forte fuerit, ut Bonifacius ap-pelletur; si timidus, Leo; si rusticus, Urbanus; si improbus, Innocentius; si fe-rox, Clemens; si male audierit, Benedictus; ut saltem nomine Pontifex sit ornamento dignitati. Addit Laur. Bank, in Roma Triumphante, c. 9. p. 155. Si ubique succubuerit, Victor; si omnis nequitiæ Sacerdos, Pius; si populum suppresserit, Nicolaus; si tristis, Hilarius; si fortunæ ludibriis ex-positus, Felix; si faciem simia habuerit similem, Formosus; si semper torvus, Gelasius. Atque jam Differt. VII. de Piis vidimus. Sed & suo jam tempore Imperator Conradinus, rectiùs Conradus, in Epistola de injuriis sibi per Pontifices Romanos inlatis ad status Imperii missa ar-que que à Goldasto constitutionibus Imperialibus inserta, queri potuit, Urbanum non urbanè se tractâsse, Clementem non clementiam, sed inclementiam operatum esse. Amant antiqua nomina, non fidem, non mores antiquos; nomina pulchra, fœda tamen patrantes; atque adeò singulis occinere licet: Diceris vivere, sed mortuus es, Apoc. III.1. Ovina sub pelle lupus, Angelus Satanæ, sed transformatus in Angelum lucis, sub nomine virtutis vitiorum servus? Amant nomina alia, alii ac planè jam mutati videri volentes. Sic ex ipsorum mente Toftatus Abulensis in 4. Reg. c. 25. qu. 15. primam transnominationis Pontificiæ causam facit; Quia nomen imponitur, & tamen qui efficitur summus Pontifex, prius erat ut homo privatus & cùm efficitur Pontifex, est ut gerens vices Dei in terris, ideò alius est, cui aliud nomen competit. Addit Papyrius Massonus: Nomina ideò mutari debent, eò quòd ad vitam perfectiorem assumantur. Sed respondet Montacutius Orig. Eccl. p. 1. p 114. Sed inprimis vita Pontificatus non est simpliciter & omnimodo perfectissima. Secundò tum qui de vita Laicali per Sacros ordines transeunt in Sacerdotium, nomina sua deberent immutare: Et quicunque cum Episcopatu Ecclesiis præficiuntur. Sed & priores Sergio, Pontifices, quique retrò, ad B. Petrum ascendendo, ad eundem modum tenerentur: imprimis autem posteri, ad illum obligarentur. Scire autem debuisset Montacutius temporis successu creditam dignitatem longè quavis aliâ majorem in assumptione ad Pontificatum ista postulare cœpisse, & jam Gentiles, Lactantio de falsa Relig. c.21. teste, nomina iis mutâsse, quos Deos inter referebant. Quos inter etiam Papas aliquo modo referri, vel sola satis probat adoratio; Cæterùm non potest non mali ominis esse, quòd Pontifices electi sic baptismalia, quibus auditis, semper fœderis cum Deo initi, nascentisque hinc commercii divinioris omnis cum fructu meminisse deberent, nomina mutant, eatenus quoque in Anti-Christorum formam, abjectis nominibus Baptismalibus, se induentes; Et quòd, nonnullis in mortis cumprimis articulo tenuitatis prioris conscientiâ ea rursus admittentibus, alii eorum repetitionem ægrè aliquando ferunt. Cujus exemplum Diar. Europ. Cent. XVII. p.65. in Alexandro VII. suppeditat, memorans, eum Patri Olivæ, Confessori suo, cùm is agoni zantem jam olim depositò Fabii nomine alloqueretur, regessisse; Sumus equidem adhuc Alexander VII. non Johannes Baptista Pansilius. Sic repetito Innocentii X. prædecessoris potiùs, quàm suo nomine, innuens, eum quidem dignitatis suæ oblitum paulò ante mortem baptismali nomine mine contentum fuisse, sibi eundem non esse animum. Quæ immodestia, an moribundo Pontifice digna fuerit, Lectori dijudicandum relinquimus.
units.tr: XXI. The names are excellent! But do the names they take suit them? Rarely. About John XII, the first author of the change, we brought forward above the testimony of Baronius, that though he changed his name, he did not put off his tyranny, and wished at least to be well spoken of by his name. The opinion of others is and has been the same. The first honour, says Polydorus Vergilius, a writer who was Catholic even before the Reformation, De inventoribus rerum, book 4, chapter 10, p. 342, is held by the Roman Pontiff, so that if he is dishonoured by an unlovely name, he may at once, once created, be allowed to change it. For example, let it not be said in jest: if a man was perhaps wicked before, let him be called Boniface; if timid, Leo; if rustic, Urban; if shameless, Innocent; if savage, Clement; if he had a bad reputation, Benedict; so that at least by his name the Pontiff may be an ornament to his dignity. Laurentius Bancus adds, in Roma Triumphans, chapter 9, p. 155: If he has everywhere been defeated, Victor; if he is a priest of all wickedness, Pius; if he has oppressed the people, Nicholas; if he is sad, Hilary; if he is exposed to the mockeries of fortune, Felix; if he has a face like an ape, Formosus; if he has always been grim, Gelasius. And we have already seen about the Pii in Dissertation VII. But in his own time the Emperor Conradin, more correctly Conrad, could also complain, in a letter on the injuries done to him by the Roman Pontiffs, sent to the states of the Empire and inserted by Goldast among the imperial constitutions, that Urban had not acted urbanely, nor Clement with clemency, but with cruelty. They love old names, not the faith, not the old morals; they commit foul deeds under fair names, and so one may sing to each of them: You are said to live, but you are dead, Rev. 3:1. A wolf under sheep's skin, an angel of Satan transformed into an angel of light, a servant of vices under the name of virtue? They love other names, wishing to appear as altogether different men. Thus, in their own view, Tostatus of Avila, on 4 Kings chapter 25, question 15, makes the first reason for papal renaming this: Because a name is imposed, and yet he who becomes supreme Pontiff was previously a private man, and when he becomes Pontiff he is one who bears the place of God on earth, therefore another name is fitting for him. Papirius Masson adds: Names ought to be changed because they are taken up for a more perfect life. But Montagu replies, in Origines Ecclesiasticae, part 1, p. 114: But above all, the life of the Pontificate is not simply and in every way most perfect. Secondly, those who pass from lay life to the priesthood through holy orders would have to change their names, and whoever is set over churches with the episcopate. But also the earlier Sergii, and the popes who went back, ascending to Blessed Peter, would be bound in the same way; and especially the later ones would be bound to it. Montagu ought to have known that over time a dignity believed to be far greater than any other began to demand these things in the assumption of the Pontificate, and that already the Gentiles, as Lactantius testifies in On the False Religion, chapter 21, had changed the names of those they counted among their gods. That the popes are in some way counted among these, adoration alone sufficiently proves. Moreover, it cannot but be a bad omen that the popes, when elected, change their baptismal names, which ought to remind them, whenever they are heard, of the covenant entered into with God and of all the fruit of the divine commerce arising from their new birth; and in this they clothe themselves in the form of Antichrists, casting off their baptismal names. Some of them, at the very point of death especially, when they recognised their former lowliness, took those names up again, and others sometimes bear it badly that they are repeated. The Diarium Europaeum, century 17, p. 65, supplies an example in Alexander VII, recording that when his confessor, Father Oliva, once addressed him at the point of death by the name Fabius, which he had long since laid aside, he replied: Truly we are still Alexander VII, not John Baptist Pansilius. Thus, by repeating the name of his predecessor Innocent X rather than his own, he implied that Innocent, who had forgotten his dignity a little before death and was content with his baptismal name, was not the mind he himself had. We leave it to the reader to judge whether this immodesty was worthy of a dying Pope.

units.la: XXII. Et tunc solet, ita pergit Sacrarum Ceremoniarum liber, subscribere constitutiones ante electionem firmatas, & juratas, & signare aliquas supplicationes. De constitutionibus illis jam Differt. IV. inter antecedentia Electionis egimus. Sciendum autem est, quòd raro subscribuntur, sive jurantur, rarius servantur. Licèt enim electus æquè ac reliqui Cardinales ante electionem earum observationem juraverit, facilè tamen Papa factus se à juramento suo dispensat, quod sive ante, sive post electionem præstitit; cùm & alios interdum ab omnibus in Electione obliquitatibus, quod in Conclavi Urbani VI. factum, statim absolvat atque dispenset. Nempe Papa nullo modo ligatus esse vult. Hinc Marcellus II. cùm initio Pontificatu, verba sunt Onuphrii in vita, à Cardinalibus rogaretur, ut priscò instituto ei diplomati subscriberet, quo juramento obligaretur, certum tantùm numerum Cardinalium esse creaturum; Id facere recusavit, affirmans, se id opere præstaturum, verbis nolle. Similiter Innocentius IX. quando ei oblata fuit Bulla Pii V. de non alienandis Ecclesiæ terris &c. juramento confirmanda, respondit: Juramus & declaramus, omnes in ea casus dubitabiles contineri. Usque adeò Pontifex est ὁ ἄνομος, & ludunt Cardinales, quando ante electionem constitutiones faciunt & juramento confirmant, quas tamen electi servare nolunt, qui proin vel maximè ludunt! Respectu supplicationum verò, de eodem Innocentio IX. Conclave narrat, eum Cardinali Cajetano, pro Antonio Ursino liberando certam pecuniæ summam offerenti, respondisse: Non vogliamo danari, mà obedienza: Id est: Nolumus argentum, sed obedientiam.
units.tr: XXII. And then it is customary, so the book of Sacred Ceremonies goes on, to subscribe to the constitutions confirmed and sworn before the election, and to sign certain supplications. We have already dealt with those constitutions among the preliminaries of the Election in Dissertation IV. But it must be known that they are rarely subscribed or sworn to, and more rarely kept. For although the one elected, like the other cardinals, swore to observe them before the election, a pope who has been made easily releases himself from his oath, whether he gave it before or after the election; and sometimes he immediately absolves and dispenses others from all the irregularities in the election, as was done in the conclave of Urban VI. Indeed the pope wishes to be bound in no way. Hence Marcellus II, when at the beginning of his pontificate, these are the words of Onuphrius in his life, was asked by the cardinals to subscribe to the old formal document by which he would be bound by oath to create only a certain number of cardinals; he refused to do this, asserting that he would do it in deed, not promise it in words. Similarly Innocent IX, when the Bull of Pius V on not alienating the lands of the Church and so on was offered to him to be confirmed by oath, replied: We swear and declare that all cases of doubt are contained in it. So far is the Pope ὁ ἄνομος [the lawless one], and the cardinals play games when before the election they make constitutions and confirm them by oath, which the elected nevertheless refuse to keep, and so they play games all the more! As for supplications, the Conclave tells of the same Innocent IX, that when Cardinal Caetani offered him a certain sum of money for the release of Antonio Orsini, he replied: Non vogliamo danari, ma obedienza: that is, We want not money but obedience.

units.la: XXIII. Interim verò, sic pergit liber Ceremoniarum, prior Diaconorum aperta Sacrarii fenestrella, quâ populus expectans videri potest, crucem profert, altâ voce clamitans. Annuncio vobis gaudium magnum: Papam habemus. Reverendissimus Dominus Cardinalis ——electus est in summum Pontificem, & elegit sibi nomen—— Populus autem, electione cognitâ, more antiquo currit ad diripiendas ædes electi. In quo etiam aliquando error fuit. Cùm enim electo Urbano VI. populo diceretur, ut iret ad S. Petrum ad audiendam pronuntiationem, ivit ad domum Cardinalis S. Petri, qui Romanus erat, qualis à populo expetebatur, & quem putabat esse indicatum; hinc diripere ripere coeperunt ejus aedes & clamare: Romanum habemus. Utidem huic respectu aedium, quod S. Severinae respectu cellulae, infortunium accidering, Authore Conclavis narrante.
units.tr: XXIII. Meanwhile, the book of Ceremonies goes on thus: the senior of the Deacons opens the little window of the sacristy, through which the waiting people can see, holds up a cross, and calls out in a loud voice: "I announce to you great joy: we have a Pope. The most reverend Lord Cardinal ——has been elected supreme Pontiff and has taken for himself the name ——". The people, once the election is known, run in the old manner to plunder the house of the newly elected man. An error once occurred in this matter. When the people of Rome were told, after Urban VI had been elected, to go to St Peter's to hear the announcement, they went instead to the house of the Cardinal of St Peter's, who was a Roman, as the people wanted, and whom they believed had been named. From there they began to plunder his house and to shout: "We have a Roman!" A similar misfortune befell the houses of S. Severina, as it did the cell of S. ... according to the author of the Conclave.

units.la: XXIV. Dum haec aguntur, sunt verba ejusdem Ceremoniarum libri, & Pontifex vestitus primo salutatur, porta Conclavis omnes aperiuntur, repagula murique ostiorum & fenestrarum deiciuntur, pulsantur campana, & signa laetitiae omnis generis eduntur. Conclave tunc quoque diripi, ex eo, quod in citato Urbano VI. Conclavi Conclavistae argentum suum, electione facta, alio portari curarunt, colligi posse videtur. Pontifex novus, ita pergit Ceremoniale, pracedente cruce, & Cardinalibus ad Ecclesiam S. Petri descendit, & prostratus ante altare sine mitra aliquandiu orat; agitque gratias Deo, & beatis Apostolis. Tum surgens a Cardinalibus super altare ad sedendum constituitur cum mitra, & prior Episcoporum genu flexu incipit. Te Deum laudamus: quem hymnum Cantores prosequuntur. Interim Cardinales pedes electi, manus, & os deosculantur, servato ordine: quod & alii, qui adsunt, pralati & nobiles faciunt. Finito hymno, idem prior Episcoporum stans a cornu sinistro altaris, ubi Epistola legitur, dicit super electum, Pater noster &c. — Tum eodem ordine revertitur ad Cameram Papalem, & ibi quiescit, & Domini Cardinales revertuntur ad propria.
units.tr: XXIV. While these things are being done, these are the words of the same book of Ceremonies, the Pope, once dressed, is first greeted; the gates of the Conclave are all thrown open, the bars and walls of the doors and windows are pulled down, the bells are rung, and signs of joy of every kind are displayed. It seems to follow from the Conclave of Urban VI already cited that the Conclave was also plundered then, since the Conclavists, once the election was made, took care to have their silver carried elsewhere. The new Pope, the ceremonial goes on, with the cross going before him and the Cardinals, goes down to the church of St Peter, and, prostrate before the altar without his mitre, prays for a while, and gives thanks to God and the blessed Apostles. Then, rising, he is placed by the Cardinals on the altar to sit, with his mitre on, and the senior of the Bishops begins, kneeling: "We praise you, O God," which the singers take up as a hymn. Meanwhile the Cardinals kiss the feet, hands and mouth of the elected man, in due order; the prelates and nobles who are present do the same.
