When the hymn is finished, the same senior of the Bishops, standing at the left horn of the altar, where the Epistle is read, says over the elected man, "Our Father," etc. — Then, in the same order, he returns to the Papal Chamber and rests there, and the Lord Cardinals return to their own homes.

units.la: XXV. Quod si esset, sic porro narrat Author, aliquis extra Collegium, & tamen in urbe, vel loco vicino, antequam patres exeant e Conclavi, vocetur nomine Collegii ab aliquibus pralatis, & introductus in Conclavi: a priore Episcoporum intimetur ei electio, & requiratur ejus consensus; quo habito, omnia fiant, quae de electo praesente superius dicta sunt. Si autem non consentiret, iterum ad novam electionem faciendam procedant. Si autem Canonice electus esset absens: ita quod per aliquot dies ejus praesentia haberi non posset: patres, publicata ejus electione, & destinata ad electum idonea legatione, Conclavi exeant: legati cum mandatis, & authenticis documentis nominato electionem insinuent, & consensum exquirant, acceptantem, summum Pontificem salutent; & habitu Pontificali exornent; referantque patribus, deinde reliqua peragantur, ut novo electo, & Collegio videbitur. Si autem acceptare noluerit, ite um Domini Cardinales in Conclave revertantur ad novam electionem peragendam. Exemplum absentis in urbe in Urbano VI. ab Urbe, in Adriano VI. datur, nullum, acceptare constanter nolentis, a multis seculis.
units.tr: XXV. But if, the author goes on, someone outside the College, yet in the city or a nearby place, were called in the name of the College by some prelates before the fathers leave the Conclave, and introduced into the Conclave, the senior of the Bishops announces the election to him and asks for his consent; once that is obtained, everything is done that was said above about the elected man when present. But if he did not consent, they proceed to a new election. If, however, someone absent had been canonically elected, so that his presence could not be had for some days, the fathers, once the election has been published and a suitable embassy sent to the chosen man, leave the Conclave; the envoys, with their commission and authentic documents, announce the election to the named man, ask for his consent, and, if he accepts, salute him as supreme Pontiff and dress him in the Pontifical habit; and they report back to the fathers, after which the rest is carried out as seems best to the new elect and the College. But if he refuses to accept, the Lord Cardinals return to the Conclave to conduct a new election. An example of an absent man in the city is given in Urban VI, from outside the city in Adrian VI; there has been no example, for many centuries, of someone who steadfastly refused to accept.

units.la: XXVI. Consequens Electionis, sub Imperatoribus Christianis primis, Regibus Italiae, & primis etiam Imperatoribus Germanis manis, quoque fuit Imperatoria Pontificum recens electorum confirmatio, quâ sine eos consecrare, vel pro Pontificibus habere nefas erat. De quo illorum temporum more eò minùs dubitare licet, quando jam Differt. IV. ostendimus, tunc Imperatores ipsum eligendi jus ab ipsis etiam Pontificibus confirmatum sæpe exercuisse. Quemadmodum etiam, quæ ibi pro jure eligendi dicta sunt, multò magis respectu juris confirmandi valent. De quo, tum ob aliorum, qui præcesserunt, labores, tum ob Pontificiorum hac in parte confessiones multis hëic agere nihil attinet. Audimus tamen primò generale Guicciardini, Pontificii Hist. Pap. l. IV. testimonium: Sine Imperatorum & Hexarchorum authoritate, inquit, quamvis Sacerdotum P. Q. R. suffragiis renuntiati, neque se pro Pontificibus gerere, neque Pontificatum capere audebant; sed maximè Onuphrium, qui in Pelag. II. Platina & morem, & moris ortum, & specialem rationem, & causas speciales ita enarrat: Gothis Italiâ omni per Narsem Patricium pulsis, eâque cum urbe Roma Orientalis Imperii parte factâ, sub Justiniano Imperatore, ex authoritate Papæ Vigilii, novus quidam in Comitiis Pontificiis mos inolevit. Morem autem antiquiorem, neque authoritate Vigilii, aut Pontificum constitutum esse, Liberii, Eulalii & Bonifacii, Symmachi & Laurentii, Felicis IV. Bonifacii II. & Sylverii exemplis, Honorii, Odoacri & Theodorici constitutionibus, ante Vigilium factis, meridiana luce clarius apparet. Sed pergit Onuphrius: Is fuit (mos,) ut, mortuo Papa, nova quidem electio more majorum, statim à Clero S. P. Q. R. fieret; Verùm electus Rom. Pontifex non ante consecrari, atque ab Episcopis ordinari posset, quàm ejus electio ab Imperatore Constantinopolitano confirmata esset: ipséque literis suis patentibus electo Pontifici licentiam concederet, ut ordinari posset; atque ita jurisdictionem Pontificatûs tum obineret; Pro qua licentia consequenda electo necesse erat, certam pecuniæ quantitatem Imperatori transmittere. Qua venia obtenta, ipse postea consecrabatur, & Romanum administrabat Pontificatum. Antea enim iidem dies comitiorum & consecrationis Pontificis renuntiati erant. Hoc autem ideò Justinianum Imp. (ante quem Imperatorum & Regum authoritatem in electione Pontificum magnam jam fuisse, allegata docent;) vel ex ejus authoritate Vigilium Papam (ergò contradicit ei, quòd ex authoritate Vigilii morem inolevisse, suprà dixerat,) instituisse credendum est, ut Imperator certus esset de conditionibus novi Pontificis: cujus tum maxima esse authoritas coeperat: Imperatoribus præsertim Italiâ absentibus, ne aliquo Pontifice factiosò, vel Imperatoris hoste ordinato, urbs urbs & Italia eo autore, ab Orientali Imperio deficeret; seque finitimis Barbaris traderet; quod Sylverium Papam aliquando quasi esse sibi persuadebat. Quaratione fiebat, ut in novis Comitiis eum Ro. Pont. crearent, quem Imperatori, à quo confirmandus erat, amicum esse scirent; de quo ille consideret, nihil in Italia contra Imperium moliturum &c.
units.tr: XXVI. Under the first Christian Emperors, the kings of Italy, and also the first German Emperors, a consequence of the election was the imperial confirmation of newly elected Popes, without which it was wrong to consecrate them or to regard them as Popes. Concerning the custom of those times there is less reason to doubt this, since we have already shown in Dissertation IV. that the Emperors often exercised the right of election, which had been confirmed by the Popes themselves. And what was said there about the right of electing applies all the more to the right of confirming. There is no need to dwell at length on this, both because of the labours of others who went before and because of the admissions of the Papists on this point. Let us hear first the general testimony of Guicciardini, a Papist, in his History of the Popes, book IV.: "Without the authority of the Emperors and the Exarchs," he says, "although they had been declared by the votes of the priests of the Roman Church, they did not dare to act as Popes or to take up the Pontificate." But above all let us hear Onofrio, who, on Pelagius II, in Platina, describes the custom, its origin, its particular reasoning and its special causes thus: "When the Goths had been driven out of all Italy by Narses the Patrician, and the city of Rome with it had become part of the Eastern Empire under the Emperor Justinian, by the authority of Pope Vigilius a new custom took hold in the Papal elections." That the older custom was not established by the authority of Vigilius or of the Popes, but earlier, is clearer than midday from the examples of Liberius, Eulalius and Boniface, Symmachus and Laurence, Felix IV, Boniface II and Silverius, and from the decrees of Honorius, Odoacer and Theodoric made before Vigilius. But Onofrio goes on: "This was the custom: when a Pope had died, a new election was made at once by the clergy of the Senate and People of Rome, in the manner of the ancestors; but the elected Roman Pontiff could not be consecrated or ordained by the Bishops until his election had been confirmed by the Emperor at Constantinople, who would himself give the elected Pontiff, by his open letters, licence to be ordained, and so he then obtained the jurisdiction of the Pontificate. To obtain this licence the elected man had to send a certain sum of money to the Emperor. Once this permission was obtained, he was consecrated and administered the Roman Pontificate. Previously the days of the election and of the consecration of the Pope had been announced together. It must be believed, however, that Vigilius the Pope instituted this (as the aforementioned facts show that the authority of the Emperors and Kings in the election of Popes was already great before Justinian; and so he contradicts himself, since he said above that the custom took hold by the authority of Vigilius), or at least by Justinian's authority, so that the Emperor could be sure of the conditions of the new Pope, whose authority had then begun to be very great, especially when the Emperors were absent from Italy; so that under some factious Pope, or one ordained by an enemy of the Emperor, the city and Italy, under his lead, might not revolt from the Eastern Empire and hand themselves over to the neighbouring barbarians, which he once thought Pope Silverius was about to do. For this reason they chose at the new elections as Roman Pontiff the man whom they knew to be a friend of the Emperor, by whom he had to be confirmed; and the Emperor would reflect that he would plan nothing in Italy against the Empire, etc."

units.la: XXVII. Hinc Pelagius II. sine Imperatoris consensu creatus, narrantibus, eodem Onuphrio & Naucl. Gener. 20. excusationem in eo quaesivit, quòd extra obsessam ab hoste (Longobardo) urbem mitti quispiam non potuerit; Atque addidit Onuphrius: Nil enim tum à Clero in eligendo Pontifice actum erat, nisi ejus electionem Imperator approbâsset. Hinc etiam Gregorius I. ipse à Clero & populo electus, sed ab onere liberari volens, ad Imperatorem scripsit, ut suam electionem non haberet ratam, Joan. Diacono in vita referente. Non enim licebat, inquit Aimonius l. 3. c. 74. tunc temporis ad Pontificatum promoveri absque jussione Principis Constantinopolitani; Quam jussionem etiam deinceps Gregorius I. l. 1. ep. 5. agnovit. Et licet Constantinus Pogonatus non tantùm tributum novi Pontificis relaxârit, sed & paulò ante obitum ipsum confirmationis suae jus Benedicto II. tum ex animi pietate, tum ne ordinationes cum damno protelarentur, condonârit; illud tamen Exarchi consensum non exclusisse, ex eo patet, quòd Conon secundus post Benedictum, ab Exarcho Theodoro, quem rogaverant, ante ordinationem ex more confirmatus apud Anastasium in Vita legitur. Sed & diu post Paschalis I. uti Platina in Vita narrat, nullâ interpositâ Imperatoris autoritate, Pontifex factus, ubi Pontificatum iniit, statim Legatos ad Ludovicum misit; qui ejus rei culpam omnem in Clerum & Populum rejicerent: quod ab his vi coactus esset, Pontificium munus obire. Quibus Imperator respondit: Majorum instituta & pacta servanda esse; caverent, ne deinde majestatem laederent. Quamobrem etiam Gregorius IV. non prius Pontificium munus obire voluit, quam à Legatis Ludovici Imperatoris ob eam causam Romam missis, qui diligenter tantam electionem discussissent, confirmatus esset. Atque fecit isthoc pius Imperator, ut Platina porrò testatur, non superbiâ motus, sed ne jura Imperii administraret. Quod autem idem Baronio ad an. 774. n. 21. electionem Romanis liberam cessisse dicitur, illud tanquam dictis contrarium, vel fabulosis ostendit, vel talibus, quibus, quem patiuntur etiam, sensus alius dari debet. Imò ipse tandem Hildebrandus, utut in caeteris atque deinceps in Imperatorum & Regum jura summe injurius, à Clero populóque Romano electus, à iuli à sui tamen, ut Acta Gregorii VII. apud Bar. ad an. 1073. n. 23. habent, ordinatione abstinuit, donec Henricus Rex suum præberet assensum.
units.tr: XXVII. Hence Pelagius II, created without the Emperor's consent, as Onofrio and Naucler, Generation 20, relate, sought an excuse for this in the fact "that someone could not be sent outside the city, which was besieged by the enemy (the Lombard)." Onofrio adds: "For nothing was then done by the clergy in electing a Pope unless the Emperor had approved the election." Hence also Gregory I, though elected by the clergy and people, wishing to be relieved of the burden, wrote to the Emperor asking him not to ratify his election, as John the Deacon reports in his life. "For it was not lawful," says Aimo, book 3, ch. 74, "at that time to be advanced to the Pontificate without the command of the Prince of Constantinople." Gregory I afterwards acknowledged this command, book 1, letter 5. And although Constantine Pogonatus not only remitted the tribute due from a new Pope, but also, shortly before his death, granted Benedict II the right of confirmation itself, partly out of piety of mind and partly so that ordinations would not be delayed to the loss of the Church, it is clear that this did not exclude the consent of the Exarch: Conon, the second after Benedict, was confirmed by the Exarch Theodore, whom they had asked, before his ordination according to custom, as is read in Anastasius in Vita. But long afterwards, as Platina in Vita relates, Paschal I, having been made Pope without any intervention of the Emperor's authority, as soon as he entered upon the Pontificate sent envoys at once to Louis, who laid the whole blame for the matter on the clergy and people: that he had been forced by them to take up the Pontifical office. To this the Emperor replied that the institutions and agreements of the ancestors were to be kept; they should take care not to injure the majesty of the Empire thereafter. For this reason also Gregory IV did not wish to take up the Pontifical office until he had been confirmed by envoys sent to Rome for this purpose by the Emperor Louis, who had carefully examined so great an election. And this, as Platina further attests, the pious Emperor did, "not moved by pride, but so that he would not administer the rights of the Empire." As for what is said of the same matter by Baronius at the year 774, n. 21, that the election was ceded freely to the Romans, he shows it either to be contrary to the facts or fabulous, or else such that another sense must be given to what they suffer. Indeed Hildebrand himself at last, though in other matters and afterwards extremely unjust toward the rights of Emperors and Kings, when elected by the clergy and Roman people, nevertheless, as the Acts of Gregory VII in Baronius at the year 1073, n. 23 report, abstained from ordination until King Henry gave his assent.

units.la: XXVIII. Hæc autem Hildebrandi, sive Gregorii VII. confirmatio ultima fuit efficax. Deinceps enim atque in secutis dissidiis Imperatores Papis Romæ creatis Anti-Papas opposuerunt; Dissidiis autem illis, ob investituram maximè susceptis, finitis, Imperatores & ab electione & paulatim etiam ab omni, quod Romæ habebant, temporali quoque jure exclusi fuerunt, Cardinalibus tandem, ut Differt. IV. pluribus ostendimus, se solos, exclusa populo, exclusis etiam Imperatoribus, Electionum Dominos constituentibus. Quin eò usque se metamorphosis illa tandem extendit, ut Imperatores jure confirmationis, quod habebant, amisso, suam jam confirmationem à jure, quod prius non habebant, & nutu Pontificio expectare, saltem ex Pontificum voluntate, Pontificiorúmque Monarchicorum hypothesi, debeant. Ita Pontificibus quæ non fuerunt, introducere, quæ fuerunt, abrogare, jus mutare Dan. VII. 26. & supra omne venerabile se efferre, 2. Thess. II. 4. solenne est! Sed redeamus ad Authorem Sacrarum Ceremoniarum;
units.tr: XXVIII. This last confirmation by Hildebrand, or Gregory VII, was effective. From then on, in the later disputes, the emperors set anti-popes against the popes created at Rome. When those disputes, chiefly over investiture, were ended, the emperors were excluded both from the election and gradually from all the temporal right they had held at Rome. Finally the cardinals, as we have shown at length in Differt. IV., made themselves alone the masters of elections, excluding the people and the emperors too. Indeed that transformation went so far that the emperors, having lost the right of confirmation they had, must now await their confirmation from a right they did not previously have, and from the pope's nod, at least by the pope's will, on the hypothesis of the Papist monarchists. Thus it is a customary practice to introduce for popes what had not been, to abolish what had been, to change times and laws, Dan. VII. 26, and to exalt himself above every so-called god, 2 Thess. II. 4! But let us return to the author of the Sacred Ceremonies.

units.la: XXIX. Ante coronationem suam, inquit porrò, electus Romanus Pontifex Consistoria tenere non consuevit, neque provisiones aliquas Ecclesiarum facere; si tamen aliquo impedimento Coronationem diutius differre oporteret, & urgeret necessitas, Ecclesiis rectè posset providere, & omnia, quæ essent pro utilitate Reipublica, peragere. Et hoc tempore Bulla plumbea literarum suarum ab una tantùm parte imprimetur, ubi sunt Capita Apostolorum: ab alia autem, ubi litera sui nominis imprimi solent, nihil erit: In principio, si prius erat Episcopus consecratus, scriberetur N. Episcopus, servus &c. ut alias. Si autem non esset consecratus Episcopus, scriberetur: N. electus, servus servorum Dei. In fine autem literarum ante datam adduntur hæc verba: Nec mireris, quòd Bulla exprimens nomen nostrum non est appensa præsentibus. Nam hii, qui fuerunt hactenus electi in Romanos Pontifices, ante suæ Consecrationis & benedictionis solemnia in suis bullandis literis modum hujusmodi observare consueverunt. In data autem dicitur loco: Pontificatûs nostri: suscepti à nobis Apostolatûs officii anno primo.
units.tr: XXIX. Before his coronation, he says further, the elected Roman Pontiff is not accustomed to hold consistories or to make any provisions for churches; yet if, by some hindrance, the coronation had to be delayed longer, and necessity pressed, he could rightly provide for the churches and carry out all things that were for the good of the commonwealth. And at this time the leaden seal of his letters is stamped on one side only, where the heads of the Apostles are; on the other side, where the letters of his name are usually stamped, there is nothing. At the beginning, if he had previously been consecrated bishop, it was written "N. Bishop, servant," etc., as in other cases. If, however, he had not been consecrated bishop, it was written "N. elect, servant of the servants of God." At the end of the letters, before the date, these words are added: "Do not be surprised that the bull expressing our name is not appended to the present letters. For those who have hitherto been elected Roman Pontiffs have been accustomed to observe this manner in sealing their letters before the solemnities of their consecration and blessing." In the date, instead of "of our pontificate," it is said, "in the first year of the apostolic office taken up by us."

units.la: XXX. Præbent ista occasionem quæstioni: Utrum Pontifex ante suam coronationem, jam sit Pontifex potestate Pontificis præditus? Ad quam variè à variis respondetur. Nos ita sentimus de Ministris Ecclesiasticis legitimis, solâ electione (quam à vocatione missione non distinguimus;) tales fieri, jubentibus nimirum nomine Dei qui, vult, ut ministeria in Ecclesia perennent, & Doctores, Rectores apti quærantur, illis, penes quos potestas est. Quòd autem ordinatio insuper apud nos etiam locum habet, electionem vel præcedens, vel sequens; illud nihil aliud dicit, quàm electos, vel eligendos in examine dignos atque aptos repertos esse, (quorum tamen aptitudo, si desit talis examinis per Ministros facultas, aliàs etiam cognosci potest;) Ministros alios iis ben precari, eorúmque laboribus, atque eos in communionem societatis Ecclesiasticæ & operis Domini recipere; Síque publicè & coram coetu fiat, coetum illorum electionem porrò probare; Quæ quidem ordinatio vel consecratio ab Apostolica per manuum impositionem confirmatione orta, sed non similiter hodie donorum extraordinariorum collatione fœcunda, si electionem sequatur, Ministrum magis declarat, quàm facit; Neque etiam, ut per Ministros fiat ordinatos, absolutè necessarium est. Pontifices autem non istis, sed suis, falsis licèt, hypothesibus metiri debemus. Statuunt quippe, potestatem non conferri, nisi à Clericis, continuâ serie inde ab Apostolis à suis similibus, vel se majoribus ordinatis, ordinatione, quæ caracterem quendam indelebilem imprimat, qui aliunde acquiri non possit, & sine quo Ministerium Ecclesiasticum exercere nefas sit. Quæ, si ad Pontifices electos vel eligendos jam applicentur, satis evincunt, neque ab ullo homine dignitatem Ecclesiasticam Pontificia infe-riorem habente, vel Episcopis communibus vel, & multò minùs, à Cardinalibus quibusvis, Presbyteris, Diaconis tantùm, imò aliquando nullis plane ordinibus initiatis; neq; ab Imperatoribus, Regibus, quos Laicos vocant, vel à plebe, juxta Electionis formas Differt.IV. ostensas, potestatem Pontificiam accipere posse, proin primò solâ per tales electione non fieri; quod tamen Hieromonarchici nostris temporibus communiter asserunt. Concordant, inquit Almaynus de pot. Eccl. & Laica quaest. 4. c. Un. Jurista & Theologi: quòd Papa, postquam est electus, habet supremam administrationem in spiritualibus & omnimodam Jurisdictionem. Atque idem probat II Cardinalismo p.3. l. 2. p. 323. primò exemplo Urbani VII. qui tot tantùm diebus, quot in vocibus, Urbano Settimo, literæ, in Pontificatu vivens atque ante Coronationem mortuus, validas tamen constitutiones fecerit, secundò verbis Bullæ: Ut is, qui electus est in Apostolatum, si juxta consuetudinem intronizari non valeat, electus tamen sicut verus Papa obtinet aucto-
units.tr: XXX. These things give rise to the question: Is the pope, before his coronation, already pope, endowed with the power of the papacy? To this different people give different answers. We hold this about lawful ecclesiastical ministers: that by election alone (which we do not distinguish from vocation and sending) they are made such, since God, who wills that ministries endure in the Church and that fit teachers and rulers be sought, commands it through those who hold the power. Moreover, that ordination also has a place among us, either preceding or following the election, means nothing other than that the elected, or those to be elected, have been found worthy and fit upon examination (whose fitness, if such examination by ministers is lacking, can also be known in other ways); that other ministers pray for them, bless their labours, and receive them into the fellowship of the Church and the work of the Lord; and that if this is done publicly and before the assembly, the assembly then approves their election. This ordination or consecration, which arose from apostolic confirmation through the laying on of hands, but which is not similarly fruitful today in the conferring of extraordinary gifts, when it follows the election, declares the minister rather than makes him. Nor is it absolutely necessary that he be ordained by ministers. But the Papists must be measured not by these principles but by their own hypotheses, false though they are. For they lay down that power is conferred only by clerics in an unbroken succession from the Apostles, by ordination from their like or their superiors, which imprints a certain indelible character that cannot be acquired otherwise, and without which it is unlawful to exercise the ecclesiastical ministry. If these principles are now applied to popes elected or to be elected, they sufficiently show that the papal power cannot be received from any man holding an ecclesiastical dignity inferior to the papacy, whether common bishops, or much less any cardinals, mere presbyters or deacons, or even men initiated into no order at all; nor from emperors and kings, whom they call laymen, nor from the people, according to the forms of election set out in Differt. IV. Hence, first, the papal power is not conferred by election alone through such persons; yet the Hieromonarchists of our times commonly assert this. The jurists and theologians agree, says Almain, De potestate ecclesiastica et laica, quaest. 4, c. Un., that the Pope, once elected, has supreme administration in spiritual matters and full jurisdiction. The same is proved in the Cardinalismus, part 3, book 2, p. 323, first by the example of Urban VII, who, living as pope for only as many days as there are letters in the words Urbano Settimo, and dying before his coronation, nevertheless issued valid constitutions; secondly, by the words of the bull: that he who has been elected to the apostolate, if he cannot be enthroned according to custom, nevertheless holds as the true pope,

units.la: Coronationem potestatem habeat; auctoritatem regendi R. Ecclesiam, & disponendi omnes facultates illius, quod B. Gregorium ante suam coronationem cognovimus fecisse &c. Tertiò anathemate Clementis V. quod dicat omnibus potestatem Pontifici electo ante Coronationem denegantibus. Quòd autem quartò dicit, Papam non ante coronationem, Imperatoris nondum coronati ad instar, electum tantum vocari, illud & in Imperatore falsâ hypothesi nititur, & numero praecedente allatis contrariantur. Sed cùm Pontificiorum nullus Papae electo, vel minimam potestatem ordinis, v. gr. Diaconi, si non habuerit jam ante electionem, ob eam adscribat, potestas autem Ecclesiastica atque spiritualis omnis simul Ecclesiae & Apostolis data sit, neque separari, aut potestas jurisdictionis, quam vocant, sine potestate ordinis, quae prior concipitur, obtingere queat, imò ipsa potestas temporalis, quam insuper Episcopi illi usurpant, sub alio, quàm quòd Episcopi sunt, respectu eis non conferatur dicere necesse habent, vel omnem planè ordinis etiam potestatem electione conferri, vel nullam planè, ex suis hypothesibus. Si confertur, quò pertinet illa distinctio n. praeted. tradita? Cur non electus Consistoria tenet & Ecclesiarum provisionis facit, etiam extrà casum necessitatis, qui sic conferre supponitur, quod ipsa non confert electio? Cur nomen suum imprimere; Cur se Episcopum vocare; Cur; anno Apostolatûs nostri; scribere, non audet? Cur rem in casu necessitatis, & extra eum, respectu jurisdictionis, sed non nomen usurpare audet? Quomodo, salvis hypothesibus Pontificiis, sola Laicorum aliquando electio, Presbyterum, imò Diaconum, imò Laicum, Episcopum, imò Pontificem summum facere potest? Cur non aliis potiùs, deficiente, vel nondum secuta ordinatione per Episcopos, potestatem multò inferiorem conferre potest? Quò sic ordinationis absoluta necessitas, quò Christianorum tam varia distinctio, quò character indelebilis ablegantur? Et quomodo ista conciliantur cum eo, quòd aliquando posteriores priorum acta, sub praetextu nondum tum habitae consecrationis, abrogârunt; & quòd aliquando Pontifices se simul consecrationem benedictionis & officii sui plenitudinem accepisse testati sunt? Si verò non confert electio potestatem, (quod & hypotheses exigere ofendimus;) cur electo communiter tribuunt supremam administrationem in spiritualibus & omnimodam jurisdictionem? Cur in omnibus tanquam Pontificem tractant eum, qui Pontifex non est? Cur suo nomine jam agit, omnia in necessitatis casu; Quid aliud est, adorare talem, quàm, ex hypothesi etiam, idololatriam foedissimam committere? Si enim potestatem Pontificiam, officium non habet, neque dignitatem habebit, quam ceu fundamentum adorationi suae substernunt. Et sic quoque irrita redduntur omnia Pontificum ante consecrationes suas decreta, acta Pontificia; Atque ex omnibus apparet, Hieromonarchicos hinc inde urgeri suarum hypothesium absurditate in istas angustias, in praecipitia ejusmodi redactos. Nobis autem liberum est, denuò redire ad Authorem librorum de Sacris Ceremoniis.
units.tr: the power of coronation; the authority to rule the Holy Church and to dispose of all its resources, which we know that Blessed Gregory did before his coronation, etc. Thirdly, by the anathema of Clement V, which condemns all who deny the power to the pope-elect before coronation. But when he says, fourthly, that the pope before coronation is called merely elect, just as an emperor not yet crowned is, this rests on a false hypothesis for the emperor too, and is contrary to the proofs adduced in the preceding paragraph. But since none of the Papists ascribes to the pope-elect even the least power of order, for instance that of a deacon, if he did not already have it before the election, and since all ecclesiastical and spiritual power was given at once to the Church and to the Apostles, and jurisdictional power, as they call it, cannot be separated from or obtained without the power of order, which is conceived as prior; and since even the temporal power, which those bishops usurp besides, is not conferred on them in some respect other than that by which they are bishops, they must say, according to their own hypotheses, either that all power of order is conferred by election, or that none is at all. If it is conferred, what does that distinction mentioned in the preceding paragraph mean? Why does the elect not hold consistories and make provision for churches even outside the case of necessity, if it is supposed that the election itself does not confer what it does? Why does he not dare to stamp his name, to call himself bishop, to write "in the year of our apostolate"? Why does he dare to usurp the thing in the case of necessity, and outside it with respect to jurisdiction, but not the name? How, with the Papist hypotheses kept intact, can the election of laymen alone sometimes make a presbyter, indeed a deacon, indeed a layman, a bishop, indeed the supreme pontiff? Why can it not rather confer a much lower power on others, when ordination by bishops is lacking or has not yet followed? Where, then, are the absolute necessity of ordination, the so varied distinction of Christians, and the indelible character banished? And how are these reconciled with the fact that later popes have sometimes annulled the acts of earlier ones on the pretext of a consecration not yet received, and that sometimes popes have testified that they received at once the consecration, the blessing, and the fullness of their office? But if election does not confer the power (as the hypotheses too, we have shown, require), why do they commonly attribute to the elect supreme administration in spiritual matters and full jurisdiction? Why do they treat in everything as pope one who is not pope? Why does he now act in his own name, in all things, in a case of necessity? What else is it to adore such a man than, even on their own hypothesis, to commit the most foul idolatry? For if he has no papal power or office, he will also have no dignity, on which they set as the foundation of their adoration. And so too all the decrees and papal acts of popes before their consecrations are rendered void. From all this it is evident that the Hieromonarchists, pressed on every side by the absurdity of their hypotheses, have been driven into these straits and into such precipices. It is for us, however, free to return again to the author of the books on the Sacred Ceremonies.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Agit ille jam Sect. 2. lib. 1. De ordinatione & consecratione summi Pontificis. Et quia liber in paucorum manibus est, ea verò, quae de his tradit, ad tractationem nostram pertinent, dictis lucem non exiguam praebent, atque varia tum superstitionis atque κακοζηλίας, tum maximae ineptarum Ceremoniarum multitudinis, tum Idololatriae, tum vanitatis atque luxus, tum neglecti à Pontificibus Officii, tum aliorum observatu dignorum documenta suppeditant; pleraque Authoris, verbis quoque ipsis retentis, cum annotationibus tamen nostris brevissimis hinc inde inspergendis exhibebimus. Caeterùm, inquit, si electus in Romanum Pontificem, non esset in Sacris ordinibus constitutus, ut de Petro Moraneo anachoreta & de quibusdam aliis patrum nostrorum memoria accidit, (vide Dissert. VII. Sect. V. n. 3.) statuta per eum die ante diem coronationis per aliquem Episcopum Cardinalem, vel alium, si magis placet, ordinetur, & ad omnes ordines etiam presbyteratum poterit in eadem die simul, vel interpellatis diebus promoveri, ut placuerit. (Ergò ex hypothesi illorum, qui Papam sola electione fieri ajunt, Papa esse potest etiam Laicus, & quod alii expresse addunt, faemina ordinis incapax! Differri enim sub praetextu potest coronatio. Et Laicus talis dignior erit omnibus toto orbe Clericis! Et omnes illi absolutè dependere possunt ab eo, qui ne minimi quidem ordinis functionem exercere potest! Et Vicarius Christi erit summúsque Ecclesiae Monarcha, Petri etiam Apostolorum Principis Successor, qui neque praedicandi, neque Sacramenta administrandi potestatem habet! Dabítque idem tamen, omnem, quaecunque in Ecclesia concipitur, potestatem! Atque, ex hypothesi omnium, uno eodémque die primò quidem Laicus & Papa, secundò Acoluthus, tertiò Lector, quartò Exorcista, quintò Ostiarius, sextò Subdiaconus, septimo Diaconus, octavò Presbyter, adeóque Protheo ipso mutabilior erit? Ei injungetur, ut Cereo accenso Diaconum conum sequatur, urceolos ac ampulas ad sacrificium, nec non luminaria præparet, exorcismos Ecclesiæ supra Catechumenos legat; & extra tempus sacrificii in Pulpito Evangelium; Quod per totam vitam neque facturus est, neque facere in animo habet! Simulque distinctiones has, ut gradatim & annorum aliquot intervallo ad diversa ministeria ascenderetur, excogitatas, meros in Papatu lusus esse, suomet tunc exemplo probabit!)
units.tr: He now deals with Section 2, Book 1, On the ordination and consecration of the Supreme Pontiff. Since the book is in the hands of few, what he delivers on these matters bears directly on our discussion. It sheds no small light on them and supplies examples of various things: superstition and misplaced zeal [κακοζηλίας], a great mass of pointless ceremonies, idolatry, vanity and luxury, the neglect of duty by the Popes, and other things worth noting. Where it is useful, I shall set out most of the author's words, keeping them unchanged, and scatter my very brief comments among them. Moreover, he says, if the man elected Roman Pontiff is not already in holy orders, as happened with Peter of Morrone the hermit and some others within our memory (see Dissertation 7, Section 5, no. 3), he is to be ordained the day before the day of coronation by some Cardinal bishop or another, if you prefer; and he may be promoted to all the orders, even to the priesthood, on the same day or on later days, as may be decided. (So, on the hypothesis of those who say that a Pope is made by election alone, a Pope can even be a layman, and, as others expressly add, a woman, who is incapable of orders! The coronation can be put off on the pretext of it. Such a layman would be worthier than all the clergy in the whole world! And all of them could depend absolutely on a man who cannot perform the function of even the lowest order! And he will be the Vicar of Christ and the supreme Monarch of the Church, the successor of Peter, the prince of the Apostles, though he has no power to preach or to administer the sacraments! Yet he will still give every power that can be conceived in the Church! And so, on everyone's hypothesis, in one and the same day he will be first a layman and Pope, second an acolyte, third a lector, fourth an exorcist, fifth a doorkeeper, sixth a subdeacon, seventh a deacon, eighth a priest, and so more changeable than Proteus himself! He will be ordered to follow the deacon with a lit taper, to prepare the cruets and flasks for the sacrifice, and the lights as well, and to read the Church's exorcisms over the catechumens, and, outside the time of the sacrifice, the Gospel from the pulpit. He will never do any of this in his whole life, nor does he intend to! At the same time he will prove, by his own example, that these distinctions, devised so that one might rise gradually to the various ministries over a number of years, are mere games played in Papacy!)

units.la: XXXII. In promotione autem, ita pergit, hac servabuntur.
units.tr: XXXII. In the promotion, he goes on, the following will be observed.

units.la: Convenient in loco, ubi ordinatio fieri debet, electus Pontifex cum duobus Diaconis, & aliquibus Presbyteris Cardinalibus, Subdiacono & acoluthis Apostolicis, & omnes convenientibus sibi & tempori paramentis ornentur. Deinde Episcopus Consecrator cum suis ministris pareatur, paretur etiam ante altare credencia pro consecratore, & credencia pro Pontifice electo cum rebus opportunis ad ordinationem. Electus ordinandus ad Subdiaconatum in sede sua in loco convenienti constituta, primo lavet manus, tum supra rochetum paretur amictu, ita tamen, ut possit imponi supra caput, cum tempus erit, alba, & cingulo, deinde pluviale, quod post collum remittit: ut totum retro dependeat: tum mitram accipiat tempori opportunam. Cum omnia parata erunt, electus accedit ad altare, procumbet ad orationem sine mitra: & surgens faciet confessionem cum ordinatore; deinde revertetur ad sedem suam & leget introitum &c. ut alias. Et ordinator procedet in missa more consueto usque ad collectam ante epistolam exclusive. Tunc electus super faldistorium procumbet sine mitra, Ordinator autem in scabello ad ejus sinistram cum mitra: & alii omnes in locis suis sine mitra: & fiet litania per Subdiaconum, & cum perventum fuerit ad locum consuetum, surget ordinator, & benedicet electum——deinde iterum procumbet, & finietur litania. Tum electus, sumta mitra revertitur ad sedem suam, & ordinator accedet ad eum: & sedenti cum mitra ipse stans cum mitra dat electo calicem vacuum cum patena: & mox urceolos cum vino, & aqua, baccale, & manutergium. Qua omnia electus tanget ambabus manibus, ordinatore dicente: hujusmodi ministerium &c.——finita oratione electus sedet sine mitra, & ordinator accepta mitra imponit amictum super caput electi, dicens: Accipe amictum &c. qui mox reassumit mitram, & ordinator imponit ei manipulum in brachio sinistro, dicens: Accipe manipulum &c. Tum surgit electus, extrahitur sibi mitra & pluviale, & ordinator induit eum tunicella, dicens: Induat te Dominus veste &c. Sedet deinde electus cum mitra, & ordinator ei tradit librum epistolarum, dicens: Accipe &c. Finita ordinatione Subdiaconatûs, si electus non vult ulterius procedere, reassumit pluviale,
units.tr: The elected Pontiff, with two deacons and some priests who are Cardinals, with the subdeacon and the Apostolic acolytes, shall assemble in the place where the ordination is to be held, and all shall be vested with the vestments suited to the occasion. Then the consecrating bishop shall be attended by his ministers, and a credence shall be prepared before the altar for the consecrator, and another credence for the elected Pontiff, with the things needed for the ordination. The elected man, to be ordained subdeacon, is seated in his chair set up in a suitable place. First he washes his hands; then over the rochet he is vested with the amice, so arranged that the alb can be placed over his head when the time comes, and with the girdle; then the pluviale, which he lets fall behind his neck so that it hangs down entirely at the back; then he takes the mitre, which is suited to the time. When all is ready, the elected man goes up to the altar and kneels to pray without his mitre; and rising he makes the confession with the ordainer; then he returns to his seat and reads the introit, etc., as elsewhere. And the ordainer proceeds with the Mass in the usual way up to the collect before the epistle, exclusive. Then the elected man kneels without his mitre on the faldstool, while the ordainer sits on a stool at his left with his mitre, and all the others in their places without mitres; and the litany is sung by the subdeacon; and when the usual place is reached, the ordainer rises and blesses the elected man, then kneels again, and the litany is finished. Then the elected man, taking his mitre, returns to his seat, and the ordainer approaches him; and while he is seated with his mitre, the ordainer, standing with his mitre, gives the elected man an empty chalice with a paten, and at once cruets with wine and water, a towel and a napkin. The elected man touches all these with both hands while the ordainer says: "a ministry of this kind," etc. When the prayer is finished, the elected man sits without his mitre, and the ordainer, taking the mitre, places the amice on the elected man's head, saying: "Receive the amice," etc., who at once puts on the mitre again; and the ordainer puts the maniple on his left arm, saying: "Receive the maniple," etc. Then the elected man rises, the mitre and the pluviale are taken off him, and the ordainer clothes him in the tunicle, saying: "May the Lord clothe you with the garment," etc. The elected man then sits with his mitre, and the ordainer hands him the book of Epistles, saying: "Receive," etc. When the ordination to the subdiaconate is finished, if the elected man does not wish to go further, he puts the pluviale back on,

units.la: Papa fit Subdiaconus; viale, & finitur missa more consueto. Et sic Papa fit Subdiaconus, id est, potestatem accipit Diacono ministrandi patinam, calicem & librum Epistolarum ei porrigendi!
units.tr: The Pope becomes a subdeacon; he puts on the pluviale, and the Mass is finished in the usual way. And so the Pope becomes a subdeacon, that is, he receives the power of handing to the deacon the paten, the chalice and the book of Epistles, and of serving him with them!

units.la: XXXIII. Si vero placuerit Papæ ad Diaconatum procedere, ordinator apud altare in suo faldistorio prosequitur collectam diei cum oratione pro ordinando sub eodem per Dominum, & dicetur epistola suo ordine. Qua finita, si electus ante electionem erat Subdiaconus, paretur in principio, sicut diximus, addito manipulo, & finita epistola, procumbat in faldistorio, & fiet litania, ut diximus. Si autem tunc ordinatus est, finita epistola surgat & deponat tunicellam, & iterum sedeat cum mitra & pluviali à collo, ordinator autem ad eum accedit, & stans cum mitra, dimissis aliis rebus, dicit: Oremus &c. Et cùm pervenerit ad: Per omnia sæcula; in præfatione deponit mitram — tunc electo sine mitra sedenti imponet ipse solus dextram manum super caput, dicens: Accipe Spiritum S. ad robur &c. Deinde prosequitur præfationem usque in finem, tunc depositò pluviali, & mitra ab assistentibus electo stanti ordinator cum mitra ponit illi stolam super humerum sinistrum dicens: Accipe &c. Deinde induit eum dalmatica dicens: Induat te &c. & mox tradit illi sedenti evangeliorum librum, dicens: Accipe potestatem &c. Quo facto electo sine mitra surgente ordinator deposita mitra versus ad altare dicit: Oremus; Et ministri; Flectamus genua. Et ipse prosequitur versus ad electum. Exaudi: Domine &c. His completis si noluerit ad ulteriora procedere, missa suo ordine finitur. Et sic Papa fit Diaconus, id est, accipit potestatem Sacerdoti sacrificanti assistendi & ministrandi, Eucharistiam distribuendi, Evangelium legendi, baptizandi, prædicandi!
units.tr: XXXIII. But if it has pleased the Pope to proceed to the diaconate, the ordainer, at the altar on his faldstool, continues the collect of the day with the prayer for the one being ordained, as before, and the epistle is read in its order. When that is finished, if the elected man was a subdeacon before the election, he is vested at the beginning, as we have said, with the maniple added, and when the epistle is finished he kneels on the faldstool, and the litany is sung, as we have said. If, however, he was ordained then, when the epistle is finished he rises and takes off the tunicle, and sits again with his mitre and the pluviale off his neck. The ordainer comes up to him and, standing with his mitre, having dismissed the others, says: "Let us pray," etc. And when he reaches "for ever and ever," in the preface he takes off the mitre; then, with the elected man seated without his mitre, he alone lays his right hand on his head, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit for strength," etc. Then he goes on with the preface to the end. Then, with the pluviale taken off and the mitre handed to the elected man by those standing by, the ordainer, with his mitre, puts the stole on his left shoulder, saying: "Receive," etc. Then he clothes him in the dalmatic, saying: "May he clothe you," etc., and at once hands him, seated, the book of the Gospels, saying: "Receive the power," etc. This done, the elected man rises without his mitre, and the ordainer, having put his mitre aside, turns toward the altar and says: "Let us pray"; and the ministers: "Let us kneel." And he himself continues, turned toward the elected man: "Hear us, Lord," etc. When these are completed, if he does not wish to proceed further, the Mass is finished in its order. And so the Pope becomes a deacon, that is, he receives the power of assisting and serving the priest who sacrifices, of distributing the Eucharist, of reading the Gospel, of baptizing, of preaching!

units.la: XXXIV. Si autem ad presbyteratum tunc erit promovendus: ordinator revertetur ad suum faldistorium, & leger graduale, & alleluja sive tractum, & postea procedet ad ordinem Sacerdotalem. Quod si prius erat Diaconus, parabuntur omnia, ut supra, & ipsi addatur stola super levam in formam Diaconi; sic paratus amictu albo, cingulo, manipulo, stola & pluviali à collo retrò pendente, procumbit super faldistorium ad letaniam, si non est facta, & illa, ut præmissum est in Subdiaconatu, finita, revertitur ad sedem suam: Ordinator verò cum mitra ad electum sedentem accedens manus ambas super caput electi detectum imponit, nihil dicens. Et idem faciunt omnes Episcopi, sive Presbyteri Cardinales præsentes, accedentes tamen cum reverentia & detectis capitibus. Deinde ordinator stans cum mitra extenta manu super electum stantem dicit; Oremus &c. Et in fine expansis manibus dicit præfationem, per omnia sæcula &c. Deinde deponitur pluviale. viale electi, & Ordinator accedens cum mitra reflectit orarium electo ante pectus in modum crucis,dicens: Accipe jugum Domini &c. & mox imponit illi casulam ad scapulas à parte anteriori pendentem,dicens: Accipe vestem Sacerdotalem &c. Post hæc depositta mitra ordinator dicit: Deus sanctificationum &c. & finita Oratione genu flexus ad altare: Veni creator &c. Et similiter electus genuflexus & dicto primo versu surgit, & alii prosequuntur; Ordinator inungit electo ambas manus de oleo sancto Catechuminum (En Papa oleo Catechumenorum inungitur!) producens cum pollice suo intincto duas lineas à pollice dextra manus electi ad indicem sinistrum, & vice versa, & mox palmas & reliqua inungit, dicens: Consecrare &c. manus electi ita perunctæ una super alteram imponuntur. Tunc ordinator deterso aliquantulum digito cum mica panis tradit in manus electi calicem cum vino & aqua, & patenam cum hostia: quæ omnia electus tangit,ordinatore dicente: Accipe potestatem offerre sa. &c. Quibus peractis electus à sede sua, & ordinator in suo saldistorio lavabunt manus cum mica panis & aqua. Deinde legatur Evangelium more solito, & liber offeretur osculandus electo. Tum ordinator dicit: Dominus vobiscum; Et offertorium. Et mox accedet ad electum sedentem cum mitra: & ipse sine mitra accipiat de ejus manibus offertorium,intorticia accensa,panem & vinum,ut est moris, & per singula osculatur manum electi offerentis: posthæc revertitur ordinatus ad saldistorium, & iterum , tam ipse quàm electus lavant manus: Et statim intrant ad altare. Electus accedit ad cornu altaris: ubi dicetur Epistola, & Presbytero Cardinale ministrante & serviente de libro stans sine mitra, voce submissa omnia dicit cum ordinatore, & cum ipso concelebrat signando: & etiam verba consecrationis cum ipso proferendo (En discendi cupidum Catechumenum Missaticum!) non tamen se movet loco suo usque ad communionem: & proceditur in missa in omnibus,ut consuetum est: & pro secreta de die, dicitur secreta de ordinato sub eodem per Dominum, postquam ordinator sumpserit Sacram Eucharistiam, & partem sanguinis Christi cum particula corporis, quæ erat intus, communicet electo stanti in ipso cornu de corpore & sanguine Christi, & postea ambo purificentur cum vino (quasi impuri facti communione!) ut eis placuerit. His peractis electus revertitur ad sedem suam cum mitra, & ordinator cum mitra lavat manus, deinde accedens ad electum stans sine mitra, dicit ad electum stantem sine mitra. Respon. Jam non dicam vos servos &c. (quasi hucusque servus fuerit Pontifex, neque dicendus sit maximè deinceps, servus servorum!) Quo finito, Ordinator imponit ambas manus super super ejus caput, dicens. Accipe Spiritum S. quorum remiseris &c. (quasi vero hominis sit, sic Spiritum dare! Et quasi vero, qui jam Papa est, Spiritum ab hoc ordinatore demum atque remittendi peccata potestatem accipere queat!) Et mox explicat casulam, quae in scapulis erat electi, dicens: Stola innocentia &c. Quibus finitis imponitur mitra electo. Et tam ordinator, quam alii Cardinales & praelati assistentes recipiuntur ad osculum manus, pedis (quod certè minùs convenire videtur cum dignitate ordinatoris, qui major ordinato!) & oris electi, posthac ordinator redibit ad altare & perficiet missam cum oratione pro ordinato & dicto; Ite, missa est, vel; benedicamus Domino: Electus crucem ante se habens stans sine mitra in medio altaris benedicet omnibus, dicendo: Sit nom n Domini &c. & mox ordinator accedens versus electum tertiò (qui numerus mysticus!) genuflexus (& hoc parùm convenit ordinatori!) cum distantia convenienti ter dicet: Ad multos annos. Et solus recipietur ad osculum oris, & sic repleta ordinatione exuet se vestibus sacris cum ordinationibus consuetis. Et sic fit Papa Presbyter, id est, accipit potestatem sacrificandi!
units.tr: XXXIV. If, however, he is then to be promoted to the priesthood, the ordainer shall return to his faldstool and read the gradual, and the alleluia or tract, and afterwards proceed to the priestly order. But if he was previously a deacon, everything is to be prepared as above, and the stole is to be placed over his left shoulder in the form of a deacon. So arrayed, with amice, girdle, maniple, stole and cope hanging behind from the neck, he kneels at the faldstool for the litany, if it has not already been done. When that is finished, as was said under the subdiaconate, he returns to his seat. The ordainer, however, approaches the seated candidate with his mitre and lays both hands upon the candidate's uncovered head, saying nothing. All the bishops or presbyter cardinals present do the same, approaching with reverence and with heads uncovered. Then the ordainer, standing with his mitre and his hand extended over the candidate standing, says: Let us pray, etc. At the end, with hands spread, he says the preface, World without end, etc. Then the candidate's cope is removed. The ordainer, coming forward with his mitre, folds the orarium in front of the candidate's breast in the form of a cross, saying: Take the yoke of the Lord, etc., and at once puts on him the chasuble, hanging from the shoulders in front, saying: Take the priestly vestment, etc. After this, the mitre being laid aside, the ordainer says: God of holiness, etc., and when the prayer is finished, kneeling at the altar: Come, Creator Spirit, etc. The candidate likewise kneels, and rises at the first verse, and the others follow. The ordainer anoints both hands of the candidate with the holy oil of the catechumens (Behold, the Pope is anointed with the oil of the catechumens!), drawing with his thumb, dipped in the oil, two lines from the thumb of the candidate's right hand to the index finger of the left, and then the other way round; and then he anoints the palms and the rest, saying: Consecrate, etc. The candidate's hands, so anointed, are laid one upon the other. Then the ordainer, having wiped his finger a little with a crumb of bread, hands to the candidate the chalice with wine and water and the paten with the host; the candidate touches all of these, while the ordainer says: Receive the power to offer the sacrifice, etc. When these things are done, the candidate rises from his seat, and the ordainer and the candidate wash their hands at the faldstool with a crumb of bread and water. Then the Gospel is read in the usual way, and the book is offered to the candidate to kiss. Then the ordainer says: The Lord be with you; and the offertory. He at once approaches the candidate seated with his mitre, and himself, without mitre, receives from his hands the offertory, the lit tapers, the bread and the wine, as is customary, and at each item kisses the hand of the candidate who offers it. Afterwards the ordained returns to the faldstool, and again both he and the candidate wash their hands; and at once they go to the altar. The candidate goes to the horn of the altar, where the Epistle is read. With a presbyter cardinal ministering and serving from the book, he, standing without mitre, says everything in a low voice along with the ordainer, and concelebrates with him by making the signs of the cross, and also pronounces the words of consecration together with him (Behold the catechumen of the Mass, eager to learn!). Yet he does not move from his place until communion. The Mass proceeds in every respect as usual; and for the secret, the secret of the ordained is said under the same, by the Lord, after the ordainer has received the holy Eucharist and, giving to the candidate standing at the horn a share of the body and blood of Christ, communicates him with the particle of the body which was within the chalice, and afterwards both are purified with wine, as they see fit (as if made unclean by communion!). When these things are done, the candidate returns with his mitre to his seat, and the ordainer, with mitre, washes his hands. Then, approaching the candidate standing without mitre, he says to him: Response: Now I will no longer call you servants, etc. (as if the Pope had hitherto been a servant, and was not henceforth to be called especially the servant of servants!). When this is finished, the ordainer lays both hands upon his head, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, etc. (as if it belonged to a man to give the Spirit in this way! And as if he who is already Pope could receive the Spirit and the power of forgiving sins from this ordainer at last!). And at once he unfolds the chasuble that was on the candidate's shoulders, saying: Stole of innocence, etc. When these are finished, the mitre is placed on the candidate. The ordainer, and the cardinals and prelates assisting, are then admitted to kiss his hand, foot (which seems scarcely consistent with the dignity of the ordainer, who is greater than the one ordained!) and mouth. Afterwards the ordainer returns to the altar and completes the Mass with the prayer for the ordained and the dismissal, Go, the Mass is ended, or Let us bless the Lord. The candidate, holding the cross before him and standing without mitre in the middle of the altar, blesses everyone, saying: The name of the Lord, etc. And at once the ordainer, approaching the candidate, kneels down a third time (which hardly suits the ordainer!) at a fitting distance, and says three times: Many years! Only he is admitted to kiss the mouth; and so, the ordination being complete, he takes off the sacred vestments with the customary rites. And thus the Pope becomes a priest, that is, receives the power of sacrificing!

units.la: XXXV. Haec, ut apparet, tantùm spectant ordines superiores.
units.tr: XXXV. These things, as is evident, concern only the higher orders.

units.la: De inferioribus ita rem paucis expedit author: Quod si forte electus in Papam esset merus laicus, (nam & laicus eligi potest, dummodo sit Christianus & Catholicus) accipiet primam tonsuram & minores ordines, ut alii inferiores, nisi quod erit indutus cum rochetto & manto post collum & mitra. Et in suo faldistorio recipiet instrumenta ordinum, & habitum, & non dicuntur monitiones, sive exhortationes (certo indicio, Papam nolle partibus officii fungi, proin tantùm ludere in illo suscipiendo) sed à substantialibus (qualia vel maximè essent monitiones) incipitur.
units.tr: The author briefly settles the matter of the lower orders as follows: If by chance the elected man should be a mere layman (for a layman too can be elected, provided he is a Christian and Catholic), he will receive the first tonsure and the minor orders, like the other lower ministers, except that he will be dressed with a rochet, a mantle down his back, and a mitre. And at his faldstool he will receive the instruments of the orders and the habit, and the monitions or exhortations are not said (a sure sign that the Pope is unwilling to perform the parts of the office and is merely playing at receiving it), but the proceedings begin with the substantial parts, of which the monitions would especially be among them.

units.la: XXXVI. De Episcopali consecratione primò notat, fieri debere secundùm majorum constitutiones eadem die, cum coronatione, sed suo jam tempore brevitatis studio alia die fieri coepisse.
units.tr: XXXVI. Concerning episcopal consecration, he first notes that it ought to take place on the same day as the coronation, according to the constitutions of the elders, but that in his own time it had begun to be done on another day, out of a desire for brevity.

units.la: Hinc etiam subjungit primò consecrationem sine benedictione & coronatione. Dicit ante omnia, privatim fieri posse, si Pontifici placeat, sed convenientiùs fieri die dominico, vel festivo modo sequenti: Parabuntur tam consecrator, quàm electus omnibus paramentis Pontificalibus, cum psalmis & orationibus consuetis. Electus chirothecas & annum tantùm non accipiet, alia autem omnia. Assistunt ad minus 2. vel 3. Diaconi & unus Presb. Cardinalis, & cum ipso consecratore, si ut Episcopus Cardinalis, (esse debet ex hypothesi, si consecratio legitima tima esse debet, licet apud Baronium ad an. 1058. 12. occurrat à Presbytero consecratus!) ut decet, duo alii Episcopi Cardinales: aliqui Subdiaconi & Acoluthi Apostolici & Prælati domestici, omnes cum paramentis sibi convenientibus. De Prælatis tamen paratis præter Cardinales, non est necessarium, sed fiet ex sententia Pontificis. Parentur dua credentia, una pro electo & altera pro consecrante, & unum altare tantùm. Pro electo paretur sedes ornata in loco competenti, & faldistorium ante altare, pro consecrante faldistorium consuetum in cornu epistolæ, pro aliis scabella consueta. In credentiis parentur opportuna ad consecrationem, & ad celebrationem Missæ, candelabráque cum luminaribus opportunis in altari, & credentia. Paratis omnibus rebus, electus accedat ad altare, & depositá mitra procumbat super faldistorium. Orabit & surget, & remoto faldistorio faciet confessionem cum consecratore à sinistra sibi assistente. (Ergò etiam confessione & absolutione ab alio opus habet, cui data est omnis & summa remittendi potestas!) Finita confessione electus cum mitra revertetur ad sedem suam. Consecrator accedet ad altare, osculabitur, incensabit, si placuerit, more solito, & reversus ad suum faldistorium, leget Introitum, & Kyrieeleison, & alia usque ad Alleluja, sive ultimum versum tractûs exclusive, & cum oratione diei dicetur oratio pro electo, ut supra. Idem faciet electus in sede cum suis assistentibus, versus ad altare.
units.tr: From this he also adds, first, a consecration without the blessing and the coronation. He says above all that it may be done privately, if it pleases the Pope, but that it is more fitting to do it on a Sunday or feast day in the following manner: Both the consecrator and the elect shall be prepared with all the pontifical vestments, with the customary psalms and prayers. The elect shall receive gloves and a ring only, but all the other things. At least two or three deacons and one presbyter cardinal assist, and along with the consecrator himself, if he is a cardinal bishop (he must be so by hypothesis, if the consecration is to be lawful, although in Baronius at the year 1058, no. 12 it is found that a man was consecrated by a presbyter!), as is fitting, two other cardinal bishops; some subdeacons and acolytes of the Apostolic See and domestic prelates, all in the vestments proper to them. Concerning the prelates, however, apart from the cardinals, who are prepared, it is not necessary, but it will be done at the discretion of the Pope. Two credence tables shall be prepared, one for the elect and the other for the consecrator, and only one altar. For the elect a decorated seat shall be prepared in a suitable place, and a faldstool before the altar; for the consecrator the customary faldstool on the epistle side; for the others the customary stools. On the credence tables shall be placed the things suitable for the consecration and for the celebration of Mass, and candelabra with suitable lights on the altar and on the credence table. When everything is ready, the elect shall approach the altar, and, laying aside the mitre, shall kneel down on the faldstool. He shall pray and rise, and, the faldstool being removed, he shall make confession with the consecrator standing on his left. (So he needs absolution and confession from another, to whom the whole and supreme power of forgiving has been given!) When the confession is finished, the elect shall return with his mitre to his seat. The consecrator shall go up to the altar, kiss it, incense it if he wishes, in the usual way, and returning to his faldstool he shall read the Introit, the Kyrie eleison, and the other things up to the Alleluia, or up to the last verse of the tract exclusive, and with the collect of the day the prayer for the elect shall be said, as above. The elect shall do the same in his seat with his attendants, turned towards the altar.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: His dictis, electus procumbet cum mitra in faldistorio ante altare, consecrator ab ejus sinistris super aliquo scabello, alii autem in suis scabellis, & per unum ex Subdiaconis fit litania, nam examinatio antiqua Sanctorum patrum, & alia præcedentia omittuntur (Belle, pulchrè scilicet! Ergò non aliis, sed Papæ facilè debent manus imponi! alii, non Papa, qui Doctor summus fieri debet, debent explorari, utrum sint apti ad docendum! Sed fallor; Papa fit Episcopus, non ut doceat! per Enthusiasmum judicat de iis, quæ non novit!) Cùm ventum fuerit ad locum, ubi dicitur; Ut hunc electum; surgit consecrator, non tamen cum baculo, & versus ad electum tertiò dicit signans; Ut hunc electum & c. Et alii omnes Episcopi Cardinales cum suis libris procumbentes, tamen erecta aliquantulum facie idem faciunt. Finita litania, surgunt omnes, & electus revertitur ad sedem suam, & sedet cum mitra. Consecrator venit ante eum, & aliis prætermissis stans cum mitra, simul adjuvantibus eum Episcopis Cardinalibus, imponit librum Evangeliorum supra cervicem electi sine mitra sedentis: nam tunc mitra ei abstrahitur, quam duo Diaconi retinent usque in finem: & Consecrator atque assistentes Episcopi ponunt ambas manus super caput electi, dicentes: Accipe Spiritum S. quod
units.tr: These things having been said, the elect shall kneel with his mitre on the faldstool before the altar, the consecrator on his left on a certain stool, and the others on their own stools, and the litany is sung by one of the subdeacons; for the ancient examination of the holy Fathers and the other preceding things are omitted (splendid, indeed, and beautifully done! Therefore hands should be laid easily on the Pope, not on the others, while the others, though the Pope, who ought to be made supreme teacher, should be examined as to whether they are fit to teach! But I am mistaken: the Pope is made a bishop, not in order to teach! By enthusiasm he judges things he does not know!). When the point is reached where it is said, "That you would bless this elect," the consecrator rises, not however with his staff, and turning to the elect he says three times, making the sign of the cross, "That you would bless this elect," etc. And all the other cardinal bishops, kneeling with their books, likewise do the same, but with their faces somewhat raised. When the litany is finished, all rise, and the elect returns to his seat and sits down with his mitre. The consecrator comes before him, and, the other things being omitted, standing with his mitre, with the cardinal bishops assisting him at the same time, he lays the book of the Gospels upon the neck of the elect, who is seated without his mitre; for then the mitre is taken from him, and two deacons keep it until the end; and the consecrator and the assisting bishops place both hands upon the head of the elect, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit," which

units.la: Consecratio ipsa, ut sola fieri solet; quod tamen Consecrator alte dicit, alii submisse, ut alia omnia. Si aderunt alii Episcopi parati, poterunt & ipsi manus imponere, & omnia legere, ut Cardinales assistentes. Deinde surgit electus, & Diaconi assistentes retinent librum super illius spatulis: Consecrator autem sine mitra dicit super eum orationem: Propiciare Domine supplicationibus &c. Deinde voce mediocri extensis manibus ante pectus dicat hanc praefationem: Per omnia saecula &c. In Oratione produnt καταξηλίαν vestitus Sacerdotalis in V. T. Ea autem finita consecrator genuflexus & sine mitra versus ad altare incipit hymnum: Veni creator; Et tam electus quam alii genuflectunt eodem modo, finito primo versu surgunt omnes, & chorus prosequitur hymnum. Interim caput electi sedentis in sua sede circum ligatur panniculo lineo subtili per Diaconum: ne oleum fluat super capillos, ita ut panniculi extremitates retro super cervicem pendeant. Deinde consecrator accedens ad electum cum mitra & intincto pollice dextra manus in Sacro Chrismate stans ungit Caput electi sedentis formans primum signum crucis, quo coronam totam amplectatur. Deinde ungat reliquum coronae, dicendo: Ungatur &c. Et abstersò aliquantulum pollice cum mica panis deposita mitra prosequatur praefationem incipiens: Hoc Domine &c. (In qua oratione petunt, ut pedes Papae speciosi sint ad evangelizandam pacem, ut accipiat ministerium reconciliationis in verbo, & in factis, in virtute signorum & prodigiorum; ut sit sermo ejus, ut praedicatio, non persuasibilibus humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in ostensione spiritus, & virtutis; ut recte utatur clavibus, non ut glorietur potestate, quam tribuat Dominus in aedificationem, non in destructionem, & ut tanquam fidelis & prudens servus de familia cibum in tempore opportuno; (Cum tamen Papa Evangelium non praedicet, miraculis non fulgeat, glorietur potestate, imo ea abutatur vel maxime ad destructionem!) Post haec consecrator inchoat Schola prosequente Antiphonam. Unguentum in capite &c. Deinde repetatur Antiphona. Unguentum in capite &c. Interim imponitur mappula ad collum electi sedentis, supra quam imponit postea manus, & consecrator inungit illi manus cum Sacro Chrismate; ut fit aliis Episcopis, dicens: Ungantur &c. In qua oratione eadem καταξηλία, respectu uncti per Samuelem Davidis. Electus manus inunctas simul junctas in mappula pendente a collo reponit: baculus non datur: sed mox consecrator deposita mitra benedicit annulum preciosum, imponendo electo, dicens: Creator &c. Electus etiam surgit, dum dicitur oratio; annulum ipsum interea tenet manu dextra aliquis acoluthus ante consecratorem genuflexus. Consecrator dicta oratione aspergit annulum aqua benedicta (ut nulla non adsit superstitio!) perstitio!) & illum imponit in digito annulari dextra manûs electi sedentis, dicens: Accipe annulum fidei &c. (quo ei Ecclesiam desponsant!) Et dum imponit, osculatur manum electi: deinde adjuvantibus Episcopis assistentibus librum Evangeliorum ab ejus spatulis removens, dat ad manus electi sedentis, dicens: Accipe Evangelium & vade praedica (facit scilicet!) populo tibi commisso &c. His peractis consecrator redit ad suum faldistorium, & lavat manus; Electo autem sedente in sua sede Diaconus Cardinalis tergit caput cum medulla panis diligenter, & cum panno mundo: Deinde cum pectine mundat & componit capillos & imponit ei mitram, & tunc electus lavat manus cum mica panis, & bene mundat. Quibus finitis, tam consecrator quàm alii omnes Cardinales praesentes osculantur pedes &c. Vide clausulam consecrationis in Presbyterum per omnia fere similem.
units.tr: The consecration itself is done alone, as is customary; the consecrator, however, says it aloud, the others quietly, as with everything else. If other bishops are present and prepared, they too may lay on hands and read everything, like the assisting cardinals. Then the elect rises, and the assisting deacons hold the book over his shoulders. The consecrator, however, without his mitre, says over him the prayer: "Be propitious, O Lord, to our supplications," etc. Then, with his hands extended before his breast, he says in a moderate voice this preface: "For ever and ever," etc. In the prayer they reveal the correspondence [καταξηλία] of the priestly vestments in the Old Testament. When this is finished, the consecrator, kneeling and without his mitre, turns to the altar and begins the hymn: "Come, Creator Spirit." Both the elect and the others kneel in the same way; when the first verse is finished, all rise, and the choir continues the hymn. Meanwhile, the head of the elect, who is seated in his chair, is bound round by a deacon with a fine linen cloth, so that the oil does not run over the hair, the ends of the cloth hanging down behind over the neck. Then the consecrator, approaching the elect with his mitre, standing, and with the thumb of his right hand dipped in the holy chrism, anoints the head of the seated elect, making first the sign of the cross, so that it embraces the whole crown. Then he anoints the rest of the crown, saying: "Let him be anointed," etc. And having wiped the thumb a little with a crumb of bread, the mitre being set down, he goes on with the preface, beginning: "O Lord, this..." (In this prayer they ask that the feet of the Pope may be beautiful for proclaiming peace, that he may receive the ministry of reconciliation in word and in deed, in the power of signs and wonders; that his speech and his preaching may be not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power; that he may use the keys rightly, not glorying in the power which the Lord has given for building up and not for destruction, and that, as a faithful and wise servant of the household, he may give food in due season. (Yet the Pope neither preaches the Gospel, nor shines with miracles, nor glories in power, but rather abuses it most of all for destruction!) After this the consecrator begins, with the choir following, the antiphon: "Ointment is on the head," etc. Then the antiphon is repeated: "Ointment is on the head," etc. Meanwhile a towel is placed about the neck of the seated elect, and upon it the consecrator afterwards lays his hands and anoints his hands with the holy chrism, as is done for the other bishops, saying: "Let them be anointed," etc. In this prayer there is the same correspondence [καταξηλία] with respect to the one anointed by Samuel, David. The elect places his anointed hands joined together in the towel hanging from his neck; no staff is given; but soon the consecrator, setting down the mitre, blesses a precious ring, placing it upon the elect, saying: "Creator," etc. The elect also rises while the prayer is said; meanwhile some acolyte, kneeling before the consecrator, holds the ring in his right hand. When the prayer is said, the consecrator sprinkles the ring with holy water (so that there may be no lack of superstition!) and places it on the ring finger of the right hand of the seated elect, saying: "Receive the ring of faith," etc. (by which they wed him to the Church!). And as he places it he kisses the hand of the elect; then, with the assisting bishops helping, he removes the book of the Gospels from his shoulders and gives it into the hands of the seated elect, saying: "Receive the Gospel and go and preach" (of course he does!) "to the people committed to you," etc. When these things are done, the consecrator returns to his faldstool and washes his hands. The elect, seated in his chair, is carefully dried on the head with the crumb of bread and a clean cloth by a cardinal deacon; then he cleans and arranges the hair with a comb and places the mitre on him; and then the elect washes his hands with a crumb of bread and cleans them well. When these things are finished, both the consecrator and all the other cardinals present kiss his feet, etc. See the conclusion of the consecration of a presbyter, which is almost entirely similar in every respect.

units.la: XXXVIII. Jam tandem exhibere incipit consecrationem cum benedictione & coronatione Romani Pontificis conjunctam.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Now at last he begins to set out the consecration, joined with the blessing and the coronation of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Monet primò, eadem servari in electo, qui priùs erat Episcopus, usque: ubi incipit, cantores. Postea subjungit: Constituto Die Dominico Pontifex è cubili summo mane ad cameram paramenti, quam Papagalli appellant, egreditur. Ibi à Diaconis Cardinalibus, Subdiaconis, Acoluthis & aliis officialibus consuetis paratur amictu albo, & longo cingulo, stola, pluviali rubeo, & mitra preciosa. Cardinales alii circumsistunt, & omnes Prälati & Officiales cum suis cappis laneis. Sic electus Pontifex paratus cruce praecedente progreditur ad Petrum ordine aliàs consueto: Diaconis Cardinalibus hinc & inde fimbrias pluvialis sustinentibus: Caudam autem pluvialis portabit nobilior laicus, qui erit in curia, etiamsi esset Imperator, vel Rex, supra eum octo nobiles, sive Oratores portant umbellum hastilibus octo sustentatam, quam hodie baldachinum appellant, ante eum duo servientes armorum portant faldistorium cum magno cussino, forerius rapetum, & parvum scabellum & cussinum. Considera, Lector, pompam, & fastum, atque obstupesce mente videns humilem hunc Christi humilis & pauperis Vicarium, vel potiùs Antichristum sese super omnia efferentem! Cum Papa electus pervenerit ad portam ultimam palati, quae est in capite porticus Ecclesiae S. Petri in Palatio apud portam, extenditur tapetum, ponitur faldistorium & super illud cussinum magnum, & ad pedes parvum scabellum: & sedens ibi electus recipit ad osculum pedis Canonicos & Capitulum Basilicae S. Petri; deinde surgens intrat Ecclesiam per portam, quae est in medio; & progressus usque ad secundum circulum porphyreticum detracta mitra orat versus ad altare supra faldistorium à supradictis ibi para-
units.tr: He first advises that the same things are observed for the one elected who was previously a bishop, up to the point where it begins, "the cantors." Afterwards he adds: On the appointed Sunday the Pontiff goes out early in the morning from his bedchamber to the room of vestments, which the Papagalli call the room. There the deacon cardinals, subdeacons, acolytes and other customary officials dress him in a white amice, a long girdle, a stole, a red cope and a precious mitre. Other cardinals stand around him, and all the prelates and officials in their woollen capes. Thus the elected Pontiff, fully vested, proceeds to St Peter's with the cross going before him, in the usual order: deacon cardinals holding the fringes of the cope on either side, and the train of the cope carried by the most noble layman at the court, even if he were an emperor or king. Above him eight nobles, or envoys, carry a canopy supported by eight poles, which today they call the baldachin. Before him two armed attendants carry a faldstool with a large cushion, a rug, and a small footstool and cushion. Consider, reader, the pomp and show, and be astonished in mind as you see this humble vicar of Christ, the lowly and poor one, or rather Antichrist, lifting himself above everything! When the elected Pope has reached the last door of the palace, which is at the head of the portico of the church of St Peter in the Palace, by the door, a carpet is spread out, a faldstool is placed, with a large cushion on it and a small footstool at his feet. Sitting there, the elected one receives the canons and chapter of the basilica of St Peter to kiss his foot. Then, rising, he enters the church by the door that is in the middle, and when he has advanced as far as the second porphyry circle, with his mitre removed, he prays towards the altar above the faldstool prepared there by those mentioned above.

units.la: Consecrationis, quae simul cum benedictione et coronatione fit, antecedentia. paratum; & tunc supra scabellum parvum ponitur parvus cussinus, facta oratione surgit, reassumit mitram, & pergit ad Capellam S. Gregorii, & sedens in sede ibi parata recipit omnes Cardinales, & alios Prælatos cum suis cappis ad reverentiam. Cardinales ad manus sub auriphrygio; Prælatos ad pedis osculum; Tunc surgens sine mitra astante cruce populo benedicit, dicens. Sit nomen &c. Subdiaconus dicturus epistolam depositá cruce post benedictionem capit omnia sua paramenta: Et simul cum eo acoluthi exuunt cappas, & induunt superpellicia, super rochetum ad partem se retrahentes: Sedet deinde electus aliquantulum cum mitra: Et iterum surgens sine mitra versus ad altare sub silentio dicit: Pater noster &c. Tum altè incipit pro tertia: Deus in adjutorium &c. Et sic stat quousque incipiatur psalmus: Legem pone. Inde sedet cum mitra, & assistentibus Episcopis cum libro: ac juvantibus hinc inde Diaconis, ut moris est, incipit Psalmum: Quàm dilecta. Interim Subdiaconus Apostolicus lecturus epistolam, ut diximus, paratus omnibus suis paramentis ex altare subministrante sacrista accipit sandalia, quæ reverenter portantur ad electum sequentibus illum acoluthis cum superpelliciis, & simul cum cubiculario camera imponit pedibus sua sanctitatis (ita audiunt impurissima sæpe omnis fœditatis mancipia, nec non Sanctissimi Patres; quando Christus ad coelestem suum Patrem simpliciter dixit: Sancte pater! Joh. XVII.11.) acoluthis circum circa fimbrias pluvialis elevantibus supra illorum capita. Impositis sandaliis Diaconus lecturus Evangelium cum duobus aliis Diaconis, qui assistent Papæ, capiunt paramenta sua, ille amictum album, stolam, cingulum, dalmaticam, manipulum vero postea accipiet in altari; Alii vero duo capient amictum, & dalmaticas tantùm; Induti reverenter simul ad electum accedent, qui finitis Psalmis, cùm dicitur Capitulum pro tertia, surgit cum mitra: & finito versiculo, depositá mitra & astantibus duobus ceroferariis dicit: Dominus vobiscum: orationem pro tertia: librum prior Episcoporum Cardinalium, qui assistere debet, sustinet supra caput. Episcopi vero assistentes juvant: Et tenent candelam accensam. Dicto; Dominus vobiscum; post orationem liber removetur, ceroferarii discedunt, & dicto à Cantoribus: Benedicamus Domino. Papa sedet cum mitra, & lavat manus Episcopo Cardinalis adjuvante, & reliqua, ut aliàs, lotis manibus Episcopus Cardinalis redit ad locum suum: & Papa deponit mitram, pluviale & stolam & Diacono lecturo Evangelium ante se stante induitur consuetis paramentis, quæ per acoluthos hoc ordine portantur ex altari, & ipsi Diacono porriguntur. Duo Diaconi assistentes, & post eos duo Subdiaconi adjuvant vestientem. Primum portatur cingulum cum succinctorio, Crux pastoralis, deinde stola, tunicella dalmatica, chirotheca, planeta, mitra auri phrygiata: annulus autem non datur, si non est consecratus Episcopus, quem, si esset consecratus, Card. Episcopus assistens imponeret.
