Postea disputat de colore, & diversos diversorum habitus recenset, atque subjungit, olim Hostiensem consecrâsse pallio indutum, Portuensi & Albanensi assistentibus, jam verò ad tollendas, ut arbitratur, contentiones introductum esse, ut prior Episcoporum Card. cum 2. senioribus munus obeat. Qui consecraturus est, ita pergit, procedat ad altare majus S. Petri, ibique ad partem capiat sandalia: & paramenta omnia Pontificalia, ac si celebraturus esset cum Psalmis & orationibus consuetis, ibique expectet Pontificem. Interim Pontifici assistet subprior Episcopus Cardinalium. Paratis omnibus ordinibus, Pontifex incensum mittet in turibulo, & prior Diaconorum cum ferula processionem ad altare majus ordinabit hoc modo; familiares Papæ, minores nobiles & cubicularii: Nobiles majores & Barones, Conservatores & Oratores Laici, & non Prælati. Secretarii & advocati mixtim, ita ut duo antiquiores ex utroque ordine sint in digniori loco, Acoluthi, Clerici Camera, Auditores, acoluthus turiferarius, acoluthi ceroferarii: qui septem numero esse deberent, Subdiaconus cum cruce Papali & aliis Subdiaconis; Subdiaconi duo Latini & Græcus cum libris Evangeliorum; Et nota quòd pro Epistola & Evangelio in lingua Græca solebant vocari in hac celebritate Monachi ex monasterio crypta ferrata; (certo indicio de aliorum hac etiam in parte ignorantia;) Dein ordinem incedendi tradit. De Pontifice: Si pedibus incedet, Diaconi assistentes fimbrias pluvialis portabunt, & major princeps Caudam; octo nobiles, seu Oratores baldachinum supra ejus Caput. De ministro Ceremoniarum: Immediatè ante Pontificem præcedit cum 2. arundinibus super alteram stuppam, super alteram verò candelam ardentem portans. Et cùm Pontifex Capellam S. Gregorii exierit, ceremoniarius ad eum conversus ignem stupæ mittit, & genuflexus alta voce dicit: Pater Sancte, sic transit gloria mundi; quod tertiò facit distincto æquali spatio, antequam perveniat ad Capellæ portam (Ergò Papæ gloria, de qua monendus est, ut clariùs etiam apparebit, est gloria mundi! Gloria, quæ citò transit, licèt Sixtus V. ad verborum horum prolationem regesserit; Sed nostra gloria nunquam peribit;) Procedunt deinde omnes per navim ipsius Capellæ S. Gregorii, ubi sepulchra sunt Rom. Pont. & cùm illam exierint, flectunt ad dextram: & per portam, quæ est ante altare, ingrediuntur Capellam, & ascendunt etiam ad dextram, antequam Papa cancellos Capellæ intret: tres ultimi Presbyteri Cardinales veniunt ei obviam: & osculantur os & pectus Pontificis à seniori incipientes: deinde ante Diaconos assistentes procedunt. Cùm autem perventum fuerit ad altare, Pontifex depositâ mitrâ facit Orationem super faldistorium, deinde surgens, remoto faldistorio facit Confessionem more solito, stans hoc ordine, à Pontificis dextra stat Episcopus Cardinalis, Consecrator, vel assistens, & post eum Diaconus Cardinalis assistens, & post eum Diaconus Cardinalis assistens, à sinistris stat Diaconus Card. lecturus Evangelium, post eum Diaconus Card. assistens: post quem genuflexus manet Subdiaconus Latinus cum libro Evmngeliorum & manipulo Pontificis, quem illi imponit dicto; Indulgentiam &c. Interim Cantores Cantant introitum Missæ, & Kyrieeleison.
units.tr: The preceding things of the consecration, which takes place together with the blessing and coronation. Then a small cushion is placed on the small footstool. When the prayer is finished he rises, puts on his mitre again, and goes to the chapel of St Gregory. Sitting in the seat prepared there, he receives all the cardinals and the other prelates in their copes, for reverence: the cardinals to the hand beneath the golden fringe, the prelates to the kiss of the foot. Then he rises without the mitre, and with the cross standing by and the people present, he blesses them, saying, "Blessed be the name of the Lord, etc." The subdeacon who is to read the epistle, after the blessing, puts down the cross and takes all his vestments. At the same time the acolytes take off their copes and put on surplices over their rochets, drawing back to one side. The elected one then sits for a little while with his mitre. Rising again without the mitre, he turns to the altar and says the Our Father in silence. Then he begins aloud the prayer for the third hour: "O God, come to my aid, etc." and stands thus until the psalm "Make me to know thy law" begins. Then he sits with his mitre, and with the bishops standing by holding the book, and with the deacons helping on either side as is customary, he begins the psalm "How lovely." Meanwhile the apostolic subdeacon, who is to read the epistle as we have said, now fully vested, receives sandals from the sacristan who serves at the altar. These are carried reverently to the elected one, with the acolytes following in surplices. Together with the chamberlain of the chamber he puts them on the feet of his holiness (so the most unclean creatures of every filth often hear it, and also the most holy Fathers, when Christ simply said to his heavenly Father, "Holy Father!" John 17:11), while the acolytes lift up the fringes of the cope around his head. When the sandals are on, the deacon who is to read the Gospel, together with two other deacons who attend the Pope, take up their vestments: he takes the white amice, stole, girdle and dalmatic, but will take the maniple afterwards at the altar; the other two take only the amice and dalmatics. Clothed, they go reverently together to the elected one. When the psalms are finished, and the chapter for the third hour is said, he rises with the mitre; and when the versicle is finished, he takes off the mitre, and with two candle-bearers standing by, says, "The Lord be with you," and the prayer for the third hour. The senior bishop cardinal, who ought to be present, holds the book above his head. The assisting bishops help, and hold a lighted candle. After "The Lord be with you" and the prayer, the book is removed, the candle-bearers depart, and the cantors sing "Let us bless the Lord." The Pope sits with his mitre and washes his hands, with the bishop cardinal assisting, and the rest as at other times. When his hands are washed, the bishop cardinal returns to his place. The Pope takes off the mitre, cope and stole, and the deacon who is to read the Gospel, standing before him, is vested in the usual vestments. These are carried in this order by the acolytes from the altar and handed to the deacon himself. Two assisting deacons, and after them two subdeacons, help in dressing him. First the girdle with its strap is carried, then the pastoral staff, then the stole, the tunicle, the dalmatic, the gloves, the chasuble, and the golden mitre with its fringe. The ring, however, is not given unless he has been consecrated a bishop; if he had been, the assisting bishop cardinal would put it on. After this he discusses the colour, and recounts the different dress of different men, and adds that formerly the bishop of Ostia used to consecrate while wearing the pallium, with the bishops of Porto and Albano assisting, but that now, as he thinks, to remove disputes it has been introduced that the senior bishop cardinal, with two of the senior cardinals, performs the office. He who is to consecrate, so he proceeds, is to go to the high altar of St Peter, and there take his sandals on one side, and all the pontifical vestments, as if he were about to celebrate with the customary psalms and prayers, and there wait for the Pontiff. Meanwhile the senior bishop cardinal is to attend the Pontiff. With all the orders ready, the Pontiff puts incense into the censer, and the senior deacon orders the procession to the high altar with the staff in this way: the household of the Pope, the lesser nobles and the chamberlains; the greater nobles and barons, the conservators and lay envoys, and not prelates. Secretaries and advocates mixed together, so that the two senior from each group are in the more honourable place; acolytes, clerks of the chamber, auditors, the acolyte who carries the censer, the acolytes with candles, who ought to number seven. The subdeacon with the papal cross and the other subdeacons; two Latin subdeacons and a Greek with the books of the Gospels. And note that for the epistle and Gospel in the Greek language, in this celebration, the monks were customarily called from the monastery of the Crypt with iron gates; (a sure sign of the ignorance of others in this respect too). Then he sets out the order of going. As for the Pontiff: if he goes on foot, the assisting deacons will carry the fringes of the cope, and the chief prince the train; eight nobles, or envoys, the canopy over his head. As for the master of ceremonies: He goes directly before the Pontiff, carrying two reeds with tow on one, and a burning candle on the other. And when the Pontiff has come out of the chapel of St Gregory, the master of ceremonies, turning to him, sets fire to the tow, and kneeling, says in a loud voice: "Holy Father, so passes the glory of the world"; which he does three times, at equal intervals, before they reach the door of the chapel. (So the Pope's glory, about which he is to be warned, as will appear more clearly, is the glory of the world! A glory that passes quickly, although Sixtus V, at the utterance of these words, retorted: "But our glory will never perish.") Then all proceed through the nave of the chapel of St Gregory itself, where the tombs of the Roman Pontiffs are, and when they have left it, they turn to the right, and through the door which is in front of the altar they enter the chapel, and go up also on the right, before the Pope enters the chancel of the chapel. The three last presbyter cardinals come to meet him, and kiss his mouth and breast, beginning with the senior. Then they proceed before the assisting deacons. When they have come to the altar, the Pontiff, with his mitre removed, offers a prayer over the faldstool; then rising, with the faldstool removed, he makes the confession in the usual way, standing in this order: on the Pontiff's right stands the bishop cardinal, the consecrator or assistant, and after him the assisting deacon cardinal, and after him another assisting deacon cardinal. On his left stands the deacon cardinal who is to read the Gospel, after him the assisting deacon cardinal, and after him, kneeling, remains the Latin subdeacon with the book of the Gospels and the Pope's maniple, which he places on him, saying, "Indulgence, etc." Meanwhile the cantors sing the introit of the Mass, and the Kyrie eleison.

units.la: XXXIX. De ipsa consecratione ita pergit:
units.tr: XXXIX. He continues thus on the consecration itself:

units.la: Cantores, ut finierint Kyrieeleison, quiescent. Electus procumbet super faldistorium ante altare, ad ejus dextram Consecrator & ad sinistram Diaconus Evangelii super scabella, Diaconi assistentes post Pontificem duo, Episcopi Cardinales seniores hinc inde super scabella, alii omnes, ut commodum erit, genuflexi procumbent omnes cum mitris in Capite: & Diaconus Evangelii incipiet sine mitra litaniam: & omnes respondent replicando. Cùm perventum fuerit ad locum, ubi dicitur: Ut hunc electum &c. & etiam tertiò dicitur ab eodem Diacono, & tam Consecrator, quàm omnes alii in Episcopali dignitate constituti præsentes, & parati erecto Capite, & extensa dextra, non tamen moventes se de locis suis benedicunt consecrandum tertiò, ut in ordinario. Finita litania omnes surgunt & Consecrator stat ad infimum gradum sedis Papalis vertens faciem versus altare, medius inter duos seniores Episcopos Cardinales: qui etiam stolam habere debent & librum. Electus Pontifex ante eum stabit medius inter assistentes Diaconos vertens faciem suam ad faciem consecrantis. Episcopi, Archiepiscopi, Patriarchæ, qui aderunt parati cum suis libris, omnes accedent & circulum facient, & omnia cum consecratore dicent, voce tamen submissa depositis mitris & omnibus stantibus. Episcopus Cardinalis à sinistris super Pontificem dicit orationem, quâ finitâ usque; in unitate &c. ponit librum Evangeliorum apertum inter cervicem & spatulas electi: quem Diaconi Cardinales retinent usque in finem; Et tam consecrator, quàm alii 2. Episc. Cardinales ponunt primò manus super ejus caput nihil dicentes, & similiter faciunt omnes præsentes parati in Episcopatûs ordine constituti. Consecrator autem extensis manibus dicit præfationem consuetam: Per omnia &c. Et ungit &c. quæ suprà tradidimus.
units.tr: When the singers have finished the Kyrie eleison, they fall silent. The elect prostrates himself on the faldstool before the altar, with the consecrator at his right hand and the deacon of the Gospel at his left, on stools. The two assisting deacons stand behind the Pope. The senior cardinal bishops sit on stools on either side, and all the others kneel, as is convenient, with their mitres on their heads. The deacon of the Gospel begins the litany without a mitre, and all respond by repeating the words. When he reaches the place where it says "that you would deign to bless this elect," and the deacon says it a third time, the consecrator and all the others present who hold episcopal rank, standing ready with heads erect and right hands extended but without moving from their places, bless the one to be consecrated a third time, as in the ordinary rite. When the litany is finished, all rise. The consecrator stands on the lowest step of the papal throne, facing the altar, between the two senior cardinal bishops, who ought also to have a stole and a book. The elect, now Pope, stands before him between the assisting deacons, facing the consecrator's face. The bishops, archbishops and patriarchs who are present, ready with their books, all come forward and form a circle, and they say everything together with the consecrator, though in a low voice, with their mitres removed and everyone standing. The cardinal bishop on the left says the prayer over the Pope. When it is finished, as far as "in unity," etc., he places the open Book of the Gospels between the neck and shoulder blades of the elect. The cardinal deacons hold it there to the end. The consecrator and the other two cardinal bishops first lay their hands on his head, saying nothing, and all the others present who hold episcopal rank do likewise. The consecrator, with hands extended, then says the usual preface: "Through all things," etc. And he anoints, etc., as we have set out above.

units.la: XL. Sequentia adhibentur, ubi Papa jam Episcopus est tantùm benedicendus & coronandus.
units.tr: XL. The following are used where the Pope is already a bishop and is only to be blessed and crowned.

units.la: Facta confessione immediatè accipit mitram & sedet in sede, sive faldistorio sibi parato inter sedem eminentem & altare re: & 3. primi Episcopi accedunt ad Pontificem, & faciem ante illius faciem tenentes sine mitra, illorum junior super Pontificem stantem sine mitra ipse in medio duorum stans primam dicit orationem, in qua precantur, ut quem indicium sua plebis elegerit, sentire faciat, se ejus munere ad hunc apicem pervenisse; Secundam secundus & ipse in medio; Tertiam prior in eodem loco, quà petunt, ut Deus, quem de humili cathedra violenter sublimatum sublimarint, (quàm egregiè ista cum dictis & probatis conveniunt!) virtutum meritis cumulet. Dictis orationibus Papa etiam sine mitra accedit ad altare, & prior Diaconorum secundo adjuvante capit pallium de altari: & imponit Pontifici, & dicit: Accipe pallium Sanctam plenitudinem Pontificalis officii ad honorem omnipotentis Dei, gloriosissimæ Virginis Mariæ, ejus Matris, B. Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, & S. Rom. Ecclesiæ; Et firmat cum spinulis. (Simile planè est Pallium hoc aliorum Episcoporum & Archiepiscoporum palliis; De quorum confectione ac superstitiosa consecratione vide Sacr. Cerem. l. 1. Sect. 10. Sunt ex lana & lino parva admodùm, sed instanter, instantiùs & instantissimè petentibus singula ditissimis Archiepiscopis 60000. jam vel 70000. ducatorum, aut carius etiam de corpore pauperis Petri sumpta Gehasi & Simonis artibus, juxta illud scilicet: Gratis accepistis gratis date; venduntur;) Accepto pallio Pontifex accedit ad altare sine mitra: illud osculatur primùm, & deinde librum Evangeliorum, quem Subdiaconus à sinistra parte offert; Imponit incensum in turibulo, Diacono Evangelii offerente naviculam, incensat altare more solito, & accepta mitra in cornu altaris stans, à Diacono incensatur, & in os recipit tunc Diaconus osculum, ut aliàs; sed ascendit ad Cathedram eminentem (an ut ministerium concionatoris ordiatur? Non;) & sedens recipit ad reverentiam Cardinales & Prælatos omnes paratos, Cardinales ad osculum pedis, manûs & oris, alios paratos, ad osculum pedis & manûs. Finitâ reverentiâ surgit Papa sine mitra, & legit introitum & Kyrieeleison, sustinente librum Cardinale Episcopo, cum aliis assistentibus (Ipse igitur non dignus est, ut accipiat librum, vel liber Orationum non dignus est, ut accipiatur ab eo; Orationum, quas Deus accipere debet;) Deinde in voce dicit: Gloria &c. & orationes opportunas, & secretè orationem pro se. Dictis orationibus sedet, & prior Diaconorum cum ferula descendit ad Confessionem B. Petri cum Subdiaconis, Auditoribus, Secretariis, & Advocatis: quibus in 2. acies distributis, ita ut in qualibet acie sint ex omnium ordine, faciunt laudes Pontifici stantes capitibus detectis, Papa & omnibus sedentibus in locis suis. Prior Diaconorum incipit solus alta voce, quasi legendo: Exaudi. Subdiaconi &c. respondent: Domino nostro N. à Deo decreto (ut caetera omnia, sed non speciali cura & approbatione dato, ut ostensum Differt. VI.) summo Pontifici, & universali Papa, vita. Et sic tertiò dicitur & respondetur. Subsequenter idem prior Diaconorum dicet: Salvator mundi; Et illi respondebunt: Tu illum ad juva. Tertiò utrumque similiter. Deinde idem: S. Maria; & illi: Tu illum adjuva. bis. Idem; S. Michael; & illi; Tu illum &c. Tunc deinceps semel S. Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Joannes Baptista, Petre, Paule, Stephane, Leo, Gregori, Benedicte, Basili, Sabba, Agnes, Cecilia, Lucia. Et ad singulos & singulas. Tu illum adjuva; (Sine ullo discrimine, praeter illud numeri, invocationis Dei & creaturarum;) Finitis laudibus dicitur Epistola Latinè & deinde Graecè (ὑστερον πρότερον! Sed Latina praeferunt! Sed Graeca non intelligunt! Latinis autem praemissis, aliquo modo, quid Graecè sequatur subolfaciunt!) & proceditur in Missa usque ad finem. Datur benedictio, sed non publicantur tunc indulgentiae. Sed proceditur ad coronationem.
units.tr: Immediately after the confession, he takes the mitre and sits on the chair, or faldstool prepared for him between the raised seat and the altar. Then the three first bishops approach the Pope and, standing face to face with him, without mitres, the youngest of them, standing above the Pope, also without a mitre, says the first prayer, in which they pray that God would make him feel, whom the judgment of his people has chosen, that he has reached this summit by their office. The second, the second bishop, also standing in the middle, says the second prayer. The first, in the same place, says the third, in which they ask that God may heap virtues upon the one whom he has violently raised from a humble chair (how admirably these words agree with the facts and with what has been proved!). When the prayers are said, the Pope, still without a mitre, goes to the altar. The senior of the deacons, with the second deacon helping, takes the pallium from the altar and places it on the Pope, saying: "Receive the pallium, the holy fullness of the pontifical office, to the honour of almighty God, of the most glorious Virgin Mary, his Mother, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of the holy Roman Church." And he fastens it with pins. (This pallium is entirely like the palliums of the other bishops and archbishops. For their making and superstitious consecration, see Sacred Ceremonies, book 1, section 10. They are very small, made of wool and linen; but to those who ask more and more urgently and most urgently, the richest archbishops are sold each one for 60,000 or even 70,000 ducats, or more dearly still, taken from the body of poor Peter, by the arts of Gehazi and Simon, namely according to that saying: "Freely you have received, freely give.") When the pallium is received, the Pope goes to the altar without a mitre. He kisses it first, and then the Book of the Gospels, which the subdeacon offers from the left side. He puts incense into the censer, the deacon of the Gospel offering the incense boat, and he incenses the altar in the usual way. Then, taking the mitre and standing at the horn of the altar, he is incensed by the deacon. The deacon then receives the kiss on the mouth, as on other occasions; but he ascends to the raised chair (in order to begin the office of preacher? No;) and, seated, he receives the reverence of all the cardinals and prelates who are ready, the cardinals with the kiss on foot, hand and mouth, and the others who are ready with the kiss on foot and hand. When the reverence is finished, the Pope rises without a mitre and reads the introit and the Kyrie eleison, the cardinal bishop holding the book with the other assistants. (He himself, then, is not worthy to take the book, or the book of prayers is not worthy to be taken by him; prayers which God ought to receive.) Then he says aloud: "Glory," etc., and suitable prayers, and privately a prayer for himself. When the prayers are said, he sits, and the senior of the deacons, with the staff, goes down to the Confession of Saint Peter with the subdeacons, auditors, secretaries and advocates. They are divided into two lines, so that each line has members of every rank, and they sing praises to the Pope, standing with heads uncovered, while the Pope and all the others sit in their places. The senior deacon begins alone in a loud voice, as if reading: "Hear." The subdeacons, etc., respond: "To our lord N., given by God (like all the rest, but not given with special care and approval, as shown in Dissertation VI), the highest Pontiff and universal Pope, life." And so it is said and answered a third time. Afterwards the same senior deacon says: "Saviour of the world"; and they answer: "Help him." Three times, both in the same way. Then the same: "Saint Mary"; and they: "Help him." Twice. The same: "Saint Michael"; and they: "Help him," etc. Then after that, once each: Saint Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, John the Baptist, Peter, Paul, Stephen, Leo, Gregory, Benedict, Basil, Sabbas, Agnes, Cecilia, Lucy; and to each one, male or female: "Help him." (Without any distinction, except that of number, between the invocation of God and of creatures.) When the praises are finished, the Epistle is read in Latin and then in Greek [hysteron proteron]! But they prefer the Latin! But they do not understand the Greek! Yet with the Latin put first, somehow they smell out what follows in the Greek! The Mass then proceeds to the end. The blessing is given, but indulgences are not then proclaimed. But they proceed to the coronation.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Pontifex reassumptis chirothecis, & annulis cum omnibus paramentis suis, in quibus celebraverat, & cum Cardinalibus, Praelatis & Officialibus omnibus, ut in Missa paratis: procedit ad suggestum supra gradus Basilicae Apostolorum Principis ex materia constructum & ornatum, ibique in sede eminenti sibi parata sedet: Et cum omnes Praelati convenerint, & populus ex Basilica in Aream exierit. Diaconus à sinistris deponit mitram consuetam è Capite Pontificis, & Diaconus à dextris Tiaram, quod Regnum appellant, & triplici corona ornatum Pontificis Capiti imponit, (Coronationis praemium vide tract. de Gard. n. 52.) populo acclamante: Kyrieeleison. Et Diaconus à dextris Latinè; à sinistris vero vulgariter publicant plenarias Indulgentias. Tum paratur pro effio ad Lateranum. Dum vero paratur, nos in coronae triplicis & coronationis consideratione paulisper morabimur.
units.tr: Having put on again his gloves and rings and all the vestments in which he had celebrated, the Pope goes with the Cardinals, Prelates and all the officials, prepared as for Mass, to a platform of timber built and decorated above the steps of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, and there sits on the eminent seat prepared for him. When all the Prelates have gathered and the people have come out of the Basilica into the square, the deacon on his left takes the customary mitre from the Pope's head, and the deacon on his right places on the Pope's head the tiara, which they call the Regnum, adorned with a triple crown (for the reward of the coronation see tract. de Gard. n. 52.), while the people acclaim: Kyrie eleison [Κύριε ἐλέησον]. Then the deacon on the right announces plenary indulgences in Latin, and the deacon on the left in the vernacular. Then preparations are made for the procession to the Lateran. While these are being made, we shall linger a little over the triple crown and the meaning of the coronation.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: De origine coronationis Pontificum primò videamus; quae non satis certa est. Certum autem illud est, Pontifices nostros neque à Christo, neque à Petro, neque etiam à primis ejus per aliquot secula successoribus, ut vocant, coronationis exemplum accepisse. Non à Christo, quem non aurea & pretiosissimis gemmis ornata, sed spinea corona in Evangelio redimitum contemplamur, licet Regem Regum & Dominum Dominantium; De quo etiam constat, eum Regnum oblatum fugisse, & coram Pontio Pilato bonam confessionem edidisse: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo; Unde eum insignia quoque Regni mundani fugiturum fuisse, facili opere colligitur; Atque maximè mirandum esse, quòd Romanus Pontifex, quando Rex terrenus pius juxta atque fortissimus Balduinus Hierosolymæ coronâ aureâ coronari noluit, ea de causa, quòd Christus ibi spineam coronam portârit, quòd Romanus, inquam, Pontifex, humilis hujus atque ab omni pompa mundana alienissimi Christi, si vera jactat, Vicarius, in ea ipsa etiam urbe, in qua crucifixus est, Apoc. XI.8. &, quod maximum, eo ipso tempore, quo Christi Vicarius fieri vult, atque in hujus Vicariatûs indicium, coronâ aureâ & pretiosissimis gemmis radiante, eáque non unicâ, sed triplici coronari velit. Quænam quæsò illa inter Principem & Vicarium conformitas? Vel annon summa diversitas suggerere deberet cogitationes de Antichristo? Petrum quod attinet, præsumi debet, eum meliùs memorem fuisse verborum sui Domini: Vos autem non sic; quàm ut in hoc etiam Regibus terræ similis, imò superior iisdem fieri voluerit; Atque quando, juxta traditionem antiquam, non erecto, ut Christus, sed terram versus demisso capite crucifigi voluit, ne quasi eodem mactaretur honore, quantò magis cogitandum est, eum spineam Christi in aureám suam & triplicem quidem coronam nunquam commutaturum fuisse? Alia ille & longè alia sectatus est: Quod & Bernhardus de Consid. l. 4. c. 3. ad Eugenium II. ita perscripsit: Pastorem te huic populo aut nega, aut exhibe. Non negabis, ne cujus sedem tenes, te neges hæredem. Petrus hic est, qui nescitur aliquando processisse vel ornatus gemmis, vel sericis; Non tactus auro, non vectus equo, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepentibus militibus septus. Absque his tamen credidit, satis impleri posse mandatum, Pasce meas oves. In his successisti non Petro, sed Constantino. Sed neque in his succedunt primis, qui dicuntur, Petri successoribus, de quibus constat, eos similiter solam immarcessibilem justitiæ coronam, coronam etiam Martyrii deamâsse. Ut non à fidis Dei servis, sed à Deorum falsorum potiùs cultoribus, Sacerdotibus nimirum gentilibus, quod facit ad an. 34. 297. Baronius, coronas portandi ritus derivandus sit; Vel, si malunt, ab Idolis ipsis, uti Romanorum veterum Rhea, vel Cybele coronâ exaltatâ, testibus Nat. Comite l. IX. 5. Mythol. & Gerh. Jo. Vossio l. 2. 54. Idol. superbiit, & Ludovico, Romano Patricio in sua navigatione l. V. 2. & Christ. Arnold. in append. Rogerii aperta janua ad occultum Ehnicism. c. 25. p. 855. notantibus, in regno Calecut Diabolus informa monstrosa triplici tamen coronâ redimitus adoratur. Romani autem suas accepisse videntur; simplicem quidem, dictam Regnum ab Anastasio Dicoro, Orientis in Seculo sexto Imperatore, qui eam Clodovæo Franciæ Regi, hic, Sigeberto Gemblacensi teste, Romano Pontifici misit, S. Petro, id est, in sacrario ejus reponendam, non Capiti Pontificis imponendam; haud magis ac Abimelech Sacerdos consecrato à Davide, atque tentorio conventûs illato Goliathi gladio se accingere debuit; Alteram verò à Bonifacio VIII. qui dare regna & auferre pro arbitrio conabatur, uti Platina loquitur, post Extravagantem; Unam Sanctam, quâ Cæsareo-Papatum suum stabilire conatur, publicatam, juxta communem opinionem. Quare & cum successoribus cum duplici corona in statuis ac imaginibus Romæ Avenionéque conspicitur; Tertiam denique à Benedicto XII. Quamvis alii antiquiorem originem assignent. Hinc ortum est triregnum, tiara, Cidaris, Dianæ (voce obscurissima) chamaurus.
units.tr: Let us first look at the origin of the papal coronation, which is not very certain. It is certain, however, that our Popes did not receive the custom of coronation from Christ, nor from Peter, nor even from his first successors for some centuries, as they are called. Not from Christ, whom the Gospel shows us crowned not with gold and most precious gems but with a crown of thorns, although he is the King of kings and Lord of lords. It is also certain that he fled when a kingdom was offered him, and before Pontius Pilate made the good confession: My kingdom is not of this world. From this it is easily gathered that he would have fled the insignia of worldly kingdoms too. And it is most astonishing that the Roman Pontiff, when the earthly king Baldwin, a man as pious as he was brave, refused to be crowned with a golden crown in Jerusalem, for the reason that Christ had worn a crown of thorns there, that this Roman Pontiff, I say, the Vicar of this humble Christ, who was most alien to all worldly pomp (if he boasts truly of being his Vicar), should wish to be crowned, in that very city where he was crucified (Rev. 11:8), and, what is greatest, at the very time when he wishes to become Christ's Vicar, and as a token of this Vicariate, with a golden crown blazing with most precious gems, and not with one crown but with three. What agreement, I ask, is there between a Prince and a Vicar? Or should not such great difference rather suggest thoughts about Antichrist? As for Peter, it must be presumed that he remembered better the words of his Lord: But it shall not be so among you; far from wanting to become like the kings of the earth in this, or even superior to them. And since, according to ancient tradition, he wished to be crucified not upright like Christ but with his head bowed towards the earth, lest he should seem to be slain with the same honour, how much more must we think that he would never have exchanged Christ's thorny crown for a golden and indeed triple crown? He followed other and very different ways. Bernard also wrote this to Eugenius II in de Consid. l. 4. c. 3.: Either deny that you are a pastor to this people, or show yourself to be one. You will not deny it, lest by denying it you deny that you are heir to the seat you hold. Peter was he who is not known ever to have gone forth adorned with gems or silks; not touched with gold, not carried on a horse, nor attended by soldiers, nor surrounded by the clamour of soldiers. Yet without these he believed the command, Feed my sheep, could be fully carried out. In these things you have succeeded not Peter but Constantine. Nor indeed do those who are said to be the first successors of Peter succeed him in these things, of whom it is established that they likewise loved only the unfading crown of righteousness and the crown of martyrdom. So the custom of carrying crowns must be derived not from the faithful servants of God but rather from the worshippers of false gods, namely the pagan priests, as Baronius shows ad an. 34. 297.; or, if they prefer, from the idols themselves, as the Roman Rhea or Cybele took pride in her raised crown, as Natalis Comes notes l. IX. 5. Mythol. and Gerhard Johannes Vossius l. 2. 54. Idol., and as Ludovicus Romanus Patricius notes in sua navigatione l. V. 2. and Christian Arnold in append. Rogerii aperta janua ad occultum Ehnicism. c. 25. p. 855.: in the kingdom of Calicut the Devil is adored in monstrous form, yet crowned with a triple crown. The Romans, however, seem to have received theirs: one simple crown, called the Regnum by Anastasius Dicorus, Emperor of the East in the sixth century, who sent it to Clovis, King of the Franks, and according to Sigebert of Gembloux, Clovis then sent it to the Roman Pontiff to be placed in the sacristy of St Peter, that is, not to be placed on the Pontiff's head; no more than Abimelech the priest, consecrated by David, ought to gird himself with the sword of Goliath, which had been brought into the tabernacle of the assembly. The other crown was introduced by Boniface VIII, who tried to give and take away kingdoms at his pleasure, as Platina says, after the Extravagant Unam Sanctam, which, according to common opinion, was published to establish his Caesaro-Papacy. Hence successors are also seen with a double crown in statues and images at Rome and Avignon. Finally, a third was added by Benedict XII, although others assign a more ancient origin. From this arose the names triregnum, tiara, Cidaris, Dianae (a most obscure word) and chamaurus.

units.la: XLIII. Pretiosissima autem est corona, auro pretiosissimisque unionibus intertexta. Et eam quidem, quæ Amadeo Sabaudiæ Duci, vocato Felici V. imposita fuit, 30000. aureis, testibus Urspergense in Paralipomenis, & Ænea Sylvio in Epistola ad Johannem de Segovia, quæ in Fasc. rer. expet. sol. 25. 26. reperitur, æstimata fuit. Clemens V. in tumultu, quem paulò post exhibebimus, amisit Carbunculum pretii 6000. aureorum, Platina teste. Qui idem Pauli II. luxui describendo vix suum stylum sufficere putavit. Vide Differt. IV. Sect. 2. n. 62. Et jam in Hadriano I. scripsit, Paulum hunc, adeò his muliebribus delinimentis delectatum esse, conquisitis undique magno pretio gemmis, & exhausto penè Ecclesia Romana ærario, ut quotiescunque in publicum prodiret, Cybeles quædam Phrygia, de qua supra, atque turrita, non mitrata videretur. Hinc etiam ibidem conjicit, partim gemmarum pondere apoplexiam ei lethalem ortam esse. Neque desunt, qui scribant (vide Mey. Theat. Hist. p. 254.) inæstimabilem Caroli Burgundi Adamantem in prælio Gransonien si amissum, à milite repertum, & primò quidem vilissimo, deinde surgente semper multùm pretio à diversis venditum, tandem à Julio II. 20000. Ducatis emptum atque Triregno insertum esse. Quod sic inæstimabilis tandem pretii factum est; quo, ut etiam triplicitate sua, singulas omnium Regum coronas multùm superare censeri debet; Atque exinde, cæteris paribus, colligi, quænam sit illa mulier inaurata auro, lapide pretioso & margaritis, Apoc. XVII. 4.
units.tr: XLIII. The crown is most precious, woven with gold and the most precious pearls. The one placed on Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, called Felix V, was valued at 30,000 gold coins, according to the Urspergensis in his Paralipomena and Aeneas Sylvius in his letter to John of Segovia, which is found in the Fasc. rer. expet. pp. 25–26. Clement V, in the tumult which we shall describe shortly, lost a carbuncle worth 6,000 gold coins, according to Platina. The same Platina thought his pen could scarcely describe the luxury of Paul II. See Dissertation IV, section 2, n. 62. And already in his life of Hadrian I he wrote that this Paul was so delighted with these womanly adornments, with gems sought out everywhere at great cost and the treasury of the Roman Church almost emptied, that whenever he came out in public he looked like some Phrygian Cybele, of whom we spoke above, and turreted rather than mitred. Hence in the same place he also conjectures that a deadly apoplexy came upon him partly from the weight of the gems. Nor are there lacking those who write (see Meyer, Theatrum Historicum p. 254) that the inestimable diamond of Charles of Burgundy, lost in the battle of Granson, was found by a soldier, first sold for a very low price, then sold by various buyers at ever higher prices, and at last bought by Julius II for 20,000 ducats and set into the triregnum. Thus it became of inestimable value, so that even apart from its triple form it ought to be judged to far exceed the single crowns of all kings. From this, other things being equal, one may infer what that "woman adorned with gold, precious stone and pearls" is, Rev. 17:4.

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Pars XLIV. Non immeritò autem quæri potest, quodnam sit hujus triregni mysterium; Atque eò majore jure de eo quæri potest, quia ei olim inscriptum fuit: Mysterium. Quod & Brocardus Pontificius in Apoc. XVII.5. & Josephus Scaliger in Notis ad N.T. ex authore fide digno ad Julium III. qui verba: Julius Pontifex maximus, substituerit, duas esse indicat; & Lessius à Jacobo Magnæ Britanniæ Rege objectum negare non fuit ausus. Quin ipsi mysterium assignant, atque triregnum isthoc faciunt Hieroglyphicum Papalis Majestatis ad Cœlestia, terrena & inferna pertinentis, uti Reinaudus apud Dianam de Ador. Papæ. p.2: loquitur; vel ad tres orbis terrarum partes, ut conjiciunt alii. Prius mysterium nimis late extendit potestatem Pontificiam, cùm alter Deus in terris cœlestia & infernalia indispensabilia noverit; Posterius nimis coarctat eandem, cùm sic recens inventa quarta orbis pars Papæ non subsit, atque illam Regi Castiliæ donando, quæ sua non sunt, etiam ex hypothesi, donârit. Sed seriò. Vana illa sunt, & à communicum ipsa corona fastu & usurpatione profecta; Quemadmodum etiam Mysteria alia apud Corn. à Lap. in Zach. VI. à ternarii numeri perfectione & S. Trinitatis figura, & triade omnium virtutum rerumque consummationem, quæ in Christo fuerit & suo modo in Pontifice esse debeat, significantem, atque etiam ab eo, quòd Pontifex sit Sponsus & Princeps Ecclesiæ Victricis, Triumphatricis & Regnatricis; inani studio conquisita. Ut si quod heic mysterium subsit, nullum aliud sit, quàm quòd sic etiam agnosci debet meretrix; quæ infronte sua scriptum habet: Mysterium Apoc. XVII.5. sed redeamus jam è diverticulo in viam. Forte jam parata est processio ad Lateranum.
units.tr: Part XLIV. Not without reason may one ask what the mystery of this triregnum is, and all the more so because it was once inscribed with the word Mysterium. Brocardus the Papist, on Rev. 17:5, and Joseph Scaliger, in his Notes on the New Testament, indicate, on the authority of a trustworthy writer, that the words Julius Pontifex maximus were substituted for this to Julius III, and that there were two such inscriptions. Lessius did not dare to deny the objection raised by James, King of Great Britain. Indeed, they themselves assign a mystery and make the triregnum a hieroglyph of papal majesty pertaining to heavenly, earthly and infernal things, as Reinaudus speaks in Diana, de Ador. Papae, p. 2; or to the three parts of the world, as others conjecture. The former mystery extends the papal power too widely, since the other God on earth is acknowledged to have an indispensable power over heavenly and infernal things; the latter restricts it too narrowly, since the fourth part of the world, recently discovered, would not be subject to the Pope, and in giving it to the King of Castile he would be giving what is not his, even on their own hypothesis. But seriously: those are empty fancies, and the crown itself was devised out of pride and usurpation. Likewise the other mysteries sought out with vain zeal by Cornelius a Lapide on Zech. 6, that it signifies the perfection of the number three and the figure of the Holy Trinity, and the triad of all virtues and the completion of all things which was in Christ and ought in its own way to be in the Pope, and also that the Pope is the Bridegroom and Prince of the Victorious, Triumphant and Reigning Church. If there is any mystery here, it is no other than this: that in this way the harlot too should be recognised, who has written on her forehead: Mystery (Rev. 17:5). But let us now return from the byway to the road. Perhaps the procession to the Lateran is now ready.

units.la: XLV. Antequam vero eam describat, sequentia adhuc narrat Author: Sed quoniam plerunque, antequam hac completa sint, hora est satis tarda; & longa ad Lateranum restat via, multâque ibi adhuc sunt peragenda: consueverunt aliquando Pontifices, & Patres sustentationis gratiâ aliquantulum cibi sumere: paratur refectio in atrio domûs Archipresbyteri Basilicæ pro Pontifice & Cardinalibus; pro aliis Prælatis in vicinis domibus Canonicorum. Coronato Pontifice veniunt ad refectionem, & interim parantur, quæ ad processionem sunt opportuna. Sumptâ refectione Pontifex & omnes descendunt ad equitandum. Quo ordine, prolixè recenset, & inter alia de scala Papæ panno rubeo cooperta, quam portet equus albus ductus per unum ex parasrenariis purpurea veste indutum; Qui postquam Papa ascenderit equum cum ista scala, vadat in ordine suo, dextra equi habenas, sinissinistra rubrum ferens baculum. Sacramentum per familiarem Sacrista equo albo mansueto, ornato, ad collum tintinabulum bene tiniens habenti impositum duci ait, quando Papæ equus per Imperatores, vel Reges ducendus aliquandiu esset! Priori Diaconorum tribuit, quòd ferulam in manu habens totam processionem ordinare debeat, & illa ordinatâ equitare in loco suo. Procedit tandem, ita pergit, summus Pontifex super equum album faleratum coopertum àparte posteriori stragiola sarmesina sub baldachino, quod 8 magni nobiles, sive oratores portant. Cùm Papa per scalam, quam superiùs diximus, ascendit equum: major princeps, qui præsens adest, etiamsi Rex esset, aut Imperator, stapham equi Papalis tenet, & deinde ducit equum per frenum aliquantulum. Si Imperator, aut Rex soli essent, id est, non esset alius Rex: soli equum ducerent cum dextra manu; Sin verò esset alius Rex, dignior à dextra, alius à sinistra frenum tenerent. Si non sunt Reges, digniores ducant equum. Et postquam Imperator, Rex, sive alius magnus princeps aliquantulum equum duxerit: Substituantur alii duo magni nobiles eorum loco & mutentur. Si verò Pontifex non equo, sed sella veheretur, 4. majores principes, etiamsi inter eos Imperator, aut quivis maximus princeps adesset in honorem Salvatoris Jesu Christi (scilicet honor ille, quem Christus se alienum esse semper voluit non institutus, imò usurpatoris in eo terminabitur!) sellam ipsam cum Pontifice humeris suis portare aliquantulum debent. Sed adeunt etiam 4. validi Pontificis familiares, qui pondus sustinent; ita ut principes ipsi in signum pia religionis, ac reverentia magis, quàm ad onus subeundum manus apposuisse videantur: qui etiam mutabuntur pro hominum & itineris dispositione. Similiter & 8. nobiles, qui Baldachinum super caput Pontificis ferunt, mutabuntur post aliquod spatium, & equos suos ascendentes in ordine suo equitabunt: eorum loco nobiles cives Romani usque ad Lateranum Baldachinum portabunt, mutabuntúrque per vices —Circa Pontificem aliquando ante, aliquando post equitabit marescallus sive soldanus Curiæ, cum 2. sacculis pecuniarum ante sellam, & ipsas pecunias projiciet super populum ad pressuram dimovendam, ut infra dicemus; Primum jactum pecuniæ faciet, cùm Pontifex incipiet se movere, alium apud pontem Hadriani, tum in Area apud montem Jordanum. Inde in Area parionis, deinde alium apud S. Marcum, postea apud S. Adrianum, & demum ubicunque magnam pressuram apud Pontificem viderit, & ut facilius possit transire, ad partem transversam jaciat pecunias. Post Pontificem &c. Vice camerarius baculum in manu portat, & pertinet ad eum curare, ut ordo à priore Diaconorum datus servetur in processione —Cùm Pontifex pervenerit ad montem Jordanum: Judæi illi obviam veniunt, genuflexi legem Pontifici offerunt: lingua Hebraica legem laudantes & hortantes Pontificem, ut illam veneretur. Pontifex verò his auditis (rectè ait, his auditis, quando vix centesimus Hebræa intelligit!) in hanc sententiam respondet: (non intellexit, & tamen respondet, dictorum planè ignarus;) S. Legem, viri Hebrai, & laudamus & veneramur, utpote qua ab omnipotente Deo per manus Moysi patribus vestris tradita est: Observantiam verò vestram & vanam interpretationem (cui simillima observantia traditionaria Pontificia!) damnamus atque improbamus &c. Sed quoniam nonnunquam accidit, ut Judæi, populi multitudine opprimantur, solent aliquando impetrare pro eorum securitate, ut hoc faciant super ante murali arcis S. Angeli in angulo ad viam, quâ itur ad palatium. Hîc autem Lectori considerandum relinquo, quantopere Judæi illi scandalizari debeant, tum hostiæ, tum ipsius etiam Pontificis Idolatrico cultu, & magna sub Christi crucifixi nomine in omni Pompa & luxu mundano hominum deceptione!
units.tr: XLV. Before describing the procession itself, the author next narrates the following: But since, for the most part, these ceremonies are not finished before the hour is quite late, and there is a long way still to go to the Lateran with much yet to be done there, the Popes and Fathers sometimes take a little food to keep up their strength. A meal is prepared in the forecourt of the house of the archpriest of the basilica for the Pope and the Cardinals; for the other prelates it is prepared in the neighbouring houses of the canons. When the Pope has been crowned, they come to the meal, and meanwhile what is needed for the procession is made ready. Once the meal is taken, the Pope and everyone go down to mount their horses. He describes the order in great detail, and among other things the Pope's ladder, covered with red cloth, which a white horse led by one of the equerries, dressed in purple, is to carry. After the Pope has mounted the horse with that ladder, he goes in his place, holding the bridle in his right hand and carrying a red staff in his left. The Sacristan, through a household servant, says that the Sacrament is to be led on a gentle white horse, decked out, with a bell ringing well hung around its neck. How long the Pope's horse would have to be led by emperors or kings! To the first of the deacons he assigns that, holding a rod in his hand, he must put the whole procession in order, and once it is ordered, ride in his own place. At last he proceeds, and goes on: the supreme Pontiff, upon a white horse, caparisoned, covered at the back with a sarmesine cloth, under a canopy, which eight great nobles, or ambassadors, carry. When the Pope mounts the horse by the ladder we mentioned above, the chief prince who is present, even if he were a king or an emperor, holds the stirrup of the papal horse and then leads the horse a short way by the bridle. If only an emperor or a king were present, that is, if there were no other king, they alone would lead the horse with the right hand; but if there were another king, the more worthy would hold the bridle on the right and the other on the left. If there are no kings, the more worthy lead the horse. And after the emperor, king, or other great prince has led the horse for a little while, two other great nobles are substituted in their place and they change. But if the Pope is carried not on a horse but in a chair, four of the greater princes, even if an emperor or some very great prince is among them, in honour of the Saviour Jesus Christ (that honour, of course, which Christ always wished to be foreign to him, not instituted, but in this case it will end in the usurper!) must carry the chair itself with the Pope on their shoulders for a little while. But four strong household servants of the Pope also come forward to bear the weight, so that the princes themselves seem to have laid their hands to it as a sign of pious religion and reverence rather than to bear the burden: who also are changed according to the disposition of the men and the journey. Likewise the eight nobles who carry the canopy over the Pope's head are changed after some interval, and, mounting their horses, ride in their own order; in their place the noble citizens of Rome carry the canopy as far as the Lateran, and they are changed in turns. Beside the Pope, sometimes before and sometimes after, rides the marshal or sultan of the Curia, with two bags of money before the chair, and he throws the money among the people to relieve the crush, as we shall say below. He will make the first throw of money when the Pope begins to move, another at the Bridge of Hadrian, then in the Square at Monte Giordano. Then in the Piazza Parione, next another at S. Marco, afterwards at S. Adriano, and finally wherever he sees a great crush around the Pope, and so that he may pass more easily, he throws the money sideways. After the Pope etc. The vice-chamberlain carries a staff in his hand, and it is his job to see that the order given by the first of the deacons is kept in the procession. When the Pope has reached Monte Giordano, those Jews come to meet him, kneel, and offer the Law to the Pope, praising the Law in the Hebrew tongue and urging the Pope to revere it. The Pope, having heard these things (he says rightly, "having heard these things," when scarcely one in a hundred understands Hebrew!), answers to this effect (he did not understand, and yet he answers, quite ignorant of what was said): "We both praise and revere the holy Law, men of Hebrew race, since it was handed down to your fathers by almighty God through the hand of Moses; but your observance and your vain interpretation (to which the traditional observance of the Papists is most like!) we condemn and reject, etc." But since it sometimes happens that the Jews are overwhelmed by the crowd of people, they are sometimes allowed, for their safety, to do this on the wall in front of the castle of S. Angelo, at the corner by the road that leads to the palace. Here I leave it to the reader to consider how greatly those Jews ought to be scandalised, both by the sacrifice and by the idolatrous worship of the Pope himself, and by the great deception of men under the name of the crucified Christ, in every worldly pomp and luxury!

units.la: XLVI. Cùm Pontifex ad Ecclesiam Lateranensem pervenerit, descendit in porticum Ecclesiæ, & à Canonicis illius Ecclesiæ honorificè paratis, excipitur cruce. Descendit Pontifex ex equo; Prior Canonicorum Lateranensium offert crucem osculandam Pontifici, quam Diaconus Cardinalis accipit, & ad os Pontifici: cui prius Tiaram extraxit: ponit. Osculata cruce Pontifici ponitur mitra, & regnum datur in manibus Auditoris: Ipse verò Pontifex à Priore & Canonicis prædictis ducitur ad marmoream sedem ante portam principalem à sinistra stantem, quæ stercoraria appellatur, & ibi eum sedere faciunt, qui ita tamen sedet, ut magis jacere videatur, ad quem mox accedentes Cardinales elevant eum honorificè, dicentes: Suscitat de pulvere egenum, & de stercore erigit pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, & solium gloriæ teneat (quæ ultima verba de suo verbis Psalmistæ addunt; cum quibus aperte ludunt, cùm Pontificis elevatio neque sit gratiosa elevatio à Deo, ut ostendimus, neque humilis & egeni, quod patet ex tractatione de Cardinalibus, & Papa nolit sedere cum Principibus, sed sedere principibus stantibus, portantibus, procumbentibus; alium verò & antiquiorem sellæ hujus usum vide (Dissert. VII. Sect. 3. n. 36. 37. 38. 39.) Surgens Pontifex, accipit de gremio Camerarii sibi assistentis, quantum pugno potest complecti pecuniarum; Ubi tamen nihil prorsus sit argenti & auri, & spargit inter populum, dicens: Argentum & aurum non est mihi: quod autem habeo hoc tibi do (qui Scripturæ abusus adhuc manifestior est, & quem vel præ-
units.tr: XLVI. When the Pope has reached the Church of the Lateran, he descends into the portico of the church, and is received with the cross by the canons of that church, who have prepared to honour him. The Pope descends from the horse; the Prior of the Lateran canons offers the cross for the Pope to kiss, which a Cardinal deacon takes and puts to the Pope's mouth, after first removing the tiara from him. After the Pope has kissed the cross, the mitre is put on him and the sceptre is given into the hands of the Auditor. The Pope himself is led by the aforesaid Prior and canons to the marble seat before the main door on the left, which is called the dung-seat, and they make him sit there, but in such a way that he seems rather to lie, and the Cardinals who approach him at once raise him up honourably, saying: "He raises the needy from the dust, and lifts the poor from the dunghill, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory" (which last words they add from their own, changing the words of the Psalmist; with which they openly mock, since the Pope's elevation is neither a gracious elevation from God, as we have shown, nor that of the humble and needy, as is clear from the treatment of the Cardinals; and the Pope does not wish to sit with princes, but to have princes stand, carry, and prostrate themselves before him; for an older and different use of this chair, see (Dissert. VII, Sect. 3, nn. 36, 37, 38, 39)). Rising, the Pope takes from the lap of the chamberlain who assists him as much money as he can grasp with his fist; although there is absolutely no silver or gold there, and he scatters it among the people, saying: "Silver and gold I have not; but what I have, that I give to you" (which abuse of Scripture is even more evident, and which especially...

units.la: Quæ apud Lateranum agantur; præmissa & sequentia clarissimè produnt, ut & cognitæ Paparum ingentes divitiæ. Cæterùm si argentum & aurum non haberet, & tantùm cuprum &c. neque tamen illud, quod in dicto Petri sequitur: Surge & ambula; præstare potest, miser certè esset Petri Successor ille, qualis revera est, atque hèic merito imitamur Germanorum illud: Kûpferin Gelt / Kûpferne Seelmessen: Cuprei Nummi, Cupreæ Missæ: Cuprei nummi, Cupreus Papa;) Pons ligneus recta linea à porta Ecclesia principali ad altare majus excitatur cum pluteis hinc indè pectoribus tenus altitudo circiter quinque pedum, latitudo sex aut septem, qui alteri ponti conjungitur simili modo constructo à porta, quâ ascenditur per Ecclesiam ad Sancta Sanctorum venienti, quod fit, ut Pontifex à populi multitudine non opprimatur, circa altare à gradibus, & supra omnia circumcirca tabulis clausa esse debent, ut per pontem tantùm Capellam intrent: Præcedentibus igitur Canonicis & cantantibus: Te Deum laudamus: Pontifex cum Cardinalibus intrat Ecclesiam, & ante altare majus supra faldistorium procumbens sine mitra aliquantulum orat. Deinde surgens benedicit populo, dicens: Sit nomen &c. Inde cum mitra ascendens ad sedem eminentem sedens recipit ad osculum pedis Canonicos Lateranenses. Deinde Pontifex per ipsum pontem ascendit ad palatium Lateranum per portam, quæ est in Ecclesia. Et cùm perventum fuerit in prima aula quæ aula Concilii appellatur; sedet Pontifex in sede sibi parata apud tabulam lapideam in Capite aulæ, quæ dicitur mensura Christi; (quam certè non habet Pontifex, licèt habere videri velit; sed contrariam potiùs habet, ut porrò ostendemus,) Et hinc inde apud eum stant Domini Cardinales. Prior verò Presbyterorum Cardinalium stans ante Papam convenienti intervallo cum Subdiaconis, auditoribus, Advocatis & Scriniariis facit laudes Domino nostro, ut fecerat Prior Diaconorum in S. Petro, incipiens: Exaudi &c. Prior Presbyterorum prædictus, & alii, qui faciunt laudes, stant detecto capite. Pontifex verò sedet cum mitra, alii Cardinales stant cum mitra. — Finitis laudibus, Papa procedit ad Capellam S. Sylvestri; Ibi ante portam Capellæ sunt duæ sedes porphyreticæ perforatæ; & ibi sedet Pontifex super primam; Ad quem prior Ecclesiæ Lateranensis accedit, & genuflexus dat Pontifici ferulam in manu in signum Correctionis & regiminis, & Claves ipsius Basilicæ, ac Palatii Lateranensis, in signum potestatis claudendi & aperiendi, ligandi atque solvendi. Surgit deinde Papa cum ferula & clavibus & sedet in altera sede porphyretica ad aliam partem, & ibi restituit eidem priori ferulam, & Claves, & ab eodem praecingitur super planetam sedens cum cingulo quodam fericeo rubro, cum burbursa etiam sericea & rubra; in qua sunt 12. Lapides pretiosi cum musco (quae & ipsa est κακοζηλία Judaica, cum illa & reliqua V. T. typica tantum fuerint, & ad Christum, Sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedek, respexerint;) Tum Pontifex praecinctus & sedens e gremio Camerarii capit denarios argenteos omnifariam, quotquot potest manu continere, & super populum spargens, dicit: Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, justitia ejus manet in seculum seculi. Et hoc tertio facit. (Ita suam ipsemet justitiam & liberalitatem praedicans. Sed vanissime; Neque enim dat pauperibus, sed projicit proximis, saepe ditissimis; Atque ex eleemosynis omnem istam pompam plus quam Regiam conficit, magno certe pauperum vere talium detrimento. Quin igitur potius dicat: Haec omnia tibi dabo, si coram me procidens adoraveris Matth. IV.9.) In istis 2. sedibus Pontifex sedet: ut in prima stercoraria. Ducitur deinde Pontifex ad Sancta Sanctorum, ubi supra faldistorium sine mitra genuflexus orat. Inde surgens cum mitra revertitur ad Capellam S. Sylvestri, in quam intrans sedet super sedem ibi paratam, tum deponit mitram, Chirothecas, Pallium, planetam, & assumit pluviale, & mitram simplicem, & sedens dat Presbyterium hoc modo; Cardinalibus 2. aureos & 2. grossos argenteos. Veniunt Cardinales, & profunde caput inclinant ante Pontificem, porriguntque ei mitram apertam, in qua Pontifex immittit pecuniam: Illi accepta pecunia manum Pontificis osculantur; pecunias caput Pontifex e gremio Camerarii. Alii Praelati genuflectunt ante Pontificem & accipiunt in mitra unum aureum, & unum grossum, & osculantur dextrum genu Papae. Alii vero Praelati & Officiales accipiunt in manu tantundem, & osculantur pedem (Et ita omnes hos sibi emit mancipia sua futura;) Dato Presbyterio, Pontifex cum Cardinalibus ascendit ad Palatium Lateranense, & si non facit solenne convivium, deponit paramenta sua, intrat Cameram, quiescit, & prandet, seu cenat. Cardinales ducuntur ad Cameras ordinatas, quiescunt, recreantur & expectant Pontificem; Si vult redire ad S. Petrum eodem die. Sin autem, revertuntur. XLVII. Et sic absolvimus Pontificiae coronationis pompam, qualis ab Authore describitur; Et quae certe magna est, & magni constat. Id quod unico Leonis X. exemplo colligi velim; in cujus coronatione tantus fastus fuit; ut uno die 100000. aureorum expenderentur. Ut potiori, quam Judas, jure quis heic atque de coronatione illius, qui aurum & argentum non habet pauperis Christi & Petri Successor, quaerere & queri posset: Quorsum ista perditio? potuissent haec dari pauperibus, & tum seriodici; Dispersit. &c. quod ubi
units.tr: What is done at the Lateran is clearly revealed by what precedes and follows it, as are the immense riches of the Popes, which are well known. Yet even if he had no silver or gold, only copper, and that could not do what Peter's words that follow say, "Rise and walk," then that successor of Peter would surely be a wretched one, as he really is. Here we rightly apply the German saying: Kûpferin Gelt / Kûpferne Seelmessen (copper coins, copper masses; copper coins, a copper Pope). A wooden bridge is built in a straight line from the main door of the principal church to the high altar, with railings on either side up to chest height, about five feet high and six or seven feet wide. It joins another bridge, similarly built, from the door by which those coming up through the church ascend to the Holy of Holies. This is done so that the Pope is not crushed by the crowd of people. Around the altar, the steps and everything else must be closed off on all sides with boards, so that people enter the chapel only by the bridge. With the canons going ahead and singing "We praise thee, O God," the Pope enters the church with the cardinals, and before the high altar, kneeling on a faldstool without his mitre, he prays for a little while. Then, rising, he blesses the people, saying, "Blessed be the name," and so on. Then, wearing his mitre, he ascends to a raised seat, sits down, and receives the kiss of the foot from the Lateran canons. Next the Pope goes by this same bridge to the Lateran palace through the door that is in the church. When he reaches the first hall, which is called the hall of the Council, the Pope sits in a seat prepared for him beside the stone tablet at the head of the hall, which is called the measure of Christ (which the Pope certainly does not have, though he wants to seem to have it; rather he has the opposite, as we will show further on). The lord cardinals stand on either side of him. The senior of the cardinal priests, standing before the Pope at a suitable distance, together with the subdeacons, auditors, advocates and notaries, offers praises to our Lord, as the senior of the cardinal deacons did at St Peter's, beginning "Hear, O..." etc. The aforesaid senior of the cardinal priests and the others who offer the praises stand with their heads uncovered. But the Pope sits with his mitre on, and the other cardinals stand with their mitres on. — When the praises are finished, the Pope proceeds to the chapel of St Sylvester. There, before the chapel door, are two perforated porphyry seats, and the Pope sits upon the first. The prior of the Lateran church approaches him, kneels, and gives the Pope a rod in his hand as a sign of correction and rule, and the keys of the basilica itself and of the Lateran palace, as a sign of the power of shutting and opening, binding and loosing. The Pope then rises with the rod and the keys and sits in the other porphyry seat on the other side. There he returns the rod and the keys to the same prior, and is girded by him, sitting in the chasuble, with a red silken girdle and also a red silken purse, in which there are twelve precious stones with musk. (This too is a Jewish kakozēlia [κακοζηλία], since all these Old Testament types were only types and looked to Christ, the priest after the order of Melchizedek.) Then the Pope, girded and seated, takes from the lap of the chamberlain silver pennies, as many as he can hold in his hand, and scattering them among the people, says, "He hath dispersed abroad, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever and ever." And he does this three times. (So he himself proclaims his own righteousness and generosity, but most vainly. For he does not give to the poor, but throws to those nearby, often the very rich; and out of alms he makes all that pomp, more than royal, to the great loss of the poor who are truly poor. Why does he not rather say: All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me, Matt. 4:9?) On these two seats the Pope sits, like the first, on a dung-heap. Then the Pope is led to the Holy of Holies, where, kneeling on a faldstool without his mitre, he prays. Then, rising, he returns with his mitre to the chapel of St Sylvester. Entering it, he sits on the seat prepared there, then takes off his mitre, gloves, pallium and chasuble, and puts on a cope and a plain mitre, and sitting he gives the presbyterium in this way: to the cardinals, two gold coins and two silver groats. The cardinals come and bow their heads deeply before the Pope, and hold out to him an open mitre, into which the Pope puts the money. Having received the money, they kiss the Pope's hand. The Pope takes the money from the lap of the chamberlain. Other prelates kneel before the Pope and receive in a mitre one gold coin and one groat, and kiss the Pope's right knee. Other prelates and officials receive the same amount in their hand and kiss the foot (and so he buys all these as his future servants). When the presbyterium has been given, the Pope goes up with the cardinals to the Lateran palace, and if he does not hold a solemn banquet, he takes off his vestments, enters his chamber, rests, and dines or sups. The cardinals are led to their assigned rooms, where they rest, refresh themselves, and wait for the Pope. If he wishes to return to St Peter's the same day, he does so; if not, they go back. XLVII. And so we have finished the pomp of the papal coronation, as the author describes it, which is certainly great and costs a great deal. I would like this to be gathered from the single example of Leo X, at whose coronation there was such display that 100,000 gold pieces were spent in one day. With greater right than Judas, one might here ask and complain about the coronation of him who has no gold or silver, the successor of the poor Christ and of Peter: "To what purpose is this waste? These things could have been given to the poor." And then the words, He hath dispersed abroad, etc., when....

units.la: Pompa hac coronationis magni constat & aliquando infelix fuit. ubi tantillum pauperibus erogatur, tantum inutili pompa consumitur, dicitur nonnisi ridicule. Sed & infelix saepe est illa coronationis pompa & cum multorum nece conjuncta. Ita enim primo de coronatione Clementis V. scribit Platina: Coronationi Pontificis interfuere & Philippus Rex Francia, ejusque frater Carolus nuper ex Italia reversus, Johannes Britannia Dux, qui ruina muri oppressus moritur, cum plerisque aliis, dum pompa Coronationis, ut fit, per urbem ducitur, Philippus quoque rex ea ruina aliqua ex parte debilitatus est. Pontifex autem in tanta trepidatione ex equo deturbatus, solum carbunculum ex tiara amisit, precu aureorum 6000. ut quidam scribunt. Recentius exemplum est Pii IV. de cujus coronatione ita Onuphrius in Vita scribit: Ei spectaculo magna vis hominum undique confluxit. Pluverat tota ea nocte & die parte, unde marmorei ante Basilicam Vaticanam gradus, & eorum pracinctiones lubrica admodum facta erant. Ea re in solenni nummorum jactu, in eadem scalis insignis hominum strages fuit, pecunias avide eripere cupientium: nam neque se eo impetu sustinere a lapsu poterant, nec, si qui paululum titubassent, haerere afflicti vestigio, aliique super alios cadentes misere perierunt. Circiter XVIII. homines ea turba necati, supra XL. luxati & elisi, quod miserabile spectaculum fuit ac a quibusdam ad ipsius Pontificatus res gestas pro omine relatum. Omen certe in his similibusque exemplis est, atque interdum sic Deus ostendit, displicere sibi mundanum fastum, illum maxime, cui nomen ejus impie praetexitur.
units.tr: This coronation pomp costs much and has sometimes been unlucky: when a tiny sum is given to the poor and so much is spent on useless show, it is rightly called ridiculous. But that coronation pomp has often also been unlucky, and joined with the deaths of many. For Platina writes thus of the coronation of Clement V: At the coronation of the Pope were present Philip, King of France, and his brother Charles, recently returned from Italy, and John, Duke of Brittany, who was crushed and died by the collapse of a wall, along with many others, while the coronation procession, as usual, was being led through the city. King Philip too was in some measure weakened by that collapse. The Pope himself, in such great alarm, was thrown from his horse and lost only a carbuncle from his tiara, worth 6000 gold pieces, as some write. A more recent example is that of Pius IV, of whose coronation Onuphrius writes thus in his Life: A great crowd of people flocked from everywhere to that spectacle. It had rained all that night and during part of the day, so the marble steps in front of the Vatican basilica and their edges had become very slippery. Because of this, when the coins were thrown on the same steps during the solemn ceremony, there was a notable slaughter of people, all eagerly trying to snatch the money. For they could not hold themselves up against that rush and fall, and those who had stumbled a little could not keep their footing once knocked down, and they fell upon one another and miserably perished. About eighteen people were killed in that crush, and more than forty were dislocated and crushed. It was a pitiable spectacle, and some regarded it as an omen for the deeds of his pontificate. Certainly there is an omen in these and similar examples, and God sometimes shows in this way that the worldly show displeases him, especially that show under which his name is impiously put forward.

units.la: XLVIII. Sed quantum fastus ille Deo displiceat, magis adhuc apparebit, si parallelismum quendam inter Christi & Petri processiones ab una, & processiones Pontificum, qui utriusque Vicariatum & successionem jactant, coronationis die institui solitas & hactenus descriptas, ab altera parte, instituerimus.
units.tr: XLVIII. But how much that pomp displeases God will become even clearer if we set up a certain parallel between the processions of Christ and Peter on one side, and those of the Popes, who boast of being the vicars and successors of both, which are customarily held on the day of coronation and have been described above, on the other.

units.la: I. Christus & Petrus illuc tantum iverunt, quo a Deo missi fuerunt; Sed Pontifices non possunt dicere, ex Dei instituto esse suas processiones coronationis die suscipi solitas, ut & ipsam coronationem a Deo non esse ostendimus; In utroque tamen haud parum situm esse censent.
units.tr: I. Christ and Peter went only where God had sent them. The Popes cannot say that their processions, customarily undertaken on the day of coronation, are by God's appointment, just as we have shown that the coronation itself is not from God. Yet they think a great deal depends on both.

units.la: II. Christus & Petrus processiones suas instituerunt, maxime ut audirentur; Pontifices contra, ut viderentur. Et quod de Paulo II. Platina habet: Inspici tum ab omnibus volebat & admirari; illud plerisque certe convenit; Atque eo etiam ipsa pompa luxuriosa spectat.
units.tr: II. Christ and Peter instituted their processions chiefly so that they might be heard; the Popes, on the contrary, so that they might be seen. What Platina says of Paul II certainly applies to most of them: He wanted to be looked at and admired by all then. Their luxurious pomp also aims at this very thing.

units.la: III. Christus & Petrus ut plurimum pedites incesserunt; Pontifices ordinario equis aut sellis vehuntur.
units.tr: III. Christ and Peter for the most part went on foot. The Popes are ordinarily carried on horses or in litters.

units.la: IV. Christus super asinum vehebatur semel; Pontifices equis albis faleratis a parte posteriori stragiola:
units.tr: IV. Christ rode on a donkey once. The Popes ride on white horses decked with trappings, with rich coverings at the rear:

units.la: Parallelismus inter processiones Christi & Petri ab una, Pontificum vero ab altera parte. gola carmesina coopertis utuntur. V. Christus & Petrus iter fecerunt in vestitu simplici atque communi; Pontificum hac etiam in parte luxus quemvis alium superat. VI. Christus & Petrus sine coronis & mitris pretiosis; Pontifices non sine illis. VII. Christus & Petrus subjdio; Pontifices semper sub baldachino per 8. portari solito. VIII. Christus & Petrus sine Sacramento, praeter quòd obvios conversos baptizârunt. Pontifices nunquam sine Sacramento, quo tanquam praesidio utuntur, licèt minùs reverenter etiam in comparatione haberi ostenderimus. IX. Christus & Petrus cum Apostolis & fidelibus Ministris aliis; Pontifices cum luxuriosis Cardinalibus, ventribus plerunque pigris. X. Christus & Petrus cum plebejis proximè junctis, eò propioribus, quò melioribus; Pontifices cum terrae magnatibus, quâ talibus propius junctis. XI. Christus & Petrus sine armata manu; Pontifices non item. XII. Christus & Petrus in suis itineribus honorificè tractârunt magistratus, nisi valdè impii fuerint; Pontifices Christianos Imperatores & Reges usque adeò non honorant, & sic Caesari, quae Caesaris sunt, dant, ut eos potiùs ad servilia ministeria sibi exhibenda damnent, & tanto ab iis cultu affici velint, quantum supremus Magistratus Dei in hac terra vicarius ne quidem à vilissimo subdito jure exigere potest. XIII. Christus & Petrus in suis processionibus usi sunt lingua nota; Pontifices utuntur plebi ignota. XIV. Christus & Petrus obambulârunt pauperes, Pontifices ditissimi; Illi acceperunt ex aliena liberalitate necessaria, hi malè projiciunt sua superflua; Illis corrumpendis bona terrestria frustrà adhibita sunt; hi non vano successu bonis terrestribus alios sibi emere student, sectatores futuros; Illorum paupertati hi in medio divitiarum suarum testimoniorum abusu illudunt. XV. Christus & Petrus in suis processionibus honorem indebitum repudiârunt, eum etiam, quem admittere potuissent, modestiâ suâ variè temperârunt; Pontifices contrà omnibus modis indebitum imò illicitum honorem affectant, laudésque locis destinatis decantandas. XVI. Christi & Petri processiones alienissimae fuerunt à fastu mundano, quem contrà processiones Pontificum ubique spirant. XVII. Christus & Petrus ita obambulârunt, ut non habuerint, quò caput reponerent, & locum paratum rarò invenerint; Pontifices contrà & sellis vecti mollissimè caput reponunt, & omnia ubique magnâ diligentiâ parata inveniunt, & ornata. XVIII. Christus & Petrus facilè sistebantur ab-auxiauxilium implorantibus miseris, Pontifices contrà negligent in suis processionibus, quos ipsi miseros fecerunt, queritantes XIX. Christus & Petrus obambulârunt, ut ministrarent, Pontifices contrà ut sibi semper & in omnibus & ab omnibus ministraretur. Hinc XX. Christi & Petri profectiones maximè aliis & variè utiles fuerunt; Pontificum contrà processiones non prosunt nisi illis, qui nummos eorum projectos excipiunt; imò & illis, quando in pressura populi calcantur, & multis aliis eodem modo, & quatenus inutilis pompæ materiam privatione propria suppeditare debent, nocent. Et cuando Christus & Petrus ille sua, hic illius potentiâ mortuis vitam dederunt, hi contrà vivis tam inutili pompâ eripiunt. Ut hic illud de Ignatio Loyola, occasione occæcati in festo Canonisatiō-nis igne artificiali nobilissimi juvenis prolatum: Alii Sancti cæcos vi-dere faciunt, Ignatius verò videntes cæcos reddit; applicare liceat. Ista nempe sunt successorum horum fictitiorum miracula & beneficia! Neque etiam prædicando ædificant, iter facientes; Non Christianos, non Judæos, quos contrà plurimùm scandalizant atque in infidelitate confirmant. Siquè Petrus concione unicâ tria Judæorum millia ad fidem Christianam adduxit, ipsi contrà tribus processionum millibus ne unicum quidem Judæum converterent. Neque enim desunt authores fide dignissimi, qui plures Romæ Christianos Judaismum, quàm Judæos Christianismum amplecti testantur. Quis igitur hos haberet pro Successoribus & Vicariis eadem potestate præditis illorum? Quis non potiùs, visâ multiplici vel in his oppositione, judicaret, eos qui Antichristi, loco Christi, esse volunt, esse Antichristos, contrà Christum, Christo dissimillimos & in omnibusferè manifeste contrarios?
units.tr: Parallelism between the processions of Christ and Peter on one side, and of the Popes on the other. They use crimson-covered throat-cloths. V. Christ and Peter travelled in simple and common clothing; in this respect too the Popes' luxury surpasses all others. VI. Christ and Peter had no crowns or precious mitres; the Popes do not go without them. VII. Christ and Peter went in the open air; the Popes are always carried under a canopy, which is customarily borne by eight men. VIII. Christ and Peter went without the Sacrament, except that they baptized the converts they met. The Popes are never without the Sacrament, which they use as a safeguard, though we have shown that they are held in less reverence even in comparison. IX. Christ and Peter were accompanied by the Apostles, faithful ministers and others; the Popes by luxurious Cardinals, mostly with sluggish bellies. X. Christ and Peter were accompanied by common people, those nearest to them being the better sort; the Popes by the great men of the land, who are joined to them the more closely the more they are such. XI. Christ and Peter had no armed hand; the Popes do not likewise. XII. Christ and Peter on their journeys honoured the magistrates, unless they were very impious. The Popes do not honour Christian emperors and kings to such a degree; so they give to Caesar what is Caesar's, that they rather condemn them to servile duties to perform for themselves, and wish to be honoured by them as much as the supreme magistrate, God's vicar on this earth, could not even demand from the lowliest subject. XIII. Christ and Peter used a known language in their processions; the Popes use one unknown to the people. XIV. Christ and Peter walked about as the poor; the Popes are very rich. The former received necessities from the generosity of others; these throw away their superfluities badly. Earthly goods were used in vain to corrupt the former; these seek by no empty success to buy followers for themselves with earthly goods. In the midst of their riches they mock the poverty of the former by abusing their testimonies. XV. Christ and Peter rejected undue honour in their processions, and even tempered by their modesty the honour they could have accepted in various ways; the Popes, on the contrary, seek undue and indeed unlawful honour in every way, and have praises to be sung in appointed places. XVI. The processions of Christ and Peter were utterly alien to worldly pomp, which the processions of the Popes, on the contrary, breathe everywhere. XVII. Christ and Peter walked about in such a way that they had nowhere to lay their head, and rarely found a prepared place; the Popes, on the contrary, when carried in litters lay their head down most softly, and find everything prepared with great care and adorned everywhere. XVIII. Christ and Peter were readily approached by wretched people imploring help; the Popes, on the contrary, in their processions neglect those whom they themselves have made wretched, complaining. XIX. Christ and Peter walked about in order to serve; the Popes, on the contrary, so that they might always and in everything and by everyone be served. XX. Hence the journeys of Christ and Peter were most useful to others and in various ways; the processions of the Popes benefit only those who catch the coins they throw, and indeed harm those who are trampled in the crush of the people, and many others in the same way, and insofar as they must supply the material of useless pomp by private deprivation, they do harm. And whereas Christ and Peter gave life to the dead, the one by his own power, the other by his, these on the contrary snatch life from the living by such useless pomp. Just as what was said here about Ignatius Loyola, on the occasion of a most noble young man being blinded by fireworks at the feast of his canonisation, may be applied: Other saints make the blind see; Ignatius makes those who see blind. Those indeed are the miracles and benefits of these fictitious successors! Nor do they edify by preaching as they travel: not Christians, not Jews, whom on the contrary they greatly scandalize and confirm in unbelief. If Peter by a single sermon brought three thousand Jews to the Christian faith, they on the contrary would not convert even one Jew with three thousand processions. For there are no lack of most trustworthy authors who testify that more Christians embrace Judaism at Rome than Jews embrace Christianity. Who then would regard these as successors and vicars endowed with the same power as those? Who would not rather judge, seeing so many oppositions even in these things, that those who wish to be Antichrists in place of Christ are Antichrists, contrary to Christ, most unlike him and almost manifestly opposed to him in everything?

units.la: XLIX. Quales etiam apparent in convivio, quod Author
