units.tr: XLIX. Such as also appear at the banquet, which the author

units.la: Libri Ceremoniarum n. 57. sub finem innuit & Sectione 3. totâ multis ita describit, ut dicat ante omnia, simile convivium feriâ quintâ in Cœna Domini celebrari solere, atque suâ ætate à Pio II. & Paulo II. celebratum esse. His præmissis, agit de paranda aula convivii aulaïs & pannis fericeis, aureisque; Et subjungit: In capite aulæ erit suggestus, ad quem triplici gradu ascenderetur, longus pro latitudine aulæ; in medio surget quadratus thalamus palmi altitudine; Super quo mensa paratur Pontificis; apud parietem erit sedes Papalis, ad quam parvo & deinde magno scabello ascendetur; ornabiturque sedes cum panno aureo pendente supra caput, mensa erit alta ad justam proportionem sedentis à sinistra sinistra super suggestum. Parabitur alia mensa pro credentia Papæ cum vasis aureis & argenteis vino & aqua & aliis consuetis——A dextra parte aulæ infra suggestum parabuntur mensæ pro Episcopis, & Presbyteris Cardinalibus, & paulò inferiùs, pro aliis Prælatis. Et pro Cardinalibus erunt aliquantò altiores, & sedilia habebunt gradum unum, super quem tenebunt pedes Cardinales. A sinistra è regione mensæ Cardinalium parabitur mensa pro Diaconis Cardinalibus ejusdem altitudinis & cum gradu. Et inferiùs alia mensa pro Oratoribus, nobilibus & officialibus in sine aulæ, vel in aula præcedente, si erit commoda, parabitur magna credentia cum pluribus gradibus ad magnificentiam, & alia super longam mensam cum vasis, quibus in communis (commune) utentur. Si huic convivio interesset Imperator, paratur pro eo sedes ad dextram Pontificis & mensa super plano suggestûs, super quam solus comedet Imperator. Sedes habebit scabellum parvum viride & erit ornata panno aureo, non tamen habebit pendentem supra caput; Similiter parabitur pro eo credentia juxta credentiam Papæ à sinistris. Si verò adesset Rex aliquis, paratur credentia pro eo paulò remotior ab ea; Sedes verò nulla paratur, quia sedet in mensa post primum Episc. Cardinalem——Cardinalibus singulis sufficiunt quaterni ministri, quorum unus vinum propinet, alter carnes concidat; alter de cultello fercula inferat, quartus prægustet vinum & aquam & alia subministret. Pontifici servire solent nobiliores, qui sunt in Curia Laici, etiamsi sint fratres aut filii Regum, præsertim in illorum præsentia. Pontifex igitur cum paramentis Pontificalibus, si celebravit illa die usque ad Dalmaticam inclusivè, & cum sandalis inclusivè; & cum sandalis indutus, supra Dalmaticam manto rubro aperto à parte anteriori & mitram habens in capite supra favonem medius inter Diaconos ducitur ad mensam. Cardinales & Prælati omnes habent superpelliceum super rochetum, sive supra vestes sui ordinis, si sint religiosi, & mitram albam in capite. Supra superpelliceum Cardinales & Prælati seculares habent mantellum sine cauda apertum à parte ante, & coloris violacei sive obscuri. Religiosi verò coloris sui ordinis, sed eodem modo apertos.—— Aderunt familiares Pontificis & alii servitores in copia. Aderunt etiam servientes armorum bene ornati cum suis baculis argenteis, qui præire debent ante portantes fercula, & removere multitudinem à via. Magister sacri hospitii & magister domûs providebant in tempore de modo & ordine ferculorum; De servitoribus, qui priùs, & qui posteriùs, & quòd quælibet mensa habeat præfectos suos. Qua verò priùs, qua deinceps, & per quos ferenda, & sic de aliis rebus opportunis. Pontifex remotá priùs mensâ ad partem, sedeat in sede cum mitra & mantum post collum aperzturu. tum, ut nihil ante pectus dependeat; Cardinales, Principes, & Prælati, & alii conviva stent ante mensas paratas. Nobilior Laicus etiam Imperator, aut Rex aquam ad lavandas Pontificis manus primò ferat hoc ordine. Magister sacri hospitii cum clerico Cerimoniarum, quem adesse oportet in ordinandis his rebus omnibus, cum servientibus armorum. Et si Imperator aut Rex aquam ferre debet cum aliquibus etiam principibus sociatis; Imperatorem aut Regem ad credentiam ducit. Si est nobilis inferior, solus erit & in credentia aquam prius à ministris probatam accipit in pelvibus, fértque consuetis Cerimoniis ad Pontificem, præeunte uno ex Auditoribus cum mantili ad tergendum manus. Prior Episcoporum Cardinalium, & duo Diaconi assistentes, depositis in manibus servitorum mantellis & mitris, sicin rochetto serviunt Papa, dum lavat, Episcopus aquam cum portante infundendo, & Diaconi mantile, quod ab Auditore acceperant, hinc inde tenendo. Dum Papa lavat manus, Prælati & Laici omnes genufiectunt, Cardinales & Prælati stant capite detecto.
units.tr: The author of the Book of Ceremonies, n. 57, hints at this near the end, and in all of section 3 he describes it at length. He says first of all that a banquet of this kind is usually held on Maundy Thursday, and that in his own time it was celebrated by Pius II and Paul II. With these preliminaries he turns to preparing the banqueting hall with hangings, silk cloths and gold, and he adds: At the head of the hall there will be a platform, reached by three steps, as long as the hall is wide. In the middle a square canopy will rise, a palm high. On it the Pope's table will be laid. Against the wall will be the Papal seat, which is climbed by a small footstool and then a large one. The seat will be adorned with a gold cloth hanging over the head. The table will be high, in due proportion to the one seated, on the left side above the platform. Another table shall be set up for the Pope's sideboard, with gold and silver vessels, wine, water and the other customary things. On the right side of the hall, below the platform, tables shall be laid for the bishops and the presbyter cardinals, and a little lower for the other prelates. For the cardinals the tables will be somewhat higher, and their seats will have one step on which the cardinals will rest their feet. On the left, opposite the cardinals' table, a table will be laid for the cardinal deacons of the same height and with a step. Lower down there shall be another table for the envoys, nobles and officials at the end of the hall, or in the preceding hall if that is convenient. A large sideboard with several steps, for show, will be set up, and another over a long table with vessels that they will use in common. If the emperor attends this banquet, a seat will be prepared for him at the Pope's right and a table on the level of the platform, at which the emperor alone will eat. His seat will have a small green footstool and will be adorned with a gold cloth, but it will have no canopy over the head. Likewise a sideboard will be prepared for him beside the Pope's sideboard on the left. If some king is present, a sideboard will be prepared for him somewhat further off. No seat is prepared for him, because he sits at the table after the first cardinal bishop. Four attendants suffice for each cardinal: one to pour the wine, another to carve the meat, a third to bring the dishes from the carving board, and a fourth to taste the wine and water and to serve other things. The Pope is usually served by the more noble laymen of the Curia, even if they are brothers or sons of kings, especially in their presence. The Pope, then, wearing his pontifical vestments (if he has celebrated that day, as far as the dalmatic inclusive, and with the sandals inclusive), and wearing sandals, with a red open cape over the dalmatic in front and a mitre on his head above the favonius, is led to the table between the deacons. All the cardinals and prelates wear a surplice over the rochet, or over the vestments of their order if they are religious, and a white mitre on the head. Over the surplice the cardinals and secular prelates wear a mantle without a train, open at the front and of a violet or dark colour. The religious wear the colour of their order, but open in the same way. The Pope's familiars and other servants will be present in numbers. Well-dressed men-at-arms will also be present with their silver staves, who must go before those carrying the dishes and clear the crowd from the way. The master of the sacred household and the master of the palace shall arrange in good time the manner and order of the dishes: which servants go first and which after, that each table has its own overseers, which dishes are carried first and which later, by whom they are to be carried, and so on for other suitable matters. The Pope, after the table has been removed to one side, shall sit in his seat with mitre and mantle, the mantle open behind the neck, so that nothing hangs before the breast. The cardinals, princes, prelates and other guests shall stand before the tables already laid.

units.la: Cùm Papa laverit, reaptetur mensa ante eum, & tres Cardinales, qui illi servierant, capiunt suos mantellos, & mitras & vadunt ad loca sua; & Imperator apud sedem suam primò stans lavetur suis Cerimoniis, deinde Cardinales Domini laventur stantes ante mensas cum mitris in capite, post eos laventur Prælati stantes sine mitris, & seculares (si qui sunt) detectis capitibus. Stabunt ante mensas lavantes eo ordine, quo sedere debent in mensa; Prior Episcoporum in Capite ad dextram: Si aderit Rex aliquis, erit in secundo loco, si plures Reges, mixti cum primis Cardinalibus, primò Cardinalis, deinde Rex successive. Si erunt mixtim Principes, aut Filii, vel Fratres Regum. Si non serviunt Papæ, debent sedere inter Diaconos Cardinales, vel post eos, pro eorum dignitate & conditione; primogenitus autem Regis, quia Rex futurus putatur: post primum Presbyterum Cardinalem erit; Sed nullo modo inter Episcopos. Et hoc tam in conviviis, quàm aliis actibus publicis: quamvis nostro tempore aliquorum sive ambitione, sive ignorantia aliquando fit servatum contrarium &c. Si qua sunt contentiones de præsidentia, componantur; si nolunt componi, ambo contendentes honestè jubeantur exire; Si tamen esset colorata contentionis causa, & non temeraria, quia tunc solus temerarius ejiciendus esset.
units.tr: When the Pope has washed, the table before him is set again, and the three cardinals who served him take up their mantles and mitres and go to their places. The emperor, standing first at his seat, is washed with his own ceremonies. Then the lord cardinals are washed, standing before the tables with mitres on their heads; after them the prelates are washed, standing without mitres, and the laymen (if any) with heads uncovered. They shall stand before the tables to wash in the order in which they are to sit at the table: the first of the bishops at the head on the right. If some king is present, he shall be in the second place; if there are several kings, mixed with the first cardinals, first the cardinal, then the king in turn. If princes, or sons or brothers of kings, are present together, and they do not serve the Pope, they must sit among the cardinal deacons or after them, according to their dignity and rank. The eldest son of a king, however, because he is thought to be the future king, shall sit after the first presbyter cardinal; but in no way among the bishops. This holds both for banquets and for other public acts, although in our time, through the ambition or ignorance of some, the contrary is sometimes observed, etc. If there are disputes about precedence, they are to be settled; if they refuse to be settled, both contending parties are to be asked honourably to withdraw. If, however, the cause of the dispute is plausible and not rash, then only the rash one should be expelled.

units.la: Tales certè Vicarius Christi non hortabitur quemadmodum Christus, ut ultimo loco assideant; Sed quia ipse primos accubitus amat, amat amantes & tolerat, & sollicitè primos accubitus disponit! Subjungit Author, Imperatorem Græcorum, ut Regem tantùm tractari. De portandis ferculis: Primum portabit nobilior Princeps, sive Imperator sive Rex sit &c. quod capit extra portam aula convivii ab aliquo familiari PontifiPontificis; alii inferiores pro ferculo ad coquinam vadunt. Magister Sacri hospitii & magister domus baculos in manibus tenentes, & in habitu sibi conveniente deducunt portantes fercula, quae quidem fercula ad Pontificem & Imperatorem tantum cooperta portari debent, Regibus & aliis debent, antequam appareant in conspectu Papae, detegi. Item in praesentia Pontificis nulli omnino fit publice praegustatio, nisi ipsi Pontifici, & Imperatori tantum. Usque in finem convivii legitur aliquid a Subdiacono de S. Scriptura. Cum Pontifex biberit, consueverunt omnes adstantes praeter Episcopos & superioris dignitatis viros genuflectere, quod servari nostris temporibus vidimus, inquit Author, quamvis in nullo cerimoniarum libro id legamus. (Huc pertinet, quod Author Vita Sixti V. testatur, bibi in sanitatem Pontificis a geniculis;) Epulis abunde submini stratis, sic pergit Author Ceremonialis, fit secunda lotio manuum: & tunc secundus nobilis laicus portat aquam consuetis cerimoniis, prior Episcoporum Card. & 2. Diaconi dimissis mantellis & mitris, ut supra, lavantur. Unus Cardinalis servit alteri de mantili. Ponuntur deinde confectiones, sive species, & demum finito convivio lector dicit: Tu autem Domine miserere nobis; nisi sit in coena Domini, quia tunc non profertur. Tu autem. Surgit Pontifex sine mitra, assistunt ei Diaconi, & reddantur gratiae, ut in ordinario. Omnibus completis, reducitur Pontifex ad Cameram suam. Ultimo dicit Author: Advertendum, quod nunquam in convivio Pontificis admittuntur mulieres, etiamsi Imperatrix, Regina, vel Pontificis consanguinea esset. Bene se res haberet, si publico privatum, manifesto occultum responderet, & non ad illegitimi tori societatem a multis admitterentur, quibus mensae publica communio denegatur! De quo Differt. VII. ubi de vitiosis eligendorum & electorum qualitatibus, visum est. Ita nempe solent hypocritae, minora eaque ex parte licita negant, graviora, & per se turpia larga manu concedunt!
units.tr: Surely the Vicar of Christ does not urge them, as Christ did, to recline in the last place. Rather, because he himself loves the first places, he loves those who love them, tolerates them, and carefully arranges the first places! The author adds: The emperor of the Greeks is to be treated only as a king. On the carrying of the dishes: The more noble prince, whether emperor or king, shall carry the first dish, which is received outside the door of the banqueting hall from some familiar of the Pope. The other lesser men go to the kitchen for dishes. The master of the sacred household and the master of the palace, holding staves in their hands and dressed fittingly, lead those carrying the dishes. The dishes are to be carried covered only to the Pope and the emperor; for the kings and others they must be uncovered before they appear in the Pope's sight. Likewise, in the Pope's presence, no one at all is given a public taste beforehand, except the Pope himself and the emperor alone. Until the end of the banquet something from Holy Scripture is read by a subdeacon. When the Pope has drunk, all who are standing near, except the bishops and men of higher rank, customarily kneel, which we have seen observed in our time, says the author, although we read this in no book of ceremonies. (To this belongs what the author of the Life of Sixtus V testifies: that they drank to the Pope's health kneeling.) With the tables abundantly laid, the ceremonial author goes on: a second washing of the hands takes place, and then the second noble layman brings water with the customary ceremonies, and the first of the cardinal bishops and two deacons, having laid aside their mantles and mitres as above, are washed. One cardinal serves another with a towel. Then the confections, or sweets, are set out, and at last, when the banquet is finished, the reader says: "But you, O Lord, have mercy on us"; except on Maundy Thursday, when it is not said. "But you." The Pope rises without a mitre, the deacons attend him, and thanks are given as usual. When everything is finished, the Pope is led back to his chamber. Finally the author says: It must be noted that women are never admitted to the Pope's banquet, even if they were an empress, a queen, or a blood relation of the Pope. It would be well if he answered for the public by the private, and for the manifest by the hidden, and did not admit to the fellowship of an illegitimate bed those whom many deny the public communion of the table! On this I treated in Dissertation VII, where the faulty qualities of those to be elected and of the elected were considered. Hypocrites are accustomed to refuse the lesser things, and those that are in some respects lawful, and to concede with a lavish hand the more serious things, which are shameful in themselves!

units.la: L. Nihil restat de ceremoniis, Pontificis Romani electionem proxime consequentibus, nisi quod Author Sect. 4. indicat, quaenam mutentur, si coronatio Pontificis fiat extra urbem. Quia autem illud ad raro contingentia pertinet; & a longo tempore nunquam contigit; & levis est in nonnullis tantum variatio breviter ab Authore ipso indigitata; eam nos innuisse contenti sumus; Quaedam duntaxat ad convivium solenne Pontificum n. praeced. descriptum brevissime adhuc annotaturi; Nempe, ut ab initio numeri diximus, porro ostendit dissimilitudinem inter Christum & Pontificem. Et quando Pontifex, qui Successor & Vicarius Christi vocari cupit, se talem cibatione, illi, quâ Christus suos Auditores bis cibavit, simili, probare posset, & maximè ab initio muneris illud facere deberet, contrà, populo Christiano vacuis ventribus & latrantibus post longiores pompæ moras stomachis dimisso, neque invitatis, quos invitandos esse Servator dixerat, cæcis &c. mundi magnatibus & otiosis Sacerdotibus convivium exhibet, in quo post longas de primo accubitu anxiè quæsito contentiones non multos paucis, sed paucos multis & abundè subministratis epulis cibat, non tantùm à miraculo, sed etiam à temperantiæ legibus alienissimus; Id in convivii sui circumstantiis omnibus unicè agens, ut sua & reliquæ rasæ cohortis præeminentia strenuè promoveatur; Quam & ita promovet magna cum Christianorum Regum, Principum & Magistratuum reliquorum injuria & ignominia sese cum suis super illos omnes longè efferens; quemadmodum & luxu Reges superare contendit, & mundano fastu, cui similem frustrà in orbe quæras. Et sic, quod ab initio Dissertationis hujus diximus, valdè vitiosa sunt Electionis Romanorum Pontificum consequentia, primò ceremonialia.
units.tr: L. Nothing remains to be said about the ceremonies that immediately follow the election of the Roman Pontiff, except what the author indicates in Sect. 4., namely which things are changed if the coronation of the Pontiff takes place outside the city. But since that concerns things that rarely happen, and have not happened for a long time, and since the variation the author himself briefly points out is slight and affects only a few details, we are content to have hinted at it. We shall add only a very brief note on the solemn banquet of the Pontiffs described in the preceding number. As we said at the beginning of the number, the author goes on to show the unlikeness between Christ and the Pontiff. If the Pontiff, who wishes to be called the successor and vicar of Christ, could prove himself such by a meal like that with which Christ fed his hearers twice, and above all ought to do so from the start of his office, then on the contrary he sends the Christian people away with empty stomachs and grumbling after long delays of pomp. He does not invite those whom the Saviour said were to be invited, but offers his banquet to the blind, etc., to the great men of the world and to idle priests. At this banquet, after long and anxious disputes about who may sit first, he feeds a few with many, and many with few, but with food served in abundance, being utterly alien not only to the miracle but also to the laws of temperance. In all the circumstances of his banquet he works solely to promote vigorously the pre-eminence of himself and of the rest of his shaven band. He promotes it in such a way, to the great injury and disgrace of Christian kings, princes and other magistrates, that he raises himself and his followers far above them all. In the same way he strives to surpass kings in luxury and in worldly pride, of which you would seek a like example in vain anywhere in the world. And so, as we said at the beginning of this Dissertation, the consequences of the election of the Roman Pontiffs are very faulty, first of all the ceremonial ones.

units.la: SECTIO POSTERIOR, In qua, De Electionis Pontificum Romanorum consequentibus à Ceremoniis diversis agitur; Breviarium.
units.tr: SECTION LAST, in which the consequences of the election of the Roman Pontiffs, other than the ceremonial ones, are discussed; a summary.

units.la: I. Transitio & divisio consequentium non-Ceremonialium; II. Consequens Electionis est, quòd ipsi etiam Pontifices mutantur; III. Causa mutationis in simulatione Electionem antecedente ostenditur; IV. Mutatio respectu Amicorum; V. Mutatio omnis deberet esse in melius, sed mutantur in deterius; VI. Quod respectu morum probatur; VII. Fidei respectu non ita mutantur, ut infallibiles fiant; VIII. Interdum pessimè mutant opiniones saniores ante Pontificatum defensas; IX. Statum ita mutant, ut miserrimi fiant; X. Mutantur etiam eorum consanguinei per Nepotismum, qui declaratur exemplis Iohannis XVI. & Nicolai III. XI. Bonifacii IX. XII. Sixti IV. XIII. Innocentii VIII. XIV. Alexandri VI. Pii III. Leonis X. Clementis VII. Pauli III. XV. Julii III. Pii IV. XVI. Gregorii XIII. XVII.
units.tr: I. Transition and division of the non-ceremonial consequences. II. A consequence of the election is that the Pontiffs themselves are changed. III. The cause of the change is shown to lie in the pretence that preceded the election. IV. The change with respect to friends. V. Every change ought to be for the better, but they change for the worse. VI. This is proved with respect to morals. VII. With respect to faith they do not change so as to become infallible. VIII. Sometimes they change for the worse, abandoning sounder opinions they had defended before the Papacy. IX. They change their condition so that they become most wretched. X. Their relatives are also changed through nepotism, which is illustrated by the examples of (1) John XVI and Nicholas III; (2) Boniface IX; (3) Sixtus IV; (4) Innocent VIII; (5) Alexander VI; (6) Pius III; (7) Leo X; (8) Clement VII; (9) Paul III; (10) Julius III; (11) Pius IV; (12) Gregory XIII.

units.la: Sect. II. COMSEQUENTIA NON-CEREMONIALIA.
units.tr: Section II. The Non-Ceremonial Consequences.

units.la: XVII. Sixti V. XVIII. Vrbani VII. Gregorii XIV. XIX. Innocentii IX. Clementis VIII. Leonis XI. XX. Pauli V. XXI. Gregorii XV. XXII. Vrbani VIII. XXIII. Innocentii X. XXIV. Alexandri VII. XXV. Nepotismus tamen à nonnullis rejectus fuit; Quod probatur exemplis; XXVI. Clementis IV. & Nicolai IV. XXVII. Benedicti XII. XXVIII. Adriani VI. XXIX. Marcelli II. XXX. Pii V. Ex recentioribus unius & alterius; Iudicium de horum abstinentia; unà cum exemplis aliis recentissimis in contrarium. XXXI. Maximè hic vitiosum, quòd tanta est Nepotum potestas, & omnia quasi soli peragunt; XXXII. Minimè plerumque apti; XXXIII. Auri cupidissimi; XXXIV. Qui multum nocent sibi & Pontificibus; XXXV. Ecclesia plurimùm; XXXVI. Brevem habent usurpationem, tristes exitus; XXXVII. Hinc, quando de aliquo eligendo agitur, prima est Nepotum consideratio; XXXVIII. Vitium in Nepotismo propius notatur; XXXIX. Mutatio rerum Electionem consequens, vitiosa & illa. XL. Conclusio totius operis.
units.tr: XVII. Sixtus V. XVIII. Urban VII. Gregory XIV. XIX. Innocent IX. Clement VIII. Leo XI. XX. Paul V. XXI. Gregory XV. XXII. Urban VIII. XXIII. Innocent X. XXIV. Alexander VII. XXV. Nepotism was nevertheless rejected by some, which is proved by examples. XXVI. Clement IV and Nicholas IV. XXVII. Benedict XII. XXVIII. Adrian VI. XXIX. Marcellus II. XXX. Pius V. Of more recent popes, one or two; judgement on their abstention from it, together with other very recent examples to the contrary. XXXI. This is most faulty here, that the power of the nephews is so great, and they almost alone carry everything through. XXXII. Mostly least suited. XXXIII. Most greedy for gold. XXXIV. Who do great harm both to themselves and to the popes. XXXV. The Church most of all. XXXVI. They have a brief tenure and sad endings. XXXVII. Hence, when someone is to be elected, the first consideration is the nephews. XXXVIII. The fault in nepotism is noted more closely. XXXIX. The change in affairs that follows the election is also faulty. XL. Conclusion of the whole work.

units.la: I. SI juxta Dissertationis hujus Sectionem priorem Ceremonialia Electionis Pontificum Romanorum consequentia eam parum commendant, haud magis certè eam ornant consequentia proxima reliqua. Quae in mutatione, quam illa post se trahere solet, nunc tandem exhiberi, instituti ratio postulat. Mutatio illa duplex animadvertitur, & personarum, & rerum. Personae, quae statim post electionem mutantur, sunt vel Pontifices, vel eorum consanguinei; De reliquis, quos recens electi Pontifices vel deprimunt, vel extollunt, ut nihil seorsim dicamus. De illorum primò mutatione agendum est, utpote quae fundamentum est mutationis in reliquis, & personis & rebus.
units.tr: I. If, according to the earlier section of this dissertation, the ceremonies that follow the election of the Roman Pontiffs commend it little, the consequences that come next certainly do not adorn it any more. The plan of this work now requires that these be set out, namely the change which the election usually drags after it. This change is seen to be twofold, of persons and of things. The persons who are changed immediately after the election are either the Pontiffs themselves or their relatives. As for the others whom the newly elected Pontiffs either lower or raise, we will say nothing of them separately. We must treat first of the change in the Pontiffs, since it is the foundation of the change in the rest, both persons and affairs.

units.la: II. Pontifices igitur recens electi mutantur. Nomina eorum mutari supra vidimus, sed in nominibus mutatio neutiquam terminatur. Ipsi etiam mutantur, non essendo medesimi huomini &c. dum non sunt iidem homines, qui eliguntur, & qui Pontifices sunt. Sed simul cum statu & nomine ipsam etiam naturam mutant. Et sape difficile esset 2. homines invenire studiis magis dissimiles, quàm à se idem differt in Cardinalatu & Papatu; ut Nobil. Sandis Relat. dello stato della Relig. c. 31. loquitur. Sic etiam Author Vita Sixti V. p. 376. testatur, quòd mutent consuetudines, volitiones & cogitationes, quas habuerant in Cardinalatu.
units.tr: II. The newly elected Pontiffs, then, are changed. We saw above that their names are changed, but the change is by no means limited to names. They themselves are also changed, not being the same men &c. since the men who are elected are not the same as those who are Pontiffs. But together with their status and name they also change their very nature. And it would often be difficult to find 2. men more unlike in their pursuits than a man is from himself when he is a Cardinal and when he is Pope, as the Noble Sandis speaks in his Relation of the State of Religion, ch. 31. So too the author of the Life of Sixtus V, p. 376, bears witness that they change the habits, wishes and thoughts which they had as Cardinals.

units.la: III. Causa mutationis est simulatio electionem antecedens; Quíque simulàrunt, ut obtinerent, alii necessariò apparere debent, postquam jam obtinuerunt, quod antea quaesiverant. Nullum enim simulatum & affectatum, ut nullum etiam violentum, est diuturnum. Mutatos igitur fuisse omnes illos praesumendum est, de quoquorum simulatione supra egimus. Et quando Sixtum V. omnibus aliis in simulando palmam praeripuisse antehac ostendimus, eundem etiam mutationis hujus exemplum jam exhibebimus; Quippe fuit, eodem Nobili Sandis. ibidem testante, il piu sommesso &c. maxime submissus & humillimus Cardinalis, Papa generosissimus & spiritus altissimos gerens. In suo Cardinalatu servus & mancipium Hispaniae; In Papatu ejusdem inimicus periculosissimus, quem unquam in mundo habuerit. Paucis, in Cardinalatu suo erat ignominiose habitus, ut vilis Monachus, in Papatu cultus tanquam Princeps magni valoris & spiritus. Addit: Nemini mirum videri debet istud discrimen; quando tam contraria sunt media consequendi & gerendi Papatum; in uno namque statu se accommodant humoribus omnium aliorum; & in altero expectant; ut omnes se accommodent humoribus suis; Quibus accedit; quod benevolentia Principum unica via est Papatum consequendi; sed eorum nimia potentia medium eundem destruendi. Atque tandem notat, mutabilitatem hanc facere, ut Principes desiderent tranquilla natura hominem, qui non sit ex metallo volatili. Et poenituit, juxta Authorem Vita Sixti V. p.2. p.160. Hispanos, quod elegerunt hominem, qui vixerat cum cruce, & videbatur mori velle cum gladio. Tunc se deceptum sentit mundus, qui decipi voluit, quia tunc nebulae simulationum abeunt! Exemplo etiam Julii II. de quo Macchiavellus Princip. cap.XVI: Apres, qu'il eut fait son prosit du nom de liberal, il en quitta depuis les actions, afin de pouvoir faire la guerre au Roy de France; Id est: Postquam ei profuisset liberalis elogium, ex illo tempore actionibus liberalibus abstinuit, ut bellum Regi Gallia inferre posset.
units.tr: III. The cause of the change is the pretence that precedes the election. Those who pretended in order to obtain it must then appear as others, once they have obtained what they had sought before. For nothing pretended and affected lasts long, just as nothing violent does. It must therefore be presumed that all those whose pretence we treated above were changed. And since we have shown above that Sixtus V surpassed all others in pretending, we shall now also set out an example of this change in him. For, as the same Noble Sandis testifies ibidem, he was the most submissive and humble Cardinal, il piu sommesso &c., and a Pope of the most generous spirit and very lofty mind. As Cardinal he was the slave and tool of Spain; as Pope he was the most dangerous enemy of the same Spain that the world has ever had. In short, as Cardinal he was treated with contempt as a worthless monk, but as Pope he was honoured as a prince of great worth and spirit. He adds: No one should think this difference strange, since the means of obtaining and exercising the papacy are so opposite; for in the one state they accommodate themselves to the moods of all others, and in the other they expect that all accommodate themselves to their moods; To this is added: that the goodwill of princes is the only way to obtain the papacy, but their excessive power is the means of destroying it. And finally he notes that this changeability makes princes desire a man of a calm nature, who is not made of volatile metal. And, according to the author of the Life of Sixtus V, vol. 2, p. 160, the Spaniards repented that they had chosen a man who had lived with the cross and seemed willing to die with the sword. Then the world, which wanted to be deceived, feels itself deceived, because then the clouds of pretences vanish! Also by the example of Julius II, of whom Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. XVI, says: After he had gained the name of liberal, he thereafter gave up liberal actions, so that he could make war on the King of France; that is: after the reputation for liberality had served him, from that time he abstained from liberal actions, so that he could wage war on the King of France.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Tunc frustra est beneficiis electos cumulasse; Tunc nihil juvat, eos amicos antea habuisse. Quod & Lottinus in Differt. de Conclavi monuit; & Author Conclavis Alexandri VII. experientia confirmatum esse docuit; L'esperienza ha dimostrato &c. Experientia ostendit, inquit, quod in Papa (qualiacunque ejus antehac facta fuerint) semper pravalet desiderium dominium Ecclesiasticum amplificandi, saltem successoribus, quaecunque acceperat; relinquendi; Addo, desiderium, suos bene ditandi. Hinc etiam Fridericus II. electione Innocentii IV. parum delectatus est, atque gratulantibus amicis, quod amicus electus esset, respondit; Sinibaldum Cardinalem ex amico optimo in hostem acerrimum ob Pontificatum mutatum esse; Platina in vita narrante. Hinc pariter de Innocentio X. Magnus Hispaniae Minister dixit; Che il Re voleva ben haverlo per amico, ma non per Papa; Id est; Regem
units.tr: It is therefore in vain to have heaped benefits on the elect, and it does no good to have had them as friends beforehand. Lottinus also warned of this in his Dissertation on the Conclave, and the author of the Conclave of Alexander VII taught that experience confirms it: L'esperienza ha dimostrato etc. Experience shows, he says, that in a Pope (whatever he had done before) the desire to enlarge ecclesiastical dominion always prevails, at least to leave to his successors whatever he had acquired; I add: the desire to enrich his own people well. Hence also Frederick II was little pleased by the election of Innocent IV, and when his friends congratulated him that a friend had been elected, he replied: Sinibaldus has changed from the best of friends into the bitterest of enemies because of the Papacy; Platina relates this in his life. Likewise, of Innocent X the great minister of Spain said: Che il Re voleva ben haverlo per amico, ma non per Papa; that is, the King (Regem)

units.la: Mutatio respectu Amicorum; gem equidem velle eum amicum habere, sed non Papam ; Sic innuens, amicum non manere Papam factum, ut nec Gallus manere dicitur vicinus factus. Quemadmodum etiam MSC. Italicum habet: Hi-spania Regem à Papa inimico mortaliter odio haberi, ab amico timeri, nunquam amari &c. Similes igitur sunt tales electi Pontifices, illi, de quo referunt, eum, postquam Magistratum adeptus esset, omnibus suis amicis pristinis renuntiasse ; Quamvis consanguineis renuntiare plane nolint. Utut autem sic amicorum & beneficiorum oblivi-scantur, injuriarum tamen contrà porrò memores perhibentur. Ita enim Macchiavellus Princip. cap. VII. occasione Caesaris Borgiae in electionem Julii II. consentientis ait: C'est une simplicité &c. simplicis est, credere, recentia beneficia apud Magnates inducere oblivionem veterum injuriarum & irarum. Proin Dux multùm in creatione Julii II. qua eum plane perdidit, aberravit.
units.tr: Change with respect to friends; would indeed have him as a friend, but not as Pope. He implies in this that a friend does not remain a friend once he has become Pope, just as a neighbour is said not to remain a neighbour once he has become a Frenchman. The Italian manuscript also has it: Spain is mortally hated by a Pope who is an enemy, feared by one who is a friend, never loved, etc. Such, then, are the elected Popes. Of one of them they report that once he had gained the office, he renounced all his former friends, though they are unwilling to renounce their relatives altogether. Yet although they forget friends and benefits in this way, they are said to remember injuries well. Machiavelli, Prince, ch. VII, says this about Caesar Borgia's consent to the election of Julius II: C'est une simplicité etc. It is a simplicity to believe that recent benefits among great men bring about the forgetting of old injuries and anger. Therefore the Duke went badly wrong in the creation of Julius II, by which he utterly ruined himself.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Quando autem mutantur electi Pontifices, utrum in melius, vel in deterius mutentur, plenius jam atque distinctius dispiciendum est. Mutationem in melius postularet utique species collati muneris. Quid enim? Annon in melius mutari debet electus in Vicarium Christi, Monarcham, Sponsum & Caput Sanctae Ecclesiae? Quando ab infimis etiam Ecclesiae Ministris requiritur, ut profectus eorum manifestus fiat omnibus; ut non frustrà donum acceperint, & ut digne ambulent vocatione tum generali, tum speciali? Sed quicquid fieri debeat; & quicquid etiam in Vigilio (vide Schisma ejus) Baronius jactet; atque quasi requiratibidem; certum est, Pontifices electos à longo tempore plerunque in deterius manifestè mutari; Nomina egregia quidem assumunt electi, sed nominibus rem saepissimè contrariari jam suprà ostendimus breviter; Atque illis proin applicari potest: Proficient in malo. Mores quod spectat primò, heic certè, si usquam alibi, valet: Horres morres; Honores mutant mores; Sed, quod ex parte Regiminis Electitii malum est, maximè ubi unus cum potestate absoluta praesse debet, in pejus. Id quod Roma jam olim experta est, Tiberii, Neronis, & aliorum, qui in privata fortuna optimi visi, potestate deinceps publica ad humani generis perniciem pessimè abusi sunt, exemplis; Et hodienum atq; ab aliquot seculis in Pontificibus saepissimè experiri debuit; neq; Roma tantùm. Et eò magis in Pontificibus, quòd ex humili saepe statu ad istam sublimitatem exaltantur, sed gravius nihil est humili, cùm surgit in altum. Fidem assertioni nostrae plenissimam equidem sácer-
units.tr: Whether elected Popes are changed for the better or for the worse must now be examined more fully and more precisely. The nature of the office conferred certainly calls for a change for the better. For what? Ought not the one elected to be changed for the better into the Vicar of Christ, Monarch, Bridegroom and Head of the holy Church? Even the lowest ministers of the Church are required to show their progress clearly to all, so that they have not received their gift in vain and so that they walk worthily in both their general and their particular calling. But whatever ought to happen, and whatever Baronius may boast of in Vigilius (see his schism), and as if he required it there too, it is certain that elected Popes have for a long time been plainly changed, for the most part, for the worse. Those elected do indeed assume noble names, but as we have shown briefly above, the reality very often contradicts the names. And so the saying can be applied to them: Proficient in malo. As for morals, the first point is that Honours change manners holds true here, if anywhere. But as far as the governing of the elective monarchy is concerned, which is an evil, it is worst where one man must rule with absolute power. Rome has already experienced this long ago, in the examples of Tiberius, Nero and others, who seemed the best in private life but afterwards, in public power, abused it most terribly to the ruin of the human race. And today, and for some centuries, it has been experienced most often in the Popes, and not in Rome alone. The more so in the Popes, because they are often exalted from a lowly state to that height, but nothing is more grievous than a man of low birth when he rises high. Of course the sacred writings give the fullest confirmation of our assertion.

units.la: Mutatio omnis in melius fieri deberet; sed mutantur in deterius; facere possunt, quæ Differt.VII. Sect.VII. de vitiosis Pontificum qualitatibus diximus; Pauca tamen adhuc eáque magis specialia heic addidisse juvabit.
units.tr: Every change should be for the better, but they are changed for the worse. They can do what we said in Dissertation VII, Section VII, on the vicious qualities of the Popes. It will nevertheless be helpful to add a few more specific points here.

units.la: VI. Eos non in melius mutari, ex eo patet, quòd de habentibus malos ante electionem affectibus, semper præsumitur atque timetur, eos illis porrò indulturos; Hinc illorum electioni ab iis, quorum ceu antehac offendentium interest, omni studio resistitur. Sic in Conclavi Pii V. noluerunt quidam Moronem, timentes, eum, cum antea ob hæresis suspicionem incarceratus fuisset, inimicitias ulturum; Quem suum metum etiam cum Pauli IV. in Caraffis exemplo defendere noverunt. Contrà manifestissimis exemplis eos in deterius mutari probatur. Nonnulla duntaxat afferre lubet. Clementi VI. Franciscus Petrarcha tribuit, eum laudatum fuisse, antequam hoc Fortuna culmen ascenderet, in quod evecti circumstrepentibus adulantium turbis veræ laudis judicium amittant. De Innocentio VII. scribit Paulus Langius in Chronico Citizensi, minus juste, minusque laudabiliter eum dominium urbis exercuisse, quoniam illa temporalium adfluentia obficiunt haud parùm spiritualibus, neque Petri Successor, ipse Papa ejusmodi periculosum temporale dominium sumpsisse debuerat. Eidem ante Papatum Cosmato dicto Janus Vitalis in suis Elogiis sequens Epitaphium posuit: Innocuus, Cosmate, venis ad pascua Petri; Ex Pastore dehinc factus es, ecce, lupus!
units.tr: VI. That they are not changed for the better is clear from this: concerning those who had bad inclinations before their election, it is always presumed and feared that they will go on indulging them. Hence those whose interest it is to resist such men, as they had before, oppose their election with all their zeal. So in the Conclave of Pius V some did not want Morone, fearing that since he had earlier been imprisoned on suspicion of heresy, he would take revenge for the enmity. They also knew how to defend this fear by the example of the Carafas under Paul IV. On the contrary, it is proved by the clearest examples that they are changed for the worse. I will mention only a few. Francis Petrarch ascribes to Clement VI that he was praised before this Fortune raised him to the summit, to which those who are carried up, amid the clamour of flattering crowds, lose the judgement of true praise. Paulus Langius, in the Citizen Chronicle, writes of Innocent VII that he exercised dominion over the city less justly and less laudably, since that flood of temporal affairs greatly obstructs spiritual ones, and the successor of Peter, the Pope himself, ought not to have assumed such a dangerous temporal dominion. Janus Vitalis, in his Elogies, placed on the same man, before his papacy, when he was called Cosmas, the following epitaph: Harmless, Cosmas, you came to the pastures of Peter; behold, from a shepherd you have become a wolf!

units.la: Ut simul Innocentius esse desierit, & vocari coeperit! Julii III. mutationem ingenuè describit ita Onuphrius in vita: Quod si vita, quam privatus egit, institutum, Pontificatum quoque adeptus, constanter quoque servavisset, multa, quæ eo tempore depravata erant, in meliorem haud dubiè formam essent restituta. Qui namque occupationibus totus intentus Cardinalis veluti furtim voluptates sequebatur, Pontifex factus, vototum jam omnium compos, abdicatâ rerum curâ hilaritati & genio suo nimiùm indulsit, usque adeò homines præmii spe potiùs ad virtutem amplectendam, quam ipsamet virtutis pulchritudine accenduntur. Paulus IV. narrante in vita Onuphrio, timentibus severam reformationem vetus illud usurpavit: Uxorem non habentes sæpe verberant. Pii IV. exemplum vide Differt.VII. Sect.7, n. 65. cui Onuphrius in Vita præter alia tribuit, quòd egregius vita famáque fuerit, quoad privatus, vel in Magistratibus prioribus sub Pontificibus vixerit. In Conclavi Sixti V. Savelli non obtinuit, quia ejus superbia, de qua præsumebant, multùm in Pontificatu auctum ftum iri, magnos & parvos deterrebat. Urbani VII. sibi antea conjun-ctissimi morte post 13. dierum Pontificatum intellectâ, Paulus Sarpius Venetus, ut in Vita p.32. habetur, senza alcun segno d'alteratione, sine ullo alterationis signo, dixit : Ideò raptus est, ne malitia mutaret intellectum ejus. In Conclavi Leonis XI. ex simulatione Baronii collegerunt, ch'ancor egli &c. ipsum quoque, si Papa factus esset, se accommodaturum fuisse communi vivendi generi, cùm illa statim dominationis vis appareat irresistibilis, ut homines plerunque morum corruptionem sequantur. In Urbano VIII. primus electionis fructus fuit, quòd mentitus est, licèt enim omnia ad electionem suam disposita noverit, tamen de nomine interrogatus respondit, se, cùm crediderit, se Cardinalem in cellam reditypum, de nomine Papa necdum cogitâsse. Sed & mutationem ejus in deterius MSC. Italicum confirmat; Videbatur, inquit Author, Angelus bene educatus & pietati consecratus; Verùm similis fuit argento buono e bello; Mà posto à Paragon poi sul'incade. Non restava alla botte di martello. Id est: Examen non sustinuit. Imò in genere subjungit: Religiosi hi in Novitiatu ne veniale quidem peccatum committunt, sed professione factâ neque abyssos mortalium, neque ipsum infernum curant; dum privati sunt, imperio digni videntur, sed in imperio, ne minimis quidem; Dum quarunt, ―― sed quam primum obtinuerunt; omnes primò Serafini videntur &c. De Alexandro VII. vide Dissert. VII. Sect. 7. n. 71. Quæ exempla non tantùm facta referunt, sed & ex parte causas atque rationes explicant. Atque ita mutantur Pontifices electi respectu morum!
units.tr: So that Innocent at once ceased to be what he was and began to be called something else! Onuphrius, in his life, describes the change of Julius III frankly as follows: If he had constantly kept the way of life he led as a private man, even after gaining the Papacy, many things that had been corrupted at that time would undoubtedly have been restored to a better form. For as a Cardinal, wholly intent on his duties, he pursued pleasures as if in secret; but once made Pope, having gained all his desires, he gave up concern for affairs and indulged too much in cheerfulness and his own inclinations, to such an extent that men are kindled to embrace virtue more by hope of reward than by the beauty of virtue itself. Onuphrius, narrating in his life that Paul IV, fearing a strict reform, took up that old saying: They often beat those who have no wife. For the example of Pius IV, see Dissertation VII, Section 7, no. 65, to which Onuphrius in his Life attributes, among other things, that he was excellent in life and reputation while he lived as a private man, or in the earlier magistracies under the Popes. In the Conclave of Sixtus V, Savelli did not succeed, because his pride, which they presumed would greatly increase in the Papacy, frightened great and small alike. When the death of Urban VII, who had been very closely united with him, was announced after thirteen days of pontificate, Paulus Sarpius of Venice, as is recorded in his Life, p. 32, said, senza alcun segno d'alteratione, without any sign of alteration: He was snatched away, so that wickedness might not change his understanding. In the Conclave of Leo XI they inferred from Baronius's dissimulation that he too, if he had become Pope, would have adapted himself to the common manner of living, since the force of domination immediately appears irresistible, so that men for the most part follow the corruption of morals. In Urban VIII the first fruit of his election was that he lied: although he knew that everything had been arranged for his election, when asked about his name he replied that he had thought he was returning to his cell as a Cardinal and had not yet thought about a papal name. The Italian manuscript also confirms his change for the worse: Angelus, the author says, seemed well brought up and consecrated to piety; but he was like good silver of fine quality; when set to the test he was found wanting. The hammer had nothing left to strike. That is: he did not stand the examination. Indeed, the author adds in general: These religious men commit not even a venial sin in the novitiate, but once they have professed, they care neither for the depths of mortals nor for hell itself; while they are private persons they seem worthy of rule, but once in rule, not even of the smallest things; while they seek it, but as soon as they have obtained it, they all at first seem like Seraphim, etc. On Alexander VII see Dissertation VII, Section 7, no. 71. These examples not only relate deeds but also in part explain the causes and reasons. And so the elected Popes are changed with respect to morals!

units.la: VII. Fidem quod attinet, sequaces, eos optimè mutari atque insigni Metamorphosi ex fallibilibus infallibiles fieri, dictitant; Sed vana certè jactantia; Quis enim infallibilitatem fidei usurpatoribus talibus atque ita electis, & quidem vi talium electionum convenire ratione illæsa arbitretur? Et quis tantum respectu fidei profectum iis tribuat, quando eos tam malè in moribus proficere manifestum est? Et quando patet, ignaros antehac, rerum Divinarum manere ignarissimos? Et quid quæsò est ex recensitis omnibus, unde quis merito tantam prærogativam derivare queat? Non, non; clamant omnia, talibus infallibilitatem fidei minimè omnium competere, Pontificum ratione fidei mutationem non ad illum terminum pertingere! Quemadmodum & ea, quæ Dissert. VII. Sect. 5. n. 15. seqq. attulimus, satis probant, Cardinales eligentes ipsos talem mutationem Pontificis futuri haud credere.
units.tr: As for faith, my opponents keep saying that such men are changed for the better and, by a remarkable metamorphosis, go from being fallible to being infallible. But that is empty boasting. For who could think that infallibility of faith, in the sound sense, belongs to such usurpers, chosen in this way, and indeed by the force of such elections? And who would credit them with any advance in faith when it is plain they make such poor progress in morals? And when it is clear that men who were ignorant before remain most ignorant of divine things? And what, I ask, is there in all that has been recounted from which anyone could rightly derive so great a prerogative? No, no: everything cries out that infallibility of faith belongs least of all to such men, and that the change in the Popes' faith does not reach that end. Our earlier arguments in Dissert. VII. Sect. 5. n. 15. seqq. sufficiently prove this, namely that the cardinals who elect them do not believe that such a change of faith comes with the Pope-to-be.

units.la: VIII. Mutantur tamen fidei etiam respectu; atque alia credere incipiunt nonnulli, saltem docere, quàm quae antehac crediderant, docuerant. De quibus egregiè M. Ant. de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. l. IV. c.10. n. 96. ubi probat, eos, qui magnum Romae Papatum suis tueantur & extollant scriptis, contrà conscientiam id facere, ita scribit: Cùm prius durissimè de Papatu sentiret, in ipsa tamen, quam liberè loquentes fugillârunt, Cathedra, absque ulla illius, quam prius franare voluerunt, potestatis correctione & moderatione, pleni Papae, ut alii, sedernt. Et aliquis eorum, etiam scriptis foedam canere palinodiam adversus propriam priùs explicatam sententiam non erubuit. Talis fuit Æneas Sylvius Bulla Retract. Pii II. tom. I. Conc. (ubi inter alia ait: Tuebamur antiquam sententiam; nempe de Conciliorum superioritate; Ita ut Pontificum fit, post electionem à sententia antiqua deficere!) Gerbertus, qui, ut vidimus, vidimus & nos, adversus Papatum serio aliquando disputavit, ad Papatum tamen evectus & factus Sylvester II. Papatum plenum exercuit. Ita Guido Viennensis, qui in Concilio Viennensi Gallicano, ut supra c. 8. n. 67. vidimus, Papae minabatur, se ab ejus obedientia discessurum, si contrà, quàm ipsi Galli statuissent, aliquid fecisset, jam factus Callistus, plenum & ipse Papatum voluit & exercere & habere. Quâ hæc hi dicentes, illa gesserint, conscientiâ, judicent pii viri, imò Deus. Addimus ex Authore des Nouvelles de la Republique des Lettres T. II. p.382. 383. de illo ipso Pio II. sive Ænea Sylvio, cujus jam jam mentio facta est, & qui in Concilio Basileensi, cujus actus duobus libris descripsit, Scriba, abbreviator literarum Apostolicarum, ex 12. illis, qui Concilii Censores instituti, unus, Concilii nomine saepius hinc inde Legatus, particeps ac Princeps omnium gestorum, Legatus etiam Felicis Papae nomine ad Imperatorem Fridericum fuit; quòd Curia Romana nihil omiserit ad missum ab Imperatore Romam in partes suas trahendum, pour gagner un Ecrivain si hardi, inquit de Varillas. La Minorité de St Louis &c. Elle l'interessa dans les abus, dont il se plaignoit &c. Utiles ei, eodem porrò narrante, fecit abusus, de quibus antea conquestus erat, dedit Beneficia, pensiones, pileum Cardinalium, & munera potiora. Ita ut sensim sine sensu animum contrà curiam mitigaret suum, atque eam ex parte, quâ placere poterat, aspicere consueverit, & jucunditates, quibus fruebatur, tandem plane omne durum in animo emollierint, & ipse plenè ad eos transierit, quibus antea infensus erat, hâc solâ, quòd non citiùs ita egerit, poenitentiâ; Neque enim tantùm deliciis Romanis inescatus in gratiam Nicolai Felicis sui abdicationem tionem cauponatus est, eam ob rem à Nicolao Episcopus, à Calixto Cardinalis creatus, sed & Papa factus in Bulla citata, cujus initium: Execrabilis, sententias suas priores & quorumvis appellationes à Papa ad Concilium vanas, execrabiles, pestiferas & irritas pronunciavit, suscipientésque nonnisi in articulo mortis absolvendos excommunicavit, Universitates etiam, Collegia & catera corpora easenus interdicto subjecit, omnésque omninò poena læsæ majestatis reis & hæreticis debita subjecit; Atque in altera, quæ incipit: In minoribus Universitati Coloniensi An. 1463. scripta, pœnitere se professus est, quòd Dialogum & alios quosdam libros scripserit pro autoritate Concilii, Ecclesiam Dei se ignoranter, sicut Paulus fecit, scilicet, persecutum fuisse, jam vero Pontificis autoritatem supra Ecclesiam declarare, eúmque supremum ejus Monarcham, cujus peccata judicio Dei relinquenda, à nemine judicanda sint.
units.tr: VIII. Yet their faith does change too, and some men begin to believe, or at least to teach, things different from what they had believed and taught before. On this matter M. Ant. de Dominis writes admirably in de Rep. Eccl. l. IV. c.10. n. 96., where he proves that those who defend and exalt the great papacy at Rome in their writings do so against their own conscience. He writes thus: Although he had once judged the papacy most harshly, yet once he sat in the very chair which, speaking freely, they had once tried to curb, without any correction or moderation of that power which they had wanted to restrain, and they sat as full Popes, like the others. And one of them did not blush to sing a shameful palinode in his writings against the opinion he had earlier set forth. Such was Aeneas Sylvius, the Bull of Retraction of Pius II, in volume I of the Councils (where, among other things, he says: We defended the old opinion, namely the superiority of Councils; so it is the way of Popes, after their election, to fall away from the old opinion!). Gerbert, who, as we have seen, and as we too have seen, once argued seriously against the papacy, yet when he was raised to the papacy and became Sylvester II, exercised the full papacy. So too Guy of Vienne, who at the Gallican Council of Vienne, as we saw above in c. 8. n. 67, threatened the Pope that he would withdraw from his obedience if he did anything contrary to what the French themselves had decided; once made Callistus, he himself wished to exercise and hold the full papacy. Let pious men judge, and indeed God, with what conscience these men did what they said and wrote. We add, from the author of the Nouvelles de la République des Lettres, vol. II, pp. 382–383, concerning that same Pius II, or Aeneas Sylvius, already mentioned, who at the Council of Basel, whose proceedings he described in two books, was secretary and abbreviator of the apostolic letters; one of the twelve censors appointed to the Council, often sent on its behalf here and there as legate, a participant and chief of all its acts, and also sent as legate of Pope Felix to the Emperor Frederick. The Roman Curia omitted nothing to draw into its own party the man sent to Rome by the Emperor, to win over such a bold writer, as de Varillas says in La Minorité de St Louis &c. It interested him in the abuses of which he had complained &c. The abuses of which he had earlier complained became useful to him, according to the same narrator; they gave him benefices, pensions, the cardinal's hat and the more important offices, so that, little by little and without his noticing, he softened his mind against the Curia and began to look on it in the part that could please him, and the pleasures he enjoyed at last softened every harshness in his mind, and he passed over completely to those whom he had once opposed; the only thing he did not do sooner was repent. For not only was he lured by Roman delights, but in return for his renunciation he was bought over to the favour of Nicholas, his Felix; for this he was made bishop by Nicholas and cardinal by Callistus, and was made Pope in the Bull cited above, which begins Execrabilis, in which he declared his earlier judgments, and all appeals from the Pope to a Council, vain, execrable, pestilent and void, and excommunicated those who accepted them, to be absolved only at the point of death; he also placed universities, colleges and other such bodies under interdict on that ground, and subjected all of them to the penalties due to offenders against majesty and to heretics. In the other Bull, which begins In minoribus, written to the University of Cologne in the year 1463, he professed that he repented that he had written his Dialogue and certain other books in support of the authority of Councils; he had persecuted the Church of God in ignorance, as Paul did; and now he declares the authority of the Pope over the Church, and that he is its supreme Monarch, whose sins are to be left to the judgment of God and are not to be judged by anyone.

units.la: Addimus Adriani VI. quem tamen non satis mutari potuisse, supra vidimus, exemplum; Mutatum enim tamen quadantenus (quis enim Papatus vi transsubstantiativæ plenè resisteret!) fuisse, arguit, quòd, nonnullis ei ob oculos ponentibus, eum antehac contra pluralitatem beneficiorum vehementer declamâsse, respondit: Cùm infans essem, loquebar ut infans & habebam proposita infantilia, sed jam postquam vir sum, ut vir loquor, & sentio. Vel potius ei, ut & reliquis, contigit idem, quòd Doctori cuidam, apud Authorem Fasc. Temp. Zelum etiam præ se ferenti atque vehementer quoque contrà eosdem abusus declamanti, contigisse ajunt; Ad consilii quippe: Date ei unam bonam præposituram, & bene pacatus erit; executionem, zelo planè extincto, atque jam alius factus statim respondit: Non bene intellexi hanc materiam, præter modò. Tale nempe est Demosthenis, vel caninum offa projectâ silentium, in justissimum, cùm manifestum sit, tales à fide optima ad pessimam, ad pessimam saltem & carni suæ, affectibus suis, usurpationi jam suæ accommodatam doctrinam transfire, similes etiamillis, qui antequam Magistratum adipiscantur, Magistratus acta quævis virgulâ censoriâ notare, ipsi electi præ aliis, saltem cum aliis impingere solent; sed in hoc dissimiles, quòd à dignitate illegitima seducuntur. Contrà non est ista, ô viri, neque illa in reliquis mutatio vestra similis mutationi Saulis, qui Rex à Vate declaratus cogitationes Regia Majestate dignas alius factus statim habuit; neque similis est mutationi Apostolorum, quorum successionem jactatis, sed quos simplices antehac piscatores, injustos ex parte publicanos, mox orbis stupens doctissimos, mos, facundissimos juxta atque piissimos Evangelii præcones audivit, vidit ; neque similis est speciatim , quicquid Pius II. impiè suprà garriverit,mutationi Saulis sub initium novæ Ecclesiæ furentis,sed in Paulum (ast quot & quanta dico, dum Paulum dico?) st:tim post vocationem mutati; neque tandem similis Cypriani, Augustini & aliorum Ecclesiæ primitivæ Doctorum mutationi ; quia nempe non ut illi,ad bona bene & à Deo vocamini.
units.tr: We add the example of Adrian VI, whom, as we saw above, could not be changed enough; yet that he was changed to some extent (for who could resist the transubstantiating force of the papacy altogether!) is shown by his answer when some people set before his eyes that he had earlier declaimed vehemently against the plurality of benefices: When I was a child, I spoke as a child, and I had childish aims; but now that I am a man, I speak and think as a man. Or rather, what befell him, as well as the others, is said to have befallen a certain doctor, reported by the author of the Fasc. Temp., who, while showing zeal and declaiming vehemently against those same abuses, was given the advice: Give him one good provostship, and he will be well content; and when this was carried out, his zeal was utterly quenched, and he at once became another man and answered: I did not understand this matter well, beyond what I have said. Such is the silence of Demosthenes, or the dog that is silenced by a morsel thrown to it, on the most just matter; since it is plain that such men pass from the best faith to the worst, or at least to a doctrine suited to their flesh, their affections and their present usurpation. They are like those who, before they attain a magistracy, are wont to mark every act of the magistrates with a censor's rod, and once elected, prefer to find fault with others, at least to strike at others; but they differ in this, that they are seduced by an illegitimate dignity. But that change of yours, gentlemen, in other matters is not like the change of Saul, who, once declared king by the seer, at once became another man and had thoughts worthy of royal majesty; nor is it like the change of the Apostles, whose succession you boast of, but who were once simple fishermen, in part tax collectors, and whom the astonished world soon heard and saw as most learned, most eloquent and most pious heralds of the Gospel; nor is it especially like the change of Saul at the beginning of the raging new Church, which is what Pius II wickedly babbled above, for Paul (but how many and how great things do I say, when I say Paul?) was changed right after his calling; nor finally is it like the change of Cyprian, Augustine and the other doctors of the primitive Church, because, unlike them, you were not called to good things well and by God.

units.la: IX. Mutationem duplicem in Pontificibus hactenus ostensam sequitur & ex parte etiam constituit mutatio statûs illorum, quâ, non quidem ex magnis in mundo maximi,ex Cardinalibus Papæ (quod facilè concipitur;) sed ex minùs miseris magis miseri, miserrimi fiunt, dum Papæ fiunt. Mirum de Capite Ecclesiæ & Vicario Christi effatum, sed vel ex ipsa Pontificum confessione verum tamen. Divitias maximas & fontes sub pietatis prætextu acquirendi inexhaustos acquirere cum Papatu videntur ; acquirunt etiam,sed quæ non sufficiunt,non satis faciunt. Crescunt equidem nummi, sed crescit etiam amor & quæsita necessitas habendi. Et, ut in hydropico:
units.tr: IX. The double change in the Popes shown so far is followed, and in part also brought about, by a change in their status: not from great to greatest in the world, from cardinals to Pope (which is easily understood), but from less wretched they become more wretched, and most wretched, when they become Popes. It is a remarkable saying about the Head of the Church and the Vicar of Christ, yet true, even from the Popes' own confession. They seem to acquire with the papacy the greatest riches and sources of wealth that can be drawn without limit under the pretext of piety; they do acquire them, but these do not suffice, they do not satisfy. Money indeed increases, but so does the love and the sought-for need of having more. And, as with the dropsical man: The more they drink, the more they thirst for water!

units.la: Quò plus sunt pota, plus sitiuntur aquæ!
units.tr: The more they drink, the more they thirst for water!

units.la: Id quod ingenuè Alexandrum V. fassum esse ajunt, quòd nempe ex Episcopo divite, Cardinalis pauper, ex paupere Cardinale Papa mendicus factus sit. Sed & reliquam miseriam conjunctam Gregorius M. jam indigitavit, & præter alios Adrianus VI. confirmavit, cujus apud Onuphrium, in Vita sequens Epitaphium : Hadrianus VI. hic situs est,qui nihil sibi infelicius in vita,quàm quòd imperaret, duxit. Quaque parte, inquit, elogium verum dixit. Quippe nunquam ei in Pontificatu ita bene fuisse annotari poterat,quin intra privatam vitam consistere, multò malle videretur. Urbanus VII. autem suprà,dum vestiretur,indigitavit ; quam neque si centum linguæ oráque centum essent,eloqui possem. Si quis negotia ipse tractare velit,quot mox molestiis obrutus erit! Brevem Papărum vitam jam alibi aliquâ ratione indicavimus. Eam peculiari operâ examinavit jam olim Petrus Damiani Opusc. 23. de Brev. Vita Pontif. R. & Divina Provid. p.593. ita scribens: Aliquando certè, si ritè teneo, à me sollicitè requisistis, quæ mihi causa videretur, cur Apostolicæ Sedis Antistes nunquam diutiùs vivat, sed intra breve temporis spatium diem claudat extremum,adeò,ut post B. Petrum Apostolum,qui per quinque circiter annorum lustra præsedit, nemo postmodum Romanorum Pontificum hoc spatium Præsulatûs æquaverit ; mo- dernis
units.tr: This is what they say Alexander V frankly admitted: that from a rich bishop he became a poor cardinal, and from a poor cardinal he became a beggar as Pope. Gregory the Great also pointed out the rest of this wretchedness, and Adrian VI, among others, confirmed it. Onuphrius, in his Life, gives his epitaph: Here lies Adrian VI, who thought nothing in his life more unhappy than that he held rule. He says the epitaph spoke truly in every respect. Indeed, it could never be said of him so well during his papacy that he did not seem to prefer, far more, to live a private life. Urban VII, however, indicated this above while he was being dressed; I could not express it even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths. If anyone wishes to manage affairs himself, how soon will he be overwhelmed by troubles! We have already indicated the brevity of the Popes' lives in another place, in some way. Peter Damian examined it with particular care long ago, Opusc. 23. de Brev. Vita Pontif. R. & Divina Provid. p.593, writing thus: Sometime, certainly, if I hold it rightly, you anxiously asked me what seemed to me the reason why the occupant of the Apostolic See never lives longer, but closes his last day within a short span of time, so that after the blessed Apostle Peter, who presided for about five lustra of years, no one of the Roman Pontiffs has afterwards equalled this length of pontificate; in modern

units.la: {y}Statum mutant, ut miserrimi fiant dernis imò temporibus vix quispiam in prædicta sedis culmen evehitur, qui metam quatuor, vel ut multum, quinque transcendat annorum. Quod considerantibus prodigialis, ut ita loquar, stupor oboritur, quoniam hac breviter vivendi necessitas, quantum ad nostram notitiam, in nulla alia totius orbis Ecclesia reperitur. Sed in quantum mortalibus divina dispensationis revelatur arcanum, videtur nobis: quia idcirco hoc judicii cœlestis ordo disponit, ut humano generi metum mortis incutiat, & quàm despicienda sit temporalis vita gloria in ipso gloria principatu evidenter ostendat; quatenus dum præcipuus hominum tam angusti temporis compendio moritur, tremefactus quisque ad præstolandi sui obitús custodiam provocetur, & arbor humani generis, dum cacumem ac verticem suum tam facile corruisse consideract, flatu concussa formidinis, in suis unque ramusculis contremiscat. Sed quispiam fortassis objiciat, cur & Regibus hac eadem vivendi brevitas non occurrat — facilè respondetur: Quia cùm unus omni mundo Papa præsideat, Regum autem plurimos in orbe terrarum sua cujusque Regni meta concludat, quia quilibet Imperator ad Papæ vestigia corruit, tanquam Rex Regum & Princeps Imperatorum cunctos in carne viventes honore ac dignitate præcellit. Unde quolibet Rege defuncto, administratione ejus regnum tantummodò, cui præerat, destituitur; Cùm verò Sedis Apostolicæ Pontifex moritur, universus tanquam communi patre mundus orbatur. Post Damianum verò Stengelius Optica Pralatorum p.11. c.20 p.268. sequentia de eadem Pontificum vitæ brevitate adjecit: Breves quidem in angustias Pontificum vitas conclusit Damianus, fateor, dum ultra quatuor quinqueve annos non extendit: in breviores tamen mihi videntur coarctata, si Pontificum historia consulantur. Antiquam memoriam replicemus, inveniemus procul dubio, veteres aliquot Pontifices, Anteros, Lucios, Xistos, Eusebios, Anastasios, Bonifacios, Adrianos, Gelasios, aliósque vix integrum annum suo in Pontificatu explevisse. Quid annum memoro, cùm ad breviores periodos nonnulli contrahantur, qui non annos, sed menses attigerunt? Agapitus I. & Lucius II. menses undecim. Leo II. & Bened. II. & Alex. V. menses decem. Clemens II. & Bonif. III. menses novem. Marcus & Johannes XIV. & Johannes XX. menses octo. Stephanus X. menses septem. Stephanus IV. & Leo VI. menses sex. Cœlestinus II. & Innocentius V. & Cœlestinus V. menses quinque. Johannes XVI. XVII. menses quatuor. Innocentius IX. nostris temporibus, non multis ab hinc annis, menses duos. Valentinus & Leo V. & Adrianus V. & Gregorius VIII. mensem unum. Proh! quæ angustia, tam amplo in principatu! Sed alii tamen angustiores ad terminos coacti non annos, aut menses, sed paucos dies in summo Pontificatu ficatu impleverunt Leo XI. nostro Seculo, dies viginti septem; Pius III. dies viginti sex; Damasus II. dies viginti tres; Marcellus II. dies viginti unum. Sisinnius, dies viginti; Coelestinus IV. dies septemdecim, Bonif. VI. dies quindecim, Urbanus VII. nostra aetate, dies septem. Stephanus II. dies quatuor. O terminni dominandi! qui etiam in extrema miseria videri possent angusti: quidni in suprema gloria angustissimi videantur? Subjungit: Rectissime igitur B. Bernardus Epist. 237. Eugenium Papam adhortatur, ut ex brevissimo suorum praedecessorum dominatu suum quoque similem fore non vanus augur meditetur, atque inter transeuntis gloria blandimenta, quae ipsa ibi Bernhardi verba, non insaniens neque stultiescens, novissima sua memoret, & se hominem esse meminerit. De Leone XI. ita scribit Author Conclavis, quod 25. Pontificatus die mortuus sit, lasciando altrui &c, aliis exemplum relinquens memorabile, quod dignitates illae eminentes, quae flamma lucida ad instar splendeant & homines splendore suo ad desiderium sui invitent, revera consumant nimis approp inquantes & se illis immergentes; quod quidem in muscis respectu flammarum proprie dictarum saepe observatur. De Joanne XXII. stultetamen sibi vitam longam promittente Platina videatur. Ajunt, recens electo acclamari etiam: S. Pater, annos Petri non videbis; Et certe nemo 25. annos, quos Petro, additis septem mensibus, tribuunt, ex dictis successoribus vidit; proximus Hadrianus I. qui annos 23. m. 10. d. 17. sedit, accessit. Hinc provocare potuit Cornelius a Lapide ad Esaj. 38. p. 312. ad 1600. annorum experientiam, qua dictum illud confirmetur. Ita ut de Pontifice, qui per 24. annos regnavit, non valeat Ciceronis illud: Nemo est tam senex, qui se annum non putet posse vivere. Et tamen Urbanus VIII. qui id forte putavit atque insuper post v ginti & duorum annorum regimen, etiam se Petri annos visurum, Bulla, quae habetur T. IV. Bullarii Magni p. 173. singulari, gravissime omnem de residuo Pontificum & consanguineorum vitae spatio divinationem quibuscunque, Marchionalis vel Ducalis etiam dignitatis existentibus, sic laesa Majestatis reis futuris, sub excommunicationis, degradationis, beneficiorum privationis, confiscationis & ultimi supplicii poena, vetuit atque interdixit. Si vero non cadat negotiis obrutus (ut multi otio & voluptatibus indulgent unice;) quis tutum ab insidiis praestabit? Quibus vel maxime impetuntur; Jam Dissert. VI. veneno & aliis modis a successionem quaerentibus occisos exhibuimus. Tota tractatio docet, quam multi violenta morte perierint; In nulla sede, in nulla Imperatoria vel Regia dignitate tot morte violenta obiisse notantur. Habet & in miseria Papatus præròﬁativam, ut in ambitione & celsitudine mundana. Gerardus Brazutus veneficus Benedicti IX. conductus tredecim annorum spatio sex Pontificibus venena porrexisse fertur. Catalogus misera morte pereuntium Paparum, Anastasii II. Vigilii, Sabiniani, Martini I. Agathonis, Eugenii II. Johanna, Formosi, Sergii III. Johannis XI. & XIII. & XV. Benedicti IX. Lucii II. Adriani IV. Innocentii IV. Johannis XXII. veneno necatorum, Cononis, Sisinnii II. Valentini I. Leonis VI. Stephani VII. Johannis XVI. Johannis XIX. Clementis II. Leonis IX. Victoris II. Stephani IX. Nicolai II. Victoris III. Gregorii IX. Coelestini IV. Benedicti XI. Urbani V. Alexandri V. & VI. Clementis VII. & Leonis X. quibus recentiores quidam addi possunt, apud Cl. Hospinianum Hist. Sacr. Part, II. p. 125. b. 126. a. habetur. Vide violentæ mortis causas; etiam omissæ vindictæ, apud Authorem Nepot. p.2. l. 1. p.39. & de insidiis in genere p 37. seqq. majoribus quorumcunque aliorum Principum, quæ adhuc majores essent successuum respectu, si, quod, Onuphrio in Vita tradente, Marcellus II. illicitum esse judicavit, militum custodia abesset. Dissertatione VII. Pauli V. anxias de morte violenta sollicitudines memoravimus; Volunt ex aureis poculis bibere, ex quibus venenum bibitur. Hinc nunquam tuti sunt. Et memorabile est, quod hoc addatur, Sixti V. exemplum, de quo in Vita p.2. p.225. legimus, quòd postquam aliquando ex improviso cum Monacho legumina comedisset, dixerit: Benedetto sia &c. Benedictus sis, summe Domine, quòd occasionem dedisti Pontifici, semel in quiete cibum sumendi; Quem eum alias non in quiete sumpsisse, arguit, quòd additur, timuisse eum, ne sibi accideret, quod multis ante eum, & sibi quoque, hinc cautissimum non permisisse ut coquus unquam culina exiret, atque continuas eidem excubias posuisse. Sed & Pius V. apud citatum Nepotismi authorem p. 42. maximè deformis, Pontifices nihil sine timore capientes pingues esse non posse, pronuntiat. Paulum IV. nonnisi reliquias ciborum ie præsente ab Aulicis consumptorum comedisse, omnes, hostias nonnisi dimidias, datis Sacristæ dimidiis, assumpsisse, ibidem p. 43.44. narratur. Sed quot præter negotia & anxias de morte violenta curas, curis aliis atque sollicitudinibus animi Pontificum continuò torqueri debent? Si cogitant, de ingressu illegitimo, de usurpatione injusta; quòd non tales sint, quales habeantur & haberi velint; quòd erroris & omnis malitiæ vani prætextus sint, quòd Idololatriæ objectum sint, quòd Christus non impunitum dimisdimissurus sit nominis sui detestandum abusum; quòd Curiae mancipia sint, quòd memoria sua in maledictione futura sit, quòd sui vix exaltati mox rursus deprimendi sint; & de aliis, quae illos, qui nondum omnem sensum amiserunt, perpetuâ carnificinâ excruciare potis sunt. Quanti verò cruciatus sunt in sola de salute consequenda desperatione, quâ Pontifices multos, quâ tales, saepe angi certò constat? Vigerius quidem Theatr. Antichr. p. 2. c. 29. narrat, Bellayum Cardinalem cuidam, qui ipsi optârat, ut Pontifex fieret, respondisse; Absit, ut unquam filius perditionis fiam! Atque regerenti, Cardinalis membra haberi corporis Pontificis, mentem suam ita explicâsse; Cardinalibus tamen reliquam esse spem demisericordia Divina, sed Pontificum hodie nemini ceu filio perditionis & Antichristo salutis januam patere. Si quis autem ista in dubium vocare velit, eum relegabimus ad similia plane ipsorum Pontificum de desperato suo statu verba, Onuphrius in Marcello II. refert; Habebat, inquit de Marcello, Anagnosten in mensa, qui Sacros libros, aut Sanctorum Patrum scripta legeret. Post longum in prandio silentium, recordatus aliquando ea Hadriani quarti Papa verba: Romano Pontifice nemo est miserabilior, conditione ejus nulla miserior; Totius ejus laetitia & felicitas amaritudo est; Cathedra Romani Pontificis est spinosa, iter undique confertum aculeis, pondus tantae molis, ut robustissimos premat & confringat humeros: manu mensam percutiens, dixit: Non vides, quomodo, qui locum hunc altissimum tenent, salvari possint. Atque notandum est, verba haec ei extorsisse S. Scripturae & Patrum Lectionem. Conferri possunt verba sequentia: Dum Monachus essem, bene de salute mea speravi; Cardinalis factus, valde dubitare coepi; Papa pene desspero; Missis autem exemplis eorum, qui Papatum consecuti atque sic in reprobam mentem magis magisque dati tandem Athei facti sunt, jam mirari subit, quòd Vicarius Christi eget gratia & gloria Christi, quòd Caput Ecclesiae, non habet partem in salute Ecclesiae! Cujus & possibilitatem Dist. 40. Can. si Papa, & veritatem de Benedicto IX. Baronius his verbis: Hunc Deus condemnatum ad inferos voluit omnibus innotescere; de Johanne XXII. ex devotissimorum fide Fasc. Temp. de Sixto V. Bellarminus apud Maresc. Syst. Theol. Loc. 17. §. 15. ita: Quantum sapio, quantum capio, quantum intelligo descendit ad inferos; de pluribus S. Brigitta Revelat. l. 7. c. 7. p. 632. Multi summi Pontifices fuerunt ante Johannem Papam, qui sunt in inferno; & necessitatem quasi, de filiis perditionis 2. Thess. II. 3. de bestia in stagnum ignis conjicienda, hactenus dicta prodiderunt. Ipse Bellar-
units.tr: In modern times the Popes change their state so that they become most wretched. Scarcely anyone is raised to that summit of the see who passes the limit of four years, or at most five. Those who consider this are seized by a kind of amazement, as I may put it, since this necessity of living briefly, so far as we know, is found in no other Church in the whole world. But as far as the secret of divine dispensation is revealed to mortals, it seems to us that this is why the order of heavenly judgment ordains it: to strike fear of death into the human race, and to show clearly how contemptible is the glory of temporal life, even in the very glory of the highest rule. For while the chief of men dies after so short a span of a narrow time, each person, trembling, is stirred to keep watch for his own death, and the tree of the human race, seeing that its crown and top have so easily fallen, shakes in the blast of fear, even in its smallest branches. But someone perhaps objects: why does this same brevity of life not also befall kings? The answer is easy. Because one Pope presides over the whole world, while the boundary of each kingdom confines most kings of the earth to their own realm, and because every emperor falls at the feet of the Pope, he, as King of kings and Prince of emperors, surpasses all living in the flesh in honour and dignity. Hence, when any king dies, only the kingdom over which he presided is left without its administration; but when the Pope of the Apostolic See dies, the whole world is bereaved, as of a common father. After Damianus, Stengelius, in the Optica Pralatorum p. 11, c. 20, p. 268, added the following on the same brevity of the Popes' lives: I admit that Damianus has indeed confined the lives of the Popes to narrow limits, since he does not extend them beyond four or five years. Yet they seem to me to be cramped into even briefer spans if we consult the history of the Popes. If we recall ancient memory, we will undoubtedly find that several early Popes, Anterus, Lucius, Xystus, Eusebius, Anastasius, Boniface, Hadrian, Gelasius, and others, scarcely completed a full year in their pontificate. Why speak of years, when some have been drawn into still shorter periods, who reached not years but months? Agapitus I and Lucius II, eleven months. Leo II, Benedict II and Alexander V, ten months. Clement II and Boniface III, nine months. Marcellus and John XIV and John XX, eight months. Stephen X, seven months. Stephen IV and Leo VI, six months. Celestine II, Innocent V and Celestine V, five months. John XVI and XVII, four months. Innocent IX, in our own times, not many years ago, two months. Valentine, Leo V, Adrian V and Gregory VIII, one month. Alas, what narrowness in so ample a principate! Yet others, driven into still narrower limits, completed not years or months but a few days in the highest pontificate: Leo XI in our century, twenty-seven days; Pius III, twenty-six days; Damasus II, twenty-three days; Marcellus II, twenty-one days; Sisinnius, twenty days; Celestine IV, seventeen days; Boniface VI, fifteen days; Urban VII in our age, seven days; Stephen II, four days.
