O dominating limits! which even in extreme misery might seem narrow: why should they not seem most narrow in supreme glory? He adds: Rightly, therefore, did St Bernard (Ep. 237) exhort Pope Eugenius, and not in vain, to consider that his own rule would be as brief as that of his predecessors, and amid the flattering enticements of passing glory, as Bernard's own words have it, not to be unwise or foolish, but to remember his last things and to remember that he is a man. Concerning Leo XI the author of the Conclave writes that he died on the twenty-fifth day of his pontificate, leaving others behind, and leaving an memorable example to others, that those high dignities, which shine like a bright flame and invite men by their splendour to desire them, in truth consume those who come too near and plunge themselves into them; which indeed is often observed in moths with respect to flames properly so called. Concerning John XXII, who nevertheless promised himself a long life, Platina seems to speak. They say that at his election this acclamation was also shouted: Holy Father, you will not see the years of Peter; and indeed no one among the said successors saw the twenty-five years, with seven months added, which they assign to Peter; the nearest was Hadrian I, who sat twenty-three years, ten months and seventeen days. From this Cornelius a Lapide (on Isaiah 38, p. 312) could appeal to an experience of 1600 years, by which that saying is confirmed. So that of a Pope who reigned for twenty-four years, that saying of Cicero does not hold: No one is so old that he does not think he can live another year. And yet Urban VIII, who perhaps thought this, and moreover, after a rule of twenty-two years, expected to see the years of Peter as well, in the bull found in T. IV, Bullarium Magnum p. 173, forbade with the greatest severity any divination whatsoever about the remaining span of life of the Popes and their kinsmen, even for those holding marquisal or ducal dignity, under the penalty of excommunication, degradation, deprivation of benefices, confiscation, and the ultimate punishment, as future guilty of treason. But if he does not fall, overwhelmed by business (as many give themselves over solely to leisure and pleasures), who will provide a safe guard against plots? These are especially aimed at the Popes. Already in Dissert. VI we have shown that they were killed with poison and other methods by those seeking the succession. The whole treatment teaches how many perished by violent death. In no see, in no imperial or royal dignity, are so many noted to have died a violent death. The papacy also has its prerogative in misery, as it does in worldly ambition and height. Gerard Brazutus, the poisoner hired by Benedict IX, is said to have given poison to six Popes over a span of thirteen years. The catalogue of Popes who perished a wretched death: Anastasius II, Vigilius, Sabinianus, Martin I, Agatho, Eugene II, Joan, Formosus, Sergius III, John XI, XIII and XV, Benedict IX, Lucius II, Adrian IV, Innocent IV, John XXII, poisoned; Conon, Sisinnius II, Valentine I, Leo VI, Stephen VII, John XVI, John XIX, Clement II, Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, Nicholas II, Victor III, Gregory IX, Celestine IV, Benedict XI, Urban V, Alexander V and VI, Clement VII and Leo X, to whom some more recent names can be added, found in Hospinian's Historia Sacramentaria, part II, p. 125b–126a. See the causes of violent death, including revenges left unperformed, in the author of Nepotismus, p. 2, l. 1, p. 39, and on plots in general p. 37 ff. The greater of all other princes, which would be even greater in respect of successions if, as Onuphrius reports in his Life, Marcellus II judged it unlawful, were not absent from the guard of soldiers. In Dissertation VII we recalled the anxious concerns of Paul V about violent death. They want to drink from golden cups, since poison is drunk from them. Hence they are never safe. And it is worth noting what is added, the example of Sixtus V, of whom we read in his Life, p. 2, p. 225, that once, after unexpectedly eating beans with a monk, he said: Blessed be you, almighty Lord, that you gave the Pope occasion once to take food in peace; that he had not taken food in peace at other times is shown by what is added, that he feared it would happen to him as it had to many before him and to himself too. Hence he most cautiously did not permit the cook ever to leave the kitchen, and posted constant guards over him. But also Pius V, in the already cited author of Nepotismus, p. 42, most shamefully declared that Popes taking nothing without fear cannot be fat. It is related in the same place, pp. 43–44, that Paul IV ate only the leftovers of food consumed by the courtiers in his presence, and took the hosts only halved, giving the halves to the sacristan. But how many concerns, beyond business and anxious cares about violent death, must constantly torment the minds of the Popes with other cares and anxieties? If they reflect on their unlawful entry, on their unjust usurpation; that they are not such as they are held to be and wish to be held; that they are the empty pretexts of error and of all malice; that they are the object of idolatry; that Christ will not let pass unpunished the detestable abuse of his name; that they are the slaves of the Curia; that their memory will be in cursing; that they, scarcely exalted, will soon be cast down again; and by others which are able to torture with perpetual slaughter those who have not yet lost all feeling. But how great are the torments in the very despair of obtaining salvation, by which many Popes, and such as they, are often certainly known to be distressed! Vigerius, indeed, in his Theatrum Antichristi p. 2, c. 29, relates that Cardinal Bellarmine, when someone wished him to become Pope, answered: Far be it that I should ever become a son of perdition! And when the other replied, Cardinals are members of the body of the Pope, he explained his mind thus: Yet to the Cardinals there remains hope in the divine mercy; but today the door of salvation lies open to no one of the Popes, as to a son of perdition and Antichrist. If anyone wishes to call this into doubt, we will refer him to similar words of the Popes themselves about their desperate state. Onuphrius, in his Life of Marcellus II, reports: He had, he said, a reader at table, who read the holy books or the writings of the holy Fathers. After a long silence at dinner, he recalled the words of Hadrian IV, the Pope: No one is more wretched than the Roman Pontiff; no condition is more miserable than his; all his joy and happiness is bitterness; the chair of the Roman Pontiff is thorny, the way on all sides crowded with thorns, the weight of so great a mass that it crushes and breaks the strongest shoulders: striking the table with his hand, he said: Do you not see how those who hold this highest place can be saved? And it should be noted that these words were wrung from him by reading Holy Scripture and the Fathers. The following words may be compared: While I was a monk, I hoped well of my salvation; made a cardinal, I began to doubt greatly; made Pope, I almost despair. Having set out the examples of those who obtained the papacy and, thus given over more and more to a reprobate mind, at last became atheists, one is now moved to wonder that the Vicar of Christ lacks the grace and glory of Christ, and that the Head of the Church has no part in the salvation of the Church! Of this possibility and truth, Dist. 40, Can. Si Papa, and concerning Benedict IX, Baronius with these words: God wished this man, condemned to hell, to be made known to all; concerning John XXII, from the faith of the most devoted, Fasc. Temp.; concerning Sixtus V, Bellarmine, quoted by Maresius in Systema Theologiae, Loc. 17, §15, thus: So far as I know, so far as I grasp, so far as I understand, he went down to hell; concerning many, St Bridget, Revelations l. 7, c. 7, p. 632: There were many supreme Popes before John the Pope who are in hell; and, as it were, of the necessity of the sons of perdition (2 Thess. 2:3) and of the beast to be cast into the lake of fire, they have set forth what has been said so far. Bellarmine himself…

units.la: Marginal notes on the left are too faint and damaged to be read reliably; they are not transcribed. Bellarminus, Fuligatto l. VI. 4. in Vita referente, ad verba adversarii, ob simplicitatem non electum esse, dicentis, in margine annotâsse fertur: Felix simplicitas, qua me tanto onere liberavit! Quemadmodum etiam, eodem p. 359. referente, hæc ejus Litania & quotidiana supplicatio fuit: A Papatu libera me Domine, & mitte quem missurus es! Si modò hæc non sub larva scripsit, & dixit, & publicavit, & prima quidem, se quoque, ceu Jesuitam & Gallis ob Scripta de potestate Papæ exosum, proin haud admittendum, solandi animo, eodemque insuper, qui vulpi in fabula tribuitur, dicenti, cùm habere non posset; Nondum matura est, nolo acerbam sumere. Quod quidem suspicari jubet ipsum Bellarmini, cùm sumpturus esset sanctissimum Domini nostri corpus, in conspectu B. Virginis Maria, & totius cœlestis curiæ apud eundem p. 353. votum; Quod si forte (quod non cupio, & precor Deum, ut non accidat) ad Pontificatum assumptus fuero, neminem ex consanguineis & affinibus exaltabo ad Cardinalatum, vel temporalem Principatum, vel Ducatum, vel Comitatum, vel quemcunque titulum, neque eos ditabo; Sed solùm eos adjuvabo, ut in statu suo civili commodè vivere possint. Amen, Amen. Talia enim in casûs difficultate spondere desiderantis est, maximè si publicentur. Ut contrà suspicioni huic non contrariatur, quòd in primis Comitiis apud eundem p. 357. dicere solitus fuit, cùm adhuc vegetus & viribus prosperis erat, fore erem fortasse pœnitendam Cardinalibus, si ipsum eligerent, qui genus ducebat ab avis adeò longævis, ut superstites fuerint usque ad extremum senium. Dixit quippe in primis Comitiis, si dixit, rémque non tanti ad eum impediendum momenti dixit, detexit, jam fortè dictam detectámque aliis. Et tamen hic Papatus, hæc tanta miseria omnium votis expetitur modis omnibus quæritur! O vanas hominum mentes & pectora caca!
units.tr: Marginal notes on the left are too faint and damaged to be read reliably; they are not transcribed. Bellarmine, as Fuligatto reports in Book VI, chapter 4 of his Life, is said to have written in the margin, in reply to his opponent's words that he was not chosen because of his simplicity: "Happy simplicity, which has freed me from so great a burden!" Likewise, as the same author reports on p. 359, his daily litany and prayer was: "Deliver me, Lord, from the Papacy, and send whom you are going to send!" If he did not write, say and publish these things under a mask, and if he first of all said them about himself, as a Jesuit and one hated by the French for his writings on the power of the Pope, and therefore not to be admitted, then he said them to console himself. He also said what is attributed to the fox in the fable when he could not reach the grapes: "It is not yet ripe; I do not want to take it when it is sour." This certainly leads one to suspect Bellarmine's own vow, made on p. 353, when he was about to receive the most holy body of our Lord in the sight of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the whole heavenly court: "If perhaps (which I do not desire, and I pray God that it does not happen) I should be raised to the Papacy, I will not exalt anyone of my kin or relatives to the cardinalate, or to temporal principality, or to a duchy, or a county, or any title whatever, nor will I enrich them; but I will only help them so that they can live comfortably in their civil condition. Amen, amen." Such promises are the sort that a man makes in a difficult situation who wishes them, especially if they are published. Nor does the suspicion contradict what he used to say at the first conclave, on p. 357, while he was still vigorous and in good strength: that if the cardinals elected him, they would perhaps have cause to repent, since he came from ancestors who lived so long that they survived to extreme old age. He said this at the first conclave, if he said it; and though it was a matter of no great importance for hindering him, he revealed and disclosed it, perhaps already said and disclosed to others. And yet this Papacy, this great misery, is sought by everyone's votes and pursued by every means! "O vain minds of men and blind hearts!"

units.la: X. Tristis est & maximè tristis in Pontificibus mutatio, lætior videri posset illa in eorum consanguineis; si quidem secundùm mundum judicaremus; Illi enim exaltantur, ditantur antehac sæpe vilissimi, pauperrimi; Exemplis illud primò confirmabimus.
units.tr: X. The change in the Popes is sad, and especially sad; it might seem happier among their kinsmen, if we judged by the world's standards. For those men are exalted and enriched, who before were often the basest and poorest. We will first confirm this by examples.

units.la: De Johanne XVI. ita scribit Platina; Merito ab ipsis Clericis odio habitus est, maximè quòd divina humanáque omnia cognatis & affinibus suis elargiebatur, posthabito Dei honore & Romana sedis dignitate, quem certè errorem ita posteris tradidit, ut ad nostram quoque ætatem pervenerit. Quâ quidem consuetudine nil certè dici perniciosius potest, cùm non ob Religionem & Dei cultum appetere Pontificatum nostri Sacerdotes videantur, sed ut fratrum, vel nepotum, vel familiarium ingluviem & avaritiam expleant, pleant. Nicolao III. idem vitio vertit,quòd suos ita amârit,ut aliunde (Stella ait, ut fit, nimium) raperet,quod eis condonaret. Nam quibusdam nobilibus Romanis Castella vi abstulit, ac suis dono dedit,maximè verò Surianum. Ubi etiam subita morte correptus fuit. Stella rursus dicit: eum sibi proposuisse, duos Reges ex sua familia creare,unum in Etruria & alium in Lombardia.
units.tr: Platina writes of John XVI as follows: "He was rightly hated even by the clergy themselves, especially because he gave away all things, divine and human, to his kin and relatives, setting aside the honour of God and the dignity of the Roman See. He handed down this error to posterity so thoroughly that it has come down even to our own age. Certainly nothing can be said to be more harmful than this custom, since our priests seem to seek the Papacy not for religion and the worship of God, but to satisfy the gluttony and greed of their brothers, nephews or household." Nicholas III was likewise faulted for loving his own so much that he took from elsewhere (Stella says, as usually happens, too much) what he might give to them. For he took castles by force from some Roman nobles and gave them as gifts to his people, above all Suriano, where he was also struck down by sudden death. Stella again says that he had planned to create two kings from his own family, one in Tuscany and another in Lombardy.

units.la: XI. Sub Bonifacio IX. multa crimina, Platina in Vita notante eodem, per Simoniacam pravitatem committebantur, petentibus contra jus fasque omnia tum fratribus, tum cognatis: quorum magna multitudo quaestûs causâ Romam venerat. Indulgentia verò & quidem plenaria ita passim vendebantur, ut jam vilesceret clavium & literarum Apostolicarum auctoritas. Revocare hac omnia Bonifacius conatus,cognatorum precibus eò identidem redire cogebatur. Unde melius actum cum Ecclesia Dei censerem, si Pontifices rejectis affinibus & cognatis,vel saltem in mediocri fortuna collocatis, Pontificiae dignitati potius, quàm carni & sanguini consulerent.
units.tr: XI. Under Boniface IX, as Platina notes in the same Life, "many crimes were committed through simoniacal depravity, since all things contrary to law and right were sought by brothers and kinsmen alike, and a great crowd of them came to Rome for profit. Indulgences, even plenary ones, were sold everywhere, so that the authority of the keys and of the apostolic letters grew cheap." Boniface tried to revoke all these things, but he was repeatedly forced back to them by the entreaties of his kin. So I would judge that the Church of God would have fared better if the Popes, rejecting relatives and kinsmen, or at least placing them in modest fortune, had looked to the Papal dignity rather than to flesh and blood.

units.la: XII. Sixti IV. Nepotismum jam supra ex parte descripsimus. De eo distinctiùs Onuphrius in vita ita loquitur: Xystus suorum indulgentissimus ac amantissimus omnium judicio est existimatus. Quorum causâ multa praeter fas jusque egisse & concessisse vitio illi datum est. Petrus ipse (Rivaria) amplissimis sacerdotiorum redditibus auctus, ita splendidus erat, ut pecunia perdenda natus esse videretur, nam eo biennio, quo tantum post ea super vixit, ducenta aureorum millia in victu absumpsisse, IX. verò millia aris alieni, argenti autem celati CCC. pondo reliquisse traditur. Obiit voluptatibus confectus, annorum XXIX. sepultus ad S. Apostolos. Paulò ante obitum creatus à Xysto fuerat totius Italiae Legatus. Qua de causa & ubique, ac Mediolani praesertim, Venetiis & Patavii honorificentissimè susceptus, Romam, ubi paulò post excessit, reversus est. Cujus frater Hieronymus ex tenui alioqui & humili fortuna, in ejus potentia locum succedens & Forocornelii ac Forolivii princeps factus, post eum rem omnem Ecclesiasticam administravit, ingenio magis severo ac voluptatibus minimum, praeter unam Venationem, deditus. Uxorem is duxit Catherinam Galeathii Insubrum ducis ex concubina filiam, cujus rei causâ filium ejus Ascanium Cardinalem Xystus postea creavit. Post hos verò Pontifex fratrum sororumque filios, quos multos habuit, ad magnos honores divitiasque provexit. Nam Leonardum fratris filium, data ei in matrimonium regis Ferdinandi filia notha urbis praefectum dixit, & in ejus defuncti locum alterius fratris filium Joannem Juliani Cardinalis (Julii II.) fratrem suffecit, Sora ac Senogallia principatu adjuncto &c. Christophorum deinde & Dominicum Ruvereos fratres—item sororis filium, & Petri Riarii sorore natum—annorum 17. &c. Cardinales dixit. Eodem, quem supra dixerat, Hieronymo Riario ceu conspirationis contra Medicæos instrumento clam, ne tam atrox scelestúmque consilium sanctis auribus admissé videretur, usum esse, paulò post indicat. Hinc etiam natus rumor in tota Europa Authori Nepotismi p. 4. l. 2. p. 109. memoratus, Chelsea città &c. Romam tot habere Papas, quot essent Sixti Nepotes. Atque ut eos satiaret, eodem p. 117. seqq. narrante, simulavit, se debita Antecessorum soluturum, & vendidit gemmas ex Tiara Pauli II. debitis nihilominus manentibus, creditoribus illusis. Ut sub hoc Sixto Nepotismus in nervum eruperit; quare etiam Il Nipotismo in eo primum ejus exemplum ostendit. In quem sane errorem, inquit Joh. Stella in Vita, multi superiorum Pontificum etiam cecidere, quod satis detestandum & reprehensibile est.
units.tr: XII. We have already described in part the nepotism of Sixtus IV. Onuphrius speaks of it more distinctly in his Life as follows: "Sixtus was judged by all to be the most indulgent and loving toward his own. For their sake he was thought to have done and granted many things beyond right and law, and he was blamed for it. Peter himself (Riario), enriched with the very large revenues of ecclesiastical offices, was so showy that he seemed born to squander money. In the two years he survived after this, he is said to have spent two hundred thousand gold pieces on his living, and to have left behind nine thousand debts and three hundred pounds of hidden silver. He died worn out by pleasures, at the age of twenty-nine, and was buried at the Holy Apostles. Shortly before his death he had been made by Sixtus legate of all Italy. For this reason he was received with the greatest honour everywhere, especially at Milan, Venice and Padua, and returned to Rome, where he died shortly after. His brother Hieronymus, from a poor and humble fortune, succeeded him in his power and was made lord of Forlì and Imola, and after him administered all ecclesiastical affairs, being of a rather severe disposition and given to pleasures only a little, apart from one hunting. He married Caterina, the illegitimate daughter of Galeazzo, Duke of the Insubrians; for this reason Sixtus later made her son Ascanio a cardinal. After these, the Pope advanced to great honours and riches the sons of his brothers and sisters, of whom he had many. For he made Leonardo, his brother's son, to whom he gave in marriage the natural daughter of King Ferdinand, prefect of the city; and in place of this same man, when he died, he put in another brother's son, Giovanni, brother of Julian, the cardinal (Julius II), together with the principality of Sora and Senigallia, and so on. Then he made Christopher and Dominic Rovere, brothers, a nephew of his sister, and a son of Peter Riario's sister, cardinals at the age of seventeen, and so on." He afterwards shows that he secretly used Hieronymus Riario, as an instrument of conspiracy against the Medici, "so that so atrocious and wicked a plan would not seem to have been admitted to holy ears." Hence the rumour spread through all Europe, as the author of the Nepotism mentioned on p. 4, book 2, p. 109, says: "The city of Chelsea ... Rome has as many Popes as Sixtus had nephews." And to satisfy them, as the same author relates on p. 117 and following, he pretended that he would pay the debts of his predecessors, and he sold the jewels from the tiara of Paul II, while the debts nonetheless remained, and the creditors were mocked. Thus under this Sixtus nepotism broke out into full strength; for this reason also the Italian term for it, Il Nipotismo, first shows its example in him. Into this error, says John Stella in his Life, "many of the earlier Popes also fell, which is certainly to be detested and condemned."

units.la: XIII. Successor Innocentius VIII. quum ante Pontificatum aliquot filios suscepisset, inquit Onuphrius in vita, duos ex his Pontificatui suo superstites magnis honoribus & opibus evexit; Nimio, ut Stella loquitur, eorum amore affectus.
units.tr: XIII. His successor, Innocent VIII, although before his Papacy he had fathered several sons, as Onuphrius says in the Life, advanced two of them who survived to his Papacy to great honours and wealth, being affected, as Stella puts it, by excessive love for them.

units.la: Nam Francisco oppida nonnulla urbi vicina dedit, Laurentiúque Medicis filiam Magdalenam, formosissimam puellam matrimonio junxit: alteram Theodorinam Gerardo Usumari Genuensi nuptam magnis divitiis cumulavit—Laurentium Cybo fratris sui nothum Archiepiscopum Beneventanum, & arcis praefectum, & Joannem Medicem Laurentii filium nurus sua fratrem vix XIII. annum agentem &c. Cardinalem.
units.tr: For he gave Francesco several towns near the city, and married to Lorenzo de' Medici his daughter Maddalena, a most beautiful girl. The other daughter, Teodorina, married to Gerardo Usodimare of Genoa, he loaded with great riches. He made Lorenzo Cibo, the natural son of his brother, Archbishop of Benevento and prefect of the citadel, and Giovanni de' Medici, son of Lorenzo and his daughter-in-law's brother, barely thirteen years old, a cardinal, and so on.

units.la: XIV. Alexandri VI. Nepotismus, vel potiùs Filiismus & Spuriismus, jam ex iis, quae Differt. VII. Sect. 6. n. 56. diximus, aliquo modo cognosci potest.
units.tr: XIV. Alexander VI's nepotism, or rather filialism and bastardism, can be understood in some measure from what we said in Differt. VII. Sect. 6. n. 56.

units.la: Bella autem ex solo, divitias & principatus spuriis acquirendi studio, perfidè suscepta, atque iniquissimè crudelissimèque gesta apud Onuphrium multis descripta legi possunt. Electo in locum ejus Pio III. cognati come api &c. loquitur Author Nepotismi p. 1. l. 2. p. 141. apum ad istar Romam Senis advolare coeperunt, sed, intellectâ non sine ingenti dolore Pontificis morte, ante ingressum in urbem iisdem equis, quibus venerant, redierunt. Atque conjicit, eum illis multum indulturum fuisse ob teneritudinem affectus erga illos. Leonis X. Nepotismum praeter alios Il Nipotismo p. 145–148. describit. Illum verò Clementis VII. ejusdem familiae suae augmentum unicè quaerentis p. 152. seqq. Post Clementem Paulus III. verba sunt Onuphrii phrii, fuit adeò erga suos sanguinis propinquitate sibi conjunctos indulgens, ut & intemperanter eis faveret, & ad summos honores, aut ad summum auctoritatis locum, stabilésque divitias eosdem proveheret. Certè suscepti GC. millibus aureorum Murinæ & Regii cum Ferrarii duce quæstionem finivit. Contrà voluntatem complurium Cardinalium Petro Luisio Parmam, & Placentiam nobilissimas Ecclesiæ Romanæ beneficiarias in Gallia Cispadana urbes vectigales, Camerino Ecclesiæ à Nepote Octavio restituto, decemque millium aureorum annuo tributo imposito addixit: &, quod antea factum non meminerant, duos Nepotes Farnesios fratres in idem Cardinalium Collegium adscivit &c. Vide plura de eo Disput.VII. Sect.6. n. 62. & II Nipotismo p.154--162.
units.tr: The wars he waged treacherously, for the sake of acquiring riches and principalities for his bastards, and carried on most unjustly and cruelly, can be read as described at length by Onuphrius. After Pius III was elected in his place, the author of Nepotismi p. 1, l. 2, p. 141, speaks of his relatives: "Like bees they began to fly to Rome from Siena, but when they learned, not without great sorrow, of the Pontiff's death, they returned on the same horses on which they had come, before entering the city." And he conjectures that "he would have indulged them greatly, out of tenderness of affection toward them." Among others, the author describes the nepotism of Leo X in Il Nipotismo p. 145–148. Clement VII, who sought only to increase his own family, is described in p. 152 ff. After Clement came Paul III, of whom Onuphrius says: "He was so indulgent toward his own kin that he favoured them to excess and advanced them to the highest honours and the supreme places of authority, and to lasting riches. Indeed, for 300,000 gold pieces he settled the dispute with Murina and Regio and with the duke of Ferrara. Against the wishes of many cardinals, he granted to Pier Luigi Parma and Piacenza, the most noble cities of the Church of Rome in Cispadane Gaul, as a fief, and Camerino, restored to the Church by his nephew Octavio, with an annual tribute of 10,000 gold pieces imposed on it. And, what had not been done before, he admitted his two nephews, the Farnese brothers, into the same college of cardinals, etc." See more on him in Disput. VII. Sect. 6. n. 62, and Il Nipotismo p. 154–162.

units.la: XV. De Julii III. Nepotismo ea paucis apud Authorem Nepotismi Ib. p. 162. seq. habentur; eum quidem, Papa potius voluptatibus indulgente, quàm suorum tantam, tanquam priores, curam habente, ad similem gradum non pervenisse, interim sub conditionibus Fratri & Nepoti maximè commodis ingentibus sumptibus Hetruria Ducem à Julio adjutum esse, qui etiam 5. Nepotes Cardinales creaverit, iisque multùm exhibuerit, licèt non prodiga Antecessorum manu; resistentibus etiam ad ulteriora tendenti Cardinalibus. Successori, Paulo IV. tribuit, quòd Nepotem statim ad Cardinalatum & non exiguam authoritatem evexerit, & Columnarum injustè sublatorum bona alii Nepoti, ejus potentiam pro virili augendo, propria fecerit, atque rursus alii Comitatum, priori Domino ejecto, vendicârit; quo facto ad tantam insolentiam proruperint & temeritatem Pontificis indulgentiâ excitatam, ut furati sint, occiderint, atque mille impostauras malo populi & Ecclesiæ commiserint, ut non tantùm orbem offenderint, sed & Pontificem ad eos Roma pellendos & omni dignitate privandos adegerint. Vide p.165 167.168. Pium IV. qui immediatè successit, severum quidem, imò perfidum in extirpando Pauli Nepotismo describit, sed subjungit: Post hac bonus Pontifex Pius, ut pietati nihil defit, consuetudinem Antecessorum secutus novum introduxit Nepotismum, dum ultrà 25. Nepotes ex fratribus & sororibus Romam ad eum venerunt, quos omnes ad ultimum usque, & quoad possibile fuit, ad altitudines honorum maxime conspicuorum evexit, & per nexus matrimoniales ditissimos reddidit; præcipuè Johannem Antonium Sarbellonem Nepotem suum unicè ascummulandis pro familia thesauro intentum; p.168.169.170. Testimonium Onuphrii vide Diss.VII.Sect.6. n. 65,
units.tr: XV. On the nepotism of Julius III, the author of Nepotismi, ibid. p. 162 f., gives a few details. He says that Julius, a pope who indulged in pleasures rather than taking such care of his own people as his predecessors had, did not reach the same level, but that under conditions most advantageous to his brother and nephew, he gave great sums of money to the Duke of Tuscany, who was also aided by Julius; that he created five nephews cardinals and treated them generously, though not with the lavish hand of his predecessors; and that he met resistance from the cardinals when he tried to go further. To his successor, Paul IV, the author ascribes this: "He immediately raised his nephew to the cardinalate and to no small authority, and as far as he could, he made his power grow by taking the goods of the Colonna, unjustly seized, and making them his own, giving them to another nephew; and then he claimed for yet another nephew the county, after its former lord had been ejected. By this, the nephews were driven to such insolence and recklessness, encouraged by the Pontiff's indulgence, that they stole, killed, and committed a thousand frauds to the harm of the people and the Church, so that they not only offended the whole world but also compelled the Pontiff to expel them from Rome and strip them of all dignity." See p. 165, 167, 168. He describes Pius IV, who immediately succeeded, as severe, indeed treacherous, in extirpating the nepotism of Paul, but adds: "After this, the good Pontiff Pius, lacking nothing in piety, followed the custom of his predecessors and introduced a new nepotism, since more than twenty-five nephews, from his brothers and sisters, came to him at Rome. He raised all of them, to the last one and as far as possible, to the heights of most conspicuous honours, and made them very rich through wealthy marriages, especially John Anthony Serbelloni, his nephew, who was devoted solely to heaping up a treasure for the family; p. 168, 169, 170." For Onuphrius' testimony, see Diss. VII, Sect. 6, n. 65.

units.la: XVI. Qui
units.tr: XVI. Who

units.la: XVI. Qui ei post Pium V. successit Gregorius XIII, ejusdem Authoris Nepotismi lb. p.171.172. testimonio adeo indulgens erga suos fuit, ut revera se Buon compagno, bonum socium exhibuerit. Electus statim Nepotem Cardinalem creavit, eique multas Abbatias, quae Antecessoris jam tempore vacaverant, dedit. Praeter hunc autem omnes suos Nepotes, ex fratribus & sororibus Romam vocavit, iisque officia, dignitates, administrationes & dominia ad eos magnos reddendos sufficientia dedit, & tantum praeter Abbatias & Praelaturas (quando Principatibus acquirendis tempora parum apta vidit) argenti, quantum volebant & desiderabant.
units.tr: XVI. Gregory XIII, who succeeded Pius V, was, by the testimony of the same author in Nepotismi lb. p. 171, 172, so indulgent toward his own that he truly showed himself a "good fellow" (buon compagno). Immediately upon his election he created a nephew a cardinal and gave him many abbeys that had already fallen vacant in his predecessor's time. Besides this one, he called all his nephews, from his brothers and sisters, to Rome, and gave them offices, dignities, administrations and lordships sufficient to make them great, and as much silver, besides abbeys and prelacies (since he saw that the times were little suited to acquiring principalities), as they wished and desired.

units.la: XVII. Post eum Sixtus V. ex pauperrima familia (domum ipse aliquando joco illustrem dixit) & ordine Francisci, ex quo etiam Sixtus IV. Nepotismi, si non author, saltem auctor, primis diebus a suis exaltandis alienior visus, eodem Authore Nepotismi p.173. seqq. referente, eos tamen postea tantum amavit, ut nullus ante eum in suis ditandis studiosior fuerit, ne ipse quidem Sixtus IV. Soror Camilla lotrix asino, quem filius ducebat, vecta Romam venit, sed in primo Pontificatus mense Nium 21. annorum Pileo ipsius Pontificis ornatum, & praeter diversas Abbatias reditibus 30000. Duplicium annuis ditatum, alium, qui Asinum duxerat, praecipuis Romae officiis honoratum & maxima pompa ditissima atque Nobilissima Romana conjugatum vidit; Ipsa annuos reditus 10000. scutorum accepit, sed naturam mutare non valens semper vitam rusticam egit. Filia dua, data singulis 100000. Scutorum dote, & adjunctis certis dignitatibus, pilco Cardinalitio, atque bonis reditibus, in familias Ursinorum & Columnarum nubendo transferunt. Filium fratris Cardinalem creatum 20000. scutorum annuis reditibus ex multis etiam Abbatiis colligendis auxit. Breviter praeter argentum praesens familia sua annuos reditus 150000. Duplicium reliquit.
units.tr: XVII. After him came Sixtus V, from a very poor family (he himself once said in jest that his house was illustrious), and of the Franciscan order, from which also Sixtus IV, if not the originator, at least the promoter of nepotism, came. In the first days he seemed rather aloof from raising his own people, but, as the same author of Nepotismi p. 173 ff. relates, he afterwards loved them so much that no one before him was more eager to enrich his kin, not even Sixtus IV. His sister Camilla, a washerwoman, came to Rome riding on a donkey which her son was leading. In the first month of his pontificate, she saw the boy, aged twenty-one, adorned with the Pontiff's own cap and enriched with various abbeys and an annual income of 30,000 double ducats. She saw the other, who had led the donkey, honoured with the chief offices at Rome and made very rich and noble through a most splendid Roman marriage. She herself received an annual income of 10,000 scudi, but unable to change her nature, she always lived a rustic life. Two daughters, each given a dowry of 100,000 scudi, together with certain dignities, a cardinal's hat, and good revenues, were married into the families of the Orsini and the Colonna. A nephew, made a cardinal, he enlarged with an annual income of 20,000 scudi, collected also from many abbeys. In short, besides the silver at hand, his family left an annual income of 150,000 double ducats.

units.la: XVIII. Urbanus VII. immediatus Sixti Successor post 13. dies Pontificatus mortuus nonnisi quibusdam legatis suis prodesse potuit; Ipsi autem magna cum pompa Genua egressi, sed cognita Pontificis morte, mox redeuntes, suis concivibus ludibrium debuerunt; p.177.178. Melior sors affulsit cognatis Gregorii XIV. Successoris Urbani, 10. mensium spatio; Nepotem Cardinalem, assignatis praeter multas Abbatias & dignitates praecipuas 12000. duplicium annuis reditibus creavit, maximam diei partem cum eo consumpsit, sine eo nihil egit, ad eum saepe dixit: Nipote fate la vostra borsa prima che io mora; Id est; Nepos, imple bursam, antequam moriar; subsequente in tantum Nepotis obedientia, ut ex singulis centenis nonnisi nonanonaginta sua fecerit, residuo in moneta pessima Ecclesiae relicto. Alium Nepotem Generalissimum S. Ecclesiae, Principi matrimonio junctum, Principem, confiscatis sub rebellionis praetextu bonis prioris, factum, ad bellum Gallicum misit; p. 178. 179. 180.
units.tr: XVIII. Urban VII, the immediate successor of Sixtus, died after thirteen days of his pontificate and could help only some of his legates. They set out from Genoa with great pomp, but when they learned of the Pontiff's death they soon returned and were made a laughing stock by their fellow citizens; p. 177, 178. A better fate shone on the relatives of Gregory XIV, Urban's successor, during the space of ten months. He created a nephew a cardinal, assigning him, besides many abbeys and chief dignities, an annual income of 12,000 double ducats. He spent most of the day with him and did nothing without him, and often said to him: "Nephew, fill your purse before I die" (Nipote fate la vostra borsa prima che io mora), that is, "Nephew, fill your purse before I die." Such was the nephew's obedience that he kept for himself only ninety-nine out of every hundred, leaving the remainder to the Church in the worst coin. He sent another nephew, the general of the Holy Church, who had been married to a prince and made a prince, after the goods of the former lord had been confiscated under the pretext of rebellion, to the war in France; p. 178, 179, 180.

units.la: XIX. Qui hunc excepit, Innocentius IX. 2, mensium spatio parum suis proficere potuit, nisi quod Pro-Nepotem Cardinalem creavit, eique Referendarii (quod tunc unice vacabat;) officium dedit; Reliquis ob inopinatam Pontificis mortem vana spe delusis, paupertate comite domum redire coacts; p. 180. 181. Successori Clementi VIII. tribuit Author, quod paulatim & minori cum scandalo suis omnibus optime satisfacere potuerit, in prima creatione 2. Cardinales Nepotes fecerit, & posthac nihil sine eis; alterum interdum idolum cordis sui vocando, atque ei omnia saepe permittendo; quod aucto salario & additis quibusdam privilegiis & praerogativis Nepotem alium Ecclesiae Generalem declaraverit; alium Marchionem absolutum, empto Marchionatu, fecerit, sed apud se beneficiorum aliorum conferendorum gratia retinuerit; eidem, haerede testamentario, quem spurium dicebat, expulso, subditis parum gaudentibus, Cardinalibus resistentibus, Ducatum Estiensem vendicare voluerit; denique Nepotem alium Cardinalem creavit, datis ei non paucis beneficiis; Sic utilis fuerit suis omnibus, bono corde, quod bono ille dabat, maxime nummos numerosos accipientibus; p. 182–188. Non similiter dare, non similiter accipere potuerant, Leo XI. qui successit, & ejus consanguinei. Brevis Pontificatus 25. dierum duntaxat magis obfuit, quam promissio de suis non ditandis, quam omnibus communem ipse etiam Sixtus IV. fecit. Vocatus quidem erat Nepos Cardinalis Romae creandus, sed creari non potuit, Papa ipso ingressus ejus in urbem die ingenti totius familiae dolore vitam & potestatem finiente p. 188. 189. 190.
units.tr: XIX. Innocent IX, who succeeded him, could do little for his own in the two months of his reign, except that he created a pro-nephew a cardinal and gave him the office of referendary, which was then vacant. The others, deceived by vain hopes at the Pontiff's unexpected death, were forced to return home in poverty; p. 180, 181. The author ascribes to his successor Clement VIII that he gradually, and with less scandal, was able to satisfy all his own very well. At his first creation he made two nephews cardinals, and afterwards did nothing without them. He often called one of them "the idol of his heart", and often allowed him everything. Having increased his salary and added certain privileges and prerogatives, he declared another nephew general of the Church. He made another an absolute marquis by buying a marquisate for him, but kept for himself the power of conferring other benefices. He wished to claim the Duchy of Este for the same nephew, whom he named as his testamentary heir, though he called him a bastard, after expelling him; the subjects were little pleased, and the cardinals resisted. Finally he created another nephew a cardinal, granting him no small benefices. Thus he was useful to all his own, with a good heart, since those who received the good things he gave, above all the numerous coins, were very glad; p. 182–188. Leo XI, who succeeded, and his relatives could not give or receive in the same way. His short pontificate of only twenty-five days harmed them more than the promise not to enrich his own, which Sixtus IV himself had made, a promise common to all. A cardinal nephew was summoned to be created at Rome, but he could not be created, since the Pope himself, who entered the city on the day of his nephew's arrival, ended his life and power to the great grief of the whole family; p. 188, 189, 190.

units.la: XX. Sed quot hunc passibus antecessit, succedens licet Paulus V. Romam burgis implevit, tot Borghesios introducendo, & quidem, quod pessimum, momento unico. Jam in Cardinalatu quasi omnia sua cognatis impendit, maxime Nepoti, quem a puerit a secum habuerat, & Papa factus statim Cardinalem, licet ex sorore, Borghesium creavit. Erat hic interpres mentis Pontificis, medium gratiae, adjutor in negotiis Ecclesiae gravissimis; Gratiae nonnisi per hunc Canalem fluebant; omnia regebat, imperabat omnibus; Quam primum beneficia vacarunt, jam Nepotum fuerunt; dignidignitates præcipuæ, cognatorum secularium; acceperunt divitias, ut usum alium nescientes ædificia superbissima, & ultra Regios sumptus, coeperint ædificare; Cardinalis Borghesius Palatium nec- dum absolutum, cùm oporteret ei dimidium quasi Papatum impendere, & solum fundamentum 200000. ducatos absumpserit; Fratres Pontificis verò 2. villas, de quarum una Minister Hispaniæ dixit: Rex meus talia his temporibus pro habitatione sua suscipere non fuisset ausus. Papæ tamen ista studium eos ditandi auxerunt, quo ne quidem opus habuerunt, dum absolutè imperantes omnia in suum commodum convertere potuerunt, quibusdam duntaxat Papæ ad renovationem ædificiorum publicorum & platearum relictis. Neque unquam antea tanta fuit Nepotum támque absoluta potestas, per 16. annos; Mortuo Papa, Princeps Nepos 100000. Duplicium annuos reditus habuit, tantum etiam Cardinales & reliqui, præter argentum præsens, quod apud solum Cardinalem millionem effecisse creditur, & Paulus tamen Ecclesiæ ne denarium quidem reliquit. p. 190–198.
units.tr: XX. But although Paul V, who succeeded him, filled Rome with burgis, introducing so many Borghesi, and that in a single moment, which is the worst of it, went before him by so many steps. Already while still a cardinal he devoted almost everything to his relatives, above all to his nephew, whom he had kept with him from boyhood; and when he became Pope he at once made Borghese a cardinal, though he was only a nephew through his sister. This man was the interpreter of the Pope's mind, the means of grace, and the helper in the Church's most serious affairs. Grace flowed only through this channel; he governed everything and commanded everyone. As soon as benefices fell vacant, they became the nephews' property; the chief dignities went to secular relatives. They received riches, and, not knowing any other use for them, began to build most proud palaces, beyond royal expenditure. Cardinal Borghese, while his palace was not yet finished, though he ought to have spent half of a papacy on it, used up 200,000 ducats on the foundation alone. The Pope's brothers had two villas, of one of which the Spanish minister said: "My king would not have dared to accept such a thing for his residence in these times." Yet these things only increased the Pope's zeal to enrich them, though they had no need of it, since, ruling absolutely, they were able to turn everything to their own advantage, with only a few things left to the Pope for the renovation of public buildings and squares. Never before was there such power of nephews, and so absolute, for sixteen years. When the Pope died, Prince Nephew had an annual income of 100,000 double ducats; the cardinals and the rest had as much, besides the ready money, which is believed to have amounted to a million for the cardinal alone; and yet Paul left the Church not even a penny. p. 190–198.

units.la: XXI. Succedens Gregorius XV. curis publicis illas de familia stabilienda præmittens, atque exemplum Leonis XI. intuens, tertio jam post promotionem suam die Nepotem Cardinalem & fratrem, licet absentem, Ecclesiæ Generalem, & paulò post Ducem, infinitis bonis stabilibus, Ecclesiæ argento emptis, simul ei assignatis, fecit. Eodem die Nepotibus & Cognatis multis aliis, absentibus & illis, multas dignitates contulit, ut Romæ tunc regnárit Nepotismus, Nepotibus urbem necdum ingressis. Cardinalis Nepos ita solus omnia direxit, ut non à Papa, sed Papa potius ab ipso dependisse dici debeat, & aliquando curiosius de statu rerum interrogans ab eo verba tumida audiverit; Che volete cercar tanta briga? Mangiate, bevete, e contentatevi d'esser servito? Quid de his solicitus es? Ede, bibe, & esto contentus, quod tibi bene servitur. Ipse autem unicè reditibus & beneficiis perpetuis corradendis intentus fuit, Papa non tantùm permittente, sed & calcaria currenti velocissimè prætereuntis occasionis mentione addente; Hinc etiam 27. mensium spatio acquisivit & mortuo Pontifice habuit præter infinita pretiosa nobilia, præter nummos ædificiis impensos & argentum præsens 250000. scutorum annuos reditus; ut hic Nepotismus, temporis brevis intuitu avidissimus fuerit, & tamen minùs vituperatus, quia Nepotes omnium benevolentiam, quoad fieri poterat, s mull captârunt, omnes honorando, serviendo omnibus; Hinc publica convitia abfuerunt p. 198--203.
units.tr: XXI. Gregory XV, who succeeded, setting public cares aside to establish his family first, and looking to the example of Leo XI, on the third day after his election made his nephew a cardinal and his brother, though absent, General of the Church, and soon after a duke, with endless landed estates bought with Church money assigned to him at the same time. On the same day he conferred many dignities on nephews and other relatives, both absent and present, so that Nepotism reigned in Rome before the nephews had even entered the city. The cardinal nephew so alone directed everything that it ought to be said that the Pope depended on him rather than he on the Pope; and when the Pope once asked him somewhat too curiously about the state of affairs, he heard from him a swelling reply: "What do you want to go to so much trouble for? Eat, drink, and be content to be served? Why are you anxious about these things? Eat, drink, and be content that you are well served." He himself was intent solely on gathering in revenues and perpetual benefices, the Pope not only permitting it but even spurring him on, mentioning the occasion that was passing swiftly by. Hence in the space of twenty-seven months he acquired, and at the Pope's death had, besides endless precious and noble things, besides money spent on buildings and ready silver, an annual income of 250,000 crowns; so that this Nepotism was most greedy in a short time, and yet was less blamed, because the nephews, as far as possible, won the goodwill of all by honouring everyone and serving everyone. Hence public insults were absent. p. 198–203.

units.la: XXII. Vigiliam hactenus habuimus, Festum sequitur; inquit Author Nepotismi l 3. p. 208. Electo Urbano VIII. Barberini apum ad instar(erat insigne familiæ)sed non sine aculeo advolârunt ad mel Ecclesiæ consumendum. Sub initium Pontifex dignum Nepotem Cardinalem fecit, anno sequente Fratrem Capucinum, Capucinorum agendi rationes omnium ludibrio difficillimè dediscentem; Alterum Fratrem Generalatu Ecclesiæ, Præfectura urbis & tot officiis honoravit, imò cumulavit, ut ea omnia ipsemet nesciverit, parùm de officio solicitus, sed beneficiis inde fluentibus maximè attentus. Post annos 4. Nepotem alium Cardinalis Nepotis fratrem creavit Cardinalem quoque; sed fratri hic dissimillimus omnes actionibus suis indignis scandalizavit deinceps à fratre mutandus. Regimen ab initio satis bonum tandem in manus Nepotum pervenit, qui Pontificis placita suis alligare nôrunt, & de solis Principatibus, familia æternisanda, & domibus duplicibus implendis cogitârunt; Abbatias, beneficia sibi statim appropriârunt, &, numero crescente, ex parte etiam Nepotibus suis scholas vix dum frequentantibus; imò contrà Pontificum decreta & magna bene meritorum desperatione, lactentibus; quid? necdum natis; conditio enim matrimonialis alicubi fuit, ut primogenitus acciperet certam Abbatiam; desperatione, inquam, bene meritorum; cùm enim Prælatus talis rogaret, dictum ei: ut patienter adhuc parùm expectet; Elapsis ex illo tempore octo annis & infinitis rursus beneficiis vacantibus familiæ Barbarinæ implantatis, tandem vacuus domum redire instituit, atque in egressu urbis, cuidam patientiam ulteriorem suadenti respondit: Sanctus, non homo, sine desperatione panem à Barberinis eripi videt; alius alii patientiæ suasori respondit: Si infiniti Papatus essent inter Barbarinos distribuendi, & præter illos adhuc unus iis non visus, spem habere possem. Sed nemo cum illis dividet unicum, quem arctissimè manu tenent. Dicit Author, se 12. magna volumina similibus exemplis implere posse, cùm tunc Prælatis nonnisi repudiata à Barbarinis viliora obtigerint; pretiosa, servientibus non Ecclesiæ, sed Barbarinis; quod & exemplis confirmat; Urbanus non erat promptus ad Cardinales creandos & tamen contrà Canones Fratres creavit, & tamen Barbarini (quot fuerunt, tot tandem Papæ fuerunt!) divitiis satiati tandem ad confirmandas partes suas Cardinalium quasi cohortes creárunt. Romani murmurárunt; Pasquinus os aperuit; maximè quando antiquissimæ structuræ ex ære Ecclesiæ Rotundæ sublatæ & partem quidem in ornamentum majoris altaris S. Petri, maximam verò partem in privata ornamenta Palatiorum conversæ fuerunt, populus per plateas clamavit: Quod non fecerunt Barbari, fecerunt Barbarini; Pasquinus, modò; muscas viscera Ecclesiæ exfugere; modò, Ecclesiam non habere unquadrino, quadrantem; quia omnia interceperit Il Barbarino; modò; cultros, gladios ad abigendas muscas emendos esse. Imò testatur Author, odium eòusque crevisse, ut, nisi quotidie Romani mortem Pontificis expectare potuissent, rebellio dubio procul oritura fuisset. Quidam numeravit muscas in insignibus & 10000. hinc inde invenit. Argento suo fidentes dimidiam sibi Italiam promiserunt, & primò quidem Ducatum Urbinensem suum facere voluerunt, sed non fecerunt, Cardinalibus se opponentibus, & consideranti-bus ipsismet, satis jam odii attractum esse; Postea appetiverunt Regnum Neapolitanum, sed audiverunt, Neapolitanos se citius Turcis daturos esse; Rursus Ducatum Parmæ & Placentiæ Possessori eripere studuerunt, sed in fugam ab eo conjecti sunt usque in ipsum Castellum Romæ, atque Româ ipsâ pelli potuissent; Denuò amorem Lucæ præ se tulerunt, sed quia loco melius aculeum excommunicationis ostenderunt, Lucenses remedia contrà futura quæsiverunt; Deinceps Papatum, cuilibet creaturarum suarum Urbem ad dies vitæ concedere, & Richeliæo Comitatum Avignonensem in hunc finem donare volentes, his adjuvantibus hæreditarium reddere conati sunt; Tandem in omnibus se delusos sentientes, ad studium opes cumulandi relapsi sunt; in quo felices esse continuârunt, tanquam experti à 20. annis Magistri. Cæterùm authoritatem Nepotum arguit, quòd Franciscus Cardinalis Patronus audire, & cum veteri re novum titulum ferre debuit; atque nihil feré ex ore Pontificis intellectum, præter; Vocate Cardinalem Patronum, loquimini cum Cardinale Patrono; videbimus cum Cardinale Patrono &c. Quod & Ministros & Principes ægre habuit, quòd nimirum Pontifex, summos Monarchas pro filiis habens, in præsentia ipsorum etiam Principum, ita Nepotem compellavit; regerente aliquando Principe Parmensi: Nullum agnosco Patronum praeter Sanct. Vestram. Titulum alium acquisiverunt tunc, Eminentia, Cardinalibus communem, sed ipsis à Pontifice primò solis destinatum. De quo Dissert. IV. sert. IV. egimus. Nunquam Rex tam absolute subditis imperavit, quàm illi Ecclesiae, castigatis vel contradicere volentibus; non ausi sunt 5. reliquae Pauli V. creaturae; Creaturae ipsorum tantùm subscribere debuerunt. Post tale regimen 23. annorum mortuus est Urbanus, infinita Ecclesiae debita, infinitos suis thesauros, quos manu capere, non pennâ numerare voluerunt, & 227. Regimina, dignitates, officia, Abbatias, Beneficia & alios titulos, quorum quidam annuatim 8000. scutorum & amplius dederunt, relinquens; ut titulosissimus etiam Hispaniae Rex ne dimidiam quidem titulorum partem habeat. Argenti praesentis abyssum sola imaginatio penetrat. Creditur, Franciscum ultra 2000000. ducatorum praeter sepulta ab Antonio & post exilii diuturni ingentes sumptus sub terra condita habuisse, & praeter missa à Thaddaeo in Palaestinam ad sepulturam similem; prout oertum habetur, in 2. noctibus 3. ultimorum mensium ultra 60. mulos nummis onustos illuc abiisse. Atque colligitur, quantum illi collegerint ex collectis ab aliis ante eos, quorum tantò brevior Pontificatus fuit; Colligit sic Author 30000000. scutorum; Subjungit Nepotismum illum adhuc durare, & duraturum, cùm tres sint Cardinales Barberini, quorum unum 3. rationibus eligendum censet; Franciscum nempe; Sed falsus fuit; noluerunt Cardinales porrò pungi ab istis Apibus; Vide Authorem à p. 203——256.
units.tr: XXII. We have had the vigil so far; the feast follows, says the author of Nepotismus, l. 3, p. 208. When Urban VIII of the Barberini was elected, the bees of that family (which was their emblem) flew in, but not without a sting, to consume the honey of the Church. At the beginning the Pope made a worthy nephew a cardinal; in the following year he made a Capuchin brother, who could most hardly unlearn the ways of the Capuchins, a laughing-stock to all. He honoured, indeed heaped upon, another brother with the generalship of the Church, the prefecture of the city and many offices, so that he himself knew none of them, little concerned about the duty but most intent on the benefices flowing from them. After four years he made another nephew, brother of the cardinal nephew, a cardinal too; but this man, most unlike his brother, scandalized everyone by his unworthy actions and was afterwards to be changed by his brother. The government, at first fairly good, at last came into the hands of the nephews, who knew how to bind the Pope's decisions to their own, and thought only of principalities, of making the family eternal, and of filling their houses twice over. They at once appropriated abbeys and benefices to themselves, and, as the number grew, partly to their nephews, who scarcely yet attended school; indeed, against the decrees of the Popes and to the great despair of the deserving, to infants at the breast, and even to unborn children. For in one place the condition of a marriage was that the firstborn should receive a certain abbey. To the despair, I say, of the deserving: when such a prelate asked for something, he was told to wait patiently a little longer. Eight years having passed since then, and endless benefices having again fallen vacant and been planted in the Barberini family, at last he resolved to return home empty-handed; and as he left the city, to someone urging him to further patience he replied: "A holy man, not a human being, sees bread snatched from the Barberini without despair." Another replied to another who urged patience: "If there were infinite papacies to be distributed among the Barberini, and besides them one more unseen by them, I could hope. But no one will share with them the one thing they hold in the tightest grip." The author says he could fill twelve great volumes with similar examples, since the prelates received only the cheaper things the Barberini rejected, while the precious things served not the Church but the Barberini. He confirms this with examples. Urban was not prompt to create cardinals, and yet, against the canons, he made his brothers cardinals; and the Barberini (as many as there were, so many popes there were!), sated with riches, at last created a sort of cohort of cardinals to strengthen their party. The Romans murmured; Pasquin opened his mouth, especially when the most ancient bronze structures of the Rotunda of the Church were removed, and part of them turned into ornament for the greater altar of St Peter, but most of them into private ornaments of the palaces. The people cried through the streets: "What the Barbarians did not do, the Barberini did." Pasquin said now: "Flies are sucking the Church's entrails"; now, that the Church does not have a farthing, a quarter, because il Barbarino has taken everything; now, that knives and swords must be bought to drive off the flies. Indeed the author testifies that the hatred had grown so far that, unless the Romans could expect the Pope's death daily, rebellion would undoubtedly have arisen. Someone counted the flies in the arms and found 10,000 here and there. Trusting in their silver, they promised themselves half of Italy, and first indeed wanted to make the Duchy of Urbino their own, but did not, the cardinals opposing them and themselves considering that enough hatred had already been drawn. Afterwards they aimed at the Kingdom of Naples, but they heard: "The Neapolitans would sooner give themselves to the Turks." Again they tried to snatch the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza from its possessor, but they were thrown into flight by him as far as the very castle of Rome, and could have been driven out of Rome itself. Again they showed their love for Lucca, but because they displayed the sting of excommunication in the wrong place, the people of Lucca sought remedies against the future. Then, wishing to make the papacy, which they gave to any of their creatures for the days of his life, and to give the Avignon county to Richelieu to this end, they tried, with his help, to make it hereditary. At last, feeling themselves deceived in everything, they relapsed into the study of piling up wealth; in which they continued to be happy, as masters experienced for twenty years. Moreover, the author proves the authority of the nephews by the fact that Francis, the Cardinal Patron, had to be heard and to bear a new title with an old thing; and that scarcely anything was understood from the Pope's mouth except: "Call the Cardinal Patron; speak with the Cardinal Patron; we will see with the Cardinal Patron, etc." This also vexed the ministers and princes, namely that the Pope, though he regarded the greatest monarchs as his sons, in their very presence addressed the nephew in this way; once the Prince of Parma replied: "I acknowledge no patron except Your Holiness." They then acquired another title, Eminence, common to cardinals, but first destined by the Pope for them alone, about which we treated in Dissertation IV, section IV. Never did a king rule his subjects so absolutely as the Barberini ruled the Church; those who were chastised or wished to contradict dared not; the five remaining creatures of Paul V did not dare; they had only to subscribe to their creatures' decisions. After such a government of twenty-three years Urban died, leaving infinite debts of the Church, infinite treasures of his own, which they wanted to grasp by hand rather than count with a pen, and 227 governorships, dignities, offices, abbeys, benefices and other titles, some of which gave 8,000 crowns a year and more; so that even the most titled King of Spain does not have half of their titles. Only imagination can penetrate the abyss of ready silver. It is believed that Francis had more than 2,000,000 ducats, apart from what Antonio had buried and the great expenses of his long exile hidden underground, and apart from what Thaddeus sent to Palestine for a similar burial; as is certainly held, in two nights of the last three months more than 60 mules laden with money went there. And from this one may gather how much they collected from what others had collected before them, whose papacies were so much shorter. The author thus reckons 30,000,000 crowns. He adds that this Nepotism still lasts and will last, since there are three Barberini cardinals, one of whom he thinks should be elected for three reasons, namely Francis. But he was wrong; the cardinals no longer wished to be stung by those bees. See the author, pp. 203–256.

units.la: XXIII. Innocentius X. statim secundum Nepotem Patronum creavit, sed minus aptum, hinc etiam minus Pontifici gratum, & minus libenter istis deditum; Maluit in conjugio vivere & Princeps Nepos audire Principem de Rossano viduam ducens; quae & eum amare coepit, ut occasio daretur, Pontificem ipsum ad amorem invitandi, eóque obtento statui Ecclesiae & Papae imperandi. Papa autem, remisso pileo, factum cognoscens, novos conjuges in exilium ire jussit; Olympiam substituens & cum ea Cognatissimum. De quo vide Dissert. VII. Sect. 6. n. 70. Tantae eum efficaciae fuisse ait Author, ut Domina ipsius Papae, Papissa, Papa verò sine ejus licentia se movere non audens nec Papa, nec homo visus sit; atque subjungit, quanto Cognatissmus ille scandalo fuerit; quomodo coactus sit, eam ex curia pellere; quomodo revocârit quidem Principem Nepotem, sed non admiserit denuò ad negotiationes; quomodo contrà Camillus Astalli Cardinalis Nepos Patronus factus, sed mortuo Cardinale Panzirolo, Patroni Patrono, urbe ipsa pulsus, Cognatissmus Innocentii X. mus Olympiæ ad eandem potestatem revocatus, & Nepotismus primus Cognatismo subjectus sit, permissâ Nepotibus aurum capiendi, sed sub Olympia, potestate; Sua autem eóusque Olympia abusa sit, ut Vigilia tantum fuerit omne illud, quod Barbarini fecerint, Cardinalatus, Abbatiæ, Episcopatus, Canonicatus & omnis generis dignitates carè venditæ, bursæ, etiam cum murmure, si modo plenæ, gratæ, bene meriti non tantum non honorati, sed & Româ pulsi fuerint; ut Papæ nulla habita ratio & quorundam murmur fuerit, fœminis Sacramentorum administrationem permittendam esse, cum Olympia Ecclesiam sine Papa gubernet; ista dicentium, quia Papam mortuum judicârint civiliter; donec etiam naturaliter mortuus sit, & cum eo potestas Olympiæ, quæ hæresis Ecclesiæ, Scandalum Christianismi & destructio populi in statu Ecclesiæ fuerit. Vide âp.256.–305.
units.tr: XXIII. Innocent X. at once made his nephew Patron, though he was less suitable, and so less pleasing to the Pope and less willingly devoted to these men. He preferred to live in marriage and to listen to the Princeps Nepos, taking as his wife the widow of the Prince of Rossano. She also began to love him, so that an opportunity would be given to draw the Pontiff himself into love and, once that was obtained, to command the Church and the Pope. The Pope, however, laying aside his skullcap and learning the facts, ordered the new spouses into exile, putting Olympia in her place and with her the Cognatissimum. On him see Dissert. VII. Sect. 6. n. 70. The author says that he had such influence that the Pope's own lady, the Popess, was thought neither Pope nor man, since the Pope did not dare to move without his permission. He adds how great a scandal this Cognatissimus was, and how he was forced to drive her from the court; how he recalled the Prince Nephew but did not admit him again to affairs; and how, on the contrary, Camillo Astalli, a cardinal, was made Nephew Patron, but after Cardinal Panzirolo, the Patron's patron, died, he was driven from the city itself, and the Cognatissimus of Innocent X., Olympia, was recalled to the same power. Nepotism was thus made subject to Cognatism, the Nephews being allowed to take gold, but under Olympia's power. Olympia abused her power to such an extent that everything the Barberini had done was but a vigil: cardinalates, abbacies, bishoprics, canonries and dignities of every kind were sold dearly for purses, even with murmuring. Whoever was full, pleasing and well deserving was not only not honoured but was even driven from Rome. The Pope was taken into no account, and there was some murmuring that women should be allowed to administer the Sacraments, since Olympia governed the Church without a Pope. Those saying this judged the Pope dead in civil terms, until he also died in fact; and with him the power of Olympia ended, which was a heresy of the Church, a scandal to Christianity and a destruction of the people in the state of the Church. See pp. 256–305.

units.la: XXIV. De Alexandri VII. Nepotismo sequentia habet; Timuisse post electionem omnes statim, Romam non capturam multitudinem Nepotum; Marium primogenitum fratrem ante depositionem vestis prioris conscenso equo festinanter iter ingressum, gratulationum verò cum titulo Excellentiæ ubique occurrentium multitudine & honorum futurorum imaginatione quasi ecstaticum inopinatò à fratre Pontifice nuntium & literas de itinere Romano omittendo accepisse, magno cum dolore noctu reversum honorem tamen à Magno Duce & dona, ut & à multis Cardinalibus aliisque Magnatibus unâ cum universa cognatione, à Venetis nobilitatem, Pontificem suâ in hac parte abstinentiâ ingentes laudes accepisse, similem tamen fuisse, illi, qui in tempestate magna vestes quidem in aquam projecerit, fune tamen in manibus retento, cum semper iis dona miserit, quotidie nova sua communicârit, al quando Duplices cerâ obductos, quod ipse viderit, & quibusdam Mulis impositos, aliâ vice sub prætextu vasium argenteorum & sericî pro certis Ecclesiis, latentes; Laborâsse interim Legatos, imò ipsos etiam Cardinales, & quòd rogari velit, notantes, pro receptione, benignius in dies auditos, juramentum de non recipiendis Romæ suis coram crucifixo factum occursu & receptione in Castello Gandolphi ex Jesuitarum & Pallavicini Confessoris consilio elusum; viginti folia ex historia Concilii Tridentini laudes Pontificis ob istam abstinentiam continentia, aliter mox ex eleemosyna collecta impressa fuisse, & ita Pontificis laudes in fumum abiisse; Succedentibus convitiis Alexandri VII. vitiis & in Arcu quodam Triumphali loco verborum: Orietur in diebus nostris justitia & abundantia pacis; levi mutatione illis; Moritur — panis; repertis; atque insignibus domûs Chigiæ respectu arboris, de cruce latronis injusti, à qua populus Romanus per manus Nepotismi suspendi debeat; respectu Stellæ, de Cometa ruinam urbis præsagiente; explicatis; quæ eò magis metuerint, quia sub tribus Alexandris Roma spoliata fuerit; Nepotismum prioribus cunctis multò pejorem proximè ex 5. Nepotibus & fratre supra memorato auri cupidissimo constitisse; usque adeò cupidum fuisse, ut nihil sine lucri respectu fecerit, semper in ore habens: Non v'é niente à guadagnare: Id est: Nullum hinc datur lucrum; atque in artibus lucrandi ipsos statim Barbarinos, (magnos artifices!) vincens; Filium Cardinalem Patronum, neglectâ negotiorum curâ sensibus & voluptatibus usq; adeò indulsisse, ut ultra sex spurios ex Meretricibus diversis susceperit; contentus ordinariâ annuâ 100000. scutorum ad voluptates istas & similes materiâ. Alium Nepotem Sigismundum 17. annos natum expectâsse jam divitem Abbatiis & beneficiis primam promotionem ad Cardinalatum; Alium Augustinum, Sigismundi fratrem majorem, Principem Nobiles ipsos non resalutantem ab omnibus ob superbiam odio haberi, sed eò magis gratum esse Pontifici, destinatum, ringentibus cum fratre Mario suis, ad familiæ propagationem, hinc Cardinalem pecuniam datâ operâ dissipare, hinc perpetuo odio utrumque ramum flagrare, & hunc collata alteri beneficia male interpretari, magis autem amari Augustinum, quia Pater Augustus Pontificem in studiis adjuverit, quod Marius tenuior opibus præstare haud potuerit; atque odium illud intestinum multùm Romæ, Ecclesiæque prodesse; nuptiis Augustini 100000. impensi esse, ultra dona ingentis pretii Sponsæ data, illo ipso tempore, quo Religio Romana in Germania peritura visa sit; Neogamo Pontificem 60000. Duplicibus terram Farnesiam emisse, Farnesio Principi futuro, atque æmulatione alterius ramî notatâ, pro hujus Nepotis divitiis augendis unicè sollicitum fuisse, pro universa autem familia, quæsivisse, ut Cardinalis Patronus Hispaniæ Protector declaretur. Vide à p.305--388. Atque hic terminavit Author suam historiam Nepotismi.
units.tr: XXIV. On the Nepotism of Alexander VII he has the following. After the election everyone feared that the crowd of Nephews would not be satisfied in Rome. Mario, the eldest brother, before he had put off his former dress, mounted a horse and set out hastily; amid the crowds meeting him everywhere with congratulations, the title of Excellency and the imagining of future honours, he received, as if in ecstasy, an unexpected message and letter from his brother the Pontiff about the Roman journey, which was to be omitted. He returned at night with great grief, yet he accepted honour from the Grand Duke and gifts, as well as from many Cardinals and other magnates, together with his whole kindred, and from the Venetians nobility. The Pontiff received great praise for his abstinence in this matter, yet he was like one who, in a great storm, indeed throws his clothes into the water but keeps a rope in his hands, since he always sent them gifts and daily communicated new ones: sometimes double sums sealed in wax, as he himself saw, and carried on certain mules; at another time, under the pretext of silver vessels and silk for certain churches, they lay hidden. Meanwhile the legates, and even the Cardinals themselves, laboured, noting that they were heard more kindly by the day, and that he wished to be asked for the reception. The oath made before the crucifix, not to receive his relatives at Rome, was eluded by the meeting and reception at the Castle of Gandolfo, by the counsel of the Jesuits and of Pallavicini, his Confessor. Twenty leaves from the history of the Council of Trent, containing praise of the Pontiff for this abstinence, were printed soon afterwards, otherwise collected by alms; and so the praises of the Pontiff went up in smoke. The abuses of Alexander VII. followed, and, in a certain triumphal arch, words were found in a place of ill omen: Orietur in diebus nostris justitia & abundantia pacis, with a slight change to them: Moritur — panis. And, with reference to the arms of the house of Chigi, the tree was explained as the cross of the unjust thief, from which the Roman people was to be hanged by the hands of Nepotism; the star as a comet presaging the ruin of the city. They feared these all the more because under three Alexanders Rome had been despoiled. Nepotism under him was far worse than all the former kinds, having consisted proximately of five Nephews and the aforementioned brother, most greedy for gold; so greedy was he that he did nothing without regard to profit, always having on his lips: Non v'é niente à guadagnare, that is, No gain is to be had here. In the arts of gaining he surpassed the Barberini themselves, great artists though they were. His Cardinal Nephew Patron, neglecting the care of affairs, so indulged his senses and pleasures that he fathered more than six bastards by different prostitutes, being content with the ordinary yearly sum of 100,000 scudi for those pleasures and similar matters. Another Nephew, Sigismund, aged seventeen, already rich in abbacies and benefices, awaited his first promotion to the cardinalate. Another, Augustine, the elder brother of Sigismund, a prince who did not return the greetings of nobles, was hated by all for his pride, yet was all the more pleasing to the Pontiff, and was destined, with his brother Mario, to the propagation of the family; hence the Cardinal deliberately squandered money, and both branches burned with perpetual hatred, and he interpreted badly the benefices conferred on the other. Augustine, however, was loved more, because Father Augustus had helped the Pontiff in his studies, which Mario, being of slenderer means, could not do. That internal hatred did much good in Rome and for the Church. For the marriage of Augustine 100,000 were spent, besides gifts of great value given to the bride, at the very time when the Roman religion seemed about to perish in Germany. The Pontiff bought for the newly married couple, for 60,000 double pistoles, the Farnese estate, for the future Prince Farnese; and, noting the rivalry of the other branch, he was solicitous only in increasing the wealth of this Nephew, while for the whole family he sought that the Cardinal Patron be declared Protector of Spain. See pp. 305–388. Here the author ended his history of Nepotism.

units.la: XXV. Multis eum Pontificibus perplacuisse ostendimus; Non tamen placuit omnibus. Atque in hoc certè non sequuntur exemplum Christi, qui neq; consobrinis suis sessionem ad dextram & ad
units.tr: XXV. We have shown that Nepotism pleased many Popes. Yet it did not please all. And in this certainly they do not follow the example of Christ, who did not grant his cousins the seat at his right hand and at his

units.la: Nepotismus tamen à nonnullis & ad sinistram indulgere voluit, neque universalem Ecclesiæ Monarcham, (ex hypothesi loquor;) constituturus alterutrum ex illis, sed Petrum elegit; Licèt Gregorius XV. ut Il Nip. p. 2 p.33. habet in suo, exemplum Christi sequi voluerit, Nepotem Ludovicum sæpissimè dilectum suum Johannem appellando; Petrum etiam consanguineis, utut sororem fœminam circumduxerit, parùm indulsisse constat. Atque idem planè constat de successoribus per aliquot secula, etiam post pacem Christianis concessam; Hinc serum satis ex Seculo X. primi notabilis Nepotis exemplum dedimus; Post quod etiam initium rarior primò Nepotismus fuit, qui deinceps quoque à multis non tantùm missus, sed & rejectus fuit. Ut exempla sequentia docebunt:
units.tr: Nepotism, however, some wished to indulge, and not to the universal Monarch of the Church (I speak on the hypothesis), who was to appoint one of them, but he chose Peter. Although Gregory XV, as Il Nip. p. 2 p.33. has it in his work, wished to follow the example of Christ, calling his nephew Ludovico very often his beloved John, it is clear that he showed little favour to kinsmen, even when he led about his sister as a woman. The same is clearly true of successors for several centuries, even after peace was granted to Christians. Hence we have given a late enough example of the first notable Nephew, from the tenth century. After this, Nepotism at first became rarer, and afterwards was not only put aside by many but also rejected. As the following examples will show:

units.la: XXVI. Seculo XII. vixit Adrianus IV. quo de Maimburgius Decadence de l'Empire, ubi ejus Elogium habet: Il tint le St Siege pres de cinq ans &c.
units.tr: XXVI. In the twelfth century lived Adrian IV, of whom Maimbourg in Decadence de l'Empire, where he gives his eulogy, says: He held the Holy See for nearly five years, etc.

units.la: Id est: In Sancta sede fuit per quinque annos, quibus dedit rara omnium virtutum Christianarum exempla, & cumprimis singularis indifferentia erga carnem & sanguinem, quanquam, ut sincerè loquar, in ea modum excessit, quem virtus in medio consistens nobis præscribit. Tantum enim abest, ut cum aliis quibusdam accusari possit nimia pro Nepotum suorum aliorúmque suorum valde pauperum agnatorum exaltatione passionis, ut potiùs meo quidem judicio inconvenienter laudetur, quòd eos usq; adeò neglexit, ut ne obolum quidem iis unquam dare voluerit, matrem suam in ætate valdè provectam extremaq; paupertate constitutam commendare contentus charitati & eleemosynis Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis, quæ eam, mortuo Pontifice, tam parùm curavit, ut ferè fame & miseria mori debuerit. Hoc est sine dubio virtutem nimium extendere, ita enim vitari vult extremum unum, ut non ideò impingatur in alterum, præcipuè quando, quemadmodum hîc, agitur contrà Legem Dei, quæ præcipit liberis, ut honorent parentes, eósque, scilicet, necessitati eximant, quando in ea hærent. Addit tamen: Mais une plus longue reflexion surce sujet seroit fort inutile, car il n'y a pas lieu de craindre, que ce mauvais exemple soit jamais suivi des autres Papes, qui auront toujours l'ame trop grande pour aller jusques à cet excez de dureté à l'egard de leurs parens. Id est. Sed longiori hîc reflexione minimè est opus, neque enim timendum est, alios Papas malum hoc exemplum esse secuturos, animo enim majori sunt, quàm qui ipsis permittat talem duritiæ erga agnatos suos excessum. Quâ ratione ab una parte docuit, Pontificum virtutem vel in defectu vel in excessu peccare, ab altera verò recentiorum indulgentiam haud obscurè sugillavit. Seculo XIII. mediâ incedere visus via CleClemens IV. qui teste in Vita Platina, bona Ecclesia ita accuratè dispensavit, ut plus Deo, quàm affinitati & cognationi tribuisse videatur. Duas habuit filias ex mortua uxore ante Pontificatum suscepta, quarum alteram in monasterium collocata triginta libras Turonensium parvorum dedit, alteram autem, quæ marito suæ conditionis nupserat, trecentas libras Turonensium dotis nomine numerari jussit: hac conditione, ne quid unquam amplius peteret. Habuit & Nepotem Clericum: quem ubi comperit tres prabendas (ita enim Canonicatus vocant) habere, optionem facere compulit, ut, quam vellet ex his, retineret, duas relinqueret. Verùm instantibus amicis, non solùm quæ habebat, nepoti dimitteret, sed majora & plura tribueret: respondit vir Sanctissimus (quem utinam nostræ ætatis Pontifices imitati essent!) se Deo, non autem carni & sanguini acquieturum esse, Deum ita velle, ut sua in pias causas erogarentur, nec esse dignum Petri Successorem, qui plus cognationi, quàm pietati & Christo tribueret. Eodem in Seculo Nicolaus IV. Joh Stella in Vita indice, non plura affinibus aut cognatis debere, aut conferre, quàm aliis bonis arbitratus est.
units.tr: That is: he was in the Holy See for five years, during which he gave rare examples of all Christian virtues, and above all a singular indifference towards flesh and blood, although, to speak frankly, he went beyond the measure which virtue, standing in the middle, prescribes for us. For it is so far from being possible to accuse him, as some others can be accused, of excessive exaltation of his nephews and other very poor kinsmen, that in my judgement he is rather praised improperly, because he so neglected them that he would never give them so much as a penny, being content to commend his mother, who was far advanced in years and in the depths of poverty, to the charity and alms of the Church of Canterbury; and that Church, after the Pope's death, cared so little for her that she nearly had to die of hunger and misery. This is without doubt to stretch virtue too far, for one extreme is avoided in such a way that one falls into the other, especially when, as here, what is at issue is contrary to the law of God, which commands children to honour their parents and to relieve them of necessity when they are in it. He adds, however: "But a longer reflection on this subject would be quite useless, for there is no reason to fear that this bad example will ever be followed by the other Popes, who will always have souls too great to go to such an excess of hardness towards their relatives." That is: "But there is no need for a longer reflection here, for we need not fear that other Popes will follow this bad example; they are of too great a spirit to permit themselves such an excess of harshness towards their kinsmen." By which reasoning he has shown on the one hand that the virtue of the Popes sins either by deficiency or by excess, and on the other hand has quite plainly cast a slur on the indulgence of more recent men. In the thirteenth century Clement IV seemed to take the middle path: CleClement IV, who, as Platina witnesses in his Life, managed the goods of the Church so carefully that he seems to have given more to God than to affinity and kinship. He had two daughters by a wife who died before his pontificate; he placed one in a monastery and gave her thirty small Tours pounds, and he ordered that three hundred Tours pounds be counted out as a dowry for the other, who had married a man of her own rank, on the condition that she never ask for anything more. He also had a nephew who was a clergyman; when he learned that the nephew held three prebends (for so they call canonries), he compelled him to make a choice, so that he might keep whichever of them he wished and give up two. But when his friends urged him, he did not merely let the nephew keep what he had, but granted him greater and more.
