The most holy man replied (would that the Popes of our age had imitated him!) that he would yield to God and not to flesh and blood; God wished that his goods be spent on pious causes, and it was not fitting for the Successor of Peter to give more to kinship than to piety and to Christ. In the same century Nicholas IV, as John Stella states in the Index to his Life, thought that he ought to owe and to confer no more on relatives and kinsmen than on other good men.

units.la: XXVII. Seculo XIV. Benedictus XII. dictus, eodem Platina in Vita narrante, Cardinales creavit viros egregios, non de sua stirpe, ut nunc fit, sed undecunque ad tantam dignitatem vocatos.
units.tr: XXVII. In the fourteenth century Benedict XII, as Platina narrates in the same Life, created cardinals who were outstanding men, not from his own stock, as happens now, but called from wherever to such dignity.

units.la: Ne tamen periculo suo nimium sit locutus, addit: Non improbo tamen eos, qui ob cognationem & affinitatem ad summos dignitatis gradus erigantur, si tanta conditione digni sint. Eidem Benedicto Loyolita Otto in Roma Gloriosa tribuit sequens ex Psalmo XVII. Hebr. XIX. symbolum: Si mei non fuerint dominati, tunc immaculatus ero.
units.tr: Yet, lest he have spoken too boldly at his own risk, he adds: "I do not, however, disapprove of those who are raised to the highest grades of dignity on account of kinship and affinity, if they are worthy of such a rank." To the same Benedict, Otto the Loyolite in Roma Gloriosa assigns the following motto from Psalm XVII (Hebrew XIX): If they have not ruled over me, then I shall be blameless.

units.la: XXVIII. Seculo XVI. Adrianus VI. notante in Vita Onuphrio, difficulter cognatos ad beneficia provexit, non quia eis candidè non faveret, si alioqui idonei fuissent, sed quia, ut dicere solet, (solebat,) ædificare Sion in sanguinibus nollet, hoc est, quia in Sacris respicere necessitudines natura nollet, ut quæ ibi locum non haberent.
units.tr: XXVIII. In the sixteenth century Adrian VI, as Onuphrius notes in his Life, promoted relatives to benefices with difficulty; not because he did not favour them kindly, if otherwise they were fit, but because, as he was accustomed to say, he did not wish to build Zion in blood, that is, because he was unwilling to take family ties into account in sacred matters, since these had no place there.

units.la: Quinimò in iis, etiam in paribus dotibus, alienorum potius quàm suorum rationem habiturus videbatur. Ex quo fuit, quòd literis magnatum quorundam inferioris Germaniæ sollicitatus, utquendam propinquum suum adolescentem & forma & ingenio præstantem, qui tum recens Magister Philosophiæ creatus, studia altiora Lovanii sequebatur, galero Cardinalitio ornaret, ex more aliorum Pontificum solenni, nequaquam voluit. Patruelis sui filium, Senæ Etruscæ in Gymnasio literis operam navantem, quòd Romam nequaquam vocatus intermissis studiis repente venerat, confestim meritorio equo impositum remisit, animi levitatem identidem objectans, & severè admonens, ut ab se modestia stia & temperantia exemplum opportunè sumeret. Alios quoque nec remoto affinitatis gradu necessarios, qui ipse celsioris fortunæ è Germania pedibus Romam venerant, mirum in modum increpavit, donatisque singulis sagis laneis, & frugi viatico, pedibus similiter in patria redire jussit. Quarum rerum testimonio superiorum Pontificum profusam erga propinquos liberalitatem, uti gravem & Reipublicæ perniciosam, detestari erat solitus.
units.tr: Indeed, he seemed to have more regard for strangers than for his own, even when their qualifications were equal. Hence, when he was urged by letters from some magnates of Lower Germany to adorn with the cardinal's hat a certain young relative, outstanding in both looks and talent, who had only recently been created Master of Philosophy and was pursuing higher studies at Louvain, he by no means wished to do so, though it was a solemn custom of other Popes. The son of his first cousin, who was devoting himself to letters in the gymnasium at Siena, had suddenly come to Rome, though not summoned, abandoning his studies; he immediately had him put on a hired horse and sent back, repeatedly reproaching him for lightness of mind and sternly admonishing him to take from himself an opportune example of modesty and self-restraint. Other kinsmen, not even distantly related, who had come to Rome on foot from Germany in the hope of higher fortune, he rebuked in a remarkable way; giving each a woollen cloak and a modest allowance for the journey, he likewise ordered them to return home on foot. As evidence of such things, he was accustomed to denounce the lavish generosity of earlier Popes towards their kin as harmful and burdensome to the commonwealth.

units.la: XXIX. Seculo eodem Marcellus II. (qui tamen 12. Pontificatûs die morbo laborare coepit, 22. mortuus est) referente in Vita Onuphrio eodem; Neminem propinquorum Romam venire voluit, ne fratrem quidem; quódque his & temporibus & moribus novum est: duos parvulos Alexandri fratris filios, quos ipse in urbe educabat, à nemine salutari, raro etiam in publicum prodire, praterquam ad sacra passus: eos verò sericeis vestibus indutos modestia admonendos curavit, nec brevi eo tempore, quo Pontifex fuit, illos unquam vidit: Interpellatus, an in Palatium ex privatis aedibus introducendi essent, respondit: Quid illis cum Palatio, eorum forte id patrimonium esse censetis? Tria sua Sacerdotia Cardinalibus duobus & Volaterano donavit &c. Paulò post inter ea multa & magna, quæ ad Apostolicæ sedis decus penè obscuratum instaurandum meditatum fuisse ferebatur, præcipuum esse dicit, quòd fratris, liberisque suis tantum largiri, quantum singuli è nobilitate homines in redditibus haberent, decreverat, nec ultrà privatorum civium conditionem se efferre passurus erat, non ad principatum & dignitates evehi, ne assem quidem de fructibus Ecclesiæ, nisi de libera omnium Cardinalium sententia, eos auferre permissurus. Id maximè percupere videbatur, ut eos Venetus Senatus in Patriciorum numerum adscriberet, summum id honoris genus, quo eos honestaret, esse reputans. XXX. Eodem adhuc Seculo Pius V. alienior quoque à Nepotismo introducendo visus fuit, dum ægrè Nepotem dignissimum Cardinalem, rogantibus Cardinalibus, fecit, atque nonnisi severæ conditionis, de non immiscendo se regimini aliter, additione. In qua abstinentia eum unus & alter ex recentissimis post Alexandrum VII. quadantenus secuti sunt; Quamvis sub immediato ejus successore Clemente IX. & Nepos Rospigliosius minoris quidem durationis, authoritatis & artis fuerit, hinc & Prædecessoribus longè inferior; Creaturas etiam & opes collectas familiæque fortunam si respicias; de quo L'Ambasciata di Romolo a' Romani hinc inde maximè nel Ritratto & nella Apologia del Cardinale. Sub Clemente X. verò Noni Successore, le Cardinal Nevéu, indice Authore de la Critiq. Gener. Lettr. Nouv. XIX. p. 619. avoit exercè une puissance absolue, & d'une maniere, qui avoit souvent chagrinè la France. Id est: Cardinalis Nepos habebat potestatem absolutam & exercebat modo sape Gallis valdè tædiofo. Innocentii XI. Successoris non minima fuit abstinentia, tamen & hic, si Gallis maximè fides haberetur, & non fefellit apparentia, satis ab aliis regebatur, & circumducebatur, relinquens post se non infortunatum Dominum Livium. Si quid autem Nepotismo sub Innocentio defuit, sub Alexandro VIII. additum vidimus nuper denuò, in additis domui Ottobonianæ intrà anni spatium opibus ferè immensis & dignitate Principali, considerante Papa, quòd breve sibi tempus superfit sine mora utendum. Innocentius XII. hactenus hæres est abstinentiæ Undecimi, ut nominis & dignitatis; & jam in moneta dixit: Hic nihil pro nobis. Quamvis & addi possit; ab Alexandro prædecessore relictum; & necessaria interdum sit, ærario à Nepotibus præeuntibus exhausto, abstinentia & de novo colligendum sequentibus; Quamvis etiam de Papis, ut de Principibus aliis, nunquam ex initiis talibus judicium ferri possit certum, neque enim semper respondent ultima primis, exemplo cumprimis Alexandri VII. pessimíque ab eo introducti Nepotismi, ab initio: Quanquam vultus erat multa & præclara minantis. Horat. sat. 3. l. 3. Quicquid sit, constat, paucissimos Nepotismum, reliquis à longo tempore tantopere deamatum, vel non, vel odio habuisse, & vix tot, quot ab inductione sècula elapsa sunt; Constat, quosdam eorum, qui abstinuerunt, haud alieniores aliis quidusdam, qui postea introduxerunt, sed brevitate vitæ, quò minùs similiter deficerent, impeditos fuisse; Constat etiam de summa hodiernæ abstinentiæ necessitate; neque enim orbis ex pristino lethargo sensim evigilans ulterius hos & similes manifestos abusus ferre posse videtur; Quamvis futurorum ignarissimi simus, & nuper Nepotismum resurgentem viderimus, utut ab Innocentio XI. sepultum, resurrecturum forte, & si denuò sepeliatur. Sed si vel plures abstinuissent, & in posterum abstinerent, illi ipsi & suo exemplo & verbis suis ad secus facientium & patientium pessimum statum eo melius cognoscendum nobis inservirent; Quem etiam illa, quæ generaliùs adhuc notanda veniunt, cognoscendum porrò sistunt.
units.tr: XXIX. In the same century Marcellus II (who, however, began to suffer from illness on the twelfth day of his pontificate, and died on the twenty-second), as Onuphrius reports in the same Life: "He did not wish any of his relatives to come to Rome, not even his brother; and what is new for these times and customs: he allowed the two little sons of his brother Alexander, whom he was bringing up in the city himself, to be greeted by no one, and seldom to appear in public, except to sacred services. He took care that they were dressed in silken garments and admonished to modesty; and during the short time that he was Pope he never once saw them. When he was asked whether they should be brought into the Palace from their private house, he replied: 'What have they to do with the Palace? Do you think that perhaps it is their patrimony?' He gave his three benefices to two cardinals and to Volterrano, etc." Shortly afterwards, among the "many great things which were said to have been planned for restoring the almost obscured dignity of the Apostolic See," he says the chief one is that he had decided to give to his brother and children only as much as individual noblemen have in revenues, and that he would not allow himself to be raised above the condition of private citizens; that he would not promote them to principalities and dignities, nor would he permit them to take away even a penny of the income of the Church without the free judgement of all the cardinals. He seemed especially eager that the Venetian Senate enrol them among the patricians, considering this the highest kind of honour by which to distinguish them. XXX. In this same century Pius V also seemed rather averse to introducing nepotism, for he made a nephew a cardinal only with reluctance, when the cardinals asked him to, and then only with the addition of a strict condition, that he should not interfere in government in any other way. Some one or two of the most recent Popes after Alexander VII have to some extent followed this abstinence. Although under his immediate successor, Clement IX, the nephew Rospigliosi was indeed of shorter duration, authority and skill, and therefore far inferior to his predecessors, if you consider the creatures and wealth he gathered and the fortune of his family; on which see L'Ambasciata di Romolo a' Romani, here and there especially in the Ritratto and in the Apologia del Cardinale. Under Clement X, the successor of Clement IX, the Cardinal Nephew (the author of the Critique générale indicates this in the Nouvelles de la République des Lettres, XIX, p. 619) exercised absolute power, in a way that often vexed France. That is: the Cardinal Nephew had absolute power and exercised it in a way often very tedious to the French. The abstinence of Innocent XI, his successor, was not small; yet even he, if one gives full credit to the French, and if appearance did not deceive, was sufficiently governed and led about by others, leaving behind him no unfortunate lord, Livio. If anything was lacking to nepotism under Innocent, we recently saw it added under Alexander VIII, when, within the span of a year, almost immense wealth and princely dignity were added to the house of Ottoboni, the Pope considering that little time remained to him and that it must be used without delay. Innocent XII, so far, is the heir of the abstinence of Innocent XI in name and dignity only; and he has already said on a coin: "Here nothing for ourselves." Although it might also be added: "left by Alexander, his predecessor"; and abstinence, which those who follow must practise anew, is sometimes necessary when the treasury has been drained by nephews who went before. Although, too, concerning Popes, as concerning other princes, a certain judgement can never be made from such beginnings, for the last things do not always correspond to the first; especially the example of Alexander VII and the very bad nepotism introduced by him from the beginning: "Although his face was that of one threatening many and splendid things." Horace, Satires, book 3. Whatever the case, it is established that very few have either abstained from nepotism, which for a long time has been so greatly loved by the rest, or have hated it; and scarcely as many as the centuries that have passed since its introduction. It is established that some of those who abstained were not less favourable to their kin than certain others who afterwards introduced nepotism, but were prevented by the shortness of their lives from failing in the same way. It is established too concerning the great necessity of abstinence today; for the world, slowly waking from its former lethargy, does not seem able to bear these and similar manifest abuses any longer. Although we are most ignorant of the future, and we have recently seen nepotism rising again, though buried by Innocent XI, it may perhaps rise again, even if it is buried again. But even if more Popes had abstained, and would abstain in future, they themselves, by their example and their words, would serve us well in understanding more clearly the worst condition of those who act otherwise and of those who suffer it; and the things which are yet to be noted more generally place this understanding before us in turn.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Illud certè præprimis, quòd tanta est Nepotum aliquando potestas, & quòd non partem tantùm, sed omnia quasi negotia maximè ardua soli tractant, Pontifices sunt, & Pontifices quasi
units.tr: Above all, this is certainly the case: the power of nephews is sometimes so great that they alone handle not just a part but almost all the most arduous business. They are Popes, and Popes in the manner of nephews.

units.la: Maxime hic vitiosum, quòd — margin note, not transcribed. quasi Nepotes. Vide ea, quæ suprà diximus, maximè in Gregorio XV. Vide etiam II Nip. p. 2. p.75. seqq. & p.292. seqq. & p. 367. Considera dein, annon causam habuerit ille p. 13. dicendi: Se nolle esse subditum Papæ, qui sit subditus suorum consanguineorum; quando etiam Papa p. 48. dixit: Cognata, conserva personam nostram, & nos tibi Pontificatum conservabimus. Annon Nepotibus, vel Cognatis talibus facile esset probatu, vel se, vel uxores, vel infantes suos esse Dominos Orbis & Ecclesiæ, dum ipsi sic pro lubitu Pontifices, id est, summos Monarchas, & Ecclesiæ Capita circumducunt, regunt, placitis suis subjicere nôrunt, ipsi modò uxoribus subjecti, modò infantibus, ne quid pejus dicam, in uxorum defectu? Et cui non absurdum videtur, Ecclesiam pro nutu talium regi debere? Atque non sufficere in Papatu, ut speciosò Ecclesiæ nomine Papa venditetur; dum Papæ etiam nomine nounisi ejus Nepotes cum concupiscentiis suis veniunt?
units.tr: Most faulty here, that [margin note, not transcribed] nephews. See what we said above, especially on Gregory XV. See also II Nip. p. 2. p. 75 ff. and p. 292 ff. and p. 367. Consider next whether that writer had cause to say, p. 13: that he was unwilling to be subject to the Pope, who is subject to his relatives; since the Pope too said, p. 48: Relative, keep our person, and we will keep the papacy for you. Would it not be easy to prove to nephews, or to such kinsmen, that they themselves, or their wives, or their children, are the lords of the world and the Church, since they lead the Popes about at their pleasure, that is, the supreme monarchs and heads of the Church, and know how to bend them to their wishes, while they themselves are now subject to wives, now to children, not to say worse, when there are no wives? And who does not find it absurd that the Church should be ruled at the nod of such people? And is it not enough in Popery that the Papacy is sold under the specious name of the Church, while under the name of the Pope only his nephews come, with their lusts?

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Nepotes minimè tantis apti; Juvenes, indocti, inexercitati, ut plurimùm, & aliis omnibus assueti. Quis tales, quis ab asinis ita ad equos, imò à vilissimis, tenuissimis, ad summa & maximè ardua, momentanea sæpe promotione, evectos, rite in tanto culmine præesse crederet? Quando necesse habet aliquis Gregorius XV. differens tractationem de arduis dicere; se expectare, donec Nepos magis Politicis negotiationibus sit assuetus p 367. Quando necesse habet aliquis Legatus interrogatus: Utrum eat ad tractandum cum Astalio Nepote? respondere; Se ire ad instituendum Nepotem? Quando Generalissimus fit, qui per totam vitam gladium non portavit? Qualis fuit & factus est sub Alexandro VII. Frater Marius. Quando Æsopum legens ad negotiationes maximè arduas vocatur? Quod in ejusdem filio, Cardinale Patrono, contigit. Vide p.266. seq. Quando Capucinus sub Urbano VIII. mox de rebus salutem orbis Christiani concernentibus agit, adhuc dum nonnisi de Clausfro suo cogitans, ut Legato Cæsareo auxilium contrà Turcas implorante, de rapis in Clausfro, carumque bonitate & præparatione loqui cœpit; ut Legatum Hispaniæ, ex quo conventu Ejus Reverenda Paternitas fit, ac si Capucinus & ipse esset, interrogavit; ut, errore animadverso fassus est, omnes obvios sibi Capucinos videri; ut neminem alio titulo quàm Paternitatis compellavit; ut aliquando Regium Ministrum usque ad portas Clausfri comitari voluit &c. Quis à tam ineptis apta & tanto culmine digna expectet? Nihil jam de Sixti V. cognatione, nihil hil de pessima talium saepe vita, post ea, quae jam diximus, dicemus.
units.tr: Nephews are by no means fit for such tasks: they are mostly young, untaught, inexperienced, and accustomed to everything else. Who would believe that such men, raised by a sudden promotion, often from asses to horses, or rather from the lowest and meanest condition to the highest and most arduous offices, could rightly preside at such a height? When Gregory XV, deferring the discussion of difficult matters, had to say that he was waiting until the nephew should be more accustomed to political negotiations, p. 367; when a certain Legate, asked, whether he was going to treat with the nephew Astalio, had to reply, that he was going to instruct the nephew; when a man who had never carried a sword his whole life was made Commander-in-Chief? Such was Brother Marius under Alexander VII, and such he became. When a man who has been reading Aesop is called to the most arduous negotiations? This happened to the son of the same man, the Cardinal Patron; see p. 266 ff. When under Urban VIII a Capuchin soon dealt with matters concerning the welfare of the Christian world, while still thinking only of his cloister: when an Imperial Legate was begging for help against the Turks, he began to speak of the grapes in his cloister, and their goodness and preparation; when he asked the Spanish Legate, from which convent Your Reverend Paternity comes, as if he too were a Capuchin; when, having noticed his error, he confessed that all the people he met seemed to him to be Capuchins; when he addressed no one by any title but Paternity; when at one point he wanted to escort a royal minister as far as the gates of the cloister, etc. Who would expect fit and worthy conduct at such a height from men so inept? I will say nothing more now of Sixtus V's kinship, nor of the wretched life of such men, which is often bad, after what we have already said.

units.la: XXXIII. Dicimus tamen rursus: Nepotes cum concupiscentiis suis; auri cupidissimos Nepotes, qui & horas audiendis Legatis destinatas horas paupertatis & miseriae vocant, utpote in quibus nihil accipiunt, & normisi de nummis cogitant; Hinc quidam volens cognoscere ex Legato Galliae: Quot ibi Protestantes essent; interrogavit; quot ibi nummi essent; quo errore animadverso, respondit Legatus; non tot Regem haereticos habere, quot Nepos nummos habeat; Hinc alius solebat nuntianti Legatum venire, respondere, collum rumpat; nunciati, Ministrum Datariae adesse; gratus erit. Hinc quidam Legatus solebat ante significare, se acturum de renunciatione certorum beneficiorum; egit etiam ab initio Audientiae, & gratus fuit. Vide haec & plura p.382--389. Confer ea, quae supra attulimus, & fidem ista impetrabunt facile. Sed quomodo rursus tales Ecclesiam bene regent?
units.tr: XXXIII. Yet I say again: nephews with their lusts; nephews most eager for gold, who call the hours set aside for hearing Legates hours of poverty and misery, since they receive nothing in them and think only of money. Hence a certain man, wishing to learn from the Legate of France how many Protestants there were there, asked how many coins there were there; when he noticed his mistake, the Legate replied, the King does not have as many heretics as the nephew has coins. Hence another used to answer, when told that the Legate was coming, may he break his neck; when told that the minister of the Datary was present, he will be welcome. Hence a certain Legate used to announce beforehand that he would speak about the renunciation of certain benefices; he did so also at the start of the audience, and was welcome. See these and more things at p. 382–389. Compare what we have brought forward above, and these things will easily win belief. But how again can such men rule the Church well?

units.la: XXXIV. Non faciunt; sed multum nocent, sibi, Pontificibus & Ecclesiae; Sibi; neque obstant honorum cumuli, acervi divitiarum; quibus & gehennam sibi aedificant, & Idola cadente cadunt Pontifice, & in vita & in morte maledictioni sunt. De quibus & egimus & agemus. Salutem quod attinet, quaesivit Author Nepotismi p.443. ex Abbate Romano, cur non Nepotes, legentes vitas Antecessorum, melius sibi consulere studeant; Respondit; nummos numerantibus tempus lectionis deesse, incipere legere deficientibus nummis, deficere demum in morte; Alius non inferior eidem dixit: Abire in purgatorium, utpote quos pudeat in Paradisum venire, ad Christum, quem hic spoliaverint, p.444. Nocent etiam Pontificibus, quibus quidem valde prodesse videntur, dum onera Papatus vel ex toto, vel ex parte in se recipiunt, dum Pontificibus occasionem, negotiationes in longum protrahendi, praebent, ipsis dicentibus: Loquimini cum Nepote; Nepotibus: Loquemur cum Avunculo. Vid. p.235. & totum fere librum tertium secundae partis; quod idem esse ait Author cum illo, quod Christus missus est a Cajapha ad Pilatum, a Pilato ad Herodem ab Herode denuo ad Pilatum &c. p.304. Nepotibus se praetextu Avunculi excusantibus, Avunculo ad Nepotes remittente, & tractationibus tandem cum Nepotibus conclusis, demum dicente: Videbimus! Hinc aliquando Legatus Lucensis ad Amicum, devotionem suam Sanctis testari volentem: Amice, si nemo tractare potest cum Barbarinis, qui loquuntur, quis tractare poterit cum Sanctis, qui non loquuntur? Si tam difficiles sunt vivi, quam difficiles erunt mortui? Porro Pontificibus utiles esse videntur in expiscandis Regnorum arcanis,dum nimirum simulare debent,se certorum Regnorum vel certi Regni partes tuituros; atque, in eum finem Urbanum VIII. 2. Nepotibus mandâsse, ut alter, simulatâ erga Gallos benevolentiâ, Gallorum, alter eadem arte Hispanorum expiscaretur arcana, Author p.66. seqq. ait & probat, Ast multùm illis revera nocent, dum malitiæ instrumenta sunt, dum potestate à Pontificibus neglecta pessimè abutuntur, semper nomine Pontificum; dum etiam Pontifices ab iis malè agere, divitias, voluptates sectari discunt. Vide exemplum Alexandri, ubi de vitiosis ejus qualitatibus egimus; & confer verba Senatoris Veneti: Sarebbe &c. Urbanus Sanctus esset, si Franciscus, Antonius & Thaddæus non Dæmones essent II Nip. p.2. p.154. dum sic Pontificum damnationem promovent,ut Pontifices illorum; Cognati Papæ, inquit Prælatus Germanus apud Authorem Nepot. p. 2. l.1. p.6. acquirunt hunc mundum indulgentiâ Pontificis, p.161. Pontifex perdit alterum vitio Nepotum.
units.tr: XXXIV. They do not; rather they do great harm: to themselves, to the Popes, and to the Church. To themselves: neither the heaps of honours nor the piles of riches stand in their way; with these they build for themselves a hell, and when the Pope falls, they fall like idols, and in life and in death they are cursed. Of these both we have spoken and we shall speak. As for their salvation, the author of Nepotismus asked a Roman Abbot, p. 443, why nephews, who read the lives of their predecessors, did not take better care of themselves. He replied: those who count money have no time to read; they begin to read when the money runs out, and at last they fail in death. Another, no less shrewd, said to the same author: they go to purgatory, since they would be ashamed to come into paradise to Christ, whom they have stripped here, p. 444. They also harm the Popes, whom indeed they seem greatly to help, since they take upon themselves the burdens of the Papacy, wholly or in part, and give the Popes the chance to drag negotiations out at length, the Popes saying, speak with the nephew, and the nephews, we will speak with the uncle. See p. 235 and nearly the whole third book of the second part. The author says this is the same as when Christ was sent by Caiaphas to Pilate, from Pilate to Herod, and from Herod back to Pilate, etc. p. 304. The nephews excuse themselves on the pretext of the uncle, the uncle refers them back to the nephews, and finally, when the negotiations have been concluded with the nephews, the uncle says at last: We shall see! Hence once the Lucchese Legate, to a friend who wished to attest his devotion to the Saints, said: Friend, if no one can treat with the Barberini, who speak, who will be able to treat with the Saints, who do not speak? If the living are so hard to deal with, how hard will the dead be? Again, they seem useful to the Popes in fishing out the secrets of kingdoms, since they must of course pretend to take up the cause of certain kingdoms or parts of a kingdom. The author, p. 66 ff., says and proves that Urban VIII commanded two nephews, so that one, with a pretended goodwill towards the French, should fish out the secrets of the French, and the other by the same art those of the Spanish. But they do the greatest harm in reality, since they are instruments of malice; since, with power neglected by the Popes, they abuse it most wickedly, always under the Popes' name; and since they teach the Popes to act badly and to pursue riches and pleasures. See the example of Alexander, where we discussed his vicious qualities, and compare the words of the Venetian Senator: It would be ... Urban would be a saint, if Francis, Antony and Thaddeus were not demons, II Nip. p. 2, p. 154. Thus they promote the damnation of the Popes just as the Popes promote theirs. "Relatives of the Pope," says the German Prelate, as cited by the author of Nepotismus, p. 2, l. 1, p. 6, "gain this world by the Pope's indulgence," p. 161, "the Pope loses the other world through the vices of the nephews."

units.la: XXXV. Ast quantum Ecclesiæ nocere dici debent! Plurimum certè; Dum sæpe tam mali, tam inepti, tam indocti, tam inexperti, tam auri cupidi omnia regunt, imò pervertunt, idque potestate illimitata sæpe.
units.tr: XXXV. But how much they must be said to harm the Church! Very much indeed: since so often such bad, inept, untaught, inexperienced, gold-greedy men rule and even pervert everything, and often with unlimited power.

units.la: Fidem sub dominio horum illæsam non manere, facilè creditur, quando omnis generis negotia fidem etiam concernentia æquali potestate interdum tractant; & quando ex principio malorum morum fidem corrumpente ad tantam potestatem admittuntur. Exemplo quantum noceant, dici satis nequit; Si enim Nepotes Pontificum, qui Sacrorum sunt arbitri, mala quævis patrant, quid non alii sibi licere putabunt? Sed quantam desolationem in Ecclesia illa, & statu cumprimis, ut vocat ur, Ecclesiæ suâ injustitiâ atque avaritiâ producunt? Levi eam, post contemplationes speciliores, obtutu contemplemur; Dicuntur Authori Nepotismi p.2.78. Messores Ecclesiæ, Principibus Ecclesiæ ceu seminatoribus oppositi; Sed nihil isti Messores relinquunt fere; Pecus non tondere tantùm, sed & deglubere Pastores illi stulti amant; Ædificant Palatia in sanguinibus; Hinc dixit Magnus Hetruriæ Dux aliquando ad religiosè peregrinantem: Roma non est Templum magis Sacrosanctum Palatio Barbarinorum, utpote tot martyrum sanguine ædificatum p.161. Hinc & populum & subditos & Christianismum & Ecclesiam, & Ecclesiasticos & Monachos, & Principes & altaria sigillatim de Nepotibus querentes introducit; Hinc, quantis & quot execrationibus, imprecationibus impetantur, p.446–448. docet; Hinc nihilominùs patientiam Romani populi in his patiendis calum obducentis p. 257. seqq. miratur; Hinc, p.50. statum Ecclesiæ dictum miserrimum pronunciat, ceu similem urbi, quam hostis, quia tenere non possit, spoliet; Et quia Nepotismum Hydræ, cujus capite amputato uno, aliud statim crescit, similem p.134. videt, atque novam imminentem, novo Pontifice electo, calamitatem, hinc etiam p.50. statuit, meliorem subditorum statum futurum, si hæreditarium regnum esset. Et cur non? Cùm post muscas ferè satiatas sitientes semper atque esurientes majori cum corporis illius molestia succedant; Hinc etiam Nepotes, qui singuli merito rei sunt violentiarum, gravaminum, vectigalium, extorsionum, latrociniorum, Simoniarum, Tyrannidum, rapinarum, injustitiarum, tòtque miseriarum, quibus persecutiones Gentilium longè superare L. Ambasc. Rom. p. 6. dicuntur. Consulta etiam, & cum præcedentibus confer ea, quæ p.13. metricè habentur, ubi de Pontificibus ceu lupis rapacibus Roma ita queritur; Che per finir discorticarmi il Gregge Chiaman da Rastri & Antri i lor Nepoti Scalzi, Birbanti, e Malandrini ignoti Senza Dio, senza fede, e senza legge. Questi cacchi ladroni e Rei fur bacci Di forche avanzo e sol resto di Roia Si spacian tutti del sangue di Troja E fanno al par dè Reggi i Principacci. Quanto di belle, e buon hanno i miei sigli, Quanto di ricco e sacro hanno i miei tempii, Tutto à forza si rubba da quest' Empii, Tutto preda divien de' loro artigli: Sotto il suo giogo ecco già spicca e langue Il mio popol piagato in mille guise, E pur mirar conviengli e tinte e trise Quelle porpore lor nel proprio sangue. E appra un Abisso, questo appena empito Sen' apre uno più vasto in un baleno E questo ancora al sin colmo e ripieno Un' altro, e à questo un altro in infinito. Italia fosse, & io, tutto un Thesoro. Mai diffamar potrei le gole immonde, Che per quelle voragini profonde Non basta il mondo distillato in oro &c.
units.tr: It is easily believed that the faith does not remain unharmed under the rule of such men, when they sometimes handle with equal power all kinds of business, even matters touching the faith, and when they are admitted to such power on the basis of a principle of bad morals that corrupts the faith. It can scarcely be said how much harm they do by example. For if the nephews of the Popes, who are the arbiters of sacred things, commit any evil whatever, who will not think it lawful for himself? But what desolation, and above all what state of the so-called Church, do they produce by their injustice and avarice? Let us look at it briefly, after more special consideration. The author of Nepotismus, p. 2, p. 78, calls them the reapers of the Church, set against the Princes of the Church as sowers. But those reapers leave almost nothing; those foolish shepherds love not only to shear the flock but to flay it. They build palaces in blood. Hence the Great Duke of Tuscany once said to a man travelling there out of religious devotion: Rome is no more sacred a temple than the palace of the Barberini, since it was built with the blood of so many martyrs, p. 161. Hence he brings in the people, the subjects, Christianity, the Church, the clergy and monks, the Princes and the altars, each complaining separately about the nephews; hence he teaches with how many and how many curses and imprecations they are assailed, p. 446–448; hence he nevertheless marvels at the patience of the Roman people in enduring these things, which draws a veil over the matter, p. 257 ff.; hence, p. 50, he pronounces the state of the Church most wretched, like a city which an enemy plunders because it cannot hold it; and since he sees Nepotism as like the Hydra, whose one head, when cut off, is immediately replaced by another, p. 134, and sees a new calamity threatening with each new Pope elected, therefore he also decides, p. 50, that the condition of the subjects would be better if the kingdom were hereditary. And why not? Since after the flies have nearly gorged themselves, the thirsty and hungry ones come next, with far greater trouble to that body. Hence also the nephews, each of whom is rightly called guilty of violence, oppression, taxes, extortions, robberies, simonies, tyrannies, plunderings, injustices, and so many miseries that the persecutions of the Gentiles are far surpassed, L. Ambasc. Rom. p. 6. Consult also, and compare with what precedes, the verses at p. 13, where Rome thus complains of the Popes as ravening wolves: Since to finish flaying the flock, they call on their barefoot nephews, rogues and bandits unknown, without God, without faith, and without law. These cackling thieves and guilty men are the scraps of the gallows and the sole remnant of Rome; they all boast of the blood of Troy and play at princes as well as kings. How much of beauty and goodness my sons have, how much of wealth and sanctity my temples have, all is robbed by force by these impious men; all becomes prey to their talons. Under their yoke my people now droops and languishes, wounded in a thousand ways, and must look upon those purples of theirs dyed in its own blood. And an abyss, scarcely filled, opens another vaster in a moment, and that too, at last full and brimming, another, and to this another, endlessly. Were Italy and I one treasure, I could never denounce those foul throats, for into those deep chasms the whole world distilled into gold is not enough, etc.

units.la: Quæ quidem brevissimè dicunt; Papas, ut planè excorient Gregem, vilissimos suos agnatos, planè impios, vocare, qui latrones omnia eximia filiis populi, omnia sacra Templis auferant, & purpuras in sanguine populi tingant, sine ullo fine, cùm abyssum abyssus excipiat, & Italia, si nonnisi thesaurus esset, immundas gulas, quibus universus orbis in aurum destillatum minimè sufficeret, explere neutiqam posset. Adde, quæ p. 67. de Alexandri VII. Nepotismo leguntur: Pose Alessandro pria che fosse spento Al clero per dici anni i sei per cento E diciò non contento Per arrichir Don Mario suo Germano Il Mantello à San Pier strappò di mano, O duro Caso e strano.
units.tr: These words say very briefly that the Popes, as they strip the flock clean, call their most worthless kinsmen (agnati) utterly impious, since they are robbers who take everything precious from the children of the people and everything sacred from the temples, and who dye their purple in the people's blood, without any end. Abyss calls to abyss, and Italy, even if it were nothing but a treasury, could never satisfy their filthy gullets, into which the whole world distilled into gold would not suffice. Add what is read at p. 67 concerning the nepotism of Alexander VII: Before he was snuffed out, Pope Alexander / Taxed the clergy six per cent for ten years, / And not content with that, / To enrich Don Mario, his German brother, / He snatched the mantle from St Peter's hand. / O hard and strange case.

units.la: Id est; Eum ante Clericatum sex pro centum non fuisse contentum, & ad ditandum fratrem duro casu S. Petro pallium eripuisse è manibus. Considera porro artificium, quo juxta p. 75. dum contrà Turcas aliquid colligendum esset, Monasteriorum & Abbatiarum ruinâ, Xenodochiorum, pauperum & Orphanorum tributis rem suam quasi unicè promovere nõrunt. Et vide p. 89. suprà memoratum Alexandri VII. fratrem in exemplum pessimi populo fratris allegatum. Vide tandem p. 243. de Barbarinis, cùm eligendus esset; Quelle Vespe homai Il sangue human' hanno succhiato assai.
units.tr: That is: before his clerical office he was not content with six per cent, and to enrich his brother he snatched the pallium from the hands of St Peter in a hard case. Consider further the trick by which, according to p. 75, when something had to be collected against the Turks, they were able to advance their own affairs almost solely by the ruin of monasteries and abbeys, and by taxes on hospitals, the poor and orphans. And see p. 89, where the aforesaid brother of Alexander VII is cited to the people as an example of the worst kind of brother. Finally see p. 243, concerning the Barberini, when one was to be elected: Those wasps by now / Have sucked human blood enough.

units.la: Id est: Vespa illa satis humani sanguinis hauserunt.
units.tr: That is: those wasps have drunk up a great deal of human blood.

units.la: XXXVI. Mirum post dicta esse non debet, quòd non manet talium potestas, non diuturna est Nepotum usurpatio, & tristis eos exitus dejicit. Jam Dissert. IV. Sect. III. n. 8.9. eorum unâ cum morte Pontificis sui mortem, id est, casum contemplati sumus; Quem hic exemplis porrò illustrare possumus. Illo Pii IV. qui, (quod ipse dicebat) ut Romanorum Pontificum propinquis salutare exemplum relinqueret, ut populos sibi creditos clementer acciperent, & publica negocia pro ecclesiæ dignitate conficerent, specie vindicandi ea crimina, quæ Carafa patruo Pontifice, & bello potissimùm Neapolitano patraverant, gravissimè in eorum etiam vitam animadvertit, ut apud Onuphrium legi potest; Alio Innocentii X. qui statim Nepotismum Antecessoris cum tanto furore persecutus est, ut licet persecutio justa fuerit, nimis tamen severa visa sit, Authore Nepot. p. 2. p. 256. testante. Quomodo autem ejusdem Nepotismus, vel potius Cognatismus, eandem post mortem ipsius aleam subire debuerit, Dissert. VII. Sect. VII. n. 70. in vitiosis ipsius Qualitatibus obiter notavimus. Qui certè casus cum similibus similium sequi necessario debuerunt, & debent, sive injustitiam & sacrilegia, sive odium populi & exectrationes frequentes; Talibus enim Deus non benedicit; & de male quaesitis non gaudet tertius haeres; Sive successorum aviditatem spectemus; Hâc fur furem spoliat; injustitia majori injustitiâ concul-catur, & quercu cadente quilibet ligna colligit; Sic vastatores vastandi sunt, & vaccæ pingues à macidis deglutiendæ; quod ita fieri ex praecedentibus liquet, ut, simili porrò coincidente, & fame maciéque harum manente in his, illas deglutitas esse, serò appareat. Confer ea, quæ Author Nepotismi p. 2. l. 3. p. 390--442. de Familiis Pontificum brevi tempore florentibus habet.
units.tr: XXXVI. It should not be surprising after what has been said that such power does not last, that the usurpation of nephews is not long-lived, and that a sad end overtakes them. We have already considered, in Dissertation IV, Section III, nn. 8–9, how their death, that is, their downfall, goes together with the death of their Pontiff; and we can illustrate this further with examples. Take Pius IV, who, (as he himself used to say) in order to leave a salutary example to the relatives of the Roman Pontiffs, that they should receive the peoples entrusted to them with mercy and conduct public affairs in a manner worthy of the Church, under the pretext of avenging the crimes that Carafa had committed against his uncle the Pope, and above all the war at Naples, punished their very lives most severely, as can be read in Onuphrius. Or take Innocent X, who at once pursued the nepotism of his predecessor with such fury that, although the prosecution was just, it seemed excessively severe, as the author of Nepotismus, p. 2, p. 256, bears witness. How the same nepotism, or rather kinship-favouritism, was bound to undergo the same risk after the Pontiff's own death, we noted in passing in Dissertation VII, Section VII, n. 70, with reference to his vicious qualities. These outcomes must necessarily have followed, and must follow, for similar cases of similar things, whether we look at injustice and sacrilege or at the hatred of the people and frequent curses. For God does not bless such men, and the third heir does not rejoice in ill-gotten goods. Or if we look at the greed of successors: a thief is robbed by a thief, injustice is trampled by a greater injustice, and when the oak falls, everyone gathers wood. Thus the destroyers must be destroyed, and the fat cows swallowed by the lean ones; that this happens in this way is clear from what has gone before, so that, when a similar succession follows and the famine and leanness of these men remain in those who come after, it becomes plain late on that the earlier men were swallowed up. Compare what the author of Nepotismus, p. 2, l. 3, pp. 390–442, says about the families of the Pontiffs who flourished for a short time.

units.la: XXXVII. Quando autem, de quo dicta fidem facere possunt, ipsi illi etiam, qui Nepotismum alienum persequuntur, proprium nequaquam meliorem introducunt, & quando eousque se extendit in Pontificibus electis amor erga consanguineos (addo, amor erga patriam; Vide Vita di Sisto V. p. 2. p. 324. & exemplum Bonifacii IX. in Roma Gloriosa. p. 506.) & consequens electionis, Lottino Dissert. de Conclavi docente, est liberalitas erga amicos, quibus nimirum amicitiam continuatam videre contingit, non enim omnes omnes statim deserunt; Mirum quoque videri non debet, quòd idem Ibidem, Cognatorum rationem habendam esse, docet, & in Conclavibus omnibus, quam primùm de aliquo eligendo agi coeptum est, prima nunc esse solet de Nepotibus, vel consanguineis, quos eligendus habeat, aliis, cogitatio, atque multi cognationis respectu repulsam ferunt, qui cæterùm omnium dignissimi omnium judicio habentur;
units.tr: XXXVII. When the very men who pursue the nepotism of others, and of whom we can speak with authority, by no means introduce a better kind of their own, and when the love of Pontiffs for their own kin extends so far (I add, love for their native land; see Life of Sixtus V, p. 2, p. 324, and the example of Boniface IX in Roma Gloriosa, p. 506), and a consequence of election, as Lottini teaches in Dissertation on the Conclave, is generosity towards friends, namely those with whom one has the chance to see a continued friendship, for not all men desert everyone at once. Nor should it seem strange that the same author, in the same place, teaches that regard must be had for kinsmen, and that in every conclave, as soon as the election of someone is taken up, the first thought is usually about the nephews or kinsmen whom the one to be elected has, and that many people are rejected on account of kinship, although in the judgment of all they are regarded as the most worthy of all.

units.la: XXXVIII. Nempe non praesumunt de Pontificibus suis, de quibus tanta tamen praesumunt! eos suos usque ad aras tantùm diligere posse! Eos Deum & justitiam plùs diligere posse! Eos cum Christo fratrum mentionem ingerentibus respondere posse: Quinam sunt fratres nostri? Fratres nostri sunt, qui faciunt voluntatem Domini. Quæ quidem verba Alexander VII. initio Pontificatûs sua facere ausus fuit, dum alii fratrem recipiendum esse suaderent, sed quo jure, vel potius hypocrisi quanta, supra allata ostendunt. Hic etenim Successores Christi esse nolunt! Imo Nepotismo suo veritatem dictorum ejus: Non potestis simul Deo servire & Mammoni; evertere conantur; Et perfidi sunt, dum bona Ecclesiae stabilia interdum etiam contra juramentum suum abalienant! Et patiuntur, imo authoritate sua muniunt abominationes, quas recensuimus, omnes, imo plures, quam dici potest. Quale hoc est principium unicum suos ditandi? Quale hoc est regnum, in quo eleemosynae, & animarum purgandarum lytra ita impenduntur, justitiae, an iniquitatis, Dei, an Mammonis? Iniquitatis certe & Mammonis, & quicquid ad ista velanda adhibetur, velamen Mysterii iniquitatis; Tristis proin & ista in Pontificum recens electorum consanguineis mutatio, & maxime tristis.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Surely they do not presume about their Pontiffs, although they presume so much! That these men can love their own kin only up to the altars! That they can love God and justice more! That when others bring up the mention of brothers, they can answer with Christ: Who are my brothers? My brothers are those who do the will of the Lord. Alexander VII dared to claim these words as his own at the start of his pontificate, when others urged that a brother should be received; but by what right, or rather how great a hypocrisy, the things quoted above show. For these men do not want to be successors of Christ! Indeed, by their nepotism they try to overturn the truth of his saying: You cannot serve God and Mammon at the same time. And they are faithless, when they sometimes alienate the stable goods of the Church, even against their own oath! And they suffer, and indeed by their authority they protect, the abominations we have listed, all of them, and more than can be told. What kind of principle is this, that they enrich only their own? What kind of kingdom is this, in which alms and the ransoms for souls to be cleansed are spent in such a way? Is it of justice or of iniquity, of God or of Mammon? Surely of iniquity and Mammon; and whatever is used to veil these things is the veil of the mystery of iniquity. Sad, therefore, and very sad, is this change among the kinsmen of recently elected Pontiffs.

units.la: XXXIX. Mutatio, quae in rebus accidere solet, haud magis certe Pontifices commendat. Novi Domini, novi Aulici, novi Consiliarii, novi Nepotes, exigunt novas volitiones, molitiones, consilia nova, novas agendi rationes. Hinc mutantur omnia; in deterius plerunque; Quod eventus docuit; Non tantum seculo decimo. De quo Baronius ad an. 1000. n. 3. Sunt haec infelicissima illa tempora, cum alter alterius res gestas, intrusus quisque Pontifex aboleret. Vide Dissert. VII. Sect. 6. n. 12. 15. 16. Nam & deinceps Innocentius VI. multas reservationes a Clemente factas, a pud Platinam in Vita, suspendisse legitur; Et Paulus IV. apud Onuphrium in Vita, publica sanctione, cuncta, quae superiores Pontifices post Julium II. concesserant, quae bona redditusque Ecclesiarum minuerent, sustulisse; Et Lege Julii III. ut habet idem in Marcello II. cautum est, ut donatio necessario facta, non ante valida censeatur, quam 2. aut 3. subsequentium Pontificum authoritas accessisset; Imo quasi ordinarium ipsis esse, statim gratias praedecessorum revocare, ex ipsa Lege ipsorum discimus. Quando autem mutatio ista statutorum atque decretorum ipsam etiam fidem spectare ex Apostasia posteriorum temporum & ex Pontificum illorum, qui, ipsis Gallis Pontificiis fatentibus, in fide erraverunt, exemplis agnoscitur, eo evidentius patet, praeter reliqua, quae hactenus a nobis enarrata sunt, Electionis Pontificum Romanorum consequentia, hoc ipsum etiam, quod in ordine considerationis nostrae ultimum esse voluimus, vitiosum, Vicariis Christi summisque Ecclesiae Monarchis indignum, & una cum reliquis totius Papatus eversivum esse.
units.tr: XXXIX. The change that usually happens in human affairs certainly does not recommend Pontiffs any more. New lords, new courtiers, new counsellors, new nephews demand new wishes, new undertakings, new plans and new ways of acting. Hence everything changes, for the most part for the worse, as events have taught; and not only in the tenth century. On this Baronius, at the year 1000, n. 3: These were the most unhappy times, when each intruded Pontiff annulled the deeds of the other. See Dissertation VII, Section VI, nn. 12, 15, 16. For we read that afterwards Innocent VI suspended many reservations made by Clement, as in Platina in his Life, the Pope suspended; and that Paul IV, as in Onuphrius in his Life, by public decree abolished all the things which the earlier Pontiffs after Julius II had granted, which diminished the goods and revenues of the Churches; and that by the law of Julius III, as the same author has it in Marcellus II, it was provided that a donation necessarily made should not be considered valid until the authority of two or three subsequent Pontiffs had been added. Indeed, we learn from their own law that it is almost customary for them to revoke at once the favours of their predecessors. When it is recognised, from the apostasy of later times and from the examples of those Pontiffs who, as even the Gallican Papists confess, erred in faith, that this change of statutes and decrees touches the faith itself, it becomes even more evident, besides the other things we have so far set out, that this consequence of the election of Roman Pontiffs, which we wished to be last in the order of our consideration, is vicious, unworthy of the Vicars of Christ and the supreme Monarchs of the Church, and, together with the rest, destructive of the whole Papacy.

units.la: Mutatio rerum electionem consequens vitiosa & illa;
units.tr: A change in affairs following the election is also vicious.

units.la: XL. Qui proin multò fortiùs evertitur per ea omnia, quæ in hisce Dissertationibus dicta sunt, simul sumpta; Dum nimirum sufficienter probatum dedimus, Apostolum Petrum, cujus successionem vanissimè jactant, dignitatem atque potestatem, quam ipsi ab eo hæreditario quasi jure ad se devolutum spectant, electionis suæ beneficio nullo modo accepisse; & potestatem Petri qualemcunque ad Pontifices nostros nulla ratione, jure nullo pertinere; & formas ipsas Electionis Pontificum nostrorum eorum pretium haud parùm imminuere; Eelectionem autem nævis plurimis & ratione eligentium, & ratione actuum eligendi, & ratione eorum, qui eligi soleant; neque paucis, ob consequentia inconvenientia, laborare; Atque ita ipsissimum Pontificatûs fundamentum loco suo movimus, cariosum, & Mysterium Iniquitatis in ipso suo initio, Authoribûsque suis tale esse, ostendimus; Quod si, occasione laboris nostri qualiscunque, & alii nobiscum agnoscant, vel magis magisque cognoscere pergant, ejus jam pretium habemus, jam scopum assecuti sumus, Dei nempe nostri in fratrum ædificatione humanáque salute gloriam, quam ei soli vendicamus omnem atque indies aûstam videre cupimus petimúsque, per Dominum nostrum & Ecclesiæ suæ unicum, ὃς ἀνομον ἀναλώσει τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ καὶ καταργήσει τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ, qui impium illum perdet Spiritu oris sui & abolebit apparitione adventûs sui, Jesum Christum! Amen!
units.tr: XL. Therefore it is overturned much more strongly by all the things said in these Dissertations taken together. For we have sufficiently proved that the Apostle Peter, whose succession they boast of most emptily, did not in any way receive by the benefit of their election the dignity and power which they claim has devolved to themselves, as if by hereditary right, from him; that the power of Peter, of whatever kind it was, belongs by no reasoning and no right to our Pontiffs; that the very forms of the election of our Pontiffs considerably diminish their worth; and that the election itself suffers from many blemishes, both in respect of the electors, and of the acts of electing, and of those who are usually elected; and not a few by the inconveniences that follow. And so we have moved the very foundation of the Papacy from its place, showing it to be rotten, and a Mystery of Iniquity from its very beginning, and such in its authors. If, by occasion of our labour, whatever it is, others agree with us, or continue to recognise more and more, we already have its reward, and have already attained our aim, namely the glory of our God in the building up of brothers and the salvation of men, which we claim for him alone, and which we desire and pray to see increased every day, through our Lord and the only one of his Church, whom [the Lord Jesus will destroy] the lawless one [with the breath of his mouth and will bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming] [ὃς ἀνομον ἀναλώσει τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ καὶ καταργήσει τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ], who will destroy that impious one with the Spirit of his mouth and abolish by the appearance of his coming, Jesus Christ! Amen!

units.la: Per Accessum Pontificem eligendi forma post Scrutinium insufficiens IV. 3. 63. quale semper fere est, 64. adhibetur; Est autem accedendi consuetudo ex Antiquitate Romana; Actus ejus diversi enumerantur, 65. Differentia inter antecedentia & actum primum accedentem numero qualis maneat, 78. Pontifices ... (continues) ... Concluditur tractatio de Scrutinio & Accessu. 74.
units.tr: Accession: the form of electing the Pontiff after an insufficient scrutiny. IV. 3. 63. Such a form is almost always used, 64. The custom of accession comes from Roman antiquity. Its various acts are enumerated, 65. How the difference between the preceding acts and the first accession stands in number, 78. Pontiffs ... (continues) ... The treatment of the scrutiny and accession is concluded. 74.

units.tr: Hadrian IV. What sort of man he was. VII. 7. 31. His pride. 34. In his judgement, no one is more wretched than the Roman Pontiff. VIII. 2. 9. He showed the opposite extreme to nepotism. 16.

units.la: Adrianus V. Constitutiones Conclaviarias revocat IV. 3. 20.
units.tr: Hadrian V. Revokes the conclave constitutions. IV. 3. 20.

units.la: Adrianus VI. absens electus. VIII. 1. 25. nomen non mutavit. 19. qualis & qui ejus nævi fuerint. VII 7.58. alia credere, vel docere saltem coepit, cum abusu Scripturæ in excusatione prioris, Papa factus. VIII.2 8. ex hypothesi & accusatione quoque Monarchicorum parum prudens, minúsque fuit aptus. VII. 8. 13. Nepotismum, exemplo etiam, detestatus est. VIII. 2. 28. ejus testimonium de Antecessoribus pessimis & corrupto Ecclesiæ statu. VII. 7. 58. de misero Pontificum statu. VIII. 2. 9. quàm ingratus, mors quàm grata fuerit. IV. 3. 5. Epitaphium ejus. VIII. 2. 9.
units.tr: Hadrian VI. Elected while absent. VIII. 1. 25. Did not change his name. 19. What his blemishes were and who they were. VII. 7. 58. Once he became Pope he began to believe or at least teach other things, with an abuse of Scripture in excusing his earlier views. VIII. 2. 8. Through his hypothesis and also his accusation of the Monarchists he was rather imprudent, and less fit. VII. 8. 13. He detested nepotism, even by example. VIII. 2. 28. His testimony about the very bad predecessors and the corrupt state of the Church. VII. 7. 58. About the wretched state of the Pontiffs. VIII. 2. 9. How ungrateful he was, how welcome his death was. IV. 3. 5. His epitaph. VIII. 2. 9.

units.la: Albanus Card. ab ambitu in Concl. Sixti V. adhuc sibi temperans, atque non ambiendum esse, juxta quosdam, judicans VI. 1. 29. in Concl. Greg. XIV. ambitioso animo residuas in extrema senectute vires ambulando ostensurus incasu interit. 25. ideo gratus fuit Gallis, quia Hispanis exosus. 29.
units.tr: Albanus, Cardinal: refrained for the time from ambition in the conclave of Sixtus V, judging, according to some, that one should not canvass. VI. 1. 29. In the conclave of Gregory XIV, with an ambitious mind, he exhausted his remaining strength in extreme old age by walking about and perished in a fall. 25. He was therefore welcome to the French because he was hated by the Spanish. 29.

units.la: Albicius Card. Simoniacis ab utraque parte artibus cedit VI. 4. 43. ejus promotioni obstitit defectus simulationis 7. ejus domus ante ingressum in Concl. instar Conclavis & nocturnarum congregationum tractationumque locus fuit: 16.
units.tr: Albicius, Cardinal, yields to simony by arts on both sides. VI. 4. 43. The lack of pretence stood in the way of his promotion. 7. His house before entering the conclave was like a conclave and a place of nightly meetings and discussions. 16.

units.la: Alexander II. P. in Schismate VII. 1. 51. 33. cum neglectu authoritatis Imperatoriæ factus.
units.tr: Alexander II. Pope, made in the schism. VII. 1. 51. 33. With neglect of imperial authority.

units.la: Alexander III. P. non, ut quidam ajunt, introduxit electionem per solos Card. sed addit constitutionem de numero duarum tertiarum necessario. IV. 2. 112. Imperatore concalcato, Cardinalium dignitatem plurimum auxit. 60. in Schismate Papa fuit. VII. 1. 7. seqq.
units.tr: Alexander III. Pope. He did not, as some say, introduce election by the cardinals alone, but added the requirement of a necessary two-thirds majority. IV. 2. 112. With the emperor trampled underfoot, he greatly increased the dignity of the cardinals. 60. He was Pope during the schism. VII. 1. 7. seqq.

units.la: Alexander V. in Schismate electus. VII. 1. 103. ejus mores, gesta, mors &c. 104. Papa fuit, semet fatente, mendicus. VIII. 2. 9.
units.tr: Alexander V was elected during the schism. VII. 1. 103. His morals, deeds, death, etc. 104. He was Pope, by his own admission, a beggar. VIII. 2. 9.

units.la: Alexander VI concordi quidem, sed pessima. VI. 4. 57. Simoniaca etiam. 35. electione Papa factus, monstrum omnis impietatis in omnibus suis actionibus. VII. 7. 56. Magiæ reus. V. 33. Cardinales ob acceptam pecuniam creavit. IV. 2. 85. imo pileum Cardinalitium pro fœmina à se stupranda venditi. IV. 2. 85. alium sub simili conditione venalem exposuit Ib. Cardinales indignis plane modis tractavit. 40. filium obsidem tanquam Legatum in Galliam misit. 55 Nepotismum potius Spuriismum introduxit, habuit. VIII. 2. 13. Papatum hæreditarium facere voluit. IV. 2. 40. vitæ tamen Scriptorem aliquem turpissime adulantem erga literatos benignior invenit. VII. 7. 75.
units.tr: Alexander VI, indeed harmonious, but most wicked. VI. 4. 57. Also simoniacal. 35. Made Pope by election, a monster of all impiety in all his actions. VII. 7. 56. Accused of magic. V. 33. He created Cardinals for money received. IV. 2. 85. Indeed he sold the Cardinal's hat for a woman whom he himself had debauched. IV. 2. 85. He put another up for sale on similar terms. Ib. He treated the Cardinals in plainly unworthy ways. 40. He sent his son as a hostage, as Legate, into France. 55. He introduced, rather than nepotism, bastardism. VIII. 2. 13. He wished to make the Papacy hereditary. IV. 2. 40. Yet he found a certain writer of his life, most basely flattering, kinder to literary men. VII. 7. 75.

units.la: Alexander VII. P. morbi lethalis ante Pontificatum interdum simulator. IV. 3. 18. detestatus Mazarini Card. Galliæ Ministri literis approbatus eligi potuit VI. 2. 28. ejus hypocrisis, dum electus non in medio, sed in angulo altaris collocari voluit. VIII. 1. 6. ab initio veri patientiam. IV 2. 37. magnificentiam Alexandri M. 81.
units.tr: Alexander VII P., at times a pretender of a deadly illness before the Pontificate. IV. 3. 18. Although he detested Mazarin, the Cardinal and minister of France, he could be elected, approved by letters. VI. 2. 28. His hypocrisy, since when elected he wanted to be placed not in the middle but in the corner of the altar. VIII. 1. 6. From the beginning, a pretence of patience. IV. 2. 37. The magnificence of Alexander the Great. 81.

units.la: dorum cupidinem 82. nec non alienum à Nepotismo animum, præ se tulit. VIII. 2. 14. pessimi author 1b. & 35 elusò etiam, quod de nunquam Romæ recipiendis Nepotibus peculiariter præstiterat, juramento 24. & adhibitis ante receptionem publicam in Nepotibus & Fratre ditando variis fraudibus, 1b. indignos ad Cardinalatum promovit. IV. 2. 88. consilium, ut quivis Card. electus tormentum bellicum magnum parari curaret, accepit. 76 pessimus factus est, pessimè imperavit. VII. 7. 71. Senensium nomen Romanis abominabile reddidit. IV. 3. 7. moribundus nomine Baptismali appellari refutavit. VIII. 1. 21. ejus funebria. 14. atque in monumento depicta immaculata B. Virginis conceptio. 1b.
units.tr: of the desire for gifts. 82. He also showed a mind far from nepotism. VIII. 2. 14. The author of the worst things. Ib. and 35. He also evaded, by an oath concerning the Nephews never to be received at Rome, which he had given specially, 24. and by various frauds, in enriching the Nephews and his Brother before their public reception. Ib. He promoted unworthy men to the Cardinalate. IV. 2. 88. He accepted a plan that every Cardinal elect should have a large piece of artillery prepared. 76. He became most wicked, and ruled most wickedly. VII. 7. 71. He made the name of the Sienese abominable to the Romans. IV. 3. 7. Dying, he refused to be called by his baptismal name. VIII. 1. 21. His funeral. 14. And in his monument is painted the immaculate conception of the Blessed Virgin. Ib.

units.tr: On Alexander VIII. VII. 7. 72. His nepotism. VIII. 2. 30.
